items.q: According to Benner’s model, which level of proficiency describes a nurse who has been in the same clinical position for 2 to 3 years, anticipates nursing care, and establishes long-range goals?
items.a: Competent
items.ex: Benner’s competent nurse has 2 to 3 years in the same position and can anticipate care and set long-range goals.
w: Advanced beginner
The advanced beginner has only some experience, possibly observational, and identifies meaningful aspects of care.
Proficient
The proficient nurse has more than 2 to 3 years in the position and perceives situations as a whole.
Expert
The expert has diverse experience and an intuitive grasp of existing or potential clinical problems.

alt.q: An operating room nurse with 15 years of experience takes a new position in home health. According to Benner, at which level does this nurse enter the home health setting?
alt.a: Novice
alt.ex: Benner’s novice is any nurse entering a situation with no previous experience, even an experienced nurse changing settings.
w: Competent
Competence requires 2 to 3 years in the same clinical position, which this nurse lacks in home health.
Proficient
Proficiency requires more than 2 to 3 years in the same position, not years in a different setting.
Expert
Expertise reflects an intuitive grasp within familiar practice, not a setting with no previous experience.

items.q: A proficient nurse focuses on managing care as opposed to managing and performing skills.
items.a: True
items.ex: Benner’s proficient nurse perceives the whole situation and focuses on managing care rather than performing skills.
items.ww: Box 1.1 states that the proficient nurse focuses on managing care, not on managing and performing skills.

alt.q: At Benner’s competent level, a nurse first perceives a patient’s situation as a whole and readily transfers knowledge from multiple previous experiences.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Perceiving the whole situation and transferring knowledge from many past experiences characterizes the proficient nurse.
alt.ww: Box 1.1 assigns these abilities to the proficient level; the competent nurse anticipates care and sets long-range goals.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient who had major surgery yesterday. Which action is an example of nursing autonomy?
items.a: Implementing coughing and deep-breathing exercises to clear secretions
items.ex: Autonomy is initiating independent nursing interventions without medical orders, such as coughing and deep-breathing exercises.
w: Starting an antibiotic for a suspected surgical wound infection
Antibiotics require a prescription, so starting one is not an independent nursing intervention.
Ordering a chest x-ray to check for postoperative pneumonia
Diagnostic tests require a health care provider’s order.
Increasing the dose of the prescribed opioid analgesic
Changing a prescribed medication dose requires a medical order.

alt.q: Later, the same postoperative patient has a fever and yellow-green drainage from the surgical wound. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
alt.a: Collaborate with health care providers to develop a treatment plan for the infection
alt.ex: When a complication arises, the nurse collaborates with other health care providers to plan the best treatment.
w: Continue the coughing exercises and recheck the wound at the end of the shift
Delaying action on signs of infection is unsafe; these findings need collaboration now.
Begin an antibiotic from unit stock to treat the suspected infection
Antibiotics require a medical order, so this exceeds independent nursing practice.
Document the drainage and wait for the surgeon’s next scheduled visit
Waiting delays treatment of a likely infection; the nurse should collaborate promptly.

items.q: Which statement best defines accountability in professional nursing practice?
items.a: Being professionally and legally responsible for the type and quality of nursing care provided
items.ex: Accountability is professional and legal responsibility for care, covering dependent, independent, and interdependent nursing actions.
w: Initiating independent nursing interventions without the need for medical orders
This defines autonomy, not accountability.
Protecting the patient’s human and legal rights and helping the patient assert them
This describes the patient advocate role.
Coordinating staff activities with personnel, policy, and budgetary responsibility
This describes the manager role.

alt.q: A new policy allows nurses on a unit to initiate more interventions independently. According to the chapter, what accompanies this increased autonomy?
alt.a: Greater responsibility and accountability for the care provided
alt.ex: The chapter states that with increased autonomy comes greater responsibility and accountability.
w: Less need to stay current in nursing and scientific knowledge
Nurses must remain current and competent in knowledge and technical skills.
Reduced legal responsibility for dependent nursing actions
Accountability includes dependent, independent, and interdependent nursing actions.
Freedom from nursing audits and standards of practice
The profession regulates accountability through nursing audits and standards of practice.

items.q: The family members of a patient speak limited English and appear worried about the patient’s treatment plan. Which action by the nurse best demonstrates the role of patient advocate?
items.a: Finding an interpreter to help the family communicate their concerns
items.ex: Advocates help patients and families assert their rights; an interpreter lets the family voice their concerns.
w: Asking the family to wait until a bilingual relative can visit
Waiting delays communication and leaves the family’s concerns unaddressed.
Explaining the treatment plan slowly and loudly in English
Speaking slowly in English does not ensure understanding for limited English speakers.
Telling the family the provider will answer questions at discharge
Deferring concerns until discharge fails to act on the family’s behalf now.

alt.q: A patient says, “I’m not sure whether I should agree to this treatment.” Which nursing action best reflects the advocate role?
alt.a: Providing additional information to help the patient make the decision
alt.ex: The chapter’s example of advocacy is giving additional information so the patient can decide about treatment.
w: Encouraging the patient to accept the treatment the provider recommends
Advocacy respects patient autonomy and self-determination rather than steering the choice.
Asking the family to make the decision on the patient’s behalf
This undermines the patient’s right to self-determination.
Telling the patient that most people in this situation agree to it
Pressure from others’ choices does not support an informed, autonomous decision.

items.q: Which situation is an example of planned, formal patient teaching?
items.a: Teaching a patient newly diagnosed with diabetes mellitus self-management strategies
items.ex: Planned teaching is formal and individualized, such as diabetes self-management; answering casual questions is informal teaching.
w: Answering a patient’s question about the reason for an intravenous infusion
Responding to a question during conversation is unplanned, informal teaching.
Discussing smoking cessation when a patient raises it in casual conversation
A topic raised in casual conversation is unplanned, informal teaching.
Responding to a visitor’s passing question about needed lifestyle changes
A passing question answered on the spot is unplanned, informal teaching.

alt.q: During morning care, a patient casually asks why the intravenous infusion is running. How should the nurse classify the teaching that follows?
alt.a: Unplanned, informal teaching
alt.ex: Teaching that arises during casual conversation, such as explaining an IV infusion, is unplanned and informal.
w: Planned, formal teaching
Formal teaching is prearranged and individualized, such as diabetes self-management education.
Staff development education
Staff development educates nurses within an agency, not patients.
Individualized teaching plan
A teaching plan is developed in advance from assessed needs, not prompted by a casual question.

items.q: Which of the following are ANA Standards of Practice? Select all that apply.
o: Assessment
Standard 1: the RN collects pertinent data about the health care consumer’s health or situation.
Outcomes identification
Standard 3: the RN identifies expected outcomes for an individualized plan.
Evaluation
Standard 6: the RN evaluates progress toward goals and outcomes.
Ethics
Ethics is a Standard of Professional Performance (Standard 7).
Resource stewardship
Resource stewardship is a Standard of Professional Performance (Standard 17).
Collaboration
Collaboration is a Standard of Professional Performance (Standard 11).
items.ex: Standards of Practice follow the nursing process, assessment through evaluation; Standards of Professional Performance cover role behaviors such as ethics, advocacy, and leadership.

alt.q: Which of the following are ANA Standards of Professional Performance? Select all that apply.
o: Advocacy
Standard 8: the RN demonstrates advocacy in all roles and settings.
Leadership
Standard 12: the RN leads within the practice setting and the profession.
Environmental health
Standard 18: the RN practices in a way that advances environmental safety and health.
Diagnosis
Diagnosis is Standard of Practice 2, part of the nursing process.
Planning
Planning is Standard of Practice 4, part of the nursing process.
Implementation
Implementation is Standard of Practice 5, part of the nursing process.
alt.ex: Correct: Advocacy; Leadership; Environmental health.

items.q: The nursing code of ethics is a statement of philosophical ideals of right and wrong that defines the principles nurses use to provide care.
items.a: True
items.ex: The chapter defines the code of ethics as philosophical ideals of right and wrong that guide the principles of patient care.
items.ww: This matches the chapter’s definition; the code is a statement of ideals, not an agency procedure manual.

alt.q: Because the profession has a code of ethics, nurses should set aside their personal values and ethics when they practice.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The chapter encourages nurses to incorporate their own values and compare their personal ethics with professional standards.
alt.ww: Personal values are not discarded; nurses explore how they compare with established professional standards.

items.q: The services that a qualified health professional is deemed competent to perform and permitted to undertake under the terms of their license make up the [[scope of practice|scope of nursing practice]].
items.ex: Professional standards and the code of ethics are both followed within the nurse’s scope of practice, defined by competence and licensure.

alt.q: A nurse follows the standards of practice and code of ethics within their [[scope of practice|scope of nursing practice]], the services they are competent and licensed to perform.
alt.ex: Professional standards and the code of ethics are both followed within the nurse’s scope of practice, defined by competence and licensure.

items.q: According to the APRN Consensus Model, which is one of the four advanced practice registered nurse roles?
items.a: Certified nurse-midwife
items.ex: The four APRN roles are clinical nurse specialist, nurse practitioner, certified nurse-midwife, and certified registered nurse anesthetist.
w: Nurse educator
Nurse educators teach in schools or agencies; this is not one of the four APRN roles.
Nurse administrator
Nurse administrators manage nursing staff; this is not one of the four APRN roles.
Nurse researcher
Nurse researchers conduct research; this is not one of the four APRN roles.

alt.q: APRN educational preparation is in at least one of six populations. Which is one of these populations?
alt.a: Adult-gerontology
alt.ex: The six populations are adult-gerontology, pediatrics, neonatology, women’s health/gender related, family/individual across the life span, and psychiatric mental health.
w: Oncology
Oncology is an example of a CNS disease specialty, not one of the six populations.
Critical care
Critical care is a practice setting, not one of the six populations.
Wound care
Wound care is a type-of-problem specialty, not one of the six populations.

items.q: A registered nurse wants to apply to a nurse anesthesia program. What experience must the nurse have before applying?
items.a: At least 1 year of critical care or emergency experience
items.ex: Applicants to nurse anesthesia programs must have at least 1 year of critical care or emergency experience.
w: At least 6 months of medical-surgical experience
The requirement is critical care or emergency experience, not medical-surgical experience.
At least 2 years of operating room experience
The requirement is 1 year in critical care or emergency, not operating room work.
At least 3 years of any acute care experience
The requirement specifies critical care or emergency experience for at least 1 year.

alt.q: Which statement about the certified registered nurse anesthetist is accurate?
alt.a: Practices both autonomously and in collaboration with the interprofessional team
alt.ex: CRNAs deliver anesthesia and pain care autonomously and collaboratively, under anesthesiologist guidance and supervision.
w: Prescribes contraceptives and manages uncomplicated childbirth
This describes the certified nurse-midwife.
Needs no anesthesia education beyond initial RN preparation
CRNAs complete advanced education in an accredited nurse anesthesia program.
Mainly consults on complex cases and drives organization-wide practice change
This describes the clinical nurse specialist.

items.q: Which activities are within the scope of practice of a certified nurse-midwife? Select all that apply.
o: Prescribing contraceptive methods
CNMs prescribe medications, including controlled substances and contraceptive methods.
Providing preconception care
Family planning services, including preconception care, are part of nurse-midwifery.
Ordering and interpreting laboratory tests
CNMs order and interpret laboratory and diagnostic tests.
Administering surgical anesthesia
Anesthesia care is the role of the certified registered nurse anesthetist.
Independently managing complicated, high-risk patients
CNMs admit, manage, and discharge uncomplicated patients.
items.ex: CNMs independently provide pregnancy, childbirth, postpartum, reproductive, gynecological, and family planning care, managing uncomplicated patients.

alt.q: A nurse is explaining the certified nurse-midwife role to a pregnant patient. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The CNM can care for you during pregnancy, childbirth, and after delivery
Nurse-midwifery includes care during pregnancy, childbirth, and the postpartum period.
The CNM is certified by the American College of Nurse-Midwives
CNMs are educated in midwifery and certified by the ACNM.
The CNM can prescribe medications, including controlled substances
CNMs prescribe medications, including controlled substances.
The CNM needs a physician to perform your physical examinations
CNMs conduct physical examinations themselves.
The CNM is prepared with an associate degree plus midwifery training
CNMs have graduate preparation, a master’s degree or doctorate, in nursing.
alt.ex: Correct: The CNM can care for you during pregnancy, childbirth, and after delivery; The CNM is certified by the American College of Nurse-Midwives; The CNM can prescribe medications, including controlled substances.

items.q: A new graduate nurse says, “I want to start a nurse practitioner program right away so I can skip bedside nursing.” Which response by the nurse mentor is best?
items.a: “Bedside practice first builds the knowledge and judgment an advanced role requires.”
items.ex: Solid bedside practice builds knowledge of disease, skills, critical thinking, and clinical judgment needed for advanced practice.
w: “That makes sense; bedside experience is not needed for graduate study.”
The chapter stresses obtaining solid bedside practice before an advanced role.
“Only clinical nurse specialists need bedside practice before graduate school.”
Bedside practice is important preparation for any advanced practice role.
“You should first spend several years in nursing administration instead.”
Administration is a separate career path; bedside practice is the recommended preparation.

alt.q: Why does the chapter recommend that new graduates obtain solid bedside clinical practice before entering an advanced practice role?
alt.a: It refines critical thinking and builds sound clinical judgment
alt.ex: Bedside practice increases knowledge of disease, builds skill and confidence, and refines critical thinking and judgment.
w: It is the main requirement for initial RN licensure
The rationale given is clinical knowledge and judgment, not a licensure requirement.
It replaces graduate courses in advanced pharmacology
APRNs still need advanced education in pathophysiology, pharmacology, and assessment.
It allows the nurse to bill for services independently
Billing relates to APRN practice under state regulation, not bedside experience.

items.q: Which description best fits the role of a clinical nurse specialist?
items.a: An expert clinician in a specialty who supports bedside nurses and drives practice change
items.ex: CNSs are expert clinicians in a specialty who support bedside nurses, drive practice change, and ensure evidence-based care.
w: An APRN educated in midwifery who provides care during pregnancy and birth
This describes the certified nurse-midwife.
An APRN with advanced anesthesia education who provides anesthesia care
This describes the certified registered nurse anesthetist.
An RN who conducts studies to define and expand nursing’s scope of practice
This describes the nurse researcher.

alt.q: A clinical nurse specialist’s specialty may be identified by the type of problem managed. Which specialty is an example of this category?
alt.a: Wound care
alt.ex: CNS specialties are identified by population, setting, disease, type of care, or type of problem such as wound or pain.
w: Geriatrics
Geriatrics identifies a specialty by population.
Critical care
Critical care identifies a specialty by setting.
Rehabilitation
Rehabilitation identifies a specialty by type of care.

items.q: Today the majority of nurses practice in hospital settings.
items.a: True
items.ex: Most nurses work in hospitals, followed by community-based care, ambulatory care, home care, and nursing homes/extended care.
items.ww: The chapter states the majority of nurses practice in hospital settings.

alt.q: Nursing homes and extended care settings now employ more nurses than hospitals do.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hospitals employ the most nurses; nursing homes and extended care settings come last in the chapter’s list.
alt.ww: The chapter lists hospitals first, ahead of community, ambulatory, home care, and nursing home settings.

items.q: Which functions are part of a nurse administrator’s role? Select all that apply.
o: Budgeting
Budgeting is a listed function of nurse administrators.
Staffing
Staffing is a listed function of nurse administrators.
Strategic planning of programs and services
Administrators plan programs and services strategically.
Employee evaluation and development
Administrators evaluate and develop employees.
Prescribing medications for patients on the unit
Prescribing belongs to APRNs, not the administrator role.
Administering anesthesia for surgical patients
Anesthesia care is the CRNA’s role.
items.ex: Nurse administrators manage nursing staff; their functions include budgeting, staffing, strategic planning, and employee evaluation and development.

alt.q: Which competencies are outlined for nurse leaders in administrative or executive practice? Select all that apply.
o: Communication and relationship management
This is one of the five administrative competencies.
Knowledge of the health care environment
This is one of the five administrative competencies.
Business skills and principles
This is one of the five administrative competencies.
Advanced physical assessment and prescribing
These are part of APRN education, not the five administrative competencies.
Research design and grant writing
These relate to the nurse researcher, not the five administrative competencies.
alt.ex: Correct: Communication and relationship management; Knowledge of the health care environment; Business skills and principles.

items.q: A nurse wants a position orienting new personnel, teaching critical care courses, and instructing staff on new equipment. Which role best matches this nurse’s goals?

items.ex: Staff development educators provide orientation, critical care courses, skill competency, safety training, and instruction on new equipment.
w: Patient education nurse educator
This educator teaches patients and families to self-manage illness, not agency staff.
Nursing faculty member
Faculty educate students in nursing programs, not agency personnel.
Nurse researcher
Researchers conduct studies and performance improvement, not staff orientation.

alt.q: What is the primary focus of a nurse educator in an agency’s patient education department, such as a wound treatment clinic?
alt.a: Teaching and coaching patients and families to self-manage illness
alt.ex: Patient education nurse educators develop therapeutic programs so patients and families can self-manage illness and improve outcomes.
w: Orienting newly hired nurses to agency policies and procedures
Orientation is the work of staff development educators.
Teaching nursing students in classroom and clinical settings
Teaching students is the role of nursing faculty.
Developing the unit budget and staffing plan for the clinic
Budgeting and staffing are nurse administrator functions.

items.q: Which statement describes Florence Nightingale’s contribution in Notes on Nursing?

items.ex: In Notes on Nursing, Nightingale established the first nursing philosophy, centered on maintaining and restoring health.
w: She became the first nursing professor at a university teachers college
Mary Adelaide Nutting became the first nursing professor, at Columbia Teachers College.
She described nursing as serving the poor in city tenement settlements
Lillian Wald and Mary Brewster’s Henry Street Settlement served tenement residents.
She created a forum to build nurses’ competence in ethics and human rights
The ANA established the Center for Ethics and Human Rights.

w: How to diagnose diseases and prescribe treatments for each one
Nightingale’s focus was health maintenance and restoration, not diagnosing and prescribing.
How to organize hospitals, ambulances, and supplies for troops
Dix and Bickerdyke organized hospitals, ambulances, and supplies in the Civil War.
How to conduct laboratory research on disease-causing organisms
Nightingale’s work used statistics on sanitation, not laboratory research.

items.q: A community health nurse analyzes local data and finds that cases of severe diarrheal illness cluster in neighborhoods with poor sanitation. This nurse is practicing a role first demonstrated by which nursing leader?
items.a: Florence Nightingale
items.ex: Nightingale was the first practicing nurse epidemiologist, using statistics to link poor sanitation with cholera and dysentery.
w: Clara Barton
Barton founded the American Red Cross and cared for soldiers on Civil War battlefields.
Isabel Hampton Robb
Robb helped found the organization that became the ANA and authored textbooks.
Mary Adelaide Nutting
Nutting was instrumental in moving nursing education into universities.

alt.q: Nightingale’s statistical analyses connected poor sanitation with the incidence of which diseases?
alt.a: Cholera and dysentery

Her analyses linked sanitation to cholera and dysentery, not smallpox and measles.
Tuberculosis and pneumonia
Her analyses linked sanitation to cholera and dysentery, not respiratory diseases.
Influenza and diphtheria
Her analyses linked sanitation to cholera and dysentery, not influenza or diphtheria.

items.q: After Nightingale improved sanitation at the Barracks Hospital in Scutari during the Crimean War, the mortality rate fell sharply within 6 months.

items.ex: Her attention to sanitation, nutrition, and basic conditions cut mortality at Scutari from 42.7% to 2.2% in 6 months.
items.ww: The chapter reports a dramatic drop in mortality as a result of her actions.

alt.q: Nightingale was called the “lady with the lamp” because she introduced improved lighting to reduce infection in battlefield hospitals.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The nickname came from her traveling the battlefield hospitals at night carrying her lamp.
alt.ww: Her reforms targeted sanitation and nutrition; the name refers to her night rounds with a lamp.

Community nursing for tenement residents is linked to the Henry Street Settlement in New York.
The first nursing journal, published for London hospital nurses
The chapter credits Robb with helping found the American Journal of Nursing, not Nightingale.
The first professional nursing organization in Great Britain
The chapter does not credit Nightingale with founding a professional organization.

alt.q: The Nightingale Training School for Nurses at St. Thomas’ Hospital in London is historically significant because it was the first:

Nightingale founded the training school at St. Thomas’ Hospital in London.
Opened a settlement house serving poor New York tenement residents

Dorothea Lynde Dix

This is Mary Adelaide Nutting’s contribution.
Organizing ambulances and supplies for wounded troops
This describes Dix and Bickerdyke in the Civil War.
Developing standards for end-of-life nursing care

The nurse corps were established as practice expanded, not through Henry Street.

Educating nurses in palliative and end-of-life care

Community nursing growth is tied to Henry Street in 1893, before the ANA was named.
After the Magnet program began in 1990
Community nursing grew significantly nearly a century earlier, after 1893.

Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross.

Lillian Wald and Mary Brewster opened the Henry Street Settlement.

Tubman is known for her work in the Underground Railroad movement.

That's milestone 2 of 6.

ord.q: Place these nursing milestones in chronological order, from earliest to most recent.
items: Nightingale volunteers in the Crimean War
Barton, Dix, and Bickerdyke care for Civil War soldiers
Wald and Brewster open the Henry Street Settlement
Nurses’ Associated Alumnae of the United States and Canada is founded
Nutting becomes the first nursing professor at Columbia Teachers College
The Magnet Recognition Program begins
ord.ex: Crimean War (1853), Civil War (1860–65), Henry Street (1893), Nurses’ Associated Alumnae (1896), Nutting’s professorship (1906), Magnet program (1990).

items.q: Which societal needs are nurses revising nursing practice and school curricula to meet in the twenty-first century? Select all that apply.
o: An aging population
An aging population is one of the needs the chapter lists.
Bioterrorism
Bioterrorism is one of the needs the chapter lists.
Emerging infections
Emerging infections are one of the needs the chapter lists.
Disaster management
Disaster management is one of the needs the chapter lists.
Longer hospital stays for low-acuity patients
The chapter cites high acuity and early discharge, not longer stays.
Declining cultural diversity
Cultural diversity is increasing and is itself one of the needs listed.
items.ex: Twenty-first-century needs include an aging population, cultural diversity, bioterrorism, emerging infections, and disaster management, along with high acuity and early discharge.

alt.q: Which factors require twenty-first-century nurses in all settings to have a strong, current knowledge base? Select all that apply.
o: Advances in technology and informatics
Technology and informatics advances demand current knowledge.
The high acuity level of hospitalized patients
High acuity requires a strong knowledge base.
Early discharge from health care institutions
Early discharge means nurses in all settings manage more complex needs.
Reduced use of technology in patient care
Technology use is advancing, not decreasing.
Longer inpatient recovery periods
The chapter cites early discharge, not longer inpatient stays.
alt.ex: Correct: Advances in technology and informatics; The high acuity level of hospitalized patients; Early discharge from health care institutions.

items.q: A nurse on an oncology unit wants education to improve the palliative and end-of-life care given to patients. Which initiative is designed for this purpose?
items.a: End-of-Life Nursing Education Consortium
items.ex: ELNEC, with the AACN and City of Hope, improves palliative care through end-of-life education for students and practicing nurses.
w: Magnet Recognition Program
Magnet designates organizations whose nursing goals improve patient outcomes, not end-of-life education.
Future of Nursing: Campaign for Action
This campaign supports nursing’s role in improving health equity.
Center for Ethics and Human Rights
This ANA center addresses ethical and human rights issues, not palliative care education.

alt.q: What is the focus of the Last Acts Campaign, in which nursing and the Robert Wood Johnson Foundation are taking a leadership role?
alt.a: Developing standards and policies for end-of-life care
alt.ex: Through the Last Acts Campaign, nursing and the RWJF lead development of end-of-life care standards and policies.
w: Increasing diversity in the nursing workforce and leadership
This is a focus of the Future of Nursing 2020-2030 initiative.
Recognizing organizations that achieve nursing excellence
This describes the Magnet Recognition Program.
Moving nursing education into university settings
This was Mary Adelaide Nutting’s contribution.

items.q: What does the Magnet Recognition Program designate?
items.a: Organizations whose nursing leaders align nursing goals to improve patient outcomes
items.ex: Magnet designates organizations where nursing leaders align nursing strategic goals to improve patient outcomes.
w: Individual nurses who reach expert-level clinical proficiency
Magnet recognizes organizations, not individual nurses’ proficiency.
Schools of nursing that offer university-based education
Magnet designates health care organizations, not schools of nursing.
Hospitals that train nurses for military service
Magnet recognizes nursing excellence, not military training.

alt.q: A nurse is considering a job at a Magnet-designated hospital. According to the chapter, what does Magnet recognition mean for nurses?
alt.a: Education and development at every career stage, leading to greater bedside autonomy
alt.ex: For nurses, Magnet means education and development through every career stage, which leads to greater autonomy at the bedside.
w: Fewer continuing education requirements, leaving more time for bedside care
Magnet emphasizes education and development, not fewer requirements.
Reduced bedside autonomy in exchange for more management oversight
Magnet recognition leads to greater, not reduced, bedside autonomy.
Guaranteed promotion to management after 2 to 3 years of service
The chapter describes development and autonomy, not guaranteed promotion.

items.q: The Nurses’ Associated Alumnae of the United States and Canada, which Isabel Hampton Robb helped found, later became the American Nurses Association.
items.a: True
items.ex: Robb helped found the Nurses’ Associated Alumnae in 1896, and it became the ANA in 1911.
items.ww: The chapter states directly that this organization became the ANA.

alt.q: Isabel Hampton Robb is best known for founding the American Red Cross during the Civil War.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Clara Barton founded the American Red Cross; Robb helped found the ANA’s forerunner and the American Journal of Nursing.
alt.ww: Robb’s contributions were organizational and educational, not founding the Red Cross.

items.q: Because her statistical analyses connected poor sanitation with cholera and dysentery, Florence Nightingale was the first practicing nurse [[epidemiologist]].
items.ex: Nightingale used statistics to link sanitation with disease, making her the first practicing nurse epidemiologist.

alt.q: Nightingale is considered the first practicing nurse [[epidemiologist]] because she used data to link poor sanitation with disease.
alt.ex: Nightingale used statistics to link sanitation with disease, making her the first practicing nurse epidemiologist.

items.q: A nurse is struggling with a complex ethical issue involving patients’ human rights and wants professional resources to build ethical competence. Which ANA resource is designed for this purpose?
items.a: The Center for Ethics and Human Rights
items.ex: The ANA’s Center for Ethics and Human Rights provides a forum on these issues and programs to increase ethical competence.
w: The Magnet Recognition Program
Magnet designates organizations for nursing excellence, not ethics education.
The Henry Street Settlement
Henry Street was an early community health settlement for the poor.
The Last Acts Campaign
The Last Acts Campaign develops end-of-life care standards and policies.

alt.q: What is the purpose of the ANA Center for Ethics and Human Rights?
alt.a: Providing a forum on ethical and human rights issues and building ethical competence
alt.ex: The center addresses complex ethical and human rights issues facing nurses and designs programs to increase ethical competence.
w: Designating health care organizations that achieve nursing excellence
This describes the Magnet Recognition Program.
Improving palliative care through end-of-life nursing education
This describes ELNEC.
Creating uniform state regulation of advanced practice nursing roles
This describes the APRN Consensus Model.

items.q: When communities face health care crises such as natural disasters or disease outbreaks, which activities have nurses established? Select all that apply.
o: Community-based immunization programs
Nurses establish immunization programs during community health crises.
Screening programs and treatment clinics
Nurses establish screening programs and treatment clinics in crises.
Health promotion activities
Nurses establish health promotion activities when public health resources are insufficient.
Closing community clinics to concentrate staff in hospitals
Nurses expand community-based services in crises rather than closing them.
Limiting care to military hospitals until the crisis ends
Military care applies to war; community crises bring community-based programs.
items.ex: Nurses respond to community crises by establishing immunization and screening programs, treatment clinics, and health promotion activities.

alt.q: In what ways have nurses historically responded to the needs of patients and communities? Select all that apply.
o: Caring for the wounded in combat zones and military hospitals
In wartime nurses meet the needs of the wounded at home and abroad.
Establishing treatment clinics during disease outbreaks
Nurses set up treatment clinics when communities face outbreaks.
Providing health promotion when public health resources fall short
Nurses establish health promotion activities when resources are insufficient.
Restricting care to hospital settings during natural disasters
Nurses establish community-based programs during disasters.
Withdrawing from community care during public health emergencies
Nurses have always responded to community needs in crises.
alt.ex: Correct: Caring for the wounded in combat zones and military hospitals; Establishing treatment clinics during disease outbreaks; Providing health promotion when public health resources fall short.

items.q: Which development characterized nursing in the last half of the twentieth century?
items.a: Creation of specialty nursing organizations such as AORN and ENA
items.ex: The late twentieth century saw creation of specialty organizations such as AACN, AORN, INS, and ENA.
w: Opening of the first organized nurse training school in London
Nightingale’s training school dates to the nineteenth century.
Founding of the Henry Street Settlement for tenement residents
Henry Street opened in 1893, in the nineteenth century.
Founding of the American Red Cross by a battlefield nurse
Clara Barton’s founding of the Red Cross is tied to the Civil War era.

alt.q: In the early twentieth century, which movement evolved in nursing?
alt.a: Developing a scientific, research-based body of nursing knowledge
alt.ex: The early twentieth century brought a movement toward a scientific, research-based body of nursing knowledge and practice.
w: Replacing hospital nursing with community settlement work
Hospital nursing continued to expand alongside community nursing.
Eliminating specialization in favor of generalist practice
Specialization began developing by the 1920s.
Shifting nursing education out of universities into hospitals
Nutting moved nursing education into universities, the opposite direction.

items.q: A nursing student asks, “Why do we need to learn nursing history if it doesn’t change how I give care today?” Which response by the instructor is best?
items.a: “It increases your understanding of the social and intellectual origins of nursing.”
items.ex: Knowing nursing history increases understanding of the social and intellectual origins of the discipline.
w: “It is mainly needed to answer exam questions about famous dates.”
The value of history is understanding nursing’s origins, not memorizing dates.
“It shows that nursing practice has stayed the same since Nightingale.”
Nursing practice continually changes to meet society’s needs.
“It is required only for nurses who plan to become researchers.”
Understanding nursing’s origins benefits every nurse, not only researchers.

alt.q: What does the chapter identify as the benefit of knowing the history of the nursing profession?
alt.a: Understanding the social and intellectual origins of the discipline
alt.ex: History increases understanding of the social and intellectual origins of nursing as a discipline.
w: Memorizing the founding dates of nursing organizations
The chapter values understanding origins, not memorizing dates.
Learning to perform procedures the way early nurses did
Practice is updated with current evidence, not copied from early nurses.
Meeting a requirement for ANA membership and certification
The chapter does not link history to membership or certification.

items.q: The Civil War stimulated the growth of nursing in the United States.
items.a: True
items.ex: The Civil War (1860–65) spurred U.S. nursing through the work of Barton, Dix, Bickerdyke, and others.
items.ww: The chapter states directly that the Civil War stimulated the growth of nursing in the United States.

alt.q: Nursing specialization did not begin to develop until the twenty-first century.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nursing specialization started to develop by the 1920s, and specialty organizations followed later in the century.
alt.ww: Specialization began in the twentieth century, long before the twenty-first.

items.q: Which is identified in the chapter as an external force affecting nursing today?
items.a: Increasing numbers of the medically underserved
items.ex: External forces include nurses’ self-care, reform and rising costs, demographic changes, human rights, and growing numbers of medically underserved.
w: Decreasing racial and ethnic diversity
The population is becoming more, not less, racially and ethnically diverse.
A shrinking older adult population
The older adult population is expanding as baby boomers age.
Steadily falling health care costs
The chapter describes rising, even skyrocketing, health care costs.

alt.q: Which external force affecting nursing involves changes in how care is paid for and delivered, along with rising expenses?
alt.a: Health care reform and costs
alt.ex: Health care reform affects how care is paid for and delivered, and rising costs challenge the whole system.
w: Demographic changes
Demographic changes refer to an aging, more diverse, more urban population.
Human rights
Human rights is a separate force, not the one about payment and delivery.
Nurses’ self-care
Self-care concerns nurses’ own physical and emotional needs.

items.q: How does compassion fatigue among nurses affect health care agencies?
items.a: It can lead to high nurse turnover and lower patient satisfaction
items.ex: Compassion fatigue changes job performance and can drive nurses to leave, raising turnover and affecting patient satisfaction.
w: It increases patient satisfaction because nurses work harder
Compassion fatigue harms care quality and patient satisfaction.
It improves retention because nurses bond more closely with patients
Compassion fatigue can make nurses want to leave the specialty or profession.
It has little effect on an agency’s ability to keep competent staff
It affects an agency’s ability to maintain a caring, competent staff.

alt.q: Which outcome is most likely when a nurse’s compassion fatigue goes unrecognized?
alt.a: A desire to leave the specialty or the profession
alt.ex: Unaddressed compassion fatigue can lead nurses to want to leave their specialty or the profession.
w: Improved job performance from heightened alertness
Compassion fatigue causes negative changes in job performance.
Greater pleasure in previously enjoyable activities
Compassion fatigue decreases pleasure in previously enjoyable activities.
Stronger engagement with each patient’s care
Compassion fatigue reduces the quality of care provided.

items.q: After months of short staffing and little support from co-workers, a nurse feels physically and mentally exhausted, irritable, restless, and unable to focus on patients. Which condition do these findings describe?
items.a: Burnout
items.ex: Burnout is physical and mental exhaustion when perceived demands outweigh resources, often with low social support and staffing pressures.
w: Lateral violence
Lateral violence is humiliating nurse-to-nurse behavior, not exhaustion.
Secondary traumatic stress
Secondary traumatic stress comes from witnessing others’ trauma, not from staffing demands.
Resilience
Resilience is a protective factor against burnout, not a state of exhaustion.

alt.q: Which definition of burnout is consistent with the chapter?
alt.a: A condition that occurs when perceived demands outweigh perceived resources
alt.ex: Burnout occurs when perceived demands outweigh perceived resources, producing physical and mental exhaustion.
w: Trauma experienced from witnessing and caring for others who suffer trauma
This defines secondary traumatic stress.
Repeated destructive actions by one nurse designed to humiliate another
This describes lateral violence.
A combined state of burnout and secondary traumatic stress
This defines compassion fatigue.

items.q: A nurse manager is teaching staff to recognize compassion fatigue. Which findings typically result from compassion fatigue? Select all that apply.
o: Feelings of hopelessness
Hopelessness is a typical result of compassion fatigue.
Decreased pleasure in previously enjoyable activities
Loss of enjoyment is a typical result of compassion fatigue.
A state of hypervigilance
Hypervigilance is a typical result of compassion fatigue.
Anxiety
Anxiety is a typical result of compassion fatigue.
Renewed energy for caring for suffering patients
Compassion fatigue reflects depletion after prolonged giving, not renewed energy.
Improved focus and engagement with patients
Exhaustion leaves nurses unable to focus and engage with patients.
items.ex: Compassion fatigue typically causes hopelessness, loss of pleasure, hypervigilance, and anxiety, and it arises from prolonged exposure to suffering.

alt.q: Which factors place a nurse at risk for compassion fatigue? Select all that apply.
o: Frequent, intense, or prolonged exposure to grief and loss
This exposure places nurses at risk for compassion fatigue.
Giving high levels of compassion over a long period to those suffering
Prolonged high-energy giving is a common cause.
Caring for suffering patients without seeing improved outcomes
It often results when outcomes do not improve.
Strong support from co-workers and management
Feeling supported improves retention and helps prevent compassion fatigue.
Regular self-care and appropriate work-life balance
Self-care and work-life balance are protective stress-management techniques.
alt.ex: Correct: Frequent, intense, or prolonged exposure to grief and loss; Giving high levels of compassion over a long period to those suffering; Caring for suffering patients without seeing improved outcomes.

items.q: An oncology nurse has cared for patients receiving long-term chemotherapy for several years. Which statement by the nurse is most concerning for compassion fatigue?

Sharing difficult stories with colleagues is a healthy coping strategy.
“I take my breaks and keep my days off for my family.”
Self-care and work-life balance help prevent compassion fatigue.

Finding meaning in work does not suggest compassion fatigue.

Added workload increases demands and worsens exhaustion.
Discourage nurses from discussing patients’ suffering during breaks
Validating experiences and sharing stories helps nurses cope.

Early recognition and prompt intervention are recommended.

Support reduces turnover rather than increasing it.
More frequent lateral violence

Less need for nurses’ self-care
Self-care remains necessary for all nurses.

items.q: Which behaviors are examples of lateral violence? Select all that apply.
o: Withholding information from a co-worker
Withholding information is a form of lateral violence.
Making snide remarks about a colleague
Snide remarks are a form of lateral violence.
Raising eyebrows or making faces at another nurse
Nonverbal expressions of disapproval are lateral violence.
Privately offering a new nurse constructive feedback
Respectful, private feedback is not designed to humiliate.
Asking a colleague to clarify an unclear order
Seeking clarification is appropriate communication, not lateral violence.
items.ex: Lateral violence includes withholding information, humiliating actions, snide remarks, and nonverbal disapproval such as eye-rolling or making faces.

Withholding information is lateral violence.

Nonverbal expressions of disapproval are lateral violence.

items.q: Which nurses are most likely to face problems with lateral, or horizontal, violence?
items.a: New graduates and nurses new to a unit

The chapter identifies new graduates and nurses new to a unit as most at risk.
Expert nurses with many years on the same unit
Experienced nurses on a familiar unit are not the group identified as most at risk.
Advanced practice nurses in primary care
The chapter identifies new graduates and nurses new to a unit as most at risk.

w: Nurses with more than 10 years on the unit
Long-tenured nurses are not the group most likely to experience lateral violence.
Charge nurses who supervise each shift
Charge nurses are not identified as the group most at risk.
Nurses who work only in leadership roles
Leaders are not identified as the group most at risk.

items.q: Building connections with colleagues to share difficult stories is a helpful stress-management technique for nurses.

items.ww: The chapter lists building connections with colleagues as a helpful stress-management technique.

alt.a: False

alt.ww: The chapter states compassion fatigue occurs without warning.

items.a: True
items.ex: Despite fear and supply shortages, camaraderie and showing up for shifts helped nurses cope and build teams.
items.ww: The chapter credits professional camaraderie with facilitating coping and team building.

alt.q: Building resilience in nurses increases their risk of burnout, anxiety, and depression.

items.q: How is health care reform expected to change where care is delivered?
items.a: More care in community settings, with hospitals treating the very seriously ill
items.ex: Reform shifts services toward community settings and prevention, while hospitals continue to manage very seriously ill patients.
w: More health promotion in hospitals, with community settings closing
Health promotion and services are expected to grow in community settings.
Less care in homes and schools, with more in large hospital centers
More nurses will be needed in homes, schools, and senior centers.
More seriously ill patients treated in community centers than hospitals
Hospitals will continue to manage the care of very seriously ill patients.

alt.q: Because of health care reform, more nurses will practice in community care centers, homes, schools, and senior centers. Which skill will these nurses especially need?
alt.a: Assessing resources, service gaps, and how patients adapt at home
alt.ex: Community-based nurses must assess resources, service gaps, and patients’ adaptation to returning to their communities.
w: Managing complex ventilator settings in critical care
Critical care skills are hospital-focused, not the community need described.
Performing surgical procedures independently in clinics
Surgery is outside the community nursing skills described.
Avoiding social workers and case managers to cut costs
Close collaboration with social workers and case managers is critical.

items.q: Which action by the nurse best demonstrates providing care in an efficient and economically sound manner?
items.a: Using supplies and equipment judiciously during patient care
items.ex: Nurses control costs by following protocols, planning timely discharge, and using supplies and equipment judiciously.
w: Opening extra dressing kits at the bedside in case they are needed
Opening unneeded supplies wastes resources.
Postponing discharge planning until the day the patient leaves
Timely, well-planned discharge is part of cost-effective care.
Departing from established protocols to save time on a busy shift
Following established protocols is part of efficient, sound care.

alt.q: A nurse is planning care for a patient expected to go home in 3 days. Which action reflects responsible use of health care resources?
alt.a: Beginning timely, well-planned discharge preparation now
alt.ex: Exercising timely, well-planned discharge is one way nurses provide efficient, economically sound care.
w: Waiting for the discharge order before starting any teaching
Late planning can delay discharge and waste resources.
Ordering extra supplies to send home just in case
Judicious use of supplies is expected; extras waste resources.
Keeping the patient an extra day to finish routine teaching
Unneeded hospital days increase costs; teaching should start early.

items.q: Which nursing response to health care reform is consistent with the chapter?
items.a: Collaborating closely with social workers and case managers
items.ex: As care moves into communities, the chapter calls close collaboration with social workers and case managers critical.
w: Keeping nursing education unchanged as care shifts to communities
The chapter calls for changing nursing education to respond to reform.
Reducing efforts to help patients adapt to new delivery methods
Nurses should help patients adapt to new health care delivery methods.
Leaving hospital staffing and management models as they are
The chapter calls for improving staffing and management models in hospitals.

alt.q: A hospital nursing department is preparing for changes from health care reform. Which plan reflects the chapter’s recommendations?
alt.a: Improving staffing models and preparing patients to return home safely
alt.ex: Nursing responds to reform by improving staffing and management models and providing care to safely return patients home.
w: Extending hospital stays so patients recover fully before discharge
Reform shifts care toward community settings and safe return home.
Limiting discharge teaching to reduce nursing workload
Helping patients adapt and return safely home requires teaching.
Ending collaboration with community agencies to control costs
Assessing community resources and collaborating are emphasized.

items.q: According to population projections cited in the chapter, what will be true by 2030?
items.a: All baby boomers will be older than 65 years of age

w: All baby boomers will be older than 75 years of age
The projection is that all baby boomers will be older than 65, not 75.
One of every ten residents will be of retirement age
The projection is one of every five residents, not one in ten.
One of every two residents will be of retirement age
The projection is one of every five residents, not one in two.

alt.q: By 2044, what change in the U.S. population is predicted?
alt.a: More than half of the population will be part of a minority group
alt.ex: Projections predict that by 2044 more than half of the U.S. population will be part of a minority group.
w: More than half of the population will live in rural areas
The population continues shifting from rural areas to urban centers.
More than half of the population will be older than 65
The projection is one in five of retirement age by 2030, not half.
Less than one-tenth of the population will be part of a minority group
The population is becoming more racially and ethnically diverse.

items.q: The U.S. population is still shifting from urban centers to rural areas.
items.a: False
items.ex: The population is still shifting from rural areas to urban centers, while more people live with chronic illness.
items.ww: The chapter describes movement from rural to urban areas, not the reverse.

alt.q: More people today want to receive outpatient and community-based care and remain in their homes or communities.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Outpatient settings are expanding, and more people prefer care that lets them remain in their homes or communities.
alt.ww: The chapter states that more people want outpatient and community-based care.

items.q: Which factors contribute to increases in the medically underserved population? Select all that apply.
o: Unemployment or underemployment
Unemployment and underemployment contribute to being medically underserved.
Inadequate health insurance
Inadequate insurance limits access to care.
Homelessness
Homelessness contributes to being medically underserved.
Mental illness
Mental illness is a listed contributing factor.
Comprehensive employer-sponsored insurance
Adequate insurance improves access; inadequate insurance is the risk factor.
Declining health care costs
Rising, not declining, costs contribute to the underserved population.
items.ex: Unemployment, underemployment, inadequate insurance, low-paying jobs, mental illness, homelessness, and rising costs all increase the medically underserved population.

alt.q: A community nurse assesses residents at a shelter. Which factors identified in the chapter would place these residents among the medically underserved? Select all that apply.
o: Low-paying jobs
Low-paying jobs are a listed contributing factor.
Rising health care costs
Rising costs contribute to the underserved population.
Homelessness
Homelessness is a listed contributing factor.
Stable full-time employment
Unemployment or underemployment, not stable employment, is the risk factor.
Adequate health insurance coverage
Inadequate insurance, not adequate coverage, is the risk factor.
alt.ex: Correct: Low-paying jobs; Rising health care costs; Homelessness.

items.q: The trauma that health care providers experience when witnessing and caring for others suffering trauma is called [[secondary traumatic stress]].
items.ex: Secondary traumatic stress, combined with burnout, makes up compassion fatigue.

alt.q: An oncology nurse who cares for patients through years of cancer treatment may develop [[secondary traumatic stress]], the trauma of witnessing others’ suffering.
alt.ex: Secondary traumatic stress, combined with burnout, makes up compassion fatigue.

items.q: A nurse says, “I skip my breaks and pick up extra shifts because my patients need me more than I need rest.” Which response by the charge nurse is best?
items.a: “You can’t give fully engaged, compassionate care when you’re depleted.”
items.ex: Nurses cannot give engaged, compassionate care when depleted, so self-care is necessary to function as healthy professionals.
w: “That kind of dedication is what makes a nurse truly professional.”
Praising self-neglect reinforces the depletion that leads to burnout.
“Self-care matters only for nurses who work in acute care.”
All nurses have self-care needs that must be met.
“Rest is less important than meeting every patient need.”
Unmet self-care needs undermine the care nurses provide.

alt.q: Why does the chapter emphasize nurses’ self-care?
alt.a: Nurses cannot give fully engaged, compassionate care when depleted
alt.ex: The chapter explains that a depleted nurse cannot give engaged, compassionate care to others.
w: Self-care is required for annual renewal of a nursing license
The chapter links self-care to quality of care, not licensure.
Self-care prevents nurses from encountering grief and loss
Nurses will still experience grief and loss; self-care helps them cope.
Self-care matters only during public health emergencies
Self-care needs exist throughout a nurse’s education and career.

items.q: Why is caring for the medically underserved population challenging?
items.a: Social, political, economic, and health literacy factors affect access to care
items.ex: These factors affect access both to care and to health care–related resources for the medically underserved.
w: This population rarely has chronic or mental health needs
Mental illness is one of the factors that contributes to being underserved.
Nursing has historically avoided advocating for this population
Nursing has a strong history of advocating for the medically underserved.
Rising health care costs have shrunk the size of this population
Rising costs increase, not decrease, the underserved population.

alt.q: A nurse plans teaching for a medically underserved patient who has difficulty understanding written health information. Which access factor identified in the chapter is the nurse addressing?
alt.a: Health literacy
alt.ex: Health literacy, along with social, political, and economic factors, affects access to care and health resources.
w: Demographic shift
Demographic shifts describe population changes, not a patient’s understanding of health information.
Lateral violence
Lateral violence is nurse-to-nurse behavior, not a patient access factor.
Compassion fatigue
Compassion fatigue affects nurses, not a patient’s access to care.

items.q: Current philosophies and definitions of nursing have a holistic focus. What does this focus address?
items.a: The whole person in all dimensions, in health and illness, with family and community
items.ex: A holistic focus addresses the whole person in all dimensions, in health and illness, and in interaction with family and community.
w: The patient’s physical illness during acute care, apart from family influences
Holism includes all dimensions and interaction with family and community.
The disease process alone, mainly during hospital stays
Holism covers health as well as illness, beyond the disease process.
The family’s needs, rather than the individual patient’s needs
Holism addresses the whole person within family and community, not family alone.

alt.q: Which nursing action best reflects the holistic focus of current nursing philosophies?
alt.a: Assessing a patient’s physical, emotional, and family needs together
alt.ex: Holistic care addresses the whole person in all dimensions and in interaction with family and community.
w: Focusing care only on the patient’s medical diagnosis
A diagnosis-only focus ignores the other dimensions of the person.
Addressing family needs only after the patient is discharged
Holistic care includes the family throughout health and illness.
Limiting assessment to vital signs and laboratory results
Physical data alone do not address the whole person.

items.q: A nurse notices that a unit’s pressure injury prevention procedure was written many years ago. Which action best reflects evidence-based practice?
items.a: Searching for the best current scientific evidence on pressure injury prevention
items.ex: Evidence-based practice means always searching for the best scientific evidence rather than relying solely on education, experience, or policy.
w: Continuing the procedure because it is official agency policy
Practice should not rely solely on agency policies and procedures.
Using the method the nurse learned in nursing school
Practice should not rely solely on information gained during education.
Following the approach experienced co-workers prefer
Practice should not rely solely on experiential knowledge.

alt.q: According to the chapter, what does it mean for nursing practice to be based on current evidence?
alt.a: Always searching for the best scientific evidence for recurrent patient problems
alt.ex: Current evidence-based practice means always seeking the best scientific evidence for recurrent patient health care problems.
w: Relying mainly on knowledge gained during nursing education
Education alone is not enough; nurses must seek current evidence.
Following agency policies and procedures without question
Agency policies alone are not a substitute for current evidence.
Basing decisions primarily on personal clinical experience
Experiential knowledge alone is not enough; nurses must seek current evidence.

items.q: When patient outcomes improve as a result of evidence, nursing practices change and become standards of care.
items.a: True
items.ex: Evidence that improves patient outcomes changes nursing practice and becomes the standard of care.
items.ww: The chapter states directly that evidence-based improvements become standards of care.

alt.q: Following agency policies and procedures alone is sufficient for evidence-based nursing practice.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses must not rely solely on agency policies; they search for the best scientific evidence.
alt.ww: The chapter warns against relying solely on education, experience, or agency policies.

items.q: According to the chapter, which core responsibility of the registered nurse is shaped by scientific and evidence-based knowledge?
items.a: Making sound clinical judgments
items.ex: Making sound clinical judgments is a core RN responsibility, and evidence-based knowledge is a critical element shaping it.
w: Writing agency policies and procedures
Policies are not the core responsibility described; practice should not rely solely on them.
Prescribing medical treatments
Prescribing is not described as the RN’s core responsibility.
Developing unit budgets
Budgeting is a nurse administrator function, not the RN’s core responsibility described.

alt.q: Clinical judgment is influenced by which critical thinking element, of which evidence-based knowledge is a critical part?
alt.a: Knowledge
alt.ex: The chapter states clinical judgment is influenced by the critical thinking element of knowledge, including evidence-based knowledge.
w: Experience
The chapter names knowledge, not experience, as the element containing evidence-based knowledge.
Attitudes
The chapter names knowledge, not attitudes, as the element shaping judgment here.
Standards
The chapter names knowledge, not standards, as the element shaping judgment here.

items.q: Health care agencies show commitment to stakeholders by implementing evidence-based practices. Which goals does this support? Select all that apply.
o: Addressing health care disparities
An equitable system addresses disparities.
Controlling health care costs
Controlling costs is part of the commitment to stakeholders.
Reducing gaps in care
Reducing gaps in care is part of the commitment.
Improving patient safety
Evidence-based practices improve patient safety.
Increasing the number of hospital admissions
More admissions are not a goal of a safe, equitable system.
Limiting services to fully insured patients
An equitable system addresses disparities rather than restricting access.
items.ex: Agencies commit to a safe, high-quality, equitable system that addresses disparities, controls costs, reduces gaps, and improves safety through evidence-based practice.

alt.q: A hospital wants to create a safe, high-quality, equitable health care system. Which strategies are consistent with the chapter? Select all that apply.
o: Implementing evidence-based practices
Evidence-based practices improve patient safety and quality.
Addressing disparities in care
An equitable system addresses disparities.
Reducing gaps in care
Reducing gaps in care is part of the commitment.
Raising costs to fund new services
The goal is to control health care costs.
Relying solely on long-standing procedures
Practice should be based on current evidence, not tradition alone.
alt.ex: Correct: Implementing evidence-based practices; Addressing disparities in care; Reducing gaps in care.

items.q: A nurse is caring for Kitty, a 10-year-old with severe developmental delay whose parents have provided all of her care. Acting as a patient advocate, which question is most appropriate for the nurse to ask the parents?
items.a: “What are your goals for Kitty’s care as she grows older?”
items.ex: Advocacy begins with knowing the family’s goals for future care so the nurse can help them achieve those goals.
w: “Have you thought about placing Kitty in a long-term care facility?”
Suggesting placement imposes the nurse’s plan before learning the family’s goals.
“Why did you choose this particular school for Kitty?”
School choice is already meeting her needs and is not the advocacy priority.
“Could you increase Kitty’s seizure medicine if you need to?”
Her seizures are controlled, and changing doses requires a prescriber.

alt.q: Kitty’s parents tell the nurse they want to keep caring for her at home as long as possible. Which nursing action best supports them as an advocate?
alt.a: Helping the parents identify resources to achieve their goal of home care
alt.ex: An advocate uses the family’s goals to help them achieve those goals while respecting their preferences.
w: Encouraging the parents to reconsider and plan for placement
This overrides the family’s stated goal rather than supporting it.
Telling the parents that home care will soon become impossible
This dismisses their goal instead of helping them reach it.
Leaving any discussion of future care to the health care provider
Advocacy is a nursing role; the nurse acts on the family’s behalf.

items.q: Why is computerized physician/provider order entry considered a critical patient safety initiative?
items.a: It improves safety in medication ordering and administration
items.ex: CPOE lets providers enter orders directly and is a critical safety initiative, especially for medication ordering and administration.
w: It replaces the need for nursing assessment of patients
Technology supports assessment but does not replace nursing assessment.
It lets patients enter their own medication orders at home
CPOE allows health care providers, not patients, to enter orders.
It eliminates the need for an electronic health record
CPOE and the EHR are both used; one does not replace the other.

alt.q: Which technology allows health care providers to enter medical orders directly?
alt.a: Computerized physician/provider order entry
alt.ex: CPOE allows health care providers to directly enter medical orders, improving medication safety.
w: Hospital Consumer Assessment of Healthcare Providers and Systems
HCAHPS is a survey measuring patients’ perspectives on hospital care.
Telehealth e-visit platform
Telehealth and e-visits open new venues for patient care, not order entry.
Hospital Compare consumer website
Hospital Compare lets consumers compare hospital performance measures.

items.q: How do emerging information technologies affect nursing practice? Select all that apply.
o: They provide more accurate, noninvasive assessment tools
Emerging technologies provide more accurate, noninvasive assessment tools.
They help nurses implement evidence-based practices automatically
Technologies help nurses implement evidence-based practices automatically.
They collect and trend patient outcome data
Technologies collect and trend patient outcome data.
They eliminate the need for patient teaching
Nurses must teach patients how to use electronic tools correctly.
They replace relationships between nurses and patients
Technologies help nurses build relationships with patients.
items.ex: Emerging technologies improve assessment, automate evidence-based practice, trend outcome data, support clinical decisions, and expand access to care.

alt.q: Which benefits of telehealth and related technologies are described in the chapter? Select all that apply.
o: Increased access to care for rural populations
Telehealth has increased access for rural populations.
Support for patients with chronic pain and other chronic conditions
Telehealth supports patients with chronic conditions.
Information and support for family caregivers in end-of-life care
Telehealth provides family caregivers end-of-life support.
Helping older adults stay home while staying connected
Technology helps older adults remain home and connected.
Ending the need for patient education about devices
Nurses must learn the tools to teach patients correct use.
Replacing care coordination by the health care team
Technology helps with decision support and care coordination.
alt.ex: Correct: Increased access to care for rural populations; Support for patients with chronic pain and other chronic conditions; Information and support for family caregivers in end-of-life care; Helping older adults stay home while staying connected.

items.q: A patient with heart failure will use a home device to phone in daily health information. Which action by the nurse is most important?
items.a: Learning how the device works so the nurse can teach correct use
items.ex: The chapter advises nurses to learn how electronic tools work so they can teach patients to use them correctly.
w: Letting the patient figure out the device after discharge
Patients need teaching to use the device correctly.
Telling the patient the device replaces follow-up care
Devices open new venues for care but do not replace follow-up.
Asking only the family to learn the device
The patient using the device needs teaching to use it correctly.

alt.q: Why should nurses learn how telehealth and e-visit tools work?
alt.a: So they can teach patients to use them correctly
alt.ex: Learning how electronic tools work allows nurses to teach patients correct use.
w: So they can replace face-to-face nursing assessments
Technology supports assessment rather than replacing nursing care.
So they can limit patients’ access to health information
These tools increase information acquisition and distribution.
So they can avoid documenting care in the record
Documentation is still required, often in the EHR.

items.q: The increased use of telehealth and telemedicine has increased access to care for rural populations.
items.a: True
items.ex: Telehealth and telemedicine have expanded rural access and support chronic condition and end-of-life care.
items.ww: The chapter states telehealth has increased access for care in rural populations.

alt.q: Technological innovations make it harder for older adults to stay in their homes because they require constant on-site monitoring.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Technology helps caregivers monitor home environments and enables older adults to stay home while connected to support.
alt.ww: The chapter describes technology as enabling older adults to remain at home.

items.q: Which definition describes genomics?
items.a: The study of the structure, function, evolution, and mapping of genomes
items.ex: Genomics is the branch of molecular biology concerned with the structure, function, evolution, and mapping of genomes.
w: The study of inheritance and how traits pass between generations
This defines genetics.
The study of how proteins made by genes direct cell activity
Genes carry instructions for proteins, but this is not the definition of genomics.
The study of how diet and activity alone influence disease rates
Genomics studies genomes; behaviors interact with genes but are not the definition.

alt.q: How does genetics differ from genomics?
alt.a: Genetics studies inheritance and how traits pass between generations
alt.ex: Genetics studies inheritance and variation of genes, while genomics maps and studies whole genomes.
w: Genetics studies the mapping and evolution of entire genomes
This describes genomics.
Genetics studies only environmental causes of disease
Genetics studies inheritance and variation of genes.
Genetics studies nucleotide sequences within a single genome
This describes genomics.

items.a: Efficient method for documenting and managing patient health care information

w: Allows health care providers to directly enter medical orders
That goes with CPOE.
Website comparing hospitals’ performance on specific diseases and procedures

Standardized survey measuring patients’ perspectives on hospital care
That goes with HCAHPS.

That goes with HCAHPS.

w: Efficient method for documenting and managing patient health care information

Website comparing hospitals’ performance on specific diseases and procedures
That goes with Hospital Compare.

alt.q: What is Telehealth?
alt.a: Remote care that has increased access for rural populations

w: Efficient method for documenting and managing patient health care information
That goes with Electronic health record.
Allows health care providers to directly enter medical orders

Website comparing hospitals’ performance on specific diseases and procedures

mt.q: Match each health care technology or consumer resource with its description.
pairs: Efficient method for documenting and managing patient health care information
Allows health care providers to directly enter medical orders
