items.q: A nurse is assessing the structure or locale of a community. Which data belong to this component? Select all that apply.
o: Water and sanitation
Water and sanitation are listed under structure in Box 3.2.
Emergency services
Emergency services are part of the community’s structure.
Transportation
Transportation is a structural element of the community.
Average household income
Economic status, such as average household income, is listed under structure.
Age distribution
Age distribution is a population characteristic.
Welfare system
The welfare system belongs to the social system component.
items.ex: Structure covers boundaries, emergency services, water and sanitation, housing, economic status, transportation, and safety.

alt.q: Which items would a nurse record under the structure component of a community assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Housing
Housing is listed under structure in Box 3.2.
Geographical boundaries
Geographical boundaries define the locale and belong to structure.
Safety
Safety is a structural element of the community.
Density
Density is a population characteristic.
Volunteer programs
Volunteer programs are part of the social system.
Predominant religious groups
Predominant religious groups are a population characteristic.
alt.ex: Correct: Housing; Geographical boundaries; Safety.

items.q: Which data describe the population component of a community assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Growth trends
Growth trends are listed under population in Box 3.2.
Education level
The education level of residents is a population characteristic.
Predominant ethnic groups
Predominant ethnic groups describe the people of the community.
Sex distribution
Sex distribution is a population characteristic.
Educational system
The educational system, such as the schools, belongs to the social system.
Housing
Housing belongs to the structure component.
items.ex: Population data include age and sex distribution, growth trends, density, education level, and predominant ethnic and religious groups.

alt.q: A nurse is compiling the population section of a community assessment. Which data should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Age distribution
Age distribution is listed under population in Box 3.2.
Density
Population density describes the people of the community.
Predominant religious groups
Predominant religious groups are a population characteristic.
Communication system
The communication system belongs to the social system.
Transportation
Transportation belongs to the structure component.
Emergency services
Emergency services belong to the structure component.
alt.ex: Correct: Age distribution; Density; Predominant religious groups.

items.q: Which elements belong to the social system component of a community assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Government
Government is listed under social system in Box 3.2.
Health system
The health system is part of the community’s social system.
Volunteer programs
Volunteer programs are part of the social system.
Communication system
The communication system is part of the social system.
Water and sanitation
Water and sanitation belong to the structure component.
Age distribution
Age distribution is a population characteristic.
items.ex: The social system includes the educational, government, communication, welfare, volunteer, and health systems.

alt.q: While assessing a community’s social system, which agencies or systems should the nurse examine? Select all that apply.
o: Educational system
Schools and the educational system are part of the social system.
Welfare system
The welfare system is listed under social system in Box 3.2.
Health system
Health care agencies make up the community’s health system.
Geographical boundaries
Geographical boundaries belong to the structure component.
Growth trends
Growth trends are a population characteristic.
alt.ex: Correct: Educational system; Welfare system; Health system.

items.q: In a community assessment, the number of residents receiving public assistance is recorded under which component?
items.a: Structure, as part of economic status
items.ex: Box 3.2 lists economic status, including household income and residents on public assistance, under structure.
w: Population, as part of demographics
Population covers age, sex, growth, density, education, ethnicity, and religion, not economic status.
Social system, as part of welfare
The welfare system itself is a social system, but residents’ economic status is a structural item.
Social system, as part of government
Government is a social system; economic status of residents is recorded under structure.

alt.q: A nurse notes that the average household income in a neighborhood is low. Under which component of the community assessment should this be recorded?
alt.a: Structure
alt.ex: Economic status, such as average household income, is listed under the structure component.
w: Population
Population data cover age, sex, growth trends, density, education, and ethnic and religious groups.
Social system
The social system covers schools, government, communication, welfare, volunteer, and health systems.
Health system
The health system is one part of the social system, not where income is recorded.

items.q: How does “education level” differ from “educational system” in a community assessment?
items.a: Education level is a population characteristic; the educational system is a social system
items.ex: Box 3.2 lists residents’ education level under population and the schools, or educational system, under social system.
w: Education level is a social system; the educational system is a structural feature
Education level describes the people, and the educational system is a social system, not structure.
Both are population characteristics recorded with age and sex distribution
Only education level is a population item; the educational system is a social system.
Both are structural features recorded with housing and transportation
Neither is a structural item; one is population and the other is social system.

alt.q: A nurse records that most adults in a community did not finish high school. Which component of the community does this finding describe?
alt.a: Population
alt.ex: Education level of residents is a population characteristic in Box 3.2.
w: Social system
The schools themselves are a social system, but residents’ education level describes the population.
Structure
Structure covers boundaries, services, housing, economics, transportation, and safety.
Welfare system
The welfare system is part of the social system and does not describe residents’ schooling.

items.q: A nurse new to a community health agency needs the age distribution and growth trends of the population. Which source should the nurse use?
items.a: Statistics from reliable websites and the local public health department
items.ex: Demographic data are obtained by accessing community statistics from reliable websites and the local public health department.
w: Observations made while driving through the neighborhood
Driving through the area is used to assess structure, not demographic statistics.
Informal conversations with patients in the clinic waiting room
A few patient conversations are not reliable population statistics.
A site visit to the local school district office
Site visits are used to learn about social systems such as schools and agencies.

alt.q: Which method is most appropriate for obtaining the demographic data needed for a community assessment?
alt.a: Accessing community statistics through the local public health department
alt.ex: Population demographics come from reliable statistical sources such as websites and the local public health department.
w: Walking the neighborhood to see where residents gather
Observing where residents meet assesses the structure or locale.
Scheduling a site visit to a local health care agency
Site visits help the nurse learn about social systems and their services.
Interviewing several residents about their family histories
Individual interviews do not provide reliable population-wide statistics.

items.q: During a walk through a neighborhood, a community health nurse notes abandoned buildings, missing sidewalks, and roads in poor repair. Which part of the community assessment is the nurse completing?
items.a: Assessment of the structure or locale
items.ex: Traveling through the community and observing its design and safety issues assesses the structure or locale.
w: Assessment of the population
Population data are demographic statistics such as age, sex, density, and education level.
Assessment of the social systems
Social systems such as schools and agencies are assessed through websites or site visits.
Assessment of the health system
The health system is a social system and is not assessed by observing roads and buildings.

alt.q: A nurse wants to assess the structure or locale of a community. Which action should the nurse take?
alt.a: Travel around the community and observe its design and where residents meet
alt.ex: Structure is assessed by traveling the area and observing its design, location of services, and meeting places.
w: Download census reports on the community’s age and sex distribution
Census data describe the population component, not the structure.
Review the websites of local schools and health care agencies
Agency websites are used to learn about the social systems.
Schedule a meeting with the director of a volunteer program
Volunteer programs are part of the social system, not the structure.

items.q: While assessing the physical environment of a community, which finding should the nurse identify as a possible environmental hazard?
items.a: Contamination of the soil near a former industrial site
items.ex: The nurse looks for possible environmental hazards in the air, water, or soil when assessing the physical environment.
w: A large proportion of residents older than 65 years
Age distribution is a population characteristic, not an environmental hazard.
A limited number of local volunteer programs
Volunteer programs are part of the social system, not the physical environment.
A high percentage of residents of one religious group
Predominant religious groups are a population characteristic, not a hazard.

alt.q: Which observation made during a community assessment represents an environmental hazard?
alt.a: Residents report a chemical odor in the local water supply
alt.ex: Environmental hazards are found in the air, water, or soil of the physical environment.
w: The community has a growing number of young families
Growth trends describe the population, not an environmental hazard.
The local school has recently changed its curriculum
The school curriculum relates to the educational system, a social system.
Most residents rely on one radio station for local news
News sources relate to the communication system, a social system.

items.q: A nurse is making a home visit to an older adult who lives alone. Which assessment best reflects evaluating the home for safety?
items.a: Checking that door locks are secure and walkway lighting works
items.ex: Home safety checks include secure door locks, intact windows, and working lighting along walkways and entryways.
w: Reviewing the patient’s list of current medications
Medication review is important but does not assess the physical safety of the home.
Asking about the patient’s preferred religious practices
Religious preferences do not address the safety of the home environment.
Recording the patient’s level of formal education
Education level does not assess the security or safety of the home.

alt.q: During a home safety assessment, which question should the nurse consider?
alt.a: Are the windows secure and intact?
alt.ex: Secure, intact windows are one of the home safety questions the book lists, along with locks and lighting.
w: Is the home close to the patient’s workplace?
Distance to work does not determine the home’s physical safety.
Does the patient prefer to cook at home?
Cooking preference does not reflect the security of the home.
How many people attend the patient’s church?
Church attendance does not address the safety of the home.

items.q: A nurse is assessing a patient’s home for safety. Which items should the nurse check? Select all that apply.
o: Door locks are secure
Secure door locks are part of the home safety assessment.
Windows are secure and intact
Intact, secure windows help protect the patient at home.
Lighting along walkways and entryways works
Working lighting on walkways and entryways is a listed safety check.
The home is decorated to the patient’s taste
Decor reflects preference, not safety.
The home is near the patient’s favorite store
Distance to a store does not determine the safety of the home.
items.ex: The book’s home safety questions cover secure door locks, secure intact windows, and working lighting along walkways and entryways.

alt.q: Which findings during a home visit indicate that the home is safe? Select all that apply.
o: The entryway light turns on and works
Operational lighting along entryways is a home safety feature.
The front door has a working, secure lock
Secure door locks protect the patient in the home.
The bedroom window closes and is unbroken
Secure, intact windows are a home safety feature.
The walkway light has been burned out for weeks
Nonworking walkway lighting is a safety concern, not a sign of safety.
A side window is cracked and will not latch
A window that is not secure or intact is a safety concern.
alt.ex: Correct: The entryway light turns on and works; The front door has a working, secure lock; The bedroom window closes and is unbroken.

items.q: A community health nurse will begin home visits in a neighborhood with frequent reports of crime. Which information is most important for the nurse to know before conducting patient assessments?
items.a: The level of community violence and the resources available when help is needed
items.ex: Knowing community violence levels and available help resources is vital when assessing patients in that community.
w: The average age of residents and the community’s overall growth trends
Age and growth data describe the population but do not prepare the nurse for violence.
The names of the predominant ethnic and religious groups in the area
These population data matter, but violence and help resources are vital for safety here.
The schedule of local volunteer programs and community meetings
Volunteer schedules do not address violence or how to get help when needed.

alt.q: Why should a nurse know the level of community violence before assessing patients in their homes?
alt.a: Patient assessment occurs in the context of the community and its available resources for help
alt.ex: Individuals are always assessed in the context of the community, including its violence level and help resources.
w: Violence levels determine which patients qualify for home care services
The book does not link violence levels to eligibility for home care.
The nurse must report community violence data to the public health department
The text does not describe the nurse reporting violence data during assessments.
Violence is the most common cause of illness in every community
The text does not identify violence as the most common cause of illness.

items.q: Why is understanding the community essential before trying to promote a patient’s health?
items.a: Efforts to promote health and bring about change are unlikely to succeed without it
items.ex: The community is where patients live, work, play, and learn, so health promotion depends on understanding it.
w: Insurers require a community assessment before paying for home visits
The text does not tie community assessment to insurer payment.
Patients cannot give consent until a community assessment is completed
Consent is not dependent on completion of a community assessment.
Community data replace the need for individual patient assessments
Individual assessments are still done, but against the community background.

alt.q: A nurse tries to change a patient’s health behaviors without first learning about the patient’s community. What outcome is most likely, according to the text?
alt.a: The effort to promote health and bring about change is unlikely to succeed
alt.ex: Without adequate understanding of the patient’s environment, health promotion and change efforts are unlikely to succeed.
w: The patient will change more quickly because the plan is simpler
Ignoring the community makes success less likely, not faster.
The outcome will be the same as with a full community assessment
The text states that understanding the environment is needed for success.
The patient will need fewer follow-up visits from the nurse
The text links missing community understanding to failed change, not fewer visits.

items.q: What does completing a community assessment require of the nurse?
items.a: Clinical judgment and critical thinking to analyze multiple sources of data
items.ex: Community assessment draws on many data sources, which the nurse analyzes using clinical judgment and critical thinking.
w: Advanced certification in epidemiology and biostatistics
The text does not require special certification to assess a community.
A single reliable source of data from the hospital
Community assessment uses multiple data sources, not one hospital source.
A physician order for each data source consulted
No health care provider order is needed to gather community data.

alt.q: A nursing student collects data from public health statistics, neighborhood observations, and agency websites. What must the student use to complete the community assessment?
alt.a: Clinical judgment and critical thinking to analyze the data together
alt.ex: Analyzing multiple sources of community data requires clinical judgment and critical thinking.
w: Only the public health statistics, because they are most objective
The assessment combines multiple data sources rather than relying on one.
Only the neighborhood observations, because they are firsthand
Firsthand observation addresses structure only; all sources are analyzed together.
A standardized score that ranks the community against others
The text does not describe ranking communities with a standardized score.

items.q: A complete community assessment examines all three community components to identify needs for health policy, health programs, and health services.
items.a: True
items.ex: Each component is examined to identify needs for health policy, health programs, and needed health services.
items.ww: The assessment does not stop at one component; all three are examined to find policy, program, and service needs.

alt.q: The main purpose of a community assessment is to diagnose the illnesses of individual residents.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A community assessment identifies needs for health policy, health programs, and health services for the population.
alt.ww: Diagnosing individual illnesses is not its purpose; it focuses on the population and its environment.

items.q: A nurse should always assess an individual patient in the context of the patient’s community.
items.a: True
items.ex: Once the nurse understands the community, individual assessments are performed against that background.
items.ww: Assessing a patient apart from the community ignores the environment that shapes the patient’s health.

alt.q: Individual patient assessments should be kept separate from community data so that the patient’s findings are not biased.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book directs nurses to perform individual assessments against the background of the community.
alt.ww: Separating them is incorrect; the individual is always assessed in the context of the community.

items.q: Demographic data about a community’s population are best gathered by walking through the neighborhood and observing residents.
items.a: False
items.ex: Demographic data come from community statistics on reliable websites and from the local public health department.
items.ww: Walking the neighborhood assesses the structure or locale, not population statistics.

alt.q: A nurse can learn about a community’s social systems, such as schools and health care agencies, by visiting their websites or scheduling a site visit.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Social system information is obtained from agency websites or site visits to learn about their services.
alt.ww: These methods are the ones the book describes for learning about social systems.

items.q: The community has three components: the structure or locale, the people, and the [[social systems|social system]].
items.ex: Structure, people (population), and social systems are the three components examined in a community assessment.

alt.q: Schools, government, welfare, and health care agencies are part of a community’s [[social system|social systems]].
alt.ex: Structure, people (population), and social systems are the three components examined in a community assessment.

items.q: A community health nurse visits a patient with a healing wound whose family is worried about the cost of supplies. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Coordinate wound care and help find low-cost dressings
items.ex: Coordinating services and locating affordable supplies brings together resources and supports continuity of care.
w: Tell the family to use any clean household cloth instead of dressings
Substituting household items is not what the book suggests; the nurse helps locate cost-effective dressings.
Advise the family to return to the hospital for every dressing change
Repeated hospital visits add cost and do not coordinate care in the community.
Leave the family to research dressing suppliers on their own
The nurse brings together resources rather than leaving the family to find them alone.

alt.q: Which nursing action best illustrates bringing together resources to improve a patient’s continuity of care in the community?
alt.a: Arranging wound care services and helping the patient locate affordable dressing supplies
alt.ex: The book gives coordinating wound care and finding cost-effective dressings as an example of improving continuity of care.
w: Performing every dressing change personally regardless of the family’s ability
Continuity of care depends on coordinating resources, not the nurse doing everything personally.
Referring the patient to several agencies that each provide wound care
Overlapping referrals create duplication of services rather than coordinated care.
Teaching wound care once and closing the case at the first visit
A single teaching session does not coordinate ongoing resources for the healing wound.

items.q: What results when a community health nurse collaborates with patients and their health care providers?
items.a: Person-centered care with less duplication of health care services
items.ex: Collaboration with patients and providers provides person-centered care and helps reduce duplicated services.
w: Faster discharge from acute care with fewer home visits
The text links collaboration to person-centered care and less duplication, not fewer visits.
Reduced need for the patient to participate in decisions
Person-centered care increases, not reduces, the patient’s involvement.
Transfer of care planning entirely to the health care provider
Collaboration shares planning; it does not hand it entirely to the provider.

alt.q: A patient is receiving the same physical therapy service from two different agencies. Which nursing action would best address this problem?
alt.a: Collaborate with the patient and the health care providers to coordinate services
alt.ex: Collaborating with patients and providers helps reduce duplication of health care services.
w: Encourage the patient to continue both services for faster progress
Continuing both services keeps the duplication the nurse should reduce.
Cancel one agency’s services without discussing it with the patient
Acting without the patient is not collaborative or person-centered.
Report the duplication to the insurer and take no other action
Reporting alone does not coordinate the patient’s care with the providers.

items.q: Which approach should a community health nurse use to promote and protect a patient’s health within the context of the community?
items.a: An evidence-based practice approach
items.ex: The book directs nurses to promote and protect health within the community using an evidence-based practice approach.
w: An acute care, disease-focused approach
Community health nursing focuses on prevention and health promotion with evidence, not acute disease care alone.
A tradition-based approach
Relying on tradition rather than evidence does not reflect the book’s guidance.
A provider-directed approach
The book stresses evidence-based, person-centered care rather than care directed only by the provider.

alt.q: A nurse plans a childhood obesity program after reviewing research showing which community strategies work. What approach does this reflect?
alt.a: Evidence-based practice
alt.ex: Basing community interventions on research findings is an evidence-based practice approach.
w: Acute care practice
Acute care focuses on illness in hospitals, not research-based community programs.
Custodial care
Custodial care provides assistance with daily needs, not research-based programs.
Crisis intervention
Crisis intervention addresses an immediate emergency, not planned prevention programs.

items.q: According to the evidence on childhood obesity in high-risk racial/ethnic minority groups, which approach best prevents obesity?
items.a: Combined physical activity and nutrition interventions
items.ex: Prevention is best achieved by combining physical activity and nutrition approaches that target obesity and its co-morbidities.
w: Nutrition counseling delivered without an activity component
Diet alone is less effective; interventions should include both diet and physical activity.
Physical activity programs delivered without diet guidance
Activity alone is less effective; nutrition must be combined with physical activity.
Weight-loss medication prescribed during school-age years
The evidence summary emphasizes lifestyle approaches, not medication.

alt.q: A nurse is designing a childhood obesity program. Which plan follows the book’s application to nursing practice?
alt.a: Include both diet and physical activity recommendations
alt.ex: Interventions need to include both diet and physical activity recommendations to reduce obesity risk factors.
w: Focus only on diet recommendations for the child
A diet-only program omits the physical activity the evidence calls for.
Focus only on increasing the child’s daily activity
An activity-only program omits the nutrition component the evidence calls for.
Focus only on monitoring the child’s weight monthly
Monitoring alone is not an intervention targeting diet and activity.

items.q: Which conditions are common co-morbidities of childhood obesity? Select all that apply.
o: Hypertension
Hypertension is listed as a common co-morbidity of childhood obesity.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Type 2 diabetes mellitus is a common co-morbidity of childhood obesity.
Fatty liver
Fatty liver is listed among the co-morbidities of childhood obesity.
Insulin insensitivity
Insulin insensitivity is a common co-morbidity of childhood obesity.
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
Type 1 diabetes is autoimmune; type 2 diabetes is the form linked to obesity.
Hypotension
Childhood obesity is associated with hypertension, not hypotension.
items.ex: Box 3.3 lists hypertension, insulin insensitivity, fatty liver, type 2 diabetes, and cardiovascular disease as common co-morbidities.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching parents about the health risks of childhood obesity. Which conditions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Cardiovascular disease
Cardiovascular disease is a co-morbidity associated with childhood obesity.
Hypertension
Hypertension is a common co-morbidity of childhood obesity.
Insulin insensitivity
Insulin insensitivity is a common co-morbidity of childhood obesity.
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
Type 2, not type 1, diabetes mellitus is associated with obesity.
Low blood pressure
Obesity is associated with high, not low, blood pressure.
alt.ex: Correct: Cardiovascular disease; Hypertension; Insulin insensitivity.

items.q: The parent of a 10-year-old with obesity says, “I’ll tell him to eat better and exercise, and he can handle it himself.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Children do best when the adults around them support the changes and model them too.”
items.ex: Asking children to change without adult support and role modeling does not lead to positive outcomes.
w: “That is a good plan, because children his age should manage their own health.”
Leaving the child alone without adult support will not produce positive outcomes.
“He should start a strict diet first and add activity later in the year.”
Diet and physical activity should be combined, not staggered.
“It would be best to wait until he is older to make any lifestyle changes.”
Delaying change ignores the risk of obesity-related co-morbidities.

alt.q: Which statement by a parent shows understanding of teaching about a child’s obesity program?
alt.a: “Our whole family will make these changes together so I can set the example.”
alt.ex: Adult support and role modeling are needed for children to succeed with lifestyle changes.
w: “My daughter is old enough to follow the plan without our help.”
Children without adult support and role modeling do not achieve positive outcomes.
“We will focus on her diet and worry about activity some other time.”
Interventions should include both diet and physical activity.
“The program only matters for her meals at home, not at school.”
Nutrition information must address both the school and home environments.

items.q: A nurse is planning a community program to reduce childhood obesity among families from ethnically diverse backgrounds. Which strategies reflect the book’s application to nursing practice? Select all that apply.
o: Include both diet and physical activity recommendations
Interventions need to address both diet and physical activity.
Provide nutrition information for both school and home environments
Nutritional information must cover both school and home settings.
Use culturally and linguistically appropriate communication
Culturally and linguistically appropriate care is essential for diverse populations.
Engage local youth as leaders through an obesity prevention curriculum
Engaging minority youth as leaders can mobilize support for obesity prevention.
Use one standard English-language handout for all families
A single English handout is not culturally or linguistically appropriate.
Limit nutrition teaching to meals eaten at home
Nutrition information must include the school environment as well as the home.
items.ex: Effective programs target modifiable risk factors with diet and activity, cover school and home, are culturally appropriate, and engage youth leaders.

alt.q: Which interventions would a community health nurse include in an evidence-based childhood obesity program? Select all that apply.
o: Design interventions that target modifiable obesity risk factors
Nurses should understand modifiable risk factors and design interventions to reduce them.
Hold community workshops to build attendance and buy-in
Workshops and media resources help gain attendance and community buy-in.
Offer materials in the families’ preferred languages
Linguistically appropriate communication is needed for ethnically diverse populations.
Ask children to make lifestyle changes on their own
Without adult support and role modeling, children do not achieve positive outcomes.
Recommend physical activity without any diet guidance
Interventions must include both diet and physical activity recommendations.
alt.ex: Correct: Design interventions that target modifiable obesity risk factors; Hold community workshops to build attendance and buy-in; Offer materials in the families’ preferred languages.

items.q: Children have greater success adhering to obesity interventions when their caregivers perceive the interventions as useful.
items.a: True
items.ex: Evidence shows that caregivers’ view of an intervention’s usefulness improves children’s adherence.
items.ww: Caregiver perception does matter; children adhere better when caregivers see the intervention as useful.

alt.q: A caregiver’s opinion of an obesity intervention has little effect on whether the child follows it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: When caregivers perceive interventions as useful, children have greater success adhering to them.
alt.ww: Caregiver views strongly influence the child’s adherence, so the statement is incorrect.

items.q: Community-based childhood obesity interventions have been effective both in reducing body mass index (BMI) and in building a sense of community and support among participants.
items.a: True
items.ex: Box 3.3 reports that community-based interventions reduce BMI and develop community and support among participants.
items.ww: These interventions provide both a physical benefit and a social benefit, so the statement is accurate.

alt.q: Community-based obesity interventions lower body mass index (BMI) but provide no social benefit to the participants.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Community-based interventions reduce BMI and also develop a sense of community and support among participants.
alt.ww: There is a social benefit as well, since participants gain a sense of community and support.

items.q: In the United States, obesity is less prevalent among children from ethnically diverse populations than among other children.
items.a: False
items.ex: Box 3.3 states that obesity is more prevalent in children from ethnically diverse populations in the United States.
items.ww: The reverse is true; prevalence is higher, which is why nurses target these health disparities.

alt.q: Obesity is more prevalent among children from ethnically diverse populations in the United States.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The evidence summary in Box 3.3 identifies higher obesity prevalence in children from ethnically diverse populations.
alt.ww: Prevalence is not lower in these groups; it is higher, creating a health disparity.

items.q: What role does public policy play in reducing childhood obesity in underserved communities?
items.a: Ensuring access to healthful food choices and improved socioenvironmental areas
items.ex: Public policy must ensure underserved communities can access healthful foods and improved socioenvironmental areas.
w: Requiring every child to complete a weight-loss program at school
The text does not describe mandatory weight-loss programs as public policy.
Making parents solely responsible for buying and preparing food
Policy is meant to improve access, not shift all responsibility to parents.
Limiting physical activity programs to children who are overweight
The text does not call for restricting activity programs to certain children.

alt.q: A family in an underserved neighborhood wants to follow the nurse’s nutrition advice but has no store nearby that sells fresh produce. Which issue does this illustrate?
alt.a: The need to ensure families have access to the recommended foods
alt.ex: Families need access to recommended foods so that healthy choices can actually be made.
w: The family’s lack of motivation to change its eating habits
The family wants to change; the barrier is access, not motivation.
The need for the child to follow the plan without adult help
Children need adult support; this situation is about food access.
The failure of physical activity programs in the community
The problem described is access to food, not physical activity.

items.q: Why might a childhood obesity program include community workshops and media resources?
items.a: To gain attendance and community buy-in
items.ex: Workshops and media resources are used in community-based obesity programs to draw attendance and build community buy-in.
w: To replace individual counseling of families
The text presents workshops as a way to engage the community, not as a replacement for counseling.
To reduce the need for diet recommendations
Diet recommendations remain a required part of the intervention.
To satisfy legal reporting requirements
The text does not connect workshops to any legal reporting requirement.

alt.q: A nurse plans to advertise a new family fitness and nutrition program through local media and host open workshops. What is the main goal of this strategy?
alt.a: Increasing attendance and community buy-in
alt.ex: Community workshops and media resources help gain attendance and community buy-in for obesity programs.
w: Limiting enrollment to the families at highest risk
Broad outreach is used to increase, not limit, participation.
Collecting body mass index data for research
The purpose described is engagement, not data collection.
Replacing home visits by community health nurses
Outreach supports the program but does not replace nursing visits.

items.q: A community health nurse is starting an obesity prevention program in a neighborhood where many families speak Spanish as their primary language. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Provide culturally and linguistically appropriate materials and communication
items.ex: Culturally and linguistically appropriate interventions are essential when caring for patients from ethnically diverse populations.
w: Use the agency’s standard English-language materials for consistency
Standard English materials are not linguistically appropriate for these families.
Ask the children to translate all teaching for their parents
Relying on children to translate is not culturally or linguistically appropriate communication.
Postpone the program until the families learn more English
Delaying care is not appropriate; the nurse adapts communication to the families.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of planning obesity interventions for ethnically diverse families?
alt.a: “I need to adapt my teaching to the families’ culture and language.”
alt.ex: The book calls for culturally and linguistically appropriate interventions and communication for ethnically diverse populations.
w: “I will use the same teaching plan for every family I see.”
A uniform plan ignores the culture and language of diverse families.
“Culture affects food choices only for older adults in a family.”
Culture shapes health views for the whole family, not just older adults.
“Language barriers rarely matter if the handouts have pictures.”
Linguistically appropriate communication is still essential, even with visual materials.

items.q: A patient works the night shift, and the patient’s parents provide child care during the day. How should the community health nurse use this information?
items.a: Adapt the timing and plan of interventions to fit the family’s daily routine
items.ex: Day-to-day family activities, such as work hours and child care, influence how the nurse adapts interventions.
w: Record it as background only, because it does not affect the care plan
Daily family activities are variables that shape how interventions are adapted.
Ask the patient to change jobs so that care can follow a standard schedule
The nurse adapts care to the patient’s life rather than asking the patient to change it.
Exclude the patient’s parents from discussions about the plan of care
Family members who provide care are part of the picture of the patient’s life.

alt.q: What does the book identify as the variables that influence how a nurse adapts interventions in community-based practice?
alt.a: The day-to-day activities of family life
alt.ex: The day-to-day activities of family life are the variables that influence how the nurse adapts interventions.
w: The policies of the nearest acute care hospital
Hospital policies are not identified as the variables that shape community interventions.
The nurse’s personal teaching preferences
Care is adapted to the patient’s life, not to the nurse’s preferences.
The standard schedule set by the home care agency
Interventions are adapted to the family’s routine, not a fixed agency schedule.

items.q: In designing person-centered community interventions, which step comes right after “Gain acceptance by the family and learn what makes the patient unique”?
items.a: Acquire a picture of the patient’s life, including daily routines and values
items.ex: That's step 3 of 4. The nurse begins with caring relationships, gains acceptance and understanding of the patient’s life, and then designs person-centered interventions.
w: Design person-centered interventions to promote health and prevent disease
That's step 4 of 4.
Establish strong, caring relationships with the patient and family
That's step 1 of 4.

alt.q: Which step comes first in designing person-centered community interventions?
alt.a: Establish strong, caring relationships with the patient and family
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 4. The nurse begins with caring relationships, gains acceptance and understanding of the patient’s life, and then designs person-centered interventions.
w: Gain acceptance by the family and learn what makes the patient unique
That's step 2 of 4.
Acquire a picture of the patient’s life, including daily routines and values
That's step 3 of 4.
Design person-centered interventions to promote health and prevent disease
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: Which step comes last in designing person-centered community interventions?
alt.a: Design person-centered interventions to promote health and prevent disease
alt.ex: That's step 4 of 4. The nurse begins with caring relationships, gains acceptance and understanding of the patient’s life, and then designs person-centered interventions.
w: Acquire a picture of the patient’s life, including daily routines and values
That's step 3 of 4.
Gain acceptance by the family and learn what makes the patient unique
That's step 2 of 4.
Establish strong, caring relationships with the patient and family
That's step 1 of 4.

alt.q: In designing person-centered community interventions, which step comes right after “Establish strong, caring relationships with the patient and family”?
alt.a: Gain acceptance by the family and learn what makes the patient unique
alt.ex: That's step 2 of 4. The nurse begins with caring relationships, gains acceptance and understanding of the patient’s life, and then designs person-centered interventions.
w: Acquire a picture of the patient’s life, including daily routines and values
That's step 3 of 4.
Design person-centered interventions to promote health and prevent disease
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: In designing person-centered community interventions, which step comes right after “Acquire a picture of the patient’s life, including daily routines and values”?
alt.a: Design person-centered interventions to promote health and prevent disease
alt.ex: That's step 4 of 4. The nurse begins with caring relationships, gains acceptance and understanding of the patient’s life, and then designs person-centered interventions.
w: Gain acceptance by the family and learn what makes the patient unique
That's step 2 of 4.
Establish strong, caring relationships with the patient and family
That's step 1 of 4.

alt.q: In designing person-centered community interventions, which step comes right before “Gain acceptance by the family and learn what makes the patient unique”?
alt.a: Establish strong, caring relationships with the patient and family
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 4. The nurse begins with caring relationships, gains acceptance and understanding of the patient’s life, and then designs person-centered interventions.
w: Acquire a picture of the patient’s life, including daily routines and values
That's step 3 of 4.
Design person-centered interventions to promote health and prevent disease
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: In designing person-centered community interventions, which step comes right before “Acquire a picture of the patient’s life, including daily routines and values”?
alt.a: Gain acceptance by the family and learn what makes the patient unique
alt.ex: That's step 2 of 4. The nurse begins with caring relationships, gains acceptance and understanding of the patient’s life, and then designs person-centered interventions.
w: Establish strong, caring relationships with the patient and family
That's step 1 of 4.
Design person-centered interventions to promote health and prevent disease
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: In designing person-centered community interventions, which step comes right before “Design person-centered interventions to promote health and prevent disease”?
alt.a: Acquire a picture of the patient’s life, including daily routines and values
alt.ex: That's step 3 of 4. The nurse begins with caring relationships, gains acceptance and understanding of the patient’s life, and then designs person-centered interventions.
w: Gain acceptance by the family and learn what makes the patient unique
That's step 2 of 4.
Establish strong, caring relationships with the patient and family
That's step 1 of 4.

ord.q: Put these steps in the order the nurse uses to arrive at person-centered interventions in community-based practice.
items: Establish strong, caring relationships with the patient and family
Gain acceptance by the family and learn what makes the patient unique
Acquire a picture of the patient’s life, including daily routines and values
Design person-centered interventions to promote health and prevent disease
ord.ex: The nurse begins with caring relationships, gains acceptance and understanding of the patient’s life, and then designs person-centered interventions.

items.q: When nurses bring together the resources a patient needs, they improve the patient’s [[continuity of care]].
items.ex: Bringing together community resources for each patient improves the patient’s continuity of care.

alt.q: Coordinating community services and supplies for a patient with a healing wound supports [[continuity of care]].
alt.ex: Bringing together community resources for each patient improves the patient’s continuity of care.

items.q: What allows a community health nurse to advise, counsel, and teach a patient and family effectively?
items.a: Gaining experience and acceptance by the family after building a caring relationship
items.ex: As the nurse gains experience and is accepted by the family, the nurse can advise, counsel, and teach effectively.
w: Providing written instructions at the first visit before any relationship forms
Effective teaching follows a caring relationship and the family’s acceptance.
Limiting conversations with the family to the patient’s medical diagnosis
Understanding the patient’s whole life, not only the diagnosis, supports effective teaching.
Making decisions for the family to reduce their stress
Community nurses partner with families; they do not make decisions for them.

alt.q: A nurse new to community health wants to teach a family about healthy eating. What should the nurse do first?
alt.a: Establish a strong, caring relationship with the patient and family
alt.ex: The book says to begin by establishing strong, caring relationships with patients and families.
w: Give the family a detailed meal plan at the first visit
Teaching is more effective after a caring relationship and family acceptance are established.
Refer the family to a dietitian without further assessment
Referral without a relationship or assessment skips understanding the patient’s life.
Tell the family which foods they must stop buying
Directing changes before building a relationship is not the book’s first step.

items.q: Which strategy is described as a potential way to mobilize support for addressing childhood obesity in racial and ethnic minority communities?
items.a: Engaging local youth as leaders through an obesity prevention curriculum
items.ex: Engaging minority youth as leaders through an obesity prevention curriculum can mobilize support for addressing obesity.
w: Assigning health care providers to lead all community decisions
The strategy described engages youth leaders, not providers directing the community.
Holding private weight checks for each child at school
Weight checks do not mobilize community support for prevention.
Sending families printed warnings about obesity risks by mail
Mailed warnings do not engage the community as active leaders.

alt.q: A nurse wants to build community support for childhood obesity prevention in a minority neighborhood. Which plan best reflects the evidence in Box 3.3?
alt.a: Train interested teens to lead obesity prevention activities for their peers
alt.ex: Engaging minority youth as leaders through an obesity prevention curriculum is a potential strategy to mobilize support.
w: Have outside experts run the program with little community input
Collaborative initiatives with community involvement have the highest success rates.
Provide diet information without involving parents or schools
Programs need adult support and must address both school and home.
Wait for families to request help before offering any program
Waiting passively does not mobilize community support for prevention.

items.q: In community-based practice, which factors about a patient’s family life should the nurse consider when adapting interventions? Select all that apply.
o: The time of day the patient goes to work
Work hours are a day-to-day factor that shapes how interventions are adapted.
Whether the spouse or the patient’s parents can provide child care
Availability of family for child care influences how care is planned.
Family values that shape views about health
Family values about health are a key factor in person-centered interventions.
The nurse’s own preferred visit schedule
Interventions are adapted to the patient’s life, not the nurse’s preferences.
A standard plan used for all patients with the same diagnosis
Person-centered care is individualized rather than standardized by diagnosis.
items.ex: Work hours, child care availability, and family health values are examples of family-life factors the nurse considers.

alt.q: A nurse is building a picture of a patient’s life to design person-centered interventions. Which information is relevant? Select all that apply.
o: The patient leaves for work at 5 a.m. each day
The time the patient goes to work influences how interventions are adapted.
The patient’s mother watches the children after school
Who provides child care is part of the family’s daily routine.
The family believes home remedies should be tried first
Family values that shape views about health guide person-centered care.
The agency prefers visits to be scheduled on Mondays
Agency convenience does not reflect the patient’s life.
The nurse usually teaches all families the same way
A uniform teaching approach ignores what makes each patient unique.
alt.ex: Correct: The patient leaves for work at 5 a.m. each day; The patient’s mother watches the children after school; The family believes home remedies should be tried first.

items.q: A systematic review on childhood obesity among racial/ethnic minority children found which type of effort to have a high success rate?
items.a: Collaborative initiatives with community involvement
items.ex: Community involvement in collaborative initiatives had a high success rate in reducing obesity and preventing co-morbidities.
w: Individual counseling of children without their families
Children need adult support; the review highlighted collaborative community initiatives.
School programs focused only on physical education
Effective prevention combines activity and nutrition with community involvement.
Medication-based weight management programs
The review emphasized community-based lifestyle initiatives, not medications.

alt.q: A nurse wants to reduce obesity and prevent co-morbidities among racial/ethnic minority children in the community. Which approach does the evidence show has a high success rate?
alt.a: Collaborative initiatives with community involvement and supervision
alt.ex: Collaborative initiatives with community involvement and supervision have high success rates in reducing obesity among these children.
w: Lifestyle rules given to children without adult role models
Without adult support and role modeling, children do not achieve positive outcomes.
Nutrition teaching limited to the school cafeteria setting
Nutrition information must address both school and home environments.
Short-term weight-loss medication for each child at risk
The evidence supports community-based lifestyle initiatives, not medications.

items.q: Which description best explains what a theory does?
items.a: Defines concepts, explains how they relate, and predicts outcomes
items.ex: A theory explains an event by defining concepts, explaining the relationships among them, and predicting outcomes.
w: Lists the procedural steps for performing a nursing skill
Procedure steps describe a skill; they do not explain or predict a phenomenon.
Records patient data in a standard documentation format
Documentation formats record data; they do not explain relationships or predict outcomes.
Provides a systematic process for delivering nursing care
This describes the nursing process, which the textbook states is not a theory.

alt.q: A nursing theory conceptualizes an aspect of nursing for which purposes?
alt.a: To describe, explain, predict, or prescribe nursing care
alt.ex: Nursing theories conceptualize an aspect of nursing to describe, explain, predict, or prescribe nursing care measures.
w: To replace clinical judgment with fixed care protocols
Theories give a framework for assessment and clinical judgment; they do not replace it.
To medically diagnose and treat a patient’s disease
Nurses do not medically diagnose; nursing theories guide nursing care.
To make nursing practice subservient to medicine
Theories distinguish nursing as a discipline distinct from medicine.

items.src: Ch 4 · Theoretical foundations of nursing practice

items.q: Which term refers to an area of study that examines how the philosophical, theoretical, and empirical components of a discipline’s knowledge relate to one another?
items.a: Metatheory
items.ex: Metatheory looks at the relationships among the components of a discipline’s knowledge and is used to derive theories and concepts.
w: Middle-range theory
Middle-range theories are limited in scope and address a specific phenomenon such as comfort or uncertainty.
Practice theory
Practice theories are narrow and guide care of a specific population at a specific time.
Descriptive theory
Descriptive theories describe phenomena and the circumstances in which they occur.

alt.q: Which statement about metatheory is accurate?
alt.a: It is used to derive theories and theoretical concepts
alt.ex: Metatheory gives a broad overview of a discipline’s knowledge and is used to derive theories and theoretical concepts.
w: It is the least abstract category of theory
Metatheory is the most abstract category; practice theory is the least abstract.
It guides care of one population at a specific time
This describes practice (situation-specific) theories.
It details interventions and their expected outcomes
This describes prescriptive theories.

w: It is a grand theory defining nursing’s domain and goals

The nursing process is a nursing system, not a borrowed theory.

items.q: A patient is 1 day postoperative and rates incisional pain as severe. The nurse planned discharge teaching for this morning. Which action should the nurse take first?

w: Begin teaching now to keep discharge on schedule

Give written materials for the patient to read now
Any teaching method still addresses a higher-level need before the basic need.
Teach the family while the patient rests in pain
Pain relief is the patient’s first priority before teaching proceeds.

alt.q: Which statement reflects how a nurse uses Maslow’s hierarchy to set priorities?

w: Self-actualization needs come first because they drive recovery

Love and belonging needs come before safety needs in most patients
Safety and security rank below physiological needs but above love and belonging.
All levels of need receive equal priority at the same time
The hierarchy ranks needs in five levels of priority.

items.q: A patient’s vital signs are stable, and the patient is safe and comfortable. The patient tells the nurse, “Nobody from my faith community knows I’m here, and I feel spiritually lost.” Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?

items.ex: When a patient has no emergent physical or safety needs, the nurse gives high priority to psychological, sociocultural, developmental, or spiritual needs.
w: Defer the concern until the patient is ready for discharge
With basic needs met, spiritual needs become a high priority now.
Tell the patient that physical needs must always be met first
Physical and safety needs are already met, so higher-level needs take priority.
Reassess vital signs hourly before discussing the concern
Vital signs are stable; there is no emergent physical need delaying care of the spiritual need.

alt.q: When does a nurse give high priority to a patient’s psychological, sociocultural, developmental, or spiritual needs?

w: Only after the patient reaches self-actualization

Only when the patient is fully dependent on others
Dependent patients especially need physiological and safety needs met first.
Only after the patient is discharged from care
Nurses address higher-level needs during care once basic needs are met.

The nurse-patient relationship itself is central; delaying it leaves anxiety unaddressed.
Perform all of the patient’s self-care activities for now
Compensating for self-care reflects Orem’s theory, not Peplau’s.

alt.q: While caring for this anxious teenager, the nurse reaches the working phase of Peplau’s relationship. Which nursing activity fits this phase?
alt.a: Carrying out therapeutic activities with the patient
alt.ex: The working phase of Peplau’s nurse-patient relationship involves therapeutic activity.
w: Gathering data before first meeting the patient
Data gathering belongs to the preorientation phase.
Defining the issue in the first discussion
Defining the issue belongs to the orientation phase.
Ending the relationship once needs are resolved
Termination belongs to the resolution phase.

items.src: Ch 4 · Theoretical foundations of nursing practice

items.q: According to Orem, when does nursing care become necessary?
items.a: When patients cannot fulfill biological, psychological, developmental, or social needs
items.ex: Orem held that nursing care is needed when patients are unable to meet their own biological, psychological, developmental, or social needs.
w: When the environment keeps nature from restoring health
This reflects Nightingale’s environmental theory.
When anxiety interferes with the nurse-patient relationship
This reflects Peplau’s interpersonal theory.
When cultural traditions conflict with the plan of care
This reflects Leininger’s culture care theory.

alt.q: Which nursing activity is central to applying Orem’s self-care deficit nursing theory?
alt.a: Continually assessing the patient’s ability to perform self-care
alt.ex: Nurses using Orem’s theory continually assess self-care ability and intervene as needed.
w: Improving ventilation, light, and hygiene in the room
Environmental improvement is central to Nightingale’s theory.
Moving through orientation, working, and resolution phases
Relationship phases are central to Peplau’s theory.
Integrating cultural values into the plan of care
Cultural integration is central to Leininger’s theory.

items.src: Ch 4 · Theoretical foundations of nursing practice

items.q: A nurse has been bathing a patient during an acute illness, and the patient’s condition is now improving. Applying Orem’s theory, which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Encourage the patient to begin bathing independently
items.ex: As the patient’s condition improves, the nurse encourages the patient to begin doing self-care activities independently.
w: Continue giving full baths until the day of discharge
Continuing full care fails to promote the patient’s improving self-care ability.
Ask the family to take over all bathing
Orem’s theory aims at the patient performing self-care, not shifting care to others.
Stop all bathing assistance immediately
The nurse evaluates how much self-care the patient can do and intervenes as needed.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a recovering patient using Orem’s theory. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
alt.a: “Doing more of my own care as I get stronger will help my recovery.”
alt.ex: Orem held that people who take part in self-care activities are more likely to improve their health outcomes.
w: “The nurses should keep doing my care until I go home.”
Orem’s theory encourages patients to resume self-care as they are able.
“My recovery depends only on the medicines I receive.”
Self-care participation improves health outcomes, not just medicines.
“I should not try any self-care until I am fully well.”
Patients begin self-care as their condition improves, not only when fully well.

items.src: Ch 4 · Theoretical foundations of nursing practice

items.q: What is the goal of nursing care in Leininger’s culture care theory?
items.a: Providing culturally specific nursing care
items.ex: The major concept of Leininger’s theory is cultural diversity, and the goal of care is culturally specific nursing care.
w: Restoring balance to the behavioral system
Restoring behavioral system balance is the focus of Johnson’s model.
Converting anxiety into constructive actions
This is a focus of Peplau’s interpersonal theory.
Improving the environment so nature can heal
This is the focus of Nightingale’s environmental theory.

alt.q: What is the major concept of Leininger’s culture care theory?
alt.a: Cultural diversity
alt.ex: Cultural diversity is the major concept; human caring varies among cultures in its expressions, processes, and patterns.
w: Self-care deficit
Self-care deficit is the central concept of Orem’s theory.
Interpersonal relations
Interpersonal relations are central to Peplau’s theory.
Environmental sanitation
Environment and sanitation are central to Nightingale’s theory.

items.src: Ch 4 · Theoretical foundations of nursing practice

items.q: A patient’s culture expects the community leader to be present for health care decisions. Which action by the health care team is most appropriate?
items.a: Reschedule rounds so the community leader can attend
items.ex: Leininger’s theory leads the team to adjust care, such as rescheduling rounds, to include the community leader.
w: Hold rounds as planned and inform the leader afterward
Proceeding without the leader ignores the patient’s cultural practice for decisions.
Ask the patient to make decisions without the leader
This disregards the culture’s expectation that the leader be present.
Have the nurse act as decision-maker in the leader’s place
The nurse should integrate, not replace, the patient’s cultural decision process.

alt.q: Applying Leininger’s theory, how should a nurse handle a patient’s cultural traditions, values, and beliefs?
alt.a: Safely integrate them into the plan of care
alt.ex: To care for patients of unique cultures, nurses safely integrate cultural traditions, values, and beliefs into the plan of care.
w: Set them aside during the hospital stay
Setting culture aside ignores its influence on health and care.
Address them only after discharge
Culture influences care throughout, not only after discharge.
Replace them with standard hospital routines
Standard routines do not provide culturally specific care.

items.src: Ch 4 · Theoretical foundations of nursing practice

items.q: A patient whose culture values stoicism rarely mentions pain after surgery. Which question by the nurse best reflects Leininger’s theory when assessing pain?
items.a: “Is the pain getting worse or remaining the same?”
items.ex: Symptom expression differs among cultures, so the nurse skillfully incorporates cultural practices when assessing pain.
w: “You don’t have any pain at all, correct?”
A leading question invites a stoic patient to deny pain.
“Why aren’t you telling us about your pain?”
A “why” question sounds judgmental and ignores cultural expression.
“People from your culture don’t feel much pain, right?”
This stereotypes the patient and dismisses pain assessment.

alt.q: Two patients from different cultures have the same surgery; one is quiet about pain and the other is very vocal. Which nursing approach is best?
alt.a: Incorporate each patient’s cultural practices when assessing pain
alt.ex: Because symptom expression differs among cultures, the nurse incorporates each patient’s cultural practices into pain assessment.
w: Assume the quiet patient has less pain than the vocal one
Stoic patients may not complain even when they have pain.
Medicate both patients on one identical fixed schedule
Identical care ignores individual and cultural differences.
Assess pain only in the patient who reports it aloud
The quiet patient may also have pain needing assessment.

items.src: Ch 4 · Theoretical foundations of nursing practice

To classify nursing theories by their level of abstraction

To set nurse staffing ratios for clinical units
The model addresses cognitive processes, not staffing.

alt.q: What does the multilayered NCSBN-CJM explain?

w: The phases of the nurse-patient relationship

items.q: The NCSBN-CJM serves as the framework for which examination?

w: Advanced practice certification exams

Hospital orientation competency tests

Nursing school admission exams
The model frames the licensure exam taken after nursing school.

alt.q: How can nursing students use the NCSBN-CJM?
alt.a: To learn to think like a nurse and make safe clinical decisions
alt.ex: Students use the model to learn to think like a nurse and make safe decisions that improve patient outcomes.
w: To replace clinical experience with classroom study
Competence grows with clinical experience and exposure, not in place of it.
To choose one theory for every patient situation
The model explains clinical judgment, not selection of one theory.
To memorize task lists without clinical reasoning
The model teaches complex decision making, not rote tasks.

w: Theoretical knowledge

Metatheoretical knowledge
Metatheory examines components of a discipline’s knowledge.
Biomedical knowledge
Biomedical knowledge comes from fields such as physiology and pharmacology.

w: It is formed only from the nurse’s own clinical experiences

Both theoretical and experiential knowledge are needed for safe care.
It is often called the art of nursing
The art of nursing refers to experiential or clinical knowledge.

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship between nursing research and nursing theory?
items.a: Research tests and modifies theory, and theory prompts research
items.ex: Research validates, refutes, supports, or modifies theory, while theory stimulates nurse scientists to explore practice issues.
w: Research replaces theory once enough studies are done
Research refines theory; it does not replace it.
Theory is fixed, so research can only confirm it
Research can also refute or modify theory.
Research and theory develop apart from practice
Their relationship builds a knowledge base that is applied to practice.

alt.q: How do the relationships among a theory’s components help nurse researchers?
alt.a: They help identify research questions and determine study design
alt.ex: The relationships among a theory’s components often help identify research questions and the overall design of a study.
w: They remove the need to collect data in a study
Research still requires data; theory shapes the questions.
They guarantee that every hypothesis is supported
Research can refute as well as support a theory.
They allow one study to test the entire theory
No single study tests all components of a theory.

items.q: Researchers used Peplau’s theory to study mental health nurses’ communication about prescription medication misuse. Nurses were comfortable with their knowledge but less comfortable communicating with other professionals. Which conclusion did the researchers reach?
items.a: Nurses need to be empowered to communicate with the interprofessional team
items.ex: Using Peplau’s theory, researchers identified a need to empower nurses to communicate with the team to reduce harm from misused medications.
w: Nurses need more knowledge about medication misuse
Nurses reported being comfortable with their knowledge.
Peplau’s theory does not apply to medication misuse
The researchers used Peplau’s theory successfully to frame the study.
Nurses should avoid discussing misuse with patients
The finding called for more communication, not less.

alt.q: Why was Peplau’s theory a fitting framework for a study of nurses’ communication about prescription medication misuse?
alt.a: It focuses on interpersonal relations and communication
alt.ex: Peplau’s theory centers on interpersonal relations, making it suited to studying how nurses communicate.
w: It focuses on environmental factors such as ventilation
Environmental factors are the focus of Nightingale’s theory.
It focuses on patients’ ability to perform self-care
Self-care is the focus of Orem’s theory.
It focuses on providing culturally specific care
Culturally specific care is the focus of Leininger’s theory.

items.q: Which statement describes theory-generating research?
items.a: The investigator observes without preconceived ideas to view a phenomenon in a new way
items.ex: Theory-generating research uses logic and observation, without preconceived ideas, to explore relationships among phenomena.
w: The investigator tests hypotheses drawn from a theory’s assumptions
Testing hypotheses from assumptions is theory-testing research.
The investigator tests every component of a theory in one study
No single study tests all components of a theory.
The investigator applies a grand theory unchanged to a new group
Generating research creates new theory rather than applying existing theory.

alt.q: Which type of theory is often developed through theory-generating research?

Metatheories
Metatheory examines the components of a discipline’s knowledge.
Shared theories

items.q: Nurse researchers use Kolcaba’s comfort theory to examine whether menthol lozenges improve comfort, thirst, and nausea after extubation following cardiovascular surgery. Which type of research is this?

Metatheory development
Metatheory examines how a discipline’s knowledge components relate.
Descriptive theory building

alt.q: Which statement describes theory-testing research?

alt.ex: Theory-testing research builds evidence for describing or predicting patient outcomes.
w: It creates a new theory from observations without preconceived ideas
This describes theory-generating research.
It tests all of a theory’s components in a single study
Researchers test a theory through a variety of studies.

Testing uses research questions or hypotheses and data.

items.q: A hospitalized patient with a terminal illness tells the nurse, “I just want to die in my own bed.” Which action best reflects an expert nurse’s creative caring?
items.a: Work with the team to find a way to honor the wish to die at home
items.ex: Creative caring takes the extra step of individualizing care, such as honoring a patient’s wish to die at home.
w: Explain that hospital policy requires care to continue on the unit
This dismisses the patient’s wish instead of individualizing care.
Document the statement and continue the current plan unchanged
Documenting alone does not individualize care to the patient’s need.
Tell the patient that home care is less safe than hospital care
This discourages the patient rather than honoring the wish.

alt.q: Which statement best describes creative caring?
alt.a: Taking the extra step of individualizing care to each patient’s needs
alt.ex: The expert nurse translates the art and science of nursing into creative caring that individualizes care.
w: Following the standard care plan exactly for every patient
Creative caring goes beyond standard care to individualize it.
Applying theory while setting aside past clinical experience
Creative caring blends the art (experience) and science of nursing.
Using research evidence while ignoring the art of nursing
Creative caring combines both the art and the science.

items.q: A patient in her first pregnancy tells the nurse she feels isolated and unsure about becoming a parent. Based on Meleis’ transitions theory, which action is most appropriate?

w: Advise her to wait until after the birth to seek support
Nurses provide professional support during the prenatal period.
Limit teaching to the physical changes of pregnancy
Education also covers expectations, coping, and relationship changes.
Tell her that her feelings will resolve without help

alt.q: Which statement by a first-time expectant parent shows understanding of the nurse’s transition teaching?

w: “Once I feel confident, it won’t change before the birth.”
Self-confidence may change during the pregnancy.

items.src: Ch 4 · Theoretical foundations of nursing practice

items.q: According to Meleis and others’ theory of transitions, when is a transition required?
items.a: When one’s reality is interrupted, requiring change and a new reality
items.ex: A transition is required when reality is interrupted, causing a need for change and the forming of a new reality.
w: Only when a person is admitted to an acute care hospital
Transitions include developmental, health-illness, situational, and organizational types.
When a patient cannot meet self-care needs independently
Self-care deficit is the focus of Orem’s theory.
When environmental factors keep nature from healing
Environmental barriers to healing are the focus of Nightingale’s theory.

alt.q: A new parent says, “Since the baby was born, nothing about my life feels the same.” Which concept from Meleis’ theory explains this experience?
alt.a: A transition, in which interrupted reality requires a new reality
alt.ex: Meleis’ theory describes a transition as an interruption of reality that requires change and a new reality.
w: A self-care deficit that requires the nurse to provide care
Self-care deficit is Orem’s concept and does not fit this experience.
An environmental imbalance that requires room changes
Environmental imbalance is Nightingale’s concept.
Anxiety that requires moving to the resolution phase
Relationship phases are Peplau’s concept.

items.q: Which description best defines evidence-based practice (EBP)?
items.a: Combining the best research evidence with clinical expertise, patient preferences and values, and available resources
items.ex: EBP is a problem-solving approach that integrates best evidence with clinician expertise, patient preferences and values, and health care resources.
w: Following agency policies and procedures exactly as they were originally written and taught
Policies are sometimes based on tradition rather than current evidence, so following them alone does not ensure EBP.
Applying the findings of the most recent single research study to every patient on the unit
EBP weighs evidence with expertise and patient values; findings are not applied uniformly to every patient.
Relying on an experienced nurse’s clinical expertise to guide each patient care decision
Clinical expertise is only one element; EBP also requires research evidence, patient preferences, and resources.

alt.q: A nurse is using evidence-based practice to make a patient care decision. Along with the best research evidence, which factors does the nurse also consider?
alt.a: Clinical expertise, patient preferences and values, and available health care resources
alt.ex: The EBP model combines research evidence with clinical expertise, patient preferences and values, and available resources.
w: Unit tradition, staff convenience, and how long a practice has been used
Tradition and convenience are what EBP replaces with current evidence.
Opinions of coworkers, the newest product available, and past unit routines
Coworker opinion and routines are not EBP elements; expertise, patient values, and resources are.
Only the statistical results reported in the research articles reviewed
Statistics are part of appraising evidence; EBP adds expertise, patient values, and resources.

items.q: A nurse reads a study showing that therapeutic touch reduced perceived abdominal pain in adults after surgery. The nurse’s postoperative patient has cultural beliefs that discourage touch. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Look for a different evidence-based pain therapy that the patient will accept
items.ex: EBP integrates evidence with patient values and preferences, so the nurse seeks another evidence-based therapy the patient accepts.
w: Use therapeutic touch because the research evidence supports its effectiveness
Evidence must be applied with the patient’s values; using touch against cultural beliefs is inappropriate.
Explain to the patient why research findings outweigh cultural beliefs
EBP respects patient values and preferences rather than trying to override them with research findings.
Set aside evidence-based approaches and manage pain by unit routine
Tradition is not a substitute for evidence; the nurse should seek another evidence-based therapy that fits the patient.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of how to apply research evidence to an individual patient?
alt.a: “Even strong evidence has to fit my patient’s values, beliefs, and preferences.”
alt.ex: Clinical expertise and attention to patient values and preferences ensure evidence is applied safely and appropriately.
w: “If a study shows an intervention works, I should use it for every patient.”
Outcomes of applying evidence differ with each patient’s health, values, and preferences, so it is not applied uniformly.
“A patient’s cultural beliefs do not change how I apply research evidence.”
Cultural beliefs, such as those discouraging touch, can make an evidence-based therapy inappropriate for a patient.
“My clinical expertise matters less once I find a well-designed study.”
Clinical expertise remains an essential EBP element alongside research evidence.
