items.q: A nurse reviews the unit’s monthly quality report and notices that patient falls have increased each month for the past quarter. What type of trigger for an EBP question does this represent?
items.a: A problem-focused trigger
items.ex: Noticing a problem trend or a recurring failure of an intervention while caring for patients is a problem-focused trigger.
w: A knowledge-focused trigger
Knowledge-focused triggers come from new information, such as a conference or guideline, not a problem trend.
A background question
A background question is a type of question asked after a trigger, not the trigger itself.
A foreground question
A foreground question is a specific question formed after a problem is identified, not the trigger.

alt.q: After attending a conference, a nurse wonders whether a new pain intervention presented there would help patients on her unit. Which type of trigger is this?
alt.a: A knowledge-focused trigger
alt.ex: New information from conferences, inservices, practice guidelines, or research publications creates a knowledge-focused trigger.
w: A problem-focused trigger
Problem-focused triggers arise from recurring failures or problem trends in patient care, not new information.
A background question
A background question asks general information about a clinical issue; it is not a trigger.
A foreground question
A foreground question is a specific, searchable question; it is not the source that prompts inquiry.

items.q: Which is an example of a foreground question?
items.a: In patients with dementia, does the use of stress reduction techniques reduce wandering?
items.ex: A foreground question focuses on specific knowledge, such as one intervention in one population, and grows out of a background question.
w: What is the best way to reduce wandering in patients with dementia?
This general question is a background question that must be answered before a specific foreground question.
Which factors cause bloodstream infections in central venous catheters?
This broad question about causes is a background question, like Cathy and Tom’s first question.
What approaches are commonly used to manage pain in older adults?
This asks general information about a clinical issue, which makes it a background question.

alt.q: How does a background question differ from a foreground question?
alt.a: It asks for general information about a clinical issue before a specific question can be posed
alt.ex: A background question gathers general information that helps the nurse form a specific, searchable foreground question.
w: It focuses on one specific intervention for one patient population
This describes a foreground question, which is specific and searchable.
It is always written using all five PICOT elements in order
PICOT format is used to state a foreground question, not a background question.
It is answered only after the foreground question has been searched
A background question must be answered before a searchable foreground question can be posed.

items.q: Which PICOT question is worded best for searching the literature?
items.a: Does chlorhexidine compared with alcohol affect the incidence of CLABSI in surgical patients?
items.ex: Box 5.1 advises a nondirectional outcome, such as “affect,” because a directional outcome may limit the articles found.
w: Does chlorhexidine compared with alcohol reduce the incidence of CLABSI in surgical patients?
“Reduce” makes the outcome directional, which may limit the articles found in a search.
What is the best way to prevent infections in patients who have central lines?
This is a broad background question without specific PICOT elements.
In surgical patients, how effective is chlorhexidine at preventing CLABSI?
It drops the comparison (alcohol) and implies a direction, which may limit search results.

alt.q: Why should the outcome in a PICOT question be stated nondirectionally?
alt.a: A directional outcome may limit the articles found in a search
alt.ex: Writing “affect” instead of “reduce” keeps the search open to all relevant articles on the outcome.
w: A nondirectional outcome guarantees a statistically significant result
Question wording does not affect study results; it affects how broadly the search captures articles.
A directional outcome is permitted only in qualitative questions
Box 5.1 recommends nondirectional outcomes in general; qualitative questions are not an exception.
A nondirectional outcome removes the need for a comparison
Comparison is a separate PICOT element; outcome wording does not determine whether one is included.

items.q: A well-designed PICOT question must include all five elements in the order P, I, C, O, T.
items.a: False
items.ex: The sequence is not required, and not every question uses I, C, or T; the aim is to include as many elements as possible.
items.ww: Saying True ignores that a meaningful question, such as a qualitative one, may contain only a P and an O.

alt.q: A meaningful qualitative question can contain only a patient population and an outcome.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: For example, “How do patients with cystic fibrosis perceive their quality of life?” contains only P and O.
alt.ww: Saying False assumes all five elements are mandatory, but the aim is simply to include as many elements as possible.

items.q: According to the hierarchy of evidence, which source provides the highest level of evidence?
items.a: A systematic review or meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials
items.ex: Level 1 includes systematic reviews or meta-analyses of RCTs, which rigorously summarize current evidence on a topic.
w: A single well-designed randomized controlled trial
A single RCT is Level 2, below systematic reviews of RCTs.
A controlled trial without randomization
A quasiexperimental study, or controlled trial without randomization, is Level 3.
A systematic review of descriptive and qualitative studies
Systematic reviews of descriptive and qualitative studies are Level 5.

alt.q: A nurse finds four sources on a PICOT question. Which source sits lowest on the hierarchy of evidence?
alt.a: A report from a committee of expert clinicians
alt.ex: Opinions of authorities and reports of expert committees are Level 7, the bottom of the evidence pyramid.
w: A single correlational study of hospitalized adults
A single nonexperimental study, such as a correlational study, is Level 4.
A single qualitative study of patient experiences
A single descriptive or qualitative study is Level 6, above expert opinion.
A controlled trial that did not randomize subjects
Controlled trials without randomization, or quasiexperimental studies, are Level 3.

items.q: In a systematic review, the researcher uses statistics to show the effect of an intervention on an outcome.
items.a: False
items.ex: A meta-analysis uses statistics to show an intervention’s effect; a systematic review draws conclusions without statistics.
items.ww: Saying True confuses the two; statistical analysis is what distinguishes a meta-analysis from a systematic review.

alt.q: The main difference between a meta-analysis and a systematic review is that a meta-analysis uses statistics to show an intervention’s effect.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Both rigorously summarize evidence on a PICOT question, but only a meta-analysis applies statistics to the effect.
alt.ww: Saying False misses that a systematic review uses no statistics to draw conclusions, unlike a meta-analysis.

items.q: Which statements describe a randomized controlled trial (RCT)? Select all that apply.
o: All subjects have an equal chance of being placed in either group
Random assignment gives every subject an equal chance of being in the control or treatment group.
The treatment group receives the experimental intervention
The intervention being tested is given to the treatment group.
The control group receives the usual standard of care
The intervention is tested against the usual standard of care given to the control group.
Both groups are measured for the same outcomes
Researchers measure both groups for the same outcomes and compare them statistically.
Subjects choose which group they want to join
Subjects are randomly assigned; letting them choose would introduce bias.
The control group receives no care at all during the study
The control group receives the usual standard of care, not an absence of care.
items.ex: In an RCT, subjects are randomly assigned, the treatment group gets the intervention, the control group gets usual care, and outcomes are compared.

alt.q: A nurse reads a study report. Which features indicate the study was a randomized controlled trial? Select all that apply.
o: Subjects were randomly assigned to a control or treatment group
Random assignment to groups is the defining feature of an RCT.
An intervention was tested against the usual standard of care
RCTs compare an experimental intervention with the usual standard of care.
Statistical tests compared outcomes between the two groups
Researchers use statistics to see whether the intervention made a significant difference.
Researchers interviewed subjects and summarized common themes
Summarizing themes from interviews describes qualitative research, not an RCT.
Researchers reported the opinions of an expert committee
Expert committee reports are Level 7 evidence, not experimental research.
alt.ex: Correct: Subjects were randomly assigned to a control or treatment group; An intervention was tested against the usual standard of care; Statistical tests compared outcomes between the two groups.

items.q: A study testing a new fall-prevention strategy reports p < 0.05 for the difference between groups. How should the nurse interpret this result?
items.a: The difference was likely due to the intervention rather than chance
items.ex: A value below p = 0.05 means less than a 5% probability that the difference was caused by chance.
w: The difference was most likely due to chance alone
p < 0.05 means less than a 5% probability that the difference occurred by chance.
The intervention reduced falls in 95% of the subjects
The p value is a probability about chance, not the percentage of subjects who improved.
The findings apply to all hospitalized patients
The p value shows statistical significance, not generalizability, which is addressed under clinical implications.

alt.q: What does the p value reported in a research article tell the reader?
alt.a: Whether a difference between groups was likely due to the intervention or to chance
alt.ex: The p value, usually set at 0.05, is a probability level indicating whether a difference was likely caused by chance.
w: How many subjects were enrolled in each study group
The number of subjects is described in the methods section, not by the p value.
Whether the study findings can be applied to other settings
Generalizability is explained under clinical implications, not by the p value.
Which level of evidence the study represents
The level of evidence depends on the study design, not on the p value.

items.q: A [[peer-reviewed|peer reviewed]] article is reviewed for accuracy, validity, and rigor and approved by experts before it is published.
items.ex: Expert review before publication helps ensure the scientific quality of research found in journals and databases.

alt.q: Before publication, experts check a [[peer-reviewed|peer reviewed]] article for accuracy, validity, and rigor.
alt.ex: Expert review before publication helps ensure the scientific quality of research found in journals and databases.

items.q: While appraising articles, a nurse wants to quickly decide whether an article is research or clinically based and whether to keep reading. Which sections should the nurse read first?
items.a: The abstract and introduction
items.ex: The abstract summarizes purpose and findings, and with the introduction it helps decide whether to read the entire article.
w: The analysis and results
These sections report statistics and findings; they are read after deciding the article is relevant.
The methods and clinical implications
Methods explain study design and implications explain application; neither is a quick screen.
The literature review and narrative
These sections give detailed background and study content, not a quick summary of relevance.

alt.q: Which section of a research article explains generalizability, or how to apply findings in practice for the type of subjects studied?
alt.a: Clinical implications
alt.ex: In the clinical implications section, the researcher explains generalizability and how to apply findings in a practice setting.
w: Abstract
The abstract briefly summarizes purpose, major findings, and implications; generalizability is detailed under clinical implications.
Literature review
The literature review synthesizes prior research to show what led to the study.
Methods or design
Methods explain how the study was organized and conducted, including study type and number of subjects.

items.q: A unit practice committee has developed a new evidence-based protocol that it plans to implement across several nursing units. Which action is best before implementing it on a large scale?
items.a: Test the change with a 3-month pilot study
items.ex: A pilot study, often 3 months, shows whether a change can be implemented easily and achieves desired outcomes before wide rollout.
w: Implement it on all units within 1 week to keep momentum
Large-scale change requires planning; a pilot first shows whether the change is feasible and effective.
Wait 12 months for the annual policy review
Policies are now updated when new evidence justifies a revision, not only at annual review.
Repeat the literature search 2 more times to confirm
The evidence has already been appraised; the next step is testing the change in practice.

alt.q: What information does a pilot study provide when a unit integrates an evidence-based practice change?
alt.a: Whether the change can be implemented easily and achieves desired outcomes
alt.ex: Pilot study results tell whether the practice change is easy to implement and produces the desired outcomes.
w: Whether the change is supported by a meta-analysis of RCTs
The level of evidence is determined during critical appraisal, before a pilot.
Whether the PICOT question was worded nondirectionally
PICOT wording is addressed in step 1; a pilot tests the change in practice.
Whether the change will work in every agency nationwide
A pilot is a small-scale test of the change locally, not across all agencies.

items.q: An ICU has implemented a bundle of interventions to prevent CLABSI. Which action best evaluates the effect of the practice change?
items.a: Compare CLABSI incidence before and after the change over several months
items.ex: Formal evaluation tracks the outcome before and after the change, such as over 3 to 6 months, to determine its effect.
w: Ask staff whether they like using the new bundle
Staff opinions do not measure the outcome; pre- and postintervention CLABSI rates are needed.
Confirm that the bundle appeared in the unit newsletter
Communicating the change is not the same as evaluating its effect on patient outcomes.
Review again the articles used to justify the change
Rereading the evidence does not show whether the change improved outcomes in practice.

alt.q: Three months after a practice change, a unit’s CLABSI rate has increased. Which action should the committee take?
alt.a: Determine whether the change needs modification or discontinuation
alt.ex: Evaluation determines whether a change was effective, needs modification, or should be discontinued.
w: Continue the change because evidence supports it
Unexpected results occur; continuing without action would allow more patients to develop CLABSI.
Stop collecting CLABSI data until staff are retrained
Monitoring must continue because evaluation guides whether to modify or stop the change.
Wait until the annual review to discuss the results
Delay exposes more patients to harm; evaluation results must be acted on.

items.q: A practice change on a medical unit has reduced patient falls. Which group should be the first to discuss the outcomes of the change?
items.a: The clinical staff on that unit
items.ex: Because unit staff participated in the change, they are the first to discuss its outcomes and must receive feedback.
w: Attendees at a national nursing conference
Broader dissemination comes later; unit staff should receive feedback first.
The hospital’s nursing research council
Sharing beyond the unit level comes after unit staff discuss the outcomes.
Readers of a peer-reviewed nursing journal
Publishing is a later way to disseminate results; unit staff are the first group.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows understanding of why unit staff should see the results of an EBP change?
alt.a: “When staff see the benefits, the change is more likely to be sustained.”
alt.ex: Staff appreciate seeing results, and a change is more sustainable when staff can see its benefits.
w: “Results should be shared with staff only after they are published.”
Unit huddles, meetings, and newsletters share results with staff without waiting for publication.
“Staff do not need feedback once the change is in place.”
Staff participated in the change, so receiving feedback is critical.
“Results matter only to the managers who approved the change.”
Clinicians enjoy and appreciate seeing results, and their feedback supports sustaining the change.

items.q: Which strategies help sustain nurses’ use of evidence-based practice? Select all that apply.
o: Forming an EBP team or journal club
Journal clubs and EBP teams help create a culture of inquiry.
Including EBP as a competency on job descriptions
This encourages nurses to attend EBP workshops and build appraisal skills.
Conducting performance audits with feedback to nurses
Audits and feedback make nurses aware of their use of EBP.
Partnering with an APRN who mentors EBP skills
Scholarly mentorship from APRNs and nurse leaders helps nurses develop EBP skills.
Limiting EBP activities to nurse researchers only
Sustained EBP depends on engaging staff nurses, not restricting it to researchers.
Introducing changes without communication from leaders
Ongoing communication from nurse leaders increases nurses’ willingness to adopt new practices.
items.ex: Box 5.2 lists journal clubs, EBP job competencies, audits with feedback, and mentorship among strategies that sustain EBP.

alt.q: A nurse manager wants staff to keep using evidence-based practices after a change. Which actions are supported by evidence? Select all that apply.
o: Encourage nurses to pursue specialty certification
Nurses with specialty certification or advanced degrees are more likely to use EBP.
Use unit-based EBP champions to support the change
Unit-based champions or facilitators help implement EBP changes at the unit level.
Engage patients and families in EBP education and decisions
Engaging patients and families helped sustain use of EBP interventions.
Discourage questions about the protocol to avoid confusion
Staff should be able to ask questions; a spirit of inquiry supports EBP.
Avoid spending money on developing an EBP culture
Agencies investing in EBP culture had less nurse turnover and better patient outcomes.
alt.ex: Correct: Encourage nurses to pursue specialty certification; Use unit-based EBP champions to support the change; Engage patients and families in EBP education and decisions.

items.q: Which features indicate that a health care agency supports a culture of evidence-based practice? Select all that apply.
o: Nurses are encouraged to question current practice
A culture of inquiry encourages nurses to question practice.
EBP mentors are identified to guide other nurses
Supportive agencies identify EBP mentors to mentor other nurses in the process.
EBP competencies are part of performance evaluations
Integrating EBP competencies in evaluations and clinical ladders supports EBP.
Policies are kept unchanged to preserve tradition
EBP replaces tradition and the status quo with current evidence.
Only physicians may suggest changes in practice
EBP culture empowers nurses to question practice and lead changes.
items.ex: Agencies supporting EBP encourage questioning, provide mentors and tools, value EBP in evaluations, and recognize nurses’ EBP work.

alt.q: A new graduate nurse is comparing employers. Which characteristics suggest an agency supports evidence-based practice? Select all that apply.
o: Policies and procedures are evidence based
Requiring evidence-based P&Ps is a key feature of a practice environment that supports EBP.
Nurse leaders value and role-model EBP
Leaders who value and model EBP support its use by staff.
Nurses are recognized for their EBP work
Recognition programs for EBP work are a feature of supportive agencies.
Practice changes are discouraged to maintain the status quo
Nurses can no longer accept traditional practices and the status quo.
Policies are revised only on a fixed annual schedule
Policies are now updated whenever new evidence justifies a revision.
alt.ex: Correct: Policies and procedures are evidence based; Nurse leaders value and role-model EBP; Nurses are recognized for their EBP work.

items.q: Quality and risk management data, such as monthly infection rates, provide the evidence needed to solve a clinical problem.

w: Analyze the literature and form a research question or hypothesis

items.q: When the nursing process is compared with the research process, which research activity corresponds to the diagnosis step?
items.a: Developing research questions or hypotheses
items.ex: Table 5.2 pairs nursing diagnosis with developing research questions or hypotheses.
w: Reviewing the literature to define the problem
Literature review aligns with assessment, where the problem is identified.
Selecting a research design and data collection methods
Choosing the design and methods aligns with planning.
Recruiting subjects and collecting the data
Conducting the study aligns with implementation.

alt.q: In the comparison of the nursing process with the scientific method, identifying independent and dependent variables is part of which step?
alt.a: Planning
alt.ex: Table 5.2 places selecting the design, sample, variables, data collection, and analysis plan under planning.
w: Assessment
Assessment corresponds to observing, asking questions, and reviewing the literature.
Implementation
Implementation corresponds to obtaining approvals, enrolling subjects, and collecting data.
Evaluation
Evaluation corresponds to analyzing results and communicating findings.

items.q: When the findings of a correctly performed study apply to similar patients, the study has [[generalizability]].
items.ex: Generalizability describes whether findings apply to similar patients beyond those studied.

alt.q: [[Generalizability]] means that a study’s findings apply to similar patients cared for in practice.
alt.ex: Generalizability describes whether findings apply to similar patients beyond those studied.

items.q: A nursing student is reviewing terms used to judge research. Which statement by the student shows understanding of reliability?
items.a: “The same results occur when the study is repeated under the same conditions.”
items.ex: Reliability means a study yields the same results when repeated under the same conditions.
w: “The findings apply to other patients similar to those studied.”
This describes generalizability.
“The study followed all steps of the scientific method without bias.”
This describes valid findings.
“The sample is large enough to represent the whole population.”
This relates to minimizing sampling error.

alt.q: A research team repeats a study under the same conditions and obtains the same results. Which quality of the study does this demonstrate?
alt.a: Reliability
alt.ex: Obtaining the same results when a study is repeated under the same conditions demonstrates reliability.
w: Validity
Valid findings come from following all steps of the scientific method without bias.
Generalizability
Generalizability means the findings apply to similar patients.
Inductive reasoning
Inductive reasoning develops generalizations from specific observations in qualitative research.

items.q: After a thorough literature search, a nurse finds no evidence that answers the unit’s PICOT question. Which is the best next option?
items.a: Conduct a research study to create new knowledge
items.ex: When no evidence supports a change, the next option is research, the process of creating new knowledge.
w: Adopt the practice most nurses on the unit prefer
Preference and tradition are not evidence; a knowledge gap is addressed through research.
Rewrite the PICOT question as a background question
Background questions come before PICOT; the gap remains unanswered without research.
Implement a change without evaluating its effects
No evidence supports such a change, and changes should never go unevaluated.

alt.q: Which situation calls for conducting research rather than completing an EBP project?
alt.a: A gap in knowledge leaves the PICOT question unanswered
alt.ex: When EBP reveals a knowledge gap that leaves the question unanswered, the best way to answer it is a research study.
w: A systematic review answers the PICOT question
Existing strong evidence is applied through EBP; new research is not needed.
Several RCTs address the clinical question
Available RCTs provide evidence to appraise and integrate through EBP.
Clinical guidelines support a specific intervention
Guidelines are evidence for EBP; research is needed when evidence is lacking.

items.q: Why do nurse researchers follow the systematic, orderly steps of the scientific method?
items.a: To minimize the chance that the researcher’s bias influences the results
items.ex: Systematic procedures reduce error and minimize the influence of a researcher’s bias or opinion on results.
w: To guarantee that the hypothesis will be supported
The method lets a hypothesis be accepted, rejected, or modified; it guarantees no result.
To eliminate any possibility of error in a study
The possibility of error always exists; orderly procedures only reduce it.
To avoid the need for a review of the literature
Gathering information through a literature review is itself a step of the method.

alt.q: Which statement about the scientific method is accurate?
alt.a: It reduces, but does not eliminate, the possibility of error
alt.ex: Although error is always possible, the scientific method’s orderly procedures reduce it and minimize bias.
w: It removes all possibility of error from a study
The book states the possibility of error always exists.
It is used only in quantitative research studies
The study step includes quantitative or qualitative experiments.
It allows the researcher’s opinion to guide conclusions
The method minimizes the influence of the researcher’s bias or opinion.

items.q: A nurse researcher wants to study nurses’ perceptions of their own grieving when caring for patients with COVID-19. Which type of study best fits this question?
items.a: A qualitative study that summarizes themes
items.ex: The research question drives the method; perceptions of grieving are best studied qualitatively by summarizing themes.
w: A randomized controlled trial with statistical analysis
Perceptions are difficult to quantify, and an RCT tests an intervention against usual care.
A case control study of past medical records
Case control studies look back for predictors of a condition, not personal experiences.
An evaluation study of a program’s success
Evaluation research tests how well a program works, not lived perceptions.

alt.q: Which research question is best answered by a quantitative study involving statistical analysis?
alt.a: Does the use of chlorhexidine reduce the incidence of CLABSI?
alt.ex: Measuring the incidence of CLABSI with and without chlorhexidine requires quantitative methods and statistical analysis.
w: What are nurses’ perceptions of caring for dying patients?
Perceptions are studied qualitatively through themes.
How do family members experience stress in the ICU?
Experiences of stress are explored qualitatively.
How do cancer survivors describe their quality of life?
Survivors’ descriptions are analyzed qualitatively by summarizing themes.

items.q: A nurse researcher wants to address a patient problem, but little has been published about it. Which approach should the researcher take first?
items.a: Conduct an exploratory study to identify associated factors
items.ex: With little literature, researchers begin with exploratory studies before attempting formal experimental studies.
w: Test an intervention in a large randomized controlled trial
Testing interventions prematurely is overly ambitious when little is known.
Develop a risk assessment tool before studying any factors
In fall research, associated factors were identified first, then tools were developed.
Write a practice guideline based on the researcher’s opinion
Opinion is the lowest level of evidence; exploratory research builds knowledge first.

alt.q: In the development of fall prevention research, what did early researchers do before testing interventions?
alt.a: Identified the factors associated with falls
alt.ex: Researchers first identified factors associated with falls, then created risk tools, then tested targeted interventions.
w: Tested exercise programs in randomized trials
Interventions were tested only after factors and risk tools were developed.
Published practice guidelines for all hospitals
Guidelines were not the first step; researchers first explored associated factors.
Surveyed nurses’ satisfaction with fall policies
Nurse satisfaction was not the early focus; factors associated with falls were.

items.q: Which characteristics describe quantitative nursing research? Select all that apply.
o: Precisely measures and quantifies study variables
Quantitative research relies on methods that precisely measure and quantify variables.
Focuses on numerical data and statistical analysis
Numerical data and statistics are central to quantitative research.
Uses controls to eliminate bias in findings
Quantitative research uses controls to eliminate bias.
Develops theories by inductive reasoning from interviews
Inductive reasoning from interviews characterizes qualitative research.
Uses transcripts of recorded interviews as the data
Interview transcripts are the data of qualitative research.
items.ex: Quantitative research is precise, systematic, and objective, focusing on numerical data, statistics, and controls to eliminate bias.

alt.q: Which studies are examples of quantitative research? Select all that apply.
o: Measuring self-reported pain severity with a new pain therapy
Pain severity is measured quantitatively in this example.
Comparing surgical dressings by measuring wound healing over time
Measuring wound healing extent is quantitative.
A survey measuring nurses’ perceptions of physicians’ willingness to collaborate
Surveys are a quantitative method with numerically coded responses.
Interviews exploring patients’ perceptions of nurses’ caring in palliative care
Exploring perceptions through interviews is qualitative research.
Interviews about stress felt by families of critically ill patients
Family members’ perceptions of stress are studied qualitatively.
alt.ex: Correct: Measuring self-reported pain severity with a new pain therapy; Comparing surgical dressings by measuring wound healing over time; A survey measuring nurses’ perceptions of physicians’ willingness to collaborate.

items.q: Which statements describe qualitative nursing research? Select all that apply.
o: Studies phenomena that are difficult to quantify, such as quality of life
Qualitative research studies phenomena like perceptions of illness or quality of life.
Typically gathers data through recorded interviews
Interviews are recorded and transcribed to serve as data.
Uses inductive reasoning to develop generalizations from observations
Qualitative research develops generalizations or theories inductively.
Includes methods such as ethnography and phenomenology
Ethnography, phenomenology, and grounded theory are qualitative methods.
Randomly assigns subjects to control and treatment groups
Random assignment is a feature of experimental research such as RCTs.
Codes responses numerically for statistical analysis
Numerical coding for statistics describes survey research, a quantitative method.
items.ex: Qualitative research describes nonnumerical data, often from interviews, to understand experiences and the contexts in which they occur.

alt.q: A nurse researcher plans a qualitative study of cancer survivors’ quality of life. Which activities fit this method? Select all that apply.
o: Conducting extensive interviews with survivors
Qualitative data are typically gathered through interviews.
Transcribing interview recordings for interpretation
Transcripts of the recordings serve as data for interpretation.
Summarizing common themes across interviews
Themes are summarized to inductively determine characteristics of quality of life.
Testing whether survivors’ scores differ at p < 0.05
Statistical significance testing belongs to quantitative research.
Controlling variables to eliminate bias in measurement
Controls to eliminate bias in measurement characterize quantitative research.
alt.ex: Correct: Conducting extensive interviews with survivors; Transcribing interview recordings for interpretation; Summarizing common themes across interviews.

items.q: Why are randomized controlled trials not always the best approach for testing nursing interventions? Select all that apply.
o: Nursing problems often require collecting subjective data
Problems like knowledge deficits and symptom management often require subjective data.
Ethical issues arise when the control group does not receive the new therapy
Withholding a new therapeutic intervention from controls creates ethical issues.
How patients experience health problems cannot always be studied by an RCT
Understanding patients’ experiences is not always possible through an RCT.
RCTs cannot investigate cause and effect
RCTs do investigate cause and effect and are excellent for testing drug therapies.
RCTs do not randomly assign their subjects
Random assignment to control and treatment groups defines an RCT.
items.ex: Nursing questions often involve subjective data, ethical concerns about control groups, and patient experiences, so descriptive studies are common.

alt.q: A nurse researcher considers an RCT for a nursing question. Which concerns may make another design more appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: The outcome of interest is the patient’s subjective experience
Experiences of health problems cannot always be addressed through an RCT.
Withholding the new intervention from controls raises ethical issues
Ethical issues develop when the control group does not receive the new intervention.
The question concerns knowledge deficits and symptom management
These nursing problems often require subjective data that RCTs may not capture well.
The intervention being tested is a new drug therapy
RCTs are excellent for testing drug therapies.
The researcher wants to test cause and effect
Investigating cause and effect is a strength of RCTs.
alt.ex: Correct: The outcome of interest is the patient’s subjective experience; Withholding the new intervention from controls raises ethical issues; The question concerns knowledge deficits and symptom management.

items.q: In a controlled trial without randomization, more older adults happen to fall into the treatment group. Why is this a concern?
items.a: Group differences, not only the intervention, may affect the results
items.ex: Without randomization, how subjects fall into groups can bias results, so the intervention may not be the only factor.
w: Older adults are not permitted to take part in research
Age is not the problem; unequal groups introduce bias into the results.
The study automatically becomes a qualitative study
Unequal groups create bias; they do not change the type of study.
Randomization would have made the groups less comparable
Random assignment gives each subject an equal chance of either group, reducing this bias.

alt.q: Which statement best describes a controlled trial without randomization?
alt.a: An intervention is tested, but subjects are not randomly assigned to groups
alt.ex: Nonrandomized controlled trials test interventions without random assignment, which introduces bias.
w: Subjects are randomly assigned, but no intervention is tested
Nonrandomized trials do test interventions; randomization is what is missing.
Recorded interviews are analyzed for common themes
This describes qualitative research.
Past records of people with and without a condition are compared
This describes a retrospective case control study.

items.q: A researcher compares children with asthma to children without asthma, reviewing past records for family history and dust exposure. Which type of study is this?
items.a: Case control study
items.ex: A case control study compares subjects with and without a condition, often retrospectively, for associations with predictor variables.
w: Randomized controlled trial
No intervention is tested and subjects are not randomly assigned.
Evaluation research
Evaluation research tests how well a program, practice, or policy is working.
Historical research
Historical research establishes facts and relationships about past events, not predictors of a condition.

alt.q: Which is a recognized weakness of case control studies?
alt.a: Small samples and other group differences create a risk of bias
alt.ex: Small numbers of subjects and groups differing in other variables, such as stress, make results harder to interpret.
w: Random assignment of subjects limits their usefulness
Case control studies do not randomly assign subjects.
They cannot be conducted by looking back in time
Case control studies are often conducted retrospectively.
They require subjects to receive an experimental treatment
Case control studies are nonexperimental and test no intervention.

items.q: In survey research, why must the portion of the population sampled be large enough?
items.a: To keep sampling error to a minimum
items.ex: A sufficiently large sample keeps sampling error, when a sample does not represent the population, to a minimum.
w: To make random assignment to treatment groups possible
Surveys describe populations; random assignment is a feature of experiments.
To ensure the researcher controls the study variable
Controlling the study variable describes experimental research.
To eliminate the need for statistical analysis
Survey data are coded numerically so they can be analyzed statistically.

alt.q: What is sampling error?
alt.a: When the sample does not represent the entire population under study
alt.ex: Sampling error occurs when a sample fails to represent the population; a large enough sample minimizes it.
w: When the same results do not occur on repeating a study
Inconsistent results on repetition is a reliability problem.
When a researcher’s opinion influences the results
A researcher’s opinion influencing results is bias.
When survey answers are coded incorrectly for analysis
Coding mistakes are not sampling error, which concerns how well the sample represents the population.

items.q: The most basic function of a survey is description.
items.a: True
items.ex: Surveys gather large amounts of data to describe a population and the topic of study.
items.ww: Saying False overlooks that surveys mainly describe practices, perceptions, opinions, and other characteristics of people.

alt.q: Surveys are mainly used to test cause-and-effect relationships between an intervention and an outcome.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Surveys describe the frequency, distribution, and interrelation of variables; RCTs investigate cause and effect.
alt.ww: Saying True confuses surveys with RCTs, which test an intervention against usual care.

items.q: A nurse extensively interviews cancer survivors and then summarizes common themes to determine the characteristics of their quality of life. Which type of reasoning is the nurse using?
items.a: Inductive reasoning
items.ex: Qualitative research uses inductive reasoning to develop generalizations or theories from specific observations or interviews.
w: Deductive reasoning
Moving from specific interviews to general themes is inductive, not deductive.
Statistical inference
Summarizing themes from interviews is qualitative analysis, not statistics.
Correlational analysis
Correlational analysis measures relationships between variables, not themes from interviews.

alt.q: Which description fits inductive reasoning in qualitative research?
alt.a: Developing generalizations or theories from specific observations or interviews
alt.ex: Inductive reasoning builds generalizations from specific observations, as when themes emerge from interviews.
w: Testing a hypothesis by measuring variables with statistics
This describes quantitative hypothesis testing.
Controlling variables and randomly assigning subjects
This describes experimental research.
Measuring how often characteristics occur in a group
This describes descriptive research.

items.q: Which description fits empirical data in research?
items.a: Data gathered through observations and assessments, such as surveys or physiological measures
items.ex: Researchers gather empirical data through observations and assessments and use them to discover new knowledge.
w: Data based on the researcher’s personal opinion of the phenomenon
Empirical data come from observation and assessment; opinion introduces bias.
Conclusions drawn only from reviewing the existing literature
The literature review guides the question; empirical data are newly gathered.
Predictions written before a study begins, such as hypotheses
A hypothesis is a testable proposed explanation, not gathered data.

alt.q: A researcher records patients’ blood pressures and survey responses during a study. What type of data are these?
alt.a: Empirical data
alt.ex: Data gathered from observations and assessments, such as physiological data and surveys, are empirical data.
w: Hypotheses
Hypotheses are testable predictions made before data collection.
Literature review
A literature review synthesizes previous research, not new observations.
Theoretical framework
A theoretical framework is formulated during assessment to frame the problem, not collected as data.

items.q: Valid findings exist when a study has followed all steps of the scientific method without bias.
items.a: True
items.ex: Validity depends on correctly following every step of the scientific method without bias.
items.ww: Saying False ignores the book’s definition linking valid findings to following all steps without bias.

alt.q: A study’s findings are valid simply because the same results occur when the study is repeated.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Repeating a study with the same results shows reliability; validity requires following all steps without bias.
alt.ww: Saying True confuses validity with reliability.

items.q: In correlational research, the researcher actively intervenes to change one variable and observes the effect on another.
items.a: False
items.ex: Correlational studies explore relationships among variables without any active intervention by the researcher.
items.ww: Saying True describes experimental research, in which the investigator controls the study variable.

alt.q: A study examining the relationship between adolescents’ age and whether they smoke is an example of correlational research.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Correlational studies describe whether, and to what extent, two variables are associated.
alt.ww: Saying False overlooks that no intervention is tested; the study only describes the relationship between two variables.

items.q: Which statement accurately describes the National Institute of Nursing Research (NINR)?
items.a: It is the one nursing institute within the National Institutes of Health
items.ex: The NINR, the only nursing institute in the NIH, leads and funds nursing research to solve health challenges.
w: It is the professional association that sets nursing’s scope and standards
Scope and standards come from the ANA; the NINR leads and funds research.
It is the state agency that licenses registered nurses
Licensing is not the NINR’s role; it leads and funds nursing research.
It is a specialty organization focused on oncology nursing
This describes the Oncology Nursing Society, which has its own research priorities.

alt.q: What is the goal of nursing research led and funded by the NINR?
alt.a: Optimizing health and advancing health equity
alt.ex: The NINR funds research to solve health challenges and inform practice and policy, optimizing health and advancing equity.
w: Accrediting nursing education programs
Accreditation is not the NINR’s role; it funds research on health challenges.
Setting hospital reimbursement rates
Reimbursement is not set by the NINR, which funds nursing research.
Licensing advanced practice nurses
Licensure is not the NINR’s role; it leads and funds nursing research.

items.q: Which are among the five areas of scientific research supported by the NINR? Select all that apply.
o: Health equity
Health equity is one of the NINR’s five research areas.
Social determinants of health
Social determinants of health is an NINR research area.
Systems and models of care
Systems and models of care is an NINR research area.
Prevention and health promotion
Prevention and health promotion is an NINR research area.
Palliative and psychosocial care in oncology
This is an Oncology Nursing Society research priority.
Hospital marketing and branding
This is not one of the NINR’s scientific research areas.
items.ex: The NINR supports health equity, social determinants of health, population and community health, prevention and health promotion, and systems and models of care.

alt.q: A nurse researcher is preparing a proposal for NINR funding. Which topics align with the NINR’s areas of scientific research? Select all that apply.
o: Population and community health
Population and community health is one of the five NINR areas.
Social determinants of health
Social determinants of health is one of the five NINR areas.
Health equity
Health equity is one of the five NINR areas.
Palliative and psychosocial care in oncology
This is an Oncology Nursing Society priority, not an NINR area.
Health care marketing strategies
Marketing is not among the NINR’s research areas.
alt.ex: Correct: Population and community health; Social determinants of health; Health equity.

items.q: Which research question reflects an administrative focus of nursing research?
items.a: What is the best mix of nurses and assistive personnel on a unit?
items.ex: Administrative research helps nurses use resources effectively, such as finding the best practice mix of nurses and assistive personnel.
w: Which teaching approach improves nursing students’ learning outcomes?
This reflects an educational focus.
Does chewing gum reduce ileus after colon surgery?
This tests a clinical nursing intervention.
How do family members perceive stress in the ICU?
This is a clinical qualitative question about experiences.

alt.q: How can nursing research with an educational focus improve professional education and practice?
alt.a: By revealing new educational approaches that improve learning outcomes
alt.ex: Educationally focused nursing research reveals new approaches that improve learning outcomes.
w: By determining the best staffing mix on a nursing unit
Staffing mix is an administrative focus.
By testing the effectiveness of clinical nursing interventions
Testing interventions is a clinical focus.
By setting priorities for federal research funding
Funding priorities are set by agencies such as the NINR.

items.q: Translational research is also called [[implementation science]].
items.ex: Translational research, also called implementation science, tests strategies to improve uptake and use of evidence.

alt.q: Research that tests strategies to improve the uptake and use of evidence in real-world settings is called translational research or [[implementation science]].
alt.ex: Translational research, also called implementation science, tests strategies to improve uptake and use of evidence.

items.q: What is the purpose of translational research?
items.a: To test implementation strategies in real-world settings to promote use of evidence
items.ex: Translational research tests implementation strategies to learn which work for whom, in what settings, and why.
w: To summarize all RCTs on a topic using statistical methods
Statistically summarizing RCTs describes a meta-analysis.
To track a hospital’s monthly quality indicator reports
Tracking quality indicators monitors problems; it does not test implementation strategies.
To describe patients’ lived experiences of an illness
Describing lived experiences is the aim of qualitative research.

alt.q: A nurse researcher tests which strategies work best to get staff in different hospitals to adopt an evidence-based protocol. Which type of research is this?
alt.a: Translational research
alt.ex: Testing implementation strategies among diverse groups and settings to promote EBP use is translational research.
w: Historical research
Historical research establishes facts and relationships about past events.
Outcomes research
Outcomes research studies benefits, risks, costs, and holistic effects of treatments on patients.
Correlational research
Correlational research describes relationships between variables without intervention.

items.q: How does translational research differ from evidence-based practice (EBP)?
items.a: It studies how to implement and sustain evidence, while EBP uses best evidence and measures outcomes
items.ex: Translational research investigates methods to move discoveries into clinical use; EBP uses best evidence and measures outcomes.
w: It uses best evidence in practice, while EBP studies how to move discoveries into care
This reverses the two approaches.
It poses no research question, while EBP always tests a formal hypothesis
Translational research poses a research question or hypothesis; EBP begins with a PICOT question.
It relies only on expert opinion, while EBP relies only on single RCTs
Translational research uses a variety of research designs and methods.

alt.q: Which activity is an example of EBP rather than translational research?
alt.a: Applying best evidence to a unit protocol and measuring patient outcomes
alt.ex: EBP focuses on using best evidence in practice and measuring outcomes.
w: Testing which strategies best move evidence into clinical use
Testing implementation strategies is translational research.
Studying how to sustain new evidence across diverse settings
Examining how to implement and sustain evidence is translational research.
Posing a hypothesis about the most effective implementation method
Hypotheses about implementation methods belong to translational research.
