items.q: A hospital wants to adopt Naylor’s Transitional Care Model, which has proven efficacy but has not been widely adopted. Which research approach would determine how best to implement it in this hospital?
items.a: Translational research
items.ex: A translational approach would test Naylor’s proven model to determine how best to implement it in a particular agency.
w: Exploratory research
Exploratory research develops phenomena when little is known; this model’s efficacy is already established.
Historical research
Historical research examines past events, not how to implement a model.
A case control study
Case control studies compare groups with and without a condition; they do not test implementation.

alt.q: Which description fits Naylor’s Transitional Care Model?
alt.a: Discharge planning and home follow-up for chronically ill older adults by a master’s-prepared nurse
alt.ex: The model prevents complications and rehospitalization through discharge planning and home follow-up coordinated by a Transitional Care Nurse.
w: Inpatient fall prevention for older adults coordinated by nursing assistive personnel
The model addresses discharge and home follow-up to prevent complications and rehospitalization.
Preoperative teaching for surgical patients delivered by unit staff nurses
The model targets chronically ill older adults after hospitalization, not preoperative teaching.
Home hospice care for terminally ill adults managed by attending physicians
The model is coordinated by a master’s-prepared Transitional Care Nurse for chronically ill older adults.

items.q: Outcomes research typically focuses on which aspects of a treatment?
items.a: Its benefits, risks, costs, and holistic effects on patients
items.ex: Outcomes research examines the benefits, risks, costs, and holistic effects of a treatment to inform decisions.
w: Its cellular mechanisms of action in laboratory models
Fundamental mechanisms of biology and disease are studied in basic research.
The historical events that led to its development
Past events are examined in historical research.
Nurses’ satisfaction with delivering the treatment
Outcomes focus on effects on patients, not on providers’ satisfaction.

alt.q: Researchers study the effects of managing Parkinson disease through videoconferencing and telemedicine to increase access to care. What type of research is this?
alt.a: Outcomes research
alt.ex: Studying the effects of a care approach on patients, such as telemedicine for Parkinson disease, is outcomes research.
w: Historical research
Historical research establishes facts about past events.
Basic research
Basic research studies fundamental mechanisms of biology, disease, or behavior.
Preclinical research
Preclinical research connects basic science with nursing and medicine to develop model interventions.

items.q: A nurse is developing outcomes for a diabetes education program. Which statement is an appropriate care delivery outcome?
items.a: Patients self-administer insulin correctly
items.ex: Care delivery outcomes focus on recipients of service, such as patients able to self-administer insulin, not on providers.
w: Nurses successfully teach insulin administration
This focuses on the provider; care delivery outcomes focus on recipients of care.
Nurses complete the education checklist for each patient
Completing a checklist is a provider task, not an effect on patients.
Providers order insulin teaching for all patients
This is a provider action, not an observable effect on patients.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows understanding of care delivery outcomes?
alt.a: “The outcome should describe the effect on the patient, family, or community.”
alt.ex: Care delivery outcomes are observable effects of interventions on recipients of service, not on providers.
w: “The outcome should describe how well nurses performed the teaching.”
Nurse performance is a provider focus, not a care delivery outcome.
“The outcome should describe the physician’s treatment decisions.”
Physicians are providers; outcomes focus on recipients of care.
“The outcome should describe which supplies the unit used.”
Supplies are resources, not observable effects on recipients of care.

items.q: A hospital identifies patient satisfaction as an outcome for a new outpatient clinic. In describing this outcome, what is the indicator?
items.a: How the outcome is observed
items.ex: An outcome’s components are the outcome itself, its indicator (how it is observed), critical characteristics (how it is measured), and range of parameters.
w: How the outcome is measured
How the outcome is measured refers to its critical characteristics.
The scale of possible responses
The scale used for responses represents the range of parameters.
The overall goal of the new clinic
The goal is not a component of the outcome; the indicator is how it is observed.

alt.q: A hospital measures patient satisfaction by having patients rate their care on a scale of 1 to 5. In outcome terms, what does this rating scale represent?
alt.a: The range of parameters
alt.ex: Patients respond to a scale, the parameter, designed to measure their degree of satisfaction.
w: The indicator
The indicator is how the outcome is observed.
The critical characteristics
Critical characteristics describe how the outcome is measured.
The outcome itself
The outcome is patient satisfaction, not the rating scale.

items.q: Nurse-sensitive indicators are outcomes that are directly influenced by nursing practice.
items.a: True
items.ex: Nurse-sensitive indicators reflect outcomes that nursing care directly affects.
items.ww: Saying False overlooks the book’s definition of nurse-sensitive indicators as outcomes directly influenced by nursing practice.

alt.q: Length of stay, mortality, and patient satisfaction are nurse-sensitive indicators that measure a direct effect of nursing care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book lists these as outcomes that do not measure a direct effect of nursing care.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores that these outcomes are influenced by many factors beyond nursing practice.

items.q: A nurse researcher is studying whether a nurse-initiated protocol improves blood glucose control in critically ill patients. Which outcome should the researcher measure?
items.a: Patients’ blood glucose ranges compared with a desired range
items.ex: Glucose ranges compared with a desired range directly show the protocol’s effect on glucose control.
w: Patient mortality during the hospital stay
Mortality is too broad and affected by factors outside the protocol, such as medical therapies and acuity.
Overall length of the hospital stay
Length of stay is influenced by many factors and does not show the protocol’s direct effect.
Patients’ satisfaction with physician care
Satisfaction with physician care does not reflect the nurse-initiated glucose protocol.

alt.q: Why would a researcher avoid using mortality to measure the success of a nurse-initiated glucose protocol?
alt.a: Mortality is too broad and influenced by factors outside the protocol
alt.ex: Mortality is affected by medical therapies and acuity of illness, so it does not isolate the protocol’s effect.
w: Mortality cannot be measured in critically ill patients
Mortality can be measured; it simply does not reflect the protocol’s direct effect.
Mortality is a nurse-sensitive indicator by definition
Mortality is listed among outcomes that do not measure a direct effect of nursing care.
Mortality data are never available to nurse researchers
Data availability is not the issue; the outcome is too broad.

items.q: Doctorally prepared nurses play a key role in conducting translational research.
items.a: True
items.ex: Doctorally prepared nurses play a key role in conducting translational research to improve health outcomes.
items.ww: Saying False overlooks the book’s statement that doctorally prepared nurses are key to translational research.

alt.q: Doctorally prepared nurses have little role in translational research, which is left mainly to staff nurses.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book identifies doctorally prepared nurses as playing a key role in conducting translational research.
alt.ww: Saying True contradicts the book, which names doctorally prepared nurses as key to conducting translational research.

items.q: An institutional review board (IRB) includes both scientists and laypeople who review studies to ensure that ethical principles and subjects’ rights are followed.
items.a: True
items.ex: An IRB of scientists and laypeople reviews all studies in the institution to protect human subjects’ rights.
items.ww: Saying False overlooks that IRBs include laypeople as well as scientists and exist to protect human subjects.

alt.q: A researcher may begin collecting data from human subjects and obtain IRB approval after the study is underway.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Approval from the IRB or human subjects committee must be obtained before conducting any study with human subjects.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores that IRB approval comes before any study involving human subjects begins.

items.q: Which elements are required for informed consent of research subjects? Select all that apply.
o: Full information about the study’s purpose, procedures, potential harm, and benefits
Subjects must receive complete information, including harms, benefits, and alternatives.
Capability to fully understand the research and the implications of participating
Subjects must be capable of fully understanding the research.
Free choice to voluntarily consent or decline participation
Subjects must have the power of free choice.
Understanding of how confidentiality or anonymity will be maintained
Subjects must understand how their confidentiality or anonymity is protected.
Agreement to remain in the study until all data are collected
Participation is voluntary; a binding commitment is not an element of informed consent.
Knowledge of which group they will be assigned to before consenting
In randomized studies, subjects are assigned to groups after they consent.
items.ex: Informed consent requires full information, capacity to understand, free choice, and understanding of confidentiality or anonymity.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing a consent form for a research study. Which items must the form address? Select all that apply.
o: Alternative methods of treatment
Subjects must be told about alternative methods of treatment.
Potential harm and benefits of participating
Potential harm and benefits are part of full information.
How the researcher protects confidentiality
Subjects must understand how confidentiality or anonymity is maintained.
A guarantee that the intervention will benefit the subject
Consent describes potential harms and benefits; no benefit is guaranteed.
A requirement to participate in order to receive standard care
Subjects have free choice to consent or decline participation.
alt.ex: Correct: Alternative methods of treatment; Potential harm and benefits of participating; How the researcher protects confidentiality.

items.q: A patient enrolled in a nursing research study asks, “Will anyone outside the study find out what I told the researchers?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Your information won’t be reported in any way that identifies you or shared outside the team.”
items.ex: Confidentiality guarantees that information is not reported in a way that identifies the subject or shared outside the research team.
w: “Your answers will be shared with your other providers to improve your care.”
Confidentiality means information is not accessible to people outside the research team.
“Your name will appear in the published results so readers can verify them.”
Confidentiality guarantees that reports will not identify the subject.
“Once you sign consent, you give up control over how your information is used.”
Informed consent requires subjects to understand how confidentiality is maintained.

alt.q: Which statement defines confidentiality in research?
alt.a: Information a subject provides is not reported in a way that identifies the subject
alt.ex: Confidentiality also means the information is not accessible to people outside the research team.
w: Subjects may decline to participate without any penalty
This describes free choice, an element of informed consent.
Scientists and laypeople review the study for ethical principles
This describes the role of the IRB.
Subjects receive full information about the study’s procedures
This describes the information element of informed consent.

items.q: Which factors are examples of study limitations? Select all that apply.
o: A small sample of subjects
A small sample limits how far findings can be generalized.
A unique setting where the study was conducted
A unique setting affects whether findings apply elsewhere.
Failure to include representative cultural or age groups
Unrepresentative samples limit generalizability.
Inconsistent documentation that makes data hard to collect
Inconsistent chart documentation was a limitation of the gum study.
Approval of the study by the IRB
IRB approval is a required ethical step, not a limitation.
Random assignment of subjects to groups
Random assignment reduces bias; it is a strength, not a limitation.
items.ex: Limitations are factors that affect study findings, such as a small sample, unique setting, or unrepresentative groups.

alt.q: The peppermint gum pilot study had limited generalizability. Which factors contributed to this? Select all that apply.
o: Only 30 patients were in each group
The small sample of 30 per group limited generalizability.
Documentation in patient charts was inconsistent
Inconsistent documentation made data collection challenging.
Subjects were randomly assigned to groups
Random assignment is a strength that reduces bias.
The study received IRB approval before enrollment
IRB approval is an ethical requirement, not a limitation.
Nausea was measured with a self-report rating scale
Using an appropriate measurement instrument was part of the design, not a cited limitation.
alt.ex: Correct: Only 30 patients were in each group; Documentation in patient charts was inconsistent.

items.q: In the peppermint gum study, subjects were randomly assigned after giving consent. What does this mean?
items.a: Each subject had a 50-50 chance of being placed in either group
items.ex: Random assignment gives each subject an equal, 50-50 chance of being in the experimental or control group.
w: The first 30 subjects enrolled formed the treatment group
Assigning by order of enrollment is not random.
Subjects chose either of the 2 groups based on preference
Letting subjects choose would introduce bias; assignment is random.
The surgeon placed the 30 highest-risk subjects in the gum group
Selecting subjects by risk is not random and would bias results.

alt.q: A patient enrolled in the gum study asks, “How will you decide whether I get the gum?” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “You have an equal 50-50 chance of being placed in either group.”
alt.ex: Random assignment means subjects have a 50-50 chance of being in each group.
w: “The first 30 patients who agree will get the gum.”
Enrollment order is not random assignment.
“You may choose either of the 2 groups you prefer.”
Subjects do not choose; random assignment prevents bias.
“Patients with the most nausea after 1 day will get the gum.”
Assignment occurs before outcomes are measured and is not based on symptoms.

items.q: Which statement best defines performance improvement (PI)?
items.a: A formal approach for analyzing health care processes at a local level
items.ex: PI analyzes processes unique to a nursing unit, agency, or health care system to improve quality.
w: A process that creates new knowledge generalizable to other settings
Creating generalizable new knowledge describes research; PI findings are not generalizable.
A problem-solving approach that introduces new evidence-based practices
Introducing new practices based on best evidence describes EBP, not PI.
A structured method used only to analyze serious adverse events
This describes root cause analysis, which is one PI model, not PI as a whole.

alt.q: In performance improvement, what does analysis at a “local” level refer to?
alt.a: Processes unique to a nursing unit, agency, or health care system
alt.ex: Local means PI examines processes specific to one unit, agency, or system, so findings are not generalized.
w: Processes shared by all hospitals within a geographic region
PI does not look across regions; it focuses on one unit, agency, or system.
Practices tested across many diverse patient groups and settings
Testing across diverse groups and settings describes translational research, not PI.
Care delivered only in community and home health settings
Local refers to the organization studied, not to community or home care settings.

items.q: PI helps organizations alter processes to achieve the “triple aim.” Which set of outcomes makes up the triple aim?
items.a: Higher-quality care, better patient experience, and lower costs
items.ex: The triple aim is higher-quality care, a better patient experience, and lower costs.
w: Fewer staff, shorter hospital stays, and higher reimbursement
Reducing staff and raising reimbursement are not the goals named in the triple aim.
New practices, published findings, and generalizable results
Publishing generalizable findings relates to research, not the triple aim of PI.
Higher-quality care, more research, and higher staffing ratios
More research and staffing ratios are not part of the triple aim.

alt.q: A PI team redesigns the discharge process to improve quality of care and lower costs. Which third goal completes the triple aim?
alt.a: A better patient experience
alt.ex: Along with higher-quality care and lower costs, the triple aim includes a better patient experience.
w: Findings that generalize to other agencies
PI findings are not generalizable, and generalizability is not part of the triple aim.
Higher reimbursement from insurance payers
Increased reimbursement is not one of the three triple aim outcomes.
More nursing research studies on the unit
Generating research is not a component of the triple aim.

items.q: How does performance improvement (PI) differ from evidence-based practice (EBP)?
items.a: PI reviews how existing interventions within a process function
items.ex: Unlike EBP, PI does not introduce new practices; it reviews how existing interventions within a process work.
w: PI introduces new practices based on the best research evidence
Introducing new evidence-based practices is the purpose of EBP, not PI.
PI produces findings that can be generalized to other settings
PI is local; its findings are not generalizable to other settings.
PI projects usually take longer to complete than EBP projects
PI projects usually occur more quickly than EBP or research projects.

alt.q: Which activity is characteristic of EBP rather than performance improvement?
alt.a: Introducing a new practice based on the best evidence
alt.ex: EBP brings new practices into care; PI reviews how existing processes function.
w: Reviewing how existing steps of medication delivery work
Reviewing how existing interventions in a process function is the focus of PI.
Mapping the current discharge process to locate delays
Mapping an existing local process is a PI activity, such as Lean value stream mapping.
Analyzing the local appointment-scheduling process
Analyzing a local system process such as scheduling is a PI activity.

items.q: A nurse on a unit PI team says, “When our project succeeds, every hospital can adopt our results.” Which response by the charge nurse is best?
items.a: “PI results apply to our own processes and are not generalizable.”
items.ex: PI analyzes processes unique to a unit, agency, or system, so its findings do not generalize to other settings.
w: “Correct, because PI findings are tested to apply anywhere.”
PI does not allow generalizability of findings to other settings.
“Only if we obtain IRB approval before we start the project.”
IRB approval protects human subjects in research; it does not make PI findings generalizable.
“Yes, as long as more than half of our units participate.”
Participation of many units does not make PI findings generalizable beyond the organization.

alt.q: Which statement about the findings of a PI project is accurate?
alt.a: They apply to the unit, agency, or system that was studied
alt.ex: PI is a local analysis, so its findings apply only to the processes studied.
w: They can be applied to similar patients in any setting
Applying findings to similar patients elsewhere is generalizability, a feature of research, not PI.
They create new knowledge for the nursing discipline
Creating new knowledge is the purpose of research; PI examines existing local processes.
They are valid only when a hypothesis has been tested
Testing hypotheses is part of the scientific method used in research, not PI.

items.q: A unit PI team examines whether nurse staffing ratios contribute to slow responses to call lights. Which type of problem is the team addressing?
items.a: A people problem
items.ex: The textbook classifies staffing ratios and communication protocols as people problems.
w: A system problem
System problems include supply delivery and appointment scheduling.
A clinical problem
Clinical problems include surgical incision infection rates and injuries from falls.
A research problem
PI classifies problems as system, people, or clinical; staffing ratios are a people problem.

alt.q: Which issue would a PI team classify as a system problem?
alt.a: Delays in appointment scheduling
alt.ex: System problems involve processes such as supply delivery and appointment scheduling.
w: Rising surgical incision infection rates
Surgical incision infection rates are an example of a clinical problem.
Unclear staff communication protocols
Communication protocols are an example of a people problem.
Patient injuries from falls on the unit
Patient injuries from falls are an example of a clinical problem.

items.q: A unit PI committee looks for the greatest opportunity to improve quality. Which activity qualifies as high volume?
items.a: An activity making up more than 50% of the unit’s activity
items.ex: High-volume activities are those making up more than 50% of a unit’s activity.
w: An activity making up more than 25% of the unit’s activity
The textbook sets high volume at greater than 50%, not 25%, of unit activity.
An activity with potential to cause trauma or death
Potential for trauma or death defines a high-risk activity, not a high-volume one.
An activity that frequently causes family complaints
An activity causing complaints is a problem area, not a high-volume activity.

alt.q: On an orthopedic unit, adults older than 80 years have more complications after hip surgery. Which PI selection criterion does this finding represent?
alt.a: High risk
alt.ex: Complications that carry potential for trauma or death make an activity high risk.
w: High volume
High volume refers to activities making up more than 50% of unit activity, such as hip surgery itself.
Sentinel event
A sentinel event is a single unexpected occurrence of death or serious injury, not a pattern of risk.
System problem
System problems involve processes such as supply delivery and scheduling.

items.q: Which occurrence on a nursing unit meets the definition of a sentinel event?
items.a: A patient dies unexpectedly after receiving the wrong medication
items.ex: A sentinel event is an unexpected occurrence involving death or serious physical or psychological injury of a patient.
w: A family complains about delays in receiving pain medication
A complaint involves no death or serious injury, so it is not a sentinel event.
Supplies arrive late to the unit for the third time this month
Late supply delivery is a system problem without patient death or serious injury.
A patient’s scheduled radiology procedure is postponed one day
A scheduling delay causes no death or serious injury, so it is not a sentinel event.

alt.q: After a patient dies unexpectedly from a medication error, which process does the unit conduct?
alt.a: A root cause analysis
alt.ex: After a sentinel event, the unit conducts a root cause analysis to learn how and why it occurred.
w: A value stream map
Value stream mapping is a Lean tool for eliminating waste, not the required review after a sentinel event.
A randomized controlled trial
A randomized controlled trial is a research design, not the review conducted after a sentinel event.
A PICOT literature search
A PICOT search starts an EBP project; a sentinel event calls for a root cause analysis.

items.q: During a root cause analysis, the team learns that a nurse gave a medication to the wrong patient. How is the nurse’s act classified?
items.a: An active error
items.ex: Active errors are the acts that personnel perform and show how an event occurred.
w: A latent error
Latent errors involve the organization or steps of the process and explain why an event occurred.
A sampling error
Sampling error is a research term about study samples, not an act by personnel.
A selection bias
Selection bias is a research concept, not a classification used in root cause analysis.

alt.q: During a root cause analysis, the team finds that the unit’s medication storage places look-alike drugs side by side. How is this finding classified?
alt.a: A latent error
alt.ex: Latent errors arise from the organization or steps of the process and explain why an event occurred.
w: An active error
Active errors are acts performed by personnel, not features of the organization or process.
A sampling error
Sampling error is a research term, not a classification used in root cause analysis.
A sentinel event
A sentinel event is the occurrence of death or serious injury, not a contributing process factor.

items.q: A nurse tells the charge nurse that she gave a scheduled dose 2 hours late, causing no harm. Which response by the charge nurse reflects a just culture?
items.a: “Thank you for reporting it; let’s look at what in the process led to it.”
items.ex: A just culture values the reporting of errors and focuses on the processes that lead to errors.
w: “This will go in your personnel file so it does not happen again.”
A just culture focuses on processes, not on blaming the individual who reports.
“Since there was no harm, there is no need to report it.”
A just culture values reporting errors so the processes behind them can be improved.
“Let’s keep this between us to avoid a formal investigation.”
Hiding errors prevents analysis of the process; a just culture encourages reporting.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse manager shows understanding of a just culture?
alt.a: “We value error reporting and focus on the processes that lead to errors.”
alt.ex: A just culture values error reporting, process analysis, and nurses’ critical thinking and problem solving.
w: “We track which nurses make errors so we can target discipline.”
Targeting individuals for blame conflicts with a just culture’s focus on processes.
“We report only the errors that cause serious patient harm.”
A just culture values reporting all errors, not only those causing serious harm.
“We rely on managers, not staff nurses, to solve process problems.”
A just culture values nurses’ critical thinking and their work on improving care processes.

items.q: An agency plans a PI project to improve its medication administration process. Which group should the PI team engage?
items.a: Prescribers, pharmacists, transporters, and nurses
items.ex: All professions involved in medication delivery, from prescribing to administration, need to be engaged in the PI process.
w: Nurses only, because nurses administer the drugs
Medication delivery involves several professions, and all of them need to be engaged.
Pharmacists and nurses only, because they handle the doses
Prescribers and transporters are also part of the process and need to be engaged.
Nurse managers and the quality department only
PI begins at the staff level and engages every profession involved in the process.

alt.q: Why do all members of the health care team collaborate in PI activities?
alt.a: Most health care processes are interprofessional
alt.ex: Many people are involved in single processes of care, so all team members collaborate in PI.
w: TJC requires every staff member to lead a project
The textbook does not state that every staff member must lead a project.
PI findings must generalize to every discipline
PI findings are local and are not generalizable.
Only physicians can approve process changes
PI begins at the staff level with all disciplines; physicians do not hold sole approval.

items.q: A newly hired nurse asks about her role in performance improvement. Which statement by the nurse shows understanding?
items.a: “I help recognize practice trends and recurring problems on my unit.”
items.ex: Nurses participate in PI by recognizing trends, identifying recurrent problems, and initiating opportunities to improve care.
w: “The quality department handles PI, so I just follow the results.”
PI begins at the staff level, and all staff share responsibility for quality.
“I only become involved in PI if a sentinel event occurs.”
PI is continuous and ongoing; nurses take part routinely, not only after sentinel events.
“My role is to design research studies that test new practices.”
Designing research studies is not the staff nurse’s PI role; PI reviews existing processes.

alt.q: Where does the PI process begin?
alt.a: At the staff level, with all disciplines identifying problems
alt.ex: PI begins at the staff level, where all disciplines become involved in identifying quality problems.
w: At the executive level, with administrators setting targets
The textbook states PI begins with staff, not with administrators.
With accreditation surveyors identifying unit problems
Surveyors do not start PI; staff members identify quality problems.
With a research team testing a formal hypothesis
Hypothesis testing is research; PI begins with staff identifying problems.

items.q: Which criteria help a unit PI committee identify the greatest opportunities for improving quality? Select all that apply.
o: High-volume activities making up most of the unit’s work
Activities making up more than 50% of unit activity offer large opportunities for improvement.
High-risk activities with potential for trauma or death
High-risk activities are a key criterion for selecting a PI focus.
Problem areas for patients, staff, or the agency
Problem areas are the third criterion for identifying improvement opportunities.
Activities supported by the largest number of published studies
The amount of published research is not a criterion for selecting a PI focus.
Activities that are the least costly to change
Cost of change is not listed as a criterion for choosing a PI focus.
items.ex: Committees consider activities that are high volume, high risk, or problem areas for patients, staff, or the agency.

alt.q: A PI committee on an orthopedic unit reviews possible projects. Which findings could each become the focus of a PI project? Select all that apply.
o: Hip surgery is the highest-volume procedure on the unit
High-volume activities are a recognized focus for PI.
Adults older than 80 have more postoperative complications
High-risk situations with potential for trauma or death are a recognized PI focus.
Families are dissatisfied with patients’ pain control
Problem areas for patients or families are a recognized PI focus.
A national study described a new type of hip implant
A new practice from published research relates to EBP, not analysis of a local process.
The unit had no injuries from falls during the past year
An area with no problem offers little opportunity for improvement.
alt.ex: Correct: Hip surgery is the highest-volume procedure on the unit; Adults older than 80 have more postoperative complications; Families are dissatisfied with patients’ pain control.

items.q: Which statements describe a well-organized PI program? Select all that apply.
o: It focuses on processes that significantly contribute to the organization’s outcomes
A PI program targets processes or systems that strongly affect outcomes.
It aims to sustain measurable improvements over time
Sustaining measurable improvement over time is a goal of a PI program.
It uses an organization-wide, systematic approach
An organization-wide approach ensures everyone supports continuous PI.
It assigns responsibility for quality only to unit managers
All staff members need to understand their responsibility for maintaining and improving quality.
It ends once a single problem has been solved
PI is a continuous and ongoing effort, not a one-time project.
items.ex: A strong PI program targets key processes, sustains measurable gains, and engages all staff in an organization-wide culture.

alt.q: A nurse educator teaches staff about performance improvement. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: PI is a continuous and ongoing effort
PI is described as continuous and ongoing, not a one-time event.
PI seeks measurable improvements in efficiency and effectiveness
PI aims for measurable gains in efficiency, effectiveness, outcomes, and other quality indicators.
TJC’s annual patient safety goals can focus PI initiatives
The Joint Commission’s patient safety goals provide an excellent focus for PI.
PI ends once the unit’s quality data return to normal
PI is ongoing and aims to sustain improvements over time.
PI is used mainly to generalize findings to other agencies
PI is local and does not allow generalizability of findings.
alt.ex: Correct: PI is a continuous and ongoing effort; PI seeks measurable improvements in efficiency and effectiveness; TJC’s annual patient safety goals can focus PI initiatives.

items.q: A PI team reviews several problems. Which would the team classify as clinical problems? Select all that apply.
o: Surgical incision infection rates
Surgical incision infection rates are a textbook example of a clinical problem.
Patient injuries from falls
Patient injuries from falls are a textbook example of a clinical problem.
Delays in supply delivery
Supply delivery is a system problem.
Inadequate staffing ratios
Staffing ratios are a people problem.
Errors in appointment scheduling
Appointment scheduling is a system problem.
items.ex: PI problems are classified as system, people, or clinical; infections and fall injuries are clinical problems.

alt.q: For which problems does the textbook specifically advise an evidence-based approach during PI? Select all that apply.
o: Rising surgical incision infection rates
This is a clinical problem, for which an evidence-based approach is advised.
Increasing patient injuries from falls
This is a clinical problem, for which an evidence-based approach is advised.
Slow delivery of supplies to the unit
This is a system problem; teams may or may not use research for it.
Unclear staff communication protocols
This is a people problem; the specific advice for an evidence-based approach applies to clinical problems.
alt.ex: Correct: Rising surgical incision infection rates; Increasing patient injuries from falls.

items.q: PI projects usually take longer to complete than EBP or research projects.
items.a: False
items.ex: PI projects usually occur more quickly than EBP or research projects.
items.ww: Calling it true reverses the textbook, which states PI projects are usually the faster process.

alt.q: Monthly trending in PI data can reveal problems that lead to EBP projects.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The same trending from PI data that prompts a PI initiative often reveals problems that lead to EBP projects.
alt.ww: Calling it false ignores that PI trending data frequently uncover problems addressed through EBP.

items.q: When an interprofessional PI team addresses a clinical problem, an evidence-based approach is advised.
items.a: True
items.ex: PI teams may or may not use research, but an evidence-based approach is advised for clinical problems.
items.ww: Calling it false ignores the textbook’s specific advice to use evidence when dealing with clinical problems.

alt.q: Interprofessional PI teams must always base every strategy on published research findings.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: PI teams may or may not use research, although an evidence-based approach is advised for clinical problems.
alt.ww: Calling it true assumes research is always required in PI, but the textbook says teams may or may not use it.

items.q: A central goal of root cause analysis is to identify which individual made the mistake.
items.a: False
items.ex: RCA identifies underlying problems that increase the likelihood of errors and avoids focusing on individuals’ mistakes.
items.ww: Calling it true contradicts RCA’s central tenet of looking at underlying process problems rather than blaming individuals.

alt.q: Root cause analysis looks for underlying problems that make errors more likely rather than focusing on individual mistakes.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: A central tenet of RCA is identifying underlying problems while avoiding the trap of focusing on individuals.
alt.ww: Calling it false treats RCA as a search for blame, which the method specifically avoids.

sections.name: The relationship among evidence-based practice, research, and performance improvement

items.q: Which statement best describes the relationship among EBP, research, and PI?
items.a: They are closely interrelated processes along a continuum of scholarship
items.ex: EBP, research, and PI overlap and exist along a continuum of clinical scholarship.
w: They are separate processes used by different disciplines
The three processes are closely interrelated and overlap, not separate.
Research replaces the need for EBP and PI on a unit
Nurses use all three processes in practice; none replaces the others.
PI provides the strongest evidence of the three processes
PI is local analysis of processes; it is not described as the strongest evidence.

alt.q: Figure 5.3 shows research, EBP, and PI as three overlapping circles. What does the overlap illustrate?
alt.a: The three processes are closely interrelated
alt.ex: The overlapping circles show that research, EBP, and PI are closely interrelated.
w: The three processes are done by the same staff
The figure shows relationships among processes, not who carries them out.
Each process replaces the other two over time
The processes complement one another; none replaces the others.
The three processes all yield generalizable results
Only research aims for generalizable findings; PI findings are local.

items.q: Which feature do EBP, research, and PI all share?
items.a: Each ultimately uses the best evidence to provide high-quality care
items.ex: All three processes require nurses to ultimately use the best evidence to provide the highest quality of care.
w: Each produces findings generalizable to other settings
PI findings are local and not generalizable to other settings.
Each introduces new practices into patient care
PI reviews existing interventions within a process and does not introduce new practices.
Each tests a hypothesis using the scientific method
Hypothesis testing with the scientific method is a feature of research.

alt.q: A nurse asks why she needs to understand EBP, research, and PI. Which response is most accurate?
alt.a: “Nurses are accountable for knowing which process fits a clinical problem.”
alt.ex: Nurses are professionally accountable to know the differences and which process to select for a clinical problem.
w: “Nurses must personally lead all three processes on every unit.”
Nurses use all three processes but are not required to lead each one.
“Only nurse researchers need to understand how they differ.”
Every nurse is accountable for knowing the differences among the processes.
“Nurses use only EBP; the others belong to other disciplines.”
Nurses use all three processes in nursing practice.

items.q: A unit team begins an EBP project to reduce catheter-associated infections. Which information should the team review first?
items.a: Research literature along with available PI data
items.ex: When implementing an EBP project, first review evidence from research literature as well as PI data.
w: Only the unit’s current policy and procedure manual
Policies and procedures may be based on tradition rather than current evidence.
Staff opinions about how care is currently given
Staff opinions alone do not provide the best evidence for an EBP change.
Results of a new research study the team designs
Research is the next option only when existing evidence does not answer the question.

alt.q: Why is reviewing PI data helpful when planning an EBP change?
alt.a: It shows how processes work within the organization
alt.ex: PI data reveal how processes work in the organization, which guides how to make EBP changes.
w: It provides findings that apply to other agencies
PI data describe local processes and are not generalizable.
It replaces the need for a literature search
PI data are reviewed along with research literature, not instead of it.
It ensures the project obtains IRB approval
Reviewing PI data has no role in obtaining IRB approval.

items.q: How do EBP and PI relate to nursing research?
items.a: They can reveal problems that create opportunities for research
items.ex: Problems uncovered through EBP and PI sometimes create opportunities for research.
w: They confirm research findings so no further study is needed
EBP and PI often uncover gaps that lead to new research rather than ending it.
They are types of research that require testing a hypothesis
EBP and PI are distinct from research and do not test hypotheses.
They replace research whenever evidence on a topic is lacking
When evidence is lacking, research is the option for creating new knowledge.

alt.q: During an EBP project, a nurse finds no evidence that answers the PICOT question. What is the best next option?
alt.a: Conduct a research study
alt.ex: When no evidence supports a practice change, the next option is research, which creates new knowledge.
w: Adopt the practice most staff prefer
Basing practice on preference or tradition does not provide evidence.
Keep the current policy unchanged
Leaving the gap unaddressed does not answer the clinical question.
Start a performance improvement project
PI reviews existing local processes and does not create new knowledge to fill an evidence gap.

items.q: A unit revised its pain-management protocol using the best evidence, yet patient satisfaction with pain management remains lower than desired. Which step is most appropriate next?
items.a: Conduct a research study on factors shaping patients’ perceptions
items.ex: When an evidence-based change does not solve the problem, staff can conduct research to investigate it further.
w: Return to the unit’s original pain-management protocol
The original protocol had already produced low satisfaction, so returning to it would not help.
Stop collecting patient satisfaction data for a year
Ongoing monitoring is needed to evaluate whether changes improve outcomes.
Implement the revised protocol on every unit in the agency
Spreading a protocol that has not solved the problem would not address it.

alt.q: In the pain-management example, what first identified factors associated with pain management on the unit?
alt.a: Analysis of PI data
alt.ex: PI data identified factors such as types of medications ordered and patient satisfaction with pain management.
w: A randomized controlled trial
A research study was conducted only after the evidence-based protocol failed to improve satisfaction.
A meta-analysis of studies
The literature review followed, rather than preceded, the analysis of PI data.
A qualitative interview study
Research came last in the example, after PI and EBP efforts.

items.q: A Nursing Practice Council notes that falls with injuries have increased on all units and that the fall prevention protocol was last reviewed 4 years ago. How should the council proceed first?
items.a: Review current fall research along with the agency’s fall PI data
items.ex: An EBP project begins by reviewing research literature and PI data to understand the extent of the problem.
w: Design a new research study to test a fall intervention
Research is the option when no evidence exists; existing evidence is reviewed first.
Remind staff to follow the existing fall protocol closely
The protocol is 4 years old and may not reflect the best current evidence.
Adopt the fall prevention measures that most staff prefer
Staff preference is not best evidence and may reflect tradition.

alt.q: Why are falls with injuries an appropriate outcome for a Nursing Practice Council to target?
alt.a: They are a nursing-sensitive outcome
alt.ex: Falls with injuries are a nursing-sensitive outcome, so nursing practice changes can influence them.
w: They are a sentinel event in every case
Only unexpected falls causing death or serious injury meet the sentinel event definition.
They are a system problem unrelated to nursing care
Patient injuries from falls are a clinical problem influenced by nursing care.
They produce findings generalizable to all agencies
Local data on falls are not generalizable; the reason to target falls is that they are nursing sensitive.

items.q: After a PI committee makes an EBP change, which action is important next?
items.a: Monitor the results and communicate them to staff in all appropriate departments
items.ex: Monitoring results and sharing them with staff in all appropriate departments helps practice changes last.
w: Close the project because the practice change is complete
Changes must be monitored and results communicated, or they are unlikely to last.
Share the results only with members of the PI committee
Results need to reach staff in all appropriate departments, not only the committee.
Wait for an accreditation survey to evaluate the change
The committee itself monitors results rather than waiting for an outside survey.

alt.q: Which approach does the textbook describe as a good way to communicate PI activities to staff?
alt.a: Regular discussion at staff meetings and in newsletters and memos
alt.ex: Staff meetings, newsletters, and memos are good strategies for regularly communicating PI activities.
w: Posting results only in the committee’s private records
Keeping results private prevents staff from learning about the change.
Sharing results only when a project has failed
Successful projects are also shared and celebrated in a culture of improvement.
Reporting results only to the agency’s senior executives
Results need to reach staff from all appropriate departments.

items.q: Why do practice changes made by PI committees often fail to last?
items.a: The committees fail to report findings and intervention results
items.ex: Practice changes are unlikely to last when PI committees fail to report findings and the results of interventions.
w: Staff are not permitted to review unit quality data
Staff are expected to know the outcomes the organization measures.
Every PI change must first receive IRB approval
IRB approval applies to research with human subjects, not to sustaining PI changes.
PI findings are generalized to other settings too quickly
PI findings are local and are not generalized to other settings.

alt.q: A unit introduced a new bedside shift report process 6 months ago, but staff are drifting back to old habits. The committee never shared results. Which action is most likely to help the change last?
alt.a: Report the results of the change to staff regularly
alt.ex: Regularly reporting findings and results helps sustain a practice change.
w: Remove the new process and restore the old one
Abandoning the change does not address the failure to communicate results.
Begin a new research study on shift report
The problem is lack of communication, not a lack of evidence.
Discipline staff who use the old process
Punishing individuals does not address the missing communication of results.

items.q: A unit team tests a new bedside shift report tool for 2 weeks, then reviews what happened to learn from the consequences. Which PDSA phase is the team in?
items.a: Study
items.ex: In the Study phase, the team observes and learns from the consequences of the test.
w: Plan
Plan involves analyzing the problem and developing a plan to test the change.
Do
Do involves carrying out the test, which the team has already completed.
Act
Act involves determining which modifications should be made to the test.

alt.q: After studying the results of a small test of change, a PI team decides which modifications to make. Which PDSA phase is this?
alt.a: Act
alt.ex: In the Act phase, the team determines which modifications should be made to the test.
w: Plan
Plan involves developing a plan to test the change before it is carried out.
Do
Do involves carrying out the test of the change.
Study
Study involves observing and learning from the consequences of the test.

items.q: Nurses want to learn why patients on their unit wait hours for discharge after discharge orders are written. Which process best fits this goal?
items.a: Performance improvement
items.ex: PI analyzes how existing local processes, such as the discharge process, function and can be improved.
w: Nursing research
Research creates new, generalizable knowledge; this goal concerns a local process.
Translational research
Translational research tests implementation strategies across settings, not a single unit’s process.
Evidence-based practice
EBP introduces new practices from the best evidence; PI reviews existing processes.

alt.q: A nurse wants to create new knowledge that can be generalized to similar patients in other settings. Which process fits this goal?
alt.a: Nursing research
alt.ex: Research creates new knowledge, and well-conducted studies produce findings that generalize to similar patients.
w: Performance improvement
PI analyzes local processes and its findings are not generalizable.
Evidence-based practice
EBP applies existing best evidence rather than creating new knowledge.
Root cause analysis
RCA analyzes a serious adverse event within one organization.

items.q: Before a nursing team conducts a study involving human subjects, approval from which group is required?
items.a: The institutional review board
items.ex: Before any study with human subjects, researchers obtain approval from the agency’s IRB or human subjects committee.
w: The unit PI committee
Unit PI committees review quality data; they do not approve research with human subjects.
The Nursing Practice Council
A practice council guides nursing practice but is not the body that approves research.
The Joint Commission
The Joint Commission sets patient safety goals; it does not approve individual studies.

alt.q: What is the purpose of an institutional review board (IRB)?
alt.a: Ensuring ethical principles and subjects’ rights are followed in studies
alt.ex: An IRB of scientists and laypeople reviews studies to ensure ethical principles and human subjects’ rights are followed.
w: Approving PI changes to unit care processes
PI changes are handled by PI committees, not by the IRB.
Selecting the PI model a unit will use
Choosing a PI model is a committee decision, not an IRB function.
Ranking research articles by level of evidence
Ranking evidence is part of appraisal in EBP, not an IRB function.

items.q: A PI study reveals information that prompts organization-wide change. Which are examples of how the organization may respond? Select all that apply.
o: Revising policies and procedures
Revising P&Ps is one way an organization responds to PI findings.
Modifying standards of care
Modifying standards of care is one way an organization responds.
Implementing new support services
New support services are one way an organization responds with resources.
Leaving the response to individual staff nurses
The organization is responsible for responding with appropriate resources.
Waiting until a research study on the topic is published
The organization responds to the problem identified rather than waiting for outside research.
items.ex: An organization must respond to PI findings with resources, such as revised P&Ps, modified standards of care, and new support services.

alt.q: Which statements about an organization’s response after a PI study shows a need for change are accurate? Select all that apply.

Revising P&Ps is a listed example of an organizational response.

An agency with a culture of improvement celebrates successful improvement projects.
Each unit must fund changes without agency support
The organization, not the individual unit, is responsible for providing resources.
Changes must be limited to the unit that did the study
PI studies often prompt organization-wide change.
alt.ex: Correct: The organization must respond with appropriate resources; Revising policies and procedures is one appropriate response; A culture of improvement celebrates successful projects.

items.q: Which statements describe how PI data contribute to an EBP project? Select all that apply.

PI data inform how processes work and how to make EBP changes.

Trending in PI data often reveals problems that lead to EBP projects.
They replace the need to review research literature
PI data are reviewed along with research literature, not instead of it.
They provide findings that generalize to other settings
PI data are local and not generalizable.
items.ex: PI data reveal problems, show their extent, and explain how local processes work, guiding how to make EBP changes.

alt.q: A nurse prepares for an EBP project on her unit. Which statements about using PI data show correct understanding? Select all that apply.

Both research literature and PI data are reviewed first in an EBP project.

PI data supplement, but do not replace, the research literature.

items.q: Which statements accurately compare EBP, research, and PI? Select all that apply.

PI reviews how existing interventions within local processes function.
Research creates new knowledge
Research is the process of creating new knowledge.
EBP introduces new practices based on the best evidence
EBP introduces new practices, unlike PI.
PI findings are generalizable to other settings
PI does not allow generalizability of findings to other settings.
Research projects usually move faster than PI projects
PI projects usually occur more quickly than EBP or research projects.
items.ex: Research creates new knowledge, EBP introduces evidence-based practices, and PI reviews existing local processes.

alt.q: A student describes the differences among EBP, research, and PI. Which statements by the student show understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “Research is the next option when no evidence supports a change.”
When evidence is lacking, research creates the needed new knowledge.

PI reviews existing interventions rather than introducing new ones.

Researchers obtain IRB approval before conducting studies with human subjects.

Creating new knowledge is the purpose of research; EBP applies existing evidence.

items.q: EBP, research, and PI are independent processes that rarely inform one another.
items.a: False
items.ex: EBP, research, and PI are closely interrelated and overlap along a continuum of clinical scholarship.
items.ww: Calling it true ignores that PI data guide EBP and that both can reveal problems leading to research.

alt.q: Problems uncovered through EBP and PI can create opportunities for research.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: EBP and PI sometimes reveal problems that then create opportunities for research.
alt.ww: Calling it false treats the processes as unconnected, when EBP and PI often lead to research questions.

items.q: Combining findings from PI efforts with EBP creates a foundation for excellent patient care and outcomes.
items.a: True
items.ex: When PI findings are combined with EBP, they create a foundation for excellent patient care and outcomes.
items.ww: Calling it false overlooks that PI data and EBP work together to improve patient care.

alt.q: PI findings should be kept separate from EBP projects because PI does not always use research.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: PI data inform how processes work and guide how to make EBP changes, so the two are combined.
alt.ww: Calling it true ignores that reviewing PI data is a first step in an EBP project.

items.q: An agency with a culture of improvement celebrates successful improvement projects.
items.a: True
items.ex: Celebrating successful projects is a feature of an agency with a culture of improvement.
items.ww: Calling it false overlooks that recognizing success is part of a culture of improvement.

alt.q: In a culture of improvement, successful projects are completed quietly so staff stay focused on remaining problems.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: An agency with a culture of improvement celebrates successful improvement projects rather than completing them quietly.
alt.ww: Calling it true contradicts the textbook, which describes celebrating successes as part of a culture of improvement.

items.q: What does the Healthy People initiative provide for the United States?
items.a: Evidence-based, 10-year national objectives for promoting health and well-being
items.ex: Healthy People sets evidence-based national objectives every 10 years to promote health and well-being.
w: Federal regulations that set licensing requirements for nurses in each state
Nurse licensing is set by state nurse practice acts, not by the Healthy People initiative.
Annual hospital quality ratings that determine Medicare payment levels
Healthy People sets national health objectives; it does not rate hospitals or set payments.
Clinical treatment guidelines for managing the most common acute diseases
Healthy People focuses on promotion and prevention rather than on treating acute disease.

alt.q: Which time span do the Healthy People national objectives cover?
alt.a: 10 years
alt.ex: Healthy People provides 10-year national objectives, such as the current Healthy People 2030.
w: 1 year
The objectives are not annual; each set spans a decade.
5 years
The objectives cover 10 years, not 5.
25 years
Each set of objectives covers 10 years, not a quarter century.

items.q: What is the main focus of the Healthy People objectives?
items.a: Health promotion, well-being, and disease prevention
items.ex: The data-driven objectives focus on promotion, well-being, and prevention instead of illness care.
w: Hospital-based treatment of acute and chronic illness
Healthy People emphasizes prevention and promotion instead of illness care.
Payment reform and reimbursement for illness care
Healthy People sets health objectives; it does not address reimbursement.
Rehabilitation after serious injury and disability
Rehabilitation is tertiary care; Healthy People centers on promotion and prevention.

alt.q: A nurse wants to design a project that fits the focus of Healthy People. Which project best matches that focus?
alt.a: A neighborhood program to prevent disease and promote well-being
alt.ex: Healthy People objectives emphasize health promotion and disease prevention rather than illness care.
w: A hospital protocol for treating acute heart failure episodes
Treating acute illness is illness care, not the promotion and prevention focus of Healthy People.
A unit audit of medication errors during inpatient stays
Inpatient safety audits are important but are not the Healthy People prevention focus.
A billing review of costs for intensive care admissions
Cost reviews of illness care do not reflect the Healthy People emphasis on prevention.

items.q: What are the leading health indicators (LHIs) identified in Healthy People 2030?
items.a: High-priority health issues in the United States
items.ex: LHIs are high-priority U.S. health issues, such as suicides, homicides, food insecurity, and youth obesity.
w: Standards that hospitals must meet to stay accredited
Accreditation standards come from accrediting bodies, not Healthy People LHIs.
Normal laboratory ranges used to screen for disease
Lab reference ranges are clinical values, not national high-priority health issues.
Measures of nursing workload on inpatient units
Staffing measures are not LHIs; LHIs are high-priority population health issues.

alt.q: Which of these is an example of a Healthy People 2030 leading health indicator?
alt.a: Suicides
alt.ex: Suicides are listed as an LHI, a high-priority health issue in the United States.
w: Average registered nurse salary by state
Salaries are workforce data, not a high-priority health issue tracked as an LHI.
Number of hospital beds per county
Bed counts describe facilities, not a high-priority health issue.
Annual enrollment in nursing programs
Nursing school enrollment is an education statistic, not an LHI.

items.q: According to the textbook, on which key measures of health and well-being does the United States fall behind other developed countries?
items.a: Life expectancy, infant mortality, and obesity
items.ex: Despite progress on the LHIs, the nation still trails other developed countries on life expectancy, infant mortality, and obesity.
w: Medical research funding, new drug approvals, and imaging
These are areas of U.S. strength, not the key health measures the book says lag behind.
Number of medical schools, specialists, and research centers
These are resources, not the health and well-being measures the book names.
Hospital technology, surgical volume, and transplant access
These describe health care capacity, not the population health measures that lag.

alt.q: Which statement about U.S. progress on the Healthy People leading health indicators is accurate?
alt.a: Great progress has been made, but the nation still trails other developed countries on key measures
alt.ex: The United States has improved on the LHIs yet lags on life expectancy, infant mortality, and obesity.
w: The nation now leads other developed countries on every key measure of health
The book states the United States falls behind other developed countries on key measures.
Little progress has been made, so the indicators were removed from the plan
The book reports great progress, and the LHIs remain part of Healthy People 2030.
Progress is judged only by the number of people who have health insurance
LHIs include issues such as suicides, homicides, food insecurity, and youth obesity.

items.q: Which idea does the Healthy People initiative emphasize about communities?
items.a: The health of communities affects the overall health status of the nation
items.ex: Healthy People stresses that community health shapes the health status of the whole nation.
w: Community health has little effect on the nation’s overall health status
Healthy People emphasizes the opposite: community health drives national health.
National policy alone determines the health of each community
Healthy People promotes cooperation among individuals, communities, and organizations, not policy alone.
Communities should rely on hospitals to manage their health needs
Healthy People focuses on promotion and prevention through broad cooperation, not hospital care.

alt.q: A nurse speaks to a neighborhood association about Healthy People. Which statement by the nurse reflects a key emphasis of the initiative?
alt.a: “When our community becomes healthier, it helps improve the health of the whole nation.”
alt.ex: Healthy People emphasizes that the health of communities affects the nation’s overall health status.
w: “Our community’s health has little effect on the health of the nation.”
This contradicts the Healthy People emphasis on community health shaping national health.
“Only hospitals and clinics are responsible for our community’s health.”
Healthy People calls for cooperation among individuals, communities, and many organizations.
“National goals apply to hospitals, not to communities or individuals.”
Healthy People objectives aim to improve the health of all people and communities.

items.q: A community health nurse wants data to explain health disparities related to household food insecurity in the region. Which resource should the nurse consult?

Agency policies guide procedures, not population data on health disparities.
A drug reference handbook for community nursing practice
Drug references give medication information, not data on food insecurity disparities.

The practice act defines nursing scope, not population health data.

alt.q: What does the Healthy People 2030 website provide?
alt.a: Data about leading health indicators that help explain existing health disparities
alt.ex: The website offers LHI data to help explain existing health disparities.
w: Billing codes that hospitals use to charge for preventive services
Healthy People does not supply billing codes; it supplies LHI data.
Licensing exam content outlines for registered nurse candidates
Exam outlines come from licensing bodies, not from Healthy People.
Drug dosing tables for common chronic disease medications
Dosing tables are clinical references, not Healthy People LHI data.

w: Offer free blood pressure checks at a local shopping center

Exercise safety does not address household food insecurity and hunger.

items.q: A nurse speaks at a city council meeting in support of funding a community food pantry for families facing hunger. Which nursing role is the nurse demonstrating?

w: Caregiver
A caregiver provides direct care; speaking for community resources is advocacy.
Educator
An educator teaches health information; this nurse is speaking on behalf of families’ needs.
Researcher
A researcher conducts studies; the nurse here is supporting the community’s needs publicly.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a community group how to plan affordable, nutritious meals on a limited budget. Which nursing role is the nurse demonstrating?

alt.ex: Teaching people how to improve their health reflects the nurse’s role as educator.
w: Advocate
Advocacy involves speaking for patients’ interests; this nurse is teaching skills.
Caregiver
Caregiving is hands-on care; teaching meal planning is education.
Researcher
Research involves studying a problem; this nurse is teaching a group.

items.q: After a nurse teaches a community group about Healthy People, which statement by a participant shows understanding?
items.a: “It sets national goals to help keep people healthy and prevent disease.”
items.ex: Healthy People provides national objectives focused on health promotion, well-being, and disease prevention.
w: “It mainly tells hospitals how to treat people once they are sick.”
Healthy People focuses on promotion and prevention instead of illness care.
“It sets new national health goals that change every single year.”
Healthy People objectives are 10-year objectives, not annual goals.
“It is a private insurance plan that pays for preventive care.”
Healthy People is a national initiative with health objectives, not an insurance plan.

alt.q: After teaching about Healthy People, which statement by a participant shows a need for further teaching?
alt.a: “It focuses mostly on improving care for people who are already ill.”
alt.ex: Healthy People emphasizes health promotion, well-being, and disease prevention instead of illness care.
w: “It sets goals for keeping people healthy over a 10-year period.”
This is accurate; the objectives span 10 years and focus on health.
“It tracks high-priority health issues such as suicide and obesity.”
This is accurate; these are examples of leading health indicators.
“It brings communities and organizations together to improve health.”
This is accurate; Healthy People encourages broad cooperation.

items.q: Which issues are given in the textbook as examples of Healthy People 2030 leading health indicators? Select all that apply.
o: Household food insecurity and hunger
Food insecurity and hunger is listed as an LHI example.
Homicides
Homicides are listed as an LHI example.
Suicides
Suicides are listed as an LHI example.
Children and adolescents with obesity
Youth obesity is listed as an LHI example.
Number of licensed hospital beds
Bed counts describe facilities, not a high-priority health issue.
Average nurse-to-patient staffing ratio
Staffing ratios are workforce measures, not LHIs.
items.ex: LHIs are high-priority U.S. health issues; the book’s examples are food insecurity, homicides, suicides, and youth obesity.

alt.q: A public health nurse reviews community data. Which items are high-priority health issues tracked as Healthy People 2030 leading health indicators? Select all that apply.
o: Suicides
Suicides are an LHI example in the book.
Homicides
Homicides are an LHI example in the book.
Household food insecurity and hunger
Food insecurity and hunger is an LHI example.
Hospital profit margins
Profit margins are financial data, not a health issue.
Nursing school enrollment
Enrollment is education data, not an LHI.
alt.ex: Correct: Suicides; Homicides; Household food insecurity and hunger.

items.q: Which statements describe the Healthy People objectives? Select all that apply.
o: They are evidence-based.
The book describes the objectives as evidence-based.
They are data-driven.
The objectives are data-driven.

Healthy People provides 10-year national objectives.

They focus on promotion, well-being, and prevention instead of illness care.
They are written for a single profession.
Healthy People uses an interprofessional approach.

Healthy People promotes broad cooperation to improve everyone’s health.
items.ex: Healthy People objectives are evidence-based, data-driven, 10-year, interprofessional, and prevention focused.

alt.q: A nurse explains Healthy People to new staff. Which features should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

Promotion and prevention are the core focus.
An interprofessional approach

Use of data to set objectives
The objectives are data-driven.
Objectives rewritten every year
The objectives span 10 years.
Primary focus on hospital treatment of illness
Healthy People focuses on prevention instead of illness care.
alt.ex: Correct: Emphasis on health promotion and disease prevention; An interprofessional approach; Use of data to set objectives.

items.q: A nurse works to support the goals of Healthy People in the community. Which nursing actions are consistent with these goals? Select all that apply.
o: Teaching families about immunizations and recommended screenings
Education about prevention supports health promotion and disease prevention.
Identifying actual and potential risk factors in a population
Nurses identify risk factors that predispose groups to illness.

Waiting to intervene until community members become ill
Healthy People emphasizes prevention rather than illness care.
Planning programs without involving community partners
Healthy People encourages cooperation among individuals, communities, and organizations.
items.ex: Nurses support Healthy People by educating, identifying risk factors, helping modify them, and working with partners.

Identifying risk factors supports prevention.
Teaching parents about healthy nutrition for children

Helping modify risk factors prevents or limits illness.

Healthy People promotes cooperation with nonprofit organizations.

items.ww: The objectives are grounded in evidence and data, not opinion or tradition.
