items.q: How does the World Health Organization (WHO) define health?
items.a: A state of complete physical, mental, and social well-being, not merely the absence of disease or infirmity
items.ex: The WHO definition includes physical, mental, and social well-being and goes beyond the absence of disease.
w: A state in which a person has no diagnosed disease, injury, or infirmity at all
WHO states health is not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
The ability to perform daily activities without assistance or medical care
Functional independence alone does not capture complete physical, mental, and social well-being.
A level of physical fitness shown by normal vital signs and laboratory values
Normal physical findings alone leave out mental and social well-being.

alt.q: Which three areas of well-being are included in the WHO definition of health?
alt.a: Physical, mental, and social
alt.ex: WHO defines health as complete physical, mental, and social well-being.
w: Physical, spiritual, and financial
Financial well-being is not part of the WHO definition.
Mental, emotional, and occupational
The WHO definition names physical, mental, and social well-being.
Physical, environmental, and economic
Environmental and economic are not the domains named by WHO.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “I don’t have any diseases, so I must be completely healthy.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Being free of disease is important, but health also includes your mental and social well-being.”
items.ex: People free from disease are not necessarily healthy; health includes physical, mental, and social well-being.
w: “That’s right; having no disease is what being healthy means.”
Health is not merely the absence of disease, so this reinforces a misconception.
“Health is determined only by your laboratory test results.”
Lab results reflect physical status only, not mental and social well-being.
“You can’t call yourself healthy until a provider confirms it.”
Health is a personal state people define; a provider’s confirmation does not define it.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows correct understanding of the definition of health?
alt.a: “A person can be free of disease and still not be healthy.”
alt.ex: The book states that people who are free from disease are not necessarily healthy.
w: “A person with no disease is healthy by definition.”
WHO says health is not merely the absence of disease or infirmity.
“Health is measured only by a person’s physical condition.”
Health includes mental and social well-being and personal definitions.
“Health means the same thing to every person.”
Each person has a personal concept of health.

items.q: According to the textbook, people define health in relation to which factors?
items.a: Their own values, personality, and lifestyle
items.ex: Health is a state of being that people define in relation to their own values, personality, and lifestyle.
w: Their provider’s diagnosis and test results
Each person has a personal concept of health, not one set by a provider.
National health statistics and norms
People define health personally, not by national averages.
Their age group’s average life expectancy
Population life expectancy does not determine a person’s own concept of health.

alt.q: Two patients have the same chronic condition. One says she feels healthy, and the other says he feels very unhealthy. Which explanation is most accurate?
alt.a: Each person defines health according to personal values, personality, and lifestyle
alt.ex: Health is a personal concept defined in relation to a person’s own values, personality, and lifestyle.
w: One of the patients must be misreporting how severe the condition is
Different views of health are expected because health is personally defined.
Health is defined only by physical findings, so both are equally healthy
Health is not defined by physical condition alone.
The patient who feels unhealthy must have an undiagnosed second illness
Different perceptions reflect personal definitions, not necessarily another disease.

items.q: One definition describes health as the actualization of inherent and acquired human potential. Through which combination is this potential realized?
items.a: Goal-directed behavior, competent self-care, and satisfying relationships with others
items.ex: Health is actualized through goal-directed behavior, competent self-care, and satisfying relationships with others.
w: Avoiding all health risks, strict medical adherence, and frequent checkups
These are not the elements named in the actualization definition.
Genetic inheritance, financial security, and easy access to hospitals
The definition centers on behavior, self-care, and relationships, not genes or money.
Absence of symptoms, normal laboratory values, and taking no medications
This describes a disease-free view of health, not actualization of potential.

alt.q: Which patient best reflects health as the actualization of human potential?
alt.a: A patient who sets fitness goals, manages self-care, and keeps close friendships
alt.ex: Goal-directed behavior, competent self-care, and satisfying relationships realize human potential.
w: A patient who has no diagnoses but has withdrawn from friends and family
Lacking satisfying relationships does not reflect actualization of potential.
A patient who relies on others for all care despite being able to do it
Competent self-care is part of actualizing potential.
A patient who has normal lab results but has no personal health goals
Goal-directed behavior is part of this definition of health.

items.q: A patient from a different cultural background tells the nurse she uses traditional family remedies before visiting a clinic. Which understanding should guide the nurse’s response?
items.a: Culture shapes where people seek health care and the treatments they prefer
items.ex: Culture influences values, how people define health, where they seek care, and the treatments they prefer.
w: Cultural practices rarely affect how people define or seek health care
The book states culture strongly influences how people define health and seek care.
Using traditional remedies shows that the patient does not value health
Culture shapes health practices; it does not mean the patient devalues health.
Patients should set aside cultural beliefs to receive effective care
Nurses consider the total person, including culture, to individualize care.

alt.q: According to the textbook, which is influenced by a person’s culture?
alt.a: How the person defines health and what the person believes about illness
alt.ex: Culture influences values, definitions of health, beliefs about illness, care-seeking, and preferred treatments.
w: The person’s inherited blood type and tissue antigens
Blood type is genetic, not shaped by culture.
The person’s biological sex assigned at birth
Biological sex is not determined by culture.
The person’s eye color and other inherited traits
Inherited physical traits are not influenced by culture.

items.q: Which statement about life conditions and health is accurate?
items.a: They can affect health positively or negatively long before people know they are ill
items.ex: Life conditions, such as environment, diet, and lifestyle, affect health long before illness is recognized.
w: They affect health only after a disease has been diagnosed by a provider
Life conditions can affect health well before a person knows of illness.
They affect health only in negative ways that lead to chronic illness
Life conditions can have positive as well as negative effects.
They influence health only during childhood and adolescence
The book places no such age limit on how life conditions affect health.

alt.q: A nurse assesses life conditions that may affect a patient’s health. Which group of variables does the nurse include?
alt.a: Environment, diet, and lifestyle practices or choices
alt.ex: Life conditions include socioeconomic variables such as environment, diet, and lifestyle practices or choices.
w: Hospital ratings, provider specialty, and bed availability
These describe health care facilities, not the patient’s life conditions.
Insurance company name, pharmacy brand, and clinic hours
These are service details, not life conditions such as diet or environment.
Nurse staffing ratios, unit layout, and visiting hours
These are hospital features, not the patient’s life conditions.

items.q: A 78-year-old patient with arthritis and high blood pressure says, “I still consider myself healthy.” Which additional statement best explains this patient’s view of health?
items.a: “I stay mentally sharp, make my own decisions, and see my friends every week.”
items.ex: Some older adults feel healthy when alert, mentally active, independent in decisions, and connected with others.
w: “I have never needed to take any medicine for my conditions.”
Taking no medication is not how the book says older adults define health.
“My provider says all my test results are perfectly normal.”
Normal test results are not the basis the book gives for older adults’ views of health.
“I never need to see a health care provider for anything.”
Avoiding providers is not among the factors older adults use to judge health.

alt.q: Which factors do some older adults use to judge that they are healthy?
alt.a: Remaining mentally alert, deciding independently, and staying connected with others
alt.ex: Older adults may feel healthy when alert, mentally active, physically maintained, independent, and connected.
w: Having no chronic diseases, taking no medications, and needing no care
Many older adults with chronic conditions still consider themselves healthy.
Matching the strength and stamina of younger adults in daily activity
The book does not describe comparison with younger adults as a basis for health.
Receiving frequent screenings and hospital checkups throughout the year
Frequent checkups are not the criteria the book gives for older adults.

items.q: Because each person’s perception of health is different, what should the nurse do when planning care?
items.a: Consider the total person, including the environment, to individualize care
items.ex: Considering the whole person and environment lets the nurse individualize care and enhance health.
w: Use one standard definition of health for every patient on the unit
Each person has a personal concept of health, so a single standard does not individualize care.
Focus the plan mainly on the patient’s diagnosed disease process
People free of disease are not necessarily healthy, so disease focus alone is too narrow.
Base goals for the patient on the nurse’s own view of health
Care is individualized to the patient’s view, not the nurse’s.

alt.q: A nurse is planning care for a patient recovering from surgery who lives in a crowded apartment with limited access to fresh food. Which action best individualizes the plan?
alt.a: Include the patient’s home environment and food access in the plan of care
alt.ex: The nurse considers the total person, including the environment, to individualize care and enhance health.
w: Focus only on the surgical incision and postoperative pain
Considering only the physical condition ignores the total person and environment.
Use the standard postoperative plan without changes for this patient
A standard plan does not account for this patient’s life conditions.
Defer questions about home life until the patient is fully healed
Life conditions affect health now and belong in the plan.

items.q: A patient newly diagnosed with diabetes changes meal times and walking schedule to fit a new night-shift job. Which concept of health does this illustrate?
items.a: Adjusting as needed to maintain optimal health in harmony with the environment
items.ex: People adjust as needed to maintain optimal health and remain in harmony with the environment.
w: Health as simply the absence of all disease and infirmity
The patient has a disease; the behavior shows adaptation, not absence of disease.
Health as a fixed state that does not change over time
Health is dynamic; people adjust to maintain it.
Health as a state that only a provider’s diagnosis can define
Health is defined personally, and this patient is adapting on his or her own.

alt.q: Which statement about how people maintain health is accurate?
alt.a: People adjust as needed to maintain optimal health and stay in harmony with the environment
alt.ex: Maintaining optimal health involves ongoing adjustment and harmony with the environment.
w: People maintain health only by avoiding any change in their routines
Health is maintained by adjusting as needed, not by avoiding change.
People maintain health only by following a provider’s orders exactly
Health also reflects personal goals, self-care, and relationships.
People maintain health only while they remain completely free of disease
People can have disease and still work to maintain optimal health.

items.q: Which statement about personal definitions of health is accurate?
items.a: They change with age and are affected by the person’s health beliefs
items.ex: Individual perceptions and definitions of health change with age and are affected by health beliefs.
w: They stay the same once they are formed in early adulthood
The book states perceptions of health change with age.
They are set by the health care provider at the time of diagnosis
Each person has a personal concept of health shaped by beliefs and values.
They are identical for all people who share the same culture
Each person has a unique concept of health, even within a culture.

alt.q: At age 25, a patient defined health as running marathons. At 75, the same patient defines health as living independently and staying active with friends. How should the nurse interpret this change?
alt.a: Definitions of health change with age and are shaped by health beliefs
alt.ex: Perceptions and definitions of health change with age and are affected by a person’s health beliefs.
w: The patient has lost interest in maintaining health over time
The patient still values health; the definition has changed with age.
The patient’s first definition was correct and the new one is not
Each personal definition is valid for the person at that point in life.
The patient must have developed a cognitive impairment with age
A changed definition of health is expected with age and is not a sign of impairment.

items.q: A patient living in unstable housing has a normal physical examination but says, “I can’t be healthy until I have a safe place to live.” What does the nurse recognize about this statement?
items.a: People sometimes define health by their life circumstances rather than by physical condition
items.ex: Some people define health by the circumstances of their lives rather than their physical condition.
w: The patient misunderstands health, which depends only on physical findings
Health is not defined only by physical findings; life circumstances shape it.
The patient is describing an illness that has not yet been diagnosed
The patient is defining health by life circumstances, not reporting hidden disease.
The patient’s housing has no bearing on health until illness appears
Life conditions can affect health long before people know they are ill.

alt.q: Which statement about how people define their health is accurate?
alt.a: Some people define health by the circumstances of their lives rather than their physical condition
alt.ex: The book notes that people sometimes define health by life circumstances rather than physical condition.
w: All people define health only by the absence of physical symptoms
People also define health by values, lifestyle, and life circumstances.
People define health only through the results of health screenings
Screening results are not the only basis for personal definitions of health.
People define health only by comparing themselves with others their age
The book describes values, lifestyle, and circumstances, not peer comparison.

items.q: According to the textbook, a person’s culture influences which of the following? Select all that apply.

Culture influences where people seek care.
The treatments the person prefers
Culture influences preferred treatments.
The types of health promotion activities the person practices
Culture influences health promotion activities.

Blood type is genetic, not cultural.

Eye color is an inherited trait, not shaped by culture.

alt.q: A nurse considers a patient’s culture when planning care. Which areas may culture influence? Select all that apply.

Culture influences values.
What the patient believes about illness
Culture shapes beliefs about illness.
Where the patient chooses to seek care
Culture influences where people seek care.
The patient’s inherited genetic traits
Genetic traits are inherited, not shaped by culture.
The patient’s natural hair color
Hair color is inherited, not cultural.
alt.ex: Correct: The patient’s values; What the patient believes about illness; Where the patient chooses to seek care.

items.q: Some older adults believe they are healthy when they can do which of the following? Select all that apply.
o: Remain alert and mentally active
Mental alertness is one way older adults judge health.
Maintain their physical health
Maintaining physical health is part of older adults’ view of health.
Make decisions that affect their lives independently
Independent decision making is part of this view.
Stay connected with others
Connections with others contribute to older adults’ sense of health.
Live completely free of chronic conditions
Older adults may feel healthy even with chronic conditions.

Avoiding care is not a criterion the book describes.

items.q: Which are examples of life conditions that can affect a person’s health? Select all that apply.

alt.ex: Correct: The patient’s home environment; The patient’s usual diet; The patient’s lifestyle choices.

items.q: Which description best defines health beliefs?
items.a: A person’s ideas, opinions, and attitudes about health and illness
items.ex: Health beliefs are a person’s ideas, opinions, and attitudes about health and illness, and they influence behavior.
w: A person’s measured health status and screening results
Measured status is objective data, not a person’s beliefs.
The provider’s diagnosis and plan for treatment
A diagnosis belongs to the provider; beliefs belong to the person.
Scientific facts about disease that a person has learned
Health beliefs can be based on facts or on misinformation and myths.

alt.q: A patient refuses an influenza vaccine because she believes it gave her the flu years ago. Which statement about health beliefs does this illustrate?
alt.a: Health beliefs can be based on misinformation or past experiences
alt.ex: Health beliefs may rest on reality or false expectations, facts or misinformation, and good or bad experiences.
w: Health beliefs are always grounded in scientific fact
Beliefs can be based on myths or misinformation, not only facts.
Health beliefs have little effect on health behaviors
Health beliefs influence health behavior, as her refusal shows.
Health beliefs come only from health care providers
Beliefs come from many sources, including personal experiences.

items.q: The Health Belief Model (HBM) is based on three components of health-related behavior. Which is one of them?
items.a: The individual’s belief that certain health choices will prevent or cure an illness
items.ex: The HBM components are the desire to avoid illness, belief that choices prevent or cure it, and likeliness of action.
w: The provider’s confidence that a prescribed treatment will succeed
The HBM focuses on the individual’s beliefs, not the provider’s confidence.
The nurse’s ability to enforce adherence to the treatment plan
The HBM addresses the person’s beliefs and behaviors, not enforcement.
The hospital’s published success rates for treating the illness
Hospital outcomes are not a component of the HBM.

alt.q: Which component of health-related behavior is part of the Health Belief Model?
alt.a: The individual’s desire to avoid illness or to recover if ill
alt.ex: The desire to avoid illness or recover is one of the three HBM components.
w: The individual’s need for love and belonging within a family
Love and belonging is a level in Maslow’s hierarchy, not an HBM component.
The individual’s balance of body, mind, and spirit
Body, mind, and spirit relate to holistic health, not the HBM.
The individual’s behavioral outcome of committing to a plan
Commitment to a plan of action is part of the Health Promotion Model.

items.q: A 60-year-old patient believes he is not at risk for colon cancer and declines screening. After a younger friend is diagnosed with advanced colon cancer, he schedules a colonoscopy. Which HBM element prompted this change?
items.a: A cue to action from the illness of a friend
items.ex: In the HBM, cues to action such as a friend’s illness increase the perceived threat of a disease.
w: A perceived barrier to preventive action
Barriers lower the likelihood of action; this event increased it.
A demographic variable such as his age
His age did not change; the friend’s illness prompted action.
A behavioral outcome from prior screening
He had no prior colonoscopy, so prior screening outcomes do not apply.

alt.q: Which is an example of a cue to action in the Health Belief Model?
alt.a: A reminder postcard from the patient’s dentist
alt.ex: Cues to action include media campaigns, advice from others, reminder postcards, and illness of family or friends.
w: The patient’s age and ethnicity
Age and ethnicity are demographic modifying factors, not cues to action.
The patient’s personality and social class
These are sociopsychological modifying factors, not cues to action.
The cost and time needed for screening
Cost and time are perceived barriers to preventive action.

items.q: In the Health Belief Model, how is the likelihood of taking preventive action determined?
items.a: Perceived benefits of preventive action minus perceived barriers to action
items.ex: The HBM weighs perceived benefits of preventive action against perceived barriers to that action.
w: Perceived barriers to action minus perceived benefits of preventive action
This reverses the model; benefits minus barriers determines likelihood of action.
Perceived susceptibility to disease plus the patient’s demographic variables
Susceptibility shapes perceived threat; likelihood comes from benefits minus barriers.
Cues to action minus the perceived seriousness of the disease
Cues to action raise perceived threat; they are not subtracted from seriousness.

alt.q: A patient agrees that mammograms detect cancer early but says, “I can’t take time off work, and I don’t have a ride.” Which HBM factor is lowering her likelihood of being screened?
alt.a: Perceived barriers to preventive action
alt.ex: Time off work and lack of transportation are barriers that are subtracted from perceived benefits.
w: Perceived seriousness of the disease
She does not question how serious cancer is; she describes obstacles.
Cues to action from other people
Cues to action prompt action; her statements describe obstacles.
Perceived susceptibility to the disease
She does not deny her risk; she describes practical obstacles.

items.q: A nurse uses the Health Belief Model to assess a patient who smokes. Which question best addresses a key element of the model?
items.a: “How likely do you think it is that you could develop lung disease?”
items.ex: Perceived susceptibility to disease is a key HBM element used to predict adoption of healthy behaviors.
w: “What brand of cigarettes do you usually smoke?”
Cigarette brand does not reveal the patient’s health perceptions.
“Which pharmacy do you use for your prescriptions?”
Pharmacy choice does not address perceived susceptibility or seriousness.
“What time of day do you usually eat your meals?”
Meal timing does not relate to the patient’s perceived threat of lung disease.

alt.q: Which key elements of the Health Belief Model does the nurse assess to determine the likelihood that a patient will adopt healthy behaviors?
alt.a: Perceived susceptibility to disease and perceived seriousness of illness
alt.ex: The book names perception of susceptibility and seriousness as key HBM elements for predicting behavior.
w: Current laboratory results and medication list
Lab results and medications are clinical data, not health perceptions.
Past surgical history and family pedigree
These are history data, not the patient’s perceptions in the HBM.
Self-actualization needs and self-esteem needs
These are Maslow levels, not key HBM elements.

items.q: How does the Health Promotion Model (HPM) define health?
items.a: A positive, dynamic state, not merely the absence of disease
items.ex: The HPM views health as a positive, dynamic state; health promotion increases a patient’s well-being.
w: A fixed state determined at birth by genetic factors
The HPM describes health as dynamic, not fixed by genetics.
The absence of disease as confirmed by screening tests
The HPM states health is not merely the absence of disease.
A balance between episodes of illness and recovery
The HPM defines health positively, not as cycles of illness and recovery.

alt.q: Which three areas does the Health Promotion Model focus on?
alt.a: Individual characteristics and experiences, behavior-specific cognitions and affect, and behavioral outcomes
alt.ex: The HPM’s three areas lead to a behavioral outcome of committing to or changing a behavior.
w: Perceived susceptibility, perceived seriousness, and cues to action leading to threat
These are elements of the Health Belief Model.
Physiological needs, safety and security needs, and love and belonging needs
These are levels of Maslow’s hierarchy of needs.
Interactions among body, mind, and spirit within the person’s environment
This describes holistic health, not the HPM.

items.q: In the Health Promotion Model, which area contains the variables that influence a patient’s motivation to change or adopt healthy behaviors?
items.a: Behavior-specific cognitions and affect
items.ex: The book states that behavior-specific knowledge and affect variables influence motivation to adopt healthy behaviors.
w: Behavioral outcomes
Behavioral outcomes are the result: committing to or changing a behavior.
Perceived threat of disease
Perceived threat is part of the Health Belief Model.
Physiological needs
Physiological needs are the base level of Maslow’s hierarchy.

alt.q: In the Health Promotion Model, what does the behavioral outcomes area result in?
alt.a: The patient committing to or changing a health behavior
alt.ex: Behavioral outcomes in the HPM result in the patient committing to or changing a behavior.
w: The patient perceiving a greater threat of disease
Perceived threat belongs to the Health Belief Model.
The patient meeting physiological needs before others
Meeting needs in order relates to Maslow’s hierarchy.
The patient receiving a medical diagnosis of illness
The HPM focuses on promoting health behaviors, not on diagnosis.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient who is tearful about missing her daughter’s wedding. The nurse notes the patient is now struggling to breathe because of thick airway secretions. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Clear the patient’s airway of secretions
items.ex: In all cases, an emergent physiological need such as oxygenation takes precedence over higher-level needs.
w: Arrange a video call with the patient’s daughter
Love and belonging needs come after an emergent physiological need.
Encourage the patient to talk about her feelings of loss
Emotional support is important but follows the emergent breathing problem.
Praise the patient’s coping to support her self-esteem
Self-esteem is a higher-level need than airway and oxygenation.

alt.q: A fire breaks out on a hospital unit. A frightened patient is also worried about how he looks to visitors. Which need takes priority?
alt.a: Physical safety from injury
alt.ex: In situations such as a fire, fear of injury and death takes priority over self-esteem needs.
w: Self-esteem related to appearance
Self-esteem is a higher-level need than physical safety in a fire.
Love and belonging with visitors
Love and belonging needs follow safety needs in an emergency.
Self-actualization and self-discovery
Self-actualization is the highest level and is not the priority during a fire.

items.q: A nurse anticipates that pain control will be the top need of a patient who had a hysterectomy for ovarian cancer. Her pain is managed with ordered analgesics, but she says she feels unlovable and worthless. Which action best reflects the textbook’s guidance on Maslow’s hierarchy?
items.a: Address her love, belonging, and self-esteem needs as her current priority
items.ex: The nurse focuses on the patient’s actual needs found on assessment rather than strict adherence to the hierarchy.
w: Keep focusing only on pain because physiological needs always come first
Only emergent physiological needs always take precedence; her pain is managed.
Postpone her emotional concerns until she is ready for discharge
Her greatest current need is love, belonging, and self-esteem, so delay is inappropriate.
Set priorities based on how other hysterectomy patients have reacted
The book warns against assuming needs because of how other patients reacted.

alt.q: When applying Maslow’s hierarchy of needs in practice, what should the nurse do?
alt.a: Focus on each patient’s needs rather than strict adherence to the hierarchy
alt.ex: It is unrealistic to expect needs to always occur in fixed order, so the nurse individualizes priorities.
w: Always meet needs in fixed order from the bottom level upward
The book states needs do not always occur in a fixed hierarchical order.
Assume a patient’s needs match those of similar past patients
The book warns not to assume needs based on other patients’ reactions.
Address self-actualization first because it is the highest need
Self-actualization is not addressed first; basic and emergent needs come before it.

items.q: A nurse is applying holistic health principles. Which action best reflects this approach?
items.a: Recognize the patient as the ultimate expert concerning their own health
items.ex: Holistic practice puts patients at the center of care and recognizes them as experts on their own health.
w: Make health decisions for the patient as the clinical expert
Holistic health empowers patients to engage in their recovery, not the reverse.
Use holistic therapies only after conventional treatment fails
Holistic therapies are used alone or with conventional medicine in all stages.
Focus care mainly on the physical aspects of the illness
Holistic nursing considers emotional, spiritual, social, cultural, and physical aspects.

alt.q: Which statement best describes holistic health?
alt.a: A system of preventive care that focuses on the health of the whole person
alt.ex: Holistic health considers social, psychological, and environmental influences and empowers patients in their recovery.
w: A system of acute care that focuses on treating one diseased organ
Holistic health addresses the whole person, not a single organ.
A system of care that replaces patients’ role with provider decisions
Holistic health empowers patients to take part in their own care.
A system of care that is used only during the final stage of illness
Holistic strategies can be used in all stages of health and illness.

items.q: An older adult with memory loss in a long-term care setting appears anxious. Which holistic intervention should the nurse consider to help relieve the anxiety?
items.a: Reminiscence about meaningful past events
items.ex: Reminiscence is a holistic intervention that sometimes helps relieve anxiety in older adults with memory loss.
w: Reorienting the patient to the date every hour
Frequent reorientation is not a holistic intervention named in the book.
Limiting visitors to reduce stimulation
Restricting visitors is not a holistic intervention and may reduce connection.
Requesting an order for a sedative medication
A sedative is a drug therapy, not a holistic intervention.

alt.q: A patient receiving chemotherapy is struggling with difficult side effects. Which holistic approach may help the patient cope?
alt.a: Meditation and mindfulness practice
alt.ex: Meditation and mindfulness sometimes help patients cope with difficult chemotherapy side effects.
w: Stopping the chemotherapy schedule
Stopping treatment is a medical decision, not a holistic coping strategy.
Avoiding all talk about side effects
Avoidance is not a holistic intervention and does not support coping.
Spending more time alone in a dark room
Isolation is not one of the holistic interventions the book describes.

items.q: Which are positive health behaviors? Select all that apply.

Immunizations help maintain health and prevent illness.
Keeping scheduled screenings such as a colonoscopy
Screenings are positive health behaviors.
Maintaining proper sleep patterns
Proper sleep is a positive health behavior.
Practicing stress management
Stress management is a positive health behavior.
Refusing to take necessary medications
Refusing needed medications is a negative health behavior.
Engaging in risky sexual behaviors
Risky sexual behavior is harmful to health.
items.ex: Positive health behaviors maintain, attain, or regain health and prevent illness.

alt.q: Which are negative health behaviors? Select all that apply.
o: Smoking
Smoking is harmful to health.
Eating a poor diet
A poor diet is a negative health behavior.
Refusing to take necessary medications
Refusing needed medications harms health.
Drug or alcohol abuse
Substance abuse is a negative health behavior.
Getting adequate exercise
Adequate exercise is a positive health behavior.
Having a scheduled mammogram
Screenings are positive health behaviors.
alt.ex: Correct: Smoking; Eating a poor diet; Refusing to take necessary medications; Drug or alcohol abuse.

items.q: In the Health Belief Model, which are modifying factors? Select all that apply.
o: Age
Age is a demographic modifying factor.
Ethnicity
Ethnicity is a demographic modifying factor.
Social class
Social class is a sociopsychological modifying factor.
Peer and reference group pressure
Peer pressure is a sociopsychological modifying factor.
Perceived barriers to preventive action
Barriers are part of the likelihood of action, not a modifying factor.
Perceived susceptibility to disease
Susceptibility is an individual perception, not a modifying factor.
items.ex: HBM modifying factors include demographic variables and sociopsychological variables such as personality and peer pressure.

alt.q: Which are examples of cues to action in the Health Belief Model? Select all that apply.

Media campaigns are cues to action.
Advice from others
Advice from others is a cue to action.
Illness of a family member or friend
Illness of someone close is a cue to action.
The patient’s age and gender

The patient’s personality
Personality is a sociopsychological modifying factor.
alt.ex: Correct: A mass media campaign; Advice from others; Illness of a family member or friend.

items.q: Which are holistic interventions described in the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Meditation
Meditation is a widely used holistic intervention.
Music therapy
Music therapy is a holistic intervention.
Guided imagery
Guided imagery is a holistic intervention.
Therapeutic touch
Therapeutic touch is a holistic intervention.
Intravenous antibiotic therapy
Antibiotics are conventional drug therapy, not a holistic intervention.
Surgical wound debridement
Debridement is a conventional procedure, not a holistic intervention.
items.ex: Widely used holistic interventions include meditation, music therapy, reminiscence, relaxation, therapeutic touch, and guided imagery.

alt.q: Holistic nursing considers the dynamic interactions among which aspects of a person’s wellness? Select all that apply.
o: Emotional
Emotional aspects are part of holistic nursing.
Spiritual
Spiritual aspects are part of holistic nursing.
Cultural
Cultural aspects are part of holistic nursing.
Physical
Physical aspects are part of holistic nursing.
Insurance status
Insurance status is not one of the aspects named.
The nurse’s personal preferences
Holistic care centers on the patient, not the nurse’s preferences.
alt.ex: Correct: Emotional; Spiritual; Cultural; Physical.

items.q: Positive health models focus on an individual’s strengths, resiliency, resources, and capabilities rather than on disease or pathology.
items.a: True
items.ex: Positive health models emphasize strengths, resiliency, resources, potential, and capabilities.

alt.q: Positive health models focus mainly on a patient’s disease and pathology rather than on strengths.

alt.ww: Disease and pathology are not the focus of positive health models.

items.q: When using Maslow’s hierarchy, the nurse should expect a patient’s needs to always occur in a fixed order.
items.a: False

items.ww: Needs vary by patient, so strict adherence to the order is not expected.

alt.a: True

alt.ww: No higher-level need outranks an emergent physiological need.

items.q: When a patient’s health views and beliefs differ from the nurse’s, the nurse should avoid making judgments.

alt.ww: Using the nurse’s beliefs ignores the patient’s unique belief system.

sections.name: Variables influencing health and health beliefs and practices

items.q: Which variable influencing health beliefs and practices is classified as an internal variable?
items.a: Perception of functioning
items.ex: Internal variables are developmental stage, intellectual background, perception of functioning, and emotional and spiritual factors.
w: Family role and practices
Family role and practices are an external variable.
Social determinants of health
Social determinants of health are external factors such as income, housing, and education.
Cultural background
Cultural background is listed among the external variables.

alt.q: Which variable influencing health beliefs and practices is classified as an external variable?
alt.a: Family role and practices
alt.ex: External variables include family practices, psychosocial and socioeconomic factors, and cultural background.
w: Developmental stage
Developmental stage is an internal variable.
Emotional factors
Stress, depression, and fear are internal emotional factors.
Spiritual factors
Spiritual factors are listed among the internal variables.

items.q: Which description best defines social determinants of health (SDOH)?
items.a: The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age
items.ex: SDOH are the social, economic, environmental, and political conditions of daily life that affect health disparities.
w: The genetic traits a person inherits from both biological parents
Inherited traits are nonmodifiable risk factors, not social determinants.
The personal beliefs a person holds about the causes of illness
Beliefs about illness causes relate to culture and health beliefs, not the definition of SDOH.
The stages of growth a person passes through across the life span
Growth stages describe developmental stage, an internal variable.

alt.q: A nurse reviews the conditions in which a patient was born, grew up, lives, works, and is aging. What is the nurse assessing?
alt.a: Social determinants of health
alt.ex: SDOH refer to the conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age.
w: Perception of functioning
Perception of functioning concerns how a patient views fatigue, breathlessness, or pain.
Developmental stage
Developmental stage concerns growth and development, not living and working conditions.
Spiritual factors
Spiritual factors concern values, beliefs, hope, and meaning in life.

items.q: A patient with a low income, high utility bills, and a large family to support has not filled a new prescription for an antihypertensive. Which factor most likely explains this behavior?
items.a: Economic status leads the patient to place food and shelter ahead of medications
items.ex: Economic stability affects adherence; a patient with limited income may give higher priority to food and shelter than to medications.
w: The patient’s developmental stage prevents understanding of the treatment
Nothing suggests a developmental limitation; the data point to economic pressures.
The patient’s spiritual beliefs forbid the use of all prescribed medicines
No religious restriction is described; the data describe financial strain.
The patient perceives physical functioning as better than it actually is
Perception of functioning is not indicated; low income and high bills explain the choice.

alt.q: A nurse learns that a patient with a low income and a large family skips special-diet foods to pay rent. What should the nurse recognize?
alt.a: Economic stability is a social determinant that affects treatment adherence
alt.ex: SDOH related to economic stability influence adherence because patients may prioritize food and shelter over treatments and special diets.
w: The patient lacks motivation and needs firmer instructions about the diet
Labeling the patient unmotivated ignores the economic barrier described.
The patient’s family practices are the main reason for nonadherence
The data describe financial limits, not family beliefs about health.
The patient’s cultural background prohibits the prescribed diet foods
No cultural restriction is described; cost is the barrier.

items.q: A nurse is assessing how a patient perceives physical functioning. Which data does the nurse gather first?
items.a: The patient’s report of fatigue and shortness of breath
items.ex: The nurse first gathers subjective data about perceived functioning, such as fatigue, shortness of breath, or pain, then obtains objective data.
w: The patient’s blood pressure and height measurements
Blood pressure and height are objective data obtained after the subjective data.
The patient’s lung sounds on auscultation
Lung sounds are objective data about actual functioning, gathered after subjective data.
The patient’s laboratory results from the last visit
Assessment of perceived functioning starts with the patient’s own report, not test results.

alt.q: After a patient describes level of fatigue and pain, the nurse obtains objective data about actual functioning. Which data does the nurse collect?
alt.a: Blood pressure, height, and lung sounds
alt.ex: Objective data about actual functioning include measurements such as blood pressure, height, and lung sounds.
w: Ratings of pain and level of fatigue
Pain and fatigue reports are subjective data about perceived functioning.
Descriptions of shortness of breath with activity
Reports of breathlessness are subjective data from the patient.
Statements about how tired daily tasks feel
The patient’s statements about tiredness are subjective, not objective, data.

items.q: A nurse is teaching a 28-year-old patient who has a developmental delay about managing a new diet. Which factor should guide the nurse’s teaching approach?
items.a: The patient’s developmental stage and ability to participate in self-care
items.ex: Developmental stage can differ from chronological age, so care is adapted to developmental stage and self-care ability.
w: The patient’s chronological age and typical adult teaching methods
Chronological age alone may not match the patient’s developmental stage.
A standard printed handout written for all adult patients
A uniform handout ignores the patient’s individual developmental needs.
The approach the patient’s parents prefer for all teaching
Family input helps, but care is adapted to the patient’s own developmental stage.

alt.q: A nurse plans physical activity teaching for an adolescent and for a middle-aged adult. Which approach is best?
alt.a: Use different teaching techniques based on each person’s developmental stage
alt.ex: Emotional and developmental stage influence health beliefs, so techniques for adolescents differ from those for adults.
w: Use the same teaching techniques because the content is identical
The textbook states techniques for adolescents differ from those used for adults.
Teach only the adult, since adolescents do not form health beliefs
Adolescents do form health beliefs, which change over time with development.
Base both plans only on chronological age and not on development
Developmental stage sometimes differs from chronological age and should guide care.

items.q: Fear and anxiety are common in children who are ill. In which situation are these reactions most likely?
items.a: When thoughts about illness or procedures are based on unclear or missing information
items.ex: Fear and anxiety increase when children’s thoughts about illness, hospitalization, or procedures rest on lack of information or unclear information.
w: When a child has received clear explanations about a planned procedure
Clear information reduces, rather than causes, fear and anxiety in ill children.
When the child’s chronological age matches the developmental stage
A match between age and stage is not described as a cause of fear.
When the child is admitted with parents who stay at the bedside
Parental presence is not identified in the text as a source of fear.

alt.q: A nurse prepares a 7-year-old for an upcoming procedure. Which nursing action best reduces the child’s fear and anxiety?
alt.a: Give clear information about the procedure suited to the child’s development
alt.ex: Fear and anxiety in ill children often stem from lack of information or unclear information, so clear, developmentally suited explanations help.
w: Avoid discussing the procedure so the child does not worry about it
Withholding information leaves the child to imagine the procedure, increasing fear.
Give a detailed technical explanation written for adult patients
Adult-level explanations lack clarity for a child and do not fit the developmental stage.
Tell the child the procedure will happen without any further details
Lack of detail and clarity is what fuels fear and anxiety in ill children.

items.q: A patient who usually becomes very anxious under stress reports chest discomfort but says, “It’s nothing; I’m not going to the doctor.” Which variable is most likely influencing this patient’s health practices?
items.a: Emotional factors
items.ex: A person unable to cope emotionally with the threat of illness may deny symptoms and not take therapeutic action.
w: Intellectual background
Intellectual background relates to knowledge and education, not an emotional reaction to threat.
Perception of functioning
The patient is not misjudging function; the denial reflects difficulty coping emotionally.
Family role and practices
No family influence is described; the response reflects the patient’s emotional coping.

alt.q: Which statement about emotional factors and health practices is accurate?
alt.a: A person who is usually calm may show little emotional response during illness
alt.ex: How people manage stress influences reactions to illness; a calm person may react little, while another may overreact or deny symptoms.
w: A person’s level of stress has little effect on health beliefs
Stress, depression, and fear do influence health beliefs and practices.
People react to the threat of illness in the same emotional way
Reactions vary; some stay calm while others overreact or deny symptoms.
Denial of symptoms usually leads to early therapeutic action
Denial may lead the person not to take therapeutic action.

items.q: A patient scheduled for surgery tells the nurse that their religious faith discourages blood transfusions. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Explore the patient’s beliefs so they can be incorporated into the plan of care
items.ex: Nurses need to understand patients’ spiritual beliefs to incorporate them effectively in nursing care.
w: Explain that a transfusion will be given regardless of the patient’s beliefs
Overriding the patient’s beliefs ignores spiritual factors and person-centered care.
Avoid any further discussion of religion to keep the conversation neutral
Avoiding the topic prevents the nurse from understanding and including the patient’s beliefs.
Ask family members to persuade the patient to accept a transfusion
Pressuring the patient through family disregards the patient’s spiritual beliefs.

alt.q: Why does a nurse assess a patient’s spiritual beliefs, including religious practices?
alt.a: Some religions restrict certain treatments, and beliefs must be included in care
alt.ex: Some religions restrict forms of treatment, so nurses must understand spiritual beliefs to incorporate them into care.
w: Religious beliefs rarely affect decisions about medical treatment
Some religions restrict treatments such as blood transfusions.
Spiritual beliefs are mainly needed to determine a patient’s diet
Spirituality affects values, relationships, hope, and treatment choices, not mainly diet.
Religion is the only way a person can express spirituality
Religious practices are one way, not the only way, people exercise spirituality.

items.q: Why should a nurse assess the health beliefs of each patient rather than relying on knowledge of the patient’s cultural group?
items.a: Health beliefs often vary among people within the same cultural group
items.ex: Beliefs vary within a cultural group, so each patient is assessed individually to avoid stereotyping.
w: Cultural groups share identical beliefs about the causes of illness
Health beliefs often vary within a cultural group, so they are not identical.
Cultural beliefs have little influence on how patients follow treatment
Cultural beliefs shape adherence to treatment and preferences for care.
Most patients adopt every belief and practice of their culture
Nurses should not assume patients adopt all cultural beliefs and practices.

alt.q: A nurse cared for several patients from the same cultural background last week. A new patient from that background is admitted. What is the nurse’s best action?
alt.a: Assess this patient’s own health beliefs and preferences for care
alt.ex: Health beliefs vary within cultural groups, so the nurse assesses each patient and avoids stereotyping.
w: Use last week’s care plans because the beliefs will be the same
Assuming shared beliefs stereotypes the patient; beliefs vary within a group.
Avoid asking about beliefs to prevent offending the patient
Recognizing a patient’s beliefs is needed for culturally competent care.
Ask a family member to describe the culture’s typical practices
Typical group practices may not reflect this patient’s individual beliefs.

items.q: According to the textbook, what happens if a nurse is not aware of their own cultural patterns of behavior and language?
items.a: The nurse has difficulty understanding patients’ behaviors and beliefs
items.ex: Without awareness of one’s own cultural patterns, the nurse struggles to interact with patients and understand their behaviors and beliefs.
w: The nurse delivers care that is free of cultural bias
Lack of self-awareness makes bias and stereotyping more likely, not less.
The nurse relies more effectively on each patient’s own reports
Lack of awareness interferes with recognizing and understanding the patient’s beliefs.
The nurse has no effect on the nurse-patient relationship
Culture influences the nurse-patient relationship, so lack of awareness affects it.

alt.q: Which action by a nurse best reflects person-centered cultural care described in the textbook?
alt.a: Recognizing personal prejudices that could lead to stereotyping
alt.ex: Nurses are to be aware of their own cultural background and recognize prejudices that lead to stereotyping and discrimination.
w: Assuming patients will follow all beliefs of their cultural group
Nurses should not assume patients adopt all cultural beliefs and practices.
Teaching all patients with one plan that ignores cultural factors
Effective interventions incorporate cultural factors into the plan of care.
Avoiding questions about what the patient believes caused the illness
Nurses recognize each patient’s perceptions about causes of illness when teaching.

items.q: A school nurse assesses a 9-year-old with obesity whose parents believe sugary drinks are a healthy choice. Which variable most likely contributes to the child’s eating habits?
items.a: Family role and practices
items.ex: Parents with misconceptions about diet quality often contribute to eating habits that lead to obesity in their children.
w: Spiritual factors
No spiritual or religious influence on eating is described.
Perception of functioning
The issue is family beliefs about food, not how the child perceives function.
Emotional factors
The data describe parental misconceptions, not stress, fear, or depression.

alt.q: A child’s parents value daily physical activity and healthy meals. How are these family beliefs likely to affect the child?
alt.a: The child may continue to practice these health beliefs
alt.ex: Family perceptions and preventive behaviors shape how members think about health; children often continue parents’ healthy practices.
w: The child will likely reject these beliefs during school age
The textbook describes children continuing, not rejecting, family health practices.
The child’s beliefs will depend only on intellectual ability
Family role and practices strongly shape how each member values health practices.
Family beliefs will have little influence on the child’s health
The roles and organization of a family influence how members define health.

items.q: How do social determinants of health related to economic stability often affect a patient’s health?
items.a: They increase disease risk and influence when the patient enters health care
items.ex: Economic SDOH increase disease risk, affect finding affordable safe housing, and influence how or when patients enter the health care system.
w: They mainly affect a patient’s spiritual beliefs about illness
Spiritual beliefs are an internal variable, not the main effect of economic SDOH.
They have little effect once a patient has health insurance
The textbook describes broad effects on risk, housing, and access, not limited by insurance.
They determine a patient’s developmental stage and cognition
Developmental stage and cognitive ability are internal variables.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows correct understanding of social determinants of health (SDOH)?
alt.a: “Where a person lives and their income can greatly affect health.”
alt.ex: External factors such as where a person lives, environment, income, education, and relationships have considerable impact on health.
w: “SDOH include only a person’s income level and job.”
SDOH also include education, health care access, community context, and the built environment.
“SDOH are internal factors such as stress and fear.”
Stress and fear are emotional factors, an internal variable.
“SDOH affect health only in rural communities.”
SDOH affect people wherever they are born, grow, live, work, and age.

items.q: Which are categories of social determinants of health (SDOH)? Select all that apply.
o: Economic stability
Economic stability is one of the five SDOH categories.
Education access and quality
Education access and quality is one of the five SDOH categories.
Health care access and quality
Health care access and quality is one of the five SDOH categories.
Neighborhood and built environment
Neighborhood and built environment is one of the five SDOH categories.
Genetic makeup and family history
Genetics and family history are nonmodifiable risk factors, not an SDOH category.
Developmental stage and cognition
These are internal variables, not SDOH categories.
items.ex: The five SDOH categories are economic stability, education, health care access, social and community context, and neighborhood and built environment.

alt.q: A community health nurse lists social determinants of health (SDOH) affecting a neighborhood. Which are examples of SDOH? Select all that apply.
o: Poverty
Poverty is given as an example of an SDOH.
Food insecurity
Food insecurity is given as an example of an SDOH.
Exposure to violence
Exposure to violence is given as an example of an SDOH.
Access to green spaces
Access to green spaces is given as an example of an SDOH.
A family history of colon cancer
Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor, not an SDOH.
A resident’s emotional response to illness
Emotional response is an internal variable, not an SDOH.
alt.ex: Correct: Poverty; Food insecurity; Exposure to violence; Access to green spaces.

items.q: Which variables are internal variables that influence health beliefs and practices? Select all that apply.
o: Developmental stage
Developmental stage is an internal variable.
Intellectual background
Intellectual background is an internal variable.
Emotional factors
Stress, depression, and fear are internal emotional factors.
Spiritual factors
Spiritual factors are an internal variable.
Cultural background
Cultural background is an external variable.
Family role and practices
Family role and practices are an external variable.
items.ex: Internal variables are developmental stage, intellectual background, perception of functioning, and emotional and spiritual factors.

alt.q: Which variables are external variables that influence health beliefs and practices? Select all that apply.
o: Family role and practices
Family practices are an external variable.
Socioeconomic factors
Psychosocial and socioeconomic factors are external variables.
Cultural background
Cultural background is an external variable.
Perception of functioning
Perception of functioning is an internal variable.
Emotional factors
Emotional factors are an internal variable.
alt.ex: Correct: Family role and practices; Socioeconomic factors; Cultural background.

items.q: Cultural health beliefs influence a patient’s responses to health, illness, and health care providers. Which responses does the textbook list? Select all that apply.
o: Eye contact
Eye contact is one response shaped by cultural health beliefs.
Response to pain and use of pain management
Pain response and pain management use are shaped by cultural beliefs.
Use of touch
Use of touch is one response influenced by culture.
Sick role behaviors
Sick role behaviors are influenced by cultural health beliefs.
Inherited risk for hereditary syndromes
Hereditary risk is genetic, not a response shaped by cultural beliefs.
Age at which heart disease risk rises
Age-related disease risk is a nonmodifiable risk factor, not a cultural response.
items.ex: Cultural beliefs shape eye contact, pain responses and management, touch, perception and treatment of mental illness, and sick role behaviors.

alt.q: Which nursing actions reflect the implications for person-centered cultural care? Select all that apply.
o: Learn how the patient’s traditions and values affect views on illness prevention
Understanding traditions and values guides culturally competent care.
Consider the patient’s beliefs about the cause of the illness when teaching
Teaching should recognize the patient’s perceptions about illness causes.
Recognize one’s own prejudices that may lead to stereotyping
Nurses are to be aware of their own cultural background and prejudices.
Assume the patient follows all practices of the cultural group
Nurses should not assume patients adopt all cultural beliefs and practices.
Base care on the most common beliefs of the patient’s culture
Beliefs vary within groups, so care is based on the individual, not stereotypes.
alt.ex: Correct: Learn how the patient’s traditions and values affect views on illness prevention; Consider the patient’s beliefs about the cause of the illness when teaching; Recognize one’s own prejudices that may lead to stereotyping.

items.q: A person’s developmental stage always matches the person’s chronological age.
items.a: False
items.ex: Developmental stage sometimes differs from chronological age, so nurses adapt care to the patient’s developmental stage.
items.ww: Calling it true would lead nurses to plan care by age alone and miss developmental differences.

alt.q: A person’s developmental stage sometimes differs from the person’s chronological age.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The textbook notes that developmental stage may differ from chronological age, which shapes how care is adapted.
alt.ww: Calling it false assumes age and development always match, which the textbook says is not always so.

items.q: Health beliefs usually influence health behaviors, which can positively or negatively affect a patient’s level of health.
items.a: True
items.ex: Health beliefs usually shape health behaviors or practices, which in turn affect the patient’s level of health.
items.ww: Calling it false ignores the textbook’s link between beliefs, behaviors, and level of health.

alt.q: A patient’s health practices are shaped only by internal variables such as emotions and development.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Both internal variables and external variables such as family, SDOH, and culture influence health beliefs and practices.
alt.ww: Calling it true ignores the external variables, such as family and culture, that the textbook describes.

items.q: Spirituality often provides motivation for people to participate in health promotion activities.
items.a: True
items.ex: Spirituality serves as an integrating theme in people’s lives and often motivates participation in health promotion.
items.ww: Calling it false overlooks the textbook’s point that spirituality frequently motivates health promotion.

alt.q: Religious practices are the only way people exercise spirituality.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Religious practices are one way, but not the only way, that people exercise spirituality.
alt.ww: Calling it true narrows spirituality to religion, though it is reflected in how people live their lives.

items.q: The conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age are called [[social determinants of health|SDOH|social determinants]].
items.ex: SDOH include social, economic, environmental, and political factors that affect health disparities.

alt.q: Poverty, food insecurity, and lack of primary health care in a community are examples of [[social determinants of health|SDOH|social determinants]].
alt.ex: SDOH include social, economic, environmental, and political factors that affect health disparities.

items.q: What does Developmental stage mean?
items.a: Perceptions of health that change over time with growth
items.ex: Internal variables arise within the person; family practices are an external variable shaping how members view health.
w: Education, traditions, and past experiences that shape knowledge
That goes with Intellectual background.
How a patient views fatigue, breathlessness, or pain
That goes with Perception of functioning.
Degree of stress, depression, or fear
That goes with Emotional factors.

That goes with Perception of functioning.

w: Perceptions of health that change over time with growth
That goes with Developmental stage.

That goes with Perception of functioning.

alt.a: Developmental stage

Intellectual background: Education, traditions, and past experiences that shape knowledge.
