sections.name: Health promotion, wellness, and illness prevention

items.q: Which is an example of a passive health promotion strategy?
items.a: Fluoridation of municipal drinking water
items.ex: Passive strategies benefit people through the activities of others, without the individual acting, such as fluoridated water.
w: A smoking-cessation program
Smoking-cessation programs require personal involvement, so they are active strategies.
A weight-reduction program
Weight-reduction programs require active participation by the individual.
A community exercise program
Exercise programs require participants to exercise, so they are active strategies.

alt.q: Which statement best describes a passive health promotion strategy?
alt.a: People benefit from the activities of others without acting themselves
alt.ex: In passive strategies, such as vitamin D–fortified milk, individuals benefit without taking action themselves.
w: People must change their own behaviors to gain the benefit
Required personal involvement describes active strategies.
People attend regular classes to learn new health skills
Attending classes requires personal action, which is an active strategy.
People with permanent disability receive rehabilitation services
Rehabilitation for permanent disability is tertiary prevention.

items.q: A nurse helps run a blood pressure screening at a community event. How does the textbook classify this activity among the three related concepts?
items.a: Illness prevention
items.ex: Illness prevention activities such as immunization programs and blood pressure screenings protect people from actual or potential health risks.
w: Health education
Health education provides information on topics such as stress management and self-responsibility.
Passive health promotion
Screening requires the person to take part, and it is named as illness prevention.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention is rehabilitation after permanent disability, not screening.

alt.q: Which activity is an example of health education as the textbook defines it?
alt.a: Providing information on stress management and self-responsibility
alt.ex: Health education provides information on topics such as physical awareness, stress management, and self-responsibility.
w: Giving immunizations at a federally funded clinic
Immunization programs are illness prevention activities.
Fortifying homogenized milk with vitamin D
Milk fortification is a passive health promotion strategy.
Teaching a patient with a spinal cord injury to use a wheelchair
Rehabilitation after permanent injury is tertiary prevention.

items.q: Which nursing activity is an example of primary prevention?
items.a: Promoting hearing protection in an occupational setting
items.ex: Primary prevention reduces the incidence of disease; promoting hearing protection at work is a textbook example.
w: Screening a patient who is obese for diabetes mellitus
Screening to find early disease is secondary prevention.
Teaching wheelchair use after a spinal cord injury
Rehabilitation after permanent injury is tertiary prevention.
Following people who were exposed to a disease
Following exposed people is secondary prevention.

alt.q: Which nursing activity is an example of secondary prevention?
alt.a: Screening a patient who is obese for hypertension
alt.ex: Secondary prevention includes screening and prompt intervention to limit disability and reduce illness severity.
w: Teaching cardiac risk-factor reduction to a healthy group
Education to reduce cardiac risk factors is primary prevention.
Giving immunizations through a federally funded program
Immunization programs are primary prevention.
Helping a person with a disability find accommodating work
Helping people with disabilities return to work is tertiary prevention.

items.q: A patient with a permanent spinal cord injury is learning to perform activities of daily living independently. Which level of prevention does this care represent?
items.a: Tertiary prevention
items.ex: Tertiary prevention occurs when disability is permanent and focuses on rehabilitation to reach the highest possible level of functioning.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention reduces the incidence of disease before it occurs.
Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention focuses on diagnosis and prompt treatment of early disease.
Passive health promotion
Passive strategies require no action by the person, while rehabilitation requires active effort.

alt.q: What is the main goal of tertiary prevention?
alt.a: Helping patients reach the highest possible level of functioning
alt.ex: Tertiary prevention minimizes effects of permanent disease or disability and helps patients function as fully as possible despite limitations.
w: Reducing the incidence of disease in a healthy population
Reducing disease incidence is the goal of primary prevention.
Detecting new cases of disease through screening programs
Detecting new cases through screening is secondary prevention.
Benefiting people without any action on their part
Benefit without personal action describes passive health promotion.

items.q: What is the focus of secondary prevention?
items.a: Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce the severity of illness
items.ex: Secondary prevention uses diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce severity and return patients to normal health as early as possible.
w: Rehabilitation to minimize the effects of a permanent disability
Rehabilitation for permanent disability is tertiary prevention.
Health education to reduce the incidence of disease in healthy people
Reducing disease incidence through education is primary prevention.
Policies that benefit people without any action on their part
Benefits without personal action describe passive health promotion.

alt.q: A nurse follows people who were exposed to tuberculosis but do not have the disease. Which level of prevention is this?
alt.a: Secondary prevention
alt.ex: Following people exposed to a disease who do not yet have it is an example of secondary prevention.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention aims to keep disease from occurring, such as immunization or education.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention addresses permanent disability through rehabilitation.
Passive health promotion
Passive promotion, such as water fluoridation, needs no individual involvement.

items.q: A nurse screens a patient who is obese for diabetes mellitus and hypertension, then teaches the patient about physical activity to prevent hypertension. What does this situation illustrate?
items.a: Screening activities may lead to primary prevention interventions
items.ex: The textbook uses this example to show that secondary prevention screening can lead to primary prevention teaching.
w: Screening is a form of tertiary prevention for chronic disease
Screening is secondary prevention; tertiary prevention is rehabilitation.
Health teaching is appropriate only after disease is diagnosed
Teaching here aims to prevent hypertension before it develops.
Primary prevention must always come before any screening
In this example the screening came first and then led to primary prevention.

alt.q: Which statement about the levels of prevention is accurate?
alt.a: Nurses care for patients at all three levels of prevention
alt.ex: Nursing care for health promotion and illness prevention is described at primary, secondary, and tertiary levels, and nurses work in all three.
w: Nurses provide care mainly at the tertiary level of prevention
The textbook states nurses care for patients at all three levels.
Screening activities never lead to primary prevention teaching
Screening may lead to primary prevention, such as teaching about activity.
Primary prevention programs rarely receive government support
Many primary prevention programs, such as immunizations, are government supported.

items.q: Which statement best describes Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs)?
items.a: They provide primary care in medically underserved communities
items.ex: FQHCs are government-supported centers in underserved communities that increase access to primary care and address causes of poor health.
w: They mainly provide rehabilitation for patients with permanent disability
FQHCs focus on primary care and causes of poor health, not mainly rehabilitation.
They serve only patients who have private health insurance
FQHCs reduce barriers such as cost and lack of insurance.
They are privately funded centers located in wealthy suburbs
FQHCs are supported by the U.S. government and located in underserved areas.

alt.q: A patient without health insurance, who speaks limited English and lives far from the nearest clinic, needs primary care. Which resource best meets these needs?
alt.a: A Federally Qualified Health Center
alt.ex: FQHCs reduce barriers to care such as cost, lack of insurance, distance, and language in underserved communities.
w: An inpatient rehabilitation facility
Rehabilitation facilities provide tertiary care, not routine primary care.
An on-site employee wellness program
Employer programs serve employees; this patient’s barriers are cost, insurance, distance, and language.
A hospital emergency department
Emergency departments do not provide ongoing primary care that addresses SDOH.

items.q: Most states allow health care providers to order naloxone without examining the patient who will need it. What is the purpose of this legislation?
items.a: To allow qualified individuals to give naloxone in an emergency
items.ex: These laws let qualified people, such as first responders and caregivers, administer naloxone during an emergency.
w: To limit naloxone to patients who have been examined in a hospital
The law removes the exam requirement to widen, not limit, access.
To reduce the number of prescriptions written for opioid pain relief
The law concerns access to naloxone, not limiting opioid prescriptions.
To allow pharmacies to sell opioids without a prescription
The law expands naloxone availability, not opioid sales.

alt.q: Which statement about naloxone legislation in the United States is accurate?
alt.a: All 50 states have passed laws that make naloxone easier to obtain
alt.ex: All 50 states have legislation that facilitates naloxone availability, especially for first responders and caregivers.
w: Fewer than 10 states have passed laws on naloxone availability
The textbook states all 50 states have passed such legislation.
About 25 states have laws, mostly limiting naloxone to hospitals
All 50 states have laws, and they expand access beyond hospitals.
All 50 states restrict naloxone to people with a prescription
State laws facilitate, rather than restrict, naloxone availability and dispensing.

items.q: A nurse is planning an obesity prevention program for Hispanic women in a rural community. Which strategy is supported by the evidence in the textbook?
items.a: Use promotoras to provide culturally appropriate teaching and social support
items.ex: Programs using promotoras with culturally sensitive education and social support helped Hispanic women in rural areas adopt healthier lifestyles.
w: Provide the same printed materials used for all adult programs
Generic materials lack the cultural tailoring shown to be effective.
Avoid discussing family or faith to keep the program neutral
Including faith and social support improves the success of lifestyle changes.
Rely on a single lecture by a health care provider from outside
Evidence favors ongoing support from role models from similar cultures.

alt.q: A nurse plans a health promotion program for an African American faith community. Which approach is best supported by evidence?
alt.a: Partner with the church and include spiritual and social support
alt.ex: Programs including spiritual and social support within African American faith communities helped people adopt exercise and healthy eating.
w: Keep the program separate from churches and faith groups
The textbook advises working with churches and faith-based organizations.
Focus only on written facts and leave out social support
Social support is a key part of effective lifestyle change programs.
Use one standard plan designed for the general population
Culturally appropriate, holistic approaches are more effective.

items.q: Which statement best describes health promotion?
items.a: A process of helping people gain control of and improve their health
items.ex: Health promotion helps people gain control of and improve health and helps them maintain or enhance their present health.
w: Activities that prevent complications after permanent disability
Preventing complications after permanent disability is tertiary prevention.
Programs that detect disease early through screening
Early detection through screening is secondary prevention.
Services that treat acute illness in hospital settings
Treating acute illness is not health promotion, which focuses on improving present health.

alt.q: A patient joins a routine exercise and nutrition program to maintain current good health. Which concept does this reflect?
alt.a: Health promotion
alt.ex: Health promotion motivates people to engage in healthy activities like routine exercise and good nutrition to reach more stable health.
w: Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention applies to permanent disability and focuses on rehabilitation.
Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention involves screening and early treatment of disease.
Passive health promotion
Exercise and nutrition programs require the person to act, so they are active.

items.q: Why does the textbook recommend improving self-management and providing preventive services?
items.a: They reduce health care needs and costs and improve overall health
items.ex: Chronic illnesses increase costs; self-management and preventive services reduce health care needs and costs and improve health.
w: They shift care for chronic illness to hospital settings
The goal is reducing health care needs, not moving care into hospitals.
They replace the need for health policies and legislation
Policies and laws remain part of public health alongside these services.
They mainly increase the use of acute care services
Preventive services reduce, not increase, health care needs.

alt.q: Which statement best describes a holistic approach to health promotion?
alt.a: It addresses body, mind, and spirit and considers culture and faith
alt.ex: Holistic strategies focus on body, mind, and spirit and take culture, spirituality, and faith into account.
w: It focuses mainly on physical symptoms and laboratory values
A holistic approach addresses all dimensions, not only physical findings.
It uses the same program for all patients regardless of culture
Culturally appropriate approaches are a key part of holistic strategies.
It avoids including faith to keep care neutral for patients
Holistic strategies include a person’s faith and spirituality.

items.q: Which statements about Federally Qualified Health Centers (FQHCs) are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They are supported by the U.S. government
FQHCs receive U.S. government support.
They are located in medically underserved communities
FQHCs are located in medically underserved communities.
They reduce barriers such as cost, distance, and language
FQHCs increase access by reducing barriers to care.
They focus on social determinants of health
Their focus on SDOH lessens environmental causes of illness.
They serve only patients with private insurance
FQHCs reduce the barrier of lack of insurance.
They provide mainly inpatient surgical care
FQHCs increase access to primary care.
items.ex: FQHCs are government-supported primary care centers in underserved areas that reduce barriers and address SDOH.

alt.q: Which causes of poor health are FQHCs designed to address? Select all that apply.
o: Diet and nutrition
Diet and nutrition are listed causes of poor health FQHCs address.
Mental illness
Mental illness is a cause of poor health FQHCs address.
Lack of housing
Lack of housing is listed among causes FQHCs address.
Need for organ transplantation
FQHCs focus on primary care and causes of poor health, not transplants.
Demand for cosmetic procedures
Cosmetic procedures are not among the causes of poor health listed.
alt.ex: Correct: Diet and nutrition; Mental illness; Lack of housing.

items.q: A nurse helps individuals make health promotion and lifestyle changes. Which evidence-based actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Use role models from similar cultures when possible
Role models from similar cultures encourage lifestyle change.
Provide interventions that include the person’s faith
Evidence-based interventions that include faith are recommended.
Provide social support during lifestyle changes
Social support helps individuals make lifestyle changes.
Work with churches and faith-based organizations
Faith-based partners help implement community health promotion.
Use one standard program for every cultural group
Culturally appropriate approaches are more effective than uniform programs.
Avoid faith topics so the program stays neutral
Including faith is recommended, not avoided.
items.ex: Box 6.2 supports culturally matched role models, faith-based interventions, social support, and partnerships with churches.

alt.q: Which statements about health promotion programs are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Support groups help people affected by cancer
Support groups are an example of programs aimed at specific problems.
Exercise programs help reduce the risk of cardiac disease
Regular exercise programs reduce cardiac disease risk.
Mindfulness programs help reduce anxiety and depression
Mindfulness programs teach coping and improve mental health.
Programs are offered only by hospitals
Some are run by agencies, others independently, and many by businesses.
Programs focus only on people who already have disease
Many programs help healthy people develop health-oriented habits.
alt.ex: Correct: Support groups help people affected by cancer; Exercise programs help reduce the risk of cardiac disease; Mindfulness programs help reduce anxiety and depression.

items.q: Which topics are included among the Healthy People 2030 health topics and objectives that guide health promotion programs? Select all that apply.
o: Physical activity
Physical activity is a listed Healthy People 2030 topic.
Tobacco use
Tobacco use is a listed Healthy People 2030 topic.
Injury and violence prevention
Injury and violence prevention is a listed topic.
Immunization and infectious diseases
Immunization and infectious diseases is a listed topic.
Hospital billing practices
Billing practices are not a Healthy People health topic.
Cosmetic surgery outcomes
Cosmetic surgery is not among the listed health topics.
items.ex: Healthy People 2030 topics include physical activity, tobacco use, injury and violence prevention, and immunization and infectious diseases.

alt.q: A wellness program director chooses focus areas from Healthy People 2030. Which are listed topics? Select all that apply.
o: Adolescent health
Adolescent health is a listed topic.
Mental health and psychiatric disorders
Mental health and psychiatric disorders is a listed topic.
Access to health services
Access to health services is a listed topic.
Hospital staffing ratios
Staffing ratios are not a Healthy People health topic.
Medical malpractice reform
Malpractice reform is not among the listed topics.
alt.ex: Correct: Adolescent health; Mental health and psychiatric disorders; Access to health services.

items.q: Health promotion, health education, and illness prevention all focus on the future.
items.a: True
items.ex: These concepts are closely related and future-focused, though they differ in motivation and goals.
items.ww: Calling it false ignores that all three are described as focusing on the future.

alt.q: Health promotion and illness prevention have identical motivations and goals.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Although closely related and future-focused, they have distinct differences in motivation and goals.
alt.ww: Calling it true overlooks that health promotion enhances present health while illness prevention protects against risks.

items.q: Health policies and laws affect people in a community only when those people are aware of them.
items.a: False
items.ex: Health policies and laws affect all people in a community, state, or country, even if they are unaware of them.
items.ww: Calling it true contradicts the textbook, which says policies affect people regardless of awareness.

alt.q: Health policies and laws affect all people in a community, even those who are unaware of them.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Policies such as naloxone access laws affect everyone in the community, whether or not they know of them.
alt.ww: Calling it false assumes awareness is required, but policies apply to all people in the population.

items.q: In tertiary prevention, activities are directed at diagnosis and treatment of new disease.
items.a: False
items.ex: Tertiary prevention activities are directed at rehabilitation rather than diagnosis and treatment.
items.ww: Calling it true confuses tertiary prevention with secondary prevention, which focuses on diagnosis and prompt intervention.

alt.q: Tertiary prevention activities are directed at rehabilitation rather than diagnosis and treatment.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Tertiary prevention occurs after permanent disability and focuses on rehabilitation and preventing complications.
alt.ww: Calling it false would place diagnosis and treatment, which belong to secondary prevention, at the tertiary level.

items.q: Trained Latino community leaders who deliver culturally appropriate health promotion education and social support are called [[promotoras|promotora|promotores]].
items.ex: Promotoras serve as culturally similar role models, and their support has improved health outcomes in Latino communities.

alt.q: A program that uses [[promotoras|promotora|promotores]] relies on trained Latino community leaders to teach healthy nutrition and exercise.
alt.ex: Promotoras serve as culturally similar role models, and their support has improved health outcomes in Latino communities.

items.q: [[Tertiary|Tertiary prevention]] prevention occurs when a defect or disability is permanent and irreversible.
items.ex: Tertiary prevention minimizes effects of long-term disease or disability through rehabilitation and preventing complications.

alt.q: Rehabilitation to help a patient function despite permanent disability is [[tertiary|tertiary prevention]] prevention.
alt.ex: Tertiary prevention minimizes effects of long-term disease or disability through rehabilitation and preventing complications.

items.q: What does Primary prevention mean?
items.a: Reduces the incidence of disease
items.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.
w: Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity
That goes with Secondary prevention.
Rehabilitation when disability is permanent
That goes with Tertiary prevention.
Benefit from others’ activities without personal action
That goes with Passive strategy.

alt.q: What does Secondary prevention mean?
alt.a: Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity
alt.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.
w: Reduces the incidence of disease
That goes with Primary prevention.
Rehabilitation when disability is permanent
That goes with Tertiary prevention.
Benefit from others’ activities without personal action
That goes with Passive strategy.

alt.q: What does Tertiary prevention mean?
alt.a: Rehabilitation when disability is permanent
alt.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.
w: Reduces the incidence of disease
That goes with Primary prevention.
Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity
That goes with Secondary prevention.
Benefit from others’ activities without personal action
That goes with Passive strategy.

alt.q: What does Passive strategy mean?
alt.a: Benefit from others’ activities without personal action
alt.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.
w: Reduces the incidence of disease
That goes with Primary prevention.
Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity
That goes with Secondary prevention.
Rehabilitation when disability is permanent
That goes with Tertiary prevention.

alt.q: What does Active strategy mean?
alt.a: Personal involvement in measures to improve wellness
alt.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.
w: Reduces the incidence of disease
That goes with Primary prevention.
Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity
That goes with Secondary prevention.
Rehabilitation when disability is permanent
That goes with Tertiary prevention.

alt.q: Which term means “Reduces the incidence of disease”?
alt.a: Primary prevention
alt.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.
w: Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention: Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention: Rehabilitation when disability is permanent.
Passive strategy
Passive strategy: Benefit from others’ activities without personal action.

alt.q: Which term means “Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity”?
alt.a: Secondary prevention
alt.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention: Reduces the incidence of disease.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention: Rehabilitation when disability is permanent.
Passive strategy
Passive strategy: Benefit from others’ activities without personal action.

alt.q: Which term means “Rehabilitation when disability is permanent”?
alt.a: Tertiary prevention
alt.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention: Reduces the incidence of disease.
Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention: Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity.
Passive strategy
Passive strategy: Benefit from others’ activities without personal action.

alt.q: Which term means “Benefit from others’ activities without personal action”?
alt.a: Passive strategy
alt.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention: Reduces the incidence of disease.
Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention: Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention: Rehabilitation when disability is permanent.

alt.q: Which term means “Personal involvement in measures to improve wellness”?
alt.a: Active strategy
alt.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention: Reduces the incidence of disease.
Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention: Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention: Rehabilitation when disability is permanent.

mt.q: Match each health promotion and prevention term with its description.
pairs: Diagnosis and prompt intervention to reduce illness severity
Benefit from others’ activities without personal action
Personal involvement in measures to improve wellness
mt.ex: Prevention levels range from stopping disease to rehabilitation; promotion strategies differ by whether the person must act.

items.q: Which statement best defines a risk factor?
items.a: Any attribute, trait, or situation that increases vulnerability to illness or accident
items.ex: A risk factor is any attribute, quality, environmental situation, or trait that increases vulnerability to an illness or accident.
w: Any agent that directly causes a specific disease to develop
Risk factors do not cause diseases; they increase the chance of them.
Any symptom that confirms a disease has already developed
Symptoms indicate existing illness; risk factors increase vulnerability before it.
Any treatment that lowers the chance of illness or accident
Measures that lower risk are prevention strategies, not risk factors.

alt.q: A nurse notes that an older adult has impaired gait, reduced vision, and lower extremity weakness. What do these findings represent?
alt.a: Risk factors for falls
alt.ex: Impaired gait, reduced vision, and lower extremity weakness are textbook examples of risk factors for falls.
w: Causes that guarantee a fall will occur
Risk factors increase the chance of a fall but do not cause it.
Signs of a fall that has already occurred
These traits increase vulnerability; they are not evidence of a past fall.
Nonmodifiable genetic risk factors
These findings are not genetic, and some can be addressed to reduce fall risk.

items.q: A nurse is teaching a parent about asthma risk across childhood. Which statement about sex differences in asthma is accurate?
items.a: After puberty, asthma becomes more prevalent and severe in females
items.ex: Asthma risk is higher in males, but after puberty asthma becomes more prevalent and severe in females.
w: Asthma risk is higher in females than males throughout life
Before puberty, asthma risk is higher in males.
Asthma risk is the same in males and females at all ages
Sex differences in asthma risk change around puberty.
After puberty, asthma becomes more severe in males
After puberty, asthma becomes more prevalent and severe in females.

alt.q: Before puberty, which group has a higher risk for asthma?
alt.a: Males
alt.ex: The risk for asthma is higher in males than females until puberty, when it shifts toward females.
w: Females
Females have more prevalent and severe asthma only after puberty.
Neither; risk is equal
The textbook describes a higher risk in males before puberty.
Only premature infants
Premature infants are more susceptible to infections, not described as the higher asthma group.

items.q: How does a female’s risk for cardiovascular disease (CVD) compare with a male’s after menopause?
items.a: The risk becomes similar between males and females
items.ex: Males have higher CVD risk than premenopausal females, but after menopause the risk is similar.
w: The risk becomes much lower in females than in males
After menopause, female risk rises to become similar to male risk.
The risk becomes much higher in females than in males
The textbook describes similar, not higher, risk after menopause.
The risk stays the same as it was before menopause
Female CVD risk rises after menopause to match that of males.

alt.q: A 42-year-old premenopausal woman asks how her heart disease risk compares with her husband’s. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “Men generally have a higher risk than women who have not reached menopause.”
alt.ex: Males have a higher risk for CVD than premenopausal females; after menopause the risks become similar.
w: “Women generally have a higher risk than men at your stage of life.”
Premenopausal females have lower CVD risk than males.
“Your risk is identical to his at every age throughout life.”
Risk differs before menopause and becomes similar only after it.
“Sex has no effect on a person’s risk for heart disease.”
Sex is a nonmodifiable risk factor that affects CVD risk.

items.q: A 58-year-old patient who is obese develops hypertension. The patient walks infrequently, both parents have hypertension, and the spouse smokes. Which health promotion strategy should the nurse focus on?
items.a: Nutrition counseling and exercise to address modifiable risk factors
items.ex: Because the exact cause cannot be determined, the nurse focuses on modifiable risk factors for obesity, such as nutrition and exercise.
w: Genetic testing to confirm the family link to hypertension
Family history cannot be changed; the focus is on modifiable risk factors.
Explaining that hypertension was caused by the spouse’s smoking
It is impossible to determine which factor caused the hypertension.
Teaching that hypertension in parents means nothing can be done
Modifiable risks like diet and activity can still be changed.

alt.q: For the 58-year-old patient with obesity, hypertension, inactivity, a family history of hypertension, and a smoking spouse, which statement about the cause is accurate?
alt.a: It is impossible to determine which risk factor caused the hypertension
alt.ex: Lifestyle, genetics, environmental toxins, or a combination may have contributed, and the nurse cannot determine which.
w: Genetics is clearly the main cause because both parents are affected
A family link may reflect genetics, lifestyle, environment, or a combination.
Secondhand smoke is clearly the single cause of the hypertension
The textbook states no single factor can be identified in this case.
Physical inactivity alone is clearly the cause of the hypertension
Inactivity is one of several possible contributing factors.

items.q: A patient with breast cancer asks the oncology nurse whether her daughters are at increased risk. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Facilitate a conversation between the patient and a genetics counselor
items.ex: Breast cancer appears to have a genetic link; oncology nurses facilitate conversations with genetics counselors about risks to family members.
w: Reassure the patient that breast cancer does not run in families
Breast, ovarian, and colon cancers appear to have a genetic link.
Tell the patient that her daughters will develop breast cancer
Risk factors increase the chance of disease but do not guarantee it.
Advise the patient to avoid discussing the cancer with her daughters
Supporting patients and families includes addressing concerns about family risk.

alt.q: Which genetics competency does the textbook expect of all nurses?
alt.a: Identify and refer appropriate patients for genetic risk assessment and counseling
alt.ex: All nurses should identify and facilitate referral of appropriate patients for genetics risk assessment and counseling.
w: Order genetic tests independently for all patients with a family history
Nurses understand the testing process and refer; they do not order tests for everyone.
Interpret genetic test results and make the final diagnosis for families
Nurses refer and support; counselors and providers interpret risk.
Record a family history that covers only the patient’s parents
Nurses collect and document a three-generation pedigree.

items.q: An 82-year-old patient takes nine prescribed medications and has had two recent episodes of confusion. Why should the nurse assess for polypharmacy?
items.a: Polypharmacy is associated with falls and confusion in older adults
items.ex: Polypharmacy is common in older adults and is linked to falls, confusion, adverse outcomes, and longer hospital stays.
w: Polypharmacy is associated with skin cancer and sunburn in older adults
Skin cancer is linked to sun exposure, not polypharmacy.
Polypharmacy is associated with asthma and wheezing in older adults
Asthma risk relates to sex and age, not polypharmacy.
Polypharmacy is uncommon in older adults and rarely causes harm
Polypharmacy is common in older adults and associated with adverse outcomes.

alt.q: Which outcome does the textbook associate with polypharmacy in older adults?
alt.a: Increased length of hospital stay
alt.ex: Polypharmacy is associated with falls, confusion, adverse outcomes, and increased length of hospital stay.
w: Shorter recovery after hospital admission
Polypharmacy is linked to longer, not shorter, hospital stays.
Improved balance and fewer falls
Polypharmacy is associated with more falls, not fewer.
Sharper memory and decision making
Polypharmacy is associated with confusion.

items.q: A nurse plans health promotion for older adults living in the community. Which strategy does the textbook identify as key to promoting and improving health?
items.a: Injury prevention, especially fall prevention
items.ex: Injury prevention, especially fall prevention, is a key strategy to promote and improve health in older adults.
w: Limiting social activities to conserve energy
Strengthening social support and decreasing isolation promote health in older adults.
Focusing only on screening for childhood illnesses
Older adult health promotion is based on their own common risk factors and conditions.
Avoiding exercise programs to prevent injury
Regular information on exercise benefits is part of holistic health promotion for older adults.

alt.q: An older adult lives alone and rarely leaves home. Which health promotion action best fits the textbook’s guidance?
alt.a: Strengthen social support and connect the patient with resources
alt.ex: Considering the social environment and strengthening social support promotes health and provides access to resources.
w: Encourage the patient to stay home to avoid any risk of falling
Isolation worsens health; programs aim to decrease social isolation.
Wait to intervene until the patient develops a chronic illness
Health promotion is proactive and based on common risk factors.
Focus teaching only on medications and skip social needs
Social connections influence health and quality of life in older adults.

items.q: When does stress become a lifestyle risk factor?
items.a: When it is severe or prolonged or the person cannot cope adequately
items.ex: Stress is a lifestyle risk factor when it is severe or prolonged or when a person is unable to cope with life events.
w: Whenever a person experiences any brief stressful event
Brief, manageable stress is not described as a lifestyle risk factor.
Only when it causes physical symptoms that require hospitalization
Stress threatens both mental and physical health before hospitalization is needed.
Only when it comes from job-related demands and not life events
Life events such as divorce or death of a spouse are also stressors.

alt.q: A patient recently went through a divorce and is having financial difficulties. During a health assessment, what should the nurse do with this information?
alt.a: Include these life stressors in the comprehensive risk factor analysis
alt.ex: Nurses should always review patients’ life stressors as part of a comprehensive risk factor analysis.
w: Leave it out because emotional stress does not affect physical health
Stress is associated with heart disease, high blood pressure, sleep and digestive problems.
Refer the patient to a counselor and omit it from the assessment
Life stressors belong in the risk factor analysis itself.
Note it only if the patient reports chest pain during the visit
Stressors are reviewed routinely, not only when symptoms appear.

items.q: Researchers cannot agree whether the high cancer rate in Cancer Alley is caused by chemical plant toxins. Why is it difficult to link environmental exposure to illness in this area?
items.a: Residents also face many social determinants of health that affect risk
items.ex: Residents are mostly low income and face many SDOH, so researchers cannot separate those effects from toxin exposure.
w: Petroleum plants in the area release no harmful substances
The area has many petroleum plants, and toxin exposure is a suspected factor.
Cancer rates in the area are lower than expected
People living there have a higher-than-expected chance of several cancers.
Environmental exposure always comes from a single known source
Exposure rarely occurs at one time, place, or source.

alt.q: Why is it often difficult to link an illness to environmental exposure?
alt.a: Exposure rarely occurs at one time, in one location, or from one source
alt.ex: People constantly interact with the environment, and many other risk factors also contribute to illness.
w: Environment has little effect on a person’s risk of illness
Where people live determines exposures, risk factors, and state of health.
Environmental illnesses always appear within a few days of exposure
Exposure is ongoing and from many sources, so timing is not clear-cut.
Only genetic factors can explain illness in a community
Environment, lifestyle, SDOH, and genetics may all contribute.

items.q: A nurse is teaching a lifeguard who works outdoors all summer. Which health promotion teaching addresses this patient’s modifiable risk?
items.a: Use adequate sunscreen and wear proper clothing to limit sun exposure
items.ex: Excessive sun exposure increases skin cancer risk, so teaching about sunscreen and proper clothing is a health promotion strategy.
w: Have genetic testing to rule out risk for skin cancer
Sun exposure is a modifiable risk factor addressed by protection, not genetic testing.
Limit outdoor work only after skin changes appear
Prevention aims to reduce exposure before skin damage develops.
Accept the risk because age and sex determine skin cancer
Sun exposure is modifiable, so the patient can reduce the risk.

alt.q: Excessive sun exposure is an example of which type of risk factor?
alt.a: A modifiable risk factor for skin cancer
alt.ex: Sun exposure can be changed through sunscreen and protective clothing, making it a modifiable risk factor.
w: A nonmodifiable risk factor for skin cancer
Nonmodifiable factors include age, sex, genetics, and family history.
A genetic risk factor for colon cancer
Sun exposure is an environmental behavior, not a genetic link to colon cancer.
A direct cause that guarantees skin cancer
Risk factors increase the chance of disease but do not cause it.

items.q: A nurse assesses a 16-year-old during a school health visit. Which finding is a modifiable risk factor for this age group?
items.a: Texting while driving
items.ex: Modifiable risks for people 10 to 24 years old include behaviors leading to injury, such as texting while driving.
w: A family history of hypertension
Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor.
Being male
Sex is a nonmodifiable risk factor.
Being in the 10- to 24-year age group
Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor.

alt.q: Which behavior is a modifiable risk factor for unintentional injury in people 10 to 24 years old?
alt.a: Driving under the influence of drugs or alcohol
alt.ex: Behaviors leading to unintentional injury, such as driving under the influence, are modifiable risks for ages 10 to 24.
w: Having a parent with colon cancer
Family history is nonmodifiable and not an injury behavior.
Having a genetic hereditary syndrome
Genetic syndromes are nonmodifiable risk factors.
Reaching puberty
Puberty is a developmental event, not a modifiable behavior.

items.q: How does the textbook advise nurses to use their understanding of a patient’s nonmodifiable risk factors?
items.a: Combine them with assessment data and preferences to select secondary prevention strategies
items.ex: Nonmodifiable risk factors, with assessment data and preferences such as motivation, guide selection of secondary prevention strategies.
w: Ignore them because they cannot be changed by the patient
Nonmodifiable factors still guide screening and secondary prevention.
Use them to explain that disease is certain to develop later
Risk factors increase the chance of disease but do not cause it.
Rely on them alone, setting aside patient preferences and motivation
Assessment data and preferences are combined with nonmodifiable risks.

alt.q: A 52-year-old patient with a strong family history of colon cancer asks why regular screenings matter. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Screenings can find problems early, since your family history can’t be changed.”
alt.ex: Family history is nonmodifiable, so nurses teach the importance of regularly scheduled screenings, a secondary prevention strategy.
w: “Screenings are not needed because family history does not affect risk.”
Colon cancer appears to have a genetic link, so family history raises risk.
“Screenings will stop you from inheriting the risk for colon cancer.”
Screening detects disease early; it cannot change inherited risk.
“You need screenings only after symptoms of cancer appear.”
Screenings are scheduled regularly, often before symptoms, to detect early disease.

items.q: A nurse is assessing an older adult for risk factors for falls. Which findings are risk factors for falls? Select all that apply.
o: Impaired gait
Impaired gait is a textbook example of a fall risk factor.
Reduced vision
Reduced vision is a textbook example of a fall risk factor.
Lower extremity weakness
Lower extremity weakness is a textbook example of a fall risk factor.
Polypharmacy
Polypharmacy in older adults is associated with falls.
Excessive sun exposure
Sun exposure is a risk factor for skin cancer, not falls.
Family history of ovarian cancer
Family history of ovarian cancer is a genetic cancer risk, not a fall risk.
items.ex: Impaired gait, reduced vision, lower extremity weakness, and polypharmacy all increase an older adult’s vulnerability to falls.

alt.q: Which statements about health promotion for older adults are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Base programs on common risk factors and chronic conditions
Programs address common risks, chronic conditions, caregiving, and injury prevention.
Creative programs such as singing or dancing can decrease isolation
Creativity programs improve well-being and independence and decrease isolation.
Social connections and access to transportation influence health
These factors affect health promotion behaviors and quality of life.
All older adults have the same health promotion needs
Every individual is unique and needs careful assessment.
Social environment has little effect on older adults’ health
Strengthening social support promotes health and access to resources.
alt.ex: Correct: Base programs on common risk factors and chronic conditions; Creative programs such as singing or dancing can decrease isolation; Social connections and access to transportation influence health.

items.q: Which are modifiable behavioral risk factors for chronic disease? Select all that apply.
o: Smoking
Smoking is a modifiable behavioral risk factor.
Physical inactivity
Physical inactivity can be changed through behavior.
Insufficient rest and sleep
Insufficient rest and sleep is a modifiable behavioral risk factor.
Consuming an unhealthy diet
An unhealthy diet is a modifiable behavioral risk factor.
Age
Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor.
Family history
Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor.
items.ex: Modifiable behavioral risks include smoking, alcohol, unhealthy diet, obesity, inactivity, and insufficient rest and sleep.

alt.q: Which are nonmodifiable risk factors? Select all that apply.
o: Age
Age cannot be changed.
Sex
Sex is listed as a nonmodifiable risk factor.
Genetics
Genetics cannot be changed.
Family history
Family history cannot be changed.
Obesity
Obesity is a modifiable behavioral risk factor.
Drinking alcohol
Alcohol use is a modifiable behavioral risk factor.
alt.ex: Correct: Age; Sex; Genetics; Family history.

items.q: Prolonged stress threatens physical well-being. Which illnesses does the textbook associate with stress? Select all that apply.
o: Heart disease
Stress is associated with heart disease.
Sleep problems
Stress is associated with sleep problems.
High blood pressure
Stress is associated with high blood pressure.
Digestive issues
Stress is associated with digestive issues.
Hereditary colon cancer
Hereditary colon cancer relates to genetics, not stress.
Neonatal infections
Neonatal infection risk relates to age and prematurity, not stress.
items.ex: Stress threatens physical well-being and is associated with heart disease, sleep problems, high blood pressure, and digestive issues.

alt.q: Which statements about stress as a risk factor are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It can threaten both mental and physical well-being
Stress causes emotional and physiological threats to health.
It can interfere with making needed lifestyle changes
Stress interferes with health promotion and lifestyle modification.
Job-related stress can lead to burnout
Job stressors affect cognition and decision making, leading to burnout.
It is a risk factor only when it causes physical illness
Stress also threatens mental health and is a risk when severe or prolonged.
Life events such as pregnancy are never stressors
Pregnancy is listed among emotional stressors from life events.
alt.ex: Correct: It can threaten both mental and physical well-being; It can interfere with making needed lifestyle changes; Job-related stress can lead to burnout.

items.q: Risk factors cause diseases and accidents.
items.a: False
items.ex: Risk factors do not cause diseases or accidents; they increase the chances that they will occur.
items.ww: Calling it true confuses increased vulnerability with direct causation, which the textbook rejects.

alt.q: Risk factors increase the chance that a person or population will experience a disease or dysfunction.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Risk factors raise the likelihood of disease or dysfunction without directly causing it.
alt.ww: Calling it false ignores the textbook definition of risk factors as increasing vulnerability.

items.q: A teenager who makes nutritional choices that lead to obesity will most likely make similar choices as an adult.
items.a: True
items.ex: Lifestyle choices affect patients across the life span; teen nutritional habits leading to obesity often continue into adulthood.
items.ww: Calling it false ignores the textbook point that lifestyle choices tend to persist across the life span.

alt.q: Lifestyle choices made during adolescence rarely carry over into adulthood.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Lifestyle choices affect people throughout the life span, and teen habits often continue into adulthood.
alt.ww: Calling it true overlooks how adolescent choices, such as poor nutrition, tend to persist.

items.q: Beginning at about 10 years of age, the risk for intentional self-harm develops and persists throughout the rest of a person’s life.
items.a: True
items.ex: Starting at age 10, children remain at risk for accidental injury, and risk for intentional self-harm develops and persists for life.
items.ww: Calling it false would lead nurses to overlook self-harm risk in preteens, teens, and adults.

alt.q: The risk for intentional self-harm ends once a person reaches middle adulthood.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Once it develops around age 10, the risk for intentional self-harm persists for the rest of a person’s life.
alt.ww: Calling it true confuses self-harm with homicide risk, which is the risk that continues until middle adulthood.

items.q: All nurses should be able to collect and document a [[three-generation|3-generation|three generation]] pedigree.
items.ex: A three-generation pedigree helps identify risk factors for hereditary syndromes and patients who need genetic referral.

alt.q: To identify hereditary risk, the nurse records a family pedigree covering [[three|3]] generations.
alt.ex: A three-generation pedigree helps identify risk factors for hereditary syndromes and patients who need genetic referral.

items.q: Which risk is associated with Premature infants and neonates?
items.a: Greater susceptibility to infections
items.ex: Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor, and susceptibility to specific illnesses and injuries shifts across the life span.
w: Accidental deaths such as drowning, and homicide
That goes with Children 1 to 9 years old.
Onset of risk for intentional self-harm
That goes with Starting at 10 years old.
Rising risk of heart disease and many cancers
That goes with Advancing age.

alt.a: Accidental deaths such as drowning, and homicide
alt.ex: Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor, and susceptibility to specific illnesses and injuries shifts across the life span.
w: Greater susceptibility to infections
That goes with Premature infants and neonates.
Onset of risk for intentional self-harm

That goes with Advancing age.

alt.a: Onset of risk for intentional self-harm
alt.ex: Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor, and susceptibility to specific illnesses and injuries shifts across the life span.
w: Greater susceptibility to infections
That goes with Premature infants and neonates.
Accidental deaths such as drowning, and homicide
That goes with Children 1 to 9 years old.
Rising risk of heart disease and many cancers
That goes with Advancing age.

alt.a: Rising risk of heart disease and many cancers
alt.ex: Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor, and susceptibility to specific illnesses and injuries shifts across the life span.
w: Greater susceptibility to infections
That goes with Premature infants and neonates.
Accidental deaths such as drowning, and homicide
That goes with Children 1 to 9 years old.
Onset of risk for intentional self-harm
That goes with Starting at 10 years old.

alt.a: Alzheimer’s disease, influenza, and pneumonia
alt.ex: Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor, and susceptibility to specific illnesses and injuries shifts across the life span.
w: Greater susceptibility to infections
That goes with Premature infants and neonates.

That goes with Starting at 10 years old.

alt.a: Premature infants and neonates
alt.ex: Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor, and susceptibility to specific illnesses and injuries shifts across the life span.
w: Children 1 to 9 years old
Children 1 to 9 years old: Accidental deaths such as drowning, and homicide.

Starting at 10 years old: Onset of risk for intentional self-harm.
Advancing age

Children 1 to 9 years old

Advancing age

alt.a: Advancing age

w: Premature infants and neonates

mt.q: Match each age group with a risk the textbook associates with it.
pairs: Accidental deaths such as drowning, and homicide

mt.ex: Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor, and susceptibility to specific illnesses and injuries shifts across the life span.

sections.name: Risk-factor identification and changing health behaviors

items.q: A patient being assessed for heart disease risk says, “There is nothing I really need to change.” Which stage of the Transtheoretical Model of Change does this statement reflect?
items.a: Precontemplation
items.ex: In precontemplation the patient has no intent to change within 6 months and is unaware of or underestimates the problem.
w: Contemplation
A patient in contemplation recognizes a problem and is considering change within 6 months.
Preparation
A patient in preparation is making small changes toward a change in the next month.
Maintenance
A patient in maintenance has sustained a change and works to prevent relapse.

alt.q: Which patient statement best reflects the contemplation stage of change?
alt.a: “I have a problem with my drinking that I think I need to work on.”
alt.ex: Contemplation is considering a change within 6 months; the person recognizes a problem but may be ambivalent.
w: “My drinking is fine, and there is nothing I need to change about it.”
Denying any need to change reflects precontemplation.
“I have not had a drink for 9 months, and I avoid going to bars now.”
Sustaining change beyond 6 months and avoiding triggers reflects maintenance.
“I am working hard every day right now to stop drinking alcohol.”
Being actively engaged in strategies to change reflects the action stage.

items.q: A patient says, “I started running once, but I didn’t keep it up. I think I might try again in a few weeks.” Which stage of change is the patient in?
items.a: Preparation
items.ex: Preparation involves making small changes toward a change in the next month; past unsuccessful attempts are common.
w: Precontemplation
Precontemplation involves no intent to change in the next 6 months.
Action
In action the patient is actively engaged in strategies to change behavior now.
Maintenance
Maintenance is sustained change over time, beginning 6 months after action started.

alt.q: Which description matches the preparation stage of the Transtheoretical Model of Change?
alt.a: Making small changes in preparation for a change in the next month
alt.ex: In preparation the patient believes advantages outweigh disadvantages and plans to change within a month.
w: Having no intent to make changes within the next 6 months
No intent to change within 6 months defines precontemplation.
Considering a change sometime within the next 6 months
Considering a change within 6 months defines contemplation.
Actively using strategies to change behavior for up to 6 months
Active engagement lasting up to 6 months defines the action stage.

items.q: According to the Transtheoretical Model of Change, how long does the action stage typically last?
items.a: Up to 6 months
items.ex: The action stage lasts up to 6 months; maintenance begins 6 months after action has started.
w: Up to 1 month
One month is the time frame for planned change in the preparation stage.
Up to 12 months
Action does not extend to 12 months; maintenance begins at 6 months.
Up to 2 years
Two years is far longer than the action stage; maintenance begins at 6 months.

alt.q: A patient began a daily walking program 3 months ago and continues it. When will the patient enter the maintenance stage if the change is sustained?
alt.a: 6 months after the action began
alt.ex: Maintenance begins 6 months after action has started and continues indefinitely.
w: 1 month after the action began
One month is the planned time frame of the preparation stage, not the start of maintenance.
3 months after the action began
At 3 months the patient is still in the action stage, which lasts up to 6 months.
12 months after the action began
Maintenance starts at 6 months, not 12 months, after action has started.

items.q: A patient who quit smoking 2 months ago tells the nurse, “I smoked again all weekend. I guess I’m just a failure.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Relapse is part of change; let’s look at what you learned for next time.”
items.ex: Relapse is a learning process, and lessons from it can be applied to the next attempt to change.
w: “You should probably wait a year before you try to quit again.”
Delaying a new attempt ignores that lessons from relapse can be applied to the next attempt.
“Relapse means this program is not the right fit for you.”
Relapse is common; people often cycle through the stages before succeeding.
“You will need to start over at the maintenance stage now.”
After relapse a person returns to contemplation or precontemplation, not maintenance.

alt.q: A patient who began an exercise program relapses to inactivity. To which stage does the patient typically return before trying again?
alt.a: Contemplation or precontemplation
alt.ex: When relapse occurs, a person returns to contemplation or precontemplation before attempting the change again.
w: Action or maintenance
Relapse moves the person back from action, not into action or maintenance.
Preparation only
The book states relapse returns a person to contemplation or precontemplation.
Maintenance only
Maintenance is sustained change; relapse means the change has not been sustained.

items.q: Which statement best describes a wellness strategy?
items.a: Any program that attempts to change unhealthy lifestyle behaviors
items.ex: Risk-factor modification, health promotion, illness prevention, or any program that changes unhealthy behaviors is a wellness strategy.
w: A treatment plan designed to cure an existing acute disease
Curing an acute disease is treatment, not a wellness strategy aimed at changing behaviors.
A form that scores a patient’s risks for future health threats
This describes a health risk appraisal form, a tool used to identify risks.
A list of nonmodifiable risk factors such as age and genetics
Nonmodifiable factors cannot be changed, so listing them is not a behavior-change program.

alt.q: A nurse enrolls a patient in a community nutrition program to reduce obesity risk. How does the textbook classify this program?
alt.a: As a wellness strategy
alt.ex: Any program that attempts to change unhealthy lifestyle behaviors is a wellness strategy.
w: As a health risk appraisal
A health risk appraisal is a form that identifies risks, not a behavior-change program.
As a nonmodifiable risk factor
A program is an intervention, not a risk factor; obesity risk is modifiable.
As an illness career
An illness career is a person’s evolving response to a chronic disease.

items.q: What is the purpose of a health risk appraisal form?
items.a: To identify health threats based on the presence of risk factors
items.ex: Health risk appraisal forms identify health threats based on the presence of various risk factors.
w: To diagnose a disease the patient already has
The form identifies risks for health threats; it does not diagnose disease.
To determine the patient’s current stage of change
Stage of change is assessed using the Transtheoretical Model, not a risk appraisal.
To document the patient’s three-generation pedigree
A pedigree records family genetic history, a separate genetics competency.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a completed health risk appraisal for a new clinic patient. What should the nurse do next with the data?
alt.a: Identify modifiable risks and plan education fitting the patient’s motivation and culture
alt.ex: Appraisal data identify modifiable risks; the nurse then uses motivation and cultural preferences to design education.
w: File the form and wait for the health care provider to plan education
Nurses use appraisal data to design individualized patient education.
Focus the education plan mainly on the patient’s nonmodifiable risks
Nonmodifiable risks cannot be changed; education targets what the patient can modify.
Give the patient a standard pamphlet that covers all chronic diseases
Education should be individualized to the patient’s risks, motivation, and culture.

items.q: A nurse identifies that a patient who is obese has several modifiable risk factors. Which action should the nurse take first to promote behavior change?
items.a: Ask the patient which changes he feels he needs or is willing to make
items.ex: Patients typically will not change unless they see a need and are motivated, so ask what changes they perceive or will accept.
w: Give the patient a detailed 1800-calorie meal plan to start today
Starting with a plan before learning the patient’s readiness ignores motivation, a key to change.
Tell the patient he must start exercising 300 minutes each week
Imposing a goal ignores whether the patient sees a need and is motivated to change.
Refer the patient to a weight-loss program designed for action
Programs for action fit only people ready to act; first learn what the patient is willing to change.

alt.q: Why does the nurse ask a patient which lifestyle changes the patient is willing to make?
alt.a: Patients rarely change unless they see a need and are motivated
alt.ex: Patients typically will not change their behaviors unless they see a need and are motivated to change.
w: Patients must choose changes before risk factors can be identified
Risk factors are identified first through interviewing and assessment.
Patients can change their nonmodifiable risks if they are willing
Nonmodifiable risks such as age and genetics cannot be changed.
Patients who are asked are less likely to ever relapse at all
Relapse is common; asking about readiness does not prevent it entirely.

items.q: A nurse is beginning a teaching session about lifestyle changes with a patient at risk for diabetes. After establishing rapport, which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Determine what the patient already knows about lifestyle-related health risks
items.ex: Teaching begins with determining what the patient knows about specific health risks related to lifestyle.
w: Have the patient start a log of diet and activity changes today
Keeping a log is useful but comes after goals for change are set.
Set the patient’s goal for strength training at 4 days a week
Goals are set with the patient, and the standard is strength training 2 days a week.
Provide printed materials written for a college reading level
Materials must match the patient’s literacy level and should follow assessment of knowledge.

alt.q: Why does the nurse ask a patient which barriers the patient perceives to diet changes and exercise?
alt.a: To plan around obstacles that could prevent the change
alt.ex: Asking about perceived barriers lets the nurse and patient plan realistic changes that address them.
w: To decide whether the patient has nonmodifiable risks
Barriers to change are not used to identify nonmodifiable risks such as age.
To determine the patient’s three-generation family history
Family history is a genetics assessment, not an assessment of barriers.
To show the patient that the change is not really necessary
Identifying barriers supports change; it does not suggest change is unnecessary.

items.q: In the patient teaching objectives for lifestyle change, how much moderate-intensity exercise is the patient’s weekly goal?
items.a: 150 to 300 minutes a week
items.ex: The objective is moderate-intensity exercise for 150 to 300 minutes a week plus strength training 2 days a week.
w: 60 to 90 minutes a week
60 to 90 minutes falls well below the 150-minute minimum in the objective.
90 to 120 minutes a week
90 to 120 minutes is below the stated objective of 150 to 300 minutes.
400 to 500 minutes a week
400 to 500 minutes exceeds the stated range of 150 to 300 minutes.

alt.q: A patient’s lifestyle plan includes strength training. How often does the teaching objective recommend strength training exercises?
alt.a: 2 days a week
alt.ex: The teaching objective includes strength training exercises 2 days a week along with 150 to 300 minutes of moderate exercise.
w: 1 day a week
One day is less than the 2 days a week in the objective.
5 days a week
Five days exceeds the objective of strength training 2 days a week.
7 days a week
Daily strength training is not the objective; it is 2 days a week.

items.q: A nurse evaluates a patient’s learning about lifestyle changes. Which nurse statement uses the teach-back method?
items.a: “Show me what you tracked in your activity and diet log this week.”
items.ex: Teach-back has the patient explain or demonstrate what was learned, such as showing the log of tracked behaviors.
w: “Do you have any questions about the diet we discussed?”
A yes/no question does not require the patient to show what was learned.
“I will explain the exercise plan again so it is clear.”
Repeating the teaching does not evaluate what the patient learned.
“You understand why tracking your diet is important, right?”
A leading question does not have the patient demonstrate learning.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient shows understanding of the lifestyle-change teaching?
alt.a: “I will aim for 150 to 300 minutes of moderate exercise each week.”
alt.ex: The teaching objective is 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity exercise weekly.
w: “I will do strength training exercises every single day.”
The objective is strength training 2 days a week, not daily.
“I will keep my exercise to 60 minutes a week at most.”
Sixty minutes is below the 150-minute minimum.
“I will skip the log because it is not needed for change.”
Keeping a log of key behavioral changes is a teaching strategy.

items.q: Most successful behavior-change programs are designed for people in which situation?
items.a: People ready to take action on their health behavior problems
items.ex: Most successful behavior-change programs target people ready to take action regarding their health behavior problems.
w: People with no intent to change within the next 6 months
This describes precontemplation; programs are mostly designed for those ready to act.
People who have sustained a change for more than a year
These people are in maintenance, not the main target of most programs.
People who have only nonmodifiable risk factors to address
Nonmodifiable risks cannot be changed by behavior-change programs.

alt.q: According to the textbook, when are health behavior changes maintained over time?
alt.a: When they are integrated into the person’s overall lifestyle
alt.ex: Changes are maintained over time only if they are integrated into an individual’s overall lifestyle.
w: When the patient avoids all relapses during the action stage
Relapse is common and is part of the process; it does not prevent later maintenance.
When the nurse sets the goals without patient involvement
Goals are set collaboratively with the patient.
When the patient completes a single educational session
One session does not maintain change; integration into lifestyle does.

items.q: A nurse plans teaching to help a patient make lifestyle changes. Which strategies are recommended? Select all that apply.
o: Practice active listening and establish rapport
Active listening and rapport are listed teaching strategies for lifestyle change.
Collaborate on safe places to exercise and timelines for change
Collaborating on safe exercise areas and timelines is a listed strategy.
Include family members, social groups, and social media for support
Family and social supports help sustain lifestyle change.
Have the patient keep a log of key behavioral changes
A log of key behavioral changes is a recommended teaching strategy.
Use the same standard handout for every patient
Materials must be tailored to the patient’s health needs, literacy, and culture.
Set the goals for the patient to save time
Goals are established with the patient, not for the patient.
items.ex: Lifestyle teaching uses rapport, collaboration, social support, behavior logs, and tailored materials.

alt.q: Which characteristics should educational materials for lifestyle change have? Select all that apply.
o: Tailored to the patient’s health needs
Materials should be tailored to the patient’s health needs.
Matched to the patient’s literacy level
Materials should meet the patient’s literacy level and be easy to understand.
Culturally appropriate
Materials should be culturally appropriate.
Written using advanced medical terminology
Materials should be easy to understand, not full of technical terms.
Identical for every patient on the unit
Materials are tailored to each patient’s needs, not standardized for all.
alt.ex: Correct: Tailored to the patient’s health needs; Matched to the patient’s literacy level; Culturally appropriate.

items.q: A patient is in the precontemplation stage of change. Which assessment findings would the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Underestimates the problem
Precontemplators may be unaware of or underestimate the problem.
May be defensive
Defensiveness is an expected finding in precontemplation.
Is not interested in the problem
Precontemplators may be uninterested in the problem.
Is making small changes for next month
Small changes toward a change next month describe preparation.
Has integrated the change into daily life
Integration into lifestyle describes maintenance.
items.ex: Precontemplation means no intent to change within 6 months; the patient may be unaware, uninterested, or defensive.

alt.q: Which statements about the Transtheoretical Model of Change are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It describes five stages of change
The model describes five stages, from precontemplation to maintenance.
People often relapse and cycle through the stages
Change is not linear; people often relapse and cycle.
Interventions should match the patient’s stage
Matching interventions to the stage makes them most effective.
People move through the stages in a straight line
Change is not a linear process.
Maintenance ends 6 months after action begins
Maintenance begins 6 months after action and continues indefinitely.
alt.ex: Correct: It describes five stages of change; People often relapse and cycle through the stages; Interventions should match the patient’s stage.

items.q: Which are examples of wellness strategies? Select all that apply.
o: Risk-factor modification
Risk-factor modification is named as a wellness strategy.
Health promotion
Health promotion is named as a wellness strategy.
Illness prevention activities
Illness prevention activities are named as wellness strategies.
Programs to change unhealthy lifestyle habits
Any program that attempts to change unhealthy behaviors is a wellness strategy.
Recording a patient’s age and sex
Age and sex are nonmodifiable risk factors, not strategies.
Ignoring risks the patient will not discuss
Ignoring risks is not a strategy to change behavior.
items.ex: Wellness strategies include risk-factor modification, health promotion, illness prevention, and any program changing unhealthy behaviors.

alt.q: A nurse helps patients change health behaviors. Which are examples of behaviors a patient may need to adopt? Select all that apply.
o: Eating a healthy diet
A healthy diet is an example of a behavior patients may need to adopt.
Exercising regularly
Exercise is an example of a behavior patients may need to adopt.
Using tobacco
Tobacco use is a behavior patients may need to stop.
Misusing alcohol
Alcohol misuse is a behavior patients may need to stop.
alt.ex: Correct: Eating a healthy diet; Exercising regularly.

items.q: Most people move through the stages of health behavior change in a straight line without returning to earlier stages.
items.a: False
items.ex: Change is not linear; people often relapse and cycle through the stages before succeeding.
items.ww: Calling it true ignores that relapse and cycling through stages are common.

alt.q: People often relapse and cycle through the stages of change before a change is maintained.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Relapse is common, and a person returns to contemplation or precontemplation before trying again.
alt.ww: Calling it false assumes change is linear, which the textbook rejects.

items.q: Precontemplation is defined as having no intent to make changes within the next 6 months.
items.a: True
items.ex: Precontemplation is no intent to change within 6 months; the patient may underestimate the problem.
items.ww: Calling it false confuses precontemplation with contemplation, which involves considering change within 6 months.

items.q: Understanding the stages of change helps the nurse time interventions so they fit the patient’s current stage.

alt.q: The same nursing interventions work equally well at every stage of change.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Interventions are most effective when chosen to match the patient’s stage of change.
alt.ww: Calling it true ignores the need to match interventions to each stage.
