items.q: Which statement best describes illness as distinct from disease?
items.a: A state in which a person’s functioning is diminished or impaired
items.ex: Illness is diminished physical, emotional, intellectual, social, developmental, or spiritual functioning; a feeling of poor health.
w: A medical condition that causes distress through its symptoms
A medical condition causing distress through symptoms is the definition of disease.
A generic term including disorders, infections, and deformities
This generic term covering all disorders and deformities is disease.
Any trait that increases a person’s vulnerability to injury
A trait that increases vulnerability is a risk factor.

alt.q: A patient has no diagnosed medical condition but reports feeling unwell and unable to function at work. Which statement is accurate?
alt.a: The patient can be experiencing illness without a disease
alt.ex: A person can feel ill even when there is no underlying medical condition.
w: The patient cannot be ill because no disease has been found
Illness can occur in the absence of disease.
The patient’s feelings must be caused by a hidden disease
A person can feel ill without any underlying medical condition.
The patient’s reports should be treated as a risk factor
Feeling unwell describes illness, not a risk factor.

items.q: Which characteristics describe an acute disease?
items.a: Reversible and short, with abrupt, intense symptoms
items.ex: Acute disease is usually reversible and short, with symptoms that appear abruptly, are intense, and subside quickly.
w: Irreversible and lasting more than 6 months
Irreversible disease lasting more than 6 months describes chronic disease.
Gradual onset with symptoms only partly relieved
Partially relieved, long-term symptoms are typical of chronic disease.
Long duration with alternating relapses
Fluctuating between maximal function and relapses describes chronic disease.

alt.q: A chronic disease usually has which characteristics?
alt.a: Lasts more than 6 months and is irreversible
alt.ex: Chronic disease usually lasts more than 6 months, is irreversible, and affects one or more body systems.
w: Lasts less than 1 month and is reversible
Short, reversible disease is acute.
Lasts less than 6 months and resolves fully
Disease that resolves within a short time is acute.
Lasts 1 to 2 weeks with intense symptoms
Brief, intense symptoms describe acute disease.

items.q: About what percentage of adults in the United States have two or more chronic health problems?
items.ex: About 60% of US adults have one chronic disease and 40% have two or more.
w: Ten percent greatly underestimates the 40% with two or more chronic problems.
Sixty percent is the share with one chronic disease.
Eighty-five percent overestimates; the textbook reports 40%.

alt.q: About what percentage of adults in the United States have one chronic disease?
alt.ex: About 60% of US adults have one chronic disease, and 40% have two or more.
w: Twenty percent underestimates the reported 60%.
Forty percent is the share with two or more chronic problems.
Ninety percent overestimates the reported 60%.

items.q: A patient with chronic arthritis whose pain is only partly relieved by therapy has begun skipping prescribed medications. What best explains this behavior?
items.a: Partial symptom relief can reduce motivation to adhere to therapy
items.ex: A patient with chronic disease and only partially relieved symptoms may not be motivated to adhere to the therapy plan.
w: Patients with chronic disease always adhere better than others
Patients with acute disease are more likely to adhere; chronic disease can lower adherence.
The patient’s arthritis must have become an acute disease
Partial relief and nonadherence are features of chronic disease, not acute disease.
Locus of control has no effect on behavior when ill
Locus of control is an internal variable that affects illness behavior.

alt.q: Which patient is more likely to seek health care and adhere to therapy?
alt.a: A patient with an acute disease
alt.ex: A patient with an acute disease is more likely to seek care and adhere to therapy.
w: A patient with a chronic disease and partial relief
Partially relieved chronic symptoms can reduce motivation to adhere.
A patient who is frustrated with ongoing treatment
Greater frustration is linked with less ready adherence.
A patient who has become less involved in care
Less involvement in care is linked with lower adherence.

items.q: A patient with a cold calls in sick and asks a coworker to cover his meeting. How does the textbook explain this illness behavior?
items.a: Illness behavior can release a person from roles and responsibilities
items.ex: When people perceive themselves to be ill, illness behaviors become coping mechanisms that can release them from roles.
w: Illness behavior is unrelated to how people use health resources
Illness behaviors affect how people monitor symptoms and use health care resources.
Illness behavior occurs only when a disease is life threatening
Illness behavior also occurs with short-term, non–life-threatening diseases.
Illness behavior is determined entirely by genetic factors
Sociocultural and psychological factors and past experiences influence illness behavior.

alt.q: Which factors influence a person’s illness behaviors?
alt.a: Personal history, social situations, social norms, and past experiences
alt.ex: Illness behaviors are influenced by personal history, social situations, social norms, and past experiences.
w: Only the specific diagnosis made by the health care provider
Many sociocultural and psychological factors shape illness behavior, not just the diagnosis.
Only the patient’s age and genetic background
Age and genetics are not the only influences; social and personal factors matter.
Only the cost of the patient’s prescribed medications
Cost is one external variable but not the only influence.

items.q: Which patient is most likely to seek health care assistance?
items.a: A patient whose symptoms disrupt the normal daily routine
items.ex: Patients who believe symptoms disrupt their routine or are serious are more likely to seek care.
w: A patient who believes symptoms are minor and harmless
Patients who see symptoms as not serious are less likely to seek care.
A patient whose symptoms do not affect daily activities
Nondisruptive symptoms make seeking care less likely.
A patient whose symptoms are mild and not visible
Symptoms that are not visible are less likely to prompt care seeking.

alt.q: Which symptom is most likely to prompt a patient to seek assistance because of its visibility?
alt.a: A high fever
alt.ex: A visible symptom such as a high fever often prompts care more than symptoms that are not visible.
w: Mild fatigue
Fatigue is a less visible symptom, like those of ovarian cancer.
Abdominal bloating
Bloating is a less visible symptom associated with ovarian cancer.
Occasional tiredness
Tiredness is not visible and is less likely to prompt care.

items.q: An 80-year-old patient with a new, persistent cough says, “I don’t want to bother anyone. I want to keep managing on my own.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Getting this checked now can help you stay independent at home.”
items.ex: Older adults seek help when they view it as a functional way of increasing their own independence.
w: “You need to let your family take over your decisions now.”
Older adults often see help-seeking as a threat to independence; this would reinforce that fear.
“Let’s wait a few days and see whether it goes away.”
Waiting delays care; older adults often underestimate the seriousness of symptoms.
“Your neighbors can help you manage this informally.”
Informal support is a common first choice but can delay needed care.

alt.q: What do older adults commonly do first when confronted with a new symptom?
alt.a: Self-assess their health to decide whether help is needed
alt.ex: Older adults commonly self-assess first, which often delays help-seeking as they underestimate seriousness.
w: Go directly to an emergency department
Older adults often delay seeking help rather than going straight to an emergency department.
Ask a health care provider before trying anything else
Formal care is often not the first choice; informal support commonly is.
Request a home health nurse for an assessment
Older adults commonly self-assess and use informal support first.

items.q: A patient seeks treatment for a minor rash in the emergency department. Which explanation for this behavior is consistent with the textbook?
items.a: The patient may not know how else to obtain services or lack access
items.ex: Some patients use the emergency department for nonemergency care because they do not know other ways to get care or lack access.
w: The patient is showing an internal variable called locus of control
Using the emergency department this way reflects health care accessibility, an external variable.
The patient is in the precontemplation stage of change
Stages of change describe readiness to change behavior, not where care is sought.
The patient believes the rash is a sign of a chronic disease
The textbook links this behavior to access to care, not to perceived chronicity.

alt.q: Why are people living in poverty especially vulnerable to disease?
alt.a: Financial difficulties delay treatment and the ability to follow therapies
alt.ex: Financial difficulties often delay access to treatment and affect the ability to carry out prescribed therapies.
w: Poverty is a nonmodifiable genetic risk factor for disease
Economic variables are social determinants of health, not genetic risk factors.
People living in poverty seek care sooner than others
Financial difficulties often lead to delays in seeking treatment.
Poverty mainly affects the visibility of disease symptoms
Poverty affects access and ability to follow treatment, not symptom visibility.

items.q: After a mastectomy, a patient refuses to look at the incision or talk about it with her partner. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Recognize withdrawal as adaptive coping and continue supportive care
items.ex: Withdrawal after a profound body image change is an adaptive coping mechanism that helps the patient adjust.
w: Insist that the patient look at the incision before discharge
Forcing confrontation ignores that withdrawal helps the patient adjust.
Begin teaching about adapting to body changes right away
Readiness to learn adaptation comes later, during rehabilitation.
Report the patient’s withdrawal as a maladaptive response
Withdrawal is described as an adaptive coping mechanism, not maladaptive.

alt.q: When is a patient with a profound change in body image generally ready to learn how to adapt to the change?
alt.a: During rehabilitation, after gradually accepting the loss
alt.ex: As the patient acknowledges the change and accepts the loss, readiness to learn develops during rehabilitation.
w: Immediately after the change, during the initial shock
Shock is the first response, when the patient is not yet ready to learn.
While anxious and withdrawn, refusing to discuss it
Withdrawal precedes acceptance and readiness to learn.
Before the change happens, while it is still impending
Shock often occurs with an impending change; learning comes during rehabilitation.

items.q: A patient’s mother had a stroke, and the patient now manages her mother’s finances, meals, and appointments. Which term describes this change?
items.a: Role reversal
items.ex: Role reversal occurs when an adult child assumes an ill parent’s responsibilities and becomes a parent to the parent.
w: Illness career
An illness career is a person’s evolving response to a chronic disease.
Locus of control
Locus of control is the degree to which people believe they control what happens to them.
Body image
Body image is the subjective concept of physical appearance.

alt.q: How do a patient and family generally adjust to long-term role changes caused by illness?
alt.a: Through an adjustment process similar to the grief process
alt.ex: Long-term role changes require an adjustment process similar to grieving, and families often need counseling.
w: Easily, because they know the change is only temporary
Easy adjustment applies to subtle, short-term changes known to be temporary.
Without any need for counseling or guidance from nurses
Patients and families often need counseling and guidance for role changes.
By returning to their former roles within a few days
Long-term changes, by definition, do not resolve in a few days.

items.q: How does the effect of illness on self-concept compare with its effect on family roles?
items.a: It is usually more complex and less readily observed
items.ex: The effect of illness on self-concept is usually more complex and less readily observed than role changes.
w: It is usually simpler and easier to observe
Self-concept effects are more complex and less visible than role changes.
It is identical in complexity and visibility
The textbook describes self-concept effects as more complex and less visible.
It is rarely relevant to family relationships
Self-concept changes can create tension or conflict with family members.

alt.q: A patient who feels like a failure because of illness no longer meets family expectations. What is a likely result?
alt.a: Tension or conflict as family members change their interactions
alt.ex: Changes in self-concept can lead to unmet expectations, tension, or conflict, and family members change how they interact.
w: No effect, because self-concept is unrelated to family life
Self-concept is important in relationships with family members.
Improved family dynamics with no need for adjustment
Unmet expectations usually lead to tension, not improvement.
A change in the patient’s nonmodifiable risk factors
Self-concept changes do not alter nonmodifiable risk factors.

items.q: Many chronic diseases are related to which modifiable health behaviors? Select all that apply.
o: Physical inactivity
Physical inactivity is one of four behaviors linked to many chronic diseases.
Poor nutrition
Poor nutrition is one of four behaviors linked to many chronic diseases.
Tobacco use and secondhand smoke exposure
Tobacco use and secondhand smoke exposure are one of the four behaviors.
Excessive alcohol use
Excessive alcohol use is one of the four behaviors.
Family history of disease
Family history is a nonmodifiable risk factor, not a behavior.
Advancing age
Age is a nonmodifiable risk factor, not a behavior.
items.ex: Physical inactivity, poor nutrition, tobacco use or secondhand smoke, and excessive alcohol use are linked to many chronic diseases.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a patient how to reduce the occurrence of chronic disease. Which behaviors should the teaching target? Select all that apply.
o: Exposure to secondhand smoke
Tobacco use and secondhand smoke exposure are linked to many chronic diseases.
Excessive alcohol use
Excessive alcohol use is a modifiable behavior linked to chronic disease.
Physical inactivity
Physical inactivity is a modifiable behavior linked to chronic disease.
Sex assigned at birth
Sex is a nonmodifiable risk factor.
Genetic makeup
Genetics is a nonmodifiable risk factor.
alt.ex: Correct: Exposure to secondhand smoke; Excessive alcohol use; Physical inactivity.

items.q: Which are external variables that influence a patient’s illness behavior? Select all that apply.
o: Visibility of symptoms
Visibility of symptoms is an external variable.
Social group and social support
Social group and social support are external variables.
Cultural background
Cultural background is an external variable.
Accessibility of the health care system
Health care accessibility is an external variable.
Locus of control
Locus of control is an internal variable.
Perception of symptom seriousness
Perceptions of symptoms are internal variables.
items.ex: External variables include symptom visibility, social group, culture, economics, health care accessibility, and social support.

alt.q: Which are internal variables that influence a patient’s illness behavior? Select all that apply.
o: Perceptions of symptoms
A patient’s perceptions of symptoms are internal variables.
Coping skills
Coping skills are internal variables.
Locus of control
Locus of control is an internal variable.
Economic variables
Economic variables are external variables.
Physical proximity to a health care agency
Proximity to care relates to accessibility, an external variable.
alt.ex: Correct: Perceptions of symptoms; Coping skills; Locus of control.

items.q: A patient is diagnosed with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS). Which emotional and behavioral changes might the nurse expect in the patient and family? Select all that apply.
o: Anxiety
Anxiety is a common response to life-threatening or chronic disease.
Denial
Denial is a common response to life-threatening or chronic disease.
Anger
Anger is a common response to life-threatening or chronic disease.
Withdrawal
Withdrawal is a common response to life-threatening or chronic disease.
Only brief, subtle irritability
Brief, subtle irritability fits a short-term illness such as a cold.
No change in family functioning
Family needs and functioning change over time with serious disease.
items.ex: Life-threatening or chronic diseases lead to anxiety, shock, denial, anger, and withdrawal, and family functioning changes over time.

alt.q: Which factors influence how a patient and family react to a change in body image? Select all that apply.
o: The type of change
Reactions depend on the type of change, such as loss of a limb.
Their adaptive capacity
Adaptive capacity influences reactions to body image change.
The rate at which changes occur
The speed of change influences reactions.
The support services available
Available support services influence reactions.
The patient’s blood type
Blood type is not a factor in body image reactions.
alt.ex: Correct: The type of change; Their adaptive capacity; The rate at which changes occur; The support services available.

items.q: Withdrawal after a profound change in body image, such as an amputation, is an adaptive coping mechanism.
items.a: True
items.ex: Withdrawal helps the patient adjust as the reality of the change is recognized.
items.ww: Calling it false treats withdrawal as maladaptive, but the textbook describes it as adaptive.

alt.q: Withdrawal after a mastectomy is a maladaptive response that the nurse should stop right away.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Withdrawal is an adaptive coping mechanism that helps the patient adjust before acceptance.
alt.ww: Calling it true misreads withdrawal, which the textbook describes as helping adjustment.

items.q: Patients and families generally adjust more easily to subtle, short-term role changes than to long-term ones.
items.a: True
items.ex: When a role change is temporary, families know it will not need prolonged adjustment.
items.ww: Calling it false ignores that long-term changes need a grief-like adjustment process.

alt.q: Long-term role changes caused by illness usually need less adjustment than short-term changes.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Long-term role changes require an adjustment process similar to grief.
alt.ww: Calling it true reverses the textbook; short-term changes are easier to adjust to.

items.q: A patient who has a disease always feels ill.
items.a: False
items.ex: Many patients with a disease feel healthy, and a person can feel ill without disease.
items.ww: Calling it true equates illness with disease, which are different concepts.

alt.q: Many patients who have a disease feel healthy.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Illness is a feeling of poor health, which can be present or absent with disease.
alt.ww: Calling it false assumes disease always causes illness, which the textbook disputes.

items.q: The degree to which people believe they control what happens to them is called [[locus of control]].
items.ex: Locus of control is an internal variable that affects a patient’s behavior when ill.

alt.q: An internal variable describing how much people believe they control what happens to them is [[locus of control]].
alt.ex: Locus of control is an internal variable that affects a patient’s behavior when ill.

w: Gradual acceptance of the loss
That's phase 3 of 4.
Readiness to learn to adapt during rehabilitation
That's phase 4 of 4.

That's phase 4 of 4.

w: Anxiety and withdrawal as reality is recognized

That's phase 1 of 4.

ord.q: Place the phases of adjustment to a profound change in body image in order.
items: Shock at the change or impending change
Anxiety and withdrawal as reality is recognized
Gradual acceptance of the loss
Readiness to learn to adapt during rehabilitation
ord.ex: Adjustment follows grief phases: shock, then anxiety and withdrawal, then acceptance, then readiness to learn in rehabilitation.

items.q: Why does the textbook stress that nurses need to take care of themselves?
items.a: To remain healthy enough to provide competent, quality, safe care
items.ex: Nurses need to care for themselves to stay healthy so they can give competent, quality, and safe care.
w: To qualify for employer-sponsored health insurance benefits
Insurance eligibility is not the reason given for nurse self-care.
To reduce the number of patients assigned to each nurse
Self-care does not change patient assignments; it keeps nurses healthy.
To avoid any emotional connection with patients and families
Self-care does not mean avoiding relationships with patients.

alt.q: A charge nurse encourages staff to attend to their own health. Which statement shows the charge nurse’s understanding?
alt.a: “Staying healthy helps us give safe, quality care.”
alt.ex: Nurses take care of themselves so they remain healthy and can provide competent, quality, safe care.
w: “Self-care matters only for nurses who work nights.”
The need for self-care applies to all nurses.
“Self-care is optional once you gain experience.”
Experience does not remove the need for nurses to care for themselves.
“Self-care mainly helps us finish charting faster.”
The purpose given is maintaining health to provide safe care.

items.q: Compassion fatigue is a combination of which two conditions?
items.a: Secondary traumatic stress and burnout
items.ex: Compassion fatigue combines secondary traumatic stress (STS) and burnout.
w: Secondary traumatic stress and depression
Depression is not one of the two named components; burnout is.
Burnout and posttraumatic stress disorder
The second component is secondary traumatic stress, not PTSD.
Burnout and chronic sleep deprivation
Sleep changes are an effect of compassion fatigue, not a component.

alt.q: A nurse experiences both secondary traumatic stress and burnout. Which term describes this combination?
alt.a: Compassion fatigue
alt.ex: Compassion fatigue is the combination of STS and burnout.
w: Role reversal
Role reversal is when an adult child takes over an ill parent’s responsibilities.
Illness career
An illness career is a person’s evolving response to chronic disease.
Locus of control
Locus of control is the degree to which people believe they control what happens to them.

items.q: What is the source of secondary traumatic stress (STS) in nurses?
items.a: Relationships with patients and families, especially when witnessing suffering
items.ex: STS develops from nurses’ relationships with patients and families, especially when they often witness suffering.
w: A chronic lack of resources such as staffing and time
A chronic lack of resources causes burnout, not STS.
Conflicts with managers over scheduling and pay rates
Work-setting conflicts relate to burnout, not STS.
Long commutes and frequent changes in work location
These are not identified sources of STS.

alt.q: What is the source of burnout in nurses?
alt.a: A chronic lack of resources such as staffing and time
alt.ex: Burnout stems from a chronic lack of resources that results in conflict or job dissatisfaction.
w: Relationships in which nurses often witness suffering
Witnessing suffering in relationships causes STS, not burnout.
A single traumatic event early in the nurse’s career
Burnout is chronic and resource related, not from a single event.
Close friendships with experienced nurse mentors
Mentor relationships help reduce burnout rather than cause it.

items.q: A nurse on a chronically understaffed unit reports constant job dissatisfaction and conflict over workloads. Which component of compassion fatigue does this most reflect?
items.a: Burnout
items.ex: Burnout stems from a chronic lack of resources, such as staffing and time, causing conflict or job dissatisfaction.
w: Secondary traumatic stress
STS comes from relationships in which nurses witness suffering, not resource shortages.
Role reversal
Role reversal describes family role changes during illness.
Precontemplation
Precontemplation is a stage of behavior change, not a component of compassion fatigue.

alt.q: A hospice nurse who often witnesses patients’ suffering feels drained by repeated exposure to their distress. Which component of compassion fatigue does this most reflect?
alt.a: Secondary traumatic stress
alt.ex: STS develops from relationships with patients and families in which nurses frequently witness suffering.
w: Burnout
Burnout stems from a chronic lack of resources, not witnessing suffering.
Illness behavior
Illness behavior is how people act when ill from a disease.
Role reversal
Role reversal describes family role changes during illness.

items.q: A charge nurse notices that a coworker has become irritable, calls patients by room number, and seems unable to feel empathy for them. What is the most likely explanation?
items.a: Compassion fatigue
items.ex: Reduced empathy, depersonalization of the patient, and irritability are signs of compassion fatigue.
w: Normal adjustment to a new unit
These changes reflect compassion fatigue, not a normal adjustment.
A temporary role reversal
Role reversal is a family role change during illness.
Precontemplation of change
Precontemplation is a stage of behavior change, not a work-related response.

alt.q: Which workplace finding in a nurse is most consistent with compassion fatigue?
alt.a: Depersonalization of patients
alt.ex: Nurses with compassion fatigue often depersonalize patients and have reduced ability to feel empathy.
w: Increased empathy for patients
Compassion fatigue reduces, not increases, the ability to feel empathy.
Improved job satisfaction
Compassion fatigue reduces job satisfaction.
Better clinical judgment
Compassion fatigue is associated with poor judgment.

items.q: After a difficult resuscitation in which a child died, which action is the best professional strategy for the nurses involved?
items.a: Participate in a debriefing about the experience
items.ex: Debriefing after difficult or traumatic patient care experiences helps combat compassion fatigue and promote resiliency.
w: Return to work without discussing the event
Avoiding discussion misses the benefit of debriefing after traumatic care.
Ask to work extra shifts to stay distracted
Extra shifts do not address the trauma and can add to burnout.
Avoid caring for children for the next year
Avoidance is not a strategy the textbook recommends.

alt.q: A nurse wants to use self-care activities during the workday to reduce compassion fatigue. Which activity is an example?
alt.a: Practicing mindfulness or meditation on a break
alt.ex: Self-care at work includes journaling, walking, mindfulness, meditation, and gratitude activities.
w: Skipping breaks to finish documentation early
Skipping breaks does not provide self-care at work.
Working through lunch to help colleagues
Working through breaks does not support self-care.
Staying late to review patient charts
Extra work time is not a self-care activity.

items.q: During a walk at work, a coworker shares details of her own past trauma and its effects. Which approach is best for the nurse?
items.a: Consider the coworker’s story in future interactions with her
items.ex: When staff share past trauma and its effects, consider their story in interactions, especially if they show compassion fatigue.
w: Tell the coworker that personal topics are not allowed
Listening to staff stories is a recommended strategy for combating compassion fatigue.
Report the coworker to the manager as unsafe to work
Sharing past trauma does not by itself mean the coworker is unsafe.
Change the subject to avoid discussing her trauma
The strategy is to listen to staff stories, not avoid them.

alt.q: Why does the textbook suggest inviting a staff member to go on a walk at work?
alt.a: To listen to their stories as a strategy against compassion fatigue
alt.ex: Walking with a coworker and listening to their stories is a professional strategy against compassion fatigue.
w: To check their compliance with workplace exercise rules
The purpose is listening and support, not checking compliance.
To leave the unit without informing the charge nurse
The strategy does not involve leaving the unit improperly.
To evaluate their clinical skills outside the unit
The walk is for listening and support, not skills evaluation.

items.q: A nurse asks how to reduce compassion fatigue outside of work. Which recommendation reflects personal strategies from the textbook?
items.a: Eat well, sleep enough, exercise, and keep work-family balance
items.ex: Personal strategies focus on health promotion: nutrition, sleep, exercise, relaxation, work-family balance, and nonwork activities.
w: Spend days off reviewing difficult patient cases
Personal strategies emphasize nonwork activities and balance, not more work.
Pick up overtime to stay busy and avoid thinking
More work hours do not promote health or work-family balance.
Cut back on sleep to make time for hobbies
Adequate, regular sleep is a personal strategy against compassion fatigue.

alt.q: On what do personal strategies for lessening compassion fatigue focus?
alt.a: Health promotion behaviors and healthy lifestyle choices
alt.ex: Personal strategies focus on health promotion behaviors and healthy lifestyle choices.
w: Reducing contact with all patients and families
Avoiding patients is not a personal strategy in the textbook.
Medication to suppress stress-related feelings
The textbook emphasizes healthy lifestyle choices, not medication.
Taking on additional leadership roles at work
Extra work roles are not personal strategies for lessening compassion fatigue.

items.q: Which activities did one study find helped nurses deal with secondary traumatic stress and burnout?
items.a: Talking with chaplains, grieving patient losses, and reflection
items.ex: Interacting with chaplains, allowing personal time to grieve patient losses, and reflection helped nurses with STS and burnout.
w: Avoiding chaplains, suppressing grief, and working more
Suppressing grief and working more are the opposite of what helped.
Changing units, avoiding families, and skipping breaks
These avoidance behaviors were not identified as helpful.
Limiting reflection, skipping debriefing, and overtime
Reflection and debriefing help; limiting them would not.

alt.q: A nurse whose long-term patient died asks for time before the next admission. Why is this request reasonable?
alt.a: Personal time to grieve patient losses helps nurses cope with STS
alt.ex: Allowing personal time for grieving the loss of patients helped nurses deal with STS and burnout.
w: Grieving patients is a sign that the nurse is unsafe to practice
Grief is a normal response, and allowing time for it is helpful.
Time off is required by law after any patient death
The textbook supports grieving time as helpful, not as a legal requirement.
Grief time prevents all future secondary traumatic stress
Grieving time helps nurses cope but is not described as preventing all STS.

items.q: A new graduate nurse feels overwhelmed by job stress. Which relationship does the textbook identify as helpful?
items.a: A mentor or experienced nurse who understands the job’s stress
items.ex: Forming a relationship with a mentor or experienced nurse who understands job stress helps reduce compassion fatigue.
w: A patient whose family can offer emotional support
Seeking support from patients’ families is not a recommended strategy.
A new graduate who has never worked as a nurse
A peer without experience lacks the understanding of job stress a mentor provides.
A manager who handles all of the nurse’s conflicts
The textbook recommends a mentor, not shifting conflicts to a manager.

alt.q: Why is forming a relationship with an experienced nurse helpful for lessening compassion fatigue?
alt.a: The experienced nurse understands the stress of the job
alt.ex: A mentor who understands job stress can support the nurse in coping with STS and burnout.
w: The experienced nurse can take over the nurse’s patient load
The value lies in understanding and support, not shifting workload.
The experienced nurse can excuse the nurse from debriefings
Debriefings are helpful; a mentor does not replace or excuse them.
The experienced nurse can prescribe medication for stress
Prescribing is not the role of a nurse mentor.

items.q: In one study, what did participating in debriefing sessions or a compassion fatigue support group allow nurses to do?
items.a: Identify stressors and develop healthy coping strategies as a group
items.ex: Debriefing or a support group allowed nurses to identify stressors and work as a group to develop healthy coping.
w: Avoid discussing difficult cases with their coworkers
Debriefing involves discussing difficult experiences, not avoiding them.
Transfer their most difficult patients to other units
Support groups focus on coping, not transferring patients.
Eliminate the need for personal health promotion
Personal health promotion remains important alongside group strategies.

alt.q: What do institutional programs on compassion fatigue typically provide for nurses?
alt.a: Education about compassion fatigue plus resources and coping tools
alt.ex: Programs teach about compassion fatigue and its effects and give tools to prevent or cope with STS and burnout.
w: Mandatory time off after every difficult patient assignment
Mandatory leave is not described as a program feature.
Proof of which program best builds long-term resiliency
Studies are still needed to identify which programs work best long term.
Removal of all patients who are suffering from assignments
Programs help nurses cope; they do not remove suffering patients.

items.q: What does the textbook say about current evidence on programs to build nurse resiliency?
items.a: Well-designed studies are urgently needed to show which programs work long term
items.ex: There is an urgent need for well-designed studies identifying which programs best improve nurse resiliency long term.
w: Studies have identified one program that works for all nurses
No single best program has been identified; more studies are needed.
Research shows resiliency programs have no benefit for nurses
Programs such as support groups have shown benefit; long-term evidence is lacking.
Evidence supports only programs that nurses complete alone
Group approaches such as debriefing and support groups have shown benefit.

alt.q: A nurse manager wants to choose a resiliency program proven to work long term. What should the manager know?
alt.a: Evidence on which programs work best long term is still lacking
alt.ex: Well-designed studies are still needed to identify which programs best improve long-term nurse resiliency.
w: Any program lasting longer than 1 year is proven to work
Program length is not identified as proof of long-term effectiveness.
Only programs led by chaplains have proven long-term results
Chaplain interaction helped in one study, but no program is proven best long term.
Resiliency cannot be improved once compassion fatigue begins
Programs and strategies aim to help nurses cope and increase resiliency.

items.q: Which effects on a nurse’s health are associated with compassion fatigue? Select all that apply.
o: Changes in sleep and eating patterns
Compassion fatigue often changes sleep and eating patterns.
Musculoskeletal issues
Musculoskeletal issues are a listed health effect.
Emotional exhaustion and irritability
Emotional exhaustion and irritability are listed effects.
Feelings of hopelessness and anxiety
Hopelessness and anxiety are listed effects.
Greater pleasure from activities
Compassion fatigue causes an inability to take pleasure from activities.
Improved ability to focus on patients
Compassion fatigue impairs the ability to focus and engage with patients.
items.ex: Compassion fatigue often causes declining health, sleep and eating changes, musculoskeletal issues, exhaustion, irritability, hopelessness, and anxiety.

alt.q: A nurse manager reviews unit data for signs of compassion fatigue among staff. Which workplace findings are associated with it? Select all that apply.
o: Chronic absenteeism
Chronic absenteeism is associated with compassion fatigue.
High turnover rates
High turnover rates are associated with compassion fatigue.
Conflict between nurses
Conflict between nurses is associated with compassion fatigue.
Rising job satisfaction scores
Compassion fatigue reduces job satisfaction.
Improved staff performance
Compassion fatigue diminishes performance.
alt.ex: Correct: Chronic absenteeism; High turnover rates; Conflict between nurses.

items.q: Which professional strategies at work help combat compassion fatigue and promote resiliency? Select all that apply.
o: Journaling or gratitude activities during the workday
Self-care activities at work include journaling and gratitude activities.
Walking with a staff member and listening to their stories
Walking with and listening to coworkers is a listed strategy.
Participating in debriefings after traumatic patient care
Debriefing after difficult or traumatic care is a listed strategy.
Taking extra shifts to avoid thinking about stressful events
Extra shifts are not a strategy and do not address stress.
Avoiding discussion of difficult patient care experiences
Discussing difficult experiences through debriefing is recommended.
items.ex: Professional strategies include self-care at work, walking and listening to coworkers, and debriefing after traumatic experiences.

alt.q: Which personal strategies help lessen compassion fatigue? Select all that apply.
o: Getting adequate sleep regularly
Regular, adequate sleep is a personal strategy.
Engaging in regular exercise and relaxation
Exercise and relaxation are personal strategies.
Engaging in regular nonwork activities
Nonwork activities support work-family balance.
Skipping meals to save time for work
A nutritious diet is recommended.
Taking work home to stay ahead
Good work-family balance is recommended, not more work at home.
alt.ex: Correct: Getting adequate sleep regularly; Engaging in regular exercise and relaxation; Engaging in regular nonwork activities.

items.q: A nursing student asks which supports can help nurses cope with secondary traumatic stress and burnout. Which supports does the textbook identify? Select all that apply.
o: Interacting with chaplains
Interacting with chaplains helped nurses deal with STS and burnout.
A mentor who understands job stress
A mentor or experienced nurse who understands job stress is helpful.
A compassion fatigue support group
Support groups helped nurses identify stressors and develop coping strategies.
Avoiding all close relationships with patients
Avoiding patient relationships is not a recommended strategy.
Keeping feelings private from all coworkers
Group strategies such as debriefing involve sharing with coworkers.
items.ex: Chaplains, mentors, debriefing, and support groups help nurses cope with STS and burnout.

alt.q: A hospital plans to reduce compassion fatigue among its nurses. Which actions are consistent with the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Offer education on the nature of compassion fatigue
Institutional programs educate nurses about compassion fatigue and its effects.
Provide tools to prevent or cope with STS and burnout
Programs give nurses resources and tools to cope with STS and burnout.
Hold debriefing sessions after traumatic events
Debriefing helps nurses identify stressors and develop coping.
Increase patient loads to build nurse toughness
A chronic lack of resources such as staffing contributes to burnout.
Discourage nurses from grieving patient deaths
Personal time to grieve patient losses helps nurses cope.
alt.ex: Correct: Offer education on the nature of compassion fatigue; Provide tools to prevent or cope with STS and burnout; Hold debriefing sessions after traumatic events.

items.q: Burnout stems from a chronic lack of resources, such as staffing and time, in the work setting.
items.a: True
items.ex: A chronic lack of resources leads to conflicts or job dissatisfaction, which produces burnout.
items.ww: Calling it false confuses burnout with STS, which arises from witnessing suffering.

alt.q: Burnout develops mainly because nurses frequently witness patients’ suffering.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Witnessing suffering causes secondary traumatic stress; burnout stems from a chronic lack of resources.
alt.ww: Calling it true mixes up the two components of compassion fatigue.

items.q: Nurses with compassion fatigue often have a reduced ability to feel empathy for patients.
items.a: True
items.ex: Reduced empathy and depersonalization of the patient are workplace effects of compassion fatigue.
items.ww: Calling it false ignores that compassion fatigue diminishes empathy.

alt.q: Compassion fatigue usually increases a nurse’s empathy because the nurse is closely involved with suffering.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Compassion fatigue reduces the nurse’s ability to feel empathy and can lead to depersonalization.
alt.ww: Calling it true reverses the textbook’s description of reduced empathy.

items.q: Research has already identified which programs best improve nurse resiliency over the long term.
items.a: False
items.ex: There is an urgent need for well-designed studies to identify which programs best improve long-term resiliency.
items.ww: Calling it true overstates the evidence, which is still lacking for long-term effects.

alt.q: Well-designed studies are still needed to identify which programs best improve nurse resiliency long term.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The textbook calls for urgent, well-designed studies on long-term resiliency programs.
alt.ww: Calling it false assumes the best programs are already known, which the textbook disputes.

items.q: The combination of secondary traumatic stress and burnout is called [[compassion fatigue]].
items.ex: Nurses are particularly susceptible to compassion fatigue, which affects their health and work performance.

alt.ex: Nurses are particularly susceptible to compassion fatigue, which affects their health and work performance.

items.q: According to Benner’s view that caring is primary, what does caring mean?
items.a: That people, events, projects, and things matter to people
items.ex: Benner describes caring as the essence of excellent nursing practice: it means that people, events, projects, and things matter; it is a word for being connected.
w: That tasks are completed efficiently within the time available
Efficient task completion is not Benner’s definition; caring is about things mattering and being connected.
That the nurse follows the treatment plan without deviation
Following a plan is not caring itself; Benner defines caring as things mattering to people.
That disease is cured before a patient’s feelings are addressed
Benner’s view centers on connection and meaning, not on curing disease first.

alt.q: Benner described caring as “a word for being” what?
alt.a: Connected
alt.ex: Benner calls caring a word for being connected, a deep human connection that improves healing.
w: Efficient
Efficiency is not part of Benner’s description; caring is about connection.
Objective
Caring is relational and personal, not detached or objective.
Obligated
Benner frames caring as things mattering to people, not as obligation.

items.q: Why does the textbook state that a treatment given without considering its meaning to the individual is unlikely to be effective?
items.a: Illness is the human experience of loss or dysfunction
items.ex: Because illness is experienced as loss or dysfunction, care must address what the condition means to the person.
w: Treatments are effective only when patients pay for them
Cost is not the reason given; the book links effectiveness to the meaning of illness.
Most treatments act mainly through a placebo effect
The book does not claim a placebo effect; it stresses the human experience of illness.
Health care providers rarely choose the correct treatment
The book does not question treatment choice; it stresses considering meaning to the patient.

alt.q: A nurse wants to fully understand the meaning and impact of a patient’s new diagnosis. Which approach does the textbook recommend?
alt.a: Develop a caring relationship and listen to the patient’s story
alt.ex: Listening to patients’ stories within a caring relationship reveals the meaning of the condition and supports person-centered care.
w: Review the diagnosis and typical disease course in a reference text
Disease information does not reveal what the illness means to this person.
Base the plan on the symptoms listed in the medical record
Selecting care only by symptoms misses the patient’s perception and meaning of the illness.
Ask the health care provider how the patient is likely coping
The patient, not the provider, is the source of the illness’s personal meaning.

items.q: Which concept is central to Leininger’s theory of caring?
items.a: Care is the domain that sets nursing apart from other disciplines
items.ex: Leininger’s transcultural view holds that care is an essential human need and the domain that distinguishes nursing.
w: Care before cure is achieved through a single caring moment
The caring moment and care before cure belong to Watson’s transpersonal caring theory.
Caring consists of five processes beginning with knowing
The five caring processes are Swanson’s theory, not Leininger’s.
Caring is the essence of practice found in expert nurses’ stories
Interpreting expert nurses’ stories is Benner’s approach, not Leininger’s.

alt.q: Which statement reflects Leininger’s transcultural view of caring?
alt.a: Caring is universal, but how it is expressed varies among cultures
alt.ex: Leininger notes caring is a universal phenomenon whose expressions, processes, and patterns differ across cultures.
w: Caring behaviors look the same for patients of every culture
Leininger stresses that expressions of caring vary by culture and person.
Cure is more important than care in improving a human condition
Leininger states care, unlike cure, helps people improve a human condition.
Caring acts are standard and do not depend on patient values
A caring act depends on the needs, problems, and values of the patient.

items.q: A nurse is admitting a patient whose cultural background is unfamiliar to the nurse. Which action best reflects culturally based caring?
items.a: Let the patient tell their story and listen to collect the history
items.ex: Box 7.1 advises collecting a culturally based nursing history by letting patients tell their stories and listening to them.
w: Use the caring behaviors the nurse would personally prefer
Caring is personal; the nurse must learn the patient’s culturally specific behaviors, not apply their own.
Assume the patient shares the typical beliefs of their culture
Assumptions ignore individual variation; the nurse learns beliefs by listening to the patient.
Delay cultural assessment until the patient is ready for discharge
Cultural beliefs affect care throughout the stay and should be learned early.

alt.q: A nurse is unsure whether presence or touch would be welcomed by a patient from another culture. Which action is most appropriate?
alt.a: Determine whether a family or cultural group member can guide these practices
alt.ex: Box 7.1 advises determining whether a family or cultural group member is the best resource to guide caring practices like presence or touch.
w: Use touch freely because touch is a universal sign of caring
Touch is interpreted differently across cultures and may feel invasive to some patients.
Avoid presence and touch for the remainder of the hospital stay
Avoiding caring practices is unnecessary; the nurse seeks guidance on appropriate use.
Follow the approach that worked with the nurse’s previous patient
Caring is specific to each encounter; another patient’s preferences do not apply.

items.q: According to Watson, which factors increase the risk for dehumanized care?
items.a: Economic pressure for productivity and shortages of health care staff
items.ex: Watson notes the changing delivery system, economic pressure for productivity, and staff shortages raise the risk for dehumanized care.
w: Lengthy conversations between nurses and their patients
Meaningful conversations protect against dehumanized care; brief disconnected ones are the concern.
Family caregivers who are involved in daily patient care
Family involvement is not listed as a cause of dehumanized care.
Nurses who use self-disclosure to build a therapeutic alliance
Appropriate self-disclosure is a carative example, not a cause of dehumanized care.

alt.q: A nurse enters a room, reads the patient’s laboratory results aloud, and leaves without inviting questions. According to Watson’s view, what does this interaction illustrate?
alt.a: Reporting information rather than holding a meaningful conversation
alt.ex: Watson notes many nurse-patient exchanges are brief and disconnected, simply reporting information rather than meaningful conversation.
w: A caring moment that transforms both nurse and patient
A caring moment requires a connection between nurse and patient, which is absent here.
A carative factor of promoting transpersonal teaching-learning
Teaching-learning involves learning together; this nurse only delivers information.
An efficient form of transpersonal caring under time pressure
Transpersonal caring requires connection and meaningful conversation, not one-way reporting.

items.q: What makes Watson’s caring model transformative?
items.a: The relationship influences both the nurse and the patient
items.ex: Watson’s model is transformative because the caring relationship influences both nurse and patient, for better or worse.
w: The nurse changes the patient’s disease through technical skill
Watson rejects the disease orientation; transformation comes from the relationship.
The patient’s family takes over the nurse’s caring role
The model focuses on the nurse-patient caring relationship, not on families replacing nurses.
The theory changes the nurse’s tasks but not the patient
The transformation affects both nurse and patient, not tasks alone.

alt.q: In Watson’s model, when is caring-healing communicated to a patient?
alt.a: During a caring moment when a connection forms between them
alt.ex: Watson describes caring-healing passing through the nurse’s consciousness in a single caring moment when a connection forms.
w: Only after the patient’s physical condition is stabilized
Watson places care before cure; caring moments are not delayed until stabilization.
When the nurse completes the documentation of care given
Documentation is not a caring moment; connection with the patient is.
Whenever the nurse enters the room to perform a procedure
Entering a room is not enough; a connection must form for a caring moment.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “I don’t know why this illness happened to me or what it means for my life.” Which carative factor is the nurse using when helping the patient find purpose and direction?
items.a: Instilling faith-hope
items.ex: Instilling faith-hope provides a connection that offers purpose and direction when the patient seeks the meaning of an illness.
w: Meeting human needs
Meeting human needs involves helping with basic needs, not finding meaning in illness.
Using creative problem-solving
Creative problem-solving applies critical thinking in the nursing process to make sound judgments.
Promoting teaching-learning
Teaching-learning focuses on helping the patient acquire self-care skills.

alt.q: A nurse creates a quiet, private, comfortable room that preserves a patient’s dignity and peace. Which carative factor does this reflect?
alt.a: Providing a supportive, protective, or corrective environment
alt.ex: This factor creates a physical and nonphysical healing environment promoting wholeness, beauty, comfort, dignity, and peace.
w: Cultivating a sensitivity to oneself and to others
This factor involves accepting oneself and others and maturing toward self-actualization.
Forming a human-altruistic value system
This factor uses loving kindness and appropriate self-disclosure to build an alliance.
Promoting and expressing positive and negative feelings
This factor supports and accepts patients’ feelings and sharing in the relationship.

items.q: A nurse caring for a mother of a young child mentions that the nurse also raised children and understands the worry. Which Watson carative factor does this appropriate self-disclosure represent?
items.a: Forming a human-altruistic value system
items.ex: Table 7.1 gives sharing a common personal experience, such as child rearing, as an example of forming a human-altruistic value system.
w: Instilling faith-hope
Instilling faith-hope offers purpose and direction in finding meaning in illness.
Meeting human needs
Meeting human needs means intentionally helping with basic needs with a caring consciousness.
Allowing for spiritual forces
This factor lets spiritual forces provide better understanding of self and patient.

alt.q: Which example in practice matches Watson’s carative factor of promoting transpersonal teaching-learning?
alt.a: Learning together as the patient acquires self-care skills
alt.ex: In this factor the nurse and patient learn together while the patient assumes responsibility for learning self-care skills.
w: Sharing a personal experience in common with the patient
Appropriate self-disclosure illustrates forming a human-altruistic value system.
Supporting and accepting the patient’s expressed feelings
This illustrates promoting and expressing positive and negative feelings.
Applying critical thinking to make sound clinical judgments
This illustrates using creative problem-solving caring processes.

items.q: From what source did Swanson develop her theory of caring?
items.a: Three perinatal studies of patients and professional caregivers
items.ex: Swanson analyzed stories from women who miscarried, NICU parents and professionals, and socially at-risk mothers receiving public health care.
w: Interpretation of stories told by expert medical-surgical nurses
Interpreting expert nurses’ stories is how Benner described caring.
Observations of caring patterns across many world cultures
Studying caring across cultures is Leininger’s transcultural focus.
A philosophy of caring-healing consciousness and carative factors
Caring-healing consciousness and carative factors belong to Watson’s model.

alt.q: How does Swanson define caring?
alt.a: A nurturing way of relating to an individual with commitment and responsibility
alt.ex: Swanson defines caring as a nurturing way of relating to someone toward whom one feels personal commitment and responsibility.
w: A domain of care that sets nursing apart from other disciplines
Care as nursing’s distinguishing domain is Leininger’s view.
A word for being connected, in which things matter to people
This describes Benner’s view that caring is primary.
A consciousness that places care before cure in all settings
Placing care before cure through consciousness is Watson’s transpersonal theory.

items.q: A nurse helps a patient newly diagnosed with diabetes mellitus choose exercises the patient can do and diet changes the patient is willing to make. Which aspect of caring is the nurse demonstrating?
items.a: Enabling
items.ex: Enabling is when the nurse and patient work together to identify alternatives in approaches to care and resources.
w: Being with
Being with means being emotionally present, not jointly identifying alternatives.
Maintaining belief
Maintaining belief sustains faith in the patient’s capacity to get through an event.
Doing for
Doing for means doing for the patient as one would for oneself, not working out options together.

alt.q: When a nurse uses enabling with a patient, what role does the nurse take on?
alt.a: Patient advocate
alt.ex: The textbook states that in enabling, the nurse becomes a patient advocate while helping identify care alternatives and resources.
w: Primary decision maker
Enabling is a partnership; the nurse does not make decisions for the patient.
Disease manager
Enabling focuses on individualized alternatives, not a disease-centered role.
Passive observer
Enabling requires active work with the patient to find alternatives.

items.q: A nurse begins caring for a patient with a newly diagnosed chronic illness. Which question best helps the nurse understand the context of the patient’s illness?
items.a: “How does your illness affect what you do each day?”
items.ex: Asking how the illness affects daily life reveals the patient’s perception and context, helping individualize interventions.
w: “Which medications did your provider order for you?”
Medication lists come from the record and do not reveal the patient’s perception of illness.
“What laboratory values did your provider tell you about?”
Laboratory values describe the disease, not how the patient experiences it.
“Do you have any allergies to foods or medications?”
Allergy screening is important but does not explore the context of the illness.

alt.q: Why does the textbook recommend learning the context of a patient’s illness before choosing interventions?
alt.a: It is more successful than choosing by symptoms or disease alone
alt.ex: Knowing the context helps individualize interventions, which works better than selecting care only from symptoms or disease process.
w: It shortens the time needed to complete the nursing assessment
The reason given is better individualized care, not a shorter assessment.
It allows the nurse to rely less on the patient’s own perceptions
Context is learned from the patient’s perceptions, so reliance on them increases.
It replaces the need to assess physical signs and symptoms
Context supplements, not replaces, assessment of signs and symptoms.

items.q: According to Box 7.2, which outcomes are associated with nurses’ caring practices? Select all that apply.
o: Increased patient satisfaction with nursing care
Evidence shows a strong, positive relationship between nurse caring behaviors and patient satisfaction.
Reduced workplace stress and greater job satisfaction for nurses
Caring practices benefit nursing staff by reducing stress and increasing job satisfaction.
Improved functional status, self-efficacy, coping, and self-care
Box 7.2 lists these patient outcomes of caring practices.
Shorter time spent with each patient during a shift
Caring is not linked to less time; presence encourages nurses to spend more time with patients.
Less need for patients to be involved in decision making
Caring promotes partnership and advocacy, increasing patient involvement.
items.ex: Box 7.2 links caring to patient satisfaction, nurse job satisfaction, less workplace stress, and better functional status and self-care.

alt.q: Based on Box 7.2, which nurse actions improve patient and family caregiver satisfaction? Select all that apply.
o: Including the patient’s specific requests in the plan of care
Incorporating patients’ specific requests improves satisfaction.
Explaining why a request cannot be met right away
Communicating reasons a request cannot be met immediately also improves satisfaction.
Listening to the patient’s stories and concerns
Patients feel care is individualized and report greater satisfaction when nurses listen.
Declining requests without explanation to save time
Evidence shows satisfaction rises when nurses explain why a request cannot be met.
Limiting family questions about the prognosis
Nurses should ask patients and families whether they have questions about illness and prognosis.
alt.ex: Correct: Including the patient’s specific requests in the plan of care; Explaining why a request cannot be met right away; Listening to the patient’s stories and concerns.

items.q: According to Box 7.2, which benefits result from nursing presence? Select all that apply.
o: Builds trust
Nursing presence builds trust between nurse and patient.
Identifies patient educational needs
Presence helps the nurse identify what the patient needs to learn.
Reduces patient fear and anxiety
Presence reduces fear and anxiety.
Elicits important health care information
Patients share important information when the nurse provides presence.
Eliminates the need for patient teaching
Presence identifies educational needs; it does not replace teaching.
Requires constant physical contact with the patient
Presence can be quietly sitting with a patient; touch is not required.
items.ex: Presence, being with and doing for a patient, builds trust, identifies educational needs, elicits information, and reduces fear and anxiety.

alt.q: A nurse wants to provide presence for an anxious patient. Which actions reflect presence as described in Box 7.2? Select all that apply.
o: Quietly sitting with the patient
Presence includes quietly sitting with a patient.
A dedicated one-on-one physical interaction
Presence can be a dedicated one-on-one physical interaction.
Doing for the patient
Being with and doing for are components of presence.
Checking the monitor from the doorway
Observing from a distance lacks the being with that defines presence.
Leaving written information and stepping out
Handing off information without being with the patient does not provide presence.
alt.ex: Correct: Quietly sitting with the patient; A dedicated one-on-one physical interaction; Doing for the patient.

items.q: Which statements describe Watson’s transpersonal caring theory? Select all that apply.
o: It places care before cure
Watson’s theory rejects the disease orientation and places care before cure.
It is a holistic model supporting a conscious intention to care
The model supports the nurse’s conscious intention to care to promote healing and wholeness.
Its major components include carative factors and connectedness
Transpersonal care, carative factors, and connectedness are its major components.
It describes five caring processes from perinatal studies
Five caring processes from perinatal studies describe Swanson’s theory.
It focuses on the disease orientation to health care
Watson’s theory explicitly rejects the disease orientation.
items.ex: Watson’s model is holistic, places care before cure, and centers on transpersonal care, carative factors, and connectedness.

alt.q: A nurse practices from Watson’s transpersonal caring perspective. Which goals guide the nurse? Select all that apply.
o: Preserving the person’s dignity and humanity
Transpersonal caring seeks to protect, enhance, and preserve dignity and humanity.
Promoting wholeness and inner harmony
The nurse looks for deeper sources of inner healing to preserve wholeness and inner harmony.
Creating a caring-healing environment
Creating caring-healing environments is crucial to the nurse-patient relationship in Watson’s model.
Focusing care mainly on curing the disease
Watson places care before cure and rejects a disease focus.
Keeping conversations brief and informational
Watson calls for meaningful conversations, not brief reporting of information.
alt.ex: Correct: Preserving the person’s dignity and humanity; Promoting wholeness and inner harmony; Creating a caring-healing environment.

items.q: Caring is often invisible when a nurse and patient share a relationship of mutual respect, but its absence is obvious.
items.a: True
items.ex: The textbook notes caring often goes unnoticed in a respectful relationship, whereas disinterest or avoidance quickly conveys an uncaring attitude.
items.ww: Patients quickly recognize when nurses fail to relate to them, so absence of caring is readily noticed.

alt.q: Patients usually cannot tell when a nurse is simply going through the motions of care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients quickly know when nurses fail to relate to them, as in the patient who sensed the nurse was always “walking out.”
alt.ww: The book’s example shows a patient readily detecting a nurse who showed little caring while teaching.

items.q: In a caring relationship, a mutual give-and-take develops as the nurse and patient come to know each other.
items.a: True
items.ex: Caring is relational, so the relationship is much more than one person doing tasks for another.
items.ww: The textbook describes caring as mutual, not a one-directional delivery of tasks.

alt.q: A caring nurse-patient relationship is mainly one person completing tasks for another.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book states a caring relationship is much more than doing tasks; a mutual give-and-take develops.
alt.ww: Caring is relational and reciprocal, so describing it as task completion misses its essence.

items.q: Because caring is universal, a caring act is the same regardless of a patient’s needs, problems, and values.
items.a: False
items.ex: Leininger states a caring act depends on the patient’s needs, problems, and values, and its expression differs for each patient.
items.ww: Caring is universal, but its expressions vary across people and cultures, so acts must be individualized.

alt.q: Nurses need to learn culturally specific behaviors and words that reflect caring in different cultures.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Leininger’s theory holds that effective caring requires learning culturally specific caring behaviors and words.
alt.ww: Because caring expressions vary by culture, using only the nurse’s own expressions may fail to meet patients’ needs.

items.q: Leininger’s theory states that care, unlike [[cure]], helps an individual or group improve a human condition.
items.ex: Leininger distinguishes care from cure, describing care as an essential human need that improves the human condition.

alt.q: Watson’s transpersonal caring theory places care before [[cure]].
alt.ex: Leininger distinguishes care from cure, describing care as an essential human need that improves the human condition.
