items.q: Research on nurse caring behaviors as perceived by patients shows what about the affective dimension of nursing care?
items.a: Patients clearly value it, and it reflects the art of nursing
items.ex: Patients still value task effectiveness, but they clearly value the affective dimension, which reflects the art of nursing.
w: Patients value it only after their physical needs are fully met
The book does not rank affective care below tasks; patients clearly value both.
Patients consider it less important than nurses’ technical skill
Patients continue to value task skill but clearly value the affective dimension as well.
Patients rarely notice it during a short hospital stay
Patients readily perceive caring behaviors, which influence their satisfaction.

alt.q: Which statement best summarizes what patients value in nursing care?
alt.a: Both effective task performance and the affective dimension of care
alt.ex: Patients value nurses’ effectiveness in tasks and clearly value the affective dimension, the art of nursing.
w: Mainly the speed with which nurses complete procedures
Speed is not what patients emphasize; they value effectiveness and the affective dimension.
Only the technical accuracy of nursing procedures
Technical skill matters, but patients also clearly value caring behaviors.
Mainly the nurse’s ability to explain medical diagnoses
Explanation is one behavior; the key finding is valuing both tasks and affective care.

items.q: A patient says to the nurse, “The nurses here really seem to know what’s important to me.” According to the Caring Behavior Inventory study, which nurse behaviors most likely contributed to this perception?
items.a: Knowing, listening, and being present
items.ex: The CBI study found that caring behaviors such as knowing, listening, and being present contributed to patient satisfaction.
w: Rapid completion of assigned tasks
Speed of tasks was not identified as the caring behavior behind the perception.
Detailed technical explanations
Technical information alone was not the behavior identified; knowing, listening, and presence were.
Strict adherence to unit routines
Following routines does not convey that nurses know what is important to the patient.

alt.q: According to the CBI study in Table 7.3, which factors had no relation to patients’ perception of nurses’ carative-caring behavior?
alt.a: Prior hospitalizations and patient income level
alt.ex: The study found prior hospitalizations and income level were unrelated to perceptions of carative-caring behavior.
w: Nurses’ listening and being present
Listening and presence did contribute to patient satisfaction.
Nurses knowing what was important
Patients perceived that nurses knew what was important to them, which affected perceptions.
Nurses’ knowing of the patient’s story
Knowing the patient was among the caring behaviors that contributed to satisfaction.

items.q: A nurse wants to truly hear a patient’s story. Which action does the textbook recommend first?
items.a: Refine listening skills and take time to sit and make eye contact
items.ex: To really hear a patient’s story, start by refining listening skills and take time to sit and make eye contact.
w: Review the chart thoroughly so the patient need not repeat details
Chart review does not replace listening to the patient’s own story.
Ask a series of closed questions to keep the story focused
Closed questions limit the story; the book emphasizes listening and presence.
Stand at the bedside so the conversation stays brief and efficient
The book specifically advises sitting and making eye contact while listening.

alt.q: Why is knowing the patient’s story critical, according to Table 7.3?
alt.a: It helps identify and correct missing information and design individualized care
alt.ex: Knowing the story helps collect clinical and personal information, correct missing information, and design individualized care.
w: It allows the nurse to skip the physical assessment
The story complements, not replaces, clinical assessment.
It reduces the need for family involvement in care
Knowing the story does not reduce family involvement; affiliation needs remain important.
It ensures the patient follows the provider’s orders
The purpose is individualized care, not simply ensuring compliance.

items.q: In the study using HCAHPS surveys, which nursing care actions significantly improved patients’ perceptions of hospitalization?
items.a: Providing presence and answering or getting answers to questions
items.ex: Care actions that improved perceptions included presence, answering questions, pain and comfort measures, respecting culture and values, and coordinating therapies.
w: Limiting visitors and shortening patient conversations
Neither action was identified; presence and communication improved perceptions.
Reducing pain assessments and comfort measures
Implementing pain and comfort measures improved perceptions, not reducing them.
Assigning a different nurse each shift for variety
Continuity, not variety, supports knowing patients; this was not a care action identified.

alt.q: When is the HCAHPS survey described in Table 7.3 given to patients?
alt.a: After discharge from the hospital
alt.ex: The HCAHPS survey was given after discharge to correlate perceptions of nursing care actions with the hospital experience.
w: On the day of admission
Admission is too early to rate the overall hospital experience.
Before each nursing procedure
The survey measures the overall hospital experience, not individual procedures.
During the initial nursing assessment
The survey is not part of assessment; it follows discharge.

items.q: When patients sense that health care providers are sensitive, empathetic, compassionate, and interested in them as people, what usually happens?
items.a: They become active partners in the plan of care
items.ex: Perceived sensitivity and genuine interest lead patients to become active partners in their care.
w: They depend more on staff for all decisions
Caring promotes partnership, not greater dependence for decisions.
They ask fewer questions about their care
Caring encourages patients to ask questions and engage in care.
They need fewer nursing interventions overall
The book links caring to partnership, not to fewer interventions.

alt.q: A nurse wants a hesitant patient to become an active partner in the plan of care. Which approach is most likely to help?
alt.a: Show sensitivity, empathy, and genuine interest in the patient as a person
alt.ex: Patients who sense providers are sensitive, empathetic, compassionate, and interested in them usually become active partners.
w: Provide a detailed written schedule of all planned treatments
Information alone does not convey the caring that draws patients into partnership.
Remind the patient that following the plan is required for discharge
Pressure does not convey caring and does not build partnership.
Make the care decisions so the patient feels less burdened
Making decisions for the patient works against active partnership.

items.q: A review of nursing interventions based on Watson’s Theory of Human Caring reported which patient outcome?
items.a: Reduced emotional strain and improved self-management confidence
items.ex: Nurse caring interventions based on Watson’s theory reduced patients’ emotional strain and improved self-management confidence.
w: Reduced need for pain medication and shorter stays
These outcomes were not reported in the review described.
Fewer family visits and less family involvement
Reduced family involvement was not an outcome; caring includes family affiliation.
Lower nurse engagement but higher patient trust
Nurse engagement and job satisfaction increased, not decreased.

alt.q: According to the review of Watson-based interventions, how were nurses and nursing students affected?
alt.a: Nurses’ job satisfaction and students’ clinical confidence increased
alt.ex: Nurses’ job satisfaction and engagement increased, and students gained clinical confidence and awareness of caring behaviors.
w: Nurses’ workload decreased and students’ grades improved
The review reported satisfaction, engagement, and confidence, not workload or grades.
Nurses’ engagement fell as documentation time increased
Nurse engagement increased rather than fell.
Students relied more on routines than caring behaviors
Students’ awareness of caring behaviors increased.

items.q: A patient who had breast cancer 2 years ago needs another breast biopsy. She is fearful and has many questions. Which response by the nurse best reflects caring based on knowing the patient?
items.a: Obtain assistance from an oncology nurse specialist to address her questions
items.ex: The textbook example shows the nurse seeking an oncology nurse specialist rather than giving a lengthy description of the procedure.
w: Give a lengthy description of why the biopsy is necessary
The book contrasts this with the caring response; a long description does not meet her needs.
Reassure her that the biopsy will most likely be negative
False reassurance dismisses her fears and cannot be promised.
Encourage her to save her questions for after the biopsy
Delaying her questions ignores her fear and expressed needs.

alt.q: What does the breast biopsy example in the textbook illustrate about caring?
alt.a: Knowing patients helps the nurse choose the caring approach that best fits them
alt.ex: Knowing patients helps nurses select caring approaches most appropriate to their needs, such as calling on a specialist.
w: Detailed procedural teaching is always the most caring response
The example shows that a lengthy explanation was not the best approach for this patient.
Nurses should avoid involving other health care professionals
The caring response involved an oncology nurse specialist.
Patients with cancer histories prefer minimal information
The example concerns individualizing care, not withholding information.

items.q: A nurse is beginning clinical practice and wants to provide the caring behaviors that matter most to each patient. What should the nurse do first?
items.a: Assess what the patient expects from the nurse
items.ex: The textbook advises assessing what your patient expects and building relationships to learn which caring behaviors matter to them.
w: Use the caring behaviors the nurse values most personally
The nurse’s preferences may differ from the patient’s; the patient’s expectations come first.
Apply the same caring behaviors to every assigned patient
Caring is individualized; behaviors that matter differ among patients.
Wait until the patient complains to adjust care
Assessment should be proactive rather than waiting for complaints.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of patients’ perceptions of caring?
alt.a: “I need to learn which caring behaviors are important to each patient.”
alt.ex: Building nurse-patient relationships helps learn which caring behaviors each patient values.
w: “Patients mostly care that I finish my tasks on time.”
Patients value task effectiveness but clearly value the affective dimension too.
“Every patient defines caring in the same way.”
Perceptions of caring differ, so the nurse assesses each patient’s expectations.
“My caring behaviors matter less than my clinical skills.”
Patients clearly value caring behaviors, which reflect the art of nursing.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “The nurses here talk openly with my wife and let her help with my care.” Which factor of the Caring Assessment Tool does this reflect?
items.a: Affiliation needs
items.ex: Affiliation needs items include being responsive to the family, talking openly with them, and allowing their involvement.
w: Basic human needs
Basic human needs items include food, sleep, and feeling less worried.
Mutual problem solving
Mutual problem solving involves exploring alternatives and figuring out questions with the patient.
Healing environment
Healing environment items include checking on the patient, comfort, privacy, and careful body handling.

alt.q: A patient states, “The nurses make sure I get my meals and help me with sleep.” Which CAT factor does this reflect?
alt.a: Basic human needs
alt.ex: Getting food, help with sleep, and feeling less worried are items under basic human needs.
w: Affiliation needs
Affiliation needs involve the family’s involvement and communication.
Attentive reassurance
Attentive reassurance includes availability, interest, hope, and anticipating needs.
Encouraging manner
Encouraging manner includes supporting beliefs and encouraging questions.

items.q: A patient says, “The nurses here ask me what I know and help me figure out what questions to ask my doctor.” Which CAT factor is the patient describing?
items.a: Mutual problem solving
items.ex: Mutual problem solving includes asking what the patient knows and helping the patient figure out questions to ask.
w: Human respect
Human respect items include listening, accepting, treating kindly, and paying attention.
Appreciation of unique meanings
This factor reflects concern for how the patient views things and what is important to them.
Attentive reassurance
Attentive reassurance includes being available, interested, and anticipating needs.

alt.q: Which patient statement reflects the CAT factor appreciation of unique meanings?
alt.a: “The nurses know what is important to me.”
alt.ex: Appreciation of unique meanings includes knowing what is important to the patient and acknowledging inner feelings.
w: “The nurses make sure I get my meals.”
Ensuring food reflects basic human needs.
“The nurses let my family be involved.”
Family involvement reflects affiliation needs.
“The nurses respect my privacy.”
Respecting privacy is an item under healing environment.

items.q: Why should a beginning nurse become familiar with instruments such as the Caring Assessment Tool and the Caring Behavior Inventory-24?
items.a: To appreciate which behaviors hospitalized patients identify as caring
items.ex: These caring assessments help beginning professionals appreciate the types of behaviors patients identify as caring.
w: To diagnose patients’ medical conditions more accurately
Caring instruments measure perceived caring, not medical diagnoses.
To replace the need for patient satisfaction surveys
They relate to satisfaction but do not replace satisfaction surveys.
To measure nurses’ technical skill in performing procedures
They measure caring behaviors as perceived by patients, not technical skill.

alt.q: A nurse manager wants to measure how patients perceive nurses’ caring on a unit. Which tool is designed for this purpose?
alt.a: Caring Assessment Tool (CAT)
alt.ex: The CAT is one of several instruments that measure caring as perceived by patients.
w: Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)
The GCS measures level of consciousness, not perceived caring.
Braden Scale (BS)
The Braden Scale assesses pressure injury risk, not caring.
Morse Fall Scale (MFS)
The Morse Fall Scale assesses fall risk, not caring.

items.q: According to Table 7.3, which nursing care actions improved patients’ perceptions of hospitalization? Select all that apply.
o: Providing presence
Presence was among the care actions that improved perceptions.
Implementing pain and comfort measures
Pain and comfort measures improved patient perceptions.
Showing respect for the patient’s culture and values
Respect for culture and values improved perceptions.
Coordinating therapies from other health care disciplines
Coordinating and managing interdisciplinary therapies improved perceptions.
Limiting answers to questions to save time
Answering or getting answers to questions improved perceptions.
Reducing time spent at the bedside
Presence, not reduced bedside time, improved perceptions.
items.ex: HCAHPS findings tied presence, answering questions, comfort measures, cultural respect, and coordination of therapies to better perceptions.

alt.q: A nurse wants to improve patients’ ratings of their hospital experience. Based on Table 7.3, which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Answer or get answers to patients’ questions
Answering or getting answers to questions improved perceptions.
Coordinate therapies with other disciplines
Coordinating and managing therapies from other disciplines improved perceptions.
Implement pain and comfort measures
Pain and comfort measures were among the effective care actions.
Focus on completing tasks rather than presence
Presence was one of the care actions that improved perceptions.
Use the same approach regardless of culture
Showing respect for the patient’s culture and values improved perceptions.
alt.ex: Correct: Answer or get answers to patients’ questions; Coordinate therapies with other disciplines; Implement pain and comfort measures.

Listening is an item under human respect.

Acceptance is an item under human respect.

alt.q: Which items belong to the CAT factor “healing environment”? Select all that apply.

Respecting privacy is a healing environment item.

Careful handling of the body is a healing environment item.
Encourage me to ask questions

Help me figure out questions to ask
This item belongs to mutual problem solving.
alt.ex: Correct: Check on me; Respect my privacy; Treat my body carefully.

“The nurses anticipate my needs.”
Anticipating needs is an attentive reassurance item.

“The nurses help me with sleep.”

items.ex: Attentive reassurance items include being available, seeming interested, supporting hope, helping belief in self, and anticipating needs.

alt.q: Which statements reflect the CAT factor “encouraging manner”? Select all that apply.

Encouraging questions is an encouraging manner item.
“The nurses help me deal with bad feelings.”

Supporting beliefs is an encouraging manner item.
“The nurses respect my privacy.”
Respecting privacy belongs to healing environment.
“The nurses are available.”
Availability belongs to attentive reassurance.
alt.ex: Correct: “The nurses encourage me to ask questions.”; “The nurses help me deal with bad feelings.”; “The nurses support my beliefs.”

alt.ww: Studies in Table 7.3 show caring behaviors contribute to patient satisfaction and ratings.
