items.q: What does the term ethic refer to?
items.a: The ideals of right and wrong behavior
items.ex: The textbook defines ethic as the ideals of right and wrong behavior.
w: The legal limits of a nurse’s scope of practice
Legal scope of practice is a legal concept, not the definition of ethic.
The policies that govern a health care agency
Agency policies are rules, not the ideals of right and wrong behavior.
The scientific evidence that guides nursing care
Scientific evidence guides practice but is not what ethic means.

alt.q: Which term refers to the ideals of right and wrong behavior?
alt.a: Ethic
alt.ex: An ethic refers to ideals of right and wrong behavior, guiding what behavior is appropriate in patient encounters.
w: Policy
A policy is an agency rule, not an ideal of right and wrong.
Standard
A standard sets expected performance, not the ideals of right and wrong.
Theory
A theory explains phenomena; it is not the term for ideals of right and wrong.

items.q: How does an ethic of care differ from decision making based only on analytical principles?
items.a: It places caring at the center of decision making
items.ex: Nurses do not decide solely on intellectual or analytical principles; an ethic of care places caring at the center.
w: It removes ethical principles from clinical decisions
An ethic of care is itself an ethical approach; it does not remove ethics.
It relies on the provider’s orders for every decision
An ethic of care centers on caring and relationships, not only on orders.
It bases decisions on agency efficiency and cost
Efficiency and cost are not the center of an ethic of care.

alt.q: A nurse facing a difficult decision considers the relationship with the patient and the patient’s unique personhood, not only analytical rules. Which approach is the nurse using?
alt.a: An ethic of care
alt.ex: An ethic of care guides decisions by attending to relationships and giving priority to each patient’s unique personhood.
w: A task-oriented approach
A task focus does not center decisions on relationships and personhood.
A disease-oriented approach
A disease focus addresses pathology, not the patient’s unique personhood.
A purely analytical approach
The nurse is going beyond intellectual or analytical principles alone.

items.q: An ethic of care is mainly concerned with which of the following?
items.a: Relationships between people and the nurse’s character and attitude
items.ex: An ethic of care concerns relationships between people and the nurse’s character and attitude toward others.
w: Efficient allocation of staff and unit resources
Resource allocation is an administrative concern, not the focus of an ethic of care.
Accurate completion of procedures and documentation
Technical accuracy matters but is not the focus of an ethic of care.
Strict application of agency rules to all patients
Uniform rule application ignores relationships and each patient’s personhood.

alt.q: Which nurse characteristic is most closely tied to functioning from an ethic of care?
alt.a: A caring attitude toward others in each relationship
alt.ex: An ethic of care is concerned with the nurse’s character and attitude toward others within relationships.
w: Speed in completing assigned procedures
Speed reflects efficiency, not the character and attitude central to an ethic of care.
Detailed knowledge of agency policy
Policy knowledge is useful but is not the focus of an ethic of care.
Skill in operating complex equipment
Technical skill is valued but does not define an ethic of care.

items.q: Nurses who function from an ethic of care are especially sensitive to which situation?
items.a: Unequal relationships that can lead to abuse of power
items.ex: An ethic of care makes nurses sensitive to unequal relationships leading to abuse of one person’s power over another, intentional or otherwise.
w: Disagreements about staffing among unit managers
Staffing disputes are not the focus; power imbalance with patients is.
Delays in receiving supplies from central supply
Supply delays are operational, not the relational concern of an ethic of care.
Changes in agency documentation requirements
Documentation changes are administrative, not about unequal relationships.

alt.q: According to the textbook, abuse of one person’s power over another in health care can be what?
alt.a: Intentional or unintentional
alt.ex: The book notes the abuse of power in unequal relationships may be intentional or otherwise.
w: Only intentional and deliberate
The book specifies abuse of power can occur intentionally or otherwise.
Only possible between two nurses
Unequal relationships most often involve patients and families with professionals.
Rare in modern health care settings
Patients are often on unequal footing with professionals, so the risk is common.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient who is in severe pain, has received little information about the diagnosis, and is in an unfamiliar hospital setting. Why is this patient at risk for an unequal relationship with health care professionals?
items.a: Illness, lack of information, pain, and unfamiliar circumstances reduce the patient’s footing
items.ex: Patients are on unequal footing because of illness, lack of information, regression from pain and suffering, and unfamiliar circumstances.
w: The patient has chosen to give up decision making to the staff
The imbalance arises from the patient’s situation, not from a choice to give up decisions.
Professionals are legally required to make decisions for patients
There is no such requirement; the imbalance comes from the patient’s circumstances.
The patient’s family has more authority than the patient
Family authority is not the reason given for unequal footing.

alt.q: Which factor does the textbook identify as causing regression that places patients on unequal footing with professionals?
alt.a: Pain and suffering
alt.ex: Regression caused by pain and suffering is one reason patients and families are on unequal footing.
w: Strong family support
Family support is not identified as a cause of regression.
Previous health care experience
Prior experience is not a cause listed for unequal footing.
Clear discharge instructions
Clear information reduces, rather than causes, inequality.

items.q: A patient on a busy unit uses the call light frequently because of high physical and emotional care needs. The nurse overhears staff saying, “It’s your turn,” and “I just did it.” Which action by the nurse best reflects an ethic of care?
items.a: Raise the concern with the team and refocus care on the patient’s needs
items.ex: An ethic of care places the nurse as the patient’s advocate and gives priority to the patient’s unique personhood.
w: Ignore the comments because the patient’s needs are being met
These comments signal care driven by convenience rather than the patient’s needs.
Suggest limiting the patient’s access to the call system
Restricting the call system abuses power over a vulnerable patient.
Ask the patient to group requests to reduce staff workload
Placing staff convenience first ignores the patient’s needs and personhood.

alt.q: In the Reflect Now scenario, staff alternate answering a frequent call light, saying “It’s your turn.” What concern does this raise from an ethic of care perspective?
alt.a: Staff convenience is placed above the patient’s needs and personhood
alt.ex: An ethic of care gives priority to each patient’s unique personhood; turn-taking remarks shift focus to staff convenience.
w: Staff are failing to document each call accurately
Documentation is not the issue; the attitude toward the patient is.
The patient is receiving more care than is needed
The patient has real physical and emotional needs, so the care is warranted.
Staff are spending too much time on emotional care
Emotional care is part of the patient’s needs, not excess.

items.q: Which role does an ethic of care place the nurse in?
items.a: The patient’s advocate
items.ex: An ethic of care places the nurse as the patient’s advocate and guides clinical judgment and decisions about ethical dilemmas.
w: The patient’s guardian
A guardian has legal decision authority; the ethic of care positions the nurse as advocate.
The agency’s representative
The nurse’s ethic of care focuses on the patient, not on representing the agency.
The provider’s assistant
An ethic of care centers on the patient relationship, not on assisting providers.

alt.q: A patient’s family is confused and intimidated during a team meeting about treatment options. Which action best reflects the nurse’s advocate role under an ethic of care?
alt.a: Help the family understand the options and voice their concerns
alt.ex: As advocate, the nurse addresses the unequal footing caused by lack of information and unfamiliar circumstances.
w: Recommend the family accept the team’s preferred option
Steering the family uses the professional’s power instead of advocating for them.
Let the team proceed because the family seems overwhelmed
Proceeding without the family’s understanding ignores the unequal relationship.
Postpone the meeting until the family stops asking questions
Discouraging questions widens the information gap.

items.q: How does an ethic of care help guide decision making about ethical dilemmas?
items.a: By attending to relationships and each patient’s unique personhood
items.ex: An ethic of care guides decisions on ethical dilemmas by attending to relationships and giving priority to each patient’s unique personhood.
w: By applying the same rule to every patient in the same situation
Uniform rules ignore unique personhood, which an ethic of care prioritizes.
By deferring the decision to the most senior health care provider
Deferring decisions does not reflect attending to the patient’s personhood.
By choosing whichever option is most efficient for the agency
Agency efficiency is not the basis for decisions under an ethic of care.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse reflects an ethic of care in clinical judgment?
alt.a: “I need to consider what matters most to this particular patient.”
alt.ex: Giving priority to each patient’s unique personhood is central to how an ethic of care influences clinical judgment.
w: “The policy is the same for everyone, so I don’t need to know him.”
Ignoring the individual contradicts giving priority to unique personhood.
“I’ll decide based only on the facts in the chart.”
Nurses do not decide solely on analytical principles under an ethic of care.
“What’s fastest for the team should guide my decision.”
Efficiency for staff is not the center of an ethic of care.

items.q: According to the textbook, between whom does caring occur?
items.a: Nurse and patient, nurse and nurse, and nurse and other health care professionals
items.ex: Caring is an interaction among nurses, patients, and health care professionals in an atmosphere of mutual respect and trust.
w: Nurse and patient only, never between members of the team
Caring also occurs between nurses and with other professionals.
Patient and family only, with the nurse as an outside observer
The nurse actively participates in caring interactions.
Nurse and health care provider only, separate from the patient
The patient is central to caring interactions.

alt.q: In what atmosphere does the textbook say caring interactions take place?
alt.a: Mutual respect and trust
alt.ex: Caring is an interaction in an atmosphere of mutual respect and trust.
w: Strict hierarchy and control
Hierarchy and control can foster unequal relationships rather than caring.
Competition and urgency
Competition does not support the collaborative environment of caring.
Neutral professional distance
Caring involves connection, not neutral distance.

items.q: In the collaborative environment described in the ethic of care, what does the nurse provide to help achieve desired outcomes?
items.a: Encouragement, hope, support, and compassion
items.ex: In this collaborative environment, the nurse provides encouragement, hope, support, and compassion to help achieve desired outcomes.
w: Instructions, rules, deadlines, and correction
These are directive and do not describe the caring collaboration in the text.
Supervision, evaluation, discipline, and reports
These are management functions, not what the nurse offers in caring.
Medications, equipment, supplies, and forms
These are resources, not the caring elements named in the text.

alt.q: A patient recovering from a stroke is discouraged about progress. Which response by the nurse best reflects the caring described in the ethic of care?
alt.a: “You have worked hard this week. Let’s look at what you can do now.”
alt.ex: Offering encouragement, hope, and support helps the patient work toward desired outcomes.
w: “Recovery is slow for everyone, so try not to think about it.”
This dismisses the patient’s feelings rather than offering support.
“You will need to work harder if you want to go home.”
This adds pressure rather than offering encouragement and compassion.
“Your therapist can answer questions about your progress.”
Redirecting avoids the nurse’s role of offering hope and support.

items.q: A nursing student asks why caring is considered more than a personal trait in professional nursing. Which response by the instructor is most accurate?
items.a: “Caring is a professional, ethical covenant that nursing has with the public.”
items.ex: The textbook describes caring as a professional, ethical covenant with the public and a standard for clinical judgment.
w: “Caring is optional once a nurse has strong technical skills.”
Caring is a covenant and a standard, not an optional extra.
“Caring matters mainly when patients are unable to speak.”
Caring applies to every patient encounter, not only nonverbal patients.
“Caring is a legal contract signed between nurse and patient.”
Caring is an ethical covenant, not a signed legal contract.

alt.q: Besides being an ethical covenant with the public, caring is also described as what in the critical thinking process?
alt.a: A standard applied in critical thinking for clinical judgment
alt.ex: Caring is a standard applied in the critical thinking process for clinical judgment.
w: A step that replaces assessment of the patient
Caring supports, not replaces, assessment in clinical judgment.
An optional step used only in end-of-life care
Caring is a standard in every patient encounter, not only end-of-life care.
A final check performed after decisions are made
Caring informs judgment throughout, not only after decisions.

items.q: A nurse explains a procedure using medical terms, and the patient, who is anxious and in an unfamiliar setting, nods but looks confused. Which action by the nurse best reflects an ethic of care?
items.a: Check the patient’s understanding and explain again in plain language
items.ex: Lack of information and unfamiliar circumstances create unequal footing, so the caring nurse closes the information gap.
w: Proceed because the patient nodded in agreement
A nod from a confused, anxious patient does not show understanding; proceeding exploits unequal footing.
Ask the family to sign for the patient instead
Bypassing the patient disregards the patient’s unique personhood.
Document that the patient received the information
Documenting does not address the patient’s lack of understanding.

alt.q: Why should a nurse working from an ethic of care make sure a confused patient understands information about care?
alt.a: Lack of information places patients on unequal footing with professionals
alt.ex: An ethic of care makes nurses sensitive to power imbalances that arise when patients lack information.
w: Patients who understand care need less nursing time
Saving time is not the ethical reason; reducing the power imbalance is.
Agency policy requires teaching before every procedure
The reason in the text is the unequal relationship, not policy alone.
Informed patients are less likely to file complaints
Avoiding complaints is not the basis of an ethic of care.

items.q: According to the textbook, why are patients and families often on unequal footing with health care professionals? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s illness
Illness places patients at a disadvantage in relation to professionals.
Lack of information
Lack of information leaves patients and families on unequal footing.
Regression caused by pain and suffering
Pain and suffering can cause regression that weakens the patient’s position.
Unfamiliar circumstances
Unfamiliar settings and events increase patients’ vulnerability.
Higher levels of formal education
Education level is not listed as a cause of unequal footing.
Frequent use of the nurse call system
Call light use is not a cause; it reflects the patient’s needs.
items.ex: Illness, lack of information, regression from pain and suffering, and unfamiliar circumstances place patients on unequal footing.

alt.q: A nurse wants to reduce the power imbalance between a newly admitted patient and the health care team. Which actions address causes named in the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Explain the diagnosis and plan in understandable terms
Providing information addresses the lack of information that creates inequality.
Orient the patient to the unit and routines
Orientation reduces the effect of unfamiliar circumstances.
Manage the patient’s pain promptly
Relieving pain addresses regression caused by pain and suffering.
Limit the patient’s questions to save time
Limiting questions increases the information gap.
Make decisions for the patient to reduce stress
Deciding for the patient reinforces the power imbalance.
alt.ex: Correct: Explain the diagnosis and plan in understandable terms; Orient the patient to the unit and routines; Manage the patient’s pain promptly.

items.q: Which effects of an ethic of care on nursing practice are described in the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Places the nurse as the patient’s advocate
An ethic of care positions the nurse as the patient’s advocate.
Influences the nurse’s clinical judgment
An ethic of care influences clinical judgment.
Helps guide decisions about ethical dilemmas
It guides decisions on ethical dilemmas by attending to relationships.
Bases decisions solely on analytical principles
Nurses do not decide solely on analytical principles; caring is at the center.
Places agency efficiency at the center of care
Caring, not efficiency, is at the center of decision making.
items.ex: An ethic of care makes the nurse an advocate, influences clinical judgment, and guides ethical decisions through attention to relationships.

alt.q: Which statements describe an ethic of care? Select all that apply.
o: It is concerned with relationships between people
An ethic of care focuses on relationships between people.
It involves the nurse’s character and attitude toward others
The nurse’s character and attitude are central to an ethic of care.
It gives priority to each patient’s unique personhood
Ethical decisions give priority to each patient’s unique personhood.
It applies identical decisions to all patients
Uniform decisions ignore unique personhood.
It is unrelated to clinical judgment
An ethic of care directly influences clinical judgment.
alt.ex: Correct: It is concerned with relationships between people; It involves the nurse’s character and attitude toward others; It gives priority to each patient’s unique personhood.

items.q: A nurse is working from an ethic of care. Which behaviors are consistent with this approach? Select all that apply.
o: Speaking up when a colleague dismisses a patient’s request
The nurse acts as advocate when unequal relationships disadvantage a patient.
Considering the patient’s unique values in a care decision
An ethic of care gives priority to the patient’s unique personhood.
Treating colleagues with mutual respect and trust
Caring includes nurse-nurse interactions in an atmosphere of mutual respect and trust.
Withholding information so the patient will not worry
Lack of information worsens unequal footing with professionals.
Deciding care based only on the most efficient option
Efficiency alone does not place caring at the center of decisions.
items.ex: An ethic of care shows in advocacy, attention to personhood, and respectful interactions with colleagues and patients.

alt.q: Which nurse behaviors conflict with an ethic of care? Select all that apply.
o: Using the patient’s lack of information to steer decisions
This abuses power in an unequal relationship.
Treating a frequent call light as a burden to pass off
This puts staff convenience above the patient’s needs.
Basing decisions only on analytical principles
An ethic of care places caring, not analysis alone, at the center.
Advocating for the patient’s expressed preferences
Advocacy is the role an ethic of care gives the nurse.
Offering encouragement and hope to the patient
Encouragement and hope are part of the caring environment.
alt.ex: Correct: Using the patient’s lack of information to steer decisions; Treating a frequent call light as a burden to pass off; Basing decisions only on analytical principles.

items.q: Nurses make professional decisions based solely on intellectual or analytical principles.
items.a: False
items.ex: The textbook states nurses do not decide solely on analytical principles; an ethic of care places caring at the center of decision making.
items.ww: Analytical principles are part of decisions, but caring must be at the center under an ethic of care.

alt.q: An ethic of care places caring at the center of a nurse’s decision making.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Instead of relying only on intellectual or analytical principles, nurses place caring at the center of decisions.
alt.ww: The textbook explicitly contrasts purely analytical decisions with an ethic of care that centers caring.

items.q: Abuse of power in a nurse-patient relationship can occur even when it is unintentional.
items.a: True
items.ex: An ethic of care makes nurses sensitive to abuse of power in unequal relationships, whether intentional or otherwise.
items.ww: The book explicitly says abuse of power may be intentional or otherwise, so good intentions do not prevent it.

alt.q: Abuse of power in health care occurs only when a professional deliberately intends to harm a patient.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The textbook states abuse of one person’s power over another can be intentional or otherwise.
alt.ww: Unintentional actions, such as withholding information, can still exploit a patient’s unequal footing.

items.q: Caring science provides a disciplinary foundation from which nurses deliver individualized patient care.
items.a: True
items.ex: The textbook describes caring science as the disciplinary foundation for individualized patient care.
items.ww: Caring science underpins individualized care, so it is foundational rather than optional.

alt.q: Caring is an interaction that occurs only between a nurse and a patient.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Caring also occurs between nurses and between nurses and other health care professionals.
alt.ww: The book lists nurse-nurse and nurse-professional interactions, not just nurse-patient ones.

items.q: An [[ethic of care]] places caring at the center of a nurse’s decision making.
items.ex: An ethic of care centers caring in decisions rather than relying solely on analytical principles.

alt.q: In health care settings, patients are often on [[unequal]] footing with professionals because of illness and lack of information.
alt.ex: An ethic of care centers caring in decisions rather than relying solely on analytical principles.

items.q: An ethic of care places the nurse as the patient’s [[advocate]].
items.ex: As advocate, the nurse attends to relationships and protects patients from unequal power.

alt.q: An ethic of care gives priority to each patient’s unique [[personhood]] when guiding decisions about ethical dilemmas.
alt.ex: As advocate, the nurse attends to relationships and protects patients from unequal power.

items.q: Which statement best describes the “being there” aspect of nursing presence?
items.a: It includes physical presence along with communication and understanding
items.ex: “Being there” is not only physical presence; it also includes communication and understanding.
w: It means remaining physically in the room while care is delivered
Physical presence alone is not enough; “being there” also requires communication and understanding.
It means completing scheduled tasks quickly so the patient can rest
Efficient task completion is not presence; presence is a person-to-person encounter conveying closeness.
It means checking on the patient from the doorway at set intervals
Brief checks from a distance do not convey the closeness and connectedness of presence.

alt.q: A nurse is described as being truly present with a patient. Which behavior shows this?
alt.a: Being available and responsive to the patient’s expressed needs
alt.ex: A present nurse is available and responsive to a patient’s expressed needs.
w: Staying in the room while charting on the bedside computer
Physical presence alone, without engagement, does not meet the definition of presence.
Limiting conversation so the patient is not overwhelmed
Presence includes communication and understanding, not limiting interaction.
Focusing on the monitor readings rather than the patient’s words
Presence centers on the patient’s expressed needs, not only on equipment data.

items.q: A patient who is awaiting a report of biopsy results tells the nurse, “I can’t stop worrying about what they’ll find.” Which response by the nurse best conveys caring presence?
items.a: Sitting with the patient, making eye contact, and listening to the patient’s concerns
items.ex: Presence during stressful events calms anxiety; eye contact, listening, and remaining at the side create openness.
w: Telling the patient that worrying will not change the biopsy results
This dismisses the patient’s feelings and does not convey closeness or understanding.
Offering to call the health care provider to rush the results
This bypasses the patient’s expressed need for support and does not provide presence.
Suggesting the patient watch television to take the mind off it
Distraction avoids the patient’s concern instead of being with the patient.

alt.q: A patient is preparing for an unfamiliar procedure and appears frightened. Which nursing action best conveys presence?
alt.a: Explaining the procedure thoroughly and coaching the patient through it
alt.ex: Thorough explanations, remaining at the side, and coaching the patient through the experience convey presence.
w: Giving a brief explanation and leaving so the patient can rest
Leaving reduces presence; staying at the patient’s side is part of conveying presence.
Telling the patient the procedure is routine and nothing to fear
Brushing off fear does not provide the reassurance and coaching that presence involves.
Asking family members to wait outside until the procedure ends
Removing support does not convey the nurse’s presence or calm the patient’s fear.

items.q: According to the textbook, which is an outcome of nursing presence?
items.a: A decreased sense of isolation and vulnerability
items.ex: Outcomes of presence include relief of suffering, a decreased sense of isolation and vulnerability, and personal growth.
w: A shorter time spent with each patient
Presence encourages nurses to spend more time with patients, not less.
A greater reliance on medications for comfort
Presence relieves suffering through connection, not by increasing reliance on medications.
A reduced need for patient education
Presence is used together with patient education; it does not replace it.

alt.q: Which outcome is associated with nursing presence for both nurses and patients?
alt.a: Improved mental well-being
alt.ex: Presence results in improved mental well-being for nurses and patients and improved physical well-being in patients.
w: Decreased patient satisfaction with care
Presence increases patient satisfaction with nursing care and the health care system.
Increased emotional detachment of the nurse
Presence involves giving of oneself; it never leaves one unaffected.
Fewer patient- and family-centered rounds
Presence is valuable during patient- and family-centered rounds; it does not reduce them.

items.q: What does Task-oriented touch mean?
items.a: Touch used while performing a task or procedure
items.ex: Contact touch may be task-oriented, caring, or protective; therapeutic touch is a separate complementary therapy.
w: Nonverbal communication such as holding a hand or giving a back massage
That goes with Caring touch.
Touch that protects the nurse or patient, such as bracing to prevent a fall
That goes with Protective touch.
Complementary therapy in which the practitioner’s hands help the patient find inner balance
That goes with Therapeutic touch.

alt.q: What does Caring touch mean?
alt.a: Nonverbal communication such as holding a hand or giving a back massage
alt.ex: Contact touch may be task-oriented, caring, or protective; therapeutic touch is a separate complementary therapy.
w: Touch used while performing a task or procedure
That goes with Task-oriented touch.
Touch that protects the nurse or patient, such as bracing to prevent a fall
That goes with Protective touch.
Complementary therapy in which the practitioner’s hands help the patient find inner balance
That goes with Therapeutic touch.

alt.q: What does Protective touch mean?
alt.a: Touch that protects the nurse or patient, such as bracing to prevent a fall
alt.ex: Contact touch may be task-oriented, caring, or protective; therapeutic touch is a separate complementary therapy.
w: Touch used while performing a task or procedure
That goes with Task-oriented touch.
Nonverbal communication such as holding a hand or giving a back massage
That goes with Caring touch.
Complementary therapy in which the practitioner’s hands help the patient find inner balance
That goes with Therapeutic touch.

alt.q: What does Therapeutic touch mean?
alt.a: Complementary therapy in which the practitioner’s hands help the patient find inner balance
alt.ex: Contact touch may be task-oriented, caring, or protective; therapeutic touch is a separate complementary therapy.
w: Touch used while performing a task or procedure
That goes with Task-oriented touch.
Nonverbal communication such as holding a hand or giving a back massage
That goes with Caring touch.
Touch that protects the nurse or patient, such as bracing to prevent a fall
That goes with Protective touch.

alt.q: Which term means “Touch used while performing a task or procedure”?
alt.a: Task-oriented touch
alt.ex: Contact touch may be task-oriented, caring, or protective; therapeutic touch is a separate complementary therapy.
w: Caring touch
Caring touch: Nonverbal communication such as holding a hand or giving a back massage.
Protective touch
Protective touch: Touch that protects the nurse or patient, such as bracing to prevent a fall.
Therapeutic touch
Therapeutic touch: Complementary therapy in which the practitioner’s hands help the patient find inner balance.

alt.q: Which term means “Nonverbal communication such as holding a hand or giving a back massage”?
alt.a: Caring touch
alt.ex: Contact touch may be task-oriented, caring, or protective; therapeutic touch is a separate complementary therapy.
w: Task-oriented touch
Task-oriented touch: Touch used while performing a task or procedure.
Protective touch
Protective touch: Touch that protects the nurse or patient, such as bracing to prevent a fall.
Therapeutic touch
Therapeutic touch: Complementary therapy in which the practitioner’s hands help the patient find inner balance.

alt.q: Which term means “Touch that protects the nurse or patient, such as bracing to prevent a fall”?
alt.a: Protective touch
alt.ex: Contact touch may be task-oriented, caring, or protective; therapeutic touch is a separate complementary therapy.
w: Task-oriented touch
Task-oriented touch: Touch used while performing a task or procedure.
Caring touch
Caring touch: Nonverbal communication such as holding a hand or giving a back massage.
Therapeutic touch
Therapeutic touch: Complementary therapy in which the practitioner’s hands help the patient find inner balance.

alt.q: Which term means “Complementary therapy in which the practitioner’s hands help the patient find inner balance”?
alt.a: Therapeutic touch
alt.ex: Contact touch may be task-oriented, caring, or protective; therapeutic touch is a separate complementary therapy.
w: Task-oriented touch
Task-oriented touch: Touch used while performing a task or procedure.
Caring touch
Caring touch: Nonverbal communication such as holding a hand or giving a back massage.
Protective touch
Protective touch: Touch that protects the nurse or patient, such as bracing to prevent a fall.

mt.q: Match each type of touch with its description.
pairs: Touch used while performing a task or procedure
Nonverbal communication such as holding a hand or giving a back massage
Touch that protects the nurse or patient, such as bracing to prevent a fall
Complementary therapy in which the practitioner’s hands help the patient find inner balance
mt.ex: Contact touch may be task-oriented, caring, or protective; therapeutic touch is a separate complementary therapy.

items.q: A nurse who feels overwhelmed by a patient’s suffering begins to distance themselves from the patient. How is this use of protective touch likely to affect the patient?
items.a: It elicits negative feelings in the patient
items.ex: When protective touch is used to withdraw emotionally from a patient, it elicits negative feelings in the patient.
w: It increases the patient’s sense of security
Emotional withdrawal does not build security; the textbook says it elicits negative feelings.
It strengthens the nurse-patient relationship
Distancing weakens connection; it does not strengthen the relationship.
It has no effect because no physical contact occurs
Protective touch used for emotional distance does affect the patient, eliciting negative feelings.

alt.q: Which is the most obvious example of protective touch?
alt.a: Holding and bracing a patient to prevent a fall
alt.ex: The most obvious form of protective touch is preventing an accident, such as bracing a patient to avoid a fall.
w: Holding a patient’s hand during a sad conversation
Holding a hand to comfort is an example of caring touch.
Inserting a nasogastric tube gently and skillfully
Touch during a procedure is task-oriented touch.
Directing the hands over a patient’s body to restore balance
This describes therapeutic touch, a complementary therapy.

items.q: A patient is anxious about having a nasogastric tube inserted. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Fully explain the procedure and what the patient will feel
items.ex: Offer comfort first through a full explanation of the procedure and what the patient will feel, then perform it skillfully.
w: Insert the tube quickly to shorten the patient’s discomfort
Speed without explanation does not address anxiety; the procedure should be explained first.
Ask the patient to stay silent during the insertion
The nurse talks quietly with the patient throughout to provide reassurance and support.
Delay the procedure until the patient’s anxiety resolves
The anxiety is addressed through explanation and support, not by postponing needed care.

alt.q: While inserting a nasogastric tube for an anxious patient, which nursing behavior conveys security and competence?
alt.a: Talking quietly with the patient while gently inserting the tube
alt.ex: Skillful, gentle performance with quiet reassurance throughout conveys security and a sense of competence.
w: Working silently so the patient can concentrate on breathing
The textbook advises talking quietly throughout a procedure to reassure and support the patient.
Saving the explanation of the procedure until it is finished
An explanation should come before the procedure, telling the patient what they will feel.
Asking another nurse to insert the tube while the nurse leaves
Leaving does not convey support; the nurse provides comfort during the procedure.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient who has a history of being abused. Before using contact touch, what should the nurse consider first?
items.a: The patient’s past experiences and cultural practices
items.ex: Before any contact touch, be aware of past experiences and culture; for abuse victims, a simple touch may feel threatening.
w: The amount of time available to complete care
Time is not the key consideration; how the patient may perceive touch is.
The nurse’s own preference for touch during care
Touch decisions focus on how the patient accepts and interprets touch, not the nurse’s preference.
Whether the touch will be documented in the record
Documentation is not the priority; understanding the patient’s perception of touch is.

alt.q: Why should a nurse use touch with discretion?
alt.a: Touch conveys many messages and may be perceived as invasive
alt.ex: Because touch conveys many messages, a simple touch may feel invasive to some or threatening to abuse victims.
w: Touch has no effect on a patient’s comfort or security
Caring touch does influence comfort and security, so this is not the reason.
Touch is permitted only when a health care provider orders it
No order is needed; discretion is about how patients perceive and accept touch.
Touch is used only for performing tasks and procedures
Touch can also be caring or protective, not only task-oriented.

items.q: Because most patients permit task-oriented touch, the nurse does not need to tell patients when touch will occur.
items.a: False
items.ex: Patients generally permit task-oriented touch, but it is still important to inform patients when touch occurs.
items.ww: Calling it true ignores the textbook’s point that patients should be informed when touch occurs.

alt.q: Even though most patients allow task-oriented touch, nurses should inform patients when touch will occur.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Patients give nurses license to enter personal space, yet nurses still inform them when touch occurs.
alt.ww: Calling it false assumes permission removes the need to inform, which the textbook does not support.

items.q: Which approach best supports effective listening to a patient?
items.a: Remaining intentionally silent and giving full, focused attention
items.ex: To listen effectively, silence yourself, keep an open mind, and give patients full, focused attention.
w: Planning a reply while the patient is still speaking
Planning replies divides attention; effective listening requires concentrating on what the patient says.
Completing other tasks in the room while the patient talks
Becoming distracted by tasks is a barrier to listening, not an effective approach.
Interrupting often to correct inaccurate statements
Listening is nonjudgmental and accepting; frequent correction blocks the patient’s story.

alt.q: Which description of listening matches the textbook?
alt.a: A planned and deliberate act done in a nonjudgmental manner
alt.ex: Listening is planned and deliberate; the listener is present and engages the patient nonjudgmentally and with acceptance.
w: A passive act that happens naturally during routine care
Listening is planned and deliberate, not passive or automatic.
A quick check of facts to complete the admission form
Listening goes beyond gathering facts; it means taking in, interpreting, and giving back understanding.
A technique used mainly to decide which advice to give
Listening aims to understand what matters to the patient, not to prepare advice.

items.q: A patient with a newly diagnosed chronic illness begins telling the nurse how the illness has changed the patient’s life. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Please go on. I’d like to hear what this has meant for you.”
items.ex: Telling the illness story helps break its distress, and attentive listening is an essential nursing intervention.
w: “Let’s focus on your medications, since that is what matters now.”
Redirecting to tasks ignores the patient’s story and what is at stake for the patient.
“Many patients have the same illness and manage quite well.”
Comparing to others minimizes the patient’s personal concerns and story.
“You should talk about this with the counselor instead.”
Deflecting the story prevents the nurse from listening and knowing the patient.

alt.q: Why is it therapeutic for a patient with a critical illness to tell the story of the illness?
alt.a: It helps the patient break the distress of the illness
alt.ex: Being able to tell the illness story and its meaning helps a patient break the distress of illness.
w: It allows the nurse to skip the physical assessment
Listening complements assessment; it does not replace it.
It lets the nurse correct the patient’s view of the illness
Listening is nonjudgmental and accepting, not a chance to correct the patient.
It shortens the time the nurse needs to spend with the patient
Listening takes time, but that time is worthwhile for the information and relationship gained.

items.q: Which two elements does the textbook identify as facilitating knowing a patient?
items.a: Continuity of care and clinical expertise
items.ex: Continuity of care and clinical expertise facilitate knowing; knowing develops over time and with specialty experience.
w: Shorter length of stay and rapid discharge
Decreased length of stay reduces nurse-patient interactions and hinders knowing.
Standardized checklists and electronic records
Knowing is more than gathering data about clinical signs and conditions.
Rotating assignments and varied units
Fragmented care limits encounters and makes it hard to recognize patient patterns.

alt.q: A nurse cares for the same patient across several shifts during a long illness. Which element of knowing the patient does this best illustrate?
alt.a: Continuity of care
alt.ex: Knowing is best demonstrated when a nurse cares for a patient over time to understand the meaning of an event.
w: Fragmented care
Fragmented care limits encounters and makes knowing the patient difficult.
Task-oriented touch
Task-oriented touch relates to procedures, not to knowing a patient over time.
Protective distancing
Distancing from a patient works against the closeness that knowing requires.

items.q: Which factors contribute to a nurse’s ability to know patients? Select all that apply.
o: Time
Time is listed as a factor that contributes to knowing patients.
Continuity of care
Continuity of care allows the nurse to recognize patient patterns over time.
Teamwork of the nursing staff
Teamwork among nursing staff contributes to knowing patients.
Trust
Trust is listed as a factor that contributes to knowing patients.
Decreased length of stay
Decreased length of stay reduces interactions and is a barrier to knowing.
Economic constraints
Time and economic constraints are barriers to knowing a patient.
items.ex: Time, continuity of care, staff teamwork, trust, and experience help nurses know patients; organizational, time, and economic constraints are barriers.

alt.q: A nurse manager wants to understand why nurses on a unit struggle to know their patients. Which are barriers to knowing patients? Select all that apply.
o: Organizational changes that reduce time with patients
Decreasing nurses’ time with patients harms nurse-patient relationships and knowing.
Decreased length of hospital stay
Shorter stays reduce the number of nurse-patient interactions.
Fragmented patient care
Fragmented care limits encounters, making patient patterns hard to recognize.
Teamwork among the nursing staff
Teamwork contributes to knowing patients; it is not a barrier.
Experience in a specific clinical area
Clinical experience helps a nurse know patients; it is not a barrier.
alt.ex: Correct: Organizational changes that reduce time with patients; Decreased length of hospital stay; Fragmented patient care.

items.q: Knowing a patient is more than gathering data about the patient’s clinical signs and condition.
items.a: True
items.ex: Knowing includes the patient’s pattern of responses and the patient as a person, developed through a caring relationship.
items.ww: Calling it false reduces knowing to data collection, which the textbook explicitly says it exceeds.

alt.q: A nurse can fully know a patient by completing a thorough admission assessment of clinical signs.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Knowing develops over time within a caring relationship and goes beyond collecting clinical data.
alt.ww: Calling it true treats knowing as one-time data gathering, but it develops over time through caring.

items.q: In acute care, not knowing patients contributes to the risk for falls.
items.a: True
items.ex: Nurses who do not know patients are less able to recognize which fall risks apply to a specific patient.
items.ww: Calling it false ignores the textbook link between not knowing patients and both fall risk and actual falls.

alt.q: Not knowing a patient may lower patient satisfaction but has little effect on safety outcomes such as falls.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Not knowing patients contributes to falls and poor understanding of discharge instructions, so it affects safety.
alt.ww: Calling it true overlooks the poor safety outcomes, such as falls, linked to not knowing patients.

items.q: What does Intrapersonal connectedness mean?
items.a: Connected with oneself
items.ex: Spirituality offers connectedness within oneself, with others and the environment, and with the unseen or a higher power.
w: Connected with others and the environment
That goes with Interpersonal.
Connected with the unseen, God, or a higher power
That goes with Transpersonal.

alt.q: What does Interpersonal connectedness mean?
alt.a: Connected with others and the environment
alt.ex: Spirituality offers connectedness within oneself, with others and the environment, and with the unseen or a higher power.
w: Connected with oneself
That goes with Intrapersonal.
Connected with the unseen, God, or a higher power
That goes with Transpersonal.

alt.q: What does Transpersonal connectedness mean?
alt.a: Connected with the unseen, God, or a higher power
alt.ex: Spirituality offers connectedness within oneself, with others and the environment, and with the unseen or a higher power.
w: Connected with oneself
That goes with Intrapersonal.
Connected with others and the environment
That goes with Interpersonal.

alt.q: Which type of connectedness means “Connected with oneself”?
alt.a: Intrapersonal
alt.ex: Spirituality offers connectedness within oneself, with others and the environment, and with the unseen or a higher power.
w: Interpersonal
Interpersonal: Connected with others and the environment.
Transpersonal
Transpersonal: Connected with the unseen, God, or a higher power.

alt.q: Which type of connectedness means “Connected with others and the environment”?
alt.a: Interpersonal
alt.ex: Spirituality offers connectedness within oneself, with others and the environment, and with the unseen or a higher power.
w: Intrapersonal
Intrapersonal: Connected with oneself.
Transpersonal
Transpersonal: Connected with the unseen, God, or a higher power.

alt.q: Which type of connectedness means “Connected with the unseen, God, or a higher power”?
alt.a: Transpersonal
alt.ex: Spirituality offers connectedness within oneself, with others and the environment, and with the unseen or a higher power.
w: Intrapersonal
Intrapersonal: Connected with oneself.
Interpersonal
Interpersonal: Connected with others and the environment.

mt.q: Match each type of spiritual connectedness with its meaning.
pairs: Connected with others and the environment
Connected with the unseen, God, or a higher power
mt.ex: Spirituality offers connectedness within oneself, with others and the environment, and with the unseen or a higher power.

items.q: In a spiritual caring relationship, how do the patient and nurse move toward healing? Select all that apply.
o: Mobilizing hope for both the patient and the nurse
Mobilizing hope for patient and nurse is part of a spiritual caring relationship.
Finding an understanding of illness that is acceptable to the patient
The interpretation of illness must be acceptable to the patient.
Assisting the patient to use social, emotional, or spiritual resources
Helping the patient use available resources supports healing.
Guiding the patient to adopt the nurse’s religious beliefs
Spiritual caring respects the patient’s own beliefs and expectations.
Avoiding discussion of emotions to keep the focus on symptoms
Spiritual caring includes understanding emotions, not avoiding them.
items.ex: Spiritual caring mobilizes hope, finds acceptable meaning, uses the patient’s resources, and connects human to human, spirit to spirit.

alt.q: A nurse wants to provide spiritual caring to a patient with a serious illness. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Helping the patient draw on social and spiritual resources
Assisting the patient in using these resources is part of spiritual caring.
Supporting hope for the patient
Mobilizing hope moves the patient and nurse toward a healing relationship.
Respecting the patient’s beliefs and expectations
Spiritual caring interventions respect the individual’s beliefs and expectations.
Offering the nurse’s interpretation of the illness as the correct one
The interpretation must be acceptable to the patient, not imposed by the nurse.
Waiting until there is more time on a lighter assignment
Nurses with early spiritual caring practices do not see time or assignment size as barriers.
alt.ex: Correct: Helping the patient draw on social and spiritual resources; Supporting hope for the patient; Respecting the patient’s beliefs and expectations.

items.q: Nursing presence is described as the [[connectedness|connection]] between a nurse and a patient.
items.ex: Presence is a person-to-person encounter conveying closeness, involving both “being there” and “being with.”

alt.q: The closeness of nursing presence is the [[connectedness|connection]] that forms between a nurse and a patient.
alt.ex: Presence is a person-to-person encounter conveying closeness, involving both “being there” and “being with.”

items.q: A nurse cares for a family whose parent with dementia lives at home. The adult children express anger, guilt, and grief. Which nursing approach is best?
items.a: Providing comfort through a listening, nonjudgmental caring presence
items.ex: The nurse cannot fix the family’s suffering but can comfort them through a listening, nonjudgmental caring presence.
w: Explaining that these emotions are not helpful to the parent’s care
This is judgmental and dismisses suffering that is emotional, social, and spiritual.
Focusing the visit only on the parent’s physical symptoms
Suffering affects family caregivers too; caring includes support for the family.
Promising the family that the parent’s condition will improve
The nurse cannot fix the situation; false promises do not provide genuine comfort.

alt.q: Parents of a newborn with multiple developmental challenges are grieving. What does the textbook say a nurse can offer?
alt.a: Comfort through a caring presence, even though the nurse cannot fix it
alt.ex: Family suffering includes anger, guilt, fear, or grief; the nurse cannot fix it but can offer a caring presence.
w: A solution that removes the family’s emotional suffering
The textbook states the nurse cannot fix this kind of suffering.
Reassurance that their feelings will soon pass on their own
This minimizes grief rather than offering a listening, nonjudgmental presence.
Referral elsewhere so the nurse avoids the family’s emotions
Avoiding the family withholds the caring presence that comforts them.

items.q: A nurse is beginning to care for a patient whose family visits often. Which action should the nurse take first to build a caring relationship with the family?
items.a: Learn who makes up the patient’s family and their roles in the patient’s life
items.ex: A relationship with the family begins by learning who makes up the family and their roles in the patient’s life.
w: Teach the family the full treatment plan before learning about them
Teaching follows knowing the family; the relationship begins by learning who they are.
Limit the family’s involvement until the patient is more stable
Families are an important resource and should be helped to be active participants.
Ask the family to share information only with the health care provider
Success with interventions often depends on the family sharing information with the nurse.

alt.q: Which nursing behavior creates the openness that enables a relationship with a patient’s family to form?
alt.a: Showing the family respect and concern for the patient
alt.ex: Showing a family that you respect, care for, and are concerned about the patient creates openness for a relationship.
w: Explaining hospital visiting policies in detail
Explaining policies does not by itself create the openness the textbook describes.
Keeping conversations with the family brief and factual
Brief, factual exchanges do not convey the care and concern that build openness.
Focusing only on the patient’s physical care needs
Caring for the family considers the stress the illness imposes on all members.

items.q: Which nurse behaviors do families of patients with cancer perceive as caring? Select all that apply.
o: Communicating honest, clear, and accurate information
Honest, clear, accurate information is a caring behavior listed in Box 7.4.
Teaching the family how to keep the patient physically comfortable
Involving and teaching the family is perceived as caring.
Helping patients do as much for themselves as possible
Supporting the patient’s self-care is listed as a caring behavior.
Advocating for the patient’s care preferences and end-of-life decisions
Advocacy for preferences and end-of-life decisions is perceived as caring.
Limiting family questions so the nurse can complete care
Families value nurses who listen to their concerns, complaints, and fears.
Performing all self-care activities for the patient
Families value helping patients do as much for themselves as possible.
items.ex: Families of patients with cancer value honest information, listening, advocacy, family involvement, comfort measures, and support of self-care.

alt.q: A nurse cares for a patient with cancer and the patient’s family. Which actions would the family likely perceive as caring? Select all that apply.
o: Assisting the family with implementing advance directives
Helping with advance directives is perceived as caring by families.
Offering the patient a warm blanket and sitting with the patient
Comfort measures such as a warm blanket or sitting with the patient are valued.
Reading cards or mail to the patient
Reading religious texts, a favorite book, cards, or mail is perceived as caring.
Keeping the family unaware of who may enter the care area
Families value being told about nursing services and the people who may enter.
Avoiding talk about whether nursing services will be available
Assuring the patient that nursing services will be available is perceived as caring.
alt.ex: Correct: Assisting the family with implementing advance directives; Offering the patient a warm blanket and sitting with the patient; Reading cards or mail to the patient.

items.q: According to the textbook, what do nurses achieve when they commit to being caring individuals?
items.a: A sense of meaning and purpose in their lives
items.ex: When nurses commit to being caring individuals, they achieve meaning and purpose in their lives.
w: A reduced need for clinical knowledge and skill
Caring is combined with growing knowledge and experience; it does not replace them.
Protection from the effects of compassion fatigue
Committed nurses can still experience compassion fatigue when torn between competing demands.
Faster completion of their assigned daily tasks
Caring is about relationships and meaning, not completing tasks faster.

alt.q: What does the textbook identify as the source of nurses’ sense of satisfaction in caring?
alt.a: Knowing they have made a difference in patients’ lives
alt.ex: Nurses gain satisfaction when they know they have made a difference in patients’ lives.
w: Finishing every task on the shift schedule
The textbook links satisfaction to making a difference, not to task completion.
Relying on technology to monitor patients
Reliance on technology is listed as something that undermines caring.
Following standardized work processes exactly
Efforts to standardize work processes are listed as undermining caring.

items.q: Which factor does the textbook identify as undermining the nature of caring?
items.a: Reliance on technology
items.ex: Reliance on technology, lack of staff, standardizing work processes, and personal stressors all undermine caring.
w: Continuity of care
Continuity of care helps nurses know patients; it supports caring.
Teamwork among nursing staff
Teamwork contributes to knowing patients; it does not undermine caring.
Trust between nurse and patient
Trust contributes to knowing patients and supports caring.

alt.q: A nurse notices that caring on the unit has declined since staffing levels dropped. Which concept from the textbook explains this?
alt.a: Lack of staff undermines the nature of caring
alt.ex: Lack of staff is one of the factors the textbook says undermines the nature of caring.
w: Lack of staff improves continuity of care
Fewer staff leaves less time with patients, making them harder to know.
Lack of staff has no effect on caring
The textbook lists lack of staff as a factor that undermines caring.
Lack of staff increases time spent with patients
Today nurses have less time with patients, not more.

items.q: Which factors undermine the nature of caring in today’s health care system? Select all that apply.
o: Reliance on technology
Reliance on technology is listed as undermining caring.
Lack of staff
Lack of staff is listed as undermining caring.
Efforts to standardize and refine work processes
Standardizing and refining work processes is listed as undermining caring.
Personal stressors
Personal stressors are listed as undermining caring.
Continuity of care
Continuity of care facilitates knowing a patient and supports caring.
A relational staff culture
A supportive relational staff culture helps nurses cope; it does not undermine caring.
items.ex: Technology reliance, short staffing, standardized work processes, and personal stressors undermine caring.

alt.q: A nurse educator discusses challenges to caring. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Nurses have less time to spend with patients
Less time with patients makes it more difficult to know them.
Efforts to standardize work processes can undermine caring
Standardizing and refining work processes is listed as undermining caring.
Personal stressors can undermine caring
Personal stressors are among the factors that undermine caring.
Greater reliance on technology strengthens caring
Reliance on technology undermines caring.
Lack of staff mainly affects costs, not caring
Lack of staff is listed as undermining the nature of caring.
alt.ex: Correct: Nurses have less time to spend with patients; Efforts to standardize work processes can undermine caring; Personal stressors can undermine caring.

items.q: Nurses have less time to spend with patients in today’s health care system. According to the textbook, how does this challenge caring?
items.a: It makes it much more difficult to know who patients are
items.ex: With less time with patients, it is much more difficult to know who they are, which is central to caring.
w: It improves care by encouraging task efficiency
Task efficiency is not caring; reduced time undermines individualized care.
It removes the need for individualized care plans
Less time makes individualized plans harder, not unnecessary.
It increases patient satisfaction with shorter visits
Knowing patients is linked to satisfaction, so less time does not increase it.

alt.q: Why does decreased time with patients threaten individualized care?
alt.a: The nurse has fewer chances to learn the patient’s patterns and preferences
alt.ex: Limited encounters make it hard to recognize patient patterns and care preferences, compromising individualized care.
w: The nurse must then rely only on the family for all decisions
Families are an important resource, but this is not why less time threatens care.
The patient no longer needs nursing presence when time is short
Presence remains important, especially during stressful events.
Individualized care is replaced by health care provider orders
Orders do not replace the nurse knowing the patient as a unique person.

items.q: When do nurses often experience compassion fatigue?
items.a: When torn between the human caring model and the task-oriented biomedical model
items.ex: Compassion fatigue arises when nurses are torn between human caring and task-oriented biomedical demands, institutional demands, and time constraints.
w: When they spend extended time sitting with patients and families
Spending time with patients supports caring and presence; it is not described as the cause.
When they develop spiritual caring practices early in their careers
Early spiritual caring practices help nurses integrate caring into routine care.
When they provide care to the same patient over several shifts
Continuity of care facilitates knowing a patient; it is not the described cause.

alt.q: A nurse wants to sit with a frightened patient but must also complete medications, documentation, and admissions with too little time. What is this nurse at risk for?
alt.a: Compassion fatigue
alt.ex: Being torn between the caring model, institutional demands, and time constraints can lead to compassion fatigue.
w: Knowing the patient
Knowing the patient is a positive caring process, not a risk.
Nursing presence
Presence is a caring intervention, not a risk from competing demands.
Spiritual caring
Spiritual caring is an intervention that supports healing, not a risk.

items.q: Which pressures contribute to compassion fatigue in nurses? Select all that apply.
o: Being torn between the human caring and task-oriented biomedical models
This conflict is a described source of compassion fatigue.
Institutional demands
Institutional demands contribute to compassion fatigue.
Time constraints
Time constraints contribute to compassion fatigue.
Support from colleagues during stressful periods
Colleague support helps nurses cope; it does not cause compassion fatigue.
Continuity in patient assignments
Continuity helps nurses know patients; it is not a listed cause.
items.ex: Compassion fatigue arises when nurses are torn between caring and biomedical models, institutional demands, and time constraints.

alt.q: A nurse is experiencing compassion fatigue. Which statements about this condition are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It negatively affects the health of health care providers
Compassion fatigue harms the health of health care providers.
It negatively affects the effectiveness of health care providers
Compassion fatigue reduces providers’ effectiveness.
It can consequently affect patient care
Because it affects providers, it consequently affects patient care.
It affects only the nurse and never reaches patients
Compassion fatigue consequently affects patient care.
It results from too much time spent with patients
It arises from competing demands and time constraints, not excess time with patients.
alt.ex: Correct: It negatively affects the health of health care providers; It negatively affects the effectiveness of health care providers; It can consequently affect patient care.

items.q: Compassion fatigue affects the nurse’s own health but has no effect on patient care.
items.a: False
items.ex: Compassion fatigue harms the health and effectiveness of health care providers and consequently patient care.
items.ww: Calling it true ignores that reduced provider effectiveness carries over into patient care.

alt.q: Because compassion fatigue reduces the effectiveness of health care providers, it also affects patient care.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Compassion fatigue negatively affects providers’ health and effectiveness and, as a result, patient care.
alt.ww: Calling it false assumes the nurse’s condition stays separate from the quality of care delivered.

items.q: Nurses torn between the human caring model and the task-oriented biomedical model often experience [[compassion fatigue]].
items.ex: Compassion fatigue also stems from institutional demands and time constraints and harms provider effectiveness and patient care.

alt.q: Time constraints and institutional demands can lead to [[compassion fatigue]], which reduces the effectiveness of health care providers.
alt.ex: Compassion fatigue also stems from institutional demands and time constraints and harms provider effectiveness and patient care.

items.q: Efforts to standardize and refine work processes are among the factors that can undermine caring.
items.a: True
items.ex: The textbook lists efforts to standardize and refine work processes with technology, short staffing, and stressors as undermining caring.
items.ww: Calling it false assumes standardization always supports caring, but the textbook lists it as undermining caring.

alt.q: Standardizing and refining work processes reliably strengthens individualized, caring nursing practice.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Efforts to standardize and refine work processes are listed as factors that undermine the nature of caring.
alt.ww: Calling it true overlooks that standardization can push care toward tasks rather than individualized caring.

items.q: A nurse on a busy unit feels emotionally depleted after several weeks of high patient acuity. Which action is best for this nurse?
items.a: Recognize the stressors and reach out to colleagues, family, and friends
items.ex: You cannot give compassionate care when depleted; recognize stressors and reach out to others to cope.
w: Keep working extra shifts until the stress passes on its own
Ignoring self-care deepens depletion; nurses must recognize stressors and seek support.
Withdraw emotionally from patients to conserve energy
Emotional distancing is protective touch that elicits negative feelings in patients.
Focus only on tasks and avoid conversations with patients
Task-only care undermines caring and does not address the nurse’s depletion.

alt.q: Why does the textbook stress self-care for nurses?
alt.a: Nurses cannot give fully engaged, compassionate care when they feel depleted
alt.ex: Recognizing your own self-care matters because depleted nurses cannot give fully engaged, compassionate care.
w: Self-care allows nurses to spend less time with patients
Self-care supports presence with patients; it is not a way to spend less time with them.
Self-care replaces the need for support from colleagues
Nurses are encouraged to reach out to colleagues, family, and friends.
Self-care is required only for nurses in end-of-life care
All nurses need self-care, not only those in end-of-life settings.

items.q: A charge nurse notices that staff are tense about rising patient acuity, difficult working relationships, and end-of-life care. Which action best reflects caring for colleagues?
items.a: Helping build a relational staff culture where staff are supported when expressing stress
items.ex: Nurses use caring behavior with colleagues by creating a relational culture that supports staff who express tension and stress.
w: Advising staff to keep their stress private to protect morale
Hiding stress is the opposite of a culture that supports staff when they express tension.
Assigning the most stressed nurses to the highest-acuity patients
This adds stress and does not provide the support a caring staff culture offers.
Reminding staff that stress is a normal part of nursing work
Normalizing stress without support does not create a relational, caring staff culture.

alt.q: Who benefits when nurses value caring, whether giving or receiving it?
alt.a: Patients, colleagues, and the health care agency
alt.ex: Whether giving or receiving care, caring benefits patients, colleagues, and the health care agency.
w: Patients only, because caring is directed at them
Caring also benefits colleagues and the agency, not only patients.
Nurses only, because it reduces their workload
Caring benefits extend to patients and the agency; it does not reduce workload.
The health care agency only, through lower costs
The textbook names patients and colleagues as well as the agency.

items.q: A nurse has only a few minutes to check on a patient. Which approach best conveys caring within the same time frame?
items.a: Sitting down, making eye contact, and asking about the patient’s concerns before checking the IV
items.ex: The chapter shows caring and noncaring approaches can take the same time; sitting, eye contact, and listening convey caring.
w: Checking the IV and monitor, then asking brief symptom questions while standing
This mirrors the less caring scenario; it lacks sitting, touch, and listening.
Reviewing the vital sign summary from the doorway and leaving quickly
Viewing data from a distance conveys no presence or connection with the patient.
Asking the family to report concerns later so the nurse can save time
Deferring concerns avoids listening and does not convey caring to the patient.

alt.q: Two nurses spend the same amount of time in a patient’s room. One sits, touches the patient’s shoulder, and listens; the other stands and asks brief questions. What does the textbook suggest?
alt.a: The patient may perceive the two visits differently, affecting satisfaction
alt.ex: Both approaches take about the same time, yet patients may perceive them differently, affecting satisfaction.
w: Both visits convey the same level of caring
The approaches differ in presence, touch, and listening, so they are perceived differently.
The standing nurse is more caring by being efficient
Efficiency without presence or listening conveys less caring.
Caring behaviors require much more time than routine checks
The textbook stresses both scenarios take about the same amount of time.

items.q: According to the textbook, where does making care an integral part of health care delivery begin?
items.a: When institutions make caring part of the workplace philosophy and environment
items.ex: Integrating care begins when institutions make caring part of the workplace philosophy and environment and incorporate it into standards.
w: When nurses increase their reliance on monitoring technology
Reliance on technology undermines caring rather than integrating it.
When agencies standardize work processes across all units
Efforts to standardize work processes are listed as undermining caring.
When patients are discharged sooner to reduce costs
Decreased length of stay reduces nurse-patient interactions and hinders knowing patients.

alt.q: A hospital wants to make health care more compassionate. Which institutional action matches the textbook’s recommendation?
alt.a: Incorporating care concepts into standards of nursing care
alt.ex: Institutions should build care concepts into standards of nursing care and guidelines for professional conduct.
w: Replacing individualized care plans with uniform checklists
Standardizing work processes can undermine caring and individualized care.
Reducing staffing to fund new monitoring equipment
Lack of staff and reliance on technology both undermine caring.
Shortening patient visits to increase productivity
Less time with patients makes it harder to know them and provide caring.

items.q: Which actions by a health care institution help make caring an integral part of health care delivery? Select all that apply.
o: Making caring part of the philosophy of the workplace
Integrating care begins when institutions make caring part of their philosophy.
Making caring part of the environment of the workplace
Institutions make caring part of the workplace environment.
Incorporating care concepts into standards of nursing care
Care concepts belong in standards of nursing care.
Incorporating care concepts into guidelines for professional conduct
Care concepts belong in guidelines for professional conduct.
Increasing reliance on technology in place of bedside time
Reliance on technology undermines the nature of caring.
Reducing staffing to improve unit productivity
Lack of staff undermines the nature of caring.
items.ex: Institutions integrate caring by building it into workplace philosophy and environment, standards of nursing care, and guidelines for professional conduct.

alt.q: A hospital task force aims to make care more compassionate. Which recommendations are consistent with the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Write care concepts into the standards of nursing care
Incorporating care concepts into standards of care makes caring integral.
Include caring in the hospital’s workplace philosophy
Making caring part of the workplace philosophy is where integration begins.
Further standardize work processes to save time
Efforts to standardize and refine work processes undermine caring.
Rely on monitoring technology to reduce bedside visits
Reliance on technology undermines caring and reduces time to know patients.
Add care concepts to guidelines for professional conduct
Guidelines for professional conduct should incorporate care concepts.
alt.ex: Correct: Write care concepts into the standards of nursing care; Include caring in the hospital’s workplace philosophy; Add care concepts to guidelines for professional conduct.

items.q: A nurse manager wants to strengthen caring on the unit in line with the textbook. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Add care concepts to the unit’s guidelines for professional conduct
items.ex: Incorporating care concepts into standards of care and guidelines for professional conduct makes caring integral to delivery.
w: Require nurses to minimize conversation to stay on schedule
Limiting conversation reduces listening and presence, which undermines caring.
Rotate nurses to new patients every shift for variety
Fragmented assignments reduce continuity and make knowing patients difficult.
Measure nurses mainly by the number of tasks completed
A task-oriented focus contributes to compassion fatigue and undermines caring.

alt.q: Which unit change would most likely support nurses’ ability to provide caring?
alt.a: Assigning nurses to the same patients over consecutive shifts
alt.ex: Continuity of care facilitates knowing patients, which supports individualized, caring practice.
w: Increasing reliance on technology for patient monitoring
Reliance on technology is listed as undermining caring.
Further standardizing and refining work processes
Efforts to standardize work processes undermine caring.
Reducing staff numbers on each shift
Lack of staff undermines the nature of caring.

That goes with NLN.

w: American Nurses Association

alt.a: American Association of Colleges of Nursing

w: American Nurses Association
That goes with ANA.

American Organization of Nurse Executives

alt.q: Which abbreviation stands for “American Nurses Association”?
alt.a: ANA
alt.ex: These organizations recommend strategies to reverse the nursing shortage, which may also create environments that support caring.
w: NLN
NLN: National League for Nursing.
AONE

AACN
AACN: American Association of Colleges of Nursing.

alt.a: NLN
alt.ex: These organizations recommend strategies to reverse the nursing shortage, which may also create environments that support caring.
w: ANA
ANA: American Nurses Association.
AONE

AACN

w: ANA
ANA: American Nurses Association.
NLN
NLN: National League for Nursing.
AACN
AACN: American Association of Colleges of Nursing.

alt.q: Which abbreviation stands for “American Association of Colleges of Nursing”?
alt.a: AACN
alt.ex: These organizations recommend strategies to reverse the nursing shortage, which may also create environments that support caring.
w: ANA
ANA: American Nurses Association.
NLN
NLN: National League for Nursing.
AONE
AONE: American Organization of Nurse Executives.

mt.q: Match each abbreviation with the professional organization that recommends strategies to reverse the nursing shortage.
pairs: American Association of Colleges of Nursing
mt.ex: These organizations recommend strategies to reverse the nursing shortage, which may also create environments that support caring.

items.q: Professional nursing organizations recommend strategies to reverse the nursing shortage. How could these strategies affect caring?
items.a: They may create work environments that let nurses show more caring behaviors
items.ex: Several strategies may improve the workforce and create work environments that enable nurses to demonstrate more caring behaviors.
w: They may replace caring with more efficient task models
The strategies aim to support caring environments, not replace caring with tasks.
They have no relationship to nurses’ caring behaviors
The textbook links these strategies to environments that enable more caring.
They may reduce the time nurses spend with each patient
Strategies that improve the workforce support caring rather than reducing patient time.

alt.q: What problem are the strategies recommended by the ANA, NLN, AONE, and AACN designed to reverse?
alt.a: The current nursing shortage
alt.ex: These organizations recommend strategies to reverse the current nursing shortage, with potential to improve caring environments.
w: The rising cost of nursing education
The textbook ties these strategies to the nursing shortage, not education costs.
The increase in malpractice claims
Malpractice claims are not what these strategies target in this chapter.
The decline in patient length of stay
The strategies address the nursing shortage, not length of stay.

items.q: Nurses gain a sense of satisfaction mainly from completing tasks efficiently during a shift.
items.a: False
items.ex: Nurses gain satisfaction when they know they have made a difference in patients’ lives.
items.ww: Calling it true confuses task efficiency with caring, which the textbook links to meaning and satisfaction.

alt.q: Nurses gain a sense of satisfaction when they know they have made a difference in patients’ lives.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The textbook links nurses’ satisfaction to knowing they have made a difference for patients.
alt.ww: Calling it false ignores that making a difference in patients’ lives gives nurses satisfaction and purpose.

items.q: The chapter warns that in a hectic, high-tech environment, nursing practice risks becoming more [[technical]] while caring is sacrificed.
items.ex: Productivity, efficiency, and time constraints threaten nurses’ chances to build therapeutic relationships, so caring may be sacrificed.

alt.q: Time constraints and environmental demands create a risk that nursing becomes more [[technical]] and caring is sacrificed.
alt.ex: Productivity, efficiency, and time constraints threaten nurses’ chances to build therapeutic relationships, so caring may be sacrificed.

items.q: Which nurse commitment does the textbook describe as necessary to provide personal, competent, compassionate, and meaningful care?
items.a: Willingness to establish relationships with patients and families
items.ex: Nurses need to be committed to caring and willing to build relationships with patients and families to provide meaningful care.
w: Willingness to rely on technology for patient assessment
Reliance on technology undermines caring rather than supporting meaningful care.
Willingness to follow standardized processes without variation
Standardizing work processes is listed as undermining caring.
Willingness to limit family involvement in patient care
Families are an important resource; nurses build relationships with them.
