sections.name: The prevalence and costs of chronic disease

items.q: Which description matches the definition of a chronic disease?
items.a: A pathophysiological condition lasting more than 1 year that requires ongoing medical care
items.ex: A chronic disease lasts more than 1 year, requires ongoing medical care, and often limits usual activities of daily living.
w: A pathophysiological condition lasting more than 1 month that resolves with treatment
A chronic disease lasts longer than 1 year and needs ongoing care rather than resolving.
A patient’s and family’s subjective experience of living with a long-term condition
Subjective experiences and responses are part of chronic illness, not the definition of chronic disease.
A sudden condition lasting less than 6 months that needs short-term hospital care
A short, sudden condition is not chronic; chronic disease lasts more than 1 year.

alt.q: A nurse reviews four patients’ problem lists. Which condition fits the definition of a chronic disease?
alt.a: Rheumatoid arthritis present for 3 years that needs ongoing medical care
alt.ex: Chronic disease lasts more than 1 year, needs ongoing medical care, and often limits activities of daily living.
w: A urinary tract infection treated with antibiotics for 7 days
A short infection that resolves with treatment does not last more than 1 year.
A fractured wrist casted 4 weeks ago that is healing as expected
A healing fracture is time limited and does not require ongoing medical care for over a year.
Seasonal influenza that resolved after 10 days of rest and fluids
Influenza that resolves in days is an acute condition, not a chronic disease.

Dietary changes are a key lifestyle modification for managing type 2 diabetes.
“Exercise should be avoided until your blood sugar is normal.”
Regular exercise is a recommended lifestyle modification for type 2 diabetes.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus about lifestyle changes. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?

items.q: A person who inherits a gene mutation for hypertension will eventually develop hypertension.
items.a: False
items.ex: Inheriting a gene mutation does not guarantee disease; multifactorial inheritance explains why a carrier may or may not develop it.
items.ww: Saying True ignores that environmental and lifestyle factors interact with genes to determine whether disease develops.

alt.q: A person who carries genetic material for a chronic illness may never be diagnosed with that illness.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Multifactorial inheritance explains why carrying a gene mutation does not guarantee that the disease will develop.
alt.ww: Saying False assumes genes alone determine disease, but environment and lifestyle also influence risk.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A woman with a strong family history of breast and ovarian cancer tests positive for a BRCA1 mutation. She asks, “Does this mean I will get cancer?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “It means your risk is higher, not that you will get cancer; it can guide your screening choices.”
items.ex: A positive BRCA screen means increased risk, not certainty, and helps guide lifestyle changes, screening frequency, or preventive therapy.
w: “Yes, a positive result means cancer will develop at some point in your life.”
A positive result indicates increased risk; it does not mean the woman will develop cancer.
“No, the result only matters for your daughters and not for your own health.”
The result guides the woman’s own decisions about screening and preventive therapy.
“The result cannot help you, so you should simply wait for symptoms to appear.”
Knowing about a BRCA mutation guides screening, lifestyle changes, and early preventive therapy.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a patient who tested positive for a BRCA2 mutation. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
alt.a: “My cancer risk is higher, so I can plan more frequent screening or preventive options.”
alt.ex: BRCA results show increased risk and support informed decisions about screening frequency, lifestyle, and early preventive surgery.
w: “Now that I know I will get cancer, I should start chemotherapy right away.”
A positive result does not mean she will develop cancer or need chemotherapy.
“Since the test was positive, screening is no longer useful for me.”
Knowing the mutation is present supports more frequent screening, not less.
“A positive result means my risk is the same as anyone else’s.”
A BRCA mutation places her at increased risk for these cancers.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: While taking a family health history, which finding should prompt the nurse to consider a referral for genetic counseling?
items.a: The same disease appearing in relatives across several generations
items.ex: Genetic counseling is often indicated when the family history shows a strong, multigenerational pattern of the same disease.
w: A single relative who had an acute infection in childhood
An isolated acute infection does not show a multigenerational disease pattern.
A family member who broke a leg in a car accident
An injury from an accident is not an inherited disease pattern.
A sibling who had a seasonal cold earlier this year
A short-term illness in one sibling is not a strong family disease pattern.

alt.q: A patient is referred for genetic counseling because of a strong family history of heart disease. Which service does the genetic counselor provide?
alt.a: Clarifying the patient’s disease risk based on the family history
alt.ex: Genetic counselors clarify risk, answer questions, recommend screening, discuss genetic testing, and recommend risk-reducing lifestyle changes.
w: Guaranteeing whether the patient will develop heart disease
Genetic information shows risk; it cannot guarantee whether disease will develop.
Performing cardiac surgery to remove the inherited risk
Counselors provide information and recommendations, not surgical treatment.
Changing the patient’s genes so the risk is removed
Genetic factors are not modifiable; counselors recommend screening and lifestyle changes.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A patient’s brother was recently diagnosed with colon cancer caused by Lynch syndrome. Which teaching should the nurse provide to the patient?
items.a: Genetic screening is recommended, with more frequent screening if the result is positive
items.ex: Screening first-degree relatives for Lynch syndrome allows more frequent screening, earlier detection, and earlier treatment to reduce deaths.
w: Screening is needed only if symptoms of colon cancer develop
Early detection improves survival, so screening should be offered before symptoms appear.
Lynch syndrome affects only the colon, so other screening is not needed
Lynch syndrome is also linked to endometrial, ovarian, pancreatic, and other cancers.
First-degree relatives are not at increased risk for this cancer
Lynch syndrome is hereditary, so first-degree relatives should be offered screening.

alt.q: A nurse teaches the sister of a patient with Lynch syndrome. Which statement by the sister shows understanding?
alt.a: “If my genetic test is positive, I will need more frequent cancer screening.”
alt.ex: A positive genetic screen for Lynch syndrome leads to more frequent screening, improving early detection and treatment.
w: “I only need testing if I start having bowel symptoms.”
Screening is offered to first-degree relatives before symptoms because early detection improves survival.
“A positive test means only my colon needs to be checked.”
Lynch syndrome is linked to other cancers, such as endometrial and ovarian cancer.
“My brother’s diagnosis does not affect my own cancer risk.”
As a first-degree relative, she may carry the hereditary Lynch syndrome gene.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A patient completed chemotherapy and radiation for cancer last year. Which residual effects should the nurse assess for? Select all that apply.
o: Peripheral neuropathy
Peripheral neuropathy can remain after cancer treatment.
Cardiac or pulmonary toxicity
Cardiac or pulmonary toxicity is a possible residual effect of cancer treatment.
Cognitive impairment called “chemo brain”
Chemotherapy-induced cognitive impairment may last for years.
Barrel chest from air trapping
Barrel chest is a chronic physical change of emphysema, not of cancer treatment.
Clubbed fingers from chronic hypoxia
Clubbed fingers are described with emphysema, not as residual cancer treatment effects.
items.ex: Physical effects vary by disease and treatment; cancer survivors may have neuropathy, cardiac or pulmonary toxicity, or chemo brain.

alt.q: A nurse assesses a patient with long-standing emphysema. Which physical findings does the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Dyspnea that may require oxygen therapy
Emphysema causes dyspnea that may need oxygen therapy.
Clubbed fingers
Clubbed fingers are a chronic physical change in emphysema.
Barrel chest
A barrel chest is a chronic physical change in emphysema.
Chemotherapy-induced cognitive impairment
“Chemo brain” is a residual effect of cancer treatment, not emphysema.
Peripheral neuropathy from radiation
Peripheral neuropathy is a residual effect of cancer treatment, not emphysema.
alt.ex: Correct: Dyspnea that may require oxygen therapy; Clubbed fingers; Barrel chest.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Antihypertensive medications such as beta-blockers and angiotensin-converting enzyme inhibitors are associated with depressive symptoms.
items.a: True
items.ex: Medications for physical illnesses can affect mental health; some antihypertensives are associated with depressive symptoms.
items.ww: Saying False ignores that drugs treating physical illness, such as antihypertensives, can affect mental health.

alt.q: Medications used to treat mental illnesses affect only mental health and do not affect a patient’s physical health.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Mental health medications affect physical health; lithium can cause nausea, vomiting, tremors, heart rate changes, and seizures.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores physical side effects of mental health medications such as lithium.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A patient works on a farm and is regularly exposed to pesticides. Which action best reflects the nurse’s role in reducing environmental exposure?
items.a: Identify the exposure and teach the patient how to avoid further contamination
items.ex: By identifying exposures and informing patients where and how contamination occurs, nurses empower patients to avoid further exposure.
w: Reassure the patient that genetic risk matters more than exposures
The interaction of toxins and genetic predisposition is probably stronger than genetic risk alone.
Wait to address exposure until the patient develops respiratory symptoms
Risk assessment and education aim to prevent chronic disease before it develops.
Tell the patient that workplace exposures cannot be changed or reduced
Exposure reduction and avoidance are goals of public health and nursing education.

alt.q: Which activities make up the nurse’s role in reducing patients’ exposure to environmental toxins?
alt.a: Risk assessment, patient education, and supporting public policy
alt.ex: The nurse reduces environmental exposure through risk assessment, patient education, and supporting public policy on exposure.
w: Chemical testing of water, removal of asbestos, and mold cleanup
Remediation is a public health activity; the nurse assesses risk, educates, and supports policy.
Genetic testing, prenatal screening, and carrier testing
These are types of genetic testing, not the nurse’s role in environmental exposure.
Prescribing medications, ordering imaging, and making diagnoses
These are provider activities; the nurse’s role is assessment, education, and policy support.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Cigarette smoking or extended exposure to secondhand smoke is the leading cause of preventable death in the United States.
items.a: True
items.ex: Smoking and secondhand smoke are the leading cause of preventable death and are linked to 16 cancers and cardiopulmonary disease.
items.ww: Saying False overlooks that tobacco use is identified as the leading preventable cause of death in the United States.

alt.q: Excessive alcohol use is the leading cause of preventable death in the United States.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Cigarette smoking or extended secondhand smoke exposure is the leading cause; excessive alcohol is linked to 1 in 10 working-adult deaths.
alt.ww: Saying True confuses alcohol with tobacco, which is the leading cause of preventable death.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Which risk factors for chronic illness are modifiable lifestyle choices? Select all that apply.
o: Smoking cigarettes
Smoking is a common modifiable risk behavior.
Exposure to secondhand smoke
Secondhand smoke exposure is listed among the most common modifiable risk factors.
Poor nutrition
Poor nutrition is a modifiable lifestyle choice that contributes to chronic illness.
Excessive alcohol consumption
Excessive alcohol use is a modifiable risk behavior.
Inherited gene mutation for cancer
Genetic factors are not modifiable; people are born with them.
A parent with an autosomal dominant disorder
Inherited genetic risk cannot be changed by lifestyle choices.
items.ex: The most common modifiable risk factors are risk behaviors such as smoking, secondhand smoke exposure, poor nutrition, and excessive alcohol.

alt.q: A nurse is planning risk-reduction teaching. Which patient risk factors can be changed through lifestyle choices? Select all that apply.
o: Sedentary lifestyle
Lack of physical activity is modifiable and linked to heart disease, diabetes, and some cancers.
Heavy alcohol intake
Excessive alcohol consumption is a modifiable risk behavior.
Tobacco use
Tobacco use is a modifiable risk behavior and the leading preventable cause of death.
Family history of hypertension
Family genetic history is not modifiable, though it guides screening.
Carrier status for sickle cell disease
Carrier status is inherited genetic material and cannot be changed.
alt.ex: Correct: Sedentary lifestyle; Heavy alcohol intake; Tobacco use.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A 15-year-old patient says, “Vaping is safe because e-cigarettes are just flavored vapor.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “E-cigarettes contain nicotine and other contaminants that can harm your health.”
items.ex: E-cigarettes contain nicotine and contaminants such as bacterial and fungal toxins that negatively affect health.
w: “E-cigarettes are safe as long as you do not also smoke regular cigarettes.”
E-cigarettes themselves contain nicotine and toxins that harm health.
“Vaping is harmful only to the environment, not to your health.”
E-cigarettes harm both health and the environment through toxins and waste.
“Vaping is fine for teens because nicotine affects only adults.”
E-cigarettes are common in teens and contain nicotine that harms health.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a group of high school students about e-cigarettes. Which statement by a student shows understanding?
alt.a: “E-cigarettes can expose me to nicotine plus bacterial and fungal toxins.”
alt.ex: E-cigarettes contain nicotine and contaminants such as bacterial and fungal toxins that negatively affect a person’s health.
w: “E-cigarettes contain only water vapor and flavoring.”
E-cigarettes contain nicotine and other contaminants, not just water vapor.
“E-cigarettes have no effect on the environment or my health.”
E-cigarettes create biohazard, plastic, and electronic waste and harm health.
“Using e-cigarettes protects me from nicotine dependence.”
E-cigarettes contain nicotine, which can lead to dependence.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: An adult patient asks how to lower the risk of osteoporosis and bone fractures. Which teaching is consistent with chronic disease prevention strategies?
items.a: Get 1000 to 1200 mg of calcium daily, plus vitamin D, sun exposure, and physical activity
items.ex: Adequate calcium (1000–1200 mg/day for adults), vitamin D, sun exposure, and strengthening activity reduce osteoporosis and fracture risk.
w: Get 300 to 400 mg of calcium daily and limit time spent in the sun
This calcium intake is too low, and sun exposure helps reduce osteoporosis risk.
Get 2500 to 3000 mg of calcium daily and avoid weight-bearing activity
Recommended adult intake is 1000–1200 mg/day, and physical activity strengthens bones.
Get 500 to 600 mg of calcium daily and rest to protect the bones
This intake is below 1000–1200 mg/day, and activity rather than rest strengthens bones.

alt.q: What daily calcium intake is recommended for adults to help reduce the risk of osteoporosis and bone fractures?
alt.a: 1000 to 1200 mg per day
alt.ex: An adequate adult calcium intake of 1000–1200 mg/day, with vitamin D, helps reduce osteoporosis and fracture risk.
w: 200 to 400 mg per day
This is well below the 1000–1200 mg/day recommended for adults.
500 to 700 mg per day
This is below the 1000–1200 mg/day recommended for adults.
2000 to 2500 mg per day
This exceeds the 1000–1200 mg/day adult intake listed in the prevention strategies.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A woman finds a lump in her breast and immediately thinks of cancer, long treatment, suffering, and an uncertain outcome, leading to anxiety and fear. Which concept does this illustrate?
items.a: Illness representation
items.ex: Illness representations are responses to bodily and functional changes from an illness that affect the ability to self-manage it.
w: Multifactorial inheritance
Multifactorial inheritance describes genetic, environmental, and lifestyle risk, not a personal response to symptoms.
Caregiver burden
Caregiver burden describes strain on a family caregiver, not the patient’s response to a symptom.
Genetic counseling
Genetic counseling is a service that clarifies inherited risk, not a patient’s response to symptoms.

alt.q: Why is a patient’s illness representation important for the nurse to assess?
alt.a: It shapes the patient’s ability to self-manage the illness
alt.ex: Each patient’s unique response to illness-related changes affects self-management, so the nurse assesses it to plan person-centered care.
w: It predicts the patient’s genetic risk for the disease
Genetic risk comes from inherited material, not the patient’s response to illness.
It is the same for every patient with the same disease
Each person with a chronic disease has a unique illness representation.
It determines the cost of the patient’s medical care
Illness representation affects self-management, not medical care costs directly.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A 75-year-old woman with heart failure lives alone in a rural area, often feels lonely, eats salty foods to cope, and says walking outside alone is unsafe. Which intervention is best?
items.a: Help her find ways to stay connected, such as video calls and scheduled family visits
items.ex: Less loneliness is linked to better adherence; nurses help isolated patients connect through technology, scheduled visits, and enjoyable activities.
w: Tell her that her diet choices are the main cause of her illness
She already blames herself; blame does not address loneliness that drives her coping.
Advise her to remain at home where her routine is more predictable
Staying home increases social isolation, which worsens health and self-management.
Focus teaching on medications and leave social concerns to her family
Assessing and addressing loneliness is part of nursing care because it affects adherence.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with a chronic illness who reports frequent loneliness. Why is addressing the loneliness a priority?
alt.a: Less loneliness is linked to better medication management and adherence
alt.ex: People who report less loneliness manage medications and adhere to treatment plans more successfully.
w: Loneliness affects only mood and has no effect on physical health
Loneliness and social isolation carry significant physical and mental health risks.
Loneliness is uncommon in people living with chronic illness
Social isolation often occurs as chronic illness becomes more advanced or severe.
Loneliness improves once the patient adjusts to a new diagnosis
Regular loneliness poses ongoing health risks and needs assessment and intervention.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: During a home visit, a woman newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes mellitus says, “I am so scared and angry. My neighbor lost both legs. I just can’t do all of this!” What should the nurse address first?
items.a: Her fear and feelings about living with diabetes
items.ex: Emotional responses affect how a person perceives and copes with illness, so the nurse explores her feelings before teaching self-care.
w: The correct technique for checking her blood glucose
Skills teaching is unlikely to succeed until her fear and anger are addressed.
A detailed low-carbohydrate meal plan for the week
Diet teaching comes after addressing the emotional response that limits her engagement.
The schedule for taking her oral hypoglycemic tablet
Medication teaching is important, but her emotional response is limiting self-care now.

alt.q: Why does the nurse explore a newly diagnosed patient’s fear and anger before teaching self-management skills?
alt.a: Emotional responses affect how the patient perceives and copes with the illness
alt.ex: A patient’s emotional response shapes coping and perceived wellness, so a therapeutic relationship helps the patient engage in self-care.
w: Fear and anger are signs that the diagnosis is incorrect
Fear and anger are common responses to chronic illness, not signs of a wrong diagnosis.
Teaching cannot legally begin until the patient feels calm
There is no such legal rule; emotions are addressed because they affect coping.
Emotional responses are the same for every patient with diabetes
Emotional responses to chronic illness vary even more than physical responses.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: An older adult with several chronic illnesses says, “Getting old just means everything falls apart.” Which nursing action is most appropriate?
items.a: Assess for symptoms of depression and explore the patient’s perception of aging
items.ex: Older adults with negative views of aging have more depressive symptoms; assessing both lays a foundation for discussing coping strategies.
w: Reassure the patient that these feelings are a normal part of aging
Dismissing the statement misses a negative perception of aging linked to depression.
Change the subject to focus on the patient’s medication schedule
Avoiding the statement misses an important cue about depression and coping.
Tell the patient that having more illnesses does not affect function
More chronic illnesses are associated with more functional limitations and depressive symptoms.

alt.q: Which statement about older adults with chronic illness is accurate?
alt.a: A negative self-perception of aging is linked to more depressive symptoms
alt.ex: Older adults with a negative self-perception of aging experience more depressive symptoms than those with a positive view.
w: Having more chronic illnesses is linked to fewer functional limitations
More chronic illnesses are associated with more functional limitations.
Changes in body image rarely affect mood in older adults
Body image changes contribute to powerlessness and depression in older adults.
Interprofessional consultation seldom improves function in older adults
Physical and occupational therapists and social workers help decrease functional limitations.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A nurse is caring for a family whose 9-year-old child has a serious chronic illness. Which effects on the family should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: The child is at risk for posttraumatic stress symptoms
Children living with chronic illness are at risk for PTSS and PTSD.
Healthy siblings may feel left out or jealous
Healthy siblings often feel left out, jealous, and neglected.
Siblings may have problems with school attendance
Both the ill child and healthy siblings often have school attendance issues.
Parents may experience anxiety, fatigue, and depression
Parents have intense psychosocial responses and increased risk for chronic physical illness.
The child’s mental health risk ends at adulthood
Children with chronic illness often go on to have depression and anxiety in adulthood.
Parental well-being has little effect on the child
Poor parental well-being negatively affects the child’s well-being and functioning.
items.ex: Childhood chronic illness affects the whole family, so the nurse uses a family-centered, interprofessional approach.

alt.q: Which nursing actions are appropriate for a child with a chronic illness and the child’s family? Select all that apply.
o: Take a family-centered approach to care
Family-centered care is essential for children and families affected by chronic illness.
Help the family understand their emotions are normal
Normalizing illness-related emotions supports children and their families.
Involve interprofessional teams to meet holistic needs
Interprofessional teams help meet the holistic needs of children and families.
Assess for mental health needs as part of the treatment plan
Mental health risks may persist into adulthood, so anticipating and assessing them is critical.
Focus care on the ill child and exclude healthy siblings
Healthy siblings are affected and may feel left out and neglected.
Discourage parents from discussing their own stress
Parental well-being is connected to the child’s health and functioning.
alt.ex: Correct: Take a family-centered approach to care; Help the family understand their emotions are normal; Involve interprofessional teams to meet holistic needs; Assess for mental health needs as part of the treatment plan.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: About what proportion of working Americans provide care for family members or friends with chronic illnesses or disabilities?
items.a: More than 1 in 6
items.ex: More than 1 in 6 Americans who work full- or part-time also provide care for a family member or friend.
w: About 1 in 50
This underestimates caregiving; more than 1 in 6 working Americans are caregivers.
About 1 in 20
This underestimates caregiving; more than 1 in 6 working Americans are caregivers.
More than 1 in 2
This overestimates caregiving; the estimate is more than 1 in 6.

alt.q: Why are more working Americans, now more than 1 in 6, providing care for family members or friends?
alt.a: Advances in disease management mean more people live longer with chronic illness
alt.ex: Because advances in disease management help people live longer with chronic illness, more than 1 in 6 workers are caregivers.
w: Fewer people are living with chronic illness than in the past
Chronic illness is increasing as people live longer with it.
Chronic illnesses now resolve more quickly with treatment
Chronic illnesses last more than 1 year and require ongoing care.
Hospitals now keep chronically ill patients for longer stays
Care shifts to family caregivers at home as people live longer with chronic illness.

items.ex: Caregiver burden rises as the patient relies more on the caregiver and when the caregiver has anxiety or depression.

alt.q: As a patient relies more heavily on a family caregiver, caregiver [[burden]] increases.
alt.ex: Caregiver burden rises as the patient relies more on the caregiver and when the caregiver has anxiety or depression.

items.ex: Nurses ensure both members of the caregiving dyad have access to respite care, social work, and counseling.

alt.q: The nurse makes sure both members of the caregiving [[dyad]], patient and family caregiver, can reach appropriate community services.
alt.ex: Nurses ensure both members of the caregiving dyad have access to respite care, social work, and counseling.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Which factors place a family caregiver at greatest risk for poor health outcomes? Select all that apply.
o: Providing care for more than a year
Caregiving lasting more than a year increases risk for poor health outcomes.
Being 65 years of age or older
Caregivers aged 65 or older are at greater risk.
Caring for someone with dementia
Caring for a person with Alzheimer disease or another dementia increases risk.
Living with the care recipient
Living with the care recipient is a risk factor for poor health outcomes.
Having strong social support and respite
Insufficient resources, including social support and respite, increase risk.
Caring for someone with few care needs
Caring for a family member with significant needs increases risk.
items.ex: Risk rises with caregiving over a year, age 65 or older, high care needs, insufficient resources, dementia care, and living together.

alt.q: A nurse screens family caregivers. Which caregivers are at increased risk for poor health outcomes? Select all that apply.
o: A caregiver who lacks knowledge and skills for needed care
Insufficient resources such as knowledge and skills increase risk.
A caregiver whose family member has significant care needs
Caring for someone with significant needs increases risk.
A caregiver who has no access to community services
Lack of community services is an insufficient resource that increases risk.
A caregiver helping a friend for 2 weeks after minor surgery
Short-term care is not a listed risk; risk increases with care over a year.
A caregiver with strong support from friends and respite care
Adequate social support and respite are resources that lower risk.
alt.ex: Correct: A caregiver who lacks knowledge and skills for needed care; A caregiver whose family member has significant care needs; A caregiver who has no access to community services.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A nurse is screening four family caregivers. Which caregiver is at greatest risk for poor health outcomes?
items.a: A 72-year-old wife who has lived with and cared for her husband with Alzheimer disease for 3 years
items.ex: Age 65 or older, dementia care, caregiving over a year, and living with the care recipient all increase risk.
w: A 40-year-old son who visits his mother twice a week to help with her groceries
He is younger, lives apart, and provides limited help, so his risk is lower.
A 35-year-old daughter caring for her father for 2 weeks after a minor surgery
Short-term care for limited needs carries less risk than long-term dementia care.
A 50-year-old neighbor who drives a friend to monthly appointments with family help
This caregiver has support, limited duties, and lives apart from the recipient.

alt.q: Which caregiver situation carries the lowest risk for poor caregiver health outcomes?
alt.a: A 45-year-old who helps a relative for 1 month and has strong respite support
alt.ex: Short duration, younger age, and adequate resources such as respite lower risk compared with long-term, high-need caregiving.
w: A 68-year-old who has lived with a spouse with dementia for 4 years
Age 65 or older, dementia care, living together, and long duration all raise risk.
A 70-year-old caring alone for a spouse with significant needs for 2 years
Older age, significant needs, insufficient support, and duration raise risk.
A 55-year-old with no community services who cares for a parent for 3 years
Insufficient resources and caregiving over a year increase risk.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: As a patient relies more heavily on the family caregiver for assistance, the burden on the caregiver increases.
items.a: True
items.ex: Caregiver burden grows with the patient’s dependence and is also higher in caregivers with anxiety and depression.
items.ww: Saying False ignores that greater dependence of the patient means greater burden on the caregiver.

alt.q: Caregiver burden usually decreases as the patient becomes more dependent because the caregiver adapts to the role.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Burden increases, not decreases, as the patient relies more heavily on the family caregiver.
alt.ww: Saying True assumes adaptation offsets demand, but burden rises as the patient becomes more dependent.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Among family caregivers, spouses report the largest impact of caregiving on their own health.
items.a: True
items.ex: Family caregivers report that their health worsens over time, and spouses report the largest impact.
items.ww: Saying False overlooks that spouse caregivers report the greatest effect of caregiving on their health.

alt.q: Family caregivers generally report that their personal health improves the longer they provide care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Family caregivers generally report that their personal health worsens over time, especially spouses.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores that most caregivers report declining health over time, though some benefit.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Some family caregivers cope successfully, report psychological benefits, and may even have improved health from caregiving.
items.a: True
items.ex: Despite the risks, some studies show caregivers cope well, gain psychological benefits, and may have improved health and reduced mortality.
items.ww: Saying False ignores evidence that caregiving can bring psychological benefits and even improved health for some.

alt.q: Caregiving always leads to poorer physical and mental health for every family caregiver.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Some caregivers cope successfully and may experience improved health and reduced mortality from caregiving.
alt.ww: Saying True overlooks studies showing some caregivers benefit psychologically and physically from caregiving.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: The daughter of a patient with dementia says she missed her own health care appointments for months and feels exhausted. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess the daughter’s health and her caregiving responsibilities
items.ex: Caring for the caregiver begins with assessing the caregiver’s health and caregiving responsibilities, since caregivers often neglect their own health.
w: Explain that her father’s needs must come before her own health
Caregivers who neglect their own health are at risk; the caregiver also needs care.
Arrange long-term placement for her father without discussion
Acting without assessment and the family’s input skips the first step.
Teach her additional care tasks to perform for her father
Adding tasks before assessing her health and burden may increase strain.

alt.q: A spouse caring for a patient with advanced heart failure says, “I can’t remember the last time I slept well or saw my own doctor.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Tell me more about your own health and what caring for him involves each day.”
alt.ex: Assessing the caregiver’s health and responsibilities, within a therapeutic relationship, identifies needs for support and resources.
w: “Caregivers rarely get sleep, so this is something to accept.”
Dismissing the concern misses signs of caregiver burden and health risk.
“Your husband is the patient, so we should focus only on him.”
The family caregiver’s health is also a nursing concern.
“You should see your doctor after his condition improves.”
Delaying care for herself adds to the risk of poor health outcomes.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Which nursing actions support family caregivers of patients with chronic illness? Select all that apply.
o: Develop a therapeutic relationship with the caregiver
A therapeutic relationship helps the nurse learn details of the caregiving experience.
Assess physical, psychosocial, and financial effects on the caregiver
The nurse assesses these effects on both patient and caregiver.
Ensure access to respite care, social work, and counseling
Both members of the caregiving dyad need appropriate community resources.
Include the caregiver as part of the interprofessional team
The patient and caregiver are included as part of the interprofessional team.
Advise the caregiver to postpone personal health care
Neglecting personal health increases caregivers’ risk for poor outcomes.
Limit the caregiver’s role in planning the patient’s care
Caregivers are included in the team, not excluded from planning.
items.ex: Caring for the caregiver includes assessment, a therapeutic relationship, community resources, education, and inclusion in the team.

alt.q: A nurse is planning care for a patient with Parkinson disease and the patient’s spouse caregiver. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Assess the spouse’s health and caregiving responsibilities
Assessing the caregiver’s health and responsibilities is essential.
Provide education to the spouse when needed
Patient and caregiver education is provided when needed.
Refer the couple to community resources such as respite care
Both members of the dyad should have access to respite, social work, and counseling.
Focus assessment only on the patient’s physical symptoms
The nurse assesses physical, psychosocial, and financial effects on both members.
Discourage the spouse from attending team meetings
The caregiver is included as part of the interprofessional team.
alt.ex: Correct: Assess the spouse’s health and caregiving responsibilities; Provide education to the spouse when needed; Refer the couple to community resources such as respite care.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A woman caring for her father says, “The hardest part is that he doesn’t recognize me anymore.” The nurse recognizes that this caregiver’s stress is most related to which factor?
items.a: The characteristics of the father’s chronic illness
items.ex: Caregiver experience relates to illness characteristics and caregiving complexity, such as cognitive changes where the patient no longer recognizes family.
w: The financial costs of the father’s medications
Her statement reflects stress from cognitive changes, not financial strain.
Her lack of skill with physical care tasks
Her distress centers on loss of recognition, not on physical care skills.
The short duration of her father’s illness
Chronic illness is long and uncertain, which adds to stress rather than reducing it.

alt.q: A nurse explains what shapes the experience of family caregivers. Which statement is accurate?
alt.a: It relates to the illness characteristics and the complexity of caregiving
alt.ex: The caregiver’s experience is related to the characteristics of the chronic illness and how complex the caregiving is.
w: It is the same for every caregiver regardless of the illness
Experiences vary with illness characteristics, care complexity, and the relationship to the patient.
It depends only on the caregiver’s income and insurance
Finances matter, but illness characteristics and care complexity shape the experience.
It improves when the patient requires more intense care
More intense care makes coping and managing caregiving more difficult.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A patient’s wife says, “Since his stroke, I feel more like his nurse than his wife.” Which nursing understanding best explains this statement?
items.a: When the caregiver is a spouse, the marital relationship may be greatly affected
items.ex: Caregiver stress relates to the relationship with the patient, and spouse caregiving can greatly affect the marital relationship.
w: Spouses rarely experience stress because they live with the patient
Living with the care recipient increases risk, and spouses report the largest health impact.
Her feelings show that she lacks the skills needed for caregiving
Her statement reflects relationship change, not a skill deficit.
Her feelings will resolve once she adjusts to the new routine
The length and uncertainty of chronic illness add to ongoing caregiver stress.

alt.q: Which factor helps explain why caregiving stress differs from one family caregiver to another?
alt.a: The person’s relationship to the patient
alt.ex: The level of stress a caregiver experiences is related to the caregiver’s relationship to the patient, such as being a spouse.
w: The certainty of the patient’s long-term outcome
Chronic illness is marked by uncertainty, which adds to stress rather than explaining differences.
The brief duration of most chronic illnesses
Chronic illnesses are long term; their length contributes to caregiver stress.
The decreasing complexity of care over time
Care often becomes more intense over time, making coping more difficult.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Which statement best explains why family caregivers’ personal health often worsens?
items.a: They give significant direct and indirect care and often neglect their own health concerns
items.ex: Family caregivers provide a lot of direct and indirect care and often fail to address their own personal and health-related concerns.
w: They receive too much respite care and lose their caregiving skills
Respite care is a resource that supports caregivers, not a cause of declining health.
They usually provide care for only a few weeks at a time
Chronic illness caregiving is long term; caring over a year increases risk.
They are rarely involved in the patient’s daily care activities
Caregivers provide significant direct and indirect daily care.

alt.q: A caregiver says, “I never have time for my own checkups because he needs me all the time.” Which risk does the nurse identify?
alt.a: Declining caregiver health from neglect of personal health concerns
alt.ex: Caregivers who provide significant care often fail to address their own health concerns, and their health worsens over time.
w: Improved caregiver health from staying physically busy
Neglecting personal health care increases risk rather than improving health.
Lower caregiver burden because routines are predictable
Increasing patient reliance raises, not lowers, caregiver burden.
No added risk because the caregiver is not the patient
Family caregivers are at risk for burden and poor health outcomes.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A nurse screens the family caregiver of a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease and finds that the caregiver has anxiety and depression. Why is this finding significant?
items.a: Caregiver burden is higher in caregivers who experience anxiety and depression
items.ex: Caregivers with anxiety and depression experience higher caregiver burden, so they need assessment and support such as counseling.
w: Anxiety and depression lower burden by increasing alertness
Anxiety and depression are linked to higher, not lower, caregiver burden.
These feelings affect only the patient and not the caregiver
The caregiver’s own anxiety and depression increase caregiver burden.
Anxiety and depression mean the caregiver should stop caregiving
The finding calls for support and resources, not automatic withdrawal from caregiving.

alt.q: Which caregiver finding indicates higher caregiver burden?
alt.a: The caregiver reports ongoing anxiety and depression
alt.ex: Caregiver burden is higher in caregivers who experience anxiety and depression.
w: The caregiver reports strong support from friends
Social support is a resource that lowers risk for caregivers.
The caregiver uses respite care twice a month
Respite care is a resource that supports caregivers.
The caregiver feels confident with care tasks
Knowledge and skills are resources that reduce risk.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Which statement by a family caregiver should concern the nurse most as a sign of risk for poor health outcomes?
items.a: “I’m 70, I live with my wife who has dementia, and I have no one to help me.”
items.ex: Age 65 or older, dementia care, living together, and insufficient social support all increase risk for poor caregiver outcomes.
w: “My sister and I take turns, and we use respite care on weekends.”
Shared care and respite are resources that lower caregiver risk.
“I help my aunt with errands once a week, and she manages well.”
Limited help for someone with few needs carries lower risk.
“Caring for my mom has been hard but also gives me a sense of purpose.”
Some caregivers report psychological benefits; this does not signal the highest risk.

alt.q: A nurse reviews notes on four caregivers. Which caregiver needs priority follow-up for risk of poor health outcomes?
alt.a: A 68-year-old who has cared for a spouse with Alzheimer disease at home for 2 years
alt.ex: Being 65 or older, caring for someone with dementia, living together, and caring over a year all raise risk.
w: A 30-year-old who helped a sibling recover from a fracture for 3 weeks
Short-term care for a healing injury is lower risk.
A 45-year-old who visits a parent weekly and uses community services
Living apart and having community services lower risk.
A 52-year-old who shares care for a parent with siblings and has respite
Shared care and respite are resources that reduce risk.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Parents of a child with a chronic illness report constant worry and exhaustion. Why should the nurse address the parents’ well-being?
items.a: Poor parental well-being negatively affects the child’s health and functioning
items.ex: Evidence connects parental well-being with children’s health; poor parental well-being harms children’s physical and psychosocial functioning.
w: Parents’ feelings have no effect on how the child functions
Parental and child well-being are connected.
Parents of chronically ill children rarely develop health problems
These parents have increased risk for anxiety, depression, and cardiovascular disease.
Addressing parents’ needs takes focus away from family-centered care
Family-centered care includes attention to the parents’ needs.

alt.q: Which risk should the nurse anticipate for parents caring for a child with a serious chronic illness?
alt.a: Increased risk for anxiety, fatigue, depression, and cardiovascular disease
alt.ex: Childhood chronic illness creates intense psychosocial responses in parents and increases their risk for chronic physical illness.
w: Decreased risk for chronic illness because parents stay active
Parents have an increased, not decreased, risk for chronic physical illness.
Improved family functioning because of unplanned hospitalizations
Unplanned hospitalizations disrupt the family and can worsen family functioning.
Fewer emotional responses because the illness is long term
The length and uncertainty of chronic illness add to stress.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A patient with heart failure is being discharged home, where his daughter will help manage medications and daily weights. Which nursing action best supports the caregiving dyad?
items.a: Include the daughter in teaching and in the interprofessional team planning
items.ex: Nurses provide education when needed and include the patient and family caregiver as part of the interprofessional health care team.
w: Give all discharge teaching to the patient alone to protect privacy
The family caregiver who will help with care should be included when appropriate.
Ask the daughter to wait outside while the team plans care
The patient and caregiver are included as part of the interprofessional team.
Provide teaching only after the first problem arises at home
Education is provided when needed, before the caregiver must perform new tasks.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse reflects best practice for working with a family caregiver?
alt.a: “The caregiver and patient are both members of our interprofessional team.”
alt.ex: Including the patient and family caregiver as part of the interprofessional team supports both members of the caregiving dyad.
w: “The caregiver should follow the plan without being part of planning.”
Caregivers are included in the team rather than excluded from planning.
“Caregiver concerns are outside the scope of nursing care.”
Caring for the family caregiver is essential in nursing care.
“Community resources are only for patients, not their caregivers.”
Both members of the caregiving dyad should have access to resources.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Which factors increase the stress experienced by a family caregiver of a patient with chronic illness? Select all that apply.
o: The length and uncertainty of the chronic illness
The length and uncertainty of chronic illness contribute to caregiver stress.
A patient who requires more intense care
More intense care makes coping and managing caregiving more difficult.
Cognitive changes so the patient no longer recognizes family
Caregivers report stress when a patient no longer recognizes family members.
Being the spouse of the patient
Stress relates to the relationship, and the marital relationship may be greatly affected.
A short, predictable course of illness
Chronic illness is long and uncertain, which increases stress.
A patient who is becoming more independent
Burden increases as the patient relies more heavily on the caregiver, not less.
items.ex: Caregiver stress relates to illness length and uncertainty, care complexity, illness characteristics, and the caregiver’s relationship to the patient.

alt.q: A nurse assesses a caregiver for sources of stress. Which findings suggest increased stress? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s care needs have become more complex
Complexity of caregiving shapes the caregiver’s experience and stress.
The illness has an uncertain, long-term course
Length and uncertainty of chronic illness add to caregiver stress.
The caregiver is the patient’s husband
Spouse caregivers may have their marital relationship greatly affected.
The patient now needs less help with daily care
Less reliance on the caregiver lowers, not raises, burden.
The caregiver uses regular respite and counseling
Respite and counseling are resources that support caregivers.
alt.ex: Correct: The patient’s care needs have become more complex; The illness has an uncertain, long-term course; The caregiver is the patient’s husband.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: When caring for a patient with a chronic illness and the family caregiver, which effects of the illness should the nurse assess?
items.a: Physical, psychosocial, and financial effects on both the patient and the caregiver
items.ex: Nurses assess the physical, psychosocial, and financial effects of chronic illness on the patient and the family caregiver.
w: Physical effects on the patient only, since the caregiver is not the patient
The caregiver is also affected; both members of the dyad are assessed.
Financial effects on the caregiver only, since costs fall on the family
Assessment covers physical, psychosocial, and financial effects on both members.
Psychosocial effects on the patient only, leaving caregivers to their own provider
Caring for the family caregiver is essential and is part of nursing assessment.

alt.q: A nurse finds that a caregiver is struggling with the costs of care and feels isolated. Which action addresses the dyad’s needs?
alt.a: Connect both patient and caregiver with resources such as social work and counseling
alt.ex: The nurse ensures both members of the caregiving dyad can access community resources including respite care, social work, and counseling.
w: Tell the caregiver that costs and isolation are expected and will pass
Dismissing these effects misses financial and psychosocial needs the nurse should address.
Refer only the patient to social work because the patient is ill
Both members of the caregiving dyad need access to resources.
Advise the caregiver to reduce visits with friends to save money
Reducing social contact worsens isolation; support and resources are needed.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A caregiver says, “I don’t know how to do his tube feedings, and there’s no one to give me a break.” The nurse recognizes this as which risk factor for poor caregiver health outcomes?
items.a: Insufficient resources
items.ex: Insufficient resources, including knowledge, skills, social support, respite, and community services, put caregivers at risk for poor outcomes.
w: Advanced caregiver age
Age 65 or older is a risk factor, but the statement describes missing knowledge and respite.
Living apart from the care recipient
Living with, not apart from, the care recipient is the listed risk factor.
Short duration of caregiving
Caring for more than a year, not a short time, increases risk.

alt.q: Which items are included in the resources whose absence puts family caregivers at risk for poor health outcomes?
alt.a: Knowledge, skills, social support, respite, and community services
alt.ex: Insufficient resources such as knowledge, skills, social support, respite, and community services increase caregivers’ risk.
w: Age, gender, marital status, and number of children
These are demographic characteristics, not the resources listed as protective.
Genetic testing, carrier screening, and prenatal care
These are genetic services, not caregiver resources.
Hospital size, bed availability, and staffing ratios
These are facility factors, not the caregiver resources described.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: What is the main purpose of the Chronic Care Model?
items.a: To provide a framework that guides health care delivery for people with chronic illness
items.ex: The Chronic Care Model is a framework guiding health care delivery for patients living with chronic illnesses.
w: To provide a system for staging how severe a chronic disease has become
The model guides care delivery; it does not stage disease severity.
To provide a formula for setting reimbursement rates for chronic disease care
The model is not a payment tool; it guides how care is delivered.
To provide a list of nursing diagnoses used for patients with chronic illness
The model is a care delivery framework, not a nursing diagnosis taxonomy.

alt.q: The Chronic Care Model illustrates how which two components interact to influence patient outcomes?
alt.a: The community and health care systems
alt.ex: The model shows how the community and health care systems interact to influence patient outcomes.
w: The patient and the family caregiver
Patients and caregivers matter, but the model’s two interacting components are community and health systems.
Acute care and long-term care settings
The model is not organized around care settings; its components are community and health systems.
Genetic factors and lifestyle behaviors
These are chronic disease risk factors, not the components of the Chronic Care Model.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: What is the focus of the community component of the Chronic Care Model?
items.a: The availability of resources and policies that can affect health
items.ex: The community component focuses on resources and policies that have the potential to impact health.
w: How providers use system resources to deliver evidence-based care
This describes the health care systems component, not the community component.
How patient health information is shared among providers
Sharing patient information describes clinical information systems within the health system.
How providers apply guidelines when teaching patients
Applying evidence-based guidelines to teaching describes the decision support element.

alt.q: What is the focus of the health care systems component of the Chronic Care Model?
alt.a: How providers can best use system resources and provide evidence-based care
alt.ex: The health care systems component focuses on using system resources well and providing evidence-based care to improve outcomes.
w: How local resources and public policies affect community health
Resources and policies are the focus of the community component.
How legislation can reduce exposure to barriers to health
Health-related legislation belongs to the community’s resources and policies focus.
How families can replace providers in managing chronic illness
The model does not have families replace providers; it coordinates care among them.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Which approach does the textbook identify as an effective method to improve preventive health practices in the community?
items.a: Public policy changes
items.ex: Public policy changes, such as nutrition and physical activity policies, effectively improve preventive health practices.
w: Longer hospital stays
Longer hospital stays are not a preventive health strategy described in the model.
More specialty clinics
Adding specialty clinics is not the community-level method the textbook describes.
Higher medication doses
Medication dosing is treatment, not a community preventive health measure.

alt.q: Which is an example of a public policy measure that can enhance preventive health in the community?
alt.a: A policy promoting nutrition and physical activity
alt.ex: Nutrition and physical activity policies are examples of policy changes that enhance prevention.
w: A policy lengthening hospital stays for chronic illness
Lengthening stays treats illness; it does not reduce high-risk behaviors.
A policy limiting outpatient follow-up visits
Limiting follow-up would reduce, not enhance, preventive care.
A policy raising the cost of health screenings
Raising screening costs creates barriers rather than decreasing them.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A patient with type 2 diabetes tells the clinic nurse, “Managing my diabetes is my doctor’s job, not mine.” Which response by the nurse best reflects self-management support?
items.a: “Let’s work together on goals you can manage in your daily life.”
items.ex: Self-management support places the patient at the center and requires collaboration that empowers the patient to take responsibility.
w: “That’s right; your provider will make the decisions for you.”
This keeps the patient passive instead of empowering them to manage their disease.
“Your family should take charge of your diabetes care at home.”
Shifting control to family does not place the patient at the center of management.
“I’ll ask your provider to handle all of your care for you.”
Handing all care to the provider removes the collaboration self-management requires.

alt.q: Which nurse action best demonstrates the self-management support element of the Chronic Care Model?
alt.a: Collaborating with the patient to set disease management goals
alt.ex: Self-management support requires collaboration that empowers patients to take responsibility for managing their chronic diseases.
w: Making treatment decisions on the patient’s behalf
Deciding for the patient removes the patient from the center of disease management.
Giving the patient a care schedule without discussion
A schedule given without discussion lacks the collaboration self-management requires.
Referring every care question to the health care provider
Referring everything away does not empower the patient to manage the illness.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Many patients at a rural clinic need nutrition classes that the clinic cannot offer. Which action by the nurse best reflects the community element of the Chronic Care Model?
items.a: Partnering with a local agency that already offers nutrition classes
items.ex: The community element develops partnerships with local, state, and national agencies to fill gaps in services.
w: Installing a new electronic system for sharing patient records
Sharing records reflects clinical information systems, not community partnerships.
Adopting guidelines that help providers plan patient teaching
Guideline-based teaching reflects decision support, not community partnerships.
Redesigning clinic appointments around expected outcomes
Planning care around expected outcomes reflects delivery system design.

alt.q: Which element of the Chronic Care Model uses partnerships between health systems and local, state, and national agencies to fill gaps in services?
alt.a: Community
alt.ex: The community element builds partnerships with agencies to fill service gaps and improve patient care.
w: Decision support
Decision support helps providers implement evidence-based guidelines and guide patient education.
Delivery system design
Delivery system design uses evidence-based care and expected outcomes to manage resources efficiently.
Clinical information systems
Clinical information systems maintain and share patient health information.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A primary care office and an oncology office have trouble sharing information about their shared patients. Which element of the Chronic Care Model most directly addresses this problem?
items.a: Clinical information systems
items.ex: Clinical information systems maintain and share patient health information among providers and patients for effective communication.
w: Self-management support
Self-management support empowers patients to manage their disease, not to share data between offices.
Decision support
Decision support helps providers implement guidelines rather than exchange patient information.
Community
The community element builds agency partnerships; information sharing is the role of clinical information systems.

alt.q: What is the purpose of the clinical information systems element of the Chronic Care Model?
alt.a: To maintain and share patient health information among providers and patients
alt.ex: Shared health information ensures effective communication and individualized patient care.
w: To help providers implement evidence-based guidelines in practice
Implementing guidelines describes the decision support element.
To build partnerships between health systems and local agencies
Agency partnerships describe the community element.
To place the patient at the center of disease management
Placing the patient at the center describes self-management support.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: How do health care providers use the decision support element of the Chronic Care Model?
items.a: To implement evidence-based guidelines, guide patient education, and encourage patient participation
items.ex: Decision support helps providers apply evidence-based guidelines, guide teaching, and encourage patients to participate in care.
w: To share health information among providers and patients in a secure record
Sharing health information is the role of clinical information systems.
To develop partnerships with agencies that fill gaps in available services
Agency partnerships are part of the community element.
To constantly improve chronic illness management with a focus on safety
Continuous improvement focused on safety and quality describes the health system element.

alt.q: A nurse uses an evidence-based heart failure guideline to plan patient teaching and invite the patient to take part in care decisions. Which element of the model is the nurse applying?
alt.a: Decision support
alt.ex: Decision support uses evidence-based guidelines to guide patient education and encourage patient participation.
w: Delivery system design
Delivery system design focuses on evidence-based care that includes expected outcomes and efficient resource use.
Clinical information systems
Clinical information systems store and share patient information.
Community
The community element focuses on resources, policies, and agency partnerships.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: Which statement describes the delivery system design element of the Chronic Care Model?
items.a: It uses evidence-based care that includes expected outcomes and efficient resource management
items.ex: Delivery system design combines evidence-based care and patient expected outcomes to maintain health and manage resources efficiently.
w: It places the patient at the center of chronic disease management
Placing the patient at the center describes self-management support.
It maintains and shares health information among providers
Sharing health information describes clinical information systems.
It develops partnerships with local and national agencies
Agency partnerships describe the community element.

alt.q: Which element of the Chronic Care Model uses evidence-based care that includes a patient’s expected outcomes to maintain optimal health and manage system resources efficiently?
alt.a: Delivery system design
alt.ex: Delivery system design links evidence-based care and expected outcomes to optimal health and efficient resource use.
w: Self-management support
Self-management support centers on collaborating with and empowering the patient.
Decision support
Decision support helps providers apply guidelines and guide patient education.
Health system
The health system element focuses on continuously improving management with attention to safety and quality.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: According to the Chronic Care Model, improved outcomes result from productive interactions between which two parties?
items.a: An informed, activated patient and a prepared, proactive practice team
items.ex: The model’s elements lead to productive interactions between an informed, activated patient and a prepared, proactive team.
w: A compliant, passive patient and a directive health care provider
The model seeks an activated patient, not a passive one following directions.
A hospital administrator and the patient’s insurance company
The model’s key interaction is between the patient and the practice team.
A family caregiver and a community volunteer agency
Caregivers and agencies help, but the key interaction is patient and practice team.

alt.q: Which description of the patient reflects the goal of the Chronic Care Model?
alt.a: Informed and activated
alt.ex: The model aims for informed, activated patients who interact productively with a prepared, proactive team.
w: Compliant and passive
A passive patient conflicts with the model’s emphasis on patient activation.
Dependent and directed
The model empowers patients rather than making them dependent on providers.
Prepared and proactive
Prepared and proactive describes the practice team, not the patient.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A nurse reviews research on using the Chronic Care Model in a primary health care setting. Which outcome was reported for patients with type 2 diabetes?
items.a: They managed their diabetes better, including a reduction in BMI
items.ex: After the model was implemented in primary care, patients with type 2 diabetes managed their disease better, including lower BMI.
w: They needed more hospital admissions to control their glucose
The research showed better self-management, not more hospital admissions.
They stopped needing follow-up visits with primary care
The model improves follow-up rather than eliminating it.
They gained weight as provider visits became less frequent
The study reported a reduction in BMI, not weight gain.

alt.q: Research on the Chronic Care Model in primary care found better coordination of care with oncology offices. What helped achieve this?
alt.a: Chronic care coordinators partnered with cancer center social workers
alt.ex: Coordinators partnering with cancer center social workers made care more routine and improved information sharing.
w: Oncology offices took over all primary care for patients with cancer
The practices coordinated care; one did not take over the other.
Patients were asked to carry their own records between offices
Information sharing improved through coordinator partnerships, not patient-carried records.
Primary care offices stopped seeing patients with cancer
Primary care stayed involved, with better coordination between the two practices.

items.src: Ch 8 · Caring for patients with chronic illness

items.q: A nurse manager plans to implement the Chronic Care Model in a clinic. Which statement by a staff nurse shows understanding of its expected benefits?
items.a: “It should improve planned interprofessional care, follow-up, and patient education.”
items.ex: The model improves coordination of planned interprofessional care, patient follow-up, and education of patients and families.
w: “It should reduce the need to teach families about managing illness.”
The model includes educating patients and families, not reducing family teaching.
“It should let each discipline plan care independently of the others.”
The model improves coordination of interprofessional care rather than independent planning.

items.q: A nurse is collecting a nursing history from a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Which question best encourages the patient to describe their experience?

w: “Do you have trouble breathing when you walk?”

“Are you using your inhalers as prescribed?”
This closed-ended question limits the patient to a yes-or-no response.
“Has your illness become worse this month?”
This closed-ended question does not let the patient tell their story.

This question invites only a yes-or-no answer.

This closed-ended question limits the patient’s response.
“Do you take your pills daily?”
This closed-ended question does not invite the patient’s story.

Wait for the patient to bring up the pain without prompting

Inspect the abdomen and auscultate bowel sounds
The abdomen is not the system most likely affected by breathing difficulty.
Test cranial nerves and pupil reactions to light

items.q: During an alcohol assessment, which patient report should lead the nurse to suspect alcohol misuse?
items.a: A woman who has 4 drinks on a typical day
items.ex: More than three drinks a day for women suggests alcohol misuse.
w: A woman who has 1 drink on a typical day
One drink a day (7 a week) is within both the daily and weekly limits for women.
A man who has 3 drinks on a typical day
Three a day is not more than four a day for men, and the weekly total stays within limits.
A man who has 2 drinks on 5 days a week
This totals 10 drinks a week, within the limits of 4 a day and 15 a week.

alt.q: A man reports drinking no more than 3 drinks a day but about 16 drinks each week. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: His weekly total exceeds the threshold, suggesting misuse
alt.ex: More than 15 drinks a week for men indicates excess total alcohol consumption.
w: His intake is acceptable because his daily amount is under 4
Misuse is also suspected when the weekly total is exceeded.
His intake is acceptable because the weekly limit for men is 21
The weekly threshold for men is more than 15 drinks, not 21.
His weekly total suggests misuse only if he is older than 65
The textbook threshold of more than 15 drinks a week is not age-specific.
