items.q: Which statement best describes a person’s worldview?
items.a: A set of assumptions, starting in childhood, that guides how a person sees and interprets the world
items.ex: Worldview begins developing in childhood and acts as a lens for how people perceive, relate to, and interpret reality.
w: A fixed set of beliefs inherited at birth that stays the same throughout life
Worldview evolves over a lifetime through interactions with family, peers, communities, media, and institutions.
A formal religious doctrine that a person chooses to follow during adulthood
Religion may shape it, but worldview is a broader set of assumptions that starts forming in childhood.
A professional code that health care providers adopt when they enter practice
Everyone has a worldview; it is not a professional code limited to health care providers.

alt.q: A nursing student asks how a person’s worldview develops. Which response by the nurse educator is accurate?
alt.a: “It evolves over a lifetime as you interact with family, peers, communities, media, and institutions.”
alt.ex: Worldview is shaped by culture and by socialization through family, peers, schooling, media, work, and institutions over a lifetime.
w: “It is fully formed in early childhood and does not change after that.”
Worldview begins in childhood but keeps evolving throughout life.
“It develops only through formal schooling and professional education.”
Schooling is one influence; family, community, media, and institutions also shape worldview.
“It is determined by biology and is not shaped by life experiences.”
Worldview comes from shared experiences and socialization, not biology.

items.q: In a cultural encounter, which term describes the insider perspective?
items.a: Emic worldview
items.ex: The emic worldview is the insider perspective of a cultural encounter.
w: Etic worldview
The etic worldview is the outsider perspective.
Biomedical worldview
A biomedical view reflects the culture of science, not the insider perspective of an encounter.
Intersectional worldview
Intersectionality is a model of overlapping social determinants, not the insider perspective.

alt.q: What does an etic worldview represent in a cultural encounter?
alt.a: The outsider perspective
alt.ex: Every cultural encounter has an insider (emic) and an outsider (etic) perspective.
w: The insider perspective
The insider perspective is the emic worldview.
The health care team’s shared policy
Worldview perspectives belong to individuals, not agency policies.
The perspective agreed on by nurse and patient
Etic refers to an outsider view, not a negotiated shared view.

items.q: Conflict arises when health care providers interpret patients’ behaviors through their own worldview lens instead of uncovering the worldview behind the behavior.
items.a: True
items.ex: The chapter names viewing patient behavior through the provider’s own lens as a source of conflict.
items.ww: The book states that conflict does arise from this; uncovering the patient’s worldview prevents it.

alt.q: The most reliable way for a nurse to avoid cultural conflict is to interpret a patient’s behavior through the nurse’s own worldview.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Interpreting behavior through one’s own lens causes conflict; the nurse should uncover the worldview guiding the patient’s behavior.
alt.ww: Using one’s own worldview is the cause of conflict, not a way to prevent it.

items.q: Healthy People 2030 defines a health disparity as a health difference closely linked with social, economic, and/or environmental [[disadvantage|disadvantages]].
items.ex: A health disparity is a particular type of health difference closely tied to social, economic, or environmental disadvantage.

alt.q: A particular type of health difference that is closely linked with social, economic, and/or environmental disadvantage is a health [[disparity|disparities|inequity]].
alt.ex: A health disparity is a particular type of health difference closely tied to social, economic, or environmental disadvantage.

items.q: After giving birth, a patient from a culture different from the nurse’s requests seaweed soup for her first meal. The agency does not stock seaweed. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Ask about the meal’s significance and offer a substitute such as other greens like kale
items.ex: Uncovering the patient’s worldview and offering a substitute such as kale respects the request when seaweed is unavailable.
w: Explain that hospital meals follow a standard postpartum menu that cannot change
Refusing to adapt ignores the meaning of the request and the patient’s worldview.
Tell the patient soup is not appropriate after delivery and bring a regular tray
This judges the request through the nurse’s own lens instead of understanding it.
Document the request as a food preference and take no further action
Documenting alone does not address the patient’s cultural need.

alt.q: A postpartum patient assumes the hospital will serve a traditional soup that it does not stock, and the nurse is puzzled by the request. What best explains this misunderstanding?
alt.a: Nurse and patient are each viewing the situation through a different worldview
alt.ex: The patient holds an outsider view of U.S. postpartum care and the nurse is unaware of the meal’s significance.
w: The patient has a knowledge deficit about postpartum nutrition
The request reflects cultural meaning, not a lack of nutrition knowledge.
The nurse is applying the agency’s dietary policy incorrectly
The issue is differing worldviews, not misuse of policy.
The patient is refusing to cooperate with the plan of care
Requesting a culturally meaningful meal is not refusal of care.

items.q: Which description best defines social determinants of health (SDOH)?
items.a: Nonmedical conditions in which people are born, grow, live, work, and age that affect health
items.ex: SDOH are the nonmedical conditions of daily life that affect health functioning and quality-of-life outcomes.
w: Genetic and biological traits a person inherits that determine disease risk
Inherited traits are biological factors, not the nonmedical conditions that make up SDOH.
Treatments and medications that providers prescribe to manage disease
Prescribed treatments are medical care, whereas SDOH are nonmedical conditions.
Laboratory values and vital signs that reflect a person’s current health
Clinical measurements reflect health status; they are not social determinants.

alt.q: A nurse is listing a patient’s social determinants of health. Which item belongs on the list?
alt.a: Access to transportation resources
alt.ex: Transportation resources are a nonmedical condition of daily life and an example of an SDOH.
w: Blood pressure reading on admission
A blood pressure reading is a clinical finding, not a social determinant.
Results of a complete blood count
Laboratory results are clinical data, not social determinants.
Dosage of a current prescribed medication
Medication dosage is part of medical treatment, not a social determinant.

items.q: Which categories of social determinants of health does Healthy People 2030 identify? Select all that apply.
o: Economic Stability
Economic Stability is one of the five Healthy People 2030 categories.
Education Access and Quality
Education Access and Quality is one of the five categories.
Neighborhood and Built Environment
Neighborhood and Built Environment is one of the five categories.
Social and Community Context
Social and Community Context is one of the five categories.
Genetic Predisposition and Heredity
Genetics is biological, not one of the five social determinant categories.
Personal Lifestyle Choices
Lifestyle choices are not one of the five named categories.
items.ex: The five Healthy People 2030 categories are Economic Stability, Education Access and Quality, Health Care Access and Quality, Neighborhood and Built Environment, and Social and Community Context.

alt.q: A community health nurse groups local needs by the Healthy People 2030 social determinant categories. Which categories can the nurse use? Select all that apply.
o: Health Care Access and Quality
Health Care Access and Quality is one of the five categories.
Economic Stability
Economic Stability is one of the five categories.
Social and Community Context
Social and Community Context is one of the five categories.
Biological Age and Sex
Age and sex are personal characteristics, not one of the five categories.
Family Medical History
Family medical history is a biological risk factor, not a social determinant category.
alt.ex: Correct: Health Care Access and Quality; Economic Stability; Social and Community Context.

items.q: Which statements are accurate examples of health disparities in the United States? Select all that apply.
o: Rural residents have a higher risk of death from heart disease and stroke than urban residents.
Box 9.1 lists higher rural risk of death from heart disease, cancer, injuries, lung disease, and stroke.
Rural residents are more likely than urban residents to smoke and be overweight.
Rural residents are more likely to smoke, be overweight, and fall short of activity recommendations.
Black, AIAN, and Latinx individuals are less likely to have health insurance.
Lower insurance rates in these groups create barriers to obtaining health care.
Black males are less likely than White males to die from cancer.
Black males are more likely than White males to die from cancer.
Rural residents generally have better health status because of lower chronic disease rates.
Rural residents generally have poorer health status due to a higher incidence of chronic diseases.
items.ex: Box 9.1 shows disparities by geography, race, and ethnicity in risk, outcomes, and access to care.

alt.q: A nurse is preparing a community presentation on health disparities. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Black and AIAN individuals live fewer years on average than White individuals.
Box 9.1 lists shorter average life spans for Black and AIAN individuals.
Black and AIAN females are more likely to have pregnancy-related complications or die during or after pregnancy.
Box 9.1 lists higher pregnancy-related complications and deaths for these groups.
About 20% of children 3 to 17 years of age have a mental, behavioral, or developmental disorder.
Box 9.1 states about 20% of children in this age group have such a disorder.
Black and AIAN adults are more likely than White adults to receive an annual flu shot.
Black, AIAN, and Latinx adults are less likely than White adults to receive an annual flu shot.
More than 75% of people in all racial and ethnic groups complete substance use disorder treatment.
Less than 50% of individuals from all racial/ethnic groups completed treatment.
alt.ex: Correct: Black and AIAN individuals live fewer years on average than White individuals; Black and AIAN females are more likely to have pregnancy-related complications or die during or after pregnancy; About 20% of children 3 to 17 years of age have a mental, behavioral, or developmental disorder.

items.q: Which statement about breast cancer disparity is accurate?
items.a: White females are more likely to develop it, but Black females are more likely to die from it
items.ex: Box 9.1 notes that White females develop breast cancer more often, yet Black females are more likely to die from it.
w: Black females are more likely both to develop it and to die from it
White females are more likely to develop breast cancer.
White females are more likely both to develop it and to die from it
Black females are more likely to die from breast cancer.
Black and White females develop it and die from it at equal rates
The rates differ: White females develop it more, Black females die from it more.

alt.q: Compared with Black females, White females are:
alt.a: More likely to develop breast cancer but less likely to die from it
alt.ex: The disparity lies in outcomes: Black females have higher breast cancer mortality despite lower incidence.
w: Less likely to develop breast cancer and less likely to die from it
White females are more likely to develop breast cancer.
More likely to develop breast cancer and more likely to die from it
Black females, not White females, are more likely to die from it.
Less likely to develop breast cancer but more likely to die from it
This reverses the disparity described in Box 9.1.

items.q: Health disparities in rural areas are increasing, partly because 135 rural hospitals closed between 2010 and 2020.
items.a: True
items.ex: The AHRQ report links rising rural disparities to the closing of 135 rural hospitals over that decade.
items.ww: The chapter states rural disparities are increasing, and hospital closures contribute to this.

alt.q: The closure of rural hospitals between 2010 and 2020 has narrowed health disparities between rural and urban areas.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Rural hospital closures have increased, not narrowed, health disparities in rural areas.
alt.ww: Fewer hospitals reduce access to care, so the closures widened rather than narrowed rural disparities.

items.q: Which description defines marginalization?
items.a: Placing or keeping someone in a powerless or unimportant position within a society or group
items.ex: Marginalization keeps people in a powerless position and involves multiple overlapping conditions that affect health outcomes.
w: Transitioning from one culture and developing the traits of another culture
This describes acculturation.
Making a judgment or opinion about a group without sufficient cause
This describes prejudice.
Factors or advantages that benefit certain individuals, groups, or populations
This describes privilege.

alt.q: A nurse is identifying groups the chapter describes as marginalized. Which group is included?
alt.a: People who are not college educated
alt.ex: The chapter lists LGBTQIA+ people, people of color, people who are physically or mentally challenged, and people without college education.
w: People with employer-sponsored health insurance
Having insurance reflects access to resources, which is linked to privilege, not marginalization.
People who live near a large medical center
Ready access to care is not an example of marginalization.
People who hold executive leadership positions
Decision-making power is the opposite of the powerless position that defines marginalization.

items.q: Ms. Millman, who has type 2 diabetes, nods during teaching about insulin and healthy food choices and says she has no questions. She has visited the emergency department three times in 6 months. What should the nurse suspect?
items.a: A possible literacy problem that limits her understanding of the teaching
items.ex: Her neutral reaction to teaching and repeat visits suggest a questionable literacy problem, one of her social determinants of health.
w: That she fully understands the teaching and needs no further instruction
Nodding without questions and repeated admissions suggest she may not understand.
That she disagrees with the plan and is choosing not to follow it
Nothing in her case suggests disagreement; social determinants and literacy are the concern.
That her repeat visits are caused mainly by an insulin allergy
Her visits relate to poor blood sugar control linked to social determinants, not an allergy.

alt.q: Ms. Millman nods silently after diabetes teaching and has no questions. Which action should the nurse take next?
alt.a: Ask her to explain in her own words how she will manage her diet
alt.ex: Asking for an explanation in her own words checks understanding when a neutral reaction suggests a literacy problem.
w: Document that she verbalized understanding of her diabetes teaching
Prior providers documented understanding, yet she kept returning; nodding does not confirm learning.
Ask her, “Do you understand everything I told you?”
Yes-or-no checks of understanding do not verify what the patient learned.
Give her a detailed written handout and end the session
A handout alone does not confirm understanding, especially with a possible literacy problem.

items.q: Which social determinants of health affect Ms. Millman’s ability to manage her diabetes? Select all that apply.
o: Loss of employment and health insurance
Her socioeconomic status limits her financial resources and access to care.
Living in shelter housing after becoming unhoused
Lack of a home is a socioeconomic determinant affecting self-management.
Using the emergency department instead of primary care
She has no access to primary care, which is a social determinant.
A questionable literacy problem
Her neutral reaction to teaching suggests a literacy problem.
An HbA1c of 11%
HbA1c is a clinical finding showing poor control, not a social determinant.
A diagnosis of type 2 diabetes 2 years ago
The diagnosis is the disease itself, not a social determinant.
items.ex: Ms. Millman’s socioeconomic status, lack of primary care, sex, and possible literacy problem all affect her diabetes management.

alt.q: A nurse assesses a patient admitted with poorly controlled hypertension. Which findings are social determinants of health? Select all that apply.
o: Has no reliable transportation to the clinic
Transportation resources are an example of an SDOH.
Lives in a rural area far from health care services
Geographic location affecting access to care is an SDOH.
Reads at a limited literacy level
Literacy level is listed as a social determinant of health.
Blood pressure of 178/96 mm Hg
A vital sign is a clinical finding, not a social determinant.
Takes two antihypertensive medications
Medication therapy is medical treatment, not a social determinant.
alt.ex: Correct: Has no reliable transportation to the clinic; Lives in a rural area far from health care services; Reads at a limited literacy level.

items.q: A nurse reviews the records of four patients. Which patient is most likely to receive adequate preventive care?
items.a: A patient who regularly visits a primary care provider
items.ex: Patients who regularly see a primary care provider are more likely to receive adequate preventive care than those without such access.
w: A patient who uses the emergency department for most health needs
Using the emergency department reflects a lack of primary care access.
A patient who seeks care only when symptoms become severe
Waiting for severe symptoms means missing routine preventive care.
A patient who recently lost employment and health insurance
Losing insurance limits access to care and preventive services.

alt.q: Why does the chapter describe access to primary care as an important indicator?
alt.a: It reflects broader access to health care services, including preventive care
alt.ex: Access to primary care signals broader access to health services, and regular primary care improves preventive care.
w: It measures how many hospital beds are available in a community
Bed numbers are not what primary care access indicates.
It shows how many specialists practice in a region
Primary care access is about regular general care, not specialist supply.
It determines eligibility for government insurance programs
Primary care access is an indicator of access, not an eligibility rule.

items.q: Intersectionality considers how interdependent social determinants of health intersect to shape the health and well-being of individuals and communities.
items.a: True
items.ex: Intersectionality is a research and policy model that studies how overlapping social determinants shape people’s lives and health.
items.ww: The model is defined by how determinants intersect, so the statement is accurate.

alt.q: Intersectionality holds that each social determinant of health affects a person’s health independently of the others.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Intersectionality looks at how interdependent determinants intersect, not at each one in isolation.
alt.ww: The model focuses on interaction among determinants; viewing them separately is the opposite of intersectionality.

items.q: In the intersectionality model, oppression results from the interaction of which two factors?
items.a: Power and prejudice
items.ex: In oppression, power (decision-making ability) interacts with prejudice, leading to discrimination against some groups and benefits for others.
w: Privilege and assimilation
Privilege is a benefit to some groups, and assimilation is cultural adaptation; neither pairing defines oppression.
Stereotyping and acculturation
Acculturation is cultural transition, not a cause of oppression.
Income and education level
These are social determinants, not the interacting factors that define oppression.

alt.q: As used in the discussion of oppression, which description defines prejudice?

w: Decision-making ability held by a person or group
This describes power.
Advantages that benefit certain individuals or groups
This describes privilege.
A system of advantages and disadvantages tied to group membership
This describes oppression.

items.q: During self-reflection, a nurse realizes she assumes older adults cannot learn new technology. On the ladder of cultural competence, which response addresses this stereotype level?
items.a: Develop self-awareness of own assumptions, values, and biases about human behavior

w: Understand the institutional forces that support or negate cultural competence

Develop appropriate interventions and techniques for group interactions
This responds to discrimination at the group/interpersonal level.
Understand the worldviews of culturally diverse patients and co-workers
This responds to bias/prejudice, the level above stereotype.

alt.q: On the ladders of oppression and cultural competence, which response corresponds to the discrimination (group/interpersonal) level?
alt.a: Develop appropriate interventions and techniques

w: Develop self-awareness of own assumptions and values
This responds to stereotype at the individual level.
Understand the worldviews of diverse patients and co-workers
This responds to bias/prejudice at the individual level.
Understand institutional forces affecting competence
This responds to oppression at the institutional level.

items.q: Why is it important for a nurse to examine their own racial, ethnic, and cultural identity?
items.a: Without it, the nurse is more likely to assess patients’ health care problems inaccurately
items.ex: Self-examination helps the nurse recognize culturally influenced behaviors; skipping it leads to inaccurate assessment.
w: It lets the nurse predict each patient’s beliefs from the patient’s cultural group
Predicting beliefs from group membership is stereotyping, which self-examination should prevent.
It is required so the nurse can document the patient’s race in the record
Self-examination is about the nurse’s own identity, not documentation of the patient.
It allows the nurse to replace patients’ beliefs with evidence-based ones
Cultural care respects patients’ beliefs rather than replacing them.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of cultural self-examination?
alt.a: “Knowing my own identity and biases helps me recognize culturally influenced behaviors.”
alt.ex: Examining one’s own identity supports understanding the cultural factors that shape a patient’s needs and behaviors.
w: “Once I know my own culture, I can assume patients from it share my views.”
Assuming shared views is stereotyping; diversity exists within cultural groups.
“Self-examination is needed only when I care for patients from other countries.”
Self-examination is needed for every patient encounter, not only with immigrants.
“My cultural background has no effect on how I assess my patients.”
The nurse’s cultural background does influence assessment, which is why self-examination matters.

items.q: Acculturation can cause stress when the values of the culture a person is transitioning from differ from those of the new culture.
items.a: True
items.ex: Acculturation involves adapting to new traditions, customs, and language, which can be stressful when values conflict.
items.ww: The chapter notes that acculturation can lead to stress when values differ.

alt.q: Acculturation is usually free of stress because a person keeps all original customs and language unchanged.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Acculturation involves adapting to a new culture’s traditions, customs, and language, which can cause stress.
alt.ww: Acculturation means developing traits of another culture, so customs do change and stress can result.

items.q: Which statement correctly distinguishes illness from disease?
items.a: Illness is how people react to disease; disease is a malfunction of biological or psychological processes
items.ex: Disease is the malfunction itself, while illness is the way individuals and families experience and react to it.
w: Disease is how people react to illness; illness is a malfunction of biological processes
This reverses the two definitions.
Illness is a short-term condition; disease is a long-term or chronic condition
The distinction is reaction versus malfunction, not duration.
Illness has a psychological cause; disease has only a physical cause
Disease includes malfunctioning of psychological processes as well as biological ones.

alt.q: What is the term for a malfunctioning of biological or psychological processes?
alt.a: Disease
alt.ex: Disease is the malfunction; illness is the individual and family reaction to that disease.
w: Illness
Illness is the way individuals and families react to disease.
Health disparity
A health disparity is a health difference linked to social, economic, or environmental disadvantage.
Cultural stigma
Cultural stigma is meaning attached to a condition, not the malfunction itself.

items.q: A patient’s symptoms resemble those of family members who died, so the patient believes the condition is untreatable. The health care provider believes aggressive therapy may cure it. What is the likely result if this difference is not addressed?
items.a: Frustration, lack of trust, poor adherence to treatment, and poor outcomes
items.ex: Differing perspectives on illness and disease frustrate both sides and foster mistrust, nonadherence, and poor health outcomes.
w: Improved adherence because the provider’s view is medically accurate
Unaddressed differences reduce adherence rather than improve it.
Faster recovery because the patient will defer to the provider
The chapter links these differences to poor outcomes, not faster recovery.
No effect, because a patient’s beliefs do not affect treatment
Beliefs about illness strongly influence trust and adherence.

alt.q: A gap exists between a patient’s beliefs about illness and the provider’s focus on disease. Which nursing approach is best?
alt.a: Consider both the disease and the patient’s experience of illness when planning care
alt.ex: Safe, quality care means taking both disease and illness into consideration.
w: Focus care on the disease because it is the measurable problem
Focusing only on disease ignores the illness experience that brought the patient for care.
Accept the patient’s view and stop recommending any treatment
Ignoring the disease is also unsafe; both perspectives must be considered.
Refer the patient to a provider who shares the patient’s culture
Referral avoids rather than bridges the gap in perspectives.

items.q: Most health care providers in the United States are educated mainly to treat disease, whereas most people seek care because of their experience with illness.
items.a: True
items.ex: This mismatch between a disease focus and the patient’s illness experience is why nurses must consider both.
items.ww: The chapter states providers are primarily educated to treat disease while patients seek care for illness.

alt.q: Most people seek health care because a provider has diagnosed a disease rather than because of their own experience of illness.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Most individuals seek care because of their experience with illness, the way they react to disease.
alt.ww: People are driven to seek care by illness experience; providers, not patients, are oriented to disease.

items.q: Cultural stigma attached to conditions such as HIV, bipolar disorder, cancer, or dementia can lead to which outcomes? Select all that apply.
o: Lack of early detection
Stigma can delay detection of the condition.
Lack of screening
Stigma can keep people from being screened.
Lack of diagnosis
Stigma can prevent a diagnosis from being made.
Increased awareness of the condition
Stigma is linked to decreased, not increased, awareness.
Earlier entry into treatment
Stigma delays detection and diagnosis, so treatment starts later, not earlier.
items.ex: Cultural interpretation and stigma can lead to lack of early detection, screening, or diagnosis and decreased awareness.

alt.q: A nurse works in a community where certain diagnoses carry strong cultural stigma. Which effects should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Delayed screening for the condition
Stigma discourages screening.
Missed or late diagnosis
Stigma can result in lack of diagnosis.
Decreased awareness of the condition
The chapter links stigma with decreased awareness.
Higher rates of early detection
Stigma reduces early detection.
More frequent preventive health visits
Stigma discourages rather than encourages seeking care.
alt.ex: Correct: Delayed screening for the condition; Missed or late diagnosis; Decreased awareness of the condition.

items.q: Which statements about the core measures are accurate? Select all that apply.

Core measures are defined as evidence-based, researched standards.
They apply to all patients regardless of cultural or socioeconomic status.
Because the standard applies to all, all patients are to be treated equally.
They are intended to help reduce health disparities.
Besides improving care, the core measures aim to reduce disparities.
A single core measure set covers both adults and children.
There are two core measure sets: one for adults and one for children.
They apply only to patients covered by Medicare or Medicaid.
The measures apply to all patients.
items.ex: Core measures hold providers accountable to evidence-based standards for every patient, which supports equal treatment and reduces disparities.

alt.q: A nurse explains core measures to a new graduate. Which points are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They help agencies improve performance and increase accountability.
Core measures are key quality indicators for performance and accountability.
They aim to reduce health care costs.
Reducing costs is one stated aim of the measures.
There are separate measure sets for adults and for children.
There are now two core measure sets.
They were developed by The Joint Commission working alone.

The measures apply to all patients.
alt.ex: Correct: They help agencies improve performance and increase accountability; They aim to reduce health care costs; There are separate measure sets for adults and for children.

items.q: A patient presents with heart failure and left ventricular systolic dysfunction. Under the core measures, which therapy should the patient receive?
items.a: A beta blocker plus either an ACE inhibitor or an ARB
items.ex: The heart failure core measure calls for beta blocker therapy plus either ACE inhibitor or ARB therapy.
w: A beta blocker alone, without an ACE inhibitor or an ARB
The measure requires an ACE inhibitor or ARB in addition to the beta blocker.
An ACE inhibitor plus an ARB, without a beta blocker
The measure includes a beta blocker and either, not both, an ACE inhibitor or ARB.
A calcium channel blocker plus a loop diuretic
These drugs are not the therapies named in the heart failure core measure.

alt.q: Which is an example of an obstetrics and gynecology core measure described in the chapter?
alt.a: Females receive breast cancer screening
alt.ex: Breast cancer screening for females is the OB-GYN core measure example the chapter gives.
w: Females receive annual bone density scans
Bone density scanning is not the OB-GYN core measure named in the chapter.
Females receive yearly thyroid testing
Thyroid testing is not the core measure example given.
Females receive routine iron supplements
Iron supplementation is not the core measure example given.

items.q: Which description best defines cultural competence?
items.a: Adapting care in a manner congruent with the patient’s culture
items.ex: Cultural competence is the adaptation of care to fit the client’s culture while keeping one’s own views from unduly affecting care.
w: Providing identical care to every patient regardless of culture
Cultural competence adapts care to the patient’s culture rather than standardizing it.
Expecting patients to adopt the health care team’s beliefs
Competence respects patients’ beliefs rather than replacing them.
Assigning patients only to nurses who share their background
Competence is a skill every nurse develops, not a matching of backgrounds.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows understanding of cultural competence?
alt.a: “Cultural competence is a lifelong journey, not a destination.”
alt.ex: Cultural competence is a self-motivated developmental process that evolves over a lifetime.
w: “Once I complete a cultural course, I will be culturally competent.”
Competence is ongoing and evolves over a lifetime, not after one course.
“Cultural competence applies to individual nurses but not to agencies.”
Individuals, health care agencies, and systems all lie on the competence continuum.
“Cultural competence means treating every patient exactly the same way.”
Competence adapts care to each patient’s culture.

items.q: Cultural desire is the pivotal construct of cultural competence because a nurse’s desire evokes the entire process.
items.a: True

alt.a: False
alt.ex: Cultural desire, not cultural skill, is the pivotal construct that evokes the whole process.
alt.ww: Cultural skill is the ability to assess; it is the nurse’s desire that drives the process.

items.q: A female patient asks that only female health care providers care for her and seems uncomfortable with male staff. Which statement by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Modesty is important to many patients. Is there some way I can make you more comfortable?”
items.ex: This combines cultural knowledge with helpfulness and flexibility while not assuming the information applies to this patient.
w: “Because of your religion, I will make sure no male staff enter your room.”
This assumes general group knowledge applies to her without asking.
“Our male staff are professionals, so there is no need to feel uncomfortable.”
This dismisses the patient’s concern instead of exploring it.
“We cannot promise female staff, so you will need to accept who is assigned.”
This ignores her preference and shows no flexibility.

alt.q: A nurse learns that a patient’s religion places high value on modesty. Which approach reflects culturally congruent care?
alt.a: Use the knowledge as a baseline, then ask the patient about her own preferences
alt.ex: Group knowledge is a starting point, but diversity within groups means the nurse confirms individual preferences.
w: Apply the group’s modesty rules to the patient without discussing them
Applying group rules without asking risks stereotyping.
Disregard the knowledge because every patient is unique
Knowledge provides a useful baseline; it should be checked, not ignored.
Ask the family to explain the religion’s rules to the staff
The patient herself should be asked about her preferences.

items.q: How does cultural humility differ from cultural competence?
items.a: Cultural humility is an ongoing process with no end point, unlike content mastery
items.ex: Cultural humility differs from the content mastery found in competence and requires lifelong self-exploration and self-critique.
w: Cultural humility is achieved once a nurse finishes cultural training
Cultural humility has no end point and is never fully achieved.
Cultural humility focuses on facts about groups rather than relationships
Humility focuses on the relationship with the person and honoring their beliefs.
Cultural humility is needed only by nurses in diverse communities
Humility applies to every patient relationship, not only certain settings.

alt.q: Which description defines cultural humility?
alt.a: A process of self-exploration and self-critique leading to understanding how culture affects another’s health behaviors
alt.ex: Cultural humility uses self-exploration and self-critique to understand how culture shapes a person’s health behaviors.
w: The motivation to “want to” engage in becoming culturally aware and skillful
This describes cultural desire.
Obtaining a sound educational base about culturally diverse groups and their beliefs
This describes cultural knowledge.
Communicating information in a way that diverse audiences easily understand
This describes linguistic competence.

items.q: Which attributes are part of cultural humility? Select all that apply.
o: Openness
Openness is an attribute of cultural humility.
Self-reflection
Self-reflection is an attribute of cultural humility.
Lifelong learning
Cultural humility requires a lifelong commitment to learning.
Empathy
Empathy is an attribute of cultural humility.
Content mastery
Content mastery is associated with cultural competence; humility is an ongoing process.
Professional detachment
Humility focuses on the relationship with the person, not detachment.
items.ex: Cultural humility includes openness, self-awareness, self-reflection, lifelong learning, empathy, compassion, and humility.

alt.q: A nurse wants to practice cultural humility. Which qualities should the nurse develop? Select all that apply.
o: Self-awareness
Self-awareness is an attribute of cultural humility.
Compassion
Compassion is an attribute of cultural humility.
Humility
Humility itself is listed as an attribute.
Certainty about each cultural group’s beliefs
Humility involves openness and self-critique, not certainty about groups.
Emotional distance from patients
Cultural humility centers on a relationship with the patient.
alt.ex: Correct: Self-awareness; Compassion; Humility.

items.q: When cultural humility permeates all five components of cultural competence, the resulting concept is called cultural [[competemility]].
items.ex: Cultural competemility blends competence and humility, letting the nurse form a meaningful relationship with the unique patient.

alt.q: The concept of cultural [[competemility]] means being engaged in becoming culturally competent while also being engaged in cultural humility.
alt.ex: Cultural competemility blends competence and humility, letting the nurse form a meaningful relationship with the unique patient.

items.q: Using the LEARN model, a nurse tells a patient, “We both want your pain controlled, even though we see its cause differently.” Which step is the nurse using?
items.a: Acknowledge
items.ex: Acknowledging recognizes differences between the two perceptions while building on similarities.
w: Listen
Listening involves hearing the patient’s perception with encouraging comments like “Tell me more.”
Explain
Explaining is when the nurse shares the nurse’s own perception of the problem.
Negotiate
Negotiating is agreeing on a treatment plan that includes aspects of the patient’s culture.

alt.q: A nurse and patient agree to schedule treatments around the patient’s daily family prayer ritual. Which LEARN step does this reflect?
alt.a: Negotiate
alt.ex: Negotiating a treatment plan incorporates selected aspects of the patient’s culture into the plan.
w: Acknowledge
Acknowledging recognizes differences and similarities but does not set the plan.
Listen
Listening is hearing the patient’s view of the problem.
Explain
Explaining is sharing the nurse’s view of the problem.

items.q: A nurse is assigned to a young patient whose beliefs about violence directly conflict with the nurse’s values. Which action reflects cultural desire?
items.a: Provide safe, quality care nonjudgmentally and with respect
items.ex: Cultural desire requires respect and acceptance of all human beings, even when their views conflict with the nurse’s.
w: Request reassignment to a patient whose values match the nurse’s
Avoiding the patient does not reflect respect and acceptance of all people.
Share personal values so the patient can reconsider those beliefs
Imposing the nurse’s values is judgmental.
Limit contact to required tasks to avoid any conflict
Minimal contact does not reflect the openness and caring of cultural desire.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse best reflects cultural desire?
alt.a: “I want to learn from my patients and understand their perspectives.”
alt.ex: Cultural desire is wanting, not having, to engage, with a willingness to learn from others as cultural informants.
w: “I attend cultural training because my employer requires it.”
Acting because one “has to” is the opposite of cultural desire.
“I already know enough about my patients’ cultures.”
Cultural desire involves ongoing openness and willingness to learn.
“I prefer caring for patients who share my background.”
Cultural desire includes accepting differences and building on similarities.

items.q: When is transcultural care considered culturally congruent?
items.a: When it fits the person’s life patterns, values, and system of meaning
items.ex: Culturally congruent care fits patterns and meanings generated by people themselves, not biased predetermined criteria.
w: When it follows predetermined criteria for the patient’s cultural group
Congruent care is not based on biased, predetermined criteria.
When it matches the nurse’s own cultural values and practices
Care must fit the patient’s values, not the nurse’s.
When it is identical to the care given to every other patient
Congruent care is individualized to the person’s values and meanings.

alt.q: The patterns and meanings that make care culturally congruent are generated by whom?
alt.a: The people receiving care themselves
alt.ex: Culturally congruent care is built on patterns and meanings people generate themselves.
w: The health care agency’s policy committee
Agency policy is not the source of a person’s patterns and meanings.
Published lists of cultural group traits
Relying on predetermined group lists can introduce bias.
The nurse’s own cultural background
Care built on the nurse’s background would not fit the patient’s meanings.

items.q: Before assessing a patient’s culture, what should a nurse do first to build cultural awareness?
items.a: Examine and understand their own cultural history, heritage, values, and beliefs
items.ex: Cultural awareness begins with self-examination of one’s own background and biases before assessing others.
w: Memorize the health beliefs of the major cultural groups in the area
Learning about other groups is cultural knowledge, which comes after self-examination.
Review the religious preference recorded in the patient’s health record
A recorded preference does not reveal the nurse’s own biases or the patient’s deeper beliefs.
Ask the patient’s family to describe the family’s traditions
Asking about traditions is part of assessment, not the self-examination that starts awareness.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of cultural awareness?
alt.a: “I need to look at my own biases and worldview before I can understand my patients’.”
alt.ex: Cultural awareness starts with self-examination of biases to understand how one perceives and engages patients.
w: “Cultural awareness means learning the customs of each patient’s culture.”
Learning other cultures’ beliefs and values is cultural knowledge.
“If I treat everyone the same, I do not need to examine my biases.”
Everyone has biases; awareness requires examining them.
“Cultural awareness begins after I finish a patient’s cultural assessment.”
Self-examination comes before assessing patients’ cultures.

items.q: During discharge teaching, a patient avoids eye contact with the nurse. Which interpretation reflects cultural awareness?
items.a: The behavior may show respect toward a person in authority in the patient’s culture
items.ex: In some cultures, avoiding eye contact is expected as a sign of respect in the presence of authority.
w: The patient is showing disinterest in the discharge instructions
Assuming disinterest interprets the behavior through the nurse’s own cultural lens.
The patient is being disrespectful toward the nurse
In some cultures, the behavior signals respect, not disrespect.
The patient cannot understand English well enough to learn
Eye contact alone does not indicate language ability.

alt.q: A nurse perceives a patient’s lack of eye contact as disrespect. What is the best explanation for this misinterpretation?
alt.a: The nurse is interpreting the behavior through the nurse’s own cultural lens
alt.ex: Without cultural awareness, the nurse reads behavior through personal norms instead of the patient’s cultural meaning.
w: The patient has a communication disorder that needs evaluation
The behavior may be a cultural sign of respect, not a disorder.
The patient is deliberately rejecting the nurse’s teaching
Assuming rejection is the same cultural misreading.
The nurse has correctly recognized a sign of disinterest
In some cultures, avoiding eye contact shows respect.

items.q: Being open to a patient’s beliefs and forming a partnership is more important than knowing everything about the patient’s specific culture.
items.a: True
items.ex: Openness and partnership matter more than complete knowledge of a culture, especially given diversity within groups.
items.ww: The chapter states that openness and partnership outweigh knowing everything about a culture.

alt.q: Knowing everything about a patient’s specific culture is more important than being open to the patient’s beliefs and forming a partnership.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The chapter ranks openness and partnership above complete knowledge of a patient’s culture.
alt.ww: No nurse can know everything about a culture; openness and partnership are what matter most.

items.q: A nurse notices that older adults on the unit often receive less pain medication than younger patients after similar surgeries. How should the nurse view this observation?
items.a: As a possible ageism bias in the workplace that care approaches should minimize
items.ex: Cultural awareness includes questioning workplace biases, such as undertreating pain in older adults.
w: As appropriate because older adults feel less pain than younger adults
Undertreatment of pain in older adults is the chapter’s example of ageism.
As an individual preference that does not require any review
A pattern across patients suggests a workplace bias, not individual preferences.
As unrelated to cultural awareness because it involves medication
Awareness includes recognizing biases in workplace practices like pain treatment.

alt.q: To gain cultural awareness, a nurse should ask whether biases exist in which places?
alt.a: In the nurse personally and in the nurse’s workplace
alt.ex: The chapter recommends asking whether you hold biases and whether biases or issues exist where you work.
w: Within the patient’s own cultural group
Awareness focuses on the nurse and the workplace, not on judging the patient’s group.
Among the patient’s family members
Awareness is self-examination, not examining the family.
In the nurse’s personal beliefs only
Awareness also includes questioning biases in the workplace.

items.q: Which description defines cultural knowledge?
items.a: Learning about the beliefs and values of other cultures and diverse ethnic groups
items.ex: Cultural knowledge is becoming educated about other cultures’ beliefs and values, including help-seeking, treatment, and recovery.
w: Examining one’s own biases toward other cultures
This describes cultural awareness.
Conducting a cultural assessment of a patient’s problem
This describes cultural skill.
Interacting face-to-face with patients from diverse backgrounds
This describes cultural encounter.

alt.q: A nurse reviews epidemiological data on disease rates among the ethnic groups the clinic serves. Which construct of cultural competence is the nurse developing?
alt.a: Cultural knowledge
alt.ex: Learning about disease incidence and prevalence in diverse groups builds cultural knowledge.
w: Cultural awareness
Awareness is self-examination of one’s own biases and background.
Cultural encounter
An encounter is direct interaction with patients, not reviewing data.
Cultural desire
Desire is the motivation to engage, not the learning itself.

items.q: When gaining cultural knowledge, which issues should the health care provider focus on? Select all that apply.
o: Health-related beliefs and cultural values
These explain how a patient interprets illness.
Disease incidence and prevalence
Disease rates differ among ethnic groups and guide treatment.
Treatment efficacy
Treatment efficacy is a critical step for caring for diverse populations.
The patient’s ability to pay for treatment
Ability to pay is not one of the issues named for cultural knowledge.
The nurse’s personal treatment preferences
Cultural knowledge is about patients’ cultures, not the nurse’s preferences.
items.ex: Providers gaining cultural knowledge focus on health-related beliefs and values, disease incidence and prevalence, and treatment efficacy.

alt.q: A nurse is building cultural knowledge about a new immigrant community the clinic serves. Which information should the nurse seek? Select all that apply.
o: How the community’s beliefs and values shape the meaning of illness
Health-related beliefs and values guide how illness is interpreted.
Which diseases are more common in the community
Disease incidence and prevalence differ among ethnic groups.
How well treatments work for members of the community
Treatment efficacy is one of the focus issues.
Which members will follow the plan without asking questions
This reflects compliance, not the cultural knowledge issues named in the chapter.
How the community’s customs compare with the nurse’s preferences
Comparing to the nurse’s preferences is not a focus of cultural knowledge.
alt.ex: Correct: How the community’s beliefs and values shape the meaning of illness; Which diseases are more common in the community; How well treatments work for members of the community.

items.q: Why should a nurse learn about a specific culture’s risks for disease?
items.a: To focus the nursing history more appropriately during the assessment
items.ex: Knowing a culture’s disease risks lets the nurse direct the nursing history appropriately.
w: To predict each patient’s diagnosis before the assessment begins
Predicting diagnoses from group membership is stereotyping, not focused assessment.
To decide which patients need fewer assessment questions
Knowledge of risk focuses the assessment; it does not shorten it.
To replace the patient’s own description of the problem
The patient’s description remains central to the assessment.

alt.q: Because disease incidence and prevalence differ among ethnic groups, what is needed to guide treatment?
alt.a: Epidemiological data
alt.ex: Epidemiological data on disease rates in different groups are needed to guide treatment.
w: Opinions of staff about the group
Staff opinions risk bias and are not data on disease rates.
Unit tradition and routine
Tradition does not reflect disease rates in specific groups.
The patient’s insurance records
Insurance records do not describe disease incidence in a population.

items.q: A patient believes their illness is caused by an excess of “cold.” Based on the hot–cold balance concept, which remedy would the patient most likely choose?
items.a: A “hot” food or medicine to restore balance
items.ex: Restoring a disturbed balance requires opposites, such as a hot remedy for a cold problem.
w: A “cold” food or medicine of the same type as the problem
Using the same type would worsen the imbalance; opposites are used.
A neutral food with neither hot nor cold properties
The concept calls for an opposite remedy, not a neutral one.
Fasting until the cold condition resolves
The concept restores balance with opposite foods and medicines, not fasting.

alt.q: In the hot–cold balance concept, how is a disturbed balance restored?
alt.a: By using opposites, such as a hot remedy for a cold problem
alt.ex: Treating with opposites, hot for cold and cold for hot, restores the naturalistic balance.
w: By using a remedy of the same type as the problem
Matching the remedy to the problem does not restore balance.
By avoiding all food until the symptoms resolve
Balance is restored with opposite foods and medicines, not by avoiding food.
By using only prescribed medicines and no foods
Both foods and medicines are classified and used to restore balance.

items.q: A patient’s nutrition plan conflicts with the patient’s belief in balancing “hot” and “cold” foods. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Support the practice and adapt the dietary plan to include it
items.ex: The chapter directs nurses to support a patient’s hot–cold practices and adapt them into the dietary plan.
w: Explain that hot and cold beliefs have no scientific basis
Dismissing the belief does not respect the patient’s health practices.
Follow the standard plan and remove the culturally based foods
Removing valued foods ignores the patient’s beliefs and may reduce adherence.
Ask the dietitian to override the patient’s food choices
Overriding choices does not partner with the patient.

alt.q: A nurse learns that a patient chooses foods to maintain hot–cold balance. What is the best way to use this information?
alt.a: Incorporate the patient’s food beliefs into the dietary plan
alt.ex: Supporting the patient’s practices and adapting them into the plan reflects cultural knowledge in action.
w: Note the belief but plan meals without considering it
Ignoring the belief fails to adapt care to the patient.
Teach the patient to stop classifying foods as hot or cold
The nurse supports, rather than discourages, the practice.
Assume the patient defines hot and cold like others from the region
Cultures define hot and cold differently, so the nurse should not assume.

items.q: Some cultures uphold the philosophical concept of [[yin]] (cold) and yang (hot).
items.ex: Yin represents cold and yang represents hot in this concept of balance.

alt.q: In the philosophical concept of balance, yin represents cold and [[yang]] represents hot.
alt.ex: Yin represents cold and yang represents hot in this concept of balance.

items.q: Why have health care providers often held a worldview that differs from that of their patients?
items.a: They were educated in traditional medicine rooted in the culture of science and biomedicine
items.ex: Provider education immersed in science and biomedicine created a worldview often different from patients’.
w: They are trained to disregard patients’ beliefs during care
Providers are not trained to disregard beliefs; their education simply has its own culture.
They usually come from the same communities as their patients
Shared communities would reduce, not create, differences in worldview.
They were educated mainly in complementary and alternative medicine
Historically, providers were educated mainly in traditional biomedicine.

alt.q: Why are more health care providers now being educated in complementary and alternative medicine?
alt.a: To offer patients a more holistic approach based on socioeconomic status and culture
alt.ex: Education in complementary and alternative approaches helps providers offer holistic care that fits patients’ culture.
w: To replace biomedical treatment with alternative therapies
The aim is a more holistic approach, not replacing biomedicine.
To reduce the need for a cultural assessment
Cultural care and assessment remain important in every encounter.
To meet a federal requirement for professional licensure
The chapter does not describe it as a licensure requirement.

items.q: What does the iceberg analogy illustrate about worldview?
items.a: Most aspects of worldview lie outside awareness and are invisible to others
items.ex: Like an iceberg mostly under water, most of a person’s worldview is hidden from the person and from others.
w: Most aspects of worldview are visible through a person’s behavior
Only behavior is visible; the beliefs guiding it are hidden.
Worldview can be fully assessed by asking about religious preference
Deeply held beliefs are not revealed by a religious preference alone.
Only patients, not nurses, have hidden aspects of worldview
Both nurse and patient act according to their own worldviews.

alt.q: In the iceberg analogy of worldview, which aspect lies above the water line?
alt.a: Behavior that others can observe
alt.ex: Behavior is the visible part; learned, largely subconscious beliefs and values lie beneath the surface.
w: Beliefs and attitudes that guide behavior
These lie beneath the surface and are not visible to others.
Knowledge gained through life experience
Knowledge and experience guiding behavior are hidden below the surface.
Values that are largely subconscious
Subconscious values are the deepest, hidden part of the iceberg.

items.q: A patient’s deeply held beliefs about removing a body part may not be revealed by simply assessing religious preference.
items.a: True
items.ex: Deep beliefs lie “underneath the iceberg” and are not obvious from a recorded religious preference.
items.ww: The chapter states such beliefs are not obvious from assessing religious preference.

alt.q: Documenting a patient’s religious preference reliably reveals the deeply held beliefs that will guide the patient’s care decisions.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Deeply held beliefs lie beneath the surface and are not revealed by a religious preference alone.
alt.ww: A recorded preference is surface information; the beliefs guiding decisions must be explored.

items.q: A patient who willingly came to the hospital now refuses the recommended surgery for religious reasons. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Explore the patient’s beliefs and what the surgery means to the patient
items.ex: Uncovering the worldview behind the behavior avoids conflict caused by judging it through the nurse’s own lens.
w: Remind the patient that coming to the hospital implied consent to surgery
Coming for help does not mean consent; the patient’s beliefs guide this decision.
Ask the chaplain to persuade the patient to proceed with surgery
Persuasion does not first explore and respect the patient’s beliefs.
Document the refusal and cancel the surgery without discussion
Canceling without discussion skips assessment of the patient’s beliefs.

alt.q: A patient refuses surgery for reasons the nurse does not understand. Which question from the cultural assessment guide best helps the nurse understand?
alt.a: “What is the difference between what we are doing and what you think we should be doing for you?”
alt.ex: This question explores the patient’s own expectations of care, revealing beliefs beneath visible behavior.
w: “What does your family like to eat, and do all members share the same tastes?”
This dietary question does not address the refusal.
“What is the composition of your family, and how many generations live together?”
Family composition does not directly reveal the patient’s view of the treatment.
“How well do you understand spoken and written English in daily life?”
Language ability matters but does not explore the patient’s beliefs about surgery.

items.q: A nurse is assessing health beliefs and practices using the cultural assessment guide. Which questions fit this category? Select all that apply.
o: “How would you define health and illness?”
Defining health and illness is a health beliefs and practices question.
“What do you usually do to treat an illness?”
Usual treatment practices fit this category.
“Do you prefer a health professional of the same gender, age, and background?”
Provider preference is listed under health beliefs and practices.
“What language do you speak in your home?”
This belongs to the language and communication category.
“Who in your family is responsible for food preparation?”
This belongs to the dietary practices category.
items.ex: Health beliefs and practices questions explore how patients define, treat, and feel about health, illness, and providers.

alt.q: Which questions from the cultural assessment guide address language and communication? Select all that apply.
o: “What language do you speak in your home?”
Home language is a language and communication question.
“Is touch an acceptable form of communication for you?”
Acceptability of touch is a communication question.
“Are there special signs of showing respect or disrespect?”
Signs of respect fit language and communication.
“Is there a significant person to whom you look for guidance?”
This belongs to faith-based influences and special rituals.
“Do you practice periods of required fasting?”
This belongs to dietary practices.
alt.ex: Correct: “What language do you speak in your home?”; “Is touch an acceptable form of communication for you?”; “Are there special signs of showing respect or disrespect?”

mt.ex: Box 9.4 groups cultural assessment questions into categories that uncover beliefs beneath visible behavior.

items.q: Which description best defines a cultural encounter?
items.a: Any direct interaction with a patient from a culturally diverse background
items.ex: Whenever a nurse directly interacts with patients from diverse backgrounds, that interaction is a cultural encounter.
w: A self-examination of one’s own cultural biases
This describes cultural awareness.
A formal course on the beliefs of other cultures
Formal learning about cultures builds cultural knowledge.
A written cultural history completed by the patient
A written history is not the direct interaction that defines an encounter.

alt.q: A nurse’s repeated interactions with patients from one community lead the nurse to revise an earlier assumption about that group. Which construct does this reflect?
alt.a: Cultural encounter
alt.ex: Cultural encounters aim to modify existing beliefs about a cultural group and prevent stereotyping.
w: Cultural awareness
Awareness is self-examination of one’s own biases and background.
Cultural desire
Desire is the motivation to engage, not the revision of beliefs through interaction.
Cultural knowledge
Knowledge comes from education about groups rather than direct interaction.

items.q: Which are goals of a cultural encounter? Select all that apply.
o: Send and receive verbal and nonverbal communication accurately in each cultural context
Accurate communication across cultural contexts is the first goal.
Validate, refine, or modify existing values, beliefs, and practices about a cultural group
Continuous interaction to refine beliefs is the second goal.
Confirm the nurse’s existing beliefs about a cultural group
Encounters aim to modify beliefs and prevent stereotyping, not confirm them.
Teach patients to adopt the health care team’s cultural values
Encounters do not aim to change patients’ cultural values.
Limit communication to verbal exchanges to avoid misunderstanding
Both verbal and nonverbal communication are part of the goal.
items.ex: Cultural encounters have two goals: accurate communication in each cultural context and continual refinement of beliefs about cultural groups.

alt.q: A nurse integrates the goals of cultural encounters into ongoing care. Which actions reflect these goals? Select all that apply.
o: Communicating in a way that generates a wide variety of responses
Generating varied responses is part of the communication goal.
Interacting continuously with diverse patients to refine beliefs about groups
Ongoing interaction to validate or modify beliefs is a goal.
Using a fixed script to obtain identical answers from every patient
The goal is a wide variety of responses, not identical answers.
Reducing contact with diverse patients to avoid stereotyping
Encounters prevent stereotyping through more contact, not less.
Relying on one encounter to set lasting beliefs about a group
Beliefs are refined through continuous interaction, not one encounter.
alt.ex: Correct: Communicating in a way that generates a wide variety of responses; Interacting continuously with diverse patients to refine beliefs about groups.

items.q: A nurse is preparing a patient for a physical examination. Which cultural assessment question addresses modesty?
items.a: “Are there restrictions related to exposure of parts of the body that we must respect?”
items.ex: Modesty restrictions, such as on exposing body parts, are explored in the health beliefs and practices questions.
w: “What does your family like to eat, and who prepares the food?”
This is a dietary practices question.
“How long do you think your current health problem will last?”
This explores the history of the current health problem.
“Are there ethnic organizations that influence your health care?”
This explores sources of support beyond the family.

alt.q: A nurse asks a patient, “Are there restrictions on exposing parts of the body or discussing sexual health that we must respect?” What is the nurse assessing?
alt.a: Restrictions imposed by modesty
alt.ex: This question identifies modesty restrictions so the nurse can respect them during care.
w: Dietary restrictions related to rituals
Dietary restrictions are assessed with food and fasting questions.
Family decision-making roles
Decision-making is assessed by asking who makes decisions in the family.
Language and literacy level
Language is assessed by asking about home language and English understanding.

items.q: Health care has its own culture of hierarchies, power, values, beliefs, and practices.
items.a: True
items.ex: Recognizing health care’s own culture helps explain why provider and patient worldviews often differ.
items.ww: The chapter describes health care as having its own culture.

alt.q: Health care is a culturally neutral setting that has no hierarchies, values, or practices of its own.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Health care has its own culture of hierarchies, power, values, beliefs, and practices.
alt.ww: Health care is not neutral; its culture shapes providers’ worldviews.

items.q: A nurse on an acute care unit admits a patient who will need extensive postoperative teaching. Time for a full cultural history is limited. Which assessment focus is best?
items.a: The patient’s and family’s language, family roles, and health care practices
items.ex: In acute care, the nurse focuses on priority needs; extensive teaching makes language, family roles, and practices priorities.
w: The patient’s complete family history across three generations
A full family history is less relevant to the immediate teaching needs.
The patient’s childhood experiences and milestone rituals
These may matter later but are not the priority for postoperative teaching.
The patient’s food preferences for holiday celebrations
Holiday food preferences are not a priority for the impending treatment plan.

alt.q: Why can a home health nurse often gather a more comprehensive cultural history than a nurse in acute care?
alt.a: The nurse can gather more information with each patient visit
alt.ex: In settings such as home health, schools, and clinics, repeated visits allow more cultural information to be gathered.
w: Home health patients do not have priority care needs
All patients have priority needs; the difference is the time available over visits.
Acute care nurses are not expected to assess culture
Acute care nurses assess culture but focus on priority needs.
Cultural assessment can be completed only in the home
Cultural assessment occurs in all settings.

items.q: Which areas are listed as considerations when performing a transcultural assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Communication
Communication, including voice quality and use of silence, is a consideration.
Space
Space, including comfort and conversational distance, is a consideration.
Time
Orientation to and view of time is a consideration.
Biological variations
Biological variations, including physical assessment, are a consideration.
Insurance coverage
Insurance is not one of the transcultural assessment considerations.
Hospital billing status
Billing status is not one of the transcultural assessment considerations.
items.ex: Box 9.5 lists communication, space, social organization, time, environmental control, and biological variations for the culturally unique individual.

alt.q: A nurse uses Box 9.5 to plan a transcultural assessment. Which areas should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Social organization
Social organization, such as marital status and number of children, is a consideration.
Environmental control
Environmental control, including locus of control and value orientation, is a consideration.
Cultural assimilation
The nurse notes cultural assimilation as part of the assessment.
Laboratory reference ranges
Lab reference ranges are not a transcultural assessment consideration.
The nurse’s preferred schedule
The nurse’s schedule is not part of the patient’s transcultural assessment.
alt.ex: Correct: Social organization; Environmental control; Cultural assimilation.

items.q: A nurse is about to meet a patient and family from a culture unfamiliar to the nurse. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Conduct a self-exploration and self-critique to identify possible bias
items.ex: Before meeting the patient and family, the nurse identifies personal bias as a cultural humility strategy.
w: Review a list of typical beliefs held by the patient’s cultural group
Relying on group lists risks stereotyping; the nurse should ask the patient.
Ask the family to choose one spokesperson for all care decisions
Family involvement should follow the patient’s wishes, not the nurse’s rule.
Set the treatment goals before the patient arrives on the unit
The patient should help set the agenda and make decisions.

alt.q: At the end of a patient and family interaction, which action reflects cultural humility?
alt.a: Ask the patient whether they felt understood or what would help
alt.ex: Asking whether the patient felt understood closes the interaction with self-critique and openness.
w: Summarize the plan and ask the patient to sign agreement
This does not check whether the patient felt understood.
Tell the family which cultural practices must stop
Humility seeks to incorporate helpful practices, not stop them.
Thank the family and leave without further questions
Leaving without asking misses the chance to learn how to improve understanding.

items.q: Which description defines health literacy?
items.a: The capacity to obtain, process, and understand basic health information and services to make health decisions
items.ex: Health literacy is the capacity to get, process, and understand health information and services needed for decisions.
w: The ability to read at or above a high school grade level in English
Even people with good literacy skills can have trouble with health information.
The ability to convey information so diverse audiences easily understand it
This describes linguistic competence.
Knowledge of medical vocabulary gained through formal health education
Health literacy is about obtaining and using health information, not formal training.

alt.q: Which statement about limited health literacy is accurate?
alt.a: Even people with good literacy skills can have trouble understanding health information
alt.ex: Limited health literacy can affect anyone, including people with good general literacy.
w: Limited health literacy affects only people who do not speak English
Limited health literacy can be a problem for anyone.
People with a college education do not have limited health literacy
Good literacy skills do not guarantee understanding of health information.
Limited health literacy is identified by asking a patient’s grade level
Validated tools and observed behaviors are used to assess health literacy.

items.q: How does storytelling help a nurse during a cultural assessment?
items.a: It helps identify the real problems affecting health and culturally appropriate ways to intervene
items.ex: A patient’s story reveals real problems affecting health status and culturally appropriate interventions.
w: It replaces the need to perform a culturally based physical assessment
Storytelling supports but does not replace the physical assessment.
It limits the patient to answering brief, closed-ended questions
Storytelling uses open-ended sharing rather than closed questions.
It lets the nurse skip asking about the patient’s home remedies
Asking about home remedies remains important in assessment.

alt.q: Which nursing action reflects the evidence on storytelling?
alt.a: Create a safe, caring, and nonjudgmental environment for the patient’s story
alt.ex: Storytelling works best in a safe, caring, nonjudgmental, participant-centered environment.
w: Interrupt the story to keep the assessment focused on facts
Storytelling should be participant-centered and allow reflection.
Use storytelling only with adult patients, not children
Storytelling can be therapeutic for children and helpful for adolescents.
Discourage expressions of emotion while the patient tells the story
Storytelling allows for the expression of emotion.

items.q: Nurses may tell their own stories about patient experiences, respecting confidentiality and staying professional, to help explain procedures or treatment plans.
items.a: True
items.ex: Sharing professional stories frames messages so they are memorable and helps explain procedures or treatments.
items.ww: The evidence-based practice box recommends nurses tell their own stories while respecting confidentiality.

alt.q: Nurses should never share stories about other patients’ experiences when explaining a procedure, even when confidentiality is protected.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses can share patient-experience stories, respecting confidentiality and professionalism, to explain procedures.
alt.ww: The chapter recommends this kind of storytelling when confidentiality is respected.

items.q: [[Linguistic competence]] is the ability to communicate effectively and convey information in a manner that is easily understood by diverse audiences.
items.ex: Linguistic competence reduces misunderstandings that create barriers to accessing health care.

alt.q: The ability to convey information so that diverse audiences easily understand it is called [[linguistic competence]].
alt.ex: Linguistic competence reduces misunderstandings that create barriers to accessing health care.

items.q: Which language assistance requirements must U.S. health care organizations meet under the National CLAS Standards? Select all that apply.
o: Provide language assistance resources at no cost to the patient
Language assistance must be free to facilitate timely access to care.
Inform patients of available language services verbally and in writing
Patients must be told clearly, in their preferred language, verbally and in writing.
Provide easy-to-understand materials and signage in commonly used local languages
Print, multimedia, and signage must be in languages common to the service area.
Use bilingual minors when trained interpreters are unavailable
The standards say not to use untrained individuals or minors as interpreters.
Charge a reduced fee for interpreter services
Language assistance must be provided at no cost.
items.ex: CLAS language standards require free, competent language assistance, notice of its availability, and understandable materials.

alt.q: A nurse cares for a patient with limited English proficiency. Which actions align with the CLAS Standards? Select all that apply.
o: Arrange a trained medical interpreter at no cost to the patient
Trained interpreters must be provided free of charge.
Tell the patient verbally and in writing about the right to language assistance
Patients must be notified both verbally and in writing.
Ensure the interpreter is competent in medical terminology
Agencies must ensure the competence of those providing language assistance.
Ask the patient’s 12-year-old child to interpret
Minors must not be used as interpreters.
Ask the patient to bring an English-speaking friend to interpret
Untrained individuals must not be used as interpreters.
alt.ex: Correct: Arrange a trained medical interpreter at no cost to the patient; Tell the patient verbally and in writing about the right to language assistance; Ensure the interpreter is competent in medical terminology.

items.q: During an assessment, which patient behaviors might reflect a health literacy deficit? Select all that apply.
o: Having difficulty completing registration forms
Difficulty with forms can signal limited health literacy.
Failing to make follow-up appointments
Missed follow-up can reflect a literacy deficit.
Asking few questions during a physical examination
Asking few questions is a possible sign of limited health literacy.
Responding simply “yes” when asked if explanations are understood
A simple “yes” does not confirm understanding.
Accurately restating instructions in their own words
Correct teach-back in their own words suggests understanding.
Correctly demonstrating how to measure a medication dose
Correct demonstration shows understanding, not a deficit.
items.ex: Difficulty with forms, missed appointments, few questions, and simple “yes” answers can signal limited health literacy.

alt.q: A nurse is screening a new clinic patient for limited health literacy. Which observations should raise concern? Select all that apply.
o: Leaves large parts of the health history form blank
Trouble completing health histories can reflect a literacy deficit.
Has missed several scheduled follow-up appointments
Failing to make follow-up appointments is a warning sign.
Says only “yes” when asked if the explanation was clear
Simple “yes” responses may hide a lack of understanding.
Asks detailed questions about medication side effects
Asking detailed questions suggests engagement, not a deficit.
Explains the treatment plan correctly in their own words
Accurate explanation shows understanding.
alt.ex: Correct: Leaves large parts of the health history form blank; Has missed several scheduled follow-up appointments; Says only “yes” when asked if the explanation was clear.
