items.q: While assessing a newborn with dark skin, the nurse notes darkly pigmented areas on the buttocks and lower back. Which action is best?
items.a: Recognize the likely congenital birthmark and avoid mistaking it for bruising
items.ex: Congenital dermal melanocytosis is a pigmented birthmark that should not be mistaken for bruising or abuse.
w: Report the areas immediately as suspected child abuse
These birthmarks are commonly misread as abuse; recognizing them prevents a false report.
Apply cold compresses to reduce the bruising
The areas are pigmented birthmarks, not bruises needing treatment.
Document the areas as bruises of unknown cause
Documenting them as bruises misinterprets a normal pigmented birthmark.

alt.q: What is congenital dermal melanocytosis?
alt.a: A darkly pigmented birthmark that may appear shortly after birth
alt.ex: It may appear on the buttocks, lower back, arms, or legs of dark skin and is not a sign of abuse.
w: A pattern of marks caused by coining or cupping
Coining and cupping marks come from cultural healing practices.
A rash caused by an imbalance of hot and cold
Hot–cold balance is a health belief, not the cause of this birthmark.
A skin sign of sickle cell anemia in infants
Sickle cell anemia is suggested by lab values, not this birthmark.

items.q: During a physical assessment, the nurse notes linear and circular marks on an adult patient’s back. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Ask the patient about home remedies and cultural healing practices
items.ex: Coining and cupping leave skin marks that can be misread as abuse or disease, so the nurse asks about home practices.
w: Report the marks to the health care provider as signs of abuse
Reporting before asking may misinterpret marks from cultural practices.
Document the marks as an unexplained skin disease
The marks may come from cultural practices, which the nurse should ask about first.
Apply a topical cream to treat the marks
Treatment is premature before the cause is assessed.

alt.q: Why do some subcultures use coining and cupping?
alt.a: To release excess force from the body and restore balance
alt.ex: These practices aim to release excess force and restore balance, leaving marks that can be misinterpreted.
w: To treat bacterial infections of the skin
Coining and cupping are not described as treatments for skin infection.
To mark family members for religious ceremonies
The practices are healing practices, not ceremonial markings.
To diagnose sickle cell anemia at home
Sickle cell anemia is identified by laboratory values.

items.q: Plain language makes information easy to read, at an [[8th|eighth|8]] grade reading level or less.
items.ex: Plain language is grammatically correct, uses complete sentences, and targets an 8th grade reading level or less.

alt.q: Information written at an 8th grade reading level or less, using correct grammar and complete sentences, is called [[plain language]].
alt.ex: Plain language is grammatically correct, uses complete sentences, and targets an 8th grade reading level or less.

items.q: A nurse has finished teaching a patient about insulin. Which statement by the nurse best uses teach-back?
items.a: “Please explain how insulin affects your blood sugar so I know I explained it clearly.”
items.ex: Teach-back uses open-ended requests to explain in one’s own words, framed as a check on the nurse’s teaching.
w: “I covered a lot today. Do you understand how your insulin affects your blood sugar?”
Asking “Do you understand?” does not verify understanding.
“Do you have any questions about how your insulin affects your blood sugar?”
Asking for questions is discouraged; patients may have none even when confused.
“You know how insulin affects your blood sugar now, right? Just nod if so.”
A leading yes-or-no question does not confirm learning.

alt.q: After diet teaching, which statement by Ms. Millman best shows that she understands?
alt.a: “At the neighborhood store, I will pick healthy foods from the meal plan we made.”
alt.ex: Describing in her own words how she will make healthy choices meets the teaching objective in Box 9.7.
w: “Yes, I understand everything you told me today about my diet.”
A simple “yes” does not confirm understanding.
“I don’t have any questions right now about changing my diet.”
Having no questions does not show she can apply the teaching.
“I will just keep eating whatever the shelter happens to serve me.”
This does not describe healthy food choices.

items.q: Teach-back is a test of the nurse’s communication, not a test of the patient’s knowledge.
items.a: True
items.ex: Treating teach-back as a test of your own communication creates a shame-free environment for patients.
items.ww: The chapter states teach-back confirms the clarity of the nurse’s communication rather than testing the patient.

alt.q: Teach-back is mainly a test of the patient’s knowledge, so an incorrect answer means the patient has failed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Teach-back confirms the clarity of the nurse’s communication; the nurse takes responsibility for success or failure.
alt.ww: An incorrect answer signals the nurse should explain differently, not that the patient failed.

items.q: A patient correctly states when and how much of a newly changed medication dose to take. Which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Ask the patient to demonstrate measuring the dose
items.ex: The show-me method matters because many patients who state a dose correctly make mistakes when demonstrating it.
w: Document that teaching is complete and understood
Stating the dose correctly does not ensure the patient can prepare it.
Ask whether the patient has any other questions
Asking for questions does not verify the skill.
Provide a handout and end the session
A handout reinforces teaching but does not confirm the patient can measure the dose.

alt.q: When should a nurse use teach-back during a teaching session?
alt.a: After each small segment of information, repeated throughout the visit
alt.ex: “Chunk and check” means teaching in small segments and using teach-back several times during the visit.
w: Only at the end of the visit, after all information is given
Waiting until the end is discouraged; chunk and check instead.
Only at the next follow-up appointment
Teach-back is used during the teaching session itself.
Only if the patient asks a question during teaching
Teach-back is used consistently, not only when questions arise.

items.q: A nurse begins a patient interview with a trained interpreter present. Which action is correct?
items.a: Look at the patient and speak in the first person in short sentences
items.ex: The nurse speaks directly to the patient in first-person statements while the interpreter is an inconspicuous participant.
w: Look at the interpreter and say, “Tell her that…”
Third-person statements and looking at the interpreter should be avoided.
Use humor to put the patient at ease during the interview
Jokes are often lost in interpretation and should be avoided.
Use medical acronyms to keep the conversation brief
Jargon and acronyms should be avoided when working with an interpreter.

alt.q: Where should an interpreter be positioned during a patient interview?
alt.a: Next to or slightly behind the patient
alt.ex: This position lets the nurse look at and speak directly to the patient.
w: Directly in front of the patient, facing them
This would draw the patient’s attention away from the nurse.
Beside the nurse, facing the patient
The interpreter sits by the patient, not the nurse.
Between the nurse and the patient
Placing the interpreter between them blocks direct communication.

items.q: A patient with limited English proficiency arrives with an adult daughter who offers to interpret. No in-person interpreter is available right now. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Use a telephone service with an on-call trained interpreter
items.ex: When an in-person interpreter is not available in time, a phone service with a trained interpreter is a feasible option.
w: Accept the daughter’s offer because she knows the patient best
Family members may add their own opinions, reducing accuracy.
Ask the patient’s 14-year-old grandson to interpret instead
Minors must not be used as interpreters.
Delay all communication until an in-person interpreter arrives
Language assistance should support timely access to care.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid using a patient’s family members as interpreters?
alt.a: They may add their own perceptions or opinions, reducing accuracy
alt.ex: Family members may include their own views, which can greatly reduce the accuracy of the interpretation.
w: They usually lack fluency in the patient’s primary language
Fluency is not the concern; adding their own views is.
Agency policy forbids family from attending patient interviews
Family may be involved in care; the issue is accuracy of interpretation.
They cannot be present when consent forms are explained
The concern is the accuracy of interpretation, not their presence.

items.q: Translators work with written words, whereas interpreters work with spoken words.
items.a: True
items.ex: The CLAS Standards provide qualified translators for written words and interpreters for verbal words.
items.ww: The chapter defines translators by written words and interpreters by verbal words.

alt.q: Interpreters convert written documents, whereas translators convey spoken conversations between nurse and patient.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: This reverses the roles: translators handle written words and interpreters handle spoken words.
alt.ww: Interpreters work with verbal words, and translators with written words.

items.q: When the main wage earner in a family loses a job, another adult in the family takes over the wage-earner role. Which family attribute does this best demonstrate?
items.a: Family resiliency
items.ex: Resiliency is shown when a family adapts to role and structural changes and crises, such as a member taking over a lost role.
w: Family durability
Durability is support and structure that lasts beyond the household over long periods, such as through divorce or remarriage.
Family diversity
Diversity is the uniqueness of each family unit, not its ability to adapt to a stressor.
Rigid family structure
A rigid structure limits who can assume a task; this family shifted the role to another member.

alt.q: Which description best defines family resiliency?
alt.a: The ability of a family to cope with expected and unexpected stressors
alt.ex: Resiliency is the family’s ability to adapt to stressors, role changes, developmental milestones, and crises.
w: The support and structure that extend beyond the walls of the household
This defines family durability, which persists through lifestyle changes over time.
The uniqueness of each family unit and the way it is made up
This defines family diversity, not the ability to cope with stressors.
The interactions among members shaped by structure and function
This describes family dynamics, not the family’s coping ability.

items.q: A nurse cares for one family in which a couple married and had children later in life, and another in which grandparents live in the home with parents and young children. Which concept explains why the nurse individualizes care for each family?
items.a: Family diversity
items.ex: Family diversity is the uniqueness of each family unit, so each family has its own needs, strengths, and challenges.
w: Family durability
Durability refers to support that lasts beyond the household through life changes, not to differences between families.
Family resiliency
Resiliency is the ability to cope with stressors, not the differing makeup of family units.
Family hardiness
Hardiness refers to a family’s internal strengths and durability, not the uniqueness of its form.

alt.q: Which statement best describes family diversity?
alt.a: Each family unit is unique in its makeup and situation
alt.ex: Diversity means no two families are alike; each has its own strengths, weaknesses, resources, and challenges.
w: Families maintain support through divorce, death, and remarriage
Continuing support through lifestyle changes describes family durability.
Families adapt when one member takes over another’s role
Adapting to role changes describes family resiliency.
Families share one traditional structure of parents and children
Diversity means families take many forms rather than one traditional structure.

items.q: During admission, a patient lists her roommate of 20 years as her emergency contact. Which question by the nurse best begins assessing the patient’s family?
items.a: “Whom do you consider to be your family?”
items.ex: A family is what the individual believes it to be, so the nurse first learns how the patient defines family.
w: “Do you have a spouse or any children?”
This assumes family means legal or biological ties and may miss people the patient considers family.
“Which of your blood relatives can we contact?”
Limiting family to blood relatives ignores relationships based on enduring commitment.
“Is your roommate legally related to you?”
Legal ties are not required; family is the set of relationships the patient identifies.

alt.q: Which assessment question best helps the nurse understand who supports a patient within the family?
alt.a: “Who provides support for you day to day?”
alt.ex: The book advises assessing who provides day-to-day support and how patients define their families.
w: “What is your current marital status?”
Marital status alone does not reveal who the patient sees as family or who gives support.
“How many children do you have?”
Counting children assumes a traditional family and may miss the actual support network.
“Who is listed as your legal next of kin?”
Legal status does not show who influences the patient’s life or provides support.

items.q: Why does the nurse need to understand family dynamics when caring for patients?
items.a: To build on the patient’s and family’s strengths and resources when managing health problems
items.ex: Knowledge of family dynamics lets the nurse build on patient and family strengths and resources while managing health problems.
w: To decide which family members should be excluded from care decisions
Family-centered care supports family participation rather than excluding members.
To replace the family’s own problem solving with the nurse’s plan
The nurse builds on the family’s problem solving and coping; the plan is not imposed.
To identify the legal next of kin for signing consent forms
Family dynamics concern interactions among members, not legal consent status.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse reflects the purpose of understanding a family’s dynamics?
alt.a: “Knowing how this family interacts helps me build on its strengths and resources.”
alt.ex: Understanding family dynamics lets the nurse build on patient and family strengths and resources in managing health problems.
w: “It tells me which relatives to exclude from care planning.”
Family-centered care includes the family rather than excluding members.
“It lets me replace the family’s coping methods with my own.”
The nurse builds on the family’s coping capacity rather than replacing it.
“It identifies which relative must sign the consent forms.”
Family dynamics concern interactions among members, not legal consent.

items.q: What is the goal of family-centered nursing care?
items.a: To address the health care needs of the family as a unit and promote the well-being of the patient and each member
items.ex: Family-centered care addresses the family unit’s needs and advocates for the health of the patient and individual members.
w: To focus on the hospitalized patient while family members manage their own needs
Family-centered care addresses the needs of the whole family, not the patient alone.
To teach family members to take over all of the patient’s care at home
Teaching may be part of care, but the goal is the health of the family and its members.
To help the health care team make care decisions on the family’s behalf
Family-centered care supports family participation in decisions rather than deciding for them.

alt.q: A student nurse says, “My job is to care for my patient; the family is someone else’s concern.” Which response by the instructor reflects family-centered care?
alt.a: “You are responsible for caring for both the patient and the family.”
alt.ex: The book states that nurses must care for both the family and the patient.
w: “That is correct; social services manages the family’s needs.”
Nurses are responsible for the family as well as the patient, not only social services.
“Families matter only when they are the legal decision makers.”
All families need care regardless of legal decision-making status.
“Focus on the family only after the patient has been discharged.”
Family-centered care begins during the patient’s care, not only after discharge.

items.q: A patient’s daughter asks why her father’s surgery was delayed. The nurse gives her a timely, complete, and unbiased explanation in terms she can use. Which core concept of person- and family-centered care is the nurse applying?
items.a: Information sharing
items.ex: Information sharing means giving timely, complete, accurate, unbiased information so families can take part in care and decisions.
w: Collaboration
Collaboration refers to working together on policy and program development, implementation, and evaluation.
Participation
Participation refers to supporting involvement in care and decisions at the level the family chooses.
Dignity and respect
Dignity and respect refers to honoring family perspectives, choices, values, and culture.

alt.q: Which nurse action best reflects the information-sharing concept of person- and family-centered care?
alt.a: Giving the family timely, accurate updates so they can take part in decisions
alt.ex: Timely, complete, and accurate information helps patients and families participate in care and decision making.
w: Sharing only the information the family specifically asks about
Information sharing calls for complete information, not only what the family thinks to ask.
Waiting to share results until the plan of care is final
Information must be timely so the family can take part in decisions.
Giving a simplified version that leaves out some care options
Leaving out options makes the information incomplete and biased.

items.q: A patient’s spouse wants to help with meals and stay informed but prefers not to make treatment decisions. Which response by the nurse best reflects person- and family-centered care?
items.a: “You can be involved in whatever way feels right to you, and we will support that.”
items.ex: Patients and families need support and encouragement to participate in care and decisions at whatever level they choose.
w: “Families are expected to take part in every treatment decision.”
Participation is at the level the family chooses, not a required level.
“It would be best to leave all of the care to the nursing staff.”
Discouraging involvement conflicts with supporting family participation in care.
“Your role should be limited to visiting during set hours.”
Restricting the spouse’s role ignores the family’s chosen level of participation.

alt.q: According to the participation concept, at what level should patients and families take part in care and decision making?
alt.a: At whatever level they choose, with ongoing support and encouragement
alt.ex: Box 10.1 states that families need ongoing support to participate in care and decisions at whatever level they choose.
w: At the level set by the health care provider’s preferences
The family, not the provider, chooses its level of participation.
Only at the level needed for legal consent to treatment
Participation includes care and decision making, not just legal consent.
Fully, in every decision, regardless of the family’s wishes
Requiring full participation ignores the family’s choice of level.

items.q: The way family is defined affects which of the following? Select all that apply.
o: Who is included on health insurance policies
The definition of family affects who is covered on health insurance policies.
Who has access to children’s school records
Access to children’s school records depends on how family is defined.
Who is eligible for sick-leave benefits
Eligibility for sick-leave benefits is affected by the definition of family.
A patient’s legal right to refuse treatment
The right to refuse treatment belongs to the individual and does not depend on family definitions.
Which vaccines a child is required to receive
Vaccine requirements are not determined by how family is defined.
items.ex: The definition of family affects insurance coverage, school records, marriage, joint tax returns, sick leave, and public assistance.

alt.q: Social scientists and legislators often debate how to define family. Which decisions can that definition affect? Select all that apply.
o: Who can join in matrimony
Who may marry is affected by the definition of family.
Who files joint tax returns
Filing joint tax returns depends on how family is defined.
Who is eligible for public assistance programs
Public assistance eligibility is linked to the definition of family.
A patient’s medical diagnosis
A medical diagnosis is based on health data, not the definition of family.
The nursing diagnoses a patient may receive
Nursing diagnoses come from assessment data, not legal definitions of family.
alt.ex: Correct: Who can join in matrimony; Who files joint tax returns; Who is eligible for public assistance programs.

items.q: According to the textbook, a family includes only people related by birth, marriage, or adoption.
items.a: False
items.ex: A family is what an individual believes it to be; some include aunts, uncles, close friends, and pets.
items.ww: Saying True ignores that family members can be related through enduring commitments rather than biology or law.

alt.q: A family can include people with no biological or legal ties if the patient identifies them as family.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Family is a set of relationships the patient identifies, whether or not there are biological or legal ties.
alt.ww: Saying False limits family to legal and biological ties, which the book does not require.

items.q: Because a family is made up of its members, the family is equal to the sum of its individual members.
items.a: False
items.ex: Families represent more than a set of individuals; a family is more than the sum of its members.
items.ww: Saying True misses that family interactions and relationships create a unit greater than its individual members.

alt.q: A family represents more than a set of individuals and is more than the sum of its individual members.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The book stresses that a family is more than a collection of individuals and deserves care as a unit.
alt.ww: Saying False treats the family as only a list of individuals, ignoring its relationships and function as a unit.

items.q: Relationships among patients, families, and health care providers are often shaped by providers’ beliefs rather than by the needs of patients and family caregivers.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book warns this often happens, so nurses must assess how patients define their families.
items.ww: Saying False overlooks the book’s caution that provider beliefs, not patient needs, often define these relationships.

alt.q: Relationships among patients, families, and health care providers are usually defined by what patients and family caregivers need.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: These relationships are often shaped by providers’ beliefs rather than by patient and family caregiver needs.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores the book’s point that providers’ beliefs frequently shape these relationships.

items.q: Family [[durability]] is a system of support and structure within a family that extends beyond the walls of the household.
items.ex: Durability lets the family persist through divorce, death, remarriage, or children leaving home.

alt.q: A family that continues to support its members through divorce and remarriage shows family [[durability]].
alt.ex: Durability lets the family persist through divorce, death, remarriage, or children leaving home.

items.q: Family [[dynamics]] are the interactions between and among family members that are affected by a family’s makeup, structure, function, problem solving, and coping capacity.
items.ex: Understanding family dynamics helps the nurse build on patient and family strengths and resources.

alt.q: The nurse studies family [[dynamics]], the interactions among family members, to build on their strengths when managing health problems.
alt.ex: Understanding family dynamics helps the nurse build on patient and family strengths and resources.

items.q: A 70-year-old patient who lives alone tells the nurse, “My neighbor and my dog are my family.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Tell me how your neighbor helps you so we can include her in your plan.”
items.ex: Family is who the patient believes it to be, so the nurse respects this definition and includes the neighbor.
w: “I meant relatives such as children, siblings, or cousins.”
This dismisses the patient’s own definition of family.
“Pets and neighbors cannot be considered part of a family.”
For some people, close friends and pets are family; the patient’s view deserves respect.
“Do you have any living relatives we could call instead?”
Seeking relatives instead ignores the support network the patient identified.

alt.q: A patient identifies a close friend as family. How should the nurse view this friend?
alt.a: As a family member, because the patient defines who family is
alt.ex: Patients have deeply ingrained values about their families, and family is what the individual believes it to be.
w: As a visitor, because the friend has no legal tie to the patient
Legal ties are not needed for someone to be family.
As a support person who is excluded from care planning
Excluding the friend ignores the patient’s definition of family.
As family only if the health care provider agrees
The patient, not the provider, defines who is family.

items.q: Which challenges does the textbook identify as facing families today? Select all that apply.
o: Effects of health and illness
Health and illness are listed among the challenges families face.
Recognition and access to health care for LGBTQIA+ families
Parental recognition and health care access for LGBTQIA+ families are named challenges.
Caring for older family members
Caring for older members is a major challenge for many families.
Changes in family structure and dynamics
Families face changes in structure and dynamics over time.
A decline in the diversity of family forms
Family forms are becoming more diverse, not less.
A shrinking number of older adults needing care
The older-adult population is growing, increasing caregiving needs.
items.ex: Families face health and illness, LGBTQIA+ recognition, childbearing and childrearing, structural changes, and care of older members.

alt.q: Which family attributes help families adapt to challenges? Select all that apply.
o: Durability
Durability gives support and structure that lasts through lifestyle changes.
Resiliency
Resiliency is the ability to cope with expected and unexpected stressors.
Diversity
Diversity reflects each family’s uniqueness, which helps it adapt in its own way.
Rigid role assignment
Rigid structures limit who can take on tasks and threaten family functioning.
Isolation from outside support
Support beyond the household strengthens families; isolation does not help them adapt.
alt.ex: Correct: Durability; Resiliency; Diversity.

items.q: Which nurse actions are consistent with the core concepts of person- and family-centered care? Select all that apply.
o: Considering the family’s values, beliefs, and culture when planning care
This reflects dignity and respect.
Encouraging the family to take part in decisions at the level they choose
This reflects the participation concept.
Including families in program development and evaluation
This reflects the collaboration concept.
Sharing only the information the nurse thinks the family can handle
Information sharing requires complete and unbiased information.
Planning care around the nurse’s view of what the family should value
Dignity and respect require honoring the family’s own perspectives and choices.
items.ex: Person- and family-centered care rests on dignity and respect, information sharing, participation, and collaboration.

alt.q: A unit is revising its visiting policy using person- and family-centered care. Which actions fit this approach? Select all that apply.
o: Inviting patients and families to help develop and evaluate the policy
Collaboration includes families in policy development and evaluation.
Honoring family perspectives and choices about visiting
Dignity and respect call for honoring family perspectives and choices.
Giving families timely, complete information about the change
Information sharing calls for timely, complete, accurate information.
Having staff alone decide the policy to avoid delays
Excluding families conflicts with collaboration in policy development.
Limiting families’ role to following the new rules
Families should participate and collaborate, not simply comply.
alt.ex: Correct: Inviting patients and families to help develop and evaluate the policy; Honoring family perspectives and choices about visiting; Giving families timely, complete information about the change.

items.q: Which activity best illustrates the collaboration concept of person- and family-centered care?
items.a: Patients and families helping to design a new unit and its programs
items.ex: Collaboration involves patients, families, and providers working together on policy, programs, research, facility design, and education.
w: A nurse explaining test results to a family in plain terms
Explaining results reflects information sharing.
A nurse honoring a family’s choice about end-of-life care
Honoring choices reflects dignity and respect.
A nurse encouraging a family to help at the level they choose
Supporting a chosen level of involvement reflects participation.

alt.q: Patients and family members serve on a committee that develops and evaluates a new discharge program. Which core concept of person- and family-centered care does this show?
alt.a: Collaboration
alt.ex: Collaboration brings patients, families, and providers together in program development, implementation, and evaluation.
w: Participation
Participation refers to involvement in the patient’s own care and decisions, not program development.
Information sharing
Information sharing refers to giving families timely, complete, and accurate information.
Dignity and respect
Dignity and respect refers to honoring family perspectives, values, and choices.

items.q: A patient’s family asks the nurse to consider their cultural beliefs about healing when planning care. Which action best reflects the dignity and respect concept?
items.a: Listen to the family’s perspective and consider their beliefs when planning care
items.ex: Dignity and respect require honoring family perspectives and choices and considering their values, beliefs, and culture in care.
w: Explain that cultural beliefs do not affect hospital care
This dismisses the family’s values rather than honoring them.
Document the request and continue the current plan unchanged
Recording the request without considering it does not honor the family’s perspective.
Ask the provider to explain why the beliefs are not relevant
This overrides the family’s beliefs instead of incorporating them.

alt.q: Which description fits the dignity and respect concept of person- and family-centered care?
alt.a: Honoring patient and family perspectives, choices, values, and culture
alt.ex: Under dignity and respect, providers listen to and honor family perspectives and consider their knowledge, values, beliefs, and culture.
w: Providing timely, complete, and unbiased information
This describes information sharing.
Supporting involvement at whatever level families choose
This describes participation.
Working together on policy and program development
This describes collaboration.

items.q: Family [[forms]] are patterns of people considered by family members to be included in a family.
items.ex: Each family form has unique challenges and strengths, so the nurse stays open about who makes up a family.

alt.q: The patterns of people that family members consider to be part of their family are called family [[forms]].
alt.ex: Each family form has unique challenges and strengths, so the nurse stays open about who makes up a family.

items.q: What term describes middle-aged adults who must meet their own needs along with those of their children and their aging parents?
items.a: The sandwich generation
items.ex: The sandwich generation balances the needs of children and aging family members, often at the expense of their own well-being.
w: The graying of America
This phrase describes the growth of the older-adult population, not the middle-aged adults caring for them.
A blended family
A blended family results from remarriage and its complex set of relationships.
A crisis-prone family
A crisis-prone family lacks, or believes it lacks, control over its environment.

alt.q: A 48-year-old patient works full time, has two teenagers at home, and helps care for her father with dementia. Which concept best describes her situation?
alt.a: She is part of the sandwich generation
alt.ex: Sandwich-generation adults balance their own needs with those of their children and aging relatives.
w: She is part of a crisis-prone family
Nothing suggests the family lacks control over its environment.
She is part of an extremely flexible family
Flexibility describes family structure, not caring for two generations at once.
She is part of a blended family
A blended family forms through remarriage, which is not described here.

items.q: In a family with a rigid structure, the mother provides all emotional support for the children and does all household chores. She is hospitalized for several weeks. Which family problem should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: No other member is considered acceptable to take over her tasks
items.ex: Rigid structures limit who may do tasks, so a change in that person’s health burdens the family.
w: Family members cannot decide who should act during the crisis
Difficulty deciding who should act results from an extremely flexible structure.
The family will readily share her tasks among other members
A rigid family does not easily shift tasks to others.
Outside helpers will take over her roles without difficulty
Rigid structures limit people outside the immediate family from assuming tasks.

alt.q: Which description best characterizes a rigid family structure?
alt.a: It specifies who does each task and limits who else may assume it
alt.ex: Rigid structures assign tasks to specific people and limit others, including outsiders, from taking them on.
w: It lacks stability, so no one is clearly responsible for acting
This describes an extremely flexible structure.
It allows different members to complete tasks and accepts outside help
This describes the flexible structure of an effective family.
It changes its membership with each new stressful event
Rigid structures resist change rather than change membership.

items.q: Why can an extremely flexible family structure cause problems for a family?
items.a: The lack of stability can keep members from deciding who should act in a crisis
items.ex: Too much flexibility removes stability, so members may not know who should act during a crisis or rapid change.
w: Only one member is allowed to perform each household task
This describes a rigid structure, not an extremely flexible one.
Members refuse all help from people outside the family
Refusing outside help is linked to rigid structures, not flexibility.
Too many rules prevent members from adapting to change
Too many rules describes rigidity; extreme flexibility lacks stability.

alt.q: A family’s members all share every role and no one is clearly in charge. When the father is suddenly hospitalized, which problem is most likely?
alt.a: Members may struggle to decide who should act during the crisis
alt.ex: An extremely flexible structure lacks stability, which can prevent members from deciding who should act.
w: No member will be considered acceptable to take over his tasks
This problem arises in rigid structures that limit who may do tasks.
The family will refuse help offered by neighbors and friends
Refusing outside help reflects a rigid structure, not a flexible one.
The family will function better because roles are interchangeable
Extreme flexibility threatens functioning because the family lacks stability.

items.q: Which statement best describes family function?
items.a: What a family does, including the processes it uses to achieve its goals
items.ex: Function includes socializing younger members, meeting economic needs, relating to society, and processes such as communication and conflict resolution.
w: The ongoing membership of the family and its pattern of relationships
This describes family structure, which is based on membership, beliefs, and relationships.
The patterns of people that members consider to be in the family
This defines family forms.
The family’s genetic susceptibility to diseases across generations
This describes genetic factors, not family function.

alt.q: Which is an example of a family function process?
alt.a: Family members resolving a conflict about household tasks
alt.ex: Function processes include communication, goal setting, conflict resolution, caregiving, nurturing, and use of resources.
w: The number of people who currently live in the household
Household membership is part of family structure.
The family’s shared belief system about family membership
Belief systems are part of family structure.
The family’s inherited risk for heart disease
Inherited risk is a genetic factor, not a family function.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a family living in poverty. Which approach by the nurse is best?
items.a: Share information on community resources and help the family decide how to obtain assistance
items.ex: Be sensitive to the family’s need for autonomy and independence while helping them obtain financial and health care resources.
w: Arrange food and energy assistance without first involving the family
Acting without the family ignores their need for autonomy and independence.
Avoid discussing finances, since the topic may embarrass the family
Helping the family obtain financial and health care resources is part of the nurse’s role.
Refer the family to the emergency department for future health care
The goal is appropriate, accessible health care resources, not reliance on the emergency department.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of care for families living in poverty?
alt.a: “I should respect the family’s independence while helping them find resources.”
alt.ex: Nurses stay sensitive to autonomy and independence while helping families obtain financial and health care resources.
w: “I should choose the assistance programs the family will use.”
Choosing for the family ignores their need for autonomy.
“Insurance through the ACA removes their barriers to health care.”
Access to appropriate care remains a challenge for families at or near poverty.
“Families in poverty are rarely at risk for being uninsured.”
People living in poverty are more likely to be uninsured.

items.q: How does chronic housing insecurity differ from transitional episodic housing insecurity?
items.a: Chronic involves using shelters for long-term housing; transitional episodic involves one short stay
items.ex: Chronic housing insecurity means relying on shelters long term, whereas transitional episodic means a single short shelter stay.
w: Chronic involves one short stay; transitional episodic involves long-term shelter use
This reverses the two definitions.
Chronic affects only adults; transitional episodic affects only children
The types are defined by length and pattern of shelter use, not age.
Chronic results from a catastrophic event; transitional episodic results from illness
The types differ by length of shelter use, not by cause.

alt.q: A young adult stays in a shelter for 2 weeks after a house fire and then moves into an apartment. Which type of housing insecurity does this describe?
alt.a: Transitional episodic housing insecurity
alt.ex: Transitional episodic housing insecurity involves needing shelter for one stay and for a short period.
w: Chronic housing insecurity
Chronic housing insecurity involves using shelters for long-term housing needs.
Rigid housing insecurity
This is not a recognized type; rigid describes a family structure.
Generational housing insecurity
This is not one of the types described; the book contrasts chronic and transitional episodic.

items.q: A family caregiver who works full time and cares for her mother says she has not seen her own health care provider or dentist in 2 years. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Your own health matters too. Let’s talk about how you can fit in your checkups.”
items.ex: Caregivers often do not treat their own health needs as a priority and miss routine primary care and dental visits.
w: “That shows how dedicated you are to your mother’s care.”
Praising the sacrifice reinforces neglect of the caregiver’s own health needs.
“Most caregivers skip checkups, so that is nothing to worry about.”
Missed screenings and visits put the caregiver’s health at risk.
“You should focus on your mother now and see your provider later.”
Delaying her own care adds to the caregiver’s health risks.

alt.q: Which risk to the caregiver’s own health does the textbook describe for family caregivers?
alt.a: Missing routine primary care visits, screenings, and dental care
alt.ex: Caregivers often fail to make their own health a priority and miss routine visits, screenings, and dental care.
w: Receiving too many screenings because of frequent health visits
Caregivers tend to miss, not overuse, routine health care.
Gaining social freedom as caregiving responsibilities grow
Caregivers often lose social, economic, and physical freedom.
Improving mental health from the demands of daily caregiving
Caregiver mental health is often at risk from anxiety, depression, and stress.

items.q: Which caregiving activity is an instrumental activity of daily living (IADL)?
items.a: Shopping for the care recipient’s groceries
items.ex: The book gives shopping and housekeeping as instrumental activities of daily living that caregivers provide.
w: Bathing the care recipient
Bathing is personal care, not an instrumental activity.
Feeding the care recipient
Feeding is personal care, not an instrumental activity.
Grooming the care recipient
Grooming is personal care, not an instrumental activity.

alt.q: Which caregiving activity is personal care rather than an instrumental activity of daily living (IADL)?
alt.a: Bathing the care recipient
alt.ex: Personal care includes bathing, feeding, and grooming; shopping and housekeeping are instrumental activities.
w: Housekeeping for the care recipient
Housekeeping is an instrumental activity of daily living.
Shopping for the care recipient
Shopping is an instrumental activity of daily living.
Monitoring the care recipient’s finances
Monitoring finances is a broader caregiving task, not personal care.

items.q: Which societal factor does the textbook link to the rising number of grandparents raising their grandchildren?
items.a: Military deployment of the children’s parents
items.ex: Grandparents raise grandchildren because of factors such as military deployment, unemployment, adolescent pregnancy, substance abuse, and divorce.
w: Rising educational levels of older adults
Higher education among older adults is a positive trend, not a cause of grandparent parenting.
Legal recognition of same-sex marriage
Same-sex marriage rulings are not listed among causes of grandparent parenting.
Falling divorce rates among younger adults
Divorce leading to single parenthood is a cause; falling divorce would not increase it.

alt.q: A grandmother is now raising her two grandchildren. Which situation is a societal factor the textbook links to this trend?
alt.a: The children’s parent has a substance abuse problem
alt.ex: Substance abuse, unemployment, adolescent pregnancy, military deployment, and divorce lead grandparents to raise grandchildren.
w: The grandmother recently completed a college degree
Increased education among older adults is a positive trend, not a cause.
The grandmother continues to work part time
Workforce participation of older adults is a positive trend, not a cause.
The family recently moved into a larger home
A larger home is not a societal factor linked to this trend.

items.q: Which statement about adolescent fathers is supported by the textbook?
items.a: They usually have poorer support systems and fewer resources to learn parenting
items.ex: Adolescent fathers often lack support and parenting resources and face lower income, education, and job opportunities.
w: They rarely experience stress when their partners become pregnant
Stressors are placed on adolescent fathers when their partners become pregnant.
They usually have more resources to learn parenting than mothers
Adolescent fathers usually have poorer support systems and fewer parenting resources.
They are linked to higher educational attainment and income
Adolescent fatherhood is linked to lower socioeconomic status and education.

alt.q: Which outcome is associated with adolescent fatherhood?
alt.a: Lower educational attainment and fewer job opportunities
alt.ex: Adolescent fatherhood is associated with lower socioeconomic status, lower education, and fewer job opportunities.
w: Higher income than peers who delay parenting
Adolescent fatherhood is associated with lower socioeconomic status.
Stronger support systems than adolescent mothers
Adolescent fathers usually have poorer support systems.
Earlier entry into stable, well-paid careers
Adolescent fathers have fewer job opportunities.

items.q: A nurse visits a 16-year-old mother who lives with her parents and her 2-week-old infant. Based on the textbook, which areas are most important for the nurse to assess?
items.a: Her knowledge of infant care and the social support available to her
items.ex: Adolescent mothers often lack knowledge about infant care and social support, which strains family relationships.
w: Her plans to move out and live on her own right away
Most adolescent mothers continue to live with their families.
Her readiness to manage parenting without family help
Adolescent parents often need family support; they are seldom ready to parent alone.
Her career goals as the family’s main wage earner
Career goals are not the priority; infant care knowledge and support are.

alt.q: Which consequence of adolescent pregnancy does the textbook describe?
alt.a: Lack of knowledge about caring for an infant and lack of social support
alt.ex: Adolescent pregnancy often leads to problems with birth, psychological well-being, infant care knowledge, support, education, and finances.
w: Improved economic stability because the family gains a member
Adolescent pregnancy often causes economic strain.
Fewer family stressors because the mother lives at home
Being a parent while still an adolescent often severely stresses family relationships.
Lower risk that the infant will later have academic problems
Children of adolescent parents are more likely to have poor academic performance.

items.q: Which statement about family caregivers is supported by the textbook?
items.a: Older caregivers tend to care for someone their own age
items.ex: Older caregivers usually care for someone their own age, while younger caregivers usually care for someone older.
w: Most family caregivers are male
Most family caregivers are female.
Few family caregivers are employed while caregiving
About 61% of caregivers were employed while caregiving.
Younger caregivers tend to care for someone younger
Younger caregivers tend to care for someone older than themselves.

alt.q: A 76-year-old woman tells the nurse she is a family caregiver. Based on caregiving trends, whom is she most likely caring for?
alt.a: Her spouse or another person about her own age
alt.ex: Older caregivers tend to care for someone their own age, while younger caregivers care for someone older.
w: A school-age grandchild living in her home
The trend described is that older caregivers care for someone their own age.
An adult child in his 40s with a disability
Older caregivers most often care for someone their own age, not a younger adult.
A young neighbor recovering from surgery
Older caregivers tend to care for someone their own age.

items.q: A nurse is assessing the health of a family caregiver. Which concerns does the textbook identify as risks for caregivers? Select all that apply.
o: Anxiety and depression
Caregivers report increased mental health issues such as anxiety and depression.
Lack of sleep and changes in eating habits
Stress-related symptoms include lack of sleep and changes in eating habits.
Loss of income and family savings
Families report lost income and savings when a member leaves work to give care.
Poor physical health
Caregivers report poor physical health along with mental health issues.
Increased social and economic freedom
Caregivers often lose social, economic, and physical freedom.
Reduced need for support from others
Social networks and support from family and friends help mediate caregiver stress.
items.ex: Box 10.2 describes caregiver mental and physical health risks, stress symptoms, and financial loss.

alt.q: Which factors help older adult caregivers overcome the distress of caregiving? Select all that apply.
o: Good coping strategies
Caregivers with good coping strategies can overcome caregiving distress.
A good relationship with the care recipient
Good relationships with care recipients help caregivers overcome distress.
Acceptance of the caregiver role
Accepting the caregiver role helps overcome physical, psychological, and social distress.
Support from family and friends
Social networks and support help mediate caregiver stress.
Withdrawing from social networks
Social networks reduce caregiver stress; withdrawal is a sign of strain.
Taking on all care tasks alone
Families need help sharing caregiving roles among members.
alt.ex: Correct: Good coping strategies; A good relationship with the care recipient; Acceptance of the caregiver role; Support from family and friends.

items.q: Children in families experiencing housing insecurity have higher rates of which problems? Select all that apply.
o: Asthma
Children experiencing housing insecurity have higher rates of asthma.
Ear infections
Ear infections are more common in these children.
Poor dental health
Poor dental health is more common in these children.
Poor immunization documentation
These children often have poor immunization documentation.
Regular well-child visits with a primary provider
The emergency department often becomes their only access to health care.
Lower rates of anxiety and depression
These children experience anxiety, depression, and withdrawal more often.
items.ex: Children with unstable housing have more asthma, ear infections, stomach problems, mental illness, poor dental health, and poor immunization documentation.

alt.q: A school nurse cares for a 7-year-old whose family lives in a shelter. Which problems is this child at increased risk for? Select all that apply.
o: Developmental delay related to hunger
Hunger increases these children’s risk for developmental delay.
Missing school because of lack of transportation
Lack of transportation, clothing, supplies, and records affect school attendance.
Stomach problems
Stomach problems are more common in children with housing insecurity.
Consistent access to a primary care provider
The emergency department often becomes their only source of care.
Complete school and immunization records
These children often lack school records and immunization documentation.
alt.ex: Correct: Developmental delay related to hunger; Missing school because of lack of transportation; Stomach problems.

items.q: Which factors are associated with family violence? Select all that apply.
o: Stress
Stress is one of the complex factors associated with family violence.
Poverty
Poverty is associated with family violence.
Social isolation
Social isolation is associated with family violence.
Learned family behavior
Violence can be a learned family behavior.
Membership in a higher social class
Abuse occurs across all social classes; higher class is not a listed factor.
A strong social support network
Social isolation, not strong support, is associated with family violence.
items.ex: Factors linked to family violence include stress, poverty, social isolation, psychopathology, and learned family behavior.

alt.q: A nurse is screening a family for risk of domestic violence. Which findings are associated factors? Select all that apply.
o: A parent with a psychiatric illness
Psychopathology is associated with family violence.
A family with few social contacts
Social isolation is associated with family violence.
A parent who witnessed violence as a child
Learned family behavior is associated with family violence.
A family with a high household income
Abuse occurs across all social classes; high income is not a listed risk factor.
A family with a large circle of supportive friends
Strong support is not an associated factor; isolation is.
alt.ex: Correct: A parent with a psychiatric illness; A family with few social contacts; A parent who witnessed violence as a child.

items.q: Emotional, physical, and sexual abuse in families occurs mainly in lower social classes.
items.a: False
items.ex: Domestic violence, including emotional, physical, and sexual abuse, occurs across all social classes.
items.ww: Saying True reflects a misconception; poverty is one associated factor, but abuse occurs in every social class.

alt.q: A child who witnesses violence in the home is at increased risk for experiencing domestic violence later in life.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: One long-term consequence of family violence is moving from one abusive situation to another.
alt.ww: Saying False ignores that negative consequences of abuse linger, including later domestic violence.

items.q: Divorce is becoming less common in younger adults but has increased in adults 50 years of age and older.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book notes declining divorce in younger adults and an increase in adults 50 and older.
items.ww: Saying False reverses the trend; divorce has risen among adults 50 years and older.

alt.q: Divorce has become more common in younger adults and less common in adults 50 years of age and older.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The trend is the reverse: divorce is less common in younger adults and has increased in adults 50 and older.
alt.ww: Saying True reverses the actual trend described in the book.

items.q: Children are the poorest age-group in America.
items.a: True
items.ex: Children remain the poorest age-group, with 15.3% at the poverty level.
items.ww: Saying False overlooks that children, not older adults, have the highest poverty level.

alt.q: Adults 65 years and older are the poorest age-group in America.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Children are the poorest age-group; older adults show positive trends such as more education and workforce participation.
alt.ww: Saying True confuses the growing older-adult population with poverty; children have the highest poverty level.

items.q: What is the primary focus of nursing care when using the approach Family as context?
items.a: The health and development of an individual member within a specific family environment
items.ex: Context focuses on the individual, patient on the family unit, and system on both together.
w: The family’s needs, processes, and relationships, such as parenting or caregiving
That goes with Family as patient.
Each family member and the family unit, using all available resources
That goes with Family as a system.

alt.q: What is the primary focus of nursing care when using the approach Family as patient?
alt.a: The family’s needs, processes, and relationships, such as parenting or caregiving
alt.ex: Context focuses on the individual, patient on the family unit, and system on both together.
w: The health and development of an individual member within a specific family environment
That goes with Family as context.
Each family member and the family unit, using all available resources
That goes with Family as a system.

alt.q: What is the primary focus of nursing care when using the approach Family as a system?
alt.a: Each family member and the family unit, using all available resources
alt.ex: Context focuses on the individual, patient on the family unit, and system on both together.
w: The health and development of an individual member within a specific family environment
That goes with Family as context.
The family’s needs, processes, and relationships, such as parenting or caregiving
That goes with Family as patient.

alt.q: Which approach to family nursing focuses on “The health and development of an individual member within a specific family environment”?
alt.a: Family as context
alt.ex: Context focuses on the individual, patient on the family unit, and system on both together.
w: Family as patient
Family as patient: The family’s needs, processes, and relationships, such as parenting or caregiving.
Family as a system
Family as a system: Each family member and the family unit, using all available resources.

alt.q: Which approach to family nursing focuses on “The family’s needs, processes, and relationships, such as parenting or caregiving”?
alt.a: Family as patient
alt.ex: Context focuses on the individual, patient on the family unit, and system on both together.
w: Family as context
Family as context: The health and development of an individual member within a specific family environment.
Family as a system
Family as a system: Each family member and the family unit, using all available resources.

alt.q: Which approach to family nursing focuses on “Each family member and the family unit, using all available resources”?
alt.a: Family as a system
alt.ex: Context focuses on the individual, patient on the family unit, and system on both together.
w: Family as context
Family as context: The health and development of an individual member within a specific family environment.
Family as patient
Family as patient: The family’s needs, processes, and relationships, such as parenting or caregiving.

mt.q: Match each approach to family nursing with its primary focus.
pairs: The health and development of an individual member within a specific family environment
The family’s needs, processes, and relationships, such as parenting or caregiving
Each family member and the family unit, using all available resources
mt.ex: Context focuses on the individual, patient on the family unit, and system on both together.

items.q: A nurse caring for David, a 35-year-old dying at home, assesses whether his wife Lisa is getting enough rest and how their oldest child is coping with anger and fear. Which approach to family nursing is the nurse using?
items.a: Family as patient
items.ex: Assessing the needs, rest, coping, and resources of the wife and children makes the family the focus of care.
w: Family as context
Family as context focuses first on David’s own needs, such as comfort, hygiene, and nutrition.
Family as a system
Family as a system combines both perspectives and the family’s resources to individualize care.
Family as caregiver
This is not one of the three approaches; the approaches are context, patient, and system.

alt.q: While caring for David at the end of life, the nurse assesses his comfort, hygiene, nutrition, and how he is coping with dying. Which approach is the nurse using?
alt.a: Family as context
alt.ex: Family as context focuses first on the individual patient’s needs within the family environment.
w: Family as patient
Family as patient would focus on the wife and children’s needs and coping.
Family as a system
Family as a system would combine individual and family needs with available resources.
Family as community
This is not one of the three approaches; the approaches are context, patient, and system.

items.q: The nurse finds that David’s family is not eating well and Lisa is exhausted. The nurse holds a family conference and sets up a schedule with Lisa’s mother and church members so Lisa can rest. Which approach to family nursing does this show?
items.a: Family as a system
items.ex: Family as a system cares for each member and the family unit while using available social and community resources.
w: Family as context
Family as context focuses on David as an individual within his family environment.
Family as patient
Family as patient focuses on family needs but does not combine both perspectives with outside resources.
Family as a unit of service
This is not one of the three approaches described in the book.

alt.q: When the nurse cares for a family as a system, what does care include?
alt.a: Care of each family member and of the family unit, using all available resources
alt.ex: Family as a system combines the context and patient perspectives with environmental, social, psychological, and community resources.
w: Care of the individual patient only, within the family environment
Focusing on the individual within the family describes family as context.
Care of family relationships only, separate from individual needs
Focusing on family processes alone describes family as patient.
Care delegated entirely to community agencies and resources
The nurse still cares for members and the unit; resources support that care.

items.q: What is the goal of family nursing?
items.a: To help a family and its members reach and maintain maximum health throughout and beyond the illness experience
items.ex: Family nursing aims for maximum health for the family and its members during and after illness.
w: To help the patient recover while family members manage on their own
Family nursing includes the health of the family and its members, not only the patient.
To prepare the family to take over all of the nursing care after discharge
Preparing caregivers is one intervention, not the overall goal.
To identify which family members are responsible for the patient’s illness
Family nursing promotes health; it does not assign blame for illness.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse reflects the goal of family nursing?
alt.a: “I help the family and each member reach maximum health during and after illness.”
alt.ex: Family nursing aims for maximum health of the family and its members throughout and beyond the illness experience.
w: “I focus on my patient’s recovery and let the family manage on its own.”
Family nursing includes the family’s health, not only the patient’s recovery.
“My goal is to have the family take over all nursing care at home.”
Preparing caregivers is one intervention, not the goal of family nursing.
“I find out which family members caused the patient’s illness.”
Family nursing promotes health rather than assigning blame.

items.q: Which characteristic describes a crisis-proof, or effective, family?
items.a: A flexible structure that lets different members complete tasks and accepts outside help
items.ex: An effective family balances stability with growth and change through a flexible structure that accepts outside help.
w: A rigid structure in which each member performs only assigned tasks
Rigid structures limit who can do tasks and threaten family functioning.
A structure so flexible that no member is responsible for any task
Too much flexibility causes a lack of cohesiveness and stability.
A belief that it has little control over its home and neighborhood
Lacking or believing it lacks control describes a crisis-prone family.

alt.q: A family tells the nurse, “There is nothing we can do about what happens to us; things just happen.” Which type of family does this statement suggest?
alt.a: A crisis-prone, or ineffective, family
alt.ex: An ineffective, crisis-prone family lacks, or believes it lacks, control over its environment.
w: A crisis-proof, or effective, family
An effective family controls and influences its immediate environment.
A hardy family with strong internal strengths
Hardiness includes knowing that life events are controllable.
A resilient family with high life satisfaction
Resilient families withstand stressors rather than feeling powerless.

items.q: Which characteristic reflects family hardiness?
items.a: Viewing challenging situations as opportunities for growth
items.ex: Hardiness includes commitment to finding meaning, knowing life events are controllable and predictable, and seeing challenges as growth opportunities.
w: Believing that life events are uncontrollable and unpredictable
Hardy families know that life events are controllable and predictable.
Avoiding challenging situations to protect family stability
Hardy families see challenges as chances to grow, not things to avoid.
Relying on one member to manage every stressful event
Relying on one member reflects rigidity, not hardiness.

alt.q: A family facing a parent’s new cancer diagnosis says, “This is hard, but we will learn from it and grow closer.” Which family characteristic does this show?
alt.a: Family hardiness
alt.ex: Seeing a challenge as an opportunity for growth and finding meaning reflects family hardiness.
w: Family rigidity
Rigidity limits who can do tasks; it does not describe viewing challenges as growth.
Crisis-prone functioning
Crisis-prone families lack, or believe they lack, control over their environment.
Family diversity
Diversity is the uniqueness of each family, not its response to stress.

items.q: Which findings demonstrate family resilience? Select all that apply.
o: A high level of spirituality
A high level of spirituality is a sign of family resilience.
High life satisfaction
Life satisfaction is a sign of family resilience.
Low levels of depression
Low depression is a sign of family resilience.
Ability to withstand life difficulties and stressors
Withstanding difficulties and stressors demonstrates resilience.
Belief that the family lacks control over its environment
This belief describes a crisis-prone family.
Frequent conflict that goes unresolved
Unresolved conflict is not a sign of resilience.
items.ex: Resilience is shown by high spirituality, life satisfaction, low depression, and the ability to withstand stressors.

alt.q: Which resources and techniques help the nurse understand a family’s level of resiliency? Select all that apply.
o: Adequate income
Resources such as adequate income help families maintain health.
Education
Education is a resource that helps show a family’s resiliency.
Coping resources
Coping resources are techniques families use to keep balance.
Isolation from community support
Isolation is not a resource that supports resiliency.
Avoidance of all health care contact
Avoiding health care is not a resource or coping technique for resiliency.
alt.ex: Correct: Adequate income; Education; Coping resources.

items.q: A parent tells the children that smoking is harmful while continuing to smoke at home. Why is this situation a concern for the children’s future health?
items.a: Health behavior reinforced in early life strongly influences later health practices
items.ex: Family environment is crucial because behaviors reinforced early in life strongly shape later health practices.
w: Children usually reject the health behaviors they see at home
Behaviors reinforced at home in early life tend to influence, not repel, later practices.
Mixed messages affect only the parent’s health, not the children’s
Mixed health messages influence the children’s later health practices.
Family health habits have little effect once children reach school age
Early family environment has a strong influence on later health practices.

alt.q: Why is the family environment considered crucial to a child’s long-term health?
alt.a: Health behaviors reinforced in early life strongly shape later health practices
alt.ex: The family is the primary social context for health promotion, and early reinforced behaviors strongly influence later practices.
w: Health practices are set mainly by peers during adolescence
The book identifies the family, not peers, as the primary context for health promotion.
Early health behaviors have little effect on adult practices
Behaviors reinforced early in life strongly influence later health practices.
Family environment matters only during an acute illness
Family environment shapes health practices throughout life and adjustment to crises.

items.q: What critical role can nurses play related to genetic factors in families?
items.a: Encouraging genetic testing in high-risk situations and supporting families with the findings
items.ex: Nurses can encourage testing, especially in high-risk situations, and then inform and support families with results.
w: Deciding for the family whether its members should have children
Families make their own informed decisions; the nurse supports them.
Discouraging genetic testing to prevent family anxiety
Encouraging testing in high-risk situations is a critical nursing role.
Withholding test results until the family requests them
Nurses inform and support families with findings rather than withholding them.

alt.q: A patient at high risk because of a strong family history of breast cancer asks the nurse about genetic testing. Which nursing action best reflects the nurse’s role?
alt.a: Encourage testing and plan to help the family understand and use the results
alt.ex: Nurses encourage testing in high-risk situations and then inform and support families with the findings.
w: Advise against testing because the results only cause worry
Encouraging testing in high-risk situations is a critical nursing role.
Decide for the patient whether she should have preventive surgery
Patients and families make informed decisions; the nurse supports them.
Explain that test results are shared only with the provider
Nurses help inform and support families with the findings.

items.q: When families know their genetic risks, they can make informed lifestyle decisions and may seek medical intervention earlier.
items.a: True
items.ex: Known risks lead families to be more vigilant about health changes and sometimes to seek intervention earlier.
items.ww: Saying False ignores that genetic knowledge helps families make informed choices and recognize changes sooner.

alt.q: All families who learn of a genetic risk for a neurological disease such as Huntington disease decide not to have children.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Some families choose not to have children, others choose not to know the risk, and others decide after learning it.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores that families make different choices; the book says such families may choose not to have children.

items.q: A patient is admitted to the intensive care unit after a serious car crash. The family has been in the waiting room for hours. Which action by the nurse best supports the family?
items.a: Offer them something to eat or drink and tell them you will stay with their loved one if they leave for a meal
items.ex: Making the family comfortable and offering to stay with the patient helps family members feel able to leave briefly.
w: Ask them to remain in the waiting room until the provider updates them
Leaving families waiting increases stress; the nurse acts to make them comfortable.
Suggest they go home and call later for information about the patient
Sending the family away does not meet their need for information and presence.
Limit updates to one family member to prevent miscommunication at the bedside
The family needs information and comfort, not restrictions on support.

alt.q: Which nurse action helps make a hospitalized patient’s family comfortable?
alt.a: Bringing the family a blanket and encouraging them to get a meal
alt.ex: The book suggests food, drink, a blanket, or encouragement to get a meal while the nurse stays with the patient.
w: Keeping the family in the waiting room until visiting hours begin
Keeping the family away does not make them comfortable.
Avoiding contact with the family so they can rest privately
The nurse should actively attend to the family’s comfort.
Telling the family that their presence increases the patient’s stress
This discourages the family rather than supporting them.

items.q: The spouse of a hospitalized patient asks the nurse a question about the expected recovery that the nurse cannot answer. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “I don’t know, but I will find someone who can answer that for you.”
items.ex: Nurses answer family questions honestly and, when they do not know, find someone who does.
w: “You will need to ask the doctor during rounds tomorrow.”
This delays the answer and shifts the responsibility to the family.
“Most patients recover well, so try not to worry about it.”
Giving a reassuring guess is not an honest answer.
“That information is not something nurses discuss with families.”
Nurses advocate for families and help them get answers.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows understanding of how to advocate for a patient’s family?
alt.a: “I answer questions honestly, and I find someone else when I don’t know.”
alt.ex: Advocacy includes honest answers, finding someone who knows, and ensuring the family knows the team.
w: “I avoid answering questions so the family won’t be upset.”
Avoiding questions does not advocate for the family.
“I give my best guess so the family is not left waiting.”
Guessing is not an honest answer to the family’s question.
“I refer every family question to the health care provider.”
Nurses answer honestly when they can and find help when they cannot.

items.q: Why is a family member’s hospitalization stressful for the whole family? Select all that apply.
o: The health care environment is foreign to them
Health care environments are unfamiliar to families.
Physicians and nurses are strangers
Families are dealing with health care providers they do not know.
Medical language is difficult to understand
Medical language is hard for families to understand or interpret.
Family members are often separated from one another
Hospitalization often separates family members.
Previous family conflicts always disappear during a crisis
Previous conflicts can rise to the surface, while others are suppressed.
Communication among family members improves from worry
Fear and worry can cause communication among members to be misunderstood.
items.ex: Foreign settings, strangers, hard medical language, and separation make hospitalization stressful for the whole family.

alt.q: During an acute health crisis, how might family members respond? Select all that apply.
o: They misunderstand one another because of fear and worry
Fear and worry can cause misunderstood communication among members.
Previous family conflicts rise to the surface
Old conflicts can resurface during an acute crisis.
They experience anxiety, frustration, and guilt
Families of seriously ill members experience anxiety, frustration, guilt, and economic burden.
They make decisions more easily when feeling powerless
Powerlessness makes important health decisions more difficult.
Their economic concerns usually disappear
Families often face economic burden during a serious illness.
alt.ex: Correct: They misunderstand one another because of fear and worry; Previous family conflicts rise to the surface; They experience anxiety, frustration, and guilt.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a family whose member is terminally ill. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Encourage the patient and family to make decisions about pain control and comfort measures
Patients and families should make decisions about care and specific therapies.
Make timely referrals for hospice, including grief support
Timely referral to hospice and grief support is part of end-of-life care.
Provide information about the dying process
Families need information about the dying process and what to do at death.
Provide privacy and time for goodbyes at the time of death
Being sensitive to family needs includes privacy and time for goodbyes.
Make care decisions for the family to reduce their burden
The nurse encourages the patient and family to make their own decisions.
Wait until the time of death to discuss what the family should do
Families should know in advance what to do at the time of death.
items.ex: End-of-life care includes shared decisions, home care setup, timely hospice and grief referrals, information, and sensitivity at death.

alt.q: Which statements about families facing end-of-life care are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Many diseases besides cancer have terminal aspects
Heart failure, pulmonary and renal diseases, dementia, and neuromuscular diseases have terminal aspects.
Each family approaches end-of-life decisions differently
Each family copes with end-of-life decisions in its own way.
Even prepared families have great need for information and support
Prepared families still need information, support, assurance, and presence.
Families who expect the death need little nursing presence
Their need for presence remains great even when they are prepared.
Hospice referral should wait until the final days of life
Referrals for hospice should be timely.
alt.ex: Correct: Many diseases besides cancer have terminal aspects; Each family approaches end-of-life decisions differently; Even prepared families have great need for information and support.

items.q: Family as context and family as patient are mutually exclusive approaches, so the nurse must choose only one.
items.a: False
items.ex: The approaches are not mutually exclusive; family as a system uses both together.
items.ww: Saying True ignores that the nurse can combine the context and patient perspectives in family as a system.

alt.q: When caring for a family as a system, the nurse cares for each family member and for the family unit.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Family as a system combines family as context and family as patient using all available resources.
alt.ww: Saying False misses that the system approach includes both the individual members and the family unit.

items.q: Many diseases other than cancer, such as heart failure and dementia, have terminal aspects that families must face.
items.a: True
items.ex: Heart failure, pulmonary and renal diseases, dementia, and neuromuscular diseases can have terminal aspects.
items.ww: Saying False reflects the common belief that terminal illness means cancer.

alt.q: Terminal illness in families is almost always related to cancer.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: People often equate terminal illness with cancer, but many diseases have terminal aspects.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores heart failure, pulmonary and renal diseases, dementia, and neuromuscular diseases.

items.q: A nurse uses a family-centered care model for a patient with an acute illness. How can the nurse involve the family during a hand-off report?
items.a: Include the patient and family in discussing the current and long-term plan of care
items.ex: Involving the family during hand-off gives them a chance to discuss the present and long-term plan of care.
w: Give the report away from the bedside so the family is not worried
Excluding the family misses an opportunity to involve them in planning.
Ask the family to leave the room until the report is finished
Family-centered care makes the family an active partner in care.
