Share only the medication schedule with the family after the report
The family should take part in discussing the full plan of care.

alt.q: In a family-centered care model for acute or chronic illness, what role do family members and surrogate decision makers have?
alt.a: They become active partners in decision making and care
alt.ex: Family-centered care makes family members and surrogate decision makers active partners in decisions and care.
w: They receive information only after the team has decided
Families take part in shared decision making, not just receive decisions.
They observe care but do not take part in decisions
Families are active partners, not observers.
They make decisions only when the patient is unconscious
Families take part in care and decisions throughout the illness.

items.q: When viewing the family as patient, what is the focus of the nurse’s assessment?
items.a: Family patterns and processes rather than the characteristics of individual members
items.ex: Family as patient focuses assessment on family patterns versus characteristics of individual members.
w: The health and development of one member within the family environment
This describes the focus of family as context.
The physical needs of the ill member, such as hygiene and nutrition
Individual physical needs are the focus of family as context.
The community resources available to replace family caregivers
Family as patient focuses on family patterns, not on replacing caregivers.

alt.q: A nurse uses a family-as-patient approach for a family caring for a member with dementia. What should the nurse determine?
alt.a: Who the family caregivers are, their roles, and how they interact to meet needs
alt.ex: With family as patient, the nurse assesses caregivers, their roles, and their interactions, which are family patterns and processes.
w: The ill member’s own hygiene, comfort, and nutrition needs only
Focusing on one member’s needs describes family as context.
Which community agency can replace the family caregivers
Family as patient focuses on family patterns, not on replacing caregivers.
The ill member’s individual developmental level only
Individual development within the family is the focus of family as context.

items.q: A family member has had multiple sclerosis for several years. Which statement best describes how chronic illness typically affects the family?
items.a: Family roles, schedules, and resources must be reorganized around the illness
items.ex: Chronic illness presents continuous challenges, so family patterns, roles, schedules, and resources are reorganized around it.
w: The family is affected only during the first weeks after diagnosis
Chronic illness presents continuous challenges for families.
The illness affects the patient but rarely the family’s finances
Disease influences the family economically, emotionally, socially, and functionally.
The family’s usual routines remain mostly unchanged over time
Routines and functions often must be reorganized around the chronic illness.

alt.q: Which statement about chronic illness in a family is accurate?
alt.a: It presents continuous challenges that require reorganizing family functions
alt.ex: Family patterns, roles, schedules, finances, and functions often must be reorganized around a chronic illness.
w: It affects the family only during periods of hospitalization
Chronic illness presents continuous challenges, not only during hospital stays.
It changes the patient’s routines but not the family’s routines
Work and household schedules of the family are reorganized around the illness.
It affects the family emotionally but not economically or socially
Disease affects the family economically, emotionally, socially, and functionally.

items.q: Family [[hardiness]] includes the internal strengths and durability of the family unit.
items.ex: Hardiness and resiliency moderate a family’s stress and thus affect the family’s health.

alt.q: The internal strengths and durability of a family unit are called family [[hardiness]].
alt.ex: Hardiness and resiliency moderate a family’s stress and thus affect the family’s health.

sections.name: Family-centered care and the nursing process

items.q: A nurse uses the nursing process to identify and organize care for the entire family rather than for one member. Which perspective does this reflect?
items.a: Family as patient
items.ex: The textbook uses the nursing process for an individual within a family (family as context) or for the entire family (family as patient).
w: Family as context
Family as context centers on one individual, with the family in the background.
Family durability
Durability describes a family's lasting system of support, not a focus of care.
Family diversity
Diversity describes the uniqueness of families, not a focus for organizing care.

alt.q: A nurse uses the nursing process to organize care for one patient while considering that patient's family. Which perspective does this reflect?
alt.a: Family as context
alt.ex: Organizing care for an individual within a family is the family-as-context perspective.
w: Family as patient
Family as patient makes the entire family the focus of care.
Family durability
Durability describes a family's lasting system of support, not a focus of care.
Family resiliency
Resiliency is a family's ability to cope, not a focus for organizing care.

items.q: In Box 10.3, what does the Family structure area determine?
items.a: Members of the family, relationships among them, and the family’s context
items.ex: Box 10.3 organizes family assessment questions into structure, development, and functioning.
w: How the family adapts during predictable and unpredictable changes
That goes with Developmental assessment.
How members behave toward one another, including routine and expressive aspects
That goes with Family functioning.

alt.q: In Box 10.3, what does the Developmental assessment area determine?
alt.a: How the family adapts during predictable and unpredictable changes
alt.ex: Box 10.3 organizes family assessment questions into structure, development, and functioning.
w: Members of the family, relationships among them, and the family’s context
That goes with Family structure.
How members behave toward one another, including routine and expressive aspects
That goes with Family functioning.

alt.q: In Box 10.3, what does the Family functioning area determine?
alt.a: How members behave toward one another, including routine and expressive aspects
alt.ex: Box 10.3 organizes family assessment questions into structure, development, and functioning.
w: Members of the family, relationships among them, and the family’s context
That goes with Family structure.
How the family adapts during predictable and unpredictable changes
That goes with Developmental assessment.

alt.q: Which family assessment area determines “Members of the family, relationships among them, and the family’s context”?
alt.a: Family structure
alt.ex: Box 10.3 organizes family assessment questions into structure, development, and functioning.
w: Developmental assessment
Developmental assessment: How the family adapts during predictable and unpredictable changes.
Family functioning
Family functioning: How members behave toward one another, including routine and expressive aspects.

alt.q: Which family assessment area determines “How the family adapts during predictable and unpredictable changes”?
alt.a: Developmental assessment
alt.ex: Box 10.3 organizes family assessment questions into structure, development, and functioning.
w: Family structure
Family structure: Members of the family, relationships among them, and the family’s context.
Family functioning
Family functioning: How members behave toward one another, including routine and expressive aspects.

alt.q: Which family assessment area determines “How members behave toward one another, including routine and expressive aspects”?
alt.a: Family functioning
alt.ex: Box 10.3 organizes family assessment questions into structure, development, and functioning.
w: Family structure
Family structure: Members of the family, relationships among them, and the family’s context.
Developmental assessment
Developmental assessment: How the family adapts during predictable and unpredictable changes.

mt.q: Match each area of the Calgary-based family assessment with what it determines.
pairs: Members of the family, relationships among them, and the family’s context
How the family adapts during predictable and unpredictable changes
How members behave toward one another, including routine and expressive aspects
mt.ex: Box 10.3 organizes family assessment questions into structure, development, and functioning.

items.q: When beginning a family assessment, what should the nurse determine first?
items.a: The patient’s definition of and attitude toward the family
items.ex: The patient’s concept of family is individualized and influences how much the nurse can include the family in care.
w: The family’s economic resources and insurance coverage
Economic resources are assessed as part of function after the patient’s definition.
The family’s power structure and division of tasks
Power structure and roles are assessed after determining who the family is.
The family’s cultural practices for caring for the sick
Culture is assessed too, but the assessment begins with the patient’s definition of family.

alt.q: A nurse is starting a family assessment with a newly admitted patient. Which question should the nurse ask first?
alt.a: “What does family mean to you, and who is part of it?”
alt.ex: The assessment begins with the patient’s definition of and attitude toward family, which guides how the family is included.
w: “Who decides where your family goes on vacation?”
Power structure questions come after the nurse learns who the family is.
“Does your family have enough income to meet its needs?”
Economic resources are assessed later as part of family function.
“What foods does your family usually eat at home?”
Cultural practice questions follow after the patient’s concept of family is known.

items.q: An older adult is being discharged home after surgery and needs daily dressing changes. The patient’s spouse says, “I can’t do the dressings.” What should the nurse do first?
items.a: Find out whether someone else in the family or support system is willing and able
items.ex: The nurse first looks for another willing, able caregiver in the support system; if none, a home care referral is arranged.
w: Arrange a home care referral for daily dressing changes
A home care referral is arranged if no one in the support system can do the dressings.
Teach the spouse the procedure until the spouse agrees to do it
The spouse has said they cannot; the nurse explores other caregivers first.
Ask the provider to delay discharge until the wound heals
Delaying discharge is not the book’s approach; the nurse finds a caregiver or referral.

alt.q: An older adult going home after surgery needs dressing changes, and no one in the family or support system is willing and able to do them. What should the nurse arrange?
alt.a: A home care referral
alt.ex: If no family or support person can perform needed care, the nurse arranges a home care referral.
w: A physical therapy referral
Physical therapy is recommended for exercise and strength training, not dressing changes.
A longer hospital stay
The book directs a home care referral rather than keeping the patient hospitalized.
A support group referral
Support groups help caregivers share feelings; they do not perform dressing changes.

items.q: A family caregiver tells the nurse, “I feel trapped by having to bathe my mother.” Which response by the nurse best reflects the evidence on caregiver mental health?
items.a: Help the caregiver reframe this as a chance to care for someone who once cared for her
items.ex: Encouraging caregivers to discuss feelings and reframe them more adaptively supports caregiver mental health.
w: Tell the caregiver that bathing is a normal task she should accept
Dismissing her feelings does not help shape a more adaptive perception.
Advise the caregiver to stop bathing her mother to avoid resentment
Stopping care does not address her perception of the caregiving role.
Change the subject to the mother’s care plan to keep the visit focused
Caregivers should be encouraged to discuss their feelings about caregiving.

alt.q: The nurse helps a caregiver reframe negative feelings about bathing her mother. Which caregiver statement shows the adaptive reframing the nurse is encouraging?
alt.a: “I now have the chance to care for someone who once cared for me.”
alt.ex: Reframing caregiving in a more adaptive way helps shape perceptions that improve caregiver mental health.
w: “I have no choice; this is simply my burden to carry now.”
This statement still frames caregiving as a trap rather than an opportunity.
“I will keep these feelings to myself so Mom won’t know.”
Caregivers are encouraged to discuss their feelings, not hide them.
“Someone else in the family should be doing this, not me.”
This shifts blame rather than reframing the caregiving role adaptively.

items.q: A married father of four sustains multiple fractures in a car crash and will be non–weight-bearing for 6 to 8 weeks. His spouse feels overwhelmed planning how to meet the family’s needs. Which nursing diagnosis is most appropriate for this family?
items.a: Impaired Family Process
items.ex: Immobility and temporary changes in family roles disrupt family processes, so Impaired Family Process applies.
w: Risk for Impaired Parent/Child Attachment
Nothing suggests a threat to the bond between parent and child.
Family Knowledge of Disease
This positive diagnosis does not describe the role changes and overwhelmed spouse.
Conflicting Caregiver Attitude
No conflicting caregiver attitudes are described in the situation.

alt.q: Nursing diagnoses that relate to a family often focus on which area?
alt.a: Changes in family processes or roles
alt.ex: Family nursing diagnoses often focus on the family’s ability to cope and on changes in family processes or roles.
w: Each member’s individual medical diagnosis
Medical diagnoses are not the focus; family coping, processes, and roles are.
The family’s legal and insurance status
Legal status is not the focus of family nursing diagnoses.
One isolated problem at a time
Assessment often identifies multiple interrelated nursing diagnoses for the family.

items.q: Which characteristics should outcomes in a family plan of care have?
items.a: Concrete, realistic, fitting members’ developmental stages, and acceptable to the family
items.ex: Outcomes must be concrete and realistic, compatible with developmental stages, and acceptable to family members and their lifestyle.
w: Broad and general so the family can interpret them as needed
Outcomes should be concrete so all members clearly understand them.
Set by the nurse alone to save time and avoid disagreement
Plans are developed with families and mutually agreed upon.
Ambitious enough to change the family’s lifestyle completely
Outcomes must be realistic and acceptable to the family’s lifestyle.

alt.q: A nurse writes this outcome for a family with toddlers and a frail grandparent: “All members will jog 5 miles daily within 1 week.” What is the main problem with this outcome?
alt.a: It is not realistic or compatible with members’ developmental stages
alt.ex: Outcomes must be realistic, fit members’ developmental stages, and be acceptable to the family and its lifestyle.
w: It is too concrete for the family to understand
Outcomes should be concrete; that is not the problem here.
It was not written by the health care provider
Nurses develop family outcomes together with the family.
It focuses on health promotion instead of illness
Health promotion outcomes are appropriate when they are realistic.

items.q: A nurse notices that a new father avoids touching his newborn’s umbilical cord during cord care. Which statement by the nurse best addresses this subtle learning need?
items.a: “I notice you are trying to avoid touching the cord. I see that a lot.”
items.ex: Respectful, nonjudgmental observations lower defenses so the parent is more willing to learn without embarrassment.
w: “You have to clean the cord properly or it could get infected.”
Speaking as an authority can raise defenses and embarrass the father.
“Let me do the cord care since you seem uncomfortable with it.”
Taking over does not meet the father’s learning need.
“Didn’t anyone show you how to do cord care before now?”
This question can embarrass the father and increase defensiveness.

alt.q: An older adult is using a cane unsafely. Which statement by the nurse is most likely to make the patient willing to learn?
alt.a: “You use the cane the way I did before I was shown a safer way; may I show you?”
alt.ex: Confident, skillful, respectful communication instead of an authoritative tone makes patients more willing to listen.
w: “You are using that cane wrong and will fall if you keep doing that.”
An authoritative, critical tone raises defenses and embarrassment.
“You should have learned to use the cane before you went home.”
Blaming statements make the patient less willing to listen.
“I will ask physical therapy to take your cane away until you learn.”
Threatening to remove the device does not address the learning need.

items.q: A couple married for 30 years is coping with the husband’s new diagnosis of heart failure. Which nursing action uses family strengths to promote health?
items.a: Point out that their marriage has endured many crises, so they can likely adapt to this one
items.ex: Helping families focus on strengths, such as past adaptation to crises, rather than problems promotes health.
w: Review each problem the couple has had during their marriage
The nurse focuses the family on strengths, not on problems and weaknesses.
Explain that heart failure will likely overwhelm their coping
This focuses on weakness rather than the couple’s strengths.
Advise the couple to rely on the health care team for all decisions
Using family strengths empowers the family rather than shifting decisions away.

alt.q: Which is an example of a family strength the nurse can help a family use?
alt.a: Clear communication and support among family members
alt.ex: Family strengths include clear communication, adaptability, healthy childrearing, support, commitment, cohesiveness, and spirituality.
w: Avoidance of discussing problems with one another
Avoidance is not one of the family strengths listed.
Rigid assignment of all tasks to a single member
Rigidity limits family functioning; adaptability is a strength.
Reliance on outside agencies for every family decision
Commitment to one another and the family unit is the strength described.

items.q: A patient will be discharged home on a daily subcutaneous injection. When and how should the nurse involve the family in teaching?
items.a: Begin teaching on admission, let the family give the injection under observation, and reinforce throughout the stay
items.ex: Because stays are short, families take active caregiving roles from admission, practice under observation, and receive ongoing reinforcement.
w: Teach the family the injection technique on the morning of discharge
Waiting until discharge leaves too little time; teaching starts on admission.
Give the family a written handout and have them read it at home
Families need opportunity to practice under observation and reinforcement.
Teach only the patient, since the family is not giving the injection yet
Including the family in care during admission prepares them for their role.

alt.q: Why should family caregivers be included in a patient’s care during the hospital admission?
alt.a: To better prepare them for their role and reduce stress after discharge
alt.ex: Including caregivers during admission prepares them for caregiving and reduces stress following discharge.
w: To reduce the number of nurses needed on the unit
The purpose is caregiver preparation, not staffing.
To allow the hospital stay to be extended for teaching
Hospital stays are shortened, which is why early inclusion matters.
To transfer legal responsibility for care to the family
Inclusion prepares caregivers; it does not transfer legal responsibility.

items.q: A nurse’s assessment shows that the relationship between a patient and the family member who plans to provide care is not supportive. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Connect the patient and family with community services to meet the patient’s caregiving needs
items.ex: When the caregiver relationship is not supportive, community services should meet the patient’s caregiving needs.
w: Assign the family member as caregiver and schedule a follow-up visit
An unsupportive relationship puts the patient at risk; community services are needed.
Teach the family member to provide care despite the relationship
Teaching does not correct an unsupportive relationship that places the patient at risk.
Delay discharge until the family relationship has improved
The book directs the nurse to arrange community services, not delay discharge.

alt.q: During discharge planning, a nurse observes the adult son who will care for his father yelling at and insulting him. Which action by the nurse is best?
alt.a: Arrange community services to provide the father’s caregiving needs
alt.ex: Negative verbal interactions are potentially harmful; an unsupportive caregiving relationship calls for community services.
w: Discharge the father home with his son as planned
An unsupportive relationship puts the older adult at risk for harmful behaviors.
Teach the son the care skills before discharge
Teaching skills does not correct an unsupportive caregiving relationship.
Tell the son that yelling is a normal caregiver reaction
Screaming, yelling, and insults are potentially harmful caregiver behaviors.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a family from a culture different from the nurse’s own. Which approach best supports culturally sensitive family-centered care?
items.a: Ask the family about their cultural background and practices instead of making assumptions
items.ex: Generalizations about cultural groups lead to stereotyping, so the nurse asks about each family’s background and practices.
w: Plan care based on general traits known for the family’s ethnic group
Categorical generalizations are often misleading and lead to stereotyping.
Avoid asking about culture so the family does not feel singled out
Asking about cultural background and practices is how the nurse learns its influence.
Assume the family shares the nurse’s own beliefs about health care
Families differ in values and beliefs, which affect care decisions.

alt.q: Which question best helps the nurse learn how culture influences a family’s care?
alt.a: “Who usually cares for sick family members in your family?”
alt.ex: Questions about cultural practices, such as who cares for the sick, show culture’s influence on the family.
w: “Your culture usually prefers family caregivers, correct?”
This question assumes a cultural generalization instead of asking.
“Do you agree with our usual unit routines for families?”
This asks about unit routines, not the family’s cultural practices.
“How long has your family lived in this country?”
This does not directly ask about cultural practices or caregiving.

items.q: Which statement best describes how the nurse evaluates care when the family is viewed as a system?
items.a: The nurse evaluates the effects of interventions on the entire family, including extended family members
items.ex: With family as a system, evaluation focuses on the effects of interventions on everyone, including extended family.
w: The nurse evaluates only whether the patient’s individual needs were met
This is closer to family as context, which compares patient and family responses to outcomes.
The nurse evaluates only the health of each member separately
Family health is more than the health of all individual members.
The nurse evaluates whether the plan was completed on schedule
Evaluation focuses on the effects of interventions, not on task completion.

alt.q: Using a family-as-system approach, a nurse cares for an older adult receiving chemotherapy for new cancer. How should the nurse evaluate interventions to improve communication and coping?
alt.a: Determine their effectiveness for the patient, spouse, children, and grandchildren
alt.ex: System-level evaluation looks at how interventions affected the entire family, including extended members.
w: Determine their effectiveness for the patient alone
Evaluating only the patient ignores the system focus on the whole family.
Compare the patient’s laboratory values with expected ranges
Laboratory values do not measure family communication and coping.
Ask the health care provider whether the goals were met
Evaluation includes the family’s perceptions and responses, not only the provider’s view.

items.q: Which teaching points should the nurse include when teaching a family about caregiver role strain? Select all that apply.
o: Signs such as changes in appetite, sleep, or leisure activities
Box 10.6 lists changes in appetite, weight, sleep, or leisure activities as signs.
Signs such as social withdrawal, irritability, and anger
Social withdrawal, irritability, and anger are signs of role strain.
Setting up alternating schedules so the primary caregiver can rest
Alternating schedules give the primary caregiver time to rest.
Calling the provider if the caregiver seems overly exhausted
Families should call if the caregiver has health problems or seems overly exhausted.
Role strain usually lessens when the patient is hospitalized
Role strain may intensify when the patient’s health changes or hospitalization is needed.
The primary caregiver should handle all care to keep routines stable
Sharing care through alternating schedules reduces strain.
items.ex: Box 10.6 teaches signs of role strain, when it intensifies, alternating schedules, community resources, and when to call the provider.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing a family caregiver for caregiver role strain. Which findings are signs of role strain? Select all that apply.
o: Loss of interest in personal appearance
Loss of interest in appearance is a sign of caregiver role strain.
Social withdrawal from friends
Social withdrawal is a sign of caregiver role strain.
Change in weight and sleeping patterns
Changes in weight and sleep are signs of role strain.
Steady appetite and regular sleep
Unchanged appetite and sleep are not signs of role strain.
Continued enjoyment of usual leisure activities
A change in leisure activities, not continued enjoyment, signals strain.
alt.ex: Correct: Loss of interest in personal appearance; Social withdrawal from friends; Change in weight and sleeping patterns.

items.q: Which nursing actions support clear communication with a family in the acute care setting? Select all that apply.
o: Using clear, plain language
Plain language helps families understand health issues and decisions.
Providing a professional interpreter when the family does not speak English
Professional interpreters ensure accurate communication.
Identifying the family’s decision maker and consistently going to that person
Consistently communicating with the decision maker keeps information clear.
Helping the family keep open lines of communication with the team
Open communication helps anticipate patient and family needs.
Using precise medical terminology to avoid oversimplifying
Clear communication clarifies medical terminology for the family.
Asking a bilingual child in the family to interpret
The book calls for professional interpreters.
items.ex: Supportive, clear, consistent communication includes plain language, professional interpreters, and a consistent decision maker.

alt.q: A patient’s large family repeatedly calls the unit for updates on her progress. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Identify who makes decisions for the family and consistently update that person
Consistently going to the decision maker keeps information clear.
Help the decision maker develop a method to share information clearly
Decision makers sometimes need help communicating decisions.
Help the family decide whether a blog or social media suits their needs
Some families use blogs or social media to share consistent information.
Give each caller a different nurse’s summary of the plan
Inconsistent messages from multiple sources reduce clarity.
Refuse to give updates until the family chooses one spokesperson
The nurse helps identify the decision maker rather than refusing updates.
alt.ex: Correct: Identify who makes decisions for the family and consistently update that person; Help the decision maker develop a method to share information clearly; Help the family decide whether a blog or social media suits their needs.

items.q: A nurse is supporting a family caregiver of a patient with dementia. Which interventions are supported by evidence? Select all that apply.
o: Teach ways to cope with and redirect behavioral disturbances
Teaching dementia caregivers to redirect behaviors reduces burden and distress.
Refer the caregiver to a support group
Support groups let caregivers share feelings and experiences with others.
Encourage the caregiver to stay engaged in care during hospitalization
Caregivers should help with mobilization, meals, and education during hospital stays.
Help the caregiver find a balance among competing needs
Finding a balance reduces stress and role strain.
Advise the caregiver to avoid discussing feelings to stay strong
Caregivers should be encouraged to discuss their feelings.
Limit teaching to the patient, since the caregiver is not ill
Education is targeted to both patient and caregiver needs.
items.ex: Box 10.5 supports tailored caregiver interventions: coping skills, support groups, engagement, balance, and emotional and financial support.

alt.q: Which nursing interventions does evidence support for reducing family caregiver burden? Select all that apply.
o: Teaching mindfulness techniques such as meditation and guided imagery
Mindfulness helps caregivers focus on the present and reduces burden.
Carefully assessing the caregiver’s mental health
Assessing caregiver mental health is a recommended practice.
Helping the family identify financial resources
Emotional support and financial resources may reduce burden and improve coping.
Discouraging caregiver help with meals during hospitalization
Caregivers should stay engaged, such as helping with meals and mobilization.
Ignoring cultural stigma linked to the patient’s illness
Nurses assess cultural implications, such as stigma with mental illness.
alt.ex: Correct: Teaching mindfulness techniques such as meditation and guided imagery; Carefully assessing the caregiver’s mental health; Helping the family identify financial resources.

items.q: Discharge planning with a family begins on the day the patient is ready to leave the health care facility.
items.a: False
items.ex: Discharge planning begins with the initiation of care and includes the family.
items.ww: Saying True ignores that early planning is needed to assess who will provide care and what will be needed at home.

alt.q: Discharge planning begins with the initiation of care and includes the family.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Early planning lets the nurse assess who will give care and what is needed at home at discharge.
alt.ww: Saying False delays planning, leaving too little time to prepare caregivers and arrange resources.

items.q: Evaluation of family-centered care begins with determining the family’s perspective of the nursing care provided.
items.a: True
items.ex: Evaluation begins by asking whether care met the family’s expectations and outcomes from their point of view.
items.ww: Saying False ignores that evaluation starts “through the patient’s and family’s eyes.”

alt.q: Evaluation of family-centered care begins with the nurse’s own judgment of whether interventions were completed as planned.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Evaluation begins with the family’s perspective of the care and whether it met their expectations.
alt.ww: Saying True overlooks that evaluation starts with the family’s perceptions, not the nurse’s task list.

items.q: Family caregivers sometimes resist help because they feel obligated to be the sole source of support for the care recipient.
items.a: True
items.ex: Some caregivers resist help from a sense of obligation, so the nurse understands family dynamics before referring.
items.ww: Saying False ignores that obligation can lead caregivers to refuse community resources.

alt.q: Family caregivers readily accept community resources because they welcome relief from caregiving.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Some caregivers resist help, so the nurse assesses family dynamics and desire for support before referral.
alt.ww: Saying True ignores that caregivers may feel obligated to be the only source of support.

items.q: The [[Synergy Model|synergy model]] recognizes the importance of the relationship between the nurse and the patient and family in creating a healing environment.
items.ex: When there is synergy between a patient, family, and nurse, optimal patient outcomes result.

alt.q: According to the [[Synergy Model|synergy model]], the needs and characteristics of a patient and family drive nursing interventions.
alt.ex: When there is synergy between a patient, family, and nurse, optimal patient outcomes result.

items.q: What is fundamental to Gesell’s theory of development?
items.a: Each child’s pattern of growth is unique and is directed by gene activity
items.ex: Gesell held that every child’s growth pattern is unique and that gene activity directs it.
w: Each child’s growth is shaped mainly by unconscious conflicts and emotion
Unconscious conflict and emotion are the basis of psychoanalytical theory, not Gesell’s biophysical theory.
Each child’s growth depends mainly on relationships with family and culture
Family and culture are emphasized in Erikson’s psychosocial theory, not Gesell’s gene-directed theory.
Each child’s growth follows a random order set by the child’s environment
Gesell described a fixed developmental sequence directed by genes, not a random environmental order.

alt.q: A nurse is explaining Gesell’s biophysical theory to parents. Which statement best reflects it?
alt.a: Your baby’s growth pattern is unique and is directed by the baby’s genes
alt.ex: Gesell’s theory states that each child’s growth pattern is unique and directed by gene activity.
w: Your baby’s growth pattern is set mostly by how you resolve toilet training
Toilet training conflicts belong to Freud’s anal stage, not Gesell’s gene-directed growth theory.
Your baby’s growth pattern is identical to that of every other baby
Gesell stressed that each child’s pattern of growth is unique, not identical.
Your baby’s growth pattern depends only on the food and care provided
Genes direct the pattern; environment influences but does not solely determine growth.

items.q: Which description best defines the cephalocaudal pattern of growth?
items.a: Growth is fastest at the top of the body and proceeds downward
items.ex: In the cephalocaudal pattern, head and brain develop faster than arm and leg coordination.
w: Growth starts at the center of the body and moves toward the extremities
This describes the proximodistal pattern, not the cephalocaudal pattern.
Growth is fastest in the arms and legs and then moves toward the head
This reverses the cephalocaudal pattern, which proceeds from head downward.
Growth occurs at the same rate in all body regions at the same time
Growth follows a set sequence; it is fastest at the top in the cephalocaudal pattern.

alt.q: Head and brain development occurring faster than arm and leg coordination is an example of which growth pattern?
alt.a: Cephalocaudal
alt.ex: Cephalocaudal growth is fastest at the top of the body, so the head and brain lead.
w: Proximodistal
Proximodistal growth moves from the center of the body to the extremities.
Psychosexual
Psychosexual refers to Freud’s stages of personality development, not physical growth.
Sensorimotor
Sensorimotor is Piaget’s first cognitive period, not a pattern of physical growth.

items.q: A parent asks why the 4-month-old infant holds up the head well but cannot yet coordinate leg movements. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Babies develop control from the head downward, so head control comes before leg coordination
items.ex: Growth is cephalocaudal: head and brain develop faster than arm and leg coordination.
w: Babies develop control from the hands and feet inward, so the legs will come first
This reverses the expected order; growth proceeds from head downward and center outward.
Babies who show this pattern usually have a delay that needs further testing
Head control before leg coordination is the expected cephalocaudal sequence, not a delay.
Babies develop all body regions at once, so leg control should appear soon
Growth follows a set sequence rather than occurring in all regions at once.

alt.q: A parent notices that the infant had good head control well before the infant could coordinate the legs. The parent asks if this is normal. Which explanation should the nurse give?
alt.a: Yes, growth normally proceeds from the head downward toward the legs
alt.ex: The cephalocaudal pattern means growth is fastest at the top, so head control precedes leg coordination.
w: No, leg coordination normally develops before control of the head
This reverses the cephalocaudal pattern, in which the head leads.
No, this pattern suggests a problem with the infant’s nervous system
Head control preceding leg coordination is the normal sequence, not a sign of a problem.
Yes, growth normally proceeds from the arms and legs toward the trunk
Proximodistal growth moves from the center outward, not from the limbs inward.

items.q: Which example illustrates the proximodistal pattern of growth?
items.a: Organ systems in the trunk develop before the arms and legs
items.ex: The proximodistal pattern starts at the center of the body and moves toward the extremities.
w: The head and brain develop before arm and leg coordination
Head-before-limbs describes the cephalocaudal pattern, not proximodistal.
The fingers and toes develop before the organs of the trunk
This reverses the proximodistal pattern, which moves from center outward.
The arms and legs develop before the head and the trunk
Growth does not begin at the extremities; it moves from the center outward.

alt.q: Organ systems in the trunk developing before the arms and legs is an example of which growth pattern?
alt.a: Proximodistal
alt.ex: Proximodistal growth begins at the center of the body and moves toward the extremities.
w: Cephalocaudal
Cephalocaudal growth proceeds from the head downward, not from center outward.
Generativity
Generativity is Erikson’s middle-age stage, not a pattern of physical growth.
Temperament
Temperament is a behavioral style affecting emotional interactions, not a growth pattern.

items.q: A school-age child with a chronic disease is shorter than both parents and siblings. The parent asks why. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: Genes set the growth pattern, but chronic disease can slow the growth rate
items.ex: Genes direct height, but growth is maximized only when conditions are adequate; chronic disease often limits growth rate.
w: Height is set only by genes, so the disease cannot be the cause
Environmental factors such as chronic disease influence growth and can result in smaller stature.
Height is set only by environment, so family height is not relevant
Genes direct the growth rate; environment influences whether that potential is reached.
Height will catch up later because disease never affects growth
The text states chronic disease often affects growth rate and results in smaller stature.

alt.q: Which situation is most likely to result in a child’s smaller stature, regardless of the child’s genetic blueprint?
alt.a: Long-term poor nutrition during childhood
alt.ex: Poor nutrition or chronic disease often slows growth and results in smaller stature despite the genetic blueprint.
w: Having parents who are both tall
Tall parents suggest a tall genetic potential, not smaller stature.
Walking independently by 10 months
Early walking reflects gross-motor progress and allows exploration; it does not limit stature.
Having an easy, even temperament
Temperament is a behavioral style and is not described as affecting stature.

items.q: A parent of a healthy, well-nourished child asks whether giving extra food and supplements will make the child grow taller than expected. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Good nutrition helps your child reach full height but cannot exceed the height set by heredity
items.ex: Adequate nutrition and absence of disease maximize growth but cannot produce height beyond what heredity determines.
w: Extra nutrition and supplements will raise your child’s height above the genetic potential
The text states nutrition cannot result in height beyond that determined by heredity.
Nutrition has no effect on height because height depends only on the genes
Poor nutrition does affect growth rate; nutrition helps reach, but not exceed, genetic potential.
Height depends only on diet, so the more food given, the taller the child grows
Genes direct the growth rate; environment influences whether the genetic potential is reached.

alt.q: Which statement by a parent shows understanding of how genes and environment affect a child’s height?
alt.a: “Good food and health help my child reach the height set by genes, but not go beyond it.”
alt.ex: Genes set the potential; adequate nutrition and freedom from disease allow that potential to be reached.
w: “If I give my child extra vitamins, my child will grow taller than the genes allow.”
Nutrition cannot produce height beyond what heredity determines.
“My child’s height depends only on genes, so diet and illness do not matter.”
Poor nutrition and chronic disease often slow growth and result in smaller stature.
“My child’s height depends only on diet, so the family’s height does not matter.”
Genes direct the growth rate in height; diet influences whether it is maximized.

items.q: Which statement best distinguishes growth from development?
items.a: Growth is physical change; development includes biological, cognitive, and socioemotional change
items.ex: Growth covers physical changes; development refers to biological, cognitive, and socioemotional changes over a lifetime.
w: Growth is cognitive change; development refers only to physical change in height
This reverses the terms; growth is physical, and development is broader.
Growth ends at birth; development refers to changes that begin in adolescence
Growth spans prenatal life to older adulthood, and development begins at conception.
Growth involves only advancement; development involves only deterioration
Growth itself shows both advancement and deterioration across the life span.

alt.q: A nurse describes changes in a patient’s thinking and social relationships over time. Which term best describes these changes?
alt.a: Development
alt.ex: Development refers to biological, cognitive, and socioemotional changes that continue throughout life.
w: Growth
Growth refers to the physical changes from the prenatal period through older adulthood.
Maturation
Maturation refers to the gene-directed sequence of physical development, not thinking and relationships.
Stature
Stature refers to physical height, not cognitive or social change.

items.q: During a well-child visit, the nurse notes that a 20-month-old child does not yet walk. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
items.a: Delayed gross-motor ability that may slow the child’s exploration of the environment
items.ex: A child not walking by 20 months shows delayed gross-motor ability that slows exploration and manipulation of the environment.
w: Expected gross-motor ability because most children walk after 2 years of age
The text uses not walking by 20 months as an example of delay, not an expected finding.
Delayed fine-motor ability that will mainly affect the child’s speech and language
Walking is a gross-motor skill; its delay affects exploration of the environment.
Advanced gross-motor ability because the child is focusing on cognitive skills
Not walking at 20 months is a delay, not an advanced skill.

alt.q: Why is walking by 10 months of age considered beneficial for a child’s development?
alt.a: The child can explore and find stimulation in the environment
alt.ex: Early walking allows exploration and stimulation, and success in one phase supports later phases.
w: The child can skip the later stages of motor development
Development follows a fixed sequence; stages are not skipped.
The child will reach a greater adult height than other children
Adult height is directed by genes, not by the age of walking.
The child no longer needs close supervision from caregivers
Walking does not remove the need for supervision; it increases exploration.

items.q: Which statement best describes biophysical development?
items.a: How the physical body grows and changes, compared against established norms
items.ex: Biophysical development is physical growth and change; providers compare changes in a growing infant against established norms.
w: How the personality forms through unconscious conflicts between pleasure and reality
This describes Freud’s psychoanalytical model, not biophysical development.
How thinking moves from reflex activity to abstract reasoning over time
This describes cognitive development, as in Piaget’s theory.
How moral reasoning moves from obedience to social contract over time
This describes Kohlberg’s moral development, not biophysical development.

alt.q: A health care provider plots an infant’s length and head size against established norms at each visit. Which type of development is being assessed?
alt.a: Biophysical development
alt.ex: Biophysical development concerns how the physical body grows and changes compared with established norms.
w: Psychosocial development
Psychosocial development concerns personality and relationships, not measured physical growth.
Moral development
Moral development concerns reasoning about right and wrong, not physical size.
Cognitive development
Cognitive development concerns thinking, not measured physical growth.

items.q: Where is sequential development most clearly evident, according to Gesell’s observations?
items.a: In the fetus, in which organ systems develop in a specified order
items.ex: Gesell noted a fixed sequence of maturation, evident in the fetus’s specified order of organ system development.
w: In the adolescent, in which body systems mature in a random order
Gesell described a fixed sequence, and the text cites the fetus as the example.
In the older adult, in which organ systems decline all at the same time
The example of sequential development given is fetal organ development, not aging.
In the toddler, in which motor skills develop in any order chosen
Maturation follows a fixed sequence; the order is not chosen.

alt.q: Gesell observed that the pattern of maturation follows which type of sequence?
alt.a: A fixed developmental sequence directed by genes
alt.ex: Gesell noted maturation follows a fixed sequence directed by gene activity, as seen in fetal organ development.
w: A flexible sequence directed by parenting style
Gesell held that genes, not parenting style, direct the fixed sequence.
A random sequence directed by the environment
The sequence is fixed and gene-directed, though environment affects outcomes.
A reversible sequence directed by the child’s choices
The maturation sequence is fixed, not chosen or reversed by the child.

items.q: Why is it important for nurses to understand normal growth and development?
items.a: To predict, detect, and prevent deviations from expected patterns that may affect health
items.ex: Knowing normal patterns helps nurses predict, detect, and prevent deviations that may affect a patient’s health.
w: To ensure every patient follows exactly the same growth pattern at the same age
Individuals have unique patterns of growth and development; the goal is not identical patterns.
To diagnose and treat genetic disorders that cause abnormal growth in children
Nurses use developmental knowledge to detect deviations, not to diagnose genetic disorders.
To replace the need for individualized assessment of each patient’s needs
Developmental theories guide individualized assessment and care rather than replacing it.

alt.q: A nurse compares a child’s growth with expected patterns at each visit. What is the main purpose of this comparison?
alt.a: To detect deviations from expected patterns early so they can be addressed
alt.ex: Understanding normal growth helps nurses predict, detect, and prevent deviations that may affect health.
w: To prove that the child’s growth matches that of the child’s siblings
Each individual’s pattern is unique; matching siblings is not the purpose.
To determine the exact adult height the child will reach in the future
Comparison detects deviations; it does not fix an exact adult height.
To decide which developmental stage the child can safely skip ahead to
Development proceeds in sequence; stages are not skipped.

items.q: Which factors can influence a child’s growth rate in height? Select all that apply.
o: Gene activity directing the growth pattern
Genes direct the growth rate in height for each individual.
Poor nutrition
Poor nutrition often slows growth and results in smaller stature.
Chronic disease
Chronic disease often affects the growth rate and results in smaller stature.
Supplements that push height past the genetic limit
Nutrition cannot result in height beyond that determined by heredity.
The child’s Freudian psychosexual stage
Psychosexual stages describe personality development, not physical growth rate.
items.ex: Genes direct the growth rate, and environmental factors such as nutrition and disease affect whether it is maximized.

alt.q: A child’s growth in height may fall short of the genetic potential because of which factors? Select all that apply.
o: Inadequate nutrition
Poor nutrition often slows the growth rate, resulting in smaller stature.
A chronic illness
Chronic disease often affects growth rate regardless of the genetic blueprint.
Adequate nutrition with no disease
Adequate conditions allow growth to be maximized, not reduced.
A slow-to-warm-up temperament
Temperament is a behavioral style and is not described as limiting height.
Environmental conditions that are not adequate
Growth is only maximized if environmental conditions are adequate.
alt.ex: Correct: Inadequate nutrition; A chronic illness; Environmental conditions that are not adequate.

items.q: Which examples reflect the normal sequence of physical growth described in biophysical theory? Select all that apply.
o: Head and brain develop faster than arm and leg coordination
This is the cephalocaudal pattern, with growth fastest at the top.
Trunk organ systems develop before the arms and legs
This is the proximodistal pattern, from center to extremities.
Fetal organ systems develop in a specified order
Gesell cited fetal organ development as evidence of a fixed sequence.
Leg coordination develops before head control
This reverses the cephalocaudal pattern.
Hands and feet develop before the trunk organs
This reverses the proximodistal pattern.
items.ex: Growth is cephalocaudal and proximodistal and follows a fixed, gene-directed sequence.

alt.q: A nurse teaches parents about the order of their infant’s physical growth. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: “Your baby will control the head before coordinating the legs.”
Cephalocaudal growth proceeds from the head downward.
“Your baby’s body develops from the center outward to the arms and legs.”
Proximodistal growth moves from the center toward the extremities.
“Your baby will coordinate the arms and legs before controlling the head.”
This reverses the head-to-toe sequence.
“Your baby’s fingers will develop before the organs in the chest.”
Trunk organ systems develop before the extremities.
“Your baby’s genes guide the order in which growth happens.”
Genes direct the sequence of development.
alt.ex: Correct: “Your baby will control the head before coordinating the legs.”; “Your baby’s body develops from the center outward to the arms and legs.”; “Your baby’s genes guide the order in which growth happens.”

items.q: Some disease processes can cause development to regress or be delayed.
items.a: True
items.ex: Development is dynamic and usually progresses, but some disease processes cause regression or delay.
items.ww: Development is not guaranteed to progress; illness can cause it to regress or be delayed.

alt.q: Once a developmental phase is achieved, disease processes cannot cause development to regress.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The text states some disease processes cause development to regress or be delayed.
alt.ww: Development can regress with disease, so achieved phases are not protected from illness.

items.q: According to Gesell, the pattern of maturation follows a fixed developmental sequence.
items.a: True
items.ex: Gesell noted maturation follows a fixed sequence, evident in the fetus’s specified order of organ development.
items.ww: Gesell did not describe a variable order; he described a fixed, gene-directed sequence.

alt.q: Gesell believed the order of maturation varies freely from child to child with no fixed sequence.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Each child’s pattern is unique, but Gesell held that maturation follows a fixed developmental sequence.
alt.ww: Uniqueness refers to the individual growth pattern; the sequence of maturation remains fixed.

items.q: In the proximodistal pattern, the arms and legs develop before the organ systems of the trunk.
items.a: False
items.ex: Proximodistal growth starts at the center of the body, so trunk organ systems develop before the extremities.
items.ww: The pattern moves from the center outward, so the extremities do not develop first.

alt.q: In the proximodistal pattern, growth starts at the center of the body and moves toward the extremities.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Proximodistal growth moves from the trunk toward the arms and legs.
alt.ww: This statement correctly defines the proximodistal pattern, so it is not false.

items.q: The growth pattern in which growth is fastest at the top of the body, with the head and brain developing faster than arm and leg coordination, is called the [[cephalocaudal]] pattern.
items.ex: Cephalocaudal growth proceeds from the head downward.

alt.q: Because growth follows the [[cephalocaudal]] pattern, an infant controls the head before coordinating the legs.
alt.ex: Cephalocaudal growth proceeds from the head downward.

items.q: The [[proximodistal]] growth pattern starts at the center of the body and moves toward the extremities.
items.ex: Proximodistal growth means trunk organ systems develop before the arms and legs.

alt.q: Organ systems of the trunk developing before the arms and legs illustrates the [[proximodistal]] growth pattern.
alt.ex: Proximodistal growth means trunk organ systems develop before the arms and legs.

items.q: What does Growth mean?
items.a: Physical changes from the prenatal period through older adulthood
items.ex: These terms describe physical growth, overall development, and the directions in which the body grows.
w: Biological, cognitive, and socioemotional changes beginning at conception
That goes with Development.
Growth fastest at the top of the body, proceeding downward
That goes with Cephalocaudal.
Growth from the center of the body toward the extremities
That goes with Proximodistal.

alt.q: What does Development mean?

items.q: A child is meeting each developmental phase successfully. According to the chapter, how does this pattern affect the child?
items.a: Repeated success promotes health and supports completing later phases
items.ex: Success within a phase affects the ability to complete later phases, and repeated success promotes health.
w: Repeated success has no effect on how later phases are completed
Success or failure within a phase affects the ability to complete subsequent phases.
Repeated success allows the child to skip the next phases entirely
Phases follow a sequence; success supports, not skips, later phases.
Repeated success leads to inadequacies in later development
Inadequacies are linked to repeated developmental failures, not repeated success.

alt.q: A child has experienced repeated developmental failures. Which outcome does the chapter associate with this pattern?
alt.a: Inadequacies may result and affect later phases
alt.ex: Repeated developmental failures sometimes result in inadequacies, since each phase affects the next.
w: Health is promoted by the extra challenges
Health is promoted by repeated success, not repeated failure.
Later phases are completed more quickly
Failure in a phase affects the ability to complete later phases.
Development is unaffected in later phases
Success or failure within a phase affects later phases.

items.q: In Freud’s psychosexual theory, during which stage does the child learn to delay gratification through toilet training to meet parental and societal expectations?
items.a: Anal stage
items.ex: In the anal stage (12 to 18 months to 3 years), toilet training teaches the child to delay gratification.
w: Oral stage
The oral stage centers on sucking and oral satisfaction in infancy.
Latency stage
In latency, children channel sexual urges into socially acceptable activities.
Phallic stage
The phallic stage focuses on the genitals and the Oedipus or Electra complex.

alt.q: A 2-year-old is being toilet trained. Which Freudian stage is the child in, and what is being learned?
alt.a: Anal stage; delaying gratification to meet expectations
alt.ex: Toilet training in the anal stage teaches the child to delay gratification to meet parental and societal expectations.
w: Oral stage; separating the parent from the self
Realizing the parent is separate from self occurs late in the oral stage.
Genital stage; forming relationships outside the family
The genital stage begins at puberty with urges directed outside the family.
Phallic stage; identifying with the same-sex parent
Identification with the same-sex parent ends the phallic stage at 3 to 6 years.

items.q: According to Freud, which component of personality represents reality and mediates conflicts between the environment and the forces of the id?
items.a: Ego
items.ex: The ego mediates between the id and the environment, helping people judge reality and regulate impulses.
w: Id
The id is the primitive part seeking immediate pleasure, not the mediator of reality.
Superego
The superego is the conscience that regulates, restrains, and prohibits actions.
Libido
Libido is not one of the three personality components the text describes.

alt.q: Which personality component is often called the conscience and is influenced by standards of outside social forces such as parents or teachers?
alt.a: Superego
alt.ex: The superego regulates, restrains, and prohibits actions and is shaped by outside social standards.
w: Ego
The ego is the reality component and sense of self, not the conscience.
Id
The id consists of basic instinctual impulses driven to achieve pleasure.
Libido
Libido is not one of the three personality components the text describes.

items.q: A 9-month-old infant is hospitalized for several days. Based on Erikson’s theory, which nursing action best supports the infant’s psychosocial development?
items.a: Arrange for a consistent caregiver who meets the infant’s needs reliably
items.ex: Resolving trust vs. mistrust requires a consistent caregiver who is available to meet the infant’s needs.
w: Rotate different staff members so the infant adapts to many caregivers
Inconsistent caregivers undermine trust, which requires a consistent available caregiver.
Offer the infant simple choices between two safe toys during care
Offering choices supports autonomy in toddlers, not trust in infants.
Delay feeding the infant to help the infant learn to tolerate waiting
Infants’ needs must be met; the id cannot tolerate delay, and trust depends on needs being met.

alt.q: Which outcome results from an infant’s successful resolution of Erikson’s trust vs. mistrust stage?
alt.a: Faith and optimism
alt.ex: The formation of trust results in faith and optimism and is the basis for future relationships.
w: Self-control and willpower
Self-control and willpower result from mastering autonomy vs. shame and doubt.
Direction and purpose
Direction and purpose result from resolving initiative vs. guilt.
Devotion and fidelity
Devotion and fidelity result from mastering identity vs. role confusion.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a hospitalized 2-year-old. Which intervention best supports the child’s stage of autonomy vs. shame and doubt?
items.a: Let the child choose which of two safe cups to drink from
items.ex: Toddlers develop autonomy by making choices, which must be simple and safe.
w: Make all care decisions for the child to avoid any frustration
Limiting choices leads to feelings of shame and doubt rather than autonomy.
Let the child choose whether or not to take the prescribed medication
Choices for a toddler must be simple and safe; refusing medication is not a safe choice.
Correct the child firmly and punish refusals to cooperate with care
Harsh punishment leads to feelings of shame and doubt.

alt.q: Which parental behavior is most likely to lead a toddler to feelings of shame and doubt?
alt.a: Limiting the toddler’s choices and using harsh punishment
alt.ex: Erikson’s theory holds that limited choices and harsh punishment lead to shame and doubt in toddlers.
w: Offering the toddler simple and safe choices about playthings
Simple, safe choices help toddlers develop autonomy.
Allowing the toddler to practice feeding and walking skills
Practicing self-care supports the newfound independence of this stage.
Modeling empathetic guidance during the toddler’s challenges
Empathetic guidance supports, rather than undermines, the toddler’s autonomy.

items.q: A 4-year-old hospitalized child is fearful about upcoming dressing changes. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate for this child’s developmental stage?
items.a: Use play in which the child applies bandages to a stuffed animal
items.ex: Play therapy helps preschoolers deal with the threats of hospitalization, and they readily treat toys as having feelings.
w: Have the child keep a written record of intake and output
Participating in routines like recording intake and output suits school-age children.
Give the child detailed information to make treatment decisions
Giving information to make some treatment decisions suits hospitalized adolescents.
Ask the child’s partner or significant other to stay at bedside
Support from a partner or significant other meets a young adult’s need for intimacy.

alt.q: Which characteristic of preschoolers makes play with dolls or stuffed animals useful in helping them cope with hospitalization?
alt.a: Animism, treating toys as if they have thoughts and feelings
alt.ex: Preschoolers engage in animism, so play with toys helps them work through hospitalization threats.
w: Abstract thinking, reasoning about hypothetical situations
Abstract thinking develops in adolescence during formal operations.
Industry, seeking praise for completing real tasks
Industry is the school-age child’s task, not the basis of preschool play.
Fidelity, devotion to others and their own ideals
Fidelity results from mastering adolescent identity vs. role confusion.

items.q: A 10-year-old child is hospitalized for several weeks. Based on Erikson’s theory, which nursing action best supports the child’s development?
items.a: Teach the child the unit routines and let the child help record intake and output
items.ex: School-age children need real achievement; understanding routines and participating in treatment builds competency.
w: Do all care for the child so the child can rest from responsibilities
Without chances for achievement, school-age children develop a sense of inadequacy and inferiority.
Give the child difficult tasks to build the child’s confidence quickly
Skills that are too difficult lead to a sense of inadequacy and inferiority.
Limit contact with peers so the child can concentrate on recovery
School-age children learn to work and play with peers, which supports this stage.

alt.q: A school-age child is not given support for learning new skills. According to Erikson, which outcome is most likely?
alt.a: A sense of inadequacy and inferiority
alt.ex: Without support or with skills that are too difficult, school-age children develop inadequacy and inferiority.
w: A sense of shame and doubt
Shame and doubt result from limited choices or harsh punishment in toddlers.
A sense of role confusion
Role confusion relates to adolescent identity development.
A sense of stagnation
Stagnation results when middle-age adults cannot contribute to the next generation.

items.q: A 16-year-old is hospitalized with a new diagnosis. Which nursing action best supports this patient’s developmental stage?
items.a: Provide enough information so the adolescent can make some decisions about the treatment plan
items.ex: Hospitalized adolescents are helped to deal with illness by receiving enough information to make some treatment decisions.
w: Direct all information to the parents so the adolescent is protected from worry
Excluding the adolescent prevents participation in decisions that support identity development.
Provide stuffed animals so the adolescent can act out the planned procedures
Play with stuffed animals suits preschoolers who engage in animism.
Assume the adolescent understands the risks of not following the treatment
Adolescents do not consistently perceive vulnerability, so risks should not be assumed understood.

alt.q: Which characteristic of adolescents contributes most to risk-taking behaviors?
alt.a: A perceived invulnerability to the risks of their actions
alt.ex: Adolescents do not consistently perceive vulnerability; this perceived invulnerability contributes to risk-taking.
w: A strong need to delay gratification to meet expectations
Delaying gratification is learned in Freud’s anal stage during toilet training.
A fear of rejection and disappointment by close partners
Fear of rejection leads to isolation in the young adult stage.
A tendency to treat objects as if they have feelings
Animism is characteristic of preschoolers, not adolescents.

items.q: In which main aspect does Erikson’s theory differ from Freud’s?
items.a: Erikson’s stages emphasize relationships to family and culture rather than sexual urges
items.ex: Erikson built on Freud but emphasized a person’s relationship to family and culture instead of sexual urges.
w: Erikson’s stages emphasize sexual urges rather than relationships to family and culture
This reverses the two theories; Freud emphasized sexual urges.
Erikson’s stages emphasize gene-directed physical growth rather than personality
Gene-directed physical growth is the focus of Gesell’s biophysical theory.
Erikson’s stages emphasize moral reasoning rather than family and cultural relationships
Moral reasoning is the focus of Kohlberg’s theory, not Erikson’s.

alt.q: Which feature of Erikson’s theory gives it a broad, life span view of development?
alt.a: Its emphasis on family relationships and culture across all ages
alt.ex: Erikson’s focus on family relationships and culture offers a broad, life span view of development.
w: Its focus on sexual pleasure in parts of the body
Pleasure in body zones is the basis of Freud’s psychosexual stages.
Its focus on gene activity directing growth patterns
Gene-directed growth is the basis of Gesell’s biophysical theory.
Its focus on stages that end with puberty and adolescence
Erikson’s stages continue through young adulthood, middle age, and old age.

items.q: A parent reports that a 6-year-old cries and complains of a stomachache every morning before school and needs time to adjust to new teachers. Which temperament does this behavior best reflect?
items.a: Slow to warm up
items.ex: Slow-to-warm-up children need time to adjust to new situations and may use somatic complaints to avoid them.
w: Easy
The easy child is even-tempered, adaptable to change, and has a typically positive mood.
Difficult
The difficult child is highly distracted, active, irritable, and irregular in habits.
Egocentric
Egocentric describes preoperational thinking, not one of the three temperament types.

alt.q: Which description best fits the easy child temperament?
alt.a: Even-tempered and adaptable, with regular habits and a typically positive mood
alt.ex: The easy child is easygoing, predictable, open to change, and shows a mild to moderately intense positive mood.
w: Uncomfortable with new situations and slow to adjust to new environments
This describes the slow-to-warm-up child.
Highly distracted, active, and irritable, with irregular daily habits
This describes the difficult child.
Avoids new situations with tears and complaints such as stomachaches
This describes the slow-to-warm-up child.

items.q: Parents describe their 5-year-old as highly distracted, active, irritable, and irregular in habits. The child will soon start kindergarten. Which suggestion by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: Practice or role-play the new school situation with the child ahead of time
items.ex: The difficult child may benefit from practice or role-playing to succeed with new skills, situations, or environments.
w: Use the same strategies that worked well with the child’s older sibling
Strategies that worked with a first child often no longer work; counseling should be individualized.
Delay kindergarten until the child’s temperament changes completely
Temperament traits endure; knowledge of temperament helps children modify responses.
Avoid discussing school until the first day so the child is not upset
The difficult child benefits from practice and role-playing before new situations.

alt.q: Parents say the strategies that worked well with their first child do not work with their second child. Which nursing response is best?
alt.a: Explain that children differ in temperament and individualize guidance for this child
alt.ex: Temperament differs among children, and individualized counseling improves parent-child interactions.
w: Advise the parents to use the first child’s strategies more consistently
Strategies that worked with one child often fail with another because temperaments differ.
Tell the parents that the second child likely has a developmental delay
Differing responses reflect temperament differences, not necessarily delay.
Recommend waiting until the child outgrows this temperament by school age
Temperament traits may continue through middle school and into adulthood.

items.q: Which criticism has been made of Freud’s psychoanalytical model of personality development?
items.a: It is based on biological determinants and ignores culture and experience
items.ex: Critics say Freud based his analysis on biological determinants and ignored the influence of culture and experience.
w: It places too much emphasis on culture and the role of family relationships
Freud is criticized for ignoring culture; Erikson is the theorist who emphasized it.
It overestimates the role of conscious thought in shaping personality
Psychoanalysts today believe conscious thought plays a much greater role than Freud imagined.
It describes development as mainly conscious and free of emotional influence
Psychoanalytical theory describes development as primarily unconscious and influenced by emotion.

alt.q: How do psychoanalysts today view the role of conscious thought compared with Freud’s view?
alt.a: Conscious thought plays a much greater role than Freud imagined
alt.ex: Modern psychoanalysts believe the role of conscious thought is much greater than Freud imagined.
w: Conscious thought plays a much smaller role than Freud imagined
This reverses the current view; conscious thought is now seen as more important.
Conscious thought plays no role at all in personality development
Current psychoanalysts give conscious thought a greater role, not none.
Conscious thought plays exactly the role that Freud described
Today’s psychoanalysts believe its role is much greater than Freud described.

items.q: Which nursing actions match the Erikson stage of the hospitalized patient? Select all that apply.
o: Offering a toddler simple, safe choices during care
Toddlers develop autonomy by making simple, safe choices.
Using play therapy with a preschooler to deal with hospitalization
Play therapy helps preschoolers deal with the threats of hospitalization.
Letting a school-age child help keep a record of intake and output
Participating in treatment gives school-age children real achievement.
Keeping a young adult’s partner away to promote rest
Young adults benefit from the support of their partner or significant other during hospitalization.
Withholding treatment information from an adolescent
Adolescents should get enough information to make some treatment decisions.
items.ex: Nursing interventions should fit each patient’s developmental task to support successful resolution of the stage.

alt.q: A nurse plans developmentally appropriate care for hospitalized patients. Which plans are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Assign a consistent caregiver to meet an infant’s needs
Infants develop trust when a consistent caregiver meets their needs.
Give an adolescent enough information to make some treatment decisions
Information helps adolescents participate in decisions about their care.
Encourage a young adult’s significant other to visit and offer support
A young adult’s need for intimacy remains present during hospitalization.
Limit a toddler’s choices to prevent the toddler from feeling overwhelmed
Limiting choices leads to shame and doubt in toddlers.
Do all self-care for a school-age child so the child does not struggle
School-age children need real achievement to develop competency.
alt.ex: Correct: Assign a consistent caregiver to meet an infant’s needs; Give an adolescent enough information to make some treatment decisions; Encourage a young adult’s significant other to visit and offer support.

items.q: A nurse is teaching parents about the three broad temperament types. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: An easy child is open and adaptable to change.
The easy child is easygoing, even-tempered, and adaptable.
A slow-to-warm-up child may complain of a stomachache to avoid school.
Somatic complaints are one way slow-to-warm-up children avoid situations.
A difficult child may benefit from practice or role-playing new situations.
Practice helps the difficult child succeed with new skills and settings.
Temperament traits identified in infancy disappear by the toddler years.
Traits may continue to influence behavior through middle school and into adulthood.
A difficult child has regular and predictable daily habits.
Regular, predictable habits describe the easy child; the difficult child is irregular.
items.ex: Most children show one of three broad temperaments, and knowing them guides individualized anticipatory guidance.

alt.q: Which statements about temperament are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Temperament is a behavioral style that affects emotional interactions with others.
This is the textbook definition of temperament.
A child’s temperament influences how others respond to the child.
Children’s individual responses significantly influence how others respond to them.
Knowledge of temperament helps nurses give parents anticipatory guidance.
Understanding temperament is critical when providing anticipatory guidance.
Parenting strategies that work for one child will work for all siblings.
Strategies that worked with a first child often do not work with a second.
Personality and temperament are unrelated to each other.
Personality and temperament are often closely linked.
alt.ex: Correct: Temperament is a behavioral style that affects emotional interactions with others; A child’s temperament influences how others respond to the child; Knowledge of temperament helps nurses give parents anticipatory guidance.

items.q: According to Freud, the id is the most primitive part of the personality, originates in the infant, and cannot tolerate delay.
items.a: True
items.ex: The id consists of basic instinctual impulses driven to achieve pleasure and demands immediate need fulfillment.
items.ww: This correctly describes the id, so it is not false.

alt.q: According to Freud, the superego is the most primitive part of the personality and demands that needs be met immediately.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The id is the most primitive part; the superego is the conscience that regulates and restrains actions.
alt.ww: The superego restrains impulses rather than demanding immediate gratification, so the statement is not true.

items.q: In Erikson’s theory, a developmental task once mastered can be challenged and tested again during new situations or times of conflict.
items.a: True
items.ex: Erikson held that mastered tasks are challenged and tested again in new situations or conflict.
items.ww: Mastered tasks are not permanently settled; they can be retested.

alt.q: In Erikson’s theory, once a person masters a stage’s task, that task is never challenged again later in life.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Erikson stated tasks once mastered are challenged and tested again during new situations or conflict.
alt.ww: Mastery is not permanent; new situations can test earlier tasks again.

items.q: In Freud’s latency stage, children repress sexual urges and channel them into productive, socially acceptable activities.
items.a: True
items.ex: During latency (6 to 12 years), urges from the oedipal stage are channeled into socially acceptable activities.
items.ww: This correctly describes latency, so it is not false.

alt.q: In Freud’s latency stage, sexual urges reawaken and are directed toward an individual outside the family circle.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Reawakened urges directed outside the family describe the genital stage, not latency.
alt.ww: In latency urges are repressed and channeled, so the statement does not describe that stage.

items.q: A preschooler who treats dolls or stuffed animals as if they have thoughts and feelings is showing [[animism]].
items.ex: Animism is a preschool developmental characteristic that makes play therapy useful during hospitalization.

alt.q: The developmental characteristic of preschoolers called [[animism]] leads them to treat toys as though they have feelings.
alt.ex: Animism is a preschool developmental characteristic that makes play therapy useful during hospitalization.
