items.q: How does current understanding of adult development differ from early studies of development?
items.a: Adults keep developing new abilities and adapting, though changes come more slowly
items.ex: Early studies focused only on childhood; now we know people keep developing and adapting throughout adulthood.
w: Adults stop developing once physical growth ends in adolescence
Development continues throughout life, not only until physical growth ends.
Adults develop new abilities faster than children do
Adult changes come more slowly than those of childhood.
Adults only lose abilities, so adult development means decline
Adults continue to develop new abilities and adapt to shifting environments.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows correct understanding of adult development?
alt.a: “Adults keep developing new abilities, but the changes come more slowly than in childhood.”
alt.ex: Development continues through adulthood, although adult changes come more slowly.
w: “Development is complete by the end of adolescence, so adults only maintain skills.”
Early studies focused on childhood, but development continues in adulthood.
“Adults develop new abilities more rapidly than children because of experience.”
Adult changes come more slowly, not more rapidly.
“Adult development is mainly a decline in abilities with no new growth.”
Adults continue to develop new abilities and adapt to shifting environments.

items.q: Which description best defines the contemporary life events approach to adult development?
items.a: It considers the variations that occur for each individual’s life events
items.ex: The contemporary life events approach accounts for individual variation, personal circumstances, and social context.
w: It assumes every adult passes through the same events at the same ages
The approach takes individual variation into account rather than assuming uniformity.
It explains adult behavior through unconscious conflicts from childhood
Unconscious conflicts are the basis of psychoanalytical theory, not the life events approach.
It measures adult development by changes in physical height and weight
Physical measurement is biophysical; the life events approach looks at circumstances and context.

alt.q: A nurse’s assessment focuses on how one patient’s life events, family support, and social context differ from another patient’s. Which approach to adult development is the nurse using?
alt.a: Contemporary life events approach
alt.ex: This approach considers individual variation, personal circumstances, adjustment to change, and social and historical context.
w: Psychosexual stage approach
Psychosexual stages are Freud’s childhood personality stages, not variations in adult life events.
Biophysical maturation approach
Biophysical theories address physical growth directed by genes.
Cognitive period approach
Cognitive periods describe changes in thinking, as in Piaget’s theory.

items.q: Which factors does the contemporary life events approach consider when assessing an adult’s development? Select all that apply.
o: Personal circumstances such as health and family support
Personal circumstances, including health and family support, are part of this approach.
How the person views and adjusts to changes
The approach considers how a person views and adjusts to change.
The current social and historical context of the person’s life
Social and historical context is included in this approach.
Only the person’s chronological age
The approach looks at individual variations, not age alone.
Psychosexual conflicts left unresolved from childhood
Psychosexual conflicts belong to Freud’s theory, not the life events approach.
items.ex: The life events approach considers personal circumstances, adjustment to change, and social and historical context.

alt.q: A nurse uses the contemporary life events approach to assess a 58-year-old patient. Which assessment questions fit this approach? Select all that apply.
o: “Who in your family is available to support you right now?”
Family support is a personal circumstance considered in this approach.
“How have you been adjusting to the recent changes in your life?”
How a person views and adjusts to change is part of this approach.
“How is your health affecting your daily life?”
Health is a personal circumstance considered in this approach.
“At what age did you complete toilet training?”
Toilet training relates to Freud’s anal stage, not adult life events.
“Do you treat objects as if they have feelings?”
Animism is a preschool characteristic, not an adult life events factor.
alt.ex: Correct: “Who in your family is available to support you right now?”; “How have you been adjusting to the recent changes in your life?”; “How is your health affecting your daily life?”

items.q: What has made the life span approach to development popular?
items.a: The increase in life expectancy
items.ex: Longer life expectancy has made the life span approach to development popular.
w: The decline in adult health screening
Health screening is not given as the reason; life expectancy is.
The focus of early studies on childhood
Early studies focused only on childhood, which the life span approach expanded.
The decrease in the number of life events
The life span approach accounts for multiple adult life events, not fewer events.

alt.q: Because people are living longer, which approach to development has become more widely used?
alt.a: The life span approach
alt.ex: The increase in life expectancy has made the life span approach to development popular.
w: The childhood-only approach
Early studies focused only on childhood; longer life spans favor a life span view.
The psychosexual approach
Freud’s psychosexual approach focuses on stages from infancy to adolescence.
The biophysical approach
Biophysical theory addresses physical growth, not the effect of longer life spans.

items.q: Which characteristics describe life span development? Select all that apply.
o: Lifelong
Life span development continues throughout life.
Multidimensional
Life span development is described as multidimensional.
Multidirectional
Life span development is described as multidirectional.
Contextual
Life span development is described as contextual.
Complete by the end of adolescence
Development continues through adulthood, not just until adolescence.
Determined by biological factors alone
Development is an interaction of biological, sociocultural, and individual factors.
items.ex: Life span development is lifelong, multidimensional, multidirectional, and contextual.

alt.q: According to the life span view, development is an interaction of which types of factors? Select all that apply.
o: Biological factors
Biological factors are one of the three interacting influences.
Sociocultural factors
Sociocultural factors are one of the three interacting influences.
Individual factors
Individual factors are one of the three interacting influences.
Only genetic factors
Development reflects several interacting factors, not genes alone.
Only childhood events
Life span development is lifelong and is not shaped by childhood events alone.
alt.ex: Correct: Biological factors; Sociocultural factors; Individual factors.

items.q: A 47-year-old patient recovering from a heart attack says, “I can’t coach my son’s team anymore, and I feel like I am not contributing to anything.” Which nursing response best supports this patient’s developmental stage?
items.a: Help the patient find other ways to contribute, such as volunteering at a local school
items.ex: Nurses help ill middle-age adults choose creative ways to foster social development and contribute to future generations.
w: Encourage the patient to focus only on recovery and avoid outside activities
Inability to contribute to the next generation leads to stagnation.
Encourage the patient to review past mistakes and accept them
Life review and acceptance relate to integrity vs. despair in old age.
Suggest the patient focus on forming a new intimate relationship
Forming an intimate relationship is the young adult task, not middle age.

alt.q: A middle-age adult is unable to play any role in the development of the next generation. According to Erikson, which outcome is most likely?
alt.a: Stagnation
alt.ex: Inability to play a role in the development of the next generation results in stagnation.
w: Isolation
Isolation results when a young adult cannot establish companionship and intimacy.
Despair
Despair results when an older adult appraises life with regret over unmet goals.
Mistrust
Mistrust results when an infant lacks a consistent caregiver.

items.q: A 26-year-old patient is admitted for surgery and is anxious. According to Erikson’s theory, which nursing action best meets this patient’s developmental needs?
items.a: Encourage the patient’s partner or significant other to be present for support
items.ex: A young adult’s need for intimacy remains during hospitalization, so support from a partner is beneficial.
w: Limit visitors to the patient’s parents to support family identity
The young adult’s task centers on intimacy with a partner, not identity within the family.
Provide a stuffed animal for the patient to use in play therapy
Play therapy with toys suits preschoolers, not young adults.
Discourage visits so the patient can develop independence from others
Isolation results when young adults cannot establish companionship and intimacy.

alt.q: According to Erikson, what results if a young adult is unable to establish companionship and intimacy?
alt.a: Isolation because of a fear of rejection and disappointment
alt.ex: Failing to establish intimacy leads to isolation stemming from fear of rejection and disappointment.
w: Stagnation because of an inability to guide the next generation
Stagnation is the negative outcome of middle-age generativity.
Despair because of regret over goals that were never achieved
Despair is the negative outcome of the old-age integrity stage.
Inferiority because of a lack of support for learning new skills
Inferiority is the negative outcome of the school-age industry stage.

items.q: An 82-year-old patient who recently retired because of illness says, “My life has been nothing but mistakes.” Which nursing intervention best promotes ego integrity?
items.a: Encourage the patient to reflect on meaningful relationships with family, community, or a higher power
items.ex: Encouraging reflection on meaningful relationships enhances feelings of integrity in older adults.
w: Change the subject to avoid dwelling on the patient’s past
Older adults often appraise their lives; guiding reflection supports integrity rather than avoiding it.
Tell the patient that most older adults feel the same way
Dismissing the feeling does not help the patient find meaning or integrity.
Advise the patient to focus on forming new intimate relationships
Intimacy vs. isolation is the young adult stage, not the older adult stage.

alt.q: Which statement by an older adult best reflects successful resolution of Erikson’s integrity vs. despair stage?
alt.a: “I made mistakes, but overall my life has had real meaning.”
alt.ex: Integrity means viewing life as a meaningful whole with satisfaction, even with its inevitable mistakes.
w: “My life was a failure, and I regret the goals I never reached.”
Seeing oneself as a failure with regret reflects despair.
“I still need to find a partner so I will not feel alone.”
Seeking intimacy to avoid isolation reflects the young adult stage.
“I can’t contribute anything to the next generation anymore.”
Concern about contributing to the next generation reflects stagnation in middle age.

items.q: Two 70-year-old patients have the same diagnosis but are adjusting very differently. Which nursing approach best reflects the contemporary life events approach?
items.a: Assess each patient’s health, family support, and how each views the changes
items.ex: The life events approach considers each individual’s personal circumstances and how the person views and adjusts to change.
w: Expect both patients to adjust the same way because they are the same age
The approach accounts for individual variation rather than assuming age-based uniformity.
Base the care plan only on the expected course of the shared diagnosis
The approach also considers personal circumstances, adjustment, and social context.
Assume the patient adjusting poorly has unresolved childhood conflicts
Unresolved childhood conflict reflects psychoanalytical theory, not the life events approach.

alt.q: Two adults of the same age experience the same life event. Which statement best explains why their development may differ?
alt.a: Each person’s circumstances, adjustment to change, and social context vary
alt.ex: The life events approach recognizes individual variation in circumstances, adjustment, and social and historical context.
w: Adults of the same age always respond identically to life events
The approach takes into account the variations that occur for each individual.
Adult development depends only on genes inherited from parents
Development is an interaction of biological, sociocultural, and individual factors.
Adult development is fixed by the end of the latency stage
Development continues throughout adulthood, well beyond latency.

items.q: Why is it important for nurses to adopt a life span perspective of human development?
items.a: It provides a knowledge base for planning health screening, health history, promotion, and teaching
items.ex: A life span perspective helps nurses plan screening and history questions, health promotion, and education for patients and families.
w: It limits developmental assessment to infants and children in pediatric settings
A life span perspective considers all developmental stages, not only childhood.
It allows nurses to use a single theory to explain all human development
Human development is complex and cannot be explained by only one theory.
It replaces the need to consider each patient’s individual circumstances
The life span view considers individual, biological, and sociocultural factors.

alt.q: A nurse is preparing health screening questions for adults of all ages. Which perspective best supports this task?
alt.a: A life span perspective that considers all developmental stages
alt.ex: Understanding development across the life span helps nurses plan screening, history, promotion, and education.
w: A childhood-focused perspective that stops at adolescence
Traditional childhood-only views do not address adult screening needs.
A single-theory perspective that explains all development
No single theory can explain the complex process of human development.
A psychosexual perspective that focuses on body zones
Freud’s psychosexual stages do not guide screening across all adult ages.

items.q: According to Erikson, how do middle-age adults achieve success in the generativity stage?
items.a: By contributing to future generations through parenting, teaching, mentoring, and community involvement
items.ex: Middle-age adults achieve generativity by supporting future generations through parenthood, teaching, mentoring, and community work.
w: By finding a partner and forming a first intimate relationship with another person
Forming an intimate relationship is the task of young adulthood.
By reviewing past life events and accepting the mistakes that were made along the way
Life review and acceptance relate to integrity vs. despair in old age.
By answering the question “Who am I?” and choosing a vocation and a life partner
Answering “Who am I?” is the adolescent identity task.

alt.q: A middle-age adult volunteers to mentor young people at a community center. Which Erikson stage task does this behavior reflect?
alt.a: Generativity vs. self-absorption and stagnation
alt.ex: Mentoring and community involvement contribute to future generations, the task of generativity.
w: Intimacy vs. isolation
Intimacy vs. isolation involves forming close relationships in young adulthood.
Integrity vs. despair
Integrity vs. despair involves appraising one’s life in old age.
Autonomy vs. sense of shame and doubt
Autonomy vs. shame and doubt involves toddlers making choices and gaining self-control.

items.q: Which statement best describes the challenges older adults face that relate to ego integrity?
items.a: Physical and social losses are met with internal struggles such as searching for meaning
items.ex: Aging brings physical and social losses; meeting these and the search for meaning can produce wisdom.
w: Physical and social losses rarely occur, so integrity develops automatically
The aging process creates physical and social losses, including loss of status and function.
Internal struggles end in old age, so only physical losses must be managed
External struggles are met with internal struggles, such as the search for meaning.
Coping strategies interfere with integrity and should be discouraged in older adults
Coping strategies promote ego integrity in older adults.

alt.q: Which basic strength can result when older adults meet the physical, social, and internal challenges of aging?
alt.a: Wisdom
alt.ex: Meeting the challenges of aging creates the potential for growth and the basic strength of wisdom.
w: Fidelity
Fidelity results from mastering the adolescent identity stage.
Willpower
Willpower results from mastering the toddler autonomy stage.
Purpose
Purpose results from resolving the preschool initiative stage.

items.q: A nurse is caring for older adults in a long-term care setting. Which interventions support ego integrity? Select all that apply.
o: Encourage reflection on relationships with family, community, or a higher power
Reflecting on meaningful relationships enhances feelings of integrity.
Support the use of coping strategies for losses of aging
Coping strategies promote ego integrity in older adults.
Help residents feel valued, appreciated, and needed
Feeling valued, appreciated, and needed supports integrity rather than despair.
Discourage residents from looking back on their lives
Older adults often appraise their lives; guided reflection supports integrity.
Focus care only on physical losses and not on meaning
Internal struggles, such as searching for meaning, must also be addressed.
items.ex: Reflection on relationships, coping strategies, and meaningful activity help older adults achieve integrity rather than despair.

alt.q: Which nursing actions help older adults feel valued and achieve integrity? Select all that apply.
o: Inviting the patient to talk about meaningful family relationships
Reflecting on meaningful relationships enhances feelings of integrity.
Helping the patient use coping strategies after retirement or illness
Coping strategies promote ego integrity in older adults.
Helping the patient feel valued, appreciated, and needed
Nurses can help people feel valued, appreciated, and needed.
Telling the patient that past mistakes define the patient’s life
Focusing on failures and regret reflects despair, not integrity.
Avoiding discussion of the patient’s spiritual relationships
Reflection on a relationship with a higher power can enhance integrity.
alt.ex: Correct: Inviting the patient to talk about meaningful family relationships; Helping the patient use coping strategies after retirement or illness; Helping the patient feel valued, appreciated, and needed.

items.q: Which statement about adult development best reflects the life span approach?
items.a: Development is an interaction of biological, sociocultural, and individual factors
items.ex: The life span approach sees development as lifelong and shaped by interacting biological, sociocultural, and individual factors.
w: Development is directed only by genes and ends when physical growth stops
Genes are one influence; development continues throughout life and is shaped by several factors.
Development is driven by unconscious conflicts resolved in early childhood
Unconscious conflict is the basis of psychoanalytical theory, not the life span approach.
Development follows the same timetable for every adult regardless of context
The life span approach is contextual and accounts for individual variation.

alt.q: A nurse considers a newly retired patient’s health, culture, family, and personal coping style when planning care. Which view of development is the nurse applying?
alt.a: Development results from interacting biological, sociocultural, and individual factors
alt.ex: The life span approach holds that development is an interaction of biological, sociocultural, and individual factors.
w: Development results mainly from gene activity that directs a fixed sequence
A fixed gene-directed sequence describes Gesell’s biophysical theory, not the life span view.
Development results mainly from pleasure focused in zones of the body
Pleasure in body zones describes Freud’s psychosexual theory.
Development results mainly from childhood events and is complete by adulthood
Life span development is lifelong and continues through adulthood.

items.q: Although adult changes come more slowly than in childhood, people continue to develop new abilities throughout adulthood.
items.a: True
items.ex: We now know people continue to develop new abilities and adapt to shifting environments in adulthood.
items.ww: Development does not stop after childhood; it only proceeds more slowly.

alt.q: Development is essentially complete by the end of adolescence, so adults only maintain existing abilities.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Early studies focused on childhood, but adults keep developing new abilities and adapting.
alt.ww: Adults continue to develop, so development is not complete after adolescence.

items.q: The contemporary life events approach assumes that all adults experience the same life events in the same way.
items.a: False
items.ex: The approach considers the variations that occur for each individual, including circumstances and context.
items.ww: The approach is built on individual variation, so it does not assume uniform experiences.

alt.q: The contemporary life events approach considers the current social and historical context in which a person is living.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Social and historical context is one of the factors the life events approach considers.
alt.ww: Context is explicitly included in this approach, so the statement is not false.

items.q: Erikson believed that problems in adult life resulted from unsuccessful resolution of earlier developmental stages.
items.a: True
items.ex: Erikson linked adult problems to earlier unresolved stages, while his family and culture focus gave a life span view.
items.ww: This reflects Erikson’s stated belief, so it is not false.

alt.q: Erikson believed that adult problems arise only from current events and are unrelated to earlier developmental stages.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Erikson believed adult problems resulted from unsuccessful resolution of earlier stages.
alt.ww: Erikson tied adult problems to earlier stages, so they are not unrelated.

items.q: Life span development is described as lifelong, multidimensional, [[multidirectional]], and contextual.
items.ex: These four features describe development as continuing, varied, and shaped by context throughout life.

alt.q: In addition to being lifelong, multidimensional, and contextual, life span development is [[multidirectional]].
alt.ex: These four features describe development as continuing, varied, and shaped by context throughout life.

items.q: The contemporary [[life events]] approach to adult development takes into consideration the variations that occur for each individual.
items.ex: This approach weighs personal circumstances, adjustment to change, and social and historical context.

alt.q: An approach to adult development that considers each person’s health, family support, and social context is the contemporary [[life events]] approach.
alt.ex: This approach weighs personal circumstances, adjustment to change, and social and historical context.

items.q: Which Erikson stage occurs during Adolescence (puberty)?
items.a: Identity vs. role confusion
items.ex: Erikson’s later stages continue development from puberty through old age.
w: Intimacy vs. isolation
That goes with Young adulthood.
Generativity vs. self-absorption and stagnation
That goes with Middle age.
Integrity vs. despair
That goes with Old age.

alt.q: Which Erikson stage occurs during Young adulthood?
alt.a: Intimacy vs. isolation

mt.ex: Erikson’s later stages continue development from puberty through old age.

items.q: An infant learns that sucking produces a pleasing result and then sucks on fingers, a blanket, and clothing. In Piaget’s theory, what is this action pattern called?
items.a: A schema
items.ex: In the sensorimotor period, infants develop schemas, or action patterns such as sucking, grasping, or kicking, for dealing with the environment.
w: Object permanence
Object permanence is knowing objects still exist when unseen, not a repeated action pattern.
Seriation
Seriation is ordering objects by quantitative dimensions, achieved in concrete operations.
Animism
Animism is giving lifelike feelings to objects, seen in the preoperational period.

alt.q: During which of Piaget’s periods do infants develop schemas such as hitting, looking, grasping, and kicking?
alt.a: Sensorimotor
alt.ex: Schemas, or action patterns for dealing with the environment, develop in the sensorimotor period from birth to 2 years.
w: Preoperational
The preoperational period (2 to 7 years) centers on symbols, mental images, and egocentric thought.
Concrete operations
Concrete operations (7 to 11 years) brings mental operations such as reversibility and conservation.
Formal operations
Formal operations (11 years to adulthood) brings abstract and theoretical reasoning.

items.q: According to Piaget, what drives individuals to move from one stage of cognitive development to the next?
items.a: Seeking cognitive equilibrium, a state of mental balance
items.ex: Piaget believed individuals move between stages seeking cognitive equilibrium and build mental structures to adapt to the world.
w: Resolving unconscious conflicts between pleasure and reality
Resolving unconscious conflicts reflects Freud’s psychoanalytical theory, not Piaget’s cognitive theory.
Avoiding punishment and gaining rewards from authority figures
Avoiding punishment describes Kohlberg’s preconventional moral reasoning, not cognitive stage movement.
Mastering a psychosocial crisis specific to each life stage
Mastering a developmental crisis at each stage is Erikson’s psychosocial theory.

alt.q: In Piaget’s theory, what is cognitive equilibrium?
alt.a: A state of mental balance that individuals seek
alt.ex: Piaget described cognitive equilibrium as a state of mental balance that motivates movement from one stage to another.
w: A fixed level of intelligence present from birth
Piaget’s theory describes changing intellectual organization, not a fixed level of intelligence.
A balance between sexual pleasure and reality
Balancing pleasure with the mandates of reality relates to Freud’s psychosexual theory.
A stage in which moral rules are fully internalized
Internalizing rules relates to moral development theory, not cognitive equilibrium.

items.q: A 4-year-old is scheduled for several blood draws during a hospital stay and is frightened. Which nursing intervention best supports the child’s cognitive development?
items.a: Use play therapy to help the child work through the procedures
items.ex: Play is a primary way preoperational children learn, and play therapy helps them work through invasive and intrusive procedures.
w: Give a detailed verbal explanation of how the laboratory tests the blood
Preoperational children think with symbols and fantasy, so detailed abstract explanations are not effective.
Ask the child to describe the steps of the procedure in reverse order
Mentally reversing a series of steps is a concrete operational skill not expected at age 4.
Schedule the blood draws without telling the child to avoid upsetting him
Avoiding preparation does not help the child understand events; play helps the child understand what is happening.

alt.q: A nurse provides medical play with a doll, bandages, and a toy syringe to a 5-year-old before surgery. What is the primary reason for this intervention?
alt.a: Play helps the child understand events taking place during hospitalization
alt.ex: In the preoperational period, play helps the child understand events and work through procedures, and it helps an ill child progress developmentally.
w: Play distracts the child so that preoperative teaching is unnecessary
Play is a means of learning and understanding, not a replacement for preparing the child.
Play tests whether the child has achieved conservation and reversibility
Conservation and reversibility are concrete operational skills; this play is meant to help understanding, not to test them.
Play allows the nurse to determine whether the child has object permanence
Object permanence is a sensorimotor achievement; it is not the purpose of medical play at age 5.

items.q: A 4-year-old tells the nurse that the IV pump “is angry and beeping at me because it wants me to stay in bed.” This statement is an example of which characteristic of preoperational thought?
items.a: Animism
items.ex: Animism is personifying objects, believing inanimate objects have lifelike thoughts, wishes, and feelings, which is typical early in the preoperational period.
w: Conservation
Conservation is seeing quantities as unchanged despite a change in appearance, a concrete operational skill.
Reversibility
Reversibility is mentally reversing steps to return to the start, achieved in concrete operations.
Personal fable
The personal fable is an adolescent’s belief that their thoughts and feelings are unique.

alt.q: Which statement by a preschool child best illustrates animism?
alt.a: “My teddy bear is sad because he had to get a shot too.”
alt.ex: Animism means believing inanimate objects, like a teddy bear, have lifelike thoughts and feelings.
w: “That tall cup has the same juice as the short one.”
Recognizing equal amounts despite different appearance is conservation, a concrete operational skill.
“Everyone at school is going to stare at my cast.”
Believing everyone is watching reflects the adolescent imaginary audience.
“I can line up these sticks from shortest to longest.”
Ordering objects by length is seriation, achieved in concrete operations.

items.q: A 15-year-old with diabetes is admitted after drinking at a party and skipping insulin. He says, “Bad things happen to other people, not to me.” Which developmental characteristic does this statement reflect?
items.a: A sense of invulnerability common in adolescence
items.ex: Adolescent egocentrism includes feelings of invulnerability, which frequently lead to risk-taking behaviors, especially in early adolescence.
w: Egocentrism typical of the preoperational period
Preoperational egocentrism is seeing only one’s own point of view, typical of ages 2 to 7.
Postformal thought typical of young adulthood
Postformal thought is recognizing that answers vary by situation, a proposed adult stage.
Instrumental relativist moral orientation
This is Kohlberg’s stage 2, based on satisfying one’s own needs, not a cognitive feeling of invulnerability.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a 15-year-old who engages in risk-taking behaviors and believes nobody understands his feelings. Which intervention is most consistent with Piaget’s theory?
alt.a: Connect him with a group of peers who have similar health experiences
alt.ex: Sharing experiences with peers helps adolescents learn that many of their thoughts and feelings are shared, so they are not so different.
w: Use simple pictures and play to explain his health condition
Play and simple symbols suit preoperational children; adolescents can reason abstractly.
Limit contact with peers until his risk-taking behavior stops
Peer sharing helps adolescents see their feelings are not unique, so limiting it removes a support.
Tell him that his feelings are unrealistic and will soon pass
Dismissing his feelings does not help him learn that others share similar thoughts and feelings.

items.q: A 14-year-old with a facial burn refuses to return to school, saying, “Everyone will be staring at me the whole day.” The nurse recognizes this as which feature of adolescent thinking?
items.a: Imaginary audience
items.ex: The imaginary audience is the adolescent’s belief that their actions and appearance are constantly being scrutinized by others.
w: Personal fable
The personal fable is the belief that one’s thoughts and feelings are unique, not that others are watching.
Object permanence
Object permanence is the infant’s understanding that objects exist when unseen.
Magical thinking
Magical thinking is a fantasy-based feature of preoperational children, not adolescent self-consciousness.

alt.q: An adolescent tells the nurse, “No one has ever felt the way I feel right now.” Which feature of adolescent egocentric thought does this statement reflect?
alt.a: Personal fable
alt.ex: The personal fable is the adolescent belief that their thoughts and feelings are unique.
w: Imaginary audience
The imaginary audience is the belief that one’s actions and appearance are always being scrutinized.
Animism
Animism is a preoperational belief that inanimate objects have feelings.
Seriation
Seriation is ordering objects by length, weight, or other characteristics in concrete operations.

items.q: A child watches the nurse pour water from a short, wide cup into a tall, thin cup and says, “It’s still the same amount of water.” The child has achieved which concept?
items.a: Conservation
items.ex: Conservation is the ability to see quantities as remaining the same despite a change in physical appearance, a concrete operations achievement.
w: Seriation
Seriation is ordering objects by quantitative dimensions such as length or weight.
Animism
Animism is believing inanimate objects have lifelike thoughts and feelings.
Object permanence
Object permanence is knowing that objects exist even when they cannot be seen, heard, or touched.

alt.q: In which of Piaget’s periods does a child typically first achieve conservation?
alt.a: Concrete operations (7 to 11 years)
alt.ex: Conservation is a major accomplishment of the concrete operations period, along with reversibility and seriation.
w: Sensorimotor (birth to 2 years)
The key sensorimotor accomplishment is object permanence, not conservation.
Preoperational (2 to 7 years)
Preoperational thinking is egocentric and magical; conservation is not yet achieved.
Formal operations (11 years to adulthood)
Conservation is achieved earlier; formal operations adds abstract and theoretical reasoning.

items.q: A nurse is preparing discharge teaching for a 45-year-old patient newly diagnosed with heart failure. Based on cognitive developmental theory, which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess the patient’s cognitive ability before planning the teaching
items.ex: Many adults may not become formal operational thinkers, so assessing cognitive ability is critical when providing health care teaching.
w: Use abstract explanations because all adults think at a formal level
Many adults remain concrete operational thinkers, so an adult’s age does not guarantee abstract thinking.
Use play and picture stories as for a preoperational child
Choosing a teaching approach before assessment is premature; assessment of cognitive ability comes first.
Provide written materials and let the patient read them alone
Giving materials without assessing cognitive ability skips the critical first step in planning teaching.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows correct understanding of adult cognitive development and patient teaching?
alt.a: “Some adults stay at the concrete stage, so I will assess how each patient thinks.”
alt.ex: Piaget noted many adults remain concrete operational thinkers, so assessing cognitive ability is critical for teaching.
w: “All adults reason abstractly, so I can teach every adult the same way.”
Many adults do not become formal operational thinkers, so teaching must fit assessed cognitive ability.
“Cognitive stages end in childhood, so I do not assess adult thinking.”
Cognitive development continues in adulthood, and assessment of cognitive ability is critical for teaching.
“Adults always reach one correct answer, so I will give one solution only.”
Research shows adults frequently accept several possible solutions rather than one answer.

items.q: Developmentalists proposed a fifth stage of cognitive development called postformal thought. Which ability characterizes this stage?
items.a: Recognizing that answers vary from situation to situation
items.ex: In postformal thought, adults recognize that answers vary by situation and that solutions need to be sensible.
w: Reasoning about abstract and theoretical possibilities
Abstract reasoning about possibilities characterizes Piaget’s formal operations period.
Mentally reversing steps to return to the starting point
Reversibility is a primary characteristic of concrete operational thought.
Thinking with the use of symbols and mental images
Thinking with symbols and mental images characterizes the preoperational period.

alt.q: A 30-year-old weighing treatment options says, “There’s no single right answer; it depends on my situation, and the plan has to be practical.” This reflects which cognitive stage?
alt.a: Postformal thought
alt.ex: Postformal thought includes recognizing that answers vary from situation to situation and that solutions need to be sensible.
w: Formal operations
Formal operations involves abstract reasoning; accepting situational, practical solutions was proposed as a later stage.
Concrete operations
Concrete operations involves mental operations on concrete objects, such as conservation and seriation.
Preoperational thought
Preoperational thought is egocentric and magical, typical of children ages 2 to 7.

items.q: William Perry studied college students. According to his findings, what did continued cognitive development in adulthood involve?
items.a: Increasing cognitive flexibility
items.ex: Perry found that continued cognitive development involved increasing cognitive flexibility, accepting that alternative explanations could be right.
w: Increasing reliance on authority for answers
Perry described moving away from accepting only one answer toward considering alternative explanations.
Decreasing use of emotion in decisions
Research shows adults incorporate emotions, logic, practicality, and flexibility when making decisions.
Increasing focus on acquiring new facts
The emphasis shifts from attaining knowledge to using knowledge for goal achievement.

alt.q: According to research on adult cognition, how does the use of knowledge change as adults develop?
alt.a: The emphasis shifts from attaining knowledge to using it for goal achievement
alt.ex: Adults change how they use knowledge, shifting from attaining knowledge or skills to using knowledge for goal achievement.
w: The emphasis shifts from using knowledge to memorizing new facts
The shift is the reverse: from attaining knowledge toward applying it to goals.
The emphasis shifts from many possible answers to one correct answer
Adults move from accepting only one answer toward accepting several possible solutions.
The emphasis shifts from flexible thinking to rigid rule following
Perry found cognitive development involves increasing, not decreasing, cognitive flexibility.

items.q: A nurse on a pediatric unit wants to improve sleep quality for hospitalized children. Which nursing action is best supported by evidence?
items.a: Group nursing interventions to reduce interruptions during the night
items.ex: Evidence supports reducing interruptions or grouping interventions, along with reducing noise and dimming lights, to promote sleep.
w: Ask parents to go home at night so the child can sleep undisturbed
Evidence supports allowing parents to sleep with their children, not sending them home.
Perform vital signs hourly so the child gets used to being awakened
Frequent interruptions for nursing interventions are a risk factor for sleep disruption.
Keep room lights on so the nurse can observe the child without waking him
Evidence supports dimming lights to promote sleep in hospitalized children.

alt.q: A housekeeper removes a “quiet time” door hanger from a hospitalized child’s room and throws it away. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
alt.a: Teach ancillary staff to maintain the quiet time door hangers
alt.ex: Evidence supports educating ancillary personnel, such as housekeeping, to maintain rather than discard quiet time door hangers.
w: Stop using the door hanger because staff do not follow it
The door hanger is a recommended sleep intervention; the solution is staff education, not abandoning it.
Wake the child so the room can be cleaned at the same time
Waking the child adds interruptions, a risk factor for sleep disruption.
Ask the parents to leave so housekeeping can finish their work
Evidence supports family-centered care and allowing parents to stay with their child.

items.q: Which nurse-specific interventions are supported by evidence to promote sleep in hospitalized children? Select all that apply.
o: Reduce noise in and around the room
Reducing noise is a recommended nurse-specific sleep intervention.
Dim the lights at night
Dimming lights is a recommended nurse-specific sleep intervention.
Group care activities to limit interruptions
Grouping interventions reduces interruptions, a known risk factor for sleep disruption.
Use a “quiet time” door hanger
A quiet time door hanger is a recommended intervention that staff should maintain.
Limit parents’ presence at night
Evidence supports allowing parents to sleep with their children and including them in sleep care.
Wake the child for all routine checks
Interruptions for nursing interventions disrupt sleep; grouping them is recommended.
items.ex: Recommended sleep interventions include reducing noise, dimming lights, grouping interventions, and using quiet time door hangers.

alt.q: A nurse identifies risk factors for sleep disruption in a hospitalized child. Which factors increase this risk? Select all that apply.
o: Environmental noise
Environmental noise is a listed risk factor for sleep disruption in hospitalized children.
Pain
Pain is a listed risk factor for sleep disruption during recovery.
Anxiety
Anxiety is a listed risk factor for sleep disruption in hospitalized children.
Interruptions for nursing care
Interruptions for nursing interventions disrupt sleep, which is why grouping care is recommended.
A parent sleeping in the room
Allowing parents to sleep with their children is a recommended intervention, not a risk factor.
Dimmed lights at night
Dimming lights is a recommended intervention to promote sleep.
alt.ex: Correct: Environmental noise; Pain; Anxiety; Interruptions for nursing care.

items.q: Which characteristics describe thinking in Piaget’s preoperational period (2 to 7 years)? Select all that apply.
o: Egocentrism, seeing objects and people only from one’s own view
Preoperational children believe everyone experiences the world exactly as they do.
Animism, believing objects have thoughts and feelings
Early in this period, children personify inanimate objects.
Thinking influenced greatly by fantasy and magic
Preoperational thinking is heavily influenced by fantasy and magical thinking.
Difficulty conceptualizing time
Children in this stage have difficulty understanding time.
Conservation of quantity despite changes in appearance
Conservation is a major accomplishment of concrete operations, after age 7.
Reasoning with respect to abstract possibilities
Reasoning about possibilities develops in formal operations, from 11 years.
items.ex: Preoperational thought is egocentric, animistic, magical, and limited in time concepts, and children learn through symbols and play.

alt.q: Which abilities are achieved in Piaget’s concrete operations period (7 to 11 years)? Select all that apply.
o: Reversibility
Mentally reversing a series of steps is a primary characteristic of concrete operational thought.
Seriation
Ordering objects by length, weight, or other characteristics is achieved in this period.
Conservation
Seeing quantities as unchanged despite a change in appearance is a major accomplishment of this stage.
Appreciating that a friend’s view differs from one’s own
Children can coordinate two concrete perspectives and appreciate others’ views.
Animism
Animism is a feature of early preoperational thought.
Object permanence as a new achievement
Object permanence is first achieved in the sensorimotor period.
alt.ex: Correct: Reversibility; Seriation; Conservation; Appreciating that a friend’s view differs from one’s own.

items.q: Which features of egocentric thought are characteristic of adolescents moving into formal operations? Select all that apply.
o: Belief that others constantly scrutinize their appearance
This is the imaginary audience, a form of adolescent self-consciousness.
Belief that their thoughts and feelings are unique
This is the personal fable described in adolescence.
Feelings of invulnerability
Adolescents often feel invulnerable, which frequently leads to risk-taking behavior.
Belief that toys and objects have feelings
Personifying objects is animism, typical of the preoperational period.
Inability to think about past events
Adolescents can think abstractly and reason about possibilities; this is not a feature of their egocentrism.
items.ex: Adolescent egocentrism includes the imaginary audience, the personal fable, and invulnerability, which can lead to risk-taking.

alt.q: A nurse caring for a 13-year-old should anticipate which thinking patterns? Select all that apply.
o: Self-consciousness about being watched by others
The imaginary audience is common as adolescents transition to formal operations.
Belief that no one has felt what they feel
The personal fable is part of adolescent egocentric thought.
Risk-taking related to feeling invulnerable
Invulnerability frequently leads to risk-taking, especially in early adolescence.
Learning mainly through motor and reflex actions
Learning through motor and reflex actions describes the sensorimotor period.
Belief that illness is caused by inanimate objects’ wishes
Attributing wishes to objects is animism, a preoperational feature.
alt.ex: Correct: Self-consciousness about being watched by others; Belief that no one has felt what they feel; Risk-taking related to feeling invulnerable.

items.q: According to Piaget, many adults never become formal operational thinkers and remain at the concrete stage.
items.a: True
items.ex: Piaget noted many adults remain concrete thinkers, so the nurse assesses cognitive ability before teaching.
items.ww: It is not false, because the text states many adults may not become formal operational thinkers.

alt.q: All healthy adults reach Piaget’s formal operations stage, so nurses can assume abstract thinking when teaching adults.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Many adults remain at the concrete stage, so assessment of cognitive ability is critical before teaching.
alt.ww: It is not true, because Piaget noted many adults do not become formal operational thinkers.

items.q: Children in the concrete operations period can appreciate the difference between their own perspective and a friend’s perspective.
items.a: True
items.ex: Concrete operational children can coordinate two concrete perspectives in social and scientific thinking.
items.ww: It is not false; seeing only one’s own view is preoperational egocentrism, which concrete operational children move beyond.

alt.q: Children in the concrete operations period still see objects and people from only one point of view, their own.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Seeing only one’s own point of view is preoperational egocentrism; concrete operational children can coordinate two perspectives.
alt.ww: It is not true, because by 7 to 11 years children appreciate how their view differs from a friend’s.

items.q: Lack of quality sleep in hospitalized children can interfere with blood glucose levels and delay healing.
items.a: True
items.ex: Poor sleep impairs biological processes and brain function, interferes with blood glucose, and may delay healing.
items.ww: It is not false; the evidence links sleep loss to altered glucose levels and delayed healing in hospitalized children.

alt.q: Sleep disruption in hospitalized children affects comfort but has little effect on healing or blood glucose.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Lack of quality sleep interferes with blood glucose levels and may delay the healing process.
alt.ww: It is not true, because sleep loss impairs biological processes, brain function, glucose control, and healing.

items.q: Piaget called the understanding that objects continue to exist even when they cannot be seen, heard, or touched [[object permanence]].
items.ex: Object permanence develops in the sensorimotor period and is considered one of the child’s most important accomplishments.

alt.q: An infant who searches for a toy hidden under a blanket shows [[object permanence]], a key sensorimotor achievement.
alt.ex: Object permanence develops in the sensorimotor period and is considered one of the child’s most important accomplishments.

items.q: Which statement best defines moral development?
items.a: Changes in thoughts, emotions, and behaviors that influence beliefs about right and wrong
items.ex: Moral development refers to changes in thoughts, emotions, and behaviors that influence beliefs about what is right or wrong.
w: Changes in how children think, reason, and perceive their physical world
This describes cognitive development, Piaget’s focus on intellectual organization.
Changes in unconscious conflicts between pleasure and the demands of reality
This describes Freud’s psychoanalytical view of personality development.
Changes in physical growth that follow a predictable, genetically set pattern
This describes biophysical development, not beliefs about right and wrong.

alt.q: Moral development encompasses which dimensions?
alt.a: Interpersonal and intrapersonal dimensions
alt.ex: Moral development has both interpersonal and intrapersonal dimensions because it governs how people interact with others.
w: Sensorimotor and preoperational dimensions
Sensorimotor and preoperational are Piaget’s cognitive periods, not dimensions of moral development.
Oral and anal dimensions
Oral and anal are Freud’s psychosexual stages.
Physical and biological dimensions
Physical and biological changes relate to biophysical development, not beliefs about right and wrong.

items.q: According to Kohlberg, at what age does his theory of moral development begin to apply?
items.a: From 4 years of age until adulthood
items.ex: Kohlberg’s theory applies from 4 years of age until adulthood; children younger than 4 do not understand morality.
w: From birth until adulthood
Kohlberg states that children younger than 4 years do not understand morality.
From 7 years of age until adulthood
The theory begins earlier, at 4 years of age.
From 11 years of age until adulthood
Age 11 marks Piaget’s formal operations, not the start of Kohlberg’s theory.

alt.q: A parent asks whether a 2-year-old who grabs toys understands that it is “wrong.” Based on Kohlberg’s theory, which response is accurate?
alt.a: Children younger than 4 years do not understand morality
alt.ex: Kohlberg’s theory applies from age 4 into adulthood because children younger than 4 do not understand morality.
w: Children this age reason at the conventional level
Conventional reasoning involves internalizing societal expectations and is not seen in toddlers.
Children this age follow a social contract orientation
Social contract orientation is stage 5, at the postconventional level.
Children this age are in the good boy–nice girl stage
Good boy–nice girl is stage 3, at the conventional level.

items.q: A 6-year-old hospitalized with pneumonia tells the nurse, “I got sick because I hit my brother.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “You did not get sick because of anything you did wrong.”
items.ex: At the preconventional level children view illness as punishment, so nurses reinforce that illness is not caused by wrongdoing.
w: “If you are nice to your brother, you will get better faster.”
This reinforces the false belief that behavior causes or cures illness.
“Hitting is wrong, so you should apologize to your brother.”
This focuses on the behavior and does not correct the belief that illness is punishment.
“Why do you think hitting your brother made you sick?”
Exploring the belief without correcting it misses the need to reinforce that illness is not punishment.

alt.q: A preschool child in the hospital asks, “Am I sick because I didn’t listen to Mommy?” The nurse recognizes this thinking is typical of which level of Kohlberg’s theory?
alt.a: Preconventional reasoning
alt.ex: At the preconventional level, thinking is egocentric, and children view illness as punishment for misbehavior.
w: Conventional reasoning
Conventional reasoning focuses on social rules and relationships, not illness as punishment.
Postconventional reasoning
Postconventional reasoning balances human rights with societal rules and defines own principles.
Postformal reasoning
Postformal thought is a proposed adult cognitive stage, not a level of moral reasoning.

items.q: A child comes home on time for supper only because he does not want to be confined to his room for the evening. This reasoning reflects which of Kohlberg’s stages?
items.a: Stage 2: Instrumental relativist orientation
items.ex: In stage 2, punishment is something to avoid, and right choices are based on satisfying one’s own needs.
w: Stage 1: Punishment and obedience orientation
In stage 1, punishment is proof of being wrong, and behavior reflects absolute obedience to authority.
Stage 3: Good boy–nice girl orientation
Stage 3 is motivated by winning approval and being seen as good.
Stage 4: Society-maintaining orientation
Stage 4 is motivated by duty, respect for authority, and maintaining social order.

alt.q: How does a child in Kohlberg’s stage 2 view punishment differently from a child in stage 1?
alt.a: As something to avoid rather than as proof of being wrong
alt.ex: In stage 1 punishment proves an act was wrong; in stage 2 it is simply something one wants to avoid.
w: As proof of being wrong rather than something to avoid
This reverses the stages; viewing punishment as proof of wrongdoing is stage 1.
As a way to win approval rather than to avoid harm
Winning approval is the focus of stage 3, the good boy–nice girl orientation.
As a societal duty rather than a personal consequence
Duty and maintaining social order are the focus of stage 4.

items.q: At Kohlberg’s conventional level, how does the focus of moral decision making change?
items.a: From “What’s in it for me?” to “How will it affect my relationships?”
items.ex: Conventional reasoning internalizes societal and others’ expectations, shifting focus from self-interest to effects on relationships.
w: From “How will it affect others?” to “What’s in it for me?”
This reverses the shift; self-interest characterizes the earlier preconventional level.
From “What does the law say?” to “What does my conscience say?”
Moving toward self-chosen principles describes the postconventional level.
From “Will I be rewarded?” to “Will I be punished?”
Both reward and punishment are preconventional concerns, not the conventional shift.

alt.q: Which statement best reflects moral reasoning at Kohlberg’s conventional level?
alt.a: “I want to meet my family’s expectations and keep their trust.”
alt.ex: Conventional reasoning is based on internalizing the expectations of family, group, or nation and maintaining relationships.
w: “I will do it because I will get a reward afterward.”
Acting for reward is preconventional reasoning based on consequences.
“I will follow my conscience even if it breaks the law.”
Following self-chosen principles over law reflects postconventional stage 6.
“I will obey so that I do not get caught and punished.”
Avoiding punishment is preconventional stage 1 reasoning.

items.q: Members of a patient’s family disagree about end-of-life decisions and are struggling with the moral dilemma. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate when providing grief support?
items.a: Assess the level of moral decision making used by each family member
items.ex: Grief support involves understanding the level of moral decision making of each family member facing end-of-life dilemmas.
w: Tell the family which decision the nurse believes is morally right
Nurses separate their own beliefs from others when helping patients and families with moral decisions.
Ask the family to choose one member to make all decisions quickly
Rushing the process ignores each member’s moral reasoning and the struggle they are experiencing.
Explain that their disagreement shows they are reasoning poorly
Judging the family does not support them; the nurse seeks to understand each member’s moral reasoning.

alt.q: Nurses commonly observe Kohlberg’s conventional level of moral reasoning in which clinical situation?
alt.a: Family members making end-of-life decisions for a loved one
alt.ex: At the conventional level, people weigh effects on relationships, which nurses see when families make end-of-life decisions.
w: A toddler grabbing a toy from another child in the playroom
Children younger than 4 do not understand morality, according to Kohlberg.
A preschooler believing illness is punishment for misbehaving
Viewing illness as punishment is typical of the preconventional level.
An infant searching for a toy hidden under a blanket
Searching for a hidden toy shows object permanence, a cognitive achievement.

items.q: A student stays after school to do odd jobs so the teacher will think she is a good person. This reasoning reflects which of Kohlberg’s stages?
items.a: Stage 3: Good boy–nice girl orientation
items.ex: In stage 3, the individual wants to win approval and maintain the expectations of the immediate group by being nice.
w: Stage 2: Instrumental relativist orientation
Stage 2 is based on satisfying one’s own needs and avoiding punishment, not winning approval.
Stage 4: Society-maintaining orientation
Stage 4 focuses on duty and social order rather than approval from one’s immediate group.
Stage 5: Social contract orientation
Stage 5 involves following societal law while recognizing that laws can be changed to improve society.

alt.q: In Kohlberg’s stage 3, how is “being good” defined?
alt.a: Having positive motives and keeping relationships through trust and loyalty
alt.ex: Stage 3 defines being good as having positive motives, showing concern, and keeping relationships through trust, loyalty, respect, and gratitude.
w: Obeying rules absolutely to avoid physical consequences
Absolute obedience to avoid punishment is stage 1 reasoning.
Following self-chosen principles such as the Golden Rule
Self-chosen abstract principles define right in stage 6.
Doing one’s duty to maintain the order of society
Doing one’s duty and maintaining social order is stage 4.

items.q: An adolescent decides not to attend a party where beer will be served, not because he fears getting caught but because he knows it is not right. This reflects which stage?
items.a: Stage 4: Society-maintaining orientation
items.ex: Stage 4 expands focus to societal concerns; right behavior is doing one’s duty, respecting authority, and maintaining social order.
w: Stage 1: Punishment and obedience orientation
Stage 1 behavior is motivated by fear of punishment, which this adolescent specifically does not cite.
Stage 2: Instrumental relativist orientation
Stage 2 decisions are based on satisfying one’s own needs.
Stage 6: Universal ethical principle orientation
Stage 6 involves abstract self-chosen principles that may lead to civil disobedience.

alt.q: In Kohlberg’s stage 4, what defines right behavior?
alt.a: Doing one’s duty, respecting authority, and maintaining the social order
alt.ex: Stage 4 moves from relationships to societal concerns, so right behavior means duty, respect for authority, and social order.
w: Winning approval and meeting the immediate group’s expectations
Seeking approval from one’s immediate group describes stage 3.
Satisfying one’s own needs and occasionally the needs of others
Satisfying one’s own needs describes stage 2.
Following conscience based on abstract self-chosen ethical principles
Conscience and self-chosen principles define right in stage 6.

items.q: A person refuses to obey a law because it treats one racial group unjustly. According to Kohlberg, this civil disobedience reflects which stage?
items.a: Stage 6: Universal ethical principle orientation
items.ex: Stage 6 defines right by conscience and self-chosen principles such as justice, so a person may not follow an unjust law.
w: Stage 5: Social contract orientation
A person in stage 5 follows the law, even if unfair, while recognizing it can be changed.
Stage 4: Society-maintaining orientation
Stage 4 emphasizes respect for authority and maintaining social order.
Stage 3: Good boy–nice girl orientation
Stage 3 focuses on winning approval from one’s immediate group.

alt.q: A citizen believes a law is unfair to a certain group but obeys it while working through the democratic process to change it. This reflects which stage?
alt.a: Stage 5: Social contract orientation
alt.ex: Stage 5 follows societal law and the democratic process but recognizes laws can be changed to improve society.
w: Stage 6: Universal ethical principle orientation
A stage 6 person may not follow a law that does not seem just to the group.
Stage 2: Instrumental relativist orientation
Stage 2 focuses on satisfying one’s own needs, not improving society.
Stage 1: Punishment and obedience orientation
Stage 1 obeys rules to avoid punishment and does not consider changing laws.

items.q: A nurse is helping a patient make a difficult treatment decision that conflicts with the nurse’s personal values. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Recognize the nurse’s own level of moral reasoning
items.ex: Recognizing your own moral developmental level is essential to separate your beliefs from others’ when helping with moral decisions.
w: Share the nurse’s values so the patient can consider them
Imposing the nurse’s beliefs interferes with the patient’s own moral decision-making process.
Ask another nurse to take over care of the patient
Transferring care avoids the issue; the nurse first examines how her own moral reasoning affects care.
Encourage the patient to choose the option the family prefers
Directing the decision does not support the patient’s own process or separate the nurse’s beliefs.

alt.q: Why is it essential for nurses to recognize their own moral developmental level?
alt.a: To separate their beliefs from patients’ beliefs during moral decision making
alt.ex: Recognizing one’s own moral level helps the nurse separate personal beliefs from others when helping patients with moral decisions.
w: To ensure patients adopt the nurse’s level of moral reasoning
The goal is to support the patient’s own decision process, not to change the patient’s reasoning.
To prove that the nurse’s moral reasoning is at stage 6
The purpose is self-awareness to separate beliefs, not reaching a particular stage.
To decide which patients deserve a higher level of care
Moral self-awareness is not used to ration care; it helps nurses separate beliefs from patients’.

items.q: During an interdisciplinary meeting, a case manager complains about the resources used for a patient who is experiencing homelessness. The nurse believes all patients deserve the same level of care. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Recognize the moral reasoning used by team members and how it influences the care plan
items.ex: Nurses recognize the level of moral and ethical reasoning used by other team members and its influence on a patient’s care plan.
w: Reduce the patient’s care to match the case manager’s preference
Simply giving up the nurse’s ethical view does not address how team reasoning affects patient care.
Avoid discussing the patient’s care with the case manager again
Avoidance prevents a unified outcome; ideally all team members work at the same level.
Report the case manager’s views to the patient and family
Sharing team conflict with the patient does not address the team’s moral reasoning or care plan.

alt.q: Ideally, how should the moral reasoning of health care team members relate to one another when planning care?
alt.a: All members are on the same level, creating a unified outcome
alt.ex: Ideally all team members share the same level of moral reasoning, creating a unified outcome for the patient.
w: Each member works at a different level to balance decisions
The book describes the ideal as members on the same level, not deliberately different levels.
Only the health care provider’s moral reasoning guides the care plan
Every team member’s moral reasoning can influence the patient’s care plan.
Members’ moral reasoning does not affect the patient’s care plan
The level of moral reasoning of team members influences a patient’s care plan.

items.q: Which statements describe criticisms of Kohlberg’s theory of moral development? Select all that apply.
o: Most research subjects were males
Critics questioned his choice of subjects, most of whom were male.
Most subjects were raised in Western philosophical traditions
Critics note his subjects mainly came from Western philosophical traditions.
Moral reasoning cannot be assumed to translate into good actions
A current criticism is that reasoning about morality does not guarantee good actions.
There may be no link between the levels and specific moral theories
Some critics claim the levels are not linked to specific moral theories.
The theory applies only to children younger than 4 years
The theory applies from age 4 into adulthood; younger children do not understand morality.
The theory ignores the role of moral dilemmas
Kohlberg built his stages by examining responses to a series of moral dilemmas.
items.ex: Critics cite male, Western subjects, the gap between reasoning and action, and a weak link between levels and moral theories.

alt.q: A nursing student is reviewing limitations of Kohlberg’s work. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: His research subjects were mostly male
Most of Kohlberg’s subjects were males, which critics question.
Moral reasoning does not necessarily lead to good actions
Critics argue that moral reasoning cannot be assumed to translate into good actions.
Other research has examined morality from a care perspective
Researchers have studied moral development through relationships and concern for others.
His subjects represented many diverse cultures equally
Most subjects were raised in Western philosophical traditions.
He is not recognized as a leader in moral theory
Kohlberg is recognized as a leader in moral developmental theory despite criticism.
alt.ex: Correct: His research subjects were mostly male; Moral reasoning does not necessarily lead to good actions; Other research has examined morality from a care perspective.

items.q: Which characteristics describe Kohlberg’s preconventional level of moral reasoning? Select all that apply.
o: Thinking is primarily egocentric
Preconventional reasoning is a premoral level with limited cognition and egocentric thinking.
Thinking is based mostly on likes and pleasures
At this level, thinking is mostly based on likes and pleasures.
The reason for acting relates to punishment or reward
The “why” of acting relates to expected consequences of punishment or reward.
Illness may be seen as punishment for misbehavior
Children at this level may view illness as punishment for fighting or disobeying.
Behavior is guided by loyalty to family, group, or nation
Loyalty to family, group, or nation characterizes the conventional level.
Right is defined by self-chosen ethical principles
Self-chosen ethical principles define right at the postconventional stage 6.
items.ex: The preconventional level is egocentric and premoral, with behavior guided by pleasure and by punishment or reward.

alt.q: Which characteristics describe Kohlberg’s postconventional level of moral reasoning? Select all that apply.
o: Balancing basic human rights with societal rules
Postconventional reasoning finds a balance between human rights and obligations and societal rules.
Defining one’s own moral values and principles
Individuals move away from authority and conformity to define their own values.
Considering what an ideal society would be like
At this level, individuals start to look at what an ideal society would be like.
Acting mainly to avoid being caught and punished
Avoiding punishment is preconventional stage 1 reasoning.
Acting mainly to win approval from one’s group
Seeking group approval is conventional stage 3 reasoning.
alt.ex: Correct: Balancing basic human rights with societal rules; Defining one’s own moral values and principles; Considering what an ideal society would be like.

items.q: Which characteristics describe Kohlberg’s conventional level of moral reasoning? Select all that apply.
o: Personal internalization of societal and others’ expectations
Conventional reasoning is based on internalizing the expectations of society and others.
Loyalty to the family, group, or nation and its order
The person develops loyalty to and actively maintains, supports, and justifies the order.
Emphasis on social rules and a community-centered approach
The conventional level emphasizes social rules and community rather than self-interest.
Concern for how a decision will affect relationships
Decision making moves from self-interest to how choices affect relationships with others.
Thinking based mostly on personal likes and pleasures
Thinking based on likes and pleasures characterizes the preconventional level.
Willingness to break an unjust law based on conscience
Civil disobedience based on conscience reflects postconventional stage 6.
items.ex: The conventional level internalizes societal expectations, values loyalty and social rules, and weighs effects on relationships.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for patients and families whose moral reasoning is at Kohlberg’s conventional level. Which statements would the nurse expect to hear? Select all that apply.
o: “I want to do what my family expects of me.”
Meeting the expectations of family or group is conventional reasoning.
“I need to think about how this affects the people I love.”
Concern for relationships replaces self-interest at the conventional level.
“It is my duty to respect the rules that keep order.”
Duty and maintaining social order describe stage 4, within the conventional level.
“I only do it if there is something in it for me.”
Self-interest characterizes the preconventional level.
“I will follow my own principles even if the law disagrees.”
Placing self-chosen principles above law reflects the postconventional level.
alt.ex: Correct: “I want to do what my family expects of me.”; “I need to think about how this affects the people I love.”; “It is my duty to respect the rules that keep order.”

items.q: Kohlberg identified six stages of moral development grouped under three levels.
items.a: True
items.ex: From responses to moral dilemmas, Kohlberg identified six stages under three levels: preconventional, conventional, and postconventional.
items.ww: It is not false; the theory has three levels, each containing two stages, for six stages in all.

alt.q: Kohlberg identified three stages of moral development grouped under six levels.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Kohlberg’s theory has three levels with two stages each, for a total of six stages.
alt.ww: It is not true, because the numbers are reversed: there are six stages under three levels.

items.q: A person in Kohlberg’s stage 5 follows the law but recognizes the possibility of changing it to improve society.
items.a: True
items.ex: Stage 5, social contract orientation, follows societal law while recognizing laws can be changed to improve society.
items.ww: It is not false; recognizing laws can be changed to improve society is the defining feature of stage 5.

alt.q: A person in Kohlberg’s stage 5 believes laws are fixed and should never be changed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Stage 5 follows the law but recognizes the possibility of changing it to improve society.
alt.ww: It is not true, because the social contract orientation accepts that laws can be changed for the better.

items.q: The level of moral reasoning used by other members of the health care team can influence a patient’s plan of care.
items.a: True
items.ex: Nurses recognize the moral and ethical reasoning of other team members and its influence on a patient’s care plan.
items.ww: It is not false; the book stresses that team members’ moral reasoning affects the patient’s care plan.

alt.q: A patient’s plan of care depends only on the nurse’s moral reasoning, not on other team members’ reasoning.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The moral reasoning of other health care team members also influences a patient’s care plan.
alt.ww: It is not true, because the reasoning of every team member can shape the patient’s plan of care.

items.q: In Kohlberg’s theory, the premoral level in which thinking is primarily egocentric and guided by punishment or reward is called [[preconventional|preconventional reasoning]].

items.q: On what basis are the stages of human growth and development organized into age-groups?
items.a: The timing and sequence of developmental tasks children accomplish
items.ex: Although the chronological division is somewhat arbitrary, stages are based on when and in what order children accomplish developmental tasks.
w: The average height and weight a child reaches each year
Height and weight are physical measures assessed within stages; they are not the basis for dividing the stages.
The grade level a child is placed in at school
School grade is a social placement; stages rest on the timing and sequence of developmental tasks.
The order in which a child receives routine immunizations
Immunization schedules are health promotion activities, not the basis for defining developmental stages.

alt.q: A nursing student asks why children are grouped into stages such as toddler and preschooler. Which explanation is most accurate?
alt.a: The groupings reflect when and in what order children typically master developmental tasks
alt.ex: Stages are organized by age but grounded in the timing and sequence of the developmental tasks children accomplish.
w: The groupings reflect the exact age at which every child changes behavior
The chronological division is described as somewhat arbitrary, so it does not mark an exact age for every child.
The groupings reflect the type of health insurance coverage at each age
Insurance coverage has nothing to do with how developmental stages are defined.
The groupings reflect the order of growth in a child’s head circumference
Head circumference is one physical measure; it does not define the developmental stages.

items.q: Dividing growth and development into stages by age is somewhat arbitrary, even though the stages follow the timing and sequence of developmental tasks.
items.a: True
items.ex: Development is continuous, so age cutoffs are approximate, but they are grounded in when children typically accomplish developmental tasks.
items.ww: Calling the age divisions exact ignores that development is continuous and that the chronological division is described as somewhat arbitrary.

alt.q: Each developmental stage begins and ends at a precise age that applies equally to every child.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The chronological division into stages is somewhat arbitrary; it reflects typical timing and sequence of tasks, not fixed cutoffs for every child.
alt.ww: Stages are approximate groupings of a continuous process, so they cannot start and stop at exact ages for all children.

items.q: For each stage of growth and development, which areas does the chapter address? (Select all that apply.)

Physical growth and change are described for every stage from conception through adolescence.
Psychosocial changes
Psychosocial development, such as trust, autonomy, and identity, is addressed for each stage.
Cognitive changes
Cognitive development, such as Piaget’s stages, is described across the age-groups.
Health risks and health promotion concerns
Each stage includes its typical health risks and health promotion concerns.
Retirement and late-life role transitions
Retirement concerns belong to older adulthood, not conception through adolescence.
Career advancement in the workplace
Career advancement is an adult concern; the chapter covers children through adolescence.
items.ex: The chapter examines physical, psychosocial, and cognitive changes plus health risks and health promotion for each stage.

alt.q: A nurse uses the chapter to prepare age-specific care for children. Which kinds of information can the nurse expect for each stage? (Select all that apply.)

Physical changes are described for each age-group.
Typical psychosocial development
Psychosocial changes are part of each stage’s description.
Health promotion concerns for that age-group
Health promotion concerns are covered for every stage.

Adult chronic disease management is not part of the stages from conception through adolescence.
Hospital staffing ratios for pediatric units
Staffing ratios are administrative issues, not developmental stage content.
alt.ex: Correct: Expected physical growth and changes; Typical psychosocial development; Health promotion concerns for that age-group.

The first 12 months of life
The first 12 months covers both the neonatal period and infancy.

Six months falls within infancy, which spans 1 month to 1 year.

24 to 60 months of age

5 to 8 years of age

2 to 6 years of age

w: Toddlerhood

School-age period
The school-age period begins at about 6 years of age.
Infancy

Toddlerhood

w: Adolescence
Adolescence has major pubertal changes, but infancy is singled out for its dramatic growth and development.
Preschool period

School-age period

alt.q: Why can a nurse most easily observe a child’s adaptive potential during the first year of life?

w: Infants are mostly reflexive and show few changes
Reflexive functioning describes the neonate; infancy is marked by rapid change toward purposeful behavior.

Interaction between infants and the environment becomes greater and more meaningful during this year.
Physical growth in infancy is slower than at any time

items.q: A nurse is preparing to assess a 9-year-old during a school health screening. Which action best reflects an age-specific approach?
items.a: Review the developmental expectations for the school-age group before the assessment

w: Use the same developmental checklist used for all pediatric patients
A single checklist ignores the different developmental expectations of each age-group.
Compare the child’s skills with those expected of an adolescent
A 9-year-old is in the school-age period, so adolescent expectations do not apply.
Base the assessment only on the child’s height and weight
Assessment includes physical, psychosocial, and cognitive development, not just measurements.

alt.q: Before assessing a 15-year-old, which preparation by the nurse is most appropriate?
