alt.ex: Age-specific assessment requires knowing the developmental expectations for the patient’s age-group, here adolescence.
w: Reviewing the developmental expectations for the school-age group
School-age expectations apply to 6 to about 12 years; a 15-year-old is an adolescent.
Reviewing an adult assessment form with no changes
Adolescents have their own developmental expectations that differ from adults.
Reviewing only the immunization record for the teen
Immunizations matter, but age-specific assessment covers the full set of developmental expectations.

items.q: The parent of a 6-month-old says, “My baby is smaller than my sister’s baby, who is the same age. Is something wrong?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Steady and proportional growth is more important than your baby’s actual size.”
items.ex: For infants, steady and proportional growth is more important than absolute growth, so the nurse focuses on the growth pattern.
w: “Your baby should be the same size as other babies of the same age.”
Children vary in size; the pattern of steady, proportional growth matters more than absolute size.
“Smaller babies usually have a developmental delay, so we will refer you.”
Smaller size alone does not indicate delay; the pattern of growth over time is what is evaluated.
“Size does not matter at all during the first year of life.”
Growth is assessed carefully in infancy; the point is that steady proportional growth matters most.

alt.q: Which statement by a parent shows understanding of how an infant’s growth is evaluated?
alt.a: “The nurse will look for steady, proportional growth over time.”
alt.ex: Steady and proportional growth of an infant is more important than absolute growth.
w: “My baby needs to be the biggest baby in the group to be healthy.”
Being larger than others is not the goal; steady, proportional growth is.
“Only my baby’s weight at this one visit really matters.”
A single measurement does not show the growth pattern over time.
“Growth is never measured once my baby leaves the hospital.”
Weight, length, and head circumference continue to be tracked to show the growth pattern.

items.q: Which statement best describes human growth and development?

They are simple processes that stop at school entry
Development continues through adolescence and is described as complex.
They are random changes with no predictable sequence
Stages are based on the predictable timing and sequence of developmental tasks.

alt.q: A parent asks whether children develop only during certain short periods. Which reply by the nurse is accurate?

“Each child develops in a completely unpredictable order.”

alt.ex: Toddlers gain independence from greater physical mobility and cognitive abilities between 12 and 36 months.

items.q: Puberty marks the end of the school-age years and the beginning of adolescence.
items.a: True
items.ex: The middle years of childhood run from 6 to about 12 years, and puberty marks their end and the start of adolescence.
items.ww: Puberty is the event that ends the middle childhood years and begins adolescence, so the statement is accurate.

alt.q: The term puberty refers to psychological maturation, whereas adolescence refers to the point at which reproduction becomes possible.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The terms are reversed: adolescence refers to psychological maturation, and puberty is the point at which reproduction becomes possible.
alt.ww: Adolescent describes psychological maturation; puberty describes reproductive capability, so the statement swaps the definitions.

items.q: Human growth and development occur in short bursts separated by long periods with no change.
items.a: False
items.ex: Growth and development are continuous processes; stages organize them but do not mean development stops between them.
items.ww: Development does not pause between stages; it is a continuous, complex process.

alt.q: Human growth and development are continuous processes, even though they are commonly divided into stages.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Stages are a convenient way to organize a continuous, complex process by age-group.
alt.ww: Stage divisions do not mean development stops and starts; the process is continuous.

items.q: Which statements about the stages of growth and development are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
o: Stages are organized by age-groups.
Development is typically divided into stages organized by age-groups.
The chronological division is somewhat arbitrary.
Age cutoffs are approximate rather than exact for every child.
Stages reflect the timing and sequence of developmental tasks.
The division is based on when and in what order tasks are accomplished.
Each stage has its own health risks and health promotion concerns.
Health risks and health promotion are addressed for each stage.
All children enter each stage on the same exact day.
Because the division is somewhat arbitrary, children do not all change on an exact date.
Development stops once a stage has been completed.
Growth and development are continuous throughout childhood.
items.ex: Stages group a continuous process by age, based on the timing and sequence of tasks, with stage-specific health concerns.

alt.q: A nurse explains developmental stages to new parents. Which points are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
o: Children accomplish developmental tasks in a predictable sequence.
Stages are based on the timing and sequence of developmental tasks.
Age cutoffs for stages are approximate.
The chronological division is somewhat arbitrary.
Each age-group has particular health promotion needs.
Health promotion concerns are described for each stage.
Stages are defined only by the child’s weight.
Stages reflect developmental tasks across physical, psychosocial, and cognitive areas, not weight alone.
Growth and development are simple, one-step processes.
Growth and development are described as continuous and complex.
alt.ex: Correct: Children accomplish developmental tasks in a predictable sequence; Age cutoffs for stages are approximate; Each age-group has particular health promotion needs.

items.q: Which term refers to the point at which reproduction becomes possible?
items.a: Puberty
items.ex: Puberty is the point at which reproduction becomes possible; its hormonal changes alter the young person’s appearance.
w: Adolescence
Adolescence usually refers to psychological maturation during the transition to adulthood.
Toddlerhood
Toddlerhood is the period from 12 to 36 months, long before reproductive maturity.
School-age period
The school-age period ends when puberty begins; it is not the point of reproductive capability.

alt.q: A 14-year-old asks the nurse, “What is the difference between being an adolescent and going through puberty?” Which answer is accurate?
alt.a: “Adolescence refers to psychological maturing; puberty is when reproduction becomes possible.”
alt.ex: Adolescent refers to psychological maturation, whereas puberty refers to the point at which reproduction becomes possible.
w: “Puberty refers to psychological maturing; adolescence is when reproduction becomes possible.”
This reverses the definitions of puberty and adolescence.
“They are two words for exactly the same thing with no difference.”
The terms differ: one describes psychological maturation and the other reproductive capability.
“Puberty happens before age 6, and adolescence starts after age 20.”
Puberty ends the school-age years, and adolescence usually spans 13 to 20 years.

items.q: Which age range does the chapter give for the school-age period, or middle childhood?
items.a: 6 to about 12 years of age
items.ex: The middle years of childhood span 6 to about 12 years, laying the foundation for adult roles in work, recreation, and social interaction.
w: 3 to 5 years of age
Ages 3 to 5 are the preschool period.
12 to 18 years of age
These years fall mainly in adolescence, which usually spans 13 to 20 years.
1 to 3 years of age
Ages 12 to 36 months are toddlerhood.

alt.q: A child is 10 years old. In which developmental period is the child?
alt.a: School-age period
alt.ex: Children 6 to about 12 years old are in the school-age period, or middle childhood.
w: Preschool period
The preschool period ends at 5 years of age.
Adolescence
Adolescence usually begins around 13 years and follows puberty.
Toddlerhood
Toddlerhood ends at 36 months.

sections.name: Selecting a developmental framework for nursing

items.q: What does a family-centered approach that incorporates knowledge of developmental stages and theories provide for the nurse?
items.a: A framework to assess and plan care that meets the needs of the child and family
items.ex: Combining family-centered care with developmental knowledge gives the nurse a framework for assessing and planning care for child and family.
w: A standard care plan that is the same for every child of any age
The framework tailors care to the child’s developmental level, not one plan for all ages.
A way to make care decisions without involving the child’s family
The approach is family-centered, so the family is included in planning care.
A method of ranking children by their academic performance
The framework guides nursing assessment and care, not academic ranking.

alt.q: A nurse wants to plan care that fits both a child’s developmental needs and the family’s needs. Which approach should the nurse use?
alt.a: A family-centered approach that applies knowledge of developmental stages and theories
alt.ex: Family-centered care grounded in developmental stages and theories provides a framework for appropriate assessment and planning.
w: A task-centered approach that applies the unit’s routine schedule
Unit routines do not address the child’s developmental level or the family’s needs.
A provider-centered approach that applies standard adult protocols
Adult protocols do not reflect a child’s developmental stage or the family’s role.
A disease-centered approach that applies the medical diagnosis only
Focusing only on the diagnosis ignores developmental and family needs.

items.q: A developmental framework encourages the nurse to organize care around which factor?
items.a: The child’s current level of functioning
items.ex: Care is organized for the child’s current level of functioning to motivate self-direction and health promotion.
w: The child’s chronological age alone
Age-groups are a guide, but care is organized around how the child is functioning now.
The parents’ preferred daily routine
Family input matters, but care is organized around the child’s current functioning.
The nurse’s own assignment schedule
Care is centered on the child’s needs, not the nurse’s workload.

alt.q: Organizing care around a child’s current level of functioning is intended to motivate which outcomes?
alt.a: Self-direction and health promotion
alt.ex: Fitting care to the child’s current functioning motivates self-direction and health promotion.
w: Dependence on caregivers and compliance
The aim is to build self-direction, not dependence on caregivers.
Faster discharge and lower hospital cost
These are not the stated goals; self-direction and health promotion are.
Quiet behavior and fewer parent visits
The framework encourages family involvement, not fewer visits.

items.q: Why does the nurse encourage a hospitalized toddler to make simple choices and feed themself?
items.a: To advance the toddler’s developing autonomy
items.ex: Toddlers are developing autonomy, so simple choices and self-feeding support this developmental task.
w: To shorten the time needed for meals
Self-feeding toddlers often take longer and spill; the goal is autonomy, not speed.
To build the toddler’s sense of trust in the nurse
Trust versus mistrust is the infant’s developmental task; toddlers are developing autonomy.
To prepare the toddler for formal school learning
Preparing for formal education is a preschool concern; the toddler goal is autonomy.

alt.q: A nurse lets a 2-year-old choose between two cups and hold the spoon at lunch. Which developmental need is the nurse supporting?
alt.a: Autonomy
alt.ex: A sense of autonomy emerges in toddlerhood, and choices and self-feeding help advance it.
w: Trust
Trust is the developmental focus in infancy, built through consistent parent-infant interaction.
Identity
Developing a sense of identity is the main psychosocial task of adolescence.
Industry
Industry is the focus of school-age children, not toddlers.

items.q: A nurse needs to give an oral medication to a 2-year-old. Which approach by the nurse is best?
items.a: “It’s time for your medicine. Would you like water or juice with it?”
items.ex: Telling the toddler it is time and offering a simple choice limits chances for a “no” and supports autonomy.
w: “Do you want to take your medicine now?”
A yes-or-no question invites the toddler’s negativism and a likely “no.”
“If you don’t take this medicine, you can’t see your mom.”
Threats increase distress and do not support the toddler’s developing autonomy.
“Would you like to take your medicine later or right now?”
Offering to delay a scheduled medication gives a choice the toddler should not have.

alt.q: Which statement by a parent of a toddler shows understanding of how to reduce negativism?
alt.a: “I’ll tell him it’s bath time and let him pick which toy to bring.”
alt.ex: Stating what must happen and offering a simple choice limits opportunities for a “no” answer.
w: “I’ll ask him if he wants a bath tonight and accept his answer.”
Asking a yes-or-no question invites a “no” and increases negativism.
“I’ll give him a bath without telling him anything first.”
Toddlers still benefit from being told what is happening and given simple choices.
“I’ll let him skip baths until he stops saying no.”
Avoiding needed care does not reduce negativism; offering simple choices does.

items.q: A 15-year-old with a new chronic illness is hospitalized, and the team is planning discharge care. Which action by the nurse best reflects developmental principles?
items.a: Include the adolescent in decisions about the plan of care
items.ex: Adolescents are developing independence and should feel empowered to participate in decisions regarding their plan of care.
w: Review the discharge plan with the parents only
Leaving the adolescent out ignores their developing independence and need to participate.
Delay teaching until the adolescent turns 18
Adolescents should be involved in their care now, as they are developing independence.
Give the adolescent a printed plan without discussion
Handing over a plan without discussion does not empower the adolescent to take part in decisions.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse caring for a 16-year-old shows the best understanding of adolescent development?
alt.a: “Let’s decide together how you will fit treatments into your school day.”
alt.ex: Because adolescents are developing independence, the nurse empowers them to participate in care decisions.
w: “Your parents will decide how your treatments fit into your day.”
This excludes the adolescent from decisions about their own care.
“You are too young to have a say in your treatment schedule.”
Adolescents should feel empowered to participate in decisions about their plan of care.
“I will set up your treatment schedule so you don’t have to.”
Making all decisions for the teen does not support developing independence.

items.q: A nurse is caring for an 8-year-old who needs to increase oral fluid intake after surgery. Which approach best supports the child’s development?
items.a: Let the child help choose the fluids and help keep a record of intake
items.ex: Illness threatens school-age children’s control, so involving them in care, such as choosing fluids and recording intake, maintains independence.
w: Have the parents record all intake without telling the child
Excluding the child removes a chance to maintain control and independence.
Give the child whatever fluid is on the tray without discussion
This removes the child’s choice when participation is developmentally appropriate.
Tell the child fluid intake is an adult responsibility only
School-age children can participate in care, which helps them maintain independence.

alt.q: Why does the nurse encourage a hospitalized school-age child to participate in personal care whenever possible?
alt.a: Illness and hospitalization threaten the child’s sense of control over personal care
alt.ex: School-age children are independent in personal care, so participation helps them keep as much independence as possible.
w: Illness and hospitalization make school-age children more willing to be dependent
Hospitalization threatens control; it does not make children want dependence.
Nursing staff are usually too busy to provide personal care for school-age children
The reason is developmental, preserving independence, not staffing.
School-age children are not yet able to bathe or dress themselves independently
Improved fine-motor skills allow school-age children to be very independent in personal care.

items.q: A nurse is about to obtain a health history from a 16-year-old who arrived with a parent. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Ask the parent to step out so the interview can be done privately
items.ex: As adolescents become more autonomous, interviews should be conducted without parents present in a private, nonthreatening setting.
w: Direct the health history questions to the parent
Adolescents should be interviewed directly and privately as they become more autonomous.
Interview the adolescent with the parent present throughout
A parent’s presence can inhibit honest answers; interviews should be private.
Have the adolescent fill out a form in the waiting room
A form in a public area does not provide the privacy and interaction recommended.

alt.q: Which setting is most appropriate for a nurse to discuss sexual health with a 15-year-old?
alt.a: A private room with the adolescent alone
alt.ex: Discussions with adolescents should be private and confidential, without parents present.
w: The waiting room with the parent nearby
A waiting room lacks privacy and may discourage honest discussion.
An exam room with the parent present
Adolescent interviews should be conducted without parents present.
A hallway between scheduled appointments
A hallway is not private or nonthreatening.

items.q: During a private interview, a 14-year-old asks, “Will you tell my parents what I say?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “What you tell me stays private, unless it involves abuse or thoughts of suicide.”
items.ex: The nurse ensures confidentiality and explains its limits, such as disclosure of abuse or suicidal ideation.
w: “Everything you say will stay private, no matter what you tell me.”
Confidentiality has limits, such as abuse or suicidal ideation, that must be explained.
“I share everything with your parents because you are a minor.”
Adolescent discussions should be confidential, with only specific stated limits.
“That depends on whether your parents ask me about it later.”
Confidentiality limits are based on safety concerns such as abuse or suicide, not on parent requests.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of confidentiality when interviewing adolescents?
alt.a: “I will explain that I must report abuse or suicidal thoughts.”
alt.ex: Nurses ensure confidentiality and explain its limitations, including disclosure of abuse or suicidal ideation.
w: “I will promise that nothing they say will ever be shared.”
Promising absolute secrecy is inaccurate because abuse and suicidal ideation must be disclosed.
“I will tell the parents everything after each interview.”
Adolescent discussions should be private and confidential.
“I will avoid discussing confidentiality so they stay relaxed.”
Explaining confidentiality and its limits builds trust and is recommended.

items.q: A 2-year-old admitted to the hospital cries whenever the parents leave. Which nursing action best supports the toddler?
items.a: Encourage the parents to stay as much as possible and help provide care
items.ex: Separation from parents is stressful for hospitalized toddlers, so nurses encourage parents to stay and actively participate in care.
w: Ask the parents to visit less often so the toddler adjusts
Fewer visits increase separation stress; parents should stay as much as possible.
Assign a different nurse each shift so the toddler meets many people
Many caregivers add stress; parent presence and participation are encouraged.
Keep the parents out of care so the toddler bonds with staff
Parents should actively participate in care; supporting them gains the toddler’s cooperation.

alt.q: Why does the nurse focus on establishing a trusting relationship with the parents of a hospitalized toddler?
alt.a: It often results in the toddler’s acceptance of treatment
alt.ex: Creating an environment that supports parents helps gain the toddler’s trust and cooperation, often leading to acceptance of treatment.
w: It allows parents to leave the toddler alone more often
The goal is parent presence and participation, not more time away.
It replaces the need to explain procedures to the toddler
Trust with parents supports cooperation but does not replace age-appropriate explanations.
It means the toddler will no longer have temper tantrums
Tantrums are normal in toddlerhood; trust with parents supports acceptance of care.

items.q: A toddler on the pediatric unit insists on holding a cup without help. Which nursing action supports independence safely?
items.a: Provide a two-handled cup with a spout and a bib with a pocket
items.ex: Toddlers should be allowed to do things that will not harm themselves or others; two-handled spouted cups and pocket bibs support this.
w: Hold the cup for the toddler so no milk is spilled
Preventing the attempt blocks the toddler’s developing independence.
Give milk only through a bottle until discharge
Returning to a bottle does not support the toddler’s drive to do things independently.
Tell the toddler cups are only for older children
This frustrates the toddler and discourages appropriate independence.

alt.q: Which guideline should caregivers follow when encouraging a toddler’s independence?
alt.a: Allow the toddler to do things that will not result in harm to self or others
alt.ex: Caregivers encourage independence appropriately by allowing activities that will not cause harm.
w: Allow the toddler to do anything the toddler chooses to try
Independence is encouraged only for activities that will not cause harm.
Allow independence only after the toddler turns 3 years old
Autonomy emerges during toddlerhood, so independence is encouraged then.
Allow independence only when no mess will be created
Some mess, such as spilled milk, is expected and managed with pocket bibs.

items.q: A newborn cries when hungry, and the parent asks how often to feed the baby. Which response by the nurse applies developmental knowledge?
items.a: “Feed your baby on demand when the baby shows hunger.”
items.ex: A newborn’s cry is generally a reflexive response to an unmet need such as hunger, so feeding on demand is advised.
w: “Feed your baby on a strict schedule every 4 hours.”
Nurses counsel feeding on demand rather than on a rigid schedule.
“Let your baby cry for a while to learn the routine.”
Crying signals an unmet need; newborns do not learn schedules this way.
“Feed your baby only when the baby stops crying.”
Crying from hunger signals the need to feed, not to wait.

alt.q: Why does the nurse advise parents to feed a crying, hungry newborn on demand rather than on a rigid schedule?
alt.a: A newborn’s cry is generally a reflexive response to an unmet need
alt.ex: Newborn behavior is mostly reflexive, and crying usually signals hunger, fatigue, or discomfort.
w: A newborn’s cry is generally a learned way to get attention
Newborn functioning is mostly reflexive; crying is not a learned behavior.
A newborn’s cry is generally a sign of a serious illness
Crying most often reflects unmet needs such as hunger, fatigue, or discomfort.
A newborn’s cry is generally caused by too much feeding
Crying when hungry signals the need to be fed.

items.q: Which nursing actions support a toddler’s developing autonomy? (Select all that apply.)
o: Offering simple choices, such as which drink to have
Simple choices advance the toddler’s developing autonomy.
Encouraging the toddler to feed themself
Self-feeding supports the toddler’s drive for independence.
Limiting opportunities for a “no” answer
Limiting yes-or-no questions reduces negativism.
Letting the toddler do tasks that will not cause harm
Independence is encouraged for activities that are safe.
Asking, “Do you want your medicine now?”
A yes-or-no question invites negativism and a likely refusal.
Doing all care for the toddler to save time
Doing everything for the toddler blocks the development of autonomy.
items.ex: Toddlers develop autonomy through safe independence and simple choices, while caregivers avoid yes-or-no questions that invite refusal.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching parents of a 20-month-old how to encourage independence. Which suggestions are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)
o: Use a two-handled cup with a spout when the toddler wants to drink alone
Adapted cups let toddlers practice safely.
State that it is time for a task, then offer a simple choice
This limits chances for a “no” and supports autonomy.
Let the toddler feed themself even if some food spills
Self-feeding supports independence; pocket bibs help with spills.
Ask yes-or-no questions about every required task
Yes-or-no questions invite negativism.
Feed and dress the toddler to avoid any frustration
Doing everything for the toddler does not support autonomy.
alt.ex: Correct: Use a two-handled cup with a spout when the toddler wants to drink alone; State that it is time for a task, then offer a simple choice; Let the toddler feed themself even if some food spills.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a 16-year-old. Which actions reflect developmentally appropriate care? (Select all that apply.)
o: Conducting the interview without parents present
As adolescents become more autonomous, interviews are done without parents.
Explaining the limits of confidentiality
The nurse explains limits such as disclosure of abuse or suicidal ideation.
Being nonjudgmental and showing interest in the teen’s view
Genuine interest and a nonjudgmental attitude support communication.
Involving the adolescent in decisions about the care plan
Adolescents should be empowered to participate in decisions.
Directing all care decisions to the parents
Excluding the adolescent ignores developing independence.
Sharing everything the teen says with the parents
Discussions with adolescents should be private and confidential.
items.ex: Adolescent care respects developing independence through privacy, confidentiality with stated limits, respect, and shared decisions.

alt.q: Which nursing approaches support an adolescent’s developing independence? (Select all that apply.)
o: Empowering the teen to take part in care decisions
Adolescents should feel empowered to participate in their plan of care.
Providing privacy and a nonthreatening environment
Privacy supports open communication with adolescents.
Helping families foster independence while keeping family structure
Nurses help families balance independence and family structure.
Making all decisions for the teen to reduce stress
Adolescents need to make choices and experience their consequences.
Interviewing the teen only with a parent present
Interviews should be conducted without parents present.
alt.ex: Correct: Empowering the teen to take part in care decisions; Providing privacy and a nonthreatening environment; Helping families foster independence while keeping family structure.

items.q: Which elements make up the framework a nurse uses to assess and plan care for a child and family? (Select all that apply.)
o: A family-centered approach
The framework is family-centered, meeting the needs of the child and family.
Knowledge of developmental stages
Knowing developmental stages guides age-appropriate care.
Knowledge of developmental theories
Developmental theories inform the nurse’s assessment and planning.
A standard adult care plan for every patient
Adult care plans do not reflect a child’s developmental level.
The nurse’s personal parenting preferences
Care is based on developmental knowledge and family needs, not personal preferences.
items.ex: Family-centered care combined with knowledge of developmental stages and theories forms the nurse’s framework.

alt.q: A nurse builds a developmental framework for a hospitalized preschooler. Which components should it include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Involvement of the child’s family
A family-centered approach meets the needs of both child and family.
Expected tasks for the preschool stage
Knowledge of developmental stages guides appropriate care.
Relevant developmental theories
Theories such as Erikson’s and Piaget’s inform care planning.
The unit’s routine for adult patients
Adult routines do not address a child’s developmental needs.
The child’s diagnosis as the only focus
Focusing only on the diagnosis omits developmental and family needs.
alt.ex: Correct: Involvement of the child’s family; Expected tasks for the preschool stage; Relevant developmental theories.

items.q: A developmental framework for nursing plans care for the child alone, apart from the family’s needs.
items.a: False
items.ex: The framework uses a family-centered approach so care meets the needs of both the child and the family.
items.ww: Leaving out the family contradicts the family-centered approach that underlies the framework.

alt.q: A family-centered approach that uses knowledge of developmental stages helps the nurse plan care for both the child and the family.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Family-centered care plus developmental knowledge provides a framework that meets the needs of child and family.
alt.ww: The framework is explicitly family-centered, so saying it ignores the family would be inaccurate.

items.q: Because adolescents are minors, the nurse should direct care decisions to parents and keep adolescents out of care planning.
items.a: False
items.ex: Adolescents are developing independence and should feel empowered to participate in decisions regarding their plan of care.
items.ww: Excluding adolescents ignores their developing independence and the recommendation to involve them in decisions.

alt.q: Adolescents should feel empowered to take part in decisions about their plan of care because they are developing independence.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Involving adolescents in care decisions supports their developing independence.
alt.ww: Keeping adolescents out of planning would ignore their developmental need for independence.

items.q: Illness and hospitalization threaten a school-age child’s control over personal care, so the nurse lets the child participate in care whenever possible.
items.a: True
items.ex: Participating in care helps school-age children maintain as much independence as possible during illness.
items.ww: School-age children are very independent in personal care, so removing their participation would increase their loss of control.

alt.q: Letting a hospitalized school-age child help with personal care is discouraged because it adds to the child’s stress.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Participation helps school-age children keep control and independence that illness threatens.
alt.ww: Participation reduces the loss of control caused by illness, so it is encouraged rather than discouraged.

items.q: Nurses encourage toddlers to make simple choices and feed themselves to advance their developing [[autonomy]].
items.ex: A sense of autonomy emerges during toddlerhood, and choices and self-feeding support it.

alt.q: Letting a 2-year-old pick between two drinks supports the toddler’s developing [[autonomy]].
alt.ex: A sense of autonomy emerges during toddlerhood, and choices and self-feeding support it.

items.q: Asking a toddler “Do you want your medicine?” invites [[negativism]], so nurses limit opportunities for a “no” answer.
items.ex: Negativism is the toddler’s tendency to answer “no”; offering simple choices instead limits it.

alt.q: The toddler behavior of answering “no” to requests is called [[negativism]].
alt.ex: Negativism is the toddler’s tendency to answer “no”; offering simple choices instead limits it.

mt.ex: Matching care to the developmental stage supports trust in infants, autonomy in toddlers, and independence in older children.

items.q: How long does a pregnancy that reaches full term last, on average?
items.a: 38 to 40 weeks
items.ex: A full-term pregnancy is calculated to last an average of 38 to 40 weeks, divided into three trimesters.
w: 28 to 32 weeks
This is well short of full term, which averages 38 to 40 weeks.
34 to 36 weeks
These weeks fall before the 38-to-40-week average for a full-term pregnancy.
42 to 44 weeks
This is longer than the 38-to-40-week average for a full-term pregnancy.

alt.q: A pregnant patient asks how pregnancy is usually divided. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “Into three trimesters, each about 3 months long”
alt.ex: Pregnancy is commonly divided into three equal phases of 3 months each, called trimesters.
w: “Into two halves, each about 5 months long”
Pregnancy is divided into three trimesters, not two halves.
“Into four quarters, each about 2 months long”
Pregnancy is divided into three trimesters of about 3 months.
“Into nine stages, each about 1 month long”
The common division is three trimesters, not monthly stages.

items.q: During which time frame does the embryonic stage occur?
items.a: From day 15 until the eighth week
items.ex: The embryonic stage follows the 14-day preembryonic stage and lasts from day 15 until the eighth week.
w: From fertilization through day 14
The first 14 days after fertilization are the preembryonic stage.
From the end of the eighth week until birth
This is the fetal stage, which follows the embryonic stage.
From the twelfth week until the twentieth week
By the twelfth week the developing child is already in the fetal stage.

alt.q: A pregnant patient is 5 weeks past fertilization. In which stage of development is the embryo?
alt.a: Embryonic stage
alt.ex: The embryonic stage lasts from day 15 until the eighth week, so 5 weeks falls within it.
w: Preembryonic stage
The preembryonic stage covers only the first 14 days after fertilization.
Fetal stage
The fetal stage begins at the end of the eighth week.
Neonatal period
The neonatal period is the first 28 days after birth.

items.q: Why is the embryonic stage the most vulnerable to teratogens?
items.a: All body organs are formed by the eighth week of gestation
items.ex: Because organs form during the embryonic stage, exposure to teratogens then can cause abnormal development of structures.
w: The placenta stops functioning during the embryonic stage
The placenta begins development during the embryonic stage; it does not stop functioning.
The embryo receives no nutrients during the embryonic stage
The embryo is nourished; vulnerability comes from rapid organ formation.
Most maternal infections occur only during the embryonic stage
Vulnerability is due to organ formation, not the timing of infections.

alt.q: A patient who is 6 weeks pregnant asks why the nurse stresses avoiding alcohol and drugs now. Which response is most accurate?
alt.a: “The baby’s organs are forming right now, so this is when they are most vulnerable.”
alt.ex: The embryonic stage is the most vulnerable because all body organs are formed by the eighth week.
w: “The baby is least affected by drugs in the first weeks of pregnancy.”
The early embryonic weeks are the most vulnerable, not the least.
“The placenta blocks most drugs until the third trimester.”
The placenta is extremely porous, so drugs pass to the embryo.
“Drugs only matter once the baby can move in the uterus.”
Teratogens have their greatest effect while organs form in the embryonic stage.

items.q: Which statement describes the role of the placenta during pregnancy?
items.a: It serves as the fetal lungs, kidneys, gastrointestinal tract, and endocrine organ
items.ex: The placenta performs these functions for the fetus and produces essential hormones that help maintain the pregnancy.
w: It serves as a complete barrier against viruses, chemicals, and drugs
The placenta is extremely porous, so these agents can pass to the fetus.
It serves as the fetal brain, spinal cord, and nervous system
The placenta acts as lungs, kidneys, GI tract, and endocrine organ, not nervous system.
It serves only as storage for maternal nutrients and fluids
The placenta does much more, including hormone production and gas exchange.

alt.q: When does the placenta begin to develop?
alt.a: At the third week of the embryonic stage
alt.ex: The placenta begins development at the third week of the embryonic stage and produces hormones that help maintain pregnancy.
w: At the first week of the preembryonic stage
Placental development begins later, at the third week of the embryonic stage.
At the end of the first trimester
The placenta begins developing well before the end of the first trimester.
At the beginning of the fetal stage
The placenta has already begun developing during the embryonic stage.

items.q: For a female at normal weight for height, what is the recommended weight gain during pregnancy?
items.a: 11 to 15 kg (25 to 35 lb) over three trimesters
items.ex: A normal-weight patient should gain 11 to 15 kg (25 to 35 lb) over the pregnancy, with attention to the pattern of gain.
w: 5 to 7 kg (11 to 15 lb) over three trimesters
This is below the recommended 11 to 15 kg for a normal-weight patient.
18 to 23 kg (40 to 50 lb) over three trimesters
This exceeds the recommended 11 to 15 kg for a normal-weight patient.
2 to 4 kg (4 to 9 lb) over three trimesters
This is far below the recommended gain needed for maternal and fetal tissue growth.

alt.q: A patient of normal weight for height gained a total of 30 lb during pregnancy. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: The gain is within the recommended 25 to 35 lb range
alt.ex: Recommended gain for a normal-weight patient is 11 to 15 kg (25 to 35 lb) over three trimesters.
w: The gain is below the recommended 40 to 50 lb range
The recommended range for normal weight is 25 to 35 lb, not 40 to 50 lb.
The gain is above the recommended 15 to 20 lb range
The recommended range is 25 to 35 lb, so 30 lb is not excessive.
The gain is above the recommended 10 to 15 lb range
The recommended range is 25 to 35 lb, so 30 lb is appropriate.

items.q: Which birth weight defines low birth weight?
items.a: Less than 2500 g (5.5 lb)
items.ex: Low birth weight is less than 2500 g (5.5 lb); infants of teenage mothers have an increased risk.
w: Less than 3500 g (7.7 lb)
Many healthy newborns weigh under 3500 g; the cutoff is 2500 g.
Less than 4000 g (8.8 lb)
4000 g is within the average newborn range, not low birth weight.
Less than 1500 g (3.3 lb)
The low birth weight cutoff is 2500 g, so this value is too low.

alt.q: A newborn weighs 2300 g (5.1 lb). How should the nurse classify this weight?
alt.a: Low birth weight, because it is less than 2500 g
alt.ex: Low birth weight is defined as less than 2500 g (5.5 lb).
w: Normal birth weight, because it is more than 2000 g
The cutoff for low birth weight is 2500 g, not 2000 g.
Normal birth weight, because it is more than 1500 g
Weights under 2500 g are low birth weight.
Low birth weight, because it is less than 3000 g
The defining cutoff is 2500 g, not 3000 g.

items.q: A nurse is completing an initial prenatal assessment. Which question is especially important to include?
items.a: “Do you use any herbal supplements or other complementary therapies?”
items.ex: Some complementary therapies, such as herbal supplements, can be harmful during pregnancy, so the nurse asks about their use.
w: “Do you prefer morning or afternoon prenatal appointments?”
Scheduling preference does not address a potential risk to the pregnancy.
“Have you chosen a name for the baby yet?”
This is a social question and does not assess health risks.
“Which hospital did your parents use for their births?”
Family birth locations do not assess current risks to the pregnancy.

alt.q: A pregnant patient says, “I take an herbal tea blend because natural products are always safe.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Some herbal supplements can be harmful in pregnancy. Let’s review what is in it.”
alt.ex: Herbal supplements can be harmful during pregnancy, so the nurse gathers information and provides accurate teaching.
w: “Natural products are safe, so you can keep using it as you like.”
Herbal supplements are not automatically safe and some can harm the pregnancy.
“Herbal products only matter after the baby is born.”
Herbal supplements can affect the pregnancy itself.
“You should stop eating all plant-based foods right away.”
Normal foods are not the concern; certain herbal supplements are.

items.q: A 16-year-old comes for her first prenatal visit at 28 weeks of gestation. Which risk to the infant should the nurse recognize?
items.a: Prematurity and low birth weight
items.ex: Pregnant adolescents often seek prenatal care late, and infants of teenage mothers have an increased risk of prematurity and low birth weight.
w: Post-term birth and high birth weight
Infants of teenage mothers are at risk for prematurity and low birth weight, not the opposite.
Chromosomal defects related to maternal age
Chromosomal defect risk rises as females age, not in adolescence.
Delayed closure of the anterior fontanel
Fontanel closure is not a risk linked to teenage pregnancy in the text.

alt.q: Which pattern of prenatal care is commonly seen in pregnant adolescents?
alt.a: They often seek prenatal care late or not at all
alt.ex: Pregnant adolescents often seek prenatal care late in the pregnancy or fail to seek it, for a variety of reasons.
w: They usually begin prenatal care before conception
Preconception care is not typical for pregnant adolescents.
They usually attend more visits than older patients
Adolescents often seek care late or not at all.
They usually begin care in the first few weeks
Pregnant adolescents often delay prenatal care.

items.q: A pregnant patient states, “I’ve already gained a lot of weight, so my baby must be getting plenty of nutrients.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Weight gain doesn’t always mean more nutrients. Let’s look at what you’re eating.”
items.ex: An increase in weight does not always indicate an increase in nutrients, and the pattern of weight gain also matters.
w: “That’s right; weight gain shows the baby is well nourished.”
Weight gain alone does not show that nutrient needs are being met.
“You should stop gaining weight for the rest of the pregnancy.”
Continued weight gain in a healthy pattern is needed for maternal and fetal tissue growth.
“The amount you gain matters, but the pattern does not.”
The pattern of weight gain is important for tissue growth in the mother and fetus.

alt.q: Which statement by a pregnant patient shows understanding of nutrition teaching?
alt.a: “How I gain weight over each trimester matters, not just the total.”
alt.ex: The pattern of weight gain is important for tissue growth in the mother and fetus.
w: “As long as the scale goes up, my baby is getting enough nutrients.”
Weight gain does not always mean an increase in nutrients.
“My eating habits before pregnancy do not affect my baby.”
Poor nutrition before pregnancy can make it hard to meet fetal needs.
“I should eat as little as possible to limit my weight gain.”
Inadequate nutrients and calories may fail to meet fetal requirements.

items.q: A patient in the first trimester reports nausea and breast tenderness and asks if something is wrong. Which nursing response is best?
items.a: Explain that these are common discomforts and teach safe self-care measures
items.ex: Nurses anticipate common discomforts, explain their physiological causes, and offer safe treatment suggestions.
w: Tell the patient to go to the emergency department right away
Nausea and breast tenderness are common pregnancy discomforts, not emergencies.
Tell the patient that these symptoms will last the whole pregnancy
This is not accurate teaching and does not help the patient manage the discomfort.
Recommend the patient start an herbal remedy for the nausea
Some herbal supplements can be harmful during pregnancy.

alt.q: Why does the nurse explain the physiological causes of common pregnancy discomforts?
alt.a: Understanding the causes and safe treatments supports the patient’s health
alt.ex: Discussing causes and safe treatments is helpful to expectant mothers and contributes to overall health during pregnancy.
w: Understanding the causes means no treatment will be needed
Explanation is paired with suggestions for safe treatment.
Understanding the causes is required before any prenatal visit
This is not a requirement; it is supportive teaching.
Understanding the causes prevents all discomforts from occurring
Fetal growth and hormonal changes often cause discomforts regardless of teaching.

items.q: A patient planning a first pregnancy at age 42 asks about age-related concerns. Which information is accurate?
items.a: As females age, the risk of chromosomal defects and infertility increases
items.ex: Maternal age can affect fertility, fetal health, and maternal health, with chromosomal defects and infertility rising with age.
w: As females age, the risk of chromosomal defects decreases
The risk of chromosomal defects increases, not decreases, with age.
As females age, fertility increases until menopause
Infertility risk increases as females age.
As females age, maternal age no longer affects the fetus
Maternal age can affect the health of the fetus.

alt.q: Which group of patients faces an increasing risk of chromosomal defects in the fetus?
alt.a: Females who become pregnant at older ages
alt.ex: As females age, the risk of chromosomal defects and infertility increases.
w: Females who become pregnant as adolescents
Adolescent pregnancy is linked to prematurity and low birth weight, not chromosomal defects.
Females who gain the recommended weight
Appropriate weight gain is not linked to increased chromosomal defects.
Females who start prenatal care early
Early prenatal care does not raise the risk of chromosomal defects.

items.q: Which factors determine the effect of a teratogen on the developing fetus? (Select all that apply.)
o: The developmental stage when exposure occurs
Timing matters; the embryonic stage is the most vulnerable.
Individual genetic susceptibility
Genetic susceptibility influences how a teratogen affects development.
The extent of the exposure
The amount or degree of exposure affects the outcome.
The sex of the fetus
Fetal sex is not listed as a factor that determines teratogen effects.
The season of the year the exposure occurs
Season is not a factor; stage, susceptibility, and extent are.
items.ex: Teratogen effects depend on the developmental stage at exposure, genetic susceptibility, and extent of exposure.

alt.q: A nurse explains why two fetuses exposed to the same drug may be affected differently. Which reasons are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
o: Exposure occurred at different developmental stages
The stage of development at exposure affects the result.
The fetuses differ in genetic susceptibility
Individual genetic susceptibility changes the effect.
The amount of exposure was different
The extent of exposure influences the outcome.
One placenta blocked the drug completely
The placenta is extremely porous, so drugs pass through it.
The drug only affects fetuses after birth
Teratogens act during development before birth.
alt.ex: Correct: Exposure occurred at different developmental stages; The fetuses differ in genetic susceptibility; The amount of exposure was different.

items.q: Which are common discomforts of pregnancy that the nurse should anticipate? (Select all that apply.)
o: Urinary frequency
Urinary frequency is a common pregnancy discomfort.
Heartburn
Heartburn is commonly reported during pregnancy.
Ankle edema
Ankle edema is a common discomfort related to pregnancy changes.
Backache
Backache is a common concern expressed by expectant mothers.
Diarrhea
Constipation, not diarrhea, is listed as a common discomfort.
Decreased urination
Urinary frequency, not decreased urination, is common.
items.ex: Fetal growth and hormonal changes often cause discomforts such as nausea, breast tenderness, urinary frequency, heartburn, constipation, ankle edema, and backache.

alt.q: A patient asks which symptoms are common in pregnancy. Which should the nurse include? (Select all that apply.)
o: Nausea and vomiting
Nausea and vomiting are common pregnancy discomforts.
Breast tenderness
Breast tenderness is commonly reported.
Constipation
Constipation is a common discomfort of pregnancy.
Increased appetite for nonfood items only
This is not listed among the common discomforts.
Decreased breast size
Breast tenderness, not decreased size, is a common change.
alt.ex: Correct: Nausea and vomiting; Breast tenderness; Constipation.

items.q: Which functions does the placenta perform for the fetus? (Select all that apply.)
o: Acts as the fetal lungs
The placenta functions as the fetal lungs.
Acts as the fetal kidneys
The placenta functions as the fetal kidneys.
Acts as the fetal gastrointestinal tract
The placenta functions as the fetal GI tract.
Produces hormones that help maintain the pregnancy
The placenta produces essential hormones that maintain pregnancy.
Filters out viruses before they reach the fetus
The placenta is extremely porous, so viruses can pass through.
Prevents maternal drugs from reaching the fetus
Drugs pass across the porous placenta and can act as teratogens.
items.ex: The placenta functions as fetal lungs, kidneys, GI tract, and endocrine organ, but its porosity lets harmful agents through.

alt.q: Which statements about the placenta are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
o: It functions as an endocrine organ
The placenta functions as the fetal endocrine organ.
It is extremely porous
Its porosity allows viruses, chemicals, and drugs to pass.
It begins developing in the embryonic stage
Placental development begins at the third week of the embryonic stage.
It blocks all chemicals from crossing to the fetus
Chemicals can pass from the mother to the fetus.
It begins developing after the eighth week
The placenta begins developing during the embryonic stage.
alt.ex: Correct: It functions as an endocrine organ; It is extremely porous; It begins developing in the embryonic stage.

items.q: The fetal stage lasts from the end of the eighth week of gestation until birth.
items.a: True
items.ex: After the preembryonic and embryonic stages, the fetal stage runs from the end of the eighth week until birth.
items.ww: The fetal stage is the final prenatal stage, beginning at the end of week 8 and ending at birth.

alt.q: The fetal stage begins on day 15 after fertilization.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Day 15 begins the embryonic stage; the fetal stage starts at the end of the eighth week.
alt.ww: Day 15 marks the start of the embryonic stage, which precedes the fetal stage.

items.q: Because the placenta is extremely porous, viruses, chemicals, and drugs can pass from the mother to the developing child.
items.a: True
items.ex: The porous placenta lets noxious materials pass, and these teratogens can cause abnormal development.
items.ww: The placenta is not a complete barrier; harmful agents do cross it.

alt.q: The placenta acts as a complete barrier that protects the fetus from drugs the mother takes.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The placenta is extremely porous, so drugs and other teratogens pass to the fetus.
alt.ww: Drugs can cross the placenta, so it does not fully protect the fetus.

items.q: Family dynamics have little effect on fetal development, so the nurse focuses only on physical health during pregnancy.
items.a: False
items.ex: Family dynamics affect fetal development, so the nurse listens to concerns of the mother and partner and offers support each trimester.
items.ww: Pregnancy is a developmental challenge with emotional and family dimensions that affect the fetus, so psychosocial support matters.

alt.q: Family dynamics affect fetal development, so the nurse listens to concerns and offers support through each trimester.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Pregnancy can be a period of conflict or support, and family dynamics influence fetal development.
alt.ww: Ignoring family dynamics would overlook a recognized influence on fetal development.

sections.name: Transition from intrauterine to extrauterine life

items.q: During what time period does the transition from intrauterine to extrauterine life occur?
items.a: The first 24 hours of life
items.ex: The transition requires profound physiological changes and occurs during the first 24 hours, so close assessment is essential.
w: The first 2 hours of life
The transition extends through the first 24 hours, not just the first 2 hours.
The first 7 days of life
The transition occurs in the first 24 hours; the neonatal period lasts longer.
The first 28 days of life
The first 28 days is the neonatal period; the transition occurs within the first 24 hours.

alt.q: Why is careful assessment of the newborn especially important during the first 24 hours of life?
alt.a: Profound physiological changes occur as the newborn adapts to extrauterine life
alt.ex: Assessment during the transition ensures that these profound changes proceed as expected.
w: Profound growth in height occurs during the first day
The concern is physiological adaptation, not growth in height.
Most newborn reflexes disappear during the first day
Newborn reflexes persist; the focus is physiological transition.
Attachment can begin only after the first day ends
Attachment begins during pregnancy and early contact is encouraged right after birth.

items.q: Which assessment tool is most widely used to evaluate a newborn’s condition immediately after birth?
items.a: Apgar score
items.ex: The Apgar score rates heart rate, respiratory effort, muscle tone, reflex irritability, and skin color to determine overall status.
w: Gestational age assessment
Gestational age is assessed after the comprehensive physical assessment, not as the immediate birth assessment.
Head circumference measurement
Head circumference is one measurement in the comprehensive assessment, not the immediate status tool.
Denver developmental screening
Developmental screening is not used to evaluate immediate physiological status at birth.

alt.q: What is the purpose of the Apgar score?
alt.a: To determine the newborn’s overall status at birth
alt.ex: The Apgar score assesses the physiological functioning of major organ systems to determine overall status.
w: To estimate the newborn’s gestational age
Gestational age is assessed separately after the physical assessment.
To predict the newborn’s adult height
The Apgar score does not predict growth.
To measure parent-newborn attachment
Attachment is assessed through parent-newborn interactions, not the Apgar score.

items.q: When is the Apgar assessment generally conducted?
items.a: At 1 and 5 minutes after birth, repeated until the newborn stabilizes
items.ex: The Apgar is done at 1 and 5 minutes and is sometimes repeated until the newborn’s condition stabilizes.
w: At 10 and 30 minutes after birth, then stopped
The Apgar is generally done at 1 and 5 minutes after birth.
At 1 and 24 hours after birth, then stopped
Apgar timing is in minutes, not hours, and can be repeated until stable.
Once, at 1 minute after birth, never repeated
It is done at both 1 and 5 minutes and sometimes repeated.

alt.q: A newborn’s condition has not stabilized after the 5-minute Apgar assessment. What should the nurse expect?
alt.a: The Apgar assessment may be repeated until the newborn stabilizes
alt.ex: The Apgar is sometimes repeated beyond 5 minutes until the newborn’s condition stabilizes.
w: The Apgar assessment is not repeated after 5 minutes
It can be repeated until the newborn’s condition stabilizes.
The Apgar assessment is replaced by a gestational age exam
Gestational age assessment does not replace evaluation of overall status.
The Apgar assessment is postponed until the next day
Ongoing assessment during the transition is essential, not delayed.

items.q: Which physiological change at birth is considered the most extreme?
items.a: Leaving the uterine circulation and developing independent circulation and respiration
items.ex: The most extreme change is the shift from uterine circulation to independent circulatory and respiratory functioning.
w: Beginning to regulate weight and grow in length after birth
Growth continues after birth, but it is not the most extreme change at birth.
Developing the first reflexes and responding to sounds after birth
Reflexes are present at birth; the greatest change is circulatory and respiratory.
Starting to digest breast milk or formula after birth
Feeding is a major change, but circulatory and respiratory independence is the most extreme.

alt.q: A nursing student asks what makes the moment of birth so physiologically demanding. Which answer is best?
alt.a: The newborn must begin breathing and circulating blood independently
alt.ex: Leaving the uterine circulation and developing independent circulatory and respiratory function is the most extreme change.
w: The newborn must begin making antibodies independently
The newborn’s immune system is immature; the most extreme change is circulatory and respiratory.
The newborn must begin walking reflexes independently
Reflexes are not the most extreme change at birth.
The newborn must begin digesting solid food independently
Newborns do not eat solid food; the main change is circulation and breathing.

items.q: Why is it essential to stabilize and maintain a newborn’s body temperature?
items.a: Hypothermia increases the newborn’s oxygen needs
items.ex: Newborns are prone to heat loss and cold stress, and hypothermia increases oxygen needs.
w: Hypothermia decreases the newborn’s oxygen needs
Hypothermia increases, not decreases, oxygen needs.
Hypothermia speeds the newborn’s weight gain
Cold stress does not promote weight gain; it raises oxygen needs.

items.q: When should the nurse perform the comprehensive assessment of a newborn?
items.a: As soon as physiological functioning is stable, generally within a few hours after birth
items.ex: A comprehensive assessment is done once the newborn is physiologically stable, generally within a few hours of birth.
w: Only after the newborn has regained birth weight in the second week
Waiting two weeks would delay the baseline needed for future comparison.
Immediately at delivery, before the newborn’s functioning has stabilized
The book directs the assessment after physiological functioning is stable.
At the first outpatient visit after discharge from the agency
Accurate measurement as soon as possible after birth gives a baseline for comparison.

alt.q: After completing a comprehensive physical assessment of a newborn, what should the nurse assess next?
alt.a: Gestational age and parent-newborn interactions that indicate attachment
alt.ex: After the physical assessment, the nurse assesses gestational age and interactions showing successful attachment.
w: Fine-motor skills such as reaching for and grasping a rattle
Grasping a rattle briefly is an infant skill at about 2 months.
Object permanence and early memory development
Object permanence develops at about 7 to 9 months.
Readiness to begin solid foods and iron supplements
Solid foods are not recommended before 6 months of age.

items.q: At what distance from the face can a newborn focus on objects?
items.a: About 20 to 30 cm (8–12 inches)
items.ex: At birth newborns focus on objects about 20 to 30 cm (8–12 inches) away and perceive forms.
w: About 5 to 10 cm (2–4 inches)
This is closer than the 20 to 30 cm focal distance described.
About 60 to 90 cm (24–36 inches)
This is farther than the 20 to 30 cm focal distance described.
About 120 to 150 cm (4–5 feet)
Newborns focus only at about 20 to 30 cm, not across a room.

alt.q: Which visual stimuli do newborns respond to best?
alt.a: Human faces, black-and-white contrasting patterns, and bright colors
alt.ex: Newborns respond to human faces, black-and-white contrasting patterns, and bright colors.
w: Pastel colors and soft, low-contrast patterns
Newborns respond to contrast and bright colors, not low-contrast pastels.
Distant moving objects across the room
Newborns focus at only about 20 to 30 cm from their faces.
Printed words and small detailed pictures
Newborns perceive forms and contrast, not fine detail or print.

items.q: Parents ask how they can promote their newborn’s cognitive development. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Talk to your baby and hold her so she can see your face.”
items.ex: Sensory stimulation such as talking and showing the parent’s face lets newborns take in stimuli and promotes cognitive development.
w: “Keep her room quiet and dim so she is not overstimulated.”
Newborns learn by taking in stimuli; parents should provide sensory stimulation.
“Place a tablet with educational videos near her crib.”
The book stresses parental interaction, and screens should not replace parent-child interaction.
“Wait until she can sit up before playing with her.”
Stimulation should begin in the newborn period, not months later.

alt.q: A nurse has taught parents about sensory stimulation for their newborn. Which statement by a parent shows understanding?
alt.a: “I’ll talk to him and hold him close enough to see my face.”
alt.ex: Talking and letting the newborn see the parent’s face provide stimulation that enhances learning.
w: “I’ll avoid talking to him until he can recognize my voice.”
Newborns already respond to the primary caregiver’s voice; talking promotes development.
“I’ll hang pastel pictures on the far wall of his room.”
Newborns focus at 20 to 30 cm and prefer contrast and bright colors.
“I’ll let him cry so he learns to soothe himself early.”
Crying communicates an unmet need; parents should learn to respond to cues.

items.q: A mother says her 2-week-old cries a lot before scheduled feedings every 4 hours. Which suggestion by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: Feed the infant on demand rather than on a rigid schedule
items.ex: Newborn crying is generally a reflexive response to an unmet need such as hunger, so on-demand feeding is advised.
w: Offer water between feedings to stretch the schedule
Infants should not receive supplemental water in addition to breast milk or formula.
Let the infant cry until the scheduled feeding time
Crying when hungry signals an unmet need that parents should meet.
Begin adding cereal to feedings to keep the infant full
Solid foods are not recommended before 6 months of age.

alt.q: A parent is frustrated because they cannot tell why their newborn is crying. Which nursing action is best?
alt.a: Help the parent learn to recognize the newborn’s cry patterns and respond
alt.ex: With the nurse’s help, parents can learn the newborn’s cry patterns and take appropriate action.
w: Explain that newborn crying has no meaning at this age
Crying is a means of communication that gives cues about needs.
Advise the parent to ignore crying to avoid spoiling the baby
Crying usually reflects an unmet need, such as hunger or discomfort.
Suggest keeping the newborn on a strict feeding schedule
On-demand feeding is advised when a newborn cries from hunger.

items.q: A newborn with a congenital heart defect tires quickly during feedings, and the parents seem discouraged. Which nursing action best supports parent-infant attachment?
items.a: Point out the newborn’s positive qualities and responses to the parents
items.ex: Nurses support attachment by pointing out positive qualities and responses and acknowledging how hard separation can be.
w: Feed the newborn in the nursery so parents can rest
Removing parents from caregiving reduces the interactions that build attachment.
Tell the parents attachment will begin once the defect is repaired
Attachment develops through early interactions; the nurse supports it now.
Explain that weak newborn cues mean bonding cannot occur
Bonding can still occur; the nurse supports it by highlighting positive responses.

alt.q: Which newborn is at greatest risk for a compromised attachment process?
alt.a: A premature newborn too weak to respond to parental cues
alt.ex: Premature newborns and those with anomalies often give weak cues, making caregiving less mutually satisfying.
w: A term newborn who watches the caregiver’s face
Watching the caregiver’s face is a normal behavior that supports attachment.
A term newborn who cries when hungry and feeds well
Crying when hungry and feeding well are normal cues that support attachment.
A term newborn whose older sibling helps with bathing
Sibling involvement in care supports growth and promotes nurturing.

items.q: Parents should keep older siblings from participating in a newborn’s care during the first month to protect the newborn.
items.a: False
items.ex: Parents can allow siblings to take part in age-appropriate aspects of care; family involvement promotes nurturing.
items.ww: The chapter encourages sibling involvement in newborn care rather than excluding siblings.

alt.q: Allowing siblings to take part in age-appropriate aspects of newborn care helps support growth and development.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Family involvement, including siblings, supports growth and development and promotes nurturing.
alt.ww: The chapter states that sibling participation in age-appropriate care is beneficial, not harmful.

items.q: What is the purpose of newborn blood screening tests performed before discharge?
items.a: To identify serious conditions such as inborn errors of metabolism before symptoms begin
items.ex: Screening detects conditions such as PKU early so treatment can prevent permanent intellectual disabilities.
w: To confirm conditions in newborns who already show clear symptoms
Screening aims to find conditions before symptoms begin.
To determine the newborn’s gestational age after the physical assessment
Gestational age is assessed clinically, not by metabolic blood screening.
To measure the newborn’s immunity before the first vaccines are given
Blood screening targets inborn errors of metabolism, not immunity.

alt.q: Which condition is a newborn blood screening test designed to detect?
alt.a: Phenylketonuria
alt.ex: Neonatal blood screening detects PKU, hypothyroidism, galactosemia, and other inborn errors of metabolism.
w: Strabismus
Strabismus is detected by vision screening in the preschool years.
Sudden infant death syndrome
SIDS is reduced through safe sleep practices; it is not screened by a blood test.
Hearing loss
Hearing loss is found through universal newborn hearing screening, not blood tests.

items.q: [[Hearing loss]] is the most common congenital abnormality in newborns, so universal screening before discharge is recommended.
items.ex: Early detection of hearing loss leads to early treatment and can prevent delays, especially in communication.

alt.q: Universal newborn screening targets [[hearing loss]], the most common congenital abnormality, before discharge or within the first month.
alt.ex: Early detection of hearing loss leads to early treatment and can prevent delays, especially in communication.

items.q: A parent plans to place the newborn’s rear-facing car seat in the front passenger seat, which has an air bag. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “A rear-facing seat in front of an air bag is extremely dangerous.”
items.ex: Placing a rear-facing restraint in the front seat with a passenger-side air bag is extremely dangerous.
w: “That works if you turn the car seat to face forward instead.”
Infants should ride rear-facing until age 2 or the seat’s limits.
“That is fine as long as the harness straps are snug.”
Snug straps do not remove the danger of a passenger-side air bag.
“Holding the baby on your lap is safer than the front seat.”
An unrestrained child is at risk of death; a federally approved car seat is essential.

alt.q: Until when should infants and toddlers ride in a rear-facing car safety seat?
alt.a: Until 2 years of age or the seat’s highest allowed weight or height
alt.ex: Children should ride rear-facing until age 2 or until they reach the manufacturer’s highest weight or height limit.
w: Until 6 months of age or the seat’s lowest allowed weight
Turning forward at 6 months is far earlier than the recommendation.
Until 12 months of age or when the child can walk
The recommendation extends to 2 years, not 1 year or walking.
Until 4 years of age or the child can sit alone
The guideline is 2 years or the seat’s limits, not 4 years.

items.q: Which practices help reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS)? Select all that apply.
o: Placing the infant on the back to sleep
Back sleeping on a firm surface decreases SIDS risk.
Using a firm sleep surface
A firm sleep surface is recommended to reduce SIDS risk.
Removing pillows, bumper pads, and stuffed animals from the crib
Removing soft objects from the crib is a listed safeguard.
Avoiding overheating the infant
Avoiding overheating is a listed SIDS safeguard.
Bed sharing with the parents
Co-sleeping or bed sharing is associated with increased SIDS risk.
Placing the infant prone on a soft blanket
Infants should be placed on their backs on a firm surface.
items.ex: Safe sleep includes back positioning, a firm surface, a bare crib, no overheating, and no smoking.

alt.q: Which factors increase an infant’s risk for SIDS? Select all that apply.
o: Smoking around the infant
Smoking during pregnancy or around the infant raises SIDS risk.
Co-sleeping with the parents
Bed sharing is associated with an increased risk for SIDS.
Crib bumper pads and pillows
Soft items in the crib should be removed to reduce risk.
Overheating the infant
Avoiding overheating is a safeguard, so overheating increases risk.
Supine sleep position
Placing infants on their backs decreases SIDS risk.
A snug-fitting crib mattress
A snug-fitting mattress is a recommended crib safety feature.
alt.ex: Correct: Smoking around the infant; Co-sleeping with the parents; Crib bumper pads and pillows; Overheating the infant.

items.q: Parents plan to use an older crib from a relative. What is the maximum safe distance between the crib slats?
items.a: 6 cm (2.4 inches)
items.ex: Parents should check that crib slats are no more than 6 cm (2.4 inches) apart.
w: 10 cm (3.9 inches)
This exceeds the 6 cm maximum slat spacing.
12 cm (4.7 inches)
This is about twice the 6 cm maximum slat spacing.
15 cm (5.9 inches)
This far exceeds the 6 cm maximum slat spacing.

alt.q: Federal safety standards recommend a crib with a flat, firm surface whose head elevates no more than how much?
alt.a: Less than 10 degrees
alt.ex: Cribs should have a flat, firm surface with a head that elevates less than 10 degrees.
w: Less than 30 degrees
Thirty degrees is far steeper than the under-10-degree standard.
Less than 45 degrees
Forty-five degrees is far steeper than the under-10-degree standard.
Less than 20 degrees
Twenty degrees is double the under-10-degree standard.

items.q: Parents should remove crib mobiles as soon as the infant can reach them.
items.a: True
items.ex: Mobiles must be firmly attached with no hanging strings and removed once the infant can reach them.
items.ww: The chapter specifically instructs parents to remove mobiles once the infant can reach them.

alt.q: An older crib that does not meet current safety standards can be made safe by adding a new, firmer mattress.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Unsafe cribs that do not meet safety standards should be disassembled and thrown away.
alt.ww: The book says unsafe cribs must be disassembled and discarded, not modified with a new mattress.

items.q: A nurse assesses a 6-hour-old newborn. Which finding is most important to report?
items.a: Movement of the right arm and leg only
items.ex: Newborn movements are sporadic but symmetrical and involve all four extremities, so one-sided movement is abnormal.
w: Bluish color of the hands and feet
Cyanosis of the hands and feet is normal for the first 24 hours.
Spontaneous yawning and sneezing
Yawning and sneezing are normal newborn reflexes.
Watching the caregiver’s face
Newborns normally watch the caregiver’s face.

alt.q: A parent notices their 10-hour-old newborn’s hands and feet look bluish. The newborn is active with symmetrical movements. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Bluish hands and feet are normal during the first 24 hours.”
alt.ex: Cyanosis of the hands and feet is a normal newborn characteristic for the first 24 hours.
w: “This is a sign of a heart defect that needs evaluation.”
Acrocyanosis in the first 24 hours is expected, not a sign of a defect.
“This means your baby needs supplemental oxygen right now.”
Bluish extremities alone in the first day are a normal finding.
“This means the baby is too cold and needs a warm bath.”
This is normal acrocyanosis, and overheating infants should be avoided.

items.q: An infant weighed 3.5 kg (7.7 lb) at birth. At 12 months, which weight reflects expected growth?
items.a: About 10.5 kg (23 lb)
items.ex: Birth weight triples by 12 months, so 3.5 kg becomes about 10.5 kg.
w: About 7 kg (15.4 lb)
Doubling birth weight is expected at about 5 months, not 12 months.
About 14 kg (30.8 lb)
This is four times birth weight; weight triples by 12 months.
About 5 kg (11 lb)
This is far below the expected tripling of birth weight by 12 months.

alt.q: At about what age does an infant’s birth weight double?
alt.a: About 5 months
alt.ex: Birth weight doubles in approximately 5 months and triples by 12 months.
w: About 2 months
Two months is too early; doubling occurs at about 5 months.
About 12 months
By 12 months birth weight triples rather than doubles.
About 9 months
Doubling occurs earlier, at about 5 months.

items.q: A parent is upset that their 6-month-old has stayed near the 20th percentile on growth charts since birth. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Steady, proportional growth over time matters more than the exact measurements.”
items.ex: Steady and proportional growth is more important than absolute values, and serial measurements best monitor growth.
w: “Your baby is underweight and needs extra cereal added to bottles.”
Consistent growth on a percentile is reassuring, and solids are not advised before 6 months.
“Only measurements above the 50th percentile are considered normal.”
Growth norms include a range; steady growth matters more than absolute values.
“One measurement today will tell us whether your baby is healthy.”
Measurements recorded over time, not single values, best identify problems.

alt.q: What is the best way for a nurse to monitor an infant’s growth and identify problems?
alt.a: Compare measurements recorded over time on age- and sex-related charts
alt.ex: Measurements recorded over time are the best way to monitor growth and identify problems.
w: Compare one measurement with the parents’ adult heights
A single comparison with parents does not track the infant’s growth pattern.
Compare current weight with that of siblings at the same age
Sibling weights are not the norms used to judge an infant’s growth.
Compare one measurement with the average for all infants
Single absolute values matter less than steady, proportional growth over time.

items.q: Blinking, yawning, and coughing are newborn reflexes that disappear after several months.

alt.q: The Moro, or startle, reflex present at birth disappears after several months.

alt.ex: Grasping, rooting, sucking, and the Moro reflex disappear after several months of infancy.
alt.ww: The chapter lists the Moro reflex among those that fade, unlike blinking or coughing.

items.q: Which fine-motor skills are expected in an infant 8 to 10 months old? Select all that apply.
o: Picks up small objects
Table 12.1 lists picking up small objects at 8 to 10 months.
Begins to use a pincer grasp
The pincer grasp begins at 8 to 10 months.
Shows hand preference
Hand preference appears at 8 to 10 months.
Draws an arc with a pencil
Drawing an arc is expected by 24 months.
Turns book pages one at a time
Turning single pages is a toddler skill; at 10–12 months infants turn several at once.

alt.q: Which fine-motor skills are expected in an infant 6 to 8 months old? Select all that apply.

Banging objects together is listed for 6 to 8 months.

Places objects into containers
