w: Holds a bottle
Holding a bottle is expected at 4 to 6 months.
Pulls feet to mouth to explore
Pulling feet to mouth is expected at 4 to 6 months.
Turns from abdomen to back
Rolling from abdomen to back is expected by 5 months.

alt.q: A nurse assesses a 10-month-old. Which finding is most important to report?
alt.a: Unable to sit alone without support
alt.ex: Sitting alone without support is expected at 6 to 8 months, so its absence at 10 months suggests delay.
w: Not yet walking alone
At 10 to 12 months infants may only attempt a first step alone.
Turns several book pages at once
Turning more than one page at a time is expected at 10 to 12 months.
Pulls self to a standing position
Pulling to stand is expected at 8 to 10 months.

items.q: A 9-month-old searches for a toy after the parent hides it under a blanket. Which milestone does this demonstrate?
items.a: Object permanence
items.ex: By 7 to 9 months infants realize unseen objects still exist, showing that memory is beginning to develop.
w: Separation and individuation
Individuation is learning where the self ends and the world begins.
Parallel play
Parallel play, playing beside another child, appears in toddlerhood.
Proximodistal development
Proximodistal describes central-to-peripheral motor development, not memory.

alt.q: Why is object permanence considered an important developmental milestone?
alt.a: It shows that the infant’s memory is beginning to develop
alt.ex: Realizing that unseen objects still exist demonstrates that memory is beginning to develop.
w: It shows that the infant can think from another’s point of view
Taking another’s view develops later; toddlers still cannot assume others’ views.
It shows that the infant has mastered cause-and-effect reasoning
Cause-and-effect awareness begins in the preschool years.
It shows that the infant is ready to begin solid foods
Solid food readiness relates to gastrointestinal maturity at 6 months.

items.q: A 4-month-old receiving tube feedings in the hospital has little energy. Which nursing action best promotes cognitive development while conserving energy?
items.a: Offer a pacifier and talk to the infant
items.ex: Offering a pacifier and talking stimulates the infant according to energy level while conserving energy.
w: Keep the infant in a quiet room without stimulation
Lack of stimulation can slow cognitive development in ill infants.
Schedule long active play sessions twice a day
Long sessions ignore the infant’s limited energy level.
Wait until discharge to provide developmental stimulation
Ill infants need stimulation now to avoid slowed cognitive development.

alt.q: According to Piaget, what is the first stage of cognitive development, which begins in infancy?
alt.a: Sensorimotor period
alt.ex: In the sensorimotor period, lasting until about the third birthday, infants explore their world through the senses.
w: Preoperational stage
The preoperational stage begins in toddlerhood as thinking becomes more symbolic.
Concrete operations stage
Concrete operations is a later school-age stage.
Formal operations stage
Formal operations is the adolescent stage of abstract thought.

items.q: Which language abilities are expected of a typical 1-year-old?
items.a: Says 3 to 5 words and understands almost 100 words
items.ex: By 1 year infants recognize their names, say 3 to 5 words, and understand almost 100 words.
w: Says about 300 words and uses two-word sentences
This describes a 24-month-old toddler.
Says about 10 words and understands about 50 words
About 10 words is expected at 18 months.
Says no words and understands about 10 words
This underestimates the 1-year-old’s expected language abilities.

alt.q: Parents ask how to help their 10-month-old’s language development. Which suggestion by the nurse is best?
alt.a: Name the objects the infant’s attention is focused on
alt.ex: Nurses promote language by encouraging parents to name objects on which the infant’s attention is focused.
w: Play recorded speech so the infant hears many words
Recorded media do not replace parent-child interaction for language development.
Avoid talking until the infant begins to say words
Waiting withholds the interaction that builds language.
Use only single sounds the infant can already make
Naming real objects builds comprehension better than limiting speech.

items.q: According to Erikson, what determines whether an infant develops trust or mistrust?
items.a: The quality of parent-infant interactions and the care the infant receives
items.ex: Infants learn to trust self, others, and the world through the parent-child relationship and the care received.
w: The infant’s rate of physical growth during the first year
Growth rate does not determine trust; relationships and care do.
The age at which the infant achieves object permanence
Object permanence is a cognitive milestone, not Erikson’s determinant of trust.
The number of toys available for solitary play
Toys support play, but trust develops through the quality of care.

alt.q: An 8-month-old is hospitalized, and the parents cannot stay at the bedside. Which nursing action best fosters the infant’s trust?
alt.a: Limit the number of different caregivers and follow the parents’ care directions
alt.ex: Fewer caregivers and following parents’ directions support continued development of trust during separation.
w: Rotate many nurses so the infant adapts to new people
More caregivers complicate attachment and undermine trust.
Schedule all painful procedures during parent visits
Linking parents with painful procedures does not foster trust; limit negative experiences.
Keep the infant in the crib and limit holding
Infants need pleasurable sensations to support psychosocial development.

items.q: Erikson described the psychosocial crisis of infancy as trust versus [[mistrust]].
items.ex: During infancy the quality of parent-infant interaction determines whether trust or mistrust develops.

alt.q: The infant’s developmental crisis is [[trust|trust versus mistrust]], learned through the parent-child relationship.
alt.ex: During infancy the quality of parent-infant interaction determines whether trust or mistrust develops.

items.q: Which findings are warning signs of child abuse? Select all that apply.
o: A delay in seeking treatment for an injury
Delayed treatment is listed in Box 12.1.
Conflicting or changing stories about the injury
Changing accounts of the trauma are a warning sign.
Injury blamed on a sibling or another party
Blaming the injury on another party is a warning sign.
Frequent visits to emergency departments at multiple facilities
Visits to many facilities is listed in Box 12.1.
A history that matches the pattern of injury
A compatible history is reassuring; an incompatible history is the warning sign.
Prompt treatment sought by a caregiver with a consistent story
Delay and inconsistency, not prompt consistent reports, raise suspicion.
items.ex: A combination of signs or a pattern of injury, such as delays and inconsistent histories, raises suspicion of maltreatment.

alt.q: A nurse evaluates a child in the clinic. Which findings should raise suspicion of abuse? Select all that apply.
o: A child brought in for a cold who has signs of physical trauma
An initial complaint unrelated to the findings is a warning sign.
An older child who looks at the caregiver before answering
This inappropriate response of the child is a warning sign.
Previous reports of abuse in the family
Prior family abuse reports are listed in Box 12.1.
Evidence of previous injuries over time
Physical evidence of injury over time is a warning sign.
A history consistent with the child’s developmental age
Histories inconsistent with developmental age, not consistent ones, raise concern.
alt.ex: Correct: A child brought in for a cold who has signs of physical trauma; An older child who looks at the caregiver before answering; Previous reports of abuse in the family; Evidence of previous injuries over time.

items.q: A caregiver brings a 6-month-old with a scald burn and says the infant turned on the hot water faucet. Which warning sign of abuse does this represent?
items.a: A history inconsistent with the child’s developmental age
items.ex: A 6-month-old cannot turn on hot water, so the history does not fit the infant’s developmental abilities.
w: Delay in seeking treatment
Nothing in the scenario suggests the caregiver delayed care.
Previous reports of abuse in the family
No prior reports are described in this situation.
Frequent visits to multiple facilities
No pattern of visits to multiple facilities is described.

alt.q: A nurse suspects that an infant’s injuries result from maltreatment. Which action is required?
alt.a: Report the suspected maltreatment to the appropriate authorities
alt.ex: Nurses are mandated reporters and must report suspected child maltreatment to authorities by law.
w: Wait for proof of abuse before reporting
The law requires reporting suspicion; proof is not needed first.
Ask the caregiver to explain before deciding to report
The nurse must report suspected maltreatment regardless of explanations.
Document the findings and discuss them at the next visit
Delaying action fails the legal duty to report suspected maltreatment.

items.q: More children suffer from neglect than from any other type of maltreatment.
items.a: True
items.ex: Neglect is the most common form of child maltreatment, and children often experience more than one type.
items.ww: The chapter states that neglect affects more children than any other type of maltreatment.

alt.q: Physical abuse is the most common type of child maltreatment, and children who are abused usually experience only one type.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Neglect is the most common type, and maltreated children often experience more than one type.
alt.ww: The chapter names neglect as most common and notes multiple types of maltreatment are frequent.

items.q: The parent of an 8-month-old who is formula fed asks about switching to whole cow’s milk. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Continue iron-fortified formula; cow’s milk is not recommended before 12 months.”
items.ex: Whole cow’s milk, 2% milk, or alternate milk products are not recommended before 12 months of age.
w: “Switch now to 2% cow’s milk to prevent obesity.”
No cow’s milk, including 2%, is recommended before 12 months.
“Whole milk is fine if you also give juice for vitamins.”
Cow’s milk is not advised before 12 months, and juice should be avoided.
“You can switch at 6 months once solid foods start.”
Cow’s milk is not recommended until 12 months, regardless of solid foods.

alt.q: A parent who cannot breastfeed asks what to feed her newborn. Which recommendation by the nurse is appropriate?
alt.a: Iron-fortified commercially prepared formula
alt.ex: When breastfeeding is not possible or desired, iron-fortified commercially prepared formula is the acceptable alternative.
w: Whole cow’s milk diluted with water
Cow’s milk is not recommended before 12 months, and supplemental water should be avoided.
Low-iron formula to prevent constipation
Formula-fed infants need iron-fortified formula throughout the first year.
An alternate milk product such as soy beverage
Alternate milk products are not recommended before 12 months.

items.q: A nurse has taught a parent about introducing solid foods. Which statement by the parent shows understanding?
items.a: “I’ll start solids at 6 months and give each new food about a week.”
items.ex: Solids start at 6 months, and introducing one food for about a week makes food sensitivities easier to identify.
w: “I’ll start rice cereal at 2 months to help her sleep.”
Solids before 6 months expose infants to food antigens that cause allergies.
“I’ll introduce three new foods each day to add variety.”
Introducing several foods together makes it hard to identify a reaction.
“I’ll give fruit juice daily once she starts eating solids.”
Fruit juices do not provide sufficient and appropriate calories for infants.

alt.q: Why are solid foods not recommended before 6 months of age?
alt.a: The gastrointestinal tract is not mature enough to handle complex nutrients
alt.ex: An immature GI tract cannot handle complex nutrients, and early solids expose infants to antigens causing food allergies.
w: Solid foods provide too much iron for young infants
Iron excess is not the reason; GI immaturity and allergy risk are.
Infants cannot swallow until the sucking reflex disappears
Swallowing is present at birth as a normal newborn reflex.
Solid foods interfere with fluoride absorption from breast milk
Breast milk lacks adequate fluoride; this is not why solids are delayed.

items.q: Which statements about infant vitamin and mineral needs are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: A breastfed infant absorbs adequate iron from breast milk for the first 4 to 6 months
Breast milk iron is well absorbed during the first 4 to 6 months.
After 6 months, iron-fortified cereal is generally an adequate iron source
Iron-fortified cereal usually meets iron needs after 6 months.
Formula-fed infants need iron-fortified formula throughout the first year
Formula iron is less readily absorbed, so fortified formula is needed all year.
Breastfed infants under 6 months generally need fluoride supplements
Fluoride supplementation is generally not needed for breastfed infants under 6 months.
Infants should receive water between breast milk feedings
Infants should not receive supplemental fluids such as water or juice.
items.ex: Iron needs are met by breast milk early, fortified cereal later, and fortified formula all year for formula-fed infants.

alt.q: A nurse teaches parents of a breastfed 3-month-old about supplements. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: “Your baby is absorbing enough iron from breast milk right now.”
Breastfed infants absorb adequate iron during the first 4 to 6 months.
“Fluoride drops are generally not needed before 6 months.”
Supplementation in breastfed infants under 6 months is generally not needed.
“Tell us about any herbal or alternative products you use.”
Nurses ask about alternative therapies to help determine their safety.
“Start iron-fortified cereal now to boost her iron.”
Iron-fortified cereal is a supplemental source after 6 months, not at 3 months.
“Give a little juice daily for extra vitamins.”
Infants should not receive juice; it lacks appropriate calories.
alt.ex: Correct: “Your baby is absorbing enough iron from breast milk right now.”; “Fluoride drops are generally not needed before 6 months.”; “Tell us about any herbal or alternative products you use.”

items.q: Which common side effects of immunizations should the nurse teach parents to expect?
items.a: Low-grade fever and tenderness at the injection site
items.ex: Minor side effects such as low-grade fever and local tenderness are common; serious reactions are rare.
w: High fever and seizures within hours
Serious reactions are rare; minor effects such as low-grade fever are common.
A widespread rash and joint swelling
These are not the common side effects the chapter describes.
Loss of appetite lasting several weeks
Common side effects are minor and short-lived, such as local tenderness.

alt.q: A nurse is about to give immunizations to a 2-month-old. Which intervention can reduce the infant’s pain?
alt.a: Have the parent breastfeed or swaddle the infant during the injections
alt.ex: Breastfeeding and swaddling are interventions to reduce or eliminate infant pain during immunizations.
w: Delay the vaccines until the infant is older
The primary series should begin soon after birth; delay is not pain relief.
Give all doses quickly without comfort measures
The book directs using interventions to reduce immunization pain.
Have the parent leave the room during the injections
Parent comfort measures such as breastfeeding help reduce pain.

items.q: By 6 months of age, most infants show nocturnal sleep patterns and sleep 9 to 11 hours at night.
items.a: True
items.ex: Many infants have days and nights reversed until 3 to 4 months, but by 6 months most sleep 9 to 11 hours at night.
items.ww: The chapter describes this nighttime pattern for most 6-month-olds.

alt.q: Most infants sleep through the night from birth, and day-night reversal is rarely seen in the first months.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Many infants have days and nights reversed until 3 to 4 months of age.
alt.ww: Day-night reversal is common early; nocturnal patterns appear by about 6 months.

items.q: Which age range defines toddlerhood?
items.a: 12 to 36 months
items.ex: Toddlerhood spans 12 to 36 months, with increased independence from greater mobility and cognitive abilities.
w: 1 to 12 months
This is infancy.
3 to 5 years
This is the preschool period.
6 to 12 months
This is the second half of infancy.

alt.q: A 30-month-old is in which developmental stage?
alt.a: Toddler
alt.ex: Toddlerhood runs from 12 to 36 months, so a 30-month-old is a toddler.
w: Infant
Infancy ends at 1 year of age.
Preschooler
The preschool period begins at 3 years of age.
Newborn
The neonatal period is only the first 28 days.

items.q: A nurse needs to give oral medication to a 2-year-old. Which approach is best?
items.a: “It’s time for your medicine. Do you want water or juice with it?”
items.ex: Limiting chances for a “no” answer while offering an acceptable choice reduces negativism and supports control.
w: “Do you want to take your medicine now?”
This invites a “no” answer, which the nurse should avoid with toddlers.
“Would you like to take your medicine later instead?”
This invites refusal and does not set a firm limit.
“If you don’t take it, you can’t see your mommy.”
Threatening separation is not an appropriate strategy and increases distress.

alt.q: Parents report frequent temper tantrums in their 2-year-old. When are these behaviors most common?
alt.a: When parents stop the toddler’s initial independent action
alt.ex: Unsuccessful attempts at control cause negative behavior, most often when parents stop initial independent actions.
w: When the toddler is offered a choice between two options
Offering choices supports control and helps reduce negativism.
When the toddler succeeds at a new self-care skill
Success pleases toddlers and leads to more attempts at control.
When the toddler plays beside another child
Parallel play is normal toddler play and does not trigger tantrums.

items.q: How much does the average toddler grow in height each year?
items.a: About 7.5 cm (3 inches), mostly through leg elongation
items.ex: Toddlers grow about 7.5 cm (3 inches) a year, mostly by leg lengthening, and gain 1.8 to 2.7 kg.
w: About 15 cm (6 inches), mostly through trunk growth
This doubles the toddler’s annual height gain and misplaces where growth occurs.
About 2.5 cm (1 inch), mostly through head growth
This is the monthly height gain in early infancy.
About 12 cm (4.7 inches), mostly through trunk growth
This overstates the gain; toddlers grow mostly through leg elongation.

alt.q: How much weight does the average toddler gain each year?
alt.a: About 1.8 to 2.7 kg (4–6 lb)
alt.ex: Toddlers gain approximately 1.8 to 2.7 kg (4–6 lb) each year.
w: About 4.5 to 5.5 kg (10–12 lb)
This exceeds the toddler’s average annual weight gain.
About 0.5 to 1 kg (1–2 lb)
This is less than the toddler’s average annual weight gain.
About 6 to 7 kg (13–15 lb)
This exceeds even infant-like growth and is not the toddler average.

items.q: Which gross-motor skills do most children achieve by their third birthday? Select all that apply.
o: Riding a tricycle
Most toddlers ride tricycles by their third birthday.
Running well
Most toddlers run well by the third birthday.
Kicking a ball
Kicking a ball is among the toddler’s locomotion skills.
Standing on one foot for several seconds
Toddlers learn to stand on one foot for several seconds.
Skipping on alternate feet
Skipping on alternate feet is usually achieved by 5 years.
Jumping rope
Jumping rope is usually achieved by 5 years.
items.ex: Toddler locomotion includes running, jumping, standing on one foot, kicking, and riding a tricycle by age 3.

alt.q: Which fine-motor skills are expected by the end of toddlerhood? Select all that apply.
o: Stacking a small tower of blocks
By 3 years children usually stack a small tower of blocks.
Holding a crayon with the fingers
Toddlers move from a fist grip to holding crayons with their fingers.
Turning book pages one at a time
Toddlers can turn pages one at a time.
Drinking from a cup without spilling
Toddlers can drink well from a cup without spilling.
Copying triangles and diamonds
Triangles and diamonds are usually mastered at 5 to 6 years.
Copying squares
Copying squares is a preschool skill.
alt.ex: Correct: Stacking a small tower of blocks; Holding a crayon with the fingers; Turning book pages one at a time; Drinking from a cup without spilling.

items.q: In language development from toddler to preschooler, which milestone comes right after “Speaks in two-word sentences”?
items.a: Uses simple sentences and learns 5 or 6 new words daily
items.ex: That's milestone 3 of 4. About 10 words at 18 months, two-word sentences at 24, simple sentences at 36, and 4- to 5-word sentences by age 5.
w: Combines 4 to 5 words into sentences
That's milestone 4 of 4.
Uses about 10 words
That's milestone 1 of 4.

alt.q: Which milestone comes first in language development from toddler to preschooler?
alt.a: Uses about 10 words
alt.ex: That's milestone 1 of 4. About 10 words at 18 months, two-word sentences at 24, simple sentences at 36, and 4- to 5-word sentences by age 5.
w: Speaks in two-word sentences
That's milestone 2 of 4.
Uses simple sentences and learns 5 or 6 new words daily
That's milestone 3 of 4.
Combines 4 to 5 words into sentences
That's milestone 4 of 4.

alt.q: Which milestone comes last in language development from toddler to preschooler?
alt.a: Combines 4 to 5 words into sentences
alt.ex: That's milestone 4 of 4. About 10 words at 18 months, two-word sentences at 24, simple sentences at 36, and 4- to 5-word sentences by age 5.
w: Uses simple sentences and learns 5 or 6 new words daily
That's milestone 3 of 4.
Speaks in two-word sentences
That's milestone 2 of 4.
Uses about 10 words
That's milestone 1 of 4.

alt.q: In language development from toddler to preschooler, which milestone comes right after “Uses about 10 words”?
alt.a: Speaks in two-word sentences
alt.ex: That's milestone 2 of 4. About 10 words at 18 months, two-word sentences at 24, simple sentences at 36, and 4- to 5-word sentences by age 5.
w: Uses simple sentences and learns 5 or 6 new words daily
That's milestone 3 of 4.
Combines 4 to 5 words into sentences
That's milestone 4 of 4.

alt.q: In language development from toddler to preschooler, which milestone comes right after “Uses simple sentences and learns 5 or 6 new words daily”?
alt.a: Combines 4 to 5 words into sentences
alt.ex: That's milestone 4 of 4. About 10 words at 18 months, two-word sentences at 24, simple sentences at 36, and 4- to 5-word sentences by age 5.
w: Speaks in two-word sentences
That's milestone 2 of 4.
Uses about 10 words
That's milestone 1 of 4.

alt.q: In language development from toddler to preschooler, which milestone comes right before “Speaks in two-word sentences”?
alt.a: Uses about 10 words
alt.ex: That's milestone 1 of 4. About 10 words at 18 months, two-word sentences at 24, simple sentences at 36, and 4- to 5-word sentences by age 5.
w: Uses simple sentences and learns 5 or 6 new words daily
That's milestone 3 of 4.
Combines 4 to 5 words into sentences
That's milestone 4 of 4.

alt.q: In language development from toddler to preschooler, which milestone comes right before “Uses simple sentences and learns 5 or 6 new words daily”?
alt.a: Speaks in two-word sentences
alt.ex: That's milestone 2 of 4. About 10 words at 18 months, two-word sentences at 24, simple sentences at 36, and 4- to 5-word sentences by age 5.
w: Uses about 10 words
That's milestone 1 of 4.
Combines 4 to 5 words into sentences
That's milestone 4 of 4.

alt.q: In language development from toddler to preschooler, which milestone comes right before “Combines 4 to 5 words into sentences”?
alt.a: Uses simple sentences and learns 5 or 6 new words daily
alt.ex: That's milestone 3 of 4. About 10 words at 18 months, two-word sentences at 24, simple sentences at 36, and 4- to 5-word sentences by age 5.
w: Speaks in two-word sentences
That's milestone 2 of 4.
Uses about 10 words
That's milestone 1 of 4.

ord.q: Place these expressive language milestones in the order they typically appear.
items: Uses about 10 words
Speaks in two-word sentences
Uses simple sentences and learns 5 or 6 new words daily
Combines 4 to 5 words into sentences
ord.ex: About 10 words at 18 months, two-word sentences at 24, simple sentences at 36, and 4- to 5-word sentences by age 5.

items.q: Which vocabulary is typical of a 24-month-old child?
items.a: Up to 300 words, often in two-word sentences
items.ex: The 24-month-old has a vocabulary of up to 300 words and usually speaks in two-word sentences.
w: About 10 words, mostly single words
About 10 words is typical at 18 months.
About 2100 words in 4- to 5-word sentences
This describes a 5-year-old preschooler.
About 3 to 5 words, mostly single words
This is typical of a 1-year-old infant.

alt.q: A parent worries that their 2-year-old understands far more than they say. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “That’s expected; toddlers understand much more speech than they can say.”
alt.ex: A toddler’s ability to understand speech is much greater than the number of words acquired.
w: “That suggests a speech delay that needs a referral.”
Comprehension exceeding speech is normal in toddlerhood.
“Children should say every word they understand by age 2.”
Toddler comprehension normally exceeds spoken vocabulary.
“Limit talking to your child so they try harder to speak.”
Talking and reading to children best promotes language.

items.q: A toddler pretends to shave like daddy and uses a finger as a pretend gun. What cognitive ability does this show?
items.a: Using symbols to represent objects, places, and people
items.ex: Toddlers use symbols, imitating earlier-seen behavior and pretending one object is another.
w: Understanding cause-and-effect relationships
Toddlers do not yet grasp cause and effect; that awareness begins in preschool.
Assuming another person’s point of view
Toddlers are unable to assume the view of another.
Reasoning from the general to the specific
This reasoning begins as children near 5 years of age.

alt.q: According to Piaget, which stage of cognitive development begins in toddlerhood?
alt.a: Preoperational stage
alt.ex: The preoperational stage begins in toddlerhood, as children think more symbolically while vocabulary develops.
w: Sensorimotor stage
The sensorimotor period begins in infancy.
Concrete operations stage
Concrete operations is a school-age stage.
Formal operations stage
Formal operations is the adolescent stage.

items.q: A nurse has taught parents of a 2-year-old about promoting language. Which statement by a parent indicates a need for further teaching?
items.a: “Tablet videos will teach him words as well as we can.”
items.ex: Screens should not replace parent-child interaction because they have been shown to delay language development.
w: “We will read books with him every day.”
Reading expands vocabulary, knowledge, and imagination, so this shows understanding.
“We will talk with him during meals and play.”
Talking with children best facilitates language development.
“We will answer when he asks, ‘What’s that?’”
Answering typical toddler questions supports symbolic thinking and language.

alt.q: How do parents best facilitate a toddler’s language development?
alt.a: By talking and reading to the child
alt.ex: Parents facilitate language best by talking and reading to children, which expands vocabulary and imagination.
w: By providing educational television programs
Screen activities should not replace parent-child interaction and can delay language.
By correcting every grammatical error
The chapter emphasizes talking and reading, not constant correction.
By limiting conversation to simple commands
Rich conversation and reading, not commands alone, build vocabulary.

items.q: According to Erikson, which psychosocial sense emerges during toddlerhood?
items.a: Autonomy
items.ex: Toddlers develop autonomy, striving to do everything for themselves and master bodily functions.
w: Trust
Trust versus mistrust is the infant’s crisis.
Initiative
Initiative versus guilt is the preschooler’s crisis.
Industry
Industry develops during the school-age years.

alt.q: A 15-month-old insists on holding a cup but spills milk. Which suggestion to parents best supports autonomy?
alt.a: Use a two-handled cup with a spout and a plastic bib with a pocket
alt.ex: Encouraging safe independence, such as a two-handled spouted cup and pocket bib, supports the toddler’s autonomy.
w: Hold the cup for the toddler until spilling stops
Taking over blocks independence and may trigger negative behavior.
Offer milk only from a bottle until age 3
This prevents the toddler from learning self-feeding skills.
Remove milk from meals until the toddler is older
Toddlers need milk in limited amounts; removing it does not support autonomy.

items.q: Parallel play, in which a toddler plays beside rather than with another child, begins during toddlerhood.
items.a: True
items.ex: Toddlers continue solitary play and begin parallel play, playing beside rather than with another child.
items.ww: The chapter describes parallel play as the new form of play in toddlerhood.

alt.q: Toddlers typically engage in associative play, sharing similar activities with other children in a group.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Toddlers engage in solitary and parallel play; associative play begins after the third birthday.
alt.ww: Associative play is a preschool development; toddlers play beside rather than with others.

items.q: A nurse makes a home visit to a family with a 22-month-old in an older house. Which finding is most important to address?
items.a: Chipping paint on the windowsills
items.ex: Lead poisoning remains a serious hazard, often from chipping lead-based paint in older homes.
w: Toys stored in a low, open bin
Accessible safe toys support exploration and are not a hazard.
A two-handled cup with a spout
A two-handled spouted cup supports toddler independence safely.
Picture books on a low shelf
Books support language development and pose no safety risk.

alt.q: Why do poisonings occur frequently in children near 2 years of age?
alt.a: They put objects and substances in their mouths to learn about them
alt.ex: Toddlers near age 2 place objects in their mouths to learn, so poisons must be removed or locked up.
w: They can read labels but ignore warnings
Toddlers cannot read; mouthing is part of exploration.
They prefer bitter tastes to sweet ones
The reason is exploratory mouthing, not taste preference.
They have mastered opening locked cabinets
Locking up poisons is an effective safety measure for toddlers.

items.q: Toddlers’ lack of awareness of the danger of water and their new walking skills make drowning a major cause of accidental death in this age-group.
items.a: True
items.ex: New mobility plus unawareness of water danger makes drowning a major cause of accidental toddler death.
items.ww: The chapter names drowning as a major cause of accidental death in toddlers.

alt.q: Because toddlers naturally fear water, drowning is an uncommon cause of accidental death in this age-group.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Toddlers lack awareness of the danger of water, so drowning is a major cause of accidental death.
alt.ww: The chapter states the opposite: toddlers are unaware of water danger, and drowning is common.

items.q: A 2-year-old is admitted to the pediatric unit and cries when the parents leave. Which nursing action is best?
items.a: Encourage the parents to stay as much as possible and help provide care
items.ex: Hospitalized toddlers are stressed by separation; parental presence and participation build trust and cooperation.
w: Ask the parents to limit visits so the toddler adjusts
Limiting visits increases separation stress for toddlers.
Have the parents leave while the toddler sleeps
Toddlers fear separation; parents should stay as much as possible.
Assign a new nurse each shift to broaden trust
Trust grows through a trusting relationship with parents, not many caregivers.

alt.q: Why does establishing a trusting relationship with the parents help when caring for a hospitalized toddler?
alt.a: It often leads to the toddler accepting treatment
alt.ex: Supporting parents gains the toddler’s trust and cooperation, often resulting in acceptance of treatment.
w: It allows the nurse to exclude the parents from care
Nurses encourage parents to participate actively in care.
It eliminates the toddler’s fear of separation
Toddlers remain strongly attached and still fear separation.

Trust supports cooperation; it does not replace explanations.

items.q: A parent reports that their pale 20-month-old drinks about 6 cups of milk a day and eats little solid food. Which recommendation by the nurse is best?
items.a: Limit milk to 2 to 3 cups per day
items.ex: More than 1 quart of milk a day decreases appetite for solids and leads to inadequate iron intake.
w: Switch to skim milk and keep the same amount
Toddlers need fat until age 2, and the volume itself is the problem.
Add a fourth daily serving of milk at bedtime
Increasing milk further worsens appetite for iron-rich solid foods.
Replace milk with fruit juice between meals
Only nutritious snacks should be offered between meals.

alt.q: Why should toddlers drink no more than 2 to 3 cups of milk each day?
alt.a: Excess milk decreases appetite for solid foods and results in inadequate iron intake
alt.ex: Drinking more than 1 quart of milk daily reduces appetite for essential solids and causes inadequate iron intake.
w: Excess milk increases the risk of lead absorption
The chapter links excess milk to poor appetite and low iron, not lead.
Excess milk provides too much fat for brain growth
Toddlers need fat for growth; whole milk is advised until age 2.
Excess milk delays the development of sphincter control
Milk intake is not linked to sphincter control in the chapter.

items.q: Children should not be offered low-fat or skim milk until 2 years of age because they need fat for satisfactory physical and intellectual growth.
items.a: True
items.ex: Dietary fat supports physical and intellectual growth, so low-fat or skim milk is withheld until age 2.
items.ww: The chapter gives this exact recommendation and rationale.

alt.q: To prevent childhood obesity, toddlers should switch to skim milk as soon as they turn 1 year old.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Toddlers need fat for physical and intellectual growth, so low-fat or skim milk waits until age 2.
alt.ww: The chapter advises against low-fat or skim milk before 2 years despite obesity concerns.

items.q: A toddler’s desire to eat one food repeatedly is called a [[food jag|food jags]].
items.ex: Food jags are common in toddlers; parents should keep offering a variety of nutritious foods.

alt.q: When a toddler wants to eat only the same food again and again, the toddler is having a [[food jag|food jags]].
alt.ex: Food jags are common in toddlers; parents should keep offering a variety of nutritious foods.

items.q: A parent is upset that their 2-year-old wants only macaroni at every meal. Which advice by the nurse is best?
items.a: Offer a variety of nutritious foods at meals and only nutritious snacks between
items.ex: Rather than becoming disturbed by food jags, parents offer varied nutritious foods and nutritious snacks.
w: Require the toddler to finish each food before leaving the table
Struggles to control intake cause problem behavior and conflict.
Serve large portions so the toddler eats enough
Small, reasonable servings allow toddlers to finish their meals.
Spoon-feed the toddler to ensure a balanced intake
Finger foods let toddlers eat independently and satisfy their need for control.

alt.q: Why are finger foods recommended for toddlers?
alt.a: They let toddlers feed themselves, meeting their need for control
alt.ex: Finger foods allow self-feeding, satisfying the toddler’s need for independence and control.
w: They provide more iron than foods eaten with a spoon
Finger foods support independence; they are not chosen for iron content.
They prevent food jags by limiting choices
Food jags are managed by offering a variety of nutritious foods.
They shorten mealtimes so toddlers eat less
Small, reasonable servings, not finger foods, control portion size.

items.q: Which factors indicate a toddler’s readiness for toilet training? Select all that apply.
o: Sphincter control has developed
Sphincter control is required for toilet training.
The child can undress
The ability to undress is a readiness factor.
The child has the necessary language and cognitive abilities
Language and cognitive abilities are needed for training.
The child is motivated to hold on to please the parent
The toddler must want to hold on to please the parent.
The child has reached exactly 18 months of age
Readiness, not a set age, determines when to begin.
The parent wants training finished before a new sibling arrives
Parental schedules do not indicate the child’s readiness.
items.ex: Toilet training depends on locomotion, undressing, sphincter control, language, cognition, and motivation to please the parent.

alt.q: A nurse teaches parents about toilet training their toddler. Which points are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Watch for your child’s patterns and urge to urinate and defecate
Recognizing these patterns helps determine readiness.
Be patient and consistent
Patience and consistency are essential to success.
Keep a calm attitude during training
A calm attitude is essential for successful toilet training.
Start on a fixed date regardless of your child’s readiness
The child’s readiness, not a calendar date, is essential.
Begin before your child can undress or communicate needs
Undressing and language abilities are needed for training.
alt.ex: Correct: Watch for your child’s patterns and urge to urinate and defecate; Be patient and consistent; Keep a calm attitude during training.

items.q: A nurse teaches parents of a 2-year-old about injury prevention. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Lock up medications and cleaning materials
Removing or locking up possible poisons creates a safer environment for exploration.
Remove or secure poisonous household plants
Plants are among the possible poisons parents should remove or lock up.
Supervise the toddler closely around water
Toddlers are unaware of water danger, so drowning is a major cause of death.
Use the car seat according to safety guidelines
Some toddler deaths occur because car seat guidelines are not followed.
Allow free exploration of rooms that are not childproofed
Toddlers always need close supervision, especially when environments are not childproof.
Rely on telling the toddler that the stove is hot
Toddlers’ curiosity outpaces understanding; limit setting and supervision are needed.
items.ex: Toddler mobility and curiosity raise injury risk, so parents lock up poisons, supervise closely, and use car seats properly.

alt.q: Which factors place toddlers at increased risk for injury? Select all that apply.
o: Newly developed locomotion abilities
New mobility increases the toddler’s risk for injury.
Insatiable curiosity
Curiosity drives exploration that increases injury risk.
Mouthing objects to learn about them
Children near 2 years put objects in their mouths, causing frequent poisonings.
Lack of awareness of the danger of water
This makes drowning a major cause of toddler accidental death.
Improved balance that makes falls rare
Falls become much less of a problem in preschoolers, not toddlers.
A well-developed understanding of cause and effect
Toddlers do not yet grasp cause and effect.
alt.ex: Correct: Newly developed locomotion abilities; Insatiable curiosity; Mouthing objects to learn about them; Lack of awareness of the danger of water.

items.q: Which statement best describes the preschool period?
items.a: Ages 3 to 5 years, when physical development slows compared with cognitive and psychosocial development
items.ex: The preschool period spans 3 to 5 years, and physical development is slower than cognitive and psychosocial development.
w: Ages 12 to 36 months, when negativism and tantrums peak in frequency
This describes toddlerhood.
Ages 1 month to 1 year, when physical growth is the most dramatic
This describes infancy.
Ages 6 to 12 years, when formal schooling has already begun
Preschoolers are still eagerly awaiting formal education.

alt.q: Why do many people consider the preschool years the most intriguing years of parenting?
alt.a: Children are less negative and share thoughts and communicate more effectively
alt.ex: Preschoolers are less negative, share thoughts more accurately, and interact and communicate more effectively.
w: Children grow faster physically than in any other period
Physical growth slows in preschool; infancy has the most dramatic growth.
Children no longer need parental supervision for safety
Parents must continue close supervision of preschoolers’ activities.
Children have completed all their fine-motor development
Fine-motor skills are still being refined; triangles come at 5 to 6 years.

items.q: Which growth pattern is typical of preschoolers?
items.a: Weight gain of about 2 to 3 kg (4.5–6.5 lb) per year
items.ex: Preschoolers gain about 2 to 3 kg (4.5–6.5 lb) and grow 6.5 to 9 cm per year.
w: Weight gain of about 5 to 6 kg (11–13 lb) per year
This exceeds the preschooler’s average annual gain.
Weight gain of about 0.5 to 1 kg (1–2 lb) per year
This is less than the preschooler’s average annual gain.
Weight gain of about 7 to 8 kg (15–18 lb) per year
This far exceeds the preschooler’s average annual gain.

alt.q: By the fifth birthday, what is the average height of a child?

w: About 85 cm (33.5 inches)
This is shorter than the average 5-year-old height of 110 cm.
About 135 cm (53 inches)
This is taller than the average 5-year-old height of 110 cm.
About 150 cm (59 inches)
This far exceeds the average 5-year-old height of 110 cm.

items.q: Which motor skills does a child usually achieve by about 5 years of age? Select all that apply.
o: Skipping on alternate feet
By 5 years children usually skip on alternate feet.
Jumping rope
Jumping rope is usually achieved by 5 years.
Copying crosses and squares
Preschoolers learn to copy crosses and squares.
Beginning to skate and swim
By 5 years children begin to skate and swim.
Mastering triangles and diamonds by age 4
Triangles and diamonds are usually mastered between 5 and 6 years.
items.ex: Preschoolers refine coordination: skipping, jumping rope, skating, swimming, and copying crosses and squares.

alt.q: A nurse assesses a 4-year-old’s development. Which findings are expected? Select all that apply.
o: Runs well
Running well is a preschool gross-motor skill.
Walks up and down steps with ease
Preschoolers walk up and down steps easily.
Learning to hop
Hopping is learned during the preschool years.
Copies a diamond accurately
Diamonds are usually mastered between 5 and 6 years.
Prints letters and numbers fluently
Scribbling and drawing build skills needed later for printing.
alt.ex: Correct: Runs well; Walks up and down steps with ease; Learning to hop.

items.q: A 4-year-old has been hospitalized for several weeks with a chronic condition. Which nursing approach to developmental needs is best?
items.a: Provide ongoing developmental opportunities suited to the child’s energy
items.ex: Children with chronic or long hospitalizations need ongoing developmental opportunities woven into daily experiences.
w: Keep the child on strict bed rest until discharge from the hospital
Rest suits acute illness; chronic or long stays need developmental exposure.
Postpone all skill practice until the child returns home to family
Postponing deprives the child of needed developmental opportunities.
Exclude the child from usual daily activities to conserve energy
Exclusion suits acute illness, not prolonged hospitalization.

alt.q: Which child benefits most from rest and exclusion from usual daily activities?
alt.a: A 4-year-old with an acute illness
alt.ex: Children with acute illnesses benefit from rest; those with chronic conditions need ongoing developmental opportunities.
w: A 4-year-old with a chronic condition
Children with chronic conditions need ongoing exposure to developmental opportunities.
A 4-year-old hospitalized for several weeks
Long hospitalizations require ongoing developmental opportunities.
A 4-year-old recovering at home after a long stay
This child needs chances to practice skills, not exclusion.

items.q: A hospitalized 4-year-old says, “I cried last night, and that’s why the nurse gave me the shot.” What does this statement illustrate?
items.a: Early causal thinking that links events related in time
items.ex: Preschoolers link events related in time or space in a causal fashion, an early form of causal thinking.
w: Reasoning from the general to the specific
That reasoning begins near age 5, as in “I get a shot twice a day.”
Belief that inanimate objects have lifelike qualities
That belief appears in statements like “Trees cry when branches break.”
Understanding that punishment is socially mediated
Preschoolers do not yet realize punishment is socially mediated.

alt.q: A 4-year-old says, “Trees cry when their branches get broken.” Which characteristic of preschool thinking does this show?
alt.a: Belief that inanimate objects have lifelike qualities
alt.ex: Preschoolers believe inanimate objects have lifelike qualities and are capable of action.
w: Magical belief that thinking something makes it happen
Magical thinking concerns wishes causing events, not objects having feelings.
Reasoning from the general to the specific
This rule-based reasoning appears near age 5 and is not shown here.
Linking two events that occur close in time
This statement assigns feelings to an object rather than linking events in time.

items.q: According to the chapter, what is the greatest fear of preschool children?
items.a: Bodily harm
items.ex: Fear of bodily harm shows in fears of the dark, animals, thunderstorms, and medical personnel.
w: Separation from peers
The chapter names bodily harm, not peer separation, as the greatest fear.
Loss of independence
Loss of independence affects health feelings, but bodily harm is the greatest fear.
Failure at school
Preschoolers have not yet begun formal schooling.

alt.q: A 4-year-old refuses to let the nurse measure blood pressure. Which nursing action is most likely to gain cooperation?
alt.a: Let the child help measure the parent’s blood pressure first
alt.ex: Preschoolers cooperate when allowed to help measure a parent’s blood pressure or handle the nurse’s equipment.
w: Hold the child still and measure quickly
Restraint increases fear of bodily harm and reduces cooperation.
Explain that the cuff will not hurt and proceed
Hands-on involvement, not reassurance alone, gains preschool cooperation.
Skip vital signs until the child is asleep
Avoiding the task misses the strategy that gains cooperation.

items.q: Which characteristics describe preschoolers’ thinking? Select all that apply.
o: They remain egocentric in communication
Preschoolers believe others think as they do.
They believe punishment automatically follows breaking a rule
They do not yet realize punishment is socially mediated.
They believe that thinking something can make it happen
Magical thinking is characteristic of preschoolers.
They link events that occur close together in time causally
Early causal thinking links events related in time or space.
They fully understand that punishment is decided by others
Preschoolers think punishment is automatically connected to an act.
They have abandoned fantasy for purely logical thought
Their rich fantasy life persists, grounded in perceived reality.
items.ex: Preschool thought is egocentric, magical, and concrete, with early causal links and automatic punishment beliefs.

alt.q: A nurse prepares to care for a 4-year-old. Which preschool beliefs should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: A broken rule brings immediate punishment
Preschoolers believe punishment results immediately when a rule is broken.
Inanimate objects have feelings and can act
Preschoolers give lifelike qualities to inanimate objects.
Others think the same way the child does
Preschoolers remain egocentric and believe others think as they do.
Wishes cannot make events happen
Preschoolers believe that thinking something will make it happen.
Punishment is a social decision made by adults
They do not yet realize punishment is socially mediated.
alt.ex: Correct: A broken rule brings immediate punishment; Inanimate objects have feelings and can act; Others think the same way the child does.

items.q: By 5 years of age, about how many words does an average child use?
items.a: About 2100 words
items.ex: By 5 years children average 2100 words and combine four to five words into sentences.
w: About 300 words
Up to 300 words is typical of a 24-month-old.
About 100 words
Understanding almost 100 words is typical of a 1-year-old.
About 5000 words
This exceeds the 2100-word average for a 5-year-old.

alt.q: How many words does a typical 5-year-old combine into sentences?
alt.a: Four to five words
alt.ex: Preschoolers combine four to five words into sentences, using pronouns, prepositions, adjectives, and verbs.
w: Two words
Two-word sentences are typical of a 24-month-old.
One word
Single words are typical of infants and early toddlers.
Eight to ten words
This exceeds what the chapter describes for preschool sentences.

items.q: A nurse is preparing a 4-year-old for a contrast imaging study. Which explanation is best?
items.a: “The doctor will put special medicine in your arm to help the pictures show up.”
items.ex: Phonetically similar words like die and dye confuse preschoolers, so avoid them and check comprehension.
w: “The doctor will put a dye in your arm to help the pictures show up.”
“Dye” sounds like “die” and can frighten a preschooler.
“The doctor will inject a radiopaque contrast medium into a vein.”
Technical language is not understandable to a 4-year-old.
“Don’t worry, you won’t feel a thing during the whole test.”
False reassurance does not prepare the child or check understanding.

alt.q: After explaining a procedure to a preschooler, what should the nurse do next?
alt.a: Assess the child’s comprehension of the explanation
alt.ex: Preschoolers may confuse similar-sounding words, so the nurse assesses comprehension of explanations.
w: Assume understanding if the child stops asking “Why?”
Preschoolers ask why repeatedly; silence does not confirm understanding.
Repeat the same explanation using medical terms
Technical terms do not help a preschooler understand.
Begin the procedure without further discussion
Comprehension should be assessed before proceeding.

items.q: According to Erikson, how can parents help a preschooler balance initiative and guilt?
items.a: Allow the child to do things on their own while setting firm limits and giving guidance
items.ex: Erikson recommends independence within firm limits and guidance to balance initiative and guilt.
w: Do most tasks for the child to prevent mistakes and feelings of failure
Taking over limits initiative, which preschoolers need to develop.
Let the child attempt any activity without limits to build confidence
Without limits, children overstep abilities and feel guilt.
Punish the child whenever an activity is beyond the child’s abilities
Guilt arises from overstepping; punishment does not build balance.

alt.q: A 4-year-old spills milk while trying to pour from a full gallon container and says, “I’m bad.” What does this reflect?
alt.a: Guilt from overstepping the limits of the child’s abilities

Mistrust relates to infancy and parent-infant interaction quality.

The scenario reflects the preschooler’s initiative-versus-guilt crisis.
Inferiority from comparison with peers at school
This preschooler has not begun formal schooling.

items.q: A 4-year-old whose baby brother is hospitalized tells the nurse, “I wished he would go away, and now he’s sick.” Which response by the nurse is best?

Children should be encouraged to talk about their feelings.
“Your brother will be fine, so you don’t need to worry.”
This does not correct the belief that the wish caused the illness.

This is a separate belief about automatic punishment.

alt.q: Which behaviors might a preschooler show during times of stress? Select all that apply.

Thumb-sucking
Thumb-sucking is a normal stress response.
Wanting parents to feed and dress them

Mastering triangles and diamonds early

items.q: A parent reports that their 4-year-old has started bed-wetting again since a new baby arrived. Which response by the nurse is best?

alt.q: Which activity gives a stressed preschooler a socially acceptable way to vent frustration or anger?
