alt.ex: That's stage 2 of 5. Infants play alone, toddlers play side by side, 3-year-olds pair up, 4-year-olds form small groups, and 5-year-olds have temporary leaders.
w: Solitary, exploratory play
That's stage 1 of 5.
Play in groups of two or three
That's stage 4 of 5.
Group play with a temporary leader for each activity
That's stage 5 of 5.

alt.q: In the development of play from infancy through the preschool years, which stage comes right before “Play in groups of two or three”?
alt.a: Cooperative play with one other child
alt.ex: That's stage 3 of 5. Infants play alone, toddlers play side by side, 3-year-olds pair up, 4-year-olds form small groups, and 5-year-olds have temporary leaders.
w: Parallel play beside another child
That's stage 2 of 5.
Solitary, exploratory play
That's stage 1 of 5.
Group play with a temporary leader for each activity
That's stage 5 of 5.

alt.q: In the development of play from infancy through the preschool years, which stage comes right before “Group play with a temporary leader for each activity”?
alt.a: Play in groups of two or three
alt.ex: That's stage 4 of 5. Infants play alone, toddlers play side by side, 3-year-olds pair up, 4-year-olds form small groups, and 5-year-olds have temporary leaders.
w: Cooperative play with one other child
That's stage 3 of 5.
Parallel play beside another child
That's stage 2 of 5.
Solitary, exploratory play
That's stage 1 of 5.

ord.q: Place these stages of play in the order children typically progress through them.
items: Solitary, exploratory play
Parallel play beside another child
Cooperative play with one other child
Play in groups of two or three
Group play with a temporary leader for each activity
ord.ex: Infants play alone, toddlers play side by side, 3-year-olds pair up, 4-year-olds form small groups, and 5-year-olds have temporary leaders.

items.q: Imaginary playmates are a sign of health and help preschoolers distinguish between reality and fantasy.
items.a: True
items.ex: Imaginary playmates serve many purposes, are a sign of health, and help children separate reality from fantasy.
items.ww: The chapter describes imaginary playmates as healthy, not as a sign of a problem.

alt.q: A preschooler who has an imaginary playmate is showing difficulty separating reality from fantasy and should be referred.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Imaginary playmates are a sign of health that helps children distinguish reality from fantasy.
alt.ww: The chapter presents imaginary playmates as healthy, so no referral is needed.

items.q: The AAP advises that preschoolers watch no more than 1 hour per day of educational, nonviolent TV programs.
items.a: True
items.ex: Limiting TV to 1 hour of educational, nonviolent viewing leaves time for reading, physical activity, and socializing.
items.ww: The chapter gives the 1-hour limit, ideally viewed with parents or responsible adults.

alt.q: Because educational programs support learning, preschoolers can safely watch up to 3 hours of TV each day.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The AAP advises no more than 1 hour per day of educational, nonviolent TV for preschoolers.
alt.ww: The limit is 1 hour; more screen time displaces reading, physical activity, and socializing.

items.q: As preschoolers become more coordinated and have better balance, falls become much less of a problem.
items.a: True
items.ex: Improved fine- and gross-motor skills and balance make falls much less of a problem in preschoolers.
items.ww: The chapter states that falls decrease as coordination and balance improve.

alt.q: Because preschoolers are more coordinated than toddlers, parents can relax close supervision of their activities.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Parents must continue close supervision, and toddler injury-prevention guidelines still apply to preschoolers.
alt.ww: The chapter stresses ongoing supervision and parental example, such as wearing a bike helmet.

items.q: A parent worries that their finicky 4-year-old eats very little. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Focus on food quality, and let your child help prepare meals.”
items.ex: Food quality matters more than quantity, and preschoolers who help prepare meals are more likely to try new foods.
w: “Serve adult-sized portions so your child gets enough.”
Preschoolers eat about half of adult portion sizes.
“Insist that your child clean the plate at every meal.”
Quality matters more than quantity, and power struggles cause conflict.
“Your child needs about 3000 calories each day.”
The average preschool daily intake is about 1800 calories.

alt.q: What is the average daily caloric intake of a preschooler?
alt.a: About 1800 calories
alt.ex: Preschoolers average about 1800 calories daily and eat about half of adult portions.
w: About 1000 calories
This is below the preschooler’s average intake of 1800 calories.
About 2500 calories
This exceeds the preschooler’s average intake of 1800 calories.
About 3000 calories
This far exceeds the preschooler’s average intake of 1800 calories.

items.q: Preschoolers need [[10 to 13|10-13]] hours of sleep per night and take infrequent naps.
items.ex: Preschool sleep needs are 10 to 13 hours, and helping children slow down before bedtime improves sleep.

alt.q: A 4-year-old should get about [[10 to 13|10-13]] hours of sleep each night.
alt.ex: Preschool sleep needs are 10 to 13 hours, and helping children slow down before bedtime improves sleep.

items.q: Early detection and treatment of strabismus must occur by 6 years of age to prevent [[amblyopia]].
items.ex: Vision screening begins in the preschool years to find nonbinocular vision, or strabismus, before amblyopia develops.

alt.q: Strabismus, or nonbinocular vision, must be found and treated by age [[6|six]] to prevent amblyopia.
alt.ex: Vision screening begins in the preschool years to find nonbinocular vision, or strabismus, before amblyopia develops.

items.q: The developmental period that includes both the school-age child and the adolescent spans which ages?
items.a: 6 to 18 years
items.ex: The book groups school-age children and adolescents together as the period between 6 and 18 years of age.
w: 3 to 12 years
Ages 3 to 5 are the preschool period, which comes before the school-age years.
6 to 12 years
This covers only the school-age (middle) years, not adolescence as well.
12 to 21 years
This omits the school-age years, which begin at about 6 years of age.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing developmental expectations for a group that includes both school-age children and adolescents. Which age range does this group cover?
alt.a: Between 6 and 18 years of age
alt.ex: Developmental changes from 6 to 18 years span the school-age and adolescent periods.
w: Between 1 and 6 years of age
Ages 1 to 6 cover toddlers and preschoolers, not school-age children and adolescents.
Between 10 and 25 years of age
School-age development begins at about 6 years, and the group ends near 18 years.
Between 4 and 14 years of age
This range includes preschoolers and leaves out older adolescents.

items.q: According to the textbook, children between 6 and 18 years of age expand, refine, and synchronize their skills mainly for which purpose?
items.a: To become accepted and productive members of society
items.ex: Children develop and synchronize physical, psychosocial, cognitive, and moral skills so they can become accepted, productive members of society.
w: To remain dependent on family for daily decision making
These years move the child toward independence, not continued dependence on family.
To master the reflexes needed for basic survival needs
Reflexes and basic survival needs are concerns of the newborn and infant, not ages 6 to 18.
To separate from peers and focus on solitary activities
Peer and group activities become more important, not less, during these years.

alt.q: A school nurse explains to parents why children aged 6 to 18 work so hard to refine their physical, cognitive, psychosocial, and moral skills. Which goal does the nurse describe?
alt.a: Becoming accepted and productive members of society
alt.ex: The book states these skills are developed so children can become accepted and productive members of society.
w: Achieving financial independence from parents by age 14
Financial independence is not the norm for adolescents in American society.
Avoiding all contact with the wider school community
The environment expands to include school and community rather than avoiding it.
Returning to the family-centered world of early childhood
Development moves outward from family to school and community, not back.

items.q: A nurse in a family clinic is seeing a 7-year-old and her 15-year-old brother for annual checkups. Which approach should the nurse use when assessing their development?
items.a: Review the developmental expectations appropriate to each child’s age-group
items.ex: Age-specific assessment requires reviewing the appropriate developmental expectations for each age-group.
w: Use the adolescent’s milestones as the standard for both children
A 7-year-old cannot be judged by adolescent milestones; each age-group has its own expectations.
Compare the younger child’s progress directly with her brother’s
Sibling comparison is not age-specific; each child is assessed against expectations for their own age-group.
Postpone developmental assessment until both children reach adulthood
Assessment is done at each age to promote healthy development, not deferred to adulthood.

alt.q: A nurse is preparing to assess a 10-year-old and a 17-year-old. Which statement by the nurse reflects the correct approach to age-specific assessment?
alt.a: “I will compare each child with the expectations for their own age-group.”
alt.ex: Age-specific assessment means reviewing the developmental expectations that fit each age-group.
w: “I will use one checklist for anyone between 6 and 18 years.”
Development from 6 to 18 is diverse, so a single checklist does not fit both ages.
“I will assess only physical growth, since that changes most.”
Development spans physical, psychosocial, cognitive, and moral areas, not physical growth alone.
“I will ask the parents to describe the expected milestones.”
The nurse, not the parents, is responsible for reviewing age-appropriate developmental expectations.

items.q: A 16-year-old with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is being discharged. Which nursing action best reflects a developmental framework for this patient?
items.a: Encourage the adolescent to participate in decisions about the plan of care
items.ex: Adolescents are developing independence and should feel empowered to participate in decisions regarding their plan of care.
w: Direct all teaching to the parents because they will manage the care
Excluding the adolescent ignores the developing independence the framework says to support.
Delay involving the adolescent until reaching legal adulthood
Adolescents should participate now; independence is developing during this stage.
Offer only simple either-or choices, as is done for toddlers
Simple choices suit toddlers developing autonomy; adolescents can share fuller decision making.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse caring for a hospitalized 15-year-old best supports this patient’s developmental needs?
alt.a: “Let’s talk about the plan together so you can help make the decisions.”
alt.ex: Nurses empower adolescents to participate in decisions about their care because they are developing independence.
w: “Your parents and I will decide the plan and let you know later.”
This removes the adolescent from decisions and undermines developing independence.
“You can choose which cup to use, but the rest is up to us.”
Limited simple choices fit a toddler’s autonomy, not an adolescent’s independence.
“You are too young to understand the details of your plan.”
Adolescents can think abstractly and should be empowered to participate in care decisions.

items.q: Which statement best compares the thinking of school-age children with that of adolescents?
items.a: School-age children think about what is; adolescents can imagine what might be
items.ex: Concrete thinkers reason about the here and now, whereas adolescents use abstract reasoning about possibilities and the future.
w: School-age children think abstractly; adolescents think only concretely
This reverses the stages; abstract thought develops in adolescence.
Both groups think mainly about what might happen in the future
Future-oriented, hypothetical thinking is typical of adolescents, not school-age children.
Both groups remain egocentric and cannot see another viewpoint
School-age children become less egocentric and begin to understand other viewpoints.

alt.q: A nurse notices that a 9-year-old focuses on the facts of today’s procedure, while her 16-year-old sister asks about many possible future outcomes. How does the nurse interpret this difference?
alt.a: It reflects concrete thinking in the child and abstract thinking in the teen
alt.ex: School-age children think logically about the here and now; adolescents consider hypothetical possibilities and the future.
w: It shows a cognitive delay in the 9-year-old that needs referral
Thinking about the here and now is expected for a school-age child, not a delay.
It shows the teenager is more anxious and needs sedation
Considering many possibilities reflects normal abstract thinking, not a need for sedation.
It reflects sensorimotor thinking in both sisters at this age
Sensorimotor thinking belongs to infancy, not to school-age children or teens.

items.q: Which pairing correctly matches each age-group with its psychosocial focus according to Erikson?
items.a: School-age: industry versus inferiority; adolescent: search for identity
items.ex: Erikson names industry versus inferiority for school-age children and the search for identity, with identity confusion as the danger, for adolescents.
w: School-age: trust versus mistrust; adolescent: industry versus inferiority
Trust versus mistrust belongs to infancy, and industry is the school-age task.
School-age: initiative versus guilt; adolescent: autonomy versus shame
Initiative and autonomy are preschool and toddler tasks, not school-age and adolescent ones.
School-age: search for identity; adolescent: industry versus inferiority
This reverses the two stages; identity is the adolescent task.

alt.q: A nurse is explaining Erikson’s stages to a parent of a 9-year-old and a 15-year-old. Which explanation is accurate?
alt.a: The younger child is building competence; the older one is forming an identity
alt.ex: School-age children strive for competence (industry), while adolescents search for a personal identity.
w: The younger child is building trust; the older one is building autonomy
Trust and autonomy are infant and toddler tasks.
Both children are working mainly on initiative versus guilt
Initiative versus guilt is the preschooler’s task.
The younger child is forming an identity; the older one is building competence
This reverses the tasks of the two age-groups.

items.q: How does the rate of physical growth in the school-age years compare with growth in adolescence?
items.a: School-age growth is slow and consistent; adolescent growth is rapid
items.ex: The school-age years are a relative calm before the adolescent growth spurt, when physical changes occur rapidly.
w: School-age growth is rapid; adolescent growth slows and stops
School-age growth is slow and steady, and adolescents have a growth spurt.
Both periods have the same steady, slow rate of growth
Adolescence brings a rapid growth spurt, unlike the slower school-age years.
Both periods have rapid growth like that seen in infancy
School-age growth slows compared with infancy and adolescence.

alt.q: The textbook describes the school-age years as “a relative calm.” What does this phrase refer to?
alt.a: Slow, steady growth before the adolescent growth spurt
alt.ex: School-age growth is slow and consistent, a relative calm before the rapid growth of adolescence.
w: A pause in all cognitive and psychosocial development
Children make great developmental strides in cognitive and psychosocial skills during these years.
The absence of stress compared with earlier generations
Today’s school-age children actually experience more stress than earlier generations.
Rapid growth that settles once puberty has begun
Growth speeds up, rather than settles, once adolescence and puberty begin.

items.q: How does a school-age child’s view of health differ from an adolescent’s view?
items.a: The child judges by functional ability; the teen also weighs feelings of well-being
items.ex: School-age children judge health by observable facts and functional ability; adolescents add feelings of well-being, normal function, and absence of symptoms.
w: The child judges by future disease risk; the teen judges by appearance only
Future risk is abstract; school-age children use observable facts such as illness, eating, and sleeping.
Both groups define health only by how they look to their peers
Neither group defines health only by appearance; function and well-being are central.
The child judges by feelings of well-being; the teen judges by grades
Adolescents, not children, evaluate well-being, and grades are not the measure of health.

alt.q: A nurse asks a 9-year-old and a 16-year-old how they know they are healthy. Which response from the 9-year-old is expected for that age?
alt.a: “I’m healthy because I can play, eat, and sleep like always.”
alt.ex: School-age children judge health by observable facts and functional ability, such as eating, sleeping, and being free of illness.
w: “I’m healthy because I’ll probably avoid heart disease later.”
Reasoning about future possibilities is typical of adolescents, not school-age children.
“I’m healthy because my doctor gave me a high score.”
School-age children rely on what they can observe in daily function, not a rating.
“I’m healthy because I make good lifestyle choices overall.”
Abstract evaluation of lifestyle reflects adolescent thinking rather than a school-age view.

items.q: A nurse is planning injury prevention teaching for families with children aged 6 to 18. Which fact should guide this teaching?
items.a: Accidents and unintentional injuries are a leading cause of death in both groups
items.ex: Accidents are a leading cause of death in school-age children, and unintentional injury is the leading cause of death in adolescents.
w: Infections are the leading cause of death in both groups
Infections cause most childhood illnesses, but accidents are the leading cause of death.
Suicide is the leading cause of death in both groups
Suicide is a major cause in older teens, but unintentional injury leads in both groups.
Cancer is the leading cause of death in both groups
The book identifies accidents and unintentional injury, not cancer, as the leading cause.

alt.q: Which statement about injury in school-age children and adolescents is accurate?
alt.a: Safety teaching is a priority because accidents are a leading cause of death
alt.ex: Because accidents and unintentional injuries are a leading cause of death from 6 to 18 years, safety is a priority teaching topic.
w: Injury risk falls to zero once motor skills are well developed
Better skills lower risk, but risk taking and less supervision still cause injuries.
Injuries matter less than infections as a cause of death
Infections cause most illnesses, but accidents are the leading cause of death.
Safety teaching is best postponed until a teen begins driving
Safety teaching starts in the school-age years, such as helmets and seat belts.

items.q: Which statement correctly compares language development in school-age children and adolescents?
items.a: Language grows rapidly in school-age years; in adolescence the focus shifts to communication skills
items.ex: School-age children show rapid language growth; by adolescence language is almost complete and communication skills become the focus.
w: Language develops slowly in school-age years and is only beginning in adolescence
Language growth is rapid in middle childhood and almost complete by adolescence.
Vocabulary stops expanding in school-age years, and adolescents focus on syntax
Vocabulary continues to expand in adolescence; school-age children learn syntax rules.
Both groups interpret words literally and cannot appreciate jokes or riddles
School-age children reason about meaning in context and enjoy jokes and riddles.

alt.q: A nurse notes that a 10-year-old loves riddles and a 16-year-old speaks differently to parents than to friends. What do these behaviors show?
alt.a: Expected language growth in the child and communication skill in the teen
alt.ex: School-age children think about language and enjoy riddles; adolescents choose different ways to communicate with different people.
w: A language delay in the child and poor social skills in the teen
Enjoying riddles and adjusting messages to the audience are expected, healthy behaviors.
Literal word use in the child and limited vocabulary in the teen
Riddles require nonliteral reasoning, and adolescent vocabulary continues to expand.
Egocentric speech in the child and regression in the teen
School-age children are becoming less egocentric, and tailoring messages is not regression.

items.q: Which statement best compares peer relationships in school-age children and adolescents?
items.a: School-age children often prefer same-sex peers; adolescents value peers more than parents
items.ex: School-age children often prefer same-sex peers and best friends; adolescents seek group identity and place more value on peers than parents.
w: School-age children prefer solitary play; adolescents avoid peer groups
Group play overshadows solitary play in school-age years, and teens seek peer groups.
School-age children value parents less; adolescents value parents more
This reverses the pattern; adolescents place more value on peers than parents.
Both groups show little interest in belonging to clubs or groups
Clubs and peer groups become prominent in school-age years, and teens seek group identity.

alt.q: A parent says, “My 8-year-old only plays with girls her age, and my 15-year-old dresses exactly like her friends.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Both behaviors are typical peer patterns for their ages.”
alt.ex: Preferring same-sex peers is common in school-age children, and similarity in dress is common in teen peer groups.
w: “Both behaviors suggest your daughters are socially isolated.”
These are typical peer behaviors, not signs of isolation.
“The 8-year-old should be encouraged to play only with boys.”
Preferring same-sex peers is common at this age and needs no correction.
“The 15-year-old needs help to stop seeking group approval.”
Teens seek group identity for self-esteem and acceptance; this is expected.

items.q: Which statements correctly compare school-age children and adolescents? Select all that apply.
o: Group identity increases as the school-age child approaches adolescence.
School-age group identity grows and leads into the adolescent search for group identity.
Puberty marks the end of the school-age years and the start of adolescence.
The book states puberty ends the middle years and begins adolescence.
Formal operations may begin around 11 years and develop in adolescence.
Piaget’s formal operations may start near 11 years and allow abstract thinking in teens.
Language development begins in adolescence after concrete thinking ends.
Language grows rapidly in middle childhood and is almost complete by adolescence.
Growth is faster in the school-age years than in adolescence.
School-age growth is slow and consistent; adolescents have a rapid growth spurt.
items.ex: School-age development builds directly toward adolescence through puberty, formal operations, and growing group identity.

alt.q: A nursing student is reviewing development from 6 to 18 years. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Puberty signals the move from the middle years into adolescence.
Puberty marks the end of the middle years and the beginning of adolescence.
Children may start to think abstractly at about 11 years.
Around 11 years, children may begin formal operations and abstract reasoning.
Group identity becomes stronger as adolescence approaches.
Group identity increases as the school-age child nears adolescence.
Adolescents grow more slowly than school-age children.
Adolescents grow rapidly; school-age growth is the slower, steadier period.
Language skills are first acquired during adolescence.
Language develops long before adolescence and is almost complete by then.
alt.ex: Correct: Puberty signals the move from the middle years into adolescence; Children may start to think abstractly at about 11 years; Group identity becomes stronger as adolescence approaches.

items.q: A nurse is caring for children and adolescents aged 6 to 18. Which actions are developmentally appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Let a hospitalized 8-year-old help choose fluids and record intake.
School-age children value independence, so participating in care preserves control.
Provide privacy when explaining a procedure to a 10-year-old.
School-age children are modest and sensitive about exposure, so privacy is needed.
Interview a 16-year-old without parents present for part of the visit.
As adolescents become more autonomous, interviews should be conducted without parents present.
Make all care decisions for a 15-year-old without discussion.
Adolescents should be empowered to participate in decisions about their care.
Expose a 9-year-old fully during an examination to save time.
School-age children are modest; the nurse always provides privacy.
items.ex: Care for ages 6 to 18 supports growing independence, modesty, and autonomy at each age.

alt.q: Which nursing actions match the developmental needs of school-age children and adolescents? Select all that apply.
o: Encourage a school-age child to take part in personal care when hospitalized.
Participation maintains the independence school-age children have developed in self-care.
Keep a 10-year-old covered during explanations of a common procedure.
Modesty is expected at this age, so privacy is always provided.
Hold part of an adolescent’s interview with the parents out of the room.
Interviews without parents support adolescent autonomy and open discussion.
Discourage a teenager from asking questions about the care plan.
Adolescents should be empowered to take part in decisions about their care.
Take over all bathing and dressing for a hospitalized 11-year-old.
Taking over self-care threatens the child’s control; independence should be maintained.
alt.ex: Correct: Encourage a school-age child to take part in personal care when hospitalized; Keep a 10-year-old covered during explanations of a common procedure; Hold part of an adolescent’s interview with the parents out of the room.

items.q: Which statements about human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccination for school-age children and adolescents are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The first dose is usually given at 11 to 12 years of age.
The CDC recommends routine HPV vaccination, usually starting at 11 to 12 years.
Vaccination can begin as early as 9 years of age.
The series may be started as early as 9 years.
It is recommended for both male and female children.
Routine HPV vaccination is recommended for male and female children.
Teens who missed the usual age can no longer receive it.
Vaccination is still recommended through 26 years for those who missed it.
It is reserved for children found to be at high risk.
Because no one can predict who will develop disease, vaccination is routine for all.
items.ex: HPV vaccination is routine for all children, usually at 11 to 12 years, with catch-up recommended through 26 years.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching parents about the HPV vaccine. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Both sons and daughters should receive the vaccine.
Males and females are both at risk, so routine vaccination includes both.
A teen who missed the vaccine at 11 or 12 can still receive it.
Vaccination is still recommended through 26 years of age.
The vaccine may be started as early as age 9.
The first dose can be given as early as 9 years of age.
The vaccine should wait until the teen becomes sexually active.
The routine first dose is at 11 to 12 years, not tied to sexual activity.
The vaccine is needed only by females to prevent cervical cancer.
Males can develop genital warts, so the vaccine is recommended for both sexes.
alt.ex: Correct: Both sons and daughters should receive the vaccine; A teen who missed the vaccine at 11 or 12 can still receive it; The vaccine may be started as early as age 9.

items.q: Between 6 and 18 years of age, the child’s developmental environment remains limited mainly to family and close friends.
items.a: False
items.ex: The environment expands and diversifies beyond family and close friends to include the child’s school and community.
items.ww: The statement would be true only for younger children; school-age children and adolescents develop within school and community as well.

alt.q: From 6 to 18 years of age, the environment in which children develop skills expands to include the school and community.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The book states the environment expands beyond family and close friends to the school and community.
alt.ww: It is not limited to the family; school and community become part of the developmental environment.

items.q: Nurses promote the health of school-age children and adolescents by helping them achieve a necessary developmental balance.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states that nurses promote health by helping children and adolescents achieve a necessary developmental balance.
items.ww: It is not false; balanced development across physical, psychosocial, cognitive, and moral areas is the nursing goal.

alt.q: Nurses promote the health of children aged 6 to 18 by focusing on physical growth, because cognitive and moral skills develop on their own.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Development spans physical, psychosocial, cognitive, and moral skills, and nurses help children achieve a balance among them.
alt.ww: It cannot be true because the nurse’s goal is balance across all areas, not physical growth alone.

items.q: Puberty marks the end of the middle years of childhood and the beginning of adolescence.
items.a: True
items.ex: The school-age (middle) years run from 6 to about 12 years and end with puberty, which begins adolescence.
items.ww: It is not false; the book uses puberty, not a set grade or birthday, as the boundary.

alt.q: The middle years of childhood end when the child enters high school, whether or not puberty has begun.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Puberty, not school entry, marks the end of the middle years and the beginning of adolescence.
alt.ww: It is not true because the transition is defined by puberty rather than by the school grade.

items.q: Children between 6 and 18 years of age develop, expand, refine, and synchronize physical, psychosocial, cognitive, and [[moral]] skills.
items.ex: The four skill areas developed from 6 to 18 years are physical, psychosocial, cognitive, and moral.

alt.q: Along with physical, psychosocial, and cognitive skills, children aged 6 to 18 refine their [[moral]] skills to become productive members of society.
alt.ex: The four skill areas developed from 6 to 18 years are physical, psychosocial, cognitive, and moral.

items.q: In Piaget’s stages of cognitive development, which stage comes right after “Preoperational”?
items.a: Concrete operations
items.ex: That's stage 3 of 4. Infants are sensorimotor, toddlers and preschoolers preoperational, school-age children concrete (about 7 years), and formal operations may begin near 11 years.
w: Formal operations
That's stage 4 of 4.
Sensorimotor
That's stage 1 of 4.

alt.q: Which stage comes first in Piaget’s stages of cognitive development?
alt.a: Sensorimotor
alt.ex: That's stage 1 of 4. Infants are sensorimotor, toddlers and preschoolers preoperational, school-age children concrete (about 7 years), and formal operations may begin near 11 years.
w: Preoperational
That's stage 2 of 4.
Concrete operations
That's stage 3 of 4.
Formal operations
That's stage 4 of 4.

alt.q: Which stage comes last in Piaget’s stages of cognitive development?
alt.a: Formal operations
alt.ex: That's stage 4 of 4. Infants are sensorimotor, toddlers and preschoolers preoperational, school-age children concrete (about 7 years), and formal operations may begin near 11 years.
w: Concrete operations
That's stage 3 of 4.
Preoperational
That's stage 2 of 4.
Sensorimotor
That's stage 1 of 4.

alt.q: In Piaget’s stages of cognitive development, which stage comes right after “Sensorimotor”?
alt.a: Preoperational
alt.ex: That's stage 2 of 4. Infants are sensorimotor, toddlers and preschoolers preoperational, school-age children concrete (about 7 years), and formal operations may begin near 11 years.
w: Concrete operations
That's stage 3 of 4.
Formal operations
That's stage 4 of 4.

alt.q: In Piaget’s stages of cognitive development, which stage comes right after “Concrete operations”?
alt.a: Formal operations
alt.ex: That's stage 4 of 4. Infants are sensorimotor, toddlers and preschoolers preoperational, school-age children concrete (about 7 years), and formal operations may begin near 11 years.
w: Preoperational
That's stage 2 of 4.
Sensorimotor
That's stage 1 of 4.

alt.q: In Piaget’s stages of cognitive development, which stage comes right before “Preoperational”?
alt.a: Sensorimotor
alt.ex: That's stage 1 of 4. Infants are sensorimotor, toddlers and preschoolers preoperational, school-age children concrete (about 7 years), and formal operations may begin near 11 years.
w: Concrete operations
That's stage 3 of 4.
Formal operations
That's stage 4 of 4.

Abstract thinking and forming hypotheses, beginning about 11 years
mt.ex: These concepts from Erikson, Piaget, and Freud describe development from the school-age years through adolescence.

items.q: The school-age period, or the “middle years” of childhood, covers which ages?
items.a: 6 to about 12 years
items.ex: The middle years run from 6 to about 12 years, ending with puberty and the start of adolescence.
w: 3 to about 6 years
Ages 3 to 6 are the preschool period.
1 to about 3 years
Ages 1 to 3 are toddlerhood.
13 to about 20 years
Ages 13 to 20 are usually adolescence.

alt.q: Which event marks the end of the school-age period?
alt.a: The onset of puberty
alt.ex: Puberty marks the end of the middle years and the beginning of adolescence.
w: Entering middle school
School grade does not define the end of the middle years; puberty does.
Reaching 10 years of age
Ten years is when puberty discussions should begin, not the end of the period.
Mastering gross-motor skills
Gross-motor skills are refined throughout the period and do not mark its end.

items.q: A parent asks why their 7-year-old looks so much slimmer than in the preschool years. Which explanation is accurate?
items.a: Changes in fat distribution and thickness make the child look slimmer
items.ex: The school-age child appears slimmer than the preschooler because of changes in fat distribution and thickness.
w: The child is losing weight because growth has stopped
Growth continues slowly, and many children double their weight during these years.
The child is in a rapid growth spurt like that of adolescence
School-age growth is slow and consistent; the growth spurt comes in adolescence.
The child is likely not eating enough and needs a diet review
A slimmer appearance is an expected change in fat distribution, not undernutrition.

alt.q: Which statement accurately describes physical growth during the school-age years?
alt.a: Growth is slow and consistent, and many children double their weight
alt.ex: School-age growth is slow and steady; many children double their weight, and most females exceed males in height and weight by the end.
w: Growth is rapid, and males usually exceed females by the end of the period
Growth is slow, and most females exceed males in height and weight by the end.
Growth stops entirely until the adolescent growth spurt begins
Growth slows but continues; it does not stop.
Growth is fastest at 6 years and is complete by 12 years
Growth is slow and consistent throughout, and adolescents keep growing afterward.

items.q: A hospitalized 9-year-old becomes upset because the nurses are managing all of the child’s fluids and personal care. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Let the child help choose the type of fluids and keep a record of intake
items.ex: Illness threatens a school-age child’s control, so the nurse allows participation in care to maintain independence.
w: Explain that the nurses must handle all care while the child is ill
Removing all control worsens the threat to independence that illness causes.
Ask a parent to take over the child’s personal care tasks
Shifting care to a parent still takes away the child’s own independence.
Distract the child with a video game until the feelings pass
Distraction does not address the child’s need for control and participation in care.

alt.q: Which statement by the parent of a hospitalized 10-year-old shows understanding of the child’s developmental needs?
alt.a: “I’ll let my son help keep track of how much he drinks each day.”
alt.ex: School-age children are independent in self-care, and participating in care preserves their sense of control during illness.
w: “I’ll do all of his bathing and dressing so he can rest.”
Taking over self-care threatens the control and independence the child has developed.
“He is too young to understand anything about his care.”
School-age children understand directions well and can participate in care.
“I’ll ask the nurses to make all of his care choices.”
Removing choices undermines independence; the child should help decide where possible.

items.q: According to the Scoliosis Research Society recommendation in the textbook, when should school-age children be screened for scoliosis?
items.a: Females twice at 10 and 12 years; males once at 13 or 14 years
items.ex: Females are screened twice (10 and 12 years) and males once (13 or 14 years), because early treatment can limit curve progression.
w: Females once at 13 or 14 years; males twice at 10 and 12 years
This reverses the schedule; females are screened twice at the younger ages.
Both sexes once at 6 years and again at 18 years
Screening is done near puberty, not at the start and end of the age range.
Both sexes every year from 8 years to 16 years
The recommendation is two screenings for females and one for males, not yearly.

alt.q: A school nurse is planning scoliosis screening. Which student is due for screening according to the recommendation?
alt.a: A 12-year-old female who was screened at age 10
alt.ex: Females are screened at 10 and again at 12 years, so a 12-year-old female needs her second screening.
w: A 10-year-old male who has never been screened
Males are screened once at 13 or 14 years, not at 10.
An 8-year-old female who has never been screened
Female screening begins at 10 years, not 8.
A 15-year-old male who was screened at age 13
Males need only one screening, which this student already had.

items.q: Which behavior shows that a school-age child has reached Piaget’s concrete operational stage?
items.a: Recognizing that a flattened ball of clay still has the same amount of clay
items.ex: Concrete operational children understand that quantity stays the same even when shape or appearance changes.
w: Insisting that a tall, thin glass holds more juice than a short, wide one
Being fooled by appearance is preoperational thinking, before concrete operations.
Forming hypotheses about many abstract future possibilities
Hypothetical, abstract thinking is formal operations, typical of adolescence.
Needing to act out an event in order to understand it
Concrete thinkers can experience events without acting them out.

alt.q: An 8-year-old proudly sorts his baseball card collection by team and then again by position. What cognitive skill does this show?
alt.a: Understanding that one item can belong to two groups at once
alt.ex: School-age children understand the same element can exist in two groups at the same time, often shown through collections.
w: Sorting objects only by a single feature such as color
Grouping by one feature is what younger children do; this child uses two.
Thinking abstractly about hypothetical outcomes
Abstract hypothetical thinking is formal operations, not this sorting skill.
Remaining egocentric and unable to see other viewpoints
School-age children become less egocentric; sorting does not show egocentrism.

items.q: A parent reports that their 10-year-old has repeatedly failed at school and sports and is now withdrawing from friends. Based on Erikson’s theory, which outcome is the child at risk for?
items.a: A sense of inferiority
items.ex: In industry versus inferiority, children faced with failure may feel unworthy, sometimes withdrawing from school and peers.
w: A sense of mistrust
Mistrust is the risk of Erikson’s infant stage.
A sense of shame and doubt
Shame and doubt are risks of the toddler stage.
A sense of identity confusion
Identity confusion is the danger of adolescence.

alt.q: Which situation best supports a sense of industry in a school-age child?
alt.a: Being praised by the coach for helping the team reach its goal
alt.ex: School-age children who are positively recognized for success feel a sense of worth, supporting industry.
w: Being told to stop asking questions during a class lesson
Discouraging participation does not build competence or recognition.
Being allowed to watch others play without taking part
Industry grows from mastering skills and contributing, not watching.
Being compared unfavorably with an older sibling’s grades
Negative comparison risks feelings of inferiority rather than worth.

items.q: Why do school-age children begin to enjoy jokes and riddles?
items.a: They begin to think about language and reason about word meaning in context
items.ex: School-age children think about language and interpret words in context rather than literally, so they appreciate jokes and riddles.
w: They interpret every word literally and enjoy the confusion it causes
School-age children are less likely to interpret words literally.
They have stopped learning rules of syntax and word order
They become more aware of syntax rules during these years.
They believe that words have fixed, absolute meanings
They realize words have arbitrary rather than absolute meanings.

alt.q: Which statement about language development in school-age children is accurate?
alt.a: Children realize that words have arbitrary rather than absolute meanings
alt.ex: School-age children accept language as subjective, recognize that meanings are arbitrary, and reason about words in context.
w: Language growth slows greatly compared with the preschool years
Language growth is rapid during middle childhood.
Children become less aware of how words link into sentences
They become more aware of syntax, how words link into phrases and sentences.
Children rely more on literal interpretation of each word
They are less likely to use literal interpretation and reason within context.

items.q: A school nurse is helping an anxious 9-year-old who worries about tests. Which intervention plan is most likely to succeed?
items.a: Teach deep breathing and imagery, involving the parent, child, and teacher
items.ex: Most children can learn deep breathing, positive imagery, and progressive relaxation; including parent, child, and teacher gives maximal success.
w: Teach relaxation to the child alone, without telling the parents
The book says to include the parent, child, and teacher for maximal success.
Advise the parents to remove the child from all testing
Removing all testing does not teach coping; the goal is to reduce stress and stress response.
Wait until the child is old enough for abstract coping skills
Most school-age children can already learn breathing, imagery, and relaxation techniques.

alt.q: Which action should the nurse take first when helping a school-age child cope with stress?
alt.a: Help the parents and child identify potential stressors
alt.ex: The nurse first helps the parents and child identify potential stressors, then designs interventions to minimize stress and the stress response.
w: Refer the child to a psychiatrist for medication
Identifying stressors and teaching coping comes before medication, which the book does not describe.
Tell the child that stress is normal and will pass
Reassurance alone does not identify stressors or teach coping.
Recommend the child spend more time alone after school
Unsupervised time alone can increase stress and the risk of injury.

items.q: A nurse is about to explain a common procedure to a 10-year-old. Which action is most important?
items.a: Provide privacy, because the child is modest about exposure
items.ex: School-age children are aware of their bodies and modest about being exposed, so the nurse always provides privacy.
w: Explain the procedure in front of the other children in the room
Explaining in front of others ignores the child’s modesty and need for privacy.
Use only abstract explanations of how the body works
School-age children think concretely about the here and now, so abstract explanations are less suitable.
Ask the parent to leave and the child’s classmates to stay
Classmates staying would violate privacy; modesty requires a private setting.

alt.q: Which behavior by a school-age child during a health examination should the nurse expect?
alt.a: Asking to stay covered while the examination is explained
alt.ex: Expect school-age children to be aware of their bodies and to be modest and sensitive about exposure.
w: Undressing freely in front of strangers without concern
School-age children are modest, so lack of concern is not expected.
Judging their health by abstract future risks
They judge health by observable facts and functional ability, not abstract risks.
Refusing to take part in any personal care tasks
School-age children are very independent in personal care and want to participate.

items.q: At what age does the textbook recommend that parents begin discussing upcoming pubertal changes with their child?
items.a: 10 years
items.ex: When a school-age child reaches 10 years, parents begin discussions to prepare for pubertal changes, including menstruation, reproduction, and STIs.
w: 6 years
Six years is the start of the school-age period, before puberty discussions are recommended.
13 years
Thirteen years is too late; discussions should come before pubertal changes begin.
16 years
By 16 most pubertal changes have occurred, so preparation would come too late.

alt.q: A parent of a 10-year-old asks when to start talking about puberty. Which topics should the nurse suggest the parent introduce now?
alt.a: Menstruation, sexual intercourse, reproduction, and STIs
alt.ex: At 10 years, introductory topics include menstruation, sexual intercourse, reproduction, and sexually transmitted infections.
w: Birth control methods only, delaying other topics until marriage
Introductory topics at 10 include menstruation, reproduction, intercourse, and STIs, not birth control alone.
Nothing yet, because children this age have no sexual curiosity
Children in middle childhood are curious about sexuality, so discussions begin at 10.
Only body changes, since STIs are not relevant until adulthood
STIs are an included introductory topic; HPV is the most common STI.

items.q: The parent of a 9-year-old asks whether the human papillomavirus (HPV) vaccine can be given now. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Yes, it can start at 9, although the first dose is usually given at 11 to 12.”
items.ex: The first HPV dose is usually given at 11 to 12 years but can be administered as early as 9 years.
w: “No, the vaccine cannot be given before 13 years of age.”
The vaccine may be given as early as 9 years of age.
“No, it is only given after a child becomes sexually active.”
Routine vaccination is given before sexual activity, usually at 11 to 12 years.
“Yes, but only if your child is female, since males are not at risk.”
Males can develop genital warts, and vaccination is recommended for both sexes.

alt.q: A parent says, “My son is 15 and missed his HPV shot, so it’s too late.” Which response by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “He can still be vaccinated; it is recommended through 26 years.”
alt.ex: For those who miss the usual age window, HPV vaccination is still recommended through 26 years of age.
w: “That’s right; the vaccine works only if given before 12.”
Catch-up vaccination is recommended through 26 years of age.
“He doesn’t need it, because only females are at risk.”
Males can develop genital warts, so vaccination is recommended for both sexes.
“He should wait until he is 26 to receive the vaccine.”
Twenty-six is the upper age for vaccination, not a reason to wait.

items.q: Which statement about virtual (online) learning for school-age children is accurate?
items.a: Students must work more independently, and they may experience social distancing
items.ex: Distance learning requires independent, actively engaged students, and children may be socially distanced because they do not always interact with classmates.
w: It removes the need for students to engage actively in their learning
Virtual students must be actively engaged in their own learning.
It always provides more peer interaction than classroom learning
Children in virtual learning often experience social distancing from peers.
It supports development without any added services for children
Virtual education needs innovative services to support growth and development needs.

alt.q: A parent says their 10-year-old will start fully online school. Which point should the nurse include when discussing development?
alt.a: Plan ways for the child to stay socially connected with other children
alt.ex: Virtual learning can create social distance, so services and activities are needed to support the child’s social development.
w: Online school removes the need for any peer interaction
Peer interaction remains important; group play and achievement matter at this age.
The child will need less independence than in a classroom
Online learners must work more independently, not less.
Online school is suitable only for children with illness
Children use virtual learning for many reasons, not only illness.

items.q: Childhood obesity places a school-age child at increased risk for which conditions? Select all that apply.
o: Hypertension
Hypertension is listed among the health risks of childhood obesity.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Obesity increases the risk for type 2 diabetes mellitus.
Sleep apnea
Sleep apnea is a pulmonary complication of childhood obesity.
Fatty liver disease
Fatty liver disease is listed among obesity-related problems.
Type 1 diabetes mellitus
Type 1 diabetes is not a listed obesity risk; type 2 diabetes is.
Hearing loss
Hearing loss is not listed among the health risks of childhood obesity.
items.ex: Childhood obesity raises the risk of hypertension, type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, sleep apnea, musculoskeletal problems, dyslipidemia, and psychological problems.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching parents about the health effects of obesity in children. Which complications should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Dyslipidemia
Dyslipidemia is a listed risk of childhood obesity.
Musculoskeletal problems
Excess weight increases musculoskeletal problems.
Psychological problems
Obesity carries the potential for psychological problems.
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism is not listed as a consequence of childhood obesity.
Scoliosis
Scoliosis is a spinal curvature screened for separately, not a listed obesity complication.
alt.ex: Correct: Dyslipidemia; Musculoskeletal problems; Psychological problems.

items.q: Which cognitive abilities are expected in a school-age child in the concrete operational stage? Select all that apply.
o: Understands that quantity stays the same when shape changes
Conservation of quantity, as with clay balls, develops in this stage.
Understands that one item can belong to two groups at once
School-age children can classify an element into two groups at the same time.
Recognizes that others may not share their thoughts and feelings
School-age children become less egocentric and begin to see other viewpoints.
Thinks logically about the here and now
Concrete operations allow logical thinking about present, concrete situations.
Must act out events in order to understand them
School-age children can experience events without acting them out.
Judges situations only by how things appear
Their thoughts are no longer dominated by perceptions.
items.ex: Concrete operational thought brings logic, conservation, classification, and reduced egocentrism to the school-age child.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing cognitive development in an 8-year-old. Which findings are expected? Select all that apply.
o: Can focus on more than one aspect of a situation
School-age children can concentrate on more than one aspect at a time.
Enjoys ordering and reordering a sticker collection
Collections reflect the new skill of classifying items into multiple groups.
Understands a friend may see a situation differently
School-age children begin to understand another viewpoint.
Believes a flattened clay ball has less clay than a round one
Concrete thinkers understand quantity is conserved despite a change in shape.
Thinks only egocentrically about events
School-age children become less egocentric.
alt.ex: Correct: Can focus on more than one aspect of a situation; Enjoys ordering and reordering a sticker collection; Understands a friend may see a situation differently.

items.q: A nurse is assessing sources of stress for a school-age child. Which sources does the textbook identify? Select all that apply.
o: Parental expectations
Parental expectations are a listed source of stress.
Peer expectations
Expectations of peers add to the child’s stress.
The school environment
The school environment is a listed stressor.
Violence in the family, school, or community
Violence in any of these settings is a source of stress.
Consistent adult supervision after school
Lack of supervision, not supervision, is linked to increased stress.
Participation in structured group play
Group play builds achievement and belonging; it is not a listed stressor.
items.ex: Stress comes from parental and peer expectations, the school environment, and violence, and is greater for children left unsupervised.

alt.q: Which factors increase stress or risk for a school-age child? Select all that apply.
o: Caring for themselves after school without adult supervision
Unsupervised children may feel more stress and are at greater risk for injury.
Violence in the community or school
Violence in family, school, or community is a source of stress.
High expectations from parents and peers
Parental and peer expectations are listed stressors.
Learning deep-breathing and relaxation techniques
These are interventions that help children cope with stress.
Including the teacher in stress-reduction plans
Involving parent, child, and teacher improves success of interventions.
alt.ex: Correct: Caring for themselves after school without adult supervision; Violence in the community or school; High expectations from parents and peers.

items.q: School-age children who are left at home without adult supervision are at greater risk for injury and unsafe behaviors.
items.a: True
items.ex: Children who care for themselves before or after school without supervision may feel more stress and have greater risk for injury and unsafe behaviors.
items.ww: It is not false; the book directly links lack of supervision with stress and injury risk.

alt.q: School-age children who care for themselves after school without supervision have lower injury risk because they become more self-reliant.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Unsupervised children feel increased stress and are at greater risk for injury and unsafe behaviors.
alt.ww: It cannot be true; self-care without supervision raises, not lowers, the risk of injury.

items.q: “Rainbow fentanyl” is made in bright colors and shapes so that it looks like candy, which makes it a particular danger to children.
items.a: True
items.ex: Drug cartels purposely made fentanyl in colors and shapes that resemble candy to attract younger children.
items.ww: It is not false; the DEA has warned that its candy-like look targets children.

alt.q: Fentanyl poses little risk to school-age children because the drug is not made to look appealing to children.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Rainbow fentanyl comes in colors and shapes that look like candy, purposely made to addict younger children.
alt.ww: It is not true; the DEA’s One Pill Can Kill campaign warns of this risk to children.

items.q: Although Freud called middle childhood the latency period, school-age children are in fact curious about their sexuality.
items.a: True
items.ex: Children show curiosity about adult magazines and sexually explicit words, so this is the time for sex education.
items.ww: It is not false; the book states children are curious despite Freud’s latency label.

alt.q: Because middle childhood is a latency period, school-age children have no interest in sexuality, and sex education should wait until adolescence.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: School-age children are curious about sexuality, and this is the time for sex education on maturation, reproduction, and relationships.
alt.ww: It is not true; the book rejects the idea that sexual interest is absent in middle childhood.

items.q: Erikson identifies the developmental task of the school-age child as industry versus [[inferiority]].
items.ex: School-age children strive for competence (industry); repeated failure can lead to feelings of inferiority.

alt.q: A school-age child who is positively recognized for success develops a sense of [[industry]] rather than inferiority.
alt.ex: School-age children strive for competence (industry); repeated failure can lead to feelings of inferiority.

items.a: Most children can hold a pencil and print letters and words

alt.a: 6 years

w: About 7 years
