items.q: How does the term adolescence differ from the term puberty?
items.a: Adolescence refers to psychological maturation; puberty is when reproduction becomes possible
items.ex: Adolescence usually refers to psychological maturation, whereas puberty is the point at which reproduction becomes possible.
w: Adolescence is when reproduction becomes possible; puberty is psychological maturation
This reverses the definitions of the two terms.
Adolescence and puberty both mean the onset of menstruation in females
Onset of menstruation is menarche, which is only one part of puberty.
Adolescence ends at 13 years; puberty describes the years after 18
Adolescence usually spans about 13 to 20 years; puberty is a reproductive milestone.

alt.q: Which term refers to the point at which reproduction becomes possible?
alt.a: Puberty
alt.ex: Puberty refers to the point at which reproduction becomes possible; adolescence refers to psychological maturation.
w: Adolescence
Adolescence refers to psychological maturation from childhood to adulthood.
Latency
Latency is Freud’s term for middle childhood.
Menarche
Menarche is the onset of menstruation, not the general point of reproductive capability.

items.q: At about what ages does peak height velocity occur in adolescents?
items.a: About 12 years in females and 14 years in males
items.ex: Females generally reach peak height velocity earlier, at about 12 years, than males, at about 14 years.
w: About 14 years in females and 12 years in males
This reverses the sexes; females have prepubescent changes before males.
About 10 years in females and 18 years in males
Peak height velocity is about 12 and 14 years; males keep growing until 18 to 20.
About 16 years in both females and males
Females reach full height by 16 to 17; peak velocity occurs earlier in both sexes.

alt.q: A 13-year-old female who had menarche last month asks how much taller she will grow. Which response is accurate?
alt.a: “Most females grow less than 5 cm (2 inches) after menarche.”
alt.ex: Females grow less than 5 cm after menarche and reach full height by 16 to 17 years.
w: “Most females grow another 20 cm (8 inches) after menarche.”
Five to 20 cm is total adolescent height gain; growth after menarche is under 5 cm.
“Most females grow another 10 to 30 cm (4 to 12 inches).”
Ten to 30 cm is the total height gain for males during adolescence.
“Most females stop growing completely (0 cm) at menarche.”
Growth slows but continues, less than 5 cm, after menarche.

items.q: A 14-year-old male is upset because he is shorter than his friends. His growth chart shows steady progress along his own curve. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Your steady progress on your own growth curve matters more than how you compare with friends.”
items.ex: An individual’s sustained progression along the growth curve is more important than comparison with the norm, and teens need reassurance of normalcy.
w: “Being shorter than friends at your age means you will stay short as an adult.”
Males continue to grow until 18 to 20 years, so current height does not predict final height.
“You should not worry about this, since looking like your peers is not important.”
Being like peers is extremely important to teens; dismissing it denies emotional support.
“Your growth is delayed, so you will need a referral for hormone testing today.”
Steady progression on his own curve is reassuring and does not indicate a delay.

alt.q: Which nursing action best supports an adolescent whose pubertal changes are occurring later than those of peers?
alt.a: Provide emotional support and reassurance about normal variation
alt.ex: Deviation in timing is very hard for teens to accept, so nurses provide emotional support for early or delayed puberty.
w: Advise the teen to avoid peers until the changes catch up
Peer relationships support self-esteem; avoiding peers is not recommended.
Tell the teen that timing differences are rare and serious
Wide variation in pubertal timing exists within and between sexes.
Compare the teen’s height with the population norm only
Sustained progression on the individual’s curve matters more than the norm.

items.q: A 16-year-old says, “I can text while driving. Accidents happen to other people, not me.” How should the nurse interpret this statement?
items.a: It reflects the adolescent belief of being unique and invincible
items.ex: Adolescents believe they are unique and the exception, which leads to risk-taking behaviors such as distracted driving.
w: It shows the teen cannot yet think abstractly about the future
Adolescents can think abstractly; they lack experience, not reasoning ability.
It shows a concrete operational focus on the here and now
Concrete operations describe school-age thinking, not this adolescent belief.
It reflects identity confusion caused by rejecting parental values
This statement shows a sense of invincibility, not identity confusion.

alt.q: Why do adolescents often engage in risk-taking behaviors even though they can think abstractly?
alt.a: They lack experience and see themselves as the exception
alt.ex: Adolescents can think as well as adults but lack experience and believe they are unique and invincible.
w: They cannot yet consider more than one possible outcome
Adolescents consider an infinite variety of causes and solutions.
They still rely on concrete thinking about the present
Adolescents move beyond concrete properties and think about the future.
They have not developed any personal value systems yet
Adolescents develop their own ethical systems based on personal values.

items.q: A 15-year-old asks the nurse, “Will you promise not to tell anyone what I say?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “What you share stays private unless you tell me about abuse or thoughts of suicide.”
items.ex: Nurses ensure confidentiality and explain its limits, such as disclosure of abuse or suicidal ideation.
w: “Yes, I promise never to share anything you tell me with anyone.”
Confidentiality has limits; abuse and suicidal ideation must be disclosed.
“No, I share everything you say with your parents after the visit.”
Adolescents are ensured confidentiality, which builds trust and openness.
“That depends on whether your parents agree to keep it private.”
Limits of confidentiality depend on safety issues, not parental agreement.

alt.q: Which information must the nurse explain to an adolescent when discussing the limits of confidentiality?
alt.a: Disclosure of abuse or suicidal ideation may need to be shared
alt.ex: Confidentiality is ensured, but its limits, such as disclosure of abuse or suicidal ideation, are explained.
w: Any discussion of school grades must be shared with parents
School performance is not a listed limit of confidentiality.
All questions about sexuality must be reported to parents
Sexual topics are discussed confidentially to open communication.
Nothing an adolescent says can ever be shared with anyone
Confidentiality has limits when safety is at risk.

items.q: According to Erikson, what is the prime danger of the adolescent stage?
items.a: Identity confusion
items.ex: Erikson saw identity or role confusion as the prime danger, with cliquish behavior and intolerance as defenses against it.
w: Inferiority
Inferiority is the risk of the school-age stage of industry versus inferiority.
Mistrust
Mistrust is the risk of the infant stage.
Guilt
Guilt is the risk of the preschool stage of initiative versus guilt.

alt.q: A parent is troubled that their teenager’s friend group excludes anyone who dresses differently. How does Erikson explain this behavior?
alt.a: As a defense against identity confusion
alt.ex: Erikson suggests cliquish behavior and intolerance of differences are defenses against identity confusion.
w: As a sign of concrete operational thinking
Concrete thinking belongs to school-age children, not this behavior.
As evidence of a sense of inferiority
Inferiority is the school-age risk, not the explanation for teen cliques.
As a lack of interest in peer acceptance
Teens strongly seek peer acceptance; cliques reflect that need.

items.q: A 17-year-old’s parent reports declining grades, withdrawal from friends, crying, and poor sleep over the past month. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Make an immediate referral to a mental health professional
items.ex: When assessment indicates depression or suicide risk, the nurse makes immediate referrals to mental health professionals.
w: Reassure the parent that these are normal teenage mood swings
These are warning signs of depression and suicide risk, not normal changes.
Schedule a follow-up visit in 6 months to reassess behavior
Delaying action is unsafe; referral should be immediate.
Suggest the teen join a sports team to improve mood
Activities may help coping later but do not replace immediate referral.

alt.q: During a sports physical, a 16-year-old says, “Sometimes I think everyone would be better off without me.” What is the nurse’s priority action?
alt.a: Refer the teen immediately to a mental health professional
alt.ex: Verbalization of suicidal thought signals suicide risk and requires immediate referral to mental health professionals.
w: Complete the physical and note the comment for the next visit
Suicidal statements require immediate action, not delay.
Keep the statement confidential as the teen requested
Suicidal ideation is a limit of confidentiality and must be acted on.
Tell the teen to focus on the positive parts of life
Guidance on positives helps, but immediate referral is the priority.

items.q: Which statement about causes of death among adolescents in the United States is accurate?
items.a: Motor vehicle accidents are the most common cause, and homicide ranks second
items.ex: Unintentional injury, mainly motor vehicle accidents, is the leading cause of death in adolescents; homicide is second.
w: Suicide is the most common cause, and motor vehicle accidents rank second
Unintentional injury is the leading cause; homicide is second.
Homicide is the most common cause, and drowning ranks second
Homicide is second, and drowning is another frequent accidental cause.
Infections are the most common cause, and firearms rank second
Infections cause most childhood illnesses, not most adolescent deaths.

alt.q: Which statement about homicide among adolescents is accurate?
alt.a: It is the leading cause of death in African-American teenagers
alt.ex: Homicide is the second leading cause of death in U.S. adolescents and the leading cause in African-American teenagers.
w: It is the leading cause of death in all U.S. adolescents
Unintentional injury, not homicide, leads for all adolescents.
It is most often committed by a stranger with a knife
Teens are most likely killed by an acquaintance or gang member, most often with a firearm.
It is rare and no longer a concern in school settings
Violence among adolescents is a national concern, including school shootings.

items.q: During a well visit for a 15-year-old, which assessment is especially important for reducing the risk of homicide and suicide?
items.a: Ask whether there is a gun in the home and discuss gun safety
items.ex: A gun in the home increases adolescent homicide and suicide risk, so assess gun presence and discuss gun safety.
w: Ask how many hours the teen spends playing video games
Video game use is not linked to homicide and suicide risk in the text.
Ask whether the teen has a part-time job after school
Part-time work supports independence and is not a homicide or suicide risk.
Ask how often the family eats dinner at home together
Family meals are not the assessment the book links to homicide and suicide risk.

alt.q: Why does the textbook recommend assessing gun presence in the home when counseling families of adolescents?
alt.a: A gun in the home increases the risk of adolescent homicide and suicide
alt.ex: Teens are most often killed with a firearm, and a gun in the home increases homicide and suicide risk.
w: Guns in the home are the main cause of motor vehicle accidents
Motor vehicle accidents relate to driving inexperience and risk taking, not guns.
Guns in the home are the leading cause of eating disorders
Eating disorders are not linked to gun presence.
A gun in the home is required to be reported to the police
Assessment is for counseling on safety, not mandatory police reporting.

items.q: A 16-year-old tells the nurse that he is gay and plans to tell his family this weekend. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Let’s talk about how you might tell them and plan for your safety if they react badly.”
items.ex: If an adolescent discloses sexual orientation, help plan how to tell family and build a safety plan in case the response is not supportive.
w: “You should keep this hidden from everyone until you are older.”
Hiding orientation to avoid stigma increases vulnerability to depression and suicide.
“Many teens feel this way, but it usually changes by adulthood.”
This dismisses the adolescent’s disclosure and is not the supportive response the book describes.
“I will need to call your parents to tell them before you do.”
Disclosure is the adolescent’s choice; the nurse helps plan it, not take over.

alt.q: Why are adolescents who keep an LGBTQIA+ orientation hidden at increased risk?
alt.a: Hiding it to avoid stigma increases vulnerability to depression and suicide
alt.ex: Teens often hide their orientation to avoid stigma, victimization, or bullying, which increases vulnerability to depression and suicide.
w: Hiding it increases the risk of developing anorexia nervosa
The book links hiding orientation to depression and suicide, not anorexia specifically.
Hiding it lowers their need for peer group acceptance
Teens still need peer acceptance; hiding orientation does not reduce that need.
Hiding it delays the physical changes of puberty
Pubertal physical changes are hormonal and not affected by disclosure.

items.q: A nurse suspects a 15-year-old in the emergency department is a victim of sex trafficking. The adult accompanying the teen refuses to leave the room. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Find a safe way to separate the teen from the adult before further questioning
items.ex: Evidence supports knowing how to safely separate the individual from the trafficker and connecting them with immediate protective resources.
w: Ask the teen about trafficking directly in front of the adult
Questioning in front of a possible trafficker is unsafe and unlikely to bring disclosure.
Discharge the teen because victims usually disclose on their own
Trafficked children often do not disclose, and victims returned without intervention stay at risk.
Wait to act until the teen clearly states that trafficking is occurring
Nurses as mandatory reporters must recognize signs and intervene without waiting for disclosure.

alt.q: Which statement about sex trafficking of minors is accurate according to the evidence-based practice box?
alt.a: Health care providers often fail to recognize victims, who then return to traffickers
alt.ex: Providers frequently do not recognize trafficking victims, so education on signs and risk factors improves early identification.
w: Most trafficked minors readily disclose that they are victims
Trafficked children often do not disclose, making recognition difficult.
The prevalence is well documented by a national tracking system
There is no uniform data system, so prevalence is largely unknown.
Only social workers need training to recognize the warning signs
Mandatory reporters, including nurses, must recognize signs and intervene.

items.q: A parent worries that her 14-year-old daughter compares herself to others on social media. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
items.a: Unhealthy social comparison may contribute to body image problems and eating disorders
items.ex: Social media can encourage unhealthy social comparisons that may play a role in body image problems and be a risk factor for eating disorders.
w: Social media use has no effect on how teens see themselves
The book notes concern about social media’s effect on teen identity.
Social comparison protects teens from forming poor peer groups
Unhealthy comparisons can make teens view others as better off than themselves.
Social media mainly affects school-age children, not adolescents
The concern described is about social media and teen identity.

alt.q: Which nursing action best promotes positive peer group selection for adolescents?
alt.a: Encourage parents to communicate with their teens and provide supervision
alt.ex: Nurses encourage parents to communicate with adolescents and provide supervision to promote selection of positive peer groups.
w: Advise parents to forbid all peer group activities
Peer groups provide belonging and approval; the goal is positive selection, not avoidance.
Tell parents that peer choices do not affect health
Poor peer selection can lead to poor decisions and negative health outcomes.
Suggest parents let teens choose friends without discussion
Communication and supervision help teens select positive peer groups.

items.q: Which are the four main physical changes of adolescence? Select all that apply.
o: Increased growth rate of the skeleton, muscle, and viscera
This is the first of the four main physical changes.
Sex-specific changes, such as shoulder and hip width
Sex-specific changes in body shape are one of the four main changes.
Alteration in the distribution of muscle and fat
Redistribution of muscle and fat is one of the four main changes.
Development of the reproductive system and secondary sex characteristics
Sexual maturation is one of the four main changes.
Slow, consistent growth like that of middle childhood
Physical changes in adolescence are rapid, not slow and consistent.
Completion of growth in both sexes by 14 years of age
Females reach full height by 16 to 17 and males grow until 18 to 20.
items.ex: The four main physical changes are faster growth, sex-specific changes, muscle and fat redistribution, and reproductive maturation.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a group of 12-year-olds about puberty. Which changes should the nurse describe? Select all that apply.
o: Changes in shoulder and hip width that differ by sex
Sex-specific changes in shoulder and hip width occur in puberty.
Changes in hair growth and voice caused by sex hormones
Estrogen and testosterone drive secondary sex characteristics such as hair growth and voice changes.
Acne and body odor linked to changing hormone levels
Changing hormone concentrations are linked to acne and body odor.
Changes that follow a different sequence in most individuals
The sequence of pubertal growth changes is the same in most individuals.
Changes that begin later in females than in males
Females generally have prepubescent changes before males.
alt.ex: Correct: Changes in shoulder and hip width that differ by sex; Changes in hair growth and voice caused by sex hormones; Acne and body odor linked to changing hormone levels.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to interview an adolescent. Which communication strategies are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Conduct the interview without parents present
As adolescents become more autonomous, interviews should be conducted without parents present.
Explain the limits of confidentiality
Ensure confidentiality and explain limits such as disclosure of abuse or suicidal ideation.
Ask open-ended questions
Open-ended questions encourage the adolescent to share their perspective.
Start with less sensitive topics before more sensitive ones
Beginning with less sensitive topics opens channels for further discussion.
Begin with questions about sexual activity to build trust
Sensitive topics come after less sensitive ones.
Promise that nothing said will ever be shared
Confidentiality has limits that must be explained.
items.ex: Effective adolescent interviews use privacy, explained confidentiality, a nonjudgmental tone, open-ended questions, and a gradual move to sensitive topics.

alt.q: Which nurse behaviors are likely to help an adolescent communicate openly? Select all that apply.
o: Showing genuine interest in the adolescent’s point of view
Being nonjudgmental and genuinely interested builds trust.
Providing a private, nonthreatening setting
Privacy and a nonthreatening environment support open communication.
Moving gradually from general topics to sex, drugs, and school
Starting with less sensitive topics opens channels for further discussion.
Expressing disapproval of risky choices the teen describes
The nurse should be nonjudgmental to keep communication open.
Using mainly yes-or-no questions to save time
Open-ended questions are recommended for adolescents.
alt.ex: Correct: Showing genuine interest in the adolescent’s point of view; Providing a private, nonthreatening setting; Moving gradually from general topics to sex, drugs, and school.

items.q: Which changes in behavior should the nurse screen for when assessing an adolescent for depression and suicide risk? Select all that apply.
o: Decrease in school performance
Declining school performance is a listed warning sign.
Withdrawal
Withdrawal and social isolation commonly precede a suicide attempt.
Appetite and sleep disturbances
Changes in appetite and sleep are listed behavior changes.
Verbalization of suicidal thought
Talking about suicide is a direct warning sign requiring referral.
Increased initiative in new activities
Loss of initiative, not increased initiative, is a warning sign.
Improved relationships with family
Improved relationships are not a sign of depression or suicide risk.
items.ex: Screen for decreased school performance, withdrawal, loss of initiative, loneliness and crying, appetite and sleep changes, and suicidal talk.

alt.q: A school nurse is reviewing reports on several students. Which findings suggest depression or suicide risk? Select all that apply.
o: A student who has lost interest and initiative in usual activities
Loss of initiative is a listed warning sign.
A student who reports loneliness, sadness, and frequent crying
Loneliness, sadness, and crying are listed behavior changes.
A student whose grades have dropped sharply this semester
A decrease in school performance is a warning sign.
A student who has joined a supportive new peer group
Supportive peer groups have a positive influence and are not a warning sign.
A student whose sleep and appetite are unchanged
Unchanged sleep and appetite are not warning signs; disturbances are.
alt.ex: Correct: A student who has lost interest and initiative in usual activities; A student who reports loneliness, sadness, and frequent crying; A student whose grades have dropped sharply this semester.

items.q: E-cigarettes are a safe alternative to conventional cigarettes for adolescents.
items.a: False
items.ex: E-cigarettes can harm adolescent brain development, impair learning and memory, increase addiction risk, and are linked to serious lung problems.
items.ww: It cannot be true; the book states e-cigarettes are not safe even if some believe they are less harmful.

alt.q: Vaping can harm adolescent brain development and impair learning, memory, and attention.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: E-cigarettes harm the developing brain, impair learning, memory, and attention, and increase the risk of addiction to other substances.
alt.ww: It is not false; the book lists these harms as reasons e-cigarettes are unsafe.

items.q: Bulimia nervosa is more difficult to detect than anorexia nervosa because it occurs within a normal weight range.
items.a: True
items.ex: Unlike anorexia, bulimia occurs within a normal weight range, so a thorough dietary history is important to detect it.
items.ww: It is not false; normal weight hides bulimia, unlike the low weight seen in anorexia.

alt.q: Adolescents with bulimia nervosa are easy to identify because they are markedly underweight.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Bulimia occurs within a normal weight range, making it much more difficult to detect.
alt.ww: It is not true; refusal to maintain minimal normal weight describes anorexia, not bulimia.

items.q: Sexually active adolescents should be screened for sexually transmitted infections (STIs) even when they have no symptoms.
items.a: True
items.ex: Because STIs affect millions of sexually active adolescents each year, screening is imperative even without symptoms.
items.ww: It is not false; the high incidence makes screening of asymptomatic sexually active teens essential.

alt.q: Sexually active adolescents need STI screening only when they report symptoms such as discharge or pain.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: STIs are so common in sexually active adolescents that screening is done even when no symptoms are present.
alt.ww: It is not true; waiting for symptoms would miss many infections in this high-incidence group.

items.q: It is illegal to sell any tobacco product, including e-cigarettes, to anyone under [[21|twenty-one]] years of age.

items.q: Which statement best describes emerging adulthood?
items.a: A phase from the late teens to mid-20s focused on identity and becoming independent
items.ex: Emerging adulthood, from the late teens to mid-20s, centers on major life transitions, identity development, and becoming independent.
w: A phase from the mid-30s to 40 focused on reexamining life goals and relationships
Vigorous examination of life goals and relationships traditionally occurs from ages 35 to 40.
A phase from the late 20s to mid-30s focused on achievement in a chosen career
Directing energy toward achievement traditionally occurs from ages 29 to 34, after emerging adulthood.
A phase from the early teens to late teens focused on developing secondary sex characteristics
Secondary sex characteristics develop during adolescence, before emerging adulthood.

alt.q: A 22-year-old who recently moved out of her parents’ home is deciding who she wants to be and how to reach her goals. Which developmental phase does this describe?
alt.a: Emerging adulthood
alt.ex: Identity development and deciding how to attain goals while becoming independent are tasks of emerging adulthood.
w: Middle adulthood
Middle adulthood spans ages 35 to 64 and centers on contributing to others and adapting to physical change.
Sandwich generation
The sandwich generation describes middle adults caring for both their children and aging parents.
Postparental family stage
The postparental stage begins in middle adulthood when children leave the household.

items.q: A 24-year-old who smokes daily and binge drinks on weekends says, “I’m young and healthy. Lung and heart disease are things older people worry about.” Which concept does this statement reflect?
items.a: Optimistic bias
items.ex: With optimistic bias, young adults do not perceive that risks for cancer and chronic cardiac and pulmonary disease will affect them.
w: Emerging adulthood
Emerging adulthood is a developmental phase, not a belief that health risks do not apply to oneself.
Health literacy
Health literacy is the skill to access, understand, and use health information, not a denial of risk.
Empty nest syndrome
Empty nest syndrome is the sadness parents feel when children leave home.

alt.q: A nurse explains optimistic bias to nursing students. Which example illustrates it?
alt.a: A young adult believes smoking will not harm his own future health
alt.ex: Optimistic bias means young adults do not perceive that the risks of behaviors like smoking will affect their health.
w: A young adult delays marriage to focus on career goals first
Delaying marriage is a common life choice of young adults, not a misperception of health risk.
A young adult relies on social media for emotional support
Reliance on social media relates to isolation risk, not to underestimating disease risk.
A young adult worries excessively about a minor family illness
Excessive worry is the opposite of optimistic bias, which underestimates personal risk.

items.q: A nurse teaches a 30-year-old smoker about the cardiac effects of nicotine. Which explanation is accurate?
items.a: Nicotine constricts the coronary arteries, raising the risk of angina and myocardial infarction
items.ex: Nicotine is a vasoconstrictor acting on the coronary arteries, increasing the risk of angina, MI, and coronary artery disease.
w: Nicotine dilates the coronary arteries, which overworks the heart and causes angina
Nicotine causes vasoconstriction, not vasodilation, of the coronary arteries.
Nicotine affects only the lungs, so the risk of heart disease is unchanged
Smoking is a documented risk factor for cardiac and vascular disease, not only lung disease.
Nicotine raises the heart rate but has no effect on the blood vessels
Nicotine’s main vascular effect is constriction of coronary and peripheral vessels.

alt.q: Which effect of nicotine explains why smokers develop peripheral vascular problems?
alt.a: Peripheral vasoconstriction
alt.ex: Nicotine causes peripheral vasoconstriction, which leads to vascular problems.
w: Peripheral vasodilation
Nicotine narrows blood vessels; it does not dilate them.
Smooth muscle relaxation
Smooth muscle relaxation is an effect of caffeine, not nicotine.
Increased gastric acid secretion
Increased gastric acid is an effect of caffeine and does not explain vascular problems.

items.q: A nurse is completing a personal lifestyle assessment for a young adult. Which data does the nurse collect? Select all that apply.
o: Use of caffeine, tobacco, alcohol, and illicit drugs
Substance and caffeine habits are core parts of the lifestyle assessment.
Occupational exposure to hazardous substances
Type of work and hazardous exposures are assessed as occupational risk factors.
Dates and locations of military assignments
Military records with dates and areas of assignment can reveal risk factors.
Hobbies, interests, and general life satisfaction
Life satisfaction, hobbies, and interests are included in the lifestyle assessment.
Childhood immunization dates
Immunization history is part of the health history, not the assessment of lifestyle habits and environment.
Grades earned in high school courses
School grades are not listed among lifestyle risk factors such as habits, home, economics, and stress.
items.ex: A lifestyle assessment covers life satisfaction, habits, home, economics, occupation, stress, and sometimes military history.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a young adult’s personal lifestyle assessment. Which findings are health risk factors? Select all that apply.
o: Binge drinks most weekends
Binge drinking is a health risk behavior common among young adults.
Works with solvents without protective equipment
Occupational exposure to hazardous substances increases disease risk.
Rarely engages in physical activity
Low physical activity is a lifestyle risk for chronic disease.
Always wears a seat belt when driving
Seat belt use is a recommended healthy lifestyle change, not a risk.
Eats a balanced diet with limited fast food
A healthy diet reduces risk; poor nutrition patterns are the risk factor.
alt.ex: Correct: Binge drinks most weekends; Works with solvents without protective equipment; Rarely engages in physical activity.

items.q: Joan, 25, comes to the clinic alone for insomnia. She speaks quietly, avoids eye contact, says her marriage is “not going well” since her husband lost his job, and has bruises and scratches on her breasts, abdomen, and back. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Privately assess Joan for intimate partner violence and ask about her safety
items.ex: Unexplained injuries, withdrawal, and a partner’s job loss suggest IPV, so a thorough assessment for violence comes first.
w: Teach Joan sleep hygiene measures to improve her insomnia
Insomnia is the presenting complaint, but injuries suggesting IPV take priority for assessment.
Suggest Joan bring her husband to the next visit for counseling
Involving a possible abuser before assessing for IPV could put Joan at greater risk.
Document the bruises and schedule a follow-up visit in 1 month
Delaying assessment overlooks signs of IPV and leaves Joan without help.

alt.q: While assessing Joan, which finding most strongly indicates the need to screen for intimate partner violence?
alt.a: Scratches and bruises on her breasts, abdomen, and back
alt.ex: Physical injuries such as bruises are direct signs of possible IPV and call for a focused assessment.
w: Difficulty falling asleep at night for several weeks
Insomnia has many causes and is not by itself a sign of violence.
She does not currently work outside of the home
Not working outside the home is a social detail, not evidence of injury.
She came to the clinic by herself for the visit
Coming alone is common and does not by itself suggest violence.

items.q: Which factors suggest a risk of perpetrating intimate partner violence? Select all that apply.
o: Adverse childhood experiences such as abuse or neglect
Adverse childhood experiences, including witnessing abuse, are risk factors for perpetrating IPV.
Heavy drinking
Drug or alcohol use, especially heavy drinking, is a risk factor for perpetration.
Unemployment
Unemployment is listed among risk factors for perpetrating IPV.
Desire for power and control in relationships
Seeking power and control in relationships is a risk factor.
High self-esteem
Low self-esteem, not high self-esteem, is a risk factor for perpetration.
Stable long-term employment
Unemployment, not stable employment, increases risk.
items.ex: IPV perpetration risks include adverse childhood experiences, substance use, unemployment, low self-esteem, gambling, and desire for control.

alt.q: A nurse screens a patient for risk factors associated with perpetrating IPV. Which findings are concerning? Select all that apply.
o: Witnessed domestic abuse as a child
Witnessing domestic abuse is an adverse childhood experience linked to perpetration.
Regular gambling
Gambling is a listed risk factor for perpetrating IPV.
Antisocial or borderline personality traits
These personality traits are risk factors for perpetration.
Abstains from alcohol and drugs
Substance use, not abstinence, is the risk factor.
Shares decision-making equally with a partner
A desire for power and control, not shared decisions, is the risk factor.
alt.ex: Correct: Witnessed domestic abuse as a child; Regular gambling; Antisocial or borderline personality traits.

items.q: A pregnant woman has a greater risk of being a victim of intimate partner violence than a nonpregnant woman.
items.a: True
items.ex: Risk of violence increases during the reproductive years, and pregnancy raises a woman’s risk of IPV.
items.ww: Saying False overlooks that pregnancy increases, not decreases, the risk of IPV.

alt.q: Pregnancy lowers a woman’s risk of intimate partner violence because partners tend to become more protective.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A pregnant woman is at greater risk of IPV, which can lead to delayed prenatal care and preterm birth.
alt.ww: Saying True reflects a common misconception; the book states pregnancy increases IPV risk.

items.ex: The opioid crisis moved from prescription opioids in the 1990s, to heroin in 2010, to synthetic opioids like fentanyl in 2013.
w: Rapid increase in overdose deaths involving heroin
That goes with Second wave (2010).
Overdose deaths involving synthetic opioids such as illicit fentanyl
That goes with Third wave (2013).

pairs: Rapid increase in overdose deaths involving heroin
Overdose deaths involving synthetic opioids such as illicit fentanyl

items.q: A nurse is completing a routine health assessment of a 21-year-old college student. Which approach to screening for substance use is best?
items.a: Ask nonjudgmentally how often in the past year the student used alcohol, tobacco, or drugs
items.ex: Nonjudgmental questions about legal and illegal substance use are a routine part of every health assessment.
w: Ask about drug use only if the student shows signs of intoxication
Substance use is hard to detect early, so screening is routine, not limited to visible signs.
Ask only about illegal drugs because legal substances pose little risk
Screening includes legal drugs such as alcohol, tobacco, and prescribed drugs as well as illegal ones.
Tell the student that substance use is wrong before asking any questions
Judgmental statements discourage honest answers; questions should be nonjudgmental.

alt.q: A young adult’s screening answers suggest risk for substance use. Which action should the nurse take next?
alt.a: Use a more detailed screening tool to further assess the risk
alt.ex: If screening suggests risk, further assessment tools such as the NM-ASSIST are available.
w: Notify law enforcement about the patient’s reported drug use
The nurse’s role is assessment and health recommendations, not reporting to police.
Repeat the same brief screening question at next year’s visit
A positive screen calls for further assessment now, not waiting a year.
Reassure the patient that substance use at this age is expected
Substance use disorder contributes to death and injury in young adults and is not dismissed.

items.q: A 26-year-old graduate student reports restlessness, irritability, muscle tremor, and heart palpitations during exam week. Which assessment question is most relevant?
items.a: “How much coffee, energy drinks, or caffeinated medicine do you use daily?”
items.ex: Large amounts of caffeine cause restlessness, irritability, tremor, and palpitations, so caffeine intake is assessed.
w: “Have you noticed any recent changes in your peripheral vision?”
Vision changes do not explain tremor, irritability, and palpitations.
“When was your last screening for sexually transmitted infections?”
STI screening matters but does not explain these stimulant-type symptoms.
“Does anyone in your family have a history of colorectal cancer?”
Family cancer history does not explain acute restlessness and palpitations.

alt.q: Which set of effects does caffeine produce?
alt.a: Increased heart rate, gastric acid secretion, and diuresis
alt.ex: Caffeine stimulates catecholamine release, increasing heart rate, gastric acid, metabolic rate, and diuresis.
w: Decreased heart rate, gastric acid secretion, and diuresis
Caffeine is a stimulant that increases, not decreases, heart rate and gastric acid.
Increased heart rate with smooth muscle contraction and urine retention
Caffeine relaxes smooth muscle and increases diuresis.
Decreased metabolic rate with drowsiness and constipation
Caffeine raises basal metabolic rate and causes restlessness and sometimes diarrhea.

items.q: Which young adults are at higher risk for human trafficking? Select all that apply.
o: Those who have run away from home
Running away from home is a listed risk for trafficking.
Those who are homeless
Homeless young adults are at high risk for trafficking.
Those with intellectual and developmental disabilities
Intellectual and developmental disabilities increase risk.
Those with histories of physical and sexual abuse
Shared histories of abuse and trauma increase risk.
Those living with supportive, financially stable families
Poverty and family instability, not stable families, increase risk.
Those with secure housing and steady employment
Homelessness and poverty, not secure housing and income, increase risk.
items.ex: Running away, homelessness, disabilities, poverty, family instability, abuse, and trauma place young adults at risk for trafficking.

alt.q: An emergency department nurse is caring for several young adults. Which patients have characteristics that place them at higher risk for human trafficking? Select all that apply.
o: An 18-year-old who recently ran away from home
Running away from home increases the risk of trafficking.
A 19-year-old who has been homeless for several months
Homelessness is a major risk for trafficking.
A 20-year-old with an intellectual disability and an unstable family
Disability and family instability both increase risk.
A 21-year-old living with supportive parents while in college
A stable, supportive home is not a listed risk factor.
A 22-year-old with a steady job and secure housing
Poverty and homelessness, not stable income and housing, increase risk.
alt.ex: Correct: An 18-year-old who recently ran away from home; A 19-year-old who has been homeless for several months; A 20-year-old with an intellectual disability and an unstable family.

items.q: A 23-year-old man comes to the clinic reporting burning on urination. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
items.a: Assess his sexual activity and be alert for a sexually transmitted infection
items.ex: Nurses are alert for STIs when young adults report urological or gynecological problems and assess sexual activity for screening.
w: Advise increasing fluid intake and returning if symptoms persist
This delays assessment of a possible STI in a high-risk age-group.
Avoid questions about sexual activity to protect his privacy
Assessing sexual activity determines appropriate STI screening and prevention.
Explain that STIs are uncommon in his age-group
Almost half of all new STIs occur in people younger than 26.

alt.q: Which statement about sexually transmitted infections in young adults is accurate?
alt.a: Almost half of all new STIs occur in people younger than 26 years
alt.ex: STIs are a major health problem in young adults, with nearly half of new infections in people under 26.
w: Almost half of all new STIs occur in people older than 50 years
New STIs are concentrated in young people, not older adults.
About one-tenth of all new STIs occur in people younger than 26 years
The proportion is much higher, close to half of new infections.
Nearly all new STIs occur in people younger than 18 years
Young adults up to 26, not only minors, account for nearly half of new infections.

items.q: A pregnant woman commonly feels big, awkward, and unattractive during the third trimester, when the fetus grows more rapidly.
items.a: True
items.ex: Table 13.2 notes that rapid fetal growth in the third trimester often leaves the woman feeling big and unattractive.
items.ww: Saying False ignores the body image changes listed for the third trimester.

alt.q: Most pregnant women feel their most attractive during the third trimester, when the fetus grows most rapidly.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: During the third trimester women often feel big, awkward, and unattractive as the fetus grows rapidly.
alt.ww: Saying True confuses the third trimester with feelings of well-being when the woman first feels the baby move.

items.q: A 28-year-old accountant reports poor sleep, skipped meals, and smoking more since a new manager started. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
items.a: Ask about her job demands, sources of work stress, and support at work
items.ex: Assessment of work-related stress includes usual work, perceived stressors, job demand changes, and sources of support.
w: Reassure her that work stress usually resolves without any changes
Unaddressed work stress affects health behaviors; it needs assessment, not dismissal.
Advise her to look for a new job as soon as possible
Interventions are person-centered and follow assessment, not an immediate job change.
Address smoking cessation only and avoid discussing work
The increased smoking is linked to work stress, so the stressors must be assessed.

alt.q: According to the World Health Organization, work-related stress occurs when:
alt.a: Work demands and pressures do not match a person’s knowledge and abilities
alt.ex: WHO defines work-related stress as the response to demands not matched to one’s knowledge and abilities that challenge coping.
w: A worker regularly works more than 40 hours in one week
Long hours alone are not the definition; the mismatch between demands and abilities is.
A worker changes jobs more than once in a single year
Frequent job changes are a feature of the labor market, not the WHO definition.
A worker receives formal feedback on job performance
Performance feedback is not the WHO definition of work-related stress.

items.q: Infertility evaluation begins after a couple has had unprotected intercourse for about [[12|twelve]] months without conceiving.
items.ex: About 12 months of unprotected intercourse without conception is the point at which infertility evaluation begins.

alt.q: A couple who has not conceived after about [[12|twelve]] months of unprotected intercourse should begin an infertility evaluation.
alt.ex: About 12 months of unprotected intercourse without conception is the point at which infertility evaluation begins.

items.q: A nurse visits a first-time breastfeeding mother 1 week after delivery. Which finding indicates the mother needs breastfeeding assistance?
items.a: The infant fails to latch onto the breast and is gaining little weight
items.ex: Failure to latch and low infant weight gain are signs the mother needs breastfeeding information and help.
w: The infant feeds well and sleeps contentedly between feedings
Good feeding and contented sleep suggest breastfeeding is going well.
The infant has gained weight steadily since hospital discharge
Steady weight gain indicates effective feeding.
The mother says breastfeeding is getting easier each day
Growing confidence suggests she is adapting well to breastfeeding.

alt.q: Which statement by a new mother suggests she needs breastfeeding information and assistance?
alt.a: “My baby keeps slipping off my breast and can’t seem to latch on.”
alt.ex: An infant who cannot latch onto the breast is a sign that the mother needs assistance.
w: “My baby latches well and has gained weight since we got home.”
Good latch and weight gain show successful breastfeeding.
“My baby feeds, then falls asleep satisfied for a few hours.”
A satisfied infant between feedings suggests effective breastfeeding.
“I was nervous at first, but breastfeeding feels natural now.”
Decreasing anxiety shows the mother is adapting well.

items.q: A nurse teaches a new mother and her partner about postpartum depression. Which statement by the partner shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I should watch for overwhelming sadness, withdrawal, or trouble bonding with the baby.”
items.ex: Common signs of postpartum depression include overwhelming sadness, mood swings, impaired sleep, withdrawal, and difficulty bonding.
w: “Mood swings after birth are normal, so we never need to report them.”
Mood swings are a sign of postpartum depression that should be recognized and reported.
“Difficulty bonding with the baby is expected and not a concern.”
Difficulty bonding with the infant is a common sign of postpartum depression.
“If she withdraws from the family, it means she is resting well.”
Withdrawal is a sign of postpartum depression, not healthy rest.

alt.q: Which findings in a postpartum woman are signs of postpartum depression?
alt.a: Mood swings, impaired sleeping, and difficulty bonding with the infant
alt.ex: Postpartum depression signs include overwhelming sadness, mood swings, impaired sleep, withdrawal, and difficulty bonding.
w: Irregular, short uterine contractions and urinary frequency
These describe Braxton Hicks contractions and urinary frequency in the third trimester.
Breast enlargement, breast tenderness, and morning sickness
These are common physiological changes of the first trimester.
Genital discharge and discomfort with urination
These are immediate physical effects of sexually transmitted infections.

items.q: A 50-year-old woman helps her teenage children with schoolwork while also managing her widowed father’s medications and appointments. Which term describes her situation?
items.a: Sandwich generation
items.ex: Middle adults who help aging parents while still responsible for their own children are in the sandwich generation.
w: Postparental family stage
The postparental stage begins after children leave the household.
Empty nest syndrome
Empty nest syndrome is sadness and loneliness when children leave home.
Emerging adulthood
Emerging adulthood is a phase from the late teens to mid-20s.

alt.q: Which description defines the sandwich generation?
alt.a: Middle adults caring for aging parents while still responsible for their own children
alt.ex: The sandwich generation is caught between the responsibilities of caring for children and caring for aging parents.
w: Middle adults whose children have left home and who are redefining their relationship
This describes the postparental family stage.
Young adults who move back to their parents’ home after finishing college
Returning home as a young adult is not the sandwich generation.
Older adults raising their grandchildren while their adult children work
The term refers to middle adults between children and aging parents.

items.q: A nurse performs a physical examination on a 52-year-old patient. Which findings are abnormal and need follow-up? Select all that apply.
o: Drooping of the upper eyelid
Ptosis is listed as an abnormal eye finding in the middle adult.
Recent increase in the size of one breast
A recent increase in size of one breast is an abnormal breast finding.
Unequal chest expansion
Unequal chest expansion is an abnormal thorax and lung finding.
Reduced peripheral vision
Reduced peripheral vision is listed as an abnormal eye finding.
Graying of the hair

items.q: Perimenopause, the period of declining ovarian function with irregular menstrual cycles, generally lasts [[1 to 3|1-3|one to three]] years.
items.ex: During perimenopause, ova diminish and cycles become irregular for about 1 to 3 years before menopause.

alt.q: Irregular menstrual cycles caused by declining ovarian function mark [[perimenopause]], which generally lasts 1 to 3 years.
alt.ex: During perimenopause, ova diminish and cycles become irregular for about 1 to 3 years before menopause.

items.q: During and after the climacteric, a man is still capable of producing fertile sperm and fathering a child.
items.a: True
items.ex: Decreased androgens cause the climacteric, but men remain able to father a child; erections are less firm and the refractory period longer.
items.ww: Saying False confuses the climacteric with menopause, which ends ovulation in women.

alt.q: The climacteric ends a man’s ability to father a child because androgen levels fall.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Although androgens decrease, a man can still produce fertile sperm during and after the climacteric.
alt.ww: Saying True assumes the climacteric ends fertility, but men remain capable of fathering a child.

items.q: The spouse of a 54-year-old patient reports that the patient has become forgetful and irritable over the past year. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Screen the patient for memory problems and report the findings
items.ex: Cognitive changes are rare in middle adults, so memory problems are screened carefully because early-onset dementia may be missed.
w: Explain that memory loss is a normal part of middle age
Cognitive changes are rare in middle adults except with illness or trauma.
Reassure the spouse that dementia does not occur before age 65
Early-onset dementia includes dementia-related conditions before age 65.
Suggest a vacation to reduce stress before any further assessment
Delaying assessment can delay diagnosis and care for early-onset dementia.

alt.q: Which statement about cognitive changes in middle adults is accurate?
alt.a: Cognitive changes are rare in middle adults except with illness or trauma
alt.ex: Middle adults continue to learn, and cognitive changes are rare without illness or trauma.
w: Cognitive decline is expected in all middle adults after age 40
Decline is not expected; middle adults continue to learn.
Middle adults generally lose the ability to learn new job skills
Many middle adults enter educational programs to gain new skills.
Memory loss in middle adults is almost always caused by normal aging
Memory loss warrants screening because early-onset dementia can occur.

items.q: A 56-year-old man taking a beta blocker and a diuretic for hypertension tells the nurse he has trouble maintaining an erection. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Some blood pressure medicines can cause this; let’s talk with your health care provider.”
items.ex: Antihypertensives, diuretics, and beta blockers can cause erectile dysfunction, so the concern is shared with the provider.
w: “This is a normal part of aging, and nothing can be done about it.”
Medication side effects are a treatable cause and should not be dismissed as aging.
“Stop taking your blood pressure medicines until the problem improves.”
Stopping antihypertensives on his own is unsafe; changes require the provider.
“Erection problems in middle age are always caused by job stress.”
Job stress is one factor, but medications and health also influence sexual function.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a middle-age man’s medication list. Which medication is most likely to contribute to erectile dysfunction?
alt.a: A beta blocker taken for hypertension
alt.ex: Antihypertensive agents, including beta blockers and diuretics, can cause erectile dysfunction.
w: A vitamin D supplement taken for a deficiency
Vitamin D supplements are not linked to erectile dysfunction in the text.
A topical cream applied for dry skin
A skin cream is not among the medications that affect sexual function.
Artificial tears used for dry eyes
Eye drops for dryness are not linked to erectile dysfunction.

items.q: For a middle adult who is widowed, separated, or divorced, resolution of grief often takes a year or more.
items.a: True
items.ex: Normal grief moves back and forth through phases, and resolution often takes a year or more.
items.ww: Saying False underestimates how long normal grief takes after a change in marital status.

alt.q: Normal grief after losing a spouse moves in a straight line through each phase and usually resolves within a few weeks.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Grief progresses back and forth through phases, and resolution often takes a year or more.
alt.ww: Saying True misrepresents grief, which is not linear and often lasts a year or more.

items.q: A 58-year-old woman working full-time is caring for her mother with dementia. She says she is exhausted and has stopped going to her own medical appointments. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Assess her physical and emotional needs and include them in the plan of care
items.ex: Nurses determine the caregiver’s physical and emotional health needs and incorporate them into the patient’s plan of care.
w: Advise her to quit her job to become a full-time caregiver
The decision to stop working is the family’s; the nurse first assesses needs and resources.
Focus the plan of care only on her mother’s needs
The health needs of both the caregiver and the parent are identified.
Tell her that caregivers should put their own health second
Neglecting caregiver health is not supported; caregiver needs are part of the plan.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse reflects best practice when meeting a middle-adult family caregiver of an aging parent?
alt.a: “Let’s look at your own health needs as well as your father’s.”
alt.ex: Nurses identify the health needs of both generations and help the family find available resources.
w: “Your father’s needs come first, so we will focus only on him.”
The caregiver’s health needs are also assessed and included in the plan.
“Your own health concerns can wait until caregiving is over.”
Caregiver health needs are addressed now, not postponed.
“Community resources are only for patients who live alone.”
Nurses help multigenerational families identify community resources.

items.q: Which exercise pattern does the textbook describe as promoting health in middle adults?
items.a: 20 to 30 minutes, 5 or 6 times a week
items.ex: Routine exercise of 20 to 30 minutes 5 or 6 times a week promotes health in middle adults.
w: 60 to 90 minutes, once a week
A single weekly session does not provide regular fitness.
10 minutes, 2 times a week
This is too brief and infrequent to meet the recommendation.
20 to 30 minutes, once a month
Monthly exercise is not routine fitness.

alt.q: A 47-year-old asks the nurse how often to exercise to stay healthy. Which response is best?
alt.a: “Aim for 20 to 30 minutes of exercise 5 or 6 times a week.”

Once weekly does not meet the routine frequency recommended.
“Aim for 10 minutes of exercise 2 times a week.”
This duration and frequency fall short of the recommendation.
“Aim for 2 hours of exercise once a month.”
Monthly exercise does not provide regular fitness.
