items.q: Routine calcium and vitamin D supplements are recommended for all middle-age women to reduce fracture risk.
items.a: False
items.ex: Supplements are recommended when a vitamin D deficiency is present; routine use does not reduce fracture risk.
items.ww: Saying True reflects outdated practice; routine supplements are no longer recommended.

alt.q: Calcium and vitamin D supplements are now recommended for middle-age women when a vitamin D deficiency is present.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: New data show supplements are indicated for vitamin D deficiency because routine use does not reduce fractures.
alt.ww: Saying False overlooks that supplements are still recommended when a deficiency exists.

items.q: A nurse wants to help a 50-year-old patient who smokes and rarely exercises form positive health habits. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Determine whether the patient is ready to make a health behavior change
items.ex: The nurse first assesses readiness to change, then provides information and positive reinforcement.
w: Give the patient a detailed exercise plan to start this week
Planning comes after assessing readiness to change.
Offer rewards only after the patient has fully quit smoking
Reinforcement is given for health-directed behaviors along the way, and readiness is assessed first.
Explain that long-standing habits cannot change in middle age
Middle adults often adopt healthier lifestyles; habits can be changed.

alt.q: Before teaching a middle adult about changing poor health habits, what should the nurse assess first?
alt.a: The patient’s readiness to change health behaviors
alt.ex: Assessing readiness for a health behavior change is the first step in promoting positive habits.
w: The patient’s preferred brand of exercise equipment
Equipment preferences are minor details, not the first assessment.
The patient’s ability to pay for a gym membership
Cost may matter later, but readiness to change is assessed first.
The patient’s family history of osteoporosis
Family history is useful but does not determine readiness to change.

items.q: Which are internal barriers to changing health habits? Select all that apply.
o: Lack of knowledge
Lack of knowledge is an internal barrier to change.
Insufficient skills to change health habits
Insufficient skills or motivation is an internal barrier.
Undefined short- and long-term goals
Undefined goals are an internal barrier.
Lack of facilities
Lack of facilities is an external barrier.
Poor access to care
Poor access to care is an external barrier.
Limited social support
Limited social support is an external barrier.
items.ex: Box 13.2 lists lack of knowledge, insufficient skills or motivation, and undefined goals as internal barriers.

alt.q: Which are external barriers to changing health habits? Select all that apply.
o: Lack of facilities
Lack of facilities is an external barrier.
Poor access to care
Poor access to care is an external barrier.
Limited social support
Limited social support is an external barrier.
Lack of resources and materials
Lack of resources and materials is an external barrier.
Lack of knowledge
Lack of knowledge is an internal barrier.
Undefined short- and long-term goals
Undefined goals are an internal barrier.
alt.ex: Correct: Lack of facilities; Poor access to care; Limited social support; Lack of resources and materials.

items.q: A 60-year-old patient for whom English is a second language is being discharged on new diabetes medications. Which action best promotes the patient’s understanding?
items.a: Use a professional interpreter and visual materials at an appropriate reading level
items.ex: People for whom English is a second language risk low health literacy; interpreters and literacy-appropriate materials improve understanding.
w: Have the patient’s teenage grandchild translate the instructions
A professional interpreter may be needed to ensure accurate understanding of health instructions.
Give detailed written English instructions for the patient to read at home
Low health literacy limits understanding of written information such as discharge teaching.
Speak louder and more slowly while reviewing the instructions in English
Volume does not overcome a language barrier or low health literacy.

alt.q: Which definition of health literacy is accurate?
alt.a: Cognitive and social skills that determine motivation and ability to access, understand, and use health information
alt.ex: Health literacy is the cognitive and social skills that let people access, understand, and use information to promote health.
w: The ability to read printed materials at or above a high school reading level
Health literacy is broader than reading level; it includes motivation and using information.
The amount of formal education a person has completed in health or science courses
Health literacy is not defined by formal education in health sciences.
A person’s knowledge of the medical terms used by health care providers and staff
Knowing terminology is not the definition; access, understanding, and use of information are.

items.q: Which are risk factors for depression in middle adults? Select all that apply.
o: Family history of depression
A family history of depression is a listed risk factor.
Being female
Being female is a risk factor for depression.
Lack of social support
Lack of social support increases the risk of depression.
Chronic illness
Chronic illness is a risk factor, and depression can aggravate it.
Being male
Being female, not male, is the listed risk factor.
Strong network of friends and family
Strong social support is protective; lack of support is the risk.
items.ex: Depression risk factors include family history, being female, LGBTQIA+ identity, lack of social support, chronic illness, and negative life events.

alt.q: A nurse screens middle adults for depression. Which findings increase a patient’s risk? Select all that apply.
o: Member of the LGBTQIA+ community
Being a member of the LGBTQIA+ community is a listed risk factor.
Recent negative stressful life event
Negative stressful life events increase depression risk.
Family history of depression
Family history is a risk factor for depression.
Steady social support from friends
Social support is protective; its lack is the risk factor.
No history of chronic illness
Chronic illness, not its absence, increases risk.
alt.ex: Correct: Member of the LGBTQIA+ community; Recent negative stressful life event; Family history of depression.

items.q: A nurse is assessing a 52-year-old patient recently diagnosed with depression. Which approach is most appropriate?
items.a: Collect assessment data from both the patient and the patient’s family
items.ex: Whatever screening tool is used, data come from both patient and family; family data are often especially important.
w: Rely only on the patient’s own report of mood and behavior
Family data are often particularly important, depending on the level of depression.
Assess only physical symptoms such as back pain and fatigue
Assessment covers mood, cognitive, behavioral, social, and physical changes.
Avoid asking about family history to protect the patient’s privacy
Individual and family history of depression is part of focused data collection.

alt.q: A nurse uses the agency’s depression screening tool for a middle adult. From whom should the nurse collect assessment data?
alt.a: Both the patient and the patient’s family
alt.ex: Data are collected from both the patient and family, and family data may be especially important.
w: The patient only
Family data are often particularly important depending on the level of depression.
The family only
The patient’s own report is also needed for a complete assessment.
The health care provider only
Assessment data come from the patient and family, not only the provider.

items.q: Which definition of early-onset dementia (EOD) is accurate?
items.a: Dementia-related conditions that begin before age 65
items.ex: EOD includes all dementia-related conditions before age 65 and can be missed because it is not expected in younger adults.
w: Dementia-related conditions that begin before age 40
The age cutoff for EOD is 65, not 40.
Dementia-related conditions that begin before age 50
The age cutoff for EOD is 65, not 50.
Dementia-related conditions that begin after age 75
EOD occurs before age 65, not late in life.

alt.q: The spouse of a 61-year-old with worsening memory loss and irritability speaks with the nurse. Which statement shows understanding of early-onset dementia?
alt.a: “Dementia can begin before age 65, so this needs to be checked.”
alt.ex: Early-onset dementia includes dementia before 65, so memory problems in middle adults are screened carefully.
w: “Dementia only starts after age 75, so this must be stress.”
Dementia can occur before 65; attributing it to stress delays diagnosis.
“Memory problems before age 70 are part of normal aging.”
Cognitive changes are rare in middle adults except with illness or trauma.
“Dementia can start before age 40 only if it runs in families.”
EOD covers all dementia-related conditions before age 65.

items.q: A 55-year-old patient is recovering from an ankle fracture. Compared with a young adult, what should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: A longer recovery period because healing processes slow
items.ex: Injuries and acute illnesses in middle adults need longer recovery because healing slows, and they more often become chronic.
w: A shorter recovery period because of greater life experience
Life experience does not speed healing; slower healing lengthens recovery.
The same recovery period with less risk of chronic problems
Acute conditions in middle adults are more likely to become chronic.
A longer recovery only if there is a family history of fractures
Slower healing in middle age, not family history, lengthens recovery.

alt.q: Which statement about acute illness in middle adults is accurate?
alt.a: Recovery takes longer, and conditions are more likely to become chronic
alt.ex: Slower healing lengthens recovery and makes acute conditions more likely to become chronic in middle adults.
w: Acute illnesses differ completely from those of young adults
Acute illnesses in middle adults are like those of young adults.
Recovery is faster than in young adults because of set routines
Healing slows in middle age, so recovery is longer, not faster.
Acute illness rarely affects stress in the sandwich generation
Stress increases as they balance work, family, and parents while recovering.

items.q: Which statement best describes the functional ability of older adults?
items.a: It varies widely, and most older adults are active and involved in their communities.
items.ex: Older adults have a wide range of functional ability, and most remain active and involved in their communities.
w: It declines in a predictable, uniform way once a person reaches 65 years of age.
Each person ages in their own way; age 65 is only a social boundary, not a point of uniform decline.
Most older adults have lost the ability to care for themselves and need residential housing.
Only a smaller number lose the ability to care for themselves and need assisted living or residential housing.
It depends mainly on chronological age rather than on health and psychosocial factors.
Chronological age often has little relation to the reality of aging for an individual older adult.

alt.q: A nursing student says, “Most older adults are frail and depend on others for their care.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
alt.a: “Most older adults are active, involved in their communities, and functionally independent.”
alt.ex: Most older adults remain functionally independent and active despite the increasing prevalence of chronic disease.
w: “That is correct; dependence on others is an expected result of normal aging.”
Normal aging changes do not equal dependence; most older adults remain functionally independent.
“Only older adults who live with a spouse or partner are able to stay independent.”
Living with a partner is linked to fewer functional difficulties, but many others also stay independent.
“Most older adults become dependent once they develop their first chronic illness.”
Most older adults remain functionally independent even though chronic disease becomes more common.

items.q: A nurse is completing an admission assessment for a 78-year-old patient with pneumonia. Which approach best reflects the textbook’s guidance on assessing older adults?
items.a: Identify the patient’s strengths and abilities and plan care that encourages independence.
items.ex: The nurse identifies strengths and abilities during assessment and makes encouraging independence an integral part of the plan of care.
w: Focus the assessment on signs of disease and decline, which matter most at this age.
Do not assume disease and decline are the only factors to assess; strengths and abilities matter too.
Assume the patient needs help with dressing and mobility because of advanced age.
Assumptions based on age are inaccurate; functional ability varies widely and must be assessed individually.
Gather most of the history from family because older adults are unreliable historians.
Older adults vary in cognitive health; the patient should be assessed as an individual rather than presumed unreliable.

alt.q: Which plan of care entry for an 80-year-old patient hospitalized with a chronic illness best reflects the textbook’s approach to older adults?
alt.a: Build on the patient’s identified strengths to encourage independence in self-care.
alt.ex: Encouraging independence and building on strengths are integral parts of the plan of care for an older adult.
w: Provide complete care for all activities to conserve the patient’s limited energy.
Doing everything for the patient undermines independence, which should be encouraged as part of the plan.
Limit assessment to the chronic illness because it explains all current findings.
Disease is not the only factor to assess; the nurse also identifies strengths and abilities.
Expect gradual loss of function and plan early placement in residential housing.
Most older adults remain functionally independent; decline should not be assumed.

items.q: A 74-year-old patient with diabetes is admitted for a minor procedure. A newly hired nurse says, “All my older patients are going to be confused and dependent.” Which response by the charge nurse is best?
items.a: “Older adults vary widely, so we need to assess each patient as an individual.”
items.ex: Older adults vary in physiological, cognitive, and psychosocial health and function, so each needs individual assessment.
w: “That is realistic, so plan extra time to do most of their care for them.”
This reinforces a stereotype; most older adults are independent and should be encouraged to stay so.
“Only patients over 85 are likely to be confused, so this patient will be fine.”
Age alone does not predict confusion; each older adult must be assessed individually.
“Confusion is normal at that age, so it does not need to be reported.”
Confusion should not be assumed to be normal; assuming decline can cause real problems to be missed.

alt.q: A nurse caring for several older adults is asked by a student why care plans for patients of the same age differ so much. Which response is best?
alt.a: “Older adults differ widely in their physical, cognitive, and psychosocial health.”
alt.ex: Variations in physiological, cognitive, and psychosocial health make each older adult’s needs unique.
w: “Care plans differ only because each patient has a different medical diagnosis.”
Diagnosis is one factor, but psychosocial health, function, and strengths also vary widely.
“Care plans for older adults are usually identical; these are unusual cases.”
Every older adult is unique, so care plans are individualized rather than identical.
“Care plans differ mainly because each patient is a different chronological age.”
Chronological age has little relation to the reality of a person’s aging.

items.q: A 77-year-old man was recently diagnosed with heart failure, and his wife died 3 months ago. He now seems withdrawn. Which interpretation by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: His losses and health changes together place him at high risk for illness and functional decline.
items.ex: Reduced stress response, multiple losses, and age-related physical and psychosocial changes combine to place older adults at high risk for illness and decline.
w: His withdrawal is an expected part of normal aging and needs no further assessment.
Withdrawal is not an expected part of aging; physical and psychosocial factors interact and need assessment.
His physical illness and his grief are separate issues that do not affect each other.
The physical and psychosocial aspects of aging are closely related and influence each other.
His heart failure is the only factor the nurse needs to assess at this time.
Disease is not the only factor to assess; psychosocial losses also affect his health and function.

alt.q: Which older adult is at greatest risk for illness and functional deterioration based on the textbook’s description of interacting factors?
alt.a: A 79-year-old with a new chronic illness who has recently lost several close family members
alt.ex: A reduced ability to respond to stress plus multiple losses and age-related changes places older adults at high risk.
w: A 72-year-old who lives with a spouse and volunteers weekly at a community center
Living with a partner and being active are linked with fewer functional difficulties.
An 81-year-old with one well-controlled chronic illness who walks daily with friends
Stable health with active social contact does not show the combined stress and losses that raise risk.
A 68-year-old who recently retired and is taking classes at a local college
Pursuing new interests after retirement does not suggest the multiple losses that raise risk.

items.q: According to the textbook, which older adults report fewer functional difficulties, such as with dressing or mobility?
items.a: Some who live with a spouse or partner
items.ex: The text notes that some older adults who live with a spouse or partner have fewer functional difficulties, such as with dressing or mobility.
w: Those who recently moved to a new city
Relocation is a change requiring adjustment; it is not linked in the text to fewer functional difficulties.
Those who live alone in a single-level home
Living alone is not identified as the factor linked to fewer functional difficulties.
Those who recently left the workforce
Retirement is a role transition; it is not the factor linked to fewer functional difficulties.

alt.q: During an assessment, a nurse learns that an 80-year-old woman lives with her long-term partner. Based on the textbook, what may this finding suggest?
alt.a: She may have fewer difficulties with tasks such as dressing or mobility.
alt.ex: Some older adults who live with a spouse or partner have fewer functional difficulties, such as with dressing or mobility.
w: She is more likely to need assisted living in the near future.
Living with a partner is linked to fewer functional difficulties, not a greater need for assisted living.
She is at greater risk for confusion and withdrawal from others.
Confusion and withdrawal are seen in a smaller number of older adults and are not linked to living with a partner.
She does not need a functional assessment during this admission.
Every older adult needs an individual assessment of function; living arrangements only offer clues.

items.q: Which older adults are most likely to need assisted living or residential housing?
items.a: Those who have lost the ability to care for themselves or to make decisions about their needs
items.ex: A smaller number of older adults lose self-care ability, become confused or withdrawn, or cannot make decisions, and need assisted living or residential housing.
w: Those who have one chronic illness that is well controlled with medication at home
Many older adults have chronic illness yet remain functionally independent.
Those who have recently retired and are adjusting to a reduced or fixed income
Retirement and income changes are developmental tasks, not reasons for residential care.
Those who have mild age-related changes in vision, hearing, or physical endurance
Normal sensory and energy changes do not by themselves mean a person cannot live independently.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing four older adults in a community clinic. Which patient’s situation most suggests a need for assisted living or residential housing?
alt.a: An 84-year-old who is confused, withdrawn, and unable to make decisions about her needs
alt.ex: Older adults who are confused or withdrawn or unable to make decisions about their needs may require assisted living or residential housing.
w: A 76-year-old with arthritis who uses a cane and drives to church activities each week
This patient shows functional independence and social involvement despite a chronic condition.
An 82-year-old who lives with her husband and needs help only with heavy housework
Living with a partner and needing minimal help suggests good functional ability.
A 70-year-old who has hypertension and diabetes and manages his own medications
Managing his own care shows independence despite multiple chronic conditions.

items.q: A nurse is assessing an 85-year-old patient who has diabetes, heart failure, and osteoarthritis. Why is the assessment of this patient likely to be more complex?
items.a: Multiple chronic illnesses interact with physical and psychosocial factors of aging.
items.ex: Chronic conditions add complexity because many older adults have multiple illnesses that interact with physical and psychosocial factors.
w: Chronic illnesses always produce classic signs that hide the effects of aging.
Chronic conditions add complexity; they do not always produce classic, easily recognized signs.
Older adults with chronic illness are usually unable to describe their symptoms.
Having chronic illness does not mean an older adult cannot participate in the assessment.
Chronic illness makes it impossible to assess this patient’s functional status.
Functional status can and should be assessed; nursing assessment reveals how disease affects function.

alt.q: Which statement about chronic illness in older adults is accurate according to the textbook?
alt.a: Many older adults have several chronic illnesses, which adds complexity to their care.
alt.ex: Older adults may have at least one chronic illness, and many have multiple illnesses that complicate assessment and care.
w: Chronic illness usually causes older adults to lose functional independence.
Most older adults remain functionally independent despite the increasing prevalence of chronic disease.
Chronic illness is rare in older adults who remain active in their communities.
Chronic illness is common among older adults, including many who remain active.
Chronic illness simplifies care because symptoms follow a predictable pattern.
Chronic conditions add to the complexity, not the simplicity, of assessment and care.

items.q: What does nursing assessment provide about the effect of disease on an older adult?
items.a: Clues to how a disease or illness affects the patient’s functional status
items.ex: Nursing assessment provides valuable clues to the effects of a disease or illness on a patient’s functional status.
w: A medical diagnosis that confirms which disease the patient has
Diagnosing disease is the health care provider’s role; nursing assessment focuses on effects on function.
Proof that functional decline is caused by normal aging alone
Assessment helps sort out effects of disease and aging; it does not assume decline is normal.
A prediction of how long the patient is likely to live
Predicting life span is not the purpose described for nursing assessment of older adults.

alt.q: A nurse notes that since developing heart failure, an older adult can no longer climb stairs to the bedroom. What is the main value of this assessment finding?
alt.a: It shows how the illness is affecting the patient’s functional status.
alt.ex: Nursing assessment gives clues to the effects of a disease or illness on functional status, which guides individualized care.
w: It confirms the medical diagnosis of heart failure for the provider.
The finding describes function; it does not confirm a medical diagnosis.
It shows that the patient now needs residential housing.
One functional change does not mean the patient can no longer live independently.
It shows the expected decline that occurs in all older adults.
Decline should not be assumed in all older adults; this change is linked to illness.

items.q: Why should the nurse avoid assuming that all of an older adult’s signs and behaviors represent disease and decline?
items.a: The assumption may cause the nurse to miss the patient’s strengths and other needs.
items.ex: The text warns not to assume all findings show disease and decline or that these are the only factors to assess; strengths and abilities matter too.
w: Older adults rarely have chronic illnesses that affect their function.
Chronic illness is common in older adults, so this is not the reason.
Signs of disease are not important to assess in older adults.
Signs of disease are important; they are just not the only factors to assess.
Functional decline is expected in every older adult and needs no assessment.
Decline is not universal; most older adults remain functionally independent.

alt.q: A nurse documents only an older adult’s symptoms and limitations. What important part of the assessment is missing?
alt.a: The patient’s strengths and abilities
alt.ex: The nurse must also identify an older adult’s strengths and abilities during assessment to support independence.
w: The patient’s exact chronological age
Chronological age often has little relation to the reality of a person’s aging.
A list of expected age-related declines
Expected declines should not be assumed; individual assessment is needed.
The family’s opinion of the patient’s abilities
Family input may help, but the missing element is the patient’s own strengths and abilities.

items.q: Two 82-year-old patients are admitted to the same unit. One leads a community garden club; the other needs help with all activities of daily living. Which conclusion by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: Function varies widely in older adults, so each needs individual assessment.
items.ex: Older adults have a wide range of functional ability, so the nurse approaches each person as an individual.
w: The garden club leader is unusual because most people that age need help.
Most older adults are active and involved in their communities, so this patient is not unusual.
Both patients will need the same plan of care because they are the same age.
Chronological age has little relation to the reality of aging; plans must be individualized.
The dependent patient is showing the expected result of normal aging.
Loss of self-care ability affects only a smaller number of older adults and is not normal aging.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for two 90-year-old patients with very different levels of independence. Which principle should guide the nurse’s care?
alt.a: Each older adult is unique and should be approached as an individual.
alt.ex: Each person ages in their own way, so the nurse approaches each older adult as an individual.
w: Patients of the same age should receive the same standard care plan.
Same age does not mean same needs; care is individualized.
The more dependent patient reflects what is typical at age 90.
Most older adults remain functionally independent, so dependence is not assumed to be typical.
The more independent patient will soon decline to the same level.
Decline should not be assumed; the nurse identifies and supports strengths.

items.q: Which factors combine to place older adults at high risk for illness and functional deterioration? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced ability to respond to stress
A reduced ability to respond to stress is one of the factors that raises risk.
Experience of multiple losses
Multiple losses combine with other aging changes to raise the risk of illness and decline.
Physical and psychosocial changes of normal aging
Normal aging changes interact with stress and losses to increase risk.
Living with a spouse or partner
Living with a partner is linked with fewer functional difficulties, not higher risk.
Active involvement in community activities
Most older adults are active in their communities; this reflects strength, not risk.
items.ex: A reduced stress response, multiple losses, and physical and psychosocial aging changes combine to place older adults at high risk.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a student why some older adults are vulnerable to illness and loss of function. Which points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Physical and psychosocial aspects of aging are closely related.
The text states the physical and psychosocial aspects of aging are closely related.
Losses such as the death of loved ones add to the risk.
Multiple losses are one of the factors that combine to raise risk.
Older adults are less able to respond to stress.
A reduced ability to respond to stress contributes to high risk.
Chronological age alone determines a person’s risk.
Chronological age often has little relation to the reality of a person’s aging.
Chronic illness always leads to loss of independence.
Most older adults remain functionally independent despite chronic disease.
alt.ex: Correct: Physical and psychosocial aspects of aging are closely related; Losses such as the death of loved ones add to the risk; Older adults are less able to respond to stress.

items.q: Which statements about older adults are accurate according to the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Most older adults are active and involved in their communities.
The text states most older adults are active and involved in their communities.
Many older adults have more than one chronic illness.
Many older adults have multiple chronic illnesses, which adds complexity to care.
Most older adults remain functionally independent.
Most remain functionally independent despite the rising prevalence of chronic disease.
Most older adults need assisted living or residential housing.
Only a smaller number lose self-care ability and need residential care.
Chronological age reliably predicts functional ability.
Chronological age often has little relation to the reality of aging.
items.ex: Older adults vary widely; most are active and independent even though many have chronic illnesses.

alt.q: A nurse is correcting misunderstandings in a staff in-service on older adults. Which statements should the nurse confirm as true? Select all that apply.
o: Older adults vary in physiological, cognitive, and psychosocial health.
Variation in these areas is what makes nursing care of older adults challenging.
Older adults have a wide range of functional ability.
The text describes a wide range of functional ability among older adults.
A smaller number of older adults cannot make decisions about their needs.
Only a smaller number become confused or unable to make decisions about their needs.
Most older adults are confused or withdrawn.
Confusion and withdrawal affect a smaller number, not most older adults.
Chronic illness causes most older adults to lose independence.
Most older adults remain functionally independent despite chronic disease.
alt.ex: Correct: Older adults vary in physiological, cognitive, and psychosocial health; Older adults have a wide range of functional ability; A smaller number of older adults cannot make decisions about their needs.

items.q: A nurse is assessing a newly admitted 81-year-old patient. Which actions reflect the textbook’s approach to older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Identify the patient’s strengths and abilities
Strengths and abilities are identified during every assessment of an older adult.
Assess how illness affects the patient’s functional status
Nursing assessment provides clues to the effects of disease on functional status.
Plan care that encourages the patient’s independence
Encouraging independence is an integral part of the plan of care.
Assume new behaviors are signs of age-related decline
The nurse must not assume all signs or behaviors represent disease and decline.
Limit the assessment to the patient’s disease symptoms
Disease is not the only factor to assess; psychosocial factors and strengths matter too.
items.ex: The nurse assesses function and strengths, avoids assuming decline, and plans care that encourages independence.

alt.q: Which nursing behaviors would interfere with an individualized assessment of an older adult? Select all that apply.
o: Assuming confusion is expected because of age
Confusion is not assumed; only a smaller number of older adults are confused.
Planning care based mainly on chronological age
Chronological age has little relation to the reality of a person’s aging.
Recording only the patient’s limitations
Omitting strengths and abilities leaves out an essential part of assessment.
Asking how illness has changed daily function
Assessing illness effects on function is an appropriate part of assessment.
Noting activities the patient still enjoys
Identifying abilities and interests supports independence and is appropriate.
alt.ex: Correct: Assuming confusion is expected because of age; Planning care based mainly on chronological age; Recording only the patient’s limitations.

items.q: Most older adults remain functionally independent even though the prevalence of chronic disease increases with age.
items.a: True
items.ex: The text states most older adults remain functionally independent despite the increasing prevalence of chronic disease.
items.ww: Chronic disease is common, but it does not cause most older adults to lose independence.

alt.q: Because chronic disease is so common with aging, most older adults lose their functional independence.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Most older adults stay functionally independent even as chronic disease becomes more common.
alt.ww: Loss of independence affects a smaller number of older adults, not most of them.

items.q: The physical and psychosocial aspects of aging are closely related.
items.a: True
items.ex: Physical and psychosocial factors interact, which is why the nurse assesses both together in older adults.
items.ww: Treating them as separate ignores how stress and losses affect physical health and function.

alt.q: Physical aging changes and psychosocial aging changes are unrelated and can be assessed as separate issues.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The text states the physical and psychosocial aspects of aging are closely related and combine to affect risk.
alt.ww: Losses and stress interact with physical changes, so they cannot be treated as unrelated.

items.q: A person’s chronological age is a reliable indicator of how that person is experiencing aging.
items.a: False
items.ex: Chronological age often has little relation to the reality of aging, because each person ages in their own way.
items.ww: Many older adults consider themselves middle aged well into their seventh decade, so age in years misleads.

alt.q: Two people of the same chronological age may be aging in very different ways.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Each person ages in their own way, so people of the same age can differ widely in health and function.
alt.ww: Age in years does not determine a person’s physical, cognitive, or psychosocial status.

items.q: Many older adults have more than one chronic illness, which adds to the complexity of their assessment and care.
items.a: True
items.ex: Older adults may have at least one chronic illness, and many have multiple illnesses that complicate care.
items.ww: Multiple chronic conditions make assessment more complex, not simpler.

alt.q: Chronic illnesses in older adults usually occur one at a time, so they seldom complicate assessment.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Many older adults have multiple chronic illnesses, which adds complexity to assessment and care.
alt.ww: Multiple coexisting illnesses are common in older adults and do complicate assessment.

items.q: [[Chronological age|chronological]] often has little relation to the reality of aging for an older adult.
items.ex: Because each person ages in their own way, age in years tells the nurse little about a person’s actual aging.

alt.q: A patient’s age in years, or [[chronological age|chronological]], does not reveal how that person is actually aging.
alt.ex: Because each person ages in their own way, age in years tells the nurse little about a person’s actual aging.

items.q: During assessment, the nurse identifies an older adult’s strengths and abilities and encourages [[independence]] as an integral part of the plan of care.
items.ex: Encouraging independence and building on strengths are central to nursing care of older adults.

alt.q: Building on an older adult’s strengths helps the nurse promote the patient’s [[independence]] in the plan of care.
alt.ex: Encouraging independence and building on strengths are central to nursing care of older adults.

items.q: Why does nursing care of older adults pose special challenges?
items.a: Older adults vary in their physiological, cognitive, and psychosocial health.
items.ex: Variations in physiological, cognitive, and psychosocial health, plus a wide range of function, make nursing care of older adults challenging.
w: Older adults all share the same predictable set of health problems.
Older adults are not alike; each is unique and ages in their own way.
Older adults are usually unable to take part in their own assessment.
Most older adults are active and independent and can take part in assessment.
Older adults rarely have chronic illnesses that need ongoing care.
Chronic illness is common, and many older adults have multiple illnesses.

alt.q: A nurse orienting to a geriatric unit asks why care plans there cannot follow one standard template. Which explanation is best?
alt.a: Older adults differ widely in health and function, so care must be individualized.
alt.ex: Older adults vary in physiological, cognitive, and psychosocial health and in functional ability, so care is individualized.
w: Templates are avoided only because older adults dislike written plans.
The reason is variability among older adults, not patient dislike of written plans.
Older adults have so few health needs that a template is unnecessary.
Older adults often have complex needs, including multiple chronic illnesses.
Each older adult’s care depends mainly on their exact chronological age.
Chronological age has little relation to the reality of a person’s aging.

items.q: [[Ageism]] is discrimination against older people because of negative and inaccurate stereotypes.
items.ex: Ageism reflects myths about older adults and leads to undervaluing them.

alt.q: Discrimination against older people that is based on negative, inaccurate stereotypes is called [[ageism]].
alt.ex: Ageism reflects myths about older adults and leads to undervaluing them.

items.q: What does Gerontology mean?
items.a: The study of aging and its effects on people as they grow older
items.ex: These key terms describe the study of aging, bias against older adults, the oldest of the old, and nursing care of older adults.
w: Discrimination against older people based on negative and inaccurate stereotypes
That goes with Ageism.
The oldest of the old, often described as optimistic with broad interests
That goes with Centenarians.
Care that addresses mutually established outcomes and goals for an older adult and family
That goes with Gerontological nursing.

items.q: In clinical judgment in assessing an older adult, which step comes right after “Objectively assess the patient’s functional, physiological, psychosocial, and emotional status”?

That's step 3 of 3.
