ord.q: Put the steps of using clinical judgment to avoid stereotypes when assessing an older adult in order.
items: Objectively assess the patient’s functional, physiological, psychosocial, and emotional status
Compare the findings with the patient’s normal status
Decide whether health problems exist
ord.ex: The nurse objectively assesses, compares findings with the patient’s normal status, and only then decides whether a health problem exists.

items.q: A nurse hears a colleague say, “Don’t bother teaching Mr. Lee about his new inhaler; at 84 he won’t learn it.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Older adults are lifelong learners; we can adapt teaching to his needs.”
items.ex: Older adults are lifelong learners; vision, hearing, or energy changes may affect learning, so teaching is adapted rather than skipped.
w: “You are right, so we should teach only his daughter about the inhaler.”
This reinforces the stereotype that older adults cannot learn; the patient should be taught.
“We should wait until he asks questions before trying to teach him.”
Delaying teaching reflects the same assumption that older adults cannot learn.
“He will need to learn it, but expect him to forget most of the details.”
Assuming forgetfulness is a stereotype; older adults can learn and remember new information.

alt.q: A 70-year-old patient says, “I’m too old to learn how to use a tablet for my telehealth visits.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Many people your age learn new skills; we can go at a pace that suits you.”
alt.ex: Older adults are lifelong learners, so the nurse encourages learning and adapts the pace to the patient.
w: “That’s understandable; I’ll arrange phone visits so you won’t need to learn it.”
This accepts the myth that older adults cannot learn new information.
“Most older adults can’t manage technology, so ask a grandchild to do it.”
This reflects the stereotype that older adults are unable to understand and learn.
“Try to learn it, but don’t worry if you can’t remember how to use it.”
This assumes forgetfulness, a common but inaccurate stereotype of older adults.

items.q: An 88-year-old patient is newly confused this morning. A staff member says, “She’s just old; that’s how they get.” Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess her current mental status and compare it with her usual baseline.
items.ex: The nurse objectively assesses status and compares it with the patient’s normal status before deciding whether a problem exists.
w: Document that the confusion is an expected part of normal aging.
Confusion is a stereotype of aging, not a normal finding; assuming so may miss a health problem.
Reorient her to the date and place and continue with routine care.
Reorienting without assessment skips the step of identifying whether a health problem exists.
Ask a family member to stay with her until the confusion clears.
Seeking supervision first delays the objective assessment needed to identify a possible problem.

alt.q: A nurse notices that an older adult who usually walks independently is now unsteady and quiet. Which nursing action best avoids stereotyping?
alt.a: Compare today’s findings with the patient’s normal status to decide if a problem exists.
alt.ex: Clinical judgment compares objective findings with the patient’s normal status, rather than attributing changes to age.
w: Attribute the change to aging and continue with the current plan of care.
Attributing change to age is stereotyping and may cause a health problem to be missed.
Restrict the patient to bed until the unsteadiness goes away on its own.
This acts without assessing the cause and limits independence unnecessarily.
Assume the patient is tired and recheck function in a few days.
Assuming a cause without assessment may delay recognition of a health problem.

items.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows correct understanding of how ageism affects older adults?
items.a: “Ageism can limit an older adult’s socialization, independence, and access to care.”
items.ex: Ageism undermines self-confidence and self-perception of aging and limits socialization, independence, and sometimes access to care.
w: “Ageism affects how others see older adults but not how they see themselves.”
Ageism also undermines older adults’ own self-confidence and self-perception of aging.
“Ageism improves care because staff give older adults extra attention.”
Ageism distorts caregivers’ understanding and negatively affects quality of care.
“Ageism is no longer an issue because age discrimination is illegal.”
Laws ban age discrimination, but ageist myths still persist among lay people and providers.

alt.q: A nurse is explaining the effects of ageism on caregivers. Which effect should the nurse identify?
alt.a: It distorts caregivers’ understanding of the uniqueness of each older adult.
alt.ex: Experts note that ageism distorts caregivers’ understanding of the uniqueness of each older adult.
w: It helps caregivers set realistic goals for most older patients.
Ageism is based on inaccurate stereotypes, so it does not support realistic goals.
It improves caregivers’ efficiency when they plan care by age group.
Planning care by age group ignores each older adult’s unique needs.
It has little effect on care because most caregivers ignore it.
Negative stereotypes held by providers often negatively affect the quality of patient care.

items.q: Which statement about the finances of older adults is supported by the textbook?
items.a: Social Security benefits are the primary source of income for most older adults.
items.ex: Social Security serves as the main income source for most older adults; beliefs that most are wealthy or poor are misconceptions.
w: Most older adults are affluent and have few financial concerns.
Believing most older adults are affluent is a misconception about their finances.
Most older adults have incomes that fall below the poverty level.
Only a minority of people over 65 have incomes below the poverty level.
Older men usually report a lower income than older women.
Older women, not men, report a significantly lower income.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing the financial resources of a 75-year-old widow. Which fact from the textbook should inform the nurse’s assessment?
alt.a: Older women report a significantly lower income than older men.
alt.ex: Older women report significantly lower incomes than men, so the nurse assesses financial resources rather than assuming affluence.
w: Older women usually have larger pensions than older men.
Older women report a significantly lower income than men.
Most older adults rely mainly on income from their investments.
Social Security, not investments, is the primary income source for most older adults.
Most older women live below the poverty level after age 65.
Only a minority of people over 65 have incomes below the poverty level.

items.q: Which characteristics do specialists in gerontology associate with centenarians?
items.a: An optimistic outlook, good memories, broad social contacts, and tolerance for others
items.ex: Gerontology specialists describe centenarians as optimistic, with good memories, broad social contacts and interests, and tolerance for others.
w: A rigid outlook, poor memories, few social contacts, and impatience with others
These traits reflect common stereotypes, the opposite of what specialists observe in centenarians.
A cautious outlook, declining memories, narrow interests, and dependence on others
Declining memory and narrow interests are stereotypes, not findings about centenarians.
A withdrawn outlook, confused thinking, limited interests, and boredom with others
Withdrawal, confusion, and boredom are stereotypes that gerontology research does not support.

alt.q: A family member says, “When people get to 100, they must be bored and forgetful.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
alt.a: “People who live to 100 often have good memories and broad interests.”
alt.ex: Specialists view centenarians as having good memories, broad social contacts and interests, and an optimistic outlook.
w: “Yes, memory and interest in others are usually lost by that age.”
This repeats the stereotype that older adults are forgetful and bored.
“Yes, but most of them are comfortable being alone and inactive.”
Centenarians are described as having broad social contacts and interests.
“Only centenarians who live with family keep their memories intact.”
Good memories are described in centenarians generally, not only those living with family.

items.q: Why is it a concern when health care providers hold negative stereotypes about aging?
items.a: Their actions often negatively affect the quality of patient care.
items.ex: When health care providers hold negative stereotypes about aging, their actions often negatively affect the quality of patient care.
w: Their stereotypes have little effect because older adults ignore them.
Ageism undermines older adults’ self-confidence and self-perception, so it does affect them.
Their stereotypes mainly affect lay people rather than patient care.
Stereotypes held by providers directly affect the care patients receive.
Their stereotypes cause them to overestimate older adults’ abilities.
Negative stereotypes portray older adults as ill and incapable, which underestimates them.

alt.q: What is a likely result when a nurse believes older adults are rigid and unable to learn?
alt.a: The nurse may provide lower-quality care, such as skipping patient teaching.
alt.ex: Negative stereotypes held by providers often negatively affect the quality of care, for example by withholding teaching.
w: The nurse will provide more complete teaching to compensate.
Believing older adults cannot learn usually leads to less teaching, not more.
The nurse will have more realistic expectations for recovery.
Stereotypes are inaccurate, so they produce unrealistic, not realistic, expectations.
The nurse’s belief will have no effect on the care given.
Provider stereotypes often negatively affect the quality of patient care.

items.q: Which belief is an example of ageism?
items.a: An older adult’s knowledge is too outdated to have any current value.
items.ex: Considering older adults’ knowledge and experience too outdated to be valuable is an ageist idea based on inaccurate stereotypes.
w: Older adults have a wide range of functional abilities.
This is an accurate statement about variability among older adults.
Older adults continue to learn throughout their lives.
This is accurate; older adults are lifelong learners.
Older adults influence public policy as voters and activists.
This is accurate; their political power challenges ageist views.

alt.q: Which statement made by a staff member reflects ageism?
alt.a: “Once people stop working, they don’t really contribute anything.”
alt.ex: Equating worth with productivity leads some to view older adults as worthless after leaving the workforce, an example of ageism.
w: “Older adults bring perspective from living through many changes.”
This values older adults’ experience, which counters ageism.
“Many retirees volunteer and start new careers or hobbies.”
This reflects the reality that retirement can be active and productive.
“Older voters have a major influence on public policy.”
This accurately describes older adults’ political power.

items.q: What did the American Psychological Association’s Resolution on Ageism recognize?
items.a: Age is a risk factor for discrimination.
items.ex: The APA resolution recognizes age as a risk factor for discrimination and promotes a more productive narrative about longer life spans.
w: Age is a reliable predictor of cognitive decline.
The resolution challenges, rather than supports, negative assumptions about aging.
Age bias is already well addressed by DEI programs.
Age bias is seldom on the radar of diversity, equity, and inclusion departments.
Age discrimination is acceptable in some workplaces.
Current laws ban age discrimination, and the resolution works against it.

alt.q: A nurse educator describes efforts by psychologists to reframe attitudes toward aging. Which goal of the APA Resolution on Ageism should the educator include?
alt.a: Advancing a more productive public narrative about the benefits of longer life spans
alt.ex: The resolution advances a more productive public narrative about longer life spans and encourages more emphasis on aging in psychology training.
w: Reducing emphasis on aging in psychology training programs
The resolution encourages more, not less, emphasis on aging in psychology training.
Promoting the view that older adults should leave the workforce early
Linking worth to work and pushing older adults out reflects ageism, which the resolution opposes.
Classifying age as a protected trait only for adults over 85
The resolution recognizes age as a risk factor for discrimination without such a limit.

items.q: Why do older adults offer a unique perspective when voting on social, economic, and technological issues?
items.a: They have experienced almost a century of developments, including recessions and wars.
items.ex: Older adults have lived through financial recessions, wars, and major technology changes, giving them a unique perspective.
w: They are less affected by economic and social policy than younger adults.
Older adults are strongly affected by policy, including changes in health care.
They usually vote the same way, which simplifies policy decisions.
The text does not describe uniform voting; their perspective comes from experience.
They rarely participate in elections, so each vote carries more weight.
Older adults are active voters with a major influence on public policy.

alt.q: Which fact helps challenge ageist views in society?
alt.a: Older adults are a significant part of the consumer economy and influence public policy.
alt.ex: The economic and political power of older adults, as consumers and voters, challenges ageist views.
w: Older adults depend on younger adults to make most of their decisions.
This is a stereotype; older adults are active consumers, voters, and activists.
Older adults have little interest in social and technological issues.
Older adults take part in voting on social, economic, and technological issues.
Older adults’ experiences are too outdated to inform current policy.
Their experience of nearly a century of developments adds a unique perspective.

items.q: A nurse is preparing discharge teaching for an 81-year-old patient who has reduced energy and some hearing loss. Which plan best reflects the textbook’s view of older adults as learners?
items.a: Adapt the teaching to his hearing and energy changes and teach him directly.
items.ex: Hearing changes and reduced energy sometimes affect learning, but older adults are lifelong learners, so teaching is adapted, not withheld.
w: Teach only his wife because his hearing loss prevents learning.
Sensory changes may affect learning but do not prevent it; the patient should be taught.
Give him written handouts and skip the verbal teaching session.
Skipping teaching assumes he cannot learn; teaching should be adapted to his needs.
Provide all the information in one long session before discharge.
Reduced energy and endurance can affect learning, so one long session is a poor fit.

alt.q: Which factors does the textbook identify as sometimes affecting the learning process in older adults?
alt.a: Changes in vision or hearing and reduced energy and endurance
alt.ex: Vision or hearing changes and reduced energy and endurance sometimes affect learning, though older adults remain lifelong learners.
w: A loss of the ability to understand any new information
Believing older adults cannot learn new information is a stereotype.
Rigid thinking and lack of interest in new information
Rigidity and boredom are stereotypes, not described influences on learning.
Confusion and forgetfulness that occur with normal aging
Confusion and forgetfulness are stereotypes, not normal parts of aging.

items.q: Which statements about older adults are facts rather than myths? Select all that apply.
o: Older adults are lifelong learners.
Gerontology specialists recognize older adults as lifelong learners.
Older women report lower incomes than older men.
Older women report a significantly lower income than men.
Vision and hearing changes sometimes affect learning.
Sensory changes and reduced energy can affect the learning process.
Most older adults live below the poverty level.
Only a minority of people over 65 have incomes below the poverty level.
Most older adults cannot understand new information.
This is a stereotype; older adults can learn new information.
items.ex: Older adults keep learning despite sensory changes, and income varies, with women reporting lower incomes; poverty and inability to learn are myths.

alt.q: Which beliefs about older adults are common stereotypes? Select all that apply.
o: Older adults are forgetful and confused.
Forgetfulness and confusion are common stereotypes of older adults.
Older adults are rigid and unfriendly.
Rigidity and unfriendliness are listed among common stereotypes.
Older adults are ill, disabled, and inactive.
These are stereotypes; most older adults are active and independent.
Older adults are a major influence on public policy.
This is accurate; older adults are influential voters and activists.
Older adults vary widely in functional ability.
This is accurate; functional ability varies widely among older adults.
alt.ex: Correct: Older adults are forgetful and confused; Older adults are rigid and unfriendly; Older adults are ill, disabled, and inactive.

items.q: Which effects of ageism on older adults are identified by gerontology experts? Select all that apply.
o: Undermines self-confidence
Ageism typically undermines older adults’ self-confidence.
Weakens self-perception of aging
Ageism undermines how older adults perceive their own aging.
Limits socialization and independence
Ageism limits older adults’ socialization and independence.
Sometimes limits access to care
At times ageism limits older adults’ access to care.
Increases access to health services
Ageism can limit, not increase, access to care.
Improves caregivers’ understanding
Ageism distorts caregivers’ understanding of each older adult’s uniqueness.
items.ex: Ageism harms older adults’ confidence, self-perception, socialization, independence, and access to care, and distorts caregivers’ views.

alt.q: A nurse is presenting on ageism to staff. Which factors that challenge ageist views should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Laws that ban age discrimination
Current laws ban age discrimination.
Older adults’ role in the consumer economy
Older adults’ economic power challenges ageist views.
Older adults’ influence as voters and activists
Older adults’ political power challenges ageist views.
Equating a person’s worth with productivity
Linking worth to productivity fuels ageism after people leave the workforce.
Society’s emphasis on youth and energy
Valuing youth, energy, and attractiveness leads to undervaluing older adults.
alt.ex: Correct: Laws that ban age discrimination; Older adults’ role in the consumer economy; Older adults’ influence as voters and activists.

items.q: Which societal beliefs contribute to the undervaluing of older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Placing high value on attractiveness, energy, and youth
A society that values youth and energy tends to undervalue older adults.
Equating a person’s worth with productivity
This leads some to view older adults as worthless after they leave the workforce.
Viewing older adults’ knowledge as outdated
Considering their experience outdated is an ageist idea.
Recognizing older adults as lifelong learners
This accurate view counters, rather than causes, undervaluing.
Valuing nearly a century of lived experience
Valuing experience counters ageist views.
items.ex: Valuing youth, linking worth to productivity, and viewing older adults’ knowledge as outdated all contribute to ageism.

alt.q: A nurse hears several comments at a staff meeting. Which comments reflect ideas that lead to undervaluing older adults? Select all that apply.
o: “Retired people don’t contribute anything anymore.”
This equates worth with productivity, an ageist idea.
“Her nursing experience from decades ago is useless now.”
Viewing older adults’ knowledge as outdated is ageist.
“It’s sad when people lose their looks and energy.”
Valuing attractiveness and youth leads to undervaluing older adults.
“He has seen huge changes in health care over his life.”
This recognizes the value of an older adult’s experience.
“Many of my older patients are eager to learn.”
This accurately reflects older adults as lifelong learners.
alt.ex: Correct: “Retired people don’t contribute anything anymore.”; “Her nursing experience from decades ago is useless now.”; “It’s sad when people lose their looks and energy.”

items.q: Myths and stereotypes about older adults persist among health care providers as well as among lay people.
items.a: True
items.ex: Despite ongoing gerontology research, myths persist among both lay people and health care providers.
items.ww: Health care providers are not immune; their stereotypes often harm the quality of patient care.

alt.q: Myths and stereotypes about aging are found among lay people but are no longer held by health care providers.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Myths and stereotypes about older adults persist among health care providers as well as lay people.
alt.ww: Ongoing research has not eliminated stereotypes, and providers who hold them can harm care quality.

items.q: Most organizations’ diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) departments actively address age bias along with racism and gender bias.
items.a: False
items.ex: DEI departments tackle issues such as racism and gender bias, but age bias is seldom on their radar.
items.ww: Age bias is often overlooked even in organizations with DEI departments.

alt.q: Although DEI departments tackle racism and gender bias, age bias is seldom on their radar.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Age bias is rarely addressed by DEI departments, even though ageism harms older adults.
alt.ww: The text notes age bias is seldom on the radar of DEI departments.

items.q: Leaving the workforce causes an older adult’s knowledge and experience to lose its current value.
items.a: False
items.ex: This belief is an ageist myth; older adults bring a unique perspective from nearly a century of developments.
items.ww: Viewing older adults’ knowledge as outdated is an example of ageism, not a fact.

alt.q: Equating a person’s worth with productivity leads some people to view older adults as worthless after they retire.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Linking worth to productivity is one way society undervalues older adults after they leave the workforce.
alt.ww: The text names this belief as a cause of undervaluing older adults.

items.q: A nurse notices that an older adult walks more slowly than other patients on the unit. To avoid stereotyping, what should the nurse compare this finding with?
items.a: The patient’s own normal status
items.ex: Clinical judgment compares objective findings with the patient’s normal status before deciding whether a health problem exists.
w: Standard norms set for younger adults
Norms based on younger adults may not apply to older adults and ignore individual baselines.
Typical findings for the patient’s age group
Comparing with an age group relies on generalizations rather than the individual’s baseline.
The family’s expectations for the patient
Family expectations are not an objective baseline for deciding whether a problem exists.

alt.q: After objectively assessing an older adult’s functional and emotional status, what should the nurse do next before deciding whether a health problem exists?
alt.a: Compare the findings with the patient’s normal status.
alt.ex: The nurse compares objective findings with the patient’s normal status, then decides whether health problems exist.
w: Attribute the findings to the patient’s chronological age.
Attributing findings to age is stereotyping and may cause problems to be missed.
Report every finding as a new health problem.
Findings are first compared with the patient’s normal status to see if they are new.
Ask the family to confirm the findings are normal for age.
Family input can help, but the comparison is with the patient’s own normal status.

items.q: Where do nurses’ attitudes toward older adults come from? Select all that apply.
o: Personal experiences with older adults
Personal experiences with older adults shape nurses’ attitudes.
Nursing education
Education contributes to nurses’ attitudes toward older adults.
Employment experiences
Work experiences with older adults shape attitudes.
Attitudes of coworkers and employing institutions
Coworkers and institutions influence how nurses view older adults.
The patient’s chronological age alone
Attitudes come from the nurse’s experiences, not from a patient’s age.
The patient’s type of health insurance
Insurance type is not identified as a source of nurses’ attitudes.
items.ex: Nurses’ attitudes come from personal experiences, education, employment experiences, and the attitudes of coworkers and institutions.

alt.q: A nurse manager is planning to improve staff attitudes toward older patients. Which influences on attitudes should the manager consider? Select all that apply.
o: The attitudes modeled by coworkers on the unit
Coworker attitudes influence how nurses view older adults.
The attitudes reflected in agency policies
Employing institutions’ attitudes shape nurses’ attitudes.
Education about aging and older adults’ needs
Education and specialized knowledge about aging shape attitudes.
Staff members’ past experiences with older adults
Personal experiences shape attitudes, positively or negatively.
The number of years until staff members retire
Years to retirement are not identified as a source of attitudes.
alt.ex: Correct: The attitudes modeled by coworkers on the unit; The attitudes reflected in agency policies; Education about aging and older adults’ needs; Staff members’ past experiences with older adults.

items.q: Which action should a nurse take first to build positive attitudes toward caring for older adults?
items.a: Assess personal attitudes toward older adults and toward their own aging.
items.ex: The text stresses assessing your own attitudes toward older adults, your own aging, and the aging of family, friends, and patients.
w: Avoid caring for older adults until feeling more comfortable.
Avoidance prevents growth; nurses in all settings care for older adults.
Adopt the views of experienced coworkers on the unit.
Coworker attitudes may be negative; nurses should question prevailing negative attitudes.
Focus only on the medical diagnoses of older patients.
Focusing on diagnoses alone ignores the attitudes that shape how care is given.

alt.q: A nurse wants to improve the care given to older adults. Which self-assessment is most important for the nurse to complete?
alt.a: Examining feelings about older adults, personal aging, and the aging of loved ones
alt.ex: Nurses assess their attitudes toward older adults, their own aging, and the aging of family, friends, and patients.
w: Reviewing the number of older adults on the current caseload
Caseload size does not reveal the nurse’s attitudes toward older adults.
Comparing skill speed with that of other nurses on the unit
Task speed is unrelated to the attitudes that affect care of older adults.
Listing the chronic illnesses most common in older adults
Knowledge of disease matters, but this does not assess personal attitudes.

items.q: Why are positive attitudes and specialized knowledge about aging a priority for all nurses?
items.a: The number of older adults in health care settings is increasing.
items.ex: Given the increasing number of older adults in health care settings, positive attitudes and knowledge about aging are priorities for all nurses.
w: Most older adults are cared for only in long-term care settings.
Older adults are found in all health care settings, not only long-term care.
Gerontological nursing is required for every nursing license.
The text bases the priority on the growing older population, not licensing rules.
Older adults have fewer health care needs than younger adults.
Older adults often have complex needs, which is why specialized knowledge is needed.

alt.q: A nurse in a pediatric clinic asks why learning about aging matters in her practice. Which response is best?
alt.a: “Older adults appear in every setting, so knowledge of aging is a priority for all nurses.”
alt.ex: With more older adults in health care settings, forming positive attitudes and gaining knowledge about aging are priorities for every nurse.
w: “It matters only if you plan to transfer to a long-term care unit someday.”
The priority applies to all nurses, not only those in long-term care.
“It is not relevant because older adults rarely visit pediatric settings.”
Older adults are present across settings, including as grandparents and caregivers.
“Only nurses certified in gerontology need to understand aging.”
Specialized knowledge about aging is a priority for all nurses.

items.q: On what are positive attitudes toward older adults based in part?
items.a: A realistic portrayal of older adults’ characteristics and health care needs
items.ex: Positive attitudes rest partly on a realistic picture of older adults’ characteristics and needs rather than on myths.
w: A belief that most older adults are fragile and need protection
This reflects a stereotype of older adults as ill and disabled, not a realistic portrayal.
A focus on the losses and declines that come with aging
Focusing only on decline ignores strengths and does not portray older adults realistically.
An assumption that older adults prefer others to decide for them
Nurses should actively involve older adults in care decisions.

alt.q: A nursing instructor wants students to develop positive attitudes toward older adults. Which teaching strategy best supports this goal?
alt.a: Present realistic information about older adults’ characteristics and health needs.
alt.ex: Positive attitudes are based in part on a realistic portrayal of older adults’ characteristics and health care needs.
w: Emphasize the most severe cases of dementia and disability seen in practice.
Focusing on extreme cases portrays older adults unrealistically as ill and dependent.
Avoid discussing aging so students do not form negative impressions.
Avoiding the topic prevents students from gaining specialized knowledge about aging.
Describe older adults mainly as patients who need protection from decisions.
This treats older adults as objects rather than involving them in decisions.

items.q: An alert 83-year-old patient and her daughter are present while discharge options are discussed. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Direct questions to the patient and involve her in decisions about discharge.
items.ex: It is critical to respect older adults and actively involve them in care decisions and activities.
w: Direct questions to the daughter because she will provide the care.
Bypassing an alert patient treats her as an object rather than an independent person.
Make the discharge decision with the health care provider to save time.
Deciding without the patient fails to involve her in her own care decisions.
Wait to discuss discharge until the daughter can meet without the patient.
Excluding the patient from the discussion fails to respect her right to take part.

alt.q: An alert 86-year-old patient’s son answers every question the nurse asks during an interview. Which action by the nurse is best?
alt.a: Politely redirect questions to the patient so she remains the primary source of information.
alt.ex: Family may add information with consent, but the older adult should remain the primary source of information whenever possible.
w: Continue interviewing the son because he seems to know her history well.
Relying on the son treats the alert patient as an object rather than an active participant.
Ask the son to complete the admission forms on her behalf.
Having the son complete forms excludes an alert patient from her own care.
End the interview and complete it later when the son has left.
Ending the interview delays care; the nurse can involve the patient now with tact.

items.q: A nurse observes a nursing assistant setting a resident’s bath and meal times without asking the resident. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Let’s ask her what times she prefers so she can take part in planning her care.”
items.ex: Respecting older adults means actively involving them in care decisions and activities rather than treating them as objects.
w: “That’s fine; a set schedule is easier for residents who are older.”
Imposing schedules without input treats residents as objects rather than independent people.
“Check with her family about her preferences before the next shift.”
The resident herself should be involved in decisions about her care when able.
“Keep the schedule, but tell her about the times once they are set.”
Informing her afterward does not actively involve her in the decision.

alt.q: A resident in a nursing center wants to choose her own clothes, though this takes longer. The nursing assistant wants to dress her quickly. Which action by the nurse is best?
alt.a: Support the resident in choosing her clothes and dressing with help as needed.
alt.ex: Involving older adults in care activities respects their independence and dignity rather than treating them as objects.
w: Choose clothes for her each day so morning care can be completed on time.
This prioritizes efficiency over the resident’s independence and dignity.
Ask her family to lay out her clothing the night before each visit.
This removes the choice from the resident rather than involving her.
Dress her quickly now and let her choose clothes on the weekends.
Limiting choice to weekends still fails to respect her daily involvement in care.

items.q: During shift report, a nurse says, “Room 12 is just another confused old lady.” Which response by the charge nurse is best?
items.a: “Let’s not assume that; what did your assessment show about her?”
items.ex: Nurses address ageism by questioning prevailing negative attitudes and stereotypes and reinforcing the realities of aging.
w: “Most of our older patients are confused, so plan care accordingly.”
This reinforces a stereotype; confusion affects only a smaller number of older adults.
“Just make sure she does not fall during your shift.”
Moving on without questioning the stereotype leaves ageism unaddressed.
“It’s best not to comment on how other staff describe patients.”
Nurses are called to question, not ignore, negative attitudes and stereotypes.

alt.q: Which action best shows a nurse addressing ageism on a hospital unit?
alt.a: Questioning a coworker’s negative comment and sharing accurate facts about aging
alt.ex: Nurses recognize and address ageism by questioning negative attitudes and stereotypes and reinforcing the realities of aging in all settings.
w: Ignoring a coworker’s negative comment to avoid conflict on the unit
Ignoring negative comments allows prevailing ageist attitudes to continue.
Agreeing that older patients usually need others to decide for them
This reinforces the stereotype rather than questioning it.
Assigning older patients only to nurses who enjoy working with them
This avoids rather than addresses ageism among all staff.

items.q: A nursing student says, “I had a bad experience caring for my grandfather, and I dread working with older patients.” Which response by the instructor is best?
items.a: “Reflecting on how that experience affects you can help you care for older adults.”
items.ex: Reflecting on positive and negative experiences with older adults helps nurses recognize how those experiences may affect future care.
w: “You should ask to be assigned only to younger patients this term.”
Avoidance prevents growth; older adults are found in all health care settings.
“Your feelings will not affect the care you give to older adults.”
Personal experiences shape attitudes, which can affect care.
“Most nurses feel that way, so there is no need to think about it.”
Nurses are encouraged to assess and reflect on their attitudes, not dismiss them.

alt.q: A nurse completes the textbook’s reflection activity on caring for older adults. What should the nurse consider?
alt.a: Positive and negative past experiences with older adults and their effect on future care
alt.ex: The reflection asks nurses to consider past experiences with older adults and how these may affect future care.
w: Which older adults on the unit need the least nursing time
Workload planning is not the focus of the reflection on attitudes.
How to avoid caring for older adults who remind them of family
The aim is to understand feelings, not to avoid caring for older adults.
Which medical diagnoses are most common among older adults
Diagnoses relate to knowledge, not to reflecting on personal attitudes.

items.q: Which statement by a new graduate nurse shows understanding of respectful care of older adults?
items.a: “I will involve my older patients in decisions about their care.”
items.ex: It is critical to respect older adults and actively involve them in care decisions and activities.
w: “I will make decisions for older patients so they are not burdened.”
Deciding for patients treats them as objects rather than independent, dignified people.
“I will speak mainly with families because they know what is best.”
Older adults should remain active participants in their own care.
“I will finish care quickly so older patients do not have to help.”
Doing everything for patients reduces their involvement and independence.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse indicates a need for further teaching about attitudes toward older adults?
alt.a: “Older patients are easier to care for when they let staff decide everything.”
alt.ex: Treating older adults as objects who should let staff decide reflects past practices nurses are called to change.
w: “I ask my older patients which care activities they want to do themselves.”
Involving patients in care activities reflects respect and needs no correction.
“I try to notice when coworkers make assumptions based on a patient’s age.”
Questioning assumptions is how nurses address ageism.
“My own feelings about aging may affect how I care for older adults.”
Recognizing personal attitudes about aging shows correct understanding.

items.q: How did agency settings such as hospitals and nursing centers often treat older adults in the past?
items.a: As objects rather than as independent, dignified people
items.ex: In the past, hospitals and nursing centers often treated older adults as objects rather than as independent, dignified people.
w: As partners who directed decisions about their own care
Older adults were not treated as partners; this is what nurses now strive for.
As teachers whose experience guided younger staff members
The text describes past treatment as objectifying, not as valuing their experience.
As consumers whose choices shaped the services offered
Past agency settings did not treat older adults as independent decision makers.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing the history of care of older adults. Which practice from the past are nurses now called to change?
alt.a: Treating older adults as objects instead of as independent, dignified people
alt.ex: Nurses are now called to respect older adults and involve them in care, unlike past agency practices.
w: Involving older adults in decisions about their own care
Involving older adults in decisions is the practice nurses should continue.
Teaching older adults about their health conditions
Teaching supports older adults as lifelong learners and should continue.
Assessing older adults’ functional abilities and strengths
Assessing strengths and function is current recommended practice.

items.q: A family member tells the nurse, “Mom is 87, so the staff should just decide what is best for her.” The mother is alert and oriented. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Your mother can share in decisions about her care, and we want her involved.”
items.ex: Nurses respect older adults and actively involve them in care decisions, rather than deciding for them based on age.
w: “You are right; at her age it is kinder not to burden her with choices.”
Excluding an alert older adult treats her as an object rather than a dignified person.
“We will let you make the decisions since you are her next of kin.”
An alert older adult should be involved in her own care decisions.
“We will decide with the health care provider and let you both know.”
Deciding without her fails to involve her actively in decisions.

alt.q: An alert 90-year-old patient is scheduled for a care conference. Which plan by the nurse best reflects respect for the patient?
alt.a: Invite the patient to attend and share her goals for her care.
alt.ex: Respecting older adults means actively involving them in care decisions and activities.
w: Hold the conference with the family and share the plan with her afterward.
Informing her afterward does not involve her in the decisions.
Let the health care team set her goals because of her advanced age.
Age alone is not a reason to exclude her from setting goals.
Ask her family to represent her views so she does not become tired.
An alert patient should speak for herself whenever possible.

items.q: Nurses’ attitudes toward older adults can be shaped by the attitudes of their coworkers and employing institutions.
items.a: True
items.ex: Coworkers and institutions are among the sources of nurses’ attitudes, along with personal experience, education, and employment.
items.ww: Attitudes are not formed only from personal experience; the work environment also shapes them.

alt.q: Nurses’ attitudes toward older adults come only from their personal experiences with older family members.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Attitudes also come from education, employment experiences, and the attitudes of coworkers and institutions.
alt.ww: Several sources shape attitudes, not personal family experiences alone.

items.a: False
items.ex: Because older adults are increasing in all health care settings, this knowledge is a priority for all nurses.
items.ww: Older adults receive care in every setting, so the priority is not limited to long-term care.

alt.q: Forming positive attitudes toward older adults and gaining knowledge about aging are priorities for all nurses.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The growing number of older adults in health care settings makes this a priority for every nurse.
alt.ww: Limiting this priority to some settings ignores that older adults are cared for everywhere.

items.q: Nurses are called to recognize and address ageism by questioning negative attitudes and reinforcing the realities of aging in all care settings.
items.a: True
items.ex: Nurses address ageism by questioning prevailing negative attitudes and stereotypes in all settings.
items.ww: Ignoring ageist attitudes allows them to continue and harm the care older adults receive.

alt.q: Nurses best address ageism by avoiding any discussion of coworkers’ attitudes toward older patients.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses address ageism by actively questioning prevailing negative attitudes and stereotypes.
alt.ww: Avoiding the topic leaves negative attitudes unchallenged.

items.q: Which nursing actions demonstrate respect for older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Asking the patient about preferences for care activities
Actively involving older adults in care activities shows respect.
Including the patient in decisions about the plan of care
Involving older adults in care decisions is critical to respectful care.
Questioning a coworker’s stereotype about an older patient
Questioning negative stereotypes is how nurses address ageism.
Making decisions for the patient to save time
Deciding for patients treats them as objects rather than independent people.
Directing questions to family instead of an alert patient
The older adult should remain the primary source of information when possible.
items.ex: Respectful care involves older adults in decisions and activities and challenges ageist stereotypes.

alt.q: Which nursing behaviors treat older adults as objects rather than as independent, dignified people? Select all that apply.
o: Setting a resident’s daily schedule without asking her
Imposing schedules without input removes the resident from decisions.
Discussing an alert patient’s care only with family
Bypassing an alert patient fails to involve her in her own care.
Choosing a resident’s clothing to finish care faster
This removes choice and independence for the sake of efficiency.
Asking a patient which activities he wants to do himself
Involving the patient in care activities respects his independence.
Inviting a patient to share goals for her care
Involving the patient in care decisions shows respect.
alt.ex: Correct: Setting a resident’s daily schedule without asking her; Discussing an alert patient’s care only with family; Choosing a resident’s clothing to finish care faster.

items.q: Which statements by nurses reflect ageist attitudes? Select all that apply.
o: “Older patients can’t really make their own decisions.”
This stereotype treats older adults as unable to direct their own care.
“There is no point teaching him; he is too old to learn.”
This reflects the myth that older adults cannot learn new information.
“She is old, so her confusion is just part of aging.”
This stereotype assumes confusion is normal and can lead to missed problems.
“I will ask her what matters most to her in her care.”
This involves the older adult in decisions, which is respectful care.
“I will compare his function today with his usual level.”
Comparing findings with the patient’s normal status avoids stereotyping.
items.ex: Ageist statements assume older adults cannot decide, learn, or think clearly; respectful statements involve and assess the individual.

alt.q: Which statements by nurses reflect positive, realistic attitudes toward older adults? Select all that apply.
o: “Most of my older patients are independent and active.”
Most older adults remain active and functionally independent.
“I involve older patients in planning their own care.”
Actively involving older adults in care decisions reflects respect.
“Older adults can keep learning new skills.”
Older adults are lifelong learners.
“Older patients are happiest when staff decide for them.”
This treats older adults as objects rather than independent people.
“Teaching older patients is usually a waste of time.”
This reflects the myth that older adults cannot learn.
alt.ex: Correct: “Most of my older patients are independent and active.”; “I involve older patients in planning their own care.”; “Older adults can keep learning new skills.”

items.q: According to the textbook, which two priorities apply to all nurses given the growing number of older adults in health care settings?
items.a: Forming positive attitudes toward older adults and gaining specialized knowledge about aging
items.ex: With more older adults in health care settings, positive attitudes and specialized knowledge about aging are priorities for all nurses.
w: Referring older adults to specialists and limiting their hospital stays
These are not the priorities the text names for all nurses.
Making care decisions for older adults and protecting them from risk
Nurses involve older adults in decisions rather than deciding for them.
Avoiding discussion of aging and focusing only on medical diagnoses
Nurses need specialized knowledge about aging, not avoidance of the topic.

alt.q: A hospital is planning staff development for nurses on all units. Which focus best matches the textbook’s priorities for caring for older adults?
alt.a: Building positive attitudes and specialized knowledge about aging and older adults’ needs
alt.ex: Positive attitudes and specialized knowledge about aging and older adults’ health care needs are priorities for all nurses.
w: Training only gerontology unit nurses on the needs of older patients
The priority applies to all nurses, not only those on gerontology units.
Teaching staff to complete care for older adults as quickly as possible
Speed is not the priority; respect and involvement of older adults are.
Reviewing the losses and declines that all older adults experience
Focusing on decline does not give a realistic portrayal of older adults.

items.q: A nurse notices feeling impatient with older patients since her own father began to decline. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Reflect on how her feelings about her father’s aging may affect her care.
items.ex: Nurses assess their attitudes toward the aging of family and friends because personal experiences shape attitudes toward patients.
w: Request assignments with only younger patients until her father improves.
Avoidance does not address the attitude; older adults are in all care settings.
Ignore the feelings because personal life does not affect patient care.
Personal experiences with older adults do shape nurses’ attitudes and care.
Share her frustration with patients so they understand her impatience.
Sharing frustration with patients is not therapeutic and does not address her attitudes.

alt.q: Why does the textbook encourage nurses to assess their attitudes toward the aging of their own family and friends?
alt.a: Personal experiences with aging shape the attitudes nurses bring to patient care.
alt.ex: Nurses’ attitudes come partly from personal experiences, so feelings about loved ones’ aging can affect how they care for older adults.
w: Nurses are expected to provide care for their own family members.
The purpose is self-awareness of attitudes, not caring for one’s own family.
Family experiences are the only source of a nurse’s attitudes.
Education, employment, and coworkers also shape attitudes.
Personal feelings about aging have no effect on patient care.
Personal experiences shape attitudes, which can affect care.

items.q: Which are developmental tasks for older adults listed in the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Adjusting to retirement and reduced or fixed income
Adjusting to retirement and income changes is a listed task for older adults.
Acceptance of self as an aging person
Accepting oneself as an aging person is a listed developmental task.
Redefining relationships with adult children and siblings
Relationships with adult children and siblings are redefined in older age.
Maintaining satisfactory living arrangements
Maintaining satisfactory living arrangements is a listed task.
Establishing a career and starting a family
Establishing a career and family are tasks of earlier adulthood.
Forming an identity separate from one’s parents
Forming a separate identity is a task of adolescence, not older adulthood.
items.ex: Box 14.1 tasks include adjusting to retirement and income, self-acceptance as aging, redefining relationships, and maintaining living arrangements.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing developmental tasks with an older adult support group. Which tasks should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Adjusting to changes in health and physical strength
Adjusting to health and strength changes is a listed developmental task.
Adjusting to the death of a spouse, siblings, or friends
Adjusting to deaths of loved ones is a listed developmental task.
Maintaining quality of life through exercise and hobbies
Maintaining quality of life through activities is a listed task.
Maintaining an optimal level of health and function
Maintaining optimal health and functional abilities is a listed task.
Choosing an occupation and completing training
Choosing an occupation is a task of young adulthood.
alt.ex: Correct: Adjusting to changes in health and physical strength; Adjusting to the death of a spouse, siblings, or friends; Maintaining quality of life through exercise and hobbies; Maintaining an optimal level of health and function.

items.q: Which changes are among the more common changes older adults experience? Select all that apply.
o: Alterations in health status
Changes in health status are among the more common changes of aging.
Loss of significant others
Losing significant others is a common change older adults face.
Decreased sense of usefulness
A decreased sense of usefulness is a common change listed in the text.
Increase in income after retirement
Income commonly decreases, not increases, for older adults.
More structure from a daily work schedule
Retirement removes the structure that a work schedule provided.
items.ex: Common changes include altered health, loss of significant others, decreased usefulness, and decreased socialization, income, and independent living.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing the losses an older adult may be facing. Which areas of decline should the nurse explore? Select all that apply.
o: Socialization
Decreased socialization is a common change for older adults.
Income
Decreased income is a common change, often linked to retirement.
Independent living
Decreased independent living is among the common changes of aging.
Need for health care services
Health care needs often increase, not decrease, with alterations in health.
Number of chronic conditions
Chronic conditions tend to increase with age rather than decrease.
alt.ex: Correct: Socialization; Income; Independent living.

items.q: Which behaviors does the textbook describe as potentially problematic ways that older adults deny their aging? Select all that apply.
o: Refusing to ask for help despite functional decline
Denying functional decline and refusing help places safety at great risk.
Avoiding senior citizens’ centers
Avoiding programs designed for them means missing their benefits.
Avoiding senior health promotion activities
Avoiding health promotion programs means not receiving their benefits.
Adopting younger styles of clothing
This shows difficulty accepting aging but is not described as a safety or benefit risk.
Using cosmetics to hide signs of aging
This shows difficulty accepting aging but is not described as potentially problematic.
items.ex: Denial becomes problematic when older adults refuse needed help or avoid programs designed for their benefit.

alt.q: Which behaviors suggest an older adult is having difficulty accepting aging? Select all that apply.
o: Understating age when asked
Understating age is a sign of difficulty accepting aging.
Wearing younger styles of clothing
Adopting younger clothing styles can signal difficulty accepting aging.
Using cosmetics to hide signs of aging
Hiding physical evidence of aging with cosmetics signals difficulty accepting aging.
Reviewing strengths and limitations realistically
A realistic review of strengths and limitations reflects acceptance of aging.
Joining a senior health promotion program
Using programs designed for older adults reflects acceptance, not denial.
alt.ex: Correct: Understating age when asked; Wearing younger styles of clothing; Using cosmetics to hide signs of aging.

items.q: The changes in appearance and body functioning that occur as body systems age are normal and are not associated with disease.
items.a: True
items.ex: Age-related physical changes are normal, though disease can alter their timing or impact on daily life.
items.ww: Normal aging changes are not disease; treating them as illness reflects a misunderstanding of aging.

alt.q: Age-related changes in appearance and body functioning are early signs of disease that require treatment.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: These changes are normal aging, not disease, although disease sometimes alters their timing or impact.
alt.ww: The text states these changes are not associated with disease.

items.q: Acceptance of personal aging means retreating into inactivity.
items.a: False
items.ex: Acceptance does not mean inactivity; it requires a realistic review of strengths and limitations.
items.ww: Older adults who accept aging can remain active while recognizing their limitations.

alt.q: Acceptance of personal aging requires a realistic review of one’s strengths and limitations.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Accepting aging involves realistically weighing strengths and limitations, not withdrawing from activity.
alt.ww: Acceptance is not retreat into inactivity, as some mistakenly believe.

items.q: A change in living arrangements usually requires an extended period of adjustment for an older adult.
items.a: True
items.ex: Relocation usually requires extended adjustment, during which support from health care providers, friends, and family is essential.
items.ww: Older adults do not usually adjust quickly to a move; ongoing support is needed.

alt.q: Most older adults adjust to a new living arrangement within a few days and need little outside support.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A change in living arrangements usually requires an extended adjustment with essential support from others.
alt.ww: Quick, unsupported adjustment is not typical; support from family, friends, and providers is essential.
