items.q: A 79-year-old patient with worsening arthritis insists on walking to the bathroom alone, saying, “I can do it myself; I don’t need help.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Let’s look at what you can do safely on your own and where some help would keep you safe.”
items.ex: Denying functional decline and refusing help risks safety; acceptance involves a realistic review of strengths and limitations.
w: “You are right; staying independent matters more than any risk of falling.”
Supporting denial of functional decline places the patient’s safety at great risk.
“From now on, you must stay in bed unless a staff member is present.”
Accepting aging does not mean retreating into inactivity; this ignores her strengths.
“At your age, you should expect to need help with everything.”
This stereotype ignores the patient’s strengths and abilities.

alt.q: An 82-year-old man denies that his vision and balance have changed and refuses help with grocery shopping. Which concern is the nurse’s priority?
alt.a: His denial of functional decline places his safety at great risk.
alt.ex: Older adults who deny functional decline and refuse help place their safety at great risk.
w: His refusal shows he has fully accepted the changes of aging.
Refusing needed help reflects denial of decline, not acceptance of aging.
His behavior is expected and needs no further assessment.
Denial that affects safety needs assessment and a realistic review of limitations.
His wish to shop alone shows he is retreating into inactivity.
He is not inactive; the concern is denial of decline that threatens safety.

items.q: A 72-year-old patient who recently retired from engineering says, “I don’t know who I am anymore without my job.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Losing your work role is a big change. What interests might give your days meaning now?”
items.ex: Retirement means losing the work role; the nurse acknowledges the loss and helps build new interests and a meaningful routine.
w: “You worked hard for this; just relax and enjoy having nothing to do.”
This reflects the myth that retirement means passivity and ignores the loss of the work role.
“Most people feel fine about retiring, so this feeling will soon pass.”
This dismisses the loss; adjustment to retirement is individualized.
“You could ask your children to fill your time with babysitting.”
Retirees may wish to pursue their own interests rather than fill time with child care.

alt.q: Which statement by a recently retired patient shows a positive adjustment to retirement as described in the textbook?
alt.a: “I plan to volunteer and take some classes at the community college.”
alt.ex: Some older adults welcome retirement as a time to pursue new interests, volunteer, continue education, or start new careers.
w: “Now that I’ve stopped working, I plan to stay home and rest.”
Associating retirement with passivity and seclusion is a common misconception.
“Without my job, I don’t see much reason to plan my days.”
Adjustment requires developing a personally meaningful schedule, not abandoning plans.
“I’ll let my children decide how I should spend my time.”
This gives up control of decision making instead of pursuing personal interests.

items.q: An 85-year-old woman moved into a nursing center last week because of physical impairments. She is tearful and says she misses her home. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Provide ongoing support, recognizing that adjusting to a new living arrangement takes time.
items.ex: A change in living arrangements usually requires an extended adjustment during which support from providers, friends, and family is essential.
w: Reassure her that most residents feel at home within a few days of moving.
Adjustment usually takes an extended period, so this reassurance is inaccurate.
Limit family visits so that she can adapt more quickly to the new setting.
Support from family members is essential during the adjustment period.
Explain that her tearfulness is a normal sign of aging that will not change.
Her distress relates to the loss and relocation, not to normal aging.

alt.q: An older adult has just moved from his house into a smaller, single-level apartment. Which plan best supports his adjustment?
alt.a: Encourage ongoing contact with family and friends during an extended adjustment period.
alt.ex: Adjustment to new living arrangements takes time, and support from family, friends, and health care providers is essential.
w: Expect him to adjust quickly because the new home is easier to manage.
Even a needed move usually requires an extended period of adjustment.
Advise him to avoid visitors until he settles into his new routine.
Support from family and friends is essential, so isolation is not advised.
Tell him the move was necessary and that he should not dwell on it.
Dismissing his feelings does not support adjustment to a significant change.

items.q: An 80-year-old man’s wife died 2 months ago, and his brother died last week. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Losing your wife and brother so close together must be very hard. Would you like to talk about them?”
items.ex: Deaths of loved ones are losses and reminders of mortality; the nurse supports the older adult through the grieving process.
w: “At your age, you must be getting used to losing the people you love.”
Coming to terms with deaths is often difficult; losses are not easier because of age.
“You should focus on staying busy so you do not think about your losses.”
Avoiding grief does not help the patient work through the grieving process.
“Your family can help you more with this than the nursing staff can.”
Nurses play a role in helping older adults through the grieving process.

alt.q: Why can the deaths of a spouse, siblings, and friends be especially difficult for older adults?
alt.a: They are both losses and reminders of the older adult’s own mortality.
alt.ex: The deaths of loved ones represent losses and reminders of personal mortality, so coming to terms with them is often difficult.
w: They usually happen suddenly and without any warning signs.
The text links the difficulty to loss and mortality, not to suddenness.
They require the older adult to move into residential housing.
Bereavement does not by itself require a change in living arrangements.
They are less painful than losses experienced earlier in life.
Coming to terms with these deaths is often difficult, not less painful.

items.q: An older adult’s daughter cares for her father while working full time and raising two children. They often disagree about his medical decisions. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Guide the father and daughter in discussing decision making and support for her caregiving.
items.ex: As adult children and aging parents negotiate changing roles, nurses are in a position to guide the family.
w: Advise the daughter to make all medical decisions for her father.
Control of decision making is a key issue; transferring all control ignores the father’s role.
Tell the father to accept his daughter’s choices because she is busy.
This dismisses the father’s role and does not help them negotiate changing roles.
Avoid involvement because family conflict is a private matter.
Nurses are in a position to guide families through changing roles.

alt.q: Which issues commonly arise as older adults and their adult children redefine their relationships?
alt.a: Control of decision making, dependence, conflict, guilt, and loss
alt.ex: Redefining relationships with adult children often raises issues of decision-making control, dependence, conflict, guilt, and loss.
w: Career choice, identity formation, peer pressure, and school stress
These are concerns of adolescence and young adulthood.
Marriage planning, first jobs, home buying, and starting families
These are tasks of young adulthood, not of aging parents and adult children.
Weight gain, sleep habits, screen time, and sports injuries
These issues are not described as arising in redefined parent–child relationships.

items.q: According to the textbook, what partly determines how issues between older adults and their adult children are resolved?
items.a: The past relationship between the older adult and the adult children
items.ex: How issues surface and are resolved depends in part on the past relationship between older adults and their adult children.
w: The number of grandchildren and siblings in the family
The text links resolution to the past relationship, not to family size.
The chronological age of the older adult and adult children
Age alone does not determine how family issues are resolved.
The distance between the older adult’s and children’s homes
The text does not identify distance as the deciding factor.

alt.q: A nurse is helping a family through conflict as an adult son becomes his mother’s caregiver. Which assessment will best help the nurse anticipate how the conflict may be resolved?
alt.a: Asking about the quality of the mother’s and son’s relationship in the past
alt.ex: The past relationship between older adults and adult children partly determines how issues surface and are resolved.
w: Asking about the son’s income and the cost of care
Finances matter, but the text ties resolution to the past relationship.
Asking how many other siblings live nearby
Number of siblings is not identified as the key factor.
Asking about the mother’s exact chronological age
Chronological age has little relation to how relationship issues are resolved.

items.q: How does the presence of disease affect the normal physical changes of aging?
items.a: It sometimes alters the timing of the changes or their impact on daily life.
items.ex: Physical changes of aging are normal, but disease sometimes alters their timing or their impact on daily life.
w: It causes the changes, since they do not occur without disease.
The changes are normal and occur without disease.
It prevents the changes from occurring until the disease resolves.
Disease does not stop aging changes; it may alter their timing or impact.
It has no effect, because aging changes and disease are unrelated.
Disease can alter when aging changes occur and how they affect daily life.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching an older adult about age-related changes. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
alt.a: “Some changes with age are normal, but an illness can make them affect me more.”
alt.ex: Age-related changes are normal, and disease sometimes alters their timing or impact on daily life.
w: “All of the changes I’m noticing must mean I have a disease.”
Physical changes of aging are normal and not associated with disease.
“My changes will happen at the same time as everyone my age.”
The extent and timing of aging changes vary by individual.
“Illness cannot change how aging affects my daily activities.”
Disease sometimes alters the timing or impact of aging changes on daily life.

items.q: Which statement about how older adults adjust to the changes and losses of aging is accurate?
items.a: Some adapt easily, while others need help from family, friends, and health professionals.
items.ex: Adjustment is individualized; some adapt easily and others need help from family, friends, and health care professionals.
w: Most adapt in the same way because the changes of aging are universal.
No two people age the same way, and adjustment is individualized.
Most need professional help because the losses of aging are too severe.
For some, adaptation and adjustment are relatively easy.
Few experience any losses because most remain active and independent.
Older adults commonly experience changes and losses even while remaining active.

alt.q: Two older adults face similar losses, but one adjusts easily while the other struggles. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: Adjustment to aging is individualized, so the nurse offers support as needed.
alt.ex: How older adults adjust to changes is individualized, and nurses should be sensitive to losses and ready to offer support.
w: The one who is struggling is likely showing early signs of disease.
Difficulty adjusting reflects individual coping, not necessarily disease.
The one who adjusted easily is probably denying the loss.
Some older adults find adaptation and adjustment relatively easy.
Both should adjust in the same time if given the same support.
Adjustment is individualized and does not follow a set timeline.

items.q: Theories of aging are closely linked to which concept?
items.a: Developmental tasks appropriate for distinct stages of life
items.ex: Theories of aging are closely linked to the concept of developmental tasks appropriate for distinct stages of life.
w: Normal laboratory values for distinct age groups
Laboratory norms are not the concept linked to theories of aging.
Chronic diseases common to distinct age groups
Theories of aging are tied to developmental tasks, not disease patterns.
Legal rights assigned to distinct age groups
Legal rights are not the concept described as linked to theories of aging.

alt.q: A nurse is using developmental theory to plan care for older adults. What should the nurse keep in mind?
alt.a: Common tasks exist, but no two people age the same way biologically or psychosocially.
alt.ex: There are common developmental tasks for older adults, yet no two individuals age in the same way.
w: All older adults complete the developmental tasks in the same order.
The text does not present the tasks as a fixed order; aging is individual.
Developmental tasks end once a person reaches 65 years of age.
Older adults have their own developmental tasks associated with change and loss.
Developmental tasks apply only to older adults who are retired.
Tasks such as accepting aging and adjusting to loss apply to all older adults.

items.q: Which retired older adult is most likely to report satisfaction with life in retirement?
items.a: A retiree in good health with sufficient income who looked forward to retiring
items.ex: Health status, sufficient income, and positive preretirement expectations influence a retired person’s satisfaction with life.
w: A retiree with a new chronic illness who has a limited fixed income
Poor health and inadequate income reduce satisfaction in retirement.
A retiree in good health who dreaded leaving work and has money worries
Negative expectations and financial stress reduce satisfaction in retirement.
A retiree with sufficient income who has declining health and no plans
Declining health lowers satisfaction even when income is sufficient.

alt.q: A nurse is helping a 63-year-old patient prepare for retirement. Which topic should the nurse include?
alt.a: Meaningful activities, social networks, income, and health promotion
alt.ex: Retirement preparation includes relationships, meaningful activities, social networks, income, health promotion, and long-range planning.
w: Ways to avoid making any new commitments during retirement
Retirement involves building new interests and social networks, not avoiding commitments.
How to spend most of the day resting to conserve energy
Associating retirement with passivity is a common misconception.
Plans to rely on adult children for all daily decisions
Retirement planning supports the retiree’s own interests and decision making.

items.q: When adult children become caregivers for their aging parents, which challenge does the textbook describe for the adult children?
items.a: Balancing their own children and careers with the demands of family caregiving
items.ex: Adult children who become caregivers must balance their own children and careers with the many challenges of family caregiving.
w: Learning to accept the parent’s complete control over their own lives
Control of decision making is negotiated, not handed fully to the parent.
Adjusting to retirement and a reduced or fixed income of their own
Retirement and fixed income are developmental tasks of the older adult.
Moving the parent into residential housing as soon as possible
Relocation is not described as the expected response to caregiving.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing an adult daughter who has become her mother’s caregiver. Which question best addresses a challenge the textbook describes?
alt.a: “How are you balancing caregiving with your job and your own children?”
alt.ex: Adult child caregivers must balance their own children and careers with the challenges of family caregiving.
w: “When do you plan to move your mother into a nursing center?”
This assumes relocation rather than assessing the caregiver’s challenges.
“Has your mother adjusted to her reduced fixed income yet?”
This addresses the mother’s task, not the caregiver’s challenge.
“Do you make all of your mother’s decisions for her now?”
This assumes the daughter has full control rather than assessing balance.

items.q: A 76-year-old patient recovering from a hip fracture tells the nurse that gardening and church choir give her life meaning. Which nursing action best supports her developmental task of maintaining quality of life?
items.a: Help her plan ways to continue gardening and choir as she recovers.
items.ex: Maintaining quality of life through hobbies and social activities is a developmental task, and quality of life is defined uniquely by each person.
w: Encourage her to give up her hobbies to avoid another injury.
Acceptance of aging does not require retreat into inactivity.
Suggest activities that most patients her age find meaningful.
What defines quality of life is unique to each person, not the same for an age group.
Focus her plan only on her hip and leave activities to her family.
Supporting quality of life is often a nursing priority for older adults.

alt.q: A nurse is planning care to help an older adult maintain quality of life. Which step should the nurse take first?
alt.a: Ask the patient what activities and relationships matter most to her.
alt.ex: Because quality of life is defined uniquely by each person, the nurse first learns what matters to the patient.
w: Choose activities based on what most older adults enjoy.
Quality of life differs for each person, so generalizing is inappropriate.
Ask the family to decide which activities she should keep.
The patient defines her own quality of life and should be involved.
Limit her activities to reduce the risk of fatigue or falls.
Limiting activity without assessment may reduce rather than maintain quality of life.

sections.name: Community-based and institutional health care services

items.q: According to the textbook, what is the best way for a patient and family to evaluate the quality of a nursing center?
items.a: Visit the center and inspect it personally
items.ex: Personally visiting and inspecting the center is described as the best way to judge its quality.
w: Read the center’s advertising brochure
A brochure is marketing material; the book recommends visiting and inspecting the center in person.
Ask the admissions director for a description
The director’s description is not a substitute for the family’s own visit and inspection.
Compare the monthly fees of nearby centers
Cost does not measure quality; a personal visit and inspection is the recommended method.

alt.q: A daughter asks the nurse how she can judge the quality of a nursing center for her father. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Visit the center together and inspect it in person.”
alt.ex: The book identifies a personal visit and inspection by the patient and family as the best way to evaluate quality.
w: “The center with the highest fees usually gives the best care.”
Fees are not an indicator of quality; visiting and inspecting the center is recommended.
“Choose the center closest to the hospital for easier follow-up.”
Location does not reflect quality; the family should visit and inspect the center.
“The admissions staff can tell you everything you need to know.”
Relying on staff descriptions replaces the family’s own inspection, which is the best evaluation.

items.q: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) rates the quality of nursing centers on the basis of which three areas?
items.a: Health inspections, staffing, and quality measures
items.ex: CMS quality ratings for nursing centers are based on health inspections, staffing, and quality measures.
w: Resident satisfaction, monthly cost, and location
Cost and location are not the CMS rating areas; ratings use inspections, staffing, and quality measures.
Bed count, building age, and physician referrals
Facility size, age, and referrals are not part of the CMS quality rating.
Accreditation, menu variety, and room size
These features are not the three areas CMS uses to rate nursing center quality.

alt.q: A family reviews a nursing center’s CMS quality rating. Besides health inspections and quality measures, which area does the rating consider?
alt.a: Staffing
alt.ex: The CMS rating combines health inspections, staffing, and quality measures.
w: Monthly fees
Cost is not one of the three areas used in the CMS quality rating.
Distance from a hospital
Location is not part of the CMS quality rating.
Number of private rooms
Room type is not one of the CMS rating areas.

items.q: Results of state and federal inspections of nursing centers are confidential and are released only to current residents.
items.a: False
items.ex: Inspection results are public and available at the nursing center, online, and at the inspectors’ offices.
items.ww: Anyone can review inspection results, so they are not limited to current residents.

alt.q: The public can review results of state and federal nursing center inspections at the center, online, and at the inspectors’ offices.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Inspection results are publicly available in all three of these places to help families compare centers.
alt.ww: Inspection results are not confidential; the book states they are available to the public.

items.q: Which situation commonly leads family caregivers to consider nursing center placement for an older adult?
items.a: Recovery after hospitalization requires more help than the family can give
items.ex: Families consider placement when convalescence needs more assistance than they can provide or in-home care becomes too difficult.
w: The older adult has reached the age of retirement eligibility
Retirement is a life transition, not a reason for nursing center placement.
The older adult notices occasional mild forgetfulness
Occasional forgetfulness is a normal aging change, not a reason for placement.
The older adult begins wearing reading glasses for presbyopia
Presbyopia is a common age-related vision change that does not require placement.

alt.q: A family caregiver tells the nurse she is thinking about a nursing center for her mother. Which situation described by the caregiver is a common reason for considering placement?
alt.a: “Caring for her at home has become increasingly difficult.”
alt.ex: Increasing difficulty providing in-home care is a common reason families consider nursing center placement.
w: “She just retired and wants a change of scenery.”
Retirement alone is not a common reason for nursing center placement.
“She sometimes misplaces her keys.”
Occasionally misplacing things is mild forgetfulness, a normal aging change.
“She prefers to eat her meals with friends.”
A wish for social meals does not indicate a need for nursing center care.

items.q: Once an older adult is admitted to a nursing center, the placement is permanent and discharge is not possible.
items.a: False
items.ex: The decision to enter a nursing center is never final; some residents are discharged home or to a less acute setting.
items.ww: Discharge to home or a less acute setting does occur, so placement is not necessarily permanent.

alt.q: A nursing center resident is sometimes discharged to home or to another less acute setting.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Although many older adults view the center as their final residence, placement is never final.
alt.ww: Residents can be discharged, so it is wrong to treat admission as permanent.

items.q: A family is touring a nursing center for their father. Which observation suggests a quality nursing center?
items.a: Residents’ rooms contain their own photos and belongings
items.ex: A quality center is a home where residents are encouraged to personalize their rooms.
w: Hallways have a strong, lingering odor of urine
A quality center is clean with no pervasive odors.
Staff ask families not to help with residents’ care
Quality centers welcome and encourage family involvement in care.
The unit looks and operates like a hospital ward
A quality nursing center does not feel like a hospital; it feels homelike.

alt.q: During a visit to a nursing center, which finding should raise the family’s concern about quality?
alt.a: Staff focus on finishing tasks rather than on the residents
alt.ex: In a quality center, staff assist residents actively and focus on the person, not on the task.
w: Residents choose from several options at mealtimes
Quality food and mealtime choices are a feature of a quality center.
Staff invite the family to a care planning meeting
Encouraging family participation in care planning is a sign of quality.
Residents decorate their rooms with family pictures
Personalized rooms show the center is a home, a sign of quality.

items.q: Which features does the textbook list for a quality nursing center? Select all that apply.
o: Is Medicare and Medicaid certified
Medicare and Medicaid certification is a listed feature of a quality center.
Has qualified staff who have passed criminal background checks
Adequate, qualified, background-checked staff are a listed quality feature.
Attends quickly to resident requests
Quick response to resident requests is a listed quality feature.
Limits family visits to protect resident routines
Quality centers welcome families and encourage their involvement.
Has a clinical, hospital-like atmosphere
A quality center does not feel like a hospital; it feels homelike.
items.ex: Box 14.2 lists certification, qualified checked staff, prompt response to requests, and a homelike, family-friendly setting as quality features.

alt.q: A family asks what makes a nursing center feel like a home. Which features of a quality center should the nurse describe? Select all that apply.
o: Residents are encouraged to personalize their rooms
A quality center is a home where residents personalize their rooms.
Residents’ privacy is respected
Respect for privacy is a listed feature of a quality center.
The center offers quality food and mealtime choices
Quality food and meal choices are a listed feature.
Meals are served at one fixed time with no choices
Quality centers offer mealtime choices rather than rigid schedules.
Personal belongings are removed to reduce clutter
Residents are encouraged to personalize rooms, not to give up belongings.
alt.ex: Correct: Residents are encouraged to personalize their rooms; Residents’ privacy is respected; The center offers quality food and mealtime choices.

items.q: Besides helping with basic activities of daily living, what do staff in a quality nursing center regularly help residents with?
items.a: Social and recreational activities
items.ex: Box 14.2 notes that staff regularly help residents with social and recreational activities in addition to ADLs.
w: Managing their bank accounts
Financial management is not the assistance the box describes; it lists social and recreational activities.
Writing their wills and directives
Legal planning is not the regular staff assistance listed; social and recreational activities are.
Selling their former homes
Selling property is not a regular staff activity; staff help with social and recreational activities.

alt.q: A family asks what help nursing center staff give besides bathing and dressing. Which response reflects a quality center?
alt.a: “Staff regularly help residents join social and recreational activities.”
alt.ex: In a quality center, staff assist with ADLs and regularly help residents with social and recreational activities.
w: “Staff focus mainly on completing medical treatments.”
A quality center does not feel like a hospital; staff also support social life.
“Staff leave all activities for families to arrange.”
Staff in a quality center regularly help residents with activities.
“Staff manage residents’ personal financial planning.”
Financial planning is not the help described; social and recreational support is.

items.q: Which health care team members are described as helping older adults and families sort through options for care?
items.a: Nurses and social workers
items.ex: Nurses and social workers provide information and answer questions as families review care options.
w: Pharmacists and dietitians
These professionals focus on medications and nutrition, not on reviewing care options.
Insurance agents and attorneys
The textbook names nurses and social workers, not agents or attorneys, for this role.
Physical and respiratory therapists
Therapists focus on function and breathing, not on helping families review care options.

alt.q: An older patient’s spouse says, “There are so many choices for care after discharge. I don’t know where to start.” Which action by the nurse is best?
alt.a: Provide information about care options and answer the spouse’s questions
alt.ex: Nurses help families by giving information and answering questions as they review care options.
w: Tell the spouse that a nursing center is the safest choice
Choosing for the family ignores their needs; the nurse informs them so they can decide.
Advise the spouse to let the health care provider decide
Deferring the decision does not help the family understand and review the options.
Suggest waiting until the patient is home to decide
Delaying leaves the family without needed information when the decision is due.

items.q: A family asks what to look for when touring a nursing center. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Notice whether staff respond quickly to residents’ requests.”
items.ex: A quality center attends quickly to resident requests, with staff focused on the person rather than the task.
w: “Look for a setting that feels as much like a hospital as possible.”
A quality nursing center does not feel like a hospital; it should feel homelike.
“Check that families may visit only at set times.”
Quality centers welcome families and encourage their involvement.
“Make sure residents’ rooms are kept bare and uniform.”
Residents in a quality center are encouraged to personalize their rooms.

alt.q: Which statement by a family member indicates understanding of how to choose a nursing center?
alt.a: “We will visit the centers ourselves and check their CMS quality ratings.”
alt.ex: Visiting in person is the best evaluation, and CMS ratings add data on inspections, staffing, and quality measures.
w: “We will pick the most hospital-like center, since Dad needs care.”
A quality center feels homelike, not like a hospital, while still providing quality care.
“We will not visit, because seeing the center might upset Mom.”
Visiting is an important step and the best way to judge quality.
“We will trust the brochure, since inspection results are private.”
Inspection results are public, and a personal visit is the best evaluation.

items.q: A quality nursing center should look and feel like a hospital so that residents receive quality care.
items.a: False
items.ex: A quality nursing center does not feel like a hospital; it is a homelike place where people live while still receiving quality care.
items.ww: Quality care does not require a hospital atmosphere; the center should feel homelike.

alt.q: A quality nursing center does not feel like a hospital, yet it still provides quality care.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Box 14.2 describes a quality center as a home that feels homelike while delivering quality care.
alt.ww: A homelike setting and quality care go together; a hospital feel is not required.

items.q: Recovery from hospitalization, called [[convalescence]], sometimes requires more assistance than the family can provide.
items.ex: When convalescence needs more help than the family can give, families may consider nursing center placement.

alt.q: When [[convalescence|recovery]] after a hospital stay needs more help than family can give, nursing center placement may be considered.
alt.ex: When convalescence needs more help than the family can give, families may consider nursing center placement.

items.q: Outside of the acute care hospital, nurses care for older adults in nursing centers, which are also called [[long-term care|long term care]] settings.
items.ex: The chapter identifies nursing centers as long-term care settings for older adults.

alt.q: Another name for long-term care is a [[nursing center|nursing home|nursing centre]], one of the residential settings where nurses care for older adults.
alt.ex: The chapter identifies nursing centers as long-term care settings for older adults.

items.q: Outside of an acute care hospital, in which settings do nurses care for older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Adult day care centers
Adult day care centers are a listed community setting for older adults.
Assisted-living residences
Assisted-living residences are a listed residential setting.
Retirement communities
Retirement communities are a listed setting for care of older adults.
Intensive care units
Intensive care units are part of the acute care hospital.
Postanesthesia care units
Postanesthesia care units are part of the acute care hospital.
items.ex: Community and residential settings include clinics, homes, retirement communities, adult day care, assisted living, and nursing centers.

alt.q: A student lists community and residential settings where nurses care for older adults. Which entries are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Clinics
Clinics are a listed setting outside the acute care hospital.
Private homes and apartments
Nurses care for older adults in their own homes and apartments.
Nursing centers
Nursing centers (long-term care) are a listed residential setting.
Hospital emergency departments
Emergency departments are part of the acute care hospital.
Hospital operating rooms
Operating rooms are part of the acute care hospital.
alt.ex: Correct: Clinics; Private homes and apartments; Nursing centers.

items.q: Admission to a nursing center is identified in the chapter as a possible cause of which condition in older adults?
items.a: Depression
items.ex: Loss of a loved one or admission to a nursing center sometimes causes depression in older adults.
w: Presbycusis
Presbycusis is an age-related hearing loss, not a result of nursing center admission.
Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis results from bone loss, not from relocation to a nursing center.
Hypertension
Hypertension is a cardiovascular condition, not described as caused by admission.

alt.q: Two weeks after admission to a nursing center, a resident has lost interest in activities she once enjoyed. Which condition should the nurse assess for?
alt.a: Depression
alt.ex: Admission to a nursing center can trigger depression; lack of interest in former activities is a warning sign.
w: Presbyopia
Presbyopia is a vision change and does not cause loss of interest in activities.
Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis affects bone density, not interest in activities.
Hypertension
Hypertension is often silent and does not explain loss of interest.

items.q: For which group of older adults do providers place special emphasis on annual influenza immunization?
items.a: Residents of nursing homes and long-term care facilities
items.ex: Annual influenza immunization is recommended for all older adults, with special emphasis on those in assisted living and long-term care.
w: Older adults who live at home with a spouse
All older adults need annual immunization, but the emphasis is on residential care settings.
Older adults who still work part time
Working status is not the basis for the special emphasis on influenza vaccination.
Older adults who exercise every day
Fitness level is not the basis for the emphasis; living in a care facility is.

alt.q: Why do providers strongly recommend annual influenza immunization for all older adults, especially those in long-term care?
alt.a: Those who die from influenza are mainly older adults
alt.ex: The chapter notes that people who die from influenza are predominantly older adults.
w: Influenza vaccine also prevents pneumonia and shingles
Separate vaccines are recommended for pneumonia and shingles.
Older adults can no longer receive other vaccines
Older adults are encouraged to receive other vaccines, including boosters.
Influenza vaccine replaces the need for handwashing
Proper handwashing remains part of good disease prevention.

items.q: In which settings does restorative care for older adults take place?
items.a: Private homes, rehabilitation facilities, and nursing centers
items.ex: Both types of restorative care take place in private homes, rehabilitation facilities, and nursing centers.
w: Intensive care units, emergency departments, and operating rooms
These are acute care areas; restorative care continues after the acute phase.
Urgent care centers, pharmacies, and physician offices
These are not the settings the chapter lists for restorative care.
Acute care units, outpatient surgery, and imaging centers
These are acute or procedural settings, not restorative care settings.

alt.q: An older adult will continue recovering from knee surgery after leaving the hospital. Where can restorative care be provided?
alt.a: At home, in a rehabilitation facility, or in a nursing center
alt.ex: Restorative care continues recovery begun in acute care and takes place in homes, rehabilitation facilities, and nursing centers.
w: In the surgical unit until the incision heals
Restorative care continues after the acute phase, outside the acute care unit.
In an intensive care unit for close monitoring
Intensive care is acute care, not a restorative care setting.
In the emergency department observation area
The emergency department is acute care, not a restorative setting.

items.q: Box 14.2 states that a quality nursing center encourages family involvement. In which ways can families be involved? Select all that apply.
o: Providing information about the resident
Staff encourage families who wish to provide information.
Participating in care planning
Family participation in care planning is encouraged.
Helping with social activities or physical care
Families may help with social activities or physical care.
Visiting only during posted hours
Quality centers welcome families when they visit rather than restricting them.
Leaving all care decisions to staff
Families are encouraged to ask questions and participate, not to step back.
items.ex: Quality centers welcome families and encourage them to give information, ask questions, join care planning, and help with care.

alt.q: A son asks how he can stay involved after his mother moves into a nursing center. Which responses reflect a quality center’s approach? Select all that apply.
o: “You are welcome to ask staff questions about her care.”
Staff encourage family members to ask questions.
“You can join meetings to plan her care.”
Families are invited to participate in care planning.
“You can help with her social activities.”
Helping with social activities is a welcomed form of involvement.
“Families should not help with physical care.”
Families may help with physical care if they wish.
“Staff will contact you only if there is an emergency.”
Quality centers provide active communication from staff to patient and family.
alt.ex: Correct: “You are welcome to ask staff questions about her care.”; “You can join meetings to plan her care.”; “You can help with her social activities.”

items.q: An older adult’s daughter wants to compare nursing centers online before visiting. Which resource should the nurse recommend?
items.a: The CMS quality ratings for nursing centers
items.ex: CMS offers quality ratings based on inspections, staffing, and quality measures, plus a nursing center checklist.
w: Reviews posted on social media
Social media posts are not the reliable resource the book recommends; CMS ratings are.
The center’s own marketing website
A center’s marketing site is promotional, not an objective quality rating.
A neighbor’s personal recommendation
A single opinion is not an objective quality rating like the CMS resource.

alt.q: Which organization provides a quality rating and a checklist to help families choose a nursing center?
alt.a: The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
alt.ex: CMS rates nursing centers on health inspections, staffing, and quality measures and offers a nursing center checklist.
w: The National Institute on Aging
The chapter names CMS, not the NIA, as the source of nursing center ratings.
The National Council on Aging
The chapter names CMS, not the NCOA, as the source of nursing center ratings.
The Alzheimer’s Association
This group supports dementia care; it does not rate nursing centers in the chapter.

items.q: The nurse’s assistance is especially valuable when patients and families must make decisions about moving to a nursing center.
items.a: True
items.ex: Sorting through care options can be overwhelming, and nurses help by providing information and answering questions.
items.ww: The chapter specifically highlights nursing center decisions as a time when the nurse’s help is valuable.

alt.q: Decisions about nursing center placement are best made by the health care team alone, without input from the patient and family.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients and families make placement decisions; nurses and social workers support them with information.
alt.ww: The book stresses supporting the patient and family as they review options and decide.

sections.name: Assessing the needs of older adults

items.q: An 82-year-old patient with heart failure tires easily during the admission history and physical examination. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Allow rest periods or complete the assessment in several sessions
items.ex: When energy or endurance is limited, allow rest periods or conduct the assessment in several sessions.
w: Finish the full assessment quickly in one session
Rushing an exhausted patient yields poor data; rest periods or several sessions are recommended.
Obtain the entire history from a family member
The older adult should remain the primary source of information whenever possible.
Skip the history and perform only the physical examination
A complete history is essential; pacing the assessment is preferred over omitting it.

alt.q: Why does a comprehensive assessment of an older adult usually take more time than that of a younger adult?
alt.a: The longer life and medical history may be complex
alt.ex: A longer life and medical history, and their potential complexity, lengthen the assessment.
w: Older adults must be examined only by specialists
No such requirement exists; the time relates to the length and complexity of history.
Most older adults are cognitively impaired
Widespread cognitive impairment is a misconception about aging.
Physical examination techniques differ completely in older adults
Techniques are adapted, but the added time reflects a longer, complex history.

items.q: During an assessment, an older adult gives answers that do not match the nurse’s questions. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Check for hearing or vision problems and ensure assistive devices are in use
items.ex: Sensory deficits can make an older adult seem confused; ensuring glasses and hearing aids are used prevents misleading data.
w: Document that the patient is confused
Concluding confusion without ruling out sensory impairment may be inaccurate.
Ask the family to answer the remaining questions
The older adult should remain the primary source whenever possible.
Begin a standardized dementia screening test
Sensory problems should be ruled out first because they can mimic confusion.

alt.q: Why must the nurse consider an older adult’s visual or hearing impairment when choosing communication techniques during an assessment?
alt.a: Missed cues can lead the nurse to wrongly conclude the patient is confused
alt.ex: If the older adult cannot perceive visual or auditory cues, assessment data become inaccurate and may suggest false confusion.
w: Sensory loss always indicates early dementia
Sensory loss is not dementia; it can only mimic confusion.
Patients with sensory loss cannot give consent
Sensory impairment does not remove the ability to consent.
Sensory deficits shorten the assessment time needed
Sensory deficits complicate data gathering; they do not shorten it.

items.q: An 84-year-old woman has a urinary tract infection. Which findings reflect an altered presentation of UTI that the nurse might see in an older adult? Select all that apply.
o: New-onset incontinence
Older adults with UTI sometimes present with incontinence instead of classic urinary symptoms.
Falls
Falls may be the presenting sign of a UTI in an older adult.
Only a slight rise in temperature within normal limits
A slight temperature elevation may be the only sign instead of fever.
High fever with shaking chills
Older adults with UTI often lack a fever; this is the classic, not altered, presentation.
Severe burning on urination with urgency
Dysuria and urgency are classic symptoms that are often absent in older adults.
items.ex: Classic signs are often absent or blunted in older adults; a UTI may appear as incontinence, falls, and minimal temperature change.

alt.q: A nurse reviews atypical presentations of illness in older adults. Which pairings are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Pneumonia: tachycardia, tachypnea, and confusion without fever
Some older adults with pneumonia lack fever and productive cough.
Myocardial infarction: sudden dyspnea with anxiety and confusion
Older adults may have dyspnea and confusion instead of crushing chest pain.
UTI: incontinence and falls
UTI may present with incontinence, falls, and only slight temperature elevation.
Pneumonia: high fever with productive cough in every case
These common symptoms are often absent in older adults with pneumonia.
Myocardial infarction: crushing chest pain with diaphoresis in every case
Classic chest pain is often replaced by sudden dyspnea in older adults.
alt.ex: Correct: Pneumonia: tachycardia, tachypnea, and confusion without fever; Myocardial infarction: sudden dyspnea with anxiety and confusion; UTI: incontinence and falls.

items.q: A 79-year-old man with a cardiac history calls the clinic reporting new shortness of breath and feeling confused. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Direct him to go to the emergency department
items.ex: Increased dyspnea and confusion are the most common signs of myocardial infarction in older adults with cardiac history.
w: Schedule a clinic appointment for later in the week
Delaying care is unsafe because these symptoms may signal a myocardial infarction.
Advise him to rest and call back if chest pain develops
Older adults often have MI without chest pain, so waiting for pain is unsafe.
Suggest he increase fluids for possible dehydration
These symptoms require emergency evaluation for MI, not home management.

alt.q: Which presentation of myocardial infarction is common in older adults?
alt.a: Sudden dyspnea accompanied by anxiety and confusion
alt.ex: Instead of crushing chest pain and diaphoresis, older adults often have sudden dyspnea with anxiety and confusion.
w: Crushing substernal chest pain with diaphoresis
This is the classic presentation, which is often absent in older adults.
High fever with productive cough and chills
These are classic pneumonia symptoms, not MI symptoms.
Painful urination with urgency and frequency
These are classic urinary tract infection symptoms.

That goes with I.
Confusion
