mt.q: Match each letter of the SPICES assessment tool with the area it represents.
mt.ex: SPICES flags sleep disorders, eating problems, incontinence, confusion, falls, and skin breakdown for in-depth assessment.

items.q: An older adult’s temperature exceeds 38.2°C (100.9°F). How should the nurse interpret this finding?
items.a: It is serious and needs immediate follow-up to find the cause
items.ex: Temperatures above 38.2°C (100.9°F) in older adults are serious and require immediate follow-up.
w: It is an expected response to aging that needs no action
An elevated temperature is significant in older adults and is never simply age-related.
It is low-grade and can be rechecked in 24 hours
Waiting is unsafe; this temperature requires immediate follow-up.
It is important only if a productive cough is present
The temperature itself is serious; older adults often lack classic symptoms.

alt.q: Why is even a small temperature elevation significant in an older adult?
alt.a: Baseline may be lower than the usual adult normal temperature
alt.ex: Thermoregulation changes can lower baseline temperature, so even a small rise may signal infection.
w: Baseline is usually higher than 37.5°C (99.5°F)
Baseline temperature tends to be lower, not higher, in older adults.
Infection always causes fever above 39°C (102.2°F)
Up to one-third of older adults with acute infections have no fever.
Oral readings run about 1°C (1.8°F) too low
Readings are not described as inaccurate; the baseline itself may be lower.

items.q: Confusion is an expected and inevitable finding in a hospitalized older adult.
items.a: False
items.ex: Confusion is not inevitable; look for acute illness, fever, a neurological event, new medications, or delirium risk factors.
items.ww: Treating confusion as expected could delay recognizing a treatable acute problem.

alt.q: When a hospitalized older adult shows new confusion, the nurse should look for acute illness, fever, a neurological event, or new medications.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Confusion signals a possible cause such as illness, fever, a neurological event, new medications, or delirium risk factors.
alt.ww: New confusion is not a normal part of aging and must be investigated.

items.q: A 77-year-old patient’s family reports that his hearing has worsened. Before assuming he has presbycusis, which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Inspect the external auditory canals for cerumen
items.ex: Impacted cerumen is a common, easily treated cause of diminished hearing that should be ruled out first.
w: Refer him for hearing aid fitting
A referral is premature until a treatable cause like cerumen is ruled out.
Document bilateral age-related hearing loss
Presbycusis should not be assumed before inspecting the ear canals.
Speak louder and use a high-pitched voice
Low-pitched tones are clearer for older adults, and the cause still needs assessment.

alt.q: Which common cause of diminished hearing in older adults is easy to treat?
alt.a: Impacted cerumen
alt.ex: Impacted cerumen is a common, easy-to-treat cause of reduced hearing acuity.
w: Presbycusis
Presbycusis is an age-related hearing loss and is not easily reversed.
Sclerosis of the inner ear
Inner ear sclerosis is an aging change that is not easily treated.
Thickening of the tympanic membrane
Tympanic membrane thickening is an aging change, not an easily treated cause.

items.q: A progressive decline in the ability of the eyes to accommodate from near to far vision is called [[presbyopia]].
items.ex: Presbyopia is a common age-related vision change; older adults also need more light for reading and ADLs.

alt.q: An age-related loss of acuity for high-pitched sounds and conversational speech is called [[presbycusis]].
alt.ex: Presbyopia is a common age-related vision change; older adults also need more light for reading and ADLs.

items.q: Hypertension is a normal, harmless change of aging.
items.a: False
items.ex: Although common, hypertension is not a normal aging change and predisposes to heart failure, stroke, and renal failure.
items.ww: Hypertension carries serious risks, so it must not be dismissed as harmless aging.

alt.q: Although hypertension is common in older adults, it is not a normal aging change.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Hypertension predisposes older adults to heart failure, stroke, renal failure, coronary heart disease, and peripheral vascular disease.
alt.ww: Calling it normal aging ignores that it is a disease with serious complications.

items.q: A previously independent 80-year-old woman suddenly cannot dress or bathe herself. How should the nurse interpret this change?
items.a: It often signals an acute illness or a worsening chronic problem
items.ex: A sudden decline in ADL ability often signals acute illness such as pneumonia or UTI, or a worsening chronic condition.
w: It is an expected change in late older adulthood
Sudden functional decline is not normal aging and needs investigation.
It shows she needs immediate nursing center placement
Placement is not the first step; the cause of the decline must be identified.
It reflects lack of motivation that requires encouragement
A sudden change is often a sign of illness, not of motivation.

alt.q: Which statement about functional status in older adults is accurate?
alt.a: It is a sensitive indicator of health or illness
alt.ex: Functional status, the safe performance of ADLs and IADLs, is a sensitive indicator of health or illness.
w: It depends only on the person’s physical strength
Functional status involves physical, psychological, cognitive, and social domains.
It declines suddenly as part of normal aging
A sudden decline signals illness rather than normal aging.
It is assessed only by asking the patient
Family caregiver input and OT and PT help ensure an accurate assessment.

items.q: Which findings in an older adult are NOT normal aging changes and require further assessment for an underlying cause? Select all that apply.
o: Getting lost in familiar places
Getting lost in familiar places signals serious cognitive impairment.
Loss of the ability to calculate
Loss of calculation ability is not a normal aging change.
Poor judgment
Poor judgment suggests serious cognitive impairment needing assessment.
Occasionally misplacing things
Occasionally misplacing items is mild forgetfulness, not a serious memory problem.
Recalling information more slowly than before
Slower recall is a normal change some older adults notice.
items.ex: Disorientation, language loss, getting lost, trouble following directions, loss of calculation, and poor judgment are not normal aging.

alt.q: A daughter describes changes in her 78-year-old father. Which findings should the nurse recognize as possible serious cognitive impairment? Select all that apply.
o: He has trouble following simple directions
Difficulty following directions is not a normal aging change.
He is disoriented about where he is
Disorientation signals serious cognitive impairment.
He has lost some language skills
Loss of language skills requires further assessment.
He once forgot to pay a bill
Occasionally forgetting a bill is mild forgetfulness.
He sometimes misplaces his glasses
Occasionally misplacing things is a normal sign of mild forgetfulness.
alt.ex: Correct: He has trouble following simple directions; He is disoriented about where he is; He has lost some language skills.

items.q: What is the typical onset of Delirium?
items.a: Sudden or abrupt onset
items.ex: Table 14.2 contrasts the abrupt onset of delirium, the slow insidious onset of dementia, and the recent onset of depression.
w: Insidious onset with slow progression over years
That goes with Dementia.
Recent onset that may occur with major life changes
That goes with Depression.

alt.q: What is the typical onset of Dementia?
alt.a: Insidious onset with slow progression over years
alt.ex: Table 14.2 contrasts the abrupt onset of delirium, the slow insidious onset of dementia, and the recent onset of depression.
w: Sudden or abrupt onset
That goes with Delirium.
Recent onset that may occur with major life changes
That goes with Depression.

alt.q: What is the typical onset of Depression?
alt.a: Recent onset that may occur with major life changes
alt.ex: Table 14.2 contrasts the abrupt onset of delirium, the slow insidious onset of dementia, and the recent onset of depression.
w: Sudden or abrupt onset
That goes with Delirium.
Insidious onset with slow progression over years
That goes with Dementia.

alt.q: Which condition has “Sudden or abrupt onset”?
alt.a: Delirium
alt.ex: Table 14.2 contrasts the abrupt onset of delirium, the slow insidious onset of dementia, and the recent onset of depression.
w: Dementia
Dementia: Insidious onset with slow progression over years.
Depression
Depression: Recent onset that may occur with major life changes.

alt.q: Which condition has “Insidious onset with slow progression over years”?
alt.a: Dementia
alt.ex: Table 14.2 contrasts the abrupt onset of delirium, the slow insidious onset of dementia, and the recent onset of depression.
w: Delirium
Delirium: Sudden or abrupt onset.
Depression
Depression: Recent onset that may occur with major life changes.

alt.q: Which condition has “Recent onset that may occur with major life changes”?
alt.a: Depression
alt.ex: Table 14.2 contrasts the abrupt onset of delirium, the slow insidious onset of dementia, and the recent onset of depression.
w: Delirium
Delirium: Sudden or abrupt onset.
Dementia
Dementia: Insidious onset with slow progression over years.

mt.q: Match each condition with its typical onset, as compared in Table 14.2.
pairs: Insidious onset with slow progression over years
Recent onset that may occur with major life changes
mt.ex: Table 14.2 contrasts the abrupt onset of delirium, the slow insidious onset of dementia, and the recent onset of depression.

items.q: A hospitalized 81-year-old suddenly becomes agitated, restless, and sees things that are not there. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Assess for signs of infection such as pneumonia or UTI
items.ex: New-onset delirium is a medical emergency and should trigger assessment for infections like pneumonia and UTI.
w: Document the behavior as worsening dementia
This abrupt change suggests delirium, which must be ruled out and treated.
Reassure the family that this is normal with aging
Delirium is not normal aging; it is a potentially reversible emergency.
Reassess the patient at the end of the shift
Delirium requires prompt assessment and intervention, not delay.

alt.q: Why is delirium considered a medical emergency in an older adult?
alt.a: It is potentially reversible if the cause is treated promptly
alt.ex: Delirium has physiological causes; prompt recognition and treatment of the cause can reverse it.
w: It always progresses to irreversible dementia
Delirium is potentially reversible; dementia is the irreversible condition.
It occurs only in patients on mechanical ventilation
Delirium occurs in any setting, though ICU patients have high rates.
It is caused mainly by normal aging of the brain
Delirium has physiological, environmental, or psychosocial causes, not normal aging.

items.q: A nursing center resident with dementia says she must leave to pick up her children from school. Which response by the nurse best follows dementia care recommendations?
items.a: Acknowledge her concern and treat the behavior as communication
items.ex: Box 14.5 advises accepting the person’s reality and viewing behavior as communication rather than reorienting.
w: Firmly remind her that her children are grown adults
Repeated reorientation is discouraged in dementia care; accept the person’s reality.
Request a sedative from the health care provider
Nonpharmacological measures should be used before medications.
Explain that she is in a nursing center and cannot leave
Correcting her reality can increase distress; recognize her behavior as communication.

alt.q: A resident with dementia begins wandering in the hallway late in the afternoon. What should the nurse consider first?
alt.a: An unmet need such as hunger, pain, or the need to void
alt.ex: Behaviors like wandering often express unmet needs such as hunger, pain, anxiety, or the need to void.
w: A need for physical restraints to prevent falls
Restraints are avoided; the nurse looks for the need behind the behavior.
A need for a sedating medication
Nonpharmacological measures come first because medications may sedate.
A deliberate attempt to disrupt staff routines
Behaviors are viewed as communication of a need, not deliberate disruption.

items.q: Which tool is an easy-to-use screening instrument for depression in older adults?
items.a: Geriatric Depression Scale
items.ex: The Geriatric Depression Scale helps nurses recognize and analyze cues related to depression in older adults.
w: Montreal Cognitive Assessment
The MoCA assesses mental status and cognition, not depression.
Mini-Mental State Examination-2
The MMSE-2 assesses mental status, not depression.
Clock drawing test
The clock drawing test assesses cognition, not depression.

alt.q: An older adult with diabetes has lost interest in former activities since his wife died. Which tool should the nurse use to screen for depression?
alt.a: Geriatric Depression Scale
alt.ex: The Geriatric Depression Scale is an easy-to-use screening tool for depression in older adults.
w: Montreal Cognitive Assessment
The MoCA screens cognition, not depression.
Mini-Mental State Examination-2
The MMSE-2 screens mental status, not depression.
Clock drawing test
The clock drawing test screens cognition, not depression.

items.q: Older adults should be screened for sexually transmitted infections regardless of age.
items.a: True
items.ex: Aging changes, reentering the dating scene, and risky behaviors create STI risk, so screening occurs regardless of age.
items.ww: Older adults remain sexually active and at risk, so age is no reason to skip screening.

alt.q: Because sexual activity declines with age, STI screening is unnecessary for adults older than 65.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Older adults have STI risk factors and often do not disclose sexual concerns, so screening occurs regardless of age.
alt.ww: Sexuality continues throughout life, and older adults have specific STI risk factors.

items.q: A nurse is teaching an older adult about home safety. At what maximum temperature should the water heater be set?
items.ex: Water heaters should not be set higher than 120°F to help prevent burns.
w: 130°F is above the recommended maximum of 120°F.
140°F is well above the recommended maximum of 120°F.
150°F is well above the recommended maximum of 120°F.

alt.q: An older adult says, “I set my water heater to 140°F so my bath stays hot.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Please lower it to no higher than 120°F.”
alt.ex: The recommended maximum water heater setting is 120°F to reduce the risk of burns.
w: “That setting is safe if you test the water first.”
140°F exceeds the safe limit of 120°F regardless of testing.
“Lower it to 130°F, which is the safe maximum.”
130°F is still above the recommended maximum of 120°F.
“Raise it to 150°F to kill bacteria in the tank.”
Raising the temperature increases burn risk; the limit is 120°F.

items.q: A nurse assesses the bathroom of an older adult who lives alone. Which features promote safety? Select all that apply.
o: Grab bars by the shower and toilet
Grab bars help with transfers and can be reached during a fall.
Nonslip surfaces on the floor and in the tub
Nonslip surfaces reduce the risk of falls.
Adequate lighting, especially at night
Good lighting, especially at night, is a key bathroom safety feature.
Throw rugs in front of the sink and tub
Rugs are obstacles that increase fall risk and should be minimized.
Supplies stored on high shelves to reduce clutter
Needed supplies should be within easy reach.
items.ex: A safe bathroom has grab bars, nonslip surfaces, supplies within reach, minimal obstacles, and adequate lighting.

alt.q: Which home features help an older adult with age-related vision changes move about safely? Select all that apply.
o: A color contrast at the edge of each stair
Contrast shows where each step ends.
Door frames that contrast with wall color
Contrasting frames and baseboards improve perception of room boundaries.
Furnishings in red, orange, and yellow
These colors are the easiest for older adults to see.
Highly polished, shiny floors
Shiny floors create glare and may appear wet.
Pastel blue and green color schemes
Older adults have difficulty distinguishing pastels and blue from green.
alt.ex: Correct: A color contrast at the edge of each stair; Door frames that contrast with wall color; Furnishings in red, orange, and yellow.

items.q: A nurse discusses end-of-life concerns with an older adult. Which concern does current evidence suggest is uncommon among older adults?
items.a: Fear of one’s own death
items.ex: Fear of one’s own death is uncommon; older adults more often fear being a burden, suffering, or being alone.
w: Fear of being a burden
Fear of being a burden is a common concern of older adults.
Fear of suffering
Fear of suffering is a common concern of older adults.
Fear of being alone
Fear of being alone is a common concern of older adults.

alt.q: Which statement about older adults’ attitudes toward death is supported by current evidence?
alt.a: Fear of their own death is uncommon
alt.ex: Older adults hold varied beliefs about death, but fear of their own death is uncommon.
w: Most are comfortable with death
The nurse should not assume an older adult is comfortable with death.
Their death is always a blessing
This is a stereotype that does not apply to every older adult.
Most have no unfinished business
Many older adults still have unfinished business as death approaches.

sections.name: Addressing the health concerns of older adults

items.q: Which Healthy People 2030 objective for older adults falls under injury prevention?
items.a: Reduce the proportion of older adults who use inappropriate medications
items.ex: Injury prevention objectives include reducing fall-related deaths, inappropriate medication use, and ED visits due to falls.
w: Reduce hospital admissions for urinary tract infections
This is an infectious disease objective, not an injury prevention objective.
Reduce vision loss from age-related macular degeneration
This is a sensory or communication disorders objective.
Reduce infections caused by Listeria
This is a foodborne illness objective, not injury prevention.

alt.q: Under which Healthy People 2030 category for older adults is the objective to reduce fall-related deaths listed?
alt.a: Injury prevention
alt.ex: Injury prevention objectives include reducing fall-related deaths, inappropriate medication use, and ED visits due to falls.
w: Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis objectives address hip fractures, screening, and treatment after fractures.
Dementias
Dementia objectives address awareness and preventing hospitalizations.
Oral conditions
Oral objectives address root decay, tooth loss, and periodontitis.

items.q: According to Box 14.6, which printed teaching materials are best for older adults with health literacy limitations?
items.a: Large black font on cream or white paper
items.ex: Box 14.6 recommends large black font on cream or white paper for older adults.
w: Small black font on bright yellow paper
Small print is hard to read; large black font on cream or white is recommended.
Large blue font on pale green paper
Older adults have difficulty with blue and green; black on cream or white is recommended.
Large white font on a glossy black page
Glossy pages create glare; black font on cream or white paper is recommended.

alt.q: A nurse prepares a medication handout for an older adult with low health literacy. Which approach is best?
alt.a: Use clear, concise language and avoid medical terminology
alt.ex: Clear, concise language without medical terms helps older adults with health literacy limitations.
w: Include detailed medical terms for accuracy
Medical terminology confuses learners; plain language is recommended.
Use small print so the handout fits on one page
Large print is recommended for older adults.
Rely on the handout alone without demonstration
Pictures and demonstrations should augment spoken and written information.

items.q: A nurse has taught an older adult how to change a wound dressing. Which statement by the nurse uses the teach-back principle to evaluate learning?
items.a: “Show me how you will change the dressing on your wound.”
items.ex: Teach-back asks the patient to explain or demonstrate what was taught, such as showing the dressing change.
w: “Do you have any questions about the dressing change?”
A yes-or-no question does not confirm what the patient learned.
“Do you understand how to change your dressing?”
Asking about understanding does not show that learning occurred.
“I will leave a handout so you can review the steps.”
Giving a handout is teaching, not evaluating learning.

alt.q: Which statement is an example of using teach-back to evaluate an older adult’s understanding of medications?
alt.a: “Show me all of your morning medications.”
alt.ex: Box 14.6 uses having the patient show the morning medications as a teach-back evaluation.
w: “Are you taking all of your medications?”
A yes-or-no question does not verify understanding.
“Your pharmacist will review your medications.”
Referral does not evaluate what the patient learned.
“Here is a list of your morning medications.”
Providing a list is teaching, not teach-back evaluation.

items.q: During a teaching session, an older adult’s daughter appears overwhelmed by information about her mother’s care. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Give her a chance to ask questions and reschedule the session if possible
items.ex: Box 14.6 advises offering overwhelmed caregivers time for questions and rescheduling the session if possible.
w: Continue so that all content is covered today
An overwhelmed learner is not ready to learn; continuing reduces learning.
Give her printed materials and end the session
Ending abruptly does not let her ask questions or return when ready.
Teach the content to another family member instead
The caregiver still needs the information; rescheduling is preferred.

alt.q: Before starting a teaching session, the nurse notes that an older adult is grimacing and appears tired. Which action is best?
alt.a: Delay teaching until the patient is ready to learn
alt.ex: Readiness to learn comes first; the nurse watches for cues of pain and fatigue before teaching.
w: Proceed quickly so the patient can rest afterward
Pain and fatigue interfere with learning, so teaching should wait.
Teach the family member and skip the patient
The patient remains the learner; teaching should wait until they are ready.
Provide written materials and leave the room
Written materials alone do not address readiness or allow questions.

items.q: Which general preventive health measures should the nurse recommend to older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Immunizations for influenza, shingles, and pneumococcal disease
These immunizations, plus tetanus, diphtheria, and pertussis, are recommended.
Seven to nine hours of good quality sleep
Good sleep of 7 to 9 hours is a listed preventive measure.
Regular primary care, dental, and vision visits
Regular primary care, dental, vision, and hearing visits are recommended.
Stopping screening activities after age 65
Screening such as blood pressure, mammography, and bone density continues as indicated by age.
Avoiding new learning to prevent stress
Learning new skills may help keep older adults cognitively healthy.
items.ex: Preventive measures include regular visits, screenings, immunizations, exercise, healthy weight and diet, good sleep, and mental and cognitive health.

alt.q: An older adult asks how to stay healthy. Which recommendations are consistent with the chapter? Select all that apply.
o: Eat plenty of fresh fruits, vegetables, and whole grains
A well-balanced diet with fruits, vegetables, and whole grains is recommended.
Stay socially connected to care for mental health
Socialization is listed as care for mental health.
Learn new skills to support cognitive health
Learning new skills may help keep older adults cognitively healthy.
Limit sleep to 5 hours to prevent daytime confusion
Good quality sleep of 7 to 9 hours is recommended.
Skip immunizations if you received them as a child
Some older adults need boosters or never had the primary series.
alt.ex: Correct: Eat plenty of fresh fruits, vegetables, and whole grains; Stay socially connected to care for mental health; Learn new skills to support cognitive health.

items.q: The concurrent use of many medications, which increases the risk for adverse drug effects, is called [[polypharmacy]].
items.ex: Polypharmacy is common with multiple chronic conditions and is linked to adverse reactions, falls, and readmissions.

alt.q: An older adult taking several medications for hypertension, diabetes, and arthritis at once is experiencing [[polypharmacy]].
alt.ex: Polypharmacy is common with multiple chronic conditions and is linked to adverse reactions, falls, and readmissions.

items.q: Exposure to fumes from hair dyes, artificial nail products, and paints can contribute to chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
items.a: True
items.ex: Inhalants such as tobacco smoke, secondhand smoke, and these fumes can injure the lungs and lead to COPD.
items.ww: The chapter lists these fumes as lung inhalants that can lead to COPD.

alt.q: Only active cigarette smoking causes chronic obstructive pulmonary disease; secondhand smoke and other fumes do not contribute.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Secondhand smoke and fumes from hair dyes, nail products, and paints can also lead to COPD.
alt.ww: Lung injury from several inhalants, not only active smoking, can cause COPD.

items.q: A 70-year-old who smokes tells the nurse he is not willing to quit. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Suggest that he at least reduce the amount he smokes
items.ex: If a patient rejects smoking cessation, the nurse suggests at least a reduction in smoking.
w: Tell him that quitting after age 50 has no benefit
Quitting after 50 reduces the risk of dying prematurely.
Stop discussing smoking at future visits
The nurse continues to support change; reduction is suggested.
Insist that he quit immediately to continue care
Coercion is not recommended; suggest reduction when cessation is refused.

alt.q: An older adult says she is ready to quit smoking. Which action should the nurse take next?
alt.a: Set a quit date and plan a follow-up visit
alt.ex: When a patient is open to quitting, set a quit or reduction date and a follow-up visit to discuss the attempt.
w: Tell her to quit on her own and call if she fails
Planned follow-up with encouragement is recommended, not leaving her alone.
Advise her to avoid including family in the plan
Family members should be included in the plan if possible.
Tell her that nicotine gum is unsafe at her age
Nicotine gum and patches are part of cessation programs.

items.q: Which findings should increase the nurse’s suspicion of alcohol abuse in an older adult? Select all that apply.
o: A history of repeated falls and accidents
Repeated falls and accidents raise suspicion of alcohol abuse.
Recurring episodes of memory loss and confusion
Recurrent memory loss and confusion are listed clues.
Skipping meals or medications
A history of skipping meals or medications raises suspicion.
Increased involvement in community activities
Social isolation, not increased involvement, raises suspicion.
Careful management of household finances
Difficulty managing household tasks and finances raises suspicion.
items.ex: Suspicion increases with repeated falls, isolation, memory loss, missed obligations, skipped meals or medications, and trouble managing finances.

alt.q: Which factors are clues that an older adult may be abusing alcohol? Select all that apply.
o: Recent loss of a loved one
Loss of a loved one is a listed clue of alcohol abuse.
Loss of a role or identity
Role and identity loss is a listed clue.
Coexisting depression or dementia
Coexisting dementia or depression is a listed clue.
A stable routine with no recent life changes
Stress and life changes, not stability, are listed clues.
Friends who discourage drinking
Encouragement or approval by friends is the listed clue.
alt.ex: Correct: Recent loss of a loved one; Loss of a role or identity; Coexisting depression or dementia.

items.q: An older adult with dementia is losing weight in a nursing center. Which intervention should the nurse include in the plan of care?
items.a: Offer small, frequent meals with finger foods
items.ex: For older adults with dementia, provide small, frequent meals and easy-to-eat finger foods, and monitor weight and intake.
w: Serve three large meals at set times only
Small, frequent meals are recommended over large, fixed meals.
Withhold supplements until meals are finished
Supplements the patient likes and can swallow easily should be offered.
Limit assistance so the patient stays independent
Assistance with eating is recommended for adequate intake.

alt.q: An older adult with dementia has trouble feeding herself with utensils. Which foods should the nurse offer?
alt.a: Finger foods such as sandwiches and cut-up fruit
alt.ex: Finger foods like chicken strips, sandwiches, and cut-up fruit and vegetables are easy for people with dementia to eat.
w: Soups and stews served in deep bowls
These require utensils, which this patient has difficulty using.
Large portions served three times a day
Small, frequent meals are recommended for older adults with dementia.
Whole steaks that must be cut with a knife
Foods needing utensils are harder to manage than finger foods.

items.q: A nurse teaches an older adult about a new walking program. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will stop and get help if I feel chest tightness or get dizzy.”
items.ex: Older adults should stop exercising and seek help for chest pain, shortness of breath, dizziness, joint pain, or palpitations.
w: “I will walk outside even on the hottest days to stay on schedule.”
Outdoor exercise in extreme temperatures should be avoided.
“I will skip water before walking so I do not need the bathroom.”
Older adults should drink water before and after exercising.
“I will start with a long, fast walk to build strength quickly.”
Programs for sedentary older adults should begin conservatively and progress slowly.

alt.q: Before a sedentary older adult begins an exercise program, which action should the nurse take?
alt.a: Collaborate with the health care provider about contraindications
alt.ex: Collaborate with the health care provider before starting a program to be sure there are no medical contraindications.
w: Begin with high-intensity training to see quick results
Programs for sedentary older adults begin conservatively and progress slowly.
Recommend exercising alone to avoid distraction
Exercising with a partner is a recommended safety measure.
Advise waiting until all chronic conditions resolve
Older adults should be as active as their abilities and conditions allow.

items.q: An older adult who limits activity because of a fear of falling lowers the risk of future falls.
items.a: False
items.ex: Fear of falling leads to unnatural walking and limited activity, reducing mobility and fitness and raising future fall risk.
items.ww: Limiting activity weakens mobility and fitness, which increases rather than lowers fall risk.

alt.q: Fear of falling after a fall can lead to reduced mobility and a higher risk of future falls.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Older adults who fear falling often limit activity, which reduces fitness and independence and raises fall risk.
alt.ww: Avoiding activity does not protect against falls; it leads to deconditioning.

items.q: What is the purpose of the Beers Criteria for older adults?
items.a: To help providers recognize potentially inappropriate medications
items.ex: The Beers Criteria guide prescribers in recognizing potentially inappropriate medications for older adults.
w: To screen older adults for symptoms of depression
Depression screening uses tools such as the Geriatric Depression Scale.
To rate the quality of care in nursing centers
CMS quality ratings, not the Beers Criteria, rate nursing centers.
To assess the risk for alcohol abuse in older adults
Alcohol screening tools are listed in the NIDA tools chart.

alt.q: Which tool helps health care providers recognize potentially inappropriate medications for older adults?
alt.a: Beers Criteria
alt.ex: The Beers Criteria guide providers in recognizing potentially inappropriate medication use in older adults.
w: SPICES tool
SPICES is a general assessment tool for areas such as sleep, falls, and skin.
Geriatric Depression Scale
This scale screens for depression, not inappropriate medications.
Montreal Cognitive Assessment
The MoCA evaluates cognition, not medication appropriateness.

items.q: When an older adult sees several specialists, each specialist should manage the medications independently without one overall coordinator.
items.a: False
items.ex: One provider should keep track of the overall medication regimen when an older adult sees several specialists.
items.ww: Independent management by multiple providers increases polypharmacy and interaction risks.

alt.q: When an older adult sees several specialists, one provider should keep track of the overall medication regimen.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: A single provider overseeing the full regimen helps prevent polypharmacy, interactions, and adverse effects.
alt.ww: Without one coordinator, medications from different specialists may interact or duplicate.

items.q: An older adult becomes confused, and the health care provider finds a urinary tract infection. Which approach to the confusion is best?
items.a: Treat the infection that is causing the confusion
items.ex: When confusion has a physiological cause, providers treat the cause rather than the confused behavior.
w: Give a sedative to control the confused behavior
Sedatives can cause or worsen confusion and increase fall risk.
Apply physical restraints until the confusion clears
Restraints increase disorientation; treating the cause is the priority.
Prescribe a tranquilizer to calm the patient
Tranquilizers can worsen confusion and lower blood pressure.

alt.q: An older adult’s confusion worsens each evening and seems related to the environment. Which intervention is best?
alt.a: Provide adequate light and encourage use of assistive devices
alt.ex: Time-related or environmental confusion is managed with nonpharmacological measures like lighting and assistive devices.
w: Request a sedative for the evening hours
Sedatives often cause or worsen confusion in older adults.
Request a beta blocker to calm the patient
Beta blockers can worsen confusion and lower blood pressure.
Limit phone calls from family in the evening
Hearing reassuring family voices is a recommended measure.

items.q: A nurse suspects that an older adult is being mistreated. The caregiver refuses to leave the room during the interview. How should the nurse interpret this behavior?
items.a: It is a red flag for possible mistreatment
items.ex: The interview should occur privately; a caregiver who refuses to leave is a red flag.
w: It shows the caregiver’s appropriate concern
Refusing to allow a private interview is a warning sign, not a sign of support.
It is required for patients with cognitive impairment
The assessment is done privately away from the caregiver when mistreatment is possible.
It has no meaning for the assessment
This refusal is specifically identified as a red flag.

alt.q: A nurse plans to screen an older adult for mistreatment. The adult’s caregiver usually attends every visit. How should the nurse conduct the interview?
alt.a: Privately, away from the caregiver
alt.ex: Screening for mistreatment requires interviewing and assessing the older adult privately, away from the caregiver.
w: With the caregiver present to confirm details
Most perpetrators are caregivers, so their presence can prevent disclosure.
By telephone with the caregiver only
The older adult must be interviewed directly and privately.
In a group with other family members
A group setting is not private and may inhibit disclosure.

items.a: Frequent reminders of person, place, and time with familiar aids
items.ex: Reality orientation reorients, validation respects feelings, reminiscence recalls the past, and touch comforts older adults.

That goes with Validation therapy.
Recalling past events and memories to bring meaning to the present
That goes with Reminiscence.
Physical contact that comforts, relaxes, and conveys warmth
That goes with Therapeutic touch.

items.q: An anxious older adult insists that today is Tuesday, although it is Thursday. Using validation therapy, which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Acknowledge the distress the patient is feeling
items.ex: Validation therapy avoids arguing and focuses on acknowledging the emotional content of the conversation.
w: Show the patient a calendar to prove it is Thursday
Insisting on the correct date reflects reality orientation, not validation.
Agree that it is Tuesday to end the conversation
Validation does not involve reinforcing the older adult’s misperceptions.
Ignore the statement and change the subject
Ignoring the patient fails to convey respect and understanding.

alt.q: Which statement about validation therapy is accurate?
alt.a: It respects the person’s feelings without reinforcing misperceptions
alt.ex: Validation reflects sensitivity to hidden meanings and feelings without reinforcing misperceptions.
w: It requires the person to agree with the correct time and place
Insisting on correct facts describes reality orientation.
It reinforces the person’s misperceptions to avoid conflict
Validation does not reinforce misperceptions.
It is used mainly to assess memory and coping
Using recall to assess memory and coping describes reminiscence.

items.q: An older adult asks which changes might be early signs of cancer. Which signs should the nurse encourage the patient to report promptly? Select all that apply.
o: A skin lesion that does not heal
Nonhealing skin lesions should be reported promptly.
A change in bowel habits
A change in bowel habits is a listed sign to report.
Unexplained weight loss
Unexplained weight loss is a listed sign of cancer.
Gray hair and facial wrinkles
These are universal aging changes, not signs of cancer.
Slower nail growth
Slower nail growth is a normal integumentary aging change.
items.ex: Older adults should report nonhealing lesions, unexpected bleeding, bowel changes, nagging cough, lumps, mole changes, dysphagia, and weight loss.

alt.q: Which findings described by an older adult are warning signs of cancer that require prompt reporting? Select all that apply.
o: “I have had a nagging cough for weeks.”
A nagging cough is a sign to report promptly.
“I found a new lump under my arm.”
A lump in the breast or another part of the body should be reported.
“It is getting harder to swallow my food.”
Difficulty swallowing is a listed warning sign.
“My skin feels drier than it used to.”
Dry skin is a normal aging change with loss of moisture.
“I need more light to read the newspaper.”
Needing more light for reading is a normal aging vision change.
alt.ex: Correct: “I have had a nagging cough for weeks.”; “I found a new lump under my arm.”; “It is getting harder to swallow my food.”

items.q: Which adverse events are older adults at increased risk for in the acute care setting? Select all that apply.
o: Delirium
The acute care setting increases the risk for delirium.
Health care–associated infections
HAIs are a listed adverse event risk in acute care.
Dehydration and malnutrition
Dehydration and malnutrition are listed acute care risks.
Presbycusis
Presbycusis is an age-related hearing change, not an acute care adverse event.
Presbyopia
Presbyopia is an age-related vision change, not an acute care adverse event.
items.ex: Acute care poses increased risk for delirium, dehydration, malnutrition, HAIs, urinary incontinence, and falls.

alt.q: A nurse plans care for a hospitalized 85-year-old. Which adverse events should the plan aim to prevent? Select all that apply.
o: Falls
Older adults in acute care are at greater risk for falls.
Urinary incontinence
Hospitalized older adults are at risk for transient urinary incontinence.
Pressure injuries
Immobility, incontinence, and malnutrition increase pressure injury risk in acute care.
Dorsal kyphosis
Kyphosis results from osteoporosis, not from hospitalization.
Cataracts
Cataracts relate to yellowing of the lens with age, not hospitalization.
alt.ex: Correct: Falls; Urinary incontinence; Pressure injuries.

items.q: Which is a nonmedical cause of delirium in a hospitalized older adult?
items.a: Separation from usual support systems
items.ex: Nonmedical causes include unfamiliar surroundings and staff, bed rest, separation from support systems, and stress.
w: Hypoxia from a lung condition
Hypoxia is a physiological, medical cause of delirium.
Dehydration from poor fluid intake
Dehydration is a physiological, medical cause of delirium.
Interactions among several drugs
Drug interactions are a medical cause of delirium.

alt.q: Which group of factors includes only nonmedical causes of delirium in hospitalized older adults?
alt.a: Unfamiliar surroundings, unfamiliar staff, and bed rest
alt.ex: Unfamiliar surroundings and staff, bed rest, separation from support, and stress are nonmedical causes of delirium.
w: Infection, dehydration, and hypoxia
These are medical, physiological causes of delirium.
Anesthesia, pain, and drug interactions
These are medical causes that increase delirium risk.
Sleep deprivation, infection, and anesthesia
Infection and anesthesia are medical causes of delirium.

items.q: Despite prevention measures, a hospitalized 80-year-old develops delirium. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Help identify and treat the cause of the delirium
items.ex: When prevention fails, nursing management begins with identifying and treating the cause of delirium.
w: Apply physical restraints to keep the patient safe
Restraints should be avoided; a restraint-free environment is safest.
Ask the family to stay away until the confusion clears
Family visits are a supportive intervention for delirium.
Request a sedative to control the behavior
Sedatives can worsen confusion; the cause must be identified and treated.

alt.q: When prevention of delirium fails in a hospitalized older adult, where does nursing management begin?
alt.a: Identifying and treating the cause of delirium
alt.ex: Delirium is potentially reversible, so management begins with identifying and treating its cause.
w: Applying restraints until the behavior improves
Every effort must be made to avoid physical restraints.
Giving a sedative at bedtime to promote sleep
Sedatives can cause or worsen confusion in older adults.
Moving the patient to a new, unfamiliar room
Unfamiliar surroundings are a nonmedical cause of delirium.

items.q: Which interventions support an older adult with delirium in the acute care setting? Select all that apply.
o: Encourage family visits
Family visits are a supportive intervention for delirium.
Compensate for vision and hearing deficits
Impaired vision or hearing worsens confusion and hinders reorientation.
Use reality orientation techniques
Reality orientation techniques are often useful in delirium.
Apply physical restraints when the patient is restless
Every effort must be made to avoid physical restraints.
Keep the room dark and quiet throughout the day
Memory cues and compensating for sensory deficits are recommended; unfamiliar surroundings and sensory impairment add to confusion.
items.ex: Supportive delirium care includes family visits, memory cues, compensating for sensory deficits, and reality orientation.

alt.q: A nurse plans care for a confused older adult on a medical unit. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Place a clock and calendar where the patient can see them
Clocks and calendars are memory cues for orientation.
Make sure the patient wears glasses and hearing aids
Compensating for sensory deficits supports reorientation.
Wear a visible name tag when caring for the patient
Name tags are a recommended memory cue.
Rotate different staff each shift for variety
Unfamiliar staff contribute to delirium; stable staffing is preferred.
Limit contact with family members
Separation from support systems is a cause of delirium.
alt.ex: Correct: Place a clock and calendar where the patient can see them; Make sure the patient wears glasses and hearing aids; Wear a visible name tag when caring for the patient.

items.q: A hospitalized older adult was kept NPO for diagnostic tests and is now drinking little. Which intervention best reduces the risk for dehydration?
items.a: Offer beverages and snacks frequently and include favorite drinks
items.ex: Frequent beverages and snacks, favorite foods and drinks, and getting out of bed reduce dehydration and malnutrition risk.
w: Wait for the patient to ask for fluids
A reduced thirst response means older adults may not ask for fluids.
Place the water pitcher on the windowsill to keep it cool
Being unable to reach beverages increases dehydration risk.
Keep the patient in bed to conserve energy
Getting the patient out of bed is a recommended intervention.

alt.q: Why are hospitalized older adults at greater risk for dehydration and malnutrition?
alt.a: Food and fluids are often limited before diagnostic tests
alt.ex: Limiting food and fluids before tests, medications that reduce appetite, and inability to reach drinks increase risk.
w: Hospital meals contain too many calories
Calorie content is not a listed reason for the increased risk.
Older adults have an increased thirst response
Older adults have a reduced, not increased, thirst response.
Hospital beverages are always available at the bedside
Inability to reach beverages increases the risk.

VAP
