alt.q: Which abbreviation stands for “Ventilator-associated pneumonia”?
alt.a: VAP
alt.ex: CLABSI, CAUTI, surgical site infection, and VAP are the most common HAIs in hospitalized patients.
w: HAI
HAI: Health care–associated infection.
CLABSI
CLABSI: Central line–associated bloodstream infection.
CAUTI
CAUTI: Catheter-associated urinary tract infection.

mt.q: Match each health care–associated infection abbreviation with its meaning.
mt.ex: CLABSI, CAUTI, surgical site infection, and VAP are the most common HAIs in hospitalized patients.

items.q: What is the leading measure for preventing health care–associated infections in hospitalized older adults?
items.a: Hand hygiene combined with proper isolation procedures
items.ex: Hand hygiene with proper isolation policies is the leading measure to prevent and control infection transmission.
w: Routine prophylactic antibiotics for all older patients
Routine antibiotics are not the leading preventive measure named.
Keeping older patients on strict bed rest
Bed rest adds risks such as delirium and pressure injury.
Inserting urinary catheters to keep skin dry
Indwelling catheters create infection risk and should be avoided.

alt.q: A nurse wants to reduce the spread of infection among older patients on a medical unit. Which action is the leading preventive measure?
alt.a: Performing hand hygiene and following isolation procedures
alt.ex: Hand hygiene combined with proper isolation policy is the leading measure to prevent HAIs.
w: Giving all older patients prophylactic antibiotics
Routine antibiotics are not the leading preventive measure named.
Keeping older patients on bed rest in their rooms
Bed rest adds risks such as delirium and pressure injuries.
Inserting urinary catheters to keep patients dry
Indwelling catheters create CAUTI risk and should be avoided.

items.q: Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter is an appropriate way to manage transient incontinence in a hospitalized older adult.
items.a: False
items.ex: Indwelling catheterization should be avoided; plan voiding opportunities and improve access to the toilet instead.
items.ww: Catheters add infection risk such as CAUTI, so individualized voiding plans are preferred.

alt.q: When a hospitalized older adult develops transient incontinence, the nurse should avoid indwelling urinary catheterization.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Planned voiding opportunities and easier toilet access are preferred over indwelling catheters.
alt.ww: Using a catheter for convenience increases infection risk and is not recommended.

items.q: A hospitalized 83-year-old who needs help walking has new episodes of urinary incontinence. Which intervention should the nurse implement?
items.a: Plan regular voiding opportunities and improve access to the toilet
items.ex: Individualized interventions include planned voiding opportunities and modifying the environment for toilet access.
w: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter
Indwelling urinary catheterization should be avoided.
Restrict fluids to reduce urine output
Fluid restriction raises dehydration risk, which is already high in older adults.
Apply incontinence briefs and change them once per shift
Briefs do not address the cause, and infrequent changes harm skin.

alt.q: Which factor can cause transient urinary incontinence in a hospitalized older adult?
alt.a: Needing assistance to get to the bathroom
alt.ex: Delirium, untreated UTIs, medications, restricted mobility, and needing help to reach the bathroom cause incontinence.
w: Increased bladder capacity with aging
Aging decreases, not increases, bladder capacity.
Use of a bedside commode within reach
Easy toilet access helps prevent incontinence.
Treatment of a urinary tract infection
Untreated, not treated, UTIs cause incontinence.

items.q: Which measures are key to preventing skin breakdown in hospitalized older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Frequent repositioning
Frequent repositioning is a key prevention measure.
Reducing shear and friction during positioning
Reducing shear and friction protects fragile aging skin.
Providing nutritional support
Nutritional support is a key point in preventing skin breakdown.
Keeping the patient on bed rest
Immobility increases the risk for pressure injuries.
Allowing moisture to remain on the skin
Meticulous skin care and moisture management are needed.
items.ex: Key points are an appropriate mattress, proper and frequent repositioning, reducing shear and friction, skin and moisture care, and nutrition.

alt.q: Which factors in the acute care setting increase an older adult’s risk for pressure injuries? Select all that apply.
o: Immobility
Immobility is a listed acute care factor for skin breakdown.
Incontinence
Incontinence increases moisture and skin breakdown risk.
Malnutrition
Malnutrition is a listed factor for pressure injury.
Frequent repositioning
Frequent repositioning prevents, not causes, pressure injuries.
Use of a pressure-appropriate mattress
An appropriate mattress helps prevent skin breakdown.
alt.ex: Correct: Immobility; Incontinence; Malnutrition.

items.q: How do diuretics increase the risk for falls in hospitalized older adults?
items.a: They increase the number of attempts to get out of bed to void
items.ex: Increased urine output from diuretics leads to more trips out of bed to void, increasing fall risk.
w: They sedate the patient, causing drowsiness and unsteadiness
Sedation is the fall mechanism of sedatives and hypnotics, not of diuretics.
They impair vision so tripping hazards are hard to see
Impaired vision is a separate fall risk, not the diuretic mechanism.
They require equipment that becomes an obstacle to walking
Equipment is a separate hazard; the diuretic risk is more trips to void.

alt.q: A hospitalized older adult started on a diuretic is now at increased risk for falls. What is the reason?
alt.a: More frequent attempts to get out of bed to void
alt.ex: The increased urine output from diuretics leads to more attempts to get out of bed, raising fall risk.
w: The diuretic sedates the patient, causing unsteadiness
Sedation is the fall mechanism of sedatives and hypnotics, not of diuretics.
The diuretic impairs vision so hazards are hard to see
Impaired vision is a separate fall risk, not the diuretic mechanism.
The diuretic raises blood pressure on standing
Orthostatic changes lower, not raise, blood pressure on rising.

items.q: Medications that cause [[orthostatic hypotension]] increase the risk for falls because blood pressure drops when an older adult gets out of a bed or chair.
items.ex: A drop in blood pressure on rising can cause dizziness and unsteadiness, leading to falls.

alt.q: When an older adult stands up and blood pressure falls, the condition is [[orthostatic hypotension|postural hypotension]], a medication effect that raises fall risk.
alt.ex: A drop in blood pressure on rising can cause dizziness and unsteadiness, leading to falls.

items.q: Physical restraints are a safe way to prevent falls in confused, hospitalized older adults.
items.a: False
items.ex: A safe environment for older adults is restraint-free, and every effort must be made to avoid physical restraints.
items.ww: Restraints increase disorientation and are not considered safe fall prevention.

alt.q: A safe environment for hospitalized older adults is a restraint-free environment.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The chapter states that every effort must be made to avoid physical restraints.
alt.ww: Restraints add harm, such as increased disorientation, rather than safety.

items.q: Ongoing care that continues recovery from acute illness or surgery and supports chronic conditions affecting daily functioning is called [[restorative care|restorative]].
items.ex: Restorative care has two types and takes place in homes, rehabilitation facilities, and nursing centers.

alt.q: Care that helps an older adult regain prior independence in ADLs after surgery is part of [[restorative care|restorative]].
alt.ex: Restorative care has two types and takes place in homes, rehabilitation facilities, and nursing centers.

items.q: Which statement describes the two types of restorative care?
items.a: Continued recovery from acute illness or surgery and support of chronic conditions
items.ex: Restorative care continues recovery begun in acute care and supports chronic conditions affecting daily functioning.
w: Emergency treatment of injuries and stabilization in intensive care
These are acute care services, not restorative care.
Comfort care at end of life and support during bereavement
These describe end-of-life and grief care, not restorative care.
Diagnostic testing and surgical intervention for new illness
These are acute care activities, not restorative care.

alt.q: What is the aim of restorative care during convalescence from acute illness or surgery?
alt.a: Regaining or improving the prior level of independence in ADLs
alt.ex: Interventions during convalescence aim to regain or improve the patient’s prior independence in ADLs.
w: Replacing the patient’s ADLs with full staff assistance
The goal is independence, not dependence on staff.
Preparing the patient for permanent nursing center placement
The goal is restoring prior function, not planning permanent placement.
Stopping all interventions begun in the acute care setting
Acute care interventions continue and are later modified.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to transfer an older adult from the hospital to home health care. Which information is most important to include in the discharge information?
items.a: Ongoing interventions such as exercise routines and wound care
items.ex: Discharge information should include required ongoing interventions so restorative care continues without interruption.
w: The names of the patient’s hospital roommates
Roommate names do not support continuing care.
A list of the hospital’s visiting hours
Visiting hours are not needed to continue restorative care at home.
The patient’s room number during the hospital stay
Room number does not guide ongoing care at home.

alt.q: Why should acute care discharge information include medication schedules and blood glucose monitoring routines?
alt.a: So interventions begun in acute care can continue in restorative care
alt.ex: Restorative care continues acute care interventions and modifies them as convalescence progresses.
w: So the patient can stop all acute care interventions at home
Interventions continue, then are modified as recovery progresses.
So home care nurses can repeat the full admission assessment
The purpose is continuity of care, not repeating admission.
So the patient can be readmitted quickly if needed
The purpose is continuing care, not planning readmission.

items.q: When restorative care addresses an older adult’s chronic conditions, what are the goals of care?
items.a: Stabilizing the condition and maximizing independence in ADLs
items.ex: For chronic conditions, restorative care aims to stabilize the condition and maximize independence in ADLs.
w: Curing the condition and stopping all medications
Chronic conditions are stabilized rather than cured.
Transferring all ADLs to family caregivers
The goal is to maximize the older adult’s own independence.
Limiting activity to prevent any possible risk
Older adults need to perform ADLs with an acceptable level of risk.

alt.q: A nurse plans restorative care for an older adult with chronic arthritis. Which outcome best reflects its goals?
alt.a: The patient dresses independently while the arthritis remains stable
alt.ex: Restorative care for chronic conditions stabilizes the condition and maximizes independence in ADLs.
w: The patient’s arthritis is permanently cured
Restorative care stabilizes rather than cures chronic conditions.
The family completes all of the patient’s ADLs
Maximizing the patient’s own independence is the goal.
The patient remains in bed to avoid joint strain
Limiting activity reduces independence rather than maximizing it.

items.q: An older adult with dementia is physically strong but cannot safely complete ADLs. Which ability does the patient most likely lack?
items.a: The ability to recognize, judge, and remember
items.ex: Cognitive ability to perform ADLs requires recognizing, judging, and remembering; dementia interferes despite physical capability.
w: Adequate strength and flexibility
Strength and flexibility are physical abilities this patient still has.
Adequate balance and coordination
Balance is a physical ability, which the patient still has.
Normal hearing and visual acuity
Sensory deficits are accommodated separately; the problem described is cognitive.

alt.q: What does the physical ability to perform ADLs require?
alt.a: Strength, flexibility, and balance
alt.ex: The physical ability to perform ADLs requires strength, flexibility, and balance.
w: Recognition, judgment, and memory
These describe the cognitive ability needed for ADLs.
Motivation, insight, and education
These are not the physical requirements listed for ADLs.
Vision, hearing, and touch
Sensory impairments are accommodated, but they are not the listed physical requirements.

items.q: An older adult recovering from a stroke struggles to dress and bathe independently. Which team member should the nurse collaborate with to select the correct assistive devices?
items.a: Occupational therapist
items.ex: Occupational therapists are trained in selecting the correct type of assistive devices and helping patients adapt.
w: Registered dietitian
Dietitians plan nutrition interventions, not assistive devices for ADLs.
Respiratory therapist
Respiratory therapists focus on breathing, not ADL assistive devices.
Pharmacist
Pharmacists review medications, not assistive devices.

alt.q: An older adult living alone can no longer manage shopping and paying bills. Which action is appropriate?
alt.a: Consult an occupational therapist and consider family help with IADLs
alt.ex: Occupational therapists help people adapt to IADL difficulties, and family caregivers may assume more IADL responsibility.
w: Recommend immediate nursing center placement
Older adults can stay at home with outside help or a support network.
Tell the patient to stop shopping and paying bills
Support for IADLs is needed, not abandoning these tasks.
Refer the patient to a respiratory therapist
Respiratory therapy does not address difficulty with IADLs.

items.q: When an older adult’s cognitive status prevents participation in health care decisions, the nurse should include family caregivers in planning care.
items.a: True
items.ex: Family and friends knew the older adult before the impairment and can explain behaviors and suggest management methods.
items.ww: Excluding family loses a rich source of data when the patient cannot take part.

alt.q: Family caregivers are a poor source of data about an older adult with cognitive impairment because they cannot be objective.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Family and friends are rich sources of data because they knew the older adult before the impairment.
alt.ww: The chapter describes family as rich sources of data, not poor ones.

items.q: Which definition of clinical judgment does the textbook present?
items.a: A conclusion about a patient’s needs or health problems that leads to taking or avoiding action
items.ex: Clinical judgment is a conclusion about patient needs that leads to taking or avoiding action, or using, modifying, or creating approaches.
w: A standard set of steps applied in the same way to every patient’s problem
Clinical judgment can mean modifying standard approaches or creating new ones based on the patient’s response.
A medical diagnosis the nurse makes after reviewing laboratory test results
Nurses do not make medical diagnoses; clinical judgment concerns the patient’s needs and health problems.
A routine task that assistive personnel perform under a nurse’s direction
Assistive personnel perform basic care; they lack the knowledge to make clinical judgments.

alt.q: How does the NCSBN describe the relationship between clinical judgment and critical thinking?
alt.a: Clinical judgment is the observed outcome of critical thinking and decision making.
alt.ex: The NCSBN defines clinical judgment as the observed outcome of critical thinking and decision making.
w: Clinical judgment is a step that must be finished before critical thinking begins.
Clinical judgments arise from critical thinking, so critical thinking comes first, not after.
Clinical judgment replaces critical thinking once a nurse gains experience.
Experienced nurses still think critically; their judgments grow out of that thinking.
Clinical judgment and critical thinking are unrelated processes used in different settings.
The two are closely linked; clinical judgment is the outcome of critical thinking.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: According to the textbook, what begins the process of clinical judgment and clinical decision making?
items.a: The patient’s health care needs
items.ex: A patient’s health care needs begin the process of clinical judgment and clinical decision making.
w: The health care provider’s written orders
Orders guide some care, but the process of clinical judgment starts with the patient’s needs.
The policies of the health care agency
Agency policies may serve as decision criteria, but they do not start the judgment process.
The nurse’s list of assigned tasks
Task lists are not the starting point; judgment begins with what the patient needs.

alt.q: In the clinical judgment model for nursing, what ultimately drives the clinical decisions a nurse makes?
alt.a: The needs of the individual patient
alt.ex: The model links critical thinking, the nursing process, and clinical judgment to decisions that respond to patient needs.
w: The routines of the nursing unit
Unit routines do not drive decisions; each patient poses a unique situation.
The preferences of the charge nurse
The model centers on the patient’s needs, not a colleague’s preferences.
The order in which patients were admitted
Admission order is not a decision criterion; patient needs and condition are.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: An RN is working with assistive personnel (AP) on a busy unit. A patient’s blood pressure has started to fall and the patient is becoming less alert. Which activity must the RN perform rather than delegate?
items.a: Analyzing why the patient’s condition is changing and choosing the actions needed
items.ex: Only the RN analyzes changes in a patient’s condition and decides which strategies are required.
w: Helping a stable patient walk down the hallway
Ambulating a stable patient is a basic aspect of care that can be delegated to AP.
Collecting a routine urine specimen from another patient
Specimen collection is a basic task the textbook describes delegating to AP.
Helping reposition a patient to make the patient more comfortable
Assisting with positioning is basic care; in the case study the nurse obtained AP help with it.

alt.q: Why does the RN, rather than assistive personnel (AP), make clinical decisions when a patient’s condition changes?
alt.a: AP lack the knowledge and experience to analyze why or when a patient’s condition changes.
alt.ex: AP perform basic aspects of care but do not have the knowledge to analyze changes or select strategies.
w: AP are not permitted to provide any direct care to patients.
AP do provide direct care; nurses direct them to perform basic aspects of care.
AP spend less time with patients than nurses do.
Time with patients is not the reason; the difference is knowledge and the ability to analyze.
AP are not allowed to speak with patients’ family members.
Communication rules are not the reason; AP lack the knowledge to analyze clinical changes.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: A nursing student asks, “What really separates a professional nurse from assistive personnel?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “The RN makes clinical decisions by analyzing changes in a patient and choosing what to do.”
items.ex: Clinical decision making separates professional nurses from technicians and AP.
w: “The RN performs hygiene and comfort measures for every assigned patient.”
Hygiene and comfort care are basic aspects of care that AP can perform.
“The RN measures vital signs more often than AP do during a shift.”
Measuring data is not what separates roles; analyzing the data and deciding is.
“The RN follows the unit’s routine task list more closely than AP do.”
Following routines is not clinical decision making, which requires analysis and judgment.

alt.q: A new graduate nurse describes the RN’s role in caring for a deteriorating patient. Which statement shows understanding of clinical decision making?
alt.a: “I observe for changes, analyze the data, identify problems, plan, and act right away if the patient worsens.”
alt.ex: An RN observes, collects and analyzes data, identifies problems, plans strategies, and takes immediate action when a condition worsens.
w: “I record the vital signs and wait for the health care provider to interpret them.”
The RN analyzes data and acts; waiting for someone else to interpret delays needed action.
“I ask the AP to decide whether the patient’s change in condition is important.”
AP lack the knowledge to analyze why or when a patient’s condition changes.
“I follow the standard care plan exactly, whatever the patient’s response.”
Clinical judgment may require modifying standard approaches based on the patient’s response.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: Research on clinical judgment shows that a nurse’s clinical judgments are influenced most by what?
items.a: The nurse’s own experience and knowledge
items.ex: Clinical judgments are influenced more by a nurse’s experience and knowledge than by the objective data at hand.
w: The objective data about the situation at hand
Research found objective data influence judgments less than the nurse’s experience and knowledge.
The written policies of the health care agency
Policies may guide decisions, but research points to experience and knowledge as the stronger influence.
The preferences of the patient’s family members
Family input is considered, but it is not identified as the main influence on judgments.

alt.q: Why can an experienced nurse often interpret a patient’s data more quickly and confidently than a new nurse?
alt.a: Years of practice help the nurse recognize patterns in the data.
alt.ex: Years of experience, especially in specialized fields, lead to recognizing patterns of data and interpreting them quickly.
w: Experienced nurses rely only on objective data and ignore context.
Clinical judgments are shaped by context and experience, not objective data alone.
Experienced nurses are allowed to make medical diagnoses.
Nurses do not make medical diagnoses, regardless of experience.
Experienced nurses apply one standard plan to all patients.
Each patient’s problems are unique; experience helps tailor care, not standardize it.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: A nurse new to a medical unit wants to strengthen the clinical judgments the nurse makes about patients. Which approach best supports this goal?
items.a: Learn each patient’s typical pattern of responses and engage patients about their concerns.
items.ex: Sound clinical judgment partly relies on knowing patients, their typical responses, and engaging with them about their concerns.
w: Rely on objective data alone and keep conversations with patients brief.
Objective data influence judgment less than knowing patients and engaging with them about concerns.
Apply the same plan of care to every patient with the same diagnosis.
Each patient’s problems are unique, so standardized plans do not build sound judgment.
Focus on finishing assigned tasks quickly so patients are not disturbed.
Task focus does not build knowledge of patients’ patterns of responses.

alt.q: Which practice helps a nurse build the ability to recognize patterns of health care problems over time?
alt.a: Practicing in one setting over time and forming therapeutic relationships with patients and families
alt.ex: Observations made over time in a setting and therapeutic relationships with patients and families build pattern recognition.
w: Rotating to a different unit every shift to see as many diagnoses as possible
Practicing in a particular setting over time, not constant rotation, builds pattern recognition.
Limiting contact with families so the focus stays on the patient’s physical data
Relationships with patients and families help build the ability to recognize patterns.
Memorizing textbook solutions for the most common patient problems
Most patients’ problems have no clear textbook solutions.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: A nurse meets a newly admitted patient whose needs are not yet clear. Which approach reflects the textbook’s guidance?
items.a: Question, wonder, and explore different perspectives and interpretations to find a solution.
items.ex: Most patients’ problems have no clear textbook solutions, so the nurse questions and explores perspectives to find what benefits the patient.
w: Apply the standard textbook solution for the patient’s medical diagnosis.
Most patients have problems for which there are no clear textbook solutions.
Wait until the health care provider explains what the patient needs.
The nurse actively explores interpretations rather than waiting to be told the patient’s needs.
Assume the patient’s needs match those of the last patient with this diagnosis.
Each patient’s health problems are unique, so assumptions from other patients can mislead.

alt.q: Why will a nurse often not have a clear picture of a patient’s needs when first meeting the patient?
alt.a: Each patient’s problems are unique and shaped by health, lifestyle, culture, relationships, and environment.
alt.ex: A patient’s problems are a product of physical health, lifestyle, culture, relationships, living environment, and experiences.
w: Patients rarely share any useful information during a first meeting.
Some patients withhold information, but the main reason given is that each patient’s problems are unique.
Nurses are not expected to assess patients until a diagnosis is confirmed.
Nurses assess from the first contact; the challenge is the uniqueness of each patient.
Patients with the same diagnosis have the same needs, which take time to look up.
Patients with the same diagnosis do not share identical problems; each is unique.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: A student worries about having to use every part of the clinical judgment model with each patient. Which response by the clinical instructor is best?
items.a: “You won’t apply every element each time; the model holds what you need to make the right decisions.”
items.ex: The model is not meant to be applied element by element to each patient, but it contains what is needed for sound decisions.
w: “Yes, every element must be applied to each patient in the same order.”
The textbook states the model is not offered for applying every element to each situation.
“The model is only for patients with complex, unstable conditions.”
The model contains elements for making the right decisions in every type of patient situation.
“The model is only for students; experienced nurses no longer use it.”
Experienced nurses apply the model spontaneously, purposefully, and effectively.

alt.q: Which statement about the clinical judgment model for nursing is accurate?
alt.a: Each patient poses a unique situation for applying the model.
alt.ex: The model applies in every type of patient situation, and each patient presents a unique situation for using it.
w: The model requires every element to be used for every patient.
The model is not offered for applying every element or component to each patient situation.
The model applies only to patients with respiratory problems.
Respiratory examples illustrate the model, which applies to every type of patient situation.
The model is a fixed protocol that replaces nursing judgment.
The model explains how critical thinking, clinical judgment, and decision making interrelate.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient who has respiratory problems because of fractured ribs. Applying the clinical judgment model, which focus is most appropriate?
items.a: Examine chest excursion and consider pain-relief approaches.
items.ex: For fractured ribs, the nurse applies knowledge of ventilation and fracture pain, examines chest excursion, and considers pain relief.
w: Use the same plan of care as for a patient with pneumonia.
Each patient poses a unique situation; the cause of the respiratory problem changes the focus.
Focus on oxygen delivery and leave pain assessment until later.
Pain from fractures affects ventilation, so pain-relief approaches are part of the focus.
Skip the patient interview because the cause of the problem is known.
Interview data are reviewed to offer person-centered care for pain relief.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a patient who has respiratory problems because of pneumonia. Applying the clinical judgment model, which focus is most appropriate?
alt.a: Listen to lung sounds and reflect on criteria for airway suctioning.
alt.ex: For pneumonia, the nurse applies knowledge of oxygenation and the disease, listens to lung sounds, and considers suctioning criteria.
w: Use the same plan of care as for a patient with fractured ribs.
The cause of the respiratory problem changes how the nurse applies the model.
Focus mainly on chest excursion and pain from rib fractures.
Chest excursion and fracture pain are the focus for fractured ribs, not pneumonia.
Skip the interview because anxiety does not affect breathing.
Interview data help the nurse ease anxiety related to shortness of breath.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: What does clinical decision making require a nurse to do?
items.a: Investigate and analyze all aspects of a problem, then apply scientific and nursing knowledge to choose the best action.
items.ex: Clinical decision making uses judgment to analyze all aspects of a problem and knowledge to choose the best course of action.
w: Choose the first workable solution so care is not delayed while analyzing the problem.
Clinical decision making requires analyzing all aspects of a problem before choosing an action.
Carry out the health care provider’s orders without analyzing the patient’s response.
The nurse analyzes the problem and patient response; decisions are not just order following.
Rely mainly on a feeling about the patient rather than on knowledge and data.
Decisions apply scientific and nursing knowledge, not feelings alone.

alt.q: A nurse investigates every aspect of a patient’s new problem and applies scientific and nursing knowledge to select the best course of action. What is the nurse doing?
alt.a: Clinical decision making
alt.ex: Using judgment to analyze a clinical problem and applying knowledge to choose the best action is clinical decision making.
w: Delegating
Delegating assigns tasks to AP; it is not the analysis and choice of a course of action.
Documenting
Documenting records care; it does not analyze a problem to choose an action.
Intuitive guessing
The nurse is reasoning with knowledge, not relying on an inner sense.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: Which sources does a nurse draw on when forming clinical judgments? Select all that apply.
o: Theoretical education and knowledge
The nurse’s knowledge base includes theoretical education and knowledge.
Clinical experience
Clinical experience is part of the knowledge base a nurse draws on.
Information from the interprofessional team
The nurse considers information from the interprofessional team.
The ability to reflect
The nurse uses the ability to reflect in forming clinical judgment.
The AP’s analysis of why a condition changed
AP lack the knowledge to analyze why or when a patient’s condition changes.
Personal opinions about a patient’s lifestyle
Personal opinions are not a source of evidence for clinical judgment.
items.ex: Clinical judgment draws on knowledge, clinical experience, reflection, and interprofessional team information.

alt.q: A nurse describes how the nurse reasons through a patient’s new problem. Which statements show appropriate use of available information? Select all that apply.
o: “I use what I learned in my nursing courses.”
Theoretical education is part of the knowledge base for clinical judgment.
“I think back on similar patients I have cared for.”
Clinical experience and reflection inform clinical judgment.
“I consider what the respiratory therapist reported.”
Information from the interprofessional team is part of clinical judgment.
“I let the AP decide if the change is significant.”
AP do not have the knowledge to analyze changes in a patient’s condition.
“I ignore data that don’t fit my first impression.”
Clinical reasoning uses all available information and evidence.
alt.ex: Correct: “I use what I learned in my nursing courses.”; “I think back on similar patients I have cared for.”; “I consider what the respiratory therapist reported.”

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: Which statements reflect research themes about clinical judgment? Select all that apply.
o: Clinical judgments are influenced by the context of the situation and the culture of the setting.
Research identified context and culture of care settings as influences.
Sound clinical judgment partly relies on knowing patients.
Knowing patients’ typical responses and engaging with them supports sound judgment.
Nurses use more than one reasoning approach at the same time.
Nurses combine approaches such as problem solving and reflection.
Most patients’ problems have clear textbook solutions.
Most patients have problems for which there are no clear textbook solutions.
Objective data influence judgment more than the nurse’s experience.
Experience and knowledge influence judgment more than objective data.
items.ex: Research shows judgment is shaped by context, knowing patients, combined reasoning, and experience, and that textbook answers are rare.

alt.q: A nurse educator corrects misconceptions about clinical judgment. Which statements should the educator identify as inaccurate? Select all that apply.
o: “Clinical judgment depends mainly on objective data, not experience.”
This is inaccurate; experience and knowledge influence judgment more than objective data.
“Most patient problems can be solved with a textbook answer.”
This is inaccurate; most patients’ problems have no clear textbook solutions.
“The culture of a care setting has no effect on judgment.”
This is inaccurate; the culture of the setting influences clinical judgment.
“Knowing a patient’s typical responses supports sound judgment.”
This is accurate; sound judgment partly relies on knowing patients.
“Nurses can combine problem solving and reflection at once.”
This is accurate; nurses use several reasoning approaches at the same time.
alt.ex: Correct: “Clinical judgment depends mainly on objective data, not experience.”; “Most patient problems can be solved with a textbook answer.”; “The culture of a care setting has no effect on judgment.”

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: In the clinical judgment model for nursing, which factors are listed under the environment component of critical thinking competence? Select all that apply.
o: Time pressure
Time pressure is an environmental factor in the model.
Interruptions
Interruptions are an environmental factor in the model.
Task complexity
Task complexity is an environmental factor in the model.
Setting
The care setting is an environmental factor in the model.
Skill competence
Skill competence belongs to the experience component.

sections.name: Critical thinking and the nursing process

items.q: How does the textbook define critical thinking?
items.a: The ability to think in a systematic and logical manner with openness to question and reflect on the reasoning process
items.ex: Critical thinking is systematic, logical thinking that stays open to questioning and reflecting on one’s reasoning.
w: The ability to reach a quick decision by relying on an inner sense without reasoning
That describes intuition, which is understanding something immediately without conscious reasoning.
The process of following a health care provider’s orders exactly as they are written
Following orders is not critical thinking, which questions and reflects on reasoning.
The skill of memorizing standard care plans for the most common medical diagnoses
Memorization is not critical thinking; most patients’ problems have no textbook solution.

alt.q: A nurse thinks through a patient’s problem in an orderly, logical way and stays willing to question and reflect on that reasoning. What is the nurse demonstrating?
alt.a: Critical thinking
alt.ex: Systematic, logical thinking with openness to question and reflect on reasoning is critical thinking.
w: Intuition
Intuition is understanding something immediately, without conscious reasoning.
Delegation
Delegation assigns tasks to others; it is not a way of reasoning.
Documentation
Documentation records care; it is not the reasoning process itself.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: A patient is 1 day after a colon resection. The patient lies supine holding the arms over the abdomen, rates incisional pain as 7 on a 0-to-10 scale, and says, “It hurts too much to move.” The as-needed analgesic, ordered every 4 hours, was last given 5 hours ago. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Administer the ordered as-needed analgesic.
items.ex: Pain is the priority and is limiting mobility; the analgesic is due, so pain relief comes first.
w: Assist the patient to walk in the hallway right away.
Pain reduces mobility, so pain is relieved first to help the patient move.
Notify the health care provider that the analgesic is not working.
The last dose was 5 hours ago and is due again; there is no evidence it failed.
Document the pain rating and reassess it in 1 hour.
Delaying treatment of severe, due-for-relief pain is not appropriate when an analgesic is ordered.

alt.q: A nurse plans care for a postoperative patient who has severe incisional pain and has not turned since the night before. Why does the nurse give pain relief before encouraging mobility?
alt.a: Pain reduces mobility, so relieving it first helps the patient move.
alt.ex: The nurse implements pain relief first so the patient can become more mobile and avoid immobility complications.
w: Mobility is not important until the patient goes home.
Early mobility after surgery matters to prevent complications such as deep vein thrombosis.
Pain medication is safer when the patient is lying still.
The reason given is that pain limits mobility, not medication safety.
Patients cannot be repositioned until pain is completely gone.
The goal is reduced pain to enable mobility, not complete absence of pain.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: When immobility after surgery is prolonged, which complications is a patient susceptible to?
items.a: Deep vein thrombosis and pneumonia
items.ex: Prolonged immobility makes patients susceptible to deep vein thrombosis and pneumonia.
w: Hypertension and hyperglycemia
These are not the immobility complications the textbook names.
Wound dehiscence and hemorrhage
These are not the complications linked to prolonged immobility in the text.
Anemia and hyperkalemia
These are not the complications the textbook links to immobility.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a postoperative patient about turning and walking. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
alt.a: “Staying in bed too long raises my risk for blood clots and pneumonia.”
alt.ex: Prolonged immobility increases the risk of deep vein thrombosis and pneumonia, so early mobility matters.
w: “Staying still helps my incision heal, so I won’t move until the pain is gone.”
Prolonged immobility causes complications; pain is relieved so the patient can move.
“Moving around only matters after I go home from the hospital.”
Early mobility after surgery is important while still in the hospital.
“Bed rest prevents pneumonia because it lets my lungs rest.”
Immobility increases, rather than prevents, the risk of pneumonia.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: What is the aim of critical thinking in nursing?
items.a: To focus on the important issues in a clinical situation so decisions produce desired patient outcomes
items.ex: Critical thinking aims to focus on what is important so the nurse’s decisions lead to desired outcomes.
w: To complete every assigned task in the shortest possible amount of time
Speed is not the aim; focusing on what matters for patient outcomes is.
To make a medical diagnosis for the health care provider to confirm later
Nurses do not make medical diagnoses; critical thinking supports nursing decisions.
To follow a single standard approach for every patient with one diagnosis
Critical thinking looks at each unique patient rather than one standard approach.

alt.q: After relieving a postoperative patient’s pain, the nurse sees that the patient now turns and walks with assistance. What does this outcome show about the nurse’s critical thinking?
alt.a: It focused on the important issues and produced a desired patient outcome.
alt.ex: Reduced pain and improved mobility are desired outcomes produced by focusing on the important issues.
w: It replaced the need to evaluate the patient’s response.
Evaluation of outcomes remains part of the nursing process.
It relied on intuition instead of systematic reasoning.
The nurse used knowledge and systematic reasoning, which is critical thinking.
It made pain relief the automatic priority for all surgery.
Priorities are individualized; no health situation produces automatic priorities.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: How does the American Nurses Association (ANA) describe the nursing process?
items.a: As the framework and essential core of practice nurses use to apply critical thinking

w: As a checklist that replaces critical thinking in routine care
The nursing process is how nurses apply critical thinking, not a substitute for it.
As a research method used only by nurse scientists in studies
That describes the scientific method; the nursing process guides everyday practice.
As a set of tasks that nurses may delegate to assistive personnel
Nursing process decisions require professional knowledge AP do not have.

alt.q: A student asks how the nursing process relates to critical thinking. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “The nursing process is the framework we use to apply critical thinking in practice.”
alt.ex: The ANA calls the nursing process the framework and essential core of practice for applying critical thinking.
w: “The nursing process is used instead of critical thinking.”
The nursing process is how critical thinking is applied, not a replacement for it.
“The nursing process is only used for documentation.”
It guides assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation, not just documentation.
“Critical thinking is only needed after the process ends.”
Critical thinking is applied throughout the nursing process.

Implementation and evaluation
Implementation and evaluation remain separate steps in the five-step process.

alt.q: Which list shows the five-step nursing process used in this textbook?

alt.ex: The textbook folds outcome identification into planning, leaving five steps.
w: Assessment, outcome identification, implementation, evaluation, reflection
Diagnosis and planning are steps; reflection is not listed as a separate step.
Recognize cues, analyze cues, take action, evaluate outcomes, document
These mix NCSBN cognitive skills with documentation; they are not the nursing process steps.
Assessment, diagnosis, delegation, implementation, evaluation
Delegation is not a step; planning is the third step.

items.a: To diagnose and treat human responses to patients’ health problems

w: To make and confirm medical diagnoses for patients
Nurses do not make medical diagnoses; they address human responses.
To carry out health care provider orders efficiently
The process centers on human responses, not simply carrying out orders.
To standardize care for patients with one diagnosis
The process individualizes care to each patient’s responses and outcomes.

alt.q: Which example is a human response that the nursing process is designed to diagnose and treat?

alt.ex: Human responses include patient symptoms and the need for knowledge.
w: The patient’s medical diagnosis of colon cancer
A medical diagnosis is the health problem, not the human response to it.
The surgeon’s choice of surgical procedure
Surgical choices are medical decisions, not human responses.
The pathology report describing the tumor cells
A pathology report is a test result, not the patient’s human response.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: While evaluating care, a nurse compares a patient’s pain rating and pain characteristics with the expected outcomes to judge whether interventions worked. Which critical thinking skill is the nurse using?
items.a: Evaluation
items.ex: Evaluation uses objective criteria such as expected outcomes and pain characteristics to determine results of nursing actions.
w: Interpretation
Interpretation involves orderly data collection and categorizing data, not judging results.
Explanation
Explanation supports findings and conclusions and chooses strategies.
Inference
Inference looks at the meaning of findings and relationships among them.

alt.q: A nurse considers what a patient’s guarding, wincing, and refusal to move mean, whether these findings are related, and whether they show that a problem exists. Which critical thinking skill is the nurse using?
alt.a: Inference
alt.ex: Inference examines the meaning and significance of findings and the relationships among them.
w: Evaluation
Evaluation uses objective criteria to determine the results of nursing actions.
Self-regulation
Self-regulation is reflecting on experiences and improving one’s own performance.
Explanation
Explanation supports findings and conclusions with knowledge and experience.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: After a difficult shift, a nurse reviews how the nurse’s actions connected with patient outcomes and identifies ways to improve the nurse’s own performance. Which critical thinking skill is this?

items.ex: Self-regulation means reflecting on experiences, connecting actions with outcomes, and identifying ways to improve.
w: Analysis
Analysis is open-minded review of patient data for problems, trends, and options.
Interpretation
Interpretation is orderly data collection, pattern finding, and categorizing data.
Inference
Inference looks at the meaning of findings and relationships among them.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a patient’s data with an open mind, avoids careless assumptions, and asks whether other options exist or more data are needed. Which critical thinking skill is the nurse using?
alt.a: Analysis
alt.ex: Analysis means being open-minded, avoiding careless assumptions, and asking about other options and needed data.
w: Self-regulation
Self-regulation is reflecting on one’s own performance and outcomes.
Explanation
Explanation supports findings and conclusions and chooses care strategies.
Evaluation
Evaluation uses objective criteria to determine results of nursing actions.

items.q: A nurse is admitting a patient and wants the assessment to support accurate clinical judgments. Which approach is best?
items.a: Complete a holistic assessment that includes both subjective and objective findings.
items.ex: Forming clinical judgments requires holistic assessments that include objective and subjective findings.
w: Rely on objective findings and set aside the patient’s own report.
Subjective findings, such as the patient’s description of pain, are needed too.
Rely on the patient’s report alone because symptoms are subjective.
Objective findings, such as observed behaviors and records, are also needed.
Limit assessment to the body system named in the medical diagnosis.
A holistic assessment looks at the whole patient, not one system.

alt.q: In the case study, the nurse observes the patient’s posture, asks the patient to describe the pain, and reviews the EHR. What does this show about the nurse’s assessment?
alt.a: It combines subjective and objective data to inform the assessment.
alt.ex: Holistic assessment includes both subjective (patient report) and objective (observation, records) findings.
w: It relies mainly on the EHR rather than the patient.
The nurse used the patient’s report and observation as well as the EHR.
It skips analysis because the problem is already known.
The nurse analyzed and interpreted data before concluding pain was the priority.
It focuses on tasks the AP can complete independently.
Assessment and analysis are the nurse’s role, not tasks for AP.

items.q: After a nurse implements care based on a clinical judgment, what does the nursing process call for next?

Repeat the same interventions for every patient with the same problem.
Each patient is unique; evaluation and reflection guide future decisions.
Hand off evaluation of the outcomes to the assistive personnel.
Evaluating outcomes requires professional judgment that AP do not have.

Ask the AP to decide whether another dose of analgesic is needed.
AP lack the knowledge to analyze the patient’s response to care.
Begin ambulating the patient without checking the patient’s response.

items.q: Which questions reflect critical thinking about a clinical situation? Select all that apply.
o: Why does the patient have this condition?
Critical thinkers ask why the condition exists.
Are there signs and symptoms associated with worsening of the condition?
Watching for signs of worsening is part of critical thinking.
Do I require more information?
Critical thinkers ask whether more information is needed.
What other ways can I collect data to understand the problem?
Seeking other ways to collect data helps understand the problem fully.
Which option will take the least of my time?
Saving time is not one of the critical thinking questions about the patient.
What did the last nurse decide, so I can repeat it?
Critical thinking examines the patient’s situation rather than copying prior decisions.
items.ex: Critical thinkers ask why, what is expected, what signals worsening, what they know, and whether more data are needed.

alt.q: A nurse caring for a patient after surgery is thinking critically. Which questions would the nurse ask? Select all that apply.

“What care options do I have?”
Considering care options is part of critical thinking.
“How can I finish this patient’s care before lunch?”
Time management is not a critical thinking question about the patient.
“Which diagnosis did the patient have last admission?”
Critical thinking focuses on the present situation, not repeating a past label.
alt.ex: Correct: “How does this condition normally affect a patient physically and psychologically?”; “Are these signs and symptoms what I would expect?”; “What care options do I have?”

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: Although decision making follows a sequence of steps, it involves moving back and forth when considering all criteria.
items.a: True
items.ex: Decision making is not strictly linear; the person revisits criteria to reach informed conclusions.
items.ww: The steps provide a sequence, but considering criteria requires going back and forth.

alt.q: Decision making is a strictly linear process in which each step is completed once and never revisited.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Decision making involves moving back and forth among criteria even though the steps follow a sequence.
alt.ww: Revisiting criteria is expected and leads to informed, evidence-based conclusions.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: Intuition is not recommended for beginning nurses because their cognitive level and clinical experience are incomplete.
items.a: True
items.ex: Beginning nurses rely more on analytic reasoning; intuition develops from experience with many patients.
items.ww: Intuition depends on experience that beginning nurses do not yet have.

alt.q: Beginning nurses should rely mainly on intuition because it allows them to act quickly.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Less experienced nurses rely on analytic reasoning; intuition is not recommended for beginners.
alt.ww: Quick action from intuition must be backed by experience and reasoning, which beginners still lack.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: Nurses make medical diagnoses when a patient’s signs and symptoms match those of a disease.
items.a: False
items.ex: Nurses compare signs and symptoms with those of a medical diagnosis but form nursing diagnoses, not medical ones.
items.ww: Making a medical diagnosis is outside the nurse’s role, though nurses monitor closely.

alt.q: Nurses compare a patient’s signs and symptoms with those common to a medical diagnosis.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Comparing findings with a medical diagnosis helps nurses monitor patients and recognize changes.
alt.ww: Nurses do this comparison even though they do not make the medical diagnosis.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: [[Diagnostic reasoning]] precedes clinical judgment and involves knowing when there is enough information to make an accurate diagnosis.
items.ex: Diagnostic reasoning corresponds to the assessment and diagnosis steps of the nursing process.

alt.q: Gathering cues until there is a pattern of data that supports an accurate diagnosis is called [[diagnostic reasoning]].
alt.ex: Diagnostic reasoning corresponds to the assessment and diagnosis steps of the nursing process.

items.q: How does the textbook describe the focus of beginning nursing students?

items.ex: Beginning students focus on skills and organizing activities rather than on each patient’s specific clinical situation.
w: They focus on each patient’s unique clinical context during every skill
Applying skills within each patient’s context develops later; beginners are task oriented.
They readily adapt procedures to meet each patient’s unique needs
Inexperience keeps beginners from anticipating how to individualize procedures.
They make most clinical decisions independently of instructors
Independent decision making is a feature of complex, not basic, critical thinking.

alt.q: A nursing student in a first clinical rotation spends most of the shift worrying about completing assigned skills on time. This behavior reflects which characteristic of beginning students?
alt.a: Being task oriented rather than focused on the patient’s clinical situation
alt.ex: Early in practice, students focus on skills and organization and worry about disrupting the unit.
w: Being committed to decisions and accountable for their results
Commitment is the highest level, not a feature of beginners.
Being creative in generating original solutions to problems
Creativity and original solutions mark complex critical thinking.
Being able to consider a wide array of clinical alternatives
Considering a wide array of alternatives describes the commitment level.

items.ex: Basic thinking is concrete and rule based, following a procedure without individualizing it.
w: Complex
A complex thinker would adapt the procedure to the patient’s needs.
Commitment
Commitment involves choosing among alternatives and accepting accountability, not rigid rule following.
Expert
Expert is not one of the three levels of critical thinking described in the chapter.

alt.a: Basic
alt.ex: At the basic level, a single solution usually resolves each problem and answers are seen as right or wrong.
w: Complex
A complex thinker considers alternative solutions such as repositioning the arm.
Commitment
The commitment level considers a wide array of alternatives before deciding.
Proficient
Proficient is not one of the three levels of critical thinking in Box 15.3.

items.a: Complex

w: Basic

Commitment

Novice
Novice is not one of the three levels of critical thinking in the chapter.

Rigid rule following without adapting reflects basic critical thinking.
Asking the instructor which single correct answer applies to a problem
Trusting experts to have the right answer reflects basic critical thinking.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: A nurse gives pain medication to a postoperative patient with an abdominal incision. Later the patient is restless and short of breath and reports “terrible pain in my chest.” Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Ask whether this pain differs from the pain felt before the medication
items.ex: Rather than assume the pain is incisional, the nurse gathers more data to recognize a possible life-threatening change.
w: Give another dose of the ordered pain medication
Medicating without assessing assumes incisional pain and could miss a pulmonary embolus.
Reposition the patient to take pressure off the incision
Repositioning treats incisional pain without first assessing a new, different symptom.
Document the pain as expected incisional discomfort
Assuming the pain is expected skips assessment of a potentially life-threatening problem.

alt.q: A postoperative patient reports new, sharper chest pain and is short of breath. The nurse finds his heart rate is now 102 and irregular; an hour ago it was 88 and regular. Which action should the nurse take next?
alt.a: Notify the physician of the change in the patient’s condition
alt.ex: New chest pain, dyspnea, and a rising irregular heart rate suggest a life-threatening problem such as pulmonary embolus.
w: Recheck the heart rate in 1 hour to confirm the trend
Delaying a report of a possible pulmonary embolus could result in harm.
Give the next scheduled dose of pain medication early
Medicating masks symptoms of a serious change that requires the physician’s evaluation.
Encourage the patient to walk to relieve his restlessness
Activity could worsen a suspected embolus; the change must be reported.

The book states reflection is not intuitive but purposeful.

Reflecting on what went well is also useful and builds confidence.
It is a formal report submitted after a critical incident
Incident discussion is a separate process; reflection is a personal or shared review.

alt.q: A nurse takes time after a shift to visualize a difficult patient situation and honestly review everything she remembers about it. What is the nurse doing?

w: Developing a concept map
A concept map is a visual diagram of a patient’s problems and interventions.
Holding a safety huddle
A safety huddle is a team meeting after a critical incident.
Writing a care plan
A care plan addresses a patient’s problems, not a review of the nurse’s experience.

items.a: The contradiction between the nurse’s vision of their performance and actual practice

w: The patient’s medical diagnosis and prescribed treatment plan
Medical diagnosis is not the focus; reflection examines the nurse’s own practice.
The staffing patterns and workload of other nurses on the unit
Reflection is focused on one’s own experiences, beliefs, and practice.
The billing codes that apply to each nursing intervention
Billing is unrelated to reflective practice.

alt.q: A nurse who believed she communicated clearly realizes, while reflecting, that her patient misunderstood her teaching. What has reflective practice helped her do?

w: Determine the patient’s medical diagnosis more accurately
Reflection focuses on the nurse’s own practice, not the medical diagnosis.
Avoid all future errors in patient teaching
Reflection supports learning, but it does not guarantee that errors never occur.
Show that the patient was responsible for the misunderstanding
Reflection examines the nurse’s own beliefs, values, and practice honestly.

Keeping entries confidential to protect patient identity is correct.
