items.q: Reflection is an intuitive process that happens automatically, without purposeful effort.
items.a: False
items.ex: Reflection is not intuitive; it is a purposeful act of visualizing and honestly reviewing a situation.
items.ww: The chapter compares reflection to instant replay that requires deliberate time and effort.

alt.q: Reflection involves purposefully visualizing a situation and taking time to honestly review everything you remember about it.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The chapter describes reflection as an instant replay that is purposeful, not intuitive.
alt.ww: Calling reflection automatic or intuitive contradicts the book’s description.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: Reflecting on clinical situations that went well can be just as useful as reflecting on things that went wrong.
items.a: True
items.ex: Reflecting on successes is rewarding and useful for building confidence.
items.ww: The chapter notes that reflections often focus on errors but that successes are equally valuable.

alt.q: Reflective journaling should focus only on clinical situations that went wrong.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Reflecting on things that went well is also rewarding and helps build confidence.
alt.ww: Limiting reflection to errors misses the value of learning from successes.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: The nursing process and the elements of critical thinking are interdependent in making the clinical judgments needed for appropriate decisions.
items.a: True
items.ex: The chapter states that the two processes are interdependent in making clinical judgments.
items.ww: Figure 15.3 shows critical thinking components synthesized with the nursing process, not used separately.

alt.q: Critical thinking and the nursing process are separate processes that nurses use independently of each other.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The two processes are interdependent and are synthesized in making clinical judgments.
alt.ww: The chapter presents them as working together, so treating them as separate is inaccurate.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: A visual, nonlinear representation of a patient’s problems or nursing diagnoses and their related interventions is called a [[concept map|concept mapping]].
items.ex: Concept maps show interrelationships of problems and interventions and support comprehensive care planning.

alt.q: To see how a patient’s multiple nursing diagnoses and interventions connect, a student can draw a nonlinear diagram called a [[concept map|concept mapping]].
alt.ex: Concept maps show interrelationships of problems and interventions and support comprehensive care planning.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: When a nurse is caring for patients, reflective reasoning improves which aspect of clinical judgment?
items.a: The accuracy of diagnostic conclusions
items.ex: Reflecting on the meaning of findings improves diagnostic accuracy and problem solving, strengthening clinical judgment.
w: The speed of documentation
Reflection is about judgment and learning, not documentation speed.
The number of tasks completed
Task completion is not what reflective reasoning improves.
The length of patient interviews
Interview length is not the benefit the chapter links to reflection.

alt.q: A nurse gathers data about a patient, reflects on what the findings mean, and explores their possible meanings. What does the chapter say this process improves?
alt.a: The nurse’s ability to problem solve
alt.ex: Gathering information, reflecting on findings, and exploring their meaning improves problem solving.
w: The nurse’s ability to avoid all errors
Reflection supports learning, but it cannot guarantee that no errors occur.
The nurse’s need to consult colleagues
Reflection complements consultation; it does not change the need for colleagues.
The nurse’s speed in performing skills
Skill speed is not the benefit the chapter links to reflection.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: According to the evidence-based practice box on active learning, which teaching approach was more effective in developing students’ critical thinking than traditional, static case studies?
items.a: Unfolding case studies
items.ex: Unfolding case studies were shown to develop critical thinking more effectively than static case studies.
w: Didactic lectures
Lectures are passive learning; the box compares active learning with didactic lecture.
Memorization drills
Memorizing is passive learning, the opposite of active learning.
Assigned reading
Passive reading is contrasted with active learning activities.

alt.q: A nurse educator wants to promote critical thinking during a post-clinical conference. Which activity is supported by the evidence in Box 15.7?
alt.a: Having students share and analyze actual cases from clinical
alt.ex: Sharing actual cases and examining how critical thinking was applied can improve learning.
w: Having students listen silently to a lecture
Passive listening does not engage students in active learning.
Having students memorize a list of definitions
Memorization is passive learning rather than active engagement.
Having students reread the textbook chapter alone
Passive reading is contrasted with active, collaborative learning.

items.src: Ch 15 · Critical thinking and clinical judgment

items.q: According to the textbook, what determines how extensive a nurse’s assessment of a patient should be?
items.a: The nurse’s judgment, based on the patient’s response, the urgency of the condition, and the time available
items.ex: The extent of assessment is a judgment triggered by presenting signs and symptoms, urgency, and the time available to gather data.
w: The agency’s admission form, which requires the same set of data for every patient
Forms organize data, but the extent of assessment is set by the nurse’s judgment of the situation.
The health care provider’s orders, which specify which body systems the nurse should examine
Nurses use their own critical thinking to decide what and how much to assess.
The patient’s medical diagnosis, which dictates a fixed list of findings to collect
Diagnosis guides questions, but extent depends on the patient’s response, urgency, and time.

alt.q: A nurse decides to perform a brief, focused assessment rather than a full review. Which set of factors should guide this decision?
alt.a: How the patient is responding, how urgent the condition is, and how much time is available
alt.ex: Presenting signs and symptoms, urgency, and available time trigger the nurse’s judgment about assessment extent.
w: The patient’s age, insurance status, and expected length of stay
These do not determine the extent of assessment; the patient’s response and urgency do.
The number of staff on the unit, the shift, and the unit’s routine
Unit routines do not set assessment extent; the patient’s presentation and urgency do.
The order of the sections on the electronic health record form
EHR forms organize data but do not decide how much assessment a situation needs.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient on postoperative day 2 after a colectomy whose priority has been incision pain. The patient suddenly reports shortness of breath and new chest pain. What should become the nurse’s assessment priority?
items.a: Oxygenation and breathing status
items.ex: Assessment is situational; when signs of a possible pulmonary embolus appear, oxygenation becomes the new priority.
w: Character and severity of incision pain
Incision pain remains important, but new breathing problems take priority over the original focus.
Bowel sounds and passage of flatus
Gastrointestinal function matters after colectomy, but airway and breathing come first.
The patient’s coping and family support
Psychosocial assessment follows once the patient’s breathing is stable.

alt.q: Which statement best explains why a nurse changed the focus of assessment when a postoperative patient developed sudden dyspnea?
alt.a: Assessment is situational, so priorities shift as the patient’s condition changes.
alt.ex: Tonya shifted from surgical recovery to oxygenation when cues of a possible pulmonary embolus appeared.
w: Assessment follows a fixed sequence that is completed in the same order each time.
A fixed sequence ignores changing cues; assessment priorities shift with the patient’s condition.
Postoperative pain is never a priority once the first day after surgery has passed.
Pain stayed a priority for Mr. Lawson; oxygenation simply became more urgent.
The nurse must finish the planned assessment before addressing any new symptom.
New urgent cues require an immediate change in focus, not completion of the old plan.

items.q: What is meant by validation of assessment data?
items.a: Comparing data with another source to determine whether the data are accurate
items.ex: Validation compares data with another source, such as the EHR, measurements, or team members, to confirm accuracy.
w: Recording assessment data in the electronic health record within the shift
Documentation records data but does not confirm their accuracy.
Grouping assessment data into patterns to name a nursing diagnosis
Clustering data is part of analysis; validation checks the accuracy of the data first.
Asking the health care provider to sign the completed nursing history
A signature does not verify accuracy; comparison with another source does.

alt.q: A nurse observes that a patient appears short of breath and then counts the respiratory rate and checks the EHR for earlier rates. What is the nurse doing?
alt.a: Validating the inference by comparing it with measurement and another data source
alt.ex: Validation compares data with another source, such as measurement or the EHR, to avoid incorrect inferences.
w: Generating solutions for a problem that has already been confirmed
Solutions come after the problem is identified; the nurse is still checking data accuracy.
Evaluating the outcome of a nursing intervention already in place
No intervention has been given; the nurse is confirming the accuracy of an observation.
Performing a comprehensive nursing history using a theory framework
Checking one observation against other sources is validation, not a full nursing history.

items.q: Which source of assessment data is considered the primary source?
items.a: The patient
items.ex: The patient is the primary source; family, health professionals, and the EHR are secondary sources.
w: The family caregiver
A family caregiver is a secondary source for alert patients who can answer questions.
The electronic health record
The EHR is a secondary source used to compare and validate data.
The hand-off report
Hand-off reports from other caregivers are secondary sources of information.

alt.q: A nurse gathers information about a patient from several places. Which one is a secondary source of data?
alt.a: The patient’s electronic health record
alt.ex: Secondary sources include family, friends, health professionals, and the EHR; the patient is the primary source.
w: The patient’s description of the pain
The patient’s own report comes from the primary source.
The patient’s answers to interview questions
Interview answers given by the patient come from the primary source.
The patient’s report of how he copes with stress
Self-reported coping is information from the primary source, the patient.

items.q: A nurse on a surgical unit is caring for several patients. One patient calls out with sudden, increased incision pain. Which assessment should the nurse perform first?
items.a: A quick screening focused on the character of the incisional pain
items.ex: A periodic problem-focused screening rules out or follows up on a priority problem such as sudden incisional pain.
w: A comprehensive nursing history using functional health patterns
A full history is not appropriate when a sudden priority problem needs a focused screening.
A complete head-to-toe physical examination of all body systems
A full examination delays attention to the priority problem; a focused screening comes first.
A health literacy screening before asking about the pain
Literacy screening is not the priority when the patient reports sudden new pain.

alt.q: What is the main purpose of the quick screenings nurses perform during rounding or while giving care?
alt.a: To rule out or follow up on patient problems
alt.ex: Periodic problem-focused assessments include quick screenings that rule out or follow up on patient problems.
w: To replace the need for a nursing history
Quick screenings supplement, not replace, the patient-centered interview and nursing history.
To collect data for the agency’s quality reports
Screenings during care focus on patient problems, not agency reporting.
To complete a full review of every body system
A full review is a comprehensive examination, not a quick screening.

items.q: For which situation does the textbook describe use of the ABCDE approach?
items.a: Rapid bedside assessment of a patient who is critically ill or quickly deteriorating
items.ex: The ABCDE principle guides rapid bedside assessment of critical physiological functions so nurses can make quick treatment decisions.
w: Routine admission history for a stable patient being admitted for elective surgery
A stable elective admission calls for a patient-centered nursing history, not emergency screening.
Screening a patient’s health literacy before giving discharge teaching materials
Health literacy is screened with tools such as SAHL-S&E or REALM-SF, not ABCDE.
Organizing a long-term care resident’s data for the Minimum Data Set review
Long-term care data follow the Minimum Data Set framework, not the ABCDE approach.

alt.q: An emergency department nurse uses the ABCDE approach with a newly arrived trauma patient. What is the main benefit of this approach?
alt.a: It lets the nurse assess critical physiological functions and make quick treatment decisions.
alt.ex: ABCDE is a quick screening approach for critical functions in emergencies, allowing fast treatment decisions.
w: It gives a holistic picture of the patient’s psychosocial and spiritual needs.
Holistic needs are assessed in a comprehensive nursing history, not in a rapid ABCDE screening.
It identifies all eleven functional health patterns during the first contact.
Functional health patterns organize a comprehensive history, not an emergency screening.
It replaces the need for any later physical examination of the patient.
ABCDE is a rapid screening; more complete assessment follows once the patient is stable.

items.q: A postoperative patient reports nausea. Which physical examination findings should the nurse focus on?
items.a: Bowel sounds and abdominal distention
items.ex: Patient symptoms direct the examination; nausea directs the nurse to assess bowel sounds and abdominal distention.
w: Lung sounds and chest excursion
Lung sounds and chest excursion are the focus for shortness of breath, not nausea.
Pupil size and hand grip strength
These are neurological findings unrelated to the symptom of nausea.
Pedal pulses and skin temperature
Leg pulses and temperature assess circulation and clot risk, not nausea.

alt.q: A patient reports new shortness of breath. Which physical examination findings should the nurse focus on?
alt.a: Lung sounds and chest excursion
alt.ex: Symptoms direct the examination; shortness of breath directs the nurse to lung sounds and chest excursion.
w: Bowel sounds and abdominal distention
Bowel sounds and distention are the focus for nausea, not shortness of breath.
Incision edges and wound drainage
Wound inspection assesses healing, not the cause of shortness of breath.
Joint range of motion and swelling
Joint assessment relates to arthritis, not shortness of breath.

items.q: A nurse knows that major abdominal surgery increases the risk for blood clots in the legs. Which assessment best reflects applying this knowledge?
items.a: Palpating the lower extremity pulses and noting skin temperature of the legs
items.ex: Knowledge of venous thrombosis risk after abdominal surgery leads the nurse to assess leg circulation by palpating pulses and skin temperature.
w: Auscultating bowel sounds and asking whether the patient is passing flatus
Bowel sounds and flatus relate to the colectomy’s effect on GI function, not clot risk.
Asking the patient to rate incision pain on a scale of 0 to 10
Pain rating addresses surgical pain, not circulation in the legs.
Inspecting the suture line for inflammation and drainage
Wound inspection assesses healing, not the risk for venous thrombosis.

alt.q: Why did Tonya assess Mr. Lawson’s bowel sounds and ask whether he was passing flatus after his colectomy?
alt.a: She knew that a colectomy alters gastrointestinal function.
alt.ex: Scientific knowledge of how colectomy affects GI function guided Tonya to assess bowel sounds and flatus.
w: She knew that a colectomy causes clots to form in the legs.
Clot risk led her to assess leg circulation, not bowel sounds.
She suspected the patient had developed a pulmonary embolus.
A suspected pulmonary embolus calls for assessment of breathing and oxygenation.
She was screening for poor health literacy before teaching.
Bowel sounds and flatus assess GI function, not health literacy.

items.q: Why does the textbook favor assessment frameworks developed from nursing theories over many EHR frameworks?
items.a: Nursing theory frameworks are more holistic and person-centered, while EHR frameworks are often medically driven.
items.ex: EHR frameworks are often medically driven; nursing frameworks give a more holistic, person-centered, comprehensive review.
w: Nursing theory frameworks are shorter and require less time to complete than EHR forms.
The advantage is holism and person-centeredness, not speed.
EHR frameworks do not allow nurses to record any subjective data from patients.
EHR forms do capture subjective data; their limitation is a medical focus.
Nursing theory frameworks focus mainly on the patient’s medical diagnosis and treatment.
That describes medically driven frameworks; nursing frameworks are holistic.

alt.q: A nurse wants a nursing history to be more person-centered than the agency’s EHR form allows. What does the textbook recommend?
alt.a: Focus on what is important to the patient.
alt.ex: To make a nursing history more person-centered, the nurse focuses on what matters to the patient.
w: Follow the EHR form strictly in its printed order.
EHR frameworks are often medically driven and less person-centered.
Limit questions to the patient’s admitting diagnosis.
A diagnosis-only focus is medically driven, not person-centered.
Let the family decide which topics to cover first.
Person-centered care focuses on what matters to the patient, not the family’s agenda.

items.q: In a problem-focused approach that begins with a patient’s presenting situation, what does the nurse do after asking follow-up questions to clarify the problem?
items.a: Performs a physical examination focused on the same problem areas to confirm observations
items.ex: After follow-up questions, the nurse examines the same problem areas to confirm observations.
w: Selects nursing interventions before examining the patient
Assessment, including physical examination, comes before choosing interventions.
Completes a full comprehensive nursing history of all patterns
A problem-focused approach stays on the problem areas rather than a full history.
Refers the patient to the health care provider for all examination
Nurses perform their own focused physical examination to confirm observations.

alt.q: A patient reports limited understanding of postoperative recovery and reduced mobility. Which sequence reflects a problem-focused assessment?
alt.a: Ask follow-up questions about these problems, then examine the same areas to confirm observations.
alt.ex: Problem-focused assessment starts with the presenting problem, clarifies it with questions, then confirms it with focused examination.
w: Examine every body system first, then decide which problems to ask the patient about.
A full examination first is comprehensive, not problem-focused.
Teach about recovery immediately, then assess mobility at the next shift.
Assessment must come before teaching or other interventions.
Review the EHR only, then document the problems without examining the patient.
Physical examination is needed to confirm what the patient reports.

items.q: A nurse is completing a problem-focused pain assessment. Which question assesses precipitating factors of the pain?
items.a: “What causes your pain to worsen during the day?”
items.ex: Precipitating factors are what cause the pain to worsen, such as movement or certain activities.
w: “Rate your pain on a scale of 0 to 10.”
A 0-to-10 rating assesses the severity of pain.
“Tell me how the pain is affecting your daily life.”
This explores the nature and impact of pain, not what triggers it.
“Describe your pain to me in your own words.”
Describing the pain assesses its nature, not its precipitating factors.

alt.q: During a problem-focused pain assessment, which physical examination action assesses the severity of pain?
alt.a: Inspect the area of discomfort and palpate it for tenderness.
alt.ex: For severity, the nurse inspects the area of discomfort and palpates for tenderness along with a 0-to-10 rating.
w: Observe for nonverbal cues while the patient walks.
Observing nonverbal signs during activity assesses precipitating factors.
Observe for grimacing or crying while the patient rests.
Nonverbal cues at rest are used to assess the nature of the pain.
Ask the patient what makes the pain worse during the day.
This is an interview question about precipitating factors, not an examination action.

items.q: A nurse is reviewing environmental factors in the critical thinking model that can affect assessment. Which factors are included? Select all that apply.
o: Time pressure
Time pressure is an environmental factor that limits how much data can be gathered.
Interruptions
Interruptions are an environmental factor that affects assessment.
Task complexity
Task complexity is listed under environment in the critical thinking model.
Setting
The care setting is an environmental factor in the model.
Perseverance
Perseverance is a critical thinking attitude, not an environmental factor.
Skill competence
Skill competence belongs to the experience component, not the environment.
items.ex: The environment component includes time pressure, setting, task complexity, and interruptions.

alt.q: Which items are critical thinking attitudes that support assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Curiosity
Curiosity is a critical thinking attitude listed in the model.
Discipline
Discipline is a critical thinking attitude that keeps assessment systematic.
Responsibility
Responsibility is a critical thinking attitude in the model.
Interruptions
Interruptions are an environmental factor, not an attitude.
Agency policies
Agency policies and procedures are standards, not attitudes.
alt.ex: Correct: Curiosity; Discipline; Responsibility.

items.q: Which of the following are among Gordon’s functional health patterns? Select all that apply.
o: Elimination
Elimination is one of Gordon’s 11 functional health patterns.
Sleep and rest
Sleep and rest is one of Gordon’s 11 patterns.
Coping and stress tolerance
Coping and stress tolerance is one of the patterns Tonya used for Mr. Lawson.
Values and beliefs
Values and beliefs is one of Gordon’s 11 patterns.
Disability and exposure
Disability and exposure are parts of the ABCDE emergency approach, not Gordon’s patterns.
Airway and circulation
Airway and circulation belong to the ABCDE approach, not Gordon’s patterns.
items.ex: Gordon’s 11 patterns include elimination, sleep-rest, coping-stress tolerance, and values-beliefs, among others.

alt.q: A nurse organizes a comprehensive nursing history with Gordon’s functional health patterns. Which categories will the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Nutritional-metabolic
Nutritional-metabolic is one of Gordon’s 11 patterns.
Roles and relationships
Roles and relationships is one of Gordon’s 11 patterns.
Self-perception and self-concept
Self-perception and self-concept is one of Gordon’s 11 patterns.
Breathing and exposure
Breathing and exposure come from the ABCDE emergency approach.
Medical diagnosis and treatment
This is a medically driven category, not a Gordon pattern.
alt.ex: Correct: Nutritional-metabolic; Roles and relationships; Self-perception and self-concept.

items.q: Making an initial inference about assessment data is an error that nurses should avoid.
items.a: False
items.ex: An initial inference is not wrong; problems arise only if the nurse fails to validate it.
items.ww: The book states inferences are acceptable when validated by measurement or questioning the patient.

alt.q: Making an initial inference is acceptable as long as the nurse validates it with measurement or by questioning the patient.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Problems result only when the nurse does not validate an inference with measurement or questioning.
alt.ww: Inferences are a normal part of interpretation; failing to validate them is the actual problem.

items.q: In home and community settings, changes in a patient’s condition are most often subtle and develop over time.
items.a: True
items.ex: Changes are sometimes acute, but most often subtle and gradual, so nurses must notice even small cues.
items.ww: Acute changes occur, but the book says most changes in these settings are subtle.

alt.q: In home and community settings, most changes in a patient’s condition are sudden and acute, so subtle cues can be ignored.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Most changes are subtle and develop over time; nurses must notice cues regardless of how subtle.
alt.ww: Subtle cues must be noticed to prevent harm and detect deterioration early.

items.q: Both the patient-centered interview and periodic assessments can be either comprehensive or problem focused.
items.a: True
items.ex: Each type of assessment is either comprehensive or problem focused and is supplemented by physical examination.
items.ww: Neither type is limited to one scope; the scope depends on the situation.

alt.q: Periodic assessments during ongoing patient contact are always comprehensive reviews of all body systems.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Periodic assessments may be comprehensive or problem focused, such as quick screenings during rounds.
alt.ww: Quick problem-focused screenings during rounding are a common form of periodic assessment.

items.q: Gordon’s model includes [[11|eleven]] functional health patterns, such as elimination, sleep and rest, and values and beliefs.
items.ex: Gordon’s 11 functional health patterns provide categories for a structured, holistic nursing history.

alt.q: A nurse organizing a nursing history with Gordon’s framework assesses [[11|eleven]] functional health patterns.
alt.ex: Gordon’s 11 functional health patterns provide categories for a structured, holistic nursing history.

items.q: [[Validation]] of assessment data is the comparison of data with another source to determine data accuracy.
items.ex: Validation prevents incorrect inferences by checking data against measurement, the EHR, team members, or family.

alt.q: To avoid incorrect inferences, the nurse performs [[validation|validating]] by comparing findings with another source to confirm accuracy.
alt.ex: Validation prevents incorrect inferences by checking data against measurement, the EHR, team members, or family.

items.q: Which finding is an example of subjective data?
items.a: The patient states, “My incision feels sore when I turn.”
items.ex: Subjective data are the patient’s own verbal descriptions, feelings, perceptions, and self-reported symptoms.
w: The nurse measures a blood pressure of 132/84 mm Hg.
A measured blood pressure is objective data based on an accepted standard.
The nurse observes slight separation of the incision.
Inspecting a wound produces objective data the nurse sees.
The nurse notes the patient guards the incision when turning.
An observed behavior is objective data, even though it suggests pain.

alt.q: Which finding is an example of objective data?
alt.a: The nurse observes the patient walking with a shuffling gait.
alt.ex: Objective data come from observation and measurement, including a specifically described observed behavior such as gait.
w: The patient says the dizziness started yesterday.
A patient’s report of symptoms is subjective data.
The patient reports feeling alone and worried.
Feelings described by the patient are subjective data.
The patient describes the pain as sharp and burning.
The patient’s description of pain is subjective data.

items.q: A nurse is assigned four patients. Which patient is likely to be the most reliable source of assessment data?
items.a: A patient who is alert, conscious, and answering questions appropriately
items.ex: Patients who are conscious, alert, and able to answer questions appropriately provide the most accurate information.
w: A patient who is easily distracted and inattentive during questioning
Inattentive or easily distracted patients can be less reliable sources.
A patient who is very anxious and fearful about upcoming surgery
Fear and anxiety can make a patient a less reliable source.
A patient who has a diagnosis of moderate dementia
Patients with dementia can be less reliable sources of information.

alt.q: A nurse is admitting a patient with dementia who cannot answer questions reliably. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Gather information from the family, preferably the identified family caregiver.
alt.ex: When a patient is not a reliable source, the nurse refers to the family, preferably the family caregiver.
w: Skip the nursing history and rely only on the physical examination.
Subjective history is still needed; the family caregiver can supply it.
Record the patient’s answers as given without seeking other sources.
Unreliable answers need another source, preferably the family caregiver.
Wait until the patient’s cognition improves before collecting any data.
Assessment cannot be delayed; family caregivers can provide information now.

items.q: A nurse is assessing a patient with heart failure. Based on the disease pathology, which physical assessment is most appropriate?
items.a: Auscultate lung sounds, assess heart rate and rhythm, and palpate the extremities for edema.
items.ex: Heart failure affects lungs, heart, and peripheral circulation, so the nurse assesses lung sounds, rate and rhythm, and edema.
w: Assess range of motion in affected and unaffected joints for stiffness and swelling.
Range of motion of joints is the focus for arthritis, not heart failure.
Inspect the incision for drainage and palpate the suture line for tenderness.
Incision assessment is for a surgical patient, not the pathology of heart failure.
Auscultate bowel sounds and ask the patient whether they are passing flatus.
Bowel sounds and flatus relate to GI surgery, not heart failure.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing a patient with arthritis. Based on the disease pathology, which physical assessment is most appropriate?
alt.a: Inspect and palpate the joints and assess range of motion of affected and unaffected joints.
alt.ex: Arthritis causes joint pain, stiffness, and swelling, so the nurse inspects, palpates, and checks range of motion of joints.
w: Auscultate lung sounds and palpate the lower extremities for peripheral edema.
Lung sounds and edema are the focus for heart failure.
Measure respiratory rate and depth and assess for trouble breathing lying down.
Breathing assessment relates to heart failure, not arthritis.
Assess only the most painful joint to avoid causing additional discomfort.
Both affected and unaffected joints are assessed for comparison.

items.q: What do health literacy universal precautions assume about patients?
items.a: All patients may have difficulty understanding health information and accessing health services.
items.ex: Universal precautions assume all patients have difficulty, so health information is presented clearly to everyone.
w: Only older patients and those with low income have difficulty understanding health information.
The precautions apply to all patients, not only selected groups.
Patients with a college education understand health information without special approaches.
Universal precautions assume everyone may struggle, regardless of education.
Patients who speak English fluently can be given standard technical explanations.
Fluent speakers can still have limited health literacy; precautions apply to everyone.

alt.q: A nurse explains health information in plain language to every patient, including a physician who is hospitalized. What principle is the nurse applying?
alt.a: Health literacy universal precautions
alt.ex: Universal precautions present information clearly to all patients because anyone may misunderstand health information.
w: Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act
HIPAA protects patient privacy; it does not address clear communication.
Teach-back confirmation of understanding
Teach-back checks understanding but is one action within universal precautions.
Functional health pattern assessment
Functional health patterns organize a nursing history, not communication of information.

items.q: A nurse is choosing printed discharge information for a patient. According to health literacy universal precautions, at what reading level should the material be written?
items.a: At or below a fifth- to sixth-grade reading level
items.ex: Printed educational information should be written at or below a fifth- to sixth-grade reading level.
w: At or below an eighth- to ninth-grade reading level
This level is too high for health literacy universal precautions.
At or below a tenth- to twelfth-grade reading level
A high school level is too difficult for many patients.
At or below a seventh- to eighth-grade reading level
This level is above the recommended fifth- to sixth-grade level.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a patient education pamphlet written at a ninth-grade level. What should the nurse conclude?
alt.a: It should be revised to a fifth- to sixth-grade level or below.
alt.ex: Universal precautions call for printed information at or below a fifth- to sixth-grade reading level.
w: It is acceptable because most adults read at a ninth-grade level.
Precautions assume all patients may struggle, so a lower level is required.
It is acceptable because the patient finished high school.
Universal precautions apply to all patients regardless of education.
It should be revised to a seventh- to eighth-grade level or below.
The target is a fifth- to sixth-grade level or below, which is lower.

items.q: Which description matches the Short Assessment of Health Literacy—Spanish and English (SAHL-S&E)?
items.a: An 18-item test in which the patient reads a term aloud and chooses the closer word in meaning from 2 options
items.ex: The SAHL-S&E has 18 items; the patient reads each term aloud and picks the closer meaning from two options.
w: A 7-item word recognition test that gives a quick estimate of health literacy
This describes the REALM-SF, not the SAHL-S&E.
A 66-item word recognition test used as the full-length literacy instrument
The 66-item tool is the full REALM, not the SAHL-S&E.
A 6-item test designed for patients facing a specific cancer situation
The CHLT-6 is the tool for a specific situation such as cancer.

alt.q: Which description matches the Rapid Estimate of Adult Literacy in Medicine—Short Form (REALM-SF)?
alt.a: A 7-item word recognition test that gives clinicians a valid quick assessment
alt.ex: The REALM-SF has 7 word-recognition items and gives results similar to the 66-item REALM.
w: An 18-item test in which the patient picks the closer word meaning from 2 options
This describes the SAHL-S&E.
A 66-item test that must be completed before any discharge teaching
The 66-item tool is the full REALM, which the short form replaces.
A 6-item test designed for patients facing a specific cancer situation
The CHLT-6 is used for a specific situation such as cancer.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to give a hand-off report to the oncoming nurse. Which approach best supports effective communication?
items.a: Give the report face-to-face in a place free from distraction, focusing on critical information.
items.ex: Determine the critical information to communicate, and use face-to-face interaction in a distraction-free place.
w: Leave a detailed written note at the nurses’ station and leave on time.
Face-to-face interaction is recommended so the receiver can clarify information.
Give the report at the busy nurses’ station so other staff can also hear it.
Hand-offs should occur in a place that is free from distraction.
Share every detail of the shift so that nothing at all is left out.
The nurse determines the critical information rather than every detail.

alt.q: How does The Joint Commission define a hand-off report?
alt.a: A transfer and acceptance of patient care responsibility achieved through effective communication
alt.ex: TJC defines a hand-off as transfer and acceptance of care responsibility through effective real-time communication.
w: A written summary of patient care placed in the health record at discharge
A hand-off is a real-time process between caregivers, not a discharge summary.
A meeting in which the health care provider reviews the treatment plan with the family
A hand-off passes responsibility between caregivers, not to the family.
A report of patient incidents sent to the risk management department
Incident reporting is a different process from a hand-off.

items.q: A patient’s chest x-ray suggests lung congestion. Which nursing action best reflects how diagnostic data direct assessment?
items.a: Auscultate the patient’s lung sounds to determine the extent of congestion.
items.ex: Diagnostic data can direct the nurse to explore further, such as auscultating lungs when an x-ray shows congestion.
w: Record the x-ray result and wait for the health care provider’s interpretation.
The data should prompt the nurse to assess the patient further, not just wait.
Ask the patient to describe any recent changes in appetite or bowel habits.
Bowel and appetite questions do not explore the lung congestion shown on x-ray.
Compare the x-ray result with the patient’s blood glucose log from home.
Home glucose values are unrelated to lung congestion.

alt.q: A nurse notes that a patient’s urine is cloudy. How can diagnostic data help the nurse with this finding?
alt.a: A urine culture can confirm whether infection is present.
alt.ex: Diagnostic data confirm observational findings, such as a culture showing whether cloudy urine reflects infection.
w: A chest x-ray can show whether the bladder is infected.
A chest x-ray examines the lungs, not the urinary tract.
A blood glucose log can explain why urine looks cloudy.
Glucose values do not confirm a urinary infection.
A pain rating can confirm the cause of cloudy urine.
A pain rating is not a diagnostic test for infection.

items.q: A nurse is interviewing an 84-year-old patient who has a hearing deficit. Which nonverbal technique best helps the nurse check whether information is understood?
items.a: Maintain eye contact with the patient while talking.
items.ex: Patient-directed eye gaze lets the speaker check understanding and signals readiness to interact.
w: Speak while facing the computer screen to save time.
Facing a screen blocks visual cues the patient needs.
Stand behind the patient and speak more loudly.
Standing out of view prevents eye contact and visual cues.
Avoid eye contact so the patient does not feel pressured.
Eye contact is recommended to check understanding with hearing deficits.

alt.q: While interviewing an older adult with a visual deficit, the nurse uses affirmative head nodding. What is the purpose of this technique?
alt.a: It regulates the interaction and supports spoken language.
alt.ex: Affirmative head nodding regulates turn-taking, supports spoken language, and allows comments on the interaction.
w: It signals that the nurse is ready to end the interview.
Nodding regulates the interaction; it is not a signal to end.
It tells the patient the nurse disagrees with what was said.
Affirmative nodding supports the interaction rather than signaling disagreement.
It replaces the need for the nurse to ask any questions.
Nodding supports spoken language but does not replace questions.

items.q: A 79-year-old patient says, “My legs ache and I’m tired all the time, but that’s just old age. Nothing can be done.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Tell me more about the aching and tiredness so we can look into it.”
items.ex: Older adults may not report symptoms because they attribute them to age, so the nurse explores the symptoms further.
w: “You’re right, aching and fatigue are expected at your age.”
Attributing symptoms to age may miss a treatable problem.
“Let’s focus instead on the reason for today’s admission.”
Dismissing the symptoms ignores important cues.
“Your family can tell me about this later, so let’s move on.”
The patient is the primary source; the nurse should explore now.

alt.q: Why should a nurse carefully explore vague complaints from an older adult patient?
alt.a: Symptoms in older adults are often muted, vague, or nonspecific.
alt.ex: Compared with younger adults, older adults often have less obvious, vague, or nonspecific symptoms.
w: Older adults usually exaggerate their symptoms.
The concern is that symptoms are muted or underreported, not exaggerated.
Vague complaints are normal changes of aging.
Vague complaints may signal illness and should not be dismissed as aging.
Older adults rarely have more than one problem.
This is not the reason; symptoms are often muted or nonspecific.

items.q: A nurse wants to ask an alert patient’s spouse about the patient’s sleep and medication habits. What should the nurse do first?
items.a: Ask the patient for permission to include the spouse.
items.ex: Patients do not always want family involved, and some agencies require the patient’s oral or written permission.
w: Interview the spouse in the hallway so the patient is not disturbed.
Collecting data from family without the patient’s permission may violate the patient’s wishes.
Ask the health care provider to approve the conversation.
The patient, not the provider, gives permission to involve family.
Interview the spouse because family always has the best information.
For alert patients, the patient is the primary source and family is secondary.

alt.q: Before Tonya updated Mrs. Lawson on her husband’s condition, she first spoke with Mr. Lawson. Why was this an appropriate action?
alt.a: Patients do not always want their families involved, so permission is needed.
alt.ex: Some agencies require patient permission to collect data from family, and some patients or cultures do not want family involved.
w: Family members may share information only with the provider.
Families can share information with nurses when the patient permits.
Family input is useful only when the patient is critically ill.
Family is also an important secondary source for alert patients.
Speaking with the patient first was required to obtain vital signs.
The purpose was to obtain consent to involve the wife, not to measure vital signs.

items.q: Which actions are part of health literacy universal precautions? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid using medical jargon.
Avoiding jargon is a core universal precaution.
Break instructions into small concrete steps.
Small concrete steps help patients understand information.
Limit the focus of a visit to three key points.
Limiting a visit to three key points relevant to the patient is recommended.
Use teach-back to assess understanding.
Teach-back confirms whether the patient understood the instruction.
Write printed material at a ninth-grade level.
Printed material should be at or below a fifth- to sixth-grade level.
Cover as many topics as possible in each visit.
Visits should be limited to three key points, not many topics.
items.ex: Universal precautions include plain language, small steps, three key points, teach-back, and low reading-level print materials.

alt.q: A nurse is applying health literacy universal precautions during a patient assessment. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Ask the patient to explain the instructions back in their own words.
This is teach-back, which assesses understanding.
Focus the visit on three key points relevant to the patient’s problem.
Limiting the focus to three key points is recommended.
Replace clinical terms with everyday words.
Avoiding medical jargon is a universal precaution.
Screen only patients who appear confused.
Screening tools are used with all patients under universal precautions.
Give long detailed explanations all at once.
Information is broken into small concrete steps instead.
alt.ex: Correct: Ask the patient to explain the instructions back in their own words; Focus the visit on three key points relevant to the patient’s problem; Replace clinical terms with everyday words.

items.q: A nurse is assessing an older adult. Which approaches are recommended? Select all that apply.
o: Routinely include a functional assessment of daily self-care ability.
Functional assessment is routinely included for older adults.
Allow pauses and give the patient time to tell their story.
Allowing pauses helps older adults share complete information.
Use short, uncomplicated questions and listen carefully.
Short, simple questions and careful listening are recommended.
Use leading questions to shorten the interview.
Questions should be short but not leading.
Assume physiological age matches chronological age.
Physiological and chronological age may not match.
Attribute vague symptoms to normal aging.
Vague symptoms may signal illness and need further exploration.
items.ex: Older adults need functional assessment, time, simple nonleading questions, and careful listening.

alt.q: Which statements about assessing older adults are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Older adults may need more time if they have hearing or cognitive impairment.
Hearing or cognitive impairment can lengthen assessment.
Changes of aging occur at different rates in different people.
Not all older adults experience the same changes at the same rate.
Family members can fill in gaps in information when appropriate.
Consulting family when appropriate fills information gaps.
Symptoms are usually more dramatic than in younger adults.
Symptoms are often muted, vague, or nonspecific.
All older adults experience the same sensory changes.
Changes vary among older adults.
alt.ex: Correct: Older adults may need more time if they have hearing or cognitive impairment; Changes of aging occur at different rates in different people; Family members can fill in gaps in information when appropriate.

items.q: For which patients are family caregivers or significant others considered primary sources of information? Select all that apply.
o: Infants and young children
Family members are primary sources for infants and children.
Patients who are critically ill
Critically ill patients often cannot provide information, so family is primary.
Patients with intellectual disabilities
Family is a primary source for patients with intellectual disabilities.
Patients with cognitive impairments
Cognitive impairment makes family a primary source.
Alert adults recovering from minor surgery
For alert patients, family is an important secondary source.
Oriented adults with stable chronic illness
Alert, oriented patients are their own primary source.
items.ex: Family is a primary source for children, critically ill patients, and those with intellectual or cognitive impairment.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for an alert, oriented adult. How can family members contribute to the assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Confirm findings the nurse has gathered
Family members can confirm findings as secondary sources.
Identify health patterns such as medication habits
Family can describe patterns such as whether medicines are taken regularly.
Describe how the patient usually copes with stress
Family can share how the patient normally copes.
Replace the patient as the primary source
For alert patients, the patient remains the primary source.
Give consent for data collection on the patient’s behalf
An alert patient gives their own permission to involve family.
alt.ex: Correct: Confirm findings the nurse has gathered; Identify health patterns such as medication habits; Describe how the patient usually copes with stress.

items.q: Only patients can provide subjective data about their own health condition.
items.a: True
items.ex: Subjective data are the patient’s own feelings, perceptions, and self-reported symptoms.
items.ww: Others can report observations, but subjective data come only from the patient.

alt.q: Family members can provide subjective data about a patient’s health condition in the same way the patient can.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Only patients provide subjective data relevant to their health condition.
alt.ww: Family members are secondary sources; they cannot report the patient’s own feelings and perceptions.

items.q: In older adults, physiological age and chronological age may not match.
items.a: True
items.ex: Not all older adults experience the same changes, and changes occur at different rates.
items.ww: Chronological age alone does not predict physiological changes.

alt.q: In older adults, chronological age is a reliable measure of physiological age.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Physiological age and chronological age may not match because changes occur at different rates.
alt.ww: Older adults vary widely, so age in years does not predict physiological status.

items.q: A patient’s health record offers both baseline and ongoing subjective and objective information about the patient’s response to illness.
items.a: True
items.ex: Health records offer baseline and ongoing subjective and objective data and help check consistency of observations.
items.ww: The record contains both types of data, not just one.

alt.q: A patient’s health record contains only objective data, such as laboratory results and vital signs.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Health records contain both subjective and objective information about the patient’s response to illness.
alt.ww: Records also include subjective data, such as summaries of ongoing assessments.

items.q: Patients’ verbal descriptions of their health problems, including feelings, perceptions, and self-reported symptoms, are called [[subjective data|subjective]].

alt.q: A patient’s self-report of incision pain is an example of [[subjective data|subjective]].

items.q: Using [[teach-back|teach back]], the nurse asks the patient to explain instructions in their own words to assess understanding.

alt.ex: Teach-back is a health literacy universal precaution that checks whether the patient understood.

items.q: A nursing student meets a patient for the first time to begin an assessment. Which action best starts a therapeutic relationship?
items.a: Introduce yourself and explain your role.
items.ex: Courtesy at the first meeting, such as an introduction and explanation of role, begins a trusting relationship.
w: Begin by reading the admission form aloud.
Starting with a form ignores the patient and does not build connection.
Address the patient by first name right away.
The nurse addresses the patient formally, then asks their preferred name.
Ask the visitors to leave without explanation.
The nurse meets and acknowledges others and asks the patient’s permission.

alt.q: A nurse enters a patient’s room for an initial interview. Which statement best reflects courtesy that supports the nurse-patient relationship?
alt.a: “I’m Julia, your nursing student today. May I ask how you are feeling?”
alt.ex: Introducing yourself, explaining your role, and asking permission show courtesy and build the relationship.
w: “I need to finish this form quickly, so please keep answers short.”
Rushing the patient conveys disinterest and hinders trust.
“Hi, honey. Let’s get your history done before lunch arrives.”
