“Your chart already has the answers, so this will be quick.”
Assuming answers ignores the patient’s story and their concerns.

items.q: What does the textbook describe as central to achieving effective person-centered relationships?
items.a: Trust
items.ex: Trust is central to person-centered relationships and needed to learn the information required to care for a patient.
w: Efficiency
Efficiency helps workflow but is not described as central to the relationship.
Formality
Stiff formality may inhibit a patient rather than build the relationship.
Documentation
Documentation records data but does not create the relationship.

alt.q: A patient refuses to share details about home life with a nurse. According to the textbook, what is most needed for the nurse to learn this information?
alt.a: A trusting relationship with the patient
alt.ex: Trust is necessary to ensure the nurse can learn the information needed to care for the patient.
w: A more detailed admission form
Forms do not replace trust in getting patients to share information.
A written consent from family
Family consent does not create the patient’s willingness to share.
A list of closed-ended questions
Closed-ended questions limit answers and do not build trust.

items.q: According to the textbook, understanding a patient is not enough. What else must the nurse convey?
items.a: That the patient is understandable and the patient’s story is acceptable
items.ex: Beyond understanding, the nurse must convey that the patient is understandable and the patient’s story is acceptable.
w: That the nurse has already identified the patient’s medical diagnosis
Conveying a diagnosis is not the goal; acceptance of the story is.
That the patient’s concerns will be handled by the health care provider
Deferring concerns does not convey acceptance of the patient’s story.
That the nurse has limited time and the story must be brief
Signaling time limits discourages the patient from sharing.

alt.q: A patient hesitantly shares a long story about fears of losing independence. Which response best conveys that the patient’s story is acceptable?
alt.a: “That sounds very hard. I’d like to hear more about what worries you.”
alt.ex: The nurse conveys that the patient is understandable and the story acceptable, encouraging the patient to share more.
w: “Many people feel that way, but it usually turns out fine.”
False reassurance dismisses the story rather than accepting it.
“Let’s stay on track and finish your admission questions.”
Redirecting away from concerns signals that the story is not welcome.
“You shouldn’t worry; your doctor will take care of that.”
Telling the patient not to worry dismisses their concerns.

items.q: A nurse begins a shift with five patients and many interruptions. How should the nurse begin learning about each patient?
items.a: Take a few minutes of quality time to be present with each patient during rounds.
items.ex: Regardless of urgency or setting, even a few minutes of quality time helps the nurse learn about each patient.
w: Wait until the end of the shift when there is time for a full interview.
Waiting delays learning about patients; quality time can occur in a few minutes.
Rely on the hand-off report and avoid interrupting the patients.
The hand-off helps, but nurses still need time with patients to know them.
Review the EHR for each patient instead of visiting the rooms.
Records do not replace being present with the patient.

alt.q: A home care nurse has only a short time for each visit. What does the textbook advise about building the relationship?
alt.a: Even a few minutes of focused, quality time with the patient helps.
alt.ex: Quality time to be present with the patient can be brief and should happen in any encounter.
w: Relationships can only be built during long, unhurried visits.
Even a few minutes of quality time is valuable.
The nurse should postpone relationship building until the patient is stable.
Quality time should occur in any encounter, regardless of urgency.
The relationship matters less in home care than in the hospital.
The relationship matters in every setting, including home visits.

items.q: A nurse is entering data into the computer while a patient describes new symptoms. The patient stops talking and looks away. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Turn from the screen, make eye contact, and note key words to document later.
items.ex: Staring at a computer screen seems uncaring; the nurse focuses on the patient and documents later.
w: Continue typing so that the data are recorded accurately.
Continued screen focus conveys disinterest and blocks connection.
Ask the patient to wait until the data entry is finished.
This interrupts the patient’s story and conveys lack of interest.
Switch to closed-ended questions to finish the form faster.
Closed-ended questions limit the story and do not repair the connection.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid talking on a phone or staring at a computer screen during an assessment interview?
alt.a: Patients will perceive the nurse as uncaring.
alt.ex: Box 16.3 warns that phones and screens make the nurse seem uncaring and harm the connection.
w: It may break patient confidentiality rules.
The main concern described is the patient perceiving the nurse as uncaring.
It makes the documentation less accurate.
The concern is the relationship, not the accuracy of entries.
It lengthens the interview for the nurse.
Time is not the issue; the patient’s perception of caring is.

items.q: According to research cited in the textbook, which experience develops a type of knowing that fosters sound clinical judgment?
items.a: Hearing patients’ illness accounts, watching them, and learning how they typically respond
items.ex: Hearing patients’ accounts, watching them, and understanding their typical responses develops knowing that supports sound judgment.
w: Memorizing normal laboratory values for each age group and gender
Lab norms are needed, but this knowing comes from experiences with patients.
Completing every section of the EHR assessment form for each patient
Completing forms does not by itself build knowledge of the patient.
Reviewing the health care provider’s orders at the start of each shift
Orders guide care but do not create knowing the patient.

alt.q: A nurse has cared for the same patient for 3 days and notices the patient is quieter than usual. Why is this nurse likely to recognize a subtle change?
alt.a: Watching the patient over time builds knowledge of how the patient typically responds.
alt.ex: Coming to understand how patients typically respond develops a type of knowing that fosters sound clinical judgment.
w: Experienced nurses rely on intuition and do not need to observe patients.
Knowing comes from hearing, watching, and understanding patients, not from skipping observation.
The patient’s chart lists every expected behavior for the diagnosis.
Records do not show how this patient typically responds.
The nurse has memorized the textbook signs of deterioration.
Knowledge helps, but knowing this patient comes from time spent with them.

items.q: A postoperative patient says to the nurse, “I feel alone—just not certain what is happening to me.” Which response by the nurse best builds the relationship and the assessment?
items.a: “Tell me how you usually cope with stress and who supports you.”
items.ex: Showing interest in the patient’s concerns, such as coping and support, connects with the patient and collects relevant data.
w: “You’re not alone; there are many nurses on this unit.”
This dismisses the feeling instead of exploring the patient’s concerns.
“Everyone feels that way after surgery; it will pass.”
Generalizing the feeling closes off further discussion.
“Let me get you something to help you sleep.”
Acting before assessing ignores the patient’s concern.

alt.q: A patient remains restless after his breathing has stabilized. Which question best shows interest in his concerns?
alt.a: “Is there anything else making you restless?”
alt.ex: Open interest in the patient’s concerns, as Tonya showed, helps reveal the true nature of the problem.
w: “Are you restless because of the pain?”
This leading question limits the answer to what the nurse suspects.
“Do you want me to call your doctor now?”
This shifts the issue to the provider without exploring the patient’s concern.
“You seem fine, so can you try to rest?”
This dismisses the patient’s restlessness without assessing it.

items.q: Why does connecting with patients by showing interest in their problems and concerns matter in assessment?
items.a: It helps the nurse collect a relevant database.
items.ex: Showing interest helps the nurse collect relevant data; patients reveal more when the nurse focuses on their concerns.
w: It reduces the need for a physical examination.
Interest improves the history but does not replace physical examination.
It shortens the time needed for the hand-off report.
Connection affects data gathering with the patient, not hand-off length.
It allows the nurse to skip validating the data.
Data still must be validated against other sources.

alt.q: A nurse notices that a patient shares more details when the nurse shows genuine interest. Which explanation from the textbook fits this observation?
alt.a: Patients are more likely to fully reveal problems when nurses focus on their concerns.
alt.ex: Patients more fully reveal the nature of health problems when nurses show interest and focus on their concerns.
w: Patients share more when the nurse asks only closed-ended questions.
Closed-ended questions limit answers rather than encouraging full disclosure.
Patients share more when the nurse is very formal and distant.
Stiff formality may inhibit patients.
Patients share more when the nurse suggests possible answers.
Suggesting answers is leading and limits what patients share.

items.q: During an interview, a patient who trusts the nurse begins asking about planned treatments and diagnostic tests. What does this behavior most likely indicate?
items.a: The patient feels comfortable partnering with the nurse in planning care.
items.ex: When trust is established, patients feel comfortable asking questions so they can partner in decisions and planning care.
w: The patient is avoiding the nurse’s assessment questions.
Asking questions after trust is built reflects partnership, not avoidance.
The patient does not understand the purpose of the interview.
These questions show engagement rather than confusion about the interview.
The patient is anxious and cannot provide reliable data.
Questions about care show partnership, not unreliability.

alt.q: What is a result of establishing trust with a patient during an interview?
alt.a: The patient feels comfortable asking questions and partnering in decisions.
alt.ex: Trust lets patients ask about treatments and testing and partner with the nurse in planning care.
w: The patient stops needing any health teaching.
Trust supports teaching; it does not eliminate the need for it.
The patient relies on the nurse to make decisions.
Trust supports partnership rather than handing decisions to the nurse.
The patient no longer needs data validated.
Data still need validation regardless of trust.

items.q: Knowing the patient and situation involves building therapeutic relationships with whom?
items.a: Patients and their support networks
items.ex: Knowing the patient involves therapeutic relationships with patients and their support networks to understand data deeply.
w: Health care providers and nurse managers
Team communication matters, but knowing the patient centers on patients and supporters.
Insurance case managers and payers
Payers are not part of knowing the patient’s situation.
Other patients on the same unit
Other patients are not part of this patient’s support network.

alt.q: A nurse includes a patient’s spouse and adult daughter in conversations about the patient’s recovery. Which concept does this best reflect?
alt.a: Building relationships with the patient’s support network
alt.ex: Building relationships with patients and their support networks gives the nurse an intimate understanding of the data.
w: Applying health literacy universal precautions
Universal precautions address clear information, not relationships with supporters.
Validating data through diagnostic test results
Diagnostic data are test results, not relationships with family.
Performing a problem-focused quick screening
Quick screenings address urgent problems, not the support network.

items.q: A new nurse says, “I build rapport with patients only during the admission interview.” Which response by the preceptor is most accurate?
items.a: “Quality time to connect should happen in any encounter with a patient.”
items.ex: Quality time should occur at admission, during rounds, at follow-up visits, and in any patient encounter.
w: “That is correct; admission is the only time rapport matters.”
Quality time is needed in every encounter, not just admission.
“Rapport is built mainly during the discharge teaching session.”
Discharge is one encounter, but rapport is built throughout care.
“Rapport matters only when the patient has an urgent problem.”
Quality time is valuable regardless of urgency.

alt.q: A nurse is planning when to spend quality time with a patient. Which time does the textbook identify?
alt.a: During rounds at the beginning of a shift
alt.ex: Quality time should occur on admission, during rounds at the start of a shift, at follow-up visits, and in any encounter.
w: Only after the patient’s condition is stable
Quality time should occur regardless of urgency or setting.
Only after the physical examination is finished
Quality time is not limited to after examination.
Only when the family is present at the bedside
Family presence is not required for quality time.

items.q: A nurse is concerned about how to come across during a first interview. Which approach does the textbook recommend?
items.a: Avoid both stiff formality and being too casual, and choose words carefully.
items.ex: Stiff formality may inhibit a patient, being too casual may not instill confidence, and careless words may upset an anxious patient.
w: Be very formal so the patient views the nurse as a professional.
Stiff formality may inhibit the patient.
Be casual and use slang so the patient relaxes quickly.
Being too casual may not instill confidence.
Use technical terms so the patient trusts the nurse’s expertise.
Medical jargon hinders understanding and should be avoided.

alt.q: Why should a nurse choose words carefully when talking with an anxious patient?
alt.a: Words the nurse thinks are harmless may seem very important to the patient.
alt.ex: An anxious patient who is trying to understand may give great weight to casual remarks.
w: Anxious patients rarely listen to what nurses say.
Anxious patients often listen closely, which is why words matter.
Careful words shorten the length of the interview.
Careful wording is about the patient’s understanding, not time.
Careful words remove the need for teach-back.
Teach-back is still used to check understanding.

items.q: Which factors does the textbook identify as making quality time with patients difficult? Select all that apply.
o: Interruptions
Interruptions are named as a barrier to quality time.
Care of other patients
Caring for other patients competes for the nurse’s time.
Other home visits
Other scheduled home visits can limit time with a patient.
Restricted time in the health care setting
Limited time allotted in the setting makes quality time difficult.
The patient’s trust in the nurse
Trust supports the relationship; it is not a barrier.
Use of therapeutic communication
Therapeutic communication supports quality time.
items.ex: Interruptions, other patients, other home visits, and restricted time can make quality time difficult.

alt.q: A nurse wants to protect time to be present with a patient. Which barriers should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Frequent interruptions on the unit
Interruptions make quality time difficult.
Competing needs of other assigned patients
Other patients’ care competes for time.
Limited time allowed for each visit
Restricted time in the setting limits quality time.
Showing interest in the patient’s concerns
Showing interest builds connection rather than blocking it.
Listening without interrupting the patient
Attentive listening supports quality time.
alt.ex: Correct: Frequent interruptions on the unit; Competing needs of other assigned patients; Limited time allowed for each visit.

items.q: Which nursing behaviors help build a connection with a patient during an assessment interview? Select all that apply.
o: Begin with open-ended questions.
Open-ended questions encourage patients to tell their stories.
Allow the patient to describe symptoms without interruption.
Uninterrupted description shows interest and gathers full data.
Note the patient’s tone of voice, posture, and energy.
Being observant is part of connecting with the patient.
Assume you know the nature of the problem.
Assuming the problem prevents listening and attentiveness.
Fill in data fields while looking at the screen.
Staring at a screen makes the nurse seem uncaring.
Dominate the discussion to keep it on track.
The nurse should not dominate; the patient’s needs guide follow-up.
items.ex: Open-ended questions, uninterrupted listening, and careful observation build connection and gather relevant data.

alt.q: Which behaviors would weaken a nurse’s connection with a patient during assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Talking on a phone during the interview
Phone use makes the patient perceive the nurse as uncaring.
Interrupting the patient’s description of symptoms
Interruptions prevent full description and harm connection.
Assuming the problem before the patient finishes
Assuming the problem replaces listening and attentiveness.
Respecting the patient’s silence
Respecting silence is a recommended connection behavior.
Letting the patient’s concerns guide follow-up questions
Following the patient’s concerns builds connection.
alt.ex: Correct: Talking on a phone during the interview; Interrupting the patient’s description of symptoms; Assuming the problem before the patient finishes.

items.q: When does the textbook say a nurse should have quality time with a patient? Select all that apply.
o: During patient admission to a hospital unit
Admission is a key time for quality time with the patient.
During rounds at the beginning of a shift
Rounds at the start of a shift are an opportunity for quality time.
During a follow-up home or clinic visit
Follow-up visits are named as times for quality time.
Only when the patient’s condition is urgent
Quality time occurs regardless of urgency, in any encounter.
Only after all documentation is complete
Quality time is not delayed until documentation is finished.
items.ex: Quality time should happen at admission, during rounds, at follow-up visits, and in any patient encounter.

alt.q: A nurse wants to build therapeutic relationships across settings. Which encounters offer opportunities for quality time? Select all that apply.
o: Admitting a patient to a medical unit
Admission is a recommended time for quality time.
Making rounds at the start of a shift
Rounds are a recommended time for quality time.
Seeing a patient at a clinic follow-up visit
Follow-up clinic visits are named in the textbook.
Only the first meeting with the patient
Quality time should occur in any encounter, not just the first.
Only when the patient asks for the nurse
The nurse seeks quality time in every encounter.
alt.ex: Correct: Admitting a patient to a medical unit; Making rounds at the start of a shift; Seeing a patient at a clinic follow-up visit.

items.q: Understanding a patient is sufficient for a therapeutic relationship, even if the nurse does not convey that understanding to the patient.
items.a: False
items.ex: The nurse must also convey that the patient is understandable and that the patient’s story is acceptable.
items.ww: Understanding alone is insufficient; the patient needs to sense acceptance.

alt.q: Besides understanding a patient, the nurse must convey that the patient’s story is acceptable.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Conveying acceptance of the patient’s story is required in addition to understanding.
alt.ww: The book states that only understanding a patient is insufficient.

items.q: Regardless of how urgent a situation is, a nurse can begin to learn about a patient by being present with the patient for even a few minutes.
items.a: True
items.ex: Even a few minutes of quality time, in any setting or level of urgency, helps the nurse learn about the patient.
items.ww: Quality time does not require a long, uninterrupted period.

alt.q: Quality time with a patient is possible only in nonurgent situations when the nurse has a long uninterrupted period.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Regardless of urgency or setting, even a few minutes of being present counts as quality time.
alt.ww: The book says quality time can be brief and should occur in any encounter.

items.q: Therapeutic communication skills and a nurse’s sincere intention to understand a patient’s concerns are critical to clinical judgment.
items.a: True
items.ex: These skills enable patients to tell their stories so the nurse understands the situation and forms sound judgments.
items.ww: Without them, the nurse gathers incomplete data and misses the patient’s real concerns.

alt.q: Clinical judgment depends mainly on physical examination findings, so the nurse-patient relationship has little effect on it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Therapeutic communication and sincere interest in the patient’s concerns are critical to clinical judgment.
alt.ww: Knowing the patient through relationships fosters sound clinical judgment.

items.q: [[Trust]] is central to achieving effective person-centered relationships with patients.
items.ex: Trust ensures the nurse can learn the information needed to care for the patient.

alt.q: Without [[trust]], a nurse may not learn the information needed to care for a patient.
alt.ex: Trust ensures the nurse can learn the information needed to care for the patient.

items.q: Effective [[communication|therapeutic communication]] is the foundation for enabling patients to tell their stories and nurses to understand their situations.
items.ex: Effective communication lets patients share their stories so nurses can understand them more fully.

alt.q: Patients can tell their stories and nurses can understand them when effective [[communication|therapeutic communication]] forms the foundation of the relationship.
alt.ex: Effective communication lets patients share their stories so nurses can understand them more fully.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “I’ve been feeling dizzy.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Describe how you feel when you are dizzy.”
items.ex: Asking the patient to describe the symptom clarifies its meaning, because dizziness can reflect many disorders.
w: “Does the room spin when you are dizzy?”
Direct questions like this often get a “yes” and may not reveal the true problem.
“Do you feel faint when you are dizzy?”
Most patients answer “yes” to direct questions, which may hide the real cause.
“It isn’t happening too often, is it?”
This leading question limits the answer to what the patient thinks the nurse wants.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid asking a patient who reports dizziness, “Does the room spin?”
alt.a: Most patients will answer yes, which may not reveal the true problem.
alt.ex: Direct questions about a symptom often get a “yes”; a full description is needed because dizziness has many causes.
w: The question is too open-ended to give useful information.
This is a closed-ended question, not an open-ended one.
Spinning is never associated with dizziness.
The issue is the question style, not whether spinning occurs.
The patient may feel the nurse is rushing to end the interview.
The concern is inaccurate data, not the patient’s sense of the ending.

items.q: Which question by the nurse is a leading question?
items.a: “That wasn’t very hard to do, do you agree?”
items.ex: Leading questions suggest an answer and can limit information to what the patient thinks the nurse wants to know.
w: “How often does the diarrhea occur?”
This is a direct closed-ended question that seeks specific information.
“What are your concerns about this?”
This open-ended question lets the patient decide what to share.
“Is there anything else you can tell me?”
This is a probing question that encourages full description.

alt.q: Which question by the nurse is a direct closed-ended question?
alt.a: “Do you have pain or cramping?”
alt.ex: Closed-ended questions limit answers to one or two words, such as yes or no, or a number or frequency.
w: “So, tell me more about your stomach trouble.”
This open-ended question invites the patient to tell the story.
“It didn’t happen too often, did it?”
This is a leading question that suggests the answer.
“What else is bothering you?”
This is a probing, open-ended question.

items.q: A nurse says, “Go on,” and “Uh-huh,” while a patient describes symptoms. Which interview technique is the nurse using?
items.a: Back channeling
items.ex: Back channeling uses active listening prompts to show interest and encourage the patient to give more details.
w: Probing
Probing uses open-ended questions such as “What else is bothering you?”
Leading
Leading questions suggest an answer to the patient.
Validation
Validation compares data with another source to confirm accuracy.

alt.q: Which nursing statement is an example of back channeling?
alt.a: “All right, go on.”
alt.ex: Back channeling includes prompts such as “all right,” “go on,” or “uh-huh” to encourage more detail.
w: “How many times a day does it occur?”
This is a closed-ended question seeking a number.
“That didn’t hurt much, did it?”
This is a leading question.
“Tell me more about your concerns.”
This is an open-ended question.

items.q: Halfway through a nursing history, a patient becomes tired and begins shifting uncomfortably. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Postpone the rest of the interview until later.
items.ex: If a patient becomes fatigued or uncomfortable, it is time to postpone; the interview need not be completed in one session.
w: Speed up by asking only yes-or-no questions to finish.
Rushing the patient yields incomplete data and ignores fatigue.
Continue because the history must be completed at once.
It is not necessary to complete the interview in one session.
Ask the family to finish answering the questions now.
The alert patient remains the primary source; postpone instead.

alt.q: Which statement about the length of an assessment interview is accurate?
alt.a: It is not necessary to complete the interview in one session.
alt.ex: To avoid tiring the patient, the nurse may finish the interview in more than one session.
w: The nursing history must always be completed on admission.
The interview may be continued later to avoid tiring the patient.
An interview should never be stopped once it has begun.
The nurse postpones when the patient becomes fatigued or uncomfortable.
A useful interview always takes at least 30 minutes.
An interview may last less than 1 minute or several minutes.

items.q: A patient says, “I can get up from the chair by myself with no trouble.” What should the nurse do next?
items.a: Observe the patient rise from the chair and begin walking.
items.ex: Subjective reports are validated with objective data, such as watching the patient rise from a chair.
w: Document that the patient is independent in transfers.
Recording the report without validation may be misleading.
Ask the family whether the statement is true.
Direct observation validates function better than another report.
Accept the report because the patient is alert.
The nurse should not rely only on what patients say they can do.

alt.q: A nurse wants to assess a patient’s ability to prepare a medication at home. Which method gives the most accurate information?
alt.a: Watching a return demonstration of the task
alt.ex: Direct observation, often during a return demonstration, is better than relying on what patients say they can do.
w: Asking the patient to describe the steps
The patient’s description may be misleading about actual function.
Reviewing the EHR for past teaching notes
Notes do not show what the patient can do now.
Asking whether the patient feels confident
Confidence does not confirm the patient’s actual ability.

items.q: What are the primary objectives when taking an initial nursing history?
items.a: Discover the patient’s concerns, explore expectations for the visit, and show genuine interest and partnership
items.ex: Primary objectives are learning concerns, exploring expectations, and displaying genuine interest and partnership.
w: Complete every EHR field, confirm the medical diagnosis, and schedule tests
These are tasks, not the primary objectives of a nursing history.
Teach about the illness, review medications, and plan the patient’s discharge
Teaching and planning come after assessment, not as history objectives.
Obtain consent, review insurance, and identify the family decision maker
These are administrative tasks, not the main history objectives.

alt.q: A nurse begins an initial nursing history by asking, “What would you like us to do for you today?” Which objective does this question best serve?
alt.a: Exploring the patient’s expectations for the health care visit
alt.ex: Exploring expectations for the visit is a primary objective of the initial nursing history.
w: Validating objective data with another source
Validation compares data with other sources; this question explores expectations.
Closing the interview with a summary
Summarizing happens in the termination phase, not at the start.
Screening the patient’s level of health literacy
Literacy screening uses specific tools, not this question.

items.q: A nurse is ending an interview and says, “I have just two more questions. We’ll be finished in a few minutes.” What is the purpose of this statement?
items.a: It helps the patient stay focused without wondering when the interview will end.
items.ex: Signaling the end helps the patient keep attention and gives a chance to ask questions or clarify information.
w: It tells the patient that the nurse is too busy to talk longer.
The purpose is to support attention, not to signal that the nurse is busy.
It prevents the patient from bringing up any new concerns.
It actually gives the patient an opportunity to ask more questions.
It replaces the need to summarize the discussion with the patient.
Summarizing is still part of the termination phase.

alt.q: During the termination phase of an interview, what should the nurse do?
alt.a: Summarize the discussion and check the accuracy of the information.
alt.ex: In termination, the nurse summarizes, checks accuracy, signals the end, and tells the patient when they will return.
w: Introduce the agenda and explain why data are being collected.
Setting an agenda happens during the orientation phase.
Ask open-ended questions about new symptoms.
Collecting new data is the work of the working phase.
Leave without telling the patient when you will return.
The nurse ends in a friendly way and says when they will return.

items.q: At the start of an interview, a patient says, “I’ve been thinking about questions I want to ask about going home.” The nurse has a standard discharge form to complete. Which response is best?
items.a: “Good. Let’s start with your questions.”
items.ex: The nurse focuses on the patient’s priorities and order, integrating standard information with the patient’s concerns.
w: “Let’s finish my form first, then we’ll get to your questions.”
This puts the nurse’s agenda ahead of the patient’s priorities.
“Your doctor will answer those questions before you leave.”
This dismisses the patient’s concerns and loses useful data.
“We don’t need to talk about going home for a few more days.”
Ignoring the patient’s priorities discourages active partnership.

alt.q: During the orientation phase, whose priorities should guide the agenda of the interview?
alt.a: The patient’s priorities, in the order the patient presents them
alt.ex: The nurse focuses on the patient’s priorities and order, not a personal agenda, and integrates standard data.
w: The nurse’s priorities, in the order of the EHR form
The nurse avoids following a personal agenda over the patient’s concerns.
The provider’s priorities, in the order of the orders
The agenda centers on the patient’s concerns.
The family’s priorities, in the order they are raised
The family may contribute, but the patient’s priorities guide the agenda.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to interview a newly admitted patient with chronic lung disease. Which topics should the nurse plan to include?
items.a: Respiratory status, effects of symptoms on lifestyle, and acceptance of the chronic disease
items.ex: A diagnosis of chronic lung disease suggests questions about breathing, lifestyle effects, and understanding of the disease.
w: Joint range of motion, hand stiffness, and swelling of the knees
These relate to arthritis, not chronic lung disease.
Bowel sounds, passage of flatus, and appearance of the incision
These relate to abdominal surgery, not chronic lung disease.
Blood glucose results, insulin use, and foot inspection habits
These relate to diabetes, not chronic lung disease.

alt.q: A nurse is preparing for an admission interview, but the EHR contains little information. What will the record most likely include?
alt.a: The admitting diagnosis and the patient’s chief complaint
alt.ex: On admission, there may be little in the record except the admitting diagnosis and chief complaint.
w: A full nursing history and the discharge plan
These are completed later, not present on admission.
Previous shift notes and hand-off reports
A new admission has no previous shift notes.
Teach-back results and literacy screening scores
These are gathered during care, not before admission.

items.q: A patient’s friend is visiting when the nurse arrives to conduct an assessment interview. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Ask the patient’s permission to conduct the interview with the visitor present.
items.ex: Box 16.3 directs the nurse to meet visitors and ask the patient’s permission to interview in a visitor’s presence.
w: Ask the visitor to leave without consulting the patient.
The patient decides whether the visitor stays.
Proceed with the interview because visitors may help.
The nurse needs the patient’s permission first.
Postpone the interview until the visitor leaves.
Postponing is unnecessary if the patient agrees to the visitor staying.

alt.q: Which action shows courtesy at the beginning of an assessment interview?
alt.a: Address the patient formally, then ask the preferred name.
alt.ex: Box 16.3 advises addressing the patient formally, then asking how the patient prefers to be addressed.
w: Call the patient by first name to build rapport quickly.
The nurse first addresses the patient formally, then asks preference.
Skip introductions to save time for questions.
Introducing yourself and your role is part of courtesy.
Ignore others in the room to keep the focus on the patient.
The nurse meets and acknowledges others in the room.

items.q: When should a nurse use direct closed-ended questions during an interview?
items.a: After the patient describes a problem, to seek more specific details about it
items.ex: Closed-ended questions follow the patient’s story to clarify specific details such as frequency or presence of a symptom.
w: At the start of the interview, to let the patient tell the full story
Open-ended questions are used at the start to let the patient tell the story.
When the nurse wants the patient to describe a problem thoroughly
Direct questions are not ideal for thorough descriptions.
When the nurse wants the patient to volunteer as much as possible
Closed-ended questions do not encourage volunteering more information.

alt.q: A patient reports indigestion, diarrhea, and loss of appetite after a series of trips. Which nursing question best clarifies the problem?
alt.a: “How often does the diarrhea occur?”
alt.ex: After the patient describes the problem, closed-ended questions clarify details such as frequency of a symptom.
w: “It isn’t too bad, is it?”
This is a leading question that suggests the answer.
“Tell me about your trips.”
This open-ended question does not clarify the symptom details.
“Uh-huh, go on.”
Back channeling encourages talk but does not clarify specific details.

items.q: Which actions by the nurse support comfort and courtesy during an assessment interview? Select all that apply.
o: Knock before entering the room.
Knocking is a basic courtesy.
Close the curtains or door to maintain privacy.
Privacy is a comfort measure.
Turn off the TV and silence phones.
Quiet supports a focused interview.
Assure the patient that information stays within the health care team.
Assuring confidentiality is a courtesy.
Fill in data fields on the screen while the patient talks.
Staring at a screen seems uncaring; document key words later.
Insist on finishing the whole interview in one session.
It is not necessary to complete the interview in one session.
items.ex: Courtesy and comfort include knocking, privacy, quiet, and confidentiality, while avoiding screens and patient fatigue.

alt.q: A nurse is planning an extended assessment interview. Which preparations are recommended? Select all that apply.
o: Plan 10 to 15 minutes with no other activities scheduled.
Box 16.3 suggests planning 10 to 15 minutes of uninterrupted time.
Provide a comfortable room temperature.
Comfortable temperature is part of comfort.
Review the patient’s EHR when information is available.
Reviewing the EHR is part of interview preparation.
Plan to type every answer word for word during the interview.
Reduce computer time; remember key words and document later.
Schedule the interview during visiting hours to save time.
Interruptions and visitors can limit focus; quiet is preferred.
alt.ex: Correct: Plan 10 to 15 minutes with no other activities scheduled; Provide a comfortable room temperature; Review the patient’s EHR when information is available.

items.q: Which outcomes does the textbook link to good interview skills? Select all that apply.
o: Improved problem detection
Good interview skills yield more data and improve problem detection.
Greater diagnostic accuracy
More complete data improve diagnostic accuracy.
Higher patient satisfaction
Patient satisfaction improves with good interview skills.
Better patient health outcomes
Good interview skills improve patient health outcomes.
Less need for physical examination
Physical examination is still needed to validate subjective data.
Fewer questions from patients
Good interviews invite patients to ask questions and partner.
items.ex: Good interview skills yield more data, improving detection, accuracy, satisfaction, and outcomes.

alt.q: An empathic, patient-centered interview benefits patients in which ways? Select all that apply.
o: Strengthens the patient’s sense of self-esteem
An empathic interview strengthens self-esteem.
Lessens feelings of helplessness during illness
It reduces feelings of helplessness during illness.
Improves the accuracy of problem identification
More data improve diagnostic accuracy.
Removes the need to validate subjective data
Subjective data still must be validated with objective data.
Lets the nurse set the agenda without patient input
The patient’s priorities, not the nurse’s agenda, guide the interview.
alt.ex: Correct: Strengthens the patient’s sense of self-esteem; Lessens feelings of helplessness during illness; Improves the accuracy of problem identification.

items.q: Which actions belong to the termination phase of an assessment interview? Select all that apply.
o: Summarize the discussion with the patient.
Summarizing is part of termination.
Check the accuracy of the information collected.
Termination includes checking accuracy.
Let the patient know the interview is ending.
Signaling the end helps the patient keep attention.
Tell the patient when you will return.
Ending in a friendly way includes saying when you will return.
Set the agenda for the interview.
Setting an agenda belongs to the orientation phase.
Ask open-ended questions to begin data collection.
Starting data collection belongs to the working phase.
items.ex: Termination includes summarizing, checking accuracy, signaling the end, and stating when the nurse will return.

alt.q: A nurse is closing an interview with a patient. Which statements are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: “Let me summarize what we discussed to make sure it is correct.”
Summarizing checks accuracy.
“Is there anything else you would like to discuss?”
Ending by inviting other topics is recommended.
“I’ll come back after I check on two other patients.”
Telling the patient when you will return ends in a friendly way.
“Let me explain why I am collecting this information.”
Explaining the purpose belongs in the orientation phase.
“We’re done; someone will see you later.”
This abrupt ending gives no chance to clarify and no return time.
alt.ex: Correct: “Let me summarize what we discussed to make sure it is correct.”; “Is there anything else you would like to discuss?”; “I’ll come back after I check on two other patients.”

items.q: In the patient-centered interview, which phase comes right after “Orientation and setting an agenda”?
items.a: Working phase: collecting assessment data
items.ex: The formal interview moves from orientation and agenda setting, to collecting data, to termination.
w: Termination of the interview
That's phase 3 of 3.

alt.q: Which phase comes first in the patient-centered interview?
alt.a: Orientation and setting an agenda
alt.ex: The formal interview moves from orientation and agenda setting, to collecting data, to termination.
w: Working phase: collecting assessment data
That's phase 2 of 3.
Termination of the interview
That's phase 3 of 3.

alt.q: Which phase comes last in the patient-centered interview?
alt.a: Termination of the interview
alt.ex: The formal interview moves from orientation and agenda setting, to collecting data, to termination.
w: Working phase: collecting assessment data
That's phase 2 of 3.
Orientation and setting an agenda
That's phase 1 of 3.

alt.q: In the patient-centered interview, which phase comes right after “Working phase: collecting assessment data”?
alt.a: Termination of the interview
alt.ex: The formal interview moves from orientation and agenda setting, to collecting data, to termination.
w: Orientation and setting an agenda
That's phase 1 of 3.

alt.q: In the patient-centered interview, which phase comes right before “Working phase: collecting assessment data”?
alt.a: Orientation and setting an agenda
alt.ex: The formal interview moves from orientation and agenda setting, to collecting data, to termination.
w: Termination of the interview
That's phase 3 of 3.

alt.q: In the patient-centered interview, which phase comes right before “Termination of the interview”?
alt.a: Working phase: collecting assessment data
alt.ex: The formal interview moves from orientation and agenda setting, to collecting data, to termination.
w: Orientation and setting an agenda
That's phase 1 of 3.

ord.q: Put the phases of a formal patient-centered interview in order.
items: Orientation and setting an agenda
Working phase: collecting assessment data
Termination of the interview
ord.ex: The formal interview moves from orientation and agenda setting, to collecting data, to termination.

items.a: Elicits the patient’s unique story in their own words
items.ex: Each interview technique serves a different purpose in exploring the patient’s story.
w: Seeks specific details with one- or two-word answers
That goes with Direct closed-ended question.
Limits answers to what the patient thinks the nurse wants
That goes with Leading question.
Active listening prompts that show interest
That goes with Back channeling.

w: Elicits the patient’s unique story in their own words

alt.ex: Each interview technique serves a different purpose in exploring the patient’s story.
w: Elicits the patient’s unique story in their own words

Seeks specific details with one- or two-word answers

Active listening prompts that show interest
That goes with Back channeling.

w: Elicits the patient’s unique story in their own words

Seeks specific details with one- or two-word answers
That goes with Direct closed-ended question.

That goes with Leading question.

w: Elicits the patient’s unique story in their own words
That goes with Open-ended question.

Limits answers to what the patient thinks the nurse wants

Leading question: Limits answers to what the patient thinks the nurse wants.

Back channeling: Active listening prompts that show interest.

alt.a: Leading question

pairs: Elicits the patient’s unique story in their own words
Seeks specific details with one- or two-word answers

Repeated prompts until the patient has nothing else to say
mt.ex: Each interview technique serves a different purpose in exploring the patient’s story.

items.q: A patient-centered interview may last less than 1 minute or several minutes.
items.a: True
items.ex: Interviews vary in length; ongoing interviews can be brief while a nursing history is the most extensive.
items.ww: There is no minimum length; even a brief interview gathers useful data.

alt.q: A patient-centered interview must last at least several minutes to gather useful information.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: An interview may last less than 1 minute or several minutes, depending on the situation.
alt.ww: Brief ongoing interviews focused on priorities are also valid patient-centered interviews.

items.q: Direct closed-ended questions are ideal when the nurse wants a patient to describe a health problem thoroughly.
items.a: False
items.ex: Closed-ended questions limit answers and are not ideal for thorough descriptions; open-ended questions are.
items.ww: Closed-ended questions do not encourage patients to volunteer more information.

alt.q: Direct closed-ended questions do not encourage patients to volunteer more information than the nurse requests.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Closed-ended questions require short answers and clarify details but limit volunteered information.
alt.ww: Open-ended questions, not closed-ended ones, invite patients to share more.

items.q: When asking how often a symptom occurs, the nurse should allow the patient to define “often.”
items.a: True
items.ex: Letting the patient define frequency avoids leading questions that limit or distort the answer.
items.ww: Suggesting a frequency leads the patient toward the nurse’s expected answer.

alt.q: Asking “It didn’t happen too often, did it?” is a good way to help a patient estimate how often a symptom occurs.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: This is a leading question; the patient should define “often” in their own words.
alt.ww: Leading questions limit information to what the patient thinks the nurse wants to hear.

items.q: Active listening prompts such as “all right,” “go on,” or “uh-huh” are called [[back channeling|backchanneling|back-channeling]].
items.ex: Back channeling shows the nurse is interested and encourages the patient to give more details.

alt.q: When a nurse says “uh-huh” to encourage more details, the technique is called [[back channeling|backchanneling|back-channeling]].
alt.ex: Back channeling shows the nurse is interested and encourages the patient to give more details.

items.q: How does clinical experience improve a nurse’s assessment of patients?
items.a: It leads to pattern recognition and the ability to quickly and confidently correlate data to form conclusions.
items.ex: Experience builds pattern recognition in assessment data, so the nurse can correlate data quickly and confidently to reach conclusions.
w: It allows the nurse to skip parts of the assessment that rarely reveal abnormal findings.
Experience helps the nurse anticipate needed assessments; it does not justify omitting assessment data.
It replaces the need to validate findings with the patient or other members of the team.
Validation of data is still required; experience does not remove the need to confirm inferences.
It lets the nurse rely on the medical diagnosis rather than on the patient’s own responses.
Assessment remains person-centered; experience helps the nurse interpret the patient’s responses, not ignore them.

alt.q: The textbook compares experience to a painter’s background. What does this background allow the nurse to do?
alt.a: Put each patient’s clinical situation into perspective
alt.ex: Just as a painter creates a background for details, a nurse uses background experiences to put each patient’s situation into perspective.
w: Apply the same plan of care to every patient
Care remains person-centered; experience provides context, not a single plan for everyone.
Avoid asking patients about their health history
Experience actually teaches which questions to ask; it does not replace the history.
Make a medical diagnosis without test results
Nurses do not make medical diagnoses; experience helps place nursing data in context.

items.q: Which statement best describes how novice nurses usually apply the nursing process?
items.a: In a linear way, focusing only on data collected rather than the whole context of the patient’s situation
items.ex: New nurses have not yet had the experiences that let them place each patient situation into context, so they tend to work linearly.
w: Intuitively, drawing on mental connections from many similar earlier patient situations
Using intuition from previous similar experiences develops as the nurse gains more clinical practice.
Holistically, pulling together all of the patient’s data into a complete clinical picture
Pulling together all of a patient’s data is a skill that grows with clinical practice.
Selectively, collecting only the data that confirm the first impression of the patient
The book describes novices as focusing only on collected data, not as seeking confirming data.

alt.q: A new graduate nurse reviews a postoperative patient’s vital signs and pain score but does not consider the patient’s recent surgery, home situation, or concerns. Which explanation from the textbook best fits this approach?
alt.a: Novice nurses have not yet had the experiences that let them place patient situations into context.
alt.ex: Novices usually apply the nursing process linearly, focusing only on collected data rather than the whole context.
w: Novice nurses are trained to focus only on objective data and to leave subjective data to others.
Assessment includes both objective and subjective data for every nurse, new or experienced.
Novice nurses are expected to defer every patient assessment to an experienced preceptor.
New nurses perform assessments; their limitation is lack of experience for context, not deferral.
Novice nurses rely too heavily on intuition and so overlook the measured findings.
Appropriate use of intuition develops with experience; novices tend to focus narrowly on collected data.

items.q: A nurse whose father died last year is caring for a patient who is grieving the recent death of a spouse. Which approach by the nurse is best?
items.a: Reflect on her own experience to help explore the patient’s situation without letting it bias her findings.
items.ex: Personal experiences can help a nurse understand a patient’s situation if the nurse does not allow them to bias findings.
w: Assume the patient is feeling the same emotions she felt and plan care around them.
Assuming the patient feels as the nurse did allows personal experience to bias the assessment.
Ask to be reassigned because personal experience will always distort her assessment.
Personal experience can help understanding; the book asks nurses to reflect on it, not avoid such patients.
Spend most of the interview describing her own loss to build rapport with the patient.
The focus of assessment is the patient’s situation; the nurse’s experience is a tool for reflection.

alt.q: A nurse who has been a caregiver for a parent with dementia admits a patient with caregiver fatigue. Which statement by the nurse shows appropriate use of personal experience?
alt.a: “My own caregiving helps me know what to ask, but I need to hear how this patient experiences it.”
alt.ex: Reflecting on personal experience helps explore the patient’s situation, provided it does not bias the findings.
w: “I know exactly how this patient feels, so I can skip the questions about coping.”
Assuming the patient’s feelings lets personal experience bias the findings and leaves out needed data.
“I should keep my own caregiving experience completely out of my thinking during care.”
The book says personal experience can help a nurse understand a patient’s situation when used without bias.
“My caregiving experience means my findings will be more accurate than the patient’s report.”
Personal experience does not make the nurse’s view more accurate than the patient’s own account.

items.q: According to the textbook, which is one of the most important sources of assessment data available to a nurse?
items.a: The nurse’s own experience in caring for patients
items.ex: Your experience in caring for patients is described as one of the most important sources of data.
w: The nurse’s memory of textbook lists of normal findings
Knowledge of normal findings is part of the knowledge base, but the book singles out experience caring for patients.
The nurse’s personal opinions about the patient’s lifestyle
Personal opinions can bias findings; they are not a source of assessment data.
The nurse’s preference for a standard set of questions
Experience teaches the nurse to choose the questions that give the most useful information, not a fixed set.

alt.q: Through clinical experience caring for patients, what does a nurse learn about asking questions during assessment?
alt.a: Which questions will provide the most useful information
alt.ex: Clinical experience teaches the types of questions to ask, choosing those that provide the most useful information.
w: That closed-ended questions should be used for every topic
Experience teaches the nurse to choose the most useful questions, not one question type for everything.
That questions are unnecessary when vital signs are normal
Normal vital signs do not replace the patient’s own account; questions remain part of assessment.
That the same questions should be asked in the same order
Experience helps the nurse select questions suited to the patient, not apply a rigid script.

items.q: A nurse has repeatedly performed a dressing change on many patients. What does this repeated experience allow the nurse to do?
items.a: Adapt the skill to a patient’s needs without sacrificing safe principles
items.ex: Performing a skill repeatedly teaches what is necessary to adapt it without sacrificing safe principles.
w: Omit steps that seem unnecessary for patients with small wounds
Adapting a skill never means sacrificing safe principles or skipping needed steps.
Perform the skill without first assessing the patient’s condition
The book stresses being thorough in assessing a patient before performing any procedure.
Delegate the skill’s assessment portion to assistive personnel
Experience improves the nurse’s own assessment; it is not a reason to hand off assessment.

alt.q: An experienced nurse modifies how a patient is positioned for a procedure because of the patient’s joint contractures. Which principle guides this modification?
alt.a: Adapting a skill is acceptable only when safe principles are not sacrificed.
alt.ex: Experience teaches what is necessary to adapt a skill while keeping safe principles intact.
w: Adapting a skill is acceptable whenever it saves the nurse time on a busy shift.
Time savings do not justify adaptation; safe principles must be kept.
Adapting a skill is never acceptable because procedures must be identical each time.
The book describes adapting skills as part of experiential knowledge, as long as safety is kept.
Adapting a skill is acceptable as long as the patient agrees to the change.
Patient agreement matters, but the guiding rule is that safe principles are not sacrificed.

items.q: Experiential knowledge with a nursing skill helps the nurse in which way before the skill is performed?
items.a: Anticipating the assessments needed and the preparation steps for competent performance
items.ex: Experiential knowledge lets the nurse anticipate needed assessments and preparation steps so the skill is performed competently.
w: Knowing that assessment can be done after the skill is completed instead of before
Thorough assessment comes before any nursing procedure, not after.
Recognizing that patient knowledge of the skill has little effect on its outcome
Patient knowledge of the skill is one of the things the nurse assesses beforehand.
Understanding that skill competence matters more than accurate assessment data
Skill experience supports accurate assessment; competence includes performing an assessment and physical examination.

alt.q: A nurse with experience inserting urinary catheters gathers the supplies needed and checks the patient’s history of urinary problems before entering the room. Which benefit of experience does this illustrate?
alt.a: Anticipating the assessments and preparation needed to perform the skill competently
alt.ex: Experience lets the nurse anticipate needed assessments and preparation steps before performing a skill.
w: Recognizing patterns in assessment data to make a medical diagnosis
Nurses do not make medical diagnoses; this nurse is preparing for a skill.
Reducing the need for a thorough assessment before the procedure begins
The nurse is still thorough in assessing before the procedure; experience guides what to assess.
Applying the nursing process in a linear way focused on collected data
Linear application describes novice nurses, not anticipatory preparation from experience.

items.q: After caring for several more patients who have had a colectomy, how does the textbook say Tonya’s practice will change?
items.a: She can use that experience as context for future patients who have a colectomy.
items.ex: Tonya’s growing experience with colectomy patients gives her context to interpret future patients’ situations.
w: She will no longer need to assess bowel sounds in patients after colectomy.
Experience guides assessment; it does not eliminate needed assessments such as bowel sounds.
She will apply the nursing process in a more linear and step-by-step way.
Linear application is typical of novices; experience helps a nurse consider the whole context.
She will base her care on the typical colectomy patient rather than on Mr. Lawson.
Experience supports person-centered decisions; it is context, not a replacement for the individual.

alt.q: Which statement by a new nurse shows understanding of how experience with a patient population builds assessment skill?
alt.a: “Each patient with this surgery I care for gives me context for the next one.”
alt.ex: Experience with similar patients provides context for future patient situations and builds the ability to make clinical judgments.
w: “Once I have cared for one patient with this surgery, I know what all of them need.”
Each patient is unique; experience provides context but does not make all patients alike.
“Experience matters less than following the electronic health record’s assessment form.”
Experience is one of the most important sources of assessment data, not secondary to a form.
“My experience with this surgery means I can rely on intuition instead of collecting data.”
Intuition is used appropriately alongside data, built from connections to previous similar experiences.

items.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows correct understanding of how intuition develops in nursing assessment?
items.a: “As I gain practice, I’ll make mental connections to similar past situations that support my intuition.”
items.ex: With more practice, nurses make mental connections from similar experiences, allowing them to use intuition appropriately in judgments.
w: “Intuition is a personality trait, so some nurses have it and others never will.”
The book links appropriate use of intuition to clinical practice and mental connections, not to a fixed trait.
“Once I have intuition, I won’t need to collect a complete set of assessment data.”
Intuition supports judgment built on data; it does not replace data collection.
“Novice nurses should rely on intuition most because they lack clinical knowledge.”
Novices lack the experiences that support intuition; it develops as clinical practice grows.

alt.q: According to the textbook, what allows an experienced nurse to appropriately use intuition to form judgments?
alt.a: Mental connections made from previous similar clinical experiences
alt.ex: As clinical practice grows, nurses connect new situations with similar past ones, which lets them use intuition appropriately.
w: Memorization of the steps of the nursing process in order
Knowing the steps is basic knowledge; intuition comes from connections to past clinical experiences.
Following the electronic health record assessment template
A template organizes data but does not create the experiential connections behind intuition.
Confidence that comes from years of formal classroom study
The book ties intuition to clinical experience, not to classroom study alone.

items.q: According to the textbook, what strengthens a nurse’s critical thinking skills?
items.a: Practical experience and the opportunity to make clinical decisions
items.ex: Practical experience and opportunities to make clinical decisions strengthen critical thinking skills.
w: Avoiding clinical decisions until all knowledge has been mastered
Making clinical decisions is itself what strengthens critical thinking; waiting does not.
Following the same assessment routine for every patient encountered
A fixed routine does not build the context and connections that strengthen critical thinking.
Relying on the judgments of experienced nurses for all decisions
Learning from others helps, but the book stresses the nurse’s own practical experience and decisions.

alt.q: A nurse educator wants students to strengthen their critical thinking. Which learning activity best reflects the textbook?
alt.a: Giving students clinical practice with opportunities to make clinical decisions
alt.ex: The book states that practical experience and the opportunity to make clinical decisions strengthen critical thinking.
w: Having students memorize lists of normal assessment findings
Normal findings are part of the knowledge base, but practice and decision making strengthen critical thinking.
Having students observe nurses without making any decisions
Observation alone lacks the decision-making opportunities the book identifies.
Having students copy completed care plans for similar patients
Copying plans does not give students their own clinical decision-making experience.

items.q: A nurse with 10 years of experience on a surgical unit is floated for the first time to a pediatric unit. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Ask for an orientation and seek help from nurses who regularly work on that unit.
items.ex: Experience in one specialty may not transfer; nurses new to an area should ask for orientation and assistance from regular staff.
w: Use her surgical experience as the context for every pediatric patient she assesses.
Experience is shaped by specialty area; surgical patterns may not fit pediatric patients.
Rely on her intuition because experienced nurses can assess any type of patient.
A nurse can be an expert in one area and a novice in another; intuition comes from similar experiences.
Limit her assessments to vital signs until she is reassigned to the surgical unit.
Patients still need a thorough assessment; limiting assessment is unsafe.

alt.q: Why might an expert surgical nurse function more like a novice when caring for patients in an unfamiliar specialty?
alt.a: Experience in practice and in specialty areas shapes how well a nurse knows patients.
alt.ex: Knowing patients and their situations is influenced by experience in practice and in specialty areas of nursing.
w: Assessment skills learned in one specialty are lost after a long period of time.
The book does not say skills are lost; the issue is lack of experience with that specialty’s patients.
Expert nurses are not permitted to use intuition outside their home unit.
No such rule exists; intuition simply depends on having similar past experiences.
Physical examination techniques are completely different in every specialty.
The issue is context and pattern recognition with those patients, not entirely different techniques.

items.q: Before her next clinical day, a nursing student plans a patient-centered interview. Which plan best reflects the textbook’s “Reflect Now” guidance?
items.a: Consider ways to connect early with the patient and which questions fit the patient’s health situation.
items.ex: The book asks students to plan how to connect early with a patient and which questions suit the patient’s health situation.
w: Prepare a standard list of questions to ask every patient in the same order.
A fixed list ignores the patient’s specific health situation, which should guide question choice.
Plan to read the medical record only and interview the patient on a later day.
The guidance is to plan the interview itself and connect early with the patient.
Plan to focus only on the physical examination and leave the interview to others.
The interview is part of the nurse’s assessment; the book asks students to plan it.

alt.q: Which question should a nursing student ask themselves when preparing a patient-centered interview?
alt.a: “In which ways can I connect early with this patient?”
alt.ex: Connecting early with a patient is one of the planning considerations the book poses for a patient-centered interview.
w: “How can I finish the interview as quickly as possible?”
Speed is not the focus; the student plans connection and appropriate questions.
“Which of my own experiences should I share first?”
The interview centers on the patient, not on sharing the nurse’s experiences.
“Which questions can I skip because the chart answers them?”
The planning question is which questions are appropriate for the health situation, not which to skip.

items.q: During assessment, which kind of personal experience does the textbook suggest a nurse consider?
items.a: Family health situations such as caregiving fatigue, loss of a loved one or job, or anxiety over the unknown
items.ex: Reflecting on personal family health situations can help the nurse understand a patient’s situation, if bias is avoided.
w: Grades earned in prerequisite science courses and nursing skills laboratories
Academic performance is part of education, not the personal experience the book describes.
Preferences about which patient populations the nurse most enjoys caring for
Personal preferences are not the experiences the book asks nurses to reflect on.
Opinions formed about patients from reading about their diagnoses before meeting them
Preformed opinions risk bias; the book refers to the nurse’s own family health situations.

alt.q: A nurse who once lost a job recognizes a patient’s worry about losing work during a long illness. How does the textbook describe the value of this personal experience?
alt.a: It can help the nurse understand the patient’s situation if it does not bias the findings.
alt.ex: Personal experiences and perceptions help nurses understand patients’ situations when they are not allowed to bias findings.
w: It allows the nurse to conclude what the patient’s main problem is without asking.
Assuming the problem lets experience bias the findings; the nurse still explores the patient’s situation.
It should be ignored because personal experience has no place in assessment.
The book encourages reflecting on personal experience to explore a patient’s situation.
It makes the nurse’s view of the situation more reliable than the patient’s view.
The patient is the primary source; personal experience aids understanding, not replacement.

items.q: Which abilities does a nurse develop through clinical experience caring for patients? Select all that apply.
o: Observing patients’ behaviors and physical signs and symptoms
Clinical experience helps the nurse observe behaviors and physical signs and symptoms.
Tracking trends in patient data
Tracking trends is one ability the book links to clinical experience.
Recognizing clinical changes and identifying cues
Experience helps the nurse recognize clinical changes and identify cues.
Making medical diagnoses from assessment data
Nurses form nursing judgments; medical diagnosis is outside nursing practice.
Omitting assessments for familiar patient conditions
Experience helps anticipate assessments; it never justifies omitting them.
items.ex: Clinical experience helps nurses observe signs, track trends, recognize changes, identify cues, and choose useful questions.

alt.q: A nurse has cared for many patients after abdominal surgery. Which skills has this experience likely strengthened? Select all that apply.
o: Recognizing subtle clinical changes in a new postoperative patient
Experience helps the nurse recognize clinical changes and identify cues.
Choosing questions that give the most useful information
Experience teaches the types of questions that provide the most useful information.
Knowing patterns of response shown by similar patients
Knowing patterns from similar patients builds the ability to know patients and make judgments.
Assuming every new patient will respond like previous patients
Experience gives context, but each patient’s situation must still be assessed individually.
Relying on intuition instead of collecting assessment data
Intuition is used appropriately alongside data, not in place of it.
alt.ex: Correct: Recognizing subtle clinical changes in a new postoperative patient; Choosing questions that give the most useful information; Knowing patterns of response shown by similar patients.

items.q: Before performing any nursing procedure, what should the nurse assess thoroughly? Select all that apply.
o: Risk factors that affect how the skill is to be performed
Risk factors can change how a skill must be carried out safely.
The patient’s knowledge of the skill
Patient knowledge of the skill is part of the pre-procedure assessment.
Patient characteristics that might influence the skill outcome
Characteristics such as condition or mobility can affect the outcome of a skill.
How long the nurse took to perform the skill last time
The book focuses on the patient’s risk factors, knowledge, and characteristics, not the nurse’s timing.
Which other nurses on the unit prefer to do the skill
Colleague preferences are not part of assessing the patient before a procedure.
items.ex: Be thorough before any procedure: assess risk factors, patient knowledge of the skill, and patient characteristics affecting outcome.

alt.q: A nurse is about to perform a procedure on a patient. Which findings should the nurse gather beforehand? Select all that apply.
o: Conditions that would change how the procedure must be done
Risk factors that affect how a skill is performed are assessed before the procedure.
What the patient already understands about the procedure
Patient knowledge of the skill is part of the pre-procedure assessment.
Patient traits that could affect how the procedure turns out
Patient characteristics that might influence the outcome are assessed beforehand.
Whether the procedure can be shortened by skipping safety steps
Safe principles are never sacrificed when adapting a skill.
Whether the patient’s roommate has had the same procedure
Another patient’s history is not part of this patient’s assessment.
alt.ex: Correct: Conditions that would change how the procedure must be done; What the patient already understands about the procedure; Patient traits that could affect how the procedure turns out.

items.q: Which elements make up the “experience” component of critical thinking in assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Personal experience
Personal experience is listed under experience in the critical thinking model for assessment.
Clinical experience in assessment and physical examination
Clinical experience in assessment, examination, and knowing what to examine is part of experience.
Skill competence
Competence with skills is part of the experience component.
Time pressure
Time pressure is an environmental factor, not part of experience.
Intellectual standards in measurement
Intellectual standards belong to the standards component.
Curiosity
Curiosity is a critical thinking attitude, not an element of experience.
items.ex: The experience component includes personal experience, clinical experience in assessment and examination, and skill competence.

alt.q: A nurse educator lists elements of the experience component in the critical thinking model for assessment. Which items belong on the list? Select all that apply.
o: Knowing what to examine
Knowing what to examine is part of clinical experience in assessment.
Competence in performing nursing skills
Skill competence is part of the experience component.
Personal experience with family health situations
Personal experience is part of the experience component.
Setting where the assessment occurs
Setting is an environmental factor.
Agency policies and procedures
Agency policies and procedures belong to the standards component.
alt.ex: Correct: Knowing what to examine; Competence in performing nursing skills; Personal experience with family health situations.

items.q: Personal experiences, such as caring for an ill family member, can help a nurse understand a patient’s situation if the nurse does not let them bias the findings.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book encourages reflecting on personal experience to explore a patient’s situation while avoiding bias.
items.ww: Personal experiences are not inherently harmful; they help understanding when they are not allowed to bias findings.

alt.q: Because personal experiences always bias assessment findings, nurses should keep them entirely out of their thinking about patients.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Personal experiences can help nurses understand patients’ situations when they are not allowed to bias findings.
alt.ww: The book tells nurses to reflect on personal experience to explore a patient’s situation, not to exclude it.

items.q: Experience with nursing skills affects only the technical performance of procedures and has little effect on the accuracy of assessment.
items.a: False
items.ex: Skill experience, including competence in assessment and physical examination, is important for accurate assessment.
items.ww: The book states experience with nursing skills is important for accurate assessment, not just technical performance.

alt.q: Experience with nursing skills, including competence in performing a physical examination, is important for accurate assessment.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Repeated practice builds the competence in assessment and physical examination that accurate assessment requires.
alt.ww: Skill experience does affect assessment accuracy, so the statement cannot be false.

items.q: A nurse should be thorough in assessing a patient before performing any nursing procedure, even a routine one.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book says to be thorough in assessing a patient prior to performing any nursing procedure.
items.ww: There is no exception for routine procedures; assessment before any procedure supports safety.

alt.q: A thorough assessment before a procedure is needed only for complex procedures, not for routine ones the nurse performs often.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Thorough assessment is needed before any nursing procedure, regardless of how routine it is.
alt.ww: Frequent performance helps the nurse anticipate assessments; it does not remove the need for them.

items.q: Experience leads to [[pattern recognition|recognition of patterns]] in assessment data, allowing a nurse to quickly correlate data to form conclusions.
items.ex: Pattern recognition from experience lets nurses quickly and confidently correlate assessment data.

alt.q: An experienced nurse can quickly and confidently reach conclusions because experience builds [[pattern recognition|recognition of patterns]] in assessment data.
alt.ex: Pattern recognition from experience lets nurses quickly and confidently correlate assessment data.

items.q: Novice nurses usually apply the nursing process in a [[linear]] way, focusing only on the data collected.
items.ex: New nurses lack the experiences needed to place each patient situation into context, so they work linearly.

alt.q: Unlike experienced nurses, new nurses tend to use the nursing process in a [[linear]] fashion without considering the whole context.
alt.ex: New nurses lack the experiences needed to place each patient situation into context, so they work linearly.
