items.q: An emergency department nurse is assessing several newly arrived patients. What should primarily guide the nurse’s assessment of each patient?
items.a: The severity of each patient’s condition
items.ex: In the emergency department, the severity of each patient’s condition guides the assessment.
w: The order in which patients arrived
Arrival order does not set priority; severity of condition does.
The patient’s social and financial needs
A broad social and financial assessment fits the home care setting more than the emergency department.
The time remaining in the nurse’s shift
Time matters, but severity of condition guides emergency assessment.

alt.q: Which description of assessment in the emergency department matches the textbook?
alt.a: Quick, organized thinking to prioritize patients’ physical and psychological needs
alt.ex: The emergency department requires quick, organized thinking to prioritize physical and psychological needs.
w: Slow, comprehensive history taking for every patient before any treatment
Emergency care calls for quick prioritization by severity, not lengthy histories first.
Focus on physical needs only, leaving psychological needs to other settings
The book states both physical and psychological needs are prioritized.
Assessment of home conditions such as finances and culture for each patient
An array of social, financial, and cultural conditions is assessed in the home care setting.

items.q: Which advantage does the home care setting offer for nursing assessment?
items.a: It permits assessing social, financial, and cultural conditions that affect the patient’s health status.
items.ex: In the home, the nurse can assess an array of conditions, such as social, financial, and cultural factors, affecting health.
w: It eliminates the need for physical assessment because the patient is stable at home.
Physical assessment remains necessary; home patients’ conditions can change, often subtly.
It allows assessment to be guided only by the patient’s acute vital sign changes.
The home setting widens the assessment beyond acute physical changes to social and cultural factors.
It requires the quick, organized prioritization of many critically ill patients.
Quick prioritization of critically ill patients describes the emergency department setting.

alt.q: A home health nurse visits a patient recovering from heart failure. Which assessment is especially well suited to this setting?
alt.a: Assessing financial, social, and cultural conditions in the home that affect the patient’s health
alt.ex: Home care permits assessment of an array of conditions, such as social, financial, and cultural factors, in the home.
w: Assessing only cardiac rhythm because other factors are addressed in the hospital
Home care allows a broader assessment, not a narrower one.
Rapidly triaging the patient by severity as in an emergency department
Rapid triage by severity describes emergency department assessment.
Postponing assessment of the home until the patient is readmitted to the hospital
The home setting is the ideal place to assess home conditions affecting health.

items.q: Which features of a hospital nursing unit does the textbook identify as affecting how a nurse performs an assessment?
items.a: How patient rooms are designed, procedures for nursing activities, and staff resources
items.ex: On a hospital unit, room design, procedures for nursing activities, and staff resources affect assessment.
w: Patient finances, cultural practices, and the condition of the home
These conditions are assessed in the home care setting.
Severity of illness, triage category, and order of patient arrival
Severity guides assessment in the emergency department setting.
The nurse’s years of experience, specialty, and personal history
These relate to the nurse’s experience, not to the unit setting.

alt.q: A nurse is assigned to a unit where patient rooms are far apart and few assistive personnel are on duty. Which environmental factor does this situation illustrate?
alt.a: Setting
alt.ex: Room design and staff resources on a hospital unit are part of the setting, which affects assessment.
w: Interruptions
Interruptions are distractions during care, such as phone calls, not unit design or staffing.
Task complexity
Task complexity refers to the patient’s condition and number of procedures.
Personal experience
Personal experience is part of the experience component, not the environment.

items.q: A nurse on a medical unit is about to help a stable patient with a bed bath when a new patient arrives on the unit. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Delegate the bed bath to assistive personnel so the nurse can assess the new patient.
items.ex: The book gives delegating a task to assistive personnel (AP) as a way to free the nurse to assess a new patient.
w: Ask assistive personnel to complete the new patient’s admission assessment.
Assessing the new patient is the nurse’s role; the task delegated is the bath.
Finish the bed bath first and then assess the new patient at the next scheduled round.
Delaying the new patient’s assessment leaves needs unidentified; delegating the bath frees the nurse.
Ask the new patient to wait in the lounge until the end of the nurse’s current tasks.
The new patient needs assessment; the nurse should rearrange work through delegation.

alt.q: Why might a nurse delegate a routine task to assistive personnel at the start of a busy shift?
alt.a: So the nurse is free to assess a newly admitted patient
alt.ex: Considering the unit setting, a nurse might delegate a task to AP so the nurse can assess a new patient.
w: So assistive personnel can interpret the assessment data
Interpreting assessment data is a nursing responsibility, not a delegated task.
So the nurse can avoid doing any patient assessments that shift
The purpose is to make time for assessment, not to avoid it.
So assistive personnel can validate the nurse’s nursing diagnoses
Validation is done with other sources such as the EHR and team members, not by delegating diagnosis.

items.q: According to the textbook, what happens when a nurse does not spend enough time on patient assessment?
items.a: The nurse will be unable to identify patient needs accurately.
items.ex: Unless enough time is spent in assessment, the nurse cannot identify patient needs accurately.
w: The nurse will complete the shift with more time for other activities.
Saving time on assessment comes at the cost of failing to identify patient needs.
The patient’s needs will be identified later during evaluation.
Evaluation depends on an accurate assessment; it does not replace it.
The nurse will rely more appropriately on pattern recognition.
Pattern recognition depends on data; too little assessment time limits accurate identification of needs.

alt.q: A nurse says, “I’m too busy today to do more than glance at my patients.” Which response by the charge nurse reflects the textbook?
alt.a: “Without enough time spent assessing, we can’t identify patients’ needs accurately.”
alt.ex: Nurses who value assessment find time for it, because inadequate assessment prevents accurate identification of needs.
w: “That’s fine; assessments can wait until the next shift has more staff.”
Postponing assessment risks missing patient needs and changes in condition.
“Ask the patients to tell you if anything changes, and skip the assessment.”
Patient reports are important, but they do not replace the nurse’s assessment.
“Just check vital signs, because they show all the needs we must address.”
Vital signs alone do not identify all patient needs.

items.q: A nurse receives hand-off report at 0700. One patient is scheduled to leave the unit for a procedure at 0745, and medications are due at 0900. Which plan best manages time for assessment?
items.a: Assess the patient going for the procedure first, then assess others around the 0900 medication pass.
items.ex: Nurses organize assessments around hand-off reports, scheduled procedures such as medications, and when patients leave the unit.
w: Assess all patients in room-number order, beginning after the 0900 medication pass.
Room order ignores the patient who must leave the unit at 0745.
Delay all assessments until the patient returns from the procedure at the end of the shift.
Delaying assessments leaves patient needs unidentified for much of the shift.
Assess only the patient going for the procedure and skip assessment of the others today.
Every patient needs assessment; time management organizes it rather than eliminating it.

alt.q: Which events does the textbook say a nurse should consider when organizing time to assess each patient?
alt.a: When hand-off reports occur, when medications are scheduled, and when patients leave the unit
alt.ex: Organizing assessments around hand-offs, scheduled procedures, and patients leaving for procedures helps manage time.
w: When family members visit, when meals arrive, and when the nurse takes breaks
These are not the events the book names for organizing assessment time.
When the health care provider rounds, when lab results post, and when shifts end
The book names hand-offs, scheduled procedures, and patient departures, not these events.
When patients call for help, when alarms sound, and when phones ring
These are unscheduled events or interruptions, not a plan for organizing assessments.

items.q: Which tips does the textbook give for managing time for assessment? Select all that apply.
o: List the care activities that need to be done, including assessment.
Listing activities, including assessment, is the first time-management tip.
Prioritize the care activities.
Prioritizing activities helps the nurse focus on what matters most.
Estimate the time needed for each activity and spend it consciously.
Estimating and consciously spending time is one of the tips.
Cautiously spend time on unscheduled activities and learn to say “no.”
Unscheduled activities can consume time needed for assessment.
Postpone assessments until all scheduled tasks are complete.
Assessment is a care activity to be listed and prioritized, not postponed.
Agree to every unscheduled request to support teamwork.
The book advises caution with unscheduled activities and learning to say “no.”
items.ex: Time-management tips: list activities including assessment, prioritize them, estimate and consciously spend time, and be cautious with unscheduled activities.

alt.q: A nurse wants to manage time better so that patient assessments get done. Which strategies are consistent with the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Include assessment on the list of activities to complete
The first tip is to list care activities, including assessment.
Rank activities by priority
Prioritizing activities is one of the textbook’s tips.
Learn to say “no” to some unscheduled activities
The book advises cautiously spending time on unscheduled activities.
Spend time on activities without estimating how long they take
The book advises estimating the time for each activity and spending it consciously.
Use only scheduled rounds, not other encounters, for assessment
Each patient encounter is a time to perform an assessment.
alt.ex: Correct: Include assessment on the list of activities to complete; Rank activities by priority; Learn to say “no” to some unscheduled activities.

items.q: According to the textbook, what enables a nurse to manage task complexity during assessment?
items.a: The ability to prioritize patient needs
items.ex: Task complexity arises from the patient’s condition, numerous procedures, or both; prioritizing patient needs helps manage it.
w: The ability to perform every procedure faster
Speed is not the strategy the book gives; prioritizing needs is.
The decision to assess only the main diagnosis
Complex patients have several actual and potential problems that must be prioritized, not ignored.
The use of the same assessment for every patient
Complex situations call for prioritizing that patient’s needs, not a uniform assessment.

alt.q: A patient’s physical condition is unstable and the patient needs several procedures during the shift. Which skill will most help the nurse perform a high-quality assessment?
alt.a: Prioritizing the patient’s needs
alt.ex: Prioritizing patient needs enables the nurse to manage task complexity.
w: Postponing assessment until procedures are done
Delaying assessment leaves clinical changes unrecognized in a complex patient.
Delegating the assessment to assistive personnel
Assessment is the nurse’s responsibility; tasks may be delegated, not assessment.
Performing all procedures before any assessment
The nurse assesses to prioritize; procedures do not replace assessment.

items.q: A patient with diabetes mellitus had a colectomy and has developed a surgical wound infection. The patient is stable, has two IV lines, and reports incisional pain. Which assessment plan is best?
items.a: Check the surgical wound and pain status frequently, and assess the response to early mobility.
items.ex: For this complex patient, the nurse checks the wound and pain often, assesses response to early mobility, and may check stable vital signs less often.
w: Check routine vital signs every hour and the wound once per shift.
Routine vital signs might be performed less often if stable; the wound needs frequent checks.
Focus only on the IV lines, since medications treat the wound infection.
The wound, pain, and cardiopulmonary risks also need assessment, not only the IV lines.
Delay mobility assessment until the wound infection has fully resolved.
The book says assessment of the patient’s response to early mobility becomes important.

alt.q: In the textbook’s example of a patient with diabetes who develops a surgical wound infection, which assessment might the nurse perform less often if the patient is stable?
alt.a: Routine vital signs
alt.ex: Routine vital signs might be performed less often if the patient is stable, while the wound and pain are checked frequently.
w: Surgical wound checks
The nurse knows to check the surgical wound frequently.
Pain status checks
Pain from the surgical wound is checked frequently.
Response to early mobility
Assessment of response to early mobility becomes important for this patient.

items.q: Why does a patient with diabetes mellitus present greater task complexity for the nurse after surgery than a patient without diabetes?
items.a: Diabetes puts the patient at risk for infection and circulatory problems.
items.ex: Infection and circulatory problems are long-term complications of diabetes, adding to the problems the nurse must assess.
w: Diabetes prevents patients from reporting pain accurately after surgery.
The book does not say this; the example patient does experience and report wound pain.
Diabetes eliminates the usual postoperative cardiopulmonary risks.
The patient has the same postsurgical cardiopulmonary risks from immobility.
Diabetes makes early mobility unsafe for postoperative patients.
The book stresses assessing the patient’s response to early mobility, not avoiding it.

alt.q: Which long-term complications of diabetes mellitus does the textbook identify as increasing a surgical patient’s risk?
alt.a: Infection and circulatory problems
alt.ex: The book names infection and circulatory problems as long-term complications of diabetes that raise risk.
w: Hearing loss and visual problems
These are not the complications named in the task complexity example.
Anxiety and caregiver fatigue
These relate to emotional or family situations, not diabetes complications.
Pulmonary embolus and pneumonia
Cardiopulmonary risks come from immobility after surgery, not from diabetes in this example.

items.q: In the textbook’s example, which factors increase the task complexity of caring for a patient with diabetes after colectomy? Select all that apply.
o: A surgical wound infection
The patient develops a surgical wound infection, adding to the assessment load.
More than one IV line for medications
Multiple IV lines add procedures the nurse must manage and assess.
Postsurgical cardiopulmonary risks from immobility
The patient has the same cardiopulmonary risks resulting from immobility.
Pain from the surgical wound
The patient also experiences pain from the surgical wound.
A home environment with fall hazards
Home hazards are not part of this hospital task complexity example.
A recent loss of a job
Personal losses are not among the factors in this example.
items.ex: The patient’s wound infection, multiple IV lines, cardiopulmonary risks, and surgical pain combine to increase task complexity.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with diabetes after colectomy who has developed complications. Which findings should the nurse prioritize in ongoing assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Condition of the surgical wound
The nurse knows to check the surgical wound frequently.
Pain status
Pain from the surgical wound is checked frequently.
Response to early mobility
Assessing the response to early mobility becomes important.
Hourly routine vital signs while the patient is stable
Routine vital signs might be performed less often if the patient is stable.
Financial resources for the hospital stay
Finances are not a priority in this complex postoperative assessment.
alt.ex: Correct: Condition of the surgical wound; Pain status; Response to early mobility.

items.q: Research on interruptions during medication administration has shown a correlation with which outcome?
items.a: Medication administration errors
items.ex: Interruptions during medication administration are correlated with medication administration errors, one form of adverse event.
w: Improved accuracy of medication documentation
Interruptions are linked to errors, not to improved accuracy.
Shorter time spent at each patient’s bedside
The research cited links interruptions with errors, not with bedside time.
Greater patient satisfaction with nursing care
Interruptions are not linked with satisfaction in the text; they are linked with errors.

alt.q: A nurse manager wants to reduce medication administration errors on the unit. Based on the textbook, which factor should the manager address?
alt.a: Interruptions of nurses during medication administration
alt.ex: Interruptions during medication administration are common and correlated with medication errors.
w: The setting’s distance from the emergency department
Distance from another unit is not the factor the book links to medication errors.
The number of nurses with home care experience
Home care experience is unrelated to the research on medication errors.
How often patients ask about their medications
Patient questions are not the factor; interruptions of the nurse are.

items.q: A nurse is performing a necessary assessment before a procedure when a colleague asks a question and the nurse’s phone rings. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Take a time-out and avoid responding until the assessment is finished.
items.ex: The nurse avoids interruptions by taking a time-out and not responding to calls or questions during a necessary assessment.
w: Answer the phone quickly, then resume the assessment from where it stopped.
Responding to the phone interrupts the nurse’s critical thinking and full attention.
Answer the colleague first, because questions from staff take priority.
During a necessary assessment, the nurse avoids responding to questions from others.
Stop the assessment and finish it later from memory after the calls.
Stopping and relying on memory risks missing subtle signs and reduces accuracy.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows understanding of how interruptions affect assessment?
alt.a: “My full attention helps me notice subtle signs of a patient’s condition.”
alt.ex: Avoiding interruptions lets the nurse observe more subtle signs and focus on the priorities selected for the assessment.
w: “Interruptions only matter when I am giving medications, not when assessing.”
Interruptions affect assessment activities as well as medication administration.
“Answering my phone during assessment shows I am available to the team.”
Responding during a necessary assessment breaks the focus needed for critical thinking.
“I can assess accurately while answering questions from other staff.”
The book advises avoiding questions from others when performing a necessary assessment.

items.q: Why does a nurse perform an assessment upon entering a patient’s room to perform a procedure?
items.a: To ensure the safety and accuracy of the procedure
items.ex: When a nurse enters a room to perform a procedure, assessment is performed to ensure safety and accuracy.
w: To document a reason for delaying the procedure
Assessment is not done to justify delay; it supports safe, accurate care.
To satisfy the requirement for a daily head-to-toe examination
The purpose described is safety and accuracy of the procedure.
To decide whether to delegate the assessment to assistive personnel
Assessment is the nurse’s responsibility and is done to ensure safety and accuracy.

alt.q: A nurse enters a patient’s room to change an IV dressing and first observes the patient’s condition and the IV site. What is the main purpose of this assessment?
alt.a: To ensure the procedure is performed safely and accurately

items.q: A patient reports incisional pain rated 6 on a 0-to-10 scale. Which action by the nurse best demonstrates the attitude of discipline?
items.a: Asking what makes the pain worse, where exactly it hurts, and how the patient would describe it
items.ex: A disciplined thinker misses few details; asking specific questions about the pain’s character identifies problems more accurately.
w: Recording the pain rating and moving on to the next patient on the assignment
Recording only the rating misses details about the character of the pain.
Assuming the pain is expected because the patient had abdominal surgery
Assuming the cause skips the systematic data collection that discipline requires.
Asking the patient to rate the pain again in an hour before asking anything else
Repeating only the rating does not gather the specific details discipline calls for.

alt.q: Why does a disciplined nurse miss few details when assessing a patient?
alt.a: The nurse is orderly, systematic, and diligent with information, resources, and time.
alt.ex: A disciplined thinker is orderly, systematic, and diligent, so few details are missed.
w: The nurse relies on intuition to fill in any data that are missing.
Intuition does not replace the systematic data collection of a disciplined thinker.
The nurse limits assessment to the patient’s most obvious problem.
Narrowing the assessment would cause details to be missed.
The nurse repeats the same questions until the patient agrees.
Discipline involves systematic, specific questioning, not repeating questions.

items.q: A patient cannot speak after throat surgery. The nurse tries a message board, and when that does not work, tries an alarm bell until communication is effective. Which attitude does this demonstrate?
items.a: Perseverance
items.ex: Perseverance means continuing to look for resources and approaches until a successful one is found.
w: Confidence
Confidence is belief in one’s own judgment and skills, not persistence in trying approaches.
Fairness
Fairness means not letting bias or prejudice affect decisions.
Humility
Humility means admitting the limits of one’s knowledge and skill.

alt.q: Which action by a nurse best demonstrates perseverance during assessment?
alt.a: Trying different approaches until finding an effective way to communicate with the patient
alt.ex: A persevering nurse is not satisfied with minimal effort and keeps trying approaches until one works.
w: Accepting the first approach that was tried even though it did not work well
Settling for an approach that fails is the opposite of perseverance.
Documenting that the patient could not communicate and ending the interview
Stopping after one barrier reflects minimal effort, not perseverance.
Asking the patient’s family to complete the assessment instead of the patient
Family can validate data, but perseverance means continuing to seek a way to reach the patient.

items.q: Which statement best describes the attitude of curiosity during assessment?
items.a: Asking “Why?” and “What if?” motivates the nurse to inquire further when data patterns are unclear.
items.ex: Curiosity drives the nurse to investigate further, such as questioning family or providers, to get all needed information.
w: Accepting assessment data at face value avoids wasting time on further questions.
Accepting data without further inquiry is the opposite of curiosity.
Following the agency form exactly ensures the nurse never needs to inquire further.
Forms organize data, but curiosity leads the nurse beyond them when patterns are unclear.
Avoiding questions about the patient’s concerns keeps the focus on physical findings.
Curiosity includes exploring a patient’s knowledge and concerns.

alt.q: A nurse notices that a patient’s data form a pattern that is not clear. Which action shows curiosity?
alt.a: Asking “What if?” and questioning the family and health care provider for more information
alt.ex: Curiosity motivates the nurse to inquire further, such as questioning family or providers or reviewing the literature.
w: Recording the data and waiting to see if the pattern becomes clearer
Waiting without inquiry does not show curiosity.
Choosing the most common explanation and planning care around it
Settling quickly on an explanation skips the inquiry curiosity calls for.
Reporting that the data are normal because no single value is abnormal
Dismissing an unclear pattern is the opposite of curious inquiry.

items.q: A nursing student notices that a patient’s breathing has changed but is not sure whether the finding is important. Which action by the student is best?
items.a: Discuss the finding with the nursing instructor right away.
items.ex: When unsure of a clinical situation’s meaning, a student should discuss it with the instructor; patient safety is a priority.
w: Wait until the end of the shift to see whether the breathing worsens.
Waiting delays recognition of a possible clinical change; safety is a priority.
Decide the finding is unimportant to avoid appearing unsure.
Confident nurses are aware of the limits of their knowledge and seek help.
Perform an unfamiliar procedure to relieve the breathing problem.
Never perform a procedure without the knowledge base and confidence to do it.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student reflects an appropriate level of confidence?
alt.a: “I know the limits of my knowledge, so I ask my instructor when I’m unsure.”
alt.ex: Confidence includes awareness of the extent and limits of one’s knowledge; students discuss uncertain findings with instructors.
w: “I perform procedures I have read about, even if I feel unsure about them.”
The book says never perform a procedure unless you have the knowledge base and feel confident.
“Asking for help would show patients that I lack confidence.”
Recognizing limitations is part of confidence; patient safety comes first.
“If I’m confident, I can make decisions without checking any data.”
Confidence rests on knowledge and reasoned judgment, not on skipping data.

items.q: As a nurse’s confidence grows with experience, how does the nurse’s focus during patient care change?
items.a: From the nurse’s own needs to the patient’s needs
items.ex: Confidence grows with experience, shifting focus from remembering data meanings or procedure steps to the patient’s needs.
w: From the patient’s needs to the unit’s needs
Confidence shifts focus toward the patient, not away from the patient.
From the patient’s needs to the nurse’s own needs
This reverses the shift; confidence moves focus toward the patient.
From the team’s needs to the nurse’s own needs
Confidence moves the nurse’s attention to the patient, not inward.

alt.q: A new nurse spends most of a patient encounter trying to remember how to perform a procedure. What does the textbook say will happen as the nurse gains confidence?
alt.a: The nurse will shift focus from personal needs to the patient’s needs.
alt.ex: As confidence grows, the nurse shifts from personal concerns, such as remembering a procedure, to the patient’s needs.
w: The nurse will no longer need to recognize personal limitations.
Confidence grows by recognizing strengths and limitations, not by ignoring them.
The nurse will rely less on assessment and more on routine.
Confidence does not reduce the need for assessment.
The nurse will become anxious and hesitate to make decisions.
Anxiety and hesitation describe a lack of confidence.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient who is overweight and realizes she holds negative personal attitudes about obesity. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Recognize the bias and keep it from influencing how she assesses and cares for the patient.

w: Limit the assessment to weight-related problems, since they explain the patient’s symptoms.
Narrowing the assessment because of a personal attitude lets bias shape the data collected.
Ask the patient to explain why weight loss efforts have failed before assessing anything else.
Leading with the nurse’s concern reflects bias rather than a fair, patient-centered assessment.
Share her personal views with the patient so the relationship is honest from the start.
Sharing personal judgments does not keep bias out of care and harms the relationship.

alt.q: Which attitude is shown by a nurse who looks at a patient’s situation objectively and does not let personal prejudice affect assessment?
alt.a: Fairness
alt.ex: Fairness means dealing with situations justly and not letting bias or prejudice affect decisions.
w: Risk taking
Risk taking is trying different ways to solve problems without harm to the patient.
Perseverance
Perseverance is persisting until an effective approach is found.
Creativity
Creativity is original thinking that leads to feasible solutions.

items.q: A nurse is tempted to prepare medication doses for several patients at once to save time. Which attitude should lead the nurse to avoid this shortcut?
items.a: Responsibility
items.ex: Responsibility means being accountable for decisions and actions and correctly performing care based on standards, without shortcuts.
w: Curiosity
Curiosity drives further inquiry into unclear data, not adherence to standards.
Creativity
Creativity finds new solutions while following standards; it does not address shortcuts here.
Confidence
Confidence is belief in one’s judgment and skills, not accountability for following standards.

alt.q: Which action by a nurse best demonstrates the attitude of responsibility?
alt.a: Identifying each patient before giving a medication rather than skipping that step
alt.ex: Responsible nurses perform care correctly based on standards of practice and avoid shortcuts such as skipping patient identification.
w: Preparing several patients’ medications together to finish the medication pass on time
Preparing doses for multiple patients at once is a shortcut the book warns against.
Skipping patient identification for patients the nurse has cared for before
Skipping identification is a work-around that violates standards of practice.
Letting the next shift decide whether a missed assessment should be completed
Responsible nurses are accountable for their own decisions and actions.

items.q: In the case study, what did Tonya do that demonstrated curiosity and discipline when Mr. Lawson became restless?

items.ex: Tonya displayed curiosity and discipline by asking Mr. Lawson questions to learn about him and the nature of his concerns.

This would not gather information; Tonya sought to learn the cause of his restlessness.
She documented his restlessness as expected anxiety and continued with routine care.
Accepting the finding without inquiry is the opposite of curiosity and discipline.
She asked the next shift to explore his concerns because she was busy with others.
Tonya pursued the information herself, showing curiosity and discipline.

alt.q: Mr. Lawson is restless, and Tonya wants to learn more. Which question would best show curiosity about his situation?

“Your vital signs are fine, so you should feel better soon, right?”
This gives false reassurance and closes off further information.
“Do you want me to call the health care provider for you?”
This does not gather information about his concerns.

items.q: Which statement best describes a nurse who thinks independently during assessment?

w: The nurse ignores the ideas of other team members and relies only on personal opinion.
Independent thinking does not mean ignoring others’ ideas; it means considering all sides.
The nurse waits for the health care provider’s direction before forming any judgment.
Waiting for direction is not independent thinking; Tonya recognized and reported changes herself.
The nurse follows the most experienced colleague’s conclusion without further thought.
Accepting another’s ideas without question is the opposite of independent thinking.

alt.q: Tonya recognized developing signs and symptoms suggesting a major breathing problem in Mr. Lawson and reported them to the physician. Which attitude does this show?
alt.a: Independent thinking
alt.ex: Tonya applied independent thinking when she recognized Mr. Lawson’s developing signs and reported them to the physician.
w: Humility

Fairness
Fairness concerns keeping bias out of decisions.
Perseverance
Perseverance is persisting with different approaches until one succeeds.

items.q: A nurse wants to try a nonpharmacological approach to pain relief that is new for a patient. Which action shows appropriate risk taking?
items.a: Following safety guidelines, analyzing possible dangers, and involving the patient in the decision
items.ex: Desirable risk taking follows safety guidelines, analyzes dangers, involves the patient, and is well reasoned.
w: Trying the approach without telling the patient so expectations do not affect results
Risk taking should involve the patient in decisions.
Trying several new approaches at once to find the best one as quickly as possible
Risk taking should be well reasoned and logical, not haphazard.
Avoiding any new approach because any risk is unacceptable in patient care
The book says risk taking can be desirable when it leads to a positive outcome without harm.

alt.q: According to the textbook, where does a nurse’s willingness to take risks without causing harm to a patient come from?

alt.ex: The willingness to take risks without harming a patient comes from experience with similar clinical problems.

Avoiding involvement of the patient

Preference is not the basis; experience with similar problems is.

items.q: While waiting for the medical team, Tonya showed discipline in further assessing Mr. Lawson. Which actions are examples of this? Select all that apply.

Talking with him helped reduce anxiety and detect changes in consciousness.

Leaving him alone so he could rest until the team arrived

Systematic rechecking helps the nurse miss few details.
Asking specific questions about the character of new pain
Specific questions about pain reflect a disciplined, thorough approach.
Observing the surgical wound and incision
Observing the wound is part of a thorough, orderly assessment.
Asking only for a 0-to-10 pain rating
A rating alone misses details a disciplined nurse would gather.

items.q: Which actions demonstrate the attitude of responsibility? Select all that apply.
o: Performing care correctly based on standards of practice
Responsible nurses perform care correctly based on standards of practice.
Knowing the limits and scope of one’s practice
Nurses are accountable for knowing the limits and scope of their practice.
Being accountable for the outcomes of one’s actions
Responsibility includes accountability for decisions and their outcomes.
Using work-arounds when the unit is busy
Shortcuts or work-arounds violate standards of practice.
Skipping patient identification for familiar patients
Skipping identification is a shortcut that responsible nurses avoid.
items.ex: Responsibility is knowing you are accountable for your decisions, actions, and critical thinking.

alt.q: A nurse is reflecting on what it means to be responsible in practice. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

Accountability for decisions and outcomes is the core of responsibility.
“I follow standards of practice rather than taking shortcuts.”
Standards set the minimum acceptable level of performance.
“I need to know the limits and scope of my practice.”
Knowing the limits and scope of practice is part of responsibility.
“Shortcuts are acceptable if no harm results.”
Shortcuts violate standards of practice even if no harm is seen.

items.q: A thorough patient assessment relies on the nurse applying all of the critical thinking attitudes.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states that a thorough assessment relies on nurses applying all critical thinking attitudes.
items.ww: No single attitude is enough; the book says all attitudes are applied.

alt.a: False
alt.ex: A thorough assessment relies on all critical thinking attitudes, not just curiosity and discipline.
alt.ww: The book says all attitudes are applied in assessment, so limiting them to two is incorrect.

items.q: Confidence grows with experience in recognizing one’s own strengths and limitations.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book links growing confidence to experience recognizing strengths and limitations.
items.ww: Confidence develops through experience and self-awareness, so the statement is accurate.

alt.q: A confident nurse does not need to acknowledge the limits of personal knowledge.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Confident nurses are always aware of the extent and limits of their knowledge.
alt.ww: Ignoring limits threatens patient safety; awareness of limits is part of confidence.

items.q: A nurse who perseveres is not satisfied with minimal effort and works to achieve the highest quality level of care.

items.ex: Perseverance means being resilient and determined to find effective solutions to care problems.

alt.q: Perseverance means continuing with the first approach chosen, even when it is not working, until the problem resolves.
alt.a: False

items.q: [[Confidence]] is the belief in oneself, one’s judgment and skills, and one’s possession of the knowledge and ability to think critically.

alt.q: A nurse who believes in her own judgment, skills, knowledge, and ability to think critically shows the attitude of [[confidence]].

items.q: A disciplined thinker is orderly, [[systematic]], and diligent with information, resources, and time when making decisions.

items.q: During a home visit, a nurse observes that a 72-year-old patient walks with an unsteady gait. Which conclusion should the nurse recognize immediately?

items.ex: The book states the nurse should immediately recognize an unsteady gait as a fall risk factor.

An unsteady gait signals fall risk; it should not be dismissed as normal.
The unsteady gait is caused by visual problems.
Vision is assessed as a possible contributor, but the cause is not assumed.
The unsteady gait means the patient needs bed rest.
The nurse assesses fall risk further; restricting activity is not the conclusion.

alt.q: A home health nurse notes that an older adult patient walks unsteadily. Which nursing concern is most directly suggested by this finding?
alt.a: Risk for falls
alt.ex: An unsteady gait is a fall risk factor, which the nurse should recognize immediately.
w: Risk for infection
Gait problems are not a sign of infection risk.
Risk for phlebitis
Phlebitis relates to IV sites, not gait.
Risk for caregiver fatigue
Caregiver fatigue relates to family caregivers, not the patient’s gait.

items.q: A home health nurse has a patient with an unsteady gait perform a Timed Up and Go test and observes the patient walking down a hallway. Which intellectual standard is the nurse applying?

items.ex: Using the Timed Up and Go test and observing gait helps the nurse be precise and specific in assessment.
w: Being broad
Broad means covering multiple viewpoints, such as patient and family.
Being plausible
Plausible means reasonable or probable, not exact measurement.
Being consistent
Consistent refers to expressing consistent beliefs or values.

alt.q: Which assessment would help a nurse be precise and specific when evaluating an older adult’s balance?

alt.ex: The Timed Up and Go test is an evidence-based clinical test for balance that makes assessment precise and specific.
w: Asking the patient if they ever feel dizzy
This is a useful question, but the book’s example of precision is the Timed Up and Go test.
Reviewing the patient’s list of current medications
Medication review is helpful but is not the precise balance test described.
Asking the family whether the patient seems steady
Family reports add data but are less precise than a standardized balance test.

items.q: A home health nurse is assessing an older adult with an unsteady gait. Which action applies the intellectual standard of relevance?

items.ex: The nurse applies relevance by assessing fall history and the home environment, which bear directly on fall risk.
w: Measuring the time the patient needs to rise, walk, and return to sitting
This is the Timed Up and Go test, used to be precise and specific.
Watching the patient walk a short distance down the hallway
Observing gait is part of being precise and specific.
Assessing the color, warmth, and drainage at the patient’s IV site
These are phlebitis criteria from professional standards, not part of this fall assessment.

alt.q: In the textbook’s home health example, assessing an older adult’s history of falls and home environment illustrates which intellectual standard?
alt.a: Relevance
alt.ex: Fall history and home environment are essential to the patient’s fall risk, illustrating relevance.
w: Precision
Precision is shown by the Timed Up and Go test and gait observation.
Clarity
Clarity refers to plain, understandable communication.
Plausibility
Plausibility means reasonable or probable, not essential to the situation.

items.q: Why does the home health nurse assess the vision of a 72-year-old patient who has an unsteady gait?

w: To determine whether the patient can read medication labels at home
Reading labels matters, but the book links vision assessment here to ambulation.
To complete the vision screening required for every home visit
The book ties this vision check to gait and fall risk, not a routine requirement.
To decide whether the patient may continue to drive a car safely

alt.q: A home health nurse assessing an older adult’s unsteady gait also checks the patient’s vision. What is the nurse looking for?

Changes that would explain the patient’s mood
The book links this vision check to ambulation, not mood.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with a peripheral IV line. Which assessment reflects the Infusion Nurses Society criteria for phlebitis?

Auscultating over the IV site and asking the patient to rate overall comfort
Auscultation is not part of the described phlebitis assessment.
Checking the infusion pump rate and counting the drops in the drip chamber
These check the infusion, not the signs of phlebitis at the site.

alt.q: A nurse inspects a patient’s IV site, notes the skin color, palpates for warmth, and looks for drainage. Which guides this assessment?

The patient’s request for a specific type of check
The assessment follows standard criteria rather than patient requests.

Broad thinking covers multiple viewpoints; this assessment follows a professional standard.

items.q: How do professional standards improve a nurse’s ability to identify patient problems during assessment?
items.a: They let the nurse compare actual findings with what the standard sets as normal or abnormal.

w: They replace the need for the nurse to gather data from the patient directly.

Validation remains necessary; standards help judge whether findings are normal.
They require the nurse to assess every body system at every encounter.
Standards guide what is normal or abnormal, not a full examination every time.

alt.q: A nurse compares a patient’s IV site findings with published criteria for phlebitis. What is the main benefit of this practice?

Standards improve accuracy, not the number of assessments.
Less need to document the IV site findings
Documentation remains necessary.
No need to report abnormal findings
Abnormal findings identified with standards still need reporting and action.

items.q: Which definition of an intellectual standard matches the textbook?

items.ex: An intellectual standard is a guideline or principle for rational thought, applied during all steps of the nursing process.

alt.q: A nurse uses principles such as accuracy, relevance, and precision to guide data collection. What are these principles called?

alt.ex: Intellectual standards are guidelines for rational thought, such as accuracy, relevance, and precision.
w: Agency policies
Agency policies are procedural rules set by an organization.
Clinical practice guidelines
Clinical practice guidelines are professional standards for specific clinical care.
Critical thinking attitudes
Attitudes include curiosity and discipline, not accuracy or precision.

items.q: According to the textbook, what does routine use of intellectual standards in clinical practice prevent?
items.a: Performing critical thinking haphazardly
items.ex: Routinely applying intellectual standards keeps critical thinking from being haphazard.

Intuition can be used appropriately; standards prevent haphazard thinking.
Delegating tasks to assistive personnel
Delegation is unrelated to intellectual standards.
Asking patients open-ended questions
Open-ended questions are a communication technique, not something standards prevent.

alt.q: A nurse says, “I use intellectual standards every day, not only for difficult cases.” What benefit does the textbook give for this routine use?
alt.a: Critical thinking is not carried out haphazardly.

w: Assessment can be shortened for stable patients.
Standards guide rational thought; they are not a reason to shorten assessment.
Professional standards are no longer needed.
Intellectual and professional standards are both used.
Data no longer need to be validated.
Validation of data is still required.

items.q: Which description of professional standards for critical thinking matches the textbook?
items.a: Ethical criteria for judgments, evidence-based criteria for evaluation, and criteria for professional responsibility
items.ex: Professional standards include ethical criteria, evidence-based evaluation criteria, and criteria for professional responsibility.
w: Personal values, preferences, and past experiences of the individual nurse
Personal experience is a separate component; standards are shared professional criteria.
Time pressure, setting, task complexity, and interruptions on the unit
These are environmental factors that affect assessment.
Perseverance, curiosity, confidence, discipline, and responsibility
These are critical thinking attitudes, not professional standards.

alt.q: A nurse uses evidence-based criteria to evaluate a patient’s IV site and considers ethical criteria when making judgments. Which component of critical thinking is the nurse applying?

w: Environment
Environment includes setting, time pressure, task complexity, and interruptions.
Attitudes
Attitudes include curiosity, discipline, and confidence.
Experience
Experience includes personal and clinical experience and skill competence.

items.q: A nurse works in a Medicare-certified long-term care agency. Which structured format will the nurse most likely use to organize residents’ assessment data?

w: The Timed Up and Go test
This is a balance test, not a database format.
The ABCDE emergency approach
ABCDE is a rapid screening for critically ill patients.
The Infusion Nurses Society criteria
These are criteria for phlebitis at IV sites.

alt.q: What does a theory or practice standard provide when a nurse uses a structured database format for a nursing history?
alt.a: The categories of information to assess

A structured database organizes nursing data; it does not provide a medical diagnosis.
The priority order of nursing interventions
Interventions are planned later; the framework sets assessment categories.
The schedule for routine vital signs
Vital sign schedules are not what the framework supplies.

items.q: Which statement describes standards of practice?

Standards set a minimum level for all nurses, not an expert-only level.
Optional suggestions nurses may follow when time permits
Nurses are responsible for performing care based on standards of practice.
Personal guidelines each nurse develops from experience
Standards are professional, not personal, criteria.

alt.q: A nurse follows standards of practice when performing care. What level of performance do these standards represent?
alt.a: The minimum level accepted to ensure high-quality care

w: The maximum level that any nurse can achieve
Standards are a minimum, not a maximum.

Standards apply to all nurses.
A level required only in acute care hospitals
Standards apply across practice settings.

items.q: A home health nurse is assessing a 72-year-old patient with an unsteady gait. Which actions are consistent with the textbook’s example? Select all that apply.
o: Having the patient perform the Timed Up and Go test
The test is an evidence-based measure of balance that makes the assessment precise.
Observing the patient walk a short distance down the hallway
Observing gait adds precise, specific data about mobility.
Assessing the patient’s vision
Visual problems might contribute to limitations in ambulation.
Assessing the patient’s history of falls and the home environment
These are relevant to fall risk.
Advising the patient to stay in bed until the next visit
Restricting activity is not part of the assessment described.
Postponing gait assessment until a provider visit
The nurse recognizes fall risk immediately and assesses it.
items.ex: The nurse uses precise tests, observes gait, checks vision, and assesses relevant fall history and home conditions.

alt.q: Which data should a nurse collect to assess fall risk in an older adult with an unsteady gait at home? Select all that apply.
o: Results of a Timed Up and Go test
This evidence-based test measures balance precisely.
Visual problems that might limit ambulation
Vision is assessed because it may contribute to limited ambulation.
Previous falls
History of falls is relevant to fall risk.
Condition of the IV site
IV site condition relates to phlebitis, not fall risk.
Skin temperature at the IV site
This is a phlebitis criterion, not a fall risk assessment.
alt.ex: Correct: Results of a Timed Up and Go test; Visual problems that might limit ambulation; Previous falls.

items.q: Which items are part of the standards component of critical thinking in assessment? Select all that apply.
o: ANA Nursing: Scope and Standards of Practice
The ANA scope and standards are part of the standards component.
Clinical practice guidelines
Clinical practice guidelines and standards of practice are included.
Intellectual standards in measurement
Intellectual standards in measurement are part of standards.
Agency policies and procedures
Agency policies and procedures are included in standards.
Skill competence
Skill competence belongs to the experience component.
Interruptions
Interruptions are an environmental factor.
items.ex: Standards include ANA scope and standards, clinical guidelines, intellectual standards, agency policies, professional and ethical standards.

alt.q: A nurse educator asks students to identify standards that guide assessment. Which answers are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Ethical standards
Ethical standards are part of the standards component.
Professional standards of care
Professional standards of care guide assessment.
Agency policies and procedures
Agency policies and procedures are included in standards.
Time pressure on the unit
Time pressure is an environmental factor.
Curiosity about patient concerns
Curiosity is a critical thinking attitude.
Personal experience with illness
Personal experience belongs to the experience component.
alt.ex: Correct: Ethical standards; Professional standards of care; Agency policies and procedures.

items.q: Which statements about using standards in assessment are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Intellectual standards influence how a nurse conducts an assessment.
The book states intellectual standards influence how assessment is conducted.
Professional standards or clinical guidelines influence assessment.
Professional standards and guidelines, such as phlebitis criteria, shape assessment.
Standards help the nurse compare findings with what is normal or abnormal.
This comparison improves problem identification.
Standards replace the need for the nurse’s clinical judgment.
Standards support judgment; the nurse still interprets and validates data.
Intellectual standards apply only to the planning step of the nursing process.
Intellectual standards apply during all steps, including assessment.
items.ex: Intellectual and professional standards guide data collection and help the nurse identify abnormal findings.

alt.q: A nurse is reflecting on the role of standards during assessment. Which statements reflect the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: “I reflect on intellectual standards to guide my data collection.”
The book advises reflecting on intellectual standards to guide data collection.
“Evidence-based criteria help me judge whether a finding is abnormal.”
Standards set what is normal or abnormal, improving problem identification.
“Professional guidelines tell me which signs to look for at an IV site.”
The Infusion Nurses Society criteria define signs of phlebitis.
“Standards matter only for new nurses who lack experience.”
Standards guide all nurses’ assessments, regardless of experience.
“Once I find one abnormal finding, standards no longer apply.”
Standards continue to guide the whole assessment.
alt.ex: Correct: “I reflect on intellectual standards to guide my data collection.”; “Evidence-based criteria help me judge whether a finding is abnormal.”; “Professional guidelines tell me which signs to look for at an IV site.”

items.q: Intellectual standards influence how a nurse conducts an assessment.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states intellectual standards influence how assessment is conducted and guide data collection.
items.ww: Intellectual standards apply during all steps of the nursing process, including assessment.

alt.q: The Timed Up and Go test is an evidence-based screening test for visual problems in older adults.

items.q: Comparing a patient’s actual assessment findings with what a standard sets as normal or abnormal improves problem identification.
items.a: True
items.ex: Standards give criteria for normal and abnormal findings, which improves problem identification.

alt.q: Experienced nurses no longer need to compare their findings with standards because their judgment identifies problems more accurately.

alt.ww: Experience supports judgment, but standards still improve problem identification for every nurse.

alt.ex: The Infusion Nurses Society has evidence-based criteria for the signs of phlebitis.

items.q: The [[Timed Up and Go|TUG|Timed Up and Go test]] test is an evidence-based clinical test for balance.
