items.q: A nurse asks a newly admitted patient why they came for care today. Which entry best documents the patient’s chief concern?
items.a: Patient states, “I’ve had a burning pain in my stomach for 3 days.”
items.ex: The chief concern is a brief statement in the patient’s own words, documented in quotation marks as subjective data.
w: Patient appears to have gastritis based on the reported symptoms.
This is the nurse’s interpretation, not the patient’s own statement of why care was sought.
Epigastric burning pain, onset 3 days ago, rated 6 out of 10.
This is the nurse’s clinical summary, not a brief statement in the patient’s own words.
Patient is a 52-year-old accountant referred by a family provider.
Age, occupation, and referral source are biographical information, not the chief concern.

alt.q: Why does the nurse place a patient’s chief concern in quotation marks when documenting it?
alt.a: To show that it is a subjective statement in the patient’s own words
alt.ex: Quotation marks indicate subjective data recorded exactly as the patient stated it.
w: To show that the nurse has confirmed it with a physical examination
Quotation marks mark the patient’s own words, not confirmation by examination.
To show that the health care provider has reviewed the statement
Quotation marks do not indicate provider review; they identify subjective patient statements.
To show that it is objective data gathered through observation
A patient’s statement is subjective data; observations are objective data.

items.q: Which set of data is classified as biographical information in the nursing health history?
items.a: Age, occupation, marital status, and referral source
items.ex: Biographical information is factual demographic data such as age, gender, address, insurance, occupation, marital status, and referral source.
w: Allergies, past surgeries, and current medications
These belong in the past health history, not biographical data.
Sleep, exercise, nutrition, and coping patterns
These lifestyle patterns are part of the past health history.
Normal function and changes in each body system
This describes the review of systems, not biographical data.

alt.q: A nurse records a patient’s address, insurance information, and working status. Which component of the health history is the nurse completing?
alt.a: Biographical information
alt.ex: Address, insurance, and working status are factual demographic data that make up biographical information.
w: Psychosocial history
The psychosocial history covers support systems, recent losses, and coping with stress and grief.
Past health history
The past health history covers hospitalizations, surgeries, medications, allergies, and habits.
Review of systems
The review of systems collects subjective data about each body system.

items.q: During the health history, a patient reports breaking out in hives after receiving penicillin and needing emergency treatment. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Record the specific reaction and its treatment on the assessment form and the allergy armband.
items.ex: For any allergy, the nurse notes the specific reaction and treatment on the assessment form and the special armband.
w: Record “penicillin allergy” and omit the details of the reaction to keep the entry concise.
Nonspecific entries leave readers with only general impressions; the reaction and treatment must be noted.
Wait to document the allergy until a family member confirms that the reaction occurred.
The patient’s report is documented now; delaying leaves the allergy unavailable to others caring for the patient.
Document the allergy only if the reaction happened within the past year.
All allergy history is relevant regardless of when the reaction occurred.

alt.q: Which allergy entry in a nursing health history is most complete?
alt.a: Latex: generalized hives, treated in emergency department; allergy armband applied.
alt.ex: A complete allergy entry includes the agent, the specific reaction, the treatment required, and the armband.
w: Latex allergy reported by patient; details unknown at this time today.
This entry lacks the specific reaction and treatment the patient could describe.
Latex: hives; patient unsure whether any treatment was given.
This omits the treatment and the special armband required for allergies.
Allergic to some medical supplies; patient will clarify later.
This is vague and does not name the agent, reaction, or treatment.

items.q: A patient says, “My chest pain gets worse when I climb stairs and goes away when I rest.” Which part of the PQRST assessment does this information address?
items.a: Provokes
items.ex: Provokes covers precipitating and relieving factors, such as what makes a symptom better or worse.
w: Quality
Quality describes what the symptom feels like, such as sharp or dull.
Radiate
Radiate describes where the symptom is located and whether it spreads.
Time
Time describes onset, duration, and how often the symptom occurs.

alt.q: Which question assesses the “R” component of the PQRST assessment?
alt.a: “Does the pain stay in one place or move anywhere else?”
alt.ex: Radiate asks where the symptom is located and whether it goes anywhere else.
w: “What makes the pain better or worse for you?”
This addresses Provokes, the precipitating and relieving factors.
“What does the pain feel like when it starts?”
This addresses Quality, what the symptom feels like.
“When did the pain first start bothering you?”
This addresses Time, the onset and duration of the symptom.

items.q: A patient reports abdominal pain but says, “I don’t know how to describe it; it just hurts.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Would you say the pain is sharp, or is it more of a dull pain?”
items.ex: When a patient has difficulty describing the quality of a symptom, the nurse offers probes such as sharp or dull.
w: “That’s fine; I will record it as a cramping type of pain.”
Quality should be in the patient’s own words; the nurse should not assign a description.
“Then let’s skip that question and talk about your medicines.”
Skipping quality leaves the symptom incompletely described; probes help the patient describe it.
“Just tell me how bad it is on a scale of 0 to 10.”
The severity rating is useful but does not describe what the pain feels like.

alt.q: A patient reports feeling “funny” when standing up but cannot explain further. Which nurse response best clarifies the quality of this symptom?
alt.a: “Do you feel light-headed, dizzy, or off-balance when you stand?”
alt.ex: Offering specific descriptive probes helps a patient who has difficulty describing a symptom’s quality.
w: “How many times a day does this happen when you stand?”
This explores timing and frequency, not what the symptom feels like.
“Rate how bad the feeling is on a scale of 0 to 10.”
This measures severity, not the quality of the symptom.
“What do you think is causing you to feel this way?”
This explores provoking factors and perceived causes, not quality.

items.q: During a comprehensive health history, the nurse asks about a patient’s self-concept, body image, mood, and coping mechanisms. Which health dimension is the nurse assessing?
items.a: Emotional
items.ex: The emotional dimension includes behavioral and emotional status, support system, self-concept, body image, mood, sexuality, and coping.
w: Intellectual
The intellectual dimension includes problem solving, educational level, communication patterns, and attention span.
Spiritual
The spiritual dimension includes beliefs and meaning, religious experiences, rituals, and practices.
Social
The social dimension includes financial status, recreational activities, primary language, and cultural heritage.

alt.q: Which data belong to the intellectual dimension of a comprehensive health history?
alt.a: Problem solving, educational level, and attention span
alt.ex: The intellectual dimension covers intellectual performance, problem solving, educational level, communication patterns, and attention span.
w: Beliefs and meaning, religious experiences, and rituals
These belong to the spiritual dimension.
Financial status, primary language, and recreation
These belong to the social dimension.
Self-concept, body image, and coping mechanisms
These belong to the emotional dimension.

items.q: What is the main objective of obtaining a patient’s family history?
items.a: To determine risk for genetic or familial illness and identify health promotion needs
items.ex: The family history identifies risk for illnesses of a genetic or familial nature and areas for health promotion and illness prevention.
w: To verify the patient’s insurance coverage and identify the referral source
Insurance and referral source are part of biographical information.
To list the patient’s past surgeries, hospitalizations, and injuries
These are part of the patient’s own past health history.
To determine which family member will make all care decisions
Decision making is explored in cultural assessment; the family history focuses on risk and family support.

alt.q: A patient’s mother and sister both had breast cancer. According to the textbook, how does this family history guide care?
alt.a: It guides risk assessment, such as annual mammograms and possible breast MRI.
alt.ex: A family history of breast cancer guides screening such as annual mammograms, often breast MRI, and genetic counseling for children.
w: It has little effect on care unless the patient already has symptoms.
Family history guides screening for at-risk patients even before symptoms appear.
It applies only to the relatives and not to the patient’s own screening.
Screening guidelines apply to the patient and to family members at risk.
It is used mainly to plan which relative will be the family caregiver.
Family structure helps plan caregiving, but this history primarily guides risk assessment.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse that his adult son is critical of him and that their conversations usually end in arguments. The nurse is planning discharge teaching. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Avoid involving the son in the patient’s care and teaching.
items.ex: If a patient’s family is not supportive, the nurse does not involve the family in care.
w: Include the son in every teaching session to improve the relationship.
Stressful family relationships can be a barrier; an unsupportive family is not involved in care.
Require the son to attend discharge teaching before the patient leaves.
Requiring an unsupportive family member’s involvement conflicts with the textbook’s guidance.
Ask the son to make the patient’s care decisions after discharge.
Giving decision making to an unsupportive family member is inappropriate and not patient centered.

alt.q: Mrs. Lawson tells Tonya, “I feel I can do whatever is needed for him.” Tonya’s assessment shows a supportive pattern. What should Tonya do with this finding?
alt.a: Include Mrs. Lawson when providing patient education.
alt.ex: Because Mrs. Lawson is supportive and able to help, Tonya includes her in patient education.
w: Exclude Mrs. Lawson so the patient learns to manage on his own.
Excluding a willing, supportive spouse removes a resource for the patient’s adjustment at home.
Teach only Mrs. Lawson because the patient may resist restrictions.
The patient remains the focus of teaching; the supportive spouse is included, not substituted.
Refer Mrs. Lawson for a caregiver stress evaluation right away.
Her statements show readiness and support, not caregiver stress needing referral.

items.q: During the psychosocial history, a patient says that walking and reading help him cope with stress at home. How can the nurse best use this information?
items.a: Use walking or reading as nursing interventions if he becomes stressed during care.
items.ex: Coping behaviors a patient uses at home can serve as nursing interventions when stress occurs during health care.
w: Record it only as background because home habits do not apply in the hospital.
The textbook states home coping behaviors can be used as nursing interventions.
Discourage these activities and teach new coping methods to replace them.
Effective existing coping behaviors are built on, not replaced.
Report it to the health care provider as a sign of ineffective coping.
Walking and reading are healthy coping strategies, not signs of ineffective coping.

alt.q: Which information is collected as part of the psychosocial history?
alt.a: Recent losses and how the patient and family cope with stress and grief
alt.ex: The psychosocial history covers support systems, recent loss, and how patient and family typically cope with stress and grief.
w: Illnesses in immediate and blood relatives that suggest inherited risk
This information belongs in the family history.
The presence or absence of problems in each body system
This information is gathered in the review of systems.
Age, address, insurance information, and working status
These are biographical data.

items.q: A patient arrives at the emergency department with sudden shortness of breath. Which approach to the review of systems is most appropriate?
items.a: A problem-focused review that prioritizes systems related to the patient’s condition
items.ex: A problem-focused review is common in emergent situations; the systems prioritized depend on the patient’s condition and urgency.
w: A comprehensive review of every body system before care begins
A comprehensive review fits a nonemergent admission or initial home visit, not an emergency.
Asking every question on the admission form for each system
With structured forms, nurses usually do not cover every question each time, especially when urgent.
Postponing the review until the physical examination is finished
Findings from the review help focus the physical examination, so it is not deferred.

alt.q: In which situation is a nurse most likely to complete a comprehensive review of all body systems?
alt.a: A nonemergent admission to a clinic
alt.ex: A comprehensive review of systems is more likely during a nonemergent clinic admission or an initial home visit.
w: A rapid response call for a patient in distress
Emergent situations call for a problem-focused review.
An emergency department visit for acute chest pain
Emergent situations call for a problem-focused review.
A brief recheck of a patient during ongoing care
Ongoing situations commonly use a problem-focused review.

items.q: A patient scheduled for a biopsy tells the nurse, “I’m not worried at all.” The nurse notes poor eye contact, shakiness, and restlessness. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Recognize that verbal and nonverbal data conflict and gather more data about anxiety.
items.ex: These behaviors suggest anxiety; conflicting verbal and nonverbal data direct the nurse to gather more objective information.
w: Document that the patient has no concerns about the upcoming procedure.
Documenting only the verbal statement ignores nonverbal cues that conflict with it.
Accept the statement because a patient’s words are the most reliable data.
The nurse determines whether observed behavior matches what the patient says.
Reassure the patient that there is nothing to worry about with a biopsy.
False reassurance does not assess the patient’s apparent anxiety.

alt.q: A patient denies concern about surgery but is restless, shaky, and avoids eye contact. What do these findings most likely suggest?
alt.a: Anxiety, with verbal and nonverbal data in conflict
alt.ex: Poor eye contact, shakiness, and restlessness suggest anxiety that conflicts with the patient’s verbal statement.
w: Calm acceptance, with verbal and nonverbal data in agreement
The behaviors contradict the patient’s statement, so the data do not agree.
Pain, with verbal and nonverbal data in agreement
The behaviors suggest anxiety, and they conflict with the patient’s words.
Confusion, with verbal data more accurate than behavior
Nothing suggests confusion; observed behaviors add depth to the objective database.

items.q: A nurse is completing an admission history with a computer at the bedside. Which behavior best displays professionalism and caring?
items.a: Positioning the computer so the nurse can face and focus on the patient
items.ex: Look at the patient rather than the screen and position the computer so it does not distract from the patient.
w: Following the screen’s data categories in order so nothing is missed
Do not let a computer program guide the assessment; focus on the patient.
Typing continuously while the patient talks to save time later
Focusing on the screen reduces patient engagement and harms rapport.
Asking short yes-or-no questions so the form is completed quickly
The nurse proceeds at a reasonable pace and asks open-ended questions.

alt.q: What can happen when a nurse focuses on the computer instead of the patient during a health history?
alt.a: Less patient engagement and a more negative rapport
alt.ex: Focusing on the computer leads to observable communication differences, including less engagement and more negative rapport.
w: More accurate data because every field is completed
Focusing on the screen harms communication; it does not improve accuracy.
Greater patient trust because the nurse appears thorough
Screen focus produces more negative rapport, not greater trust.
Shorter interviews with no effect on the relationship
Screen focus does affect the relationship by reducing engagement.

items.q: Which items should the nurse include in a complete medication history? Select all that apply.
o: Prescribed medications the patient takes now
Current prescribed medications are part of a complete medication history.
Prescribed medications the patient took in the past
Past as well as current prescriptions are included.
Over-the-counter medications
Over-the-counter medications are part of a complete medication history.
Herbal supplements
Herbal supplements are included in the medication history.
Only medications ordered by the current health care provider
Limiting the history to one provider’s orders misses past, OTC, and herbal products.
Medications taken by immediate family members
Relatives’ medications are not part of the patient’s medication history.
items.ex: A complete medication history includes past and current prescribed and over-the-counter medications and any herbal supplements.

alt.q: A patient says, “I only take my blood pressure pill.” Which follow-up questions help complete the medication history? Select all that apply.
o: “Do you take any over-the-counter medicines?”
Over-the-counter medications belong in a complete medication history.
“Do you use any herbal supplements?”
Herbal supplements belong in a complete medication history.
“What medications have you taken in the past?”
Past prescribed medications are part of a complete history.
“Which medicines does your spouse take?”
A spouse’s medications are not part of the patient’s medication history.
“Has your provider ever changed your insurance?”
Insurance is biographical information, not medication history.
alt.ex: Correct: “Do you take any over-the-counter medicines?”; “Do you use any herbal supplements?”; “What medications have you taken in the past?”

items.q: A nurse assesses a patient’s expectations of health care. Which expectations do patients typically have? Select all that apply.
o: Information about their treatments and prognosis
Patients typically expect information about treatments and prognosis.
A plan of care for their return home
Inpatients and outpatients alike expect a plan of care for going home.
Relief of pain and other symptoms
Patients typically expect relief of pain and other symptoms.
Caring expressed by health care providers
Patients expect providers to express caring.
Discharge within 24 hours of admission
The textbook does not list a set length of stay as a typical expectation.
No involvement in decisions about their care
Patients expect information and a plan of care, not exclusion from their care.
items.ex: Patients typically expect information about treatment, prognosis, and a home care plan, symptom relief, and caring from providers.

alt.q: Which statements about assessing patient expectations are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Unmet expectations can lead patients to perceive poor satisfaction.
Patients may perceive satisfaction as poor when expectations are not met.
The nurse assesses expectations at the start of care.
Initial expectations are assessed so they can be revisited later.
After care, the nurse assesses whether expectations changed or were met.
Initial expectations are used later to judge whether they were met or changed.
Expectations are assessed only for inpatients, not outpatients.
Both inpatients and outpatients have expectations, such as a plan for returning home.
Expectations are assessed only once, at the time of discharge.
Expectations are assessed initially and reassessed after care is provided.
alt.ex: Correct: Unmet expectations can lead patients to perceive poor satisfaction; The nurse assesses expectations at the start of care; After care, the nurse assesses whether expectations changed or were met.

items.q: Which nurse actions reflect a culturally competent, person-centered approach to the health history? Select all that apply.
o: Using a qualified professional interpreter when there is a language difference
The textbook calls for a qualified professional interpreter for language differences.
Removing barriers to family presence when the patient wants family involved
When patients desire family involvement, the nurse removes barriers to having families present.
Explaining the intent of questions the nurse asks
Explaining the intent of questions provides clarity.
Showing genuine curiosity about the patient’s beliefs and values
Genuine curiosity builds a trusting nurse-patient relationship.
Asking the patient’s 10-year-old child to interpret during the interview
A qualified professional interpreter, not a child, is used for language differences.
Assuming a patient who is obese does not exercise regularly
Stereotype-based assumptions lead to collecting inaccurate information.
items.ex: Person-centered cultural assessment uses professional interpreters, includes desired family, explains questions, and shows curiosity without bias.

alt.q: Which questions help a nurse determine a patient’s health beliefs and practices? Select all that apply.
o: “What do you do at home to care for yourself and stay healthy?”
This explores the patient’s health practices.
“Tell me what your beliefs are about pain and the best way to treat it.”
This explores health beliefs about pain and its treatment.
“Do you prefer a caregiver who is of the same gender identity as you?”
This explores care preferences tied to health beliefs.
“People from your background usually avoid medicine, right?”
This leading question relies on a stereotype and can yield inaccurate data.
“You don’t use any home remedies, do you?”
This leading question imposes the nurse’s view instead of exploring beliefs.
alt.ex: Correct: “What do you do at home to care for yourself and stay healthy?”; “Tell me what your beliefs are about pain and the best way to treat it.”; “Do you prefer a caregiver who is of the same gender identity as you?”

items.q: Because most health history forms are structured, the nurse explores every component in equal detail for every patient.
items.a: False
items.ex: Interview findings show the nurse which components to explore fully; patient needs and available time determine completeness.
items.ww: A structured form does not mean equal depth; the nurse adjusts detail to each patient’s needs and priorities.

alt.q: A patient’s priorities and needs, and the time available, determine how complete a nursing health history will be.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The completeness of a history varies with the patient’s priorities and needs and the time the nurse has.
alt.ww: Histories are not uniformly complete; the textbook ties completeness to patient needs and available time.

items.q: If a nurse does not document an assessment finding or suspected problem, the information is lost to others caring for the patient.
items.a: True
items.ex: Undocumented findings are unavailable to the rest of the team, so timely, clear documentation is required.
items.ww: Verbal knowledge does not reach all caregivers; only documented findings are available to others.

alt.q: Accurate data collection and documentation are dependent nursing functions that require a health care provider’s order.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurse practice acts and the ANA Nursing’s Social Policy Statement require these as independent functions of the professional nurse.
alt.ww: Data collection and documentation are independent nursing functions, so no provider order is needed.

items.q: Cultural humility requires the nurse to recognize the limits of their own knowledge and cultural perspective and remain open to new perspectives.
items.a: True
items.ex: Without cultural humility, a nurse can be biased and misinterpret assessment findings.
items.ww: Cultural humility is defined by acknowledging one’s limits and staying open, which prevents biased interpretation.

alt.q: Assumptions based on stereotypes help the nurse collect assessment data more efficiently and accurately.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Stereotype-based assumptions, such as believing obese patients do not exercise, lead to inaccurate information.
alt.ww: Stereotypes distort the history; nurses ask constructive, probing questions to learn who the patient truly is.

items.q: The [[chief concern|chief complaint]] is a brief statement in the patient’s own words about the reason for seeking health care.

items.q: Tonya finds a 1.2-cm separation of Mr. Lawson’s incision with serosanguinous drainage, inflammation, and tenderness. Which additional assessment best validates her concern about infection?
items.a: Measuring the patient’s body temperature
items.ex: Tonya validated the inflamed open area by measuring temperature, which was slightly above the patient’s average.
w: Inspecting the IV site in the patient’s left forearm
The IV inspection rules out phlebitis; it does not validate the wound finding.
Asking the patient to rate his current pain level
His pain rating was unchanged and reflects stability rather than confirming infection.
Reviewing the patient’s dietary intake for the day
Dietary intake does not confirm or refute a suspected surgical site infection.

alt.q: After seeing an inflamed open area of the incision, Tonya measures Mr. Lawson’s temperature. This action is an example of which part of assessment?
alt.a: Validation
alt.ex: Validating an observation with further assessment, such as a temperature, prevents incorrect inferences.
w: Selecting a nursing diagnosis
Nursing diagnoses are identified after data are interpreted and validated.
Evaluating an intervention
No intervention has been given yet; Tonya is still collecting data.
Documenting a baseline
Documentation records data; measuring a confirming sign is validation.

items.q: A nurse observes a postoperative patient who lies still with arms along his sides, says he has not turned for some time, and rates his pain as 7. Which statement is an inference rather than a cue?
items.a: Pain limits the patient’s ability to move and reposition himself.
items.ex: An inference is the nurse’s interpretation of cues; the other statements are observed or reported data.
w: The patient lies still in bed with his arms along his sides.
This is an observed sign, which is a cue.
The patient states that he has not turned for some time.
This is a patient report gathered during assessment, which is a cue.
The patient rates his pain at 7 on a scale of 0 to 10.
This is a measured symptom rating, which is a cue.

alt.q: Which statement about a postoperative patient is a cue rather than an inference?
alt.a: The patient reports pain at 7 on a scale of 0 to 10.
alt.ex: Cues are signs and symptoms obtained through observation and measurement, such as a pain rating.
w: The patient’s pain is severe enough to need attention.
Judging pain as severe is an inference drawn from the cues.
The patient’s pain limits his ability to reposition himself.
This interpretation of the cues is an inference.
The patient’s wound healing appears to be altered now.
This is an interpretation of wound cues, not a cue itself.

items.q: Which principle should guide a nurse before making an inference during assessment?
items.a: Always have supporting signs and symptoms before making an inference.
items.ex: Inferences must rest on supporting signs and symptoms, and they then direct further questions.
w: Make an inference early so the remaining assessment can be skipped.
Inferences direct further questions; they do not end the assessment.
Base the inference on the patient’s medical diagnosis alone.
Inferences come from the patient’s own cues, not a diagnosis alone.
Rely on the first finding because later data tend to confuse.
Additional data may confirm or refute a pattern, so later data matter.

alt.q: What does it mean for a nurse to critically anticipate during assessment?
alt.a: Continuously think about what the data show and decide whether more data are needed
alt.ex: Critically anticipating means ongoing thinking about the data and judging whether more data are needed.
w: Predict the patient’s nursing diagnoses before meeting the patient
Anticipating is not guessing diagnoses in advance; it is ongoing analysis of collected data.
Follow the admission form strictly without changing the order of questions
Critical anticipation adapts questions to the data rather than following a fixed order.
Collect every possible piece of data before thinking about its meaning
The nurse thinks about meaning continuously as data are collected.

items.q: A postoperative patient rates his surgical pain as 7. The nurse then asks, “When is the last time you turned?” and he replies, “Not since the nurses turned me last night.” Which pattern is the nurse exploring?
items.a: Limited mobility
items.ex: In the branching example, questions about turning and getting up in a chair explore a pattern of limited mobility.
w: Developing infection
Infection is explored by inspecting the incision, not by asking about turning.
Chronic pain
Asking where pain is located helps distinguish acute from chronic pain.
Knowledge deficit
The question about turning targets mobility, not the patient’s learning needs.

alt.q: In a branching assessment, a nurse asks to look at a patient’s incision and finds a 1.2-cm separation with slight serosanguinous drainage. Which pattern is the nurse exploring?
alt.a: Developing infection
alt.ex: Inspecting a separated incision with drainage explores whether infection is developing.
w: Limited mobility
Mobility is explored by asking when the patient last turned or got up.
Acute pain
Pain patterns are explored by asking about location and severity.
Anxiety
Anxiety is explored through behavior such as restlessness and poor eye contact.

items.q: Why should a nurse validate assessment information before completing data interpretation?
items.a: To avoid incorrect inferences and inaccurate problem identification
items.ex: Without validation of an initial inference through further assessment, inaccurate problem identification can result.
w: To meet a billing requirement before the patient is admitted
Validation is a clinical reasoning step, not a billing requirement.
To end data collection once the first inference is confirmed
Validation often opens the door for gathering more data.
To replace the need for a physical examination of the patient
Validation may require more physical examination data, not less.

alt.q: Which statement about validation is accurate?
alt.a: It often leads to gathering more data because it clarifies vague data.
alt.ex: Validation involves clarifying vague or unclear data and may require reassessing the history or examination.
w: It is completed only after nursing diagnoses have been selected.
Validation occurs before data interpretation is complete, before diagnoses are chosen.
It relies only on the nurse’s own physical examination findings.
Validation also uses the EHR, other team members, and family or friends.
It closes data collection once the first inference is recorded.
Validation opens the door for gathering more assessment data.

items.q: A nurse infers that a postoperative patient’s restlessness is caused by incisional pain. Which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Validate the inference by gathering more data from the patient.
items.ex: An initial inference must be validated with further assessment to avoid inaccurate problem identification.
w: Document acute pain as the patient’s problem right away.
Documenting a problem before validating the inference risks an inaccurate conclusion.
Tell the oncoming nurse that pain is the cause of restlessness.
Passing on an unvalidated inference spreads a possibly incorrect conclusion.
Ignore further findings that suggest a different cause.
Different findings may refute the inference and must be considered.

alt.q: Besides the EHR and other health care team members, which source does the textbook note may help validate assessment information?
alt.a: The patient’s family or friends
alt.ex: Family or friends can often validate assessment information alongside the EHR and team members.
w: A standard care plan from a reference book
A generic care plan does not validate data about this specific patient.
The nurse’s memory of similar past patients
Experience helps, but it cannot validate this patient’s data.
Diagnoses already listed on the problem list
Existing labels are not a source for validating new assessment findings.

items.q: Tonya assesses Mr. Lawson on his third postoperative day. Which finding is most important to report to the health care provider?
items.a: A 1.2-cm wound separation with drainage and inflammation
items.ex: Wound separation with drainage, inflammation, and tenderness are cues to altered healing and possible infection, which Tonya reports.
w: An intact IV site with no signs of phlebitis
An intact IV site meets standard criteria for ruling out phlebitis.
A pain rating of 4, unchanged from earlier
An unchanged pain level shows stability rather than a new problem.
A heart rate of 88 beats/min and regular rhythm
This vital sign is normal and reflects stability.

alt.q: Mr. Lawson’s IV site is intact with no signs of phlebitis. Why does Tonya still inspect it during her assessment?
alt.a: Any open site, including an IV site, can lead to infection.
alt.ex: Tonya’s knowledge that any open wound, such as an IV site, can lead to infection guides her to inspect it.
w: IV sites must be inspected only when the patient reports pain there.
Tonya inspects the site routinely, not only when pain is reported.
Phlebitis is the most likely cause of his slightly raised temperature.
The IV site showed no phlebitis; the temperature confirmed the wound concern.
Inspecting the IV site replaces the need to assess the incision.
Tonya assesses both the incision and the IV site.

items.q: When initiating a concept map with assessment data, what is the nurse’s first step?
items.a: Organize the data by placing cues into clusters that form patterns.
items.ex: The first step of a concept map is organizing assessment data and clustering cues into patterns.
w: Select nursing diagnoses for each of the patient’s problems.
Selecting nursing diagnoses is the next step after clustering cues into patterns.
Write outcomes and interventions for each health problem.
Planning interventions follows identification of nursing diagnoses.
Evaluate the patient’s response to nursing interventions.
Evaluation comes much later, after care has been provided.

alt.q: After Tonya clusters Mr. Lawson’s cues into patterns on her concept map, what is the next step?
alt.a: Identifying specific nursing diagnoses
alt.ex: After cues are clustered into patterns, the next step in developing the concept map is selecting nursing diagnoses.
w: Collecting the first set of data
Data collection comes before cues can be clustered.
Discharging the patient home
Discharge is not a step in developing a concept map.
Evaluating his expected outcomes
Evaluation follows diagnosis, planning, and implementation.

items.q: A nursing student asks why concept mapping is used in clinical courses. Which response by the instructor is most accurate?
items.a: “It helps you understand the relationships among a patient’s problems.”
items.ex: Concept maps build clinical judgment by showing relationships among patient problems and giving a holistic view.
w: “It replaces the need to identify nursing diagnoses.”
Concept mapping leads into, rather than replaces, selecting nursing diagnoses.
“It is the legal record of the patient’s assessment.”
The EHR is the record; a concept map is a learning and thinking strategy.
“It lets you focus on one problem at a time in isolation.”
Concept maps show how problems relate rather than isolating them.

alt.q: Which outcome does the textbook link to the use of concept maps?
alt.a: A holistic perspective on patient needs that supports better clinical decisions
alt.ex: Concept mapping gives a holistic perspective on the patient’s needs, leading to better clinical decisions.
w: A shorter assessment because fewer cues need to be collected
Concept mapping organizes data; it does not reduce the data needed.
A standard format that is the same in every educational setting
Formats vary and may include spider maps, hierarchical maps, or flowcharts.
A replacement for physical examination in stable patients
Concept maps organize assessment data; they do not replace examination.

items.q: In Tonya’s concept map for Mr. Lawson, assessment cues are aligned with potential patterns. What do the dotted lines between the patterns show?
items.a: Relationships between the patterns
items.ex: Dotted lines in the concept map show how the patterns relate to one another.
w: The order in which to give interventions
Interventions are planned later; the lines show relationships among patterns.
Cues that have been ruled out by the nurse
Ruled-out cues are not mapped; the lines link related patterns.
Nursing diagnoses that have been resolved
Diagnoses are selected in the next step; the lines show relationships.

alt.q: Why does clustering cues into patterns help a nurse build a concept map?
alt.a: It shows cues and patterns that relate to more than one health problem.
alt.ex: Clustering cues lets the nurse readily identify data cues and patterns that relate to more than one health problem.
w: It removes the need to validate any of the assessment data.
Clustering does not replace validation of data before interpretation.
It limits the map to a single problem so the plan is simpler.
Clustering reveals links among several problems, not just one.
It lets the nurse skip collecting data on other body systems.
Clustering organizes collected data; it does not shorten data collection.

items.q: A nurse notes several cues that suggest a pattern of fluid volume excess, then finds a new assessment finding that does not fit the pattern. Which action reflects sound clinical judgment?
items.a: Reconsider the pattern and refute it if the new finding does not support it.
items.ex: A pattern can be confirmed by adding more data or refuted on the basis of a different assessment finding.
w: Disregard the new finding because a pattern has already formed.
Ignoring conflicting data can lead to incorrect inferences and problems.
Document fluid volume excess as a nursing diagnosis right away.
Diagnoses are identified only after data are interpreted and validated.
Stop collecting data until the health care provider reviews it.
Data collection is continuous and evolving during clinical judgment.

alt.q: A nurse sees an emerging pattern in a patient’s signs and symptoms. Which action can the nurse take to confirm the pattern?
alt.a: Add more assessment data that support the pattern.
alt.ex: Nurses confirm a pattern by adding more data or refute it on the basis of a different finding.
w: Rely on the first cue noticed during the shift.
A single early cue cannot confirm a pattern; more supporting data are needed.
Ask the patient to agree with the nurse’s conclusion.
Seeking agreement is not the same as gathering supporting data.
Compare the pattern with a textbook care plan.
A generic care plan does not supply this patient’s supporting data.

items.q: According to clinical standards, which findings are signs of a surgical site infection? Select all that apply.
o: Inflammation of the incision
Inflammation is a standard sign of surgical site infection.
Tenderness at the incision
Tenderness is a standard sign of surgical site infection.
Abnormal appearance of drainage
Abnormal-appearing drainage is a standard sign of surgical site infection.
Wound edges that are closed and intact
Closed, intact edges suggest normal healing rather than infection.
A pain rating unchanged from the previous assessment
An unchanged pain level reflects stability, not infection.
items.ex: Clinical standards list inflammation, tenderness, and abnormal appearance of drainage as signs of surgical site infection.

alt.q: Which of Mr. Lawson’s findings are cues suggesting a problem with wound healing and potential infection? Select all that apply.
o: A 1.2-cm separation of the wound between two sutures
An open wound is a potential source of infection.
A small amount of serosanguinous drainage
Drainage from the separated incision is a data cue for infection.
An inflamed, tender area of the incision
Inflammation and tenderness are standard signs of surgical site infection.
A temperature slightly above his average temperature
The slight rise confirms an early indication of infection.
An intact IV site with no signs of phlebitis
This finding meets standard criteria for ruling out phlebitis.
A blood pressure of 110/78 mm Hg
This vital sign is normal and shows stability.

items.q: Which actions help a nurse validate assessment findings? Select all that apply.
o: Comparing findings with data in the EHR
Comparing data in the EHR is a way to validate findings.
Consulting with other nurses or health care team members
Other team members can help validate findings.
Asking family or friends about the patient’s usual condition
Family or friends may validate assessment information.
Measuring a related sign to confirm an observation
Tonya validated an inflamed wound by measuring body temperature.
Accepting the first inference without further assessment
Unvalidated inferences can lead to inaccurate problem identification.
Documenting the suspected problem as a final diagnosis
Validation occurs before interpretation is complete and diagnoses are chosen.
items.ex: Validation uses the EHR, team members, family or friends, and further assessment to confirm findings before interpretation.

alt.q: A nurse suspects that an older patient’s confusion is new. Which actions would validate this finding? Select all that apply.
o: Asking the patient’s daughter whether this behavior is usual for him
Family members can validate assessment information.
Reviewing earlier mental status findings in the EHR
Comparing data in the EHR validates current findings.
Consulting with the nurse who cared for him on the previous shift
Consulting other nurses helps validate findings.
Documenting acute confusion as the problem before checking further
Documenting an unvalidated inference risks inaccurate problem identification.
Starting interventions based only on the first impression
Acting on an unvalidated inference may target the wrong problem.
alt.ex: Correct: Asking the patient’s daughter whether this behavior is usual for him; Reviewing earlier mental status findings in the EHR; Consulting with the nurse who cared for him on the previous shift.

items.q: Which statement best defines a medical diagnosis?
items.a: Identification of a disease condition based on signs and symptoms, medical history, and diagnostic test results
items.ex: A medical diagnosis identifies a disease from physical signs and symptoms, the medical history, and diagnostic tests and procedures.
w: A clinical judgment that classifies a person’s, family’s, or community’s response to illness
This describes a nursing diagnosis, which names a response to illness rather than the disease itself.
A potential problem managed with both independent and provider-prescribed interventions
This describes a collaborative problem, which focuses on monitoring and preventing complications.
A judgment that a patient has an increased potential to develop a problem or complication
This describes a risk nursing diagnosis, not the identification of a disease condition.

alt.q: A health care provider confirms rheumatoid arthritis after reviewing the patient’s symptoms, history, and laboratory results. What type of diagnosis has been made?
alt.a: Medical diagnosis
alt.ex: Identifying a disease condition from signs, symptoms, history, and test results is a medical diagnosis.
w: Nursing diagnosis
A nursing diagnosis names the patient’s response to the disease, such as pain or impaired mobility.
Collaborative problem
A collaborative problem is a potential complication monitored by the nurse, not the disease itself.
Risk diagnosis
A risk diagnosis names a susceptibility to a problem that does not yet exist.

items.q: Which health care professionals are licensed to treat conditions described in medical diagnostic terms?
items.a: Physicians and advanced practice registered nurses
items.ex: Physicians and APRNs, such as nurse practitioners, are licensed to treat diseases described by medical diagnoses.
w: Registered nurses and licensed practical nurses
Registered nurses cannot treat medical diagnoses; they treat patients’ responses to health conditions.
Registered dietitians and physical therapists
These professionals recommend therapies but are not licensed to treat medical diagnoses.
Registered nurses with several years of experience
Experience does not change scope; only APRNs among nurses treat medical diagnoses.

alt.q: A patient with diabetes mellitus needs an HbA1c test and insulin. Which member of the health care team may order these?
alt.a: The nurse practitioner
alt.ex: Only advanced practice registered nurses, such as nurse practitioners, among nurses can treat medical diagnoses and order HbA1c or insulin.
w: The staff registered nurse
Registered nurses educate about diabetes medication and diet but cannot order insulin or HbA1c tests.
The registered dietitian
A dietitian recommends therapeutic diets but does not order medications or laboratory tests.
The charge nurse
A charge nurse is a registered nurse and is not licensed to treat medical diagnoses.

items.q: Which statement best defines a nursing diagnosis?
items.a: A clinical judgment that classifies an individual’s, family’s, or community’s response to illness
items.ex: A nursing diagnosis names a response to illness so all nurses understand the patient’s specific health care needs.
w: The identification of a disease based on physical signs and diagnostic test results
This defines a medical diagnosis, which names the disease rather than the response to it.
A potential complication that requires both medical and nursing interventions to manage
This defines a collaborative problem, in which the nurse mainly monitors and prevents complications.
A list of nursing interventions planned to correct a patient’s health problem
Interventions are planned after a nursing diagnosis is identified; they are not the diagnosis itself.

alt.q: A nurse documents “Acute Pain” for a patient after hip surgery. What does this entry represent?
alt.a: The nurse’s clinical judgment about the patient’s response to a health condition
alt.ex: Acute Pain is a nursing diagnosis, a clinical judgment about the patient’s response that nurses are licensed to treat.
w: The identification of the disease causing the patient’s symptoms
Naming the disease is a medical diagnosis; Acute Pain names the patient’s response.
A potential complication that only a health care provider can treat
Nurses independently treat pain with interventions such as heat, cold, and positioning.
A nursing intervention that the nurse will carry out for the patient
Acute Pain is a diagnosis; interventions are selected afterward to address it.

items.q: A registered nurse is caring for a patient with rheumatoid arthritis who reports joint pain and stiffness. Which action is within the nurse’s independent scope of practice?
items.a: Apply heat or cold to the painful joints
items.ex: Nurses treat responses such as pain with independent interventions like heat or cold, not the disease itself.
w: Prescribe a new medication to slow the disease
Registered nurses cannot order medications to treat rheumatoid arthritis; that is a medical treatment.
Order laboratory tests to confirm disease activity
Ordering diagnostic tests to manage a disease is the role of physicians and APRNs.
Change the dose of the prescribed arthritis drug
Adjusting medical treatment of the disease is outside the registered nurse’s scope.

alt.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis has limited mobility. Which intervention may the registered nurse provide independently?
alt.a: Implement an early mobility protocol
alt.ex: Improving mobility through early mobility protocols is a nursing intervention for the patient’s response to the disease.
w: Order a disease-modifying medication
Medications to treat the disease must be ordered by a physician or APRN.
Order joint imaging to evaluate the disease
Diagnostic tests for the disease are ordered by health care providers, not registered nurses.
Discontinue the patient’s prescribed medication
Changing medical therapy is not within the registered nurse’s independent scope.

items.q: Which statement best describes a collaborative problem?
items.a: A potential problem managed with both nursing and provider-prescribed interventions, focused on monitoring and prevention
items.ex: Collaborative problems need medical and nursing interventions; the nurse monitors the condition and works to prevent the complication.
w: A problem the nurse can prevent or treat entirely with independent nursing interventions
If the nurse can prevent or primarily treat the problem independently, it is a nursing diagnosis.
A disease condition identified from signs, symptoms, history, and diagnostic test results
This describes a medical diagnosis, which physicians and APRNs treat.
A desire or ability to improve health status through a positive behavioral change
This describes a health promotion or positive nursing diagnosis.

alt.q: For a collaborative problem, what is the main focus of the nursing aspect of care?
alt.a: Monitoring the patient’s condition and preventing the potential complication
alt.ex: In collaborative problems, nursing care centers on monitoring the condition and preventing the complication from developing.
w: Prescribing the medical treatment that resolves the complication
Medical treatment is prescribed by health care providers; the nurse monitors and prevents.
Treating the complication independently without provider orders
Collaborative problems require provider-prescribed interventions in addition to nursing interventions.
Confirming the medical diagnosis through diagnostic testing
Confirming a disease through testing is part of medical diagnosis, not nursing care.

items.q: A patient comes to a clinic with an infected leg wound. The health care provider prescribes antibiotics and a dietitian recommends a high-protein diet. Which action reflects the nurse’s role in managing this collaborative problem?
items.a: Monitor for fever and provide wound care
items.ex: In this example, the nurse monitors for fever and provides wound care while other team members contribute their own interventions.
w: Select the antibiotic and its dosage
Prescribing antibiotics is the health care provider’s role in this collaborative problem.
Design the patient’s therapeutic diet
The registered dietitian recommends the high-protein therapeutic diet.
Leave wound management to the provider
The nurse actively contributes by monitoring and giving wound care; the problem is shared.

alt.q: In the case of a patient with an infected leg wound, which team member’s contribution is matched correctly?
alt.a: Nurse: monitors for fever and provides wound care
alt.ex: The nurse monitors for fever and gives wound care, while the provider prescribes antibiotics and the dietitian recommends the diet.
w: Nurse: prescribes antibiotics for the infection
Antibiotics are prescribed by the health care provider, not the nurse.
Dietitian: monitors for fever and wound drainage
Monitoring for fever is the nurse’s role; the dietitian recommends a high-protein diet.
Provider: teaches hand hygiene and wound care
In this example, the patient collaborates by learning hand hygiene and wound care practices.
