items.q: A nurse writes the diagnosis Lack of Knowledge for a patient but includes no related factor. What is the main effect on care planning?
items.a: Other nurses have less direction about which interventions are needed
items.ex: A related factor adds clarity and directs the type of interventions appropriate for the patient.
w: The diagnosis can no longer be entered in the EHR
A diagnosis can be documented; it is simply less clear for planning.
The diagnosis automatically becomes a collaborative problem
Omitting a related factor does not change the type of problem.
Outcomes must be chosen by the health care provider
Nurses still plan outcomes; the diagnosis is just less specific.

alt.q: Tonya enters “Lack of Knowledge regarding postoperative care related to inexperience with surgery” in Mr. Lawson’s plan of care. What does adding the related factor accomplish?
alt.a: It directs other nurses to the scope of patient education required
alt.ex: The book states this wording directs other nurses to the scope of teaching Mr. Lawson needs.
w: It proves that inexperience directly caused his infection
A related factor shows association, not cause and effect, and is not about infection.
It turns the diagnosis into a risk diagnosis
Risk diagnoses have no related factors; this is a problem-focused diagnosis.
It replaces the need to list assessment findings
Assessment findings can still be listed to add clarity and guide evaluation.

items.q: Two patients have the nursing diagnosis Anxiety. Patient A’s anxiety is related to uncertainty about surgery; Patient B’s is related to losing a job that was the family’s main income. Which intervention is most appropriate for Patient B?
items.a: Consult with a social worker to arrange job counseling
items.ex: Interventions differ by related factor; job loss calls for social work referral for job counseling.
w: Provide detailed instruction about surgery and recovery
This fits anxiety related to uncertainty over surgery, which is Patient A.
Plan a formal time to ask questions about surgery
This addresses surgical uncertainty, Patient A’s related factor.
Administer an analgesic 30 minutes before exercise
This fits impaired mobility related to acute pain, not anxiety from job loss.

alt.q: A patient has Impaired Mobility related to acute pain and rates pain 7 on a scale of 1 to 10. Which intervention best matches this related factor?
alt.a: Administer an analgesic 30 minutes before planned exercise
alt.ex: When pain limits mobility, giving analgesia before activity targets the related factor.
w: Instruct the patient on a 3-point crutch gait
Crutch gait training fits mobility impaired by a musculoskeletal injury.
Consult a social worker for job counseling
This addresses anxiety related to job loss, not pain-related mobility.
Plan formal time for questions about surgery
This addresses anxiety from surgical uncertainty, not acute pain.

items.q: Tonya plans to teach Mr. Lawson about incision care, but he is restless, says he is worried, and rates his pain as high. Which action should Tonya take first?
items.a: Relieve his pain and anxiety before beginning the teaching
items.ex: Tonya knows that unless his pain and anxiety are relieved, he will not respond to instruction.
w: Begin the full teaching session as planned
Teaching while pain and anxiety are high is unlikely to be effective.
Give him written materials to read on his own
Written materials do not address the pain and anxiety blocking learning.
Postpone all teaching until after he is discharged
He needs this knowledge before discharge; pain and anxiety should be relieved first.

alt.q: Why did Tonya consider Mr. Lawson’s pain and anxiety when prioritizing his diagnosis of Lack of Knowledge?
alt.a: He will not respond to teaching until pain and anxiety are relieved
alt.ex: The diagnoses affect each other, so relieving pain and anxiety makes teaching effective.
w: Pain and anxiety are collaborative problems needing orders
Pain and anxiety are nursing diagnoses; the issue is their effect on learning.
Lack of Knowledge always has the lowest priority
Priorities depend on the patient’s situation, not a fixed rule.
Teaching would make his pain and anxiety worse
The concern is that pain and anxiety block learning, not that teaching worsens them.

items.q: A patient’s condition changes during a shift: one nursing diagnosis has resolved and new assessment cues suggest a different problem. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Update the nursing diagnoses and revise the care plan priorities
items.ex: The nursing process is dynamic; changing conditions bring new or resolved diagnoses that change the plan of care.
w: Keep the original care plan unchanged until discharge
A static plan ignores new or resolved diagnoses and changing priorities.
Wait for the health care provider to revise the plan
Nurses are accountable for revising nursing diagnoses and the nursing care plan.
Remove the care plan from the patient’s record
The plan should be revised, not removed, as priorities change.

alt.q: Which statement best explains why a care plan must be revised during a patient’s stay?
alt.a: As the patient’s condition changes, priorities and diagnoses change
alt.ex: New or resolved nursing diagnoses and shifting priorities affect the plan of care.
w: Care plans expire automatically after each shift
Revision is driven by changes in the patient, not by time limits.
Each nurse must write a new plan with new terms
Standardized terms stay consistent; changes reflect the patient’s condition.
Medical diagnoses change daily in most patients
Revision reflects changes in human responses and priorities, not daily medical diagnoses.

items.q: A nurse is developing a care plan for a bedridden patient at risk for pressure injuries. How should this problem be listed?
items.a: As a nursing diagnosis, because nurses can prevent it independently
items.ex: When nurses can independently prevent or treat a complication, it is a nursing diagnosis such as Risk for Pressure Ulcer.
w: As a collaborative problem, because it needs a provider order
Nurses can prevent pressure injuries independently, so it is a nursing diagnosis.
As a medical diagnosis, because it involves the skin
The patient’s risk is a human response nurses manage, not a medical diagnosis.
As a collaborative problem, because a dietitian may help
Help from other disciplines does not make it collaborative when nurses can prevent it.

alt.q: A postoperative patient may develop hemorrhage, which nurses monitor for but cannot prevent independently. How should this be listed in the plan of care?
alt.a: As a collaborative problem managed with nursing and medical interventions
alt.ex: Problems nurses cannot prevent, such as hemorrhage and seizures, are collaborative problems.
w: As a nursing diagnosis treated only by nursing interventions
Nurses cannot independently prevent hemorrhage, so it is not a nursing diagnosis.
As a health promotion diagnosis for the patient
Health promotion diagnoses describe readiness to improve health, not complications.
As a medical diagnosis requiring no nursing monitoring
Nurses monitor collaborative problems and help prevent complications.

items.q: Why are unclear, nonstandard terms a problem when nurses write care plans?
items.a: They cause inconsistencies in naming needs, interventions, and outcomes
items.ex: Unclear wording creates inconsistent naming of diagnoses, interventions, and expected outcomes.
w: They speed up communication with other disciplines
Unclear terms hinder communication across disciplines.
They improve the accuracy of documentation
Standardized terms, not unclear wording, improve accuracy.
They increase use of evidence-based guidelines
Standard terminologies support evidence-based guidelines; vague terms do not.

alt.q: Which benefit of standardized nursing terminology supports clear care planning?
alt.a: Agreed-upon definitions that represent the knowledge behind terms
alt.ex: Standard terminologies include agreed-upon definitions, so all disciplines understand the patient’s needs.
w: Freedom for each nurse to invent new labels
Inventing labels creates inconsistency; standard terms use agreed definitions.
Removal of the need for interprofessional input
Standard terms improve collaboration rather than remove it.
Labels that apply only within one care setting
Standard terms are meant to be understood across settings and disciplines.

items.q: Mr. Lawson’s plan of care states: “Lack of Knowledge regarding postoperative care related to inexperience with surgery as evidenced by frequent questions about postoperative routines.” Which part is the related factor?
items.a: Inexperience with surgery
items.ex: The related factor follows “related to” and directs the type of interventions needed.
w: Lack of Knowledge
This is the diagnostic label, the name of the nursing diagnosis.
Frequent questions about postoperative routines
This is the major assessment finding that follows “as evidenced by.”
Postoperative care
This specifies the topic of the knowledge problem, not the related factor.

alt.q: In Mr. Lawson’s diagnosis, which part will best guide Tonya in evaluating whether her teaching was effective?
alt.a: Frequent questions about postoperative routines
alt.ex: Listing major assessment findings offers guidelines for evaluating the effectiveness of nursing care.
w: Inexperience with surgery
This related factor directs interventions; findings guide evaluation.
Lack of Knowledge
The label names the problem but does not supply measurable evidence.
Lack of Knowledge regarding postoperative care
This names the problem and its topic but is not the evidence used to evaluate.

items.q: Mr. Lawson’s breathing has stabilized over 24 hours after a pulmonary embolus, with no additional emboli. How did Tonya handle his breathing in his plan of care?
items.a: She continued monitoring without selecting a breathing diagnosis
items.ex: With his breathing stable, Tonya chose not to add a breathing diagnosis but continues to monitor.
w: She made breathing his highest priority nursing diagnosis
His breathing had stabilized, so she did not select a breathing diagnosis.
She stopped assessing his respiratory status
She continues monitoring even though no breathing diagnosis was selected.
She replaced Acute Pain with a breathing diagnosis
Acute Pain remained relevant; no breathing diagnosis was added.

alt.q: Which statement best explains Tonya’s decision about Mr. Lawson’s stabilized breathing problem?
alt.a: A stable problem may need monitoring rather than a nursing diagnosis
alt.ex: Diagnoses reflect current data; his stable breathing warranted continued monitoring, not a new diagnosis.
w: Breathing problems are never nursing diagnoses
Breathing responses can be nursing diagnoses when the data support them.
A pulmonary embolus is a nursing diagnosis
A pulmonary embolus is a medical diagnosis, not a nursing diagnosis.
Once stable, a problem needs no further assessment
Tonya continues to monitor; stability does not end assessment.

items.q: Accurate nursing diagnoses allow the resulting care plan to do which of the following? Select all that apply.
o: Communicate the patient’s responses to all health care professionals
The book states the care plan communicates the patient’s responses to all professionals.
Help ensure high-quality care
Accurate diagnoses lead to a care plan that ensures high-quality care.
Demonstrate the nurse’s accountability for care
The care plan demonstrates accountability for patient care.
Replace the need for ongoing assessment
The nursing process is dynamic; ongoing assessment is still required.
Substitute for the health care provider’s medical plan
The nursing care plan complements, not replaces, medical treatment.
items.ex: An accurate care plan acts as a road map, communicates responses to the team, and supports high-quality, accountable care.

alt.q: A nurse explains to a student why accurate nursing diagnoses matter for the care plan. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
o: “The plan becomes a road map for delivering our care.”
The care plan guides the delivery of nursing care.
“The plan lets every discipline understand the patient’s responses.”
Accurate diagnoses let the plan communicate responses to all professionals.
“The plan shows we are accountable for the patient’s care.”
The care plan demonstrates nursing accountability.
“Once the plan is written, we no longer need to reassess.”
Diagnoses and priorities change, so reassessment continues.
“The plan is only meant to be read by nurses.”
The plan communicates with all health care professionals.
alt.ex: Correct: “The plan becomes a road map for delivering our care.”; “The plan lets every discipline understand the patient’s responses.”; “The plan shows we are accountable for the patient’s care.”

items.q: A patient has an infected leg wound, a collaborative problem. Which actions are part of managing this problem as described in the book? Select all that apply.
o: The health care provider prescribes antibiotics
Prescribed antibiotics are the medical part of collaborative management.
The nurse monitors for fever and provides wound care
Monitoring and wound care are the nursing part of management.
A registered dietitian recommends a high-protein diet
The dietitian contributes a therapeutic diet high in protein.
The patient learns hand hygiene and wound care
The patient collaborates by learning hygiene and wound care.
The nurse independently prescribes antibiotics
Antibiotics are prescribed by the health care provider, not independently by the nurse.
The dietitian takes over all wound care
Wound care is provided by the nurse; the dietitian recommends diet.
items.ex: Collaborative problems combine provider-prescribed, therapist-recommended, and nursing interventions, with the patient also participating.

alt.q: Which statements about collaborative problems in a care plan are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They require both medical and nursing interventions
Collaborative problems need both medical and nursing interventions.
The nursing focus is monitoring and preventing complications
Nurses monitor the condition and help prevent complications.
Seizures and hemorrhage are examples
The book lists seizures and hemorrhage as collaborative problems.
Nurses can prevent them independently
If nurses can prevent a problem independently, it is a nursing diagnosis.
Pressure injuries are a typical example
Nurses can prevent pressure injuries, so these are nursing diagnoses.
alt.ex: Correct: They require both medical and nursing interventions; The nursing focus is monitoring and preventing complications; Seizures and hemorrhage are examples.

items.q: Interprofessional collaboration in care planning offers which benefits, according to the book? Select all that apply.
o: Involves patients and families in decisions about their care
Collaboration ensures patients and families take part in decision making.
Improves coordination between disciplines
Collaboration improves coordination among different disciplines.
Improves access to health interventions
The book lists improved access to health interventions as a benefit.
Enhances delivery of person-centered care
Team collaboration enhances person-centered care.
Lets each discipline plan care without consulting others
Collaboration means disciplines communicate and consider each other’s views.
Removes the need for nursing diagnoses
Nursing diagnoses are used to communicate within collaborative care.
items.ex: Interprofessional collaboration involves patients, improves access and coordination, and enhances person-centered care and outcomes.

alt.q: A nurse joins a discharge planning conference with a physical therapist and social worker. Which practices reflect effective interprofessional collaboration? Select all that apply.
o: Using nursing diagnoses to convey the patient’s problems
Standard nursing diagnoses communicate patient problems clearly across disciplines.
Considering the other professionals’ perspectives
Collaboration relies on considering one another’s unique perspectives.
Including the patient and family in decisions
Collaboration ensures patients and families are involved in decision making.
Keeping the nursing plan separate from the team
Separating plans undermines coordination between disciplines.
Using personal shorthand instead of standard terms
Nonstandard wording causes inconsistencies and confusion.
alt.ex: Correct: Using nursing diagnoses to convey the patient’s problems; Considering the other professionals’ perspectives; Including the patient and family in decisions.

items.q: By making accurate nursing diagnoses, the nurse’s care plan communicates the patient’s health care responses to all health care professionals.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states the care plan communicates a patient’s responses to problems to all health care professionals.
items.ww: The care plan is not limited to nurses; it informs the whole team.

alt.q: A nursing care plan is intended to communicate the patient’s responses only to other nurses.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The care plan communicates the patient’s responses to all health care professionals, supporting collaboration.
alt.ww: Nursing diagnosis is a standardized language used across health care disciplines.

items.q: Risk nursing diagnoses do not include related factors because the problem does not yet exist.
items.a: True
items.ex: Risk diagnoses identify susceptibility to a potential problem, so there is no existing etiology to relate.
items.ww: Related factors apply to existing problems; a risk diagnosis uses risk factors instead.

alt.q: Every nursing diagnosis in a care plan, including a risk diagnosis, must include a related factor.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Risk diagnoses have no related factors because the problem has not yet developed.
alt.ww: Only problem-focused diagnoses use related factors to direct interventions.

items.q: Listing major assessment findings in a diagnostic statement provides guidelines for evaluating how effective nursing care has been.
items.a: True
items.ex: Major findings give measurable evidence, such as weight loss, that later outcomes can be compared against.
items.ww: The findings shape outcomes, such as a target weight gain, used to evaluate care.

alt.q: Major assessment findings in a diagnostic statement are used to choose medical treatments rather than to evaluate nursing care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Highlighting major findings offers guidelines for evaluating the efficacy of nursing care.
alt.ww: The book links listed findings to planning outcomes and evaluating nursing care, not medical treatment.

items.q: The care plan is a [[road map|roadmap]] for delivering nursing care and demonstrates the nurse’s accountability for patient care.
items.ex: The book compares the care plan to a road map because it directs how nursing care is delivered.

alt.q: Because it guides how nurses deliver care, the care plan is described as a [[road map|roadmap]].
alt.ex: The book compares the care plan to a road map because it directs how nursing care is delivered.

items.q: What is a clinical decision support (CDS) system?
items.a: Software designed to guide nurses in clinical decision making
items.ex: CDS systems are software that help nurses make clinical decisions by matching data to a knowledge base.
w: A paper system for storing scanned patient records
CDS is decision-guiding software, not a storage system for records.
A billing program that codes nursing services
CDS supports clinical decisions; it is not a billing tool.
A messaging tool used for hand-off reports
Hand-off communication is separate; CDS guides decision making.

alt.q: How does a clinical decision support system help a nurse?
alt.a: It matches a patient’s assessment findings to a computerized knowledge base
alt.ex: The system compares a patient’s findings with its clinical knowledge base and presents recommendations.
w: It records vital signs automatically from bedside monitors
Automatic vital sign capture is not how the book defines CDS.
It replaces the nurse’s assessment with a computer exam
The nurse still assesses; CDS uses the nurse’s entered findings.
It schedules the nurse’s patient assignments for each shift
Staffing tools are separate; CDS supports clinical decisions.

items.q: A clinical decision support system suggests the diagnosis Risk for Infection for a postoperative patient. Which statement by the nurse reflects appropriate use of the system?
items.a: “The suggestion helps me, but I still apply my own clinical judgment.”
items.ex: CDS presents patient-specific recommendations to assist decision making, not to replace the nurse’s judgment.
w: “The system has decided, so I will enter it without review.”
CDS assists decisions; the nurse remains responsible for confirming the diagnosis.
“The system only suggests medical diagnoses, so I will ignore it.”
CDS can suggest nursing diagnoses and interventions, so it should be considered.
“The suggestion means I do not need to assess the incision.”
Recommendations depend on accurate assessment data, which the nurse still gathers.

alt.q: After matching a patient’s findings to its knowledge base, what does a clinical decision support system present to the clinician?
alt.a: Patient-specific recommendations, such as diagnoses and interventions
alt.ex: CDS presents individualized recommendations to assist the clinician’s decision making.
w: A final diagnosis that the nurse must accept
Recommendations assist decisions; they are not binding final diagnoses.
A generic care plan used for all patients
Recommendations are patient specific, not one plan for everyone.
A list of the patient’s insurance billing codes
CDS provides clinical recommendations, not billing codes.

items.q: According to current evidence, what is a benefit of using standardized nursing diagnostic terms in the EHR?
items.a: Improved documentation accuracy and communication between disciplines
items.ex: Standard diagnostic terms in EHRs improve accuracy and communication about the patient’s condition and response to therapy.
w: Elimination of the need for nursing assessment
Assessment data are still required to select and support diagnoses.
Replacement of the hand-off report between nurses
Hand-off reports are still needed to confirm diagnoses and progress.
Removal of the need to collaborate with other disciplines
Standard terms support collaboration rather than replacing it.

alt.q: A nurse documents using standardized nursing diagnostic terms in the EHR rather than free-form descriptions. Which outcome does evidence support?
alt.a: Clearer communication about the patient’s response to therapies
alt.ex: Standardized terms facilitate communication between nurses and other disciplines about the patient’s condition and responses.
w: Less need to record supporting assessment data
Assessment data confirming the diagnosis must still be documented.
Fewer nursing diagnoses identified per patient
Standard terms improve accuracy, not reduce the number of diagnoses.
Diagnoses chosen by the EHR vendor rather than the nurse
Nurses select diagnoses; standard terms make them clearer.

items.q: A nurse works at an agency whose clinical decision support system was built with the vendor using medical diagnoses only. The system offers no nursing diagnoses. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Identify the patient’s relevant nursing diagnoses herself
items.ex: When nursing terminology is not integrated into the CDS, nurses must specifically identify relevant nursing diagnoses.
w: Document only the medical diagnoses the system lists
Medical diagnoses do not describe the patient’s human responses that nurses treat.
Wait for the vendor to add nursing terms before diagnosing
Patient care cannot wait; the nurse identifies the diagnoses now.
Omit nursing diagnoses because the system lacks them
Nursing diagnoses remain the nurse’s responsibility even without system support.

alt.q: What does the book say about how agencies build the standard language used in their clinical decision support systems?
alt.a: It may be based only on medical diagnoses and staff expertise
alt.ex: Agencies work with EHR vendors, and the terms are sometimes based only on medical diagnoses and staff opinions.
w: It must always include ICNP® nursing diagnoses
Nursing terminology may or may not be integrated into a CDS system.
It is identical in every health care agency
Agencies create language unique to the institution with their vendors.
It is written by the patient’s health care provider
Agencies and EHR vendors build it, sometimes with staff input.

items.q: A busy nurse enters only part of a patient’s assessment findings into the clinical decision support system. What is the most important concern?
items.a: Poor data quality reduces the quality of decision support
items.ex: The book stresses accurate, thorough data entry because the quality of data affects the quality of decision support.
w: The system will automatically fill in the missing findings
The system relies on the nurse’s entries; it cannot supply missing findings.
The nurse will not be able to log out of the EHR
Logging out is unrelated to the concern about data quality.
Partial entry is acceptable if the shift is short-staffed
Accurate, complete data entry is required regardless of workload.

alt.q: Why does the book advise nurses to be accurate and thorough when entering data into a clinical decision support system?
alt.a: The quality of the data affects the quality of the decision support
alt.ex: Incomplete or inaccurate entries lead to less reliable recommendations from the system.
w: The system penalizes nurses for incomplete entries
The concern is the quality of recommendations, not penalties.
Thorough entry replaces the need for hand-off reports
Hand-off reports are still required to confirm diagnoses.
Detailed entries make the system choose medical treatments
CDS assists nursing decisions; data quality affects its recommendations.

items.q: According to Box 17.3, which description matches an effectively implemented clinical decision support system?
items.a: The right information to the right audiences, in the right ways, at the right times
items.ex: Effective CDS delivers appropriate information to the right people in the right ways at the right times.
w: All available information to every user, at all times
Overloading every user with all information is not effective decision support.
Information only to health care providers, at discharge
Effective CDS serves the right audiences, including nurses, when the information is needed.
The same alerts to every nurse, whatever the patient
Effective CDS is patient specific rather than identical for every patient.

alt.q: A CDS system integrates nursing diagnostic categories with a database of nursing interventions and clinical guidelines. What result does Box 17.3 describe?
alt.a: A greater chance that an evidence-based guideline will be used
alt.ex: Linking diagnostic categories with interventions or guidelines increases the chance evidence-based guidelines are used.
w: A lower need for nurses to enter assessment data
Data entry remains essential; quality data drive quality support.
Guaranteed improvement in every patient outcome
Evidence on patient outcomes from CDS has been mixed.
Elimination of standardized nursing terminology
Integration relies on standardized nursing terminology rather than eliminating it.

items.q: Using ICNP® terminology in an EHR sometimes requires what to ensure accuracy?
items.a: The use of free text
items.ex: The book notes ICNP® terminology sometimes requires free text to ensure documentation accuracy.
w: A health care provider’s cosignature
A provider cosignature is not what the book says ICNP® sometimes requires.
Conversion into medical diagnosis codes
ICNP® describes nursing practice and is not converted to medical codes for accuracy.
A separate paper backup record
The book does not describe paper backups; free text is the stated need.

alt.q: Which terminology does the book say has a standardized format that can improve nurses’ ability to find diagnoses and interventions within the EHR?
alt.a: NANDA-I
alt.ex: NANDA-I’s standardized format helps nurses find diagnoses and interventions in the EHR.
w: ICNP®
ICNP® links well with other systems but sometimes requires free text for accuracy.
Medical diagnosis codes
Medical codes do not organize nursing diagnoses and interventions.
Free-text nurses’ notes
Free text lacks a standardized format for locating diagnoses.

items.q: After a nurse enters a patient’s nursing diagnoses into the EHR, what determines how the diagnoses are disseminated throughout the record?
items.a: The agency’s information system
items.ex: The agency information system dictates where diagnoses appear, such as care plans, task sheets, or notes.
w: The patient’s health care provider
The provider does not control how the information system disseminates nursing diagnoses.
The nurse manager’s personal preference
Dissemination is set by the agency’s information system, not individual preference.
The patient’s insurance company
Insurers do not determine how the EHR displays nursing diagnoses.

alt.q: Which is an example of where an agency information system may place a patient’s nursing diagnoses after they are entered?
alt.a: A daily task sheet
alt.ex: Diagnoses may appear in a formal care plan, a daily task sheet, or nurses’ notes.
w: The pharmacy dispensing log
The book lists care plans, task sheets, and nurses’ notes, not pharmacy logs.
The laboratory requisition form
Laboratory forms are not where the book says diagnoses are disseminated.
The patient’s hospital billing statement
Billing statements are not among the places the book lists.

items: The nurse enters assessment data into the EHR
The software organizes the data into patterns
The nurse selects accurate nursing diagnoses
The system directs the nurse to evidence-based outcome and intervention options
The nurse selects outcomes and interventions for the individual patient
ord.ex: Advanced systems pattern the nurse’s assessment data to support diagnosis, then offer evidence-based options for individualized care.

items.q: According to the book, many state-of-the-art EHRs contain which nursing content?
items.a: NANDA-I diagnoses, related factors, defining characteristics, NIC, and NOC
items.ex: Advanced EHRs often include full NANDA-I diagnostic content along with NIC interventions and NOC outcomes.
w: Medical diagnoses, laboratory reference ranges, and billing codes only
This omits the nursing diagnoses, interventions, and outcomes the book describes.
Free-text nurses’ notes without standardized nursing terms
State-of-the-art EHRs use standardized terminology such as NANDA-I, NIC, and NOC.
Physician order sets, pharmacy records, and imaging reports only
These lack the nursing diagnostic content the book says advanced EHRs contain.

alt.q: What does the ICNP® develop for specified health situations to help build health information systems?
alt.a: Catalogs, which are nursing data subsets
alt.ex: ICNP® catalogs are nursing data subsets used to build information systems for many practice settings.
w: Medication order sets for prescribers
Order sets are not what ICNP® develops; it develops nursing catalogs.
Billing codes for nursing services
ICNP® catalogs are nursing data subsets, not billing codes.
Patient education videos for discharge
ICNP® develops terminology catalogs, not teaching videos.

items.q: A nurse receives a hand-off report on a patient with the nursing diagnosis Acute Pain. Which action follows the book’s documentation guidance?
items.a: Confirm the diagnoses now and report the patient’s progress at end of shift
items.ex: The book advises confirming diagnoses during hand-off and communicating the patient’s progress at the end of the shift.
w: Accept the diagnoses as given and review them the next day
Diagnoses should be confirmed at hand-off, not deferred.
Delete the previous diagnoses and write new ones
The nurse confirms existing diagnoses rather than discarding them.
Report progress only if the patient’s pain worsens
Progress is communicated at the end of every shift, not only with worsening.

alt.q: At the end of the shift, a nurse prepares to give hand-off report on a patient whose diagnoses she confirmed at the start of the shift. What should she communicate?
alt.a: The patient’s progress on the identified nursing diagnoses
alt.ex: After confirming diagnoses at hand-off, the nurse communicates the patient’s progress at the end of the shift.
w: Only the patient’s medical diagnoses and orders
Nursing diagnoses and progress must be communicated, not only medical information.
Her personal opinion of the patient’s family
Report focuses on diagnoses and progress, not personal opinions.
A list of tasks she did not have time to chart
All care should be documented; report conveys the patient’s progress.

items.q: During an assessment, a nurse identifies that a patient has a new nursing diagnosis, Risk for Fall. How should the nurse document this?
items.a: Enter the diagnosis promptly in the EHR with the supporting assessment data
items.ex: The nurse should communicate diagnoses accurately and in a timely way and document the confirming assessment data.
w: Enter the diagnosis label alone at the end of the week
Diagnoses must be timely and supported by documented assessment data.
Tell the next nurse verbally without documenting it
Priority information must be documented and accessible to the whole team.
Wait until the health care provider confirms it
Nursing diagnoses are the nurse’s responsibility and should be entered promptly.

alt.q: Why does the book stress entering the right data into the EHR despite its ease and convenience?
alt.a: So all health care providers have an accurate database
alt.ex: Accurate entries give every provider an accurate database for decisions and communication.
w: So the agency can bill for every nursing action
The book’s reason is accuracy of the shared database, not billing.
So nurses can skip the hand-off report
Hand-off reports remain necessary to confirm diagnoses.
So the system can diagnose without nurses
Nurses still select diagnoses; accurate data support that decision.

items.q: Which findings about clinical decision support systems are reported in Box 17.3? Select all that apply.
o: They can increase adherence to clinical guidelines
Studies show CDS can increase adherence to clinical guidelines.
They are a tool to increase the accuracy of nursing diagnoses
A systematic review found CDS increases nursing diagnosis accuracy.
They reduced decision time in one study
CDS improved adherence to recommendations and reduced decision time.
They consistently improved every patient outcome
Effects on decision making, care delivery, and outcomes were mixed.
They eliminated the need for nursing judgment
CDS supports, rather than replaces, nurses’ clinical judgment.
items.ex: Evidence shows CDS can improve guideline adherence, diagnostic accuracy, and decision time, though outcome effects are mixed.

alt.q: A nurse reviews evidence on clinical decision support systems. Which conclusions are supported by Box 17.3? Select all that apply.
o: CDS can improve adherence to recommended diagnoses and treatments
Studies found CDS improved adherence to recommendations.
Effects on patient outcomes have been mixed
One study found mixed effects on decision making, care, and outcomes.
Predictive models using common nursing data elements show potential
Predictive CDS using standard terminology may provide valuable health status information.
CDS works well regardless of data quality
Data quality affects the quality of decision support.
CDS removes the need for continuing education
Nurses should attend ongoing education to use CDS well.
alt.ex: Correct: CDS can improve adherence to recommended diagnoses and treatments; Effects on patient outcomes have been mixed; Predictive models using common nursing data elements show potential.

items.q: Which nursing implications for clinical decision support systems are listed in Box 17.3? Select all that apply.
o: Be accurate and thorough when entering data
Data quality affects the quality of decision support.
Use informational standards such as ICNP® terminology
Information standards help ensure safe, effective nursing care.
Attend ongoing continuing education on the system
Education improves data entry, accuracy, and clinical judgment.
Accept system recommendations without review
CDS assists decisions; nurses still apply clinical judgment.
Limit data entry to save documentation time
Limited entry lowers data quality and decision support.
items.ex: Box 17.3 advises accurate data entry, use of information standards such as ICNP®, and ongoing education.

alt.q: A unit educator reviews best practices for the new clinical decision support system. Which statements by nurses reflect the nursing implications in Box 17.3? Select all that apply.
o: “I enter complete, accurate data because the support depends on it.”
Quality of data affects the quality of decision support.
“I use ICNP® terms so the information meets a standard.”
Using information standards such as ICNP® supports safe, effective care.
“I attend the update classes on the system each year.”
Ongoing education improves data entry, accuracy, and clinical judgment.
“I accept whatever the system recommends without question.”
CDS assists decision making; the nurse still uses clinical judgment.
“I skip optional fields so I can finish charting faster.”
Incomplete entries lower the quality of decision support.
alt.ex: Correct: “I enter complete, accurate data because the support depends on it.”; “I use ICNP® terms so the information meets a standard.”; “I attend the update classes on the system each year.”

items.q: A nurse documents a patient’s nursing diagnoses in the EHR. Which actions follow the book’s tips for accurate documentation? Select all that apply.
o: Document the assessment data that confirm each diagnosis
Supporting assessment data should be documented with the diagnosis.
Communicate the patient’s progress at the end of the shift
Progress is reported at the end of the shift after confirming diagnoses.
Document priority information where the whole team can access it
Priority information must be easily accessible to all team members.
Enter diagnoses without supporting data to save time
Diagnoses must be backed by documented assessment data.
Share diagnoses with nurses only, not other professionals
Nurses collaborate with all professionals using nursing diagnoses.
items.ex: Accurate EHR documentation includes supporting data, timely updates, progress reports, and accessible priority information.

alt.q: Which statements by a nurse show correct use of the EHR for nursing diagnoses? Select all that apply.
o: “I enter his new diagnosis now with the findings that support it.”
Timely entry with confirming data matches the book’s guidance.
“I confirmed his diagnoses during the hand-off report.”
Confirming diagnoses at hand-off is recommended.
“I use his nursing diagnoses when talking with the therapist.”
Nursing diagnoses convey patient problems to all professionals.
“I will chart his diagnoses later this week when it is quieter.”
Diagnoses should be documented in a timely manner.
“I keep his priority concerns on a note in my pocket.”
Priority information must be accessible to all team members.
alt.ex: Correct: “I enter his new diagnosis now with the findings that support it.”; “I confirmed his diagnoses during the hand-off report.”; “I use his nursing diagnoses when talking with the therapist.”

items.q: Research shows that the effects of clinical decision support systems on decision making, care delivery, and patient outcomes have been mixed.
items.a: True
items.ex: Box 17.3 reports mixed effects, although CDS improved adherence to recommendations and reduced decision time.
items.ww: Evidence does not show consistent improvement in all outcomes.

alt.q: Research shows that clinical decision support systems consistently improve all patient outcomes.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Studies found mixed effects on decision making, care delivery, and patient outcomes.
alt.ww: CDS shows benefits such as guideline adherence, but outcome effects are not consistent.

items.q: The ICNP® standardized terminology has been developed for various populations and settings and links well with other health-related terminology systems.
items.a: True
items.ex: ICNP® supports accurate, consistent sharing of information across settings and links with other terminologies.
items.ww: ICNP® is not limited to one setting; it was developed for various populations and settings.

alt.q: The ICNP® was developed for a single type of hospital unit and does not link with other health-related terminologies.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: ICNP® was developed for various populations and settings and links well with other terminology systems.
alt.ww: Its broad development and linkage support consistent information sharing across settings.

items.q: A clinical decision support system can be designed with rules based on current literature and practice or on patient needs.
items.a: True
items.ex: CDS rules can reflect current evidence, practice, or patient needs, supporting individualized care.
items.ww: The book describes designing CDS rules from literature, practice, or patient needs.

alt.q: Clinical decision support rules are fixed by the vendor and cannot be based on current literature or patient needs.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: CDS can be designed with rules based on current literature and practice or patient needs.
alt.ww: Agencies work with vendors to shape the system, including evidence-based rules.

items.q: Using [[standardized language|standardized terminology|standard language]] helps ensure accuracy and consistency in the way information is shared among health care providers.
items.ex: Accuracy and consistency in sharing information are essential, and standardized language helps ensure both.

alt.q: Accuracy and consistency of information shared in the EHR are supported by using [[standardized language|standardized terminology|standard language]] such as ICNP® or NANDA-I.
alt.ex: Accuracy and consistency in sharing information are essential, and standardized language helps ensure both.

items.q: [[Clinical decision support|CDS|clinical decision support system]] systems are software designed to guide nurses in their clinical decision making by matching assessment findings to a knowledge base.
items.ex: Clinical decision support systems compare a patient’s findings with a computerized knowledge base and present recommendations.

alt.q: Software that matches a patient’s assessment findings to a computerized clinical knowledge base and suggests diagnoses is a [[clinical decision support|CDS]] system.
alt.ex: Clinical decision support systems compare a patient’s findings with a computerized knowledge base and present recommendations.

items.q: What does critical thinking offer a nurse during the planning step of the nursing process?
items.a: A methodical way to avoid routine plans and create an individualized, patient-centered plan
items.ex: Critical thinking helps the nurse avoid routine plans of care and build an individualized plan developed with the patient’s involvement.
w: A quick way to copy a standard plan of care for patients with the same diagnosis
Routine, copied plans are exactly what critical thinking is meant to help the nurse avoid.
A method for the nurse to plan care without needing the patient’s input
The patient must be involved in decision making; planning is not done without the patient.
A way to replace the nursing diagnoses with a list of medical orders
Accurate nursing diagnoses guide planning; they are not replaced by a list of medical orders.

alt.q: A nurse uses the same preprinted plan for every patient after abdominal surgery without changes. Which feedback from the nurse educator reflects critical thinking in planning?
alt.a: “Each plan should be individualized and developed with the patient’s involvement.”
alt.ex: Critical thinking offers a methodical way to avoid routine plans and instead create an individualized, patient-centered plan.
w: “Using one plan for all patients ensures the most consistent care.”
Consistency does not replace individualization; routine plans ignore each patient’s unique needs.
“Standard plans are fine as long as the health care provider signs them.”
A provider’s signature does not make a routine plan person-centered or individualized.
“Plans only need to be individualized for patients who ask for changes.”
Every patient needs a person-centered plan, not only those who request changes.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A nurse with 15 years of experience on a surgical unit says, “I’ve cared for hundreds of colectomy patients, so I’ll just use my usual plan.” Which response by the charge nurse is best?
items.a: “Your experience speeds planning, but the plan still needs to fit this patient and involve him.”
items.ex: For experienced nurses planning occurs quickly and almost automatically, but it must still be person-centered for each unique patient.
w: “That is fine; experienced nurses no longer need to involve patients in planning.”
The patient must be involved in decision making regardless of the nurse’s experience.
“You should start over and write the plan as if you were a new graduate.”
Experience is an asset that makes planning faster; it does not need to be discarded.
“Use your usual plan and change it only if the health care provider asks.”
Individualizing the plan is the nurse’s responsibility, not something done only on request.

alt.q: Which statement about how experience affects planning is accurate?
alt.a: Planning becomes rapid for experienced nurses, yet it must remain person-centered.
alt.ex: Experienced nurses familiar with a diagnosis plan quickly, but each plan is still tailored to the unique patient.
w: Planning becomes rapid for experienced nurses, so patient involvement is optional.
The patient must always be involved in the decision-making process.
Planning stays slow for all nurses because each plan is written from scratch.
For experienced nurses, planning is a conscious process that occurs rather quickly.
Planning becomes automatic for experienced nurses, so plans can be standardized.
Even when planning feels automatic, the plan must be individualized for each patient.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: Which approach does the textbook describe as a way to promote person-centered care during planning?
items.a: Using a collaborative, partnership consultation style that involves patients in their care
items.ex: Forming a collaborative/partnership consultation style involves patients in their care and supports person-centered planning.
w: Using a directive style in which the nurse decides and then informs the patient
A directive style leaves the patient out; the patient must be involved in decision making.
Using a delegation style in which assistive personnel set the patient’s outcomes
Assistive personnel do not set outcomes; the nurse partners with the patient in planning.
Using a protocol style in which the agency’s standard plan is followed unchanged
Following a standard plan unchanged leads to routine care rather than person-centered care.

alt.q: A nurse sits with a patient and his wife to discuss goals before choosing interventions. Which planning approach is the nurse using?
alt.a: A collaborative, partnership consultation style
alt.ex: Involving the patient and family in decisions reflects the partnership consultation style that supports person-centered planning.
w: A directive, nurse-centered planning style
In a directive style the nurse decides alone, which this nurse is not doing.
A routine, protocol-driven planning style
Routine protocol plans are not individualized through discussion with the patient.
A delegated, team-assigned planning style
The nurse is not delegating; the nurse is partnering directly with the patient and family.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: The textbook calls education of the patient or family caregivers a fundamental part of any care plan. Which knowledge does the nurse need to plan that education?
items.a: Cultural caring, the teaching-learning process, and family dynamics
items.ex: Because teaching is part of every plan, the nurse needs knowledge of cultural caring, the teaching-learning process, and family dynamics.
w: Staffing levels, unit workflow, and the model for delivering care
These are environmental factors that affect timing of care, not the knowledge base for teaching.
Agency policies, infusion standards, and practice guidelines
These are standards the nurse applies, not the knowledge needed to plan patient education.
Skill competence, personal experience, and clinical experience
These belong to the experience component of critical thinking, not knowledge for teaching.

alt.q: A nurse plans discharge teaching for a patient whose adult children will help at home. Why does the nurse consider family dynamics in this plan?
alt.a: Teaching patients and family caregivers is a fundamental part of every plan of care.
alt.ex: Education of the patient or family caregivers is fundamental to any plan, which requires knowledge of family dynamics.
w: Family dynamics matter only when the patient cannot learn the material.
Teaching involves the patient and family caregivers as a fundamental part of every plan.
Family dynamics are assessed only by social workers, not by nurses.
Nurses use knowledge of family dynamics as part of their own knowledge base in planning.
Family dynamics replace the need to teach the patient directly.
The patient is still taught; family caregivers are included, not substituted.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A home health nurse is planning a day of patient visits. Which factor from the home health environment most directly affects how this nurse prioritizes care?
items.a: The distance the nurse must travel between scheduled visits
items.ex: In home health, the number of visits, travel distance, and availability of family caregivers and home resources affect prioritization.
w: The nursing unit’s workflow routine and shift report times
Unit workflow routines are hospital environmental factors, not home health factors.
The nurse’s years of clinical experience in home care
Years of experience belong to the experience component, not the environment.
The agency’s policies for documenting each home visit
Agency policies are part of the standards component, not the care environment.

alt.q: A hospital nurse notices that the unit is short two nurses today. Which component of critical thinking in planning does this factor represent?
alt.a: Environment
alt.ex: Staffing levels are an environmental factor that affects the minute-by-minute determination of patient care priorities.
w: Experience
Experience refers to the nurse’s personal and clinical experience and skill competence, not staffing.
Standards
Standards include practice guidelines, agency policies, and ethical standards, not staffing levels.
Attitudes
Attitudes include perseverance, responsibility, discipline, and creativity, not unit staffing.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A patient’s priority after hip replacement surgery is early mobility. When planning interventions, which question best shows the nurse anticipating environmental factors?
items.a: “Does this unit have a physical therapist or trained technicians to help with early ambulation?”
items.ex: The nurse anticipates environmental factors such as availability of personnel when identifying interventions in the plan of care.
w: “What is the pathophysiology of healing after hip replacement surgery?”
This question draws on the knowledge base, not on environmental factors.
“Have I ever helped a patient walk after hip replacement before?”
This question reflects the experience component, not the care environment.
“What does the clinical guideline say about early mobility after surgery?”
Clinical guidelines are part of the standards component, not the environment.

alt.q: Which planning decision shows that a hospital nurse is accounting for the care environment?
alt.a: Scheduling a patient’s ambulation for a time when trained staff are available to assist
alt.ex: Availability of personnel and resources affects timing and efficiency of a plan, so the nurse plans around it.
w: Reviewing the pathophysiology of the patient’s condition before choosing interventions
Reviewing pathophysiology uses the knowledge base rather than the environment.
Reviewing the clinical practice guideline for preventing bloodstream infection
Using a clinical guideline applies the standards component rather than the environment.
Reflecting on past patients who responded well to the same intervention
Reflecting on past patients uses the experience component rather than the environment.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A newly graduated nurse is planning care that includes a procedure the nurse has never performed. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Ask an experienced colleague for assistance with planning and performing the procedure.
items.ex: The nurse asks for assistance when experience with a patient problem or recommended intervention is limited, because competence affects outcomes.
w: Leave the procedure out of the plan until the nurse gains more experience.
Omitting a needed intervention harms the patient; the nurse should seek help instead.
Perform the procedure alone using memory of a classroom demonstration.
Limited competence can affect patient outcomes, so the nurse should ask for assistance.
Delegate the procedure to assistive personnel who have done it before.
Lack of nurse experience is not a reason to delegate; the nurse should seek help from a colleague.

alt.q: Why does a nurse’s competence in performing skills matter when planning care?
alt.a: Interventions often include skills, and the nurse’s competence affects patient outcomes.
alt.ex: Interventions in a plan often include skills or procedures, and competence in performing them affects outcomes.
w: Skills are seldom part of a plan of care, so competence matters little.
Interventions chosen for a plan of care often include nursing skills or procedures.
Competence affects only the nurse’s speed, not the patient’s outcomes.
The textbook states that skill competence affects patient outcomes.
Competence matters only for skills the health care provider has ordered.
Competence matters for all skills in the plan, including independent nursing skills.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A nurse is planning care for a patient receiving intravenous therapy. Which source of standards should guide interventions such as cleansing the IV site and changing the dressing?
items.a: The Infusion Nurses Society standards of practice for IV therapy
items.ex: The Infusion Nurses Society has standards of practice used when planning interventions for patients receiving IV therapy.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A patient’s family asks the nurse to plan care without telling the patient about a treatment option they dislike. Which question reflects the ethical standards the nurse applies in planning?

“Which option has the nurse performed most often before?”

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: Which definition describes clinical or practice autonomy?

w: The ability to plan care without sharing the plan with other health care providers
Nurses are responsible for sharing their plan of care with all health care providers.
The patient’s right to refuse any intervention that the nurse recommends
This describes patient autonomy, not the nurse’s clinical or practice autonomy.
The ability to carry out medical orders without questioning their purpose
Accountable decision making includes judgment, not following orders without thought.

alt.q: A nurse independently selects nursing interventions, collaborates with the team, and accepts accountability for the decisions. Which concept does this describe?
alt.a: Clinical or practice autonomy
alt.ex: Practice autonomy is independent, interdependent, and accountable decision making for the immediate benefit of patients.
w: Interprofessional consultation
Consultation is seeking expert advice from another professional, not the nurse’s own decision making.
Cognitive shifting
Cognitive shifts are changes in attention between patients, not accountable decision making.
Priority setting
Priority setting is ordering nursing diagnoses, not the overall ability to make accountable decisions.

Send the plan to the health care provider, who becomes responsible for it.
The nurse remains responsible for sharing the plan and keeping it relevant.

Asking the patient to keep a copy instead of sharing it with staff

items.q: Which statement best defines priority setting in nursing care?
items.a: The preferred ordering of nursing diagnoses or problems that guides timely selection of interventions
items.ex: Priority setting orders nursing diagnoses or patient problems, which then guides the selection and timely implementation of interventions.
w: The ordering of the care tasks listed in the patient’s electronic health record
Priority setting is not the ordering of a list of care tasks in the EHR.
The ranking of patients by the order in which their admissions occurred
Priorities depend on patients’ conditions and needs, not on admission order.
The fixed ranking of nursing diagnoses that is set once on admission
Priorities change as patients’ conditions change, sometimes within minutes.

alt.q: A nursing student says, “I set my priorities by working down the task list in the EHR.” Which response by the nursing instructor is best?
alt.a: “Priorities come from the patient’s current condition, treatment timing, and desired outcomes.”
alt.ex: Priorities are based on the patient’s current condition, the timing of ordered treatments, and desired outcomes, not a task list.
w: “That works well, because the EHR lists tasks in order of importance.”
Priority setting is not ordering a list of care tasks documented in the EHR.
“Priorities come from the order in which the health care provider wrote orders.”
The order of written orders does not determine the patient’s priority needs.
“Priorities come from whichever tasks take the least amount of time.”
Task length does not determine priority; the patient’s condition and outcomes do.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A nurse begins a shift caring for a patient whose plan of care was written two days ago. Which action should the nurse take first to establish today’s priorities?
items.a: Assess the patient to determine which nursing diagnoses are currently relevant.
items.ex: Ongoing assessment determines the current relevance of a patient’s diagnoses, so priorities are reviewed each time care begins.
w: Follow the priority order written in the plan two days ago.
Priorities can change within minutes, so an old ranking may no longer be accurate.
Complete the scheduled tasks before reviewing the plan of care.
Priority setting is based on the patient’s condition, not on completing a task list.
Ask assistive personnel which problems they think are the priority.
The nurse determines priorities through assessment; this is not delegated to assistive personnel.

alt.q: Why should a nurse review a patient’s priority diagnoses at the start of each shift or clinic visit?
alt.a: Patients’ conditions change, so the order for addressing diagnoses also changes.
alt.ex: As patients’ conditions change, the order for addressing diagnoses changes, sometimes within a matter of minutes.
w: Agency policy requires that diagnoses be renumbered at each shift.
The reason is the patient’s changing condition, not a renumbering policy.
Nursing diagnoses expire after each shift and must be rewritten.
Diagnoses do not expire; their relevance is confirmed through ongoing assessment.
Priorities are set by the previous nurse and cannot be changed later.
Each nurse reassesses and may change priorities as the patient’s condition changes.

Risk for Constipation

alt.q: Which principle should guide a nurse ranking a patient’s problem-focused and health promotion diagnoses?

w: Health promotion diagnoses generally take priority over problem-focused diagnoses.
This reverses the principle; actual problems generally come first.
At-risk diagnoses generally take priority over problem-focused diagnoses.
At-risk diagnoses generally rank below actual problem-focused diagnoses.
All types of diagnoses carry equal priority until the patient decides.
The nurse uses principles to rank diagnoses; they are not all equal.

items.q: Tonya has been focusing on Mr. Lawson’s postoperative teaching. He suddenly reports chest pain and difficulty breathing. Which action should Tonya take?
items.a: Act immediately on the warning signs of a possible pulmonary embolus.
items.ex: Chest pain and difficulty breathing are triggers of a possible pulmonary embolus, which requires immediate action.
w: Finish the discharge teaching, then reassess his breathing.
Teaching is not the priority when warning signs of a life-threatening complication appear.
Document the findings and recheck them at the next scheduled assessment.
Delaying action on signs of pulmonary embolus could result in serious harm.
Offer relaxation exercises to reduce his anxiety about surgery.
Treating anxiety ignores warning signs of a possible pulmonary embolus.

alt.q: Why did Mr. Lawson’s new chest pain and difficulty breathing change Tonya’s priorities?
alt.a: They were warning signs of a possible complication that required immediate action.
alt.ex: Knowledge triggers such as new clinical signs tell the nurse which symptom patterns need action and when.
w: They showed that his teaching needs were finally being met.
New chest pain and dyspnea are warning signs of a complication, not signs of learning.
They were expected findings that needed no change in the plan.
These signs suggested a pulmonary embolus, a complication of surgery needing urgent action.
They meant his Lack of Knowledge was now the highest priority.
A possible pulmonary embolus threatens breathing and circulation, which outrank teaching needs.

Anxiety about returning to work on time
This concern is low priority while he can attend to teaching and needs more assessment.
Risk for Infection with a healing incision
This is intermediate priority unless the condition of his wound worsens.

Tonya had identified four nursing diagnoses for Mr. Lawson.
Pain relief removed the need to teach him before discharge.
Teaching remained necessary; it became a greater priority once pain was controlled.

Unrelated to any current health needs of the patient

Focused only on the patient’s long-term health needs

Only when the health care provider writes an order for it
The nurse sets priorities for nursing diagnoses based on assessment, not an order.
Never, because psychosocial diagnoses are always low priority

alt.q: Which statement best describes low-priority nursing diagnoses?

w: They have no effect on the patient’s future health or well-being.

items.q: A dying patient with Acute Pain says, “Please hold my pain medicine for now. I need to talk about my fears first.” Which response by the nurse is best?

“Pain always comes first, so I need to give the medicine now.”
A dying patient’s fear may take precedence over pain when the patient requests it.
“Your fears can wait until the chaplain visits later today.”
The patient’s fear is the priority now; delaying it ignores the patient’s expressed need.

alt.q: When ethical issues cloud a patient’s priorities, which action should the nurse take?

alt.ex: When ethical issues cloud priorities, the nurse keeps an open dialogue with the patient, family members, and other providers.
w: Follow the physiological priorities and avoid discussing the issue.
Ethical concerns require open dialogue, not avoidance.
Let the family decide the priorities without involving the patient.
The patient’s expectations are central; dialogue includes the patient.

w: Agreeing to every request for help as soon as it is made

Completing all documentation before any patient care begins
Care is organized by patient priorities, not by finishing documentation first.
Following the morning priorities without revision all shift

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: How does the textbook define an outcome?
items.a: The effect of a health care service or intervention on a patient’s health or behavior
items.ex: An outcome is the effect of a health care service or intervention, including results in health status, quality of life, attitudes, and behavior.
w: The list of nursing interventions the nurse plans to deliver to a patient during a shift
A list of interventions describes nursing actions, not their effect on the patient.
The medical diagnosis that the health care provider confirms during a hospital stay
A medical diagnosis identifies disease; an outcome is the effect of care.
The nursing diagnosis label that best fits the cues found during the assessment
A nursing diagnosis identifies the problem; the outcome is the effect of care on it.

alt.q: A nurse positions a patient to reduce pain, and the patient reports less pain. What does the reduced pain represent?
alt.a: An outcome of the intervention
alt.ex: An outcome is the effect of a health care intervention; positioning aims to meet the outcome of pain reduction.
w: The nursing intervention itself
Positioning is the intervention; the reduced pain is its effect.
A nursing diagnosis for pain
A nursing diagnosis names the problem, such as Acute Pain, not the result of care.
The scientific rationale for care
A rationale explains why an intervention works, not the result in the patient.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A patient with a pressure injury has a nursing diagnosis of Impaired Skin Integrity. Which statement is a correctly written person-centered outcome?
items.a: “Pressure injury reduces in diameter by discharge.”
items.ex: A person-centered outcome reflects the patient’s response, not the nurse’s goals or the delivery of an intervention.
w: “Hydrogel dressing applied to pressure injury daily.”
This describes delivery of a nursing intervention, not the patient’s response.
“Nurse will turn patient every 2 hours.”
This is a nursing action, not a patient outcome.
“Nurse will teach patient about skin care.”
This states the nurse’s goal rather than a change in the patient.

alt.q: Which statement written in a care plan is an intervention rather than an expected outcome?
alt.a: “Ambulate patient in the hall.”
alt.ex: Writing an intervention in place of an outcome is a common error; outcomes describe patient behavior or response.
w: “Patient ambulates in the hall 3 times a day by 4/22.”
This is a correctly written outcome describing a specific patient behavior.
“Patient reports pain at a level of 3 or less by discharge.”
This is an outcome describing the patient’s report of pain.
“Patient’s wound shows no purulent drainage by discharge.”
This is an outcome describing a physiological response.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A nurse writes the outcome, “Patient’s lungs are clear to auscultation, and respiratory rate is 24 breaths/min by 8/22.” On 8/22 the lungs are clear but the respiratory rate is 28 breaths/min. What is the problem with this outcome?
items.a: It combines two responses, so the nurse cannot decide whether it was met.
items.ex: An outcome addresses only one behavior or response; combining two makes evaluation impossible when only one part is met.
w: It lacks a time frame, so the nurse cannot judge progress.
The statement does include a date, so timing is not the problem.
It uses vague terms, so the nurse cannot measure the result.
Both parts are measurable; the problem is that two responses are combined.
It describes a nursing intervention instead of a patient response.
Both parts describe patient responses; the problem is that there are two of them.

alt.q: Which expected outcome is written correctly as a single, specific response?
alt.a: “Patient’s respiratory rate is 16 to 20 breaths/min by 8/22.”
alt.ex: Each outcome should address only one behavior or response so the nurse can evaluate it and decide whether to modify the plan.
w: “Patient’s lungs are clear, and pulse is 60 to 100 beats/min by 8/22.”
This combines two responses, which makes evaluation difficult.
“Patient’s cough decreases, and appetite improves by 8/22.”
This combines two responses, so it could be partly met.
“Patient walks 20 feet, and temperature is below 37°C by 8/22.”
This combines two unrelated responses in one outcome.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: Which expected outcome should the nurse revise because it uses a vague qualifier?
items.a: “Patient’s vital signs will be stable by discharge.”
items.ex: Vague terms such as normal, acceptable, or stable lead to guesswork in judging the patient’s response.
w: “Patient’s pain is less than 4 on a 0-to-10 scale in 48 hours.”
This outcome uses a pain-rating scale that allows objective measurement.
“Apical pulse will remain between 60 and 100 beats/min.”
This outcome gives a measurable range for the pulse.
“Body temperature will remain below 37°C (98.6°F).”
This outcome gives a specific, measurable temperature value.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid words such as “normal” or “acceptable” in an expected outcome?
alt.a: They lead to guesswork when the nurse evaluates the patient’s response.
alt.ex: Vague terms result in guesswork; terms describing quality, quantity, frequency, length, or weight allow precise evaluation.
w: They make the outcome too long to document in the EHR.
The problem is imprecise evaluation, not the length of the statement.
They are reserved for outcomes written by health care providers.
No discipline should use vague qualifiers; the issue is measurability.
They prevent the patient from agreeing to the outcome.
The problem is that the outcome cannot be measured precisely, not patient agreement.

items.q: A patient with weakness has a nursing diagnosis of Self-Care Deficit: Hygiene. The nurse proposes the outcome, “Patient will wash hands and face in 72 hours.” How should the nurse confirm that this outcome is realistic?

items.ex: Assessment and collaboration with occupational therapy determine whether the outcome is realistic for the patient’s weakness.
w: Assume the outcome is realistic because it is a simple hygiene task.
Outcomes are set within the patient’s limitations, which must be assessed.
Change the time frame to 24 hours so it can be met more quickly.
A shorter time frame does not make the outcome more realistic for a weak patient.
Ask assistive personnel to decide whether the outcome is reasonable.
The nurse uses assessment and interprofessional collaboration, not AP judgment.

alt.q: When setting a realistic outcome, which factor should the nurse consider?
alt.a: Whether the patient has a reliable family caregiver to help at home
alt.ex: Realistic outcomes consider the patient’s preferences, needs, and resources, including reliable family caregivers.
w: Whether the outcome matches the outcomes of other patients on the unit
Outcomes are individualized; other patients’ outcomes do not determine realism.
Whether the outcome can be met without involving the patient
Outcomes are set with the patient and depend on the patient’s abilities.
Whether the outcome avoids any mention of cost or resources

Continue the same plan without any changes.

Every outcome should have a time for it to be met.

w: Patients should set all priorities, and the nurse carries them out.
The nurse remains responsible for acting in the patient’s best interests.
Patients should not be involved because their priorities may differ.

Patients should be involved only after the nurse finalizes priorities.

items.q: Tonya taught Mr. Lawson the signs of wound infection and used teach-back. Which statement by Mr. Lawson shows that he understood the teaching?

“I’ll call if I feel tired, lose my appetite, or have trouble sleeping.”

items.q: A nurse reviewing new orders notices a medication dose that seems much higher than usual for the patient’s condition. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Clarify the order before giving the medication
items.ex: Whenever a nurse is unsure about an order, it must be clarified before proceeding; clarifying orders protects the patient and team.
w: Give the dose as written because the prescriber is responsible
A nurse who carries out an incorrect order shares the error and is legally responsible for complications.
Give half the dose until the prescriber can be reached
Changing a dose independently is not within nursing scope; the order must be clarified first.
Document the concern after giving the scheduled dose
Documenting after administration does not prevent harm; clarification must come before giving the drug.

alt.q: A nurse is unsure whether a newly transcribed order for a feeding tube insertion is correct for the patient. Which statement by the nurse reflects competent practice?
alt.a: “I need to clarify this order before I proceed.”
alt.ex: Orders can be miswritten or mistranscribed, so the nurse clarifies any uncertain order before carrying it out.
w: “The provider wrote it, so the risk is the provider’s.”
A nurse who carries out an incorrect order shares the error and its legal responsibility.
“I will insert the tube now and ask about it later.”
Uncertain orders must be clarified before, not after, patient care.
“I will skip this order and leave it for the next shift.”
Ignoring the order delays care; the correct step is to clarify it now.

items.ww: The nurse is accountable for recognizing and clarifying errors, so responsibility is not limited to the prescriber.

alt.q: A nurse who carries out an inappropriate intervention is legally responsible for complications that result from the error.

alt.ww: Nurses cannot shift accountability to the prescriber; they must determine whether each therapy is appropriate.

Interventions are not chosen by label alone; the related factors differ.

Textbook order is not a selection factor; outcomes, evidence, and feasibility are.
