alt.q: A nurse is selecting interventions for a patient’s plan of care. Which considerations are among the six factors in Box 18.3? Select all that apply.
o: Research-based knowledge for the intervention
Research evidence shows the intervention’s effectiveness for certain types of patients.
Feasibility of carrying out the intervention
Feasibility includes interactions with other therapies, cost, time, and patient limitations.
The nurse’s own competency to perform it
The nurse must understand the rationale and have the necessary skills.
Whether the intervention was used for the last patient
Interventions must fit this patient’s diagnosis and related factors.
Whether the intervention can be completed by one nurse alone
Collaboration with others is often needed and is not a reason to reject an intervention.
alt.ex: Correct: Research-based knowledge for the intervention; Feasibility of carrying out the intervention; The nurse’s own competency to perform it.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: For a nursing diagnosis whose related factor cannot be changed, where should the nurse direct interventions?
items.a: Toward treating the signs and symptoms of the diagnosis
items.ex: When the related factor cannot change, interventions target the defining characteristics, or signs and symptoms.
w: Toward eliminating the risk factors for the diagnosis
Targeting risk factors is the approach for Risk diagnoses, not unchangeable related factors.
Toward revising the medical diagnosis with the provider
Medical diagnoses are not the focus of nursing interventions for this situation.
Toward removing the nursing diagnosis from the plan
The diagnosis still requires care; interventions shift to its signs and symptoms.

alt.q: A patient has the nursing diagnosis Risk for Infection. Where should the nurse direct interventions?
alt.a: Toward altering or eliminating the risk factors
alt.ex: For Risk diagnoses, interventions target the risk factors, such as keeping an incision clean and maintaining good nutrition.
w: Toward treating the defining characteristics
Risk diagnoses have no defining characteristics yet; the risk factors are targeted.
Toward relieving the existing signs of infection
A Risk diagnosis means the problem has not developed, so risk factors are addressed.
Toward changing the patient’s medical diagnosis
Medical diagnoses are not altered by nursing interventions for Risk diagnoses.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A nurse cannot find research evidence for an intervention being considered for a patient. What does Box 18.3 recommend?
items.a: Use scientific principles or consult a clinical expert
items.ex: When research is not available, the nurse relies on scientific principles (such as infection control or learning) or a clinical expert.
w: Choose the intervention the patient’s family prefers
Family preference matters but does not replace a scientific basis for the intervention.
Delay all interventions until research is published
Care cannot wait for new studies; scientific principles or an expert guide the choice.
Use the intervention that is the least costly
Cost relates to feasibility but does not substitute for a scientific basis.

alt.q: Which statement about the research base for nursing interventions is accurate?
alt.a: Research evidence indicates how effective an intervention is with certain types of patients
alt.ex: Nurses use research evidence for the appropriate patient group or setting because it shows effectiveness with certain patients.
w: Research evidence applies equally to every patient group and setting
Evidence must be applied to the appropriate patient group and setting.
Research evidence is needed only for dependent interventions
Evidence supports the selection of all intervention types, including independent ones.
Research evidence replaces the need for clinical judgment in selection
Evidence is combined with patient knowledge and experience in clinical judgment.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A nurse plans to get a patient up into a chair 3 times a day, but the patient is becoming weaker and few staff are available to help with transfers. Which Box 18.3 factor is the nurse considering?
items.a: Feasibility
items.ex: Feasibility includes the patient’s strengths and limitations, cost, staff, and time needed to carry out an intervention.
w: Acceptability to the patient
Acceptability concerns the patient’s choices, values, and culture, not staffing or weakness.
Research base
The research base concerns evidence of effectiveness, not available staff or patient strength.
Capability of the nurse
Nurse capability concerns the nurse’s knowledge and skills, not staffing or patient condition.

alt.q: A nurse asks, “Do I understand the scientific rationale for this intervention, and do I have the psychomotor skills to perform it?” Which Box 18.3 factor is the nurse considering?
alt.a: Capability of the nurse
alt.ex: Nurse capability includes understanding the rationale, having psychosocial and psychomotor skills, and using resources in the setting.
w: Feasibility
Feasibility addresses interactions, patient limitations, cost, and time rather than the nurse’s own skills.
Acceptability to the patient
Acceptability concerns patient choice, values, and culture.
Desired patient outcomes
Outcomes are criteria for judging efficacy, not the nurse’s competency.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A patient with chronic back pain says, “I don’t want to just be told what to do.” Which nursing action best promotes acceptability of the plan?

items.ex: Acceptability is promoted by offering choices and giving information about each intervention and the patient’s expected participation.
w: Choose the most effective intervention and begin it right away
Selecting for the patient without offering choices does not promote informed choice.
Ask the health care provider to decide which interventions to use
Shifting the decision to the provider bypasses the patient’s participation.
Use the agency’s standard plan without changes to save time
Standard plans should be customized; offering choices respects patient preferences.

alt.q: A nurse plans care for a patient whose cultural beliefs shape health practices. Which action best reflects the Box 18.3 guidance on acceptability?
alt.a: Consider the patient’s values, beliefs, and culture when selecting interventions
alt.ex: A person-centered approach considers values, beliefs, and culture so the patient accepts and participates in interventions.
w: Choose interventions that fit the unit routine, then explain them
Unit routine does not ensure the patient will accept the interventions.
Select interventions that worked for patients of the same age
Age-based choices ignore the individual’s values, beliefs, and culture.
Avoid discussing the plan so the patient is not overwhelmed
Patients need information about each intervention to make informed choices.

alt.q: In the NIC model, which level comes right before “Classes”?
alt.a: Domains

w: Interventions

alt.a: Classes

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

alt.ex: NIC level 1 uses seven broad domains to organize its 30 classes and 614 interventions.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: In the NIC taxonomy, what is “Physical Comfort Promotion”?

w: A domain at the highest level
Domains are the broad level 1 terms, such as safety and basic physiological.
A single nursing intervention
Interventions are level 3 items listed within the class, such as Nausea Management.
A nursing activity within an intervention
Activities are specific actions within an intervention, such as adjusting room temperature.

alt.q: A patient has the nursing diagnosis Acute Pain. Within the NIC class Physical Comfort Promotion, which is an example of an intervention?
alt.a: Pain Management: Acute
alt.ex: Pain Management: Acute is a level 3 intervention in the Physical Comfort Promotion class, with 20 recommended activities.
w: Basic physiological
Basic physiological is a broad level 1 domain, not an intervention.
Safety
Safety is a level 1 domain used to organize classes and interventions.
Acute Pain
Acute Pain is a nursing diagnosis linked to the class, not an intervention.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: NIC interventions can be used only with NANDA nursing diagnoses.
items.a: False
items.ex: As standard terminologies, NIC interventions can be used with several diagnostic classifications, including ICNP and NANDA.
items.ww: NIC is linked to more than one diagnostic system, so it is not limited to NANDA.

alt.q: NIC interventions can be used with various diagnostic classifications, including ICNP and NANDA.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: NIC provides standardized interventions usable across classifications to enhance communication and compare outcomes.
alt.ww: Restricting NIC to one system would defeat its purpose of standardizing communication across settings.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A patient’s plan of care includes the NIC intervention Comfort Management. Which nursing activities belong to this intervention? Select all that apply.
o: Adjust the room temperature to the patient’s comfort
Adjusting room temperature is a listed comfort management activity.
Determine sources of discomfort, such as a damp dressing
Identifying discomfort sources like damp dressings or wrinkled linen is listed.
Keep the nurse call system within reach and answer it promptly
Prompt attention to a call system within reach is a listed activity.
Keep the room brightly lit to help the patient stay alert
The activities call for a calm environment that supports quiet and rest.
Apply skin products freely to mucous membranes
Comfort management includes avoiding exposing skin or mucous membranes to irritants.
items.ex: Box 18.5 activities include adjusting temperature, a calm and clean environment, finding sources of discomfort, positioning, and a reachable call system.

alt.q: Which actions are examples of Comfort Management activities from Box 18.5? Select all that apply.
o: Provide a single room if the patient prefers quiet and rest
Offering a single room by preference is a listed activity.
Position the patient to facilitate comfort
Positioning for comfort is a listed comfort management activity.
Provide a safe, clean, calm, and airy environment
A safe, clean, calm, airy environment is a listed activity.
Check on the patient’s call light only at scheduled times
The activity calls for prompt attention to the nurse call system.
Leave wrinkled linen to avoid disturbing the patient
Wrinkled linen is named as a source of discomfort to correct.
alt.ex: Correct: Provide a single room if the patient prefers quiet and rest; Position the patient to facilitate comfort; Provide a safe, clean, calm, and airy environment.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: An experienced nurse knows how to adapt time-tested interventions when a patient has unique characteristics or problems.
items.a: True
items.ex: Experience teaches how interventions modify related factors, so expert nurses adapt proven interventions to unique patients.
items.ww: Experience is a critical thinking factor that supports adapting, not rigidly repeating, interventions.

alt.q: Once a nurse has seen an intervention succeed, it should be repeated exactly the same way for every patient with that diagnosis.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Experienced nurses reuse successful interventions when appropriate but adapt them when a patient poses unique characteristics.
alt.ww: Interventions must be individualized; the same label does not mean identical care for every patient.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: Which statement accurately describes The Joint Commission (TJC) requirement for a plan of care?

items.ex: TJC requires a plan of care for every patient in all settings but leaves its documentation or communication to each organization.
w: A plan of care is required only for hospitalized patients, using a TJC-supplied form
TJC requires a plan in all health care settings and does not mandate a particular form.
A plan of care is required only for surgical patients, using a critical pathway
The requirement covers every patient in all settings, not only surgical patients.
A plan of care is recommended but optional, depending on the patient’s condition
TJC requires, rather than recommends, a plan of care for each patient.

alt.q: A nurse in an outpatient clinic asks whether TJC requires a plan of care for clinic patients. Which response is accurate?

alt.ex: The TJC requirement applies to each patient in every health care setting, not only inpatient units.
w: “No. TJC requires plans of care only for hospital inpatients.”
The requirement extends to all health care settings.
“No. TJC requires plans of care only for patients on critical pathways.”
Every patient needs a plan of care, whatever form it takes.
“Yes, but only when the clinic uses TJC’s standard care plan form.”
TJC leaves the documentation format up to each organization.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: According to TJC, a care plan refers to the process of planning and implementing coordinated, person-centered care rather than to a particular document.
items.a: True
items.ex: TJC describes the treatment or care plan as a process; organizations choose how to document it.
items.ww: TJC does not specify a document, so equating the care plan with one form is incorrect.

alt.q: TJC defines a care plan as a specific standardized form that every accredited agency must use.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A care plan is the process of coordinated, person-centered care; it may take forms such as an EHR plan, standardized plan, ERAS, or pathway.
alt.ww: TJC leaves the format up to each organization rather than mandating one form.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: What is the purpose of an enhanced recovery after surgery (ERAS) pathway?
items.a: To reduce surgical stress response, optimize physiologic function, and facilitate recovery
items.ex: An ERAS is an interprofessional, evidence-based pathway designed to lower surgical stress, optimize function, and speed recovery.
w: To replace individualized care plans with one fixed surgical routine
Care must still be individualized; clinical judgment outranks the pathway.
To document each patient’s nursing diagnoses and their rationales
Rationales with references are a feature of student care plans, not ERAS.
To determine which patients qualify for elective surgery
ERAS guides recovery for a planned surgery rather than surgical eligibility.

alt.q: A nurse explains to a patient scheduled for a specific surgery that an interprofessional team created an ERAS pathway. Which statement best describes it?
alt.a: It plots the expected hourly or daily progress from home through surgery and back home
alt.ex: An ERAS sets time frames for each discipline’s responsibilities across the whole perioperative continuum.
w: It lists the nursing diagnoses a student must address during the stay
Student care plans list diagnoses; ERAS plots expected progression for a surgery.
It covers only the time the patient spends in the operating room
ERAS spans the entire perioperative period, from home back to home.
It is written by nurses alone to direct nursing care only
ERAS is developed by an interprofessional team and identifies each discipline’s responsibilities.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: An ERAS pathway sets expected time frames for which patient care events? Select all that apply.
o: Progressing with mobility
ERAS sets when patients are to progress with mobility.
Advancing the diet
Diet advancement is timed within an ERAS.
Receiving specific types of medications
ERAS sets when patients receive specific types of medications.
Discontinuing therapies such as a Foley catheter
ERAS times the discontinuation of therapies like IV lines and Foley catheters.
Choosing the patient’s surgeon
ERAS guides care for a planned surgery; it does not select providers.
items.ex: An ERAS plots hourly or daily progression, setting when patients advance mobility and diet, get medications, and stop therapies.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a patient’s ERAS pathway after surgery. Which elements would the nurse expect it to include? Select all that apply.
o: When intravenous therapy is to be discontinued
ERAS sets time frames for discontinuing therapies such as IV lines.
When the patient should advance with mobility
Mobility progression is a timed element of an ERAS.
Each discipline’s responsibilities, such as treatments and diagnostics
ERAS forms an integrated continuum identifying each discipline’s responsibilities.
A guarantee that every patient will follow the pathway
Not every patient fits a pathway; clinical judgment outranks it.
Scientific rationales with cited references for each nursing action
Cited rationales are a feature of student care plans.
alt.ex: Correct: When intravenous therapy is to be discontinued; When the patient should advance with mobility; Each discipline’s responsibilities, such as treatments and diagnostics.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A patient on a total hip replacement ERAS pathway is not ready to advance activity on the day the pathway specifies because of new dizziness. Which action by the nurse is best?

items.ex: Not every patient fits a pathway; clinical judgment outranks the care path, and care must still be individualized.
w: Advance activity as scheduled because the pathway is evidence based
Following the pathway despite a change in condition ignores clinical judgment and patient safety.
Remove the patient from all planned care until the dizziness ends
Stopping all care is unnecessary; the plan is individualized to the patient’s status.
Wait to update the plan until the next scheduled care conference
Nurses revise the plan when the patient’s status changes, not at a later meeting.

alt.q: Which statement about critical pathways and ERAS is accurate?

alt.ex: Pathways support consistent workflow, but nurses must individualize care because not every patient fits a pathway.
w: Every patient with the condition will fit the pathway
The book cautions that not every patient will fit an ERAS or pathway.

Pathways and ERAS need routine updating as new evidence emerges.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: Critical pathways and ERAS have traditionally been developed for conditions that are high volume and relatively predictable, such as total hip replacement.

items.ww: Pathways rely on predictable courses, so they are built for common, consistent conditions rather than rare ones.

alt.q: Critical pathways are mainly developed for rare conditions with unpredictable courses, where standard workflows are not possible.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Pathways are developed for high-volume, consistent, relatively predictable medical and surgical conditions.
alt.ww: A pathway plots expected progression, which requires a predictable course rather than an unpredictable one.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: Standardized care plans follow a standard format, but the nurse can individualize each plan to a patient’s unique needs.

items.ww: The book stresses that nurses customize standardized plans, so they are not fixed.

alt.q: Because standardized care plans are developed by agency clinical experts, nurses should not alter them for individual patients.
alt.a: False

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: For which types of expertise are nurses consulted? Select all that apply.

Patient education skills
Patient education skills are a reason nurses are consulted.
Staff education skills
Nurses are consulted for staff education skills.
Writing orders for invasive procedures
Ordering procedures is a health care provider’s role, not a reason nurses are listed as consultants.
Prescribing changes to medications

items.ex: Nurses serve as consultants for their clinical expertise, patient education skills, and staff education skills.

alt.q: Which statements about consultation in nursing are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Nurses in practice frequently consult with dietitians, therapists, and pharmacists

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: A newly licensed nurse is caring for a patient whose symptoms the nurse cannot identify. Which action is best?
items.a: Consult an experienced nurse on the unit
items.ex: An experienced nurse is a valuable consultant in unfamiliar situations, such as unidentified symptoms or a new procedure.
w: Wait to see whether the symptoms resolve on their own
Waiting delays needed care when the nurse cannot identify the problem.
Search online for the symptoms before taking any action
Consulting an experienced colleague gives timely, situation-specific expertise.
Document the symptoms and leave them for the next shift
Passing an unidentified problem along delays care that consultation could provide.

alt.q: A nurse is assigned a patient who needs a procedure the nurse has never performed. Which statement by the nurse reflects appropriate consultation?

“I will skip the procedure until someone else is assigned.”

“I will ask the patient to explain how it is usually done.”
The patient is not the appropriate source of procedural expertise.

items.src: Ch 18 · Planning and outcomes identification in nursing care

items.q: What advantage does an objective consultant bring to an unclear clinical situation?

Ability to approve changes without informing the nurse
Consultants share findings and recommendations with the nurse, who incorporates them.
Guarantee that the first recommendation will solve the problem
Recommendations are tried, and the nurse gives feedback on their outcome.

Nurses remain available to discuss findings and recommendations.

Wait for the dietitian to revise the nursing care plan
The nurse incorporates the recommendations; the consultant does not take over.

w: Follow the protocol exactly as written, because standard interventions cannot be changed.
Standard interventions guide care, but the nurse must still tailor them to the individual patient.
Stop using the protocol, because it does not fit this particular patient.
The protocol still provides effective, evidence-based care; it is adapted, not abandoned.
Ask the patient to wait until the protocol is formally revised by the expert team.
Waiting for a formal revision delays person-centered care the nurse is accountable to provide now.

“Standard interventions are written only for rare and unusual health problems.”

“Standard interventions are chosen mainly by individual staff nurses on each shift.”
Expert clinical teams review scientific evidence and current practices to form standard interventions.

This describes a standing order, which is a list of medical orders rather than evidence-based recommendations.
Specific interventions unique to one clinical setting that staff in that setting must follow
This describes a protocol, which is unique to a setting; guidelines address recurring problems more broadly.
A standardized language that nurses use to name and organize the treatments they perform
This describes the Nursing Interventions Classification (NIC), not clinical practice guidelines.

alt.q: Recommendations intended to optimize patient care, informed by a systematic review of evidence and an assessment of benefits and harms of alternative care options, are called:

Standing orders are lists of medical orders signed by a prescriber, not evidence-review recommendations.
Care plans
A care plan is an individual patient’s plan, not a set of evidence-based recommendations for a condition.
Critical pathways

items.ex: The recommendations combine the evidence with value judgments about benefits and harms of alternative options.
w: The systematic review of evidence
The systematic review summarizes current research and the strength of the evidence, not value judgments.
The agency’s standing orders
Standing orders are separate medical orders, not one of the two parts of a guideline.
The patient’s nursing care plan
The care plan is individual; the guideline’s two parts are the evidence review and the recommendations.

The expected outcomes in the nursing care plan

Protocols include specific interventions that are set in place and must be followed.

This resembles a standing order; protocols are setting-specific sets of interventions.

A standing order is a list of medical orders signed by a prescriber for specific clinical problems.
Nursing diagnosis
A nursing diagnosis names a patient problem; it is not a set of required interventions.

The point of a bundle is that its interventions work better collectively.
“Bundles are designed mainly to shorten the time nurses spend on documentation.”
Bundles are designed to improve quality by preventing the most common complications.
“Bundles let nurses skip the interventions that seem least important to them.”

“That is fine because bundles have not been shown to change outcomes.”

Perform only the bundle intervention with the strongest evidence.
Bundle interventions have more impact together than any single intervention alone.
Use the bundle only when the patient shows signs of infection.
Bundles are designed to prevent common complications, so they are used before problems appear.

Give the medication and record it without ever notifying the health care provider.

“I never need to tell the health care provider about care given under a standing order.”

items.q: A nurse is applying evidence about care bundles to practice. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Perform the full set of interventions in the bundle
Every component must be consistently implemented to optimize effectiveness.
Adapt each intervention to the clinical setting where it is performed
Interventions should be adapted to the clinical setting.
Document and evaluate all bundle interventions
Documentation and evaluation show improved adherence by the health care team.
Use the bundle to support communication among care teams
Bundles facilitate communication between teams and individuals involved in care.
Omit bundle elements when the unit is short staffed
Omitting elements reduces effectiveness; the full set is performed.
Use the bundle only after a complication develops
Bundles are designed to prevent common complications.
items.ex: Nurses perform the full bundle, adapt it to the setting, document and evaluate it, and use it to improve communication.

alt.q: Which nursing actions would reduce the effectiveness of a care bundle? Select all that apply.
o: Skipping one bundle element when busy
Every component must be consistently implemented for bundles to work.
Carrying out bundle elements only occasionally
Bundles improve outcomes when performed collectively and reliably.
Doing only the element with the best evidence
Bundle elements have greater impact together than individually.
Documenting each bundle element performed
Documenting all interventions is recommended to show adherence.
Adapting elements to the clinical setting
Adapting interventions to the setting is a recommended practice.
alt.ex: Correct: Skipping one bundle element when busy; Carrying out bundle elements only occasionally; Doing only the element with the best evidence.

items.q: For which purposes is the Nursing Interventions Classification (NIC) system used? Select all that apply.
o: Care planning
NIC is used for care planning.
Clinical documentation
NIC is used for clinical documentation.
Communication across care settings
NIC enhances communication of nursing care across settings.
Effectiveness research
NIC supports effectiveness research and outcome comparison.
Prescribing medications under standing orders
Standing orders are signed by prescribers; NIC does not authorize prescribing.
Replacing nursing diagnoses with medical diagnoses
NIC classifies nursing interventions; it does not replace nursing diagnoses.
items.ex: NIC supports care planning, documentation, communication across settings, data integration, research, productivity measurement, and competency evaluation.

alt.q: Which statements describe features of the Nursing Interventions Classification (NIC)? Select all that apply.
o: It provides a nursing language for health care information software.
NIC provides a nursing language for health care information systems.
It organizes knowledge so it can be retrieved to aid decision making.
NIC organizes knowledge for management and retrieval to facilitate decisions.
It is used in competency evaluation and productivity measurement.
Both uses are listed among NIC features.
It lists the three to five steps of each care bundle.
Care bundles are a separate form of clinical guideline.
It is used only within a single hospital unit.
NIC enhances communication of nursing care across settings.
alt.ex: Correct: It provides a nursing language for health care information software; It organizes knowledge so it can be retrieved to aid decision making; It is used in competency evaluation and productivity measurement.

items.q: Clinical protocols are unique to a clinical setting and include specific interventions that must be followed.
items.a: True
items.ex: Protocols are setting-specific and required, and they often incorporate aspects of clinical guidelines.
items.ww: Protocols are not optional suggestions; they set specific required interventions for that setting.

alt.q: Clinical protocols are identical in every agency because they are copied directly from national guidelines.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Protocols are unique to each clinical setting, though agencies often incorporate aspects of guidelines into them.
alt.ww: Agencies do draw on guidelines, but each protocol is unique to its own setting.

items.q: A nurse must contact the health care provider before giving a medication covered by a standing order.
items.a: False
items.ex: The standing order covers the nurse’s action, so the nurse gives the medication first and notifies the provider afterward.
items.ww: Requiring prior contact would defeat the purpose of standing orders in rapidly changing, urgent situations.

alt.q: After completing a standing order, the nurse notifies the health care provider.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The nurse acts under the standing order and then notifies the health care provider.
alt.ww: Standing orders do not eliminate communication; the provider is informed once the order is carried out.

items.q: A review of many studies found that the effect of care bundles on patient outcomes is still uncertain and needs more research.
items.a: True
items.ex: Although some studies show benefits, a review of 37 studies reported that the effect of bundles is uncertain.
items.ww: Some single studies showed benefit, but the overall evidence on outcomes is not yet conclusive.

alt.q: Research has firmly established that care bundles improve patient outcomes in every condition studied.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Some studies show promising benefits, but reviews report the effect of bundles on outcomes remains uncertain.
alt.ww: Promising single studies do not outweigh reviews finding the overall effect uncertain.

items.q: A [[standing order]] is a standard list of medical orders for routine therapies, monitoring guidelines, or diagnostic procedures for patients with specific clinical problems.
items.ex: Standing orders are signed by licensed prescribers and let nurses act promptly in specific clinical settings.

items.q: Which description best fits reflection-in-action?
items.a: Reading the patient during care and modifying interventions as needed
items.ex: Reflection-in-action involves self-awareness and the ability to read, assess, and modify interventions while caring for a patient.
w: Reviewing the outcomes of care afterward to guide future practice
This is reflection-on-action, which is retrospective.
Following the agency protocol exactly without any changes to it
Reflection-in-action involves making necessary modifications, not rigid adherence.
Writing the nursing care plan before meeting the patient for care
Planning ahead is part of preparation, not reflection while acting.

alt.q: While bathing a patient, a nurse notices the patient wincing and changes the plan to reposition the patient more slowly. This is an example of:
alt.a: Reflection-in-action
alt.ex: Reading the patient and modifying the intervention during care is reflection-in-action.
w: Reflection-on-action
Reflection-on-action is retrospective and happens after care is completed.
Standing order use
A standing order is a prescriber’s list of medical orders, not a reflective process.
Delegation of care
Delegation assigns tasks to others; this nurse is adapting their own care.

items.q: After a shift, a nurse reviews why a patient did not learn the planned teaching and decides to use shorter sessions in the future. Which process is the nurse using?
items.a: Reflection-on-action
items.ex: Reflection-on-action is retrospective; the nurse processes outcomes of care to influence future practice.
w: Reflection-in-action
Reflection-in-action occurs during care, as the nurse reads and adapts to the patient.
Nonanalytical reasoning
Nonanalytical reasoning is quick and reflexive, not a deliberate review after care.
Standard intervention
A standard intervention is a set of care measures, not a reflective process.

alt.q: Which statement best describes reflection-on-action?
alt.a: A retrospective review of care outcomes that shapes future practice
alt.ex: In reflection-on-action, the nurse looks back on the outcomes of care to influence future nursing practice.
w: An immediate change in care based on the patient’s response
Adapting care in the moment is reflection-in-action.
A prescriber-approved list of orders for urgent situations
This describes a standing order, not a reflective process.
A set of three to five interventions performed together
This describes a care bundle, not reflection.

items.q: A nurse is preparing medications on a busy unit with frequent phone calls. Which action best applies critical thinking about the environment?
items.a: Prepare the medications in a No-Interruption Zone and mute the phone.
items.ex: Eliminating distractions during medication preparation helps the nurse attend to the task and ensure accuracy.
w: Prepare the medications quickly between calls to keep up with the workload.
Working between interruptions increases distraction and the chance of error.
Ask the assistive personnel to prepare the medications while the nurse answers calls.
Medication preparation is the nurse’s responsibility; delegation does not remove the distraction problem.
Prepare all patients’ medications at the start of the shift to save time later.
This does not address interruptions and is not the safety strategy the text describes.

alt.q: Which nursing action reflects attention to task complexity and interruptions during implementation?
alt.a: Temporarily turning off the phone while preparing medications
alt.ex: Eliminating distractions helps ensure accuracy when administering interventions.
w: Answering every call immediately during medication preparation
Responding to interruptions during preparation increases the risk of error.
Preparing medications at the busy nurses’ station counter
A busy area adds distractions; a No-Interruption Zone is recommended.
Talking with visitors while drawing up an injection
Conversation adds distraction during a task that requires accuracy.

items.q: A nursing student is assigned to perform a procedure that the student has practiced only in the simulation lab. Which action should the student take first?
items.a: Reflect on personal competency and obtain resources such as an experienced nurse.
items.ex: For a new procedure, reflect on competency and knowledge, obtain resources, and refer to the policy and procedure manual.
w: Perform the procedure alone because it was practiced successfully in simulation.
Simulation practice alone may not ensure safe performance on a real patient.
Refuse the assignment until the procedure has been seen several more times.
Refusing is unnecessary; obtaining guidance and resources supports safe performance.
Ask the patient whether the procedure can be postponed to another shift.
Postponing care is not the recommended response; preparation and support are.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student about performing a new procedure on a patient shows correct understanding?
alt.a: “I will review the procedure manual and ask an experienced nurse to help me.”
alt.ex: Skill competence for a new procedure is supported by reviewing policy and procedures and obtaining an experienced nurse.
w: “I passed it in the simulation lab, so I can do it on my own.”
Simulation practice does not replace reflecting on competency and obtaining resources.
“I will watch an online video while I perform the procedure.”
Reviewing resources happens before care, not during the procedure.
“I will let the patient guide me since the patient has had it before.”
The nurse, not the patient, is responsible for competent, safe performance.

items.q: A nurse is walking a postoperative patient in the hallway when the patient becomes dizzy and the gait becomes unsteady. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Sit the patient in a chair.
items.ex: The nurse anticipates hypotension or unsteady gait and adjusts by sitting the patient in a chair when symptoms develop.
w: Continue walking slowly back to the room.
Continuing to walk a dizzy patient increases the risk of a fall.
Leave the patient to get a wheelchair.
Leaving a dizzy patient standing alone is unsafe.
Ask the patient to walk faster to finish.
Increasing activity during symptoms worsens the risk of falling.

alt.q: Adjusting an intervention to a patient’s changing status, such as sitting a patient down when hypotension develops during ambulation, reflects which intellectual standard?
alt.a: Relevance
alt.ex: Table 19.1 links adapting an intervention to the patient’s changing status with the intellectual standard of relevance.
w: Creativity
Creativity is an attitude, shown by adapting care to a physical limitation, not an intellectual standard.
Confidence
Confidence is an attitude that builds trust, not the intellectual standard in this example.
Experience
Experience is a separate critical thinking element, not an intellectual standard.

items.q: A nurse who uses surgical asepsis for a hospitalized patient’s dressing change is preparing the family caregiver to change the dressing at home. Which technique should the nurse teach?
items.a: Clean technique
items.ex: Interventions are adapted to the setting: surgical asepsis in the hospital and clean technique for family caregivers at home.
w: Surgical asepsis
Surgical asepsis is used in the hospital; the intervention is adapted for the home setting.
Sterile gloving
Sterile gloving is part of surgical asepsis, which is adapted for home use.
No hand hygiene
Clean technique still requires hand hygiene to reduce infection risk.

alt.q: Using surgical asepsis for a dressing change in the hospital but teaching clean technique for the home illustrates which critical thinking element?
alt.a: Environment: health care setting
alt.ex: Table 19.1 lists adapting an intervention to conditions within a setting under the environment element.
w: Knowledge: pathophysiology
Pathophysiology guides choices such as suction frequency in pneumonia, not setting adaptations.
Attitudes: confidence
Confidence relates to calm, clear instructions that build patient trust.
Standards: intellectual standards
Intellectual standards guide precision and relevance, not adapting care to the setting.

items.q: Tonya administers the anticoagulant ordered for Mr. Lawson after his pulmonary embolus has stabilized. What type of nursing function is this?
items.a: A dependent function
items.ex: Giving a prescribed anticoagulant is a dependent function because it requires a health care provider’s order.
w: An independent function
Independent functions are nurse-initiated; this medication requires a provider’s order.
A delegated function
Medication administration here is performed by the RN, not delegated to others.
A standing order function
No standing order is described; the anticoagulant was ordered for Mr. Lawson.

alt.q: Why did Tonya choose not to identify a nursing diagnosis for Mr. Lawson’s pulmonary embolus, even though she continues to monitor his vital signs?
alt.a: The condition has stabilized, and she continues the provider-ordered care.
alt.ex: Once the acute problem stabilized, Tonya monitored vital signs and gave the ordered anticoagulant rather than adding a diagnosis.
w: The condition was never considered serious enough to monitor.
The embolus required immediate action and continued monitoring.
Nurses are not allowed to monitor patients with emboli.
Tonya continues to monitor vital signs as part of care.
The patient asked her not to address the condition.
The decision was based on his stabilized condition, not a patient request.

items.q: Tonya teaches Mr. Lawson relaxation exercises, which help both his anxiety and his acute pain. What does this illustrate?
items.a: One planned intervention can treat more than one health problem.
items.ex: Nursing diagnoses are interrelated, so a single intervention such as relaxation can modify more than one problem.
w: Each nursing diagnosis must have its own separate interventions.
Diagnoses are interrelated, and one intervention can address several problems.
Relaxation exercises replace the need for analgesics after surgery.
Relaxation is used with analgesics, not as a replacement for them.
Anxiety must be resolved before pain can be treated.
The example shows both problems being treated by the same intervention.

alt.q: Which statement about Mr. Lawson’s nursing diagnoses is accurate?
alt.a: His diagnoses are interrelated, so some interventions address more than one.
alt.ex: Relaxation exercises, for example, help both anxiety and acute pain.
w: His diagnoses are independent, so each needs a separate plan.
The diagnoses are interrelated, and interventions can overlap.
His diagnoses stay fixed in priority throughout the stay.
Lack of Knowledge became a priority as discharge approached.
His diagnoses should be addressed one at a time in order.
Interrelated diagnoses are often treated together by shared interventions.

items.q: A nursing student is unsure how to carry out a planned intervention. What does the textbook recommend?
items.a: Seek supervision from faculty or experienced nurses, or review agency policy and procedures.
items.ex: Beginning students seek supervision or review policies and procedures to guide implementation decisions.
w: Perform the intervention as best as possible and ask questions afterward.
Acting without needed knowledge risks patient safety; seek guidance first.
Skip the intervention and document that it was not needed.
Omitting care and documenting it inaccurately is unsafe and inappropriate.
Ask the patient’s family how they would prefer it be done.
Family input matters, but the student needs professional guidance for the intervention.

alt.q: Which action by a beginning nursing student shows sound clinical judgment before implementing an unfamiliar intervention?
alt.a: Asking the faculty member for supervision before starting
alt.ex: Seeking supervision from faculty or experienced nurses guides the student’s implementation decisions.
w: Starting the intervention to avoid delaying the patient’s care
Starting without needed knowledge places the patient at risk.
Asking another student to perform it instead
Another student may lack competence; supervision by faculty is appropriate.
Waiting until the next clinical day to attempt it
Delay is unnecessary when supervision and resources are available.

items.q: Which attitude in performing interventions builds trust with patients?
items.a: Confidence
items.ex: The text states that confidence in performing interventions builds trust with patients.
w: Discipline
Self-discipline guides reviewing, modifying, and implementing interventions.
Creativity
Creativity helps the nurse adapt interventions, such as for physical limitations.
Independence
Independent thinking is an attitude, but the text links trust to confidence.

alt.q: Before teaching, a nurse reflects on why the patient is receiving an intervention and then gives clear, calm instructions about how the patient can participate. Which attitude is the nurse demonstrating?
alt.a: Confidence
alt.ex: Table 19.1 pairs confidence with reflecting first and then giving clear, calm, confident instructions.
w: Creativity
Creativity is shown by adapting interventions to physical limitations.
Responsibility
Responsibility is an attitude, but this example illustrates confidence.
Discipline
Discipline guides reviewing and modifying interventions, not this example.

items.q: What does recognizing a patient’s changing clinical condition during implementation require of the nurse?
items.a: Knowing the patient and situation and responding in a timely manner
items.ex: Recognizing clinical change requires knowing the patient and situation and responding promptly by adapting interventions.
w: Following the original plan of care until the next scheduled evaluation
Waiting for scheduled evaluation delays the timely response that changing conditions require.
Relying only on standard protocols rather than on the individual patient
Protocols help, but recognizing change depends on knowing the individual patient and situation.
Delegating reassessment of the patient to the assistive personnel
Recognizing and responding to clinical change requires the nurse’s own clinical judgment.

alt.q: A nurse notices that a patient’s condition is changing during care. Which approach best reflects critical thinking in implementation?
alt.a: Consider which assessments to gather, which findings to expect, and how to adapt interventions.
alt.ex: The nurse considers needed assessments, expected findings, and adaptations, drawing on knowledge and past experience.
w: Continue the planned interventions unchanged until the shift ends.
A changing condition calls for a timely response and possible adaptation of interventions.
Stop all interventions until the health care provider makes rounds.
Stopping care and waiting is not a timely response to clinical change.
Repeat the same intervention more often to see if it starts working.
The nurse adapts interventions based on assessment rather than simply repeating them.

items.q: Which attitudes are part of critical thinking in implementation? Select all that apply.
o: Independent thinking
Thinking independently is listed among the attitudes.
Responsibility
Responsibility is an attitude that guides implementation.
Creativity
Creativity helps the nurse adapt interventions to the patient.
Confidence
Confidence in performing interventions builds trust.
Skill competence
Skill competence is part of the experience element.
Task complexity
Task complexity is an environmental factor.
items.ex: The attitudes are independent thinking, responsibility, creativity, discipline, and confidence.

alt.q: Which items belong to critical thinking elements other than attitudes? Select all that apply.
o: Previous patient care experiences
This belongs to the experience element.
Agency policies and procedures
This belongs to the standards element.
Time pressure on the unit
This belongs to the environment element.
Discipline
Discipline is one of the attitudes.
Creativity
Creativity is one of the attitudes.
alt.ex: Correct: Previous patient care experiences; Agency policies and procedures; Time pressure on the unit.

items.q: Which environmental factors influence critical thinking during implementation? Select all that apply.
o: Time pressure
Time pressure is an environmental factor.
Interruptions
Interruptions are an environmental factor that threatens accuracy.
Care delivery model on the nursing unit
The care delivery model is part of the environment.
Health care resources such as equipment and personnel
Available resources are an environmental factor.
Knowledge of successful interventions
This belongs to the experience element.
Ethical standards
Ethical standards belong to the standards element.
items.ex: Environment includes time pressure, setting, task complexity, the care delivery model, interruptions, and resources.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing factors in the work setting that may affect implementation. Which factors should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.
o: Task complexity
Task complexity is an environmental factor.
Interruptions during care
Interruptions are an environmental factor.
Available equipment and personnel
Health care resources are part of the environment.
The ANA scope and standards of practice
These are part of the standards element.
The nurse’s skill competence
Skill competence is part of the experience element.
alt.ex: Correct: Task complexity; Interruptions during care; Available equipment and personnel.

items.q: Which tips help a nurse form judgments and make decisions during implementation? Select all that apply.
o: Review the set of all possible interventions for the problem
Reviewing all possible interventions is the first tip listed.
Review all possible consequences of each nursing action
Consequences include relief, little effect, or an adverse reaction.
Determine the probability of each possible consequence
Estimating risk helps decide whether to continue or change interventions.
Judge the value of the consequence to the patient
The nurse weighs how the consequence benefits the patient.
Choose the intervention used most often on the unit
Frequency of use on the unit does not replace patient-specific judgment.
Implement first and consider consequences afterward
The nurse thinks before acting and weighs consequences beforehand.
items.ex: The nurse reviews possible interventions and consequences, estimates their probability, and judges their value to the patient.

alt.q: For Mr. Lawson’s pain, Tonya considers that an analgesic might relieve pain, have little effect, or cause sedation and fall risk. Which decision-making activities is she using? Select all that apply.
o: Reviewing all possible consequences of the action
Listing relief, little effect, or adverse reaction reviews possible consequences.
Considering the risk of an adverse outcome
Sedation and fall risk are possible adverse consequences she weighs.
Reviewing alternative pain interventions
She also considered positioning, splinting, and relaxation.
Delegating the decision to the assistive personnel
Clinical judgment about interventions remains the nurse’s responsibility.
Giving the analgesic before considering outcomes
The nurse thinks before acting and weighs consequences first.
alt.ex: Correct: Reviewing all possible consequences of the action; Considering the risk of an adverse outcome; Reviewing alternative pain interventions.

items.q: Reflection-on-action is a retrospective process in which the nurse uses the outcomes of care to influence future practice.
items.a: True
items.ex: Reflection-on-action looks back on care so the nurse can improve future practice.
items.ww: Reflection during care is reflection-in-action; reflection-on-action happens afterward.

alt.q: Reflection-on-action occurs while the nurse is giving care and involves changing interventions in the moment.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Changing interventions during care is reflection-in-action; reflection-on-action is retrospective.
alt.ww: Adapting care in the moment describes reflection-in-action, not reflection-on-action.

items.q: Professional and agency standards of practice offer guidelines on whether interventions can be delegated.
items.a: True
items.ex: Standards guide the selection of interventions, their frequency and timing, and whether they can be delegated.
items.ww: Standards address delegation as well as selection, frequency, and timing of interventions.

alt.q: Agency standards guide which interventions to select but do not address their timing or whether they can be delegated.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Standards guide selection, frequency, timing, and whether interventions can be delegated.
alt.ww: The standards cover timing and delegation as well as selection.

items.q: Health literacy limitations are a patient characteristic that may require the nurse to adapt interventions.
items.a: True
items.ex: Adaptations are needed for older adults and for common problems such as mobility limits, symptoms, and health literacy limitations.
items.ww: Health literacy affects how patients understand care, so interventions are adapted to it.

alt.q: Nurses need to adapt interventions only for older adults, since other patient characteristics do not change how care is delivered.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Mobility restrictions, symptoms such as pain or nausea, and health literacy limitations also require adaptations.
alt.ww: Older adults are one example, but several other patient characteristics also call for adaptations.

items.q: [[Intellectual standards|intellectual standard]] are guidelines for rational thought and responsible action that help the nurse be precise and logical during implementation.
items.ex: Applying intellectual standards helps the nurse make instructions relevant, clear, logical, and complete.

alt.q: Before teaching, Tonya makes her instructions relevant, clear, logical, and complete by applying [[intellectual standards|intellectual standard]].
alt.ex: Applying intellectual standards helps the nurse make instructions relevant, clear, logical, and complete.

items.q: After reassessing a patient, a nurse identifies a new nursing diagnosis. Which action is appropriate when revising the plan of care in the electronic health record (EHR)?
items.a: Add the new diagnosis with appropriate outcomes and date the revisions.
items.ex: The nurse adds new diagnoses, selects outcomes, revises related interventions, and dates any revisions.
w: Delete the earlier diagnoses so only the newest problem is listed.
Existing diagnoses are revised as needed, not deleted to make room for new ones.
Wait until the end of the shift to tell the team about the change.
The team is informed of significant changes and the time they occurred.
Add the new interventions but leave the diagnoses and outcomes unchanged.
Diagnoses and outcomes are revised in the EHR along with interventions.

alt.q: Why is it important to keep a patient’s nursing care plan current?
alt.a: An out-of-date or incorrect care plan compromises the quality of nursing care.
alt.ex: Review and revision let the nurse provide more appropriate and timely interventions.
w: A care plan is legally required only at admission and discharge.
The plan is revised whenever reassessment shows a need, not only at admission.
Revising the plan removes the need to communicate verbally.
Changes are conveyed both verbally and in the health record.
Care plans are used mainly for billing rather than care.
Care plans guide appropriate, timely interventions for the patient.

items.q: A patient with an indwelling urinary catheter develops a catheter-associated urinary tract infection that an accepted prevention strategy could have avoided. How does the AHRQ classify this adverse event?

w: Ameliorable adverse event

Negligence involves care below expected standards, such as heat applied too long.

Failure to use an accepted prevention strategy makes this a preventable event.

Ameliorable events were not preventable but could have been less harmful.
Expected side effect of therapy
Exceeding the ordered time falls below the standard of care.

Review the care plan and consider whether interventions need revision

Implement the intervention correctly

items.q: How does reassessment during implementation differ from evaluation?
items.a: It gathers new data to decide whether diagnoses are current or new problems exist.
items.ex: Reassessment collects additional information to keep the plan complete, current, and appropriate; evaluation judges response to care.
w: It repeats an earlier assessment to judge the patient’s response to care.
Repeating an assessment to judge response to an intervention is evaluation.
It is done once at admission and is not repeated during the hospital stay.
Assessment is continuous and occurs each time the nurse interacts with the patient.
It focuses on revising the medical diagnosis written by the provider.
Reassessment focuses on whether nursing diagnoses are current or new problems exist.

alt.q: A nurse gathers additional information from a patient to find out whether existing nursing diagnoses are still current. This activity is called:
alt.a: Reassessment
alt.ex: Reassessment determines whether diagnoses are current or new problems have developed.
w: Evaluation
Evaluation determines a patient’s response to an intervention or whether outcomes were met.
Delegation
Delegation assigns tasks to other team members; it does not gather new data.
Documentation
Documentation records care; it is not the process of collecting new data.

items.q: Tonya is explaining lifting restrictions to Mr. Lawson. He appears more anxious after hearing that his employer called and cannot teach back the information. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Redirect the discussion to his concerns about returning to work.
items.ex: Tonya needs an attentive learner, so she lets him express work concerns and then links restrictions to his routines.
w: Repeat the lifting restrictions until he can teach them back.
An anxious patient is not an attentive learner; repetition does not address the anxiety.
Give the written booklet to his wife and end the session.
Including his wife helps, but ending the session leaves his anxiety and learning needs unaddressed.
Postpone all teaching until the morning of his discharge.
Delaying teaching does not address his anxiety and reduces time to learn before discharge.

alt.q: A patient becomes visibly worried during discharge teaching and cannot repeat the information. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Tell me more about what is worrying you right now.”
alt.ex: Letting the patient express concerns helps create an attentive learner before teaching continues.
w: “Let’s keep going; we need to finish before you leave.”
Continuing ignores the anxiety that is blocking learning.
“Don’t worry, everything will be fine after you go home.”
False reassurance dismisses the patient’s concerns.
“I will just give you the handout to read later.”
A handout alone does not address the anxiety or confirm learning.

items.q: Which component of a nurse’s time refers to the sequential ordering of care activities during the daily routines of a practice setting?
items.a: Sociological
items.ex: The sociological component is the sequential ordering of care activities within the daily routines of the setting.
w: Physical
The physical component is the amount of time needed to complete nursing activities.
Psychological
The psychological component is how the nurse’s care affects what patients experience.
Organizational
Organizational is not one of the three components of time described in the text.

alt.q: Which component of a nurse’s time describes the impact of care on what and how patients experience interventions?
alt.a: Psychological
alt.ex: The psychological component concerns how the nurse’s care shapes the patient’s experience of interventions.
w: Physical
The physical component is the amount of time spent completing nursing activities.
Sociological
The sociological component is the sequential ordering of activities in the daily routine.
Financial
Financial is not one of the three components of time described in the text.

items.q: A nurse is gathering supplies for a sterile dressing change. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Keep extra supplies nearby but open them only if they are needed.
items.ex: Keeping unopened extras on hand covers mishaps while controlling costs; unopened supplies are returned afterward.
w: Open extra supplies ahead of time so they are ready if needed.
Opening supplies that may not be needed wastes them and increases costs.
Bring only the exact supplies needed, with no extras available.
Extra supplies should be available in case of errors or mishaps.
Discard all unused supplies after the procedure for infection control.
Unopened supplies are returned to storage after the procedure.

alt.q: After completing a procedure, a nurse has several unopened packages of gauze left at the bedside. Which action is best?
alt.a: Return the unopened supplies to the storage area.
alt.ex: Returning unopened supplies controls costs and shows fiscal responsibility.
w: Discard them because they were in the patient’s room.
Unopened supplies are returned to storage, not discarded.
Open them to restock the bedside dressing cart.
Supplies are not opened unless they are needed.
Leave them at the bedside for the next shift.
The text directs returning unopened supplies to storage areas.

items.q: A patient asks the nurse for a bedpan. The assistive personnel (AP) assigned to the patient is in another room, and the nurse has time. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Help the patient with the bedpan now.
items.ex: Staff work together as patient needs demand; the nurse helps the patient rather than searching for the AP.
w: Find the AP and ask the AP to come back.
Searching for an AP in another room delays care the nurse has time to give.
Ask the patient to wait until the AP returns.
Making the patient wait is unnecessary when the nurse is available.
Ask the charge nurse to reassign the AP.
Reassignment is unnecessary; the nurse can meet the need directly.

alt.q: Which statement by a new nurse shows understanding of teamwork during implementation?
alt.a: “If I have time, I help a patient with feeding instead of looking for the AP.”
alt.ex: Patient care staff work together as patient needs demand, and colleagues respect initiative and collaboration.
w: “Feeding is assigned to the AP, so I should always wait for the AP.”
Nurses help patients directly when they have time rather than waiting.
“I should never ask an AP to help me with a dressing change.”
For complex or difficult interventions, the nurse needs help from colleagues.
“Delegated tasks are no longer part of my responsibility.”
Nurses remain responsible and assist as patient needs change.

items.q: A nurse plans to teach a postoperative patient who reports moderate pain. Which action best prepares the patient for teaching?
items.a: Give an analgesic dose that relieves pain without impairing mental faculties.
items.ex: When a patient must be alert, the nurse relieves discomfort without impairing the ability to follow instruction.
w: Give the strongest available analgesic dose before teaching starts.
A dose strong enough to impair mental faculties interferes with learning.
Begin teaching now and give the analgesic afterward as a reward.
Pain interferes with concentration, so comfort measures come before interventions.
Withhold analgesics so the patient stays fully alert for teaching.
Untreated pain interferes with concentration and cooperation.

alt.q: A patient is scheduled to walk in the hallway but reports feeling very fatigued after a diagnostic test. Which action is best?
alt.a: Delay the walk until the patient has had a chance to rest.
alt.ex: If a patient is fatigued, delay ambulation or transfer until after rest, and plan only tolerable activity.
w: Walk the patient now to keep to the schedule.
Fatigue interferes with cooperation and safety; activity is delayed until after rest.
Cancel all ambulation for the rest of the day.
Ambulation is delayed until after rest, not cancelled entirely.
Walk the patient twice as far to build endurance.
Plan only the amount of activity the patient can tolerate comfortably.

items.q: A patient who is obese has uncontrolled postoperative pain and refuses to change position. Which complication should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: Pressure injury
items.ex: Uncontrolled pain makes the patient unwilling or unable to reposition, which raises the risk of pressure injury.
w: Aspiration
Aspiration risk is linked to giving oral medications to patients with dysphagia.
Urinary tract infection
UTI risk is linked to indwelling urinary catheters.
Low potassium
Low potassium was linked to a diuretic without follow-up laboratory testing.

alt.q: A patient who is obese has uncontrolled postoperative pain and avoids turning. Which nursing actions best prevent a complication?
alt.a: Anticipate pain, give ordered analgesics, and consult a wound care specialist.
alt.ex: Controlling pain and using a pressure-relief device recommended by a specialist reduce pressure injury risk.
w: Restrict all movement until the pain has fully resolved.
Immobility increases pressure injury risk rather than preventing it.
Wait for a reddened area to appear before acting.
Expert nurses anticipate complications before signs develop.
Hold analgesics to keep the patient alert to reposition.
Uncontrolled pain is the reason the patient avoids repositioning.

items.q: A nurse needs to turn and reposition a patient who is overweight and immobile, but no other staff member is available right now. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Wait to obtain additional personnel and transfer equipment before turning the patient.
items.ex: The nurse does not take shortcuts when help is unavailable, because shortcuts risk injury to the nurse and patient.
w: Turn the patient alone, using good body mechanics to prevent injury.
Taking shortcuts without assistance risks injury to both nurse and patient.
Ask the patient’s visitor to help pull the patient up in bed.
Visitors are not trained staff; additional personnel and equipment are needed.
Skip repositioning for the shift and document the patient’s refusal.
The patient did not refuse; documenting this would be inaccurate.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows correct planning for assistance with a patient who is overweight and immobile?
alt.a: “I will decide ahead of time how many staff and what transfer equipment I need.”
alt.ex: Determining the number of additional personnel in advance supports safe turning and positioning.
w: “I will start turning the patient and call for help if it gets difficult.”
Need for assistance is identified before care begins, not partway through.
“I will turn the patient alone if no one is free right away.”
Do not take shortcuts when assistance is not immediately available.
“I will ask the patient to turn without help to save time.”
An immobile patient cannot safely turn without assistance.

That's step 1 of 4.
