alt.a: Seek the information needed to be competent to perform the procedure
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 4. The nurse first gains knowledge, organizes equipment, considers consequences, and then performs the skill with an experienced nurse’s guidance.
w: Consider the consequences of performing the procedure on this patient
That's step 3 of 4.
Have an experienced nurse provide assistance and guidance
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: In performing a new procedural skill, which step comes right before “Consider the consequences of performing the procedure on this patient”?
alt.a: Collect all equipment needed to be organized before the procedure
alt.ex: That's step 2 of 4. The nurse first gains knowledge, organizes equipment, considers consequences, and then performs the skill with an experienced nurse’s guidance.
w: Seek the information needed to be competent to perform the procedure
That's step 1 of 4.
Have an experienced nurse provide assistance and guidance
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: In performing a new procedural skill, which step comes right before “Have an experienced nurse provide assistance and guidance”?
alt.a: Consider the consequences of performing the procedure on this patient
alt.ex: That's step 3 of 4. The nurse first gains knowledge, organizes equipment, considers consequences, and then performs the skill with an experienced nurse’s guidance.
w: Collect all equipment needed to be organized before the procedure
That's step 2 of 4.
Seek the information needed to be competent to perform the procedure
That's step 1 of 4.

ord.q: A nurse must perform a new procedural skill for the first time. Put the recommended steps in order.
items: Seek the information needed to be competent to perform the procedure
Collect all equipment needed to be organized before the procedure
Consider the consequences of performing the procedure on this patient
Have an experienced nurse provide assistance and guidance
ord.ex: The nurse first gains knowledge, organizes equipment, considers consequences, and then performs the skill with an experienced nurse’s guidance.

items.q: Which features of evidence-based design (EBD) are ambient features? Select all that apply.
o: Noise
Noise is an ambient feature of EBD.
Air quality
Air quality is an ambient feature of EBD.
Light
Light is an ambient feature of EBD.
Temperature
Temperature is an ambient feature of EBD.
Signage
Signage is part of interior design.
Room dimensions
Room dimensions are part of physical construction.
items.ex: EBD includes physical construction, ambient features (noise, air quality, light, temperature), and interior design.

alt.q: Which items are part of the interior design component of evidence-based design? Select all that apply.
o: Furniture
Furniture is part of interior design.
Signage
Signage is part of interior design.
Artwork
Artwork is part of interior design.
Door and window placement
This is part of physical construction.
Air quality
Air quality is an ambient feature.
alt.ex: Correct: Furniture; Signage; Artwork.

items.q: Which physical environmental factors promote patient healing? Select all that apply.
o: Standardized patient rooms and equipment
Standardization makes routine tasks simpler and decreases errors.
Improved lighting where medications are dispensed
Better illumination in medication areas is a listed healing factor.
Acuity-adaptable rooms
These limit the need to transfer patients when conditions worsen.
Decentralized nurses’ stations and supply rooms
Decentralization lets nurses spend less time walking and more time treating patients.
Shared multiple-bed patient rooms
Privacy and single-patient rooms are the features that promote healing.
One centralized supply room for the whole unit
Decentralized supply rooms reduce walking and promote efficient care.
items.ex: Standardization, good lighting, air filtration, fall-reducing design, patient control, adaptable rooms, privacy, and decentralization promote healing.

alt.q: A hospital is redesigning a nursing unit. Which features would the nurse recommend to reduce patient falls? Select all that apply.
o: Floors that are not slippery
Nonslip floors are a fall-reducing room feature.
Correct toilet and furniture height
Correct height of toilets and furniture reduces falls.
Correct placement of rails and accessories
Properly placed rails and accessories reduce falls.
Narrow door openings
Appropriate door openings are the listed fall-reducing feature.
Rooms crowded with extra furniture
Removing clutter and unnecessary furniture makes the environment safer.
alt.ex: Correct: Floors that are not slippery; Correct toilet and furniture height; Correct placement of rails and accessories.

items.q: A nurse is preparing the environment before ambulating a patient who has a visual impairment. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Remove clutter and unnecessary equipment
Removing clutter makes the environment safer.
Create a clear path for walking
Clear paths help patients ambulate safely.
Provide the patient’s eyeglasses
Providing assistive devices prevents injury in patients with sensory deficits.
Rearrange furniture as needed for the walk
Rearranging furniture and equipment is recommended when ambulating a patient.
Move personal items out of the patient’s reach
Personal items should be easily accessible.
Keep the room dim to help the patient rest
A dim room adds risk for a patient with a visual impairment.
items.ex: Removing clutter, clearing paths, providing assistive devices, and rearranging furniture prevent injury.

alt.q: Which nursing actions make the environment conducive to care? Select all that apply.
o: Close curtains before exposing body parts
Privacy helps the patient relax during care.
Reduce distractions during teaching
Fewer distractions enhance learning opportunities.
Check that bath water is not too warm
Checking water temperature prevents injury.
Ask visitors to stay during a bed bath
Visitors are asked to leave as care is completed.
Leave the door open during wound care
Doors or curtains are closed when exposing the body.
alt.ex: Correct: Close curtains before exposing body parts; Reduce distractions during teaching; Check that bath water is not too warm.

items.q: Reassessment during implementation is the same as repeating a previous assessment to evaluate a patient’s response to an intervention.
items.a: False
items.ex: Reassessment gathers additional data to see whether diagnoses are current or new problems exist; evaluation judges response.
items.ww: Repeating an assessment to judge response is evaluation, which differs from reassessment.

alt.q: Reassessment gathers additional information to determine whether nursing diagnoses are current or new problems have developed.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Reassessment keeps the plan complete, current, and appropriate.
alt.ww: Reassessment is distinct from evaluation, which judges the patient’s response to an intervention.

items.q: Psychomotor skills require the integration of cognitive and motor activities.
items.a: True
items.ex: Giving an injection, for example, requires knowledge of anatomy and pharmacology plus coordination and precision.
items.ww: Psychomotor skills combine knowledge with motor ability, not motor ability alone.

alt.q: Psychomotor skills depend on motor coordination alone and do not require cognitive knowledge.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Psychomotor skills integrate cognitive knowledge, such as anatomy and pharmacology, with motor activity.
alt.ww: Without cognitive knowledge, the nurse cannot perform an injection safely and correctly.

items.q: The decision to delegate an intervention should be based mainly on the task the patient requires.
items.a: False
items.ex: Delegation is based on the patient’s condition, team competence, task complexity, and the supervision required.
items.ww: The task alone does not determine delegation; the nurse judges the patient and team as well.

alt.q: A licensed nurse decides whether to delegate based on the patient’s condition, staff competence, task complexity, and the supervision needed.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: These factors, along with the health care environment, guide delegation decisions.
alt.ww: Basing delegation on the task alone ignores patient condition and staff competence.

items.q: An [[adverse event]] is a harmful and negative outcome, such as a fall or wrong medication, that happens when a patient has been provided with medical care.
items.ex: Adverse events can be avoided or minimized with proper preparation and implementation.

alt.q: A patient who falls or receives the wrong medication while receiving care has experienced an [[adverse event]].
alt.ex: Adverse events can be avoided or minimized with proper preparation and implementation.

items.q: Which activity is an example of an activity of daily living (ADL)?
items.a: Eating a meal
items.ex: ADLs are essential tasks needed regularly for basic survival and well-being, such as eating, toileting, dressing, and bathing.
w: Paying monthly bills
Paying bills is an instrumental activity of daily living, oriented toward interacting with the environment.
Shopping for groceries
Shopping is an instrumental activity of daily living, which is more complex than an ADL.
Caring for a pet
Caring for pets is an instrumental activity of daily living that supports daily life in the environment.

alt.q: A home care nurse lists a patient’s activities. Which one is an ADL rather than an instrumental activity of daily living?
alt.a: Getting into and out of the bathtub
alt.ex: Functional mobility, such as getting into or out of a bed or bathtub, is listed among the ADLs.
w: Taking daily medications
Taking medications is listed as an instrumental activity of daily living.
Preparing the evening meal
Preparing meals is an instrumental activity of daily living, not an ADL.
Cleaning the kitchen
Housecleaning is an instrumental activity of daily living, not an ADL.

items.q: A nurse is helping a patient with dementia get dressed. Which actions reflect recommended ways to assist with ADLs? Select all that apply.
o: Divide the activity into small tasks and complete one task at a time.
Breaking an activity into understandable tasks helps the patient with dementia succeed.
Explain each step in simple words and allow time for a response.
Simple, easy-to-understand steps with time to respond support the patient’s ability.
Prepare the clothing and supplies before involving the patient.
Preparing for the activity first avoids confusion once the patient is involved.
Point out errors right away so the patient can learn the correct way.
The nurse should not point out mistakes to a patient with dementia.
Offer several clothing choices to promote independence in decisions.
Giving too many choices confuses a patient with dementia and should be avoided.
Explain why dressing matters and what happens if it is not done.
Explanations of why a job is needed or consequences of not doing it should be avoided.
items.ex: Assisting a patient with dementia means matching help to ability, preparing first, simplifying steps, and avoiding mistakes, choices, and long explanations.

alt.q: Which approaches should a nurse avoid when helping a patient with dementia perform ADLs? Select all that apply.
o: Asking several questions about how the patient would like to proceed
Confusing or unnecessary questions should be avoided with a patient with dementia.
Telling the patient when a step has been done incorrectly
Pointing out mistakes should be avoided.
Explaining the health consequences of skipping the task
Explanations of what will happen if a job is not done should be avoided.
Matching the level of assistance to the patient’s current ability
Planning assistance to match ability is a recommended approach.
Completing one simple task before moving to the next
Getting one task done at a time is a recommended approach.
alt.ex: Correct: Asking several questions about how the patient would like to proceed; Telling the patient when a step has been done incorrectly; Explaining the health consequences of skipping the task.

items.q: In dementia ADL assistance, which stage comes right after “Remind the patient to perform the overall task”?
items.a: Stay at the patient’s side in case problems arise
items.ex: Assistance progresses from a simple reminder, to being present in case of problems, to cueing each specific step such as soap, wash, then rinse.
w: Remind the patient to do each specific step of the task
That's stage 3 of 3.

alt.q: Which stage comes first in dementia ADL assistance?
alt.a: Remind the patient to perform the overall task
alt.ex: Assistance progresses from a simple reminder, to being present in case of problems, to cueing each specific step such as soap, wash, then rinse.
w: Stay at the patient’s side in case problems arise
That's stage 2 of 3.
Remind the patient to do each specific step of the task
That's stage 3 of 3.

alt.q: Which stage comes last in dementia ADL assistance?
alt.a: Remind the patient to do each specific step of the task
alt.ex: Assistance progresses from a simple reminder, to being present in case of problems, to cueing each specific step such as soap, wash, then rinse.
w: Stay at the patient’s side in case problems arise
That's stage 2 of 3.
Remind the patient to perform the overall task
That's stage 1 of 3.

alt.q: In dementia ADL assistance, which stage comes right after “Stay at the patient’s side in case problems arise”?
alt.a: Remind the patient to do each specific step of the task
alt.ex: Assistance progresses from a simple reminder, to being present in case of problems, to cueing each specific step such as soap, wash, then rinse.
w: Remind the patient to perform the overall task
That's stage 1 of 3.

alt.q: In dementia ADL assistance, which stage comes right before “Stay at the patient’s side in case problems arise”?
alt.a: Remind the patient to perform the overall task
alt.ex: Assistance progresses from a simple reminder, to being present in case of problems, to cueing each specific step such as soap, wash, then rinse.
w: Remind the patient to do each specific step of the task
That's stage 3 of 3.

alt.q: In dementia ADL assistance, which stage comes right before “Remind the patient to do each specific step of the task”?
alt.a: Stay at the patient’s side in case problems arise
alt.ex: Assistance progresses from a simple reminder, to being present in case of problems, to cueing each specific step such as soap, wash, then rinse.
w: Remind the patient to perform the overall task
That's stage 1 of 3.

ord.q: Put in order the progression of assistance a patient with dementia typically needs for an ADL such as bathing, from earliest to latest.
items: Remind the patient to perform the overall task
Stay at the patient’s side in case problems arise
Remind the patient to do each specific step of the task
ord.ex: Assistance progresses from a simple reminder, to being present in case of problems, to cueing each specific step such as soap, wash, then rinse.

items.q: A patient with moderate dementia becomes frustrated while trying to make a sandwich. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Break the activity into single steps, such as first opening the containers.
items.ex: Dividing an activity into tasks the patient can understand and completing one at a time supports the patient with dementia.
w: Explain why eating lunch is important for the patient’s overall health.
Explanations of why a task is needed should be avoided with a patient with dementia.
Point out which step the patient did wrong so it can be corrected.
The nurse should not point out mistakes to a patient with dementia.
Offer the patient a list of several sandwich options to choose from.
Too many choices confuse a patient with dementia and should be avoided.

alt.q: A nurse is coaching a patient with dementia through bathing. Which statement by the nurse is most appropriate?
alt.a: “Now put soap on the washcloth.”
alt.ex: Simple, one-step directions in plain words help a patient with dementia complete a task.
w: “You missed your left arm again; let’s try to remember it.”
Pointing out mistakes should be avoided with a patient with dementia.
“Would you prefer a bath, a shower, or a sponge bath, and when?”
Too many choices and confusing questions should be avoided.
“If you don’t rinse well, your skin will get irritated and itchy.”
Explaining consequences of not doing a task should be avoided.

items.q: A patient with chronic lung disease becomes short of breath and fatigued at mealtimes and has begun skipping meals. Which intervention is most appropriate?
items.a: Set up the meal tray, offer to cut the food, and plan smaller, more frequent meals.
items.ex: Setting up meals, cutting food, and offering smaller, more frequent meals helps a fatigued patient maintain nutrition.
w: Encourage the patient to eat three full meals without assistance to build endurance.
Fatigue from shortness of breath signals a need for ADL assistance, not more demands.
Delay meals until the patient asks for food so the patient can rest undisturbed.
Waiting allows the patient to keep avoiding eating, which threatens nutrition.
Feed the patient every meal completely to save all the patient’s energy for breathing.
Patients should participate to the level possible; total care is not needed here.

alt.q: Which patient finding most clearly indicates a probable need for assistance with ADLs?
alt.a: The patient reports fatigue and pain when moving from bed to chair.
alt.ex: Fatigue, limited mobility, confusion, or pain suggest that a patient probably needs help with ADLs.
w: The patient reports eating breakfast independently each morning.
Independent eating does not show a need for ADL assistance.
The patient asks for a newspaper and reading glasses after lunch.
Requesting reading materials does not indicate difficulty with ADLs.
The patient walks to the bathroom without dizziness or shortness of breath.
Walking without symptoms shows independent toileting and mobility.

items.q: If a patient is stable and alert and the patient and family are willing, it is appropriate for family members to help with the patient’s ADLs.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states that family may help with care when the patient is stable and alert and both patient and family are willing.
items.ww: Family involvement is appropriate under these conditions, and some cultures prefer family to provide ADL assistance.

alt.q: Because ADLs are nursing care, the nurse should always perform them rather than allow family members to help, regardless of the patient’s preferences.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses respect patients’ wishes; some cultures prefer family to assist with ADLs, and family may help when appropriate.
alt.ww: Family may assist a stable, alert patient when patient and family are willing, so the nurse need not always do it.

items.q: [[Instrumental activities of daily living|IADLs|IADL|instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs)]] are activities such as shopping, paying bills, and housecleaning that support daily life and involve interacting with the environment.
items.ex: IADLs are more complex than ADLs, are oriented toward the environment, and are generally managed by occupational therapists.

alt.q: Preparing meals, home maintenance, and taking medications are examples of [[instrumental activities of daily living|IADLs|IADL|instrumental ADLs]].
alt.ex: IADLs are more complex than ADLs, are oriented toward the environment, and are generally managed by occupational therapists.

items.q: A hospitalized patient recovering from a stroke will be discharged home, where they live alone. Which nursing action best addresses the patient’s instrumental activities of daily living?
items.a: Anticipate how the illness will affect tasks like cooking and arrange referrals.
items.ex: In acute care the nurse anticipates how illness affects IADLs and makes referrals so the patient has needed resources at home.
w: Wait until a home care visit to determine whether the patient can manage tasks.
Needs should be anticipated in acute care so resources are in place before discharge.
Focus only on bathing and toileting because IADLs are not a nursing concern.
Nurses help patients adapt IADLs and arrange referrals, even though OTs generally manage them.
Advise the family to take over all household tasks for the patient permanently.
The goal is helping the patient retain a level of independence, not removing all tasks.

alt.q: A home care nurse visits a patient with arthritis who has trouble reaching pots stored on high shelves. Which action best supports the patient’s independence?
alt.a: Help the patient rearrange the kitchen so cookware is easier to reach.
alt.ex: Home and community nurses help patients adapt how they perform IADLs, such as rearranging a kitchen, to retain independence.
w: Recommend that the patient stop cooking and rely on frozen meals.
Stopping the activity reduces independence instead of adapting how it is done.
Tell the patient that only an occupational therapist can address this.
Although OTs generally manage IADLs, nurses in home care frequently help patients adapt them.
Suggest the patient move into a facility where meals are provided.
This removes independence rather than adapting the environment so the patient can stay independent.

items.q: Which requirements apply to all physical care techniques? Select all that apply.
o: Use safe patient-handling techniques.
All physical care techniques require safe patient handling.
Follow proper infection control practices.
Infection control is required with all hands-on procedures.
Protect yourself and the patient from injury.
Preventing injury to nurse and patient is required for all techniques.
Stay organized and follow applicable practice guidelines.
Organization and adherence to practice guidelines are required.
Skip assessment when the procedure has been done many times before.
Assessments before, during, and after a skill are always needed, and past responses should be considered.
items.ex: Physical care techniques require protecting from injury, safe patient handling, infection control, organization, and following practice guidelines.

alt.q: Before performing a physical care procedure, which things is the nurse responsible for knowing? Select all that apply.
o: The associated risks of the procedure
The nurse must know the procedure’s risks.
The standard frequency of the procedure
The nurse must know how often the procedure is standardly done.
Needed assessments before, during, and after the procedure
Assessments and evaluations around the skill are the nurse’s responsibility.
The billing code assigned to the procedure
Billing is not among the nurse’s listed knowledge responsibilities for a procedure.
How other patients on the unit responded to it
The nurse considers how this patient responded in the past, not other patients.
alt.ex: Correct: The associated risks of the procedure; The standard frequency of the procedure; Needed assessments before, during, and after the procedure.

items.q: A nurse is about to ambulate a postoperative patient for the first time. Which statement by the nurse is best?
items.a: “We’ll walk to the doorway, and you can sit and rest there. Tell me if you feel dizzy or short of breath.”
items.ex: Before ambulating, discuss how far to walk, chances to rest, and ask the patient to report dizziness or shortness of breath.
w: “Let’s walk down the hall as far as you can go before you need to stop for the day.”
Distance and rest plans should be agreed on beforehand, not left open-ended.
“Hold on to the rail and keep walking even if you start to feel a bit lightheaded.”
The patient should report dizziness, not keep walking through it.
“Walking is ordered every shift, so we will just get going without any planning.”
The nurse discusses expected outcomes and plans with the patient before the procedure.

alt.q: Before helping a patient walk, a nurse plans with the patient. Which plan reflects the textbook’s guidance?
alt.a: Agree on the distance, identify places to stop, and ask the patient to report dizziness.
alt.ex: Knowing expected outcomes means discussing distance, rest opportunities, and symptoms to report before ambulation.
w: Walk the greatest distance possible, since longer walks always speed recovery.
The nurse sets a specific distance based on the patient’s condition and response.
Avoid mentioning symptoms so the patient does not become anxious about walking.
The nurse asks the patient to tell if dizziness or shortness of breath occurs.
Let the patient walk alone first to see how far they can independently go.
The plan should be discussed and safety ensured, not tested by walking alone.

items.q: A nurse finds a patient unresponsive and not breathing. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Stay with the patient, begin support, and have another staff member get experienced help.
items.ex: In an emergency, the nurse stays with the patient, maintains support, and has another staff member obtain an experienced professional.
w: Leave the patient briefly to locate the charge nurse and the emergency cart.
The nurse should not leave; another staff member obtains help.
Telephone the health care provider from the nurses’ station for orders first.
Leaving the bedside to call delays support; the nurse stays with the patient.
Document the time and findings in the EHR before beginning any intervention.
Documentation is not the priority during a life-threatening event.

alt.q: A patient with a history of depression tells the nurse of a plan to end their life tonight. Which nursing action is best?
alt.a: Remain with the patient and have a colleague contact a crisis counselor immediately.
alt.ex: Lifesaving measures include referring a suicidal patient to a crisis counselor quickly while the nurse stays with the patient.
w: Schedule a social work consult for the next business day.
A suicidal patient needs referral to a crisis counselor as quickly as possible.
Leave the room to give the patient privacy to calm down.
The nurse stays with the patient in an emergency rather than leaving.
Reassure the patient that things will look better in the morning.
False reassurance does not protect the patient; a lifesaving referral is needed.

items.q: Which nursing actions are examples of lifesaving measures? Select all that apply.
o: Starting cardiopulmonary resuscitation
CPR restores physiological homeostasis when it is threatened.
Administering emergency medications
Emergency medications are a lifesaving measure.
Intervening to protect a patient who is violent
Protecting a confused or violent patient is listed as a lifesaving measure.
Referring a severely anxious patient to a crisis counselor
Quick referral of a severely anxious or suicidal patient is a lifesaving measure.
Transcribing a new medical order
Order transcription is an indirect care activity, not a lifesaving measure.
Teaching a patient about a new medication
Teaching is a direct care method, not a lifesaving measure.
items.ex: Lifesaving measures restore physiological or psychological homeostasis when it is threatened.

alt.q: A nursing student is reviewing lifesaving measures. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They are used when a patient’s physiological or psychological state is threatened.
Lifesaving measures respond to threats to physiological or psychological state.
Their purpose is to restore homeostasis.
The purpose of lifesaving measures is to restore physiological or psychological homeostasis.
They include protecting a patient who is confused.
Intervening to protect a confused or violent patient is a lifesaving measure.
They are limited to physical threats such as cardiac arrest.
Psychological threats, such as suicidal thoughts, also call for lifesaving measures.
They should wait until the health care provider arrives.
The nurse stays with the patient and maintains support while help is obtained.
alt.ex: Correct: They are used when a patient’s physiological or psychological state is threatened; Their purpose is to restore homeostasis; They include protecting a patient who is confused.

items.q: How does counseling differ from teaching as a direct care method?
items.a: Counseling develops new attitudes, behaviors, and feelings; teaching builds knowledge or psychomotor skills.
items.ex: Both need interpersonal skills, but counseling targets attitudes, behaviors, and feelings while teaching targets knowledge and skills.
w: Counseling builds psychomotor skills; teaching develops new attitudes, behaviors, and feelings.
This reverses them; teaching builds knowledge and psychomotor skills.
Counseling is done only by psychiatrists; teaching is done only by nurses.
Nurses counsel patients with normal adjustment difficulties and also teach.
Counseling requires interpersonal skills; teaching relies only on written handouts.
Both counseling and teaching require good interpersonal skills.

alt.q: A nurse helps a patient learn to inject insulin and then helps the patient work through anger about the diagnosis. Which statement correctly classifies these actions?
alt.a: Injection practice is teaching; working through anger is counseling.
alt.ex: Teaching focuses on knowledge and psychomotor skills; counseling develops new attitudes, behaviors, and feelings.
w: Injection practice is counseling; working through anger is teaching.
This reverses the methods; skill building is teaching.
Both actions are counseling because they involve the patient’s feelings.
Learning a psychomotor skill is teaching, not counseling.
Both actions are indirect care because they prepare for discharge.
Both involve direct interaction with the patient, so they are direct care.

items.q: Nurses can counsel patients and families who have normal adjustment difficulties and are upset or frustrated but are not psychologically disabled.
items.a: True
items.ex: Nurses counsel people with normal adjustment difficulties; those with psychiatric diagnoses also need specialized therapy.
items.ww: The book specifically identifies normal adjustment difficulties as within the nurse’s counseling role.

alt.q: A general staff nurse’s supportive counseling is sufficient therapy for a patient with a psychiatric diagnosis.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients with psychiatric diagnoses need therapy from mental health nurses, social workers, psychiatrists, or psychologists plus supportive nursing care.
alt.ww: Supportive nursing care is added to, not a replacement for, specialized psychiatric therapy.

items.q: A woman caring for her aging mother at home tells the nurse she is exhausted and overwhelmed. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
items.a: Provide information about respite care and help her manage her caregiving stress.
items.ex: Nurses counsel caregivers with normal adjustment difficulties, such as giving information about respite care, a break from caregiving.
w: Refer her to a psychiatrist because caregiver stress is a psychiatric disorder.
Normal adjustment difficulties can be counseled by nurses; she is not psychologically disabled.
Advise her that the stress will pass once she gets used to the routine.
This dismisses her concerns rather than helping her examine alternatives and resources.
Tell her to place her mother in long-term care to end the stress.
Counseling helps people examine alternatives and choose; the nurse does not decide for her.

alt.q: Which outcome shows that counseling a stressed family caregiver has been effective?
alt.a: The caregiver examines options, chooses respite care, and reports feeling more in control.
alt.ex: Counseling helps people examine alternatives; doing so builds a sense of control and better stress management.
w: The caregiver agrees to follow every suggestion the nurse makes without question.
Counseling encourages the person to examine alternatives and decide, not simply comply.
The caregiver correctly demonstrates how to transfer her mother to a chair.
Demonstrating a psychomotor skill reflects teaching, not counseling.
The caregiver states she no longer needs to discuss her feelings with anyone.
Avoiding discussion does not show improved stress management or problem solving.

items.q: Patient education should begin at admission to the health care agency and take place with every direct encounter.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book’s patient education tips include providing education with every direct encounter, beginning with admission.
items.ww: Teaching is an ongoing process of keeping patients informed throughout care, not a single event.

alt.q: To avoid overwhelming patients, the nurse should save patient education for a single session on the day of discharge.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Teaching is ongoing and occurs with every encounter, beginning with admission.
alt.ww: Waiting until discharge contradicts the guidance to teach with every direct encounter.

items.q: A patient seems uneasy and refuses a scheduled breathing treatment. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Can you tell me what concerns you about the treatment?”
items.ex: Asking what concerns the patient gives the nurse a chance to provide further teaching and correct knowledge deficits.
w: “The health care provider ordered it, so you really need to take it.”
Pressuring the patient misses the chance to learn and address the concern.
“That’s fine; I will document that you refused and let it go.”
The nurse should first explore concerns, which may reveal a teaching need.
“Most patients feel nervous, but they all end up feeling better afterward.”
This generalizes and reassures without finding out the patient’s actual concern.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a patient how to use a new glucose meter. Which action best confirms the patient understands?
alt.a: Have the patient demonstrate the test and explain the steps back.
alt.ex: Routinely using return demonstration and teach-back shows whether the explanation was understood.
w: Ask the patient whether there are any questions before leaving.
A yes or no answer does not confirm understanding.
Give the patient a detailed brochure written in medical terms.
Instruction should avoid medical jargon and does not confirm understanding.
Repeat the explanation twice to be sure it is remembered.
Repetition by the nurse does not show what the patient understands.

items.q: A nurse applies a moist heat compress to a patient’s leg. How often should the nurse inspect the area for an adverse reaction after application?
items.a: Every 5 minutes
items.ex: Inspecting every 5 minutes allows early detection of excessive reddening from heat or maceration from moisture.
w: Every 30 minutes
Waiting 30 minutes risks a burn or maceration going unnoticed.
Every 15 minutes
The book directs inspection every 5 minutes, not 15.
Only after 60 minutes
Waiting until removal does not prevent adverse skin reactions.

alt.q: Five minutes after a nurse applies a moist heat compress, which finding most indicates an adverse reaction?
alt.a: Excessive reddening of the skin under the compress
alt.ex: Excessive reddening from heat or maceration from moisture signals an adverse reaction to a heat compress.
w: Mild warmth of the skin under the compress
Warmth is the expected effect of a heat compress.
Patient report of a soothing sensation
Comfort is an expected outcome, not an adverse reaction.
Skin that is intact and slightly pink
Intact skin with slight color change does not indicate harm.

items.q: After a third dose of penicillin, a patient with no known allergies develops hives. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
items.a: Stop further doses, document the reaction, and consult the health care provider.
items.ex: With an adverse reaction, the nurse documents it, stops the drug, consults the provider, and gives an ordered antihistamine.
w: Give the next scheduled dose and recheck the skin in 1 hour.
Continuing the drug risks worsening the allergic response.
Give diphenhydramine from stock and continue the penicillin.
An antihistamine requires an order, and the causative drug must be stopped.
Apply a cool compress and reassess at the end of the shift.
This delays stopping the drug and consulting the provider.

alt.q: A patient develops hives after receiving an antibiotic. The nurse stops the drug and consults the provider. Which medication would the nurse expect to give to relieve the reaction?

w: Acetaminophen, an analgesic and antipyretic
Acetaminophen treats pain and fever, not an allergic response.
Furosemide, a loop diuretic for fluid excess
A diuretic does not counteract hives or itching.
Morphine, an opioid analgesic for severe pain
Morphine does not treat an allergic reaction and can itself cause itching.

items.q: Which statement best defines indirect care measures?
items.a: Treatments or procedures that benefit a patient without face-to-face contact
items.ex: Indirect care measures benefit the patient but do not involve face-to-face contact, such as managing the care environment.
w: Treatments or procedures performed through direct interaction with patients
This describes direct care, such as ADL assistance or teaching.
Treatments performed only when a patient’s condition becomes life threatening
This describes lifesaving measures, a type of direct care.
Procedures that the health care provider performs instead of the nurse
Indirect care is performed by nurses and the team without face-to-face contact.

alt.q: A nurse spends part of a shift on activities that benefit patients without face-to-face contact. What type of care is this?
alt.a: Indirect care
alt.ex: Activities that benefit patients without face-to-face contact, such as documentation, are indirect care.
w: Direct care
Direct care involves direct interaction with patients.
Preventive care
Preventive interventions promote health and prevent illness, often with patient contact.
Lifesaving care
Lifesaving measures are physical care techniques done with the patient in an emergency.

items.q: Which activities are examples of indirect care? Select all that apply.
o: Documenting care in the electronic health record
Documentation is listed as an indirect care activity.
Collecting, labeling, and transporting specimens
Specimen handling is an indirect care activity.
Telephone consultation with a health care provider
Telephone consultations with providers are indirect care.
Transcribing a medical order
Medical order transcription is an indirect care activity.
Counseling a patient who is anxious about surgery
Counseling occurs through direct interaction, so it is direct care.
Assisting a patient with bathing
Help with ADLs is hands-on direct care.
items.ex: Indirect care includes documentation, delegation, order transcription, infection control, safety management, consultation, hand-offs, specimens, and transport.

alt.q: Which nursing activities are classified as direct care rather than indirect care? Select all that apply.
o: Teaching a patient how to use an inhaler
Teaching happens through direct interaction with the patient.
Starting cardiopulmonary resuscitation
CPR is a lifesaving measure, a form of direct care.
Helping a patient eat lunch
ADL assistance is direct care.
Giving a hand-off report to the oncoming nurse
Hand-off reports to team members are indirect care.
Making a patient’s room environmentally safe
Environmental safety management is indirect care.
alt.ex: Correct: Teaching a patient how to use an inhaler; Starting cardiopulmonary resuscitation; Helping a patient eat lunch.

items.q: During a shift, a nurse properly stores sterile supplies and sets up protective isolation for a patient’s room. How are these activities classified?

w: Direct care involving physical care techniques
Physical care techniques are hands-on procedures done with the patient.
Direct care involving lifesaving measures
Lifesaving measures respond to a threatened physiological or psychological state.
Indirect care involving delegation to staff
Delegation is directing another person to perform tasks, not storing supplies.

alt.q: A nurse transports a patient to the radiology department for a procedure. According to the textbook, this is an example of which type of care?

w: Direct physical care
Transport is listed as an indirect care activity, not a physical care technique.
Preventive care
Preventive interventions promote health and prevent illness.
Counseling
Counseling helps patients manage stress through problem solving.
