items.q: What is a main purpose of documenting a nursing intervention in the electronic health record?
items.a: It validates that the procedure was done and informs later caregivers.
items.ex: The record validates that the nurse performed a procedure and tells subsequent caregivers what approaches lead to successful care.
w: It replaces the need for a verbal hand-off report between nurses.
Hand-off communication is still needed when care is transferred.
It is used mainly to calculate the cost of each nursing procedure.
The book describes validation and information for caregivers, not cost calculation.
It allows the nurse to delegate the nursing process to assistive personnel.
The nursing process cannot be delegated, regardless of documentation.

alt.q: An oncoming nurse reads in the EHR that a patient’s pain improved most with repositioning plus ice. How does this documentation help care?
alt.a: It guides later caregivers on approaches that lead to successful care.
alt.ex: Documentation gives subsequent caregivers valuable information about which approaches succeed with the patient.
w: It proves that the previous nurse delegated the intervention correctly.
The entry records the intervention and response, not the delegation process.
It means the oncoming nurse no longer needs to assess the patient’s pain.
Documentation informs care but does not replace ongoing assessment.
It serves only as legal protection and has little use for patient care.
The record gives valuable information to subsequent caregivers.

items.q: When a nurse documents an individualized nursing intervention in the EHR, what does the EHR usually allow the nurse to add?
items.a: A brief description of pertinent assessment findings and the patient’s response
items.ex: For individualized interventions, the EHR usually offers space for pertinent assessment findings and the patient’s response.
w: A full copy of the patient’s medical history and admission database
The entry is a brief description of findings and response, not the full history.
The names of all staff members who were working on the unit
Staff lists are not part of documenting an individualized intervention.
A list of standardized interventions that were not performed
The focus is on the intervention done and the patient’s response.

alt.q: A nurse uses guided imagery with a patient who is anxious before surgery. Which EHR entry best reflects the textbook’s guidance on documenting an individualized intervention?
alt.a: Patient tense with rapid speech; after guided imagery, states feeling calmer.
alt.ex: Documentation of an individualized intervention includes pertinent assessment findings and the patient’s response.
w: Guided imagery done per routine; see standard care plan for details.
This omits assessment findings and the patient’s response.
Patient seemed fine; nurse plans to try guided imagery again tomorrow.
This is vague and does not state findings or response to the intervention.
Guided imagery provided; patient had no complaints during the shift.
This does not describe pertinent findings or how the patient responded.

items.q: According to the textbook, what is often the root cause of most reported adverse or sentinel events in health care organizations?
items.a: Miscommunication
items.ex: Miscommunication is often the root cause of most reported adverse or sentinel events.
w: Equipment failure
The book names miscommunication, not equipment failure, as the common root cause.
Patient nonadherence
Nonadherence affects outcomes but is not named as the root cause of sentinel events.
Staffing shortages
The book identifies miscommunication as the common root cause.

alt.q: A hospital reviews a sentinel event in which a patient received a duplicate dose of medication. Based on the textbook, which underlying cause is most likely?
alt.a: Ineffective communication between caregivers
alt.ex: Miscommunication is often the root cause of adverse events and can lead to needlessly duplicated interventions.
w: Lack of documentation software on the unit
The book points to communication, not software, as the usual root cause.
Too many health care providers on the team
Team size is not named; communication quality is the key issue.
The patient’s failure to report the first dose
Patient factors are not the root cause named for sentinel events.

items.q: Which outcomes can result from ineffective or incomplete communication among caregivers? Select all that apply.
o: Uninformed caregivers
Incomplete communication leaves caregivers uninformed.
Needlessly duplicated interventions
Poor communication can cause interventions to be repeated unnecessarily.
Delayed procedures
Procedures can be delayed when information is not shared.
Tasks that are left undone
Communication gaps can leave tasks undone.
Fewer adverse events
Effective communication, not ineffective communication, reduces adverse events.
items.ex: Ineffective or incomplete communication often causes uninformed caregivers, duplicated interventions, delayed procedures, or tasks left undone.

alt.q: Which characteristics should a nurse’s communication with other health care professionals have? Select all that apply.
o: Timely
Communication should be timely.
Accurate
Communication should be accurate.
Relevant to the patient’s clinical situation
Communication should be relevant to the clinical situation.
Lengthy and detailed in all background information
Nurses should be clear, concise, and to the point.
Limited to written messages only
Interventions are communicated in electronic, written, or oral formats.
alt.ex: Correct: Timely; Accurate; Relevant to the patient’s clinical situation.

items.q: When communicating nursing interventions, the nurse should be clear, concise, and to the point.
items.a: True
items.ex: Clear, concise communication that is timely, accurate, and relevant reduces errors and adverse events.
items.ww: The book directs nurses always to be clear, concise, and to the point.

alt.q: Giving every possible background detail, even if unrelated, makes communication of nursing interventions safer than a concise report.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Communication should be concise and relevant to the patient’s clinical situation.
alt.ww: Unrelated detail works against clear, concise, relevant communication.

items.q: Why are hand-off reports, hourly rounding, and consultation considered critical indirect care activities?
items.a: They help ensure direct care is planned, coordinated, and done with proper resources.
items.ex: Communicating patient information ensures direct care activities are planned, coordinated, and performed with the proper resources.
w: They replace the need for the nurse to provide most direct care.
They support direct care rather than replacing it.
They allow the nurse to transfer accountability for care to others.
The RN retains responsibility and accountability for nursing practice.
They are required mainly for billing and reimbursement purposes.
Their purpose is coordination of care, not billing.

alt.q: An oncoming nurse receives a thorough hand-off report about a patient scheduled for a procedure. What is the main benefit of this communication?
alt.a: Care can be coordinated and performed with the right resources.
alt.ex: Communicating patient information ensures care is planned, coordinated, and performed with proper resources.
w: The oncoming nurse can skip the initial patient assessment.
Hand-off information supports, but does not replace, assessment.
The off-going nurse is no longer accountable for earlier care.
Hand-off is about coordination, not removing accountability for care given.
The patient no longer needs to be told about the procedure.
Patients still need teaching about procedures.

items.q: [[Delegation]] is the process for a nurse to direct another person to perform nursing tasks and activities.
items.ex: Delegation is an indirect care activity in which the RN directs another person while retaining accountability.

alt.q: When an RN directs an assistive personnel to perform nursing tasks, the process is called [[delegation|delegating]].
alt.ex: Delegation is an indirect care activity in which the RN directs another person while retaining accountability.

items.q: When an RN delegates a care task, the RN retains responsibility and accountability for the provision of nursing practice.
items.a: True
items.ex: RNs can delegate tasks but retain responsibility and accountability for nursing practice.
items.ww: Delegating a task never transfers the RN’s accountability for nursing practice.

alt.q: An RN may delegate the nursing process, including assessment and evaluation, to an experienced assistive personnel.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: An RN can delegate care tasks but not the nursing process.
alt.ww: Even an experienced AP cannot be delegated the nursing process; only tasks may be delegated.

items.q: An RN is caring for four patients with assistive personnel (AP). Which task is most appropriate to delegate to the AP?
items.a: Measuring vital signs for a stable patient recovering from knee surgery
items.ex: Noninvasive, repetitive tasks such as vital signs for stable patients can be delegated to APs.
w: Assessing a newly admitted patient who reports chest pain
Assessment is part of the nursing process, which cannot be delegated.
Evaluating a patient’s response to a new pain medication
Evaluation is part of the nursing process, which the RN keeps.
Teaching a patient how to self-administer insulin injections
Patient teaching requires nursing judgment and is not a noninvasive, repetitive task.

alt.q: Which task should the RN NOT delegate to assistive personnel?
alt.a: Developing the nursing care plan for a new patient
alt.ex: Planning is part of the nursing process, which an RN cannot delegate.
w: Providing skin care to a stable patient
Skin care is a noninvasive, repetitive task that can be delegated.
Helping a stable patient transfer to a chair
Transfer and mobility skills can be delegated to APs.
Assisting a stable patient with morning hygiene
Hygiene is a noninvasive, repetitive task that can be delegated.

items.q: Which interventions can an RN typically assign to certified nurse assistants and other assistive personnel? Select all that apply.
o: Skin care
Skin care is a noninvasive, repetitive intervention suitable for APs.
Transfer and mobility skills
Transfers and mobility are listed as delegable to APs.
Hygiene
Hygiene is a noninvasive, repetitive intervention.
Vital signs for patients who are stable
Vital signs may be delegated when patients are stable.
Evaluating whether patient outcomes were met
Evaluation is part of the nursing process, which cannot be delegated.
Initial assessment of a newly admitted patient
Assessment is part of the nursing process retained by the RN.
items.ex: APs can be assigned noninvasive, repetitive interventions such as skin care, transfers, hygiene, and vital signs for stable patients.

alt.q: An RN is planning assignments. Which activities should the RN keep rather than assign to assistive personnel? Select all that apply.
o: Evaluating a patient’s response to care
Evaluation is part of the nursing process, which cannot be delegated.
Developing the patient’s plan of care
Planning is part of the nursing process.
Assessing a patient whose condition is unstable
Vital signs and care tasks are delegated only for stable patients; assessment stays with the RN.
Helping a stable patient with hygiene
Hygiene is a noninvasive, repetitive task that can be delegated.
Repositioning a stable patient for skin care
Skin care and mobility tasks can be delegated.
alt.ex: Correct: Evaluating a patient’s response to care; Developing the patient’s plan of care; Assessing a patient whose condition is unstable.

items.q: An RN delegates blood pressure checks for a stable patient to an assistive personnel (AP). Which instruction best reflects effective delegation communication?
items.a: “Take Mr. Kim’s blood pressure at 2 PM with the manual cuff and report it to me by 2:15.”
items.ex: The RN communicates the data to collect, the method, and the time frame for reporting results.
w: “Check Mr. Kim’s blood pressure sometime this afternoon when you have a chance.”
This omits the method and a time frame for reporting results to the RN.
“Take Mr. Kim’s blood pressure and just chart it; I’ll look later if I have time.”
The RN must set a time frame for reporting results and supervise.
“Let me know if anything looks off with Mr. Kim while you are in the room.”
This gives no specific data to collect, method, or reporting time.

alt.q: After an RN delegates a task, the AP asks, “Should I use the bed scale or the standing scale for the weight?” How should the RN view this question?
alt.a: As expected two-way communication that clarifies the delegated task
alt.ex: Two-way communication is essential, including the delegatee asking clarifying questions.
w: As a sign the AP is not competent and should not do the task
Asking clarifying questions is an expected part of delegation, not a sign of incompetence.
As unnecessary because the RN already gave the instruction
Delegation includes the delegatee asking clarifying questions.
As a reason to transfer accountability for the task to the AP
The RN retains accountability regardless of the questions asked.

items.q: Effective delegation includes two-way communication in which the delegatee can ask clarifying questions.
items.a: True
items.ex: Two-way communication is essential, with the RN giving specific instructions and the delegatee asking questions.
items.ww: The book states that two-way communication, including clarifying questions, is essential in delegation.

alt.q: Once an RN gives instructions for a delegated task, communication with the delegatee is one-way, and the delegatee should not question them.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Delegation requires two-way communication, including the delegatee asking clarifying questions.
alt.ww: Clarifying questions from the delegatee are an expected part of delegation.

items.q: An AP tells the RN that a delegated patient ambulation has been completed. What is the RN’s responsibility now?
items.a: Make sure the task was done correctly, documented, and evaluated.
items.ex: The RN supervises delegated tasks and ensures each is completed correctly, documented, and evaluated.
w: Nothing further, because responsibility moved to the AP once the task was done.
The RN retains responsibility and accountability for delegated care.
Repeat the entire ambulation to confirm the AP did it properly.
Supervision means verifying the task, not redoing it.
Ask the AP to document it and then delegate the evaluation to the AP.
Evaluation is part of the nursing process and cannot be delegated.

alt.q: Which RN action best demonstrates appropriate supervision of a task delegated to an AP?
alt.a: Checking that the AP finished the task on time and without difficulty
alt.ex: Ongoing supervision confirms that the AP performed the task on time without difficulty and according to the standard of care.
w: Assuming the task was completed because the AP has years of experience
The RN must be sure the delegated action was completed correctly.
Waiting until the end of the shift to ask the AP about the task
Ongoing supervision is needed, not a check only at shift’s end.
Letting the AP decide whether the task needs to be reported
The RN sets the reporting time frame and evaluates the task.

items.q: Which statement about delegating direct care interventions is correct?
items.a: They are delegated only to personnel who are competent to perform them.
items.ex: The nurse delegates direct care interventions only to competent personnel and ensures each task is assigned appropriately.
w: They are delegated to whichever staff member is least busy on the unit.
Delegation depends on competence, not availability alone.
They can be delegated without instructions if the task is routine.
The RN must communicate specific instructions for any delegated activity.
They are delegated only to other RNs, never to LPNs or APs.
RNs may delegate to other RNs, LPNs, or APs.

alt.q: Before delegating a dressing change, what must the RN confirm about the delegatee?
alt.a: That the delegatee is competent to perform the task
alt.ex: Direct care interventions are delegated only to competent personnel.
w: That the delegatee has worked on the unit the longest
Seniority does not establish competence for a task.
That the delegatee has a lighter assignment than others
Workload alone does not make a delegation appropriate.
That the delegatee will accept accountability for the outcome
The RN retains accountability for delegated care.

items.q: According to the textbook, what often determines the frequency and way nursing care activities are delegated?
items.a: The nursing unit’s delivery-of-care model
items.ex: How often and how care is delegated often depends on the nursing unit delivery-of-care model.
w: The patient’s preference for staff
Patient preference is not named as what determines delegation patterns.
The health care provider’s orders
Provider orders do not set how nursing tasks are delegated.
The number of years of AP service
The book names the unit delivery-of-care model, not AP seniority.

alt.q: Two units in the same hospital delegate tasks to APs differently. Which factor most likely explains this difference?
alt.a: Each unit uses a different delivery-of-care model.
alt.ex: The frequency and way care activities are delegated often depends on the unit delivery-of-care model.
w: Each unit serves patients with different insurance plans.
Insurance is not named as a factor in delegation.
Each unit has a different number of visitors each day.
Visitor numbers do not determine how delegation occurs.
Each unit has a different documentation system in place.
Documentation systems are not what shapes delegation patterns.

items.q: How does appropriate delegation to assistive personnel benefit patient care?
items.a: The right care provider performs the right tasks, so the team works efficiently.
items.ex: Correct delegation ensures the right provider does the right tasks, so nurse and APs work together efficiently for the patient.
w: The RN no longer needs to supervise or evaluate the delegated tasks.
The RN must supervise and ensure delegated tasks are completed, documented, and evaluated.
The AP becomes accountable for the nursing care of that patient.
The RN retains responsibility and accountability for nursing practice.
The RN can hand off assessment and planning to free up more time.
The nursing process cannot be delegated; only care tasks can.

alt.q: An RN delegates hygiene for two stable patients to an AP. Which outcome shows the main benefit of delegation?
alt.a: The RN has more time to focus on patient teaching and assessment.
alt.ex: Delegation lets the nurse use time more wisely, for example to focus on patient education, while others assist.
w: The RN no longer has to check on those two patients during the shift.
The RN must still supervise and evaluate delegated care.
The AP takes over accountability for those patients’ outcomes.
Accountability stays with the RN who delegates.
The AP begins evaluating the patients’ responses to treatment.
Evaluation is part of the nursing process and is not delegated.

items.q: Which list correctly names the categories of factors that influence patient adherence?
items.a: Condition/disease, patient, social and economic, system and health care team, and therapeutic factors
items.ex: Adherence is influenced by the condition or disease, the patient, social and economic conditions, system and team factors, and therapeutic factors.
w: Patient, family, nurse, and health care provider factors only, with no system or economic factors
Adherence also depends on the condition, social and economic, system, and therapeutic factors.
Patient knowledge and motivation alone, since nonadherence is a person-centered problem
Focusing only on patient factors ignores the other dimensions that influence adherence.
Medication cost, insurance coverage, and pharmacy access, which are purely economic factors
Cost matters, but disease, patient, system, and therapeutic factors also influence adherence.

alt.q: A nurse reviews why Mr. Lawson may or may not follow his treatment plan. Which approach reflects the textbook’s view of adherence?
alt.a: Consider his condition, personal traits, social and economic situation, care team, and therapy.
alt.ex: Many dimensions influence adherence, such as pain and complications, anxiety, wife’s support, employment, and the nurse relationship.
w: Focus only on his motivation, because nonadherence is mainly a patient problem.
Viewing nonadherence only as a patient problem ignores system and provider factors.
Focus only on his surgery, because the condition decides whether he adheres.
The condition is only one of several dimensions affecting adherence.
Focus only on his income, because cost is the single cause of nonadherence.
Cost is significant, but several other dimensions also influence adherence.

items.q: A nurse carefully plans and delivers interventions for a patient with diabetes, yet the patient’s outcomes are not met. Which factor does the textbook say influences success despite the nurse’s efforts?
items.a: The patient’s adherence to the agreed-upon regimen
items.ex: Despite careful planning and implementation, success in meeting outcomes is influenced by patient adherence.
w: The length of the nurse’s written care plan
A longer plan does not determine success; the patient’s adherence does.
The number of interventions documented per shift
Documentation volume does not determine whether outcomes are met.
The time of day the interventions are delivered
Timing is not named; adherence influences success in meeting outcomes.

alt.q: Which statement about meeting expected patient outcomes is consistent with the textbook?
alt.a: Even with good planning and implementation, patient adherence influences success.
alt.ex: Success in meeting outcomes depends partly on whether the patient follows the agreed-upon regimen.
w: Good planning and implementation always guarantee outcomes are met.
Patient adherence also influences whether outcomes are met.
Outcomes depend only on the number of interventions provided.
Adherence, not just the number of interventions, influences success.
Patient behavior has little effect once the care plan is written.
The patient’s behaviors following the regimen strongly influence outcomes.

items.q: What is the main aim when a nurse delivers a nursing intervention?
items.a: To achieve expected outcomes that manage or eliminate the patient’s nursing diagnoses
items.ex: Interventions aim to achieve expected patient outcomes that manage or eliminate nursing diagnoses or problems.
w: To complete every task on the care plan before the end of the shift
Task completion is not the aim; achieving the patient’s outcomes is.
To document care thoroughly enough to meet agency accreditation rules
Documentation supports care but is not the purpose of intervening.
To deliver one intervention at a time for each patient problem identified
Most situations need multiple interventions to achieve select outcomes.

alt.q: A nurse is evaluating why an intervention was chosen for a patient with impaired mobility. Which reason fits the textbook?
alt.a: It helps meet expected outcomes to manage the mobility problem.
alt.ex: The aim of an intervention is to achieve expected outcomes that manage or eliminate a nursing diagnosis.
w: It is the only intervention needed to resolve the problem.
Most clinical situations require multiple interventions to achieve outcomes.
It fills the time between scheduled medication passes.
Interventions are chosen to achieve outcomes, not to fill time.
It is the same intervention used for all patients on the unit.
Interventions are individualized to the patient’s problems and outcomes.

items.q: Why does the textbook emphasize applying care coordination principles during implementation?
items.a: Patients’ conditions can change minute by minute, and multiple interventions are often needed.
items.ex: Changing conditions and the need for multiple interventions make time management, organization, and resource use essential.
w: Patients’ conditions are stable, so interventions can be planned once per shift.
Conditions often change minute by minute, requiring ongoing coordination.
A single intervention usually resolves each nursing diagnosis completely.
Most clinical situations require multiple interventions to achieve outcomes.
Care coordination replaces the need to set priorities among diagnoses.
Priority setting remains critical to successful implementation.

alt.q: A nurse’s postoperative patient develops new pain while another patient needs discharge teaching. Which principle best helps the nurse meet both patients’ outcomes?
alt.a: Applying time management, organization, and priority setting
alt.ex: Care coordination principles and priority setting help the nurse deliver interventions effectively when conditions change.
w: Completing tasks in the order they appear on the care plan
Care must be sequenced by priority, not by list order.
Delaying all care until the health care provider gives direction
Nurses coordinate and prioritize care themselves using clinical judgment.
Finishing the discharge teaching before assessing the new pain
Assessing a change in condition generally takes priority over routine teaching.

items.q: Which care coordination principles help a nurse deliver interventions effectively and meet desired outcomes? Select all that apply.
o: Good time management
Time management is a named care coordination principle.
Organizational skills
Organization helps the nurse deliver multiple interventions effectively.
Appropriate use of resources
Using resources appropriately is a care coordination principle.
Performing every intervention personally
Nurses coordinate and delegate; they do not personally perform all interventions.
Following a fixed routine regardless of changes
Conditions change minute by minute, so care must adapt.
items.ex: Care coordination relies on time management, organizational skills, and appropriate use of resources.

alt.q: A charge nurse observes a new nurse who is falling behind. Which behaviors would show the new nurse is applying care coordination principles? Select all that apply.
o: Grouping care activities to use time efficiently
This reflects good time management.
Gathering needed supplies before entering the room
This reflects organizational skills.
Asking an available AP to help with a stable patient’s hygiene
This reflects appropriate use of resources.
Completing tasks strictly in the order written on the care plan
Priority setting, not list order, guides the sequence of care.
Ignoring a new change in a patient to stay on schedule
Conditions change and care must adapt to them.
alt.ex: Correct: Grouping care activities to use time efficiently; Gathering needed supplies before entering the room; Asking an available AP to help with a stable patient’s hygiene.

items.q: How does prioritizing nursing diagnoses and outcomes help the nurse during implementation?
items.a: It helps the nurse anticipate and sequence interventions when there are multiple problems.
items.ex: Prioritizing diagnoses and outcomes helps anticipate and sequence interventions for multiple nursing diagnoses and collaborative problems.
w: It removes the need to reassess the patient once care has started.
Conditions change minute by minute, so ongoing assessment is still needed.
It allows lower-priority diagnoses to be dropped from the care plan.
Priorities guide sequencing; they do not mean other problems are discarded.
It ensures that every intervention can be delegated to support staff.
Prioritizing guides sequencing, not which tasks may be delegated.

alt.q: A patient has acute pain, risk for infection, and a knowledge deficit. Which nursing approach reflects the textbook’s guidance?
alt.a: Prioritize the diagnoses so interventions can be anticipated and sequenced.
alt.ex: Priority setting is critical; ranking diagnoses helps the nurse anticipate and sequence interventions.
w: Address each diagnosis in alphabetical order to be consistent.
Sequencing should be based on priority, not alphabetical order.
Treat only the first diagnosis listed until it is fully resolved.
Multiple interventions are often needed at once for several problems.
Wait for the patient to choose which problem to address each day.
The nurse sets priorities with the patient, using clinical judgment.

items.q: Patient [[adherence]] is the extent to which a patient’s behaviors follow an agreed-upon prescription or therapeutic regimen.
items.ex: Success in meeting outcomes is influenced by patient adherence to the agreed-upon treatment plan.

alt.q: The extent to which a patient follows an agreed-upon therapeutic regimen is called patient [[adherence]].
alt.ex: Success in meeting outcomes is influenced by patient adherence to the agreed-upon treatment plan.

items.q: Which factors appear to be critical facilitators of medication adherence from the patient’s perspective? Select all that apply.
o: Information and knowledge about diseases and treatments
Knowledge of diseases and treatments was identified as a key facilitator.
Communication and trust in the patient-provider relationship
Trust and communication with providers facilitate adherence.
Support
Support was identified as a critical facilitator.
Adequate resources
Adequate resources facilitate medication adherence.
A generic list of what the patient must not do
Simple lists of restrictions are less meaningful than person-centered teaching.
Warnings that nonadherence is the patient’s own fault
Treating nonadherence as only a patient problem ignores system and provider factors.
items.ex: From the patient’s perspective, information, communication and trust, support, and adequate resources facilitate medication adherence.

alt.q: A nurse wants to improve a patient’s medication adherence. Which actions address factors the textbook identifies as facilitators? Select all that apply.
o: Building a trusting relationship with open communication
Communication and trust in the patient-provider relationship facilitate adherence.
Connecting the patient with resources to obtain medications
Adequate resources are a critical facilitator.
Arranging consented phone call or text reminders
Consented reminders could enhance medication adherence.
Giving the same standard handout used for every patient
Education alone has not been shown to improve adherence unless person-centered.
Labeling the patient as noncompliant in the record
Labeling does not address the factors that facilitate adherence.
alt.ex: Correct: Building a trusting relationship with open communication; Connecting the patient with resources to obtain medications; Arranging consented phone call or text reminders.

items.q: A patient with hypertension tells the nurse, “I stopped refilling my blood pressure pills because they cost too much.” Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Work with the team to find resources that lower the medication’s cost.
items.ex: Cost of therapies significantly influences adherence, and adequate resources facilitate it.
w: Repeat the teaching about why blood pressure control is important.
Education alone does not address the cost barrier the patient described.
Document that the patient is choosing to be nonadherent.
Treating nonadherence only as a patient problem ignores system factors like cost.
Warn the patient that stopping the pills could cause a stroke.
Warnings do not resolve the cost barrier preventing adherence.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing reasons patients do not follow medication regimens. Which statement about cost is consistent with the textbook?
alt.a: Cost of therapies is a significant influence on adherence.
alt.ex: The book identifies cost of therapies as a significant influence on adherence.
w: Cost rarely affects adherence when a patient understands the drug.
Cost is a significant influence regardless of the patient’s knowledge.
Cost affects adherence only for patients without health insurance.
The book names cost as a significant influence without limiting it to the uninsured.
Cost is a patient factor that nurses cannot help address.
Nurses can address system and resource factors, not only patient factors.

items.q: Nonadherence has traditionally been considered a person-centered problem, so interventions have mainly focused on patient factors.
items.a: True
items.ex: Because nonadherence was viewed as a patient problem, interventions largely ignored health care system and provider factors.
items.ww: The book states that interventions have mainly focused on patient factors and largely ignored other dimensions.

alt.q: Health care systems and providers play little role in patient adherence, so focusing only on patient factors is sufficient.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Adherence is influenced by condition, patient, social and economic, system and team, and therapeutic factors.
alt.ww: Ignoring system and provider dimensions leaves out important influences on adherence.

items.q: Education alone, without being person-centered, has been shown to consistently improve patient adherence.
items.a: False
items.ex: In several studies education alone did not improve adherence; person-centered, targeted education had a favorable impact.
items.ww: Studies found education alone did not positively affect adherence, so the statement is false.

alt.q: Patient education that is person-centered and targeted to the patient’s unique situation has a favorable impact on adherence.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Person-centered education tailored to the patient’s situation has been shown to have a favorable impact on adherence.
alt.ww: Targeted, person-centered education is what improves adherence, unlike education alone.

items.q: A nurse is teaching a patient who works in construction about postoperative lifting restrictions. Which approach is most likely to improve adherence?
items.a: Explain how lifting at work could strain the wound and delay his return to the job.
items.ex: Linking restrictions to the patient’s own daily activities and goals makes them more meaningful and relevant.
w: Give him a printed list of activities he must avoid after surgery.
A simple list of what not to do is less meaningful than linking restrictions to his life.
Tell him firmly that the surgeon requires the restrictions.
Stressing authority does not tie the restrictions to his personal situation.
Describe how wound healing works at the cellular level.
Technical detail without a link to his daily life does not make teaching person-centered.

alt.q: Tonya teaches Mr. Lawson about his postoperative restrictions. Which statement by Mr. Lawson shows the teaching was made meaningful to him?
alt.a: “If I lift my grandchild, the strain could open my wound farther.”
alt.ex: Tying restrictions to his own activities, such as lifting a grandchild, shows he understands why they matter.
w: “I have a sheet listing what not to do, so I will read it later.”
Having a list does not show he relates the restrictions to his own life.
“The restrictions are just hospital rules that everyone has to follow.”
This shows he does not see the personal relevance of the restrictions.
“I can lift heavy groceries as long as my wound is not painful.”
Lifting groceries could stress the wound and cause it to open farther.

items.q: According to the textbook, when is a patient more likely to adhere to a treatment?
items.a: When the patient sees the treatment as beneficial and improving quality of life
items.ex: Adherence is more likely when a treatment is seen as beneficial and making a difference in quality of life.
w: When the patient receives the treatment information in a single session
Education alone has not been shown to improve adherence.
When the patient is told the treatment is required by the provider
Adherence relates to the patient’s beliefs and values, not authority alone.
When the patient is offered a treatment that costs more than others
Cost is a significant barrier, not a promoter, of adherence.

alt.q: Which patient statement suggests the greatest likelihood of adhering to a new exercise program?
alt.a: “Since I started walking, I can play with my kids without getting winded.”
alt.ex: Patients who see a treatment as beneficial and improving quality of life are more likely to adhere.
w: “My doctor says I have to walk, so I guess I’ll try it for a while.”
Following orders without valuing the benefit suggests weaker adherence.
“I don’t see how walking will make any difference for my heart.”
Not seeing a benefit makes adherence less likely.
“I’ll start walking once things settle down at work in a few months.”
This suggests the patient is not ready for change, which makes changes harder.

items.q: A patient newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes says, “I’m just not ready to change how I eat yet.” What should the nurse recognize?
items.a: Diet changes may seem more challenging when a patient is not ready for change.
items.ex: If a patient is not ready for change, alterations to health routines such as diet may seem more challenging.
w: The patient’s readiness has no effect on adherence to diet changes.
Readiness for change does affect how challenging routine changes seem.
Repeating the same teaching more often will overcome the reluctance.
Education alone has not been shown to improve adherence.
The patient should be labeled noncompliant in the care plan.
Labeling ignores the many factors that influence adherence.

alt.q: Which factor described in the textbook can make changes in diet, exercise, or medication use seem more challenging to a patient?
alt.a: The patient not being ready for change
alt.ex: When a patient is not ready for change, alterations to health routines may seem more challenging.
w: The patient having strong family support
Support is a facilitator of adherence, not a barrier.
The patient trusting the health care provider
Trust in the patient-provider relationship facilitates adherence.
The patient seeing the treatment as beneficial
Seeing a treatment as beneficial makes adherence more likely.

items.q: From a community health perspective, which strategy could enhance medication adherence?
items.a: Using consented reminders such as phone calls or text messages
items.ex: Active and passive communication, including consented reminders like phone calls or texts, could enhance medication adherence.
w: Sending reminders to patients without asking their permission
The book specifies consented reminders, which respect the patient’s choice.
Limiting contact with patients until their next scheduled visit
Ongoing communication, not reduced contact, could enhance adherence.
Focusing education efforts only on patients, not on providers
Improving both providers’ and patients’ education is recommended.

alt.q: A clinic wants to improve medication adherence among its patients. Which plan reflects the community health strategies in the textbook?
alt.a: Educate both providers and patients and offer opt-in text reminders.
alt.ex: Improving provider and patient education and using consented reminders could enhance adherence.
w: Educate only patients and send reminders to everyone automatically.
Both providers and patients need education, and reminders should be consented.
Educate only providers and avoid contacting patients between visits.
Patient education and consented reminders are also recommended.
Rely on patients to remember doses without any added communication.
Active and passive communication could enhance adherence.

items.q: Strengthening partnerships between providers’ organizations and faith-based and community organizations could help drive patient adherence.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book notes that partnerships with faith-based and community organizations could drive adherence.
items.ww: Community partnerships are named as a way to drive adherence, so they are not irrelevant.

alt.q: Efforts to improve adherence should stay within the health care organization, because faith-based and community groups have no effect on it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Partnerships with faith-based and community organizations could drive adherence.
alt.ww: Community and faith-based partnerships are named as a way to strengthen adherence.

items.q: A patient is being discharged from the hospital to a rehabilitation agency. Which nursing action best promotes a smooth transition?
items.a: Begin timely discharge planning that includes patient and family education and resources.
items.ex: Adequate, timely discharge planning with collaborative education and community resources promotes smooth transitions between settings.
w: Wait until the day of discharge to begin planning so plans are current.
Discharge planning must be adequate and timely, not left to the last day.
Teach the patient alone so the family does not become confused.
Education should be collaborative and include the family.
Choose interventions the team prefers, whether or not the patient agrees.
Interventions should be ones the patient is willing and able to follow.

alt.q: Which discharge plan best supports a smooth transition from hospital to home?
alt.a: Interventions the patient is willing and able to follow, with family teaching and community resources
alt.ex: Smooth transitions depend on interventions the patient will follow, collaborative education, and arranged community resources.
w: A standard set of interventions given to all patients with the same diagnosis
Care should be individualized to the patient’s beliefs, culture, and lifestyle.
Complex interventions that require frequent clinic visits the patient cannot reach
Interventions should be ones the patient is able to follow.
Instructions given only to the patient on the morning of discharge
Planning should be timely and include collaborative patient and family education.

items.a: Extent to which a patient’s behaviors follow an agreed-upon regimen
items.ex: These concepts help nurses deliver interventions effectively and support patients in meeting expected outcomes.
w: Teaching targeted to a patient’s unique situation
That goes with Person-centered education.
Phone calls or text messages a patient agrees to receive
That goes with Consented reminders.
Arranging education and community resources for a smooth transition
That goes with Discharge planning.

w: Extent to which a patient’s behaviors follow an agreed-upon regimen

Teaching targeted to a patient’s unique situation
That goes with Person-centered education.
Arranging education and community resources for a smooth transition

w: Extent to which a patient’s behaviors follow an agreed-upon regimen

That goes with Consented reminders.

alt.q: Which description fits Care coordination?

w: Extent to which a patient’s behaviors follow an agreed-upon regimen
That goes with Patient adherence.
Teaching targeted to a patient’s unique situation
That goes with Person-centered education.
Phone calls or text messages a patient agrees to receive
That goes with Consented reminders.

w: Patient adherence
Patient adherence: Extent to which a patient’s behaviors follow an agreed-upon regimen.
Consented reminders
Consented reminders: Phone calls or text messages a patient agrees to receive.
Discharge planning
Discharge planning: Arranging education and community resources for a smooth transition.

alt.q: Which term is described as “Phone calls or text messages a patient agrees to receive”?
alt.a: Consented reminders
alt.ex: These concepts help nurses deliver interventions effectively and support patients in meeting expected outcomes.
w: Patient adherence
Patient adherence: Extent to which a patient’s behaviors follow an agreed-upon regimen.
Person-centered education
Person-centered education: Teaching targeted to a patient’s unique situation.
Discharge planning

alt.a: Discharge planning

w: Patient adherence

Person-centered education

Consented reminders

mt.q: Match each term related to achieving patient outcomes with its description.
pairs: Extent to which a patient’s behaviors follow an agreed-upon regimen
Teaching targeted to a patient’s unique situation
Phone calls or text messages a patient agrees to receive
Arranging education and community resources for a smooth transition
Using time management, organization, and resources to deliver interventions
mt.ex: These concepts help nurses deliver interventions effectively and support patients in meeting expected outcomes.

items.q: A patient with heart failure reports, “I weighed myself every morning this week and called when I gained 2 pounds.” Which response by the nurse best supports continued adherence?
items.a: “You followed your plan exactly and caught the change early. Well done.”
items.ex: Reinforcing successes with the treatment plan encourages a patient to keep following the care plan.
w: “Good, but remember you also need to cut down on salt much more.”
Shifting to a criticism misses the chance to reinforce the success.
“That’s what you were told to do, so it is expected of you.”
This dismisses the achievement instead of reinforcing it.
“You can probably weigh yourself less often now that you know how.”
This undermines the plan rather than reinforcing successful behavior.

alt.q: Which nursing action does the textbook identify as encouraging a patient to follow the care plan?
alt.a: Reinforcing the patient’s successes with the treatment plan
alt.ex: Reinforcing successes with the treatment plan encourages the patient to follow the care plan.
w: Pointing out each time the patient misses a treatment
Focusing on failures is not the strategy named; reinforcing successes is.
Providing the same information at every visit
Education alone has not been shown to improve adherence.
Reducing contact once the patient has started treatment
Ongoing communication and support facilitate adherence.

items.q: A patient’s cultural diet includes foods high in sodium, and the patient needs a low-sodium diet. Which approach best reflects the textbook’s guidance on individualizing care?
items.a: Work with the patient to adapt familiar foods to fit the diet plan.
items.ex: Individualized care considers factors that influence a patient’s health beliefs, culture, and lifestyle, which supports adherence.
w: Give the patient a standard low-sodium menu used for all patients.
Standard plans ignore the patient’s culture and lifestyle.
Tell the patient to stop eating all traditional foods permanently.
This disregards culture and is unlikely to be followed.
Leave the diet out of the plan because culture cannot be changed.
Care should be adapted to the patient’s culture, not left unaddressed.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse best reflects individualized care to support a patient’s adherence after discharge?
alt.a: “Let’s plan your medication times around your work schedule and family routines.”
alt.ex: Individualizing care to the patient’s beliefs, culture, and lifestyle helps the patient follow the plan.
w: “Everyone with your condition takes the medication at 8 AM and 8 PM.”
A standard schedule ignores the patient’s lifestyle.
“Your schedule is not my concern; the plan comes first.”
This disregards the lifestyle factors that influence adherence.
“You will need to change your job to fit this treatment plan.”
Interventions should fit what the patient is willing and able to follow.

sections.name: Clinical judgment and critical thinking in evaluation

items.q: During the evaluation step of the nursing process, what is the nurse’s “action” in clinical judgment?
items.a: Deciding whether to continue, revise, or discontinue an intervention
items.ex: In evaluation, the clinical judgment action is determining whether an intervention should be continued, revised, or discontinued.
w: Selecting the nursing diagnoses that best fit the assessment cues
Selecting nursing diagnoses is part of the diagnosis step, not the action taken during evaluation.
Delivering the interventions written in the plan of care
Delivering interventions is implementation; evaluation judges whether those interventions worked.
Collecting the baseline data used to identify patient problems
Collecting baseline data to identify problems is assessment, which comes before interventions.

alt.q: A nurse rechecks a patient after a series of interventions and concludes that one approach is no longer needed. Which clinical judgment decision does this represent?
alt.a: Determining whether to continue, revise, or discontinue the intervention
alt.ex: Evaluation leads the nurse to decide whether each intervention should be continued, revised, or discontinued.
w: Generating new hypotheses about the patient’s medical diagnosis
Generating hypotheses about the cause of problems precedes care; this decision is about an intervention already given.
Recognizing cues that define the patient’s original health problem
Recognizing cues to define the original problem occurs during assessment, not when judging an intervention’s results.
Prioritizing which nursing diagnoses to address during the shift
Prioritizing diagnoses occurs in planning; this nurse is judging whether an intervention is still needed.

items.q: A nurse applies a warm compress to a patient’s wound. What is the purpose of the nurse’s evaluative measures afterward?
items.a: To determine whether the patient met the expected outcomes
items.ex: Evaluative measures, such as reinspecting the wound, show whether expected outcomes were met, not whether interventions were completed.
w: To confirm that every ordered intervention was completed
Evaluation focuses on the patient’s response; completing interventions does not prove they worked.
To identify which new health problems the patient has
Identifying what problems exist is the purpose of assessment rather than evaluation.
To decide which compress to apply at the next treatment
Choosing the compress type is part of planning and implementing, not the purpose of evaluative measures.

alt.q: Which documentation entry best reflects true evaluation of wound care?
alt.a: “Wound reinspected; drainage decreased from moderate to scant.”
alt.ex: Evaluation reports the patient’s response compared with expected outcomes, such as a decrease in wound drainage.
w: “Warm compress applied to wound as ordered at 1000.”
This entry documents that an intervention was done, not whether the wound improved.
“Wound care supplies gathered and brought to bedside.”
Gathering supplies is preparation for care and says nothing about the patient’s outcome.
“Wound care completed per protocol; patient in bed.”
Completing a protocol shows the task was done, not whether the expected outcome was achieved.

items.q: Which actions reflect competency in performing evaluation, as identified in a review of critical thinking indicators? Select all that apply.
o: Examining the results of care according to clinical data collected
Examining results against collected clinical data is one of the four evaluation competencies.
Comparing achieved effects with expected outcomes
Comparing achieved and expected outcomes is central to evaluation and requires in-depth knowledge.
Recognizing errors or omissions in care
Recognizing errors or omissions, and their consequences, is one of the four competencies.
Confirming that each intervention was completed on schedule
Evaluation judges patient outcomes, not whether tasks were finished on time.
Repeating the same plan of care until discharge
Evaluation may lead to revising or discontinuing care, so the plan is not simply repeated.
items.ex: The four competencies are examining results, comparing achieved with expected outcomes, recognizing errors or omissions, and understanding, reflecting on, and correcting errors.

alt.q: A nurse is mentoring a new graduate in evaluation. Which behaviors by the graduate show evaluation competency? Select all that apply.
o: Reflects on the patient situation and corrects errors that are found
Understanding the situation, reflecting on it, and correcting errors is one of the four competencies.
Compares the patient’s achieved outcomes with the expected outcomes
Comparing achieved effects with expected outcomes is an evaluation competency.
Examines results of care using clinical data collected after care
Examining results based on collected clinical data is an evaluation competency.
Assumes outcomes are met when all interventions are charted as done
Charting completed interventions does not show the patient met expected outcomes.
Relies on what usually happens to patients with the same diagnosis
Clinical judgments should be based on the specific patient, not on patients in general.
alt.ex: Correct: Reflects on the patient situation and corrects errors that are found; Compares the patient’s achieved outcomes with the expected outcomes; Examines results of care using clinical data collected after care.

items.q: A patient with pneumonia completed a course of antibiotics. How does the health care provider evaluate whether the pneumonia has resolved?
items.a: By repeating the original assessments and comparing the new findings
items.ex: Comparing original assessment data with repeated measures after treatment, such as chest x-ray, cough, and temperature, shows the patient’s status.
w: By confirming that the patient took every dose of the antibiotic
Taking all doses shows the treatment was given, not whether the pneumonia resolved.
By using new tests that were not part of the original workup
Evaluation repeats the original assessments so that before and after findings can be compared.
By asking the patient whether the antibiotic had any side effects
Side effects are worth noting but do not show whether the pneumonia itself resolved.

alt.q: Which approach does the textbook describe as informing the nurse of a patient’s status during evaluation?
alt.a: Continually comparing original assessment data with repeated measures
alt.ex: Continually comparing the original assessment data with evaluation data obtained after an intervention informs the nurse of a patient’s status.
w: Reviewing the list of interventions that were completed each shift
A list of completed interventions does not show how the patient responded to them.
Relying on the health care provider’s orders to judge progress
Orders direct treatment; the nurse judges progress by comparing before and after data.
Collecting a single set of data at the time of discharge only
Evaluation is continuous; one set of data at discharge cannot show change over time.

items.q: Mr. Lawson’s diagnosis of Acute Pain was based on a pain rating of 7, splinting of his incision, and unwillingness to move in bed. Which evaluative measures should the nurse use to judge whether his pain is relieved?
items.a: Ask him to rate his pain and observe his movements and breathing
items.ex: Outcomes focus on relieving the original cues, so the nurse checks his pain rating, splinting, movement, and breathing.
w: Check how many doses of analgesic he has received since surgery
The number of doses given does not show whether the cues of pain were relieved.
Review his laboratory results for signs of surgical complications
Laboratory results do not measure the cues used to form the Acute Pain diagnosis.
Ask his wife whether he seems to be in less pain than yesterday
Family input helps, but the patient’s own rating and observed movement are the direct measures.

alt.q: Mr. Lawson’s expected outcomes include a pain rating of 4 or less, no splinting of the incision, and moving freely in bed. Which finding best shows the outcomes are being met?
alt.a: He rates pain at 3 and moves in bed without splinting his incision
alt.ex: The outcomes were designed to remove the original cues, so a low pain rating and free movement show progress.
w: He rates pain at 5 and moves in bed only when his wife helps him
A rating of 5 exceeds the outcome of 4 or less, and he is not moving freely.
He rates pain at 3 but still holds a pillow over his incision to move
Continued splinting means one of the expected outcomes has not been met.
He requested every available dose of his prn analgesic overnight
Medication use alone does not show his pain rating or movement outcomes were met.

items.q: What are the criterion-based standards a nurse uses during evaluation?
items.a: The expected outcomes identified during planning
items.ex: Expected outcomes, based on the patient’s nursing diagnoses and assessment findings, serve as the criterion-based standards for evaluation.
w: The interventions listed in the nursing care plan
Interventions are the actions delivered; outcomes are the standards used to judge them.
The health care provider’s orders for treatment
Orders direct therapy but are not the criteria used to judge the patient’s response.
The nursing diagnoses selected during assessment
Diagnoses state the problem; the outcomes linked to them are the evaluation standards.

alt.q: A patient has a staged pressure injury (PI). What does the nurse use as outcome criteria to monitor the patient’s response to treatment?
alt.a: The PI staging criteria, such as appearance and wound size
alt.ex: Once a PI is staged, staging criteria from the clinical practice guideline become the outcome criteria for monitoring treatment response.
w: The number of dressing changes completed each day
Counting dressing changes measures interventions, not how the wound responds.
The patient’s report of comfort during each dressing change
Comfort matters, but the staging criteria are the standard for judging wound change.
The type of dressing ordered by the health care provider
The dressing type is an intervention; staging criteria are the outcome measures.

items.q: Knowledge is the critical thinking element the textbook describes as central to evaluation.
items.a: True
items.ex: The nurse’s knowledge base acts as a data bank used to recognize when patients progress, when problems worsen, and when to rethink care.
items.ww: Experience, standards, attitudes, and environment all matter, but knowledge is identified as central to evaluation.

alt.q: Because evaluation relies mainly on intuition, knowledge of a patient’s pathophysiology adds little to judging outcomes.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Knowledge of pathophysiology and normal findings lets the nurse recognize improvement, worsening, and complications.
alt.ww: Evaluation draws on a knowledge base; it is not mainly intuition, and pathophysiology is part of that base.

items.q: Which statement best describes clinical deterioration?
items.a: A dynamic state that compromises hemodynamic stability with physiological decompensation
items.ex: Clinical deterioration is a dynamic state marked by physiological decompensation with subjective or objective findings that compromise hemodynamic stability.
w: A slow, predictable decline that develops only in chronic illness
Deterioration can move a patient to a worse state quickly; it is not limited to chronic illness.
A stable condition in which outcomes are met more slowly than expected
A stable condition with delayed progress does not involve physiological decompensation.
An expected response to treatment that resolves without intervention
Deterioration increases the risk for numerous problems and needs early recognition.

alt.q: Why are nurses described as playing a critical role in recognizing clinical deterioration early?
alt.a: They spend more time at the patient’s bedside than other providers
alt.ex: Because nurses spend more time at the bedside than other providers, they are positioned to recognize early changes.
w: They are responsible for ordering diagnostic tests when changes occur
Ordering tests is not the reason; their bedside presence lets them notice change.
They review the patient’s history only at the time of admission
Nurses must understand the patient’s history and current condition continually, not only at admission.
They rely on monitoring equipment rather than direct observation
Recognizing deterioration depends on assessing and knowing the patient, not equipment alone.

items.q: Which themes were identified for recognizing patient deterioration? Select all that apply.
o: Assessing the patient
Assessing the patient is one of the three key themes for recognizing deterioration.
Knowing the patient
Knowing the patient gives familiarity and heightened awareness of subtle changes.
Education
Nurses with more ongoing education and skills training seem more perceptive of change.
Delegating vital signs
Delegating vital signs was not identified as a theme for recognizing deterioration.
Standardized care for all
Treating all patients the same can cause errors in judgment; care should be patient specific.
items.ex: Assessing the patient, knowing the patient, and education were the three key themes for recognizing deterioration.

alt.q: Which factors help a nurse recognize subtle changes in a patient’s condition? Select all that apply.
o: Experience caring for similar patients or the same patient over time
Knowing the patient through experience heightens awareness of subtle changes.
Full understanding of the patient’s medical history and current condition
Nurses recognize deterioration by fully understanding the history and current condition.
Ongoing clinical education and skills training
Nurses with more ongoing education and training seem more perceptive of clinical change.
Caring for a different group of patients every shift
Constantly changing assignments limits the familiarity that comes from knowing the patient.
Focusing on what happens to patients with the diagnosis in general
Judgments should be based on what is occurring with the specific patient.
alt.ex: Correct: Experience caring for similar patients or the same patient over time; Full understanding of the patient’s medical history and current condition; Ongoing clinical education and skills training.

items.q: A new graduate nurse is unsure whether a patient’s data are sufficient to decide that an expected outcome was met. Which approach reflects the critical thinking attitude the textbook emphasizes here?
items.a: Acknowledge the uncertainty and gather more information before deciding
items.ex: Humility is important when the nurse is unsure whether there is adequate information to decide if outcomes were met.
w: Document the outcome as met because most patients improve by this point
Assuming improvement based on typical patients ignores the need for adequate patient-specific data.
Rely on the first finding obtained to avoid delaying the documentation
One finding may be insufficient; humility means recognizing when more information is needed.
Document the outcome as unmet so the plan of care continues unchanged
Labeling the outcome without adequate data is inaccurate, whether marked met or unmet.

alt.q: Which critical thinking attitude is most important when a nurse is unsure whether there is enough information to decide if a patient met an outcome?
alt.a: Humility
alt.ex: Humility helps the nurse recognize limits in available information before judging outcome achievement.
w: Creativity
Creativity helps in adapting approaches, but recognizing the limits of one’s information reflects humility.
Perseverance
Perseverance keeps the nurse working on a problem, but the attitude for uncertainty here is humility.
Confidence
Confidence is useful in evaluation, but uncertainty about adequate data calls for humility.

items.q: Which competencies are included in the ANA standards for the evaluation step of the nursing process? Select all that apply.
o: Being systematic and using criterion-based evaluation
ANA evaluation competencies include systematic, criterion-based evaluation.
Collaborating with patients and health care providers
Collaboration with patients and providers is an ANA evaluation competency.
Using ongoing assessment data to revise the plan
Ongoing assessment data are used to revise the plan of care.
Communicating results to patients and families
ANA standards include communicating results of care to patients and families.
Limiting evaluation to the day of discharge
Evaluation is ongoing and occurs with every patient contact, not just at discharge.
Leaving evaluation decisions to the health care provider
Nurses are responsible for evaluating the efficacy of their own care.
items.ex: ANA competencies include systematic criterion-based evaluation, collaboration, revising the plan using ongoing data, and communicating results to patients and families.

alt.q: A nurse manager reviews how staff evaluate care. Which staff behaviors meet ANA evaluation standards? Select all that apply.
o: Uses ongoing assessment data to revise a patient’s plan of care
Revising the plan with ongoing assessment data is an ANA evaluation competency.
Shares the results of care with the patient and family
Communicating results to patients and families is part of the ANA standards.
Delivers interventions so as to minimize unwarranted treatment
The standards focus on responsible care that minimizes unwarranted or unwanted treatment.
Continues every intervention unchanged until the patient is discharged
Evaluation leads to continuing, revising, or discontinuing interventions as needed.
Evaluates care only when the patient voices a complaint
Evaluation is systematic and ongoing, not triggered only by complaints.
alt.ex: Correct: Uses ongoing assessment data to revise a patient’s plan of care; Shares the results of care with the patient and family; Delivers interventions so as to minimize unwarranted treatment.

items.q: For which interventions does the textbook stress that evaluating efficacy is especially important?
items.a: Medications, blood products, and intravenous fluids
items.ex: The nurse is responsible for evaluating efficacy of care, especially critical interventions such as medications, blood products, and IV fluids.
w: Hygiene, bed making, and routine positioning
These are important but are not the critical interventions the textbook singles out.
Discharge teaching, referrals, and patient education
Teaching outcomes are evaluated, but the critical interventions named are medications, blood products, and IV fluids.
Vital signs, intake and output, and daily weights
These are measurements used in evaluation, not critical interventions being evaluated.

alt.q: A nurse has just started a blood transfusion. Why is it essential to return and evaluate the patient’s response?
alt.a: Blood products are critical interventions whose efficacy the nurse must evaluate
alt.ex: Nurses are responsible for evaluating efficacy of care, which is especially important for critical interventions such as blood products.
w: The health care provider evaluates transfusions, so the nurse only documents
The nurse is responsible for evaluating the efficacy of care, including transfusions.
Evaluation is needed only if the patient reports a reaction during the transfusion
Evaluation should not wait for complaints; critical interventions require active evaluation.
Agency policy requires a signature after transfusions are finished
Documentation is required, but the reason to evaluate is the critical nature of the intervention.

items.q: Clarity, precision, accuracy, and significance are examples of [[intellectual standards]] that make evaluative measures comprehensive.
items.ex: Applying intellectual standards for measurement helps ensure that evaluation is thorough and accurate.

alt.q: The [[intellectual standards]] of clarity, precision, accuracy, and significance help make a nurse’s evaluative measures comprehensive.
alt.ex: Applying intellectual standards for measurement helps ensure that evaluation is thorough and accurate.

items.q: A nurse on a busy unit administers a prn analgesic and is quickly called to another patient. Which action shows sound evaluation practice?
items.a: Plan a time to return and reassess the patient’s pain response
items.ex: Delivering interventions automatically without returning to evaluate outcomes is irresponsible; anticipating the need to evaluate fits it into care.
w: Assume the analgesic worked unless the patient uses the call light
Waiting for a call light is not evaluation; the nurse must actively return to reassess.
Document that the medication was effective to save time later
Documenting an outcome that was not evaluated is inaccurate and unsafe.
Wait until the next scheduled dose to ask about the patient’s pain
Waiting for the next dose delays evaluation of whether the first dose worked.

alt.q: Which strategy helps a nurse manage the care environment so that evaluation is not neglected?
alt.a: Anticipate the need to evaluate and fit it in with other care activities
alt.ex: Nurses minimize distractions, anticipate when evaluation is needed, and plan how it fits with other activities.
w: Evaluate interventions only when there is time left at the end of the shift
Leaving evaluation until spare time risks omitting it; it should be planned.
Focus planning time on interventions rather than on their evaluation
Treating evaluation as less important than interventions is a problem, not a strategy.
Complete evaluation quickly by checking only whether the patient is stable
Evaluation is methodical and more than a quick check of stability.

items.q: Delivering interventions in an automatic fashion, without returning to evaluate the patient’s outcomes, is irresponsible practice.
items.a: True
items.ex: Taking time to evaluate is critical because only evaluation shows whether interventions were sufficient or beneficial.
items.ww: Automatic care without evaluation cannot show whether care helped, so it is not acceptable practice.

alt.q: When time and resources are limited, it is acceptable practice to deliver routine interventions without returning to evaluate their outcomes.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Limited time does not justify skipping evaluation; delivering interventions without evaluating outcomes is irresponsible.
alt.ww: Research notes evaluation is sometimes deprioritized, but the textbook calls skipping it irresponsible, not acceptable.
