mt.q: Match each element of critical thinking in evaluation with an example of it.
pairs: Pathophysiology of the patient’s health condition
mt.ex: Each critical thinking element contributes to evaluation: knowledge, experience, environment, standards, and attitudes.

items.q: Knowing a patient, gained by caring for similar patients or the same patient over time, heightens a nurse’s awareness of subtle changes in status.
items.a: True
items.ex: Knowing the patient gives familiarity that helps the nurse notice subtle changes and early deterioration.
items.ww: Familiarity from experience helps, not hinders, recognition of subtle changes in a patient’s status.

alt.q: Nurses with less ongoing clinical education tend to be more perceptive in recognizing clinical change because they rely on fresh observation.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses with more ongoing clinical education and skills training seem to be more perceptive in recognizing change.
alt.ww: More education and skills training, not less, is linked to better recognition of clinical change.

items.q: A nurse caring for a postoperative patient notices evaluation findings that the nurse has not seen before and senses the patient may be worsening. What should the nurse do first?
items.a: Ask a more experienced nurse to help evaluate the patient’s response
items.ex: Use available resources, including experienced nurses, especially when sensing a worsening condition or unfamiliar evaluation data.
w: Document the findings and recheck them at the next scheduled time
Waiting delays recognition of possible deterioration when early detection is needed.
Continue the plan of care because most patients improve after surgery
Judgments must be based on this patient’s findings, not on patients in general.
Wait to see whether the findings become clearer over the next shift
Unfamiliar findings with a sense of worsening call for prompt help, not waiting.

alt.q: A student nurse is unsure how to interpret a patient’s unexpected evaluation findings. Which response by the instructor is best?
alt.a: “Let’s ask the experienced nurse caring for this patient to evaluate with us.”
alt.ex: Seeking help from more experienced nurses is recommended when evaluation data are unfamiliar or suggest worsening.
w: “Record the findings, and the next shift will decide whether they matter.”
Passing the findings on without evaluation delays recognition of possible deterioration.
“These findings are probably normal because the patient was stable earlier.”
Earlier stability does not rule out change; unfamiliar findings need careful evaluation.
“Compare the findings with what typically happens to patients after surgery.”
Evaluation must be based on this patient’s data, not on patients in general.

items.q: Before discharge, Tonya asks Mr. and Mrs. Lawson to explain the signs of wound infection and the activities he must avoid. What is Tonya doing?
items.a: Gathering evaluative measures to judge the effectiveness of her care
items.ex: Assessing pain, inspecting the wound, and obtaining patient and wife feedback are evaluative measures of her interventions.
w: Completing an initial assessment to identify new nursing diagnoses
Mr. Lawson’s problems were identified earlier; Tonya is now evaluating the effect of her care.
Delivering the first teaching session on postoperative wound care
Asking the Lawsons to explain information checks learning rather than delivering new teaching.
Delegating discharge teaching to Mr. Lawson’s family caregiver
Tonya is not delegating; she is gathering feedback to judge whether outcomes were met.

alt.q: Which set of actions by Tonya best represents evaluative measures for Mr. Lawson before discharge?
alt.a: Assessing pain, inspecting the wound, and obtaining feedback from the Lawsons
alt.ex: Tonya gathered evaluative measures by assessing pain, inspecting the wound, and obtaining patient and wife feedback.
w: Reviewing orders, calling the pharmacy, and printing his medication list
These are discharge tasks, not measures of Mr. Lawson’s response to care.
Removing his IV line, packing his belongings, and arranging transport
These are discharge activities that do not show whether outcomes were met.
Listing his interventions, counting doses, and signing the care plan
Counting completed interventions does not evaluate the patient’s outcomes.

items.q: How does a nurse become more expert in evaluation?
items.a: By witnessing the effects of past interventions and clinical changes
items.ex: Expertise in evaluation grows as a nurse witnesses the effects of interventions and clinical changes, such as a developing pressure injury.
w: By memorizing the interventions listed in standard care plans
Knowing standard interventions helps planning, but expertise in evaluation comes from witnessing responses and change.
By delegating evaluation of routine care to assistive personnel
Delegating evaluation removes the nurse from the observations that build expertise.
By relying on the health care provider’s judgment of outcomes
Nurses are responsible for evaluating their own care and build expertise by observing change.

alt.q: Tonya recognized Mr. Lawson’s pulmonary embolus 24 hours after surgery from its physical signs and symptoms. What made this recognition possible?
alt.a: Her knowledge combined with her clinical experience
alt.ex: Tonya’s ability to recognize the symptoms of clinical deterioration resulted from her knowledge and experience.
w: A routine laboratory test ordered by the health care provider
The textbook credits her recognition of physical signs to her knowledge and experience.
A family member’s report of a change in his behavior
Tonya recognized the physical signs and symptoms herself through knowledge and experience.
An automated alert from the electronic health record
Her recognition came from her own knowledge and experience, not an automated alert.

items.q: During teach-back, Mr. Lawson correctly states he must avoid heavy lifting. His wife then mentions he loves picking up their 3-year-old grandchild. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Revise the teaching to stress why he cannot lift his grandchildren
items.ex: Tonya adapted her instruction to emphasize that he cannot lift his grandchildren, making her approach more comprehensive.
w: Document that the activity outcome is fully met and end teaching
His wife’s comment reveals a risk the teaching has not yet addressed.
Tell the wife to remind him not to lift heavy objects at home
Shifting responsibility to the wife does not address his understanding of the restriction.
Repeat the same general instruction about avoiding heavy lifting
He already knows the general rule; teaching must address his specific situation.

alt.q: Why did Tonya revise her teaching after hearing that Mr. Lawson enjoys picking up his grandchildren?
alt.a: The new information revealed a gap that could keep him from meeting the outcome
alt.ex: Evaluation through teach-back and family comments revealed a specific risk, so Tonya adapted her interventions.
w: He was unable to state any of his activity restrictions
He correctly stated he should avoid heavy lifting; the gap was specific to his grandchildren.
His physician changed his activity restrictions before discharge
The restrictions were unchanged; the revision responded to new patient information.
Agency policy requires teaching to be repeated before discharge
The revision was based on evaluation findings, not on a policy requirement.

items.q: How do evaluative measures differ from assessment measures?
items.a: They are made after interventions to judge whether problems changed
items.ex: Assessment identifies what problems exist; evaluative measures, made after interventions, show whether problems stayed the same, improved, or changed.
w: They use completely different skills from those used in assessment
The same skills, such as observation and measurement scales, are often used in both steps.
They are collected before interventions to identify a patient’s problems
Identifying problems before interventions describes assessment, not evaluation.
They rely only on patient self-report rather than on physical findings
Evaluative measures include observation, physiological measurements, scales, and interviews.

alt.q: After tracheal suctioning, which comparison best evaluates the efficacy of the procedure?
alt.a: Post-suctioning oxygen saturation compared with pre-suctioning and expected levels
alt.ex: The nurse compares the saturation after suctioning with the presuctioning level and the anticipated level, such as at least 95%.
w: Post-suctioning oxygen saturation compared with the previous day’s levels
Yesterday’s value is not the baseline for this intervention; compare with presuctioning data.
The amount of secretions removed compared with the amount expected
Secretion amount alone does not show the patient’s oxygenation response.
The length of the procedure compared with the agency’s suctioning policy
Procedure length describes the intervention, not the patient’s response to it.

items.q: A 60-year-old patient begins an early ambulation protocol after surgery. Using the formula age-predicted HR max = 208 − (0.7 × Age), what is the patient’s safe maximal heart rate?
items.a: 166 beats/min
items.ex: 208 − (0.7 × 60) = 208 − 42 = 166 beats/min; the pulse should remain below this during exercise.
w: 160 beats/min
This result comes from subtracting age from 220, not the formula in the textbook.
148 beats/min
This value does not result from the formula; 0.7 × 60 is 42, so 208 − 42 = 166.
178 beats/min
This value does not result from the formula; correctly calculated, the maximum is 166.

alt.q: A 70-year-old patient is ambulating after surgery. Which heart rate stays below the age-predicted HR max calculated as 208 − (0.7 × Age)?
alt.a: 157 beats/min
alt.ex: 208 − (0.7 × 70) = 208 − 49 = 159 beats/min, so 157 stays below the safe maximum.
w: 160 beats/min
The safe maximum for age 70 is 159 beats/min, so 160 exceeds it.
165 beats/min
The safe maximum for age 70 is 159 beats/min, so 165 exceeds it.
172 beats/min
The safe maximum for age 70 is 159 beats/min, so 172 exceeds it.

items.q: After surgery, a patient’s baseline heart rate is 88/min and respirations 18/min. The expected outcomes for early ambulation are that pulse returns to baseline within 10 minutes and respirations stay within two breaths of baseline. Which finding shows an outcome was NOT met?
items.a: Pulse is 104/min 15 minutes after the patient stops walking
items.ex: Pulse should return to the resting baseline within 10 minutes after exercise; 104/min at 15 minutes is not at baseline.
w: Respirations are 19/min while the patient is walking
A rate of 19 is within two breaths of the baseline of 18.
Pulse is 88/min 8 minutes after the patient stops walking
The pulse returned to baseline within 10 minutes, so the outcome was met.
The patient denies feeling breathless during the walk
Denying breathlessness is one of the expected outcomes for this protocol.

alt.q: A patient with a baseline respiratory rate of 16/min ambulates as part of an early ambulation protocol. Which respiratory rate during exercise meets the expected outcome?
alt.a: 17/min
alt.ex: The expected outcome is a respiratory rate within two breaths of baseline, so 17/min meets it.
w: 20/min
A rate of 20 is four breaths above baseline, outside the two-breath range.
22/min
A rate of 22 is six breaths above baseline, outside the two-breath range.
24/min
A rate of 24 is eight breaths above baseline, well outside the expected range.

items.q: A single observation showing that a pressure injury looks smaller is enough to conclude that the injury is healing.
items.a: False
items.ex: Evaluative measures must be collected over time to show a consistent pattern of improvement; one observation is insufficient.
items.ww: Healing is judged by trends, such as gradual decrease in size and drainage over days, not one observation.

alt.q: In home care or nursing home settings, it may take weeks or even months to determine whether interventions led to a pattern of improvement.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Collecting evaluative measures over time reveals trends; in home and nursing home settings this can take weeks or months.
alt.ww: Patterns of change in these settings are not seen in a single visit; they emerge over an extended time.

Vital signs: Hemodynamic change.
Pressure injury staging system
Pressure injury staging system: Whether a treated pressure injury has changed.

mt.q: Match each evaluative measure with what it is the standard for evaluating.
pairs: Pain severity and change over time
Whether a treated pressure injury has changed
mt.ex: Using the right evaluative measure for an outcome makes it more likely that the nurse accurately identifies a change in condition.

items.q: Evaluation of behavioral change is more difficult than evaluation of physiological change.
items.a: True
items.ex: Behavioral information, such as taking medications correctly or following a diet, often relies on the patient’s self-report.
items.ww: Physiological change has standard measures like vital signs, while behavior often depends on self-report, making it harder.

alt.q: Behavioral change is easier to evaluate than physiological change because the nurse can directly observe whether a patient follows a diet at home.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Behavioral change is harder to evaluate because information such as following a diet often relies on patient self-report.
alt.ww: Nurses usually cannot directly observe home behaviors, so evaluation relies on self-report and is more difficult.

items.q: What is a patient’s self-report?
items.a: A measure of health status that comes directly from the patient without clinician interpretation
items.ex: Self-report reflects the patient’s own perceptions or beliefs, given without interpretation by a clinician or anyone else.
w: A clinician’s summary of how the patient appears to be responding to care
A clinician’s interpretation is exactly what self-report excludes.
A family caregiver’s description of the patient’s behavior at home
Self-report comes directly from the patient, not from family members.
A standardized physical measure of the patient’s functional performance
Physical measures are objective data; self-report is the patient’s own perception.

alt.q: A nurse uses open-ended questions to obtain a patient’s self-report about adherence to a diet. What is important for the nurse to ensure?
alt.a: The patient hears and understands the questions and why a response matters
alt.ex: With open-ended self-report questions, the patient must hear and understand the questions and why a verbal response is important.
w: The patient’s family answers for the patient to improve accuracy
Self-report comes directly from the patient, not from family interpretation.
The nurse rephrases the patient’s answer before recording it
Self-report is recorded without interpretation of the response by a clinician.
The patient answers using only yes or no to keep data objective
Open-ended questions invite description; yes-or-no answers limit the self-report.

items.q: Which are examples of Health Behavior measures used in self-management evaluation? Select all that apply.
o: Pill count to check adherence to medications
Pill counts measure adherence to medication administration, a health behavior indicator.
Demonstration of a self-injection or dressing change
Demonstrated psychomotor skill is a health behavior measure.
Adherence to medical follow-up visits
Keeping follow-up visits is listed as a health behavior measure.
Blood glucose control measured by HbA1c
HbA1c is a clinical indicator of Physical Health Status.
Readmission to the hospital within 30 days
Readmission measures Health Service Utilization, not health behavior.
Score on the General Self-Efficacy Scale
The General Self-Efficacy Scale measures Self-Efficacy.
items.ex: Health behavior indicators include medication adherence such as pill counts, demonstrated psychomotor skills, and adherence to follow-up visits.

alt.q: A home health nurse evaluates a patient with diabetes. Which measures reflect Physical Health Status or Health Service Utilization indicators? Select all that apply.
o: HbA1c showing blood glucose control
Blood glucose control by HbA1c is a Physical Health Status clinical indicator.
Blood pressure control over several visits
Blood pressure control is a Physical Health Status clinical indicator.
Admission to the emergency department in the past month
Emergency department admission is a Health Service Utilization measure.
Count of remaining pills in the medication bottle
A pill count is a Health Behavior measure of adherence.
Perceived stress score on a validated survey
Perceived stress is a Psychological Indicator.
alt.ex: Correct: HbA1c showing blood glucose control; Blood pressure control over several visits; Admission to the emergency department in the past month.

items.q: How does the textbook define functional status?
items.a: A person’s ability to perform ADLs and IADLs independently
items.ex: Functional status measures a person’s ability to perform activities of daily living and instrumental activities of daily living independently.
w: A person’s level of knowledge about the illness and its treatment
Knowledge is one indicator of self-management, not the definition of functional status.
A person’s score on scales measuring perceived stress and self-control
Perceived stress and self-control are psychological indicators, not functional status.
A person’s pattern of using hospital and emergency services
Service use reflects health service utilization rather than functional status.

alt.q: A home health nurse uses the OASIS instrument for a patient recovering from a stroke. What is the nurse evaluating?
alt.a: The patient’s ability to perform daily activities independently
alt.ex: OASIS is an instrument for measuring functional status, the ability to perform ADLs and IADLs independently.
w: The patient’s risk for intravenous site phlebitis
IV site phlebitis is evaluated with Infusion Nurses Society criteria.
The stage and size of the patient’s pressure injury
Pressure injuries are evaluated with the PI staging system.
The patient’s hemodynamic response to medications
Vital signs are the standard for determining hemodynamic change.

items.q: How does the Nursing Outcomes Classification (NOC) add objectivity when evaluating a patient’s progress?
items.a: Its specific, measurable indicators are rated on 5-point Likert scales
items.ex: NOC indicators are specific and measurable and are rated on 5-point Likert-format scales, adding objectivity to evaluation.
w: Its broad outcome categories replace the need for specific indicators
Outcome categories are broad; the specific, measurable indicators are what are rated.
Its outcomes are written by each nurse in personal, nonstandard terms
NOC is a standard nursing language used across a health care system.
Its outcomes are used only during planning and not during evaluation
NOC outcomes are selected in planning and used as criteria during evaluation.

alt.q: Within the NOC system, which statement about outcomes and indicators is accurate?
alt.a: Outcome categories are broad, while indicators are specific and measurable
alt.ex: NOC outcome categories are broadly defined; indicators, the same as expected outcomes, are specific and measurable.
w: Indicators are broad, while outcome categories are specific and measurable
This reverses them; the indicators are the specific, measurable part.
Outcomes and indicators are both broad and require nurse interpretation
Indicators are specific and measurable, which adds objectivity.
Indicators are used only with NANDA-I diagnoses and not with ICNP
NOC indicators are also appropriate for use with ICNP diagnoses.

items.q: A nursing-sensitive outcome is a state, behavior, or perception that is measured along a [[continuum]] in response to a nursing intervention.
items.ex: Nursing-sensitive outcomes, such as NOC indicators, are measured along a continuum so the nurse can judge degrees of progress.

alt.q: A state, behavior, or perception measured along a continuum in response to a nursing intervention is called a [[nursing-sensitive outcome|nurse-sensitive outcome]].
alt.ex: Nursing-sensitive outcomes, such as NOC indicators, are measured along a continuum so the nurse can judge degrees of progress.

items.q: In interpreting and summarizing evaluation findings, which step comes right after “Evaluate the patient’s actual behavior or response”?
items.a: Compare the outcome criteria with the actual behavior or response
items.ex: That's step 3 of 5. Interpreting findings moves from identifying desired responses, to observing actual responses, comparing and judging agreement, then explaining any gap.
w: Judge the degree of agreement between outcome criteria and actual behavior
That's step 4 of 5.
Examine the outcome criteria to identify the exact desired behavior or response
That's step 1 of 5.
If there is no or partial agreement, identify the reason and the next action
That's step 5 of 5.

alt.q: Which step comes first in interpreting and summarizing evaluation findings?
alt.a: Examine the outcome criteria to identify the exact desired behavior or response
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 5. Interpreting findings moves from identifying desired responses, to observing actual responses, comparing and judging agreement, then explaining any gap.
w: Evaluate the patient’s actual behavior or response
That's step 2 of 5.
Compare the outcome criteria with the actual behavior or response
That's step 3 of 5.
Judge the degree of agreement between outcome criteria and actual behavior
That's step 4 of 5.

alt.q: Which step comes last in interpreting and summarizing evaluation findings?
alt.a: If there is no or partial agreement, identify the reason and the next action
alt.ex: That's step 5 of 5. Interpreting findings moves from identifying desired responses, to observing actual responses, comparing and judging agreement, then explaining any gap.
w: Judge the degree of agreement between outcome criteria and actual behavior
That's step 4 of 5.

Evaluate the patient’s actual behavior or response
That's step 2 of 5.

ord.q: Put the steps for interpreting and summarizing evaluation findings in order.
items: Examine the outcome criteria to identify the exact desired behavior or response
Evaluate the patient’s actual behavior or response
Compare the outcome criteria with the actual behavior or response
Judge the degree of agreement between outcome criteria and actual behavior
If there is no or partial agreement, identify the reason and the next action
ord.ex: Interpreting findings moves from identifying desired responses, to observing actual responses, comparing and judging agreement, then explaining any gap.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient to use an incentive spirometer and immediately watches the patient’s technique to decide whether to adjust the instruction. Which type of reflection is this?
items.a: Reflection-in-action
items.ex: Reflection-in-action occurs when observable outcomes are recognized during or immediately after an action so care can be modified.
w: Reflection-on-action
Reflection-on-action occurs later, when the nurse revisits outcomes to influence future interventions.
Reflective summarizing
This is not a term the textbook uses for evaluation during care.
Retrospective review
A retrospective review occurs after care, not while observing the patient during the action.

alt.q: A nurse returns to a patient the next day to see whether yesterday’s teaching changed the patient’s self-care. Which type of reflection is this?
alt.a: Reflection-on-action
alt.ex: Reflection-on-action occurs later, when delayed effects require the nurse to revisit the patient to judge outcomes.
w: Reflection-in-action
Reflection-in-action happens during or immediately after an action, not a day later.
Reflective summarizing
This is not a term the textbook uses for revisiting outcomes later.
Concurrent review
A concurrent review happens during care, not when the nurse returns later.

items.q: When a nurse reviews a patient’s progress and finds that planned interventions were delayed, not done, or not completed, this is an example of missed nursing care.
items.a: True
items.ex: Missed nursing care is planned care that was delayed, not done, or not completed, and evaluation helps reveal it.
items.ww: The textbook defines missed nursing care as exactly this: planned interventions delayed, omitted, or incomplete.

alt.q: Because patients with the same health problem respond alike, a nurse can evaluate a patient by relying on what typically happens to similar patients.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients with the same problem are not treated the same; treating them alike causes errors in judgment.
alt.ww: Judgments must be based on observations of the specific patient, not on what happens to patients in general.

items.q: In which situations is reassessment of the patient necessary? Select all that apply.
o: An expected outcome was not met
Unmet outcomes require reassessment before modifying the plan.
An expected outcome was only partially met
Partially met outcomes also require reassessment.
A new patient problem has developed
Reassessment is needed when a new problem develops.
The patient met the outcome and agrees it was met
A met, confirmed outcome leads to maintaining or discontinuing that part of care.
Interventions were completed on schedule
Completing interventions on time is not a trigger for reassessment.
items.ex: Reassessment is necessary for unmet or partially met outcomes or a new problem, and it keeps the database accurate and current.

alt.q: When revising a patient’s expected outcomes, which questions should the nurse ask? Select all that apply.
o: Does the time frame for the outcome need to be revised?
Reviewing the time frame is part of revising outcomes.
Has reassessment revealed that an outcome is unrealistic?
Unrealistic outcomes must be identified and changed.
Is a more specific measure needed to judge achievement?
A more specific measure may be needed to determine outcome achievement.
Can more nursing diagnoses be added to the care plan?
Accuracy of diagnoses is more important than the number selected.
Were the interventions charted as completed each shift?
Charting completed tasks does not address whether an outcome is appropriate.
alt.ex: Correct: Does the time frame for the outcome need to be revised?; Has reassessment revealed that an outcome is unrealistic?; Is a more specific measure needed to judge achievement?.

items.q: While teaching self-administration of insulin, a nurse finds that the patient has developed a medication-related tremor and cannot safely draw up or inject insulin. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Teach a family caregiver and revise the outcomes to reflect the caregiver’s role
items.ex: Because the original outcomes cannot be met, the nurse adds new interventions for a caregiver and revises outcomes accordingly.
w: Continue the original teaching until the patient can inject independently
The tremor makes the original outcomes unattainable, so repeating the same teaching is inappropriate.
Discontinue insulin teaching because the patient has not met the outcomes
Unmet outcomes call for revising the plan, not abandoning teaching.
Increase the frequency of teaching sessions with the patient
More sessions will not overcome a tremor that prevents safe injection.

alt.q: Why did a nurse change the outcome “Patient administers insulin injection independently” to “Family caregiver administers insulin injection correctly”?
alt.a: A new problem, a tremor, made the original outcome impossible to meet
alt.ex: When a new problem makes outcomes unattainable, the nurse adds new interventions and revises the outcomes.
w: The patient had already met the original outcome successfully
A met outcome would lead to maintaining or discontinuing care, not reassigning it.
The family caregiver asked to take over the patient’s care
The change was made because the patient’s tremor made safe injection impossible.
Agency policy requires a family member to give all injections
The textbook ties the revision to the patient’s new problem, not to policy.

items.q: When evaluating interventions in a care plan, which two factors does the nurse examine?
items.a: The appropriateness of the intervention and its correct application
items.ex: Nurses examine whether the intervention selected was appropriate and whether it was applied correctly.
w: The cost of the intervention and the time needed to perform it
Cost and time are not the two factors the textbook names for evaluating interventions.
The patient’s preference for the intervention and its convenience
Preferences matter in planning, but the two factors are appropriateness and correct application.
The number of interventions and how often each was documented
The number of interventions does not show whether they were appropriate or applied correctly.

alt.q: How does a nurse determine whether a selected intervention is appropriate?
alt.a: By comparing it with the nursing standards of care for the health problem
alt.ex: Appropriateness is determined using standards of care, the minimum level of care accepted to ensure high-quality care.
w: By asking whether the intervention is the one used most often on the unit
Frequent use on a unit does not establish that an intervention meets the standard of care.
By choosing the intervention that takes the least nursing time
Time savings do not define appropriateness; standards of care do.
By checking whether the intervention was charted as completed
Charting completion shows it was done, not that it was appropriate.

items.q: A patient’s care plan states “Provide walker for ambulation,” but the patient is unsteady and cannot walk safely with the walker alone. How should the nurse revise this intervention?
items.a: Change the action verb to “Assist patient during ambulation”
items.ex: To change the level of care, substitute a different action verb; assisting provides more help than providing a device.
w: Change the action verb to “Instruct patient on walker use”
Instructing alone does not increase the hands-on help an unsteady patient needs.
Keep the intervention and document the patient’s unsteadiness
An inappropriate level of care needs revision, not just documentation.
Discontinue ambulation until the patient can walk independently
Stopping ambulation does not adjust the level of care to the patient’s needs.

alt.q: A patient cannot perform a dressing change after the nurse explained the steps. Which revision of the intervention changes the level of care appropriately?
alt.a: Replace “Instruct” with “Demonstrate” for the dressing change
alt.ex: Demonstration requires showing how a skill is performed rather than only explaining it, a higher level of care.
w: Replace “Demonstrate” with “Instruct” for the dressing change
This lowers the level of care; the patient needs more support, not less.
Replace “Assist” with “Provide” for the dressing change
Providing suggests the patient is more independent, which does not fit this situation.
Keep “Instruct” but repeat the explanation more slowly
The verb, and thus the level of care, must change when the current level is inappropriate.

items.q: After instruction, a patient correctly explains how to recognize signs of wound infection, meeting the expected outcome. What should the nurse do next?
items.a: Confirm with the patient and discontinue that part of the care plan
items.ex: When an outcome is met, the nurse confirms with the patient and discontinues that part of the plan; further instruction is not needed.
w: Repeat the same instruction daily until the patient is discharged
Further instruction is not needed once the patient demonstrates knowledge.
Perform a complete reassessment of the related nursing diagnosis
Complete reassessment is required for unmet or partially met outcomes, not met ones.
Revise the outcome to a more difficult knowledge goal
A met outcome leads to maintaining or discontinuing care, not automatically making it harder.

alt.q: A patient continues to have congested lung sounds despite coughing and deep-breathing exercises every 4 hours. Which revision of the plan is most appropriate?
alt.a: Increase the frequency of the exercises and add positioning
alt.ex: Adjusting the frequency of interventions based on the patient’s response, and adding positioning, helps clear the airway.
w: Discontinue the exercises because they have not been effective
Partial response calls for adjusting frequency, not stopping a needed intervention.
Continue the same schedule and reevaluate at discharge
An unfavorable response requires changing the plan and reevaluating promptly.
Decrease the frequency so the patient is less fatigued
Persistent congestion calls for more frequent airway clearance, not less.

items.q: Why are documentation and reporting considered important parts of evaluation?
items.a: They share the patient’s progress so the team can make ongoing decisions
items.ex: Accurate, timely information lets nurses and other team members know whether a patient is progressing and make clinical decisions.
w: They prove to the agency that every intervention was performed
Documentation records interventions, but its evaluative value is in showing patient progress.
They replace the need for verbal hand-off between nurses
Information must be in the EHR and also shared during hand-off and ongoing communication.
They are needed mainly for billing and insurance purposes
The textbook stresses sharing patient progress with the team, not billing.

alt.q: A charge nurse reviews why evaluation findings must be entered promptly in the EHR. Which explanation is most accurate?
alt.a: Team members need current progress data to make clinical decisions
alt.ex: Accurate, timely documentation lets the health care team know whether a patient is progressing and make ongoing decisions.
w: Prompt entries mainly protect the nurse from legal action
The textbook’s emphasis is sharing progress with the team for decision making.
Prompt entries let the nurse skip reporting at hand-off
Information is shared both in the EHR and during hand-off communication.
Prompt entries are needed only when a patient’s condition worsens
Progress should be documented consistently, whether improving or worsening.

items.q: When documenting a patient’s response to interventions, which elements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: The interventions that were delivered
Thorough documentation describes the interventions provided.
The evaluative measures used
Documentation describes the evaluative measures used to judge response.
The outcomes achieved
The outcomes achieved show whether the patient is progressing.
The continued plan of care
Documenting the continued plan tells others what care comes next.
The nurse’s opinion of the patient’s motivation
Personal opinions are not part of evaluating outcomes; documentation should rest on evaluative data.
A list of every routine task done that shift
Thorough evaluative notes focus on response to care, not an inventory of tasks.
items.ex: A thorough evaluation note describes the interventions, evaluative measures, outcomes achieved, and continued plan of care.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a colleague’s evaluation note. Which features show the note is thorough? Select all that apply.
o: It names the evaluative measures used to judge the response
Evaluative measures are a required element of an evaluation note.
It states which outcomes were achieved
Achieved outcomes show the patient’s progress.
It describes the continued plan of care
The continued plan tells other team members what care follows.
It states only that care was given per protocol
Stating that care was given does not show the response or outcomes.
It includes guesses about the patient’s home situation
Notes should present a clear argument from evaluative data, not guesses.
alt.ex: Correct: It names the evaluative measures used to judge the response; It states which outcomes were achieved; It describes the continued plan of care.

items.q: Which documentation entry best reflects evaluation of a patient’s response to teaching?
items.a: “Taught signs of infection; patient listed 3 signs; will review dressing change tomorrow.”
items.ex: This entry gives the intervention, the evaluative measure and outcome, and the continued plan of care.
w: “Taught signs of infection to patient; patient tolerated the session well.”
“Tolerated well” does not state an evaluative measure or whether the outcome was met.
“Patient seems to understand wound care and is eager to be discharged.”
This is a vague impression without the intervention, measure, or plan of care.
“Teaching on signs of infection was completed as ordered at 1400.”
This records that teaching was done, not how the patient responded.

alt.q: A nurse writes: “Instructed on low-sodium diet.” Which addition would best turn this into an evaluation note?
alt.a: “Patient selected 3 low-sodium foods from a menu; will review labels tomorrow.”
alt.ex: Adding the evaluative measure, the outcome achieved, and the continued plan makes the note an evaluation of care.
w: “Patient was given a low-sodium diet handout to keep at the bedside.”
Giving a handout is another intervention, not evidence of the patient’s response.
“Patient appeared attentive and pleasant throughout the instruction.”
Attentiveness alone does not show whether the knowledge outcome was met.
“Instruction was given according to the unit standard of care.”
Following a standard describes the intervention, not the patient’s outcome.

items.q: In which situation is consistent, thorough documentation of a patient’s progress toward expected outcomes especially important?
items.a: When the same nurse will not care for the patient throughout the stay
items.ex: When different nurses care for a patient, consistent documentation lets each know the patient’s progress toward outcomes.
w: When the patient has only one nursing diagnosis on the care plan
The number of diagnoses does not determine the need for consistent documentation.
When the patient is expected to be discharged within 24 hours
Short stays still need documentation, but the textbook stresses changes in caregivers.
When the patient’s family is present during most of the care
Family presence does not replace consistent documentation for the care team.

alt.q: A patient will be cared for by several different nurses during a 5-day stay. Why is consistent documentation of progress toward outcomes essential?
alt.a: Each nurse needs to know how the patient is progressing toward the outcomes
alt.ex: Without the same nurse throughout a stay, consistent and thorough documentation is how progress toward outcomes is shared.
w: Each nurse must repeat all interventions that were already completed
Documentation prevents unnecessary repetition rather than requiring it.
Each nurse will write a new care plan at the start of every shift
Nurses build on the documented plan rather than rewriting it each shift.
Each nurse is responsible only for the care given on that shift
Continuity of care requires each nurse to know prior progress, not only their own shift.

items.q: What is a potential benefit of using nursing diagnostic language, NIC, and NOC in electronic health record systems?
items.a: Improved quality, consistency, and accuracy of documentation
items.ex: Using standardized nursing languages in EHRs can improve the quality, consistency, and accuracy of what is documented.
w: Elimination of the need for nurses to evaluate outcomes
Standardized language supports evaluation; it does not replace the nurse’s judgment.
Removal of the need for hand-off communication between shifts
Hand-off communication is still needed along with documentation.
Shorter notes that leave out the continued plan of care
Thorough notes still include the continued plan of care.

alt.q: A hospital adds NOC outcomes and indicators to its EHR. Which result would the textbook most expect?
alt.a: Easier interpretation of whether interventions led to expected outcomes
alt.ex: Electronic systems provide linkages that make it easier to interpret cues about whether interventions led to expected outcomes.
w: Less need for nurses to gather evaluative measures at the bedside
Bedside evaluative measures are still needed to enter accurate data.
Fewer nursing diagnoses listed on each patient’s care plan
Standardized language aims at accuracy, not at reducing the number of diagnoses.
Automatic discontinuation of all interventions after 24 hours
Discontinuing care is a nursing decision based on whether outcomes are met.

items.q: Electronic systems provide linkages that make it easier to interpret cues about whether interventions led to expected patient outcomes.
items.a: True
items.ex: EHR linkages connect interventions and outcomes, helping nurses interpret whether care was effective.
items.ww: Electronic systems support interpretation of outcomes, so this is not a false claim.

alt.q: Once a nursing diagnosis is revised, documenting new expected outcomes is unnecessary because the change is shared verbally at hand-off.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Clearly documented outcomes for new or revised nursing diagnoses are necessary so all team members are aware of the revised plan.
alt.ww: Verbal hand-off alone is not enough; revised outcomes must be clearly documented in the EHR.

items.q: Tonya’s documentation states that Mr. Lawson should avoid lifting any object over [[9 kg|20 lb|9 kg (20 lb)|20 pounds]] to reduce strain on his suture line.
items.ex: Mr. Lawson was taught to avoid lifting objects over 9 kg (20 lb), including his grandchildren, groceries, and trash.

alt.q: To protect his suture line, Mr. Lawson must not lift objects heavier than [[20 lb|9 kg|20 pounds|9 kg (20 lb)]], including his grandchildren.
alt.ex: Mr. Lawson was taught to avoid lifting objects over 9 kg (20 lb), including his grandchildren, groceries, and trash.

items.q: Tonya’s note ends with “Will recommend to home health nurse the need to observe patient and wife perform wound care at home.” Which element of an evaluation note does this statement provide?
items.a: The continued plan of care
items.ex: Documentation should include the continued plan of care so others know what follow-up is needed.
w: The evaluative measure used
The evaluative measures were asking the patient and wife to describe and demonstrate.
The outcome already achieved
This statement describes future follow-up, not an outcome already met.
The initial assessment cue
It does not describe original assessment data but the next step in care.

alt.q: In Tonya’s note, which statement documents an outcome that was achieved?
alt.a: “Wife demonstrated proper handwashing technique.”
alt.ex: The wife’s correct demonstration documents an achieved outcome of the handwashing instruction.
w: “Instructed patient on importance of handwashing.”
This statement documents the intervention, not the outcome.
“Provided patient a pamphlet outlining wound care.”
Providing a pamphlet is an additional intervention, not an outcome.
“Will recommend home health nurse observe wound care.”
This is the continued plan of care, not an achieved outcome.

items.q: Tonya asks Mr. and Mrs. Lawson when they should call the physician about his wound. Which response, as documented in her note, shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “We should call if there are signs of infection or if pain develops.”
items.ex: The Lawsons verbalized signs of infection and occurrence of pain as reasons to notify the physician, which Tonya documented.
w: “We should call only if the stitches come out completely.”
Waiting for the stitches to come out would miss earlier signs of infection or pain.
“We should wait for the home health nurse to decide.”
The Lawsons were taught to recognize reasons to call the physician themselves.
“We should call only if he has trouble lifting objects.”
He is to avoid lifting heavy objects; trouble lifting is not a reason taught for calling.

alt.q: Which finding did Tonya document as the Lawsons’ reasons to notify the physician about the wound?
alt.a: Signs of infection and occurrence of pain
alt.ex: Tonya documented that the patient and wife verbalized signs of infection and occurrence of pain as reasons to call.
w: Mild itching and dry skin around the incision
These were not the reasons documented for notifying the physician.
Tiredness and a decreased appetite at home
These were not documented as reasons to call about the wound.
Difficulty with handwashing and dressing supplies
The wife demonstrated handwashing; supply issues were not reasons to call.

items.q: A study of medical records attributed inadequate documentation of nursing diagnoses and outcomes to which factors? Select all that apply.
o: Nurses’ perception of having many non-nursing duties
Perceived non-nursing duties were linked to inadequate documentation.
Use of manual documentation
Manual documentation was identified as a contributing factor.
Lack of standards for documenting patient progress notes
A lack of documentation standards contributed to poor documentation.
Too many nursing diagnoses on each care plan
The study did not attribute inadequate documentation to excess diagnoses.
Patients refusing to share health information
Patient refusal was not identified as a cause of inadequate documentation.
items.ex: Inadequate documentation was attributed to perceived non-nursing duties, manual documentation, and a lack of standards for progress notes.

alt.q: A nurse manager wants to improve documentation of patient outcomes. Based on the evidence summary, which barriers should be addressed? Select all that apply.
o: Reliance on manual documentation
Manual documentation was linked to inadequate documentation.
No standards for documenting patient progress
A lack of standards for progress notes contributed to poor documentation.
Nurses’ sense of being burdened with non-nursing duties
Perceived non-nursing duties were a contributing factor.
Nurses documenting patient outcomes too frequently
The problem identified was too little outcome documentation, not too much.
Use of standardized nursing language in the EHR
Standardized language is expected to improve documentation quality.
alt.ex: Correct: Reliance on manual documentation; No standards for documenting patient progress; Nurses’ sense of being burdened with non-nursing duties.

items.q: Documentation is the primary source of evidence used to continuously measure performance outcomes against predetermined standards.
items.a: True
items.ex: Because documentation is the main evidence for measuring performance, accurate entries are essential.
items.ww: Documentation, not memory or informal report, is the primary evidence for performance measurement.

alt.q: Performance outcomes are measured mainly through informal staff reports, so documentation plays only a minor role in measuring care quality.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Documentation is the primary source of evidence used to measure performance outcomes against predetermined standards.
alt.ww: Informal reports are not the main source; documented evidence is used to measure performance.

items.q: According to the evidence summary in Box 20.1, what effect has electronic health record use been found to have on clinicians?
items.a: It takes attention away from patients and slows down practice
items.ex: EHR use was found to take clinicians’ attention from patients and slow practice, which may include patient evaluation.
w: It eliminates time spent on organizational documentation
Community nurses still reported organizational documentation, which they found redundant.
It guarantees that all patient outcomes are documented
EHRs do not guarantee complete outcome documentation; improvements are still needed.
It increases the time nurses spend at the bedside
The finding was that EHR use takes attention away from patients.

alt.q: Which recommendation for practice follows from the evidence on barriers to documenting evaluation?
alt.a: Integrate clinical documentation into individual patient care and improve EHRs
alt.ex: The evidence calls for integrating documentation into individual patient care and improving electronic health records.
w: Return to manual documentation to save clinicians’ time
Manual documentation was linked to inadequate documentation, not improvement.
Reduce documentation of patient outcomes to focus on tasks
Outcomes should be documented; too little outcome documentation was the problem.
Limit EHR entries to health care providers rather than nurses
Both providers and nurses must enter notes accurately for decision making.

items.q: Why must health care providers and nurses enter notes into the electronic health record accurately?
items.a: To support accurate medical and nursing decision making
items.ex: Accurate EHR notes facilitate accurate medical and nursing decision making.
w: To reduce the time needed for patient evaluation
Accuracy supports decisions; it is not mainly a way to reduce evaluation time.
To limit what information families can request
Sharing with families follows regulations and agency guidelines, not documentation accuracy.
To replace communication during hand-off reports
Information is shared in both the EHR and hand-off communication.

alt.q: A nurse documents that a patient’s pain outcome was met, but the patient actually rated pain at 8. What is the greatest risk of this inaccurate entry?
alt.a: Other team members may make care decisions based on false data
alt.ex: Accurate notes are needed for accurate medical and nursing decision making; false data can lead to inappropriate care.
w: The entry will make the note longer than the agency requires
Length is not the concern; the inaccuracy misleads decision making.
The entry will need to be signed by the charge nurse
Signature requirements are not the risk the textbook emphasizes.
The entry will delay the patient’s billing for the visit
Billing is not the concern; inaccurate data affect clinical decisions.

items.q: A patient’s family member asks the nurse about the patient’s latest diagnostic findings. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Follow agency guidelines on what clinical information may be shared
items.ex: Nurses keep families informed but must know agency guidelines on the types of clinical information they can communicate.
w: Share all results immediately because families have a right to know
Results are shared according to federal and state regulations and agency guidelines.
Refuse to discuss the patient’s progress with family at any time
ANA standards call for sharing results of care with patients and families.
Tell the family to read the results in the patient’s chart
Directing family to the chart bypasses the regulations and guidelines for sharing information.

alt.q: Which statement reflects the ANA standard for sharing evaluation results?
alt.a: Results of care are shared with patients and families according to regulations
alt.ex: An ANA evaluation standard is sharing results of care with patients and families according to federal and state regulations.
w: Results of care are shared only with other health care providers
Patients and families should be kept informed of the patient’s progress.
Results of care are shared with families only after discharge
Families are kept informed about progress, not only after discharge.
Results of care are shared with anyone who asks the nurse
Sharing follows federal and state regulations and agency guidelines.

items.q: Nurses should keep patients and families informed about the patient’s progress while following agency guidelines on what clinical information can be communicated.
items.a: True
items.ex: ANA standards call for sharing results with patients and families, within regulations and agency guidelines.
items.ww: Keeping families informed is a standard, but it is limited by regulations and agency guidelines.

alt.q: ANA standards direct nurses to withhold the results of care from patients and families until the health care provider discusses them at discharge.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: One ANA evaluation standard is to share results of care with patients and families according to federal and state regulations.
alt.ww: Nurses keep patients and families informed about progress; results are not withheld until discharge.

items.q: What should a nurse’s documentation of evaluation present?
items.a: A clear argument from the evaluative data about whether the patient is progressing
items.ex: Documentation should present a clear, data-based argument showing whether a patient is progressing.
w: A complete list of the interventions performed during the shift
Listing interventions does not show whether the patient is progressing.
The nurse’s general impression of the patient’s attitude
Impressions are not evaluative data and do not show progress toward outcomes.
A copy of the original care plan with no changes noted
Documentation should reflect current progress and any revisions to the plan.

alt.q: Which feature makes an evaluation note most useful to the next nurse?
alt.a: It uses evaluative data to show clearly whether the patient is progressing
alt.ex: A note that argues from evaluative data whether a patient is progressing lets others make ongoing clinical decisions.
w: It repeats the admission assessment word for word
Repeating admission data does not show progress after interventions.
It lists each task completed without describing responses
Tasks without responses do not show whether outcomes were met.
It summarizes the nurse’s opinions about the family
Opinions about the family are not evaluative data on the patient’s progress.

items.q: A nurse confirms with a patient that the outcome for a teaching plan has been met and discontinues that part of the care plan. Why is documenting the discontinuation important?
items.a: It keeps other nurses from providing unnecessary interventions
items.ex: Documenting a discontinued plan ensures other nurses do not provide unnecessary care and supports continuity of care.
w: It requires the health care provider to write a new order
Discontinuing a nursing care plan item does not depend on a new provider order.
It allows the outcome to be reopened automatically later
Documentation communicates the change; it does not automatically reopen outcomes.
It shows that the patient was discharged from the unit
Discontinuing part of a plan is not the same as discharge.

alt.q: What happens when a nurse does not communicate achieved outcomes to other nurses?
alt.a: Time and energy are wasted on care that is no longer needed
alt.ex: Failing to communicate achieved outcomes wastes time and energy because others may continue unneeded interventions.
w: The patient’s nursing diagnoses are automatically resolved
Diagnoses are not resolved automatically; communication is needed.
The care plan is updated by the EHR without nursing input
The nurse must document the change for others to know.
The patient’s outcomes are reevaluated by the provider instead
Evaluating nursing outcomes remains the nurse’s responsibility.

items.q: A nurse revises a patient’s nursing diagnosis after new assessment cues appear. What should the nurse do to ensure the team follows the revised plan?
items.a: Clearly document the outcomes for the revised diagnosis in the EHR
items.ex: Clearly documented outcomes for new or revised nursing diagnoses make all team members aware of the revised care plan.
w: Mention the revision only to the next nurse at hand-off
Verbal report alone does not inform the whole team; the revision must be documented.
Keep the original outcomes so the record stays consistent
Outcomes must match the revised diagnosis for the plan to be accurate.
Wait until the patient meets the outcomes before documenting
Documenting only after outcomes are met leaves the team unaware of the new plan.

alt.q: A nurse adds a new nursing diagnosis to a patient’s care plan. Which action best supports team awareness of this change?
alt.a: Document clear expected outcomes for the new diagnosis
alt.ex: Clear documentation of outcomes for new diagnoses ensures all team members know about the revised care plan.
w: Tell the patient so the patient can inform other staff
Staff should not rely on the patient to communicate care plan changes.
Write the diagnosis on the whiteboard without outcomes
A diagnosis without documented outcomes gives the team no criteria for evaluation.
Hold the change until the weekly care conference
Delaying documentation leaves the team unaware of the revised plan.

items.q: Which statement from Tonya’s note is an example of the Intervention?
items.a: Instructed patient on handwashing and daily wound observation
items.ex: A thorough evaluation note describes interventions, evaluative measures used, outcomes achieved, and the continued plan of care.
w: Asked patient to describe when to call the physician about the wound
That goes with Evaluative measure.
Patient verbalized several examples of objects not to lift
That goes with Outcome achieved.
Will recommend that the home health nurse observe wound care
That goes with Continued plan of care.

alt.q: Which statement from Tonya’s note is an example of the Evaluative measure?
alt.a: Asked patient to describe when to call the physician about the wound
alt.ex: A thorough evaluation note describes interventions, evaluative measures used, outcomes achieved, and the continued plan of care.
w: Instructed patient on handwashing and daily wound observation
That goes with Intervention.
Patient verbalized several examples of objects not to lift
That goes with Outcome achieved.
Will recommend that the home health nurse observe wound care
That goes with Continued plan of care.

alt.q: Which statement from Tonya’s note is an example of the Outcome achieved?
alt.a: Patient verbalized several examples of objects not to lift
alt.ex: A thorough evaluation note describes interventions, evaluative measures used, outcomes achieved, and the continued plan of care.
w: Instructed patient on handwashing and daily wound observation
That goes with Intervention.
Asked patient to describe when to call the physician about the wound
That goes with Evaluative measure.
Will recommend that the home health nurse observe wound care
That goes with Continued plan of care.

alt.q: Which statement from Tonya’s note is an example of the Continued plan of care?
alt.a: Will recommend that the home health nurse observe wound care
alt.ex: A thorough evaluation note describes interventions, evaluative measures used, outcomes achieved, and the continued plan of care.
w: Instructed patient on handwashing and daily wound observation
That goes with Intervention.
Asked patient to describe when to call the physician about the wound
That goes with Evaluative measure.
Patient verbalized several examples of objects not to lift
That goes with Outcome achieved.

alt.q: Which element of an evaluation note does “Instructed patient on handwashing and daily wound observation” represent?
alt.a: Intervention
alt.ex: A thorough evaluation note describes interventions, evaluative measures used, outcomes achieved, and the continued plan of care.
w: Evaluative measure
Evaluative measure: Asked patient to describe when to call the physician about the wound.
Outcome achieved
Outcome achieved: Patient verbalized several examples of objects not to lift.
Continued plan of care
Continued plan of care: Will recommend that the home health nurse observe wound care.

alt.q: Which element of an evaluation note does “Asked patient to describe when to call the physician about the wound” represent?
alt.a: Evaluative measure
alt.ex: A thorough evaluation note describes interventions, evaluative measures used, outcomes achieved, and the continued plan of care.
w: Intervention
Intervention: Instructed patient on handwashing and daily wound observation.
Outcome achieved
Outcome achieved: Patient verbalized several examples of objects not to lift.
Continued plan of care
Continued plan of care: Will recommend that the home health nurse observe wound care.

alt.q: Which element of an evaluation note does “Patient verbalized several examples of objects not to lift” represent?
alt.a: Outcome achieved
alt.ex: A thorough evaluation note describes interventions, evaluative measures used, outcomes achieved, and the continued plan of care.
w: Intervention
Intervention: Instructed patient on handwashing and daily wound observation.
Evaluative measure
Evaluative measure: Asked patient to describe when to call the physician about the wound.
Continued plan of care
Continued plan of care: Will recommend that the home health nurse observe wound care.

alt.q: Which element of an evaluation note does “Will recommend that the home health nurse observe wound care” represent?
alt.a: Continued plan of care
alt.ex: A thorough evaluation note describes interventions, evaluative measures used, outcomes achieved, and the continued plan of care.
w: Intervention
Intervention: Instructed patient on handwashing and daily wound observation.
Evaluative measure
Evaluative measure: Asked patient to describe when to call the physician about the wound.
Outcome achieved
Outcome achieved: Patient verbalized several examples of objects not to lift.

mt.q: Match each element of an evaluation note with the matching statement from Tonya’s documentation for Mr. Lawson.
pairs: Instructed patient on handwashing and daily wound observation
Asked patient to describe when to call the physician about the wound
Patient verbalized several examples of objects not to lift
Will recommend that the home health nurse observe wound care
mt.ex: A thorough evaluation note describes interventions, evaluative measures used, outcomes achieved, and the continued plan of care.

items.q: At the end of a shift, a nurse gives hand-off report on a patient whose care plan was revised. Which information is most important to share?
items.a: The patient’s progress toward expected outcomes and the revised plan
items.ex: Hand-off should share whether the patient is progressing and any revisions so the next nurse can make ongoing decisions.
w: The list of supplies used during the patient’s care that shift
Supplies used do not tell the next nurse whether the patient is progressing.
The nurse’s personal opinions about the patient’s family
Opinions are not evaluative data and do not support clinical decisions.
The times each routine task was finished during the shift
Task times do not convey outcomes or the revised plan of care.

alt.q: Which statement during hand-off best communicates evaluation findings?
alt.a: “His pain outcome is met, but the plan now adds teaching for his wife.”
alt.ex: This statement conveys outcome achievement and the revised plan so the next nurse can continue appropriate care.
w: “He had a quiet shift and did not use the call light very often.”
A quiet shift does not show whether specific outcomes were met.
“I gave all of his scheduled medications on time today.”
Giving medications on time shows interventions were done, not outcomes.
“His wife visited for most of the afternoon and evening.”
Visiting times do not communicate progress toward expected outcomes.

items.q: According to the textbook, person-centered care is achieved only when which condition is met?
items.a: The patient and family are actively involved with providers in evaluation
items.ex: Person-centered care requires the patient and family to be active partners with health care providers in the evaluation process.
w: The nurse independently judges whether every outcome was met
Evaluating alone excludes the patient and family, so the care is not person centered.
The health care provider approves each revised expected outcome
Provider approval does not create person-centered care; active patient and family involvement does.
The care plan follows the nursing unit’s standard of care exactly
Standards of care guide interventions, but person-centered care depends on patient and family involvement.

alt.q: A nurse wants evaluation of a patient’s care to be person centered. Which approach best achieves this?
alt.a: Asking the patient and family whether expected outcomes are being met
alt.ex: Person-centered care is achieved when the patient and family actively take part with providers in evaluation.
w: Basing conclusions only on the nurse’s objective measurements
Objective data matter, but leaving out the patient and family prevents person-centered evaluation.
Letting the health care provider decide which outcomes were met
Handing evaluation to the provider alone excludes the patient and family from the process.
Sharing the evaluation results with the family after discharge
Informing the family afterward is not the same as involving them actively in evaluation.

items.q: Research cited in the chapter links respectful communication between nurses and patients with which results? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced patient uncertainty
Respectful communication is reported to reduce patient uncertainty.
Greater patient engagement in decision making
Respectful communication enhances patient engagement in decisions about care.
Improved adherence to treatment plans
Patients who experience respectful communication adhere better to their treatment plans.
Higher patient satisfaction with care
Increased satisfaction is one of the listed results of respectful communication.
Less need for objective evaluative measures
Communication adds patient perspective but never replaces objective evaluative measures.
Fewer family members involved in care
Collaboration aims to involve the family more, not less.
items.ex: Respectful nurse–patient communication reduces uncertainty and improves engagement, adherence, social support, safety, and satisfaction.

alt.q: A nurse focuses on respectful communication while evaluating care with patients. Which outcomes can the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Increased social support for the patient
Increased social support is a reported result of respectful communication.
Improved patient safety
Respectful communication is linked with increased patient safety.
Better adherence to the treatment plan
Patients adhere better to treatment plans when communication is respectful.
Shorter documentation time for each patient
Documentation time is not a reported result of respectful communication.
Elimination of the need for reassessment
Reassessment is still needed when outcomes are unmet; communication does not replace it.
alt.ex: Correct: Increased social support for the patient; Improved patient safety; Better adherence to the treatment plan.

items.q: A nurse is evaluating pain management for a patient on the first day after surgery. Which question by the nurse best obtains the patient’s perspective on the intervention?
items.a: “Are you receiving the type of pain relief you expect?”
items.ex: Asking whether the patient is getting the relief they expect lets the patient say whether the intervention is meeting their outcomes.
w: “You are feeling more comfortable now, aren’t you?”
This leading question suggests the answer instead of eliciting the patient’s own view.
“Did you take the pain pill I brought you earlier?”
This checks that an intervention was completed, not whether the expected outcome was achieved.
“Should I call your surgeon about the pain medicine?”
This skips evaluation of the patient’s response and moves to action without data.

alt.q: A patient will change a surgical dressing at home after discharge. Which question by the nurse best evaluates the patient’s readiness from the patient’s point of view?
alt.a: “What additional information do you need to change your dressing at home?”
alt.ex: This open question invites the patient to identify unmet learning needs before discharge.
w: “You understand the dressing instructions, right?”
A leading yes-or-no question does not reveal what the patient still needs to learn.
“Did the nurse give you the dressing supply list?”
This confirms a task was done rather than evaluating the patient’s readiness.
“Has your wife already watched the dressing video?”
This checks completion of an activity, not the patient’s own perception of readiness.

items.q: The textbook states that the patient knows best about which of the following outcomes?
items.a: Whether breathing has become easier
items.ex: Patients can best report subjective outcomes such as whether pain has lessened or breathing is easier.
w: Whether the incision edges are approximated
Wound edge approximation is an objective finding the nurse inspects.
Whether oxygen saturation is within range
Oxygen saturation is a physiological measurement obtained with equipment.
Whether lung sounds have become clear
Lung sounds are evaluated by the nurse through auscultation.

alt.q: A nurse wants to know whether a patient’s pain has lessened 30 minutes after an analgesic. According to the textbook, who knows this best?
alt.a: The patient
alt.ex: A patient knows best whether pain has lessened, so the patient’s own report is essential.
w: The health care provider
The provider did not experience the pain; the patient’s report is the best source.
The family caregiver
Family members notice behavior changes, but the patient knows best whether pain has lessened.
The nursing assistant
Others can observe pain behaviors, but only the patient knows the pain experience.

items.q: The wife of an older adult patient tells the nurse, “He has been awake most of the night since his new medicine started. At home he always sleeps straight through.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Thank you for telling me. Describe how his sleep has changed.”
items.ex: Family members often recognize behavior changes such as altered sleep sooner than the nurse, so the nurse explores the cue.
w: “Sleep often changes in the hospital, so this is expected.”
Dismissing the cue ignores family insight that may reveal a medication effect.
“I checked on him at night and he seemed asleep each time.”
Brief nurse checks are less reliable than the family’s familiarity with the patient’s usual pattern.
“Let’s see whether the problem continues after he goes home.”
Delaying evaluation misses a chance to adjust care while the patient is still hospitalized.

alt.q: A daughter tells the nurse that her mother “isn’t herself today” and seems more withdrawn than usual. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
alt.a: Ask the daughter what specific changes she has noticed
alt.ex: Families often recognize changes in patient behavior sooner than nurses because of their familiarity with the patient.
w: Reassure the daughter that her mother’s vital signs are stable
Stable vital signs do not rule out the behavioral change the family has noticed.
Tell the daughter that mood changes are common in older adults
Generalizing ignores the patient-specific cue that the family has identified.
Document the concern and wait for the next scheduled assessment
Waiting delays evaluation of a possible change that the family recognized early.

items.q: Because of their familiarity with the patient, family members often recognize changes in patient behavior, such as a change in sleep pattern, sooner than the nurse can.
items.a: True
items.ex: The textbook notes that family familiarity lets them notice behavior changes, such as sleep pattern changes, sooner than the nurse.
items.ww: Nurses are skilled observers, but families know the patient’s usual behavior and often detect changes first.

alt.q: Because nurses are trained observers, they typically recognize changes in a patient’s behavior, such as a new sleep pattern, before family members do.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Families often recognize behavior changes before the nurse because they know the patient’s usual patterns.
alt.ww: Training does not replace a family’s long familiarity with the patient’s usual behavior.

items.q: According to the textbook, what does evaluating a patient’s expectations accomplish?
items.a: It determines satisfaction with care and strengthens partnering
items.ex: Evaluating patient expectations reveals satisfaction with care and builds the nurse–patient partnership.
w: It replaces the objective evaluative measures the nurse collects
Patient input adds to, but does not replace, objective evaluative measures.
It confirms that the selected nursing diagnoses are accurate
Diagnosis accuracy is checked by reassessing cues, not by evaluating expectations.
It fulfills the agency’s requirement for reimbursement of care
Reimbursement is not the purpose the textbook gives for evaluating expectations.

alt.q: A nurse asks a patient, “What is your most important need before going home?” What is the main benefit of asking this type of question?
alt.a: It reveals whether expectations are met and builds partnership
alt.ex: Asking about expectations shows whether they are met, determines satisfaction, and strengthens partnering with the patient.
w: It allows the nurse to skip the discharge teaching plan
Teaching is still needed; the question guides it rather than replacing it.
It gives the nurse objective data about wound healing
A patient’s stated needs are subjective data, not objective wound findings.
It transfers responsibility for outcomes to the patient
Responsibility for outcomes is shared; it is not transferred to the patient.

items.q: Health care professionals involved in a patient’s care share responsibility for achieving the patient’s outcomes.
items.a: True
items.ex: The textbook states that professionals share responsibility in achieving patient outcomes, which is why collaboration matters.
items.ww: Outcomes are a shared responsibility, so no single professional carries them alone.

alt.q: Because evaluation is a nursing step, findings gathered by other health care team members are not used when judging whether outcomes were met.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Team members who contribute to care gather valuable evaluative findings that the nurse uses in evaluation.
alt.ww: Excluding team findings would leave out valuable evaluative data about the patient’s responses.

items.q: A nurse is evaluating the walking ability of a patient recovering from hip surgery. Which action best reflects collaboration in evaluation?
items.a: Asking the physical therapist how the patient’s gait looked in therapy
items.ex: Team members who contribute to care gather valuable evaluative findings, so the nurse collaborates to stay informed.
w: Relying only on her own observation at the start of the shift
A single observation by one nurse misses findings gathered by other team members.
Waiting until discharge to read the therapy progress notes
Collaboration requires routine and timely interaction, not review at the end of the stay.
Asking the patient to rate overall satisfaction with the hospital
General satisfaction does not provide evaluative data about the patient’s walking.

alt.q: Which statement best describes successful collaboration with the health care team during evaluation?
alt.a: It involves routine, timely interaction with all professionals in the patient’s care
alt.ex: Successful collaboration requires routine and timely interactions with all professionals involved in the patient’s care.
w: It involves contacting other disciplines only when a problem occurs
Collaboration is routine and ongoing, not limited to times when problems arise.
It involves sharing evaluation findings with nurses but not other disciplines
All members of the team, not just nurses, contribute valuable evaluative findings.
It involves reviewing team notes once the patient has been discharged
Collaboration must be timely so the nurse stays informed during care.

items.q: The ANA standards describe competencies for the evaluation step of the nursing process. Which actions reflect these competencies? Select all that apply.
o: Using criterion-based evaluation in a systematic way
Systematic, criterion-based evaluation is an ANA evaluation competency.
Collaborating with patients and health care providers
Collaboration with patients and providers is part of the ANA evaluation standard.
Using ongoing assessment data to revise the plan
Revising the plan with ongoing assessment data is an ANA evaluation competency.
Communicating results to patients and families
Sharing results with patients and families is part of the ANA evaluation standard.
Evaluating whether interventions were completed on time
Evaluation judges whether outcomes were met, not whether interventions were completed.
Withholding progress reports until discharge
The standards call for keeping patients and families informed about progress.
items.ex: ANA evaluation competencies include systematic criterion-based evaluation, collaboration, revising plans with ongoing data, and communicating results.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing the ANA standard for evaluation. Which nursing actions meet this standard? Select all that apply.
o: Sharing evaluation results with the patient’s family as regulations allow
The ANA standard includes sharing results with patients and families per federal and state regulations.
Comparing patient responses against the expected outcomes
Criterion-based evaluation uses expected outcomes as the standard.
Working with the health care team to judge the patient’s progress
Collaboration with health care providers is an evaluation competency.
Delivering interventions automatically without returning to evaluate
Delivering interventions without evaluating outcomes is described as irresponsible practice.
Keeping the plan unchanged even when new assessment data appear
The standard calls for using ongoing assessment data to revise the plan.
alt.ex: Correct: Sharing evaluation results with the patient’s family as regulations allow; Comparing patient responses against the expected outcomes; Working with the health care team to judge the patient’s progress.

items.q: A nurse determines that a patient has met the expected outcome of independently self-injecting insulin. Which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Confirm with the patient that the outcome has been met
items.ex: When outcomes are met, the nurse confirms the evaluation with the patient when possible before discontinuing that part of the plan.
w: Remove the insulin teaching from the plan without discussion
The textbook directs the nurse to confirm with the patient first, then discontinue if both agree.
Continue the same insulin teaching every day until discharge
Further instruction is not needed once a patient demonstrates the skill.
Complete a full reassessment of all the patient’s diagnoses
Complete reassessment is needed for unmet outcomes or new problems, not a met outcome.

alt.q: A nurse and patient agree that the patient has met the outcome for safe use of a walker. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Discontinue and document that part of the care plan
alt.ex: Documenting a discontinued plan prevents other nurses from providing unnecessary interventions.
w: Keep the walker teaching active in case it is needed later
Continuing unneeded interventions wastes time and energy and disrupts continuity of care.
Report the achievement verbally but leave the plan unchanged
Without documentation, other nurses may repeat interventions that are no longer needed.
Add a new nursing diagnosis about walker safety
A met outcome does not call for a new diagnosis about the same problem.

items.q: A patient’s son asks the nurse whether his father’s diagnostic test results show improvement. What should guide the nurse’s response?
items.a: Agency guidelines on which clinical information the nurse may share
items.ex: Nurses share results with families according to federal and state regulations and follow agency guidelines on what can be communicated.
