w: The son’s position as the patient’s oldest child
Family position does not determine what clinical information the nurse may share.
Whether the health care provider is on the unit today
Provider availability does not determine what the nurse is permitted to communicate.
Whether the test results are normal or abnormal
Agency guidelines, not whether results are favorable, determine what may be shared.

alt.q: One ANA standard for evaluation concerns sharing results of care with patients and families. According to the textbook, how is this sharing done?
alt.a: According to federal and state regulations
alt.ex: The ANA standard calls for sharing results with patients and families according to federal and state regulations.
w: Only after the patient has been discharged
Patients and families should be kept informed about progress during care.
Only when the health care provider is present
The standard does not require the provider’s presence to share results.
Only when every expected outcome has been met
Progress, including unmet outcomes, is shared to keep patients and families informed.

items.q: During discharge teaching, a patient with a new abdominal incision has a lifting restriction. His wife says, “He can’t wait to pick up our 3-year-old grandson.” Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Revise teaching to explain why he must not lift the grandson for several weeks
items.ex: The family’s comment revealed a cue, so the nurse adapts teaching to the patient’s situation, as Tonya did with Mr. Lawson.
w: Document that the activity teaching outcome has been fully met
The comment suggests a risk of not following the restriction, so the outcome is not yet met.
Tell the wife to keep the grandchildren away from the home
This does not address the patient’s understanding of why lifting is restricted.
Ask the surgeon to repeat the activity restrictions to the patient
The nurse can adapt her own teaching; referral is not needed for this cue.

alt.q: While evaluating a patient’s understanding of activity restrictions, the nurse learns from the family that the patient often lifts heavy objects at home. What is the purpose of revising the teaching plan in response?
alt.a: To make the instruction fit the patient’s actual situation
alt.ex: Family input revealed a factor that could prevent outcome achievement, so the nurse makes her approach more comprehensive.
w: To transfer responsibility for the restriction to the family
The patient still needs to understand and follow the restriction himself.
To shorten teaching because the patient already knows the rules
Knowing the rule is not enough when the family describes behavior that conflicts with it.
To close the activity outcome so discharge is not delayed
The outcome is not met when cues suggest the patient may not follow the restriction.

items.q: How does information from a patient and family about whether interventions helped relate to the nurse’s objective evaluative measures?
items.a: It adds to the objective evaluative measures
items.ex: The patient and family can tell the nurse how interventions helped, and this information adds to objective measures.
w: It replaces objective measures when the two disagree
Patient and family input supplements objective data rather than overriding it.
It is collected only after the patient is discharged
Patient and family input is gathered throughout care to guide revisions.
It is less valid and is not used in revising the plan
The textbook values this input when deciding to continue, revise, or discontinue care.

alt.q: A nurse is deciding whether to continue, revise, or discontinue a plan of care. Which statement best describes the role of the patient’s report about how interventions helped?
alt.a: It supplements the objective data the nurse has collected
alt.ex: Patients and families can say how interventions helped, which adds to the nurse’s objective evaluative measures.
w: It is the only data needed to make the decision
Objective evaluative measures are still needed alongside the patient’s report.
It matters only when the objective data are missing
The patient’s report is valuable even when objective data are available.
It should be ignored when vital signs are normal
Normal vital signs do not make the patient’s perspective irrelevant.

items.q: After delivering an intervention, a nurse gathers data to examine its results. Which sources of evaluative data does the textbook describe? Select all that apply.
o: Subjective reports from the patient
Patients share their perspective on whether an intervention worked.
Observations from family members
Family members often notice behavior changes sooner than the nurse.
Findings from other health care team members
Team members who contribute to care gather valuable evaluative findings.
Objective measurements by the nurse
Physiological measures and observation are core evaluative measures.
Outcomes of other patients with the same diagnosis
Judgments must be based on the specific patient, not on patients in general.
Opinions of visitors who are not involved in care
Data come from the patient, family, and team members as appropriate, not unrelated visitors.
items.ex: Evaluative data come from the patient, family, and health care team members along with the nurse’s own objective measures.

alt.q: A nurse wants a complete picture of a patient’s response to a new mobility plan. From whom should the nurse gather evaluative data? Select all that apply.
o: The patient
The patient can report whether the intervention is meeting expectations.
The patient’s spouse who visits daily
Family familiarity helps detect changes in the patient’s behavior.
The physical therapist working with the patient
Team members contributing to care provide valuable evaluative findings.
A roommate’s family members
People not involved in the patient’s care are not appropriate sources of evaluative data.
Published averages for similar patients
Evaluation relies on patient-specific measures rather than what happens to patients in general.
alt.ex: Correct: The patient; The patient’s spouse who visits daily; The physical therapist working with the patient.

items.q: Care that is achieved only when the patient and family are actively involved with health care providers in evaluation is called [[person-centered|person centered|patient-centered|patient centered]] care.
items.ex: Person-centered care depends on active partnership of the patient and family with providers during evaluation.

alt.q: When a patient and family actively partner with providers in evaluating outcomes, the nurse is delivering [[person-centered|person centered|patient-centered|patient centered]] care.
alt.ex: Person-centered care depends on active partnership of the patient and family with providers during evaluation.

items.q: A measure of health status that comes directly from the patient, without interpretation by a clinician, is called a patient [[self-report|self report]].
items.ex: Self-report captures the patient’s own perceptions, which is why patients can tell the nurse whether interventions are working.

alt.q: When Tonya asked Mr. Lawson to describe his activity restrictions in his own words, she used the evaluative measure of patient [[self-report|self report]].
alt.ex: Self-report captures the patient’s own perceptions, which is why patients can tell the nurse whether interventions are working.

items.q: Effective communication is required for patients and families to be actively involved in the evaluation process.
items.a: True
items.ex: Active patient and family involvement in evaluation, the basis of person-centered care, requires effective communication.
items.ww: Without effective communication, patients and families cannot share their perspectives on outcomes.

alt.q: Person-centered evaluation is achieved when the nurse evaluates outcomes alone and then informs the family of the conclusions.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Person-centered care requires the patient and family to be actively involved in evaluation, not just informed afterward.
alt.ww: Informing the family of conclusions is not the same as involving them in the evaluation.

items.q: When evaluating outcomes in partnership with a patient, which factors does the textbook direct the nurse to consider?
items.a: The patient’s values, preferences, and expressed needs
items.ex: Considering what matters to the patient, including values, preferences, and expressed needs, supports partnership in evaluation.
w: The patient’s insurance, income, and occupation
Financial and job details are not the factors the textbook names for partnering in evaluation.
The unit’s staffing, census, and budget
Unit resources affect the environment but are not what is important to the patient.
The provider’s preferences, schedule, and orders
Partnership in evaluation centers on the patient’s own priorities, not the provider’s.

alt.q: A patient says that being able to attend his daughter’s wedding next month matters most to him. How should the nurse use this information during evaluation?
alt.a: Include it when judging whether outcomes meet his expressed needs
alt.ex: The nurse considers the patient’s values, preferences, and expressed needs when evaluating outcomes with the patient.
w: Set it aside because it is not a clinical finding
What is important to the patient is a key part of person-centered evaluation.
Refer it to social work instead of discussing it
The nurse partners with the patient directly on what matters to him.
Use it only if the provider writes a related order
Considering the patient’s expressed needs does not depend on a provider order.

items.q: A float nurse caring for a patient for the first time is unsure whether the patient’s level of confusion has changed since yesterday. Which action is best?
items.a: Ask a colleague who knows the patient to confirm the finding
items.ex: When a nurse has not cared for a patient over time, asking familiar colleagues to confirm findings improves evaluation.
w: Document the current confusion as the patient’s baseline
Labeling an unverified finding as baseline could hide a real change in condition.
Wait until the next shift for another nurse to reassess
Delaying evaluation could miss early signs of deterioration.
Assume no change because no one has reported concerns
Absence of reports is not evidence; patient-specific evaluation is required.

alt.q: Why does the textbook recommend asking colleagues who are familiar with a patient to help confirm evaluation findings?
alt.a: Their familiarity helps detect subtle changes a new nurse may miss
alt.ex: Knowing a patient over time heightens awareness of subtle changes, so familiar colleagues strengthen evaluation.
w: Their confirmation transfers accountability for the findings
The nurse remains responsible for evaluating the efficacy of care.
Their input replaces the need for patient self-report
Colleague input adds to, but does not replace, the patient’s own report.
Their review is required before any finding is documented
Confirmation helps when the nurse is unfamiliar with the patient; it is not required for all documentation.

items.q: What is the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) policy regarding “never events”?
items.a: CMS does not reimburse agencies for the costs of treating them
items.ex: CMS will not pay health care agencies for the costs of treating never events.
w: CMS reimburses the costs at a reduced rate after review
CMS provides no reimbursement for treating never events, not a reduced rate.
CMS reimburses the costs only when reported within 24 hours
Prompt reporting does not make never-event treatment costs reimbursable.
CMS bills the patient directly for the costs of treatment
The policy is nonpayment to the agency, not billing the patient.

alt.q: Which organization does not reimburse health care agencies for the costs associated with treating never events?
alt.a: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
alt.ex: CMS does not reimburse agencies for treating never events, giving agencies a strong reason to prevent them.
w: National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators
NDNQI is a nursing quality measurement program, not a payer.
American Nurses Association
The ANA sets professional standards and established NDNQI; it does not reimburse care.
Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality
AHRQ is a research and quality agency, not the payer that denies reimbursement.

items.q: Never events are defined by specific characteristics. Which characteristics describe a never event? Select all that apply.
o: Unambiguous, meaning clearly identifiable and measurable
Never events are unambiguous, meaning they can be clearly identified and measured.
Serious, meaning resulting in death or significant disability
Never events are serious, causing death or significant disability.
Usually preventable
Never events are usually preventable, which is why they should never occur.
Minor and self-limiting
Never events are serious, resulting in death or significant disability.
Rare and impossible to predict
Never events are usually preventable, so they are not considered unpredictable.
items.ex: Never events are adverse events that are unambiguous, serious, and usually preventable.

alt.q: A quality committee is deciding whether an adverse event meets the definition of a never event. Which features support classifying it as one? Select all that apply.
o: It can be clearly identified and measured
Being clearly identifiable and measurable makes the event unambiguous.
It resulted in significant disability
A serious outcome such as death or significant disability is required.
It could usually have been prevented
Never events are usually preventable.
It caused no harm to the patient
Events without serious harm do not meet the never-event definition.
It was a known, unavoidable side effect of therapy
Never events are usually preventable, not unavoidable expected effects.
alt.ex: Correct: It can be clearly identified and measured; It resulted in significant disability; It could usually have been prevented.

items.q: Which situations are examples of never events described in the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Serious injury associated with a medication error
Death or serious injury from a medication error is a listed never event.
Administration of incompatible blood products
Giving incompatible blood products is a listed never event.
A fall while being cared for in a health care setting
A fall during care in a health care setting is a listed never event.
A stage 3 pressure ulcer acquired after admission
Stage 3, stage 4, and unstageable pressure ulcers acquired after admission are never events.
A stage 2 pressure injury acquired after admission
Only stage 3, stage 4, or unstageable pressure ulcers acquired after admission are listed.
A pressure ulcer documented on the admission assessment
An ulcer present on admission was not acquired after admission to the agency.
items.ex: Listed never events include medication-error injury, incompatible blood, falls during care, and stage 3, 4, or unstageable ulcers acquired after admission.

alt.q: A hospital reviews adverse events from the past month. Which would be classified as never events? Select all that apply.
o: An unstageable pressure ulcer that developed during the stay
Unstageable pressure ulcers acquired after admission are never events.
A stage 4 pressure ulcer that developed after admission
Stage 4 pressure ulcers acquired after admission are never events.
A patient death associated with a medication error
Death associated with a medication error is a never event.
A stage 1 pressure injury noted on the third hospital day
Stage 1 injuries are not among the pressure ulcer stages listed as never events.
A dose given 30 minutes late without any harm
A never event must be serious, resulting in death or significant disability.
alt.ex: Correct: An unstageable pressure ulcer that developed during the stay; A stage 4 pressure ulcer that developed after admission; A patient death associated with a medication error.

items.q: A nurse completes skin assessments on patients admitted to a medical unit. Which finding would be classified as a never event?
items.a: A stage 3 sacral pressure injury first found on hospital day 4
items.ex: Stage 3, stage 4, or unstageable pressure ulcers acquired after admission are never events.
w: A stage 2 heel pressure injury first found on hospital day 4
Stage 2 injuries are not among the pressure ulcer stages listed as never events.
A stage 3 sacral pressure injury found on the admission assessment
An injury present on admission was not acquired after admission.
A stage 1 reddened area over the coccyx found on hospital day 4
Stage 1 injuries are not among the pressure ulcer stages listed as never events.

alt.q: A patient is admitted with an unstageable pressure injury documented on the admission skin assessment. Why is this injury not counted as a never event?
alt.a: It was not acquired after admission to the agency
alt.ex: Pressure ulcers count as never events only when acquired after admission to a health care agency.
w: Unstageable injuries are excluded from never events
Unstageable pressure ulcers acquired after admission are listed as never events.
Only stage 4 injuries are counted as never events
Stage 3, stage 4, and unstageable ulcers acquired after admission all count.
Pressure injuries are not nursing-sensitive outcomes
Pressure injuries are nursing-sensitive outcomes and appear on the NDNQI list.

items.q: Never events are adverse events that are usually preventable.
items.a: True
items.ex: Never events are unambiguous, serious, and usually preventable adverse events.
items.ww: Because they are usually preventable, evidence-based interventions can keep them from occurring.

alt.q: Any adverse event that occurs in a hospital, regardless of its severity, is classified as a never event.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Never events must be serious, causing death or significant disability, as well as unambiguous and usually preventable.
alt.ww: Minor adverse events do not meet the never-event criterion of being serious.

items.q: Why does the textbook describe nursing-sensitive quality outcomes such as falls and pressure ulcers as significant health care problems?
items.a: They increase suffering, prolong hospital stays, and raise costs
items.ex: These outcomes increase patient pain and suffering, prolong hospital stays, and increase health care costs.
w: They reduce nurse staffing levels and limit new admissions
Staffing and admissions are not the consequences the textbook names.
They affect accreditation scores but rarely harm patients
These outcomes cause real patient pain and suffering.
They shorten hospital stays but increase readmission rates
These outcomes prolong, rather than shorten, hospital stays.

alt.q: A unit’s rate of falls with injury has risen. Which consequence does the textbook associate with nursing-sensitive outcomes like this?
alt.a: Longer hospital stays for affected patients
alt.ex: Nursing-sensitive quality outcomes prolong hospital stays, increase suffering, and increase costs.
w: Lower overall health care costs
These outcomes increase, not lower, health care costs.
Reduced patient pain and suffering
These outcomes increase patient pain and suffering.
Faster recovery for affected patients
These outcomes prolong stays rather than speeding recovery.

items.q: A nurse on a medical unit learns that the unit’s rate of catheter-associated urinary tract infections has risen. Which action reflects the nurse’s role described in the textbook?
items.a: Implement the unit’s evidence-based catheter care bundle consistently
items.ex: Practicing nurses implement clinical guidelines, care bundles, and evidence-based interventions to prevent nursing-sensitive outcomes.
w: Wait for the annual quality report before changing practice
Units evaluate progress regularly; data are gathered monthly, not just annually.
Leave infection prevention to the infection control department
Bedside nurses directly affect preventable outcomes through their own interventions.
Report the infection rate to CMS to obtain reimbursement
Reporting does not prevent infections, and CMS does not pay for never events.

alt.q: A nurse caring for a patient on a ventilator wants to help reduce the unit’s ventilator-associated pneumonia rate. Which approach is most consistent with the textbook?
alt.a: Apply the evidence-based care bundle for ventilated patients
alt.ex: Nurses use clinical guidelines, care bundles, and evidence-based interventions to prevent nursing-sensitive outcomes.
w: Rely on personal routines from past experience alone
Prevention relies on evidence-based guidelines and bundles, not routine alone.
Focus only on patients who already show infection signs
Prevention bundles are applied before infection develops to prevent the outcome.
Leave prevention measures to the respiratory therapist
The textbook describes nurses as implementing interventions to prevent these outcomes.

items.q: All patient care units regularly evaluate their progress in reducing preventable outcomes and carry out ongoing quality improvement efforts.
items.a: True
items.ex: The textbook states that all patient care units regularly evaluate progress and implement ongoing quality improvement.
items.ww: Quality evaluation is an ongoing activity on every unit, not a one-time or selective process.

alt.q: Only units that have reported a never event are expected to evaluate their progress in reducing preventable outcomes.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: All patient care units, not just those with a never event, regularly evaluate progress and pursue quality improvement.
alt.ww: Waiting for a never event would make quality evaluation reactive rather than ongoing.

items.q: Health care organizations gather [[monthly]] data on the rates of nursing-sensitive preventable outcomes.
items.ex: Monthly data collection lets units regularly track progress in reducing preventable outcomes.

alt.q: Rates of nursing-sensitive preventable outcomes are collected by health care organizations every [[month]].
alt.ex: Monthly data collection lets units regularly track progress in reducing preventable outcomes.

items.q: Which organization established the National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators (NDNQI)?
items.a: American Nurses Association (ANA)
items.ex: The NDNQI was established by the ANA.
w: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS)
CMS is the payer that denies reimbursement for never events, not the NDNQI founder.
Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality (AHRQ)
AHRQ is a federal research agency; it did not establish the NDNQI.
Infusion Nurses Society (INS)
INS sets criteria for evaluating IV sites; it did not establish the NDNQI.

alt.q: Which description of the National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators (NDNQI) is accurate?
alt.a: It is the only voluntary, proprietary nursing quality measurement program
alt.ex: The ANA-established NDNQI is the only voluntary, proprietary nursing quality measurement program.
w: It is a federal program that sets Medicare payment rates
Medicare payment is a CMS function; NDNQI measures nursing quality.
It is a mandatory state reporting system for all hospitals
NDNQI participation is voluntary, although Magnet hospitals must report.
It is an accrediting body that inspects hospital units
NDNQI provides performance reports; it is not an accrediting body.

items.q: Participation in the NDNQI is mandatory for every hospital in the United States.
items.a: False
items.ex: The NDNQI is a voluntary program, although hospitals that achieve Magnet Status must gather and report its data.
items.ww: Only Magnet hospitals are required to report NDNQI data; participation is otherwise voluntary.

alt.q: Hospitals that achieve Magnet Status are required to gather and report NDNQI data.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The textbook states that Magnet hospitals must gather and report NDNQI data.
alt.ww: Although NDNQI is voluntary for most hospitals, Magnet Status makes reporting a requirement.

items.q: What type of quality performance report does the NDNQI provide to hospitals?
items.a: Unit-level reports on outcomes such as falls
items.ex: NDNQI provides unit-level quality performance reports on outcomes such as falls, falls with injury, and restraint use.
w: Individual nurse annual performance reviews
NDNQI reports outcomes by unit, not reviews of individual nurses.
Physician-level reports on prescribing rates
NDNQI focuses on nursing-sensitive outcomes, not physician prescribing.
Patient-level billing and payment summaries
NDNQI reports quality outcomes, not billing information.

alt.q: A nurse manager uses NDNQI data to compare her unit’s fall rate. At which levels does the NDNQI allow comparison?
alt.a: Within the agency and at state, regional, and national levels
alt.ex: NDNQI unit-level reports allow comparison within an agency and at state, regional, and national levels in the United States.
w: Only between units within the same agency
Comparison extends beyond the agency to state, regional, and national levels.
Only with hospitals located outside the United States
NDNQI comparisons are within the agency and across levels within the United States.
Only among hospitals that share the same owner
Comparison is not limited to hospitals with common ownership.

items.q: Which outcomes are listed as NDNQI nursing-sensitive outcomes in Box 20.2? Select all that apply.
o: Catheter-associated urinary tract infections
CAUTI is a listed NDNQI nursing-sensitive outcome.
Central line–associated bloodstream infections
CLABSI is a listed NDNQI nursing-sensitive outcome.
Physical restraint prevalence
Physical restraint prevalence is a listed NDNQI outcome.
Failure to rescue
Failure to rescue is a listed NDNQI outcome.
Average length of hospital stay
Length of stay is not among the NDNQI outcomes in Box 20.2.
Number of nursing diagnoses per patient
Diagnosis counts are not an NDNQI outcome; accuracy matters more than number.
items.ex: Box 20.2 lists infections, failure to rescue, medication errors, falls, pressure injuries, pain cycles, restraints, VAP, and psychiatric assaults.

alt.q: A unit council is reviewing its NDNQI nursing-sensitive outcomes. Which outcomes will appear on the report? Select all that apply.
o: Ventilator-associated pneumonia rates
VAP rates are a listed NDNQI outcome.
Psychiatric patient assault rates
Psychiatric patient assault rates are a listed NDNQI outcome.
Pain assessment, intervention, and reassessment cycles completed
Completed pain assessment and reassessment cycles are a listed NDNQI outcome.
Patient falls with injury
Falls and falls with injury are listed NDNQI outcomes.
Hospital readmission within 30 days
Readmission is a self-management health service indicator, not an NDNQI outcome in Box 20.2.
alt.ex: Correct: Ventilator-associated pneumonia rates; Psychiatric patient assault rates; Pain assessment, intervention, and reassessment cycles completed; Patient falls with injury.

items.q: A nurse manager reviews the unit’s NDNQI report and finds that the rate of falls with injury is higher than that of comparable units nationally. Which response best reflects the textbook?
items.a: Start a quality improvement effort using evidence-based fall prevention
items.ex: Units evaluate progress on preventable outcomes and implement ongoing quality improvement with evidence-based interventions.
w: Increase use of physical restraints to prevent further falls
Restraint prevalence is itself an NDNQI quality indicator, so restraints are not the answer.
Conclude that national data cannot be compared and take no action
NDNQI is designed to allow comparison at national levels.
Report each nurse involved in a fall to the state board
Quality improvement focuses on unit processes and prevention, not individual punishment.

alt.q: A medical unit’s pressure injury rate has been above the national comparison for 3 months. What is the purpose of the unit regularly evaluating this rate?
alt.a: To track progress and guide ongoing quality improvement
alt.ex: Units regularly evaluate progress in reducing preventable outcomes so they can implement ongoing quality improvement.
w: To decide which patients may be refused admission
Quality data guide improvement, not decisions to refuse patients.
To obtain CMS payment for treating the injuries
CMS does not reimburse costs of treating never events such as stage 3 or 4 ulcers.
To rank individual nurses for annual raises
NDNQI reports unit-level outcomes, not individual nurse rankings.

items.q: Which statement by a new graduate nurse shows understanding of how bedside nurses affect their agency’s quality outcomes?
items.a: “Evaluating whether my interventions work helps reduce preventable outcomes.”
items.ex: Nurses who deliver person-centered care and continually evaluate interventions make a significant impact on preventable outcomes.
w: “Quality outcomes depend on administrators rather than bedside nurses.”
Bedside nurses significantly affect preventable outcomes through care and evaluation.
“Unit data are reviewed only yearly, so daily care has little effect.”
Data are gathered monthly, and daily nursing care directly affects outcome rates.
“Never events cannot be avoided, so evaluating care will not reduce them.”
Never events are usually preventable, and evaluation helps prevent them.

alt.q: According to the textbook, what does a nurse gain by learning what is effective for individual patients?
alt.a: Knowledge of evidence-based and practical approaches to quality care
alt.ex: Learning what works for individual patients builds knowledge of evidence-based and practical ways to improve quality of care.
w: Freedom to stop following the agency’s clinical guidelines
Individual learning complements, rather than replaces, clinical guidelines.
A way to avoid reporting outcomes on the NDNQI report
Learning from patients does not change unit outcome reporting.
Proof that every patient with one diagnosis needs identical care
Patients with the same problem are not treated the same way.

items.q: Why is accurate documentation essential to evaluating the quality of nursing care?
items.a: It is the primary evidence used to measure performance against standards
items.ex: Documentation is the primary source of evidence used to continuously measure performance outcomes against predetermined standards.
w: It selects the patient’s nursing diagnoses automatically
Documentation records diagnoses; the nurse selects them through clinical judgment.
It removes the need for unit-level quality reports
Unit-level reports depend on documentation; documentation does not replace them.
It is needed only for patients who experience never events
All care and outcomes must be documented, not only never events.

alt.q: A unit’s quality committee measures performance outcomes against predetermined standards. What is the primary source of evidence for this measurement?
alt.a: Nursing documentation in the patient record
alt.ex: Documentation is the primary source of evidence used to measure performance outcomes against predetermined standards.
w: Staff recollection gathered at monthly meetings
Memory is unreliable; documented records are the primary evidence.
Patient satisfaction comments posted online
Online comments are not the primary evidence for measuring performance outcomes.
Verbal reports given at shift hand-off
Hand-off communication is important, but documentation is the primary evidence source.

items.q: How do health care agencies use patient-reported outcome measures (PROMs) in evaluating care?
items.a: To measure outcome-based performance and quality of care
items.ex: PROMs capture patients’ reports of their outcomes, which agencies use to measure outcome-based performance and quality.
w: To set nurse-to-patient staffing ratios for each unit
PROMs capture patient-reported outcomes; they are not staffing tools.
To determine CMS reimbursement for never events
CMS does not reimburse never events, regardless of PROM results.
To replace clinician measurement of vital signs
PROMs capture patient perceptions and do not replace physiological measures.

alt.q: A hospital asks discharged patients to complete a survey describing their own health outcomes. What is this type of tool called?
alt.a: Patient-reported outcome measure
alt.ex: PROMs capture patients’ own reports of outcomes, which agencies use to measure performance and quality of care.
w: Nursing Interventions Classification
NIC is a standard language for nursing interventions, not a patient survey of outcomes.
Clinical practice guideline
A clinical practice guideline directs care; it does not capture patient reports.
Care bundle checklist
A care bundle is a set of evidence-based interventions, not a patient outcome survey.

items.q: A nurse reviewing a patient’s progress finds that planned turning every 2 hours was delayed or not done during the night shift. How does the textbook describe this situation?
items.a: Missed nursing care
items.ex: Planned interventions that are delayed, not done, or not completed are an example of missed nursing care.
w: A never event
Never events are serious adverse outcomes, such as a fall, not delayed interventions alone.
A collaborative problem
A collaborative problem is a patient health problem, not an omission in care.
Reflection-in-action
Reflection-in-action is recognizing a patient’s response during care, not an omission.

alt.q: Which situation is an example of missed nursing care?
alt.a: Planned mouth care for a patient with mucositis was not completed
alt.ex: Missed nursing care occurs when planned interventions are delayed, not done, or not completed.
w: A patient refuses ambulation after it is offered and documented
The intervention was offered and documented; the patient exercised the right to refuse.
A patient’s pain rating falls from 7 to 3 after an analgesic
This is an evaluative finding showing that an outcome is improving.
A nurse increases coughing exercises because lung sounds are congested
Adjusting frequency based on response is appropriate revision of the plan.

items.q: Adverse events that are serious, clearly identifiable, and usually preventable, and whose treatment costs CMS does not reimburse, are called [[never events|never event]].
items.ex: Never events are unambiguous, serious, usually preventable adverse events that CMS will not reimburse agencies for treating.

alt.q: CMS will not pay agencies to treat [[never events|never event]], such as a fall during care or administration of incompatible blood products.
alt.ex: Never events are unambiguous, serious, usually preventable adverse events that CMS will not reimburse agencies for treating.

w: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services

w: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services

National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators
That goes with NDNQI.
Patient-reported outcome measures

alt.q: What does PROMs mean?
alt.a: Patient-reported outcome measures
alt.ex: These organizations and tools support measuring outcomes, standards, and nursing quality in health care agencies.
w: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services

National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators
That goes with NDNQI.
American Nurses Association

alt.q: What does NOC mean?
alt.a: Nursing Outcomes Classification
alt.ex: These organizations and tools support measuring outcomes, standards, and nursing quality in health care agencies.
w: Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
That goes with CMS.
National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators
That goes with NDNQI.
American Nurses Association
That goes with ANA.

alt.q: Which abbreviation means “Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services”?
alt.a: CMS
alt.ex: These organizations and tools support measuring outcomes, standards, and nursing quality in health care agencies.
w: NDNQI
NDNQI: National Database of Nursing Quality Indicators.
ANA
ANA: American Nurses Association.
PROMs

items.q: According to the textbook, what is perhaps the most important responsibility of the nurse executive?
items.a: Establishing a philosophy for nursing that enables managers and staff to provide quality care
items.ex: The nurse executive’s key responsibility is a nursing philosophy that enables managers and staff to deliver quality nursing care.
w: Submitting staffing schedules and conducting routine staff evaluations for each unit
Staffing schedules and staff evaluations are listed among the nurse manager’s responsibilities.
Coordinating discharge planning and follow-up for patients with complex problems
Coordinating care across settings and discharge planning is the work of the case manager.
Providing direct care to a caseload of patients from admission to discharge
Caring for a caseload from admission to discharge describes primary nursing, not an executive role.

alt.q: Which member of the agency is described as a clinical and business leader who balances quality of care and cost-effectiveness with staff satisfaction?
alt.a: The nurse executive
alt.ex: The nurse executive, often a chief nursing officer, unites agency strategy with nursing values while balancing quality, cost, and staff satisfaction.
w: The nurse manager
The nurse manager directs and supports a unit’s staff in applying the agency’s nursing philosophy.
The case manager
The case manager coordinates services for patients across levels of care rather than leading nursing agency-wide.
The staff nurse
Staff nurses participate in decisions through shared governance but do not set the agency’s nursing direction.

items.q: A newly hired nurse manager wants to lead the unit using transformational leadership. Which action best reflects this style?
items.a: Spending time on the unit sharing ideas with staff and recognizing a job well done
items.ex: Transformational leaders are present on the unit, share ideas, empower staff, show appreciation, and hold team members accountable.
w: Making unit decisions alone to give staff clear direction during change
Transformational leaders empower staff and develop the team rather than deciding alone.
Limiting time on the unit to focus on budget reports and meetings
Transformational leaders spend time on their units with the staff.
Avoiding holding staff accountable in order to protect unit morale
Transformational leaders hold team members accountable while recognizing good work.

alt.q: Which focus best describes a nurse manager who uses transformational leadership?
alt.a: Change and innovation through team development
alt.ex: The transformational nurse manager focuses on change and innovation through team development and mentors staff.
w: Stable routines maintained through close supervision
Close supervision of fixed routines does not describe the change-focused transformational leader.
Cost control through centralized decision making
Transformational leaders empower staff; centralized control is not their focus.
Task completion through detailed written rules
A task-and-rules focus does not reflect mentoring and team development.

items.q: Which statement by a nurse manager best reflects servant leadership?
items.a: “I place each nurse in the position that makes the best use of their strengths.”
items.ex: Servant leaders learn each member’s strengths and weaknesses and ensure nurses work in positions that best use their strengths.
w: “I take credit for our unit’s successes so administration sees my value.”
Servant leaders practice humility and give credit to their staff for successes.
“As the leader, I am expected to know the answer to every question.”
Servant leaders understand that they do not know all the answers.
“I chose to become a leader first and then learned how to serve others.”
Servant leaders choose to serve others before they decide to become leaders.

alt.q: Which characteristic distinguishes a servant leader from other leadership styles?
alt.a: Putting the needs of others first while practicing humility
alt.ex: Servant leaders prioritize meeting employees’ highest priority needs, promote growth and autonomy, and remain modest.
w: Choosing a leadership style that is consistent with one’s personality
Choosing a style consistent with one’s personality describes authentic leadership.
Keeping decision making at the top of the organization
Centralized decision making is not a feature of relationship-based servant leadership.
Focusing on personal advancement within the agency
Servant leaders focus on others’ growth and autonomy, not their own advancement.

items.q: A medical unit organizes care so that an RN leads a group made up of other RNs, LPNs, and assistive personnel (APs) who provide care together. Which nursing care delivery model is the unit using?
items.a: Team nursing
items.ex: In team nursing, care is provided by a group led by an RN and requires effective leadership, collaboration, and communication.
w: Primary nursing
In primary nursing one RN is responsible for a caseload of patients from admission to discharge.
Total patient care
In total patient care an RN handles all aspects of care for one or more patients during a shift.
Case management
Case management coordinates services across levels of care; case managers do not provide direct care.

alt.q: On a unit that uses primary nursing, the RN who has cared for a patient since admission is not scheduled to work tomorrow. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Leave directions in the plan of care for the other RNs to follow.
alt.ex: In primary nursing, when the nurse is off the unit, directions are left (e.g., in the plan of care) for other RNs.
w: Assign the patient’s care to an AP until the nurse returns.
Primary nursing is an all-RN model, and APs are never given sole responsibility for patients.
Transfer the patient to the case manager for direct care.
Case managers do not provide direct care; they coordinate services.
Ask the nurse manager to provide the patient’s care.
The model relies on other RNs following the primary nurse’s directions, not the manager.

items.q: A patient with heart failure will be discharged from the hospital to a rehabilitation facility. Which activity would the case manager most likely perform?
items.a: Coordinate discharge planning and arrange needed services and equipment.
items.ex: Case managers coordinate discharge planning, ensure services are available, and make cost-efficient choices rather than giving direct care.
w: Provide the patient’s daily medications and wound care.
Case managers do not provide direct care; direct care providers do.
Perform the patient’s physical assessment each shift.
Shift assessments are direct care performed by the nurses assigned to the patient.
Lead a team of LPNs and APs caring for the patient.
Leading an RN-led care team describes team nursing, not case management.

alt.q: A nurse explains the case manager’s role to the family of a patient with a traumatic brain injury. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “The case manager coordinates services across settings but does not provide direct care.”
alt.ex: Case managers link and coordinate services across levels of care and collaborate with direct care providers.
w: “The case manager will give all of the patient’s nursing care while in the hospital.”
Case managers collaborate with direct care providers instead of giving direct care.
“The case manager’s involvement ends on the day the patient is discharged.”
Case managers follow up with patients after discharge to home, rehabilitation, or long-term care.
“The case manager focuses on quality and is not responsible for costs.”
Case managers are accountable for both cost management and quality.

items.q: A nurse delegates measuring vital signs to an AP. The AP reports that the patient’s temperature is elevated. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Verify the temperature and give acetaminophen as ordered.
items.ex: The nurse remains accountable for delegated care, including recognizing abnormal vital signs and providing appropriate care.
w: Document the reading, since the AP is accountable for the vital signs.
Delegating responsibility does not transfer accountability; the nurse remains accountable.
Ask the AP to recheck the temperature at the next scheduled time.
Waiting delays appropriate care; the nurse must recognize and act on the abnormal value.
Report the finding to the nurse manager for follow-up.
The nurse, not the manager, is accountable for responding to the patient’s findings.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse about delegating vital signs to an AP shows a correct understanding of accountability?
alt.a: “I remain accountable for knowing whether the values are expected and for acting on them.”
alt.ex: Even when delegating, the nurse is accountable for knowing normal values, recognizing changes, and providing appropriate care.
w: “Once I delegate the task, the AP is accountable for the patient’s outcome.”
The nurse delegates responsibility but remains accountable for the delegated care.
“I am accountable for vital signs only when I measure them myself.”
Accountability for delegated care stays with the nurse who delegated it.
“The nurse manager is accountable for all tasks delegated on the unit.”
Each nurse is answerable for their own actions, including the care they delegate.

items.q: A nurse learns that the registered dietitian did not complete the discharge teaching listed on a patient’s plan of care. The nurse consults the dietitian and reviews the plan to ensure the teaching is done. Which element of decision making is the nurse using?
items.a: Authority
items.ex: Authority is the legal ability to perform a task and gives the nurse power to make final decisions and give instructions.
w: Autonomy
Autonomy is freedom of choice and responsibility for those choices, such as planning independent interventions.
Responsibility
Responsibility refers to the duties and activities a nurse is employed to perform.
Accountability
Accountability means being answerable for one’s own actions and evaluating their effectiveness.

alt.q: While managing a patient’s care, a nurse discovers that the physical therapist did not complete the gait training listed on the plan of care. Using authority, what should the nurse do?
alt.a: Consult the therapist about why it was not done and review the plan.
alt.ex: Authority lets the nurse determine whether collaboration succeeded by consulting the team member and reviewing the established plan.
w: Perform the gait training in place of the therapist.
Taking over another discipline’s intervention does not determine why the plan was not followed.
Document the omission and take no further action.
Documenting alone does not ensure the recommended care is completed.
Remove gait training from the patient’s plan of care.
Removing the intervention ignores the patient’s need; the nurse reviews the plan instead.

items.q: Which situation is an example of work autonomy rather than clinical autonomy?
items.a: A nurse makes decisions about the unit’s scheduling.
items.ex: Work autonomy involves independent decisions about the work of the unit, such as scheduling or unit governance.
w: A nurse develops a discharge teaching plan for a patient.
Developing a patient teaching plan is clinical autonomy over patient care.
A nurse implements an independent nursing intervention.
Independent nursing interventions are an example of clinical autonomy.
A nurse plans care within the scope of nursing practice.
Planning patient care within professional scope is clinical autonomy.

alt.q: Which situation is an example of clinical autonomy?
alt.a: A nurse develops a discharge teaching plan based on the patient’s needs.
alt.ex: Clinical autonomy means making independent decisions about patient care within the scope of professional practice.
w: A nurse takes part in decisions about unit governance.
Decisions about unit governance are work autonomy.
A nurse creates a work schedule on a self-scheduling unit.
Scheduling decisions are an example of work autonomy.
A nurse helps decide how unit committees are organized.
Decisions about how the unit operates reflect work autonomy.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient whose family asks about recent test results. The nurse makes sure the patient and family receive timely, complete, and accurate information so they can take part in decisions. Which core concept of patient- and family-centered care is the nurse applying?
items.a: Information sharing
items.ex: Information sharing means providers share timely, complete, and accurate information so patients and families can participate effectively.
w: Respect and dignity
Respect and dignity means care includes the patient’s and family’s knowledge, values, beliefs, and culture.
Participation
Participation means patients and families are encouraged and supported in taking part in care and decisions.
Collaboration
Collaboration involves patients and families in policy and program development, implementation, and evaluation.

alt.q: Which nursing action best demonstrates the patient- and family-centered care concept of information sharing?
alt.a: Giving the family complete, accurate test results in time for decisions
alt.ex: Sharing timely, complete, and accurate information allows patients and families to participate in care and decision making.
w: Building the family’s cultural beliefs into the plan of care
Incorporating values, beliefs, and culture reflects respect and dignity.
Inviting family members to help develop unit programs
Involving families in policy and program development reflects collaboration.
Encouraging the patient to help with daily care activities
Supporting patients in taking part in care reflects participation.

items.q: A nurse manager plans to change how hand-off report is given on a large unit. Which approach best prevents mistrust among the staff?
items.a: Share the plan through several methods, such as newsletters, minutes, and staff meetings.
items.ex: Lack of communication about planned changes often leads to mistrust, so effective managers use a variety of communication approaches.
w: Announce the change on the day it takes effect to avoid debate.
Withholding information about planned changes often leads to mistrust among staff.
Send a single e-mail and assume all staff will read it.
One message rarely ensures consistent, timely information reaches every staff member.
Discuss the plan only with the RNs who give report.
All staff, including LPNs, APs, and unit secretaries, need to be kept informed.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse manager reflects effective staff communication?
alt.a: “Each committee member will share updates directly with an assigned group of staff.”
alt.ex: When units have committees, each member communicates with a select number of staff so everyone can give input.
w: “I am solely responsible for all communication that happens on this unit.”
A manager cannot assume total responsibility for all communication.
“Committee minutes stay private until any planned changes are final.”
Minutes are usually kept accessible to all staff or sent by e-mail.
“Staff will learn about the change once the new policy is in place.”
Failing to communicate planned changes often leads to mistrust.

items.q: A nurse uses knowledge of the nurse’s own role and the expertise of the pharmacist and respiratory therapist to address a patient’s health outcomes. Which Interprofessional Education Collaborative (IPEC) competency does this demonstrate?
items.a: Roles and responsibilities
items.ex: The roles and responsibilities competency uses knowledge of one’s own role and team members’ expertise to address health outcomes.
w: Values and ethics
Values and ethics involves maintaining shared values, ethical conduct, and mutual respect.
Communication
Communication involves responsive, responsible, respectful, and compassionate exchanges with team members.
Teams and teamwork
Teams and teamwork applies principles of team science to adapt one’s role in different team settings.

alt.q: A nurse wants to strengthen the IPEC competency of roles and responsibilities. Which action fits this competency best?
alt.a: Learning each team member’s expertise to address patient outcomes
alt.ex: Knowing one’s own role and other members’ expertise is the core of the roles and responsibilities competency.
w: Speaking with team members in a compassionate, respectful way
Respectful, compassionate exchanges describe the communication competency.
Maintaining a climate of shared values and ethical conduct
Shared values and ethical conduct describe the values and ethics competency.
Applying team science principles to adapt to new team settings
Adapting one’s role using team science describes the teams and teamwork competency.

items.q: Which characteristics describe effective leaders according to the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Allow vulnerabilities to show
Effective leaders are aware of their strengths and weaknesses and allow vulnerabilities to show.
Rebound from setbacks with positivity
Rebounding from setbacks with positivity is listed among effective leader characteristics.
Take responsibility for decisions
Effective leaders take responsibility for the decisions they make.
Use different leadership styles appropriately
Effective leaders use transformational, authentic, or value-based styles as appropriate.
Rely on one leadership style in every situation
Effective leaders adapt by using different leadership styles appropriately.
Hide personal weaknesses to maintain authority
Effective leaders know their weaknesses and allow vulnerabilities to show.
items.ex: Effective leaders show self-awareness, resilience, responsibility, and flexibility in leadership style.

alt.q: A nurse manager is reflecting on effective leadership behaviors. Which behaviors should the manager adopt? Select all that apply.
o: Seek multiple perspectives when solving problems
Effective leaders seek multiple perspectives and opinions to generate options and solutions.
Schedule time to reflect, recharge, and reframe
Regularly scheduling time to reflect and recharge is an effective leader characteristic.
Understand what can and cannot be changed
Effective leaders recognize what they can and cannot change.
Make decisions alone during times of uncertainty
Effective leaders take initiative and sustain motivation while seeking others’ perspectives.
Avoid change to keep the unit stable
Effective leaders identify the need for change and support it effectively.
alt.ex: Correct: Seek multiple perspectives when solving problems; Schedule time to reflect, recharge, and reframe; Understand what can and cannot be changed.

items.q: Which are Model Components of the Magnet Recognition Program® framework? Select all that apply.
o: Transformational Leadership
Transformational Leadership is one of the 5 Model Components.
Structural Empowerment
Structural Empowerment is one of the 5 Model Components.
Exemplary Professional Practice
Exemplary Professional Practice is one of the 5 Model Components.
Empirical Quality Results
Empirical Quality Results is one of the 5 Model Components.
Centralized Decision Making
Magnet® hospitals empower nurses with autonomy and control over practice, not centralized decisions.
Cost Containment
The fifth component is New Knowledge, Innovation, & Improvements, not cost containment.
items.ex: The 5 Model Components are Transformational Leadership, Structural Empowerment, Exemplary Professional Practice, New Knowledge/Innovation/Improvements, and Empirical Quality Results.

alt.q: Which features would a nurse expect to find in a Magnet®-certified hospital? Select all that apply.
o: Nurses with professional autonomy over their practice
Magnet® nurses have autonomy over practice and control over the practice environment.
Clinical promotion systems for nurses
Magnet® hospitals typically have clinical promotion systems.
Research- and evidence-based practice programs
Magnet® hospitals typically have research- and evidence-based practice programs.
Practice decisions made only by the nurse executive
Professional nurse councils at organizational and unit levels create an empowerment model.
A culture focused mainly on cost rather than patients
The Magnet® culture focuses on concern for patients.
alt.ex: Correct: Nurses with professional autonomy over their practice; Clinical promotion systems for nurses; Research- and evidence-based practice programs.

items.q: Which activities are responsibilities of a nurse manager? Select all that apply.
o: Recruit, interview, and hire new employees
Recruiting new employees is listed among nurse manager responsibilities.
Submit staffing schedules for the unit
Nurse managers submit the unit’s staffing schedules.
Establish and monitor a quality improvement plan
Nurse managers establish, monitor, and implement a QI plan for the unit.
Advocate for nursing staff to administration
Nurse managers advocate for their staff to the agency’s administration.
Provide direct care to an assigned caseload of patients
A caseload of direct care describes primary nursing, not the manager role.
Follow patients after discharge to long-term care
Follow-up across care settings is the work of the case manager.
items.ex: Nurse managers handle hiring, staffing, quality improvement, and staff advocacy for their unit.

alt.q: A new nurse manager reviews the responsibilities of the role. Which activities should the manager expect to perform? Select all that apply.
o: Conduct regular staff meetings
Conducting regular staff meetings is a nurse manager responsibility.
Review and recommend new equipment for the unit
Nurse managers review and recommend new unit equipment.
Make rounds with health care providers
Making rounds with health care providers is listed in the manager’s responsibilities.
Write the state’s scope of practice for nurses
Scope of practice is set by the state’s Nurse Practice Act, not the manager.
Coordinate services for patients across all levels of care
Coordinating services across levels of care is the case manager’s role.
alt.ex: Correct: Conduct regular staff meetings; Review and recommend new equipment for the unit; Make rounds with health care providers.

items.q: Interprofessional rounding is used to involve patients and families in planning care and to improve care coordination.
items.a: True
items.ex: Agencies focused on patient- and family-centered care use interprofessional rounding to involve patients and families and enhance team communication.
items.ww: Rounding is designed to include patients and families, coordinate care, and focus the team on shared goals.

alt.q: Interprofessional rounding is limited to health care professionals, so patients and families are not involved in planning care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Interprofessional rounding is used specifically to involve patients and families in planning their care.
alt.ww: Including patients and families is a key purpose of interprofessional rounding, along with care coordination.

items.q: Achieving Magnet Status is a formal process that can take a full year or longer.
items.a: True
items.ex: Hospitals must take the initiative and complete a formal process that can take a year or longer to achieve Magnet Status.
items.ww: Magnet Status is not quick or automatic; it requires a lengthy formal process.

alt.q: Magnet Status is granted automatically to hospitals that meet state licensing requirements.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hospitals must take the initiative and undergo a formal process lasting a year or longer to achieve Magnet Status.
alt.ww: Licensing alone does not confer Magnet Status; it requires a formal application process.

items.q: A nurse is accountable for the overall outcomes of patient care.
items.a: False
items.ex: Nurses are accountable for what they do, such as performing the nursing process and procedures correctly, not overall outcomes.
items.ww: The text states that nurses are not accountable for the overall outcomes of patient care, only for their own actions.

alt.q: A nurse is accountable for performing nursing procedures correctly and for staying current on nursing practice issues.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Accountability covers what the nurse does: the nursing process, correct procedures, effective communication, and staying current.
alt.ww: Being answerable for one’s own actions, including procedures and knowledge, is the meaning of accountability.

items.q: [[Shared governance|professional governance]] is the typical decentralized structure used in health care agencies today to involve staff in decision making.
items.ex: Shared governance moves decision making to the lowest level possible and promotes accountability and empowerment in staff nurses.

alt.q: Also called professional governance, [[shared governance]] promotes decision making, accountability, and empowerment among staff nurses.
alt.ex: Shared governance moves decision making to the lowest level possible and promotes accountability and empowerment in staff nurses.
