alt.ex: Team and primary nursing are classic models; patient- and family-centered care and case management are more common today.
w: Team nursing
Team nursing: A group of RNs, LPNs, and APs provides care under an RN leader.
Primary nursing
Primary nursing: One RN is responsible for a caseload of patients from admission to discharge.
Total patient care
Total patient care: An RN is responsible for all aspects of care for patients during a shift.

mt.q: Match each nursing care delivery model with its description.
pairs: A group of RNs, LPNs, and APs provides care under an RN leader
One RN is responsible for a caseload of patients from admission to discharge
An RN is responsible for all aspects of care for patients during a shift
Care is coordinated across all levels of care while streamlining costs
The patient or family is the source of control and a full partner in care
mt.ex: Team and primary nursing are classic models; patient- and family-centered care and case management are more common today.

items.q: A patient returns to the room short of breath after walking down the hall. At the same time, the dietary assistant arrives with the patient’s lunch tray. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Position the patient comfortably in bed and evaluate the breathlessness.
items.ex: High-priority physiological needs come first; the patient can eat after breathing is evaluated and comfort is restored.
w: Set up the meal tray so the patient can eat while the food is warm.
Nutrition can wait; shortness of breath is a higher-priority physiological need.
Ask the dietary assistant to help the patient start eating.
Eating while short of breath delays evaluation of the priority problem.
Document the distance the patient walked in the health record.
Documentation does not address the patient’s immediate breathing problem.

alt.q: A nursing student finds a patient short of breath after ambulating just as lunch arrives. Which statement by the student shows correct priority setting?
alt.a: “I will evaluate the breathing first; the patient can eat once comfortable.”
alt.ex: When patients have diverse needs, the nurse focuses on basic needs, evaluating breathlessness before helping with the meal.
w: “I will help with the meal first so the food does not get cold.”
Breathing is a higher priority than the timing of a meal.
“I will let the patient eat and check the breathing at the next rounds.”
Delaying action on a breathing problem could lead to serious complications.
“I will ask the dietary assistant to watch the breathing during the meal.”
Evaluating a change in breathing is the nurse’s responsibility and cannot be handed off this way.

items.q: After hand-off report, a nurse is assigned four patients. Using the ABC+VL approach, which patient should the nurse assess first?
items.a: A patient with labored breathing and a falling oxygen saturation
items.ex: Airway, breathing, circulation, vital sign, and life-threatening laboratory problems are first-level priorities to attend to immediately.
w: A patient who has become newly confused since the morning
A change in mental status is a second-level problem that follows first-level problems.
A patient with acute incisional pain after surgery yesterday
Acute pain is a second-level problem, addressed after airway and breathing concerns.
A patient whose family is having difficulty coping with a diagnosis
Family coping is a third-level problem.

alt.q: Which patient problem is classified as a second-level priority?
alt.a: Acute pain after surgery
alt.ex: Second-level problems include mental status changes, untreated medical issues, acute pain, acute elimination problems, abnormal lab results, and risks.
w: Partial airway obstruction
Airway problems are first-level priorities in the ABC+VL approach.
A life-threatening potassium level
Life-threatening laboratory values are first-level priorities.
Long-term health management needs
Long-term health management issues are third-level problems.

items.q: A nurse begins bathing a stable patient who is eager to visit with family. An x-ray technician arrives for a routine chest x-ray and offers to return later. Which action is best?
items.a: Complete the patient’s hygiene and have the technician return later.
items.ex: With a stable patient and a routine order, hygiene and comfort before the family visit is the higher priority.
w: Stop the bath so the x-ray can be taken right away.
A routine x-ray for a stable patient can wait when the technician is willing to return.
Ask the family to postpone their visit until testing is done.
The patient’s needs stay at the center; delaying the visit for a routine test does not serve the patient.
Ask the health care provider to cancel the x-ray order.
The x-ray is still needed; it is simply rescheduled for later.

alt.q: A nurse is bathing a patient who had symptoms earlier in the shift that led to orders for a chest x-ray and blood work. The x-ray technician and phlebotomist arrive. Which action is best?
alt.a: Pause the bath so the diagnostic tests can be completed.
alt.ex: Keeping the patient’s needs central means ensuring tests ordered for earlier symptoms are completed promptly.
w: Ask both staff members to return after the bath is finished.
Tests ordered for new symptoms are a higher priority than completing hygiene.
Finish the bath and then call the staff members back later.
Delaying tests ordered for symptoms could delay needed treatment.
Allow only the blood draw and reschedule the x-ray for tomorrow.
Both diagnostic tests were ordered for the patient’s symptoms and need to be completed.

items.q: A nursing student assesses a patient and detects a change from baseline but is not sure what is happening. Which action is best?
items.a: Consult an experienced RN to confirm the findings.
items.ex: Recognizing personal limitations and using professional resources confirms findings and ensures the proper course of action.
w: Continue to monitor and reassess at the end of the shift.
Waiting delays action on a change in condition; never hesitate to ask for help.
Document the findings and wait for the next scheduled assessment.
Documentation alone does not ensure the patient receives the proper care.
Ask the AP to recheck the patient’s vital signs in an hour.
Interpreting a change in condition requires nursing judgment and timely consultation.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows correct use of professional resources?
alt.a: “When I am unsure about a change in a patient, I ask an experienced RN.”
alt.ex: Leaders know their limitations and seek professional colleagues for guidance and support.
w: “Asking for help shows I am not ready to lead a team.”
Seeking guidance is what effective leaders do when they reach their limits.
“I should handle changes alone so I learn faster.”
Never hesitate to ask for assistance when a patient’s condition changes.
“I ask for help only after the patient becomes unstable.”
Consulting early prevents delays that could lead to serious complications.

items.q: A nurse is due to administer an IV antibiotic to a patient whose IV tubing is also due to be changed. Which plan makes the best use of time?
items.a: Change the tubing and assess the IV site while giving the antibiotic.
items.ex: Good time management combines activities that can be done together while in the patient’s room.
w: Give the antibiotic now and come back later for the tubing and site.
Separate trips waste time when the activities could be combined in one visit.
Change the tubing at the end of the shift after other care is done.
Tubing changes are scheduled by policy, and combining them saves time.
Ask the AP to assess the IV site during routine vital signs.
Assessment is nursing judgment and is never delegated to APs.

alt.q: While giving oral medications to a patient, which activity can a nurse combine with this task to use time efficiently?
alt.a: Teaching about the medications and using the teach-back method
alt.ex: Efficient nurses combine activities, such as teaching and assessing understanding while administering medications.
w: Discussing unit issues with colleagues at the bedside
Socializing should not interrupt important activities like medication administration.
Starting another patient’s dressing change at the same time
Completing one patient’s activity before moving on reduces fragmentation and errors.
Completing the shift documentation for other patients
Documenting for other patients distracts from the patient receiving medications.

items.q: A nurse planned discharge teaching for 1000. At 1000 the patient reports nausea. Which action is best?
items.a: Postpone the teaching until the nausea is relieved.
items.ex: A patient who is nauseated or in pain is not ready to learn, so teaching is timed around the patient’s condition.
w: Begin the teaching because discharge is already scheduled.
Teaching while the patient is nauseated is not effective use of time.
Leave written instructions for the patient to read alone.
Leaving materials does not provide teaching or evaluate understanding.
Ask a family member to teach the patient later instead.
Patient teaching is the nurse’s responsibility and is simply rescheduled.

alt.q: A nurse decides when to schedule teaching, ambulation, and rest periods based on what is known about the patient’s condition. Which principle of time management is the nurse applying?
alt.a: Priority setting
alt.ex: Priority setting places established patient priorities within set time frames, such as timing teaching around nausea or pain.
w: Goal setting
Goal setting reviews the outcomes and care that need to be accomplished for the day.
Time analysis
Time analysis is reflecting on and tracking how time is used in different activities.
Interruption control
Interruption control keeps socializing from disrupting important care activities.

items.q: A nurse administers an oral pain medication. When should the nurse plan to return to evaluate the patient’s response?
items.a: In about 30 minutes
items.ex: The textbook gives 30 minutes after an oral medication as an example time to return and evaluate care.
w: In about 5 minutes
Five minutes is too soon for an oral medication to take effect.
In about 15 minutes
Fifteen minutes is the example given for evaluating after an IV fluid begins infusing.
In about 60 minutes
Sixty minutes is the example given for evaluating after discharge instructions.

alt.q: A nurse starts an IV fluid infusion. When should the nurse plan to return to the bedside to evaluate the patient?
alt.a: In about 15 minutes
alt.ex: The textbook gives 15 minutes after an IV fluid begins infusing as an example time to evaluate care.
w: In about 30 minutes
Thirty minutes is the example for evaluating after an oral medication.
In about 60 minutes
Sixty minutes is the example for evaluating after discharge instructions.
In about 120 minutes
Waiting 2 hours is too long to evaluate the response to a new IV infusion.

items.q: Alex, a nurse, calls the health care provider about Ms. Martin’s uncontrolled postoperative pain and ends by saying, “Would you like to change Ms. Martin’s pain medication order?” Which part of SBAR is this statement?
items.a: Recommendation
items.ex: The recommendation states what the nurse is requesting or suggesting, here a change in the pain medication order.
w: Situation
The situation identifies the caller and patient and states the current problem.
Background
The background gives history, such as the diagnosis, surgery, and medication order.
Assessment
The assessment reports the nurse’s findings, such as pain rating and behavior.

alt.q: During an SBAR call, a nurse states, “Ms. Martin has ovarian cancer and had tumor debulking surgery yesterday. Her pain medicine is ordered every 6 hours as needed.” Which part of SBAR is this?
alt.a: Background
alt.ex: The background provides relevant history, including the diagnosis, surgery, and current medication order.
w: Situation
The situation identifies the caller and patient and describes the current problem.
Assessment
The assessment describes current findings, such as the pain rating and behavior.
Recommendation
The recommendation is the nurse’s request, such as changing the order.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a stable patient on a medical unit. Which task is appropriate to delegate to an AP?
items.a: Measuring the patient’s vital signs
items.ex: For a stable patient, the nurse can delegate vital signs to the AP while remaining responsible for ongoing assessment.
w: Teaching the patient about a new medication
Patient teaching is part of nursing judgment and is never delegated to APs.
Evaluating the patient’s response to pain medication
Evaluation is a step of the nursing process and cannot be delegated to APs.
Completing the patient’s admission assessment
Assessment requires nursing judgment and is never delegated to APs.

alt.q: A nurse is planning care for a stable patient. Which task should the nurse keep rather than delegate to an AP?
alt.a: Teaching the patient about wound care at home
alt.ex: Clinical reasoning, nursing judgment, and patient teaching are never delegated to APs.
w: Helping the patient with morning hygiene
APs attend to basic needs such as hygiene.
Assisting the patient with meals
Meal assistance is a basic need that APs can provide.
Walking the patient in the hallway
Ambulation is a basic need that APs can assist with.

items.q: A nurse learns that a newly hired AP measured a patient’s blood pressure incorrectly. Which approach to feedback is best?
items.a: Give specific feedback in private about how to avoid the mistake.
items.ex: Feedback given privately preserves dignity and is specific, focused on one issue, and on what can be changed.
w: Correct the AP in front of the patient so the error is fixed at once.
Feedback given in public does not preserve the staff member’s dignity.
Review all of the AP’s errors from the week in one meeting.
Effective feedback addresses only one issue at a time.
Ask another nurse to pass the feedback along to the AP.
Instructions and feedback are never given through another staff member.

alt.q: An AP’s performance has not met expectations on several shifts. Which response by the nurse is most appropriate?
alt.a: Review the procedure with the AP and offer a demonstration.
alt.ex: Poor performance often results from inadequate training or too many tasks, so the nurse reviews the procedure or recommends training.
w: Stop delegating to the AP and complete all tasks alone.
Withdrawing delegation does not address the likely cause, such as inadequate training.
Report the AP to the nurse manager without discussing it first.
The nurse first gives constructive feedback and addresses training needs.
Assign the AP additional tasks to build experience quickly.
Too many delegated tasks can itself cause poor performance.

items.q: During a busy shift, a nurse notices a colleague is overwhelmed, offers to help, and later speaks up when the colleague’s patient is at risk of harm. Which TeamSTEPPS® skill does this demonstrate?
items.a: Mutual support
items.ex: Mutual support means team members assist each other, give and receive feedback, and advocate when patient safety is threatened.
w: Situation monitoring
Situation monitoring is actively scanning behaviors and the environment to understand what is happening.
Team leadership
Team leadership ensures members understand goals and roles and manages conflict.
Communication
Communication is the verbal and nonverbal exchange of information among team members.

alt.q: Which action by a nurse best demonstrates the TeamSTEPPS® skill of mutual support?
alt.a: Advocating for a patient when safety is threatened
alt.ex: Mutual support includes assisting teammates, giving and receiving feedback, and advocating when patient safety is threatened.
w: Scanning the unit to anticipate teammates’ needs
Scanning to anticipate needs describes situation monitoring.
Making sure all members understand team goals
Ensuring members understand goals and roles describes team leadership.
Exchanging information clearly and accurately
Clear, accurate exchange of information describes the communication skill.

items.q: Which actions reflect the five rights of delegation? Select all that apply.
o: Delegate tasks only when the patient’s condition is stable
The right circumstance requires a stable patient.
Give a clear description of the task, its limits, and expectations
Right directions and communication require a clear, concise description of the task.
Follow up with the delegatee at the end of the activity
Right supervision and evaluation includes follow-up to evaluate outcomes.
Delegate any task the delegatee feels comfortable performing
The right task must be in the job description or agency policies and procedures.
Delegate patient teaching to an experienced AP
Patient teaching is nursing judgment and is never delegated to APs.
items.ex: The five rights are right task, circumstance, person, directions and communication, and supervision and evaluation.

alt.q: A nurse is deciding whether to delegate care to an AP. Which considerations are consistent with the five rights of delegation? Select all that apply.
o: The task is included in the AP’s job description or agency policy
The right task is in the job description or agency policies and procedures.
The AP has the knowledge and skills to perform the task
The right person has the required knowledge and skills.
The nurse is available to intervene if needed
Right supervision requires the nurse to be available and ready to intervene.
The patient’s condition has just changed
A change in condition requires the nurse to reassess; delegation needs a stable patient.
Instructions can be passed along by another nurse
Instructions are never given through another staff member.
alt.ex: Correct: The task is included in the AP’s job description or agency policy; The AP has the knowledge and skills to perform the task; The nurse is available to intervene if needed.

items.q: A nurse delegates ambulation of a patient to an AP. Which actions reflect effective communication with the AP? Select all that apply.
o: Describe the task, the desired outcome, and when it must be done
Clear directions include the task, desired outcome, and time frame.
Ask the AP to report back after completing the task
The nurse asks the AP to report back after the task is complete.
Begin the request with “please” and end with “thank you”
Courtesy helps APs feel they are part of the team.
Listen to the AP’s questions and requests for clarification
Listening attentively confirms the AP understands the request.
Relay the instructions through the charge nurse
Instructions are never given through another staff member.
Give feedback only if the outcome is poor
Feedback is always given, regardless of outcome, including thanks for a job well done.
items.ex: Effective delegation communication is clear, courteous, two-way, and includes reporting back and feedback.

alt.q: Which statements by a nurse delegating to an AP are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: “Please check his blood pressure before he stands.”
Specific instructions describe exactly what the AP needs to do.
“Please tell me when you have finished.”
Asking the AP to report back supports supervision and evaluation.
“Thank you for your help with Mr. Floyd.”
A thank-you makes the AP feel part of the team and increases future help.
“Teach him how to use his walker at home.”
Patient teaching is never delegated to APs.
“Decide whether he is well enough to keep walking.”
Clinical judgment and decision making are never delegated to APs.
alt.ex: Correct: “Please check his blood pressure before he stands.”; “Please tell me when you have finished.”; “Thank you for your help with Mr. Floyd.”

items.q: Which strategies support good time management? Select all that apply.
o: Make a to-do list that sequences nursing activities
A to-do list sequencing activities is a useful time-management skill.
Complete an activity with one patient before starting the next
Finishing one activity first makes care less fragmented and reduces errors.
Keep the work area clean and clutter free
A clean, uncluttered work area is a time-management strategy.
Decrease interruptions while completing tasks
Reducing interruptions helps the nurse complete tasks efficiently.
Plan less time for activities that need help from other staff
Activities needing other staff usually take longer because of their schedules.
Chat with colleagues during medication administration
Socializing should not interrupt important activities like medication administration.
items.ex: Lists, finishing tasks, an organized work area, and fewer interruptions support effective time management.

alt.q: Which actions reflect the principles of time management? Select all that apply.
o: Reflect at the end of the day on how well time was used
Evaluation means reflecting on how effectively time was used.
Keep track of time spent on different activities
Time analysis tracks how time is used to identify areas to improve.
Plan time to help colleagues that fits the care schedule
Interruption control includes planning help that complements your schedule.
Schedule teaching while the patient is in pain to save time
A patient in pain or nauseated is not ready for teaching.
Keep difficulties to yourself rather than involve an instructor
Difficulties are discussed with an instructor or experienced staff member.
alt.ex: Correct: Reflect at the end of the day on how well time was used; Keep track of time spent on different activities; Plan time to help colleagues that fits the care schedule.

items.q: Setting priorities is a dynamic process, and priorities change as a patient’s condition changes.
items.a: True
items.ex: Priorities do not remain stable; the nurse stays flexible and revises them as patient needs change.
items.ww: Priorities are not fixed for the shift; they change frequently with the patient’s condition.

alt.q: Once priorities are set from the hand-off report, they should remain the same for the rest of the shift.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Priority setting is dynamic; priorities change often as patients’ conditions change.
alt.ww: Hand-off report helps set initial priorities, but they must be revised as conditions change.

items.q: When a nurse delegates a task, accountability for that task transfers to the person who performs it.
items.a: False
items.ex: Delegation transfers responsibility and authority for the task, but the delegating nurse remains accountable.
items.ww: The textbook states that even though delegation transfers responsibility and authority, the nurse remains accountable.

alt.q: Delegation transfers responsibility and authority for a task, but the nurse who delegates remains accountable for it.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The nurse who delegates stays accountable for the delegated task and must supervise and evaluate it.
alt.ww: Accountability does not move to the delegatee; it stays with the delegating nurse.

items.q: Opportunities for professional learning occur with each patient interaction and each encounter with a colleague.
items.a: True
items.ex: A leader recognizes there is always something new to learn, both formally and informally, from patients and colleagues.
items.ww: Learning is not limited to classes; everyday interactions with patients and colleagues also build knowledge.

alt.q: Lifelong learning comes mainly from formal classes, so informal encounters with colleagues add little to a nurse’s competence.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses actively pursue both formal and informal learning, valuing what colleagues share in every encounter.
alt.ww: Learning also occurs with each patient interaction and each encounter with colleagues, not only in classes.

items.q: The CUS tool communicates a change in a patient’s condition: I am Concerned, I am Uncomfortable, and this is a [[Safety]] issue.
items.ex: CUS is a TeamSTEPPS® tool for voicing worries about a patient using escalating statements ending with a safety concern.

alt.q: When using the CUS tool, a nurse states, “I am Concerned, I am [[Uncomfortable]], and this is a Safety issue.”
alt.ex: CUS is a TeamSTEPPS® tool for voicing worries about a patient using escalating statements ending with a safety concern.

items.q: In priority setting, which level comes right after “Airway, breathing, circulation, vital sign, and life-threatening laboratory value problems”?

w: Long-term health management, rest, and family coping issues
That's level 3 of 3.

w: Long-term health management, rest, and family coping issues
That's level 3 of 3.

alt.q: In priority setting, which level comes right before “Long-term health management, rest, and family coping issues”?
alt.a: Mental status changes, untreated medical issues, acute pain, and acute elimination problems
alt.ex: First-level ABC+VL problems are addressed immediately, then second-level problems, then third-level problems.
w: Airway, breathing, circulation, vital sign, and life-threatening laboratory value problems
That's level 1 of 3.

ord.q: Put these categories of patient problems in the order a nurse should address them when setting priorities.
items: Airway, breathing, circulation, vital sign, and life-threatening laboratory value problems
Mental status changes, untreated medical issues, acute pain, and acute elimination problems
Long-term health management, rest, and family coping issues
ord.ex: First-level ABC+VL problems are addressed immediately, then second-level problems, then third-level problems.

items.q: How do ethical issues differ from legal issues in health care?
items.a: Ethics has a broader focus on behavior and character than the law.
items.ex: Laws are concrete and publicly determined, whereas ethics has a broader base of interest centered on behavior and character.
w: Ethics relies on concrete rules that are publicly determined.
Concrete, publicly determined rules describe laws, not ethics.
Ethical violations always lead to a public penalty such as a fine.
Public consequences such as tickets or jail time follow from breaking laws.
Ethics applies only to decisions that courts have already reviewed.
Ethics refers broadly to behavior and character, not only to court-reviewed matters.

alt.q: Which feature is characteristic of a legal issue rather than an ethical issue?
alt.a: It is resolved by reference to concrete, publicly determined rules.
alt.ex: Legal issues are settled by laws that are usually concrete and publicly determined, and breaking them has public consequences.
w: It concerns the ideals of right and wrong behavior and character.
The ideals of right and wrong behavior and character are the concern of ethics.
It reflects a person’s judgment about behavior based on beliefs.
Judgment about behavior based on specific beliefs describes morals.
It reflects deeply held personal beliefs about the worth of an idea.
Deeply held beliefs about worth describe values, not legal issues.

items.q: A nursing student asks how the terms morals and ethics differ. Which explanation is accurate?
items.a: Morals are judgments about behavior based on beliefs; ethics is the study of ideals of right and wrong.
items.ex: Although the terms are often used interchangeably, morals refer to belief-based judgments and ethics to the study of right and wrong behavior.
w: Morals are the study of right and wrong; ethics are judgments about one person’s behavior.
This reverses the definitions; ethics is the study and morals are the judgments.
Morals are publicly determined rules; ethics are private feelings about behavior.
Publicly determined rules describe laws, and ethics is a field of study, not private feelings.
Morals apply only to health care; ethics apply only outside of health care.
Neither term is limited to a setting; bioethics is the branch of ethics within health care.

alt.q: Which term refers to the study of the ideals of right and wrong behavior?
alt.a: Ethics
alt.ex: Ethics is the study of the ideals of right and wrong behavior and concerns our obligations to individuals, groups, and society.
w: Morals
Morals refer to judgment about behavior based on specific beliefs.
Values
Values are deeply held beliefs about the worth of an idea, custom, or object.
Laws
Laws are concrete, publicly determined rules with public consequences when broken.

items.q: Which development prompted the growth of bioethics as a field of study in the United States?
items.a: Scarce kidneys for transplant compared with the number of patients in need
items.ex: When kidney transplant procedures were perfected, too few kidneys were available, and this scarcity became an immediate ethical concern.
w: Passage of federal laws protecting the privacy of health records
Privacy legislation such as HIPAA came much later and is not described as the origin of bioethics.
Creation of whistle-blower protections for health care employees
Whistle-blower protections relate to professional autonomy, not to the emergence of bioethics.
Introduction of the informed consent signature for surgery
Informed consent shows respect for autonomy but is not described as starting bioethics.

alt.q: Which statement best describes bioethics?
alt.a: A branch of ethics within health care that addresses issues raised by medical technology
alt.ex: Bioethics is the branch of ethics within health care; changing technologies such as organ transplant raise questions it addresses.
w: A set of state laws that define penalties for unsafe clinical practice
Laws with penalties are legal matters; bioethics is a branch of ethics.
A personal judgment about behavior based on one’s religious beliefs
Judgment about behavior based on specific beliefs describes morals.
A national set of patient safety goals for health care agencies
National patient safety guidelines are set by The Joint Commission, not by bioethics.

items.q: Before obtaining a patient’s blood pressure, the nurse explains the procedure and asks whether the patient has any questions. Which ethical principle is the nurse demonstrating?
items.a: Autonomy
items.ex: Explaining nursing procedures and supporting patients’ questions are ways nurses show respect for patient autonomy.
w: Justice
Justice concerns fairness and the distribution of resources.
Nonmaleficence
Nonmaleficence is the avoidance of harm, not involving the patient in care.
Fidelity
Fidelity is faithfulness and keeping promises, such as following through on a care plan.

alt.q: A patient asks the nurse why a new medication has been prescribed before taking it. Which response by the nurse best respects the patient’s autonomy?
alt.a: “Let me explain what this medication is for so you can decide with me.”
alt.ex: Respecting autonomy means supporting patients who raise questions and making sure they get the information they request.
w: “Your health care provider knows best, so you should just take it.”
This reflects paternalistic care, which respect for autonomy moves away from.
“It is better if you do not worry about the details of your care.”
Withholding requested information fails to include the patient in decisions about care.
“I will ask your family to decide whether you should take it.”
Shifting the decision to family bypasses the patient’s right to make autonomous decisions.

items.q: A nurse is assigned to assist with a procedure that conflicts with the nurse’s religious beliefs. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Request reassignment through agency policy while ensuring another qualified nurse provides care.
items.ex: Agencies respect professional autonomy by reassigning duties, but the patient must be protected from abandonment and care must not be compromised.
w: Leave the procedure room once it begins and notify the charge nurse afterward.
Leaving during care risks abandonment; fidelity requires arranging an equally qualified replacement first.
Complete the assignment without telling anyone about the conflict.
Agency policies exist to accommodate such conflicts, so the nurse can raise it and seek reassignment.
Ask the patient to choose another treatment that fits the nurse’s beliefs.
Pressuring the patient to change treatment violates the patient’s autonomy.

alt.q: Which statement best describes how agencies show respect for the professional autonomy of a nurse whose personal beliefs conflict with an assigned duty?
alt.a: They reassign the duty in a way that protects the patient from abandonment.
alt.ex: Agency policies accommodate professional autonomy by reassigning duties while ensuring patient care is not compromised.
w: They require the nurse to perform the duty regardless of personal belief.
Agencies respect professional autonomy by finding a way to reassign duties.
They allow the nurse to leave the patient as soon as the conflict arises.
Reassignment must protect the patient from abandonment.
They let the nurse decide which patients the agency will accept for care.
Professional autonomy does not extend to choosing which patients the agency serves.

items.q: A nurse believes a unit practice is unsafe but fears retaliation for reporting it. Which agency feature supports this nurse in making a report?
items.a: An anonymous reporting system with whistle-blower protections
items.ex: Anonymous reporting and whistle-blower protections prohibit retaliation for legitimate safety reports and express respect for professional autonomy.
w: A just distribution of scarce resources across hospital units
Distribution of scarce resources relates to justice, not to protecting employees who report.
An informed consent form signed by the patient before care
Informed consent shows respect for patient autonomy, not protection for reporting staff.
A policy requiring the nurse to report only to the patient’s family
Reporting safety concerns to family does not protect the nurse or address agency practice.

alt.q: Which concept do agency whistle-blower protections represent, according to the textbook?
alt.a: Respect for professional autonomy
alt.ex: Protections that prohibit retaliation for legitimate safety reports express respect for the autonomy of health care professionals.
w: Respect for patient confidentiality
Confidentiality concerns protecting patients’ private health information.
Commitment to distributive justice
Justice concerns fairness and distribution of health care resources.
Commitment to paternalistic care
Paternalism, where providers make all decisions, is what autonomy moves away from.

items.q: What does the nurse’s agreement to act with beneficence imply?
items.a: The best interests of the patient remain more important than self-interest.
items.ex: Beneficence means taking positive actions to help others, so the patient’s best interests outweigh the nurse’s self-interest.
w: The nurse avoids every treatment that could cause the patient discomfort.
Avoiding harm is nonmaleficence, which still requires balancing risks and benefits.
The nurse distributes care equally among all patients on the unit.
Fair distribution of resources relates to justice.
The nurse keeps every promise made to the patient during the shift.
Keeping promises is fidelity.

alt.q: Which principle refers to taking positive actions to help others?
alt.a: Beneficence
alt.ex: Beneficence, fundamental to nursing and medicine, refers to taking positive actions to help others.
w: Nonmaleficence
Nonmaleficence is the avoidance of harm or hurt.
Autonomy
Autonomy is freedom from external control.
Accountability
Accountability means answering for one’s own actions.

items.q: A patient is considering a bone marrow transplant that may cure the disease but involves periods of suffering. Which principle most directly requires the team to weigh the risks and benefits to do the least harm possible?
items.a: Nonmaleficence
items.ex: Nonmaleficence is the commitment to avoid harm, which requires balancing risks and benefits while doing the least harm possible.
w: Justice
Justice addresses fairness and distribution of resources rather than the harm of a treatment.
Fidelity
Fidelity concerns faithfulness and keeping promises.
Confidentiality
Confidentiality concerns keeping patients’ health information private.

alt.q: How does the principle of nonmaleficence guide health care professionals?
alt.a: They balance the risks and benefits of care while doing the least harm possible.
alt.ex: Ethical practice requires an equal commitment to do no harm, so professionals try to minimize harm while weighing benefit.
w: They refuse to offer any treatment that causes suffering to the patient.
Treatments such as transplant cause suffering yet may be offered after weighing risks and benefits.
They allocate scarce treatments to patients who have earned them.
Allocation of scarce resources is a question of justice.
They keep the patient’s health information private from others.
Keeping information private is confidentiality.

items.q: A committee is discussing how to allocate a limited number of donor organs among patients waiting for transplant. Which ethical principle is central to this discussion?
items.a: Justice
items.ex: Justice refers to fairness and the distribution of resources and is cited in discussions of organ transplants and scarce services.
w: Fidelity
Fidelity is faithfulness and keeping promises to patients, the agency, and oneself.
Autonomy
Autonomy is freedom from external control, not the distribution of scarce resources.
Beneficence
Beneficence is taking positive actions to help others.

alt.q: Why is the principle of justice described as open to interpretation?
alt.a: People interpret fairness differently, such as by earned access, equal shares, or need.
alt.ex: Justice raises questions of whether resources go to those who earned them, are shared equally, or go to those in greater need.
w: Laws about health insurance change frequently, such as by state, year, or agency.
Justice is an ethical principle; its ambiguity comes from differing views of fairness, not changing laws.
Patients define their own goals differently, such as by values, culture, or family.
Differing patient goals relate to autonomy, not to how fairness in distribution is interpreted.
Agencies report safety errors differently, such as by phone, form, or e-mail.
Error reporting relates to just culture, not to differing interpretations of fairness.

items.q: A nurse reports a near-miss medication error on a unit that practices a just culture. Which response by the nurse manager reflects this approach?
items.a: “Thank you for reporting it; let’s look at what in the system contributed to it.”
items.ex: Just culture promotes open discussion without fear of retaliation and withholds blame so system issues can be investigated.
w: “This will be noted in your file as a disciplinary warning.”
Disciplining a nurse for reporting discourages open discussion, the opposite of just culture.
“Since no harm occurred, there is no need to discuss it further.”
Just culture includes errors that nearly occur, so near misses are discussed openly.
“Please keep this between us so the staff do not find out.”
Just culture fosters open discussion so the team can design systems that prevent harm.

alt.q: What is the main purpose of withholding blame in a just culture?
alt.a: To allow system issues that contributed to an error to be investigated
alt.ex: Blame is withheld so the system’s contributions to an error can be examined and new systems designed to prevent harm.
w: To protect the agency from legal consequences of the error
Just culture aims at open learning about errors, not legal protection of the agency.
To keep information about errors confidential from staff
Just culture promotes open discussion of errors among the team.
To ensure that the patient is not told about the error
Just culture concerns open discussion, not withholding information from patients.

items.q: A nurse assesses a patient’s pain and tells the patient about a plan to manage it. To honor the standard of fidelity, what should the nurse do next?
items.a: Begin the planned interventions as soon as possible and monitor the patient’s response.
items.ex: Fidelity, the agreement to keep promises, encourages starting the pain interventions promptly and monitoring the response.
w: Wait until the next scheduled assessment to begin the planned interventions.
Delaying the plan does not keep the promise made to the patient.
Ask the family to decide whether the pain plan should be started.
Fidelity concerns the nurse following through, and the decision belongs with the patient.
Document the plan and leave its implementation for the next shift.
Passing the plan on without acting fails to honor the promise to the patient.

alt.q: A nurse must remove herself from a patient’s care because of a personal conflict. Which action best demonstrates fidelity to the patient?
alt.a: Finding an equally qualified professional to provide the care before stepping away
alt.ex: Fidelity demands that the nurse not abandon the patient but find an equally qualified professional to provide the care.
w: Telling the patient to request a different nurse from the charge nurse
Placing the burden on the patient risks a gap in care and abandonment.
Leaving the assignment once the conflict is documented in the record
Leaving without a qualified replacement abandons the patient.
Continuing care but limiting contact to required tasks only
Fidelity requires excellent care for all patients, including those whose values differ.

items.q: Which actions by a nurse demonstrate respect for patient autonomy? Select all that apply.
o: Explaining a procedure before administering a medication
Explaining nursing procedures is one way nurses show respect for autonomy.
Helping a patient articulate preferences, values, and goals
Clarifying what is important to patients is a key step in autonomous decisions.
Ensuring a patient receives the information requested about a procedure
Supporting patients’ questions and requests for information respects autonomy.
Choosing the treatment the team believes is best without patient input
Making decisions without the patient reflects paternalism, which autonomy rejects.
Limiting information about risks so the patient does not become anxious
Informed consent requires informing patients of risks and benefits.
items.ex: Respect for autonomy includes patients in all decisions about their care through information, explanation, and clarifying goals.

alt.q: A patient is preparing to consent to surgery. Which elements of the informed consent process reflect respect for the patient’s autonomy? Select all that apply.
o: Informing the patient about the risks and benefits of options
The team’s role is to inform patients of risks and benefits.
Planning care with the patient that matches the patient’s goals
The plan is determined with the patient to match the patient’s goals and values.
Documenting the patient’s consent with the patient’s signature
For surgery and procedures, consent is often documented by the patient’s signature.
Allowing the surgical team to choose the procedure for the patient
Rather than the team choosing, the patient decides with the team.
Asking a co-worker to sign for the patient to save time
Consent is the patient’s own decision and signature.
alt.ex: Informed consent respects autonomy because the patient, informed of risks and benefits, determines the plan of care with the team.

items.q: Which actions demonstrate a nurse’s fidelity? Select all that apply.
o: Finding an equally qualified nurse before withdrawing from a patient’s care
Fidelity demands that the nurse not abandon the patient.
Seeking to correct an agency procedure that is not appropriate
Fidelity to the agency includes improving policies that are inappropriate.
Attending continuing education and seeking mentoring
Fidelity to oneself includes attending to needs for support, mentoring, and education.
Giving less attention to a patient whose lifestyle the nurse disapproves of
Fidelity means providing excellent care to all patients regardless of their choices.
Ignoring agency policies the nurse personally finds inconvenient
Fidelity to the agency means following its policies or working to correct them.
items.ex: Fidelity is faithfulness to patients, to the employing agency, and to oneself.

alt.q: To whom does the nurse owe a duty of fidelity, according to the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: The patients the nurse cares for
Nurses must be faithful to their patients, including keeping promises.
The health care agency that employs the nurse
Fidelity to the agency means following or improving its policies.
The nurse personally
Fidelity to oneself is honored by meeting needs for support and education.
Only patients who share the nurse’s values
Fidelity applies to all patients, including those whose values differ.
Only the health care provider who wrote the orders
The textbook names patients, the agency, and oneself, not a single provider.
alt.ex: The duty of fidelity extends to patients, the employing agency, and oneself.

items.q: Which issues commonly involve the principle of justice? Select all that apply.
o: Allocation of donor organs for transplant
Organ transplants are among issues that cite justice.
Access to health insurance
Health insurance discussions involve fair access to care.
Locations of hospitals and the services they offer
Hospital locations and services affect the distribution of resources.
Explaining a dressing change before starting it
Explaining procedures shows respect for autonomy.
Returning promptly with promised pain medication
Keeping promises reflects fidelity.
items.ex: Justice concerns fairness and the distribution of scarce services and resources.

alt.q: A nurse joins a community discussion about health care reform. Which questions reflect the principle of justice? Select all that apply.
o: Should resources go to those who have earned them?
Whether resources should be earned is one interpretation of justice.
Should health care resources be distributed equally?
Equal distribution is another interpretation of fairness.
Should those with greater need receive more resources?
Distribution by need is also debated under justice.
Should patients sign consent before diagnostic procedures?
Consent concerns respect for patient autonomy.
Should nurses keep promises made to patients?
Keeping promises reflects fidelity.
alt.ex: Justice questions ask how scarce resources should be fairly distributed, by merit, equally, or by need.

items.q: Respect for patient autonomy reflects a movement toward paternalistic care in which health care providers make all decisions.
items.a: False
items.ex: Respect for autonomy reflects a movement away from paternalism; involving patients in decisions is now standard practice.
items.ww: The statement is false because autonomy moves away from, not toward, providers making all decisions.

alt.q: Involving patients in decisions about their care is now standard practice and a key feature of person-centered care.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Respect for patient autonomy, including patients in all aspects of care, is a key feature of person-centered care.
alt.ww: It is not false, because the textbook states involving patients in decisions is now standard practice.

items.q: Ethical health care practice involves an equal commitment to do no harm as well as the will to do good.
items.a: True
items.ex: Nonmaleficence requires not only the will to do good but an equal commitment to do no harm.
items.ww: It is not false, because the textbook pairs beneficence with an equal commitment to avoid harm.

alt.q: Nonmaleficence requires health care professionals to avoid any treatment that could cause a patient suffering.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nonmaleficence means balancing risks and benefits to do the least harm possible, even when a treatment involves suffering.
alt.ww: It is not true, because treatments like bone marrow transplant cause suffering yet may offer a chance at cure.

items.q: Autonomy in health care applies only to patients and not to health care professionals.
items.a: False
items.ex: Autonomy also applies to agency respect for health care professionals, such as reassignment and whistle-blower protections.
items.ww: The statement is false because the textbook describes respect for professional autonomy as well as patient autonomy.

alt.q: Agency policies that reassign a nurse’s duties when they conflict with a personal belief show respect for professional autonomy.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Reassignment that still protects the patient from abandonment is an expression of respect for professional autonomy.
alt.ww: It is not false, because such policies are the textbook’s example of respect for professional autonomy.

items.q: [[Autonomy]] refers to freedom from external control.
items.ex: Autonomy means freedom from external control and in health care applies to respect for patients and professionals.

alt.q: Respecting a patient’s [[autonomy]] means including the patient in decisions about all aspects of care.
alt.ex: Autonomy means freedom from external control and in health care applies to respect for patients and professionals.

items.q: [[Fidelity]] refers to faithfulness or the agreement to keep promises.
items.ex: Fidelity is faithfulness, owed to patients, to the employing agency, and to oneself.

alt.q: When a nurse follows through promptly on a promised pain plan, the nurse honors the principle of [[fidelity]].
alt.ex: Fidelity is faithfulness, owed to patients, to the employing agency, and to oneself.

items.q: What does Autonomy mean?
items.a: Freedom from external control
items.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.
w: Taking positive actions to help others
That goes with Beneficence.
Avoidance of harm or hurt
That goes with Nonmaleficence.
Fairness and the distribution of resources
That goes with Justice.

alt.q: What does Beneficence mean?
alt.a: Taking positive actions to help others
alt.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.
w: Freedom from external control
That goes with Autonomy.
Avoidance of harm or hurt
That goes with Nonmaleficence.
Fairness and the distribution of resources
That goes with Justice.

alt.q: What does Nonmaleficence mean?
alt.a: Avoidance of harm or hurt
alt.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.
w: Freedom from external control
That goes with Autonomy.
Taking positive actions to help others
That goes with Beneficence.
Fairness and the distribution of resources
That goes with Justice.

alt.q: What does Justice mean?
alt.a: Fairness and the distribution of resources
alt.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.
w: Freedom from external control
That goes with Autonomy.
Taking positive actions to help others
That goes with Beneficence.
Avoidance of harm or hurt
That goes with Nonmaleficence.

alt.q: What does Fidelity mean?
alt.a: Faithfulness or the agreement to keep promises
alt.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.
w: Freedom from external control
That goes with Autonomy.
Taking positive actions to help others
That goes with Beneficence.
Avoidance of harm or hurt
That goes with Nonmaleficence.

alt.q: Which term means “Freedom from external control”?
alt.a: Autonomy
alt.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.
w: Beneficence
Beneficence: Taking positive actions to help others.
Nonmaleficence
Nonmaleficence: Avoidance of harm or hurt.
Justice
Justice: Fairness and the distribution of resources.

alt.q: Which term means “Taking positive actions to help others”?
alt.a: Beneficence
alt.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.
w: Autonomy
Autonomy: Freedom from external control.
Nonmaleficence
Nonmaleficence: Avoidance of harm or hurt.
Justice
Justice: Fairness and the distribution of resources.

alt.q: Which term means “Avoidance of harm or hurt”?
alt.a: Nonmaleficence
alt.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.
w: Autonomy
Autonomy: Freedom from external control.
Beneficence
Beneficence: Taking positive actions to help others.
Justice
Justice: Fairness and the distribution of resources.

alt.q: Which term means “Fairness and the distribution of resources”?
alt.a: Justice
alt.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.
w: Autonomy
Autonomy: Freedom from external control.
Beneficence
Beneficence: Taking positive actions to help others.
Nonmaleficence
Nonmaleficence: Avoidance of harm or hurt.

alt.q: Which term means “Faithfulness or the agreement to keep promises”?
alt.a: Fidelity
alt.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.
w: Autonomy
Autonomy: Freedom from external control.
Beneficence
Beneficence: Taking positive actions to help others.
Nonmaleficence
Nonmaleficence: Avoidance of harm or hurt.

mt.q: Match each ethical principle with its meaning.
pairs: Taking positive actions to help others
Fairness and the distribution of resources
Faithfulness or the agreement to keep promises
mt.ex: These five principles are applied during the ethical decision-making process.

items.q: Which statement best defines a code of ethics?
items.a: A set of guiding principles that all members of a profession accept
items.ex: A code of ethics is a collective statement of a group’s expectations and standards of behavior that all members accept.
w: A set of laws that impose public penalties on professionals who break them
Rules with public penalties are laws, not a code of ethics.
A personal belief about the worth of an idea, a custom, or an object
A deeply held personal belief about worth is a value.
A set of national patient safety guidelines issued for health care agencies
National patient safety guidelines are established by The Joint Commission.

alt.q: A collective statement of a profession’s expectations and standards of behavior is called a:
alt.a: Code of ethics
alt.ex: A code of ethics is the profession’s collective statement of the group’s expectations and standards of behavior.
w: Bill of rights
A bill of rights lists entitlements of a group rather than a profession’s standards of behavior.
Scope of practice
Scope of practice defines legal limits of practice, not a collective ethical statement.
Values clarification
Values clarification is a process of identifying values, not a profession’s code.

items.q: Which organization established and periodically revises the Code of Ethics for Nurses in the United States?
items.a: American Nurses Association
items.ex: The ANA established its first Code of Ethics for Nurses and has continued to review and revise it periodically.
w: The Joint Commission
The Joint Commission establishes national patient safety guidelines, not the nursing code.
U.S. Department of Health and Human Services
DHHS is associated with HIPAA privacy regulation, not the nursing code.
State boards of nursing
State boards regulate licensure; the Code of Ethics for Nurses is from the ANA.

alt.q: Which statement about the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses is accurate?
alt.a: It has been reviewed and revised periodically since it was established.
alt.ex: The ANA has continued to review and revise the Code periodically since establishing its first version.
w: It has remained unchanged since it was first established.
The ANA has revised the Code periodically.
It is federal legislation enforced with fines for violations.
Federal legislation with fines describes HIPAA, not the Code.
It applies only to nurses in management positions.
A code of ethics is accepted by all members of a profession.

items.q: Which key principles are named in the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses?
items.a: Advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality
items.ex: The textbook identifies advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality as key principles of the Code.
w: Utilitarianism, deontology, casuistry, and feminist ethics
These are philosophical approaches to ethics, not the Code’s key principles.
Delegation, prioritization, documentation, and supervision
These are nursing management skills, not the key ethical principles of the Code.
Diagnosis, prescribing, licensure, and reimbursement
These are practice and regulatory matters, not the Code’s key principles.

alt.q: Which principle is identified as a key principle of the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses?
alt.a: Advocacy
alt.ex: Advocacy, along with responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality, is a key principle in the Code.
w: Paternalism
Paternalism, where providers make all decisions, is what modern ethics moves away from.
Utilitarianism
Utilitarianism is a philosophical approach to ethics, not a key Code principle.
Retaliation
Retaliation against reporting employees is prohibited by whistle-blower protections.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse that he no longer wants to continue a treatment, but the team keeps encouraging him to proceed. Which action by the nurse best demonstrates advocacy?
items.a: Share the patient’s wishes with the team and support his right to refuse treatment.
items.ex: Nurses advocate for patients’ rights, including the right to refuse treatment, and help others understand the patient’s view.
w: Encourage the patient to follow the team’s recommendation without question.
Pressuring the patient does not advocate for his right to refuse treatment.
Tell the patient that refusing treatment is not permitted in the hospital.
Patients have a right to refuse treatment that nurses advocate for.
Avoid discussing the patient’s wishes so the team is not disrupted.
Advocacy requires applying the nurse’s knowledge on the patient’s behalf.

alt.q: Why is the nurse in a unique position to advocate for patients?
alt.a: The nurse’s special relationship with patients gives insight into the patient’s point of view.
alt.ex: The nurse’s relationship with patients provides role-specific knowledge to make a unique contribution to understanding the patient’s view.
w: The nurse has legal authority to make treatment decisions for patients.
Advocacy supports patients’ own rights rather than giving nurses decision authority.
The nurse is the only team member who can access patient records.
Others involved in care also access records; this is not why nurses advocate uniquely.
The nurse sets national safety standards for the health care agency.
National safety standards are set by agencies such as The Joint Commission.

items.q: A patient’s neighbor calls the unit and asks the nurse how the patient is doing after surgery. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “I can only share a patient’s information with those involved in the patient’s care.”
items.ex: HIPAA prohibits sharing a patient’s medical or personal information with anyone not involved in the patient’s care.
w: “The patient is recovering well and should go home in a day or two.”
Sharing condition details with someone not involved in care violates confidentiality.
“I can give you the information if you confirm the patient’s birth date.”
Knowing personal details does not give the neighbor a right to know.
“Since you are a neighbor, I can tell you the patient’s general condition.”
Being a neighbor does not make the caller involved in the patient’s care.

alt.q: A nurse on another unit asks about a friend who is a patient on your unit. The nurse is not involved in the friend’s care. Which action is correct?
alt.a: Decline to share the information because the nurse has no right to know.
alt.ex: Under HIPAA’s right to know, information is shared only with those involved in the patient’s care, regardless of profession.
w: Share the information because the colleague is also a licensed nurse.
Being a nurse does not create a right to know without involvement in the care.
Share only the diagnosis because it is not considered personal information.
Medical condition information is protected and cannot be shared with uninvolved people.
Allow the colleague to read the record while the nurse is present.
Access to medical records is also regulated by HIPAA and limited to those involved in care.

items.q: A nurse is asked to perform a procedure the nurse has not done before and feels unsure of the steps. Which action best reflects professional responsibility?
items.a: Seek guidance before performing the procedure.
items.ex: Responsibility includes maintaining competence and seeking guidance when uncertain of one’s skills and knowledge.
w: Perform the procedure and review the steps afterward.
Acting without needed knowledge risks harm and does not meet professional responsibility.
Delegate the procedure to assistive personnel instead.
The nurse remains responsible for delegated tasks and must not hand off uncertainty.
Postpone the procedure without notifying anyone.
Following through on obligations is part of responsibility; delaying silently does not.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse best demonstrates responsibility as described in the Code of Ethics?
alt.a: “I keep my skills current and apply our agency’s policies to my care.”
alt.ex: Responsibility includes maintaining competence and applying the workplace’s policies and procedures to care.
w: “Once I delegate a task, the outcome is no longer my concern.”
Nurses are responsible for the tasks they delegate to others.
“I protect patients’ privacy by limiting who can see their records.”
Protecting privacy describes confidentiality rather than responsibility.
“I speak up for patients’ rights when they cannot speak for themselves.”
Speaking up for patients’ rights describes advocacy.

items.q: A nurse delegates obtaining vital signs to assistive personnel (AP). Which statement about the nurse’s responsibility is accurate?
items.a: The nurse remains responsible for the tasks delegated to the AP.
items.ex: As a nurse you are responsible for your actions, the care you provide, and the tasks that you delegate to others.
w: The AP becomes solely responsible for the task once it is assigned.
Delegation does not remove the nurse’s responsibility for the task.
The nurse manager becomes responsible for all delegated tasks.
The delegating nurse, not the manager, is responsible for tasks the nurse delegates.
Responsibility for delegated tasks shifts to the health care provider.
The nurse who delegates retains responsibility for the delegated tasks.

alt.q: Which term refers to a willingness to respect one’s professional obligations and to follow through?
alt.a: Responsibility
alt.ex: Responsibility is the willingness to respect professional obligations and follow through, including for delegated tasks.
w: Accountability
Accountability refers to answering for your own actions.
Advocacy
Advocacy is applying one’s skills and knowledge for the benefit of another.
Confidentiality
Confidentiality is the obligation to respect patient privacy.

items.q: What does accountability mean in professional nursing practice?
items.a: Answering for your own actions so they are explainable to patients and employers
items.ex: Accountability means answering for your own actions and ensuring your professional actions are explainable to patients and your employer.
w: Applying your skills and knowledge for the benefit of another person
Applying skills for another’s benefit is advocacy.
Respecting each patient’s right to keep health information private
Respecting privacy is confidentiality.
Keeping promises made to patients, the agency, and yourself
Keeping promises is fidelity.

alt.q: After a patient questions why a dose was held, the nurse explains the assessment findings and reasoning behind the decision. Which principle does this demonstrate?
alt.a: Accountability
alt.ex: Explaining one’s professional actions to patients reflects accountability, answering for one’s own actions.
w: Justice
Justice concerns fairness and distribution of resources.
Advocacy
Advocacy applies the nurse’s knowledge for the patient’s benefit, not explaining one’s own actions.
Confidentiality
Confidentiality concerns protecting a patient’s private information.

items.q: How do health care agencies exercise accountability?
items.a: By monitoring individual and agency adherence to national standards
items.ex: Agencies exercise accountability by monitoring adherence to national standards established by agencies such as The Joint Commission.
w: By reassigning duties that conflict with an employee’s beliefs
Reassignment of duties reflects respect for professional autonomy.
By withholding blame when errors or near misses occur
Withholding blame to examine system issues describes a just culture.
By allowing employees to report unsafe practices anonymously
Anonymous reporting supports professional autonomy and whistle-blower protection.

alt.q: What is the role of The Joint Commission (TJC) as described in the chapter?
alt.a: Establishing national patient safety guidelines for consistent, effective practice
alt.ex: TJC establishes national patient safety guidelines to ensure patient and workplace safety through consistent, effective nursing practices.
w: Writing and revising the Code of Ethics for Nurses
The ANA established and revises the Code of Ethics for Nurses.
Fining individuals who share protected health information
Fines for privacy violations are established by HIPAA legislation.
Setting standards for interprofessional communication
The ANA sets standards for collaborative interprofessional communication.

items.q: Why is confidentiality considered essential in nursing practice?
items.a: It is a fundamental part of the trusting nurse–patient relationship.
items.ex: Confidentiality, the team’s obligation to respect patient privacy, is fundamental to the trusting relationship between nurse and patient.
w: It allows the nurse to share information freely with the patient’s friends.
Confidentiality limits sharing to those involved in the patient’s care.
It ensures scarce resources are distributed fairly among patients.
Fair distribution of resources is justice.
It allows the nurse to make decisions on the patient’s behalf.
Making decisions for patients is paternalism, not confidentiality.

alt.q: Which term refers to the health care team’s obligation to respect patient privacy?
alt.a: Confidentiality
alt.ex: Confidentiality is the team’s obligation to respect the patient’s right to keep personal health information private.
w: Fidelity
Fidelity is faithfulness and keeping promises.
Accountability
Accountability is answering for one’s own actions.
Beneficence
Beneficence is taking positive actions to help others.

items.q: Which statement accurately describes the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA)?
items.a: It is federal legislation that mandates protection of patients’ personal health information.
items.ex: HIPAA mandates confidentiality, defines patients’ privacy rights, and establishes fines for violations.
w: It is a voluntary guideline that agencies may choose to follow.
HIPAA is federal legislation that mandates confidentiality and sets fines.
It is the nursing profession’s code describing duties to society.
The ANA Code of Ethics describes the nurse’s duties to the profession and society.
It is a set of national goals for preventing medication errors.
National patient safety guidelines are established by The Joint Commission.

alt.q: What does HIPAA call the principle that patient information may be shared only with those involved in the patient’s care?
alt.a: The right to know
alt.ex: HIPAA calls the limit on sharing information to those involved in the patient’s care the “right to know.”
w: The right to refuse
The right to refuse treatment is a patient right nurses advocate for.
The just culture
Just culture refers to open discussion of errors without fear of retaliation.
The informed consent
Informed consent is how patients agree to treatment after learning risks and benefits.

items.q: Which actions demonstrate a nurse’s professional responsibility? Select all that apply.
o: Maintaining competence to provide care
Responsibility includes maintaining competence.
Seeking guidance when uncertain of skills or knowledge
Seeking guidance when unsure is part of responsibility.
Applying the workplace’s policies and procedures to care
Applying agency policies demonstrates responsibility.
Accepting responsibility for tasks delegated to others
Nurses are responsible for the tasks they delegate.
Performing unfamiliar skills without help to avoid delays
Responsibility requires seeking guidance when uncertain.
Letting assistive personnel answer for tasks the nurse delegated
The delegating nurse remains responsible for those tasks.
items.ex: Responsibility is a willingness to respect professional obligations and follow through on them.

alt.q: A nurse manager is evaluating new graduates. Which behaviors show that a graduate understands professional responsibility? Select all that apply.
o: Asks a preceptor for help before a first-time procedure
Seeking guidance when uncertain reflects responsibility.
Follows the agency’s procedure when caring for a central line
Applying workplace policies shows responsibility.
Follows up on care the graduate delegated to an AP
Nurses remain responsible for delegated tasks.
Skips a mandatory skills update because the graduate is busy
Maintaining competence is part of responsibility.
Assumes the AP is responsible for delegated vital signs
Delegation does not transfer the nurse’s responsibility.
alt.ex: Responsibility includes maintaining competence, seeking guidance, following policies, and owning delegated tasks.

items.q: Which statements accurately describe HIPAA? Select all that apply.
o: It mandates confidentiality of patients’ personal health information.
HIPAA mandates confidentiality and protection of health information.
It defines patients’ rights and privileges for protection of privacy.
The legislation defines rights and privileges for privacy.
It establishes fines for privacy violations.
HIPAA establishes fines for violations.
It regulates communication of information in medical records.
HIPAA also regulates communication of information in records.
It permits nurses to share information with any licensed staff member.
Information is shared only with those involved in the patient’s care.
It sets national patient safety guidelines for health care agencies.
National patient safety guidelines come from The Joint Commission.
items.ex: HIPAA is federal legislation that mandates confidentiality, defines privacy rights, sets fines, and regulates record communication.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a new staff member about HIPAA. Which statements by the new staff member show correct understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “I can discuss a patient’s condition only with people involved in the care.”
HIPAA’s right to know limits sharing to those involved in care.
“There can be fines if patient privacy is violated.”
HIPAA establishes fines for violations.
“HIPAA also covers how information in medical records is communicated.”
HIPAA regulates communication of information in medical records.
“I can tell a patient’s friends about the diagnosis if they ask kindly.”
Friends not involved in care have no right to know.
“HIPAA applies only to paper records, not to conversations.”
HIPAA prohibits sharing condition information with uninvolved people, not just records.
alt.ex: HIPAA limits sharing to those involved in care, sets fines, and regulates communication of record information.

items.q: What do the provisions of the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses describe? Select all that apply.
o: The nurse’s obligation to the patient
The provisions describe the nurse’s obligation to the patient.
The nurse’s role as a member of the health care team
The provisions describe the nurse’s role on the team.
The nurse’s duties to the profession and to society
The provisions include duties to the profession and to society.
Fines for nurses who violate patient privacy
Fines for privacy violations are established by HIPAA.
National patient safety guidelines for agencies
National safety guidelines are set by The Joint Commission.
items.ex: The Code’s provisions address obligations to patients, the health care team, the profession, and society.

alt.q: A nursing student reviews the ANA Code of Ethics. To whom does the Code describe the nurse’s obligations or duties? Select all that apply.
o: Patients
The Code describes the nurse’s obligation to the patient.
The nursing profession
The Code describes duties to the profession.
Society
The Code describes duties to society.
Insurance companies
The Code does not describe duties to insurers.
Pharmaceutical suppliers
The Code does not describe duties to suppliers.
alt.ex: The Code addresses the nurse’s obligations to patients, the team, the profession, and society.

items.q: Accountability refers to answering for your own actions.
items.a: True
items.ex: Accountable nurses ensure their professional actions are explainable to patients and employers.
items.ww: It is not false, because answering for one’s own actions is the textbook’s definition of accountability.

alt.q: Accountability applies only to individual nurses and not to health care agencies.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Agencies also exercise accountability by monitoring individual and agency adherence to national standards.
alt.ww: It is not true, because health care agencies are also accountable for meeting national standards such as TJC’s.

items.q: A nurse may share a patient’s medical information with a co-worker who is not involved in the patient’s care, as long as the co-worker is a licensed nurse.
items.a: False
items.ex: HIPAA permits sharing information only with those involved in the patient’s care, regardless of their license.
items.ww: It is not true, because professional status does not give someone a right to know without involvement in care.

alt.q: Under HIPAA, a nurse may share a patient’s medical condition only with those involved in the patient’s care.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: HIPAA calls this limit the right to know and mandates protection of personal health information.
alt.ww: It is not false, because HIPAA restricts sharing to those involved in the patient’s care.

items.q: As a patient advocate, a nurse supports a patient’s right to refuse treatment.
items.a: True
items.ex: Nurses advocate for patients’ health, safety, and rights, including the right to privacy and to refuse treatment.
items.ww: It is not false, because the right to refuse treatment is among the rights nurses advocate for.

alt.q: As a patient advocate, the nurse’s main duty is to persuade patients to accept the treatment the team recommends.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Advocacy applies the nurse’s skills for the patient’s benefit, including supporting the right to refuse treatment.
alt.ww: It is not true, because advocacy protects the patient’s rights rather than securing agreement with the team.

items.q: [[Advocacy]] refers to the application of one’s skills and knowledge for the benefit of another person.
items.ex: Like lawyers advancing clients’ interests, nurses advocate for patients’ health, safety, and rights.

alt.q: When a nurse uses expertise to protect a patient’s right to privacy, the nurse is practicing [[advocacy]].
alt.ex: Like lawyers advancing clients’ interests, nurses advocate for patients’ health, safety, and rights.

items.q: Federal legislation known as [[HIPAA|Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act]] mandates confidentiality and protection of patients’ personal health information.
items.ex: HIPAA defines patients’ privacy rights, establishes fines for violations, and regulates communication of medical record information.

alt.q: The federal law that limits sharing of patient information to those with a “right to know” is [[HIPAA|Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act]].
alt.ex: HIPAA defines patients’ privacy rights, establishes fines for violations, and regulates communication of medical record information.

items.q: What does Advocacy mean?

The team’s obligation to respect patient privacy

w: Applying one’s skills and knowledge for the benefit of another
That goes with Advocacy.
Willingness to respect professional obligations and follow through
That goes with Responsibility.
The team’s obligation to respect patient privacy
That goes with Confidentiality.

w: Applying one’s skills and knowledge for the benefit of another
That goes with Advocacy.
Willingness to respect professional obligations and follow through
That goes with Responsibility.
Answering for your own actions
That goes with Accountability.

w: Responsibility

Accountability

Confidentiality

alt.q: Which term means “Willingness to respect professional obligations and follow through”?
alt.a: Responsibility

w: Advocacy

Accountability

Confidentiality

alt.q: Which term means “Answering for your own actions”?
alt.a: Accountability

Responsibility

Confidentiality
