mt.q: Match each key principle of the nursing code of ethics with its meaning.
pairs: Applying one’s skills and knowledge for the benefit of another
Willingness to respect professional obligations and follow through
The team’s obligation to respect patient privacy
mt.ex: Advocacy, responsibility, accountability, and confidentiality are key principles in the ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses.

items.q: Which definition of a value is consistent with the textbook?
items.a: A deeply held belief about the worth of an idea, attitude, custom, or object that affects choices
items.ex: A value is a deeply held belief about worth that affects a person’s choices and behaviors.
w: A view or idea that is not necessarily based on facts and changes with each situation
A view not necessarily based on facts describes an opinion.
A statement supported by objective data that can be verified by others
A statement supported by objective data is a fact.
A set of guiding principles that all members of a profession agree to accept
Principles accepted by all members of a profession form a code of ethics.

alt.q: A deeply held belief about the worth of an idea, attitude, custom, or object that affects choices and behaviors is called a:
alt.a: Value
alt.ex: Values are deeply held beliefs about worth that shape a person’s choices and behaviors.
w: Fact
A fact is supported by objective data.
Opinion
An opinion is a view not necessarily based on facts.
Law
A law is a concrete, publicly determined rule with public consequences.

items.q: How does the nurse–patient relationship differ from other intimate relationships such as friendship or marriage?
items.a: The nurse provides care based solely on the patient’s need for nursing services.
items.ex: In most intimate relationships people choose partners with aligned values, but nurses care for patients solely based on need.
w: The nurse chooses patients whose values align with the nurse’s own values.
Nurses do not choose patients by shared values; care is based on need.
The nurse expects that the patient will adopt the nurse’s values over time.
Nurses respect patients’ differing values rather than expecting them to change.
The nurse limits contact with the patient to the physical aspects of care.
Nursing involves physical, emotional, psychological, and spiritual contact.

alt.q: Which ethical concepts shape the practice of health care and distinguish it from friendship, marriage, and employer–employee relationships?
alt.a: Beneficence and fidelity
alt.ex: Beneficence and fidelity commit the nurse to help and remain faithful to patients regardless of shared values.
w: Justice and confidentiality
These are important principles, but the textbook names beneficence and fidelity as distinguishing health care relationships.
Autonomy and accountability
These principles do not distinguish health care relationships in the textbook.
Advocacy and responsibility
These are key Code principles but are not the concepts named for this distinction.

items.q: A nurse is assigned to a patient whose lifestyle choices conflict with the nurse’s personal values. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Provide the same quality of care given to any other patient with similar needs.
items.ex: Nurses care for patients based on need and apply the same skills regardless of background, lifestyle, or choices.
w: Ask to be reassigned to a patient whose values better match the nurse’s.
Value differences alone are not a reason to withdraw; care is based on the patient’s need.
Explain to the patient why the nurse’s values are the better choice.
Imposing one’s values becomes judgmental and intensifies conflict.
Limit care to essential tasks until the patient changes the behavior.
Fidelity requires excellent care for all patients, including those with different values.

alt.q: A nurse notices feeling irritated while caring for a patient whose beliefs differ from her own. What is the best first step for the nurse?
alt.a: Recognize that her own values are one individual perspective.
alt.ex: Appreciating your values as your own individual perspective is the first step to working with people whose values differ.
w: Avoid the patient as much as possible to prevent conflict.
Avoidance compromises care that nurses provide based on patient need.
Tell the patient that the patient’s beliefs are not based on fact.
Judgmental statements about another’s values intensify conflict.
Treat her own values as facts that guide the patient’s care.
Treating values as facts is a source of conflict, not a way to resolve it.

items.q: A nursing student notices that some personal values have changed since starting the nursing program. Which explanation is most accurate?
items.a: Values can change over time as people become part of different groups.
items.ex: Although values reflect cultural and social influences, they change as individuals join groups, such as the nursing profession.
w: Values are fixed in childhood, so the student is only changing opinions.
The textbook states that values can change over time.
Values change only when they are proven false by objective data.
Values are beliefs about worth, not claims tested by objective data like facts.
Values change only through formal values clarification tools.
Values also change through education, experiences, and new group membership.

alt.q: Where do a nurse’s professional values come from, according to the textbook?
alt.a: Membership in the nursing profession and the health care team
alt.ex: Nurses bring personal values from family and experience, then develop professional values as members of nursing and the team.
w: Inborn traits that are present from birth
Values reflect cultural and social influences and change over time, not inborn traits.
Objective data gathered during patient assessment
Objective data support facts rather than form values.
Laws that are concrete and publicly determined
Laws are legal rules; professional values develop through group membership.

items.q: The textbook compares recognizing your own values to “seeing the bubble you live in.” What does this comparison mean?
items.a: People usually view the world through their values without acknowledging them.
items.ex: Values are intrinsic to our view of the world, so we usually look through them without noticing them.
w: People usually change their values whenever they enter a new setting.
Values can change over time, but the bubble refers to not noticing them.
People usually share the same values as everyone in their community.
Values differ among people; the comparison is about not seeing one’s own values.
People usually keep their values separate from their daily decisions.
Values affect choices and behaviors rather than staying separate from them.

alt.q: Why is learning to recognize your own values important for a nurse?
alt.a: It is the first step to working effectively with people whose values differ.
alt.ex: Appreciating your values as your own perspective is the first step in working with professionals, patients, and families who differ.
w: It allows the nurse to replace patients’ values with professional values.
Nurses respect patients’ values rather than replacing them.
It ensures the nurse will avoid all ethical conflicts with patients.
Health care relationships sometimes occur in the presence of conflicting values.
It proves which values are facts and which are merely opinions.
Values are distinct from facts and opinions; recognizing them does not make them facts.

items.q: When does an ethical dilemma almost always occur, according to the textbook?
items.a: In the presence of conflicting values
items.ex: Ethical dilemmas almost always occur when values conflict, so clarifying values is key to resolving them.
w: In the presence of conflicting laws
Conflicting laws are legal issues resolved by reference to the law.
In the presence of missing lab data
Missing data can be resolved by gathering information and is not itself a dilemma.
In the presence of shared values
Shared values are the basis of ethical codes, not the source of dilemmas.

alt.q: To resolve an ethical conflict, what must a person distinguish among?
alt.a: Value, fact, and opinion
alt.ex: Resolving ethical conflicts requires distinguishing among value, fact, and opinion.
w: Law, policy, and procedure
Distinguishing laws and policies does not address the conflicting values at the root of dilemmas.
Diagnosis, outcome, and plan
These are nursing process elements, not the distinction used in values clarification.
Morals, ethics, and bioethics
These are terms in ethics, but the textbook names value, fact, and opinion.

items.q: During a discussion about a patient’s care, which statement is a fact?
items.a: “His hemoglobin A1C result this morning was 9%.”
items.ex: Facts are supported by objective data, such as a measured laboratory result.
w: “Teenagers with diabetes never follow their diet.”
This is an opinion, a view not necessarily based on facts.
“Patients should always put their health first.”
This expresses a belief about worth, which is a value.
“His parents care more than he does about this.”
This is an opinion that is not supported by objective data.

alt.q: A nurse says, “Patients who refuse treatment are just being difficult.” How should this statement be classified?
alt.a: An opinion
alt.ex: An opinion is a view or idea that is not necessarily based on facts.
w: A fact
A fact is supported by objective data, which this statement lacks.
A law
A law is a concrete, publicly determined rule.
A code
A code of ethics is a set of principles accepted by a profession.

items.q: During a care conference, a patient’s daughter suddenly raises her voice and becomes tearful when hospice is mentioned. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: The daughter’s strong reaction may signal that her values feel threatened.
items.ex: A strong emotional reaction is often a sign that a person’s values are threatened, so exploring them is helpful.
w: The daughter’s reaction shows she lacks the facts and needs more data only.
More data alone does not address values that feel threatened.
The daughter’s reaction means she should be excluded from further discussion.
Families are welcome participants; exploring values helps resolve conflict.
The daughter’s reaction shows that her opinion is supported by objective data.
An emotional reaction does not make a view a fact supported by data.

alt.q: What is often indicated when a person expresses a strong emotional reaction during an ethical discussion?
alt.a: The person’s values are threatened.
alt.ex: When people react with strong emotion, it is often a sign that their values are threatened.
w: The person has accepted the facts.
Strong emotion signals threatened values, not acceptance of facts.
The person lacks any values.
Strong emotion suggests deeply held values rather than an absence of values.
The person has resolved the issue.
Strong emotion usually means conflict is still present.

items.q: A co-worker says, “That patient’s decision is just wrong, and I won’t pretend otherwise.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Let’s talk about the values behind his choice and the values behind our reaction.”
items.ex: Clarifying values of patients and co-workers is an effective part of ethical discourse and reduces judgmental conflict.
w: “You are right, and we should make sure he knows how wrong he is.”
Being judgmental about values intensifies conflict.
“Your values are facts, so the patient will have to accept them.”
Treating values as facts is a common source of conflict.
“Let’s not bring it up, since values do not matter in health care.”
Values play an important role in ethics and must be clarified, not ignored.

alt.q: What can happen when people are so passionate about their values that they become judgmental?
alt.a: Conflict intensifies.
alt.ex: Passion about values can make people judgmental in a way that intensifies conflict.
w: Conflict resolves.
Judgmental attitudes intensify rather than resolve conflict.
Facts become clearer.
Judgment tends to blur the line between values and facts.
Values become shared.
Judging others does not create shared values.

items.q: Whose values should be clarified as part of effective ethical discourse?
items.a: The nurse’s, the patients’, and co-workers’ values
items.ex: Clarifying values, including your own, your patients’, and your co-workers’, is an important and effective part of ethical discourse.
w: Only the patients’ values, because the nurse’s are professional
Nurses must also clarify their own values, which shape how they see a situation.
Only the nurse’s values, because patients’ are private
Clarifying patients’ values supports person-centered decision making.
Only the health care provider’s values, because they decide care
Ethical discourse includes all involved, not only the provider.

alt.q: A nurse is preparing for an ethics discussion about a patient’s care. Which action reflects effective values clarification?
alt.a: Reflecting on her own values as well as those of the patient and team
alt.ex: Effective ethical discourse clarifies the nurse’s own values along with those of patients and co-workers.
w: Focusing only on the team’s professional values and policies
Patients’ and personal values must also be clarified.
Treating her strongest values as established facts for the group
Strong values are not facts; confusing them intensifies conflict.
Avoiding personal values so that only laws guide the discussion
Ethical problems involve values, so ignoring them does not resolve conflict.

items.q: What is the purpose of values clarification tools used with patients during illness?
items.a: To support a person-centered decision-making process
items.ex: Values clarification tools help patients consider their values systematically and support person-centered decisions during illness.
w: To persuade patients to accept the team’s treatment plan
Persuasion is not the goal; the tools center decisions on the patient’s values.
To determine patients’ eligibility for scarce resources
Allocating scarce resources is a question of justice.
To document patients’ legal consent for procedures
Documenting consent is part of informed consent, not values clarification.

alt.q: A nurse helps a patient with advanced heart failure systematically identify what matters most to him before a family meeting. How does this help?
alt.a: It supports better advance care planning discussions with family and providers.
alt.ex: Values clarification supports better advance health care planning discussions among patients, family caregivers, and providers.
w: It removes the need for the patient to discuss wishes with family.
Values clarification improves, rather than replaces, discussions with family.
It allows the nurse to decide the plan of care for the patient.
Decisions remain person-centered and made with the patient.
It ensures the patient’s values will match the provider’s values.
The goal is to understand the patient’s values, not to align them with others’.

items.q: Which statements about values are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They reflect cultural and social influences.
Values reflect cultural and social influences.
They can change over time as people join different groups.
Values change as individuals become part of new groups.
They affect a person’s choices and behaviors.
A value is a belief that affects choices and behaviors.
They are supported by objective data.
Being supported by objective data defines a fact.
They are usually noticed and acknowledged by the person.
We usually view the world through our values without acknowledging them.
items.ex: Values are deeply held, socially shaped beliefs that can change and that guide choices, often without our awareness.

alt.q: A nurse educator is teaching about values. Which statements by students show correct understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “My values were shaped by my family and education.”
Personal values come from family, education, and other experiences.
“I will develop professional values as a member of nursing.”
Nurses develop professional values as members of the profession.
“My values influence the choices I make.”
Values affect choices and behaviors.
“Once formed in childhood, my values cannot change.”
Values can change over time as people join different groups.
“If I feel strongly about a value, it is a fact.”
Strongly held values are sometimes mistaken for facts but are not facts.
alt.ex: Values come from family, education, experience, and professional membership, and they can change over time.

items.q: Which sources contribute to the values a nurse holds? Select all that apply.
o: Family
Personal values come partly from family.
Education
Education contributes to personal values.
Membership in the nursing profession
Nurses develop professional values as members of the profession.
Objective laboratory data
Objective data support facts, not values.
Publicly determined laws
Laws govern legal issues; they are not described as a source of values.
items.ex: Nurses hold personal values from family, education, and experience, plus professional values from nursing and the team.

alt.q: A nurse reflects on where her values come from. Which influences does the textbook describe? Select all that apply.
o: Life experiences
Other experiences shape personal values.
Cultural and social influences
Values reflect cultural and social influences.
Belonging to the health care team
Professional values develop as a member of the team.
Inherited genetic traits
Values reflect social influences and change over time, not genetics.
Measurements of vital signs
Measurements are objective data supporting facts.

items.q: How does deontology determine whether an action is right or wrong?
items.a: By its adherence to rules and principles such as truthfulness and justice
items.ex: Deontology looks at the act itself and judges its rightness by the rules or principles, such as fidelity and justice, that it upholds.

alt.ex: Deontology examines a situation for essential right or wrong based on principles rather than looking at consequences.
w: Utilitarianism
Utilitarianism measures the effect an act will have, focusing on consequences.
Casuistry

Ethics of care

items.q: A nurse caring for Stella, an older adult with dementia, decides to negotiate an exception to the visitation policy for her son David so that the unit stays free of conflict for other patients and staff. Which approach to ethics is the nurse applying?
items.a: Utilitarianism

w: Deontology

Casuistry
Casuistry would compare this case with similar past cases rather than weigh unit-wide outcomes.
Ethics of care
Ethics of care would first explore the relationships involved rather than the effect on the whole unit.

alt.q: A nurse caring for Stella believes the right action is to seek help enforcing the visitation policy because making an exception for David when other families follow the rules would be unjust. Which approach is the nurse applying?

Feminist ethics
Feminist ethics would look for power imbalances among the people involved.
Casuistry
Casuistry would look to precedent cases rather than the duty created by the policy.

items.q: A nurse deciding whether David may stay at Stella’s bedside during change of shift recalls past situations in which families made similar requests and compares Stella’s prognosis and David’s ability to help with her care. Which approach is the nurse using?
items.a: Casuistry
items.ex: Casuistry, or case-based reasoning, finds similar precedent cases and compares details to identify the closest match.
w: Deontology
Deontology judges actions by the principles they uphold rather than by precedent.
Utilitarianism
Utilitarianism weighs the consequences of the action for the greatest number.
Feminist ethics
Feminist ethics asks about relationships and power imbalance, not prior cases.

alt.q: What is a key step when applying casuistry to an ethical problem?
alt.a: Comparing details of the current case with prior cases to find the closest match
alt.ex: In casuistry, details such as prognosis and family contribution are compared with precedent cases to choose the closest match.
w: Predicting which option brings the most benefit to the most people
Predicting the greatest good for the most people is the utilitarian method.
Identifying the rule or principle that the proposed action would uphold
Identifying principles an action upholds is the deontological method.
Looking for a power imbalance among the people involved in the case
Seeking power imbalances is characteristic of feminist ethics.

items.q: A nurse caring for Stella wonders whether David’s presence is intimidating to her and whether staff enforcing the policy are taking a position of unjustified power over David. Which approach to ethics do these questions reflect?

items.ex: Feminist ethics asks about the people involved and their relationships, such as power imbalances, rather than underlying principles.
w: Deontology
Deontology asks which rules and principles an action upholds.
Utilitarianism
Utilitarianism asks which outcome gives the greatest good to the greatest number.
Casuistry
Casuistry asks which precedent case most closely matches the current one.

alt.q: A nurse using feminist ethics in the situation of Stella and David would most likely do what?

Acting on duty to agency rules reflects deontology.
Choose whichever option causes the least conflict on the unit
Choosing the option with the best overall outcome reflects utilitarianism.
Find a past case with similar details and follow its outcome
Following a similar precedent case reflects casuistry.

items.q: How does the ethics of care differ from feminist ethics?

Basing decisions on precedent cases describes casuistry.

alt.q: In which two approaches to ethics is the decision maker described as detached and objective?

Both of these focus on relationships, and ethics of care stresses the decision maker’s involvement.

Ethics of care emphasizes the decision maker’s engaged role, not detachment.

Utilitarianism weighs outcomes for the greatest number rather than exploring the specific relationships.
Deontology
Deontology examines which principles an action upholds rather than its impact on relationships.
Casuistry

alt.q: A nurse applying the ethics of care to Stella and David’s situation would first do what?

alt.ex: Ethics of care first explores the relationships involved and then chooses the action that best supports them.
w: Review the visitation policy to identify the duty it creates
Identifying duties created by rules reflects deontology.
Recall similar past cases to identify the closest precedent
Recalling precedent cases reflects casuistry.
Choose the option least disruptive to other patients on the unit
Choosing the least disruptive option for the most people reflects utilitarianism.

items.q: Which criticism does the textbook raise about utilitarianism?
items.a: It can be taken too far, as when the ends are used to justify the means

Difficulty finding precedent is the weakness of casuistry.
Without traditional principles, decisions rely too much on subjective judgment
Overreliance on subjective judgment is the criticism of feminist ethics.
Respecting autonomy is complicated when patients cannot voice preferences
This complication is described for deontology’s principle of autonomy.

alt.q: What limitation of deontology does the situation of Stella and David illustrate?
alt.a: Adhering to a principle alone does not always give clear answers in complicated situations
alt.ex: Respect for autonomy guides deontology, but applying a principle alone can leave confusion, such as when a patient cannot voice preferences.
w: Predicting the greatest good is impossible when people define good differently
Conflicting definitions of the greatest good is a limitation of utilitarianism.
Finding a precedent case with matching details is often very difficult
Difficulty finding a precedent is the weakness of casuistry.
Focusing on relationships leaves decisions too dependent on subjective judgment
Dependence on subjective judgment is the criticism raised about feminist ethics.

items.q: Stella, who has dementia, had always stated clearly that she wanted her son David at her bedside. A nurse guided by respect for autonomy should take which action?
items.a: Advocate for an exception to the visitation policy
items.ex: If Stella clearly desired David’s presence, respect for her autonomy becomes the guiding principle, and the nurse should advocate for an exception.

Respect for Stella’s known wishes, not agency rules, is the guiding principle in this version of the case.
Ask David to leave so that the unit remains free of conflict

Delay any action until a similar precedent case can be found

alt.q: Why can the principle of autonomy become complicated when using deontology?

Autonomy can be considered only after precedent cases have been reviewed
Reviewing precedent cases is casuistry and is not a requirement of deontology.

items.q: According to feminist ethics, what is the basis for moral behavior?
items.a: The natural caring for others

w: Fidelity to promises and rules

The greatest good for the most people
The greatest good for the greatest number guides utilitarianism.
Precedent set by similar prior cases

alt.q: What do critics of feminist ethics argue?

Finding a precedent case is difficult in complex situations with unique features
Difficulty finding precedent is the weakness of casuistry.
Strict adherence to rules makes it impossible to consider any patient preferences

Nurses must follow agency rules without exception in every situation
Strict rule following reflects deontology and does not explain the appeal of the ethics of care.
Nurses usually base decisions on how prior similar cases were managed
Basing decisions on prior cases describes casuistry.

alt.q: What makes it difficult for people using a utilitarian approach to agree on the right action?
alt.a: Differing ideas of what counts as the greatest good

w: Differing interpretations of the agency’s rules
Interpreting rules and principles is the work of deontology.
Differing choices about which precedent case fits
Choosing a matching precedent case is the work of casuistry.
Differing views about who holds power in the situation

alt.q: Which approach to ethics focuses on “Natural caring for others and attention to power imbalance”?
alt.a: Feminist ethics
alt.ex: Each approach offers a different lens on an ethical problem, and none guarantees agreement in complicated situations.
w: Deontology
Deontology: Adherence to rules and principles such as truthfulness and justice.
Utilitarianism
Utilitarianism: The greatest good for the greatest number of people.
Casuistry
Casuistry: Details of similar precedent cases and how they were managed.

alt.q: Which approach to ethics focuses on “Relationships and context, emphasizing the decision maker’s role”?
alt.a: Ethics of care
alt.ex: Each approach offers a different lens on an ethical problem, and none guarantees agreement in complicated situations.
w: Deontology
Deontology: Adherence to rules and principles such as truthfulness and justice.
Utilitarianism
Utilitarianism: The greatest good for the greatest number of people.
Casuistry
Casuistry: Details of similar precedent cases and how they were managed.

mt.q: Match each approach to ethics with its main focus.
pairs: Adherence to rules and principles such as truthfulness and justice
The greatest good for the greatest number of people
Details of similar precedent cases and how they were managed
Natural caring for others and attention to power imbalance
Relationships and context, emphasizing the decision maker’s role

items.q: Why may patients and families feel more comfortable revealing information to nurses than to other health care providers?
items.a: Nurses engage with patients over longer periods and provide intimate physical care
items.ex: Longer contact and intimate acts such as bathing and feeding lead patients to share details with nurses they have not shared with others.
w: Nurses are the only team members bound by patient confidentiality
All health care professionals are bound by confidentiality; this is not the reason given.
Nurses make the final decisions about the patient’s treatment plan
Nurses collaborate with the team; they do not make all final treatment decisions.
Nurses have less contact with other members of the health care team
Nurses collaborate closely with interprofessional team members.

alt.q: A nurse learns about a patient’s fears, coping style, and family life during morning care. Which factor best explains why nurses gain this special knowledge?
alt.a: Their longer time with patients and involvement in intimate care
alt.ex: Nurses spend more time with patients and perform intimate care, so patients often reveal details not shared with others.
w: Their responsibility to obtain informed consent for procedures
Informed consent is not given as the reason nurses learn these personal details.
Their role in managing the agency’s distribution of resources
Managers and administrators contribute knowledge of systems and resource distribution.
Their authority to approve exceptions to agency policies
Approving policy exceptions is not the reason patients confide in nurses.

items.q: A patient refuses all morning pills until given “hormone medicine,” which is not among the prescribed drugs. A team member suggests the nursing student say one pill is the hormone pill. The student feels torn because giving the medications benefits the patient but lying violates trust. Which ethical problem is the student experiencing?
items.a: Ethical dilemma
items.ex: A dilemma exists when two opposing courses of action, here beneficence and truthfulness, can both be justified by ethical principles.
w: Moral distress
Moral distress involves feeling compelled to take one specific action while believing it is wrong, not two justifiable options.
Moral resilience
Moral resilience is the ability to grow from adverse ethical problems, not an ethical problem.
Communication problem
The conflict is between two justifiable ethical options, not a misunderstanding.

alt.q: A health care provider directs a nursing student to tell a patient that a pill is “hormone medicine” when it is not. The medications are overdue, no one else is available, and the student believes lying is wrong but feels compelled to do it. Which ethical problem is the student at risk for?
alt.a: Moral distress
alt.ex: In moral distress, the nurse feels the need to take a specific action while believing that action to be wrong.
w: Ethical dilemma
A dilemma involves two opposing options that are both justifiable, not pressure toward one action believed wrong.
Moral resilience
Moral resilience is the ability to grow from ethical adversity, not the problem itself.
Just culture
Just culture is open discussion of errors without fear of retaliation, not an ethical problem.

items.q: When an ethical problem is identified as a dilemma, what does applying the nursing process often include?
items.a: Identifying more options than the two opposing ones
items.ex: With two opposing but justifiable options, the nursing process often includes looking for additional options.
w: Choosing whichever option can be completed fastest
Speed is not the basis for resolving a dilemma.
Following the advice of the most senior team member
Deferring to seniority does not resolve the ethical conflict.
Referring the problem directly to the board of nursing
Boards of nursing address scope of practice and competency questions, not routine dilemmas.

alt.q: A nurse recognizes a situation that is creating moral distress. What does the textbook recommend?
alt.a: Discuss the situation with another person
alt.ex: Situations that generate moral distress should be discussed with another person when they are identified.
w: Keep the concern private to avoid conflict
Keeping silent prevents colleagues and managers from addressing contributing factors.
Take the action despite believing it wrong
Acting against one’s values is what produces moral distress.
Request a transfer to another nursing unit
Transfer is not the recommended response; discussion and shared resources are.

items.q: A nursing student faces an older adult who refuses morning medications until given a “hormone pill” that is not prescribed. Which action by the student best resolves the dilemma without lying?
items.a: Spend time at the bedside to build trust with the patient
items.ex: Building trust by spending time at the bedside may allow the student to give the ordered medications without lying.
w: Tell the patient that one of the pills is the hormone pill
Lying to the patient violates autonomy and betrays trust.
Hide the pills in the patient’s food without telling the patient
Concealing medications is deceptive and also violates the patient’s autonomy.
Leave the room and record that all medications were refused
Leaving without trying other options does not give the patient the benefit of the medications.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of how to resolve an ethical dilemma?
alt.a: “I should look for other options besides the two that conflict.”
alt.ex: When a dilemma presents two opposing justifiable options, identifying more options often leads to resolution.
w: “I must pick one of the two conflicting options right away.”
Choosing quickly between two options overlooks other possible actions.
“A dilemma means I am forced to act against my values.”
Feeling compelled to act against one’s values describes moral distress.
“Only the ethics committee can resolve an ethical dilemma.”
Nurses can resolve many dilemmas using colleagues and other resources.

items.q: How does processing an ethical problem differ from the nursing process?
items.a: It requires negotiating differences of opinion where there may be no single right answer
items.ex: Both are methodical, but ethical problem solving involves negotiating differing opinions and situations without one right answer.
w: It does not use a methodical approach to the clinical issue
Resolving an ethical problem is like the nursing process in its methodical approach.
It excludes family members to protect the patient’s privacy
Welcome participation of families and primary caregivers is essential to the process.
It always ends with one correct solution that all accept
Ethical problems may have no single right answer, and consensus is not guaranteed.

alt.q: A nurse feels uncertain about a conflict with a family but finds that speaking openly and listening resolves it. What does this suggest about the situation?
alt.a: It was a communication problem that looked like an ethical problem
alt.ex: Sometimes communication problems look like ethical problems, and open speaking and listening achieve resolution.
w: It was an ethical dilemma that required an ethics committee
Resolution through open conversation suggests a communication problem, not a dilemma needing a committee.
It was moral distress caused by the work environment
Moral distress involves feeling compelled to do something believed wrong.
It was a legal issue that required reference to the law
Legal issues are resolved by reference to laws, not by open conversation.

items.q: A nurse caring for Miguel, an 18-year-old with type 1 diabetes, has confirmed that an ethical problem exists and is now gathering information. Which strategy is most important at this step?
items.a: Ask open-ended questions and take time to listen
items.ex: A key strategy in gathering information is asking open-ended questions and listening to hear others’ perspectives.
w: Remove the snacks before talking with anyone
Acting before gathering information skips the steps that lead to a sound plan.
Choose an action plan before reviewing the chart
Creating an action plan comes after gathering information and identifying options.
Report Miguel’s diet choices to the ethics committee
Referral is not the information-gathering strategy and is not the first step here.

alt.q: Why does the textbook stress focused interaction when gathering information about an ethical problem?
alt.a: Our interpretation of a situation is based on our own values
alt.ex: Because we interpret situations through our own values, focused interaction is needed to hear others’ perspectives.
w: Patients rarely know their own values and goals
Patients’ values and perspectives are a key source of information.
Clinical information alone resolves most ethical problems
Ethical problems involve values and obligations that clinical facts alone may not resolve.
Colleagues’ views are less useful than written policies
The views of colleagues are listed as pertinent information.

items.q: During which step of resolving an ethical dilemma does the nurse clarify values, recognize the principles involved, and distinguish among facts, opinions, and values?
items.a: Identifying the ethical elements
items.ex: Step 3 identifies the ethical elements by clarifying values, recognizing principles, and distinguishing facts, opinions, and values.
w: Naming the problem
Naming the problem (Step 4) creates a clear, simple statement after the ethical elements are identified.
Identifying courses of action
Identifying courses of action (Step 5) lists possible options with input from others.
Evaluating the action plan
Evaluating (Step 7) decides whether further action is needed after the plan is carried out.

alt.q: While gathering information about an ethical problem, a nurse examines personal values. What does this help the nurse do?
alt.a: Differentiate between fact and opinion
alt.ex: Examining personal values helps differentiate fact from opinion, an important part of processing an ethical problem.
w: Predict the final outcome of the case
Examining values does not predict outcomes; it clarifies one’s own perspective.
Determine the agency’s legal liability
Legal liability is not the purpose of examining personal values.
Avoid involving the patient’s family
Families’ values and perspectives are part of the information gathered.

items.q: Miguel, an 18-year-old with type 1 diabetes, is eating snacks that contradict his prescribed diet. Which ethical principle supports respecting his right to choose his diet once he is informed of the risks and benefits?
items.a: Autonomy
items.ex: Autonomy supports actions that respect the patient’s right to make personal choices.
w: Beneficence
Beneficence, the obligation to do good, supports seeking the action best for Miguel’s health.
Fidelity
Fidelity to the health care team supports adhering to the current treatment plan.
Justice
Justice concerns fairness and the distribution of resources, not Miguel’s personal choices.

alt.q: In Miguel’s case, which ethical principle supports actions that adhere to his current treatment plan?
alt.a: Fidelity to the health care team
alt.ex: Fidelity to the health care team supports actions that keep to the current treatment plan.
w: Respect for patient autonomy
Autonomy supports Miguel’s right to make his own choices.
Beneficence toward the patient
Beneficence supports seeking the action that is best for Miguel.
Justice in resource distribution
Justice concerns fairness in distributing resources, not adherence to the plan.

items.q: In Step 4 of resolving an ethical dilemma, why is it helpful to name the problem aloud with a colleague?
items.a: Speaking aloud encourages the right language and allows feedback from others
items.ex: Naming the problem is harder than it sounds; speaking aloud helps find the right words and invites feedback.
w: A colleague is legally required to approve every problem statement
No legal approval is required; involving others simply improves the statement.
Naming the problem alone is not possible without an ethics committee
A statement can be developed alone, but speaking aloud with others helps.
A colleague can decide the final action plan on the nurse’s behalf
Colleagues help articulate the issue; they do not take over the decision.

alt.q: After talking with a colleague, the nurse caring for Miguel names the problem. Which statement correctly names it?
alt.a: An ethical dilemma between beneficence and respect for Miguel’s autonomy
alt.ex: The nurse concludes the conflict is between acting with beneficence to protect Miguel’s health and respecting his autonomy.
w: Moral distress between fidelity to the team and justice
The nurse identifies a dilemma involving beneficence and autonomy, not fidelity and justice.
A legal conflict over whether Miguel can give consent
Miguel is an adult; the problem named is ethical, not a consent dispute.
An ethical dilemma between justice and nonmaleficence
Justice and nonmaleficence are not the principles named in Miguel’s case.

items.q: A nurse’s action plan for an ethical problem is to ask the unit manager for help first. According to the textbook, what is a helpful way to structure this step?
items.a: Also decide what to do next, such as consulting the ethics committee, if the first step fails
items.ex: Rather than a single action, select what to do first and what to do later if the first step does not achieve resolution.
w: Commit to the manager’s advice as the only action to be taken
Planning only one action leaves no alternative if it does not resolve the problem.
Delay all action until every member of the team fully agrees
Waiting for full agreement is not the textbook’s approach; action requires courage.
Avoid planning further steps so that the plan stays flexible
Planning a backup action is recommended in case the first step is ineffective.

alt.q: A nurse is about to carry out the action plan for an ethical problem and feels nervous and fearful. Which approach does the textbook recommend?
alt.a: Focus on the desired outcome, which is resolution of the ethical issue
alt.ex: Because this step requires courage, focusing on the desired outcome of resolution helps the nurse enact the plan.
w: Postpone the plan until the unpleasant emotions have passed
Fear and anger are expected; the nurse acts with courage rather than waiting.
Hand the plan to a colleague who feels more comfortable
Colleagues may help plan words, but the nurse still carries out the plan.
Change to a different plan that avoids talking with the patient
Avoiding the patient does not address the ethical issue.

items.q: The adult daughter of a patient disagrees with the team about her parent’s treatment and asks the nurse whether she can bring her concern to the ethics committee. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Yes. Patients and family members may request access to the ethics committee.”
items.ex: In most agencies, anyone seeking ethical advice, including patients and family members, can request access to an ethics committee.
w: “Only physicians and health care providers may contact the ethics committee.”
Access is not limited to providers; patients and families may also request it.
“Only the nurse manager can decide whether the committee will hear a case.”
Nurses, patients, and families can request access without a manager’s decision.
“The ethics committee only writes policies and does not hear individual cases.”
Clinical ethics consultation is one of the committee’s three major functions.

alt.q: Who may request access to the ethics committee in most health care agencies?
alt.a: Any person seeking ethical advice, including patients and families
alt.ex: Nurses, physicians, health care providers, patients, and family members can request access to an ethics committee.
w: Only physicians and other health care providers on the case
Patients, families, and nurses may also request access.
Only nurse managers and agency administrators
Access is not limited to managers and administrators.
Only the patient’s legal representative or attorney
Any person seeking ethical advice may request access, not only legal representatives.

items.q: Which elements does the textbook identify as essential to finding clarity and consensus when processing an ethical problem? Select all that apply.
o: Presumption of goodwill on the part of all participants
Assuming all participants want to do good is essential.
Strict adherence to confidentiality
Strict confidentiality is an essential element of the process.
Person-centered decision making
Decisions centered on the person are essential to the process.
Welcome participation of families and primary caregivers
Families and primary caregivers are welcomed into the process.
Deferring to the most senior health care provider present
Every perspective should be heard; deferring to seniority is not an essential element.
items.ex: Goodwill, confidentiality, person-centered decisions, and family participation keep the process productive.

alt.q: A nurse is preparing for a family conference about an ethical problem. Which approaches support clarity and consensus? Select all that apply.
o: Assuming that all participants want to do good
The presumption of goodwill is essential, even when participants have different ideas of good.
Keeping all discussion strictly confidential
Strict adherence to confidentiality is essential.
Making decisions centered on the patient as a person
Person-centered decision making is an essential element.
Limiting the family’s role to receiving the final decision
Families and primary caregivers should be welcomed as participants.
Settling the issue quickly so emotions do not arise
Ethical problems can raise troubling emotions; rushing is not an essential element.
alt.ex: Presumed goodwill, confidentiality, and person-centered decisions, with families welcomed, help reach clarity and consensus.

items.q: Which are major functions of a hospital ethics committee? Select all that apply.
o: Providing clinical ethics consultation
Clinical ethics consultation is one of the three major functions.
Developing or revising policies pertaining to clinical ethics
Committees develop or revise policies such as those on advance directives.
Facilitating education about topical issues in clinical ethics
Education about current clinical ethics issues is a major function.
Disciplining staff who violate the code of ethics
Discipline is not listed among the committee’s functions.
Issuing legally binding orders for patient treatment
Committees facilitate discussion and may reach consensus but do not issue binding orders.
items.ex: Ethics committees provide consultation, develop and revise policies, and facilitate education about clinical ethics.

alt.q: An ethics committee is developing and revising agency policies related to clinical ethics. Which topics are examples of such policies? Select all that apply.
o: Advance directives
Advance directives are an example of a clinical ethics policy.
Withholding and withdrawing life-sustaining treatments
Policies on withholding and withdrawing treatment are named examples.
Informed consent
Informed consent is listed as a policy area.
Organ procurement
Organ procurement is listed as a policy area.
Nurse salary scales
Salary scales are not clinical ethics policies.
alt.ex: Ethics committees develop or revise policies on advance directives, life-sustaining treatment, informed consent, and organ procurement.

items.q: Which strategies does the textbook recommend to reduce moral distress among nurses? Select all that apply.
o: Develop and practice skilled communication with the team, patients, and families
Professional communication open to others’ views can prevent conflicts and reduce moral distress.
Find out whether the agency has an ethics committee and how to consult it
Identifying available resources helps reduce moral distress.
Find a mentor skilled in examining ethical problems
A mentor or leader can help process ethical situations.
Practice self-care skills such as mindfulness and self-compassion
Self-care skills such as mindfulness and breathing are recommended.
Avoid discussing ethical concerns with colleagues to prevent conflict
Discussing distressing situations with others is recommended, not avoided.
items.ex: Communication, knowing resources, mentoring, and self-care help reduce moral distress and build moral resilience.

alt.q: Which factors are identified as causes of moral distress among nurses? Select all that apply.
o: Psychological distress such as depression and emotional exhaustion
Depression and emotional exhaustion are listed among the causes.
Job dissatisfaction
Job dissatisfaction is listed among the causes.
Dysfunctional interprofessional communication
Poor interprofessional communication is listed among the causes.
Strong work-related quality of life
Diminished, not strong, work-related quality of life is listed.
Supportive debriefing with the interprofessional team
Debriefing is a support strategy for addressing moral distress, not a cause.
alt.ex: Evidence links moral distress to psychological distress, job dissatisfaction, poor communication, and diminished work-related quality of life.

items.q: Moral distress often shows itself as anger or frustration.
items.a: True
items.ex: The textbook notes that moral distress often manifests as anger or frustration.
items.ww: Anger and frustration are named as common signs of moral distress.

alt.q: In an ethical dilemma, the nurse feels compelled to take one specific action while believing that action is wrong.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: That describes moral distress; a dilemma involves two opposing courses of action that can both be justified.
alt.ww: A dilemma is defined by two justifiable but opposing options, not pressure toward one wrong action.

items.q: If an ethical concern does not directly affect patient care, the nurse may document the discussion in meeting minutes or in an e-mail to those involved.
items.a: True
items.ex: Concerns not directly affecting patient care may be documented in meeting minutes or e-mail to participants.
items.ww: The EHR is required when a family caregiver conference or treatment plan change is involved, not for every discussion.

alt.q: When an ethics discussion leads to changes in the treatment plan, the nurse documents it only in meeting minutes, not in the EHR.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Family caregiver conferences or treatment plan changes are documented in the EHR, sometimes on an ethics consultation form.
alt.ww: Treatment plan changes directly affect patient care, so all relevant information belongs in the EHR.

items.q: An ethics committee meeting that ends without a clear plan can still be valuable if participants gain a better understanding of one another’s perspectives.
items.a: True
items.ex: A successful meeting is one in which every perspective is heard, even if no clear plan results.
items.ww: The textbook notes some meetings end without a plan but with improved understanding of perspectives.

alt.q: An ethics committee meeting is successful only if it produces consensus on a specific course of action.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Success means every perspective is heard; some meetings end without consensus but with better mutual understanding.
alt.ww: Consensus sometimes occurs, but it is not the textbook’s measure of a successful meeting.

items.q: [[Moral resilience|resilience]] is the ability to grow and even gain confidence from adverse and complex ethical problems.
items.ex: Building moral resilience may reduce nurses’ susceptibility to moral distress.

alt.q: Deliberate attention to building moral [[resilience]] may reduce nurses’ susceptibility to moral distress.
alt.ex: Building moral resilience may reduce nurses’ susceptibility to moral distress.

Professional organizations

alt.a: Professional organizations

items.q: A nurse wants to post a photo of a patient’s healing wound on social media, cropped so that no name or face shows. Which response by the charge nurse is best?
items.a: “Posting patient pictures violates confidentiality even without identifiers.”
items.ex: Posting information or pictures about patients, even without specific identifiers, is a violation of confidentiality.
w: “It is acceptable as long as the patient’s name is not visible.”
Removing the name does not prevent a breach; any patient photo violates confidentiality.
“It is acceptable if your account is set to private for friends.”
Privacy settings do not make posting patient information acceptable.
“It is acceptable if you post it after the patient is discharged.”
Discharge does not change the confidentiality violation.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows understanding of patient privacy on social media?
alt.a: “I will not post about patients even if I leave out their names.”
alt.ex: Posting patient information or pictures, even without specific identifiers, violates confidentiality.
w: “I can post patient stories if I change the patient’s name.”
Changing names does not prevent a confidentiality violation.
“I can share patient photos with friends in a private group.”
Sharing patient photos in any online group violates confidentiality.
“I can post about patients once my shift has ended.”
Timing of the post does not change the privacy violation.

items.q: A patient currently on the unit sends the nurse a “friend” request on a social media site. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Decline the request, because it crosses the professional boundary
items.ex: Online friendship with a patient makes the relationship more personal and crosses the patient–professional boundary.
w: Accept the request but avoid discussing the patient’s health
Even without health talk, online friendship risks objectivity and reveals the relationship to others.
Accept the request, because it supports the patient emotionally
Social media can support patients through friends and family, not through friendship with their nurse.
Accept the request and limit the visibility of the friendship
Limiting visibility does not remove the boundary problem or the risk to objectivity.

alt.q: Why is online “friendship” between a nurse and a patient problematic?
alt.a: It risks clouding the nurse’s objectivity in clinical perceptions
alt.ex: Online friendship can cloud objectivity and crosses the professional boundary, making the relationship more personal.
w: It is the only acceptable way to provide emotional support
Social media support for patients comes from friends and loved ones, not their nurse.
It is required to follow up on care after discharge
Follow-up care does not require social media friendship.
It improves the nurse’s objectivity about the patient
Online friendship threatens, rather than improves, objectivity.

items.q: According to the textbook, a nurse’s use of social media should be in line with what?
items.a: The agency’s values and policies and the professional code of conduct
items.ex: Social media usage should align with the health care agency’s values, policies, and professional code of conduct.
w: The privacy settings and terms of service of each website
Website settings do not set the professional standard for nurses’ online conduct.
The preferences of patients who request online contact with nurses
Patient requests do not override professional boundaries and agency policy.
The number of followers the nurse has on each platform
Audience size is unrelated to professional standards for social media.

alt.q: A nurse has questions about when and where it is appropriate to use social media. Which resources does the textbook identify?
alt.a: Workplace policies and the ANA’s principles for nurses’ social media use
alt.ex: Workplace policies and the ANA’s social media principles help answer questions about appropriate use.
w: Patients’ comments and the advice of other social media users
Patients and the public do not set professional standards for nurses.
The default privacy settings on each social media platform
Platform settings do not define professional conduct.
Personal preference alone, since social media is used off duty
Off-duty use must still align with agency policies and the professional code.

items.q: For what purpose do health care researchers use quality-of-life measures?
items.a: To scientifically define the value and benefits of medical interventions using statistics
items.ex: Quality-of-life measures help researchers statistically define the value and benefits of interventions.
w: To determine which patients are eligible for health insurance coverage
Insurance eligibility is not the stated purpose of quality-of-life measures.
To replace patients’ own descriptions of what matters most to them
Researchers increasingly add patient self-reports rather than replacing them.
To decide which patients may request a consultation with the ethics committee
Anyone seeking ethical advice may request an ethics consultation.

alt.q: What limitation of statistical analysis of quality of life does the textbook identify?
alt.a: It is more difficult when the outcome cannot be quantified
alt.ex: Statistical analysis becomes more difficult when outcomes cannot be measured in numbers.
w: It cannot be applied to any medical intervention
Researchers do use statistics to define the value of interventions.
It always ignores the burden of the intervention
Burden and benefit are part of weighing interventions.
It can only be done using patient self-reports
Both observed measures and patient self-reports are used.

items.q: Why is the pain of a flu vaccine injection considered an acceptable burden?
items.a: Its short-term burden is offset by the large benefit of avoiding or spreading the flu
items.ex: Any intervention creates a burden that must be offset by its benefit; the brief pain of a flu shot is outweighed by preventing flu.
w: Vaccines create no burden for the patient or the family
Every intervention creates some burden, including the pain of an injection.
The patient’s quality of life is not considered for vaccines
Quality of life is considered; avoiding the flu prevents a low-quality experience.
Its burden is equal to that of a long course of chemotherapy
A 6-month course of chemotherapy creates a much greater burden.

alt.q: A patient is considering a 6-month course of chemotherapy, a greater burden than a simple injection. When is this burden considered acceptable?
alt.a: When the expected outcome is a return to quality of life as the patient defines it
alt.ex: A greater burden is acceptable if treatment returns the patient to a quality of life acceptable by the patient’s own definition.
w: When the health care team believes the treatment is worth any burden
Acceptability is based on the patient’s definition of quality, not the team’s view.
When the burden lasts a shorter time than a flu vaccine injection
Chemotherapy’s burden is longer and greater; duration alone is not the test.
When statistics show the treatment works for most other patients
The test is a return to quality of life as this patient defines it.

items.q: A patient newly diagnosed with cancer is weighing treatment options and asks the nurse what to do. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “What matters most to you as you think about these choices?”
items.ex: Nurses facilitate conversations about treatment choices by encouraging patients to articulate their own definition of quality of life.
w: “Most patients your age choose the most aggressive treatment.”
Quality of life is deeply personal and should not be based on what others choose.
“Your health care provider knows which option is best for you.”
This dismisses the patient’s own priorities and definition of quality of life.
“Your family should decide since this choice is so difficult.”
Family values influence quality of life, but the patient’s own definition guides choices.

alt.q: How can a nurse best facilitate conversations about a patient’s treatment choices?
alt.a: Encourage the patient to articulate a personal definition of quality of life
alt.ex: Because quality of life is deeply personal, nurses help patients express what quality means to them.
w: Explain the statistical outcomes the patient should accept
Statistics alone cannot capture a patient’s personal definition of quality.
Recommend the option the nurse would choose for themselves
The nurse’s own preferences do not define the patient’s quality of life.
Use only objective measures such as age and independence
Subjective measures of what matters to the patient are also important.

items.q: Why are conflicts about end-of-life care common in health care?
items.a: Views about death and dying are part of deeply held spiritual and cultural beliefs
items.ex: Because views on death and dying stem from deeply held spiritual and cultural beliefs, end-of-life conflicts are common.
w: Everyone agrees on what a good death looks like for each patient
Although all agree a good death is desirable, opinions differ on what it looks like.
Health care providers can always predict exactly when death will occur
Predictions about health outcomes are not always accurate.
Conflicts occur only between patients and their family members
Conflicts also occur among team members and between families and the team.

alt.q: Why may health care providers have difficulty telling a patient with serious illness that the end of life is coming soon?
alt.a: Predictions about health outcomes are not always accurate
alt.ex: Because predictions about outcomes are not always accurate, communicating that death is near is difficult.
w: Patients with serious illness have no goals for end of life
Patients and families often have goals, such as pain control or being with family.
Providers are not permitted to discuss prognosis with patients
No such restriction is described; the difficulty lies in uncertain predictions.
Everyone has the same view of what a good death looks like
There are a variety of opinions about what a good death looks like.

items.q: A patient is dying with little or no hope of recovery, and the family and team agree that further aggressive interventions would be futile. How does this agreement help?
items.a: It helps everyone turn to palliative care measures as a more constructive approach
items.ex: Agreeing that an intervention is futile can help patients, families, and the team turn to palliative care.
w: It requires the team to stop all symptom management and comfort measures
Symptom management and comfort measures continue; they are not considered futile.
It transfers all decisions about care to the hospital ethics committee
The agreement redirects care toward palliation; it does not transfer decisions.
It means the patient no longer needs nursing care or assessment
Patients receiving palliative care continue to need nursing care.

alt.q: For a patient who is dying with little or no hope of recovery, which interventions are generally seen as futile?
alt.a: Almost any intervention beyond symptom management and comfort measures
alt.ex: When recovery is not expected, interventions beyond symptom management and comfort are unlikely to produce benefit.
w: Pain control and other measures aimed at the patient’s comfort
Symptom management and comfort measures are not considered futile.
Palliative care measures requested by the patient and family
Palliative care is the more constructive approach, not a futile one.
Allowing family members to remain with the patient at the bedside
Being with family is a common end-of-life goal, not a futile intervention.

items.q: The questions “Is health care a right that everyone can claim?” and “How can we best divide the health care resources we have?” involve which ethical principle?
items.a: Justice
items.ex: Access to health care is an ethical issue of justice, involving fairness and the distribution of resources.
w: Autonomy
Autonomy concerns freedom from external control and respect for patients’ choices.
Fidelity
Fidelity is faithfulness and the agreement to keep promises.
Nonmaleficence
Nonmaleficence is the avoidance of harm.

alt.q: Which nursing action best reflects an ethical commitment to justice regarding access to health care?
alt.a: Staying knowledgeable about affordable care options in the community
alt.ex: Knowing affordable care in the community helps nurses advocate for patients and reflects a commitment to justice.
w: Explaining each nursing procedure before performing it
Explaining procedures demonstrates respect for autonomy.
Starting the pain management plan as soon as possible
Promptly initiating a promised plan reflects fidelity.
Balancing the risks of care to do the least harm possible
Doing the least harm reflects nonmaleficence.

items.q: What was the purpose of the Affordable Care Act (ACA) passed in 2010?
items.a: To create regulations that control costs and improve the availability of insurance
items.ex: The ACA created regulations to control costs and improve insurance availability, improving access for millions of uninsured people.
w: To make Medicare available to all adults regardless of their age
Medicare is a federal program for individuals aged 65 and older.
To end employer-based health insurance as a benefit of employment
Employer-based insurance continues as one way people obtain coverage.
To limit insurance to urgent services and remove preventive care
The ACA aimed to expand access to less expensive preventive services.

alt.q: What was the aim of the ACA’s changes in payment for services?
alt.a: To expand access to preventive care and reduce expensive, burdensome chronic illness
alt.ex: Rewarding practices that reduce harm and promote quality aimed to expand preventive care and reduce costly chronic illness.
w: To reward practices that perform the most expensive procedures
Payment changes rewarded harm reduction and quality outcomes, not expensive procedures.
To shift payment for preventive care entirely to patients
The aim was to expand access to less expensive preventive services.
To pay practices based only on the number of patients seen
Payment changes rewarded quality outcomes, not volume alone.

items.q: According to the 2022 National Healthcare Quality and Disparities Report, what is the most significant contributing factor to poor quality of care?
items.a: Lack of health insurance
items.ex: The QDR reports that lack of health insurance is the most significant contributor to poor quality of care.
w: Low health literacy
Health literacy is not identified in the report as the most significant factor.
Distance from hospitals
Location affects coverage rates, but lack of insurance is named as the main factor.
Shortage of providers
Provider shortage is not identified as the most significant factor.

alt.q: A nurse reviewing health disparities data wants to identify the factor most strongly linked to poor quality of care. Which factor should the nurse identify?
alt.a: Being uninsured
alt.ex: Lack of health insurance is the most significant contributing factor to poor quality of care.
w: Living in a suburban area
Suburban residence is not named; inner-city and rural communities have lower coverage.
Receiving employer-based coverage
Having insurance is protective rather than a cause of poor care.
Enrolling in Medicare at age 65
Medicare provides insurance coverage, not a contributing factor to poor care.

items.q: Which statements about social media and nursing are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Social media can be a supportive source of information about patient care or professional nursing activities.
Social media can share useful information about patient care and nursing.
Social media can provide nurses emotional support during hardships at work.
It can offer nurses emotional support when they face hardships.
Social media can help patients connect with loved ones who cannot be physically present.
Patients can use it to stay connected with friends and family.
Removing names from patient photos makes posting them acceptable.
Posting patient information or pictures, even without identifiers, violates confidentiality.
Online friendship with patients strengthens the professional boundary.
Online friendship crosses the professional boundary and makes the relationship personal.
items.ex: Social media offers support and information, but the risk to patient privacy and professional boundaries is great.

alt.q: Which are risks of social media use identified by the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Violating patient confidentiality by posting information or pictures
Posting about patients, even without identifiers, violates confidentiality.
Clouding the nurse’s objectivity through online friendship with a patient
Online friendship risks the nurse’s objectivity in clinical perceptions.
Other users learning about a patient’s health from visible nurse–patient interactions
The public nature of online interaction can reveal the relationship and the patient’s health.
Patients becoming unable to connect with loved ones who are far away
Social media helps patients connect with loved ones; this is a benefit, not a risk.
Nurses losing access to professional information about patient care
Social media can be a source of professional information, not a loss of it.
alt.ex: The textbook identifies privacy breaches, boundary crossing, and public exposure of patients’ health as social media risks.

items.q: Which are objective measures of quality of life? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s age
Age is listed as an objective measure.
The patient’s ability to live independently
Ability to live independently is an objective measure.
The ability to contribute to society in a gainful way
Gainful contribution to society is an objective measure.
What the patient enjoys doing
What the patient enjoys is a subjective measure obtained by asking the patient.
What matters most to the patient
What matters most is a subjective measure based on the patient’s own priorities.
items.ex: Objective measures include age, independent living, and gainful contribution; subjective measures come from asking patients.

alt.q: Which are subjective measures of quality of life? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s stated priorities
Asking patients to identify their priorities is a subjective measure.
What the patient enjoys
What the patient enjoys is a subjective measure.
What matters most to the patient
Asking what matters most is a subjective measure.
The patient’s age
Age is an objective measure.
The patient’s ability to live independently
Ability to live independently is an objective measure.
alt.ex: Subjective measures ask patients about priorities, enjoyment, and what matters most to them.

items.q: Which statements reflect the implications for person-centered care related to access to affordable health care? Select all that apply.
o: Health outcomes often correlate directly to health care access.
The textbook states that health outcomes often correlate directly to access.
Issues of justice help inform discussion about access to care.
Justice and just distribution of resources inform discussions about access.
Nurses identify culturally appropriate resources for patients in their communities.
Identifying culturally appropriate community resources is a listed implication.
Nurses know and respect patients’ cultural practices about health promotion.
Respecting cultural practices regarding health care needs is a listed implication.
Low-income and rural communities are now as likely as others to be insured.
These communities remain significantly less likely to have health insurance.
items.ex: Access, justice, cultural practices, and culturally appropriate resources all shape person-centered care.

alt.q: According to the 2022 QDR, which groups are significantly less likely to have health insurance coverage? Select all that apply.
o: Low-income households
Low-income households are significantly less likely to be insured.
Minority communities
Minority communities are significantly less likely to be insured.
Rural communities
Rural communities are significantly less likely to be insured.
Inner-city communities
Inner-city communities are significantly less likely to be insured.
Adults aged 65 and older
Adults aged 65 and older are eligible for Medicare, a federal insurance program.
alt.ex: Despite the ACA, low-income, minority, inner-city, and rural communities are significantly less likely to be insured.

items.q: A person’s definition of quality of life can change over time and can be influenced by family and community values.
items.a: True
items.ex: Quality of life is deeply personal and shaped by personal, family, and community values that may change over time.
items.ww: The textbook states that a person’s definition of quality can change over time.

alt.q: Once a person defines quality of life, that definition stays fixed and is unaffected by family or community values.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Quality of life can change over time and is influenced by personal, family, and community values.
alt.ww: A fixed definition contradicts the textbook, which notes definitions shift and reflect family and community values.

items.q: Medicare is a federal insurance program available to all individuals aged 65 and older.
items.a: True
items.ex: Medicare is a federal program for all individuals aged 65 and older; Medicaid is state based and based on need.
items.ww: Medicare is defined by age, not by financial need.

alt.q: Medicaid is a federal insurance program available to all individuals aged 65 and older regardless of need.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Medicaid programs are state based and based on need; the federal program for those 65 and older is Medicare.
alt.ww: Medicaid eligibility is based on need, and the age-based federal program is Medicare.

items.q: Patient-Reported Outcomes are patient self-reports about quality of life and other outcomes that scientists increasingly include alongside observed measurements.
items.a: True
items.ex: Scientists increasingly add patient self-reports, called Patient-Reported Outcomes, to observed measures.
items.ww: The textbook describes Patient-Reported Outcomes as self-reports added to observed measurement.

alt.q: Quality-of-life research relies only on observed measurements, because patient self-reports are considered too subjective to include.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Scientists increasingly incorporate Patient-Reported Outcomes, or patient self-reports, along with observed measurement.
alt.ww: Self-reports are increasingly included, not excluded, in quality-of-life research.

items.q: In health care discussions, the term [[futile]] refers to interventions unlikely to produce benefit for a patient.
items.ex: Futile means hopeless or serving no useful purpose; in health care, it describes interventions unlikely to benefit the patient.

alt.q: An intervention that is hopeless or unlikely to benefit a dying patient is described as [[futile]].
alt.ex: Futile means hopeless or serving no useful purpose; in health care, it describes interventions unlikely to benefit the patient.

items.q: Access to health care is an ethical issue of [[justice]], involving fairness and the distribution of resources.
items.ex: Questions of who can claim health care and how resources are divided involve fairness and justice.

alt.q: Debates over how to fairly divide limited health care resources involve the ethical principle of [[justice]].
alt.ex: Questions of who can claim health care and how resources are divided involve fairness and justice.
