items.q: A patient’s right to refuse treatment, even when the nurse disagrees with the decision, is an example of which source of law?
items.a: Constitutional law
items.ex: The right to refuse treatment is a constitutional right afforded to every U.S. citizen, derived from federal and state constitutions.
w: Case law
Case law consists of decisions made in individual legal cases that were resolved in courts.
Administrative law
Administrative law clarifies expectations of statutes, such as what a nurse’s duty to care includes.
Common law
Common law arises from decisions made in the absence of law, such as early patient confidentiality.

alt.q: Which example best illustrates constitutional law in nursing practice?
alt.a: A patient’s right to refuse treatment
alt.ex: Every U.S. citizen has a constitutional right to refuse treatment, and agencies interpret such laws in their policies.
w: A nurse practice act defining scope of practice
A nurse practice act is a civil statutory law passed by a state legislature.
A regulation defining a nurse’s duty to care
Regulations that define duty are administrative, or regulatory, law.
A jury award in a malpractice trial
A decision reached in a court case is an example of case law.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: Nurse practice acts are classified as which type of law?
items.a: Civil statutory law
items.ex: Nurse practice acts are civil state laws passed by legislatures that define nursing and the standards nurses must meet.
w: Criminal statutory law
Criminal laws protect society and punish crimes, such as criminal mistreatment of vulnerable adults.
Common law
Common law arises in the absence of law; nurse practice acts are passed by state legislatures.
Federal constitutional law
Nurse practice acts are state statutes, not provisions of a constitution.

alt.q: Which law is a civil statute that defines nursing and the standards nurses must meet within a state?
alt.a: The nurse practice act
alt.ex: Each state’s nurse practice act defines scope of practice, educational requirements, and how to obtain licensure.
w: The criminal mistreatment statute
Criminal mistreatment statutes are criminal laws that punish harm to vulnerable adults.
The ANA Code of Ethics for Nurses
The code of ethics is a professional document developed by the ANA, not a statute.
The agency policy and procedure manual
Agency policies implement standards and must conform to laws, but they are not statutes.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: An alert, competent adult patient declines a blood transfusion that the nurse believes is needed. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “You have the right to refuse. Can you tell me more about your decision?”
items.ex: Patients have a constitutional right to refuse treatment, and nurses must respect it even when they disagree.
w: “You have to accept it because your provider has ordered it.”
A provider’s order does not remove a patient’s constitutional right to refuse treatment.
“I will ask your family to make this decision for you instead.”
A competent adult makes their own decisions; family members cannot take over that right.
“If you refuse, you will need to be discharged later today.”
Threatening discharge is coercive; refusing one treatment does not end other supportive care.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of a patient’s right to refuse treatment?
alt.a: “I must respect a patient’s refusal even when I disagree with it.”
alt.ex: Nurses must understand and respect patients’ constitutional right to refuse treatment, regardless of personal agreement.
w: “A patient may refuse only if the health care provider agrees.”
The right to refuse belongs to the patient and does not depend on provider approval.
“Once a patient consents, the patient cannot refuse later.”
Patients keep the right to refuse, even after a procedure has begun.
“Patients may refuse treatment only for religious reasons.”
The right to refuse applies broadly; religious refusal is only one example upheld by courts.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: A nurse observes a colleague repeatedly providing unsafe, incompetent care and decides not to report it. Which type of law has the nurse violated?
items.a: Regulatory law
items.ex: Regulatory law describes the process for reporting incompetent or unethical conduct; a nurse who does not report it violates regulatory law.
w: Common law
Common law comes from decisions made in the absence of law, such as early patient confidentiality.
Case law
Case law consists of decisions made in legal cases resolved in courts.
Constitutional law
Constitutional law comes from federal and state constitutions, such as the right to refuse treatment.

alt.q: Which action would place a nurse in violation of regulatory law?
alt.a: Failing to report a colleague’s unethical conduct to the board
alt.ex: Regulations require nurses to report incompetent or unethical nursing conduct to the state board of nursing or nursing commission.
w: Appealing a violation to the state board of nursing
Nurses are permitted to appeal violations to the state board or nursing commission.

items.q: A nurse with a hearing disability is hired on a medical unit. Under the ADA, which action is required of the employer?

w: Requiring the nurse to disclose the disability to all coworkers

Assigning the nurse only to tasks that involve no patient care

Requiring the nurse to pass an extra state licensing exam

An exemption from all workplace safety and practice standards
Accommodations allow nurses to practice safely within standards.

Accommodations support the person in the job they are qualified to hold.

The capable patient’s decision stands; family agreement is not required.
“The surgeon will decide, since the two of you disagree.”
The capable patient, not the surgeon, decides whether to proceed.

alt.q: When can a person named as a DPAHC begin making health care decisions for a patient?

Whenever family members disagree with the patient’s treatment choices
Family disagreement does not override a patient who has decisional capacity.
Only after the patient’s death, to arrange after-life care

A terminal diagnosis alone does not create a DNR order.

alt.q: Which statement about CPR and DNR orders is accurate?

w: CPR requires written consent from the patient before it begins.
CPR is an emergency treatment provided without patient consent.
A family’s verbal request is enough to withhold CPR.
Only a written DNR order in the medical record allows CPR to be withheld.
Patients with a terminal diagnosis are presumed to decline CPR.

items.q: Legally, a license to practice nursing is considered a privilege rather than a right.
items.a: True
items.ex: A nursing license is a privilege granted by the state that permits offering special skills and protects the public.
items.ww: States issue and enforce licenses, and boards can restrict, suspend, or revoke them.

alt.q: Because a nursing license is a legal right, a state board of nursing cannot restrict or revoke it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A license is a privilege; the board may investigate, suspend, or revoke it after notice and due process.
alt.ww: Boards regularly restrict, suspend, or revoke licenses when conduct violates the nurse practice act.

w: It requires a separate license from each participating state.

w: The nurse must first obtain a license in the patient’s state.

Telehealth across state lines is not allowed under the NLC.
The NLC specifically facilitates telehealth across state lines.

Explaining risks and alternatives is the responsibility of the person performing the procedure.
The nurse guarantees the patient understands every possible complication
A witness does not guarantee understanding; the nurse reports doubts to the provider.
The nurse agrees that the procedure is the best medical option
Witnessing does not express the nurse’s opinion of the procedure.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse about witnessing a consent form is accurate?
alt.a: “My signature shows the patient signed the form in my presence.”
alt.ex: Witnessing confirms the patient signed in the nurse’s presence and appeared to consent voluntarily and capably.
w: “My signature means I explained the procedure’s risks.”
The person performing the procedure explains risks and obtains consent.
“My signature confirms the procedure is the best option.”
A witness signature does not endorse the procedure.
“My signature shows I obtained the patient’s informed consent.”
Obtaining informed consent usually is not the nurse’s responsibility.

w: “I can witness it if my instructor cosigns afterward.”

“I can witness it because the patient seems to understand.”
Students should not witness consent forms regardless of patient understanding.
“I’ll witness it and note that I am a nursing student.”
Identifying as a student does not make witnessing acceptable.

alt.q: Why should nursing students not be asked to witness the signing of consent forms?
alt.a: Because of the legal nature of the consent document
alt.ex: Nursing students cannot and should not witness consent forms under any circumstances because of the document’s legal nature.
w: Because students cannot read medical terminology
The reason given is the legal nature of the document, not reading ability.
Because only physicians may witness consent forms

Because patients prefer licensed staff to be present
Patient preference is not the stated reason.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: A nurse stops at a highway crash and applies pressure to a victim’s bleeding leg wound. Which action protects the nurse from a claim of patient abandonment?
items.a: Staying with the victim until care is handed off to emergency medical technicians
items.ex: Once committed to emergency care, a nurse must stay until care can be safely transferred to a capable person such as EMTs.
w: Leaving the scene as soon as the bleeding has stopped
Leaving before a safe hand-off can create liability for patient abandonment.
Asking an untrained bystander to take over the care
Care must be transferred to someone who can provide needed care, such as EMTs.
Performing an advanced procedure to stabilize the victim first
Procedures beyond the nurse’s scope and training remove Good Samaritan protection.

alt.q: Which action would remove Good Samaritan protection from a nurse giving care at an accident scene?
alt.a: Performing a procedure beyond the nurse’s scope and training
alt.ex: Nurses are liable for injury from procedures that exceed their scope of practice and for which they have no training.
w: Applying pressure to a wound without sterile supplies
Appropriate care without proper equipment is still within accepted standards.
Staying with the victim until EMTs arrive and take over
Staying until a safe hand-off is required and prevents abandonment claims.
Giving care consistent with the nurse’s knowledge and experience
Care consistent with the nurse’s knowledge and experience is protected.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: A home health nurse notices that an older adult has untreated pressure injuries and appears underweight. The patient’s daughter, the caregiver, says she is doing her best. The nurse is unsure whether neglect is occurring. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Report the suspected neglect as required by state law
items.ex: Nurses are mandatory reporters when they have reasonable suspicion, and patient safety comes before the caregiver.
w: Wait until there is proof of neglect before reporting
The standard to report is reasonable suspicion, not proof.
Avoid reporting to protect the relationship with the caregiver
Nurses must place the patient’s health and safety above the caregiver.
Ask the daughter for permission before making a report
Mandatory reporting does not require the caregiver’s permission.

alt.q: What standard triggers a nurse’s legal duty to report suspected abuse or neglect?
alt.a: Reasonable suspicion that the person may be at risk of harm
alt.ex: The standard of proof for reporting abuse or neglect is a reasonable suspicion that the person may be at risk of harm.
w: Clear evidence that the person was harmed on purpose
Proof of intentional harm is not required before reporting.
A confession from the suspected caregiver or family member
A confession is not required; reasonable suspicion is enough.
A health care provider’s written confirmation of the abuse
The nurse reports on reasonable suspicion without waiting for confirmation.

w: Cardiopulmonary standard

Terminal disease standard
A terminal disease is one expected to cause death within 6 months, not a standard of death.
Decisional capacity standard

alt.q: Under laws similar to the Uniform Determination of Death Act, how may health care providers determine death?

w: Using only the cardiopulmonary standard

Using only the whole-brain standard
The act permits either standard, not only the whole-brain one.
Using both standards together in every case
Providers may use either definition; both are not required.

items.q: Under state statutory guidelines, which minors are generally considered emancipated and may consent to their own medical treatment? Select all that apply.
o: A 16-year-old who is married
Minors who are married, divorced, or widowed are emancipated.
A 17-year-old in active military service
Minors in active military service are emancipated.
A minor designated emancipated by a court order
A court order can designate a minor as emancipated.
A 17-year-old who works part-time and lives with parents
Having a job does not make a minor emancipated.
A 15-year-old who wants elective cosmetic surgery
Ordinarily, minors cannot consent to treatment without a parent.
items.ex: Emancipated minors include those emancipated by court order; those married, divorced, or widowed; and those in active military service.

alt.q: Which individuals may generally consent to medical treatment under state statutory guidelines? Select all that apply.
o: A competent adult 18 years of age or older, for self
Any competent adult 18 or older may consent for themselves.
A parent, for an unemancipated minor child
Parents may consent for their unemancipated minor children.
A grandparent, for a minor grandchild in an emergency when parents are absent
Grandparents may consent in an emergency if parents are not present.
An adult sibling, for a minor sibling during routine care with parents present
Adult siblings may consent only in an emergency when parents are absent.
A neighbor, for a minor child who lives next door
Neighbors are not among those who may legally consent.
alt.ex: Those who may consent include competent adults, parents, guardians, and, in emergencies without parents, adult siblings or grandparents.

Substance abuse treatment
Minors may consent to substance abuse treatment.

Elective cosmetic surgery
Ordinarily minors cannot consent to treatment without a parent.
Elective knee surgery
Elective surgery is not among the conditions minors may consent to alone.
items.ex: Unemancipated minors may consent for pregnancy, care of a custodial child, STIs, substance abuse, and outpatient mental health treatment.

items.q: Which information is a key element of informed consent? Select all that apply.

The patient receives an explanation of the procedure or treatment.
The names and qualifications of people performing and assisting
The patient is told who will perform and assist and their qualifications.
Alternative therapies and the risks of doing nothing
The patient learns alternatives and the risks of no treatment.
The right to refuse even after the procedure has begun
The patient may refuse even after the procedure has started.
A guarantee that the outcome will be successful
Consent discloses risks, including serious harm and death, not guarantees.
Agreement that refusing will end all other supportive care
Patients may refuse without discontinuing other supportive care.
items.ex: Informed consent includes an explanation, who performs it, serious risks, alternatives, and the right to refuse at any time.

Patients may refuse even after a procedure has begun.

“Once I sign the form, I cannot withdraw my consent.”
Patients keep the right to refuse at any point.
“I won’t be told who is assisting with the procedure.”
Patients receive the names and qualifications of those assisting.
alt.ex: Patients must learn risks and who is involved, and they may refuse at any time without losing other care.

items.q: A medical-surgical nurse is told to float to the pediatric unit for the shift but has never cared for children. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Inform the supervisor that the nurse lacks the education and experience to care for pediatric patients
items.ex: A nurse asked to float must tell the supervisor when the nurse lacks the education or experience needed for the assigned patients.
w: Accept the assignment and ask the pediatric nurses for help only if a problem arises
Waiting until problems arise puts patients at risk; the supervisor must first know of the gap in preparation.
Leave the hospital after explaining that floating is not part of the nurse’s usual role
Leaving without addressing the assignment with the supervisor does not protect patients and is not the book’s guidance.
Report the staffing shortage to the state board of nursing before going to the unit
The board of nursing is not the first contact; the immediate supervisor handles assignment concerns.

alt.q: A nurse who usually works in an adult intensive care unit is asked to float to labor and delivery and has no obstetric experience. Which statement by the nurse is most appropriate?
alt.a: “I need to let you know I have no obstetric training or experience for these patients.”
alt.ex: The floating nurse must inform the supervisor of missing education or experience so assignments can be adjusted safely.
w: “I will take the patients and look up any procedures I do not know as I go.”
Learning on the job while caring for patients without preparation risks unsafe care.
“I am refusing to float anywhere because it is not in my job description.”
A blanket refusal without specific reasons is not the expected response; nurses learn floating policies before employment.
“I will float, but only if another nurse documents that I objected.”
The key step is telling the supervisor about the lack of preparation, not having another nurse document an objection.

The book describes agency nursing committees, not the board of nursing, determining staffing in these states.
The agency budget office sets staffing from projected revenue

items.q: Which situation does the textbook describe as giving rise to legal issues related to staffing?
items.a: Too few nurses to provide competent care, or nurses working excessive overtime
items.ex: Legal issues occur when there are not enough nurses to give competent care or when nurses work excessive overtime.
w: Too many experienced nurses scheduled on a unit with low patient acuity
Overstaffing may be inefficient, but the book links legal issues to understaffing and excessive overtime.
Traveling nurses being given orientation materials before they arrive
Sharing orientation materials with travelers before arrival is a recommended integration strategy, not a legal problem.
Staff nurses joining a committee that recommends safe staffing levels
Staffing committees determine safe staffing; participating in them is not described as creating legal issues.

alt.q: A nurse has worked several double shifts this week because the unit is short staffed. Why does this situation raise a legal concern?
alt.a: Excessive overtime can lead to care that is not competent and safe
alt.ex: Short staffing and excessive overtime threaten competent care, and poor care from insufficient staffing has led to lawsuits.
w: Overtime hours automatically transfer the nurse’s liability to the agency
Overtime does not shift a nurse’s accountability; the concern is unsafe care from fatigue and short staffing.
Nurses who work overtime may not delegate any tasks to assistive personnel
Working overtime does not change delegation rules; the risk is impaired, unsafe care.
Overtime work is prohibited by federal law for all registered nurses
The book does not state that overtime is prohibited; it warns that excessive overtime creates legal issues.

items.q: Which statement best defines patient abandonment?
items.a: A nurse refuses to provide care after a nurse-patient relationship has been established
items.ex: Abandonment occurs when care is refused after the nurse-patient relationship exists; refusal before that point can be appropriate for valid reasons.
w: A nurse refuses an assignment before accepting report on the patients
Refusal before the relationship is established, for valid reasons, is not abandonment.
A nurse floats to another unit when the home unit is short staffed
Floating is a staffing practice, not a refusal to provide care.
A nurse delegates hygiene care for a patient to assistive personnel
Appropriate delegation with supervision is not refusing care for the patient.

alt.q: A nurse accepts report on four patients, begins care, and then leaves the unit midshift after a disagreement with the charge nurse. What legal problem has the nurse created?

Invasion of privacy

Defamation of character
Defamation is publishing false statements that damage a person’s reputation.

items.q: A nurse decides to refuse an assignment for a valid reason before accepting report. What should the nurse tell the immediate supervisor?

items.q: In general, what does nurse delegation mean?

w: An RN transfers full responsibility for a patient’s care to an LPN for the shift
The RN retains responsibility to communicate, supervise, and reassess whether delegation remains appropriate.
A nursing student performs any task learned in class while employed as assistive personnel
Students may do only tasks in their job description and allowed by the nurse practice act.
A supervisor assigns a floating nurse to a unit where the nurse does not usually work

alt.q: After delegating vital signs to assistive personnel, what responsibility does the RN keep?

alt.ex: The RN retains responsibility to communicate clearly, supervise care, and periodically reassess whether nurse delegation continues to be appropriate.
w: None, because accountability for the task passes fully to the assistive personnel
Responsibility does not pass entirely to the delegatee; the RN keeps supervision and reassessment.
Only signing the shift report to verify that the vital signs were completed
Signing a report is not the supervision and periodic reassessment the RN retains.
Only repeating the vital signs personally to confirm each value is accurate
The RN supervises and reassesses appropriateness; redoing every task is not the described responsibility.

items.q: Beyond basic care such as hygiene and vital signs, which task does the textbook say RNs can usually delegate to LPNs?

w: Reassessing whether delegation remains appropriate

The RN retains responsibility to supervise delegated care.

alt.q: An LPN is delegating care to a certified nursing assistant (CNA). Which task is typical of what LPNs delegate?

Removing a surgical drain
The book gives removing a surgical drain as care that may exceed a nurse practice act.
Deciding whether delegation is still appropriate

items.q: A nursing student gives a patient care that exceeds the student’s preparation, and the patient is harmed. According to the textbook, who generally shares liability?

items.ex: When a student harms a patient, liability is generally shared among the student, instructor, agency, and university.
w: Only the clinical instructor, because students practice under the instructor’s license
Students are liable for actions that exceed their scope of practice and harm patients.
Only the health care agency, because students are agency employees
Students are not agency employees, although the agency must monitor their acts.
Only the student, because the student chose to perform the task
Liability is generally shared, not borne by the student alone.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of student liability?
alt.a: “I am held to the standard of a professional nurse when I give patient care.”
alt.ex: Students are expected to perform as professional nurses would in providing safe patient care and are liable when they exceed their scope.
w: “My instructor is liable for anything I do, so I cannot be held responsible.”
Students are liable for harm when actions exceed their scope of practice.
“If I meant well, I cannot be liable for harm I cause a patient.”
Students are expected to know what they can and cannot do regardless of intent.
“The hospital has no duty to watch my care because I am not an employee.”
Although students are not employees, the agency has a responsibility to monitor their acts.

items.q: A nursing student who works as a medication technician learned to give intramuscular (IM) injections in nursing class. Learning a skill in class does not permit doing it outside the job description and nurse practice act.
Give the injection if the staff nurse stays in the room to supervise

Ask the clinical instructor to approve the injection by telephone
The instructor cannot expand the student employee’s job description; the supervisor must reassign the task.

Perform the task because it is listed in the job description

Delegate the task to another assistive personnel on the unit

sections.name: Legal implications and reducing your legal risks

items.q: A patient refuses an x-ray. The nurse tells the patient, “If you don’t cooperate, I’ll have to restrain you for the x-ray.” Which tort has the nurse committed?
items.a: Assault
items.ex: Assault is an intentional threat that places a person in reasonable fear of harmful or unwelcome contact; no contact is needed.
w: Battery
Battery requires actual offensive touching without consent; here there was only a threat.
Libel
Libel is written defamation of character, such as false charting.
Negligence
Negligence is an unintentional tort; a deliberate threat is an intentional tort.

alt.q: Which feature distinguishes assault from battery?
alt.a: Assault does not require any actual physical contact
alt.ex: Assault is a threat creating reasonable fear of contact, while battery is actual offensive touching without consent.
w: Assault requires that the patient be physically injured
Assault requires no contact at all, so injury is not required.
Assault can only be committed by a health care provider
Assault also occurs when a patient threatens a nurse.
Assault is an unintentional tort, unlike battery
Assault and battery are both intentional torts.

items.q: A patient signs consent for an appendectomy, and the surgeon also removes the patient’s tonsils during the operation. Which tort has occurred?
items.a: Battery
items.ex: A procedure beyond the scope of the patient’s consent is battery; the key component is the patient’s consent.
w: Assault
Assault is a threat of contact without actual touching; here contact occurred.
False imprisonment
False imprisonment is restraining a patient without a legal reason.
Invasion of privacy
Invasion of privacy involves releasing health information to unauthorized people.

alt.q: A nurse gives an injection to a patient who has clearly refused it. Why is this action considered battery?
alt.a: The nurse touched the patient without consent or lawful justification
alt.ex: Battery is any intentional offensive touching without consent or lawful justification, even if no injury occurs.
w: The nurse threatened the patient before giving the injection
A threat alone describes assault, not battery.
The nurse released the patient’s information without permission
Unauthorized release of information is invasion of privacy.
The nurse kept the patient confined to the bed during the injection
Confining a patient without a legal reason is false imprisonment.

items.ex: People who insist on information without patient consent must be referred to a supervisor; deciding disclosure is outside the nurse’s scope.
w: Share only the diagnosis, since the employer is paying for health insurance
Releasing information to an employer without consent is invasion of privacy.
Confirm the diagnosis if the caller can state the patient’s birth date
Knowing identifying data does not authorize release without the patient’s permission.
Tell the caller to e-mail the request so the nurse can reply in writing
E-mail is also confidential communication and cannot be released without permission.

alt.q: A reporter arrives on the unit and repeatedly demands information about a well-known patient. What is the nurse’s best response?

w: “I can tell you the patient’s condition is stable, but nothing else.”
Releasing any health information to the press without consent is invasion of privacy.
“I will ask the family whether I can share the diagnosis with you.”
Permission must come from the patient, and the request goes to a supervisor.
“I can share details after the patient is discharged from the unit.”
Discharge does not end confidentiality; release still requires the patient’s permission.

Malpractice requires that the patient was injured by the breach of duty.
Malpractice applies only to physicians

The visitor cannot be liable because they lack a medical license

w: The EHR will automatically lock the patient record for the rest of the shift
The concern is legal: changes are tracked and may look like record alteration.
Only the health care provider is allowed to change nursing documentation
Nurses can amend their entries correctly, as identified late or amended notes.
Deleted notes are sent to the state board of nursing for review
The issue is that altered records suggest hiding information from a court.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: In a malpractice suit, against what standard is a nurse’s actual conduct compared?
items.a: What a reasonably prudent nurse would do under the same or similar circumstances
items.ex: Courts compare the nurse’s conduct with what any reasonably prudent nurse would do in similar circumstances in that geographic area.
w: What the most experienced nurse in the agency would do in any circumstance
The standard is the reasonably prudent nurse, not the most expert nurse.
What the patient and family expected the nurse would do for the patient
Patient expectations do not set the legal standard of care.
What the health care provider ordered, regardless of nursing standards
Nursing conduct is measured against nursing standards of care, not orders alone.

alt.q: A patient falls while walking from the bathroom to bed. How is negligence by the nurse typically determined?
alt.a: By reviewing whether the nurse followed the fall prevention policy and transfer procedure
alt.ex: Negligence is judged by whether the nurse followed correct fall prevention policy and transfer procedure, as a prudent nurse would.
w: By determining whether the patient was injured badly enough to need surgery
Injury severity affects damages, but negligence depends on whether standards were followed.
By asking the patient whether the nurse seemed caring during the hospital stay
Patient perceptions of caring do not determine whether standards of care were met.
By counting how many falls occurred on the unit in the previous year
Unit fall rates suggest systemic issues but do not establish this nurse’s conduct.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: A nurse relies on the hospital’s malpractice insurance. A patient files a lawsuit, and a complaint is also filed with the state licensing board. What does the textbook say about this situation?
items.a: Malpractice insurance does not cover the licensing board complaint
items.ex: Malpractice insurance covers costs of a patient’s suit but not a licensing board complaint, so nurses should carry licensure defense coverage too.
w: The hospital’s lawyer will represent the nurse’s personal interests in both actions
The agency’s lawyer represents the employer, not the nurse.
Malpractice insurance automatically covers both the lawsuit and the board complaint
These are two different actions governed by different laws; malpractice insurance covers only the lawsuit.
Board complaints are dismissed whenever the employer has malpractice insurance
Employer insurance has no effect on a separate licensing board action.

alt.q: Why is it often recommended that nurses carry their own professional liability insurance?
alt.a: Employer coverage is often inadequate and the employer’s lawyer represents the employer
alt.ex: Relying on employer insurance is often inadequate; its lawyer represents the employer and covers nurses only within the scope of employment.
w: Employers are not permitted to carry insurance that covers nurses’ actions
Agencies do carry insurance covering nurses working within the scope of employment.
Personal insurance prevents patients from filing lawsuits against nurses
Insurance pays defense and settlement costs; it does not prevent lawsuits.
Personal insurance replaces the need to follow agency policies and procedures
Following policies remains essential for reducing legal risk regardless of insurance.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: An 18-year-old patient in a new leg cast reports numbness, and his toes are swollen and discolored. The nurse has called the health care provider twice with no response. Which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Notify the charge nurse or nursing supervisor to follow the chain of command
items.ex: When a provider does not respond, nurses must act for the patient’s safety by following the chain of command.
w: Document the findings and wait for the provider to return the calls
Waiting without escalating made nurses liable in the landmark cast case.
Reassure the patient that swelling is expected after cast application
Swelling, discoloration, and numbness signal impaired circulation that must be reported.
Remove the cast to relieve pressure on the patient’s leg
Removing the cast is not the nurse’s step; escalating to get appropriate care is.

alt.q: In the landmark case of a patient whose cast caused gangrene and amputation, why were the nurses held liable along with the physician?
alt.a: They failed to use the chain of command when the physician did not respond
alt.ex: The nurses recognized impaired circulation but did not escalate to the supervisor and others when the physician failed to respond.
w: They applied the cast without enough padding
The physician applied the cast; the nurses were liable for failing to monitor and report.
They failed to recognize the signs of impaired circulation
The nurses did recognize the signs but did not escalate.
They refused to provide care for the patient after admission
The nurses did not refuse care; they failed to follow the chain of command.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: A nurse is involved in a medication error on the unit. What is true about the occurrence report the nurse completes?
items.a: It is confidential and separate from the health record, but discoverable by court order
items.ex: Occurrence reports are kept separate from the health care record but can be obtained by court order in legal proceedings.
w: It is filed in the patient’s health record so all providers can review it
The report is confidential and separate from the health care record.
It is always protected from use in any legal proceeding
Occurrence reports are discoverable by court order during a legal proceeding.
It is completed by the risk manager after interviewing the nurse
The health care worker most directly involved completes the report.

alt.q: A visitor slips on the unit and injures an ankle. Who should complete the occurrence report?
alt.a: The health care worker most directly involved in the occurrence
alt.ex: The worker most directly involved completes the report, which alerts risk management and helps prevent recurrence.
w: The nurse manager who is responsible for the unit
Managers may review reports, but the most directly involved worker completes them.
The risk manager assigned to the hospital
Risk managers use the reports; they do not complete them for staff.
The health care provider who examines the visitor
The person most directly involved, not the examining provider, completes the report.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: An operating room nurse compares the signed consent form with the prepped surgical site before an operation. What is the purpose of the Joint Commission’s Universal Protocol that guides this check?
items.a: To prevent wrong-patient, wrong-procedure, and wrong-site surgery
items.ex: The Universal Protocol, with its mandatory time-out, prevents patients from undergoing the wrong operation or wrong-site surgery.
w: To prevent surgical site infections after the procedure
Infection prevention is important, but the protocol targets wrong-procedure and wrong-site errors.
To prevent delays in starting surgery on schedule
The protocol adds a mandatory time-out; it is about safety, not schedule.
To prevent patients from refusing surgery after consenting
The protocol verifies the correct procedure and site; it does not address withdrawal of consent.

alt.q: A nurse in an outpatient clinic is assisting with an invasive procedure. Which requirement of the Universal Protocol applies?
alt.a: A mandatory time-out before the procedure begins
alt.ex: Nurses implement the Universal Protocol, including a mandatory time-out, for any invasive surgical procedure regardless of setting.
w: A risk manager present in the room during the procedure
The protocol requires a time-out, not a risk manager’s presence.
An occurrence report completed before the procedure begins
Occurrence reports document events after they happen, not before every procedure.
A court reporter to record the consent discussion
Court reporters transcribe depositions, not surgical consent.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: Which elements must be shown to prove negligence against a nurse? Select all that apply.
o: The nurse owed a duty of care to the patient
A duty of care is the first element of proof.
The nurse breached that duty of care
Failing to use ordinary skill under similar circumstances is a breach.
The breach caused the patient physical injury or harm
The patient must be harmed because of the breach.
The injury resulted in compensable damages
Damages such as medical bills, lost wages, and pain and suffering are required.
The nurse intended to cause harm to the patient
Negligence is unintentional; intent to harm is not required.
The nurse had been disciplined by the board before
Prior discipline is not an element of proving negligence.
items.ex: Proof of negligence requires a duty, a breach of that duty, harm caused by the breach, and compensable damages.

alt.q: A patient sues a nurse for malpractice. Which must the patient’s side establish? Select all that apply.
o: The nurse had a duty of care to the patient
Duty of care is required to establish malpractice.
The patient was injured as a result of the breach
Injury caused by the breach is required.
Damages are allowed under state law to make the person whole
State law must allow damages or remedies.
The nurse deliberately chose to harm the patient
Malpractice does not require intent to harm.
The patient complained to the nurse during the stay
Patient complaints during care are not a required element.
alt.ex: Malpractice requires a duty, a breach, injury resulting from the breach, and damages allowed under state law.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: Which are common negligent acts that have resulted in lawsuits against nurses? Select all that apply.
o: Failing to communicate important information during shift handoffs
Failure to communicate and report is a common source of negligence.
Failing to assess and monitor a patient and report significant findings
Failure to assess, monitor, and report is a common source.
Failing to initiate the chain of command for a safety concern
Not using the chain of command is a common negligent act.
Failing to follow the fall prevention protocol
Not following policies and procedures is a common source of negligence.
Refusing an assignment before accepting report for a valid reason
Valid refusal before a relationship is established is not negligence.
Using teach-back to confirm a patient understands instructions
Teach-back is a recommended way to reduce legal risk.
items.ex: Common sources include failures to communicate, assess and monitor, ensure safety, rescue, give medications correctly, use the chain of command, and follow policies.

alt.q: A risk manager reviews claims filed against nurses. Which actions would the risk manager expect to find among common sources of negligence? Select all that apply.
o: Not following the rights of medication administration
Failure to administer medications correctly is a common source.
Failure to rescue a deteriorating patient
Failure to rescue is listed among common negligent acts.
Improper or negligent performance of a treatment
Improper treatment is a common source of negligence.
Clarifying an unclear medical order before acting
Clarifying unclear orders reduces legal risk.
Documenting patient education and the patient’s understanding
Documenting patient understanding is a risk-reduction practice.
alt.ex: Medication errors, failure to rescue, and improper treatment are common sources of negligence, while clarifying orders and documenting teaching reduce risk.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: Which actions by a nurse help reduce personal legal risk? Select all that apply.
o: Using teach-back to verify the patient understands instructions
Teach-back confirms understanding of patient education.
Conducting and documenting one’s own assessment instead of copying the previous one
Documenting your own assessment ensures accuracy.
Continually assessing the patient rather than relying entirely on monitors
No monitor is reliable all the time, so continual assessment is needed.
Clarifying unclear medical orders before carrying them out
Clarifying unclear orders is a listed risk-reduction action.
Posting a description of a difficult shift without patient names on social media
Nurses should avoid posting about patients or the workplace on social media.
Waiting until the end of the shift to report a significant change in condition
Significant changes must be reported to the health care provider in a timely manner.
items.ex: Teach-back, accurate own assessments, continual assessment, and clarifying orders reduce risk; social media posts and delayed reporting increase it.

alt.q: A new graduate asks how to lower the risk of a malpractice claim. Which practices should the preceptor recommend? Select all that apply.
o: Know and follow the agency’s policies and procedures
Following agency policies keeps care consistent with prudent colleagues.
Explain tests and treatments in language the patient understands
Clear communication with patients helps avoid malpractice.
Speak up when there is a concern about patient safety
Speaking up about safety concerns is a recommended practice.
Rely on alarms to detect changes so assessments can be less frequent
Monitors are not always reliable; continual assessment is needed.
Avoid documenting patient education to keep notes brief
Patient education and understanding should be documented.
alt.ex: Following policies, communicating clearly with patients, and speaking up about safety all reduce the risk of malpractice claims.

items.q: A nurse can commit assault without ever touching the patient.
items.a: True

items.ww: It is not false, because touching is what defines battery, not assault.

alt.a: False

items.ww: It is not true, because legal resolution is decided by the judge or jury, not the expert.

alt.q: A nurse expert witness gives an opinion on whether the nurse met standards of care but does not make legal decisions.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Experts compare the nurse’s care with standards from practice acts, TJC, policies, and evidence; courts make legal decisions.
alt.ww: It is not false, because the expert’s role is limited to applying standards of care to the facts.

items.src: Ch 23 · Legal implications in nursing practice

items.q: Nurses who were unaware of a current standard of care can use that lack of knowledge as a defense against malpractice.
items.a: False
items.ex: Ignorance of the law or of standards of care is not a defense; nurses must know current standards and agency policies.
items.ww: It is not true, because nurses are required to know the evidence and standards that apply to their practice.

alt.q: Ignorance of the law or of standards of care is not a defense against malpractice.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: All nurses are required to know current standards of care and their employing agency’s policies and procedures.
alt.ww: It is not false, because lack of knowledge does not excuse care that falls below the standard.

items.q: A nursing student feels anxious before caring for a patient with a complex diagnosis. Which thought is an example of positive self-talk?
items.a: “This is my chance to learn about this patient, and I can ask for help if I need it.”
items.ex: Positive self-talk reframes fear into an opportunity and acknowledges asking for help, which builds confidence for difficult situations.
w: “I am not ready to care for a patient this complex, so I will probably fail.”
This negative self-talk is a cognitive distortion that lowers self-esteem and confidence.
“I should avoid this assignment until I have a lot more experience.”
Avoidance does not build confidence; positive self-talk mentally rehearses how to handle the situation.
“If I make one mistake, everyone on the unit will know I am incompetent.”
This catastrophic thinking is a cognitive distortion that positive self-talk is meant to reduce.

alt.q: How does positive self-talk help a nurse in professional practice?
alt.a: It provides a mental rehearsal for difficult tasks or situations
alt.ex: Positive self-talk mentally rehearses difficult tasks so the nurse handles them more effectively and with more confidence.
w: It replaces the need to ask for help with unfamiliar tasks
The book’s example of positive self-talk includes knowing you can ask for help when needed.
It ensures patients perceive messages exactly as intended
Self-talk is inner communication; it cannot guarantee how others interpret messages.
It allows the nurse to avoid challenging patient assignments
Positive self-talk prepares the nurse to face difficult situations, not to avoid them.

items.q: Which level of communication is used most often in nursing situations and lies at the heart of nursing practice?
items.a: Interpersonal communication
items.ex: One-on-one interpersonal communication between a nurse and another person is the level most frequently used in nursing.
w: Intrapersonal communication
Intrapersonal communication is self-talk, the nurse’s own inner thoughts.
Small-group communication
Small-group communication occurs in committees and care conferences, not in most daily nursing interactions.
Public communication
Public communication is interaction with an audience, such as a community presentation.

alt.q: Which description defines interpersonal communication?
alt.a: One-on-one interaction between a nurse and another person, in person or electronically
alt.ex: Interpersonal communication is one-on-one interaction, face to face or by text or other electronic format, within a social context.
w: Interaction with an audience such as a community group or a class
Interaction with an audience describes public communication.
Inner thoughts that a nurse uses to rehearse difficult situations
Inner thoughts and mental rehearsal describe intrapersonal communication, or self-talk.
Outcome-oriented interaction among a few people meeting together
Outcome-oriented interaction among a small number of people is small-group communication.

items.q: A nurse uses the teach-back method after explaining a new medication to a patient. What is the main purpose of this method?
items.a: To verify how well the nurse explained the information
items.ex: Teach-back verifies how well the nurse explained the information and clarifies misinterpretations; it does not test the patient’s knowledge.
w: To formally test and score the patient’s knowledge of the drug
The book states teach-back does not test the patient’s knowledge.
To replace written discharge instructions about the drug
Teach-back checks understanding of an explanation; it does not replace other teaching materials.
To let the patient practice giving the drug independently
Teach-back uses questions to assess understanding rather than skill practice.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse about the teach-back method is accurate?
alt.a: “It checks the clarity of my explanation, not the patient’s knowledge.”
alt.ex: Teach-back asks the patient to restate information so the nurse can assess understanding and correct misinterpretations of the explanation.
w: “It tests whether the patient studied the teaching materials.”
Teach-back is not a test of the patient’s knowledge or study habits.
“It is used only with patients who have low literacy.”
The book presents teach-back as a way to validate meaning when providing health information, not only for low literacy.
“It lets me skip asking questions about the patient’s concerns.”
Teach-back relies on asking the patient questions to assess understanding.

items.q: A nurse attends an interprofessional patient care conference. How should communication in this setting be conducted?
items.a: Organized, concise, and complete, with all disciplines contributing
items.ex: Small-group communication should be organized, concise, and complete, and all participating disciplines are encouraged to contribute and give feedback.
w: Informal and lengthy, with the physician providing all input
All participating disciplines, not one, are encouraged to contribute and provide feedback.
Limited to nursing input so the meeting stays focused
Small-group communication encourages every discipline to contribute, not just nursing.
Detailed and unstructured to allow free-flowing discussion
Small-group communication is outcome oriented and should be organized and concise.

alt.q: Which activity is an example of small-group communication?
alt.a: Serving on a committee with participants from other disciplines
alt.ex: Committees and patient care conferences use small-group communication, which is outcome oriented and requires understanding group dynamics.
w: Presenting scholarly work to colleagues at a national conference
Presenting to an audience is public communication.
Sending a secure message to a patient through a patient portal
Secure messaging through a portal is electronic communication.
Taking a health history from a patient at the bedside
One-on-one history taking is interpersonal communication.

items.q: A nurse is replying to a patient’s question sent through the patient portal. Which practice follows professional guidelines for electronic communication?
items.a: Signing the message with professional credentials
items.ex: Professional electronic communication avoids all-capital text, uses language the patient understands, and is signed with professional credentials.
w: Typing the key instructions in all capital letters
Text written in all capital letters should be avoided in electronic messages.
Using medical terminology to keep the message precise
Messages should use language the patient will understand rather than medical jargon.
Leaving off a signature to keep the reply brief
Nurses should sign electronic messages with their professional credentials.

alt.q: Which is a recognized challenge of communicating with patients through an electronic portal?
alt.a: Maintaining the empathetic nature of the therapeutic relationship
alt.ex: Portals keep patients engaged and informed, but conveying the empathy of the therapeutic relationship may be more challenging.
w: Keeping patients engaged and informed about their care
Portals are described as enabling patients to stay engaged and informed.
Allowing frequent and timely contact with the care team
Frequent and timely communication is an advantage of secure messaging.
Giving patients a way to message their nurse or physician
Messaging the nurse or physician is the purpose of a portal, not a challenge.

items.q: Which critical thinking attitude motivates a nurse to communicate with and learn more about a patient as a person?
items.a: Curiosity
items.ex: Curiosity motivates the nurse to learn more about a person, and patients communicate more with nurses who show interest in them.
w: Humility
Humility helps the nurse recognize when communication must improve, especially related to cultural needs.
Integrity
Integrity helps the nurse recognize conflicting opinions and communicate to reach mutually beneficial decisions.
Self-confidence
Self-confidence helps the nurse convey comfort and establish a caring relationship more readily.

alt.q: A nurse recognizes the need to communicate better with a patient because of the patient’s cultural needs. Which critical thinking attitude is the nurse showing?
alt.a: Humility
alt.ex: Humility allows a nurse to recognize when communication and intervention need improvement, especially related to cultural needs.
w: Curiosity
Curiosity motivates learning more about a person but is not the recognition of one’s own limits.
Perseverance
Perseverance motivates more thorough assessment and finding innovative solutions.
Independence
An independent attitude encourages sharing ideas about interventions with colleagues.

items.q: A nurse explains a prescribed diet differently to a newly diagnosed patient than to a patient who has repeatedly chosen not to follow diet restrictions. What principle explains this?
items.a: Clinical decision making about communication is contextual
items.ex: The unique features of each situation shape what, when, where, why, and how the nurse conveys a message.
w: Teaching must be identical for all patients to be safe
The book uses this example to show that explanations differ by situation, not that they must be identical.
Patients who do not follow a diet need no more teaching
The patient who has not followed restrictions still receives an explanation, adapted to the situation.
Only newly diagnosed patients benefit from diet teaching
Both patients receive an explanation; only its approach differs with the context.

alt.q: How does the text describe effective communication techniques?
alt.a: Easy to learn but difficult to apply
alt.ex: Choosing which technique fits each unique situation requires critical thinking, making application harder than learning the techniques.
w: Difficult to learn but easy to apply
The book states the reverse: techniques are easy to learn but their application is difficult.
Easy to learn and automatic once memorized
Applying techniques requires critical thinking about what fits each situation, so it is never automatic.
Best learned by reading rather than practice
The book states the best way to develop communication skills is through practice and role-play.

items.q: A nurse assumes that an older patient from a particular cultural group will not want to take part in care decisions and does not ask. What does this assumption represent?
items.a: A stereotype that can distort how messages are interpreted
items.ex: Stereotypes and perceptual biases interfere with accurately perceiving and interpreting messages; critical thinking helps overcome them.
w: An example of cultural humility in nursing practice
Cultural humility recognizes incomplete understanding and explores the patient’s views instead of assuming.
Appropriate use of knowledge from prior experience
Assuming one understands a culture is a common error that distorts information.
A form of positive self-talk before a difficult task
Positive self-talk is inner rehearsal by the nurse, not an assumption about a patient.

alt.q: Which action best helps a nurse overcome perceptual biases when interacting with patients?
alt.a: Applying critical thinking during all patient interactions
alt.ex: Critical thinking during every interaction helps the nurse overcome biases and stereotypes and accurately interpret messages.
w: Relying on first impressions formed during admission
First impressions can carry biases; accurate interpretation requires critical thinking.
Assuming an understanding of the patient’s culture
People often incorrectly assume they understand a person’s culture, which distorts information.
Focusing on information that fits expectations
People tend to ignore information that conflicts with expectations; this is the bias to overcome.

items.q: Effective interpersonal communication requires a sense of mutuality. What does mutuality mean?
items.a: The nurse-patient relationship is a partnership of equal participants
items.ex: Mutuality is the belief that the nurse-patient relationship is a partnership in which both are equal participants.
w: The nurse directs decisions because of greater expertise
Directing decisions for the patient contradicts a partnership of equals.
The nurse and patient share the same cultural background
Mutuality concerns partnership, not shared culture; nurses work with people unlike themselves.
Both parties avoid expressing negative feelings
Caring nurses encourage expression of both positive and negative feelings.

alt.q: A nurse views the relationship with a patient as a partnership in which both are equal participants. Which quality of interpersonal communication does this reflect?
alt.a: Mutuality
alt.ex: Mutuality is the belief that nurse and patient are equal partners in the relationship.
w: Authenticity
Authenticity means being oneself in the relationship.
Initiative
Initiative is taking the lead in establishing and maintaining communication.
Assertiveness
Assertiveness is expressing oneself directly; it is not the belief in equal partnership.

items.q: A nurse plans to involve a patient in a discussion of the plan of care at the bedside of a semiprivate room. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Provide privacy before starting the discussion
items.ex: Person-centered bedside conversations about care contribute to a culture of safety, and providing privacy for them is essential.
w: Postpone involving the patient until discharge
Involving patients in conversations about their care should not be delayed; it supports safety.
Discuss the plan only with the family in the hallway
The patient should be involved in conversations about care, with privacy provided.
Speak quietly and proceed without other changes
Lowering the voice does not provide the privacy the book calls essential.

alt.q: According to the text, what does involving patients in conversations about their care contribute to?
alt.a: A culture of safety
alt.ex: Person- and family-centered communication, such as involving patients in conversations about care, contributes to a culture of safety.
w: A reduced need for team handoffs
Handoffs remain necessary; the book links patient involvement to safety culture.
Less need for documentation
Documentation is still required throughout the nursing process.
A complementary role relationship
A complementary relationship places one person above the other, the opposite of partnership.

items.q: A nurse on a short-staffed oncology unit has bonded with a dying patient’s family and reports emotional exhaustion. Which problem is the nurse at risk for?
items.a: Compassion fatigue
items.ex: Nurses may experience grief and compassion fatigue from emotional exhaustion, especially after bonding with patients or families.
w: Lateral violence
Lateral violence involves hostile behavior among colleagues, not exhaustion from caring.
Perceptual bias
Perceptual bias distorts interpretation of messages; it is not caused by emotional exhaustion.
Stereotyping
Stereotyping is a preconceived belief about a group, unrelated to caregiver exhaustion.

alt.q: Which factor does the text link to nurses experiencing grief and compassion fatigue?
alt.a: Developing a bond with patients or families
alt.ex: Grief and compassion fatigue arise from emotional exhaustion, especially when nurses have bonded with patients or families.
w: Using positive self-talk before difficult tasks
Positive self-talk builds confidence and self-esteem rather than causing exhaustion.
Taking part in bedside interprofessional rounds
Bedside rounding is linked to improved satisfaction and safety.
Using the teach-back method with patients
Teach-back verifies the nurse’s explanation and is not linked to compassion fatigue.

items.q: Which nursing actions reflect caring in nurse-patient relationships? Select all that apply.
o: Instilling faith and hope
Instilling faith and hope is listed among caring nursing actions.
Promoting patient advocacy
Advocacy for the patient is a caring nursing action.
Being present and encouraging expression of positive and negative feelings
Presence and encouraging all feelings demonstrate caring.
Respecting and allowing for spiritual expression
Respecting spiritual expression is a caring action.
Limiting talk about negative feelings to keep the patient positive
Caring encourages expression of negative as well as positive feelings.
Making care decisions for the patient to reduce the patient’s burden
Skilled communication empowers patients to make their own choices.
items.ex: Caring is shown by being with, doing for, and promoting well-being, including presence, hope, advocacy, and spiritual respect.

alt.q: A nurse wants to demonstrate caring through communication. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Developing healing relationships
Developing healing relationships is a caring nursing action.
Promoting interpersonal teaching and learning
Interpersonal teaching and learning reflects caring.
Providing for nursing care needs in a supportive way
Supportive provision of care needs is a caring action.
Discouraging spiritual expression during acute illness
Caring respects and allows for spiritual expression.
Using persuasion to pressure the patient into compliant choices
Nurses must not use communication to manipulate or coerce patients.
alt.ex: Caring actions include healing relationships, interpersonal teaching, and supportive care, never manipulation or coercion.

items.q: Which patient situations does the text identify as challenging communication situations? Select all that apply.
o: A patient who is angry and cannot listen to explanations
Angry or confrontational people who cannot listen are listed as challenging.
A patient with dementia who is confused and disoriented
Cognitive disorders such as dementia make communication challenging.
A patient who is flirtatious or sexually inappropriate
Flirtatious or sexually inappropriate behavior is a listed challenge.
A patient who understands little English
Language barriers are listed as a challenging situation.
A patient who calmly restates the care plan correctly
A calm patient who understands the plan does not present a communication challenge.
items.ex: Box 24.2 lists situations, such as anger, confusion, language barriers, and inappropriate behavior, that require careful therapeutic techniques.

alt.q: A nurse is preparing to role-play challenging communication situations. Which patient behaviors should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Being silent or withdrawn with difficulty expressing needs
Silent or withdrawn people are listed as challenging.
Being demanding and expecting others to meet requests
Demanding people are a listed communication challenge.
Being talkative or lonely and wanting constant company
Talkative or lonely people who want constant company are listed.
Being frightened and having difficulty coping
Frightened, anxious people with difficulty coping are listed.
Being relaxed and asking relevant questions about care
A relaxed patient asking relevant questions is not a challenging situation.
alt.ex: Role-playing Box 24.2 situations before clinical practice is recommended because communication skills develop best through practice.

items.q: Meaningful interpersonal communication results in which outcomes? Select all that apply.
o: Exchange and clarification of ideas
Exchange and clarification of ideas result from meaningful interpersonal communication.
Problem solving
Problem solving is a listed result.
Expression of feelings
Expression of feelings is a listed result.
Team building
Team building is a listed result.
No further need to validate meaning
Meaning resides in people, so nurses continue to validate or negotiate meaning.
Identical interpretation of messages by all receivers
Each person interprets messages differently; received messages can differ from intended ones.
items.ex: Meaningful interpersonal communication leads to idea exchange, problem solving, feelings expression, decisions, outcomes, team building, and growth.

alt.q: A nurse and patient engage in meaningful interpersonal communication. Which results can the nurse expect? Select all that apply.
o: Decision making
Decision making is a listed result of meaningful interpersonal communication.
Achieving outcomes
Achieving outcomes is a listed result.
Personal growth
Personal growth is a listed result.
Messages always received exactly as intended
Received messages are sometimes different from intended messages.
Less need to consider differing values
Nurses work with people with different values and must validate meaning.
alt.ex: Interpersonal communication supports decision making, outcomes, and personal growth, but meaning must still be validated.

items.q: Because meaning resides in people rather than in words, a received message is sometimes different from the intended message.
items.a: True
items.ex: Meaning lies in people, so nurses validate or mutually negotiate meaning when communicating.
items.ww: Words do not carry fixed meanings; each receiver brings different opinions, experiences, and values.

alt.q: Because words carry fixed meanings, a clearly worded message is always received exactly as the sender intended.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Meaning resides in people, not words, so received messages can differ from intended ones.
alt.ww: A clear message can still be misread because each person brings different experiences and values.

items.q: Like any powerful therapeutic agent, a nurse’s communication can cause harm as well as good.
items.a: True
items.ex: Every posture, gesture, word, and attitude can hurt or heal, so nurses have an ethical duty to do no harm.
items.ww: The book states communication can result in both harm and good, so it is not automatically helpful.

alt.q: Because therapeutic communication is a caring behavior, a nurse’s words and gestures cannot harm a patient.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Communication is a powerful therapeutic agent that can harm as well as heal.
alt.ww: Careless communication can hurt, manipulate, or coerce, which is why nurses must respect its power.

items.q: Communication skills are used mainly during assessment and have little role in the evaluation step of the nursing process.
items.a: False
items.ex: Communication is integrated in every step, including evaluation, where the nurse gathers feedback and explains care plan revisions.
items.ww: Box 24.1 lists communication activities in evaluation, such as acquiring verbal and nonverbal feedback.

alt.q: Nurses use communication skills to accomplish the work of every step of the nursing process.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Communication is used to gather, analyze, and interpret information throughout assessment, diagnosis, planning, implementation, and evaluation.
alt.ww: Box 24.1 shows communication activities in each step, not only during assessment.

items.q: Intrapersonal communication, a powerful form of communication that strongly influences perceptions and self-esteem, is also called [[self-talk|self talk]].
items.ex: Intrapersonal communication is self-talk; positive self-talk provides mental rehearsal and diminishes cognitive distortions.

alt.q: Transforming “I’m scared” into “This is my opportunity to learn” is an example of positive [[self-talk|self talk]].
alt.ex: Intrapersonal communication is self-talk; positive self-talk provides mental rehearsal and diminishes cognitive distortions.
