items.q: One patient presses the call light because of difficulty breathing; another asks for pain medication. In the circular transactional model, the breathing difficulty and the pain are examples of the:
items.a: Referent
items.ex: The referent is the stimulus, such as a sensation or idea, that motivates a person to communicate.
w: Channel
The channel is the sensory route, visual, auditory, or tactile, used to send a message.
Feedback
Feedback is the message the sender receives back from the receiver.
Message
The message is the content of the communication, not what prompts it.

alt.q: Why is it useful for a nurse to know the referent that initiated a patient’s communication?
alt.a: It helps the nurse develop and organize messages more efficiently
alt.ex: Knowing what prompted communication lets the nurse organize an appropriate response, such as reacting differently to dyspnea than to pain.
w: It shows which sensory channel the patient prefers to use
Channels are the sensory routes of a message; the referent is what motivates communication.
It shows how well the patient decoded the nurse’s message
How well a message was understood is shown by feedback.
It identifies the setting where the interaction takes place
The setting for the interaction is the environment.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient how to use a new inhaler. Which type of role relationship does this interaction represent?
items.a: Complementary
items.ex: In a complementary relationship one person holds an elevated position, as when a nurse educates a patient.
w: Symmetrical
Symmetrical relationships are more equal, such as patients discussing discharge plans together.
Reciprocal
The circular transactional model describes role relationships as complementary or symmetrical.
Mutual
Mutuality is a belief about partnership, not the role relationship of the transactional model.

alt.q: Which situation is an example of a symmetrical role relationship?
alt.a: A group of patients discussing their plans after discharge
alt.ex: Symmetrical relationships are more equal, such as patients sharing their discharge plans with one another.
w: A nurse teaching a patient about a new therapy
Nurse-to-patient teaching places the nurse in an elevated, complementary role.
A nurse explaining a new medication to a patient
Medication education is the book’s example of a complementary relationship.
A charge nurse directing a newly hired nurse
A charge nurse directing a new nurse holds an elevated position, a complementary relationship.

items.q: A nurse tells a patient, “Your incision is healing well without purulent drainage.” Which revision best improves the message?
items.a: “The edges of your wound are closed and there’s no drainage, so I see no signs of infection.”
items.ex: Effective messages use understandable language; plain words convey the same meaning to a patient without health care literacy.
w: “Your incision shows no purulent exudate and is approximating well.”
This version adds more medical jargon, making the message harder to understand.
“Your surgical site is healing by primary intention without complication.”
Technical phrases such as primary intention are unfamiliar to most patients.
“Your incision looks fine, right? Okay? Any drainage is normal, okay?”
Adding “right” or “Okay?” does not create clarity and the drainage claim is misleading.

alt.q: Which qualities describe an effective message?
alt.a: Clear, direct, timely, and in understandable language
alt.ex: Effective messages are clear, direct, timely, and understandable, expressed calmly and in a manner familiar to the patient.
w: Lengthy, thorough, and in precise medical terms
Medical terms and long explanations hinder understanding for many patients.
Brief, indirect, and delivered when convenient
Effective messages are direct and timely, not indirect or based on convenience.
Formal, scripted, and given only in writing
Messages can be spoken or written; the key is that the patient understands them.

items.q: A nurse wants to increase the chance that a patient understands how to change a dressing at home. Which approach best applies knowledge of communication channels?
items.a: Explain the steps, show pictures, and let the patient handle the supplies
items.ex: Messages are usually understood more clearly when the sender uses more channels, such as auditory, visual, and tactile.
w: Give a written handout for the patient to read alone
A handout alone uses one channel and gives no chance to clarify understanding.
Explain the steps aloud once while the television is on
One auditory channel with environmental distraction reduces understanding.
Send the instructions later through the patient portal
A delayed written message uses a single channel and misses immediate clarification.

alt.q: Which statement about communication channels is accurate?
alt.a: A message is usually understood better when more channels are used
alt.ex: Individuals usually understand a message more clearly when the sender uses more visual, auditory, and tactile channels.
w: Touch sends messages through the auditory channel
Touch uses the tactile channel; spoken words use the auditory channel.
Facial expressions send messages through the tactile channel
Facial expressions send visual messages.
Using one channel prevents confusing the receiver
Using more channels, not fewer, usually improves understanding.

items.q: What does feedback indicate in the communication process?
items.a: The extent to which the receiver understood the message
items.ex: Feedback is the message a sender receives from the receiver, showing how well the meaning was understood.
w: The stimulus that motivated the sender to communicate
The stimulus that starts communication is the referent.
The setting in which the interaction takes place
The setting for interaction is the environment.
The sensory route used to transmit the message
The sensory route is the channel.

alt.q: After explaining a procedure, a nurse notices the patient frowning and asks, “What questions do you have about the steps?” Which element of communication is the nurse seeking?
alt.a: Feedback
alt.ex: A sender seeks verbal and nonverbal feedback to evaluate the receiver’s response and the effectiveness of the message.
w: Referent
The referent is the cue that starts communication, not the receiver’s response.
Channel
The channel is the sensory route of the message, not the receiver’s response.
Environment
The environment is the setting, not the receiver’s response to the message.

items.q: A nurse says to a quiet patient, “You haven’t been talking much since your family left. Is something on your mind?” The patient replies sharply, “That’s my business.” What best explains this response?
items.a: The patient perceived the question as an invasion of privacy
items.ex: Perception is an interpersonal variable; one patient may see this question as caring while another sees it as intrusive.
w: The nurse’s message lacked clarity and directness
The question was clear and direct; the difference lies in the patient’s perception.
The environment was too noisy for the patient to hear
Nothing suggests noise; the patient heard and responded to the question.
The nurse and patient have a symmetrical role relationship
Role relationships do not explain why a patient interprets a caring question as intrusive.

alt.q: Which interpersonal variable provides a uniquely personal view of reality formed by a person’s culture, expectations, and experiences?
alt.a: Perception
alt.ex: Perception gives each person a unique view of reality, so each person interprets messages differently.
w: Referent
The referent is the stimulus that motivates communication.
Feedback
Feedback is the receiver’s response to the sender’s message.
Channel
A channel is the sensory route through which a message travels.

items.q: What does cultural humility allow a nurse to do when communicating with patients?
items.a: Recognize an incomplete understanding of the patient’s culture and explore what affects communication
items.ex: Cultural humility recognizes that the nurse does not completely understand a patient’s culture and allows exploring interpersonal variables.
w: Assume full understanding of the patient’s culture after a single careful assessment
Cultural humility rests on recognizing that you do not completely understand another culture.
Apply the same communication approach to every patient from one cultural group
Treating all members of a group the same reflects stereotyping, not humility.
Avoid discussing sociocultural background so the patient is not offended
Cultural humility explores sociocultural background rather than avoiding it.

alt.q: A nurse caring for a patient from an unfamiliar culture says, “I don’t fully understand your traditions. Can you tell me what is important to you?” What does this reflect?
alt.a: Cultural humility
alt.ex: Recognizing limited understanding and asking the patient to explain reflects cultural humility.
w: Stereotyping
Stereotyping assumes knowledge about a group; this nurse asks instead of assuming.
Perceptual bias
Perceptual bias distorts interpretation; the nurse is seeking accurate information.
A complementary role relationship
Complementary relationships involve one person in an elevated position, unrelated to exploring culture.

items.q: A nurse needs to discuss a new diagnosis with a patient in a semiprivate room where the television is loud and the roommate has visitors. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Arrange a quiet, private setting before beginning the discussion
items.ex: An effective setting provides physical and emotional comfort and safety; noise and lack of privacy create confusion and tension.
w: Speak louder so the patient can hear over the noise
Speaking louder does not remove distractions or provide privacy.
Begin the discussion and ask visitors to stay quiet
Visitors present still prevent privacy for a sensitive discussion.
Leave written information for the patient to read later
Written material alone does not address the patient’s questions or need for a supportive setting.

alt.q: Which description fits an effective communication environment?
alt.a: It provides physical and emotional comfort and safety
alt.ex: An effective setting gives participants physical and emotional comfort and safety, free of noise and distractions.
w: It allows open access to the patient’s space for efficiency
Lack of privacy or space creates confusion, tension, and discomfort.
It keeps the room cool and busy so the patient stays alert
Temperature extremes and distractions interfere with communication.
It includes background activity to ease tension
Noise and distractions increase tension rather than ease it.

items.q: A nurse begins discharge teaching for a patient who reports severe pain and is drowsy after receiving an opioid. Why is the patient unlikely to absorb the teaching?
items.a: Pain and medication effects are interpersonal variables that affect communication
items.ex: Illness-related interpersonal variables such as pain, anxiety, and medication effects affect nurse-patient communication.
w: The referent for the teaching is unclear to the patient
The referent is what prompted the communication; the barrier here lies within the patient.
The nurse is using too many channels to send the message
Using more channels usually improves understanding.
Feedback from the patient is not needed in this situation
Feedback is always needed to evaluate whether a message was understood.

alt.q: Which interpersonal variables are associated with a patient’s illness?
alt.a: Pain, anxiety, and medication effects
alt.ex: Pain, anxiety, and medication effects are illness-related interpersonal variables that affect nurse-patient communication.
w: Noise, temperature, and lack of privacy
These are environmental factors, not variables within the patient.
Visual, auditory, and tactile senses
These are communication channels.
Sights, sounds, and ideas that prompt talking
Cues that prompt communication are referents.

items.q: According to the text, what increases the likelihood that a sender and receiver will accurately perceive one another’s meaning?
items.a: Having more in common and a closer relationship
items.ex: The more the sender and receiver share and the closer their relationship, the more accurately they perceive meaning.
w: Using more technical vocabulary
Technical vocabulary makes messages harder for many patients to understand.
Saving feedback for the end of the talk
Feedback occurs continuously and is needed to clarify messages.
Keeping a strictly formal relationship
A closer relationship, not a more distant one, improves accurate perception.

alt.q: A nurse wants to improve the accuracy of communication with a newly admitted patient. Which action is most effective?
alt.a: Establishing rapport with the patient
alt.ex: Establishing rapport ensures more effective communication, which improves clinical judgment and decision making.
w: Using precise medical terminology
Medical jargon sounds foreign to patients and hinders understanding.
Keeping conversations brief and formal
A formal, distant approach does not build the closeness that improves accurate perception.
Waiting to seek feedback until teaching ends
Feedback is sought continuously to clarify messages.

items.q: Which statement accurately describes the circular transactional model of communication?
items.a: Each person is both speaker and listener and can send and receive messages at the same time
items.ex: In this model communication is continuous and interactive; both parties simultaneously send and receive messages.
w: The sender transmits a message and the receiver listens without responding
A one-way process ignores the continuous, interactive exchange the model describes.
Communication ends as soon as the sender finishes delivering the message
Communication is continuous; feedback keeps the process going.
Only the nurse gives feedback to correct or validate the message
Feedback comes from the receiver or environment and flows between both parties.

alt.q: During a conversation, a nurse and patient switch back and forth between sending and receiving messages. Which concept does this describe?
alt.a: Transactional communication
alt.ex: Transactional communication involves the sender and receiver roles switching back and forth between nurse and patient.
w: Linear communication
A linear process moves one way; the model described is circular and transactional.
Complementary role relationship
A complementary relationship refers to one person holding an elevated position.
Intrapersonal communication
Intrapersonal communication is self-talk within one person.

items.q: Which are elements of the circular transactional model of communication? Select all that apply.
o: Referent
The referent motivates communication and is an element of the model.
Channels
Channels are the sensory routes for messages in the model.
Feedback
Feedback lets communicators correct or validate communication.
Interpersonal variables
Interpersonal variables within sender and receiver are part of the model.
Teach-back
Teach-back is a teaching method, not an element of the model.
Territoriality
Territoriality is a form of nonverbal communication, not a model element.
items.ex: The model includes referent, sender and receiver, message, channels, environment, feedback, and interpersonal variables.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing the circular transactional model. Which elements should the nurse identify? Select all that apply.
o: Sender and receiver
Sender and receiver are elements of the model.
Message
The message, the content of communication, is an element.
Environment
The environment, or context, is an element of the model.
Mutuality
Mutuality is a belief about partnership, not an element of the model.
Self-talk
Self-talk is intrapersonal communication, a level of communication.
alt.ex: Sender and receiver, message, and environment are among the seven elements of the circular transactional model.

items.q: Which interpersonal variables can affect how a patient communicates? Select all that apply.
o: Educational and developmental level
Education and developmental level are listed interpersonal variables.
Sociocultural background
Sociocultural background influences how a patient communicates.
Values and beliefs
Values and beliefs are listed interpersonal variables.
Emotions
Emotions are listed interpersonal variables.
Noise level in the room
Noise is an environmental factor, not a variable within the person.
Number of channels used by the nurse
Channels are a separate element of the communication model.
items.ex: Interpersonal variables lie within the sender and receiver and include education, culture, values, emotions, gender, health, and roles.

alt.q: A nurse assesses factors within a patient that may influence communication. Which should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.
o: Gender
Gender is a listed interpersonal variable.
Physical health status
Physical health status is a listed interpersonal variable.
Roles and relationships
Roles and relationships are listed interpersonal variables.
Room temperature
Temperature extremes are environmental factors.
Lack of privacy
Lack of privacy is an environmental factor.
alt.ex: Factors within the person, such as gender, health status, and roles, are interpersonal variables, unlike environmental conditions.

items.q: Which environmental factors interfere with communication between a nurse and patient? Select all that apply.
o: Noise
Noise creates confusion, tension, and discomfort.
Temperature extremes
Temperature extremes interfere with communication.
Distractions
Distractions are common in health care settings and interfere with messages.
Lack of privacy or space
Lack of privacy or space creates tension and discomfort.
Physical and emotional comfort
Comfort and safety describe an effective communication setting.
items.ex: Noise, temperature extremes, distractions, and lack of privacy or space create confusion, tension, and discomfort.

alt.q: A nurse is preparing to talk with a patient about test results. Which actions help create a favorable communication environment? Select all that apply.
o: Turning off the television
Reducing noise and distractions supports effective communication.
Closing the door or curtain
Providing privacy supports comfort and safety.
Adjusting the room temperature for comfort
Avoiding temperature extremes promotes physical comfort.
Holding the talk in a busy hallway
A busy hallway adds distractions and removes privacy.
Talking while the roommate’s visitors are present
Visitors present reduce privacy and add distraction.
alt.ex: Nurses control the environment as much as possible to provide comfort, privacy, and safety for effective communication.

items.q: Active listening is important for the receiver to accurately decode and understand a message.
items.a: True
items.ex: Decoding is the receiver interpreting the meaning of word symbols, and active listening supports accurate decoding.
items.ww: Without active listening, the receiver is less likely to interpret the sender’s meaning correctly.

alt.q: Decoding is the sender’s task of putting a message into verbal and nonverbal symbols the receiver can understand.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Putting a message into symbols is encoding by the sender; decoding is the receiver interpreting the message.
alt.ww: The receiver, not the sender, decodes the message by interpreting its symbols.

items.q: Patients with cognitive disorders such as dementia may need aids like hearing aids, interpreters, or pictures to understand messages.
items.a: True
items.ex: People with cognitive disorders or communication barriers may need assistance to clarify messages sent and received.
items.ww: Assistance such as pictures or interpreters helps these patients understand, so it is not unnecessary.

alt.q: Pictures and other aids are of little use for confused patients because they cannot understand messages.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients with confusion or dementia may need aids such as pictures to help them understand messages.
alt.ww: The book recommends assistance to help these patients understand, rather than assuming they cannot.

items.q: Feedback occurs only after the sender has finished delivering the entire message.
items.a: False
items.ex: Feedback occurs continuously between sender and receiver, allowing them to correct or validate communication.
items.ww: Communication in the transactional model is continuous, so feedback is not limited to the end.

alt.q: Feedback occurs continuously between a sender and a receiver.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Feedback flows continuously, letting the sender evaluate the receiver’s response and clarify messages.
alt.ww: Feedback does not wait until the message ends; it is part of the ongoing, interactive process.

items.q: The [[sender]] is the person who encodes and delivers a message, and the [[receiver]] is the person who receives and decodes it.
items.ex: The sender encodes the message into verbal and nonverbal symbols; the receiver decodes, or interprets, those symbols.

alt.q: A nurse who explains a procedure acts as the [[sender]], and the patient who interprets the explanation acts as the [[receiver]].
alt.ex: The sender encodes the message into verbal and nonverbal symbols; the receiver decodes, or interprets, those symbols.

items.q: Factors within both the sender and receiver that influence communication, such as perception, emotions, and culture, are called [[interpersonal variables|interpersonal variable]].
items.ex: Interpersonal variables include perception, education, culture, values, emotions, gender, health status, and roles.

alt.q: Pain, anxiety, and medication effects are illness-related [[interpersonal variables|interpersonal variable]] that affect nurse-patient communication.
alt.ex: Interpersonal variables include perception, education, culture, values, emotions, gender, health status, and roles.

items.q: What is the Referent in the communication process?
items.a: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate
items.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Person who encodes and delivers a message
That goes with Sender.
Person who receives and decodes a message
That goes with Receiver.
Sensory route used to send and receive a message
That goes with Channel.

alt.a: Person who encodes and delivers a message
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate
That goes with Referent.
Person who receives and decodes a message
That goes with Receiver.
Sensory route used to send and receive a message
That goes with Channel.

alt.q: What is the Receiver in the communication process?
alt.a: Person who receives and decodes a message
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate
That goes with Referent.
Person who encodes and delivers a message
That goes with Sender.
Sensory route used to send and receive a message
That goes with Channel.

alt.q: What is the Channel in the communication process?
alt.a: Sensory route used to send and receive a message
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate
That goes with Referent.
Person who encodes and delivers a message
That goes with Sender.
Person who receives and decodes a message
That goes with Receiver.

alt.q: What is the Feedback in the communication process?
alt.a: Message the sender receives back from the receiver
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate
That goes with Referent.
Person who encodes and delivers a message
That goes with Sender.
Person who receives and decodes a message
That goes with Receiver.

alt.q: What is the Environment in the communication process?
alt.a: Setting for the sender-receiver interaction
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate
That goes with Referent.
Person who encodes and delivers a message
That goes with Sender.
Person who receives and decodes a message
That goes with Receiver.

alt.q: Which element of communication is the “Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate”?
alt.a: Referent
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Sender
Sender: Person who encodes and delivers a message.
Receiver
Receiver: Person who receives and decodes a message.
Channel
Channel: Sensory route used to send and receive a message.

alt.q: Which element of communication is the “Person who encodes and delivers a message”?
alt.a: Sender
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Referent
Referent: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate.
Receiver
Receiver: Person who receives and decodes a message.
Channel
Channel: Sensory route used to send and receive a message.

alt.q: Which element of communication is the “Person who receives and decodes a message”?
alt.a: Receiver
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Referent
Referent: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate.
Sender
Sender: Person who encodes and delivers a message.
Channel
Channel: Sensory route used to send and receive a message.

alt.q: Which element of communication is the “Sensory route used to send and receive a message”?
alt.a: Channel
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Referent
Referent: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate.
Sender
Sender: Person who encodes and delivers a message.
Receiver
Receiver: Person who receives and decodes a message.

alt.a: Feedback
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Referent
Referent: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate.
Sender
Sender: Person who encodes and delivers a message.
Receiver
Receiver: Person who receives and decodes a message.

alt.q: Which element of communication is the “Setting for the sender-receiver interaction”?
alt.a: Environment
alt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.
w: Referent
Referent: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate.
Sender
Sender: Person who encodes and delivers a message.
Receiver
Receiver: Person who receives and decodes a message.

mt.q: Match each element of the circular transactional model with its description.
pairs: Stimulus that motivates a person to communicate
Person who encodes and delivers a message
Person who receives and decodes a message
Sensory route used to send and receive a message
Message the sender receives back from the receiver
mt.ex: Each element of the circular transactional model influences how accurately messages are sent, understood, and validated.

items.q: A nurse admits a patient who speaks little English. The patient’s 12-year-old grandson offers to translate. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Arrange for a professional interpreter
items.ex: When a patient speaks another language, a professional interpreter is necessary for successful communication.
w: Allow the grandson to interpret the admission history
The book states a professional interpreter is necessary, not a family member.
Speak louder and more slowly in English
Volume and pace do not overcome a language barrier.
Use gestures alone to complete the assessment
Gestures alone cannot accurately convey a full admission history.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of communicating with a patient who speaks another language?
alt.a: “I’ll request a professional interpreter for our conversations.”
alt.ex: Communication fails if sender and receiver cannot translate each other’s words, so a professional interpreter is necessary.
w: “I’ll ask a bilingual relative to interpret for us.”
The book specifies a professional interpreter is necessary.
“I’ll use medical terms since they’re universal.”
Medical jargon sounds foreign even to patients who share the nurse’s language.
“I’ll talk quickly so we finish before she tires.”
Rapid speech conveys unintended messages and does not bridge a language barrier.

items.q: A provider tells a family that their father is in “serious condition,” and the family begins grieving as if death is near. This misunderstanding involves which aspect of verbal communication?
items.a: Connotative meaning
items.ex: Connotative meaning is the interpretation of a word shaped by people’s thoughts and feelings about it, such as “serious.”
w: Denotative meaning
Denotative meaning is the meaning shared by people who use a common language.
Pacing
Pacing is the speed and rhythm of speech, not the interpretation of a word.
Intonation
Intonation is tone of voice; the family’s distress stems from what the word meant to them.

alt.q: Health care providers share the understanding that the word “code” means cardiac arrest. Which type of meaning does this illustrate?
alt.a: Denotative meaning
alt.ex: Denotative meaning is shared by those who use a common language, such as “code” among health care providers.
w: Connotative meaning
Connotative meaning is a personal interpretation influenced by thoughts and feelings about a word.
Inappropriate affect
Inappropriate affect is a facial expression that does not match a verbal message.
Metacommunication
Metacommunication refers to all factors that influence communication.

items.q: A nurse is about to measure a 6-year-old child’s vital signs. Which statement is most appropriate?
items.a: “I’m going to check your blood pressure, heart rate, and temperature.”
items.ex: Familiar phrases like “take your vital signs” may confuse or frighten a child, so naming each measurement is clearer.
w: “I’m going to take all of your vital signs now, okay?”
This common phrase may be unfamiliar to adults and frightening to a child.
“I need to assess your hemodynamic status and perfusion.”
Medical jargon sounds like a foreign language to patients.
“Let’s get your vitals and your temp done quickly, okay?”
Abbreviated jargon and a tag “okay?” do not achieve clarity.

alt.q: Why should a nurse limit the use of medical jargon to conversations with other health care team members?
alt.a: Patients unfamiliar with health care may not understand it
alt.ex: Medical jargon is technical terminology that patients unfamiliar with health care settings often cannot understand.
w: It is not allowed even among health care team members
The book recommends limiting jargon to conversations with team members, where it is appropriate.
It makes nurses seem less professional to their colleagues
The concern is patient understanding, not how colleagues view the nurse.
It is understood only by patients who are older adults
Age does not ensure understanding; jargon confuses many patients.

items.q: Which nurse behavior may give a patient the impression that the nurse is hiding the truth?
items.a: Long pauses and rapid shifts to another subject
items.ex: Long pauses and rapid subject changes during conversation can suggest the nurse is concealing the truth.
w: Speaking moderately slowly and enunciating clearly
Moderately slow, clear speech is the recommended pacing.
Using brief examples to explain a procedure
Brief examples make explanations easier to understand.
Repeating important parts of the message
Repeating key points clarifies communication.

alt.q: What should a nurse do to improve the pacing of conversation with patients?
alt.a: Think before speaking and be aware of speech rhythm
alt.ex: Thinking before speaking and attending to the rhythm of speech improves pacing.
w: Speak rapidly to cover all teaching points
Talking rapidly conveys an unintended message.
Speak very slowly and deliberately at all times
Excessively slow, deliberate speech also conveys an unintended message.
Pause often while changing topics quickly
Awkward pauses and rapid topic shifts suggest hiding the truth.

items.q: Which question about pain best demonstrates clarity and brevity?
items.a: “Where is your pain?”
items.ex: Effective communication is simple, brief, and direct, expressing an idea in as few words as needed.
w: “Could you describe for me where your discomfort is located?”
This wordy phrasing is less direct than a simple question.
“Where does it hurt, right? Okay?”
Adding “right” or “Okay?” does not achieve clarity.
“Would you tell me about the area that is uncomfortable?”
This roundabout wording is less clear than asking directly.

alt.q: A nurse is explaining a procedure to an older adult. Which approach best supports clarity?
alt.a: Use fewer words, speak slowly, and repeat key points
alt.ex: For older adults, fewer words create less confusion; slow, clear speech and repeating key points clarify messages.
w: Add “Okay?” after each sentence to check understanding
Phrases such as “Okay?” after every sentence do not achieve clarity.
Give a detailed explanation with many technical terms
Lengthy, technical explanations create more confusion.
Speak quickly so the explanation stays short
Speaking slowly and enunciating clearly aids understanding.

items.q: A patient is about to have emergency surgery and is visibly anxious. Which topic is most relevant for the nurse to address?
items.a: The patient’s fears and the presurgical procedures
items.ex: Messages relevant to the situation are more effective; before emergency surgery, explaining procedures and clarifying fears matters most.
w: The long-term health risks of the patient’s smoking
The book gives smoking risks as less relevant than presurgical explanations in this situation.
A detailed diet plan for after discharge
Discharge diet teaching is not relevant to the immediate situation.
Routine teaching about home medication storage
Routine teaching is poorly timed when a patient faces emergency surgery.

alt.q: A nurse plans routine teaching for a patient who is in severe pain. Which action is best?
alt.a: Delay the teaching until the patient’s pain is relieved
alt.ex: Poor timing prevents a clear message from being effective; routine teaching should not begin during severe pain.
w: Begin the teaching now to stay on schedule
Teaching during severe pain is poorly timed and ineffective.
Provide the teaching in written form only
A written handout does not fix the poor timing of teaching during severe pain.
Shorten the teaching and proceed while the patient is in pain
Brevity does not overcome poor timing during severe pain.

items.q: When a patient’s verbal and nonverbal messages are incongruent, how does the receiver usually respond?
items.a: Gives more weight to the nonverbal message
items.ex: Nonverbal communication is unconsciously motivated, so when messages conflict the receiver usually “hears” the nonverbal message.
w: Believes the spoken words over the body language
The receiver usually relies more on the nonverbal message when the two conflict.
Ignores both messages until they are clarified
Receivers do not ignore incongruent messages; they tend to favor the nonverbal one.
Gives equal weight to both of the messages
The nonverbal message usually carries more weight for the receiver.

alt.q: A young patient sits rigidly and says in a sharp voice, “Going to surgery is no big deal.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “You say surgery doesn’t bother you, but you seem tense. Tell me how you’re feeling.”
alt.ex: Noticing the mismatch between words, tone, and posture lets the nurse explore the patient’s feelings and concerns.
w: “I’m glad you’re not worried. Let’s review your consent form.”
This accepts the words and ignores the conflicting nonverbal cues.
“Everyone gets nervous, but there’s nothing to worry about.”
False reassurance closes off exploration of the patient’s feelings.
“Why are you saying that when you’re obviously upset?”
A confrontational “why” question puts the patient on the defensive.

items.q: A patient with depression has an expressionless face that reveals little about what he is thinking or feeling. What term describes this?
items.a: Flat affect
items.ex: An expressionless face that reveals little about thoughts or feelings is called flat affect.
w: Inappropriate affect
Inappropriate affect is an expression that does not match the verbal message.
Metacommunication
Metacommunication refers to all factors that influence communication.
Territoriality
Territoriality is the need to gain, maintain, and defend one’s space.

alt.q: A patient smiles while describing the recent death of her spouse. Which term describes this facial expression?
alt.a: Inappropriate affect
alt.ex: Inappropriate affect is a facial expression that does not match the content of the verbal message.
w: Flat affect
Flat affect is an expressionless face, not an expression that conflicts with the words.
Connotative meaning
Connotative meaning concerns personal interpretation of a word.
Denotative meaning
Denotative meaning is the shared meaning of a word in a common language.

items.q: A nurse notices that a patient from a culture that views direct eye contact as intrusive looks away during the interview. Which interpretation is best?
items.a: The behavior may reflect cultural preference rather than a problem
items.ex: Some cultures consider eye contact intrusive or threatening, so the nurse considers culture before interpreting it.
w: The patient is being defensive and should be confronted
Lack of eye contact can reflect culture; confronting the patient is inappropriate.
The patient lacks confidence and needs reassurance
Assuming low confidence ignores the cultural meaning of eye contact.
The patient is not ready to communicate at all
Avoiding eye contact in this culture does not mean unwillingness to communicate.

alt.q: Which statement about eye contact is accurate?
alt.a: Its meaning depends on the person’s culture and preferences
alt.ex: Always consider a person’s culture and personal preferences when interpreting eye contact.
w: Lack of eye contact always signals anxiety or defensiveness
Lack of eye contact sometimes, not always, indicates anxiety; it may reflect culture.
All cultures view steady eye contact as a sign of respect
Some cultures consider eye contact intrusive, threatening, or harmful.
Eye contact has no effect on readiness to talk
People signal readiness to communicate through eye contact.

items.q: A patient sitting in bed is angry about a delayed discharge. Where should the nurse position herself while talking with the patient?
items.a: At the same eye level as the patient
items.ex: Interacting at the same eye level indicates equality and, with an angry person, helps establish autonomy over the concern.
w: Standing over the patient to show authority
Looking down on a person establishes authority, which can escalate anger.
Out of the patient’s line of sight
Avoiding eye contact limits engagement and the ability to observe the patient.
Across the room at public distance
Public distance of 12 feet or more is for speeches, not personal conversation.

alt.q: What does looking down on a person during an interaction communicate?
alt.a: Authority over the person
alt.ex: Looking down on a person establishes authority, whereas interacting at the same eye level indicates equality.
w: Equality in the relationship
Equality is conveyed by interacting at the same eye level.
Respect and willingness to listen
Maintaining eye contact, not looking down, shows respect and willingness to listen.
Readiness to communicate
Readiness to communicate is signaled through eye contact, not looking down.

items.q: A patient moans while turning in bed. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “I notice you moaning as you turn. Are you having pain?”
items.ex: Sounds have several possible meanings, so the nurse validates the nonverbal message to interpret it accurately.
w: “You’re moaning, so I’ll get your pain medicine now.”
Acting before validating assumes the meaning of the moan, which may differ.
“Moaning means you’re uncomfortable, so try to relax.”
Moaning can convey pleasure or suffering; the nurse should validate rather than assume.
“Let me know later if you need anything at all.”
This ignores the nonverbal cue instead of validating it.

alt.q: Why should a nurse validate the meaning of a patient’s sounds, such as moaning or crying?

w: Sounds are not a true form of communication
Sounds such as sighs and sobs do communicate feelings and thoughts.
Sounds always signal physical pain
Moaning can convey pleasure as well as suffering.
Crying always signals sadness or grief
Crying can communicate happiness, sadness, or anger.

A quick, purposeful gait communicates well-being and confidence.
Leaning forward
Leaning forward conveys attention.

items.q: A nursing student is getting ready for a clinical shift. Which actions follow typical health care agency dress code policies? Select all that apply.

items.q: Territory is important because it provides people with a sense of which needs? Select all that apply.

Identity
Territory provides a sense of identity.
Security
Territory provides a sense of security.
Control
Territory provides a sense of control.
Dependence
Territory supports independence-related needs such as control, not dependence.
Isolation
Territory provides privacy, not isolation.
items.ex: Territoriality is the need to gain, maintain, and defend one’s space, which provides privacy, identity, security, and control.

alt.q: Which statements about personal space are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It is invisible and travels with the person
Personal space is invisible, individual, and travels with a person.
Comfortable distance varies with culture, relationship, and situation
Interpersonal distance depends on culture, relationship, and situation.
People respond defensively when it is threatened
Threatened personal space leads to defensiveness and less effective communication.
It is marked by visible boundaries such as fences
Visible boundaries mark territory; personal space is invisible.
It is the same distance for all people
Distances vary by culture, relationship, and situation.
alt.ex: Personal space is invisible and individual; nurses convey respect for privacy when caregiving requires entering it.

items.q: Nonverbal communication is unconsciously motivated and more accurately indicates a person’s intended meaning than spoken words.
items.a: True
items.ex: Because nonverbal behavior is unconsciously motivated, it is a more accurate indicator of intended meaning than words.
items.ww: Spoken words are not the more accurate indicator; receivers usually trust nonverbal cues when the two conflict.

alt.q: Spoken words reveal a person’s intended meaning more accurately than nonverbal behavior because words are chosen consciously.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nonverbal communication is unconsciously motivated and more accurately indicates intended meaning than spoken words.
alt.ww: The book states nonverbal behavior, not consciously chosen words, better reflects intended meaning.

items.q: Tone of voice changes how a message sounds but does not change its meaning.
items.a: False
items.ex: Intonation dramatically affects meaning; the same words can express enthusiasm, anger, concern, or indifference.
items.ww: A patronizing tone, for example, can make a message seem condescending and inhibit communication.

alt.q: A patient’s tone of voice can give the nurse information about the patient’s emotional state or energy level.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Intonation conveys meaning, and a patient’s tone of voice reveals emotional state or energy level.
alt.ww: Tone is a meaningful part of the message, not just a feature of how it sounds.

items.q: A nurse who frowns in concentration while performing a procedure may be perceived by the patient as angry or disapproving.
items.a: True
items.ex: Patients closely observe nurses and may misread unintended facial expressions such as a frown of concentration.
items.ww: People are often unaware of the messages their expressions convey, and patients do notice them.

alt.q: Patients rarely notice a nurse’s facial expressions while care is being provided.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients closely observe nurses, and even slight changes in the eyes, lips, or facial muscles reveal feelings.
alt.ww: Because patients watch nurses closely, nurses try to avoid showing shock, disgust, or dismay.

items.q: [[Metacommunication]] is a broad term that refers to all factors that influence communication.
items.ex: Awareness of factors such as tone and nonverbal behavior helps people better understand what is communicated.

alt.q: Noticing that a patient’s tense posture contradicts his words is an example of awareness of [[metacommunication]].
alt.ex: Awareness of factors such as tone and nonverbal behavior helps people better understand what is communicated.

items.q: In the nurse-patient helping relationship, which phase comes right after “Orientation phase”?

items.q: During which phase of the helping relationship does the nurse first let the patient know when to expect the relationship to end?
items.a: Orientation phase
items.ex: In orientation the nurse sets the tone, clarifies roles, forms contracts, and tells the patient when termination is expected.
w: Preinteraction phase
Preinteraction occurs before the nurse meets the patient, when the nurse reviews data and plans the setting.
Working phase
The working phase focuses on solving problems and accomplishing outcomes together.
Termination phase
In termination the nurse reminds the patient the end is near; the expected end was set during orientation.

alt.q: Before meeting a new patient, a nurse reviews the medical record, talks with other caregivers, and chooses a private place to talk. Which phase of the helping relationship is this?
alt.a: Preinteraction phase
alt.ex: Preinteraction happens before meeting the patient and includes reviewing data, talking to caregivers, and planning a private setting and enough time.
w: Orientation phase
Orientation begins when the nurse and patient meet and get to know each other.
Working phase
The working phase is when the nurse and patient work together toward outcomes.
Termination phase
Termination is the ending of the relationship, with evaluation and transition to other caregivers.

items.q: During a friendly conversation, a patient asks a nursing student, “Where do you live? Do you have kids?” Which response by the student is best?
items.a: “I live nearby. Now tell me how your breathing has been today.”
items.ex: The book advises giving minimal information or deflecting with gentle humor, then refocusing the conversation on the patient.
w: “I live on Elm Street with my husband and our two girls, 4 and 7.”
Sharing detailed personal information shifts the focus from the patient to the student.
“I’m not allowed to answer any personal questions from patients.”
An abrupt refusal is not required; the student uses judgment and gently refocuses.
“Why do you want to know about my family and where I live?”
“Why” questions can feel accusatory and do not return the focus to the patient.

alt.q: What does the textbook recommend when a patient asks a nurse personal questions during social conversation?
alt.a: Give minimal information or deflect with gentle humor, then refocus on the patient
alt.ex: Professional judgment guides what to share; minimal information or gentle humor keeps the focus on the patient.
w: Share detailed personal information to build a friendship with the patient
The relationship is professional; the patient’s needs, not the nurse’s, take priority.
Refuse firmly and end the conversation to protect professional boundaries
Ending the conversation is unnecessary; a gentle deflection and refocus is recommended.
Report the questions to the charge nurse as inappropriate patient behavior
Personal questions are common in social conversation and are not a behavior to report.

items.q: Which statement best describes nonjudgmental acceptance in a nurse-patient relationship?
items.a: Being willing to hear a message or acknowledge feelings without necessarily agreeing
items.ex: Acceptance conveys willingness to hear a message or acknowledge feelings; it does not mean agreeing with or approving of decisions.
w: Agreeing with the patient’s decisions so that trust is not damaged
Acceptance does not mean the nurse always agrees with the patient.
Approving of the patient’s actions as long as they are legal and safe
Acceptance does not mean approving of a patient’s decisions or actions.
Avoiding any discussion of the patient’s choices to prevent conflict
Acceptance involves hearing the patient’s message, not avoiding the topic.

alt.q: A nurse disagrees with a patient’s decision to stop chemotherapy but listens to his reasons and acknowledges his feelings. What is the nurse demonstrating?
alt.a: Nonjudgmental acceptance
alt.ex: Listening and acknowledging feelings without requiring agreement is nonjudgmental acceptance, an important part of the caring relationship.
w: Sympathy
Sympathy is concern or pity that can cause overidentification, not the listening described here.
Approval
Approval implies agreement with the decision, which the nurse does not have.
Self-disclosure
Self-disclosure is sharing the nurse’s own personal experiences with the patient.

items.q: A nurse encourages a patient to describe what her breast cancer diagnosis means in her daily life. What is the main benefit of this narrative interaction?
items.a: Understanding the context of her life and what is meaningful to her
items.ex: Listening to stories reveals the context of patients’ lives and what matters to them, information a standard history form rarely shows.
w: Collecting answers faster than with a standard history form
Stories take time; their value is depth, not speed of data collection.
Giving the nurse a chance to share similar personal experiences
Narrative interaction centers on the patient’s story, not the nurse’s.
Confirming the medical diagnosis using the patient’s own words
The purpose is understanding the patient’s perspective, not confirming a diagnosis.

alt.q: What is the term for encouraging patients to share their personal stories with the nurse?
alt.a: Narrative interaction
alt.ex: Sharing stories is called narrative interaction and helps the nurse learn what is meaningful from the patient’s perspective.
w: Motivational interviewing
Motivational interviewing is a goal-oriented technique to encourage behavior change.
Therapeutic confrontation
Confrontation points out inconsistencies in feelings, beliefs, or behaviors.
Social conversation
Social conversation is superficial small talk used early to help people relax.

items.q: Using motivational interviewing, a nurse hears a patient say, “I used to walk every day before my knee surgery, but now I just sit at home.” Which response shows reflective listening?
items.a: “Since your surgery, it’s been hard to stay as active as you were.”
items.ex: Reflective listening restates in the nurse’s own words what the patient is trying to convey.
w: “Why did you stop walking every day after your knee surgery?”
MI avoids “why” questions; this does not reflect the patient’s message.
“You showed real determination getting through that surgery.”
Acknowledging a patient’s strengths is an affirmation, not reflective listening.
“So you need to start walking again every day starting tomorrow.”
Giving a directive does not reflect what the patient conveyed.

alt.q: A nurse says to a patient, “It took real effort to come to this appointment while you were in so much pain.” Which part of the OARS model is the nurse using?
alt.a: Affirmations
alt.ex: Affirmations find and acknowledge the patient’s strengths, such as the effort to attend despite pain.
w: Open-ended questions
Open-ended questions cannot be answered with a single yes or no; this is a statement.
Reflective listening
Reflective listening restates the patient’s own message in the nurse’s words.
Summarizing
Summarizing reviews several points of the interview to verify understanding.

items.q: A nurse using motivational interviewing wants to explore a patient’s feelings about smoking. Which question is most appropriate?
items.a: “What concerns you most about your smoking?”
items.ex: Open-ended questions that avoid “why” help develop empathy and let the patient explore motivation.
w: “Why do you keep smoking when you know it hurts you?”
MI avoids “why” questions, which can feel judgmental and accusatory.
“Do you want to quit smoking in the next month?”
This yes-or-no question limits the patient’s response.
“How many cigarettes do you smoke each day?”
This closed question gathers a fact but does not explore feelings.

alt.q: Why does motivational interviewing focus on drawing out the patient’s own motivation to change?
alt.a: Change is more likely when the patient decides it is important
alt.ex: MI rests on the understanding that change is more likely when the patient determines that making a change is important.
w: Patients change more when the nurse gives firm directions
MI is collaborative and person-centered rather than directive.
The nurse is responsible for choosing the patient’s health goals
In MI the nurse and patient collaborate; the patient’s priorities guide the plan.
Patients follow advice better when the nurse is critical
MI uses a noncritical, nonjudgmental approach to support change.

items.q: At the end of an I-PASS hand-off report, the oncoming nurse restates the key points of the report. What is the purpose of this step?
items.a: To confirm the report was received and understood and allow questions
items.ex: Synthesis by the receiver ensures the information was received and understood and gives a chance to clarify and ask questions.
w: To document the full report in the patient’s health record
The step is a verbal summary to check understanding, not documentation.
To identify each nurse’s role when they do not know each other
Introducing oneself and one’s role is the Identify step of ISBAR.
To rank the patient’s illness severity for the next shift
Illness severity is stated by the reporting nurse at the start of I-PASS.

alt.q: Which step of I-PASS is carried out by the nurse receiving the report rather than the nurse giving it?
alt.a: Synthesis by receiver
alt.ex: In synthesis by receiver, the oncoming nurse summarizes the report to confirm understanding and clarify information.
w: Situational awareness and contingency planning
The reporting nurse describes concerns to anticipate, such as fall risk.
Action items
The reporting nurse lists tasks that need to be done during the shift.
Illness severity
The reporting nurse begins by stating how stable the patient is.

items.q: When is the Identify step that some organizations add to SBAR (ISBAR) especially used?
items.a: When the health care providers do not actively know one another
items.ex: The Identify step adds an introduction, location, and role when providers do not know each other.
w: When the patient’s condition is critical and unstable
Identify is added for unfamiliar providers, not because of patient acuity.
When the report is given at the patient’s bedside
Bedside reporting is a setting, not the reason for the Identify step.
When the receiver must summarize the report back
Summarizing back is synthesis by the receiver in I-PASS.

alt.q: A nurse calls a health care provider she has never worked with about a patient’s change in condition. Using ISBAR, what should the nurse do first?
alt.a: Introduce herself, her location, and her role in the patient’s care
alt.ex: ISBAR begins with Identify: an introduction, location, and role when providers do not know one another.
w: Describe the patient’s current situation and vital signs
Situation follows the Identify step in ISBAR.
Recommend the treatment change she believes is needed
Recommendation is the final step of ISBAR.
Summarize the patient’s background and medical history
Background comes after Identify and Situation.

items.q: A charge nurse often rolls her eyes and criticizes a new nurse in front of others without offering solutions. Which action by the new nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: Calmly address the behavior when it occurs and ask for it to stop
items.ex: The book advises addressing lateral violence calmly when it happens, describing its effect, and asking for it to stop.
w: Discuss the charge nurse’s behavior with other nurses on the unit
Nurses experiencing lateral violence should avoid gossiping about the situation or person.
Record each incident in detail in the assigned patient’s chart
Incidents are documented in personal notes, never in patient records.
Ignore the behavior to avoid conflict with a more senior nurse
There must be zero tolerance of lateral violence; it should be addressed.

alt.q: A nurse who is being bullied by a colleague wants to keep a record of the incidents. Where should the nurse document them?
alt.a: In detailed personal notes
alt.ex: Incidents of lateral violence are documented in detail in personal notes, not in patient records.
w: In the patient’s electronic health record
Patient records are for patient care, not for workplace conflicts.
In a shared log that the whole unit can read
Sharing incidents widely invites gossip, which the nurse should avoid.
In an email sent to coworkers on the unit
Telling coworkers about the situation is gossip, which should be avoided.

items.q: How does lateral violence jeopardize patient safety?
items.a: Intimidated nurses are less likely to report near misses or question orders
items.ex: Intimidation decreases the likelihood that a nurse will report a near-miss event, question an order, or act to improve care.
w: Bullied nurses spend more time documenting incidents than giving care
The book links safety risk to intimidation silencing nurses, not documentation time.
Patients who see bullying often refuse care from the nurses involved
The safety risk described is nurses not speaking up, not patients refusing care.
Units with bullying are assigned more patients per nurse each shift
Staffing ratios are not described as an effect of lateral violence.

alt.q: Which outcome of lateral violence affects the nursing work environment, according to the textbook?
alt.a: Poor retention of qualified nurses
alt.ex: Lateral violence leads to job dissatisfaction, a decreased sense of value, poor teamwork, poor retention, and nurses leaving the profession.
w: Stronger teamwork as nurses unite against a bully
Lateral violence leads to poor teamwork, not stronger teamwork.
Higher job satisfaction among experienced nurses
Lateral violence causes job dissatisfaction.
Fewer nurses leaving the nursing profession
Lateral violence contributes to nurses leaving the profession.

items.q: According to the textbook, what is the best way for a nurse acting as a community change agent to prevent errors, reduce resistance, and promote change?
items.a: Provide clear and accurate information to members of the public
items.ex: Clear, accurate public information is described as the best way to prevent errors, reduce resistance, and promote change.
w: Limit health information to people with medical training
Community nurses share information widely with the public, not only professionals.
Rely on a single channel so that messages stay consistent
The book lists many channels, from newsletters to radio and websites.
Present personal opinions persuasively to win public support
The emphasis is on clear and accurate information, not persuasion by opinion.

alt.q: A nurse wants to share information about a community vaccination clinic. Which channels does the textbook identify for community communication?
alt.a: Neighborhood newsletters, health fairs, and radio
alt.ex: Community channels include newsletters, health fairs, bulletin boards, newspapers, radio, television, and electronic sites.
w: Hand-off reports given at each change of shift
Hand-off reports communicate among the health care team, not the community.
Individual patients’ electronic health records
Health records are confidential and are not public communication channels.
Process recordings of nurse-patient conversations
Process recordings are used to evaluate a nurse’s own communication.

items.q: Which behaviors are examples of lateral violence among nurses? Select all that apply.
o: Withholding information from a colleague
Withholding information is listed as a lateral violence behavior.
Being hypercritical of a coworker’s work
Being hypercritical is a form of workplace bullying.
Excluding a nurse from unit activities
Excluding colleagues is a lateral violence behavior.
Raising eyebrows or making faces in disapproval
Nonverbal expressions of disapproval are included in lateral violence.
Offering constructive feedback with possible solutions
Lateral violence involves criticizing without solutions; feedback with solutions is professional.
Asking a colleague to clarify an unclear order
Seeking clarification is safe practice, not bullying.
items.ex: Lateral violence includes withholding information, hypercriticism, put-downs, criticism without solutions, exclusion, and nonverbal disapproval.

alt.q: A nurse is experiencing lateral violence from a coworker. Which actions does the textbook recommend? Select all that apply.
o: Describe how the behavior affects your functioning
Explaining the effect of the behavior is a recommended technique.
Notify the manager to get support
Notifying the manager provides support for the situation.
Plan for taking action in the future
Planning future action is one of the recommended techniques.
Avoid gossiping about the situation with other staff
Gossip spreads conflict; the nurse should avoid it.
Respond with the same behavior so the coworker stops
Retaliating continues the cycle; assertive communication is recommended.
Document the incidents in the patient’s medical record
Incidents are documented in personal notes, not patient records.
alt.ex: Recommended actions include addressing behavior calmly, describing its effect, asking it to stop, notifying the manager, avoiding gossip, and planning ahead.

items.q: Which outcomes have been associated with bedside nursing hand-off reporting? Select all that apply.
o: Fewer patient falls
Bedside hand-off reporting reduced the incidence of falls.
Fewer pressure injuries
Bedside hand-off reporting reduced the incidence of pressure injuries.
Fewer medication errors
Bedside hand-off reporting reduced medication errors.
Improved communication
Bedside reporting improved communication in addition to safety outcomes.
Less need for nurse training on hand-off
Effective bedside reporting requires education and training on a standardized approach.
Elimination of standard hand-off guidelines
Bedside reporting works best when guidelines and expectations are set and followed.
items.ex: An integrative review found bedside hand-off reporting reduced falls, pressure injuries, and medication errors and improved communication.

alt.q: A nurse is preparing to give a bedside hand-off report. Which actions help make the environment right for the report? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the environment calm and quiet
A calm, quiet environment is conducive to bedside reporting.
Protect the patient’s privacy
Ensuring privacy is part of a respectful bedside report.
Invite the patient and family caregivers to participate
Bedside reporting gives patients and families a chance to take part.
Give the report in the hallway so the patient can rest
Hand-off reporting should occur at the patient’s bedside.
Ask the family to leave so the report is not interrupted
Families should have the opportunity to participate in the report.
alt.ex: Bedside hand-off should occur in a calm, quiet, respectful, private setting that lets patients and families participate.

items.q: Which nursing actions belong to the orientation phase of the helping relationship? Select all that apply.
o: Clarify the patient’s and the nurse’s roles
Clarifying roles is an orientation phase task.
Form contracts that specify who will do what
Contracts are formed during orientation.
Assess the patient’s health status
Assessment of health status occurs during orientation.
Expect the patient to test the nurse’s competence
Patients often test the nurse’s competence and commitment early on.
Evaluate achievement of expected outcomes with the patient
Evaluating outcomes with the patient occurs in the termination phase.
Review the medical record before meeting the patient
Reviewing data before meeting is a preinteraction phase task.
items.ex: Orientation is when the nurse and patient meet, build trust, assess, prioritize, clarify roles, and form contracts.

alt.q: Which nursing actions belong to the working phase of the helping relationship? Select all that apply.
o: Encourage the patient to express feelings about health
Helping the patient express feelings is a working phase task.
Provide information needed to change behavior
Giving information to understand and change behavior occurs in the working phase.
Use appropriate self-disclosure and confrontation
These techniques are used during the working phase.
Reminisce about the relationship with the patient
Reminiscing is part of the termination phase.
Plan enough time for the first interaction
Planning time for the initial meeting is a preinteraction task.
Tell the patient when the relationship will end
Letting the patient know when to expect termination occurs in orientation.
alt.ex: In the working phase, the nurse and patient solve problems together and work toward the outcomes they set.

items.q: Even a brief nurse-patient interaction uses an abbreviated version of the preinteraction, orientation, working, and termination phases.
items.a: True
items.ex: During a clinical day the nurse prepares, meets the patient, works toward outcomes, and says goodbye, a short version of all four phases.
items.ww: The phases are not limited to long relationships; brief contacts follow an abbreviated version of them.

alt.q: The phases of the helping relationship apply only to long-term relationships, such as weeks of home care visits.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Even a brief interaction, such as one clinical day, uses an abbreviated version of all four phases.
alt.ww: The book states that even brief interactions use the phases in abbreviated form.

items.q: Social conversation is easy and superficial, whereas therapeutic interactions are often more intense, difficult, and uncomfortable.
items.a: True
items.ex: Socializing helps people relax and lays a foundation, but therapeutic interactions address deeper health concerns.
items.ww: The book contrasts superficial social talk with more intense therapeutic interaction.

alt.q: Because social conversation builds trust, the nurse should keep interactions social rather than moving to health concerns.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Social talk establishes trust, but the nurse must move beyond it to discuss issues affecting the patient’s health.
alt.ww: Staying at a social level prevents the nurse from addressing the patient’s health concerns.

items.q: Motivational interviewing can be effective even when caring for patients who may not seem ready to change their behavior.
items.a: True
items.ex: Because MI accepts the patient’s feelings and draws out their own motivation, it works even with patients who seem not ready to change.
items.ww: MI is not limited to motivated patients; it is designed to evoke motivation and address ambivalence.

alt.q: Motivational interviewing should be reserved for patients who have already decided to change their behavior.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: MI is effective even with patients who do not seem ready, because it draws out motivation and explores ambivalence.
alt.ww: The book states MI is effective even when patients may not seem ready to change.

items.q: Withholding information, being hypercritical, and excluding colleagues are behaviors of [[lateral violence|workplace bullying|horizontal violence]].
items.ex: Lateral violence, or workplace bullying among colleagues, harms teamwork, retention, and patient safety.

alt.q: There must be zero tolerance of [[lateral violence|workplace bullying|horizontal violence]], which can be a precursor to compassion fatigue.
alt.ex: Lateral violence, or workplace bullying among colleagues, harms teamwork, retention, and patient safety.
