ord.q: Place the steps of the AIDET communication technique in order.
items: Acknowledge the person
Introduce yourself and your role
Give the duration of the procedure or wait
Explain what the patient will experience
Thank the patient
ord.ex: AIDET stands for Acknowledge, Introduce, Duration, Explain, and Thank you.

items.q: When using AIDET, why does the nurse tell the patient how long a procedure will take?
items.a: To keep the patient informed of any delays that may occur
items.ex: Giving the duration of a procedure or test results keeps patients informed of delays.
w: To obtain the patient’s informed consent for the procedure
Informed consent is not the purpose of the Duration step.
To identify the nurse’s role in the patient’s care
Stating one’s role is part of the Introduce step.
To inform the patient of the safety precautions needed
Safety precautions are covered in the Explain step.

alt.q: What does the “D” in AIDET stand for?
alt.a: Duration
alt.ex: The D is Duration: telling the patient how long a procedure or test results may take.
w: Documentation
Documentation is not one of the AIDET steps.
Delegation
Delegation is a management skill, not part of AIDET.
Diagnosis
AIDET is a service communication technique, not a diagnostic step.

items.q: A nurse is preparing a patient for a CT scan using AIDET. Which statement fits the Explain step?
items.a: “The table moves slowly, and this strap keeps you from sliding.”
items.ex: Explain describes what the patient will experience and informs the patient of safety precautions.
w: “Hello, Ms. Lee. I’m Dana, the RN caring for you today.”
Giving your name and role is the Introduce step.
“The scan takes about 20 minutes; results take a few hours.”
Telling how long things will take is the Duration step.
“Thank you for choosing us; I enjoyed working with you.”
Thanking the patient is the final Thank you step.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse reflects the Introduce step of AIDET?
alt.a: “I’m Sam, the nurse who will be caring for you until 7 tonight.”
alt.ex: In Introduce, the nurse gives their name and explains their role in the person’s care.
w: “Good morning! Please have a seat and make yourself comfortable.”
Greeting the person warmly and making them comfortable is Acknowledge.
“Your test should take about 30 minutes, and then you can eat.”
Telling how long a test will take is the Duration step.
“You will feel a cool gel on your skin, but it will not hurt.”
Describing what the patient will experience is the Explain step.

items.q: A nurse meets Mr. Robert Hayes, age 68, on admission. Which greeting is most appropriate?
items.a: “Good morning, Mr. Hayes. I’m Jo Lin, your registered nurse.”
items.ex: Nurses usually use the last name at first and state their own name and status, which conveys respect.
w: “Good morning, Robert. I’m Jo, and I’ll be helping you today.”
First names are used only if the patient requests it; status is also missing.
“Good morning, dear. I’m your nurse for today’s shift here.”
Terms of endearment should be avoided, and the nurse gives no name.
“Good morning. Are you the new patient in bed 4 by the window?”
Identifying patients by bed or room number is demeaning.

alt.q: When may a nurse appropriately begin calling an adult patient by the first name?
alt.a: When the patient requests it
alt.ex: Nurses use the last name initially and switch to the first name if the patient requests it.
w: After the first full shift of care
Time spent together does not replace the patient’s stated preference.
When the patient is alert and oriented
Alert adults are addressed by last name unless they prefer otherwise.
After the admission assessment is done
Completing assessment does not change how the patient prefers to be addressed.

items.q: At the bedside, a nurse says to a family member, “The hip fracture in room 12 is doing well today.” Why is this inappropriate?
items.a: It is demeaning and implies the nurse does not know the patient as a person
items.ex: Referring to patients by diagnosis or room number is demeaning and suggests the nurse does not care to know the individual.
w: It uses medical terminology the family may not understand
The problem is depersonalizing the patient, not the vocabulary used.
It fails to state the patient’s age and admitting diagnosis
Adding details would not fix the lack of respect for the person.
It gives the family too much detail about the patient’s progress
The issue is labeling the patient by diagnosis and room.

alt.q: Which practice reflects respectful use of names in professional communication?
alt.a: Asking patients and co-workers how they prefer to be addressed
alt.ex: The nurse asks how people prefer to be addressed and honors their preferences, conveying respect for dignity.
w: Calling older patients “grandma” or “grandpa” to show warmth
Terms such as grandma are terms of endearment that should be avoided.
Referring to patients by room number during bedside report
Using room numbers is demeaning and impersonal.
Using first names for all adult patients to seem friendly
Last names are used initially unless the patient asks otherwise.

items.q: Which nurse behavior is most likely to foster a patient’s trust?
items.a: Consistently following through on what the nurse says
items.ex: Trust is fostered by warmth, consistency, reliability, honesty, competence, and respect.
w: Sharing stories about other patients’ situations
Gossiping about others signals that the nurse cannot be trusted.
Withholding bad news to protect the patient’s feelings
Withholding key information violates legal and ethical standards.
Telling the patient about personal problems at home
Sharing personal information damages trust and shifts the focus.

alt.q: A nurse tells a patient about another patient’s difficult family situation. What message does this send?
alt.a: That the nurse cannot be trusted
alt.ex: Gossiping about others sends the message that the nurse cannot be trusted and damages relationships.
w: That the nurse is open and honest
Sharing others’ private information is a breach, not honesty.
That the nurse is empathetic toward patients
Empathy focuses on this patient’s feelings, not others’ private lives.
That the patient is not alone in their struggles
Sharing other patients’ stories breaks confidentiality and damages trust.

items.q: What is a likely result when trust is not established in a nurse-patient relationship?
items.a: The relationship rarely moves beyond social interaction and superficial care
items.ex: Without trust, a nurse-patient relationship rarely progresses beyond social interaction and superficial care.
w: The patient shares more personal stories to test the nurse
Patients are more likely to share stories when trust exists.
The patient becomes more assertive in expressing needs
Trust fosters open expression of needs; its absence limits it.
The relationship moves quickly into the termination phase
Lack of trust keeps the relationship superficial rather than ending it sooner.

alt.q: Which outcome is more likely when trust exists between a nurse and a patient?
alt.a: The patient shares personal stories
alt.ex: When trust exists, patients are more likely to share their stories and express feelings, thoughts, and needs.
w: The patient avoids expressing needs
Trust enhances, rather than limits, expression of needs.
The nurse withholds key information
Withholding information is dishonest and destroys trust.
The relationship stays at a social level
A relationship stays social when trust is missing.

items.q: A nurse takes the initiative to solve a problem with a patient’s discharge plan and accepts responsibility for the outcome. Which element of professional communication is shown?
items.a: Autonomy and responsibility
items.ex: Autonomous nurses are self-directed, take initiative in problem solving, and accept responsibility for the outcomes of their actions.
w: Courtesy
Courtesy involves polite behaviors such as knocking, greeting, and saying please and thank you.
Trustworthiness
Trustworthiness means helping others without hesitation, not self-directed problem solving.
Acceptance
Acceptance is a willingness to hear a message or acknowledge feelings.

alt.q: Besides being self-directed themselves, professional nurses recognize and advocate for which aspect of their patients?
alt.a: Autonomy
alt.ex: It is important for professional nurses to recognize and advocate for their patients’ autonomy.
w: Dependence
Nurses support patients’ self-direction rather than dependence.
Compliance
Advocacy centers on the patient’s right to choose, not compliance.
Anonymity
Anonymity is not described as an element of professional communication.

items.q: A colleague keeps asking a nurse to cover her breaks, leaving the nurse’s own patients unattended. Which response by the nurse is assertive?
items.a: “I need to stay with my patients, so I can’t cover your break today.”
items.ex: Assertive responses use “I” messages to express needs and set limits without judging or hurting others.
w: “Fine, I’ll do it again, even though I’m already far behind.”
Giving in while resenting it is a passive response that avoids the issue.
“You always dump your work on me, and it is completely unfair.”
Blaming the other person is an aggressive response.
“Why do you keep asking me instead of someone else on the unit?”
A “why” question does not state the nurse’s needs or limits.

alt.q: Which phrase most often begins an assertive response?
alt.a: “I feel…”
alt.ex: Assertive responses contain “I” messages such as I want, I need, I think, or I feel.
w: “You always…”
“You always” statements blame the other person and are aggressive.
“You should…”
“Should” statements are judgmental rather than assertive.
“Why don’t you…”
“Why” questions can sound accusatory and do not express the speaker’s needs.

items.q: A nursing student arrives to take vital signs on a patient whose hospital room door is closed. What should the student do first?
items.a: Knock on the door before entering the room
items.ex: Common courtesy includes knocking before entering a patient’s room, then greeting, introducing, and stating the purpose.
w: Enter quietly so the patient is not disturbed
Entering without knocking is discourteous and invades privacy.
Begin the vital signs and then introduce herself
The student introduces herself and her purpose before starting care.
Ask the patient’s visitors to step out of the room
The student must first knock and introduce herself before any request.

alt.q: How do others often perceive a nurse who is discourteous?
alt.a: As rude or insensitive
alt.ex: Discourteous or unprofessional nurses are perceived as rude or insensitive, creating barriers and team friction.
w: As efficient and focused
Discourtesy is not seen as efficiency; it creates barriers to helping relationships.
As confident and competent
Professional behavior, not discourtesy, conveys confidence and competence.
As busy but still caring
Discourtesy sends the message of insensitivity, not caring.

items.q: Which description matches the textbook’s expectations for a nurse’s professional appearance?
items.a: Clean, neat, well groomed, conservatively dressed, and odor free
items.ex: Professional appearance helps establish trustworthiness and competence.
w: Fashionably dressed with bold accessories to seem approachable
Professionals are expected to dress conservatively.
Casually dressed so that patients feel relaxed and at ease
Professional appearance, not casual dress, establishes trust and competence.
Wearing a strong fragrance to cover unpleasant hospital odors
Professionals are expected to be odor free.

alt.q: Which behavior communicates professionalism, according to the textbook?
alt.a: Arriving on time, organized, and well prepared
alt.ex: Being on time, organized, well prepared, and equipped for the role communicates professionalism.
w: Speaking loudly so everyone can hear clearly
Professionals speak in a clear, well-modulated voice.
Leaving off the name badge to seem friendly
Health care workers should always wear a name badge.
Using casual slang to put patients at ease
Professionals use good grammar.

items.q: A new nurse sees an experienced health care provider make a medication error but hesitates to speak up. What does the textbook identify as a common reason assertiveness is difficult in such situations?
items.a: Fear of retaliation
items.ex: Ethical issues such as identifying another provider’s error can make assertiveness difficult for fear of retaliation.
w: Lack of knowledge about the error
The nurse recognized the error; the barrier described is fear of retaliation.
Policies that forbid reporting errors
Agencies expect errors to be reported; no such policy is described.
The patient’s request for secrecy
The book attributes hesitation to fear of retaliation, not patient requests.

alt.q: Which characteristic describes assertive individuals?
alt.a: They can say no and set limits
alt.ex: Assertive individuals deal with criticism and manipulation, say no, set limits, and resist intentionally imposed guilt.
w: They avoid conflict by agreeing with others
Avoiding conflict by going along is passive, not assertive.
They put others down to get their way
Putting others down is aggressive; assertiveness respects others.
They accept guilt that others impose on them
Assertive people resist intentionally imposed guilt.

items.q: Which behaviors are part of assertive communication? Select all that apply.
o: Appropriate eye contact
Appropriate eye contact is listed as assertive behavior.
Spontaneous verbal responses in a confident voice
A confident voice with spontaneous responses reflects assertiveness.
Culturally sensitive use of touch and space
Assertive behavior includes culturally sensitive touch and space.
Nonverbal cues that show interest and active listening
Nonverbal communication reflecting interest and listening is assertive.
Raising the voice to make a point
Raising the voice is aggressive rather than assertive.
Agreeing with others to keep the peace
Going along to avoid conflict is passive behavior.
items.ex: Assertive behavior expresses feelings and ideas confidently while respecting others’ feelings, ideas, and choices.

alt.q: What are the benefits of assertive behavior for a nurse? Select all that apply.
o: Increased self-esteem
Assertive behavior increases self-esteem.
Increased self-confidence
Assertiveness increases self-confidence.
Greater ability to develop satisfying relationships
Assertive behavior improves interpersonal relationships.
Increased outcome attainment
Assertiveness increases outcome attainment.
Avoidance of all conflict with colleagues
Assertive nurses manage criticism and conflict rather than avoiding it.
Greater reliance on others to make decisions
Assertive people make decisions and control their lives more effectively.
alt.ex: Assertive behavior increases self-esteem, self-confidence, satisfying relationships, and outcome attainment.

items.q: Which actions demonstrate common courtesy in professional nursing communication? Select all that apply.
o: Knocking before entering a patient’s room
Knocking before entering is a basic courtesy.
Addressing people by name
Using names is part of courteous communication.
Saying “please” and “thank you” to team members
Courtesy extends to team members as well as patients.
Stating your purpose for being in the room
Stating your purpose is part of practicing courtesy.
Skipping introductions when the unit is busy
Always introduce yourself; failing to do so conveys a lack of caring.
Referring to the patient by room number
Identifying patients by room number is demeaning.
items.ex: Courtesy includes knocking, greeting and saying goodbye, stating your purpose, using names, introducing yourself, and saying please and thank you.

alt.q: A nurse wants to recognize a patient as a unique individual. Which behaviors help? Select all that apply.
o: Making eye contact
Eye contact is a way to recognize others.
Smiling
Smiling is a way to recognize others.
Addressing the patient by preferred name
Using names conveys respect for dignity and uniqueness.
Calling the patient “sweetheart”
Terms of endearment should be avoided.
Referring to the patient by diagnosis
Labeling patients by diagnosis is demeaning.
alt.ex: Eye contact, smiling, and using preferred names recognize the patient as a unique person.

items.q: For which people is using a first name generally appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Infants
First names are appropriate for infants.
Young children
Young children are usually addressed by first name.
Patients who are confused or unconscious
First names are appropriate for confused or unconscious patients.
Close team members
First names are appropriate among close team members.
An alert older adult at the first meeting
Last names are used in the initial interaction unless the patient prefers otherwise.
Any adult patient, to seem more friendly
Last names are respectful in most cultures and used initially with adults.
items.ex: First names fit infants, young children, confused or unconscious patients, and close team members; otherwise follow the patient’s preference.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for several patients. Which patients may the nurse appropriately address by first name without being asked? Select all that apply.
o: A 3-year-old admitted with asthma
First names are appropriate for young children.
An unconscious adult after a head injury
First names are appropriate for unconscious patients.
A confused older adult with delirium
First names are appropriate for confused patients.
An alert 75-year-old admitted for surgery
Alert adults are addressed by last name unless they request otherwise.
A 40-year-old attorney meeting the nurse for the first time
Last names are used in the initial interaction with adults.
alt.ex: First names are appropriate for young children and patients who are confused or unconscious; alert adults choose how to be addressed.

items.q: Failing to give your name and status, such as nursing student or RN, conveys an impersonal lack of commitment or caring.
items.a: True
items.ex: Not introducing yourself creates uncertainty about the interaction and seems impersonal and uncaring.
items.ww: The book says to always introduce yourself and state your title.

alt.q: Because patients can read name badges, nurses do not need to introduce themselves verbally or state their title.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses should always introduce themselves and state their status, in addition to wearing a name badge.
alt.ww: Failing to give name and status creates uncertainty and conveys a lack of caring.

items.q: Terms of endearment such as “honey” or “sweetheart” help older patients feel cared for and are encouraged.
items.a: False
items.ex: Terms of endearment such as honey, dear, grandma, or sweetheart should be avoided.
items.ww: Addressing people by their preferred name, not pet names, conveys respect for dignity.

alt.q: Even the closest nurse-patient relationships rarely progress to identities beyond first names.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Professional relationships stay professional, so nurses avoid pet names even in close relationships.
alt.ww: The book states close relationships rarely go beyond first names.

items.q: Withholding key information from a patient violates both legal and ethical standards of practice.
items.a: True
items.ex: Withholding key information, lying, or distorting the truth violates legal and ethical standards and destroys trust.
items.ww: Honesty is required; withholding key information is a form of dishonesty.

alt.q: Withholding key information from a patient is acceptable when the nurse believes the truth would upset the patient.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses avoid dishonesty at all costs; withholding key information violates legal and ethical standards.
alt.ww: Distressing information is shared with sensitivity, not withheld.

items.q: [[Autonomy]] is being self-directed and independent in accomplishing outcomes and advocating for others.
items.ex: Autonomous nurses make choices, take initiative in problem solving, and accept responsibility for outcomes.

alt.q: A nurse who is self-directed and independent in accomplishing outcomes is demonstrating [[autonomy]].
alt.ex: Autonomous nurses make choices, take initiative in problem solving, and accept responsibility for outcomes.

items: Assessment
Analysis and nursing diagnosis
Planning and outcomes identification
Implementation
Evaluation
ord.ex: The nurse assesses factors affecting communication, identifies diagnoses, plans outcomes, implements techniques, and evaluates effectiveness.

items.q: A patient who is endotracheally intubated is alert and appears anxious. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Establish an alternate way for the patient to communicate needs
items.ex: Patients who cannot speak are at risk for injury unless the nurse identifies an alternate communication method.
w: Ask the patient to speak slowly and clearly
Intubation prevents air from moving past the vocal cords, so speech is not possible.
Wait until extubation to assess the patient’s needs
Delaying communication leaves the patient unable to report emergent needs.
Tell the patient that everything will be fine soon
This is false reassurance and does not let the patient express needs.

alt.q: Why must the nurse identify an alternate communication method for a patient who cannot speak?
alt.a: The patient is at risk for injury without one
alt.ex: A patient unable to speak cannot report emergent needs, so an alternate method keeps the patient safe.
w: It is required before any medication is given
Safety, not medication policy, is the reason given.
It removes the need for a nursing diagnosis
Impaired Verbal Communication is still identified and addressed.
It replaces the need for a nurse call system
Keeping the call system in reach remains essential.

items.q: An older adult with hearing loss says “What?” after the nurse explains a procedure. What should the nurse do next?
items.a: Rephrase the explanation using short sentences
items.ex: For hearing impairment, rephrase rather than repeat if misunderstood, and use short sentences about one topic.
w: Repeat the same explanation in a louder voice
Speak at a normal volume and rephrase rather than repeat; do not shout.
Exaggerate lip movements to aid lip reading
Speak clearly but do not exaggerate lip movement.
Document that the patient is being uncooperative
Do not assume a patient who does not reply is uncooperative.

alt.q: Which approach is recommended when communicating with an older adult who has hearing loss?
alt.a: Face the patient at eye level with your mouth visible
alt.ex: Facing the patient at eye level with the mouth visible, without chewing gum, helps the patient receive the message.
w: Speak very slowly and exaggerate each word
Speak a little slower, not excessively slowly, and do not exaggerate lip movement.
Ask several related questions at once to save time
Ask one question at a time and keep communication short.
Choose a dim room to reduce glare on your face
Choose a quiet, well-lit environment with minimal distractions.

items.q: The evening before surgery, a patient says, “I’m scared the surgeon will find cancer.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Waiting to learn what the surgeon finds must be very hard. How can I help?”
items.ex: This empathetic response acknowledges the patient’s feelings and invites further expression.
w: “Don’t worry; I’m sure everything will turn out just fine.”
False reassurance not supported by facts blocks expression of feelings.
“Why are you already thinking about cancer before surgery?”
“Why” questions are often heard as accusations and cause resentment.
“Let’s talk about your diet after surgery instead of that.”
Changing the subject is rude and blocks further communication.

alt.q: A patient who just learned she needs a mastectomy is crying. Which response shows empathy rather than sympathy?
alt.a: “Losing a breast is a major change. Can we talk about how it may affect you?”
alt.ex: Empathy acknowledges the patient’s reality and invites discussion while the nurse stays objective.
w: “I’m so sorry about this; you must feel completely devastated.”
This is sympathy, a subjective response that can make the nurse lose objectivity.
“I know exactly how you feel; my aunt had the same surgery.”
This shifts the focus to the nurse and assumes the patient’s feelings.
“You’ll be fine; most women adjust very quickly afterward.”
This is false reassurance that discourages expression of feelings.

items.q: A patient who speaks only Spanish needs to give a health history, and no on-site interpreter is available. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Use a telephone interpretation service
items.ex: If on-site interpreters are unavailable, use telephone interpretation; family, friends, or bilingual staff are strongly discouraged.
w: Ask the patient’s 12-year-old son to interpret
Family members, especially children, should not be used as interpreters.
Ask a bilingual staff member to interpret
Use of bilingual staff members to interpret is strongly discouraged.
Speak slowly in English and watch for nodding
Nodding or saying “okay” does not necessarily mean the patient understands.

alt.q: A professional interpreter is present for a patient’s assessment. To whom should the nurse direct the questions?
alt.a: Directly to the patient
alt.ex: The nurse speaks directly to the patient, even when an interpreter is present.
w: Directly to the interpreter
The interpreter conveys the message, but the nurse addresses the patient.
To an adult family member
The patient is the focus; family should not replace the patient or interpreter.
To whoever answers first
Questions are directed to the patient, who is the source of the history.

items.q: A nurse plans a 30-minute discussion with a patient about lifestyle changes after a heart attack. What should the nurse do before starting?
items.a: Make sure symptoms are controlled and elimination needs are met
items.ex: Address physical care priorities first before lengthy interactions so the discussion is not interrupted.
w: Turn on the television to help the patient relax
Distractions such as television should be minimized for communication.
Invite several visitors to join the discussion
A quiet, private place free from distractions such as visitors is preferred.
Schedule the talk for when the meal tray arrives
Competing activities interrupt the discussion; meet comfort needs first.

alt.q: A patient has impaired airway clearance and is very frightened. How does the textbook advise the nurse to plan priorities?
alt.a: Plan to ease the patient’s fear while starting airway interventions
alt.ex: Physiological needs and communication can go hand in hand, so the nurse allays fear while initiating airway care.
w: Address the fear only after the airway is fully managed
The book says to plan to allay fear simultaneously, not afterward.
Manage the fear completely before any airway care begins
An urgent airway problem cannot wait until anxiety is resolved.
Ask the family to manage the fear while the nurse works
The nurse plans both needs together as part of the care plan.

items.q: A patient has not touched the lunch tray. Which statement by the nurse shares an observation rather than making an assumption?
items.a: “I see you haven’t eaten anything.”
items.ex: Stating what the nurse sees is a gentle observation that invites the patient to explain without being contradicted.
w: “You must not be hungry today.”
This draws a conclusion without validating it, which is an assumption.
“You don’t care about your diet goals.”
Assuming lack of interest in nutrition goals is an unvalidated conclusion.
“You must not like hospital food.”
This interprets the untouched tray without checking with the patient.

alt.q: Why is sharing observations a safer technique than making assumptions?
alt.a: Assumptions force the patient to contradict the nurse
alt.ex: Making assumptions draws unvalidated conclusions and puts the patient in the position of having to contradict the nurse.
w: Observations always lead to a nursing diagnosis
Observations start conversation; they do not automatically produce a diagnosis.
Assumptions take longer to document in the record
Documentation time is not the reason given.
Assumptions are only appropriate with quiet patients
Observations, not assumptions, help start conversation with quiet patients.

items.q: A patient with aphasia after a stroke has difficulty forming words. Which team member should the nurse collaborate with?
items.a: Speech-language pathologist
items.ex: Speech-language pathologists help patients with aphasia and dysphagia communicate.
w: Mental health nurse specialist
Mental health nurse specialists help angry or highly anxious patients communicate.
Professional interpreter
Interpreters are needed for patients who speak a foreign language.
Physical therapist
Physical therapists address mobility, not communication strategies.

alt.q: A highly anxious patient cannot communicate needs effectively. Which team member does the textbook suggest can help?
alt.a: Mental health nurse specialist
alt.ex: Mental health nurse specialists help angry or highly anxious patients communicate more effectively.
w: Speech-language pathologist
Speech-language pathologists help patients with aphasia and dysphagia.
Professional interpreter
Interpreters help patients who speak a foreign language.
Respiratory therapist
Respiratory therapists are not described as communication experts.

items.q: A patient who cannot speak after laryngeal surgery is frustrated using pen and paper because his handwriting is shaky. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Revise the care plan to try a picture board
items.ex: When a method frustrates the patient, the nurse identifies the cause and modifies the plan, such as switching to a picture board.
w: Encourage him to keep practicing with pen and paper
Continuing a method that frustrates the patient does not meet the outcome.
Ask his family to speak for him at all times
The goal is for the patient to convey his own messages.
Limit communication to only his essential needs
Limiting communication does not address the barrier.

alt.q: When a patient’s expected communication outcomes are not met, what should the nurse do?
alt.a: Determine which factors influenced the outcomes
alt.ex: If outcomes are not met, the nurse determines which factors influenced them and modifies the plan of care.
w: Continue the same plan unchanged for another week
Unsatisfactory progress calls for modifying the plan.
Document that the patient is being uncooperative
The nurse explores contributing factors rather than labeling the patient.
Drop the outcome from the patient’s care plan
The nurse revises interventions so the outcome can still be met.

items.q: A nurse notes that a patient has severe pain and is short of breath during an interview. In which context of communication do these factors belong?
items.a: Psychophysiological context
items.ex: Physiological status such as pain and dyspnea is an internal factor in the psychophysiological context.
w: Relational context
The relational context is the nature of the relationship, such as trust and power.
Situational context
The situational context is the reason for communicating, such as information exchange.
Environmental context
The environmental context is the physical surroundings, such as noise and privacy.

alt.q: Privacy level and noise level belong to which context of communication?
alt.a: Environmental context
alt.ex: The environmental context is the physical surroundings, including privacy, noise, comfort, safety, and distraction levels.
w: Cultural context
The cultural context includes education level, language, customs, and expectations.
Relational context
The relational context concerns trust, caring, self-disclosure, and power.
Psychophysiological context
This context includes internal factors such as pain, emotions, and self-esteem.

items.q: Using the SURETY model for active listening, how should the nurse be seated?
items.a: At a slight angle facing the patient
items.ex: Sitting at a slight angle is nonconfrontational and shows the nurse is there to listen.
w: Directly across with arms crossed
Crossed arms convey a defensive, closed attitude.
Behind the computer while charting
Talking while working at a computer is distracting and hinders listening.
At the foot of the bed, standing
SURETY begins with sitting at an angle facing the patient.

alt.q: What does the “Y” in the SURETY model stand for?
alt.a: Your intuition
alt.ex: Y reminds the nurse to trust intuition to individualize and adapt communication techniques.
w: Yielding to silence
Silence is a separate technique, not part of SURETY.
Your posture
Posture is addressed by S (sit at an angle) and U (uncross legs and arms).
Yes-or-no questions
Closed questions are not part of the SURETY model.

items.q: A nurse reviews a patient’s medication record before an interview. Which drug classes may cause the patient to slur words or use incomplete sentences? Select all that apply.
o: Opiates
Opiates may cause slurred words or incomplete sentences.
Antidepressants
Antidepressants are listed as affecting speech.
Neuroleptics
Neuroleptics may cause slurred speech.
Sedatives
Sedatives may cause slurred words or incomplete sentences.
Topical antibiotics
Topical antibiotics are not listed as affecting speech.
Stool softeners
Stool softeners are not listed as affecting speech.
items.ex: Opiates, antidepressants, neuroleptics, hypnotics, and sedatives may cause slurred words or incomplete sentences.

alt.q: A patient’s speech is slurred during the admission interview. Which medications in the record might explain this finding? Select all that apply.
o: A hypnotic taken at bedtime
Hypnotics may cause slurred words.
An opiate for postoperative pain
Opiates may cause slurred speech or incomplete sentences.
An antidepressant taken daily
Antidepressants are listed as affecting speech.
An antacid taken after meals
Antacids are not listed as affecting speech.
A topical antifungal cream
Topical antifungals are not listed as affecting speech.
alt.ex: Reviewing the medication record reveals drugs such as hypnotics, opiates, and antidepressants that may impair speech.

items.q: Which actions are appropriate when communicating with a patient who is unresponsive? Select all that apply.
o: Call the patient by name during interactions
Calling the patient by name is recommended.
Explain all procedures and sensations
Explaining procedures and sensations is recommended for unresponsive patients.
Speak to the patient as though they can hear
Speak as though the patient can hear.
Communicate both verbally and by touch
Both verbal communication and touch are recommended.
Discuss the patient’s condition with family at the bedside
Avoid talking about the patient to others in the patient’s presence.
Skip explanations because the patient cannot respond
All procedures and sensations should still be explained.
items.ex: Treat the unresponsive patient as able to hear: use the name, touch, explanations, and orientation, and avoid talking about them.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a heavily sedated patient on a ventilator. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Orient the patient to person, place, and time
Orientation is recommended for unresponsive patients.
Tell the patient before turning and repositioning
All procedures and sensations should be explained.
Use the patient’s name when speaking
Calling the patient by name is recommended.
Avoid touch so the patient is not startled
Communicate both verbally and by touch.
Talk with colleagues about the prognosis at the bedside
Avoid talking about the patient to others in their presence.
alt.ex: Heavily sedated patients should be addressed by name, oriented, touched, and told about procedures as though they can hear.

items.q: Which approaches support communication with a patient who has a cognitive impairment? Select all that apply.
o: Use simple sentences
Simple sentences without long explanations aid understanding.
Ask one question at a time
Asking one question at a time reduces confusion.
Include family and friends in conversations
Family and friends help, especially on subjects the patient knows.
Use pictures or gestures that mimic the action
Visual cues and gestures support understanding.
Give long, detailed explanations
Long explanations should be avoided.
Approach from behind to avoid startling the patient
Approach the patient from the front.
items.ex: With cognitive impairment, keep messages simple, ask one question at a time, allow time, and use family, pictures, and gestures.

alt.q: Using the ABC mnemonic, a nurse wants to “behave calmly” with a patient who has dementia. Which actions fit? Select all that apply.
o: Approach the patient from the front
Behaving calmly includes approaching from the front.
Position yourself at the patient’s eye level
Being at eye level conveys respect.
Avoid making sudden movements
Sudden movements should be avoided.
Stand close over the patient to hold attention
Respect the patient’s personal space.
Ask several questions together to save time
Use short, simple questions and allow time to respond.
alt.ex: Behave calmly means approaching from the front, respecting space, being at eye level, avoiding sudden moves, and staying calm.

items.q: In general, the nurse should allow the patient to break a silence, particularly when the patient started it.
items.a: True
items.ex: Silence lets the patient think and gain insight, so the nurse usually lets the patient break it.
items.ww: The book advises allowing the patient to break the silence, especially when they initiated it.

alt.q: When a patient becomes silent, the nurse should fill the pause quickly so the patient does not feel uncomfortable.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Silence gives time to sort out feelings and gain insight; the nurse generally lets the patient break it.
alt.ww: Filling every pause cuts off the patient’s thinking; silence is a therapeutic technique.

items.q: Therapeutic confrontation should be used only after trust is established and done gently with sensitivity.
items.a: True
items.ex: Confrontation helps the patient see inconsistencies, but it requires established trust and a gentle approach.
items.ww: The book specifies trust must come first and confrontation must be gentle.

alt.q: Therapeutic confrontation is most effective early in the orientation phase, before trust develops.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Confrontation is used only after trust is established, typically in the working phase.
alt.ww: Confronting a patient before trust exists can damage the relationship.

items.q: Dark coping humor used by staff within earshot of patients or their loved ones can cause great emotional distress.
items.a: True
items.ex: Coping humor is easily misinterpreted as uncaring by people not involved in the situation.
items.ww: The book warns that coping humor overheard by patients or families causes great distress.

alt.q: Joking about a patient’s cultural attributes is acceptable once a strong therapeutic relationship has formed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: It is never appropriate, with any patient, to joke about race, disability, sexual orientation, economic status, or culture.
alt.ww: A strong relationship does not make such jokes appropriate.

items.q: The primary nursing diagnostic label for a patient with limited or no ability to communicate verbally is [[Impaired Verbal Communication]].
items.ex: Impaired Verbal Communication applies when a patient has trouble receiving, processing, transmitting, or using symbols.

alt.q: A patient with aphasia who has difficulty forming words and comprehending fits the nursing diagnosis [[Impaired Verbal Communication]].
alt.ex: Impaired Verbal Communication applies when a patient has trouble receiving, processing, transmitting, or using symbols.

items.q: Written records of a nurse’s verbal and nonverbal interactions with patients, used to evaluate communication, are called [[process recordings|process recording]].
items.ex: Analyzing process recordings shows missed cues and whether responses facilitated or blocked communication.

alt.q: Analyzing a [[process recording|process recordings]] helps a nurse identify missed cues and whether responses facilitated or blocked communication.
alt.ex: Analyzing process recordings shows missed cues and whether responses facilitated or blocked communication.

items.q: Which example shows False reassurance?
items.a: “Don’t worry; everything will be just fine.”
items.ex: Nontherapeutic techniques block communication and discourage further expression of feelings and ideas.
w: “Why are you so upset today?”
That goes with Asking for explanations.
“No one on this staff would ever lie to you.”
That goes with Defensive response.
“If I were you, I’d move your father to a nursing home.”
