items.q: What is the primary goal of patient education?
items.a: Helping individuals, families, or communities achieve optimal levels of health
items.ex: Patient education aims first at helping individuals, families, or communities reach their optimal level of health.
w: Shortening hospital stays so that acute care beds open more quickly
Shorter stays may follow good teaching, but the book names optimal health as the primary goal.
Ensuring patients carry out every order from the health care provider
Education supports active participation and decision making, not simple compliance with orders.
Transferring responsibility for documenting care from nurses to patients
Documentation stays a nursing responsibility; education aims at optimal health.

alt.q: A new graduate nurse asks why patient education is a core nursing activity. Which response reflects the book’s primary purpose?
alt.a: “It helps patients and families reach their best possible level of health.”
alt.ex: The primary goal of patient education is helping individuals, families, or communities achieve optimal health.
w: “It protects the hospital by showing that information was handed out.”
Handing out material is not the goal; optimal health through active participation is.
“It mainly reduces the number of questions patients ask the staff.”
Education encourages patients to ask questions and participate, not to ask fewer.
“It replaces the need for follow-up visits after discharge.”
Education does not replace follow-up care; it helps patients reach optimal health.

items.q: What is the goal of primary prevention in patient education?
items.a: Promoting health and reducing disease
items.ex: Primary prevention teaching gives information and skills that help patients adopt healthier behaviors to promote health and reduce disease.
w: Diagnosing illness early and treating it promptly
Early diagnosis and prompt treatment describe secondary prevention.
Rehabilitating patients with permanent impairments
Rehabilitation is the focus of tertiary prevention.
Limiting disability after an acute injury
Limiting disability to return to normal health is part of secondary prevention.

alt.q: A school nurse teaches healthy eating and exercise to students who have no illness. Which level of prevention is this?
alt.a: Primary prevention
alt.ex: Teaching healthy people to adopt healthier behaviors promotes health and reduces disease, the goal of primary prevention.
w: Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention addresses early diagnosis and prompt treatment of illness.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention addresses rehabilitation after illness or injury with lasting effects.
Quaternary prevention
The book describes three levels of prevention: primary, secondary, and tertiary.

items.q: Which focus best describes secondary prevention?
items.a: Early diagnosis and prompt treatment of illness while limiting disability
items.ex: Secondary prevention aims to detect and treat illness early and limit disability so patients return to normal health quickly.
w: Promoting healthy behaviors in people who are not yet ill
Promoting health in well people is primary prevention.
Rehabilitation of patients with irreversible chronic conditions
Rehabilitation for irreversible conditions is tertiary prevention.
Teaching new ways to perform activities after permanent loss of function
Adapting to permanent loss of function is tertiary prevention.

alt.q: A patient is recovering from an acute injury and asks the home health nurse how to care for the wound and regain strength. Which level of prevention guides this teaching?
alt.a: Secondary prevention
alt.ex: Patients recovering from acute illness or injury need information and self-care skills to regain health, which is secondary prevention.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention promotes health before disease occurs.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention addresses permanent impairments and rehabilitation, not recovery from an acute injury.
Health maintenance only
This is not a level of prevention; recovery from acute injury falls under secondary prevention.

items.q: What is the focus of tertiary prevention?
items.a: Rehabilitation to regain function or cope with permanent changes
items.ex: Tertiary prevention focuses on rehabilitation rather than disease detection and treatment for patients with temporary or permanent impaired function.
w: Screening to detect illness at an early stage
Screening and early detection belong to secondary prevention.
Promoting health to reduce the risk of disease
Health promotion and disease reduction are primary prevention.
Prompt treatment of a newly diagnosed acute illness
Prompt treatment of illness is secondary prevention.

alt.q: A patient lost the ability to speak after surgery on the larynx and is learning new ways to communicate. Which level of prevention does this teaching represent?
alt.a: Tertiary prevention
alt.ex: Learning to cope with a permanent loss of function, such as speech after larynx surgery, is rehabilitation in tertiary prevention.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention promotes health before disease develops.
Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention centers on early diagnosis and prompt treatment.
Health promotion
Health promotion belongs to primary prevention, not rehabilitation after a permanent loss.

items.q: A nurse is preparing discharge teaching for an older patient recovering from a fractured hip. The patient’s adult son is visiting. Which action should the nurse take first regarding the son?
items.a: Assess the relationship between the patient and the son
items.ex: The book warns not to assume a family caregiver should be involved; assess the patient-family relationship before teaching caregivers.
w: Include the son in all teaching sessions starting today
Automatically including family assumes involvement is wanted before assessing the relationship.
Exclude the son so that the patient stays independent
Excluding a needed family caregiver from teaching can cause conflicts.
Give the son written instructions to take home tonight
Teaching the son before assessing the patient-family relationship skips a needed assessment.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows correct understanding of involving family caregivers in teaching?
alt.a: “I will assess the patient-family relationship before I teach the daughter.”
alt.ex: Family caregivers are often vital, but the nurse assesses the patient-family relationship before including them in education.
w: “Family members should always attend teaching, whatever the patient prefers.”
Assuming family should be involved ignores the need to assess the relationship first.
“Leaving the family out of teaching avoids conflicts at home.”
The book states that excluding a family caregiver from the plan can cause conflicts.
“Family caregivers need much less teaching than the patient does.”
Family caregivers usually require as much education as patients.

items.q: A patient recovering from a myocardial infarction seems uninterested when the nurse begins teaching about diet changes. Which approach by the nurse is best?
items.a: Assess the patient’s willingness to learn and find ways to motivate interest
items.ex: Some patients find healthy behaviors hard to adopt and lose interest; nurses identify willingness to learn and motivate interest.
w: Postpone all teaching until the patient asks for information
Waiting passively misses the nurse’s role in motivating a patient’s interest in learning.
Give the written diet plan only to the family and skip the patient
The patient still needs education; family teaching does not replace it.
Warn the patient that refusing to learn will cause another heart attack
Threats do not motivate learning; the nurse assesses willingness and builds interest.

alt.q: Which nursing skill does the book emphasize for patients who find it difficult to adopt healthy behaviors after an acute illness?
alt.a: Identifying willingness to learn and motivating interest in learning
alt.ex: Nurses learn to identify patients’ willingness to learn and motivate their interest when patients become disinterested in learning.
w: Repeating the same information until the patient agrees
Repetition alone does not address willingness or motivation to learn.
Referring the patient to a dietitian instead of teaching
Referral does not replace the nurse’s role in assessing and motivating the learner.
Teaching the family caregiver in place of the patient
Family teaching supports, but does not replace, motivating the patient to learn.

items.q: A patient had a stroke and will need help at home. When should education for the patient’s family begin?
items.a: As soon as the nurse identifies the patient’s needs and the family shows willingness to help
items.ex: Family education begins as soon as patient needs are identified and the family displays willingness to help.
w: On the day of discharge, once the discharge order is written
Waiting until discharge delays teaching the family needs to support major changes.
After the patient has reached the maximum level of recovery
Families need teaching early so they can understand and accept changes in the patient.
Only after the family formally requests written instructions
The nurse starts teaching once needs are known and the family is willing, not only on request.

alt.q: The family of a patient with a spinal cord injury wants to help with care at home. Which teaching is appropriate for health care management?
alt.a: Giving medications through a gastric tube and doing passive range-of-motion exercises
alt.ex: The book lists gastric tube medications and passive range of motion as health care management skills taught to families.
w: Adjusting the patient’s prescribed medication doses as symptoms change
Changing prescribed doses is not a family skill; families learn to give medications safely.
Interpreting the patient’s diagnostic imaging results
Interpreting diagnostic results is not a family health care management skill.
Deciding when the patient no longer needs rehabilitation
This decision belongs to the health care team, not to family teaching.

items.q: How does the nurse identify a patient’s deficits and learning needs when planning a teaching program?
items.a: By comparing the patient’s realistic desired level of health with the actual state of health
items.ex: Comparing realistic desired health with actual health reveals deficits and needs for an effective teaching plan.
w: By reviewing which teaching pamphlets the unit has available
Available materials do not reveal the patient’s deficits and needs.
By asking the family which topics they would like covered
Family input helps, but deficits are found by comparing desired and actual health.
By teaching the standard content for the patient’s diagnosis
Standard content ignores the individual gap between desired and actual health.

alt.q: A nurse compares what a patient realistically hopes to achieve after a stroke with the patient’s current abilities. What is the purpose of this comparison?
alt.a: To identify deficits and needs so effective teaching can be planned
alt.ex: The gap between realistic desired health and actual health shows the deficits and needs that the teaching plan addresses.
w: To decide whether the patient qualifies for long-term care placement
Placement decisions are not the purpose described for this comparison.
To document that the patient’s goals are unrealistic
The comparison uses realistic goals to plan teaching, not to label goals.
To determine which family member is legally responsible for care
Legal responsibility is not determined by this comparison.

items.q: According to the book, when does success in patient education occur?
items.a: When patients incorporate knowledge and skills into their routine life activities
items.ex: Teaching succeeds when patients build the new knowledge and skills into daily life to promote their health.
w: When patients sign the form stating they received teaching
A signature documents teaching was given, not that it changed daily behavior.
When patients repeat the information correctly once before discharge
A single correct repetition does not show the knowledge is part of daily routines.
When all of the planned teaching materials have been handed out
Distributing materials does not show the patient applies the learning.

alt.q: An adolescent with diabetes was taught insulin self-injection. Which finding best shows that this teaching was successful?
alt.a: The adolescent safely self-administers daily injections as part of a normal routine
alt.ex: Success occurs when patients incorporate knowledge and skills into routine life activities, such as safe daily self-injection.
w: The adolescent watches a parent prepare and give each injection
Watching a parent shows dependence, not that the adolescent incorporated the skill.
The adolescent reads the insulin package insert in the clinic
Reading material is exposure to information, not use of the skill in daily life.
The adolescent describes insulin action but avoids giving injections
Knowledge without performing the skill means it is not part of daily routines.

items.q: Families of patients with cognitive disorders, intellectual disability, or terminal illness need which type of skills to adapt to these chronic conditions?
items.a: Communication and relational skills
items.ex: These families need communication and relational skills to adapt to emotional effects and to provide psychosocial support.
w: Advanced physical assessment skills
Physical assessment is not what the book identifies for adapting to emotional effects.
Diagnostic testing skills
Diagnostic testing is not a family role; the book stresses communication and relational skills.
Medication dose adjustment skills
Adjusting doses is not a family skill; the emphasis is on emotional and psychosocial support.

alt.q: Why does the family of a patient with a terminal illness need communication and relational skills?
alt.a: To adapt to the emotional effects of the condition and provide psychosocial support
alt.ex: Communication and relational skills help families cope emotionally and give psychosocial support that facilitates the patient’s health.
w: To take over the patient’s legal decision making right away
Legal decision making is not the stated purpose of these skills.
To replace the hospice team’s role in symptom management
Families support the patient but do not replace the health care team.
To limit visitors so the patient can rest without interruption
Limiting visitors is not the purpose the book gives for these skills.

items.q: After a childbearing class, which statement by an expectant mother shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I plan to eat healthy foods, stay active, and avoid substances that can harm my baby.”
items.ex: Mothers who apply knowledge from childbearing classes are more likely to eat well, exercise, and avoid substances that harm the fetus.
w: “I can keep drinking small amounts of wine because the placenta filters it out.”
Avoiding substances that can harm the fetus is a key teaching point.
“I should stop all exercise until after my baby is born.”
Teaching encourages physical exercise during pregnancy rather than stopping it.
“Eating for two means I can eat whatever foods I want now.”
Teaching promotes eating healthy foods, not unrestricted intake.

alt.q: A nurse teaches expectant parents about normal physical and psychological changes of pregnancy. Which outcome shows this primary prevention teaching worked?
alt.a: The mother eats healthy foods, exercises, and avoids substances harmful to the fetus
alt.ex: Applying new knowledge about normal childbearing leads to healthier eating, exercise, and avoiding harmful substances.
w: The mother attends every class but keeps smoking during the pregnancy
Attendance without behavior change does not show the teaching was applied.
The mother can list pregnancy changes but has not changed her diet
Knowledge that is not applied does not show successful teaching.
The father agrees to handle all of the mother’s meal planning
Delegating meals does not show the mother applied the new knowledge.

items.q: Which teaching activities are examples of tertiary prevention? Select all that apply.
o: Teaching a patient new ways to communicate after larynx surgery
Coping with permanent loss of speech is rehabilitation, the focus of tertiary prevention.
Teaching a stroke patient’s family to give medications through a gastric tube
Teaching families care skills after serious disability supports rehabilitation in tertiary prevention.
Teaching passive range-of-motion exercises to the family of a patient with a spinal cord injury
Helping families manage permanent physical changes is tertiary prevention.
Teaching expectant parents about normal changes of pregnancy
Childbearing classes that promote healthy behaviors are primary prevention.
Teaching a patient what to expect during a cancer screening test
Screening for early diagnosis is secondary prevention.
items.ex: Tertiary prevention focuses on rehabilitation for patients who must regain function or cope with permanent health alterations.

alt.q: A nurse works on a rehabilitation unit. Which teaching activities fit the tertiary prevention focus of the unit? Select all that apply.
o: Helping a patient with a permanent impairment relearn activities of daily living
Regaining function to continue ADLs is a tertiary prevention goal.
Teaching a patient after laryngectomy an alternative way to communicate
Coping with a permanent change in function is rehabilitation.
Teaching the family of a stroke patient how to provide passive range of motion
Family care skills after serious disability support rehabilitation.
Teaching high school students about the dangers of smoking
Preventing disease in healthy people is primary prevention.
Teaching a patient to prepare for screening mammography
Screening for early detection is secondary prevention.
alt.ex: Tertiary prevention teaching helps patients with lasting impairments regain function or cope with permanent changes.

items.q: Which statements about family caregivers in patient education are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Family caregivers are often a vital part of a patient’s return to health.
The book describes family caregivers as often vital to recovery.
Family caregivers usually need as much education as the patient.
Caregivers usually require as much education as patients.
Excluding a family caregiver from the teaching plan can lead to conflicts.
The book warns that leaving out a family caregiver can cause conflicts.
A family caregiver should always be included without further assessment.
The nurse assesses the patient-family relationship before teaching caregivers.
The nurse decides which people count as the patient’s family.
Family is defined by the patient, not by the nurse.
items.ex: Family caregivers are vital and need thorough teaching, but the nurse assesses the patient-family relationship first.

alt.q: A nurse is planning teaching that may involve a patient’s family. Which actions follow the book’s guidance? Select all that apply.
o: Assess the patient-family relationship before teaching the family
Do not assume involvement; assess the relationship first.
Plan for the family caregiver to receive as much teaching as the patient
Family caregivers usually require as much education as patients.
Let the patient define who is considered family
The book refers to the family as defined by the patient.
Leave the family out of the plan to keep teaching simple
Excluding a family caregiver can create conflicts.
Teach any relative who visits, whatever the patient prefers
Teaching relatives without assessing the relationship ignores the patient’s wishes.
alt.ex: Good family teaching respects the patient’s definition of family, assesses relationships first, and gives caregivers thorough education.

items.q: Which outcomes of patient education does the book describe? Select all that apply.
o: Lower health care costs for individuals through preventive education
Education about preventive health care can reduce health care costs for individuals.
Prevention of chronic disease through lifestyle changes
Patients learn lifestyle changes such as diet, exercise, and stopping smoking to prevent chronic disease.
Reduced effects of chronic illnesses and associated medical care
Lifestyle changes reduce the effects of chronic illness and the medical care it needs.
Safe, person-centered care through active patient participation
Education with active participation and decision making is essential for safe, person-centered care.
Elimination of the need for routine health screening
Education does not replace screening; screening is part of secondary prevention.
items.ex: Patient education supports safe person-centered care, prevents and lessens chronic disease, and can lower health care costs.

alt.q: A community nurse explains the benefits of teaching patients about diet, exercise, and smoking cessation. Which benefits are supported by the book? Select all that apply.
o: It can reduce individuals’ health care costs.
Preventive education can reduce health care costs for individuals.
It helps prevent chronic disease.
Lifestyle changes are taught to prevent chronic disease.
It can reduce the effects of existing chronic illness.
Lifestyle changes reduce the effects of chronic illnesses and related care.
It guarantees patients will never need hospital care.
Education lowers risk but cannot guarantee that hospital care is never needed.
It removes the need for follow-up with the health care provider.
Education supports, but does not replace, ongoing health care.
alt.ex: Lifestyle teaching can prevent chronic disease, lessen its effects, and reduce individuals’ health care costs.

items.q: Providing education about preventive health care can reduce health care costs for individuals.
items.a: True
items.ex: Preventive teaching helps patients change lifestyles to prevent chronic disease, which reduces related medical care and costs.
items.ww: The book directly states that preventive health education can reduce individuals’ health care costs.

alt.q: Preventive health education has little effect on individual health care costs because most costs come from acute care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book states preventive health education can reduce costs by preventing chronic disease and its associated care.
alt.ww: Preventive teaching lowers costs by preventing chronic disease and reducing the effects of chronic illness.

items.q: A nurse should assume that a family caregiver will be involved in a patient’s teaching plan.
items.a: False
items.ex: The book warns not to assume family involvement; the nurse assesses the patient-family relationship before teaching caregivers.
items.ww: Involving family without assessment ignores the patient’s relationships and wishes, which the nurse must assess first.

alt.q: Before providing education to family caregivers, the nurse assesses the patient-family relationship.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Assessing the patient-family relationship comes before including family caregivers in teaching.
alt.ww: Skipping this assessment risks teaching people the patient does not want involved.

items.q: The focus of tertiary prevention is disease detection and prompt treatment.
items.a: False
items.ex: Tertiary prevention focuses on rehabilitation; detection and prompt treatment belong to secondary prevention.
items.ww: Detection and treatment describe secondary prevention, not the rehabilitation focus of tertiary prevention.

alt.q: The focus of tertiary prevention is rehabilitation for patients with temporary or permanent impaired function.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Tertiary prevention helps patients regain previous function or cope with permanent health alterations.
alt.ww: Tertiary prevention is about rehabilitation, not early detection or prompt treatment.

items.q: The goal of [[primary]] prevention is to promote health and reduce disease.
items.ex: Primary prevention teaching helps people adopt healthier behaviors in schools, homes, and clinics.

alt.q: Teaching healthy adolescents to avoid smoking is an example of [[primary]] prevention, which promotes health and reduces disease.
alt.ex: Primary prevention teaching helps people adopt healthier behaviors in schools, homes, and clinics.

items.q: The focus of tertiary prevention is [[rehabilitation]] rather than disease detection and treatment.
items.ex: Tertiary prevention helps patients regain function or cope with permanent health alterations.

alt.q: Helping a patient learn new ways to communicate after larynx surgery is an example of [[rehabilitation]], the focus of tertiary prevention.
alt.ex: Tertiary prevention helps patients regain function or cope with permanent health alterations.

items.q: Which teaching example illustrates Primary prevention?
items.a: Teaching expectant parents to eat well and avoid substances harmful to the fetus
items.ex: Primary prevention promotes health, secondary addresses early diagnosis and recovery from acute illness, and tertiary focuses on rehabilitation.
w: Teaching self-care to a patient recovering from an acute injury
That goes with Secondary prevention.
Teaching a patient new ways to communicate after larynx surgery
That goes with Tertiary prevention.

alt.q: Which teaching example illustrates Secondary prevention?
alt.a: Teaching self-care to a patient recovering from an acute injury
alt.ex: Primary prevention promotes health, secondary addresses early diagnosis and recovery from acute illness, and tertiary focuses on rehabilitation.
w: Teaching expectant parents to eat well and avoid substances harmful to the fetus
That goes with Primary prevention.
Teaching a patient new ways to communicate after larynx surgery
That goes with Tertiary prevention.

alt.q: Which teaching example illustrates Tertiary prevention?
alt.a: Teaching a patient new ways to communicate after larynx surgery
alt.ex: Primary prevention promotes health, secondary addresses early diagnosis and recovery from acute illness, and tertiary focuses on rehabilitation.
w: Teaching expectant parents to eat well and avoid substances harmful to the fetus
That goes with Primary prevention.
Teaching self-care to a patient recovering from an acute injury
That goes with Secondary prevention.

alt.q: Which level of prevention does this teaching illustrate: “Teaching expectant parents to eat well and avoid substances harmful to the fetus”?
alt.a: Primary prevention
alt.ex: Primary prevention promotes health, secondary addresses early diagnosis and recovery from acute illness, and tertiary focuses on rehabilitation.
w: Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention: Teaching self-care to a patient recovering from an acute injury.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention: Teaching a patient new ways to communicate after larynx surgery.

alt.q: Which level of prevention does this teaching illustrate: “Teaching self-care to a patient recovering from an acute injury”?
alt.a: Secondary prevention
alt.ex: Primary prevention promotes health, secondary addresses early diagnosis and recovery from acute illness, and tertiary focuses on rehabilitation.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention: Teaching expectant parents to eat well and avoid substances harmful to the fetus.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention: Teaching a patient new ways to communicate after larynx surgery.

alt.q: Which level of prevention does this teaching illustrate: “Teaching a patient new ways to communicate after larynx surgery”?
alt.a: Tertiary prevention
alt.ex: Primary prevention promotes health, secondary addresses early diagnosis and recovery from acute illness, and tertiary focuses on rehabilitation.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention: Teaching expectant parents to eat well and avoid substances harmful to the fetus.
Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention: Teaching self-care to a patient recovering from an acute injury.

mt.q: Match each level of prevention with an example of teaching at that level.
pairs: Teaching expectant parents to eat well and avoid substances harmful to the fetus
Teaching self-care to a patient recovering from an acute injury
Teaching a patient new ways to communicate after larynx surgery
mt.ex: Primary prevention promotes health, secondary addresses early diagnosis and recovery from acute illness, and tertiary focuses on rehabilitation.

items.q: Which description of teaching matches the textbook?
items.a: A conscious, deliberate set of actions that helps people gain knowledge, change attitudes, adopt behaviors, or perform skills
items.ex: Teaching imparts knowledge through directed activities that help individuals gain knowledge, change attitudes, adopt behaviors, or perform new skills.
w: A permanent change in behavior that results from a meaningful experience in the learner’s life
A permanent change in behavior from an experience describes learning, not teaching.
An informal exchange of information that happens whenever a nurse and patient talk together
Teaching is a conscious and deliberate set of actions, not any casual exchange.
A one-time presentation of facts that the learner is expected to memorize without any help
Teaching guides learners and sets the pace; it is not a one-time fact delivery.

alt.q: According to the book, when do teaching and learning begin?
alt.a: When a person identifies a need to know or to acquire an ability
alt.ex: Teaching and learning begin when a person identifies a need for knowing or acquiring an ability to do something.
w: When the health care provider writes an order for teaching
A provider order is not what starts the teaching-learning process.
When the patient has been told the discharge date
Discharge planning does not define when learning begins.
When the nurse finishes writing a formal teaching plan
A plan responds to a need; the identified need starts the process.

items.q: A nurse taught a patient a new daily medication regimen. Which observation best shows that learning has occurred?
items.a: The patient correctly sets up a 7-day pill organizer and takes the medications each day
items.ex: Learning means understanding and applying new concepts, shown by setting up the organizer and adhering to the regimen.
w: The patient says the printed medication sheet was easy to read
Finding a sheet readable does not show understanding or application.
The patient nods and smiles while the nurse explains each drug
Nodding is not evidence of understanding or applying the information.
The patient asks that the medication list be given to the spouse
Handing the list to a spouse does not show the patient learned the regimen.

alt.q: Which definition of learning matches the textbook?
alt.a: An experience that causes a permanent change in behavior, skill, emotional functioning, or mental processing
alt.ex: Learning is a lifelong, dynamic process in which an experience produces a permanent change in behavior, skills, emotions, or thinking.
w: A deliberate set of actions an educator uses to impart knowledge to others
Deliberate actions to impart knowledge describe teaching, not learning.
A temporary ability to repeat information right after hearing it
Learning is a permanent change, not short-term repetition.
A one-time event that ends when formal schooling is complete
Learning is lifelong and dynamic, not limited to formal schooling.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to teach a patient newly diagnosed with heart failure. How should the nurse determine what to teach?
items.a: Ask the patient questions and find out the patient’s interests
items.ex: Teaching is most effective when it responds to learner needs, which the educator assesses by asking questions and determining interests.
w: Use the standard heart failure teaching packet without changes
Standard content may not respond to this learner’s needs and interests.
Teach whatever topics the nurse believes are most interesting
Teaching is based on the learner’s needs, not the nurse’s preferences.
Wait for the health care provider to list the teaching topics
The nurse assesses learner needs directly through questions and interests.

alt.q: When is teaching most effective, according to the book?
alt.a: When it responds to the learner’s needs
alt.ex: An educator assesses learner needs by asking questions and determining interests, making teaching responsive and effective.
w: When it covers every topic related to the diagnosis
Covering everything does not ensure the learner’s needs are met.
When it is delivered in a single long session
Session length does not make teaching effective; responding to needs does.
When it follows the same script for every patient
A fixed script ignores individual learner needs.

items.q: A nurse hears a colleague say, “That patient can’t read well, so I won’t bother with discharge teaching.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Nurses are legally responsible for teaching every patient, so we need to adapt teaching to the patient’s literacy.”
items.ex: Nurses are legally responsible for educating all patients regardless of age, culture, literacy level, religion, or other characteristics.
w: “That makes sense; written handouts can be mailed to the patient later.”
Skipping teaching for low literacy violates the nurse’s legal responsibility to teach all patients.
“Teaching is optional for patients who have limited literacy.”
Teaching is required for all patients, whatever their literacy level.
“Only the health care provider is responsible for teaching this patient.”
Nurses themselves are legally responsible for patient education.

alt.q: Which statement about the nurse’s responsibility for patient education is accurate?
alt.a: Nurses are legally responsible for educating all patients regardless of their characteristics
alt.ex: The legal duty to teach applies to every patient, regardless of gender, culture, age, literacy, religion, or other characteristics.
w: Nurses teach only patients who request information
The duty covers all patients, not only those who ask.
Nurses teach only patients who meet a minimum literacy level
Literacy level does not limit the nurse’s responsibility to teach.
Nurses teach only when the health care provider orders it
Patient education is a nursing responsibility, not dependent on an order.

items.q: What is the purpose of the American Hospital Association’s document The Patient Care Partnership?
items.a: To outline patients’ rights and responsibilities and what to expect during a hospital stay
items.ex: The Patient Care Partnership explains patient rights and responsibilities, including participation in informed decisions about care.
w: To set legal staffing ratios for nurses on hospital units
Staffing ratios are not the subject of this document.
To describe the steps nurses follow when writing teaching plans
It addresses patient rights, not how nurses write teaching plans.
To list the fees that hospitals may charge for patient education
Fees are not the focus; Medicare standards address being informed of fees in nursing centers.

alt.q: According to The Patient Care Partnership, information that patients need to make informed decisions must have which qualities?
alt.a: Accurate, complete, and relevant to the patient’s needs, language, and health literacy
alt.ex: Information for informed decisions must be accurate, complete, and relevant to the patient’s needs, language, and health literacy.
w: Brief, technical, and identical for every patient on the unit
Identical technical information ignores language and health literacy.
Written only in English to keep the medical record consistent
Patients have the right to information that fits their language.
Limited to facts the health care provider believes are essential
The information must be complete and relevant to the patient’s needs.

items.q: A hospitalized patient says, “I don’t want to bother the nurses by asking about this new pill.” Which response by the nurse reflects The Joint Commission’s Speak Up guidance?
items.a: “Please ask about anything you don’t understand, and ask again if it still isn’t clear.”
items.ex: Speak Up encourages patients to voice questions or concerns and to ask again if they still do not understand.
w: “The nurses check everything, so you do not need to ask about your medicines.”
Speak Up tells patients to pay attention to their care and not assume anything.
“It is best to save your questions for the health care provider’s visit.”
Patients are encouraged to ask questions whenever concerns arise.
“Your family can ask the questions for you after you go home.”
An advocate can help, but the patient is encouraged to speak up and participate now.

alt.q: What is the main purpose of The Joint Commission’s Speak Up campaigns?
alt.a: To help patients understand their rights and become active participants in their care by asking questions
alt.ex: Speak Up makes patients more aware of their rights and more involved, increasing the chance they get needed care on time.
w: To teach nurses how to document patient complaints for accreditation surveys
Speak Up is aimed at patients, not at nurse documentation.
To train patients to perform their own treatments while in the hospital
The campaign promotes participation and questions, not self-performed treatments.
To reduce the number of questions patients ask hospital staff
Speak Up encourages patients to ask more questions, not fewer.

items.q: According to the Speak Up guidance, why should patients learn about their new medicines and why they take them?
items.a: Medication errors are the most common health care mistakes
items.ex: Speak Up advises patients to know their medicines because medication errors are the most common health care mistakes.
w: Patient falls are the most common health care mistakes
The guidance names medication errors, not falls, as the most common mistakes.
Wrong-site surgery is the most common health care mistake
Speak Up identifies medication errors as most common.
Health care–associated infections are the most common health care mistakes
The guidance links knowing medicines to medication errors being most common.

alt.q: After teaching based on Speak Up guidance, which statement by a patient shows understanding?
alt.a: “I will learn what each new medicine is for and why I take it.”
alt.ex: Knowing new medicines and their purpose helps patients catch errors, since medication errors are the most common mistakes.
w: “I will trust the staff to give the right medicines without asking.”
Speak Up tells patients not to assume anything and to pay attention to their care.
“I will avoid asking about tests so the staff are not interrupted.”
Patients are encouraged to learn about tests and treatment to make informed decisions.
“I will let the health care team make my care decisions for me.”
Patients are told to participate in all decisions; they are the center of the team.

items.q: A nurse has finished teaching a patient with heart failure about new medications. Which action best evaluates the patient’s understanding?
items.a: Ask the patient to explain in their own words when to take each medication and its side effects
items.ex: Teach-back asks patients to explain information in their own words, the standard approach for evaluating understanding.
w: Ask the patient, “Do you understand everything I just told you?”
A yes-or-no question does not reveal what the patient actually understands.
Have the patient sign a form stating teaching was received
A signature documents teaching, not the patient’s understanding.
Ask the patient’s spouse whether the explanation made sense
Understanding is checked with the learner, in the learner’s own words.

alt.q: Which nurse statement is an appropriate teach-back question?
alt.a: “To be sure I explained clearly, can you tell me in your own words the benefits and risks of your treatment?”
alt.ex: Teach-back questions ask patients to restate information in their own words, and the nurse takes responsibility for clarity.
w: “You understand the risks and benefits of your treatment now, right?”
A leading yes-or-no question does not let the patient show understanding.
“Do you have any questions about your treatment before I leave the room?”
Asking for questions does not check what the patient understood.
“Would you like me to read the treatment information to you once more?”
Rereading information does not evaluate the patient’s understanding.

items.q: During teach-back, a patient incorrectly describes when to take a new medication. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “I must not have done a good job explaining. Let me try again.”
items.ex: When teach-back shows misunderstanding, the nurse takes responsibility for the explanation and reteaches in another way.
w: “You need to listen more carefully this time.”
Blaming the patient discourages learning; the nurse owns the explanation.
“That’s close enough; the label on the bottle will remind you.”
Accepting a misunderstanding about medications is unsafe; reteaching is needed.
“I’ll explain it to your daughter so she can remind you.”
Teaching the family does not address the patient’s misunderstanding.

alt.q: A patient’s teach-back shows confusion about how to use a new inhaler. What should the nurse do next?
alt.a: Present the information another way, such as with different words, pictures, or a model
alt.ex: After misunderstanding, the nurse provides information in another way and then asks the patient to explain again.
w: Repeat the same explanation slowly, using exactly the same words as before
Repeating the same explanation may not fix the misunderstanding; use a different approach.
Document that the patient refused the teaching and notify the provider
The patient did not refuse; the nurse needs to reteach.
Move on to the next topic and return to this one at a later session
Moving on leaves an unsafe gap; reteach and check understanding now.

items.q: In the teaching process, what role do learning objectives play?
items.a: They describe the behaviors the learner will show after successful instruction
items.ex: Learning objectives describe the learner’s expected behaviors after instruction and serve the same role as outcomes in nursing care.
w: They list the teaching materials the nurse will use
Materials are teaching resources; objectives describe learner behaviors.
They record how long each teaching session lasts
Session length is not what objectives describe.
They describe the nurse’s actions during the teaching session
Objectives describe what the learner will do, not the nurse’s actions.

alt.q: In the comparison of teaching to communication, which statement is accurate?
alt.a: The nurse is the sender, the patient is the receiver, and learning objectives act like outcomes
alt.ex: The nurse conveys the message to the patient, and objectives serve the same role as outcomes in nursing care.
w: The patient is the sender and the nurse is the receiver of the teaching message
In patient education the nurse sends the message and the patient receives it.
Feedback is unnecessary because teaching flows in one direction only
Feedback between sender and receiver is essential in teaching.
Learning objectives are written after teaching to explain what happened
Objectives are identified before instruction to describe expected learner behaviors.

items.q: A patient correctly performs a return demonstration of an insulin injection after teaching. What should the nurse do next?
items.a: Provide reinforcement
items.ex: When feedback shows learning occurred, the nurse provides reinforcement, which supports continued self-management.
w: Repeat the entire demonstration again
Repeating the demonstration is needed when learning was not successful.
Change to a different teaching approach
The approach is adapted only when feedback shows learning was unsuccessful.
End the session without commenting on performance
The nurse gives feedback that affirms success in meeting the objectives.

alt.q: A patient’s return demonstration of a dressing change shows several errors. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Adapt the approach and provide further instruction
alt.ex: If feedback does not show learning, the nurse adapts the teaching approach and gives further instruction.
w: Provide reinforcement for completing the demonstration
Reinforcement is given when feedback shows learning; this feedback does not.
Document that the teaching objectives were met
The objectives were not met when the demonstration contains errors.
Ask the patient to keep practicing alone at home
Unsupervised practice does not correct errors; the nurse needs to reteach.

items.q: Which rights do patients have according to The Joint Commission’s guidance? Select all that apply.
o: Obtaining information about care in their preferred language
Patients have a right to information in their preferred language.
Knowing the names of their caregivers
Patients are advised they have the right to know caregivers’ names.
Receiving treatment for pain
Treatment for pain is listed among patient rights.
Receiving an up-to-date list of current medications
Patients have the right to an up-to-date list of current medications.
Choosing which nurse is assigned to them each shift
Selecting nurse assignments is not a right listed in the guidance.
items.ex: Patients have the right to be informed in their language, know caregivers, receive pain treatment and medication lists, and be respected.

alt.q: Medicare standards protect residents’ rights in nursing centers. Which rights are included? Select all that apply.
o: Being informed about their health status and medical condition
Residents have the right to be informed about health status and medical condition.
Being informed about their medications
Information about medications is part of the right to proper medical care.
Being informed about services and fees
Residents have the right to be informed about services and fees.
Being guaranteed a private room at no extra charge
A free private room is not among the rights described.
Choosing which staff members work in the center
Staffing choices are not a resident right described in the text.
alt.ex: Medicare standards include the right to proper care, with information about health status, condition, medications, services, and fees.

items.q: Which patient factors influence the ability to receive and understand a teaching message? Select all that apply.
o: Anxiety
Anxiety is listed as influencing the ability to receive and understand a message.
Physical symptoms
Physical symptoms can interfere with receiving and understanding teaching.
Health literacy
Health literacy affects the ability to understand health information.
Values
A patient’s values influence how a message is received and understood.
The nurse’s years of clinical experience
This is not a patient factor; the list concerns the learner’s own variables.
The type of health insurance the patient has
Insurance type is not among the factors the book lists.
items.ex: Attitudes, anxiety, physical symptoms, education, health literacy, and values affect a patient’s ability to receive and understand a message.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing whether a patient is able to learn about a new diagnosis. Which factors affect the patient’s ability to learn? Select all that apply.
o: Emotional and physical health
The ability to learn depends on emotional and physical health.
Stage of development
Developmental stage influences the ability to learn.
Cultural perspective
Cultural perspective is listed as affecting the ability to learn.
Previous knowledge
What the patient already knows affects new learning.
The size of the patient’s hospital room
Room size is not a factor the book lists for the ability to learn.
alt.ex: The ability to learn depends on emotional and physical health, education, culture, values, developmental stage, and previous knowledge.

items.q: In which teaching situations does the book recommend using the teach-back method? Select all that apply.
o: Providing information about medications
Teach-back is recommended when teaching about medications.
Teaching how to use a new medical device
Teach-back is recommended for using a new medical device.
Explaining the next steps in the patient’s care
Teach-back is recommended when explaining next steps in care.
Teaching only patients with documented low health literacy
Teach-back supports patients at all degrees of health literacy.
Teaching only after a patient has been readmitted
Teach-back is used before discharge to help prevent readmissions.
items.ex: Teach-back is recommended for complex chronic illness teaching, especially medications, home care, new devices, and next steps in care.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with a complex chronic illness. Which teaching topics call for teach-back? Select all that apply.
o: Home care instructions
Teach-back is recommended for home care instructions.
The patient’s medication schedule and side effects
Medication teaching is a key use of teach-back.
Use of a new home glucose meter
Teach-back is recommended when teaching use of a new medical device.
Routine greetings when the nurse enters the room
Greetings are not teaching content that needs evaluation.
Small talk about the patient’s plans for the weekend
Casual conversation is not teaching content that needs evaluation.
alt.ex: Teach-back fits complex chronic illness teaching, such as medications, home care, new devices, and next steps in care.

items.q: According to the book, teaching cannot be separated from learning.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states that it is impossible to separate teaching from learning; teaching aims at producing learning.
items.ww: Teaching exists to produce learning, so the two are treated as inseparable.

alt.q: Teaching is complete once the nurse has delivered the content, whether or not the patient learned it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Teaching and learning are inseparable; the nurse evaluates learning and adapts instruction when learning has not occurred.
alt.ww: Delivery alone is not enough; feedback must show learning, or the nurse reteaches.

items.q: Learning can change a person’s thoughts, feelings, or attitudes, not only knowledge and skills.
items.a: True
items.ex: Learning can alter thoughts, feelings, or attitudes, and changes behavior, skill, emotional functioning, or mental processing.
items.ww: The definition of learning includes changes in attitudes and emotional functioning, not just knowledge.

alt.q: Learning refers only to gaining new facts; a change in attitude is not considered learning.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Learning includes changes in thoughts, feelings, and attitudes as well as knowledge and skills.
alt.ww: The book’s definition of learning explicitly includes emotional functioning and attitudes.

items.q: The nurse gives feedback to the learner only at the end of a teaching session.
items.a: False
items.ex: Feedback is provided both during and at the completion of each instructional encounter.
items.ww: Waiting until the end misses chances to correct and reinforce during instruction.

alt.q: The nurse provides feedback both during and at the completion of each teaching encounter.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Ongoing feedback affirms progress toward objectives and shows whether instruction needs to change.
alt.ww: Feedback limited to the end would miss errors and reinforcement during teaching.

items.q: Using [[five|5]] or more teach-back questions after patient education is more effective in identifying misunderstanding.

alt.ex: Several teach-back questions more accurately reveal what the patient misunderstands and what further education is needed.

ord.q: Put the steps of using the teach-back method in order.
items: Teach the patient the needed information
Ask the patient to explain the information in their own words
If the patient misunderstands, say you may not have explained it well
Present the information another way, using different words, pictures, or a model
Ask the patient again to explain it in their own words
ord.ex: Teach-back checks understanding in the patient’s words, then the nurse reteaches differently and rechecks when misunderstanding appears.

items.q: A patient with a new colostomy is learning to accept the change in body image. Which domain of learning does this involve?
items.a: Affective
items.ex: Learning coping skills to accept a changed body image involves attitudes and feelings, the affective domain.
w: Cognitive
The cognitive domain covers understanding, such as how diet affects the ostomy.
Psychomotor
The psychomotor domain covers skills, such as changing the pouch.
Perceptual
Perception is a level within the psychomotor domain, not one of the three domains.

alt.q: A patient with a new ostomy learns how diet, medications, and activity affect the ostomy. Which domain of learning does this involve?
alt.a: Cognitive
alt.ex: Gaining understanding of how diet, medications, and activity affect the ostomy is cognitive learning.
w: Affective
The affective domain involves attitudes, such as accepting the body image change.
Psychomotor
Psychomotor learning involves skills such as changing the pouch and skin care.
Characterizing
Characterizing is the highest affective behavior, not a domain of learning.

items.q: According to the book, when does the most effective learning take place?
items.a: When all three domains of learning are used
items.ex: The most effective learning occurs when cognitive, affective, and psychomotor domains are all used.
w: When teaching focuses on the cognitive domain alone
Using only one domain is less effective than merging all three.
When the psychomotor domain is mastered before others
The book does not require one domain to come first; it emphasizes using all three.
When the affective domain is left until after discharge
Delaying affective learning ignores a domain the patient needs now.

alt.q: While changing a patient’s ostomy pouch, the nurse explains each step and also asks how the patient feels about the ostomy. What does this approach demonstrate?
alt.a: Merging learning domains during instruction
alt.ex: Explaining steps while exploring feelings combines cognitive, psychomotor, and affective learning, which makes learning most effective.
w: Focusing teaching on the psychomotor domain only
The nurse also explains and explores feelings, which goes beyond psychomotor learning.
Delaying affective learning until skills are mastered
Exploring feelings during the skill addresses affective learning now.
Using a lecture to control the teaching session
Lecture is a formal cognitive method; this approach merges domains.

items.q: A nurse is teaching a parent to give a child subcutaneous injections at home. Which teaching method fits this learning best?
items.a: Demonstration followed by return demonstration
items.ex: Psychomotor skills are taught by demonstration, practice, and return demonstration, which lets the nurse observe the patient perform the skill.
w: Lecture with written handouts
Lecture is a cognitive method; it does not let the parent perform the skill.
Group discussion about feelings
Group discussion supports affective learning, not motor skill performance.
Question-and-answer session
Question-and-answer sessions address concerns and apply knowledge, not motor skills.

alt.q: Which teaching method is the best way to determine whether a patient can correctly perform a skill?
alt.a: Return demonstration
alt.ex: Return demonstration lets the patient perform the skill as the nurse observes and gives excellent feedback and reinforcement.
w: Lecture
Lecture is educator controlled and builds knowledge, not skill performance.
Role-play
Role-play applies knowledge or expresses feelings, not observed skill performance.
One-on-one discussion
Discussion allows sensitive topics to be explored but does not show skill performance.

items.q: A patient newly diagnosed with breast cancer wants to talk privately about fears related to body image. Which teaching method is most appropriate?
items.a: One-on-one discussion
items.ex: One-on-one discussion allows patients to discuss personal, sensitive topics of interest or concern in the affective domain.
w: Group discussion
Group discussion offers peer support but is not private for sensitive personal topics.
Lecture
Lecture is educator controlled and builds knowledge rather than exploring feelings.
Return demonstration
Return demonstration evaluates psychomotor skills, not feelings.

alt.q: A patient adjusting to a new diagnosis of diabetes would benefit from hearing how others have coped. Which teaching method best meets this need?
alt.a: Group discussion
alt.ex: Group discussion lets patients receive support from others and learn from others’ experiences in the affective domain.
w: Lecture
Lecture is educator controlled and does not offer peer experiences or support.
Demonstration
Demonstration presents skills, not others’ experiences of coping.
Independent computer-assisted project
Independent projects are self-paced and do not provide group support.

items.q: Which teaching method is more formal because it is controlled by the educator?
items.a: Lecture
items.ex: Lecture is a formal, educator-controlled cognitive method that helps learners acquire new knowledge and comprehension.
w: Group discussion
Discussion promotes active participation and peer support rather than educator control.
Role-play
Role-play lets the patient actively apply knowledge in a controlled situation.
Independent project
Independent projects let the patient take responsibility and work at their own pace.

alt.q: Which cognitive teaching method allows a patient to take responsibility for completing learning activities at their own pace?
alt.a: Independent project such as computer-assisted instruction
alt.ex: Independent projects let patients work at their own pace and promote analysis, synthesis, and evaluation of information.
w: Lecture given to a group of patients
Lecture is educator controlled, so the pace is set by the educator.
Demonstration of a procedure by the nurse
Demonstration is a psychomotor method led by the nurse.
Question-and-answer session with the nurse
Question-and-answer sessions address specific concerns rather than self-paced work.

items.q: In Bloom’s revised taxonomy, which cognitive behavior is the simplest, and which is the most complex?
items.a: Remembering is simplest; creating is most complex
items.ex: Bloom’s revised taxonomy rises from remembering through understanding, applying, analyzing, and evaluating to creating.
w: Understanding is simplest; evaluating is most complex
Remembering comes before understanding, and creating is above evaluating.
Remembering is simplest; evaluating is most complex
In the revised taxonomy, creating is the highest level, above evaluating.
Applying is simplest; analyzing is most complex
Applying and analyzing are middle levels of the hierarchy.

alt.q: Why must a learner master remembering before mastering understanding in Bloom’s revised taxonomy?
alt.a: Each simpler skill is a prerequisite to mastering the next more complex one
alt.ex: The taxonomy is a hierarchy of increasing complexity in which each simpler skill must be mastered before the next.
w: Each level is learned separately and in any order
The levels build on one another in a set order of complexity.
Remembering is the most complex skill in the hierarchy
Remembering is the simplest level; creating is the most complex.
Understanding requires psychomotor skill to be mastered first
The prerequisite is the lower cognitive level, not a psychomotor skill.

items.q: A patient with diabetes uses what was learned to design a new weekly meal plan that fits the patient’s work schedule and dietary restrictions. Which cognitive behavior does this show?
items.a: Creating
items.ex: Creating means putting elements together into a coherent whole or new pattern through generating, planning, or producing.
w: Remembering
Remembering is recalling knowledge from memory, not producing a new plan.
Applying
Applying is carrying out a known procedure, not generating a new structure.
Understanding
Understanding is constructing meaning, such as explaining or summarizing information.

alt.q: A patient reviews a week of blood glucose readings and judges whether they meet the targets the health care provider set. Which cognitive behavior does this show?
alt.a: Evaluating
alt.ex: Evaluating means making judgments based on criteria and standards through checking and critiquing.
w: Remembering
Remembering is recognizing or recalling knowledge, not judging against criteria.
Creating
Creating means producing a new whole or pattern, not judging against standards.
Applying
Applying is executing a procedure, not judging results against criteria.

items.q: A patient with diabetes states, “Checking my feet every day is important to me now, and I’m committed to doing it.” Which affective learning behavior does this show?
items.a: Valuing
items.ex: Valuing is attaching worth to acquired knowledge, shown through acceptance, preference, or commitment.
w: Receiving
Receiving is passive willingness to receive information without active engagement.
Responding
Responding is active attention and motivation to learn, not commitment to a value.
Characterizing
Characterizing is acting consistently from a fully internalized value system, the highest level.

alt.q: During a teaching session, a patient asks questions, nods, and says, “I want to learn how to do this.” Which affective learning behavior does this show?
alt.a: Responding
alt.ex: Responding requires active participation, with verbal and nonverbal responses to stimuli and motivation to learn.
w: Receiving
Receiving is alert and willing but passive, without active participation.
Valuing
Valuing shows commitment or preference for the knowledge, beyond active participation.
Organizing
Organizing is developing a value system, not participating in a session.

items.q: In the psychomotor domain, which behavior is the simplest, and which is the most complex?
items.a: Fundamental is simplest; origination is most complex
items.ex: Psychomotor behaviors range from fundamental movements up to origination, which creates new movement patterns.
w: Perception is simplest; adaptation is most complex
Perception follows fundamental, and origination is above adaptation.
Guided response is simplest; mechanism is most complex
Guided response and mechanism are middle levels.
Fundamental is simplest; complex overt response is most complex
Adaptation and origination rank above complex overt response.

alt.q: A patient who performs wound care well modifies the technique when a dressing unexpectedly sticks to the wound. Which psychomotor behavior does this show?
alt.a: Adaptation
alt.ex: Adaptation means motor skills are well developed and movements can be modified when unexpected problems occur.
w: Guided response
Guided response is early learning through imitation and practice under guidance.
Mechanism
Mechanism is gaining confidence and proficiency, not modifying for unexpected problems.
Perception
Perception is taking in sensory information and reacting, not modifying a mastered skill.

items.q: A nurse is about to teach a patient how to use a walker. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess whether the patient can walk independently or bear weight
items.ex: Before teaching, the nurse assesses the patient’s current level, starting with fundamental skills such as walking and bearing weight.
w: Have the patient walk the hallway alone with the walker
Independent use comes later, after guided response and growing confidence.
Demonstrate how to adapt the walker for stairs and curbs
Adapting the skill is an advanced level; assess fundamental skills first.
Give the patient written instructions on walker use to read
Written material does not establish the patient’s current psychomotor level.

alt.q: A patient is using a walker while the nurse provides assistance and guidance. Which psychomotor behavior is the patient showing?
alt.a: Guided response
alt.ex: Guided response is the early stage of learning a skill under an instructor’s guidance through imitation and practice.
w: Mechanism
Mechanism shows confidence and proficiency, which comes after guided use.
Fundamental
Fundamental skills are basic movements such as walking and bearing weight, assessed before walker teaching.
Origination
Origination is creating new movement patterns, the most complex level.

items.q: A nurse is teaching a patient to perform a psychomotor skill. Which teaching methods are appropriate for this domain? Select all that apply.
o: Demonstration
Demonstration presents the skill and lets the patient model the nurse’s behavior.
Practice
Practice lets the patient perform skills with equipment in a controlled setting with repetition.
Return demonstration
Return demonstration lets the nurse observe the patient performing the skill.
Independent projects or games
These promote adaptation and origination and let the learner use new skills.
Lecture
Lecture is a cognitive method for acquiring knowledge, not motor skills.
Group discussion
Group discussion supports cognitive and affective learning, not skill performance.
items.ex: Psychomotor methods are demonstration, practice, return demonstration, and independent projects or games.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a parent how to use a nebulizer for a child at home. Which methods match this type of learning? Select all that apply.
o: Demonstrating the nebulizer setup while the parent watches
Demonstration lets the parent model the nurse’s behavior.
Letting the parent practice with the equipment in a controlled setting
Practice gives repetition with the equipment.
Watching the parent set up the nebulizer alone
Return demonstration shows whether the parent can perform the skill correctly.
Giving a lecture on how the medication works in the lungs
Lecture builds knowledge, not the motor skill of using the device.
Holding a one-on-one discussion of the parent’s feelings
One-on-one discussion is an affective method, not a skill method.
alt.ex: Using a nebulizer is a psychomotor skill learned through demonstration, practice, and return demonstration.

items.q: Which teaching methods are listed for the affective domain of learning? Select all that apply.
o: Role-play

Group discussion
Group discussion offers support and learning from others’ experiences.
One-on-one discussion
One-on-one discussion allows personal, sensitive topics to be explored.

Return demonstration is a psychomotor method for evaluating skills.
Lecture

items.ex: Affective methods, role-play and group or one-on-one discussion, let patients express and examine values, feelings, and attitudes.

alt.q: A patient is struggling to accept a new diagnosis of a chronic illness. Which teaching methods would best support this patient’s affective learning? Select all that apply.

A support group discussion with other patients
Group discussion offers support and learning from others’ experiences.
A private one-on-one discussion with the nurse

Lecture builds cognitive knowledge rather than addressing attitudes.
Practice with equipment in a skills lab
Practice is a psychomotor method.
alt.ex: Coping and acceptance are affective learning, supported by role-play and group or one-on-one discussion.

items.q: A patient had surgery for colon cancer and has a new ostomy. Which learning needs belong to the cognitive domain? Select all that apply.
o: How diet affects the ostomy
Understanding the effect of diet is cognitive learning.
How medications affect the ostomy
Understanding medication effects is cognitive learning.
How activity affects the ostomy
Understanding the effect of activity is cognitive learning.
Changing the ostomy pouch
Changing the pouch is a psychomotor skill.
Coping with the change in body image
Accepting body image change is affective learning.
items.ex: Understanding how diet, medications, and activity affect the ostomy is cognitive; pouch changes are psychomotor and coping is affective.

alt.q: The same patient with a new ostomy has several learning needs. Which needs belong to the psychomotor domain? Select all that apply.
o: Changing the ostomy pouch
Changing the pouch is a manual skill in the psychomotor domain.

Skin care is a physical skill in the psychomotor domain.
Understanding how diet affects the ostomy

Accepting the change in body image
Accepting body image change is affective learning.
Understanding how medications affect output
This is cognitive learning about understanding.
alt.ex: Pouch changes and skin care are psychomotor skills; understanding effects is cognitive and accepting body image is affective.

items.q: In Bloom’s revised taxonomy, each simpler cognitive skill is a prerequisite to mastering the next more complex skill.
items.a: True
items.ex: The taxonomy is a hierarchy of increasing complexity that builds higher-order thinking on lower-level skills.
items.ww: The levels are not independent; mastery of each lower level is needed before the next.

alt.q: The levels of Bloom’s revised taxonomy are independent, so a learner can master creating before remembering.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Each simpler skill is a prerequisite for the next, so remembering must be mastered before higher levels.
alt.ww: The hierarchy requires mastering lower levels such as remembering before more complex ones.

items.q: Values clarification is an example of affective learning.

alt.a: False
