items.q: Which statement best describes the purpose of motivational interviewing (MI) in patient education?
items.a: It helps patients resolve ambivalence and find their own internal motivation to change.
items.ex: MI is person centered; the motivation for change must come from the patient, with the clinician acting as a guide.
w: It gives patients a complete plan the nurse has designed to solve their problem.
The objective of MI is not to solve the patient’s problem or to develop a plan for the patient.
It persuades patients to accept what the provider believes they need to learn.
Teaching that does not match the patient’s own goals or values is often ineffective; MI evokes the patient’s goals.
It tests patients on their knowledge of their disease before discharge.
MI is a counseling technique that evokes conversation about change, not a knowledge test.

alt.q: A nurse uses motivational interviewing with a patient who is unsure about starting an exercise program. Which nurse behavior is consistent with MI?
alt.a: Listening to the patient’s concerns and boosting confidence in the ability to change
alt.ex: In MI the clinician guides by clarifying strengths and aspirations, listening to concerns, and boosting confidence before collaborating on a plan.
w: Telling the patient the exercise plan the nurse has chosen for the patient
MI encourages patient autonomy in decision making rather than nurse-chosen plans.
Warning the patient firmly about complications of remaining inactive
MI relies on the patient’s own motivation, not on the clinician’s pressure or warnings.
Postponing all discussion until the patient states a firm commitment
MI works well with patients who start off unmotivated; the interviewer evokes the conversation about change.

items.q: Which patient is likely to have the strongest motivation to learn?
items.a: A patient who needs the information to survive a newly diagnosed illness
items.ex: Patients who need knowledge for survival have a stronger motivation to learn than those who need it for health promotion.
w: A healthy patient who is offered general information on wellness
Knowledge needed only to promote health produces weaker motivation than knowledge needed for survival.
A patient who does not see a disease as a personal threat
Many people do not change behaviors unless they perceive a disease as a threat.
A patient who doubts that the prescribed therapy will help
Therapy is more effective when the person believes it will improve health.

alt.q: According to the textbook, which belief most strengthens a patient’s motivation to adopt a new health behavior?
alt.a: Believing that health is important and the therapy will improve it
alt.ex: A person’s therapy is more effective when the person believes health is important and that the therapy will improve health.
w: Believing that the disease poses little personal threat
People usually do not change behavior unless they perceive the disease as a threat.
Believing that the barriers to change are too great
Patients must overcome barriers to change health practices before adopting new behaviors.
Believing that the benefits of the change are uncertain
Patients need to see the benefits of a healthy behavior before they adopt it.

items.q: A patient newly diagnosed with cancer says, “I’m fine; nothing is wrong with me,” and refuses to look at the teaching booklet. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Remain available, and explain each procedure in the present tense as it is done.
items.ex: In denial the patient is not prepared to deal with the problem, so the nurse offers support and explains current care in the present tense.
w: Explain the long-term effects of the diagnosis so the patient accepts reality.
Trying to convince a patient in denial about the illness results in further anger or withdrawal.
Insist that the patient read the booklet before the next treatment.
Forcing information during denial causes withdrawal; give only information the patient pursues or requires.
Begin teaching the future self-care skills needed after discharge.
Teaching future skills fits the acceptance stage, when the patient is more easily motivated to learn.

alt.q: A patient with a new diagnosis of chronic heart failure begins to ask questions and says, “I guess things have really changed for me.” Which nursing action is most appropriate at this stage?
alt.a: Find out what the patient wants to learn and set times for discussion.
alt.ex: In resolution the patient perceives a need for help and is ready to be responsible for learning, so formal teaching begins.
w: Provide only the information the patient absolutely requires.
Limiting information to what is absolutely required fits the denial stage, not resolution.
Avoid arguing and reassure the family that the anger is normal.
Not arguing and reassuring the family describes the anger stage.
Introduce only reality and teach in the present tense.
Introducing only reality with present-tense teaching fits the bargaining stage.

items.q: A nurse plans to teach a postoperative patient how to splint the incision. The patient rates incisional pain as 7 on a 0-to-10 scale. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Give the prescribed analgesic and begin teaching about 30 minutes later.
items.ex: Physical discomfort impairs attention; providing an analgesic 30 minutes before a session enhances the attention of a patient in pain.
w: Start the session now so the patient learns a way to reduce pain.
A patient in significant pain cannot focus; comfort must be addressed before teaching begins.
Give the patient a pamphlet to read while the pain subsides.
Pain interferes with concentration whether teaching is verbal or written.
Teach the family caregiver instead and skip teaching the patient.
A caregiver may receive teaching when a patient cannot attend, but this pain can be relieved first.

alt.q: A patient with a new patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) pump is in moderate pain. Which teaching topic is the patient most receptive to at this time?
alt.a: How to use the patient-controlled analgesia pump
alt.ex: A patient in pain is receptive to simple, immediately useful facts, such as PCA use, but not to unrelated skills.
w: How to walk with crutches at home
The book states a patient in pain is not receptive to learning crutch walking.
How to plan meals for the coming weeks
Long-term topics are not a priority when discomfort limits the ability to attend.
How to perform postoperative home exercises
Detailed skill teaching is not appropriate while pain limits attention.

items.q: A patient spent the entire morning undergoing rigorous diagnostic studies. The nurse planned to teach a new home medication schedule that afternoon. Which action is best?
items.a: Postpone the teaching until the patient is rested and able to participate.
items.ex: Fatigue depletes energy and impairs learning; a patient who has had rigorous studies all morning is unlikely to learn that day.
w: Teach the full schedule now because discharge may be soon.
Teaching a fatigued patient is ineffective; energy-depleting conditions impair the ability to learn.
Shorten the content and teach only during the evening meal.
Mealtime does not resolve fatigue and adds distraction to the session.
Teach now and plan to repeat the content at a later visit.
Teaching while the patient is exhausted wastes the session; better outcomes come when patients can participate.

alt.q: During a teaching session, a patient’s answers become brief and the patient stops asking questions or initiating activity. Which action should the nurse take?
alt.a: Temporarily stop teaching and allow the patient to rest.
alt.ex: Willingness to communicate, activity initiated, and responses to questions reflect energy level; stop teaching temporarily if the patient needs rest.
w: Speed up the session so all content is covered quickly.
Rushing content to a tired patient does not produce learning.
Switch to a written handout for the patient to study now.
A fatigued patient cannot attend to written material either.
Continue because short answers show the patient understands.
Decreased communication and activity indicate low energy, not understanding.

items.q: How does a patient’s level of anxiety affect learning?
items.a: Mild anxiety can help learning, but high anxiety prevents it.
items.ex: As anxiety increases, attention often decreases; a mild level can be conducive to learning, while a high level prevents learning.
w: Any level of anxiety prevents learning from occurring.
The book states a mild level of anxiety can be conducive to learning.
High anxiety improves attention and speeds learning.
High anxiety prevents learning because attention decreases as anxiety rises.
Anxiety has little effect when information is written.
Anxiety reduces the ability to concentrate regardless of the teaching method.

alt.q: A patient scheduled for a procedure is mildly anxious and asking many questions. How should the nurse interpret this level of anxiety in relation to teaching?
alt.a: It is a level that can be conducive to learning.
alt.ex: Mild anxiety can be conducive to learning; only high anxiety prevents learning from occurring.
w: It is a level that prevents any learning.
High, not mild, anxiety prevents learning.
It requires teaching to be delayed until tomorrow.
Mild anxiety does not require postponing teaching.
It means only the family should be taught.
A family caregiver is taught when the patient cannot attend, which is not the case here.

items.q: A nurse is preparing a toddler for an examination. Which teaching method is most appropriate for this developmental stage?
items.a: Let the child apply a bandage to a doll and handle the equipment.
items.ex: Box 25.3 recommends play, such as handling equipment or bandaging a doll, plus simple words to teach toddlers.
w: Explain the anatomy involved using correct medical terms.
Toddlers need simple words such as “cut” instead of “laceration.”
Use problem solving to let the child choose among options.
Problem solving to make choices is recommended for adolescents.
Teach the psychomotor skills needed to maintain health.
Teaching health-maintenance psychomotor skills fits school-age children.

alt.q: Which teaching method from Box 25.3 is recommended for adolescents?
alt.a: Use teaching as a collaborative activity and allow health decisions.
alt.ex: Adolescents benefit from collaborative teaching, problem solving, and making decisions about health and health promotion.
w: Use role-play, imitation, and play to make learning fun.
Role-play, imitation, and play are recommended for preschoolers.
Offer picture books about children in the hospital.
Picture books about hospitalized children are recommended for toddlers.
Keep routines such as feeding and bathing consistent.
Consistent routines are a method for infants.

items.q: A nurse instructs an adult to avoid lifting more than 10 pounds for 6 weeks after surgery. Which action best applies adult learning principles?
items.a: Ask which daily activities might conflict with the restriction and plan around them.
items.ex: Adults learn best when information is personally relevant; learn which normal activities conflict with restrictions and find ways to help adherence.
w: Give a detailed lecture on wound healing before discussing the restriction.
Adults learn best by applying knowledge to real-life problems, not from background lectures.
Tell the patient the restriction firmly and avoid discussing exceptions.
Adults need help resolving needs they perceive as important; mutual objectives improve outcomes.
Provide the same handout given to every surgical patient on the unit.
Generic teaching ignores the adult’s personal situation and previous experience.

alt.q: Which approach is most effective for teaching an adult learner?
alt.a: Setting mutual objectives that relate to the patient’s daily life
alt.ex: Assessing what the adult knows and wants to know and setting mutual objectives improves patient education outcomes.
w: Setting objectives for the patient based only on the protocol
Adults are self-directed and do best with mutual learning objectives.
Presenting theory first and real-life application later
Adults do best when applying new knowledge to solve real-life problems.
Avoiding reference to the patient’s past experiences
Adult learners do best when asked to use their previous experiences.

items.q: Which statement best describes self-efficacy?
items.a: A person’s perceived ability to successfully complete a task
items.ex: Self-efficacy, a concept in social learning theory, is a person’s perceived ability to successfully complete a task.
w: A person’s mental state that allows focus on a learning activity
This describes an attentional set, not self-efficacy.
A person’s willingness to engage in a learning activity
Willingness to engage in learning describes readiness to learn.
A person’s ability to read and understand health information
This describes part of health literacy, not self-efficacy.

alt.q: A patient says, “I know I can learn to give my own insulin; I’ve mastered harder things.” Which concept does this statement reflect?
alt.a: Self-efficacy
alt.ex: Believing one can achieve a behavior reflects self-efficacy, which makes consistent and correct performance more likely.
w: Attentional set
An attentional set is the mental state that allows focus on a learning activity.
Cognitive dissonance
Cognitive dissonance is mental discomfort from conflicting attitudes, beliefs, or behaviors.
Negative reinforcement
Negative reinforcement is a stimulus such as criticism used to decrease an undesired response.

items.q: A patient recovering from a stroke tells the nurse, “Now that I’ve accepted what happened, I want to learn everything I need to manage at home.” Which stage of adaptation does this reflect?
items.a: Acceptance
items.ex: In acceptance the patient recognizes reality, actively pursues information, and strives for independence, so teaching focuses on future skills.
w: Bargaining
In bargaining the patient offers to live a better life in exchange for better health.
Anger
In anger the patient blames and directs anger toward the nurse or others.
Denial
In denial the patient avoids discussion of the illness and disregards restrictions.

alt.q: A patient in the acceptance stage of adaptation to a new chronic illness is preparing for discharge. Which teaching focus is most appropriate?
alt.a: Future skills and knowledge, with the family involved in discharge teaching
alt.ex: Acceptance reflects willingness to deal with the illness, so focus on future skills and involve family or significant others.
w: Only present-tense explanations of procedures being done now
Present-tense teaching only is used in denial, anger, and bargaining.
Only the information the patient absolutely requires today
Limiting to absolutely required information fits denial.
Reassurance to the family that the patient’s anger is normal
Reassuring the family about anger fits the anger stage.

items.q: Which physical characteristics does a patient need to learn psychomotor skills? Select all that apply.
o: Size that matches the task or equipment
The patient’s height and weight should match the task or equipment used.
Strength for the activity required
Strength, such as the ability to follow an exercise program, is required.
Coordination for complicated motor skills
Dexterity is needed for skills such as changing a bandage.
Sensory acuity to receive the messages taught
Visual, auditory, tactile, and other senses are needed to receive and respond to teaching.
A high school reading level
Reading level affects written learning but is not one of the physical characteristics listed.
A family caregiver at home
A caregiver is a resource for learning, not a physical characteristic of the learner.
items.ex: Size, strength, coordination, and sensory acuity are the physical characteristics needed to learn psychomotor skills.

alt.q: A nurse is deciding whether a patient is physically able to learn a psychomotor skill. Which findings suggest the patient is not yet able to learn it? Select all that apply.
o: Insufficient upper body strength for a bed-to-wheelchair transfer
It is useless to teach a transfer when the patient lacks upper body strength.
Poor eyesight and a weak grasp when learning to apply an elastic bandage
An older patient with poor eyesight or a weak grasp cannot learn to apply an elastic bandage.
A high fever and respiratory difficulty
Teaching is postponed when illness is aggravated by complications such as high fever or respiratory difficulty.
Mild anxiety with frequent questions
Mild anxiety can be conducive to learning.
Alertness and good hand coordination
Alertness and coordination support, rather than prevent, learning psychomotor skills.
alt.ex: Lack of strength, poor sensory acuity or grasp, and acute complications such as fever or respiratory difficulty prevent psychomotor learning.

items.q: Which cultural phenomena does Giger and Davidhizar’s Transcultural Assessment Model ask the nurse to consider? Select all that apply.
o: Communication
Communication is one of the six cultural phenomena in the model.
Space
Space is one of the six cultural phenomena.
Time
Time is one of the six cultural phenomena.
Environmental control
Environmental control is one of the six cultural phenomena.
Educational level
Educational level is not one of the six phenomena; the others are social organization and biological variations.
Income
Income is not one of the six cultural phenomena in the model.
items.ex: The six phenomena are communication, space, social organization, time, environmental control, and biological variations.

alt.q: A nurse uses Giger and Davidhizar’s model to plan education for a patient from another culture. Which phenomena are part of this model? Select all that apply.
o: Social organization
Social organization is one of the six cultural phenomena.
Biological variations
Biological variations are one of the six cultural phenomena.
Communication
Communication is one of the six cultural phenomena.
Religious denomination
Religious denomination is not listed among the six phenomena.
Occupation
Occupation is not one of the six cultural phenomena in the model.
alt.ex: Giger and Davidhizar’s model includes communication, space, social organization, time, environmental control, and biological variations.

items.q: Which features of a learning environment promote learning? Select all that apply.
o: Good lighting
A well-lit room lets the patient watch demonstrations and see visual aids.
Good ventilation and a comfortable temperature
A cold, hot, or stuffy room makes the patient too uncomfortable to focus.
Privacy with infrequent interruptions
A quiet, private setting with few interruptions is best.
Group seating that lets participants observe one another
Observing others’ verbal and nonverbal interactions enhances group learning.
A darkened room to keep the patient relaxed
A darkened room interferes with watching the nurse’s actions and visual aids.
A large room for a small group to reduce crowding
The size of the room should not overwhelm the group.
items.ex: The ideal setting is well lit, ventilated, comfortable, quiet, and private, and suits the size of the group.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a patient in a busy hospital room. Which actions improve the learning environment? Select all that apply.
o: Close the cubicle curtains
Closing curtains provides privacy even in a busy hospital.
Turn off the loud television
Distractions and persistent noise impair focus; a quiet area is essential.
Adjust a stuffy, warm room to a comfortable temperature
A hot or stuffy room makes patients too uncomfortable to focus.
Dim the lights before demonstrating a skill
A darkened room interferes with watching a demonstration.
Keep several visitors talking in the room for support
Several people talking create distraction; privacy and quiet are best.
alt.ex: Privacy, quiet, good lighting, and comfortable temperature help the patient focus on learning.

items.q: According to the CDC, health information should be accurate, accessible, and actionable.
items.a: True
items.ex: The three As require information that is accurate without being dumbed down, easy to access and scan, and focused on what people need to do.
items.ww: The textbook lists accurate, accessible, and actionable as the three As of health information.

alt.q: For health information to be accurate under the CDC’s three As, it must be simplified, even if that means leaving out content.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Accurate information is presented in ways people understand without “dumbing down” the information.
alt.ww: The book specifies accurate information does not dumb down content; it is presented so people can understand it.

items.q: Although adults are generally self-directed learners, they often become dependent in new learning situations such as a new diagnosis.
items.a: True
items.ex: Adults tend to be self-directed but often become dependent when facing new situations such as a new diagnosis or medication.
items.ww: The textbook states adults often become dependent in new learning situations despite being self-directed.

alt.q: Because adults are self-directed, they remain independent learners even when they receive a new diagnosis or new medication.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Adults often become dependent in new learning situations such as a new diagnosis or new medication.
alt.ww: Self-direction does not prevent dependence; new learning situations often make adults dependent learners.

items.q: A person who reads well and works easily with numbers can still have poor health literacy.
items.a: True
items.ex: Poor health literacy is especially likely when people do not understand how their bodies work, are unfamiliar with medical terms, or are anxious after diagnosis.
items.ww: The book states that even people who can read and work with numbers can have poor health literacy.

alt.q: Health literacy refers only to a person’s ability to read printed health information.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Health literacy also includes the skills to problem solve, articulate a problem, and make well-informed health decisions.
alt.ww: Health literacy is broader than reading; it includes problem solving, describing problems, and decision making.

items.q: Which organization is an example of an accrediting agency that sets standards for patient education in health care institutions?
items.a: The Joint Commission
items.ex: Accrediting agencies such as The Joint Commission set guidelines or standards for patient education in health care institutions.
w: The state board of pharmacy
A state pharmacy board regulates pharmacy practice and is not the accrediting agency named for patient education.
The local public health department
Public health departments are not the accrediting agency the book names.
The hospital’s nursing union
Unions do not accredit health care institutions or set patient education standards.

alt.q: Standards set by The Joint Commission require which action of nurses and all health care providers?
alt.a: Assess patients’ learning needs and provide education
alt.ex: TJC standards require providers to assess learning needs and educate on topics such as medications, nutrition, equipment, pain, and the plan of care.
w: Delegate routine teaching to assistive personnel
TJC standards require providers themselves to assess needs and educate; delegation is not the standard.
Teach only when a provider writes an order
Patient teaching is within the scope of nursing practice and does not require a teaching order.
Provide education only at the time of discharge
Teaching needs are identified as early as possible after admission, not only at discharge.

items.q: As a nurse gains experience in patient education, what does that experience allow the nurse to do?
items.a: Match educational needs with the right approaches and choose the best time to teach.
items.ex: Experience allows the nurse to match a patient’s educational needs with the right instructional approaches and best timing.
w: Use one standard teaching plan for all patients with the same diagnosis.
Effective teaching is individualized to the patient, not standardized by diagnosis alone.
Skip assessment of what the patient already knows to save time.
Effective educators always determine what patients already know and need to know.
Rely mainly on passing on facts about the patient’s condition.
An effective educator does more than just pass on facts.

alt.q: What is required for a nurse to provide effective individualized patient information?
alt.a: Knowing both the patient and the information to be taught
alt.ex: Effective individualized education requires knowing both your patient and the information you plan to teach.
w: Knowing the patient’s diagnosis and the standard handout
A diagnosis and a handout alone do not individualize teaching to the patient.
Knowing the topics the nurse prefers to teach
Teaching is based on the patient’s needs, not the nurse’s preferences.
Knowing the length of stay the insurer will cover
Length of stay affects time to teach but does not individualize the content.

items.q: A patient is scheduled for an elective total joint replacement next week. When should the nurse begin education about postoperative guidelines?
items.a: Before the surgery occurs
items.ex: Patients with routine conditions such as joint replacement have specific guidelines, so nurses begin education before surgery.
w: On the day before discharge
Waiting until the day before discharge wastes the limited time available in acute care.
At the first home health visit
Home health reinforces and adds teaching but does not replace preoperative teaching.
Once the patient is alert after surgery
Postoperative alertness takes hours, and discharge may already be scheduled by then.

alt.q: A patient will be discharged 6 to 8 hours after an outpatient knee replacement. Why does the nurse provide most teaching preoperatively?
alt.a: The patient will not be alert enough to learn until shortly before discharge.
alt.ex: It takes hours after surgery for the patient to be alert enough to learn, and discharge follows soon after.
w: Postoperative teaching is the responsibility of the surgeon.
Patient teaching falls within the scope of nursing practice.
The patient will not need any teaching after surgery.
The nurse still teaches priority safety topics immediately after surgery.
Preoperative patients are always less anxious than postoperative patients.
The rationale is limited postoperative time and alertness, not lower anxiety.

items.q: A patient is admitted to an acute care unit with a complicated condition. Which action by the nurse early in the admission best prepares the patient for discharge?
items.a: Identify the patient’s family caregivers and involve them in instruction early.
items.ex: In acute care, identify resources such as family caregivers as early as possible and engage them early in instruction.
w: Wait until the discharge order to begin teaching the caregivers.
Time for teaching in acute care is very limited, so waiting for the discharge order is too late.
Postpone identifying caregivers until learning needs are obvious.
Resources should be identified as early as possible, even when needs are unclear.
Teach only the patient so information remains confidential.
With the patient’s agreement, family caregivers are engaged early as resources.

alt.q: Which question best helps a nurse in acute care confirm learning priorities with a patient and family caregiver?
alt.a: “What is most important for you both to learn before going home?”
alt.ex: Confirm with patients and caregivers what is most important for them to learn to be prepared to return home.
w: “Would you like to read the full booklet on your condition?”
Offering all content does not confirm priorities and may overwhelm the learners.
“Has your health care provider explained everything to you?”
This closed question does not identify what the patient and family need to learn.
“Can we discuss teaching once your discharge is ordered?”
Delaying teaching until discharge wastes the limited time available in acute care.

items.q: Why is the time available for patient teaching in acute care settings very limited?
items.a: Lengths of stay have declined, and patients are sicker when hospitalized.
items.ex: Declining lengths of stay and sicker hospitalized patients leave very limited time for teaching in acute care.
w: Patient teaching is outside the scope of acute care nursing.
All state nurse practice acts recognize patient teaching as within nursing practice.
Accrediting agencies limit teaching to outpatient settings.
Accrediting agencies require education in health care institutions, including hospitals.
Most hospitalized patients have no learning needs.
Patients have learning needs in all settings; time, not need, is limited.

alt.q: Because acute care time is limited, what must the nurse do to meet patients’ learning needs?
alt.a: Identify potential learning needs as early as possible after admission.
alt.ex: Managing limited acute care time requires identifying potential learning needs as early as possible following admission.
w: Delay all teaching until the patient’s first clinic visit.
Patients need essential information to return home safely, so acute care teaching cannot be delayed entirely.
Present all available information during one long session.
Large amounts of information overwhelm patients; teaching should focus on priorities.
Leave teaching to the health care provider at discharge.
Patient teaching is within nursing practice, and nurses are primarily responsible for meeting education needs.

items.q: In which settings do nurses usually have more time to identify learning needs and provide comprehensive, ongoing education?
items.a: Clinic, home care, and rehabilitation settings
items.ex: Clinic, home care, and rehabilitation settings allow more time for identifying needs and providing comprehensive ongoing education.
w: Emergency, surgical, and intensive care settings
These acute settings have sicker patients and very limited time for teaching.
Same-day surgery and observation units
Short-stay settings limit teaching time even more than inpatient units.
Acute medical and surgical inpatient units
Shorter lengths of stay and sicker patients limit teaching time on inpatient units.

alt.q: A nurse moves from an acute care unit to a home care agency. How is patient education likely to differ in the new setting?
alt.a: There is more time to identify needs and give ongoing education.
alt.ex: Home care, clinic, and rehabilitation nurses have more time to identify learning needs and provide comprehensive ongoing education.
w: There is less time because each visit is brief.
Home care allows more, not less, time for comprehensive education than acute care.
Learning needs must all be met at the first visit.
Home care allows ongoing education and reinforcement across visits.
Family caregivers are no longer part of teaching.
Family caregivers often share in discussions in the home setting.

items.q: A patient is being discharged a few hours after outpatient knee replacement. The home health nurse will visit tomorrow. Which teaching topic is the priority before the patient leaves?
items.a: Signs and symptoms to report right away
items.ex: Immediately after surgery the nurse focuses on what the patient and caregiver need to safely assume care until home health visits.
w: How to change the surgical dressing
Dressing changes are a less immediate need addressed by the home health team.
How to prevent constipation at home
Constipation prevention is a less immediate topic for the home health team.
How to perform the full exercise program
Postoperative exercises are taught later by the home health team and physical therapist.

alt.q: For a patient discharged the same day after knee replacement, which topic should the nurse include in teaching before discharge?
alt.a: How to use the toilet or a commode safely
alt.ex: Before discharge, teach safe transfers, walker use, toileting, pain medication management, and signs and symptoms to report.
w: How to change the dressing each day
Dressing changes are addressed later by the home health team.
How to add fiber to prevent constipation
Preventing constipation is a less immediate need covered by home health.
How to progress the home exercise routine
Postoperative exercises are a less immediate need covered after discharge.

items.q: Besides accreditation standards, which source of standards often identifies education topics that are standards of care for select patient conditions?
items.a: Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines and protocols
items.ex: Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines and protocols often include education topics that are standards of care for select conditions.
w: Commercial pharmaceutical advertising materials
Advertising is not a standard used to guide patient education.
Individual patients’ online search results
Online searches are information sources, not professional standards.
Hospital billing and reimbursement codes
Reimbursement codes do not define education standards of care.

alt.q: A nurse wants to know which education topics are standard of care for a patient with heart failure. Which resource is most appropriate?
alt.a: A professional organization’s clinical practice guideline
alt.ex: Clinical guidelines and protocols from professional organizations often include education topics that are standards of care.
w: A family member’s past experience with heart failure
Personal experience is not a professional standard of care.
The state’s motor vehicle safety regulations
Motor vehicle regulations do not address heart failure education.
The insurer’s list of covered diagnoses
Coverage lists do not define the education standard of care.

items.q: A patient is highly anxious and must be prepared quickly for an emergent diagnostic procedure. Which teaching approach should the nurse use?
items.a: Telling
items.ex: Telling is used when time is limited or a highly anxious patient needs vital information; give simple, explicit instructions.
w: Participating
Participating involves mutual content decisions and discussion, which requires more time.
Entrusting
Entrusting gives a patient who has knowledge the opportunity to manage self-care over time.
Simulation
Simulation poses problems to solve, which suits problem-solving practice rather than emergent preparation.

alt.q: What is a limitation of the telling approach used when time for teaching is limited?
alt.a: There is no opportunity for feedback.
alt.ex: With telling, the nurse outlines needed information with simple, explicit instructions, but there is no opportunity for feedback.
w: It cannot be used with highly anxious patients.
Telling is effective for a highly anxious patient when information is vital.
It requires the patient to choose the content.
Patient choice of content describes the participating approach.
It takes several sessions to complete.
Telling is used precisely because time for teaching is limited.

items.q: What leads a nurse to decide what information to teach a patient and how best to teach it?
items.a: Knowledge of the patient’s condition and the patient’s assessment data
items.ex: Knowledge of the health condition combined with information gained from assessment leads the nurse to decide what and how to teach.
w: The order in which topics appear in the agency handout
Handout order does not reflect what the individual patient needs.
The topics the nurse feels most comfortable teaching
Content is chosen from the patient’s needs, not the nurse’s comfort.
The amount of time left before the end of the shift
Time affects how much is taught, but assessment determines what to teach.

alt.q: Which nurse statement reflects critical thinking and clinical judgment in patient education?
alt.a: “I’ll find out what my patient already knows before I decide what to teach.”
alt.ex: Effective educators determine what patients already know, what they need to know, and their learning preferences.
w: “I’ll give my patient every handout we have on this diagnosis.”
Providing all available material ignores the patient’s needs and may overwhelm the patient.
“I’ll teach everything now, whether or not my patient is ready.”
Teaching is timed for when patients are ready to learn.
“I’ll cover the facts quickly because that is what teaching is.”
Effective education requires more than passing on facts.

items.q: According to the textbook, critical thinking in patient education involves applying which of the following?
items.a: Standards
items.ex: Critical thinking in patient education involves applying standards such as nurse practice acts, accreditation standards, and clinical guidelines.
w: Personal preferences
Personal preferences of the nurse are not the basis of critical thinking in patient education.
Billing codes
Billing codes do not guide the critical thinking used in patient teaching.
Unit traditions
Unit traditions are not standards for patient education.

alt.q: Which outcome does the textbook link to successfully implementing patient education standards through collaboration among health care professionals?
alt.a: Enhanced patient safety
alt.ex: Implementing patient education standards requires collaboration among health care professionals and enhances patient safety.
w: Shorter teaching sessions
Collaboration is not described as a way to shorten teaching sessions.
Lower staffing needs
The book does not link education standards to staffing levels.
Fewer learning needs
Standards guide meeting learning needs; they do not reduce them.

items.q: A nurse on a busy acute care unit has limited time to teach a patient who will be discharged tomorrow. Which approach to the teaching plan is best?
items.a: Keep the plan concise and focused on priority learning needs.
items.ex: Because acute care time is limited, teaching plans must be concise and focused on the patient’s priority learning needs.
w: Cover every topic in the agency’s complete teaching plan.
Trying to cover everything in limited time overwhelms the patient and dilutes priorities.
Begin with detailed background on the disease process.
Background information is less critical than what the patient needs to manage safely.
Defer all teaching to the patient’s first home care visit.
Patients need essential safety information before they leave the hospital.

alt.q: Why are teaching plans in home care and outpatient clinics usually more comprehensive than those in acute care?
alt.a: Nurses have more time, and patients are often less anxious.
alt.ex: Home care and clinic plans are more comprehensive because nurses often have more time and patients are often less anxious.
w: Patients in these settings are usually sicker.
Patients are sicker in acute care, which limits teaching time there.
Accrediting standards apply only in these settings.
Education standards also apply in hospitals and other health care institutions.
Family caregivers cannot be involved in acute care.
Family caregivers are engaged early in acute care instruction.

items.q: Which topics do The Joint Commission standards require health care providers to address in patient education? Select all that apply.
o: Medications
Medications are among the topics listed in TJC education standards.
Nutrition
Nutrition is a required education topic.
Use of medical equipment
Use of medical equipment is a required topic.
Pain management
Pain management is a required topic.
Hospital staffing ratios
Staffing ratios are not a patient education topic.
Health care providers’ credentials
Provider credentials are not listed among required education topics.
items.ex: TJC standards require education on topics including medications, nutrition, medical equipment, pain management, and the patient’s plan of care.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing accreditation standards for patient education. Which topics should the nurse plan to address with patients? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s plan of care
The plan of care is among the required education topics.
Pain management
Pain management is a required education topic.
Medications
Medications are a required education topic.
The hospital’s budget process
Budget processes are not patient education topics.
Other patients’ diagnoses on the unit
Other patients’ information is confidential and not an education topic.
alt.ex: TJC standards include education on medications, nutrition, equipment use, pain management, and the plan of care.

items.q: Which decisions does a nurse’s clinical judgment guide in patient education? Select all that apply.
o: What information to teach
Knowledge of the condition and assessment data lead the nurse to decide what to teach.
The best time for teaching
Clinical judgment allows the nurse to determine the best time for teaching.
The resources to use
Clinical judgment helps determine the resources to use.
How to engage the patient
Clinical judgment helps determine how to engage the patient.
Which medications the patient is prescribed
Prescribing is the health care provider’s role, not a teaching decision.
Whether teaching is within nursing scope
Nurse practice acts already establish that teaching is within nursing practice.
items.ex: Clinical judgment helps the nurse decide what and how to teach, when to teach, which resources to use, and how to engage the patient.

alt.q: A nurse prepares to teach a patient with a new diagnosis. Which information should the nurse determine before teaching? Select all that apply.
o: What the patient already knows
Effective educators determine what patients already know.
What the patient needs to know
Effective educators determine what patients need to know.
The patient’s learning preferences
Learning preferences guide the choice of instructional approach.
Whether the patient is ready to learn
Teaching is timed for when patients are ready to learn.
Which topics the nurse prefers to teach
Teaching content is driven by the patient’s needs, not the nurse’s preferences.
alt.ex: Before teaching, determine what the patient knows, needs to know, prefers, and whether the patient is ready to learn.

items.q: Which statements about the health care environment and patient education are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Patients are sicker when hospitalized, which limits teaching time
Sicker patients and shorter stays leave very limited time for acute care teaching.
Learning needs are easier to identify for conditions seen routinely on a unit
Identifying early needs is easier for routinely seen conditions such as joint replacement.
Home care nurses often have more time for comprehensive education
Clinic, home care, and rehabilitation settings allow more time for ongoing education.
Learning needs are always obvious on the day of admission
Complicated or unclear conditions may not have obvious learning needs until a day before discharge.
Hospital lengths of stay have been increasing for many years
Lengths of stay in acute care have been declining for many years.
items.ex: Shorter stays and sicker patients limit acute care teaching, while outpatient and home settings allow more comprehensive education.

alt.q: A nurse compares patient education across settings. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Rehabilitation settings allow more time for ongoing education
Rehabilitation, clinic, and home care settings give nurses more time to teach.
Patients with unclear conditions may not show learning needs until near discharge
Complicated or unclear conditions may not reveal learning needs until a day before discharge.
In acute care, family caregivers should be engaged early in instruction
Identify and engage resources such as family caregivers as early as possible.
Acute care settings allow the most time for comprehensive teaching
Acute care has the least time because stays are short and patients are sicker.
Teaching in acute care should wait until learning needs are certain
Potential learning needs are identified as early as possible after admission.
alt.ex: Acute care demands early identification of learning needs and resources, while other settings allow fuller education.

items.q: To be an effective educator, a nurse must do more than just pass on facts to the patient.
items.a: True
items.ex: Effective educators determine what patients know, need to know, and prefer, and teach when the patient is ready.
items.ww: The textbook states that to be an effective educator you need to do more than just pass on facts.

alt.q: Effective patient education consists mainly of accurately passing on facts about the patient’s condition.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Effective education also requires assessing what patients know, their needs and preferences, and their readiness to learn.
alt.ww: Passing on facts alone is not enough; the nurse must individualize teaching and time it to readiness.

items.q: Patients whose conditions are complicated or unclear may not have obvious learning needs until a day before discharge.
items.a: True
items.ex: Unlike routine conditions such as joint replacement, complicated conditions may not reveal learning needs until shortly before discharge.
items.ww: The textbook contrasts routine conditions with complicated ones whose learning needs may not appear until a day before discharge.

alt.q: For every hospitalized patient, learning needs can be fully identified on the day of admission.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients with complicated or unclear conditions may not have obvious learning needs until a day before discharge.
alt.ww: Early identification is easier only for routine conditions; complicated conditions may reveal needs much later.

items.q: Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines and protocols are among the standards that guide patient education.
items.a: True
items.ex: Besides nurse practice acts and accreditation standards, clinical guidelines often include education topics that are standards of care.
items.ww: The textbook lists professional organizations’ clinical guidelines and protocols as standards used in patient education.

alt.q: The Joint Commission is the only source of standards that guide nurses in patient education.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurse practice acts and professional organizations’ clinical guidelines and protocols also guide patient education.
alt.ww: Patient education standards also come from state nurse practice acts and professional clinical guidelines.

items.q: All state [[nurse practice acts|nurse practice act]] recognize that patient teaching falls within the scope of nursing practice.
items.ex: Because nurse practice acts include teaching in nursing’s scope, nurses are responsible for patient education.

alt.q: Patient teaching is part of the scope of nursing practice as recognized by every state’s [[nurse practice act|nurse practice acts]].
alt.ex: Because nurse practice acts include teaching in nursing’s scope, nurses are responsible for patient education.

items.q: What do State nurse practice acts contribute to patient education?
items.a: Recognize patient teaching as within the scope of nursing practice
items.ex: Patient education is guided by nurse practice acts, accrediting agency standards, and professional clinical guidelines and protocols.
w: Require institutions to assess learning needs and educate on set topics
That goes with Accrediting agencies such as The Joint Commission.
Identify education topics that are standards of care for select conditions
That goes with Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines.

alt.q: What do Accrediting agencies such as The Joint Commission contribute to patient education?
alt.a: Require institutions to assess learning needs and educate on set topics
alt.ex: Patient education is guided by nurse practice acts, accrediting agency standards, and professional clinical guidelines and protocols.
w: Recognize patient teaching as within the scope of nursing practice
That goes with State nurse practice acts.
Identify education topics that are standards of care for select conditions
That goes with Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines.

alt.q: What do Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines contribute to patient education?
alt.a: Identify education topics that are standards of care for select conditions
alt.ex: Patient education is guided by nurse practice acts, accrediting agency standards, and professional clinical guidelines and protocols.
w: Recognize patient teaching as within the scope of nursing practice
That goes with State nurse practice acts.
Require institutions to assess learning needs and educate on set topics
That goes with Accrediting agencies such as The Joint Commission.

alt.q: Which source of standards does this: “Recognize patient teaching as within the scope of nursing practice”?
alt.a: State nurse practice acts
alt.ex: Patient education is guided by nurse practice acts, accrediting agency standards, and professional clinical guidelines and protocols.
w: Accrediting agencies such as The Joint Commission
Accrediting agencies such as The Joint Commission: Require institutions to assess learning needs and educate on set topics.
Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines
Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines: Identify education topics that are standards of care for select conditions.

alt.q: Which source of standards does this: “Require institutions to assess learning needs and educate on set topics”?
alt.a: Accrediting agencies such as The Joint Commission
alt.ex: Patient education is guided by nurse practice acts, accrediting agency standards, and professional clinical guidelines and protocols.
w: State nurse practice acts
State nurse practice acts: Recognize patient teaching as within the scope of nursing practice.
Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines
Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines: Identify education topics that are standards of care for select conditions.

alt.q: Which source of standards does this: “Identify education topics that are standards of care for select conditions”?
alt.a: Professional organizations’ clinical guidelines
alt.ex: Patient education is guided by nurse practice acts, accrediting agency standards, and professional clinical guidelines and protocols.
w: State nurse practice acts
State nurse practice acts: Recognize patient teaching as within the scope of nursing practice.
Accrediting agencies such as The Joint Commission
Accrediting agencies such as The Joint Commission: Require institutions to assess learning needs and educate on set topics.

mt.q: Match each source of standards with what it contributes to patient education.
pairs: Recognize patient teaching as within the scope of nursing practice
Accrediting agencies such as The Joint Commission
Require institutions to assess learning needs and educate on set topics
Identify education topics that are standards of care for select conditions
mt.ex: Patient education is guided by nurse practice acts, accrediting agency standards, and professional clinical guidelines and protocols.

items.q: Which statement defines learning needs?
items.a: The gaps between the knowledge a learner has and the knowledge and skills needed
items.ex: Learning needs are gaps between actual knowledge and the knowledge and skills needed to perform a task or make a decision.
w: The topics the nurse believes every patient with a diagnosis must learn
Learning needs are individual gaps, not a standard list chosen by the nurse.
The patient’s willingness to engage in a learning activity
Willingness to engage in learning defines readiness to learn.
The patient’s preferred way of receiving new information
Preferred ways of receiving information describe learning style.

alt.q: During assessment, what is most important for the nurse to determine about a patient’s learning needs?
alt.a: What the patient wants to know or any goal for learning
alt.ex: When assessing learning needs, apply motivational interviewing; it is most important to determine what the patient wants to know.
w: Which handout the unit usually gives for the diagnosis
Standard handouts do not reveal the patient’s own learning goals.
How much time remains before the patient’s discharge
Time affects planning but is not the most important assessment finding.
Which topics the health care provider wants covered
The patient’s own goals for learning are most important to determine.

items.q: A postoperative patient rates pain as 8 on a 0-to-10 scale. The nurse had planned to teach incision care. The patient’s nursing diagnoses include Acute Pain. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Delay teaching until the pain is controlled.
items.ex: When a diagnosis such as Acute Pain creates a barrier to learning, teaching is inappropriate until the problem is controlled.
w: Teach incision care now and recheck the pain afterward.
Teaching while a barrier such as acute pain exists is inappropriate.
Give a written handout to read while the pain persists.
Severe pain interferes with attention for written teaching as well.
Teach the content more quickly to shorten the session.
Speeding up teaching does not remove the pain that blocks learning.

alt.q: A patient has a nursing diagnosis of Activity Intolerance and becomes short of breath with minimal exertion. How should this diagnosis affect the teaching plan?
alt.a: Teaching is delayed until the problem is controlled.
alt.ex: Activity Intolerance is a condition that creates a barrier to effective learning, so teaching waits until it is resolved or controlled.
w: Teaching is shortened but given as originally planned.
Teaching is inappropriate when a barrier to learning is present.
Teaching is given only to the family from now on.
Family may be taught when needed, but the plan is to delay teaching until the problem is controlled.
Teaching continues because this diagnosis does not affect learning.
The book names Activity Intolerance as a barrier to effective learning.

items.q: A patient newly diagnosed with coronary artery disease has two learning outcomes: taking nitroglycerin correctly for chest pain and developing a diet low in saturated fat. Which should the nurse teach first?
items.a: How to take nitroglycerin and when to call for help
items.ex: Chest pain is an emergency, so survival-related teaching about nitroglycerin comes before diet and exercise changes.
w: How to plan meals low in saturated fat
Diet changes are addressed after basic survival priorities are met.
How to start a regular exercise program
Exercise is discussed after the patient can respond to an emergency.
How coronary arteries become narrowed
Background information is less critical than knowing how to respond to chest pain.

alt.q: Which factors determine teaching priorities for a patient? Choose the best answer.
alt.a: Patient perceptions, anxiety or pain, time available, and self-care needs
alt.ex: Priorities depend on what the patient sees as important, anxiety or pain, time available, and what is needed for safe self-care.
w: The order of topics in the agency’s standard teaching plan
Standard plans provide structure, but priorities are individualized with the patient.
The amount of background content the nurse can provide
Providing a lot of background can overwhelm patients; focus on critical information.
The topics the nurse covered with the previous patient
Priorities are based on this patient’s diagnoses and outcomes.

items.q: Which schedule of teaching sessions is easiest for patients to tolerate while retaining interest in the material?
items.a: Frequent sessions lasting 10 to 15 minutes
items.ex: Patients tolerate and retain interest better during frequent sessions lasting 10 to 15 minutes.
w: One session lasting 60 to 90 minutes
Long single sessions are harder to tolerate, though sometimes needed with short stays.
Weekly sessions lasting 45 to 60 minutes
Long intervals risk forgetting, and long sessions reduce attention.
Daily sessions lasting 30 to 45 minutes
Shorter, frequent sessions of 10 to 15 minutes are easier to tolerate.

alt.q: A nurse is planning teaching for a child newly diagnosed with diabetes mellitus. Which principle should guide the frequency of sessions?
alt.a: Frequency depends on the learner’s abilities and the complexity of the material.
alt.ex: Newly diagnosed children need more visits than experienced adults, and intervals must not be so long that information is forgotten.
w: Frequency should match that of adults who have managed diabetes for years.
Children newly diagnosed require more visits than adults experienced in self-management.
Frequency should be weekly, regardless of how much the child forgets.
Intervals should not be so long that the patient forgets information.
Frequency should be limited to one session to avoid overwhelming the child.
Complex material and a new diagnosis require more, not fewer, sessions.

items.q: What group size is most effective for group instruction?
items.a: Six or fewer participants
items.ex: Learning in a group of six or fewer is most effective and avoids distracting behaviors.
w: Ten to twelve participants
Larger groups are more likely to produce distracting behaviors.
Fifteen to twenty participants
Groups this large reduce active participation and increase distractions.
Twenty-five or more participants
Very large groups suit lectures but not effective group learning.

alt.q: Why does a lecture to a group of patients need to be followed by discussion and practice?
alt.a: A lecture does not ensure learners are actively thinking about the material.
alt.ex: Lectures efficiently present standard content, but discussion and practice let learners share ideas and seek clarification.
w: A lecture is too unstructured to present standard content.
Lectures are highly structured and efficient for standard content.
A lecture cannot be used for groups of patients.
Group instruction often involves both lecture and discussion.
A lecture is the least economical way to teach groups.
Group teaching, including lectures, is an economical way to teach several patients.

items.q: A nurse wants to evaluate whether a patient understood teaching about stroke warning signs. Which statement by the nurse best uses the teach-back method?
items.a: “I want to be certain I taught this well. Can you describe some symptoms of a stroke?”
items.ex: Teach-back uses nonjudgmental language so patients do not feel tested, and asks them to explain in their own words.
w: “Do you understand the symptoms of a stroke that I just explained?”
A yes-or-no question does not let the nurse determine what the patient remembers.
“Let’s see if you passed: name five symptoms of a stroke for me.”
Teach-back avoids language that makes patients feel tested.
“Do you have any questions about the stroke symptoms we covered?”
Asking for questions does not confirm that the patient can restate the information.

alt.q: Which prompt is an example of the teach-back method?
alt.a: “Tell me in your own words how you will take this medication at home.”
alt.ex: Teach-back asks the patient to explain material or demonstrate a skill so the nurse can judge retention and understanding.
w: “This medication is taken twice daily; is that clear to you?”
A yes-or-no check does not show that the patient can restate the information.
“Here is a handout on this medication to read at home.”
Giving a handout provides information but does not evaluate understanding.
“You understand how to take this medication, don’t you?”
A leading question does not evaluate retention in the patient’s own words.

items.q: During teach-back, a patient cannot recall the symptoms of a stroke that the nurse just explained. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “I must not have explained stroke symptoms very well. Let me try again.”
items.ex: The nurse takes ownership of the teaching, then modifies and repeats the content and reassesses retention.
w: “You need to listen more carefully when I am explaining things.”
Blaming the patient is judgmental; the nurse takes ownership of the teaching.
“That’s okay; the information is in your discharge folder.”
The nurse must modify and repeat content until the patient understands.
“Let’s move on, and your family can learn the symptoms instead.”
Skipping reteaching leaves the patient without critical safety information.

alt.q: When is a patient’s understanding confirmed with the teach-back method?
alt.a: When the patient accurately restates the information in their own words
alt.ex: Patient understanding is confirmed when the patient can accurately restate the information in their own words.
w: When the patient says the information is clear
Stating that something is clear does not show retention or understanding.
When the patient signs the education record
A signature documents teaching but does not confirm understanding.
When the patient repeats the nurse’s words exactly
Teach-back looks for accurate restatement in the patient’s own words, not memorized phrases.

items.q: Which learning objective is written correctly for a patient learning colostomy care?
items.a: The patient will empty the colostomy bag correctly in 3 days.
items.ex: Outcomes describe specific behaviors the patient must perform under realistic conditions and time frames.
w: The patient will understand colostomy care well.
“Understand” is not observable and gives no time frame or criteria.
The nurse will teach colostomy care before discharge.
Learning objectives describe patient behaviors, not nurse actions.
The patient will feel comfortable with the colostomy.
This is not a specific, measurable behavior with a time frame.

alt.q: Which outcome statement correctly considers the conditions under which a patient will perform a behavior?
alt.a: The patient will walk from bedroom to bathroom using crutches by the end of the day.
alt.ex: Outcomes consider the conditions under which the patient will typically perform the behavior, with a realistic time frame.
w: The patient will know how to use crutches safely.
“Know” is not a specific behavior and lacks conditions or a time frame.
The nurse will demonstrate crutch walking to the patient.
Outcomes describe the patient’s behavior, not the nurse’s action.
The patient will be independent with all mobility soon.
This outcome is vague and lacks realistic conditions and time frame.

items.q: A patient has poor reading comprehension and needs to learn about a new medication. Which teaching tool is the best choice?
items.a: A streaming video about the medication
items.ex: A printed pamphlet is not the best tool for poor reading comprehension; audiovisual materials suit patients with reading problems.
w: A printed pamphlet about the medication
Printed materials require reading ability the patient lacks.
A programmed instruction workbook
Programmed instruction is a written sequential format that depends on reading.
A computer instruction module
Computer instruction requires reading comprehension and computer familiarity.

alt.q: A patient needs to learn a skill using equipment that is too small to see easily. Which teaching tool is most useful?
alt.a: A model of the equipment
alt.ex: Models are useful when real objects are too small, large, or complicated, and they let learners handle what they will use.
w: A bar graph of the steps
Graphs present numerical data, not physical equipment.
A written list of the steps
Written lists do not let learners manipulate the equipment.
A podcast describing the skill
Audio alone does not provide a visible, handled object.

items.q: A nurse uses social praise after an adult patient correctly checks a blood glucose level. What makes this reinforcement most effective?
items.a: Giving the praise closely after the desired behavior
items.ex: Reinforcement must closely follow the behavior so a clear correlation between the behavior and the reward is established.
w: Giving the praise at the end of the week
Delayed reinforcement weakens the link between the behavior and the reward.
Pairing the praise with criticism of errors
Negative reinforcement can discourage participation and cause withdrawal.
Giving a toy or food as a tangible reward
Material reinforcers work well with young children; most reinforcers with adults are social.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid relying on negative reinforcement, such as frowning or criticism, during patient teaching?
alt.a: It can discourage participation and cause the learner to withdraw.
alt.ex: Negative reinforcement may decrease an undesired response, but its effects are less predictable and often undesirable.
w: It always increases the desired behavior too quickly.
Negative reinforcement is unpredictable and does not reliably promote desired behaviors.
It works only with young children who need rewards.
Material rewards, not negative reinforcement, work well with young children.
It requires a therapeutic relationship to be used.
Trust makes reinforcement more effective in adults, but negative reinforcement still risks withdrawal.

items.q: A nurse is teaching a patient who has low health literacy. Which strategies should the nurse use? Select all that apply.
o: Use simple words such as “belly” instead of “abdomen”
Use common, one- or two-syllable words to explain medical information.
Emphasize one to three key points
Keep sessions short, put key information first, and emphasize one to three points.
Provide materials written at about a fifth-grade reading level
Fifth-grade reading level is generally recommended for adult learners.
Ask the patient to teach back the information
Teach-back and return demonstration check comprehension.
Use long sessions so all content is covered at once
Sessions should be short and to the point, scheduled at frequent intervals.
Use medical terms so the patient learns the vocabulary
Medical jargon makes information too complex to understand.
items.ex: Plain language, few key points, simple materials, and teach-back help patients with literacy or learning disability problems.

alt.q: A patient with a learning disability needs teaching about a new treatment. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Face the patient and sit at the patient’s level
Facing the patient and maintaining eye contact supports communication.
Use simple pictures that show only important concepts
Graphics should show only the needed concepts, without unneeded detail.
Teach in increments organized into sections
Teaching in increments organized into sections aids understanding.
Speak quickly to keep the session brief
Speak slowly and invite participation; fast speech limits processing.
Include detailed anatomy in each drawing
Detailed anatomy that is not needed should be left out of pictures.
alt.ex: Face the patient, use simple graphics, and teach in increments for patients with literacy or learning disability problems.

items.q: A nurse is planning education for an older adult. Which strategies from Box 25.8 should the nurse use? Select all that apply.
o: Use black 14-point print on matte white paper
Large print that contrasts with the background aids reading.
Present information slowly in a clear, low tone
A slow, clear, low tone accommodates hearing loss.
Keep sessions short and allow frequent breaks
Short sessions with breaks support learning in older adults.
Give concise, step-by-step directions and check each step
Assess understanding of each step before moving ahead.
Print handouts in blue and green for easy reading
Blues and greens become harder to distinguish with age.
Speak in a loud, high-pitched voice
A clear, low tone, not a loud or high-pitched voice, accommodates hearing loss.
items.ex: Older adults learn best with large high-contrast print, a slow low voice, short sessions, and step-by-step instructions.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching an older adult who has hearing loss and wears glasses. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Face the patient directly when speaking
Directly facing the learner helps a patient with hearing loss hear or lip-read.
Eliminate extraneous noise in the room
Removing background noise accommodates hearing loss.
Encourage the patient to wear glasses and a working hearing aid
Ensure prostheses are worn, fit properly, and work.
Cover the mouth with a hand while talking
A hand near the mouth interferes with hearing or lip-reading.
Provide bright lighting with strong glare
Lighting should be sufficient but with low glare.
alt.ex: For older adults with sensory changes, face the patient, reduce noise, ensure prostheses are used, and provide low-glare lighting.

items.q: Which guidelines should the nurse follow when giving preparatory instruction before a procedure? Select all that apply.
o: Describe the physical sensations the patient will feel
Describe sensations, such as a sticking feeling as the needle punctures the skin.
Explain the cause of each sensation
Explaining the cause prevents misinterpretation of the experience.
Prepare the patient for aspects others commonly notice
Prepare patients only for what others have commonly noticed.
Tell the patient when results will be available and who will give them
Patients should know when and from whom they will receive results.
Describe every rare sensation that could possibly occur
Preparation is limited to sensations others commonly notice.
Avoid mentioning discomfort to keep the patient calm
The known is less threatening than the unknown; describe sensations honestly.
items.ex: Preparatory explanations describe common sensations and their causes and tell patients when and from whom results will come.

alt.q: A nurse prepares a patient for a blood draw. Which statements reflect correct preparatory instruction? Select all that apply.
o: “You will feel a sticking sensation as the needle goes in.”
Describing the physical sensation helps the patient know what to expect.
“It may burn because the alcohol enters the puncture site.”
Explaining the cause of a sensation prevents misinterpretation.
“Your hand may tingle and feel numb from the tight tourniquet.”
This prepares the patient for a sensation others commonly notice.
“You won’t feel anything, so there is nothing to prepare for.”
Withholding expected sensations removes the sense of control preparation provides.
“I can’t tell you when your results will be ready.”
Patients should know when results will be available and who will provide them.
alt.ex: Describing sensations, their causes, and common experiences enhances the patient’s sense of control and lowers anxiety.

items.q: Because health literacy screening tools rely on self-report, nurses should combine them with interviews and observation to fully assess health literacy.
items.a: True
items.ex: Self-report tools give subjective information, so other methods such as interviews and observations are needed.
items.ww: The book states screening tool data are subjective and must be supplemented by other assessment methods.

alt.q: Health literacy screening tools such as REALM-SF provide objective results, so no other assessment method is needed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: These tools rely on self-report and are subjective, so they are combined with interviews and patient observations.
alt.ww: Screening tool results are subjective; interviews and observation are also needed for a full assessment.

items.q: Patients are more likely to remember information taught early in a teaching session, so essential content should come first.
items.a: True
items.ex: Begin with high-priority content, such as monitoring an incision for infection, and finish with less critical information.
items.ww: The textbook advises beginning instruction with essential content because early information is better remembered.

alt.q: Essential content is best saved for the end of a teaching session because patients remember the last information they hear.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients remember information taught early in a session, so begin with essential, high-priority content.
alt.ww: The book directs nurses to start with essential content and end with less critical information.

items.q: In the telling approach to teaching, the nurse gives simple, explicit instructions, and there is no opportunity for feedback.
items.a: True
items.ex: Telling suits limited time or high anxiety but offers no opportunity for feedback, unlike participating.
items.ww: The textbook states there is no opportunity for feedback with the telling approach.

alt.q: The entrusting approach gives the patient regular opportunities to decide content together with the nurse and revise the teaching plan.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Mutual content decisions and plan revision describe participating; entrusting lets the patient manage self-care while the nurse observes.
alt.ww: Deciding content together and revising the plan is the participating approach, not entrusting.

items.q: Teach-back is a [[closed-loop]] communication technique that evaluates the patient’s retention of information given during teaching.
items.ex: In teach-back the patient explains or demonstrates what was taught, closing the loop so the nurse can verify understanding.

alt.q: The [[teach-back|teach back]] method asks patients to explain or demonstrate what was taught in their own words to confirm understanding.
alt.ex: In teach-back the patient explains or demonstrates what was taught, closing the loop so the nurse can verify understanding.
