items.q: Which are purposes of the data entered into a patient’s health record? Select all that apply.
o: Documenting patient care activities
The record documents the care activities provided to the patient.
Facilitating interprofessional communication
The record lets all members of the health care team communicate about the patient.
Providing a legal record of the care provided
The record serves as legal evidence of the care that was delivered.
Justifying billing and reimbursement of care
Documentation supports financial billing and reimbursement for services.
Supplying health details to a patient’s employer
Patient information is confidential and is shared only with those involved in the patient’s care.
Recording staff opinions about coworkers’ performance
Critical comments about other professionals do not belong in the record and can be used as evidence of unprofessional behavior.
items.ex: Health record data document care, support team communication, provide a legal record, and justify billing and reimbursement.

alt.q: A nurse orientation class discusses why accurate health records matter. Which uses of the record should the educator include? Select all that apply.
o: Auditing and evaluating care for quality improvement
Record data are used to audit, monitor, and evaluate care for quality and performance improvement.
Serving as a resource for education
Health records are a resource for nursing and health care education.
Providing data for research
Health records supply data for research when privacy and ethical considerations are met.
Advertising the agency’s services to the public
Marketing is not a purpose of the confidential health record.
Allowing any agency employee to review any patient’s care
Only team members directly involved in a patient’s care have legitimate access to the record.
alt.ex: Beyond care, communication, legal, and billing purposes, the record supports auditing, education, and research.

items.q: Which statement best defines documentation in a patient’s health record?
items.a: A written account of pertinent patient data, clinical decisions and interventions, and patient responses
items.ex: Documentation is a key communication strategy that produces a written account of patient data, decisions, interventions, and responses.
w: A verbal summary of the patient’s status given to the oncoming nurse at shift change
A verbal summary at shift change is a hand-off report, not documentation.
A list of the health care provider’s orders that nurses transcribe at the end of a shift
Orders are only one part of the record; documentation covers data, decisions, interventions, and responses.
A private journal in which the nurse records personal impressions of each patient
The record is a legal, shared account of objective care, not personal impressions.

alt.q: Health care documentation consists of which information?
alt.a: All information entered into a health record, whether electronic, paper, or both
alt.ex: Health care documentation includes everything entered into a health record, in electronic, paper, or combined formats.
w: Only the information entered by the health care provider in the medical history
Documentation includes entries by all members of the team, not only the provider.
Only the information stored on paper forms kept at the nurses’ station
Records may be electronic, paper, or a combination of both formats.
Only the information that insurance companies need to approve payment
Documentation serves many purposes beyond reimbursement, including care and communication.

items.q: A patient is admitted from a nursing home with a stage 3 pressure injury on the sacrum. Which nursing action is most important for the health record?
items.a: Describe the pressure injury accurately in the admission assessment documentation
items.ex: Accurate documentation on admission shows the injury was present before hospitalization, which matters for clinical care and reimbursement.
w: Wait to document the injury until the wound care nurse confirms its stage
Delaying documentation risks the injury appearing to be hospital acquired; document status on admission.
Document the injury only if it worsens during the hospital stay
Status on admission must be documented so the course of the injury can be tracked.
Record only the treatment plan and omit a description of the wound
The record must reflect the patient’s actual status, not only the plan of care.

alt.q: A nurse is completing documentation as a patient is transferred to another unit. Why is accurate documentation of the patient’s status especially important at this time?
alt.a: It shows the patient’s progress and how events developed, which affects care and reimbursement
alt.ex: The book stresses accurate status documentation on admission, transfer, or discharge because tracking how events develop affects care and hospital reimbursement.
w: It replaces the need to give a verbal report to the receiving nurse
Documentation complements, but does not eliminate, communication with the receiving team.
It is the only time the nurse is legally required to document assessments
Nurses document all nursing care throughout the stay, not only at transfer.
It allows the sending unit to close the patient’s health record permanently
The EHR is a continuous lifetime record; it is not closed at transfer.

items.q: Which hospital-acquired conditions are considered “nurse-sensitive” never events for which CMS no longer reimburses hospitals? Select all that apply.
o: Stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries
Stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries are among the four nurse-sensitive preventable adverse events.
Falls with injury
Falls with injury are a nurse-sensitive never event.
Catheter-associated urinary tract infections
CAUTIs are a nurse-sensitive never event.
Central line–associated bloodstream infections
CLABSIs are a nurse-sensitive never event.
Stage 1 pressure injuries
Only stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries are listed as nurse-sensitive never events.
Postoperative nausea after anesthesia
Postoperative nausea is not one of the four nurse-sensitive never events.
items.ex: The four nurse-sensitive never events are stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries, falls with injury, CAUTIs, and CLABSIs.

alt.q: A quality improvement committee reviews nurse-sensitive never events on a medical unit. Which events should the committee track? Select all that apply.
o: A patient who fell and fractured a hip
Falls with injury are a nurse-sensitive never event.
A patient who developed a CLABSI
Central line–associated bloodstream infections are nurse-sensitive never events.
A patient who developed a stage 4 pressure injury
Stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries are nurse-sensitive never events.
A patient whose surgery was rescheduled
A rescheduled surgery is not a hospital-acquired condition.
A patient admitted with community-acquired pneumonia
A condition present on admission is not hospital acquired.
alt.ex: Nurse-sensitive never events include falls with injury, stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries, CAUTIs, and CLABSIs.

items.q: CMS continues to reimburse hospitals for treating “never events” as long as the care is documented accurately.
items.a: False
items.ex: Since 2008, CMS no longer reimburses hospitals for treating specific hospital-acquired conditions, or never events.
items.ww: Accurate documentation does not restore payment; CMS does not pay for treatment of these preventable adverse events.

alt.q: Under CMS policy, hospitals are no longer reimbursed for treating certain preventable hospital-acquired conditions.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: CMS stopped reimbursing hospitals for treatment of 11 specific hospital-acquired conditions, commonly called never events.
alt.ww: These preventable adverse events are not paid for, which makes accurate documentation of patient status crucial.

items.q: What are diagnosis-related groups (DRGs)?
items.a: Classifications based on primary and secondary medical diagnoses used to set Medicare reimbursement
items.ex: DRGs classify patients by primary and secondary medical diagnoses and form the basis for Medicare reimbursement to agencies.
w: Groups of nursing diagnoses used to decide nurse staffing levels for each unit
DRGs are based on medical diagnoses and set reimbursement, not nurse staffing.
Categories of patients grouped by age used to assign them to hospital units
DRGs are based on medical diagnoses, not patient age or unit placement.
Lists of abbreviations that agencies approve for use in documentation
Approved abbreviation lists are a TJC requirement unrelated to DRGs.

alt.q: How does Medicare reimburse a health care agency for care provided under a diagnosis-related group?
alt.a: With a predetermined dollar amount for each DRG
alt.ex: Health care agencies are reimbursed a predetermined dollar amount by Medicare for each DRG.
w: With the full amount the agency bills for each day of care
DRG payment is a predetermined amount, not whatever the agency bills.
With an amount based on the number of nurses assigned
Reimbursement is tied to the DRG classification, not nurse assignments.
With an amount set by the patient’s private insurer
Medicare sets the predetermined DRG amount; private insurers review records separately.

items.q: [[Diagnosis-related groups|DRGs|diagnosis related groups|DRG]] are classifications based on a patient’s primary and secondary medical diagnoses that serve as the basis for Medicare reimbursement.
items.ex: Medicare pays a health care agency a predetermined dollar amount for each DRG.

alt.q: Medicare reimburses an agency a predetermined dollar amount for each [[diagnosis-related group|DRG|diagnosis related group]], a classification based on primary and secondary medical diagnoses.
alt.ex: Medicare pays a health care agency a predetermined dollar amount for each DRG.

items.q: A nurse uses several specialty dressings, a wound vacuum device, and extra supplies while caring for a patient with a complex wound. Why should the nurse document the supplies and equipment used?
items.a: It clarifies the treatment given and supports accurate, timely reimbursement
items.ex: Documenting nursing services, supplies, and equipment clarifies the treatment received and supports accurate and timely reimbursement.
w: It allows the unit to restock supplies without filing a separate order
Restocking is a supply-chain process; documentation supports care and reimbursement.
It proves the patient’s wound developed before admission to the hospital
Supply use does not show when a wound developed; the admission assessment does.
It is needed only when the patient has private insurance coverage
Medicare, private insurers, and federal auditors all review records to determine reimbursement.

alt.q: Which information do insurance companies obtain from documentation by all members of the health care team to determine payment?
alt.a: Severity of illness, intensity of services, and quality of care
alt.ex: Team documentation shows the severity of illness, intensity of services, and quality of care during an episode of care.
w: Number of visitors, length of visits, and family satisfaction
Visitor information is not used to determine reimbursement.
Staff salaries, unit budgets, and overtime hours
Agency finances are not drawn from patient documentation.
Patient’s employer, income, and credit history
Reimbursement is based on care provided, not the patient’s finances.

items.q: A quality improvement (QI) nurse reviews a unit’s health records to see whether nurses consistently document implementation of fall precautions. Which purpose of the health record does this review serve?
items.a: Auditing and monitoring
items.ex: Record audits show whether providers follow standards of care and identify areas for improvement and staff development.
w: Research
Research uses de-identified data with IRB approval to answer study questions, not to check unit practice.
Reimbursement
Reimbursement review determines payment, not whether nurses follow fall precautions.
Education
Educational review helps a nurse learn about patients, not monitor unit compliance.

alt.q: What information do audits of health records provide to a health care agency?
alt.a: Recurrent problems, specific incidents, and whether standards of care are followed
alt.ex: Audits reveal recurrent health care problems, patient incidents, and adherence to standards of care.
w: Each nurse’s personal opinions about the care given on the unit
Audits review documented care, not personal opinions.
The predetermined Medicare payment for each patient’s diagnosis
Payment amounts are set by DRG classification, not by audits.
The names of patients eligible for upcoming research studies
Audits evaluate quality of care, not research recruitment.

items.q: A chart audit shows that nurses on a surgical unit often fail to document evaluation of pain management interventions. What should happen next with these findings?
items.a: Share the deficiencies with all nursing staff so practice or policy can change
items.ex: Deficiencies identified in audits are shared with all nursing staff so that changes in policy or practice can occur.
w: Keep the findings confidential within the quality improvement department
Findings are shared with staff, because hidden findings cannot change practice.
Ask the nurses to add late pain entries to every audited record
Adding entries to make records look complete does not address the practice gap.
Report each nurse involved to the state board of nursing
The book describes using audits for improvement and staff development, not board reporting.

alt.q: Which regulatory bodies require health care agencies to monitor and evaluate the quality and appropriateness of patient care?
alt.a: The Joint Commission and the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services
alt.ex: Regulations from TJC and CMS require agencies to monitor and evaluate the quality and appropriateness of care.
w: The American Nurses Association and the state boards of nursing
These groups set practice standards and licensure, not the cited monitoring regulations.
The Institutional Review Board and the Department of Justice
IRBs approve research; the cited monitoring requirement comes from TJC and CMS.
Private insurance carriers and hospital pharmacy committees
Insurers review records for payment; the monitoring requirement is from TJC and CMS.

items.q: Each nurse is held accountable for the accuracy of the documentation that the nurse enters into the patient’s record.
items.a: True
items.ex: As a member of the interprofessional team, you are accountable for the accuracy of what you document.
items.ww: Accountability for an entry rests with the person who made it, not with the provider or the unit.

alt.q: The health care provider is accountable for the accuracy of all nursing entries in a patient’s record.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Each nurse is accountable for the accuracy of the documentation that nurse enters.
alt.ww: Nurses, not providers, are responsible for the accuracy of their own entries; you chart only for yourself.

items.q: A nursing student reads the health record of an assigned patient before providing care. What is the main educational benefit of this review?
items.a: Learning the patient’s condition, response to treatment, and care likely needed
items.ex: Reading the record of an assigned patient is an effective way to learn the condition, treatment response, and care needed.
w: Gathering identifiable patient data to use in a class presentation
Patient data used for school must be de-identified and never removed with identifiers.
Checking whether other nurses’ entries meet accreditation standards
Monitoring compliance is the role of audits, not a student’s preparation.
Reviewing records of other patients on the unit for comparison
Students may access only records of patients they are assigned to care for.

alt.q: Over time, a nurse reviews the records of many patients with similar diagnoses. How does this help the nurse’s practice?
alt.a: It helps the nurse identify patterns and anticipate the assessments and care needed
alt.ex: Patterns found in records of similar patients help the nurse anticipate assessments, care, and responses to treatment.
w: It allows the nurse to skip assessments that are usually normal
Recognizing patterns guides assessment; it does not justify omitting assessments.
It provides identifiable data the nurse can publish without approval
Research use requires de-identified data and IRB approval.
It replaces the need to read the current patient’s health record
Each patient’s own record is still reviewed to provide safe care.

items.q: What is de-identification of health record data?
items.a: A process that prevents a person’s identity from being connected with information
items.ex: De-identification keeps a person’s identity from being linked to data, such as using a random number instead of a name.
w: A process that removes all clinical data from a patient’s record after discharge
De-identification removes identifiers, not clinical data, and records are not purged at discharge.
A process that verifies a patient’s identity before treatments are given
Verifying identity before care is a safety check, not de-identification.
A process that blocks unauthorized users from logging into the record
Blocking unauthorized log-ins is done with passwords and access codes.

alt.q: A nurse collecting research data replaces each patient’s name and Social Security number with a random number on the data form. Which process is the nurse using?
alt.a: De-identification
alt.ex: Using a random number instead of identifiers prevents the patient’s identity from being linked to the data.
w: Authentication
Authentication uses access codes and passwords to confirm authorized users.
Interoperability
Interoperability is the exchange of information among health care providers.
Back-timing
Back-timing is entering a late note at the appropriate time and date.

items.q: Using a random number instead of a patient’s name on a research data form is an example of [[de-identification|deidentification]].
items.ex: De-identification prevents a person’s identity from being connected with information taken from a health record.

alt.q: Health record data used for statistical analysis in research must undergo [[de-identification|deidentification]] so the patient’s identity cannot be linked to it.
alt.ex: De-identification prevents a person’s identity from being connected with information taken from a health record.

items.q: A nurse is collecting data from health records for an evidence-based practice project on postoperative complications. Which action best protects patient privacy?
items.a: Label each data form with a random number instead of the patient’s name
items.ex: De-identified data, labeled with random numbers rather than names or Social Security numbers, can be used for analysis.
w: Label each data form with the patient’s name and date of birth
Names and birth dates are identifiers that must not appear on research forms.
Label each data form with the patient’s Social Security number
A Social Security number identifies the patient and must be replaced by a random number.
Label each data form with the patient’s room number and diagnosis
Room numbers are identifiers that can connect data to a specific person.

alt.q: A nurse researcher suspects that early ambulation lowers postoperative complication rates and wants to review surgical patients’ records. What must the researcher do first?
alt.a: Obtain approval from the agency’s institutional review board
alt.ex: Nurse researchers must obtain IRB approval before reviewing health records for a study.
w: Obtain verbal approval from the charge nurse on each unit
A charge nurse cannot authorize research access to records; an IRB must.
Obtain a list of the patients’ home addresses for follow-up
Collecting identifiers conflicts with de-identification and does not authorize access.
Obtain copies of the records to review at home
Records must not be printed and removed; IRB approval comes first.

items.q: De-identified data from health records can be used for statistical analysis of which items? Select all that apply.
o: Frequency of clinical disorders
Frequency of clinical disorders is listed as a use of de-identified data.
Complications of illness or treatment
Complication rates can be analyzed with de-identified data.
Clinical outcomes achieved for specific illnesses
Clinical outcomes are an example of de-identified data analysis.
Patient mortality
Patient mortality is listed among analyses of de-identified data.
Contact information for recruiting individual patients
De-identified data cannot be linked to individuals, so they cannot be used to contact patients.
Billing statements for individual patients
Billing uses identified records for reimbursement, not de-identified research data.
items.ex: De-identified data support analysis of disorders, complications, therapies, outcomes, and mortality for research, EBP, and QI.

alt.q: A QI team plans to analyze de-identified health record data. Which questions could the team answer with these data? Select all that apply.
o: How often a specific complication occurs after surgery
Complication frequency is a typical analysis of de-identified data.
How often specific nursing therapies are used
Use of specific medical and nursing therapies can be analyzed.
What outcomes patients with a specific illness achieve
Clinical outcomes for specific illnesses are a listed use.
Which named patient had the longest hospital stay
De-identified data cannot reveal a specific patient’s identity.
What each patient’s home telephone number is
Telephone numbers are identifiers that are removed from de-identified data.
alt.ex: Analyses of de-identified data address clinical patterns, therapies, and outcomes without revealing who the patients are.

items.q: De-identified data from health records can contribute to evidence-based practice and quality improvement projects.
items.a: True
items.ex: Analysis of de-identified record data supports research, EBP, and QI, contributing to high-quality health care.
items.ww: Records are a recognized resource for research and QI when data are de-identified and approved.

alt.q: Health record data may be used only for direct patient care and never for research or quality improvement.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: With de-identification and approval, record data are used in research, EBP, and QI projects.
alt.ww: Research and QI are listed purposes of the health record, subject to privacy and ethical safeguards.

items.ex: The health record supports auditing, reimbursement, education, research, and legal purposes in addition to care and communication.

w: A QI nurse checks whether fall precautions are documented

An insurer reviews a record to decide on payment: Reimbursement.

mt.q: Match each use of the health record with the purpose it serves.
pairs: A QI nurse checks whether fall precautions are documented
An insurer reviews a record to decide on payment
A student reads an assigned patient’s record before care
A nurse compares complication rates using de-identified data
A record shows in court that standards of care were met
mt.ex: The health record supports auditing, reimbursement, education, research, and legal purposes in addition to care and communication.

items.q: A nurse educator wants to use a recent patient’s health record as a teaching case for a nursing class. Which action best addresses privacy and ethical considerations?
items.a: Remove all patient identifiers from the case before presenting it
items.ex: Records can serve education only when privacy and ethical considerations are met, so identifiers are removed.
w: Present the full record because the students are health care learners
Being a learner does not give students a right to identifiable patient data.
Present the record with the patient’s name but omit the room number
The name is an identifier that still links the data to the patient.
Ask the students to keep the patient’s name private after class
Relying on students’ discretion does not protect the patient; identifiers must be removed.

alt.q: Which statement about using health records for nursing education and research is accurate?
alt.a: Privacy and ethical considerations must be addressed before records are used
alt.ex: Health records are a resource for education and research, but privacy and ethical considerations must be addressed.
w: Records may be used freely because education benefits future patients
Educational value does not override the patient’s right to privacy.
Records may never be used for any purpose other than direct care
Records are a recognized resource for education and research with safeguards.
Records may be used only after the patient has been discharged
Discharge status does not remove the need for privacy safeguards.

items.q: A physical therapist reads the nurse’s entry describing how far a patient walked and how the patient tolerated it before planning therapy. Which purpose of the health record does this illustrate?
items.a: Interprofessional communication
items.ex: The record allows members of the interprofessional team to communicate about patient problems and responses to care.
w: Reimbursement
Reimbursement concerns payment for services, not planning therapy.
Auditing and monitoring
Auditing evaluates quality and compliance across records, not planning individual care.
Research
Research uses de-identified data under IRB approval, not routine care planning.

alt.q: A dietitian, a nurse, and a health care provider all read and add to the same patient’s record to coordinate care. Which purpose of the record are they using?
alt.a: Facilitating communication among health care providers
alt.ex: Facilitating interprofessional communication is a core purpose of data entered into the health record.
w: Justifying billing for the agency
Billing justification is a different purpose that supports reimbursement.
Providing data for statistical research
Research uses de-identified data, not coordination of one patient’s care.
Evaluating staff for performance reviews
The record is not described as a tool for staff performance reviews.

sections.name: Interprofessional communication within the health record

items.q: When should a nurse document assessment findings and patient information in the health record?
items.a: In real time or as soon as possible after providing care
items.ex: Documenting in real time or immediately after care enhances communication and promotes safe patient care.
w: At the end of the shift so all entries are made together
Waiting until shift’s end delays communication and increases the chance of forgotten details.
Before the care is provided so the plan is visible to the team
Documenting care before it is given is inaccurate; entries describe care already provided.
Only when a finding is abnormal or the patient’s condition changes
All nursing care is documented, not only abnormal findings.

alt.q: A nurse completes a patient assessment at 0900. To best support communication with the team, when should the nurse document it?
alt.a: Immediately after completing the assessment
alt.ex: Documenting immediately after an assessment keeps the record current and supports safe, timely decisions.
w: During the hand-off report at 1900
Delaying until hand-off leaves the record out of date for other team members.
After all morning medications are given
Postponing entries risks forgetting information and delays team access.
When the health care provider asks for the findings
The record must be current for everyone, not only on request.

items.q: When a plan of care is not communicated to all members of the health care team, care becomes fragmented and delays or omissions often occur.
items.a: True
items.ex: Poor communication of the plan leads to fragmented care, repeated tasks, and delays or omissions in care.
items.ww: The book directly links failure to communicate the plan with fragmented, repeated, or omitted care.

alt.q: If each team member knows his or her own tasks, communicating the overall plan of care to the whole team has little effect on patient care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Without a shared plan, care becomes fragmented, tasks are repeated, and delays or omissions occur.
alt.ww: The quality of care depends on communication among all team members, not only individual task knowledge.

items.q: Which information is contained in all health records? Select all that apply.
o: Informed consent for treatment and procedures
Informed consent is part of every health record.
Therapeutic orders, including code status
Orders such as do-not-resuscitate status are part of the record.
Patient education
Patient education is recorded in every health record.
Discharge summary and plan
The discharge summary and plan are standard record content.
The nurse’s personal opinions about the family
Personal opinions are subjective and do not belong in the record.
Unit staffing assignments for the shift
Staffing assignments are unit management information, not patient record content.
items.ex: All health records include identification, consents, orders, care plans, assessments, results, education, and discharge information.

alt.q: A nursing student reviews an assigned patient’s record. Which items should the student expect to find? Select all that apply.
o: Patient identification and demographic data
Identification and demographics appear in all health records.
Existence of a living will or durable power of attorney for health care
Advance directive documents are noted when applicable.
Diagnostic study results
Diagnostic results are part of every health record.
Summary of operative procedures
Operative summaries are included in the record.
Comments about errors made by other staff
Critical comments about other professionals must not be documented.
alt.ex: The record contains identification, advance directive status, consents, results, operative summaries, and more.

items.q: A nurse documenting on a paper record realizes an entry was written for the wrong time. Which action is correct?
items.a: Draw a single line through the error, write “error” above it, initial it, and chart correctly
items.ex: A single line, the word error, and the nurse’s initials keep the original readable and show no attempt to hide information.
w: Cover the error with correction fluid, then write the correct entry over it
Correction fluid makes charting illegible and looks like an attempt to hide information.
Scratch out the error completely so it cannot be misread, then write the entry
Scratching out errors appears to deface the record or hide information.
Erase the error carefully and rewrite the entry in the same space
Erasing is not permitted because it appears to alter the legal record.

alt.q: A nurse uses paper documentation at an agency. Which practice follows legal guidelines?
alt.a: Writing legibly in black pen and never erasing entries
alt.ex: Paper documentation uses black pen and legible handwriting; erasing, correction fluid, or scratching out are not allowed.
w: Writing in pencil so that errors can be corrected neatly
Pencil can be erased, which undermines the integrity of the legal record.
Using correction tape so that the record stays tidy
Correction tape hides the original entry and appears to deface the record.
Writing in any ink color as long as entries are legible
The book specifies a black pen for paper documentation.

items.q: A nurse believes an analgesic order is incorrect and calls the health care provider. Which documentation is appropriate?
items.a: “Provider was called to clarify order for analgesic.”
items.ex: Document that you sought clarification; a nurse who carries out an order known to be incorrect is equally liable.
w: “Provider made error in analgesic order.”
Documenting “provider made error” is a critical comment that should be avoided.
“Provider wrote another careless analgesic order.”
Retaliatory or critical comments can be used as evidence of nonprofessional behavior.
“Analgesic given as ordered despite concerns.”
Giving a medication known to be incorrect makes the nurse as liable as the provider.

alt.q: Why should a nurse question and clarify a health care provider’s order that appears incorrect before carrying it out?
alt.a: A nurse who performs an incorrect order is as liable as the provider
alt.ex: If you perform an order known to be incorrect, you are just as liable for prosecution as the health care provider.
w: Only the provider is liable for harm from an incorrect order
The nurse who carries out a known incorrect order shares liability.
Agency policy requires clarification only for verbal orders
Any order the nurse questions should be clarified and documented.
A pharmacist must cosign every order the nurse questions
The guideline is to seek and document clarification from the provider.

items.q: A nurse who cared for a patient earlier has left the unit for the day and calls with information that needs to be documented. Which action by the nurse receiving the call is correct?
items.a: Document the information, naming the caller as the source and noting it was received by telephone
items.ex: The exception to charting only for yourself requires naming the source and noting the information came by telephone.
w: Document the information under the other nurse’s name using that nurse’s log-in
Using another person’s log-in violates security; each user’s ID is an electronic signature.
Refuse to document the information because nurses chart only for themselves
The book allows this exception when the source and telephone method are documented.
Document the information as the receiving nurse’s own direct observation
Recording someone else’s findings as your own is inaccurate; the source must be named.

alt.q: Why does a nurse chart only for himself or herself and never for someone else?
alt.a: Each nurse is accountable for information that he or she enters into the chart
alt.ex: You are accountable for what you enter, so you never chart care that someone else provided or observed.
w: Charting for others takes more time than charting for oneself
The rule is about accountability, not time.
Only charge nurses are allowed to chart care given by others
No nurse charts for another; accountability rests with the person entering data.
Each nurse’s entries are billed separately to the patient
The guideline is based on accountability for entries, not billing.

items.q: Which nursing note best meets legal guidelines for documentation?
items.a: “Patient refused morning medications, stating, ‘I don’t want any more pills today.’”
items.ex: Objective descriptions of behavior with the patient’s comments in quotation marks are legally sound.
w: “Patient was uncooperative and rude all morning and had a bad day.”
Judgmental, vague phrases are subjective and do not describe the patient’s actual behavior.
“Status unchanged since last shift; no new concerns noted.”
Generalized, empty phrases do not reflect a patient assessment.
“Night nurse again failed to give the patient’s ordered medications.”
Critical comments about other professionals can be used as evidence of nonprofessional behavior.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid documenting phrases such as “had good day” or “status unchanged”?
alt.a: They are subjective and do not reflect a patient assessment
alt.ex: Generalized, empty phrases are subjective; use complete, concise descriptions so documentation is objective and factual.
w: They are too long and slow down documentation
These phrases are short; the problem is that they lack assessment content.
They are on TJC’s official “do not use” list
The “do not use” list covers abbreviations, not these phrases.
They can be documented only by the health care provider
No one should use these phrases because they do not describe the patient’s status.

items.q: Which documentation mistakes can result in malpractice? Select all that apply.
o: Failing to document medication administration
Missing medication administration entries is a listed malpractice risk.
Failing to document discontinued medications
Not documenting discontinued medications can lead to malpractice.
Keeping incomplete or illegible records
Incomplete or illegible records are a listed documentation mistake.
Failing to document a change in the patient’s condition
Not recording changes in condition or medication reactions is a malpractice risk.
Documenting care in real time
Timely documentation reduces errors and is recommended practice.
Using the patient’s exact words in quotation marks
Quoting the patient is a recommended way to record subjective data.
items.ex: Malpractice can result from failing to document key information, nursing actions, medications, reactions, or changes, or from incomplete or illegible records.

alt.q: A nurse manager reviews documentation risks with new graduates. Which omissions should the manager identify as possible causes of malpractice? Select all that apply.
o: Not recording a patient’s reaction to a medication
Failing to document medication reactions is a listed malpractice risk.
Not recording nursing actions that were performed
Failing to document nursing actions can result in malpractice.
Not recording pertinent health or medication information
Omitting pertinent health or medication information is a listed mistake.
Not recording the patient’s favorite television shows
Irrelevant details are not required and should be avoided.
Not recording opinions about the patient’s family
Personal opinions do not belong in the record at all.
alt.ex: Documenting nursing actions, medications, reactions, and pertinent information limits liability.

items.q: Once logged on to the electronic health record, a nurse may leave the screen unattended briefly as long as the nurse stays on the unit.
items.a: False
items.ex: Do not leave the computer screen unattended once logged on, because entries are tied to your user identification.
items.ww: Any unattended log-in allows others to view PHI or enter data under your electronic signature.

alt.q: A nurse’s electronic signature is associated with the nurse’s user identification and password, so the nurse uses only his or her own log-in.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Each user log-in is an electronic signature, so you protect your ID and password and use only your own.
alt.ww: Sharing or borrowing log-ins would attach entries to the wrong person and breach security.

items.q: Before electronic health records, why did paper health records jeopardize patient safety?
items.a: Each visit had a separate record, so allergies and medications were lost between visits
items.ex: Episode-oriented paper records made previous information hard to review, so key data were lost from one episode to the next.
w: Paper records could be read by only one health care provider per day
The safety problem was separate records per episode, not daily access limits.
Paper records did not include the patient’s identification data
Paper records contained identification; the issue was data lost between episodes.
Paper records were required to be destroyed after each discharge
Paper records were not destroyed; they were episode oriented and hard to link.

alt.q: What is a unique feature of an electronic health record (EHR) compared with episode-oriented paper records?
alt.a: It integrates all patient information into one record across every encounter
alt.ex: An EHR integrates all patient information into one record regardless of how many times the patient enters the system.
w: It creates a new record for each hospital admission or clinic visit
A separate record for each visit describes the older paper system.
It limits access to one health care provider at a time
EHRs allow multiple providers customized access at the same time.
It stores only the current admission’s data to protect privacy
An EHR is a lifetime record linking all previous encounters.

items.ex: These terms describe the electronic record and the security mechanisms that protect patient information.

That goes with Electronic health record system (EHRS).
Individually identifiable information about past, present, or future health status
That goes with Protected health information (PHI).
Hardware and software that protect a private network from outside hackers
That goes with Firewall.

items.q: A nurse explains to a new graduate the key advantages of the electronic health record (EHR) for nursing. Which statement is accurate?
items.a: “It lets nurses compare current data with data from previous encounters.”
items.ex: Key EHR advantages for nursing include comparing current with past data, ongoing symptom management, and an ongoing education record.
w: “It eliminates the need to protect patient privacy and confidentiality.”
EHRs must support confidentiality, privacy, and audit trails.
“It allows anyone in the agency to view any patient’s record.”
Only team members directly involved in a patient’s care have legitimate access.
“It removes the need for nurses to document in real time.”
Real-time documentation remains essential with an EHR.

alt.q: Which feature does an electronic health record (EHR) provide that supports ongoing patient teaching?
alt.a: An ongoing record of education provided and the patient’s response
alt.ex: The EHR keeps an ongoing record of health education and the patient’s response, a key advantage for nursing.
w: A separate teaching record that is deleted after each discharge
EHR data are linked across encounters rather than deleted at discharge.
Automatic teaching that replaces the nurse’s instruction
The EHR records teaching; it does not replace the nurse’s instruction.
A list of teaching topics available only to the provider
EHR information is available to authorized members of the whole team.

items.q: Which attributes are electronic health records (EHRs) expected to have? Select all that apply.
o: A lifetime record linking all previous encounters
EHRs link all patient data from previous encounters into a lifetime record.
A problem list showing current problems and their status
A problem list with occurrences and status is an expected component.
Support for confidentiality, privacy, and audit trails
EHRs must support confidentiality, privacy, and audit trails.
Continuous access for multiple authorized users at the same time
Multiple providers can access customized views at the same time.
Access limited to one provider at a time
EHRs allow simultaneous access by multiple authorized providers.
A separate new record for each episode of care
Separate episode records describe old paper systems, not EHRs.
items.ex: EHR attributes include a lifetime record, problem list, privacy and audit support, continuous shared access, decision tools, and cost and quality measures.

alt.q: An agency is evaluating whether its EHR meets agreed-on standards. Which features should the EHR include? Select all that apply.
o: Support for decision analysis tools
EHRs should support the use of decision analysis tools.
Direct entry of patient data by providers
Direct data entry by providers is an expected attribute.
Mechanisms for measuring the cost and quality of care
EHRs include ways to measure cost and quality.
A method to document clinical reasoning for diagnoses
EHRs document the rationale for diagnoses so decision making can be tracked.
Removal of all past data at each new admission
EHRs keep a lifetime record linking all previous encounters.
alt.ex: Standard EHRs support decision tools, direct provider entry, documentation of reasoning, and measurement of cost and quality.

items.q: A nurse needs a patient’s home telephone number to reschedule an appointment. Under the HIPAA Privacy Rule, what information should the nurse access?
items.a: Only the patient’s telephone information
items.ex: The Privacy Rule limits disclosure or requests to the specific information required for a particular purpose.
w: The patient’s complete health record
Accessing the full record exceeds what is needed for rescheduling.
The patient’s problem list and telephone number
Clinical problems are not needed to reschedule an appointment.
The telephone numbers of all patients due for follow-up
Other patients’ information is not needed for this purpose.

alt.q: Which requirement is part of the HIPAA Privacy Rule?
alt.a: Requests for health information are limited to what a purpose requires
alt.ex: Under the Privacy Rule, disclosure or requests are limited to the specific information needed for a particular purpose.
w: Safeguards are specified for 18 elements of electronic PHI
Safeguards for electronic PHI are specified by the Security Rule.
Patients may not read or copy their own health records
Patients have the right to request copies of and read their records.
All employees may access any record for continuing education
Access requires appropriate permission and a legitimate need.

items.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of patient confidentiality during clinical practice?
items.a: “I will copy only de-identified data into my notebook while viewing the record.”
items.ex: Students transcribe needed information directly from the screen and de-identify all data used for clinical assignments.
w: “I will print the patient’s record so I can finish my care plan at home.”
Never print information from the record to take away for assignments or personal use.
“I will look up my roommate’s record because she was admitted to this unit.”
Viewing records of patients not in your care is unethical and traceable through log-ins.
“I will include the room number and birth date on my care plan for accuracy.”
Room numbers and birth dates are identifiers that must not appear in student work.

alt.q: A nursing student is assigned to care for one patient on a busy unit. Which action by the student is appropriate?
alt.a: Reviewing only that patient’s record and interprofessional plan of care
alt.ex: Students review records only for information needed to provide safe and effective care to assigned patients.
w: Reviewing other patients’ records to learn about their conditions
Accessing other patients’ records is unethical and can lead to dismissal.
Sharing the patient’s diagnosis with classmates during lunch
Patient information is shared with classmates only during clinical conferences.
Printing the patient’s laboratory results to study at home
Information printed must be for professional use only and not removed with identifiers.

items.q: Patients have the right to request copies of their health record and read the information in it.
items.a: True
items.ex: Patients may request copies and read their records; agency policies describe how records are shared.
items.ww: The book states this right directly; written permission is usually needed for release to others.

alt.q: Patients may not read their own health records without a court order.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients have the right to request copies of their health record and read the information.
alt.ww: No court order is needed; agency policy guides how records are shared with patients.

items.q: The HIPAA [[Security Rule]] specifies administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for protected health information in electronic form.
items.ex: The Security Rule protects 18 specific elements of electronic PHI, whereas the Privacy Rule limits disclosures to what is needed.

alt.q: Administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for 18 elements of electronic PHI are set by HIPAA’s [[Security Rule]].
alt.ex: The Security Rule protects 18 specific elements of electronic PHI, whereas the Privacy Rule limits disclosures to what is needed.

items.q: A nurse must fax protected health information (PHI) to a clinic the unit has never sent records to before. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Verify the number by sending a test fax before sending PHI
items.ex: For any new recipient, verify the fax number with a test fax before sending PHI.
w: Send the PHI and call the clinic afterward to confirm receipt
Verification occurs before PHI is sent, so it cannot go to the wrong number.
Send the PHI without a cover page to reduce the number of pages
A cover page should always be used when faxing PHI.
Send the full record in case the clinic needs more information
Faxed information should not exceed what was requested or clinically needed.

alt.q: Which practice enhances the security of faxing protected health information (PHI)?
alt.a: Using a fax machine in a secure, nonpublic area used only for PHI
alt.ex: PHI fax machines are located in secure, nonpublic areas designated exclusively for PHI and kept separate from others.
w: Using any available fax machine on the unit to save time
PHI should be sent from a designated, secure machine, not any machine.
Leaving faxed documents in the tray for the recipient to collect
Faxes with PHI must be stored or disposed of according to policy.
Sending all information in the record to avoid repeat requests
Information sent should not exceed what was requested or required.

items.q: A coworker asks a nurse for the nurse’s password to look up a lab result quickly because the coworker forgot their own. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “I can’t share my password; please use your own log-in or ask the system administrator.”
items.ex: Never share your computer password with anyone under any circumstances; entries are tied to your user identification.
w: “Sure, just log out when you finish so no one else sees the screen.”
Sharing a password is never allowed, even briefly or with precautions.
“I’ll log in for you, and you can look up the result yourself.”
Letting another person work under your log-in attaches their actions to your electronic signature.
“Use it this once, and I’ll change it at the end of the shift.”
Changing the password later does not make sharing it acceptable.

alt.q: Which practice describes a strong, secure password system for an electronic health record?
alt.a: Combining letters, numbers, and symbols and changing passwords frequently
alt.ex: Strong passwords combine letters, numbers, and symbols, and good systems require frequent changes.
w: Using the nurse’s birth date so it is easy to remember
Personal dates are easy to guess and weaken security.
Keeping the same password for years to avoid confusion
Good systems require frequent changes to prevent tampering.
Sharing the password with the charge nurse in case of emergency
Passwords are known only to the user and system administrators.

items.q: At the end of the shift, a nurse has a printed nursing activities work list containing patient information. What should the nurse do with it?
items.a: Shred it or place it in a locked receptacle for shredding
items.ex: Printed PHI is destroyed by shredding or placing it in a locked receptacle once it is no longer needed.
w: Place it in the regular trash can at the nurses’ station
Regular trash exposes PHI to unauthorized persons.
Take it home to review before the next shift
Printed information must not leave the agency.
Leave it at the station for the oncoming nurse to use
PHI must not be left in view of unauthorized persons; it is destroyed when no longer needed.

alt.q: Historically, what has been the primary source of accidental, unauthorized disclosure of protected health information (PHI)?
alt.a: Information printed from the record or faxed to other providers
alt.ex: Printed and faxed information has been the main source of accidental disclosure, so such papers are destroyed after use.
w: Information spoken aloud during hand-off report
The book identifies printed and faxed information as the primary source.
Information viewed through computer privacy filters
Privacy filters are a protective measure, not a source of disclosure.
Information stored behind the agency firewall
Firewalls protect networks from outside hackers and misuse.

sections.name: Standards and guidelines for quality nursing documentation

items.q: Current documentation standards require that patients admitted to a health care agency be assessed for which needs? Select all that apply.
o: Psychosocial needs
Psychosocial needs are part of the required admission assessment.
Spiritual and cultural needs
Spiritual and cultural needs must be assessed on admission.
Knowledge level
Knowledge level is a required admission assessment area.
Discharge planning needs
Discharge planning needs are assessed from admission.
Political beliefs
Political beliefs are not part of the required admission assessment.
Family members’ employment history
Family employment history is not listed among required assessment areas.
items.ex: Standards require assessment of physical, psychosocial, environmental, self-care, spiritual, cultural, knowledge level, and discharge planning needs.

alt.q: A nurse completes an admission assessment that meets accreditation documentation standards. Which areas must be included? Select all that apply.
o: Physical needs
Physical needs are part of the required admission assessment.
Environmental needs
Environmental needs must be assessed on admission.
Self-care needs
Self-care needs are a required assessment area.
The patient’s credit history
Financial history is not part of the required nursing admission assessment.
The nurse’s opinion of the patient’s lifestyle
Personal opinions are not documented; assessments are objective.
alt.ex: Admission assessments cover physical, psychosocial, environmental, self-care, spiritual, cultural, knowledge, and discharge needs.

items.q: A nurse is documenting care for a patient who reports feeling nervous. Which entry is most factual?
items.a: “Heart rate 110, respirations 22 and slightly labored; patient states, ‘I feel very nervous.’”
items.ex: Factual entries combine objective measurements with the patient’s exact words in quotation marks.
w: “Patient seems anxious and appears to be worried about tomorrow’s test results.”
“Seems” and “appears” state an opinion and do not describe observable behavior.
“Patient is apparently nervous today, so reassurance was provided as needed.”
“Apparently” is vague and the entry gives no objective signs of anxiety.
“Patient is anxious as usual and is being difficult with staff this shift.”
This entry is judgmental and subjective, with no measurable data.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid terms such as “appears,” “seems,” and “apparently” in documentation?
alt.a: They suggest an opinion rather than communicating facts
alt.ex: Vague terms suggest opinion and do not inform other caregivers about the patient’s actual behaviors.
w: They are on TJC’s official “do not use” list
The “do not use” list includes abbreviations, not these words.
They make entries too long to read quickly
The problem is vagueness, not length.
They are permitted only in subjective data sections
The only subjective data recorded are the patient’s own statements.

items.q: Which entry about a patient’s fluid intake is most accurate?
items.a: “Intake, 360 mL of water.”
items.ex: Exact measurements establish accuracy and help show whether a condition has changed.
w: “Patient drank an adequate amount of fluid.”
“Adequate” is vague and cannot be compared over time.
“Patient drank a good amount of water.”
“A good amount” is not a measurement.
“Patient drank most of the water pitcher.”
“Most of the pitcher” is an estimate, not an exact measurement.

alt.q: Which description of a surgical incision is most accurate?
alt.a: “Approximated, 5 cm long, without redness, drainage, or edema.”
alt.ex: Exact size and specific findings make an incision description accurate and comparable over time.
w: “Large abdominal incision healing well, no problems.”
“Large” and “healing well” are vague and not measurable.
“Incision looks good and seems to be closing nicely.”
“Looks good” and “seems” express opinion rather than fact.
“Incision about the usual size, healing normally.”
“Usual size” and “normally” do not give exact data.

items.q: How should a nurse document subjective data provided by a patient?
items.a: Record the patient’s exact words in quotation marks, with supporting objective data
items.ex: Subjective data are the patient’s statements, documented in quotation marks and supported by objective findings.
w: Summarize the patient’s feelings in the nurse’s own words without quotation marks
The patient’s exact words in quotation marks are documented whenever possible.
Record only the nurse’s interpretation of what the patient meant
Interpretations are opinions; the record contains the patient’s actual statements.
Omit subjective statements because only objective data belong in the record
Patient statements are the subjective data included in the record.

alt.q: Which subjective data belong in a patient’s health record?
alt.a: Statements made by the patient
alt.ex: The only subjective data included in the record are statements made by the patient.
w: Statements about the patient made by visitors
Visitor opinions are not the patient’s subjective data.
The nurse’s impression of the patient’s mood
The nurse’s impressions are opinions, not patient statements.
Comments from staff about the patient’s attitude
Staff opinions about the patient do not belong in the record.

items.q: Words such as “appears,” “seems,” and “apparently” should be avoided in documentation because they suggest the nurse is stating an opinion.
items.a: True
items.ex: Vague terms suggest opinion and do not accurately communicate the patient’s behaviors to other caregivers.
items.ww: Factual records contain clear, objective descriptions, so opinion-signaling words are avoided.

alt.q: Using qualifiers such as “appears” and “seems” makes documentation more factual because it avoids overstating findings.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Qualifiers such as “appears” and “seems” signal opinion and make documentation less factual.
alt.ww: Factual documentation describes what was observed and measured, not impressions softened by qualifiers.

items.q: Which do-not-use abbreviation is written out as “unit” because it can be mistaken for 0, 4, or “cc”?
items.a: U, u
items.ex: TJC lists U or u for unit as do not use; write “unit” because it is mistaken for 0, 4, or cc.
w: IU
IU is mistaken for IV or the number 10; write “International Unit.”
QD
QD is mistaken for QOD; write “daily.”
MS
MS can mean morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate; write the full name.

alt.q: In addition to the “do not use” list, what does The Joint Commission require each health care agency to develop?
alt.a: A list of standard abbreviations, symbols, and acronyms for all team members
alt.ex: TJC requires agencies to develop a list of standard abbreviations, symbols, and acronyms used by the whole team.
w: A list of medications that may be ordered only by telephone
This is not a TJC requirement described for abbreviations.
A list of nurses approved to create new abbreviations
Agencies set one standard list for everyone rather than letting individuals create abbreviations.
A list of abbreviations that may be used only on paper records
The standard list applies to documenting and communicating care in any format.

items.q: A nurse reads a handwritten order for “MS 4 mg IV every 4 hours as needed for pain.” What is the safety concern with this order?
items.a: MS can mean either morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate
items.ex: MS is on TJC’s do-not-use list because it can mean morphine sulfate or magnesium sulfate.
w: MS can be mistaken for the number 10 or for IV
Being mistaken for IV or 10 is the problem with IU.
MS can be mistaken for the abbreviation QOD
QD and QOD are mistaken for each other, not MS.
MS is missing the leading zero needed for the dose
Leading zeros apply to doses less than 1, not the drug name.

alt.q: What should be written instead of “MSO4” or “MgSO4” in medication orders?
alt.a: “Morphine sulfate” or “magnesium sulfate”
alt.ex: Because these abbreviations are confused for one another, the full drug names are written out.
w: “MS” for morphine and “MG” for magnesium
Shortened forms remain confusing; the full names are required.
“Morph” for morphine and “Mag” for magnesium
Informal shortened names do not eliminate the risk of confusion.
The drug class and dose without the drug name
The drug name must be written out completely.

items.q: A trailing zero, such as writing “5.0 mg,” may be used in medication orders to show the precision of a dose.
items.a: False
items.ex: Trailing zeros may not be used in medication orders or medication-related documentation because the decimal point can be missed.
items.ww: A missed decimal in 5.0 mg could be read as 50 mg, so trailing zeros are prohibited for medications.

alt.q: A trailing zero may be used to show precision for values such as laboratory results or catheter sizes, but not in medication orders.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: TJC allows trailing zeros only where precision must be shown, such as lab results, lesion sizes, or tube sizes.
alt.ww: The exception for precision never extends to medication orders or medication documentation.

items.q: Writing “0.5 mg” rather than “.5 mg” uses a [[leading zero]] so that the decimal point is not missed.
items.ex: Lack of a leading zero is on TJC’s do-not-use list; write 0.X mg.

alt.q: TJC prohibits omitting the [[leading zero]] in doses such as .5 mg because the decimal point can be missed.
alt.ex: Lack of a leading zero is on TJC’s do-not-use list; write 0.X mg.

items.q: A nursing student is documenting care on a paper record. How should the student sign each entry?
items.a: With full name and the nursing student abbreviation, such as NS or SN
items.ex: Students documenting on paper write their full name and the nursing student abbreviation, NS or SN.
w: With first name only, because students cannot use credentials
Each entry must clearly identify the author with name and role.
With the clinical instructor’s name and credentials
Students chart for themselves; no one signs another person’s name.
With initials only, with no full name in the record
If initials are used, the full name and role must appear at least once.

alt.q: A nurse documenting on paper uses initials to sign entries. What else is required?
alt.a: The full name and credentials must appear at least once in the record
alt.ex: When initials are used, the full name and credentials/title/role are documented at least once so others can identify the author.
w: A witness must countersign each initialed entry
Countersigning is not required; the full name must appear at least once.
The initials must be written in red ink
Paper documentation uses black pen.
Initials may be used only for entries made after midnight
Initials are allowed anytime if the full name appears once.

items.q: Which activities or findings should a nurse document at the time they occur? Select all that apply.
o: Vital signs
Vital signs are documented at the time of occurrence.
Pain assessment
Pain assessments are documented when they occur.
Administration of medications and treatments
Medications and treatments are documented at the time given.
Change in status and who was notified
Status changes, treatment, and who was notified are documented right away.
Teaching the nurse plans to provide later in the week
Documentation records care that has occurred, not future plans as completed care.
Comments about a coworker’s performance
Critical comments about coworkers should never be documented.
items.ex: Vital signs, pain, medications, status changes, preoperative preparation, admission or discharge, and responses are documented when they occur.

alt.q: A nurse uses a workstation on wheels to document in real time. Which events should be documented at the time they occur? Select all that apply.
o: Preoperative checklist completion
Preparation for surgery, including the preoperative checklist, is documented at the time.
A patient’s transfer to another unit
Admission, transfer, discharge, or death is documented at the time of occurrence.
The patient’s response to an intervention
Patient responses to treatment are documented when they occur.
Hygiene supplies needed for tomorrow
Supply planning is not a patient care event to document.
The nurse’s break times during the shift
Staff break times are not patient documentation.
alt.ex: Timely entries of key events prevent unsafe care caused by delayed documentation.

items.q: A nurse administers a medication at 10:22 p.m. How is this time documented in military time?
items.ex: In military time, p.m. hours add 12, so 10:22 p.m. is written as 2222.
w: 1022 is 10:22 a.m. in military time.
2022 is 8:22 p.m. in military time.
0222 is 2:22 a.m. in military time.

alt.q: In military time, how is 1 minute after midnight written?
alt.ex: The military clock ends at midnight as 2400 and begins 1 minute after midnight as 0001.
w: The military clock ends at 2400; the next minute starts the new day at 0001.
1201 is 1 minute after noon in military time.
0101 is 1:01 a.m. in military time.

items.q: In military time, 3:45 p.m. is documented as [[1545]].
items.ex: Military time uses one 24-hour cycle, so p.m. hours add 12 to avoid confusing a.m. and p.m.

alt.q: A nurse documenting a dressing change done at 3:45 p.m. writes the time in military format as [[1545]].
alt.ex: Military time uses one 24-hour cycle, so p.m. hours add 12 to avoid confusing a.m. and p.m.

items.q: At 1500, a patient reports a throbbing headache rated 6 on a 0-to-10 scale, and the nurse gives acetaminophen 650 mg PO. Which documentation is most complete?
items.a: Time, drug, dose, route, pain rating before, and pain rating 30 minutes after
items.ex: Medication documentation includes time, name, dose, route, preliminary assessment, and the patient’s response.
w: Time and drug name only, because the dose and route appear in the order
Dose, route, assessment, and response are all part of medication documentation.
Drug, dose, and route, with the pain rating added at the end of shift
Pain assessment and response are documented at the time, not at shift’s end.
Patient’s pain rating only, because the bar-code system logs the drug
The nurse documents the complete medication entry and the patient’s response.

alt.q: When using a bar-code medication administration program, when should the nurse document a medication?
alt.a: At the time of administration or immediately after
alt.ex: Medication administration is documented when given, or immediately after, to keep the record current and safe.
w: At the end of the medication pass for all patients
Delaying documentation risks errors such as repeated doses.
Before preparing the medication at the dispensing cabinet
Documenting before giving a drug records care that has not happened.
Only if the patient experiences a reaction
Every administration is documented, not only those with reactions.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient how to use an inhaler. Which entry best documents the teaching?
items.a: Inhaler use taught by demonstration and booklet; patient did a correct return demonstration
items.ex: Teaching documentation includes the information presented, the method used, and the patient’s response, such as return demonstration.
w: Inhaler teaching completed; patient seemed to understand all of the instructions
“Seemed to understand” is vague and gives no evidence of learning.
Patient was given an inhaler booklet to read later at home after discharge
This entry omits the patient’s response and evidence of understanding.
Inhaler teaching planned; will review with the patient on a future shift
This entry describes a plan rather than teaching that occurred.

alt.q: Which evidence of understanding should a nurse document after patient and family teaching?
alt.a: Teach-back, return demonstration, or change in behavior
alt.ex: Teaching entries include the patient’s response, such as questions and evidence of understanding like teach-back.
w: The nurse’s belief that the patient will comply
A belief is an opinion, not evidence of understanding.
The number of minutes spent in the teaching session
Time spent does not show whether the patient learned.
A note that the booklet was placed at the bedside
Providing materials alone does not show understanding.

items.q: A nurse documents discharge planning for a patient going home after surgery. Which content best meets the criteria for discharge planning documentation?
items.a: Measurable expected outcomes and the need for referrals
items.ex: Table 26.2 lists measurable expected outcomes and need for referrals as criteria for discharge planning documentation.
w: General statements that the patient is doing well
Vague statements are not measurable and do not meet documentation criteria.
The nurse’s opinion about the family’s ability to cope
Opinions are not documented; criteria call for measurable outcomes.
A list of the patient’s visitors during the stay
Visitor lists are irrelevant to discharge planning criteria.

alt.q: Which outcome statement in a discharge plan is written in measurable terms?
alt.a: “Patient will walk 300 feet without assistance before discharge.”
alt.ex: Discharge planning documentation includes measurable expected outcomes that can be evaluated.
w: “Patient will feel better about walking before discharge.”
Feeling better cannot be measured objectively.
“Patient will understand the importance of walking soon.”
Understanding is not stated in an observable, measurable way.
“Patient will try to walk more often when at home.”
Trying more often has no measurable criterion.

items.q: A nurse needs to document a complex situation in which a patient fell, was assessed, and then received treatment. What should the nurse do before entering the note?
items.a: Think about the situation and decide what information and words to include
items.ex: Organized notes come from thinking through the situation first and then entering information in a logical order.
w: Enter each detail in the order the nurse happens to recall it
Random order makes notes disorganized and hard to follow.
Copy the previous shift’s note and change the time
Copying notes is inaccurate and does not describe the current situation.
Wait until the next day to document a calmer summary
Delays in documentation can lead to unsafe care; entries must be current.

alt.q: Which example shows an organized documentation entry about pain?
alt.a: Pain described, then the assessment and interventions, then the patient’s response
alt.ex: An organized entry describes the pain, the nurse’s assessment and interventions, and the patient’s response, in logical order.
w: The patient’s response first, then the pain, then the interventions
A logical entry follows the sequence of events from problem to response.
Interventions only, because pain is listed in the flow sheet
An organized entry links the problem, actions, and response.
Pain rating only, with interventions recorded on another day
Entries should be current and complete, not split across days.

items.q: Misspelled terms can cause serious treatment errors because some medication names, such as hydromorphone and hydrocodone, are similar.
items.a: True
items.ex: Similar terms and drug names are easily misinterpreted, so careful spelling and transcription prevent errors.
items.ww: Spelling errors are not merely cosmetic; similar drug names can lead to the wrong medication being given.

alt.q: Spelling errors in documentation are a cosmetic problem that does not affect patient safety.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Similar terms such as dysphagia and dysphasia, or drug names like lamotrigine and lamivudine, make spelling errors dangerous.
alt.ww: Correct spelling shows competency and prevents serious treatment errors.

items.q: How does a health care agency choose its documentation system?
items.a: It selects a system that reflects the agency’s philosophy of nursing
items.ex: Each agency selects a documentation system reflecting its nursing philosophy and uses it throughout the agency.
w: Each nurse chooses the format that best fits his or her style
Individual nurses do not choose; one system is used throughout the agency.
Each unit chooses a different system based on its patients
The same system is used throughout a specific agency.
The patient’s insurer chooses the system used for that patient

alt.q: A nurse who floats between units in the same agency notices that every unit documents the same way. Why?

Float nurses must use their home unit’s system everywhere

items.q: In the electronic health record, how are flow sheets for routine assessment data organized?

By medical diagnosis, navigated through a printed paper index

By health care provider, navigated through each provider’s orders
Flow sheets are organized by body system, not by provider.

Incident reports

The health care provider’s plan for surgery

When the patient requests a copy of the flow sheet
