items.q: In focus charting, what does the “A” in a DAR note represent?
items.a: Action or nursing intervention
items.ex: DAR stands for data, action or nursing intervention, and response of the patient.
w: Assessment of the problem
Assessment is the A in a SOAP note, not a DAR note.
Allergies of the patient
Allergies are not a component of DAR notes.
Approval by the provider
DAR notes do not include provider approval.

alt.q: In focus charting, what does the “R” in a DAR note represent?
alt.a: Response of the patient
alt.ex: The R in DAR is the patient’s response to the nursing action.
w: Reason for admission
The reason for admission is not a DAR component.
Recommendation of the nurse
DAR ends with the patient’s response, not a recommendation.
Result of laboratory tests
Lab results may be data, but R is the patient’s response.

items.q: Which progress note format is used by all health care disciplines?
items.a: SOAP
items.ex: SOAP notes, identifying interprofessional problems, are used by all health care disciplines.
w: PIE
PIE notes have a specific nursing focus.
DAR
DAR is the format for focus charting, used to report patient concerns.
Flow sheet
Flow sheets document routine data, not progress notes for all disciplines.

alt.q: A nurse wants to write a progress note with a specific nursing focus on a nursing diagnosis, interventions, and evaluation. Which format fits?
alt.a: PIE
alt.ex: PIE notes identify the nursing problem, interventions, and nursing evaluation.
w: SOAP
SOAP notes identify interprofessional problems and are used by all disciplines.
DAR
DAR uses data, action, and response rather than a nursing diagnosis structure.
Narrative
Narrative notes use a storylike format rather than a structured nursing focus.

items.q: A nurse writes a DAR note for a patient with a deep vein thrombosis who says, “My leg is so swollen. I’m worried about this blood clot.” Where does this statement belong?
items.a: Data
items.ex: The D in DAR contains subjective and objective data, such as the patient’s statement.
w: Action
Action contains the nursing interventions, such as providing a brochure.
Response
Response describes the patient’s reaction after the intervention, such as teach-back.
Assessment
Assessment is a SOAP component, not part of a DAR note.

alt.q: In a SOAP note for a patient with a deep vein thrombosis, where does the nurse document “Patient lacks knowledge regarding anticoagulation therapy”?
alt.a: Assessment
alt.ex: The A in SOAP is the assessment, the nurse’s conclusion about the patient’s problem.
w: Subjective
Subjective data are the patient’s own statements.
Objective
Objective data are observations such as alertness and behavior.
Plan
Plan contains the teaching and interventions to address the problem.

items.q: In an electronic health record, when is narrative documentation typically used?
items.a: Only in critical situations
items.ex: Narrative notes in an EHR, entered by free text or menu selection, are typically used only in critical situations.
w: For every routine vital sign
Routine vital signs are entered on flow sheets.
Only for discharge teaching
Narrative notes are not limited to discharge teaching.
Only by health care providers
Nurses and health care providers both use narrative documentation.

alt.q: How is narrative documentation entered in an electronic health record?
alt.a: By free text entry or menu selections
alt.ex: In an EHR, the storylike narrative format is entered using free text or menu selections.
w: By checkboxes on graphic flow sheets only
Flow sheet checkboxes are not narrative documentation.
By scanned handwritten notes only
Narrative in an EHR is entered as free text or menu selections.
By voice messages to the provider only
Voice messages are not narrative documentation in the record.

items.q: Focus charting DAR notes address patient concerns such as a sign or symptom, a behavior, a significant event, or a change in condition.
items.a: True
items.ex: DAR notes address signs or symptoms, conditions, nursing diagnoses, behaviors, significant events, or changes in condition.
items.ww: DAR notes are not limited to medical diagnoses; they focus on any patient concern.

alt.q: DAR notes in focus charting are limited to medical diagnoses identified by the health care provider.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Focus charting addresses many patient concerns, including symptoms, behaviors, nursing diagnoses, and significant events.
alt.ww: Medical diagnoses are only one possible focus; DAR covers a broad range of concerns.

items.q: Flow sheet sections of the EHR are designed mainly for checkboxes and drop-down lists, but they allow short narrative comments.
items.a: True
items.ex: Flow sheets mainly use checkboxes or drop-down lists, with space for short, descriptive narrative comments.
items.ww: The book describes both features: structured entries plus brief narrative comments.

alt.q: EHR flow sheets do not allow narrative comments, so all added detail must be entered on paper.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Flow sheets allow short narrative comments, and detailed notes are entered as narrative progress notes in the EHR.
alt.ww: Free-text narrative is available within flow sheets and progress notes in the EHR.

items.q: A health care agency uses the same documentation system throughout the agency, and sometimes throughout an entire health care system.
items.a: True
items.ex: The agency’s chosen documentation system is used throughout that agency and sometimes across the health care system.
items.ww: Units do not choose their own systems; one system reflects the agency’s nursing philosophy.

alt.q: Each nursing unit within an agency selects its own documentation format based on staff preference.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: One documentation system reflecting the agency’s nursing philosophy is used throughout the agency.
alt.ww: Staff preference does not determine format; the agency selects a single system.

items.q: When entering a narrative progress note in the EHR, which items should the nurse describe clearly and accurately? Select all that apply.
o: Subjective assessment findings
Narrative notes clearly describe subjective findings.
Objective assessment findings
Narrative notes clearly describe objective findings.
Interventions to resolve patient problems
Interventions to resolve problems are part of the note.
Interventions to maintain patient safety
Safety interventions are documented in narrative notes.
The nurse’s opinion of the patient’s character
Personal opinions are subjective and do not belong in the record.
Routine details unrelated to the plan of care
Irrelevant details are avoided unless significant to status or care.
items.ex: Narrative notes clearly describe subjective and objective findings and interventions for problems and safety.

alt.q: A nurse writes a narrative note after a patient’s sudden change in condition. Which content should the note include? Select all that apply.
o: What the patient said about the symptoms
Subjective findings are described clearly in the note.
Measured findings such as vital signs
Objective findings are described accurately.
Actions taken to keep the patient safe
Interventions to maintain safety belong in the note.
Speculation about what caused the change
Entries must be factual; do not speculate or guess.
Blame directed at the previous shift
Critical comments about others are never documented.
alt.ex: Clear narrative notes help providers find details about changes in a patient’s condition.

items.q: [[Narrative documentation|narrative|narrative charting]] uses a storylike format to document patient assessment, clinical decisions, and care provided.
items.ex: Narrative notes may be entered by free text or menu selection and are typically used in critical situations in an EHR.

alt.q: A progress note written in a storylike format, entered as free text in the EHR, is an example of [[narrative documentation|narrative|narrative charting]].
alt.ex: Narrative notes may be entered by free text or menu selection and are typically used in critical situations in an EHR.

items.q: A nurse writes the following note: “P: Lack of Knowledge related to inexperience with disease condition.” What should the next part of this note contain?
items.a: Interventions that will be used to address the problem
items.ex: In PIE format, the problem is followed by interventions and then the nursing evaluation.
w: Objective data such as vital signs and alertness
Objective data are the O in SOAP, not the next PIE component.
The patient’s response to the teaching provided
The patient’s response belongs in the E, which comes after interventions.
The health care provider’s plan for discharge
PIE notes have a nursing focus and move from problem to interventions.

alt.q: In a PIE note about anticoagulation teaching, where does the nurse record that the patient could teach back the plan for warfarin therapy?
alt.a: Evaluation
alt.ex: The patient’s ability to teach back shows the nursing evaluation of the response to teaching.
w: Problem
The problem section states the nursing diagnosis.
Intervention
The intervention section records the teaching provided.
Data
Data is a DAR component, not part of a PIE note.

items.q: A patient’s condition changes during the shift. Why should the nurse’s documentation clearly describe the findings and interventions?
items.a: Providers review nursing documentation for details about changes in condition
items.ex: Health care providers review nursing documentation for details about changes in a patient’s condition.
w: Providers use nursing documentation only for billing
Providers use nursing notes to understand changes in condition.
Providers do not read nursing notes during a hospital stay
The book states that providers review nursing documentation.
Detailed nursing notes are needed only after discharge
Detailed notes support communication during the stay.

alt.q: How do EHRs that make narrative notes and flow sheet data easy to retrieve support patient care?
alt.a: They augment clinician communication and support continuity of care
alt.ex: Easy retrieval of narrative and flow sheet data improves interprofessional understanding and continuity of care.
w: They eliminate the need for nursing assessments
Assessments are still needed; retrieval improves communication.
They allow nurses to skip documenting routine care
Routine care is still documented on flow sheets.
They restrict information to the nurse who entered it
EHRs make information available to all authorized team members.

items.q: Which statements describe the SOAP note format? Select all that apply.
o: It is used by all health care disciplines
SOAP notes are used by all disciplines.
It identifies interprofessional problems
SOAP notes identify interprofessional problems.
It ends with a plan section
P, the final component, is the plan.
It is limited to nursing diagnoses
A nursing-only focus describes PIE notes.
It has three components: data, action, response
Data, action, and response describe DAR notes in focus charting.
items.ex: SOAP notes, used by all disciplines, include subjective, objective, assessment, and plan sections for interprofessional problems.

alt.q: A nurse compares progress note formats. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: PIE notes have a specific nursing focus
PIE notes identify nursing problems, interventions, and evaluation.
DAR notes are used in focus charting
Focus charting uses the DAR format.
SOAP notes include an assessment section
The A in SOAP is assessment.
PIE notes are used by all health care disciplines
SOAP is the format used by all disciplines; PIE has a nursing focus.
Narrative notes use only checkboxes
Narrative notes use a storylike format, not checkboxes.
alt.ex: SOAP is interprofessional, PIE is nursing focused, DAR is focus charting, and narrative is storylike.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient receiving a heparin infusion for deep vein thrombosis about the plan for anticoagulation. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching documented in the note?
items.a: “The heparin will stop when my PT/INR is therapeutic on warfarin.”
items.ex: The documented teach-back shows heparin stops when PT/INR is therapeutic on warfarin, which continues for about 6 months.
w: “The heparin will continue for about 6 months after discharge.”
Warfarin, not heparin, is expected to continue about 6 months after discharge.
“I will no longer need blood tests once the heparin is started.”
Daily blood tests check anticoagulation levels during therapy.
“I should walk as much as possible while the heparin is infusing.”
The teaching stressed the importance of bed rest during treatment.

alt.q: In the narrative note example, which method did the nurse use to validate the patient’s understanding of anticoagulation teaching?
alt.a: Teach-back
alt.ex: The nurse used the teach-back method, and the patient described when heparin would stop and how long warfarin would continue.
w: Written test
No written test was used; understanding was validated through teach-back.
Return demonstration
Return demonstration suits skills; this teaching was validated by teach-back.
Family interview
The patient’s own explanation was used to validate understanding.

sections.name: Common record-keeping forms within the electronic health record

items.q: Which statement best describes the philosophy behind charting by exception (CBE)?
items.a: All standards for normal findings and routine care are met unless otherwise documented
items.ex: CBE assumes normal assessment standards and routine care were met; the nurse documents only exceptions to them.
w: Every assessment finding is described in a full narrative note each shift
Writing every finding in narrative form is the opposite of an exception-based approach.
Only care given by the health care provider needs to be documented
CBE applies to nursing assessments and routine nursing care, not just provider care.
Normal findings are documented only when the patient requests it
Normal findings are covered by predefined WDL criteria, not by patient request.

alt.q: In an exception-based documentation system, what does selecting “within defined limits” (WDL) for a body system indicate?
alt.a: The findings meet the written criteria for a normal assessment of that system
alt.ex: WDL statements are predefined written criteria describing a normal assessment for each body system.
w: The system was not assessed during the shift
WDL means the system was assessed and met the normal criteria, not that it was skipped.
The findings are abnormal but expected for the diagnosis
Findings that deviate from the WDL definition are documented as exceptions, not as WDL.
The health care provider must review the findings
WDL signals normal findings; it does not trigger provider review.

items.q: A nurse using an exception-based EHR finds new crackles in the lower lobes of a patient whose lungs were clear earlier. Which documentation action is best?
items.a: Select the abnormal finding and add a narrative note on the change, actions taken, and response
items.ex: Changes in status need a narrative note describing their effects, the interventions taken, and the patient’s response.
w: Select WDL for the respiratory system because the other findings are normal
WDL would falsely state the lungs meet normal criteria when an exception exists.
Mention the crackles only in the verbal hand-off report at the end of shift
A hand-off report does not replace documentation of a change in the health record.
Check the box for crackles and leave the note section blank to save time
Checkbox entries alone cannot adequately capture a significant change and the nurse’s response to it.

alt.q: A patient’s condition changes, and the nurse’s CBE note on the exception has little description of key findings and no mention of periodic checks. What is the main risk?
alt.a: A lawyer could claim the nurse was negligent
alt.ex: When an exception occurs, a sparse note lacking key findings or periodic checks invites a claim of nursing negligence.
w: The acuity rating will automatically drop to level 1
Acuity reflects the type and number of interventions, not the length of an exception note.
The note will be removed from the health record
Inadequate notes remain in the record; their weakness is the legal exposure.
The care summary will stop updating for that patient
The patient care summary updates automatically regardless of note quality.

items.q: Why does an exception-based documentation system still require narrative notes?
items.a: Some changes in status, interventions, and responses cannot be captured by flow sheet entries alone
items.ex: Narrative notes record significant changes, subsequent interventions, and the patient’s response that standard flow sheet entries cannot capture adequately.
w: Narrative notes replace flow sheets for all routine body system assessments
Routine normal findings are documented with WDL statements on flow sheets, not narrative notes.
Accrediting agencies forbid the use of drop-down menus for abnormal findings
Drop-down menus are used to describe findings that deviate from WDL definitions.
Flow sheets are not part of the electronic health record
Well-designed flow sheets are a key part of exception-based documentation within the EHR.

alt.q: Which component is described as a key part of a good exception-based documentation system within the EHR?
alt.a: Well-designed flow sheets
alt.ex: Well-designed flow sheets let nurses select WDL statements or drop-down choices for findings and routine care.
w: Daily handwritten narrative summaries
Narrative notes are added for exceptions; they are not the core of an exception-based system.
Incident reports filed for every exception
Incident reports are for events outside routine care and are not part of the health record.
Acuity ratings entered by each nurse
Acuity ratings determine staffing and are not part of the health record.

items.q: In charting by exception, the predefined written criteria for a normal assessment of each body system are called [[within defined limits|WDL|within normal limits|WNL]].
items.ex: WDL or WNL statements define a “normal” assessment for each body system so only deviations need detailed description.

alt.q: When a body system meets its written criteria for a normal assessment, the nurse selects the statement [[within defined limits|WDL|within normal limits|WNL]].
alt.ex: WDL or WNL statements define a “normal” assessment for each body system so only deviations need detailed description.

items.q: The SBAR or ISBAR format is a commonly used framework for writing a narrative note when an exception occurs.
items.a: True
items.ex: SBAR and ISBAR organize narrative notes about exceptions and are also popular formats for verbal reports.
items.ww: The book specifically names SBAR and ISBAR as frameworks for narrative notes when exceptions occur.

alt.q: SBAR and ISBAR are formats for verbal reports only and should not be used to structure a written narrative note.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: SBAR and ISBAR are popular for verbal reporting and are also commonly used for narrative notes when exceptions occur.
alt.ww: The book names both as frameworks for written narrative notes as well as verbal reports.

items.q: In the ISBAR format, which part comes right after “Situation”?
items.a: Background
items.ex: That's part 3 of 5. ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.
w: Assessment
That's part 4 of 5.
Identify
That's part 1 of 5.
Recommendation
That's part 5 of 5.

alt.q: Which part comes first in the ISBAR format?
alt.a: Identify
alt.ex: That's part 1 of 5. ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.
w: Situation
That's part 2 of 5.
Background
That's part 3 of 5.
Assessment
That's part 4 of 5.

alt.q: Which part comes last in the ISBAR format?
alt.a: Recommendation
alt.ex: That's part 5 of 5. ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.
w: Assessment
That's part 4 of 5.
Background
That's part 3 of 5.
Situation
That's part 2 of 5.

alt.q: In the ISBAR format, which part comes right after “Identify”?
alt.a: Situation
alt.ex: That's part 2 of 5. ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.
w: Background
That's part 3 of 5.
Assessment
That's part 4 of 5.
Recommendation
That's part 5 of 5.

alt.q: In the ISBAR format, which part comes right after “Background”?
alt.a: Assessment
alt.ex: That's part 4 of 5. ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.
w: Recommendation
That's part 5 of 5.
Situation
That's part 2 of 5.
Identify
That's part 1 of 5.

alt.q: In the ISBAR format, which part comes right after “Assessment”?
alt.a: Recommendation
alt.ex: That's part 5 of 5. ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.
w: Background
That's part 3 of 5.
Situation
That's part 2 of 5.
Identify
That's part 1 of 5.

alt.q: In the ISBAR format, which part comes right before “Situation”?
alt.a: Identify
alt.ex: That's part 1 of 5. ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.
w: Background
That's part 3 of 5.
Assessment
That's part 4 of 5.
Recommendation
That's part 5 of 5.

alt.q: In the ISBAR format, which part comes right before “Background”?
alt.a: Situation
alt.ex: That's part 2 of 5. ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.
w: Identify
That's part 1 of 5.
Assessment
That's part 4 of 5.
Recommendation
That's part 5 of 5.

alt.q: In the ISBAR format, which part comes right before “Assessment”?
alt.a: Background
alt.ex: That's part 3 of 5. ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.
w: Situation
That's part 2 of 5.
Identify
That's part 1 of 5.
Recommendation
That's part 5 of 5.

alt.q: In the ISBAR format, which part comes right before “Recommendation”?
alt.a: Assessment
alt.ex: That's part 4 of 5. ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.
w: Background
That's part 3 of 5.
Situation
That's part 2 of 5.
Identify
That's part 1 of 5.

ord.q: Put the parts of an ISBAR narrative note in the order the format presents them.
items: Identify
Situation
Background
Assessment
Recommendation
ord.ex: ISBAR stands for identify, situation, background, assessment, and recommendation, in that order.

items.q: What is the main purpose of the admission nursing history form?
items.a: To guide a comprehensive assessment that gives baseline data for later comparison
items.ex: The admission history guides a comprehensive assessment to identify nursing diagnoses and provides baseline data for comparison when the condition changes.
w: To give the patient written instructions for care at home
Written home instructions belong to the discharge summary given to the patient.
To determine the number of staff needed on the next shift
Staffing needs are determined with an acuity rating system.
To record the hand-off report given at the end of each shift
The patient care summary is the worksheet used for giving the hand-off report.

alt.q: On the third hospital day, a nurse wonders whether a patient’s confusion is new. Which document provides the best baseline for comparison?
alt.a: The admission nursing history form
alt.ex: Completing the admission nursing history provides baseline data used for comparison when a patient’s condition changes.
w: The discharge summary form
The discharge summary is prepared for discharge, not as an admission baseline.
The standardized care plan
A standardized care plan lists interventions and outcomes, not the baseline assessment.
The incident report file
Incident reports are not part of the health record and do not hold admission baseline data.

items.q: At the start of a shift, a nurse reviews an EHR document that automatically updates and is used as a worksheet for organizing care and giving the hand-off report. Which document is this?
items.a: Patient care summary
items.ex: The patient care summary updates automatically with the latest EHR entries and serves as a shift worksheet and hand-off tool.
w: Admission nursing history form
The admission history is completed once on admission to provide baseline data.
Discharge summary form
The discharge summary is printed and given to the patient at discharge.
Occurrence report
An occurrence report documents an unexpected event and is filed with risk management.

alt.q: Why can a nurse rely on the patient care summary for the most current information at hand-off?
alt.a: It automatically updates with the newest information entered into the EHR
alt.ex: The patient care summary automatically updates, giving the most current information that was entered into the EHR.
w: It is rewritten by hand by the charge nurse every shift
The summary is generated by the EHR, not rewritten by hand.
It is reviewed and signed by the health care provider hourly
Provider co-signature applies to telephone and verbal orders, not the care summary.
It contains only information entered on the day of admission
The summary reflects current orders and data, not only admission data.

items.q: A nurse prints a patient care summary to organize care for the shift. Which information would the nurse expect to find on it? Select all that apply.
o: Allergies
Allergies are listed on the patient care summary.
Emergency code status, such as a do-not-resuscitate order
The summary includes code status for emergencies.
Scheduled tests and procedures
Scheduled tests and procedures help the nurse organize the shift.
Copies of incident reports involving the patient
Incident reports are confidential and not part of the health record.
Nearest relative or health care power of attorney to contact
The emergency contact or designated health care power of attorney is included.
The unit’s patient-to-staff ratio for the shift
Staffing ratios come from unit acuity data, not the individual care summary.
items.ex: The care summary gathers demographics, diagnoses, orders, care plan, tests, precautions, contacts, code status, and allergies.

alt.q: Which items are usually included in an EHR-generated patient care summary? Select all that apply.
o: Medical and surgical history
Medical and surgical history is part of the summary.
Current orders from the health care provider
Current orders such as dressing changes or glucose monitoring are included.
Factors that affect independence with activities of daily living
ADL independence factors are listed to guide care.
Safety precautions used in the patient’s care
Safety precautions are included so staff can maintain them.
Risk management’s analysis of near misses on the unit
Incident and near-miss analysis is confidential QI material, not part of the patient’s summary.
The patient’s acuity rating history
Acuity ratings are not part of the patient’s health record.
alt.ex: The care summary includes history, orders, nursing care plan and orders, precautions, ADL factors, contacts, code status, and allergies.

items.q: A newly hired nurse says, “The EHR already has a standardized care plan for pneumonia, so I don’t need to individualize it.” Which response by the precepting nurse is best?
items.a: “Standardized plans don’t replace your judgment; select patient-specific interventions and outcomes.”
items.ex: Nurses remain responsible for individualized care; standardized care plans cannot replace clinical judgment and are individualized for each patient.
w: “That’s right; the standardized plan already covers every pneumonia patient.”
Standardized plans must still be individualized to the patient.
“Only the health care provider is allowed to change a standardized plan.”
Nurses select and modify standardized plans as part of individualized care.
“Individualize it only if the patient develops a complication.”
Individualization begins when the nurse selects plans after the assessment, not only after complications.

alt.q: Which statement about the nurse’s responsibility when using standardized care plans is accurate?
alt.a: The nurse remains responsible for providing individualized care to each patient
alt.ex: Standardized care plans support consistent care, but nurses remain responsible for individualized care and clinical judgment.
w: The nurse is released from responsibility for decisions the plan covers
Using a standardized plan does not shift responsibility away from the nurse.
The nurse may not modify a plan once it has been selected
Most EHRs allow plans to be modified with patient-specific interventions and outcomes.
The nurse uses the plan instead of performing an assessment
The nurse completes an assessment first and then selects appropriate plans.

items.q: Which benefit of standardized care plans is described in the textbook?
items.a: They are useful for QI audits and improve continuity of care among nurses
items.ex: Standardized care plans help with quality improvement audits and improve continuity of care among professional nurses.
w: They eliminate the need to update the care plan during the stay
Nurses update care plans regularly to keep them appropriate and evidence based.
They remove the need for nursing assessment on admission
An assessment comes first; plans are selected based on identified problems.
They replace the need for interprofessional discharge planning
Discharge planning is a separate interprofessional process that begins at admission.

alt.q: A quality improvement nurse plans an audit of care for patients with the same nursing diagnosis. Which feature of the EHR is especially useful for this audit?
alt.a: Standardized care plans based on agency standards and evidence-based guidelines
alt.ex: Standardized care plans are useful when conducting QI audits because they reflect agency standards and evidence-based guidelines.
w: Incident reports stored within each patient’s health record
Incident reports are not stored in the health record.
Acuity ratings entered into each patient’s health record
Acuity ratings are not part of the health record.
Printed hand-off worksheets kept at the nurses’ station
Printed worksheets contain PHI and are not the audit tool described.

items.q: After completing a nursing assessment on admission, which step does the nurse take next when using standardized care plans in the EHR?
items.a: Identify the nursing problems or diagnoses
items.ex: After the assessment, the nurse identifies nursing problems or diagnoses and then selects the appropriate standardized plans.
w: Print the discharge summary for the patient
The discharge summary is printed and given to the patient at discharge.
Ask the health care provider to co-sign the plan
Provider co-signature applies to telephone and verbal orders.
Select every available plan for the medical diagnosis
Plans are chosen for the patient’s identified nursing problems, not every plan for a medical diagnosis.

alt.q: A nurse has identified a patient’s nursing diagnoses in the EHR. What is the nurse’s next action with the standardized care plans?
alt.a: Select the appropriate plans and individualize their interventions and outcomes
alt.ex: The nurse selects standardized plans appropriate for the patient and individualizes them with patient-specific interventions and outcomes.
w: Accept the default plan for the unit without changes
Plans are individualized with patient-specific interventions and outcomes.
Wait until discharge to choose care plans
Plans are selected after the assessment to guide care throughout the stay.
Repeat the admission history before choosing plans
The completed assessment is the basis for selecting plans; repeating it is unnecessary.

items.q: Once standardized care plans are selected on admission, they remain unchanged for the rest of the hospital stay.
items.a: False
items.ex: Nurses update care plans on a regular basis to ensure they stay appropriate and evidence based.
items.ww: Care plans are living documents that the nurse revises as the patient’s needs change.

alt.q: Nurses update care plans regularly to ensure that the documents remain appropriate and evidence based.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Regular updates keep care plans appropriate to the patient and consistent with current evidence.
alt.ww: Leaving plans unchanged would let them become outdated and no longer fit the patient.

items.q: The categories or data fields in EHR record-keeping forms are usually derived from agency standards of practice or accrediting agency guidelines.
items.a: True
items.ex: Form fields reflect agency standards of practice or guidelines from accrediting agencies.
items.ww: Forms are not designed by individual preference; they follow agency and accreditation standards.

alt.q: Each nurse chooses the data fields on EHR documentation forms to fit a personal charting style.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Form categories are usually derived from agency standards of practice or accrediting agency guidelines.
alt.ww: Personal preference does not determine form fields; agency and accrediting standards do.

items.q: Which information about a patient’s discharge does the nurse document in the health record?
items.a: The actual time of discharge, mode of transportation, and who accompanied the patient
items.ex: Box 26.2 directs the nurse to record the discharge time, how the patient left, and who went with the patient.
w: The planned time of discharge, the room number, and the last nurse on duty
The actual, not planned, discharge time is recorded along with transportation and companion.
The patient’s acuity level, staffing ratio, and charge nurse on duty
Acuity and staffing data are not part of the health record.
The incident reports filed, the near misses, and the risk manager notified
Incident reports are never referenced in the health record.

alt.q: A patient leaves the unit by wheelchair to a car driven by her daughter at 1430. Which entry completes the required discharge documentation?
alt.a: “Discharged at 1430 by wheelchair to private car, accompanied by daughter.”
alt.ex: The health record includes the actual time of discharge, mode of transportation, and who accompanied the patient.
w: “Discharged this afternoon; patient stable and happy to go home.”
This omits the exact time, transportation mode, and companion.
“Discharge planned for today per provider; family to pick up patient.”
This describes a plan, not the actual time, mode, and companion.
“Discharged at 1430; see incident report regarding wheelchair.”
It omits transport details and references an incident report, which is avoided.

items.q: A patient is admitted today for a scheduled hip replacement. When should the nurse begin discharge planning with the patient and family?
items.a: Now, at the time of admission
items.ex: Discharge planning ideally begins at admission, partnering with the patient and family to identify outcomes and discharge needs.
w: After surgery, once the patient is stable
Waiting until after surgery delays identifying needs, services, and equipment.
The day before the expected discharge
Last-minute planning does not allow time to arrange resources and teaching.
Only if the patient will need home care
All patients need discharge planning to the appropriate level of care.

alt.q: Which statement about discharge planning is accurate?
alt.a: It ideally begins at admission and involves the patient and family
alt.ex: Starting at admission and partnering with the patient and family helps ensure a safe, effective, and timely discharge.
w: It is completed by the health care provider alone on the day of discharge
Discharge planning is an interprofessional process that starts at admission.
It begins only after the patient’s acuity level reaches 1
Discharge planning is not triggered by an acuity score.
It is limited to reviewing the medication list with the patient
Planning also covers outcomes, level of care, support services, and equipment.

items.q: A nurse is preparing written discharge instructions. Which actions follow the textbook’s discharge summary guidelines? Select all that apply.
o: Use clear, concise descriptions in the patient’s own language
Instructions should be understandable in the patient’s own language.
Provide a detailed list of all prescribed medications
A complete list of prescribed medications is included.
Review signs and symptoms of complications to report to the health care provider
Patients need to know which complications to report.
Use precise medical terminology so the instructions are exact
Medical terms can confuse patients; use clear language the patient understands.
List only the medications that are new since admission
The list includes all prescribed medications, not only new ones.
Record the actual time of discharge, mode of transportation, and who accompanied the patient
These discharge details are documented in the health record.
items.ex: Discharge information is clear, complete, and practical, covering medications, precautions, restrictions, complications, contacts, and follow-up.

alt.q: Which items belong in a patient’s discharge summary information? Select all that apply.
o: Step-by-step description of procedures the patient will perform at home
Procedures such as home medication administration are described step by step.
Restrictions on activities such as bathing, lifting, and driving
Activity restrictions related to ADLs are reviewed.
Names and phone numbers of providers and community resources
Patients need contacts for questions or help after discharge.
Unresolved problems with plans for follow-up
Unresolved problems and follow-up plans are identified.
The patient’s acuity level on the day of discharge
Acuity ratings guide staffing and are not part of discharge teaching.
A copy of any incident report filed during the stay
Incident reports are confidential and are not shared through the discharge summary.
alt.ex: Discharge information includes procedures, precautions, activity restrictions, complications, contacts, and unresolved problems with follow-up plans.

items.q: Which considerations are part of developing a comprehensive interprofessional discharge plan? Select all that apply.
o: Identifying key clinical outcomes and timelines for reaching them
Outcomes and timelines are part of the discharge planning process.
Determining the appropriate level of care for discharge
Planning identifies the right level of care after discharge.
Deciding whether health care equipment is needed in the home
Home equipment needs are considered during planning.
Identifying needed support services such as home care or physical therapy
Support services are considered for a safe transition.
Waiting to involve the family until the day of discharge
The patient and family are partners from admission onward.
items.ex: Discharge planning covers outcomes and timelines, level of care, support services, equipment, and all necessary resources.

alt.q: Which statements about discharge planning are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It relies on interprofessional collaboration
Developing a safe discharge plan relies on interprofessional planning.
Involving the family caregiver helps ensure they have needed information and resources
Family involvement prepares caregivers for the next level of care.
Safe, timely discharge supports cost-effective care and appropriate reimbursement
The book links timely discharge with cost-effective care and reimbursement.
The nurse plans discharge alone once the health care provider writes the order
Planning is interprofessional and begins at admission.
Planning focuses only on medications and ignores community resources
Community resources and support services are part of the plan.
alt.ex: Interprofessional discharge planning that starts at admission and involves the family supports safe, cost-effective transitions.

items.q: A nurse completes discharge teaching for a patient going home after surgery. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the discharge information?
items.a: “If I have questions at home, I’ll call the person listed on my discharge papers.”
items.ex: Discharge documentation names a person to contact for questions or emergencies, so this patient knows how to get help.
w: “Since nobody mentioned it, I can drive and lift whatever I want right away.”

“I’ll only keep taking the new pills and stop my usual medicines.”
The discharge list includes all prescribed medications, not just new ones.
“I won’t need to report any symptoms because my surgery went well.”
Patients are taught signs and symptoms of complications to report.

alt.q: What happens to the discharge summary document when a patient leaves the agency?

w: It is deleted from the EHR once the patient signs it
The summary remains in the EHR as a record of the teaching provided.
It is sent only to the risk-management department
Risk management receives incident reports, not discharge summaries.
It is kept in the EHR but not given to the patient
The patient receives a printed copy to take home.

sections.name: Documenting communication with providers and unique events

items.q: A nurse phones a health care provider about a patient’s new chest pain. Which elements must the nurse include when documenting the call? Select all that apply.
o: When the call was made
The time of the call is documented.
Who made the call and who was called
Both the caller and the person called are recorded.
What information was given
The information reported to the provider is documented.
What information was received
Orders or responses received are documented.
The nurse’s opinion of the provider’s tone
Personal opinions about the provider are not part of call documentation.
items.ex: Phone call documentation covers when, who called, who was called, to whom information was given, and what was given and received.

alt.q: Which statements about documenting a phone call to a health care provider are accurate? Select all that apply.

The exact health care provider’s name is included in the note

Every call is documented, whether or not an order results.
The nurse types their own name and credentials at the end of the EHR note
The nurse’s name and credentials autogenerate with a time stamp when signing.

items.q: In which situation is accepting a verbal order most appropriate?
items.a: A patient’s condition is deteriorating and the provider is managing an emergency at the bedside
items.ex: Verbal orders are discouraged except in urgent or emergent situations because they are error prone.
w: The provider is standing at the desk and finds typing orders inconvenient
Verbal orders should never be used just for the provider’s convenience.
The provider is finishing rounds and wants to save time before leaving
Saving the provider time is not an urgent need that justifies a verbal order.
The provider prefers to dictate all routine orders for stable patients
Routine orders for stable patients should be entered directly, not given verbally.

alt.q: Why are verbal orders considered error prone?
alt.a: They can be misheard, misunderstood, or transcribed incorrectly
alt.ex: Accents, dialects, and drug name pronunciations make verbal orders easy to mishear, misunderstand, or transcribe incorrectly.
w: They cannot legally be co-signed by the provider
Verbal orders are co-signed by the provider within the agency’s time frame.
They are never entered into the computer system
Verbal orders are entered into CPOE as soon as possible.
They are always given by unlicensed personnel
Verbal orders are given by a health care provider to an RN.

items.q: A health care provider phones a new medication order to an RN. After writing down the complete order, what should the nurse do next?
items.a: Read the written order back to the provider
items.ex: TJC requires the receiver to document the order and read it back, confirming both hearing and transcription.
w: Repeat each word aloud while the provider is still speaking
Repeating as the order is spoken does not verify what was transcribed; the order is read back after writing.
Ask a pharmacist to call the provider to confirm
Verification is done by the receiving nurse reading the order back to the provider.
Give the medication and then document the call
The order must be documented and read back before acting on it.

alt.q: According to TJC, why must a nurse read back a telephone order rather than simply repeat it?
alt.a: Reading back confirms that the order was heard and transcribed accurately
alt.ex: Reading back what was written checks both correct hearing and accurate transcription of the order.
w: Reading back replaces the need for the provider to co-sign
The provider still co-signs the order within the agency’s time frame.
Reading back allows the nurse to skip entering the order in CPOE
The order is still entered into CPOE as soon as possible.
Reading back lets any staff member accept the order
Only authorized staff identified by agency policy may receive these orders.

items.q: A health care provider sends a medication order to the nurse through the agency’s secure messaging application. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Follow agency policy and obtain the order in a way that allows read-back
items.ex: At most agencies, orders cannot be received through secure messaging because it does not allow read-back.
w: Enter the order immediately because secure messages are encrypted
Security of the message does not solve the lack of read-back.
Text the order back to the provider as a read-back
Messaging applications do not allow a true read-back of the order.
Ask a second nurse to read the message and co-sign it
A second nurse reviewing a message does not replace read-back with the provider.

alt.q: Why can orders not be received through secure messaging applications at most agencies?
alt.a: These applications do not allow for read-back
alt.ex: Read-back is required to verify orders, and text-style secure messaging does not allow it.
w: These applications do not protect patient information
Secure messaging is designed for team communication; the barrier is the lack of read-back.
These applications are not available to nurses
Secure messaging is available to members of the health care team at some agencies.
These applications delete messages after each shift
Message retention is not the reason given; lack of read-back is.

items.q: Within what time frame does a health care provider usually co-sign a telephone or verbal order?
items.a: Within 24 hours
items.ex: The provider co-signs each TO and VO within the agency’s required time frame, usually 24 hours.
w: Within 1 hour
One hour is shorter than the usual agency time frame for co-signature.
Within 8 hours
The usual co-signature time frame is longer than 8 hours.
Within 72 hours
Seventy-two hours exceeds the usual 24-hour time frame.

alt.q: Who legally verifies a telephone order by co-signing it?
alt.a: The health care provider who gave the order
alt.ex: The prescribing provider legally verifies a TO or VO by co-signing it within the agency’s time frame.
w: The nurse who received the order
The receiving nurse documents and reads back the order but does not legally verify it.
The charge nurse on the next shift
The charge nurse does not verify another provider’s order.
The pharmacist who dispenses the medication
Pharmacists do not co-sign provider orders.

items.q: When signing a telephone order, the nurse documents “TORB,” which stands for telephone order [[read back|read-back]].
items.ex: TORB shows the order was read back to the provider who gave it, confirming accurate hearing and transcription.

alt.q: The abbreviation that shows a phone order was verified by reading it back to the provider is [[TORB]].
alt.ex: TORB shows the order was read back to the provider who gave it, confirming accurate hearing and transcription.

items.q: Some agency policies require a second person to listen on the telephone line while a health care provider gives a telephone order.
items.a: True

items.ww: The book describes a second listener as wise and sometimes required, not prohibited.

alt.q: Having a second nurse listen to a telephone order is unsafe and should be avoided because it causes confusion.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A second person listening as a TO is given is wise in some situations and required by some agencies.
alt.ww: A second listener adds a check against error rather than causing it.

items.q: A nurse takes a telephone order. Which information must the nurse document according to the guidelines for telephone and verbal orders? Select all that apply.

The patient’s name and the complete order
The full order and patient name are recorded.
The name and credentials of the provider giving the order
The ordering provider is identified with credentials.
The nurse’s own name and credentials
The receiving nurse is identified.
The reason the provider could not come in person
The provider’s reason for phoning is not a required element.
items.ex: TO/VO documentation includes the order type, date and time, patient, complete order, provider, and receiving nurse.

alt.q: Which actions follow the guidelines for telephone and verbal orders? Select all that apply.
o: Only staff authorized by written agency policy receive the order
Each agency identifies who may receive TOs and VOs.
Clearly identify the patient’s name, birth date, and diagnoses
Clear identification prevents orders for the wrong patient.
Ask the provider to repeat a word or phrase if needed
Clarification questions prevent misunderstanding.
Have two nurses review and sign the order when agency policy requires it
Some agencies require review by two nurses.
Avoid clarification questions so the provider’s time is not wasted
Clarification questions are encouraged to avoid misunderstandings.
Let whichever staff member answers the phone accept the order
Only authorized staff identified in agency policy may receive orders.
alt.ex: Authorized staff identify the patient clearly, clarify unclear words, read back orders, and follow agency signing policy.

items.q: Which event is an example of an incident that requires an occurrence report?
items.a: A visitor loses consciousness in the patient’s room
items.ex: Incidents are events inconsistent with routine care or standard procedures; a visitor losing consciousness is a listed example.
w: A patient receives scheduled pain medication on time
On-time scheduled care is routine and expected.
A patient walks in the hall with assistance as ordered
Ordered ambulation is routine, expected care.
A health care provider changes a diet order during rounds
Changing an order is a normal part of care, not an incident.

alt.q: Which situation is NOT considered an incident?
alt.a: A dressing is changed according to the provider’s order
alt.ex: An incident is an event that is not consistent with routine, expected care; an ordered dressing change is routine.
w: A nurse sustains a needlestick injury
Needlestick injuries are listed as incidents.
An ordered therapy is accidentally omitted
Accidental omission of ordered therapies is an incident.
A patient falls while getting out of bed
Patient falls are a common example of an incident.

items.q: A nurse prepares a medication and, while checking the label at the bedside, discovers it is the wrong dose. The medication is not given and the patient is unharmed. How is this event classified?
items.a: A near miss
items.ex: A near miss exposes a patient to a hazardous situation that could cause harm, but no harm occurs because of luck or early detection.
w: A sentinel event
A sentinel event is a serious event; here the error was caught and no harm occurred.
A routine occurrence that needs no report
Near misses are reportable because they pose a risk for patient injury.
An acuity change
Acuity reflects care needs for staffing, not an error event.

alt.q: Which description best fits the term “near miss”?
alt.a: Exposure to a hazard that could have caused harm, but no harm occurred
alt.ex: There is consensus that a near miss means potential for harm with no harm, owing to luck or early detection.
w: An error that caused temporary harm that was quickly treated
When harm occurs, the event is not a near miss.
An event that caused permanent harm to a patient
Permanent harm is the opposite of a near miss.
A routine procedure completed according to policy
Routine care is not an incident or near miss.

items.q: A nurse finds a patient on the floor beside the bed, assesses the patient, and notifies the health care provider. Which health record entry is most appropriate?
items.a: “Found patient sitting on floor beside bed at 0200; no visible injury. Provider notified at 0205.”
items.ex: The record should give an objective description of what happened, what was observed, and follow-up actions including provider notification.
w: “Patient fell; incident report completed and sent to risk management.”
The health record must not reference the incident report.
“Near miss: patient slipped because evening staff left the rails down.”
Labeling it a near miss and assigning blame are not objective documentation.
“Patient apparently tried to climb out of bed again, as usual.”
This is speculation rather than an objective description of what was observed.

alt.q: After documenting an incident in the health record, what else must the nurse evaluate and document there?
alt.a: The patient’s response to the incident
alt.ex: Nurses evaluate and document the patient’s response to the incident in the health record.
w: The incident report number for reference
Referring to the incident report in the record is avoided.
The name of the staff member at fault
Blaming others is not part of objective documentation.
The sentinel event classification
The record must not label the event as an incident, near miss, or sentinel event.

items.q: Why should a nurse avoid referring to an incident report in the patient’s health record?
items.a: A lawyer could more easily argue the report is part of the record and admissible
items.ex: Mentioning the report in the record helps a lawyer argue it is part of the record and therefore admissible.
