That's stage 1 of 4.

alt.q: In child passenger safety, which stage comes right before “Forward-facing car safety seat with a harness”?
alt.a: Rear-facing car safety seat
alt.ex: That's stage 1 of 4. The AAP recommends rear-facing as long as possible, then a harnessed forward-facing seat, then a booster until the vehicle belt fits properly.
w: Belt-positioning booster seat
That's stage 3 of 4.
Vehicle lap and shoulder seat belt alone
That's stage 4 of 4.

alt.q: In child passenger safety, which stage comes right before “Belt-positioning booster seat”?
alt.a: Forward-facing car safety seat with a harness
alt.ex: That's stage 2 of 4. The AAP recommends rear-facing as long as possible, then a harnessed forward-facing seat, then a booster until the vehicle belt fits properly.
w: Rear-facing car safety seat
That's stage 1 of 4.
Vehicle lap and shoulder seat belt alone
That's stage 4 of 4.

alt.q: In child passenger safety, which stage comes right before “Vehicle lap and shoulder seat belt alone”?
alt.a: Belt-positioning booster seat
alt.ex: That's stage 3 of 4. The AAP recommends rear-facing as long as possible, then a harnessed forward-facing seat, then a booster until the vehicle belt fits properly.
w: Forward-facing car safety seat with a harness
That's stage 2 of 4.
Rear-facing car safety seat
That's stage 1 of 4.

ord.q: Put the types of vehicle restraint in the order a child should progress through them while growing.
items: Rear-facing car safety seat
Forward-facing car safety seat with a harness
Belt-positioning booster seat
Vehicle lap and shoulder seat belt alone
ord.ex: The AAP recommends rear-facing as long as possible, then a harnessed forward-facing seat, then a booster until the vehicle belt fits properly.

items.q: A parent asks the nurse when their child can stop using a belt-positioning booster seat. Which response is consistent with AAP recommendations?
items.a: When the vehicle belt fits properly, often at 4 feet 9 inches tall and age 9 to 12 years
items.ex: Children use a booster until the lap and shoulder belt fits properly, often at least 144.8 cm (4 feet 9 inches) and 9 to 12 years old.
w: When the child turns 5 years old and starts attending kindergarten
Age 5 is far too young; the belt must fit properly, often at 9 to 12 years.
When the child is 3 feet 6 inches tall and age 6 to 7 years
Most children this size are too small for the vehicle belt to fit properly.
When the child weighs 29.5 kg, the limit of many harnessed seats
About 29.5 kg (65 lb) is a common forward-facing harness limit, which signals moving to a booster.

alt.q: A 7-year-old who is 3 feet 11 inches tall has outgrown a forward-facing harnessed car seat. Which restraint should the child use?
alt.a: A belt-positioning booster seat until the vehicle belt fits properly
alt.ex: Children who exceed harness limits use a booster until the vehicle lap and shoulder belt fits, often at 4 feet 9 inches.
w: The vehicle lap and shoulder belt alone in the front seat
The belt will not fit properly yet, and children 12 and younger ride in the rear seat.
A rear-facing car safety seat with a harness
Rear-facing seats are for infants and toddlers within the seat’s limits.
The vehicle lap belt alone without the shoulder belt
Children who use the vehicle belt should always use both lap and shoulder belts.

items.q: Per mile driven, teen drivers have a fatal crash rate almost 3 times as high as that of drivers age 20 and older.
items.a: True
items.ex: The CDC reports that teen drivers have a fatal crash rate per mile almost 3 times higher than drivers 20 and older.
items.ww: Teens underestimate hazards, speed, drive at night, and have the lowest seat belt use, so their risk is not equal to older drivers’.

alt.q: Per mile driven, teen drivers have about the same fatal crash rate as drivers age 20 and older.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Teen drivers’ fatal crash rate per mile is almost 3 times that of drivers age 20 and older.
alt.ww: Risk-taking, inexperience recognizing hazards, and low seat belt use make teen drivers much more likely to crash fatally.

items.q: The nurse teaches an 80-year-old patient about safe driving. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will plan to drive during daylight hours and in good weather.”
items.ex: Driving in daylight and good weather helps compensate for age-related decline in vision and cognitive functioning.
w: “I will have my eyes checked every 3 to 5 years.”
Older drivers should have their eyes checked at least once a year.
“I will stay close behind the car ahead to keep up with traffic.”
Older drivers should leave a large following distance.
“I will review my own medications so I don’t bother my pharmacist.”
Ask the health care provider or pharmacist to review prescription and OTC medications.

alt.q: Which recommendation should the nurse include when counseling an older adult about staying a safe driver?
alt.a: Have an eye examination at least once a year
alt.ex: Yearly eye checks and wearing prescribed corrective lenses help offset age-related vision decline.
w: Choose routes that avoid intersections with left-turn arrows
Older drivers should choose routes that include left-turn arrows, good lighting, and easy parking.
Play the radio loudly to stay alert on long drives
A loud radio is a distraction older drivers should avoid.
Limit exercise so fatigue does not affect driving
Regular exercise increases the strength and flexibility needed for driving.

items.q: Which age-group is at greatest risk for accidental poisoning in the home?
items.a: Toddlers, preschoolers, and young school-age children
items.ex: Curiosity leads toddlers, preschoolers, and young school-age children to ingest cleaners, medications, and hygiene products.
w: Adolescents who experiment with peers
Adolescent poisonings are more often tied to drug experimentation or suicide attempts, not curiosity at home.
Young adults living on their own
Young adults are not identified as the group at greatest risk.
Middle-age adults with busy schedules
Middle-age adults are not identified as the group at greatest risk.

alt.q: Why does packaging medications in multiple-dose containers increase the poisoning risk for young children?
alt.a: A child who opens one container can reach many tablets or capsules
alt.ex: Because medications come in multiple-dose containers, a child who opens one has access to many doses.
w: Multiple-dose containers are never made with safety caps
The issue is access to many doses once opened, not missing caps.
Each tablet in a large container is more concentrated
Container size does not change tablet strength.
Large containers are labeled only for adult readers
Labeling is not the reason; access to multiple doses is.

items.q: A [[poison control center|poison control]] is the best resource for patients and parents who need information about treating an accidental poisoning.
items.ex: Poison control centers have the information needed to treat poisonings; the national hotline is 1-800-222-1222.

alt.q: Parents seeking advice after a child swallows a household chemical should contact a [[poison control center|poison control]], reachable nationwide at 1-800-222-1222.
alt.ex: Poison control centers have the information needed to treat poisonings; the national hotline is 1-800-222-1222.

items.q: Why are fetuses, infants, and young children more vulnerable to lead poisoning than adults?
items.a: Their bodies absorb lead more easily and are more sensitive to its effects
items.ex: Young bodies absorb lead more easily, and small children are more sensitive to its damaging effects.
w: Their kidneys excrete lead too quickly to protect the brain
The problem is greater absorption and sensitivity, not rapid excretion.
They are exposed to lead only through breast milk
Lead is swallowed or inhaled from paint, dust, soil, and water.
Their immune systems form antibodies that bind lead
Lead toxicity is not an immune reaction.

alt.q: A nurse cares for a 3-year-old who lives in an older home with peeling paint. Which effect of excessive lead exposure should the nurse explain to the parents?
alt.a: Learning and behavioral problems with possible brain and kidney damage
alt.ex: Excess lead affects a child’s growth and causes learning and behavioral problems and brain and kidney damage.
w: Improved appetite with rapid weight gain and growth
Lead impairs a child’s growth; it does not speed it.
Burns on the skin where painted surfaces were touched
Lead poisoning occurs from swallowing or inhaling lead, not skin burns.
Sudden infant death during sleep in the first year
SIDS is not an effect of lead exposure in a 3-year-old.

items.q: A patient is found sitting on the bedside mat after sliding off the bed while reaching for a cup. How should the nurse classify this event?
items.a: As a fall, because the patient unintentionally came to rest on a lower surface
items.ex: A fall is an unintentional change in position coming to rest on the ground, floor, or another surface such as a bedside mat.
w: As a near miss, because the patient never reached the floor
Coming to rest on another surface such as a bedside mat still counts as a fall.
As a fall only if the patient sustained an injury
Injury is not required; the unintentional change in position defines a fall.
As a voluntary position change, because the patient was reaching
The patient did not intend to land on the mat, so the change was unintentional.

alt.q: Which statement correctly defines a fall?
alt.a: An unintentional change in position ending on the ground, floor, or another surface
alt.ex: A fall can end on the ground, floor, or another surface, such as a bed, chair, or bedside mat.
w: Any change in position that results in a fracture or bleeding
Injury is a possible result, not part of the definition.
An intentional move from the bed to the floor by a confused patient
Falls are unintentional changes in position.
A collapse that can occur only from a standing position
Falls can also occur from a bed or chair.

items.q: Four older adults on a medical unit are at risk for falling. If a fall occurs, which patient is at greatest risk for a serious injury?
items.a: A 79-year-old with osteoporosis who takes an anticoagulant
items.ex: Patients with osteoporosis or bleeding tendencies from disease or treatment are most at risk for fractures or internal bleeding.
w: A 70-year-old with seasonal allergies who uses a nasal spray
Allergies do not increase the risk of fracture or bleeding after a fall.
A 68-year-old with a healed ankle sprain who uses a cane
A healed sprain does not create the bone fragility or bleeding risk that worsens injury.
A 75-year-old with mild hearing loss who wears hearing aids
Hearing loss can affect safety but does not make injuries from a fall more severe.

alt.q: Why does the nurse consider a patient’s bleeding tendency when planning fall prevention?
alt.a: A fall can cause internal bleeding that is more serious in these patients
alt.ex: Bleeding tendencies from disease or medical treatment place patients most at risk for serious injury such as internal bleeding.
w: Bleeding tendencies cause the dizziness behind most falls
The concern is injury severity after a fall, not the cause of the fall.
Bleeding tendencies prevent patients from using walkers
Bleeding tendencies do not limit use of assistive devices.
Bleeding tendencies make fall risk tools inaccurate
Fall risk tools remain valid; bleeding raises the risk of serious injury.

items.q: Up to 70% of individuals with a recent fall report a fear of falling, and many of them limit physical or social activities.
items.a: True
items.ex: Up to 70% of recent fallers fear falling, and half of these limit or exclude physical or social activities.
items.ww: Fear of falling is common, not rare, and it often leads older adults to restrict activity.

alt.q: Fear of falling seldom changes the daily activities of community-dwelling older adults who have fallen.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Many older adults avoid activities out of fear; about half of those who fear falling limit physical or social activities.
alt.ww: Fear of falling frequently restricts activity, which is why it is a recognized concern for older adults.

items.q: What does Pathogen mean?
items.a: Any microorganism capable of producing an illness
items.ex: These terms describe key environmental threats: pathogens, poisons, infections acquired during care, and biological agents used as weapons.
w: Any substance that impairs health or causes death when ingested, inhaled, injected, or absorbed
That goes with Poison.
An infection not present on admission that develops during the stay
That goes with Health care–acquired infection.
Use of microbes or toxins as weapons to further personal or political agendas
That goes with Bioterrorism.

alt.q: What does Poison mean?
alt.a: Any substance that impairs health or causes death when ingested, inhaled, injected, or absorbed
alt.ex: These terms describe key environmental threats: pathogens, poisons, infections acquired during care, and biological agents used as weapons.
w: Any microorganism capable of producing an illness
That goes with Pathogen.
An infection not present on admission that develops during the stay
That goes with Health care–acquired infection.

alt.q: What does Health care–acquired infection mean?
alt.a: An infection not present on admission that develops during the stay

w: Any microorganism capable of producing an illness
That goes with Pathogen.
Any substance that impairs health or causes death when ingested, inhaled, injected, or absorbed
That goes with Poison.
Use of microbes or toxins as weapons to further personal or political agendas
That goes with Bioterrorism.

w: Any microorganism capable of producing an illness

Any substance that impairs health or causes death when ingested, inhaled, injected, or absorbed

An infection not present on admission that develops during the stay
That goes with Health care–acquired infection.

alt.a: Pathogen
alt.ex: These terms describe key environmental threats: pathogens, poisons, infections acquired during care, and biological agents used as weapons.
w: Poison
Poison: Any substance that impairs health or causes death when ingested, inhaled, injected, or absorbed.
Health care–acquired infection
Health care–acquired infection: An infection not present on admission that develops during the stay.
Bioterrorism
Bioterrorism: Use of microbes or toxins as weapons to further personal or political agendas.

alt.a: Poison
alt.ex: These terms describe key environmental threats: pathogens, poisons, infections acquired during care, and biological agents used as weapons.
w: Pathogen
Pathogen: Any microorganism capable of producing an illness.
Health care–acquired infection
Health care–acquired infection: An infection not present on admission that develops during the stay.
Bioterrorism
Bioterrorism: Use of microbes or toxins as weapons to further personal or political agendas.

alt.a: Health care–acquired infection
alt.ex: These terms describe key environmental threats: pathogens, poisons, infections acquired during care, and biological agents used as weapons.
w: Pathogen
Pathogen: Any microorganism capable of producing an illness.
Poison
Poison: Any substance that impairs health or causes death when ingested, inhaled, injected, or absorbed.
Bioterrorism

w: Pathogen

Poison
Poison: Any substance that impairs health or causes death when ingested, inhaled, injected, or absorbed.
Health care–acquired infection
Health care–acquired infection: An infection not present on admission that develops during the stay.

mt.q: Match each environmental safety term with its meaning.
pairs: Any microorganism capable of producing an illness
Any substance that impairs health or causes death when ingested, inhaled, injected, or absorbed
An infection not present on admission that develops during the stay
Use of microbes or toxins as weapons to further personal or political agendas
mt.ex: These terms describe key environmental threats: pathogens, poisons, infections acquired during care, and biological agents used as weapons.

items.q: Which statement accurately compares the bioterrorism agents anthrax and smallpox?
items.a: Anthrax spreads through aerosolized spores, whereas smallpox spreads person to person
items.ex: Anthrax, a bacterium, is not communicable by direct contact but spreads in aerosolized spores; smallpox, a virus, spreads readily person to person.
w: Smallpox spreads through aerosolized spores, whereas anthrax spreads person to person
This reverses the two agents’ modes of transmission.
Both spread readily through direct person-to-person contact with victims
Anthrax is not communicable from direct contact.
Both are rarely lethal and cause symptoms only after 30 days
Both can be lethal, and symptoms generally occur within 7 days of exposure.

alt.q: A family member asks whether they can catch anthrax by touching a relative exposed in a bioterrorist attack. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “Anthrax is not passed by direct contact; it spreads through spores in the air.”
alt.ex: Anthrax is not communicable from direct contact; it is transmitted in spores that become aerosolized.
w: “Yes, anthrax spreads easily by touch, just like smallpox does.”
Smallpox spreads person to person, but anthrax does not.
“Anthrax spreads only through contaminated food and water.”
Anthrax is transmitted in aerosolized spores.
“Anthrax cannot cause serious illness, so contact is no concern.”
Anthrax can be lethal.

items.q: A hospital accredited by The Joint Commission (TJC) is updating its emergency management (EM) program. Which plans must the program include? Select all that apply.
o: Communications
Communication plans are a required part of the EM program.
Staffing
Staffing plans are required so care continues during a disaster.
Disaster recovery
Plans must address recovery after the disaster.
Staff education and training
Staff must be educated and trained in disaster responses.
Marketing the hospital’s disaster readiness to the public
Marketing is not part of the required EM program.
A plan for only the single most likely local hazard
The EM program must include all types of hazards.
items.ex: TJC requires an all-hazards EM program overseen by senior leadership, with plans for communications, staffing, recovery, training, and more.

alt.q: Which statements about hospital disaster preparedness are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The EM program must be overseen by senior leadership
Senior leadership oversight is required.
Plans must address essential and critical utilities
Essential and critical utilities are a required plan area.
Testing and evaluation are part of the required plans
The program must be tested and evaluated.
Routine disaster drills help ensure staff are trained
Agencies hold routine drills so staff know appropriate responses.
Plans may be limited to natural disasters such as floods
Hospitals must plan for all types of hazards, including bioterrorism.
Drills are unnecessary once a written plan exists
Routine drills are needed to ensure staff are educated and trained.
alt.ex: Hospital EM programs need leadership oversight, all-hazards planning, utilities and continuity plans, testing, and routine drills.

items.q: A nurse teaches family caregivers how to reduce the spread of infection at home. Why does the nurse emphasize hand hygiene above other measures?
items.a: Touch is the most common way pathogens are transmitted
items.ex: The most common means of pathogen transmission is touch, so hand hygiene is the most effective way to limit spread.
w: Most pathogens spread through contaminated air vents
Touch, not air vents, is the most common route of transmission.
Hand hygiene replaces the need for immunizations
Immunizations remain essential to prevent vaccine-preventable diseases.
Most pathogens spread through contaminated tap water
Touch, not water supply, is the most common route of transmission.

alt.q: Which practice is the most effective method for limiting the transmission of pathogens in health care settings?
alt.a: Hand hygiene
alt.ex: The medically aseptic practice of hand hygiene is the most effective method for limiting pathogen transmission.
w: Wearing a surgical mask
Masks have specific uses but are not the most effective overall method.
Routine antibiotic use
Antibiotics treat infection; they are not a method for limiting transmission.
Private rooms for all
Room assignment does not replace hand hygiene as the most effective method.

items.q: Which immunization recommendations should the nurse include when teaching adults? Select all that apply.
o: Older adults should be immunized regularly against COVID-19, flu, and pneumonia
Older adults not regularly immunized for these are at risk for infectious disease.
Healthy adults 50 years and older should ask about the shingles vaccine
The shingles vaccine is recommended for healthy adults 50 years and older.
Health care workers exposed to blood should receive the three-dose hepatitis B series
Workers at risk of exposure to blood or body fluids need the three-dose series.
The shingles vaccine is reserved for adults older than 80 with chronic illness
It is recommended for healthy adults 50 years and older.
Health care workers need hepatitis B vaccine only after a needlestick injury
At-risk workers should receive the series in advance, not only after exposure.
items.ex: Adults need vaccines based on age, job, lifestyle, travel, and health conditions, including specific recommendations for older adults and health care workers.

alt.q: A healthy 55-year-old emergency department nurse asks which vaccines to discuss with a health care provider. Which vaccines are recommended for this nurse? Select all that apply.
o: Shingles vaccine
Shingles vaccination is recommended for healthy adults 50 years and older.
Three-dose hepatitis B series
Health care workers at risk of blood or body fluid exposure need the three-dose series.
A single hepatitis B dose instead of the series
The recommendation is the three-dose series.
The childhood combined 7-vaccine series
That series is completed in childhood by age 24 months.
alt.ex: This nurse qualifies for shingles vaccine by age and for the three-dose hepatitis B series because of occupational exposure.

items.q: A parent of a 2-month-old says, “I’m afraid the shots will cause autism or SIDS, so I want to skip them.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Studies have found no link between vaccines and autism or SIDS.”
items.ex: Studies show vaccines are not linked to autism and do not cause SIDS, even though SIDS often occurs at the age of early vaccines.
w: “Those risks are real but rare, so the benefits are worth it.”
Research shows no link to autism or SIDS, so calling the risks real is inaccurate.
“You can safely wait until your baby is 2 years old to start.”
Delaying leaves the child undervaccinated and at risk of contracting and spreading disease.
“If you are worried, it is fine to skip the vaccines entirely.”
Undervaccinated children are at increased risk of contracting and spreading infectious disease.

alt.q: Why do some parents mistakenly link the 2-month and 4-month vaccinations to sudden infant death syndrome?
alt.a: SIDS commonly occurs during the same time frame as these vaccinations
alt.ex: SIDS commonly occurs around the ages of the 2- and 4-month vaccines, but studies show vaccines do not cause it.
w: Vaccines given at these ages contain ingredients that cause SIDS
Studies show vaccines do not cause and are not linked to SIDS.
SIDS occurs only in infants who received these vaccines
SIDS is not linked to vaccination; the concern stems from timing overlap.
Infants sleep more deeply for weeks after these vaccines
This is not the reason; the concern comes from the shared time frame.

items.q: The nurse teaches new parents about safe sleep. Which statement by a parent shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “We will lay the baby on her back on a firm crib mattress with nothing else in the crib.”
items.ex: A safe sleep environment places the infant on the back on a firm mattress in a safety-approved crib free of pillows, toys, and blankets.
w: “We will put a soft pillow and blanket in the crib so she stays comfortable.”
Pillows, toys, and blankets in the crib are suffocation hazards.
“She can nap with me on the sofa as long as I stay awake.”
Parents should avoid sleeping with an infant in bed, on the sofa, or on the floor.
“We will lay her on her stomach so she does not choke if she spits up.”
A safe sleep environment places the infant on the back.

alt.q: During a home visit, which observation requires the nurse to intervene to promote infant sleep safety?
alt.a: The infant is asleep on the couch beside a parent
alt.ex: Sleeping with an infant on a sofa, in an adult bed, or on the floor is a hazard parents should be taught to avoid.
w: The infant is asleep on her back in a safety-approved crib
Back sleeping in a safety-approved crib is the recommended practice.
The crib mattress is firm and covered with a fitted sheet
A firm mattress with a fitted sheet reduces suffocation risk.
The crib is free of toys, pillows, and loose blankets
Keeping these items out of the crib removes suffocation hazards.

items.q: A school nurse is identifying students at risk for involvement in school violence. Which findings are individual risk factors for violence? Select all that apply.
o: History of early aggressive behavior
Early aggressive behavior is an individual risk factor.
Involvement with drugs, alcohol, or tobacco
Substance involvement is an individual risk factor.
History of violent victimization
Having been a victim of violence is an individual risk factor.
High emotional distress
High emotional distress is an individual risk factor.
Strong commitment to school and good grades
Low commitment to school and poor performance are risk factors; strong commitment is not.
Living in a community with many youth activities
Few community activities for young people is the risk factor.
items.ex: Individual violence risk factors include victimization, attention or learning disorders, early aggression, substance use, poor control, and high distress.

alt.q: Which community characteristics increase the risk for youth violence? Select all that apply.
o: High rates of violence and crime
Communities with high violence and crime rates increase risk.
High unemployment rates
High unemployment is a community risk factor.
Few community activities for young people
A lack of youth activities is a community risk factor.
Socially disorganized neighborhoods
Social disorganization is a community risk factor.
High levels of community participation
Low levels of community participation are the risk factor.
Stable housing where families stay for years
Unstable housing with frequent moves is the risk factor.
alt.ex: Community risk factors include violence and crime, limited economic opportunity, unemployment, poverty, unstable housing, few youth activities, and low participation.

items.q: A school nurse is assessing a 15-year-old for possible substance abuse. Which finding should the nurse recognize as a possible clue?
items.a: Wearing long-sleeved shirts in hot weather
items.ex: Long sleeves in hot weather are an environmental clue to substance abuse, along with drug paraphernalia and liquor bottles.
w: Joining a new school sports team
Joining a team is not identified as a clue to substance abuse.
Spending weekends at family events
Family involvement is not a substance abuse clue; isolation is.
Improved attendance at school
Absenteeism, not improved attendance, is a psychosocial clue.

alt.q: Parents of a 16-year-old ask what signs might suggest their teen is using drugs. Which psychosocial clues should the nurse include?
alt.a: Failing grades, absenteeism, and withdrawal into isolation
alt.ex: Psychosocial clues include failing grades, change in dress, absenteeism, isolation, and changes in interpersonal relationships.
w: Greater interest in family dinners and outings
Increased family involvement is not a clue to substance abuse.
Steady grades and regular school attendance
Stable grades and attendance do not suggest substance abuse.
Some emotional separation from parents toward peers
Emotional separation and stronger peer influence are normal in adolescence.

items.q: Which factors place an adolescent at risk for suicide? Select all that apply.
o: A recent death of a close friend
A recent or serious loss is a suicide risk factor.
A prior suicide attempt
Prior attempts increase suicide risk.
Access to weapons or pills at home
Access to lethal means is a risk factor.
Being a victim of bullying
Being bullied is a known suicide risk factor.
Strong connections with family and community members
Strong connections help minimize suicide risk rather than raise it.
Good problem-solving skills for peer conflict
Good problem-solving abilities help reduce suicide risk.
items.ex: Adolescent suicide risk factors include loss, psychiatric disorders, prior attempts, substance use, bullying, lack of support, and access to lethal means.

alt.q: A nurse reviews the history of a 14-year-old admitted for a sports injury. Which findings should prompt further assessment for suicide risk? Select all that apply.
o: Diagnosed with depression last year
A mood disorder such as depression is a suicide risk factor.
Family history of suicide
A family history of suicide increases risk.
Reports feeling isolated with no adult support
Lack of social support from adults and friends is a risk factor.
Plays on a school soccer team
Team sports participation is not a suicide risk factor.
Recently earned a driver’s license
Getting a license is not a suicide risk factor.
alt.ex: Depression, family history of suicide, and isolation without support are risk factors that warrant further suicide assessment.

items.q: Once an older adult falls, the risk of falling a second time is doubled.
items.a: True
items.ex: A previous fall doubles the risk of another fall, which is why fall history is central to risk assessment.
items.ww: A first fall does not leave risk unchanged or lower it; it doubles the likelihood of another fall.

alt.q: A previous fall has little effect on an older adult’s risk of falling again.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Once a patient falls, the risk of falling a second time is doubled.
alt.ww: Fall history is a major risk factor, which is why it appears on fall risk assessment tools.

items.q: A patient with dementia walks aimlessly up and down the hallway and tries to enter a staff-only area. Which description fits this behavior?
items.a: Wandering caused by spatial disorientation and impaired navigation
items.ex: Dementia causes spatial disorientation and impaired navigation, leading to wandering, an aimless, purposeless movement that risks falls and injury.
w: Mind wandering caused by a task needing little attention
Mind wandering is unfocused thought, not aimless physical movement.
Purposeful exercise to rebuild strength and endurance
Wandering is aimless and purposeless, not planned exercise.
Normal age-related forgetfulness, such as misplacing keys
Misplacing keys is a normal change, unlike dementia-related wandering.

alt.q: Why should the nurse avoid abruptly interrupting a patient with dementia who is wandering?
alt.a: Interrupting a wandering patient can increase the patient’s distress
alt.ex: Interrupting wandering can increase distress, so caregivers apply safety principles to reduce wandering and keep surroundings safe.
w: Wandering is harmless and needs no intervention
Wandering exposes patients to falls, injuries, and leaving the unit.
Interrupting wandering makes the patient fall asleep
Interruption increases distress; it does not cause sleep.
Wandering patients cannot hear staff who speak to them
Wandering stems from disorientation, not hearing loss.

items.q: A nurse in occupational health learns that staff rarely wear N95 respirators because the unit often runs out of them. Which category of factors affecting PPE adherence does this represent?
items.a: Environmental factors
items.ex: Environmental factors include the availability of equipment and negative-pressure rooms.
w: Individual factors
Individual factors are knowledge, beliefs, attitudes, and perception of risk.
Organizational factors
Organizational factors are management expectations, feedback, policies, and training.
Lifestyle factors
Lifestyle is an individual safety risk, not one of the three PPE adherence categories.

alt.q: Staff report that managers never give feedback on PPE use and that PPE training is rarely offered. Which category of PPE adherence factors needs attention?
alt.a: Organizational factors
alt.ex: Organizational factors include management’s expectations, performance feedback, workplace policies, and training programs.
w: Individual factors
Individual factors concern the worker’s own knowledge, beliefs, and risk perception.
Environmental factors
Environmental factors concern equipment and negative-pressure room availability.
Sociodemographic factors
Sociodemographics fall under individual factors.

items.q: A patient being discharged home after hip surgery says, “I’ve lived alone for 30 years. I know how to keep myself safe.” Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess the patient’s understanding of the specific safety risks after surgery
items.ex: Never assume a patient’s knowledge; one of the first areas to assess is the patient’s understanding of safety risks and how to minimize them.
w: Skip home safety teaching because the patient is experienced
Never assume a patient’s knowledge about a safety topic.
Hand the patient a safety pamphlet and complete the discharge
Teaching should follow assessment of what the patient understands.
Tell the patient that living alone is unsafe after surgery
Dismissing the patient’s view does not assess understanding of risks.

alt.q: Which behavior reflects a patient’s lack of safety awareness?
alt.a: Storing medicines on a low shelf within a toddler’s reach
alt.ex: Not keeping medicines or poisons away from children is an example of a lack of safety awareness.
w: Checking expiration dates before using food products
Reading expiration dates shows safety awareness.
Wearing required safety equipment while at work
Using safety equipment at work shows safety awareness.
Keeping cleaning products in a locked cabinet
Locking up cleaning products shows safety awareness.

items.q: Which description defines a medical error?
items.a: A planned action not completed as intended, or use of a wrong plan of care
items.ex: Medical errors occur when planned actions are not completed as intended or wrong plans of care are used, in all health care settings.
w: Any poor outcome that occurs despite correct care
A poor outcome after correct care is not an error in planning or execution.
An injury that happens only in an operating room
Medical errors occur in all health care settings.
A complaint a patient files about the quality of care
A complaint is not the definition of a medical error.

alt.q: A medication was ordered correctly, but a nurse gave it to the patient in the next room. How is this event classified?
alt.a: A medical error, because the planned action was not completed as intended
alt.ex: A planned action that is not completed as intended is a medical error.
w: A nurse-sensitive indicator, because a nurse directly caused it
Nurse-sensitive indicators are hospital-acquired conditions such as falls and pressure injuries.
An unanticipated physiological event that could not be predicted
This term describes unpredictable falls from seizures or strokes, not care errors.
An equipment-related accident caused by poor device design
No equipment failure was involved; the planned action was carried out wrongly.

items.q: Under CMS rules, hospitals receive no additional payment for which conditions when they were not present on admission? Select all that apply.
o: Stage III or IV pressure injury
Stage III and IV pressure injuries are on the CMS list.
Fall resulting in a hip fracture
Falls and trauma such as fractures are on the CMS list.
Catheter-associated urinary tract infection
CAUTIs are on the CMS list.
Foreign object retained after surgery
Retained foreign objects are on the CMS list.
Stage 1 pressure injury
Only stage III and IV pressure injuries are on the CMS list.
Pneumonia diagnosed in the emergency department before admission
A condition present on admission is not hospital acquired.
items.ex: CMS does not pay extra for selected hospital-acquired conditions not present on admission, such as falls with trauma, stage III/IV pressure injuries, and CAUTIs.

alt.q: Which hospital-acquired conditions are on the CMS present-on-admission indicator list? Select all that apply.
o: Air embolism
Air embolism is on the CMS list.
Blood incompatibility
Blood incompatibility is on the CMS list.
Hypoglycemic coma from poor glycemic control
Manifestations of poor glycemic control are on the CMS list.
Iatrogenic pneumothorax with venous catheterization
Iatrogenic pneumothorax with venous catheterization is on the CMS list.
Seasonal influenza acquired before admission
A condition present on admission is not hospital acquired.
Stage 2 pressure injury
Only stage III and IV pressure injuries are listed.
alt.ex: The CMS list includes air embolism, blood incompatibility, poor glycemic control, iatrogenic pneumothorax, and other preventable conditions.

items.q: Hospital-acquired conditions such as falls and stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries are [[nurse-sensitive indicators|nurse-sensitive indicator|nurse sensitive indicators|nurse sensitive indicator]], meaning a nurse directly affects their development.
items.ex: Because nurses directly affect these conditions, they are the focus of nursing performance improvement efforts.

alt.q: Because a nurse directly influences whether conditions like falls develop, they are called [[nurse-sensitive indicators|nurse-sensitive indicator|nurse sensitive indicators|nurse sensitive indicator]] and are targets of nursing performance improvement.
alt.ex: Because nurses directly affect these conditions, they are the focus of nursing performance improvement efforts.

items.q: A nurse discovers that a patient received a medication dose intended for another patient. After ensuring the patient is safe and notifying the health care provider, which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Complete an incident report that fully describes the event
items.ex: When an actual or potential adverse event occurs, the nurse involved completes a confidential incident or occurrence report.
w: Wait to see whether harm occurs before reporting the event
Actual or potential adverse events are reported whether or not harm occurs.
Mention the event only verbally to the nurse manager
A written incident report lets the organization identify trends and areas to improve.
Correct the medication record so the error is not visible
Hiding the event prevents the organization from learning and improving.

alt.q: Why does focusing on the root cause of an error, rather than on the individual involved, improve patient safety?
alt.a: It identifies what contributed to the error and promotes a culture of safety
alt.ex: Focusing on the root cause instead of the individual promotes a culture of safety and pinpoints what contributed to an error.
w: It ensures the staff member involved is disciplined fairly
A culture of safety is blame free; discipline is not the purpose.
It removes the need to complete an incident report
Incident reports are still completed so trends can be identified.
It allows the agency to avoid reporting events to regulators
TJC-accredited agencies must analyze serious events and monitor corrective plans.

items.q: A nurse finds that an infusion pump is not delivering fluid at the programmed rate. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Replace it with a working pump, tag it, take it out of service, and report it
items.ex: Replace faulty equipment, tag it, take it out of service, and promptly report the malfunction to the appropriate department.
w: Keep using it while checking the infusion more often
Faulty equipment must be removed from service, not used with closer monitoring.
Try to repair the pump at the bedside before telling anyone
Do not operate or repair equipment without proper instruction; report it.
Return the pump to the supply room for the next user
Untagged faulty equipment could harm another patient.

alt.q: A patient dies, and the investigation suggests a malfunctioning medical device was involved. To whom must the agency report the death?
alt.a: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the product manufacturer
alt.ex: Agencies must report all suspected medical device–related deaths to the FDA and the product manufacturer.
w: The Occupational Safety and Health Administration only
OSHA addresses worker safety; device deaths go to the FDA and manufacturer.
The patient’s insurance company and the billing office
Insurers are not the required recipients of device-related death reports.
The National Quality Forum and the local newspaper
The NQF endorses standards; device deaths are reported to the FDA and manufacturer.

items.q: A nurse is about to perform a high-risk procedure that the nurse has done only once before. Which action best reduces the risk of a procedure-related accident?
items.a: Take a short time-out to review the steps and the agency procedure manual
items.ex: For high-risk or less familiar procedures, take a time-out, reflect, review knowledge, and refer to the policy and procedure manual if needed.
w: Perform the procedure quickly to limit the patient’s anxiety
Rushing increases error risk; a time-out to review is safer.
Answer pages and phone calls while performing the procedure
Distractions and interruptions contribute to procedure-related accidents.
Ask the patient to explain how the procedure was done last time
The patient is not the source for procedure standards; the policy manual is.

alt.q: A nurse is preparing an IV medication when a colleague repeatedly interrupts with questions. Why should the nurse limit these interruptions?
alt.a: Distractions and interruptions contribute to procedure-related accidents
alt.ex: Distractions and interruptions must be limited, especially during high-risk procedures such as IV medication administration.
w: Colleagues are not allowed to ask questions during a shift
Collaboration is encouraged; the issue is interruption during high-risk tasks.
Interruptions affect only the time needed for documentation
Interruptions raise the risk of errors in the procedure itself.
IV medications must legally be prepared in complete silence
No such law exists; limiting interruptions reduces accident risk.

items.q: A nurse is splashed on the arm with a disinfectant while cleaning equipment. Which resource provides first aid guidelines for this exposure?
items.a: The safety data sheet for the chemical
items.ex: Safety data sheets describe a chemical’s hazards, safe handling, first aid guidelines, and containment and removal of spills.
w: The agency’s fall prevention policy
Fall policies do not cover chemical exposure.
The patient’s medication administration record
The MAR lists patient medications, not chemical first aid.
The list of serious reportable events
The SRE list names adverse events; it gives no first aid guidance.

alt.q: Which information does a safety data sheet (SDS) provide?
alt.a: Health hazards, safe handling precautions, first aid, and spill cleanup steps
alt.ex: SDSs are required resources detailing a chemical’s hazards, safe handling and use, first aid, and spill containment and removal.
w: Patient fall risk scores and prevention strategies
Fall risk scores come from fall risk assessment tools.
Dosage ranges and side effects of patient medications
Drug references, not SDSs, provide dosing information.
Staff schedules for fire and disaster drills
Drill schedules are not part of an SDS.

items.q: In fall prevention, which step comes right after “Assess the patient’s fall risk”?
items.a: Develop a personalized fall prevention plan
items.ex: Fall prevention is a three-step process: assess fall risk, develop a personalized prevention plan, and consistently carry it out.
w: Consistently execute the plan
That's step 3 of 3.

alt.q: Which step comes first in fall prevention?
alt.a: Assess the patient’s fall risk
alt.ex: Fall prevention is a three-step process: assess fall risk, develop a personalized prevention plan, and consistently carry it out.
w: Develop a personalized fall prevention plan
That's step 2 of 3.
Consistently execute the plan
That's step 3 of 3.

alt.q: Which step comes last in fall prevention?
alt.a: Consistently execute the plan
alt.ex: Fall prevention is a three-step process: assess fall risk, develop a personalized prevention plan, and consistently carry it out.
w: Develop a personalized fall prevention plan
That's step 2 of 3.
Assess the patient’s fall risk
That's step 1 of 3.

alt.q: In fall prevention, which step comes right after “Develop a personalized fall prevention plan”?
alt.a: Consistently execute the plan
alt.ex: Fall prevention is a three-step process: assess fall risk, develop a personalized prevention plan, and consistently carry it out.
w: Assess the patient’s fall risk
That's step 1 of 3.

alt.q: In fall prevention, which step comes right before “Develop a personalized fall prevention plan”?
alt.a: Assess the patient’s fall risk
alt.ex: Fall prevention is a three-step process: assess fall risk, develop a personalized prevention plan, and consistently carry it out.
w: Consistently execute the plan
That's step 3 of 3.

alt.q: In fall prevention, which step comes right before “Consistently execute the plan”?
alt.a: Develop a personalized fall prevention plan
alt.ex: Fall prevention is a three-step process: assess fall risk, develop a personalized prevention plan, and consistently carry it out.
w: Assess the patient’s fall risk
That's step 1 of 3.

ord.q: Put the steps of the fall prevention process in order.
items: Assess the patient’s fall risk
Develop a personalized fall prevention plan
Consistently execute the plan
ord.ex: Fall prevention is a three-step process: assess fall risk, develop a personalized prevention plan, and consistently carry it out.

items.q: Which description fits an Accidental fall?
items.a: Patient slips or trips, such as on spilled water or IV tubing
items.ex: Universal Fall Precautions prevent accidental falls, tailored interventions prevent anticipated falls, and unanticipated physiological falls cannot be predicted.
w: Caused by underlying symptoms or conditions such as gait instability or urinary frequency
That goes with Anticipated fall.
Cannot be predicted, such as from an undiagnosed seizure or a stroke
That goes with Unanticipated physiological fall.

alt.q: Which description fits an Anticipated fall?
alt.a: Caused by underlying symptoms or conditions such as gait instability or urinary frequency
alt.ex: Universal Fall Precautions prevent accidental falls, tailored interventions prevent anticipated falls, and unanticipated physiological falls cannot be predicted.
w: Patient slips or trips, such as on spilled water or IV tubing
That goes with Accidental fall.
Cannot be predicted, such as from an undiagnosed seizure or a stroke
That goes with Unanticipated physiological fall.

alt.q: Which description fits an Unanticipated physiological fall?
alt.a: Cannot be predicted, such as from an undiagnosed seizure or a stroke
alt.ex: Universal Fall Precautions prevent accidental falls, tailored interventions prevent anticipated falls, and unanticipated physiological falls cannot be predicted.
w: Patient slips or trips, such as on spilled water or IV tubing
That goes with Accidental fall.
Caused by underlying symptoms or conditions such as gait instability or urinary frequency
That goes with Anticipated fall.

alt.q: Which type of fall is described as “Patient slips or trips, such as on spilled water or IV tubing”?
alt.a: Accidental fall
alt.ex: Universal Fall Precautions prevent accidental falls, tailored interventions prevent anticipated falls, and unanticipated physiological falls cannot be predicted.
w: Anticipated fall
Anticipated fall: Caused by underlying symptoms or conditions such as gait instability or urinary frequency.
Unanticipated physiological fall
Unanticipated physiological fall: Cannot be predicted, such as from an undiagnosed seizure or a stroke.

alt.q: Which type of fall is described as “Caused by underlying symptoms or conditions such as gait instability or urinary frequency”?
alt.a: Anticipated fall
alt.ex: Universal Fall Precautions prevent accidental falls, tailored interventions prevent anticipated falls, and unanticipated physiological falls cannot be predicted.
w: Accidental fall
Accidental fall: Patient slips or trips, such as on spilled water or IV tubing.
Unanticipated physiological fall
Unanticipated physiological fall: Cannot be predicted, such as from an undiagnosed seizure or a stroke.

alt.q: Which type of fall is described as “Cannot be predicted, such as from an undiagnosed seizure or a stroke”?
alt.a: Unanticipated physiological fall
alt.ex: Universal Fall Precautions prevent accidental falls, tailored interventions prevent anticipated falls, and unanticipated physiological falls cannot be predicted.
w: Accidental fall
Accidental fall: Patient slips or trips, such as on spilled water or IV tubing.
Anticipated fall
Anticipated fall: Caused by underlying symptoms or conditions such as gait instability or urinary frequency.

mt.q: Match each type of fall with its description.
pairs: Patient slips or trips, such as on spilled water or IV tubing
Caused by underlying symptoms or conditions such as gait instability or urinary frequency
Cannot be predicted, such as from an undiagnosed seizure or a stroke
mt.ex: Universal Fall Precautions prevent accidental falls, tailored interventions prevent anticipated falls, and unanticipated physiological falls cannot be predicted.

items.q: Universal Fall Precautions apply to all patients regardless of their fall risk.
items.a: True
items.ex: Universal Fall Precautions keep the environment safe and comfortable and prevent accidental slips and trips for every patient.
items.ww: They are not limited to high-risk patients; tailored interventions are added on top for patient-specific risks.

alt.q: Universal Fall Precautions are reserved for patients who score as high risk on a fall risk assessment tool.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Universal Fall Precautions apply to every patient; those at higher risk also receive tailored interventions.
alt.ww: Limiting them to high scorers would leave other patients exposed to accidental slips and trips.

items.q: Intrinsic fall risk factors are environmental factors, such as hospital working processes, that increase a patient’s susceptibility to falling.
items.a: False
items.ex: Intrinsic factors are patient-related predisposing factors; extrinsic factors relate to the hospital environment and working processes.
items.ww: Environmental and work-process factors are extrinsic, not intrinsic.

alt.q: Patient-related predisposing factors are intrinsic fall risk factors, whereas hospital environment and working-process factors are extrinsic.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Fall risk factors fall into two categories: patient-related (intrinsic) and environment and working-process related (extrinsic).
alt.ww: Swapping the labels is a common misconception; intrinsic factors come from the patient.

items.q: In health care settings, which statement describes the most common pattern of workplace violence?
items.a: Patients or visitors toward workers, most often by a person with altered mental status
items.ex: The most common type is patient/visitor to worker, and the most common perpetrator characteristic is altered mental status.
w: Workers toward patients, most often by staff who are understaffed
Patient/visitor-to-worker violence is the most common type.
Workers toward coworkers, most often during change-of-shift report
Patient/visitor-to-worker violence is the most common type.
Visitors toward other visitors, most often in crowded waiting rooms
Most violence is directed at workers, not other visitors.

alt.q: An emergency department nurse reviews conditions on the unit. Which finding increases the risk for workplace violence?
alt.a: Long wait times in a crowded waiting area
alt.ex: Stressful conditions such as long waits and crowding are risk factors for workplace violence.
w: Bright lighting in the parking area
Poor lighting, not bright lighting, is a risk factor.
Restricted access to patient care areas
Unrestricted access to rooms and clinics is the risk factor.
Adequate staffing on every shift
Understaffing, not adequate staffing, is a risk factor.

sections.name: Nursing process: patient safety and quality

items.q: Which elements belong in a person-centered safety assessment? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s own perceptions of risk factors
Patient perceptions of risk are part of a person-centered assessment.
The patient’s values and beliefs about safety
Values and beliefs shape how the patient views safety.
The patient’s previous experience with accidents
Information about past accidents is included.
The patient’s knowledge of how to adapt to safety risks
Knowledge of adapting to risks is part of the assessment.
The nurse’s personal view of what a safe home looks like
Nurses cannot base decisions on their own bias about what is safe.
An assumption that adults already know basic safety rules
Never assume a patient’s knowledge about a safety topic.
items.ex: A person-centered assessment covers perceptions of risk, values and beliefs, concerns about the setting, knowledge to adapt, and past accidents.

alt.q: A nurse completes a safety assessment for a newly admitted patient who recently immigrated and speaks limited English. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Ask, “What does it mean for you to be safe?”
This question reveals the patient’s own perception of safety.
Use a professional interpreter during the assessment
A professional interpreter is critical to learn how the patient perceives safety precautions.
Ask about the patient’s concerns about being in the hospital
Concerns about the health care setting are part of a person-centered assessment.
Judge the patient’s risks using only the nurse’s own standards
Individuals perceive safety differently, so the nurse’s bias cannot guide decisions.
Skip the cultural review because hospital rules apply to everyone
Assessment must include the patient’s cultural perspective and health literacy.
alt.ex: Person-centered assessment explores the patient’s meaning of safety, concerns, and cultural perspective, using a professional interpreter when needed.

items.q: A patient admitted with pneumonia tells the nurse, “I walk just fine on my own at home.” How should the nurse assess the patient’s gait and balance?
items.a: Observe the patient walking in the room
items.ex: Assess balance and gait by watching the patient walk; do not rely on self-report.
w: Document the patient’s report that walking is normal
Self-report of walking ability is often misleading.
Rely on a relative’s description instead of watching
Families provide useful history, but gait must be directly observed.
Use the gait findings from the last admission
Earlier findings may not reflect the patient’s current status.

alt.q: A home health nurse plans a fall risk assessment for a patient recovering from a stroke. Why does the nurse watch the patient walk rather than ask about walking ability?
alt.a: Patients’ self-reports of their ability to walk are often misleading
alt.ex: Experience shows self-reported walking ability is often misleading, so assessment must involve observing the patient walk.
w: Patients after a stroke are unable to answer questions
Many stroke patients can answer questions; the issue is accuracy of self-report.
Observing gait is required only for billing purposes
Observation is done for accurate fall risk assessment, not billing.
Watching the patient walk replaces the fall history
Fall history is still gathered; observation complements it.

items.q: A patient has the nursing diagnosis Risk for Fall, with visual impairment as the risk factor. Which intervention best addresses this risk factor?
items.a: Keep the room well lit and the patient’s eyeglasses clean and within reach
items.ex: Interventions must target the identified risk factor; for visual impairment, good lighting, orientation, and accessible eyeglasses reduce fall risk.
w: Perform range-of-motion exercises with the patient twice daily
ROM exercises address altered mobility, not visual impairment.
Increase the frequency of supervised walks in the hallway
More supervised ambulation targets altered mobility.
Teach the patient how to use a cane on the stronger side
Cane teaching addresses mobility, not vision.

alt.q: A patient at risk for falls routinely has orthostatic hypotension. Which intervention is tailored to this risk factor?
alt.a: Have the patient dangle the feet at the bedside for 3 to 5 minutes before walking
alt.ex: With orthostatic hypotension, place the bed low and have the patient dangle 3 to 5 minutes before ambulating.
w: Provide a bedside commode for 3 to 5 days instead of walking
A bedside commode is tailored to urinary urgency or incontinence.
Keep 2 night-lights on to brighten the path to the bathroom
Lighting addresses visual impairment, not blood pressure drops.
Apply 1 yellow wristband and take no further action
A wristband communicates risk but does not address orthostatic hypotension.

items.a: Evaluate gait and balance if no sign of fall severity is present
items.ex: That's step 3 of 4. Screening questions lead to a fall severity check, then gait and balance testing, then a multifactorial assessment when gait or balance is impaired.
w: Complete a multifactorial fall risk assessment if gait or balance is impaired
That's step 4 of 4.
Screen with three key questions about falls, unsteadiness, and worry
That's step 1 of 4.
