ord.q: Following the World Falls guideline for community-dwelling older adults, put these steps of fall risk evaluation in order.
items: Screen with three key questions about falls, unsteadiness, and worry
Assess fall severity in those who answer yes to any question
Evaluate gait and balance if no sign of fall severity is present
Complete a multifactorial fall risk assessment if gait or balance is impaired
ord.ex: Screening questions lead to a fall severity check, then gait and balance testing, then a multifactorial assessment when gait or balance is impaired.

items.q: A primary care nurse screens a 70-year-old for fall risk using the World Falls guideline. Which key questions should the nurse ask? Select all that apply.
o: Have you fallen in the past year?
A fall in the past year is one of the three key questions.
Do you feel unsteady when standing or walking?
Unsteadiness is one of the three key questions.
Are you worried about falling?
Worry about falling is one of the three key questions.
Do you use a cane or walker at home?
Assistive device use is not one of the three key screening questions.
How many prescription medications do you take?
Medication count is not one of the three key screening questions.
items.ex: The guideline screens adults 65 and older with three questions; a yes to any one prompts assessment of fall severity.

alt.q: An older adult answers yes to a fall screening question. Which findings indicate fall severity under the World Falls guideline? Select all that apply.
o: An injury from the fall
Injury is a sign of fall severity.
Two or more falls in the last year
Two or more falls in a year indicates fall severity.
Frailty
Frailty is a fall severity criterion.
Inability to get up after lying on the floor
Being unable to get up from the floor indicates fall severity.
A single fall without injury while gardening
One noninjurious fall does not meet a fall severity criterion.
Wearing glasses for reading
Reading glasses are not a fall severity criterion.
alt.ex: Fall severity includes injury, two or more falls in a year, frailty, inability to get up, and loss of consciousness or suspected syncope.

items.q: Once a fall risk assessment is completed on admission, it needs to be repeated only if the patient actually falls.
items.a: False
items.ex: At minimum, fall risk is assessed on admission, after a change in condition, after a fall, and when the patient is transferred.
items.ww: Hospitalized patients’ conditions often change, so reassessment is also needed after condition changes and transfers.

alt.q: At a minimum, fall risk is assessed on admission, after a change in the patient’s condition, after a fall, and on transfer.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: These minimum assessment points capture changing risk, and at-risk patients need ongoing assessment during their stay.
alt.ww: Assessing only on admission would miss new risks that develop as the patient’s condition changes.

items.q: Which expected outcome is written correctly for a patient with the nursing diagnosis Risk for Fall?
items.a: Patient remains free of falls for the next 1 month
items.ex: Outcomes should be measurable, realistic, time limited, and focused on removing risks or managing contributing factors.
w: Patient will understand fall risks better within 1 month
“Understand” is not measurable; outcomes must be observable.
Nurse will place the bed in low position for 1 month
This is a nursing intervention, not a patient outcome.
Patient will walk without a walker 1 day after a stroke
This outcome is not realistic for the patient’s condition.

alt.q: Mrs. Cohen, 10 days after a stroke, is at high risk for falls. Why did Kylie set the outcome “Patient will not fall in 1 month” rather than a longer time frame?
alt.a: Fall risk is highest early in recovery, so a realistic short time frame fits
alt.ex: Kylie hopes to extend the time frame later, but Mrs. Cohen’s high early fall risk makes a 1-month outcome realistic.
w: Agency rules require every outcome to be met within 1 month
Time frames are individualized to the patient, not fixed by rule.
Mrs. Cohen will no longer be at risk for falls after 1 month
Her risk will persist; Kylie hopes to extend the time frame later.
Home health visits end after 1 month for all stroke patients
Visit limits are not the reason given for the time frame.

items.q: A parent of a 1-year-old asks how to avoid accidentally leaving the child in a hot car. Which suggestion should the nurse give?
items.a: Keep an item such as a purse or phone in the back seat with the child
items.ex: Putting a purse or phone in the back serves as a reminder; a change in routine is a major risk for hot-car deaths.
w: Crack the windows open when parking for a short errand
Never leave a child alone in a car, even briefly; heatstroke can develop quickly.
Park only in shaded areas when the child is in the car
Heatstroke deaths occur even in shaded vehicles and at temperatures as low as 57°F.
Leave the car unlocked so a passerby can help if needed
Lock the car when not in use so children cannot climb in.

alt.q: Why are young children left in a parked vehicle at risk for heatstroke even on a mild day?
alt.a: Their body temperature rises 3 to 5 times faster than an adult’s
alt.ex: Children’s body temperature rises 3–5 times faster than adults’, and heatstroke deaths occur even at 57°F (13.9°C).
w: They sweat 3 to 5 times more than adults and dehydrate
The danger is a rapid rise in body temperature, not excess sweating.
Car interiors heat up only when it is above 100°F outside
Heatstroke deaths have occurred at outside temperatures as low as 57°F.
Their body temperature rises half as fast as an adult’s
Children’s temperature rises 3 to 5 times faster, not slower.

items.q: An 82-year-old patient takes several medications. Which medication classes does the nurse recognize as increasing this patient’s fall risk? Select all that apply.
o: Diuretics
Diuretics increase voiding frequency and fall risk.
Antihypertensives
Antihypertensives can cause dizziness and hypotension.
Anxiolytic and hypnotic agents
Anxiolytics and hypnotics are listed as increasing fall risk.
Anticholinergics
Anticholinergics are listed as increasing fall risk.
Calcium supplements
Calcium is not among the medications listed as increasing fall risk.
Topical skin moisturizers
Topical moisturizers are not among the listed fall-risk medications.
items.ex: Anticholinergics, diuretics, anxiolytics, hypnotics, antidepressants, antihypertensives, vasodilators, analgesics, and laxatives pose or increase fall risk in older adults.

alt.q: Which physiological changes of aging increase an older adult’s safety risk? Select all that apply.
o: Slowed reaction time
Slowed reaction time is an age-related change affecting safety.
Decreased flexibility and strength
Reduced flexibility and strength affect safety.
More frequent nocturia and incontinence
Nocturia and incontinence increase nighttime fall risk.
Slowed reflexes
Reflexes slow with aging.
Faster response to multiple stimuli
The ability to respond to multiple stimuli slows with aging.
Improved hearing and night vision
Older adults experience visual and hearing alterations.
alt.ex: Aging brings vision and hearing changes, slowed reactions and reflexes, reduced flexibility and strength, memory changes, and nocturia that raise safety risks.

items.q: Thawing frozen meat on the kitchen counter is safe as long as the meat is cooked within 2 hours.
items.a: False
items.ex: Never thaw frozen food on the counter; refrigerate perishables within 2 hours and keep the refrigerator below 40°F.
items.ww: Counter thawing is ruled out by the Chill principle no matter how soon the food is cooked.

alt.q: Under the Chill principle of food safety, perishables are refrigerated within 2 hours and the refrigerator is kept below 40°F.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The CDC Chill tip calls for a working refrigerator below 40°F, refrigerating perishables within 2 hours, and never thawing food on the counter.
alt.ww: Longer delays or warmer storage do not meet the CDC Chill guidance for preventing foodborne illness.

items.q: A parent calls the clinic and says their 3-year-old just swallowed some liquid household cleaner. The child is awake, alert, and breathing normally. Which instruction by the nurse is appropriate?
items.a: “Call the poison control center now for specific guidance.”
items.ex: For a conscious, alert person, contact poison control before trying any intervention; never induce vomiting after household cleaner ingestion.
w: “Make your child vomit to empty the stomach.”
Never induce vomiting after ingestion of household cleaners.
“Give a dose of ipecac syrup from your medicine cabinet.”
Ipecac is no longer recommended for routine home treatment of poisoning.
“Wait an hour to see whether any symptoms appear.”
First aid within seconds to minutes makes a difference; get guidance now.

alt.q: A person who swallowed an unknown substance collapses, has a seizure, and cannot be awakened. Which action should the nurse take first?
alt.a: Call 9-1-1 immediately
alt.ex: Collapse, seizure, trouble breathing, or inability to awaken calls for 9-1-1 immediately, with CPR if indicated.
w: Call the poison control center for advice
Poison control is for conscious, alert persons; collapse or seizure needs 9-1-1.
Give a small amount of milk to drink
Fluids are given only to a conscious person able to swallow.
Induce vomiting to remove the substance
Inducing vomiting is not recommended and risks aspiration.

items.q: A nurse receiving a newly transferred patient notices a yellow wristband. Under the standardized color scheme recommended by the American Hospital Association, what does it indicate?
items.a: The patient is at risk for falling
items.ex: The AHA recommended red for allergy, yellow for fall risk, and purple for do not resuscitate.
w: The patient has an allergy
Red wristbands indicate allergies.
The patient has a do-not-resuscitate order
Purple wristbands indicate do not resuscitate.
The patient needs isolation precautions
Yellow indicates fall risk, not isolation.

alt.q: A patient wearing a yellow fall-risk wristband has improved, and the nurse wonders whether the band is still accurate. Which action is best?
alt.a: Verify that the wristband reflects the patient’s current condition
alt.ex: Wristbands can be missed or outdated, so always verify that the alert band reflects the patient’s current condition.
w: Rely on the wristband because it was applied on admission
A wristband applied earlier may no longer reflect current risk.
Remove all wristbands because they are hard to see in low light
Wristbands remain a communication tool; verify rather than remove them all.
Assume the wristband now signals a latex allergy instead
Yellow signals fall risk; allergy is red.

items.q: An older adult patient who is confused keeps pulling at the IV line in the forearm. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Camouflage the IV line with a stockinette sleeve or clothing
items.ex: Try restraint alternatives first; camouflaging IV lines keeps the patient from focusing on and dislodging them.
w: Apply wrist restraints to both of the patient’s arms
Restraints are used only after alternatives fail, choosing the least restrictive type.
Give a sedative to calm the patient’s behavior
Using medication to manage behavior is a chemical restraint, not a first-line alternative.
Raise all four side rails on the patient’s bed
Full side rails can act as a restraint and increase fall risk.

alt.q: Alternatives have failed, and a confused patient keeps pulling at a nasogastric feeding tube. The health care provider orders a restraint. Which type should the nurse use?
alt.a: The least restrictive device, such as a soft mitt
alt.ex: If a restraint is required, always use the least restrictive type, such as a soft mitt rather than a limb restraint.
w: A jacket restraint to keep the patient in bed
Many agencies have eliminated vest restraints, and they are not least restrictive.
Four-point limb restraints for full immobilization
Choose the least restrictive type, such as a mitt, not limb restraints.
All side rails raised plus a sedative as needed
Chemical restraint and full side rails are not the least restrictive option.

items.q: What is the restraint order time limit for Adults 18 years and older?
items.a: 4 hours
items.ex: Restraint orders last 4 hours for adults, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, and 1 hour under 9, renewable up to 24 consecutive hours.
w: 2 hours
That goes with Children 9 through 17 years.
1 hour
That goes with Children younger than 9 years.

alt.q: What is the restraint order time limit for Children 9 through 17 years?
alt.a: 2 hours
alt.ex: Restraint orders last 4 hours for adults, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, and 1 hour under 9, renewable up to 24 consecutive hours.
w: 4 hours
That goes with Adults 18 years and older.
1 hour
That goes with Children younger than 9 years.

alt.q: What is the restraint order time limit for Children younger than 9 years?
alt.a: 1 hour
alt.ex: Restraint orders last 4 hours for adults, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, and 1 hour under 9, renewable up to 24 consecutive hours.
w: 4 hours
That goes with Adults 18 years and older.
2 hours
That goes with Children 9 through 17 years.

alt.q: Which age-group has a restraint order time limit of “4 hours”?
alt.a: Adults 18 years and older
alt.ex: Restraint orders last 4 hours for adults, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, and 1 hour under 9, renewable up to 24 consecutive hours.
w: Children 9 through 17 years
Children 9 through 17 years: 2 hours.
Children younger than 9 years
Children younger than 9 years: 1 hour.

alt.q: Which age-group has a restraint order time limit of “2 hours”?
alt.a: Children 9 through 17 years
alt.ex: Restraint orders last 4 hours for adults, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, and 1 hour under 9, renewable up to 24 consecutive hours.
w: Adults 18 years and older
Adults 18 years and older: 4 hours.
Children younger than 9 years
Children younger than 9 years: 1 hour.

alt.q: Which age-group has a restraint order time limit of “1 hour”?
alt.a: Children younger than 9 years
alt.ex: Restraint orders last 4 hours for adults, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, and 1 hour under 9, renewable up to 24 consecutive hours.
w: Adults 18 years and older
Adults 18 years and older: 4 hours.
Children 9 through 17 years
Children 9 through 17 years: 2 hours.

mt.q: Match each patient age-group with the time limit for each original restraint order or renewal in a hospital.
mt.ex: Restraint orders last 4 hours for adults, 2 hours for ages 9 to 17, and 1 hour under 9, renewable up to 24 consecutive hours.

items.q: A health care provider may write a restraint order on an as-needed (prn) basis so nurses can apply the restraint if behavior escalates.
items.a: False
items.ex: Restraints are never ordered prn; an order must follow a face-to-face assessment and specify type, location, duration, and circumstances.
items.ww: A prn order would bypass the required assessment and time-limited renewal that protect patients.

alt.q: A restraint order must be based on a face-to-face assessment and must state the restraint type, location, duration, and circumstances of use.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Restraint use must be clinically justified, with a current order specifying type, location, duration, and circumstances; prn orders are not allowed.
alt.ww: Vague or as-needed orders do not meet regulatory standards for restraint use.

items.q: In which situation are raised side rails NOT considered a physical restraint?
items.a: Only the two upper rails are raised, leaving the lower bed open for exit
items.ex: When a patient has a route to exit the bed safely and move freely within it, side rails are not a restraint.
w: All four rails are raised for a patient who wants to get up
Blocking all exits keeps a patient who wants to get up in bed, which restrains them.
Rails are raised so an alert patient cannot leave bed at will
Rails that prevent a willing patient from leaving the bed act as a restraint.
All rails are raised and the bed is placed in its highest position
This restricts exit and raises fall injury risk; the bed should be low.

alt.q: A confused patient keeps trying to climb out of bed and has not voided in several hours. Which action should the nurse take first?
alt.a: Assess and address the cause, such as a need to use the toilet
alt.ex: Focus first on the cause of confusion or bed exits, such as toileting needs, pain, dehydration, or a new medication.
w: Raise all four side rails to keep the patient in bed
Side rails alone for a disoriented patient often increase confusion and lead to falls over the rail.
Apply a vest restraint until the confusion clears
Restraints are a last resort after addressing causes and trying alternatives.
Raise the bed to its highest position to deter climbing
The bed should be in its lowest position to reduce injury from a fall.

items.q: A nurse discovers a small fire in a wastebasket in a patient’s room. The patient is in bed beside it. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Remove the patient from the room
items.ex: RACE sets priorities: Rescue patients in immediate danger, Activate the alarm, Confine the fire, then Extinguish it.
w: Activate the fire alarm
The alarm is activated after rescuing patients in immediate danger.
Close the doors and turn off oxygen
Confining the fire comes after rescue and activating the alarm.
Put out the fire with an extinguisher
Extinguishing is the last step of RACE.

alt.q: After moving a patient away from a small fire, a nurse sees an extinguisher nearby. What should the nurse do before trying to put out the fire?
alt.a: Activate the fire alarm
alt.ex: Always activate the alarm before attempting to extinguish even a minor fire.
w: Document the event in the record
Documentation comes later; activating the alarm comes first.
Call the patient’s family members
Notifying family is not a RACE priority.
Open windows to vent the smoke
Confining the fire involves closing, not opening, doors and windows.

items.q: A patient in bed begins having a generalized tonic-clonic seizure. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Stay with the patient, note the time, and call for help
items.ex: When a seizure begins, note the time, stay with the patient, and call for help; never restrain or force objects into the mouth.
w: Place a tongue depressor between the clenched teeth
Never force objects into the mouth when the teeth are clenched.
Hold the arms and legs firmly to stop the jerking
Do not restrain the patient; hold limbs loosely.
Leave the room to get seizure medication from supply
Stay with the patient and call for help instead of leaving.

alt.q: During a tonic-clonic seizure, a patient who was sitting in a chair is eased to the floor. Which nursing action is appropriate?
alt.a: Turn the patient onto one side with the head tilted slightly forward
alt.ex: Side-lying with the head tilted forward supports ventilation and drainage of oral secretions.
w: Lift the patient back to bed while the seizure continues
Do not lift a patient from floor to bed during a seizure.
Give sips of water to keep the airway moist
Give nothing by mouth until the person is awake.
Restrain the patient’s limbs to prevent injury
Do not restrain; hold limbs loosely and clear hard objects.

items.q: Prolonged or repeated seizures indicate [[status epilepticus]], a medical emergency requiring intensive monitoring and treatment.
items.ex: Status epilepticus is an emergency; a seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer or seizures without regaining consciousness require emergency help.

alt.q: A seizure that lasts too long, or seizures that occur one after another, signal [[status epilepticus]], which requires emergency treatment.
alt.ex: Status epilepticus is an emergency; a seizure lasting 5 minutes or longer or seizures without regaining consciousness require emergency help.

items.q: A father yells at the nurse that his child, who has leukemia, is not getting proper care. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “This must be very frightening for you. Tell me what worries you most.”
items.ex: Focusing on feelings with supportive words such as “That must be scary” shows understanding and helps de-escalate.
w: “You need to calm down, or I will call security right now.”
Threats escalate the situation; set clear, reasonable limits with a positive choice.
“I am doing my job correctly, and you are being unreasonable.”
A defensive, judgmental reply does not respect the person’s feelings.
“I will come back later when you are ready to be polite.”
Walking away ignores the person instead of working together on the problem.

alt.q: A patient in the emergency department becomes belligerent about waiting. Which nonverbal approach should the nurse use?
alt.a: Keep a neutral voice tone and expression and respect personal space
alt.ex: A patient losing control reacts to nonverbal cues, so keep tone, expression, and movements neutral and allow personal space.
w: Stand close to the patient to show authority
Respect personal space; closeness can increase anxiety and risk.
Raise your voice so the patient hears over the noise
A raised voice is threatening; keep voice tone neutral.
Cross your arms and hold a firm, steady stare
This posture is threatening; use nonthreatening nonverbal communication.

sections.name: Skill 27.1 · Fall prevention in health care settings

items.q: Which fall prevention task must the registered nurse perform rather than delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Assessing the patient’s fall risks and communicating them to the team
items.ex: Assessing and communicating fall risk requires nursing judgment and cannot be delegated; the prevention measures themselves can be.
w: Locking the bed in the low position after giving care
Keeping the bed low and locked is a prevention measure that AP can carry out.
Placing the nurse call system within the patient’s reach
Positioning the call system is an environmental safety measure that can be delegated.
Putting skid-proof footwear on the patient before walking
Applying proper footwear is a prevention measure that AP can perform.

alt.q: A nurse is directing assistive personnel (AP) who care for a patient at high risk for falls. Which patient behavior should the nurse tell the AP to report immediately?
alt.a: The patient becomes disoriented and starts wandering
alt.ex: Disorientation and wandering are precursors to falls, so AP report them to the RN immediately.
w: The patient asks to have the call light moved closer
Moving the call light is a routine request the AP can simply meet.
The patient asks for help walking to the bathroom
Asking for help is the desired safe behavior, not a precursor to a fall.
The patient asks for an extra blanket at bedtime
A comfort request is not a fall precursor that needs immediate reporting.

items.q: The nurse reviews the EHR of a patient admitted after a fall at home. Which conditions increase this patient’s risk of a serious injury, such as fracture or internal hemorrhage, from a fall? Select all that apply.
o: Age over 85 years with frailty
Advanced age or frailty is the A in the ABCS factors for serious fall injury.
Osteoporosis with bone metastasis
Bone disorders make a fracture from a fall more likely.
Daily anticoagulant therapy
Anticoagulant use is a coagulation risk that increases bleeding after a fall.
Recent abdominal surgery
Thoracic or abdominal surgery is the S in the ABCS factors.
Well-controlled seasonal allergies
Seasonal allergies are not among the ABCS factors for serious fall injury.
A normal platelet count
A normal count does not raise bleeding risk; thrombocytopenia does.
items.ex: The ABCS factors (age over 85 or frailty, bone disorders, coagulation disorders, surgery) make an injury from a fall more serious.

alt.q: Using the ABCS criteria, which patients are at increased risk of serious injury if they fall? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with leukemia and thrombocytopenia
Coagulation disorders raise the risk of hemorrhage after a fall.
A patient recovering from a lower limb amputation
Lower limb amputation is one of the surgeries named in the ABCS factors.
A patient with a recent hip fracture
A recent fracture is a bone disorder that raises the risk of injury.
A 40-year-old patient admitted with a migraine
This patient has none of the ABCS factors for serious fall injury.
A 50-year-old patient with a healed ankle sprain
An old, healed sprain is not one of the ABCS injury-risk factors.
alt.ex: Age over 85 or frailty, bone disorders, coagulation disorders, and certain surgeries increase the risk of fracture or hemorrhage from a fall.

items.q: A patient scored as low fall risk on admission returns from surgery after general anesthesia. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?
items.a: Repeat the fall risk assessment because the patient’s condition has changed
items.ex: Fall risk is reassessed on admission, on transfer between units, after a significant change in condition, and after a fall.
w: Keep the admission fall risk score until the patient is discharged
Risk changes during a stay; a significant change in condition requires reassessment.
Wait to reassess fall risk until the patient falls on the unit
Reassessment after a fall is required, but waiting for a fall misses prevention.
Reassess fall risk only if the family voices a safety concern
Reassessment is triggered by clinical events, not only by family concerns.

alt.q: In a general acute care setting, which event requires the nurse to perform a new fall risk assessment?
alt.a: Transfer of the patient from one unit to another
alt.ex: Fall risk assessment is done on admission, on transfer between units, with a significant change in condition, or after a fall.
w: Each routine change of the patient’s bed linens
A linen change does not alter the patient’s fall risk.
Each visit to the patient by a family member
Visits are not one of the triggers for a fall risk assessment.
Each delivery of the patient’s meal tray
Meal delivery is not a trigger for repeating the assessment.

items.q: An 82-year-old patient says, “I walk just fine at home, so I don’t need help getting to the bathroom.” Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Observe the patient walking in the room to assess gait objectively
items.ex: Older adults often overestimate their walking ability, so the nurse checks self-report against objective observation.
w: Document that the patient is independent with ambulation
Documenting independence from self-report alone ignores possible decline in motor performance.
Activate a bed alarm so the patient cannot get up unnoticed
An alarm does not assess the patient’s actual mobility and is not the first step.
Tell the patient to stay in bed for the rest of the stay
Prolonged bed rest causes deconditioning and does not assess mobility.

alt.q: Why does the nurse compare a patient’s own description of walking ability with an objective mobility assessment?
alt.a: Patients, especially older adults, often overestimate their walking ability
alt.ex: Patients may not recognize declining motor performance, so the nurse does not rely only on what the patient says.
w: Patients usually underestimate their walking ability out of fear
The book warns of overestimation, which leads to unassisted walking and falls.
Objective tools are needed mainly for billing and records
Objective assessment guides safe mobility, not billing.
Patients’ views of their ability are never assessed at all
Patient perception is assessed; it simply must be checked against objective findings.

items.q: During a fall risk assessment, the nurse screens for polypharmacy. Which medication history best fits this term?
items.a: Five or more medications, including redundant drugs for the same condition
items.ex: Polypharmacy is unnecessary use of five or more and/or redundant medications, or drugs inappropriate for the condition.
w: Two medications that were prescribed by different providers
Two drugs from different prescribers do not meet the five-or-more threshold.
One over-the-counter herbal product taken once a day
A single herbal product is reviewed for fall risk but is not polypharmacy.
One medication taken at a higher than usual dose
A single high-dose drug is not the use of multiple medications.

alt.q: How many medications does the nurse use as the threshold for polypharmacy when assessing fall risk?
alt.a: 5 or more
alt.ex: Polypharmacy is the unnecessary use of 5 or more medications, and falls rise with the number of drugs taken.
w: 2 or more
Two drugs is below the threshold the book uses for polypharmacy.
3 or more
Three drugs is below the five-drug threshold for polypharmacy.
4 or more
Taking 1 to 4 drugs is described separately from polypharmacy.

items.q: The nurse reviews a patient’s medications for fall risk. Which drug classes should the nurse flag? Select all that apply.
o: Benzodiazepines
Benzodiazepines commonly cause drowsiness and increase fall risk.
Opioids
Opioids cause drowsiness and further increase fall risk.
Antipsychotics
Antipsychotics are listed among drugs that create risk for falls.
Anticonvulsants
Anticonvulsants are listed among drugs that create risk for falls.
Topical skin moisturizers
Topical moisturizers do not cause drowsiness or fall risk.
Daily multivitamin supplements
A multivitamin is not among the fall-risk drug classes in the book.
items.ex: Benzodiazepines, antipsychotics, antidepressants, opioids, barbiturates, and anticonvulsants commonly cause drowsiness and create fall risk.

alt.q: A 78-year-old patient takes several medications. Which actions belong in the nurse’s medication review for fall risk? Select all that apply.
o: Include over-the-counter drugs and herbal products
OTC and herbal products are reviewed along with prescribed drugs.
Compare fall-risk drugs with the AGS Beers Criteria lists
Beers Criteria list drugs that may not be the safest options for older adults.
Assess for polypharmacy and redundant drugs
Falls increase with the number of medications a person takes.
Review only the prescription drugs ordered this admission
Home, OTC, and herbal products also contribute to fall risk.
Stop any drug the nurse believes is unsafe
The nurse discusses risky drugs with the provider and teaches; the nurse does not stop them.
alt.ex: A complete medication review includes OTC and herbal products, Beers Criteria comparison, and a check for polypharmacy.

items.q: The nurse assesses for orthostatic hypotension in a patient who is 65 or older, has a history of a fall, or takes multiple medications.
items.a: True
items.ex: Orthostatic hypotension is common in older adults due to nervous and vascular changes and is linked to polypharmacy and frailty.
items.ww: These groups are specifically identified for orthostatic hypotension assessment as part of fall prevention.

alt.q: Orthostatic hypotension is uncommon in older adults, so the nurse assesses for it only in patients taking blood pressure medicines.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Orthostatic hypotension is common in older adults, so assess those 65 and older, with a fall history, or on multiple drugs.
alt.ww: Age-related nervous and vascular changes, polypharmacy, immobility, and frailty all contribute, not only blood pressure medicines.

items.q: A nurse caring for patients at risk for falls conducts hourly purposeful rounds. Which action best reflects the purpose of these rounds?
items.a: Proactively offering toileting help and checking pain, position, and personal items
items.ex: Purposeful rounds address pain, toileting, comfort of position, and reach of personal items, reducing unassisted activity that leads to falls.
w: Checking that patients are asleep and turning off all room lights
Rounds are proactive needs checks; glare-free lighting and a night light reduce falls.
Measuring and recording full vital signs on every patient each hour
Hourly rounds focus on pain, toileting, position, and items, not routine vital signs.
Reminding each patient to stay in bed for the rest of the shift
Rounding meets needs so patients need not get up alone; it does not enforce bed rest.

alt.q: Why do hourly purposeful rounds help reduce falls in hospitalized patients?
alt.a: Patients’ needs are met before they try to get up without assistance
alt.ex: Rounding reduces falls related to patients performing activities, such as toileting, without assistance.
w: Patients are kept awake so that they remain alert
Rounds are not meant to keep patients awake; comfort and rest are supported.
Staff can apply restraints sooner to restless patients
Restraints are a final option; rounding is a restraint alternative.
Patients are encouraged to walk alone more often
Rounding lessens the need for patients to get up independently.

items.q: A patient in a four-side-rail bed is able to get out of bed independently. How should the nurse position the side rails?
items.a: Leave the two upper side rails up
items.ex: Two upper rails aid turning, comfort, and call-system access while allowing a safe exit from the bed.
w: Raise all four side rails
Rails that restrict freedom of movement act as a restraint and block a safe exit.
Lower all four side rails
Upper rails help with turning, security, and access to bed controls.
Raise only the two lower side rails
Raised lower rails block the exit route at the foot of the bed.

alt.q: A patient in a two-side-rail bed is able to get out of bed independently. How should the nurse position the side rails?
alt.a: Keep only one side rail up
alt.ex: In a two-rail bed, one rail up allows safe exit for an independent patient; both rails up is for dependent patients.
w: Keep both side rails up
Both rails up is used for dependent, less mobile patients and restricts an independent patient.
Keep both side rails down
One rail still supports turning and gives easy access to the call system.
Keep both rails up and pad them
Padding does not change that both rails up restricts this patient’s movement.

items.q: Which observation indicates that a patient’s wheelchair fits correctly?
items.a: Two finger widths of space between the patient and the side of the chair
items.ex: A correctly fitted chair is comfortable, so the patient is less likely to try to exit it without help.
w: The chair back reaches only to the patient’s lower back
The back of the chair should come up to mid-shoulder.
The patient’s knees sit higher than the hips, feet dangling
Thighs should be level with the feet flat on the floor.
The patient leans sideways to rest an elbow on the armrest
Elbows should rest on armrests without leaning over or tucking arms in.

alt.q: Why does the nurse make sure a high-fall-risk patient’s wheelchair fits well and limit how long the patient sits in it?
alt.a: Discomfort and restlessness can lead the patient to exit the chair without help
alt.ex: Pain, discomfort, fatigue, and boredom can prompt an unassisted wheelchair exit, so fit and sitting time are managed.
w: A well-fitted chair can then be used for sitting all day
Wheelchairs are for transport, not for sitting an extended time.
A snug chair removes the need for any staff monitoring
Fit reduces exit attempts but does not replace monitoring.
A fitted chair can be pushed front wheels first into elevators
Wheelchairs are backed into elevators, large rear wheels first.

items.q: When taking a patient in a wheelchair into an elevator, the nurse backs the chair in, leading with the large rear wheels.
items.a: True
items.ex: Leading with the large rear wheels keeps the small front wheels from catching in the gap and tipping the chair.
items.ww: Going in forward lets the small front wheels catch in the crack between elevator and floor.

alt.q: Pushing a wheelchair forward into an elevator, small front wheels first, is safest because they roll easily over the gap.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The chair is backed in with large rear wheels first because small front wheels can catch in the gap and tip the chair.
alt.ww: Small front wheels are the ones that catch in the crack, so they should not lead.

items.q: Which actions make the immediate environment safer for a patient at high risk for falls? Select all that apply.
o: Place the walker on the exit side of the bed
Assistive devices on the exit side give support when transferring out of bed.
Provide glare-free lighting and a night light
Glare troubles older adults’ vision, and a night light lights the way at night.
Coil and secure excess cords and tubing
Securing cords and tubing reduces tripping and entanglement.
Lock the wheels on the bed and wheelchair
Locks prevent the device from moving during a transfer.
Keep the IV pole in the path to the bathroom
The path to the bathroom should be kept free of obstacles such as IV poles.
Store personal items on a shelf across the room
Items out of reach lead to falls from reaching; keep them within easy reach.
items.ex: A safe environment has clear floors, secured cords, good lighting, locked equipment, and devices and items within easy reach.

alt.q: Which measures are part of Universal Fall Precautions? Select all that apply.
o: Bed in the low position with wheels locked
A low, locked bed lets the patient get in and out easily and safely.
Properly fitted skid-proof footwear
Skid-proof footwear prevents slipping on the floor.
Orientation to the room and nurse call system
Orientation provides familiarity with the environment and how to call for help.
Smooth socks without treads for comfort
Socks without treads promote slipping; skid-proof footwear is used.
Wet-floor signs left up after the floor dries
The sign is removed once the floor is dry.
alt.ex: Universal Fall Precautions include a low, locked bed, skid-proof footwear, orientation, and the call system within reach.

items.q: The nurse finds a patient lying on the floor beside the bed. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Call for assistance and stay with the patient while assessing for injury
items.ex: Calling for help and assessing for injury while staying with the patient come before notification, reporting, and the postfall huddle.
w: Help the patient back into bed before others arrive
Moving the patient before assessing could worsen an injury.
Complete the incident report while details are fresh
Reporting comes after the patient is assessed and the provider is notified.

items.q: To reduce nighttime fall risk, when should the nurse schedule oral medications for a patient at high risk for falls?

w: Within 15 minutes before bedtime

At least 30 minutes before bedtime
Thirty minutes is less than the 2-hour lead time the book advises.
At 2 a.m. during night rounds
Waking the patient for oral drugs at night adds bathroom trips and fall risk.

alt.q: What is the rationale for giving a high-fall-risk patient’s oral medications at least 2 hours before bedtime?

alt.ex: Medications can increase the need to use the bathroom at night, which raises fall risk.
w: It lets the patient sleep through hourly rounds
Hourly rounding continues regardless of medication timing.
It allows absorption before the evening meal is served
Timing is tied to bedtime bathroom needs, not to meals.
It allows the nurse to skip overnight safety checks
Overnight checks and rounding continue for high-risk patients.

items.q: A nurse is considering a bed alarm for a cognitively impaired patient at high risk for falls. Which concern should guide the nurse’s judgment?

w: Alarms prevent falls without any need for staff response
An alarm only alerts staff; the patient is safe only if staff respond.
Alarms are never permitted for cognitively impaired patients
Alarms are allowed; the nurse uses judgment about their effects.
Alarms should replace hourly purposeful rounding
Rounding continues; alarms are one measure among many.

alt.q: The nurse thinks about using a wedge cushion to keep a high-fall-risk patient from sliding out of a chair. Why should the nurse consult therapy services first?

w: The cushion tilts the patient forward out of the chair
The wedge tilts the pelvis toward the back of the chair, not forward.
The cushion is classified as a chemical restraint
A cushion is a physical device, not a medication.
The cushion is meant only for patients with head injury

items.q: The nurse uses teach-back after fall prevention teaching. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I will press the call button and wait for help before getting up to the bathroom.”
items.ex: Using the call system and waiting for help before getting up is a key fall prevention behavior.
w: “I can take my sleeping pill and still walk to the bathroom alone at night.”
Sedating drugs cause drowsiness and raise fall risk, so the patient should call for help.
“I will wear my regular smooth socks so my feet stay warm on the floor.”
Properly fitted skid-proof footwear, not smooth socks, prevents slipping.
“I will keep my glasses in the drawer since I am mostly lying in bed.”
Glasses should be clean and available so the patient stays alert to surroundings.

alt.q: A family caregiver cannot correctly teach back why the patient is at risk for falling. What should the nurse do next?
alt.a: Revise the instruction or plan revised teaching for the caregiver
alt.ex: When teach-back is incorrect, the nurse revises instruction now or develops a plan for revised teaching.
w: Document that fall prevention teaching is complete
Teaching is not complete until the caregiver can explain the risks.
Repeat the same explanation word for word
Unchanged repetition does not revise the instruction that failed.
Postpone all teaching until the day of discharge
Delaying teaching leaves the patient at risk during the stay.

items.q: Which task related to physical restraints may the nurse delegate to trained assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Routine checking of a restraint that is already applied
items.ex: Applying and routinely checking a restraint can be delegated; assessing behavior, orientation, and need for restraint cannot.
w: Assessing whether the patient still needs restraints
Determining need for restraint requires nursing assessment and cannot be delegated.
Evaluating the patient’s orientation to the environment
Assessing orientation and behavior is a nursing responsibility.
Deciding whether restraint use is appropriate
Judging appropriate restraint use cannot be delegated to AP.

alt.q: Which finding should the nurse instruct AP to report as a sign that a patient is not tolerating a restraint?
alt.a: The patient keeps trying to remove the restraint
alt.ex: Confusion, agitation, and attempts to remove restraints signal that the patient is not tolerating the restraint.
w: The patient asks for a drink of water
A request for fluids is a basic need the AP meets, not intolerance.
The patient asks to use the bedpan
Toileting is a routine need the AP is directed to provide.
The patient sleeps quietly between checks
Calm rest does not suggest intolerance of the restraint.

items.q: A patient’s level of consciousness changes abruptly and the patient begins pulling at medical devices. Which underlying causes should the nurse assess for? Select all that apply.
o: Hypoglycemia or hyperglycemia
Blood glucose imbalance can quickly alter cognition.
Fever and sepsis
Infection and sepsis can cause sudden confusion.
Alcohol or substance withdrawal
Withdrawal is a listed cause of abrupt change in mental status.
Fluid and electrolyte imbalance
Fluid and electrolyte imbalances can cause sudden confusion.
Chronic, stable knee osteoarthritis
A stable chronic joint condition does not cause abrupt cognitive change.
items.ex: Respiratory and neurological changes, sepsis, glucose and electrolyte imbalance, and withdrawal can cause sudden confusion; treating them may avoid restraints.

alt.q: Which laboratory values should the nurse review because abnormal results can cause sudden confusion in older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Serum electrolytes
Electrolyte imbalance can cause sudden confusion.
Blood glucose
A blood glucose imbalance can cause sudden confusion.
Urinalysis
Urinalysis may reveal an infection that causes confusion.
Lipid panel
A lipid panel is not among the values reviewed for acute confusion.
Bone density score
Bone density is not a laboratory value tied to sudden confusion.
alt.ex: Electrolytes, blood glucose, blood culture, and urinalysis can reveal imbalances or infection that cause sudden confusion.

items.q: An older adult who was calm yesterday is suddenly restless, disoriented, and pulling at an IV line. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess for physiological causes such as hypoglycemia or fluid imbalance
items.ex: Abrupt cognitive change can stem from treatable problems; identifying them may remove the need for restraints.
w: Apply soft wrist restraints to protect the IV line
Restraints are a last resort; possible causes are assessed first.
Ask the provider for an as-needed restraint order
Restraints cannot be ordered PRN, and assessment comes first.
Place hand mitts tethered to the bed frame
Tethered mitts are a restraint, and assessment of causes comes first.

alt.q: After finding a patient’s abrupt change in mental status and abnormal physiological findings, what should the nurse do next?
alt.a: Notify the health care provider of the changes
alt.ex: The health care provider must determine whether the change in status causes behavior that needs temporary restraint.
w: Apply the least restrictive restraint before calling
Restraint requires a provider’s order, and the cause needs evaluation first.
Document the change and recheck it at end of shift
An abrupt change needs prompt reporting, not delayed recheck.
Ask the family to stay with the patient overnight
Family presence may help, but the provider must be informed of the change.

w: 2 hours
That goes with Children and adolescents 9 to 17 years.
1 hour
That goes with Children under 9 years.

w: 4 hours

1 hour

w: 4 hours

2 hours

w: Children and adolescents 9 to 17 years
Children and adolescents 9 to 17 years: 2 hours.
Children under 9 years

Adults 18 years and older: 4 hours.

alt.q: Which age group has a violent-behavior restraint order time limit of 1 hour?

w: Adults 18 years and older
Adults 18 years and older: 4 hours.
Children and adolescents 9 to 17 years
Children and adolescents 9 to 17 years: 2 hours.

mt.q: Match each age group with the time limit for a restraint order used for violent or self-destructive behavior.
mt.ex: Violent or self-destructive restraint orders are renewed within these limits, for a maximum of 24 consecutive hours.

items.q: A patient is placed in restraints for violent behavior that endangers staff. Within what time must the patient be evaluated in person?
items.a: Within 1 hour of starting the restraint
items.ex: A licensed independent provider, or a trained RN, APRN, or physician assistant, evaluates the patient in person within 1 hour.
w: Within 4 hours of starting the restraint
Four hours is the adult order time limit, not the in-person evaluation time.
Within 8 hours of starting the restraint
Eight hours is far beyond the required 1-hour evaluation.
Within 24 hours of starting the restraint
Twenty-four hours is the maximum renewal period, not the evaluation time.

alt.q: For a patient restrained for violent or self-destructive behavior, for how many consecutive hours at most may time-limited orders be renewed?
alt.a: 24 hours
alt.ex: Orders are renewed within the age-based time limits for a maximum of 24 consecutive hours.
w: 12 hours
Renewal can continue beyond 12 hours, up to 24 consecutive hours.
48 hours
Forty-eight hours exceeds the 24-hour maximum.
72 hours
Seventy-two hours exceeds the 24-hour maximum.

items.q: A health care provider may write a restraint order on an as-needed (PRN) basis.
items.a: False
items.ex: Restraints cannot be ordered PRN; if behavior after release again requires restraint, a new order is needed.
items.ww: PRN restraint orders are not allowed, so the statement cannot be true.

alt.q: If a patient recently released from restraint again shows behavior that only restraint can manage, a new order is required.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Because restraints cannot be ordered PRN, reapplication after release requires a new order.
alt.ww: Reapplying without a new order would amount to a PRN order, which is not permitted.

items.q: A current health care provider’s order for a restraint must include which elements? Select all that apply.
o: Purpose of the restraint
The order states why the restraint is being used.
Type of restraint
The order names the type, which must be the least restrictive.
Location of the restraint
The order specifies where the restraint is applied.
Time or duration of the restraint
The order sets the time or duration of use.
Instructions to reapply as needed
Restraints cannot be ordered on an as-needed basis.
Name of the AP who will apply it
The order does not name the staff member who applies the restraint.
items.ex: The order includes purpose, type, location, and time or duration, and must be for the least restrictive restraint.

alt.q: Before applying a restraint to a patient for whom restraint alternatives have failed, which actions should the nurse complete? Select all that apply.
o: Confer with the health care provider
When alternatives fail, the nurse confers with the provider about restraint.
Review agency policies and state laws on restraints
Restraint use must follow agency policy and state law.
Review manufacturer instructions and choose the right size
Incorrect sizing or application can cause injury or death.
Obtain an order to use the restraint as needed
Restraints cannot be ordered PRN.
Apply the restraint first and request an order later
A current provider’s order is obtained before applying the restraint.
alt.ex: Before applying a restraint, the nurse confers with the provider, follows policy and law, obtains a current order, and reviews device instructions.

items.q: Under which condition are hand mitts considered a restraint?
items.a: The mitts are pinned or attached to the bed or bedding
items.ex: Mitts become a restraint if tethered, used with wrist restraints, too tight or bulky, or not easily removable by the patient.
w: The mitts are loose and the patient can remove them
Untethered mitts the patient can remove are a restraint alternative.
The patient can still use the hands freely in the mitts
Unrestricted hand use makes mitts an alternative, not a restraint.
The mitt’s Velcro strap is placed around the wrist
Placing the strap at the wrist, not the forearm, is correct application.

alt.q: Which description of hand mitt use meets the criteria for a restraint alternative rather than a restraint?
alt.a: Untethered mitts that the patient is able to remove
alt.ex: Mitts are an alternative if untethered, fingers are not immobilized, hand use is unrestricted, and the patient can remove them.
w: Mitts tied to the bed frame during the night
Attaching mitts to the bed makes them a restraint.
Mitts used together with wrist restraints
Using mitts with wrist restraints makes them a restraint.
Mitts so bulky that the hands cannot be used
Bulky mitts that greatly reduce hand use are a restraint.

items.q: A nurse applies an elbow restraint (freedom splint). Which device is this restraint most effective at protecting?
items.a: A nasogastric tube near the patient’s face
items.ex: Because patients have difficulty bending their arms, the splint makes it hard to remove devices near the face or neck.
w: An indwelling urinary catheter
The splint does not impede removal of urinary devices.
An abdominal surgical drain
The splint does not impede removal of abdominal devices.
A peripheral IV line in the arm
Freedom splints may not prevent a patient from removing IV lines.

alt.q: How should the nurse apply an elbow restraint (freedom splint)?
alt.a: Center it over the elbow with the opening facing away from the patient
alt.ex: The splint is centered over the elbow, opening and Velcro straps away from the patient, and clamped to the gown sleeve.
w: Center it over the wrist with the opening facing the patient
The splint goes over the elbow, with the opening facing away.
Attach its straps to the moving part of the bed frame
The freedom splint is the exception that is not secured to the bed frame.
Wrap it tightly around the forearm and tie it in a knot
It closes with hook-and-loop straps threaded through a buckle, not a knot.

items.q: Why is a self-releasing roll belt considered a restraint alternative?
items.a: The patient can easily undo its self-releasing buckle and Velcro
items.ex: Because the patient can release it, the roll belt does not restrict freedom the way a restraint does.
w: It is tied to the side rails so it cannot slip
Belt straps attach to a moveable part of the bedframe, never the side rails.
It is fastened tightly enough to limit chest movement
The belt must be snug but must not restrict breathing.
It keeps the patient from turning over in bed
A properly applied roll belt allows the patient to turn in bed.

alt.q: When applying a self-releasing roll belt, which finding shows correct application?
alt.a: The belt is snug at the waist but does not restrict breathing
alt.ex: The belt sits at waist level, snug without restricting breathing, with bedframe straps snug so they don’t slide.
w: The belt is fastened tightly across the chest
The belt goes at waist level and must not restrict breathing.
The belt straps are looped around the side rails
Straps are looped around a moveable part of the bedframe.
The belt straps slide when the bed is adjusted
Bedframe straps should be snug and not slide when the bed moves.

items.q: An enclosure bed is being considered on a medical unit. For which patients is this bed not intended? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with multiple IV lines and drainage tubes
The bed is not intended for patients with multiple lines or tubes.
A patient who is suicidal
Suicidal or self-destructive patients should not be placed in the bed.
A patient who is claustrophobic
Claustrophobia is a listed reason not to use the bed.
A patient who is violent and combative
Violent or combative patients should not be placed in the bed.
An agitated, cognitively impaired patient at high fall risk
The bed may be appropriate for agitated, cognitively impaired patients at high fall risk.
items.ex: Enclosure beds are not for patients with multiple lines or tubes, or who are violent, suicidal, claustrophobic, or outside weight limits.

alt.q: Which statements about enclosure beds are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The enclosure bed is considered a restraint
It restricts the patient from voluntarily getting out of bed.
All staff must be fully trained in its use
Staff training is required before using the bed.
Family should be told about the bed and why it is used
Family and caregivers are informed about the bed and its purpose.
It may be combined with wrist restraints for added safety
Other restraint devices are not used in an enclosure bed.
It should be used solely to prevent falls
The bed should not be used solely for fall prevention.
alt.ex: An enclosure bed is a restraint used with trained staff, informed family, and no other restraints, and never solely for fall prevention.

items.q: After securing a soft extremity restraint, the nurse inserts [[two|2]] fingers under it to make sure it is not too tight.
items.ex: A restraint secured snugly but not tightly allows two fingers underneath; tight application impairs circulation and can cause neurovascular injury.

alt.q: To check a wrist restraint for constriction, the nurse should be able to slide [[two|2]] fingers under the secured restraint.
alt.ex: A restraint secured snugly but not tightly allows two fingers underneath; tight application impairs circulation and can cause neurovascular injury.

items.q: A patient has both wrist and ankle restraints. How should the nurse position the patient?
items.a: In a lateral position or with the head of the bed elevated
items.ex: A patient restrained at the wrists and ankles is at risk for aspiration if left supine.
w: Supine with the arms and legs fully extended
The supine position puts a patient with four-point restraints at risk for aspiration.
Prone with the face turned to one side
Prone positioning is not the position the book recommends for restrained patients.
Supine with the knees raised for comfort
Raising the knees does not change the aspiration risk of lying supine.

alt.q: Why does the nurse avoid placing a patient with wrist and ankle restraints in the supine position?
alt.a: The patient is at risk for aspiration
alt.ex: Supine positioning with wrist and ankle restraints risks aspiration, so lateral or head-elevated positions are used.
w: The patient is at risk for orthostatic hypotension
Orthostatic hypotension is not the stated risk of the supine position here.
The restraint straps will loosen when supine
Position does not loosen properly secured straps.
The restraints cannot be checked when supine
Restraints can be checked in any position; aspiration is the concern.

items.q: The nurse finds that an AP has tied a patient’s wrist restraint strap to the side rail. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Reattach the strap with a quick-release buckle to a moveable part of the bedframe
items.ex: Straps on the moving bedframe don’t tighten when the bed is adjusted, and a quick-release buckle allows rapid release in an emergency.
w: Leave the strap tied to the rail but loosen the knot slightly
Straps are never attached to side rails or tied in knots.
Move the strap to the fixed frame at the head of the bed
Straps go on the part that moves with the head of the bed so they don’t tighten.
Retie the strap to the rail with a firmer double knot
Knots prevent quick release in an emergency, and rails are never used.

alt.q: Why does the nurse attach restraint straps to the part of the bedframe that moves when the head of the bed is raised?
alt.a: The strap will not tighten and restrict circulation when the bed is adjusted
alt.ex: A properly positioned strap does not tighten and restrict circulation when the bed is raised or lowered.
w: The strap will be within the patient’s reach to release
The buckle is kept out of the patient’s reach.
The strap will hold the side rail in the raised position
Straps are never attached to side rails.
The strap will keep the bed from being lowered
The bed is placed in its lowest position after restraint application.

items.q: Restraint straps are secured to the bedframe with a quick-release buckle rather than tied in a knot.
items.a: True
items.ex: A quick-release buckle, kept out of the patient’s reach, allows the patient to be released quickly in an emergency.
items.ww: Knots can’t be undone quickly, which delays release and evacuation in an emergency.

alt.q: Tying restraint straps to the bedframe with a firm knot is preferred because the patient cannot undo it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Straps are secured with a quick-release buckle, not a knot, so staff can release the patient quickly in an emergency.
alt.ww: Keeping the buckle out of reach, not knotting, prevents patient release while allowing emergency release.

items.q: In applying a physical restraint, which step comes right after “Apply the selected restraint device”?
items.a: Attach straps to the part of the bedframe that moves with the head of the bed
items.ex: That's step 5 of 8. Baseline assessment and padding precede application; straps are then secured safely, rechecked for circulation, and the bed made safe.
w: Secure the straps with a quick-release buckle out of the patient’s reach
That's step 6 of 8.
Pad skin and bony prominences that will be under the restraint
That's step 3 of 8.
Recheck with two fingers and assess pulses, skin color, temperature, and sensation
That's step 7 of 8.

alt.q: Which step comes first in applying a physical restraint?
alt.a: Adjust the bed height and lower the side rail on the near side
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 8. Baseline assessment and padding precede application; straps are then secured safely, rechecked for circulation, and the bed made safe.
w: Inspect the area and assess skin, sensation, circulation, and joint motion
That's step 2 of 8.
Pad skin and bony prominences that will be under the restraint
That's step 3 of 8.
Apply the selected restraint device
That's step 4 of 8.

alt.q: Which step comes last in applying a physical restraint?
alt.a: Raise side rails as appropriate and place the bed in the lowest position
alt.ex: That's step 8 of 8. Baseline assessment and padding precede application; straps are then secured safely, rechecked for circulation, and the bed made safe.
w: Recheck with two fingers and assess pulses, skin color, temperature, and sensation
That's step 7 of 8.
Secure the straps with a quick-release buckle out of the patient’s reach
That's step 6 of 8.
Attach straps to the part of the bedframe that moves with the head of the bed
That's step 5 of 8.
