ord.q: Put these implementation steps for applying a physical restraint in the correct order.
items: Adjust the bed height and lower the side rail on the near side
Inspect the area and assess skin, sensation, circulation, and joint motion
Pad skin and bony prominences that will be under the restraint
Apply the selected restraint device
Attach straps to the part of the bedframe that moves with the head of the bed
Secure the straps with a quick-release buckle out of the patient’s reach
Recheck with two fingers and assess pulses, skin color, temperature, and sensation
Raise side rails as appropriate and place the bed in the lowest position
ord.ex: Baseline assessment and padding precede application; straps are then secured safely, rechecked for circulation, and the bed made safe.

items.q: How is a patient monitored while in both restraints and seclusion for violent, self-destructive behavior?
items.a: Continuously, by way of video and audio
items.ex: Violent or self-destructive patients in restraint and seclusion are monitored continuously, unlike nonviolent patients.
w: Every 2 hours, during routine rounds
Every 2 hours applies to nonviolent patients, not violent patients in seclusion.
Every 4 hours, when the order is renewed
Four hours is the adult order limit, not the monitoring frequency.
Every 8 hours, by the charge nurse
Monitoring this infrequently is unsafe for a violent patient in seclusion.

alt.q: A nonviolent patient has soft wrist restraints. At a minimum, how often should the nurse release the restraints and evaluate toileting, nutrition, fluids, and hygiene needs?
alt.a: At least every 2 hours
alt.ex: Releasing the restraint at least every 2 hours prevents injury and attends to basic needs.
w: At least every 4 hours
Four hours is longer than the 2-hour minimum for release and evaluation.
At least every 8 hours
Eight hours leaves basic needs and skin unattended far too long.
At least every 24 hours
Once a day risks injury and neglect of basic needs.

items.q: A temporary, directly supervised release of a restraint for toileting or range-of-motion exercises counts as discontinuing the restraint.
items.a: False
items.ex: A temporary, directly supervised release to meet care needs is not considered a discontinuation of the restraint.
items.ww: Short supervised releases for care are expected parts of restraint use, not an end to it.

alt.q: Briefly removing a restraint under direct supervision to take vital signs is not considered discontinuing the restraint.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Temporary, directly supervised releases for vital signs, toileting, feeding, or range of motion are not discontinuation.
alt.ww: Calling it a discontinuation would wrongly imply a new order is needed after each care release.

items.q: A patient in a soft wrist restraint reports tingling and numbness, and the hand is pale and cool. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Remove the restraint immediately and stay with the patient
items.ex: Neurovascular injury requires immediate removal, staying with the patient, notifying the provider, and protecting the extremity.
w: Loosen the restraint slightly and recheck it in 1 hour
Signs of neurovascular injury require immediate removal, not loosening.
Elevate the arm on a pillow and reassess at the next check
Delaying removal allows neurovascular injury to progress.
Add extra padding under the restraint and leave it on
Padding reduces friction but does not relieve neurovascular compromise.

alt.q: A restraint has caused an injury to a patient’s wrist. To whom should the nurse report it, and when?
alt.a: To the RN in charge and the health care provider, immediately
alt.ex: Any injury resulting from a restraint is reported immediately to the RN in charge and the health care provider.
w: To the oncoming AP, during the next hand-off
AP are not the ones who must be notified, and waiting delays care.
To the family caregiver, at their next visit
Family may be informed, but the RN in charge and provider are told at once.
To the unit manager, in the weekly safety report
A weekly report delays required immediate reporting.

items.q: A restrained patient becomes more confused and agitated. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
items.a: Determine the cause of the behavior and consult the health care provider
items.ex: Rising confusion calls for finding and removing the cause, adjusting stimulation, reorienting, and trying restraint-free options.
w: Add a second type of restraint to further limit movement
More restraint does not address the cause and increases risk of injury.
Remove all stimulation by darkening the room completely
Stimulation is adjusted and made meaningful, not removed entirely.
Leave the patient alone so the behavior can settle down
An agitated restrained patient needs assessment, reorientation, and support.

alt.q: A patient in alcohol withdrawal is struggling against wrist restraints. Which complication should the nurse watch for?
alt.a: Rhabdomyolysis
alt.ex: Resisting restraints during alcohol withdrawal can raise body temperature, cause rhabdomyolysis, and lead to physical injury.
w: Hypothermia
Struggling against restraints raises body temperature rather than lowering it.
Bradycardia
A slow heart rate is not the complication the book links to resisting restraints.
Constipation
Constipation is not an acute effect of resisting restraints.

items.q: Which statement best describes an infection?
items.a: A pathogen invades tissues and begins growing within a host
items.ex: Infection results when a pathogen invades tissues and grows within the host, unlike colonization, which involves no tissue invasion.
w: Microorganisms grow on a host without any tissue invasion or damage
Growth without tissue invasion or damage describes colonization, not infection.
A pathogen is present on the skin after contact with a contaminated object
The mere presence of a pathogen does not mean an infection will occur.
Normal flora survive and multiply on the skin without causing illness
This describes resident (normal) flora, which do not cause illness in their usual site.

alt.q: A nurse explains the term infection to a student. Which description should the nurse use?
alt.a: Pathogens invade the tissues and grow within the host
alt.ex: An infection requires tissue invasion and growth of the pathogen within the host.
w: Microorganisms are present and growing without damaging tissue
Presence and growth without tissue invasion or damage is colonization.
Transient organisms attach to the hands during routine care
Transient flora picked up during care are removed by hand hygiene and are not an infection.
Resident organisms live on the skin and maintain health
Resident organisms are normal flora that survive and multiply without causing illness.

items.q: Which term describes the presence and growth of microorganisms within a host without tissue invasion or damage?
items.a: Colonization
items.ex: Colonization is the presence and growth of microorganisms in a host without tissue invasion or damage.
w: Infection
Infection requires that a pathogen invade tissues and grow within the host.
Communicable disease
A communicable disease is an infection that can be transmitted directly from one person to another.
Symptomatic illness
A symptomatic infection is one in which multiplying pathogens cause clinical signs and symptoms.

alt.q: A nurse reads that colonization has occurred. What does this mean?
alt.a: Microorganisms are present and growing but have not invaded or damaged tissue
alt.ex: Colonization involves microorganism presence and growth without tissue invasion or damage.
w: Pathogens have invaded tissue and are causing clinical symptoms
Tissue invasion with symptoms describes a symptomatic infection, not colonization.
Pathogens have invaded tissue but are not yet causing any symptoms
Tissue invasion without symptoms is an asymptomatic infection, not colonization.
Microorganisms have been destroyed by a bactericidal agent
Destruction of bacteria by temperature or chemicals is a bactericidal effect.

items.q: When microorganisms are present and growing within a host but there is no tissue invasion or damage, the condition is called [[colonization|colonisation]].
items.ex: Colonization differs from infection because the organisms do not invade or damage tissue.

alt.q: A culture shows bacteria growing on a patient’s skin with no tissue invasion or damage; this is termed [[colonization|colonisation]].
alt.ex: Colonization differs from infection because the organisms do not invade or damage tissue.

items.q: Disease or infection results only if pathogens multiply and alter normal tissue function.
items.a: True
items.ex: Pathogens must multiply and alter normal tissue function before disease or infection results.
items.ww: Merely being present is not enough; infection requires multiplication that changes normal tissue function.

alt.q: Finding a pathogen within a host means that an infection has occurred.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The presence of a pathogen does not mean infection will occur; infection requires tissue invasion and altered function.
alt.ww: A pathogen can colonize a host without invading tissue, so presence alone does not equal infection.

items.q: Which term describes an infectious disease that can be transmitted directly from one person to another?
items.a: Communicable disease
items.ex: An infectious disease that can be transmitted directly from one person to another is termed a communicable disease.
w: Colonization
Colonization is organism growth without tissue invasion or damage.
Suprainfection
Suprainfection develops when broad-spectrum antibiotics eliminate normal flora, allowing other organisms to multiply.
Iatrogenic infection
An iatrogenic infection is an HAI caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure.

alt.q: A nurse describes a disease as communicable. What does this term mean?
alt.a: It can be transmitted directly from one person to another
alt.ex: Communicable diseases are infectious diseases that pass directly from person to person.
w: It is caused by a procedure performed in a health care agency
Infection caused by an invasive procedure is iatrogenic.
It is caused by overgrowth of the patient’s own normal flora
Overgrowth of a patient’s own altered flora is an endogenous infection.
It produces clinical signs and symptoms in the infected person
Producing clinical signs and symptoms makes an infection symptomatic, not communicable.

items.q: If an infectious disease can be transmitted directly from one person to another, it is termed a [[communicable disease|communicable]].
items.ex: Communicable diseases such as HBV, HCV, HIV, and TB require emphasis on infection prevention and control techniques.

alt.q: Hepatitis C is an example of a [[communicable disease|communicable]] because it can pass directly from one person to another.
alt.ex: Communicable diseases such as HBV, HCV, HIV, and TB require emphasis on infection prevention and control techniques.

items.q: A patient’s pathogens are multiplying and the patient has fever and a painful, reddened wound. How is this infection classified?
items.a: Symptomatic
items.ex: When pathogens multiply and cause clinical signs and symptoms, the infection is symptomatic.
w: Asymptomatic
An asymptomatic infection has no clinical signs or symptoms present.
Colonized
Colonization involves no tissue invasion or damage, so it does not cause these findings.
Convalescent
Convalescence is the stage when acute symptoms of infection disappear.

alt.q: An infection is described as asymptomatic. What does this indicate?
alt.a: Clinical signs and symptoms of the illness are not present
alt.ex: An illness without clinical signs and symptoms is termed asymptomatic.
w: Microorganisms are present without invading any tissue
Presence without tissue invasion is colonization, not an asymptomatic infection.
The illness cannot be transmitted to other people
Asymptomatic infections such as HCV can still be transmitted to others.
The acute symptoms of the infection have just disappeared
Disappearance of acute symptoms marks the convalescence stage.

items.q: A nurse sustains a needlestick from a used needle while caring for a patient with hepatitis C virus (HCV) who has no symptoms. Which statement by the nurse shows correct understanding?
items.a: I am at risk because HCV spreads through blood even when the source has no symptoms
items.ex: HCV is most efficiently transmitted by percutaneous passage of blood into the skin, even when the source patient is asymptomatic.
w: I am not at risk because the patient has an asymptomatic infection
HCV can be transmitted even if the source patient is asymptomatic.
I am at risk only if the patient later develops signs of illness
Transmission risk exists at the time of the percutaneous exposure regardless of the patient’s symptoms.
I am not at risk because HCV spreads mainly through respiratory droplets
HCV is spread most efficiently by direct passage of blood into the skin, not droplets.

alt.q: A student asks why sharps precautions matter when caring for a patient with HCV who feels well. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: HCV can pass through a needlestick even if the patient has no symptoms
alt.ex: HCV is efficiently transmitted by percutaneous blood exposure, even from an asymptomatic source patient.
w: HCV only spreads when the patient has active symptoms of illness
HCV transmission does not require the source patient to be symptomatic.
HCV is spread mainly by touching contaminated linens and surfaces
HCV is most efficiently spread by direct passage of blood into the skin.
HCV is a low-risk disease that does not pose a risk to caregivers
HCV is a communicable disease that poses a risk through percutaneous exposure.

items.q: By which route is hepatitis C virus (HCV) most efficiently transmitted?
items.a: Direct passage of blood into the skin through a percutaneous exposure
items.ex: HCV is most efficiently transmitted by direct passage of blood into the skin from a percutaneous exposure.
w: Inhalation of droplet nuclei suspended in the air
Droplet nuclei carry airborne organisms such as those aerosolized by equipment or construction dust.
Ingestion of improperly stored or undercooked food
Contaminated food is a vehicle for organisms such as Salmonella, not the main HCV route.
Contact with large droplets from a cough or sneeze
Droplets from coughing spread organisms such as pertussis within about 6 feet.

alt.q: Which exposure carries the greatest risk for a nurse to acquire hepatitis C virus?
alt.a: A puncture of the skin with a needle used on an infected patient
alt.ex: Percutaneous passage of blood into the skin is the most efficient way HCV is transmitted.
w: Standing within 3 feet of an infected patient who is coughing
HCV is not spread mainly by respiratory droplets.
Touching an infected patient’s intact skin with clean hands
Intact skin contact does not involve passage of blood into the skin.
Sharing a meal tray area with an infected patient’s visitor
HCV is a bloodborne pathogen and is not efficiently spread this way.

items.q: Which statements about hepatitis C virus (HCV) are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It is a communicable disease
HCV can be transmitted directly from one person to another.
It can be asymptomatic
HCV is an example of a communicable disease that can be asymptomatic.
It is efficiently spread by percutaneous blood exposure
Direct passage of blood into the skin is HCV’s most efficient route.
It cannot spread from a patient without symptoms
HCV can be transmitted even when the source patient is asymptomatic.
It is spread mainly by large respiratory droplets
HCV is a bloodborne pathogen, not a droplet-spread organism.
items.ex: HCV is a communicable, sometimes asymptomatic disease spread most efficiently by percutaneous blood exposure.

alt.q: A nurse teaches new staff about HCV exposure risk. Which points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: A needlestick from an infected patient can transmit HCV
Percutaneous exposure is the most efficient HCV transmission route.
An infected patient may have no signs or symptoms
HCV infection can be asymptomatic.
Risk exists even when the source patient feels well
HCV is transmitted even if the source patient is asymptomatic.
HCV is a low-risk illness that poses no risk to caregivers
HCV is a communicable disease requiring infection prevention measures.
Precautions are needed only after symptoms appear
Asymptomatic patients can still transmit HCV, so precautions are always needed.
alt.ex: Staff must handle sharps safely because HCV spreads by blood exposure even from asymptomatic patients.

items.q: Some infectious diseases, such as viral meningitis and pneumonia, have a low risk or no risk for transmission to others.
items.a: True
items.ex: Viral meningitis and pneumonia can be serious for patients but have low or no risk for transmission to caregivers.
items.ww: The book names these illnesses as serious for the patient yet low or no risk for others.

alt.q: Because viral meningitis is a serious illness, it poses a high transmission risk to caregivers.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Viral meningitis can be serious for the patient but has a low or no risk for transmission.
alt.ww: Severity for the patient does not determine transmission risk; viral meningitis has low or no risk to others.

items.q: A culture shows that a patient's skin carries a microorganism, but the tissue shows no invasion or damage and the patient has no signs of infection. How should the nurse describe this finding?
items.a: Colonization
items.ex: Colonization is the presence and growth of microorganisms in a host without tissue invasion or damage.
w: Infection
Infection requires pathogens to invade tissues and multiply.
Symptomatic infection
Symptomatic infection produces clinical signs and symptoms, which are absent here.
Communicable disease
A communicable disease is an infection transmitted from person to person.

alt.q: A pathogen has invaded a patient's tissues and is multiplying, but the patient has no clinical signs or symptoms. Which term describes this?
alt.a: Asymptomatic infection
alt.ex: When pathogens multiply and invade tissue but cause no clinical signs or symptoms, the infection is asymptomatic.
w: Colonization
Colonization involves no tissue invasion or damage.
Symptomatic infection
Symptomatic infection has clinical signs and symptoms.
Convalescence
Convalescence is the recovery stage after acute symptoms.

items.q: What does Infection mean?
items.a: A pathogen invades tissues and grows within a host
items.ex: Infection requires tissue invasion; colonization does not; communicable diseases spread person to person, with or without symptoms.
w: Microorganisms grow in a host without tissue invasion or damage
That goes with Colonization.
An infectious disease transmitted directly from person to person
That goes with Communicable disease.
Multiplying pathogens cause clinical signs and symptoms
That goes with Symptomatic.

alt.q: What does Colonization mean?
alt.a: Microorganisms grow in a host without tissue invasion or damage
alt.ex: Infection requires tissue invasion; colonization does not; communicable diseases spread person to person, with or without symptoms.
w: A pathogen invades tissues and grows within a host
That goes with Infection.
An infectious disease transmitted directly from person to person
That goes with Communicable disease.
Multiplying pathogens cause clinical signs and symptoms
That goes with Symptomatic.

alt.q: What does Communicable disease mean?
alt.a: An infectious disease transmitted directly from person to person

items.q: Which statements correctly distinguish infection from colonization? Select all that apply.
o: Infection involves pathogens invading tissue
An infection results when a pathogen invades tissues and grows within the host.
Colonization involves no tissue damage
Colonization is growth of organisms without tissue invasion or damage.
Both involve microorganisms growing within a host
Organisms grow within the host in both infection and colonization.
Colonization always causes clinical signs and symptoms
Colonization involves no tissue invasion or damage, so it does not cause infection symptoms.
Infection is present whenever a pathogen is found
The presence of a pathogen does not mean an infection will occur.
items.ex: Both involve organism growth, but only infection involves tissue invasion and altered tissue function.

alt.q: A nurse reviews culture results with a student. Which explanations about colonization are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Organisms are present and growing within the host
Colonization is the presence and growth of microorganisms within a host.
Tissue has not been invaded by the organisms
Colonization occurs without tissue invasion.
Tissue has not been damaged by the organisms
Colonization occurs without tissue damage.
The organisms have multiplied and altered tissue function
Multiplication that alters tissue function results in disease or infection.
The patient has a symptomatic infection
A symptomatic infection involves tissue invasion with clinical signs and symptoms.
alt.ex: Colonization means organisms are present and growing but have not invaded or damaged tissue.

items.q: A wound culture grows bacteria. Which assessment finding best indicates the patient has an infection rather than colonization?
items.a: Redness, warmth, and tenderness at the wound site
items.ex: Localized signs such as pain, tenderness, warmth, and redness show pathogens are invading tissue and altering its function.
w: Bacteria detected on the surface of the wound
Bacteria may be present and growing without tissue invasion, which is colonization.
Wound edges that are intact and pale pink
Intact, normal-appearing tissue shows no sign of tissue invasion or damage.
Normal flora found on the skin around the wound
Normal skin flora survive and multiply without causing illness.

alt.q: Which finding would suggest only colonization of a patient’s wound?
alt.a: Bacteria grow in a culture but the tissue shows no damage
alt.ex: Colonization is the growth of microorganisms without tissue invasion or damage.
w: Purulent drainage with redness and swelling at the site
Purulent drainage with inflammation signals tissue invasion and infection.
Pain and warmth spreading around the wound edges
Pain and warmth are localized signs of infection.
Fever and an elevated white blood cell count
Fever and leukocytosis suggest a systemic response to infection.

items.q: Why does the nurse use infection prevention measures with every patient, including those who show no signs of disease?
items.a: People without signs of disease can be carriers who transmit microorganisms
items.ex: Human reservoirs include people who show no signs of disease but carry it, and they can still transmit organisms.
w: Every patient without symptoms has a communicable infection
Not every asymptomatic patient is infected; some simply have no infection.
Asymptomatic patients are the only ones who transmit pathogens
People with acute or symptomatic disease also transmit microorganisms.
Colonized patients always develop a symptomatic infection
Colonization does not always progress; infection requires tissue invasion and altered function.

alt.q: A nurse cares for a patient whose infection is asymptomatic. Which statement about this patient is accurate?
alt.a: The patient can still transmit the pathogen to others
alt.ex: Humans can transmit microorganisms whether they have symptomatic disease or show no signs of disease.
w: The patient cannot spread infection until symptoms appear
Asymptomatic carriers and patients with infections such as HCV can transmit pathogens.
The patient has colonization rather than an infection
An asymptomatic infection still involves tissue invasion; colonization does not.
The patient no longer needs Standard Precautions
Standard Precautions apply because asymptomatic people may still transmit organisms.

items.q: A person whose infection causes no clinical signs or symptoms can still transmit the pathogen to others.
items.a: True
items.ex: HCV, for example, can be transmitted even when the source patient is asymptomatic.
items.ww: Absence of symptoms does not remove transmission risk; carriers and asymptomatic patients can spread organisms.

alt.q: A patient with an asymptomatic infection cannot spread the infection to caregivers.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Asymptomatic infections such as HCV can be transmitted to caregivers through percutaneous exposure.
alt.ww: Humans transmit microorganisms whether or not they show signs of disease.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with a positive skin culture whose skin is intact and shows no redness, warmth, or drainage. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
items.a: The patient has colonization because no tissue invasion is evident
items.ex: Colonization is growth of microorganisms without tissue invasion or damage; no tissue changes are evident here.
w: The patient has a localized infection that needs immediate treatment
A localized infection causes signs such as pain, warmth, and redness, which are absent.
The patient has a systemic infection that may become fatal
Systemic infection affects the entire body and produces signs such as fever.
The patient has no microorganisms present on the skin
The positive culture shows organisms are present and growing.

alt.q: A culture is positive, but the patient’s tissues show no invasion or damage. Which conclusion is correct?
alt.a: Colonization is present, which is not the same as infection
alt.ex: Organisms growing without tissue invasion or damage indicate colonization, not infection.
w: A symptomatic infection is present in the tissue
A symptomatic infection requires tissue invasion and clinical signs.
The patient has a communicable disease
Communicable disease refers to an infection that spreads directly from person to person.
The culture result must be a laboratory error
Organisms can be present and growing without causing infection.

items.q: A nurse cares for a patient with pneumonia and another with hepatitis C. Which statement best explains the difference in transmission risk to caregivers?
items.a: Hepatitis C is communicable through blood, whereas pneumonia has low or no transmission risk
items.ex: HCV is a communicable disease spread by percutaneous blood exposure; pneumonia is listed as low or no transmission risk.
w: Pneumonia is more communicable because it is more serious for the patient
Seriousness for the patient does not make pneumonia a transmission risk to others.
Both carry equal risk because both are serious infectious diseases
Some serious infections, such as pneumonia, pose low or no risk to others.
Hepatitis C poses no risk because the patient may have no symptoms
HCV can be transmitted even when the source patient is asymptomatic.

alt.q: Which patient poses the greater risk of transmitting infection to a nurse through a needlestick?
alt.a: A patient with hepatitis C who has no symptoms
alt.ex: HCV is efficiently transmitted by percutaneous exposure, even from an asymptomatic source patient.
w: A patient with viral meningitis who has a headache
Viral meningitis is described as having low or no risk for transmission.
A patient with pneumonia who has a cough
Pneumonia is described as having low or no risk for transmission.
A patient with skin colonization and intact skin
Colonization involves no tissue invasion and is not a bloodborne exposure risk.

items.q: Which statements about communicable diseases are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They can be transmitted directly from one person to another
This is the definition of a communicable disease.
They can be present without symptoms
HCV is a communicable disease that can be asymptomatic.
Bloodborne examples include HBV, HCV, and HIV
The chapter names HBV, HCV, and HIV as communicable diseases spread through blood.
They always produce clinical signs and symptoms
Communicable diseases such as HCV can be asymptomatic.
They pose no risk to caregivers
Communicable diseases require emphasis on infection prevention and control to protect others.
items.ex: Communicable diseases spread directly between people, may be asymptomatic, and include HBV, HCV, and HIV.

alt.q: A nurse explains communicable diseases to a patient’s family. Which statements should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: A communicable disease can pass directly between people
Direct person-to-person transmission defines a communicable disease.
A person can spread some communicable diseases without feeling ill
Asymptomatic communicable diseases such as HCV still spread.
Hepatitis C is an example of a communicable disease
The book uses HCV as an example of a communicable disease.
Any serious infectious illness is communicable
Serious illnesses such as viral meningitis and pneumonia can have low or no transmission risk.
Colonization is the same as a communicable disease
Colonization is growth without tissue invasion; it is not a disease.
alt.ex: Communicable diseases pass between people even without symptoms, but not every serious infection is communicable.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with Clostridium difficile and has just finished cleaning the patient after a diarrheal episode. Which hand hygiene action should the nurse take?
items.a: Wash hands with soap and water
items.ex: Soap and water is preferred when hands are visibly soiled or care is given to a patient with C. difficile.
w: Apply an alcohol-based hand rub
Alcohol rub is acceptable only when hands are not visibly soiled and C. difficile is not involved.
Remove gloves and proceed to the next patient
Hand hygiene is still required after glove removal to remove transient organisms.
Wipe hands with a dry paper towel
Drying without washing does not remove transient organisms or C. difficile spores.

alt.q: A nurse takes the blood pressure of a patient without C. difficile; the nurse’s hands are not visibly soiled. Which hand hygiene method is acceptable?
alt.a: An alcohol-based hand product or soap and water
alt.ex: If hands are not visibly soiled, alcohol-based hand products or soap and water are both acceptable.
w: Soap and water only, because alcohol products are ineffective
Alcohol-based products are acceptable when hands are not visibly soiled.
No hand hygiene, because the hands are not soiled
Transient organisms adhere to hands during contact and must be removed.
A surgical hand scrub before every patient contact
Routine hand hygiene, not a surgical scrub, is needed after this contact.

items.q: Which action is the most effective way to break the chain of infection?
items.a: Hand hygiene
items.ex: Hand hygiene is the most effective way to break the chain of infection.
w: Isolation of every patient
Isolation is used when necessary but is not identified as the most effective measure.
Broad-spectrum antibiotics
Broad-spectrum antibiotics can eliminate normal flora and contribute to resistance.
Daily linen changes
Linen can be a fomite, but hand hygiene is the most effective measure.

alt.q: What is the major route of transmission for pathogens in the health care setting?
alt.a: Unwashed hands of the health care worker
alt.ex: The unwashed hands of health care workers are the major route of pathogen transmission in health care.
w: Water supplied to the patient care unit
Water can be a vehicle but is not the major route in health care.
Insects that enter the health care agency
Vectors such as flies are not the major health care route.
Food served from the hospital kitchen
Food can be a vehicle but is not the major health care route.

items.q: Which statement about resident skin microorganisms is accurate?
items.a: They are not virulent but can cause infection when invasive procedures allow entry into deep tissues
items.ex: Resident flora are not virulent but can cause serious infection after surgery or invasive procedures or in severe immunocompromise.
w: They attach to the skin temporarily and are removed easily with hand hygiene
This describes transient microorganisms acquired during contact.
They are highly virulent and cause most health care–associated infections
Resident skin flora are not virulent; they survive without causing illness.
They never cause infection because they are part of normal flora
They can cause serious infection when invasive procedures let them enter deep tissues.

alt.q: A nurse touches a contaminated gauze dressing. Which type of microorganisms adhere to the nurse’s skin?
alt.a: Transient microorganisms
alt.ex: Transient organisms attach to skin during contact with people or objects and are readily transmitted unless removed by hand hygiene.
w: Resident microorganisms
Resident organisms are permanent normal flora of the skin, not acquired from a dressing.
Normal flora
Normal flora are resident organisms that live permanently on the skin.
Anaerobic microorganisms
Anaerobes thrive where little or no oxygen exists, such as deep tissues.

items.q: The potential for microorganisms to cause disease depends on which factors? Select all that apply.
o: Number of microorganisms present
A larger number of organisms increases disease potential.
Virulence of the microorganisms
Virulence is the ability to produce disease.
Ability to enter and survive in a host
Organisms must enter and survive in a host to cause disease.
Susceptibility of the host
A susceptible host is needed for infection to develop.
Color of the microorganism colonies
Colony color is not a factor in disease potential.
Season in which exposure occurs
The book does not list season as a factor in disease potential.
items.ex: Disease potential depends on the number of organisms, their virulence, their ability to enter and survive, and host susceptibility.

alt.q: A nurse explains why some exposures lead to infection and others do not. Which factors should the nurse identify? Select all that apply.
o: How many organisms the person is exposed to
Infection develops when a host is susceptible to the numbers of organisms.
The organisms’ ability to produce disease
Virulence affects whether organisms cause disease.
The person’s resistance to the organisms
Susceptibility depends on the person’s degree of resistance.
Whether the person has ever been colonized
Prior colonization is not listed as a factor in disease potential.
Whether the organisms are visible on the skin
Microorganisms are not visible, and visibility is not a factor.
alt.ex: Exposure leads to infection depending on organism number, virulence, survival in the host, and host resistance.

items.q: Which item is an example of a fomite?
items.a: A contaminated bedside commode
items.ex: Fomites are organic matter on inanimate surfaces; equipment such as a commode often becomes a source of transmission.
w: A mosquito carrying a parasite
A mosquito is a vector that transmits organisms internally.
A carrier with no signs of disease
A carrier is a human reservoir, not an inanimate surface.
Large droplets from a sneeze
Droplets are a mode of transmission, not an inanimate surface.

alt.q: A stethoscope that is not cleaned between patients carries organisms. This stethoscope is best described as what?
alt.a: A fomite acting as a reservoir
alt.ex: Organic matter on inanimate surfaces (fomites) is a common reservoir, and equipment such as stethoscopes often transmits pathogens.
w: A vector acting as a host
Vectors are living carriers such as flies, mosquitoes, lice, fleas, and ticks.
A portal of entry
A portal of entry is the route by which organisms enter a host’s body.
A susceptible host
A susceptible host is a person whose resistance is inadequate to prevent infection.

items.q: What is the ideal temperature range for growth of most human pathogens?
items.ex: Most human pathogens grow best at 20°C to 43°C (68°F to 109°F).
w: Cold temperatures tend to prevent bacterial growth and reproduction (bacteriostasis).
This range is above the ideal growth range for most human pathogens.
This range is below the ideal growth range for most human pathogens.

alt.q: Most microorganisms prefer an environment within which pH range?
alt.ex: Most microorganisms prefer a pH of 5.0 to 7.0, although bacteria thrive in alkaline urine.
w: A gastric pH of 1 to 2 is deleterious to many microbial pathogens.
This range is above the pH most microorganisms prefer.
This range is more acidic than most microorganisms prefer.

items.q: Cold temperatures tend to prevent the growth and reproduction of bacteria, a process called bacteriostasis.
items.a: True
items.ex: Bacteriostasis is the prevention of bacterial growth and reproduction, as occurs with cold temperatures.
items.ww: Cold does not destroy bacteria; it prevents growth, which is bacteriostasis rather than a bactericidal effect.

alt.q: Refrigerating food destroys the bacteria in it, which is called a bactericidal effect.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Cold temperatures prevent bacterial growth (bacteriostasis); a bactericidal agent destroys bacteria.
alt.ww: Cold inhibits rather than kills bacteria, so refrigeration is bacteriostatic, not bactericidal.

items.q: A temperature or chemical that destroys bacteria is described as [[bactericidal]].
items.ex: Bactericidal agents destroy bacteria, whereas bacteriostasis only prevents their growth and reproduction.

alt.q: An agent that kills bacteria, rather than simply stopping their growth, has a [[bactericidal]] effect.
alt.ex: Bactericidal agents destroy bacteria, whereas bacteriostasis only prevents their growth and reproduction.

items.q: Which statement about the oxygen needs of microorganisms is accurate?
items.a: Anaerobic bacteria typically cause infections deep within the pleural cavity, a joint, or a sinus tract
items.ex: Anaerobes thrive where little or no free oxygen is available, so they typically cause deep infections.
w: Anaerobic organisms cause more infections in humans than aerobic organisms do
Aerobic organisms cause more human infections than anaerobic organisms.
Staphylococcus aureus is an example of an anaerobic organism found in the colon
S. aureus is aerobic; Bacteroides fragilis is the anaerobe of the colon.
Aerobic bacteria thrive best where little or no free oxygen is available
Aerobic bacteria require oxygen for survival and multiplication.

alt.q: Bacteroides fragilis is normal flora of the colon. Under which circumstance can it cause infection?
alt.a: When it is displaced into the bloodstream or tissue after surgery or injury
alt.ex: This anaerobe of the normal colon flora causes infection when displaced into the bloodstream or surrounding tissue.
w: When the patient breathes air with a high oxygen content
Oxygen exposure does not trigger infection by this anaerobic organism.
When the patient’s urine becomes more acidic than normal
Urine pH relates to bacterial growth in urine, not B. fragilis infection.
When the patient is exposed to cold temperatures
Cold temperatures prevent bacterial growth rather than cause infection.

items.q: Why is Clostridium difficile able to live on inanimate surfaces for long periods?
items.a: It forms spores that resist drying
items.ex: Some bacteria form spores that resist drying and survive on surfaces for long periods; C. difficile is a common example.
w: It is normal flora of the skin
C. difficile is not described as skin flora; resident skin flora are not virulent.
It requires no water for growth
Most organisms require moisture; spores resist drying but do not grow without water.
It thrives in alkaline urine
Bacteria thriving in alkaline urine relates to pH, not survival on surfaces.

alt.q: Which spore-forming bacterium causes antibiotic-induced diarrhea?
alt.a: Clostridium difficile
alt.ex: C. difficile is a common spore-forming bacterium that causes antibiotic-induced diarrhea.
w: Clostridium perfringens
C. perfringens thrives on organic matter and causes gas gangrene.
Escherichia coli
E. coli consumes undigested foodstuff in the bowel.
Staphylococcus aureus
S. aureus is given as an example of an aerobic organism.

items.q: Which are portals of exit for microorganisms? Select all that apply.
o: Respiratory tract
Pathogens such as influenza leave the body when an infected person sneezes or coughs.
Blood
Organisms exit from wounds, venipuncture sites, hematemesis, and bloody stool.
Breaks in skin and mucous membranes
Any break in skin or mucous membrane integrity allows pathogens to exit.
Transplacental route
Organisms can pass from mother to fetus across the placenta.
Intact, unbroken skin
It is a break in skin integrity, not intact skin, that allows pathogens to exit.
Insect vectors
Vectors such as mosquitoes are a mode of transmission, not a portal of exit.
items.ex: Portals of exit include blood, skin and mucous membranes, respiratory, GU, and GI tracts, and the transplacental route.

alt.q: A nurse identifies how pathogens may leave a patient’s body. Which are portals of exit? Select all that apply.
o: Urination in a patient with a UTI
Normally sterile urine carries organisms out during a UTI.
Emesis and bowel elimination
These are gastrointestinal portals of exit.
Purulent drainage from a wound
Purulent drainage shows pathogens exiting through broken skin.
Contaminated soiled linen
Soiled linen is a fomite involved in indirect contact transmission.
Food that was improperly stored
Improperly stored food is a reservoir and vehicle, not a portal of exit.
alt.ex: Portals of exit are body sites such as urine, GI losses, and wound drainage through which organisms leave.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with pertussis who is coughing frequently. How are the organisms most likely to reach another person?
items.a: Through droplets that travel short distances, within about 6 feet
items.ex: Coughing or sneezing creates droplets that carry germs about 6 feet to a susceptible person’s eyes, nose, or mouth.
w: Through droplet nuclei that remain suspended in air for long distances
Suspended droplet nuclei describe airborne transmission, such as Aspergillus from construction dust.
Through a vector such as a flea, louse, or tick that bites the person
Vector transmission involves insects, not coughing.
Through a contaminated vehicle such as blood, drugs, or water
Vehicle transmission involves contaminated items, not respiratory droplets.

alt.q: A visitor sits about 3 feet from a patient with pertussis who sneezes, and droplets land on the visitor’s nose. Which mode of transmission does this represent?
alt.a: Droplet
alt.ex: Droplets from coughing or sneezing travel short distances (about 6 feet) and land on a person’s eyes, nose, or mouth.
w: Airborne
Airborne transmission involves droplet nuclei or residue suspended in air.
Vector
Vector transmission involves flies, mosquitoes, lice, fleas, or ticks.
Indirect contact
Indirect contact involves touching a contaminated inanimate object.

items.q: A nurse is about to perform a venipuncture. Which action best prevents organisms from entering the patient through this portal of entry?
items.a: Perform proper skin preparation before the needle pierces the skin
items.ex: During venipuncture, organisms enter the body if proper skin preparation is not performed first.
w: Choose the arm with the most visible veins
Vein selection does not prevent organisms from entering through the puncture.
Apply a tourniquet before cleaning the site
A tourniquet helps locate veins but does not prevent organism entry.
Insert the needle quickly to reduce pain
Speed of insertion does not prevent pathogens from entering the body.

alt.q: Which statement about portals of entry is accurate?
alt.a: Organisms enter the body through the same routes they use for exiting
alt.ex: Portals of entry mirror portals of exit, such as skin, respiratory, GI, and GU routes.
w: Organisms can enter the body only through broken skin
Organisms can also enter through the respiratory, GI, and GU tracts.
Organisms enter mainly through intact mucous membranes
Intact mucosa is a mechanical barrier; it is not the main route of entry.
A strong immune system increases the chance of entry
A depressed immune system, not a strong one, enhances the chance of entry.

items.q: Which factors affect a person’s susceptibility to infection? Select all that apply.
o: Age
Age is a risk factor affecting resistance to infection.
Nutritional status
Nutritional status affects susceptibility.
Presence of chronic disease
Chronic disease affects susceptibility to infection.
Smoking
Smoking is a risk factor affecting susceptibility.
Eye color
Eye color has no effect on resistance to infection.
Blood type
Blood type is not listed as a factor affecting susceptibility.
items.ex: Natural defenses and risk factors such as age, nutrition, chronic disease, trauma, and smoking affect susceptibility.

alt.q: A nurse assesses a patient’s risk of becoming a susceptible host. Which findings increase the risk? Select all that apply.
o: Recent traumatic injury
Trauma is a risk factor that affects resistance.
Poor nutritional status
Poor nutrition reduces resistance to infection.
Depressed immune system
A depressed immune system reduces body defenses.
Regular hand hygiene by caregivers
Hand hygiene breaks the chain of infection rather than increasing susceptibility.
Intact skin and mucous membranes
Intact skin and mucosa are barriers against microorganisms.
alt.ex: Trauma, poor nutrition, and impaired immunity lower a person’s resistance and increase susceptibility.

items.q: Antimicrobial resistance occurs when infectious organisms develop the ability to defeat the drugs designed to kill them.
items.a: True
items.ex: Antimicrobial resistance has evolved from inappropriate antibiotic prescribing and lack of infection control actions.
items.ww: This is the definition of antimicrobial resistance (AR) used in the chapter.

alt.q: Antimicrobial resistance has developed mainly because patients receive too few antibiotics during hospital stays.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Resistance has evolved because of historically inappropriate prescribing of antibiotics and lack of infection control actions.
alt.ww: The book attributes resistance to inappropriate prescribing and poor infection control, not too few antibiotics.

items.q: A human can serve as a reservoir for infection even when showing no signs of disease.
items.a: True
items.ex: Human reservoirs include people with symptomatic disease and carriers who show no signs, and both can transmit organisms.
items.ww: Carriers without signs of disease can still transmit microorganisms.

alt.q: Only people with acute, symptomatic disease can serve as human reservoirs of infection.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Carriers who show no signs of disease are also human reservoirs that can transmit microorganisms.
alt.ww: Humans transmit microorganisms whether they are symptomatic or asymptomatic carriers.

items.q: A [[reservoir]] is a place where microorganisms survive, multiply, and await transfer to a susceptible host.
items.ex: Common reservoirs include humans, animals, insects, food, water, and fomites.

alt.q: Health care workers’ hands, patients, equipment, and the environment are frequent [[reservoirs|reservoir]] for health care–associated infections.
alt.ex: Common reservoirs include humans, animals, insects, food, water, and fomites.

items.q: A nurse removes a patient’s dressing and finds moist drainage on a wound kept under a dark, occlusive cover. Why does this environment favor microorganism growth?
items.a: Organisms thrive in moist, dark environments such as under dressings
items.ex: Most organisms need moisture, and microorganisms thrive in dark places such as under dressings and within body cavities.
w: Organisms need bright light to multiply in a wound
Microorganisms thrive in dark environments, not bright light.
Organisms need a dry surface to attach to tissue
Most organisms require water or moisture; moist wound drainage favors them.
Organisms need a very acidic pH below 2 to grow
Most microorganisms prefer pH 5.0 to 7.0; pH 1 to 2 is harmful to them.

alt.q: Which environment is most favorable to the growth of microorganisms?
alt.a: A moist, dark area under a dressing at body temperature
alt.ex: Moisture, darkness, and temperatures of 20°C to 43°C favor growth of most human pathogens.
w: A dry, cold surface exposed to bright light
Dryness, cold, and light do not favor most organisms.
A refrigerated area with a very acidic pH
Cold prevents growth, and a very acidic pH is harmful to many pathogens.
A heated area well above 45°C that is dry
Most human pathogens grow best at 20°C to 43°C and need moisture.

items.q: In the course of infection, which stage comes right after “Prodromal stage”?
items.a: Illness stage
items.ex: That's stage 3 of 4. Infections progress from incubation to prodromal symptoms, then specific illness, then recovery during convalescence.
w: Convalescence
That's stage 4 of 4.
Incubation period
That's stage 1 of 4.

alt.q: Which stage comes first in the course of infection?
alt.a: Incubation period
alt.ex: That's stage 1 of 4. Infections progress from incubation to prodromal symptoms, then specific illness, then recovery during convalescence.
w: Prodromal stage
That's stage 2 of 4.
Illness stage
That's stage 3 of 4.
Convalescence
That's stage 4 of 4.

alt.q: Which stage comes last in the course of infection?
alt.a: Convalescence
alt.ex: That's stage 4 of 4. Infections progress from incubation to prodromal symptoms, then specific illness, then recovery during convalescence.
w: Illness stage
That's stage 3 of 4.
Prodromal stage
That's stage 2 of 4.
Incubation period
That's stage 1 of 4.

alt.q: In the course of infection, which stage comes right after “Incubation period”?
alt.a: Prodromal stage
alt.ex: That's stage 2 of 4. Infections progress from incubation to prodromal symptoms, then specific illness, then recovery during convalescence.
w: Illness stage
That's stage 3 of 4.
Convalescence
That's stage 4 of 4.

alt.q: In the course of infection, which stage comes right after “Illness stage”?
alt.a: Convalescence
alt.ex: That's stage 4 of 4. Infections progress from incubation to prodromal symptoms, then specific illness, then recovery during convalescence.
w: Prodromal stage
That's stage 2 of 4.
Incubation period
That's stage 1 of 4.

alt.q: In the course of infection, which stage comes right before “Prodromal stage”?
alt.a: Incubation period
alt.ex: That's stage 1 of 4. Infections progress from incubation to prodromal symptoms, then specific illness, then recovery during convalescence.
w: Illness stage
That's stage 3 of 4.
Convalescence
That's stage 4 of 4.

alt.q: In the course of infection, which stage comes right before “Illness stage”?
alt.a: Prodromal stage
alt.ex: That's stage 2 of 4. Infections progress from incubation to prodromal symptoms, then specific illness, then recovery during convalescence.
w: Incubation period
That's stage 1 of 4.
Convalescence
That's stage 4 of 4.

alt.q: In the course of infection, which stage comes right before “Convalescence”?
alt.a: Illness stage
alt.ex: That's stage 3 of 4. Infections progress from incubation to prodromal symptoms, then specific illness, then recovery during convalescence.
w: Prodromal stage
That's stage 2 of 4.
Incubation period
That's stage 1 of 4.

ord.q: Place the stages in the course of an infection in order.
items: Incubation period
Prodromal stage
Illness stage
Convalescence
ord.ex: Infections progress from incubation to prodromal symptoms, then specific illness, then recovery during convalescence.

items.q: A patient reports malaise, a low-grade fever, and fatigue, but no specific symptoms of illness yet. Which stage of infection is the patient most likely in?
items.a: Prodromal stage
items.ex: The prodromal stage runs from nonspecific signs such as malaise, low-grade fever, and fatigue to more specific symptoms.
w: Incubation period
Incubation is the interval before the appearance of any first symptoms.
Illness stage
During the illness stage, signs and symptoms specific to the infection appear.
Convalescence
During convalescence, acute symptoms disappear and the patient recovers.

alt.q: A patient with herpes simplex reports itching and tingling at a site where no lesion has yet appeared. Which statement about this stage is accurate?
alt.a: The patient may be capable of spreading the disease to others
alt.ex: In the prodromal stage, microorganisms grow and multiply, and the patient may spread disease to others.
w: The pathogen has not yet entered the patient’s body
The pathogen has entered; symptoms appear only after the incubation period.
The patient is recovering as acute symptoms disappear
Disappearance of acute symptoms describes convalescence.
The patient cannot transmit infection until a lesion forms
Patients may spread disease during the prodromal stage, before specific signs.

items.q: What is the incubation period of an infection?
items.a: The interval between entrance of the pathogen into the body and appearance of the first symptoms
items.ex: Incubation is the time from pathogen entry until first symptoms appear, such as 1 to 4 days for influenza.
w: The interval from nonspecific signs and symptoms to more specific symptoms
This interval is the prodromal stage.
The interval when the patient shows signs specific to the type of infection
This interval is the illness stage.
The interval when acute symptoms disappear and the patient recovers
This interval is convalescence.

alt.q: A patient was exposed to influenza 2 days ago and has no symptoms yet. Which statement about this patient is accurate?
alt.a: The patient may still be in the incubation period for influenza
alt.ex: Influenza has an incubation period of 1 to 4 days, so a symptom-free patient at day 2 may still be incubating.
w: The patient cannot have influenza because symptoms appear within 24 hours
Influenza incubation is 1 to 4 days, not within 24 hours.
The patient is in the convalescence stage of influenza
Convalescence follows the illness stage, after acute symptoms disappear.
The patient cannot have influenza because incubation lasts 10 to 12 days
An incubation of 10 to 12 days is given for measles, not influenza.

items.q: A patient with mumps has a high fever and swelling of the parotid glands. Which stage of infection does this represent?
items.a: Illness stage
items.ex: In the illness stage the patient manifests signs and symptoms specific to the infection, such as parotid swelling in mumps.
w: Incubation period
During incubation, no symptoms have appeared yet.
Prodromal stage
The prodromal stage involves nonspecific signs such as malaise and fatigue.
Convalescence
Convalescence is when acute symptoms disappear.

alt.q: What determines the length of the convalescence stage of an infection?
alt.a: Severity of the infection and the patient’s host resistance
alt.ex: Recovery length depends on the infection’s severity and the patient’s host resistance and may take days to months.
w: Length of the incubation period for that pathogen
Incubation length is not identified as what determines recovery time.
Number of nonspecific symptoms during the prodromal stage
Prodromal symptoms do not determine the length of recovery.
Whether the infection was transmitted by droplets
The mode of transmission does not determine recovery length.

items.q: A patient has a surgical wound infection. Which finding would indicate the infection has become systemic?
items.a: Fever with a white blood cell count of 18,000/mm3
items.ex: Systemic inflammation produces fever and leukocytosis; WBCs typically rise to 15,000 to 20,000/mm3 or higher.
w: Warmth and redness at the incision site
Warmth and redness are localized signs of infection.
Tenderness when the wound is palpated
Tenderness is a localized sign at the wound site.
Mild swelling along the incision edges
Swelling at the site is a localized sign of inflammation.

alt.q: A patient with a localized wound infection is being monitored. Which finding most needs to be reported because it suggests spread to the entire body?
alt.a: New fever, malaise, and enlarged lymph nodes
alt.ex: Fever, malaise, and lymph node enlargement are systemic signs; systemic infection can be fatal if undetected and untreated.
w: Pain and tenderness at the wound site
Pain and tenderness are expected localized signs of wound infection.
Redness limited to the wound edges
Redness at the wound is a localized sign.
Warmth over the wound when touched
Warmth at the site is a localized sign.

items.q: What is the normal serum white blood cell (WBC) count in an adult?
items.ex: The normal adult WBC count is 5000 to 10,000/mm3; it typically rises to 15,000 to 20,000/mm3 or higher during inflammation.
w: This range is typical during inflammation, not a normal value.
This range is below the normal adult WBC count.
This range is well above the normal adult WBC count.

alt.q: A patient with inflammation has leukocytosis. Which WBC count range is typical during inflammation?
alt.a: 15,000 to 20,000/mm3 or higher
alt.ex: During inflammation, WBCs typically increase from a normal 5000 to 10,000/mm3 to 15,000 to 20,000/mm3 or higher.
w: 5000 to 10,000/mm3 or lower
5000 to 10,000/mm3 is the normal adult WBC range.
1000 to 4000/mm3 or lower
A low count is the opposite of leukocytosis.
10,000 to 12,000/mm3 or lower
This is below the range typically seen during inflammation.

items.q: An increase in the number of circulating white blood cells during inflammation is called [[leukocytosis]].
items.ex: Leukocytosis is the body’s response to WBCs leaving blood vessels to reach the site of inflammation.

alt.q: A WBC count that rises from 8000 to 18,000/mm3 during an infection is an example of [[leukocytosis]].
alt.ex: Leukocytosis is the body’s response to WBCs leaving blood vessels to reach the site of inflammation.

items.q: Which are signs of localized inflammation? Select all that apply.
o: Swelling
Fluid accumulation in interstitial spaces causes localized edema.
Redness
Increased local blood flow from vasodilation causes redness.
Heat
Increased local blood flow causes localized warmth.
Loss of function of the affected part
Swelling and pain cause temporary loss of function.
Fever
Fever is a systemic sign of inflammation.
Lymph node enlargement
Lymph node enlargement is a systemic sign.
items.ex: Localized inflammation causes swelling, redness, heat, pain or tenderness, and loss of function in the affected part.

alt.q: A patient’s inflammation has become systemic. Which signs and symptoms may develop? Select all that apply.
o: Fever
Fever develops when inflammation becomes systemic.
Increased white blood cells
Leukocytosis is a systemic sign.
Anorexia, nausea, and vomiting
These GI symptoms can develop with systemic inflammation.
Redness limited to the injured site
Redness at the site is a localized sign.
Stiffness of a single swollen finger joint
Stiffness of an inflamed joint is a localized loss of function.
alt.ex: Systemic inflammation causes fever, increased WBCs, malaise, anorexia, nausea, vomiting, lymph node enlargement, or organ failure.

items.q: During the vascular response of acute inflammation, what causes redness and localized warmth at the site?
items.a: Vasodilation that increases local blood flow
items.ex: Rapid vasodilation delivers more blood near the injury, causing redness and localized warmth.
w: Swelling that presses on nerve endings
Pressure on nerve endings from swelling causes pain.
Release of pyrogens that reset the hypothalamus
Pyrogens raise the hypothalamic set point, causing fever.
Formation of a meshlike matrix of platelets
The platelet and fibrinogen matrix prevents spread of inflammation.

alt.q: What causes the pain associated with inflammation?
alt.a: Swelling of inflamed tissues that increases pressure on nerve endings
alt.ex: Inflammatory swelling increases pressure on nerve endings, causing pain.
w: Vasodilation that increases blood flow to the injured area
Increased local blood flow causes redness and warmth.
Phagocytes that ingest and destroy microorganisms
Phagocytosis destroys organisms but is not described as causing pain.
Lymphatic drainage that removes inflammatory exudate
Lymphatic drainage clears exudate rather than causing pain.

items.q: Which white blood cells ingest and destroy microorganisms through phagocytosis?
items.a: Neutrophils and monocytes
items.ex: Specialized WBCs called neutrophils and monocytes ingest and destroy microorganisms or other small particles.
w: Platelets and fibrinogen
Platelets and fibrinogen form a meshlike matrix that prevents spread of inflammation.
Red blood cells and plasma
Red blood cells make exudate sanguineous; they do not ingest organisms.
Granulation and scar cells
Granulation tissue fills tissue defects in chronic inflammation.

alt.q: What is phagocytosis?
alt.a: Destruction and absorption of bacteria by specialized white blood cells
alt.ex: Through phagocytosis, neutrophils and monocytes ingest and destroy microorganisms or other small particles.
w: Formation of a meshlike matrix by platelets at the inflamed site
The platelet and plasma protein matrix prevents the spread of inflammation.
Movement of fluid and protein into the interstitial spaces
Fluid movement into interstitial spaces causes edema.
Replacement of damaged cells with healthy new cells over time
Replacing damaged cells is part of tissue repair.

items.q: What does Serous exudate look like or contain?
items.a: Clear, like plasma
items.ex: Exudate forms from fluid, dead cells, and WBCs and may be serous, sanguineous, or purulent.
w: Contains red blood cells
That goes with Sanguineous.
Contains white blood cells and bacteria
That goes with Purulent.

alt.q: What does Sanguineous exudate look like or contain?
alt.a: Contains red blood cells
alt.ex: Exudate forms from fluid, dead cells, and WBCs and may be serous, sanguineous, or purulent.
w: Clear, like plasma
That goes with Serous.
Contains white blood cells and bacteria
That goes with Purulent.

alt.q: What does Purulent exudate look like or contain?
alt.a: Contains white blood cells and bacteria
alt.ex: Exudate forms from fluid, dead cells, and WBCs and may be serous, sanguineous, or purulent.
w: Clear, like plasma
That goes with Serous.
Contains red blood cells
That goes with Sanguineous.

alt.q: Which type of exudate is “Clear, like plasma”?
alt.a: Serous
alt.ex: Exudate forms from fluid, dead cells, and WBCs and may be serous, sanguineous, or purulent.
w: Sanguineous
Sanguineous: Contains red blood cells.
Purulent
Purulent: Contains white blood cells and bacteria.

alt.q: Which type of exudate is “Contains red blood cells”?
alt.a: Sanguineous
alt.ex: Exudate forms from fluid, dead cells, and WBCs and may be serous, sanguineous, or purulent.
w: Serous
Serous: Clear, like plasma.
Purulent
Purulent: Contains white blood cells and bacteria.

alt.q: Which type of exudate is “Contains white blood cells and bacteria”?
alt.a: Purulent
alt.ex: Exudate forms from fluid, dead cells, and WBCs and may be serous, sanguineous, or purulent.
w: Serous
Serous: Clear, like plasma.
Sanguineous
Sanguineous: Contains red blood cells.

mt.q: Match each type of inflammatory exudate with its description.
pairs: Contains white blood cells and bacteria
mt.ex: Exudate forms from fluid, dead cells, and WBCs and may be serous, sanguineous, or purulent.

items.q: A patient receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics for pneumonia develops a new infection caused by a different organism. Which explanation is most accurate?
items.a: The antibiotics eliminated normal flora, allowing other microorganisms to multiply
items.ex: A suprainfection develops when broad-spectrum antibiotics eliminate normal flora, reducing body defenses and allowing pathogens to multiply.
w: The antibiotics strengthened the normal flora, which then caused illness
Antibiotics eliminate rather than strengthen normal flora.
The pneumonia was transmitted to a new body site by droplets
This describes a new organism due to flora disruption, not droplet spread.
The antibiotics caused the patient’s inflammation to stop too quickly
The new infection results from lost normal flora, not stopped inflammation.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a patient about suprainfection. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
alt.a: Strong antibiotics can kill my helpful bacteria, so other germs may grow
alt.ex: Broad-spectrum antibiotics eliminate a wide range of normal flora, reducing defenses and letting disease-producing organisms multiply.
w: Antibiotics only kill the germs that are causing my current infection
Broad-spectrum antibiotics eliminate many normal flora, not just the infecting organisms.
My normal bacteria are what cause most of my infections
Normal flora usually help maintain health in their usual area.
Suprainfection happens only when I stop my antibiotics too early
Suprainfection results from flora elimination by broad-spectrum antibiotics.

items.q: Normal flora, body system defenses, and inflammation are nonspecific defenses that protect against microorganisms regardless of prior exposure.
items.a: True
items.ex: These nonspecific defenses protect the body regardless of prior exposure; if they fail, infection usually occurs.
items.ww: These defenses work without prior exposure, which is why they are called nonspecific.

alt.q: Inflammation protects the body only against microorganisms to which a person was previously exposed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Inflammation is a nonspecific defense that protects regardless of prior exposure.
alt.ww: Nonspecific defenses such as inflammation do not depend on previous exposure.

items.q: A patient takes antacids daily. Which natural defense against infection is most affected?
items.a: Acidity of gastric secretions
items.ex: Gastric fluid with a pH of 1 to 2 is harmful to many pathogens; antacids alter this defense.
w: Flushing action of urine flow
Urine flow is altered by obstruction, catheters, or delayed micturition.
Cilia lining the upper airway
Cilia are altered by smoking, high oxygen, low humidity, and cold air.
Shedding of outer skin cells
Skin shedding is altered by failure to bathe or improper handwashing.

alt.q: Which factor may alter the respiratory tract’s cilia and mucus defense against infection?
alt.a: Smoking
alt.ex: Smoking, high oxygen and carbon dioxide concentrations, decreased humidity, and cold air may alter ciliary defenses.
w: Antacids
Antacids alter the acidity of gastric secretions.
Delayed micturition
Delayed micturition alters the flushing action of urine.
Excessive bathing
Excessive bathing alters the skin’s fatty acid defense.

items.q: A patient has an indwelling urinary catheter. How does the catheter increase the risk of infection?
items.a: Catheter movement in the urethra can help organisms migrate to the bladder
items.ex: Introducing a catheter and its continual movement in the urethra impair the urinary epithelium and facilitate organism migration.
w: The catheter makes the urine too acidic for normal flora to survive
The book does not describe catheters altering urine acidity.
The catheter increases urine flow and flushes bacteria upward
Flushing urine flow washes organisms away; catheters obstruct normal flow.
The catheter causes rapid peristalsis that retains bacteria
Peristalsis is a GI tract defense unrelated to urinary catheters.

alt.q: How does the flushing action of urine flow protect against infection?
alt.a: It washes microorganisms away from the bladder and urethra lining
alt.ex: Urine flow washes away microorganisms on the lining of the bladder and urethra.
w: It kills microorganisms with its strongly acidic pH
Bacteria actually thrive in alkaline urine; flushing works mechanically.
It traps microorganisms in mucus to be expectorated
Trapping in mucus is the respiratory cilia defense.
It engulfs and destroys microorganisms in the bladder
Engulfing organisms is the role of macrophages and phagocytes.

items.q: A nurse plans care for a patient with an active infection. Which nursing responsibilities apply? Select all that apply.
o: Properly administering antibiotics
Nurses administer antibiotics properly as part of infection care.
Monitoring the response to drug therapy
Monitoring drug response is a nursing responsibility.
Providing adequate nutrition and rest
Supportive therapy bolsters body defenses.
Following Standard Precautions
Standard Precautions are always part of infection control.
Limiting fluids and food to slow organism growth
Adequate nutrition supports defenses; restriction weakens them.
Stopping antibiotics as soon as symptoms disappear
The nurse administers antibiotics properly and monitors response, not stopping early.
items.ex: Nurses implement infection control, give antibiotics properly, monitor response, perform hand hygiene, use precautions, and support nutrition and rest.

alt.q: Which supportive measures help bolster a patient’s defenses against an infectious process? Select all that apply.
o: Adequate nutrition
Adequate nutrition bolsters the body’s defenses.
Adequate rest
Rest bolsters the body’s defenses against infection.
Proper hand hygiene by caregivers
Hand hygiene prevents further spread of infection.
Restricting the patient’s food intake
Restricting intake reduces nutrition needed for defenses.
Keeping the patient awake to monitor symptoms
Supportive therapy includes adequate rest, not sleep deprivation.
alt.ex: Supportive therapy includes adequate nutrition and rest to bolster defenses against infection.

items.q: Scar tissue that forms after chronic inflammation is as strong as the normal tissue it replaces.
items.a: False
items.ex: Scar and surrounding tissues are not as strong as normal tissue and are more susceptible to pressure, shear, or friction injury.
items.ww: Scar tissue is weaker than normal tissue, increasing the risk for pressure injury.

alt.q: Scar tissue is weaker than normal tissue and is more susceptible to injury from pressure, shear, or friction.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Because scar tissue is weaker, it increases the risk for pressure injury development.
alt.ww: Scar tissue never regains full normal strength, so it is more vulnerable to pressure injury.

items.q: Platelets and plasma proteins such as fibrinogen form a meshlike matrix at a site of inflammation to prevent its spread.
items.a: True
items.ex: Platelets and fibrinogen form a meshlike matrix that keeps inflammation from spreading.
items.ww: This matrix is described as a mechanism that limits the spread of inflammation.

alt.q: Inflammatory exudate is usually cleared away by phagocytes in the bloodstream rather than by the lymphatic system.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Exudate is usually cleared away through lymphatic drainage.
alt.ww: The book states that lymphatic drainage, not bloodstream phagocytes, usually clears exudate.

items.q: Fever during inflammation is caused by phagocytic release of [[pyrogens|pyrogen]] from bacterial cells, which raises the hypothalamic set point.
items.ex: Pyrogens increase the hypothalamic set point, producing fever.

alt.q: The hypothalamic set point rises during infection because phagocytes release [[pyrogens|pyrogen]] from bacterial cells.
alt.ex: Pyrogens increase the hypothalamic set point, producing fever.

items.q: A patient with a localized infection of the hand has swollen, painful, discolored fingers with stiff joints. Which statement by the nurse best explains the stiffness?
items.a: Swelling makes the joints stiff, and function usually returns as the inflammation subsides
items.ex: Inflammation can cause temporary loss of function; finger function returns when inflammation subsides.
w: The infection has permanently destroyed the joints of your fingers
Loss of function from inflammation is temporary, not permanent.
The stiffness means the infection has now spread to your whole body
Joint stiffness from local swelling is a localized sign, not a systemic one.
The stiffness comes from scar tissue that has already formed in your hand
Scar formation occurs at the completion of healing after chronic inflammation, not acutely.

alt.q: Which statement about loss of function during inflammation is accurate?
alt.a: It is usually temporary and improves when the inflammation subsides
alt.ex: The physiological inflammatory response may cause temporary loss of function that returns as inflammation subsides.
w: It is permanent once the tissue becomes swollen
Function returns when inflammation subsides.
It occurs only when inflammation becomes systemic
Loss of function is a sign of localized inflammation.
It is caused by phagocytes destroying healthy tissue
Swelling and pain, not phagocytes, cause the temporary loss of function.

items.q: Which nursing practice, when performed improperly, increases a patient’s risk for all types of health care–associated infections?
items.a: Hand hygiene
items.ex: Improperly performing hand hygiene increases patient risk for all types of HAIs.
w: Perineal hygiene
Improper perineal hygiene is a specific cause of urinary tract HAIs.
Airway suctioning
Nonaseptic suctioning is a specific cause of respiratory tract HAIs.
IV port access
Improper IV port access is a specific cause of bloodstream HAIs.

alt.q: A nurse caring for patients with catheters, IV lines, and surgical wounds wants one practice that lowers risk for every type of HAI. Which practice should the nurse emphasize?
alt.a: Proper hand hygiene before and after patient contact
alt.ex: Improper hand hygiene increases risk for all types of HAIs, so proper hand hygiene protects against each type.
w: Repeated irrigation of each urinary catheter
Repeated catheter irrigations increase the risk of urinary HAIs.
Adding stopcocks to each IV line for access
Adding connecting tubes or stopcocks increases bloodstream HAI risk.
Shaving each surgical site before procedures
Shaving rather than clipping is improper skin preparation that raises wound HAI risk.

items.q: Why should a nurse treat feces, urine, and wound drainage from every patient with infection prevention precautions?
items.a: These body substances contain potentially infectious microorganisms
items.ex: Body substances such as feces, urine, and wound drainage contain potentially infectious microorganisms, putting health care workers at risk.
w: These body substances are sterile only in older adults
Body substances are potentially infectious in patients of all ages.
These body substances are infectious only after diagnosis
They contain potentially infectious organisms whether or not infection is known.
These body substances are infectious only in the home setting
Workers are at risk of exposure in both hospital and home settings.

alt.q: What is the purpose of meticulous infection prevention practices when caring for a patient with a known or suspected infection?
alt.a: To reduce cross-contamination and transmission to noninfected patients
alt.ex: Meticulous use of infection prevention practices reduces cross-contamination and transmission to noninfected patients.
w: To replace the need for antibiotic therapy in the infected patient
Prevention practices limit spread; they do not replace treatment.
To keep family members from visiting the infected patient
Isolation disrupts relationships; the goal is to prevent transmission, not to stop visits.
To shorten the incubation period of the patient’s infection
Prevention practices do not change the incubation period.

items.q: Which statement best defines a health care–associated infection (HAI)?
items.a: An infection that results from the delivery of health services in a health care agency
items.ex: HAIs result from the delivery of health services in a health care agency.
w: An infection present in a patient before admission to a health care agency
HAIs result from health care delivery, not from infections present before care.
An infection that is transmitted only between members of the same family
HAIs are linked to health care services, not family transmission.
An infection caused only by organisms that are resistant to antibiotics
MDROs contribute to HAIs, but HAIs are not limited to resistant organisms.

alt.q: Which factor increases a hospitalized patient’s risk of acquiring an HAI?
alt.a: Greater number of invasive procedures performed
alt.ex: The type and number of invasive procedures, therapy, staff contacts, and length of stay influence HAI risk.
w: Shorter length of hospitalization
A longer, not shorter, hospitalization increases HAI risk.
Fewer health care employees in direct contact
More employees with direct contact increase risk.
Consistent infection prevention activities
Breaks in infection prevention increase risk; consistent practice reduces it.

items.q: Which infection is an example of an exogenous infection?
items.a: Salmonella acquired from a source outside the patient
items.ex: Exogenous infections come from organisms outside the individual, such as Salmonella, that do not exist as normal flora.
w: Staphylococci overgrowing after antibiotics alter the flora
Overgrowth of a patient’s own altered flora is an endogenous infection.
Yeast overgrowth after broad-spectrum antibiotic therapy
Yeast overgrowth from altered normal flora is endogenous.
Enterococci moving from one body site to another site
Flora moving from one site to another causes endogenous infection.

alt.q: A patient receiving broad-spectrum antibiotics develops an overgrowth of streptococci from the patient’s own flora. How is this infection classified?
alt.a: Endogenous
alt.ex: An endogenous infection occurs when part of the patient’s flora becomes altered and overgrows, often after broad-spectrum antibiotics.
w: Exogenous
Exogenous infections come from organisms outside the individual that are not normal flora.
Communicable
A communicable disease passes directly from one person to another.
Colonization
Colonization involves no tissue invasion; this patient has an infection.

items.q: A patient develops pneumonia after undergoing a bronchoscopy. How is this infection best classified?
items.a: Iatrogenic infection
items.ex: Iatrogenic infections are HAIs caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure such as bronchoscopy.
w: Exogenous infection from normal flora
Exogenous organisms come from outside the patient and are not normal flora.
Communicable disease from a visitor
The infection followed a procedure, not person-to-person transmission from a visitor.
Colonization without tissue invasion
Pneumonia is an infection with tissue invasion, not colonization.

alt.q: What is an iatrogenic infection?
alt.a: An HAI caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure
alt.ex: Iatrogenic infections are a type of HAI caused by invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedures.
w: An infection caused by organisms that are not normal flora
Infection from organisms outside the patient is exogenous.
An infection that spreads from one person to another
Direct person-to-person spread defines a communicable disease.
An infection from overgrowth of the patient’s own flora
Overgrowth of the patient’s own altered flora is endogenous.

items.q: A health care–associated infection caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure is called an [[iatrogenic]] infection.
items.ex: Procedures such as bronchoscopy and treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics increase the risk for iatrogenic infections.

alt.q: An infection that develops because of a procedure such as a bronchoscopy is described as [[iatrogenic]].
alt.ex: Procedures such as bronchoscopy and treatment with broad-spectrum antibiotics increase the risk for iatrogenic infections.

items.q: What is a(n) Exogenous infection?
items.a: Comes from organisms outside the individual that are not normal flora
items.ex: HAIs may be exogenous or endogenous; iatrogenic infections are HAIs caused by invasive procedures.
w: Overgrowth of the patient’s own altered normal flora
That goes with Endogenous.
