Caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure
That goes with Iatrogenic.
Results from the delivery of health services in an agency
That goes with Health care–associated.

alt.q: What is a(n) Endogenous infection?
alt.a: Overgrowth of the patient’s own altered normal flora
alt.ex: HAIs may be exogenous or endogenous; iatrogenic infections are HAIs caused by invasive procedures.
w: Comes from organisms outside the individual that are not normal flora
That goes with Exogenous.
Caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure
That goes with Iatrogenic.
Results from the delivery of health services in an agency
That goes with Health care–associated.

alt.q: What is a(n) Iatrogenic infection?
alt.a: Caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure
alt.ex: HAIs may be exogenous or endogenous; iatrogenic infections are HAIs caused by invasive procedures.
w: Comes from organisms outside the individual that are not normal flora
That goes with Exogenous.
Overgrowth of the patient’s own altered normal flora
That goes with Endogenous.
Results from the delivery of health services in an agency
That goes with Health care–associated.

alt.q: What is a(n) Health care–associated infection?
alt.a: Results from the delivery of health services in an agency
alt.ex: HAIs may be exogenous or endogenous; iatrogenic infections are HAIs caused by invasive procedures.
w: Comes from organisms outside the individual that are not normal flora
That goes with Exogenous.
Overgrowth of the patient’s own altered normal flora
That goes with Endogenous.
Caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure
That goes with Iatrogenic.

alt.q: Which type of infection “Comes from organisms outside the individual that are not normal flora”?
alt.a: Exogenous
alt.ex: HAIs may be exogenous or endogenous; iatrogenic infections are HAIs caused by invasive procedures.
w: Endogenous
Endogenous: Overgrowth of the patient’s own altered normal flora.
Iatrogenic
Iatrogenic: Caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure.
Health care–associated
Health care–associated: Results from the delivery of health services in an agency.

alt.q: Which type of infection “Overgrowth of the patient’s own altered normal flora”?
alt.a: Endogenous
alt.ex: HAIs may be exogenous or endogenous; iatrogenic infections are HAIs caused by invasive procedures.
w: Exogenous
Exogenous: Comes from organisms outside the individual that are not normal flora.
Iatrogenic
Iatrogenic: Caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure.
Health care–associated
Health care–associated: Results from the delivery of health services in an agency.

alt.q: Which type of infection “Caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure”?
alt.a: Iatrogenic
alt.ex: HAIs may be exogenous or endogenous; iatrogenic infections are HAIs caused by invasive procedures.
w: Exogenous
Exogenous: Comes from organisms outside the individual that are not normal flora.
Endogenous
Endogenous: Overgrowth of the patient’s own altered normal flora.
Health care–associated
Health care–associated: Results from the delivery of health services in an agency.

alt.q: Which type of infection “Results from the delivery of health services in an agency”?
alt.a: Health care–associated
alt.ex: HAIs may be exogenous or endogenous; iatrogenic infections are HAIs caused by invasive procedures.
w: Exogenous
Exogenous: Comes from organisms outside the individual that are not normal flora.
Endogenous
Endogenous: Overgrowth of the patient’s own altered normal flora.
Iatrogenic
Iatrogenic: Caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure.

mt.q: Match each type of infection with its description.
pairs: Comes from organisms outside the individual that are not normal flora
Overgrowth of the patient’s own altered normal flora
Caused by an invasive diagnostic or therapeutic procedure
Results from the delivery of health services in an agency
mt.ex: HAIs may be exogenous or endogenous; iatrogenic infections are HAIs caused by invasive procedures.

items.q: A nurse finds a patient’s urinary drainage bag resting on the bed above the level of the bladder. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Lower the drainage bag below bladder level so urine cannot flow back
items.ex: Allowing urine in the catheter or tubing to reenter the bladder (reflux) and improper tubing position are causes of urinary HAIs.
w: Irrigate the catheter to clear any urine backing up
Repeated catheter irrigations are themselves a cause of urinary tract HAIs.
Disconnect the tubing and drain the urine into the toilet
Disconnecting the catheter and tubing is a cause of urinary HAIs.
Place the drainage bag on the floor beside the bed
A bag port touching a contaminated surface such as the floor causes HAIs.

alt.q: Which nursing action helps prevent a health care–associated urinary tract infection in a patient with an indwelling catheter?
alt.a: Keep the drainage system closed and the tubing positioned to drain freely
alt.ex: Open drainage, improper tubing position, and obstructed drainage are listed causes of urinary HAIs.
w: Irrigate the catheter several times each day
Repeated catheter irrigations increase the risk of urinary HAIs.
Open the system to collect each urine specimen
Open drainage systems and improper specimen collection cause urinary HAIs.
Rest the drainage bag port on the floor for easy emptying
A drainage port touching a contaminated surface causes urinary HAIs.

items.q: Which practices increase a patient’s risk for a health care–associated urinary tract infection? Select all that apply.
o: Unsterile insertion of a urinary catheter
Unsterile insertion is a listed cause of urinary HAIs.
Using an open drainage system
Open drainage systems increase urinary HAI risk.
Allowing urine in the tubing to reflux into the bladder
Reflux of urine into the bladder is a listed cause.
Improper perineal hygiene
Improper perineal hygiene contributes to urinary HAIs.
Performing hand hygiene before catheter care
Hand hygiene reduces risk; improper hand hygiene increases risk for all HAIs.
Keeping urine draining freely without obstruction
Obstructing or interfering with drainage, not free drainage, increases risk.
items.ex: Box 28.3 lists unsterile insertion, open drainage, reflux, irrigations, disconnection, and poor perineal hygiene as urinary HAI causes.

alt.q: A nurse reviews care of a patient with an indwelling catheter. Which observations show a risk for a urinary HAI? Select all that apply.
o: The catheter and drainage tube have become disconnected
Disconnection of the catheter and tube is a listed cause.
The drainage bag port is touching the floor
A port touching a contaminated surface is a listed cause.
The catheter has been irrigated repeatedly
Repeated irrigations are a listed cause.
The closed drainage system is intact
An intact closed system is protective; open systems cause HAIs.
Urine flows freely into the drainage bag
Free flow is protective; obstructed drainage is a cause.
alt.ex: Disconnection, contaminated drainage ports, and repeated irrigations all increase urinary HAI risk.

items.q: A patient is scheduled for surgery tomorrow. Which preoperative skin preparation practice reduces the risk of a surgical wound HAI?
items.a: Clipping hair rather than shaving and having the patient bathe or shower
items.ex: Improper skin preparation, such as shaving versus clipping or omitting a preoperative bath or shower, is a cause of wound HAIs.
w: Shaving the surgical site with a razor the night before
Shaving rather than clipping is listed as improper skin preparation.
Skipping the preoperative bath to avoid skin irritation
Not performing a preoperative bath or shower increases wound HAI risk.
Using the open antiseptic bottle left from the previous day
Use of contaminated antiseptic solutions causes surgical wound HAIs.

alt.q: Which practice increases a patient’s risk for a surgical or traumatic wound HAI?
alt.a: Failing to use aseptic technique during dressing changes
alt.ex: Failure to use aseptic technique during operative procedures and dressing changes is a listed cause of wound HAIs.
w: Clipping hair at the incision site before surgery
Clipping is preferred over shaving for preoperative skin preparation.
Having the patient shower before surgery
A preoperative bath or shower is recommended; omitting it raises risk.
Cleaning the skin surface properly before incision
Failure to clean the skin properly, not proper cleaning, raises risk.

items.q: Which practices increase the risk for a health care–associated bloodstream infection? Select all that apply.
o: Adding connecting tubes or stopcocks to an IV system
Adding connectors or stopcocks is a listed cause.
Improper care of the needle insertion site
Improper site care is a listed cause.
Failing to change IV access at the first sign of infection
Not changing IV access at the first sign of infection is a listed cause.
Improperly accessing an IV port
Improper IV port access is a listed cause.
Performing hand hygiene before accessing the IV line
Hand hygiene reduces risk for all types of HAIs.
Using sterile needles and catheters
Contaminated, not sterile, needles and catheters cause bloodstream HAIs.
items.ex: Box 28.3 lists IV additives, connectors, poor site care, contaminated devices, and improper port access as bloodstream HAI causes.

alt.q: A nurse cares for patients on a respiratory unit. Which practices increase the risk of a respiratory tract HAI? Select all that apply.
o: Using contaminated respiratory therapy equipment
Contaminated respiratory equipment is a listed cause.
Suctioning the airway without aseptic technique
Failure to use aseptic technique while suctioning is a listed cause.
Disposing of secretions improperly
Improper disposal of secretions is a listed cause.
Performing hand hygiene before suctioning
Hand hygiene reduces HAI risk.
Using sterile technique when suctioning
Aseptic technique prevents respiratory HAIs.
alt.ex: Contaminated equipment, nonaseptic suctioning, and improper secretion disposal increase respiratory HAI risk.

items.q: Major sites for health care–associated infections include surgical or traumatic wounds, the urinary and respiratory tracts, and the bloodstream.
items.a: True
items.ex: Box 28.3 lists wounds, urinary tract, respiratory tract, and bloodstream as major HAI sites.
items.ww: These four sites are identified as the major sites for HAIs.

alt.q: The skin of the hands and feet is the major site for health care–associated infections.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Major HAI sites are surgical or traumatic wounds, the urinary and respiratory tracts, and the bloodstream.
alt.ww: Hands are a major reservoir and route of transmission, but they are not listed as a major HAI site.

items.q: Which term describes the age-related functional deterioration of the immune system that increases an older adult’s susceptibility to infection?
items.a: Immune senescence
items.ex: Immune senescence is age-related functional deterioration of immune function that increases susceptibility and slows immune response.
w: Suprainfection
Suprainfection results from broad-spectrum antibiotics eliminating normal flora.
Bacteriostasis
Bacteriostasis is prevention of bacterial growth, such as by cold temperatures.
Leukocytosis
Leukocytosis is an increase in circulating WBCs during inflammation.

alt.q: A nurse explains immune senescence to an older adult’s family. Which statement is accurate?
alt.a: Older adults produce fewer lymphocytes, and their antibody response lasts a shorter time
alt.ex: Older adults produce fewer lymphocytes, and when antibodies are made, their response is shorter with fewer cells.
w: Older adults produce more antibodies, which last longer than in younger adults
Antibody response in older adults is shorter, with fewer cells produced.
Older adults have a faster immune response than younger adults
Immune senescence slows the overall immune response.
Older adults no longer need influenza or pneumonia vaccines
Flu and pneumonia vaccinations are recommended for older adults.

items.q: Which findings increase an older adult’s risk for developing a health care–associated infection? Select all that apply.
o: Low serum albumin level
Low serum albumin is a listed risk for HAIs in older patients.
Unintentional weight loss
Unintentional weight loss is a listed risk.
Lack of exercise
Lack of exercise is a listed risk.
Poor social support
Poor social support is a listed risk.
Up-to-date influenza and pneumonia vaccines
Vaccinations reduce older adults’ risk for infectious diseases.
Consistent hand hygiene by family members
Proper hand hygiene reduces the risk for infections.
items.ex: Box 28.4 lists poor nutrition, unintentional weight loss, lack of exercise, poor social support, and low serum albumin as risks.

alt.q: A nurse teaches an older adult and family how to reduce infection risk. Which points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Receive the recommended influenza vaccination
Flu vaccination is recommended to reduce older adults’ infection risk.
Receive the recommended pneumonia vaccination
Pneumonia vaccination is recommended for older adults.
Use proper hand hygiene practices
Teaching hand hygiene reduces the risk for infections.
Limit protein intake to protect the kidneys
Poor nutrition and low albumin increase infection risk.
Reduce physical activity to conserve energy
Lack of exercise is a risk factor for infection.
alt.ex: Older adults should receive flu and pneumonia vaccines and use proper hand hygiene to reduce infection risk.

items.q: A nurse is assessing an 82-year-old patient admitted for hip surgery. Which finding most increases the patient’s risk for a health care–associated infection?
items.a: Serum albumin below normal and recent unintentional weight loss
items.ex: Poor nutrition, unintentional weight loss, and low serum albumin are risks for HAIs in older patients.
w: Daily walking program before admission and good appetite
Exercise and good nutrition are protective; lack of exercise is a risk.
Supportive family who visit and help with daily care
Poor social support, not strong support, is a listed risk.
Current influenza and pneumonia vaccinations on record
Vaccinations reduce older adults’ risk for infectious diseases.

alt.q: Which statement by an older adult shows understanding of teaching about infection risk?
alt.a: I will get my flu and pneumonia shots and wash my hands properly
alt.ex: Flu and pneumonia vaccines and proper hand hygiene reduce older adults’ risk for infection.
w: I can skip the flu shot because older people make longer-lasting antibodies
Older adults’ antibody response is shorter, so vaccination is recommended.
I will eat less protein so I lose some weight before surgery
Poor nutrition and unintentional weight loss increase infection risk.
I will stay in bed most of the day to save my energy
Lack of exercise increases infection risk in older adults.

items.q: Why do invasive devices such as IV catheters and indwelling urinary catheters increase the risk of HAIs?
items.a: They impair or bypass the body’s natural defenses against microorganisms
items.ex: Invasive treatment devices impair or bypass the body’s natural defenses against microorganisms.
w: They increase the patient’s production of normal flora
Devices do not increase normal flora; they bypass natural defenses.
They cause immune senescence in patients of all ages
Immune senescence is age-related immune deterioration, not a device effect.
They are always contaminated before they are inserted
Devices are not always contaminated; risk comes from bypassing defenses and technique.

alt.q: Which patient is most susceptible to an HAI?
alt.a: A critically ill patient with cancer, diabetes, and an IV catheter
alt.ex: Underlying conditions impair immunity, devices bypass defenses, and critical illness increases susceptibility, especially to MDROs.
w: A healthy adult admitted overnight for observation
A healthy patient with a short stay has fewer risk factors.
An adult with a minor sprain treated in the clinic
This patient has no invasive devices or underlying conditions.
A well-nourished adult walking the halls after surgery
Good nutrition and activity reduce, rather than increase, susceptibility.

items.q: Which intervention is identified as helping to prevent HAIs in critically ill patients?
items.a: Bathing patients with chlorhexidine washes
items.ex: Meticulous hand hygiene, CHG washes for bathing, ICU infection prevention advances, and evidence-based bundles help prevent HAIs.
w: Giving broad-spectrum antibiotics to all patients
Broad-spectrum antibiotics alter normal flora and can cause endogenous infections.
Increasing staff with direct patient contact
More staff with direct contact increases infection risk.
Extending the length of hospitalization
Longer hospitalization increases the risk of infection.

alt.q: Why does prevention of HAIs have a beneficial financial impact on health care agencies?
alt.a: Costs for treating HAIs are often not reimbursed
alt.ex: HAIs extend stays and increase costs, and these costs are often not reimbursed, so prevention saves money.
w: HAIs shorten hospital stays and reduce antibiotic costs
HAIs extend stays and increase antibiotic costs.
Medicare pays agencies more for patients with HAIs
Costs for HAIs are often not reimbursed.
HAIs occur mainly in younger, low-cost patients
Older adults have increased susceptibility to HAIs.

items.q: An exogenous infection is caused by microorganisms that are part of the patient’s own normal flora.
items.a: False
items.ex: Exogenous infections come from organisms outside the individual, such as Salmonella and Aspergillus, that do not exist as normal flora.
items.ww: Overgrowth of a patient’s own flora is endogenous; exogenous organisms come from outside the patient.

alt.q: An endogenous infection can develop when enough microorganisms normally found in one body site move to another site.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Movement of sufficient normal flora from one body site to another produces an endogenous infection.
alt.ww: The book describes endogenous infection as arising from the patient’s own flora, including movement to a new site.

items.q: The number of microorganisms needed to cause an HAI depends on the organism’s virulence, the host’s susceptibility, and the body site affected.
items.a: True
items.ex: Virulence, host susceptibility, and the body site determine how many organisms are needed to cause an HAI.
items.ww: The book names these three factors as determining the number of organisms needed for an HAI.

alt.q: The same fixed number of microorganisms causes an HAI in every patient, regardless of the body site affected.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The number of organisms needed varies with virulence, host susceptibility, and body site.
alt.ww: There is no fixed number; it varies with the organism, host, and site.

items.q: A patient on contact isolation tells the nurse, “Everyone who comes in here puts on gloves and a gown. They must think I’m dirty.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Explain how the infection spreads and why the gown and gloves protect everyone
items.ex: Discussing the disease process and maintaining a friendly, understanding manner reduce feelings of rejection about isolation.
w: Tell the patient that the precautions are hospital policy and cannot be discussed
Refusing to discuss the precautions does not address the patient’s feelings of rejection.
Stop wearing a gown and gloves in the room so the patient feels accepted
Isolation precautions must be maintained to prevent transmission.
Limit time spent in the room so the patient is not reminded of isolation
Less contact worsens loneliness; isolation already disrupts social relationships.

alt.q: The family of a patient with an HAI avoids visiting because they fear catching the infection. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Discuss the disease process with the family in a friendly, understanding manner
alt.ex: Discussing the disease process and being friendly and understanding help patients and families reduce fear and isolation.
w: Advise the family to stay away until the patient is discharged
Avoiding contact worsens the patient’s isolation and loneliness.
Tell the family that infections cannot spread to visitors
This may be inaccurate; precautions exist to prevent transmission.
Avoid discussing the infection to protect the patient’s privacy
Discussing the disease process helps reduce anxiety and fear.

sections.name: Factors influencing infection prevention and control

items.q: A new mother asks the nurse why breastfeeding may help protect her infant from infection. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Your baby receives your antibodies through the breast milk.”
items.ex: Breastfed infants often have greater immunity than bottle-fed infants because maternal antibodies pass through breast milk.
w: “Breast milk stimulates your baby to make all the immunoglobulins needed.”
An infant’s immune system cannot yet produce the immunoglobulins and WBCs needed to fight some infections.
“Breastfed babies no longer need routine childhood vaccines.”
Breastfeeding does not replace vaccination; children remain susceptible to vaccine-preventable diseases if not vaccinated.
“Breast milk raises your baby’s white blood cell count right away.”
The benefit described is transfer of the mother’s antibodies, not an immediate rise in the infant’s WBCs.

alt.q: Why is a newborn especially vulnerable to some infections?
alt.a: It has only maternal antibodies and cannot yet make enough immunoglobulins and WBCs
alt.ex: Infants are born with only the mother’s antibodies; their immature immune system cannot adequately produce immunoglobulins and WBCs.
w: Its cell-mediated immunity has declined with structural skin changes
Declining cell-mediated immunity and thinning skin describe older adults, not newborns.
High estrogen levels suppress its immune responses after birth
The text states estrogens promote, not suppress, immune responses.
Its adrenal glands release excess cortisone during feeding
Elevated cortisone relates to prolonged stress, not to normal infant feeding.

items.q: According to the text, what is the most common cause of communicable illness in young and middle-age adults?
items.a: Viruses
items.ex: Young and middle-age adults have refined defenses, and viruses are their most common cause of communicable illness.
w: Fungi
Fungal infections are linked in the chapter to drugs such as corticosteroids and TNF inhibitors, not named as most common in this age group.
Parasites
Parasitic infection is not named as the leading cause of communicable illness in young adults.
Gram-negative bacteria
Gram-negative bacilli are mentioned under rings and hand hygiene, not as the main cause of adult communicable illness.

alt.q: Which group does the text identify as most likely to develop UTIs, vaginal yeast infections, and HPV?
alt.a: Young females
alt.ex: The text states young females are most likely to develop urinary tract infections, vaginal yeast infections, and human papillomavirus.
w: Infants who are bottle-fed
Bottle-fed infants lack breast-milk antibodies but are not the group named for these infections.
Older adult males
UTIs are relatively uncommon in males; the text links males to prostatitis instead.
School-age children
Children are described as susceptible to colds, intestinal infections, mumps, measles, and chickenpox.

items.q: Which age-related change in the skin of older adults increases the potential for invasion by pathogens?
items.a: Loss of turgor and thinning of the epithelium make skin easier to tear
items.ex: Thinner, less elastic skin tears or abrades more easily, opening a route for pathogens to invade.
w: Thickening of the epithelium traps bacteria in deeper skin layers
The epithelium thins with age; it does not thicken.
Increased oil production supports growth of skin flora
The text does not describe increased oil production as an age-related change.
Faster skin cell turnover leaves gaps between new cells
Faster turnover is not the age-related change described; thinning and lost turgor are.

alt.q: Which part of the immune response does the text say particularly declines in older adults?
alt.a: Cell-mediated immunity
alt.ex: The immune response, particularly cell-mediated immunity, declines with age, making infection in older adults dangerous.
w: Maternal antibody immunity
Maternal antibodies protect newborns, not older adults.
Estrogen-driven immunity
Estrogens are discussed under sex differences, not as the main age-related decline.
Ciliary clearance in the bronchi
Impaired ciliary action is linked to emphysema and bronchitis, not named as the key age-related immune decline.

items.q: A nurse manager at a residential care facility wants to reduce transmission of influenza to older adult residents. Which measure does the text identify as reducing this transmission?
items.a: Ensuring health care workers are vaccinated against influenza
items.ex: Older adults in hospitals or care facilities are at risk for airborne infections; vaccinating health care workers against influenza reduces transmission to them.
w: Moving all residents into private negative-pressure rooms
Negative-pressure rooms are for Airborne Precautions in known or suspected cases, not routine influenza prevention.
Restricting residents’ intake of protein during flu season
Reduced protein intake weakens defenses; it does not prevent influenza.
Limiting residents’ physical activity to conserve energy
Exercise and rest together help prevent infection; restricting activity is not the measure named.

alt.q: Why are older adults living in assisted-living or residential care facilities a particular concern during flu season?
alt.a: They are at risk for airborne infections spread in these settings
alt.ex: The text notes hospitalized or institutionalized older adults are at risk for airborne infections such as influenza.
w: Their maternal antibodies have recently worn off
Maternal antibodies relate to infants, not older adults.
They cannot receive any form of vaccine
Older adults are encouraged to receive vaccines such as influenza and shingles vaccines.
Their estrogen levels sharply increase with age
This is not the reason given; the concern is airborne spread in group living.

items.q: Estrogens tend to promote immune responses during infection and after vaccination, whereas androgens tend to suppress them.
items.a: True
items.ex: Differing sex steroid hormone levels help explain sex-based differences in immune responses; estrogens promote and androgens suppress them.
items.ww: The text states estrogens promote immune responses; it is androgens that suppress them.

alt.q: Androgens enhance immune responses after vaccination, while estrogens dampen them.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The text states the opposite: estrogens promote immune responses and androgens suppress them.
alt.ww: Saying this is true reverses the hormone effects described in the text.

items.q: The ability of an antigen to provoke an immune response in the human body is called [[immunogenicity]].
items.ex: Sex-related differences have been observed in the immunogenicity and effectiveness of several vaccines in adults.

alt.q: Differences between males and females have been seen in vaccine [[immunogenicity]], the capacity of an antigen to trigger an immune response.
alt.ex: Sex-related differences have been observed in the immunogenicity and effectiveness of several vaccines in adults.

items.q: Which patient has the greatest added nutritional risk for infection because of increased protein requirements?
items.a: A patient with extensive burns
items.ex: Extensive burns and febrile conditions increase protein requirements, placing the patient at further risk for infection.
w: A patient with a healed laceration
A healed wound does not create the increased protein demand described.
A patient with seasonal allergies
Seasonal allergies are not named as increasing protein requirements.
A patient with a sprained ankle
A sprain is not described as a condition raising protein needs.

alt.q: A patient is recovering from abdominal surgery. Why does the text single out surgical patients when discussing nutrition and infection?
alt.a: Patients who have undergone surgery require increased protein
alt.ex: Surgery increases protein needs; poor protein intake reduces defenses against infection and impairs wound healing.
w: Surgery permanently lowers protein requirements
The text states surgical patients need more protein, not less.
Surgical patients should avoid carbohydrates and fats
Decreased intake of carbohydrates and fats also reduces defenses.
Surgery eliminates the need for a diet history
A thorough diet history is necessary for patients at risk.

items.q: A postoperative patient reports nausea and painful sores in the mouth and is eating very little. Which action should the nurse take first to address the patient’s infection risk?
items.a: Obtain a diet history of usual daily intake and problems altering it
items.ex: Assessment comes first: determine normal intake and whether nausea or oral pain alters food intake before planning nutritional care.
w: Restrict fluids until the nausea resolves
Restricting fluids does not address nutrition and is not supported by the text.
Teach the patient to avoid protein-rich foods
Protein needs increase after surgery; avoiding protein worsens infection risk.
Document that the patient prefers not to eat
Documenting alone ignores a nutritional risk that weakens defenses against infection.

alt.q: A nurse has completed a diet history for a febrile patient with poor intake. Which collaborative action does the text recommend next?
alt.a: Confer with a registered dietitian to calculate the calorie count of foods eaten
alt.ex: The text recommends conferring with a registered dietitian to help calculate the calorie count of foods ingested.
w: Ask the pharmacist to prescribe a high-protein diet
Pharmacists do not prescribe diets; the text names the registered dietitian.
Ask the physical therapist to measure food intake
Physical therapists help with mobility, not calorie counts.
Ask the family to stop bringing food from home
This does not assess or improve intake and is not recommended.

items.q: According to the text, what is the effect of continued or intense stress on resistance to infection?
items.a: Elevated cortisone levels decrease resistance to infection
items.ex: If stress continues or becomes intense, elevated cortisone levels result in decreased resistance to infection.
w: Lower glucose levels increase resistance to infection
ACTH increases, not lowers, serum glucose during stress.
Increased anti-inflammatory responses speed healing
Cortisone release decreases unnecessary anti-inflammatory responses.
A slower basal metabolic rate preserves immune cells
The basal metabolic rate increases during the alarm stage.

alt.q: During the alarm stage of the general adaptation syndrome, what does adrenocorticotropic hormone do?
alt.a: Raises serum glucose and decreases unnecessary antiinflammatory responses
alt.ex: ACTH increases serum glucose and, through cortisone release, decreases unnecessary antiinflammatory responses.
w: Lowers serum glucose and stimulates antibody production
ACTH raises, not lowers, serum glucose.
Slows metabolic rate and restores energy stores
The basal metabolic rate rises as the body uses energy stores.
Blocks cortisone release and boosts WBC production
ACTH works through the release of cortisone.

Alarm stage: basal metabolic rate rises as energy stores are used

items.q: Which conditions does the text describe as diseases of the immune system that weaken a host’s defenses against infectious organisms? Select all that apply.
o: Leukemia
Patients with leukemia cannot produce enough WBCs to fight off infection.
Aplastic anemia
Aplastic anemia is listed with conditions that compromise the host by weakening defenses.
Lymphoma
Lymphoma is named among immune system diseases that weaken defenses.
Emphysema
Emphysema raises risk by impairing ciliary action and thickening mucus, a body system defense, not as an immune disease.
Peripheral vascular disease
Peripheral vascular disease raises risk by reducing blood flow to injured tissue, not by weakening the immune system.
items.ex: Leukemia, AIDS, lymphoma, and aplastic anemia compromise the host by weakening defenses against infectious organisms.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing patient histories. Which conditions are named as immune system diseases that place patients at particular risk for infection? Select all that apply.
o: AIDS
Patients with HIV often cannot ward off simple infections and are prone to opportunistic infections.
Leukemia
Leukemia limits production of WBCs needed to fight infection.
Chronic bronchitis
Bronchitis impairs ciliary action and thickens mucus; it is a body system defense problem.
Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis raises risk through general debilitation and nutritional impairment, not as an immune disease.
Aplastic anemia
Aplastic anemia is listed among conditions that weaken host defenses.
alt.ex: AIDS, leukemia, lymphoma, and aplastic anemia weaken host defenses; bronchitis and multiple sclerosis increase risk by other mechanisms.

mt.q: Match each condition with how the text says it increases susceptibility to infection.
pairs: Impairs ciliary action and thickens mucus
Reduces blood flow to injured tissues
Causes general debilitation and nutritional impairment
mt.ex: Each condition weakens a different defense, from ciliary clearance and blood flow to the skin barrier and WBC production.

items.q: A patient with HIV has had several infections that a healthy person would easily resist. How does the text describe this risk?
items.a: Patients with HIV are prone to opportunistic infections
items.ex: Patients with HIV are often unable to ward off simple infections and are prone to opportunistic infections.
w: Patients with HIV are protected by excess WBC production
HIV weakens defenses; it does not cause protective WBC overproduction.
Patients with HIV only develop infections from burns
Burns are a separate risk factor; HIV weakens defenses broadly.
Patients with HIV have improved ciliary action
Ciliary action relates to emphysema and bronchitis, not HIV.

alt.q: Which phrase best describes the infections that patients with HIV are prone to, according to the text?
alt.a: Opportunistic infections that a weakened host cannot ward off
alt.ex: Weakened defenses leave patients with HIV unable to fight simple infections and prone to opportunistic ones.
w: Infections limited to the skin over pressure points
The text does not limit HIV-related infections to the skin.
Infections caused only by vaccine-preventable diseases
HIV-related infections are not limited to vaccine-preventable diseases.
Infections that occur only during the alarm stage of stress
The alarm stage relates to stress, not to HIV.

items.q: The greater the depth and extent of a patient’s burns, the higher the risk for infection.
items.a: True
items.ex: Burns damage skin surfaces, so deeper and more extensive burns create greater susceptibility to infection.
items.ww: The text directly links greater burn depth and extent to higher infection risk.

alt.q: Burn depth has little effect on infection risk once the burn is covered with a dressing.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The text states that deeper and more extensive burns carry a higher risk for infection.
alt.ww: Saying this is true ignores the direct link between burn depth and extent and infection risk.

items.q: A nurse is planning care for an older adult who is receiving chemotherapy for a recent cancer diagnosis. Which factors increase this patient’s risk for infection? Select all that apply.
o: Age-related decline in cell-mediated immunity
Older adults have decreased or delayed immune responses, especially cell-mediated immunity.
Cancer that alters the immune response
The text lists cancer as a disease that alters immune response.
Thinning skin that tears or abrades easily
Thinner skin with lost turgor makes invasion by pathogens easier.
Stress of a new diagnosis with elevated cortisone
Continued stress raises cortisone levels and decreases resistance to infection.
Mature adult defenses typical of middle age
Refined defenses describe young and middle-age adults, not older adults on chemotherapy.
items.ex: Age, cancer, skin changes, and stress each add risk; when several factors combine, susceptibility often increases.

alt.q: Which findings in an older adult on chemotherapy would the nurse identify as infection risk factors? Select all that apply.
o: Poor protein intake because of nausea
Decreased protein intake reduces defenses and impairs wound healing.
Anxiety and ongoing stress about the diagnosis
Prolonged stress raises cortisone levels and lowers resistance.
Up-to-date influenza vaccination
Vaccination protects against infection; it is not a risk factor.
Fragile skin with reduced turgor
Thin, less elastic skin is easier to tear, allowing pathogen entry.
Regular balanced exercise and adequate sleep
Rest and regular exercise help prevent infection.
alt.ex: Poor nutrition, stress, and fragile skin raise risk; vaccination, rest, and exercise are protective.

items.q: Prostatitis is more common in males older than 50 years than in younger males.
items.a: False
items.ex: Prostatitis affects males of all ages but tends to be more common in those younger than 50 years.
items.ww: The text links prostatitis to males younger than 50, not older males.

alt.q: Although UTIs are relatively uncommon in males, prostatitis affects males of all ages and is more common in those younger than 50.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The text describes prostatitis as affecting all ages but more common in males younger than 50.
alt.ww: Calling this false reverses the age pattern given in the text.

items.q: Which patient is likely at greatest risk for developing an infection?
items.a: An older adult with diabetes who had surgery and eats poorly
items.ex: When more than one risk factor is present, susceptibility often increases; this patient has age, chronic disease, surgery, and poor nutrition.
w: A healthy young adult with a minor cold and no other conditions
A young adult has refined defenses and only one minor factor.
A breastfed infant who is up to date on all recommended vaccines
Breastfeeding and vaccination both strengthen defenses.
A middle-age adult who exercises regularly and eats a varied diet
Regular exercise helps prevent infection; no risk factors are present.

alt.q: Why does the text stress assessing whether several infection risk factors occur together?
alt.a: Combined factors often raise susceptibility and prolong recovery
alt.ex: Combined factors raise susceptibility and affect length of stay, recovery time, and overall health after illness.
w: Multiple factors cancel out each other’s effects
Factors combine to increase, not cancel, susceptibility.
Only one factor can be documented per patient
Nothing limits documentation to one factor; all are assessed.
Risk factors matter only for children
Risk factors apply across the life span, including older adults.

items.q: Why are patients with chronic diseases such as diabetes mellitus and multiple sclerosis more susceptible to infection?
items.a: General debilitation and nutritional impairment
items.ex: The text attributes the increased susceptibility of these chronic diseases to general debilitation and nutritional impairment.
w: Inability to produce any WBCs
Inability to produce enough WBCs describes leukemia.
Damage to skin surfaces from burns
Skin surface damage describes burns.
Thickened mucus and impaired cilia
Impaired ciliary action and thick mucus describe emphysema and bronchitis.

alt.q: Kathy reviews how type 2 diabetes mellitus affects Mrs. Andrews after spinal surgery. Which concern does this reading most directly support?
alt.a: Diabetes impairs wound healing and raises infection risk
alt.ex: Kathy reviews how diabetes affects wound healing and nutrition because diabetes increases susceptibility to infection.
w: Diabetes protects the incision from bacterial invasion
Diabetes increases, not decreases, infection risk.
Diabetes eliminates the need for a nutrition plan
Kathy reads about nutrition in diabetes to help select foods for healing.
Diabetes speeds the inflammatory response at the incision
The text links diabetes to debilitation and poor healing, not faster healing.

items.q: Why do surgery and trauma create a double threat to a patient’s defenses against infection?
items.a: They increase both nutritional requirements and physiological stress
items.ex: The same conditions that raise nutritional requirements, such as surgery or trauma, also increase physiological stress.
w: They reduce protein needs while increasing cortisone
Surgery increases protein needs; it does not reduce them.
They block the alarm stage and the immune response
Stress triggers the alarm stage; it does not block it.
They restore energy stores but thin the epithelium
Stress depletes energy stores; epithelial thinning is an aging change.

alt.q: A trauma patient has elevated cortisone levels and increased nutritional needs. Which statement explains why this combination concerns the nurse?
alt.a: Both reduce the body’s resistance to infection
alt.ex: Prolonged stress lowers resistance through cortisone, and unmet nutritional needs reduce defenses and impair healing.
w: Both improve the inflammatory response at the wound
Cortisone decreases antiinflammatory responses and poor nutrition impairs healing.
Both are signs of a resolving infection
These are risk factors, not signs of resolving infection.
Both affect only children and young adults
Surgery and trauma affect patients of any age.

items.q: Infants are born with only the [[antibodies|antibody]] provided by the mother, so they have immature defenses against infection.
items.ex: An infant cannot yet produce enough immunoglobulins and WBCs, so it depends on maternal antibodies.

alt.q: Because a newborn’s immune system is immature, its protection comes from maternal [[antibodies|antibody]] received before birth or through breast milk.
alt.ex: An infant cannot yet produce enough immunoglobulins and WBCs, so it depends on maternal antibodies.

sections.name: Nursing process: infection prevention and control

items.q: An 82-year-old patient admitted with pneumonia has no fever or chills. Which finding is most important for the nurse to report?
items.a: New confusion with an unexplained rise in heart rate
items.ex: Older adults may lack typical signs; an unexplained increase in heart rate, confusion, or fatigue may be the only clues to pneumonia.
w: Temperature of 37.1°C (98.8°F)
A normal temperature is expected; older adults often have a reduced fever response.
Mild dryness of the lips
Dry lips call for lip care but do not signal advancing infection.
Report of sleeping well overnight
Restful sleep is reassuring, not a sign of worsening infection.

alt.q: A nursing home resident develops new urinary incontinence and agitation but has no fever. What should the nurse suspect?
alt.a: An infection presenting with atypical symptoms
alt.ex: Confusion, incontinence, or agitation may be the only symptoms of infection in older adults because of reduced inflammatory and immune responses.
w: Normal aging requiring no further assessment
New behavior changes warrant assessment for infection.
Dehydration only from low fluid intake
Atypical symptoms of infection should not be dismissed without assessment.
A side effect of seasonal influenza vaccination
Nothing links these symptoms to vaccination in the text.

items.q: A nurse suspects a patient’s localized infection has become systemic. Which findings support this? Select all that apply.
o: Fever and malaise
Systemic infections cause generalized symptoms such as fever, fatigue, and malaise.
Enlarged, tender lymph nodes draining the area
Lymph nodes draining the infected area often enlarge and become tender.
Nausea and vomiting
Nausea and vomiting are listed among systemic symptoms.
Rising blood pressure
Systemic infection can lead to low, not high, blood pressure.
Increased heart and respiratory rates
Elevated temperature can lead to increased heart and respiratory rates.
items.ex: Systemic infection produces generalized signs: fever, fatigue, nausea, malaise, enlarged nodes, tachycardia, tachypnea, and low blood pressure.

alt.q: Which findings suggest an infection is systemic rather than only localized? Select all that apply.
o: Fatigue and malaise
Generalized symptoms such as fatigue and malaise indicate systemic infection.
Redness limited to the wound edge
Redness at the site reflects local inflammation.
Low blood pressure with fever
As systemic infection develops, fever can be accompanied by low blood pressure.
Swelling confined to the incision
Localized swelling reflects local inflammation.
Productive cough with purulent sputum
Involvement of a major body system, such as the lungs, produces specific symptoms.
alt.ex: Generalized symptoms and major body system involvement point to systemic infection; signs confined to the site point to local infection.

items.q: An older adult without urinary symptoms has bacterial growth in a urine culture. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: Bacterial growth without symptoms does not always mean a UTI
items.ex: Laboratory values alone are not enough; in older adults, bacteria in urine without symptoms does not always indicate UTI.
w: The culture confirms a UTI that requires isolation
A culture alone does not confirm infection, and UTIs do not require isolation.
The result proves the specimen was contaminated
Contamination is possible but not proven; assess other clinical signs.
Normal urine always contains some bacterial growth
Urine is normally sterile without microorganism growth.

alt.q: A blood sample drawn from an IV line shows abnormal values. Which nursing action reflects the text’s guidance on laboratory data?
alt.a: Assess other clinical signs before concluding infection is present
alt.ex: Specimens can be contaminated by poor technique, such as mixing with IV fluid, so assess other clinical signs of infection.
w: Treat the values as definitive proof of infection
Laboratory values are not enough to detect infection.
Ignore laboratory values when the patient has an IV
Review results as soon as available, but interpret them with clinical signs.
Apply another agency’s normal ranges to the result
Know the standard ranges for your own agency’s laboratory.

That goes with Neutrophils.
20% to 40%; increased in chronic bacterial and viral infection
That goes with Lymphocytes.

items.q: Which patients require Airborne Precautions? Select all that apply.
o: Patient with pulmonary tuberculosis
Mycobacterium tuberculosis is spread by small droplets that stay suspended in air.
Patient with measles
Measles (rubeola) requires Airborne Precautions.
Patient with chickenpox
Varicella is listed under Airborne Precautions.
Patient with influenza
Influenza is spread by large droplets and requires Droplet Precautions.
Patient with C. difficile diarrhea
C. difficile requires Contact Precautions.
items.ex: Airborne Precautions apply to measles, varicella, disseminated herpes zoster, and TB, requiring a negative-pressure room and N95 respirator.

alt.q: A nurse is assigning rooms. Which patients need an airborne infection isolation room with negative-pressure airflow? Select all that apply.
o: Patient with disseminated herpes zoster
Disseminated herpes zoster is listed under Airborne Precautions.
Patient with MRSA wound colonization
MRSA requires Contact Precautions.
Patient with suspected tuberculosis
Known or suspected TB requires a negative-pressure room.
Patient with pertussis
Pertussis requires Droplet Precautions.
Patient with rubeola
Rubeola (measles) requires Airborne Precautions.
alt.ex: Negative-pressure airborne isolation is used for measles, varicella, disseminated zoster, and TB; MRSA and pertussis use other precautions.

Positive pressure describes a protective environment.

Gown and gloves are the Contact Precautions requirement.

alt.q: Which feature describes a protective environment used for a highly susceptible patient such as an organ transplant recipient?

w: Negative airflow with air exhausted directly outside
Negative airflow describes an airborne infection isolation room.
Standard room with a surgical mask within 3 feet
This describes Droplet Precautions.
Shared room with gown and gloves for all contact
Gown and gloves describe Contact Precautions.

items.q: A nurse has finished caring for a patient with C. difficile diarrhea. Which hand hygiene action is most appropriate?

Skip hand hygiene because gloves were worn
Hand hygiene is required after glove removal.
Wipe hands with a dry paper towel
Wiping does not remove organisms like washing does.

alt.q: For a patient with suspected C. difficile, which temperature measurement practice does the text recommend?

Patients on contact isolation need dedicated or disposable equipment.
Avoid measuring temperature until diarrhea stops
Vital signs are still assessed using appropriate equipment.

items.q: Double bagging all contaminated linen is recommended to prevent infection transmission.
items.a: False
items.ex: Double bagging is not recommended; a single intact, standard-size bag that is not overfilled and tied securely is adequate.

alt.q: A single intact, standard-size linen bag that is not overfilled and is tied securely is adequate to prevent infection transmission.

items.q: Before a sterile dressing change, the nurse notes the patient has a respiratory infection and coughs often. Which action should the nurse take?

w: Ask the patient to hold the breath during the procedure
Breath-holding throughout a procedure is unsafe and unrealistic.

Cover the sterile field with the patient’s gown
The patient’s gown is not sterile and contaminates the field.

alt.q: A patient in pain is scheduled for a lengthy sterile procedure. Which preparation does the text recommend?

w: Give the ordered analgesic after the field is set up

Withhold analgesics so the patient stays alert

Give the ordered analgesic 3 hours before the procedure
The text recommends about a half hour before.

items.q: Which actions help control or eliminate reservoirs of infection at the bedside? Select all that apply.
o: Date bottled solutions when opened and discard in 24 hours
Opened solutions can harbor microorganisms; date and discard them in 24 hours.
Empty all drainage systems each shift unless ordered otherwise
Emptying drainage removes fluids that harbor microorganisms.
Keep a urinary drainage bag below the drained site unless clamped
Raising an unclamped bag lets drainage flow back into the patient.
Leave bottled solutions uncapped for quick access
Keep solutions tightly capped; open bottles become reservoirs.
Change dressings that become wet or soiled
Wet or soiled dressings are reservoirs for microorganisms.
items.ex: Eliminating reservoirs means removing fluids, drainage, and solutions that could harbor microorganisms.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing practices for reducing reservoirs of infection. Which practices are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Place needles in puncture-proof containers at the site of use
Sharps containers at the point of use are required.
Keep table surfaces clean and dry
A clean, dry bedside unit reduces reservoirs.
Raise the urinary drainage bag to the bed rail to reduce clutter
Never raise a drainage system above the drained site unless clamped.
Keep opened solution bottles for up to 1 week
Opened bottles are dated and discarded within 24 hours.
Place soiled dressings in fluid-resistant bags
Contaminated articles go in fluid-resistant bags for disposal.
alt.ex: Sharps containers, clean dry surfaces, and bagged soiled items reduce reservoirs; raised drainage bags and old solutions add risk.

items.q: A nurse sustains a needlestick from a used needle. Which action should the nurse take first?

Delay postpones testing and time-sensitive prophylaxis.

All contaminated needlesticks are reported, regardless of known status.
Recap the needle and finish patient care first
Recapping risks more injury; report the exposure immediately.

alt.q: After an exposure that meets CDC criteria for HIV postexposure prophylaxis (PEP), when should PEP begin?

Nail length matters regardless of polish; long nails harbor more bacteria.

alt.q: Why does the nurse inspect the condition of the fingernails before hand hygiene?
alt.a: Subungual areas harbor high concentrations of bacteria
alt.ex: Areas under the nails hold many bacteria; long nails and chipped or old polish increase the bacterial count.
w: Fresh nail polish blocks the action of alcohol rubs
The text links chipped or old polish, not fresh polish, to more bacteria.
Short nails are needed to operate faucet handles
Faucets are turned off with a paper towel, not nails.
Long nails make lotion absorb poorly into the skin
Lotion absorption is not the rationale for nail inspection.

items.q: Before starting a shift, a nurse notices a small open cut on a finger. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Cover the cut with a dressing before providing care
items.ex: Open cuts can harbor high concentrations of microorganisms, so cover skin lesions with a dressing before care.
w: Apply extra alcohol rub to the cut before each patient
Alcohol does not substitute for covering an open lesion.
Wear gloves only for patients on isolation precautions
The lesion must be covered for all patient care.
Proceed with care because hand hygiene removes the risk
Open lesions still harbor microorganisms and must be covered.

alt.q: A nurse has a large open lesion on the hand that cannot be covered. What does the text say may happen?
alt.a: The nurse may be restricted from direct patient care
alt.ex: If lesions are too large to cover, agency policy may restrict the nurse from direct patient care, especially high-risk patients.
w: The nurse may continue care after washing twice as long
Longer washing does not remove the risk from an uncovered lesion.
The nurse must switch to soap-only hand hygiene
Changing products does not address the uncovered lesion.
The nurse should wear rings to protect the lesion
Rings increase bacterial counts and should be avoided.

items.q: Why are alcohol-based hand rubs preferred over soap and water when hands are not visibly soiled?
items.a: Greater microbiocidal activity, less skin drying, and convenience
items.ex: Approved alcohol-based products are preferred because of superior microbiocidal activity, reduced drying of skin, and convenience.
w: They remove visible dirt better than soap and water
Alcohol rubs are ineffective on visibly dirty hands.
They are the only products that kill spore-forming organisms
Spore exposure calls for handwashing with soap and water.
They need no rubbing because they work on contact
Hands must be rubbed until the alcohol is dry.

alt.q: A nurse is about to take the pulse of a patient. The nurse’s hands are not visibly soiled. Which hand hygiene method is preferred?
alt.a: Alcohol-based hand rub
alt.ex: Without visible soiling, an alcohol-based rub is preferred over antimicrobial or plain soap and water.
w: Surgical hand antisepsis with a brush
Surgical antisepsis is for surgical personnel before surgery.
Rinsing hands under cold running water
Rinsing alone does not provide antimicrobial action.
Wiping hands with a dry paper towel
Wiping does not decontaminate hands.

items.q: After emptying a bedpan, a nurse sees stool on the hand after removing gloves. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Wash hands with soap and water
items.ex: Visible soiling requires handwashing with soap and water; alcohol rubs are ineffective on visibly dirty hands.
w: Apply an alcohol-based rub until dry
Alcohol rubs are not effective on visibly soiled hands.
Apply clean gloves over the soiled hand
Gloves do not replace hand hygiene and would trap contamination.
Apply hand lotion from a shared dispenser
Lotion does not clean hands, and shared lotion can grow organisms.

alt.q: Which finding during the assessment phase of hand hygiene means the nurse must use soap and water rather than a hand rub?
alt.a: Visible soiling on the hands
alt.ex: Inspecting for visible soiling decides the method; visibly soiled hands require handwashing with soap and water.
w: Short, smooth fingernails
Short nails are the expected finding, not a reason for soap and water.
No rings or wristwatch in the way
Removing jewelry is preparation, not a reason to change methods.
Hands that feel dry after a previous rub
Dryness is managed with approved lotion after care.

items.q: Why does the nurse regulate the water to a warm, rather than hot, temperature for handwashing?
items.a: Warm water removes fewer protective oils than hot water
items.ex: Warm water strips fewer protective oils than hot water, helping maintain skin integrity.
w: Warm water kills spores better than hot water
Water temperature is not used to kill spores.
Hot water causes soap to lather too much
Lather is not the reason for avoiding hot water.
Warm water dries hands more quickly afterward
Hands are dried with a paper towel; drying speed is not the rationale.

alt.q: A nurse’s hands have become chapped from frequent washing. Which handwashing adjustment is supported by the skill?
alt.a: Use warm water instead of hot water
alt.ex: Warm water removes fewer protective oils than hot water, so it is gentler on skin used frequently.
w: Use hot water to remove more bacteria
Hot water removes more protective oils and worsens dryness.
Skip rinsing to leave soap on the skin
Thorough rinsing and drying help prevent dermatitis.
Use extra antiseptic soap for each wash
Avoid excessive amounts of soap or antiseptic.

items.q: During handwashing, why does the nurse keep the hands and forearms lower than the elbows?
items.a: Water flows from the least to the most contaminated area into the sink
items.ex: Hands are the most contaminated parts; keeping them low lets water carry microorganisms off the fingertips into the sink.
w: It prevents the water from splashing the floor
Splash avoidance protects the uniform, but it is not the rationale here.
It keeps soap from running onto the wrists
Wrists are washed as well; this is not the rationale.
It allows the alcohol to evaporate more quickly
Alcohol evaporation relates to hand rubs, not handwashing.

alt.q: During a surgical hand scrub the hands are held above the elbows, but during routine handwashing they are kept below. What explains routine positioning?
alt.a: Hands are the most contaminated area and water should rinse off them
alt.ex: In routine handwashing, hands are most contaminated, so water flows from forearms down to the fingertips and into the sink.
w: Hands are the cleanest area and must stay highest
In routine handwashing the hands are the most contaminated part.
Elbows must be wet first to hold the soap
Elbow wetting is not part of the rationale.
Keeping hands low prevents touching the faucet
Faucet contact is avoided with knee pedals or paper towels.

items.q: In which direction should the nurse dry the hands after handwashing, and why?
items.a: From fingers to wrists, cleanest to least clean
items.ex: Drying from the cleanest area (fingertips) to the least clean (wrists) avoids contamination.
w: From wrists to fingers, so water drips off the tips
Drying wrist to fingers moves organisms toward the cleanest area.
From palms outward, so nails are dried last
The direction given is fingers to wrists.
In any direction, as long as the towel is clean
Direction matters to avoid recontaminating the fingers.

alt.q: A student dries the hands by starting at the wrists and moving toward the fingertips. Why should the nurse correct this?
alt.a: It carries microorganisms from a less clean area to the cleanest area
alt.ex: The fingertips are cleanest after washing; drying from wrists toward them recontaminates the hands.
w: It causes the paper towel to tear more easily
Towel tearing is not the concern.
It leaves the wrists wet, which causes dermatitis
The issue is the direction of contamination, not wet wrists.
It wastes paper towels compared with air drying
Paper towel use is not the reason for correction.

items.q: Why does the nurse use a clean, dry paper towel to turn off a hand-operated faucet after washing?
items.a: Faucet handles are likely contaminated with microorganisms
items.ex: Faucet handles are often contaminated; using a clean, dry paper towel prevents recontaminating clean hands.
w: Wet hands would slip on the smooth metal faucet handle
Grip is not the rationale given.
The paper towel helps the faucet close tightly and stop dripping
Closing force is not the concern.
Paper towels disinfect the faucet handle for the next user
A paper towel only provides a barrier; it does not disinfect.

alt.q: Why does the nurse discard a wet paper towel and use a clean, dry one to turn off the faucet?
alt.a: A wet towel can transfer pathogens from the faucet by capillary action
alt.ex: Wet towels and hands allow pathogens on the faucet to pass through by capillary action.
w: A wet towel cannot grip the faucet handle firmly enough
Grip is not the rationale; contamination is.
A wet towel leaves water spots on the sink and counter
Appearance is not the reason given.
A wet towel adds soap residue to the faucet handle
Soap residue is not the stated concern.

items.q: While washing, a nurse’s hands accidentally touch the inside of the sink. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Repeat the handwashing sequence
items.ex: The inside of the sink is contaminated; if hands touch it during handwashing, repeat the sequence.
w: Continue and rinse the hands longer
A longer rinse does not correct the contamination; repeat the sequence.
Apply an alcohol rub without washing again
The skill directs repeating the handwashing sequence.
Dry hands and put on gloves to cover them
Gloves do not replace proper hand hygiene.

alt.q: Why does the nurse stand in front of the sink and keep hands and uniform away from the sink surface?
alt.a: The inside and edge of the sink are contaminated
alt.ex: The sink is a contaminated area; reaching over it increases the risk of touching the contaminated edge.
w: The sink is sterile and must not be touched
The sink is contaminated, not sterile.
Standing close helps control water temperature
Distance is about contamination, not temperature.
Leaning on the sink speeds the wash time
Leaning on the sink causes contamination.

items.q: A nurse with dry, chapped hands asks when to apply hand lotion during the shift. Which response is best?
items.a: “Use a small amount from an individual-use container after patient care.”
items.ex: Organisms can grow in lotion, so use a small amount of agency-approved lotion from an individual container after care.
w: “Apply lotion from the shared bottle before each patient contact.”
Shared lotion can grow organisms, and lotion is applied after care.
“Apply plenty of any lotion before putting on gloves.”
Use only agency-approved products, and only after care is complete.
“Avoid hand hygiene until your skin heals.”
Hand hygiene is not optional; dermatitis is managed with approved products.

alt.q: Why must nurses use only hand lotions or barrier creams approved by their health care agency?
alt.a: Approved products are selected not to interact with hand sanitizers
alt.ex: Agency-approved lotions are chosen so they do not interfere with hand sanitizing products.
w: Approved products are the only ones that are sterile
Sterility is not the rationale given.
Approved products replace the need for hand hygiene
Lotion never replaces hand hygiene.
Approved products may be applied before each patient contact
Lotion is applied after patient care activities are complete.

items.q: A nurse observes an assistive personnel (AP) leave a patient’s room without performing hand hygiene. Which action reflects the delegation guidance for this skill?
items.a: Remind the AP to perform hand hygiene
items.ex: Hand hygiene is performed by all caregivers; team members serve as role models and provide reminders when it is missed.
w: Ignore it because AP are not responsible for hand hygiene
Hand hygiene is not optional for any caregiver.
Perform hand hygiene for the AP’s next patient instead
Each caregiver must perform their own hand hygiene.
Document the omission in the patient’s chart
Hand hygiene is not documented; the AP needs a reminder.

alt.q: According to the delegation guidance for Skill 28.1, who is responsible for performing hand hygiene?
alt.a: All caregivers on the health care team
alt.ex: Hand hygiene is performed by all caregivers and is not optional; team members model it and remind one another.
w: Only RNs who perform sterile procedures
Hand hygiene applies to all caregivers, not only RNs.
Only staff caring for patients on isolation
Hand hygiene applies to all patient care.
Only assistive personnel after delegation by the RN
It is not a delegated task; everyone performs it.

items.q: A home health nurse finds that a patient’s home has no warm running water near the patient’s bed. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Plan to use alcohol-based hand rubs or detergent-containing towels
items.ex: Evaluate home facilities and anticipate alternative products such as alcohol-based rubs or detergent-containing towels.
w: Skip hand hygiene during home visits
Hand hygiene remains required in the home.
Use cold standing water in a basin for every wash
The text recommends alternative products, not standing water.
Ask the patient to buy sterile gloves for each visit
Gloves do not replace hand hygiene.

alt.q: During a home care visit, which action does the skill recommend for teaching hand hygiene to the patient and caregiver?
alt.a: Teach technique and situations for handwashing, then confirm with teach-back
alt.ex: Instruct the patient and caregiver on proper technique and when to wash, using teach-back to confirm learning.
w: Give a pamphlet and skip demonstration
The text directs teaching and teach-back, not a pamphlet alone.
Teach only the caregiver, not the patient
Both the patient and primary caregiver are taught.
Teach the steps once without checking understanding
Teach-back is used to confirm learning.

items.q: Which factors determine whether a nurse uses an antiseptic soap or an alcohol-based hand rub? Select all that apply.
o: Whether hands are visibly soiled
Visible soiling requires soap and water.
The type of infectious microorganism
Spore-forming organisms call for handwashing.
The procedure to be performed
The planned procedure is part of the decision.
The patient’s immune status
Patient immune status influences the choice.
The nurse’s personal product preference
The decision rests on clinical factors, not personal preference.
items.ex: The choice depends on visible soiling, organism type, the procedure, and the patient’s immune status.

alt.q: A nurse is deciding how to perform hand hygiene. Which considerations does the skill list for this decision? Select all that apply.
o: Patient’s immune status
Immune status is one of the listed factors.
Time remaining in the shift
Shift time is not a clinical factor in the choice.
Visibly soiled hands
Visible soiling requires soap and water.
Type of microorganism involved
Organism type influences the choice.
Distance to the nearest sink
Convenience does not determine the clinical choice.
alt.ex: Visible soiling, organism type, procedure, and immune status guide the choice; time and convenience do not.

items.q: Which actions are part of correct handwashing technique with soap and water? Select all that apply.
o: Use plenty of lather and friction for at least 20 seconds
Friction and adequate time remove dirt and transient bacteria.
Interlace fingers and rub palms and backs of hands with circular motion
Interlacing ensures all surfaces are cleaned.
Keep fingertips pointed down
Fingertips down helps remove microorganisms into the sink.
Regulate the water as hot as can be tolerated
Warm water is used; hot water removes protective oils.
Clean under fingernails with the other hand’s nails or a nail cleaner
Areas under nails are often soiled and highly contaminated.
items.ex: Proper technique uses warm water, lather, friction, interlaced fingers, fingertips down, nail cleaning, and at least 20 seconds.

alt.q: A nurse is evaluating a student’s handwashing. Which actions show correct technique? Select all that apply.
o: Leans against the sink to reach the faucet
Touching the sink contaminates the hands and uniform.
Rubs palms and backs of hands at least five times each
Circular rubbing at least five times each ensures coverage.
Rinses with hands down and elbows up
Rinsing hands down washes microorganisms away.
Lathers for only 5 seconds when busy
Lather and friction are needed for at least 20 seconds.
Turns off the faucet with a clean, dry paper towel
This avoids recontaminating clean hands.
alt.ex: Correct technique includes thorough rubbing, rinsing with hands down, and turning off the faucet with a dry towel.

items.q: A nurse develops cracked skin from repeated use of soaps and antiseptics. Which interventions does the skill recommend? Select all that apply.
o: Rinse and dry hands thoroughly after using soap and water
Thorough rinsing and drying reduce irritation.
Avoid excessive amounts of soap or antiseptic
Using only the needed amount limits skin damage.
Try various hand hygiene products
Trying different products is a listed intervention.
Stop performing hand hygiene until the skin heals
Hand hygiene is not optional.
Use approved lotions or barrier creams
Approved products will not interfere with sanitizers.
items.ex: Dermatitis is managed with thorough rinsing and drying, less product, product trials, and approved lotions; report it to employee health.

alt.q: Which actions are appropriate when a nurse has dermatitis from frequent hand hygiene? Select all that apply.
o: Report the dermatitis to employee health or infection control
Dermatitis, psoriasis, and cuts are reported.
Switch to hot water to remove more product residue
Hot water removes protective oils and worsens dryness.
Apply any lotion brought from home before patient care
Use only approved lotions, and only after care.
Avoid excessive amounts of soap or antiseptic
Less product reduces skin irritation.
Rinse and dry hands thoroughly after washing
Thorough rinsing and drying help prevent cracked skin.
alt.ex: Report dermatitis and protect skin with thorough rinsing, drying, and less product; avoid hot water and unapproved lotions.

items.q: The skin underneath rings carries a higher bacterial count, so rings should be avoided or removed during hand hygiene.
items.a: True
items.ex: Skin under rings carries more bacteria, including gram-negative bacilli and S. aureus, so rings are avoided or removed.
items.ww: The skill explicitly says to avoid rings and remove them during hand hygiene because of higher bacterial counts.

alt.q: Rings may stay on during hand hygiene because friction washes away bacteria beneath them.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Skin under rings carries higher bacterial counts; rings should be avoided or removed during hand hygiene.
alt.ww: Calling this true ignores the higher bacterial count under rings.

items.q: After applying an alcohol-based hand rub, the nurse should let the hands dry completely before applying gloves.
items.a: True
items.ex: Rubbing until the alcohol is dry gives the product enough time to work before gloves are applied.
items.ww: The skill directs rubbing until dry and allowing hands to dry completely before gloving.

alt.q: Gloves should be applied while the alcohol rub is still wet to trap the antiseptic against the skin.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hands are rubbed until the alcohol is dry so the product has time to work.
alt.ww: Saying this is true contradicts the step to let hands dry completely before gloving.

items.q: The nurse must document each episode of hand hygiene in the patient’s record.
items.a: False
items.ex: It is not necessary to document hand hygiene; dermatitis, psoriasis, or cuts are reported to employee health or infection control.
items.ww: The skill states that documenting this procedure is not necessary.

alt.q: Hand hygiene does not need to be documented, but dermatitis, psoriasis, or cuts are reported to employee health or infection control.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Hand hygiene is not charted; skin conditions that raise transmission risk are reported.
alt.ww: Calling this false implies hand hygiene must be charted, which the skill says is unnecessary.

items.q: When hands are visibly soiled, wash with soap and water using lather and friction for at least [[20|twenty]] seconds.
items.ex: Washing for at least 20 seconds gives adequate time to expose skin to the cleansing agent and remove microorganisms.

alt.q: Hands should be washed with soap and water for a minimum of [[20|twenty]] seconds before eating and after using the restroom.
alt.ex: Washing for at least 20 seconds gives adequate time to expose skin to the cleansing agent and remove microorganisms.

items.a: Clean under the fingernails

w: Rinse hands and wrists, keeping hands down and elbows up
That's step 6 of 8.
Wet hands and wrists, keeping hands lower than elbows
That's step 3 of 8.

sections.name: Skill 28.2 · Preparation of a sterile field

items.q: A nurse is preparing a sterile field for a urinary catheter insertion. Which task can the nurse assign to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Helping position the patient and obtaining supplies
items.ex: Preparing a sterile field cannot be delegated; AP may help with positioning and obtain needed supplies.
w: Opening the sterile kit on the bedside table
Opening the kit is part of preparing the field, which cannot be delegated.
Adding sterile items to the opened field
Adding items is part of field preparation, which the nurse performs.
Pouring sterile solution into the kit’s cup
Pouring is part of field preparation and is not delegated.

alt.q: An AP offers to set up the sterile field while the nurse gathers medications. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “I need to prepare the field, but please help position the patient.”
alt.ex: Sterile field preparation cannot be delegated to AP; the nurse can direct AP to help with positioning and supplies.
w: “Yes, just be sure to wear sterile gloves.”
Gloves do not make this delegable; the skill cannot be delegated.
“Yes, if you check the expiration date first.”
Checking dates does not make field preparation delegable.
“Yes, but only open the outermost flap.”
Any part of preparing the field remains the nurse’s responsibility.

items.q: Why does the nurse verify in the agency procedure manual that an ordered procedure requires surgical aseptic technique?
items.a: Some procedures require medical asepsis rather than surgical asepsis
items.ex: Not all procedures need sterile technique; verifying ensures the correct level of asepsis is used.
w: All bedside procedures require a sterile field
Some procedures require only medical asepsis.
The manual lists the patient’s latex allergies
Latex allergies are found in the EHR and by asking the patient.
The manual decides whether the patient needs analgesia
Comfort and analgesia are assessed with the patient.

alt.q: A nurse is unsure whether a dressing change needs a sterile field. Which action is most appropriate before preparing supplies?
alt.a: Check agency policy to confirm whether surgical asepsis is required
alt.ex: Verifying policy confirms whether the procedure requires surgical aseptic technique or medical asepsis.
w: Use a sterile field for every procedure to be safe
Some procedures need medical asepsis; policy guides the choice.
Ask the AP which technique they usually use
Policy, not AP habit, determines the required technique.
Ask the patient which technique they prefer
The procedure manual determines the required technique.

items.q: Why does the nurse anticipate the number and variety of supplies needed before beginning a sterile procedure?
items.a: Leaving the sterile field to get supplies increases risk for contamination
items.ex: Kits may lack enough supplies; leaving the field to get more raises the risk of contamination.
w: Extra supplies can be stored on the sterile field
Only items needed are placed on the field; extras are kept nearby.
Sterile kits always contain more supplies than needed
Not all kits contain enough or the right supplies.
The AP is not allowed to bring supplies to the room
AP can obtain supplies; the concern is leaving the field.

alt.q: During a sterile procedure, a nurse realizes an item is missing. Why is preventing this situation important?
alt.a: Leaving a sterile field unattended risks undetected contamination
alt.ex: Failing to have supplies causes the nurse to leave the field, increasing the risk for contamination.
w: The procedure must be documented as incomplete
Documentation is not the primary concern.

alt.q: How high above the sterile receiving container should the bottle lip be held when pouring?

items.q: While pouring solution, the nurse splashes liquid onto the sterile drape and it soaks through. What should the nurse do?

items.q: Before a sterile procedure, the nurse uses teach-back. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?

items.q: According to the skill guidelines, to whom may surgical hand antisepsis be delegated?
items.a: A properly trained surgical technologist or licensed practical nurse

Only a registered nurse with operating room experience

alt.q: A trained surgical technologist performs surgical hand antisepsis before a case. What is the nurse’s responsibility regarding this delegated skill?

items.q: According to the evidence cited for the surgical scrub, which antimicrobial agent is more effective than povidone-iodine?

Plain soap only removes microorganisms mechanically; it is used for the prescrub wash, not the antimicrobial scrub.
Sterile normal saline
Saline has no antimicrobial action and is not a surgical scrub agent.
Hydrogen peroxide
Hydrogen peroxide is not the scrub agent the book identifies as more effective than povidone-iodine.

alt.q: A scrub nurse asks why the agency prefers chlorhexidine gluconate over povidone-iodine for surgical scrubs. Which response is accurate?

w: Povidone-iodine is no longer approved for any hand antisepsis.

Chlorhexidine does not need to be rinsed off after scrubbing.

Povidone-iodine can only be applied with a scrub brush.

items.q: Before surgical hand antisepsis, what is the maximum fingernail length the nurse should have?

6 mm

10 mm

alt.q: A nurse’s nail polish is intact but was applied 5 days ago. What should the nurse do before scrubbing?

Polish worn longer than 4 days must be removed even if it is intact.
Apply a fresh top coat over the old polish

Use a scrub brush to clean around the polish

items.q: While preparing for a surgical scrub, a nurse notices a fresh tattoo on the forearm that is oozing serum. Which action is most appropriate?

Longer scrubbing does not make an oozing lesion safe; it may damage the skin further.
Apply alcohol-based rub to the tattoo and proceed

Wear a second pair of sterile gloves and proceed

alt.q: A surgical technologist reports an open hangnail at the cuticle before scrubbing for a case. Why is this a concern?

A hangnail makes the fingernail longer than 2 mm

items.q: Why does the skill direct the nurse not to use a brush for the surgical hand scrub?

Agent absorption is not the reason; the brush injures the skin surface.
A brush splashes water onto the nurse’s surgical attire

items.q: During the surgical scrub and rinse, why does the nurse keep the hands elevated and the elbows down?
