It reduces arm fatigue during a long scrub
Comfort is not the reason; position keeps contaminated water away from the hands.
It lets the circulating nurse inspect the hands

alt.q: When rinsing after the sponge scrub, how should the nurse direct the water?

This carries water from the less clean elbows onto the hands.
From the fingertips to the elbows in short back-and-forth passes
Moving back and forth returns water from the elbows to the hands; one continuous motion is used.
Forearms first, then hands, with the hands held below the elbows

items.q: During the sponge scrub, a nurse splashes water onto the front of the surgical attire. What should the nurse do?

Splashing causes contamination; covering it does not make the attire clean.
Blot the attire with the sterile towel after drying the hands

Contamination must be corrected before the procedure, not reported afterward.

alt.q: Why must the nurse avoid splashing the surgical attire during the scrub?
alt.a: Splashing contaminates the attire, which then must be changed
alt.ex: Splashing causes contamination and requires changing the gown, so the nurse avoids it.
w: Splashing dilutes the antimicrobial agent on the hands
The book’s rationale is contamination of attire, not dilution of the agent.
Wet attire makes the cap and mask slip out of place
Slipping cap or mask is not the reason given; splashing contaminates attire.
Splashing wastes the antimicrobial scrub agent
Waste is not the concern; contaminated attire must be changed.

items.q: After the surgical scrub, how does the nurse dry the first hand with the sterile towel?
items.a: From the fingers to the elbow in a rotating motion
items.ex: Drying moves from the cleanest area (hands) to the least clean area (elbows).
w: From the elbow to the fingers in a rotating motion
This moves from the least clean area back to the cleanest area.
By patting the palm and back of the hand only
The whole hand and arm to the elbow must be dried thoroughly.
From the fingers to the elbow, then back to the fingers
Returning to the fingers brings elbow contamination back onto the hand.

alt.q: Why does the nurse use the opposite end of the sterile towel to dry the second hand?
alt.a: To avoid moving microorganisms from the elbow to the other hand
alt.ex: The first end has touched the elbow, so using the other end avoids transferring microorganisms to the second hand.
w: Because the first end is too wet to absorb more water
Wetness is not the reason; the first end has contacted the less clean elbow.
Because the first end touched the sterile field
The towel should not touch the field; the concern is elbow contamination.
To keep the towel from dropping below waist level
Waist level matters, but the opposite end is used to avoid elbow-to-hand transfer.

items.q: After applying an alcohol-based surgical hand rub, a nurse is about to enter the operating room while the hands are still damp. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Keep rubbing until the hands are completely dry
items.ex: The rub is continued until completely dry because wet hands promote the growth of microorganisms.
w: Dry the hands with a sterile towel
The spongeless rub is rubbed until dry; towel drying is used after the sponge scrub, not the rub.
Enter and let the gloves absorb the moisture
Gloving wet hands traps moisture that promotes microbial growth.
Rinse the hands under running water
Rinsing removes the antimicrobial product before it has finished working.

alt.q: What is the rationale for rubbing an alcohol-based surgical hand rub until the hands are completely dry?
alt.a: Wet hands promote the growth of microorganisms
alt.ex: The book’s rationale for rubbing until dry is that wet hands promote microbial growth.
w: Dry hands are easier to inspect for cuts
Inspection for cuts occurs during assessment, before the scrub.
Alcohol must evaporate before the water is turned off
The water is turned off before the rub is applied.
Moist product stains the sterile gown
Staining is not the reason; moisture promotes microbial growth.

items.q: Two days after surgery, the nurse assesses a patient’s incision. Which finding is most important to report?
items.a: Redness and warmth with purulent drainage
items.ex: Redness, heat, swelling, pain, and purulent drainage at the operative site indicate a surgical site infection.
w: Wound edges well approximated
Approximated edges are an expected finding, not a sign of infection.
Dressing dry and intact
A dry, intact dressing is an expected finding.
Pain controlled with prescribed analgesic
Controlled pain does not suggest infection; purulent drainage with redness and warmth does.

alt.q: According to the skill’s evaluation section, when does a surgical site infection usually occur?
alt.a: 2 to 3 days after surgery
alt.ex: The nurse monitors for surgical site infection, which usually occurs 2 to 3 days after surgery.
w: Within 6 hours after surgery
Infection takes time to develop; the book gives 2 to 3 days.
7 to 10 days after surgery
The book states infection usually appears earlier, at 2 to 3 days.
1 month after surgery
The book states infection usually appears at 2 to 3 days.

items.q: After removing gloves following a surgical procedure, a nurse notices cracked, reddened skin on both hands. Which action is best?
items.a: Report the dermatitis to employee health or infection control
items.ex: Skin dermatitis is reported to employee health or infection control per agency policy.
w: Document the finding in the surgical patient’s record
The nurse’s skin condition is not patient documentation; it is reported to employee health.
Use a scrub brush for future scrubs to clean more deeply
Brushes damage skin and would worsen dermatitis.
Continue scrubbing as usual because gloves cover the skin
Broken skin increases risk of transmitting microorganisms and must be reported.

alt.q: Why does the nurse inspect the hands for dermatitis or cracked skin after the procedure?
alt.a: Broken skin increases risk of transmitting microorganisms in future care
alt.ex: Breaks in skin integrity increase the risk of transmitting microorganisms during later care activities.
w: Cracked skin shows the scrub time was too short
Dermatitis is not a measure of scrub time; it is a transmission risk.
Dermatitis must be documented in the patient’s record
Dermatitis is reported to employee health, not documented for the patient.
Cracked skin means the gloves were the wrong size
The concern is transmission through broken skin, not glove size.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to perform surgical hand antisepsis. Which actions are appropriate before the prescrub wash? Select all that apply.
o: Remove rings, bracelets, and watches
Jewelry harbors microorganisms and protects them from removal.
Confirm fingernails are short, clean, and healthy
Long nails harbor pathogens and can puncture gloves.
Inspect hands and forearms for cuts or open lesions
Open lesions may ooze serum containing pathogens.
Apply shoe covers, cap, mask, and eyewear
Protective wear is applied during planning, before the scrub begins.
Keep artificial nails if they are trimmed to 2 mm
Artificial nails are never worn; they harbor gram-negative organisms and fungus.
Leave intact polish on regardless of how long it has been worn
Polish worn longer than 4 days must be removed.
items.ex: Preparation removes jewelry, checks nails and skin, and applies protective attire before scrubbing.

alt.q: Which findings should keep a nurse from scrubbing until they are corrected or healed? Select all that apply.
o: Artificial nail extenders on two fingers
Extenders harbor gram-negative microorganisms and fungus and are never worn.
A fresh tattoo on the forearm oozing serum
Oozing lesions may contain pathogens; no patient contact until healed.
Chipped nail polish
Chipped polish is likely to harbor microorganisms and must be removed.
Short, clean nails with no polish
Short (2 mm), clean, healthy nails meet the requirement.
Intact skin on hands and forearms
Intact skin is the expected finding before scrubbing.
alt.ex: Artificial nails, chipped polish, and oozing lesions harbor or release microorganisms; short clean nails and intact skin are acceptable.

items.q: Which findings at an operative site suggest a surgical site infection? Select all that apply.
o: Redness
Redness at the operative site is a sign of infection.
Heat
Local warmth is a sign of infection.
Swelling
Swelling at the site is a sign of infection.
Purulent drainage
Purulent drainage at the operative site indicates infection.
Well-approximated wound edges
Approximated edges are an expected healing finding.
Dry, intact dressing
A dry, intact dressing does not suggest infection.
items.ex: Signs of surgical site infection include redness, heat, swelling, pain, and purulent drainage at the operative site.

alt.q: Which actions reflect the skill’s guidance for evaluating and documenting the surgical patient? Select all that apply.
o: Document the area and description of the surgical site after surgery
This provides a baseline for monitoring the wound.
Monitor for infection signs, which usually appear 2 to 3 days after surgery
Surgical site infection usually occurs 2 to 3 days postoperatively.
Individualize interventions such as wound care or antibiotic therapy if infection develops
The book directs interventions based on the patient’s situation.
Document the nurse’s surgical scrub time in the patient record
Documentation is not required for surgical hand antisepsis.
Stop monitoring the incision after the first 24 hours
Infection usually appears at 2 to 3 days, so monitoring continues.
alt.ex: The nurse documents the site as a baseline, monitors for infection at 2 to 3 days, and individualizes interventions.

items.q: What are advantages of approved brushless, alcohol-based surgical hand-rub products? Select all that apply.
o: They limit damage to the user’s skin
Added emollients help protect the skin.
They improve adherence to hand antisepsis protocols
The book lists improved adherence as a benefit.
They simplify the application technique
Brushless rubs simplify the technique.
They reduce waste of water, brushes, and packaging
Less material waste is a listed benefit.
They eliminate the need to clean under the nails
Nails are still cleaned with a nail pick before applying the rub.
They allow the prescrub wash to be skipped
The spongeless rub is performed after the prescrub wash.
items.ex: Brushless alcohol-based rubs with emollients protect skin, improve adherence, simplify technique, and reduce waste.

alt.q: Which statements about the spongeless surgical hand scrub with an alcohol-based rub are correct? Select all that apply.

Nails are cleaned and hands rinsed before application.
Hands are dried with a paper towel before the product is applied
Hands are dried thoroughly with a paper towel and the water turned off.
The product is used in the manufacturer’s recommended volume and time
Application follows manufacturer instructions for volume and time.
Hands are dried with a sterile towel after the product is applied
The product is rubbed in until completely dry; no towel is used.
The product is worked into the skin with a stiff brush
Brushes are not used because they damage skin.
alt.ex: The rub follows a prescrub wash, nail cleaning, and drying, then is applied per manufacturer and rubbed until dry.

items.q: When rinsing after the surgical scrub, the nurse runs water from the elbows down to the fingertips.

items.q: Artificial nails are acceptable for scrub staff as long as they are kept short and clean.

alt.q: Artificial nails harbor gram-negative microorganisms and fungus, so they are never worn for surgical hand antisepsis.

alt.ex: The book states artificial nails harbor gram-negative microorganisms and fungus and must never be worn.

items.q: The nurse must document the surgical hand antisepsis in the patient’s medical record.
items.a: False
items.ex: Documentation is not required for surgical hand antisepsis; the surgical site is documented instead.

items.q: Which task related to sterile gloving may the nurse delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Helping position the patient during a sterile-glove procedure
items.ex: AP may assist with positioning or handing off supplies, but most procedures that require sterile gloves cannot be delegated.
w: Performing a sterile dressing change with sterile gloves
Most procedures requiring sterile gloves cannot be delegated to AP.
Inserting a urinary catheter while wearing sterile gloves
Sterile procedures such as catheter insertion are not delegated to AP.
Applying sterile gloves to begin the sterile procedure
Applying sterile gloves for a sterile procedure remains the nurse’s responsibility.

alt.q: The nurse asks an AP to help with a procedure that requires sterile gloves. Which instruction is most important to give the AP?

Most procedures requiring sterile gloves cannot be delegated, so AP does not perform them.
How to document the nurse’s application of sterile gloves
Glove application does not need to be documented.
How to remove the nurse’s gloves after the procedure ends
The nurse removes the gloves; the AP assists with positioning and supplies.

items.q: Before a sterile dressing change, the nurse finds a dry water stain on the sterile glove package. Which action should the nurse take?

w: Use the gloves, because the package is now dry
A dry stain still shows prior water contamination.
Use the gloves if the inner wrapper looks unstained
The whole package is considered contaminated once water stains appear.
Wipe the package with alcohol before opening it
Wiping does not restore sterility of a water-contaminated package.

alt.q: Why is a sterile glove package with water stains considered unsafe to use?
alt.a: Water stains indicate the package was previously contaminated by water
alt.ex: Torn or wet packages are considered contaminated, and stains show the package was once wet.
w: Water stains show the gloves were made with powder
Stains do not reveal powder; they reveal past exposure to water.
Water weakens the gloves so they tear during use
The concern is contamination, not glove strength.
Water stains make the right and left gloves hard to identify
Identification is not the issue; the package is contaminated.

items.q: Why does the nurse use nonpowdered sterile gloves?

w: Powder makes the gloves more likely to tear during use
Tearing is not the reason given; the ban is due to allergic reactions.
Powder keeps the gloves from fitting over a gown cuff
Fit over gown cuffs is unrelated; the concern is hypersensitivity.
Powder inactivates the antiseptic used for hand hygiene
The book’s reason is the FDA ruling on allergic reactions.

alt.q: A student asks whether powdered sterile gloves can be used for a patient with no latex allergy. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

items.q: A nurse measures a heart rate of 128 beats/min in a resting patient whose usual rate is 76 beats/min. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Have another nurse repeat the measurement to verify the reading

A significant change must be verified and reported immediately, not held until hand-off.

Recheck the rate at the next routine vital sign time

Record the value in the EHR without telling anyone

A patient who briefly lost consciousness 10 minutes ago

items.q: Why should a nurse know a patient’s usual range of vital signs?

alt.q: A nurse is measuring the blood pressure of an overweight adult. Which equipment choice is most appropriate?
alt.a: A cuff appropriate for the patient’s arm size
alt.ex: Select equipment on the basis of the patient’s characteristics; do not use a small cuff on an overweight adult.
w: A small cuff because it is easier to apply
A small cuff on an overweight adult is specifically warned against.
A child-size cuff to keep pressure low
A child-size cuff does not fit an adult’s arm.
Any cuff, since size does not affect results
Equipment must be appropriate for the patient’s size and characteristics.

items.q: A nurse measures a patient’s temperature while the patient is in a warm, humid room. Why is the nurse concerned about this reading?
items.a: The environment may cause a value that is not a true indicator of the patient’s condition
items.ex: Environmental factors affect VS, so the nurse controls or minimizes them to obtain accurate values.
w: Humidity damages electronic thermometers and stops them from working
The concern is the environment’s effect on the body’s temperature, not equipment damage.
A warm room always lowers body temperature below the expected range
A warm environment tends to raise, not lower, the measured temperature.
Temperature must be measured only in rooms with no air movement
The guideline is to control environmental factors that affect VS, not to avoid air movement.

alt.q: Which situation is most likely to produce a temperature value that does not truly reflect the patient’s condition?
alt.a: Measuring the temperature in a warm, humid room
alt.ex: A warm, humid environment can give a temperature that is not a true indicator of the patient’s condition.
w: Using a clean, calibrated electronic thermometer
Clean, functional, calibrated equipment supports accuracy.
Using the same site as the previous measurement
Using one site consistently helps the nurse monitor true trends.
Following a step-by-step approach for the measurement
An organized, systematic approach ensures accuracy.

items.q: A patient is scheduled for a bronchoscopy. When should the nurse measure vital signs in relation to this procedure?
items.a: Before, during, and after the procedure
items.ex: VS are measured before, during, and after an invasive procedure; the preprocedure set is the baseline.
w: Only after the procedure is completed
Without a preprocedure measurement there is no baseline for comparison.
Only before the procedure begins
VS are also monitored during and after an invasive procedure.
Only if the patient reports discomfort afterward
VS are routinely measured around invasive procedures, not only for symptoms.

alt.q: What is the main purpose of obtaining vital signs before a cardiac catheterization?
alt.a: To provide a baseline for comparing values during and after the procedure
alt.ex: A baseline measurement before an invasive procedure is the starting point for identifying changes.
w: To decide whether assistive personnel may perform the procedure
Preprocedure VS do not determine who performs a catheterization.
To replace vital sign checks after the procedure is done
VS are still measured during and after the procedure.
To meet billing rules for invasive procedures
The reason is clinical: establishing a baseline for later comparison.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “I just feel funny, different somehow.” The patient has no other specific complaints. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Measure the patient’s vital signs
items.ex: Nonspecific symptoms of physical distress, such as feeling “funny” or “different,” are an indication to measure VS.
w: Reassure the patient and return in an hour
Delaying assessment could miss an early change in condition.
Document the statement and continue rounds
The report calls for assessment, not only documentation.
Ask the patient to describe the feeling at the next meal
Waiting delays the assessment that the report warrants.

alt.q: A patient who has been on bed rest for several days is getting up to walk for the first time. When should the nurse measure vital signs?
alt.a: Before and after the patient walks
alt.ex: Nursing interventions that influence VS, such as ambulation after bed rest, call for measurement before and after.
w: Only after the walk is finished
A measurement before ambulation is needed for comparison.
Only if the patient asks to stop walking
VS are measured around the activity, not only when symptoms occur.
At the next routine scheduled time
The activity itself is an indication to measure before and after.

items.q: Why should a nurse follow agency policy for cleaning vital sign equipment between patients?
items.a: Stethoscopes and other VS equipment can transmit multidrug-resistant organisms
items.ex: Research shows VS equipment such as stethoscopes is a source of MDRO transmission, so cleaning reduces infection risk.
w: Cleaning keeps the equipment calibrated for accurate readings
Calibration is a separate requirement; cleaning is about infection risk.
Cleaning is needed only when equipment is visibly soiled
Equipment is cleaned between patients per policy, not only when soiled.
Cleaning prevents the patient from feeling cold equipment
Comfort is not the reason for cleaning between patients.

alt.q: A nurse finishes taking vital signs on one patient and moves to the next room. Which action best reduces the risk of infection?
alt.a: Clean the equipment according to agency policy before using it again
alt.ex: Following agency policy for cleaning equipment between patients reduces transmission of multidrug-resistant organisms.
w: Wipe the equipment only at the end of the shift
Cleaning must occur between patients, not just at shift end.
Use the equipment again if it looks clean
Organisms can be present on equipment that appears clean.
Ask the next patient whether they mind shared equipment
Patient permission does not reduce the infection risk.

items.q: According to the normal adult vital sign ranges, which pulse oximetry value is normal?
items.a: SpO2 of 95% or higher
items.ex: The normal adult SpO2 is 95% or greater.
w: SpO2 of 85% or higher
An SpO2 below 90% is considered a medical emergency.
SpO2 of 88% or higher
88% is below normal and below the emergency threshold of 90%.
SpO2 of 90% or higher
Values from 90% to 94% are still below the normal value of 95% or higher.

alt.q: An adult patient’s SpO2 is 93%. How should the nurse interpret this value?
alt.a: It is below the normal adult value of 95% or higher
alt.ex: Normal adult SpO2 is 95% or greater, so 93% is below normal and warrants further assessment.
w: It is within the normal adult range of 90% or higher
Normal SpO2 is 95% or higher, not 90%.
It is a critical value of 75% or lower
A critical value is 75% or lower; 93% is well above that.
It is normal because any value above 85% is acceptable
Values below 90% are an emergency, and normal is 95% or higher.

items.q: Which value is the normal range for end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) measured by capnography?
items.a: 35 to 45 mm Hg
items.ex: Normal EtCO2 is 35 to 45 mm Hg, approximating the PaCO2 in a healthy patient.
w: 30 to 50 mm Hg
30 to 50 mm Hg is the normal pulse pressure.
60 to 100 mm Hg
60 to 100 is the normal adult pulse rate range in beats/min.
12 to 20 mm Hg
12 to 20 is the normal adult respiratory rate in breaths/min.

alt.q: A normal range of 35 to 45 mm Hg applies to which adult measurement?
alt.a: End-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2)
alt.ex: Capnography’s EtCO2 is normally 35 to 45 mm Hg.
w: Pulse pressure (systolic minus diastolic)
Normal pulse pressure is 30 to 50 mm Hg.
Diastolic blood pressure (lower value)
Normal diastolic pressure is less than 80 mm Hg.
Systolic blood pressure (upper value)
Normal systolic pressure is less than 120 mm Hg.

items.q: In which situations should a nurse measure a patient’s vital signs? Select all that apply.
o: On admission to a health care agency
Admission VS establish the patient’s baseline.
Before, during, and after a blood transfusion
Any blood product transfusion requires VS before, during, and after.
When the patient’s general condition changes, such as loss of consciousness
A change in physical condition is an indication to measure VS.
Before and after range-of-motion exercises
Nursing interventions that influence VS call for measurement before and after.
Only after, not before, a blood transfusion
VS are needed before the transfusion as a baseline and during it as well.
Only when the patient specifically requests it
VS are measured on schedule and whenever condition or treatment warrants, not on request alone.
items.ex: Box 29.2 lists admission, routine schedules, procedures, transfusions, VS-affecting therapies or interventions, nonspecific distress, and condition changes.

alt.q: A nurse is planning care for the day. Which events call for vital sign measurement? Select all that apply.
o: A home care visit to assess a patient
VS are measured when assessing a patient during home care visits.
Administration of a drug that affects respiratory function
Medications affecting cardiovascular, respiratory, or temperature control need VS before, during, and after.
A patient reporting increased intensity of pain
Increased pain intensity is a change in condition that calls for VS.
A patient finishing a phone call with family
A routine social activity is not an indication for VS.
A patient choosing items from the meal menu
Menu selection does not influence vital signs.
alt.ex: VS are measured during home visits, around VS-affecting therapies, and when the patient’s condition changes.

items.q: Which characteristics should vital sign equipment have before a nurse uses it? Select all that apply.
o: Clean
Clean equipment reduces the risk of transmitting infection.
Functional
Equipment must work properly to give a valid reading.
Properly calibrated
Calibration ensures accurate measurement.
Appropriate for the patient’s size and age
Equipment must fit the patient’s size, age, condition, and characteristics.
Shared among patients without cleaning if used briefly
Equipment is cleaned between patients according to agency policy.
The same cuff size for every adult
Cuff size must match the patient, not be standard for all adults.
items.ex: VS equipment must be clean, functional, calibrated, and appropriate for the patient’s size, age, condition, and characteristics.

alt.q: A nurse checks a blood pressure device before use. Which findings indicate a problem that must be corrected? Select all that apply.
o: The device has not been calibrated
Uncalibrated equipment can give inaccurate values.
The cuff was used on another patient and not cleaned
Equipment must be cleaned between patients to reduce infection risk.
The only cuff available is adult size for a small child
An adult cuff is not appropriate for a child.
The device is clean and working properly
Clean, functional equipment is what the guidelines require.
The cuff size matches the patient’s arm
A properly sized cuff meets the guideline.
alt.ex: Uncalibrated, uncleaned, or wrongly sized equipment violates the guidelines for VS equipment.

items.q: Before interpreting a patient’s vital signs, which information should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s health history
Some illnesses cause predictable changes in VS.
Prescribed and over-the-counter medications
Some medications affect one or more vital signs.
Current therapies the patient is receiving
Some treatments cause predictable changes in VS.
The patient’s usual range of vital signs
Usual values are the baseline for detecting change.
The vital signs of the patient in the next bed
Another patient’s values are irrelevant to this patient’s interpretation.
The AP’s opinion of whether the values are normal
The nurse is responsible for interpreting the significance of VS data.
items.ex: Results are analyzed on the basis of the patient’s condition, history, therapies, medications, and usual values.

alt.q: A patient’s pulse is lower than the adult range. Which factors might explain this and should be reviewed? Select all that apply.
o: A medication the patient takes that slows heart rate
Some medications affect vital signs and can explain a low value.
The patient’s documented usual pulse range
The patient’s usual value may differ from the general acceptable range.
A medical condition known to change heart rate
Some illnesses cause predictable changes in VS.
The time the patient’s visitors arrived
Visitor timing is not a factor the guidelines identify for interpreting VS.
The color of the patient’s hospital gown
Clothing color has no bearing on interpreting a pulse.
alt.ex: Medications, conditions, and the patient’s usual range all inform interpretation of a VS value.

items.q: When a nurse delegates vital sign measurement to assistive personnel, responsibility for interpreting the values transfers to the assistive personnel.
items.a: False
items.ex: Measuring VS remains the nurse’s responsibility, including reviewing and interpreting the data and deciding on interventions.
items.ww: The nurse may delegate the measurement only; interpretation and decisions about intervention stay with the nurse.

alt.q: A nurse remains responsible for reviewing and interpreting vital sign data even when measurement is delegated.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Delegation covers the task of measuring; the nurse still reviews the data and decides on interventions.
alt.ww: Responsibility for interpretation does not pass to assistive personnel with the task.

items.q: A patient’s usual vital sign values can differ from acceptable ranges because of age, response to treatment, or medical condition.
items.a: True
items.ex: Usual values may fall outside acceptable ranges and serve as the patient’s baseline for detecting change.
items.ww: Acceptable ranges are general; individual baselines vary with age, treatment, and condition.

alt.q: Any vital sign outside the acceptable adult range always indicates a new change in the patient’s condition.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A value outside the range may be the patient’s usual value; change is judged against the patient’s baseline.
alt.ww: Usual values can differ from acceptable ranges, so an out-of-range value is not automatically a new change.

items.q: The frequency of vital sign measurement is determined by the specific patient’s condition.
items.a: True
items.ex: The nurse uses clinical judgment to decide which VS to measure, when, and how often, based on the patient’s condition.
items.ww: VS frequency is individualized, not identical for every patient.

alt.q: All patients on a nursing unit should have vital signs measured at the same frequency.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Frequency depends on each patient’s condition and the nurse’s clinical judgment.
alt.ww: A uniform schedule ignores that unstable or changing patients need more frequent measurement.

items.q: Vital signs obtained during a routine physical examination serve as a [[baseline]] for future assessments.
items.ex: Establishing a database of VS gives a starting point for identifying and interpreting later changes.

alt.q: A set of vital signs measured before an invasive procedure provides a [[baseline]] for comparison during and after it.
alt.ex: Establishing a database of VS gives a starting point for identifying and interpreting later changes.

items.q: The normal adult pulse rate is 60 to [[100]] beats/min, strong and regular.
items.ex: Box 29.1 lists 60 to 100 beats/min as the normal adult pulse.

alt.q: A normal adult pulse is strong and regular, with a rate of [[60]] to 100 beats/min.
alt.ex: Box 29.1 lists 60 to 100 beats/min as the normal adult pulse.

w: 60 to 100 beats/min
That goes with Pulse.

alt.q: What is the normal adult value for End-tidal CO2 (EtCO2)?
alt.a: 35 to 45 mm Hg

w: 60 to 100 beats/min
That goes with Pulse.
12 to 20 breaths/min

95% or higher

alt.ex: Box 29.1 lists these normal adult values for comparison with patient findings.
w: 60 to 100 beats/min
That goes with Pulse.
12 to 20 breaths/min
That goes with Respirations.
95% or higher
That goes with Pulse oximetry (SpO2).

alt.a: Pulse
alt.ex: Box 29.1 lists these normal adult values for comparison with patient findings.
w: Respirations
Respirations: 12 to 20 breaths/min.
Pulse oximetry (SpO2)

Pulse pressure

alt.a: Respirations
alt.ex: Box 29.1 lists these normal adult values for comparison with patient findings.
w: Pulse
Pulse: 60 to 100 beats/min.
Pulse oximetry (SpO2)
Pulse oximetry (SpO2): 95% or higher.
Pulse pressure
Pulse pressure: 30 to 50 mm Hg.

alt.q: Which measurement has a normal adult value of “95% or higher”?
alt.a: Pulse oximetry (SpO2)
alt.ex: Box 29.1 lists these normal adult values for comparison with patient findings.
w: Pulse
Pulse: 60 to 100 beats/min.
Respirations

Pulse pressure

alt.a: Pulse pressure
alt.ex: Box 29.1 lists these normal adult values for comparison with patient findings.
w: Pulse
Pulse: 60 to 100 beats/min.
Respirations
Respirations: 12 to 20 breaths/min.
Pulse oximetry (SpO2)
Pulse oximetry (SpO2): 95% or higher.

alt.a: End-tidal CO2 (EtCO2)

w: Pulse
Pulse: 60 to 100 beats/min.
Respirations
Respirations: 12 to 20 breaths/min.
Pulse oximetry (SpO2)
Pulse oximetry (SpO2): 95% or higher.

alt.q: Which measurement has a normal adult value of “37.5°C (99.5°F)”?
alt.a: Average rectal temperature
alt.ex: Box 29.1 lists these normal adult values for comparison with patient findings.
w: Pulse
Pulse: 60 to 100 beats/min.
Respirations

Pulse oximetry (SpO2)

mt.q: Match each adult measurement with its normal value.
mt.ex: Box 29.1 lists these normal adult values for comparison with patient findings.

items.q: Which temperature measurement site reflects surface rather than core body temperature?
items.a: Axillary
items.ex: Axillary temperatures measure the body’s surface temperature, whereas pulmonary artery, esophageal, and bladder sites are core.
w: Pulmonary artery
Pulmonary artery catheter measurements are core temperatures.
Esophagus
Esophageal catheter measurements are core temperatures.
Urinary bladder
The bladder reflects core temperature and is a reliable indicator.

alt.q: Which site reflects core body temperature and is a more reliable indicator than surface sites?
alt.a: Urinary bladder
alt.ex: Sites reflecting core temperature, such as rectal and bladder, are more reliable than surface sites.
w: Axillary
The axilla measures surface temperature.
Skin of the forearm
Skin temperature fluctuates with the environment and is a surface measure.
Chemical patch on the abdomen
Temperature-sensitive patches are screening tools affected by environmental temperature.

items.q: When nerve cells in the anterior hypothalamus become heated beyond the set point, which response does the body initiate?
items.a: Sweating and vasodilation of blood vessels
items.ex: The anterior hypothalamus controls heat loss through sweating, vasodilation, and inhibition of heat production.
w: Shivering and voluntary muscle contraction
Shivering produces heat; it is triggered when temperature is below the set point.
Vasoconstriction of skin and extremity vessels
Vasoconstriction conserves heat and is triggered by the posterior hypothalamus.
Increased secretion of heat-producing hormones
Increasing heat production is the opposite of what overheating triggers.

alt.q: The posterior hypothalamus senses that body temperature is below the set point. Which response follows?
alt.a: Vasoconstriction that reduces blood flow to the skin
alt.ex: The posterior hypothalamus controls heat production and conservation, starting with vasoconstriction, then shivering if needed.
w: Sweating to promote evaporative heat loss
Sweating is a heat-loss mechanism controlled by the anterior hypothalamus.
Vasodilation of surface blood vessels
Vasodilation increases heat loss and occurs when temperature is above the set point.
Inhibition of muscle activity and shivering
Shivering is stimulated, not inhibited, when temperature is low.

items.q: A patient lies uncovered in a cool operating room during surgery. Through which mechanism is heat loss likely to be considerable?
items.a: Radiation
items.ex: Radiation heat loss can be considerable during surgery, when the patient’s skin is exposed to a cool environment.
w: Conduction
Conduction requires direct contact with a cooler object, such as an ice pack.
Convection
Convection is heat loss through air movement, such as from a fan.
Evaporation
Evaporation is heat loss as liquid, such as sweat, changes to a gas.

alt.q: A nurse removes the blankets from a patient who has a fever. This intervention mainly promotes heat loss through which mechanism?
alt.a: Radiation
alt.ex: Removing clothing or blankets promotes radiant heat loss from the body’s surface without direct contact.
w: Conduction
Conduction would involve contact with a cooler object, such as a cool cloth.
Convection
Convection depends on air movement, such as a fan.
Evaporation
Evaporation depends on moisture changing to a gas, such as sweat.

items.q: An 84-year-old patient has an oral temperature of 36°C (96.8°F) and no other abnormal findings. How should the nurse interpret this value?
items.a: It is within the average range for older adults
items.ex: The average body temperature of older adults is about 35° to 36.1°C (95° to 97°F).
w: It indicates hypothermia that requires active rewarming
Hypothermia is a core temperature below 35°C (95°F).
It indicates the beginning of a fever in an older adult
36°C is below, not above, the usual adult value.
It indicates the thermometer must be malfunctioning
This value is expected in older adults, so equipment failure is not implied.

alt.q: What is the approximate average body temperature of older adults?
alt.ex: Older adults have a lower, narrower temperature range because of changes in temperature regulation.
w: This is higher than the average for older adults.
This is the protected newborn range, not the older adult average.
This range is classified as mild hypothermia.

items.q: A parent reports a child’s temperatures. Which reading meets the fever cutoff for the site used?
items.a: Axillary 37.4°C (99.3°F)
items.ex: In children, an axillary temperature of 37.2°C (99°F) or higher meets the fever cutoff.
w: The oral cutoff is 37.8°C (100°F) or higher.
Rectal 37.8°C (100°F)
The rectal cutoff is 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher.
Forehead 37.6°C (99.7°F)
The forehead cutoff is 38.0°C (100.4°F) or higher.

alt.q: Which oral temperature in a child meets the cutoff for fever?
alt.ex: The oral fever cutoff for children is 37.8°C (100°F) or higher.
w: 37°C is the average normal oral temperature.
37.2°C is the cutoff for axillary, not oral, temperature.
37.5°C is below the oral fever cutoff of 37.8°C.

items.q: A patient’s temperature chart shows fever spikes and falls but never returns to an acceptable level. Which fever pattern is this?
items.a: Remittent
items.ex: A remittent fever spikes and falls without returning to acceptable temperature levels.
w: Intermittent
An intermittent fever returns to an acceptable value at least once in 24 hours.
Sustained
A sustained fever stays continuously above 38°C with little fluctuation.
Relapsing
A relapsing fever alternates febrile episodes with periods of acceptable temperature.

alt.q: A patient has fever spikes, but the temperature returns to an acceptable value at least once every 24 hours. Which fever pattern is this?
alt.a: Intermittent
alt.ex: Intermittent fever has spikes interspersed with usual temperature levels, returning to normal at least once in 24 hours.
w: Remittent
A remittent fever does not return to acceptable levels.
Sustained
A sustained fever remains continuously elevated with little fluctuation.
Relapsing
Relapsing fever has febrile and normal periods often longer than 24 hours.

items.q: A construction worker is brought in confused after working in the sun. His temperature is 40.6°C (105°F). Which finding best supports heatstroke rather than heat exhaustion?
items.a: Hot, dry skin
items.ex: The most important sign of heatstroke is hot, dry skin; patients do not sweat because of electrolyte loss and hypothalamic malfunction.
w: Profuse diaphoresis
Profuse diaphoresis is characteristic of heat exhaustion.
Dizziness
Dizziness occurs with deficient fluid volume in heat exhaustion as well.
Hypotension
Hypotension can occur in both heatstroke and heat exhaustion.

alt.q: A nurse finds a person with suspected heatstroke at an outdoor event. Which first aid action should the nurse take first?
alt.a: Move the person to a cooler environment
alt.ex: First aid for heatstroke starts with moving the patient to a cooler environment, then removing clothing and cooling the skin.
w: Offer hot liquids such as soup
Hot liquids are used for hypothermia, not heatstroke.
Wrap the person in dry blankets
Wrapping in blankets conserves heat and is used for hypothermia.
Have the person rest in the sun
Staying in the heat continues to overwhelm heat-loss mechanisms.

items.q: A man is brought to the emergency department after falling through ice on a lake. He is shivering and his clothes are wet. Which nursing action is the priority?
items.a: Remove the wet clothes and replace them with dry ones
items.ex: The priority in hypothermia is preventing further heat loss by removing wet clothing, applying dry clothes, and wrapping in blankets.
w: Give him a cup of hot coffee
Caffeinated fluids should be avoided; warm noncaffeinated liquids like soup are preferred.
Give him a small amount of brandy
Alcohol should be avoided in hypothermia.
Recheck his temperature in an hour
Waiting while he stays wet allows further heat loss.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a family how to care for someone with mild hypothermia before help arrives. Which statement shows understanding?
alt.a: “We will give warm soup and avoid alcohol and caffeine.”
alt.ex: A conscious patient benefits from hot liquids such as soup while avoiding alcohol and caffeinated fluids.
w: “We will give a strong cup of coffee to warm him.”
Caffeinated fluids should be avoided.
“We will give a little whiskey to help him warm up.”
Alcohol should be avoided in hypothermia.
“We will leave his head uncovered so he does not overheat.”
Keeping the head covered helps, because the head and neck lose heat quickly.

items.q: A febrile patient has orders for blood cultures and an IV antibiotic. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Obtain the blood culture specimens
items.ex: Cultures are obtained before antibiotics begin so the causative microorganism can be identified.
w: Start the IV antibiotic infusion
Giving antibiotics first can interfere with identifying the organism.
Apply ice packs to the axillae and groin
Ice packs cause shivering and are no longer recommended.
Give a tepid sponge bath
Tepid sponge baths lead to shivering and are avoided.

alt.q: When is the best time to obtain blood culture specimens from a febrile patient, according to agency policy?
alt.a: To coincide with temperature spikes
alt.ex: Blood cultures timed with temperature spikes capture the antigen-producing organism when it is most prevalent.
w: When the temperature is at its lowest
The organism is most prevalent during spikes, not low points.
After the first dose of antibiotics
Cultures are obtained before beginning antibiotics.
Only after the fever has broken
After the fever breaks, the organism is less likely to be captured.

items.q: The parent of a 4-year-old with a fever asks whether aspirin can be given at home. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Do not give aspirin to children because of its link to Reye syndrome.”
items.ex: Medications containing salicylates, such as aspirin, should never be given to children because of the association with Reye syndrome.
w: “Aspirin is the preferred fever reducer for young children.”
Aspirin is contraindicated in children.
“Aspirin is safe if you give it with food.”
Food does not remove the Reye syndrome risk.
“Aspirin is fine if the fever is above 39°C.”
No temperature level makes aspirin safe for children.

alt.q: A patient taking corticosteroids for a chronic condition is admitted with possible infection. Why does the nurse monitor this patient closely?
alt.a: Corticosteroids can mask signs and symptoms of infection
alt.ex: Corticosteroids reduce heat production by interfering with the hypothalamic response, masking signs of infection.
w: Corticosteroids cause high fevers with every infection
Steroids tend to blunt, not exaggerate, the fever response.
Corticosteroids are the antipyretic of choice
Corticosteroids are not used to treat fever.
Corticosteroids increase sweating and fluid loss
The concern is masking infection, not increased sweating.

items.q: A nurse screens a child’s temperature with a chemical dot thermometer, and the result will guide a treatment decision. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Confirm the reading with an electronic thermometer
items.ex: Chemical dot thermometers often underestimate oral temperature by 0.4°C or more, so an electronic reading confirms them.
w: Accept the reading because chemical dots are exact
Chemical dots often underestimate oral temperature.
Add 1°C to the reading to correct it
Readings are confirmed with an electronic thermometer, not adjusted by a fixed amount.
Repeat the reading with the same dot strip
Most chemical dot thermometers are single use and still underestimate.

alt.q: For which patient is a chemical dot thermometer especially useful?
alt.a: A patient on protective isolation
alt.ex: Chemical dot thermometers avoid taking electronic instruments into isolation rooms and are useful for patients with mouth sores.
w: A patient needing a treatment decision based on an exact value
Chemical dots underestimate, so an electronic reading is needed for treatment decisions.
A patient who needs continuous core temperature monitoring
Continuous core readings come from invasive devices such as pulmonary artery catheters.
A patient whose rectal temperature must be measured
Chemical dot thermometers are for oral use.

items.q: Which nursing interventions are appropriate for a febrile patient, unless contraindicated? Select all that apply.
o: Allow rest periods and limit physical activity
Reducing activity minimizes heat production and oxygen demand.
Reduce external coverings without causing shivering
Removing coverings maximizes heat loss; shivering would increase heat production.
Provide fluids for patients with normal cardiac and renal function
Fluids replace losses from insensible water loss and sweating.
Encourage oral hygiene
Oral mucous membranes dry easily from dehydration.
Give a tepid sponge bath
Tepid sponge baths cause shivering and are avoided.
Apply ice packs to the axillae and groin
Ice packs lead to shivering, which raises body temperature.
items.ex: Box 29.5 interventions minimize heat production, maximize heat loss, meet metabolic needs, and promote comfort without inducing shivering.

alt.q: A nurse is planning care for a patient with a fever. Which actions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the patient, clothing, and bed linen dry
Keeping the patient dry maximizes heat loss and comfort.
Control room temperature at 21° to 27°C (70° to 80°F)
Box 29.5 recommends this environmental temperature range.
Review previous temperatures for trends
Examining trends identifies onset and duration of febrile phases.
Encourage frequent ambulation to burn off heat
Activity increases heat production and oxygen demand.
Bathe the patient with an alcohol-water solution
Alcohol-water baths cause shivering and are avoided.
alt.ex: Fever care keeps the patient dry, controls the environment, tracks trends, and limits activity.

items.q: Which findings are signs and symptoms of heatstroke? Select all that apply.
o: Hot, dry skin
Hot, dry skin is the most important sign of heatstroke.
Confusion or delirium
Central nervous system abnormalities occur with heatstroke.
Excessive thirst
Excessive thirst is listed among heatstroke symptoms.
Muscle cramps
Muscle cramps are a sign of heatstroke.
Profuse sweating
People with heatstroke do not sweat; profuse diaphoresis suggests heat exhaustion.
Slowed heart rate
Heatstroke causes an increase, not a decrease, in heart rate.
items.ex: Heatstroke presents with temperature of 40°C or more, hot dry skin, CNS changes, thirst, nausea, cramps, tachycardia, and low BP.

alt.q: Which patients are at increased risk for heatstroke? Select all that apply.
o: An athlete training hard in hot weather
Exertional heatstroke develops in able-bodied people doing rigorous activity.
An older adult with cardiovascular disease
Nonexertional heatstroke can develop in elderly people with comorbidities.
A patient taking a diuretic
Diuretics decrease the body’s ability to lose heat.
A young adult resting in an air-conditioned room
A cool environment and rest do not overwhelm heat-loss mechanisms.
A patient with a core temperature of 34°C
34°C is hypothermia, not a heatstroke risk.
alt.ex: Risk includes exertion in heat, older age with comorbidities, and medications that impair heat loss.

items.q: Which individuals are at risk for hypothermia? Select all that apply.
o: An older adult living in a home with inadequate heating
Older adults and people with inadequate home heating are at risk.
A person who is intoxicated with alcohol
Drug or alcohol intoxication increases hypothermia risk.
A patient debilitated by sepsis
Sepsis is listed among debilitating conditions that increase risk.
A newborn exposed to a cool environment
The very young have immature temperature control.
A healthy young adult exercising in hot weather
This person is at risk for heat-related illness, not hypothermia.
An adult resting in a warm, well-heated room
A warm environment protects against heat loss.
items.ex: Those at risk include the very young and very old and people debilitated by trauma, stroke, diabetes, intoxication, or sepsis.

alt.q: Which factors contribute to the risk of frostbite? Select all that apply.
o: Fatigue
Fatigue contributes to frostbite risk.
Malnutrition
Malnutrition contributes to frostbite risk.
Hypoxemia
Hypoxemia contributes to frostbite risk.
Wearing several layers of clothing
Layers reduce conductive heat loss and protect against cold injury.
Staying in a warm room
A warm environment prevents rather than causes frostbite.
alt.ex: Fatigue, dark skin color, malnutrition, and hypoxemia contribute to frostbite risk.

items.q: Tepid sponge baths and ice packs to the axillae and groin are recommended to reduce fever.
items.a: False
items.ex: These therapies lead to shivering, which raises body temperature, and have no advantage over antipyretics.
items.ww: They were used in the past, but the book now says to avoid them because they cause shivering.

alt.q: Cooling measures that cause shivering should be avoided because shivering increases energy expenditure, oxygen demand, and body temperature.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Shivering is counterproductive in fever, so nursing cooling measures must not stimulate it.
alt.ww: Shivering produces heat, so it works against fever reduction rather than helping.

items.q: In healthy people, body temperature usually reaches its daily maximum at about 4:00 p.m.
items.a: True
items.ex: Body temperature rises steadily during the day to a maximum at about 4:00 p.m., then declines.
items.ww: Peak temperature occurs in the late afternoon, not the early morning.

alt.q: A person who starts working nights reverses the circadian temperature pattern within 1 to 2 days.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: It takes 1 to 3 weeks for the circadian temperature cycle to reverse in night workers.
alt.ww: Temperature patterns are not automatically reversed; the change takes weeks, not days.

items.q: Rectal temperatures are usually about 0.5°C (0.9°F) higher than oral temperatures.
items.a: True
items.ex: Average rectal temperature is 37.5°C compared with an average oral temperature of 37°C.
items.ww: Rectal readings are higher, not lower, than oral readings.

alt.q: Oral temperatures are usually about 0.5°C (0.9°F) higher than rectal temperatures.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Rectal temperatures are usually 0.5°C higher than oral temperatures, not lower.
alt.ww: The rectal site gives the higher reading of the two.

items.q: Hypothermia is a core body temperature of less than [[35]]°C (95°F).
items.ex: A core temperature below 35°C means heat loss has overwhelmed the body’s ability to produce heat.

alt.q: A core temperature below 35°C (95°F) is defined as [[hypothermia]].
alt.ex: A core temperature below 35°C means heat loss has overwhelmed the body’s ability to produce heat.

ord.q: Put the phases of a febrile episode in order, from onset to resolution.
items: Hypothalamus raises the set point; the patient has chills and shivers while temperature rises

The set point drops; the skin becomes warm and flushed and diaphoresis occurs

items.q: What does Radiation mean as a mechanism of heat loss?
items.a: Transfer of heat between surfaces without direct contact
items.ex: Radiation, conduction, convection, and evaporation account for constant normal heat loss from the skin.
w: Transfer of heat from one object to another through direct contact
That goes with Conduction.
Transfer of heat away from the body by air movement
That goes with Convection.
Transfer of heat energy when a liquid changes to a gas
That goes with Evaporation.

items.q: A patient’s condition suddenly worsens, and the nurse cannot palpate the radial pulse. Which site should the nurse use to quickly assess the pulse?
items.a: Carotid
items.ex: When cardiac output declines and peripheral pulses weaken, the carotid site is recommended for quickly finding the pulse.
w: Dorsalis pedis
This distal site weakens early when cardiac output falls.
Posterior tibial
This distal site is used to assess circulation to the foot, not in sudden deterioration.
Ulnar
The ulnar site assesses circulation to the hand and is not used for rapid assessment in collapse.

alt.q: Why is the carotid artery recommended for assessing the pulse when cardiac output declines significantly?
alt.a: The heart continues to deliver blood to the brain through it as long as possible
alt.ex: Peripheral pulses weaken first, but blood flow to the brain through the carotid persists as long as possible.
w: It is the only pulse site that can be auscultated
The apical pulse is the site auscultated with a stethoscope.
It reflects circulation to the lower leg and foot
Popliteal, posterior tibial, and dorsalis pedis sites reflect lower limb circulation.
It is the easiest site for patients to check on themselves
The radial pulse is used to teach patients self-monitoring.

items.q: Which site is best for assessing the pulse rate of a 9-month-old infant?
items.a: Apical
items.ex: The brachial or apical pulse is best in infants and young children because other peripheral pulses are deep and hard to palpate.
w: Radial
The radial pulse is deep and difficult to palpate accurately in an infant.
Femoral
The femoral site is used in shock or cardiac arrest, not for routine infant pulse rates.
Dorsalis pedis
This site assesses circulation to the foot, not the infant’s pulse rate.

alt.q: A nurse wants to palpate a peripheral pulse in an 8-month-old infant. Which site is best?
alt.a: Brachial
alt.ex: The brachial pulse, like the apical, is the best site in infants because other peripheral pulses are deep.
w: Radial
The radial pulse is difficult to palpate accurately in infants.
Popliteal
The popliteal site assesses circulation to the lower leg.
Posterior tibial
This site assesses circulation to the foot.

items.q: A patient takes a medication that affects heart rate, and the nurse palpates an irregular radial pulse. Which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Auscultate the apical pulse
items.ex: If the radial pulse is abnormal or the patient takes drugs affecting HR, the apical pulse gives a more accurate rate.
w: Palpate the radial pulse on the other wrist instead
An abnormal radial pulse calls for apical auscultation, not another peripheral site.
Record the radial rate and recheck at the next scheduled time
Delaying misses the more accurate apical assessment needed now.
Count the radial pulse for 15 seconds and multiply by 4
A short peripheral count is less accurate when the rhythm is irregular.

alt.q: A patient has a cast covering the wrist. Which site should the nurse use to assess the pulse rate?
alt.a: Apical
alt.ex: When the radial pulse is inaccessible because of a dressing or cast, assess the apical pulse.
w: Ulnar
The ulnar pulse is also at the wrist, under the cast.
Temporal
The temporal site is mainly used to assess pulse in children.
Popliteal
The popliteal site assesses circulation to the lower leg, not the routine pulse rate.

items.q: A nurse and a colleague count a patient’s pulses at the same time. The apical rate is 96 beats/min and the radial rate is 80 beats/min. What is the pulse deficit?
items.a: 16 beats
items.ex: The pulse deficit is the difference between the apical and radial rates: 96 − 80 = 16.
w: 8 beats
This is half the actual difference between the two rates.
80 beats
80 is the radial rate, not the deficit.
176 beats
Adding the two rates does not give the deficit.

alt.q: How should a nurse assess a patient for a pulse deficit?
alt.a: Two nurses count the apical and radial rates at the same time and compare them
alt.ex: A pulse deficit is found by simultaneous apical and radial counts by two people, then calculating the difference.
w: One nurse counts the radial rate, then the apical rate 10 minutes later
Counts must be simultaneous to compare the same heartbeats.
One nurse compares the left and right radial pulses at the same time
This assesses equality, not a pulse deficit.
One nurse compares the carotid pulses on both sides at the same time
Carotid pulses are never assessed simultaneously.

items.q: A patient’s heart rate is 80 beats/min and the stroke volume is 70 mL/beat. What is the cardiac output?
items.a: 5600 mL/min
items.ex: Cardiac output is HR multiplied by stroke volume: 80 × 70 = 5600 mL/min.
w: 150 mL/min
Adding HR and SV does not give cardiac output.
4900 mL/min
4900 mL/min results from a HR of 70, not 80.
5100 mL/min
5100 mL/min results from 60 beats/min × 85 mL/beat.

alt.q: Which statement correctly defines cardiac output?
alt.a: The volume of blood the heart pumps in 1 minute
alt.ex: Cardiac output is the product of HR and ventricular stroke volume, normally about 5000 mL/min in an adult.
w: The volume of blood ejected with each ventricular contraction
That is the stroke volume, about 60 to 70 mL.
The number of pulsing sensations felt in 1 minute
That is the pulse rate.
The difference between the apical and radial rates
That is the pulse deficit.

items.q: A patient’s stroke volume cannot change, and the heart rate increases. Which effect does the nurse expect?
items.a: BP decreases because ventricular filling time is shorter
items.ex: As HR increases, the ventricles have less time to fill; when SV cannot change, BP decreases.
w: BP increases because filling time is longer
Filling time lengthens when HR slows, not when it increases.
BP stays the same because output never changes
When SV is fixed, a change in HR changes cardiac output.
Stroke volume rises to match the faster rate
The stem states SV cannot change, so it cannot rise.

alt.q: A patient’s heart rate slows. What happens to ventricular filling time and blood pressure?
alt.a: Filling time increases, and BP increases
alt.ex: A slower HR gives the ventricles more time to fill, and BP increases.
w: Filling time decreases, and BP decreases
This describes a faster heart rate.
Filling time increases, and BP decreases
More filling time leads to higher, not lower, BP.
Filling time decreases, and BP increases
A slower rate lengthens, not shortens, filling time.

items.q: While assessing a 5-year-old, the nurse notes the heart rate speeds up with inspiration and slows with expiration. Which action is best?
items.a: Have the child hold their breath and recheck the rhythm
items.ex: Sinus dysrhythmia is a normal finding in children; the HR usually becomes regular when the child holds their breath.
w: Report a dangerous dysrhythmia to the provider at once
Sinus dysrhythmia in children is a normal finding, not an emergency.
Request a 24-hour Holter monitor for the child
A normal childhood finding does not require Holter monitoring.
Recount the rate using the radial pulse
The radial pulse is hard to palpate in young children and does not verify the finding.

alt.q: A parent asks why their child’s heartbeat speeds up when breathing in. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “This is a normal finding in children called sinus dysrhythmia.”
alt.ex: Sinus dysrhythmia is an irregular heartbeat with inspiration and expiration that is normal in children.
w: “This means your child needs an urgent heart evaluation.”
Sinus dysrhythmia is normal and does not need urgent evaluation.
“This means your child has a pulse deficit.”
A pulse deficit is a difference between apical and radial rates.
“This happens only when a child has a fever.”
Sinus dysrhythmia relates to breathing, not fever.

items.q: A nurse observes a student assessing a patient’s pulses. Which action by the student requires the nurse to intervene?
items.a: Palpating both carotid arteries at the same time
items.ex: Carotid pulses are never measured simultaneously because excessive pressure occludes blood supply to the brain.
w: Palpating both radial pulses at the same time
Symmetrical pulses other than the carotid are assessed simultaneously.
Comparing the strength of both dorsalis pedis pulses
Comparing symmetrical pulses assesses equality and is correct.
Assessing the apical pulse with a stethoscope
Auscultating the apical pulse is an appropriate technique.

alt.q: Why should a nurse never palpate both carotid pulses at the same time?
alt.a: Excessive pressure can occlude the blood supply to the brain
alt.ex: Simultaneous carotid palpation risks occluding cerebral blood flow, so carotids are assessed one side at a time.
w: It prevents the nurse from counting the heart rate
The concern is reduced blood flow to the brain, not counting.
Carotid pulses are too weak to feel bilaterally
Carotid pulses are strong and easily accessible.
It always causes a falsely high pulse rate
The danger is occluding cerebral blood flow, not a false reading.

items.q: A nurse palpates a radial pulse that is diminished and barely palpable. How should the nurse document its strength?
items.ex: Pulse strength is graded 0 to 4; diminished or barely palpable is documented as 1.
w: A grade of 0 means the pulse is absent.
A grade of 2 is normal and expected.
A grade of 3 is full or strong.

alt.q: A nurse documents a patient’s pulse strength as 3. What does this mean?
alt.a: Full or strong
alt.ex: On the 0 to 4 scale, a pulse of 3 is full or strong.
w: Bounding
Bounding is graded 4.
Normal and expected
Normal and expected is graded 2.
Diminished or barely palpable
Diminished or barely palpable is graded 1.

items.q: A nurse measures resting heart rates on four adult patients. Which value meets the definition of tachycardia?
items.a: 112 beats/min
items.ex: Tachycardia is an abnormally elevated HR, above 100 beats/min in adults.
w: 64 beats/min
64 beats/min is within the adult range of 60 to 100.
88 beats/min
88 beats/min is within the adult range.
96 beats/min
96 beats/min is high-normal but not above 100.

alt.q: A nurse measures resting heart rates on four adult patients. Which value meets the definition of bradycardia?
alt.a: 52 beats/min
alt.ex: Bradycardia is a slow rate, below 60 beats/min in adults.
w: 62 beats/min
62 beats/min is within the adult range of 60 to 100.
78 beats/min
78 beats/min is within the adult range.
104 beats/min
104 beats/min is tachycardia, not bradycardia.

items.q: A nurse is using the bell of a stethoscope to listen to low-pitched heart sounds. Which technique is correct?
items.a: Rest the bell lightly on the skin
items.ex: The bell is applied lightly; pressing it firmly creates a “diaphragm of skin” and reduces low-pitched sounds.
w: Press the bell firmly against the skin
Firm pressure converts the bell into a diaphragm and reduces low-pitched amplification.
Hold the bell in place with the thumb
The nurse may hear their own pulse through the thumb.
Place the bell over the patient’s gown
Clothing obscures sound, so the chest piece goes directly on skin.

alt.q: A nurse is auscultating a patient’s bowel sounds. Which technique is correct?
alt.a: Press the diaphragm firmly on bare skin with a tight seal
alt.ex: The diaphragm transmits high-pitched sounds and is placed directly on skin, pressed firmly to make a tight seal.
w: Rest the bell lightly over the patient’s gown
Clothing obscures sound, and the diaphragm is preferred for bowel sounds.
Hold the diaphragm in place with the thumb
The nurse may hear their own pulse through the thumb.
Use the bell pressed lightly on the abdomen
Bowel sounds are high pitched and are auscultated with the diaphragm.

items.q: Which factors increase a patient’s pulse rate? Select all that apply.
o: Fever
Fever and heat increase the pulse rate.
Hemorrhage
Blood loss increases sympathetic stimulation and pulse rate.
Anxiety
Anxiety increases sympathetic stimulation, which affects HR.
Acute pain
Acute pain increases sympathetic activity and HR.
A beta-adrenergic blocker
Beta blockers are negative chronotropic drugs that decrease HR.
Hypothermia
Hypothermia decreases the pulse rate.
items.ex: Table 29.5 lists short-term exercise, fever, acute pain, anxiety, hemorrhage, standing, and positive chronotropes as increasing pulse rate.

alt.q: Which factors decrease a patient’s pulse rate? Select all that apply.
o: Hypothermia
Low body temperature decreases HR.
Lying down
HR decreases when lying compared with standing or sitting.
Digitalis
Digitalis is a negative chronotropic drug.
Epinephrine
Epinephrine is a positive chronotropic drug that increases HR.
Short-term exercise
Short-term exercise increases pulse rate.
alt.ex: Hypothermia, lying down, a conditioned heart, and negative chronotropes such as digitalis lower the pulse rate.

items.q: A nurse is assessing a patient’s radial pulse. Which characteristics should the nurse assess? Select all that apply.
o: Rate
Rate is part of radial pulse assessment.
Rhythm
Rhythm is part of radial pulse assessment.
Strength
Strength reflects the volume ejected and arterial condition.
Equality
Radial pulses are compared on both sides for equality.
Pulse pressure
Pulse pressure is a blood pressure value, not a pulse characteristic.
Oxygen saturation
SpO2 is measured with a pulse oximeter, not by palpation.
items.ex: Radial pulse assessment includes rate, rhythm, strength, and equality.

alt.q: A nurse is auscultating a patient’s apical pulse. Which characteristics does the nurse assess? Select all that apply.
o: Rate
Rate is assessed when auscultating the apical pulse.
Rhythm
Rhythm is assessed when auscultating the apical pulse.
Strength
Strength is assessed by palpating a peripheral pulse, not by apical auscultation.
Equality
Equality compares symmetrical peripheral pulses.
Pulse deficit alone, without a radial count
A deficit requires simultaneous apical and radial counts.
alt.ex: When auscultating an apical pulse, assess rate and rhythm only.

items.q: In which situations should a nurse assess peripheral pulses such as the brachial or femoral? Select all that apply.
o: During a complete physical examination
Other peripheral pulses are assessed during a complete physical.
After surgery that may have impaired blood flow to a limb
Surgery or treatment that impairs blood flow calls for peripheral pulse checks.
When there are clinical signs of impaired peripheral blood flow
Clinical indications of impaired flow warrant peripheral pulse assessment.
Every time routine vital signs are measured
Assessing other peripheral pulses is unnecessary for routine VS.
Whenever the radial pulse is regular and strong
A normal radial pulse does not by itself call for other sites.
items.ex: Peripheral pulses beyond the radial are assessed in a complete physical, after treatment that impairs flow, or with signs of impaired flow.

alt.q: Which patients most need an assessment of pulses beyond the radial pulse? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with a new leg cast who reports numb toes
Signs of impaired peripheral blood flow call for distal pulse checks.
A patient after femoral artery catheterization
A procedure that may impair blood flow to a limb calls for peripheral pulse checks.
A patient admitted for a full physical assessment
A complete physical includes other peripheral pulses.
A stable patient having routine 4-hour vital signs
Routine VS need only the usual pulse site.
A patient being taught to count their own radial pulse

items.q: A Holter monitor allows immediate treatment when a patient’s heart rhythm becomes erratic.
items.a: False
items.ex: A Holter monitor records 24 hours of activity that is not available until the recording is reviewed.
items.ww: Immediate response is possible with telemetry, which transmits continuously to a stationary monitor.

alt.q: Cardiac telemetry provides continuous monitoring that allows immediate treatment if the rhythm becomes unstable.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Telemetry transmits the heart’s electrical activity continuously to a monitor during all daily activities.
alt.ww: Unlike a Holter monitor, telemetry data are seen in real time.

items.q: If a nurse detects an abnormal rate while palpating a peripheral pulse, the next step is to assess the apical rate.

items.ex: Auscultating the apical rate provides a more accurate assessment of cardiac contraction.
items.ww: A peripheral count alone may miss beats that do not produce a pulse wave.

alt.q: For a patient taking a medication that affects heart rate, the radial pulse gives a more accurate rate than the apical pulse.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: When a patient takes medication that affects HR, the apical pulse is more accurate.
alt.ww: The apical site, not the radial, is preferred when drugs affect heart rate.

items.q: Heart rate temporarily increases when a person changes from a lying to a standing position.
items.a: True
items.ex: Postural changes alter blood volume and sympathetic activity, raising HR when sitting or standing.
items.ww: Standing increases rather than decreases the pulse rate.

alt.q: Heart rate temporarily decreases when a person changes from a lying to a sitting position.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: HR temporarily increases, not decreases, with a change from lying to sitting or standing.
alt.ww: Lying down is the posture associated with a lower pulse rate.

items.q: The difference between the apical and radial pulse rates is the [[pulse deficit]].
items.ex: A pulse deficit reflects heart contractions that fail to transmit a pulse wave to the periphery.

alt.q: Inefficient contractions that fail to reach the radial site create a [[pulse deficit]], found by comparing apical and radial rates.
alt.ex: A pulse deficit reflects heart contractions that fail to transmit a pulse wave to the periphery.

items.q: The volume of blood entering the aorta with each ventricular contraction, about 60 to 70 mL, is the [[stroke volume|SV]].
items.ex: Each stroke volume ejection distends the aorta and creates the pulse wave.

alt.q: Cardiac output equals heart rate multiplied by [[stroke volume|SV]].
alt.ex: Each stroke volume ejection distends the aorta and creates the pulse wave.
