items.q: Which process of respiration is the movement of oxygen and carbon dioxide between the alveoli and the red blood cells?
items.a: Diffusion
items.ex: Diffusion is the movement of O2 and CO2 between the alveoli and red blood cells.
w: Ventilation
Ventilation is the mechanical movement of gases into and out of the lungs.
Perfusion
Perfusion is the distribution of red blood cells to and from the pulmonary capillaries.
Exhalation
Exhalation is one part of ventilation, not gas exchange at the alveoli.

alt.q: Which description defines ventilation?
alt.a: Mechanical movement of gases into and out of the lungs
alt.ex: Ventilation is assessed by respiratory rate, depth, rhythm, and EtCO2.
w: Movement of gases between alveoli and red blood cells
This is diffusion.
Distribution of red blood cells to and from pulmonary capillaries
This is perfusion.
Release of oxygen from hemoglobin into the tissues
This is oxygen delivery at the tissues, not ventilation.

items.q: What is the most important factor in the control of ventilation in a healthy person?
items.a: The level of carbon dioxide in the arterial blood
items.ex: An elevated CO2 level causes the brain to increase the rate and depth of breathing.
w: The level of oxygen in the arterial blood
Low O2 drives breathing mainly in patients with chronic lung disease.
The hemoglobin level in the blood
Hemoglobin affects oxygen-carrying capacity, not the main control of ventilation.
The temperature of the inhaled air
Air temperature is not a factor in the control of ventilation.

alt.q: In a patient with chronic lung disease and ongoing hypercarbia, what helps control ventilation?
alt.a: Hypoxemia sensed by chemoreceptors in the carotid artery and aorta
alt.ex: In chronic lung disease, chemoreceptors become sensitive to low arterial O2 and signal the brain to increase ventilation.
w: Rising carbon dioxide levels sensed by the brainstem
These patients have ongoing hypercarbia, so CO2 is no longer the main drive.
Stretch receptors sensing a tidal volume of 500 mL
The book does not identify tidal volume as the drive for these patients.
Decreased hemoglobin levels sensed by the kidneys
Hemoglobin levels are not the ventilatory drive described for chronic lung disease.

items.q: A nurse assesses four patients. Which respiratory finding is most important to report to the health care provider?
items.a: A patient with head trauma whose respiratory rate has fallen from 16 to 9 breaths/min
items.ex: A decrease in respirations after head trauma often signifies injury to the brainstem, where the respiratory center is located.
w: A patient whose rate is 22 breaths/min right after walking in the hall
Exercise increases rate and depth; this is an expected response.
A patient whose rate is 14 breaths/min and deep after a bronchodilator
Bronchodilators slow rate and improve depth; this shows an effective response.
A resting patient whose rate is 18 breaths/min and regular
18 breaths/min and regular is within the adult range.

alt.q: Which adult finding is a better predictor of cardiac arrest within 72 hours than heart rate or blood pressure?
alt.a: A respiratory rate greater than 27 breaths/min
alt.ex: Respiratory rate is the most sensitive indicator of acute deterioration; a rate above 27 predicts cardiac arrest within 72 hours.
w: A respiratory rate of 12 to 20 breaths/min
12 to 20 breaths/min is the normal adult range.
A respiratory rate of 15 to 20 breaths/min
This is within the normal adult range.
A respiratory rate of 20 to 25 breaths/min
This range is mildly elevated but not the threshold cited for predicting arrest.

items.q: Which action by the nurse best ensures an accurate respiratory rate?
items.a: Count respirations right after the pulse, with the hand still on the wrist over the chest
items.ex: Counting without the patient’s awareness prevents the patient from changing the rate and depth of breathing.
w: Tell the patient to breathe normally while the nurse counts
Awareness of the assessment can change the patient’s breathing.
Estimate the rate by watching the patient briefly from the doorway
Respirations must never be estimated.
Use the pulse oximeter reading in place of counting the rate
SpO2 should not take the place of assessing respiratory rate.

alt.q: Why does a nurse avoid letting a patient know that respirations are being assessed?
alt.a: The patient can change the rate and depth of breathing
alt.ex: When aware of the assessment, a patient can alter breathing, giving an inaccurate measurement.
w: The patient may stop breathing until the count is complete
The concern is a voluntary change in rate and depth, not apnea.
The patient’s pulse rate will become irregular
Awareness affects breathing, which is what is being measured.
The patient may refuse all further vital sign checks
The reason relates to accuracy, not refusal.

items.q: An adult’s respirations are irregular at about 26 breaths/min. How long should the nurse count the respirations?
items.a: 60 seconds
items.ex: High and irregular rates require a full 60-second count; 15- and 30-second counts are unreliable.
w: 15 seconds, then multiply by 4
Short counts lead to rounding errors, especially with high rates.
30 seconds, then multiply by 2
30-second counts are unreliable with high or irregular rates.
10 seconds, then multiply by 6
Very short counts multiply any error and are not recommended.

alt.q: Which statement by a new nurse shows understanding of counting respirations?
alt.a: “I count for a full minute when the rate is irregular or outside 12 to 20.”
alt.ex: A full minute count is needed when rhythm is irregular and rate is below 12 or above 20.
w: “I count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 for every patient.”
15-second counts are unreliable, especially at higher rates.
“I estimate the rate if the patient looks comfortable.”
Respirations should never be estimated.
“I use the SpO2 value when I am short on time.”
Pulse oximetry should not replace assessing respiratory rate.

items.q: During a normal, relaxed breath, a person inhales about 500 mL of air. What is this volume called?
items.a: Tidal volume
items.ex: The 500 mL inhaled during a normal, relaxed breath is the tidal volume.
w: Stroke volume
Stroke volume is the blood ejected with each ventricular contraction.
Cardiac output
Cardiac output is blood pumped by the heart per minute.
Eupnea
Eupnea is the normal rate and depth of ventilation, not a volume.

alt.q: About how much air does an adult inhale during a normal, relaxed breath?
alt.a: 500 mL
alt.ex: Tidal volume, the air inhaled in a normal relaxed breath, is about 500 mL.
w: 70 mL
About 60 to 70 mL is the stroke volume of blood, not air.
2 L is the fluid that can be lost in sweat per hour of exercise in heat.
5000 mL per minute is the normal adult cardiac output.

items.q: Which statement accurately describes expiration during normal breathing?
items.a: It is a passive process in which the diaphragm relaxes
items.ex: During expiration the diaphragm relaxes and the lungs and chest wall return to a relaxed position.
w: It is an active process driven by the phrenic nerve
Phrenic nerve impulses cause diaphragm contraction during inspiration.
It requires visible use of the neck accessory muscles
Accessory muscle use is not visible during quiet breathing.
It moves the abdominal organs downward and forward
Abdominal organs move down and forward during inspiration.

alt.q: Which event occurs during inspiration?
alt.a: The respiratory center sends impulses along the phrenic nerve, and the diaphragm contracts
alt.ex: Inspiration is active: the diaphragm contracts and abdominal organs move downward and forward.
w: The diaphragm relaxes, and abdominal organs return to their positions
This describes expiration.
The lungs and chest wall return to a relaxed position
This describes expiration.
The intercostal spaces retract as air leaves the lungs
Intercostal retraction is abnormal and occurs with obstruction.

items.q: A patient’s SpO2 falls to 89%. How should the nurse interpret this value?
items.a: It is considered a medical emergency
items.ex: Normal saturation is greater than 95%, and a saturation below 90% is considered a medical emergency.
w: It is a normal value for an adult
Normal SpO2 is greater than 95%.
It is low but not a concern until below 80%
A saturation below 90% is already an emergency.
It is the critical value at which tissues cannot extract oxygen
The critical value is 75% or less.

alt.q: At what SpO2 value are the tissues considered unable to extract enough oxygen for vital functions?
alt.a: 75% or less
alt.ex: An SpO2 of 75% or less is a critical value.
w: Less than 95%
Less than 95% is below normal but not the critical value.
Less than 90%
Below 90% is a medical emergency, but the critical value is 75% or less.
85% or less
85% is an emergency value but above the 75% critical threshold.

items.q: A patient rescued from a house fire has an SpO2 reading of 99%. How should the nurse interpret this reading?
items.a: It may be falsely elevated by carbon monoxide
items.ex: Carbon monoxide from smoke inhalation absorbs light like oxygen and artificially elevates SpO2.
w: It confirms that oxygenation is adequate
Carbon monoxide can make SpO2 appear normal when it is not.
It is falsely lowered by soot on the skin
The concern with smoke inhalation is a falsely high reading.
It shows the probe is placed too tightly
A tight probe records venous pulsations; it does not explain this reading.

alt.q: A patient received methylene blue dye during a procedure. How does this affect pulse oximetry?
alt.a: It artificially lowers the SpO2 reading
alt.ex: Intravascular dyes such as methylene blue absorb light like deoxyhemoglobin and artificially lower saturation.
w: It artificially raises the SpO2 reading
Carbon monoxide, not methylene blue, raises SpO2.
It has no effect on the SpO2 reading
The dye interferes with light absorption.
It improves accuracy at low saturations
The dye interferes with, rather than improves, the reading.

items.q: A patient with hypothermia has cold fingers, and the finger probe gives a poor signal. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Apply an earlobe or forehead sensor
items.ex: For decreased peripheral perfusion, an earlobe or forehead sensor is used; earlobe probes are least affected by vasoconstriction.
w: Tighten the finger probe to improve contact
A tight probe records venous pulsations that compete with arterial pulsations.
Move the probe to a finger with dark nail polish
Black or brown nail polish interferes with light absorption.
Accept the reading displayed on the oximeter
Reduced blood flow at the site makes the reading unreliable.

alt.q: Why is an earlobe probe preferred for a patient with heart failure and decreased peripheral perfusion?
alt.a: It is more accurate at lower saturations and least affected by vasoconstriction
alt.ex: Earlobe probes have greater accuracy at lower saturations and are least affected by peripheral vasoconstriction.
w: It is the only probe that measures exhaled carbon dioxide
Exhaled CO2 is measured by capnography.
It is the only probe unaffected by patient movement
Patient motion interferes with oximetry at any site.
It measures venous rather than arterial saturation
Pulse oximetry measures arterial pulsatile flow, not SvO2.

items.q: After a nurse suctions secretions from a patient’s airway, which finding shows the intervention was effective?
items.a: Respiratory rate decreases and depth increases
items.ex: After suctioning, the respiratory rate should decrease and depth should increase, and SpO2 may improve.
w: Respiratory rate increases and depth decreases
Faster, shallower breathing suggests worsening, not improvement.
Respiratory rate and depth both decrease
Shallower breathing does not indicate a cleared airway.
Intercostal retractions appear during inspiration
Retractions indicate obstruction to air movement.

alt.q: A patient receives a bronchodilator. Which change in respirations indicates an effective response?
alt.a: Respiratory rate decreases and depth improves
alt.ex: Bronchodilators relax constricted airways, which can reduce respiratory rate and improve depth.
w: Respiratory rate increases and breathing becomes shallow
This pattern suggests worsening respiratory status.
Expiration becomes longer than before the dose
A prolonged expiration occurs when outward airflow is obstructed.
Neck accessory muscles become more visible
Accessory muscle use indicates labored breathing.

items.q: Which factors increase a patient’s respiratory rate? Select all that apply.
o: Anemia
Decreased hemoglobin reduces oxygen-carrying capacity and increases respiratory rate.
Increased altitude
Higher altitude lowers saturated hemoglobin, increasing rate and depth.
Anxiety
Sympathetic stimulation increases rate and depth.
Exercise
Exercise increases rate and depth to meet oxygen needs and remove CO2.
Opioid analgesics
Opioids depress the rate and depth of respirations.
Bronchodilators
Bronchodilators slow the rate by dilating the airways.
items.ex: Box 29.6 lists exercise, anxiety, anemia, altitude, and abnormal blood cell function as increasing respiratory rate.

alt.q: Which medications depress the rate and depth of respirations? Select all that apply.
o: Opioid analgesics
Opioids depress respiratory rate and depth.
General anesthetics
General anesthetics depress respiratory rate and depth.
Sedative hypnotics
Sedative hypnotics depress respiratory rate and depth.
Amphetamines
Amphetamines sometimes increase rate and depth.
Cocaine
Cocaine sometimes increases rate and depth.
alt.ex: Opioids, general anesthetics, and sedative hypnotics depress breathing, while amphetamines and cocaine can increase it.

items.q: Which factors interfere with arterial pulsations and affect the accuracy of pulse oximetry? Select all that apply.
o: Peripheral vascular disease
Atherosclerosis reduces pulse volume.
Hypotension
Low cardiac output and hypotension decrease flow to peripheral arteries.
Peripheral edema
Edema obscures arterial pulsation.
Epinephrine infusion
Pharmacological vasoconstrictors decrease peripheral pulse volume.
Jaundice
Jaundice interferes with light transmission, not arterial pulsations.
Outside light sources
Outside light interferes with light processing, not arterial pulsations.
items.ex: Box 29.8 lists PVD, hypothermia at the site, vasoconstrictors, low output and hypotension, edema, and a tight probe as interfering with pulsations.

alt.q: Which factors interfere with light transmission during pulse oximetry? Select all that apply.
o: Patient motion
Motion interferes with processing reflected light.
Black nail polish
Dark nail polish interferes with light absorption.
Jaundice
Jaundice interferes with processing reflected light.
Peripheral edema
Edema interferes with arterial pulsation, not light transmission.
Hypotension
Hypotension reduces arterial flow rather than interfering with light.
alt.ex: Outside light, carbon monoxide, motion, jaundice, dyes, nail polish or thick nails, and dark skin pigment affect light transmission.

items.q: Which findings indicate labored or obstructed breathing? Select all that apply.
o: Visible use of accessory muscles in the neck
Labored respirations usually involve visible accessory muscles.
Intercostal spaces retracting during inspiration
Retractions occur when something obstructs air movement.
A prolonged expiration phase
Longer expiration is evident when outward airflow is obstructed, as in asthma or COPD.
Chest wall gently rising and falling
Gentle chest movement is normal quiet breathing.
A regular interval after each respiratory cycle
A regular interval is a normal finding.
items.ex: Accessory muscle use, intercostal retractions, and prolonged expiration signal labored or obstructed breathing.

alt.q: Which findings are expected during normal quiet breathing in an adult? Select all that apply.
o: The chest wall gently rises and falls
During quiet breathing the chest wall gently rises and falls.
Accessory muscle contraction is not visible
Neck and shoulder muscles are not visibly used at rest.
A regular time interval follows each cycle
Normal breathing has a regular interval after each respiratory cycle.
Intercostal spaces retract during inspiration
Retractions indicate obstruction to airflow.
Expiration is markedly longer than inspiration
A prolonged expiration indicates obstructed outflow.
alt.ex: Quiet breathing is smooth and regular without visible accessory or intercostal muscle use.

items.q: A pulse oximetry reading can take the place of counting a patient’s respiratory rate.
items.a: False
items.ex: SpO2 is a component of respiratory assessment but should not replace assessing respiratory rate.
items.ww: Respiratory rate is the most sensitive indicator of acute deterioration and must still be counted.

alt.q: Pulse oximetry values are part of respiratory assessment but should not replace measuring the respiratory rate.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Respiratory rate is often neglected or substituted with SpO2, but it must be assessed directly.
alt.ww: Changes in respiratory rate can signal deterioration before oxygenation values decline.

items.q: Healthy men and children usually demonstrate diaphragmatic breathing, which is best observed by watching abdominal movements.
items.a: True
items.ex: Diaphragmatic breathing comes from diaphragm contraction and relaxation, seen best in the abdomen.
items.ww: It is women who tend to use thoracic muscles, observed in the upper chest.

alt.q: Women tend to use diaphragmatic breathing, which the nurse assesses by watching the abdomen.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Women tend to use thoracic muscles to breathe, assessed by observing the upper chest.
alt.ww: Diaphragmatic breathing is typical of healthy men and children, not women.

items.q: Venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) is usually lower than arterial saturation, at about 65% to 75%.
items.a: True
items.ex: Tissues remove some oxygen from hemoglobin, so SvO2 is lower than arterial saturation, which is normally above 95%.
items.ww: Venous blood has already given oxygen to the tissues, so its saturation cannot be higher.

alt.q: Venous oxygen saturation (SvO2) is normally higher than arterial saturation because blood picks up oxygen in the tissues.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Tissues remove oxygen from hemoglobin, so SvO2 is lower, usually 65% to 75%.
alt.ww: Blood gives up, not picks up, oxygen in the tissues.

items.q: Which event produces the systolic blood pressure?
items.a: Contraction of the ventricles forcing blood into the aorta
items.ex: Systolic pressure is the peak pressure, occurring when the ventricles contract and push blood under high pressure into the aorta.
w: Relaxation of the ventricles as the heart fills
Ventricular relaxation and filling correspond to diastolic pressure, the minimal pressure.
Constriction of peripheral arterioles during rest
Arteriolar tone determines peripheral vascular resistance, not the systolic peak itself.
Closure of the cuff valve during deflation
The cuff valve is part of the measuring equipment, not a cardiac event that creates pressure.

alt.q: Which statement best describes diastolic blood pressure?
alt.a: The minimal pressure on arterial walls while the ventricles relax
alt.ex: Diastolic pressure is the minimal pressure exerted against the arterial walls at all times, present when the ventricles relax and fill.
w: The peak pressure on arterial walls while the ventricles contract
Peak pressure during ventricular contraction is the systolic pressure.
The difference between the systolic and the lowest arterial pressure
The difference between systolic and diastolic pressure is the pulse pressure.
The pressure the cuff must reach before the radial pulse disappears
That palpated value estimates systolic pressure and guides cuff inflation.

items.q: A patient’s blood pressure is 136/84 mm Hg, so the pulse pressure is [[52|52 mm Hg]] mm Hg.
items.ex: Pulse pressure is systolic minus diastolic pressure: 136 − 84 = 52.

alt.q: The difference between the systolic and the diastolic pressure is called the [[pulse pressure]].

items.q: An adult’s average blood pressure over two visits is 126/84 mm Hg. How should the nurse classify this reading?
items.a: Stage 1 hypertension
items.ex: A DBP of 80–89 is stage 1, and when SBP and DBP fall in two categories the patient is placed in the higher one.
w: Elevated blood pressure
Elevated requires a DBP below 80; this DBP of 84 places the patient higher.
Normal blood pressure
Normal requires an SBP below 120 and a DBP below 80.
Stage 2 hypertension
Stage 2 requires an SBP of 140 or more or a DBP of 90 or more.

alt.q: An adult’s average blood pressure over two visits is 124/76 mm Hg. How should the nurse classify this reading?

alt.ex: Elevated BP is an SBP of 120–129 and a DBP below 80, a high-risk group that benefits from early healthy lifestyle changes.
w: Normal blood pressure
Normal requires an SBP below 120; 124 is above that.

items.q: Which change in the hemodynamic variables would cause arterial blood pressure to rise?
items.a: A rising hematocrit that increases blood viscosity
items.ex: Higher hematocrit makes blood more viscous; flow slows and the heart contracts more forcefully, so arterial BP increases.
w: Dilation of arterioles that lowers resistance
When vessels dilate and peripheral resistance falls, arterial BP falls.
Loss of circulating volume from hemorrhage
A fall in circulating blood volume, as in hemorrhage or dehydration, lowers BP.
A very rapid heart rate that shortens filling time
A rapid HR decreases ventricular filling and volume, so BP decreases.

alt.q: A patient has arteriosclerosis with loss of arterial elasticity. Which blood pressure change does the nurse expect?
alt.a: Systolic pressure rises more than diastolic pressure
alt.ex: Rigid vessels no longer yield when the ventricle ejects its stroke volume, so systolic pressure is elevated more than diastolic.
w: Diastolic pressure rises more than systolic pressure
Reduced elasticity affects systolic pressure more significantly than diastolic pressure.
Both pressures fall because vessels cannot constrict
Inelastic vessels increase resistance to flow, so pressure rises rather than falls.
Pressures stay unchanged because blood volume is constant
Elasticity changes alter BP independently of blood volume; rigid walls raise systemic pressure.

items.q: A rapid or significant increase in heart rate always raises blood pressure because cardiac output increases.
items.a: False
items.ex: A rapid or significant HR increase shortens filling time, decreasing left ventricular volume, so BP decreases.
items.ww: Although higher cardiac output raises BP, a very rapid rate reduces filling, so BP does not always rise.

alt.q: A very rapid heart rate can lower blood pressure because it shortens the time the heart has to fill.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Reduced filling time lowers the volume in the left ventricle, so less blood is ejected and BP decreases.
alt.ww: Faster rates do not always raise BP; when filling time is cut short, BP falls.

items.q: Which errors in blood pressure assessment produce a false-high reading? Select all that apply.
o: Using a cuff that is too narrow
A cuff that is too narrow or too short gives a false-high reading.
Positioning the arm below heart level
An arm below heart level produces a false-high reading.
Leaving the arm unsupported
An unsupported arm produces a false-high reading.
Wrapping the cuff too loosely
A cuff wrapped too loosely or unevenly produces a false-high reading.
Using a cuff that is too wide
A bladder or cuff that is too wide gives a false-low reading.
Positioning the arm above heart level
An arm above heart level produces a false-low reading.
items.ex: Narrow or loose cuffs and an arm that is low or unsupported all falsely raise the reading.

alt.q: Which errors in blood pressure assessment produce a false-low reading? Select all that apply.
o: Using a cuff that is too wide
A bladder or cuff that is too wide gives a false-low reading.
Positioning the arm above heart level
An arm above heart level produces a false-low reading.
Inflating the cuff to an inadequate level
Inadequate inflation gives a false-low systolic reading.
Using a cuff that is too narrow
A cuff that is too narrow or too short gives a false-high reading.
Leaving the arm unsupported
An unsupported arm produces a false-high reading.
Positioning the arm below heart level
An arm below heart level produces a false-high reading.
alt.ex: Wide cuffs, a raised arm and inadequate inflation all falsely lower the reading.

items.q: How wide should a blood pressure cuff ideally be?
items.a: 40% of the circumference of the midpoint of the limb
items.ex: Cuff size is proportional to limb circumference: width about 40% of circumference, with the bladder encircling at least 80% of the upper arm.
w: 20% of the circumference of the midpoint of the limb
20% is how much wider than the limb diameter the cuff should be, not the share of circumference.
60% of the circumference of the midpoint of the limb
A cuff this wide is too wide and produces a false-low reading.
80% of the circumference of the midpoint of the limb
80% is the minimum share of the upper arm the bladder should encircle, not the cuff width.

alt.q: A frail older adult has lost upper arm mass. Which cuff choice reflects correct technique?
alt.a: A smaller cuff sized to the patient’s actual arm circumference
alt.ex: Cuff size is chosen in proportion to limb circumference; frail older adults with lost arm mass often need a smaller cuff.
w: The standard adult cuff used for most adult patients
A regular cuff may be too wide for a thin arm and give a false-low reading.
A large adult cuff to avoid a false-high reading
An oversized cuff is too wide and produces a false-low reading.
A regular cuff placed on the forearm instead of the arm
Forearm use is not recommended and can overestimate systolic BP by up to 20 mm Hg.

items.q: During an initial assessment the nurse obtains 148/88 mm Hg in the right arm and 132/80 mm Hg in the left arm. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Report the difference to the health care provider or nurse in charge
items.ex: A normal difference between arms is 5–10 mm Hg; differences greater than 10 mm Hg indicate vascular problems and are reported.
w: Average the two readings and document 140/84 mm Hg
Averaging hides a between-arm difference that suggests a vascular problem needing report.
Document only the left arm reading as the true baseline
Subsequent readings use the higher arm, and this difference must be reported, not ignored.
Recheck both arms in 1 year at the next routine visit
A difference over 10 mm Hg indicates a vascular problem that needs prompt reporting.

alt.q: On admission a patient’s blood pressure is 128/78 mm Hg in the right arm and 122/76 mm Hg in the left arm. How should the nurse measure blood pressure afterward?
alt.a: Use the right arm, the arm with the higher pressure
alt.ex: A 5–10 mm Hg difference between arms is normal; subsequent assessments use the arm with the higher pressure.
w: Use the left arm, the arm with the lower pressure
Subsequent assessments use the arm that had the higher reading, not the lower.
Alternate arms each time and average the results
Consistency is needed for comparison; the higher-reading arm is used for subsequent assessments.
Measure both arms at every assessment from now on
Both arms are needed only on the initial assessment; afterward the higher arm is used.

items.q: When auscultating an adult’s blood pressure, which Korotkoff sound marks the diastolic pressure?
items.a: The fifth sound, when the sounds disappear
items.ex: In adolescents and adults the fifth sound, the disappearance of sound, corresponds with the diastolic pressure.
w: The first sound, a clear rhythmic tapping
Onset of the first sound corresponds to the systolic pressure.
The second sound, a blowing or swishing
The second sound reflects turbulent flow as the artery distends, not diastolic pressure.
The fourth sound, a muffled low-pitched tone
The fourth sound marks diastolic pressure in infants and children, not adults.

alt.q: When auscultating a 6-year-old child’s blood pressure, which Korotkoff sound marks the diastolic pressure?
alt.a: The fourth sound, when the tapping becomes muffled
alt.ex: The muffled, low-pitched fourth sound is the diastolic pressure in infants and children.
w: The fifth sound, when the sounds disappear
The fifth sound marks diastolic pressure in adolescents and adults.
The first sound, when the tapping begins
Onset of the first sound corresponds to the systolic pressure.
The third sound, when the tapping is crispest

items.q: A patient with hypertension may have an auscultatory gap. How does the nurse make sure the true systolic pressure is not missed?
items.a: Palpate the radial pulse and inflate 30 mm Hg above where it disappears
items.ex: Palpating the radial artery shows how high to inflate; inflating 30 mm Hg above that point captures systolic pressure before the gap.
w: Deflate the cuff faster through the expected gap
Deflating too quickly gives a false-low systolic and false-high diastolic reading.
Inflate the cuff 10 mm Hg above the usual reading
The book’s guide is 30 mm Hg above the palpated systolic point, not 10 above the usual value.
Record the fourth sound as the systolic pressure
The fourth sound relates to diastolic pressure; systolic is the onset of the first sound.

alt.q: What is the risk of not recognizing an auscultatory gap in a patient with hypertension?
alt.a: Underestimating the systolic pressure
alt.ex: The gap, usually between the first and second sounds, spans about 40 mm Hg and can cause systolic to be underestimated.
w: Overestimating the systolic pressure
Missing the gap makes the examiner hear the first sound too low, so systolic is underestimated.
Underestimating the diastolic pressure
The gap leads to overestimation of diastolic pressure, not underestimation.
Overestimating the pulse rate
The auscultatory gap affects pressure readings, not the counted pulse rate.

items.q: A patient’s blood pressure is 132/80 mm Hg supine. After standing for 1 minute it is 108/72 mm Hg and the patient reports light-headedness. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Help the patient to a lying position
items.ex: This drop of 24 mm Hg systolic with symptoms is orthostatic hypotension; help the patient lie down, then notify the provider or nurse in charge.
w: Have the patient keep standing for another reading
Continued standing risks a fall; the patient is helped to lie down first.
Walk the patient to the bathroom to stretch the legs
Ambulating a symptomatic patient raises fall risk; orthostatic hypotension is a high-risk factor for falls.
Record the readings and recheck at the next scheduled time
Symptomatic orthostatic hypotension needs immediate action and notification, not just documentation.

alt.q: While walking in the hall, a patient suddenly reports dizziness and blurred vision consistent with orthostatic hypotension. What should the nurse do first?
alt.a: Assist the patient to a chair immediately
alt.ex: If orthostatic hypotension occurs while walking, the nurse assists the patient to a chair immediately to prevent a fall.
w: Walk the patient quickly back to bed
Continuing to walk while symptomatic risks a fall; sit the patient down at once.
Leave to get the electronic blood pressure monitor
Leaving a symptomatic patient standing risks a fall; safety comes before measurement.
Ask the patient to walk slowly while you measure the pulse
Measuring while the patient remains upright delays the safety action of sitting the patient down.

items.q: Orthostatic blood pressure measurement can be delegated to assistive personnel when the patient is stable.
items.a: False
items.ex: Orthostatic BP measurement cannot be delegated because it needs ongoing assessment and judgment about the response to position changes.
items.ww: Even in a stable patient, the nurse must anticipate and judge the physiologic response to position changes.

alt.q: Measuring orthostatic blood pressure stays with the nurse because it requires ongoing assessment and clinical judgment.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The nurse anticipates the response to changing from lying to sitting to standing, so this skill is not delegated.
alt.ww: It is not an AP task; position-change responses require the nurse’s ongoing assessment.

items.q: Which patients are not appropriate candidates for electronic (oscillometric) blood pressure measurement? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with an irregular heart rate
Irregular heart rate is listed as inappropriate for electronic BP devices.
A patient who is shivering
Shivering, seizures and excessive tremors interfere with the device.
A patient whose systolic pressure is below 90 mm Hg
BP less than 90 mm Hg systolic is not appropriate for electronic measurement.
A patient with peripheral vascular obstruction
Clots or narrowed vessels make electronic measurement inappropriate.
A patient who needs readings during IV heart medication therapy
Electronic devices are particularly useful when therapies such as IV heart and BP drugs need frequent monitoring.
items.ex: Box 29.10 lists irregular heart rate, known hypertension, vascular obstruction, shivering, seizures, tremors, inability to cooperate and SBP below 90.

alt.q: A nurse is choosing between manual auscultation and an electronic BP device. Which patients should have a manual measurement? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with known hypertension
Known hypertension is listed as not appropriate for electronic measurement.
A patient having seizures or excessive tremors
Seizures and tremors are listed conditions that interfere with electronic devices.
A patient who is unable to cooperate
Inability to cooperate is listed as inappropriate for electronic BP measurement.
A stable patient who needs readings every 15 minutes after a procedure
Electronic devices are particularly useful when frequent BP checks are needed after procedures.
A patient with a regular rhythm and normal blood pressure
A regular rhythm and normal BP are not contraindications for an electronic device.
alt.ex: Hypertension, seizures, tremors and inability to cooperate call for manual auscultation; frequent checks in stable patients suit electronic devices.

items.q: The nurse is caring for four patients. Which finding is most important to report to the health care provider immediately?
items.a: BP 88/54 mm Hg with pallor, clammy skin and new confusion
items.ex: Hypotension with pallor, clamminess, confusion, rising HR or low urine output is life threatening and is reported immediately.
w: BP 132/84 mm Hg right after walking to the bathroom
Exertion raises BP temporarily; recheck at rest rather than report urgently.
BP 104/66 mm Hg in a patient whose usual BP is 100/64
This reading matches the patient’s baseline trend and is not an acute change.
A 6 mm Hg difference in systolic pressure between arms
A 5–10 mm Hg difference between arms is normal; only more than 10 is reported.

alt.q: Which systolic blood pressure meets the book’s definition of hypotension in an adult?
alt.a: 90 mm Hg or below
alt.ex: Hypotension is present when systolic BP falls to 90 mm Hg or below; for most people it is an abnormal finding linked to illness.
w: 100 mm Hg or below
100 mm Hg is above the hypotension threshold of 90 or below.
110 mm Hg or below
110 mm Hg is well above the hypotension threshold of 90 or below.
80 mm Hg or below
Hypotension starts at 90 mm Hg or below, not only at 80.

items.q: The nurse teaches a patient to measure blood pressure at home. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I will sit in a dining chair with my back supported and my feet flat.”
items.ex: Sitting with the back straight and supported, feet flat and legs uncrossed gives accurate home readings.
w: “I will roll my sleeve down and put the cuff over it so it is snug.”
Measurements are never taken over clothing, which distorts cuff fit and sounds.
“I will check it at a different time each day to see the full range.”
Readings are taken at the same time each day, in the same position and arm.
“I will relax on the sofa with my legs crossed while it inflates.”
A sofa does not support the back, and the legs should not be crossed.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient learning home blood pressure monitoring shows correct technique?
alt.a: “I will take two or three readings 1 minute apart and write each one down.”
alt.ex: Teaching includes taking two or three readings 1 minute apart and documenting each result.
w: “I will take one reading and repeat it only if it feels high.”
Hypertension is usually without symptoms; two or three readings are taken each time.
“I will use whichever arm is easiest each time I check it.”
The same arm and position are used each time for meaningful comparison.
“I will check it right after my walk so I am warmed up.”
Measure after a brief rest; exertion falsely raises readings.

items.q: A single blood pressure reading of 150/90 mm Hg is enough to diagnose hypertension.
items.a: False
items.ex: One high reading does not qualify; diagnosis needs the average of two or more readings at each of two or more visits.
items.ww: BP varies beat to beat, so diagnosis relies on averaged readings across visits, not one value.

alt.q: Diagnosing hypertension requires the average of two or more readings taken at each of two or more visits after screening.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Because BP varies continually, trends from averaged readings over several visits are required for diagnosis.
alt.ww: A single high reading is not diagnostic; repeated averaged readings over separate visits are required.

items.q: A patient’s blood pressure is in the normal range. According to the follow-up recommendations, when should it be rechecked?
items.a: In 1 year
items.ex: For a normal initial blood pressure the recommended follow-up is a recheck in 1 year.
w: In 1 month
A 1-month interval is used for hypertension follow-up, not for a normal reading.
In 1 week
Evaluation within 1 week is for very high stage 2 pressures, depending on the situation.
In 5 years
Normal BP is rechecked yearly, not every 5 years.

alt.q: A patient’s blood pressure is 190/116 mm Hg. Which follow-up is recommended?
alt.a: Evaluate and treat immediately or within 1 week
alt.ex: For pressures above 180/110 mm Hg, evaluate and treat immediately or within 1 week depending on the clinical situation.
w: Recheck in 1 year after lifestyle changes
A yearly recheck is for normal BP, not severe stage 2 hypertension.
Recheck in 3 to 6 months with lifestyle advice
A 3–6 month recheck is for elevated BP, not pressures above 180/110.
Evaluate therapy within 6 months
Pressures above 180/110 need evaluation and treatment immediately or within 1 week.

items.q: Which factors tend to increase a patient’s blood pressure? Select all that apply.
o: Acute pain or anxiety
Pain and emotional stress cause sympathetic stimulation, raising HR, cardiac output and resistance.
Smoking a cigarette
Nicotine is a potent vasoconstrictor; BP rises and returns to baseline about 15 minutes after smoking.
Rapid, uncontrolled infusion of IV fluids
Excess IV fluid increases blood volume and therefore BP.
Decreased elasticity of arteries with aging
Older adults may have increased systolic pressure from decreased vessel elasticity.
Receiving an opioid analgesic
Opioid analgesics are a class of medication that lowers BP.
Completing a period of moderate exercise
Moderate exercise can reduce BP for several hours afterward.
items.ex: Sympathetic stimulation, vasoconstriction, more volume and stiffer arteries all raise BP.

alt.q: Which factors or medications tend to lower a patient’s blood pressure? Select all that apply.
o: A diuretic such as furosemide
Diuretics reduce sodium and water resorption by the kidneys, lowering circulating volume.
A beta-adrenergic blocker such as metoprolol
Beta blockers block sympathetic response, reducing HR and cardiac output.
An opioid analgesic
Opioid analgesics are a class of medication that lowers BP.
A calcium channel blocker such as diltiazem
Calcium channel blockers reduce peripheral resistance through systemic vasodilation.
Nicotine from cigarette smoking
Nicotine causes vasoconstriction, which raises BP.
A vasoconstrictor medication
Vasoconstrictors increase BP.
alt.ex: Diuretics, beta blockers, calcium channel blockers and opioids lower BP; nicotine and vasoconstrictors raise it.

items.q: A nurse delegates temperature measurement for a patient to assistive personnel (AP). Which instruction is appropriate?
items.a: “Use the rectal route with the patient side-lying, and report the value to me.”
items.ex: The nurse communicates the route, device and frequency, any positioning precautions, and asks the AP to report values and changes.
w: “Choose whichever route seems easiest and record it when you can.”
Selecting the route and device is the nurse’s responsibility and is communicated to the AP.
“Only tell me about the temperature if it is above 39°C.”
The AP reports temperature values and any changes, not only very high values.
“If the patient is febrile, decide whether an antipyretic is needed.”
Deciding on treatment requires nursing judgment and is not delegated to AP.

alt.q: Which part of temperature measurement remains the nurse’s responsibility when the skill is delegated to AP?
alt.a: Deciding the route, device and frequency of measurement
alt.ex: The nurse communicates the appropriate route, device and frequency; the AP measures and reports values and changes.
w: Sliding a disposable cover over the probe stem
Applying the probe cover is part of the measurement the AP performs.
Recording the measured value on the flow sheet
AP can record and report the temperature values they obtain.
Positioning the patient side-lying for a rectal reading
AP can position the patient once the nurse explains the precautions needed.

items.q: While reviewing the EHR, the nurse identifies patients at risk for temperature alterations who need more frequent temperature checks. Which conditions apply? Select all that apply.
o: Immunosuppressive drug therapy
Immunosuppression is listed as a risk for temperature alterations.
A white blood cell count of 13,500/mm3
A WBC above 12,000/mm3 or below 5000/mm3 is a listed risk.
Infusion of a blood product
Blood product infusion is a listed risk for temperature alteration.
Injury to the hypothalamus
The hypothalamus regulates temperature, so injury to it is a listed risk.
A white blood cell count of 8000/mm3
8000/mm3 falls between 5000 and 12,000, so it is not a listed risk.
items.ex: Infection, wounds or burns, abnormal WBC, immunosuppression, hypothalamic injury, temperature extremes, blood products and hypo- or hyperthermia therapy raise risk.

alt.q: Which patients have a condition the book lists as a risk for temperature alteration? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with open burn wounds
Open wounds or burns are listed risks for temperature alterations.
A patient receiving hypothermia therapy
Hypothermia or hyperthermia therapy is a listed risk.
A patient with a white blood cell count of 4200/mm3
A WBC below 5000/mm3 is a listed risk.
A patient with a white blood cell count of 9000/mm3
9000/mm3 is between 5000 and 12,000 and is not a listed risk.
A patient with a healed, closed surgical scar
Open wounds are the listed risk, not healed, closed incisions.
alt.ex: Open wounds or burns, temperature therapies and WBC below 5000 or above 12,000 are listed risks.

items.q: Before measuring an oral temperature, verify that the patient has not eaten, had a drink, chewed gum or smoked within the past [[20|twenty]] minutes.
items.ex: Oral food and fluids, smoking and gum can alter oral temperature, so the nurse waits 20 minutes.

alt.q: A patient who just finished a cup of coffee should wait [[20|twenty]] minutes before an oral temperature is taken.
alt.ex: Oral food and fluids, smoking and gum can alter oral temperature, so the nurse waits 20 minutes.

items.q: A patient is receiving oxygen by nasal cannula at 8 L/min. Which approach to temperature measurement is best?
items.a: Choose a site other than the oral route
items.ex: Nasal cannula oxygen above 6 L can make oral readings inaccurate, so another site is chosen.
w: Take the oral reading and add 0.5°C to correct it
No correction factor is given; the oral route is avoided at this flow rate.
Remove the cannula for 20 minutes, then take an oral reading
Stopping prescribed oxygen is unsafe; simply choose another site.
Take the oral reading as usual since oxygen has no effect
Nasal cannula oxygen above 6 L can produce inaccurate oral readings.

alt.q: A patient is receiving oxygen through a face mask. Which statement about oral temperature measurement is accurate?
alt.a: The oral route can be used because face mask oxygen does not cause clinically significant changes
alt.ex: Supplemental oxygen by face mask or endotracheal tube does not cause clinically significant oral temperature changes.
w: The oral route cannot be used because any oxygen falsely lowers readings
Only nasal cannula flow above 6 L is linked to inaccurate oral readings.
The mask must be off for 20 minutes before any oral temperature is taken
Removing prescribed oxygen is unnecessary because face mask oxygen does not alter oral readings significantly.
The oral reading must be confirmed rectally because face masks cool the mouth
No routine rectal confirmation is required for face mask oxygen.

items.q: Where does the nurse place an electronic thermometer probe for an oral temperature?
items.a: In the posterior sublingual pocket lateral to the center of the lower jaw
items.ex: Heat from superficial blood vessels in the posterior sublingual pocket gives the reading; it is significantly warmer than under the front of the tongue.
w: Under the front of the tongue near the lower teeth
The area under the front of the tongue reads significantly lower than the posterior pocket.
Between the cheek and the upper gum near the molars
The cheek pocket lacks the sublingual blood supply used for oral readings.
On top of the tongue at the center of the mouth
The probe goes under the tongue, where superficial blood vessels supply heat.

alt.q: After placing an oral thermometer probe, why does the nurse ask the patient to keep the lips closed and not talk?
alt.a: To keep the probe in proper position until the reading is complete
alt.ex: Closed lips and no talking maintain the probe’s position in the sublingual pocket during recording.
w: To keep saliva from shorting out the electronic probe
The plastic probe cover protects the probe; the purpose is position, not electrical safety.
To prevent the probe cover from being swallowed
The soft cover locks in place; closing the lips maintains probe position.
To let the thermometer measure exhaled air temperature
The reading comes from blood vessels in the sublingual pocket, not exhaled air.

items.q: Before placing an oral thermometer, the nurse notes that the patient has mucositis. Which action is best?
items.a: Consider an alternate temperature route
items.ex: An oral inflammatory process such as mucositis can falsely elevate oral temperature, so an alternate route is considered.
w: Place the probe under the front of the tongue instead
Moving the probe forward gives lower readings and does not remove the inflammation effect.
Take the oral reading and subtract 1°C from it
No correction factor is given; an alternate site is chosen instead.
Wait 20 minutes and then take the oral temperature
Waiting does not resolve inflammation, which keeps falsely raising oral readings.

alt.q: Why is the oral route avoided in a patient with oral mucositis?
alt.a: Oral inflammation can cause a falsely elevated reading
alt.ex: Inflammatory processes in the mouth add local heat, falsely raising the oral temperature.
w: Oral inflammation causes a falsely low reading
Inflammation raises local temperature, producing false elevations, not low readings.
The probe cover will not lock in an inflamed mouth
Cover locking happens on the probe stem before insertion, unrelated to the mouth.
Mucositis prevents the patient from closing the lips
The concern stated is false elevation from inflammation, not lip closure.

Attach the rectal (red-tip) probe stem to the thermometer unit

items.q: Rectal temperatures are routinely taken in infants younger than 1 month because this route is the most accurate.
items.a: False
items.ex: Rectal temperatures should not be routinely taken in infants younger than 1 month because of the risk of rectal perforation.
items.ww: Accuracy does not outweigh the risk of rectal perforation in young infants.

alt.q: Rectal temperatures should not be taken routinely in infants younger than 1 month because of the risk of rectal perforation.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Young infants are at risk of rectal perforation, so the rectal route is not routine for them.
alt.ww: The rectal route is avoided routinely in infants under 1 month to prevent perforation.

items.q: While inserting a rectal thermometer probe, the nurse feels resistance. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Remove the thermometer and consider another method
items.ex: If the probe cannot be inserted adequately or resistance is felt, remove it and use an alternative method; never force it.
w: Apply firmer pressure until the probe advances
The thermometer is never forced because forcing can injure the rectal mucosa.
Rotate the probe while advancing it to the full depth
Advancing against resistance is unsafe; the probe is removed instead.
Leave the probe at the current depth and take the reading
Inadequate insertion does not give a reliable reading; remove it and choose another method.

alt.q: Which statement about inserting a rectal thermometer is correct?
alt.a: The probe is never forced if resistance is felt
alt.ex: Resistance means the nurse removes the probe and considers an alternative method, protecting the rectal mucosa.
w: The probe is advanced past resistance to 5 cm in adults
Adult insertion depth is 3.5 cm, and the probe is never forced.
Resistance is overcome by asking the patient to bear down
The patient is asked to breathe slowly and relax, and the probe is never forced.
Resistance is expected and requires more lubricant before pushing
The guidance is to remove the probe and choose another method, not push further.

items.q: How far and in which direction does the nurse insert a rectal thermometer probe in an adult?
items.a: 3.5 cm (1½ inches) toward the umbilicus
items.ex: In adults the lubricated probe is inserted gently 3.5 cm toward the umbilicus for exposure to rectal wall blood vessels.
w: 1.25 cm (½ inch) toward the umbilicus
1.25 to 2.5 cm is the insertion depth for an infant or child.
3.5 cm (1½ inches) toward the coccyx
The probe is directed toward the umbilicus, not the coccyx.
6 cm (2½ inches) toward the umbilicus
6 cm exceeds the 3.5 cm recommended for adults.

alt.q: What is the recommended rectal probe insertion depth for an infant or child?
alt.a: 1.25 to 2.5 cm (½ to 1 inch)
alt.ex: For an infant or child the probe is inserted 1.25 to 2.5 cm, and never forced.
w: 3.5 to 4 cm (1½ inches)
3.5 cm is the adult insertion depth.
5 to 6 cm (2 to 2½ inches)
This exceeds even the adult depth and risks injury.
0.25 to 0.5 cm (⅛ to ¼ inch)
This is too shallow to reach rectal wall blood vessels for a reading.

items.q: How does the nurse straighten the ear canal of an adult before taking a tympanic temperature?
items.a: Pull the pinna backward, up and out
items.ex: Pulling the adult pinna backward, up and out straightens the canal for maximal exposure of the tympanic membrane.
w: Pull the pinna down and back
Down and back is used for children younger than 3 years.
Pull the earlobe straight down
Pulling the lobe down does not straighten the adult canal as the book describes.
Press the tragus forward over the canal
Covering the canal blocks the speculum; the pinna is pulled backward, up and out.

alt.q: How does the nurse position the ear of a 2-year-old child for a tympanic temperature?
alt.a: Pull the pinna down and back
alt.ex: For children younger than 3 years, pull the pinna down and back and point the probe toward the midpoint between eyebrow and sideburns.
w: Pull the pinna backward, up and out
Backward, up and out is used for adults.
Pull the pinna up and back
Up and back is used for children older than 3 years.
Leave the pinna in its natural position
The pinna is tugged to straighten the canal and expose the tympanic membrane.

Axillary: Probe in the center of the axilla with the arm across the chest.
Tympanic
Tympanic: Speculum fitted snugly in the canal, pointing toward the nose.

alt.q: Which temperature site uses this technique: “Lubricated probe inserted 3.5 cm toward the umbilicus in adults”?
alt.a: Rectal
alt.ex: Each site has its own placement so the sensor contacts the blood supply that reflects core temperature.
w: Oral
Oral: Probe in the posterior sublingual pocket with lips closed.
Axillary

Tympanic
Tympanic: Speculum fitted snugly in the canal, pointing toward the nose.

alt.q: Which temperature site uses this technique: “Probe in the center of the axilla with the arm across the chest”?
alt.a: Axillary

w: Oral

Rectal

w: Oral
Oral: Probe in the posterior sublingual pocket with lips closed.
Rectal

Axillary

mt.q: Match each temperature site with the correct technique.
pairs: Probe in the posterior sublingual pocket with lips closed
Lubricated probe inserted 3.5 cm toward the umbilicus in adults

Sensor slid across the forehead, then touched behind the earlobe
mt.ex: Each site has its own placement so the sensor contacts the blood supply that reflects core temperature.

items.q: A patient has been lying on the right side. When preparing to take a tympanic temperature, which action is correct?
items.a: Use the upper (left) ear
items.ex: Heat trapped in the ear facing down causes a falsely high reading, so the upper ear is used.
w: Use the lower (right) ear
The ear that was facing down traps heat and gives a falsely high reading.
Use either ear because position does not matter
Lying on one side traps heat in the lower ear, so position matters.
Average readings from both ears
The upper ear is chosen; averaging includes the falsely high lower-ear value.

alt.q: While preparing to take a tympanic temperature, the nurse sees obvious cerumen in the ear canal. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Switch to the other ear or choose another site
alt.ex: Cerumen impedes the lens cover of the speculum, so the nurse uses the other ear or an alternate site.
w: Take the reading and add 0.5°C for the cerumen
There is no correction factor; cerumen blocks the optical path.
Press the speculum harder to get past the cerumen
Force does not clear the optical path and may injure the canal.
Take the reading and repeat it in 2 minutes
Repeating in an ear with cerumen still gives an obstructed reading.

items.q: If a tympanic reading is abnormal, the nurse may repeat it right away in the same ear with the same probe cover.
items.a: False
items.ex: Replace the probe cover and wait 2 minutes before repeating in the same ear, or use the other ear.
items.ww: The ear canal needs time to regain its usual temperature and the lens cover must be clean.

alt.q: When a second tympanic reading is needed, the nurse replaces the probe cover and waits 2 minutes before using the same ear again.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The wait lets the ear canal regain its usual temperature, and a new cover keeps the optical path clear.
alt.ww: An immediate repeat in the same ear with the old cover risks an inaccurate result.

items.q: A diaphoretic patient needs a temporal artery temperature. Which action ensures an accurate reading?
items.a: Dry the forehead with a towel before scanning
items.ex: Moisture and diaphoresis interfere with the temporal artery sensor, so the forehead is dried first.
w: Scan the forehead quickly while it is still damp
Moisture interferes with the sensor, so the forehead must be dry.
Hold the sensor slightly above the skin surface
The sensor is placed firmly on the skin to avoid measuring ambient temperature.
Scan only behind the earlobe and skip the forehead
The scan sweeps the forehead first; behind the earlobe verifies the reading.

alt.q: Why does the nurse touch the temporal artery thermometer to the neck just behind the earlobe after sweeping the forehead?
alt.a: The area is less affected by sweating and verifies the temperature
alt.ex: The skin behind the earlobe is less affected by diaphoresis, so touching it confirms the forehead reading.
w: The area is warmer because it contains the tympanic membrane
The tympanic membrane is inside the ear canal and is not touched here.
The area resets the sensor for the next patient
Cleaning the sensor with alcohol prepares it for the next patient.
The area provides the core reading so the forehead is optional
The forehead sweep is required; behind the earlobe verifies it.

items.q: The nurse is preparing to take an axillary temperature and sees skin lesions in the patient’s axilla. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Select a different temperature site
items.ex: Skin lesions can alter local temperature and the area may be painful to touch, so the axilla is not used.
w: Dry the axilla and proceed with the reading
Drying addresses perspiration, not lesions; lesions mean the axilla is not used.
Place the probe at the edge of the axilla
The probe belongs in the center of the axilla, and lesions rule this site out.
Hold the arm away from the torso during the reading
The probe must be held close to the torso; lesions require another site.

alt.q: How does the nurse position the patient’s arm once the axillary probe is in place?
alt.a: Lower the arm over the probe and place it across the chest
alt.ex: Holding the probe close to the torso keeps it against axillary blood vessels for an accurate reading.
w: Raise the arm above the head during the reading
The arm is lowered over the probe to hold it against the torso.
Extend the arm straight out to the side
An extended arm lets the probe move away from axillary blood vessels.
Let the arm hang loosely off the side of the bed
The arm is placed across the chest so the probe stays close to the torso.

items.q: A patient’s temperature is 1°C (1.8°F) above the usual range. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Cool the room and reduce external coverings
Reducing the environment’s heat and coverings promotes heat loss.
Keep clothing and bed linen dry
Dry clothing and linen are part of fever care.
Administer antipyretics as ordered
Antipyretics are given as ordered to lower temperature.
Increase fluid intake to at least 3 L daily unless contraindicated
Fever increases fluid needs; the book recommends at least 3 L daily.
Apply warm blankets and offer warm liquids
Warm blankets and liquids are used when temperature is below the usual range.
items.ex: For fever, cool the environment, keep linen dry, apply a hypothermia blanket if ordered, give antipyretics and increase fluids.

alt.q: A patient’s temperature is 1°C (1.8°F) below the usual range. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Apply warm blankets
Warm blankets reduce heat loss in a low temperature.
Offer warm liquids unless contraindicated
Warm liquids help raise body temperature.
Remove wet clothing or linen
Wet clothing increases heat loss and is removed.
Cool the room and reduce coverings
Cooling is used when the temperature is above the usual range.
Apply a hypothermia blanket if ordered
A hyperthermia blanket, not a hypothermia blanket, is used for low temperature.
alt.ex: For low temperature, apply warm blankets, offer warm liquids, remove wet linen and use a hyperthermia blanket if ordered.

items.q: A febrile patient receives an antipyretic. When should the nurse recheck the temperature?
items.a: About 30 minutes after the antipyretic, then every 4 hours until stable
items.ex: Rechecking about 30 minutes after an antipyretic and every 4 hours shows whether temperature falls in response to therapy.
w: About 5 minutes after the antipyretic, then every hour until stable
Five minutes is too soon to show a response; the book specifies about 30 minutes.
About 2 hours after the antipyretic, then every 8 hours until stable
The book specifies about 30 minutes, then every 4 hours.
About 30 minutes after the antipyretic, then once a day until stable
Readings continue every 4 hours, not daily, until temperature stabilizes.

alt.q: A patient’s first oral reading is abnormally high. Why does the nurse take a second measurement?
alt.a: To confirm the abnormal finding, since placement errors cause inaccuracies
alt.ex: Improper placement or movement of the thermometer can cause inaccuracies; a second oral or rectal reading confirms the abnormal value.
w: To establish the high value as the patient’s new baseline
Only a reading within the acceptable range is established as a baseline.
To meet a requirement that every reading be taken twice
A second reading is used to confirm abnormal findings, not for every reading.
To find the average of the morning and evening readings
The repeat confirms an abnormal value; it is not a daily average.

items.q: A temperature that is within the acceptable range for a younger adult may reflect a fever in an older adult.
items.a: True
items.ex: Older adults have a narrower temperature range and decreased thermoregulation, so a “normal” value may be a fever.
items.ww: No single temperature is normal for everyone; older adults often run lower.

alt.q: Older adults have a wider normal temperature range than younger adults, so small elevations are rarely significant.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Older adults have a narrower range; small changes can signal fever and should be noticed.
alt.ww: Because their range is narrower and baseline lower, subtle rises are significant in older adults.

items.q: The nurse teaches family caregivers why older adults are at high risk for hypothermia. Which reasons should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Loss of subcutaneous fat
Less insulating fat increases heat loss in older adults.
Diminished sensation to cold
Older adults may not sense cold, delaying protective action.
Abnormal vasoconstrictor responses
Impaired vasoconstriction reduces heat conservation.
Impaired shivering
Reduced shivering limits heat production.
Increased basal metabolic rate
Higher metabolism would raise heat production; it is not a listed hypothermia risk.
items.ex: Older adults lose subcutaneous fat, sense cold less, vasoconstrict abnormally and shiver less, raising hypothermia risk.

alt.q: The nurse teaches a family about risk factors for heatstroke. Which factors should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Strenuous exercise in hot, humid weather
Heavy exertion in heat and humidity is a listed heatstroke risk.
Wearing tight-fitting clothing in hot environments
Tight clothing in heat limits heat loss.
Sudden exposure to a hot climate
Sudden exposure without acclimation is a listed risk.
Poor fluid intake before, during and after exercise
Inadequate fluids reduce the ability to cool the body.
Exercising in a well-ventilated area
Exercising in poorly ventilated areas is the listed risk, not well-ventilated ones.
alt.ex: Heatstroke risks include hot humid exertion, tight clothing, poor ventilation, sudden heat exposure and poor fluid intake.

sections.name: Skill 29.2 · Assessing apical and radial pulse

items.q: Which pulse assessment should the nurse perform personally rather than delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: A pulse taken to evaluate the response to a heart-rate medication
items.ex: Radial pulse can be delegated for stable patients, but not when evaluating response to a treatment or medication or when the patient is unstable.
w: A routine radial pulse on a stable patient before discharge
Routine radial pulse in a stable patient can be delegated to AP.
A radial pulse on a stable patient with a sprained ankle
A stable patient’s radial pulse is appropriate to delegate.
A morning radial pulse for a stable postoperative patient
Stable patients’ routine radial pulses can be delegated.

alt.q: A nurse is assigning vital signs. Which radial pulse measurement is appropriate to delegate to AP?
alt.a: A routine pulse on a patient whose condition is stable
alt.ex: AP can measure radial pulse when the patient’s condition is stable, after the nurse reviews the usual rate and changes to report.
w: A pulse on a patient with new chest pain and dysrhythmia
An unstable patient at risk for serious cardiac problems needs the nurse’s assessment.
A pulse to judge the effect of a newly given cardiac medication
Evaluating response to a medication is not delegated.
A pulse on a patient with acute bleeding after surgery
An unstable patient with hemorrhage requires the nurse’s assessment.

items.q: Which findings in a patient’s EHR indicate a need to assess the pulse because of risk for pulse alterations? Select all that apply.
o: History of peripheral vascular disease
Peripheral vascular disease often alters pulse rate and quality.
Recent invasive cardiovascular diagnostic test
Invasive cardiovascular tests are a listed risk for pulse alterations.
Infusion of a large volume of IV fluid
Large IV fluid volumes are a listed risk.
Medications that alter cardiac function
Drugs affecting cardiac function are a listed risk.
History of seasonal allergic rhinitis
Allergic rhinitis is not a listed risk for pulse alterations.
items.ex: Heart disease, PVD, dysrhythmia, sudden pain, invasive tests, surgery, large IV volumes, hemorrhage and cardiac drugs raise risk.

alt.q: A nurse reviews several EHRs. Which patients have a listed risk for pulse alterations? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with a cardiac dysrhythmia
Dysrhythmias are a listed risk for pulse alterations.
A patient with internal hemorrhage
Internal or external hemorrhage is a listed risk.
A patient with sudden onset of acute pain
Sudden chest pain or acute pain from any site is a listed risk.
A patient who has just had surgery
Surgery is a listed risk for pulse alterations.
A patient with a healed minor skin abrasion
A healed abrasion is not a listed risk for pulse alterations.
alt.ex: Dysrhythmia, hemorrhage, acute pain and surgery are all listed risks for pulse alterations.

items.q: Which factor would the nurse expect to decrease a patient’s heart rate?
items.a: Hypothermia
items.ex: Heart rate declines with hypothermia, while fever and warm environments increase it.
w: Fever
Fever or exposure to warm environments increases heart rate.
Anxiety
Anxiety stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, increasing heart rate.
Caffeine
Central nervous system stimulants such as caffeine can increase heart rate.

alt.q: Which situation would the nurse expect to temporarily increase a patient’s heart rate?
alt.a: Changing from a lying to a standing position
alt.ex: Heart rate increases temporarily when changing from lying to sitting or standing.
w: Receiving large doses of opioid analgesics
Large doses of opioid analgesics can slow heart rate.
Receiving a general anesthetic
General anesthetics slow heart rate.
Developing hypothermia
Heart rate declines with hypothermia.

items.q: A patient has just finished a cup of coffee and a cigarette outside. How long should the nurse wait before assessing the pulse?
items.a: 15 minutes
items.ex: After smoking or ingesting caffeine, wait 15 minutes so the pulse reflects a resting value.
w: 2 minutes
Two minutes is too short for the effects of caffeine and nicotine to subside.
5 minutes
Five to 10 minutes is the wait after activity, not after smoking or caffeine.
60 minutes
The book recommends 15 minutes, not an hour.

alt.q: A patient has just walked back from the bathroom. How long should the nurse wait before assessing the pulse?
alt.a: 5 to 10 minutes
alt.ex: After activity, wait 5 to 10 minutes so the pulse is assessed at rest for objective comparison.
w: 1 to 2 minutes
One to 2 minutes is not enough time for the rate to return to rest.
15 to 20 minutes
Fifteen minutes is the wait after smoking or caffeine, not activity.
30 to 45 minutes
A wait this long is not required after routine activity.

items.q: Before obtaining an apical pulse, which safety check should the nurse complete?
items.a: Determine whether the patient has a latex allergy and use a latex-free stethoscope
items.ex: When obtaining an apical pulse, check for latex allergy and ensure the stethoscope is latex free.
w: Determine whether the patient has eaten within the past 20 minutes
The 20-minute wait applies to oral temperatures, not apical pulse.
Determine whether the patient has a cerumen buildup in either ear
Cerumen matters for tympanic temperature, not for the apical pulse.
Determine whether the patient can hold the breath for 60 seconds
Breath holding is not part of apical pulse preparation.

alt.q: Why does the nurse clean the stethoscope before using it on each patient?
alt.a: To limit contamination of the stethoscope with multidrug-resistant organisms
alt.ex: Stethoscope hygiene per agency policy limits contamination with MDROs; cleaning before use with each patient is recommended.
w: To warm the diaphragm so the patient is not startled
Warming is done by holding the diaphragm in the palm for 5 to 10 seconds.
To improve the pitch of high-frequency heart sounds
Cleaning does not change sound pitch; it reduces microorganism transmission.
To remove latex residue for patients with a latex allergy
Latex allergy is managed by using a latex-free stethoscope, not by cleaning.

items.q: In apical pulse assessment, which step comes right after “Move fingers laterally to the left midclavicular line”?
items.a: Feel for a light tap at the point of maximal impulse
items.ex: That's step 5 of 8. Anatomical landmarks guide correct placement over the apex; the rate is counted only after S1 and S2 are clearly heard.
w: Warm the stethoscope diaphragm in the palm for 5 to 10 seconds
That's step 6 of 8.
Move fingers down the left side of the sternum to the fifth intercostal space
That's step 3 of 8.
Place the diaphragm over the PMI and listen for S1 and S2
That's step 7 of 8.

ord.q: Put these steps for locating and auscultating the apical pulse in order.
items: Find the angle of Louis just below the suprasternal notch
Slip fingers down each side of the angle to the second intercostal space
Move fingers down the left side of the sternum to the fifth intercostal space
Move fingers laterally to the left midclavicular line
Feel for a light tap at the point of maximal impulse
Warm the stethoscope diaphragm in the palm for 5 to 10 seconds
Place the diaphragm over the PMI and listen for S1 and S2
Begin counting when the second hand reaches a number
ord.ex: Anatomical landmarks guide correct placement over the apex; the rate is counted only after S1 and S2 are clearly heard.

items.q: Where is the point of maximal impulse (PMI) normally located in an adult?
items.a: Fifth intercostal space at the left midclavicular line
items.ex: The PMI, or apical impulse, is at the fifth ICS at the left MCL, reflecting the apex of the heart.
w: Second intercostal space at the left sternal border
The second ICS is found from the angle of Louis as a landmark, not the PMI.
Fifth intercostal space at the right midclavicular line
The heart’s apex lies to the left, so the PMI is at the left MCL.
Third intercostal space at the left anterior axillary line
The PMI is at the fifth ICS at the left MCL, not the third ICS.

alt.q: The nurse is unable to palpate the PMI with the patient supine. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Reposition the patient on the left side
alt.ex: If the PMI cannot be palpated, turning the patient onto the left side brings the apex closer to the chest wall.
w: Reposition the patient on the right side
The book directs repositioning to the left side, not the right.
Use the radial pulse and skip the apical assessment
The nurse repositions the patient to locate the PMI rather than abandoning the apical assessment.
Place the stethoscope at the second intercostal space
The second ICS is a landmark; the PMI is near the fifth ICS.

items.q: Normal heart sounds S1 and S2 are high pitched and best heard with the [[diaphragm]] of the stethoscope.
items.ex: High-pitched sounds are heard best with the diaphragm, which is warmed in the palm first for comfort.

alt.q: Before placing it on the chest, the nurse warms the stethoscope [[diaphragm]] in the palm for 5 to 10 seconds.
alt.ex: High-pitched sounds are heard best with the diaphragm, which is warmed in the palm first for comfort.

items.q: When counting a pulse, timing begins with zero, and the first beat after timing begins is counted as one.
items.a: True
items.ex: Pulse timing starts at zero when the second hand hits a number, and the first beat afterward is one.
items.ww: Pulse counting starts at zero; starting at one would add an extra beat.

alt.q: When counting a pulse, the first beat felt after timing begins is counted as zero.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Timing itself begins at zero; the first beat palpated or heard after timing begins is counted as one.
alt.ww: Counting the first beat as zero would drop a beat and underestimate the rate.

items.q: A patient with a regular apical rhythm is receiving a cardiovascular medication. How should the nurse count the apical rate?
items.a: Count for a full 60 seconds
items.ex: When HR is irregular or the patient receives cardiovascular medication, count for a full minute for accuracy.
w: Count for 30 seconds and multiply by 2
A 30-second count is used only for regular rates without cardiovascular medication.
Count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4
A 15-second count is not the method described for apical pulse.
Count for 10 seconds and multiply by 6
Short counts are not used; this patient needs a full minute.

alt.q: A patient with no cardiac medications has a regular apical rhythm. How should the nurse count the rate?
alt.a: Count for 30 seconds and multiply by 2
alt.ex: A regular apical rate can be assessed accurately within 30 seconds and doubled.
w: Count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4
The book describes a 30-second count for a regular rate.
Count for 10 seconds and multiply by 6
Ten seconds is not the method described for apical pulse.
Count for 2 full minutes
A full minute is needed only for irregular rates or cardiac medications; 2 minutes is not required.

items.q: What does a pulse strength of 4+ mean?
items.a: Bounding
items.ex: Strength reflects the volume of blood ejected against the arterial wall; standard terms improve communication among providers.
w: Full or strong
That goes with 3+.
Normal
That goes with 2+.
Barely palpable, diminished
That goes with 1+.

alt.q: What does a pulse strength of 3+ mean?
alt.a: Full or strong
alt.ex: Strength reflects the volume of blood ejected against the arterial wall; standard terms improve communication among providers.
w: Bounding
That goes with 4+.
Normal
That goes with 2+.
Barely palpable, diminished
That goes with 1+.

alt.q: What does a pulse strength of 2+ mean?
alt.a: Normal
alt.ex: Strength reflects the volume of blood ejected against the arterial wall; standard terms improve communication among providers.
w: Bounding
That goes with 4+.
Full or strong
That goes with 3+.
Barely palpable, diminished
That goes with 1+.

alt.q: What does a pulse strength of 1+ mean?
