items.q: Why does the nurse palpate a radial pulse with the fingertips rather than the thumb?
items.a: The thumb has its own pulsation that interferes with accuracy
items.ex: Fingertips are the most sensitive parts of the hand, and the thumb’s own pulsation can be mistaken for the patient’s.
w: The thumb presses too lightly to feel the pulse
The concern is the thumb’s own pulsation, not too little pressure.
The thumb cannot fit into the groove on the wrist
The thumb’s pulsation, not its size, makes it unsuitable.
The thumb occludes the radial artery completely
Excess pressure from any finger can occlude flow; the thumb’s issue is its own pulse.

alt.q: When palpating a radial pulse, the nurse first compresses the artery against the radius until the pulse disappears, then relaxes pressure. Why?
alt.a: Moderate pressure is more accurate, while too much pressure occludes the pulse
alt.ex: Lightly compressing then relaxing finds a moderate pressure; too much pressure occludes the pulse and impairs blood flow.
w: Firm pressure is needed throughout to count the beats
Too much pressure occludes the pulse and impairs blood flow.
Losing the pulse confirms the patient has peripheral vascular disease
Losing it initially is part of technique, not a sign of disease.
Relaxing pressure lets the nurse count respirations instead
The purpose is finding an easily palpable pulse, not counting respirations.

items.q: A nurse auscultates an apical rate that is irregular and slower than the patient’s baseline. What should the nurse do next?
items.a: Repeat the measurement or have another nurse measure it
items.ex: If the apical rate is abnormal or irregular, repeat it or have another nurse measure it, because the original may be incorrect.
w: Document the rate and recheck it at the next scheduled time
Abnormal findings are confirmed with a second measurement, not left until the next routine check.
Count the radial pulse for 30 seconds and multiply by 2
An irregular rate requires a full minute; a 30-second radial count is inaccurate.
Delegate a repeat radial pulse to the AP in 1 hour
An abnormal finding is confirmed promptly by a nurse, not delegated later.

alt.q: A patient’s radial pulse is irregular. In addition to counting for a full 60 seconds, what should the nurse assess?
alt.a: The pattern of irregularity and the radial pulses on both sides
alt.ex: Assess frequency and pattern of irregularity and compare radial pulses bilaterally; a marked difference may mean compromised arterial flow.
w: The pulse in one wrist only, counted for 30 seconds
An irregular pulse needs 60 seconds and comparison of both radial sites.
The temperature in the axilla on the same side
Temperature does not help evaluate an irregular pulse pattern.
The pulse after having the patient walk briefly
Activity alters the rate; pulse is assessed at rest.

items.q: A patient’s radial pulse is weak, thready and difficult to palpate. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Assess both radial pulses and compare findings
Comparing both sides helps determine whether flow to one extremity is compromised.
Observe for pallor and cool skin distal to the weak pulse
These are symptoms of ineffective tissue perfusion.
Check for a dressing or cast that may impede blood flow
Swelling or an encumbrance can impede blood flow to the wrist.
Use a Doppler or ultrasound stethoscope
Doppler detects low-velocity blood flow that is hard to palpate.
Record the pulse as absent and continue routine care
A weak pulse is not absent; further assessment, including the apical pulse, is needed.
items.ex: A weak radial pulse calls for bilateral comparison, perfusion checks, looking for encumbrances, Doppler use and apical auscultation.

alt.q: An adult’s radial pulse is 52 beats/min. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Assess for medications such as beta blockers
Beta blockers and antiarrhythmics decrease heart rate.
Auscultate the apical pulse
Auscultating the apical pulse confirms an abnormal radial rate.
Compare the rate with the patient’s baseline
Comparison with baseline shows whether the rate has changed.
Give the patient’s scheduled beta blocker right away
A beta blocker would lower the rate further; first assess the cause.
Have the patient exercise briefly, then recount
Pulse is assessed at rest; exercise does not clarify bradycardia.
alt.ex: For bradycardia, assess for rate-lowering drugs, auscultate the apical pulse and compare with baseline.

items.q: An AP reports that an adult patient’s radial pulse is 112 beats/min and regular. The patient has just reported acute pain. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Assess for factors that raise heart rate and auscultate the apical pulse
items.ex: A rate above 100 is tachycardia; assess for fever, pain, anxiety, exercise, low BP, blood loss or poor oxygenation, and auscultate apically.
w: Ask the AP to recount the radial pulse in 4 hours
A rate over 100 in an adult needs the nurse’s assessment now, not hours later.
Document the rate as within normal limits for an adult
The adult range is 60 to 100; 112 is tachycardia.
Give a beta blocker to slow the heart rate
Treatment decisions follow assessment and orders; first assess the cause.

alt.q: Which adult pulse rate meets the book’s definition of bradycardia?
alt.a: Less than 60 beats/min
alt.ex: In an adult, a rate below 60 beats/min is bradycardia and above 100 beats/min is tachycardia.
w: Less than 70 beats/min
Rates of 60 to 69 are within the adult range.
Less than 80 beats/min
Rates below 80 include many normal adult values.
Less than 50 beats/min
Bradycardia begins below 60, not only below 50.

items.q: Which signs and symptoms indicate altered cardiac function that may affect pulse rate and rhythm? Select all that apply.
o: Dyspnea
Dyspnea is a listed sign of altered cardiac function.
Palpitations
Palpitations are a listed symptom of altered cardiac function.
Edema of dependent body parts
Dependent edema is a listed sign of altered cardiac function.
Syncope
Syncope is a listed symptom of altered cardiac function.
Thickened nails and decreased hair growth
These are signs of peripheral vascular disease, not of altered cardiac function.
items.ex: Dyspnea, fatigue, chest pain, orthopnea, syncope, palpitations, dependent edema, cyanosis and pallor suggest altered cardiac function.

alt.q: Which findings suggest peripheral vascular disease that alters local arterial blood flow? Select all that apply.
o: Pale, cool extremities
Pale, cool extremities are listed signs of peripheral vascular disease.
Thin, shiny skin with decreased hair growth
These skin changes are listed signs of peripheral vascular disease.
Thickened nails
Thickened nails are a listed sign of peripheral vascular disease.
Orthopnea
Orthopnea is a sign of altered cardiac function, not peripheral vascular disease.
Palpitations
Palpitations are a sign of altered cardiac function, not peripheral vascular disease.
alt.ex: Pale cool extremities, thin shiny skin with decreased hair, and thickened nails suggest peripheral vascular disease.

items.q: The nurse uses teach-back with a patient going home on new cardiac medications. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “My beta blocker can slow my heart rate, so I will check my pulse.”
items.ex: Beta blockers decrease heart rate; patients on certain cardiac drugs learn to check their pulse to detect side effects.
w: “My heart medicine speeds up my pulse, so a fast rate is expected.”
Beta blockers and antiarrhythmics lower rather than raise heart rate.
“I only need to check my pulse if I start having chest pain.”
Patients on these drugs assess their pulse to detect side effects, not only with symptoms.
“I should press on both sides of my neck to find my pulse.”
Patients are taught to palpate one carotid artery, not both.

alt.q: A patient in cardiac rehabilitation explains why pulse self-checks matter. Which statement shows understanding?
alt.a: “Checking my pulse shows how my heart responds to exercise.”
alt.ex: Patients in cardiac rehabilitation assess their own pulse to determine their response to exercise and return to resting rate.
w: “Checking my pulse tells me exactly what my blood pressure is.”
Pulse rate does not give a blood pressure value.
“Checking my pulse is only needed on days I skip exercise.”
The point is to assess the response to exercise, so it is done with exercise.
“Checking my pulse replaces the need to see my provider.”
Self-monitoring supports, not replaces, follow-up with the provider.

items.q: A well-conditioned patient may have a slower-than-usual resting heart rate that returns to resting rate more quickly after exercise.
items.a: True
items.ex: Physical conditioning lowers the resting HR and speeds the return to the resting rate after activity.
items.ww: Conditioning does not slow recovery; well-conditioned patients return to resting rate faster.

alt.q: A well-conditioned patient’s heart rate takes longer than usual to return to resting rate after exercise.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A well-conditioned patient’s heart rate returns more quickly to the resting rate after exercise.
alt.ww: Slower recovery is described for older adults, not for well-conditioned patients.

items.q: When teaching a patient to obtain a carotid pulse rate, the nurse instructs the patient to palpate one carotid artery.
items.a: True
items.ex: Patients and caregivers are taught to palpate one carotid artery to obtain the carotid pulse rate.
items.ww: Palpating a single carotid is what is taught; it is not done on both sides at once.

alt.q: Patients are taught to palpate both carotid arteries at the same time to get a stronger carotid pulse.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Teaching specifies palpating one carotid artery to obtain the carotid pulse rate.
alt.ww: The instruction is to use one carotid artery, not both together.

items.q: A patient is sitting in a chair. How should the nurse position the arm to assess the radial pulse?
items.a: Bend the elbow 90 degrees and support the lower arm on the chair or nurse’s arm
items.ex: For a sitting patient, bending the elbow 90 degrees with the lower arm supported gives easy access to the radial pulse.
w: Extend the arm straight up over the patient’s head
Raising the arm overhead is not described and does not support the forearm.
Let the arm hang straight down at the patient’s side
The lower arm is supported with the elbow bent 90 degrees.
Place the arm palm up across the patient’s back
The wrist is placed with the palm down and the lower arm supported.

alt.q: A patient is lying supine. How should the nurse position the arm to assess the radial pulse?
alt.a: Place the forearm straight alongside or across the lower chest or upper abdomen
alt.ex: For a supine patient, the forearm lies straight alongside the body or across the lower chest or upper abdomen.
w: Raise the forearm straight up with the elbow locked
An elevated, unsupported arm is not the described position.
Bend the elbow 90 degrees over the edge of the bed
The 90-degree bend is used for a sitting patient with the arm supported.
Tuck the forearm under the patient’s lower back
Tucking the arm under the body hides the wrist and is not described.

items.q: Which patient’s respiratory rate should the nurse count personally rather than delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: A patient who states feeling short of breath
items.ex: Counting respirations can be delegated unless the patient is unstable, such as having dyspnea or reporting shortness of breath.
w: A stable patient awaiting discharge with clear lungs
A stable patient’s respiratory count can be delegated to AP.
A stable patient recovering from a knee arthroscopy
Stable patients’ routine respiratory counts can be delegated.
A stable patient admitted for observation of a rash
A stable patient without breathing difficulty is appropriate to delegate.

alt.q: Which instruction should the nurse give when delegating respiratory rate measurement for a stable patient to AP?
alt.a: Report any unusual respiratory values or significant changes to me
alt.ex: The nurse communicates measurement frequency and risk factors and reviews unusual values or changes the AP must report.
w: Give oxygen if the respiratory rate goes above 20
Providing oxygen as ordered is a nursing intervention, not part of the AP’s count.
Decide whether the patient needs a respiratory therapist
Collaborating with pulmonary providers is the nurse’s role.
Wake the patient and tell them you are counting
Awareness of monitoring alters the rate; respirations are counted inconspicuously.

items.q: While reviewing a patient’s EHR, the nurse looks for factors that can increase respiratory rate. Which factors apply? Select all that apply.
o: Fever
Fever increases oxygen demand and raises respiratory rate and depth.
Anxiety
Anxiety stimulates the sympathetic nervous system, increasing rate and depth.
Use of amphetamines or cocaine
Amphetamines and cocaine increase respiratory rate and depth.
Decreased hemoglobin level
Less hemoglobin carries less oxygen, so rate increases to raise oxygen delivery.
Recent dose of an opioid analgesic
Opioid analgesics depress respiratory rate and depth.
Damage to the brainstem
Brainstem damage impairs the respiratory center and inhibits rate and rhythm.
items.ex: Fever, anxiety, stimulants and low hemoglobin raise respiratory rate; opioids and brainstem injury depress it.

alt.q: Which factors can decrease a patient’s respiratory rate? Select all that apply.
o: General anesthetics
General anesthetics depress respiratory rate and depth.
Sedative hypnotics
Sedative hypnotics depress respiratory rate and depth.
Bronchodilators
Bronchodilators dilate airways, which ultimately slows respiratory rate.
Exercise
Exercise increases rate and depth to meet oxygen needs and remove carbon dioxide.
Fever
Fever increases oxygen demand and respiratory rate.
alt.ex: Anesthetics, sedative hypnotics and bronchodilators slow respiration; exercise and fever speed it.

items.q: The nurse finds that a patient’s pulse oximetry reading is 88%. How should the nurse interpret this value?
items.a: It is a clinical emergency
items.ex: Normal SpO2 is 95% to 100%; a value below 90% is a clinical emergency and often comes with respiratory changes.
w: It is a normal finding for most adults
Normal SpO2 is 95% to 100%, so 88% is well below normal.
It is a mild drop that needs no follow-up
Below 90% is an emergency, not a minor finding.
It is acceptable if the respiratory rate is 16
SpO2 below 90% is an emergency regardless of the counted rate.

alt.q: Which pulse oximetry (SpO2) range does the book give as normal?
alt.ex: Normal SpO2 is 95% to 100%; less than 90% is a clinical emergency.
w: Values below 90% are a clinical emergency.
These values fall below the normal range of 95% to 100%.
80–100 is the normal PaO2 range in mm Hg, not SpO2.

items.q: A patient’s hemoglobin has dropped from 14 to 9 g/100 mL. Which respiratory change does the nurse anticipate?
items.a: An increased respiratory rate
items.ex: Decreased hemoglobin lowers the oxygen carried in blood, so respiratory rate increases to raise oxygen delivery.
w: A decreased respiratory rate
Less oxygen-carrying capacity drives the rate up, not down.
No change in rate, only in depth
The book describes an increase in respiratory rate with low hemoglobin.
Periods of apnea lasting several seconds
Apnea signals underlying disease and is not the expected response to low hemoglobin.

alt.q: Why does a low hemoglobin level increase a patient’s respiratory rate?
alt.a: Less oxygen is carried in the blood, so breathing speeds up to deliver more
alt.ex: Hemoglobin carries oxygen; when it falls, respiratory rate rises to increase oxygen delivery.
w: Low hemoglobin directly stimulates the brainstem through anxiety
The mechanism is reduced oxygen-carrying capacity, not anxiety.
Low hemoglobin narrows the airways and raises resistance
Hemoglobin affects oxygen transport, not airway diameter.
Low hemoglobin raises carbon dioxide production in the lungs
The book links low hemoglobin to reduced oxygen carried, not more carbon dioxide.

items.q: How should the nurse position a patient without breathing difficulty before counting respirations?
items.a: Sitting, or lying with the head of the bed raised 45 to 60 degrees
items.ex: Sitting erect promotes full ventilatory movement; a position of discomfort makes the patient breathe faster.
w: Lying flat with the head of the bed at 0 degrees
Lying flat prevents full chest expansion.
Slumped forward with the head of the bed at 15 degrees
A stooped or slumped posture impairs ventilatory movement.
Side-lying with the head of the bed raised 10 degrees
Side-lying with low elevation does not promote full ventilatory movement as erect sitting does.

alt.q: A patient with heart failure has dyspnea. How should the nurse position this patient for respiratory assessment?
alt.a: In the position of greatest comfort for the patient
alt.ex: Patients with dyspnea, such as those with heart failure, ascites or late pregnancy, are assessed in the position of greatest comfort to lessen work of breathing.
w: Flat on the back to see chest movement clearly
Lying flat prevents full chest expansion and increases work of breathing.
Prone so the posterior chest is visible
The book directs the position of greatest comfort, not prone.
Side-lying with the head of the bed flat
A flat position worsens dyspnea; use the patient’s position of comfort.

items.q: Why does the nurse count respirations immediately after the pulse while keeping the fingers on the patient’s wrist?
items.a: So the patient does not consciously alter the rate or depth of breathing
items.ex: Inconspicuous assessment prevents the patient from consciously or unintentionally changing breathing; awareness lowers the rate by about 2 breaths/min.
w: So both values can be counted together in one 30-second period
Pulse and respirations are counted separately; the goal is that the patient stays unaware.
So the pulse can be used to calculate the respiratory rate
Respiratory rate is counted directly, not calculated from the pulse.
So the patient’s arm stays warm during the assessment
Arm position keeps the count inconspicuous, not warm.

alt.q: How does a patient’s awareness of having respirations counted affect the result?
alt.a: It reduces the respiratory rate by about 2 breaths/min
alt.ex: Patient awareness of monitoring reduces the respiratory rate by about 2 breaths/min, so the count is done inconspicuously.
w: It raises the respiratory rate by about 2 breaths/min
Awareness lowers, rather than raises, the rate.
It reduces the respiratory rate by about 8 breaths/min
The reported effect is about 2 breaths/min.
It has no effect on the rate but increases the depth
Awareness changes the rate, so counting is kept inconspicuous.

items.q: When counting respirations, the nurse begins timing with a count of zero, the same as for the pulse.

items.ex: Respirations occur more slowly than the pulse, so the count begins with one at the first full respiratory cycle.

alt.ex: Timing starts when the sweep hand hits a number, and the first full cycle is counted as one.
alt.ww: Respiratory counting does not start at zero the way pulse counting does.

items.q: In the first 30 seconds of counting, the nurse counts 11 regular breaths in an adult (22 breaths/min). What should the nurse do?
items.a: Count for a full 1 minute
items.ex: Count for a full minute if the rhythm is irregular or the rate is below 12 or above 20; short counts overestimate rate.
w: Record 22 breaths/min from the 30-second count
A rate above 20 requires a full-minute count for accuracy.
Count for another 15 seconds and add the results
Rates above 20 require a full 60-second count.
Record 11 breaths/min from the 30-second count
A 30-second count must be multiplied by 2; here a full minute is required.

alt.q: A patient is breathing rapidly. Why does the nurse count respirations for 60 seconds instead of 15 or 30 seconds?
alt.a: Shorter counts are unreliable when the respiratory rate is high
alt.ex: With a high rate, 15- and 30-second counts are unreliable and can overestimate respiratory rate by 2–4 breaths.
w: Shorter counts underestimate a high rate by about 10 breaths
Short counts overestimate rate by about 2–4 breaths, not underestimate by 10.
A 60-second count lets the patient forget the nurse is there
The reason given is reliability of the count, not patient distraction.
A 60-second count is required for every adult patient
A regular rate between 12 and 20 can be counted for 30 seconds and doubled.

items.q: One complete respiratory cycle consists of one inspiration and one [[expiration|exhalation]].
items.ex: The rate is accurate only after viewing a complete cycle; inspiration is about half as long as expiration.

alt.q: An inspiratory breath is about [[half|one half|1/2]] as long as an expiratory breath.
alt.ex: The rate is accurate only after viewing a complete cycle; inspiration is about half as long as expiration.

items.q: How does the nurse assess and describe the depth of a patient’s respirations?
items.a: Observe chest wall movement while counting and describe it as shallow, normal or deep
items.ex: Depth is noted by the degree of chest wall movement, confirmed by palpating excursion or auscultating after counting, and described as shallow, normal or deep.
w: Count the breaths for 15 seconds and describe them as slow, regular or fast
Rate and depth are separate; depth is described as shallow, normal or deep.
Ask the patient to breathe deeply and describe it as easy or labored
Asking for deep breaths alters the natural pattern being assessed.
Read the pulse oximeter and describe it as adequate or inadequate
SpO2 is correlated with breathing, but depth is judged from chest wall movement.

alt.q: When does the nurse palpate chest wall excursion or auscultate the posterior thorax to assess respiratory depth?
alt.a: After counting the respiratory rate
alt.ex: Depth is observed while counting, then palpation or auscultation of the posterior thorax is done after the rate is counted.
w: Before observing the first respiratory cycle
Touching or listening first would make the patient aware and alter breathing.
Instead of counting the respiratory rate
Palpation and auscultation add to, and do not replace, the rate count.
Only when the rate is below 12 breaths/min
These techniques are part of depth assessment, not limited to slow rates.

items.q: While counting respirations, the nurse notices the patient occasionally takes a single deep breath, then resumes a regular pattern. How should the nurse interpret this?
items.a: As normal sighing that expands small airways
items.ex: People periodically take single deep breaths or sighs to expand small airways prone to collapse; sighing is not an abnormal rhythm.
w: As Cheyne-Stokes respirations requiring notification
Cheyne-Stokes is a distinct abnormal pattern, not occasional single sighs.
As apnea that requires immediate intervention
Apnea is cessation of breathing for several seconds, not a deep breath.
As Kussmaul respirations from metabolic acidosis
Kussmaul is a sustained abnormal pattern, not an occasional sigh.

alt.q: Which statement about respiratory rhythm is accurate?
alt.a: Normal breathing is regular and uninterrupted, and occasional sighs are normal
alt.ex: Normal breathing is regular and uninterrupted; periodic sighs help expand small airways and are not confused with abnormal rhythm.
w: Any single deep breath means the rhythm is irregular and must be reported
Occasional sighs are normal and should not be confused with an abnormal rhythm.
Normal breathing includes brief pauses of several seconds
Cessation of respiration for several seconds is apnea, a sign of underlying disease.
Rhythm cannot be judged unless the patient is lying flat
Rhythm is observed in a comfortable position, preferably sitting.

items.q: While counting respirations in an adult, the nurse observes periods with no breathing lasting several seconds. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Report the finding to the health care provider or nurse in charge
items.ex: Irregular patterns or periods of apnea in adults are symptoms of underlying disease and are reported; further assessment and intervention are often needed.
w: Record it as normal sighing and continue routine care
Sighing is a single deep breath; pauses in breathing are apnea and must be reported.
Ask the AP to recount the respirations in 4 hours
Apnea needs prompt reporting and nursing assessment, not a delayed recount.
Wake the patient and tell them to breathe more regularly
Apnea reflects underlying disease and is reported for further assessment.

alt.q: An adult patient demonstrates Biot respirations. What is the appropriate nursing action?
alt.a: Notify the health care provider for further evaluation
alt.ex: Kussmaul, Cheyne-Stokes or Biot respirations require notifying the provider for additional evaluation and possible medical intervention.
w: Document the pattern and reassess at the next shift
These abnormal patterns need prompt provider notification, not routine reassessment.
Teach the patient deep breathing to correct the pattern
These patterns reflect underlying disease and need medical evaluation.
Count respirations for 15 seconds and multiply by 4
Irregular patterns need a full-minute count and provider notification.

items.q: An adult patient’s respiratory rate is 26 breaths/min and the patient reports dyspnea. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Assess for related factors such as obstructed airway and abnormal breath sounds
Related factors help identify the cause of tachypnea.
Help the patient to a semi- or high-Fowler position unless contraindicated
Supported sitting promotes full ventilatory movement.
Provide oxygen as ordered
Oxygen is provided as ordered for an altered respiratory rate.
Assess for environmental factors such as secondhand smoke or fumes
Environmental irritants can influence respiratory rate.
Lay the patient flat to reduce the work of breathing
Lying flat prevents full chest expansion and worsens dyspnea.
items.ex: For bradypnea or tachypnea, assess causes, position upright, give ordered oxygen, check the environment and notify if it continues.

alt.q: An adult patient’s respiratory rate is 10 breaths/min. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Assess for related factors such as restlessness and confusion
Related factors help identify the cause of bradypnea.
Notify the health care provider if the alteration continues
A persistent change needs to be reported.
Compare the rate with the patient’s baseline
Comparison with baseline shows whether a change has occurred.
Recount in 4 hours because a change of a few breaths is minor
Changes of 3 to 5 breaths/min can be the first sign of deterioration.
Count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4 to confirm
A rate below 12 requires a full 1-minute count.
alt.ex: A rate below 12 is bradypnea; assess related factors, compare with baseline and notify if it continues.

items.q: A change in respiratory rate of as little as 3 to 5 breaths/min can indicate a change in the patient’s condition.
items.a: True
items.ex: Small changes of 3 to 5 breaths/min are often the first sign of deterioration and need follow-up.
items.ww: Small changes are clinically meaningful and should not be dismissed.

alt.q: A change of 3 to 5 breaths/min is normal variation and does not need to be reported.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Such changes are often the first sign of deterioration; the nurse notifies the provider if the alteration continues.
alt.ww: Even small changes can signal deterioration and must be followed up.

items.q: Chronic smoking changes the pulmonary airways, resulting in an increased respiratory rate at rest even when the person is not smoking.
items.a: True
items.ex: Chronic smoking alters the airways, so the resting rate is higher even between cigarettes.
items.ww: The effect of chronic smoking persists when the person is not actively smoking.

alt.q: Chronic smoking affects respiratory rate only while the person is actively smoking.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Chronic smoking changes the airways and increases the resting rate even when not smoking.
alt.ww: The airway changes from chronic smoking persist, so the effect is not limited to active smoking.

items.q: Which findings are signs and symptoms of respiratory alterations? Select all that apply.
o: Cyanotic nail beds and lips
A bluish or cyanotic appearance of nail beds, lips and skin signals a respiratory alteration.
New restlessness, irritability or confusion
Restlessness, confusion and reduced consciousness can reflect inadequate oxygenation.
Use of accessory muscles
Accessory muscle use indicates labored breathing.
Thick, frothy or blood-tinged sputum
Thick, frothy, blood-tinged or copious sputum is a listed sign.
Pink nail beds with regular breathing
Pink nail beds and regular breathing are normal findings.
items.ex: Cyanosis, mental status changes, labored breathing, orthopnea, accessory muscle use and abnormal sputum indicate respiratory alterations.

alt.q: A nurse assesses several patients. Which findings suggest a respiratory alteration? Select all that apply.
o: Orthopnea
Orthopnea, difficulty breathing when lying flat, is a listed sign.
Pain during inspiration
Pain during inspiration is a listed sign of respiratory alteration.
Labored or difficult breathing
Labored breathing is a listed sign.
An occasional single deep sigh
Periodic sighs expand small airways and are normal.
A regular rate of 16 breaths/min at rest
A regular rate of 16 at rest is within the adult range of 12 to 20.
alt.ex: Orthopnea, pain on inspiration and labored breathing indicate alteration; occasional sighs and a regular rate of 16 are normal.

items.q: A patient has a painful upper abdominal incision after surgery. Which breathing pattern does the nurse anticipate?
items.a: Shallow breathing with splinting of chest wall movement
items.ex: Pain increases oxygen demand and alters rate and rhythm; breathing becomes shallow and the patient splints the chest or abdomen.
w: Deep, slow breathing with full chest expansion
Pain in the chest or abdomen makes breathing shallow, not deep.
Regular breathing with occasional deep sighs
Sighing is a normal pattern; pain causes shallow, splinted breathing.
Periods of apnea lasting several seconds
Apnea signals underlying disease; incisional pain causes shallow, splinted breathing.

alt.q: A patient has a tight, constrictive abdominal dressing. How might this affect respirations?
alt.a: It can restrict the patient’s ability to breathe deeply
alt.ex: Constrictive chest or abdominal dressings restrict the ease with which a patient can breathe deeply.
w: It slows the rate by depressing the respiratory center
Respiratory center depression comes from drugs or brainstem injury, not dressings.
It dilates the airways and slows the respiratory rate
Airway dilation is the effect of bronchodilators, not dressings.
It has no effect because dressings do not touch the chest
Abdominal dressings can restrict deep breathing as well as chest dressings.

items.q: After counting respirations, the nurse correlates the rate, depth and rhythm with pulse oximetry and ABG results. What is the rationale?
items.a: Ventilation, perfusion and diffusion are interrelated
items.ex: Evaluations of ventilation, perfusion and diffusion are interrelated, so breathing pattern is interpreted alongside SpO2 and ABGs.
w: ABG results replace the need to count the respiratory rate
ABGs complement, not replace, observing rate, depth and rhythm.
Pulse oximetry measures respiratory rate more accurately
Pulse oximetry measures oxygen saturation, not respiratory rate.
ABGs are needed before respirations can be documented
Respirations are documented regardless; correlation is used if ABGs are available.

alt.q: Which finding often accompanies an SpO2 below 90%?
alt.a: Changes in respiratory rate, depth and rhythm
alt.ex: An SpO2 below 90% is often accompanied by changes in respiratory rate, depth and rhythm.
w: A pH within 7.35 to 7.45 with no symptoms
An SpO2 below 90% is an emergency and often comes with respiratory changes.
A slower, deeper and more regular breathing pattern
Low saturation is linked to altered patterns, not a calmer one.
No change in breathing because the body compensates
Low SpO2 is often accompanied by changes in rate, depth and rhythm.

items.q: The nurse delegates spot-check SpO2 measurement for a stable postoperative patient to assistive personnel (AP). Which instruction should the nurse include?
items.a: Report any reading below 95%, or below this patient’s set value, right away.
items.ex: The nurse tells the AP to notify the nurse immediately of any SpO2 below 95% or below the value set for that patient.
w: Use the oximeter’s pulse display in place of counting the radial pulse.
AP are cautioned not to use the oximeter for heart rate because it will not detect an irregular pulse.
Place the finger probe on the arm with the automatic BP cuff.
Cuff inflation briefly stops blood flow to that finger, causing inaccurate readings and false alarms.
Use a disposable adhesive sensor even if the patient reports latex allergy.
Disposable adhesive sensors may contain latex, so they are avoided in a patient with latex allergy.

alt.q: Unless a patient-specific value has been set, below which SpO2 reading should the AP notify the nurse immediately?
alt.ex: The book directs the AP to notify the nurse immediately of any reading lower than 95% or the value set for that patient.
w: 85% is the manufacturer’s preset low alarm limit for continuous monitoring, not the AP reporting threshold.
Below 90% is an unexpected outcome needing intervention; the AP reports earlier, below 95%.
Readings of 95% or higher are not the ones the AP is told to report immediately.

items.q: Before attaching a finger probe, the nurse finds the patient’s capillary refill in that finger is 4 seconds. Which action is best?
items.a: Select an alternative probe site with better perfusion.
items.ex: The sensor needs a pulsating vascular bed; if capillary refill is greater than 2 seconds, the nurse selects an alternative site.
w: Attach the probe and accept the first number displayed.
Poor perfusion at the site makes the reading unreliable, and the first number may not be a constant value.
Switch to an adhesive sensor on the same finger.
Changing the sensor type does not fix poor perfusion at that site.
Document that SpO2 cannot be measured on this patient.
Other sites such as toe, earlobe, forehead, or nose can be evaluated first.

alt.q: A critically ill patient is receiving vasopressors. Which probe site does the book prefer for this patient?
alt.a: Forehead
alt.ex: Patients on vasopressors or who are critically ill may have increased peripheral capillary refill, so forehead sensors are preferred.
w: Finger
Peripheral perfusion is reduced in these patients, making finger readings less reliable.
Toe
The toe is also a peripheral site affected by reduced capillary refill.
Earlobe
The book names forehead sensors, not earlobe sensors, as preferred for critically ill or vasopressor patients.

items.q: A patient wearing dark brown nail polish needs a finger SpO2 reading. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Remove the polish from that digit with acetone or polish remover first.
items.ex: Black or brown nail polish alters readings, so the nurse removes polish from the digit before attaching a finger probe.
w: Attach the probe and add a note about the polish to the reading.
The reading would still be falsely altered; documenting it does not make it accurate.
Proceed, because only red nail polish affects the sensor.
The book specifically states black or brown nail polish alters readings.
Apply an adhesive sensor over the polished nail instead.
Polish under any finger sensor still falsely alters the saturation reading.

alt.q: Why does the nurse remove fingernail polish before placing a finger probe?
alt.a: Nail polish falsely alters the saturation reading.
alt.ex: The rationale for removing polish is that it falsely alters saturation by interfering with light absorption by the sensor.
w: Nail polish contains latex that reacts with the sensor.
Latex is a concern with disposable adhesive sensors, not nail polish.
The clip-on probe slides off polished nails.
Fit of the probe is not the reason given; polish changes the reading itself.
Acetone disinfects the digit before probe contact.
Infection control is achieved by hand hygiene and sensor cleaning, not polish removal.

items.q: A patient has an automatic BP cuff cycling on the left arm and needs continuous SpO2 monitoring. Where should the nurse place the finger sensor?
items.a: A finger with intact skin on the right hand
items.ex: The sensor is not placed on the same extremity as an electronic BP cuff because cuff inflation interrupts blood flow and triggers inaccurate alarms.
w: The left index finger, closest to the monitor
Each cuff inflation temporarily interrupts blood flow to that finger, causing inaccurate readings.
A left-hand finger, since the cuff inflates only periodically
Even periodic inflation interrupts flow and can trigger false alarms.
An edematous finger on the right hand
The probe is not attached to a finger that is edematous or has compromised skin.

alt.q: An adult patient has a history of peripheral vascular disease. Which sensor site should the nurse select?
alt.a: Earlobe or bridge of the nose
alt.ex: The book directs selecting the ear or bridge of the nose for an adult with peripheral vascular disease because peripheral perfusion is reduced.
w: Index finger of the dominant hand
Peripheral vascular disease reduces finger perfusion, making readings unreliable.
Great toe of either foot
The toe is a peripheral site even more affected by vascular disease.
Any fingertip after removing nail polish
Removing polish does not overcome poor peripheral blood flow.

items.q: How should the nurse position the patient before measuring SpO2?
items.a: Sitting, or lying with the head of the bed elevated 45 to 60 degrees
items.ex: Sitting erect promotes full ventilation; a position of discomfort makes the patient breathe more rapidly.
w: Lying flat with the head of the bed at 0 degrees
A flat position does not promote full ventilation.
Lying with the head of the bed elevated 10 to 15 degrees
This is too low to promote the full ventilation of sitting erect.
Trendelenburg with the head 15 to 20 degrees below the feet
Head-down positioning hinders ventilation and may cause discomfort and rapid breathing.

alt.q: Why does the nurse explain the importance of breathing normally until the SpO2 reading is complete?
alt.a: It prevents large changes in minute ventilation that cause reading errors.
alt.ex: Breathing normally prevents large fluctuations in minute ventilation and possible error in SpO2 readings, and promotes cooperation.
w: It keeps the clip-on probe from slipping off the finger.
Movement of the probe relates to motion artifact, not breathing pattern.
It slows the heart rate so the pulse display is steady.
The goal is to avoid swings in ventilation, not to change heart rate.
It makes the oximeter’s audible beep easier to hear.
The beep signals a valid pulse; breathing instructions are about ventilation.

items.q: After turning on the oximeter, the nurse notes a displayed pulse rate of 58, but the patient’s radial pulse is 92. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Reassess the sensor placement site before accepting the reading.
items.ex: Correlating oximeter and radial pulse rates ensures accuracy; a difference requires reassessment of the sensor placement site.
w: Record the oximeter pulse because the device is more precise.
A mismatch signals a possible invalid signal; the oximeter may not detect every pulse.
Report bradycardia to the health care provider immediately.
The patient’s actual radial rate is 92; the discrepancy points to the sensor, not bradycardia.
Increase the oxygen flow rate to raise the saturation.
Nothing yet shows low saturation; the sensor must be checked first, and oxygen changes need an order.

alt.q: Why does the nurse compare the oximeter pulse rate with the patient’s radial pulse?
alt.a: Matching rates confirms that the oximeter reading is accurate.
alt.ex: Correlating pulse rates ensures oximeter accuracy, because the device must be detecting a valid pulse to read SpO2 correctly.
w: The radial pulse is used to set the SpO2 alarm limits.
Alarm limits are set for SpO2 and pulse by the patient’s condition, not by one radial count.
It replaces the need to watch the pulse waveform.
The nurse still observes the waveform and beep to detect a valid pulse.
It establishes the first baseline heart rate for the shift.
The comparison checks oximeter accuracy; it is not how a pulse baseline is set.

items.q: For a spot-check, how long does the nurse leave the sensor in place before reading the SpO2?
items.a: 10 to 30 seconds, or until the readout is constant and the pulse display is at full strength
items.ex: The sensor stays on 10 to 30 seconds or until the value is constant and the pulse display reaches full strength each cardiac cycle.
w: 2 to 5 seconds, or until the first number appears on the display
The first number may not be a stable, valid value.
3 to 5 minutes, so the sensor has time to warm to skin temperature
This is longer than needed; the book uses a constant readout as the endpoint.
10 to 15 minutes, or until the patient’s breathing slows down
Breathing normally is requested, but the endpoint is a constant readout, not slower breathing.

alt.q: What does the pitch of the oximeter’s audible beep reflect?
alt.a: The SpO2 value
alt.ex: The beep and waveform confirm a valid pulse, and the pitch of the beep is proportional to the SpO2 value.
w: The respiratory rate
The oximeter does not measure breathing; pitch tracks saturation.
The strength of the pulse
Pulse strength is shown on the waveform/intensity display, not by pitch.
The remaining battery charge
Pitch is proportional to SpO2, not device power.

items.q: When starting continuous SpO2 monitoring, the nurse verifies the manufacturer’s preset alarm limits. What are they?
items.a: Low of 85% and high of 100%
items.ex: The nurse verifies preset limits of 85% low and 100% high, then sets limits for SpO2 and pulse rate based on the patient’s condition.
w: Low of 90% and high of 98%
These are not the manufacturer presets the book describes.
Low of 80% and high of 95%
An 80% low limit is below the 85% preset and 95% is not the high limit.
Low of 95% and high of 100%
95% is the AP reporting threshold, not the preset low alarm limit.

alt.q: During continuous SpO2 monitoring, how often does the nurse assess skin under the probe and relocate the sensor?
alt.a: Assess skin every 2 hours; relocate at least every 4 hours
alt.ex: Skin under the probe is assessed every 2 hours and the sensor relocated at least every 4 hours, more often if skin or perfusion is compromised.
w: Assess skin every 4 hours; relocate at least every 8 hours
These intervals are too long to prevent sensor-related skin injury.
Assess skin every 8 hours; relocate every 24 hours
Leaving a sensor this long risks pressure and adhesive injury.
Assess skin every hour; relocate only if the alarm sounds
Sensors are relocated on a schedule, not just when alarms occur.

items.q: An obese postoperative patient on nasal oxygen has an SpO2 of 87%. The sensor is properly applied and oxygen is flowing as ordered. Which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Assist the patient to a high-Fowler position and encourage slow, deep breaths.
items.ex: For SpO2 below 90%, the nurse positions the patient to maximize ventilatory effort, such as high-Fowler for an obese patient, and encourages slow, deep breaths.
w: Lower the head of the bed flat to improve peripheral perfusion.
A flat position limits ventilation, especially in an obese patient.
Remove the oxygen briefly to obtain a room-air baseline.
Removing oxygen from a patient with low saturation is unsafe.
Recheck the SpO2 at the next scheduled vital signs in 4 hours.
SpO2 below 90% needs prompt intervention and reporting, not delay.

alt.q: A patient’s SpO2 on continuous monitoring drops to 86%. Which action should the nurse take first?
alt.a: Verify that the sensor is intact and properly applied.
alt.ex: The first intervention for SpO2 below 90% is verifying the sensor is intact and properly applied, since a dislodged sensor gives a false low.
w: Turn off the alarm and recheck the reading in an hour.
Silencing and delaying ignores a possibly true drop that needs prompt follow-up.
Reset the low alarm limit to 80%.
Lowering limits hides the problem instead of assessing it.
Increase the oxygen flow rate on the flowmeter to 6 L/min.
Oxygen is adjusted as ordered; the nurse first confirms the reading is valid.

items.q: During continuous monitoring with a disposable adhesive sensor, the nurse sees erythema and blistering under the sensor. What do these findings indicate?
items.a: Medical adhesive–related skin injury
items.ex: Erythema, blistering, and excoriation under a disposable sensor are signs of medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI) caused by the adhesive.
w: Central cyanosis from low saturation
Cyanosis is a bluish color of lips, nail beds, or membranes, not blistering.
Motion artifact at the sensor site
Motion artifact causes inaccurate readings, not skin changes.
An expected effect needing no action
These are signs of skin injury that require a change in sensor site or type.

alt.q: An oximetry sensor has caused pressure injury at the site. Which intervention is appropriate?
alt.a: Rotate probe sites more often and change the sensor type or location.
alt.ex: For sensor-related pressure or tissue injury, the nurse rotates sites more frequently, changes sensor type or location, and increases skin assessment.
w: Pad the sensor with gauze and leave it on the same site.
Padding interferes with the sensor and leaves pressure on injured skin.
Assess the skin under the sensor less often to avoid irritation.
Skin assessment frequency should increase, not decrease.
Tape the clip-on sensor more tightly so it cannot move.
Added tension increases pressure on the tissue.

items.q: Why does the nurse correlate the SpO2 reading with the SaO2 from arterial blood gas (ABG) results when available?
items.a: It documents the reliability of the noninvasive measurement.
items.ex: Comparing SpO2 with ABG-derived SaO2 documents the reliability of the noninvasive pulse oximetry assessment.
w: It establishes the patient’s first SpO2 baseline.
The baseline is the first SpO2 within acceptable range, not an ABG value.
It shows the SpO2 alarm limits are set correctly.
Alarm limits are set from the patient’s condition, not checked against ABGs.
It replaces the need to assess respiratory rate and depth.
SpO2 is also correlated with respiratory assessment because ventilation and perfusion are interrelated.

alt.q: When comparing a new SpO2 reading with the patient’s baseline, which factor does the book say the nurse must note because it can affect SpO2?
alt.a: Use of oxygen therapy
alt.ex: During evaluation the nurse notes oxygen therapy, which can affect SpO2, and documents the type and amount of oxygen used.
w: Time of the last meal
Meals are not listed among factors influencing SpO2.
The patient’s height
Height is not a factor the book lists for SpO2.
Which hand is dominant
Hand dominance does not alter saturation readings.

items.q: Pulse oximetry can be delegated to assistive personnel even when the patient is unstable.
items.a: False
items.ex: SpO2 measurement can be delegated to AP unless the patient is unstable; an unstable patient needs the nurse’s assessment.
items.ww: The book limits delegation to stable patients, so the statement cannot be true.

alt.q: SpO2 measurement may be delegated to assistive personnel for a stable patient but not for an unstable one.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Delegation is allowed unless the patient is unstable, in which case the nurse performs the measurement.
alt.ww: Stating it is false would ignore that the book permits delegation for stable patients.

items.q: The pulse rate shown on an oximeter is a reliable substitute for counting the pulse in a patient with an irregular rhythm.
items.a: False
items.ex: AP are cautioned not to use pulse oximetry for heart rate because the oximeter will not detect an irregular pulse.
items.ww: An oximeter does not detect irregular pulses, so it cannot replace a manual count.

alt.q: The nurse cautions AP not to use the pulse oximeter to obtain heart rate because it will not detect an irregular pulse.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: This caution is part of the delegation instructions for SpO2 measurement.
alt.ww: Calling it false would suggest the oximeter detects irregular rhythms, which it does not.

items.q: A standard clip-on finger probe may be too small for a patient who is obese.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book notes a clip-on probe may be too small for an obese patient, so probe choice must fit the patient.
items.ww: Probe size matters; an ill-fitting probe can give inaccurate readings.

alt.q: A standard clip-on finger probe fits every adult, including patients who are obese.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A clip-on probe may be too small for a patient who is obese, so a patient-appropriate probe is chosen.
alt.ww: Saying it is true ignores the book’s warning about probe size in obesity.

items.q: When SpO2 is assessed for the first time, the nurse establishes it as the baseline only if it is within the acceptable range.
items.a: True
items.ex: A first SpO2 within acceptable range becomes the baseline used to compare future measurements.
items.ww: An abnormal first value signals a problem to address, not a normal baseline.

alt.q: The first SpO2 reading is always recorded as the patient’s baseline, even if it is below the acceptable range.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The first reading becomes the baseline only if it is within the acceptable range.
alt.ww: Treating an abnormal reading as baseline could hide a real oxygenation problem.

items.q: Before measuring SpO2, the nurse reviews the EHR. Which conditions place the patient at risk for decreased oxygen saturation? Select all that apply.
o: Recovery from conscious sedation
Sedation can reduce ventilation and lower saturation.
Traumatic injury to the chest wall
Chest wall trauma can impair ventilation.
Collapse of lung tissue
Collapsed lung reduces area for gas exchange.
A recent change in oxygen therapy
Changing oxygen therapy can alter saturation.
Healed fracture of the wrist
A healed limb fracture does not reduce ventilation or perfusion.
Corrected nearsightedness
Vision problems do not affect oxygen saturation.
items.ex: Conditions that reduce ventilation or perfusion, such as sedation, chest trauma, lung collapse, ventilator dependence, or oxygen changes, place patients at risk.

alt.q: Which patients are at risk for decreased oxygen saturation because of reduced ventilation or perfusion? Select all that apply.
o: A patient recovering from general anesthesia
Anesthesia recovery can depress ventilation.
A patient who is ventilator dependent
Ventilator dependence is listed as a risk condition.
A patient with chronic compromised respiratory function
Acute or chronic respiratory compromise lowers saturation.
A patient with a sprained ankle
An ankle sprain does not affect ventilation or perfusion.
A patient with mild seborrheic dermatitis
A skin condition of the scalp does not lower saturation.
alt.ex: Anesthesia recovery, ventilator dependence, and compromised respiratory function reduce ventilation or perfusion and increase risk for low SpO2.

items.q: Which factors can influence the measurement of SpO2? Select all that apply.
o: Hemoglobin level
The sensor detects light-absorbing hemoglobin, so hemoglobin level affects SpO2.
Hypotension
Low BP reduces the pulsating flow the sensor needs.
Bronchodilator medications
Bronchodilators are listed among factors that influence SpO2.
Postural drainage and percussion
Respiratory therapy can change saturation.
The patient’s shoe size
Shoe size has no effect on saturation readings.
The time of the last bowel movement
Bowel elimination does not influence SpO2 measurement.
items.ex: Factors such as oxygen therapy, respiratory therapy, hemoglobin, hypotension, temperature, nail polish, and medications influence SpO2 measurement.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing factors that could alter a patient’s SpO2 reading. Which factors apply? Select all that apply.
o: Supplemental oxygen therapy
Oxygen therapy affects SpO2 and must be noted.
Body temperature
Temperature is listed among factors influencing SpO2; cold fingers are avoided.
Black nail polish on the probe digit
Dark polish falsely alters readings.
The patient’s eye color
Eye color has no effect on SpO2.
The patient’s blood type
Blood type is not a factor that influences SpO2 measurement.
alt.ex: Oxygen therapy, body temperature, and nail polish influence SpO2 readings and must be considered when interpreting values.

items.q: Which sensor placement decisions follow the book’s clinical judgment guidance? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid a finger that is edematous
Probes are not attached to edematous areas or compromised skin.
Avoid earlobe and nose-bridge sensors for toddlers
Infant and toddler skin is fragile at these sites.
Avoid fingers that are hypothermic
Cold fingers have poor perfusion and give inaccurate readings.
Avoid disposable adhesive sensors in latex allergy
Disposable adhesive sensors may contain latex.
Use the finger on the arm with the BP cuff
Cuff inflation interrupts flow and causes inaccurate readings and alarms.
Use a nose-bridge sensor for an infant
Earlobe and nose-bridge sensors are not used for infants due to fragile skin.
items.ex: Sensors avoid edematous, hypothermic, or injured sites, the BP-cuff limb, fragile infant sites, and latex-containing adhesives in latex allergy.

alt.q: A nurse is choosing an SpO2 sensor site. Which choices are unsafe or likely inaccurate? Select all that apply.
o: A finger on the arm with an inflating electronic BP cuff
Cuff inflation interrupts finger blood flow and triggers alarms.
An earlobe sensor for a 2-year-old
Earlobe sensors are avoided in toddlers due to skin fragility.
A disposable adhesive sensor for a latex-allergic patient
The adhesive sensor may contain latex.
The earlobe of an adult with peripheral vascular disease
Ear or nose bridge is the recommended site in this case.
A finger with capillary refill under 2 seconds
Brisk capillary refill indicates adequate perfusion for a finger sensor.
alt.ex: The BP-cuff limb, toddler earlobes, and latex-containing adhesive sensors in latex allergy are avoided; adult earlobe in PVD and well-perfused fingers are appropriate.

items.q: [[Motion artifact|Motion|Movement artifact]] is the most common cause of inaccurate pulse oximetry measurements.
items.ex: Movement of the sensor or patient interferes with signal detection, making motion artifact the leading cause of inaccurate SpO2 readings.

alt.q: The most common cause of an inaccurate SpO2 reading is [[motion|movement]] artifact.
alt.ex: Movement of the sensor or patient interferes with signal detection, making motion artifact the leading cause of inaccurate SpO2 readings.

That's step 5 of 7.
Position patient sitting or with head of bed elevated 45 to 60 degrees

ord.q: Put these implementation steps for a pulse oximetry spot-check in order.
items: Perform hand hygiene
Position patient sitting or with head of bed elevated 45 to 60 degrees
Attach sensor to the chosen site, removing nail polish if using a finger
Turn on oximeter, observe waveform and beep, and correlate with radial pulse
Leave sensor in place 10 to 30 seconds until readout is constant, then read SpO2
Remove probe, turn oximeter off, and clean and store sensor
Help patient to a comfortable position
ord.ex: Hand hygiene and positioning come first; the sensor is attached, the device verified against the radial pulse, the value read, and the equipment cleaned before comfort measures.

items.q: The nurse is assigning BP measurements. Which patient’s BP should the nurse measure rather than delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: A postoperative patient whose BP has dropped to 82/48 mm Hg
items.ex: BP measurement can be delegated unless the patient is unstable, such as hypotensive; this patient needs the nurse’s assessment.
w: A patient with diabetes whose BP has been 128/78 mm Hg all day
This patient is stable, so BP measurement can be delegated.
An ambulatory patient awaiting discharge with BP of 124/80 mm Hg
A stable patient’s routine BP may be delegated.
A patient with renal disease whose BP is steady at 138/86 mm Hg
A steady reading in a stable patient can be delegated with clear reporting parameters.

alt.q: When delegating BP measurement to AP, which direction by the nurse is appropriate?
alt.a: Specify the limb, cuff size, and type of equipment to use.
alt.ex: The nurse explains which limb, cuff size, and manual or electronic equipment to use, plus frequency, risks, and values to report.
w: Let the AP choose whichever cuff is closest at hand.
Cuff size must fit the extremity; an improper cuff causes measurement errors.
Have the AP report only systolic values above 180 mm Hg.
The nurse reviews the patient’s usual values and the significant changes to report.
Tell the AP to use whichever arm the patient prefers.
The nurse identifies the limb, since some limbs must be avoided.

items.q: A patient has IV fluids infusing in the right arm. The left arm has no restrictions. Where should the nurse measure BP?
items.a: Left upper arm
items.ex: The cuff is not applied to an extremity with IV fluids infusing because inflation impairs flow; the unrestricted arm is used.
w: Right upper arm above the IV site
Inflating the cuff on the infusing arm impairs flow in that extremity.
Right forearm below the IV site
Any part of the extremity with the infusion is avoided.
Either ankle using the dorsalis pedis artery
Lower extremities are used only when the brachial arteries are inaccessible.

alt.q: A patient had a left mastectomy and has lymphedema in the left arm; the right arm is in a cast. Where should the nurse measure BP?
alt.a: A lower extremity, preferably the ankle
alt.ex: When both brachial sites are inaccessible, lower extremities are used; the ankle is preferred because it is more comfortable.
w: Left upper arm, since the surgery is healed
The involved arm is not used when lymphedema is present.
Right upper arm above the cast
A cast or bulky bandage makes that extremity unsuitable for a cuff.
Left forearm below the affected area
The arm with lymphedema is avoided entirely.

items.q: A patient returns from a walk and smoked a cigarette 10 minutes ago. The nurse needs a sitting BP. Which action is best?
items.a: Wait until 30 minutes have passed since smoking, then have the patient rest at least 5 minutes.
items.ex: Exercise, caffeine, or smoking within 30 minutes falsely elevates BP, and the patient rests at least 5 minutes before a sitting BP.
w: Measure now after 1 minute of rest and note the smoking.
Smoking and recent exercise falsely raise BP; noting it does not correct the reading.
Wait 5 minutes, then measure the BP with the patient standing.
Five minutes is too short after smoking, and a sitting BP was needed.
Measure right away at the ankle to avoid nicotine effects.
Nicotine causes vasoconstriction throughout the body regardless of site.

alt.q: Before measuring BP, how long should the patient rest for lying or sitting and for standing measurements?
alt.a: At least 5 minutes before lying or sitting; 1 minute before standing
alt.ex: The book directs at least 5 minutes of rest before lying or sitting BP and 1 minute before standing BP.
w: At least 1 minute before lying or sitting; 5 minutes before standing
The times are reversed.
At least 10 minutes before lying or sitting; 10 minutes before standing
These times exceed the book’s guidance.
At least 30 seconds before lying or sitting; none before standing
Too little rest allows anxiety and activity to raise BP.

items.q: In the two-step method, why does the nurse first estimate systolic pressure by palpation?
items.a: To find the maximal inflation point and prevent a false-low systolic reading
items.ex: Estimating systolic pressure by palpation determines the maximal inflation point, preventing false-low readings.
w: To measure diastolic pressure, which palpation detects best
Palpation identifies systolic pressure only.
To skip auscultation when the patient is stable
The two-step method still requires auscultation after palpation.
To warm and dilate the artery before auscultation
Palpation estimates pressure; it does not change the artery.

alt.q: During the palpation step of the two-step method, to what level does the nurse rapidly inflate the cuff?
alt.a: 30 mm Hg above the point at which the pulse disappears
alt.ex: The cuff is inflated 30 mm Hg above where the palpated pulse disappears, then slowly deflated to note where it reappears.
w: 10 mm Hg above the point at which the pulse disappears
10 mm Hg is not the book’s inflation target and risks missing true systolic pressure.
60 mm Hg above the point at which the pulse disappears
Overinflating adds discomfort without benefit; the book uses 30 mm Hg.
200 mm Hg regardless of where the pulse disappears
The target is set from the palpated pulse, not a fixed number.

items.q: A nurse lets the manometer needle fall about 8 mm Hg per second during auscultation. What effect does this have on the reading?
items.a: Systolic reads too low and diastolic reads too high
items.ex: Deflation that is too rapid decreases the systolic and increases the diastolic measurement.
w: Systolic reads too high and diastolic reads too low
That pattern results from placing the stethoscope under the cuff.
Both systolic and diastolic read too high
Rapid deflation lowers systolic, not raises it.
Neither value changes if the sounds are clear
Clear sounds do not prevent errors from rapid deflation.

alt.q: At what rate should the nurse release the valve so the manometer needle falls during auscultation?
alt.a: 2 to 3 mm Hg per second
alt.ex: A slow, steady fall of 2 to 3 mm Hg per second avoids the false-low systolic and false-high diastolic of rapid deflation.
w: 5 to 6 mm Hg per second
This is too fast and distorts both values.
8 to 10 mm Hg per second
This is far too fast for accurate readings.
0.5 to 1 mm Hg per second
Deflating too slowly causes arterial occlusion with numbness and tingling.

items.q: When auscultating BP in an adult, at which point does the nurse record the diastolic pressure?
items.a: The point at which the sounds disappear
items.ex: In adults, the beginning of the last or fifth sound, where sounds disappear, indicates diastolic pressure.
w: The first clear tapping sound
The first clear sound reflects systolic pressure.
The point where sounds first become distinctly muffled
Distinct muffling indicates diastolic pressure in children, not adults.
The point where the sounds are loudest
Sound intensity peaks partway through; it does not mark diastolic pressure.

alt.q: When auscultating BP in a child, which sound indicates diastolic pressure?
alt.a: The distinct muffling of sounds
alt.ex: In children, distinct muffling of sounds indicates diastolic pressure, whereas in adults the disappearance of sounds is used.
w: The first clear tapping sound
The first clear sound reflects systolic pressure in all ages.
The complete disappearance of sounds
Disappearance marks diastolic pressure in adults.
The point where the sounds are loudest
Peak intensity does not mark diastolic pressure.

items.q: According to the American Heart Association guidance in the skill, how should the nurse obtain a reliable BP value?
items.a: Take two sets 2 minutes apart and use the second set as baseline.
items.ex: Two sets 2 minutes apart prevent false-positive readings from the alert reaction; the second set is used as baseline.
w: Take one set and repeat it only if it seems high.
A single reading may be elevated by anxiety, so two sets are recommended.
Take two sets 10 minutes apart and use the first set.
The first reading is often higher due to anxiety, so the second set is used.
Take three sets 30 seconds apart and use the highest.
Using the highest value increases false-positive readings.

alt.q: A patient’s first BP set is 152/90 mm Hg and the second, 2 minutes later, is 144/86 mm Hg. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Obtain additional readings because the sets differ by more than 5 mm Hg.
alt.ex: If the two sets differ by more than 5 mm Hg, additional readings are necessary before a baseline is set.
w: Record 152/90 mm Hg as baseline because the first set is most accurate.
The first reading is often higher because of anxiety.
Record 144/86 mm Hg as baseline without further readings.
A difference over 5 mm Hg requires more readings first.
Average the two sets and record 148/88 mm Hg as baseline.
The sets differ by more than 5 mm Hg, so more readings are needed.

items.q: On a first assessment, a patient’s BP is 146/86 mm Hg in the right arm and 136/82 mm Hg in the left arm. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Use the right arm for repeated measurements.
items.ex: A 5 to 10 mm Hg difference between arms is normal; the arm with the higher pressure is used for repeated measurements.
w: Use the left arm because the lower value is more accurate.
The book directs using the arm with the higher pressure.
Report a circulatory problem because the arms differ.
A difference of 5 to 10 mm Hg between arms is normal.
Alternate arms with each future measurement.
Consistent use of the higher-pressure arm allows valid comparison.

alt.q: Why does the nurse measure BP in both arms during a patient’s first assessment?
alt.a: Comparing both arms can detect circulatory problems.
alt.ex: Comparing BP in both arms or legs detects circulatory problems; a 5 to 10 mm Hg difference between arms is normal.
w: It confirms the cuff size is correct for each arm.
Cuff size is chosen by mid-arm circumference before measuring.
It reduces anxiety so the reading is lower.
Two sets 2 minutes apart address anxiety, not bilateral checks.
It lets the nurse use the lower arm as baseline.
The arm with the higher pressure is used for repeated readings.

items.q: The nurse cannot obtain a BP reading on a postoperative patient using the usual site. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Obtain the pulse and respiratory rate to rule out an immediate crisis.
items.ex: When BP cannot be obtained, the nurse first determines that no immediate crisis exists by obtaining pulse and respiratory rate.
w: Try again with a larger cuff on the same arm.
Equipment changes come after confirming the patient is not in crisis.
Document that BP was not obtainable and recheck later.
Delaying risks missing a crisis such as decreased cardiac output.
Measure BP on the ankle with a Doppler device.
Alternative sites come after checking pulse and respirations for a crisis.

alt.q: An AP reports being unable to hear any BP sounds on a patient. What is the nurse’s first priority?
alt.a: Check the patient’s pulse and respirations for an immediate crisis.
alt.ex: The first intervention is to determine that no immediate crisis exists by obtaining pulse and respiratory rate.
w: Replace the stethoscope with one that has a bell.
Equipment can be changed after the patient’s status is confirmed.
Palpate the systolic BP at the radial artery.
Palpation is an alternative method used after excluding a crisis.
Ask the AP to retry the BP in 30 minutes.
Waiting could miss decreased cardiac output needing immediate notification.

items.q: A patient’s BP is 80/50 mm Hg; the baseline was 124/76 mm Hg. The patient is pale and dizzy. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Place the patient supine and restrict activity.
items.ex: For hypotension the nurse positions the patient supine to enhance circulation, restricts activity, assesses, and reports the BP.
w: Raise the patient to high-Fowler to ease breathing.
Upright positioning can worsen low BP; supine enhances circulation.
Have the patient stand to check for orthostatic changes.
Standing a hypotensive, dizzy patient risks a fall.
Walk the patient to the bathroom to empty the bladder.
Activity is restricted in a hypotensive patient.

alt.q: A patient taking antihypertensives becomes lightheaded after standing, consistent with orthostatic hypotension. What should the nurse do first?
alt.a: Return the patient to a safe position in bed or a chair.
alt.ex: For orthostatic hypotension the nurse returns the patient to a safe position and instructs not to get up without assistance.
w: Encourage the patient to keep walking to build tolerance.
Continuing to walk while lightheaded risks a fall.
Leave to get the BP machine while the patient stands.
Leaving a lightheaded patient standing is unsafe.
Have the patient stand still and breathe deeply.
Remaining upright does not protect the patient from falling.

items.q: The nurse teaches a patient taking BP medications about standing up. Which statement shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I’ll get up slowly because my BP pills can make me dizzy.”
items.ex: Teach-back confirms the patient knows BP medications can cause dizziness when standing too fast, so rising slowly prevents falls.
w: “I should stand up quickly so my blood doesn’t pool.”
Rising quickly increases the risk of orthostatic dizziness.
“Feeling dizzy when I stand is normal, so I’ll ignore it.”
Dizziness on standing signals orthostatic hypotension and needs caution.
“I’ll skip my BP pills on days when I feel dizzy.”
Stopping medications on one’s own is unsafe; the goal is slow position changes.

alt.q: A patient will monitor BP at home. Which statement shows understanding of the teaching?
alt.a: “I need a cuff that is the right size for my arm.”
alt.ex: Home care teaching stresses an appropriate-size cuff, a quiet room, and accurate electronic or aneroid devices.
w: “A finger BP monitor will give me the most accurate readings.”
Finger BP monitors are inaccurate.
“Any standard adult cuff will work for my arm.”
Improper cuff size causes measurement errors.
“I’ll take my BP in the kitchen while the TV is on.”
The quietest room is chosen for assessing BP.

items.q: Which conditions found in the EHR place a patient at risk for BP alterations? Select all that apply.
o: Renal disease
Renal disease is listed as a risk factor for BP alteration.
Increased intracranial pressure
Increased ICP is a listed risk factor.
Rapid IV infusion of blood products
Rapid fluid or blood infusion can alter BP.
Gestational hypertension
Gestational hypertension is a listed risk factor.
Corrected nearsightedness
Vision problems do not alter BP.
Healed ankle fracture from 5 years ago
A remote healed fracture is not a BP risk factor.
items.ex: Cardiovascular and renal disease, diabetes, shock, pain, rapid IV infusion, increased ICP, postoperative status, and gestational hypertension place patients at risk.

alt.q: A nurse reviews several patients’ records. Which patients are at risk for BP alterations? Select all that apply.
o: A patient in septic shock
All types of circulatory shock alter BP.
A patient with diabetes mellitus
Diabetes is a listed risk factor.
A patient on the first postoperative day
Postoperative status is a listed risk factor.
A patient with acute pain
Acute or chronic pain alters BP.
A patient with a healed childhood tonsillectomy
A remote minor surgery is not a BP risk factor.
alt.ex: Shock, diabetes, postoperative status, and pain are listed risk factors for BP alterations; a remote healed surgery is not.

items.q: On which extremities should the nurse avoid applying a BP cuff? Select all that apply.
o: Arm with IV fluids infusing
Cuff pressure impairs flow and the infusion.
Arm with an arteriovenous fistula
Inflation can compromise the shunt or fistula.
Arm with a peripherally inserted central catheter
PICC or midline catheter limbs are avoided.
Arm in a cast
A cast or bulky bandage prevents proper cuff use.
Arm opposite the side of breast surgery
Only the arm on the side of breast or axillary surgery is avoided.
Upper arm under a thin sleeve with stethoscope on skin
Thin clothing under 5 mm does not affect readings if the stethoscope is on skin.
items.ex: Inflating a cuff on a limb with an IV, shunt or fistula, PICC or midline, cast, trauma, or same-side breast surgery can impair blood flow.

alt.q: A nurse is selecting a BP site. Which sites should be avoided? Select all that apply.
o: Leg with a bulky bandage
Bulky bandages interfere with cuff application and sounds.
Traumatized extremity
Cuff pressure can further compromise impaired circulation.
Arm on the same side as axillary surgery
The side of breast or axillary surgery is avoided.
Arm with lymphedema after lumpectomy
The involved arm is not used when lymphedema is present.
Ankle when both brachial arteries are inaccessible
Lower extremities, especially the ankle, are used when arms cannot be.
Arm opposite an IV infusion
The arm without the IV is an appropriate site.
alt.ex: Bandaged, traumatized, lymphedematous, and same-side surgical limbs are avoided; the ankle and the arm opposite an IV are acceptable.

items.q: Which errors can produce a falsely high BP reading? Select all that apply.
o: Cuff wrapped too loosely
A loose-fitting cuff causes false-high readings.
Arm hanging below heart level
An arm below heart level creates a false-high reading.
Legs crossed at the knees
Crossed legs can significantly increase BP.
Talking with the patient during measurement
Talking increases both systolic and diastolic BP.
Arm raised above heart level
An arm above heart level causes a false-low reading.
Deflating the cuff too rapidly
Rapid deflation lowers systolic, though it raises diastolic.
items.ex: Loose cuffs, dependent arms, crossed legs, talking, unsupported back or arm, and lack of rest falsely elevate BP.

alt.q: Which errors can produce a falsely low systolic reading? Select all that apply.
o: Arm positioned above heart level
Placement above heart level causes a false-low reading.
Deflating the cuff faster than 3 mm Hg per second
Rapid deflation decreases the systolic measurement.
Stethoscope positioned so sounds are muffled
Muffled sounds often result in false-low systolic readings.
Patient’s back unsupported while sitting
An unsupported back raises BP.
Patient has a full bladder
A full bladder increases systolic and diastolic BP.
Cuff wrapped too loosely
A loose cuff causes false-high readings.
alt.ex: Arm above heart level, rapid deflation, and muffled sounds from poor stethoscope placement produce false-low systolic readings.

items.q: A BP cuff may be placed over a thin sleeve as long as the stethoscope rests on the skin.
items.a: True
items.ex: Thin clothing under 5 mm does not affect cuff inflation or BP readings if the stethoscope contacts skin.
items.ww: The book permits a thin sleeve, so calling it false is incorrect.

alt.q: A BP cuff must never be placed over any clothing, even a thin sleeve.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Thin clothing under 5 mm does not affect readings, so a cuff may go over a thin sleeve if the stethoscope is on skin.
alt.ww: Saying it is true ignores evidence that thin clothing does not alter readings.

items.q: Hypertension is often asymptomatic until the pressure is very high.
items.a: True
items.ex: Hypertension frequently causes no symptoms until very high, which is why measurement and risk review matter.
items.ww: Many patients with high BP feel well, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Hypertension reliably causes headache and flushing even when BP is only mildly elevated.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hypertension is often asymptomatic until very high; occipital headache, flushing, and nosebleed may occur at higher levels.
alt.ww: Relying on symptoms would miss most hypertension, which is often silent.

items.q: When lower extremity BP is needed, the ankle is the preferred site because it is more comfortable, especially for overweight patients.
items.a: True
items.ex: The ankle is preferred for lower extremity BP because it is more comfortable, particularly for overweight patients.
