items.q: A patient arrives at the emergency department during a severe asthma episode. Which assessment approach should the nurse use first?
items.a: Focus on the pulmonary and cardiovascular systems so treatment can begin immediately
items.ex: In a severe asthma episode, a focused examination of the pulmonary and cardiovascular systems comes first so treatment is not delayed.
w: Complete a full head-to-toe examination before any treatment is started
A comprehensive examination waits until the patient is no longer at risk for a poor outcome.
Begin with a neurological examination to establish a cognitive baseline
The neurological system is not the system most at risk during an asthma episode.
Obtain a complete health history before examining any body system
A lengthy history before assessing breathing would delay urgently needed treatment.

alt.q: A nurse has completed a focused pulmonary and cardiovascular assessment on a patient with severe asthma. When should the nurse perform a more comprehensive examination of the other body systems?
alt.a: When the patient is no longer at risk for a poor outcome or injury
alt.ex: A comprehensive examination of the remaining systems follows once the patient is stable and no longer at risk.
w: Before any bronchodilator therapy is given to the patient
Treatment for the acute problem should begin immediately, not wait for a full examination.
Only after the patient is discharged from the hospital
The comprehensive examination is done once the patient is stable, not deferred until discharge.
At the same time as the first focused respiratory assessment
The acute problem is addressed first; other systems are examined after the risk has passed.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which are uses of the physical examination described in the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Gathering baseline data about the patient’s health status
Baseline data allow later findings to be compared and changes detected.
Supplementing, confirming, or refuting subjective data
Objective findings are used to check what the patient reported in the history.
Identifying and confirming nursing diagnoses
Examination findings support identification and confirmation of nursing diagnoses.
Evaluating the outcomes of care
Repeat examination shows whether the patient’s condition has improved as expected.
Replacing the need for a nursing health history
The history and the examination work together; the history helps focus the examination.
Establishing the patient’s medical diagnosis for the health care provider
The nurse uses the examination to identify and confirm nursing diagnoses, not medical diagnoses.
items.ex: The physical examination gathers baseline data, checks subjective data, supports nursing diagnoses, guides decisions about changing status, and evaluates outcomes.

alt.q: A nurse explains to a student why the physical examination matters throughout a hospital stay. Which reasons should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: It helps make clinical decisions about a patient’s changing health status
Ongoing examination findings guide decisions about changes in status and management.
It shows whether the outcomes of care have been met
Examination is used to evaluate the outcomes of care.
It can confirm or refute what the patient reported in the history
Objective findings supplement, confirm, or refute subjective data.
It is needed only on admission and not again during the stay
Reassessment is done as a patient’s condition changes and at least daily in many settings.
It is used mainly to determine the patient’s insurance coverage
Insurance eligibility is one reason for some examinations, not the main purpose during hospital care.
alt.ex: During a hospital stay the examination guides clinical decisions, checks subjective data, and evaluates outcomes of care.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “My ankles have not been swelling at all.” On examination the nurse finds bilateral pitting edema of the ankles. Which purpose of the physical examination does this illustrate?
items.a: Supplementing, confirming, or refuting subjective data
items.ex: The objective finding of edema refutes the patient’s subjective report, which the examination is designed to check.
w: Gathering baseline data about the patient’s health status
Baseline data are a starting point for comparison, not a check of what the patient said.
Evaluating the outcomes of care already delivered
Evaluating outcomes compares findings with expected results after interventions.
Determining eligibility for health insurance coverage
Insurance eligibility is a reason for some examinations but is unrelated to this finding.

alt.q: A patient reports shortness of breath, and the nurse auscultates crackles in both lung bases. Which purpose of the physical examination is the nurse fulfilling?
alt.a: Confirming the subjective data obtained during the history
alt.ex: The objective finding of crackles confirms the patient’s subjective report of shortness of breath.
w: Evaluating the outcomes of an intervention already given
No intervention has been evaluated; the finding checks the patient’s report.
Determining the patient’s eligibility for military service
Eligibility screening is a different reason for performing an examination.
Establishing the patient’s medical diagnosis of pneumonia
The nurse uses findings to confirm data and nursing diagnoses, not to make a medical diagnosis.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: For hospitalized patients, the nurse integrates collection of physical assessment data into routine care, such as noticing swallowing difficulty while giving medications.
items.a: True
items.ex: Nurses gather assessment data during routine care and validate it with what is known from the health history.
items.ww: Assessment is not limited to scheduled examinations; observations during care, like swallowing problems, are valuable data.

alt.q: A nurse should collect physical assessment data only during a scheduled, formal head-to-toe examination, not during routine care activities.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses integrate data collection into routine care, such as observing sadness cues on entering a room.
alt.ww: Waiting for a formal examination would miss cues noticed during care, such as swallowing difficulty during medication administration.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which situations are reasons nurses conduct physical examinations? Select all that apply.
o: Initial evaluation during triage for emergency care
Triage requires an initial evaluation to decide on emergency care.
Routine screening to promote wellness and preventive care
Screening examinations support wellness behaviors and preventive health care.
Determining eligibility for a new job or military service
Examinations are used to determine eligibility for jobs, military service, or health insurance.
Admitting a patient to a long-term health care agency
Admission to a hospital or long-term care agency includes a physical examination.
Deciding which pharmacy a patient should use
Choice of pharmacy is not a reason for a physical examination.
items.ex: Examinations are done for triage, routine screening, eligibility determination, and admission to a hospital or long-term care agency.

alt.q: A nurse works in a community clinic. Which patients are coming in for an examination for a reason the textbook identifies? Select all that apply.
o: A man who needs an examination to qualify for health insurance
Determining eligibility for health insurance is a recognized reason.
A healthy woman seeking routine preventive screening
Routine screening promotes wellness and preventive health care.
A young adult who must be cleared before entering military service
Eligibility for military service is a recognized reason.
A patient requesting a review of the clinic’s billing statement
A billing review does not require a physical examination.
A patient who wants a prescription refill with no change in health
A simple refill request is not one of the listed reasons for a physical examination.
alt.ex: Eligibility for insurance or military service and routine wellness screening are reasons nurses conduct examinations.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: What is the main difference between the data gathered in the health history interview and the data gathered in the physical examination?
items.a: The history gathers subjective data; the examination gathers objective data
items.ex: The interview yields subjective data reported by the patient, while observation and examination yield objective data.
w: The history gathers objective data; the examination gathers subjective data
This reverses the two; the patient’s report is subjective and examination findings are objective.
Both the history and the examination gather only subjective data
Examination findings such as inspection and auscultation results are objective data.
The history gathers baseline data; the examination gathers no new data
The examination gathers additional objective data, focusing on problem areas.

alt.q: How does the nursing health history help the nurse conduct the physical examination?
alt.a: It helps focus the examination on the patient’s problem areas
alt.ex: Data from the history help the nurse focus the physical examination appropriately.
w: It replaces the need to examine body systems the patient did not mention
Additional objective data are still gathered through a body system review.
It provides the objective data that the examination cannot obtain
The history provides subjective data; the examination supplies objective data.
It tells the nurse which nursing diagnoses to finalize without examining
Diagnoses are identified and confirmed using all gathered data, including examination findings.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is preparing to examine a patient from a cultural background different from the nurse’s own. Which action best demonstrates cultural humility?
items.a: Recognizing gaps in personal knowledge about the patient’s culture
items.ex: Cultural humility includes recognizing your own knowledge deficits about different cultures.
w: Assuming the patient shares the beliefs common to the patient’s ethnic group
Assuming shared beliefs is stereotyping, which the nurse should avoid.
Using the same approach and expected findings for every patient
Cultural factors affect both the nurse’s approach and the findings to expect.
Avoiding questions about health beliefs to prevent offending the patient
Health beliefs and alternative therapies should be considered during the history and examination.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows a correct understanding of culturally aware physical assessment?
alt.a: “I need to tell apart the patient’s cultural traits and physical characteristics.”
alt.ex: There is a difference between cultural and physical characteristics, and stereotyping based on cultural factors should be avoided.
w: “I can predict the patient’s health beliefs from the patient’s race.”
Predicting beliefs from race is stereotyping, which the nurse must avoid.
“Cultural factors affect the history but not the physical findings.”
Cultural factors affect both the approach and the type of findings expected.
“Physical variations such as skin findings are the same in all groups.”
Nurses must recognize variations in physical characteristics such as skin and musculoskeletal findings.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which patient factors should the nurse consider to provide culturally sensitive care during the history and examination? Select all that apply.
o: Health beliefs
Health beliefs influence patient behaviors and the nurse’s approach.
Use of alternative therapies
Alternative therapies may affect findings and care planning.
Comfort with physical closeness
Comfort with closeness affects how the patient experiences touch during the examination.
Relationships with family
Family relationships influence decision making and who should be present.
The nurse’s preferred examination sequence
This is the nurse’s routine, not a patient cultural factor.
The patient’s insurance provider
Insurance status is not a cultural factor listed for consideration.
items.ex: Health beliefs, alternative therapies, nutritional habits, family relationships, and comfort with physical closeness all influence the examination.

alt.q: A nurse prepares to examine a newly admitted patient. Which cultural considerations will affect the nurse’s approach? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s nutritional habits
Nutritional practices are listed among cultural factors to consider.
The patient’s preferred mode of communication
Mode of communication is a cultural consideration for the assessment.
Adaptations needed for the physical assessment
The nurse considers adaptations needed to respect cultural needs.
Stereotypes about the patient’s education level
The nurse avoids stereotyping based on education or other cultural factors.
The nurse’s personal comfort with the patient’s religion
The focus is the patient’s needs, not the nurse’s personal comfort.
alt.ex: The nurse considers communication mode, nutritional practices, and needed adaptations while avoiding stereotypes.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Addressing culturally appropriate care shows respect for each patient’s uniqueness and leads to higher-quality care and improved clinical outcomes.
items.a: True
items.ex: Culturally appropriate care respects uniqueness and is linked to higher-quality care and better outcomes.
items.ww: The textbook links culturally appropriate care directly to improved quality and outcomes.

alt.q: Because cultural differences mainly affect communication, they have little influence on patient behaviors during a physical examination.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Cultural differences influence patient behaviors and affect both the nurse’s approach and expected findings.
alt.ww: Culture shapes behaviors such as comfort with closeness, so it does influence the examination.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: The distress a person feels because of a mismatch between the personal sense of gender and the sex assigned at birth is called gender [[dysphoria]].
items.ex: Gender dysphoria describes distress from a mismatch between gender identity and sex assigned at birth.

alt.q: When gender identity does not match the sex assigned at birth, the resulting distress is called [[gender dysphoria]].
alt.ex: Gender dysphoria describes distress from a mismatch between gender identity and sex assigned at birth.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is admitting a transgender patient whose identification band shows a legal name different from the name the patient uses. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Ask the patient’s name and pronouns and use them during the examination
items.ex: A gender-affirming approach affirms identity by using the person’s correct name and pronouns.
w: Use the legal name on the identification band for every interaction
Using a name the patient does not use fails to affirm gender identity.
Avoid using any name or pronoun so as not to cause offense
Avoiding names entirely does not affirm identity; using the correct name and pronouns does.
Refer to the patient by the sex assigned at birth to ensure accuracy
Using the sex assigned at birth is not gender affirming and can cause harm.

alt.q: Which nursing action reflects a gender-affirming approach when examining a patient who identifies as transgender and gender nonconforming (TGNC)?
alt.a: Using the patient’s correct name and pronouns throughout the examination
alt.ex: Affirming gender identity means referring to the person by correct name and pronouns.
w: Asking the patient to explain why the patient chose to transition
Questioning the patient’s choice is not affirming and is not required for the examination.
Using the pronouns that match the patient’s physical findings
Pronouns should reflect the patient’s identity, not physical findings.
Skipping assessment of mental health to avoid upsetting the patient
TGNC patients have a high potential for mental health issues and self-harm, so assessment is important.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: When caring for a patient who identifies as TGNC, which risk should the nurse be especially alert to during assessment?
items.a: Mental health issues and self-harm
items.ex: Nurses should be aware of the high potential for mental health issues and self-harm among TGNC patients.
w: Latex allergy and anaphylaxis
Latex allergy risk is unrelated to gender identity.
Hearing loss and vision changes
Sensory changes are not the risk highlighted for TGNC patients.
Joint deformities and arthritis
Joint problems are not identified as a particular risk for TGNC patients.

alt.q: A nurse caring for a TGNC patient notes the patient seems withdrawn. Why is careful assessment of this finding important?
alt.a: TGNC patients have a high potential for mental health issues and self-harm
alt.ex: Awareness of the high potential for mental health issues and self-harm guides the nurse to assess further.
w: TGNC patients rarely experience bias, so withdrawal is usually physical
TGNC patients experience health disparities and bias, which affect mental health.
Withdrawal is an expected effect of all gender-affirming medications
Withdrawal is not described as an expected medication effect; it warrants assessment.
Withdrawal shows the patient prefers a nurse of a different gender
Assuming a staffing preference misses the risk of mental health issues and self-harm.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Throughout the assessment of a TGNC patient, the nurse should consider the patient’s prior negative experiences with health care, including discrimination and abuse.
items.a: True
items.ex: Prior discrimination and physical or emotional abuse in health care can affect how a TGNC patient experiences an examination.
items.ww: Past negative experiences are a key consideration because TGNC patients face bias in health care settings.

alt.q: Assessment of transgender patients is the same regardless of where the patient is in the transition process.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Assessment related to transgender care differs depending on where patients are in the transition process.
alt.ww: The stage of transition changes which assessments and findings are relevant.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which constructs are measured by assessment tools developed for people who identify as TGNC? Select all that apply.
o: Impact of discrimination
Tools assess how discrimination affects the person.
Minority stress
Minority stress is one of the constructs measured.
Positive aspects of a TGNC identity
Tools also measure positive aspects of identity, not only problems.
Psychosocial aspects of a medical transition
Psychosocial aspects of transition are among the constructs.
Family history of genetic disorders
Genetic family history is not one of the listed TGNC constructs.
Preferred learning style
Learning style is not a construct of TGNC assessment tools.
items.ex: Besides gender dysphoria, TGNC tools measure discrimination, minority stress, positive identity aspects, and psychosocial aspects of transition.

alt.q: A nurse researcher reviews tools for assessing the psychological experience of TGNC individuals. Which constructs should the tools include? Select all that apply.
o: Gender dysphoria
Gender dysphoria is a core construct measured.
Minority stress
Minority stress is a recognized construct.
Impact of discrimination
The effect of discrimination is measured.
Blood pressure trends
Blood pressure is a physical finding, not a psychological construct.
Ability to perform instrumental activities of daily living
IADLs are emphasized for older adults, not listed as a TGNC construct.
alt.ex: TGNC tools address gender dysphoria, minority stress, discrimination, positive identity, and psychosocial aspects of transition.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: On entering a patient’s room to give morning medications, the nurse notices that the patient is tearful and avoids eye contact. What is the best interpretation of this observation?
items.a: It is a behavioral cue that should be validated with the patient’s history
items.ex: Nurses integrate observations during routine care and validate findings with what is known about the patient’s history.
w: It is irrelevant because no formal examination is in progress
Data collected during routine care are valid assessment findings.
It confirms a medical diagnosis of depression without further assessment
A single cue requires validation, and nurses do not make medical diagnoses.
It should be ignored until the scheduled daily examination
Cues noticed during care should be acted on and validated, not postponed.

alt.q: While giving oral medications, the nurse observes that a patient coughs and has trouble swallowing. How should the nurse view this finding?
alt.a: As physical assessment data gathered during routine care
alt.ex: Nurses integrate physical assessment into routine care, such as noticing swallowing difficulty during medication administration.
w: As a finding that counts only if seen during a formal examination
Findings observed during care are valid and should be validated, not dismissed.
As subjective data because the patient did not report it
An observed finding is objective data, whether or not the patient reports it.
As a reason to stop collecting assessment data that day
The finding should prompt further assessment, not end data collection.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which example illustrates the purpose “Gathering baseline data”?

A neurological examination before inspecting the heel
The neurological system is not the area of concern for this complaint.
No examination until the health care provider orders one
Nurses select and perform focused examinations based on the patient’s condition.

Form order guides documentation, not whether the exam is focused.

items.q: Recognizing common characteristics and disorders among the ethnic populations in a community helps the nurse provide culturally aware assessment.

items.ww: This knowledge supports awareness of variations, as long as it is not used to stereotype individual patients.

alt.q: Avoiding stereotypes means the nurse should not learn about disorders that are common in particular ethnic populations.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses should recognize common disorders among ethnic populations while still avoiding stereotyping individuals.
alt.ww: Knowledge of population patterns is encouraged; stereotyping applies assumptions to an individual without assessment.

Documentation is required, but the goal of assessment is an individualized plan of care.
Confirming the health care provider’s medical diagnosis
Nurses use data to identify nursing diagnoses and plan nursing care.

Discharge planning is only one part; the main goal is an individualized care plan.

alt.q: Which outcome results when a nurse makes clinical judgments using accurate history and examination data?

w: A standardized care plan used for all patients with the same condition

A complete list of medical orders for the health care provider to sign
Nurses plan nursing care; they do not write medical orders from assessment data.
A finished assessment that will not need to be repeated during the stay
Reassessment continues as the patient’s condition changes.

items.q: A nurse is about to examine a patient who is confused and pulling at the bedrails. The nurse realizes the stethoscope was left at the nurses’ station. What should the nurse do?

items.ex: Safety of a confused patient is a priority; never leave a confused or combative patient alone during an examination.
w: Raise the bedrails and quickly go get the stethoscope
Leaving a confused patient alone, even briefly, is unsafe.
Ask the patient to stay still while the nurse steps out
A confused patient cannot be relied on to follow instructions for safety.
Continue the examination and skip the auscultation steps
Skipping essential assessments leads to incomplete findings.

alt.q: Which principle should guide a nurse preparing to examine a combative patient?
alt.a: Never leave the patient alone during the examination
alt.ex: Safety is the priority, and a confused or combative patient must never be left alone during an examination.
w: Perform the examination only when the patient is asleep
Waiting for sleep is not the guidance; supervision and safety are the priority.
Ask the patient to undress without assistance for privacy
A combative patient needs supervision for safety rather than being left to undress alone.
Complete the examination as quickly as possible to limit risk
Speed does not replace constant supervision and a safe, organized approach.

w: Clean gloves only, because Standard Precautions require nothing more
Excessive drainage or splash risk calls for additional PPE beyond gloves.
Sterile gloves only, because the wound is open
Clean gloves reduce contact with contaminants; splash risk needs gown and eye protection.
No gloves, because hand hygiene alone is sufficient
Gloves are worn when an open sore or microorganism is present.

alt.q: When is it necessary for the nurse to add an isolation gown or eye shield during a physical examination?
alt.a: When a wound has excessive drainage or there is a risk of splashing
alt.ex: Additional PPE is added when excessive drainage or splashing could expose the nurse to contaminants.
w: Whenever the patient has intact skin and no open lesions
Intact skin without drainage does not require additional PPE.
Only when the patient requests that the nurse wear it
PPE is based on exposure risk, not patient request.
Whenever the nurse is examining a patient older than 65
Age alone does not determine the need for PPE.

alt.a: False

items.q: A patient has a known latex allergy. Which substitutes are appropriate for the nurse to use during care? Select all that apply.
o: Nitrile gloves in place of latex disposable gloves
Vinyl, nitrile, or neoprene gloves replace latex gloves.
Silicone catheters in place of latex catheters
Silicone catheters are a nonlatex alternative.
A covered blood pressure cuff
Covered cuffs prevent contact with latex in the cuff.
Nonlatex tape in place of adhesive tape
Adhesive tape may contain latex; nonlatex tapes are the substitute.
A rubber tourniquet applied over a thin gown
Latex-free or cloth-covered tourniquets are the recommended substitute.
items.ex: Nonlatex gloves, silicone catheters, covered cuffs and tubing, and nonlatex tapes reduce exposure to natural rubber latex.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a patient with latex allergy how to avoid latex at home. Which statements by the patient show understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “I will choose Mylar balloons instead of regular party balloons.”
Mylar balloons are a nonlatex alternative.
“I will use vinyl gloves when washing dishes.”
Vinyl gloves replace latex dishwashing gloves.
“I will use nonlatex condoms.”
Nonlatex condoms are recommended for people with latex allergy.
“Rubber bands are safe because they are not medical products.”
Rubber bands contain latex; string or latex-free bands are alternatives.
“Carpeting is always latex free, so I need not consider it.”
Carpeting can contain latex; other types of flooring are substitutes.
alt.ex: Household latex sources include balloons, dishwashing gloves, condoms, rubber bands, and carpeting, each with nonlatex substitutes.

A quiet, uninterrupted setting supports privacy and accurate findings.

Privacy helps patients feel comfortable discussing their condition.
Leaving the door open so staff can check on progress
An open door compromises privacy and invites interruptions.
Keeping the bed at its lowest height during the examination
Raise the bed so the nurse can reach the patient comfortably.
items.ex: A good examination environment provides privacy, adequate lighting, quiet, freedom from interruptions, and warmth.

alt.q: A nurse will examine a patient at home. Which preparations are appropriate? Select all that apply.

Home examinations are performed where privacy can be established.

Warmth and elimination of drafts maintain comfort.

Adequate lighting is necessary to illuminate body parts.
Examining the patient in the living room with family watching television
This setting lacks privacy and has noise and interruptions.
Turning off the lights so the patient feels more relaxed
Lighting is needed to see body parts properly.
alt.ex: Home examinations need a private, warm, quiet, well-lit space such as the patient’s bedroom.

items.a: It allows information to be documented in the same sequence it is gathered
items.ex: A standard form lets findings be documented in the same order in which they were collected, supporting organization.
w: It allows the nurse to skip body systems that seem normal
Skipping systems risks missing important findings.
It allows documentation to be finished before the examination
Findings are documented during and after, not before, the examination.
It allows the nurse to use personal abbreviations freely
Common and accepted medical terms and abbreviations should be used.

alt.q: A nurse documents examination findings in the electronic health record. Which practice keeps the notes accurate, brief, and concise?
alt.a: Using common and accepted medical terms and abbreviations
alt.ex: Common and accepted terms and abbreviations keep documentation accurate, brief, and concise.
w: Using abbreviations the nurse invented for speed
Unaccepted abbreviations may be misread and are not recommended.
Writing long narrative descriptions of normal findings
Notes should be brief and concise while using specific terms.
Recording general impressions such as “normal exam”
Assessments should be documented in specific terms.

Auscultation is not identified as the technique usually completed last.

w: Palpation

Auscultation is not the technique usually completed first.

items.q: Which physical assessment technique uses looking, listening, and smelling to distinguish normal from abnormal findings?
items.a: Inspection
items.ex: To inspect, the nurse carefully looks, listens, and smells to distinguish normal from abnormal findings.
w: Palpation
Palpation uses the sense of touch.
Percussion
Percussion involves tapping the skin to vibrate underlying tissues.
Auscultation
Auscultation is listening to internal body sounds, usually with a stethoscope.

alt.q: A nurse notes a patient’s facial expression, gait, and a fruity breath odor. Which technique is the nurse using?
alt.a: Inspection
alt.ex: Inspection includes observing nonverbal expressions and movements and noticing odors.
w: Palpation
Palpation requires touch to assess characteristics.
Percussion
Percussion produces sounds by tapping over body areas.
Auscultation
Auscultation uses a stethoscope to hear internal sounds.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which guidelines help the nurse achieve the best results during inspection? Select all that apply.
o: Use a direct light source such as a penlight to inspect body cavities
Direct lighting is needed to see inside body cavities.
Inspect each area for size, shape, color, symmetry, position, and abnormality
These are the characteristics assessed on inspection.
Compare each area with its match on the opposite side
Side-to-side comparison checks symmetry.
Validate findings with the patient
Validating findings confirms their accuracy.
Keep body parts covered so privacy is never compromised
Body parts are exposed as needed while still maintaining privacy.
Dim the lights to reduce glare on the skin
Adequate lighting is required for inspection.
items.ex: Good inspection requires adequate lighting, systematic assessment of characteristics, side-to-side comparison, proper exposure, and validation.

alt.q: A nursing student is inspecting a patient’s skin and oral cavity. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Ensuring adequate direct or indirect lighting
Adequate lighting is necessary for inspection.
Using a penlight to inspect the mouth
A direct light source is used for body cavities.
Exposing only the area being inspected while maintaining privacy
Expose body parts as needed while preserving privacy.
Ignoring personal vision deficits during inspection
Nurses must be aware of their own visual, hearing, or olfactory deficits.
Inspecting only the side with a reported problem
Each area is compared with its match on the opposite side.
alt.ex: Inspection uses adequate and direct lighting, appropriate exposure, side comparisons, and awareness of personal sensory deficits.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: While assessing a patient, a nurse notices a sweet, fruity odor on the patient’s breath. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Assess the patient for signs of diabetes mellitus
items.ex: A sweet, fruity breath odor from ketones suggests diabetic acidosis, so the nurse assesses for signs of diabetes.
w: Assess the patient for signs of a urinary tract infection
Ammonia-smelling urine, not fruity breath, suggests a urinary tract infection.
Assess the patient for signs of a bowel obstruction
A fecal odor of vomitus or breath suggests a bowel obstruction.
Provide mouth care for poor oral hygiene
Halitosis, not a sweet fruity odor, reflects poor oral hygiene.

alt.q: A patient’s breath has a sweet, fruity odor. Which condition does this odor most likely indicate?
alt.a: Diabetic acidosis
alt.ex: A sweet, fruity odor from ketones in the oral cavity is associated with diabetic acidosis.
w: Uremic acidosis
Uremic acidosis causes a stale urine odor on the skin.
Bowel obstruction
Bowel obstruction causes a fecal odor of vomitus or the oral cavity.
Gum disease
Gum disease causes halitosis, not a sweet, fruity odor.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which part of the hand should the nurse use to assess a patient’s skin temperature?
items.a: The dorsal surface of the hand
items.ex: The dorsum, or back, of the hand is used to assess temperature variations in the skin.
w: The palmar surface of the fingers
The palmar surface is used for texture, moisture, and vibration.
The fingertips grasping the skin
Grasping with fingertips assesses turgor and elasticity.
The ulnar surface of the hand
The ulnar surface is used to detect fremitus on the thorax.

alt.q: A nurse wants to compare the warmth of a patient’s two feet. Which technique is correct?
alt.a: Place the back of the hand on each foot
alt.ex: The dorsal surface of the hand detects temperature variations in the skin.
w: Press the fingertips firmly into each foot
Fingertip pressure does not assess temperature; the dorsum of the hand does.
Grasp the skin of each foot between the fingers
Grasping assesses turgor, not temperature.
Tap each foot with the fingertips
Tapping is percussion, which assesses density, not temperature.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is palpating a patient’s chest to detect vibration. Which part of the hand is best for this purpose?
items.a: The palmar surface of the hand and fingers
items.ex: Vibration is best felt on the palmar surface of the hand and fingers, including the bony part at the base of the fingers.
w: The dorsal surface of the hand
The dorsal surface is used to assess temperature.
The tips of the fingernails
Fingernails are kept short and are not used to sense vibration.
The thumb and index finger pinching the skin
Grasping the skin assesses turgor, not vibration.

alt.q: Which part of the hand is described as more sensitive than the fingertips and used to determine texture, size, consistency, masses, and crepitus?
alt.a: The palmar surface of the hand and finger pads
alt.ex: The palmar surface and finger pads are more sensitive than the fingertips for these characteristics.
w: The dorsal surface of the hand
The dorsal surface is best for temperature.
The ulnar edge of the hand
The ulnar surface is used for fremitus, not texture and masses.
The knuckles of a closed fist
Knuckles are not used to assess these characteristics.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Tense muscles make palpation more difficult, so the nurse should help the patient relax by having the patient take slow, deep breaths with arms at the sides.
items.a: True
items.ex: Relaxation measures such as slow, deep breaths and arms along the sides make palpation easier.
items.ww: Tension interferes with palpation, so promoting relaxation is part of the technique.

alt.q: Tender areas should be palpated first so the nurse can identify the problem before the patient becomes tired.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Tender areas are palpated last, after asking the patient to point to sensitive areas.
alt.ww: Palpating tender areas first can cause pain and muscle tension that interfere with the rest of the examination.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient reports abdominal pain in the right lower quadrant. How should the nurse plan palpation of the abdomen?
items.a: Palpate the other quadrants first and the tender area last
items.ex: Ask the patient to point to sensitive areas, watch for nonverbal discomfort, and palpate tender areas last.
w: Begin deep palpation directly over the tender area
Deep palpation is used with caution in areas of discomfort, and tender areas are palpated last.
Palpate only the tender quadrant to avoid extra discomfort
All areas are assessed, with the tender area left until last.
Palpate the tender area first to locate the problem quickly
Palpating tender areas first causes pain and muscle tension.

alt.q: Which preparation for palpation is correct?
alt.a: Warm the hands, keep fingernails short, and use a gentle approach
alt.ex: Preparation for palpation includes warming hands, short fingernails, and a gentle, slow, deliberate approach.
w: Cool the hands, keep fingernails long, and use firm, quick pressure
Cold hands, long nails, and quick pressure cause discomfort and tension.
Wear gloves at all times and use rapid pressure to save time
Palpation proceeds slowly and gently; gloves are worn based on infection risk.
Ask the patient to hold the breath and tense the abdomen
Tense muscles make palpation more difficult.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: How deep does the nurse press during light palpation?
items.a: About 1 cm (½ inch)
items.ex: Light palpation presses inward about 1 cm, letting the patient identify areas of tenderness.
w: About 4 cm (2 inches)
Four centimeters is the depth for deep palpation.
About 6 cm (3 inches)
This exceeds both light and deep palpation depths.
About 0.25 cm (⅛ inch)
This is less than the light palpation depth described.

alt.q: How deep does the nurse depress the area during deep palpation of the abdomen?
alt.a: About 4 cm (2 inches)
alt.ex: Deep palpation depresses the area about 4 cm, using one or both hands, to examine organs.
w: About 1 cm (½ inch)
One centimeter is the depth for light palpation.
About 8 cm (3 inches)
This depth exceeds the described deep palpation depth.
About 2 cm (¾ inch)
This is less than the described deep palpation depth.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: When using bimanual palpation, the relaxed [[sensing|sensing hand]] hand rests lightly on the skin while the [[active|active hand]] hand applies pressure to it.
items.ex: The sensing hand does not exert pressure directly, so it stays sensitive to organ characteristics.

alt.q: In bimanual palpation, the lower hand that rests lightly on the skin and does not press directly is called the [[sensing|sensing hand]] hand.
alt.ex: The sensing hand does not exert pressure directly, so it stays sensitive to organ characteristics.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse plans deep palpation of the abdomen of a patient who reports moderate discomfort in that area. What should the nurse keep in mind?
items.a: Deep palpation should be used with caution in an area of discomfort
items.ex: For safety, deep palpation is used with caution in a patient with discomfort in the area to be palpated.
w: Deep palpation is most accurate when started over the painful area
Tender areas are palpated last, and deep palpation is used cautiously there.
Deep palpation should always replace light palpation in painful areas
Light palpation first lets the patient identify tenderness.
Deep palpation requires the patient to tense the abdominal muscles
Tense muscles make palpation more difficult.

alt.q: What is the purpose of light palpation of the abdomen?
alt.a: To give the patient a chance to identify areas of tenderness
alt.ex: Light, superficial palpation lets the patient identify tender areas, which are then assessed further.
w: To determine the size of the liver and other deep organs
Organ condition is examined with deep palpation.
To produce sounds that reflect the density of tissue
Sounds that reflect tissue density are produced by percussion.
To detect internal sounds made by moving blood and air
Internal sounds are detected by auscultation.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: During percussion, how does the density of the underlying tissue affect the sound produced?
items.a: The denser the tissue, the quieter the sound
items.ex: The character of the percussion sound reflects tissue density; denser tissue produces a quieter sound.
w: The denser the tissue, the louder the sound
This reverses the relationship; denser tissue is quieter.
Density has no effect on the sound produced
The sound’s character directly reflects the density of the tissue.
The less dense the tissue, the shorter and quieter the sound
Less dense tissue produces a louder sound, not a quieter one.

alt.q: A nurse percusses over an area and hears an unexpected sound for that location. What might this indicate?
alt.a: A mass or a substance such as air or fluid in an organ or cavity
alt.ex: An abnormal percussion sound suggests a mass or substance such as air or fluid within an organ or body cavity.
w: Normal vibration of the heart valves closing
Heart valve closure is heard by auscultation, not percussion.
Poor hygiene of the skin over the area
Hygiene problems are detected by inspection and odor, not percussion.
Skin temperature changes from inflammation
Temperature is assessed by palpation with the dorsal hand.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Percussion is used more often by advanced practice registered nurses than by nurses in daily practice at the bedside.
items.a: True
items.ex: The skill of percussion is used more often by advanced practice registered nurses.
items.ww: Bedside nurses use inspection, palpation, and auscultation more routinely than percussion.

alt.q: Percussion is the assessment technique bedside nurses use most often in daily practice to locate organs.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Percussion is used more often by advanced practice registered nurses than by bedside nurses.
alt.ww: Although percussion can map organs, it is not a routine daily bedside technique for most nurses.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to auscultate a patient’s bowel sounds. Which part of the stethoscope should the nurse use?
items.a: The diaphragm, which is best for high-pitched sounds
items.ex: The diaphragm is best for high-pitched sounds such as bowel and lung sounds.
w: The bell, which is best for high-pitched sounds
The bell is best for low-pitched sounds.
The bell, which is best for bowel and lung sounds
Bowel and lung sounds are high pitched and best heard with the diaphragm.
The diaphragm, which is best for low-pitched sounds
The diaphragm is for high-pitched sounds; the bell is for low-pitched sounds.

alt.q: A nurse wants to listen for low-pitched vascular sounds over an artery. Which part of the stethoscope is best?
alt.a: The bell
alt.ex: The bell is best for hearing low-pitched sounds such as vascular and certain heart sounds.
w: The diaphragm
The diaphragm is best for high-pitched sounds such as bowel and lung sounds.
The tubing
The tubing carries sound; touching it creates extraneous sounds.
The earpieces
The earpieces deliver sound to the ears; they do not pick up body sounds.

items.q: A nurse describes a heart sound as having a blowing character. Which sound characteristic is the nurse describing?
items.a: Quality
items.ex: Quality describes sounds of similar frequency and loudness from different sources, using terms such as blowing or gurgling.
w: Frequency
Frequency refers to the number of sound wave cycles per second, or pitch.
Loudness

Duration
Duration refers to how long the sound vibrations last.

alt.q: Why do sounds from deep internal organs often have a shorter duration when auscultated?
alt.a: Layers of soft tissue dampen the duration of the sounds
alt.ex: Duration is the length of time vibrations last, and layers of soft tissue dampen sounds from deep organs.
w: Deep organs vibrate at a higher frequency
Frequency affects pitch, not how tissue dampens duration.
Stethoscope tubing shortens all sounds equally
Tubing does not explain the dampening of deep organ sounds.
Deep organs produce only soft-quality sounds
Quality describes the character of the sound, not its duration.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which actions reflect correct use and care of the stethoscope? Select all that apply.
o: Place the earpieces with the tips turned toward the face
Earpieces turned toward the face give clearer sounds.
Clean the diaphragm and bell before using on another patient
Cleaning between patients reduces transfer of bacteria such as MRSA.
Let the tubing hang free during auscultation
Touching or moving the tubing creates extraneous sounds.
Remove and clean the earpieces regularly to remove cerumen
Earpieces collect cerumen and bacteria and need regular cleaning.
Drape the stethoscope around the neck next to the skin
Body oils damage the tubing; avoid draping it next to the skin.
Talk with the patient while listening to lung sounds
Both the patient and the examiner need to remain quiet during auscultation.
items.ex: Proper stethoscope use includes correct earpiece position, free-hanging tubing, quiet surroundings, and regular cleaning between patients.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a student about stethoscope infection control. Which statements by the student show understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “I will wipe the diaphragm with isopropyl alcohol between patients.”
Isopropyl alcohol reduces bacterial colonies on the stethoscope.
“Hand foam can be used to clean the diaphragm and bell.”
Hand foam effectively reduces bacterial colonies on the chest piece.
“I will perform hand hygiene before and after patient contact.”
Hand hygiene reduces transfer of microorganisms from the nurse’s ears to the patient.
“Earpieces cannot carry bacteria, so they never need cleaning.”
Earpieces are sources of transferable bacteria.
“I only need to clean the stethoscope once a week.”
Clean it daily or after soiling and before reuse on another patient.
alt.ex: Stethoscope infection control includes cleaning between patients, cleaning earpieces, and hand hygiene before and after contact.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: While auscultating lung sounds, a student hears rubbing noises each time the stethoscope tubing brushes the bed rail. What is the best explanation?
items.a: Contact with the tubing creates extraneous sounds
items.ex: Extraneous sounds created by rubbing against the tubing or chest piece interfere with auscultation of organ sounds.
w: The sounds are abnormal breath sounds from the patient
The noise is linked to tubing contact, not the patient’s lungs.
The diaphragm is turned to the wrong position
An incorrect chest piece position makes sounds barely audible, not rubbing noises.
The earpieces are turned toward the face
Earpieces toward the face give clearer sound; this does not cause rubbing.

alt.q: Why should a nurse deliberately produce extraneous sounds while practicing with a stethoscope?
alt.a: To learn to recognize and disregard them during an examination
alt.ex: Deliberately producing extraneous sounds teaches the nurse to recognize and disregard them.
w: To check whether the patient can hear the stethoscope
The exercise trains the examiner, not the patient.
To test whether the earpieces need replacement
The purpose is recognizing extraneous sounds, not checking earpieces.
To warm the diaphragm before placing it on the skin
Warming is done between the hands, not by producing sounds.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse lightly blows into the diaphragm of the stethoscope and the sound is barely audible. What should the nurse conclude?
items.a: The bell is in position for use
items.ex: Sound passes through only one part of the chest piece at a time; if the diaphragm is barely audible, the bell is in position.
w: The diaphragm is in position for use
If the diaphragm were in position, the sound would be greatly amplified.
The earpieces are facing the correct direction
Earpiece direction affects clarity but does not explain a barely audible diaphragm.
The stethoscope tubing is cracked and must be replaced
A barely audible diaphragm usually means the bell is the active side.

alt.q: A nurse with a mild hearing deficit wants to improve auscultation. Which option does the textbook describe?
alt.a: Obtaining a stethoscope with extra sound amplification
alt.ex: Nurses with hearing disorders can obtain stethoscopes with extra sound amplification.
w: Relying on percussion instead of auscultation
Percussion does not replace auscultation of internal sounds.
Asking the patient to describe the internal sounds
Patients cannot hear their own internal sounds for the nurse.
Pressing the bell more firmly against the skin
Extra pressure is not described as the solution for hearing deficits.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient walks into the examination room grimacing, bent forward, and splinting the right side of the abdomen. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Examine the abdomen and the painful area before other body systems
items.ex: Obvious signs of distress such as grimacing and splinting call for setting priorities and examining the related areas first.
w: Begin the head-to-toe examination with the head and neck
A routine sequence delays assessment of the area causing obvious distress.
Complete the full dietary and weight history before examining
A detailed history can wait; signs of distress set the examination priority.
Measure height and weight before addressing the complaint
Routine measurements are not the priority when the patient shows signs of pain.

alt.q: During the general survey, a patient is short of breath and has sternal retractions. How should the nurse proceed?
alt.a: Set priorities and assess the respiratory system first
alt.ex: Signs of difficulty breathing indicate distress, so the nurse examines the related physical areas first.
w: Finish the general survey of dress and grooming first
Grooming observations are low priority when breathing is impaired.
Follow the usual head-to-toe order without changes
Signs of distress require setting priorities rather than following a routine order.
Measure the patient’s weight on a standing scale first
Weighing does not address the patient’s difficulty breathing.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A woman with bruises at different stages of healing says she “fell down the stairs” while her partner answers most questions for her. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Find a way to interview the patient privately, without the partner present
items.ex: Patients are more likely to reveal abuse when the suspected abuser is absent from the room.
w: Ask the partner to describe exactly how the fall happened
The partner may be the abuser; questioning the partner does not give the patient a safe chance to speak.
Ask the patient about abuse while the partner is in the room
Victims seldom disclose abuse in front of the suspected abuser.
Document the fall as described and continue the examination
An explanation that does not fit the injuries needs follow-up, not simple acceptance.

alt.q: A nurse suspects that an older adult is being neglected by an adult child who accompanies the patient. Which approach is most likely to help the patient disclose problems?
alt.a: Interviewing the patient alone, away from the adult child
alt.ex: Interviewing in private increases the chance that a patient will reveal abuse or neglect.
w: Interviewing the patient and adult child together
The suspected abuser’s presence discourages the patient from disclosing.
Interviewing only the adult child about the patient’s care
This leaves out the patient, who is the person at risk.
Waiting for the patient to report the abuse spontaneously
Victims often do not report abuse, so the nurse must create a safe opportunity.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A hospitalized patient weighed 72.0 kg yesterday and weighs 73.2 kg this morning on the same scale at the same time. What does this change most likely indicate?
items.a: A fluid-retention problem
items.ex: A weight gain of 0.9 to 1.4 kg (2–3 lb) in 1 day indicates fluid retention.
w: A normal daily weight variation
Some daily variation is normal, but a gain of over 1 kg in a day points to fluid retention.
An improvement in nutritional reserves
Gains in nutritional reserves occur gradually, not over a single day.
An inaccurate scale that needs calibration
The same scale and time were used, so the gain is likely real.

alt.q: Which 1-day weight change in a hospitalized patient indicates a fluid-retention problem?
alt.a: A gain of 0.9 to 1.4 kg (2–3 lb)
alt.ex: A gain of about 2 to 3 lb in a single day suggests the patient is retaining fluid.
w: A gain of 0.1 to 0.2 kg (¼–½ lb)
Small daily changes reflect normal fluid loss or retention.
A loss of 0.1 to 0.2 kg (¼–½ lb)
A small daily loss is within normal variation.
A loss of 0.3 to 0.4 kg (¾–1 lb)
A small loss does not indicate fluid retention.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: When is a patient’s weight loss considered significant enough to need medical evaluation?
items.a: Loss of more than 5% of body weight in 6 months to a year
items.ex: Losing more than 5% of body weight in 6 to 12 months is significant and requires evaluation.
w: Loss of more than 1% of body weight in 6 months to a year
A 1% loss is within normal fluctuation and is not the stated threshold.
Loss of more than 15% of body weight in 2 years
Waiting for a 15% loss would miss a significant problem; the threshold is lower and over a shorter time.
Loss of more than 2% of body weight in 2 years
This small, slow loss does not meet the threshold for significant weight loss.

alt.q: A patient weighed 80 kg last year and now weighs 74 kg without trying to lose weight. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: It is a significant loss of more than 5% that needs medical evaluation
alt.ex: A 6-kg loss is 7.5% of body weight, exceeding the 5% in 6 to 12 months threshold.
w: It is a normal daily fluctuation caused by fluid shifts
Daily fluid shifts are small; this is a sustained loss over a year.
It is an insignificant loss of less than 5% of body weight
The 6-kg loss equals 7.5%, which is above the 5% threshold.
It is significant only if the loss happened within one week
Loss of more than 5% over 6 months to a year is already significant.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Why are a hospitalized patient’s daily weights measured at the same time of day on the same scale?
items.a: To allow an objective comparison of weights from day to day
items.ex: Consistent timing and the same scale allow objective comparison, which matters because drug and care decisions are based on changes.
w: To shorten the time needed to calibrate the scale
Calibration is not the reason; consistency allows valid comparison.
To ensure the patient has an empty stomach each time
Fasting is not the stated reason; comparability of weights is.
To let the patient choose the most convenient time
The time is standardized for accuracy, not set for patient convenience.

alt.q: A nurse weighs a patient on a bed scale at 0600 one day and on a standing scale at 1400 the next. What is the main problem with this practice?
alt.a: The weights cannot be compared objectively
alt.ex: Daily weights must be taken at the same time on the same scale so that changes reflect the patient, not the method.
w: The bed scale is not allowed for hospitalized patients
Bed scales are appropriate for patients who cannot bear weight.
A standing scale is always less accurate than a bed scale
Neither scale is inherently less accurate; switching between them is the problem.
Weights should only be measured at bedtime
No specific hour is required, only the same time each day.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Why should the nurse measure vital signs before beginning positional changes during the examination?
items.a: Measurements are more accurate before the patient changes position or moves
items.ex: Vital sign measurement is more accurate when completed before positional changes or movements.
w: Measurements are faster to obtain once the patient is lying down
Speed is not the reason; movement can alter readings.
Measurements are required before any history questions are asked
The general survey and history come before vital signs.
Measurements must be taken before pain is assessed as the fifth vital sign
Pain is assessed together with vital signs, not after them.

alt.q: A nurse doubts the accuracy of a blood pressure measured at the start of an examination. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Recheck the vital signs later during the examination
alt.ex: If initial vital signs might be inaccurate, recheck them during the rest of the examination.
w: Record the first reading and ignore the doubt
A possibly inaccurate value should be rechecked, not simply recorded.
Skip the vital signs until the next shift
Vital signs are part of this examination and should be rechecked, not delayed.
Estimate the value from the patient’s usual readings
Vital signs must be measured, not estimated.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which posture is a common normal finding in an older adult during the general survey?
items.a: Stooped and forward bent, with hips and knees somewhat flexed
items.ex: Changes in older adult physiology often produce a stooped, forward-bent posture with flexed hips, knees, and elbows.
w: Rigidly erect, with hips and shoulders hyperextended
Hyperextension is not the typical posture associated with aging.
Upright, with the shoulders held completely straight when sitting
Even normal sitting posture involves some rounding of the shoulders.
Leaning sideways, with one shoulder lower than the hip
A lateral lean is not described as a normal aging change.

alt.q: A nurse observes an 82-year-old patient standing with a stooped, forward-bent posture, knees slightly flexed, and elbows bent. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: It is a common posture change with aging
alt.ex: Aging physiology often results in a stooped, forward-bent posture with flexed hips, knees, and elbows.
w: It is a sign of acute respiratory distress
Respiratory distress shows with shortness of breath and retractions, not this typical aging posture.
It always indicates depression
Slumped posture may reflect mood, but this pattern is typical of normal aging.
It indicates an acute fracture of the hip
This posture is a common aging finding, not a sign of fracture.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which description reflects a normal gait observed during the general survey?
items.a: Smooth walking with arms swinging freely and heel-to-toe placement
items.ex: A person normally walks smoothly, arms swinging freely, each leg moving heel to toe, with the head and face leading.
w: Shuffling steps with the arms held stiffly at the sides
Shuffling and stiff arms are not part of a normal gait.
Walking with one foot dragging slightly along the floor
Dragging a foot is an abnormal finding to note.
Walking with the trunk leading and the head bent down
Normally the head and face lead the body.

alt.q: While observing a patient walk into the room, which finding should the nurse note as abnormal?
alt.a: Dragging of one foot along the floor
alt.ex: The nurse notes whether the feet touch the floor correctly or whether a foot drags, which is abnormal.
w: Arms swinging freely at the sides
Free arm swing is part of a normal gait.
Heel-to-toe placement of each foot
Heel-to-toe placement is normal.
Head and face leading the body
This is the normal alignment while walking.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse suspects that a patient’s inconsistent behavior during a clinic visit is related to substance abuse. Which approach is best?
items.a: Approach the patient in a caring, nonjudgmental way and do a focused history
items.ex: Substance abuse involves emotional and lifestyle issues, so the nurse investigates with a caring, nonjudgmental focused history and examination.
w: Confront the patient directly with the suspicion of drug use
Confrontation is judgmental and discourages honest disclosure.
Ignore the behavior because one visit cannot reveal a problem
One visit may not reveal it, but unusual behaviors should still be investigated.
Assume substance abuse only occurs in low-income patients
Substance abuse affects all socioeconomic groups.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student about assessing for substance abuse needs correction?
alt.a: “Substance abuse is limited to patients in low socioeconomic groups.”
alt.ex: Substance abuse affects all socioeconomic groups, so this statement is incorrect.
w: “I should approach the patient in a caring, nonjudgmental way.”
This is correct because substance abuse involves emotional and lifestyle issues.
“A single clinic visit may not reveal the problem.”
This is correct; one visit does not always reveal substance abuse.
“Unusual behaviors need a focused history and examination.”
This is correct; unusual behaviors should be investigated further.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: An older adult arrives at the clinic on a warm day wearing a heavy sweater and a coat. What is the most likely explanation for this finding?
items.a: Older adults may wear extra clothing because of sensitivity to cold
items.ex: An older adult might wear extra clothing because of increased sensitivity to cold.
w: Extra clothing always indicates a mental illness
Depression or mental illness can affect dress, but older adults often wear extra layers due to cold sensitivity.
Extra clothing always indicates financial hardship
Socioeconomic level affects clothing choice, but this does not explain dressing warmly in heat.
Extra clothing is a sign of substance intoxication
Dressing warmly is not listed as an indicator of substance abuse.

alt.q: When assessing a patient’s dress during the general survey, what is the nurse mainly judging?
alt.a: Whether the clothing is appropriate for the temperature, weather, or setting
alt.ex: Culture and preference affect clothing, but the nurse assesses whether it suits the temperature, weather, or setting.
w: Whether the clothing reflects current fashion trends
Fashion is personal preference and not the focus of assessment.
Whether the clothing matches the patient’s cultural background
Culture influences dress; the nurse does not judge it.
Whether the clothing is expensive or inexpensive
Socioeconomic level affects clothing but is not what the nurse evaluates.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which patient behaviors, especially in combination or repeated, should prompt further assessment for substance abuse? Select all that apply.
o: Frequently misses appointments
Frequent missed appointments are an indicator of possible substance abuse.
Reports lost prescriptions for pain medications
Reporting lost prescriptions or requesting frequent refills is a red-flag behavior.
Brings in medication bottles from several different providers
Changing providers or having prescriptions from many providers is an indicator.
Has frequent emergency department visits
Frequent ED visits are listed among indicators of substance abuse.
Keeps a consistent relationship with one primary provider
Stable care with one provider is not an indicator; changing providers is.
Takes prescribed medications exactly as directed
Correct medication use does not suggest substance abuse.
items.ex: Repeated patterns such as missed appointments, lost prescriptions, multiple providers, and frequent ED visits suggest possible substance abuse.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a patient’s history for indicators of substance abuse. Which findings support further assessment? Select all that apply.
o: History of pancreatitis and gastrointestinal bleeding
GI bleeding, ulcers, pancreatitis, and cellulitis are listed indicators.
Repeated admissions to rule out heart attacks
Chest pain complaints with admissions to rule out MI are an indicator.
Frequent requests for written excuses from work
Frequent requests for absence excuses are an indicator.
Regular attendance at scheduled annual checkups
Keeping appointments is not an indicator; missing them is.
No family history of addiction
A family history of addiction, not its absence, is a risk indicator.
alt.ex: Medical problems such as GI bleeding, repeated rule-out MI admissions, and frequent absence excuses are substance abuse indicators.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which findings in an adult are clinical indicators of possible physical abuse? Select all that apply.
o: Injuries that do not match the reported cause
Injuries inconsistent with the explanation are a key indicator of abuse.
X-ray films showing fractures in different stages of healing
Old and new fractures together suggest repeated trauma.
Burns from cigarettes
Cigarette burns are listed among physical indicators of abuse.
Strangulation marks or bruises on the neck
Neck marks, throat pain, and voice changes can indicate strangulation.
A single healed scar from a childhood appendectomy
A surgical scar with a clear cause is not an abuse indicator.
Calluses on the palms of a manual laborer
Occupational calluses are explained by their cause and do not suggest abuse.
items.ex: Injuries inconsistent with the story, fractures in different healing stages, cigarette burns, and strangulation marks suggest abuse.

alt.q: A nurse examines an older adult who depends on a caregiver. Which findings suggest possible elder abuse or neglect? Select all that apply.
o: Bruises at various stages of resolution
Hematomas and bruises in different stages suggest repeated injury.
Chafing and excoriation on the wrists from restraints
Restraint marks on wrists or legs are indicators of abuse.
A prolonged interval between injury and treatment
Delay in seeking care for an injury is an indicator.
Pressure injuries (bedsores) and extreme thirst
Bedsores and extreme thirst are signs of neglect.
Clean clothing and well-managed medications
Good care is not an indicator; overmedication or undermedication is.
alt.ex: Bruises in different stages, restraint marks, delayed treatment, bedsores, and dehydration suggest elder abuse or neglect.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which factors increase an older adult’s risk for developing alcohol-related problems? Select all that apply.
o: Social isolation and loneliness
Isolation and loneliness are listed risk factors in older adults.
Recent bereavement
Loss of a loved one increases risk for alcohol-related problems.
Chronic or acute pain
Pain is a listed risk factor for older adults.
Sleep disorders
Sleep disorders increase the risk for alcohol-related problems.
Regularly sharing meals with family and friends
Shared meals promote dietary intake; social isolation, not connection, is the risk.
Absence of chronic medical disorders
Chronic medical disorders, not their absence, increase risk.
items.ex: In older adults, chronic medical disorders, sleep disorders, isolation, loneliness, bereavement, and pain raise the risk of alcohol problems.

alt.q: A nurse screens a 78-year-old for alcohol misuse. Which patient details are risk factors for alcohol-related problems? Select all that apply.
o: Lives alone since spouse died last year
Bereavement and social isolation are risk factors.
Has chronic back pain
Chronic pain increases risk for alcohol problems in older adults.
Has insomnia most nights
Sleep disorders are a risk factor.
Attends a weekly community group with friends
Social engagement is not a risk; isolation is.
Reports no chronic illnesses
Chronic medical disorders, not their absence, raise risk.
alt.ex: Bereavement, isolation, chronic pain, and sleep problems are risk factors for alcohol-related problems in older adults.
