items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is weighing an infant on a platform scale. Which action best prevents an accidental fall?
items.a: Hold a hand lightly above the infant while the infant is on the scale
items.ex: Holding a hand lightly above the infant detects movement and prevents accidental falls.
w: Place a light cloth cover on the scale before weighing
The cover prevents cross-infection, not falls.
Zero the scale with a dry diaper on it before weighing
Zeroing excludes the diaper’s weight; it does not prevent falls.
Keep the room warm while the infant is undressed
A warm room prevents chills, not falls.

alt.q: Why does the nurse place a dry diaper on an infant scale and zero the scale before weighing the infant?
alt.a: So the weight of items on the scale is not counted in the infant’s weight
alt.ex: Zeroing with the diaper on the scale removes its weight from the infant’s measured weight.
w: So the infant does not become chilled during weighing
A warm room prevents chills; zeroing relates to accuracy.
So the infant cannot roll off the scale platform
A hand held above the infant prevents falls.
So urine or feces do not spread infection to others
A light cloth or paper cover prevents cross-infection.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse needs to assess a patient with dark skin for cyanosis. Which site is most appropriate?
items.a: The buccal mucosa
items.ex: In dark skin, assess for cyanosis where pigmentation is least, such as conjunctiva, sclera, buccal mucosa, tongue, lips, nail beds, palms, and soles.
w: The skin of the forehead
Facial skin is pigmented and sun exposed, making cyanosis hard to see.
The skin over the upper back
Pigmented skin surfaces hide color changes such as cyanosis.
The skin on the back of the hand
This pigmented area is not where cyanosis is best detected in dark skin.

alt.q: In a patient with dark skin, why does the nurse inspect the conjunctiva, tongue, and palms for cyanosis?
alt.a: These areas have the least pigmentation
alt.ex: Cyanosis is assessed where pigmentation occurs least so that color changes are visible.
w: These areas are the warmest parts of the body
Temperature is not the reason; low pigmentation makes color changes visible.
These areas are exposed to the most sunlight
Sun-exposed areas are darker and less useful for color assessment.
These areas contain the most melanin
More melanin would hide cyanosis; these sites have the least.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which site is best for the nurse to inspect for jaundice?
items.a: The sclera
items.ex: The sclera is the best site to inspect for the yellow-orange discoloration of jaundice.
w: The palms
Palms are useful for many color changes, but the sclera is the best site for jaundice.
The nail beds
Nail beds are used to assess cyanosis and pallor.
The sacrum
The sacrum is a common site for erythema from pressure.

alt.q: A patient with liver disease has yellow-orange skin. Which condition does this color represent?
alt.a: Jaundice from increased bilirubin in the tissues
alt.ex: Jaundice is a yellow-orange color from increased bilirubin deposits, caused by liver disease or red blood cell destruction.
w: Cyanosis from increased deoxygenated hemoglobin
Cyanosis is a bluish color associated with hypoxia.
Erythema from increased visibility of oxyhemoglobin
Erythema is redness from dilation or increased blood flow.
Pallor from reduced amount of oxyhemoglobin
Pallor is a decrease in color, often from anemia.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse suspects inflammation over a patient’s sacrum but has difficulty seeing erythema because the patient has dark skin. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Palpate the area for warmth and compare it with another skin area
items.ex: Erythema is hard to see in dark skin, so palpate for heat and compare with a different area to detect a temperature difference.
w: Document that no erythema is present
Absence of visible redness does not rule out inflammation in dark skin.
Wait to reassess the area under brighter light tomorrow
Delaying assessment risks missing a developing problem; palpation gives information now.
Assess the area for tenting by pinching the skin
Tenting assesses turgor and hydration, not inflammation.

alt.q: In a patient with dark skin, which assessment finding helps the nurse detect a stage 1 pressure injury early?
alt.a: Warmth over the area when compared with surrounding skin
alt.ex: Warmth over an area of erythema helps identify a stage 1 pressure injury, especially when redness is hard to see.
w: Coolness over the area compared with surrounding skin
Coolness reflects decreased blood flow; inflammation produces warmth.
Rapid return of the skin after pinching
Normal turgor does not identify pressure injury.
A shiny, translucent appearance of the skin
Shiny, translucent skin describes atrophy.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which site is most appropriate for assessing skin turgor in an adult?
items.a: The back of the forearm
items.ex: Turgor is assessed by pinching skin on the back of the forearm or the sternal area.
w: The back of the hand
Skin on the back of the hand is normally loose and thin, so turgor is not reliable there.
The palm of the hand
Palm skin is normally thick; turgor is assessed on the forearm or sternal area.
The skin of the earlobe
The earlobe is not a recommended site for assessing turgor.

alt.q: Why is skin turgor not assessed reliably on the back of the hand?
alt.a: The skin there is normally loose and thin
alt.ex: Because the skin on the back of the hand is loose and thin, it does not reflect hydration reliably.
w: The skin there is normally thick and callused
Thick skin is found on the palms and soles, not the back of the hand.
The skin there is too sensitive to pinch
Sensitivity is not the reason; the loose, thin skin is.
The skin there is darker than other areas
Pigmentation does not affect turgor assessment.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse presses firmly on a patient’s edematous ankle for several seconds and releases it, leaving an indentation 6 mm deep. How should the nurse document this?
items.a: 3+ pitting edema
items.ex: Pitting depth determines the grade: 1+ is 2 mm, 2+ is 4 mm, 3+ is 6 mm, and 4+ is 8 mm.
w: 1+ pitting edema
1+ edema equals a 2-mm depth.
2+ pitting edema
2+ edema equals a 4-mm depth.
4+ pitting edema
4+ edema equals an 8-mm depth.

alt.q: Which depth of indentation corresponds to 2+ pitting edema?
alt.a: 4 mm
alt.ex: 2+ pitting edema leaves a 4-mm indentation after firm pressure.
w: 2 mm
A 2-mm depth is 1+ edema.
6 mm
A 6-mm depth is 3+ edema.
8 mm
An 8-mm depth is 4+ edema.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which part of the hand should the nurse use to assess skin temperature?
items.a: The dorsum, or back, of the hand
items.ex: Skin temperature is assessed accurately with the dorsum of the hand while comparing symmetrical body parts.
w: The palm of the hand
The palm is not the surface recommended for temperature.
The fingertips
Fingertips are used to assess moisture and texture.
The ulnar side of the hand
The ulnar surface is used for vibration such as fremitus.

alt.q: A nurse wants to compare skin temperature in a patient’s legs after vascular surgery. Which technique is correct?
alt.a: Palpate both legs with the back of the hand and compare sides
alt.ex: Temperature is assessed with the dorsum of the hand, comparing symmetrical parts, especially after vascular surgery.
w: Palpate one leg with the fingertips only
Fingertips assess texture; temperature needs the back of the hand and side-to-side comparison.
Pinch the skin of each leg and release it
Pinching assesses turgor, not temperature.
Press the skin with the thumb for several seconds
Firm thumb pressure assesses pitting edema.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient with diabetes mellitus about nail and foot care. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I will file my nails rather than cut them.”
items.ex: Patients with diabetes are told to file rather than cut their nails.
w: “I will soak my feet for 10 minutes before trimming my nails.”
Soaking is avoided in diabetes because it causes maceration and infection.
“I will put lotion between my toes to keep them soft.”
Moisture between the toes allows microorganisms to grow.
“I will use an over-the-counter product for my corns.”
Patients are cautioned against OTC preparations for corns and calluses.

alt.q: Which instruction should the nurse include when teaching foot care to a patient with diabetes mellitus?
alt.a: Inspect your feet each day in good lighting for dry places and cracks
alt.ex: Daily foot inspection in good lighting helps detect dry places and cracks early in patients with diabetes.
w: Soak your feet in warm water before cutting your nails
Soaking causes maceration and dry, cracked skin that leads to infection.
Apply lotion between your toes after bathing
Lotion between the toes keeps moisture there and promotes infection.
Dig under your toenails with a sharp tool to clean them
Sharp objects under nails or around cuticles cause injury.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse observes that a patient’s nail beds have an angle greater than 180 degrees with softened, flattened nails and enlarged fingertips. What does this finding most likely indicate?
items.a: Chronic lack of oxygen from heart or pulmonary disease
items.ex: Clubbing, an angle larger than 180 degrees with nail bed softening, results from chronic lack of oxygen.
w: Iron deficiency anemia
Iron deficiency causes koilonychia, or spoon-shaped concave nails.
A local infection at the base of the nail
Local infection causes paronychia, inflammation at the nail base.
A recent severe systemic infection
Temporary disturbance from severe illness causes Beau lines.

alt.q: What is the normal angle between the nail plate and the nail?
alt.a: About 160 degrees
alt.ex: Normal nails have a nail bed angle of about 160 degrees; a larger angle suggests chronic oxygenation problems.
w: About 90 degrees
This angle is far smaller than normal.
About 120 degrees
This is smaller than the normal nail angle.
About 200 degrees
An angle beyond 180 degrees indicates clubbing.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A parent is embarrassed after the school nurse finds head lice on the child. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Lice spread easily among children who play closely; it does not mean poor hygiene.”
items.ex: The presence of lice does not mean poor hygiene; lice spread easily among children who play closely together.
w: “Lice usually mean the child needs to bathe more often.”
Lice are not a sign of poor hygiene.
“Lice will go away on their own if you wait a few weeks.”
Lice require immediate treatment once discovered.
“Lice are only a concern if the child has body lice too.”
Head lice alone require immediate treatment.

alt.q: A nurse finds small oval particles attached to a child’s hair shafts and small red pustules behind the ears. Which action is most appropriate?
alt.a: Arrange for immediate treatment because lice are present
alt.ex: Lice eggs attach to hair, and red pustular eruptions behind the ears suggest infestation that requires immediate treatment.
w: Recommend a dandruff shampoo for dry scalp
Lice eggs resemble dandruff but cling to hair; treating dandruff misses the infestation.
Tell the parent the child needs better hygiene
Lice do not indicate poor hygiene.
Recheck the scalp at the next annual visit
Lice require immediate treatment, not delayed follow-up.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which statement about basal cell carcinoma is accurate?
items.a: It almost never spreads to other parts of the body
items.ex: Basal cell carcinoma occurs in sun-exposed, sun-damaged areas and almost never spreads to other parts of the body.
w: It develops from melanocytes in a changing mole
Melanoma, not basal cell carcinoma, develops from melanocytes.
It often travels to lymph nodes and throughout the body
Squamous cell carcinoma, not basal cell, may spread to lymph nodes and the body.
It occurs mostly on skin never exposed to the sun
Basal cell carcinoma is most common in sun-exposed areas.

alt.q: Which skin cancer develops from melanocytes and often begins as a mole that has changed in appearance?
alt.a: Malignant melanoma
alt.ex: Melanoma develops from melanocytes and often starts as a mole that changes in appearance.
w: Basal cell carcinoma
Basal cell carcinoma is a crusted lesion with a rolled border in sun-damaged skin.
Squamous cell carcinoma
Squamous cell carcinoma develops in outer layers of sun-exposed skin as a scaly lesion.
Senile keratosis
Senile keratosis is a benign age-related skin thickening.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse finds a moist, draining lesion on a patient’s leg. Which action should the nurse take before palpating it?
items.a: Put on disposable gloves
items.ex: Gloves are worn to palpate lesions that are open, moist, or draining.
w: Palpate with ungloved fingertips to assess texture
Ungloved palpation is used for intact skin, not draining lesions.
Apply firm pressure to measure lesion depth
Lesions are palpated gently, not with firm pressure.
Cover the lesion with a dressing before inspection
The lesion must be inspected in good light before it is covered.

alt.q: Which findings call for the nurse to wear gloves when palpating the skin or scalp?
alt.a: Open lesions, drainage, or lice
alt.ex: Gloves are needed when lesions are open, moist, or draining, or when lice are found.
w: Dry, intact skin of an older adult
Intact skin is palpated with ungloved fingertips.
Freckles and cherry angiomas
These common lesions are not open or draining.
Normal moisture in the axillae
Normal skinfold moisture does not require gloves.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which features should the nurse look for when using the ABCDE method to assess a mole for cancer? Select all that apply.
o: One half of the mole does not match the other half
Asymmetry is the A in ABCDE.
Edges that are blurred, notched, or ragged
Border irregularity is the B.
Variegated areas of blue, black, and brown
Nonuniform color is the C.
Diameter greater than 6 mm
Diameter larger than a pencil eraser is the D.
A uniform tan color that has stayed the same for years
Uniform, unchanging color is reassuring; change over time (Evolution) is concerning.
A diameter of 3 mm with smooth borders
Small size and smooth borders do not meet the ABCDE warning criteria.
items.ex: ABCDE stands for Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter over 6 mm, and Evolution over time.

alt.q: A patient asks which mole changes should prompt a visit to a health care provider. Which should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: The mole has changed in appearance over time
Evolution, or change over time, is a warning sign.
The mole has become larger than a pencil eraser
Diameter over 6 mm is a warning sign.
The mole has started to bleed or ulcerate
Ulceration and bleeding are ominous signs in melanoma.
The mole is symmetric with sharp, smooth edges
Symmetry and regular borders are not warning signs.
The mole has been the same color since childhood
Unchanging uniform color is not a warning sign.
alt.ex: Change in appearance, size over 6 mm, ulceration, and bleeding of a mole should be reported.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which findings in a patient’s history are risk factors for skin cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Fair, freckled complexion with a tendency to burn easily
Fair skin that burns easily is a risk factor for skin cancer.
Regular use of tanning parlors or sunlamps
Overexposure to these irritants can cause skin cancer.
Work involving coal, tar, or arsenic compounds
Exposure to these agents creates risk for skin cancer.
Light-colored hair or eyes
Light hair or eye color is a skin cancer risk factor.
Daily use of broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30
Sunscreen use is protective, not a risk factor.
Working indoors with little sun exposure
Excessive time outdoors, not indoor work, increases risk.
items.ex: Fair complexion, light hair or eyes, burning easily, tanning devices, and exposure to coal, tar, or arsenic increase skin cancer risk.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a community group about preventing skin cancer. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Use broad-spectrum sunscreen with an SPF of 30 or higher.
The ACS recommends broad-spectrum sunscreen with SPF 30 or higher.
Avoid sunbathing and indoor tanning.
Sun safety includes avoiding sunbathing and tanning beds.
Examine your skin completely every month.
A monthly skin self-examination is recommended.
Tanning pills are a safe substitute for sun exposure.
Tanning pills are listed as an irritant that can cause skin cancer.
Skin cancer usually develops suddenly, so checks are unnecessary.
Most skin changes develop gradually, so regular checks are needed.
alt.ex: Prevention includes SPF 30 or higher broad-spectrum sunscreen, avoiding tanning, and monthly skin self-examination.

items.q: Which instructions about hair and scalp care should the nurse include in patient teaching? Select all that apply.
o: Wash your hair with lukewarm water
Hot water removes the protective oils from the scalp.
Use a comb rather than a brush on wet hair
Wet hair should never be brushed; use a comb instead.
Choose a brush with ball-tipped bristles
Ball-tipped bristles reduce breakage from brushing.
Consider leaving hair loose at night
Ponytails and braids can break hair and damage roots.
Wash your hair with hot water to remove excess oil
Hot water strips protective scalp oils.
Brush your hair vigorously while it is still wet
Brushing wet hair snaps it off; a comb should be used.
items.ex: Hair care teaching includes lukewarm water, combing wet hair, ball-tipped brushes, and avoiding tight ponytails or braids.

alt.q: After teaching about hair and scalp care, which patient statements show understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “Losing some hair each day is normal.”
Average normal hair loss is 50 to 100 hairs per day.
“I’ll use a hairspray with sun protection.”
Sun damages hair and scalp, so sun-protective hairspray is advised.
“I’ll pick a quieter blow dryer.”
Loud blow dryers can affect hearing with prolonged exposure.
“I’ll brush my hair right after I shower.”
Wet hair should be combed, not brushed.
“Hot water will help my scalp stay healthy.”
Hot water removes protective oils from the scalp.
alt.ex: Understanding includes accepting normal daily hair loss, sun protection for hair, quiet blow dryers, and combing wet hair.

items.q: A patient’s visual acuity is documented as 20/40. What does this result mean?
items.a: The patient reads at 20 feet what a normal eye reads at 40 feet
items.ex: The numerator is the testing distance; the denominator is the distance from which a normal eye can read that line.
w: The patient reads at 40 feet what a normal eye reads at 20 feet
This reverses the numerator and denominator.
The patient has 40% loss of vision in each eye
The fraction compares distances; it is not a percentage of loss.
The patient read 20 of 40 letters correctly
The numbers refer to distances in feet, not letter counts.

alt.q: Which Snellen result indicates the poorest visual acuity?
alt.ex: The larger the denominator, the poorer the patient’s visual acuity.
w: 20/20 is normal visual acuity.

alt.q: A nurse examines an infant’s ear with an otoscope. How should the auricle be pulled?
alt.a: Down and back
alt.ex: For infants, the auricle is pulled down and back to straighten the canal.
w: Up and back
Up and back is used for adults and older children.
Up and forward
This direction does not straighten an infant’s canal.
Straight forward
Forward traction is not recommended.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse performs the Weber test on a patient with a conduction hearing loss in the left ear. Where will the patient hear the sound best?
items.a: In the left (impaired) ear
items.ex: In conduction deafness, the Weber sound lateralizes to the impaired ear.
w: In the right (normal) ear
Sound is heard better in the normal ear with sensorineural loss.
Equally in both ears
Equal sound in both ears is the normal finding.
In neither ear
The vibrating fork is heard by bone conduction in the Weber test.

alt.q: During the Weber test, a patient hears the sound better in the normal right ear. Which type of hearing loss in the left ear does this suggest?
alt.a: Sensorineural hearing loss
alt.ex: In sensorineural loss, the Weber sound is heard better in the normal ear.
w: Conduction hearing loss
With conduction loss the sound is louder in the impaired ear.
Normal hearing
Normal hearing produces equal sound in both ears.
Cerumen impaction
Cerumen impaction causes conduction loss, which lateralizes to the impaired ear.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: What is the normal finding of the Rinne test?
items.a: Air conduction is heard about twice as long as bone conduction
items.ex: Normally air-conducted sound is heard twice as long as bone-conducted sound, a 2:1 ratio.
w: Bone conduction is heard about twice as long as air conduction
Longer bone conduction indicates conduction deafness.
Air and bone conduction are heard for exactly the same time
Normally air conduction lasts longer than bone conduction.
Air conduction is heard only half as long as bone conduction
This reversed pattern suggests conduction loss.

alt.q: During the Rinne test, a patient hears the fork longer by bone conduction than by air conduction in the right ear. What does this suggest?
alt.a: Conduction deafness in the right ear
alt.ex: In conduction deafness, the patient hears bone conduction longer than air conduction in the affected ear.
w: Sensorineural loss in the right ear
In sensorineural loss, air conduction is still longer, but at less than a 2:1 ratio.
Normal hearing in the right ear
Normal hearing has air conduction lasting twice as long as bone conduction.
Mixed hearing loss in both ears
One test result in one ear does not indicate bilateral mixed loss.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient reports ear pain. When the nurse gently pulls the auricle and presses on the tragus, the pain increases. What does this most likely indicate?
items.a: An external ear infection
items.ex: If palpating the external ear increases pain, an external ear infection is likely.
w: A middle ear infection
Middle ear infection is suspected when manipulating the auricle and tragus does not change pain.
Mastoiditis
Mastoiditis causes tenderness over the mastoid process.
Cerumen impaction
Impaction causes conduction hearing loss, not pain worsened by tragus pressure.

alt.q: A patient with ear pain has tenderness when the nurse palpates behind the ear over the mastoid process. What does this suggest?
alt.a: Mastoiditis
alt.ex: Tenderness in the mastoid area indicates mastoiditis.
w: External ear infection
External ear infection causes pain with pulling the auricle or pressing the tragus.
Middle ear infection
Middle ear infection does not cause pain with manipulation of external structures.
Frostbite of the auricle
Frostbite causes extreme pallor of the auricle.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A postoperative patient receiving opioids has pupils that are pinpoint in size. What do these pupils commonly indicate?
items.a: Opioid intoxication
items.ex: Pinpoint pupils are a common sign of opioid intoxication; drugs such as morphine constrict pupils.
w: Opioid withdrawal
Withdrawal from opioids causes dilated pupils.
Glaucoma
Glaucoma is associated with dilated pupils.
Use of atropine eyedrops
Atropine dilates the pupils.

alt.q: Which condition or drug is associated with dilated pupils?
alt.a: Atropine eye medication
alt.ex: Dilated pupils result from glaucoma, trauma, neurological disorders, atropine, or opioid withdrawal.
w: Pilocarpine eye medication
Pilocarpine constricts the pupils.
Morphine administration
Morphine causes constricted pupils.
Inflammation of the iris
Iris inflammation causes constricted pupils.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse teaches the parents of a child who has frequent nosebleeds. Which statement by a parent shows understanding?
items.a: “I’ll have her sit up and lean forward while I pinch the front of her nose.”
items.ex: Sitting up and leaning forward avoids aspiration of blood while pressure is applied to the anterior nose.
w: “I’ll have her lie flat while I pinch the front of her nose.”
Lying flat increases the risk of aspirating blood.
“I’ll tilt her head back while I pinch the front of her nose.”
Tilting the head back allows blood to drain into the throat.
“I’ll put ice on her nose first and pinch it only if that fails.”
Pressure comes first; ice is used if pressure fails to stop bleeding.

alt.q: Pressure on the anterior nose has not stopped a child’s nosebleed. What should the parent do next?
alt.a: Apply ice or a cold cloth to the bridge of the nose
alt.ex: If pressure fails, ice or a cold cloth on the bridge of the nose is added.
w: Have the child lie down flat on the back
Lying flat risks aspiration; the child should sit up and lean forward.
Tilt the child’s head back to slow the flow
Tilting back lets blood run into the throat.
Pack the nostril with a cotton-tipped applicator
Inserting objects is not part of the teaching for nosebleeds.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Where should the nurse place the tongue depressor to inspect a patient’s pharynx?
items.a: On the middle third of the tongue
items.ex: Placing the depressor on the middle third gives a clear view without eliciting the gag reflex.
w: On the anterior third of the tongue
Too far anterior makes the back of the tongue mound up and block the view.
On the posterior third of the tongue
Placement on the posterior tongue elicits the gag reflex.
Under the tip of the tongue
This does not depress the tongue to expose the pharynx.

alt.q: A nurse places a tongue depressor on the posterior part of a patient’s tongue. What is the likely result?
alt.a: The gag reflex is elicited
alt.ex: Placing the tongue depressor on the posterior tongue elicits the gag reflex.
w: The tongue mounds up and blocks the view
Mounding occurs when the depressor is too far anterior.
The uvula fails to rise
Uvula movement reflects vagus nerve function, not depressor placement.
The lower lip is pressed against the teeth
This results from careless technique, not posterior placement.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: While examining the neck, the nurse finds several lymph nodes. Which finding is most important to report to the health care provider?
items.a: A large, fixed lymph node
items.ex: Large, fixed, inflamed, or tender nodes indicate a problem such as infection, systemic disease, or neoplasm.
w: A small, mobile, nontender node
Small, mobile, nontender nodes are common and normal.
Nodes that are not visible on inspection
Nodes are normally not visible.
Nodes that are not easily palpable
Normally lymph nodes are not easily palpable.

alt.q: Which instruction should the nurse give a patient about self-assessment of the neck?
alt.a: Call a health care provider if you notice a fixed, enlarged lump in the neck
alt.ex: Patients are taught to report a fixed, enlarged lump or mass in the neck.
w: Wait a year before reporting any lump that does not hurt
Fixed, enlarged lumps should be reported promptly whether or not they hurt.
Report every small, soft, movable node you can feel
Small, mobile, nontender nodes are common.
Massage any enlarged node until it shrinks
Massage is not recommended; a fixed, enlarged lump should be reported.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse notes thick white patches on the buccal mucosa of a patient who smokes heavily. What should the nurse suspect?
items.a: Leukoplakia, a precancerous lesion
items.ex: Thick white patches (leukoplakia) are often precancerous lesions seen in heavy smokers and alcohol users.
w: Fordyce spots, a normal finding
Fordyce spots are small yellow-white raised ectopic sebaceous glands.
Normal hyperpigmentation with aging
Hyperpigmentation appears as darker shading, not thick white patches.
Exostosis of the hard palate
Exostosis is a bony growth between the palates.

alt.q: A nurse sees small, yellow-white raised spots on a patient’s buccal mucosa and lips. What are these most likely?
alt.a: Fordyce spots
alt.ex: Small, yellow-white raised lesions on the buccal mucosa and lips are commonly Fordyce spots, or ectopic sebaceous glands.
w: Leukoplakia
Leukoplakia appears as thick white patches and is precancerous.
Varicosities
Varicosities are swollen, tortuous veins under the tongue.
Dental caries
Caries appear as chalky white, brown, or black areas on teeth.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which early warning signs of oral cavity and pharynx cancer should the nurse teach a patient to have checked by a health care professional? Select all that apply.
o: A mouth sore that does not heal
A nonhealing mouth sore is an early warning sign.
A lump or mass in the cheek area
A lump in the cheek should be checked.
Pain or difficulty swallowing, chewing, or speaking
Difficulty with these functions is a warning sign.
Numbness of the tongue or another area of the mouth
Oral numbness is a warning sign of cancer.
Pink, moist, glistening buccal mucosa
This describes normal mucosa.
Small, mobile, yellow-white spots on the lips
These describe common Fordyce spots, a normal finding.
items.ex: Warning signs include a nonhealing sore, a cheek lump, difficulty swallowing or speaking, wartlike growths, and oral numbness.

alt.q: Which factors increase a patient’s risk for oral or pharyngeal cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Use of smokeless tobacco
Tobacco in any form, including smokeless, increases oral cancer risk.
Both smoking and drinking alcohol
Combined smoking and drinking raises risk about 15 times.
History of human papillomavirus 16 (HPV-16)
HPV-16 contributes to oral cancers, especially in the posterior mouth.
Use of fluoride toothpaste
Fluoride toothpaste is a dental hygiene practice, not a cancer risk.
Dental examinations every 6 months
Regular dental visits are recommended, not a risk factor.
alt.ex: Tobacco in any form, alcohol combined with smoking, and HPV-16 increase the risk for oral and pharyngeal cancer.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which behaviors suggest that a patient may have a hearing loss? Select all that apply.
o: Failing to respond when spoken to
Failure to respond is a behavioral cue of hearing loss.
Asking others to repeat comments
Frequent requests to repeat are a sign of hearing loss.
Leaning forward to hear
Leaning forward helps people with hearing loss compensate.
A child speaking in a monotonous voice tone
Inattentiveness or a monotonous voice in a child may indicate hearing loss.
Responding promptly to whispered numbers
Correctly repeating whispered numbers indicates normal hearing.
Turning toward a speaker who calls from behind
Responding to sound from behind suggests intact hearing.
items.ex: People with hearing loss cope through cues such as not responding, asking for repetition, leaning forward, and, in children, monotonous speech.

alt.q: A nurse teaches the family of an older adult with hearing loss how to communicate. Which instructions are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Speak more slowly
Slower speech improves understanding.
Use lower tones of voice
Older adults lose high-frequency sounds first, so lower tones help.
Make sure the patient can see your face
Seeing the speaker’s face aids understanding.
Shout so the patient can hear clearly
Family members should avoid shouting.
Speak in a higher-pitched voice
High-frequency sounds are the hardest for older adults to hear.
alt.ex: Families should speak slowly in lower tones, avoid shouting, and ensure the patient can see the speaker’s face.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which precautions should the nurse teach an older adult because of normal age-related vision changes? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid or use caution when driving at night
Normal vision changes make night driving more hazardous.
Increase the lighting in the home
Better lighting reduces the risk of falls.
Paint the first and last steps of stairs a bright color
Bright step edges aid depth perception.
Wear protective eyewear around debris and splashes
Protective eyewear prevents eye injury.
Use dim lighting at night to reduce glare
Increased lighting, not dim lighting, reduces fall risk.
Paint stair edges a dark color to reduce glare
Steps should be painted a bright color such as yellow.
items.ex: Older adults should be cautious with night driving, increase home lighting, mark step edges brightly, and wear protective eyewear.

alt.q: After teaching about eye safety, which statements by an older adult show understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “I’ll add brighter lights in my hallway.”
Increased home lighting reduces fall risk.
“I’ll paint the edges of my stairs yellow.”
Bright step edges help depth perception.
“I’ll be careful about driving after dark.”
Night driving should be avoided or done with caution.
“I’ll keep the lights low to protect my eyes.”
Low lighting increases the risk of falls.
“I only need an eye examination if I go blind.”
Regular eye examinations are recommended.
alt.ex: Understanding includes brighter home lighting, bright step edges, caution with night driving, and regular eye examinations.

items.q: If the pupils are equal, round, reactive to light, and accommodate, the nurse may document PERRLA.
items.a: True
items.ex: PERRLA stands for pupils equal, round, reactive to light, and accommodation and is used when all tests are normal.
items.ww: PERRLA is the accepted abbreviation for normal pupillary findings.

alt.q: The nurse may document PERRLA even if one pupil reacts sluggishly to light, as long as both are round.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: PERRLA is documented only when pupillary reaction is normal in all tests.
alt.ww: A sluggish or unequal reaction is abnormal and must be described rather than recorded as PERRLA.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Patients should avoid cleaning the ear canal with cotton-tipped applicators.
items.a: True
items.ex: Cotton-tipped applicators and sharp objects can cause trauma or push cerumen deep into the canal.
items.ww: Applicators are not safe because they can injure the canal and impact cerumen.

alt.q: Cotton-tipped applicators are the safest way for patients to remove cerumen from deep in the ear canal.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Cotton-tipped applicators can cause trauma or impaction of cerumen deep in the canal.
alt.ww: They push wax deeper and injure the canal; patients should clean only the outer ear.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Having the patient swallow water while the nurse observes the lower neck helps reveal an abnormally enlarged thyroid.
items.a: True
items.ex: Swallowing while the nurse observes the neck helps visualize an enlarged thyroid; a normal thyroid cannot be seen.
items.ww: The swallow maneuver is the recommended way to inspect for thyroid enlargement.

alt.q: A normal thyroid gland is easily seen moving under the skin when the patient swallows.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Normally the thyroid cannot be visualized; seeing it on swallowing suggests enlargement.
alt.ww: Visibility of the gland during swallowing is abnormal, not expected.

items.ex: Nystagmus results from local injury to eye muscles or a disorder of the cranial nerves that innervate them.

alt.q: Having a patient gaze to the far left or right can initiate [[nystagmus]], a rhythmical oscillation of the eyes.
alt.ex: Nystagmus results from local injury to eye muscles or a disorder of the cranial nerves that innervate them.

items.q: What landmark does the nurse locate to begin counting the ribs and intercostal spaces?
items.a: The angle of Louis, where the second rib meets the sternum
items.ex: The angle of Louis at the manubriosternal junction is where the second rib articulates, so counting starts there.
w: The xiphoid process, where the seventh rib meets the sternum
Counting is not started from the xiphoid; the angle of Louis marks the second rib.
The suprasternal notch, where the first rib meets the sternum
The notch is a landmark, but counting begins at the angle of Louis.
The costal angle, where the tenth rib meets the sternum
The costal angle is between the costal margins, not a rib-counting start point.

alt.q: Posteriorly, at about which rib level does the inferior tip of the scapula lie?
alt.a: The seventh rib
alt.ex: The tip of the scapula lies at about the seventh rib, from which the nurse counts upward.
w: The second rib
The second rib is located anteriorly at the angle of Louis.
The fourth rib
The scapular tip lies lower, at about the seventh rib.
The tenth rib
The 10th rib is where the thumbs are placed for posterior excursion.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: What is the normal anteroposterior (AP) diameter of an adult’s chest?
items.a: One-third to one-half of the transverse diameter
items.ex: Normally the AP diameter is one-third to one-half of the side-to-side diameter.
w: Equal to the transverse diameter
An AP diameter equal to the transverse diameter is a barrel chest.
Twice the transverse diameter
The AP diameter is smaller than the transverse diameter.
One-tenth of the transverse diameter
This is far narrower than normal.

alt.q: A nurse notes that an older adult with chronic lung disease has an AP chest diameter equal to the transverse diameter. How is this described?
alt.a: Barrel-shaped chest
alt.ex: A barrel chest, with AP equal to transverse diameter, characterizes aging and chronic lung disease.
w: Normal adult chest contour
Normally the AP diameter is one-third to one-half of the transverse.
Splinting of the chest wall
Splinting is holding the chest due to pain.
Reduced costal angle
Costal angle is the angle between the costal margins.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: During palpation of the posterior thorax, a patient reports pain and tenderness over the ribs after a fall. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Avoid deep palpation of the area
items.ex: Deep palpation is avoided when there is pain because fractured rib fragments could be displaced against vital organs.
w: Palpate deeply to locate the exact fracture site
Deep pressure could displace rib fragments against vital organs.
Measure chest excursion with firm pressure first
Firm pressure on a tender chest risks further injury.
Ask the patient to cough forcefully during palpation
Coughing adds stress and does not make palpation safer.

alt.q: Why does the nurse avoid deep palpation of the chest wall in a patient who reports chest tenderness?
alt.a: Fractured rib fragments could be displaced against vital organs
alt.ex: Deep palpation over a painful area risks pushing broken rib fragments into vital organs.
w: Deep palpation always triggers a coughing spell
Forceful pressure on the trachea, not the chest wall, elicits coughing.
Deep palpation interferes with tactile fremitus
Fremitus is palpated with a firm, light touch; the concern here is injury.
Deep palpation measures excursion inaccurately
The concern is displacement of fractured ribs, not accuracy.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse palpates tactile fremitus and finds that vibrations are absent over the right lower lobe. Which condition could explain this finding?
items.a: Collapse of lung tissue in that area
items.ex: Mucus accumulation, collapsed lung tissue, or lung lesions block vibrations from reaching the chest wall.
w: Normal speech in a crying infant
Crying infants produce strong vibrations, not absent ones.
A normal finding near the tracheal bifurcation
Fremitus is strongest near the tracheal bifurcation.
Shallow breathing in a healthy adult
Fremitus depends on transmitted voice vibrations, not depth of breathing.

alt.q: Where on the posterior chest are tactile fremitus vibrations normally strongest?
alt.a: At the top, near the level of the tracheal bifurcation
alt.ex: Normally fremitus is symmetrical and strongest at the top, near the tracheal bifurcation.
w: At the lung bases near the diaphragm
Vibrations are weaker over the lower thorax.
Over the scapulae
Bone and muscle dampen vibrations over the scapulae.
Only on the right side of the chest
Normal fremitus is symmetrical on both sides.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse auscultates soft, breezy, low-pitched sounds over the periphery of the lungs, with inspiration three times longer than expiration. What are these sounds?
items.a: Vesicular breath sounds
items.ex: Vesicular sounds are soft, breezy, low pitched, heard over the lung periphery, with inspiration three times longer than expiration.
w: Bronchial breath sounds
Bronchial sounds are loud, high pitched, and heard over the trachea.
Bronchovesicular breath sounds
Bronchovesicular sounds are medium pitched with equal inspiration and expiration.
Rhonchi
Rhonchi are loud, low-pitched, rumbling adventitious sounds.

alt.q: Where are bronchovesicular breath sounds normally heard best?
alt.a: Posteriorly between the scapulae
alt.ex: Bronchovesicular sounds are best heard posteriorly between the scapulae and anteriorly beside the sternum at the first and second intercostal spaces.
w: Over the lung periphery
Vesicular sounds are heard over the lung periphery.
Only over the trachea
Bronchial sounds are heard only over the trachea.
Over the lower lateral anterior chest
Pleural friction rubs are loudest over the lower lateral anterior surface.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which description fits normal bronchial breath sounds?
items.a: Loud, high pitched, and hollow, with expiration longer than inspiration
items.ex: Bronchial sounds are loud, high pitched, and hollow, heard over the trachea, with a 3:2 expiration-to-inspiration ratio.
w: Soft, low pitched, and breezy, with inspiration longer than expiration
This describes vesicular sounds.
Medium pitched and blowing, with equal inspiration and expiration
This describes bronchovesicular sounds.
Dry and grating, without change after coughing
This describes a pleural friction rub.

alt.q: A nurse hears loud, high-pitched, hollow sounds over the lower lung periphery of a patient. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: Abnormal, because bronchial sounds are normally heard only over the trachea
alt.ex: Bronchial sounds are normal only over the trachea; elsewhere they are abnormal, as with consolidation.
w: Normal, because bronchial sounds are expected over the lung bases
Vesicular, not bronchial, sounds are expected over the periphery.
Normal, because the patient is breathing deeply
Deep breathing does not make bronchial sounds normal at the periphery.
Abnormal, because these sounds indicate pleural inflammation
Pleural inflammation produces a dry, grating friction rub.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient with asthma has high-pitched, continuous musical sounds heard over all lung fields, louder on expiration. Which adventitious sound is this?
items.a: Wheezes
items.ex: Wheezes are high-pitched, continuous musical sounds from airflow through severely narrowed airways, common in asthma.
w: Crackles
Crackles are short, interrupted sounds from reinflation of alveoli.
Rhonchi
Rhonchi are loud, low-pitched, rumbling sounds over the trachea and bronchi.
Pleural friction rub
A friction rub is a dry, grating sound from inflamed pleura.

alt.q: What causes the wheezes heard in a patient with bronchitis?
alt.a: High-velocity airflow through severely narrowed or obstructed airways
alt.ex: Wheezes result from high-velocity airflow through severely narrowed or obstructed airways.
w: Sudden reinflation of groups of alveoli
Alveolar reinflation causes crackles.
Parietal pleura rubbing against visceral pleura
Rubbing pleura causes a pleural friction rub.
Fluid or mucus in the larger airways
Fluid or mucus in large airways causes rhonchi.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient has loud, low-pitched, rumbling sounds over the trachea and bronchi. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: Ask the patient to cough and then auscultate again
items.ex: Rhonchi come from fluid or mucus in larger airways and are sometimes cleared by coughing.
w: Document the sound as a pleural friction rub
A friction rub is dry and grating and does not clear with coughing.
Document the sound as normal vesicular breathing
Vesicular sounds are soft and breezy, not loud and rumbling.
Stop auscultation because the sound is normal
Rumbling sounds are adventitious and need further assessment.

alt.q: Which adventitious breath sound is sometimes cleared by coughing?
alt.a: Rhonchi
alt.ex: Rhonchi, caused by fluid or mucus in larger airways, are sometimes cleared by coughing.
w: Fine crackles
Fine crackles are usually not cleared with coughing.
Coarse crackles
Coarse crackles are not cleared with coughing.
Pleural friction rub
A friction rub does not clear with coughing.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse has difficulty hearing breath sounds in a patient who is obese. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Ask the patient to breathe harder and faster temporarily
items.ex: If sounds are faint, as in obesity, the patient breathes harder and faster temporarily to make them audible.
w: Use the bell of the stethoscope over the posterior chest
The bell works best in children; the diaphragm is used for adults.
Ask the patient to breathe shallowly through the nose
Shallow nasal breathing makes sounds even fainter.
Listen only during expiration at each site
An entire inspiration and expiration is heard at each site.

alt.q: Which part of the stethoscope works best for auscultating breath sounds in a young child, and why?
alt.a: The bell, because of the child’s small chest
alt.ex: The bell works best in children because of their small chests; their sounds are louder due to thin chest walls.
w: The bell, because children’s breath sounds are faint
Children’s breath sounds are actually louder because of thin chest walls.
The diaphragm, because children have thick chest walls
Children have thin chest walls, and the bell is preferred.
The diaphragm, because the bell cannot detect breath sounds
The bell does detect breath sounds and is preferred in children.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient has smoked 1½ packs of cigarettes per day for 20 years. How many pack-years should the nurse document?
items.a: 30 pack-years
items.ex: Pack-years equal number of years smoking multiplied by packs per day: 20 × 1.5 = 30.
w: 13 pack-years
This divides years by packs instead of multiplying.
21.5 pack-years
This adds years and packs instead of multiplying.
40 pack-years
This would require 2 packs per day for 20 years.

alt.q: A patient smoked 2 packs per day for 15 years. What is the smoking history in pack-years?
alt.a: 30 pack-years
alt.ex: Multiply number of years smoking by packs per day: 15 × 2 = 30 pack-years.
w: 17 pack-years
This adds years and packs instead of multiplying.
7.5 pack-years
This divides years by packs.
15 pack-years
This ignores that the patient smoked 2 packs per day.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which symptoms are warning signals of lung cancer that the nurse should teach patients? Select all that apply.
o: A persistent cough
A persistent cough is a warning sign of lung cancer.
Sputum streaked with blood
Blood-streaked sputum is a warning sign.
Chest pain
Chest pain is listed among lung cancer warning signs.
Recurrent attacks of pneumonia or bronchitis
Repeated pneumonia or bronchitis is a warning sign.
Clear nasal discharge with sneezing
This suggests allergy, not lung cancer.
Increased appetite and weight gain
Weight gain is not a lung cancer warning sign.
items.ex: Lung cancer warning signs include persistent cough, blood-streaked sputum, chest pain, and recurrent pneumonia or bronchitis.

alt.q: Which factors increase a patient’s risk for lung cancer or chronic lung disease? Select all that apply.
o: Exposure to secondhand smoke
Secondhand smoke exposure is a risk factor.
Exposure to radon or asbestos
Radon and asbestos exposure increase risk.
Work involving soot, tar, nickel, or chromium
These metals and chemical mixtures are risk factors.
Receiving annual influenza vaccination
Vaccination is a preventive measure, not a risk factor.
Use of pursed-lip breathing exercises
This is a COPD self-care technique, not a risk factor.
alt.ex: Secondhand smoke, radon, asbestos, and exposure to metals or soot and tar increase the risk of lung disease.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which patient history findings are risk factors for tuberculosis (TB)? Select all that apply.
o: Known human immunodeficiency virus (HIV) infection
HIV infection is a TB risk factor.
Being homeless or living in a shelter
Homelessness and shelter residence increase TB risk.
Working in a nursing home
Residents and employees of nursing homes are at risk.
Recent immigration from a country where TB is prevalent
Immigrants from high-prevalence countries are at risk.
Living alone in a single-family home with no TB contacts
This is not listed as a TB risk factor.
A recent negative TB skin test
A negative test is not a risk factor.
items.ex: TB risk factors include HIV, substance abuse, low income, homelessness, nursing home or shelter exposure, prison, TB contacts, and immigration from high-prevalence areas.

alt.q: A patient reports several symptoms. Which ones are risk factors for both TB and HIV infection? Select all that apply.
o: Night sweats
Night sweats are listed as a risk factor for TB and HIV.
Unexplained weight loss
Unexplained weight loss is listed for both.
Hemoptysis
Hemoptysis is a listed risk factor for TB and HIV.
Chronic hoarseness
Hoarseness indicates a laryngeal disorder or cocaine or opioid sniffing.
Seasonal sneezing and itchy eyes
These suggest allergies, not TB or HIV.
alt.ex: Persistent cough, hemoptysis, unexplained weight loss, fatigue, night sweats, and fever are risk factors for both TB and HIV.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Before the thoracic examination, which signs in other body systems suggest that a patient has an oxygenation problem? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced mental alertness
The brain is very sensitive to oxygen, so alertness decreases with hypoxia.
Nasal flaring
Nasal flaring signals increased effort to breathe.
Somnolence
Sleepiness is an assessed sign of oxygenation problems.
Cyanosis
Bluish color reflects deoxygenated hemoglobin.
Pink, moist oral mucosa
Pink, moist mucosa is a normal finding.
Respiratory rate of 16 breaths per minute
A rate of 12 to 20 is normal for adults.
items.ex: Reduced alertness, nasal flaring, somnolence, and cyanosis are signs outside the chest that suggest oxygenation problems.

alt.q: Which findings during inspection of the thorax suggest that a patient is working hard to breathe? Select all that apply.
o: Bulging of the intercostal spaces during expiration
Bulging indicates great effort to breathe.
Use of the sternocleidomastoid and trapezius muscles
Accessory muscle use shows increased breathing effort.
A grunting sound with breathing
Some patients who require great effort produce a grunting sound.
Quiet breathing barely audible near the open mouth
Quiet, barely audible breathing is normal.
Equal bilateral chest expansion with each breath
Equal expansion is normal.
alt.ex: Intercostal bulging, accessory muscle use, and grunting indicate great effort to breathe.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Chest excursion is assessed on the posterior and anterior chest but not on the lateral chest.
items.a: True
items.ex: The nurse measures excursion posteriorly and anteriorly; excursion is not assessed laterally.
items.ww: Lateral examination uses inspection, palpation, and auscultation, but excursion is not measured there.

alt.q: The nurse measures chest excursion on the lateral chest after examining the posterior thorax.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Excursion is not assessed laterally; it is measured on the posterior and anterior chest.
alt.ww: Lateral assessment includes inspection, palpation, and auscultation, but not excursion.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Fine crackles are usually not cleared by coughing.
items.a: True
items.ex: Fine crackles from alveolar reinflation are heard at the end of inspiration and usually do not clear with coughing.
items.ww: Clearing with cough is typical of rhonchi, not crackles.

alt.q: Crackles usually disappear after the patient coughs, so they are not a significant finding.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Crackles are usually not cleared by coughing; rhonchi are the sounds that sometimes clear.
alt.ww: Crackles reflect alveolar reinflation and persist after coughing, so they remain significant.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: In older adults, chest excursion normally declines because of costal cartilage calcification and respiratory muscle atrophy.
items.a: True
items.ex: Aging calcifies costal cartilage and weakens respiratory muscles, reducing chest movement.
items.ww: Reduced excursion is an expected aging change, though pain, posture, or fatigue can also reduce it.

alt.q: Chest excursion normally increases in older adults as the chest becomes barrel shaped.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Excursion normally declines with age because of costal cartilage calcification and muscle atrophy.
alt.ww: A barrel chest does not increase excursion; aging reduces chest movement.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Where does the nurse expect to palpate the point of maximal impulse (PMI) in a healthy adult?
items.a: Fourth to fifth intercostal space just medial to the left midclavicular line
items.ex: The apex touches the chest wall at about the fourth to fifth intercostal space just medial to the left midclavicular line.
w: Second intercostal space just to the right of the sternal border
The second right intercostal space is the aortic area, not the apex.
Second intercostal space just to the left of the sternal border
The second left intercostal space is the pulmonic area, not the apex.
Sixth to seventh intercostal space at the left anterior axillary line
A PMI this far left and low suggests an enlarged heart, not a normal adult apex.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing the apical impulse of a healthy 6-month-old infant. Where is the infant’s apex expected to be found?
alt.a: Third or fourth intercostal space just left of the midclavicular line
alt.ex: An infant’s heart lies more horizontally, so the apex is at the third or fourth intercostal space just left of the midclavicular line.
w: Fifth or sixth intercostal space well left of the midclavicular line
This low, lateral position suggests cardiac enlargement, not a normal infant heart.
Second or third intercostal space just right of the sternal border
The apex is on the left; the right second space is the aortic area.
Sixth or seventh intercostal space at the left midaxillary line
This position is far too low and lateral for an infant’s apex.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which event in the cardiac cycle produces the first heart sound (S1)?
items.a: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
items.ex: As systole begins, rising ventricular pressure closes the mitral and tricuspid valves, producing S1 (“lub”).
w: Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves
Aortic and pulmonic valve closure produces S2 (“dub”).
Atrial contraction against a stiff ventricle
Atrial contraction pushing into a resistant ventricle produces an S4.
Rapid filling of an already distended ventricle
Filling of a distended ventricle produces an S3.

alt.q: A nurse hears the second heart sound (S2) most clearly at the aortic area. What causes this sound?
alt.a: Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves
alt.ex: When ventricular pressure falls below aortic and pulmonary artery pressure, the aortic and pulmonic valves close, causing S2.
w: Closure of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Mitral and tricuspid closure produces S1, heard best at the apex.
Opening of the mitral and tricuspid valves
Valve opening for ventricular filling is normally silent.
Contraction of the atria during late diastole
Atrial contraction against a resistant ventricle produces an S4.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse auscultates an irregular apical rate of 104 beats/min and then immediately palpates a radial rate of 82 beats/min. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Report the pulse deficit to the health care provider immediately
items.ex: A radial rate slower than the apical rate is a pulse deficit, and the book directs the nurse to report it immediately.
w: Document the radial rate as the patient’s heart rate for the shift
The radial rate misses ineffective beats; the difference itself must be reported.
Recheck the radial pulse in 4 hours with the next set of vital signs
Waiting delays reporting a finding the book says to report immediately.
Count the radial pulse for 15 seconds and multiply the count by 4
An irregular pulse is counted for a full minute, and the deficit still needs reporting.

alt.q: Why is the radial pulse slower than the apical pulse in a patient with a pulse deficit?
alt.a: Ineffective contractions fail to send pulse waves to the periphery
alt.ex: Some contractions are too weak to produce a pulse wave that reaches the radial artery, so fewer beats are felt there.
w: The radial artery is narrowed by plaque from atherosclerosis
Atherosclerosis causes diminished or unequal pulses, not a beat-by-beat deficit.
The stethoscope picks up extra sounds from breath and room noise
A pulse deficit is a real difference in beats, not artifact from noise.
The examiner counts the radial pulse for a shorter time period
Counting errors are avoided by counting both rates for a full minute.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse hears an extra heart sound just after S2 that, with S1 and S2, sounds like “Ken-TUCK-y.” What is this sound?
items.a: An S3, or ventricular gallop
items.ex: S3 follows S2 and results from a premature rush of blood into a stiff or dilated ventricle.
w: An S4, or atrial gallop
An S4 occurs just before S1 and sounds like “TEN-nes-see.”
A systolic murmur
A murmur is a sustained swishing or blowing sound, not a short extra beat.
A carotid bruit
A bruit is a blowing sound heard over a narrowed artery, not over the heart.

alt.q: Which extra heart sound occurs just before S1 and has a “TEN-nes-see” cadence?
alt.a: An S4, or atrial gallop
alt.ex: S4 occurs just before ventricular systole when the atria contract against a ventricle that is not accepting blood.
w: An S3, or ventricular gallop
An S3 occurs after S2 and sounds like “Ken-TUCK-y.”
A diastolic murmur
A diastolic murmur is a sustained swishing sound between S2 and the next S1.
A friction rub
The book lists rubs as low-pitched extra sounds but describes the TEN-nes-see rhythm only for S4.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: During a routine examination of a 66-year-old patient, the nurse hears an S4 at the apex with the patient lying on the left side. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Report the S4 to the health care provider
items.ex: Although S4 is often heard in healthy older adults, it is not normal in adults and indicates an abnormal condition to report.
w: Document it as an expected finding of aging and take no further action
The book states S4 is not normal in adults and should be reported.
Reposition the patient supine so the extra sound is no longer heard
Changing position to lose the sound does not address the abnormal finding.
Switch to the diaphragm to confirm it is a high-pitched sound
S3 and S4 are low-pitched sounds heard with the bell.

alt.q: A nurse hears an S3 in a 45-year-old patient with heart failure. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
alt.a: It is abnormal because S3 is not expected in adults over 31
alt.ex: An S3 is abnormal in adults over 31 and occurs when the heart tries to fill an already distended ventricle, as in heart failure.
w: It is normal because S3 is common in adults of any age
S3 can be normal in children and young adults but is abnormal after age 31.
It is normal because it is an expected sound of late pregnancy
S3 can occur late in pregnancy, but this patient is a 45-year-old with heart failure.
It is abnormal because it shows the mitral valve failed to open
S3 reflects rapid filling of a distended ventricle, not a valve that will not open.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which patient position is best for hearing low-pitched heart sounds during diastole?
items.a: Left lateral recumbent
items.ex: The left lateral recumbent position is good for all areas and best for low-pitched diastolic sounds.
w: Sitting up and leaning forward
Sitting and leaning forward is best for high-pitched murmurs.
Prone with arms at the sides
Prone is not one of the three positions used for heart auscultation.
Supine with the head flat
Supine is good for all areas but is not singled out for low-pitched diastolic sounds.

alt.q: A nurse wants to listen for a high-pitched murmur. Which position should the nurse ask the patient to assume?
alt.a: Sitting up and leaning forward
alt.ex: Sitting up and leaning forward is good for all areas and helps the nurse hear high-pitched murmurs.
w: Left lateral recumbent
Left lateral recumbent is best for low-pitched diastolic sounds.
Right side-lying
Right side-lying is not one of the positions described for heart auscultation.
Trendelenburg
Trendelenburg is not used for heart auscultation.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nursing student prepares to assess an older adult’s carotid pulses by placing fingers on both sides of the neck at the same time. Which action by the supervising nurse is best?
items.a: Stop the student and have them palpate one carotid artery at a time
items.ex: Occluding both carotids at once can cause loss of consciousness from inadequate blood flow to the brain.
w: Have the student press firmly to compare the strength of both sides
Firm bilateral pressure can occlude flow and stimulate the carotid sinus.
Have the student massage the arteries gently to bring out the pulse
Massaging the carotids stimulates the carotid sinus and can cause syncope.
Allow the student to continue because comparing sides at once saves time
Simultaneous palpation risks loss of consciousness and is never done.

alt.q: Why does the nurse avoid vigorous palpation or massage of the carotid arteries, especially in older adults?
alt.a: Stimulating the carotid sinus causes a reflex drop in heart rate and blood pressure
alt.ex: The carotid sinus sends impulses along the vagus nerve; stimulating it lowers heart rate and blood pressure and can cause syncope.
w: Vigorous palpation dislodges plaque that causes an immediate carotid bruit
The book’s reason is the carotid sinus reflex, not plaque causing a bruit.
Pressure on the artery triggers a reflex rise in heart rate and blood pressure
The reflex is a decrease in heart rate and blood pressure, not a rise.
Firm pressure compresses the trachea and briefly blocks the patient’s airway
The concern is the carotid sinus reflex, not airway compression.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is auscultating the carotid arteries of a 70-year-old patient with suspected cerebrovascular disease. Which technique is correct?
items.a: Place the bell over the artery and ask the patient to hold the breath briefly
items.ex: The bell picks up the low-pitched bruit, and holding the breath keeps breath sounds from obscuring it.
w: Place the diaphragm over the artery while the patient breathes deeply
Deep breathing creates breath sounds that can obscure a bruit.
Place the bell over both arteries at once while the patient talks
Talking adds noise, and each artery is examined separately.
Place the diaphragm over the artery while the patient coughs
Coughing adds noise and does not help detect a bruit.

alt.q: What does the nurse suspect when a blowing or swishing sound is heard over a carotid artery?
alt.a: A narrowed vessel lumen causing turbulent blood flow
alt.ex: A bruit is the blowing sound created when blood passes turbulently through a narrowed section of artery.
w: Normal blood flow through a healthy, elastic carotid artery
Normally no sounds are heard during carotid auscultation.
Closure of the aortic and pulmonic valves radiating to the neck
Valve closure produces S2, not a continuous swishing sound over the carotid.
Distention of the internal jugular vein from high venous pressure
Jugular venous distention is inspected, not heard as a blowing sound.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse observes that a patient’s jugular veins remain distended while the patient sits upright. Which condition does raised jugular venous pressure reflect?
items.a: Right-sided heart failure
items.ex: The internal jugular vein acts like a manometer for right atrial pressure, and raised venous pressure reflects right-sided heart failure.
w: Carotid artery stenosis
Carotid stenosis causes a bruit or diminished carotid pulse, not jugular distention.
Arterial insufficiency of the legs
Arterial insufficiency causes pale, cool extremities with weak pulses.
Dehydration with low blood volume
Low blood volume lowers, not raises, jugular venous pressure.

alt.q: Which vein does the nurse examine to best reflect pressure in the right atrium?
alt.a: Right internal jugular vein
alt.ex: The right internal jugular vein follows a more direct path to the right atrium, so its blood column reflects right atrial pressure.
w: Left external jugular vein
The external jugular lies superficially and is not the preferred vein for reflecting atrial pressure.
Right great saphenous vein
Leg veins are assessed for varicosities and phlebitis, not right atrial pressure.
Left subclavian vein
The book names the right internal jugular vein as the best vein to examine.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse assesses a patient’s lower leg and finds pale skin that worsens with elevation, cool temperature, absent pedal pulses, and thin, shiny, hairless skin. Which problem do these findings suggest?
items.a: Arterial insufficiency
items.ex: Pallor on elevation, coolness, decreased or absent pulses, and thin shiny skin with little hair are signs of arterial insufficiency.
w: Venous insufficiency
Venous insufficiency causes normal pulses, marked edema, and brown pigmentation at the ankles.
Superficial phlebitis
Phlebitis causes localized redness, warmth, tenderness, and swelling over a vein.
Dependent pitting edema
Dependent edema leaves a depression on pressure; it does not cause pallor and absent pulses.

alt.q: A patient’s lower legs show brown pigmentation around the ankles, marked edema, normal temperature, and normal pulses. Which problem do these findings suggest?
alt.a: Venous insufficiency
alt.ex: Venous insufficiency causes normal or cyanotic color, normal temperature and pulses, marked edema, and brown pigmentation around the ankles.
w: Arterial insufficiency
Arterial insufficiency causes cool, pale skin with decreased or absent pulses and little edema.
Acute arterial occlusion
Occlusion causes pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesias, and paralysis.
Carotid artery disease
Carotid disease affects neck pulses and causes bruits, not ankle pigmentation.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse grades a patient’s dorsalis pedis pulse as 1 on the 0 to 4 scale. What does this rating mean?
items.a: Pulse diminished, barely palpable
items.ex: On the 0 to 4 scale, 1 means the pulse is diminished and barely palpable.
w: Pulse absent, not palpable
An absent, nonpalpable pulse is rated 0.
Pulse expected, normal
A normal, expected pulse is rated 2.
Pulse full, increased
A full, increased pulse is rated 3.

alt.q: Which rating does a nurse use on the 0 to 4 scale to document a bounding pulse?
alt.ex: A rating of 4 describes a bounding, aneurysmal pulse.
w: A rating of 1 means the pulse is diminished and barely palpable.
A rating of 2 means the pulse is expected and normal.
A rating of 3 means the pulse is full and increased but not bounding.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which symptoms are key signs of heart disease that the nurse asks about in the nursing history? Select all that apply.
o: Chest pain or discomfort
Chest pain is a key symptom of heart disease.
Palpitations
Palpitations are listed as a key symptom of heart disease.
Orthopnea
Difficulty breathing lying flat is a key cardiac symptom.
Edema of the feet
Foot edema is listed among key symptoms of heart disease.
Increased appetite
Appetite change is not listed among key cardiac symptoms.
Ringing in the ears
Tinnitus relates to ear assessment, not heart disease.
items.ex: Key cardiac symptoms include chest pain, palpitations, fatigue, cough, dyspnea, leg cramps, foot edema, cyanosis, fainting, and orthopnea.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a patient about risk factors for heart disease. Which factors should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Smoking
Smoking is a risk factor; nicotine causes vasoconstriction.
Lack of regular aerobic exercise
Physical inactivity increases heart disease risk.
High dietary intake of saturated fat
Saturated fat and cholesterol intake raise risk.
Stressful lifestyle
Repeated exposure to stress increases risk for heart disease.
Regular intake of whole grains
Whole grains are part of the recommended heart-healthy diet.
Use of nontropical vegetable oils
Nontropical vegetable oils are part of a healthy diet, not a risk.
alt.ex: Box 30.19 lists high saturated fat, inactivity, smoking, excess weight, stress, hypertension, and family history as heart disease risk factors.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient who had vascular surgery on the leg develops a sudden arterial occlusion. Which findings make up the five Ps that characterize occlusion? Select all that apply.
o: Pain
Pain distal to the occlusion is one of the five Ps.
Pallor
Pallor results from blocked arterial flow.
Pulselessness
Loss of pulse below the blockage is one of the five Ps.
Paresthesias
Altered sensation is one of the five Ps.
Pitting edema
Pitting edema is a sign of venous insufficiency or right-sided heart failure.
Petechiae
Petechiae are not one of the five Ps of arterial occlusion.
items.ex: The five Ps of arterial occlusion are pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesias, and paralysis.

alt.q: Which findings would the nurse expect in a leg with an acute arterial occlusion? Select all that apply.
o: Paralysis below the blockage
Paralysis is one of the five Ps of occlusion.
Pain distal to the occlusion
Pain occurs below the blocked artery.
Absent pulse below the blockage
Pulselessness is one of the five Ps.
Brown pigmentation around the ankle
Brown ankle pigmentation is a sign of venous insufficiency.
Marked edema of the foot
Marked edema suggests venous problems; arterial problems cause little or no edema.
alt.ex: Pain, pallor, pulselessness, paresthesias, and paralysis characterize an arterial occlusion.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is teaching a patient with vascular insufficiency in the legs. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid sitting with your legs crossed
Crossing the legs impairs venous return.
Elevate your feet when sitting
Elevating the feet is recommended for lower-extremity vascular insufficiency.
Walk regularly
Regular walking is a listed teaching strategy.
Stop using nicotine products, including patches and gum
Nicotine from any source causes vasoconstriction.
Wear tight-fitting socks to support the veins
Tight clothing and hosiery over the legs impair circulation.
Stand in one place for long periods to rest the legs
Prolonged standing or sitting should be avoided.
items.ex: Patients with vascular insufficiency avoid tight clothing, prolonged sitting or standing, and crossed legs, walk regularly, elevate feet, and avoid nicotine.

alt.q: Which statements by a patient with lower-extremity vascular insufficiency show understanding of the teaching? Select all that apply.
o: “I will stop chewing tobacco because nicotine narrows my blood vessels.”
Nicotine causes vasoconstriction, so all nicotine products are avoided.
“I will put my feet up when I sit down.”
Elevating the feet when sitting is a listed strategy.
“I will take a walk every day.”
Regular walking is recommended.
“I will wear garters to keep my stockings snug.”
Tight garters and hosiery impair venous return.
“I will sit with my legs crossed to keep them warm.”
Crossing the legs impairs venous return.
alt.ex: Understanding is shown by avoiding nicotine and constriction, walking regularly, and elevating the feet when sitting.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A positive Homan sign is not enough to confirm deep vein thrombosis; other diagnostic tests are used.
items.a: True
items.ex: The Homan sign is unreliable and occurs in other conditions, so other tests confirm DVT even when it is positive.
items.ww: Treating a positive Homan sign as proof of DVT ignores that it is present in other conditions.

alt.q: A positive Homan sign is a reliable finding that confirms a patient has deep vein thrombosis.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The Homan sign is not a reliable indicator of phlebitis or DVT; other diagnostic tests confirm DVT.
alt.ww: The book states the sign appears in other conditions, so it cannot confirm DVT on its own.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: When blood pressure readings differ between the arms, the nurse documents the higher reading.
items.a: True
items.ex: Readings between arms can vary by as much as 10 mm Hg, and the higher reading is always documented.
items.ww: Documenting the lower value would underestimate the patient’s blood pressure.

alt.q: When blood pressure readings differ between the arms, the nurse documents the lower reading because it is usually more accurate.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book directs the nurse to always document the higher reading.
alt.ww: Arm readings vary by up to 10 mm Hg, and the higher one is recorded.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A normal carotid pulse does not change in quality as the patient breathes or moves from sitting to supine.
items.a: True
items.ex: The normal carotid pulse is localized, strong, and thrusting, and its quality does not change with breathing, neck rotation, or position.
items.ww: Changes with breathing or position are not features of a normal carotid pulse.

alt.q: A normal carotid pulse becomes weaker when the patient inhales and stronger when the patient lies supine.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: No change in the carotid impulse occurs with breathing or with moving from sitting to supine.
alt.ww: Normal carotid pulses stay the same in quality with respiration and position changes.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

alt.ex: Refill longer than 2 seconds signals a problem with vascular flow to the digits.
