items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which woman meets American Cancer Society criteria for a yearly breast MRI along with a mammogram?
items.a: A 34-year-old with a known BRCA1 gene mutation
items.ex: Women with a known BRCA1 or BRCA2 mutation are high risk and should have an annual MRI with a mammogram.
w: A 34-year-old who gave birth to her first child at age 24
First birth before age 30 is not a high-risk criterion.
A 34-year-old who had a chest x-ray for pneumonia last year
The criterion is chest radiation therapy between ages 10 and 30, not a diagnostic x-ray.
A 34-year-old whose aunt had fibrocystic breast disease
Benign breast disease in an aunt does not meet high-risk criteria.

alt.q: A woman asks why her health care provider ordered a yearly breast MRI in addition to a mammogram. Which history best explains this order?
alt.a: She received radiation therapy to the chest at age 16
alt.ex: Radiation therapy to the chest between ages 10 and 30 places a woman at high risk and calls for annual MRI with mammography.
w: She started taking a daily multivitamin at age 30
Vitamin use is not a breast cancer risk criterion.
She noticed one breast is slightly smaller at age 16
Slight size difference between breasts is common and normal.
She had her tonsils removed at age 6 in childhood
Tonsillectomy has no link to high breast cancer risk.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A menstruating patient chooses to perform breast self-examination (BSE). When should the nurse advise her to perform it?
items.a: On the fourth through seventh days of the menstrual cycle
items.ex: BSE is best done on days 4 to 7 of the cycle or right after menses, when breasts are no longer swollen or tender.
w: On the day before the menstrual period is expected to start
Hormone elevations before menses make breasts swollen and tender.
On the first day of the menstrual period as bleeding begins
Breasts are still affected by hormone changes at the start of menses.
At mid-cycle, about 14 days after the menstrual period starts
The book recommends days 4 to 7, not mid-cycle.

alt.q: A postmenopausal patient who wants to perform BSE asks when she should do it. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Check your breasts on the same day each month.”
alt.ex: Women who do not menstruate, such as after menopause or during pregnancy, check their breasts on the same day each month.
w: “Check your breasts only once a year before your mammogram.”
Once a year is not the monthly schedule the book describes for BSE.
“Check your breasts every day so you notice changes sooner.”
The book recommends a monthly check, not a daily one.
“You no longer need to check because your risk has dropped.”
Risk rises with age, and older women often ignore breast changes.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Why is a woman taught to palpate her breasts while lying down during breast self-examination?
items.a: Breast tissue spreads evenly over the chest wall and is as thin as possible
items.ex: Lying down flattens breast tissue evenly over the chest wall, making it easier to feel all of the tissue.
w: Breast tissue gathers into the center of the chest, so it is easier to grasp
Lying down spreads the tissue out; it does not gather it centrally.
The chest wall muscles contract, so any dimpling becomes more visible
Pressing hands on the hips while standing contracts the chest muscles.
The lymph nodes in the axilla move forward so they are easier to feel
The underarm is examined sitting or standing with the arm slightly raised.

alt.q: During BSE, why does a woman press her hands firmly down on her hips while standing in front of a mirror?
alt.a: It contracts the chest wall muscles and enhances any breast changes
alt.ex: Pressing on the hips contracts the chest wall muscles, which makes changes in size, shape, contour, or dimpling easier to see.
w: It flattens the breast tissue so the deeper tissue is easier to feel
Flattening tissue for palpation is the reason for lying down.
It relaxes the chest wall muscles so the lymph nodes are easier to feel
Pressing on the hips contracts, not relaxes, the chest muscles.
It raises the breasts so the inframammary ridge is easier to inspect
The maneuver is used to bring out changes in contour and dimpling.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: During breast inspection, the nurse asks the patient to raise her arms overhead, press her hands against her hips, and lean forward. What is the purpose of these maneuvers?
items.a: Contracting the pectoral muscles to accentuate any retraction
items.ex: Each position contracts the pectoral muscles, bringing out retraction or changes in breast shape.
w: Relaxing the pectoral muscles to make palpation more comfortable
These positions contract the muscles and are used for inspection, not palpation.
Moving breast tissue away from the axilla to expose the lymph nodes
Lymph nodes are palpated with the arm supported and abducted.
Increasing blood flow to the breasts to show the venous pattern
Venous pattern is inspected directly; these maneuvers target retraction.

alt.q: What causes the retraction or dimpling of breast skin that a nurse may see during inspection?
alt.a: Tumor invasion of ligaments that fibrose and pull the skin inward
alt.ex: Tumors can invade underlying ligaments, which fibrose and pull the overlying skin inward toward the tumor.
w: Rubbing of skin surfaces under large breasts that causes redness
Rubbing causes redness and excoriation, not retraction.
Weakening of supporting ligaments with age that causes sagging
Aging ligaments cause sagging and lower nipples, not dimpling.
Hormone changes before menses that cause swollen, tender tissue
Premenstrual swelling does not pull the skin inward.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse examines the breasts of a 52-year-old patient. Which finding is most important to report to the health care provider?
items.a: Nipple that turned inward over the past month
items.ex: A recent inversion or inward turning of the nipple indicates an underlying growth.
w: Nipple that has been inverted since puberty
Lifelong inversion is not the concerning finding; recent inversion is.
One breast that is slightly smaller than the other
It is common for one breast to be smaller than the other.
A firm ridge along the lower curve of each breast
The firm lower edge is the normal inframammary ridge.

alt.q: Which breast finding does the nurse recognize as normal?
alt.a: Clear yellow nipple discharge 2 days after childbirth
alt.ex: Clear yellow discharge 2 days after childbirth is common; other discharge, rashes, or ulcerations are not normal.
w: A rash with ulceration around the areola
Rashes or ulcerations are not normal on the breast or nipple.
Bloody discharge from one nipple
Bleeding or discharge from the nipple must be noted as abnormal.
Dimpling of the skin in the outer quadrant
Dimpling can result from a tumor pulling on ligaments.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: In which part of the breast is most of the glandular tissue located?
items.a: Upper outer quadrant and tail
items.ex: The largest part of the glandular tissue lies in the upper outer quadrant and the tail of each breast.
w: Lower inner quadrant
The book identifies the upper outer quadrant and tail as having the most glandular tissue.
Area just under the areola
Ducts open onto the nipple, but most glandular tissue is in the upper outer quadrant.
Lower outer quadrant
The upper, not lower, outer quadrant holds the largest part of glandular tissue.

alt.q: A nurse describes a breast finding located in the part of the breast that extends outward from the upper outer quadrant toward the axilla. What is this area called?
alt.a: Axillary tail of Spence
alt.ex: Each breast’s tail of Spence extends outward from the upper outer quadrant and holds much glandular tissue.
w: Inframammary ridge
The inframammary ridge is the firm lower edge of the breast.
Areolar margin
The areola surrounds the nipple at the center of the breast.
Supraclavicular area
The supraclavicular area holds lymph nodes above the clavicle, not breast tissue.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse palpates a breast mass that is hard, fixed, nontender, and irregular in shape and is found in only one breast. How should the nurse interpret these characteristics?
items.a: They are typical of a cancerous lesion
items.ex: Cancerous lesions are hard, fixed, nontender, irregular in shape, and usually unilateral.
w: They are typical of a benign fibrocystic cyst
Fibrocystic cysts are soft, well differentiated, movable, and often painful.
They are typical of the normal inframammary ridge
The inframammary ridge is a firm band at the lower edge of both breasts.
They are typical of normal glandular lobules
Normal glandular tissue feels lobular, dense, and elastic, not like a fixed mass.

alt.q: A patient reports bilateral lumpy, painful breasts that worsen during her menstrual period. The nurse palpates soft, movable, well-differentiated lumps. Which condition do these findings suggest?
alt.a: Fibrocystic breast disease
alt.ex: Fibrocystic disease causes bilateral lumpy, painful breasts that worsen with menses; the cysts are soft, well differentiated, and movable.
w: Breast cancer
Cancerous lesions are hard, fixed, nontender, irregular, and usually unilateral.
Axillary node metastasis
Metastatic nodes feel hard, tender, and immobile in the axilla.
Normal pregnancy changes
Pregnancy enlarges the breasts and darkens the areolas but does not cause painful cysts.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: During a breast examination, a patient says, “I feel a hard ridge along the bottom of both breasts. Is that a tumor?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “That firm band is the normal inframammary ridge. Let me guide your hand so you can feel it.”
items.ex: The firm lower edge of each breast is the normal inframammary ridge, and guiding the patient’s hand teaches normal variations.
w: “Any hard area in the breast needs a biopsy, so I will schedule one for you today.”
The inframammary ridge is normal and does not need a biopsy.
“That firm band is common in older women and usually means fibrocystic disease.”
Fibrocystic cysts are soft and movable; the ridge is normal tissue.
“Hard areas in both breasts are expected, so you can stop examining that area.”
The patient should still examine all breast tissue, including the lower edge.

alt.q: A nurse teaching BSE wants to help the patient recognize normal tissue variations. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
alt.a: “A firm ridge in the lower curve of each breast is normal.”
alt.ex: Feeling a firm ridge in the lower curve of each breast is normal; anything else unusual is reported.
w: “A firm lump in one breast that does not move is normal.”
A fixed, hard, unilateral mass is typical of cancer and must be reported.
“A nipple that has recently turned inward is normal.”
Recent nipple inversion suggests an underlying growth.
“Scaly skin on one nipple is normal after age 40.”
Scaliness of the nipple is a potential sign of breast cancer.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse palpates a patient’s axillae. Which finding is considered normal?
items.a: One small, soft, nontender node
items.ex: Normally lymph nodes are not palpable, but one or two small, soft, nontender nodes are normal.
w: One hard, tender, immobile node
An abnormal node feels like a small hard, tender, immobile mass.
Several large, firm, fixed nodes
Multiple enlarged, fixed nodes suggest infection or metastasis.
A cluster of hard nontender nodes
Hard nodes are abnormal even when they are not tender.

alt.q: Which axillary lymph node finding should the nurse report as abnormal?
alt.a: A small node that is hard, tender, and immobile
alt.ex: An abnormal palpable node feels like a small mass that is hard, tender, and immobile.
w: A small node that is soft, nontender, and movable
One or two small, soft, nontender nodes are normal.
No palpable nodes in any area of the axilla
Normally lymph nodes are not palpable.
Two small nodes that are soft and nontender
One or two small, soft, nontender nodes are a normal finding.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A 58-year-old man whose mother and sister had breast cancer asks about screening. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Routine mammograms may be recommended for men with your family history.”
items.ex: Routine mammograms may be recommended for men whose mothers or sisters have had breast cancer.
w: “Men have no breast glandular tissue, so screening is not needed.”
Men have a small amount of glandular tissue that can develop cancer.
“Men should perform breast self-examination every month.”
Because male breast cancer is rare, routine self-examinations are unnecessary.
“Men are not at risk because breast cancer only affects women.”
Men can develop breast cancer, and family history is a risk factor.

alt.q: Why do men with breast cancer have a lower survival rate than women?
alt.a: Their breast tumors are often not found until late
alt.ex: Breast tumors in men are often not found until late, which lowers survival compared with women.
w: Their tumors are usually painful and are often mistaken for injury
Most men present with painless lumps.
Their breast tissue is mostly glandular and spreads disease quickly
Men have only a small amount of glandular tissue.
Their breast cancer never involves the nearby lymph nodes
About half of men have at least one involved lymph node at diagnosis.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient with benign (fibrocystic) breast disease. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “Cutting back on caffeine may ease my breast symptoms.”
items.ex: Reducing caffeine intake, though controversial, can reduce symptoms of benign (fibrocystic) breast disease.
w: “Drinking more coffee will help my cysts go away.”
Caffeine contributes to fibrocystic changes, so intake should be reduced.
“My symptoms will be worst a week after my period.”
Symptoms are more apparent during the menstrual period.
“Lumps in both breasts mean I have breast cancer.”
Bilateral lumpy, painful breasts are typical of fibrocystic disease.

alt.q: Which factors in a patient’s history can cause fibrocystic changes in the breast?
alt.a: Hormones and caffeine
alt.ex: The nursing history notes that hormones and caffeine cause fibrocystic changes in the breast.
w: Exercise and fiber
Physical activity and fiber are not listed causes of fibrocystic changes.
Aspirin and antacids
These drugs are not listed as causing breast changes.
Diuretics and calcium
Diuretics are listed as a cause of nipple discharge, not fibrocystic change.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which findings in a woman’s nursing history are risk factors for breast cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Menstrual periods that started early in life
A long menstrual history is a breast cancer risk factor.
Never having given birth
Never having children is a listed risk factor.
Use of menopausal hormone therapy
Menopausal hormone therapy increases risk.
Tall adult height
Tall adult height is listed as a risk factor.
Menstrual periods that started late in life
Early, not late, onset of periods adds to risk.
First child born at age 22
First birth after age 30, not at 22, is the listed risk factor.
items.ex: Breast cancer risks include age over 40, family history, BRCA mutations, long menstrual history, no children or late first birth, hormone use, excess weight, and tall height.

alt.q: A nurse reviews lifestyle factors linked to breast cancer incidence. Which factors should the nurse identify? Select all that apply.
o: Being overweight or obese
Incidence correlates with excess weight.
Physical inactivity
Incidence correlates with physical inactivity.
Consumption of alcoholic beverages
Alcohol consumption correlates with breast cancer incidence.
Regular aerobic exercise
Inactivity, not exercise, is linked to higher incidence.
A low-fat diet with lean meats
A low-fat diet is part of breast health teaching, not a risk factor.
alt.ex: Breast cancer incidence correlates with excess weight, menopausal hormone therapy, physical inactivity, and alcohol use.

items.q: A nurse palpates a breast mass. Which characteristics should the nurse document? Select all that apply.

Masses are described by their location in the breast quadrants.
Diameter in centimeters
Size is measured in centimeters.
Consistency, such as soft, firm, or hard
Consistency helps distinguish types of masses.
Mobility
Whether a mass moves or is fixed is documented.
Weight in grams
Masses are not weighed during palpation.
Temperature of the mass
Temperature is not one of the listed mass characteristics.
items.ex: Abnormal masses are described by location, diameter, shape, consistency, tenderness, mobility, and discreteness.

alt.q: Which features help the nurse describe a palpable breast mass accurately? Select all that apply.
o: Shape, such as round or discoid
Shape is a listed characteristic.
Tenderness
Tenderness is documented for each mass.
Discreteness of the boundaries
Whether boundaries are clear or unclear is documented.
Color of the mass under a light
Color of a palpated mass is not a listed characteristic.
Sound heard over the mass with the bell
Breast masses are palpated, not auscultated.
alt.ex: Shape, tenderness, and discreteness, along with location, size, consistency, and mobility, describe a breast mass.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which breast changes are normal in older adulthood? Select all that apply.
o: Breasts become elongated and pendulous
Glandular tissue atrophy makes the breasts elongated, pendulous, and flaccid.
Nipples become smaller and flatter
Nipples become smaller and flatter and lose erectile ability.
Skin of the breasts wrinkles and appears loose
Breast skin tends to wrinkle and look loose.
Areolas darken and superficial veins become prominent
These changes occur during pregnancy.
A hard, fixed mass develops in one breast
A hard, fixed mass is a sign of cancer, not normal aging.
items.ex: In older adults glandular atrophy makes breasts elongated and flaccid, with wrinkled skin and smaller, flatter nipples.

alt.q: Which breast changes are normal during pregnancy? Select all that apply.
o: Breast size increases to 2 to 3 times the previous size
Breasts gradually enlarge 2 to 3 times during pregnancy.
Areolas darken and increase in diameter
Areolas darken and enlarge in pregnancy.
Nipples expel a yellowish fluid called colostrum
Colostrum is expelled from the nipples during pregnancy.
Nipples become smaller, flatter, and inverted
These are older-adult changes from shrinkage and fibrosis.
Breast tissue shrinks and becomes soft and flabby
Shrinking and softening occur at menopause.
alt.ex: Pregnancy enlarges the breasts and nipples, darkens and widens the areolas, makes veins prominent, and produces colostrum.

alt.a: False

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Why does the nurse auscultate the abdomen before palpating it?
items.a: Palpation can alter the frequency and character of bowel sounds
items.ex: Manipulating the abdomen alters bowel sounds, so auscultation comes before palpation.
w: Auscultation detects tender areas that must be avoided during palpation
Tender areas are found by asking the patient and by light palpation.
Palpation causes pain that makes the patient unable to lie still
The reason given is that palpation changes bowel sounds.
Auscultation warms the skin so palpation is more comfortable
Warm hands and stethoscope help relaxation, but that is not why the order changes.

alt.q: A nurse is about to perform an abdominal assessment. Which technique does the nurse perform last?
alt.a: Palpation
alt.ex: Completing palpation last reduces the chance of altering the frequency and character of bowel sounds.
w: Inspection
Inspection begins the abdominal examination.
Auscultation
Auscultation follows inspection and precedes palpation.
Observation of contour
Contour is inspected at the start of the examination.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient lying supine for an abdominal examination places both arms under the head. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Ask the patient to place the arms at the sides
items.ex: Arms under the head tighten the abdominal muscles, which hinders palpation; arms belong at the sides.
w: Begin deep palpation while the arms are raised
Tight abdominal muscles make palpation difficult and inaccurate.
Ask the patient to straighten the knees fully
Knees are kept slightly bent with a small pillow to help relax the abdomen.
Ask the patient to raise the head off the pillow
Raising the head is used to check for hernias, and it tightens the muscles.

alt.q: Which preparation helps a patient’s abdominal muscles relax for the abdominal examination?
alt.a: Small pillows under the slightly bent knees
alt.ex: Supine positioning with arms at the sides and knees slightly bent on small pillows helps relax the abdominal muscles.
w: Arms folded under the head
Arms under the head tighten the abdominal muscles.
Legs straight with knees locked
Knees should be slightly bent to relax the abdomen.
A cool room with the abdomen uncovered
The room should be warm, with the chest and legs draped.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Before an abdominal examination, a patient reports pain in the right lower quadrant. How should the nurse plan the examination?
items.a: Assess the right lower quadrant last
items.ex: Tender areas are assessed last to minimize the patient’s discomfort and anxiety.
w: Assess the right lower quadrant first
Starting with the painful area increases discomfort and anxiety.
Use deep palpation over the tender area
Deep palpation is never used over tender organs.
Skip auscultation to shorten the exam
Auscultation is still needed and is done before palpation.

alt.q: Why does the nurse ask a patient to point out tender areas before the abdominal examination begins?
alt.a: So painful areas can be assessed last to limit discomfort and anxiety
alt.ex: Knowing tender areas in advance lets the nurse examine them last, reducing discomfort and anxiety.
w: So painful areas can be examined first while the patient is still calm
Painful areas are assessed last, not first.
So deep palpation can be focused directly on each of the painful areas
Deep palpation is not used over tender organs.
So auscultation can be skipped over the areas that are already painful
All four quadrants are auscultated so no sounds are missed.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: What is the normal frequency of bowel sounds in an adult?
items.a: 5 to 35 times per minute
items.ex: Normal bowel sounds are soft gurgling or clicking sounds that occur irregularly 5 to 35 times per minute.
w: 1 to 4 times per minute
Sounds this infrequent would be hypoactive.
40 to 60 times per minute
This exceeds the normal range and suggests hyperactivity.
60 to 100 times per minute
This is an adult heart rate range, not a bowel sound frequency.

alt.q: A nurse auscultates the abdomen and hears soft gurgling sounds about every 10 to 15 seconds. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: Normal bowel sounds
alt.ex: It normally takes 5 to 20 seconds to hear a bowel sound, and sounds occur 5 to 35 times per minute.
w: Hyperactive bowel sounds
Hyperactive sounds are loud, growling borborygmi, not soft gurgles.
Hypoactive bowel sounds
Sounds every 10 to 15 seconds fall within the normal range.
Absent bowel sounds
Sounds are present, so they are not absent.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse auscultates the right lower quadrant of a postoperative patient and hears no bowel sounds after 1 minute. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Continue listening for a total of 5 minutes before documenting absent sounds
items.ex: It takes 5 minutes of continuous listening before determining that bowel sounds are absent.
w: Document bowel sounds as absent in the right lower quadrant
One minute is not long enough to determine that sounds are absent.
Palpate the abdomen deeply to stimulate the bowel sounds
Palpation alters bowel sounds, and deep palpation is not used over incisions.
Notify the health care provider of a suspected bowel obstruction
The nurse must first listen long enough to confirm absent sounds.

alt.q: How long must a nurse listen continuously before concluding that bowel sounds are absent?
alt.a: 5 minutes
alt.ex: The book states that 5 minutes of continuous listening is needed before determining bowel sounds are absent.
w: 30 seconds
This is far too short; normal sounds may take up to 20 seconds to occur.
1 minute
One minute is too short to conclude that sounds are absent.
15 minutes
The book specifies 5 minutes, not 15.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse hears loud, growling bowel sounds in a patient who has been taking large amounts of laxatives. What term describes these sounds?
items.a: Borborygmi
items.ex: Hyperactive, loud growling sounds are called borborygmi and indicate increased GI motility.
w: Bruits
Bruits are blowing vascular sounds over narrowed arteries.
Rebound sounds
Rebound tenderness is pain on release of pressure, not a sound.
Peristaltic rubs
This is not a term the book uses for bowel sounds.

alt.q: What do loud, growling borborygmi indicate?
alt.a: Increased GI motility
alt.ex: Borborygmi are hyperactive sounds that reflect increased GI motility from causes such as diarrhea, anxiety, or laxatives.
w: Lack of peristalsis
Absent sounds, not borborygmi, indicate a lack of peristalsis.
Narrowed abdominal blood vessels
Narrowed vessels produce bruits.
Fluid collecting in the flanks
Fluid causes bulging flanks, not hyperactive sounds.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient has a distended abdomen. When the patient rolls onto one side, a protuberance forms on the dependent side. What is the most likely cause of the distention?
items.a: Fluid in the abdominal cavity
items.ex: When fluid causes distention, the flanks bulge and a protuberance forms on the dependent side.
w: Intestinal gas
When gas causes distention, the flanks do not bulge.
Obesity
Obesity causes rolls of adipose tissue along the flanks without tightness.
Abdominal wall hernia
A hernia is a localized protrusion through the muscle wall.

alt.q: A nurse notes generalized abdominal distention with taut skin, but the flanks do not bulge. Which cause is most likely?
alt.a: Intestinal gas
alt.ex: When gas causes distention, the flanks do not bulge; fluid causes bulging flanks.
w: Ascites fluid
Fluid in the abdominal cavity causes the flanks to bulge.
Obesity
Obesity causes rolls of adipose tissue along the flanks and no sense of tightness.
An enlarged liver
An enlarged organ shows as a bulge below the ribs on deep inspiration.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: While palpating the upper abdomen of an older adult, the nurse feels a pulsation that expands laterally. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Stop deep palpation and refer the finding to the health care provider
items.ex: A laterally expanding pulsation suggests an aneurysm; the nurse does not palpate a pulsating mass deeply and refers the finding.
w: Palpate deeply with both hands to measure the size of the pulsation
Deep palpation of a pulsating mass is not done.
Test for rebound tenderness over the area of the pulsation
Deep pressure and quick release over a possible aneurysm is unsafe.
Document the finding as a normal aortic pulsation
A normal aortic pulsation is transmitted forward, not laterally.

alt.q: How does a normal aortic pulsation feel when the nurse palpates the upper abdomen just left of midline?
alt.a: The pulsation is transmitted forward
alt.ex: Normally the aortic pulsation is transmitted forward; lateral expansion suggests an aneurysm.
w: The pulsation expands laterally
Lateral expansion suggests an enlarged aorta from an aneurysm.
The pulsation cannot be felt
A pulsation is normally felt when palpating deeply near the midline.
The pulsation feels like a thrill
A thrill is a palpable vibration, not the normal aortic pulsation.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse auscultates a blowing sound over the epigastric region with the bell of the stethoscope. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Report the bruit immediately to the health care provider
items.ex: Abdominal bruits can reveal aneurysms or stenotic vessels and are reported immediately.
w: Document normal vascular sounds over the aorta
Normally no vascular sounds are heard over the aorta.
Palpate the area deeply to locate the source
Deep palpation over a possible aneurysm is not done.
Recheck the area at the next routine assessment
Waiting delays a finding the book says to report immediately.

alt.q: Where can a nurse listen for renal artery bruits?
alt.a: Over each upper quadrant anteriorly or the costovertebral angle posteriorly
alt.ex: Renal artery bruits are heard over each upper quadrant anteriorly or over the costovertebral angle posteriorly.
w: Over each lower quadrant anteriorly or the symphysis pubis
Lower quadrants are where the femoral arteries are heard.
Over the umbilicus anteriorly or the sacrum posteriorly
These are not the sites described for renal artery bruits.
Over the xiphoid process anteriorly or the scapula posteriorly
These are not the sites described for renal artery bruits.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: How does the nurse test a patient for rebound tenderness?
items.a: Press slowly and deeply into the area, then let go quickly
items.ex: Pain when the pressing hand is released quickly is a positive test, which occurs with peritoneal irritation.
w: Press lightly about 1 cm, then release the pressure slowly
This describes light palpation, not the rebound test.
Percuss the costovertebral angle with the side of the fist
Percussion at the costovertebral angle checks for kidney tenderness.
Have the patient raise the head while the nurse watches
Raising the head shows hernias and muscle separations.

alt.q: A patient has positive rebound tenderness. Which condition does this finding suggest?
alt.a: Peritoneal irritation, as in appendicitis
alt.ex: Rebound tenderness occurs with peritoneal irritation, as in appendicitis, pancreatitis, or peritoneal injury.
w: Hyperactive bowel, as in diarrhea
Diarrhea causes hyperactive bowel sounds, not rebound tenderness.
Kidney inflammation, as in pyelonephritis
Kidney inflammation causes tenderness on costovertebral angle percussion.
Ascites, as in fluid in the abdomen
Ascites causes bulging flanks and taut, shiny skin.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: How deep does the nurse depress the abdomen during light palpation?
items.a: About 1.3 cm (½ inch)
items.ex: Light palpation uses a gentle dipping motion about 1.3 cm (½ inch) deep to detect tenderness.
w: About 2.5 cm (1 inch)
This is the start of the deep palpation range.
About 5 cm (2 inches)
This depth is within the deep palpation range.
About 7.5 cm (3 inches)
This is the upper limit of deep palpation.

alt.q: How deep does an experienced nurse depress the abdomen during deep palpation?
alt.a: About 2.5 to 7.5 cm (1 to 3 inches)
alt.ex: Deep palpation depresses the abdomen about 2.5 to 7.5 cm (1 to 3 inches) to delineate organs and masses.
w: About 0.5 to 1 cm (¼ to ½ inch)
This shallow depth is less than even light palpation.
About 1.3 cm (½ inch) only
This is the depth used for light palpation.
About 10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 inches)
This exceeds the depth the book describes.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: In which situations does the nurse avoid deep abdominal palpation? Select all that apply.
o: Over a surgical incision
Deep palpation is never used over an incision.
Over tender organs
Deep pressure over tender organs is avoided.
Over an abnormal mass
Abnormal masses are not palpated deeply.
Over a pulsating abdominal mass
A pulsating mass may be an aneurysm and is palpated only lightly.
Over the lower quadrants of a relaxed, healthy patient
With experience, deep palpation is used in relaxed patients to detect less obvious masses.
Over nontender areas to delineate organ borders
Deep palpation is used in relaxed patients to delineate organs and masses.
items.ex: Deep palpation is never used over incisions, tender organs, or abnormal masses, and pulsating masses are palpated only lightly.

alt.q: In a healthy patient, where can deep abdominal pressure normally cause tenderness? Select all that apply.
o: Over the cecum
Deep pressure over the cecum causes tenderness in healthy people.
Over the sigmoid colon
The sigmoid colon is tender to deep pressure in healthy people.
Over the aorta
The aorta is tender to deep pressure in healthy people.
Over the midline near the xiphoid process
This area is tender to deep pressure in healthy people.
Over the kidneys at the costovertebral angle
Tenderness on percussion here suggests kidney inflammation.
alt.ex: In healthy patients, deep pressure causes tenderness over the cecum, sigmoid colon, aorta, and midline near the xiphoid.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which factors can cause hyperactive bowel sounds? Select all that apply.
o: Anxiety
Anxiety is a listed cause of hyperactive bowel sounds.
Diarrhea
Diarrhea increases GI motility.
Excessive ingestion of laxatives
Laxative overuse increases motility.
Inflammation of the bowel
Bowel inflammation causes hyperactive sounds.
Paralytic ileus
Paralytic ileus causes absent sounds from lack of peristalsis.
Late-stage bowel obstruction
Late-stage obstruction causes absent bowel sounds.
items.ex: Hyperactive sounds come from bowel inflammation, anxiety, diarrhea, bleeding, laxative overuse, and reactions to certain foods.

alt.q: Which conditions can cause absent bowel sounds? Select all that apply.
o: Paralytic ileus
Paralytic ileus stops peristalsis.
Peritonitis
Peritonitis can cause a lack of peristalsis.
Late-stage bowel obstruction
Late-stage obstruction can stop peristalsis.
Anxiety
Anxiety causes hyperactive sounds.
Diarrhea
Diarrhea causes hyperactive sounds.
alt.ex: Absent sounds indicate a lack of peristalsis, possibly from late-stage obstruction, paralytic ileus, or peritonitis.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which findings in a patient’s history are risk factors for hepatitis B virus (HBV) exposure? Select all that apply.

Receives hemodialysis
Hemodialysis is a listed risk factor.
Uses intravenous drugs
IV drug use is a listed risk factor.

International travel to a high-rate area is a risk factor.

Family history of heart disease relates to other risks, not HBV exposure.
items.ex: HBV exposure risks include health care work, hemodialysis, IV drug use, sexual contact with a carrier, multiple partners, and travel to high-rate areas.

Melena is a listed sign of GI alteration.
Bloody emesis
Hematemesis indicates a GI alteration.

Dysphagia is a listed GI symptom.
Heartburn

Ringing in the ears
Tinnitus is not a GI symptom.
Blurred vision
Blurred vision is not a GI symptom.
alt.ex: Difficulty swallowing, belching, gas, hematemesis, melena, heartburn, diarrhea, and constipation indicate GI alterations.

items.ww: Eversion is not a normal variant; it is a sign of distention.

alt.q: A normal umbilicus is everted, and a flat or concave umbilicus suggests an underlying mass.
alt.a: False

alt.ww: Flat or concave is normal, so eversion, not flatness, points to a problem.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.ww: The evidence summary warns that relying on bowel sounds alone misses complications.

alt.q: A complete GI assessment uses subjective data and several objective techniques rather than bowel sounds alone.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Box 30.24 recommends a complete assessment with history, inspection, auscultation, palpation, and ordered tests.
alt.ww: Using one component, such as bowel sounds alone, is not a good indicator of complications.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: When distention is expected, the nurse measures abdominal girth with a tape measure at the level of the umbilicus and marks the tape position.

alt.q: When distention is expected, the nurse measures abdominal girth at the level of the xiphoid process, choosing a new level each time.

A female attendant is always required with a male examiner.

alt.q: Which statement about attendants during a pelvic examination is accurate?
alt.a: A female examiner may choose to work alone
alt.ex: Only a male examiner always needs a female attendant; a female examiner may work alone unless the patient prefers otherwise.
w: A female examiner must always have a male attendant
There is no requirement for a male attendant.
A male examiner may choose to work alone
A male examiner always needs a female attendant present.
Attendants are needed only for adolescent patients
The attendant rule applies to all patients examined by a male examiner.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Why does the nurse ask a patient to empty her bladder before a pelvic examination?
items.a: So the uterus and ovaries are readily palpable

w: So the speculum can be inserted without lubricant
Bladder emptying is not related to speculum insertion.
So the urethral meatus can be inspected for color
The meatus is inspected regardless of bladder volume.
So the patient can lie flat without any discomfort
The book’s stated reason is palpation of the pelvic organs.

alt.q: Before a pelvic examination, the nurse asks the patient to void. Which additional task is often done at this time?
alt.a: Collecting a urine specimen
alt.ex: Before the examination the patient empties her bladder, and it is often necessary to collect a urine specimen.
w: Collecting a Pap specimen
The Pap specimen is collected by the examiner during the speculum examination.
Inserting a urinary catheter
Voiding before the examination does not call for a catheter.
Drawing a blood specimen
Blood collection is not part of the described preparation.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient with severe arthritis in her hips cannot assume the lithotomy position for a pelvic examination. Which alternative position should the nurse help her assume?
items.a: Left side-lying with the right thigh and knee drawn up to the chest
items.ex: Patients who cannot assume lithotomy can lie on the left side with the right thigh and knee drawn up to the chest.
w: Right side-lying with both legs fully extended and straight
The book describes left side-lying with the right knee drawn up.
Prone with a pillow under the hips and both legs straight
Prone does not give access for a pelvic examination.
High-Fowler’s with the legs hanging over the bed’s edge
High-Fowler’s is not an alternative described for a pelvic examination.

alt.q: A patient with painful joints cannot place both legs in stirrups. Which option does the textbook describe?
alt.a: Have the patient abduct only one leg
alt.ex: The patient can abduct only one leg, or another person can assist in separating the thighs.
w: Have the patient keep both legs together
The thighs must be separated for the examination.
Cancel the examination for another day
Alternative positions allow the examination to proceed.
Have the patient stand at the bedside
Standing is not a described position for the pelvic examination.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is about to inspect a patient’s external genitalia. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Touch the patient’s inner thigh before touching the perineum
items.ex: The perineum is sensitive and tender, so the nurse warns the patient and touches the inner thigh first.
w: Spread the labia quickly so the patient is not uncomfortable long
Touching the perineum suddenly without warning should be avoided.
Insert a speculum to view the cervix before the external exam
Speculum examination is done by advanced practitioners after external inspection.
Remove the drape fully so the whole perineum is clearly visible
The drape over the perineum is lifted while the rest of the patient stays covered.

alt.q: Why does the nurse avoid touching a patient’s perineum suddenly during the genital examination?
alt.a: The perineum is sensitive and tender
alt.ex: Because the perineum is sensitive and tender, the nurse warns the patient and touches the inner thigh first.
w: The perineum is usually inflamed
The perineum is normally free of inflammation.
Sudden touch spreads infection
Gloves and standard precautions prevent spread of infection.
The perineum has no sensation
The perineum is sensitive, which is why sudden touch is avoided.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which finding during inspection of the clitoris is within normal limits?
items.a: Length of 1.5 cm and width of 0.4 cm
items.ex: The clitoris normally does not exceed 2 cm in length and 0.5 cm in width.
w: Length of 3 cm and width of 0.4 cm
A length of 3 cm exceeds the normal 2 cm limit.
Length of 1.5 cm and width of 1 cm
A width of 1 cm exceeds the normal 0.5 cm limit.
Length of 1.5 cm, bright cherry red
A bright cherry red clitoris indicates inflammation.

alt.q: A nurse notes that a patient’s clitoris is bright cherry red. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
alt.a: The clitoris is inflamed
alt.ex: A bright cherry red clitoris indicates inflammation.
w: The clitoris is atrophied
Atrophy is a different finding and does not cause bright red color.
The clitoris is normal
Normal tissue is not bright cherry red.
The clitoris is enlarged
Size is measured; color does not indicate enlargement.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: During inspection of a young woman’s external genitalia, the nurse sees small open ulcers on the clitoris that drain serous material. Which condition does the nurse suspect?
items.a: Syphilitic chancres
items.ex: Chancres from syphilis appear as small open ulcers that drain serous material, and the clitoris is a common site in young women.
w: Genital warts
Warts appear as small bumpy spots that enlarge to cauliflower-like lesions.
Atrophic changes
Atrophy is thinning of tissue, not draining ulcers.
Normal variation
Open draining ulcers are never a normal finding.

alt.q: A nurse teaches genital self-examination. How should the nurse describe the appearance of genital warts?
alt.a: Small bumpy spots that enlarge to fleshy, cauliflower-like lesions
alt.ex: Warts appear as small, bumpy spots and enlarge to fleshy, cauliflower-like lesions.
w: Small open ulcers that drain serous material
This describes syphilitic chancres.
A bright cherry red, swollen, tender clitoris
This describes inflammation of the clitoris.
Thinned, atrophied labia in an older woman
This describes normal aging changes after menopause.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Where does the nurse expect to find the urethral meatus when inspecting the female external genitalia?
items.a: Anterior to the vaginal orifice, as a small pink slit
items.ex: The urethral meatus is anterior to the vaginal orifice, pink, and appears as a small slit or pinhole just above the vaginal canal.
w: Posterior to the vaginal orifice, as a dark red ring
The meatus lies anterior, not posterior, to the vaginal opening and is pink.
Directly on the clitoris, as a pale round opening
The meatus lies below the clitoris, above the vaginal canal.
Next to the anus, as a thin vertical slit
The anus is posterior; the vaginal orifice is the thin vertical slit.

alt.q: A nurse inspects the vaginal orifice of an adult patient. Which appearance is normal?
alt.a: A thin, vertical slit with moist tissue
alt.ex: Normally the vaginal opening is a thin, vertical slit, and the tissue is moist.
w: A wide, round opening with dry tissue
The normal opening is a thin slit with moist tissue.
A horizontal slit with yellow discharge
Discharge is noted as abnormal, and the slit is vertical.
A pinhole opening above the clitoris
A pinhole describes the urethral meatus, which lies below the clitoris.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A parent asks the nurse when the HPV vaccine should be given to a preteen. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “It is recommended at age 11 or 12, before becoming sexually active.”
items.ex: The HPV vaccine is recommended for preteen boys and girls at age 11 or 12, before sexual activity begins.
w: “It is recommended at age 18, once a teen becomes sexually active.”
The vaccine is given before sexual activity, at age 11 or 12.
“It is recommended at age 21, along with the first pelvic exam.”
Age 21 relates to pelvic exams, not the recommended vaccine age.
“It is recommended only for girls at age 15, before menarche.”
The vaccine is recommended for both boys and girls at 11 or 12.

alt.q: A 24-year-old woman who never received the HPV vaccine asks whether she can still get it. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Yes, young women can get the vaccine through age 26.”
alt.ex: People who did not start or finish the series as preteens can still receive the HPV vaccine as young adults, through age 26.
w: “No, the vaccine is given only at age 11 or 12.”
Those who did not start or finish the series can still get it.
“No, catch-up vaccination ends at age 18.”
Catch-up vaccination continues into young adulthood, through age 26.
“Yes, but only if you have never been sexually active.”
The book does not limit catch-up vaccination to people who were never sexually active.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient asks how often she needs a pelvic examination. According to the textbook, which women need one yearly?
items.a: Women who are sexually active or over the age of 21
items.ex: A pelvic examination is needed yearly for women who are sexually active or over 21; risk factors call for more frequent screening.
w: Women who have had at least one pregnancy
Pregnancy history is not the criterion for yearly examination.
Women who have reached the age of menopause
Yearly exams begin with sexual activity or age 21, not menopause.
Women who report symptoms of an infection
Yearly examinations are routine preventive care, not only for symptoms.

alt.q: Which patient is likely to be screened more often than the routine schedule for gynecological examination?
alt.a: A 30-year-old who smokes and has multiple sex partners
alt.ex: Screening is more frequent with risk factors such as a weak immune system, multiple partners, smoking, or a history of HPV.
w: A 30-year-old who exercises daily and does not smoke
These are not listed risk factors for more frequent screening.
A 30-year-old in one long-term relationship
A single long-term partner is not a listed risk factor.
A 30-year-old who completed the HPV vaccine series
Vaccination is protective, not a reason for more frequent screening.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nursing student is assigned to a patient having a speculum examination performed by a nurse practitioner. Which task is appropriate for the student?
items.a: Help the patient with positioning and provide emotional support
items.ex: Students observe or assist by helping with positioning, handing off specimen supplies, and providing emotional support.
w: Insert the speculum to view the cervix for the examiner
Speculum examination requires advanced skill and is done by advanced practitioners.
Collect the Pap specimen from the cervix for the examiner
The examiner collects the Pap specimen during the speculum examination.
Inspect the cervix for color, size, and surface characteristics
The examiner inspects the cervix through the speculum.

alt.q: Who performs the speculum examination of the internal genitalia?
alt.a: Advanced nurse practitioners and primary care providers
alt.ex: The internal speculum examination requires much skill and is performed by advanced nurse practitioners and primary care providers.
w: Nursing students under the guidance of an instructor
Students observe or assist; they do not perform the examination.
Assistive personnel trained in perineal hygiene
Assistive personnel do not perform internal examinations.
Registered nurses during routine hygiene measures
Nurses can inspect external genitalia during hygiene, but not perform the speculum exam.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A 62-year-old patient who went through menopause 10 years ago reports recent vaginal bleeding. Why is this finding important?
items.a: It is a warning sign for cervical and endometrial cancer
items.ex: Bleeding outside the normal menstrual period or after menopause is a warning sign for cervical and endometrial cancer.
w: It is a normal sign of hormone changes after menopause
Bleeding after menopause is a warning sign, not a normal change.
It is an expected result of labia majora atrophy with age
Labial atrophy is a normal aging change and does not cause bleeding.
It is a risk factor for breast but not reproductive cancer
The book lists postmenopausal bleeding as a warning sign for reproductive cancers.

alt.q: Which history finding should the nurse recognize as a warning sign for cervical or endometrial cancer?
alt.a: Bleeding between menstrual periods
alt.ex: Bleeding outside of the normal menstrual period or after menopause warns of cervical and endometrial cancer.
w: Menarche at age 12
Age at menarche is part of the menstrual history, not a warning sign.
Regular 28-day cycles
Regular cycles reflect normal reproductive health.
Thinning labia majora at age 70
Thinning and atrophy of the labia are normal with aging.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is positioning a patient in stirrups for a pelvic examination. Where should the nurse instruct the patient to place her arms?

w: Raised above her head on the table
Raising the arms tightens the abdominal muscles.
Gripping the sides of the stirrups
This is not the position described and may increase tension.
Placed under the small of her back
This is not the position described for the examination.

alt.q: During a pelvic examination, why is the patient asked to keep her arms at her sides or folded across her chest?
alt.a: To prevent tightening of the abdominal muscles
alt.ex: This arm position keeps the abdominal muscles from tightening during the examination.
w: To keep the drape in place over her knees
The drape corners fall over the knees without holding.
To keep her from reaching toward the examiner
The book’s reason is muscle relaxation, not restraint.
To raise her blood pressure during the exam
Arm position is not used to change blood pressure.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is teaching a patient about the warning signs of sexually transmitted infections (STIs). Which signs should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

Pain or burning on urination is a listed STI warning sign.
Pain during sex
Pain during sex is a listed warning sign.
Bleeding between menstruation
Intermenstrual bleeding is a listed warning sign.
Abnormal vaginal discharge
Abnormal discharge is a listed warning sign.
Regular menstrual cycles
Regular cycles reflect normal reproductive health.
Increased appetite
Appetite change is not an STI warning sign.
items.ex: STI warning signs include burning on urination, pain during sex, pelvic pain, intermenstrual bleeding, itchy rash, and abnormal discharge.

alt.q: Which measures should the nurse teach to help a patient prevent STIs? Select all that apply.

Condom use by the male partner prevents STIs.
Restricting the number of sexual partners
Fewer partners lowers STI risk.
Avoiding sex with people who have several other partners
This is a listed prevention measure.

Douching is not a prevention measure taught in the book.
Stopping condom use once symptoms resolve
Condom use continues to prevent transmission.
alt.ex: STI prevention includes condom use by the male partner, restricting partners, avoiding partners with several others, and perineal hygiene.

Multiple partners is a listed risk factor.

A strong family history of breast or ovarian cancer increases risk.
alt.ex: Ovarian cancer risks include BRCA mutations, personal or family history, PID, Lynch syndrome, hormone therapy, heavier weight, and taller height.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

Late menopause

Nulliparity is a listed risk factor.

Insufficient, not regular, physical activity is a risk.

items.ex: Endometrial cancer risks include excess weight, inactivity, menopausal estrogen, late menopause, no children, PCOS, Lynch syndrome, and type 2 diabetes.

alt.q: Which medical conditions in a patient’s history increase the risk for endometrial cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Lynch syndrome
Lynch syndrome increases endometrial cancer risk.
Type 2 diabetes
Type 2 diabetes is listed as increasing risk.
Polycystic ovary syndrome
PCOS is a listed risk factor.
Seasonal allergies
Allergies are not a listed risk factor.

alt.a: False

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is preparing a male patient for a genitalia examination. Which action should the nurse take before beginning the examination?

Keep the room warm and leave the patient fully undraped

The genitalia must be exposed for inspection, and the room should be warm.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A 19-year-old male college student asks why a genital examination is part of his routine health maintenance visit. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “The rate of sexually transmitted infections is high in your age-group.”
items.ex: Because STI incidence is high in adolescents and young adults, genital assessment is a routine part of their health maintenance examination.
w: “Prostate cancer screening begins in the late teenage years.”
Prostate screening with DRE and PSA is discussed for men age 50 and older.
“Hernias develop only in men younger than 20 years.”

“It is needed only because you have reported symptoms.”
The examination is routine for this age-group, not only when symptoms are present.

alt.q: For which group does the textbook stress that genital assessment needs to be a routine part of every health maintenance examination?
alt.a: Adolescent and young adult males
alt.ex: STI incidence is high in adolescents and young adults, so genital assessment is routine for this age-group.
w: Older adult males in long-term care
The rationale given is the high STI incidence in adolescents and young adults.
Preadolescent boys before puberty
The emphasis is on adolescents and young adults because of their high STI incidence.
Middle-aged males with hypertension

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is teaching a young man about warning signs of sexually transmitted infections. Which signs should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Pain on urination
Painful urination is a warning sign of an STI.
Abnormal penile discharge that differs from usual
A change in penile discharge is a warning sign of an STI.
Swollen lymph nodes
Swollen lymph nodes are listed among STI warning signs.
A rash or ulcer on the skin or genitalia
Rashes and ulcers on skin or genitalia are STI warning signs.
Left testicle hanging lower than the right
The left testicle normally hangs lower than the right.
A small amount of white, thick material under the foreskin
Smegma sometimes collects normally under the foreskin.
items.ex: STI warning signs include painful urination or sex, abnormal discharge, swollen lymph nodes, and rash or ulcer on skin or genitalia.

alt.q: A patient asks what changes should prompt him to seek care for a possible STI. Which findings should the nurse mention? Select all that apply.
o: Pain during sex
Pain during sexual activity is an STI warning sign.
An ulcer on the penis
Genital ulcers are a warning sign of an STI.
Discharge from the penis that is different from usual
Abnormal penile discharge is a warning sign of an STI.
Scrotum shrinking slightly in cold weather
The dartos muscle normally contracts in cold, changing scrotal size.
Scrotal skin that is darker than other body skin
Scrotal skin is normally more deeply pigmented than body skin.
alt.ex: Pain during sex, genital ulcers, and abnormal discharge are STI warning signs; scrotal size and color changes described are normal.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which measures should the nurse teach a patient to prevent sexually transmitted infections? Select all that apply.
o: Use condoms
Condom use is a key measure to prevent STIs.
Receive HPV immunization
HPV immunization is included in STI prevention teaching.
Restrict the number of sexual partners
Limiting partners reduces exposure to STIs.
Avoid sex with people who have multiple partners
Partners with multiple partners raise the risk of infection.
Delay telling partners about an STI until treatment ends
Patients with an STI should tell their partners of the need to be examined.
Rely on monthly self-examination instead of condoms
Self-examination detects signs but does not prevent transmission.
items.ex: STI prevention includes HPV immunization, condoms, fewer partners, avoiding infected partners or those with multiple partners, and perineal hygiene.

alt.q: A patient newly diagnosed with an STI asks how to prevent further infections. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Tell your sexual partners that they need to be examined
Partners of a patient with an STI need examination.
Avoid sex with a partner who is infected
Avoiding sex with an infected partner prevents transmission.
Practice regular perineal hygiene
Regular perineal hygiene is listed among STI prevention measures.
Resume sex with partners once symptoms fade, even if untreated
Symptoms can be absent while infection persists; men often have an STI without knowing it.
Seek treatment only if a partner develops symptoms twice
Treatment is sought as soon as possible if a partner becomes infected.
alt.ex: Patients with an STI inform partners, avoid sex with infected partners, use perineal hygiene, and seek prompt treatment if a partner is infected.

items.q: According to the patient teaching guidance in the chapter, at what age is the HPV vaccine recommended for preteen boys?
items.a: Age 11 or 12
items.ex: The HPV vaccine is recommended for preteen boys and girls at age 11 or 12, before sexual activity begins.
w: Age 6 or 7
This is younger than the preteen age recommended for HPV vaccination.
Age 15 or 16
Vaccination is recommended earlier, at the preteen age of 11 or 12.
Age 18, at high school graduation
Vaccination is recommended earlier, at the preteen age of 11 or 12.

alt.q: Why is the HPV vaccine recommended at age 11 or 12?
alt.a: To protect before sexual activity begins
alt.ex: Giving the vaccine at 11 or 12 provides protection before any exposure to HPV through sexual activity.
w: Because the vaccine is not safe for older teens
The vaccine can still be given later; the preteen timing is for protection before exposure.
Because HPV infection is curable after age 12
HPV is a virus and cannot be cured, which is why prevention matters.
Because boys do not need it after puberty
Boys and young men still benefit; the preteen age gives protection before exposure.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: The nurse teaches a 17-year-old male patient genital and testicular self-examination. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will do the examination every month after a warm shower.”
items.ex: Men 15 and older perform the examination monthly after a warm bath or shower, when scrotal skin is less thick.
w: “I will do the examination once a year before my physical.”
Self-examination is done monthly, not yearly.
“I will do the examination every month after a cold shower.”
A warm bath or shower thins the scrotal skin for easier palpation.
“I will start doing the examination when I turn 30.”
All men 15 years and older should perform the examination.

alt.q: A patient who is learning testicular self-examination says, “I felt a cordlike structure on the top and back of my testicle.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “That is the epididymis, which is a normal structure and not a lump.”
alt.ex: The epididymis is a cordlike structure on the top and back of the testicle; it is not a lump.
w: “That is a hernia, so you need to see your provider today.”
A hernia is a protrusion of intestine through the inguinal wall or canal, not a cord on the testicle.
“That is a sebaceous cyst, which is common in the testicle.”
Sebaceous cysts are common lumps in the scrotal skin, not a cord on the testicle.
“That is a tumor, so stop examining the area until seen.”
A cordlike structure on the top and back is the normal epididymis.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Normally the left testicle hangs lower than the right testicle.
items.a: True
items.ex: On inspection the left testicle is normally lower than the right.
items.ww: Asymmetry in testicle height is normal, with the left lower; it is not an abnormal finding.

alt.q: Normally the right testicle hangs lower than the left testicle, so a lower left testicle should be reported.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The left testicle normally hangs lower than the right, so this finding does not need to be reported.
alt.ww: The book states the left testicle is normally lower, so a lower right testicle is not the expected finding.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: What are the most common symptoms of testicular cancer?
items.a: Painless enlargement of one testis and a small, hard, pea-sized lump
items.ex: Testicular cancer most commonly causes painless enlargement of one testis and a small, hard lump on the front or side of the testicle.
w: Painful swelling of both testes and a soft, tender scrotal mass
Abnormal lumps are usually painless, and enlargement typically involves one testis.
Burning on urination and a thick, white penile discharge
Burning and discharge suggest an STI, not testicular cancer.
Loose, wrinkled scrotal skin and a resilient epididymis
Loose, wrinkled scrotal skin and a resilient epididymis are normal findings.

alt.q: Which age-group is most commonly affected by testicular cancer?
alt.a: Young men ages 18 to 34 years
alt.ex: Testicular cancer is a solid tumor common in young men ages 18 to 34 years.
w: Boys ages 8 to 12 years
Testicular cancer is common in young men 18 to 34, not preadolescent boys.
Middle-aged men ages 45 to 60 years
The common age range given is 18 to 34 years.
Older men ages 70 to 85 years
In older men the testicles shrink and soften; cancer is most common at 18 to 34.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: While examining a 24-year-old male patient, the nurse notes several findings. Which finding is most important to report to the health care provider?
items.a: A small, hard, painless lump on the front of the right testicle
items.ex: A small, hard, painless pea-sized lump on the front or side of a testicle is a common sign of testicular cancer.
w: A small amount of white, thick smegma under the foreskin
Smegma sometimes collects normally under the foreskin.
A scrotum that becomes smaller in a cool examination room
The dartos muscle contracts in cold, so scrotal size normally changes with temperature.
Testes that feel smooth, rubbery, and free of nodules
Smooth, rubbery testes without nodules are a normal finding.

alt.q: A 30-year-old man tells the nurse he has noticed a feeling of heaviness in his scrotum. Which additional finding from his history should most concern the nurse?
alt.a: Painless enlargement of one testis
alt.ex: Heaviness and painless testicular enlargement are early warning signs of testicular cancer.
w: Scrotal skin that wrinkles in cold weather
Wrinkling and contraction in cold are normal effects of the dartos muscle.
A dorsal vein that is visible on the penis
The dorsal vein is normally apparent on inspection.
Testes that are sensitive but not tender
Testes are normally sensitive but not tender.

items.ex: Because testicular cancer peaks in young adulthood, nurses teach testicular self-examination during the genital examination.

alt.q: Young men between ages 18 and [[34|thirty-four]] are the age-group in which testicular cancer, a solid tumor, is common.
alt.ex: Because testicular cancer peaks in young adulthood, nurses teach testicular self-examination during the genital examination.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: When inspecting the glans penis, where does the nurse expect to find the urethral meatus?
items.a: On the ventral surface, a few millimeters from the tip of the glans
items.ex: The meatus is slitlike and positioned on the ventral surface just millimeters from the tip of the glans.
w: On the dorsal surface, at the base of the penile shaft
The dorsal vein, not the meatus, is apparent on the dorsal surface.
On the ventral surface, at the junction with the scrotum
A meatus displaced along the shaft suggests a congenital condition.
On the lateral surface, just below the corona
The meatus is normally on the ventral surface near the tip.

alt.q: Which finding of the urethral meatus is normal?
alt.a: A slitlike, glistening pink opening without discharge
alt.ex: Compressing the glans opens the meatus, which is normally slitlike, glistening, pink, and free of discharge.
w: A round, dry red opening with scant discharge
Discharge and redness suggest inflammation or infection and warrant a culture.
A slitlike, pale opening with clear discharge
Any abnormal discharge is not normal and is cultured.
A round opening located midway along the shaft
A meatus displaced along the shaft occurs in some congenital conditions.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: In an uncircumcised patient, which area does the nurse inspect closely because it is a common site for venereal lesions?
items.a: The area between the foreskin and the glans
items.ex: The area between the foreskin and glans is a common site for venereal lesions, so the foreskin is retracted for inspection.
w: The posterior surface of the scrotum
The posterior scrotum is inspected for lesions and edema but is not named as the common site.
The area around the external inguinal ring
The inguinal ring is inspected for hernias, not as the common lesion site.
The skin over the dorsal vein of the shaft
The dorsal vein is a normal visible structure, not the common lesion site.

alt.q: Why does the nurse retract the foreskin of an uncircumcised patient during genital inspection?
alt.a: To inspect the glans and meatus, a common site for venereal lesions
alt.ex: Retracting the foreskin reveals the glans and meatus; the area between foreskin and glans commonly harbors venereal lesions.
w: To check the dartos muscle for response to temperature
The dartos muscle is in the scrotum, not under the foreskin.
To palpate the vas deferens toward the inguinal ring
The vas deferens is palpated in the scrotum along the spermatic cord.
To measure the testes, which are normally 2 to 4 cm
Testicular size is assessed by palpating the scrotum, not by retracting the foreskin.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: After inspecting the glans of an uncircumcised patient, the nurse pulls the foreskin back down to its original position.
items.a: True
items.ex: Once inspection and palpation of the glans are complete, the foreskin is returned to its original position.
items.ww: Leaving the foreskin retracted is not the correct practice; the nurse restores it after inspecting the glans.

alt.q: Once the foreskin of an uncircumcised patient is retracted, it is left retracted after the examination so the glans can air-dry.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The foreskin is pulled back down to its original position as soon as inspection and palpation of the glans are complete.
alt.ww: There is no recommendation to leave the foreskin retracted; it is restored to its original position.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse notes that a patient’s scrotum is smaller and more wrinkled than it was earlier in a warm room. What best explains this change?
items.a: The dartos muscle contracts in cold temperatures
items.ex: Scrotal size normally changes with temperature because the dartos muscle contracts in cold and relaxes in warm temperatures.
w: Scrotal edema develops in cold temperatures
Edema causes tightening of the skin and loss of wrinkling, not increased wrinkling.
An inguinal hernia enters the scrotum in the cold
A hernia enlarges the scrotum and is unrelated to temperature.
The testes shrink from an early testicular tumor
Testicular cancer causes painless enlargement, not shrinking with cold.

alt.q: Which scrotal finding indicates edema?
alt.a: Tightening of the skin with loss of wrinkling
alt.ex: Scrotal skin is normally loose and coarse; tightening of the skin or loss of wrinkling reveals edema.
w: Loose skin with a coarse surface
Loose, coarse scrotal skin is the normal finding.
Skin that is darker than other body skin
Scrotal skin is normally more deeply pigmented than body skin.
Size that changes with room temperature
Temperature-related size change is a normal dartos muscle response.

items.q: A patient reports a swelling in his groin that appears when he lifts heavy objects. How should the nurse proceed with the inguinal examination?
items.a: Have the patient stand and bear down while the nurse inspects for bulging
items.ex: With the patient standing, straining or bearing down makes a hernia more visible as a bulge in the inguinal area.
w: Have the patient lie prone and hold his breath while the nurse inspects
The patient stands for this part of the examination, and bearing down is the maneuver used.
Have the patient lie supine and relax completely while the nurse inspects
Relaxing supine makes a hernia less visible; standing and straining reveal it.
Have the patient sit and cough twice while the nurse palpates the testes
Testicular palpation does not reveal an inguinal hernia, and the patient should stand.

alt.q: What is the purpose of asking a male patient to strain or bear down during inspection of the inguinal area?
alt.a: To make a hernia more visible
alt.ex: Bearing down increases pressure so that a hernia through the inguinal wall or canal becomes more visible as a bulge.
w: To make the inguinal lymph nodes easier to palpate
Lymph nodes are palpated afterward and are not affected by straining.
To reveal internal hemorrhoids and fissures
That purpose applies to bearing down during the rectal examination.
To relax the dartos muscle of the scrotum
The dartos muscle relaxes with warmth, not with bearing down.

items.q: Which change in the testicles does the nurse expect when examining an older adult male?
items.a: The testicles decrease in size and are less firm
items.ex: In older adults the testicles decrease in size and feel less firm on palpation.
w: The testicles increase in size and become harder
Painless enlargement and hardness suggest testicular cancer, not aging.
The testicles become tender and nodular
Testes are normally sensitive but not tender, and nodules are abnormal.
The left testicle rises higher than the right
The left testicle normally stays lower than the right.

alt.q: A nurse palpates small, less firm testicles in an 82-year-old man with no other abnormal findings. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: As an expected age-related change
alt.ex: Testicles normally decrease in size and become less firm in older adults.
w: As an early warning sign of testicular cancer
Testicular cancer causes painless enlargement or a hard lump, not small, soft testes.
As a sign of an inguinal hernia
A hernia appears as a bulge in the inguinal area, not small testes.
As evidence of a current sexually transmitted infection
STIs cause signs such as discharge, lesions, or ulcers, not age-related shrinkage.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Small, nontender, mobile, horizontal inguinal lymph nodes are normally palpable.
items.a: True
items.ex: Small, nontender, mobile horizontal inguinal nodes are a normal palpable finding.
items.ww: These nodes are normal; only an abnormality in the nodes suggests infection or malignancy.

alt.q: Any palpable inguinal lymph node indicates local or systemic infection.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Small, nontender, mobile nodes are normally palpable; only abnormal nodes suggest infection or malignant disease.
alt.ww: Palpable nodes alone are not abnormal; their size, tenderness, and mobility determine whether they are normal.

items.q: When taking a nursing history before a male genitalia examination, the nurse reviews medications. Which medications should the nurse ask about because they influence sexual performance? Select all that apply.
o: Diuretics
Diuretics are listed among medications that influence sexual performance.
Antihypertensives
Antihypertensives can influence erection and ejaculation.
Sedatives
Sedatives are listed as influencing sexual performance.
Tranquilizers
Tranquilizers are listed as influencing sexual performance.
Iron preparations
Iron is reviewed in the rectal history because it turns stools black.
Calcium supplements
Calcium is discussed for osteoporosis prevention, not sexual performance.
items.ex: Diuretics, sedatives, antihypertensives, and tranquilizers can affect erection or ejaculation, so they are reviewed in the male genital history.

alt.q: A patient reports difficulty achieving an erection. Which of his current medications could be contributing? Select all that apply.
o: An antihypertensive for blood pressure
Antihypertensives influence sexual performance.
A diuretic for fluid retention
Diuretics influence sexual performance.
A sedative taken at bedtime
Sedatives influence sexual performance.
A laxative taken occasionally
Laxatives are reviewed for bowel effects, not sexual performance.
A fiber supplement taken daily
Fiber supports bowel health and is not linked to sexual performance in the text.
alt.ex: Antihypertensives, diuretics, sedatives, and tranquilizers can impair erection or ejaculation.
