alt.ex: That's step 5 of 6. The self-examination starts after warm bathing, moves from the head of the penis to the meatus and shaft, and ends at the base under the pubic hair.
w: Look at the urethral meatus for discharge
That's step 4 of 6.
Inspect and palpate the entire head of the penis in a clockwise motion
That's step 3 of 6.
Stand in front of a mirror and examine the head of the penis, pulling back the foreskin if uncircumcised
That's step 2 of 6.

ord.q: Put these steps of male genital self-examination in the order the textbook presents them.
items: Take a warm bath or shower so the scrotal skin is less thick
Stand in front of a mirror and examine the head of the penis, pulling back the foreskin if uncircumcised
Inspect and palpate the entire head of the penis in a clockwise motion
Look at the urethral meatus for discharge
Look along the entire shaft of the penis
Separate the pubic hair at the base of the penis and examine the skin underneath
ord.ex: The self-examination starts after warm bathing, moves from the head of the penis to the meatus and shaft, and ends at the base under the pubic hair.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: When during the physical examination is a good time to perform the rectal examination?
items.a: After the genital examination
items.ex: The rectal examination is conveniently performed right after the genital examination.
w: Before the head and neck examination
The rectal examination follows the genital examination, not the head and neck.
During the initial general survey
The general survey is an overall observation, not a time for a rectal examination.
Immediately after the lung examination
The rectal examination follows the genital examination.

alt.q: Which part of the physical examination does the rectal examination usually follow?
alt.a: The genital examination
alt.ex: A good time to perform the rectal examination is after the genital examination.
w: The neurological examination
The neurological examination is not the part that the rectal examination follows.
The thorax and lung examination
The rectal examination is not paired with the thorax and lungs.
The musculoskeletal examination
The musculoskeletal examination is not the part that the rectal examination follows.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which statement about the purpose of the rectal examination is accurate?
items.a: It detects colorectal cancer in its early stages and prostatic tumors in men
items.ex: The rectal examination detects early colorectal cancer and, in men, prostatic tumors.
w: It detects inguinal hernias and testicular tumors in men
Hernias and testicular tumors are found in the male genital examination.
It detects ovarian cysts and cervical cancer in women
These are assessed during the female genitalia and reproductive tract examination.
It detects kidney stones and bladder infections in adults
The rectal examination is not used to detect urinary tract conditions.

alt.q: For which patient is a rectal examination usually not performed?
alt.a: A healthy 13-year-old adolescent
alt.ex: The rectal examination usually is not performed for young children or adolescents.
w: A 52-year-old man with a family history of colon polyps
Family history of polyps is a colorectal cancer risk factor, so examination is appropriate.
A 60-year-old woman who reports rectal bleeding
Rectal bleeding is a warning sign of colorectal cancer, so examination is appropriate.
A 70-year-old man with a weak urine stream
A weak stream is a warning sign of prostate cancer in an adult man.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which findings in a patient’s history are warning signs of colorectal cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Bleeding from the rectum
Rectal bleeding is a warning sign of colorectal cancer.
Black or tarry stools
Melena is a warning sign of colorectal cancer or other GI alterations.
A change in bowel habits
New constipation or diarrhea is a warning sign of colorectal cancer.
Rectal pain
Rectal pain is listed as a warning sign.
Moist, hairless anal tissue
Moist, hairless anal tissue is a normal finding.
Perianal skin darker than skin of the buttocks
Perianal skin is normally more pigmented than buttock skin.
items.ex: Rectal bleeding, melena, rectal pain, and a change in bowel habits are warning signs of colorectal cancer.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing warning signs of colorectal cancer with a patient. Which statements by the patient indicate correct understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “I should report blood coming from my rectum.”
Rectal bleeding is a warning sign of colorectal cancer.
“I should report a change to constipation or diarrhea.”
A change in bowel habits is a warning sign.
“I should report stools that look black and tarry.”
Melena is a warning sign of colorectal cancer.
“I should report a weak or interrupted urine stream.”
A weak or interrupted stream is a warning sign of prostate cancer, not colorectal cancer.
“I should report a painless lump on my testicle.”
A painless testicular lump suggests testicular cancer.
alt.ex: Colorectal cancer warning signs include rectal bleeding, change in bowel habits, melena, and rectal pain.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which factors in a patient’s history increase the risk for colorectal cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Excess body weight
Excess body weight is a colorectal cancer risk factor.
Physical inactivity
Being physically inactive is a colorectal cancer risk factor.
Long-term smoking
Long-term smoking is a colorectal cancer risk factor.
Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Type 2 diabetes is listed among colorectal cancer risk factors.
High intake of fruits, vegetables, and fiber
Low, not high, intake of fruits, vegetables, and fiber is the risk factor.
Adequate calcium intake
Low calcium intake is the risk factor.
items.ex: Colorectal cancer risk rises with excess weight, inactivity, smoking, red or processed meat, low calcium, heavy alcohol, low fiber, and type 2 diabetes.

alt.q: A nurse is collecting a rectal and anal nursing history. Which findings should the nurse identify as colorectal cancer risk factors? Select all that apply.
o: A strong family history of colorectal polyps
Personal or strong family history of polyps increases risk.
Chronic inflammatory bowel disease
Chronic inflammatory bowel disease is a colorectal cancer risk factor.
A diet high in red or processed meats
High consumption of red or processed meat is a risk factor.
Heavy alcohol consumption
Heavy alcohol consumption is a colorectal cancer risk factor.
Regular annual fecal occult blood testing
Screening reflects preventive care; it is not a risk factor.
A diet low in fat and high in fiber
Bowel cancer is linked to high fat and insufficient fiber, not the reverse.
alt.ex: Family history of polyps, inflammatory bowel disease, red or processed meat, and heavy alcohol use are colorectal cancer risk factors.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient taking ferrous sulfate for anemia tells the nurse, “My stools have turned very dark.” Why does the nurse ask about iron preparations in the rectal history?
items.a: Iron turns the color of feces black and tarry
items.ex: Iron preparations turn feces black and tarry, which the nurse considers when evaluating dark stools.
w: Iron causes repeated diarrhea and loss of muscle tone
That effect results from repeated use of laxatives or cathartics.
Iron causes constipation and rectal fissures
Codeine, not iron, is the drug noted for causing constipation.
Iron causes bright red bleeding from the rectum
Iron darkens stool; it does not cause rectal bleeding.

alt.q: Why does the nurse ask about repeated use of laxatives or cathartics in the rectal and anal history?
alt.a: Repeated use causes diarrhea and eventual loss of intestinal muscle tone
alt.ex: Repeated laxative or cathartic use causes diarrhea and, over time, loss of intestinal muscle tone.
w: Repeated use turns the stool black and tarry
Iron preparations, not laxatives, turn stool black and tarry.
Repeated use causes painless enlargement of the prostate
Laxatives are not linked to prostate enlargement.
Repeated use protects against colorectal cancer
Laxative use is not described as protective against cancer.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: The nurse asks about codeine use in the rectal and anal history because codeine causes constipation.
items.a: True
items.ex: Codeine causes constipation, so its use is assessed when reviewing bowel patterns.
items.ww: Codeine’s effect on the bowel is constipation, which makes it relevant to the rectal history.

alt.q: The nurse asks about codeine use in the rectal history because codeine turns the stool black and tarry.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Codeine causes constipation; it is iron preparations that turn the stool black and tarry.
alt.ww: Black, tarry stool is the effect of iron, not codeine, so the statement confuses the two drugs.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: According to the American Cancer Society guidelines in the chapter, at what age should men and women of average risk begin regular colorectal cancer screening?
items.a: Age 45
items.ex: Beginning at age 45, men and women of average risk should undergo regular colorectal cancer screening.
w: Age 35
Screening for average-risk adults begins at 45, not 35.
Age 55
Waiting until 55 is later than the recommended start at 45.
Age 65
Age 65 is the age for routine osteoporosis screening in women, not colorectal screening.

alt.q: A 46-year-old woman with no risk factors asks whether she needs colorectal cancer screening yet. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “Yes, regular screening is recommended beginning at age 45.”
alt.ex: Average-risk adults begin regular colorectal cancer screening at age 45.
w: “No, regular screening is recommended beginning at age 50.”
The ACS guideline in the chapter begins screening at 45.
“No, regular screening is recommended beginning at age 60.”
Screening starts well before 60 for average-risk adults.
“No, regular screening is recommended only with symptoms.”
Screening is recommended for average-risk adults without symptoms.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

That goes with Stool DNA test.
Every 5 years

Every 10 years

alt.q: How often is the Stool DNA test recommended for colorectal cancer screening?

w: Every year

Every 5 years
That goes with Flexible sigmoidoscopy.
Every 10 years
That goes with Colonoscopy.

alt.q: How often is the Flexible sigmoidoscopy recommended for colorectal cancer screening?

alt.ex: ACS screening options include FOBT or FIT yearly, stool DNA every 3 years, sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, and colonoscopy every 10 years.
w: Every year
That goes with Fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test.
Every 3 years
That goes with Stool DNA test.
Every 10 years
That goes with Colonoscopy.

alt.q: How often is the Colonoscopy recommended for colorectal cancer screening?
alt.a: Every 10 years
alt.ex: ACS screening options include FOBT or FIT yearly, stool DNA every 3 years, sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, and colonoscopy every 10 years.
w: Every year
That goes with Fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test.
Every 3 years
That goes with Stool DNA test.
Every 5 years
That goes with Flexible sigmoidoscopy.

alt.q: Which screening test is recommended “Every year”?
alt.a: Fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test
alt.ex: ACS screening options include FOBT or FIT yearly, stool DNA every 3 years, sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, and colonoscopy every 10 years.
w: Stool DNA test
Stool DNA test: Every 3 years.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy: Every 5 years.
Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy: Every 10 years.

alt.q: Which screening test is recommended “Every 3 years”?
alt.a: Stool DNA test
alt.ex: ACS screening options include FOBT or FIT yearly, stool DNA every 3 years, sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, and colonoscopy every 10 years.
w: Fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test
Fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test: Every year.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy: Every 5 years.
Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy: Every 10 years.

alt.q: Which screening test is recommended “Every 5 years”?
alt.a: Flexible sigmoidoscopy
alt.ex: ACS screening options include FOBT or FIT yearly, stool DNA every 3 years, sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, and colonoscopy every 10 years.
w: Fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test
Fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test: Every year.
Stool DNA test
Stool DNA test: Every 3 years.
Colonoscopy
Colonoscopy: Every 10 years.

alt.q: Which screening test is recommended “Every 10 years”?
alt.a: Colonoscopy
alt.ex: ACS screening options include FOBT or FIT yearly, stool DNA every 3 years, sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, and colonoscopy every 10 years.
w: Fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test
Fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test: Every year.
Stool DNA test
Stool DNA test: Every 3 years.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy
Flexible sigmoidoscopy: Every 5 years.

mt.q: Match each colorectal cancer screening test with its recommended interval.
pairs: Fecal occult blood test or fecal immunochemical test
mt.ex: ACS screening options include FOBT or FIT yearly, stool DNA every 3 years, sigmoidoscopy every 5 years, and colonoscopy every 10 years.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: After teaching about colorectal cancer screening, the nurse evaluates a 50-year-old patient’s understanding. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “If I choose a colonoscopy, it is repeated every 10 years.”
items.ex: Colonoscopy is recommended every 10 years for average-risk adults who choose that screening option.
w: “If I choose a colonoscopy, it is repeated every 2 years.”
Colonoscopy is repeated every 10 years, not every 2 years.
“If I choose a stool DNA test, it is repeated every 10 years.”
The stool DNA test is repeated every 3 years.
“If I choose a fecal occult blood test, it is done every 5 years.”
FOBT or FIT is done annually.

alt.q: A patient chose the fecal immunochemical test for colorectal cancer screening. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
alt.a: “I will repeat this test every year.”
alt.ex: The FOBT or FIT is performed annually for colorectal cancer screening.
w: “I will repeat this test every 3 years.”
Every 3 years is the interval for the stool DNA test.
“I will repeat this test every 5 years.”
Every 5 years is the interval for flexible sigmoidoscopy or CT colonoscopy.
“I will repeat this test every 10 years.”
Every 10 years is the interval for colonoscopy.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A 64-year-old man is having a rectal and anal assessment. Which reports should the nurse recognize as warning signs of prostate cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Weak or interrupted urine flow
A weak or interrupted stream is a warning sign of prostate cancer.
Difficulty starting or stopping urine flow
Difficulty starting or stopping flow is listed as a warning sign.
Continuing pain in the lower back, pelvis, or upper thighs
Persistent pain in these areas is a warning sign of prostate cancer.
Blood in the urine
Hematuria is listed among prostate cancer warning signs.
Black stools while taking iron
Iron normally darkens stool and is not a prostate warning sign.
A visible dorsal vein on the penis
The dorsal vein is normally apparent on inspection.
items.ex: Prostate cancer warning signs include urine flow problems, nocturia, polyuria, hematuria, dysuria, and continuing pain in the lower back, pelvis, or upper thighs.

alt.q: Which urinary symptoms reported by a male patient may suggest prostate cancer, infection, or prostate enlargement? Select all that apply.
o: Nocturia
Nocturia is a warning sign of prostate cancer and also suggests enlargement or infection.
Dysuria
Painful urination is listed among the warning signs.
Inability to urinate
Inability to urinate is listed as a warning sign.
A scrotum that shrinks in the cold
Scrotal contraction in the cold is a normal dartos muscle response.
Testes that are sensitive but not tender
Sensitive, nontender testes are normal.
alt.ex: Nocturia, dysuria, and inability to urinate may signal prostate cancer, infection, or prostate enlargement.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which statement reflects the ACS prostate cancer screening guidance described in the chapter?
items.a: Men 50 and older with at least a 10-year life expectancy should make an informed decision about screening
items.ex: Men 50 and older with a life expectancy of at least 10 years should decide with their provider about DRE and PSA screening.
w: Men 40 and older with any life expectancy should have yearly screening without discussion
Screening starts at 50 and involves an informed decision about benefits, risks, and uncertainties.
Men 45 and older should have colonoscopy as the main screening test for prostate cancer
Colonoscopy screens for colorectal cancer; DRE and PSA are the prostate tests.
Men 65 and older should have screening only after symptoms of urinary retention appear
Screening is discussed from age 50 and is not reserved for symptomatic men.

alt.q: Which tests are discussed with men age 50 and older for early detection of prostate cancer?
alt.a: Digital rectal examination and prostate-specific antigen test
alt.ex: For men 50 and older, DRE and the PSA test are the prostate cancer screening options discussed.
w: Fecal immunochemical test and stool DNA test
These are colorectal cancer screening tests.
Flexible sigmoidoscopy and CT colonoscopy
These visualize the colon and screen for colorectal cancer.
Testicular self-examination and urine culture
These do not screen for prostate cancer.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A 72-year-old man with severe arthritis cannot stand for his rectal examination. Which position should the nurse use?
items.a: Lateral recumbent position
items.ex: A male patient who cannot stand is examined in the lateral recumbent position.
w: High Fowler’s position
Sitting upright does not expose the anal area for examination.
Prone position with arms raised
Prone positioning is not the alternative the book gives for men who cannot stand.
Standing and bent over the table
This is the preferred position for men, but this patient cannot stand.

alt.q: What is the best position for the rectal examination of a male patient who is able to stand?
alt.a: Standing, bent forward with hips flexed and upper body resting across the table
alt.ex: Men are best examined standing and bending forward with hips flexed and the upper body resting across an examination table.
w: Lying supine with knees bent and feet flat on the table
This dorsal recumbent position is used for female patients after the genital examination.
Lying on the side, used for all men regardless of ability
Side-lying is used for men who cannot stand, not as the best position for all.
Sitting upright on the table with legs hanging over the side
Sitting does not expose the anus and perianal area.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A female patient has just completed her genitalia examination. Which position is appropriate for her rectal examination?
items.a: Remain in the dorsal recumbent position or assume a side-lying position
items.ex: Female patients stay in the dorsal recumbent position after the genital examination or assume a side-lying position.
w: Stand and bend over the table with hips flexed
Standing and bending over is the preferred position for men.
Sit upright in the examination chair with feet on the floor
Sitting does not allow inspection of the perianal area.
Lie prone with a pillow under the abdomen
Prone positioning is not the position described for women.

alt.q: Which type of gloves does the nurse use for the rectal examination?
alt.a: Nonlatex clean gloves
alt.ex: The rectal examination is performed with nonlatex clean gloves.
w: Latex sterile gloves
Sterile gloves are not required, and nonlatex gloves are specified.
Nonlatex sterile gloves
Clean, not sterile, gloves are used for this examination.
No gloves for inspection only
Gloves are worn for the rectal examination.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: During inspection of the anus, the nurse asks the patient to bear down as though having a bowel movement so that internal hemorrhoids or fissures can appear.
items.a: True
items.ex: Bearing down causes internal hemorrhoids or fissures to appear during inspection.
items.ww: Bearing down is a recommended step because it reveals internal hemorrhoids and fissures.

alt.q: The nurse should tell the patient not to bear down during anal inspection because straining hides internal hemorrhoids.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Bearing down makes internal hemorrhoids or fissures appear, so the nurse asks the patient to do it.
alt.ww: Straining reveals internal hemorrhoids rather than hiding them, which is why the maneuver is used.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: External [[hemorrhoids|hemorrhoid]] are dilated veins that appear as reddened protrusions around the anus.
items.ex: External hemorrhoids are seen on inspection; internal hemorrhoids may appear when the patient bears down.

alt.q: Dilated veins that appear as reddened protrusions at the anus are called external [[hemorrhoids|hemorrhoid]].
alt.ex: External hemorrhoids are seen on inspection; internal hemorrhoids may appear when the patient bears down.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: While inspecting a patient’s anus, the nurse notes a reddened protrusion. How should the nurse describe the location of this finding in the documentation?
items.a: By using clock referents, such as 3 o’clock
items.ex: Clock referents, such as 3 o’clock or 8 o’clock, are used to describe the location of anal findings.
w: By using body quadrants, such as left upper
Quadrants describe abdominal findings, not anal findings.
By using dermatome zones, such as S4
Dermatomes map sensory innervation, not anal lesion location.
By using distance from the umbilicus
The umbilicus is not a reference point for anal findings.

alt.q: Why does the nurse use clock referents when documenting an anal finding?
alt.a: To describe the exact location of the finding
alt.ex: Clock referents such as 3 o’clock or 8 o’clock describe where an anal finding is located.
w: To record how long the patient bore down
Clock referents describe location, not timing.
To grade how severe the finding is
Clock referents do not grade severity.
To show what time the examination occurred
Clock referents refer to position around the anus, not time of day.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which inspection finding of the perianal and anal area is normal?
items.a: Moist, hairless anal tissue with no protrusion of tissue
items.ex: Anal tissues are normally moist and hairless, the external sphincter holds the anus closed, and no tissue protrudes.
w: Dry, hair-covered anal tissue with a slight protrusion
Anal tissue is normally moist and hairless, and protrusion is abnormal.
Moist, reddened tissue with small fissures
Fissures and inflammation are abnormal findings.
Perianal skin paler and smoother than the buttocks
Perianal skin is more pigmented and coarser than buttock skin.

alt.q: How does normal perianal skin compare with the skin over the buttocks?
alt.a: It is smooth, more pigmented, and coarser
alt.ex: Perianal skin is normally smooth, more pigmented, and coarser than the skin over the buttocks.
w: It is rough, less pigmented, and thinner
Perianal skin is smooth and more, not less, pigmented.
It is moist, paler, and finer
Perianal skin is darker and coarser than buttock skin.
It is identical in color and texture
Perianal skin differs, being more pigmented and coarser.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A new graduate nurse asks who performs digital palpation of the prostate gland. Which response by the nurse educator is accurate?
items.a: “Advanced practice registered nurses perform this examination.”
items.ex: Examination of the prostate gland by digital palpation is performed by advanced practice registered nurses.
w: “Nursing assistants perform this examination.”
Prostate examination is not delegated to assistive personnel.
“Any registered nurse performs this on admission.”
The text states that APRNs perform prostate palpation.
“Patients perform this examination monthly at home.”
Monthly self-examination applies to genital and testicular self-examination.

alt.q: A patient is anxious about his rectal examination. Which nursing approach is best?
alt.a: Explain all steps and use a calm, slow-paced, gentle approach
alt.ex: The rectal examination is uncomfortable, so explaining each step and using a calm, slow, gentle approach helps the patient relax.
w: Proceed quickly without explanation to shorten the discomfort
Explaining all steps helps the patient relax; rushing increases anxiety.
Ask the patient to bear down throughout the whole examination
Bearing down is used briefly during inspection, not to relieve anxiety.
Postpone the examination until the patient is no longer anxious
Anxiety is managed with explanation and a gentle approach, not routine postponement.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Why does the nurse ask whether a patient has undergone colorectal cancer screening, such as a fecal occult blood test or colonoscopy?
items.a: It reflects the patient’s understanding of and adherence with preventive health care
items.ex: Having completed colorectal screening reflects understanding and adherence with preventive health care measures.
w: It confirms that the patient has no risk factors for colorectal cancer
Past screening does not remove risk factors such as family history or diet.
It shows that the patient no longer needs a rectal examination
Prior screening does not replace the rectal examination.
It identifies whether the patient has used laxatives for a long time
Laxative use is assessed separately in the medication history.

alt.q: A patient says, “I had a colonoscopy 4 years ago and a stool test last year.” What does this history mainly tell the nurse?
alt.a: The patient adheres to preventive health care measures
alt.ex: Undergoing colorectal screening reflects understanding and adherence with preventive health care.
w: The patient has a strong family history of polyps
Screening history does not reveal family history; that is asked separately.
The patient has warning signs of colorectal cancer
Warning signs include bleeding, melena, pain, or bowel changes, not screening history.
The patient is at increased risk for prostate cancer
Colorectal screening history does not indicate prostate cancer risk.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Flexible sigmoidoscopy is a visual inspection of the rectum and lower colon with a hollow, lighted tube, recommended every 5 years.
items.a: True
items.ex: Flexible sigmoidoscopy uses a hollow, lighted tube to view the rectum and lower colon and is done every 5 years.
items.ww: The description and 5-year interval match the ACS screening options presented in the chapter.

alt.q: Flexible sigmoidoscopy is a stool test for hidden blood that is repeated every year.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The yearly stool test for hidden blood is the FOBT or FIT; flexible sigmoidoscopy is a visual inspection every 5 years.
alt.ww: This confuses sigmoidoscopy with fecal occult blood testing, which is the annual stool test.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: On what does the assessment of musculoskeletal function focus?
items.a: Range of joint motion, muscle strength and tone, and joint and muscle condition
items.ex: The musculoskeletal assessment focuses on ROM, muscle strength and tone, and joint and muscle condition.
w: Reflex grading, sensory dermatomes, and cranial nerve function
These are parts of the neurological assessment.
Skin turgor, capillary refill, and peripheral pulse strength
These belong to the skin and vascular assessments.
Bowel sounds, abdominal girth, and liver span
These belong to the abdominal assessment.

alt.q: Why might a nurse perform a neurological assessment at the same time as the musculoskeletal assessment?
alt.a: Because muscular disorders are often the result of neurological disease
alt.ex: Muscular disorders often result from neurological disease, so the two assessments can be performed together.
w: Because bone disorders are often the result of kidney disease
The text links muscle disorders with neurological, not kidney, disease.
Because joint disorders are often the result of skin disease
Skin disease is not the reason given for combining assessments.
Because muscle disorders are often the result of heart disease
The stated reason is the link to neurological disease.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is reviewing a patient’s history for osteoporosis risk factors. Which findings place the patient at risk? Select all that apply.
o: Long-term corticosteroid therapy
Long-term corticosteroid use is a risk factor for osteoporosis.
Low body weight and small, thin frame
Being small and thin is an osteoporosis risk factor.
Removal of ovaries before natural menopause
Early ovary removal increases osteoporosis risk.
Heavy alcohol consumption
Heavy alcohol use is an osteoporosis risk factor.
Regular weight-bearing exercise
Weight-bearing exercise reduces bone loss; inactivity is the risk factor.
Calcium intake of 1200 mg daily
Not getting enough calcium, less than 500 mg, is the risk factor.
items.ex: Osteoporosis risk factors include age, female sex, small frame, early ovary removal, smoking, heavy alcohol, inactivity, low calcium, and certain medications.

alt.q: Which medications in a patient’s history increase the risk for osteoporosis? Select all that apply.
o: Proton pump inhibitors
Long-term proton pump inhibitor use is an osteoporosis risk factor.
Phenytoin
Antiseizure medicines such as phenytoin increase osteoporosis risk.
Cancer chemotherapeutic drugs
Chemotherapeutic drugs are listed as osteoporosis risk factors.
Vitamin D supplements
Vitamin D aids calcium absorption and helps prevent bone loss.
Calcium supplements
Calcium supplements are recommended to reduce osteoporosis risk.
alt.ex: Long-term corticosteroids, proton pump inhibitors, antiseizure drugs like phenytoin or phenobarbital, and chemotherapy increase osteoporosis risk.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Why does the nurse observe a patient’s gait as the patient enters the examination room?
items.a: Gait is more natural when the patient is unaware of being observed
items.ex: When the patient is unaware of the nature of the observation, gait is more natural.
w: Gait cannot be assessed later in the examination
The patient is also asked later to walk in a straight line away and back.
Gait is assessed only to estimate the patient’s height
Gait observation looks at walking pattern, not height.
Gait is more accurate when the patient is tired
Fatigue is not the reason; natural, unobserved movement is.

alt.q: After observing the patient’s gait on entry, which additional gait assessment should the nurse perform?
alt.a: Have the patient walk in a straight line away from and back to the starting point
alt.ex: The patient walks in a straight line away from and returning to the point of origin while the nurse observes.
w: Have the patient walk in a circle around the room with eyes closed
Walking in a circle with eyes closed is not the described gait test.
Have the patient run a short distance down the hallway
Running is not part of the gait assessment.
Have the patient walk backward toward the examination table
Walking backward is not the described gait test.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which gait finding is expected in a healthy adult?
items.a: Arms swinging freely, feet placed heel to toe, and the head leading the body
items.ex: Normal gait has arms swinging freely at the sides, feet placed one at a time heel to toe, and the head leading.

Normal placement is heel to toe, with the head leading.

As evidence of a recent hip fracture
Smaller steps with a wider base are a common age-related change.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: What is frequently the first clinical sign of osteoporosis?
items.a: Loss of height
items.ex: Loss of height from vertebral fracture and collapse in the trunk is frequently the first clinical sign of osteoporosis.
w: Joint swelling
Swollen, stiff joints in older adults result from cartilage erosion and synovial fibrosis.
Muscle weakness
Muscle weakness reflects loss of muscle mass, not the first sign of osteoporosis.
Lateral spinal curve
A lateral curve is scoliosis, not the first sign of osteoporosis.

alt.q: A 68-year-old woman says her current height is about 4 cm shorter than her maximum adult height. What does this finding most likely suggest?
alt.a: Vertebral fracture and collapse from osteoporosis
alt.ex: Height loss in the trunk from vertebral fracture and collapse is frequently the first sign of osteoporosis.
w: Lordosis from weak abdominal muscles
Lordosis is increased lumbar curvature and is not described as causing height loss.
Osteoarthritis of the knees and hips
Joint changes are not described as the cause of height loss.
Normal shrinking that needs no follow-up
Height loss is a screening tool for osteoporosis and warrants referral for bone density testing.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A 66-year-old woman tells the nurse she has never been screened for bone loss. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: Refer her to her health care provider for a bone density examination
items.ex: Women 65 and older are recommended for routine osteoporosis screening and are referred for a bone density examination.
w: Reassure her that screening begins at age 75
Routine screening is recommended at 65, so she is already due.
Teach her that screening is only for women with fractures
Screening is recommended for all women 65 and older.
Tell her men are screened, but women her age are not
Women 65 and older are routinely screened; men are also recommended for screening.

alt.q: A 70-year-old man asks whether osteoporosis screening applies to him. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Men are also at risk as they age, so screening is recommended for you as well.”
alt.ex: Men are recommended for osteoporosis screening because they are also at risk as they age.
w: “Men are not at risk, so screening is recommended only for women.”
Men are at risk for osteoporosis as they age.
“Men are at risk only after a hip fracture, so you do not need screening now.”
Screening is recommended for men without waiting for a fracture.
“Men are at risk only if they take calcium, so you need to stop it first.”
Calcium helps prevent bone loss; it is not a risk factor.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is teaching an older adult how to prevent osteoporosis. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Do weight-bearing, muscle-strengthening, and balance exercises three or more times a week
This exercise program reduces bone demineralization.
Take no more than 500 mg of calcium at one time
Calcium supplements are taken in doses of no more than 500 mg at once.
Include vitamin D because it aids calcium absorption
Increased vitamin D aids calcium absorption.
Pace activities to compensate for loss in muscle strength
Older patients pace activities as muscle strength declines.
Take the full daily calcium dose at once at bedtime
No more than 500 mg of calcium should be taken at one time.
Limit exercise to once a week to protect the bones
Exercise is recommended three or more times a week.
items.ex: Osteoporosis prevention includes regular weight-bearing, strengthening, and balance exercise, adequate calcium and vitamin D, divided calcium doses, and paced activity.

alt.q: Which activities should the nurse recommend to an older adult with osteoporosis to minimize trauma and fractures? Select all that apply.
o: Walking
Walking is a moderate weight-bearing exercise recommended for osteoporosis.
Swimming
Swimming is listed as a recommended moderate exercise.
Range-of-motion exercises
ROM exercises are recommended along with proper body mechanics.
Heavy lifting to build bone mass rapidly
Lifting heavy objects is a cause of musculoskeletal problems, and only moderate exercise is advised.
Complete bed rest to avoid falls
Inactivity increases bone loss and fracture risk.
alt.ex: Proper body mechanics, ROM, and moderate weight-bearing exercise such as swimming and walking minimize trauma and fractures.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Calcium supplements are recommended for adults over age 25 at a dose of [[1000 to 1500|1000-1500|1,000 to 1,500]] mg/day.
items.ex: Calcium supplements help meet the recommended daily allowance, but no more than 500 mg is taken at one time.

alt.q: For adults over age 25, the recommended amount of supplemental calcium is [[1000 to 1500|1000-1500|1,000 to 1,500]] mg per day, taken in divided doses.
alt.ex: Calcium supplements help meet the recommended daily allowance, but no more than 500 mg is taken at one time.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: The nurse teaches a 62-year-old patient with osteopenia about calcium supplements. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will split my calcium into doses of no more than 500 mg each.”
items.ex: No more than 500 mg of calcium is taken at one time, so the daily amount is divided.
w: “I will take my full 1500 mg of calcium in one dose each morning.”
Taking more than 500 mg at once is not recommended.
“I will avoid vitamin D because it blocks calcium absorption.”
Vitamin D aids calcium absorption.
“I will stop walking so I do not fracture a bone.”
Moderate weight-bearing exercise such as walking is recommended.

alt.q: Which teach-back request would best evaluate a patient’s learning about osteoporosis prevention?
alt.a: “Describe for me what therapies you use for preventing osteoporosis.”
alt.ex: Asking the patient to describe the therapies used to prevent osteoporosis is a teach-back evaluation.
w: “Do you understand everything I told you about osteoporosis?”
A yes-or-no question does not let the patient demonstrate learning.
“Would you like a pamphlet to read about osteoporosis later?”
Offering a pamphlet does not evaluate learning.
“Have you heard of osteoporosis before today?”
This asks about prior awareness, not what the patient learned.

items.q: Measuring range of motion in all joints is not necessary when the patient demonstrates good joint movement and no problems have been identified.
items.a: True
items.ex: ROM is measured in all joints only when needed; good movement with no identified problems makes full measurement unnecessary.
items.ww: The book does not require measuring every joint when movement is good and no problems are found.

alt.q: During every physical examination the nurse must measure range of motion in all joints, even when no problems are identified.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Measuring ROM in all joints is not necessary if the patient shows good joint movement and no problems have been identified.
alt.ww: Full ROM measurement is not required for every patient; it focuses on joints showing limitation.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: While the nurse passively moves a patient’s shoulder through its range of motion, the patient grimaces and says, “That hurts.” Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Stop the movement and do not force the joint into a painful position
items.ex: A joint is never forced into a painful position during ROM assessment.
w: Continue moving the joint gently to its full normal range
Continuing into pain forces the joint and risks injury.
Ask the patient to relax so the joint can be pushed farther
Relaxation helps passive ROM, but the joint is not forced into pain.
Repeat the movement rapidly to judge muscle tone
Rapid movement into pain is unsafe and does not assess the painful joint correctly.

alt.q: Which technique is correct when assessing passive range of motion?
alt.a: Ask the patient to relax, then move the extremity through its range without forcing it
alt.ex: For passive ROM, the patient relaxes while the nurse moves the extremity through its range and never forces a painful joint.
w: Ask the patient to tense the muscle, then move the extremity rapidly
The patient relaxes for passive ROM, and movement is not rapid or forced.
Ask the patient to move the joint alone while the nurse watches
Moving the joint alone is active, not passive, ROM.
Ask the patient to resist while the nurse pushes against the limb
Resisting the nurse’s pressure tests muscle strength, not passive ROM.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient is scheduled for knee replacement surgery next week. Why does the nurse assess the range of motion of the patient’s knee before surgery?
items.a: To determine a baseline for assessing later change
items.ex: When a patient is scheduled for joint surgery, the nurse assesses normal range to establish a baseline for later comparison.
w: To confirm that the surgery is still needed
Deciding on surgery is not the purpose; the measurement provides a baseline.
To strengthen the knee before the operation
Assessment measures motion; it is not a strengthening intervention.
To grade the patellar reflex before anesthesia
Reflex grading is part of the neurological examination, not ROM.

alt.q: Which instrument is used mainly by physical and occupational therapists to measure the precise degree of joint motion?
alt.a: Goniometer
alt.ex: A goniometer has two flexible arms and a 180-degree protractor and measures the precise degree of joint motion.
w: Tuning fork
A tuning fork tests vibration sense and hearing.
Reflex hammer
A reflex hammer elicits deep tendon reflexes.
Tape measure
A tape measure compares muscle circumference, not joint angles.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A goniometer is mainly used for patients who have a suspected reduction in joint movement.
items.a: True
items.ex: A goniometer measures the precise degree of joint motion and is mainly used when joint movement is suspected to be reduced.
items.ww: The goniometer is not a routine screening tool; it is reserved mainly for suspected reduced movement.

alt.q: A goniometer is routinely used to measure the range of every joint during a basic physical examination.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A goniometer is mainly for patients with a suspected reduction in joint movement, not routine screening of every joint.
alt.ww: Routine measurement of all joints is not needed when movement is good, so the goniometer is used selectively.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse supports a patient’s relaxed arm and moves it passively. The arm feels flabby and hangs loosely in a position determined by gravity. How should the nurse document this finding?
items.a: Hypotonicity
items.ex: A muscle with little tone feels flabby, and the extremity hangs loosely in a position determined by gravity.
w: Hypertonicity
Hypertonicity causes considerable resistance to sudden passive movement.
Atrophy
An atrophied muscle is reduced in size and feels soft and boggy; it is defined by size, not tone.
Normal tone
Normal tone gives mild, even resistance through the entire range.

alt.q: When the nurse suddenly moves a patient’s elbow passively, there is considerable resistance that eventually relaxes with continued movement. What does this finding indicate?
alt.a: Hypertonicity
alt.ex: Increased tone, or hypertonicity, causes considerable resistance to sudden passive movement until the muscle eventually relaxes.
w: Hypotonicity
Hypotonicity feels flabby with little resistance.
Normal tone
Normal tone gives only mild, even resistance through the entire range.
Atrophy
Atrophy is reduced muscle size, felt as a soft, boggy muscle.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: The arm on the dominant side is normally stronger than the arm on the nondominant side.
items.a: True
items.ex: Muscle strength normally is greater on the dominant side.
items.ww: Equal strength is not the expected finding; the dominant arm is normally stronger.

alt.q: In older adults, bilateral loss of muscle mass means the dominant arm is no longer stronger than the nondominant arm.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Older adults have bilateral weakness from muscle loss, but strength remains greater in the dominant arm or leg.
alt.ww: Age-related muscle loss is bilateral, so the dominant side still stays stronger.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse finds that a patient’s right calf is weaker than the left. Which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Measure the circumference of both calves with a tape measure
items.ex: When weakness is found, the nurse compares the muscle with its counterpart by measuring circumference with a tape measure.
w: Measure the angle of the ankle joint with a goniometer
A goniometer measures joint motion, not muscle size.
Tap the Achilles tendon with a reflex hammer
Reflex testing assesses the reflex arc, not muscle size.
Apply a vibrating tuning fork to the great toe
A tuning fork tests vibration sense, not muscle size.

alt.q: How does a muscle that has atrophied feel when the nurse palpates it?
alt.a: Soft and boggy
alt.ex: An atrophied muscle is reduced in size and feels soft and boggy on palpation.
w: Firm and even
Normal muscles feel firm on palpation.
Warm and tender
Warmth and tenderness suggest inflammation, not atrophy.
Hard and nodular
A hard, nodular feel is not how atrophy is described.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which findings during palpation and inspection of the musculoskeletal system are normal? Select all that apply.
o: Muscles feel firm
Muscles should be firm on palpation.
The patient feels no discomfort when bones and joints are palpated
There should be no discomfort with pressure on bones and joints.
Extremities are symmetric in length and circumference
Bilateral symmetry in length, circumference, and alignment is normal.
Joints are free from stiffness and swelling
Joints are typically free from stiffness, instability, swelling, or inflammation.
A joint feels warm and appears swollen
Warmth and swelling suggest inflammation, which is abnormal.
A muscle feels soft and boggy
A soft, boggy muscle suggests atrophy.
items.ex: Normal musculoskeletal findings include firm muscles, no tenderness, bilateral symmetry, and joints without stiffness or swelling.

alt.q: Which musculoskeletal findings are expected changes in older adults? Select all that apply.
o: A stooped, forward-bent posture with hips and knees somewhat flexed
Older adults tend to assume a stooped, forward-bent posture.
Swollen, stiff joints with reduced range of motion
Cartilage erosion and synovial fibrosis cause these joint changes.
Bilateral weakness from loss of muscle mass
Loss of muscle mass causes bilateral weakness in older adults.
A dominant arm that is weaker than the nondominant arm
Strength remains greater in the dominant arm in older adults.
A lateral spinal curvature as a universal aging change
Scoliosis is a postural abnormality, not a universal aging change.
alt.ex: Older adults often show a stooped posture, stiff swollen joints with reduced ROM, and bilateral weakness while the dominant side stays stronger.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which scale does the nurse use to compare symmetrical muscle pairs for strength?
items.a: A grading scale of 0 to 5
items.ex: Muscle strength is graded on a scale of 0 to 5 and compared between symmetrical muscle pairs.
w: A grading scale of 0 to 4+
A 0 to 4+ scale is used to grade reflexes.
A grading scale of 3 to 15
A 3 to 15 range is the total Glasgow Coma Scale score.
A grading scale of 0 to 10
A 0 to 10 range is not the scale used for muscle strength.

alt.q: Which technique is correct when the nurse assesses the strength of a muscle group?
alt.a: Have the patient flex the muscle, then resist an opposing force without moving the joint
alt.ex: The patient flexes the muscle and resists the nurse’s gradually increasing opposing force, without allowing the joint to move.
w: Have the patient relax the muscle while the nurse moves the joint quickly
Moving a relaxed limb passively assesses tone, not strength.
Have the patient move the joint freely while the nurse applies no pressure
Free movement without resistance tests ROM, not strength.
Have the patient flex the muscle while the nurse taps its tendon briskly
Tapping a tendon elicits a reflex rather than testing strength.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which patient most clearly needs a complete neurological review?
items.a: A patient with a headache and a recent loss of function in one arm
items.ex: Patients with a headache or a recent loss of function in an extremity need a complete neurological review.
w: A patient with a minor skin abrasion on the knee
A minor abrasion does not suggest a neurological problem.
A patient requesting a routine seasonal vaccine
A routine vaccine visit does not call for a full neurological review.
A patient with a sore throat and mild cough
These symptoms do not indicate a need for complete neurological review.

alt.q: Which factor most influences a patient’s ability to follow directions during the neurological examination?
alt.a: Level of consciousness
alt.ex: A patient’s level of consciousness influences the ability to follow directions during the examination.
w: Dietary preferences
Diet does not determine the ability to follow directions.
Handedness
Handedness affects strength comparisons, not the ability to follow directions.
Height
Height does not affect the ability to follow directions.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient’s eyes open to speech, the patient is confused when answering questions, and the patient localizes pain. What is this patient’s Glasgow Coma Scale score?
items.ex: Eyes opening to speech scores 3, confused verbal response scores 4, and localizing pain scores 5, for a total of 12.
w: This total undercounts the scores; 3 plus 4 plus 5 equals 12.
A 14 would require higher scores, such as spontaneous eye opening.
This total undercounts the motor score of 5 for localizing pain.

alt.q: A patient’s eyes open only to pain, the patient uses inappropriate words, and the patient shows flexion withdrawal to pain. What is this patient’s Glasgow Coma Scale score?
alt.ex: Eyes to pain score 2, inappropriate words score 3, and flexion withdrawal scores 4, for a total of 9.
w: This total undercounts; 2 plus 3 plus 4 equals 9.
This total overcounts; flexion withdrawal scores 4, not 6.
A 12 would require higher eye and verbal scores.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A patient is not conscious enough to follow commands. How should the nurse attempt to elicit a pain response?
items.a: Apply firm pressure with the thumb over the root of a fingernail
items.ex: If the patient cannot follow commands, the nurse applies firm thumb pressure over the root of the fingernail.
w: Apply a cold test tube to the inner aspect of the arm
Cold tubes test temperature sensation, not response to pain.
Stroke the lateral aspect of the sole with a hammer handle
This elicits the plantar reflex, not the pain response.
Touch the cornea lightly with a wisp of cotton
This assesses the corneal reflex of the trigeminal nerve.

alt.q: A patient with a head injury shows no muscle tone in the extremities when a painful stimulus is applied. How should the nurse interpret this flaccid response?
alt.a: As severe injury to brain tissue
alt.ex: A flaccid response indicates absence of muscle tone in the extremities and severe injury to brain tissue.
w: As a normal response to painful stimuli
The normal response to pain is withdrawal of the body part.
As mild sedation that will soon wear off
A flaccid response reflects severe brain injury, not mild sedation.
As expected relaxation before reflex testing
Flaccidity with pain is not a normal relaxed state; it signals severe injury.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: An 81-year-old patient who was alert and oriented on admission becomes suddenly confused and restless on the second evening after surgery. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Review the history for drug toxicity, infection, metabolic disturbance, and other causes
items.ex: Sudden acute confusion in an older adult is delirium, which is potentially reversible once the underlying cause is found and treated.
w: Document the change as sundown syndrome expected with aging
Labeling delirium as sundown syndrome or normal aging leads to misdiagnosis.
Tell the family the patient has developed Alzheimer disease
Dementia is progressive; sudden confusion suggests delirium with a treatable cause.
Apply restraints to prevent the patient from getting out of bed
Restraint use can contribute to delirium and does not identify its cause.

alt.q: Which statement best distinguishes delirium from dementia?
alt.a: Delirium develops over hours to days and often reverses when its cause is treated
alt.ex: Delirium is an acute disturbance that develops quickly, fluctuates, and often reverses; dementia is a more progressive organic disorder.
w: Delirium develops over many years and steadily worsens without remission

items.q: Which features match the clinical criteria for delirium? Select all that apply.
o: Develops over a short period, usually hours to days
Delirium develops quickly over hours to days.
Tends to fluctuate during the day
Delirium tends to fluctuate during the day.
Impaired ability to focus, sustain, or shift attention
Questions must be repeated because attention is impaired.
Perceptual disturbances such as visual hallucinations
Misinterpretations, delusions, and hallucinations can occur.
Gradual onset over several years
Slow, progressive onset describes dementia, not delirium.
Caused by a preexisting or evolving dementia
By definition delirium is not caused by a preexisting or evolving dementia.
items.ex: Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of consciousness with impaired attention, cognitive change, and possible perceptual disturbances.

alt.q: A nurse suspects delirium in a hospitalized patient. Which findings support this suspicion? Select all that apply.
o: Disorientation to time, place, or person
Disorientation usually occurs in delirium.
Recent memory impairment
Recent memory commonly is affected.
Easy distraction by irrelevant stimuli
Irrelevant stimuli easily distract a person with delirium.
Rambling speech
Language disturbance can include rambling speech.
Steady, unchanged mental status for many months
Delirium is acute and fluctuating, not stable over months.
Clear awareness of the environment
Delirium reduces clarity of awareness of the environment.
alt.ex: Disorientation, recent memory loss, distractibility, and rambling speech support delirium.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Delirium is a potentially reversible condition that often resolves when the underlying cause is correctly assessed and treated.
items.a: True
items.ex: Delirium often reverses once its cause, such as a metabolic, CNS, or cardiopulmonary disorder, is identified and treated.
items.ww: Delirium is not permanent like a progressive dementia; it is potentially reversible.

alt.q: Confusion that worsens at night in an older adult is a normal part of aging and does not need further assessment.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nighttime worsening is often delirium mislabeled as sundown syndrome; it needs assessment for an underlying cause.
alt.ww: Mistaking delirium for normal aging leads to misdiagnosis, so the nurse assesses mental status for a cause.

This patient’s comprehension is intact, so the problem is expressive only.

w: Expressive aphasia
In expressive aphasia comprehension is intact but speaking or writing is impaired.
Motor aphasia
Motor aphasia is another name for expressive aphasia.
Abstract aphasia
This is not a type of aphasia described in the text.

One to two digits
One to two digits is below the normal backward range.
Nine to eleven digits
Nine to eleven digits exceeds the normal backward range.

This relevant interpretation shows intact abstract thinking.

This interpretation shows an ability to grasp the abstract meaning.

This answer reflects normal abstract thinking.

alt.q: Which finding during assessment of abstract thinking suggests altered mental status?
alt.a: The patient interprets a common saying literally

w: The patient explains the meaning behind a common saying
Explaining the meaning shows intact abstract thinking.
The patient names three unrelated objects later in the exam
Recalling three objects tests recent memory, not abstract thinking.
The patient gives a logical reason for seeking health care
A logical reason reflects intact judgment.

items.q: A nurse is testing a patient’s sensory function. Which technique is correct?
items.a: Have the patient close the eyes and apply stimuli in a random order
items.ex: Sensory testing is done with eyes closed and stimuli applied randomly so the patient cannot detect a predictable pattern.
w: Have the patient watch each stimulus and apply them in a set order
Watching and a predictable order let the patient anticipate stimuli.
Have the patient close the eyes and apply stimuli to one side only
Symmetrical areas on both sides are compared.
Have the patient keep the eyes open and apply stimuli quickly
The eyes are closed so the patient cannot see when or where touch occurs.

alt.q: A patient has reduced sensation in both feet. Which nursing action is most important?
alt.a: Assess the skin of both feet for signs of breakdown
alt.ex: Impaired sensation raises the risk of skin breakdown, so the nurse assesses the affected skin and teaches avoidance of trauma.
w: Apply hot packs to both feet to restore sensation
Heat on numb skin risks thermal trauma, which the patient is taught to avoid.
Retest sensation daily without examining the skin
A skin assessment of the affected area is needed because breakdown risk is higher.
Encourage snug footwear to sharpen the sense of touch
Pressure is a source of trauma that patients with impaired sensation should avoid.

items.q: The temperature sensation test can be omitted if the patient’s pain sensation is normal.
items.a: True
items.ex: Table guidance states to omit the temperature test when pain sensation is normal.
items.ww: Temperature testing is not mandatory in every patient; normal pain sensation allows it to be omitted.

alt.q: The temperature sensation test must always be performed, even when pain sensation is normal.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The temperature test may be omitted when pain sensation is normal.
alt.ww: Normal pain sensation makes temperature testing unnecessary, so it is not always required.

items.q: A nurse performs a Romberg test on a 75-year-old patient. Which finding should the nurse report as abnormal?
items.a: The patient loses balance and falls to the side with eyes closed
items.ex: A loss of balance causing the patient to fall to the side is a positive Romberg test.
w: The patient sways slightly with eyes closed
Slight swaying is expected during the Romberg test.
The patient keeps the feet together without breaking stance
Normally the patient does not break the stance.
The patient stands upright with arms at the sides
Standing with arms at the sides is the correct test position.

alt.q: What is the nurse’s main safety action while a patient performs the Romberg test?
alt.a: Stand at the patient’s side to protect against a fall
alt.ex: The nurse protects the patient’s safety by standing at the side while observing for swaying.
w: Stand across the room to observe overall posture
Standing far away cannot protect the patient from falling.
Have the patient hold the bed rail during the test
Holding a rail would invalidate the test; the nurse stands at the side instead.
Ask the patient to keep the eyes open throughout
The test is done with eyes open and closed; safety comes from standing beside the patient.

w: Absent reflexes
No response, graded 0, is not the expected finding with intoxication.
Diminished reflexes
