Normal 2+ reflexes
Intoxication with cocaine causes hyperactive, not expected, reflexes.

alt.q: A nurse assesses the deep tendon reflexes of an 84-year-old patient with no neurological disease. Which finding is expected?
alt.a: Diminished reflexes
alt.ex: Normally the older adult presents with diminished reflexes.
w: Hyperactive reflexes
Hyperactive reflexes occur with alcohol, cocaine, or opioid intoxication.
Reflexes with clonus
Clonus is part of a 4+ brisk, hyperactive grade.
Reflexes stronger on one side
Responses on corresponding sides are compared and should be equal.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: The nurse strokes the lateral aspect of a patient’s sole from heel to ball of the foot, curving toward the big toe. Which response is normal?
items.a: Plantar flexion of all toes
items.ex: The normal plantar reflex is plantar flexion of all toes.
w: Extension of the lower leg
Extension of the lower leg is the normal patellar reflex.
Dorsiflexion of the ankle
Dorsiflexion is the position used before striking the Achilles tendon.
Flexion of the arm at the elbow
Elbow flexion is the normal biceps reflex.

alt.q: The nurse taps a patient’s patellar tendon just below the patella with the knee flexed. Which response is normal?
alt.a: Extension of the lower leg
alt.ex: Tapping the patellar tendon normally causes extension of the lower leg.
w: Plantar flexion of the foot
Plantar flexion of the foot is the normal Achilles reflex.
Extension at the elbow
Extension at the elbow is the normal triceps reflex.
Plantar flexion of all toes
Plantar flexion of the toes is the normal plantar reflex.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: The nurse is teaching an older adult and family caregiver after a neurological assessment. Which teaching points are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Plan enough time to complete tasks because reaction time is slow
Older adults are taught to allow extra time because reaction time slows.
Observe skin surfaces for trauma because pain perception is reduced
Reduced pain perception means injuries may go unnoticed.
Use glasses, hearing aids, or ambulation aids to stay safe
Sensory and motor impairments call for safety measures such as these aids.
Avoid safety bars in the bathroom to maintain independence
Safety bars are recommended for patients with sensory or motor impairments.
Hurry through daily tasks to keep reflexes sharp
Older adults should allow more time because reaction time is slow.
items.ex: Neurological teaching for older adults covers extra time for tasks, regular skin inspection, and safety aids for sensory or motor deficits.

alt.q: Which statements by a patient show understanding of neurological safety teaching? Select all that apply.
o: “I will check my skin regularly since I may not feel injuries.”
Inspecting skin is taught because pain perception is reduced.
“I will use the safety bars when I get in and out of the tub.”
Safety bars help prevent injury with motor or sensory limits.
“I will give myself extra time to get dressed in the morning.”
Slow reaction time means planning more time for tasks.
“I will stop wearing my glasses so my eyes get stronger.”
Wearing glasses is a safety measure for sensory impairment.
“I will hurry down the stairs before my legs get tired.”
Rushing increases fall risk; tasks should be paced.
alt.ex: Understanding is shown by regular skin checks, using safety aids, and allowing extra time for tasks.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: While completing a head-to-toe assessment, the nurse palpates a firm mass in the patient’s abdomen. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Consult the patient’s health care provider before revealing the finding
items.ex: Serious abnormalities such as a mass are discussed with the health care provider before they are revealed to the patient.
w: Tell the patient that the mass is most likely a tumor
Naming a likely cause is a medical diagnosis, which is the health care provider’s responsibility.
Reassure the patient that all findings were within normal limits
Giving false reassurance is dishonest and withholds a significant abnormal finding.
Document the mass and wait for the next scheduled visit
Significant findings must be communicated, not simply recorded and left for a later visit.

alt.q: During an examination the nurse detects a highly irregular heart rate. The patient asks, “Is my heart okay?” Before discussing this finding with the patient, what should the nurse do?
alt.a: Consult the patient’s health care provider about the finding
alt.ex: A highly irregular heart rate is a serious abnormality, so the health care provider is consulted before it is revealed.
w: Explain to the patient which heart disease is causing it
Making a definitive medical diagnosis is the health care provider’s responsibility, not the nurse’s.
Tell the patient the rhythm is normal to prevent anxiety
False reassurance is inaccurate and does not address the serious finding.
Ask assistive personnel to recheck and explain the rhythm
Interpreting and explaining abnormal findings cannot be delegated to assistive personnel.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: After consulting the health care provider about a breast mass found during the examination, the nurse speaks with the patient. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
items.a: “I felt a lump in your breast, and your health care provider will examine it further.”
items.ex: The nurse explains the type of abnormality found and the need for the health care provider to conduct an additional examination.
w: “The lump I felt is most likely a benign cyst, so try not to worry.”
Offering a likely diagnosis oversteps the nurse’s role; definitive diagnoses belong to the health care provider.
“I cannot tell you anything about your examination until you are discharged.”
The nurse should explain the type of abnormality and the need for further examination, not withhold everything.
“The lump appears to be cancer, and your provider will discuss treatment.”
Stating a cancer diagnosis is a definitive medical diagnosis, which only the health care provider makes.

alt.q: A nurse found a highly irregular heart rate and has already notified the health care provider. Which statement to the patient best follows the book’s guidance?
alt.a: “Your heartbeat is irregular, and your provider will examine you further.”
alt.ex: The nurse describes the type of abnormality and explains that the health care provider needs to conduct an additional examination.
w: “Your heartbeat is irregular because you are having a heart attack.”
Naming the cause is a definitive medical diagnosis, which is the health care provider’s responsibility.
“Everything sounded fine, but your provider wants to stop by anyway.”
This falsely reassures the patient and hides the abnormality that was found.
“I am not allowed to discuss anything about your heart with you.”
The nurse explains the type of abnormality and the need for further examination rather than refusing to discuss it.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse finishes a physical examination and is about to help the patient dress when the nurse realizes the breath sounds in one lung base were not clearly heard. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Auscultate the lung base again before helping the patient dress
items.ex: Reviewing all findings before the patient dresses lets the nurse recheck information or gather additional data.
w: Help the patient dress and record the breath sounds as normal
Recording a finding that was not clearly assessed creates an inaccurate record.
Help the patient dress and recheck the lungs on the next shift
Rechecking before dressing avoids an incomplete assessment and having to redo the preparation later.
Document that the lung base could not be assessed at all
The nurse can still recheck the finding while the patient remains undressed.

alt.q: Why does the nurse review all assessment findings before helping the patient dress?
alt.a: In case any information needs rechecking or more data must be gathered
alt.ex: Reviewing findings while the patient is still undressed allows rechecking or additional data collection without repeating preparation.
w: So the patient can sign the assessment form before dressing
Patients do not sign physical examination findings; the review is for completeness and accuracy.
So the health care provider can make a diagnosis right away
The review is done by the nurse to ensure complete data, not to speed a diagnosis.
So the nurse can delegate the documentation to assistive personnel
Documenting assessment findings is not delegated to assistive personnel.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse is documenting findings on a tablet while performing a physical examination. Which behavior shows that the nurse is documenting correctly?
items.a: Looking up from the tablet to watch the patient’s face during palpation
items.ex: Documenting during an examination must not distract the nurse from observing the patient’s response to each technique.
w: Typing notes while palpating without looking at the patient
Focusing on the screen keeps the nurse from observing the patient’s response to the technique.
Recording only the findings that appear to be abnormal
A complete assessment is documented, not just abnormal findings.
Asking the patient to wait silently until all notes are typed
The nurse attends to the patient and does not let documentation interrupt the examination.

alt.q: A student nurse charts each finding during the examination. Which observation by the instructor indicates a need for further teaching?
alt.a: The student keeps eyes on the screen while percussing the abdomen
alt.ex: If documenting during an examination, the nurse must still attend to the patient to observe responses to each technique.
w: The student pauses charting to watch the patient’s expression
Watching the patient’s response during techniques is correct practice.
The student uses the agency’s electronic assessment form
Special electronic and printed forms are available for documenting assessment data.
The student reviews the charted entries for accuracy afterward
Reviewing documentation for accuracy and thoroughness is correct practice.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: After a physical examination, which task may the nurse delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Cleaning up the examination area
items.ex: The nurse may delegate cleanup of the examination area to assistive personnel if needed.
w: Sharing a summary of findings with the patient
Explaining assessment findings requires nursing knowledge and is not delegated.
Reporting significant findings to the provider
Communicating significant findings is the nurse’s responsibility, not that of assistive personnel.
Reviewing the assessment record for accuracy
The nurse reviews documentation for accuracy and thoroughness; this is not delegated.

alt.q: A busy nurse has just completed a bedside examination. Which activity is appropriate to assign to assistive personnel?
alt.a: Removing soiled items from the bedside table
alt.ex: Cleanup of the examination area can be delegated to assistive personnel, using infection control practices for soiled items.
w: Rechecking an unclear finding before the patient dresses
Rechecking assessment data is part of the nurse’s assessment and is not delegated.
Explaining an abnormal finding to the patient
Explaining abnormalities is a nursing responsibility after consulting the health care provider.
Integrating findings into the plan of care
Integrating assessment findings into the plan of care is a nursing responsibility.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse completes a physical examination at a hospitalized patient’s bedside and helps the patient back to bed. Before leaving the room, which action is most important for the patient’s safety?
items.a: Place the nurse call system within reach and raise side rails as appropriate
items.ex: Keeping the call system within reach and using side rails as appropriate protects the patient after the examination.
w: Dim the lights and close the door so the patient can rest quietly
Rest supports comfort, but access to the call system is the safety priority.
Leave the examination equipment at the bedside for the next assessment
Soiled items are removed from the bedside using infection control practices.
Ask the patient to stay awake until the findings are documented
This does not promote safety and is not part of the book’s guidance.

alt.q: Assistive personnel report that cleanup after a bedside examination is finished. Which observation requires the nurse to intervene?
alt.a: The nurse call system is resting on a chair across the room
alt.ex: The nurse call system must be within the patient’s reach after the examination so the patient can summon help.
w: The bed linen is dry and clean
Dry, clean linen is an expected part of bedside cleanup.
Soiled items are gone from the bedside table
Clearing soiled items from the bedside table is expected after an examination.
The patient is wearing a clean gown
Patients appreciate a clean gown after an examination, so this is appropriate.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A male nurse is preparing to perform a physical examination on a female patient whose cultural norms discourage examination by a person of the opposite gender. Which action is best?
items.a: Have a female staff member or culturally approved family member present
items.ex: Another person of the patient’s gender or a culturally approved family member should be in the room, which also provides a witness.
w: Proceed alone but explain each step in detail first
Explanation helps, but it does not meet the patient’s cultural need for another person present.
Skip the examination and document that it was refused
The examination can proceed respectfully once an appropriate person is present.
Ask the patient to undress fully so the exam is faster
Rushing and full exposure ignore the patient’s privacy and cultural needs.

alt.q: Why does the book recommend having a person of the patient’s gender in the room when a nurse of the opposite gender performs an examination?
alt.a: It shows cultural awareness and provides a witness to the examination
alt.ex: This step respects the patient’s individual cultural needs and gives a witness to the conduct of examiner and patient.
w: It allows the second person to perform the documentation
The second person is present for cultural awareness and as a witness, not to document.
It is required so the second person can interpret the findings
Interpreting findings is not the role of the second person in the room.
It allows the nurse to leave the room during sensitive steps
The nurse performs the examination; the second person does not replace the nurse.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: When is it most appropriate for the nurse to share a summary of the assessment findings with the patient?
items.a: After the patient has dressed and is comfortable
items.ex: After giving the patient time to dress and helping as needed, the nurse shares a summary once the patient is comfortable.
w: While the patient is still positioned on the examination table
The patient is first given time to dress and get comfortable before findings are summarized.
Only after the health care provider has reviewed every finding
Only serious abnormalities require consulting the provider first; a summary of findings can be shared by the nurse.
Only at discharge, after the entire stay is documented
There is no need to delay; the summary is shared once the patient is comfortable after the examination.

alt.q: A nurse has just completed an examination that revealed no serious abnormalities. The patient is still undressed and draped on the table. What should the nurse do before sharing a summary of the findings?
alt.a: Give the patient time to dress and become comfortable
alt.ex: The book directs the nurse to let the patient dress and get comfortable before sharing a summary of findings.
w: Obtain the health care provider’s permission to share any findings
Provider consultation is needed first only when findings reveal serious abnormalities.
Finish documenting the complete assessment in the record
Documentation is required, but the summary is shared once the patient is dressed and comfortable.
Have assistive personnel explain the normal findings
Sharing assessment findings is the nurse’s role, not a task for assistive personnel.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse identifies a significant change during a physical examination. How should the nurse communicate this finding?
items.a: Verbally or in the patient’s written care plan to appropriate personnel
items.ex: Significant findings are communicated to appropriate personnel either verbally or in the patient’s written care plan.
w: Only to the patient, who can tell the provider at the next visit
The nurse is responsible for communicating significant findings to appropriate personnel.
Only in the nurse’s personal notes until the finding is confirmed
Personal notes are not part of the record and do not reach the care team.
Only at the next scheduled interprofessional team meeting
Waiting for a meeting can delay care for a significant finding.

alt.q: Which action by the nurse best ensures that significant physical assessment findings reach the health care team?
alt.a: Reporting them verbally or recording them in the written care plan
alt.ex: The book states significant findings are communicated to appropriate personnel verbally or in the patient’s written care plan.
w: Telling the patient to mention them to each new caregiver
Communicating findings to the team is a nursing responsibility, not the patient’s.
Recording them on a sticky note placed on the patient’s chart
Informal notes can be lost and are not part of the official record.
Waiting until the findings are confirmed at the next examination
Significant findings should be communicated promptly, not delayed for another examination.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Midway through a physical examination, an older adult patient becomes tearful and says, “I’m so tired.” Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Pause, ask how the patient is tolerating it, and postpone if needed
items.ex: The nurse paces the examination for weak or older patients and postpones it when needed; findings are more accurate when the patient can relax.
w: Continue quickly so the examination is finished on schedule
The nurse should not force a patient to cooperate based on the nurse’s schedule.
Skip the remaining body systems and document them as normal
Recording unassessed systems as normal creates inaccurate documentation.
Ask the patient to stay quiet so the examination can be finished
The nurse encourages comments on discomfort rather than discouraging communication.

alt.q: A frail patient appears fatigued and anxious partway through a physical examination. Which statement by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Let’s rest a moment. Do you feel able to continue, or should we stop for now?”
alt.ex: Pausing at intervals to ask how the patient is tolerating the examination respects the patient and supports accurate findings.
w: “We only have a few systems left, so let’s keep going and finish.”
Pushing on ignores the patient’s fatigue; the examination should be paced or postponed.
“I need to finish this before my next patient arrives, so please hold still.”
The nurse should not force cooperation based on the nurse’s own schedule.
“There is nothing to be anxious about, so please try to relax.”
Dismissing the patient’s feelings does not assess tolerance or adjust the pace.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse completes a physical examination at a patient’s bedside. Which actions are appropriate afterward? Select all that apply.
o: Clear soiled items away from the bedside table
Soiled items are cleared from the bedside table after a bedside examination.
Make sure the bed linen is dry and clean
The nurse checks that bed linen is dry and clean after the examination.
Offer a clean gown and a chance to wash face and hands
Patients appreciate a clean gown and the opportunity to wash the face and hands.
Perform hand hygiene after finishing
Hand hygiene is performed afterward to prevent the spread of microorganisms.
Leave used instruments on the bedside table for later
Soiled instruments are removed promptly using infection control practices.
Lower all side rails so the patient can get up freely
Side rails are raised as appropriate for the patient’s safety, not lowered by default.
items.ex: Bedside cleanup includes removing soiled items, ensuring clean dry linen, offering a clean gown and washing, and performing hand hygiene.

alt.q: The nurse delegates cleanup after a bedside examination to assistive personnel. Which instructions should the nurse give? Select all that apply.
o: Use infection control practices when removing soiled materials
Materials soiled with potentially infectious wastes are removed using infection control practices.
Check that the bed linen is clean and dry
Ensuring dry, clean linen is part of bedside cleanup.
Place the nurse call system within the patient’s reach
The call system is placed within reach so the patient can summon help.
Tell the patient what the nurse found during the examination
Sharing assessment findings is the nurse’s responsibility and is not delegated.
Recheck any findings the nurse was unsure about
Rechecking assessment findings is a nursing assessment task and is not delegated.
alt.ex: Assistive personnel can clean up using infection control practices, check linen, and place the call system within reach; assessment tasks stay with the nurse.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: Which practices reflect correct documentation of a physical examination? Select all that apply.
o: Documenting findings during or after the examination
Findings may be documented either during the examination or after it is completed.
Using special electronic or printed assessment forms
Special forms are available to document data electronically and on paper.
Reviewing the documentation for accuracy and thoroughness
The nurse reviews documents for accuracy and thoroughness.
Documenting a complete assessment, not just problem areas
The book stresses documenting a complete assessment.
Recording only the findings that are abnormal
A complete assessment is documented, including normal findings.
Leaving documentation for the health care provider to finish
The nurse documents the nursing assessment the nurse performed.
items.ex: Documentation may occur during or after the examination on special forms, must be complete, and is reviewed for accuracy and thoroughness.

alt.q: A nursing student asks about documenting a physical examination. Which statements by the student show correct understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “If I chart during the exam, I still need to watch the patient’s responses.”
Documenting during an examination must not distract the nurse from observing the patient.
“I should reread my entries to make sure they are accurate and thorough.”
Reviewing documents for accuracy and thoroughness is required.
“My findings should be integrated into the patient’s plan of care.”
Physical assessment findings are integrated into the plan of care.
“I only need to chart findings that the provider asks about.”
The nurse documents a complete assessment, not selected findings.
“Charting during the exam is never allowed.”
The book allows documenting during the examination as long as it does not distract the nurse.
alt.ex: Correct understanding includes attending to the patient while charting, reviewing entries, and integrating findings into the plan of care.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A 38-year-old woman arrives by wheelchair sitting in a fetal position, pressing her arms into her abdomen. Her companion says she has stomach pain and cannot get to the table. Which nursing actions promote her safety and person-centered care during the examination? Select all that apply.
o: Help her onto the examination table to prevent injury
Helping patients on and off examination tables helps avoid injury.
Ask her to point out tender areas and assess those areas last
Assessing painful areas last minimizes discomfort and anxiety.
Watch her facial expressions and body movements for distress
Observing emotional and nonverbal responses helps the nurse detect fear, concern, or discomfort.
Pace the examination and pause to ask how she is tolerating it
Pacing the examination respects the patient and supports accurate findings.
Ask her to place her arms under her head during palpation
Placing the arms under the head tightens the abdominal muscles and hinders palpation.
Palpate the most painful area first to locate the problem quickly
Tender areas are assessed last to minimize discomfort and anxiety.
items.ex: For this patient the nurse assists transfers safely, assesses tender areas last, observes nonverbal cues, and paces the examination.

alt.q: A patient with severe abdominal pain is about to have an abdominal examination. Which actions by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Ask the patient to void before the examination begins
The book directs the nurse to have the patient void first to support relaxation, since tense abdominal muscles hinder palpation.
Ask the patient to identify tender areas before starting
Knowing the tender areas lets the nurse assess them last.
Warm the hands and stethoscope before touching the abdomen
Warm hands and stethoscope promote relaxation of the abdominal muscles.
Begin with deep palpation over the painful area
Palpation is done last and tender areas are examined last.
Continue the exam even if the patient asks to rest
The nurse paces the exam and postpones it when needed rather than forcing cooperation.
alt.ex: Voiding first, identifying tender areas, and warming hands and equipment promote comfort and accurate abdominal findings.

items.a: False

items.ww: Telling the patient a likely diagnosis oversteps the nurse’s role and occurs before the provider is consulted.

alt.q: Making a definitive medical diagnosis based on physical examination findings is the health care provider’s responsibility.
alt.a: True

alt.ww: The nurse identifies and reports abnormal findings but does not make definitive medical diagnoses.

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

items.q: A nurse may document physical assessment findings either during the examination or after it is completed.

items.ww: The book allows documentation at either time; what matters is continuing to observe the patient’s responses.

alt.q: To avoid errors, physical examination findings must never be documented until the entire examination is completed.
alt.a: False

items.src: Ch 30 · Health assessment and physical examination

alt.a: False
alt.ex: Soiled items are cleared from the bedside table using infection control practices, even when the bedside is the examination site.

items.q: Which was the first American law to regulate medications?
items.a: The Pure Food and Drug Act
items.ex: The Pure Food and Drug Act was the first U.S. law regulating medications and required them to be free of impure products.
w: The Controlled Substances Act
This act controls opioids and other controlled substances; it was not the first medication law.
The state nurse practice act
Nurse practice acts define the scope of nursing practice, not medication purity.
The MedWatch reporting act
MedWatch is a voluntary FDA reporting program begun in 1993, not the first medication law.

alt.q: What did the first American law regulating medications, the Pure Food and Drug Act, require?
alt.a: That all medications be free of impure products
alt.ex: The Pure Food and Drug Act required medications to be free of impure products; later laws added safety, potency, and efficacy standards.
w: That all opioids be stored in locked cabinets
Locked opioid storage is an agency guideline for controlled substances, not the focus of this law.
That nurses report all serious adverse events
Reporting serious harm is encouraged through the voluntary MedWatch program.
That states write their own medication standards
State laws must conform to federal legislation; this law did not delegate standards to states.

items.q: Which agency currently enforces the medication laws ensuring that medications undergo vigorous testing before they are sold to the public?
items.a: U.S. Food and Drug Administration
items.ex: The FDA enforces medication laws so that all marketed medications are vigorously tested before public sale.
w: Institute for Safe Medication Practices
The ISMP publishes safety guidance such as confused-name lists; it does not enforce medication laws.
State board of nursing
Boards of nursing oversee nursing practice under the nurse practice act, not medication testing.
United States Adopted Names Council
The USAN Council approves generic names; it does not enforce testing laws.

alt.q: Which responsibility belongs to the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA)?
alt.a: Enforcing laws that require medications to be tested before sale
alt.ex: The FDA enforces medication laws ensuring medications are vigorously tested before they reach the public.
w: Defining the scope of practice for registered nurses
State nurse practice acts define the scope of nursing practice.
Regulating local use of alcohol and tobacco
Local governmental bodies regulate the use of alcohol and tobacco.
Setting each hospital’s narcotic stop-order policy
Individual agencies set policies such as automatic narcotic discontinuation.

items.q: Which official publications set standards for medication strength, quality, purity, packaging, safety, labeling, and dose form?
items.a: The United States Pharmacopeia and the National Formulary
items.ex: The USP and the National Formulary are official publications that set these medication standards.
w: The MedWatch form and the MedWatch website
MedWatch is a voluntary program for reporting serious harm, not a standards publication.
State nurse practice acts and agency policy manuals
These define nursing scope and agency rules, not medication purity and dose-form standards.
The ISMP confused-name list and tall-man guide
ISMP lists address look-alike names, not strength, purity, and packaging standards.

alt.q: A nursing student asks what the United States Pharmacopeia (USP) and the National Formulary do. Which answer is accurate?
alt.a: They set standards for medication strength, quality, purity, packaging, safety, labeling, and dose form
alt.ex: These official publications set medication standards; the generic name of a medication is also listed in the USP.
w: They define the legal scope of nursing functions and responsibilities in each state
That is the role of each state’s nurse practice act.
They collect voluntary reports of serious harm caused by medications and products
Voluntary reporting of serious harm is done through the FDA’s MedWatch program.
They regulate local sales of alcohol and tobacco products within a community
Local governmental bodies regulate alcohol and tobacco use.

items.q: A patient develops a serious, harmful reaction after receiving a newly approved medication. The nurse wants to report the event to the FDA. Which action is appropriate?
items.a: Complete the FDA MedWatch form
items.ex: MedWatch encourages nurses and other professionals to report when a medication, product, or event causes serious harm.
w: Notify the United States Pharmacopeia
The USP sets standards for strength and purity; it does not collect harm reports.
File a report with the state board of nursing
The board of nursing regulates nursing practice, not medication safety reporting.
Contact the local government health office
Local bodies regulate alcohol and tobacco; the FDA program for harm reports is MedWatch.

alt.q: What is the purpose of the FDA MedWatch program?
alt.a: To encourage voluntary reporting when a medication or product causes serious harm
alt.ex: MedWatch, begun in 1993, is a voluntary program for reporting serious harm from medications, products, or medical events.
w: To require pharmacists to count controlled substances at each shift change
Running counts of opioids are agency controlled-substance procedures, not MedWatch.
To approve generic names for newly developed medications
Generic names are approved by the United States Adopted Names Council.
To list medication names that are frequently confused with one another
The ISMP publishes the list of commonly confused medication names.

items.q: Reporting serious medication-related harm through the FDA MedWatch program is mandatory for all nurses.
items.a: False
items.ex: MedWatch is a voluntary program that encourages nurses and other health care professionals to report serious harm.
items.ww: The program relies on voluntary reports; it is not a legal mandate for each nurse.

alt.q: MedWatch is a voluntary FDA program that encourages nurses to report when a medication, product, or medical event causes serious harm to a patient.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The FDA instituted MedWatch so health care professionals can voluntarily report serious harm using the MedWatch form.
alt.ww: MedWatch is neither limited to physicians nor mandatory; nurses are specifically encouraged to report.

items.q: State and local medication laws must conform to federal medication legislation.
items.a: True
items.ex: State and local laws must conform to federal law, although states often add controls of their own.
items.ww: States cannot override federal medication law; they can only add controls such as regulating substances the federal government does not.

alt.q: A state may loosen federal controls on a medication as long as its own legislature approves the change.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: State laws must conform to federal legislation; states can add controls but cannot weaken federal ones.
alt.ww: States may add controls, including on substances not federally regulated, but must still conform to federal law.

items.q: Which type of regulation is usually handled by local governmental bodies?
items.a: Use of alcohol and tobacco
items.ex: Local governmental bodies regulate the use of alcohol and tobacco.
w: Testing of new medications
Medication testing before sale is enforced at the federal level by the FDA.
Scope of nursing practice
Each state’s nurse practice act defines the scope of nursing practice.
Standards for medication purity
Purity standards are set by the USP and the National Formulary.

alt.q: Which statement about state and local medication regulation is accurate?
alt.a: States can control substances that the federal government does not regulate
alt.ex: States often add controls, including control of substances not regulated by the federal government.
w: States can approve medications that the FDA has not tested
State laws must conform to federal legislation, which requires FDA testing.
Local governments set dose-form standards for medications
Dose-form standards are set by the USP and the National Formulary.
Local governments define the scope of nursing practice
Nursing scope is defined by state nurse practice acts.

items.q: A patient’s opioid order has been automatically discontinued under agency policy after a set number of days, and the patient now reports pain. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Contact the health care provider to review whether the opioid should be reordered
items.ex: Automatic stop policies require the provider to review the need for the opioid; the provider can reorder it.
w: Continue giving the opioid until the provider makes rounds tomorrow
Once discontinued, the order is no longer valid and the opioid cannot be given.
Give the opioid because the original order was valid when written
The stop policy ended the order; giving it would be administering without a valid order.
Tell the patient that opioids cannot be ordered again during this stay
The provider can reorder the opioid after reviewing the patient’s need.

alt.q: What is the main purpose of an agency policy that automatically discontinues narcotics after a set number of days?
alt.a: It makes the provider regularly review the need, limiting unnecessarily prolonged therapy
alt.ex: Automatic stop orders help control unnecessarily prolonged therapy by requiring regular provider review of the narcotic.
w: It prevents a health care provider from ever reordering the same narcotic
The provider can reorder the narcotic after reviewing the patient’s need.
It satisfies a federal law requiring narcotics to stop after a set number of days
This is an agency policy, often more restrictive than governmental controls.
It reduces the time nurses spend counting narcotics during each shift
Running counts are still required; the policy targets prolonged therapy.

items.q: Health care agency medication policies are often more restrictive than governmental controls.
items.a: True
items.ex: Agencies set policies to meet federal, state, and local rules, and these policies are often stricter, such as automatic narcotic stop orders.
items.ww: Agency policies cannot be looser than the law, and they are frequently stricter than it.

alt.q: Because federal law is the highest authority, agency medication policies cannot be stricter than governmental controls.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Agency policies must meet regulations but are often more restrictive, as with automatic discontinuation of narcotics.
alt.ww: Agencies may go beyond legal minimums; the book gives automatic narcotic stop orders as an example.

items.q: What is the primary intent of a state nurse practice act (NPA)?
items.a: To protect the public from unskilled, undereducated, and unlicensed personnel
items.ex: NPAs define nursing scope of practice primarily to protect the public from unqualified personnel.
w: To protect nurses from lawsuits filed by patients and their families
NPAs exist to protect the public, not to shield nurses from liability.
To set purity and packaging standards for the medications nurses give
Medication standards are set by the USP and the National Formulary.
To list the medications each agency allows nurses to administer
Agencies interpret actions under the NPA; the act itself is broad.

alt.q: Why are most state nurse practice acts written in purposefully broad terms?
alt.a: So that nurses’ professional responsibilities are not limited
alt.ex: NPAs are purposefully broad so that nursing’s professional responsibilities are not restricted.
w: So that agencies can expand the act to fit their needs
Agencies can interpret but cannot modify, expand, or restrict the act’s intent.
So that federal agencies can define nursing duties
Nurse practice acts are state laws that define nursing scope.
So that nurses can perform any physician function
NPAs define nursing functions; broad wording does not grant medical practice.

items.q: A hospital is writing a policy about which medication-related actions nurses may perform under the state nurse practice act. Which statement describes the hospital’s authority?
items.a: It may interpret specific actions allowed but cannot modify, expand, or restrict the act’s intent
items.ex: Agencies can interpret actions allowed under the NPA, but they cannot change the intent of the act.
w: It may expand nursing actions beyond the act if staff receive training
Agencies cannot expand the intent of the nurse practice act.
It may restrict the act’s intent if the change improves patient safety
Agencies cannot restrict the intent of the act, although their policies can be strict.
It must adopt the act’s wording without any interpretation for its setting
Agencies are allowed to interpret the specific actions permitted under the act.

alt.q: Which action falls within a health care agency’s authority regarding the state nurse practice act?
alt.a: Interpreting which specific actions nurses may perform in that agency
alt.ex: Agencies interpret specific actions under the NPA but cannot modify, expand, or restrict its intent.
w: Expanding the act so nurses can prescribe opioids
Agencies cannot expand the intent of the act.
Rewriting the act’s definition of nursing practice
Agencies cannot modify the nurse practice act.
Removing functions the act grants to all nurses
Agencies cannot restrict the intent of the act.

items.q: A nurse is found to have violated the Controlled Substances Act. Which consequences can result? Select all that apply.
o: Fines
Violations of the Controlled Substances Act are punishable by fines.
Imprisonment
Violations can lead to imprisonment.
Loss of nurse licensure
A nurse who violates the act can lose licensure.
A warning letter with no further penalty
The act carries serious penalties, not just a warning.
Reassignment to another unit as the only penalty
Penalties include fines, imprisonment, and loss of licensure.
items.ex: Opioids are tightly controlled by federal and state guidelines, and violations bring fines, imprisonment, and loss of licensure.

alt.q: Which statements about nurses and controlled substances are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Nurses must follow legal provisions when giving opioids
Opioids are controlled through federal and state guidelines that nurses must follow.
Violations can cost a nurse their license
Loss of nurse licensure is one penalty for violating the Controlled Substances Act.
Agencies have policies for storing and distributing narcotics
Hospitals set policies for proper storage and distribution of narcotics.
Controlled substances are regulated only by agency policy
Controlled substances are regulated by federal and state guidelines.
Violations are handled only through agency discipline
Violations are punishable by fines and imprisonment, not just agency action.
alt.ex: Nurses follow federal, state, and agency rules for opioids; violations carry legal and licensure penalties.

items.q: While counting opioids at the end of the shift, the nurse finds the count does not match the inventory record. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Report the discrepancy immediately and correct it
items.ex: Box 31.1 directs nurses to report a count discrepancy immediately and correct it.
w: Document the difference and recount at the next shift
Delaying the report until the next shift does not follow the guideline to report immediately.
Adjust the record so it matches the cabinet contents
Changing the record to match hides the discrepancy instead of reporting it.
Ask the pharmacy to restock the missing doses later
Restocking does not address the discrepancy, which must be reported immediately.

alt.q: A nurse removes morphine from the computerized cabinet and is prompted to count the remaining doses. Why does the agency require this count?
alt.a: To keep a running count of opioids whenever they are dispensed
alt.ex: Counting at each dispensing keeps an accurate running count of opioids used, wasted, and remaining.
w: To check the expiration dates of the remaining opioids
The count tracks the number of doses, not their expiration dates.
To confirm the patient’s identity before the opioid is given
Patient identification is a separate safety check, not the purpose of the count.
To calculate how many doses the pharmacy will reorder
The count controls opioid use and detects discrepancies, not reordering.

items.q: The nurse gives 2 mg of hydromorphone from a 4-mg container. Which action is correct for the remaining 2 mg?
items.a: Have a second nurse witness disposal of the unused portion
items.ex: When only part of a controlled-substance dose is given, a second nurse witnesses disposal of the unused part.
w: Place the unused portion in the sharps container
Box 31.1 states not to place wasted parts of medications in sharps containers.
Return the unused portion to the locked cabinet
Partial doses are wasted per agency policy, not saved in the cabinet.
Label and save the unused portion for the next dose
Saving a partial dose violates the rules for wasting controlled substances.

alt.q: An agency uses a paper opioid record. After two nurses waste part of a dose of a controlled substance, who signs the record?
alt.a: Both the nurse who wasted the dose and the witnessing nurse
alt.ex: When paper records are kept, both nurses sign the form; computerized systems record their names electronically.
w: Only the nurse who gave the dose to the patient
The witness must also sign to confirm the disposal of the unused part.
Only the pharmacist who dispensed the controlled substance
The nurses who wasted and witnessed the disposal sign the record.
The charge nurse at the end of the shift for all wastes
Each waste is signed by the two nurses involved at the time.

items.q: Which actions follow the guidelines for safe opioid administration and control? Select all that apply.
o: Store opioids in a locked, secure cabinet, preferably computerized
Opioids are stored in locked, secure cabinets; computerized locked cabinets are preferred.
Use tamper-evident syringes when available
Tamper-evident syringes, such as for hydromorphone, are used when available.
Record the patient’s name, date, time, medication, and dosage
The inventory record documents these details each time an opioid is dispensed.
Count opioids whenever they are dispensed
A running count is kept by counting opioids whenever they are dispensed.
Discard wasted opioid portions in the sharps container
Wasted parts of medications are not placed in sharps containers.
Count opioids only once a week if a computer is used
A running count is maintained at each dispensing, even with computerized systems.
items.ex: Box 31.1 calls for locked storage, tamper-evident syringes, running counts, and complete records of each dispensed opioid.

alt.q: A nurse orientee is learning the agency’s controlled-substance procedures. Which actions by the orientee are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Follows agency policy when wasting part of an opioid dose
Unused portions are wasted according to agency policy.
Has a second nurse witness disposal of a partial dose
A second nurse witnesses disposal when only part of a dose is given.
Reports a count discrepancy immediately
Count discrepancies are reported immediately and corrected.
Leaves the opioid cabinet unlocked during busy medication passes
Opioids must always be kept in a locked, secure cabinet.
Records an opioid dose only when the patient asks about it
Every dispensed opioid is recorded on the inventory record.
alt.ex: Safe control of opioids includes proper waste with a witness, immediate reporting of discrepancies, and secure storage.

items.q: Which areas do federal medication laws control? Select all that apply.
o: Medication sales and distribution
Federal laws control how medications are sold and distributed.
Testing, naming, and labeling of medications
Federal laws control medication testing, naming, and labeling.
Use of controlled substances
Federal laws, with state guidelines, control controlled substances such as opioids.
Local use of alcohol and tobacco
Local governmental bodies regulate alcohol and tobacco use.
The scope of nursing practice in each state
State nurse practice acts define nursing scope.
items.ex: Federal medication laws control sales and distribution; testing, naming, and labeling; and controlled substances.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing which level of government regulates which aspects of medications. Which items are controlled by federal medication laws? Select all that apply.
o: Requiring testing before a medication is sold
The FDA enforces laws requiring vigorous testing before medications are sold.
Labeling of medications
Federal laws control medication labeling.
Distribution of medications
Federal laws control medication sales and distribution.
Automatic stop orders for narcotics in a hospital
Automatic stop orders are agency policies.
Defining which actions nurses may legally perform
Nursing actions are defined by state nurse practice acts.
alt.ex: Federal law governs medication testing, labeling, distribution, and controlled substances; agencies and states handle other areas.

items.q: The FDA’s voluntary [[MedWatch|Med Watch]] program encourages nurses to report when a medication, product, or medical event causes serious harm to a patient.
items.ex: MedWatch, instituted by the FDA in 1993, collects voluntary reports of serious harm through its MedWatch form.

alt.q: A nurse who sees serious harm caused by a medication can report it by completing the FDA’s [[MedWatch|Med Watch]] form.
alt.ex: MedWatch, instituted by the FDA in 1993, collects voluntary reports of serious harm through its MedWatch form.

items.q: State [[nurse practice acts|nurse practice act|NPAs|NPA]] define the scope of nurses’ professional functions and responsibilities.

alt.ex: Nurse practice acts are state laws defining nursing scope, written broadly and intended to protect the public.

items.q: A nurse receives a computerized prompt after wasting part of an opioid dose with a witness. Why does the nurse not need to sign a paper form?

Every waste of a controlled substance is documented, with a witness.
The pharmacist signs the paper form for all opioid waste
The nurses involved, not the pharmacist, are recorded as wasting and witnessing.

The pharmacist enters the nurse’s name

items.q: Which medication name gives an exact description of the medication’s composition and molecular structure?

items.ex: The chemical name precisely describes composition and molecular structure; nurses rarely use it in practice.
w: Generic name

Trade name
The trade name is the proprietary name a manufacturer uses to market the medication.
Class name

items.q: A nurse is preparing a medication whose name looks very similar to that of another medication on the unit. Which action is most important before giving it?

alt.q: Why does the ISMP recommend tall-man (mixed-case) lettering such as aMILoride versus amLODIPine?

items.a: False

items.q: What does a medication’s classification indicate?

w: Its exact chemical composition and molecular structure
That is described by the chemical name.
The manufacturer that first developed and named it
The developing manufacturer gives the generic name; classification reflects effect.
The form in which it is prepared and its route

alt.q: Patients with asthma often take beta2-adrenergic agonists, a class containing more than 15 medications. What does this illustrate about classification?
alt.a: A class usually contains more than one medication used for the same type of problem
alt.ex: Each class usually contains several medications used for the same type of health problem.
w: Each class contains only one medication for each health problem
The beta2-adrenergic class alone contains more than 15 medications.
A medication can belong to only one classification
Some medications, such as aspirin, belong to more than one class.
Classes are organized by the manufacturer’s trade name
Classes reflect effect, symptoms relieved, or desired effect, not trade names.

items.q: Aspirin is an example of a medication that belongs to more than one class. Which classes does aspirin belong to? Select all that apply.
o: Analgesic
Aspirin relieves pain, making it an analgesic.
Antipyretic
Aspirin reduces fever, making it an antipyretic.
Antiinflammatory
Aspirin reduces inflammation, making it an antiinflammatory.
Beta2-adrenergic agonist
Beta2-adrenergic agonists are a class used for asthma, not aspirin.
Opioid
Aspirin is not an opioid; morphine is an example of an opioid.
items.ex: Aspirin is an analgesic, an antipyretic, and an antiinflammatory, showing that one medication can fit several classes.

alt.q: Which statements about medication classification are accurate? Select all that apply.

A class usually contains more than one medication
The beta2-adrenergic class contains more than 15 medications.
Classification can reflect the symptoms a medication relieves
Classification indicates body-system effect, symptoms relieved, or desired effect.
Classification describes a medication’s molecular structure
Molecular structure is described by the chemical name.
Each health problem is treated by a single class of medication

alt.ex: Classes group several medications by effect or use, and one medication can belong to several classes.

items.q: What determines the route by which a medication is administered?
items.a: The form of the medication

w: The trade name of the medication

Classification reflects effect or use; the form determines the route.
The chemical name of the medication
The chemical name describes structure, not route.

alt.q: A medication comes as tablets, an elixir, and suppositories. Why must the nurse be sure to use the proper form?

All forms share the same generic name; the form determines the route.
Because each form belongs to a different medication class
Different forms of the same medication share its classification.
Because the form determines which manufacturer made the medication
Many companies make the same medication; the form determines route.

items.q: A patient asks why the tablet the nurse is giving has a special coating. Which response by the nurse is best?

Enteric coatings are designed not to dissolve in the stomach.
“The coating lets the tablet dissolve in your mouth like a lozenge.”
Troches or lozenges dissolve in the mouth; enteric-coated tablets do not.
“The coating releases the medicine slowly through your skin all day.”
Slow release through the skin describes a transdermal disk or patch.

Settling is an expected property of suspensions, not a storage problem.
The bottle holds an aqueous solution that has separated from its syrup
A solution has the substance dissolved and does not normally settle.

sections.name: Pharmacokinetics as the basis of medication actions

items.q: Which definition best describes pharmacokinetics?
items.a: The study of how medications enter the body, reach their site of action, metabolize, and exit the body
items.ex: Pharmacokinetics describes the movement of medications through the body, from entry to exit.
w: The study of the expected physiological response a medication produces in the body
That is the therapeutic effect of a medication.
The study of how medications are named, classified, and listed in official publications
Naming and classification are pharmacological concepts, not pharmacokinetics.
The study of laws that regulate how medications are tested, sold, and labeled

alt.q: A nurse uses knowledge of pharmacokinetics in which aspect of practice?

w: Choosing which trade name to order from the pharmacy each day
Trade names are marketing names and are not a pharmacokinetic concern.
Defining the legal scope of practice for medication administration
Scope of practice is defined by the state nurse practice act.
Reporting serious medication harm to the FDA through MedWatch
MedWatch reporting addresses adverse events, not how drugs move in the body.

alt.ex: That's process 1 of 4. A medication is absorbed into the blood, distributed to its site of action, metabolized to a less active form, then excreted.
w: Metabolism
That's process 3 of 4.
Excretion
That's process 4 of 4.

alt.q: In pharmacokinetics, which process comes right before “Metabolism”?
alt.a: Distribution
alt.ex: That's process 2 of 4. A medication is absorbed into the blood, distributed to its site of action, metabolized to a less active form, then excreted.
w: Absorption
That's process 1 of 4.
Excretion
That's process 4 of 4.

alt.q: In pharmacokinetics, which process comes right before “Excretion”?
alt.a: Metabolism
alt.ex: That's process 3 of 4. A medication is absorbed into the blood, distributed to its site of action, metabolized to a less active form, then excreted.
w: Distribution
That's process 2 of 4.
Absorption
That's process 1 of 4.

ord.q: Place the pharmacokinetic processes in the order in which a medication moves through the body.
items: Absorption
Distribution
Metabolism
Excretion
ord.ex: A medication is absorbed into the blood, distributed to its site of action, metabolized to a less active form, then excreted.

w: Oral
That's route 4 of 4.
Intravenous
That's route 1 of 4.

ord.q: Arrange these routes from the most rapid absorption to the slowest overall absorption.
items: Intravenous
Intramuscular
Subcutaneous
Oral
ord.ex: IV gives the most rapid absorption; IM enters the blood faster than subcutaneous, and both are faster than oral.

items.q: Why does intravenous (IV) injection produce the most rapid absorption of any route?
items.a: The medication is available immediately when it enters the systemic circulation
items.ex: IV medications enter the systemic circulation directly, so they are available immediately.
w: The medication must first pass through the gastrointestinal tract
Passing through the GI tract is why oral absorption is usually slow.
The medication dissolves slowly in the muscle before entering the blood
This would slow absorption; IV medication bypasses tissue absorption.
The medication binds to albumin before it reaches the bloodstream
Albumin binding affects distribution and reduces activity, not speed of entry.

alt.q: A patient needs a medication to take effect as quickly as possible. Which route provides the most rapid absorption?
alt.a: Intravenous
alt.ex: IV injection gives the most rapid absorption because the medication enters the systemic circulation immediately.
w: Intramuscular
IM absorption is faster than subcutaneous or oral but slower than IV.
Subcutaneous
Subcutaneous absorption is slower than IM and IV.
Oral
Oral medications pass through the GI tract, so absorption is usually slow.

items.q: Why are medications placed on mucous membranes and respiratory airways absorbed quickly?
items.a: These tissues contain many blood vessels
items.ex: Mucous membranes and airways are highly vascular, so medications placed there are absorbed quickly.
w: These tissues have a thick protective outer layer
A thick physical barrier, like skin, slows absorption.
These tissues bind medications to serum albumin
Albumin binding is a distribution factor that reduces activity.
These tissues contain the enzymes that metabolize drugs
Most metabolism occurs in the liver; vascularity explains fast absorption.

alt.q: Which route of administration has slow absorption because of the physical makeup of the tissue?
alt.a: Application to the skin
alt.ex: Absorption through the skin is slow because of the skin’s physical makeup.
w: Application to mucous membranes
Mucous membranes have many blood vessels and absorb quickly.
Inhalation into the respiratory airways
Airways are highly vascular and absorb medications quickly.
Intravenous injection into a vein
IV injection produces the most rapid absorption.

items.q: Which factors influence how a medication is absorbed? Select all that apply.
o: Route of administration
Each route has a different rate of absorption.
Blood flow at the site of administration
The richer the blood supply, the faster the absorption.
Body surface area the medication encounters
A larger surface area speeds absorption.
Lipid solubility of the medication
Highly lipid-soluble medications cross cell membranes easily and are absorbed quickly.
Serum albumin level
Albumin affects distribution through protein binding, not absorption.
Rate of glomerular filtration
Kidney function affects excretion, not absorption.
items.ex: Route, ability to dissolve, blood flow at the site, body surface area, and lipid solubility all influence absorption.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing why a patient’s oral medication may be absorbed poorly. Which factors can impair or alter oral absorption? Select all that apply.
o: Food in the stomach
Food can change a medication’s structure and impair its absorption.
Another medication given at the same time that interferes with it
Some medications given together impair each other’s absorption.
A tablet form instead of a liquid form
Solutions and suspensions are absorbed more readily than tablets or capsules.
High lipid solubility of the medication
High lipid solubility speeds absorption across cell membranes.
A rich blood supply at the absorption site
A rich blood supply speeds absorption.
alt.ex: Food, interacting medications, and the medication’s form all affect how readily an oral medication is absorbed.

items.q: Medications that are basic are absorbed rapidly through the gastric mucosa.
items.a: False
items.ex: Basic medications are not absorbed before reaching the small intestine; acidic medications pass through the gastric mucosa rapidly.
items.ww: It is acidic, not basic, medications that cross the gastric mucosa rapidly.

alt.q: Acidic medications pass through the gastric mucosa rapidly, whereas basic medications are not absorbed until they reach the small intestine.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Acidity affects where an oral medication is absorbed: acidic ones in the stomach, basic ones in the small intestine.
alt.ww: Basic medications are not absorbed in the stomach; they wait until the small intestine.

items.q: Why are most medications absorbed in the small intestine rather than the stomach?
items.a: The small intestine provides a much larger surface area
items.ex: Medications are absorbed faster when they encounter a large surface area, as in the small intestine.
w: The small intestine has less blood flow than the stomach
Less blood flow would slow absorption, not speed it.
The small intestine contains the enzymes for biotransformation
Most biotransformation occurs in the liver.
The small intestine binds medications to serum albumin
Albumin binding occurs in the blood and affects distribution.

alt.q: A medication encounters a large surface area at its absorption site. How does this affect absorption?
alt.a: It is absorbed at a faster rate
alt.ex: Large surface areas increase the rate of absorption, which is why most medications are absorbed in the small intestine.
w: It is absorbed at a slower rate
Surface area and absorption rate increase together.
It is excreted before absorption
Surface area affects absorption speed, not excretion.
It becomes bound to albumin
Protein binding is part of distribution, not a result of surface area.

items.q: A patient is prescribed two oral medications that impair each other’s absorption, and both are scheduled for 0900. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Collaborate with the pharmacist or provider to schedule them at different times
items.ex: Interacting medications are not given at the same time; the nurse consults the pharmacist or provider to set times.
w: Give both at 0900 with extra water to improve absorption
Water does not prevent the interaction that impairs both medications’ absorption.
Crush both medications together so they dissolve faster
Combining them does not prevent their interference with each other.
Skip one medication each day so they are never given together
Omitting doses is not appropriate; times are adjusted in collaboration instead.

alt.q: A patient’s oral medication is absorbed better when taken between meals because food alters its structure. Which nursing action best promotes optimal absorption?
alt.a: Plan the administration time around meals according to agency policy
alt.ex: Nurses plan administration times around meals when medications interact with food to promote optimal absorption.
w: Give the medication with the largest meal of the day
Food impairs this medication’s absorption, so giving it with a meal is not optimal.
Give the medication with a second drug to speed absorption
Some medications given together impair each other’s absorption.
Change the medication to a different form without an order
Changing form requires a provider order; timing around meals is the nursing action.

items.q: A patient with heart failure is receiving a medication whose expected effect is slower than usual. Which explanation is most accurate?
items.a: Impaired circulation slows delivery of the medication to its site of action
items.ex: Conditions that limit blood flow inhibit distribution, so effects in heart failure are often delayed or altered.
w: The heart failure increases protein binding of the medication
Low albumin, not heart failure, changes protein binding in the book’s examples.
The heart failure makes the medication more lipid soluble
Lipid solubility is a property of the medication, not of the patient’s heart.
The heart failure speeds excretion of the medication by the lungs
Only gaseous and volatile compounds exit through the lungs; circulation is the issue here.

alt.q: How quickly a medication reaches a tissue after entering the bloodstream depends mainly on which factor?
alt.a: The vascularity of the tissue or organ
alt.ex: Once in the bloodstream, a medication reaches tissues at a speed that depends on their vascularity.
w: The trade name of the medication
Names do not affect distribution.
The amount of food in the stomach
Food affects oral absorption, not distribution.
The rate of peristalsis in the bowel
Peristalsis affects excretion through the feces.

items.q: Why do central nervous system infections often require antibiotics injected directly into the subarachnoid space?
items.a: The blood-brain barrier allows only fat-soluble medications to pass into the brain
items.ex: Because the blood-brain barrier admits only fat-soluble medications, many antibiotics must be injected into the subarachnoid space.
w: Antibiotics are inactivated by the liver before reaching the brain
Liver metabolism is not the reason given; the blood-brain barrier blocks passage.
The brain has too little blood flow for antibiotics to reach it
The limiting factor is membrane permeability, not low blood flow.
Antibiotics bind to albumin and cannot leave the bloodstream
Protein binding reduces activity but the barrier is what blocks entry to the CNS.

alt.q: An older adult becomes confused after receiving a fat-soluble medication. Which pharmacokinetic change helps explain this response?
alt.a: Altered blood-brain barrier permeability allows easier passage of fat-soluble drugs
alt.ex: Some older adults have more permeable blood-brain barriers, so fat-soluble drugs pass easily and cause effects such as confusion.
w: Increased serum albumin binds more of the drug in the bloodstream
Older adults have decreased, not increased, albumin.
Faster peristalsis moves the drug out of the bowel more quickly
Faster peristalsis speeds excretion and would not cause confusion.
Improved liver function converts the drug into an active form
Liver function often declines with age, and metabolism usually inactivates drugs.

items.q: A nurse reviews the laboratory results of an older adult with malnutrition and notes a low serum albumin level. The patient receives a medication that is highly bound to albumin. Which outcome should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: Increased medication activity and risk of toxicity
items.ex: With less albumin, more medication is unbound, and the free form is active, raising activity and toxicity risk.
w: Decreased medication activity and slower onset
Less albumin leaves more free, active medication, not less.
Faster excretion of the medication through the lungs
Only gaseous and volatile compounds exit through the lungs.
No change, because albumin does not affect distribution
Protein binding directly affects distribution and activity.

alt.q: Which patients are at increased risk for medication toxicity because they have decreased serum albumin?
alt.a: Older adults and patients with liver disease or malnutrition
alt.ex: These patients have decreased albumin, so more medication is unbound and active, increasing toxicity risk.
w: Young adults and patients with high fluid intake
These groups are not described as having low albumin.
Patients with asthma or acute muscle injury
These conditions are not linked to low albumin in the book.
Patients with rapid peristalsis or recent enemas
Rapid peristalsis speeds fecal excretion, not albumin loss.

items.q: The unbound, or “free,” portion of a medication in the blood is its active form.
items.a: True
items.ex: Medication bound to albumin has reduced activity, while unbound medication is the active form.
items.ww: Binding to albumin reduces pharmacological activity, so only the free portion is active.

alt.q: The portion of a medication bound to serum albumin is its pharmacologically active form.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Binding to albumin reduces a medication’s ability to act; the unbound, free portion is active.
alt.ww: Bound medication is the less active portion, which is why low albumin increases drug activity.

items.q: Which patients have decreased serum albumin that places them at risk for increased medication activity or toxicity? Select all that apply.
o: An older adult
Older adults have decreased albumin, leaving more medication unbound.
A patient with liver disease
Liver disease decreases albumin and also slows metabolism.
A patient with malnutrition
Malnutrition lowers albumin, increasing the free, active medication.
A patient taking a laxative
Laxatives speed fecal excretion; they do not lower albumin.
A healthy adult with adequate fluid intake
Adequate fluid intake supports excretion and does not lower albumin.
items.ex: Older adults and patients with liver disease or malnutrition have less albumin, so more drug is unbound and active.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for several patients who receive highly protein-bound medications. Which statements about protein binding are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Most medications partially bind to albumin
Partial binding to albumin is common and reduces drug activity.
Binding to albumin reduces the drug’s pharmacological activity
Bound medication cannot exert its full pharmacological effect.
Low albumin can lead to toxicity
With less albumin, more drug is free and active.
Albumin binding speeds a drug’s passage into the brain
Only fat-soluble medications cross the blood-brain barrier; binding does not speed this.
Bound medication is excreted unchanged by the lungs
Gaseous and volatile compounds exit through the lungs, not bound drugs.
alt.ex: Protein binding to albumin reduces activity; when albumin is low, more active drug circulates and toxicity risk rises.

items.q: [[Biotransformation|metabolism]] occurs under the influence of enzymes that detoxify, break down, and remove biologically active chemicals, mostly in the liver.
items.ex: Biotransformation converts a medication into a less active or inactive form that is easier to excrete.

alt.q: Most medication [[biotransformation|metabolism]] takes place in the liver, although the lungs, kidneys, blood, and intestines also contribute.
alt.ex: Biotransformation converts a medication into a less active or inactive form that is easier to excrete.

items.q: A patient with liver disease receives a small sedative dose of a barbiturate. One hour later, which finding is most important for the nurse to report?
items.a: The patient is difficult to arouse and responds only to painful stimuli
items.ex: Decreased liver function slows elimination; a small barbiturate dose can cause coma in liver disease, so deep sedation must be reported.
w: The patient reports a dry mouth and asks for water
Dry mouth is minor and not a sign of dangerous accumulation.
The patient is asleep but awakens easily when spoken to
Easy arousal to voice is an expected response to a sedative.
The patient asks for an extra blanket because the room is cool
This comfort request does not suggest medication toxicity.

alt.q: Why is a patient with liver disease at risk for medication toxicity?
alt.a: The medication is eliminated more slowly and can accumulate
alt.ex: When liver function decreases, medications are usually eliminated more slowly, so they accumulate and can become toxic.
w: The liver excretes medications faster into the bile
Liver disease slows rather than speeds medication elimination.
Medications bind more strongly to albumin
Liver disease lowers albumin, leaving more unbound medication.
Medications are absorbed more slowly from the gut
The concern is slowed metabolism and accumulation, not slow absorption.

items.q: After surgery under general anesthesia, the nurse encourages a patient to deep breathe and cough. What is the pharmacokinetic reason for this intervention?
items.a: It helps the patient eliminate anesthetic gases through the lungs more rapidly
items.ex: Gaseous and volatile compounds exit through the lungs, so deep breathing and coughing speed elimination of anesthetic gases.
w: It increases absorption of oral pain medications in the stomach
Deep breathing affects lung excretion, not GI absorption.
It raises serum albumin so less anesthetic is active
Breathing exercises do not change albumin levels.
It speeds liver biotransformation of the anesthetic gases
The lungs, not the liver, eliminate volatile anesthetic gases.

alt.q: Which substances exit the body mainly through the lungs?
alt.a: Gaseous and volatile compounds such as nitrous oxide and alcohol
alt.ex: The chemical makeup of a medication determines its excretion organ; gases and volatile compounds exit through the lungs.
w: Lipid-soluble medications excreted through sweat glands
Lipid-soluble medications are excreted by the exocrine glands.
Medications excreted unchanged into the urine
Medications that escape metabolism exit through the kidneys.
Medications broken down by the liver and released in bile
Medications released in bile enter the intestines.

items.q: Which statements about medication excretion are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The kidneys are the main organs of medication excretion
The kidneys excrete most medications, some unchanged and some after biotransformation.
Lipid-soluble medications are excreted by the exocrine glands
Exocrine glands excrete lipid-soluble medications, sometimes irritating the skin.
A medication excreted in breast milk may be ingested by a nursing infant
Excretion through mammary glands puts nursing infants at risk.
Inactivity and improper diet speed excretion through the feces
Factors that slow peristalsis, such as inactivity, often prolong medication effects.
Medications excreted in bile leave the body without any resorption
After entering the intestines through the bile, chemicals are resorbed by the intestines.
items.ex: Medications exit through kidneys, liver, bowel, lungs, and exocrine glands, with the kidneys as the main route.

alt.q: A patient’s medication is excreted through the sweat glands. Which nursing actions or teaching points are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Assess the patient’s skin for irritation
Excretion through sweat glands often irritates the skin.
Teach the patient good hygiene practices
Hygiene teaching helps manage skin irritation from excreted medication.
Check the medication’s safety if the patient is breastfeeding
Any medication used by a breastfeeding woman is checked because mammary excretion can reach the infant.
Encourage the patient to limit bathing to prevent dryness
Good hygiene is taught because excreted medication can irritate the skin.
Explain that sweat is the main route of medication excretion
The kidneys are the main organs of medication excretion.
alt.ex: Exocrine excretion of lipid-soluble drugs can irritate the skin, so nurses assess skin and teach good hygiene.

items.q: Factors that increase peristalsis, such as laxatives and enemas, prolong the effects of a medication.
items.a: False
items.ex: Increased peristalsis accelerates medication excretion through the feces; slowed peristalsis prolongs medication effects.
items.ww: Laxatives and enemas speed fecal excretion, which shortens rather than lengthens medication effects.

alt.q: Factors that slow peristalsis, such as inactivity and improper diet, often prolong the effects of a medication.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: When peristalsis slows, medications leave through the feces more slowly, so their effects last longer.
alt.ww: Slowed peristalsis delays fecal excretion, so effects are prolonged rather than shortened.

items.q: A patient’s laboratory results show declining renal function. Which change to medication therapy should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: The health care provider will likely reduce medication doses
items.ex: When renal function declines, the kidneys cannot adequately excrete medications, toxicity risk rises, and providers usually reduce doses.
w: The health care provider will likely increase medication doses
Higher doses would worsen accumulation when excretion is impaired.
The medications will be excreted mainly through the lungs instead
Only gaseous and volatile compounds exit through the lungs.
No change is needed because the liver excretes most medications
The kidneys are the main organs of medication excretion.

alt.q: Which organs are the main route of medication excretion?
alt.a: The kidneys
alt.ex: The kidneys are the main organs of excretion; some medications exit unchanged in the urine.
w: The lungs
The lungs excrete gaseous and volatile compounds such as nitrous oxide.
The sweat glands
Exocrine glands excrete lipid-soluble medications, but they are not the main route.
The mammary glands
Excretion in breast milk can affect infants, but it is not the main route.

items.q: Which term describes the expected or predicted physiological response caused by a medication?
items.a: Therapeutic effect
items.ex: The therapeutic effect is the desired, predicted response, such as nitroglycerin reducing cardiac workload.
w: Side effect
A side effect is a predictable but unintended adverse effect at a usual dose.
Idiosyncratic reaction
An idiosyncratic reaction is an unpredictable overreaction, underreaction, or abnormal response.
Synergistic effect
A synergistic effect is a combined effect of two drugs greater than each alone.

alt.q: Prednisone decreases swelling, inhibits inflammation, reduces allergic responses, and prevents transplant rejection. What does this illustrate?
alt.a: A medication can have more than one therapeutic effect
alt.ex: Some medications, such as prednisone, have several therapeutic effects, which the nurse must know to teach and evaluate.
w: A medication can have several unpredictable idiosyncratic effects
These are expected therapeutic effects, not unpredictable reactions.
A medication’s side effects can negate its therapeutic action
The listed actions are desired effects, not side effects.
A medication can develop tolerance after repeated doses
Tolerance is a need for higher doses over time, not multiple effects.

items.q: Which description fits a(n) Side effect?
items.a: Predictable, often unavoidable adverse effect at a usual therapeutic dose
items.ex: Medications produce intended effects and a range of unintended actions that the nurse must recognize.
w: Harm from prolonged intake or accumulation of a medication in the blood
That goes with Toxic effect.
Unpredictable overreaction, underreaction, or abnormal reaction
That goes with Idiosyncratic reaction.
Immune response in which the medication acts as an antigen
That goes with Allergic reaction.

mt.q: Match each type of medication action with its description.
pairs: Predictable, often unavoidable adverse effect at a usual therapeutic dose
