items.q: A child who receives diphenhydramine, an antihistamine, becomes extremely agitated and excited instead of drowsy. Which type of medication action is this?
items.a: Idiosyncratic reaction
items.ex: An idiosyncratic reaction is an unpredictable overreaction, underreaction, or reaction different from normal.
w: Toxic effect
Toxic effects result from prolonged intake or accumulation, not a paradoxical response.
Medication tolerance
Tolerance develops over time and requires higher doses for the same effect.
Synergistic effect
A synergistic effect requires two medications whose combined effect is greater.

alt.q: Which statement about idiosyncratic reactions is accurate?
alt.a: It is currently not possible to predict whether a patient will have one
alt.ex: Idiosyncratic reactions are unpredictable; at present, no one can predict who will have them.
w: They occur only after prolonged intake of a medication
Effects after prolonged intake describe toxic effects.
They are predictable effects that occur at usual doses
Predictable effects at usual doses are side effects.
They occur only when two medications are taken together
Effects from two drugs together are medication interactions.

items.q: Which statement best defines a side effect?
items.a: A predictable, often unavoidable adverse effect produced at a usual therapeutic dose
items.ex: Side effects are predictable and often unavoidable at usual doses, ranging from harmless to serious.
w: An unpredictable response in which a patient overreacts to a usual dose
This describes an idiosyncratic reaction.
A harmful effect from a medication that has accumulated in the blood
Accumulation causing harm describes a toxic effect.
An immune response in which the medication acts as an antigen
This describes an allergic reaction.

alt.q: A man taking an antihypertensive medication at the usual dose develops impotence. How should the nurse classify this effect?
alt.a: Side effect
alt.ex: Impotence from some antihypertensives is a predictable, often unavoidable effect at usual doses, which defines a side effect.
w: Toxic effect
Toxic effects come from prolonged intake or accumulation, not usual dosing.
Allergic reaction
Allergic reactions are immune responses, such as hives or anaphylaxis.
Therapeutic effect
The therapeutic effect of an antihypertensive is lowering blood pressure.

items.q: Which side effects are the most common reasons patients stop taking their medications? Select all that apply.
o: Anorexia
Anorexia is one of the most common side effects.
Nausea and vomiting
Nausea and vomiting are among the most common side effects.
Constipation or diarrhea
Both constipation and diarrhea are among the most common side effects.
Drowsiness
Drowsiness is a common side effect that leads patients to stop medications.
Severe respiratory depression
Severe respiratory depression is a toxic effect of opioids such as morphine.
Edema of the pharynx and larynx
Pharyngeal and laryngeal edema is a sign of an anaphylactic reaction.
items.ex: The most common side effects are anorexia, nausea, vomiting, constipation, drowsiness, and diarrhea.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching about the side effects of a newly prescribed medication. Which statements about side effects are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They are predictable effects at usual doses
Side effects occur predictably at usual therapeutic doses.
They range from harmless to serious
Side effects range from harmless to causing serious symptoms or injury.
They can lead the provider to discontinue the medication
If side effects negate the benefit, the provider discontinues the medication.
They occur only when a dose is higher than prescribed
Side effects occur at usual therapeutic doses.
They can always be avoided by taking the medication with food
Side effects are often unavoidable.
alt.ex: Side effects are predictable, often unavoidable, vary in severity, and may lead to discontinuation.

items.q: Which patients are most at risk for adverse medication reactions? Select all that apply.
o: A 2-month-old infant
The very young are at increased risk for adverse reactions.
A pregnant woman
Pregnant women are among those most at risk.
A patient taking several medications
Taking multiple medications increases the risk of adverse reactions.
A patient with renal disease
Renal or liver disease increases the risk of adverse reactions.
A 30-year-old of average weight with no health problems
This patient has none of the listed risk factors.
A patient taking a single short-term medication
Risk rises with multiple medications, not a single one.
items.ex: Risk is highest in the very young, older adults, pregnant women, patients on multiple medications, extremes of weight, and renal or liver disease.

alt.q: A nurse is screening patients for increased risk of adverse medication effects. Which patients have a risk factor? Select all that apply.
o: An 88-year-old patient
Older adults are among those most at risk.
A patient who is extremely underweight
Extremely underweight or overweight patients are at increased risk.
A patient with liver disease
Liver disease increases risk for adverse reactions.
A 25-year-old taking one vitamin daily
This patient has no listed risk factor.
A patient whose only medication is a long-standing one
Unusual responses are especially watched for with newly prescribed drugs.
alt.ex: Age extremes, pregnancy, polypharmacy, extreme weight, and renal or liver disease raise adverse reaction risk.

items.q: A patient receiving morphine has a respiratory rate of 6 breaths/min and is difficult to arouse. The nurse suspects opioid toxicity. Which medication should the nurse anticipate giving?
items.a: Naloxone
items.ex: Naloxone is an opioid antagonist that reverses opioid toxicity, such as severe respiratory depression from morphine.
w: Diphenhydramine
Diphenhydramine is an antihistamine and can add to central nervous system depression.
Prednisone
Prednisone is a steroid used for inflammation, not opioid reversal.
Nitroglycerin
Nitroglycerin reduces cardiac workload and does not reverse opioids.

alt.q: What is the most dangerous effect of toxic levels of morphine?
alt.a: Severe respiratory depression that can lead to death
alt.ex: Toxic opioid levels cause severe respiratory depression and death; naloxone reverses opioid toxicity.
w: Hives with reddened margins and pale centers
Urticaria is a mild allergic reaction, not opioid toxicity.
Agitation and excitement instead of drowsiness
A paradoxical response like this is an idiosyncratic reaction.
Clear, watery nasal discharge with swelling
Rhinitis is a mild allergic reaction.

items.q: Toxic effects often develop after prolonged intake of a medication or when it accumulates in the blood because of impaired metabolism or excretion.
items.a: True
items.ex: Toxicity results from prolonged intake or from accumulation when the body cannot metabolize or excrete the drug.
items.ww: Toxicity is not limited to a single large dose; accumulation over time from impaired elimination also causes it.

alt.q: Toxic effects occur only after a single accidental overdose, not from medications taken as prescribed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Toxic effects often follow prolonged intake or accumulation when metabolism or excretion is impaired.
alt.ww: Prescribed medications can reach toxic levels when liver or kidney function is impaired.

items.q: Shortly after an IV antibiotic infusion begins, a patient develops severe wheezing, shortness of breath, and a feeling of throat tightness. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Stop the infusion and obtain immediate medical attention
items.ex: These are signs of anaphylaxis, a life-threatening reaction; the medication is stopped and immediate medical treatment is needed.
w: Slow the infusion rate and recheck the patient in 30 minutes
Continuing the antibiotic during anaphylaxis is dangerous and delays urgent treatment.
Document the reaction and complete a MedWatch report
Reporting comes later; the life-threatening reaction must be treated first.
Apply a cool compress and give the next dose by mouth
Anaphylaxis needs immediate medical attention, and the drug must be avoided.

alt.q: A patient receiving a medication for the first time develops a few hives but no breathing problems, while another patient develops severe wheezing and laryngeal edema. Which patient needs immediate medical attention?
alt.a: The patient with severe wheezing and laryngeal edema
alt.ex: Bronchiolar constriction, laryngeal edema, and severe wheezing signal anaphylaxis, which is life threatening and needs immediate treatment.
w: The patient with a few hives and no breathing problems
Urticaria alone is a mild allergic reaction and is less urgent.
Both patients need the same level of urgency
Anaphylaxis is life threatening; mild hives are not.
Neither patient needs attention until the next dose
Allergic reactions require assessment, and anaphylaxis requires immediate care.

items.q: Which findings characterize a severe, or anaphylactic, reaction? Select all that apply.
o: Sudden constriction of bronchiolar muscles
Bronchiolar constriction is a hallmark of anaphylaxis.
Edema of the pharynx and larynx
Pharyngeal and laryngeal edema is characteristic of anaphylaxis.
Severe wheezing and shortness of breath
Severe wheezing and shortness of breath accompany anaphylaxis.
Itching of the skin with a mild rash only
Pruritus and rash alone are mild allergic reactions.
Drowsiness after a usual dose
Drowsiness is a common side effect, not anaphylaxis.
items.ex: Anaphylaxis is life threatening, with bronchiolar constriction, pharyngeal and laryngeal edema, and severe wheezing and dyspnea.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing allergic reactions with a group of new graduates. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Antibiotics cause a high incidence of allergic reactions
Among medication classes, antibiotics cause many allergic reactions.
The medication acts as an antigen that triggers antibody release
Allergic reactions occur when the drug or chemical acts as an antigen.
Anaphylactic reactions require immediate medical attention
Anaphylaxis is life threatening and must be treated immediately.
Allergic reactions are predictable from the medication dose
Allergic reactions are unpredictable responses.
Mild allergic reactions always progress to anaphylaxis
Mild reactions such as hives or rhinitis do not always progress.
alt.ex: Allergic reactions are unpredictable immune responses; antibiotics commonly cause them, and anaphylaxis is an emergency.

items.q: Which description fits Urticaria?
items.a: Raised, irregular eruptions with reddened margins and pale centers
items.ex: Mild allergic reactions include urticaria, rash, pruritus, and rhinitis.
w: Small, raised, usually reddened vesicles often over the entire body
That goes with Rash.
Itching of the skin that accompanies most rashes
That goes with Pruritus.
Inflamed nasal mucosa with swelling and clear, watery discharge
That goes with Rhinitis.

alt.q: Which description fits Rash?
alt.a: Small, raised, usually reddened vesicles often over the entire body
alt.ex: Mild allergic reactions include urticaria, rash, pruritus, and rhinitis.
w: Raised, irregular eruptions with reddened margins and pale centers
That goes with Urticaria.
Itching of the skin that accompanies most rashes
That goes with Pruritus.
Inflamed nasal mucosa with swelling and clear, watery discharge
That goes with Rhinitis.

alt.q: Which description fits Pruritus?
alt.a: Itching of the skin that accompanies most rashes
alt.ex: Mild allergic reactions include urticaria, rash, pruritus, and rhinitis.
w: Raised, irregular eruptions with reddened margins and pale centers
That goes with Urticaria.
Small, raised, usually reddened vesicles often over the entire body
That goes with Rash.
Inflamed nasal mucosa with swelling and clear, watery discharge
That goes with Rhinitis.

alt.q: Which description fits Rhinitis?
alt.a: Inflamed nasal mucosa with swelling and clear, watery discharge
alt.ex: Mild allergic reactions include urticaria, rash, pruritus, and rhinitis.
w: Raised, irregular eruptions with reddened margins and pale centers
That goes with Urticaria.
Small, raised, usually reddened vesicles often over the entire body
That goes with Rash.
Itching of the skin that accompanies most rashes
That goes with Pruritus.

alt.q: Which mild allergic reaction is described as “Raised, irregular eruptions with reddened margins and pale centers”?
alt.a: Urticaria
alt.ex: Mild allergic reactions include urticaria, rash, pruritus, and rhinitis.
w: Rash
Rash: Small, raised, usually reddened vesicles often over the entire body.
Pruritus
Pruritus: Itching of the skin that accompanies most rashes.
Rhinitis
Rhinitis: Inflamed nasal mucosa with swelling and clear, watery discharge.

alt.q: Which mild allergic reaction is described as “Small, raised, usually reddened vesicles often over the entire body”?
alt.a: Rash
alt.ex: Mild allergic reactions include urticaria, rash, pruritus, and rhinitis.
w: Urticaria
Urticaria: Raised, irregular eruptions with reddened margins and pale centers.
Pruritus
Pruritus: Itching of the skin that accompanies most rashes.
Rhinitis
Rhinitis: Inflamed nasal mucosa with swelling and clear, watery discharge.

alt.q: Which mild allergic reaction is described as “Itching of the skin that accompanies most rashes”?
alt.a: Pruritus
alt.ex: Mild allergic reactions include urticaria, rash, pruritus, and rhinitis.
w: Urticaria
Urticaria: Raised, irregular eruptions with reddened margins and pale centers.
Rash
Rash: Small, raised, usually reddened vesicles often over the entire body.
Rhinitis
Rhinitis: Inflamed nasal mucosa with swelling and clear, watery discharge.

alt.q: Which mild allergic reaction is described as “Inflamed nasal mucosa with swelling and clear, watery discharge”?
alt.a: Rhinitis
alt.ex: Mild allergic reactions include urticaria, rash, pruritus, and rhinitis.
w: Urticaria
Urticaria: Raised, irregular eruptions with reddened margins and pale centers.
Rash
Rash: Small, raised, usually reddened vesicles often over the entire body.
Pruritus
Pruritus: Itching of the skin that accompanies most rashes.

mt.q: Match each mild allergic reaction with its description.
pairs: Raised, irregular eruptions with reddened margins and pale centers
Small, raised, usually reddened vesicles often over the entire body
Itching of the skin that accompanies most rashes
Inflamed nasal mucosa with swelling and clear, watery discharge
mt.ex: Mild allergic reactions include urticaria, rash, pruritus, and rhinitis.

items.q: A patient can have an allergic response to a medication’s chemical preservatives or to one of its metabolites, not only to the medication itself.
items.a: True
items.ex: After sensitization, a patient can react to the medication, its chemical preservatives, or a metabolite.
items.ww: Allergic responses can be triggered by preservatives and metabolites as well as by the active medication.

alt.q: A patient who took the first dose of a medication without any problems cannot later become allergic to it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients can be sensitized by an initial dose and then develop an allergic response with repeated administration.
alt.ww: Allergy often develops after sensitization, so a reaction can appear with later doses.

items.q: Which class of medications causes a high incidence of allergic reactions?
items.a: Antibiotics
items.ex: Among the different classes of medications, antibiotics cause a high incidence of allergic reactions.
w: Nitrates
Nitrates are noted for producing tolerance, not a high incidence of allergy.
Diuretics
Diuretics are given as an example of a beneficial combination with vasodilators.
Opioid antagonists
Opioid antagonists such as naloxone reverse opioid toxicity.

alt.q: A nurse is about to give a patient’s first dose of a new medication. Which medication class should prompt the nurse to watch especially closely for an allergic reaction?
alt.a: An antibiotic
alt.ex: Antibiotics cause a high incidence of allergic reactions, and unusual responses are watched for with new medications.
w: A nitrate
Nitrates are known for producing tolerance over time.
A vasodilator
Vasodilators are mentioned as part of a beneficial combination for high blood pressure.
An opioid antagonist
Opioid antagonists reverse opioid toxicity and are not singled out for allergy.

items.q: A patient who had an anaphylactic reaction to penicillin is being discharged. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will avoid penicillin and wear an allergy bracelet.”
items.ex: A patient with a known medication allergy should avoid the drug and wear an ID bracelet or medal to alert caregivers.
w: “I can take penicillin again if I take an antihistamine first.”
A patient with a known allergy needs to avoid that medication in the future.
“I only need to mention the allergy if I am having surgery.”
The allergy is relevant whenever the patient receives medical care.
“My allergy will go away if I take smaller doses of penicillin.”
Repeated exposure does not remove the allergy; the drug must be avoided.

alt.q: Why should a patient with a known medication allergy wear an identification bracelet or medal?
alt.a: It alerts care providers to the allergy if the patient cannot communicate
alt.ex: An allergy bracelet or medal warns nurses and other providers when the patient is unable to communicate during care.
w: It allows the patient to receive the medication in smaller doses
Patients with a known allergy need to avoid the medication completely.
It replaces the need to record the allergy in the health record
The bracelet supplements, not replaces, documentation of the allergy.
It shows the patient has developed tolerance to the medication
Tolerance is a different concept from allergy.

items.q: When two medications have a [[synergistic|synergistic effect]] effect, their combined effect is greater than the effect of the medications given separately.
items.ex: A synergistic effect is a medication interaction in which the combined effect exceeds that of each drug alone.

alt.q: Alcohol has a [[synergistic|synergistic effect]] effect on antihistamines and narcotic analgesics, so together they cause greater central nervous system depression.
alt.ex: A synergistic effect is a medication interaction in which the combined effect exceeds that of each drug alone.

items.q: A patient taking a narcotic analgesic for back pain says, “I like to have a few drinks with dinner.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Alcohol greatly increases the depressant effect of your pain medicine, so avoid it.”
items.ex: Alcohol is a central nervous system depressant with a synergistic effect on narcotic analgesics, making the combined effect greater.
w: “A few drinks are fine because alcohol speeds excretion of the medicine.”
Alcohol does not speed excretion; it intensifies the narcotic’s depressant effect.
“Alcohol will block your pain medicine, so take a higher dose with dinner.”
Alcohol does not block the narcotic; together they cause greater depression.
“Alcohol is safe as long as you take the medicine on an empty stomach.”
Food timing does not prevent the synergistic depressant effect.

alt.q: With which medications does alcohol have a synergistic effect?
alt.a: Antihistamines, antidepressants, barbiturates, and narcotic analgesics
alt.ex: As a central nervous system depressant, alcohol has a synergistic effect on these medications.
w: Antibiotics, diuretics, vasodilators, and nitrates
These are not listed as medications with which alcohol is synergistic.
Opioid antagonists, steroids, antipyretics, and antibiotics
These are not the book’s examples of alcohol synergy.
Beta2-adrenergic agonists, nitrates, diuretics, and steroids
These are not the CNS-depressant combinations described.

items.q: Which example shows a medication interaction that health care providers intentionally create for a beneficial effect?
items.a: Combining diuretics and vasodilators to control high blood pressure
items.ex: Providers often combine medications so they act together, such as diuretics and vasodilators when one drug alone is not effective.
w: Combining alcohol and barbiturates to deepen a patient’s sleep
Alcohol and barbiturates have a dangerous synergistic depressant effect.
Giving two oral medications together that impair each other’s absorption
Interfering medications are given at different times, not combined.
Giving naloxone along with morphine for every scheduled pain dose
Naloxone reverses opioid effects and is used for toxicity, not routinely with morphine.

alt.q: What is a medication interaction?
alt.a: A situation in which one medication modifies the action of another
alt.ex: An interaction occurs when one medication increases, diminishes, or alters the absorption, metabolism, or elimination of another.
w: A situation in which a patient overreacts to a single medication
Overreacting to a single drug describes an idiosyncratic reaction.
A situation in which a patient needs higher doses over time
Needing higher doses over time describes tolerance.
A situation in which a medication acts as an antigen
A medication acting as an antigen causes an allergic reaction.

items.q: How is medication tolerance usually noted clinically?
items.a: The patient needs higher and higher doses to achieve the same therapeutic effect
items.ex: Tolerance develops over time and is seen when increasing doses are needed for the same effect.
w: The patient has intense physical disturbance when the medication is stopped
Intense physical disturbance on withdrawal describes physical dependence.
The patient desires the medication for a benefit other than its intended effect
This describes psychological dependence.
The patient overreacts or underreacts unpredictably to the first dose
Unpredictable reactions to a dose describe idiosyncratic reactions.

alt.q: Which group of substances is known to produce tolerance?
alt.a: Opium alkaloids such as morphine, nitrates, and ethyl alcohol
alt.ex: Opium alkaloids, nitrates, and ethyl alcohol are listed as medications that produce tolerance.
w: Antibiotics, antihistamines, and opioid antagonists such as naloxone
These are not the book’s examples of tolerance-producing substances.
Diuretics, vasodilators, and steroids such as prednisone
These are not listed as producing tolerance.
Beta2-adrenergic agonists, antipyretics, and antibiotics such as penicillin
These are not the listed examples of tolerance.

items.q: Patients hospitalized for acute illnesses usually develop medication tolerance within a few days.
items.a: False
items.ex: Hospitalized patients with acute illnesses usually do not develop tolerance; it may take a month or longer to occur.
items.ww: Tolerance develops over time, often a month or longer, so it is uncommon during short acute stays.

alt.q: Medication tolerance develops over time and may take a month or longer to occur.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Tolerance occurs over time, which is why patients hospitalized for acute illness usually do not develop it.
alt.ww: Tolerance is not immediate; it typically needs a month or longer to develop.

items.q: Which statement describes physical dependence on a medication?
items.a: A physiological adaptation that causes intense physical disturbance when the medication is withdrawn
items.ex: Physical dependence is a physiological adaptation shown by intense physical disturbance on withdrawal.
w: A desire for the medication for a benefit other than its intended effect
This describes psychological dependence.
A need for higher doses over time to achieve the same therapeutic effect
This describes medication tolerance, which differs from dependence.
An unpredictable overreaction to a usual dose of the medication
This describes an idiosyncratic reaction.

alt.q: A patient takes a sedative not for sleep but because it “makes everything feel better.” Which type of medication dependence does this describe?
alt.a: Psychological dependence
alt.ex: In psychological dependence, the patient desires the medication for a benefit other than the intended effect.
w: Physical dependence
Physical dependence shows as intense physical disturbance on withdrawal.
Medication tolerance
Tolerance means needing higher doses for the same effect.
Synergistic effect
A synergistic effect involves two medications acting together.

items.q: A patient’s serum level of a medication is below the minimum effective concentration (MEC). What does the nurse expect?
items.a: The medication will not produce its therapeutic effect
items.ex: The MEC is the plasma level below which the effect of the medication does not occur.
w: The patient is at high risk for toxic effects
Toxic effects occur at the toxic concentration, which lies above the therapeutic range, not below the MEC.
The medication is at its peak concentration
The peak is the highest serum level between doses, not a level below the MEC.
The medication has reached a steady plateau
A plateau is a level maintained within the therapeutic range by repeated fixed doses.

alt.q: Which term describes the plasma level of a medication below which the medication’s effect does not occur?
alt.a: Minimum effective concentration
alt.ex: Below the minimum effective concentration, the medication does not produce its effect.
w: Trough concentration
The trough is the lowest serum level reached just before the next dose, ideally still therapeutic.
Toxic concentration
The toxic concentration is the level at which toxic effects occur.
Biological half-life
Half-life is the time for excretion to lower the serum concentration by half, not a level.

items.q: When a medication is prescribed, the goal is to keep the blood level within which range?
items.a: Between the minimum effective concentration and the toxic concentration
items.ex: The safe therapeutic range falls between the MEC and the toxic concentration.
w: Between the trough concentration and the minimum effective concentration
Levels below the MEC produce no effect, so this range is not therapeutic.
Between the toxic concentration and the peak concentration
Levels at or above the toxic concentration cause toxic effects.
Between the onset of action and the biological half-life
Onset and half-life are time intervals, not plasma concentration levels.

alt.q: A medication’s therapeutic range is best described as the serum levels that lie between which two points?
alt.a: The level where effects begin and the level where toxic effects occur
alt.ex: The therapeutic range is above the minimum effective concentration and below the toxic concentration.
w: The level just before a dose and the level 30 minutes after a dose
These describe trough and peak timing, not the limits of the therapeutic range.
The level after the first dose and the level after the last dose
Therapeutic range is defined by effect and toxicity, not by first and last doses.
The level where toxic effects occur and twice that level
Any level at or above the toxic concentration is unsafe.

items.q: A patient receives IV vancomycin every 12 hours, and the next dose is due at 1000. A trough level is ordered. When should the nurse expect the trough level to be drawn?
items.a: At 0930, about 30 minutes before the dose
items.ex: The trough level is generally drawn 30 minutes before the medication is given, when the serum level is lowest.
w: At 1030, about 30 minutes after the dose
Shortly after an IV dose the level is near its peak, not its lowest point.
At 1000, immediately after the dose is hung
Right after an IV dose the level rises quickly toward its peak.
At 1600, halfway between the two doses
Midway between doses does not capture the lowest level, which occurs just before the next dose.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a patient whose vancomycin dose is adjusted using serum levels. When is the peak level drawn?
alt.a: When the medication is expected to reach its highest concentration
alt.ex: The peak level is drawn whenever the medication is expected to reach peak concentration, which varies with its pharmacokinetics.
w: Exactly 30 minutes before the next scheduled dose
Drawing 30 minutes before the dose measures the trough, not the peak.
At the same clock time every morning regardless of dosing
Peak timing depends on when the dose was given and the drug’s pharmacokinetics.
Only after the medication has been discontinued
Peak levels guide ongoing dosing, so they are drawn during therapy.

items.q: What is the biological half-life of a medication?
items.a: The time for excretion processes to lower the serum concentration by half
items.ex: All medications have a half-life, the time it takes excretion to reduce serum concentration by 50%.
w: The time for a medication to reach half of its highest concentration
Time to highest concentration relates to peak action, not half-life.
The time for half of an oral tablet to dissolve in the stomach
Half-life refers to serum concentration falling through excretion, not tablet dissolution.
The time for a medication to produce half of its therapeutic effect
Time to produce a therapeutic effect is the onset of action.

alt.q: A medication’s serum concentration falls from 40 mcg/mL to 20 mcg/mL in 6 hours because of excretion. What does the 6 hours represent?
alt.a: The medication’s biological half-life
alt.ex: Half-life is the time it takes excretion to lower the serum concentration by half.
w: The medication’s duration of action
Duration is how long the drug stays at a concentration great enough to produce a response.
The medication’s onset of action
Onset is the time after administration for the drug to produce a response.
The medication’s plateau
Plateau is a concentration maintained after repeated fixed doses, not a time for the level to halve.

items.q: A patient with cancer pain has been given oral opioid doses only when the patient asks for them, and the pain is poorly controlled. Which change should the nurse discuss with the health care provider?
items.a: Giving the pain medication on a fixed around-the-clock schedule
items.ex: A regular around-the-clock schedule maintains an almost constant medication level, which is often most effective for cancer pain.
w: Waiting until the pain is severe before giving each dose
Irregular dosing when pain occurs lets levels fall, making pain control less effective.
Giving the medication only at bedtime to promote sleep
A single daily dose cannot maintain a constant therapeutic level for ongoing pain.
Skipping doses whenever the patient is sleeping
Skipping doses lets serum levels fall below the therapeutic range.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a patient with cancer about an around-the-clock (ATC) pain medication schedule. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
alt.a: “Taking my doses on schedule keeps a steady level of medicine in my body.”
alt.ex: Regular fixed doses maintain an almost constant level and a therapeutic plateau.
w: “I should wait to take a dose until my pain becomes hard to bear.”
Waiting for pain to build describes irregular as-needed dosing, which is less effective for cancer pain.
“I can take two doses together if I forget one earlier in the day.”
Doubling doses can push levels toward toxicity; regular intervals are needed.
“The schedule matters less than how much I take at one time.”
Patients must follow prescribed doses at correct intervals to keep a steady level.

items.q: At 0900 a nurse is scheduled to give a medication the agency has identified as time critical. Within which time window must the nurse give it?
items.a: Between 0830 and 0930
items.ex: Time-critical medications must be given within 30 minutes before or after the scheduled time.
w: Between 0700 and 1100
A 1- to 2-hour window applies to non–time-critical medications.
Between 0800 and 1000
A 1-hour window is allowed only for non–time-critical medications.
Between 0845 and 1000
The window for time-critical medications is 30 minutes on either side of the scheduled time.

alt.q: Why must time-critical medications be given within 30 minutes of the scheduled time?
alt.a: Late or early doses are likely to cause harm or subtherapeutic effects
alt.ex: Time-critical medications most likely cause harm or have subtherapeutic effects if not given on time.
w: Late or early doses must be documented as a medication error
The reason for the window is patient harm, not documentation rules.
Late or early doses always lower the drug’s biological half-life
Timing of a dose does not change a medication’s half-life.
Late or early doses always cause the patient an allergic reaction
Timing errors risk harm or subtherapeutic effect, not allergy.

items.q: Within what time frame does the nurse give medications that the agency has classified as non–time critical?
items.a: Within 1 to 2 hours before or after the scheduled time
items.ex: Non–time-critical medications most likely do not cause harm if given within 1 to 2 hours of the scheduled time.
w: Within 30 minutes before or after the scheduled time
The 30-minute window applies to time-critical medications.
Within 4 to 6 hours before or after the scheduled time
A window this wide exceeds the 1 to 2 hours allowed by guidelines.
Within 10 minutes before or after the scheduled time
Even time-critical medications have a 30-minute window.

alt.q: A once-daily vitamin scheduled for 0900 is non–time critical. Which administration time is acceptable?
alt.ex: Non–time-critical medications may be given within 1 to 2 hours before or after the scheduled time.
w: 1230 is 3.5 hours late, beyond the 1- to 2-hour window.
0530 is 3.5 hours early, beyond the 1- to 2-hour window.
1400 is 5 hours late, far outside the allowed window.

items.q: An agency gives once-daily medications at 0800. A patient has a once-daily medication that works better when taken before bedtime. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Adjust the dose to bedtime following agency policy
items.ex: Nurses can change the agency schedule based on knowledge of a medication, following agency policy.
w: Give it at 0800 because agency times cannot change
Agency schedules can be adjusted when knowledge of the drug supports a different time.
Give half the dose at 0800 and half at bedtime
Splitting the dose changes the prescribed dose, which the nurse cannot do.
Omit the dose until a new agency schedule is created
Omitting a dose deprives the patient of therapy; the nurse adjusts the time instead.

alt.q: Which statement about agency medication administration schedules is accurate?
alt.a: Nurses may adjust a scheduled time based on knowledge of the medication
alt.ex: Agencies set schedules, but nurses can adjust times based on medication knowledge and agency policy.
w: Nurses must always follow agency times without exception
The book allows adjusting times, such as moving a dose to bedtime when it works better then.
Patients choose all their own medication times in acute care
Agencies set schedules, and nurses adjust them based on knowledge of the drug.
Pharmacists set an individual time for every single dose
Agencies usually set schedules; nurses may adjust them per policy.

items.q: A nurse is teaching an older adult about a new medication ordered twice daily. Which instruction is best?
items.a: “Take one dose in the morning and another in the evening.”
items.ex: Using familiar language, the nurse teaches twice-daily dosing as morning and evening.
w: “Take this medication BID as prescribed by your doctor.”
Abbreviations such as BID are unfamiliar to many patients.
“Take one dose whenever you feel you need it during the day.”
This describes as-needed (prn) dosing, not twice-daily dosing.
“Take two doses together with breakfast every morning.”
Taking both doses at once is not twice-daily dosing and changes the interval.

alt.q: Why does the nurse teach a patient to take a BID medication “in the morning and again in the evening”?
alt.a: Familiar language helps the patient follow the dosage schedule
alt.ex: When teaching dosage schedules, nurses use familiar language so patients understand and follow them.
w: Morning and evening are the only times oral drugs are absorbed
Absorption is not limited to these times; the wording simply makes BID easy to follow.
Medical abbreviations must never appear on any medication order
The point is understandable teaching, not a ban on abbreviations in orders.
Twice-daily drugs must always be taken exactly 12 hours apart
The teaching uses everyday times rather than exact clock intervals.

items.q: How do serum levels behave with an IV infusion compared with medications given by other routes?
items.a: The peak occurs quickly, and the level begins to fall immediately
items.ex: With IV infusions the peak concentration occurs quickly, but the serum level also begins to fall immediately.
w: The peak occurs slowly, and the level stays high for days
IV medications enter the bloodstream and act immediately, so the peak is rapid.
The peak never occurs because the drug bypasses the blood
IV medications go directly into the bloodstream.
The peak occurs only after the drug is absorbed from the gut
IV medications do not need GI absorption; they enter the blood directly.

alt.q: Which statement about medications given intravenously is accurate?
alt.a: They enter the bloodstream and act immediately
alt.ex: IV medications act immediately, whereas other routes take time to enter the bloodstream.
w: They take longer than oral drugs to enter the bloodstream
Oral drugs take time to be absorbed; IV drugs enter the blood directly.
They maintain a constant peak level for the entire day
After the rapid peak, IV serum levels begin to fall immediately.
They never require scheduled dosing intervals
Repeated IV doses still need correct intervals to maintain therapeutic levels.

items.q: After an initial dose, when does a patient on a regular schedule receive each successive dose to maintain a therapeutic plateau?
items.a: When the previous dose reaches its half-life
items.ex: To maintain a therapeutic plateau, each successive dose is given when the previous dose reaches its half-life.
w: When the previous dose reaches its toxic concentration
Reaching the toxic concentration causes toxic effects and must be avoided.
When the patient first notices the drug’s effects
Noticing effects reflects onset, not the timing for a successive dose.
When the drug has been completely excreted from the body
Waiting for complete excretion lets levels drop below the MEC.

alt.q: A nurse explains why a medication must be given at regular fixed intervals. Which explanation is accurate?
alt.a: Regular doses maintain a therapeutic plateau
alt.ex: Regular fixed doses keep the serum concentration at a plateau within the therapeutic range.
w: Regular doses prevent the medication from ever reaching a peak
Serum levels still fluctuate between peak and trough with repeated doses.
Regular doses shorten the medication’s biological half-life
Dosing intervals do not change a drug’s half-life.
Regular doses allow the drug to stay above the toxic level
Levels above the toxic concentration cause toxic effects.

items.q: Which time intervals should the nurse know to anticipate a medication’s effect? Select all that apply.
o: Onset of action
Onset is the time after administration for the medication to produce a therapeutic effect.
Peak action
Peak is the time for the medication to reach its highest effective concentration.
Duration of action
Duration is how long the drug stays at a concentration great enough to have an effect.
Plateau
Plateau is the level reached and maintained after repeated fixed doses.
Absorption rate of the oral tablet coating
This is not one of the listed time intervals of medication action.
Length of the patient’s hospital stay
Hospital stay length does not describe medication action.
items.ex: Onset, peak, trough, duration, and plateau are the time intervals that help nurses anticipate medication effects.

alt.q: A patient receives repeated doses of an antibiotic. Which statements about its serum levels are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Serum levels fluctuate between doses
When a drug is given repeatedly, its serum level rises and falls between doses.
The highest level is the peak concentration
The highest serum level between doses is called the peak.
The lowest level is the trough concentration
The lowest serum level, just before the next dose, is the trough.
The trough is the highest level reached after each dose
The trough is the lowest level, not the highest.
Serum levels stay exactly the same once given
Levels change constantly as the drug is distributed and excreted.
alt.ex: With repeated dosing, levels fluctuate between a peak (highest) and a trough (lowest).

items.q: Which statements about time-critical and non–time-critical medications are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Health care agencies determine which medications are time critical
Per CMS and ISMP guidelines, agencies decide which medications are time critical.
Time-critical medications are given within 30 minutes of the scheduled time
They must be given within 30 minutes before or after the scheduled time.
Non–time-critical medications are given within 1 to 2 hours of the scheduled time
These are unlikely to cause harm if given within 1 to 2 hours.
Time-critical medications may be given up to 2 hours late
A 2-hour delay could cause harm or subtherapeutic effects for time-critical drugs.
Non–time-critical medications may be given at any time of the day
They still must be given within 1 to 2 hours of the scheduled time.
items.ex: Agencies classify medications; time-critical drugs need a 30-minute window, non–time-critical drugs a 1- to 2-hour window.

alt.q: A nurse reviews agency timing policy. Which actions follow the guidelines? Select all that apply.
o: Giving a time-critical medication scheduled at 1200 at 1215
1215 is within 30 minutes of the scheduled time.
Giving a non–time-critical medication scheduled at 0900 at 1000
1000 is within the 1- to 2-hour window.
Following the agency’s policy on medication timing
Nurses follow agency policies so patients receive medications at the right time.
Giving a time-critical medication scheduled at 0800 at 0930
0930 is 90 minutes late, beyond the 30-minute window for time-critical drugs.
Giving a non–time-critical medication scheduled at 0900 at 1400
1400 is 5 hours late, beyond the 1- to 2-hour window.
alt.ex: Time-critical drugs are given within 30 minutes and non–time-critical drugs within 1 to 2 hours of the scheduled time.

items.q: Medications are ordered at various times. On which factors is the timing of doses based? Select all that apply.
o: When the medication’s response begins
Timing considers onset, when the response begins.
When the response becomes most intense
Timing considers peak, when the response is most intense.
When the response ceases
Timing considers when the response ends, its duration.
The color of the medication tablet
Tablet color has no bearing on when doses are ordered.
The time the patient’s visitors arrive
Visiting hours do not determine medication timing.
items.ex: Medications are ordered at times based on when their response begins, becomes most intense, and ceases.

alt.q: A nurse explains to a student why the times of medication doses vary. Which explanations are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Quantity of medication in body compartments changes constantly
Medication distribution changes constantly, so timing matters.
Routes other than IV take time to enter the bloodstream
Non-IV routes need time to reach the blood and have an effect.
Each drug differs in when its effect begins, peaks, and ends
Doses are timed by onset, peak, and end of response.
All medications reach their peak at exactly the same time
Time to peak varies with each drug’s pharmacokinetics.
Doses are timed only to match the nurse’s break schedule
Timing is based on drug action, not staff schedules.
alt.ex: Dose timing depends on drug distribution, the route, and when the response begins, peaks, and ends.

items.q: With repeated doses, the trough concentration is the lowest serum level, reached just before the next scheduled dose.
items.a: True
items.ex: The trough is the minimum serum concentration reached just before the next dose.
items.ww: This is accurate; the highest level between doses is the peak, and the lowest is the trough.

alt.q: The trough concentration is the highest serum level a medication reaches after each dose.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The highest level is the peak; the trough is the lowest level, just before the next dose.
alt.ww: It is false because the highest level is called the peak concentration, not the trough.

items.q: Oral medications enter the bloodstream and act as immediately as intravenous medications.
items.a: False
items.ex: Only IV medications act immediately; medications given by other routes take time to enter the bloodstream.
items.ww: It is false because oral drugs must be absorbed before they enter the blood, unlike IV drugs.

alt.q: Medications given by routes other than IV take time to enter the bloodstream and have an effect.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: IV drugs enter the bloodstream directly, whereas drugs given by other routes need time to reach it.
alt.ww: This is accurate; only IV medications enter the bloodstream and act immediately.

items.q: Doses of some medications, such as vancomycin, are based on peak and trough serum levels.
items.a: True
items.ex: Peak and trough levels guide dosing of some medications such as vancomycin.
items.ww: This is accurate; the book names vancomycin as a drug dosed by peak and trough levels.

alt.q: Vancomycin doses are set once and are not adjusted according to serum drug levels.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Vancomycin doses are based on peak and trough serum levels.
alt.ww: It is false because peak and trough levels are used to guide vancomycin dosing.

items.q: The time it takes for excretion processes to lower the serum medication concentration by half is called the biological [[half-life|half life]].
items.ex: Every medication has a half-life; successive doses are timed to it to maintain a plateau.

alt.q: After an initial dose, each successive dose is given when the previous dose reaches its [[half-life|half life]].
alt.ex: Every medication has a half-life; successive doses are timed to it to maintain a plateau.

items.q: A patient has a nasogastric tube connected to gastric suction. A new order is written for an oral tablet. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Contact the health care provider to discuss another route
items.ex: Oral medications cannot be given when patients have gastric suction, so the nurse works with the provider to choose a route.
w: Crush the tablet and give it through the suction tube
Medication given into a tube on suction would be removed before it acts.
Give the tablet by mouth with a small sip of water
Oral administration is not possible with gastric suction in place.
Hold the medication until the patient’s next shift
Simply holding the drug delays therapy without resolving the route problem.

alt.q: For which patient is the oral route of medication administration appropriate?
alt.a: A patient who is alert and able to swallow
alt.ex: The oral route is easy, convenient, and economical for alert patients who can swallow.
w: A patient who is unconscious after a head injury
Oral medications are contraindicated in patients who are unconscious.
A patient who is vomiting after surgery
The oral route is avoided when GI function is altered by nausea or vomiting.
A patient with an esophageal stricture
Patients unable to swallow because of esophageal strictures cannot take oral drugs.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient about sublingual nitroglycerin. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I will let the tablet dissolve under my tongue and not drink until it’s gone.”
items.ex: Patients must not swallow a sublingual medication or drink anything until it is completely dissolved.
w: “I will swallow the tablet with a full glass of water.”
Swallowing a sublingual tablet prevents the intended absorption under the tongue.
“I will hold the tablet against my cheek until it is gone.”
Placing a tablet against the cheek describes the buccal route.
“I will chew the tablet so it dissolves under my tongue faster.”
Chewing leads to swallowing; the tablet should dissolve under the tongue.

alt.q: Where does the nurse place a medication ordered by the sublingual route?
alt.a: Under the tongue until it dissolves
alt.ex: Sublingual medications such as nitroglycerin are absorbed after dissolving under the tongue.
w: Against the mucous membranes of the cheek
This describes buccal administration.
On the back of the tongue to be swallowed
Sublingual drugs are not swallowed.
Inside the lower eyelid like a contact lens
This resembles intraocular disk placement.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient about a buccal medication. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I will place each dose in the opposite cheek from the last one.”
items.ex: Patients alternate cheeks with each dose to avoid mucosal irritation.
w: “I will chew the tablet before placing it against my cheek.”
Patients should not chew buccal medications.
“I will drink water while the tablet dissolves in my cheek.”
Patients should not take liquids with a buccal medication.
“I will put every dose in my right cheek so I remember it.”
Using the same cheek each time causes mucosal irritation.

alt.q: Why does the nurse instruct a patient to alternate cheeks with each dose of a buccal medication?
alt.a: To avoid irritating the mucosa
alt.ex: Alternating cheeks with each subsequent dose prevents mucosal irritation.
w: To speed the medication’s onset of action
Alternating cheeks protects the mucosa; it is not meant to speed onset.
To prevent the tablet from being swallowed
Alternating sites does not prevent swallowing; patients are told not to swallow it.
To improve the medication’s unpleasant taste
Taste is not the reason; mucosal irritation is.

items.q: A patient has a bleeding tendency. Which route should the nurse anticipate the health care provider will avoid for a new medication?
items.a: Intramuscular
items.ex: Subcutaneous, IM, and intradermal routes are avoided in patients with bleeding tendencies.
w: Oral
The oral route does not involve a needle stick, so bleeding risk is not a contraindication.
Transdermal
Transdermal patches are applied to the skin without injection.
Inhalation
Inhaled medications are not injected and do not risk bleeding at a site.

alt.q: Which group of routes is avoided in patients with bleeding tendencies?
alt.a: Subcutaneous, intramuscular, and intradermal
alt.ex: Injections into tissue are avoided in patients with bleeding tendencies because of tissue bleeding risk.
w: Oral, buccal, and sublingual
These routes are given by mouth and do not puncture tissue.
Topical, transdermal, and inhalation
These routes do not involve needlesticks into tissue.
Eyedrops, eardrops, and nose drops
Instillations into body cavities do not puncture tissue.

items.q: A critically ill patient has poor peripheral perfusion. Which route does the nurse expect for parenteral medications?
items.a: Intravenous
items.ex: When peripheral perfusion is poor, the IV route is preferred over injections.
w: Intramuscular
Poor perfusion reduces absorption from muscle, so IV is preferred.
Subcutaneous
Poor perfusion limits absorption from subcutaneous tissue.
Intradermal
The intradermal route absorbs slowly and is not used for critical illness therapy.

alt.q: Which is an advantage of IV infusion compared with other parenteral injections?
alt.a: It delivers medication when a patient is critically ill
alt.ex: IV infusion provides medication delivery during critical illness or long-term therapy and when perfusion is poor.
w: It carries no risk of introducing infection
All parenteral routes carry a risk of introducing infection.
It has a lower absorption rate than IM injection
IV and IM routes have higher absorption rates, raising reaction risk.
It rarely causes anxiety in patients or children
Parenteral routes often cause considerable anxiety, especially in children.

items.q: A patient receives a continuous intraarterial infusion of a clot-dissolving agent. Which nursing action is the priority?
items.a: Monitor the integrity of the infusion system to prevent disconnection
items.ex: The nurse monitors the system carefully because an inadvertent disconnection can cause bleeding.
w: Teach the patient to adjust the infusion rate as needed
The nurse manages the infusion; patients do not adjust clot-dissolving infusions.
Remove the arterial catheter at the end of each shift
The catheter remains in place while the continuous infusion runs.
Flush the catheter with the agent every hour for patency
Unordered flushing with a clot-dissolving drug is unsafe and not described.

alt.q: Why does the nurse carefully monitor the system delivering an intraarterial clot-dissolving infusion?
alt.a: A disconnection could lead to bleeding
alt.ex: Inadvertent disconnection of an intraarterial system with a clot-dissolving agent can cause bleeding.
w: A disconnection could cause an air embolism in the brain
The book’s stated concern is bleeding from disconnection.
A disconnection could make the medication toxic
Disconnection does not change drug toxicity; it risks bleeding.
A disconnection could convert it to an oral dose
The route does not change; disconnection risks bleeding.

items.q: In which situation is the intraosseous route used most often?
items.a: An infant whose intravascular space is hard to access
items.ex: Intraosseous infusion into bone marrow is used most in infants and toddlers with poor access or in emergencies when IV access is impossible.
w: A teenager who needs long-term pain control at home
Long-term pain control is more often given intrathecally or by other routes.
An adult receiving regional analgesia for surgery
Regional surgical analgesia is given by the epidural route.
A patient who needs chemotherapy in the pleural space
Medications into the pleural space are given by the intrapleural route.

alt.q: A nurse explains intraosseous medication administration. Where is the medication infused?
alt.a: Directly into the bone marrow
alt.ex: Intraosseous administration infuses medication directly into the bone marrow.
w: Into the subarachnoid space
Medication into the subarachnoid space is intrathecal.
Into the peritoneal cavity
Medication into the peritoneal cavity is intraperitoneal.
Into the epidural space
Medication into the epidural space is given by the epidural route.

items.q: How do oral medications compare with parenteral medications?
items.a: They have a slower onset and a more prolonged effect
items.ex: Oral medications have a slower onset of action and a more prolonged effect than parenteral medications.
w: They have a faster onset and a shorter effect
Parenteral routes, not oral, have faster absorption.
They have a faster onset and a more prolonged effect
Oral drugs take time to be absorbed, so onset is slower.
They have a slower onset and a shorter effect
Oral drugs have a more prolonged effect than parenteral drugs.

alt.q: Which statement about the oral route is accurate?
alt.a: It is the easiest and most often used route
alt.ex: The oral route is the easiest and most often used, and patients generally prefer it.
w: It is the fastest route to produce an effect
Oral drugs have a slower onset than parenteral drugs.
It is the route patients like least
Patients generally prefer the oral route.
It is the most expensive route to use
The oral route is economical; some parenteral drugs are expensive.

items.q: Why are inhaled medications absorbed readily and work rapidly?
items.a: The alveolar-capillary network is richly vascular
items.ex: The deeper respiratory passages provide a large surface area and a rich alveolar-capillary network for absorption.
w: The upper airway mucosa has few blood vessels
Absorption is rapid because of rich vascularity, not sparse vessels.
The medications are swallowed into the stomach
Inhaled drugs are absorbed in the lungs, not the stomach.
The medications bypass the circulation entirely
Inhaled drugs are absorbed into the pulmonary circulation and can act systemically.

alt.q: Which statement about the inhalation route is accurate?
alt.a: Inhaled medications can have local or systemic effects
alt.ex: Many inhaled medications have local or systemic effects because absorption is rapid.
w: Inhaled medications can be given only through the nose
They can be given through nasal and oral passages or endotracheal and tracheostomy tubes.
Inhaled medications are absorbed slowly in the lungs
The large, vascular surface of the lungs allows rapid absorption.
Inhaled medications never cause systemic effects
Some inhaled local agents cause serious systemic effects.

items.q: A patient with an eye infection has a new order for an intraocular medication disk. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Clarify the order because the disk is contraindicated in eye infections
items.ex: Intraocular disks are contraindicated in eye infections, so the nurse checks the order with the provider.
w: Insert the disk and leave it in place for up to 1 week
Inserting it would ignore the contraindication of an eye infection.
Insert the disk into the eye that does not have the infection
The order should be clarified rather than altered by the nurse.
Teach the patient to insert the disk after the first dose
Teaching is premature when the disk is contraindicated.

alt.q: Which is an advantage of an intraocular medication disk over eyedrops?
alt.a: It does not require frequent administration
alt.ex: The disk stays in place for up to 1 week, so it avoids the frequent administration eyedrops need.
w: It is less expensive than eyedrops
Intraocular disk medication is expensive.
It is safe to use in eye infections
Disks are contraindicated in eye infections.
It causes no local reactions in the eye
Local reactions are possible with intraocular disks.

items.q: A physician instills a medication into the pleural space to help resolve a persistent pleural effusion by promoting adhesion of the visceral and parietal pleura. What is this procedure called?
items.a: Pleurodesis
items.ex: Pleurodesis promotes adhesion between the visceral and parietal pleura to resolve persistent pleural effusion.
w: Paracentesis
Paracentesis is not the intrapleural procedure the book describes for adhering the pleura.
Pleural irrigation
Irrigation flushes a cavity without retaining fluid and does not describe adhering the pleura.
Thoracic instillation
This is not the book’s term for promoting pleural adhesion.

alt.q: Which medications are most commonly given by the intrapleural route?
alt.a: Chemotherapeutic agents
alt.ex: Chemotherapeutic agents are the most common medications given intrapleurally by syringe and needle or chest tube.
w: Clot-dissolving agents
Clot-dissolving agents are typically given by the intraarterial route.
Regional anesthetics
Regional analgesia is given by the epidural route.

Eye medications are given by eyedrops or an intraocular disk.

items.q: Which practices help prevent errors when writing or reading metric doses? Select all that apply.
o: Placing a zero in front of a decimal, such as 0.25
A leading zero makes the decimal point more visible.
Writing whole-number doses without a trailing zero, such as 5
Trailing zeros risk a tenfold overdose if the decimal is missed.
Converting fractions to decimals, such as 0.5 g
Fractions are converted to decimals to prevent errors.
Writing doses as fractions, such as ½ g
Fractions are a source of medication errors and should be avoided.
Adding a zero after the decimal, such as 5.0
Trailing zeros should never be used.
items.ex: Use leading zeros, avoid trailing zeros, and convert fractions to decimals to prevent dose errors.

alt.q: A nurse reviews orders for safe notation. Which doses are written correctly? Select all that apply.

This decimal has a leading zero rather than a fraction.

A leading zero is missing, so the decimal may be overlooked.
2.0 mg
The trailing zero could be misread as 20 mg.
alt.ex: Correct doses use leading zeros, no trailing zeros, and decimals instead of fractions.

items.q: A nurse teaches a family caregiver about measuring oral liquid medications at home. Which teaching points are accurate? Select all that apply.

Household measures are convenient but inaccurate.
Choose a device marked only in teaspoons and tablespoons
Devices should display only the metric scale.
items.ex: Caregivers should measure liquids with metric-only devices, never household spoons or cups.

alt.q: Which statements about household measurements are accurate? Select all that apply.

items.q: Which benefits of computerized physician order entry (CPOE) are supported by evidence? Select all that apply.
o: Standardizes practice
CPOE helps standardize practice.
Improves legibility of orders
CPOE reduces errors from poorly handwritten orders.
Alerts providers to side effects and drug-drug interactions
CPOE alerts and updates providers on side effects, interactions, and new orders.
Removes the need for nurses to check orders

Replaces the need for bar-code scanning at the bedside
Bar coding remains a last opportunity to identify an error.

alt.q: Which types of medication errors does CPOE help reduce? Select all that apply.

Work-arounds caused by a poorly designed BCMA system

items.q: Which actions help prevent medication errors in children? Select all that apply.

alt.q: Which statements about the formula method are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The formula must be memorized
Using the formula method requires memorizing the formula.
All measures must be in the same units and system
Convert measures to the same system before calculating.
The amount to administer is in the same unit as the amount on hand
Always express the amount to administer in the amount-on-hand unit.
The estimate is skipped because the formula is exact
Estimate first and compare it with the calculated answer.
The dose on hand is the amount the provider ordered
The dose ordered is what the provider prescribed; the dose on hand is what pharmacy supplied.
alt.ex: The formula method needs a memorized formula, matching units, and an answer in the amount-on-hand unit.

items.q: Which statements about choosing a dose calculation method are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Ratio and proportion, formula, and dimensional analysis are all acceptable
These three methods are described for dose calculation.
Use the method that is most logical and comfortable for you
Nurses use the method that makes most sense to them.
Use the same method consistently
Consistency with one method enhances accuracy.
Practice calculations to build confidence and reduce anxiety
Practice increases confidence in math skills.
Change methods with each problem to cross-check every dose
The book advises using the same method consistently.
Only dimensional analysis may be used for pediatric doses
Any of the three methods can be used for weight-based pediatric doses.
items.ex: Choose the most comfortable method, use it consistently, and practice to improve accuracy.

alt.q: Why do nurses need clinical calculation skills? Select all that apply.
o: Medications are not always dispensed in the ordered unit
Drugs come in standard dosages, such as 40-mg vials for a 20-mg order.
Nurses calculate intake and output
Equivalents are used when calculating intake and output.
Nurses calculate IV flow rates
Equivalents are used for IV flow rate calculations.
Pharmacists never provide conversion help
The pharmacist is a good resource for conversions.
Agencies do not provide equivalence tables
Tables of equivalent measurements are available in all agencies.
alt.ex: Nurses convert available units to desired doses and use equivalents for I&O and IV rates.

items.q: Dimensional analysis requires the nurse to memorize a formula before calculating a dose.
items.a: False
items.ex: Dimensional analysis needs no memorized formula; one equation and the same steps solve every problem.
items.ww: It is false because the formula method, not dimensional analysis, requires memorizing a formula.

alt.q: In dimensional analysis, the same steps are used to solve every medication calculation.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Dimensional analysis uses one equation and the same steps for every calculation.
alt.ww: This is accurate; no formula must be memorized.

items.q: When using the formula method, the nurse always expresses the amount to administer in the same unit as the amount on hand.
items.a: True
items.ex: The amount to administer is expressed in the same unit as the amount on hand, such as mL.
items.ww: This is accurate; mismatched units would produce a wrong or unlabeled dose.

alt.q: In the formula method, the amount to administer may be expressed in any unit the nurse prefers.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The amount to administer must be in the same unit as the amount on hand.
alt.ww: It is false because the unit must match the amount on hand.

items.q: To convert milligrams to grams, the nurse divides by 1000 and moves the decimal point 3 places to the left.
items.a: True
items.ex: Dividing by 1000 moves the decimal 3 places left, so 1000 mg = 1 g.
items.ww: This is accurate; multiplying by 1000 would convert grams to milligrams instead.

alt.q: To convert liters to milliliters, the nurse divides by 1000 and moves the decimal 3 places to the left.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: To convert liters to milliliters, multiply by 1000 and move the decimal 3 places to the right.
alt.ww: It is false because liters to milliliters requires multiplying, so 1 L = 1000 mL.

items.q: Dimensional analysis is also called the [[factor-label|unit-factor]] method.

alt.q: Another name for dimensional analysis is the [[unit-factor|factor-label]] method.
alt.ex: Dimensional analysis, or the factor-label method, uses one equation and the same steps for every calculation.

items.q: Which health care team member is authorized to prescribe medications by writing an order in the patient’s electronic health record?
items.a: Advanced practice registered nurse
items.ex: Physicians, advanced practice registered nurses, and physician’s assistants prescribe medications.
w: Licensed practical nurse
Practical nurses give medications under supervision; they do not prescribe.
Hospital pharmacist
Pharmacists prepare and dispense prescribed medications; they do not write the orders.
Staff registered nurse
Staff RNs administer and monitor medications but do not prescribe them.

alt.q: A new graduate nurse asks who may write medication orders on the unit. Which team member should the charge nurse name?
alt.a: Physician’s assistant
alt.ex: A physician, advanced practice registered nurse, or physician’s assistant may prescribe medications.
w: Pharmacy technician
Pharmacy technicians help stock and refill medications; they do not prescribe.
Charge nurse
A charge nurse administers and coordinates care but cannot prescribe medications.
Clinical pharmacist
Pharmacists dispense and give information about medications rather than writing orders.

items.q: How does computerized physician order entry (CPOE) prevent incomplete or illegible medication orders?
items.a: The provider must complete every required field before the order can be filled
items.ex: In CPOE the health care provider completes all computerized fields before the order is filled, so orders are complete and legible.
w: The pharmacist completes any missing fields before the order reaches the unit
Pharmacists check orders but do not fill in missing parts of a provider’s order.
The nurse rewrites each order on a paper form so it can be read clearly
CPOE removes the need to rewrite orders by hand; rewriting adds transcription risk.
The system sends every new order to a second provider who must cosign it
Cosigning applies to verbal and telephone orders, not routine CPOE entries.

alt.q: According to the chapter, which type of medication error is CPOE especially designed to reduce?
alt.a: Transcription errors from poorly handwritten orders
alt.ex: CPOE reduces ordering errors (wrong drug, dose, frequency) and transcription errors from poorly handwritten orders.
w: Errors from giving drugs to a patient with the same name
Patient identification errors are prevented by two identifiers and bar-code scanning.
Errors from crushing tablets that should be swallowed whole
Crushing errors are prevented by checking references or the pharmacist, not by order entry.
Errors from giving oral liquids by the intravenous route
Wrong-route oral liquid errors are reduced by enteral syringes and pharmacy preparation.

items.q: A health care provider standing at the bedside tells the nurse to give a medication and asks the nurse to enter it. What type of order is this?
items.a: A verbal order
items.ex: An order given in person by speaking to the nurse is a verbal order.
w: A telephone order
A telephone order is given over the phone, not in person.
A standing order
A standing order continues until canceled or a set number of days pass; it describes duration, not how it was given.
A STAT order
STAT describes urgency (give immediately, once), not the way an order was communicated.

alt.q: A health care provider calls the unit from home and orders a new medication for a patient. What type of order is this?
alt.a: A telephone order
alt.ex: An order for a medication or treatment made over the telephone is called a telephone order.
w: A verbal order
A verbal order is spoken to the nurse in person rather than given by phone.
A now order
A now order describes timing (within 90 minutes), not how it was communicated.
A prescription
A prescription is written for medications the patient will take outside the agency.

items.q: A nurse has just written down a telephone order for a new antibiotic. Which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Read the complete order back and receive confirmation from the provider
items.ex: After writing the order, the nurse reads it back and gets the provider’s confirmation to make sure it is accurate.
w: Give the first dose and then call the provider to confirm it
The order must be confirmed by read-back before any medication is given.
Ask another nurse to listen in and take the order instead
The nurse who took the order is the one who reads it back and confirms it.
Wait for the provider to cosign before writing anything down
The nurse documents the order now; the provider cosigns later, usually within 24 hours.

alt.q: A provider phones and says, “Give furosemide 40 mg IV now for Mr. Lee in room 12.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “I’ll read that back: furosemide 40 mg IV now for Mr. Lee, room 12. Is that correct?”
alt.ex: Reading back the complete order with patient identifiers and getting confirmation prevents misunderstandings.
w: “Got it, I’ll give the furosemide right away and chart it later on.”
Accepting an order without read-back and confirmation risks an error.
“Please text the order to the unit secretary so she can enter it.”
Only authorized staff take orders, and read-back with confirmation is required.
“I’ll give it once the pharmacist calls you back to confirm it.”
The receiving nurse, not the pharmacist, reads back and confirms the order.

items.q: Within what time frame does the health care provider usually countersign a telephone or verbal order?
items.a: Within 24 hours
items.ex: The provider countersigns telephone or verbal orders later, usually within 24 hours, per agency policy.
w: Within 1 hour
One hour is shorter than the usual time frame the book describes.
Within 8 hours
Eight hours is not the usual time frame; it is usually 24 hours.
Within 72 hours
Seventy-two hours exceeds the usual 24-hour time frame.

alt.q: After a nurse documents a verbal order and signs it, who must sign the order later, and usually when?

alt.ex: The health care provider who gave the order cosigns it, usually within 24 hours.

The provider who gave the order, not another nurse, must countersign it.
The pharmacist, usually within 12 hours
Pharmacists check orders but do not countersign a provider’s verbal order.
The provider who gave it, usually within 7 days

items.q: A nursing student caring for a patient answers the phone, and the patient’s health care provider begins to give a new medication order. Which response by the student is best?

“Go ahead; I’ll write it as a verbal order and give the first dose.”

“I’ll take the order now and have the pharmacist verify it later.”
Pharmacist review does not make it acceptable for a student to take an order.

alt.q: A nursing student sees a new medication order on a patient’s record. When may the student give the medication?
alt.a: After a registered nurse has written and verified the order
alt.ex: Students give newly ordered medications only after an RN has written and verified the order.
w: As soon as the student reads the order back to the provider
Students cannot take or confirm orders; an RN must write and verify them.
After the pharmacist has delivered the medication to the unit
Delivery of the drug does not mean an RN has verified the order.
After the student’s instructor enters the order into the record

alt.q: Nursing students give a newly ordered medication only after a registered nurse has written and verified the order.

alt.ww: Students cannot take orders and must wait for RN verification of new orders.

items.q: A nurse authorized by agency policy is receiving a telephone order. Which actions follow the guidelines for telephone and verbal orders? Select all that apply.

Clear identification prevents giving the order for the wrong patient.
Read back the entire order to the health care provider
Read-back confirms that the order was heard and recorded correctly.

The provider’s name and the nurse’s name are both signed on the order.

items.q: An order reads “Insulin regular 4 U subcut before meals.” Why is the abbreviation “U” on the do-not-use list?

Write “IU” after the number
