That's step 4 of 5.
Provider countersigns the order, usually within 24 hours
That's step 5 of 5.

alt.q: In taking a telephone order, which step comes right before “Nurse records the time and the provider’s name and signs”?
alt.a: Provider confirms the order is accurate
alt.ex: That's step 3 of 5. The nurse records and reads back the order, gets confirmation, documents and signs, and the provider countersigns later.
w: Nurse reads the order back to the provider
That's step 2 of 5.
Nurse writes or enters the complete order
That's step 1 of 5.
Provider countersigns the order, usually within 24 hours
That's step 5 of 5.

alt.q: In taking a telephone order, which step comes right before “Provider countersigns the order, usually within 24 hours”?
alt.a: Nurse records the time and the provider’s name and signs
alt.ex: That's step 4 of 5. The nurse records and reads back the order, gets confirmation, documents and signs, and the provider countersigns later.
w: Provider confirms the order is accurate
That's step 3 of 5.
Nurse reads the order back to the provider
That's step 2 of 5.
Nurse writes or enters the complete order
That's step 1 of 5.

ord.q: Put the steps for handling a telephone order in the order the chapter describes.
items: Nurse writes or enters the complete order
Nurse reads the order back to the provider
Provider confirms the order is accurate
Nurse records the time and the provider’s name and signs
Provider countersigns the order, usually within 24 hours
ord.ex: The nurse records and reads back the order, gets confirmation, documents and signs, and the provider countersigns later.

items.q: A nurse is accepting a verbal order during a busy shift. Which agency practice may also be required, depending on agency policy?
items.a: Documenting the read-back or having two nurses review and sign
items.ex: Some agencies require documentation of the read-back or two nurses to review and sign telephone or verbal orders.
w: Having the pharmacist cosign the order within 1 hour
Pharmacists do not cosign orders; the provider does, usually within 24 hours.
Recording the order only after the first dose is given
The order is documented and confirmed before the medication is given.
Having the patient sign the order to show agreement
Patients do not sign medication orders; the provider and nurse do.

alt.q: Who determines which staff members are authorized to receive and document telephone or verbal orders?
alt.a: The health care agency, in writing
alt.ex: The agency identifies in writing which staff are authorized to receive telephone or verbal orders.
w: The individual provider, by phone
Authorization is set by agency policy, not by each provider at the time of a call.
The charge nurse, at each shift
The charge nurse follows agency policy rather than setting authorization each shift.
The pharmacist, after each order
Pharmacists check orders but do not authorize who may receive them.

items.q: A nurse reviews new orders. Which orders contain an error-prone designation that needs clarification? Select all that apply.
o: Digoxin .125 mg PO daily
A missing leading zero lets .125 be misread as 125.
Lorazepam 1.0 mg IV once
A trailing zero lets 1.0 mg be read as 10 mg.
Insulin regular 6 U subcut before meals
“U” can be misread as 0 or 4, causing an overdose.
Heparin 5,000 units subcut every 12 hours
“Units” is written out in full, which is the safe form.
Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV every 2 hours as needed
The drug name is spelled out and the dose has no trailing zero.
items.ex: Missing leading zeros, trailing zeros, and the abbreviation U are on the do-not-use list.

alt.q: Which order entries follow the safe abbreviation and dose guidelines? Select all that apply.
o: Magnesium sulfate 2 g IV over 1 hour
The complete drug name is written, avoiding MgSO4 confusion.
Vitamin D 1,000 international units PO daily
International unit and daily are both written out in full.
Furosemide 0.5 mg/kg IV every other day
A leading zero is used and every other day is spelled out.
MSO4 2 mg IV every 2 hours as needed
MSO4 can be confused with magnesium sulfate; write the full name.
Levothyroxine 50 mcg PO QD
QD is prohibited; “daily” should be written instead.
alt.ex: Safe orders spell out drug names and frequencies, use leading zeros, and avoid trailing zeros and banned abbreviations.

sections.name: Types of orders in acute care agencies

items.q: Which description fits a standing order?
items.a: It is carried out until canceled by another order or a set number of days passes
items.ex: A standing order continues until the provider cancels it or the prescribed number of days has elapsed.
w: It is given once immediately and then automatically canceled
A single immediate dose describes a STAT order.
It is given only when the patient’s condition requires it
Giving a drug only when needed describes a prn order.
It is given once within 90 minutes of being received
Giving a drug once within 90 minutes describes a now order.

alt.q: A patient has the order “Decadron 10 mg daily × 5 days.” How is this order classified?
alt.a: Standing order
alt.ex: Standing orders may list a final date or number of doses, as this 5-day order does.
w: Single order
A single order is given once at a specified time, not daily for 5 days.
prn order
A prn order is given only when needed, not on a fixed daily schedule.
Now order
A now order is given once within 90 minutes, not for several days.

items.q: A patient’s blood pressure rises suddenly, and the health care provider orders “Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT.” How should the nurse carry out this order?
items.a: Give a single dose immediately and only once
items.ex: A STAT order means a single dose is given immediately and only once, often in emergencies.
w: Give a single dose within the next 90 minutes
Up to 90 minutes is allowed for a now order, not a STAT order.
Give the dose every hour until the pressure falls
STAT orders are one-time doses, not repeated until an effect occurs.
Give the dose when the patient next asks for it
Giving a drug when the patient needs it describes a prn order.

alt.q: Which situation most commonly leads a health care provider to write a STAT order?
alt.a: A sudden change in the patient’s condition
alt.ex: STAT orders are often written for emergencies when a patient’s condition changes suddenly.
w: A test that is scheduled for later in the week
Medications before a diagnostic test are usually single (one-time) orders.
A medication the patient will take after discharge
Medications for use outside the agency are ordered by prescription.
Ongoing treatment of a long-term condition
Ongoing scheduled treatment is ordered as a standing or routine order.

items.q: When a nurse receives a now order, what is the maximum time allowed to give the medication?
items.a: Up to 90 minutes
items.ex: A now order allows the nurse up to 90 minutes to give the medication, one time only.
w: Up to 15 minutes
Fifteen minutes is shorter than the time allowed for a now order.
Up to 30 minutes
Thirty minutes is the window for time-critical scheduled medications, not now orders.
Up to 4 hours
Four hours is much longer than the 90 minutes allowed for a now order.

alt.q: At 1300 a nurse receives the order “Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now.” By what time should the dose be given?
alt.ex: A now order must be given within 90 minutes, so 1300 plus 90 minutes is 1430.
w: This applies a much shorter window than the 90 minutes allowed.
Thirty minutes is too short; now orders allow up to 90 minutes.
Four hours exceeds the 90-minute limit for a now order.

items.q: A patient has the order “Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI.” How is this order classified?
items.a: Single (one-time) order
items.ex: A single order is given once at a specified time, as is common before diagnostic examinations.
w: Standing (routine) order
Standing orders repeat until canceled or until a set number of days passes.
prn (as-needed) order
A prn order depends on the patient’s need, not on a scheduled event.
STAT (immediate) order
A STAT order is given immediately, not when another department calls.

alt.q: For which purpose are single (one-time) orders commonly written?
alt.a: Preoperative medications or medications before diagnostic examinations
alt.ex: Single orders are common for preoperative medications and medications given before diagnostic examinations.
w: Emergency medications needed for a sudden change in condition
Emergency single doses given immediately are STAT orders.
Medications the patient will continue taking at home
Home medications are ordered by prescription.
Medications given only when the patient reports symptoms
Medications given when symptoms occur are prn orders.

items.q: Which example matches a STAT order?
items.a: Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT
items.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.
w: Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now
That goes with Now order.
Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI
That goes with Single order.
Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain
That goes with prn order.

alt.q: Which example matches a Now order?
alt.a: Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now
alt.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.
w: Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT
That goes with STAT order.
Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI
That goes with Single order.
Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain
That goes with prn order.

alt.q: Which example matches a Single order?
alt.a: Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI
alt.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.
w: Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT
That goes with STAT order.
Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now
That goes with Now order.
Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain
That goes with prn order.

alt.q: Which example matches a prn order?
alt.a: Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain
alt.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.
w: Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT
That goes with STAT order.
Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now
That goes with Now order.
Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI
That goes with Single order.

alt.q: Which example matches a Standing order?
alt.a: Tetracycline 500 mg PO q6h
alt.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.
w: Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT
That goes with STAT order.
Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now
That goes with Now order.
Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI
That goes with Single order.

alt.q: Which type of order is “Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT”?
alt.a: STAT order
alt.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.
w: Now order
Now order: Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now.
Single order
Single order: Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI.
prn order
prn order: Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain.

alt.q: Which type of order is “Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now”?
alt.a: Now order
alt.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.
w: STAT order
STAT order: Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT.
Single order
Single order: Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI.
prn order
prn order: Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain.

alt.q: Which type of order is “Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI”?
alt.a: Single order
alt.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.
w: STAT order
STAT order: Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT.
Now order
Now order: Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now.
prn order
prn order: Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain.

alt.q: Which type of order is “Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain”?
alt.a: prn order
alt.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.
w: STAT order
STAT order: Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT.
Now order
Now order: Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now.
Single order
Single order: Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI.

alt.q: Which type of order is “Tetracycline 500 mg PO q6h”?
alt.a: Standing order
alt.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.
w: STAT order
STAT order: Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT.
Now order
Now order: Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now.
Single order
Single order: Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI.

mt.q: Match each type of medication order with its example from the chapter.
pairs: Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI
Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain
mt.ex: Orders are classified by the frequency and urgency of administration.

items.q: A patient has “Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain.” The last dose was given 1 hour ago, and the patient now reports severe incisional pain. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Contact the health care provider to obtain a STAT order
items.ex: When a patient needs a medication before the prn interval has elapsed, the nurse may need to obtain a STAT order.
w: Give 2 mg now because the order says as needed
The q2h order requires at least 2 hours between doses.
Give 1 mg now and 1 mg at the 2-hour mark
The nurse cannot change the ordered dose or interval without a new order.
Tell the patient to wait another hour for a dose
Ignoring severe pain is not appropriate; the provider should be contacted.

alt.q: What does the order “Morphine sulfate 2 mg IV q2h prn for incisional pain” allow the nurse to do?
alt.a: Give a dose for incisional pain, at least 2 hours apart
alt.ex: The patient may receive the drug for incisional pain but must wait at least 2 hours between doses.
w: Give a dose every 2 hours around the clock
prn means as needed, not on a fixed schedule.
Give a dose for any pain, at least 1 hour apart
The order is for incisional pain and requires a 2-hour interval.
Give one dose within 2 hours, then stop
This describes a one-time order rather than a repeating prn order.

items.q: A patient with a prn analgesic order asks for pain medication. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess the severity of the patient’s pain
items.ex: Objective and subjective assessment, such as pain severity, guides the decision to give a prn medication.
w: Give the dose because the patient requested it
The nurse uses assessment and clinical judgment before giving a prn drug.
Document that the dose was given for pain
Documentation follows assessment and administration, not before them.
Call the provider to confirm the prn order
A valid prn order does not need confirmation; assessment comes first.

alt.q: After giving a prn medication, what must the nurse document in addition to the time it was given?
alt.a: Assessment findings that show why it was needed
alt.ex: Documentation of prn doses includes assessment findings that show the need and the time given.
w: The name of the pharmacist who dispensed it
The pharmacist’s name is not part of prn documentation.
The time the next scheduled dose is due
prn doses are not scheduled; the nurse documents need and response.
The amount of drug left in the dispensing system
Inventory counts are not the documentation required for prn doses.

items.q: Which actions are part of safely administering prn medications? Select all that apply.
o: Use subjective and objective assessment to decide whether the dose is needed
Assessment and clinical judgment determine the need for a prn dose.
Document assessment findings that show why the dose was given
Documentation must show why the patient needed the medication.
Document the time the medication was administered
The time of administration is recorded for every prn dose.
Frequently evaluate and document the medication’s effectiveness
Evaluating effectiveness is required after giving a prn medication.
Give the medication at the same times each day so levels stay steady
Fixed scheduling describes standing orders, not prn orders.
Give the next dose as soon as the patient asks, regardless of the interval
The ordered interval between doses must be followed.
items.ex: Safe prn use requires assessment, documentation of need and time, and evaluation of effect.

alt.q: A nurse is deciding whether to give a prn medication. Which data can guide the decision? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s rating of pain severity
Subjective data such as pain severity guide prn decisions.
The patient’s measured body temperature
Objective data such as temperature guide decisions about prn antipyretics.
The time the last dose was given
The ordered interval must have elapsed before a prn dose is given.
The number of doses left in the patient’s drawer
Drug supply does not show whether the patient needs the medication.
The time the next standing medication is due
Standing medication times do not determine the need for a prn dose.
alt.ex: The nurse uses subjective and objective findings and the ordered interval to decide whether a prn dose is needed.

items.q: Range orders for prn medications, such as “morphine sulfate IM 5–10 mg every 4–6 hours,” are a source of medication errors.
items.a: True
items.ex: Unclear prn range orders are a known source of medication errors, so they must follow agency policy.
items.ww: Wide dose and time ranges leave the nurse uncertain how much to give and when.

alt.q: Range orders such as “morphine 5–10 mg every 4–6 hours” prevent errors because the nurse can choose any dose within the range.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Unclear range orders are a source of errors; a safer order ties the dose change to pain scale scores.
alt.ww: Choosing freely within a wide range is exactly what makes these orders error-prone.

items.q: Which prn order is written in the safer range format described in the chapter?
items.a: Increase morphine dose 50% to 100% if pain is moderate to severe on the agency pain scale
items.ex: Linking the dose increase to a pain scale rating gives clear criteria and is safer than a broad dose and time range.
w: Morphine sulfate 5–10 mg IM every 4–6 hours as needed for pain
This is the chapter’s example of an unclear range order that causes errors.
Morphine sulfate 2–8 mg IV every 1–3 hours as needed for pain
Broad ranges in both dose and interval are unclear and error-prone.
Morphine sulfate 4–10 mg PO every 3–6 hours when pain is reported
This still gives open ranges without criteria for choosing a dose.

alt.q: A nurse receives a prn order that includes a dose range. Which action should the nurse take?
alt.a: Make sure the order follows agency policy for range orders
alt.ex: If a range order is written, the nurse ensures it follows agency policy for these orders.
w: Always give the lowest dose in the range to be safe
The nurse follows agency policy rather than choosing a dose by habit.
Always give the highest dose in the range for comfort
Choosing the top dose without criteria can cause harm.
Ask the pharmacist to pick a single dose from the range
Pharmacists do not alter a provider’s order; agency policy guides range orders.

items.q: A patient has orders for “Docusate 100 mg PO TID prn constipation for two days and if no results then administer magnesium hydroxide 30 mL PO prn constipation.” The patient has taken docusate for 2 days without a bowel movement. Which action is appropriate?
items.a: Give magnesium hydroxide 30 mL PO as ordered
items.ex: The order states that magnesium hydroxide is given if docusate produces no results after 2 days.
w: Give both drugs together at the next scheduled time
The order uses the drugs in sequence, not together.
Continue docusate for 2 more days before anything else
The order specifies switching to magnesium hydroxide after 2 days.
Hold both drugs and wait for a new order
The existing order already says what to give when docusate fails.

alt.q: Why must orders for two prn medications with the same action specify when to use each one?
alt.a: So the nurse knows which drug to use and how they relate
alt.ex: Orders for multiple prn drugs with the same action identify when to use each and how to use them in relation to each other.
w: So the pharmacist can stock both drugs in one drawer
Stocking is not the reason; clear direction for the nurse is.
So the patient can choose whichever drug they prefer
The order, not patient preference, determines which drug is used.
So the nurse can give both drugs at the same time
The orders clarify the relationship, which often means not giving both at once.

items.q: A now order is given only one time.
items.a: True
items.ex: Now medications are administered only once, within 90 minutes of the order.
items.ww: A now order is not repeated; ongoing doses require a standing or prn order.

alt.q: A now order may be repeated every 90 minutes until the patient’s condition improves.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Now medications are given one time only, within up to 90 minutes.
alt.ww: The 90 minutes is the time allowed to give the single dose, not a repeat interval.

items.q: In some agencies, a patient’s preoperative medication orders are discontinued automatically, and the provider writes new orders after surgery.
items.a: True
items.ex: Some conditions, such as surgery, automatically change the status of medication orders in some agencies.
items.ww: Surgery can automatically end prior orders, so nurses follow agency policy for new orders.

alt.q: After surgery, all of a patient’s preoperative medication orders automatically resume in every agency.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: In some agencies preoperative orders are discontinued automatically and new orders are written after surgery.
alt.ww: Policies vary, and surgery can end prior orders rather than resume them.

items.q: How does a now order differ from a STAT order?
items.a: A now order is needed quickly; a STAT dose is given immediately
items.ex: A now order is used when a drug is needed quickly but not right away and allows up to 90 minutes.
w: A now order repeats; a STAT dose is given only once
Both now and STAT orders are given only one time.
A now order is for emergencies; a STAT dose is routine
STAT orders, not now orders, are used in emergencies.
A now order needs a cosign; a STAT dose does not
The difference between them is timing, not cosigning.

alt.q: A patient suddenly develops a life-threatening reaction, and the provider needs a drug given right away. Which order type fits this need?
alt.a: STAT order
alt.ex: A STAT order means a single dose is given immediately and is often used in emergencies.
w: Now order
A now order allows up to 90 minutes, which is too slow for an emergency.
Single order
A single order is given at a specified time, such as before a test.
Standing order
A standing order is for repeated doses, not an immediate emergency dose.

items.q: Why does a prescription include more detailed information than a medication order written in the hospital?
items.a: The patient must know how to take it and when to refill it
items.ex: Prescriptions are for use outside the agency, so the patient needs to understand how to take and refill the drug.
w: The pharmacist must know which nurse will give each dose
At home the patient, not a nurse, takes the medication.
The provider must document the patient’s diagnosis for billing
Billing is not the reason the book gives for added detail.
The nurse must know the patient’s scheduled hospital doses
Prescriptions are for medications outside the agency, not inpatient doses.

alt.q: A health care provider writes a prescription for an opioid. What may some agencies require for this prescription?
alt.a: A special prescription pad that differs from the usual pad
alt.ex: Some agencies require controlled substance prescriptions on a special pad, such as one of a different color.
w: A verbal order given to the nurse at discharge
A prescription is written; a verbal order is used within the agency.
A STAT order entered before the patient leaves
STAT orders are for immediate inpatient doses, not discharge prescriptions.
A pharmacist’s signature beside the provider’s
Agencies may require a special pad, not a pharmacist’s signature.

items.q: Which statements about standing orders are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They continue until the provider cancels them with another order
A standing order stays active until canceled.
They may end when a prescribed number of days has elapsed
Some standing orders run for a set number of days.
Some state a final date or number of doses
Some standing orders specify a final date or number of treatments.
Nurses need to know agency policy on discontinuing them
Agency policies govern when standing orders are discontinued.
They expire automatically at the end of each nursing shift
Standing orders last until canceled or until the time limit is reached.
They are given only when the patient asks for the drug
Giving a drug only when needed describes a prn order.
items.ex: Standing orders run until canceled or until a set time or number of doses is reached, per agency policy.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a patient’s orders. Which ones are standing (routine) orders? Select all that apply.
o: Tetracycline 500 mg PO q6h
A scheduled drug that repeats until canceled is a standing order.
Decadron 10 mg daily × 5 days
A standing order may list a set number of days.
Hydralazine 10 mg IV STAT
This is a STAT order given once immediately.
Lorazepam 1 mg IV on call to MRI
This is a single order given once before a test.
Vancomycin 1 g IV piggyback now
This is a now order given once within 90 minutes.
alt.ex: Standing orders are repeating scheduled orders, sometimes with a final date or number of doses.

items.q: An order for a medication to be given only when the patient requires it is called a [[prn|PRN|as-needed|as needed]] order.
items.ex: prn orders depend on assessment and clinical judgment of the patient’s need.

alt.q: Morphine ordered “q2h [[prn|PRN|as needed|as-needed]] for incisional pain” is given only when the patient needs it, at least 2 hours apart.
alt.ex: prn orders depend on assessment and clinical judgment of the patient’s need.

items.q: Which types of medication orders are given only one time? Select all that apply.
o: STAT order
A STAT order is a single dose given immediately and only once.
Now order
A now order is given once within up to 90 minutes.
Single order
A single order is given once at a specified time.
Standing order
A standing order repeats until canceled or a set time passes.
prn order
A prn order may be repeated whenever needed within the ordered interval.
items.ex: STAT, now, and single orders are one-time orders; standing and prn orders can be repeated.

alt.q: Which types of medication orders may result in more than one dose? Select all that apply.
o: Standing order
Standing orders continue until canceled or a set number of days passes.
prn order
prn doses can be repeated when needed, respecting the interval.
STAT order
A STAT order is given immediately and only once.
Now order
Now medications are given one time only.
Single order
A single order is given once at a specified time.
alt.ex: Standing and prn orders can produce repeated doses; STAT, now, and single orders are one time only.

items.q: What forms the basis for classifying medication orders in acute care agencies?
items.a: The frequency and urgency of administration
items.ex: The frequency and urgency of medication administration form the basis for types of medication orders.
w: The route and dosage form of the drug
Route and form are parts of an order but do not define the order type.
The cost and availability of the drug
Cost and supply do not determine the type of order.
The patient’s age and body weight
Age and weight affect dosing, not whether an order is STAT, prn, or standing.

alt.q: A hospitalized patient asks the nurse for the acetaminophen they take at home, but no order exists. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “I need an order from your health care provider before I can give it.”
alt.ex: A medication cannot be given to a patient without a health care provider order.
w: “I can give it once, since you take it at home already.”
Home use does not replace the need for a provider order.
“I’ll give it if the pharmacist says it is safe for you.”
Pharmacists do not write orders; a provider order is required.
“You can take your own supply as long as I chart it.”
Self-supplied drugs still require a provider order and agency policy.

items.q: A preoperative medication is ordered “on call.” When should the nurse give it?
items.a: When the operating room staff notify the nurse that they are coming
items.ex: An on-call medication is given when the operating room staff notify the nurse they are coming to get the patient.
w: At the exact time surgery is scheduled to begin
On-call timing depends on notification, not the scheduled start time.
As soon as the nurse receives the order
Giving it immediately describes a STAT order, not an on-call order.
After the patient arrives in the operating room
The dose is given on the unit when the call comes, before transport.

alt.q: A patient is ordered “Midazolam 2 mg IV on call to OR.” Which event signals the nurse to give the dose?
alt.a: A call from operating room staff saying they are coming
alt.ex: On-call doses are given when operating room staff notify the nurse they are coming for the patient.
w: The surgeon’s arrival at the hospital that morning
The surgeon arriving does not signal that the patient is about to be transported.
The patient’s request for something to help them relax
A dose given on patient request describes a prn order.
The start of the nurse’s morning medication pass
On-call timing is not tied to routine medication times.

items.q: What does the chapter identify as the pharmacist’s main task?
items.a: Dispensing the correct drug in the proper dose and amount with an accurate label
items.ex: Dispensing the correct medication, in the proper dosage and amount, with an accurate label is the pharmacist’s main task.
w: Writing medication orders after reviewing the patient’s health history
Writing orders is the role of the physician, APRN, or physician’s assistant.
Giving medications to patients and monitoring their effects at the bedside
Administering and monitoring medications is the nurse’s role.
Mixing most tablets and liquid compounds in the hospital pharmacy
Agency pharmacists rarely mix compounds except IV solutions.

alt.q: A team member’s main task is dispensing the correct medication in the proper dosage and amount with an accurate label. Who is this?
alt.a: The pharmacist
alt.ex: This is the pharmacist’s main task, distinct from prescribing and administering.
w: The health care provider
The health care provider prescribes medications rather than dispensing them.
The registered nurse
The nurse administers medications and monitors their effects.
The assistive personnel
Assistive personnel may not take part in medication administration.

items.q: Which type of preparation do pharmacists in health care agencies still commonly mix?
items.a: Intravenous solutions
items.ex: Agency pharmacists rarely mix compounds or solutions, except IV solutions.
w: Oral tablets
Medication companies deliver tablets ready for use.
Oral capsules
Capsules arrive from manufacturers in a ready-to-use form.
Topical ointments
Agency pharmacists rarely compound products other than IV solutions.

alt.q: Why do pharmacists in health care agencies rarely mix compounds or solutions?
alt.a: Most medications arrive from companies ready for use
alt.ex: Most medication companies deliver medications in a form ready for use, so mixing is rarely needed.
w: Nurses mix most compounds on the patient care unit
Nurses do not take over compounding; the drugs arrive ready to use.

w: Prescribes medications by writing orders

w: Prescribes medications by writing orders

Registered nurse: Administers medications and monitors their effects.

Pharmacist: Prepares, dispenses, and labels prescribed medications.

mt.q: Match each team member with their role in medication administration.
pairs: Prepares, dispenses, and labels prescribed medications
Administers medications and monitors their effects
Gives new medications only after an RN verifies the order

items.q: Pharmacists are responsible for making sure that the prescriptions they fill are valid.
items.a: True
items.ex: Pharmacists fill prescriptions accurately and are responsible for being sure prescriptions are valid.
items.ww: Checking validity is part of the pharmacist’s duty, not only the prescriber’s.

alt.q: Checking that a prescription is valid is solely the prescriber’s responsibility, so the pharmacist simply fills what is written.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Pharmacists are responsible for both filling prescriptions accurately and ensuring they are valid.
alt.ww: The pharmacist shares responsibility for validity rather than filling orders blindly.

items.q: Pharmacists work with nurses, physicians, and other health care providers to evaluate how well patients’ medications are working.
items.a: True
items.ex: Evaluating medication effectiveness is a shared role that includes pharmacists.
items.ww: Pharmacists collaborate beyond dispensing to evaluate effectiveness.

alt.q: Once a medication is dispensed, the pharmacist has no further role in evaluating its effectiveness.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Pharmacists work with the team to evaluate the effectiveness of patients’ medications.
alt.ww: The pharmacist’s role continues after dispensing through collaboration with the team.

items.q: A nurse must give medications through a patient’s feeding tube and is unsure whether a tablet can be crushed. Which action is best?
items.a: Check with the pharmacist before crushing the tablet
items.ex: A pharmacist advises whether a medication can be crushed or dissolved for enteral administration.
w: Crush the tablet, since most can be given by tube
Some tablets must not be crushed; verify before altering any form.
Hold the drug and record it as refused
The patient did not refuse; the nurse needs information, not to omit the dose.
Ask assistive personnel to dissolve it in water
Medication preparation cannot be delegated to assistive personnel.

alt.q: A patient with an enteral tube needs a medication available only as a tablet. Which action fits the chapter’s guidance?
alt.a: Ask the pharmacy whether a liquid form is available
alt.ex: Nurses check with pharmacy for liquid preparations; the provider may need to change the dosage form.
w: Crush the tablet and flush it through the tube
The nurse first checks whether a liquid form is available or crushing is safe.
Give the tablet by mouth instead of by tube
Changing the route without an order is a medication error.
Skip the dose until the patient can swallow
Omitting a dose is an error when a safe alternative may exist.

items.q: A patient takes a medication that interacts with food. Whom should the nurse consult when setting the administration times?
items.a: The health care provider or a pharmacist
items.ex: Nurses consult the provider or a pharmacist when setting medication times to achieve the therapeutic effect.
w: The dietary aide who delivers meal trays
Dietary aides do not give guidance on drug-food interactions.
The unit clerk who enters the orders
Clerical staff do not plan medication timing.
The assistive personnel who feed patients
Assistive personnel do not take part in medication administration.

alt.q: Before giving a new medication, a nurse wants to identify any medication-medication interactions. Which resources are appropriate?
alt.a: Drug references, package inserts, or a pharmacist
alt.ex: Nurses check pharmacology books, references, or package inserts, or consult pharmacists, to identify interactions.
w: The patient’s family members or visitors
Family may know the patient’s medications but are not a source of interaction data.
Assistive personnel or the unit clerk
These staff do not provide medication information.
The patient’s insurance formulary list
A formulary shows coverage, not drug interactions.

items.q: Which information do pharmacists provide to nurses and other health care providers? Select all that apply.
o: Medication side effects
Pharmacists provide information about side effects.
Medication toxicity
Pharmacists provide information about toxicity.
Drug interactions
Pharmacists provide information about interactions.
Drug incompatibilities
Pharmacists provide information about incompatibilities.
Medical diagnoses
Diagnosing is not part of the pharmacist’s role.
New medication orders
Health care providers, not pharmacists, write orders.
items.ex: Pharmacists provide information about side effects, toxicity, interactions, and incompatibilities.

alt.q: Which responsibilities belong to the pharmacist? Select all that apply.
o: Filling prescriptions accurately
Accurate filling is a core pharmacist duty.
Making sure prescriptions are valid
Pharmacists are responsible for prescription validity.
Dispensing drugs with an accurate label
Correct drug, dose, amount, and label is the main task.
Writing orders for new medications
Physicians, APRNs, and physician’s assistants write orders.
Giving medications at the bedside
Nurses administer medications and monitor effects.
alt.ex: Pharmacists fill and dispense prescriptions accurately with correct labels and ensure they are valid.

items.q: Why does the ISMP recommend that pharmacists, rather than nurses, prepare oral liquid medications that are not commercially available as unit products?
items.a: To lower the risk of giving an oral liquid by the wrong route, such as IV
items.ex: Oral liquids drawn into syringes by nurses carry a high risk of wrong-route (IV) administration, which can be fatal.
w: To lower the cost of oral liquids by buying them in bulk
The recommendation is about patient safety, not cost.
To lower the time nurses spend at the bedside during care
The aim is preventing wrong-route errors, not saving nursing time.
To lower the risk of bacterial contamination of the liquid
The chapter cites wrong-route errors, not contamination, as the reason.

alt.q: A nurse works where nurses must prepare oral liquid medications. Which equipment should the nurse use?
alt.a: Enteral syringes such as ENFit
alt.ex: If nurses must prepare oral medications, they use only enteral syringes to prevent wrong-route errors.
w: Standard Luer-lock syringes
Luer syringes fit IV lines and increase wrong-route risk.
Tuberculin syringes
Tuberculin syringes are parenteral syringes that can connect to IV lines.
Insulin syringes
Insulin syringes are for subcutaneous injection, not oral liquids.

items.q: Medication reconciliation is a process in which nurses, pharmacists, and other providers compare what the patient is taking with what the patient should be taking.
items.a: True
items.ex: During reconciliation, nurses, pharmacists, and other providers compare current, intended, and newly ordered medications.
items.ww: Reconciliation is interprofessional and includes the pharmacist.

alt.q: Medication reconciliation is a nursing-only task, so pharmacists are not consulted during transitions in care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Accurate reconciliation requires consulting the patient, family, other clinicians, and pharmacists.
alt.ww: Pharmacists are named as part of the reconciliation process.

items.q: After the nurse and pharmacist determine that a medication order is safe and appropriate, where is the order placed?
items.a: On the medication administration record (MAR)
items.ex: Once an order is judged safe and appropriate, it is placed on the MAR or eMAR, which nurses use to give medications.
w: On the patient’s discharge prescription form
Prescriptions are for medications taken outside the agency.
On the agency’s occurrence (incident) report
Occurrence reports document errors, not new orders.
On the patient’s nursing care plan (Kardex)
The MAR is the form used each time a dose is prepared.

alt.q: Who checks medication orders for accuracy and thoroughness several times during the transcription process?
alt.a: Nurses and pharmacists
alt.ex: Nurses and pharmacists check all medication orders for accuracy and thoroughness during transcription.
w: Unit clerks and pharmacy technicians
Clerical and technical staff do not carry this checking responsibility.
Nursing students and their instructors
Students cannot take medication orders.
Assistive personnel and nurses
Assistive personnel may not take part in medication administration.

items.q: A nurse must convert a home medication dose from metric to household measures. Besides an agency table of equivalents, which resource does the chapter recommend?
items.a: The pharmacist
items.ex: Tables of equivalent measurements are available in agencies, and the pharmacist is also a good resource.
w: The patient’s family member
Family members are not a reliable source for dose conversions.
The assistive personnel
Assistive personnel do not take part in medication administration.
The unit secretary
Clerical staff do not provide dose calculation help.

alt.q: A nurse must calculate a child’s medication dose using body surface area (BSA). Whom should the nurse consult?
alt.a: The health care provider or the pharmacist
alt.ex: Consult the provider or the pharmacist and a pediatric or pharmacology resource for BSA-based doses.
w: The child’s parent or guardian
Parents are not a source for BSA calculations.
Another nursing student
Calculations are checked with qualified staff, not students.
The unit charge clerk
Clerical staff do not help with dose calculations.

items.q: In a unit-dose system, what does the pharmacist supply to the nursing unit?
items.a: Single-unit packages holding the ordered dose for one administration
items.ex: Pharmacists provide single-unit packages containing the dose the patient receives at one time.
w: Bulk stock bottles that nurses pour from for each patient
Pouring from stock bottles is what the unit-dose system avoids.
A 7-day supply of each patient’s drugs in labeled bags
Unit-dose systems usually keep no more than a 24-hour supply.
Unlabeled tablets sorted into each patient’s drawer
Each unit-dose tablet or capsule is wrapped and labeled separately.

alt.q: In a unit-dose system, who distributes the single-unit medication packages to patients?
alt.a: Nurses
alt.ex: Pharmacists provide the single-unit packages, and nurses distribute the medications to patients.
w: Pharmacists
Pharmacists prepare and supply the packages but do not give them to patients.
Pharmacy technicians
Technicians may refill cart drawers but do not give medications.
Assistive personnel
Medication administration cannot be delegated to assistive personnel.

items.q: A pharmacist calls to tell the nurse that a newly ordered drug may interact with one the patient already takes. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Hold the drug and contact the health care provider about the order
items.ex: If an order may be inappropriate, the nurse consults the provider and does not give it until the seven rights are met.
w: Give the drug as ordered, since the provider wrote it
The nurse is legally responsible and must clarify a possibly unsafe order.
Ask the pharmacist to change the drug to a safer one
Only the prescriber can change a medication order.
Give half the dose and monitor the patient closely
Changing the dose without an order is a medication error.

alt.q: Which statement best describes how the pharmacist and nurse work together to keep medication orders safe?
alt.a: Both consider the patient’s problems, labs, and other drugs when checking orders

w: The pharmacist checks the orders so the nurse need not verify them

The nurse checks the orders so the pharmacist need not review them

items.q: In which situations should the nurse consult a pharmacist? Select all that apply.

Checking whether two IV medications are compatible
Pharmacists provide information about incompatibilities.
Converting a dose between measurement systems
The pharmacist is a good resource for conversions.
Obtaining a new order for an earlier analgesic dose
A new or STAT order must come from the health care provider.
Receiving a telephone order for a new medication
Telephone orders come from the provider and are taken by authorized nurses.
items.ex: Pharmacists advise on crushing, compatibility, and conversions; orders come from the health care provider.

alt.q: A nurse has several questions during a shift. Which ones are appropriate to direct to the pharmacist? Select all that apply.
o: Whether a capsule’s contents can be opened for a tube
Nurses consult the pharmacist about expressing capsule contents.
What the toxic effects of a new drug are
Pharmacists provide information about toxicity.
How a drug may interact with a patient’s meals
Pharmacists help identify medication-food interactions.
Whether to increase a patient’s ordered dose
Dose changes require an order from the health care provider.
Whether a nursing student may take a verbal order
Students may never take orders; this is not a pharmacy question.
alt.ex: Pharmacists answer questions about drug forms, toxicity, and interactions; order changes come from the provider.

items.q: Dispensing the correct medication in the proper dosage and amount with an accurate [[label|labeling]] is the pharmacist’s main task.

alt.q: The pharmacist’s main task is [[dispensing|to dispense]] the correct medication, in the proper dose and amount, with an accurate label.
alt.ex: An accurate label is part of correct dispensing, which is the pharmacist’s main task.

items.q: A nurse finds a unit-dose package from the pharmacy whose label is smeared and cannot be read. Which action is best?

Appearance is not a safe way to identify a medication.

alt.q: Why is an accurate label on each dispensed medication essential to the nurse?

alt.ex: Nurses compare the medication label with the MAR to verify the right drug and dose before administration.
w: The label replaces the need for a provider order
A provider order is required for every medication given.
The label lets the patient refill it in the hospital
Refill instructions apply to prescriptions for home use.
The label shows which nurse prepared the dose
The pharmacy label identifies the drug, not the nurse.

items.q: A nurse is about to give a medication that is unfamiliar. Which action best meets the nurse’s responsibility to know about each medication?
items.a: Review drug references and consult the pharmacist as needed
items.ex: Nurses gather drug information from references, package inserts, and pharmacists before giving medications.
w: Give the drug, since the pharmacist already checked it
The nurse is responsible for knowing about each drug given.
Ask the patient to explain what the drug is for
Patients can share history but are not the nurse’s drug reference.
Delay the drug until the next shift’s nurse can give it
Delaying care is unnecessary when information is readily available.

alt.q: Which list contains only resources the chapter names for gathering medication information?

alt.ex: The chapter lists pharmacology textbooks, medication manuals, journals, the PDR, package inserts, and pharmacists.
w: Package inserts, family members, and unit clerks
Family members and unit clerks are not named drug resources.
Pharmacists, assistive personnel, and visitors
Assistive personnel and visitors are not medication resources.
Pharmacology texts, social media, and visitors
Social media and visitors are not reliable medication resources.

items.q: A nurse and pharmacist are checking a new medication order during transcription. Which factors do they take into account? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s current problems
Current problems are considered when checking an order.
The patient’s treatments
Current treatments are considered when checking an order.
The patient’s laboratory values
Lab values are considered when checking an order.
The patient’s other prescribed medications
Other medications are considered when checking an order.
The patient’s room preference
Room preference has no bearing on the safety of an order.
The patient’s insurance carrier
Insurance coverage is not part of checking an order for safety.
items.ex: Nurses and pharmacists consider problems, treatments, lab values, and other medications before placing an order on the MAR.

alt.q: Before a new order is placed on the MAR, which checks do the nurse and pharmacist perform? Select all that apply.
o: Check the order for accuracy
Orders are checked for accuracy several times during transcription.
Check the order for thoroughness
Orders are checked to make sure they are complete.
Consider the patient’s lab values and other drugs
Labs and other medications affect whether an order is safe.
Rewrite the dose to match pharmacy stock
Only the provider may change an order; concerns are clarified.
Ask assistive personnel to confirm the order
Assistive personnel have no role in verifying medication orders.
alt.ex: Nurses and pharmacists check orders for accuracy and thoroughness, considering labs and other medications, before the MAR.

items.q: Which description fits a unit-dose system?
items.a: Single-unit packages containing the dose a patient receives at one time
items.ex: In a unit-dose system pharmacists provide single-unit packages of the ordered dose for one administration.
w: Large stock bottles from which nurses pour each patient’s dose
Stock bottles are what unit-dose systems replace.
Weekly blister packs that patients keep at the bedside
Unit-dose systems usually hold no more than a 24-hour supply.
Bulk bins of tablets that pharmacists sort at the bedside
Unit-dose tablets are individually wrapped, not sorted from bins.

alt.q: A nurse opens a patient’s drawer and finds each tablet and capsule wrapped separately with the ordered dose. Which system is in use?
alt.a: A unit-dose system
alt.ex: Unit-dose systems supply each tablet or capsule wrapped separately in the ordered dose.
w: A stock-supply system
Stock supply uses bulk containers, not individually wrapped doses.
A bar-code system
Bar-code medication administration is a scanning system, not a packaging method.
A CPOE system
CPOE is an electronic ordering system, not a way of packaging drugs.

items.q: In a unit-dose system, how much of each patient’s medication is usually available at one time?
items.a: No more than a 24-hour supply
items.ex: Usually no more than a 24-hour supply of medication is available at any given time.
w: No more than an 8-hour supply
The book describes a 24-hour supply, not one shift’s worth.
No more than a 72-hour supply
Three days exceeds the usual 24-hour supply.
No more than a 7-day supply
A week’s supply would defeat the goal of limiting stock on the unit.

alt.q: How often are the drawers in a unit-dose cart usually refilled?
alt.a: Once each day at a designated time
alt.ex: At a designated time each day, the pharmacist or a technician refills the drawers with a fresh supply.
w: Once each shift at shift change
Refilling occurs once daily, matching the 24-hour supply.
Once each week on a set day
A weekly refill does not match the 24-hour supply.
Only when a nurse reports a drawer empty
Refilling is scheduled daily, not on request.

items.q: Who refills the drawers in a unit-dose medication cart with a fresh supply?
items.a: The pharmacist or a pharmacy technician
items.ex: At a designated time each day the pharmacist or a pharmacy technician refills the cart drawers.
w: The charge nurse or the staff nurse
Nurses distribute the medications but do not restock the drawers.
The unit secretary or the clerk
Clerical staff do not handle medication supplies.
The assistive personnel on the unit
Assistive personnel may not take part in medication handling.

alt.q: How is each drawer in a unit-dose cart labeled?
alt.a: With the patient’s name and designated room
alt.ex: Each drawer is labeled with the patient’s name and the patient’s designated room.
w: With the nurse’s name and shift
Drawers are organized by patient, not by nurse.
With the drug’s name and dose
Drawers hold a patient’s drugs; individual packages carry drug labels.
With the provider’s name and date
Drawers are labeled for the patient, not the prescriber.

items.q: A nurse is preparing an opioid for a patient whose medications are in a unit-dose cart. Where will the nurse find the opioid?
items.a: In a larger locked drawer separate from patient drawers
items.ex: Controlled substances are not kept in individual patient drawers but in a larger locked drawer for security.
w: In the patient’s own labeled drawer with other drugs
Controlled substances are never kept in individual patient drawers.
In the open stock shelf of the cart for prn use
Controlled substances require locked, secure storage.
In the patient’s bedside table for easy access
Bedside storage would not keep controlled substances secure.

alt.q: Why are controlled substances kept in a separate, larger locked drawer of the unit-dose cart?
alt.a: To keep them secure
alt.ex: Controlled substances are kept in a larger locked drawer to keep them secure and prevent diversion.
w: To keep them cool
The chapter gives security, not temperature, as the reason.
To keep them dry
Moisture protection is not the reason for separate storage.
To keep them sterile
Sterility is not the purpose of the locked drawer.

items.q: Which benefits of the unit-dose system does the chapter describe? Select all that apply.
o: It reduces medication errors
Single labeled doses reduce errors.
It decreases the amount of medication stocked on units
Only about a 24-hour supply is kept.
It saves time for nurses and pharmacists
Prepackaged doses save time for both groups.
It removes the need to compare labels with the MAR
Nurses still check each label against the MAR.
It allows a week of medications to be kept on the unit
Usually no more than a 24-hour supply is available.
items.ex: The unit-dose system reduces errors, decreases stock in patient care areas, and saves time.

alt.q: Which features describe a unit-dose cart system? Select all that apply.
o: Each tablet or capsule is wrapped separately
Individual wrapping is a defining feature.
Each patient drawer is labeled with name and room
Drawers are labeled with the patient’s name and room.
The cart holds limited prn and stock medications
Limited prn and stock drugs are kept for special situations.
Controlled substances go in each patient’s drawer
Controlled substances are kept in a larger locked drawer.
Nurses repackage each dose for the next day
The pharmacist or technician restocks the drawers daily.
alt.ex: Unit-dose carts hold individually wrapped doses in labeled drawers, plus limited prn and stock drugs.

items.q: Medication storage areas must be locked when they are unattended.

alt.q: A medication cart may be left unlocked in the hallway as long as it is within sight of the nurses’ station.

alt.ww: Being visible from a distance does not mean attended; the cart must be locked.

items.q: While preparing medications at a portable cart in the hallway, a nurse is called into a room to help a patient. Which action should the nurse take first?

items.ex: Medication storage areas must be locked when unattended.
w: Ask a visitor to watch the cart until the nurse returns
Visitors cannot be responsible for securing medications.
Push the cart closer to the nurses’ station and leave it
An unattended cart must be locked wherever it is placed.
Take the opened medications along and leave the cart
The cart itself still needs to be locked when unattended.

alt.q: Which storage area for medications is consistent with the chapter’s guidelines?
alt.a: A computerized cabinet that stays locked when unattended
alt.ex: Computerized cabinets are a medication storage area, and all storage must be locked when unattended.
w: An open shelf at the nurses’ station for quick access
Open shelving does not keep medications secured when unattended.
A cart left unlocked in the hall during the med pass
An unattended cart must be locked.
A patient’s bedside drawer used for all scheduled drugs
Bedside drawers are not listed as secure agency storage areas.

items.q: How does a nurse gain access to an automated medication dispensing system (AMDS)?

w: By using a key kept by the charge nurse, with a sign-out log
AMDSs use security codes and bio-identification, not shared keys.
By calling the pharmacy, which opens the drawer remotely
The nurse accesses the system directly with a security code.
By scanning the patient’s armband, with no code required
A personal security code is required for each nurse.

alt.q: Before an AMDS dispenses a medication, what must the nurse select?
alt.a: The patient’s name and medication profile
alt.ex: The nurse selects the patient’s name and medication profile before the AMDS dispenses a medication.
w: The pharmacist’s name and phone number
The nurse selects the patient, not the pharmacist.
The provider’s name and order date
Selection begins with the patient’s name and profile.
The nurse’s shift and unit number
The nurse logs in with a code, then selects the patient.

items.q: In using an AMDS, which step comes right after “Select the patient’s name and medication profile”?

items.ex: That's step 3 of 4. The nurse logs in, selects the patient, then the medication; the system then opens, records, and charges.
w: The drawer opens, records the removal, and charges the patient
That's step 4 of 4.
Enter a personal security code or bio-identification
That's step 1 of 4.

alt.q: Which step comes first in using an AMDS?
alt.a: Enter a personal security code or bio-identification
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 4. The nurse logs in, selects the patient, then the medication; the system then opens, records, and charges.
w: Select the patient’s name and medication profile
That's step 2 of 4.
Select the drug, dosage, and route from the list
That's step 3 of 4.
The drawer opens, records the removal, and charges the patient
That's step 4 of 4.

alt.q: Which step comes last in using an AMDS?
alt.a: The drawer opens, records the removal, and charges the patient

The pharmacist’s name and the drug’s lot number
The book lists drug name, dose, time, and nurse’s name.
The patient’s response to the medication
The nurse evaluates and documents the patient’s response.

alt.q: After the nurse selects a medication in an AMDS, what does the system do?

w: Prints a new order and sends it to the provider

The drawer opens for the nurse after proper selection.
Gives the dose through the patient’s IV line
An AMDS dispenses medications; it does not administer them.

items.q: What does bar-code medication administration (BCMA) require the nurse to scan?
items.a: The patient, the medication, and the nurse’s identification tag
items.ex: BCMA requires scanning bar codes to identify the patient, the medication, and the nurse’s ID before documenting.
w: The patient, the MAR, and the pharmacist’s badge
The pharmacist’s badge is not part of BCMA scanning.
The medication, the cart, and the provider’s order
Scanning includes the patient and the nurse, not the cart.
The nurse’s badge, the room, and the provider’s ID
The patient and the medication must be scanned.

alt.q: How does bar coding medications linked to patient identification bracelets improve safety?
alt.a: It provides one last chance to catch an error
alt.ex: Bar coding linked to ID bracelets provides one last opportunity to identify a medication error.
w: It replaces the need to use two patient identifiers
Nurses still use at least two identifiers along with bar coding.
It lets the pharmacist give the dose remotely
Bar coding verifies doses; nurses still administer them.
It removes the need to check the label against the MAR
Label checks with the MAR are still required.

items.q: A nurse scans a patient’s armband, and the BCMA scanner will not read it. Which action is best?

items.ex: Nurses follow agency policies when technology cannot be used; work-arounds increase medication errors.
w: Override the alert, since the nurse knows the patient well
Overriding alerts without thinking is a work-around that causes errors.
Scan a spare copy of the bar code kept on the cart instead
Scanning a copy away from the patient defeats the purpose of BCMA.
Give the dose now and scan the armband at the end of the shift
Delayed scanning bypasses the safety check before the dose is given.

alt.q: Why do work-arounds of bar-code scanning increase medication errors?
alt.a: They bypass the safety checks the system provides
alt.ex: When nurses work around technology, such as overriding alerts, medication errors occur.
w: They slow down the medication pass too much
The concern is lost safety checks, not speed.
They create too many scanner alerts
Work-arounds bypass alerts rather than create more of them.
They require extra pharmacist review
The danger is missed checks, not added review.

items.q: Automated medication dispensing systems control the dispensing of all medications, including narcotics.

alt.q: AMDSs dispense routine medications, but narcotics must always be obtained directly from the pharmacy.

alt.ex: AMDSs control the dispensing of all medications, including narcotics.

items.q: When a poorly designed BCMA system interrupts workflow, work-arounds and policy deviations increase medication errors.

items.ww: Bypassing a flawed system adds risk; well-designed BCMA reduces work-arounds.

items.q: Which description best defines a controlled substance?
items.a: A medication that has a potential for abuse
items.ex: Controlled substances are medications with potential for abuse, so their storage and use are legally regulated.
w: A medication that must be given only by the IV route
Controlled substances come in many forms and routes; the defining feature is abuse potential.
A medication that has a narrow therapeutic range
A narrow therapeutic range calls for careful monitoring but does not make a drug a controlled substance.
A medication that can be bought over the counter
OTC medications are sold without a prescription; controlled substances are tightly regulated.

alt.q: A nursing student asks why opioids are classified as controlled substances. Which answer is accurate?
alt.a: They have a potential for abuse, so federal and state laws regulate them
alt.ex: Opioids have abuse potential, so their storage, dispensing, and administration are controlled by federal and state guidelines.
w: They are always given by injection, so they need sterile handling
Opioids are given by several routes; classification is based on abuse potential.
They are new medications that are still being tested by the FDA
Controlled status reflects abuse potential, not whether a drug is still in testing.
They are too expensive to be stocked in patient care areas
Cost is not the reason; abuse potential and risk of diversion drive the controls.

items.q: What is the main reason controlled substances must be properly stored in a health care agency?
items.a: To prevent diversion of the medications
items.ex: Proper storage of controlled substances prevents diversion, the misdirection of these drugs away from their intended use.
w: To keep the medications at the right temperature
Temperature control applies to some drugs, but controlled substance storage rules target diversion.
To protect the medications from light exposure
Light protection is a product-specific concern, not the purpose of controlled substance storage.
To allow patients to reach their own doses quickly
Controlled substances are locked away from patients, not stored for patient access.

alt.q: A nurse explains why opioids are kept in a locked, computerized cabinet. Which statement best describes the purpose?
alt.a: Secure storage helps prevent the drugs from being diverted
alt.ex: Locked, secure storage and tracking of controlled substances are designed to prevent diversion.
w: Secure storage keeps the drugs from losing their potency
Potency depends on storage conditions such as temperature, not on locking the cabinet.
Secure storage lets the pharmacy bill the drugs faster
Charging is a side function of AMDSs; locking aims to prevent diversion.
Secure storage lets assistive personnel retrieve doses safely
Assistive personnel do not take part in medication administration.

items.q: A nurse violates the Controlled Substances Act. Which consequences may result? Select all that apply.
o: Fines
Violations of the Controlled Substances Act are punishable by fines.
Imprisonment
Violations can lead to imprisonment.
Loss of nursing licensure
A nurse who violates the act can lose licensure.
Required transfer to a different nursing unit
Unit transfer is not a legal penalty named for violations of the act.
Automatic closure of the agency’s pharmacy
The penalties named apply to the violator: fines, imprisonment, and license loss.
items.ex: Violating the Controlled Substances Act can bring fines, imprisonment, and loss of the nurse’s license.

alt.q: Which statements about the Controlled Substances Act are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Nurses must follow its legal provisions when giving opioids
Nurses are responsible for following all legal regulations when administering controlled substances.
A violation can lead to imprisonment
Imprisonment is one possible penalty for violating the act.
A violation can cost a nurse their license
Loss of license is a possible consequence of violating the act.
It applies only to pharmacists who dispense opioids
Nurses who administer controlled substances must also follow its provisions.
Agencies may ignore it if they use computerized cabinets
Computerized systems help agencies comply; they do not replace the law.
alt.ex: Nurses must follow the act when giving controlled substances, and violations can bring fines, imprisonment, and license loss.

items.q: While counting opioids at the start of a shift, a nurse finds that the count does not match the inventory record. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Report the discrepancy immediately and correct it
items.ex: A running count is kept for opioids, and any discrepancy must be reported immediately and corrected.
w: Recount the drawer at the end of the shift and report then
Delaying the report allows a possible diversion to go unaddressed; report it immediately.
Adjust the record to match the number of doses present
Changing the record hides the discrepancy instead of reporting and correcting it.
Ask the patients on the unit if they received extra doses
Questioning patients does not address the count; the discrepancy must be reported.

alt.q: A nurse removes a dose of oxycodone from the automated system and notices the drawer holds one fewer tablet than the screen shows. Which action is correct?
alt.a: Report the count discrepancy right away so it can be corrected
alt.ex: Discrepancies in an opioid count must be reported immediately and corrected.
w: Take the dose and note the difference at the next scheduled count
Count discrepancies are reported immediately, not held until a later count.
Return the dose and choose a different opioid from the cabinet
Switching drugs does not address the discrepancy and changes the ordered medication.
Ignore the difference because computerized counts are often wrong
Every discrepancy is reported; it may signal diversion or a dispensing error.

items.q: A nurse gives 2 mg of a 4-mg vial of morphine as ordered. What should the nurse do with the remaining 2 mg?
items.a: Have a second nurse witness disposal of the unused part
items.ex: When only part of a controlled substance dose is given, a second nurse witnesses disposal of the unused part.
w: Save the remaining amount in the vial for the next dose
Unused portions of controlled substances are wasted with a witness, not saved.
Return the vial to the pharmacy without documenting it
Waste of a controlled substance must be witnessed and recorded, not returned undocumented.
Discard the remainder in the sharps container alone
Wasted opioids must not go in sharps containers, and a second nurse must witness the waste.

alt.q: A nurse must waste half of a hydromorphone dose. The agency uses paper records. Which action is required?
alt.a: Waste the drug with a second nurse, and both nurses sign the form
alt.ex: With paper records, the nurse who wastes the drug and the witnessing nurse both sign the form.
w: Waste the drug alone, then sign the form as the only nurse
Partial-dose disposal requires a second nurse as witness.
Ask assistive personnel to watch the waste and sign the form
A second nurse, not assistive personnel, witnesses controlled substance waste.
Waste the drug and ask the pharmacist to sign it next week
The waste is witnessed and signed at the time of disposal by a second nurse.

items.ex: Wasted portions of medications must not be placed in sharps containers; follow agency policy for appropriate waste.

alt.q: Nurses follow agency policy for wasting unused portions of opioids and do not place the wasted medication in a sharps container.

alt.ww: Sharps containers are not an approved disposal site for wasted opioids, even when another nurse watches.

items.q: A patient refuses a dose of oxycodone that the nurse has already removed from the dispensing system. Which action should the nurse take?

items.ex: When a patient refuses an opioid or any controlled substance, someone else must witness the wasted medication per agency procedure.
w: Return the tablet to the dispensing drawer for another patient
Refused medications are not returned to stock; a refused controlled substance is wasted with a witness.
Keep the tablet in the patient’s room in case they change their mind
Leaving a controlled substance unattended risks diversion and violates storage rules.
Discard the tablet alone and document the refusal later
Controlled substance waste needs a witness and timely documentation.

alt.q: Which statement by a new nurse about a refused dose of morphine shows correct understanding?
alt.a: I need another nurse to witness me wasting the refused dose
alt.ex: A refused opioid must be wasted per agency procedure with someone else witnessing the waste.
w: I can put the refused dose back in the cabinet if it is unopened
Only unopened non-controlled unit doses may be saved; a refused opioid is wasted with a witness.
I can give the refused dose to another patient with the same order
Giving one patient’s dispensed dose to another bypasses controls and identification checks.
I can flush the refused dose without telling anyone
Wasting a controlled substance always requires a witness and documentation.

items.q: Which type of storage does the textbook prefer for opioids in a health care agency?
items.a: Computerized, locked cabinets
items.ex: All opioids are stored in a locked, secure cabinet or container, and computerized, locked cabinets are preferred.
w: Unlocked carts kept at the nurses’ station
Opioids must always be locked and secure, never kept in unlocked carts.
Individual patient drawers in the unit-dose cart
Controlled substances are kept in a larger locked drawer, not individual patient drawers.
Bedside cabinets in each patient’s room
Bedside storage does not provide the secure, tracked storage opioids require.

alt.q: A nurse manager is choosing storage for opioids on a new unit. Which option best meets textbook guidelines?
alt.a: A computerized cabinet that locks and tracks each opioid dispensed
alt.ex: Computerized, locked cabinets are preferred because they secure opioids and track dispensing.
w: A shelf in the clean supply room that is checked once a shift
An open shelf is not locked or secure enough for controlled substances.
A drawer in each patient’s unit-dose cart labeled with their name
Controlled substances are not kept in individual patient drawers.
A sealed box at the bedside of each patient who uses opioids
Bedside storage is not locked, centralized, or tracked as required.

items.q: Why does the textbook recommend tamper-evident syringes for drugs such as hydromorphone?
items.a: They show whether the controlled substance has been tampered with
items.ex: Tamper-evident syringes are used when available for opioids so any tampering with the controlled substance is visible.
w: They deliver the controlled substance faster than standard syringes
Tamper-evident design addresses security, not delivery speed.
They allow the nurse to skip counting the controlled substance
Opioids are still counted whenever they are dispensed.
They allow the unused portion to be saved for a later dose
Unused opioid portions are wasted with a witness, not saved.

alt.q: Which opioid does the textbook give as an example of a drug for which tamper-evident syringes should be used when available?
alt.a: Hydromorphone
alt.ex: The opioid guidelines list hydromorphone as an example of a drug supplied in tamper-evident syringes.
w: Insulin
Insulin is a time-critical medication but is not a controlled substance.
Phenytoin
Phenytoin is an anticonvulsant used as an example of agency dose limits, not tamper-evident syringes.
Vancomycin
Vancomycin is an antibiotic, not a controlled substance.

items.q: Which information is recorded on the special inventory record each time an opioid is dispensed? Select all that apply.
