The record includes the name of the patient who receives the opioid.
Date and time of administration
The date and time the opioid was given are recorded.
Name of the medication
The medication name is documented on the record.
Dosage given
The dosage is recorded so the ongoing count stays accurate.
Patient’s admitting diagnosis
The diagnosis is in the health record, not the opioid inventory record.
Name of the pharmacist who filled the drawer
The record identifies the nurse dispensing the drug, not the pharmacist who stocked it.
items.ex: Each opioid entry records the patient’s name, date, time, medication name, and dosage.

alt.q: A nurse documents a dose of morphine on the opioid record. Which entries are required? Select all that apply.
o: Morphine as the medication name
The name of the medication is a required entry.
The dose given
Dosage is part of every opioid record entry.
The patient’s name
The patient’s name identifies who received the opioid.
The patient’s pain score before the dose
Pain scores belong in the patient’s health record, not the inventory record.
The patient’s room number
The record calls for the patient’s name, date, time, medication, and dosage.
alt.ex: The opioid record lists the patient’s name, date, time, medication name, and dosage given.

items.q: In a unit-dose system, controlled substances are kept in each patient’s individual medication drawer.
items.a: False
items.ex: Controlled substances are not kept in individual patient drawers; they are kept in a larger locked drawer for security.
items.ww: Individual drawers hold routine unit doses; controlled substances need a separate, larger locked drawer.

alt.q: In a unit-dose cart, controlled substances are kept in a larger locked drawer instead of individual patient drawers.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: A larger locked drawer keeps controlled substances secure, separate from each patient’s drawer.
alt.ww: Patient drawers are refilled with routine doses; storing opioids there would not keep them secure.

items.q: When should a nurse count opioids to maintain the running count?
items.a: Whenever opioids are dispensed
items.ex: A running count is maintained by counting opioids whenever they are dispensed.
w: Only once at the end of each week
Weekly counts would miss discrepancies; opioids are counted whenever dispensed.
Only when the pharmacy restocks the cabinet
Restocking is not the only time; every dispensing event is counted.
Only when a discrepancy is suspected
Counts are routine with every dispensing, not just when a problem is suspected.

alt.q: A nurse asks why the automated cabinet asks her to count the remaining tablets every time she removes an opioid. Which explanation is correct?
alt.a: Counting with every dispensing keeps a running count of opioids
alt.ex: Counting opioids whenever they are dispensed maintains an accurate running count so discrepancies are found quickly.
w: Counting with every dispensing replaces the need for a witness when wasting
A witness is still needed for wasted opioids regardless of counts.
Counting with every dispensing lets the cabinet calculate the patient’s dose
Dose calculation is the nurse’s responsibility; counts track inventory.
Counting with every dispensing is needed only for IV opioids
All opioids are counted whenever dispensed, regardless of route.

items.q: An agency uses a computerized system to dispense opioids. How is the dispensing nurse identified on the inventory record?
items.a: The computer records the nurse’s name
items.ex: With computerized systems, the nurse’s name is recorded electronically; with paper records, the dispensing nurse signs the record.
w: The nurse signs a paper copy at the end of the shift
Signing applies to paper records; computerized systems record the name automatically.
The charge nurse enters the name at the end of the day
Each dispensing nurse is recorded by the system, not entered later by another nurse.
The pharmacist adds the name when restocking the cabinet
The pharmacist does not record which nurse dispensed each dose.

alt.q: An agency keeps paper records for opioids. Who signs the record when an opioid is dispensed?
alt.a: The nurse who dispenses the medication
alt.ex: On paper records, the nurse dispensing the opioid signs the record; computerized systems record the name instead.
w: The pharmacist who delivered the medication
The pharmacist stocks medications but does not sign for each dose dispensed.
The health care provider who ordered the medication
The prescriber orders the drug but does not sign the dispensing record.
The patient who received the medication
Patients do not sign the opioid inventory record.

items.q: Many agencies automatically discontinue narcotic orders after a set number of days. What is the purpose of this policy?
items.a: It makes the health care provider regularly review the need for the drug
items.ex: Automatic discontinuation controls unnecessarily prolonged therapy because the provider must reorder and review the narcotic’s continued need.
w: It stops patients from ever receiving narcotics for more than a few days
The provider can reorder the narcotic; the policy forces review, not a ban.
It lets nurses decide when a narcotic is no longer needed
The decision to reorder belongs to the health care provider.
It keeps the pharmacy from running out of narcotic stock
The policy addresses prolonged therapy, not supply levels.

alt.q: A patient’s opioid order was automatically discontinued after the set number of days, and the patient still has pain. Which action is appropriate?
alt.a: Contact the health care provider to review the need and reorder the opioid
alt.ex: The provider can reorder a discontinued narcotic; the policy ensures the need for it is regularly reviewed.
w: Continue giving the opioid because the patient still has pain
A discontinued order is no longer valid; giving the drug requires a new order.
Give the patient leftover doses from another patient’s supply
Using another patient’s supply bypasses orders and controlled substance safeguards.
Tell the patient that opioids can no longer be ordered
The provider can reorder the opioid after reviewing the need.

items.q: Controlled substances must be properly stored to prevent [[diversion]].
items.ex: Proper storage keeps controlled substances from being diverted from their intended use.

alt.q: Locked storage and running counts of opioids help agencies prevent drug [[diversion]].
alt.ex: Proper storage keeps controlled substances from being diverted from their intended use.

items.q: Medications with potential for abuse are called [[controlled substances|controlled substance|controlled drugs]].
items.ex: Controlled substances, such as opioids, are regulated because they can be abused.

alt.q: Opioids are an example of [[controlled substances|controlled substance|controlled drugs]], which nurses must handle according to legal regulations.
alt.ex: Controlled substances, such as opioids, are regulated because they can be abused.

items.q: A nurse is reviewing safe opioid control on a busy unit. Which actions follow the textbook’s guidelines? Select all that apply.
o: Keeping all opioids in a locked, secure cabinet
All opioids are stored in a locked, secure cabinet or container.
Counting opioids whenever they are dispensed
A running count is kept by counting with each dispensing.
Using tamper-evident syringes when available
Tamper-evident syringes are recommended for drugs such as hydromorphone.
Asking assistive personnel to remove opioids from the cabinet
No part of medication administration is delegated to assistive personnel.
Leaving the opioid drawer unlocked during the morning medication pass
Medication storage areas must be locked when unattended.
items.ex: Opioid control relies on locked storage, a running count, and tamper-evident syringes when available.

alt.q: Which practices would violate safe opioid handling? Select all that apply.
o: Correcting a count discrepancy without reporting it
Discrepancies must be reported immediately as well as corrected.
Wasting part of a dose without a second nurse present
Partial-dose disposal requires a second nurse as witness.
Placing a wasted opioid in a sharps container
Wasted portions of opioids must not go in sharps containers.
Recording the patient’s name and dosage on the inventory record
This is required documentation, not a violation.
Storing opioids in a computerized, locked cabinet
Computerized, locked cabinets are the preferred storage.
alt.ex: Unreported discrepancies, unwitnessed waste, and sharps-container disposal all violate opioid handling guidelines.

items.q: Health care agency policies on controlled substances can be more restrictive than federal and state regulations.
items.a: True
items.ex: Agencies set policies to meet regulations, and these policies are often more restrictive than governmental controls.
items.ww: Agencies cannot loosen legal requirements but commonly add stricter rules, such as automatic narcotic discontinuation.

alt.q: A health care agency may set controlled substance policies that are less restrictive than federal law if it uses computerized cabinets.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Agency policies must meet federal, state, and local regulations and are often more restrictive, never less.
alt.ww: Technology helps agencies comply but never permits policies looser than the law.

items.q: A nurse accesses an automated medication dispensing system to obtain a dose of morphine. Which step is required before the drawer opens?
items.a: Entering a personal security code and selecting the patient’s profile
items.ex: Each nurse accesses the AMDS with a security code, sometimes bio-identification, and selects the patient’s profile before a drug is dispensed.
w: Entering the charge nurse’s code and selecting any open drawer
Each nurse uses their own code; sharing codes defeats tracking of controlled substances.
Scanning the pharmacy invoice and selecting the patient’s room
Access is by the nurse’s code and the patient’s profile, not invoices or room numbers.
Entering the patient’s code and selecting the medication by color
Medications are chosen by name, dose, and route from the patient’s profile.

alt.q: Some automated dispensing systems require more than a security code. Which additional method does the textbook describe?
alt.a: Bio-identification by placing a finger on the screen
alt.ex: Some systems require bio-identification, in which the nurse places a finger on the screen to access the computer.
w: A signed note from the charge nurse
Access is controlled electronically, not by paper notes.
A verbal password given to the pharmacist
The system uses codes and bio-identification, not verbal passwords.
A key kept by the nursing supervisor
Computerized systems replace keys with codes and bio-identification.

items.q: Some agencies require health care providers to write prescriptions for controlled substances in a special way. What does the textbook describe?
items.a: Using a special prescription pad that differs from the one for other drugs
items.ex: Some agencies require controlled substance prescriptions on a special pad, such as one of a different color.
w: Using a verbal order that the nurse writes down for the provider
Prescriptions for controlled substances are written by the provider, not transcribed verbal orders.
Using the standard pad but adding the patient’s room number
Room numbers are not used as identifiers and do not make a prescription special.
Using a pharmacist’s pad that the pharmacist then signs
The provider writes the prescription; the special pad belongs to the prescriber.

alt.q: A patient going home with an opioid prescription notices the prescription paper is a different color from the others. Which explanation is best?
alt.a: Some agencies use a special pad for controlled substance prescriptions
alt.ex: Agencies may require a distinct prescription pad, such as a different color, for controlled substances.
w: The different color means the prescription cannot be refilled
Refill information is written on the prescription; color identifies the special pad.
The different color shows the drug is an over-the-counter product
OTC products do not need prescriptions; this pad marks a controlled substance.
The different color means the dose is higher than usual
The pad identifies a controlled substance prescription, not the dose size.

items.q: How do chemotherapy (antineoplastic) drugs act against cancer?
items.a: By killing cells that divide rapidly
items.ex: Chemotherapy kills rapidly dividing cells, a main property of most cancer cells, by causing DNA damage.
w: By blocking the blood supply to the tumor only
The book describes chemotherapy as killing rapidly dividing cells, not cutting off tumor blood flow.
By strengthening the patient’s immune cells
Chemotherapy damages DNA in dividing cells; it can actually cause immune dysfunction in exposed people.
By killing only cells that are already cancerous
Chemotherapy is toxic to normal cells too, not just cancer cells.

alt.q: Why is chemotherapy toxic to normal cells as well as cancer cells?
alt.a: It damages DNA in rapidly dividing cells, whether or not they are cancerous
alt.ex: Chemotherapy causes DNA damage that leads to cell death or growth arrest in any rapidly dividing cell.
w: It is given in doses too high for the body to excrete
Toxicity comes from DNA damage, not from failure to excrete the drug.
It is absorbed only by normal cells near the tumor
Chemotherapy acts on rapidly dividing cells throughout the body.
It blocks hormones that all cells need to function
The book describes DNA damage, not hormone blocking, as the mechanism.

items.q: Which statement about who may administer chemotherapy is accurate?
items.a: Any RN may give oral chemotherapy, but IV chemotherapy requires certification
items.ex: Nurses must be certified to give IV chemotherapy, whereas oral chemotherapy can be administered by any RN.
w: Only certified nurses may give either oral or IV chemotherapy
Certification is required for IV chemotherapy; any RN may give oral forms.
Any RN may give IV chemotherapy, but oral forms require certification
This reverses the rule: IV chemotherapy requires certification.
Assistive personnel may give oral chemotherapy if supervised by an RN
Medication administration is never delegated to assistive personnel.

alt.q: A newly hired RN without chemotherapy certification is assigned a patient receiving chemotherapy. Which medication may this nurse administer?
alt.a: An oral chemotherapy tablet
alt.ex: Oral chemotherapy can be given by any RN; IV chemotherapy requires certification.
w: An IV chemotherapy infusion
IV chemotherapy may be given only by nurses who have completed certification.
An IV push of a chemotherapy agent
Any IV chemotherapy requires certification.
An IV chemotherapy piggyback
IV piggyback chemotherapy is still IV chemotherapy and requires certification.

items.q: Oral chemotherapy poses less exposure risk to nurses and family caregivers than IV chemotherapy.
items.a: False
items.ex: Oral chemotherapy carries the same exposure risks to health care providers, patients, and family caregivers as IV forms.
items.ww: Even touching a chemotherapy tablet is dangerous, so oral forms are no safer to handle.

alt.q: Oral chemotherapy has the same exposure risks to health care providers and family caregivers as IV chemotherapy.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The textbook states oral chemotherapy carries the same exposure risks as IV forms.
alt.ww: Believing oral forms are safer leads to unprotected handling of tablets, which is dangerous.

items.q: Why might the harm from occupational exposure to chemotherapy not be recognized for months or years?
items.a: The injuries can include cancer, birth defects, or immune dysfunction
items.ex: Exposure injuries such as cancer, birth defects, or immune dysfunction can take months or years to appear.
w: The drugs are not absorbed through the skin or mucous membranes
Touching chemotherapy tablets is dangerous, so absorption by contact is a real risk.
The drugs lose their toxicity soon after they leave the patient
Patients excrete active chemotherapy in body fluids, which remain hazardous.
The injuries appear only in people who handle IV forms
Oral forms carry the same exposure risks as IV forms.

alt.q: A nurse who handled chemotherapy without gloves says, “I feel fine, so there was no harm.” Which response is most accurate?
alt.a: Effects of exposure such as cancer or birth defects may not appear for months or years
alt.ex: Chemotherapy exposure injuries may be delayed, so feeling well now does not mean no harm occurred.
w: Effects of exposure always appear within the first 24 hours
Injuries from exposure can be delayed for months or years.
Effects of exposure occur only after IV contact with the drug
Touching oral chemotherapy tablets is also dangerous.
Effects of exposure are limited to a mild skin rash
Exposure can cause cancer, birth defects, or immune dysfunction.

items.q: A patient is taking oral chemotherapy at home. Which statement by the family caregiver shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: We will flush the toilet twice after each use until 48 hours after the last dose
items.ex: Toilets are double-flushed during chemotherapy and for 48 hours after it is discontinued because the drugs are excreted in body wastes.
w: We will flush the toilet twice after each use until the day of the last dose
Double-flushing continues for 48 hours after chemotherapy is discontinued, not just until the last dose.
We will flush the toilet once after each use for 48 hours after the last dose
Toilets are flushed twice, not once, after each use.
We will flush the toilet twice after each use for 24 hours after the first dose
Double-flushing continues throughout therapy and for 48 hours after it stops.

alt.q: How long after a patient stops taking chemotherapy should the family keep double-flushing the toilet?
alt.a: 48 hours
alt.ex: Double-flushing continues during chemotherapy and for 48 hours after it is discontinued.
w: 12 hours
Twelve hours is too short; the precaution lasts 48 hours.
24 hours
Twenty-four hours is too short; the precaution lasts 48 hours.
7 days
The textbook specifies 48 hours, not 7 days.

items.q: Through which body substances does a patient excrete chemotherapy chemicals? Select all that apply.
o: Urine
Chemotherapy is excreted in urine, which is why toilets are double-flushed.
Stool
Stool contains excreted chemotherapy chemicals.
Vomit
Vomit is a route of chemotherapy excretion.
Saliva
Saliva contains excreted chemotherapy chemicals.
Only blood drawn from an IV line
Chemotherapy is excreted in several body fluids, not only blood.
items.ex: Patients excrete chemotherapy in urine, stool, vomit, sweat, and saliva, so these fluids are hazardous.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a family caregiver which body fluids of a patient on chemotherapy can expose others to the drug. Which should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Sweat
Chemotherapy is excreted in sweat.
Urine
Urine is a route of chemotherapy excretion.
Stool
Stool contains excreted chemotherapy.
Only the tablets themselves, not body fluids
Body fluids also carry chemotherapy chemicals and are hazardous.
Only fluids produced during the first dose
Excretion continues during therapy, and precautions continue for 48 hours after it stops.
alt.ex: Sweat, urine, and stool, along with vomit and saliva, all carry excreted chemotherapy.

items.q: How often should gloves be changed when handling chemotherapy medications, unless the manufacturer recommends differently?
items.a: Every 30 minutes
items.ex: Gloves tested for chemotherapy use are changed every 30 minutes unless manufacturer guidelines say otherwise.
w: Every 2 hours
Two hours is too long; gloves are changed every 30 minutes.
Every 60 minutes
Sixty minutes is too long; gloves are changed every 30 minutes.
Every 8-hour shift
A whole shift is far too long; gloves are changed every 30 minutes.

alt.q: A nurse has been wearing chemotherapy gloves for 30 minutes while preparing several doses. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Change the gloves now, unless the manufacturer recommends a different interval
alt.ex: Chemotherapy gloves are changed every 30 minutes unless manufacturer guidelines recommend differently.
w: Keep the gloves on until all doses are prepared, unless they tear
Gloves are changed every 30 minutes, not only when torn.
Wash the gloves with soap and keep wearing them, unless they are soiled
Gloves are single-use and are replaced, not washed.
Remove the outer gloves and keep wearing them later, unless they look wet
Protective clothing is single use and is not reused.

items.q: A nurse is double gloving to prepare chemotherapy. When should the nurse put on the gown?
items.a: Before applying the second pair of gloves
items.ex: When double gloving, the gown is placed on before the second pair of gloves.
w: After applying both pairs of gloves
The gown goes on before the second pair of gloves, not after both.
Before performing hand hygiene
Hand hygiene is performed before glove application; the gown goes on before the second pair.
After preparing the medication
The gown must be on before handling chemotherapy, ahead of the second pair of gloves.

alt.q: A nurse puts on a gown, then a second pair of chemotherapy gloves. Which statement about this sequence is correct?
alt.a: It is correct, because the gown goes on before the second pair of gloves
alt.ex: Guidelines direct the nurse to put the gown on before applying the second pair of gloves.
w: It is incorrect, because the gown should go on after both pairs of gloves
The book places the gown before the second pair of gloves.
It is incorrect, because double gloving is never needed for chemotherapy
Double gloving is used when indicated for chemotherapy handling.
It is correct, because hand hygiene is not needed when double gloving
Hand hygiene is still required before and after glove application.

items.q: A family caregiver asks how to wash sheets soiled with the body fluids of a patient receiving chemotherapy. Which instruction is correct?
items.a: Wash them twice in hot water with regular detergent, apart from other clothes
items.ex: Soiled linens are machine-washed twice in hot water with regular detergent and not with other laundry.
w: Wash them once by hand in cold water with bleach
Linens are washed in a machine, not by hand, and twice in hot water.
Wash them twice in a machine together with the family’s laundry
Soiled linens must not be washed with other clothes.
Wash them once in warm water and hang them outside to dry
The book calls for two hot-water machine washes.

alt.q: A patient’s pajamas become soiled with vomit during chemotherapy, but the family cannot wash them right away. What should the family do?
alt.a: Seal them in a plastic bag until they can be washed
alt.ex: If soiled clothes cannot be washed right away, they are sealed in a plastic bag.
w: Soak them in the sink until they can be washed
Handling soiled items by hand in a sink increases exposure; seal them in a bag.
Put them in the hamper with the other laundry
Soiled items must be kept apart from other clothes.
Rinse them by hand and hang them to dry
Soiled items should not be washed by hand.

items.q: Chemotherapy tablets may be split in half if the patient has trouble swallowing the whole tablet.
items.a: False
items.ex: Chemotherapy drugs must not be crushed, cut, or split because doing so increases exposure to the hazardous drug.
items.ww: Swallowing problems are reported to the provider; splitting chemotherapy tablets is never an acceptable fix.

alt.q: Chemotherapy drugs should not be crushed, cut, or split.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The handling guidelines prohibit crushing, cutting, or splitting chemotherapy drugs.
alt.ww: Altering chemotherapy tablets releases hazardous drug particles, so it is not allowed.

items.q: Which device must nurses now use when administering IV chemotherapy?
items.a: A closed-system transfer device
items.ex: Nurses must use closed-system transfer devices when administering IV chemotherapy to limit exposure.
w: An enteral syringe
Enteral syringes are for oral or enteral medications, not IV chemotherapy.
A standard open IV tubing set
Open systems increase exposure; closed-system transfer devices are required.
A shared pill-crushing device
Chemotherapy is not crushed, and IV chemotherapy requires closed-system transfer devices.

alt.q: A nurse certified in chemotherapy prepares to give an IV antineoplastic drug. Which equipment choice follows current guidelines?
alt.a: Separate equipment and a closed-system transfer device
alt.ex: Chemotherapy uses separate equipment from regular medications, and IV chemotherapy requires closed-system transfer devices.
w: The same equipment used for the patient’s other IV drugs
Separate equipment is used for chemotherapy and regular medications.
A standard syringe with the cap removed
IV chemotherapy requires closed-system transfer devices.
An open tubing set changed every 30 minutes
Glove changes are every 30 minutes; IV chemotherapy needs a closed system.

items.q: How should a nurse dispose of a disposable gown worn while handling chemotherapy?
items.a: As cytotoxic waste according to local waste regulations
items.ex: Disposable protective clothing is single use and is discarded as cytotoxic waste per local waste regulations.
w: As regular trash after it is folded inside out
Items used with chemotherapy are cytotoxic waste, not regular trash.
As reusable laundry after a hot-water wash
Disposable protective clothing is single use and is not laundered.
As sharps waste in the nearest sharps container
Gowns are disposed of as cytotoxic waste, not sharps waste.

alt.q: A nurse wants to reuse a chemotherapy gown that is not visibly soiled for the next patient’s dose. Which response is correct?
alt.a: The gown is a single-use item and must be discarded as cytotoxic waste
alt.ex: All disposable protective clothing used with chemotherapy is single use and discarded as cytotoxic waste.
w: The gown may be reused if it was worn for less than 30 minutes
Protective clothing is single use regardless of wear time.
The gown may be reused if it is stored in a sealed bag
Sealing in a bag applies to home laundry, not reuse of protective clothing.
The gown may be reused if no chemotherapy spilled on it
All disposable protective clothing is single use.

items.q: A nurse is teaching a patient who will take oral chemotherapy at home with a toddler and a dog. Which hazard should the nurse specifically point out?
items.a: The toilet, because excreted chemotherapy can expose children and pets
items.ex: Patients excrete chemotherapy in urine and stool, and toilets are named as a hazard for children and pets.
w: The kitchen sink, because tap water inactivates chemotherapy
Tap water does not inactivate chemotherapy; the toilet is the named hazard.
The washing machine, because it spreads chemotherapy to all laundry
Soiled items are washed separately; the toilet is the named hazard for children and pets.
The refrigerator, because chemotherapy must be kept cold at home
Storage temperature is not the hazard described for children and pets.

alt.q: Why are patients taking chemotherapy at home taught to double-flush the toilet?
alt.a: Chemotherapy excreted in urine and stool can expose others, including children and pets
alt.ex: Double-flushing reduces exposure to excreted chemotherapy, and toilets are a hazard for children and pets.
w: Chemotherapy causes constipation that blocks the toilet
Double-flushing addresses exposure to excreted drug, not constipation.
Chemotherapy makes urine change color and stain the toilet
Staining is not the reason; excreted drug exposure is.
Chemotherapy is only active in the body for the first hour
Precautions continue for 48 hours after therapy stops.

items.q: Which actions follow guidelines for safely handling chemotherapy in a health care agency? Select all that apply.
o: Storing cytotoxic agents in a designated area apart from noncytotoxic agents
Cytotoxic agents are stored in a designated area, separate from other drugs.
Using gloves tested for chemotherapy or hazardous medication use
Only gloves tested for hazardous drug use provide adequate protection.
Performing hand hygiene before and after applying gloves
Thorough hand hygiene is done before and after glove application.
Using the same pill crusher for chemotherapy and regular tablets
Chemotherapy is never crushed, and separate equipment is used.
Storing chemotherapy with the unit’s regular stock medications
Cytotoxic agents must be separated from noncytotoxic agents.
items.ex: Safe handling includes separate storage, chemotherapy-tested gloves, and hand hygiene before and after gloving.

alt.q: Which practices would increase a nurse’s risk of chemotherapy exposure? Select all that apply.
o: Wearing the same gloves for 2 hours while preparing doses
Gloves should be changed every 30 minutes.
Using standard exam gloves not tested for hazardous drugs
Gloves must be tested for chemotherapy or hazardous drug use.
Preparing chemotherapy with equipment used for regular drugs
Separate equipment must be used for chemotherapy.
Performing hand hygiene after removing gloves
Hand hygiene after glove removal reduces exposure.
Discarding the gown as cytotoxic waste
Disposing of protective clothing as cytotoxic waste is the correct practice.
alt.ex: Overlong glove use, untested gloves, and shared equipment all increase the risk of chemotherapy exposure.

items.q: Which instructions should the nurse give a family caregiver of a patient taking oral chemotherapy at home? Select all that apply.
o: Double-flush the toilet after the patient uses it
Excreted chemotherapy in urine and stool makes double-flushing necessary.
Wash soiled sheets twice in hot water in a washing machine
Soiled linens are machine-washed twice in hot water.
Keep soiled linens separate from the rest of the laundry
Soiled items are not washed with other clothes.
Handle the tablets with bare hands since they are taken by mouth
Touching chemotherapy tablets is dangerous; oral forms carry the same risks as IV.
Crush the tablet into food if the patient has trouble swallowing
Chemotherapy is never crushed, cut, or split.
items.ex: Home teaching covers double-flushing, washing soiled linens twice in hot water, and keeping them separate from other laundry.

alt.q: A home health nurse reviews chemotherapy safety with a family. Which statements by the family show a need for more teaching? Select all that apply.
o: We can stop double-flushing on the day of the last dose
Double-flushing continues for 48 hours after chemotherapy stops.
We will hand-wash the soiled sheets in the bathtub
Soiled linens are washed in a machine, not by hand.
We can cut the tablet in half if it is too big
Chemotherapy tablets must never be cut or split.
We will seal soiled clothes in a plastic bag if we cannot wash them right away
This is correct; soiled items are bagged until they can be washed.
We will wash soiled sheets apart from our other clothes
This is correct; soiled items are not washed with other clothes.
alt.ex: Stopping precautions early, hand-washing linens, and cutting tablets are errors that need more teaching.

items.q: Chemotherapy drugs cause [[DNA]] damage, leading to cell death or cell growth arrest.
items.ex: DNA damage explains why chemotherapy harms rapidly dividing normal cells as well as cancer cells.

alt.q: Antineoplastic drugs harm both cancer cells and normal cells by damaging their [[DNA]].
alt.ex: DNA damage explains why chemotherapy harms rapidly dividing normal cells as well as cancer cells.

items.q: A nurse is about to give an oral chemotherapy tablet. Which action is most important?
items.a: Wear gloves while handling the tablet
items.ex: Gloves must be worn when administering an oral chemotherapy drug because touching the tablet is dangerous.
w: Perform hand hygiene and hand the tablet to the patient barehanded
Hand hygiene alone does not protect the nurse; gloves are required.
Crush the tablet and mix it in a small amount of applesauce
Chemotherapy tablets must never be crushed.
Cut the tablet in half to make it easier to swallow
Chemotherapy tablets must never be cut or split.

alt.q: A nursing student says, “It’s only a pill, so I don’t need gloves to give oral chemotherapy.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: Touching a chemotherapy tablet is dangerous, so gloves are required
alt.ex: Oral chemotherapy carries the same exposure risk as IV forms, and gloves must be worn to handle it.
w: You are right, because only IV chemotherapy is hazardous
Oral forms have the same exposure risks as IV chemotherapy.
You only need gloves if the tablet must be crushed
Chemotherapy is never crushed, and gloves are always needed.
You only need gloves if the patient has an infection
Gloves protect against the hazardous drug itself, not only infection.

items.q: Every health care agency that handles chemotherapy must have a spill policy in place.
items.a: True
items.ex: Handling guidelines require the agency to have a spill policy for chemotherapy.
items.ww: A spill policy is mandatory, not optional, because spills cause hazardous exposure.

alt.q: A spill policy is optional for agencies that give only oral chemotherapy, since tablets cannot spill hazardous drug.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The agency must have a spill policy, and oral chemotherapy carries the same exposure risks as IV forms.
alt.ww: Oral forms are equally hazardous, so the spill policy requirement applies to all chemotherapy handling.

items.q: During which activities can accidental exposure to hazardous chemotherapy agents occur?
items.a: Unpacking, storage, handling, administration, and disposal
items.ex: Accidental exposure can occur at every stage of handling, from unpacking through disposal.
w: Administration only, when the drug enters the patient
Exposure can occur long before and after administration, including unpacking and disposal.
Preparation of IV forms only, not tablets
Oral tablets carry the same exposure risks as IV forms.
Disposal only, once the drug is in the waste bin
Exposure can happen during unpacking, storage, handling, and administration as well.

alt.q: A pharmacy technician unpacks a shipment of oral chemotherapy. Which statement about exposure risk is accurate?
alt.a: Exposure can occur during unpacking, so protective techniques are needed
alt.ex: Accidental exposure to hazardous agents can occur during unpacking, storage, handling, administration, and disposal.
w: Exposure cannot occur until a package is opened at the bedside
Unpacking and storage are named as points of possible exposure.
Exposure cannot occur with oral forms that are still packaged
Oral chemotherapy has the same exposure risks as IV forms.
Exposure cannot occur if the shipment is stored with other drugs
Cytotoxic agents must be stored separately, and storage is a point of exposure.

items.q: Where should cytotoxic agents be stored in a health care agency?
items.a: In a designated area separate from noncytotoxic agents
items.ex: Cytotoxic agents are stored in a designated area per the manufacturer’s instructions, separate from noncytotoxic agents.
w: In each patient’s unit-dose drawer with their other drugs
Cytotoxic agents are kept separate from noncytotoxic drugs.
In the controlled substance drawer with the opioids
Cytotoxic agents need their own designated area, not the opioid drawer.
In the general stock area with the unit’s routine drugs
Storing chemotherapy with routine drugs increases exposure risk.

alt.q: A nurse finds an oral chemotherapy drug mixed in with the unit’s routine stock medications. Which action is correct?
alt.a: Move it to the designated area for cytotoxic agents
alt.ex: Cytotoxic agents must be stored in a designated area apart from noncytotoxic agents.
w: Leave it there because oral forms are not hazardous
Oral chemotherapy has the same exposure risks as IV forms.
Place it in the sharps container for disposal
The drug should be stored correctly, not discarded in sharps.
Put it in the patient’s bedside drawer for convenience
Cytotoxic agents belong in a designated area per manufacturer’s instructions.

items.q: According to the textbook, what is the first thing a nurse determines in the medication administration process?
items.a: That the medication ordered is the correct medication
items.ex: The nurse first determines that the ordered medication is correct, then assesses, administers, and monitors.
w: That the patient’s family agrees with the medication
Family input matters for teaching, but the nurse first verifies the ordered medication is correct.
That assistive personnel can give the medication
No part of medication administration is delegated to assistive personnel.
That the medication has produced its desired effect
Monitoring effects comes after the medication is given, not first.

alt.q: A nurse receives a new medication order. Which nursing responsibility comes before administering the medication?
alt.a: Verifying that the ordered medication is correct
alt.ex: Nurses first determine that the ordered medication is correct before deciding to give it.
w: Monitoring the patient for the medication’s effects
Monitoring follows administration.
Teaching the patient about the medication’s side effects at discharge
Teaching is important but does not replace verifying the order first.
Asking assistive personnel to prepare the medication
Medication preparation cannot be delegated.

items.q: Which responsibilities belong to the nurse’s role in medication administration? Select all that apply.
o: Assessing the patient’s ability to self-administer medications
The nurse assesses whether a patient can safely self-administer.
Determining whether a patient should receive a medication at a given time
The nurse decides if the medication should be given now based on assessment.
Closely monitoring the medication’s effects
Monitoring effects after administration is a core nursing responsibility.
Teaching patients and family caregivers about their medications
Patient and family caregiver education is an integral part of the role.
Delegating oral medication administration to assistive personnel when busy
No part of medication administration may be delegated to assistive personnel.
Changing a dose on the nurse’s own judgment without an order
A medication order is required; the nurse clarifies concerns with the provider.
items.ex: The nurse assesses self-administration ability, decides whether to give a dose, monitors effects, and teaches patients and families.

alt.q: A nurse orientation class reviews the nurse’s role with medications. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Use the nursing process to integrate medication therapy into care
The nursing process guides integration of medication therapy into care.
Begin teaching about home medications as soon as possible
Early teaching benefits the patient more than teaching only on discharge day.
Administer medications correctly
Correct administration is a central nursing responsibility.
Allow assistive personnel to prepare medications for the nurse to give
Nurses administer only medications they prepare, and preparation is not delegated.
Assume an ordered dose is correct because the provider wrote it
Nurses are responsible for knowing ordered medications and doses are correct.
alt.ex: The nurse uses the nursing process, teaches early, administers correctly, and never delegates or assumes an order is correct.

items.q: A busy nurse has five patients due for oral medications. Assistive personnel (AP) offers to hand out the pills. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Thank you, but I must give the medications. Please tell me if anyone reports side effects.”
items.ex: Medication administration cannot be delegated to AP, but AP can report side effects or changes in condition to the nurse.
w: “Yes, please give them, as long as you check each patient’s armband.”

“Yes, I will prepare them, and you can give them to each patient.”
Nurses administer only the medications they prepare, and AP cannot give them.
“Please give only the vitamins, and I will give the other pills.”
No part of medication administration is delegated to AP, including vitamins.

alt.q: Which task related to oral medications may the nurse direct assistive personnel to perform?
alt.a: Report a patient’s new itching or rash after a medication to the nurse
alt.ex: AP cannot administer medications but are directed to report possible side effects or changes in condition to the nurse.
w: Give a patient’s scheduled oral pills while the nurse is busy
Administering oral medications cannot be delegated to AP.
Crush a patient’s tablets and mix them into applesauce
Preparing medications is part of administration and cannot be delegated.

Obtaining medications is part of the process the nurse must do.

items.q: A nurse may delegate administering oral medications to assistive personnel if the nurse prepares the medications first.
items.a: False
items.ex: No part of the medication administration process may be delegated to assistive personnel.
items.ww: Preparation by the nurse does not change the rule; the nurse who prepares must also administer.

alt.q: No part of the medication administration process may be delegated to assistive personnel.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The textbook states nurses do not delegate any part of medication administration to AP.
alt.ww: Even simple steps such as handing out pills remain nursing responsibilities and are not delegated.

items.q: When should a nurse begin teaching a hospitalized patient about medications the patient will take at home?
items.a: As soon as possible during the hospital stay
items.ex: Begin teaching about home medications as soon as possible; waiting until discharge day limits the patient’s benefit.
w: On the day of discharge, when the final list is ready
Teaching often happens on discharge day, but starting sooner benefits the patient.
At the first follow-up visit after discharge
Teaching must begin before the patient goes home.
Only after the patient asks about the medications
The nurse starts teaching proactively, not only when asked.

alt.q: A nurse learns on the second hospital day which medications a patient will take at home. Which action is best?
alt.a: Start teaching the patient and family caregiver about those medications now
alt.ex: Teaching about home medications should begin as soon as the information is available, not wait until discharge day.
w: Wait to teach until the discharge orders are signed
Waiting until discharge reduces the time the patient has to learn.
Give the patient written handouts on the day of discharge only
Handouts at discharge do not replace early, ongoing teaching.
Ask the pharmacist to do all teaching after discharge
Patient education is an integral part of the nurse’s role.

items.q: Although medication teaching often does not happen until the day of discharge, the patient benefits if the nurse starts it sooner.
items.a: True
items.ex: The textbook notes teaching often waits until discharge day, but earlier instruction benefits the patient.
items.ww: Delaying teaching to discharge is common practice, not the recommended practice.

alt.q: Medication teaching is most effective when it is saved for the day of discharge, after all orders are final.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Teaching about home medications should begin as soon as possible, not be saved for discharge day.
alt.ww: Teaching on discharge day is common, but the book recommends starting as soon as possible.

items.q: Which framework does the nurse use to integrate medication therapy into a patient’s care?

items.ex: Nurses use the nursing process to integrate medication therapy into patient care.
w: The chain of command

The unit-dose system
The unit-dose system is a medication distribution method.
The pharmacist’s formulary

alt.q: A nurse assesses a patient, identifies a medication-related nursing diagnosis, plans teaching, gives medications, and evaluates the response. What is the nurse using?
alt.a: The nursing process
alt.ex: Assessing, diagnosing, planning, implementing, and evaluating are the steps of the nursing process.
w: Medication reconciliation
Reconciliation compares medication lists during care transitions.
Bar-code medication administration
BCMA is a technology for verifying identity and medications.
The seven rights of medication administration
The rights guide safe administration, not the full care framework.

items.q: A nurse is about to give a scheduled antihypertensive. Which action best reflects the nurse’s role in deciding whether the patient should receive the medication at this time?

Ask assistive personnel to give the medication if the patient feels well
Medication administration cannot be delegated to AP.
Give half the dose to see how the patient responds
Changing a dose without an order is not within the nurse’s role.

alt.q: A patient scheduled for an oral medication is actively vomiting. Which action by the nurse is best?

A vomiting patient cannot keep down oral medications.

Crushing does not help a patient who cannot tolerate oral intake.
Give the dose by injection instead
Changing the route requires an order from the provider.

items.q: After administering a new medication, what is the nurse’s next responsibility?

The nurse actively monitors effects rather than waiting for complaints.

Documentation is done immediately after giving the dose, and monitoring continues.

The nurse actively reassesses rather than relying only on the patient to call.

items.q: Why do nurses administer only medications they have prepared themselves?

The rule rests on the nurse’s responsibility for errors, not pharmacy labeling.

Expiration is not the reason; accountability for errors is.

The reason is accountability, not access restrictions.

alt.q: A colleague hands a nurse a cup of pills she poured for the nurse’s patient and says, “I got these ready for you.” Which response is best?

items.q: A nurse is assigned a patient who is ordered a newly approved medication the nurse has never given. Which action should the nurse take first?

w: Give the medication because the provider ordered it

Patient input helps, but the nurse must consult a reliable professional source.

alt.q: Which statement by a new nurse shows correct understanding of the nurse’s accountability for medications?

items.q: A nurse who gives an ordered medication that is not appropriate for the patient is accountable for that action.

alt.a: False

items.q: A nurse determines that an older patient with arthritis cannot safely draw up insulin at home. Which action is most appropriate?

Reading the label correctly supports safe self-administration.
The patient shows how to measure a dose with a metric spoon
Correct demonstration shows the patient can measure doses.

items.q: Which tasks may the nurse direct assistive personnel (AP) to do for a patient receiving oral medications? Select all that apply.

Tell the nurse if the patient’s condition changes or worsens

Hand the patient the pills the nurse has poured
No part of medication administration, including handing out pills, is delegated to AP.
Crush tablets and mix them into the patient’s pudding
Preparing medications is part of administration and cannot be delegated.
Decide whether to hold a dose if the patient seems drowsy
Deciding whether to give a dose requires nursing judgment.
items.ex: AP may report side effects and changes in condition, but cannot prepare, give, or decide on medications.

“Please give Mr. Lee his 0900 pills while I chart.”
Administering medications cannot be delegated to AP.

Obtaining and preparing medications is part of the process the nurse performs.

items.q: Which statement best explains why medication administration requires a nurse rather than assistive personnel?

Time is not the reason; the task requires nursing knowledge and judgment.

w: Giving medications is only legal for pharmacists and physicians
Nurses legally administer medications; AP cannot because it requires nursing judgment.
Giving medications requires a security code that AP cannot learn
Access codes are not the reason; nursing knowledge and judgment are.
Giving medications is only risky for IV routes, so oral is fine
No route of medication administration is delegated to AP.

items.q: A patient says, “I take so many pills at home, I can’t keep track of them.” Which nursing action best reflects the nurse’s education role?

w: Tell the patient to take all the pills at once each morning

alt.q: Which statement by a patient after medication teaching shows the nurse’s teaching was effective?

“I will stop my pills once I start feeling better.”

items.q: How does the textbook define a medication error?
items.a: Any preventable event that may cause inappropriate medication use or patient harm
items.ex: A medication error is any preventable event that may cause or lead to inappropriate medication use or patient harm.
w: Any expected side effect that occurs after a correct dose
Expected side effects of correctly given drugs are not preventable errors.
Any allergic reaction that occurs with a new medication
A first-time allergic reaction is an adverse effect, not necessarily a preventable error.
Any event in which a patient refuses a prescribed medication
Refusal is a patient right, not a preventable error.

alt.q: Which situation meets the definition of a medication error?
alt.a: A nurse gives a scheduled dose 4 hours late because it was overlooked
alt.ex: Giving a medication at the wrong time interval is a preventable event and therefore a medication error.
w: A patient refuses a dose after the nurse explains its purpose
Patients have the right to refuse medications.
A patient has mild nausea after a correctly given antibiotic
A side effect from a correct dose is not a preventable error.
A nurse holds a dose after finding a low blood pressure
Holding a dose based on assessment is sound judgment, not an error.

items.q: Which events are examples of medication errors? Select all that apply.
o: Giving a medication by the wrong route
Wrong-route administration is a medication error.
Administering an extra dose
Extra doses are listed as medication errors.
Failing to give a prescribed medication
Omitting a medication is a medication error.
Inaccurate prescribing by the health care provider
Prescribing errors are included in the definition.
A patient refusing a medication after teaching
Refusing medication is a patient right, not an error.
A predictable side effect from a correctly given dose
A side effect from a correct dose is not a preventable error.
items.ex: Medication errors include inaccurate prescribing, wrong medication, wrong route or time, extra doses, and omitted doses.

alt.q: A unit’s safety committee reviews last month’s events. Which should be classified as medication errors? Select all that apply.
o: A heparin dose was given 2 hours late

An oral liquid was given intravenously
Wrong-route administration is a medication error.
A patient received a dose meant for a roommate
Giving the wrong medication to a patient is an error.
A patient declined a sleeping pill at bedtime
Patients have the right to refuse medications.
A dose was held after the nurse found a low pulse
Holding a dose based on assessment is appropriate judgment.
alt.ex: Late doses, wrong routes, and wrong-patient doses are errors; refusals and assessment-based holds are not.

items.q: A nurse realizes that a patient received a dose of a medication ordered for another patient. Which action should the nurse take first?

items.ex: When an error occurs, the patient’s safety is the top priority, so the nurse first assesses the patient’s condition.
w: Complete an occurrence report
The report is filed as soon as possible, but only after the patient is assessed and stable.
Notify the nurse manager
The manager is notified once the patient is stable.
Document the error in the patient’s EHR
The patient’s safety comes first; occurrence reports are not referenced in the EHR.

alt.q: A nurse discovers she gave a patient twice the ordered dose of a medication. Which action is the priority?
alt.a: Examine the patient for effects of the extra dose
alt.ex: Patient safety and well-being come first, so the nurse assesses the patient before reporting.
w: Fill out the occurrence report while details are fresh
Reporting follows patient assessment and provider notification.
Call the supervisor to explain what happened
The supervisor is informed once the patient is stable.

items.q: An occurrence report about a medication error is placed in the patient’s EHR as a permanent record.

alt.ww: Mentioning the report in the EHR would undo the legal protection the separate report provides.

items.q: Which information belongs in an occurrence report for a medication error? Select all that apply.

alt.q: A nurse is writing an occurrence report. Which entries are appropriate? Select all that apply.

items.q: A patient allergic to sulfa is ordered trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole. The nurse calls the provider before giving it and obtains a different order. How should this event be handled?

items.q: According to Box 31.4, how many times should a nurse compare a medication label with the MAR?

alt.q: According to Box 31.4 on preventing medication errors, at which points should the nurse read the medication label against the MAR?

items.q: While a nurse is giving medications to a patient, a coworker interrupts to ask about another patient’s lab results. Which action is best?

Talking while giving medications divides attention and increases error risk.

Leaving medications unattended is unsafe, and the interruption should wait.

alt.q: Which practice from the textbook helps prevent medication errors related to the environment?

items.q: A nurse cannot read the handwritten dose on a medication order. Which action is correct?

alt.q: A nurse cannot reach the health care provider to clarify an unclear medication order. What should the nurse do?

The nurse must pursue resolution through the chain of command.
Ask the patient what dose they think is correct
The patient cannot resolve an unclear order; the chain of command is used.

items.q: A nurse is about to give medications to a patient. Which pair of identifiers is acceptable to confirm the patient’s identity?

items.ex: Acceptable identifiers include the patient’s name, agency medical record number, or telephone number.
w: The patient’s name and room number
Room numbers are not acceptable patient identifiers.
The patient’s room number and diagnosis
Neither room number nor physical complaint is an acceptable identifier.
The patient’s diagnosis and bed location
Diagnosis and location do not reliably identify a patient.

alt.q: A nurse checks a patient’s armband before giving medications and finds it smudged and unreadable. Which action is correct?
alt.a: Obtain a new identification bracelet before giving the medications
alt.ex: If an identification bracelet is smudged, illegible, or missing, the nurse obtains a new one.
w: Use the room number on the door as the second identifier
Room numbers are never acceptable identifiers.
Give the medications because the nurse knows the patient’s face
Recognition is unreliable; two identifiers are required.
Ask the roommate to confirm the patient’s name
A roommate is not an acceptable means of identification.

items.q: Within what time frame should a nurse give a time-critical medication such as a scheduled antibiotic?
items.a: Within 30 minutes before or after the scheduled time

Within 4 hours before or after the scheduled time

Within 15 minutes after the scheduled time only
The window is 30 minutes before or after, not 15 minutes after only.

alt.q: Within what time frame are routinely ordered non–time-critical medications usually given?
alt.a: Within 1 to 2 hours before or after the scheduled time
alt.ex: Non–time-critical medications are given within 1 to 2 hours of the scheduled time or per agency policy.
w: Within 30 minutes before or after the scheduled time
The 30-minute window is for time-critical medications.
Within 6 hours before or after the scheduled time
Six hours is not the textbook’s window.
Within 10 minutes before or after the scheduled time

items.q: As the nurse prepares to give a patient’s 0900 medications, the patient says, “That pill looks different from the one I take at home.” Which action should the nurse take?

w: Reassure the patient that hospital brands often look different
The nurse must not ignore concerns; the pill could be the wrong drug.
Give the medication because it was scanned correctly
Patient concerns are addressed before giving the drug, even after scanning.

The patient raised a concern, not a refusal; the nurse must recheck the order.

alt.q: A family caregiver tells the nurse that the patient never takes a blue pill in the morning. Which response is best?

“Hospital medications often look different, so it’s fine.”

“You can bring the home pills if you prefer those.”

items.q: Enteral syringes such as ENFit have tips that will not connect to parenteral administration systems.
items.a: True
items.ex: Enteral syringes cannot connect to IV systems or accept needles, which prevents wrong-route errors with oral liquids.

alt.q: When a nurse must prepare an oral liquid in a syringe, a standard parenteral syringe is safe if it is labeled “oral.”
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses who prepare oral medications use only enteral syringes, which cannot connect to IV lines.

items.q: A medication error that is caught before it reaches the patient is called a [[near miss|near-miss]].
items.ex: Near misses are reported so the agency can learn why the mistake occurred and prevent similar errors.

w: Give the propofol because drug allergies differ from food allergies

alt.q: Why should a patient with a soy allergy not receive propofol?

w: Its active sedative is extracted from soybeans
The concern is the inactive ingredients, egg lecithin and soybean oil, not the active drug.

The issue is an allergic reaction to an ingredient, not altered metabolism.
Soy allergy makes patients resistant to sedation
The issue is allergy to soybean oil in the product, not resistance to its effect.

items.q: At 0900 a patient’s blood pressure is 178/98 mm Hg. Scheduled oral medications include an antihypertensive, a multivitamin, and a stool softener. Which action is best?

w: Give the multivitamin first because it was ordered first

Hold all of the medications and recheck the pressure in 1 hour

Give the stool softener first because it acts most slowly

alt.q: A patient rates incision pain as 8 out of 10, is due for several routine medications, and has a prn analgesic ordered. How should the nurse prioritize?
alt.a: Give the analgesic as soon as possible
alt.ex: When a patient is in pain, the book directs the nurse to provide pain medication as soon as possible.
w: Give all routine medications first, then the analgesic
Routine medications do not take priority over relieving significant pain.
Wait to give the analgesic at the next scheduled pass
A prn analgesic is given when needed; pain should be treated promptly.
Reassess the pain in 2 hours before giving anything

items.q: A patient newly prescribed insulin has limited time for teaching before discharge. Which topic should the nurse teach first?

w: How to rotate injection sites within one body area
Site rotation matters but is less urgent than managing life-threatening hypoglycemia.
How to keep a daily log of insulin and glucose results

How to store insulin in its original labeled container

alt.q: Why does the nurse teach hypoglycemia management before injection technique to a patient starting insulin?

w: Injection technique is learned better in the home setting

The book bases this order on clinical priority, not on a legal rule.

items.q: A patient admits skipping doses to make each bottle of medication last longer. The nurse identifies Nonadherence related to financial barriers. Which intervention best addresses the related factor?
items.a: Collaborate with a social worker or case manager on affordable resources
items.ex: When nonadherence is related to finances, the nurse collaborates with social workers, case managers, or agencies for resources.
w: Implement a detailed teaching plan about the medication’s action
A teaching plan addresses lack of knowledge, not an inability to afford medication.
Ask the health care provider to double the prescribed dose
Changing the dose does not solve the cost barrier and could cause harm.
Teach the patient to take the medication only when symptomatic
Taking medication only with symptoms changes the regimen unsafely and ignores the cost problem.

alt.q: A patient’s Nonadherence is related to lack of knowledge about the medication regimen. Which intervention fits this related factor?
alt.a: Implement a teaching plan with appropriate follow-up
alt.ex: The related factor drives the intervention; lack of knowledge calls for a teaching plan with follow-up.
w: Refer the patient to community agencies for financial help
Financial referral fits a cost-related factor, not a knowledge deficit.
Ask the pharmacist to switch to a less costly product
Cost changes do not correct the patient’s lack of knowledge.
Have a family caregiver make all medication decisions
Removing the patient from decisions does not address the knowledge gap.

items.q: A nursing student answers the unit phone, and a health care provider begins giving a new medication order. Which response by the student is best?
items.a: Ask the provider to hold while the student gets an RN
items.ex: Nursing students are prohibited from receiving or transcribing verbal and telephone orders.
w: Write the order down and read it back to the provider
Read-back is correct for an RN, but students may not receive telephone orders.
Enter the order in the MAR and have the RN cosign it
Students are prohibited from transcribing orders, even with a cosignature.
Accept the order if the provider will sign within 24 hours
The signature rule applies to orders an RN receives; students cannot receive them.

alt.q: An RN receives a telephone medication order. What should the RN do to make sure the correct order was obtained?
alt.a: Read the order back to the health care provider
alt.ex: Nurses read back verbal or telephone orders to the health care provider to confirm the correct order.
w: Repeat only the medication name to the provider
The whole order, including dose, route, and frequency, must be confirmed.
Ask the pharmacist to call the provider later
Confirmation happens at the time of the call through read-back.
Wait to write the order until the provider arrives
Telephone orders are received, read back, and documented per agency policy.

items.q: A nurse is giving an oral tablet to a 5-year-old child. Which statement by the nurse is best?
items.a: “It’s time for your pill. Do you want it with water or juice?”
items.ex: Offering a real choice, without the option of refusing, gives the child some control and improves success.
w: “Would you like to take your pill now or maybe later?”
This offers the option of not taking the medication, which the nurse should avoid.
“If you don’t take your pill, you can’t go to the playroom.”
Threats do not provide supportive care; praise and simple rewards are recommended after dosing.
“Let me explain in detail how this pill works in your body.”
Long explanations increase a child’s anxiety; use brief words at the child’s level.

alt.q: Why should the nurse avoid asking a child, “Do you want to take your medicine now?”
alt.a: It gives the child the option of not taking the medication
alt.ex: Choices such as which drink to use are helpful, but the child should not be offered the option to refuse.
w: Children cannot understand any questions about medication
Children can make simple choices, which often improves cooperation.
It increases the risk that the child will aspirate
The wording of a question does not affect aspiration risk.
Parents must make every choice for young children
Children may be given appropriate choices to gain cooperation.

items.q: Which component of a medication order makes it a legal request?
items.a: Signature of the health care provider
items.ex: Box 31.10 states that the provider’s signature makes the order a legal request.
w: Date and time the order was written
Date and time clarify when an order starts and stops.
Patient’s medical record number
The record number helps distinguish patients with the same name.
Route of administration
The route ensures the patient receives the drug by the intended route.

alt.q: Why does a medication order include the date and time it was written?
alt.a: It clarifies when the order starts and stops
alt.ex: Designating the time an order is written clarifies start and stop times and helps document any incident.
w: It makes the order a legal request
The provider’s signature, not the date and time, makes the order legal.
It distinguishes patients with the same name
The full name and medical record number distinguish patients.
It sets the routine schedule for each dose
The time and frequency of administration set the dosing schedule.

items.q: While preparing medications, the nurse notices that the MAR lists a different dose from the health care provider’s original order. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Consult the health care provider before giving the medication
items.ex: If the MAR and original order differ, the nurse consults the provider and gives nothing until all seven rights can be met.
w: Give the dose on the MAR because pharmacy verified it
A discrepancy must be resolved first; the nurse is responsible for any error given.
Give the lower of the two doses to be safe
Guessing a dose is unsafe; the correct dose must be clarified.
Give the original dose and correct the MAR afterward
The discrepancy is clarified with the provider before any dose is given.

alt.q: A nurse gives an incorrect dose because the transcribed MAR was wrong. Who is legally responsible for the error?
alt.a: The nurse who gave the incorrect dose
alt.ex: The book states that when you give the wrong medication or an incorrect dose, you are legally responsible.
w: Only the pharmacist who verified the MAR
The administering nurse is responsible for verifying every medication against the order.
Only the provider who wrote the order
The nurse must verify the MAR against the order before giving the drug.
The agency rather than any individual
The book places legal responsibility on the nurse who gives the wrong dose.

items.q: Why are older adults at risk for high blood levels of water-soluble drugs such as digoxin?
items.a: Total body water declines with aging
items.ex: Declining total body water raises the concentration of water-soluble drugs such as digoxin, which can cause heart dysfunction.
w: Adipose stores decrease with aging
Adipose stores increase with aging while lean body mass falls.
Gastric emptying speeds up with aging
Gastric emptying and GI motility slow with aging.
Plasma protein levels rise with aging
Plasma protein decreases, raising free levels of protein-bound drugs.

alt.q: Hepatic changes slow drug metabolism in older adults to about what fraction of a young adult’s rate?
alt.a: One-half to two-thirds
alt.ex: Liver mass, blood flow, and enzyme activity decline, so metabolism drops to one-half to two-thirds of a young adult’s rate.
w: One-tenth to one-fifth
This is far lower than the decline the book describes.
Three-quarters to equal
Metabolism falls more than this, to one-half to two-thirds.
One and a half to two times
Metabolism slows with aging; it does not speed up.

items.q: An older adult has trouble swallowing a large tablet. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?
items.a: Ask the provider whether a liquid form can be substituted
items.ex: Box 31.12 advises asking the health care provider to substitute a liquid medication when swallowing tablets is difficult.
w: Have the patient tilt the head back to swallow
Tilting the head back increases aspiration risk; a chin-down position is recommended.
Have the patient drink through a straw
Straws decrease control over the volume swallowed and increase aspiration risk.
Place the tablet far back on the tongue
The book advises placing the medication on the front of the tongue.

alt.q: Which instruction helps an older adult who has trouble swallowing a capsule?
alt.a: Place it on the front of the tongue, then swallow fluid
alt.ex: Placing medication on the front of the tongue and swallowing fluid helps wash it to the back of the throat.
w: Place it at the back of the throat, then swallow
The book directs placement on the front of the tongue, not the throat.
Lie flat and swallow it with a small sip
Lying flat increases aspiration risk; an upright position is used.
Swallow it dry, then drink fluid afterward
Fluid is used to help wash the medication back, not withheld.

items.q: Which type of measure does the nurse most commonly use to evaluate a patient’s response to medication?
items.a: Physiological measures such as blood pressure
items.ex: The book states the most common evaluative measure is physiological, such as blood pressure, heart rate, or visual acuity.
w: Rating scales such as a nausea scale
Rating scales are used but are not the most common type.
Behavioral responses such as agitation
Behavioral responses are used but are not the most common type.
Written measures such as a dose schedule
Written measures evaluate knowledge, not the most common measure of response.

alt.q: To evaluate an antihypertensive, a nurse checks the patient’s blood pressure. Which type of evaluative measure is this?
alt.a: Physiological measure
alt.ex: Blood pressure is a direct physiological measure, the most common type of evaluative measure.
w: Behavioral response
Behavioral responses are observed actions such as agitation.
Rating scale
Rating scales are patient ratings such as a pain or nausea score.
Anecdotal note
Anecdotal notes are logs, such as a caregiver’s adherence record.

items.q: Which practices are recommended when giving oral medications to children? Select all that apply.
o: Use a plastic oral syringe to measure a 5-mL liquid dose
An oral syringe is the most accurate device, especially for doses under 10 mL.
Mix the medication with only a small amount of food or liquid
A child may refuse to finish a larger mixture.
Mix the medication into the child’s favorite food
The medication can alter the taste, and the child may later refuse that food.
Choose a liquid form rather than a pill when possible
Liquids are safer to swallow than pills and reduce aspiration risk.
Measure the dose with a household teaspoon
Cups, teaspoons, and droppers are inaccurate for measuring liquid doses.
items.ex: Box 31.11 favors liquids, accurate oral syringes, and small mixtures that avoid favorite foods.

alt.q: Which practices are recommended when giving an injection to a child? Select all that apply.
o: Wake a sleeping child before giving the injection
Box 31.11 says to always wake a sleeping child first.
Have the parent act as comforter rather than restrainer
Another nurse restrains if needed; the parent comforts.
Distract the child with bubbles, a toy, or conversation
Distraction reduces pain perception.
Give the injection while the child sleeps to avoid fear
A sleeping child is always awakened before an injection.
Give a long, detailed explanation before the injection
Long explanations increase anxiety, especially before painful procedures.
alt.ex: Pediatric injections require waking the child, distraction, and a parent who comforts rather than restrains.

items.q: Which factors increase a patient’s risk for polypharmacy? Select all that apply.
o: Frequent use of over-the-counter medications
Frequent OTC use is a listed risk factor.
Visiting several health care providers for different illnesses
Multiple prescribers increase the risk of overlapping medications.
Incorrect beliefs about medications
Incorrect beliefs and lack of knowledge increase risk.
Having one health care provider manage all illnesses
Fewer prescribers and good communication lower the risk.
Taking a single medication for one diagnosed illness
One medication matched to a diagnosis is not polypharmacy.
items.ex: OTC use, multiple providers, lack of knowledge, and incorrect beliefs all raise polypharmacy risk.

alt.q: Which situations suggest polypharmacy? Select all that apply.
o: Taking two drugs from the same chemical class for one illness
This is the book’s example of polypharmacy.
Mixing herbal products or supplements with medications
Combining supplements or herbs with medications is a warning sign.
Taking a medication that does not match any diagnosis
A medication without a matching diagnosis fits the definition.
Taking one prescribed medication exactly as ordered
A single appropriate medication taken correctly is not polypharmacy.
Taking an antibiotic for a diagnosed infection
A medication that matches a diagnosis is appropriate use.
alt.ex: Polypharmacy includes duplicate drug classes, mixing herbals with medications, and drugs that do not match a diagnosis.

items.q: Which actions help the nurse assess a patient’s health literacy about medications? Select all that apply.
o: Have the patient explain the medication schedule for a typical day
Explaining a typical day shows understanding of the schedule.
Have the patient read a medication label and explain it
Reading and explaining a label tests understanding of written information.
Have the patient show how to give a dose that requires splitting a pill
Health literacy includes numeracy, which this demonstration tests.
Ask only yes-or-no questions about the medications
Yes-or-no answers do not reveal whether the patient truly understands.
Give the patient a pamphlet and assume it was understood
Understanding must be assessed, not assumed.
items.ex: Having patients explain a schedule, read a label, and demonstrate a dose assesses literacy and numeracy.

alt.q: Which questions belong in a nursing assessment of a patient’s medications? Select all that apply.
o: “Have you ever stopped taking your medications? If so, why?”
Box 31.7 includes this question about past nonadherence.
“How do you pay for your medications?”
Box 31.7 asks about cost and stretching the budget.
“What do you do to help remember to take your medications?”
Box 31.7 asks about memory strategies.
“You take all your pills exactly as ordered, right?”
A leading question discourages honest answers about adherence.
“Would you like me to choose your medications for you?”
Assessment explores the patient’s own routines, beliefs, and concerns.
alt.ex: Box 31.7 asks open questions about stopping medications, cost, memory aids, side effects, and allergies.

items.q: Adverse medication events occur in 22% or more of older-adult patients presenting to health care agencies.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book reports adverse medication events in at least 22% of older adults presenting for care.
items.ww: The statement matches the book’s figure, so calling it false would understate the risk in older adults.

alt.q: Skin rash is the most common serious manifestation of adverse medication events in older adults.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The most common serious manifestations are falls, orthostatic hypotension, heart failure, and delirium.
alt.ww: Rash is not listed; the book names falls, orthostatic hypotension, heart failure, and delirium.

items.q: When a patient refuses a medication, the nurse explains the reason the dose was not given in the nurses’ notes.
items.a: True
items.ex: Refused or missed doses are documented with the reason, and some agencies require circling the time or notifying the provider.
items.ww: Leaving a refused dose unexplained hides a missed dose that may affect conditions such as hypertension or diabetes.

alt.q: A dose missed because the patient was away for a diagnostic test does not need to be documented.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Doses missed for tests or procedures are documented with the reason in the nurses’ notes.
alt.ww: Missed doses can affect conditions such as diabetes, so the reason must be recorded.

items.q: Nurses standing inside a No-Interruption Zone around a medication cart should not be interrupted.
items.a: True
items.ex: NIZs, marked by signs, red tape, or borders, reduce distractions that increase medication errors.
items.ww: The purpose of an NIZ is to prevent interruptions during medication preparation.

alt.q: Answering text messages while preparing medications is acceptable if the nurse double-checks the MAR afterward.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Distractions during preparation increase errors, so the nurse avoids texts and calls during medication administration.
alt.ww: A later check does not undo errors caused by distraction during preparation.

items.q: [[Polypharmacy]] is the use of multiple medications, potentially inappropriate or unnecessary medications, or a medication that does not match a diagnosis.
items.ex: Polypharmacy raises the risk of adverse reactions and interactions with other medications and food.

alt.q: Taking two medications from the same chemical class to treat the same illness is an example of [[polypharmacy]].
alt.ex: Polypharmacy raises the risk of adverse reactions and interactions with other medications and food.
