items.q: A patient with dysphagia after a stroke has left-sided weakness and needs oral tablets. Which action best reduces aspiration risk?
items.a: Place each tablet on the right, stronger side of the mouth
items.ex: With unilateral weakness, medication is placed in the stronger side of the mouth to reduce aspiration.
w: Give all the tablets together in one spoonful of applesauce
Pills are given one at a time, confirming each is swallowed.
Have the patient tilt the head back to swallow each tablet
A chin-down position reduces aspiration; tilting the head back increases it.
Offer thin water through a straw after each tablet
Straws reduce control of volume, and thin liquids may need thickening.

alt.q: Which position does the nurse use to protect a patient from aspiration when giving oral medications, if not contraindicated?
alt.a: Seated upright at 90 degrees with chin slightly down
alt.ex: An upright 90-degree position with the head slightly flexed chin-down reduces aspiration.
w: Semi-Fowler at 30 degrees with head tilted back
The head should not tilt back, and 90 degrees is preferred.
Side-lying at 45 degrees with the neck extended
Neck extension increases aspiration risk; upright chin-down is preferred.
Supine at 0 degrees with head turned to one side
Lying flat greatly increases aspiration risk during swallowing.

items.q: Before giving medications through a nasogastric feeding tube, the nurse checks the pH of the aspirate. Which result best indicates the tube tip is in the stomach?
items.a: pH 4.0
items.ex: A gastric pH less than 5.0 is a good indicator that the tube tip is correctly placed in the stomach.
w: pH 6.5
This is above 5.0, so it does not confirm gastric placement.
pH 7.4
A neutral pH does not indicate acidic gastric contents.
pH 8.0
An alkaline pH suggests the tip is not in the stomach.

alt.q: Which gastric aspirate pH value is a good indicator of correct stomach placement of a feeding tube?
alt.a: Less than 5.0
alt.ex: Acidic aspirate with a pH under 5.0 indicates the tube tip is in the stomach.
w: Between 6.0 and 7.0
This range is above the 5.0 cutoff for gastric placement.
Exactly 7.4
A pH of 7.4 is not acidic enough to indicate stomach contents.
Greater than 8.0
Alkaline aspirate does not indicate gastric placement.

items.q: Before giving medications through a gastrostomy tube, the nurse measures a gastric residual volume of 550 mL. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Hold the medication and contact the health care provider
items.ex: When GRV exceeds 500 mL, the feeding is held and rechecked; with excessive GRV, the nurse holds the medication and contacts the provider.
w: Give the medication with an extra 60-mL water flush
Adding volume to an already full stomach is unsafe with excessive residual.
Give the medication slowly over 10 minutes instead
Slowing administration does not address the excessive residual volume.
Resume the feeding at a higher rate after the medication
Excessive residual calls for holding the feeding, not increasing it.

alt.q: A gastric residual volume above which amount signals the nurse to hold the tube feeding for 2 hours and recheck?
alt.a: 500 mL
alt.ex: If GRV exceeds 500 mL, the feeding is held for 2 hours and rechecked per agency policy.
w: 50 mL
This small volume is not the threshold for holding a feeding.
150 mL
This is below the 500-mL threshold the book gives.
250 mL
This is below the 500-mL threshold the book gives.

items.q: A nurse is about to apply a new fentanyl transdermal patch to a patient. Which action is most important?
items.a: Ask about and remove any existing patch first
items.ex: Old patches still contain drug; leaving them on has caused overdose with respiratory depression, coma, and death.
w: Apply the new patch directly over the previous site
The old patch must be found and removed; layering patches risks overdose.
Apply the new patch without gloves for better adhesion
Clean gloves are worn when removing and applying transdermal patches.
Skip documenting the site because the patch is visible
The body location of the patch is documented on the MAR.

alt.q: Why does the nurse fold the sticky sides of a removed transdermal patch together before disposing of it?
alt.a: Medication remains on the patch and can harm others
alt.ex: Used patches still contain drug; children have been harmed by accidental exposure to improperly discarded fentanyl patches.
w: Folding activates a layer that neutralizes the drug
Patches have no neutralizing layer; folding limits exposure to remaining drug.
Folded patches can be safely reapplied later
Used patches are discarded, never reapplied.
Folding shows the patch was worn for its full duration
Folding is for safe disposal, not for recording duration.

items.q: A nurse is instilling eardrops in a 2-year-old child. How should the nurse straighten the ear canal?
items.a: Pull the pinna down and back
items.ex: For children under age 3, the pinna is pulled down and back to the 6- to 9-o’clock position.
w: Pull the pinna up and back
Up and back is used for adults and children older than 3 years.
Pull the pinna straight forward
Pulling forward does not straighten the ear canal.
Press the tragus inward first
Pressure on the tragus is applied after drops are instilled.

alt.q: For an adult receiving eardrops, how does the nurse straighten the ear canal?
alt.a: Pull the pinna up and back
alt.ex: For adults and children older than 3, the pinna is pulled up and back toward the 10-o’clock position.
w: Pull the pinna down and back
Down and back is used for children younger than 3 years.
Pull the earlobe straight down
This does not straighten the adult ear canal.
Push the pinna forward and up
Pushing forward does not straighten the canal.

items.q: A nurse is inserting a rectal suppository in an adult. Which technique is correct?
items.a: Insert it past the internal sphincter against the rectal wall, 10 cm
items.ex: In adults the suppository goes 10 cm past the internal sphincter and against the rectal wall.
w: Insert it into the mass of stool so it dissolves, 10 cm
Placing a suppository in feces reduces its effectiveness.
Insert it just inside the anal opening, about 1 cm
It must pass the internal sphincter or it may be expelled.
Insert it past the sphincter about 20 cm with the patient prone
Adults need 10 cm, with the patient in left side-lying position.

alt.q: How far does the nurse insert a rectal suppository in an infant or child?
alt.a: 5 cm (2 inches)
alt.ex: Rectal suppositories are inserted 5 cm in infants and children and 10 cm in adults.
w: 1 cm (½ inch)
This would not pass the internal sphincter.
10 cm (4 inches)
This is the adult depth.
15 cm (6 inches)
This exceeds the depth used for any age.

items.q: A patient’s MDI contains 120 puffs, and the prescription is 2 puffs twice a day. How many days will the canister last?
items.a: 30 days
items.ex: 2 puffs × 2 times a day = 4 puffs per day; 120 ÷ 4 = 30 days.
w: 15 days
This divides by 8 puffs per day instead of 4.
60 days
This divides by only 2 puffs per day.
24 days
This does not follow from dividing total puffs by daily puffs.

alt.q: A patient’s MDI will run out in 25 days. When should the nurse teach the patient to refill it?
alt.a: At least 7 to 10 days before it runs out
alt.ex: Patients refill an inhaler at least 7 to 10 days before it runs out so they do not go without medication.
w: On day 25, when the counter reads 0
Waiting until empty risks being without rescue or maintenance medication.
1 to 2 days before it runs out
This leaves too little time; the book advises 7 to 10 days.
Only after 30 days of use
The canister would already be empty after 25 days.

items.q: A nurse is preparing regular insulin and NPH insulin in one syringe. Which insulin is drawn into the syringe first?
items.a: Regular insulin, to keep it free of NPH
items.ex: Regular insulin is prepared first so it does not become contaminated with the intermediate-acting insulin.
w: NPH insulin, because it must be resuspended
NPH is rolled to resuspend it, but it is drawn up second.
Either one, because the order does not matter
Order matters when mixing regular with intermediate-acting insulin.
NPH insulin, because its vial gets air first
Air goes into the NPH vial first, but regular is withdrawn first.

alt.q: When mixing regular and NPH insulin, into which vial does the nurse inject air first?
alt.a: The intermediate-acting NPH vial
alt.ex: Air equal to the NPH dose is injected into the NPH vial first, without withdrawing, then regular is drawn up.
w: The short-acting regular vial
Air goes into the regular vial second, just before withdrawing its dose.
Whichever vial is fuller
The type of insulin, not fullness, determines the sequence.
Neither vial, because insulin needs no air
Vials are closed systems; air prevents a vacuum during withdrawal.

items.q: At a subcutaneous injection site, the nurse can grasp 5 cm (2 inches) of tissue. At which angle should the needle be inserted?
items.a: 90 degrees
items.ex: If you can grasp 2 inches of tissue, insert at 90 degrees; if 1 inch, insert at 45 degrees.
w: 15 degrees
A 15-degree angle is used for intradermal injections.
30 degrees
This angle is not used for subcutaneous injections in the book.
45 degrees
45 degrees is used when only 1 inch of tissue can be grasped.

alt.q: At a subcutaneous injection site, the nurse can grasp only 2.5 cm (1 inch) of tissue. At which angle should the needle be inserted?
alt.a: 45 degrees
alt.ex: With 1 inch of tissue, a 45-degree angle keeps the medication in subcutaneous tissue.
w: 90 degrees
90 degrees is used when 2 inches of tissue can be grasped.
15 degrees
This shallow angle is for intradermal injections.
5 degrees
This shallow angle is used for intradermal injections.

items.q: After injecting a tuberculin skin test, the nurse sees no bleb, and the site bleeds after the needle is withdrawn. What does this most likely mean?
items.a: The drug entered subcutaneous tissue, so results are invalid
items.ex: No bleb or bleeding suggests the medication went into subcutaneous tissue, making the test results invalid.
w: The drug was absorbed correctly into the dermis
A correct intradermal injection produces a small bleb like a mosquito bite.
The patient is having a positive reaction to the test
A missing bleb reflects technique, not a test result.
The needle was inserted at too shallow an angle
A missing bleb suggests the needle went too deep, into subcutaneous tissue.

alt.q: Which angle of insertion does the nurse use for an intradermal injection?
alt.a: 5 to 15 degrees with the bevel up
alt.ex: ID injections use a 5- to 15-degree angle with the bevel pointing up to form a bleb.
w: 45 degrees with the bevel up
45 degrees is a subcutaneous angle.
90 degrees with the bevel down
90 degrees is used for IM and some subcutaneous injections.
5 to 15 degrees with the bevel down
The bevel should point up for an ID injection.

items.q: Before giving an IV push medication through a saline lock, the nurse notes the insertion site is reddened and edematous. Which action is appropriate?
items.a: Do not give the IV push through this site
items.ex: Never give an IV push if the site appears edematous or reddened; injection into surrounding tissue can cause sloughing and abscesses.
w: Give the push slowly over twice the usual time
Slowing the rate does not make an infiltrated or inflamed site safe.
Dilute the medication further and then give it
Dilution does not correct a compromised IV site.
Flush with heparin first, then give the push
Flushing does not make a reddened, edematous site safe to use.

alt.q: Which finding at an IV site must be present before the nurse gives an IV push medication through the existing infusion?
alt.a: Fluids flowing at the ordered rate without redness or swelling
alt.ex: Placement is confirmed first; an IV push is never given if fluids do not flow at the ordered rate or the site is edematous or red.
w: Fluids flowing slowly with mild swelling at the site
Swelling and poor flow are reasons not to give an IV push.
Redness at the site with fluids flowing freely
A reddened site is a reason to withhold the IV push.
No flow in the line but a dry, intact dressing
Fluids must flow at the ordered rate before an IV push.

items.q: Why does the primary infusion stop flowing while an IV piggyback medication infuses?
items.a: A back-check valve in the primary line stops its flow
items.ex: The back-check valve stops the primary infusion while the piggyback flows and reopens when the piggyback level falls.
w: The nurse clamps the primary tubing during the infusion
No clamp is needed; the back-check valve stops the primary flow.
The piggyback bag hangs lower than the primary bag
The piggyback hangs higher than the primary bag.
The infusion pump alternates between the two bags
Flow is controlled by the back-check valve, not alternating pump cycles.

alt.q: In a piggyback setup, where is the piggyback bag hung in relation to the primary bag?
alt.a: Higher than the primary infusion bag
alt.ex: It is called a piggyback because the small bag is higher than the primary infusion bag.
w: Lower than the primary infusion bag
A lower bag would not flow ahead of the primary infusion.
At the same height as the primary bag
The piggyback must be higher for the back-check valve to work.
Below the level of the patient’s heart
The piggyback is hung above the primary bag, not below the heart.

items.q: Which actions protect a patient from aspiration during oral medication administration? Select all that apply.
o: Give pills one at a time, ensuring each is swallowed
Box 31.13 advises one pill at a time.
Thicken liquids if the patient cannot tolerate thin liquids
Thickened liquids or nectars are easier to control.
Time medications for mealtimes or when the patient is rested
A rested, awake patient swallows more safely.
Have the patient drink through a straw
Straws decrease control over volume and increase aspiration risk.
Remind the patient to tilt the head backward to swallow
The patient should flex the head chin-down, not tilt it back.
items.ex: Box 31.13 includes one pill at a time, thickened liquids, good timing, chin-down positioning, and no straws.

alt.q: Which findings are signs of dysphagia? Select all that apply.
o: Coughing when swallowing
Cough is a listed sign of dysphagia.
Change in voice quality after swallowing
A change in voice tone or quality is a sign.
Pocketing of food in the mouth
Incomplete oral clearance or pocketing is a sign.
Regurgitation
Regurgitation is a listed sign.
Rapid, complete clearing of the mouth
Complete clearance is normal; incomplete clearance suggests dysphagia.
Increased appetite at mealtimes
Appetite is not a sign of dysphagia.
alt.ex: Signs of dysphagia include cough, voice change, delayed swallowing, pocketing of food, and regurgitation.

items.q: Which practices help prevent needlestick injuries? Select all that apply.
o: Do not recap needles after medication administration
Recapping is a common cause of needlesticks.
Report all needlestick injuries immediately per agency policy
Prompt reporting is required.
Plan safe handling and disposal before starting the procedure
Box 31.22 recommends planning disposal in advance.
Push a needle into a full sharps container if it fits
Never force a needle into a full disposal receptacle.
Leave a used syringe on the meal tray to discard later
Used needles never go on a meal tray, in a pocket, or at the bedside.
items.ex: Box 31.22 recommends no recapping, planned disposal, puncture-proof containers, and immediate reporting.

alt.q: Which actions prevent infection during an injection? Select all that apply.
o: Swab the site from the center outward in a 5-cm radius
Box 31.19 directs cleaning from center outward.
Draw up medication quickly and do not let ampules stand open
Speed prevents contaminating the solution.
Avoid touching the length of the plunger or inner barrel
This prevents syringe contamination.
Swab the site from the outer edge toward the center
Cleaning moves from the center outward, not inward.
Perform hand hygiene for about 5 seconds
Hand hygiene lasts a minimum of 20 seconds.
alt.ex: Box 31.19 covers quick drawing up, untouched sterile parts, center-outward skin prep, and 20-second hand hygiene.

items.q: Which actions are correct when giving low-molecular-weight heparin (enoxaparin) subcutaneously? Select all that apply.
o: Inject on the right or left abdomen at least 5 cm from the umbilicus
The “love handles” area at least 2 inches from the umbilicus is used.
Pinch the injection site as the needle is inserted
The book directs pinching the site during insertion.
Give it in its prefilled syringe with the attached needle
LMWH is given in its prefilled syringe.
Expel the air bubble from the syringe before injecting
The air bubble is not expelled before giving LMWH.
Inject within 1 cm of the umbilicus
The site must be at least 5 cm (2 inches) from the umbilicus.
items.ex: LMWH is given in the abdomen at least 5 cm from the umbilicus, site pinched, prefilled syringe, air bubble kept.

alt.q: Which insulin injection practices does the book recommend? Select all that apply.
o: Use the abdomen first for rapid-acting insulin
Absorption is fastest through the abdominal wall.
Do not aspirate when injecting insulin
Aspiration is avoided, especially with pens, to prevent leakage.
Keep an insulin pen needle in place for 10 seconds
This prevents leakage after injection.
Shake cloudy insulin vials to mix them
Cloudy insulin is rolled, not shaken, because bubbles alter the dose.
Reuse the same injection site within 1 week
Sites are not reused for at least 1 month.
alt.ex: Insulin guidelines include abdomen first for rapid-acting insulin, no aspiration, holding pens 10 seconds, rolling not shaking.

items.q: Floating a metered-dose inhaler in water is a reliable way to check how much medication remains.
items.a: False
items.ex: Extra propellant can make the canister float even when no medication remains, so floating is not recommended.
items.ww: Floating gives misleading results because propellant remains after the medication is gone.

alt.q: Extra propellant can make an empty MDI canister float even when no medication remains.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: This is why floating an MDI is not recommended; dividing doses by daily use estimates how long it lasts.
alt.ww: The book states propellant causes floating even without medication.

items.q: Overuse of decongestant nasal sprays can cause a rebound effect in which nasal congestion worsens.
items.a: True
items.ex: Patients are cautioned about overuse because it leads to rebound congestion.
items.ww: The book specifically warns that overuse worsens congestion through a rebound effect.

alt.q: Sympathomimetic decongestant drops such as oxymetazoline are safer than saline drops for children.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Saline drops are safer for children; swallowed decongestant can cause serious systemic effects.
alt.ww: The book states saline drops are the safer choice for children.

items.q: A nurse may add a medication to an IV bag that is already hanging if the bag is mixed well afterward.
items.a: False
items.ex: Medications are added only to new IV bags because the concentration in a hanging bag cannot be determined.
items.ww: Mixing does not reveal how much fluid remains, so the exact concentration is unknown.

alt.q: When a nurse must add a medication to IV fluid, it is added only to a new IV bag.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Adding medication to a new bag ensures a known concentration; hanging bags are never used.
alt.ww: The book prohibits adding medications to bags already hanging.

items.q: When withdrawing medication from a glass ampule, the nurse uses a [[filter needle|filter]] to keep glass particles out of the syringe.
items.ex: A filter needle is used to prepare ampule medication but is replaced with an appropriate needle before injection.

alt.q: A [[filter needle|filter]] is used to draw medication from an ampule but is never used to inject the medication.
alt.ex: A filter needle is used to prepare ampule medication but is replaced with an appropriate needle before injection.

items: Select the medication and compare its label with the MAR (first check)

items.q: Which instruction should the nurse give to assistive personnel (AP) caring for a patient who just received oral medications?
items.a: Report any rash, itching, or worsening pain after the medications
items.ex: Oral medication administration cannot be delegated; AP report side effects or changes such as pain, itching, or rash.
w: Give the patient’s noon oral medications if the nurse is busy
Administering oral medications cannot be delegated to AP.
Crush the patient’s tablets if swallowing seems difficult
Preparing medications is a nursing responsibility, and not all drugs can be crushed.
Offer the patient’s prn pain tablet whenever it is requested
AP cannot give medications, including prn doses.

alt.q: Which team member can assist a patient with impaired swallowing by teaching swallowing techniques?
alt.a: Speech pathologist
alt.ex: Skill 31.1 notes that a speech pathologist can teach swallowing techniques to patients with impaired swallowing.
w: Assistive personnel
AP report changes to the nurse but do not teach swallowing techniques.
Pharmacist
The pharmacist advises on drug forms, not swallowing techniques.
Respiratory therapist
Swallowing techniques are taught by a speech pathologist in this skill.

items.q: Why does the nurse compare the MAR with the health care provider’s written order before giving oral medications?
items.a: The order is the most reliable source and only legal record
items.ex: The order sheet is the most reliable source and only legal record of medications, and transcription errors cause medication errors.
w: The MAR is the only legal record of medications
The provider’s order, not the MAR, is the legal record.
The pharmacist requires a recheck of every order
The check is done because the order is the legal source and transcription errors occur.
The written order lists the patient’s allergic reactions
Allergies are confirmed separately with the patient and the EHR.

alt.q: Comparing the MAR with the provider’s original order helps the nurse catch which known source of medication errors?
alt.a: Transcription errors
alt.ex: Transcription errors are a source of medication errors, so the MAR is checked against the original order.
w: Bar-code scanning errors
Scanning happens at the bedside, not during the MAR-to-order comparison.
Look-alike packaging errors
Label comparison during preparation addresses packaging mix-ups.
Dropped-tablet errors
A dropped tablet is discarded during administration, not caught on the MAR.

items.q: A patient on continuous gastric suction has an oral medication ordered. Why should the nurse notify the health care provider?
items.a: The medication would be suctioned out before it is absorbed
items.ex: Patients with GI suction do not receive oral medications because the drugs are removed before absorption.
w: Gastric suction increases the potency of oral drugs
Suction removes the drug; it does not increase potency.
Suction makes the tablet dissolve too slowly
The problem is removal of the drug, not dissolution speed.
Oral medications damage the suction tubing
Tubing damage is not the reason oral drugs are contraindicated.

alt.q: Which finding is a contraindication to oral medications that the nurse should report to the health care provider?
alt.a: Decreased level of consciousness
alt.ex: Decreased LOC is a listed contraindication because it increases aspiration risk.
w: Preference for juice instead of water
A fluid preference is accommodated if compatible with the medication.
Ability to sit upright in a chair
Sitting upright is the desired position for oral medications.
History of controlled hypertension
Controlled hypertension does not prevent oral administration.

items.q: As the nurse hands over oral medications, the patient says, “I’ve never taken a yellow pill before.” Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Hold the pill, explore the concern, and verify the order
items.ex: If a patient questions a medication, do not give it; explore the concern and verify the order, which may prevent an error.
w: Explain that generic pills often change color, then give it
The nurse must verify before giving; the patient’s concern may reveal an error.
Give the pill and recheck the order after the medication pass
Verification must occur before administration, not after.
Document that the patient refused the medication
The patient raised a concern, not a refusal; the order needs verification.

alt.q: Why should the nurse withhold a medication when a patient questions whether it is correct?
alt.a: Listening to the concern may prevent a medication error
alt.ex: The patient may notice a real error, so the nurse verifies the order before giving the drug.
w: Patients have the legal right to choose their own doses
The reason is error prevention, not patient dose selection.
Questioned medications must go back to pharmacy
The nurse verifies the order; returning the drug is not required.
The concern means the patient is allergic to it
A concern does not indicate allergy; it may signal an error.

items.q: While the nurse is giving a patient’s tablets, one falls onto the floor. Which action is correct?
items.a: Discard the tablet and repeat the preparation
items.ex: A tablet that falls to the floor is contaminated, so it is discarded and a new dose prepared.
w: Wipe the tablet with an alcohol swab and give it
Wiping does not remove contamination from the floor.
Give it if it landed on a clean, dry floor
Any tablet that touches the floor is contaminated.
Return the tablet to the stock bottle for later
Returning it would contaminate the stock supply.

alt.q: Why is a tablet that falls to the floor discarded rather than given?
alt.a: The tablet is contaminated
alt.ex: The drug is contaminated once it touches the floor, so preparation is repeated.
w: The fall changes the tablet’s dose
The issue is contamination, not a change in dose.
The patient will refuse to take it
Patient preference is not the reason for discarding it.
Controlled substance rules require it
The rule applies to all dropped tablets because of contamination.

items.q: A patient needs half of a tablet. Which approach follows best practice in a health care agency?
items.a: Have the pharmacy split, label, and package the dose
items.ex: In health care agencies, only pharmacy should split tablets to ensure patient safety.
w: Split the tablet with a knife at the bedside
A knife is not a clean pill-cutting device, and pharmacy should split doses.
Split an unscored tablet with a pill cutter
Only tablets prescored by the manufacturer may be cut.
Have the patient bite the tablet in half
Biting does not give an accurate half dose.

alt.q: If the nurse must split a tablet, which tablets may be cut?
alt.a: Only tablets prescored by the manufacturer
alt.ex: Only tablets with a manufacturer score line across the center are cut, using a clean gloved hand and clean cutter.
w: Any tablet smaller than 10 mg
Tablet strength does not determine whether it can be split.
Any tablet with an enteric coating
Coating type does not make a tablet safe to cut; prescoring does.
Only capsules with a gel coating
Capsules are not split; only prescored tablets are cut.

items.q: A patient’s morning medications include digoxin, which requires an apical pulse check before administration. How should the nurse prepare it?
items.a: Place it in a separate cup with the wrapper intact
items.ex: Drugs needing preadministration assessment go in a separate cup as a reminder and so they are easy to withhold.
w: Place it in the same cup as the other medications
Mixing it with the others makes withholding it harder.
Remove the wrapper and crush it with the others
Wrappers stay on, and crushing is not indicated here.
Give it first, then check the pulse afterward
The assessment must come before giving the drug to decide whether to withhold it.

alt.q: Why does the nurse keep medications that require preadministration assessment in a separate cup?
alt.a: It serves as a reminder and makes withholding easier
alt.ex: A separate cup reminds the nurse to assess first and allows the drug to be held if needed.
w: Those drugs react chemically with other tablets
The reason is assessment and withholding, not chemical reaction.
Pharmacy policy requires one cup per medication
Other tablets share one cup; only assessed drugs are separated.
It speeds absorption when taken separately
Separation does not change absorption.

items.q: Why does the nurse use a syringe designed for oral use, rather than a hypodermic syringe, to measure a liquid oral medication?
items.a: It prevents accidental parenteral administration of the drug
items.ex: Hypodermic syringes risk parenteral administration, and a cap or needle could be dislodged and aspirated.
w: Hypodermic syringes cannot measure amounts under 1 mL
Hypodermic syringes can measure small amounts; the risk is wrong-route use.
Oral syringes keep the liquid sterile until it is given
Oral medications are not sterile; the concern is route safety.
Hypodermic syringes absorb part of the medication
The concern is accidental parenteral use, not absorption by the syringe.

alt.q: A liquid oral medication is supplied in a single-dose cup containing the correct dose. How should the nurse give it?
alt.a: Give it directly from the single-dose cup
alt.ex: Unit-dose liquids are given directly from their single-dose cup, which provides the most accurate dose.
w: Pour it into a calibrated medication cup first
Pouring into another cup is not done and may lose part of the dose.
Draw it into a hypodermic syringe first
Hypodermic syringes are never used for oral liquids.
Mix it into a full glass of juice first
Diluting it in a large volume risks an incomplete dose.

items.q: Thirty minutes after an oral antibiotic, a patient develops urticaria, rhinitis, and wheezing. Which action is appropriate?
items.a: Withhold further doses and notify the provider and pharmacy
items.ex: These signs suggest an allergic reaction; withhold doses, notify the provider and pharmacy, and assess vital signs.
w: Give the next dose with a full glass of water
Further doses are withheld when an adverse reaction occurs.
Document the reaction at the end of the shift
The provider and pharmacy are notified immediately, not later.
Encourage the patient to finish the full course
Continuing the drug despite an allergic reaction is unsafe.

alt.q: Which symptoms after an oral medication suggest an allergic reaction that may require emergency medications?
alt.a: Urticaria, pruritus, and wheezing
alt.ex: Urticaria, rash, pruritus, rhinitis, and wheezing may indicate an allergic reaction needing emergency medications.
w: Mild drowsiness and dry mouth
These are common side effects, not signs of allergy.
Slight nausea after an empty-stomach dose
Nausea is a GI side effect, not an allergic sign.
Bitter taste and increased thirst
These are not listed signs of an allergic reaction.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient about sublingual nitroglycerin. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I will let the tablet dissolve under my tongue without swallowing it.”
items.ex: Sublingual drugs dissolve under the tongue and are absorbed by vessels there; swallowing them prevents a therapeutic level.
w: “I will swallow the tablet with a full glass of water.”
Swallowed, the drug is destroyed by gastric juices or detoxified by the liver.
“I will chew the tablet and hold it against my cheek.”
Holding against the cheek is buccal use; sublingual tablets go under the tongue.
“I will sip water while the tablet is dissolving.”
Nothing is taken by mouth until the sublingual tablet fully dissolves.

alt.q: Why must a patient avoid swallowing a sublingual tablet?
alt.a: Gastric juices or the liver would inactivate the drug
alt.ex: If swallowed, the drug is destroyed by gastric juices or rapidly detoxified by the liver, preventing a therapeutic level.
w: Swallowing makes the drug act too quickly
Swallowing reduces the effect; it does not speed it up.
The tablet would irritate the esophagus
The reason is drug inactivation, not esophageal irritation.
The tablet is too large to pass the throat
Sublingual tablets are small; size is not the concern.

items.q: A nurse is giving an oral chemotherapy tablet. Which technique is correct?
items.a: Tip it from the cup into the mouth, or wear gloves
items.ex: Oral chemotherapy can go from the cup directly into the mouth, or the nurse applies gloves before handling it.
w: Hand the tablet to the patient with bare fingers
Bare hands must never touch chemotherapy drugs because residue absorbs through skin.
Wash hands after touching it with bare fingers
Skin contact must be prevented; washing afterward is not enough.
Wear gloves only if the patient has mouth drainage
Gloves are required for handling oral chemotherapy regardless of drainage.

alt.q: Why must the nurse never touch an oral chemotherapy medication with bare hands?
alt.a: Drug residue can be absorbed through the skin
alt.ex: Chemotherapy residue can be absorbed through the nurse’s skin, so gloves or a no-touch method is used.
w: Skin oils inactivate the chemotherapy drug
The concern is the nurse’s exposure, not drug inactivation.
Touching it breaks the enteric coating
The concern is skin absorption of hazardous residue.
Bare hands spread the drug’s odor
Odor is not the reason; skin absorption of residue is.

items.q: Which findings are contraindications to oral medication administration that the nurse should report to the health care provider? Select all that apply.
o: NPO status
Being NPO is a listed contraindication.
Nausea and vomiting
A vomiting patient cannot retain oral medications.
Recent gastrointestinal surgery
Recent GI surgery is a listed contraindication.
Decreased level of consciousness
Decreased LOC increases aspiration risk.
Preference for taking pills with juice
Fluid preference is accommodated if compatible with the drug.
Blood pressure within normal limits
Normal blood pressure does not prevent oral administration.
items.ex: Skill 31.1 lists NPO status, inability to swallow, vomiting, bowel problems, recent GI surgery, gastric suction, and decreased LOC.

alt.q: Which patients are at increased risk for aspirating oral medications? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with an impaired gag reflex
An impaired gag reflex increases aspiration risk.
A patient with a tracheostomy
Patients with a tracheostomy are at risk for aspiration.
A patient with impaired cognition
Impaired cognition increases aspiration risk.
An alert patient sitting upright with an intact gag reflex
This patient has no listed aspiration risk factors.
A patient who prefers water over juice
Fluid preference does not affect aspiration risk.
alt.ex: Altered swallowing, impaired gag reflex, tracheostomy, impaired cognition, and decreased LOC raise aspiration risk.

items.q: Which steps are correct for giving an orally disintegrating tablet? Select all that apply.
o: Remove it from the packet just before use
These tablets are thin and fragile, so removal is done just before use.
Place it on top of the patient’s tongue
The tablet dissolves when placed on the tongue.
Caution the patient against chewing it
The patient lets it dissolve rather than chewing it.
Push the tablet through the foil backing
Pushing through foil can break the fragile tablet.
Give a full glass of water to wash it down
Water is not needed because the tablet dissolves on the tongue.
items.ex: Orally disintegrating tablets are removed carefully just before use, placed on the tongue, and not chewed.

alt.q: Which practices are correct when preparing solid oral medications? Select all that apply.
o: Place unit-dose tablets in the cup without removing the wrapper
Wrappers keep the tablet clean and identify the drug for teaching.
Pour stock-bottle tablets into the bottle cap first
This avoids touching the medication and wasting it.
Pop blister-pack doses through the backing into a cup
Blister packs are popped through the foil or paper backing.
Count stock tablets into your palm before placing them in the cup
Medication is never touched with the fingers.
Return a dropped tablet to the stock bottle
A dropped tablet is contaminated and discarded.
alt.ex: Solid medications stay wrapped, are poured via the bottle cap, and are never touched by hand.

items.q: A patient refuses a scheduled oral medication. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Assess why the patient is refusing
Understanding the reason guides the response.
Provide further instruction about the medication
Further teaching may address the patient’s concerns.
Notify the health care provider
The provider is notified of a refused medication.
Document the reason the dose was withheld
Withheld doses are documented with the reason per agency policy.
Hide the medication in the patient’s food
Patients are never forced or tricked into taking medications.
Document the dose as given to avoid a gap
Documenting an ungiven dose falsifies the record.
items.ex: For refusal, the nurse assesses the reason, teaches, does not force the drug, notifies the provider, and documents.

alt.q: Which items does the nurse document after giving oral medications? Select all that apply.
o: Drug, dose, route, and time, with initials or signature
These are documented immediately after administration.
The patient’s response to the medication
Response to the medication is documented.
The evaluation of patient learning
The nurse documents evaluation of patient learning.
The administration time, entered before the dose is given
Documentation occurs after administration, not before.
The names of other patients on the medication pass
Other patients’ information does not belong in this record.
alt.ex: Documentation includes drug, dose, route, time, response, learning, adverse effects, and reasons for withheld doses.

items.q: Water is needed to help an orally disintegrating tablet dissolve on the tongue.

items.ww: The skill states water is not needed for orally disintegrating tablets or strips.

alt.ww: The skill explicitly says water is not needed.

items.q: Sublingual medications act in about 15 minutes, while most oral medications act in 30 to 60 minutes.

items.ww: The skill’s evaluation step gives these onset times for timing reassessment.

alt.q: Most oral medications act within 5 minutes, so the nurse evaluates their effects right away.
alt.a: False

items.q: The nurse offers a high-fat snack with aspirin because fat speeds drug absorption.
items.a: False

alt.q: For highly acidic medications such as aspirin, the nurse offers a nonfat snack such as crackers if not contraindicated.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: A nonfat snack reduces gastric irritation without the fat that delays absorption.
alt.ww: The skill recommends a nonfat snack for acidic medications.

items.q: Time-critical scheduled medications are given no more than [[30]] minutes before or after the scheduled dose.
items.ex: Early or late doses of time-critical drugs such as antibiotics, anticoagulants, and insulin beyond 30 minutes may cause harm.

alt.ex: Early or late doses of time-critical drugs such as antibiotics, anticoagulants, and insulin beyond 30 minutes may cause harm.

Any blurred vision after eyedrops is a medical emergency
Temporary blurring is an expected effect, not an emergency.

items.q: Why does the nurse clean the eyelid from the inner to the outer canthus before instilling eye medication?

alt.q: A patient has dried crusts along the eyelid margins before eyedrop instillation. Which action is correct?

Instill the drops directly over the crusts
Crusts are cleaned off first so the medication reaches the eye.
Press firmly on the eyelid to loosen the crusts
Pressure on the eye is avoided; soaking loosens crusts.

items.q: Why does the nurse ask the patient to look at the ceiling before instilling eyedrops?
