w: It opens the nasolacrimal duct to absorb the drops
Looking up does not open the duct; duct pressure limits absorption.
It dilates the pupil so the drug acts faster
Gaze direction does not dilate the pupil.
It tightens the eyelid so the dropper can rest on it
The dropper never touches the eye or eyelid.

alt.q: How far above the conjunctival sac does the nurse hold the eyedropper?
alt.a: 1 to 2 cm (¼ to ½ inch)
alt.ex: Holding the dropper 1 to 2 cm above the sac prevents contact with the eye and contamination of the sterile dropper.
w: 0 cm (resting on the lower lid)
The dropper must not touch the eye or eyelid.
4 to 5 cm (1½ to 2 inches)
This is too high for accurate placement in the sac.
8 to 10 cm (3 to 4 inches)
This height makes it hard to land drops in the sac.

items.q: As the nurse instills an eyedrop, the patient blinks and the drop lands on the outer lid margin. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Repeat the instillation into the conjunctival sac
items.ex: If drops land on the outer lid margins, the procedure is repeated because effect occurs only in the sac.
w: Count the dose as given and document it
The drug did not enter the sac, so the dose was not received.
Wipe the drop into the eye with a cotton ball
This risks contamination and does not deliver an accurate dose.
Wait until the next scheduled dose to try again
The missed drop is repeated now rather than skipped.

alt.q: Why does the nurse repeat an eyedrop that landed on the outer eyelid margin?
alt.a: Drugs act only when drops enter the conjunctival sac
alt.ex: The therapeutic effect is obtained only when drops enter the conjunctival sac.
w: Drops on the eyelid cause systemic toxicity
The concern is lack of effect, not toxicity.
The lid margin absorbs the drug too quickly
Drops on the lid do not deliver the drug to the eye.
Eyedrops must always be given in pairs
The prescribed number of drops is given, not always two.

items.q: Why does the nurse press gently on the nasolacrimal duct after instilling eyedrops that can cause systemic effects?
items.a: To prevent absorption into the systemic circulation
items.ex: Pressure prevents overflow into nasal and pharyngeal passages and absorption into systemic circulation.
w: To move the drops across the cornea
Closing the eyes gently distributes the drug, not duct pressure.
To keep the patient from blinking
Looking up reduces the blink reflex; duct pressure has another purpose.
To speed the drug into the tear duct
The goal is to keep the drug out of the duct and nasal passages.

alt.q: How long does the nurse apply pressure to the nasolacrimal duct after instilling eyedrops with systemic effects?
alt.a: 30 to 60 seconds over each eye
alt.ex: Gentle pressure is applied for 30 to 60 seconds over each eye, one at a time, avoiding the eyeball.
w: 5 to 10 seconds over both eyes at once
This is too brief, and each eye is done one at a time.
2 to 3 minutes directly on the eyeball
Pressure on the eyeball is always avoided.
10 to 15 minutes over each eye
The book specifies 30 to 60 seconds.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient receiving mydriatic eyedrops. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I should not drive until my vision and light sensitivity return to normal.”
items.ex: Mydriatics temporarily blur vision and cause light sensitivity, so driving and machinery are avoided until vision normalizes.
w: “My vision will be sharper than usual right after these drops are put in.”
Mydriatics blur vision temporarily; they do not sharpen it.
“Looking at bright lights will help these drops work faster in my eyes.”
Mydriatics cause light sensitivity; bright light causes discomfort.
“If my vision blurs afterward, I should rub my eyes firmly to clear it.”
Pressure on the eyes is avoided; blurring clears on its own.

alt.q: Which effects should the nurse prepare a patient to expect after receiving mydriatic eyedrops?
alt.a: Temporary blurred vision and sensitivity to light
alt.ex: Pupil-dilating drops temporarily blur vision and cause sensitivity to light.
w: Permanent improvement in near vision
The blurring is temporary; vision does not permanently improve.
Constricted pupils and tearing for a week
Mydriatics dilate pupils; effects are temporary.
Loss of the blink reflex for several hours
Mydriatics do not abolish the blink reflex.

items.q: A patient with a cervical spine injury needs eyedrops. How should the nurse adjust the usual positioning?
items.a: Avoid hyperextending the patient’s neck
items.ex: The usual position slightly hyperextends the neck, but this is not done with a cervical spine injury.
w: Hyperextend the neck farther to open the eye
Neck hyperextension is avoided with cervical spine injury.
Place the patient prone with the head turned
Prone positioning does not give access to the conjunctival sac.
Have the patient tilt the head toward one shoulder
Moving the neck risks further injury; the neck is not repositioned.

alt.q: What is the usual position for a patient receiving eye medications when no injury limits movement?
alt.a: Supine or sitting back with the neck slightly hyperextended
alt.ex: This position gives easy access to the eye and minimizes drainage of medication into the tear duct.
w: Side-lying with the affected eye facing down
This position lets the medication drain away.
Sitting forward with the chin on the chest
Looking down hinders access to the conjunctival sac.
Prone with the face turned to one side
Prone positioning blocks access to the eye.

items.q: After timolol eyedrops, a patient’s heart rate falls from 78 to 50 beats/min and blood pressure drops. Which action is appropriate?
items.a: Notify the provider immediately, stay, and assess vital signs
items.ex: Systemic effects such as decreased heart rate and blood pressure from timolol require immediate notification, monitoring, and withholding doses.
w: Dim the room lights and reassess in 1 hour
Dimming lights is for local burning, not systemic cardiovascular effects.
Give the next dose early to stabilize the effect
Further doses are withheld when systemic effects occur.
Apply a warm compress over the closed eye
A compress does not address systemic effects on heart rate and blood pressure.

alt.q: Which finding after epinephrine eyedrops is a systemic effect the nurse should report immediately?
alt.a: Increased heart rate and blood pressure
alt.ex: Epinephrine drops can raise heart rate and blood pressure, a systemic effect requiring immediate notification.
w: Brief stinging in the treated eye
Temporary burning is an expected local effect.
Mild redness of the eyelid
This is a local effect, not a systemic one.
A small amount of drug on the cheek
Escaped medication is absorbed by the cotton ball; it is not a systemic effect.

items.q: A patient complains of burning and eye irritation after eyedrops. Which nursing action is appropriate?
items.a: Dim the lights and notify the provider about adjusting the drug
items.ex: For local side effects, dim lights to reduce glare and notify the provider about possible changes in drug or dose.
w: Withhold all future eye medications permanently
The provider decides on adjustments; the nurse does not stop therapy permanently.
Rinse the eye with tap water and give a double dose
Doubling the dose is unsafe, and tap water is not sterile.
Tell the patient this means the drops are working
Burning may mean drops hit the cornea or the dropper touched the eye.

alt.q: Which technique error may cause burning or pain after eyedrops?
alt.a: Instilling the drops directly onto the cornea
alt.ex: Drops on the cornea, which has many pain fibers, or a dropper touching the eye can cause burning and pain.
w: Instilling the drops into the lower conjunctival sac
This is the correct placement.
Holding the dropper 1 to 2 cm above the eye
This is the correct dropper height.
Asking the patient to look at the ceiling
This correctly moves the cornea away from the drops.

items.q: After inserting an intraocular disk and pulling the lower lid over it, the nurse can still see the disk. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Repeat pulling the lower lid out and over the disk
items.ex: The disk should not be visible after the lid is pulled over it; if it can be seen, the step is repeated.
w: Leave it because it will settle within an hour
A visible disk is not correctly placed and needs repositioning now.
Press the disk firmly against the cornea
The disk rests on the sclera, and pressure on the eye is avoided.
Remove it and document that the dose was refused
The patient did not refuse; the placement simply needs correction.

alt.q: Where is an intraocular disk placed?
alt.a: In the conjunctival sac, on the sclera between iris and lower lid
alt.ex: The disk floats on the sclera between the iris and lower eyelid within the conjunctival sac.
w: Directly on the cornea, centered over the pupil
The cornea is sensitive; the disk sits on the sclera.
Under the upper eyelid, near the tear gland
The disk is placed in the lower conjunctival sac.
In the inner canthus, over the lacrimal duct
The disk goes in the lower sac, not the inner canthus.

items.q: How does the nurse apply ophthalmic ointment?
items.a: A thin ribbon along the inner lower lid, inner to outer canthus
items.ex: A thin ribbon along the inner edge of the lower lid from inner to outer canthus distributes the drug evenly.
w: A thick ribbon along the upper lid, outer to inner canthus
Ointment goes on the lower lid, thin, from inner to outer canthus.
A single dab on the cornea at the center of the eye
Medication is never placed directly on the sensitive cornea.
A thin ribbon on the outer skin of the lower eyelid
Ointment goes on the conjunctiva at the inner lid edge, not the skin.

alt.q: After applying ophthalmic ointment, what does the nurse ask the patient to do?
alt.a: Close the eye and rub the lid lightly in a circular motion
alt.ex: Light circular rubbing with a cotton ball, if not contraindicated, further distributes the ointment without trauma.
w: Blink rapidly several times to clear the ointment
Rapid blinking does not distribute the drug as intended.
Squeeze the eyelids tightly shut for 1 minute
Squeezing forces medication out of the eye.
Keep the eye open and look at a bright light
Light exposure does not distribute ointment and may cause discomfort.

items.q: A nurse documents eyedrop administration. Which entries are complete and correct? Select all that apply.
o: Timolol 0.5%, 1 drop, left eye, at 0900, with initials
This lists drug, concentration, number of drops, eye, time, and initials.
Right eye slightly red, no drainage; patient reports mild itching
Objective and subjective eye findings are documented.
Patient correctly demonstrated eyedrop instillation
Evaluation of patient learning is documented.
Eyedrops given
This omits drug, concentration, number of drops, eye, and time.
Will give drops at 0900, charted at 0845
Documentation is done after administration, never before.
items.ex: Documentation includes drug, concentration, number of drops, which eye, time after administration, findings, and learning.

alt.q: Which items does the nurse document after giving ophthalmic medications? Select all that apply.
o: Site of application: left, right, or both eyes
The specific eye is documented.
Number of drops and concentration of the drug
Concentration, dose or strength, and number of drops are recorded.
Subjective data such as pain, itching, or altered vision
Subjective findings are documented.
The time the dose was prepared, entered before giving it
Documentation occurs immediately after administration, not before.
The temperature of the drops when they were instilled
Drop temperature is not a documentation item.
alt.ex: Ophthalmic documentation covers drug, concentration, drops, eye, time, eye findings, response, and patient learning.

items.q: A patient shows systemic effects from eyedrops. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Notify the health care provider immediately
Systemic effects require immediate notification.
Remain with the patient and assess vital signs
The nurse stays and monitors vital signs.
Withhold further doses
Doses are withheld until the provider responds.
Dim the lights and continue the scheduled drops
Dimming lights is for local discomfort; doses are withheld here.
Give the next dose to compare the response
Giving more drug could worsen systemic effects.
items.ex: Systemic effects call for immediate notification, staying with the patient, assessing vital signs, and withholding doses.

alt.q: A patient cannot explain the steps for eyedrops and has trouble handling the dropper. Which actions fit? Select all that apply.
o: Repeat the instructions
Instructions are repeated when understanding is incomplete.
Include the family caregiver as appropriate
A caregiver may assist with home administration.
Include a return demonstration
Return demonstration confirms technique.
Give written instructions only and end the teaching
Teaching continues until the patient or caregiver can perform it.
Note the problem but make no change to teaching
Teaching is revised when teach-back is not successful.
alt.ex: When teach-back fails, repeat instructions, involve the family caregiver, and use return demonstration.

items.q: Which techniques are correct when instilling eyedrops? Select all that apply.
o: Rest the dominant hand on the patient’s forehead
This steadies the hand holding the dropper.
Drop the medication into the lower conjunctival sac
The lower sac is the target for drops.
Press downward against the bony orbit, not the eyeball
This exposes the sac without pressure on the eye.
Touch the dropper tip to the lower lid to steady it
The dropper must not touch the eye; ophthalmic drugs are sterile.
Ask the patient to squeeze the eyes shut afterward
Squeezing forces medication out; the patient closes the eyes gently.
items.ex: Steady the hand on the forehead, expose the sac against the bony orbit, drop into the lower sac, and avoid contact.

alt.q: Which assessments does the nurse complete before instilling eye medications? Select all that apply.
o: Condition of the external eye structures
This gives a baseline and shows whether cleaning is needed.
Symptoms such as blurred vision, burning, or itching
Eye medications may lessen or increase these symptoms.
Level of consciousness and ability to follow directions
A restless patient may move and injure the eye.
Ability to manipulate and hold the dropper
This reflects ability to learn self-administration.
Hearing acuity in both ears
Hearing is assessed for ear medications, not eye medications.
alt.ex: Pre-instillation assessment includes external eye condition, symptoms, LOC, and ability to handle the dropper.

items.q: When exposing the conjunctival sac, the nurse presses downward against the bony orbit, never directly on the eyeball.
items.a: True
items.ex: Pressing against the bony orbit prevents pressure and trauma to the eyeball.
items.ww: The skill states never to press directly against the patient’s eyeball.

alt.q: Gentle pressure directly on the eyeball helps open the conjunctival sac for eyedrops.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Pressure is applied to the bony orbit below the lid; direct pressure on the eyeball is always avoided.
alt.ww: Pressure on the eyeball can cause trauma, so it is never used.

items.q: Eyedrops kept in the refrigerator are rewarmed to room temperature before instillation unless directed otherwise.
items.a: True
items.ex: Eye medications should be at room temperature unless specifically directed otherwise.
items.ww: The skill directs rewarming refrigerated drops to room temperature.

alt.q: Eyedrops should be instilled cold, straight from the refrigerator, to reduce burning.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Eyedrops are rewarmed to room temperature before administration unless directed otherwise.
alt.ww: The skill says to verify preparations are at room temperature.

items.q: An eye patch should be taped with firm pressure over the eye to hold the medication in place.
items.a: False
items.ex: A clean eye patch covers the entire eye and is taped securely without applying pressure to the eye.
items.ww: Pressure on the eye is avoided throughout the skill.

alt.q: An eye patch is taped securely so the entire eye is covered without pressure on the eye.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: A clean patch over the whole eye reduces infection risk without pressing on the eye.
alt.ww: The skill directs taping securely without applying pressure.

items.q: The nurse instills eyedrops into the lower [[conjunctival sac|conjunctival]], which normally holds 1 or 2 drops.
items.ex: The lower conjunctival sac holds 1 or 2 drops and gives even distribution of the medication across the eye.

alt.q: After eyedrops that may cause systemic effects, the nurse presses gently on the [[nasolacrimal duct|nasolacrimal]] for 30 to 60 seconds.
alt.ex: The lower conjunctival sac holds 1 or 2 drops and gives even distribution of the medication across the eye.

items.q: Why does the nurse do this: Assess level of consciousness?
items.a: A restless patient may move and injure the eye
items.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.
w: Absorbs medication that escapes the eye
That goes with Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid.
Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out
That goes with Ask the patient to close the eyes gently.
Shows ability to learn self-administration
That goes with Assess ability to hold the dropper.

alt.q: Why does the nurse do this: Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid?
alt.a: Absorbs medication that escapes the eye
alt.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.
w: A restless patient may move and injure the eye
That goes with Assess level of consciousness.
Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out
That goes with Ask the patient to close the eyes gently.
Shows ability to learn self-administration
That goes with Assess ability to hold the dropper.

alt.q: Why does the nurse do this: Ask the patient to close the eyes gently?
alt.a: Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out
alt.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.
w: A restless patient may move and injure the eye
That goes with Assess level of consciousness.
Absorbs medication that escapes the eye
That goes with Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid.
Shows ability to learn self-administration
That goes with Assess ability to hold the dropper.

alt.q: Why does the nurse do this: Assess ability to hold the dropper?
alt.a: Shows ability to learn self-administration
alt.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.
w: A restless patient may move and injure the eye
That goes with Assess level of consciousness.
Absorbs medication that escapes the eye
That goes with Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid.
Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out
That goes with Ask the patient to close the eyes gently.

alt.q: Why does the nurse do this: Apply a clean eye patch?
alt.a: Reduces the risk of infection
alt.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.
w: A restless patient may move and injure the eye
That goes with Assess level of consciousness.
Absorbs medication that escapes the eye
That goes with Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid.
Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out
That goes with Ask the patient to close the eyes gently.

alt.q: Which action has this rationale: “A restless patient may move and injure the eye”?
alt.a: Assess level of consciousness
alt.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.
w: Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid
Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid: Absorbs medication that escapes the eye.
Ask the patient to close the eyes gently
Ask the patient to close the eyes gently: Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out.
Assess ability to hold the dropper
Assess ability to hold the dropper: Shows ability to learn self-administration.

alt.q: Which action has this rationale: “Absorbs medication that escapes the eye”?
alt.a: Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid
alt.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.
w: Assess level of consciousness
Assess level of consciousness: A restless patient may move and injure the eye.
Ask the patient to close the eyes gently
Ask the patient to close the eyes gently: Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out.
Assess ability to hold the dropper
Assess ability to hold the dropper: Shows ability to learn self-administration.

alt.q: Which action has this rationale: “Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out”?
alt.a: Ask the patient to close the eyes gently
alt.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.
w: Assess level of consciousness
Assess level of consciousness: A restless patient may move and injure the eye.
Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid
Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid: Absorbs medication that escapes the eye.
Assess ability to hold the dropper
Assess ability to hold the dropper: Shows ability to learn self-administration.

alt.q: Which action has this rationale: “Shows ability to learn self-administration”?
alt.a: Assess ability to hold the dropper
alt.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.
w: Assess level of consciousness
Assess level of consciousness: A restless patient may move and injure the eye.
Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid
Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid: Absorbs medication that escapes the eye.
Ask the patient to close the eyes gently
Ask the patient to close the eyes gently: Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out.

alt.q: Which action has this rationale: “Reduces the risk of infection”?
alt.a: Apply a clean eye patch
alt.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.
w: Assess level of consciousness
Assess level of consciousness: A restless patient may move and injure the eye.
Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid
Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid: Absorbs medication that escapes the eye.
Ask the patient to close the eyes gently
Ask the patient to close the eyes gently: Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out.

mt.q: Match each action in Skill 31.2 with its rationale.
pairs: A restless patient may move and injure the eye
Hold a cotton ball below the lower lid
Absorbs medication that escapes the eye
Ask the patient to close the eyes gently
Distributes the drug; squeezing forces it out
Assess ability to hold the dropper
mt.ex: Each step in Skill 31.2 has a safety or effectiveness rationale given in the skill’s rationale column.

sections.name: Skill 31.3 · Using metered-dose inhalers (MDIs), dry powder inhalers (DPIs), or soft mist inhalers (SMIs)

items.q: A patient using a beta-adrenergic metered-dose inhaler (MDI) reports light-headedness and nearly faints after a dose. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Withhold further doses of the medication
items.ex: Light-headedness or syncope suggests a cardiac dysrhythmia from beta-adrenergic drugs, so the nurse withholds further doses, evaluates cardiac and pulmonary status, and notifies the provider.
w: Have the patient take one more puff to finish the dose
More drug could worsen the dysrhythmia; further doses are withheld.
Teach the patient to shake the inhaler longer
Inhaler technique does not explain a possible dysrhythmia.
Have the patient rinse the mouth with warm water
Rinsing prevents fungal infection from steroids; it does not treat dysrhythmia.

alt.q: Which finding in a patient using a beta-adrenergic MDI calls for the nurse to withhold further doses?
alt.a: Light-headedness with a fainting episode
alt.ex: Light-headedness and syncope point to a cardiac dysrhythmia, an unexpected outcome that requires withholding the drug and notifying the provider.
w: A gagging sensation after a puff
Gagging comes from droplets on the pharynx when the drug is inhaled incorrectly; it calls for teaching.
A peak flow reading that improves after a dose
Improved peak flow shows the drug is working as intended.
Use of the inhaler every 4 to 6 hours
Beta-adrenergic MDIs are used as needed or regularly every 4 to 6 hours.

items.q: A patient with asthma says, “Lately I need my bronchodilator inhaler every 2 to 3 hours.” Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Notify the health care provider so the medication and delivery method can be reassessed
items.ex: Needing a bronchodilator more than every 4 hours may indicate a respiratory problem, so the drug and delivery method are reassessed with the provider.
w: Tell the patient to take two extra puffs with each use
Patients are taught not to repeat inhalations beyond the prescribed schedule.
Advise the patient to wait 2 to 5 minutes between puffs
Wait times do not address the increased need, which may signal a respiratory problem.
Reassure the patient that this frequency is expected
Use more often than every 4 hours is an unexpected outcome that must be reported.

alt.q: Which patient report about bronchodilator use should the nurse report to the health care provider?
alt.a: Needing the bronchodilator more often than every 4 hours
alt.ex: Bronchodilator need more often than every 4 hours may indicate a respiratory problem and requires reassessment of drug and delivery method.
w: Using the bronchodilator every 4 to 6 hours as prescribed
Beta-adrenergic MDIs are commonly used regularly every 4 to 6 hours.
Rinsing the mouth after using the steroid inhaler
Rinsing after steroids is correct practice that reduces fungal infection.
Waiting 2 to 5 minutes before using a second medication
This is the correct wait between two different inhaled medications.

items.q: A patient is prescribed a bronchodilator MDI and an inhaled steroid MDI at the same time. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I’ll use my bronchodilator first, wait a few minutes, then use the steroid.”
items.ex: Bronchodilators are given before steroids so they open the airways, and 2 to 5 minutes separate different medications.
w: “I’ll use the steroid first so it coats my airways before the bronchodilator.”
The bronchodilator goes first so it can open airway passages for the steroid.
“I’ll take both medications back to back without waiting between them.”
Different inhaled medications are separated by 2 to 5 minutes.
“I’ll use the steroid first and rinse my mouth before the bronchodilator.”
Steroid goes second; rinsing is done about 2 minutes after the last dose.

alt.q: Why does the nurse teach the patient to use the bronchodilator before the inhaled steroid?
alt.a: The bronchodilator opens the airways so the steroid can reach them
alt.ex: Inhaled drugs are taken in sequence, with bronchodilators first so airway passages are open for the steroid.
w: The steroid irritates the throat unless the bronchodilator numbs it
Bronchodilators dilate airways; they do not numb the throat.
The bronchodilator prevents fungal infection caused by the steroid
Rinsing the mouth after steroids reduces fungal infection risk.
The steroid blocks absorption of a bronchodilator given afterward
The reason given is airway opening, not blocked absorption.

items.q: How long should a patient wait between inhalations of the same medication from an inhaler?
items.a: 20 to 30 seconds
items.ex: Patients wait 20 to 30 seconds between puffs of the same drug so medications are inhaled sequentially.
w: 2 to 5 seconds
This is too short; the book specifies 20 to 30 seconds for the same drug.
2 to 5 minutes
This is the wait between two different medications.
10 to 15 minutes
This is longer than the book specifies for either situation.

alt.q: How long should a patient wait between inhalations of two different medications?
alt.a: 2 to 5 minutes
alt.ex: Different inhaled medications are separated by 2 to 5 minutes; puffs of the same drug are 20 to 30 seconds apart.
w: 20 to 30 seconds
This is the wait between puffs of the same medication.
5 to 10 seconds
This is too short for either situation.
30 to 60 minutes
This is far longer than the book specifies.

items.q: A patient using an inhaled corticosteroid asks why the nurse wants them to rinse their mouth afterward. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Rinsing lowers your risk of a fungal infection in your mouth.”
items.ex: Steroids can alter the normal flora of the oral mucosa, and rinsing reduces the risk of fungal infection.
w: “Rinsing helps the medicine reach your lower airways faster.”
Rinsing removes drug from the mouth; it does not speed airway delivery.
“Rinsing stops the gagging feeling caused by the spacer.”
Gagging comes from droplets on the pharynx with incorrect technique, not the reason for rinsing.
“Rinsing clears bacteria that build up on the mouthpiece.”
Mouthpiece bacteria are removed by cleaning the device, not by rinsing the mouth.

alt.q: When and how should a patient rinse after the last dose of an inhaled steroid?
alt.a: About 2 minutes after the last dose, then spit the water out
alt.ex: Rinsing with warm water about 2 minutes after the last dose and spitting it out reduces fungal infection risk.
w: Just before the first puff, then swallow the water
Rinsing is done after dosing to remove steroid from the mouth.
About 2 minutes after the last dose, then swallow the water
The water is spit out, not swallowed.
Only if the patient notices a gagging sensation
Rinsing is routine after steroid use, not limited to gagging.

items.q: Without a spacer, which MDI position does the book describe as the best way to deliver medication?
items.a: Mouthpiece 2 to 4 cm in front of a widely opened mouth
items.ex: Holding the mouthpiece 2 to 4 cm (1 to 2 inches) from a wide-open mouth, aimed at the back of the throat, is the best method without a spacer.
w: Mouthpiece 10 to 15 cm in front of closed lips
The mouth must be widely open and the distance is 2 to 4 cm.
Mouthpiece against closed lips, aimed at the palate
The opening is aimed toward the back of the throat, not the palate.
Mouthpiece under the tongue with lips slightly open
The tongue and teeth must not block the mouthpiece.

alt.q: A patient holds the MDI mouthpiece 2 to 4 cm from a widely opened mouth. Which instruction is correct?
alt.a: Aim the opening toward the back of the throat without touching the lips
alt.ex: In this position the lips should not touch the inhaler, and the opening is directed toward the back of the throat.
w: Close the lips around the mouthpiece once the puff is released
In the open-mouth method the lips do not touch the inhaler.
Aim the opening toward the roof of the mouth
The spray is directed toward the back of the throat to reach the airway.
Exhale through the mouth while pressing the canister
The canister is pressed during a slow, deep inhalation.

items.q: Which hand position makes it easier for a patient to activate an MDI canister?
items.a: Thumb at the mouthpiece with index and middle fingers on top
items.ex: The three-point or bilateral hand position, thumb at the mouthpiece and index and middle fingers at the top, makes MDIs easier to activate.
w: Index finger alone pressing the top of the canister
The book recommends the three-point position for easier activation.
Palm wrapped around the canister with mouthpiece facing up
The mouthpiece faces the mouth; the palm grip is not the described position.
Little finger on top with thumb under the canister base
This is not the three-point position the book describes.

alt.q: What is the purpose of teaching a patient the three-point hand position for an MDI?
alt.a: It makes the canister easier to activate
alt.ex: Holding the MDI with thumb at the mouthpiece and two fingers on top makes activation easier.
w: It primes the canister before each dose
Priming is a test spray into the air for a new or unused MDI.
It keeps the spacer exhalation slots open
Exhalation slots are kept clear by not covering them with the lips.
It counts the number of doses remaining
Some DPIs have an external counter that shows remaining doses.

items.q: Why does the nurse teach the patient to exhale slowly through the nose or pursed lips after an MDI dose?
items.a: It keeps small airways open during exhalation
items.ex: Slow exhalation through the nose or pursed lips after removing the MDI keeps small airways open.
w: It pushes leftover medication out of the airways
The goal is to keep the drug in the airways, not expel it.
It prevents the medication from reaching the stomach
This is not the rationale given for slow exhalation.
It primes the inhaler for the next puff
Priming is a test spray for a new or unused MDI.

alt.q: After holding the breath for about 10 seconds following an MDI puff, what should the patient do next?
alt.a: Remove the MDI and exhale slowly through the nose or pursed lips
alt.ex: The MDI is removed before exhaling, and slow exhalation through the nose or pursed lips keeps small airways open.
w: Exhale forcefully through the mouthpiece to clear it
The patient removes the MDI before exhaling and exhales slowly.
Take a second puff right away without exhaling
Puffs of the same drug are separated by 20 to 30 seconds.
Rinse the mouth before letting the breath out
Rinsing is done about 2 minutes after the last steroid dose.

items.q: Which instruction is specific to using a dry powder inhaler (DPI)?
items.a: Do not shake the device, and inhale quickly and deeply
items.ex: DPIs are not shaken; forceful, quick, deep inhalation creates the aerosol from the powder.
w: Shake it five or six times, then inhale slowly
Shaking and slow inhalation are MDI steps; a DPI is not shaken.
Spray one puff into a spacer, then inhale slowly
Spacers are used with MDIs, not DPIs.
Breathe out fully into the mouthpiece before inhaling
The patient exhales away from a DPI to prevent loss of powder.

alt.q: A patient breathes out into the mouthpiece of a dry powder inhaler just before inhaling. Why does the nurse correct this?
alt.a: Exhaling into the device causes loss of the powder
alt.ex: The patient exhales away from the DPI because breathing into it blows the powder out.
w: Exhaling into the device primes it too early
DPIs are loaded per manufacturer directions, not primed by exhaling.
Exhaling into the device damages the external counter
The counter shows doses remaining; this is not the concern.
Exhaling into the device keeps the airways from opening
The concern is lost powder, not airway opening.

items.q: A patient’s soft mist inhaler (SMI) has not been used for more than 3 days. What should the nurse instruct the patient to do before the next dose?
items.a: Repeat the priming process
items.ex: If an SMI has not been used for more than 3 days, it must be primed again before use.
w: Shake the inhaler five or six times
Shaking is an MDI step; the SMI needs priming.
Take two extra puffs to make up for missed doses
Patients do not repeat inhalations to make up doses.
Discard the inhaler and obtain a new one
The SMI can be reprimed and used.

alt.q: After how long without use must a soft mist inhaler be primed again?
alt.a: More than 3 days
alt.ex: An SMI not used for more than 3 days needs the priming process repeated.
w: More than 1 day
The book sets the limit at more than 3 days.
More than 7 days
Waiting this long without repriming exceeds the 3-day limit.
More than 30 days
Priming is needed after more than 3 days, much sooner than this.

items.q: Which instruction can the nurse give assistive personnel (AP) caring for a patient who uses an MDI?
items.a: Report audible wheezing or coughing to the nurse
items.ex: Administering MDIs cannot be delegated, but AP report breathing difficulty and side effects to the nurse.
w: Teach the patient how to use the spacer
Teaching is the nurse’s role; a respiratory therapist can also guide the patient.
Give the scheduled MDI dose
Administering MDIs cannot be delegated to AP.
Evaluate the patient’s inhaler technique
Evaluation requires nursing judgment and cannot be delegated.

alt.q: A patient has difficulty manipulating and correctly using an MDI. Which team member can help guide the patient?
alt.a: Respiratory therapist
alt.ex: The book states a respiratory therapist can guide the patient and family caregiver who have trouble using an MDI.
w: Assistive personnel
AP do not teach or administer MDIs; they report breathing problems.
Unit clerk
Clerical staff do not provide inhaler instruction.
Dietitian
Dietitians do not teach inhaler technique.

items.q: Which instructions apply when a patient uses an MDI with a spacer device? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid covering the small exhalation slots with the lips
Lips are kept off the exhalation slots so medication does not escape.
Depress the canister once, spraying one puff into the spacer
One puff is sprayed into the spacer, which holds the fine spray for inhalation.
Breathe in slowly and fully through the mouth for about 5 seconds
Slow, full inhalation distributes particles to deeper airways.
Insert the mouthpiece well beyond the raised lip
The mouthpiece is not inserted beyond the raised lip.
Do not shake the inhaler before inserting it into the spacer
The MDI is shaken 2 to 5 seconds to mix the medication.
items.ex: With a spacer, the MDI is shaken, one puff is released into the chamber, and the patient breathes in slowly and holds the breath.

alt.q: Which assessment findings suggest that a patient may need a spacer with an MDI? Select all that apply.
o: Hand tremors
Tremors interfere with depressing the canister, so a spacer is often necessary.
Impaired grasp
Impaired grasp interferes with manipulating the inhaler.
Difficulty depressing the canister
Trouble activating the canister is the problem a spacer helps solve.
Peak flow that improves after the dose
Improved peak flow shows the drug is effective.
Correct teach-back of cleaning steps
Correct teach-back shows learning, not a need for a spacer.
alt.ex: Impaired grasp or hand tremors interfere with depressing the canister, so a spacer device is often necessary.

items.q: Which teaching points about cleaning an MDI are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Once a day, remove the canister and run warm tap water through the mouthpiece for 30 to 60 seconds
Daily rinsing removes medication that builds up around the mouthpiece.
Clean the mouthpiece twice a week with mild dishwashing soap
Soap cleaning gives better antimicrobial removal; pressurized MDIs can harbor bacteria.
Let the inhaler dry completely before reusing it
The inhaler must be fully dry before use or storage.
Soak the canister in warm water to clean the valve
Water damages the canister valve; never wash or immerse the canister.
Run hot water through the canister weekly
The canister valve must never get wet.
items.ex: The plastic mouthpiece is rinsed daily and soap-washed twice weekly, while the canister is kept dry to protect its valve.

alt.q: Which patient statements show correct understanding of MDI care? Select all that apply.
o: “I’ll take the canister out before I rinse the mouthpiece.”
The canister is removed so it does not get wet.
“I’ll wash the mouthpiece with mild dish soap twice a week.”
Twice-weekly soap cleaning reduces bacteria in the device.
“I’ll let the mouthpiece dry fully before putting it back together.”
The inhaler must be completely dry before reuse.
“I’ll soak the whole inhaler, canister and all, in water.”
Immersing the canister damages the valve mechanism.
“I only need to clean it when it stops spraying.”
Cleaning is routine; buildup interferes with medication delivery.
alt.ex: Patients remove the canister, rinse the mouthpiece daily, wash it with soap twice a week, and dry it fully; the canister never gets wet.

items.q: A patient receiving a beta-adrenergic MDI develops light-headedness and syncope. Which interventions does the book list? Select all that apply.
o: Withhold all further doses of the medication
Possible dysrhythmia requires stopping the drug.
Evaluate cardiac and pulmonary status
Assessment determines the effect of the suspected dysrhythmia.
Notify the health care provider to reassess the medication and delivery method
The provider reassesses the drug choice and device.
Give an extra puff to relieve breathing difficulty
More beta-adrenergic drug could worsen the dysrhythmia.
Have the patient rinse the mouth with warm water
Rinsing prevents fungal infection; it does not address dysrhythmia.
items.ex: Dysrhythmias with beta-adrenergic drugs call for withholding doses, evaluating cardiac and pulmonary status, and notifying the provider.

alt.q: A patient’s respirations become rapid and shallow with wheezing after MDI use. Which interventions does the book list? Select all that apply.
o: Evaluate vital signs and respiratory status
Assessment comes first to judge severity.
Notify the health care provider
Worsening respiratory status must be reported.
Reassess the type of medication and delivery method
The drug or device may need to change.
Have the patient repeat the inhalation before the next scheduled dose
Patients are taught not to repeat inhalations early.
Place the patient flat in bed to rest
Sitting upright supports breathing; lying flat does not help.
alt.ex: Rapid, shallow breathing with wheezing calls for assessing vital signs and respiratory status, notifying the provider, and reassessing drug and delivery method.

items.q: A patient who was previously taught to use an inhaler should still be asked to demonstrate the technique.
items.a: True
items.ex: Patients with adequate understanding may forget the procedure, so ongoing assessment of technique identifies needs for reinforcement.
items.ww: Prior teaching does not guarantee correct use; technique is reassessed each time.

alt.q: A patient previously taught to use an MDI can be assumed to use correct technique, so a demonstration is unnecessary.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients may forget inhaler technique, so the nurse has them demonstrate it to find areas needing reinforcement.
alt.ww: Assuming correct technique misses errors that reduce drug delivery.

items.q: MDI administration is documented immediately after the dose is given, including the number of inhalations.
items.a: True
items.ex: The drug, dose or strength, number of inhalations, and time are documented immediately after administration, not before.
items.ww: Documenting before giving the dose risks recording a dose that was not taken.

alt.q: To save time, the nurse documents the MDI dose before the patient takes the inhalations.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Documentation is done immediately after administration, never before.
alt.ww: Charting in advance could record a dose that was refused or not given.

items.q: A gagging sensation during MDI use comes from droplets of medication on the pharynx or tongue when the drug is sprayed and inhaled incorrectly.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book warns patients that droplets landing on the pharynx or tongue from incorrect technique cause gagging.
items.ww: Gagging is linked to incorrect spraying and inhaling, not to a drug allergy.

alt.q: A gagging sensation during MDI use signals an allergic reaction, so the medication must be withheld.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Gagging results from droplets on the pharynx or tongue when the drug is inhaled incorrectly; it calls for technique review.
alt.ww: The book attributes gagging to incorrect technique, not allergy.

items.q: If an MDI is new or has not been used for several days, the patient pushes a [[test spray]] into the air to prime it.
items.ex: A test spray into the air primes the device, confirming the MDI is patent and the canister is positioned properly.

alt.q: Before using a new MDI, the patient [[primes|primes it|prime]] the device by pushing a test spray into the air.
alt.ex: A test spray into the air primes the device, confirming the MDI is patent and the canister is positioned properly.

items.q: Which technique fits a MDI without spacer?
items.a: Inhale slowly and deeply for 3 to 5 seconds while pressing the canister

sections.name: Skill 31.4 · Preparing injections: Ampules and vials

items.q: While drawing medication from an inverted ampule, the nurse notices air bubbles in the syringe. Which action is correct?
items.a: Remove the needle from the ampule before expelling the air
items.ex: Air is expelled only after the needle is out of the ampule, because air pushed into the ampule forces fluid out and the drug is lost.
w: Expel the air back into the ampule and keep drawing
Air pressure would force medication out of the ampule.
Discard the ampule and open a new one
Bubbles are expelled and medication added until the dose is correct.
Inject the dose with the bubbles since they are small
Air displaces medication and causes dose errors.

alt.q: Why should the nurse not expel air bubbles into an opened ampule?
alt.a: Air pressure forces fluid out of the ampule and medication is lost
alt.ex: An ampule is an open system; air pushed into it forces medication out.
w: Air carries glass fragments into the medication
Glass fragments are removed by the filter needle.
Air dilutes the concentration of the medication
Air does not dilute the drug; the concern is lost fluid.
Air clogs the filter needle
This is not the rationale given.

items.q: Why does the nurse wrap the neck of an ampule with a small gauze pad rather than an opened antiseptic swab?
items.a: Antiseptic from the swab may leak into the ampule
items.ex: Gauze protects the fingers when the glass tip breaks, while an opened antiseptic swab could leak antiseptic into the medication.
w: Gauze absorbs fluid that collects in the neck
Tapping, not gauze, moves fluid out of the neck.
Antiseptic swabs dull the scored neck of the ampule
This is not the reason given.
Gauze keeps the opened ampule sterile
The broken rim is considered contaminated regardless.

alt.q: What does the nurse place around the neck of an ampule before snapping it?
alt.a: A small gauze pad
alt.ex: A small gauze pad protects the fingers from the glass; an opened antiseptic swab is avoided because antiseptic may leak in.
w: An opened antiseptic swab
Antiseptic may leak into the ampule.
A folded clean glove
The book specifies a small gauze pad.
A filter needle cap
A cap does not protect the fingers when the neck breaks.

items.q: A nurse has drawn up medication from an ampule with a filter needle. What must the nurse do before injecting the patient?
items.a: Replace the filter needle with a regular SESIP needle
items.ex: Filter needles remove glass fragments but cannot be used for injection, so a regular safety needle is attached.
w: Inject with the filter needle to trap any glass
Filter needles cannot be used for injection.
Wipe the filter needle with an antiseptic swab
Wiping does not make a filter needle usable for injection.
Recap the filter needle and inject through the cap
Injection requires a regular SESIP needle.

alt.q: What is the purpose of a filter needle when drawing medication from an ampule?
alt.a: It filters out fragments of glass
alt.ex: Snapping an ampule can leave glass fragments, which the filter needle removes during aspiration.
w: It sharpens the bevel for injection
Filter needles cannot be used for injection.
It prevents negative pressure in the ampule
Negative pressure is a concern with vials, managed by injecting air.
It measures the dose more precisely
Dose accuracy depends on reading the syringe, not the needle.

items.q: Why does the nurse inject air into a vial equal to the volume of medication to be withdrawn?
items.a: To prevent buildup of negative pressure in the vial
items.ex: Injected air prevents a vacuum from forming as fluid is removed, so medication flows into the syringe.
w: To dilute the medication to the right concentration
Air does not dilute medication; diluent does.
To sterilize the rubber seal of the vial
The seal is cleaned with an antiseptic swab.
To remove air bubbles from the syringe barrel
Bubbles are removed by tapping and ejecting air.

alt.q: Where should the nurse inject air into a vial, and why?
alt.a: Into the air space, to prevent bubbles and an inaccurate dose
alt.ex: Injecting into the air space above the fluid prevents bubbles that would make the dose inaccurate.
w: Into the solution, to mix the medication
Injecting into fluid creates bubbles and an inaccurate dose.
Into the solution, to prevent coring of the stopper
Coring is prevented by entering the center with firm pressure.
Into the air space, to sterilize the medication
Air does not sterilize the medication.

items.q: Why does the nurse remove the needle from a vial by pulling back on the syringe barrel rather than the plunger?
items.a: Pulling the plunger can separate it from the barrel, losing medication
items.ex: Pulling on the barrel keeps the plunger in place so the drawn-up dose is not lost.
w: Pulling the plunger dulls the beveled tip
The rubber stopper, not the plunger, dulls the bevel.
Pulling the barrel prevents coring of the stopper
Coring is prevented during insertion, not removal.
Pulling the plunger injects air into the vial
Pulling the plunger draws in, not injects, air or fluid.

alt.q: A nurse is ready to take the needle out of a vial after drawing up a dose. Which technique is correct?
alt.a: Pull back on the barrel of the syringe
alt.ex: Removing the needle by the barrel prevents the plunger from separating and spilling medication.
w: Pull back on the plunger of the syringe
The plunger can separate from the barrel.
Twist the vial while pushing the plunger
Pushing the plunger would inject medication back.
Hold only the needle hub and pull it out
The book specifies pulling back on the barrel.

items.q: After withdrawing medication from a vial, why does the nurse change to a new needle before injecting it into the patient?
items.a: The stopper dulls the bevel, and drug on the shaft tracks through tissue
items.ex: A new, sharper needle with no medication on its shaft enters tissue easily and does not leave medication along the needle track.
w: The used needle is too long for any injection route
Needle length is chosen by route; dulling and tracking are the reasons.
The vial needle cannot hold the ordered volume
Needles do not hold the dose; the syringe does.
The used needle has been filtered and is now blocked
Filter needles are changed because they cannot be used for injection.

alt.q: Which problem is prevented by changing the needle after drawing medication from a vial?
alt.a: Tracking medication through tissue on a dull needle
alt.ex: Passing through the stopper dulls the bevel and coats the shaft, so a new needle prevents tracking and eases insertion.
w: Negative pressure building up in the vial
Injecting air into the vial prevents negative pressure.

Rubber particles entering the vial

items.q: A single-dose vial labeled 2 mL appears to contain slightly more fluid. The order is for 2 mL. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Draw up only the ordered 2 mL
items.ex: Manufacturers often add extra liquid to allow for loss during preparation, so the nurse draws up only the desired volume.
w: Draw up the entire contents of the vial
The extra fluid is overfill; drawing it all would overdose the patient.
Return the vial to pharmacy as mislabeled
Slight overfill is expected and does not mean mislabeling.
Add diluent so the volume matches the label
Adding diluent would change the concentration.

alt.q: Why should the nurse not assume the volume on a single-dose vial label is the total volume in the vial?
alt.a: Manufacturers may add extra liquid to allow for loss during preparation
alt.ex: Single-dose vials may contain overfill, so only the ordered volume is drawn up.
w: Labels list volume before reconstitution only
This applies to powders; the point here is overfill.
Fluid evaporates once the cap is removed
The concern is manufacturer overfill, not evaporation.
The label shows the concentration, not the volume
The label lists a volume, but the vial may hold more.

items.q: A nurse has just injected diluent into a vial of powdered medication and removed the needle. Which action comes next?

w: Shake the vial vigorously until the powder dissolves
Shaking forms air bubbles; the vial is rolled instead.
Inject air equal to the dose before withdrawing
No air is added when drawing up reconstituted medication.
Draw up the medication immediately without mixing
The medication must be fully dispersed first.

alt.q: Why is reconstituted medication rolled between the palms rather than shaken?

alt.ex: Rolling ensures proper dispersal throughout the solution and prevents air bubbles.
w: To keep the rubber seal from becoming contaminated
Contamination is prevented by swabbing the seal.
To warm the medication to body temperature
Warming is not the rationale given.
To change the concentration of the medication
Concentration is set by the diluent volume, not by mixing.

items.q: What must the nurse write on the label of a multidose vial that has just been opened?

These are not the items the book lists.

Concentration and initials are required, not volume removed.

alt.q: A nurse reconstitutes a multidose vial for future doses. Why is the date of opening and concentration recorded on the label?

w: So the pharmacy can bill for each dose

items.q: In a procedural area, a nurse prepares several syringes of medication for use during a procedure. Which action is required?

alt.q: When is it not necessary to label a syringe of prepared medication?

items.q: Which actions are correct when withdrawing medication from an ampule? Select all that apply.
o: Tap the top until fluid moves out of the neck
Tapping moves all solution into the lower chamber.
Snap the neck quickly and firmly away from the hands
Snapping away protects fingers and face from shattering glass.
Keep the needle tip under the surface of the liquid
This prevents aspiration of air bubbles.
Let the needle shaft rest on the rim to steady it
The broken rim is contaminated and must not be touched.
Aspirate with a regular SESIP needle
A filter needle is used to aspirate from an ampule.
items.ex: Ampule technique keeps fluid in the lower chamber, protects the nurse from glass, and avoids contamination and air.

alt.q: Which actions by a nurse preparing medication from an ampule need correction? Select all that apply.
o: Wrapping the neck with an opened antiseptic swab
Antiseptic may leak into the ampule; gauze is used.
Expelling air bubbles back into the ampule
Air forces fluid out and medication is lost.
Injecting the patient with the filter needle
Filter needles cannot be used for injection.
Tapping the top of the ampule before snapping it
Tapping correctly moves fluid down from the neck.
Holding the syringe vertically to expel air
Vertical positioning correctly lets air rise for removal.
alt.ex: Using an antiseptic swab on the neck, expelling air into the ampule, and injecting with a filter needle are all errors.

items.q: Which actions help prevent errors while preparing injections? Select all that apply.
o: Check the previous count before preparing a controlled substance
Controlled substance laws require careful monitoring of dispensed narcotics.
Check the expiration date on each medication
Expired medications may be inactive, less effective, or harmful.
Keep medications in sight and never leave them unattended
The nurse is responsible for safekeeping of medications.
Ask assistive personnel to draw up the dose while the nurse checks the MAR
Preparing injections cannot be delegated to AP.
Use an independent double check for every medication
Independent double checks are reserved for selected high-alert medications.
items.ex: Safe preparation includes checking counts, expiration dates, and keeping medications secure; independent double checks are reserved for high-alert drugs.

alt.q: Which actions reduce interruptions and errors when preparing injections? Select all that apply.
o: Follow the agency No-Interruption Zone policy
Interruptions contribute to medication errors.
Look at only one patient’s electronic MAR at a time
Keeping one patient’s records together prevents mix-ups.
Calculate the dose and double-check the calculation
Double-checking calculations may help reduce error.
Take phone calls while drawing up to save time
Phone calls are avoided during preparation.
Prepare several patients’ medications at once
Records and medications for one patient are kept together.
alt.ex: A quiet, interruption-free setting, one patient’s MAR at a time, and double-checked calculations reduce preparation errors.

items.q: A nurse realizes the dose drawn into a syringe is incorrect. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Discard the prepared dose
An incorrect dose is discarded.
Prepare a correct new dose
A new, correct dose is prepared.
Give the dose and document the difference
An incorrect dose is never administered.
Return the excess back into the multidose vial
Returning drawn-up medication risks contaminating the vial.
Ask another nurse to cosign the incorrect dose
A cosignature does not correct an incorrect dose.
items.ex: When the wrong dose is prepared, the nurse discards it and prepares a correct new dose.

alt.q: Air bubbles remain in a syringe after the nurse draws up a dose. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

Add medication until the correct dose is prepared
Medication is added after expelling air to reach the correct dose.

Air causes dose errors and is removed first.

The air is expelled and the dose corrected.
Shake the syringe to dissolve the bubbles
Tapping the barrel, not shaking, moves bubbles to the top.
alt.ex: Remaining air bubbles are expelled and medication is added until the correct dose is prepared.

w: It creates the zigzag path that seals the needle track
The Z-track is made by pulling the skin aside.
It numbs the tissue before the medication is injected
Aspiration does not reduce pain.
It removes air bubbles from the syringe
Air is removed during preparation, before injection.

items.q: A nurse prepares to give an IM immunization to an adult. Which statement about aspiration is correct?
items.a: Do not aspirate when giving an immunization
items.ex: The CDC no longer recommends aspiration when administering immunizations.
w: Aspirate for 5 to 10 seconds before injecting
This applies to non-vaccine IM medications, not immunizations.
Aspirate after injecting to confirm placement
Aspiration is not done for immunizations at any point.
Aspirate only if the patient is obese
Body size does not change the no-aspiration rule for vaccines.

alt.q: For which IM injection should the nurse skip aspiration before injecting?
alt.a: An adult immunization
alt.ex: Per the CDC, aspiration is not done when administering immunizations.
w: An IM antibiotic
Non-vaccine IM drugs are aspirated for 5 to 10 seconds.
An IM hormonal agent
Non-vaccine IM drugs are aspirated before injection.
An IM medication in aqueous solution
Only immunizations are exempt from aspiration.

items.q: While giving a tuberculin skin test, the nurse feels no resistance as the solution is injected and no bleb forms. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Remove the needle and begin again because the needle is too deep
items.ex: Resistance is normally felt in the tight dermis; no resistance means the needle is too deep.
w: Keep injecting slowly until a bleb appears on the skin
Medication below the dermis will not form a bleb and gives inaccurate results.
Massage the site gently to spread the solution in the dermis
Massaging an ID site alters test results.
Advance the needle farther into the skin and keep injecting
The needle is already too deep.

alt.q: Which finding shows that an intradermal injection was placed correctly?
alt.a: A bleb about 6 mm across, like a mosquito bite
alt.ex: A small bleb about 6 mm (¼ inch) indicates the medication is in the dermis.
w: A bleb about 25 mm across
A correct bleb is about 6 mm.
No visible change at the site
A missing bleb suggests the needle was too deep.
Fluid leaking back from the site
Leakage suggests incorrect placement, not correct ID technique.

items.q: A patient who is HIV positive has 7 mm of induration at the tuberculin skin test site at 48 hours. How should the nurse interpret this result?
items.a: Positive, because 5 mm or more is positive for this patient
items.ex: For patients who are HIV positive or immunosuppressed, 5 mm or more of induration is positive.
w: Not positive, because 10 mm or more is needed
The 10-mm cutoff applies to groups such as recent immigrants.
Not positive, because 15 mm or more is needed
The 15-mm cutoff applies to people with no known risk factors.
Unreadable, because 48 hours is too early to read
TB tests are read at 48 to 72 hours.

alt.q: A patient with no known risk factors for tuberculosis has 12 mm of induration at 72 hours. How should the nurse interpret this result?
alt.a: Not positive, because 15 mm or more is needed for this patient
alt.ex: For patients with no known risk factors, induration of 15 mm or more is positive.
w: Positive, because 10 mm or more is positive
The 10-mm cutoff is for groups such as recent immigrants and IV drug users.
Positive, because 5 mm or more is positive
The 5-mm cutoff is for HIV-positive or immunosuppressed patients.
Unreadable, because 72 hours is too late to read
The test is read at 48 to 72 hours.

items.q: For IM injections in adults, which site does the book identify as preferred?
items.a: Ventrogluteal
items.ex: The ventrogluteal site is the preferred IM site for adults and is used if possible.
w: Deltoid
The deltoid is used for adult vaccines in the CDC table, not as the preferred general IM site.
Vastus lateralis
The anterolateral thigh can be used for children, but it is not the adult preferred site.
Dorsogluteal
The book names the ventrogluteal site as preferred.

alt.q: A nurse plans a series of IM injections, such as antibiotics, for an adult. Which approach follows the book?
alt.a: Use the ventrogluteal site if possible and rotate sites
alt.ex: The ventrogluteal site is preferred for adult IM injections, and frequent injections require site rotation.
w: Use the same deltoid site each time to track reactions
Frequent injections require rotating sites.
Use the abdomen at least 5 cm from the umbilicus
This describes subcutaneous insulin or heparin sites.
Use the forearm below the antecubital space
This is an intradermal site.

items.q: According to the immunization table based on CDC guidelines, which site and needle length are used for an IM vaccine in an adult weighing 65 kg?
items.a: Deltoid muscle, 1-inch needle
items.ex: The immunization table lists the deltoid with a 1-inch (25-mm) needle for adults weighing 60 to 70 kg.
w: Ventrogluteal muscle, 1½-inch needle
The vaccine table lists the deltoid for adults, not the ventrogluteal.
Vastus lateralis, ⅝-inch needle
The vaccine table pairs the adult thigh with a 1½-inch needle.
Deltoid muscle, 1½-inch needle
1½-inch deltoid needles are for heavier adults, such as men over 118 kg.

alt.q: According to the immunization table based on CDC guidelines, which site and needle length are used for an IM vaccine in a 6-month-old infant?
alt.a: Vastus lateralis, 1-inch needle
alt.ex: For infants 1 to 12 months, the immunization table lists the vastus lateralis on the anterolateral thigh with a 1-inch needle.
w: Deltoid muscle, 1-inch needle
The vaccine table uses the deltoid for older children and adults.
Ventrogluteal muscle, ⅝-inch needle
The vaccine table lists the vastus lateralis for infants.
Vastus lateralis, 1½-inch needle
This length is listed for older children and adults, not infants.

items.q: To check that a subcutaneous needle is the right size, the nurse grasps a skinfold and measures it. How long should the needle be?
items.a: One-half the length of the skinfold
items.ex: A needle half the length of the skinfold helps ensure medication goes into subcutaneous tissue, not muscle.
w: Equal to the length of the skinfold
A needle this long could reach muscle.
Twice the length of the skinfold
This would place medication deep into muscle.
One-quarter the length of the skinfold
The book specifies one-half the length of the fold.

alt.q: A patient’s skinfold at a subcutaneous site measures 1 inch from top to bottom. Which needle length fits the book’s guideline?
alt.a: ½ inch
alt.ex: The needle should be one-half the length of the skinfold, so a 1-inch fold calls for a ½-inch needle.
w: 1 inch
This equals the fold length and risks injecting into muscle.
¼ inch
This is one-quarter of the fold, shorter than the guideline.
2 inches
This is twice the fold and would reach muscle.

items.q: When giving subcutaneous heparin, which site should the nurse choose first?
items.a: Right or left abdomen at least 5 cm from the umbilicus
items.ex: For insulin or heparin, abdominal sites are used first, at least 5 cm (2 inches) away from the umbilicus.
w: Abdomen within 2 cm of the umbilicus
Sites must be at least 5 cm from the umbilicus.
Ventrogluteal area of the hip
This is an IM site, not a subcutaneous heparin site.
Inner forearm below the antecubital space
This is an intradermal site.

alt.q: For subcutaneous insulin or heparin, which order of sites does the book recommend?
alt.a: Abdomen first, then thigh
alt.ex: Abdominal sites are used first, followed by the thigh, when giving insulin or heparin.
w: Thigh first, then abdomen
The abdomen is used before the thigh.
Upper arm first, then abdomen
The book names abdomen first, then thigh.
Upper back first, then thigh
The upper back is an alternative intradermal site.

items.q: Minutes after an IM injection, a patient develops urticaria, pruritus, wheezing, and dyspnea. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Notify the health care provider immediately
items.ex: These are signs of an adverse reaction; the provider is notified immediately and agency policy for medication reactions is followed.
w: Apply a warm compress to the injection site
Warm compresses are for bruising or induration, not systemic reactions.
Document the reaction and recheck in 30 minutes
Wheezing and dyspnea can be life threatening and need immediate action.
Massage the site to disperse the medication
Massage causes tissue damage and does not treat a reaction.

alt.q: Which signs after an injection indicate a severe anaphylactic reaction?
alt.a: Dyspnea, wheezing, and circulatory collapse
alt.ex: Dyspnea, wheezing, and circulatory collapse signal anaphylaxis, a life-threatening emergency, so the nurse stays and observes after injection.
w: Slight burning and stinging at the site
Patients are told an injection causes slight burning or sting.
A small bleb at an intradermal site
A bleb is the expected result of an ID injection.
Mild soreness at the site
Mild soreness is not a sign of anaphylaxis.

items.q: Thirty minutes after an IM injection, a patient reports numbness and tingling at the injection site. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Assess the site, document findings, and notify the health care provider
items.ex: Localized numbness or tingling may indicate nerve or tissue injury, which requires assessment, documentation, and reporting.
w: Massage the site to restore sensation
Massage causes underlying tissue damage.
Reassure the patient that this is expected
Continued numbness or tingling is an unexpected outcome.
Apply ice and give the next dose in the same site
This ignores possible nerve injury.

alt.q: Why does the nurse return 15 to 30 minutes after an injection to ask about pain, burning, numbness, or tingling?
alt.a: Continued discomfort may indicate injury to underlying nerves, bones, or tissue
alt.ex: Ongoing discomfort after an injection can signal injury to underlying tissue, bones, or nerves.
w: To decide whether the site should be massaged to ease pain
Injection sites are not massaged.
To read the results of each injection as with a skin test
Only skin tests are read for results.
To decide whether to repeat the dose when pain is mild
Pain is not an indication to repeat a dose.

items.q: Which instruction should the nurse give assistive personnel (AP) after administering an injection?
items.a: Report any change in vital signs or level of consciousness
items.ex: Injections cannot be delegated, but AP report side effects, allergic responses, and changes in vital signs or LOC.
w: Read the tuberculin skin test in 48 hours
Reading skin tests requires nursing assessment.
Give the next scheduled subcutaneous insulin
Administering injections cannot be delegated to AP.
Massage the injection site if it is sore
Injection sites are not massaged.

alt.q: Which task related to injections must remain with the nurse rather than assistive personnel?
alt.a: Administering a subcutaneous injection
alt.ex: The skill of administering injections cannot be delegated to AP.
w: Reporting sedation after an injection
AP can report changes in level of consciousness.
Reporting changes in vital signs
AP report vital sign changes to the nurse.
Reporting signs of an allergic response
AP are taught to report allergic responses.

items.q: Which actions are correct when giving subcutaneous heparin? Select all that apply.
o: Inject the medication over 30 seconds
The book directs heparin to be injected over 30 seconds.
Continue pinching the skin while injecting
This is an option when giving heparin or using an injection pen.
Do not aspirate after inserting the needle
Aspiration is not recommended for heparin or insulin.
Massage the site after withdrawing the needle
Massage causes underlying tissue damage.
Insert the needle at a 5- to 15-degree angle
This is the ID angle; subcutaneous uses 45 to 90 degrees.
items.ex: Heparin is injected slowly over 30 seconds without aspiration, the skin may stay pinched, and the site is not massaged.

alt.q: Which teaching points about subcutaneous insulin injections are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Rotate sites systematically within one anatomical area
Systematic rotation within an area such as the abdomen is recommended.
Avoid areas with masses, tenderness, or bruising
Abnormal sites interfere with absorption.
Do not pull back on the plunger after inserting the needle
Aspiration is not recommended for insulin.
Use the same spot each time to reduce bruising
Repeated use causes lipohypertrophy.
Massage the site to speed absorption
Massage causes underlying tissue damage.
alt.ex: Insulin sites are rotated systematically, abnormal areas are avoided, aspiration is not done, and sites are not massaged.

items.q: Which items must be documented in the patient’s EHR when an immunization is given? Select all that apply.
o: Vaccine manufacturer and lot number
Required for immunization records.
Vaccine expiration date
Required for immunization records.
Date the vaccine information statement was given
The VIS, its print date, and date given are documented.
Name and title of the person who gave the vaccine
The administrator’s name and title are recorded.
Patient’s blood type
Blood type is not part of immunization documentation.
Patient’s preferred pharmacy
This is not required immunization documentation.
items.ex: Immunization records include date, manufacturer, lot number, expiration date, administrator, agency address, and VIS details.

alt.q: Which items does the nurse document after any injection? Select all that apply.
o: Medication, dose, route, site, time, and date
These are documented immediately after administration.
Patient teaching and validation of understanding
Teaching and teach-back results are documented.
Patient’s response to the medication
The response to medication is recorded.
The planned dose, charted before giving it
Documentation is done after administration, not before.
Only reactions, leaving out routine doses
Every administered dose is documented.
alt.ex: After any injection, the nurse documents the drug details, teaching and understanding, and the patient’s response, immediately after giving it.

items.q: Which factors should the nurse assess as possible contraindications to an IM injection? Select all that apply.
o: Muscle atrophy
Atrophied muscle absorbs medication poorly.
Reduced blood flow to the muscle
Poor blood flow impairs absorption.
Circulatory shock
Shock interferes with blood flow and absorption.
A recent meal
Meals do not affect IM absorption.
Patient preference for the arm
Preference is not a contraindication.
items.ex: Muscle atrophy, reduced blood flow, and circulatory shock impair absorption of IM medications.

alt.q: Which factors should the nurse assess as possible contraindications to a subcutaneous injection? Select all that apply.
o: Circulatory shock
Reduced perfusion interferes with absorption and distribution.
Reduced local tissue perfusion
Poor perfusion impairs absorption.
Inadequate subcutaneous adipose tissue
Aging or illness can reduce the subcutaneous tissue available.
Normal blood glucose level
A normal glucose is a baseline, not a contraindication.
Well-hydrated skin
Hydrated skin does not interfere with absorption.
alt.ex: Circulatory shock, reduced local perfusion, and inadequate adipose tissue interfere with subcutaneous absorption.

items.q: After an injection, the nurse massages the site to help the medication absorb.
items.a: False
items.ex: The nurse applies gentle pressure without massage, because massage damages underlying tissue and alters ID test results.
items.ww: Massage causes tissue damage and is never part of the injection procedure.

alt.q: After withdrawing the needle, the nurse applies gentle pressure to the site and does not massage it.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Gentle pressure is applied; massage would damage tissue and disperse ID medication, altering results.
alt.ww: Massaging the site causes underlying tissue damage.

items.q: A patient who does not return within 72 hours to have a tuberculin skin test read needs the test repeated.
items.a: True
items.ex: TB tests are read at 48 to 72 hours; past 72 hours the test must be repeated.
items.ww: A reading after 72 hours is outside the valid window.

alt.q: A tuberculin skin test can still be read accurately at 5 days because induration persists.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The test is read at 48 to 72 hours; a patient who misses this window needs the test repeated.
alt.ww: The book requires a repeat test when it is not read within 72 hours.

items.q: The book recommends the Z-track method for all IM injections.
items.a: True
items.ex: Z-track creates a zigzag path that seals the needle track and is used for all IM injections.
items.ww: The book does not limit Z-track to certain drugs.

alt.q: The Z-track method is used only for IM medications that stain or irritate tissue.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book directs using Z-track for all IM injections to seal the needle track.
alt.ww: Z-track is applied to every IM injection, not just irritating drugs.

items.q: A tuberculin skin test is read at [[48 to 72|48-72]] hours after injection.
items.ex: The site is inspected for induration at 48 to 72 hours; a patient who misses 72 hours needs a repeat test.

alt.q: When reading a TB test, the nurse looks for a hard, dense, raised area called [[induration]].
alt.ex: The site is inspected for induration at 48 to 72 hours; a patient who misses 72 hours needs a repeat test.

items.q: What is the insertion angle for a(n) Intradermal injection?
