sections.name: Skill 31.6 · Administering medications by intravenous push

items.q: A patient has parenteral nutrition infusing through one IV line and a patent saline lock in the other arm. An IV push medication is ordered. Which access should the nurse use?
items.a: The saline lock, after confirming patency
items.ex: IV medications are never given through tubing that is infusing blood, blood products, or parenteral nutrition.
w: The port closest to the patient on the nutrition tubing
Medications are never pushed through parenteral nutrition tubing.
The port farthest from the patient on the nutrition tubing
No port on parenteral nutrition tubing is used for IV push.
Either line, since the drug enters the vein directly
Parenteral nutrition tubing is excluded regardless of port.

alt.q: Through which IV tubing must the nurse never give an IV push medication?
alt.a: Tubing infusing blood or blood products
alt.ex: IV medications are never given through tubing infusing blood, blood products, or parenteral nutrition.
w: Tubing infusing a compatible IV solution
Compatible IV fluids may be used with the port closest to the patient.
A saline lock that flushes easily
A patent saline lock is an appropriate route.
Tubing with a needleless injection port
Needleless ports are the preferred ports for IV push.

items.q: A nurse occludes the IV tubing and aspirates but gets no blood return from a small-gauge catheter. The site shows no signs of infiltration, and IV fluid infuses without difficulty. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Give the IV push medication
items.ex: Small-gauge catheters may not yield blood return even when patent; if the site is normal and fluid flows easily, the push is given.
w: Remove the catheter and start a new IV
A patent line with no infiltration does not need replacing.
Hold the dose and notify the health care provider
The book permits giving the push when these findings are present.
Flush forcefully to clear the catheter
Forceful flushing is not indicated for a line that infuses easily.

alt.q: Which findings allow the nurse to give an IV push through a small-gauge catheter without blood return?
alt.a: No signs of infiltration, and IV fluid infusing without difficulty
alt.ex: Small-gauge catheters may not show blood return even when patent, so a normal site and free flow confirm the line can be used.
w: Mild swelling at the site, and fluid infusing slowly
Swelling suggests infiltration.
Redness at the site, and the patient denies pain
Redness may signal phlebitis; the drug is not given.
Puffiness above the catheter, and a strong pulse
Puffiness suggests infiltration.

items.q: During an IV push, the patient suddenly becomes short of breath and begins wheezing. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Stop delivering the medication immediately
items.ex: With an adverse reaction, delivery is stopped at once, then agency protocol is followed and the provider notified immediately.
w: Finish the push more slowly, then notify the provider
Continuing gives more of the drug causing the reaction.
Flush the line rapidly with normal saline
Flushing would push the remaining drug into the patient.
Document the reaction and recheck in 15 minutes
Dyspnea and wheezing need immediate action, not delayed reassessment.

alt.q: After stopping an IV push because of an allergic reaction, which additional actions does the book list?
alt.a: Notify the provider immediately and add the allergy to the EHR
alt.ex: The provider is notified of adverse effects immediately, agency reaction policy is followed, and the allergy is added to the EHR.
w: Restart the push at half the rate after 10 minutes
The drug is not resumed after an allergic reaction.
Remove the IV and wait for the next shift to report
Adverse effects are reported immediately.
Give the rest of the dose by IM injection
The drug causing the reaction is not given by another route.

items.q: While flushing a saline lock before an IV push, the nurse notices puffiness of the skin above the catheter. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Stop and remove the catheter, then restart the IV in another site
items.ex: Swelling during a flush suggests infiltration, which requires stopping, removing the access device, and restarting elsewhere.
w: Continue flushing with more force
Force would push more fluid into the tissue.
Give the medication, then reassess the site
Medication is not given into an infiltrated site.
Apply a warm compress and keep using the site
An infiltrated site is not used for medication.

alt.q: Which finding during a saline flush of an IV lock suggests infiltration?
alt.a: Puffiness or swelling of the skin above the catheter
alt.ex: Puffiness or swelling as the site is flushed indicates infiltration and requires catheter removal.
w: Blood return on aspiration
Blood return indicates the catheter is in the vein.
Saline flowing without resistance
Easy flushing indicates a patent line.
No change in the skin over the catheter
An unchanged site is the expected finding.

items.q: Why does the nurse use a watch to time an IV push medication?
items.a: Many medication errors occur when IV pushes are given too quickly
items.ex: Rapid IV injection can be fatal, so the push is timed to the rate set by policy, the pharmacist, or a drug reference.
w: To record the exact time for the medication count
Timing protects the injection rate, not a count.
To measure how long blood return takes to appear
Blood return is checked by aspiration, not timed.
To decide when to recap the needle
Needles are never recapped.

alt.q: A drug reference states an IV push medication must be given over 5 minutes. Which equipment is essential?
alt.a: A watch with a second hand
alt.ex: A watch with a second hand is listed equipment so the push is delivered over the recommended time.
w: A filter needle
Filters are used only when the drug requires one.
A heparin flush syringe
Heparin flush is used only if agency policy calls for it.
A tuberculin syringe
Syringe size depends on volume, not timing.

items.q: Why does the nurse dilute a very small IV push dose, such as less than 1 mL, in about 5 mL of normal saline or sterile water?
items.a: To keep the medication from collecting in dead spaces of the IV system
items.ex: Tiny volumes can stay in dead spaces such as the Y-site port or IV cap instead of reaching the patient.
w: To make the medication compatible with blood products
IV drugs are never given through blood tubing.
To slow absorption once the drug reaches the vein
Dilution here ensures delivery, not slower absorption.
To prevent the need to time the injection
Every IV push is still timed.

alt.q: Before diluting an IV push medication, what should the nurse do?
alt.a: Verify with agency policy or pharmacy that dilution is permitted
alt.ex: Some IV drugs require dilution, but the nurse verifies that dilution is permitted before doing it.
w: Ask assistive personnel to prepare the diluent
IV push administration cannot be delegated to AP.
Dilute it in heparin flush solution
Normal saline or sterile water is used for dilution.
Dilute it only if the patient reports pain
Dilution depends on the drug and policy, not pain.

items.q: An IV push medication is incompatible with the IV fluid infusing through the existing line. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Stop the fluids, clamp the line, and flush with 10 mL before and after the push
items.ex: Flushing with 10 mL of normal saline or sterile water before and after lets the bolus be given without mixing incompatible drugs.
w: Push the medication quickly so the drugs do not mix
Rapid IV injection can be fatal.
Use the port farthest from the patient
Port location does not prevent incompatibility.
Add the medication to the IV bag instead
This changes the ordered route and does not solve incompatibility.

alt.q: When an IV push medication is incompatible with the running IV fluid, how much flush is given before and after the push?
alt.a: 10 mL of normal saline or sterile water
alt.ex: The line is flushed with 10 mL before the bolus and another 10 mL after, at the same rate as the medication.
w: 2 to 3 mL of normal saline
This is the volume per syringe for a saline lock flush.
5 mL of heparin flush
Heparin is not used to separate incompatible drugs.
50 mL of the infusing IV fluid
The infusing fluid is the incompatible solution.

items.q: After pushing a medication through an existing IV line, which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Withdraw the syringe and recheck the IV fluid infusion rate
items.ex: Injecting a bolus may alter the infusion rate, and rapid fluid infusion can cause circulatory fluid overload.
w: Increase the IV rate to flush the medication through
Rapid fluid infusion can cause fluid overload.
Recap the needle before discarding it
Recapping increases needlestick risk.
Massage the IV site to speed absorption
Massage has no role in IV push administration.

alt.q: Why does the nurse recheck the IV infusion rate after giving a push through an existing line?
alt.a: The bolus may change the rate, and rapid infusion can cause fluid overload
alt.ex: A bolus injection can alter the drip rate, so the rate is rechecked to prevent fluid overload.
w: To confirm that blood return is still present in the line
Blood return is checked before the push.
To decide when the next saline flush should be scheduled
This is not the rationale given.
To confirm the medication was compatible with the fluid
Compatibility is checked before the push.

items.q: A patient has a continuous IV medication infusing, and an IV push is ordered. Agency policy does not allow the continuous infusion to be stopped. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Start a new IV site and give the push by the IV lock method
items.ex: If the hanging IV is a medication that cannot be stopped, a new site is started to avoid a sudden bolus of the infusing drug.
w: Push through the port closest to the patient
This would flush a sudden bolus of the infusing medication.
Raise the infusion rate to carry the push in
This would deliver a bolus of the infusing medication.
Mix the push medication into the infusion bag
This changes the ordered route and timing.

alt.q: Why does the nurse avoid pushing a medication through a line that is infusing another medication?
alt.a: It would give the patient a sudden bolus of the infusing medication
alt.ex: Pushing into a medication line flushes the infusing drug into the patient as a bolus.
w: It would dilute the push medication too much
The concern is a bolus of the infusing drug.
It would prevent the nurse from timing the push
The push can still be timed; the risk is a bolus.
It would require a filter needle
Filters are not the issue here.

items.q: Which instruction should the nurse give assistive personnel (AP) caring for a patient receiving IV push medications?
items.a: Report any complaints of moisture or discomfort around the IV site
items.ex: IV push cannot be delegated, but AP report moisture or discomfort at the IV site, side effects, and vital signs.
w: Flush the saline lock before the nurse arrives
Flushing an IV lock is part of IV push and cannot be delegated.
Time the IV push using a watch
Giving the push, including timing it, is the nurse’s role.
Check the IV line for blood return
Checking placement is part of the nurse’s skill.

alt.q: Which task related to IV push medications cannot be delegated to assistive personnel?
alt.a: Giving an IV push medication through a saline lock
alt.ex: Administering IV bolus medications cannot be delegated to AP.
w: Obtaining vital signs and reporting them
AP can obtain and report required vital signs.
Reporting moisture around the IV site
AP report moisture or discomfort at the site.
Reporting medication side effects
AP are directed to report side effects immediately.

items.q: After giving an IV push antiarrhythmic, which assessment should the nurse prioritize to evaluate the drug’s effect?
items.a: Blood pressure and heart rate monitoring
items.ex: Vasopressors and antiarrhythmics can rapidly change physiological status and require blood pressure and heart rate monitoring.
w: Partial thromboplastin time
Laboratory studies are needed after heparin.
Peak expiratory flow rate
Peak flow monitors inhaled bronchodilator response.
Skinfold thickness at the site
Skinfold size guides subcutaneous needle length.

alt.q: Why can some IV push medications be given only in units such as the intensive care unit?
alt.a: The patient must be monitored continuously for dysrhythmias and blood pressure changes
alt.ex: Some IV pushes are safe only with continuous monitoring for dysrhythmias, blood pressure changes, or other adverse effects.
w: Only critical care nurses may use saline locks
Saline locks are used on many units.
These drugs must be diluted by a pharmacist at the bedside
Dilution is not the reason for unit restriction.
These drugs must be pushed through blood tubing
IV drugs are never given through blood tubing.

items.q: Which risk factors for medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI) should the nurse look for in the EHR before an IV push? Select all that apply.
o: Dehydration
Dehydration is listed as a MARSI risk factor.
Malnutrition
Malnutrition is listed as a MARSI risk factor.
Exposure to radiation therapy
Radiation therapy is listed as a MARSI risk factor.
Edema of the skin
Skin edema is listed as a MARSI risk factor.
A patent saline lock
Patency is not a skin injury risk factor.
Normal vital signs
Normal vital signs are not a MARSI risk factor.
items.ex: Adhesive may stabilize the catheter, so age, dehydration, malnutrition, radiation, chronic conditions, and skin edema are reviewed as MARSI risks.

alt.q: Which patient conditions increase the risk for medical adhesive–related skin injury? Select all that apply.
o: Diabetes mellitus
Chronic conditions such as diabetes are MARSI risk factors.
Immunosuppression
Immunosuppression is a listed chronic condition.
History of malnutrition
Malnutrition increases MARSI risk.
Recent influenza vaccination
Vaccination is not a listed risk factor.
Use of a needleless injection port
Port type does not affect skin injury risk.
alt.ex: Chronic conditions such as diabetes and immunosuppression, plus malnutrition, increase the risk for medical adhesive–related skin injury.

items.q: Which assessments should the nurse complete before giving an IV push through an existing IV line? Select all that apply.
o: Compatibility of the drug with the IV fluid and additives
Incompatible drugs may require flushing or a new site.
The IV site for signs of infiltration or phlebitis
Medication is not given into an edematous or inflamed site.
Patency of the IV line
The line must be patent for the drug to reach circulation.
Peak expiratory flow rate
This monitors inhaled bronchodilator therapy.
Skinfold thickness over the site
This guides subcutaneous needle length.
items.ex: Before an IV push, the nurse checks drug compatibility, the site for infiltration or phlebitis, and line patency.

alt.q: Before an IV push, which findings at the IV site mean the nurse should not give the medication there? Select all that apply.
o: Edema around the insertion site
An edematous site suggests infiltration.
Inflammation at the insertion site
Inflammation suggests phlebitis.
Swelling when the line is flushed
Swelling during flushing indicates infiltration.
Saline flushes without resistance
Easy flushing indicates a patent line.
Blood return on aspiration
Blood return confirms the catheter is in the vein.
alt.ex: Edema, inflammation, or swelling with flushing signal infiltration or phlebitis, so the medication is not given at that site.

items.q: An IV site shows signs of infiltration after an IV push. Which interventions does the book list? Select all that apply.
o: Stop the infusion or remove the access device and restart in another site
The infiltrated site is not used further.
Determine how much damage the drug can cause in subcutaneous tissue
Tissue damage potential guides follow-up care.
Provide extravasation care per policy and consult the pharmacist
Follow-up care is guided by policy, references, and the pharmacist.
Push the remaining medication quickly to finish the dose
More drug would enter the tissue.
Massage the swollen area to spread the fluid
Massage is not a listed intervention.
items.ex: For infiltration or phlebitis, the nurse stops or restarts the IV, judges tissue damage risk, and gives extravasation care with pharmacist input.

alt.q: Which actions help the nurse detect infiltration of an IV site during and after an IV push? Select all that apply.
o: Observe the site during the injection for sudden swelling
Swelling during injection indicates infiltration.
Continue observing the site for 48 hours
Signs of infiltration may not appear for 48 hours.
Encourage the patient to report discomfort at the IV site
Patient reports help detect infiltration early.
Stop observing once the medication has been flushed
Infiltration signs can be delayed for up to 48 hours.
Check the site only at the next scheduled dose
The site is observed during and after the push.
alt.ex: The nurse watches the site during injection and for 48 hours afterward, and patient reports of discomfort help detect infiltration early.

items.q: After an IV push through an IV lock, the nurse flushes with saline at the same rate the medication was given.
items.a: True
items.ex: Flushing at the same rate delivers any medication remaining in the catheter at the correct rate and prevents occlusion.
items.ww: A faster flush would push leftover medication in too quickly.

alt.q: After an IV push through an IV lock, the nurse flushes rapidly so the remaining medication clears the catheter quickly.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The flush is given at the same rate as the medication so leftover drug is delivered at the correct rate.
alt.ww: A rapid flush effectively gives the remaining drug as a rapid push.

items.q: After an IV push, the nurse recaps the needle before discarding it in the sharps container.
items.a: False
items.ex: The uncapped or safety-shielded needle and syringe are discarded directly, because recapping increases needlestick risk.
items.ww: Recapping is avoided because it increases the risk for needlestick injury.

alt.q: After an IV push, the nurse discards the uncapped or safety-shielded needle with its syringe in a puncture- and leak-proof receptacle.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Direct disposal without recapping prevents needlestick injury to patients and staff.
alt.ww: Recapping needles increases the risk for needlestick injury.

items.q: Normal saline is the preferred flush for keeping a peripheral IV lock patent.
items.a: True
items.ex: Saline keeps IV locks patent and is compatible with a wide range of medications; many agencies no longer use heparin for peripheral lines.
items.ww: The book calls the saline flush method the preferred method.

alt.q: Heparin is the preferred flush for peripheral IV locks because saline is incompatible with many medications.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Saline is preferred and compatible with a wide range of drugs; many agencies no longer use heparin flush for peripheral lines.
alt.ww: Saline, not heparin, is the preferred flush for peripheral locks.

items.q: For the saline flush method, the nurse prepares two syringes filled with [[2 to 3|2-3]] mL of normal saline.
items.ex: Saline flushing uses two 2- to 3-mL syringes, before and after the drug; if heparin flush is used, 10 units/mL is most common.

alt.q: If an agency still uses heparin flush, the most common concentration is [[10]] units/mL.
alt.ex: Saline flushing uses two 2- to 3-mL syringes, before and after the drug; if heparin flush is used, 10 units/mL is most common.

sections.name: Skill 31.7 · Administering intravenous medications by piggyback and syringe pumps

items.q: Several minutes after starting an IV piggyback antibiotic, the nurse is still at the bedside observing the patient. Which finding suggests a severe anaphylactic reaction?
items.a: Wheezing with shortness of breath
items.ex: Dyspnea, wheezing, and circulatory collapse are signs of a severe anaphylactic reaction, so the nurse stays and watches for them.
w: Pallor and coolness at the IV site
This is a local IV site problem to assess, not a sign of anaphylaxis.
Mild discomfort at the insertion site
Site discomfort should be reported, but it points to a local IV problem rather than anaphylaxis.
Dampness under the IV dressing
Moisture around the site suggests a local site problem, not a systemic allergic reaction.

alt.q: Why does the nurse stay with the patient for several minutes after starting an IV piggyback medication?
alt.a: IV medications act rapidly, and an allergic response can be immediate
alt.ex: IV administration can cause a rapid response, so the nurse observes for allergic reactions right after the infusion begins.
w: The pump must be watched until its first alarm check is done
The book's reason is rapid drug action and possible allergy, not pump checks.
The patient must sign that the medication was received
No signature is required; the nurse documents administration with initials or signature.
The primary infusion has to be restarted by hand
The primary infusion resumes automatically once the piggyback is empty.

items.q: Before hanging a scheduled IV piggyback, the nurse assesses the patient's existing IV site and finds it edematous and inflamed. Which action is appropriate?
items.a: Do not give the medication through this IV site
items.ex: The book directs the nurse not to administer medication if the IV site is edematous or inflamed.
w: Flush the site with saline, then start the piggyback
Flushing does not make an edematous, inflamed site safe to use.
Start the piggyback at a slower rate than ordered
A slower rate does not make an inflamed site safe and the ordered rate would be violated.
Apply a warm compress, then begin the infusion
The medication should not be given through an edematous or inflamed site at all.

alt.q: While assessing the IV line before an IV piggyback dose, which finding means the nurse should not administer the medication through that site?
alt.a: Edema and inflammation around the insertion site
alt.ex: An edematous or inflamed site is unsafe for IV medication administration.
w: A dry, intact dressing over the site
A dry, intact dressing is an expected, normal finding.
Saline that flushes easily without resistance
Easy flushing shows the line is patent and usable.
A patient who denies pain at the site
Absence of discomfort is reassuring, not a reason to withhold the dose.

items.q: A patient's only IV line is infusing a unit of packed red blood cells, and an IV piggyback antibiotic is now due. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Not connect the antibiotic to the tubing carrying the blood
items.ex: IV medications are never given through tubing that is infusing blood, blood products, or parenteral nutrition.
w: Connect the piggyback to the upper Y-port of the blood tubing
Medications must never enter tubing infusing blood or blood products.
Pause the blood, run the piggyback through that tubing, then resume
Pausing the blood does not make its tubing acceptable for IV medications.
Slow the transfusion and run both through the same tubing
Running both through the same tubing is exactly what the book prohibits.

alt.q: A patient has several IV lines. Through which one may the nurse NOT give an IV piggyback medication?
alt.a: The tubing infusing parenteral nutrition
alt.ex: Tubing infusing parenteral nutrition, blood, or blood products must never be used for IV medications.
w: A continuous normal saline line checked for compatibility
A compatible primary line is an acceptable route for a piggyback.
A saline lock that flushes without resistance
A patent saline lock is an acceptable route for an intermittent infusion.
A primary line whose fluid and additives are compatible
Once compatibility is confirmed, an existing primary line may be used.

items.q: A patient has a saline lock, and the nurse is about to connect IV piggyback tubing to it. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Clean the port with an antiseptic swab, let it dry, and flush it with saline
items.ex: Cleaning the port and flushing with sterile sodium chloride confirms the lock is patent before the medication is connected.
w: Insert the piggyback tubing and open the regulator clamp
Connecting without checking patency risks infusing into a blocked or misplaced line.
Wipe the port and insert the tubing before it dries
The port should be allowed to dry after cleaning before it is accessed.
Flush the lock only after the medication has finished
The lock is flushed before the infusion to ensure patency and again afterward.

alt.q: What is the purpose of flushing a saline lock before connecting an IV piggyback to it?
alt.a: To make sure the lock is patent before the medication is given
alt.ex: Flushing the lock before connecting the piggyback ensures patency so the medication enters the vein.
w: To dilute the medication inside the piggyback bag
The flush stays in the lock and vein; it does not dilute the bag contents.
To prevent medication from building up in the lock
That is the reason for flushing after the infusion, not before.
To prime the piggyback tubing with saline
The tubing is primed with medication solution from the bag, not with the flush.

items.q: The nurse has taught a patient about an IV piggyback medication infusing through an existing IV line. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: I'll tell the nurse if my IV site starts to hurt or feels wet
items.ex: Patients who report pain or discomfort at the IV site help the nurse detect infiltration early, limiting tissue damage.
w: Some burning at the IV site is normal, so I won't mention it
Site discomfort should be reported because it can signal infiltration.
When the small bag empties, I'll turn off the big bag myself
The primary infusion restarts automatically; the patient should not adjust clamps.
If the drip looks slow, I'll open the clamp a little more
Only the nurse regulates the flow rate based on the medication reference or policy.

alt.q: During teach-back, the nurse asks a patient why they are getting an IV medication and what to report. Which reply shows understanding?
alt.a: It's for my infection, and I should report pain at my IV site
alt.ex: The teach-back checks that the patient knows the medication's purpose and reports symptoms such as site discomfort.
w: It's for my infection, and there is nothing I need to report
Patients are taught to report side effects and discomfort at the IV site.
It's for my infection, and I'll report problems after it finishes
Symptoms and site discomfort should be reported as they occur, not later.
It's for my infection, and I can speed it up if I feel fine
The infusion rate is set by the nurse for safe administration.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient receiving an IV piggyback medication with help from assistive personnel (AP). Which instruction to the AP is appropriate?
items.a: Tell me right away if the patient reports dampness or pain at the IV site
items.ex: The AP cannot administer IV piggyback medications but is directed to report site moisture or discomfort to the nurse.
w: When the piggyback bag empties, restart the primary fluid
Managing the infusion is part of IV medication administration, which cannot be delegated.
If the IV pump alarms, flush the saline lock with saline
Flushing an IV lock is part of the nurse's skill and is not delegated to AP.
Lower the piggyback bag if the infusion seems too fast
Adjusting the infusion is the nurse's responsibility, not the AP's.

alt.q: Which action by assistive personnel (AP) caring for a patient with an IV piggyback infusion requires the nurse to intervene?
alt.a: The AP disconnects the empty piggyback and flushes the saline lock
alt.ex: Administering IV medications by piggyback, including disconnecting and flushing the lock, cannot be delegated to AP.
w: The AP reports that the patient's blood pressure has dropped
Reporting changes in condition or vital signs is exactly what the AP is directed to do.
The AP reports the patient's complaint of a wet IV dressing
Reporting moisture or discomfort at the IV site is an appropriate AP action.
The AP reports a new rash noticed during morning care
Reporting possible side effects to the nurse is part of the AP's instructions.

items.q: Why does the nurse hang the piggyback medication bag higher than the primary fluid bag?
items.a: The height of a fluid bag affects its rate of flow to the patient
items.ex: Bag height drives the flow rate, so the higher piggyback bag infuses first while the primary is held back.
w: It lets the medication mix with the primary fluid before infusing
The back-check valve keeps the primary fluid from flowing while the medication infuses.
It keeps air from entering the piggyback tubing
Air is removed by filling the tubing with solution before connecting it.
It lets gravity flush the saline lock between doses
A saline lock is flushed with a syringe of sterile sodium chloride, not by bag height.

alt.q: A piggyback bag cannot be hung any higher on the IV pole. Which option does the book describe for getting the correct bag positions?
alt.a: Use a hook to lower the main fluid bag
alt.ex: The piggyback must sit above the primary bag; a hook can lower the main bag to create that height difference.
w: Hang both bags at the same level on the pole
Equal heights do not give the piggyback the height advantage it needs to infuse first.
Lower the piggyback bag below the main bag
The piggyback must be above the primary bag, not below it.
Clamp the primary tubing below the Y-port
Clamping below the Y-port would also stop the medication from reaching the patient.

items.q: During an IV piggyback infusion into a continuous primary line, what does the back-check valve on the piggyback set do?
items.a: It stops the primary solution from flowing until the medication has infused
items.ex: The back-check valve holds the primary infusion until the medication infuses, and the primary then restarts automatically.
w: It filters particles out of the medication before it enters the vein
Filtering is done with a filter when the medication reference requires one, not by the valve.
It sounds an alarm when the piggyback bag is empty
The valve has no alarm; the nurse checks the primary flow rate after the medication infuses.
It sets the piggyback flow rate automatically
The nurse sets the rate with the regulator clamp or IV pump.

alt.q: A piggyback medication has just finished infusing into a continuous primary IV line. What happens next?
alt.a: The primary infusion restarts by itself, and the nurse checks its flow rate
alt.ex: Once the piggyback empties, the primary infusion begins automatically; the nurse checks and regulates its rate to the order.
w: The nurse must open the primary clamp to restart the main fluid
The primary infusion begins automatically once the piggyback solution is empty.
The primary fluid stays off until the next dose is hung
The back-check valve releases the primary flow as soon as the piggyback empties.
The pump stops both lines until the nurse resets them
Nothing requires a reset; the primary flow resumes automatically.

items.q: When using a volume-control administration set such as a Volutrol, how much IV fluid does the nurse let into the chamber before adding the medication?
items.a: 50 to 100 mL
items.ex: A small volume of 50 to 100 mL dilutes the medication and reduces the risk of fluid infusing too rapidly.
w: 5 to 10 mL
This volume is too small to dilute the medication properly.
150 to 250 mL
This is more than the small volume the book specifies for the chamber.
250 to 500 mL
This is far more than the small volume the book specifies for the chamber.

alt.q: Why is only a small volume of IV fluid (50 to 100 mL) placed in a Volutrol with the medication?
alt.a: It dilutes the medication and lowers the risk of fluid infusing too fast
alt.ex: The small, measured volume dilutes the medication and limits how much fluid could infuse too rapidly.
w: It keeps the medication concentrated so it acts faster
The purpose is to dilute the medication, not keep it concentrated.
It allows the chamber to be used without a label
The Volutrol is always labeled with the medication, dose, volume, and time.
It lets the main bag keep infusing at the same time
The clamp between the Volutrol and main bag is closed after filling.

items.q: When is the third check for accuracy performed during IV piggyback administration?
items.a: At the bedside, comparing the MAR with the medication labels and patient name
items.ex: The third check happens at the bedside, where the MAR is compared again with labels and the patient's name.
w: When the medication is removed from storage
This is the first check for accuracy.
After the medication is prepared, before leaving the medication area
This is the second check for accuracy.
After the infusion is documented in the EHR
Checks are done before administration, not after documenting.

alt.q: During IV piggyback preparation, when are the first and second checks for accuracy done?
alt.a: When the medication is removed from storage and after it is prepared
alt.ex: The label is checked against the MAR when removed from storage and after preparation; the bedside check is third.
w: After preparation and again at the bedside
The bedside comparison is the third check, not the second.
At the bedside and after the infusion is complete
Checks occur before administration; the bedside check is the third one.
When the order is written and when the patient is identified
The first two checks compare the medication label with the MAR during preparation.

items.q: A patient develops hives and wheezing during an IV piggyback infusion. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Stop the medication infusion immediately
Stopping the infusion right away is the first response to an adverse or allergic reaction.
Follow agency policy for treating the reaction, such as an antihistamine or epinephrine
Agency guidelines direct the response, which may include diphenhydramine or epinephrine.
Notify the health care provider immediately
The health care provider is told of adverse effects immediately.
Add the allergy information to the patient's EHR per agency policy
The new allergy must be recorded so the drug is not given again.
Slow the infusion and recheck the patient in 30 minutes
An allergic reaction calls for stopping the infusion, not slowing it.
Let the infusion finish so the full dose is received
Continuing the drug worsens the reaction; the infusion is stopped immediately.
items.ex: For an adverse or allergic reaction, stop the infusion, follow agency policy, notify the provider, and record the allergy.

alt.q: A patient receiving an IV medication by syringe pump suddenly becomes short of breath with a new rash. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Stop the infusion right away
The medication infusion is stopped immediately for an allergic reaction.
Notify the health care provider immediately
Adverse effects are reported to the provider immediately.
Record the allergy in the patient's EHR per agency policy
Adding the allergy to the record prevents repeat exposure.
Restart the pump at half the rate once symptoms ease
The drug causing the reaction is not restarted at a lower rate.
Wait until the dose is finished before calling the provider
The provider is notified immediately, and the infusion is stopped, not completed.
alt.ex: An allergic reaction requires stopping the infusion, notifying the provider immediately, and documenting the allergy.

items.q: An IV piggyback medication has not infused within its expected time frame. Which possible reasons should the nurse look for? Select all that apply.
o: An improperly calculated flow rate
Wrong flow-rate calculation is one reason the book lists for a delayed infusion.
Poor positioning of the IV needle at the insertion site
A poorly positioned catheter can slow or stop the infusion.
Infiltration of the IV site
Infiltration is a listed cause of failure to infuse on time.
The piggyback bag hung higher than the primary bag
This is correct technique and lets the piggyback infuse first.
The back-check valve holding back the primary fluid
This is the valve's normal function and does not slow the medication.
items.ex: When a medication does not infuse on time, the nurse determines the reason, such as flow-rate error, catheter position, or infiltration, and corrects it.

alt.q: Half of a piggyback dose is still in the bag well past the time it should have finished. Which findings could explain this? Select all that apply.
o: Swelling of the tissue around the IV site
Infiltration can stop the medication from infusing as planned.
A flow rate that was set from a calculation error
Improper flow-rate calculation can make the infusion run too slowly.
An IV catheter that is poorly positioned at the site
Poor needle or catheter positioning can impede the infusion.
A label on the tubing showing the time it was hung
Labeling prevents errors and has no effect on flow.
Hand hygiene performed before connecting the tubing
Hand hygiene reduces microorganisms and does not affect flow.
alt.ex: The book lists improper flow-rate calculation, poor catheter positioning, and infiltration as reasons an infusion runs late.

items.q: The IV site shows signs of infiltration while a piggyback medication is infusing. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Stop the IV infusion and discontinue the access device
Infiltration requires stopping the infusion and removing the access device.
Treat the IV site as directed by agency policy
Site care follows agency policy.
Insert a new IV catheter if therapy is to continue
A new catheter is placed if the patient still needs IV therapy.
Give extravasation care, such as phentolamine, per policy or pharmacist advice
For infiltration, the nurse judges tissue harm and provides extravasation care, such as phentolamine, per policy.
Flush the catheter and restart the infusion in the same site
An infiltrated site must not be used; the access device is discontinued.
Increase the rate so the dose finishes before moving the IV
Speeding the infusion pushes more medication into the tissue.
items.ex: For infiltration, stop the infusion, remove the device, treat the site per policy, restart IV access elsewhere, and give extravasation care as indicated.

alt.q: A patient's IV site shows signs of phlebitis during an intermittent IV medication infusion. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Stop the infusion and discontinue the access device
Signs of phlebitis require stopping the infusion and removing the device.
Treat the site as indicated by agency policy
Site treatment follows agency policy.
Insert a new IV catheter if IV therapy continues
Continued therapy needs a new IV access site.
Keep the infusion running and recheck the site at the end of the shift
Phlebitis calls for stopping the infusion now, not later reassessment.
Flush the line with saline and resume the medication
The affected site is not reused; the access device is discontinued.
alt.ex: Signs of phlebitis or infiltration mean stopping the infusion, removing the device, treating the site, and starting a new IV if needed.

items.q: When an IV medication will be given through an existing IV line, the nurse first checks that the medication is compatible with the IV fluid and any additives in it.
items.a: True
items.ex: An IV medication is sometimes incompatible with the IV solution or its additives, so compatibility is checked before using the line.
items.ww: Compatibility checking is a listed assessment step whenever an existing IV line is used.

alt.q: Any IV piggyback medication can be given through an existing primary line, because the primary fluid dilutes it enough to prevent problems.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Medications may be incompatible with the IV solution or additives, so compatibility must be confirmed first.
alt.ww: Dilution does not prevent incompatibility; the book requires checking compatibility with the fluid and additives.

items.q: To reduce administration set misconnections, the nurse traces every catheter, administration set, and add-on device from the patient to the container before connecting and at each care transition.
items.a: True
items.ex: Misconnections happen when connections are not checked before connecting or reconnecting, so lines are traced each time.
items.ww: Tracing lines at every connection and care transition is the book's step for preventing misconnections.

alt.q: Once IV tubing has been traced at the start of an infusion, it does not need to be traced again when care is handed off to another nurse.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Lines are traced before connecting or reconnecting and at each care transition, including handoffs.
alt.ww: Misconnections can occur at any reconnection or transition, so tracing is repeated, not done just once.

items.q: Documentation of an IV piggyback or Volutrol infusion includes the volume of fluid in the medication bag or Volutrol.
items.a: True
items.ex: The nurse documents the fluid volume in the bag or Volutrol along with medication, dose, route, rate, and time.
items.ww: The book specifically lists the volume of fluid in the bag or Volutrol as a documentation item.

alt.q: Because IV piggyback doses run over time, the nurse may wait until the end of the shift to document them with the other medications.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The medication, dose, route, infusion rate, and date and time are documented immediately.
alt.ww: The book directs immediate documentation, not delaying until the end of the shift.

items.q: After an intermittent infusion through a saline lock, the nurse disconnects the tubing, cleans the port, and flushes with [[2 to 3|2-3|two to three]] mL of sterile 0.9% sodium chloride.
items.ex: Flushing the lock with 2 to 3 mL of sterile saline after the infusion prevents medication buildup in the lock device.

alt.q: To check patency of a saline lock before connecting a piggyback, the nurse cleans the port and flushes it with [[2 to 3|2-3|two to three]] mL of sterile sodium chloride.
alt.ex: Flushing the lock with 2 to 3 mL of sterile saline after the infusion prevents medication buildup in the lock device.

items.q: Which description best defines a complementary therapy?
items.a: A therapy used together with the conventional treatment recommended by the health care provider
items.ex: Complementary therapies are used alongside, not instead of, conventional treatment; they complement it.
w: A therapy used in place of the conventional treatment recommended by the health care provider
Replacing conventional treatment makes a therapy alternative, not complementary.
A therapy that must be prescribed and administered only by a licensed physician
Many complementary therapies, such as guided imagery and breathwork, are easily learned and used by nurses.
A therapy whose effectiveness has been proven by large randomized controlled trials
Evidence for many complementary therapies is still limited, and more randomized trials are needed.

alt.q: A patient stops prescribed analgesics and manages chronic pain with yoga and lifestyle changes alone. How is yoga classified in this situation?
alt.a: As an alternative therapy
alt.ex: When a nonpharmacological therapy replaces conventional medical treatment, it becomes an alternative therapy.
w: As a complementary therapy
Yoga would be complementary only if used together with the prescribed analgesics.
As an integrative nursing intervention
Integrative care brings conventional and complementary therapies together rather than replacing one with the other.
As a biologically based therapy
Biologically based therapies are natural products such as herbs and supplements, not movement practices like yoga.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: A patient from another culture uses traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) instead of biomedical care. How does the textbook classify whole medical systems used this way?
items.a: Always as alternative, because they rest on philosophies completely different from allopathic medicine
items.ex: Whole medical systems such as TCM, Ayurveda, and naturopathy used in place of biomedicine are always considered alternative.
w: Always as complementary, because they have been used by cultures for thousands of years
A long history of use does not make a system complementary when it replaces biomedical care.
As integrative, because the patient’s cultural beliefs are being respected by the team
Integrative care combines conventional and complementary therapies; a replacement system is alternative.
As conventional, because they are widely practiced and accepted in their home countries
These systems evolved independently of conventional biomedicine and are not classified as conventional.

alt.q: Which group lists whole medical systems that the textbook says are used as alternative systems of care?
alt.a: Traditional Chinese medicine, Ayurveda, and naturopathy
alt.ex: TCM, Ayurveda, and naturopathy are complete systems of theory and practice outside conventional biomedicine.
w: Guided imagery, breathwork, and progressive relaxation
These are nursing-accessible mind-body techniques, not whole medical systems.
Probiotics, macrobiotic diet, and dietary supplements
These are biologically based therapies (natural products), not whole systems of care.
Therapeutic touch, reiki, and healing touch therapy
These are biofield (energy) therapies, not complete medical systems.

items.q: Which complementary therapy does the textbook identify as one that is NOT applied by nurses because it requires special training?
items.a: Chiropractic therapy

w: Guided imagery
Guided imagery is easily learned and can be applied in nursing practice.
Breathwork
Breathwork is easily learned and can be used in nursing practice.
Relaxation
Relaxation techniques are nursing-accessible therapies nurses can use independently.

alt.q: What does chiropractic therapy aim to do?
alt.a: Normalize the relationship between body structure and function through joint manipulations
alt.ex: Chiropractic therapy is a manipulative, body-based therapy that manipulates joints to normalize structure and function.
w: Redirect qi along meridians by inserting thin needles at acupoints
This describes acupuncture, not chiropractic therapy.
Balance the patient’s energy field with the practitioner’s open palms
This describes therapeutic touch, a biofield therapy.
Give feedback about muscle tension and heart rate using instruments
This describes biofeedback, a mind-body technique.

items.q: Which symptoms do integrative therapies help relieve in patients with medical conditions? Select all that apply.
o: Fatigue
Integrative therapies help relieve symptoms by reducing fatigue.
Nausea
Reducing nausea is one of the symptom benefits named for integrative therapies.
Pain
Integrative therapies are often used to reduce pain in conditions such as chronic pain and cancer.
Anxiety
Integrative therapies reduce anxiety as part of symptom relief.
Bacterial infection
Integrative therapies relieve symptoms; they do not treat bacterial infections.
Bone fractures
Fractures require conventional medical treatment, not symptom-relief therapies.
items.ex: Integrative therapies relieve symptoms of medical conditions by reducing fatigue, nausea, pain, and anxiety.

alt.q: In which conditions does the textbook say integrative therapies are often used? Select all that apply.
o: Cancer
Cancer is one of the conditions in which integrative therapies are often used.
Fibromyalgia
Fibromyalgia is listed among conditions commonly managed with integrative therapies.
Diabetes
Diabetes is named among conditions where integrative therapies are often used.
Chronic fatigue
Chronic fatigue is listed among these conditions.
Acute appendicitis
Signs of appendicitis require prompt consultation with a health care provider, not integrative therapy.
Acute anaphylaxis
Anaphylaxis is a medical emergency needing conventional treatment.
alt.ex: Integrative therapies are often used in cancer, chronic fatigue, chronic pain, fibromyalgia, diabetes, and other conditions.

items.q: A patient with advanced cancer and very low energy reserves asks for help with stress. Which relaxation approach is most appropriate?
items.a: Passive relaxation or guided imagery
items.ex: Active progressive relaxation needs moderate energy and increases fatigue, so passive relaxation or guided imagery is better.
w: Active progressive relaxation training
This requires moderate energy and is inappropriate for advanced disease with low energy reserves.
A vigorous yoga program done daily
Vigorous activity would increase fatigue in a patient with low energy.
Tensing all muscle groups at once
Tensing muscles costs energy and is not recommended for low energy reserves.

alt.q: For which patient is active progressive relaxation training inappropriate?
alt.a: A patient with advanced AIDS who tires easily
alt.ex: Active progressive relaxation needs moderate energy, so it is inappropriate for advanced disease or decreased energy reserves.
w: A healthy adult with work-related tension
A healthy adult usually has the energy for active progressive relaxation.
A college student with test anxiety
This student has no energy limitation preventing active relaxation.
A nurse with stress from shift work
Nurses without energy limits can benefit from relaxation techniques.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: During the second week of relaxation training, a patient reports new chest discomfort that was not present before. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Completely assess the new symptom and then notify the health care provider of the findings
items.ex: New symptoms may signal disease progression or a new illness, so assess fully and notify the health care provider.
w: Reassure the patient that increased body awareness is normal early in training
Increased sensitivity is minor, but new symptoms may indicate a new illness and need assessment.
Switch the patient to passive relaxation and continue the sessions
Changing techniques without assessment could miss a progressing condition.
Tell the patient to practice longer so the symptom resolves
Longer practice does not address a possible new illness.

alt.q: Early in relaxation training, a patient notices muscle tension more easily than before. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “This increased sensitivity is common at first and usually resolves as you continue.”
alt.ex: Increased sensitivity in detecting tension is usually minor and resolves with continued training.
w: “You should stop the training because it is making your symptoms worse.”
Increased awareness is expected early and is not a reason to stop.
“This means you have a new illness that needs immediate treatment.”
Increased sensitivity is expected; new or intensifying symptoms are what require assessment.
“You are doing the technique wrong, so you need a new technique.”
Detecting tension is part of learning, not a sign of incorrect technique.

items.q: How does meditation differ from relaxation?
items.a: The purpose of meditation is to become mindful and escape destructive patterns of negativity
items.ex: Meditation falls under mindfulness and aims to increase the ability to live freely and escape negative patterns.
w: Meditation requires tightening and relaxing muscle groups in a set order
Tensing muscle groups describes active progressive relaxation.
Meditation uses instruments to give feedback on brain-wave patterns
Instrument feedback describes biofeedback.
Meditation must be led by a certified practitioner in a clinic
Most meditation activities are easy to learn and can be self-directed.

alt.q: Which practices fall under the umbrella of mindfulness meditation?
alt.a: Loving-kindness, mindfulness breathing, and mantras or phrases of focus
alt.ex: Meditation can include compassion or loving-kindness practices, mindfulness breathing, and mantras.
w: Cupping, moxibustion, and tui na massage
These are TCM therapeutic modalities.
Acupressure, reflexology, and chiropractic care
These are body-based methods, not meditation practices.
Probiotics, mycotherapies, and herbal teas
These are biologically based natural products.

Meditation directs attention to a single focus.

Meditation uses relaxed breathing, not forceful breathing.
Electronic monitoring equipment

items.ex: The five features of meditation are a quiet space, comfortable position, receptive attitude, focus of attention, and relaxed breathing.

Use relaxed breathing

A receptive attitude is a feature of meditation.
Memorize a detailed procedure first

Meditation limits stimulus input; a quiet space is needed.
alt.ex: Meditation needs a quiet space, comfortable position, receptive attitude, focus of attention, and relaxed breathing.

Session length needs shortening when hypertension develops.

Forcing meditation ignores acceptance, which is essential for effective outcomes.
Meditation is safe because it has no effect on mental state
Meditation does affect the mind; that is why this patient may resist it.

items.q: Why should the nurse individualize the scenario used in a guided imagery session?
items.a: To ensure the image does not evoke negative memories or feelings for the patient

w: To keep the session shorter than the usual 15 to 20 minutes
Session length relates to meditation, not the reason for individualizing imagery.
To avoid using any senses other than vision during the session
Imagery may use auditory, proprioceptive, gustatory, and olfactory senses.
To make sure the practitioner, not the patient, controls the image
Patients control their images; individualization reflects their preferences.

alt.q: A nurse plans guided imagery with ocean waves, but the patient nearly drowned as a child. What should the nurse do?

alt.ex: Imagery must be individualized so the image does not evoke negative memories or feelings.
w: Continue with the ocean image to help the patient face the fear
Using an image linked to trauma may evoke negative memories.
Cancel imagery and use active progressive relaxation instead
Imagery can still be used with an image the patient finds pleasing.
Use the ocean image but shorten the session to 5 minutes
Shortening the session does not prevent negative memories.

items.ex: Creative visualization uses a clear, pleasing image practiced often, especially before bedtime or on awakening when the mind is relaxed.
w: “I will picture a different scene each time so I don’t get bored with it.”
Patients are taught to frequently visualize the same clear image.
“I will imagine my goals as things that might happen someday in the future.”

“I will only use the image when I am very anxious or in pain.”
Visualization is used during relaxing states and throughout the day.

alt.q: Which teaching strategy for creative visualization helps the patient alleviate doubts about achieving goals?

w: Visualizing the image only once a week
The patient should visualize the image frequently.
Picturing past failures to learn from them
Creative visualization focuses on positive images and desired change.
Avoiding imagery near bedtime or on waking
Bedtime and awakening are the recommended times because the mind is relaxed.

items.q: How does biofeedback help a patient gain control over physiological responses?
items.a: Instruments give immediate feedback about body functions so the patient learns which relaxation behaviors work
items.ex: Biofeedback instruments display physiological information so patients learn self-regulation and which stress-relaxation behaviors work best.
w: Needles inserted along meridians release blocked energy so the patient feels calmer
Needling along meridians describes acupuncture.
The practitioner’s hands redirect the energy field so the body heals on its own
Redirecting the energy field describes therapeutic touch.
Medications are adjusted automatically by the device in response to vital signs
Biofeedback teaches voluntary self-control; it does not adjust medications.

alt.q: A patient using biofeedback hears a tone when the pulse rate rises above the therapeutic zone. What is the purpose of the tone?
alt.a: To make the patient aware so breathing, relaxation, or imagery can be used to gain control
alt.ex: Feedback signals increase awareness of internal processes so the patient can use techniques to gain voluntary control.
w: To alert the nurse that the patient needs an antiarrhythmic
The signal is for the patient’s self-regulation, not a medication alert.
To end the session because the therapy is no longer safe
The tone is feedback to help the patient regulate, not a stop signal.
To show that the device has a technical malfunction
The tone reflects the patient’s physiological change, not device failure.

Bruxism
