Benefits and risks must be clearly and fully disclosed.
Tell patients complementary care is always safer
All therapies carry some risk, especially with conventional therapies.
alt.ex: Nurses fully disclose benefits and risks, include safety precautions, and discuss all options to support informed decisions.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: Before using a complementary therapy in practice, a nurse should understand the state nurse practice act and practice only within its scope.
items.a: True
items.ex: Nurses must understand their state nurse practice act regarding complementary therapies and practice within those laws.
items.ww: Scope of practice is defined by state law, which applies to complementary therapies too.

alt.q: A nurse may perform any complementary therapy once a patient requests it, regardless of the state nurse practice act.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nurses practice complementary therapies only within the scope of their state nurse practice act and training.
alt.ww: Patient requests do not expand a nurse’s legal scope of practice.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: Why are nurses in a unique position to recommend complementary therapies that fit a patient?
items.a: They work closely with patients and become familiar with patients’ spiritual and cultural viewpoints
items.ex: Close relationships help nurses learn patients’ spiritual and cultural views and recommend therapies aligned with these beliefs.
w: They are licensed to prescribe herbal medicines and supplements independently
RNs do not prescribe herbs; their advantage is familiarity with patients’ beliefs.
They are automatically certified in all training-specific therapies
Training-specific therapies require added education and certification.
They spend less time with patients than other providers
Nurses work very closely with patients, which is their advantage.

alt.q: Which statement describes how integrative care fits nursing?
alt.a: It is consistent with nursing’s person-centered, relationship-based legacy focused on whole-person well-being
alt.ex: The integrative approach aligns with nursing’s person-centered, relationship-based focus on whole-person health.
w: It conflicts with nursing’s focus on following provider orders without question
Integrative care matches nursing’s holistic legacy.
It replaces nursing’s focus on evidence with a focus on tradition alone
Integrative nurses use evidence to inform traditional and emerging interventions.
It limits nursing to acute care tasks such as administering medications
Integrative nursing addresses the whole person across settings.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: Which complementary practices does the textbook say many nurses already use?
items.a: Touch, relaxation techniques, imagery, and breathwork
items.ex: Many nurses already practice touch, relaxation, imagery, and breathwork using integrative nursing principles.
w: Acupuncture, cupping, moxibustion, and qi gong
These TCM therapies require specific training and are not routine nursing practice.
Chiropractic manipulation and spinal adjustments
Chiropractic therapy is not applied by nurses.
Homeopathic remedies and naturopathic purgatives
These whole-system therapies are not described as common nursing practices.

alt.q: A nurse uses a calm presence, gentle touch, and slow breathing with an anxious patient before a procedure. How is this practice best described?
alt.a: Integrative nursing using nursing-accessible therapies
alt.ex: Touch, presence, and breathwork are nursing-accessible therapies many nurses use as part of integrative nursing.
w: Alternative therapy that replaces the procedure
These therapies complement the procedure rather than replace it.
Training-specific therapy requiring certification
Breathing, presence, and simple touch are nursing-accessible and need no extra certification.
A whole medical system such as traditional Chinese medicine
These are individual techniques, not a whole medical system.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: A 48-year-old patient with breast cancer is readmitted for a wound infection. She is withdrawn, fears “one hospital visit after another,” and is tired of feeling drowsy from pain medication. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
items.a: Offer guided imagery and relaxation along with her prescribed pain management
items.ex: Imagery and relaxation reduce pain, anxiety, and opioid use and complement, not replace, prescribed analgesia.
w: Stop her pain medication and use complementary therapies instead
Stopping prescribed analgesics makes therapies alternative; the provider manages medication changes.
Begin active progressive relaxation using vigorous muscle tensing
Active progressive relaxation increases fatigue in advanced disease; passive methods fit better.
Refer her for acupuncture and avoid discussing her fears
Avoiding her fears ignores her needs; nursing-accessible therapies can address them now.

alt.q: A patient with cancer fears the future and says, “I just keep imagining things getting worse.” Which nursing-accessible therapy best helps her view the future more positively?
alt.a: Creative visualization with encouraging statements
alt.ex: Creative visualization pictures a desired future and uses encouraging statements, evoking positive emotions and well-being.
w: Electroacupuncture at specific acupoints
Electroacupuncture is training-specific and does not target future-focused thinking.
Active progressive relaxation of all muscles
This targets muscle tension and may tire a patient with cancer.
Biofeedback of her skin temperature
Biofeedback is training-specific and targets physiological control, not future outlook.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: Nurses should encourage open, honest dialogue with patients about their use of complementary therapies.
items.a: True
items.ex: All providers, including nurses, need to encourage open, honest discussion about complementary therapy use.
items.ww: Open dialogue reveals therapies that may interact with conventional care.

alt.q: Nurses should avoid discussing complementary therapies with patients because only physicians can address them.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: All providers, including nurses, need to encourage open, honest dialogue about complementary therapies.
alt.ww: Nurses have a key role in discussing therapies and helping patients make informed decisions.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: A patient asks a nurse to recommend a practitioner for traditional Chinese medicine and acupuncture. Which action is best?
items.a: Refer the patient to a qualified practitioner, such as one listed by the NCCAOM
items.ex: Nurses should know credentialing processes and refer patients to competent providers, such as NCCAOM-certified practitioners.
w: Advise the patient to choose any practitioner advertising online
Advertising does not verify training or credentials.
Perform acupuncture for the patient after reviewing a video
Acupuncture requires specific training and often licensure.
Tell the patient that TCM practitioners are all state regulated
TCM is not regulated in most states, though acupuncture is.

alt.q: Why should a nurse know about credentialing processes for complementary practitioners?
alt.a: To refer patients to competent providers
alt.ex: Knowing credentialing processes lets nurses refer patients to competent providers.
w: To license complementary practitioners in the state
Nurses do not license practitioners; state agencies do.
To perform any therapy without additional training
Training-specific therapies still require added education and certification.
To ensure herbal products have FDA approval
Herbal products are not approved as drugs by the FDA.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: Why does the textbook stress that nurses be knowledgeable about the evidence for different complementary therapies?
items.a: So they can make appropriate recommendations and give accurate information to patients and colleagues
items.ex: Knowing the evidence lets nurses recommend useful therapies and provide accurate information to patients and other professionals.
w: So they can prescribe complementary therapies without a provider’s involvement
Evidence knowledge supports recommendations and teaching, not independent prescribing.
So they can replace conventional treatments that have weaker evidence
Integrative care combines therapies rather than replacing conventional care.
So they can perform training-specific therapies without certification
Training-specific therapies still require additional education and certification.

alt.q: A nurse plans to incorporate a new complementary modality into practice. What should the nurse do first?
alt.a: Become familiar with the evidence for that modality
alt.ex: Nurses should familiarize themselves with the evidence for each modality they incorporate into practice.
w: Use it on all patients to see who responds
Nurses need to know which patients are most likely to benefit before using it.
Wait for patients to request it by name
Nurses actively discuss options; waiting for requests is not the first step.
Teach it to family caregivers before patients
Learning the evidence comes before teaching anyone.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: Which outcome best reflects the goal of integrative care as described in the textbook?
items.a: Preventing disease and improving whole-person well-being with the full spectrum of therapies
items.ex: Providers engage patients in integrative care to prevent disease, manage illness, and improve well-being using all possible therapeutics.
w: Relying solely on surgery and drugs to treat the patient’s underlying disease
Integrative care uses the full spectrum of therapies rather than solely surgery or drugs.
Replacing all prescribed medications with natural products the patient chooses
Replacing conventional care is an alternative approach.
Treating only the physical symptoms of the patient’s chronic condition
Integrative care addresses the whole person, including mind and spirit.

alt.q: A nurse explains integrative care to a patient with chronic disease. Which statement is most accurate?
alt.a: “We will combine conventional treatments with complementary therapies that fit you.”
alt.ex: Integrative care brings conventional and complementary therapies together to support whole-person well-being.
w: “We will stop your medications and use complementary therapy only.”
Stopping conventional treatment is an alternative approach.
“We will rely on surgery and drugs because they have the most evidence.”
Integrative care uses the full spectrum rather than relying solely on surgery or drugs.
“We will use complementary therapies only after all other options fail.”
Complementary therapies are integrated into care, not reserved as a last resort.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: The Joint Commission requires accredited agencies to offer [[nonpharmacological|complementary|nonpharmacologic]] therapy to effectively manage patients’ pain.
items.ex: Joint Commission pain standards require that nonpharmacological (complementary) options be offered for pain management.

alt.q: Accredited agencies must offer [[nonpharmacological|complementary|nonpharmacologic]] therapies for pain under Joint Commission standards.
alt.ex: Joint Commission pain standards require that nonpharmacological (complementary) options be offered for pain management.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: A patient taking several prescribed drugs plans to start an herbal supplement. Which nursing action reflects the integrative nursing role?
items.a: Examine the herb for interactions with the patient’s prescribed and over-the-counter drugs
items.ex: As with any medication, herbs must be checked for interaction and compatibility with other substances being used.
w: Approve the supplement because herbal products are natural
Natural does not mean safe; herbs can interact with drugs.
Tell the patient to stop all prescribed drugs while using the herb
Stopping prescribed drugs is unsafe and would make the herb an alternative therapy.
Ignore the supplement because it is not a medication
Patients may view herbs as foods, but they still need interaction checks.

alt.q: A patient taking digoxin and an antihypertensive wants to try licorice root for gastric ulcers. What is the nurse’s priority concern?
alt.a: Licorice root may interact with digoxin and antihypertensive drugs
alt.ex: Table 32.2 lists digoxin, antihypertensives, and corticosteroids as potential licorice root interactions.
w: Licorice root may interact with antirejection drugs
Antirejection drug interactions are listed for echinacea.
Licorice root may interact with finasteride
Finasteride interactions are listed for saw palmetto.
Licorice root may interact with loop diuretics
Furosemide and loop diuretic interactions are listed for aloe vera.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: Many patients view herbs as teas, powders, or dietary additives rather than as over-the-counter medications.
items.a: True
items.ex: Because patients may not see herbs as medications, nurses must ask about the full complement of therapies.
items.ww: Patients often do not count herbal products as medicines, so they may not report them unless asked.

alt.q: Patients reliably report herbal teas and supplements when asked only about their medications.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients often consider herbs teas or supplements rather than medications, so nurses must ask about them specifically.
alt.ww: Asking only about medications misses herbs that patients do not consider medicines.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: A patient with cancer says, “I want to stop my chemotherapy and just use herbs instead.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Let’s review the benefits and risks of both options so you can make an informed choice.”
items.ex: Nurses discuss the full range of biomedical and complementary options, fully disclosing benefits and risks, so patients make informed decisions.
w: “Herbs are natural, so they are a safe replacement for chemotherapy.”
Natural does not mean safe, and the nurse must disclose risks fully.
“You are not allowed to use any herbs while you are in treatment.”
Integrative care respects patient choice and discusses options rather than forbidding them.
“That is a question for your provider, so I cannot discuss it with you.”
Nurses need enough knowledge to discuss options and encourage open dialogue.

alt.q: Why does a nurse need enough knowledge to discuss both biomedical and complementary options with patients?
alt.a: To help patients make informed health care decisions
alt.ex: Knowledge of the full range of options lets nurses help patients make informed decisions.
w: To persuade patients to choose complementary care over medicine
The nurse informs; the goal is not to steer patients away from conventional care.
To prescribe herbal products in place of medications
RNs do not prescribe herbs to replace medications.
To avoid having to refer patients to other providers
Nurses also refer patients to competent providers when appropriate.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: For the readmitted patient with breast cancer who fears the future and feels drowsy from pain medication, which complementary approaches are appropriate for the nurse to offer? Select all that apply.
o: Guided imagery to reduce pain and anxiety
Imagery helps control pain and reduces stress-related symptoms.
Passive relaxation with slow abdominal breathing
Passive relaxation suits patients with limited energy reserves.
Mindfulness meditation for anxiety and distress
Patients with cancer using mindfulness often have less depression, anxiety, and distress.
Creative visualization of a positive future
Creative visualization of a desired future evokes positive emotions and improves well-being.
Active progressive relaxation with vigorous muscle tensing
This needs moderate energy and increases fatigue in advanced disease.
Chaparral tea for its anticancer effects
Chaparral is an unsafe herb with no proven efficacy and can cause severe liver toxicity.
items.ex: Imagery, passive relaxation, mindfulness, and creative visualization are nursing-accessible therapies suited to a fatigued, anxious patient with cancer.

alt.q: A patient with cancer wants to reduce reliance on sedating pain medication. Which nursing-accessible therapies could the nurse integrate with her prescribed care? Select all that apply.
o: Relaxation combined with imagery
Relaxation with imagery reduces pain, opioid use, and anxiety.
Slow, deep abdominal breathing
Breathing techniques aid in reducing pain and improving comfort.
Music during relaxation sessions
Relaxation with music reduces pain, opioid use, and anxiety.
Electroacupuncture performed by the nurse
Acupuncture is training-specific and not a nursing-accessible therapy.
Stopping all analgesics immediately
Medication changes are made by the health care provider; therapies complement analgesia.
alt.ex: Relaxation, imagery, breathing, and music are nursing-accessible therapies that can reduce pain and opioid use alongside prescribed care.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: After teaching guided imagery to a patient with chronic pain, which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I can use imagery along with my pain medication to help me feel more in control.”
items.ex: Imagery complements prescribed analgesia and helps patients exert control over pain and stress.
w: “I can stop taking my pain medication now that I know imagery.”
Medication changes are made by the provider; imagery complements, not replaces, analgesia.
“I only need to practice imagery once, and it will keep working.”
Imagery requires frequent practice to be effective.
“I should picture my worst hospital experience to face my fears.”
Images should be positive and should not evoke negative memories.

alt.q: A patient asks why the nurse suggests relaxation before a painful dressing change. Which response is best?
alt.a: “Relaxing before the procedure can lower your pain and anxiety during it.”
alt.ex: Nurses use clinical judgment to time relaxation, for example before a painful procedure, to reduce pain and anxiety.
w: “Relaxing will make the procedure unnecessary.”
Relaxation complements care; it does not replace needed procedures.
“Relaxing will replace your need for any pain medicine.”
Relaxation may reduce opioid use but does not automatically replace analgesics.
“Relaxing is only helpful after the procedure is done.”
Relaxation is often best used before a painful procedure or diagnostic test.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: Integrative care encourages using the full spectrum of possible therapeutics rather than relying solely on surgery or drugs.
items.a: True
items.ex: Providers engage patients in integrative care using the full spectrum of therapeutics, not only surgery or drugs.
items.ww: Integrative care adds complementary options to conventional treatment rather than excluding them.

alt.q: Integrative care means relying solely on surgery and drugs, with complementary therapies used only by alternative practitioners.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Integrative care employs the full spectrum of therapeutics, combining conventional and complementary approaches.
alt.ww: Relying solely on surgery or drugs is exactly what integrative care moves beyond.

items.src: Ch 32 · Complementary, alternative, and integrative therapies

items.q: How does the textbook distinguish self-concept from self-esteem?
items.a: Self-concept is how one thinks about oneself; self-esteem is how one feels about oneself
items.ex: Self-concept is a person’s view of self (thoughts), and it directly affects self-esteem (feelings about self).
w: Self-concept is how one feels about oneself; self-esteem is how one thinks about oneself
This reverses the terms; thinking about self is self-concept and feeling about self is self-esteem.
Self-concept is how others view a person; self-esteem is how the person views others
Both terms describe a person’s own view of self, not others’ views.
Self-concept is a conscious judgment only; self-esteem is an unconscious drive only
Self-concept mixes conscious and unconscious thoughts; the terms differ by thinking versus feeling.

alt.q: A patient says, “I see myself as a capable mother, and that makes me feel worthwhile.” Which part of this statement reflects self-esteem?
alt.a: Feeling worthwhile
alt.ex: Self-esteem is how one feels about oneself, so feeling worthwhile reflects self-esteem.
w: Seeing herself as a mother
How she sees herself in a role reflects self-concept and role performance, not self-esteem.
Viewing herself as capable
Viewing or thinking about oneself is self-concept, which then shapes self-esteem.
Naming her parenting role
Identifying a role relates to role performance, a component of self-concept.

items.q: A nursing student asks why nurses must differentiate self-concept from self-esteem. Which statement by the student shows understanding?
items.a: “Separating them lets me assess the patient completely and individualize the plan of care.”
items.ex: The book states nurses differentiate the two so they can correctly and completely assess and plan individualized care.
w: “Separating them is only needed when the patient has a psychiatric diagnosis.”
Understanding self-concept is a necessary part of all nursing care, not only psychiatric care.
“Separating them matters mostly for documentation and billing in the record.”
The purpose is accurate assessment and individualized care, not billing.
“Separating them is unnecessary because both terms mean the same thing.”
The terms are often used interchangeably, but nurses need to differentiate them.

alt.q: Why does the textbook say understanding a patient’s self-concept is necessary?
alt.a: It is a necessary part of all nursing care and supports holistic, high-quality care
alt.ex: Understanding self-concept gives nurses a holistic view that meets each patient’s and family’s self-concept needs.
w: It is needed only for patients admitted to behavioral health units
The book says it is part of all nursing care, not one setting.
It replaces the need for a physical assessment of the patient
Self-concept assessment complements, never replaces, physical assessment.
It is required only when a patient has a visible body change
Many threats to self-concept, such as chronic illness or job loss, are not visible.

items.q: A patient with long-standing heart failure says several things during an assessment. Which statement most suggests that chronic illness is affecting the patient’s identity and body image?
items.a: “I can’t stand to look at myself anymore.”
items.ex: The book gives this statement as an example of chronic illness affecting identity and body image.
w: “I can get through anything.”
This reflects positive thoughts about personal health, which enhance self-concept.
“I’ve never been sick a day in my life.”
This shows positive beliefs about personal health, not a threatened body image.
“I want to learn more about my medicines.”
Seeking information shows engagement, not a disturbance in identity or body image.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient reflects positive thoughts about personal health that enhance self-concept?
alt.a: “I can get through anything.”
alt.ex: A patient’s belief in personal health often enhances self-concept, as this statement shows.
w: “It’s not worth it anymore.”
This reflects a negative perception of health status.
“I’m a burden to my family.”
This is a negative perception that suggests lowered self-esteem.
“I’ll never get any better.”
This verbalization reflects chronic illness affecting identity and body image.

items.q: A hospitalized patient with a poor self-concept cannot decide what to order from the menu and asks the nurse to choose. How should the nurse interpret this behavior?
items.a: Poor self-concept often leaves people feeling out of control and unworthy of care, hindering decisions
items.ex: People with poor self-concept often do not feel in control or worthy of care and have trouble with even simple decisions.
w: The patient is probably confused and needs a full neurological assessment right away
The book links difficulty with simple decisions to poor self-concept, not primarily to neurological change.
The patient is showing trust in the nurse, a sign of a healthy self-concept
Difficulty deciding reflects lack of control linked to poor self-concept, not healthy trust.
The patient has no food preferences, which is expected during most hospital stays
Inability to make simple choices is a cue to a poor self-concept, not an expected norm.

alt.q: Which behavior does the textbook describe as typical of a patient with a poor self-concept?
alt.a: Having difficulty making even simple decisions, such as what to eat
alt.ex: Poor self-concept affects feelings of control and worth, which influences health care decisions.
w: Making health decisions quickly and with strong confidence
Confident decision making reflects a positive self-concept.
Insisting on full control over every aspect of the care plan
Patients with poor self-concept often do not feel in control.
Seeking out more social contact than usual with hospital staff
Poor self-concept is more often linked to withdrawal than to increased contact.

items.q: What does research suggest about how young children rate themselves compared with how they rate other children?
items.a: They rate themselves more highly, suggesting a positively inflated view of self
items.ex: Young children tend to rate themselves above other children, showing an inflated, positive view of self.
w: They rate themselves lower, suggesting an early tendency toward low self-esteem
The book says young children rate themselves more highly, not lower.
They rate themselves the same, suggesting a realistic and balanced view of self
Realistic self-views develop later; young children’s views are inflated.
They cannot rate themselves until adolescence, when abstract thinking begins
Young children do rate themselves, and they do so favorably.

alt.q: A 5-year-old says, “I’m the best runner and the smartest kid in my class.” How should the nurse interpret this statement?
alt.a: It reflects the positively inflated self-view typical of young children
alt.ex: Young children tend to rate themselves more highly than other children, so this is an expected inflated view.
w: It signals a disturbed self-concept that needs referral
An inflated self-rating is expected in young children, not a disturbance.
It shows the child has reached a realistic view of self
Shifts toward realistic self-information occur later and may lower self-esteem.
It means the child is being bullied and is overcompensating
Nothing in this statement points to bullying; inflated self-views are typical.

items.q: According to the textbook, which group’s self-esteem is more strongly and adversely affected by the adolescent experience?
items.a: Females
items.ex: The adolescent experience can adversely affect self-esteem, often more strongly for females than for males.
w: Males
Males often have a better overall self-concept than females during adolescence.
Only children
The book compares the effect by sex, not by sibling status.
Athletes
Group activities such as sports can foster, not lower, adolescent self-esteem.

alt.q: In which domains do adolescent males often have a better self-concept than females?
alt.a: Physical and social domains
alt.ex: Males often have a better overall self-concept than females, particularly in physical and social domains.
w: Academic and verbal domains
The book names the physical and social domains, not academic ones.
Moral and spiritual domains
These domains are not where the book reports a male advantage.
Family and career domains
The book identifies physical and social domains for this difference.

items.q: A 15-year-old girl tells the nurse she feels worthless when her online posts get few responses. How should the nurse interpret this statement?
items.a: Many youths base their self-concept on their popularity and on what others say on social media
items.ex: The book notes many youths rate their self-concept on social media popularity and comments from unknown responders.
w: Social media use has little effect on how adolescents perceive themselves
The book says adolescent social media use greatly affects self-perception and self-esteem.
Her statement reflects the expected positive inflation of self seen in adolescence
Inflated self-ratings describe young children; this statement shows lowered self-worth.
Adolescent girls are less sensitive about popularity than adolescent boys are
During puberty, girls are more sensitive about popularity and how others view them.

alt.q: Which statement about adolescent social media use is supported by the textbook?
alt.a: Its ongoing, somewhat addictive nature greatly affects youths’ self-perception and self-esteem
alt.ex: Adolescent social media use greatly affects the youth’s perception of self, self-esteem, and self-concept.
w: Its effects on self-concept are limited to youths who are bullied online by peers
The book describes broad effects, including ratings based on popularity, not only bullying.
It mainly strengthens self-concept because it widens a youth’s social network
The book stresses that popularity-based self-ratings can harm self-concept.
It affects body image in adults but has little effect on adolescent identity
The book highlights adolescents and youths as strongly affected.

items.q: During adolescence, what becomes a core developmental task influenced by biological and psychosocial changes?
items.a: The search for an enduring sense of self
items.ex: Adolescents search for an enduring sense of self, rethinking earlier self-views and trying new roles and life plans.
w: The search for a lifelong intimate partner
Forming intimate relationships is a task of young adulthood.
The guidance of the next generation
Guiding the next generation reflects generativity in middle adulthood.
The acceptance of one’s life and its meaning
Feeling positive about life’s meaning reflects integrity in older adulthood.

alt.q: Which is an example of a psychosocial change that influences adolescent identity development?
alt.a: New interactions with peers
alt.ex: The book lists new peer interactions and changing parent-adolescent relationships as psychosocial changes.
w: The onset of puberty
Puberty is the book’s example of a biological change, not a psychosocial one.
Changes in body fat distribution
This is a physical change of maturation, not a psychosocial one.
Development of secondary sex characteristics
This is a hormonal, biological change of adolescence.

items.q: A 50-year-old patient who was laid off 3 months ago has stopped seeing friends and seems depressed. What does the nurse recognize as the likely link to self-concept?
items.a: Loss of job identity can diminish the sense of self and alter self-perceptions and self-care
items.ex: Job loss can reduce the sense of self and social motivation and lead to depression as job identity is lost.
w: Job loss in adulthood rarely affects self-concept because adult identity is fixed
The book describes job loss diminishing the sense of self even in adulthood.
Withdrawal after job loss is a normal stage that resolves without assessment
Depression and withdrawal signal an altered self-perception that needs nursing attention.
Job loss mainly affects body image because physical activity usually declines
Job loss primarily threatens identity and self-perception, not body image.

alt.q: Which outcome does the textbook link to losing a job?
alt.a: A diminished sense of self and reduced motivation to be socially active
alt.ex: When people lose a job, their sense of self diminishes, and they may withdraw socially and become depressed.
w: An improved sense of self from having more personal free time
The book links job loss to a diminished, not improved, sense of self.
A stronger job identity as the person searches for new work
People lose their job identity when they lose a job.
Greater self-concept clarity from reassessing career goals
Self-concept clarity is promoted by self-enhancing work opportunities, not job loss.

items.q: What does the textbook identify as a developmental goal of adulthood and older adulthood?
items.a: Establishing a stable sense of self that transcends relationships and situations
items.ex: Adults aim for a stable sense of self that holds across relationships and situations.
w: Establishing a sense of self that depends on approval from close relationships
The goal is a self that transcends relationships, not one dependent on them.
Rethinking the previous sense of self and experimenting with new roles
Experimenting with roles and rethinking the self is typical of adolescence.
Distinguishing the self from the environment through consistent caregiving
This describes the infant task of trust versus mistrust.

alt.q: Which adult shows progress toward the developmental goal of adulthood described in the textbook?
alt.a: A woman whose sense of who she is stays stable across work, family, and friendships
alt.ex: A stable sense of self that transcends relationships and situations is a developmental goal of adulthood.
w: A man whose sense of who he is changes depending on which friends he is with
A self-view that shifts with relationships does not transcend them.
A woman who defines herself mainly by the approval of her co-workers
Basing the self on others’ approval is not a stable, transcendent sense of self.
A man who keeps trying out new life plans to discover who he really is
Experimenting with new roles and life plans describes adolescence.

items.q: Which work experiences predict job satisfaction and promote self-concept clarity and self-esteem, including in older adults?
items.a: Exploring new ideas, solving problems creatively, and learning new skills
items.ex: The book calls these self-enhancing opportunities that predict job satisfaction and commitment.
w: Repeating familiar tasks, avoiding change, and limiting new responsibility
Avoiding new challenges is the opposite of the self-enhancing opportunities described.
Working longer hours, taking extra shifts, and skipping personal time
Overextension relates to role overload, not self-enhancement.
Competing with peers, seeking praise, and comparing pay with others
Social comparison is not among the self-enhancing opportunities the book lists.

alt.q: An older adult volunteer is offered several options. Which choice best fits what the textbook says promotes self-concept clarity and self-esteem?
alt.a: Joining a team that learns new skills to solve problems in creative ways
alt.ex: Learning new skills and solving problems creatively are self-enhancing opportunities that promote self-concept clarity.
w: Doing the same simple filing task each week with no new demands
Unchanging routine tasks do not offer self-enhancing opportunities.
Stepping back from all decisions so others can take the lead
Withdrawing from problem solving does not promote self-concept clarity.
Taking a role chosen mainly for its status rather than its interest
The book emphasizes exploring ideas and learning skills, not status.

items.q: What does the textbook say about the relationship between self-esteem and health?
items.a: Lower self-esteem is a risk factor for health problems; higher self-esteem and strong social ties support good health
items.ex: How people view themselves is closely linked to perceived health, and low self-esteem increases health risk.
w: Higher self-esteem is a risk factor for health problems because it leads to overconfidence about health
The book identifies lower, not higher, self-esteem as the health risk factor.
Self-esteem has little relationship to health; social relationships alone determine health outcomes
The book links both self-esteem and social relationships to health.
Self-esteem affects mental health only and has no effect on physical health or self-care
Self-esteem and self-concept affect physical and emotional self-care.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a community group. Which statement by a participant shows understanding of the link between self-esteem and health?
alt.a: “Low self-esteem can put me at risk for health problems, but good relationships help keep me healthy.”
alt.ex: Lower self-esteem is a risk factor for health problems, whereas higher self-esteem and strong social relationships support health.
w: “High self-esteem is risky because people with it ignore their health problems.”
The book names low, not high, self-esteem as a health risk factor.
“How I feel about myself has nothing to do with how I take care of my body.”
Self-esteem and self-concept affect how people approach self-care.
“Strong relationships matter for health only when self-esteem is already high.”
Strong social relationships support good health in their own right.

items.q: Which variables does the textbook identify as affecting self-concept and self-esteem during adolescence? Select all that apply.
o: School
School is named as a variable affecting adolescent self-concept.
Sports and after-school activities
Group activities such as sports can foster adolescent self-esteem.
Family
Family is among the variables listed for adolescence.
Friends
Friends and peer relationships affect adolescent self-concept.
Menopause
Menopause affects body image in middle-aged and older females, not adolescents.
Retirement
Retirement is a later-life change, not an adolescent variable.
items.ex: Adolescence is a critical period in which school, activities, family, and friends shape self-concept and self-esteem.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing a 14-year-old’s self-concept. Which areas of the teen’s life should the nurse explore because they affect adolescent self-esteem? Select all that apply.
o: Experiences at school
School strongly influences adolescent self-concept.
Participation in sports or clubs
Group activities can foster adolescent self-esteem.
Relationships with friends
Peers and friends affect adolescent self-concept.
Social media use
Adolescent social media use greatly affects self-perception and self-esteem.
Job satisfaction
Job satisfaction is linked to self-esteem in adulthood, not early adolescence.
Loss of a spouse
Spousal loss is a self-esteem stressor of older adulthood.
alt.ex: School, activities, friends, family, and social media all shape self-concept and self-esteem in adolescence.

items.q: Which patient statements reflect negative perceptions about health that suggest a threatened self-concept? Select all that apply.
o: “It’s not worth it anymore.”
The book gives this as a negative perception of health status.
“I’m a burden to my family.”
This statement reflects a negative view of health and self-worth.
“I’ll never get any better.”
This verbalization shows chronic illness affecting identity and body image.
“I can get through anything.”
This reflects positive thoughts about personal health.
“I’ve never been sick a day in my life.”
This shows a positive belief about personal health.
items.ex: Statements of hopelessness or being a burden signal negative health perceptions affecting self-concept.

alt.q: A nurse is screening patients with chronic illness. Which statements should the nurse recognize as positive beliefs about personal health? Select all that apply.
o: “I can get through anything.”
A belief in personal health like this often enhances self-concept.
“I’ve never been sick a day in my life.”
This reflects positive thoughts about personal health.
“I’m a burden to my family.”
This is a negative perception of health status.
“I can’t stand to look at myself anymore.”
This reflects chronic illness affecting body image and identity.
“It’s not worth it anymore.”
This reflects a negative perception of health status.
alt.ex: Positive statements about personal health suggest an enhanced self-concept; hopeless statements suggest a threatened one.

items.q: How can chronic illness affect a person’s self-concept, according to the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: It can affect the ability to provide financial support
Chronic illness often affects financial support, which then affects self-esteem.
It can affect the ability to maintain relationships
Strained relationships from chronic illness affect self-esteem and roles.
It can alter perceived identity and roles
The book links chronic illness to changes in perceived identity and roles.
It can affect body image
Chronic illness affects identity and body image.
It usually strengthens self-esteem through added sick-role support
The book describes chronic illness as a threat to, not a boost for, self-esteem.
It affects self-concept only when the illness is visible to others
Effects on roles, finances, and identity occur whether or not illness is visible.
items.ex: Chronic illness affects finances, relationships, roles, identity, and body image, which then affect self-esteem.

alt.q: A patient with advancing kidney disease can no longer work full-time. Which effects on self-concept should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Lowered self-esteem from reduced ability to provide financial support
Loss of financial support affects self-esteem.
Changes in the patient’s perceived roles and identity
Chronic illness alters perceived identity and roles.
Strain on the patient’s ability to maintain relationships
Chronic illness often affects maintaining relationships.
Improved self-concept clarity from having fewer responsibilities
Reduced role ability usually threatens, not clarifies, self-concept.
No change in self-concept because the illness is internal
Internal chronic illnesses still alter roles, identity, and self-esteem.
alt.ex: Chronic illness can lower self-esteem by affecting finances, relationships, roles, and identity.

items.q: Because the terms are often used interchangeably, nurses do not need to distinguish self-concept from self-esteem when assessing a patient.
items.a: False
items.ex: Nurses must differentiate self-concept and self-esteem to assess patients completely and individualize care.
items.ww: The book directly states the two must be differentiated despite common interchangeable use.

alt.q: Self-concept, or how a person thinks about oneself, directly affects self-esteem, or how a person feels about oneself.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The book describes self-concept as directly affecting self-esteem.
alt.ww: Self-esteem is not independent of self-concept; thoughts about self shape feelings about self.

items.q: Research suggests that self-concept clarity can be transmitted from parents to their children.
items.a: True
items.ex: Parents influence self-concept development, and research suggests self-concept clarity passes from parents to children.
items.ww: The book reports parental transmission of self-concept clarity, so parents do play a role.

alt.q: Self-concept and self-esteem are fully formed in early childhood and do not continue to develop across the life span.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Self-concept and self-esteem begin developing young and continue to develop across the life span.
alt.ww: The book describes development continuing through adolescence, adulthood, and older age.

items.q: In adolescents and females in particular, culture, class, and self-esteem serve as protective factors against risk-taking behaviors such as unhealthy sexual behaviors.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book identifies culture, class, and self-esteem as protective factors against adolescent risk taking.
items.ww: These factors protect against risk taking; they do not increase it.

alt.q: In adolescent females, higher self-esteem is a risk factor that increases unhealthy sexual behaviors.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Self-esteem protects against risk-taking behaviors; low self-esteem is linked to risky behavior.
alt.ww: The book lists self-esteem as protective against unhealthy sexual behaviors.

items.q: [[Self-concept]] is an individual’s subjective view of self, involving a complex mixture of conscious and unconscious thoughts, attitudes, and perceptions.
items.ex: Self-concept is how one thinks about oneself; it shapes self-esteem and health behaviors.

alt.q: How a person thinks about oneself, called [[self-concept]], is subjective and includes both conscious and unconscious thoughts.
alt.ex: Self-concept is how one thinks about oneself; it shapes self-esteem and health behaviors.

items.q: Self-concept, or how one thinks about oneself, directly affects [[self-esteem]], or how one feels about oneself.
items.ex: Self-esteem is the feeling component that follows from self-concept.

alt.q: How a person feels about oneself is called [[self-esteem]], and it is directly affected by self-concept.
alt.ex: Self-esteem is the feeling component that follows from self-concept.

mt.q: Match each of Erikson’s stages with the age range given in Box 33.1.
mt.ex: Box 33.1 links each developmental stage to an age range and specific self-concept tasks.

items.q: Which self-concept task belongs to the stage of autonomy versus shame and doubt?
items.a: Begins to communicate likes and dislikes
items.ex: Toddlers (18 months to 3 years) begin expressing likes and dislikes and show independence.
w: Is highly imaginative and identifies with a gender
These are tasks of initiative versus guilt (3 to 5 years).
Incorporates feedback from peers and teachers
This is a task of industry versus inferiority (6 to 12 years).
Accepts body changes and maturation
This is a task of identity versus role confusion (12 to 19 years).

alt.q: A 4-year-old is highly imaginative, identifies with a gender, and is learning to name feelings. Which stage is the child working through?
alt.a: Initiative versus guilt
alt.ex: Initiative versus guilt (3 to 5 years) includes imagination, gender identification, and growing language for feelings.
w: Autonomy versus shame and doubt
This stage (18 months to 3 years) focuses on likes, dislikes, and self-control.
Industry versus inferiority
This stage (6 to 12 years) focuses on skill mastery and feedback.
Trust versus mistrust
This infant stage focuses on trusting caregivers and distinguishing self from environment.

items.q: A 9-year-old is hospitalized for several weeks and is missing school. Which nursing approach best supports the child’s self-concept for this developmental stage?
items.a: Provide chances to master new skills, such as schoolwork, and give positive feedback
items.ex: In industry versus inferiority, self-esteem increases with new skill mastery and feedback from others.
w: Provide consistent caregivers so the child learns to trust others
Trust through consistent caregiving is the infant task.
Encourage the child to explore future goals and personal values
Establishing goals and values is the adolescent identity task.
Encourage the child to reflect on a legacy for the next generation
Providing a legacy is a task of integrity versus despair.

alt.q: Which developmental task does the textbook list for industry versus inferiority (6 to 12 years)?
alt.a: Increases self-esteem with new skill mastery, such as reading and sports
alt.ex: School-age children build self-esteem by mastering skills and become aware of strengths and limitations.
w: Develops trust following consistency in caregiving and nurturing
This is the task of trust versus mistrust in infancy.
Examines attitudes, values, and beliefs and sets future goals
This is a task of identity versus role confusion in adolescence.
Reassesses life goals and shows contentment with aging
These are tasks of generativity versus self-absorption.

items.q: According to Box 33.1, what helps an infant develop trust?
items.a: Consistency in caregiving and nurturing interactions
items.ex: Infants develop trust following consistent caregiving and nurturing interactions.
w: Early opportunities to choose clothing and food
Choosing and expressing likes belongs to the toddler’s autonomy stage.
Feedback on new skills from peers and teachers
Peer and teacher feedback is part of the school-age industry stage.
Exposure to many different caregivers each day
Trust grows from consistency, not from frequently changing caregivers.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a 6-month-old infant whose parents cannot stay at the hospital. Which plan best supports the infant’s developing sense of self?
alt.a: Assign the same nurses whenever possible to give consistent, nurturing care
alt.ex: Trust develops through consistency in caregiving and nurturing interactions.
w: Rotate many staff members so the infant adapts to new faces
Changing caregivers works against the consistency needed for trust.
Encourage the infant to feed independently to build self-control
Self-control and independence are toddler tasks of autonomy.
Offer imaginative play to help the infant identify feelings
Imagination and naming feelings are preschool initiative tasks.

items.q: Which self-concept task does Box 33.1 list for intimacy versus isolation (young adult to mid-40s)?
items.a: Has stable, positive feelings about self and makes successful role transitions
items.ex: Young adults show stable, positive self-feelings and successful role transitions with increased responsibility.
w: Accepts changes in appearance and physical endurance with aging
This belongs to generativity versus self-absorption.
Feels positive about life and its meaning and plans a legacy
These tasks belong to integrity versus despair.
Examines attitudes and beliefs and accepts maturational body changes
These are tasks of identity versus role confusion.

alt.q: A 30-year-old has taken on a new job and become a parent and reports feeling confident and positive about these changes. Which stage’s tasks is this person achieving?
alt.a: Intimacy versus isolation
alt.ex: Stable positive feelings and successful role transitions with more responsibility mark intimacy versus isolation.
w: Identity versus role confusion
This adolescent stage focuses on body changes, values, and future goals.
Generativity versus self-absorption
This mid-40s to mid-60s stage focuses on accepting aging and reassessing goals.
Industry versus inferiority
This school-age stage focuses on skill mastery and feedback.

items.q: A 55-year-old tells the nurse, “I’m slowing down and getting gray, but I’ve set new goals and I’m content with getting older.” Which stage does this reflect?
items.a: Generativity versus self-absorption
items.ex: Accepting changes in appearance and endurance, reassessing goals, and contentment with aging mark generativity.
w: Integrity versus despair
This stage (mid-late 60s to death) focuses on life’s meaning and leaving a legacy.
Intimacy versus isolation
This stage focuses on stable self-feelings and role transitions in young adulthood.
Identity versus role confusion
This adolescent stage focuses on maturation and establishing values and goals.

alt.q: Which task does Box 33.1 list for generativity versus self-absorption (mid-40s to mid-60s)?
alt.a: Able to accept changes in appearance and physical endurance
alt.ex: Middle adults accept changes in appearance and endurance, reassess goals, and show contentment with aging.
w: Interested in providing a legacy for the next generation
Providing a legacy is listed under integrity versus despair.
Feels positive about an expanded sense of self
This is a task of identity versus role confusion.
Distinguishes self from the environment
This is a task of trust versus mistrust in infancy.

items.q: A 78-year-old patient spends time telling the nurse about wanting to leave family stories for the grandchildren. Which stage task does this reflect?
items.a: Integrity versus despair: interest in providing a legacy for the next generation
items.ex: Older adults in integrity versus despair feel positive about life’s meaning and want to leave a legacy.
w: Generativity versus self-absorption: reassessing life goals in midlife
Reassessing goals is a midlife task; legacy is listed under integrity.
Intimacy versus isolation: affiliation and successful role transitions
This young adult stage focuses on stable self-feelings and roles.
Identity versus role confusion: establishing goals for the future
Setting future goals is an adolescent identity task.

alt.q: Which tasks does Box 33.1 list for integrity versus despair?
alt.a: Feels positive about life and its meaning and wants to leave a legacy
alt.ex: Integrity versus despair (mid-late 60s to death) involves positive feelings about life and interest in a legacy.
w: Accepts changes in appearance and endurance and reassesses goals
These tasks belong to generativity versus self-absorption.
Has stable, positive feelings about self and handles role transitions
These tasks belong to intimacy versus isolation.
Engages in tasks and incorporates feedback from peers and teachers
These tasks belong to industry versus inferiority.

items.q: According to the textbook, at what ages does self-esteem usually peak?
items.a: Between 60 and 70 years
items.ex: Self-esteem rises through young and middle adulthood and peaks between 60 and 70 years of age.
w: Between 12 and 19 years
Self-esteem fluctuates or remains constant in adolescence rather than peaking.
Between 20 and 30 years
Self-esteem strongly increases in young adulthood but continues rising afterward.
Between 80 and 90 years
Self-esteem diminishes or stays constant in old age, with a sharp decline in very old age.

alt.q: How does self-esteem usually change in very old age?
alt.a: It declines sharply
alt.ex: After peaking at 60 to 70 years, self-esteem diminishes or stays constant, then declines sharply in very old age.
w: It peaks for the first time
Self-esteem peaks earlier, between 60 and 70 years of age.
It strongly increases
Strong increases occur in young adulthood, not very old age.
It fluctuates widely
Fluctuation is described for adolescence, not very old age.

items.q: Why do children often report high self-esteem that later declines periodically?
items.a: Their sense of self is inflated by very positive sources, and declines reflect shifts to more realistic self-information
items.ex: Positive sources inflate children’s self-esteem, and periodic declines may reflect a more realistic view of self.
w: Their sense of self is accurate early on, and declines reflect a loss of parental love as they age
The book explains declines as shifts toward realism, not loss of parental love.
Their sense of self is low at birth, and reported high scores reflect a desire to please adults
Children’s self-views are inflated by positive sources, not low and masked.
Their sense of self depends on peers only, and declines reflect the start of school bullying
The book attributes declines to more realistic self-information, not bullying.

alt.q: A parent worries that a 10-year-old who used to say “I’m the best at everything” now says, “I’m good at reading but not at sports.” Which explanation by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “This often reflects a shift to a more realistic view of self, which is expected.”
alt.ex: Periodic declines in childhood self-esteem may be associated with shifts to more realistic information about the self.
w: “This shows your child has a disturbed self-concept that needs counseling.”
A more realistic self-view is an expected developmental shift, not a disturbance.
“This means your child has stopped trusting the adults in the family.”
Trust is an infant task; this change reflects realism about abilities.
“This is a sign of early depression that will worsen in adolescence.”
The book describes such declines as a normal move toward realism.

items.q: Based on Erikson’s stages, what does the textbook say a decline in self-concept in later adulthood reflects?
items.a: A diminished need for self-promotion and a shift to a more modest, balanced view of self
items.ex: Erikson’s view links later-life decline to less need for self-promotion and a more modest, balanced self-view.
w: A failure to master the tasks of generativity and an inability to guide others
The book does not attribute later-life decline to failed generativity.
A return to the inflated self-view of early childhood and a loss of realism
Later-life change is toward a modest view, not an inflated one.
A sign that self-concept clarity is always lost with normal aging
Older adults with self-concept clarity demonstrate psychological well-being.

alt.q: What explains the increase in self-esteem and self-concept in middle adulthood, according to Erikson’s theory?
alt.a: Being productive and creative at work while guiding the next generation
alt.ex: Erikson’s generativity stage explains rising self-esteem through productivity and guiding the next generation.
w: Searching for an enduring sense of self through new roles
Searching for an enduring self is the adolescent task.
Receiving consistent, nurturing care from trusted caregivers
Consistent caregiving builds trust in infancy.
Experiencing praise for mastering reading and sports
Skill mastery and feedback build self-esteem in school age.

items.q: An 82-year-old patient’s declining health has reduced independence and self-esteem. On what should nursing interventions focus, according to the textbook?
items.a: Health behavior changes that promote self-care and self-concept
items.ex: When aging brings health deterioration, interventions must focus on health behavior changes to promote self-care and self-concept.
w: Taking over self-care so the patient can conserve energy
Doing tasks for the patient undermines self-care and independence.
Accepting that self-concept always fails in very old age
Older adults with self-concept clarity show psychological well-being.
Limiting discussion of losses to avoid lowering mood
Losses of friends, function, and independence relate to declining self-esteem and need attention.

alt.q: Which factors does the textbook closely relate to the decline in self-esteem in very old age?
alt.a: Loss of friends and loved ones, functional status, and independence
alt.ex: The decline in self-esteem in old age is closely related to losses of friends, function, and independence.
w: Loss of popularity on social media and peer approval
Social media popularity is linked to adolescent self-concept.
Harsh criticism, inconsistent discipline, and sibling rivalry
These are self-esteem stressors in children.
Role ambiguity from changing jobs and specialized workplaces
Role ambiguity in organizations is an adult employment stressor.

items.q: During a crisis, an adult patient begins behaving in ways typical of an earlier developmental stage. Why is it important for the nurse to recognize this regression?
items.a: It allows the nurse to individualize care and choose appropriate interventions
items.ex: Recognizing developmental challenges or regression lets the nurse individualize care and select interventions.
w: It confirms the patient has a permanent developmental disorder
Regression during a crisis does not by itself indicate a permanent disorder.
It shows the patient should be cared for as a child from now on
The aim is individualized care, not treating the adult as a child.
It means the patient can skip the tasks of the current stage
Each stage builds on the previous one; tasks are not skipped.

alt.q: What does the textbook say nurses should learn to recognize when assessing a patient’s developmental stage?
alt.a: Challenges in achieving an age-appropriate stage or regression to an earlier stage in crisis
alt.ex: Recognizing developmental challenges and crisis regression helps individualize care and determine interventions.
w: The exact age at which every patient will complete each stage
The book stresses individual challenges, not fixed completion ages.
Which stage a patient can permanently skip under stress
Stages build on each other; the concern is regression, not skipping.
The single factor that fully determines a patient’s self-concept
Self-concept is influenced by many factors and is always changing.

items.q: Which factors does the textbook list as bases on which self-concept can change? Select all that apply.
o: Sense of competency
Competency is listed as a factor in self-concept.
Perceived reactions of others to one’s body
Others’ perceived reactions to the body shape self-concept.
Socioeconomic status
Socioeconomic status is among the listed factors.
Cultural identity
Cultural identity is a listed factor influencing self-concept.
Blood type and genetic markers
Biological markers like blood type are not among the listed factors.
Favorite foods and leisure hobbies
Food and hobby preferences are not among the listed factors.
items.ex: Self-concept is always changing and draws on competency, others’ reactions, relationships, status, mastery, and culture.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing what shapes an adult patient’s self-concept. Which factors from the textbook’s list should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.
o: Personal and professional relationships
Relationships are listed as a basis for self-concept.
Academic and employment-related identity
Academic and job identity are listed factors.
Mastery of prior and new experiences
Mastery of experiences is a listed factor.
Perceptions of events that have an impact on self
Perceptions of impactful events are listed.
Number of hospital admissions in the past year
Admission counts are not among the listed factors.
alt.ex: Relationships, academic and job identity, mastery of experiences, and perceptions of events all shape self-concept.

items.q: Which tasks does Box 33.1 list for identity versus role confusion (12 to 19 years)? Select all that apply.
o: Accepts body changes and maturation
Adolescents work to accept maturational body changes.
Examines attitudes, values, and beliefs
Examining values and beliefs is an adolescent identity task.
Establishes goals for the future
Setting future goals is part of this stage.
Feels positive about an expanded sense of self
A positive expanded sense of self is listed for adolescence.
Shows contentment with aging
Contentment with aging belongs to generativity versus self-absorption.
Distinguishes self from environment
This is an infant task of trust versus mistrust.
items.ex: Adolescents accept body changes, sexual maturity, examine values, set goals, and expand their sense of self.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a 16-year-old. Which behaviors show the teen is meeting identity versus role confusion tasks? Select all that apply.
o: Talking about career goals after graduation
Establishing future goals is an adolescent identity task.
Questioning and examining family beliefs and values
Examining attitudes, values, and beliefs is part of this stage.
Accepting growth and body changes of puberty
Accepting body changes and maturation is listed.
Wanting to leave a legacy for younger relatives
Providing a legacy is a task of integrity versus despair.
Reassessing life goals after a long career
Reassessing life goals belongs to generativity in midlife.
alt.ex: Setting goals, examining values, and accepting body changes reflect adolescent identity tasks.

items.q: Which statements describe the usual pattern of self-esteem across the life span? Select all that apply.
o: It usually increases in early and middle childhood
Self-esteem usually rises in early and middle childhood.
It fluctuates or remains constant in adolescence
Adolescent self-esteem fluctuates or stays constant.
It strongly increases in young adulthood
Young adulthood brings a strong increase in self-esteem.
It peaks during adolescence and then slowly declines
Self-esteem peaks between 60 and 70 years, not in adolescence.
It declines steadily from young adulthood onward
Self-esteem continues to increase in middle adulthood.
items.ex: Self-esteem rises in childhood, varies in adolescence, rises in adulthood, peaks at 60 to 70, then declines in very old age.

alt.q: Which statements about self-esteem in adulthood and older age are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It continues to increase in middle adulthood
Self-esteem keeps rising through middle adulthood.
It peaks between 60 and 70 years of age
The peak occurs between 60 and 70 years.
It declines sharply in very old age
Very old age brings a sharp decline.
It is highest in young adulthood and lowest in middle age
Self-esteem keeps increasing through middle adulthood.
It never changes after age 40
Self-esteem continues to change, peaking at 60 to 70 and later declining.
alt.ex: Adult self-esteem rises through middle age, peaks at 60 to 70 years, and declines sharply in very old age.

items.q: In Erikson’s theory, each developmental stage builds on the tasks of the previous stage, and successful mastery of each stage leads to a solid sense of self.
items.a: True
items.ex: Box 33.1 is based on this principle: stages build on each other and mastery leads to a solid self.
items.ww: Stages are not independent; earlier mastery supports later development.

alt.q: In Erikson’s theory, each stage is independent, so difficulty with an earlier stage does not affect later stages.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Each stage builds on the previous one, so earlier difficulties affect later development.
alt.ww: The book states that stages build on previous tasks rather than standing alone.

items.q: Although it varies, the general life-span pattern of self-esteem holds true across gender, socioeconomic status, and culture.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states the pattern generally holds across gender, socioeconomic status, and culture.
items.ww: The pattern is described as broadly consistent, not limited to one group.

alt.q: The life-span pattern of self-esteem applies mainly to one gender and does not hold across cultures or socioeconomic groups.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The pattern varies but generally holds across gender, socioeconomic status, and culture.
alt.ww: The book describes the pattern as generally consistent across these groups.

items.q: Self-concept is always changing and continues to develop throughout life.
items.a: True
items.ex: The development of self-concept is a complex lifelong process, and self-concept is always changing.
items.ww: Self-concept is not fixed; it responds to competency, relationships, events, and culture.

alt.q: Once a person completes adolescence, self-concept becomes fixed and no longer changes.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Self-concept development is a lifelong process and is always changing.
alt.ww: Adults continue to change self-concept through role transitions, aging, and life events.

items.q: Erikson’s emphasis on the [[generativity]] stage explains the increase in self-esteem and self-concept in adulthood.
items.ex: In generativity, adults are productive and creative at work while guiding the next generation.

alt.q: Being productive at work while guiding the next generation reflects Erikson’s [[generativity]] stage, which explains rising adult self-esteem.
alt.ex: In generativity, adults are productive and creative at work while guiding the next generation.

sections.name: Components and interrelated terms of self-concept

items.q: What are the three components of self-concept identified in the textbook?
items.a: Identity, body image, and role performance
items.ex: The book names identity, body image, and role performance as the components of self-concept.
w: Identity, self-esteem, and sick role
Self-esteem is an interrelated term and sick role is a role concept, not a component.
Body image, ideal self, and role strain
Ideal self and role strain are related terms, not the three components.
Role performance, culture, and self-worth
Culture influences self-concept but is not one of the three components.

alt.q: A nurse assesses a patient’s sense of individuality, feelings about appearance, and ability to fulfill roles. Which concept is the nurse assessing?
alt.a: Self-concept
alt.ex: Identity, body image, and role performance together make up self-concept.
w: Sick role
The sick role is society’s expectations of how an ill person behaves.
Role overload
Role overload is having more roles or responsibilities than are manageable.
Ideal self
The ideal self is the aspirations and standards a person strives to attain.

items.q: What does Identity mean?
items.a: Internal sense of individuality, wholeness, and consistency over time
items.ex: Identity, body image, and role performance are the components; self-esteem is the closely related feeling about self.
w: Attitudes related to physical appearance, structure, or function
That goes with Body image.
How people perceive their ability to conduct significant roles
That goes with Role performance.
An individual’s perception and acceptance of the self
That goes with Self-esteem.

alt.q: What does Body image mean?
alt.a: Attitudes related to physical appearance, structure, or function
alt.ex: Identity, body image, and role performance are the components; self-esteem is the closely related feeling about self.
w: Internal sense of individuality, wholeness, and consistency over time
That goes with Identity.
How people perceive their ability to conduct significant roles
That goes with Role performance.
An individual’s perception and acceptance of the self
That goes with Self-esteem.

alt.q: What does Role performance mean?
alt.a: How people perceive their ability to conduct significant roles
alt.ex: Identity, body image, and role performance are the components; self-esteem is the closely related feeling about self.
w: Internal sense of individuality, wholeness, and consistency over time
That goes with Identity.
Attitudes related to physical appearance, structure, or function
That goes with Body image.
An individual’s perception and acceptance of the self
That goes with Self-esteem.

alt.q: What does Self-esteem mean?
alt.a: An individual’s perception and acceptance of the self
alt.ex: Identity, body image, and role performance are the components; self-esteem is the closely related feeling about self.
w: Internal sense of individuality, wholeness, and consistency over time
That goes with Identity.
Attitudes related to physical appearance, structure, or function
That goes with Body image.
How people perceive their ability to conduct significant roles
That goes with Role performance.

alt.q: Which term means “Internal sense of individuality, wholeness, and consistency over time”?
alt.a: Identity
alt.ex: Identity, body image, and role performance are the components; self-esteem is the closely related feeling about self.
w: Body image
Body image: Attitudes related to physical appearance, structure, or function.
Role performance
Role performance: How people perceive their ability to conduct significant roles.
Self-esteem
Self-esteem: An individual’s perception and acceptance of the self.

alt.q: Which term means “Attitudes related to physical appearance, structure, or function”?
alt.a: Body image
alt.ex: Identity, body image, and role performance are the components; self-esteem is the closely related feeling about self.
w: Identity
Identity: Internal sense of individuality, wholeness, and consistency over time.
Role performance
Role performance: How people perceive their ability to conduct significant roles.
Self-esteem
Self-esteem: An individual’s perception and acceptance of the self.

alt.q: Which term means “How people perceive their ability to conduct significant roles”?
alt.a: Role performance
alt.ex: Identity, body image, and role performance are the components; self-esteem is the closely related feeling about self.
w: Identity
Identity: Internal sense of individuality, wholeness, and consistency over time.
Body image
Body image: Attitudes related to physical appearance, structure, or function.
Self-esteem
Self-esteem: An individual’s perception and acceptance of the self.

alt.q: Which term means “An individual’s perception and acceptance of the self”?
alt.a: Self-esteem
alt.ex: Identity, body image, and role performance are the components; self-esteem is the closely related feeling about self.
w: Identity
Identity: Internal sense of individuality, wholeness, and consistency over time.
Body image
Body image: Attitudes related to physical appearance, structure, or function.
Role performance
Role performance: How people perceive their ability to conduct significant roles.

mt.q: Match each self-concept term with its description.
pairs: Internal sense of individuality, wholeness, and consistency over time
Attitudes related to physical appearance, structure, or function
How people perceive their ability to conduct significant roles
An individual’s perception and acceptance of the self
mt.ex: Identity, body image, and role performance are the components; self-esteem is the closely related feeling about self.

items.q: According to the textbook, how does a child first form an identity?
items.a: By identifying first with parenting figures and later with role models such as teachers or peers
items.ex: Children learn values and roles through identification and modeling, starting with parents and then others.
w: By identifying first with peers and later with parenting figures and teachers
The order is reversed; parenting figures come first.
By forming a fixed identity at birth that later role models do not change
Identity develops through identification and modeling over time.
By relying only on self-observation without input from what others say
Children gain identity from self-observation and from what others tell them.

alt.q: To form an identity, what must a child be able to do?
alt.a: Bring learned behaviors and expectations together into a coherent, consistent, unique whole
alt.ex: Identity formation requires integrating learned behaviors and expectations into a coherent, unique whole.
w: Copy the behaviors of one role model exactly without changes
Identity is a unique whole, not an exact copy of one model.
Separate learned behaviors from others’ expectations entirely
Identity integrates behaviors and expectations rather than separating them.
Reject the values of parenting figures to become independent
Children first identify with parenting figures as part of identity.

items.q: How does the textbook distinguish gender identity from gender role?
items.a: Gender identity is a private view of maleness or femaleness; gender role is the masculine or feminine behavior exhibited
items.ex: Gender identity is internal, whereas gender role is the outward behavior; both depend on cultural values.
w: Gender identity is the masculine or feminine behavior exhibited; gender role is a private view of oneself
This reverses the definitions.
Gender identity is assigned at birth by others; gender role is chosen freely without cultural influence
Both depend on culturally determined values; neither is free of culture.
Gender identity and gender role are the same thing and depend only on physical sexual characteristics
The book defines them separately and ties both to culture.

alt.q: A patient describes a private sense of being male or female. Which term describes this?
alt.a: Gender identity
alt.ex: Gender identity is a person’s private view of maleness or femaleness.
w: Gender role
Gender role is the masculine or feminine behavior a person exhibits.
Body image
Body image involves attitudes about appearance, structure, and function.
Role performance
Role performance is how a person perceives the ability to carry out significant roles.

items.q: How does the focus of sexuality, as part of identity, change as an adult ages?
items.a: It shifts from procreation to companionship, intimacy, and pleasure seeking
items.ex: Sexuality is part of identity, and its focus shifts with age from procreation toward companionship and intimacy.
w: It shifts from companionship to procreation and family building
The direction is reversed; the shift is away from procreation.
It disappears as part of identity after middle adulthood
Sexuality remains part of identity; only its focus changes.
It stays focused on procreation throughout the life span
The book describes a change in focus as an adult ages.

alt.q: Why is achieving identity necessary for developing intimate relationships?
alt.a: Individuals express identity in their relationships with others
alt.ex: People express identity in relationships with peers, colleagues, and social groups, so identity precedes intimacy.
w: Intimate relationships replace the need for a personal identity
Relationships express identity; they do not replace it.
Identity forms only after an intimate relationship is established
Identity achievement is needed first for intimate relationships.
Identity limits relationships to people from the same culture
The book does not restrict relationships by culture.

items.q: A nurse is completing a social history for a 13-year-old. According to Box 33.2, which action is a priority?
items.a: Assess the teen’s coping, conflict resolution, and stress management related to social media and texting
items.ex: Box 33.2 names assessment of coping, conflict resolution, and stress management with social media and texting as a priority.
w: Advise the parents to remove all electronic devices from the home to prevent bullying
The book prioritizes assessment of coping, not removing devices.
Document the teen’s cultural group and avoid discussing cultural practices further
Nurses should keep an open, nonrestrictive attitude toward cultural practices.
Focus the history on physical growth because self-concept is assessed in adulthood
Self-concept assessment is important in children and adolescents too.

alt.q: Why does the textbook stress assessing youth about electronic bullying?
alt.a: Electronic bullying threatens young people’s self-concept and is increasing, especially among youth of color
alt.ex: Bullying, including cyberbullying, threatens self-concept and well-being, and it is increasing nationwide.
w: Electronic bullying has decreased nationwide, so it is now rare among adolescents
The book says electronic bullying is increasing.
Electronic bullying affects only adults in the workplace, not youth
The book describes it as a type of youth violence.
Electronic bullying mainly affects physical health and rarely self-concept
Bullying threatens a young person’s self-concept and well-being.

items.q: During an assessment, the nurse notes several findings in a 15-year-old. Which finding is most important to address as a self-concept concern?
items.a: Healed and fresh cuts on the forearms
items.ex: Self-harm such as cutting can indicate self-concept and self-esteem issues that warrant nursing intervention.
w: Concern about mild facial acne
Concern about appearance is common in adolescence and is less urgent than self-harm.
Preference for time with peers
Peer involvement is expected in adolescence and can foster self-esteem.
Interest in a new sport team
Group activities such as sports can foster adolescent self-esteem.

alt.q: An adolescent female who is at a healthy weight repeatedly describes herself as fat. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
alt.a: It suggests a distorted body image that can signal an eating disorder
alt.ex: A distorted view of oneself as fat can signal an eating disorder and warrants further assessment.
w: It is a normal comparison that needs no follow-up
The book identifies this distortion as a possible sign of an eating disorder.
It reflects an accurate body image for her age
Seeing herself as fat at a healthy weight is a distortion, not accuracy.
