It is caused only by situational loss of a body part
Eating disorders have deep psychological origins, not situational body part loss.

items.q: Which statement about body image distortions is supported by the textbook?
items.a: Some have deep psychological origins, such as anorexia nervosa; others result from situational events like losing a body part
items.ex: The book contrasts distortions with psychological origins with those caused by situational events such as body part loss.
w: All result from situational events, such as surgery, and none have psychological origins
Some distortions, such as anorexia nervosa, have deep psychological origins.
All have deep psychological origins, and situational events rarely affect body image
Situational events such as body part loss also alter body image.
They occur only in adolescents and are uncommon in adults with health changes
Adults often exaggerate body image disturbances when health status changes.

alt.q: What does the textbook say about how people react to body image when their health status changes?
alt.a: They often exaggerate disturbances in body image
alt.ex: Individuals often exaggerate body image disturbances when a change in health status occurs.
w: They usually minimize body image changes
The book says people tend to exaggerate, not minimize, disturbances.
They rarely notice any body image change
Most people already have some body dissatisfaction, and health changes heighten it.
They ignore feedback from others about the body
The way others view a person’s body and their feedback are influential.

items.q: Which aspect of self-concept do normal developmental changes such as puberty and aging affect most visibly?
items.a: Body image
items.ex: Puberty and aging have a more apparent effect on body image than on other aspects of self-concept.
w: Identity
Identity is affected, but the book says body image shows the more apparent effect.
Role performance
Role performance changes with maturation, but body image is most visibly affected.
Ideal self
The ideal self is a related concept, not the aspect most visibly affected by puberty and aging.

alt.q: Which changes associated with aging does the textbook say affect body image in middle-aged and older females?
alt.a: Menopause, wrinkles, graying hair, and decreased vision, hearing, and mobility
alt.ex: These aging-related changes affect body image in middle-aged and older females.
w: Secondary sex characteristics, body fat changes, and growth spurts
These are adolescent changes driven by puberty hormones.
Highly imaginative play and early identification with a gender
These are preschool developmental tasks, not aging changes.
Role ambiguity, role strain, and role overload at work and home
These are role performance stressors, not physical aging changes.

items.q: What must a person do to function effectively in multiple roles, according to the textbook?
items.a: Know the expected behavior and values, desire to conform to them, and be able to meet role requirements
items.ex: Effective role functioning requires knowing expectations, wanting to conform, and being able to meet requirements.
w: Meet every ideal societal role expectation fully and without any compromise
Successful adults distinguish ideal role expectations from realistic possibilities.
Give up personal needs entirely so that no two roles ever conflict
Roles and personal needs sometimes conflict; giving up all needs is not the requirement.
Change role patterns often in adulthood to keep up with new expectations
Adult role patterns are stable and change only minimally.

alt.q: What happens when a person has difficulty or fails to meet role expectations?
alt.a: It often contributes to decreased self-esteem or altered self-concept
alt.ex: Failing to meet role expectations leads to deficits and often lowers self-esteem or alters self-concept.
w: It usually enhances the sense of self through new learning
Fulfilling, not failing, role expectations enhances the sense of self.
It has no effect once role patterns are stable in adulthood
Role failure can lower self-esteem at any age.
It mainly affects body image rather than self-esteem
Role failure affects self-esteem and self-concept, not mainly body image.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient whose self-concept closely matches the patient’s ideal self. Which level of self-esteem does the nurse expect?
items.a: High self-esteem
items.ex: A person whose self-concept closely matches the ideal self generally has high self-esteem.
w: Low self-esteem
Low self-esteem occurs when self-concept varies widely from the ideal self.
Fluctuating self-esteem
Fluctuation is described in adolescence, not as a result of close matching.
Absent self-esteem
Everyone has some level of self-esteem; close matching predicts high self-esteem.

alt.q: A patient states, “I’m nowhere near the person I want to be.” Based on the relationship between self-concept and ideal self, what does the nurse expect?
alt.a: Low self-esteem
alt.ex: When self-concept varies widely from the ideal self, self-esteem tends to be low.
w: High self-esteem
High self-esteem occurs when self-concept closely matches the ideal self.
Stable identity
This statement reflects a gap between self-concept and ideal self, not identity stability.
Role overload
Role overload is having too many roles or responsibilities, not a self-ideal gap.

items.q: A patient who is a victim of intimate partner violence (IPV) has low self-esteem. Which nursing approach is essential to gain the patient’s trust?
items.a: Showing sensitivity, respect, and confidentiality
items.ex: Sensitivity, respect, and confidentiality are essential in gaining trust with a patient who is a victim of IPV.
w: Confronting the patient about staying with the partner
Confrontation does not build trust; the book stresses sensitivity and respect.
Sharing the patient’s story with family to build support
Breaking confidentiality undermines trust.
Waiting for the patient to request help before raising IPV
People with low self-esteem experiencing IPV are less likely to seek help.

alt.q: Why might a person with low self-esteem who experiences intimate partner violence not get help?
alt.a: People with low self-esteem who experience IPV are less likely to seek help
alt.ex: The book links low self-esteem to risk-prone occurrences, including not seeking help for IPV.
w: People with low self-esteem who experience IPV usually report it at once
The book says they are less likely to seek help.
People with high self-esteem are the group least likely to seek help
Low, not high, self-esteem is linked to not seeking help.
People with low self-esteem rarely experience IPV in the first place
The book does not say low self-esteem protects against IPV.

items.q: What does the textbook say happens to self-esteem when cultural identity is central to self-concept and is positive?
items.a: Cultural pride and self-esteem tend to be strong
items.ex: Positive, central cultural identity is linked to strong cultural pride and self-esteem.
w: Cultural pride rises but self-esteem tends to fall
The book links positive cultural identity to strong pride and self-esteem together.
Self-esteem depends only on socioeconomic status
Socioeconomic status predicts self-image, but cultural identity also matters.
Social isolation and low self-concept tend to result
Isolation results from internalized prejudice, not positive cultural identity.

alt.q: What can result from internalizing prejudice and devaluing one’s own ethnic or racial minority group?
alt.a: Social isolation that negatively influences self-concept
alt.ex: Internalized prejudice can lead to social isolation, which negatively influences self-concept.
w: Stronger cultural pride and higher self-esteem
Strong pride and self-esteem follow positive cultural identity, not internalized prejudice.
A more stable and clearly defined identity
Devaluing one’s group undermines, rather than stabilizes, identity.
Better adherence to recommended health regimens
Threats to self-concept tend to reduce adherence to health regimens.

items.q: Which actions does Box 33.2 recommend to promote self-concept and self-esteem in culturally diverse patients? Select all that apply.
o: Develop an open, nonrestrictive attitude toward cultural practices
An open attitude helps assess and encourage cultural practices that improve self-concept.
Ask patients what they think is important to help them feel better
Asking patients what matters to them builds a stronger sense of self.
Offer treatment choices and collaborate about self-care practices
Collaboration and choices encourage cultural identity and pride.
Facilitate culturally sensitive health promotion for at-risk behaviors
Box 33.2 recommends culturally sensitive activities for risks such as vaping.
Encourage patients to adopt the dominant culture’s self-care practices
This discourages cultural identity, which supports self-esteem when positive.
Avoid discussing cultural practices to prevent bias in the care plan
Nurses should assess and encourage cultural practices, not avoid them.
items.ex: Box 33.2 promotes openness, asking patients, collaboration with choices, and culturally sensitive health promotion.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for an adolescent from a minority cultural group. Which nursing actions support the teen’s cultural identity and self-concept? Select all that apply.
o: Asking the teen what would help them gain a stronger sense of self
Box 33.2 recommends asking patients what is important to them.
Collaborating with the teen and family on self-care practices
Collaboration encourages cultural identity and pride.
Offering choices among treatment options
Offering treatment choices encourages cultural identity and pride.
Telling the teen to set aside family traditions during treatment
Cultural pride and identity support strong self-esteem.
Limiting questions about social media to avoid embarrassment
Assessing coping with social media is a priority nursing action.
alt.ex: Asking, collaborating, and offering choices support cultural identity and pride, which strengthen self-esteem.

items.q: According to the textbook, in which cultures is body image more favorable among females? Select all that apply.
o: Cultures with more reasonable views about physical appearance
Reasonable views about appearance are linked to more favorable body image.
Cultures with less social pressure for thinness
Less pressure for thinness supports more favorable body image.
Cultures with less tendency to base self-esteem on body image
Not basing self-esteem on body image supports a favorable body image.
Cultures with strong internalization of the thin ideal
Internalizing the thin ideal increases susceptibility to body image issues.
Cultures that emphasize youth, beauty, and wholeness
The book notes American society emphasizes these values, and Western cultures dread aging.
items.ex: Body image is more favorable where appearance views are reasonable, thinness pressure is low, and self-esteem is not tied to body image.

alt.q: Which factors does the textbook link to greater susceptibility to body image issues? Select all that apply.
o: Low self-concept clarity
Low self-concept clarity increases susceptibility to body image issues.
Internalization of the thin ideal
Internalizing the thin ideal increases susceptibility.
Appearance-related social comparisons
Appearance comparisons contribute to negative body image.
Less social pressure for thinness
Less pressure for thinness is linked to more favorable body image.
Viewing aging positively, as in Eastern cultures
Eastern cultures’ positive view of aging is not described as a risk factor.
alt.ex: Low self-concept clarity, the thin ideal, and appearance comparisons increase body image problems.

items.q: Which feelings does the textbook include in feelings about body image? Select all that apply.
o: Sexuality
Feelings about sexuality are part of body image.
Femininity and masculinity
Body image includes feelings of femininity and masculinity.
Youthfulness
Youthfulness is part of body image feelings.
Health and strength
Feelings about health and strength are included.
Job satisfaction
Job satisfaction relates to self-esteem and role, not body image feelings.
Academic achievement
Academic achievement relates to identity and self-esteem, not body image.
items.ex: Body image feelings include sexuality, femininity and masculinity, youthfulness, health, and strength.

alt.q: A threat to body image and overall self-concept can affect a patient’s adherence to which health regimens? Select all that apply.
o: Diet
Body image threats can affect adherence to recommended diets.
Exercise
Exercise adherence can be affected by threats to body image.
Health screening practices
Screening practices may be affected by body image threats.
Taking medications as prescribed
Medication adherence can be affected.
Blood type compatibility
Blood type is a fixed biological trait, not a health regimen.
Genetic inheritance patterns
Inheritance is not a health regimen that adherence affects.
alt.ex: Threats to body image can affect adherence to diet, exercise, screening, and medications.

items.q: A person’s mental image of the body is not always consistent with the person’s actual physical structure or appearance.
items.a: True
items.ex: Body image is a set of attitudes and mental images that may not match actual appearance.
items.ww: Body image can be distorted, as in anorexia nervosa, so it does not always match reality.

alt.q: A person’s body image always accurately reflects the person’s actual physical appearance.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Mental images of the body are not always consistent with actual structure or appearance.
alt.ww: Body image distortions, such as in eating disorders, show body image can differ from reality.

items.q: Western cultures have been socialized to dread the normal aging process, whereas Eastern cultures view aging positively and respect older adults.
items.a: True
items.ex: Cultural values shape body image, including attitudes toward aging.
items.ww: The book contrasts Western dread of aging with Eastern respect for older adults.

alt.q: Eastern cultures have been socialized to dread the normal aging process, whereas Western cultures view aging positively.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book describes Western cultures dreading aging and Eastern cultures viewing it positively.
alt.ww: This reverses the cultural contrast; American society emphasizes youth, beauty, and wholeness.

items.q: Once established, basic feelings about the self tend to be constant, although a situational crisis can temporarily affect self-esteem.
items.a: True
items.ex: Basic self-feelings are relatively stable, but a situational crisis may cause a temporary change in self-esteem.
items.ww: Self-esteem is not permanently reset by one crisis; basic feelings tend to remain constant.

alt.q: A single situational crisis permanently lowers a person’s established basic feelings about the self.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Basic feelings about self tend to be constant; a crisis affects self-esteem only temporarily.
alt.ww: The book describes situational effects on self-esteem as temporary.

items.q: The [[ideal self]] consists of the aspirations, goals, values, and standards of behavior that a person considers ideal and strives to attain.
items.ex: Comparing self-concept with the ideal self helps explain a person’s level of self-esteem.

alt.q: A person whose self-concept closely matches the [[ideal self|ideal-self]] generally has high self-esteem.
alt.ex: Comparing self-concept with the ideal self helps explain a person’s level of self-esteem.

items.q: How does the textbook define a self-concept stressor?
items.a: Any real or perceived change that threatens identity, body image, or role performance
items.ex: A stressor may be real or only perceived, and it threatens one or more components of self-concept.
w: Any real physical injury that permanently changes the appearance of the body
Stressors include perceived changes and threats to identity and roles, not only physical injury.
Any perceived criticism from others that lowers self-esteem for a short time
Stressors are any changes threatening identity, body image, or role performance.
Any diagnosed psychiatric illness that alters a patient’s mood or behavior
Stressors are far broader than psychiatric illness.

alt.q: What does the textbook identify as the most important factor in determining a person’s response to a self-concept stressor?
alt.a: The individual’s perception of the stressor
alt.ex: How a person perceives a stressor matters most in determining the response.
w: The number of people who notice the change
Others’ reactions influence self-concept, but perception of the stressor is most important.
The cost of treating the underlying condition
Cost is not named as the key factor in response to a stressor.
The age at which the stressor first occurs
Age affects susceptibility, but perception is the most important factor.

items.q: Which factors does the textbook relate to a person’s ability to reestablish balance after a self-concept stressor?
items.a: Number of stressors, duration of the stressor, and health status
items.ex: The ability to reestablish balance is related to how many stressors, how long they last, and health status.
w: Number of siblings, birth order, and parenting style
These family factors are not the ones named for regaining balance.
Height, weight, and visible changes in appearance
Visible changes can be stressors but are not the factors for regaining balance.
Education level, job title, and type of insurance
These are not the factors the book relates to reestablishing balance.

alt.q: A patient is coping with a new amputation, a recent divorce, and a job loss, all within a month. Why is this patient at greater risk for difficulty adapting?
alt.a: The number of stressors affects the ability to reestablish balance
alt.ex: Multiple stressors at once challenge adaptive capacity and make balance harder to restore.
w: Divorce is the only stressor that affects self-concept
Body image and identity stressors also threaten self-concept.
Amputation affects only role performance, not self-concept
Amputation is a body image stressor that affects self-concept.
Job loss in adulthood does not threaten identity
Job loss is listed as an identity stressor.

items.q: A newly hired nurse in a rapidly changing, highly specialized unit says, “I’m never sure what I’m supposed to be doing or how to do it.” Which role stressor is the nurse experiencing?
items.a: Role ambiguity
items.ex: Role ambiguity involves unclear role expectations and is common in complex, rapidly changing, specialized organizations.
w: Role conflict
Role conflict involves two or more inconsistent or mutually exclusive roles.
Role overload
Role overload is having more roles or responsibilities than are manageable.
Sick role
The sick role is society’s expectations of how an ill person behaves.

alt.q: A 16-year-old feels pressured by parents and media to act like an adult but lacks the resources to move beyond being a dependent child. Which stressor does this describe?
alt.a: Role ambiguity
alt.ex: Role ambiguity is common in adolescence, when unclear expectations create stress and confusion.
w: Role strain
Role strain combines conflict and ambiguity and is felt as inadequacy for a role.
Role overload
Role overload involves too many roles or responsibilities to manage.
Identity confusion
Identity confusion is loss of a clear, consistent sense of identity, not unclear role expectations.

items.q: A woman caring for her husband with dementia says, “I feel so frustrated. I’m just not cut out for this.” Which role stressor does this most likely reflect?
items.a: Role strain
items.ex: Role strain combines conflict and ambiguity and is felt as frustration when unsuited to a role, such as dementia care.
w: Role ambiguity
Role ambiguity alone is unclear expectations, not feeling inadequate for the role.
Sick role
The sick role is society’s expectations of how an ill person behaves.
Role performance
Role performance is a component of self-concept, not a stressor.

alt.q: Which term does the textbook use for having more roles or responsibilities within a role than are manageable?
alt.a: Role overload
alt.ex: Role overload is common when someone tries to meet work and family demands while carving out personal time.
w: Role strain
Role strain combines role conflict and role ambiguity.
Role ambiguity
Role ambiguity involves unclear role expectations.
Role conflict
Role conflict involves roles that are inconsistent or mutually exclusive.

items.q: What is identity confusion?
items.a: Failure to maintain a clear, consistent, and continuous consciousness of personal identity
items.ex: Identity confusion results when a person cannot keep a clear, consistent, continuous sense of identity.
w: Unclear expectations about how to carry out a work or family role
This describes role ambiguity.
A distorted mental image of the body’s size, shape, or function
This describes a body image disturbance.
Assuming two or more roles that are inconsistent or contradictory
This describes role conflict.

alt.q: When can identity confusion develop, according to the textbook?
alt.a: At any stage of life when a person cannot adapt to identity stressors
alt.ex: Inability to adapt to identity stressors can result in identity confusion regardless of stage of life.
w: Only during adolescence, because adults have fixed identities
Adults have more stable identities but can still develop identity confusion.
Only in older adults who have lost a spouse or partner
Spousal loss can cause loss of identity, but confusion can occur at any age.
Only in children who cannot meet parental expectations
These are childhood self-esteem stressors, not the only cause of identity confusion.

items.q: Compared with personal stressors, which stressors have more impact on an adult’s identity?
items.a: Cultural and social stressors
items.ex: Adults have more stable identities, and cultural and social stressors affect their identity more than personal ones.
w: Biological and hormonal stressors
Biological changes such as puberty affect adolescent identity.
Academic and school stressors
Academic competence is emphasized for adolescents, not adult identity.
Online popularity stressors
Social media popularity is described as an adolescent identity stressor.

alt.q: Which example does the textbook give of a cultural or social identity stressor in an adult?
alt.a: Choosing whether to honor religious traditions from one’s family of origin
alt.ex: Balancing career and family or choosing about family religious traditions are adult cultural and social stressors.
w: Adjusting to physical changes of increasing maturity and puberty
These are adolescent identity stressors.
Receiving too few online responses and negative posted comments
Social media negativity is described as an adolescent stressor.
Coping with harsh criticism and inconsistent discipline at home
These reduce self-worth in children.

items.q: A patient 1 week after colostomy surgery says, “Nobody can even tell when I’m dressed, so I shouldn’t be this upset.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Even changes others can’t see can strongly affect how you feel about your body.”
items.ex: Colostomy and mastectomy changes are not apparent when dressed but still significantly affect the individual.
w: “You’re right; since it’s hidden, it shouldn’t really affect how you see yourself.”
Hidden changes still significantly affect body image, so this dismisses the patient.
“Let’s focus on your discharge teaching now and talk about feelings another day.”
Postponing feelings ignores a significant body image stressor.
“Most patients forget about these changes within a few days after they go home.”
This gives false reassurance and minimizes the patient’s experience.

alt.q: Why do mastectomy and colostomy significantly affect body image even though they are often not apparent to others?
alt.a: They alter the appearance and function of the body, which the individual is aware of
alt.ex: Even if undetected by others, changes in appearance and function significantly affect the individual.
w: They only affect body image when others notice and comment on them
The book stresses these changes affect the person even when undetected.
They mainly affect role performance rather than body image
These procedures alter appearance and function, which are body image stressors.
They cause anorexia nervosa, which then distorts body image
Anorexia nervosa has deep psychological origins, not surgical causes.

items.q: An older adult has repeated physical complaints, and a thorough assessment finds no physical explanation. According to Box 33.3, what should the nurse do next?
items.a: Encourage the patient to talk about concerns such as anxiety, fear, insecurity, or loneliness
items.ex: Box 33.3 advises thorough assessment of physical complaints and, if none is found, encouraging verbalization of concerns.
w: Tell the patient that the complaints are imaginary and need no further attention
This dismisses concerns that may reflect threatened self-esteem.
Repeat the full physical examination until a physical cause is found
After thorough assessment finds no cause, the next step is exploring emotional concerns.
Limit time spent with the patient to discourage attention-seeking behavior
Box 33.3 advises taking time to actively listen and accept feelings.

alt.q: What does Box 33.3 recommend first when an older adult reports physical complaints?
alt.a: Thoroughly assess the physical complaints before exploring emotional concerns
alt.ex: Box 33.3 lists thorough assessment of physical complaints, then encouraging verbalization if no physical cause exists.
w: Assume the complaints are emotional and refer the patient to counseling
Physical complaints must be assessed before attributing them to emotional concerns.
Ask the family to decide whether the complaints are worth assessing
The nurse should assess the complaints thoroughly.
Reassure the patient that complaints are normal with aging
Reassurance without assessment could miss a real physical problem.

items.q: A patient in the early stage of dementia is admitted to a long-term care facility. Which statement about the patient’s self-concept guides nursing care?
items.a: Self-concept in early dementia is largely intact, so interventions should support it
items.ex: Box 33.3 notes that self-concept in early dementia is largely intact and interventions should be modified to support it.
w: Self-concept is lost early in dementia, so self-concept care is no longer useful
Self-concept remains largely intact in early dementia.
Self-concept in dementia depends only on the family, so the nurse need not address it
Nurses should modify interventions to support the patient’s self-concept.
Self-concept in dementia improves on its own, so no change in care is needed
Interventions must be modified to support self-concept, not left unchanged.

alt.q: Which nursing action from Box 33.3 helps enhance self-esteem in an older adult?
alt.a: Encouraging storytelling and review of old photographs
alt.ex: Storytelling and reviewing photographs support self-esteem in older adults.
w: Completing tasks quickly for the patient to save time
Box 33.3 advises allowing extra time and reinforcing independence.
Avoiding talk about losses to prevent sadness
The box advises discussing life changes, losses, and their meaning.
Discouraging physical exercise to prevent falls
Encouraging exercise enhances well-being and successful aging.

items.q: According to the textbook, which age group has the highest rates of depression, which negatively affects self-esteem and self-efficacy?
items.a: Young adults aged 18 to 29 years
items.ex: Young adults 18 to 29 years of age have the highest rates of depression, harming self-esteem and self-efficacy.
w: Adolescents aged 12 to 17 years
The book identifies 18 to 29, not adolescents, as having the highest rates.
Adults aged 45 to 64 years
Self-esteem continues to increase in middle adulthood.
Older adults aged 65 to 75 years
Self-esteem peaks between 60 and 70 years of age.

alt.q: Which group of children and adolescents does the textbook say is particularly at risk for low self-esteem?
alt.a: Female children and adolescents with chronic illness
alt.ex: Female children and adolescents with chronic illness are particularly at risk for low self-esteem.
w: Male children and adolescents in team sports
Group activities such as sports can foster self-esteem.
Children who rate themselves above their peers
Inflated self-ratings are typical of young children, not a risk group.
Adolescents with strong cultural identity
Positive cultural identity supports strong self-esteem.

items.q: A patient recovering from a long illness is about to return to work and says, “I should be happy, but I feel more stressed than when I was sick.” How should the nurse interpret this statement?
items.a: A shift from illness to wellness can be as stressful as a shift from wellness to illness
items.ex: The book stresses that moving along the continuum from illness to wellness is as stressful as the reverse.
w: Stress during recovery means the illness is likely to recur soon
Recovery itself is a stressful transition; it does not predict recurrence.
Only the shift from wellness to illness causes real role stress
Both directions along the continuum are stressful.
The patient has developed identity confusion and needs referral
Transition stress is expected and is not by itself identity confusion.

alt.q: Which statement about role transitions is supported by the textbook?
alt.a: Moving from illness to wellness is as stressful as moving from wellness to illness
alt.ex: Any role transition, including recovery, may lead to role conflict, ambiguity, strain, or overload.
w: Moving from illness to wellness causes little stress for most people
The book says recovery is as stressful as becoming ill.
Only negative events such as death or divorce cause role transitions
Marriage, moving, and job changes are also situational transitions.
Role transitions occur mainly in childhood and rarely in adulthood
People undergo numerous role changes throughout life.

items.q: According to the textbook, how do people with high self-esteem generally compare with those with low self-esteem?
items.a: They are more resilient and better able to cope with demands and stressors
items.ex: High self-esteem supports resilience and coping with demands and stressors.
w: They are less resilient and more easily overwhelmed by demands and stressors
This describes low, not high, self-esteem.
They are equally resilient, because coping does not depend on self-esteem
The book links higher self-esteem to better coping.
They are more likely to feel unfulfilled and disconnected from others
Low self-worth contributes to feeling unfulfilled and disconnected.

alt.q: Which outcome does the textbook link to decreased self-worth?
alt.a: Depression and unremitting uneasiness or anxiety
alt.ex: Decreased self-worth can result in depression and persistent uneasiness or anxiety.
w: Greater resilience and stronger coping skills
Resilience is linked to high, not low, self-esteem.
Improved self-concept clarity and well-being
Self-concept clarity is linked to psychological well-being, not low self-worth.
Fewer risky behaviors such as substance abuse
Low self-esteem is linked to more risky behaviors.

items.q: Which conditions does Figure 33.3 list as body image stressors? Select all that apply.
o: Amputation
Amputation is an obvious change in appearance and a body image stressor.
Mastectomy
Mastectomy alters body appearance and is a body image stressor.
Scarring
Scars, such as from burns, are body image stressors.
Incontinence
Incontinence is listed as a body image stressor.
Empty nest
Empty nest is listed as a role performance stressor.
Job loss
Job loss is listed as an identity stressor.
items.ex: Figure 33.3 places changes in body appearance, structure, or function, such as amputation and scarring, under body image.

alt.q: Which situations does Figure 33.3 list as role performance stressors? Select all that apply.
o: Empty nest
Empty nest is listed as a role performance stressor.
Promotion or demotion
Promotion or demotion changes role performance.
Transition from school to work setting
This transition is listed under role performance.
Assuming responsibility for an aging parent
Caring for an aging parent is a role performance stressor.
Colostomy
Colostomy is listed as a body image stressor.
Repeated failures
Repeated failures are listed as an identity stressor.
alt.ex: Role performance stressors involve role changes such as empty nest, promotion, new work settings, and caregiving.

items.q: Which self-esteem stressors does the textbook identify for older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Health problems
Health problems are self-esteem stressors in older adults.
Declining socioeconomic status
Declining socioeconomic status affects older adults’ self-esteem.
Loss of spouse and friends
Loss of loved ones is a key self-esteem stressor in older adults.
Declining social support
Declining social support is listed for older adults.
Unresolved sibling rivalry
Sibling rivalry is a self-esteem stressor in children.
Inconsistent discipline
Inconsistent discipline reduces self-worth in children.
items.ex: Older adults’ self-esteem is threatened by health problems, declining status and function, and loss of loved ones and support.

alt.q: Which self-esteem stressors does the textbook identify for children? Select all that apply.
o: Perceived inability to meet parental expectations
This reduces self-worth in children.
Harsh criticism
Harsh criticism is listed as a childhood self-esteem stressor.
Inconsistent discipline
Inconsistent discipline reduces children’s self-worth.
Unresolved sibling rivalry
Unresolved sibling rivalry is a childhood self-esteem stressor.
Failure in work
Work failure is an adult self-esteem stressor.
Loss of spouse and friends
Loss of spouse and friends is an older adult stressor.
alt.ex: Children’s self-worth is lowered by unmet parental expectations, harsh criticism, inconsistent discipline, and sibling rivalry.

items.q: A nurse is planning care to enhance self-esteem in an older adult who recently moved to assisted living. Which interventions from Box 33.3 are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Allow additional time to complete tasks
Box 33.3 advises allowing extra time for tasks.
Reinforce the patient’s efforts at independence
Reinforcing independence supports self-esteem.
Help the patient identify positive coping mechanisms
Identifying effective coping and why it works is recommended.
Encourage regular physical exercise
Exercise enhances well-being needed for successful aging.
Perform self-care for the patient to prevent frustration
Taking over self-care undermines independence and self-esteem.
Avoid discussing the move to keep conversations positive
The box advises clarifying what life changes mean and their effect on self-esteem.
items.ex: Box 33.3 supports independence, extra time, positive coping, and exercise to enhance older adults’ self-esteem.

alt.q: Which nursing actions does Box 33.3 recommend for enhancing self-esteem in older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Actively listen to and accept the patient’s feelings
Active listening and acceptance are recommended.
Encourage storytelling and review of old photographs
Storytelling and photographs support self-esteem.
Help the patient identify negative coping and why it is ineffective
Recognizing ineffective coping is part of Box 33.3.
Praise healthy behaviors respectfully
Respectful praise of healthy behaviors is recommended.
Change the topic when the patient mentions bereavement
Nurses should allow discussion of spousal loss and bereavement.
alt.ex: Listening, storytelling, identifying coping patterns, and praising healthy behaviors enhance older adults’ self-esteem.

items.q: What does Role conflict mean?
items.a: Simultaneously holding two or more inconsistent or mutually exclusive roles
items.ex: Role transitions can produce role conflict, ambiguity, strain, or overload, each with a distinct meaning.
w: Unclear role expectations that leave people unsure what to do
That goes with Role ambiguity.
A combination of role conflict and role ambiguity
That goes with Role strain.
More roles or responsibilities within a role than are manageable
That goes with Role overload.

alt.q: What does Role ambiguity mean?
alt.a: Unclear role expectations that leave people unsure what to do
alt.ex: Role transitions can produce role conflict, ambiguity, strain, or overload, each with a distinct meaning.
w: Simultaneously holding two or more inconsistent or mutually exclusive roles
That goes with Role conflict.
A combination of role conflict and role ambiguity
That goes with Role strain.
More roles or responsibilities within a role than are manageable
That goes with Role overload.

alt.q: What does Role strain mean?
alt.a: A combination of role conflict and role ambiguity
alt.ex: Role transitions can produce role conflict, ambiguity, strain, or overload, each with a distinct meaning.
w: Simultaneously holding two or more inconsistent or mutually exclusive roles
That goes with Role conflict.
Unclear role expectations that leave people unsure what to do
That goes with Role ambiguity.
More roles or responsibilities within a role than are manageable
That goes with Role overload.

alt.q: What does Role overload mean?
alt.a: More roles or responsibilities within a role than are manageable
alt.ex: Role transitions can produce role conflict, ambiguity, strain, or overload, each with a distinct meaning.
w: Simultaneously holding two or more inconsistent or mutually exclusive roles
That goes with Role conflict.
Unclear role expectations that leave people unsure what to do
That goes with Role ambiguity.
A combination of role conflict and role ambiguity
That goes with Role strain.

alt.q: Which term means “Simultaneously holding two or more inconsistent or mutually exclusive roles”?
alt.a: Role conflict
alt.ex: Role transitions can produce role conflict, ambiguity, strain, or overload, each with a distinct meaning.
w: Role ambiguity
Role ambiguity: Unclear role expectations that leave people unsure what to do.
Role strain
Role strain: A combination of role conflict and role ambiguity.
Role overload
Role overload: More roles or responsibilities within a role than are manageable.

alt.q: Which term means “Unclear role expectations that leave people unsure what to do”?
alt.a: Role ambiguity
alt.ex: Role transitions can produce role conflict, ambiguity, strain, or overload, each with a distinct meaning.
w: Role conflict
Role conflict: Simultaneously holding two or more inconsistent or mutually exclusive roles.
Role strain
Role strain: A combination of role conflict and role ambiguity.
Role overload
Role overload: More roles or responsibilities within a role than are manageable.

alt.q: Which term means “A combination of role conflict and role ambiguity”?
alt.a: Role strain
alt.ex: Role transitions can produce role conflict, ambiguity, strain, or overload, each with a distinct meaning.
w: Role conflict
Role conflict: Simultaneously holding two or more inconsistent or mutually exclusive roles.
Role ambiguity
Role ambiguity: Unclear role expectations that leave people unsure what to do.
Role overload
Role overload: More roles or responsibilities within a role than are manageable.

alt.q: Which term means “More roles or responsibilities within a role than are manageable”?
alt.a: Role overload
alt.ex: Role transitions can produce role conflict, ambiguity, strain, or overload, each with a distinct meaning.
w: Role conflict
Role conflict: Simultaneously holding two or more inconsistent or mutually exclusive roles.
Role ambiguity
Role ambiguity: Unclear role expectations that leave people unsure what to do.
Role strain
Role strain: A combination of role conflict and role ambiguity.

mt.q: Match each role performance stressor with its description.
pairs: Simultaneously holding two or more inconsistent or mutually exclusive roles
Unclear role expectations that leave people unsure what to do
A combination of role conflict and role ambiguity
More roles or responsibilities within a role than are manageable
mt.ex: Role transitions can produce role conflict, ambiguity, strain, or overload, each with a distinct meaning.

items.q: Identity stressors affect people throughout life, but adolescents are particularly susceptible to them.
items.a: True
items.ex: Adolescents must adjust to physical, emotional, and mental changes of maturity, which can create insecurity and anxiety.
items.ww: The book singles out adolescents as especially susceptible to identity stressors.

alt.q: Compared with adolescents, adults generally have a less stable identity and a less firmly developed self-concept.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Adults generally have a more stable identity and more firmly developed self-concept than adolescents.
alt.ww: The book states adults have the more stable identity, which is why adolescents are more susceptible.

items.q: Because mastectomy and colostomy changes are usually not apparent when a person is dressed, they have little effect on body image.
items.a: False
items.ex: Although others may not detect them, these changes significantly affect the individual’s body image.
items.ww: The book emphasizes that hidden changes in appearance and function still significantly affect the person.

alt.q: Even elective changes, such as breast augmentation or reduction, can affect body image.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The book notes that some elective changes still affect body image.
alt.ww: Body image changes do not need to be unwanted or caused by illness to affect self-concept.

items.q: An essential process in adjusting to loss is the development of a new self-concept.
items.a: True
items.ex: Adjusting to losses, such as a partner or body function, requires developing a new self-concept.
items.ww: The book names developing a new self-concept as essential to adjusting to loss.

alt.q: Adjusting to a major loss requires returning to one’s previous self-concept rather than developing a new one.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book says developing a new self-concept is essential to adjusting to loss.
alt.ww: Loss changes identity and self-esteem, so a new self-concept must develop.

items.q: The [[sick role]] involves the expectations of others and society regarding how an individual behaves when sick.
items.ex: Role conflict occurs when sick-role expectations to rest collide with co-workers’ expectations to get the job done.

alt.q: When society expects an ill person to rest but co-workers expect work to get done, the patient’s [[sick role]] creates role conflict.
alt.ex: Role conflict occurs when sick-role expectations to rest collide with co-workers’ expectations to get the job done.

sections.name: The effect of family on self-concept development

items.q: From whom does a child first develop a basic sense of who they are?
items.a: Family caregivers
items.ex: The family plays a key role in creating self-concept; children gain their basic sense of self from family caregivers.
w: Classroom teachers
Teachers become role models later; the basic sense of self comes first from family caregivers.
School-age peers
Peers grow in influence during adolescence, after the family has shaped the basic sense of self.
Health care providers
Health care providers can support self-concept, but children develop their basic sense of self from family.

alt.q: Besides a basic sense of self, what else does a child gain from family members?
alt.a: Accepted norms for thinking, feeling, and behaving
alt.ex: Family members pass on accepted norms for how to think, feel, and behave along with a basic sense of self.
w: A fixed self-concept that cannot change later in life
Self-concept develops and changes across the life span; it is not fixed in childhood.
Immunity to the influence of peers and social media
Adolescents are strongly influenced by peers and social media despite family influence.
A body image that is independent of later physical change
Body image changes with puberty, aging, illness, and injury throughout life.

items.q: Which parental response pattern does the textbook link to a child’s positive self-esteem and school achievement?
items.a: Firm, consistent, and warm
items.ex: Parents who respond in a firm, consistent, and warm manner foster a child’s positive self-esteem and school achievement.
w: Permissive, flexible, and warm
Firmness and consistency are part of the pattern that fosters self-esteem, not permissiveness.
Firm, strict, and emotionally distant
Warmth is an essential part of the pattern; distance does not foster self-esteem.
Harsh, consistent, and demanding
Harsh parenting is linked to negative self-concepts in children.

alt.q: Which parental pattern is most likely to foster a negative self-concept in a child?
alt.a: Harsh, inconsistent responses from a parent with low self-esteem
alt.ex: Parents who are harsh, inconsistent, or have low self-esteem themselves often foster negative self-concepts in their children.
w: Firm limits applied the same way each time with warmth
Firm, consistent, warm responses foster positive self-esteem and school achievement.
High levels of parental support combined with monitoring
High support and monitoring are related to higher self-esteem and fewer risky behaviors.
Positive communication and steady social support at home
Positive communication and social support foster self-esteem and well-being in adolescence.

items.q: A nurse teaches parents of a 9-year-old about building their child’s self-esteem. Which statement by a parent shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “We will set clear rules, enforce them the same way each time, and show our affection.”
items.ex: Firm, consistent, and warm responses from parents foster a child’s positive self-esteem and school achievement.
w: “We will relax the rules on stressful days so our child never feels upset with us.”
Inconsistent limits are linked to negative self-concepts rather than positive self-esteem.
“We will point out every mistake sharply so our child learns to do better quickly.”
Harsh criticism reduces a child’s self-worth and fosters a negative self-concept.
“We will stay out of our child’s activities so our child can learn independence alone.”
Low parental monitoring and support are associated with lower self-esteem and more risky behavior.

alt.q: A parent says, “I yell at my son when he fails and ignore it other times, and honestly I don’t think much of myself either.” Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?
alt.a: This parenting pattern places the child at risk for a negative self-concept.
alt.ex: Harsh, inconsistent parenting by a parent with low self-esteem often fosters negative self-concepts that can lead to negative health practices.
w: This parenting pattern will strengthen the child’s resilience over time.
Harsh, inconsistent parenting fosters negative self-concepts rather than resilience.
This parenting pattern mainly affects the child’s physical growth.
The concern is the child’s self-concept and later health practices, not physical growth.
This parenting pattern has no effect once the child begins school.
Family influence on self-concept continues through childhood and adolescence.

items.q: High levels of parental support and parental monitoring are related to which outcomes in children and adolescents?
items.a: Higher self-esteem and reduced risky behaviors
items.ex: The textbook links high parental support and monitoring to higher self-esteem and fewer risky behaviors.
w: Lower self-esteem and greater dependence on parents
Support and monitoring are associated with higher, not lower, self-esteem.
Higher self-esteem but more rebellious risky behaviors
Support and monitoring are linked to reduced, not increased, risky behaviors.
Reduced risky behaviors but lower school achievement
Positive parenting is associated with better self-esteem and school achievement, not lower achievement.

alt.q: Which parental approach is most likely to reduce an adolescent’s risky behaviors?
alt.a: Providing high levels of support while monitoring activities
alt.ex: High parental support and monitoring are related to higher self-esteem and reduced risky behaviors.
w: Allowing full freedom with little monitoring of activities
Low monitoring is not the pattern associated with reduced risky behaviors.
Monitoring closely while withholding warmth and support
Support is part of the protective pattern; monitoring without warmth is not described as protective.
Responding with harsh punishment after each mistake
Harsh parenting fosters negative self-concepts, which can lead to substance abuse.

items.q: According to the evidence on adolescents, how does a low self-concept relate to risky behavior?
items.a: It may precede or increase risky behaviors such as substance and alcohol use.
items.ex: A low self-concept may precede or perhaps increase risky behavior, including substance and alcohol abuse and risky sexual activity.
w: It develops only after an adolescent begins using substances.
Low self-concept may come before, not only after, risky behavior begins.
It protects adolescents by making them avoid peer activities.
Low self-concept is a risk, not a protective factor, for risky behavior.
It has no measurable link to drinking or drug use in teens.
The evidence links low self-concept with substance use and other risky behaviors.

alt.q: Why does helping youth develop a healthy self-concept matter for substance abuse prevention?
alt.a: A healthy self-concept and behaviors can prevent risky behaviors and their future health impact.
alt.ex: Because low self-concept may precede risky behavior, building a healthy self-concept can prevent those risks and later health effects.
w: A healthy self-concept guarantees an adolescent will never try alcohol.
Self-concept reduces risk but does not guarantee any adolescent will avoid alcohol.
A healthy self-concept matters only after substance use has begun.
The aim is prevention, before risky behaviors start.
A healthy self-concept mainly improves physical growth during puberty.
The concern is risky behavior and health, not physical growth.

items.q: Why are adolescents particularly vulnerable to changes in self-concept?
items.a: They face rapid changes in appearance, social interactions, confidence, and independence.
items.ex: Adolescent changes in appearance, social life, confidence, and independence can feel overwhelming and can influence self-concept.
w: They are no longer influenced by peer group acceptance.
Adolescents are very influenced by peer group acceptance.
Their family no longer affects their self-concept.
Family, social, and behavioral factors remain important in preadolescence and adolescence.
Their self-concept has become fixed by early adolescence.
Self-concept continues to change over time, especially during adolescence.

alt.q: A 15-year-old says, “If my friends don’t accept me, I’m nothing.” Which developmental influence does this statement best reflect?
alt.a: Strong influence of peer group acceptance on adolescent self-concept
alt.ex: Adolescents are very influenced by peer group acceptance, which affects their self-concept.
w: Stable identity achieved before entering adolescence
Adolescents are still forming identity; the statement shows reliance on peers, not stability.
Rejection of the importance of social interactions
The adolescent places great importance on social acceptance, not less.
Self-concept based mainly on parental expectations
The statement centers on friends, not on parents.

items.q: A school nurse plans a prevention program for middle school students at risk for substance use. Which nursing action does the textbook identify as a priority?
items.a: Assessing the coping strategies of the children and adolescents
items.ex: A priority nursing action is assessment of child and adolescent coping strategies.
w: Lecturing students on national substance use statistics
Statistics alone are not the priority; assessing coping strategies guides effective prevention.
Screening students only after a first substance use
Prevention requires early identification of risk and coping before use begins.
Referring every student to an addiction specialist
Universal referral is not indicated; assessment of coping comes first.

alt.q: Which group of techniques does the textbook list as appropriate coping strategies for children and adolescents?
alt.a: Effective communication, conflict resolution, and stress management
alt.ex: Appropriate coping techniques for youth include effective communication, conflict resolution, and stress management.
w: Avoidance of conflict, isolation, and screen time
Avoidance and isolation are not the coping techniques recommended for youth.
Strict dieting, competition, and social media use
These are not listed coping techniques and may harm self-concept.
Suppressing emotions, self-reliance, and silence
Suppression and silence do not build the communication skills the textbook recommends.

items.q: A 13-year-old with low self-esteem tells the nurse, “I don’t really fit in anywhere.” Which suggestion by the nurse best supports the adolescent’s self-concept?
items.a: Joining a youth sports or physical exercise program
items.ex: Physical exercise and youth sports help adolescents gain peer support and improve coping strategies and self-concept.
w: Spending more time alone until feeling more confident
Isolation does not build the peer support that improves self-concept.
Gaining approval through popularity on social media
Rating self-worth on social media popularity tends to harm, not help, adolescent self-concept.
Avoiding group activities that might cause embarrassment
Group activities such as sports foster self-esteem and peer support.

alt.q: What benefit of youth sports programs does the textbook describe for adolescents?
alt.a: Gaining peer support and improving coping strategies and self-concept
alt.ex: Participation in physical exercise and youth sports helps adolescents gain peer support and improve coping and self-concept.
w: Reducing the need for any family involvement in their lives
Family factors remain important to address in adolescence.
Replacing the need to learn stress management skills
Stress management remains an important part of prevention efforts.
Ensuring that they will not experiment with alcohol
No program guarantees avoidance of alcohol; sports improve coping and self-concept.

items.q: Which two elements does the textbook say substance abuse prevention efforts should include?
items.a: Stress management and improvement in self-esteem
items.ex: Prevention efforts should include stress management and improvement in self-esteem.
w: Drug testing and loss of school privileges
Punitive measures are not the elements the textbook recommends for prevention.
Peer avoidance and strict curfew enforcement
Peer support is helpful; avoiding peers is not a recommended prevention element.
Genetic testing and medication management
Genetic predisposition is a risk factor to identify, but prevention focuses on stress and self-esteem.

alt.q: A community health nurse designs an alcohol prevention program for teens. Which program component best fits the textbook’s recommendations?
alt.a: Sessions that teach stress management and build self-esteem
alt.ex: Including stress management and self-esteem improvement in prevention efforts addresses the self-concept link to risky behaviors.
w: Sessions that describe the legal penalties for underage drinking
Legal warnings do not address the self-concept and stress factors behind risky behaviors.
Sessions that rank students by academic performance
Ranking students does not build self-esteem or coping skills.
Sessions that separate teens from their peer groups
Peer support through programs like youth sports improves coping and self-concept.

items.q: The parents of a 16-year-old ask how they can help protect their teen from drinking and drug use. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Providing social support that builds your teen’s personal pride and life satisfaction can help.”
items.ex: Teaching families to give social support that instills pride and life satisfaction promotes self-concept and protective factors against substance use.
w: “At this age, your teen’s friends matter more, so your support makes little difference.”
Family factors remain important to address throughout preadolescence and adolescence.
“Strict punishment for every mistake will show your teen that you are serious.”
Harsh parenting fosters negative self-concepts, which can influence substance abuse.
“Most teens drink anyway, so it is best not to discuss it with your teen.”
Positive communication and social support foster adolescent self-esteem and well-being.

alt.q: Whom does the textbook say nurses should help learn to provide social support that promotes adolescent self-concept?
alt.a: Families, peers, and teachers
alt.ex: Helping families, peers, and teachers provide social support promotes self-concept and protective factors against risky behaviors.
w: Only the adolescent’s parents
Peers and teachers are also included as sources of social support.
Only school counselors and coaches
Families and peers are key sources of support, not only school staff.
Only health care providers
The textbook names families, peers, and teachers as the people to teach.

items.q: How does culture relate to the influence of parents on a child’s development?
items.a: Parents are important influences, but parenting approaches vary by culture.
items.ex: Parents are important influences on development, yet variations in parenting approach depend on the culture.
w: Culture determines a child’s self-concept, so parents have little influence.
Parents are important influences on a child’s development regardless of culture.
All cultures use the same parenting approach to build self-esteem.
Parenting approaches vary across cultures.
Culture affects parenting only after the child reaches adolescence.
Cultural variation in parenting applies throughout childhood, not only in adolescence.

alt.q: A nurse notices that a family from another culture disciplines their child differently than the nurse’s own family did. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
alt.a: Parenting approaches vary by culture, so the nurse assesses rather than judges.
alt.ex: Variations in parenting approach depend on culture; the nurse assesses the family’s pattern rather than assuming it is harmful.
w: Different discipline always means the child has a negative self-concept.
A culturally different approach is not, by itself, evidence of a negative self-concept.
The family should be told to adopt the nurse’s parenting approach.
Imposing the nurse’s values ignores cultural variation in parenting.
Culture has no bearing on how parents influence a child.
The textbook states that parenting approaches vary by culture.

items.q: According to the textbook, change in a patient’s self-concept requires which approach?
items.a: An evidence-based practice approach supported by the entire health care team
items.ex: Change in self-concept demands an evidence-based approach supported by the whole health care team.
w: A single counseling session led by the primary nurse
Self-concept change takes time and the support of the entire team.
A family-only approach without health care team involvement
The textbook calls for the entire health care team to support the approach.
A medication-based approach directed by the health care provider
The textbook describes an evidence-based team approach, not a medication-based one.

alt.q: A teen with low self-esteem is using alcohol. Which plan best reflects the textbook’s guidance on changing self-concept?
alt.a: An evidence-based plan that the whole health care team supports
alt.ex: Changing self-concept demands an evidence-based practice approach supported by the entire health care team.
w: A plan carried out by the school nurse working alone
One team member alone does not provide the team-wide support the textbook calls for.
A plan based on the nurse’s personal parenting experience
Personal experience does not replace an evidence-based approach.
A plan that waits for the teen to outgrow the behavior
Waiting ignores the need for active, evidence-based intervention.

items.q: Which factors does the textbook say health care providers must prioritize when identifying risk for early drug and alcohol use? Select all that apply.
o: Genetic predisposition
Genetic predisposition is a listed risk factor for early drug and alcohol use.
Family environment
The family environment is a listed risk factor that providers must identify.
Cultural identity
Cultural identity is included among the risk factors to identify.
Participation in youth sports
Youth sports are protective because they build peer support, coping, and self-concept.
High levels of parental monitoring
Parental monitoring is associated with reduced risky behaviors, so it is protective.
items.ex: Identifying risk factors such as genetic predisposition, family environment, and cultural identity must be a priority for providers.

alt.q: Which factors are protective against risky behaviors such as adolescent drinking and drug use? Select all that apply.
o: High parental support and monitoring
High support and monitoring are related to higher self-esteem and reduced risky behaviors.
Participation in physical exercise and youth sports
Sports build peer support, coping strategies, and self-concept.
Social support that instills personal pride
Support from families, peers, and teachers that builds pride promotes protective factors.
Harsh and inconsistent parenting
Harsh, inconsistent parenting fosters negative self-concepts that can influence substance abuse.
Low self-concept during adolescence
A low self-concept may precede or increase risky behavior.
alt.ex: Parental support and monitoring, youth sports, and social support that builds pride all protect against risky behaviors.

items.q: Which skills or relationships does the evidence suggest may reduce risky behaviors in adolescents when strengthened? Select all that apply.
o: Self-compassion
Learning self-compassion skills may reduce risky behaviors.
Resiliency
Resiliency is among the skills that may reduce risky behaviors.
Self-worth
Increasing self-worth may reduce risky adolescent behaviors.
Relationships with family, teachers, and peers
Improving these relationships may reduce risky behaviors.
Competitive ranking against classmates
Ranking is not among the skills the evidence links to reduced risky behavior.
Withdrawal from peer groups
Peer support helps; withdrawal does not reduce risky behaviors.
items.ex: Opportunities to build self-compassion, self-esteem, resiliency, self-worth, and better relationships may reduce adolescent risky behaviors.

alt.q: A nurse designs a youth program to reduce risky behaviors. Which goals fit the textbook’s evidence? Select all that apply.
o: Increase participants’ self-esteem
Building self-esteem is part of reducing risky behaviors.
Teach skills that build resiliency
Resiliency skills may reduce risky behaviors.
Improve relationships with family members
Better family relationships may reduce risky behaviors.
Encourage rating self-worth by online popularity
Basing self-worth on social media popularity harms adolescent self-concept.
Discourage contact with teachers and coaches
Improving relationships with teachers is one of the protective goals.
alt.ex: Programs that build self-esteem, resiliency, and family relationships may reduce adolescent risky behaviors.

items.q: Which family experiences reduce a child’s level of self-worth? Select all that apply.
o: Harsh criticism
Harsh criticism reduces a child’s self-worth.
Inconsistent discipline
Inconsistent discipline reduces a child’s self-worth.
Unresolved sibling rivalry
Unresolved sibling rivalry is a self-esteem stressor for children.
Perceived inability to meet parental expectations
Feeling unable to meet parental expectations reduces a child’s self-worth.
Warm, consistent parental responses
Warm, consistent responses foster positive self-esteem.
Positive communication within the family
Positive communication fosters self-esteem and well-being.
items.ex: Harsh criticism, inconsistent discipline, sibling rivalry, and unmet parental expectations are childhood self-esteem stressors.

alt.q: Which family behaviors foster a positive self-concept in children and adolescents? Select all that apply.
o: Responding in a firm, consistent, and warm manner
This pattern fosters positive self-esteem and school achievement.
High parental support and monitoring
Support and monitoring relate to higher self-esteem.
Positive communication and social support
These foster self-esteem and well-being in adolescence.
Harsh criticism after every failure
Harsh criticism reduces a child’s self-worth.
Discipline that changes with the parent’s mood
Inconsistent discipline reduces a child’s self-worth.
alt.ex: Firm, consistent, warm, supportive parenting with positive communication fosters a positive self-concept.

items.q: Well-meaning statements or advice from family members can sometimes cultivate a negative self-concept in a child.
items.a: True
items.ex: Even well-intended family statements or advice can foster negative self-concepts in children.
items.ww: Good intentions do not prevent a statement from harming how a child sees themselves.

alt.q: Because family advice is well-intentioned, it cannot contribute to a negative self-concept in a child.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Well-meaning statements or advice can still cultivate negative self-concepts in children.
alt.ww: Children absorb family messages; intent does not guarantee a positive effect on self-concept.

items.q: Positive communication and social support foster self-esteem and well-being in adolescence.
items.a: True
items.ex: Adolescent self-esteem and well-being are fostered by positive communication and social support.
items.ww: The textbook directly links positive communication and social support to adolescent self-esteem.

alt.q: Once peers become important in adolescence, family communication and support no longer affect self-esteem.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Family, social, and behavioral factors remain important in preadolescence and adolescence.
alt.ww: Positive family communication and support continue to foster adolescent self-esteem and well-being.

items.q: Negative self-concepts fostered by harsh or inconsistent parenting can influence negative health practices such as substance abuse.
items.a: True
items.ex: Harsh, inconsistent parenting fosters negative self-concepts, which can lead to negative health practices like substance abuse.
items.ww: The textbook links negative self-concept from parenting to negative health practices.

alt.q: A child’s self-concept affects emotional well-being but has no connection to later health practices such as substance use.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Negative self-concepts can influence negative health practices, including substance abuse.
alt.ww: Self-concept and health behaviors are linked; low self-concept may precede risky behavior.

items.q: A child’s positive self-esteem and school achievement are fostered by parents who respond in a firm, consistent, and [[warm]] manner.
items.ex: Warmth combined with firmness and consistency is the parental pattern linked to positive self-esteem and school achievement.

alt.q: Parents who respond in a firm, [[consistent]], and warm manner foster a child’s positive self-esteem and school achievement.
alt.ex: Warmth combined with firmness and consistency is the parental pattern linked to positive self-esteem and school achievement.

items.q: High levels of parental support and parental [[monitoring]] are related to higher self-esteem and reduced risky behaviors.
items.ex: Parental support together with monitoring is associated with higher self-esteem and fewer risky behaviors in youth.

alt.q: High levels of parental [[support]] and parental monitoring are related to higher self-esteem and reduced risky behaviors.
alt.ex: Parental support together with monitoring is associated with higher self-esteem and fewer risky behaviors in youth.

sections.name: Nurse’s effect on a patient’s self-concept

items.q: A patient is 2 days post mastectomy. During the dressing change the patient watches the nurse’s face closely. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Calmly looking at the incision and saying, “This incision is healing nicely.”
items.ex: Showing acceptance of the scar and affirming statements such as “healing nicely” positively influence the patient’s body image.
w: Looking away from the incision to spare the patient’s feelings
Avoiding the scar suggests the nurse cannot accept it and can foster negative body image.
Saying, “Try not to look; it will look better in a few months.”
This implies the scar is unacceptable and does not affirm the patient’s body image.
Working quickly and silently to finish the dressing change
Silence and haste convey discomfort; patients watch nurses’ responses to their wounds.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with a large abdominal scar after trauma surgery. Which nurse behavior is most likely to contribute to a negative body image?
alt.a: Showing a shocked facial expression when uncovering the wound
alt.ex: A shocked or disgusted expression contributes to negative body image because patients watch others’ reactions to their wounds.
w: Telling the patient, “This tissue looks healthy.”
Statements like this are affirmations that support the patient’s body image.
Using a positive, matter-of-fact approach during care
A matter-of-fact approach models acceptance for the patient and family.
Sitting down to listen to the patient’s concerns
Listening and forming a therapeutic relationship promote positive change.

items.q: A nurse feels uncomfortable while caring for a patient’s foul-smelling wound. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Anticipate and acknowledge the reaction, then focus on the patient rather than the task
items.ex: Anticipate personal reactions, acknowledge them, and focus on the patient instead of the unpleasant task or situation.
w: Ask another nurse to provide all of this patient’s wound care
Avoiding the patient does not address the reaction or support the patient’s self-concept.
Tell the patient honestly that the wound is difficult to look at
Expressing distress to the patient fosters a negative body image.
Hide the reaction by avoiding eye contact during the procedure
Avoiding eye contact is a nonverbal message that can lower the patient’s self-esteem.

alt.q: Why should a nurse put themselves in the situation of a patient with a disfiguring wound?
alt.a: To include measures that ease embarrassment, frustration, anger, and denial
alt.ex: Nurses who put themselves in the patient’s situation incorporate measures to ease embarrassment, frustration, anger, and denial.
w: To decide which coping strategies the patient should be using
The nurse collaborates with the patient on coping rather than deciding for them.
To determine whether the patient’s distress is excessive
Empathy aims to ease feelings, not to judge whether they are excessive.
To avoid showing any emotion while providing wound care
Empathy guides caring responses; it is not about suppressing all emotion.

items.q: Why is self-awareness essential for a nurse caring for patients with altered self-concept?
items.a: It is critical to understanding and accepting others.
items.ex: Self-awareness of one’s own feelings, values, and judgments is critical in understanding and accepting others.
w: It allows the nurse to share personal values with patients.
The goal is to recognize how one’s values affect patients, not to share them.
It helps the nurse avoid forming relationships with patients.
A therapeutic relationship is central; self-awareness supports it.
It ensures that patients adopt healthy lifestyle choices.
Self-awareness helps the nurse accept patients; it does not control patients’ choices.

alt.q: A nurse reflects on personal beliefs about obesity before caring for a patient after bariatric surgery. What is the main purpose of this reflection?
alt.a: To recognize personal judgments that could affect acceptance of the patient
alt.ex: Remaining aware of one’s own feelings, values, and judgments is critical to understanding and accepting others.
w: To decide whether the patient deserves extra support
Every patient deserves a nonjudgmental, accepting approach.
To prepare advice based on the nurse’s own lifestyle
The nurse examines how personal values affect patients, not how to impose them.
To identify which nursing diagnosis the patient has
Nursing diagnoses come from patient assessment data, not self-reflection.

items.q: A patient who has been working on healthier eating has lost 4 kg (8.8 lb) since the last visit. Which response by the nurse best supports the patient’s self-concept?
items.a: “I noticed you have lost 4 kg since your last visit; your changes are working.”
items.ex: When you observe a positive change, acknowledge it and tell the patient the specific positive change you observed.
w: “You still have 20 kg to lose, so keep working at it.”
Focusing on what remains overlooks the progress the nurse should acknowledge.
“Weight often comes back, so don’t celebrate too soon.”
This discourages the patient rather than reinforcing the positive change.
“Let’s wait until you lose 10 kg before we review it.”
Delaying feedback misses the chance to acknowledge the change now.

alt.q: Why does a nurse use a positive, matter-of-fact approach with a patient whose body appearance has changed?
alt.a: It provides a model for the patient and family to follow.
alt.ex: A positive, matter-of-fact approach to care provides a model for the patient and family to follow.
w: It keeps the patient from discussing difficult feelings.
The nurse wants patients to express feelings; the approach models acceptance.
It shortens the time needed to complete physical care.
The purpose is modeling acceptance, not saving time.
It shows the patient that the change is not important.
The approach conveys acceptance, not that the change is unimportant.

items.q: Which nurse action most enhances a patient’s self-concept and self-esteem?
items.a: Building a trusting relationship that includes the patient and family in decisions
items.ex: A trusting nurse-patient relationship that includes both patient and family in decision making enhances self-concept and self-esteem.
w: Making care decisions for the patient to reduce the patient’s stress
Removing the patient from decision making does not build self-esteem.
Limiting family involvement so the patient can focus on recovery
Including the family in decision making enhances self-concept.
Focusing care on physical needs until the patient is discharged
Including self-concept issues in care planning influences positive outcomes.

alt.q: A patient with a new spinal cord injury and the family meet with the nurse about the plan of care. Which nurse action best enhances the patient’s self-esteem?
alt.a: Inviting the patient and family to share in decisions about care
alt.ex: Incorporating both the patient and family in decision making within a trusting relationship enhances self-concept and self-esteem.
w: Presenting a finished plan for the patient and family to sign
A finished plan leaves out the patient’s participation in decisions.
Asking the family to decide while the patient rests
Excluding the patient from decisions does not enhance the patient’s self-esteem.
Deferring all self-esteem concerns until rehabilitation
Self-concept issues belong in the planning and delivery of care now.

items.q: How can a nurse individualize care to support a patient’s self-concept?
items.a: Highlight unique needs and include alternative practices or spiritual expression
items.ex: Individualize your approach by highlighting unique needs and incorporating alternative health care practices or methods of spiritual expression.
w: Use the same standard care plan for every patient with low self-esteem
A standard plan does not address the patient’s unique needs.
Avoid spiritual topics because they may upset some patients
Methods of spiritual expression can be incorporated into the plan of care.
Limit care to practices ordered by the health care provider
The textbook encourages including alternative practices to individualize care.

alt.q: A patient with a new amputation finds strength in daily prayer and meditation. Which nursing action best individualizes the plan of care?
alt.a: Building time for prayer and meditation into the daily plan of care
alt.ex: Incorporating methods of spiritual expression into the plan highlights the patient’s unique needs and supports self-concept.
w: Scheduling prayer only after all physical care is complete
Treating the practice as optional fails to incorporate it into the plan.
Referring the patient elsewhere to keep spiritual practices private
The nurse can incorporate spiritual expression into the plan rather than separate it.
Suggesting the patient replace meditation with physical therapy
Spiritual expression supports self-concept and need not be replaced.

items.q: Which factors does the textbook say can help protect nurses from burnout and emotional exhaustion?
items.a: Positive self-esteem, interprofessional collaboration, and counseling support
items.ex: Positive self-esteem, interprofessional collaboration, and counseling support services help protect nurses from burnout and emotional exhaustion.
w: Working extra shifts, independent practice, and limited breaks
Extra shifts and isolation are not protective; collaboration and support are.
Emotional distance, strict routines, and avoiding team meetings
Distance and avoidance do not protect against burnout.
Suppressing feelings, high workloads, and minimal feedback
Suppressing feelings is not listed as protective; counseling support is.

alt.q: Why does protecting nurses from burnout matter for patients?
alt.a: It helps nurses deliver high-quality patient care.
alt.ex: Protecting nurses from burnout and emotional exhaustion assists them to deliver high-quality patient care.
w: It reduces the need for patient teaching.
Burnout prevention supports quality care; it does not replace teaching.
It allows nurses to care for more patients per shift.
The benefit described is quality of care, not higher patient loads.
It removes the need for interprofessional collaboration.
Collaboration is itself one of the protective factors.

items.q: Why is any patient with an actual change in or threat to self-concept considered at risk?
items.a: The change can cause stress, leading to anxiety, depression, and other problems.
items.ex: Threats to self-concept or self-esteem create stress that can result in anxiety, depression, and other physical and psychosocial problems.
w: The change always causes a permanent loss of personal identity.
Self-concept can improve over time; permanent identity loss is not inevitable.
The change prevents the patient from making any decisions about care.
Patients can and should participate in decisions about their care.
The change only affects patients who had low self-esteem earlier.
Any patient facing a threat to self-concept is at risk, not only those with prior issues.

alt.q: A patient facing a below-the-knee amputation says, “I won’t be the same person anymore.” What is the patient at greatest risk for?
alt.a: Stress that can lead to anxiety and depression
