alt.ex: A threat to self-concept places the patient at risk for stress, which can result in anxiety, depression, and other problems.
w: Improved self-esteem due to the surgery
A perceived threat to identity is a stressor, not a source of improved self-esteem.
Loss of all previous coping abilities
Patients often use familiar coping patterns; they do not lose them all.
A rapid and complete adjustment within days
Adjustment to major self-concept changes often takes a year or longer.

items.q: In the critical thinking model for self-concept assessment, which attitude applies when a nurse’s beliefs and values differ from the patient’s?
items.a: Using integrity
items.ex: The model lists using integrity when your beliefs and values differ from your patient’s.
w: Using perseverance
Perseverance appears in planning and evaluation because self-concept changes happen slowly.
Using creativity
Creativity is the attitude for planning interventions.
Using confidence
Confidence is the attitude for evaluating outcomes.

alt.q: Which attitude does the self-concept assessment model describe as displaying curiosity?
alt.a: Considering why a patient may have certain behaviors
alt.ex: Curiosity in assessment means considering why a patient may behave in certain ways.
w: Choosing the nursing diagnosis before the assessment
Curiosity explores causes of behavior; it does not presume a diagnosis.
Sharing personal values to build the relationship
Integrity, not sharing values, guides the nurse when values differ.
Waiting for the patient to explain all behaviors
Curiosity is an active stance of considering reasons for behavior.

items.q: Before caring for Mrs. Johnson after her mastectomy, Kathryn reviews literature on psychological adjustment and contacts the American Cancer Society. What does this preparation reflect?
items.a: Recognition that the surgery has psychosocial as well as physiological effects
items.ex: Kathryn recognized that mastectomy has many psychosocial as well as physiological implications and expanded her knowledge base.
w: A plan to refer all of the patient’s emotional care to others
Kathryn prepared to address psychosocial needs herself, not to hand them off.
A belief that the patient’s physical needs come last
Kathryn also reviewed physical care; she addressed both kinds of needs.
A need to confirm the patient’s medical diagnosis
The medical diagnosis was known; she sought to understand psychosocial adjustment.

alt.q: A nurse will care for a patient with new facial burns. Which preparation best builds the knowledge base for assessing the patient’s self-concept?
alt.a: Reviewing the impact of illness on self-concept and nonverbal signs of distress
alt.ex: The assessment knowledge base includes the impact of illness on self-concept and nonverbal indicators of distress.
w: Reviewing the unit’s staffing and visitor policies only
Staffing and visitors are environmental factors, not the self-concept knowledge base.
Reviewing the patient’s insurance and billing records
Billing records do not inform self-concept assessment.
Reviewing the patient’s laboratory values only
Lab values alone do not address psychosocial effects on self-concept.

items.q: A nurse prepares to assess self-concept in a patient recovering from trauma. Which finding is an environmental factor in the critical thinking model that could affect this assessment?
items.a: Frequent unplanned interruptions and excessive visitors
items.ex: Environmental factors include noise, excessive visitors, risk for lack of privacy, and unplanned interruptions.
w: Previous experience caring for patients with burns
Prior experience caring for such patients is part of the experience component.
Knowledge of therapeutic communication skills
Communication skills belong to the knowledge base component.
Agency policies and procedures for documentation
Agency policies are part of the standards component.

alt.q: Which item belongs to the experience component of the critical thinking model for self-concept?
alt.a: Personal or family illnesses that affected self-concept
alt.ex: The experience component includes personal experiences with altered self-concept and personal or family illnesses that affect it.
w: Risk for lack of privacy on the unit
Risk for lack of privacy is an environmental factor.
ANA standards for psychiatric/mental health nursing
ANA standards are part of the standards component.
Nonverbal indicators of patient distress
Nonverbal indicators of distress belong to the knowledge base.

items.q: Which self-concept issues should a nurse assess and clarify about themselves before caring for patients? Select all that apply.
o: Thoughts and feelings about lifestyle, health, and illness
Nurses clarify their own thoughts about lifestyle, health, and illness.
Awareness of how their nonverbal communication affects patients
Nonverbal communication affects patients and families, so nurses assess this awareness.
Ability to convey a nonjudgmental attitude
Conveying a nonjudgmental attitude toward patients and families is a listed self-assessment item.
Preconceived attitudes toward differences in self-esteem
Nurses examine preconceived attitudes toward differences in self-concept and self-esteem.
Ability to persuade patients to share the nurse’s values
Nurses examine how their values affect patients, not how to persuade patients to adopt them.
Preference for patients whose beliefs match their own
The goal is to accept differences in health beliefs, not to prefer similar patients.
items.ex: Nurses clarify their own attitudes, values, nonverbal communication, and ability to accept differences before caring for patients.

alt.q: A nursing student completes a self-assessment before a clinical rotation on a burn unit. Which questions fit the textbook’s self-assessment of self-concept issues? Select all that apply.
o: “Can I accept health beliefs and values that differ from mine?”
Ability to accept differences in health beliefs and values is a listed item.
“How do my personal values and expectations affect patients?”
Nurses examine how their values and expectations affect patients.
“How might my facial expressions affect patients and families?”
Awareness of how nonverbal communication affects patients is a listed item.
“How can I avoid caring for patients whose injuries upset me?”
Nurses anticipate and acknowledge reactions rather than avoid patients.
“How can I get patients to adopt my view of health?”
Nurses accept patients’ beliefs rather than convert them.
alt.ex: Self-assessment covers accepting differences, the effect of personal values, and awareness of nonverbal communication.

Self-concept stressors are part of the knowledge base.
Therapeutic communication skills
Therapeutic communication skills are in the knowledge base.

Developmental and cultural factors are listed in the knowledge base.

Noise and interruptions are environmental factors.
items.ex: The assessment knowledge base includes self-concept components, stressors, communication skills, and developmental and cultural factors.

alt.q: Which items does the self-concept assessment model list under environment? Select all that apply.

Risk for lack of privacy
Risk for lack of privacy is an environmental factor.
Unplanned interruptions

items.q: Which factors does the textbook say enhance a nurse’s own self-concept and professional identity? Select all that apply.
o: The public’s perception of nurses’ image
Public perception of nursing is listed as enhancing professional identity.
The nurse’s work environment
The work environment influences a nurse’s self-concept and professional identity.
The nurse’s education
Education is among the listed influences.
Professional, social, and cultural values
These values also shape a nurse’s professional identity.
The number of patients assigned per shift
Patient load is not one of the listed influences on professional identity.
Avoidance of interprofessional collaboration
Collaboration helps protect nurses from burnout; avoiding it is not listed as enhancing identity.
items.ex: Public perception, work environment, education, and professional, social, and cultural values enhance a nurse’s self-concept and identity.

alt.q: Which statements about nurses’ own self-concept are supported by the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Positive self-esteem helps protect nurses from burnout.
Positive self-esteem is listed as protective against burnout.
Counseling support services help prevent emotional exhaustion.
Counseling support services help protect nurses.
Education influences a nurse’s professional identity.
Education is among the factors that enhance professional identity.
A nurse’s own values have no effect on patients.
Nurses must assess how their personal values and expectations affect patients.
Burnout has little effect on the quality of patient care.
Protecting nurses from burnout assists them to deliver high-quality care.
alt.ex: Nurses’ self-esteem, support services, and education shape their identity and protect the quality of care.

items.q: Patients with a change in body appearance often watch the reactions of others to their wounds and scars closely.
items.a: True
items.ex: Patients closely watch others’ reactions to their wounds, so nurses must be aware of their own responses.
items.ww: The textbook stresses that patients are sensitive to the health care team’s verbal and nonverbal responses.

alt.q: Patients with altered appearance attend mainly to what nurses say, so the nurse’s facial expression during wound care has little effect.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Nonverbal behaviors convey caring; a shocked or disgusted expression contributes to a negative body image.
alt.ww: Patients are extremely sensitive to both verbal and nonverbal responses from the health care team.

items.q: A nurse’s acceptance of a patient with an altered self-concept can often be shown simply by sitting, listening, and forming a therapeutic relationship.
items.a: True
items.ex: Acceptance that promotes positive change often simply involves sitting and listening and forming a therapeutic relationship.
items.ww: The textbook describes listening and a therapeutic relationship as the core way acceptance is shown.

alt.q: A nurse’s acceptance has little influence on an altered self-concept; only formal counseling can promote positive change.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The nurse’s acceptance of a patient with an altered self-concept can promote positive change.
alt.ww: Nurses significantly affect patients by conveying genuine interest and acceptance.

items.q: Including self-concept and self-esteem issues in the planning and delivery of care influences positive patient outcomes.
items.a: True
items.ex: Health care providers need to understand how self-esteem affects outcomes and include it in care planning.
items.ww: The textbook directly states that addressing self-concept in care influences positive outcomes.

alt.q: Self-esteem has little effect on patient outcomes, so care planning can focus only on physical needs.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Providers must understand the degree to which self-esteem affects patient outcomes and include it in care.
alt.ww: Self-concept profoundly influences a person’s response to illness and patient outcomes.

items.q: When assessing self-concept and self-esteem, what should the nurse focus on first?
items.a: Each component of self-concept: identity, body image, and role performance
items.ex: Focus first on each component of self-concept, then determine the patient’s perceptions of them to reveal the level of self-esteem.
w: The patient’s level of self-esteem as rated on a scale
Self-esteem is revealed after assessing the patient’s perceptions of each component.
The patient’s coping resources and past coping patterns
Coping is assessed, but the components of self-concept are the first focus.
The family’s description of the patient’s personality
Family input is valuable, but the components of self-concept come first.

alt.q: How does a nurse determine a patient’s level of self-esteem during assessment?
alt.a: By determining the patient’s perceptions of identity, body image, and role performance
alt.ex: After focusing on each component, the patient’s perceptions of those components reveal the level of self-esteem.
w: By counting the behaviors from a list of altered self-concept signs
Behaviors are observed, but self-esteem is revealed through perceptions of the components.
By asking family members to rate the patient’s confidence
Family insights help, but the patient’s own perceptions reveal self-esteem.
By reviewing the patient’s medical diagnosis and prognosis
The medical diagnosis alone does not reveal the patient’s self-esteem.

items.q: On the first postoperative day after mastectomy, a patient is curled up in a darkened room, crying, and rates incisional pain 9 out of 10. She has not requested analgesia for 12 hours. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Offer and administer the prescribed analgesic for the pain
items.ex: Pain at 9 out of 10 is a priority; Kathryn relieved pain first, which allowed Mrs. Johnson to then discuss her feelings.
w: Begin a discussion about her feelings about her body image
Severe pain limits her ability to engage; managing pain comes first.
Encourage her to look at the incision to begin acceptance
Forcing confrontation with a body change before readiness delays acceptance.
Open the curtains and turn on the lights to lift her mood
Changing the room does not address the priority problem of severe pain.

alt.q: After the analgesic takes effect, Mrs. Johnson’s pain is 3 out of 10. What does Kathryn do before the physical assessment?
alt.a: Asks whether Mrs. Johnson is willing to talk about what she is feeling
alt.ex: Kathryn explained she wanted to hear what Mrs. Johnson was feeling before physical care and asked if she was willing to talk.
w: Asks Mr. Johnson to leave so the assessment stays private
Mrs. Johnson asked to have her husband remain, and Kathryn honored that.
Removes the dressing so Mrs. Johnson can see her incision
Mrs. Johnson was not ready to view the incision; forcing it delays acceptance.
Provides teaching about reconstruction options and timelines
She already felt overwhelmed by too much information; listening came first.

items.q: A patient expresses fear, uncertainty, and indecision. Which additional findings most support the nursing diagnosis Anxiety rather than Situational Low Self Esteem?
items.a: Increased muscle tension, shakiness, and restlessness
items.ex: Muscle tension, shakiness, feeling unsure, and restlessness form a cluster that suggests Anxiety.
w: Negative self-appraisal and inability to cope with events
Negative self-appraisal and inability to cope point to Situational Low Self Esteem.
Difficulty making decisions and feelings of uselessness
These findings support Situational Low Self Esteem rather than Anxiety.
Long-standing negative views of self since childhood
A long-standing negative self-view suggests Chronic Low Self Esteem.

alt.q: A patient states, “I can’t cope with any of this, and I can’t make even simple decisions anymore.” Which nursing diagnosis do these findings most support?
alt.a: Situational Low Self Esteem
alt.ex: Negative self-appraisal, inability to cope with events, and difficulty making decisions suggest Situational Low Self Esteem.
w: Anxiety
Anxiety is supported by findings such as muscle tension, shakiness, and restlessness.
Acute Pain
Acute Pain is supported by reports of pain, not by negative self-appraisal.
Disturbed Personal Identity
The findings describe coping and decision making, not confusion about identity.

items.q: A nurse suspects a patient is anxious. Which statement by the nurse best validates this nursing diagnosis?
items.a: “I noticed you jumped when I touched your arm. Are you feeling uneasy today?”
items.ex: Sharing observations and letting the patient verify perceptions validates the diagnosis and often yields more data.
w: “You seem anxious today, so I will ask the provider for a sedative.”
This acts on an unvalidated conclusion instead of letting the patient verify it.
“Everyone feels nervous in the hospital, so you shouldn’t worry.”
Reassurance dismisses feelings and does not let the patient verify perceptions.
“I have charted that you have anxiety, so the team will know.”
Documenting before validating skips the patient’s confirmation of the diagnosis.

alt.q: What is the main benefit of validating a nursing diagnosis by sharing observations with the patient?
alt.a: The patient often provides additional data that clarifies the situation.
alt.ex: Allowing the patient to verify perceptions often results in additional data that further clarifies the problem.
w: The patient accepts the diagnosis without further discussion.
Validation invites discussion; it does not seek passive acceptance.
The nurse no longer needs to collect assessment data.
Validation often produces more data, so assessment continues.
The diagnosis can be documented before the assessment.
Diagnoses are validated after assessment data are analyzed.

items.q: A patient with a new colostomy has refused to look at the stoma. Which finding best indicates that the patient is becoming receptive to accepting the change?
items.a: The patient asks how to empty the pouch.
items.ex: Asking how to manage an aspect of the change or looking at the changed area signals readiness to accept it.
w: The patient asks the nurse to keep the stoma covered.
Asking to keep it covered shows continued avoidance, not readiness.
The patient turns away during pouch changes.
Turning away suggests the patient is not yet ready to integrate the change.
The patient says the family will handle the pouch.
Handing off care suggests avoidance rather than acceptance.

alt.q: While Kathryn provides hygiene, she notices Mrs. Johnson glancing at the surgical area for the first time. Which response is most appropriate?
alt.a: Continue care without comment and let her look as she is comfortable
alt.ex: Kathryn chose not to comment and let Mrs. Johnson look as she was comfortable, respecting her level of acceptance.
w: Encourage her to look closely at the entire incision now
Forcing confrontation before the patient is ready likely delays acceptance.
Cover the area quickly so that she does not become upset
Covering the area interrupts the patient’s own early steps toward acceptance.
Point out that she is finally ready to view the incision
Calling attention to it may pressure her; Kathryn chose not to comment.

items.q: A patient who had a facial reconstruction begins asking how other people have adjusted to similar changes. Which action should the nurse take next?
items.a: Tell the patient about available support groups and offer to make the initial contact
items.ex: As the patient expresses readiness to integrate the change, share available support groups and offer to make the first contact.
w: Wait until after discharge to discuss support resources
Readiness is the cue to share resources; shortened stays make follow-up and referral essential.
Show the patient photographs of others with severe scarring
Forcing confrontation with change before the patient is ready can delay acceptance.
Tell the patient that most people adjust within a few weeks
Adjustment to major self-concept changes often takes 1 year or longer.

alt.q: Why are follow-up and referrals, including home care, essential for patients adapting to an altered body image after surgery?
alt.a: Shortened lengths of stay make these needs difficult to address in acute care.
alt.ex: Because hospital stays are short, body image adaptation often cannot be completed in acute care, so follow-up is essential.
w: Body image needs are not appropriate to address during acute care.
Acute care nurses do address body image; time is the limitation.
Home care nurses are the only nurses trained in body image care.
All nurses address body image; referral is needed because stays are short.
Patients cannot begin adapting until they return home.
Adaptation can begin in acute care, as Mrs. Johnson’s case shows.

items.q: A patient has Situational Low Self Esteem related to a recent job layoff. Which expected outcome is most appropriate?
items.a: Patient describes three areas of her life in which she is functioning well.
items.ex: Outcomes should be individualized, realistic, and measurable; naming three areas of good functioning shows improved self-esteem.
w: Patient will feel better about herself soon.
This outcome is vague and cannot be measured.
Patient will find a new job before discharge.
This is not realistic or within the patient’s control during care.
Patient will never think about the layoff again.
This is unrealistic and does not measure self-esteem.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient laid off from work best shows that an outcome for Situational Low Self Esteem has been met?
alt.a: “Losing my job does not reflect my worth as a person.”
alt.ex: Stating that the job loss is not reflective of personal worth is a listed outcome supporting self-esteem.
w: “I will never be able to work at that level again.”
This is negative self-appraisal, indicating low self-esteem persists.
“I’m sure the layoff happened because I’m not good enough.”
Linking the layoff to personal inadequacy shows continued low self-esteem.
“I don’t want to talk to anyone until I find new work.”
Withdrawal suggests the outcome has not been met.

items.q: Why does the nurse ask how a patient has dealt with stressors in the past?
items.a: Patients often use a familiar coping pattern for newly encountered stressors.
items.ex: Past coping gives insight into coping style because patients often apply familiar patterns to new stressors.
w: Past coping patterns always predict how a patient will cope now.
Patients do not address all issues the same way; patterns are often, not always, repeated.
Past coping patterns are required to choose a medical diagnosis.
Coping assessment informs nursing care, not the medical diagnosis.
Past coping patterns are healthy and should always be reinforced.
Some past patterns, such as alcohol use, create more problems.

alt.q: A patient says, “When things get bad, I usually have a few drinks to calm down.” What is the best interpretation of this coping pattern?
alt.a: It is likely to create additional stressors for the patient.
alt.ex: Using drugs or alcohol during times of stress often creates additional stressors, so this pattern is not healthy.
w: It is a healthy pattern because it reduces the patient’s stress.
Alcohol use during stress often creates more stressors, not healthy functioning.
It is unrelated to the patient’s self-concept.
Coping patterns affect self-concept and are part of the assessment.
It shows the patient has no coping resources at all.
The patient has a pattern, but it is maladaptive rather than absent.

items.q: A nurse plans to include a patient’s family in the plan of care for an altered self-concept. What should the nurse consider first?
items.a: The patient’s wishes for their involvement and cultural norms about decision making
items.ex: Before including family, consider the patient’s desires for their involvement and cultural norms about who makes decisions.
w: The family’s schedule and availability to attend teaching sessions
Availability matters later; the patient’s wishes and cultural norms come first.
Which family member lives closest to the patient’s home
Proximity is not the textbook’s first consideration.
Whether the family agrees with the health care provider’s plan
The patient’s wishes guide family involvement, not the family’s agreement with the plan.

alt.q: A patient asks the nurse not to share details of her body image concerns with her adult children. Which nurse response is most appropriate?
alt.a: Respect the request and include only the people the patient chooses
alt.ex: The patient’s desires for family involvement must be considered before including any family member or significant other.
w: Explain that family must be included for the plan to work
Family involvement depends on the patient’s wishes.
Share the concerns so the family can provide support
Sharing against the patient’s wishes violates her privacy and preferences.
Ask the children privately how to handle her concerns
Consulting family without consent disregards the patient’s request.

items.q: A young teacher visits a clinic with insomnia and anxiety. She reports little rest, a recent breakup and relocation, and heavy alcohol use. What do these data together most suggest?
items.a: Actual or potential self-concept disturbances
items.ex: Too little rest, simultaneous life changes, and excessive alcohol use together suggest actual or potential self-concept disturbances.
w: A normal adjustment that needs no follow-up
Several stressors with unhealthy practices put self-concept at risk and need follow-up.
A sleep disorder that is unrelated to self-concept
The cluster of lifestyle data points to self-concept risk, not just sleep.
Chronic low self-esteem dating from childhood
The data reflect recent life changes, not long-standing negative self-views.

alt.q: After identifying the teacher’s risky lifestyle practices, which action should the nurse take next?
alt.a: Determine how she views these lifestyle elements, then refer or teach as needed
alt.ex: Exploring how the patient views lifestyle elements builds insight; then make referrals or provide needed teaching.
w: Tell her to stop drinking alcohol before discussing anything else
Directing her without exploring her views does not build insight.
Document the findings and schedule a visit in 6 months
Waiting delays needed referral or teaching.
Advise her to move back to her previous home
The nurse helps the patient gain insight rather than prescribing life choices.

items.q: During evaluation, what are the key observational indicators of a patient’s self-concept?
items.a: Nonverbal behaviors
items.ex: Nonverbal behaviors, such as more frequent eye contact, are key observational indicators of self-concept.
w: Laboratory values
Laboratory values do not directly indicate self-concept.
Vital sign trends
Vital signs do not serve as key indicators of self-concept.
Length of hospital stay
Length of stay is not an indicator of self-concept.

alt.q: A patient who initially avoided eye contact now makes frequent eye contact during conversation. How should the nurse interpret this change?
alt.a: It shows a more positive self-concept.
alt.ex: Nonverbal behavior is a key indicator; increased eye contact demonstrates a more positive self-concept.
w: It shows increasing anxiety about discharge.
Increased eye contact reflects improved self-concept, not anxiety.
It shows the patient is hiding true feelings.
There is no basis to interpret improved eye contact as concealment.
It shows no meaningful change in self-concept.
Nonverbal changes are key indicators of self-concept.

items.q: Which behaviors suggest an altered self-concept? Select all that apply.
o: Avoidance of eye contact
Avoiding eye contact is a behavior suggestive of altered self-concept.
Slumped posture
Slumped posture is listed as suggestive of altered self-concept.
Being overly apologetic
Overly apologetic behavior suggests altered self-concept.
Difficulty making decisions
Difficulty making decisions is listed as suggestive of altered self-concept.
Readily offering opinions and ideas
Readily offering opinions reflects increasing self-esteem.
Participating actively in self-care
Adequate self-care indicates progress toward a positive self-concept.
items.ex: Avoiding eye contact, slumped posture, excessive apology, and indecision are behaviors suggestive of altered self-concept.

alt.q: A nurse assesses a patient after a disfiguring injury. Which findings should the nurse recognize as suggestive of an altered self-concept? Select all that apply.
o: Unkempt appearance
An unkempt appearance is listed as suggestive of altered self-concept.
Hesitant speech
Hesitant speech suggests altered self-concept.
Excessive dependence on others
Being excessively dependent is listed as suggestive of altered self-concept.
Self-harm behaviors
Self-harm behaviors are listed and require further assessment.
Making frequent eye contact
Frequent eye contact indicates a more positive self-concept.
Showing interest in daily events
Lack of interest, not interest, suggests altered self-concept.
alt.ex: Unkempt appearance, hesitant speech, excessive dependence, and self-harm suggest altered self-concept.

items.q: Which strategies are included in patient teaching for alterations in self-esteem? Select all that apply.
o: Explain how stressors influence self-esteem
Explaining the effect of stressors on self-esteem is a listed strategy.
Have the patient identify strengths and weaknesses and reinforce strengths
Identifying strengths and reinforcing successes is a listed strategy.
Discuss situations in which the patient’s stress may intensify
Discussing situations that may intensify stress is a listed strategy.
Explore coping resources the patient can apply now
Exploring coping resources for the current problem is a listed strategy.
Avoid mentioning depression or anxiety during sessions
Symptoms such as depression and anxiety should be incorporated into teaching plans.
Make care decisions for the patient to reduce stress
The nurse collaborates with the patient to build decision-making skills.
items.ex: Teaching explains stressors, reinforces strengths, anticipates stressful situations, and explores coping resources.

alt.q: A home care nurse uses teach-back to evaluate teaching about situational low self-esteem. Which prompts fit this evaluation? Select all that apply.
o: “Describe the new communication skills you have tried since we last met.”
This is a teach-back prompt for evaluating new communication skills.
“Tell me about the decisions about your care that you made this week.”
This evaluates the patient’s decision making.
“Which coping strategies are you using now?”
This evaluates current coping strategies.
“Do you understand everything I have taught you?”
A yes-or-no question does not use teach-back.
“Would you like me to make your care decisions this week?”
This undermines the goal of building the patient’s decision making.
alt.ex: Teach-back asks the patient to describe new skills, decisions, and coping strategies in their own words.

items.q: Which findings during evaluation indicate progress toward a more positive self-concept? Select all that apply.
o: Increased social interaction
Social interaction indicates progress in self-concept.
Adequate self-care
Adequate self-care indicates progress.
Acceptance of changes resulting from surgery
Accepting changes from illness or operations indicates progress.
More readily offering opinions and ideas
A hesitant patient offering views more readily reflects increasing self-esteem.
Increased reliance on staff for decisions
Excessive dependence suggests altered self-concept.
Continued refusal to look at the changed area
Avoiding the changed area shows that acceptance has not yet occurred.
items.ex: Social interaction, adequate self-care, acceptance of change, and offering opinions all indicate improving self-concept.

alt.q: Which findings in an older adult are evidence of self-esteem and self-efficacy? Select all that apply.
o: Investing in satisfying hobbies
Satisfying hobbies are evidence of self-esteem in older adults.
Engaging in physical exercise
Physical exercise is evidence of self-esteem and self-efficacy.
Exerting choices in daily life
Exerting choices reflects self-efficacy in older adults.
Withdrawing from usual social contacts
Withdrawal suggests altered self-concept rather than self-esteem.
Letting others make daily decisions
Exerting one’s own choices, not deferring them, reflects self-efficacy.
alt.ex: Hobbies, exercise, and exerting choices in daily life are evidence of self-esteem and self-efficacy in older adults.

items.q: Forcing a patient to confront a change in body appearance before the patient is ready will likely delay acceptance.
items.a: True
items.ex: Remain sensitive to the patient’s level of acceptance, because forcing confrontation before readiness likely delays it.
items.ww: The textbook warns that early forced confrontation delays, rather than speeds, acceptance.

alt.q: Having a patient view a changed body area as soon as possible after surgery speeds acceptance of the change.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Forcing confrontation with a change before the patient is ready will likely delay acceptance.
alt.ww: The nurse waits for signs of readiness, such as questions or looking at the area.

items.q: A single assessment finding can be relevant to more than one nursing diagnosis.
items.a: True
items.ex: Findings such as fear, indecision, and inadequacy can support both Anxiety and Situational Low Self Esteem.
items.ww: The textbook explains that cues often overlap, so the nurse must differentiate the underlying problems.

alt.q: Each assessment finding supports only one nursing diagnosis, so differentiating diagnoses is rarely necessary.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Findings can suggest more than one diagnosis, which guides the nurse to validate and differentiate the problems.
alt.ww: Overlapping cues, such as indecision and fear, require the nurse to differentiate between diagnoses.

items.q: Maintaining a patient’s privacy must be a priority of care, especially after trauma or major surgery.
items.a: True
items.ex: Patient privacy is essential, and protecting it is a priority, especially following trauma or major surgery.
items.ww: The textbook names privacy as a care priority because self-concept alterations are personal and private.

alt.q: Privacy is a lower priority after major surgery because frequent monitoring makes it difficult to protect.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Privacy must be a priority, especially after trauma or major surgery; nurses proactively resolve privacy risks.
alt.ww: Difficulty protecting privacy is a reason to be proactive, not to lower its priority.

items.q: Adjustment to major changes in self-concept can often take [[1 year|one year|a year]] or longer.
items.ex: Teach patients and families that a long adjustment period does not mean the patient is having a problem adjusting.

alt.q: The nurse teaches the family that adjusting to a major change in self-concept often takes 1 [[year]] or longer, which is not a sign of a problem.
alt.ex: Teach patients and families that a long adjustment period does not mean the patient is having a problem adjusting.

items: Assessment

items.q: A parent asks the nurse what most determines whether a preschooler keeps repeating a sexual behavior, such as touching the genitals in public. Which factor does the chapter identify?
items.a: How caregivers respond to the behavior
items.ex: Young children imitate others, and whether they repeat a sexual behavior is often related to how caregivers respond.
w: The child’s assigned sex at birth
Assigned sex does not determine whether a behavior is repeated; caregiver response does.
The number of siblings in the home
Family size is not named; children imitate others and react to caregiver responses.
The child’s eventual sexual orientation
Early sexual behavior is not indicative of sexual orientation.

alt.q: Which statement best describes how young children learn about sexuality?
alt.a: They learn through their senses, such as touch, and by imitating others
alt.ex: Young children are curious about physical differences, learn through the senses, and imitate other children and adults.
w: They learn mainly from formal sexual health lessons at school
School-based sexual health education targets older children, not the early years.
They learn mainly through puberty-related hormonal changes
Puberty occurs in the school-age years, not in infancy and early childhood.
They learn mainly from peer groups outside the family
Powerful peer groups characterize adolescence; young children imitate caregivers and other children.

items.q: The parent of a 9-year-old describes several behaviors noticed at home. Which behavior should the nurse identify as a problematic sexual behavior rather than typical sex play?
items.a: Planning and forcing a sexual act on a younger cousin
items.ex: Intrusive, planned, forced, or aggressive sexual acts are not part of typical childhood sex play and are problematic.
w: Asking questions about how bodies change at puberty
School-age children normally have questions about the physical and emotional aspects of sex.
Showing curiosity about differences between boys and girls
Curiosity about physical differences is a normal part of childhood sexual development.
Playing mostly with friends of the same sex
Preadolescent children often segregate by sex; this is expected.

alt.q: Which behavior by a school-age child is consistent with typical, normal childhood sex play?
alt.a: Curious looking during play with a same-age friend
alt.ex: Because school-age children remain curious, typical childhood sexual play is normal when it is not intrusive or forced.
w: Preoccupation with sexual activity throughout the day
School-age children do not normally obsess about sexual activity.
Attempting oral sex with a classmate
Advanced behaviors such as oral sex or intercourse are not typical of school-age children.
Aggressively pressuring a younger child into touching
Aggressive or forced acts are problematic sexual behaviors, not normal play.

items.q: Same-sex sexual behavior among preadolescents who segregate by sex is a reliable early indicator of their sexual orientation.
items.a: False
items.ex: Preadolescents often segregate by sex, which facilitates same-sex behavior that does not indicate sexual orientation.
items.ww: The chapter states that this early sexual behavior is not indicative of sexual orientation.

alt.q: Same-sex sexual behavior among preadolescents who segregate by sex does not indicate their sexual orientation.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Segregation by sex in preadolescence facilitates same-sex behavior, but this early behavior does not predict orientation.
alt.ww: Treating early same-sex play as a predictor of orientation contradicts the chapter, which says it is not indicative.

items.q: Why do school-age children often obtain inaccurate information about sex and bodily changes?
items.a: Parents often feel uncomfortable discussing these topics with them
items.ex: Parental discomfort leads children to turn to other youth, movies, song lyrics, the Internet, and television.
w: Schools are prohibited from discussing puberty with them
The chapter notes sex education is insufficient, not prohibited; parental discomfort drives the problem.
Children of this age have no questions about sex
School-age children do have questions about the physical and emotional aspects of sex.
Health care providers refuse to discuss puberty with them
Providers are not described as refusing; children turn away from uncomfortable parents.

alt.q: A parent says, “I just can’t bring myself to talk to my 10-year-old about puberty.” Which outcome is the nurse most concerned about?
alt.a: The child may rely on peers and media for misleading information
alt.ex: When parents avoid the topic, children often turn to other youth and media that give inaccurate information and troublesome values.
w: The child will be unable to enter puberty on schedule
Lack of discussion does not alter the physical timing of puberty.
The child will lose all curiosity about the body
Children remain curious; they seek information elsewhere.
The child will develop a fixed sexual orientation early
Parental silence is not linked to orientation; the concern is inaccurate information.

items.q: Which concern best captures the almost constant anxiety adolescents feel within their peer group?
items.a: “Am I normal, and will I be accepted?”
items.ex: Adolescents function within a powerful peer group with ongoing anxiety about being normal and being accepted.
w: “Will I be able to reproduce someday?”
Fertility is not the anxiety the chapter describes for adolescents.
“Is my body losing its attractiveness?”
Concern about declining attractiveness is described in middle adulthood.
“Will my partner stay now that the children have left?”
Relationship change after children leave home occurs later in adulthood.

alt.q: A 15-year-old repeatedly asks the school nurse whether their body changes are like everyone else’s. The nurse recognizes this as reflecting which typical adolescent concern?
alt.a: Worry about being normal and being accepted by peers
alt.ex: Within a powerful peer network, adolescents commonly worry whether they are normal and will be accepted.
w: Worry about loss of sexual function with aging
Age-related sexual changes are concerns of middle and older adulthood.
Worry about the onset of menopause
Menopause is a midlife and older-adult change, not an adolescent concern.
Worry about adjusting to an empty nest
Adjusting to children leaving home occurs later in adult life.

items.q: An adolescent needs accurate information to make sound decisions. Which topics does the chapter identify as information adolescents need? Select all that apply.
o: Body changes
Adolescents need accurate information about the changes in their bodies.
Emotional responses within sexual relationships
Emotional aspects of sexual relationships are a listed need.
Contraception and pregnancy
Contraception and pregnancy are among the topics adolescents need to understand.
Sexually transmitted infections
STIs are a listed topic for adolescent education.
Managing postejaculatory refractory periods
A longer refractory period is an aging change in men, not an adolescent topic.
Coping with decreasing estrogen levels
Decreasing estrogen is a perimenopausal change in middle adulthood.
items.ex: Adolescents need accurate information on body changes, sexual activity and identity, emotional responses, STIs, contraception, and pregnancy.

alt.q: A school nurse is planning a comprehensive sexual health program for adolescents. Which statements reflect the chapter’s guidance? Select all that apply.
o: Include sexual identity and emotional responses within relationships
Adolescents need information on sexual identity and emotional responses as well as STIs and pregnancy.
Address physical, mental/emotional, social, and sexual domains together
These health domains are interrelated, so education must be comprehensive in scope and sequence.
Focus the program solely on STI/HIV and pregnancy facts
Goals cannot be achieved by focusing education solely on STI/HIV and pregnancy.
Rely on social media sites as the main teaching resource
Adolescents often land on unreliable, inaccurate social media sites.
Include accurate information about contraception
Contraception is one of the topics adolescents need accurate information about.
alt.ex: Adolescent sexual health education must be comprehensive across interrelated domains, not limited to STI/HIV and pregnancy facts.

items.q: What does the chapter state about adolescents with developmental disabilities and sexual health education?
items.a: They are less likely to receive developmentally appropriate sexual education
items.ex: Many such adolescents wish to date, yet they are less likely to have been given developmentally appropriate sexual education.
w: They rarely wish to date or have intimate relationships
Many adolescents with developmental disabilities may wish to date or be in intimate relationships.
They are more likely than peers to receive all 20 CDC topics
Sexual health education is insufficient in many areas, especially for youth with disabilities.
Their sexual development is unaffected by their condition
Developmental disabilities and medical conditions can affect children’s sexual development.

alt.q: The parent of a 16-year-old with a developmental disability says, “My son wants to ask a classmate on a date. Is that unusual?” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Many such teens want to date; he needs sexual education suited to his development.”
alt.ex: Many adolescents with developmental disabilities wish to date and need developmentally appropriate sexual education.
w: “That is unusual, so try to redirect him to other activities.”
Wanting to date is common among adolescents with developmental disabilities.
“He will not need sexual education until he is an adult.”
These youth are already underserved and need developmentally appropriate education now.
“His disability means his sexual development will not progress.”
Disabilities can affect sexual development but do not stop it.

items.q: Higher rates of STIs in some racial or ethnic minority groups are caused by social conditions such as poverty, income gaps, fewer jobs, and low education levels.
items.a: True
items.ex: The chapter emphasizes that these disparities stem from social conditions that make staying sexually healthy harder, not from heritage.
items.ww: Attributing the higher rates to ethnicity itself contradicts the chapter, which names social conditions as the cause.

alt.q: Higher rates of STIs in some racial or ethnic minority groups are caused mainly by their ethnicity or genetic heritage.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The chapter states the higher rates are not caused by ethnicity or heritage but by social conditions such as poverty.
alt.ww: Social conditions such as poverty, income gaps, fewer jobs, and low education levels drive the disparity, so this statement is wrong.

items.q: The nurse is teaching parents about adolescent sexuality. Which statement by a parent shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “Even if we guide her well, she will make her own choices and be accountable for them.”
items.ex: Parents need to know that, even with the best guidance, adolescents make their own decisions and must be held accountable.
w: “If we never mention sex, she will not become curious about it.”
Adolescence is marked by increased sexual interest; parents should provide factual information.
“Risky habits she starts now will usually fade on their own later.”
A pattern of risk-taking established in adolescence tends to continue throughout life.
“We can assume she agrees we have already covered these issues.”
Teens and parents often disagree about whether they talked, so clear communication is needed.

alt.q: A father says, “My son is just experimenting. Whatever risks he takes now won’t matter once he grows up.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Risk-taking patterns started in adolescence tend to continue into adult life.”
alt.ex: If an adolescent practices a pattern of risk-taking behavior, it tends to be established and continue throughout life.
w: “You are right; adolescent risk-taking rarely affects adult behavior.”
This contradicts the chapter, which says risk patterns tend to persist.
“Experimenting is harmless as long as he avoids social media.”
Risky sexual behaviors can cause STIs and unintended pregnancy regardless of social media use.
“He is too young to make his own decisions about sex.”
Adolescents do make their own decisions and need to be held accountable for them.

items.q: A 50-year-old perimenopausal woman reports pain during intercourse. Which physiological change most likely explains this symptom?
items.a: Decreasing estrogen reducing vaginal lubrication and elasticity
items.ex: Falling estrogen in perimenopause diminishes vaginal lubrication and elasticity, often leading to dyspareunia.
w: Increasing estrogen thickening the vaginal walls
Estrogen decreases, not increases, during perimenopause.
Increased pelvic blood flow from rising hormone levels
Increased pelvic blood flow occurs in the second trimester of pregnancy.
A shortened excitement phase with faster orgasm
With aging the excitement phase lengthens and orgasm takes longer.

alt.q: Which change is a result of decreasing estrogen levels in perimenopausal women?
alt.a: Decreased desire for sexual activity
alt.ex: Decreasing estrogen may decrease sexual desire and reduces vaginal lubrication and elasticity.
w: Increased vaginal elasticity
Decreasing estrogen decreases vaginal elasticity.
Increased vaginal lubrication
Decreasing estrogen diminishes vaginal lubrication.
Earlier onset of menarche
Menarche is the onset of menstruation in girls, not a perimenopausal change.

items.q: Pain that occurs during sexual intercourse is called [[dyspareunia]].
items.ex: Dyspareunia often follows the decreased vaginal lubrication and elasticity caused by falling estrogen levels in perimenopause.

alt.q: A perimenopausal woman with reduced vaginal lubrication who reports painful intercourse is experiencing [[dyspareunia]].
alt.ex: Dyspareunia often follows the decreased vaginal lubrication and elasticity caused by falling estrogen levels in perimenopause.

items.q: As men move through middle adulthood, which sexual change does the chapter describe as normal?
items.a: A longer postejaculatory refractory period
items.ex: Aging men commonly experience an increased postejaculatory refractory period and delayed ejaculation.
w: A shorter postejaculatory refractory period
The refractory period increases, not decreases, with age.
Earlier, more rapid ejaculation
Ejaculation tends to be delayed with aging.
Increased levels of sex hormones
Both males and females experience reduced availability of sex hormones with aging.

alt.q: A 58-year-old man says, “It takes me longer to ejaculate than it used to.” How should the nurse interpret this statement?
alt.a: It is a normal age-related change in sexual function
alt.ex: Delayed ejaculation and a longer refractory period are expected changes as men age.
w: It is an early sign of prostate cancer
The chapter describes delayed ejaculation as a normal aging change, not a cancer sign.
It indicates a sexually transmitted infection
STIs are not associated with this normal aging change.
It means his testosterone has risen sharply
Sex hormone availability decreases with aging.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman tells the nurse that intercourse has become uncomfortable since her periods became irregular. Which nursing intervention is most appropriate?
items.a: Provide anticipatory guidance and suggest vaginal lubrication
items.ex: Anticipatory guidance about normal changes, vaginal lubrication, and time for caressing ease concerns about sexual functioning.
w: Advise her to stop sexual activity until menopause ends
Avoidance is not recommended; lubrication and guidance address the normal change.
Tell her the discomfort is psychological and will pass
Discomfort reflects real estrogen-related changes in lubrication and elasticity.
Recommend shorter encounters with less foreplay
The chapter recommends creating time for caressing and tenderness, not less.

alt.q: Which teaching helps ease a middle-aged couple’s concerns about age-related changes in sexual functioning?
alt.a: Allow more time for caressing and tenderness
alt.ex: Creating time for caressing and tenderness, using lubrication, and anticipatory guidance ease concerns about normal changes.
w: Avoid using vaginal lubricants
Vaginal lubrication is specifically recommended for these changes.
Treat the changes as signs of serious illness
These are normal age-related changes, best addressed with anticipatory guidance.
Limit intimacy to brief encounters
Brief encounters work against the extra time older partners often need.

items.q: When children move away from home, intimate relationships between partners usually change.
items.a: True
items.ex: Children leaving home brings either renewed intimacy or the realization that partners no longer share interests.
items.ww: The chapter states that in either case intimate relationships usually change when children leave home.

alt.q: When children move away from home, partners’ intimate relationships usually stay the same.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The empty nest usually changes relationships, leading to renewed intimacy or to partners realizing they lack common interests.
alt.ww: This is wrong because the chapter says that when children leave home, intimate relationships usually change.

items.q: Which statements about sexuality in older adults are accurate according to the chapter? Select all that apply.
o: Continued interest in sex is usually associated with good physical health
Box 34.1 links continued sexual interest in later life with good physical health.
Problems with the aging sexual response often relate to illness or medications
Illnesses and medication side effects commonly underlie these problems.
Older adults are often reluctant to discuss sexual problems with providers
Reluctance to raise sexual concerns is common among older adults.
Most older adults stop being sexually active
Many older adults remain sexually active.
Extended care facilities usually increase residents’ privacy
Residents of extended care facilities often lose their privacy.
items.ex: Box 34.1 shows that older adults often remain sexually active, are reluctant to raise concerns, and face illness- and medication-related changes.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing sexuality in older adults. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Treatments for sexual dysfunction help many stay sexually active
Increased availability of treatments such as those for erectile dysfunction supports continued activity.
Assisted-living residents often have more privacy and may live as couples
Assisted-living facilities offer more privacy than extended care facilities.

Older adults engage in high-risk encounters, and HIV and STI rates are steadily rising.
“It might be best to avoid a sexual relationship at your age.”
Sexual activity is normal in later years; the nurse should convey that nonjudgmentally.

The chapter attributes the risk to lack of protection, not immune status.

items.q: Which sexual changes are normal with aging? Select all that apply.

Refractory time following orgasm lengthens with age.

Erections in older men are often less firm and shorter lasting.
Availability of sex hormones increases
Both males and females experience reduced availability of sex hormones.

Women usually do not have difficulty unless a medical condition impairs sexual activity.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching an older couple about normal sexual changes with aging. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.

Older men often have less firm, shorter-lasting erections.

Refractory time after orgasm becomes longer with aging.

Women usually maintain sexual function unless a medical condition interferes.

It usually takes longer to reach orgasm with aging.
alt.ex: Aging slows arousal and orgasm, lengthens recovery, and softens erections, but women usually keep sexual function unless illness interferes.

Estrogen levels decline, not rise, after menopause.

Menopause involves cessation of periods; incontinence does not restore them.

Self-disclosure is not the purpose; the goal is open, supportive relationships.

items.a: Ask whether he is still taking the medication as prescribed
items.ex: It is important to ask whether patients continue to take medications that are causing sexual side effects.
w: Tell him the effect is unrelated to his medication
Antihypertensives commonly cause sexual dysfunction.
Advise him to stop the medication right away
Stopping is not the nurse’s decision; assess adherence and inform the provider.
Reassure him and change the subject to his diet
Avoiding the concern misses an adherence risk that needs assessment.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching about a new antidepressant. Which approach is most likely to improve adherence?
alt.a: Discuss possible sexual side effects with both partners
alt.ex: Patients adhere better when sexual side effects are discussed with both partners and they make an informed decision.
w: Avoid mentioning sexual side effects to prevent worry
Omitting side effects prevents an informed decision and reduces adherence.
Discuss side effects only if the patient raises them
The chapter directs nurses to include sexual side effects in teaching.
Tell the patient sexual effects never occur with antidepressants
Antidepressants are a common cause of sexual dysfunction.

items.q: A patient is more likely to adhere to a treatment plan when the nurse discusses medication-related sexual side effects with both partners.
items.a: True
items.ex: Discussing sexual side effects with both partners allows an informed decision and improves adherence.
items.ww: The chapter states patients adhere better when sexual side effects are discussed with both partners.

alt.q: To protect adherence, nurses should avoid discussing a medication’s sexual side effects with the patient’s partner.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Including both partners in discussing sexual side effects supports informed decisions and improves adherence.
alt.ww: Avoiding the discussion is wrong because the chapter says adherence improves when both partners are informed.

items.q: Menarche is occurring at an earlier age in the United States.

items.ex: The chapter notes the onset of the menstrual cycle in girls is occurring earlier, a hormonally driven developmental stressor.
items.ww: The chapter states menarche is occurring at an earlier, not later, age in the United States.

alt.q: Menarche is occurring at a later age in the United States than in the past.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Menarche, the onset of the menstrual cycle, is occurring at an earlier age in the United States.
alt.ww: This is wrong because the chapter states menarche is occurring earlier, not later.

items.q: The onset of the menstrual cycle in girls is called [[menarche]].

alt.q: A 10-year-old girl having her first menstrual period is experiencing [[menarche]].
alt.ex: Menarche is a hormonally stimulated developmental change and a stressor affecting sexuality, now occurring earlier in the United States.

items.q: A nurse is teaching adolescents how to reduce their risk of STIs and unplanned pregnancy. Which strategy should the nurse include?
items.a: Consistent use of latex condoms
items.ex: Mutually monogamous relationships, delayed sexual debut, and consistent latex condom use reduce STI and unplanned pregnancy risk.
w: Occasional use of latex condoms
Protection requires consistent, not occasional, condom use.
Earlier sexual debut
A delayed sexual debut, not an earlier one, reduces risk.
Multiple short-term partners
Mutually monogamous relationships reduce risk; multiple partners increase it.

alt.q: Which statement by an adolescent shows understanding of teaching about STI prevention?
alt.a: “Waiting to have sex and staying with one faithful partner lower my risk.”
alt.ex: Delayed sexual debut and mutually monogamous relationships, plus consistent latex condoms, reduce STI risk.
w: “STIs spread only through vaginal sex, so oral sex is safe.”
STIs spread through oral, anal, or vaginal sexual contact.
“Using condoms now and then is enough to protect me.”
Condom use must be consistent to reduce risk.
“Having several partners is fine if they are my age.”
Mutual monogamy, not partner age, reduces risk.

items.q: A woman arrives at the clinic with her partner, who answers all questions for her and refuses to leave the room. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Arrange to interview the woman privately
items.ex: Controlling behaviors suggest violence; interview privately because a patient will rarely admit abuse with the abuser present.
w: Ask the woman about abuse in front of her partner
A patient will probably not admit abuse with the abuser present.
Document that the partner seems supportive
Speaking for the person and refusing to leave are controlling behaviors suggesting violence.
Discharge her quickly to avoid a confrontation
Patient safety is the most important factor; suspected violence must be assessed.

alt.q: While interviewing a patient privately, the nurse suspects sexual abuse. Which question is most appropriate?
alt.a: “Are you in a relationship in which someone is hurting you?”
alt.ex: Questions about suspected abuse should be direct yet compassionate.
w: “Why haven’t you left the person who hurts you?”
This question blames the patient rather than being compassionate.
“Did you do something to cause these injuries?”
This implies fault and discourages disclosure.
“Is everything fine at home, as I assume it is?”
This leading question is neither direct nor open to disclosure.

items.q: Which findings in an adult patient suggest possible current or past sexual violence? Select all that apply.
o: Wounds that do not match the patient’s story
Table 34.1 lists wounds inconsistent with the patient’s account.
Multiple bruises in various stages of healing
Bruises in different stages of healing suggest repeated injury.
Fractures of the face, nose, ribs, or arms
Table 34.1 lists these fractures as possible signs in adults.
Depression and panic attacks
Depression and panic attacks are listed behavioral signs in adults.
A single bruise consistent with a reported fall
An injury that matches the patient’s story is not a listed warning sign.
items.ex: Table 34.1 lists physical signs such as mismatched wounds, bruises in different healing stages, and fractures, plus behavioral signs like depression.

alt.q: Which findings in a child suggest possible sexual violence? Select all that apply.
o: Bruises, bleeding, or irritation of the external genitalia
Table 34.1 lists genital bruising, bleeding, or irritation in children.
Recurrent urinary tract infections
Recurrent UTIs are a listed physical sign in children.
Excessive masturbation or sexual acting out
These behaviors are listed signs in children.
Poor school performance and peer relationships
Table 34.1 lists poor school performance and peer relationships.
Age-appropriate curiosity about body differences
Curiosity about physical differences is normal in childhood.
alt.ex: Signs in children include genital injury, recurrent UTIs, sexual acting out, and poor school and peer functioning.

items.q: Which statement about the influence of society on sexuality is accurate?
items.a: Society shapes sexual values and attitudes and supports specific expressions of sexuality
items.ex: Each cultural and social group has rules and norms that guide sexual behavior, sexual health, and willingness to discuss it.
w: Society has little effect compared with a person’s biology
The chapter states society plays a powerful role in shaping sexual values and attitudes.
Cultural norms affect partner choice but not sexual frequency
Cultural norms influence how often people have sex as well as partner choice.
All cultural groups share one set of rules for sexual behavior
Each cultural and social group has its own set of rules and norms.

alt.q: According to the chapter, cultural norms influence which aspect of sexuality?
alt.a: How people find and choose partners and how often they have sex
alt.ex: Cultural norms influence how people find partners, whom they choose, how they relate, how often they have sex, and what they do.
w: Only the age at which puberty physically begins
Puberty timing is hormonal; the chapter lists partner and behavior norms.
Only whether a person can reproduce
Reproductive capability is biological, not a cultural norm.
Only the sex a person is assigned at birth
Assigned sex is given at birth and is not what cultural norms govern.

items.q: In the United States, which group has the highest rate of HIV infection?

Older adults have rising STI rates but not the highest HIV rate.

Asian students were less likely than other groups to engage in risky sexual behaviors.

w: Women older than 50 years
This group is not identified as having the highest rate.

Abstinent adolescents are not at sexual risk for HIV.
Married heterosexual couples
This group is not identified as having the highest rate.

items.q: According to Box 34.2, which racial or ethnic group has the largest number of HIV diagnoses in the United States?

Hispanic/Latino individuals rank second in number of diagnoses.
White individuals

Asian individuals

items.ex: Participants linked HIV disparities to insurance, access, environmental hazards, poverty, unemployment, mistrust, and few African American professionals.

items.q: The CDC system that monitors health risk behaviors contributing to the leading causes of death and disability among youth is the [[Youth Risk Behavior Surveillance System|YRBSS]].

Substance use combined with sex increases risk.

LGBQIA+ students were more likely to have been forced.

Asian individuals are not named as having the largest incidence.

Programs target the most affected communities, not the nurse’s background.

items.q: A nurse is about to discuss contraception and STI prevention with a newly admitted patient. According to Box 34.2, what should the nurse do first?
items.a: Establish a therapeutic relationship with the patient
items.ex: Box 34.2 directs nurses to establish a therapeutic relationship with the patient and family before discussing sexual health.
w: Give written materials and leave the room
Written materials support teaching but come after a therapeutic relationship is established.
Order combined HIV and STI laboratory tests
Ordering tests is not the nurse’s first step and does not build trust.

Detailed sexual questions should follow establishing a therapeutic relationship.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of person-centered sexual health care?

w: “I should cover sexual health in the first minute of the admission.”
A therapeutic relationship should come before discussing sexual health.
“I only need to give teaching to female patients.”
Both males and females need written and verbal information.
“Verbal teaching alone is enough for every patient.”
Box 34.2 calls for both written and verbal information.

items.q: A Spanish-speaking patient with limited English needs teaching about contraception and HIV testing. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Provide written and verbal information in Spanish
items.ex: Box 34.2 recommends written and verbal information in the patient’s primary language for both males and females.
w: Provide written information in English only
Information should be in the patient’s primary language.
Provide verbal information only, in English
Both written and verbal information in the primary language are recommended.
Delay teaching until the patient learns English
Teaching should not be delayed; provide it in the primary language.

alt.q: Which person-centered strategy does Box 34.2 recommend for HIV risk-reduction education?
alt.a: Culture-specific and bilingual multimedia community education
alt.ex: Culture-specific, bilingual multimedia and community education promote HIV risk reduction.
w: A single English-language pamphlet for all groups
Education should be culture-specific and bilingual.
Education limited to hospitalized patients
The box calls for community education.
Teaching directed only at female patients
Both males and females should receive information.

items.q: A nurse at a community clinic wants more patients to accept HIV testing. Which strategy is best?
items.a: Offer combined laboratory work for STIs and HIV

w: Offer HIV testing only at hospital emergency departments
The box recommends increasing testing at community clinics.
Test only patients who request HIV testing by name
Waiting for requests does not promote acceptance; combined testing does.
Require a separate visit for each sexually transmitted infection
Combining STI and HIV lab work, not separating it, promotes acceptance.

alt.q: Why does Box 34.2 recommend offering combined laboratory work for STIs and HIV at community clinics?

alt.ex: Combining STI and HIV lab work at community clinics is meant to increase acceptance of HIV testing.
w: To reduce the need for patient consent
Combining tests does not remove consent; its purpose is acceptance.
To replace the need for patient teaching
Teaching is still needed; combined testing promotes acceptance.
To limit testing to high-risk adults only
The aim is to increase testing and acceptance, not restrict it.

Increase HIV testing at community clinics
Increasing community clinic HIV testing is listed.
Discuss sexual health before building a therapeutic relationship
A therapeutic relationship should come before discussing sexual health.
Give contraception information only to female patients
Both males and females should receive information.
items.ex: Box 34.2 emphasizes trust first, primary-language teaching for all, adolescent skills, community testing, culture-specific education, and supportive policy.

Give written and verbal information in Spanish
Information should be in the primary language.
