items.q: Why do nurses often avoid discussing sexual issues with patients?
items.a: They lack information or hold values different from their patients
items.ex: Sexuality is emotionally charged, and nurses often avoid it because they lack information or have different values.
w: Patients rarely have sexual concerns to share
Patients often share concerns when sexuality is addressed in a relaxed manner.
Sexual health is unrelated to physical health
Sexuality and physical health are connected, as the chapter emphasizes.
Agency policies forbid discussing sexuality
Policies are not cited; lack of information and differing values are.

alt.q: A nurse avoids asking a patient about sexual concerns because the patient’s lifestyle conflicts with the nurse’s values. Which reason for avoidance does this illustrate?
alt.a: Holding values that differ from the patient’s
alt.ex: Nurses often avoid sexual topics because they lack information or have values different from their patients.
w: Lacking knowledge of sexual health
This scenario centers on conflicting values, not missing knowledge.
Lacking organizational support
Organizational support is a perceived barrier not described in this scenario.
Lacking time during the shift
Time is a perceived barrier not described in this scenario.

items.q: What is the likely consequence when a nurse is uncomfortable discussing topics related to sexuality?
items.a: The patient is unlikely to share sexual concerns
items.ex: If the nurse is uncomfortable discussing sexuality, the patient is unlikely to share sexual concerns.
w: The patient will share more concerns to ease tension
Nurse discomfort discourages, not encourages, patient disclosure.
The patient will raise concerns with family instead
The chapter states the patient is unlikely to share, not that they redirect.
The patient will be unaffected by the nurse’s comfort
The nurse’s comfort directly affects whether the patient shares concerns.

alt.q: A nurse appears tense and quickly changes the subject when a patient mentions intimacy. Which outcome is most likely?
alt.a: The patient withholds further sexual concerns
alt.ex: Nurse discomfort makes patients unlikely to share sexual concerns.
w: The patient describes concerns in more detail
Visible discomfort discourages patients from sharing.
The patient asks for a sexual health referral
Discomfort tends to shut down, not open, the discussion.
The patient feels reassured about the topic
Avoidance conveys discomfort, not reassurance.

items.q: A nursing student realizes they feel very uncomfortable discussing sexuality with patients. What should the student do first?
items.a: Explore their personal level of discomfort and plan how to address it
items.ex: Nurses need to explore their personal level of discomfort and develop a plan to address it.
w: Avoid the topic until a patient raises it directly
Avoidance leaves concerns unaddressed; patients may hesitate to raise them.
Ask another nurse to handle all sexual topics permanently
Referral may be needed for specific concerns, but discomfort itself must be addressed.
Hide the discomfort and proceed with a script
The discomfort should be explored and addressed, not hidden.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of preparing to discuss sexuality with patients?
alt.a: “I need to examine my own beliefs about sexuality before discussing it with patients.”
alt.ex: Nurses need to be aware of their personal beliefs before discussing sexuality with patients.
w: “My own beliefs are irrelevant when I talk about sexuality.”
Personal beliefs influence these discussions and must be examined.
“I should wait until patients bring up sexual topics themselves.”
Patients often hesitate, so nurses should address sexuality.
“I can skip this topic if it makes me uncomfortable.”
Discomfort should be explored and addressed, not used to avoid the topic.

items.q: Sexual assessment and person-centered interventions related to sexuality are consistently adopted throughout health care.
items.a: False
items.ex: Although sexuality is a significant part of each person, sexual assessment and interventions are not always adopted.
items.ww: The chapter states that sexual assessment and person-centered interventions are not always adopted in health care.

alt.q: Despite the importance of sexuality, sexual assessment and person-centered interventions are not always adopted in health care.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Factors such as knowledge, attitudes, comfort, and perceived barriers limit sexual health care.
alt.ww: Claiming they are always adopted is wrong; the chapter says they are not always adopted.

items.q: The area of sexuality is often emotionally charged for both nurses and patients.
items.a: True
items.ex: Because sexuality is emotionally charged for both, nurses must examine their own discomfort and beliefs.
items.ww: The chapter describes sexuality as emotionally charged for both nurses and patients.

alt.q: Sexuality is emotionally charged for patients but rarely for nurses.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Sexuality is often emotionally charged for both nurses and patients.
alt.ww: This is wrong because nurses also find the topic emotionally charged and often avoid it.

items.q: Patients who hesitate to raise sexual concerns often share their feelings when a nurse addresses sexuality in a relaxed, matter-of-fact manner.
items.a: True
items.ex: A relaxed, matter-of-fact approach helps hesitant patients share their sexual concerns.
items.ww: The chapter says patients often share feelings when sexuality is addressed in a relaxed, matter-of-fact manner.

alt.q: Nurses should wait for patients to bring up sexual concerns, because raising the topic makes patients less willing to share.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients may hesitate to raise concerns but often share when the nurse addresses sexuality in a relaxed, matter-of-fact way.
alt.ww: Waiting is wrong; patients often hesitate, so the nurse should raise the topic matter-of-factly.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient newly diagnosed with diabetes. Which statement by the nurse best opens a discussion of sexual health?
items.a: “Many people with diabetes notice changes in sexual function. Have you had any concerns?”
items.ex: A relaxed, matter-of-fact approach that normalizes the topic encourages hesitant patients to share.
w: “You probably don’t have any sexual problems, do you?”
This leading question discourages disclosure.
“I have to ask this, but it’s really none of my business.”
This conveys discomfort and implies the topic is unimportant.
“We don’t usually talk about sex unless you bring it up.”
This places the burden on a hesitant patient and shuts down discussion.

alt.q: A nurse is completing an admission history with a patient starting antihypertensive therapy. Which approach to sexual health is best?
alt.a: Raise sexual function calmly as a routine part of the history
alt.ex: Addressing sexuality in a relaxed, matter-of-fact manner helps patients share concerns.
w: Skip the topic unless the patient appears distressed
Patients are often hesitant; the nurse should raise the topic.
Lower the voice and apologize before asking
Apologizing conveys discomfort, making the patient less likely to share.
Ask the patient’s visitor whether there are problems
Sexual concerns should be discussed with the patient privately.

items.q: A patient asks the nurse a detailed question about a sexual concern that the nurse does not have the knowledge to answer. Which action is best?
items.a: Arrange a consultation with a professional who specializes in this area
items.ex: Nurses who lack comfort or knowledge for a patient’s concern should be prepared to consult a specialist.
w: Change the subject to the patient’s other health needs
Avoiding the concern leaves it unaddressed.
Give the best guess to avoid disappointing the patient
Guessing risks giving inaccurate information.
Tell the patient the concern is not a nursing issue
Sexual health is part of holistic nursing care.

alt.q: When should a nurse be prepared to make a consultation to another professional about a patient’s sexual concern?
alt.a: When the nurse is uncomfortable or lacks the knowledge to address it
alt.ex: If you are not comfortable or lack knowledge to discuss a concern, consult a professional who specializes in this area.
w: Only when the patient is older than 65 years
Age is not the criterion; nurse comfort and knowledge are.
Only after the patient has asked the nurse twice
Consultation depends on the nurse’s ability, not repeated requests.
Whenever a patient mentions any sexual topic
Many concerns can be addressed by the nurse directly.

items.q: A patient in a busy emergency department begins to mention a sexual concern. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Move the conversation to a quiet, private area
items.ex: Patients are more comfortable discussing sexual concerns in a quiet, private environment than a busy emergency room.
w: Continue the discussion at the busy nursing station
A busy, public setting discourages patients from sharing.
Ask the patient to save the concern for another visit
Postponing may cause the concern to go unaddressed.
Invite family members in to support the patient
Privacy, not added listeners, helps patients discuss sexual concerns.

alt.q: Which environment is most likely to help a patient feel comfortable discussing sexual concerns?
alt.a: A quiet, private room
alt.ex: The health care environment affects comfort; quiet, private settings encourage sharing.
w: A busy emergency department bay
Busy settings make patients less comfortable discussing sexual concerns.
A shared room with the curtain open
Lack of privacy discourages disclosure.
A hallway during shift change
Public, busy areas undermine privacy and comfort.

items.q: To feel comfortable addressing sexuality, nurses use [[therapeutic communication]] skills along with knowledge about all aspects of sexuality.
items.ex: Therapeutic communication skills and sexual knowledge help nurses address sexuality comfortably.

alt.q: Along with knowledge of sexuality, nurses rely on [[therapeutic communication]] skills to discuss sexual concerns comfortably.
alt.ex: Therapeutic communication skills and sexual knowledge help nurses address sexuality comfortably.

items.q: A 74-year-old patient seems embarrassed when the nurse begins a sexual health assessment. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Many people your age remain sexually active. Do you have any concerns about intimacy?”
items.ex: Older adults are often reluctant to discuss sexual problems; a nonjudgmental attitude conveys that sexual activity in later years is normal.
w: “At your age, I assume this topic doesn’t apply to you.”
Many older adults remain sexually active; this assumption is judgmental.
“Let’s skip this, since older adults rarely have sexual concerns.”
Older adults do have concerns but are often reluctant to raise them.
“You should talk about this with your children first.”
Sexual concerns are discussed with the patient, not routed through family.

alt.q: Which nursing approach best supports sexual health discussions with older adults?
alt.a: Maintain a nonjudgmental attitude and convey that sexual activity is normal in later years
alt.ex: Older adults are often reluctant to discuss sexual problems, so nurses convey acceptance and normalcy.
w: Wait for older adults to raise sexual concerns themselves
Older adults are often reluctant to raise these concerns.
Assume older adults are no longer sexually active
Many older adults remain sexually active.
Limit discussion to medication side effects only
Assess sexual interest, functioning, and perception of sexual health broadly.

items.q: Which actions help a nurse prepare to discuss sexual issues with patients? Select all that apply.
o: Becoming aware of personal beliefs about sexuality
You need to be aware of your personal beliefs before discussing sexuality.
Exploring personal discomfort and planning to address it
Nurses need to explore discomfort and develop a plan to address it.
Building knowledge about sexual health
Lack of knowledge is a key factor limiting sexual health education.
Avoiding the topic until the patient raises it
Patients are often hesitant; avoidance leaves concerns unaddressed.
Planning to share personal opinions about patients’ choices
Nurses should not convey negative feelings and must respect patients’ values.
items.ex: Preparation includes self-awareness of beliefs, addressing discomfort, and building knowledge so patients feel safe sharing.

alt.q: Which nursing behaviors encourage patients to discuss sexual concerns? Select all that apply.
o: Addressing sexuality in a relaxed, matter-of-fact manner
Patients often share feelings when the nurse is relaxed and matter-of-fact.
Holding the discussion in a quiet, private setting
Quiet, private settings increase patient comfort.
Maintaining a nonjudgmental attitude
A nonjudgmental attitude encourages disclosure, especially in older adults.
Showing visible discomfort when the topic arises
Nurse discomfort makes patients unlikely to share.
Conveying disapproval through facial expressions
Nurses must not convey negative feelings verbally or nonverbally.
alt.ex: Relaxed, private, nonjudgmental communication encourages patients to share sexual concerns.

items.q: A nurse recognizes that personal values about sexuality conflict with a patient’s values. Which critical thinking attitude requires the nurse to recognize this conflict and proceed in a mutually beneficial way?
items.a: Integrity
items.ex: Integrity requires recognizing when personal opinions and values conflict with the patient’s and proceeding in a mutually beneficial way.
w: Curiosity
Curiosity means considering why a patient behaves or responds in a particular way.
Discipline
Discipline involves thoroughness, not resolving value conflicts.
Risk taking
Taking risks involves exploring personal and patient sexual issues, not reconciling value conflicts.

alt.q: What does the attitude of integrity require of a nurse whose values about sexuality differ from a patient’s?
alt.a: Recognizing the conflict and proceeding in a mutually beneficial way
alt.ex: Integrity means recognizing conflicting values and choosing a path that benefits both nurse and patient.
w: Persuading the patient to adopt the nurse’s values
Professional standards require respect for each patient as an individual.
Ignoring the conflict and continuing as usual
Integrity requires recognizing, not ignoring, the conflict.
Refusing to care for the patient
Integrity calls for a mutually beneficial approach, not refusal of care.

items.q: Which influences shape the values systems of both patients and health care providers regarding sexuality? Select all that apply.
o: Religious teachings
Religious teachings influence values for both patients and providers.
Cultural influences on male or female roles
Cultural views of gender roles shape values systems.
Beliefs about sexual orientation
Beliefs about orientation influence values for both groups.
Social and environmental climates
Social and environmental climates also shape values systems.
The patient’s current laboratory results
Laboratory results are clinical data, not influences on values.
The nurse’s assigned shift and unit
Work assignments do not shape values about sexuality.
items.ex: Religion, cultural gender roles, beliefs about orientation, and social climate shape both patients’ and providers’ values about sexuality.

alt.q: A nurse reflects on where personal values about sexuality come from before talking with patients. Which sources does the chapter identify? Select all that apply.
o: Religious teachings
Religious teachings shape values about sexuality.
Beliefs about sexual orientation
Beliefs about orientation shape values about sexuality.
Cultural influences on gender roles
Cultural views of male and female roles shape values.
The agency’s staffing ratios
Staffing is a workplace factor, not a source of sexual values.
The patient’s medication schedule
Medication schedules are clinical details, not sources of values.
alt.ex: Knowing that religion, culture, and beliefs shape one’s values helps a nurse recognize how they may affect discussions.

items.q: While a patient describes having several sexual partners, the nurse notices frowning and crossing the arms. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Adopt a neutral, open posture and continue listening without judgment
items.ex: Nurses must not convey negative feelings verbally or nonverbally, because judgment discourages patients from sharing.
w: Tell the patient that this lifestyle is unhealthy and wrong
Conveying negative judgments verbally discourages disclosure and disrespects the patient.
End the interview because the topic is uncomfortable
Discomfort should be addressed, not used to end the discussion.
Continue frowning so the patient senses the risk involved
Negative nonverbal messages discourage patients from sharing concerns.

alt.q: Which nursing behavior is most likely to discourage a patient from sharing sexual concerns?
alt.a: Conveying disapproval through facial expressions
alt.ex: Negative feelings conveyed verbally or nonverbally make patients less willing to express sexual concerns.
w: Using a relaxed, matter-of-fact tone
A relaxed, matter-of-fact tone encourages patients to share.
Holding the discussion in a private room
Privacy increases patient comfort.
Explaining why sexual history is important
Explaining the importance of disclosure supports sharing.

items.q: How can a nurse’s own sexuality, sexual experiences, and communication style affect discussions with patients?
items.a: They are valuable in understanding the patient’s experiences
items.ex: The chapter notes a nurse’s own sexuality, experiences, and communication style help in understanding patients’ experiences.
w: They should be shared in detail with every patient
They inform the nurse’s understanding; detailed self-disclosure is not advised.
They have no bearing on professional care
Professional behavior and personal attitudes influence patients’ willingness to share.
They allow the nurse to judge patients’ choices
Nurses respect each patient and must not convey negative feelings.

alt.q: Besides personal experience, what does the chapter say nurses use to develop trust with current patients around sexual concerns?
alt.a: What they have learned from working with other patients
alt.ex: Nurses draw on lessons from caring for other patients, along with personal experience, to build trust.
w: Their personal opinions about patients’ lifestyles
Nurses avoid conveying personal opinions or negative feelings.
Information shared by the patient’s family
Trust is built with the patient directly, not through family reports.
Standard scripts that avoid sexual topics
Avoiding sexual topics prevents, rather than builds, trust.

items.q: Nurses need to explore their personal level of [[discomfort]] with sexuality and develop a plan to address it.
items.ex: Exploring discomfort matters because a nurse’s discomfort makes patients unlikely to share sexual concerns.

alt.q: Because patients withhold concerns from uneasy nurses, each nurse should examine their own [[discomfort]] with sexual topics and plan to address it.
alt.ex: Exploring discomfort matters because a nurse’s discomfort makes patients unlikely to share sexual concerns.

items.q: According to the WHO, which statement best describes sexual health?
items.a: A state of physical, emotional, mental, and social well-being related to sexuality
items.ex: The WHO defines sexual health as well-being in relation to sexuality, not merely the absence of disease or dysfunction.
w: The absence of sexually transmitted infections and dysfunction
Sexual health is not merely the absence of disease or dysfunction.
The ability to reproduce and bear healthy children
Sexual health concerns well-being, not reproductive capability alone.
A person’s private view of maleness and femaleness
That is the definition of gender identity.

alt.q: A nurse explains sexual health to a patient. Which statement is consistent with the WHO definition?
alt.a: “Sexual health includes safe, pleasurable experiences free of coercion and violence.”
alt.ex: Sexual health requires a positive, respectful approach and safe, pleasurable experiences free of coercion, discrimination, and violence.
w: “Sexual health simply means you have no infections.”
Sexual health is more than the absence of disease.
“Sexual health only matters if you want to have children.”
Sexual health is about well-being, not only reproduction.
“Sexual health is the same as your sexuality.”
The chapter states that sexuality differs from sexual health.

items.q: A patient who takes oral contraceptive pills asks whether she still needs condoms with a new partner. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Yes. The pill prevents pregnancy but does not protect you from sexually transmitted infections.”
items.ex: Oral contraceptives are effective birth control but give no STI protection, so a latex condom is needed with each act of intercourse.
w: “No. The pill protects you from both pregnancy and most sexually transmitted infections.”
The pill provides no protection from STIs.
“Only if you miss a pill, because otherwise the pill protects you from infections.”
Even perfect pill use does not reduce the risk of STIs.
“Only if your partner has symptoms, because infections without symptoms do not spread.”
Many STIs cause no symptoms yet are still transmitted.

alt.q: A patient who has an intrauterine device (IUD) says she no longer needs condoms. Which teaching point should the nurse include?
alt.a: A latex condom used with each act of intercourse reduces the risk of STIs.
alt.ex: An IUD is effective birth control but does not protect against STIs, so a latex condom is still needed every time.
w: An IUD blocks infections because it seals the cervical opening.
An IUD sits in the uterus and offers no protection from STIs.
Condoms are needed only during the first month after IUD insertion.
STI risk continues for as long as unprotected intercourse occurs.
Condoms are needed only if her partner has had an infection before.
Partners may be infected without knowing it, so condoms are needed each time.

items.q: A patient who uses a diaphragm has had a change in weight since her last fitting. After what weight change does she need to be refitted?
items.a: A gain or loss of 4.5 kg (10 lb)
items.ex: A diaphragm must be refitted after a significant weight change of about 4.5 kg (10 lb) or after a pregnancy.
w: A gain or loss of 1 kg (2 lb)
This small change does not require a new fitting.
A gain or loss of 13.6 kg (30 lb)
Refitting is needed well before a 30-lb change.
A gain or loss of 22.7 kg (50 lb)
Waiting for a 50-lb change would leave the diaphragm poorly fitted.

alt.q: Besides a significant change in weight, which event requires a woman to be refitted for a diaphragm?
alt.a: A pregnancy
alt.ex: A woman needs a new diaphragm fitting after pregnancy or a 4.5-kg (10-lb) weight gain or loss.
w: A new sexual partner
Changing partners does not change the size of the cervix or vagina.
A course of antibiotics
Antibiotics do not change diaphragm fit.
Each menstrual period
Monthly menstruation does not require a new fitting.

items.q: Other than abstinence, which contraceptive method is the most effective?
items.a: Surgical sterilization
items.ex: Sterilization, such as tubal ligation or vasectomy, is the most effective contraception method other than abstinence.
w: Spermicidal foam
Spermicides are most effective when combined with condoms and are less effective than sterilization.
The cervical cap
The cervical cap is a barrier method that is less effective than sterilization.
The basal body temperature method
Fertility-based methods depend on abstaining during fertile periods and are less effective.

alt.q: A couple asks the nurse about vasectomy. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “It is usually considered permanent, although reversal is possible and pregnancies have been reported.”
alt.ex: Vasectomy cuts and ties the vas deferens; it is usually permanent, but reversal is possible and unintended pregnancies occur.
w: “It removes the testicles so that sperm are no longer produced by the body.”
Vasectomy cuts and ties the vas deferens; the testicles are not removed.
“It is fully reversible at any time without any change in fertility afterward.”
Vasectomy is considered a permanent procedure, not an easily reversible one.
“It involves cutting and tying the fallopian tubes to block passage of sperm.”
Cutting the fallopian tubes describes female sterilization, or tubal ligation.

items.q: What is the primary mechanism by which both copper and hormone-releasing IUDs prevent pregnancy?
items.a: Stopping sperm from fertilizing an egg
items.ex: The primary action of both types of IUDs is preventing sperm from fertilizing an egg.
w: Stopping the ovaries from releasing eggs
Preventing ovulation is a main effect of hormonal contraception such as injections, not the IUD’s primary action.
Covering the cervix with a rubber barrier
This describes the diaphragm or cervical cap.
Permanently blocking the fallopian tubes
Blocking the tubes describes tubal ligation.

alt.q: A patient asks how her copper IUD works. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “It mainly works by stopping sperm from fertilizing an egg.”
alt.ex: Copper and hormonal IUDs both prevent pregnancy mainly by keeping sperm from fertilizing an egg.
w: “It mainly works by releasing estrogen to stop ovulation.”
IUDs contain copper or progesterone, and their primary action is on sperm, not ovulation.
“It mainly works by forming a barrier over the cervix.”
A barrier over the cervix describes the diaphragm or cervical cap.
“It mainly works by killing sperm in the vagina.”
Killing sperm in the vagina describes spermicidal products.

items.q: A patient with an unplanned pregnancy tells the nurse she is thinking about an abortion but is unsure what to do. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Provide a private setting to explore her options openly and without judgment
items.ex: The nurse provides an environment where the patient can discuss the issue openly and explore options in a nonjudgmental manner.
w: Share the nurse’s personal view on abortion to help guide her choice
Personal views should not steer a patient’s decision.
Tell her abortion is no longer legal anywhere in the United States
Abortion is legal in some states but not in others.
Advise her to delay any decision until the pregnancy is further along
Abortions are safer and less costly when done early in pregnancy.

alt.q: Which statement by the nurse best supports a patient who is considering ending a pregnancy?
alt.a: “Let’s talk about the options you are considering and what matters most to you.”
alt.ex: Open, nonjudgmental exploration of options, including religious, social, and personal issues, supports the patient’s decision.
w: “I would never make that choice myself, so please think it over carefully.”
Sharing personal judgment is not a nonjudgmental approach.
“Most women regret that choice, so you should continue the pregnancy.”
This pressures the patient instead of allowing open exploration of options.
“We cannot discuss this topic until your partner is present with you.”
The patient needs an environment where she can discuss the issue openly.

items.q: A nurse’s personal beliefs oppose abortion. Which approach does the textbook support?
items.a: Choose a specialty or workplace where personal values are not compromised and patient care is not jeopardized
items.ex: Nurses are entitled to their views and should work where their values are not compromised and patient care is not jeopardized.
w: Assist with every procedure because personal values have no place in nursing practice
Nurses should not be forced to take part in procedures contrary to their beliefs.
Refuse care to any patient who has had an abortion, even when the patient needs care
The care of a patient in need of health care must not be jeopardized.
Counsel each patient to continue the pregnancy so the nurse’s values are respected
Counseling must be nonjudgmental, not directed by the nurse’s values.

alt.q: Which statement about a nurse’s personal values and abortion care is accurate?
alt.a: A nurse should not be forced to participate in counseling or procedures contrary to personal beliefs.
alt.ex: Nurses are entitled to personal views and should not be forced into counseling or procedures that conflict with their values.
w: A nurse must set aside personal beliefs and assist with any abortion procedure.
The textbook states nurses should not be forced to participate against their beliefs.
A nurse may share personal beliefs to influence a patient’s final decision.
Discussion with patients must be nonjudgmental.
A nurse may withhold needed care from a patient whose choice conflicts with personal beliefs.
Patient care must never be jeopardized by the nurse’s values.

items.q: Which characteristic is shared by the people most likely to be infected with an STI?
items.a: Unprotected sex with multiple partners
items.ex: The key characteristic of people most likely to be infected with an STI is unprotected sex with multiple partners.
w: Use of oral contraceptive pills
Oral contraceptives do not protect against STIs, but their use is not the key risk characteristic.
A history of urinary tract infections
Urinary tract infections are not identified as the key STI risk.
Living in a rural community
Place of residence is not the key characteristic identified.

alt.q: Which patient is at greatest risk for acquiring an STI?
alt.a: A 22-year-old who has unprotected sex with several partners
alt.ex: Unprotected sex with multiple partners is the key characteristic of people most likely to be infected.
w: A 30-year-old in a monogamous relationship who uses condoms
Condom use with one partner lowers STI risk.
A 45-year-old who has abstained from intercourse for years
Abstinence avoids sexual exposure to STIs.
A 50-year-old with one long-term partner after a vasectomy
One long-term partner lowers risk; the vasectomy does not affect STI risk.

items.q: A patient had a possible HIV exposure 2 weeks ago and asks when HIV antibodies would appear in the blood. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
items.a: “About 6 weeks to 3 months after infection.”
items.ex: HIV antibodies appear in the blood about 6 weeks to 3 months after infection.
w: “Within 24 to 48 hours after infection.”
Antibodies take weeks to months to appear, not hours.
“About 7 to 10 days after infection.”
This is too early; antibodies appear about 6 weeks to 3 months after infection.
“About 1 to 2 years after infection.”
This is too late; antibodies appear within about 3 months.

alt.q: Which time frame describes when HIV antibodies usually become detectable in the blood?
alt.a: 6 weeks to 3 months after infection
alt.ex: Antibodies develop during the weeks after the primary infection stage, about 6 weeks to 3 months after infection.
w: 1 to 2 days after infection
Antibodies are not present this early.
12 to 18 months after infection
Antibodies appear much sooner, within about 3 months.
10 years after infection
About 10 years is the survival time for untreated people who develop AIDS.

items.q: For which group does the CDC recommend annual chlamydia screening?
items.a: All sexually active women up to age 25
items.ex: Because chlamydia causes few symptoms, the CDC recommends yearly screening for all sexually active women up to age 25.
w: All sexually active women over age 40
The recommendation targets younger women, up to age 25.
All men over age 50
Men who have sex with men are high risk, but annual screening is recommended for young women.
Women over age 65 who are not sexually active
Screening is recommended for sexually active women, not those without sexual activity.

alt.q: Why does the CDC recommend annual chlamydia screening for young sexually active women?
alt.a: Most infected people do not realize they are infected because symptoms are few
alt.ex: Chlamydia often causes few symptoms, so screening finds infections that could lead to PID, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility.
w: Chlamydia is caused by a virus that cannot be cured with medication
Chlamydia is caused by a bacterium and is usually curable with antibiotics.
Chlamydia is spread mainly through shared drinking glasses and towels
Chlamydia is spread by contact with fluids from the infected site.
Chlamydia always causes severe pelvic pain early in the infection
Chlamydia usually causes few symptoms, which is why screening matters.

items.q: The parent of an 11-year-old declines the HPV vaccine, saying it will encourage the child to become sexually active. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Evidence shows the vaccine does not increase sexual activity or risky behaviors.”
items.ex: Sharing evidence that the vaccine does not increase sexual activity reduces parental concerns and supports vaccine acceptance.
w: “It is best to wait to give the vaccine until your child becomes sexually active.”
The vaccine works best when given before sexual activity or exposure.
“The vaccine is recommended only for girls, so your son can skip it.”
The vaccine is recommended for both males and females.
“The vaccine also prevents pregnancy, which makes it worth the risk.”
The HPV vaccine protects against HPV infections, not pregnancy.

alt.q: Which nursing action is recommended to improve HPV vaccination rates among preteens?
alt.a: Recommend the HPV vaccine on the same day as other routine vaccines at age 11 or 12
alt.ex: Recommending HPV vaccination the same way and day as other routine preteen vaccines encourages acceptance.
w: Delay the HPV vaccine until the teen reports sexual activity at age 16 or 17
The vaccine is most effective before sexual activity begins.
Offer the HPV vaccine only to females between 11 and 12 years of age
The vaccine is recommended for males and females.
Avoid digital reminders for families of children aged 11 or 12 years
Digital reminders to adolescents and parents may improve vaccination rates.

items.q: How many doses of the 9-valent HPV vaccine are recommended for a healthy 11-year-old?
items.a: Two doses
items.ex: Two doses of the 9-valent HPV vaccine are recommended for preteens; older adolescents and young adults need three.
w: One dose
A single dose is not the recommended series for preteens.
Three doses
Three doses are advised for older adolescents and young adults, not preteens.
Four doses
No age group requires four doses.

alt.q: A 20-year-old who has never received the HPV vaccine asks how many doses are needed. Which response is accurate?
alt.a: Three doses
alt.ex: Older adolescents and young adults need three doses, whereas preteens need two.
w: One dose
A single dose is not the recommended catch-up series.
Two doses
Two doses are recommended for preteens, not young adults.
Four doses
No age group requires four doses.

items.q: Which sexually transmitted infections are caused by viruses and cannot be cured? Select all that apply.
o: Herpes simplex virus type 2
HSV is a viral infection that cannot be cured.
Human papillomavirus
HPV is a virus; viral STIs such as HPV cannot be cured.
Human immunodeficiency virus
HIV is viral and incurable, though treatment makes it a manageable chronic illness.
Gonorrhea
Gonorrhea is bacterial and usually curable with antibiotics.
Chlamydia
Chlamydia is bacterial and usually curable with antibiotics.
Syphilis
Syphilis is bacterial and usually curable with antibiotics.
items.ex: HSV, HPV, and HIV are viral and cannot be cured, whereas bacterial STIs are usually curable with antibiotics.

alt.q: Which STIs are caused by bacteria and are usually curable with antibiotics? Select all that apply.
o: Gonorrhea
Gonorrhea is bacterial, although resistant strains are emerging.
Chlamydia
Chlamydia trachomatis is a bacterium treated with antibiotics.
Syphilis
Treponema pallidum is a bacterium, although resistant strains are emerging.
Human papillomavirus
HPV is a virus and cannot be cured with antibiotics.
Herpes simplex virus type 2
HSV is a virus and cannot be cured.
Human immunodeficiency virus
HIV is a virus and cannot be cured.
alt.ex: Gonorrhea, chlamydia, and syphilis are bacterial and usually curable when the full course of antibiotics is taken.

items.q: Which behaviors reflect responsible sexual behavior? Select all that apply.
o: Knowing one’s sexual partner and the partner’s sexual history
Knowing a partner’s history is part of responsible sexual behavior.
Openly discussing drug use history with a partner
Open discussion of drug use history is part of responsible behavior.
Using STI and contraceptive protective devices
Protective devices reduce the risk of STIs and pregnancy.
Not letting alcohol or drugs influence sexual decisions
Drugs and alcohol should not influence decision making and sexual practices.
Skipping condoms when a partner has no visible symptoms
Many STIs cause no symptoms, so the absence of symptoms is not protective.
Drinking alcohol beforehand to ease sexual anxiety
Alcohol should not be allowed to influence decision making and sexual practices.
items.ex: Responsible sexual behavior includes knowing partners and their histories, discussing drug use, avoiding substance influence, and using protection.

alt.q: A nurse teaches an adolescent about responsible sexual behavior. Which statements show understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “I’ll ask about my partner’s sexual history before we have sex.”
Knowing the partner’s sexual history is part of responsible behavior.
“I’ll use a condom along with my birth control.”
Using both STI and contraceptive protection is responsible behavior.
“I’ll talk openly with my partner about any drug use.”
Discussing drug use history with a partner is part of responsible behavior.
“If my partner looks healthy, we don’t need a condom.”
STIs are often asymptomatic, so appearance does not indicate safety.
“A couple of drinks will help me decide more freely.”
Alcohol should not influence decision making about sex.
alt.ex: Statements about knowing partners, discussing drug use, and using STI and contraceptive protection show understanding.

items.q: Which findings are common symptoms of an STI? Select all that apply.
o: Discharge from the vagina, penis, anus, or throat
Discharge from these sites is a common STI symptom.
Pain during sex
Pain during intercourse is a common STI symptom.
Pain when urinating
Painful urination is a common STI symptom.
Unexplained rash or lesions
Rashes or lesions are common STI symptoms.
Excessive thirst
Excessive thirst is not listed as an STI symptom.
Bilateral ankle swelling
Ankle swelling is not listed as an STI symptom.
items.ex: Common STI symptoms are discharge, pain during sex or urination, and unexplained rash or lesions.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a sexually active patient about body areas that can be sites of STIs. Which sites should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Perineum
The perineum is named as a potential STI site.
Anus and rectum
The anus and rectum are potential STI sites.
Throat
Discharge from the throat can be an STI symptom after oral contact.
Fingernail beds
The nail beds are not identified as STI sites.
Soles of the feet
The soles of the feet are not identified as STI sites.
alt.ex: Because sexual behavior involves the whole body, the perineum, anus, rectum, and throat can be STI sites.

items.q: Using a vaginal spermicide together with a condom is more effective at preventing pregnancy than using either one alone.
items.a: True
items.ex: Spermicides and condoms work best when instructions are followed, and their combined use is more effective than either alone.
items.ww: Combined use adds protection beyond a single method, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Combining a condom with a vaginal spermicide adds no pregnancy protection beyond using a condom alone.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The combined use of condoms and spermicides is more effective than either one alone.
alt.ww: The book states the combination is more effective, so this statement cannot be true.

items.q: STIs are often present without symptoms, which is especially common in women.
items.a: True
items.ex: Some people do not know they are infected because symptoms are absent or unnoticed, especially women.
items.ww: Absent or unnoticed symptoms are a recognized challenge in finding STIs, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: When STI symptoms go away on their own, it means the infection has cleared.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Symptoms can go away even though the infection remains.
alt.ww: Symptoms resolving does not prove the infection is gone, so the statement is not true.

items.q: Some bacterial STIs, such as gonorrhea and syphilis, are developing antibiotic-resistant strains.
items.a: True
items.ex: Antibiotic-resistant strains of gonorrhea and syphilis are an emerging concern.
items.ww: Resistance is identified as an emerging concern, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Because bacterial STIs are curable, patients may stop antibiotics once their symptoms resolve.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients need to take antibiotics for the full course of treatment.
alt.ww: Stopping early is unsafe because the full course is required, so the statement is not true.

items.q: The most reported bacterial STI in the United States is [[chlamydia|Chlamydia trachomatis]].
items.ex: Chlamydia, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, is the most reported bacterial STI and can cause PID, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility.

alt.q: Untreated [[chlamydia|Chlamydia trachomatis]], the most commonly reported bacterial STI, can cause PID, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility.
alt.ex: Chlamydia, caused by Chlamydia trachomatis, is the most reported bacterial STI and can cause PID, ectopic pregnancy, and infertility.
