items.q: A couple who has been unable to conceive says they feel their bodies are defective and want to talk with others in the same situation. Which referral is most appropriate?
items.a: RESOLVE: The National Infertility Association
items.ex: RESOLVE is a national support group for people with infertility that provides support and referral sources.
w: North American Menopause Society
This organization addresses menopause, not infertility.
National Multiple Sclerosis Society
This group serves people with multiple sclerosis.
A local women’s shelter
Shelters serve people at risk of continued physical or sexual abuse.

alt.q: What does RESOLVE: The National Infertility Association offer?
alt.a: Support and referral sources for people with infertility
alt.ex: RESOLVE is a national infertility support group that offers support and referrals.
w: A safe place for people at risk of continued abuse
This describes women’s shelters.
Education about menopause symptoms and treatment
This describes the North American Menopause Society.
Free STI treatment and contraceptive services
This describes health departments and community clinics.

items.q: A patient’s partner answers every question for the patient, will not leave the room, and seems very attentive. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: Controlling behavior can be a cue of possible sexual violence
items.ex: Extreme jealousy and controlling behavior raise the question of sexual violence, even when the partner appears caring.
w: The partner’s behavior shows a healthy, supportive relationship
An attentive appearance can hide a very different underlying reason.
The partner is probably the patient’s legal health care proxy
Nothing in the behavior indicates legal authority to answer for the patient.
An attentive partner lowers the patient’s risk of being abused
A concerned appearance does not reduce risk and may mask abuse.

alt.q: Which partner behavior should raise the nurse’s concern about possible sexual violence?
alt.a: Extreme jealousy and controlling behavior
alt.ex: Extreme jealousy and controlling behavior are cues that raise a question of sexual violence.
w: Asking questions about discharge medications
Asking about medications is an expected caregiver behavior.
Visiting during usual visiting hours
Regular visiting is not a cue of abuse.
Bringing favorite foods from home
Bringing comfort items is not a cue of abuse.

items.q: During an assessment, a nurse suspects that a patient is a victim of sexual abuse. Which action is required?
items.a: Report the suspected abuse to the proper authorities per state law
items.ex: Nurses are mandated reporters who must report suspected sexual violence or abuse per state laws.
w: Wait until the patient confirms the abuse before making any report
Suspected abuse must be reported; confirmation is not required.
Confront the suspected abuser about the behavior during the visit
Confrontation may endanger the patient and is not the required action.
Document the suspicion in the record but take no further action
Documentation alone does not meet the duty to report.

alt.q: Why must a nurse report suspected sexual abuse even when the patient has not disclosed it?
alt.a: Nurses are mandated reporters under state laws
alt.ex: As mandated reporters, nurses must report suspected sexual violence or abuse to authorities per state law.
w: Hospital policy forbids nurses from keeping patient information private
Confidentiality still applies; the duty comes from mandated-reporter laws.
The patient’s insurer requires a report of every injury
Insurers are not the basis for reporting abuse.
Reporting is needed only to protect the nurse from lawsuits
The purpose is protecting the victim, as required by state law.

items.q: According to the textbook, sexual violence is most often committed by whom?
items.a: An intimate partner or family member
items.ex: Sexual violence most often occurs at the hands of an intimate partner or family member.
w: A stranger in a public place
Strangers are not the most common perpetrators.
A coworker or employer
Coworkers are not identified as the most common perpetrators.
An acquaintance met online
Online acquaintances are not identified as the most common perpetrators.

alt.q: When screening for sexual violence, which relationship should the nurse recognize as the most common source of abuse?
alt.a: The patient’s intimate partner or a family member
alt.ex: Most sexual violence is committed by an intimate partner or family member, so the nurse explores these relationships.
w: A health care provider the patient sees
Health care providers are not identified as the most common source.
A stranger the patient does not know
Strangers are not the most common perpetrators.
A neighbor living near the patient
Neighbors are not identified as the most common source.

items.q: When abuse is suspected or recognized, which nursing action reflects the textbook’s guidance for the family?
items.a: Mobilize support for the victim and family, since all members usually need therapy
items.ex: When abuse is suspected, mobilize support; all family members usually need therapy to promote healthy relationships.
w: Focus only on the victim, since other family members are not affected by abuse
Abuse affects the whole family, and all members usually need therapy.
Advise the family to resolve the matter privately without any outside services
The nurse mobilizes support and educates about community services.
Delay any referrals until the victim has fully recovered from the experience
Support is mobilized when abuse is suspected or recognized, not delayed.

alt.q: Why does the nurse recommend therapy for all members of a family in which sexual abuse occurred?
alt.a: Therapy promotes healthy interactions and relationships among family members
alt.ex: All family members usually need therapy to promote healthy interactions and relationships.
w: Therapy determines which family member caused the abuse
The purpose of therapy is healthy relationships, not assigning blame.
Therapy replaces the need to report the abuse to authorities
Nurses must still report suspected abuse per state law.
Therapy is required before the victim can receive medical care
Medical care is not delayed for family therapy.

items.q: The parents of a 7-year-old who was sexually molested ask how they can help their child. Which statement by a parent shows understanding of the nurse’s teaching?
items.a: “How we respond will affect how our child reacts and adapts.”
items.ex: Parents need to understand that their response is critical to how the child reacts and adapts.
w: “We should avoid talking about it so our child forgets sooner.”
Children need to be able to share their story.
“Our child must have done something to invite this to happen.”
Children need to know they are not at fault.
“Our reaction will not matter as long as therapy starts soon.”
The parents’ response is critical to the child’s adaptation.

alt.q: What do children who have been sexually molested need, according to the textbook?
alt.a: To be identified, share their story, and know they are not at fault
alt.ex: Molested children need to be identified, be able to tell their story, and know they are not to blame.
w: To avoid discussing the event so they do not relive it
Children need to be able to share their story.
To be told the event was probably a misunderstanding
Minimizing the event does not help the child know they are not at fault.
To be separated from both parents during recovery
Parents’ supportive response is critical to how the child adapts.

items.q: The partner of a patient who was raped asks the nurse why the patient now pulls away from hugs. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “She needs to work through the crisis before she feels comfortable with intimate affection.”
items.ex: Patients who have been raped need to work through the crisis before feeling comfortable with intimate expressions of affection.
w: “Pulling away means she no longer cares about your relationship.”
Withdrawal reflects the crisis, not a loss of caring.
“Insisting on affection will help her recover from the crisis faster.”
Pressuring for affection does not support her through the crisis.
“This behavior shows that she was not truly harmed by the assault.”
Sexual violence has far-ranging physical and psychological effects.

alt.q: Which statement by the partner of a rape survivor shows understanding of the nurse’s teaching?
alt.a: “I’ll support her and let her work through the crisis at her own pace.”
alt.ex: The partner needs to know how to help and support the patient while she works through the crisis.
w: “If we resume intimacy right away, she will forget it sooner.”
The patient needs to work through the crisis before intimacy feels comfortable.
“She should feel comfortable with affection again within a few days.”
Working through the crisis takes time and has no set timeline.
“I’ll avoid learning about this so that I don’t upset her.”
The partner needs to know how to help and support the patient.

items.q: A patient who takes an antidepressant tells the nurse that it has become difficult to reach orgasm. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
items.a: “Some people taking antidepressants report that their ability to reach orgasm is affected.”
items.ex: Some women and men taking antidepressants report a negative effect on their ability to reach orgasm.
w: “Antidepressants improve sexual response, so another cause must be found.”
Antidepressants are linked to negative, not improved, effects on orgasm.
“This effect of antidepressants is reported only by women, not men.”
Both women and men report this effect.
“Difficulty reaching orgasm is never related to any prescribed medication.”
Many medications, including antidepressants, affect sexual health.

alt.q: Which medication class does the textbook specifically link to a negative effect on the ability to reach orgasm?
alt.a: Antidepressants
alt.ex: Some people taking antidepressants report that their ability to reach orgasm is negatively affected.
w: Bronchodilators
Bronchodilators are not the class the textbook links to orgasm problems.
Topical antifungal creams
Topical antifungals are not the class the textbook links to orgasm problems.
Proton pump inhibitors
Proton pump inhibitors are not the class the textbook links to orgasm problems.

items.q: Risk factors for erectile dysfunction (ED) are similar to those for which condition?
items.a: Heart disease
items.ex: ED risk factors such as diabetes, hyperlipidemia, hypertension, smoking, and obesity are similar to those for heart disease.
w: Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis risk factors are not the comparison the textbook makes.
Asthma
Asthma risk factors are not the comparison the textbook makes.
Glaucoma
Glaucoma risk factors are not the comparison the textbook makes.

alt.q: A 38-year-old man with diabetes and hypertension who smokes asks whether he is too young to have ED. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “ED can occur in men under 40, and your conditions are risk factors for it.”
alt.ex: Although ED increases with age, it can occur under 40, and diabetes, hypertension, and smoking are risk factors.
w: “ED does not occur in men under 40, so another problem must be present.”
ED can occur in men under 40.
“ED in men under 40 is always caused by psychological factors only.”
ED is often multifactorial and has physical risk factors.
“Your health conditions lower your risk of ED before age 40.”
Diabetes, hypertension, and smoking increase ED risk.

items.q: Which age-related change contributes to erectile dysfunction in older men?
items.a: A decrease in testosterone that reduces the tone of erectile tissues
items.ex: An age-related decrease in testosterone often results in decreased tone of the erectile tissues.
w: An increase in testosterone that overstimulates the erectile tissues
Testosterone decreases, not increases, with age.
A decrease in estrogen that thins the skin covering the penis
Estrogen loss is not the cause identified for ED.
An increase in prostate fluid that blocks blood flow to the penis
This is not a mechanism described for age-related ED.

alt.q: What is the effect of an age-related decrease in testosterone in men?
alt.a: Decreased tone of the erectile tissues
alt.ex: Lower testosterone with aging often decreases the tone of erectile tissues, contributing to ED.
w: Increased tone of the erectile tissues
Lower testosterone decreases, not increases, tissue tone.
Increased production of sperm cells
Lower testosterone does not increase sperm production.
Increased interest in sexual activity
Lower testosterone is not linked to increased sexual interest.

items.q: Which statement about the cause of erectile dysfunction is accurate?
items.a: It is often multifactorial, with neurogenic, medication, endocrine, or psychogenic causes
items.ex: The etiology of ED is often multifactorial, including neurogenic problems, medications, and endocrine or psychogenic factors.
w: It is almost always psychological and unrelated to physical disease
Physical factors such as diabetes and hypertension often contribute.
It results only from aging and cannot occur in younger men
ED can occur in men under 40.
It is caused mainly by too much regular physical exercise
Lack of exercise, not exercise, is a risk factor.

alt.q: A man with ED asks what usually causes the problem. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “Several factors, such as nerve problems, medications, hormones, or emotions, often combine.”
alt.ex: ED is often multifactorial, with neurogenic, medication, endocrine, or psychogenic causes.
w: “It is nearly always caused by stress alone and has no physical cause.”
Physical causes such as nerve, hormone, and medication effects are common.
“It is caused only by low testosterone and is treated with hormones alone.”
Low testosterone is one factor among several.
“It is caused only by aging and develops in every man after age 60.”
ED can occur in men under 40 and does not affect every older man.

items.q: A 52-year-old woman who was treated for breast cancer tells the nurse she has little interest in sexual intimacy. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
items.a: “Chronic conditions such as breast cancer can contribute to decreased sexual desire.”
items.ex: Breast or gynecological cancers, hormonal changes, pain, depression, and anxiety can contribute to decreased sexual interest.
w: “Loss of desire is uncommon in women and suggests a psychiatric illness.”
Hypoactive sexual desire disorder is one of the most common problems in women.
“Sexual desire is not affected by cancer or its treatment in women.”
Chronic conditions such as breast cancer can decrease sexual interest.
“Decreased desire after cancer is caused only by low hormone levels.”
Biological, organic, and psychosocial factors can all contribute.

alt.q: Which factors can contribute to hypoactive sexual desire disorder in women?
alt.a: Pain, depression, anxiety, and hormonal fluctuations
alt.ex: HSDD can stem from biological, organic, or psychosocial factors such as pain, mood disorders, and hormonal changes.
w: Regular exercise, good sleep, and balanced meals
These healthy habits are not listed as contributors to HSDD.
Open communication and a supportive partner
Supportive relationships are not contributors to HSDD.
Use of water-based lubricants and condoms
These safe-sex measures are not contributors to HSDD.

items.q: Which are risk factors for erectile dysfunction? Select all that apply.
o: Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes is a risk factor shared with heart disease.
Hyperlipidemia
Hyperlipidemia is an ED risk factor.
Smoking
Smoking is an ED risk factor.
Lack of exercise
Lack of exercise is an ED risk factor.
Regular aerobic exercise
Lack of exercise, not regular exercise, is the risk factor.
Normal body weight
Obesity, not normal weight, is the risk factor.
items.ex: ED risk factors resemble those for heart disease, including diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, obesity, and inactivity.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a man about factors that raise his risk of ED. Which factors should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Hypertension
Hypertension is an ED risk factor.
Obesity
Obesity is an ED risk factor.
Alcohol abuse
Alcohol abuse is an ED risk factor.
Chronic renal failure
Chronic renal failure is an ED risk factor.
A low-fat diet
A low-fat diet does not raise ED risk; hyperlipidemia does.
Moderate daily walking
Exercise lowers risk; lack of exercise is the risk factor.
alt.ex: Hypertension, obesity, alcohol abuse, and chronic renal failure are among the ED risk factors shared with heart disease.

items.q: Which medication classes are listed as affecting sexual health? Select all that apply.
o: Antihypertensives
Antihypertensives are listed in Box 34.4.
Antidepressants
Antidepressants are listed and can affect orgasm.
Diuretics
Diuretics are listed in Box 34.4.
Antipsychotics
Antipsychotics are listed in Box 34.4.
Daily multivitamins
Multivitamins are not listed as affecting sexual health.
Topical skin moisturizers
Moisturizers are not listed as affecting sexual health.
items.ex: Many drug classes, including antihypertensives, antidepressants, diuretics, and antipsychotics, can affect sexual health.

alt.q: Which illnesses are listed as affecting the sexual health of men and women? Select all that apply.
o: Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes is listed in Box 34.4.
Spinal cord injury
Spinal cord injury is listed in Box 34.4.
Depression
Depression is listed in Box 34.4.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
COPD is listed in Box 34.4.
Seasonal allergies
Seasonal allergies are not listed as affecting sexual health.
Mild sunburn
Mild sunburn is not listed as affecting sexual health.
alt.ex: Illnesses such as diabetes, spinal cord injury, depression, and COPD can affect sexual health.

items.q: Which statements about sexual violence are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It occurs in all socioeconomic, age, and ethnic groups.
Sexual violence is widespread across all groups.
It affects men and women regardless of sexual identity.
Both men and women of any sexual identity experience it.
It often starts subtly and worsens over time.
Sexual violence often begins subtly and escalates.
It has far-ranging physical and psychological effects.
Its effects extend to physical and psychological functioning.
It is committed mainly by strangers.
It is most often committed by an intimate partner or family member.
It usually begins with a single severe episode.
It often starts subtly and worsens over time.
items.ex: Sexual violence crosses all groups and genders, often escalates gradually, and has broad physical and psychological effects.

alt.q: Which statements by nursing students show accurate understanding of sexual violence? Select all that apply.
o: “An abuser may appear to be a very caring and concerned partner.”
A caring appearance can hide a very different underlying reason.
“Over half of women have experienced sexual violence with physical contact.”
Over half of women and 1 in 3 men have experienced it.
“Nurses can educate victims about community services.”
Nurses help patients confront stressors and learn about community services.
“Sexual violence happens only in low-income families.”
It occurs in all socioeconomic groups.
“Family members rarely commit sexual violence.”
Intimate partners and family members are the most common perpetrators.
alt.ex: Students should know abusers may appear caring, sexual violence is common, and nurses connect victims with community services.

items.q: Sexual dysfunction is more prevalent in people with poor emotional and physical health and increases with age.
items.a: True
items.ex: Sexual dysfunction occurs in both men and women and is more common with poor health and older age.
items.ww: The textbook links dysfunction to poor health and increasing age, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Sexual dysfunction becomes less common as people grow older.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Sexual dysfunction increases with age, as shown by rising ED rates in older men.
alt.ww: Prevalence rises rather than falls with age, so the statement is not true.

items.q: Sex that passes smoothly through each physiological stage and ends in orgasm is more the exception than the rule.
items.a: True
items.ex: The idealized sequence is uncommon; many patients have problems with desire, the act itself, or feelings afterward.
items.ww: The textbook calls the smooth sequence the exception, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Most sexual encounters pass smoothly through every physiological stage and end in orgasm.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: In reality the smooth sequence is more the exception than the rule.
alt.ww: Problems with one or more stages are common, so the statement is not true.

items.q: The exact cause of sexual dysfunction can always be identified with a thorough evaluation.
items.a: False
items.ex: Sometimes the exact cause of sexual dysfunction cannot be determined.
items.ww: The textbook states the cause is sometimes undeterminable, so the statement cannot be true.

alt.q: Sometimes the exact cause of a patient’s sexual dysfunction cannot be determined.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Sexual dysfunction is often multifactorial, and its exact cause sometimes cannot be found.
alt.ww: The textbook acknowledges undetermined causes, so the statement is not false.

items.q: Infertility is the inability to conceive after [[1 year|one year|12 months|a year]] of unprotected intercourse.
items.ex: Infertility is defined as not conceiving after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.

alt.q: A couple meets the definition of infertility when no pregnancy occurs after [[1 year|one year|12 months|a year]] of unprotected intercourse.
alt.ex: Infertility is defined as not conceiving after 1 year of unprotected intercourse.

items.q: One of the most common problems affecting women of all ages is [[hypoactive sexual desire disorder|HSDD]].
items.ex: Hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) is common in women and has biological, organic, or psychosocial causes.

alt.q: Biological, organic, or psychosocial factors can contribute to [[hypoactive sexual desire disorder|HSDD]], a common problem in women of all ages.
alt.ex: Hypoactive sexual desire disorder (HSDD) is common in women and has biological, organic, or psychosocial causes.

sections.name: The nurse’s influence on the patient’s sexuality

items.q: Which factor does the textbook identify as influencing how willing a patient is to express sexual concerns?
items.a: The nurse’s professional behavior
items.ex: A nurse’s professional behavior influences a patient’s willingness to express sexual concerns and partner in care.
w: The patient’s insurance coverage
Insurance coverage is not identified as the influencing factor.
The number of nurses on the unit
Staffing levels are not identified as the influencing factor.
The length of the hospital stay
Length of stay is not identified as the influencing factor.

alt.q: Why does a nurse reflect on personal knowledge and values about sexuality before caring for patients?
alt.a: The nurse’s professional behavior affects whether patients share sexual concerns
alt.ex: Professional behavior shapes how willing patients are to express concerns and work with providers on interventions.
w: The nurse must share these values to guide the patient’s choices
Nurses should not impose their values on patients.
The nurse’s values determine which patient concerns are acceptable
Professional standards require respect for each patient’s values.
The nurse must teach these values as part of every assessment
Reflection is for self-awareness, not for teaching personal values.

items.q: A patient asks a new graduate nurse detailed questions about a sexual problem the nurse feels unprepared to address. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Arrange a consultation with a professional who specializes in sexual health
items.ex: If not comfortable or knowledgeable enough, the nurse should consult health care professionals who specialize in this area.
w: Change the subject to avoid giving the patient incorrect information
Avoiding the topic leaves the patient’s concern unaddressed.
Give a best-guess answer so that the patient continues to trust the nurse
Guessing risks misinformation; consultation is appropriate.
Tell the patient that sexual topics fall outside the scope of nursing care
Sexual health is part of nursing care, even when referral is needed.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse reflects appropriate professional practice regarding patients’ sexual concerns?
alt.a: “If I lack the knowledge to address a concern, I consult a specialist.”
alt.ex: Nurses recognize their competency limits and make consultations to professionals who specialize in sexual health.
w: “I avoid sexual topics because patients find them embarrassing.”
Avoidance prevents patients from getting help with concerns.
“I answer every sexual question myself to maintain trust.”
Nurses are not expected to answer every concern and should consult when needed.
“I share my own beliefs so patients know where I stand.”
Nurses must be aware of their biases, not impose them.

items.q: A patient in a busy emergency department hints that he has a sexual concern. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Continue the discussion in a quiet, private area
items.ex: Patients are more comfortable discussing sexual concerns in a quiet, private environment than in a busy emergency room.
w: Discuss the concern quickly at the nurses’ station
The nurses’ station is not private and discourages disclosure.
Ask him to describe it while the curtain is open
An open curtain does not provide privacy for a sensitive topic.
Ignore the hint until he raises the topic directly
Hints are clues to concerns and should be followed up.

alt.q: In which setting is a patient likely to feel most comfortable discussing sexual concerns?
alt.a: A quiet, private room free from interruptions
alt.ex: The health care environment affects comfort, and a quiet, private setting encourages discussion of sexual concerns.
w: A shared room with the roommate present
A roommate’s presence limits privacy.
A busy emergency department treatment bay
A busy emergency setting discourages discussion.
A hallway outside the patient’s room
A hallway lacks privacy for sensitive topics.

items.q: A patient often makes jokes whenever the nurse raises sexual health topics, and the nurse considers why the patient responds this way. Which critical thinking attitude is the nurse demonstrating?
items.a: Curiosity
items.ex: Curiosity means considering why a patient behaves or responds in a particular way.
w: Integrity
Integrity involves recognizing conflicts between the nurse’s values and the patient’s.
Risk taking
Taking risks involves exploring personal and patient sexual issues even when uncomfortable.
Perseverance
Perseverance involves recognizing that changes in sexuality may happen slowly.

alt.q: Which nurse behavior reflects the critical thinking attitude of curiosity during a sexuality assessment?
alt.a: Considering why the patient behaves or responds in a particular way
alt.ex: In the critical thinking model, curiosity is shown by considering why a patient behaves or responds as they do.
w: Recognizing conflicts between personal values and the patient’s values
This reflects integrity.
Exploring personal sexual issues even when the topic is uncomfortable
This reflects taking risks.
Following agency policies about privacy and confidentiality
This reflects applying standards.

items.q: Which professional standard should guide a nurse who is planning care for a patient who is transgender?
items.a: Standards of Care for the Health of Transgender and Gender Diverse People
items.ex: The textbook names these Standards of Care as a professional standard for planning and providing care.
w: Nursing Outcomes Classification labels for sexual functioning
NOC labels describe outcomes, not standards specific to transgender care.
The PLISSIT levels of intervention for sexual counseling
PLISSIT is an assessment and intervention model, not this professional standard.
Guidelines for teaching breast and testicular self-examination
Self-examination teaching is not the standard for transgender care.

alt.q: A nurse is applying the Standards of Care for the Health of Transgender and Gender Diverse People. In which situation are they most applicable?
alt.a: Planning care for a patient who is gender diverse
alt.ex: These standards guide planning and providing care for transgender and gender diverse patients.
w: Teaching testicular self-examination to a teenager
This teaching is not the focus of these standards.
Fitting a patient for a contraceptive diaphragm
Diaphragm fitting is not the focus of these standards.
Screening a pregnant patient for syphilis
Prenatal syphilis screening is not the focus of these standards.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to assess an older couple who seem embarrassed about a sexual concern. Which approach is best?
items.a: Use a caring approach with a mix of direct and open-ended questions
items.ex: A caring, compassionate approach combining direct and open-ended questions lets the couple express concerns.
w: Use only yes-or-no questions so the interview stays short
Closed questions alone limit the couple’s chance to express concerns.
Skip sexual topics because older adults rarely have concerns
Older adults have sexual concerns but are sometimes hesitant to discuss them.
Give them a written form and leave the room to avoid embarrassment
A therapeutic relationship, not avoidance, helps hesitant patients share.

alt.q: Why did Joshua plan to combine direct and open-ended questions when assessing Mr. and Mrs. Clements?
alt.a: To let the couple express concerns and identify factors affecting their sexual functioning
alt.ex: Combining question types gives the couple the opportunity to express concerns and helps identify contributing factors.
w: To shorten the interview so that a physical assessment is not needed
Joshua planned a physical assessment in addition to the interview.
To decide which partner is responsible for the sexual difficulty
The goal is understanding concerns, not assigning blame.
To avoid building a relationship that could embarrass the couple
Joshua planned to develop a therapeutic relationship with the couple.

items.q: Why does a nurse need a thorough understanding of safe sex practices and of behaviors associated with sexual problems?
items.a: To anticipate how to assess a patient and interpret findings
items.ex: Understanding safe sex practices and risk behaviors helps the nurse anticipate how to assess and interpret findings.
w: To replace the need for referrals to sexual health specialists
Nurses still consult specialists when concerns exceed their competency.
To share personal opinions about which practices are acceptable
Nurses should not convey personal judgments to patients.
To avoid discussing sexuality with patients who are at low risk
Sexuality is part of every patient’s health assessment.

alt.q: Which statement describes the knowledge a nurse applies when considering a patient’s sexuality?
alt.a: Knowledge from nursing and other disciplines is integrated
alt.ex: In sexuality care, the nurse integrates knowledge from nursing and other disciplines.
w: Only nursing knowledge is used
Knowledge from other disciplines is also integrated.
Only the medical diagnosis is considered
Many factors beyond the medical diagnosis affect sexuality.
Only personal experiences are used
Personal experiences supplement, not replace, professional knowledge.

items.q: How can a nurse’s own sexuality and sexual experiences be useful in patient care?
items.a: They help the nurse understand the patient’s experiences
items.ex: A nurse’s own sexuality, experiences, and communication style are valuable in understanding patients’ experiences.
w: They should be shared in detail to build rapport
Sharing personal details is not how these experiences are used.
They define which patient values are acceptable
Professional standards require respect for each patient’s values.
They must be ignored because they always cause bias
The textbook describes them as valuable, while warning about bias.

alt.q: A nurse recalls the challenges of intimacy while a partner was ill. How does this experience help the nurse care for patients?
alt.a: It adds to the nurse’s understanding of sexual challenges during illness
alt.ex: Personal experiences help the nurse understand challenges of sexual interactions when the patient or partner is ill.
w: It tells the nurse exactly how the patient should cope
Each patient’s experience is individual and not dictated by the nurse’s.
It replaces the need to assess the patient’s concerns
Assessment is still required to identify the patient’s concerns.
It allows the nurse to skip referrals to specialists
Referral is still needed when concerns exceed the nurse’s competency.

items.q: A patient describes sexual practices that differ from the nurse’s own values, and the nurse feels uncomfortable. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Keep a neutral expression and avoid conveying negative feelings
items.ex: Nurses should not convey negative feelings to patients verbally or nonverbally.
w: Tell the patient that these practices conflict with the nurse’s beliefs
Expressing disapproval conveys negative feelings and discourages disclosure.
End the conversation and document that the patient was inappropriate
Ending the talk and labeling the patient conveys judgment.
Advise the patient to adopt more conventional sexual practices
Professional standards require respect for each patient’s values.

alt.q: Which nurse behavior is most likely to discourage a patient from sharing sexual concerns?
alt.a: Frowning and looking away while the patient speaks
alt.ex: Negative nonverbal cues convey disapproval and reduce a patient’s willingness to share.
w: Sitting at eye level and maintaining a calm tone
These behaviors convey respect and encourage sharing.
Closing the door to provide privacy
Privacy encourages patients to discuss sexual concerns.
Asking open-ended questions about concerns
Open-ended questions invite patients to express concerns.

items.q: According to the textbook, sound clinical judgment applied through the nursing process involves which activities?
items.a: Anticipating needed information, analyzing data, and making clinical decisions
items.ex: Sound clinical judgment involves anticipating information needed, analyzing assessment data, and making appropriate decisions.
w: Following routine orders without analyzing individual patient data
Clinical judgment requires analyzing each patient’s assessment data.
Relying on personal opinion rather than on patient information
Judgment synthesizes knowledge and patient data, not opinion.
Completing tasks quickly without anticipating the patient’s needs
Anticipating needed information is part of clinical judgment.

alt.q: Which elements does successful clinical judgment synthesize?
alt.a: Knowledge, experience, patient information, attitudes, and standards
alt.ex: Clinical judgment synthesizes knowledge, experience, patient information, critical thinking attitudes, and standards.
w: Agency staffing, budgets, and the length of stay
These administrative factors are not the components of clinical judgment.
Personal opinions, routines, and family preferences
Personal opinions and routines are not the basis of clinical judgment.
Medical orders, billing codes, and insurance rules
These are not the components clinical judgment synthesizes.

items.q: Which nurse action demonstrates the critical thinking attitude of taking risks in a sexuality assessment?
items.a: Exploring personal sexual issues and concerns as well as the patient’s
items.ex: Taking risks, if necessary, means exploring personal sexual issues and concerns and those of the patient.
w: Considering why the patient responds in a certain way
This reflects curiosity.
Recognizing that personal values differ from the patient’s
This reflects integrity.
Following the agency’s policy on privacy and confidentiality
This reflects applying standards.

alt.q: A nurse asks a patient about a sensitive sexual concern even though the nurse feels uneasy. Which critical thinking attitude does this show?
alt.a: Taking risks
alt.ex: Taking risks means exploring sexual issues and concerns even when the topic is uncomfortable.
w: Curiosity
Curiosity means considering why a patient behaves a certain way.
Integrity
Integrity means recognizing conflicts between personal and patient values.
Humility
Humility is not the attitude described for exploring sensitive concerns.

items.q: Which factor in the critical thinking model for sexuality assessment refers to the availability of personnel with specialized knowledge related to sexuality?
items.a: Health care resources
items.ex: Health care resources, an environmental factor, refers to the availability of personnel with specialized sexuality knowledge.
w: Patient observations
Patient observations are what the nurse notices, not staff availability.
Cultural considerations
Cultural considerations relate to the patient’s culture, not staff.
Time pressure
Time pressure relates to the nurse’s available time, not specialized staff.

alt.q: A nurse notes that the agency has a sex therapist available for consultation. Which environmental factor in the critical thinking model does this represent?
alt.a: Health care resources
alt.ex: The availability of personnel with specialized knowledge related to sexuality is a health care resource.
w: Setting
Setting refers to how the care environment affects the patient’s ability to communicate.
Time pressure
Time pressure refers to limits on the nurse’s time.
Patient observations
Patient observations are cues the nurse gathers from the patient.

items.q: Which items are part of the knowledge base in the critical thinking model for sexuality assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Ways to phrase questions related to sexuality
Phrasing sexual questions is part of the knowledge base.
Effects of illness, injury, and medications on sexual function
These effects are part of the knowledge base.
Behaviors suggestive of sexual abuse
Recognizing abuse behaviors is part of the knowledge base.
Safe sex practices and contraceptive methods
Safe sex and contraception are part of the knowledge base.
Time pressure on the nursing unit
Time pressure is an environmental factor.
Agency policies and procedures
Agency policies are standards.
items.ex: The knowledge base covers question phrasing, effects of illness and medications, abuse behaviors, and safe sex practices.

alt.q: A nurse reviews what knowledge to apply before a sexuality assessment. Which items belong in the knowledge base? Select all that apply.
o: Effect of self-concept on sexuality
Self-concept effects are part of the knowledge base.
Influence of the patient’s culture and sexual orientation
Culture and orientation are part of the knowledge base.
Factors affecting sexuality based on developmental age
Developmental factors are part of the knowledge base.
Previous experiences developing rapport with patients
Previous experiences belong to the experience component.
Ethical standards of practice
Ethical standards belong to the standards component.
alt.ex: Self-concept, culture and sexual orientation, and developmental factors are part of the knowledge base.

items.q: Which nurse actions are likely to encourage a patient to discuss sexual concerns? Select all that apply.
o: Providing a quiet, private setting
Privacy increases comfort in discussing sexual concerns.
Maintaining a nonjudgmental attitude
Avoiding negative verbal and nonverbal cues encourages sharing.
Using caring direct and open-ended questions
This combination gives patients the chance to express concerns.
Being aware of personal biases
Awareness of bias helps the nurse respond respectfully.
Showing discomfort through facial expression
Negative nonverbal cues discourage disclosure.
Discussing concerns at a busy nurses’ station
A busy, public setting discourages discussion.
items.ex: Privacy, a nonjudgmental attitude, caring questions, and self-awareness all promote discussion of sexual concerns.

alt.q: Which nurse behaviors are likely to discourage a patient from sharing sexual concerns? Select all that apply.
o: Conveying disapproval through tone of voice
Negative verbal cues discourage disclosure.
Holding the discussion in a crowded hallway
Lack of privacy discourages discussion of sexual concerns.
Steering the patient toward the nurse’s own values
Imposing values ignores respect for the patient as an individual.
Offering privacy before asking sensitive questions
Privacy encourages patients to share concerns.
Using a caring, matter-of-fact approach
A caring approach supports open discussion.
alt.ex: Disapproval, lack of privacy, and imposing personal values discourage patients from sharing concerns.

items.q: Which factors are part of the environment component of the critical thinking model for sexuality assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Time pressure
Time pressure is an environmental factor.
A health care setting that may affect the patient’s ability to communicate
The setting is an environmental factor.
Cultural considerations
Cultural considerations are listed under environment.
Patient observations
Patient observations are listed under environment.
Ethical standards
Ethical standards belong to the standards component.
Previous experiences developing rapport
Previous experiences belong to the experience component.
items.ex: The environment component includes time pressure, setting, cultural considerations, patient observations, and health care resources.

alt.q: A nurse considers environmental influences before assessing a patient’s sexual concerns. Which factors should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.
o: Availability of personnel with specialized knowledge of sexuality
Health care resources are an environmental factor.
Limited time available for the discussion
Time pressure is an environmental factor.
Whether the care setting allows the patient to communicate comfortably
The setting can affect the patient’s ability to communicate.
Agency policies and procedures
Agency policies belong to the standards component.
Knowledge of safe sex practices
Safe sex knowledge belongs to the knowledge base.
alt.ex: Health care resources, time pressure, and the care setting are environmental factors in the critical thinking model.

items.q: Nurses use what they have learned from working with other patients to develop trust with current patients.
items.a: True
items.ex: Along with personal experiences, nurses draw on experience with other patients to build trust.
items.ww: Experience with previous patients is described as a resource, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Nurses should set aside lessons learned from previous patients so that those lessons do not influence current care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Experience with other patients helps nurses develop trust and care for patients more reflectively.
alt.ww: The textbook encourages using previous experiences, so the statement is not true.

items.q: Professional standards require respect for each patient as an individual, even when the patient’s customs differ from the nurse’s.
items.a: True
items.ex: Patients have customs and values different from the nurse’s, and standards require respecting each patient as an individual.
items.ww: Respect for individual values is a professional requirement, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: When a patient’s sexual values differ from the nurse’s, the nurse should encourage the patient to adopt the nurse’s values.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The nurse seeks a mutually beneficial way to proceed while respecting the patient’s values.
alt.ww: Imposing personal values violates professional standards, so the statement is not true.

items.q: A nurse’s attitude about masturbation may stem from personal experience or from values communicated by other people.
items.a: True
items.ex: Attitudes about masturbation can come from personal experience or from others’ values and beliefs.
items.ww: The textbook names both sources, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: A nurse’s attitudes about sexuality come only from formal nursing education.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Attitudes also come from personal experiences, others’ values, and early exploration.
alt.ww: Many sources shape sexual attitudes, so the statement is not true.

items.q: The critical thinking attitude of [[integrity]] requires the nurse to recognize when personal opinions and values conflict with those of the patient.
items.ex: Integrity means recognizing value conflicts and deciding how to proceed in a mutually beneficial way.

alt.q: When a nurse recognizes that personal values conflict with a patient’s and seeks a mutually beneficial approach, the nurse shows [[integrity]].
alt.ex: Integrity means recognizing value conflicts and deciding how to proceed in a mutually beneficial way.

items.q: Which example belongs to the Knowledge base component?
items.a: Effect of self-concept on sexuality
items.ex: The model combines what the nurse knows, the setting, past experiences, professional standards, and critical thinking attitudes.
w: Time pressure on the nurse
That goes with Environment.
Personal sexual experiences and responses
That goes with Experience.
Right to privacy and confidentiality

items.q: A nurse suspects that a patient is experiencing sexual violence. The patient’s partner stays at the bedside during the admission interview. Which action should the nurse take?

items.q: A nurse is beginning the sexual health portion of a nursing history. Which statement by the nurse is best?

alt.q: Why does a nurse use an opening statement before asking sexual health assessment questions?

“That’s funny. Let’s get you ready for breakfast.”

items.q: Which teaching points should the nurse include to help a patient prevent HIV? Select all that apply.

Use PEP as a routine method of HIV prevention

mt.ex: Each nursing diagnosis in the concept map links to interventions aimed at its specific cause.

items.q: The word spirituality comes from the Latin word spiritus. What does spiritus refer to?
items.a: Breath or wind
items.ex: Spiritus refers to breath or wind; the spirit gives life to a person.
w: Belief or faith
Faith is a separate concept of spiritual health; spiritus means breath or wind.
Prayer or worship
Prayer and worship are practices; spiritus means breath or wind.
Soul or afterlife
The chapter defines spiritus as breath or wind, not soul or afterlife.

alt.q: Which statement best describes what the spirit signifies, according to the chapter?
alt.a: Whatever is at the center of all aspects of a person’s life
alt.ex: The spirit gives life to a person and signifies whatever is at the center of all aspects of life.
w: A person’s membership in an organized religious community
Membership in a religious community describes religion, which is narrower than spirit.
The rituals a person performs to express religious beliefs
Rituals are religious practices, not the center of a person’s life.
The part of a person that becomes active only near death
The spirit gives life throughout life, not only near death.

items.q: Which definition of spirituality reflects current thinking described in the chapter?
items.a: An awareness of one’s inner self and a sense of connection to a higher being, nature, or a purpose greater than oneself
items.ex: Spirituality today is defined as awareness of the inner self and connection to a higher being, nature, or a greater purpose.
w: An organized, institution-related practice commonly associated with certain identified beliefs
This describes religion, which is narrower than spirituality.
A system of organized beliefs and worship that a person practices to outwardly express faith
This describes religion, an outward system of worship practices.
A firm belief in a higher power despite a complete lack of physical evidence for it
This describes faith, one construct of spirituality, not spirituality as a whole.

alt.q: A patient says, “I don’t go to church, but I feel deeply connected to nature and to my purpose as a teacher.” How should the nurse interpret this statement?
alt.a: The patient is describing spirituality, which does not depend on religious practice
alt.ex: Spirituality is connection to nature or a purpose greater than oneself and does not require religious practice.
w: The patient lacks spirituality because there is no religious affiliation
Spirituality exists in all people regardless of religious beliefs.
The patient is describing religion, an organized system of worship practices
The patient rejects organized worship; the statement describes connection, not religion.
The patient is describing agnosticism, the belief there is no known ultimate reality
The patient said nothing about ultimate reality; the statement reflects spirituality.

mt.q: Match each term with its meaning as used in the chapter.

items.q: How do atheists typically search for meaning in life, according to the chapter?
items.a: Through their work and their relationships with others
items.ex: Atheists do not believe in God but search for meaning through work and relationships with others.
w: Through organized worship and religious rituals
Organized worship reflects religion, which atheists do not practice.
Through belief in a transcendent higher power
Atheists do not believe in the existence of God or a higher power.
Through scripture reading and daily prayer
Scripture and prayer are religious practices, not the atheist’s source of meaning.

alt.q: A patient who identifies as agnostic says, “I don’t think there’s any grand plan behind things.” Where does this patient most likely find meaning?
alt.a: In what they do and how they live in the here and now
alt.ex: Agnostics find no ultimate meaning, so they discover meaning in what they do and how they live now.
w: In a relationship with a personal God or higher power
Agnostics believe no ultimate reality is known, so meaning does not come from God.
In the promise of an afterlife described by a religion
Belief in an afterlife reflects religious doctrine, not the agnostic view.
In following the doctrines of an organized religion
Religious doctrine is not the agnostic’s source of meaning.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “I’m an atheist, so don’t send a chaplain. I don’t need any of that spiritual stuff.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “I’ll respect that. Can you tell me what gives your life meaning right now?”
items.ex: Spirituality matters regardless of religious belief; the nurse respects the wish and explores sources of meaning.
w: “Everyone needs God during an illness, so I will call the chaplain anyway.”
This imposes the nurse’s beliefs and ignores the patient’s stated wishes.
“Then I will leave spiritual care out of your plan of care entirely.”
Spirituality is important even for atheists, who find meaning in work and relationships.
“Maybe you will feel differently once your illness gets worse.”
This dismisses the patient’s beliefs instead of accepting them.

alt.q: A patient who is agnostic faces a long recovery after surgery. Which nursing action best supports this patient’s spirituality?
alt.a: Exploring how the hospitalization affects the daily activities that give the patient meaning
alt.ex: Agnostics find meaning in what they do and how they live, so the nurse explores those activities.
w: Arranging a daily chaplain visit so the patient can discuss religious faith
Chaplain visits about faith do not fit a patient who finds no ultimate reality.
Documenting that spiritual care does not apply to this patient’s plan of care
Spirituality is important regardless of religious beliefs.
Encouraging the patient to consider joining a local religious community
This imposes religion rather than supporting the patient’s own spirituality.

items.q: Which statement accurately distinguishes religion from spirituality?
items.a: Religion is organized and institution-related; spirituality centers on a person’s connection to something greater
items.ex: Religion is an organized practice tied to identified beliefs; spirituality is a broader individual connection to something greater.
w: Religion is broader and more unifying than spirituality, which is a part of religion
Spirituality is the broader, more unifying concept.
Spirituality and religion are interchangeable terms that describe the same concept
The terms are often interchanged, but they are not synonymous.
Spirituality requires active membership in an organized faith community to exist
Spirituality exists in all people, including atheists and agnostics.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows correct understanding of spirituality and religion?
alt.a: “Spirituality is a broader, more unifying concept than religion.”
alt.ex: Spirituality focuses on connection to something greater, while religion is a narrower, organized practice.
w: “Religion and spirituality mean the same thing, so I can use either term.”
The concepts are often interchanged but are not the same.
“Only patients who belong to a religion have spiritual needs.”
Spirituality is important regardless of a person’s religious beliefs.
“Spirituality is a part of religion, so I assess it through worship habits.”
Religion is the narrower concept; spirituality is not limited to worship.

items.q: Spirituality is important to a person regardless of religious beliefs, including for people who are atheist or agnostic.
items.a: True
items.ex: Atheists find meaning through work and relationships and agnostics through the here and now, so spirituality matters to everyone.
items.ww: The chapter states spirituality is important regardless of a person’s religious beliefs.

alt.q: Because atheists do not believe in God, they have no spiritual needs for the nurse to address.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Atheists search for meaning in life through work and relationships, so spiritual needs remain.
alt.ww: Spirituality exists in all people; atheists still seek meaning that the nurse can support.

items.q: Which barriers to providing spiritual care have nurses and health care providers identified? Select all that apply.
o: Lack of time
Lack of time is a commonly identified barrier to spiritual care.
Lack of education
Lack of education about spiritual care is an identified barrier.
Confusion with terminology
Confusion over terms such as religion and spirituality is a barrier.
Fear of offending patients
Fear of offending patients keeps some providers from offering spiritual care.
Belief that spirituality worsens health outcomes
Research shows spirituality enhances health outcomes; this is not an identified barrier.
Lack of patient interest in spiritual topics
This is not a listed barrier; talking about spirituality often builds trust.
items.ex: Providers report lack of time, lack of education, confusion with terminology, and fear of offending patients as barriers.

alt.q: Why do nurses and other health care providers too often fail to recognize the spiritual dimension of patients? Select all that apply.
o: Spirituality is viewed as not scientific enough
Spirituality is often seen as not scientific enough to address.
Spirituality has many definitions
Its many definitions make spirituality hard to pin down.
Spirituality is difficult to measure
Difficulty measuring spirituality contributes to it being overlooked.
Spirituality applies only to religious patients
Spirituality is important regardless of religious beliefs.
Spirituality has no relationship with health
Research links spirituality with better physical and psychological health.
alt.ex: Providers overlook spirituality because it seems unscientific, has many definitions, and is difficult to measure.

items.q: Which belief did Florence Nightingale hold about spirituality?
items.a: Caring for spiritual needs is as essential as caring for physical needs
items.ex: Nightingale believed caring for a person’s spiritual needs was just as essential as caring for physical needs.
w: Spiritual needs should be met by clergy rather than by nurses
Nightingale saw spiritual care as an essential part of nursing care.
Spiritual needs become important only at the end of life
Nightingale viewed spirituality as essential to health, not only at death.
Spiritual care should begin once physical needs are fully met
She considered spiritual care just as essential, not secondary to physical care.

alt.q: Florence Nightingale viewed spirituality as a force that did what?
alt.a: Provided energy needed to promote a healthy hospital environment
alt.ex: Nightingale believed spirituality was a force providing the energy needed for a healthy hospital environment.
w: Replaced the need for medical treatment of illness
Nightingale saw spirituality as essential alongside, not instead of, physical care.
Belonged only to patients of a particular religion
Nightingale viewed spiritual care as essential for every person.
Distracted patients from following their plan of care
She saw spirituality as an energizing, health-promoting force.

items.q: A nurse’s personal spiritual health can influence the nurse’s attitudes toward spiritual care, professional commitment, and caring.
items.a: True
items.ex: The nurse’s own spiritual health shapes values and beliefs and influences attitudes toward spiritual care and caring.
items.ww: The chapter links the nurse’s spiritual health to attitudes about spiritual care, commitment, and caring.

alt.q: To remain objective, a nurse should set aside awareness of their own spirituality when assessing a patient’s spiritual needs.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Awareness of one’s own spirituality helps the nurse recognize and analyze cues of spiritual problems in patients.
alt.ww: Self-awareness supports accurate spiritual assessment; it is not something to set aside.

items.q: Why does the chapter say nurses need to be aware of their own spirituality?
items.a: It helps them recognize and analyze cues of spiritual problems in patients
items.ex: Knowing one’s own spirituality helps the nurse recognize and analyze cues and provide relevant spiritual care.
w: It allows them to share their beliefs to guide patients’ choices
Nurses should not impose their beliefs or guide patients toward them.
It qualifies them to replace chaplains in providing religious care
Self-awareness supports spiritual care but does not replace pastoral care.
It lets them decide which patients do not need spiritual care
Spirituality matters to all patients; self-awareness is not used to exclude them.

alt.q: Which nursing ability most determines how well a nurse can learn the importance spirituality holds for a patient?
alt.a: Developing caring relationships with patients
alt.ex: Determining the importance of spirituality to patients depends on the nurse’s ability to develop caring relationships.
w: Knowing the doctrines of every major religion
Religious knowledge helps, but caring relationships are the key ability.
Sharing the same religion as the patient
Nurses provide spiritual care to patients of any belief through caring relationships.
Using standardized spiritual scoring tools
Tools assist assessment, but the chapter emphasizes caring relationships.

items.q: A patient with cancer asks, “Do you think my faith can really help me get better?” Which response by the nurse is most consistent with the chapter?
items.a: “Research shows spirituality can enhance health and adaptation to illness, so your beliefs are a real resource.”
items.ex: Spirituality enhances physical and psychological health and adaptation; inner beliefs are powerful resources for healing.
w: “There is no scientific evidence that faith has any effect on health.”
Research shows spirituality positively affects health, quality of life, and adaptation.
“Your faith will cure the cancer if you believe strongly enough.”
This promises a cure; the relationship between spirituality and healing is not fully understood.
“Faith affects only your emotions, not your physical health.”
Spirituality enhances both physical and psychological health.

alt.q: Which statement about the relationship between spirituality and healing is accurate?
alt.a: It is not fully understood, but a person’s intrinsic spirit seems important in healing
alt.ex: The relationship is not completely understood, yet the intrinsic spirit appears to be an important factor in healing.
w: It is fully explained by research on how the brain responds to prayer
The chapter states the relationship is not completely understood.
It has been shown to be unrelated to physical health outcomes
Research shows spirituality enhances physical and psychological health.
It applies only to patients who practice an organized religion
Spirituality is important regardless of religious beliefs.

items.q: Research shows that spirituality positively affects which outcomes? Select all that apply.
o: Physical health
Spirituality positively affects and enhances physical health.
Quality of life
Spirituality enhances quality of life.
Adaptation to illness
Spirituality improves adaptation to illness.
Accuracy of laboratory test results
Spirituality affects health and coping, not the accuracy of laboratory tests.
Inherited genetic risk
Spirituality affects health, quality of life, and coping, not inherited genetic risk.
items.ex: Research shows spirituality enhances physical and psychological health, quality of life, and adaptation to illness.

alt.q: Spirituality has a positive impact on coping with anxiety, stress, and depression in which groups? Select all that apply.
o: Family caregivers
Family caregivers cope better with stress when spirituality is supported.
Patients in critical care
Spirituality helps critical care patients cope with anxiety and stress.
Nurses and nursing students
Spirituality supports coping in nurses and nursing students.
Patients living with cancer
Spirituality helps patients with cancer cope with anxiety and depression.
Only patients who belong to a religion
Spirituality benefits people regardless of religious beliefs.
Only patients at the end of life
Benefits are described across many groups, not only dying patients.
alt.ex: Spirituality improves coping with anxiety, stress, and depression in caregivers, critical care patients, nurses, students, and patients with cancer.

items.q: Which are integrative body-mind techniques named in the chapter? Select all that apply.
o: Prayer
Prayer is an integrative body-mind technique.
Meditation
Meditation is an integrative body-mind technique.
Distraction
Distraction is listed among integrative body-mind techniques.
Deep breathing
Deep breathing is an integrative body-mind technique.
Sedative medication
Medications are pharmacological, not integrative body-mind techniques.
Surgical intervention
Surgery is a medical treatment, not a body-mind technique.
items.ex: Integrative body-mind techniques include prayer, meditation, spirituality, relaxation, distraction, and deep breathing.

alt.q: A nurse plans integrative body-mind techniques for an anxious patient. Which techniques fit this category? Select all that apply.
o: Relaxation
Relaxation is an integrative body-mind technique.
Spirituality
Spirituality itself is listed among integrative body-mind techniques.
Deep breathing
Deep breathing is an integrative body-mind technique.
Antianxiety medication
Medication is a pharmacological therapy, not a body-mind technique.
Restricting all visitors
Restricting visitors is not a body-mind technique and may reduce support.
alt.ex: Relaxation, spirituality, and deep breathing are integrative body-mind techniques that use inner resources for healing.

items.q: According to nursing research, what can spiritual care provided with a holistic approach promote for patients at the end of life?
items.a: A dignified end of life
items.ex: Nursing research shows holistic spiritual care can promote a dignified end for patients at the end of life.
w: A longer survival time
The research cited links holistic spiritual care with dignity, not longer survival.
Avoidance of all grief
Spiritual care supports patients through grief; it does not eliminate it.
Less need for family involvement
Spiritual care often involves family; it does not reduce their role.

alt.q: Research shows that when patients with cancer participate in religious and spiritual activities, which outcome occurs?
alt.a: They remain socially engaged and keep satisfying relationships
alt.ex: Patients with cancer who join religious and spiritual activities stay socially engaged and maintain satisfying relationships.
w: They withdraw from social life to focus on worship
Research shows these patients remain actively engaged socially.
They more often decline further cancer treatment
The chapter does not link spiritual activity with declining treatment.
They no longer need psychological support
Spiritual activity supports, but does not replace, psychological care.

items.q: According to the chapter, a person’s health depends on a balance among which factors?
items.a: Physical, psychological, sociological, cultural, developmental, and spiritual factors
items.ex: Health depends on balancing physical, psychological, sociological, cultural, developmental, and spiritual factors.
w: Physical, genetic, environmental, financial, and occupational factors
This list omits the psychological, cultural, developmental, and spiritual factors named.
Religious, cultural, educational, and economic factors in a community
These are not the factors the chapter lists; spiritual factors are broader than religion.
Physical and psychological factors, with spirituality as a separate concern
Spirituality is part of the balance needed for health, not separate from it.

alt.q: What role does spirituality play in maintaining health, according to the chapter?
alt.a: It helps individuals achieve balance and cope with changes in health status
alt.ex: Spirituality helps people achieve the balance needed for health and cope with changes in health status.
w: It replaces the need for physical and psychological care
Spirituality is one of several factors in the balance, not a replacement.
It matters only when a person faces a terminal illness
Spirituality supports health and coping throughout life.
It affects health only for people who follow a religion
Spirituality is important regardless of religious beliefs.

items.q: The husband of a patient receiving chemotherapy tells the nurse he feels anxious and exhausted but says, “My faith gets me through each day.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Tell me more about how your faith helps you cope right now.”
items.ex: Spirituality helps family caregivers cope with anxiety and stress, so the nurse supports and explores it.
w: “You should focus on practical help instead of relying on faith.”
This dismisses a resource that helps caregivers cope with stress.
“Let’s talk about your wife’s chemotherapy schedule instead.”
Changing the subject ignores the caregiver’s expressed coping resource.
“Many caregivers feel this way, and it will pass with time.”
False reassurance closes the conversation instead of supporting coping.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows correct understanding of spirituality and family caregivers?
alt.a: “Supporting a caregiver’s spirituality can help the caregiver cope with stress and anxiety.”
alt.ex: Spirituality positively affects the ability of family caregivers to cope with anxiety, stress, and depression.
w: “Spirituality helps patients cope but has no effect on family caregivers.”
Research shows spirituality helps family caregivers cope.
“Only patients in critical care benefit from spiritual support.”
Benefits extend to caregivers, nurses, students, and patients with cancer.
“Spiritual support for caregivers is the chaplain’s job, not the nurse’s.”
Nurses support the spirituality of patients and families.

items.q: A nurse whose religious beliefs differ from a patient’s is caring for that patient. Which approach reflects the chapter’s guidance?
items.a: Care for the whole person and accept the patient’s beliefs and experiences
items.ex: Nurses care for the whole person and accept each patient’s beliefs and experiences.
w: Gently share personal beliefs that might bring the patient comfort
Sharing the nurse’s beliefs risks imposing them on the patient.
Refer all spiritual matters to the chaplain without discussion
Spiritual care is part of nursing’s holistic care, not only the chaplain’s.
Focus on physical care and avoid the topic of spirituality
Avoiding spirituality ignores part of caring for the whole person.

alt.q: A patient says, “My beliefs are probably strange to you.” Which response best reflects acceptance of the patient’s beliefs?
alt.a: “Your beliefs matter to your care. Will you tell me more about them?”
alt.ex: Accepting beliefs and inviting the patient to share builds the caring relationship needed for spiritual care.
w: “They are a bit unusual, but I will try my best to respect them.”
Labeling the beliefs unusual conveys judgment rather than acceptance.
“Let’s keep the focus on your physical recovery for today.”
This avoids spirituality instead of accepting the patient’s beliefs.
“I can explain what most people believe about illness.”
This imposes others’ beliefs instead of accepting the patient’s.

items.q: A person who believes that there is no known ultimate reality is described as [[agnostic|an agnostic]].
items.ex: Agnostics find meaning in the here and now because they see no ultimate meaning for the way things are.

alt.q: A patient who says no one can know any ultimate reality holds an [[agnostic]] view and finds meaning in the here and now.
alt.ex: Agnostics find meaning in the here and now because they see no ultimate meaning for the way things are.

items.q: Healing often takes place because of believing, and a person’s inner beliefs and convictions are powerful resources for healing.
items.a: True
items.ex: The chapter states healing often occurs because of believing and inner beliefs are powerful healing resources.
items.ww: The chapter directly describes inner beliefs as powerful resources for healing.

alt.q: Because spirituality is difficult to measure, research has found no association between spirituality and health.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Research shows spirituality enhances physical and psychological health, quality of life, and adaptation to illness.
alt.ww: Despite measurement challenges, research links spirituality with better health outcomes.

items.q: Which description best defines spiritual health?
items.a: A balance between one’s values, goals, and beliefs and one’s relationships within the self and with others
items.ex: Spiritual health is finding balance between values, goals, and beliefs and relationships with self and others.
w: Regular attendance at religious services and strict adherence to a faith’s rules
Attendance and rules describe religious practice, not spiritual health itself.
Freedom from all doubt, anger, and questioning about one’s personal beliefs
Spiritually healthy people may still question; health is about balance.
A firm belief in a higher power despite a lack of any physical evidence
This describes faith, one construct of spirituality.

alt.q: A spiritually healthy patient experiences a sudden loss. Which response is most likely?
alt.a: The patient finds ways of responding or adjusting, often through spiritual beliefs
alt.ex: In times of stress or loss, a spiritually healthy person often finds ways to adjust through spiritual beliefs.
w: The patient feels no stress because spiritual health prevents distress
Spiritual health supports coping but does not prevent stress.
The patient abandons prior beliefs in order to adapt to the loss
Coping styles often lie within existing spiritual beliefs.
The patient avoids reflecting on what the loss means
Spiritually healthy people seek meaning rather than avoid it.

Identity vs. identity confusion (adolescence): Questions spiritual practices and occasionally discards parents’ beliefs.

alt.q: In which developmental stage is this spiritual belief typical: “Recites prayers and imitates parents’ religious actions without understanding them”?
alt.a: Autonomy vs. shame and doubt (18 to 36 months)
alt.ex: Table 35.1 shows spirituality developing from parent-provided trust in infancy to questioning in adolescence and reflection in middle age.
w: Trust vs. mistrust (birth to 18 months)
Trust vs. mistrust (birth to 18 months): Spiritual well-being is provided by parents; trust is the basis for hope.
Industry vs. inferiority (6 to 12 years)
Industry vs. inferiority (6 to 12 years): Demands proof of reality and believes literal meanings of spiritual stories.
Identity vs. identity confusion (adolescence)
Identity vs. identity confusion (adolescence): Questions spiritual practices and occasionally discards parents’ beliefs.

alt.a: Industry vs. inferiority (6 to 12 years)
alt.ex: Table 35.1 shows spirituality developing from parent-provided trust in infancy to questioning in adolescence and reflection in middle age.
w: Trust vs. mistrust (birth to 18 months)
Trust vs. mistrust (birth to 18 months): Spiritual well-being is provided by parents; trust is the basis for hope.
Autonomy vs. shame and doubt (18 to 36 months)
Autonomy vs. shame and doubt (18 to 36 months): Recites prayers and imitates parents’ religious actions without understanding them.
Identity vs. identity confusion (adolescence)
Identity vs. identity confusion (adolescence): Questions spiritual practices and occasionally discards parents’ beliefs.

alt.a: Identity vs. identity confusion (adolescence)
alt.ex: Table 35.1 shows spirituality developing from parent-provided trust in infancy to questioning in adolescence and reflection in middle age.
w: Trust vs. mistrust (birth to 18 months)
Trust vs. mistrust (birth to 18 months): Spiritual well-being is provided by parents; trust is the basis for hope.
Autonomy vs. shame and doubt (18 to 36 months)
Autonomy vs. shame and doubt (18 to 36 months): Recites prayers and imitates parents’ religious actions without understanding them.
Industry vs. inferiority (6 to 12 years)
Industry vs. inferiority (6 to 12 years): Demands proof of reality and believes literal meanings of spiritual stories.

alt.q: In which developmental stage is this spiritual belief typical: “Reviews value system during crisis and embraces people of different faiths”?
alt.a: Generativity vs. stagnation (middle age)
alt.ex: Table 35.1 shows spirituality developing from parent-provided trust in infancy to questioning in adolescence and reflection in middle age.
w: Trust vs. mistrust (birth to 18 months)
Trust vs. mistrust (birth to 18 months): Spiritual well-being is provided by parents; trust is the basis for hope.
Autonomy vs. shame and doubt (18 to 36 months)
Autonomy vs. shame and doubt (18 to 36 months): Recites prayers and imitates parents’ religious actions without understanding them.
Industry vs. inferiority (6 to 12 years)
Industry vs. inferiority (6 to 12 years): Demands proof of reality and believes literal meanings of spiritual stories.

mt.q: Match each Erikson developmental stage with a spiritual belief typical of that stage.
pairs: Spiritual well-being is provided by parents; trust is the basis for hope
Autonomy vs. shame and doubt (18 to 36 months)
Recites prayers and imitates parents’ religious actions without understanding them
Demands proof of reality and believes literal meanings of spiritual stories
