items.q: The parent of a 2-year-old says, “She keeps telling me she got sick because she was naughty.” How should the nurse interpret this?
items.a: It is a typical belief at this age, when children often link illness to bad behavior
items.ex: Toddlers (18 to 36 months) often believe illness is related to bad behavior as they learn right from wrong.
w: It suggests the child has been punished harshly and needs a referral
This belief is developmentally expected and does not by itself suggest harsh punishment.
It shows the child has fully mastered the difference between right and wrong
Toddlers are only beginning to learn the difference between right and wrong.
It is a sign of spiritual distress that requires a chaplain visit
Linking illness to bad behavior is typical for this stage, not distress.

alt.q: Which spiritual characteristic does the nurse expect in a child 18 to 36 months of age?
alt.a: Fascination with magic and mystery
alt.ex: Table 35.1 lists fascination with magic and mystery for the autonomy vs. shame and doubt stage.
w: Questioning spiritual practices and forming own opinions
Questioning practices is typical of adolescence.
Demanding proof of reality behind spiritual stories
Demanding proof is typical of school-age children, 6 to 12 years.
Reviewing the personal value system during a crisis
Reviewing values during crisis is typical of middle-age adults.

items.q: A 16-year-old patient tells the nurse, “I’m not sure I believe what my parents taught me about God anymore.” What is the nurse’s best interpretation?
items.a: Such questioning is expected as adolescents form their own spiritual opinions
items.ex: Adolescents begin to question spiritual practices, form their own opinions, and occasionally discard parents’ beliefs.
w: It indicates spiritual distress that requires an immediate referral
Questioning beliefs is developmentally expected in adolescence.
It shows the teen has fully completed spiritual development
Spirituality continues to grow throughout adulthood.
It signals a complete loss of connectedness with the family
Adolescents often gain spirituality through connectedness with family.

alt.q: Which spiritual characteristic is typical of young adulthood?
alt.a: Forming independent beliefs, attitudes, and lifestyles
alt.ex: Young adults establish self-identity and a world view and form independent beliefs, attitudes, and lifestyles.
w: Imitating parents’ religious actions without understanding them
Imitating without understanding is typical of toddlers.
Believing that illness is caused by bad behavior
Linking illness to bad behavior is typical of toddlers.
Relying on parents to provide spiritual well-being
Parents provide spiritual well-being in infancy.

items.q: Which are among the five constructs that define spirituality? Select all that apply.
o: Connectedness
Connectedness within oneself, with others, and with a higher power is a construct.
Faith and hope
Faith and hope together form one of the five constructs.
Inner strength and peace
Inner strength and peace is one of the five constructs.
Meaning and purpose in life
Finding meaning and purpose in life events is a construct.
Religious affiliation and worship
Religion is an organized system of practice, not a construct of spirituality.
Moral rules and obedience
Obedience to rules is not one of the five constructs.
items.ex: The five constructs are self-transcendence/transcendence, connectedness, faith and hope, inner strength and peace, and meaning and purpose.

alt.q: Which statements about the constructs of spirituality are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Connectedness can be intrapersonal, interpersonal, and transpersonal
Connectedness occurs within oneself, with others and the environment, and with a higher power.
Spirituality helps people find meaning in both positive and negative events
Meaning and purpose apply to both positive and negative life events.
Inner peace fosters calm feelings despite chaos, fear, and uncertainty
Inner peace brings calm and comfort even in great distress.
Faith exists only within religious beliefs
Faith also exists without religious beliefs.
Hope is oriented mainly toward past experiences
Hope is oriented toward future goals and outcomes.
alt.ex: The constructs overlap, and spirituality is the integrating theme that unifies them.

items.q: Which statement best describes self-transcendence?
items.a: A sense of authentically connecting to one’s inner self
items.ex: Self-transcendence is authentic connection to one’s inner self, a positive force allowing new perspectives.
w: Belief that a force greater than the person exists beyond the material world
This defines transcendence, which contrasts with self-transcendence.
Connection with God or an unseen higher power
This describes transpersonal connectedness.
Firm belief held despite a lack of physical evidence
This describes faith.

alt.q: A patient states, “I believe a power far greater than me exists beyond this physical world.” Which concept does this statement reflect?
alt.a: Transcendence
alt.ex: Transcendence is the belief that a force outside of and greater than the person exists beyond the material world.
w: Self-transcendence
Self-transcendence is connecting authentically to one’s inner self.
Intrapersonal connectedness
Intrapersonal connectedness is connection within oneself.
Inner strength
Inner strength is used when making difficult decisions.

items.q: A patient says, “When I pray, I feel that God is right here with me.” Which type of connectedness is the patient describing?
items.a: Transpersonal
items.ex: Transpersonal connectedness is connection with God or an unseen higher power.
w: Intrapersonal
Intrapersonal connectedness is being connected within oneself.
Interpersonal
Interpersonal connectedness is connection with others and the environment.
Communal
Communal is not one of the three types the chapter names.

alt.q: A patient says, “My friends and the time I spend in my garden keep me grounded.” Which type of connectedness is this?
alt.a: Interpersonal
alt.ex: Interpersonal connectedness is being connected with others and the environment.
w: Intrapersonal
Intrapersonal connectedness is connection within oneself.
Transpersonal
Transpersonal connectedness is connection with God or a higher power.
Transcendent
Transcendence is belief in a force beyond the material world, not a type of connectedness.

items.q: Faith can exist without religious beliefs; for example, a person may have faith that all people are good without practicing a religion.
items.a: True
items.ex: Faith allows firm beliefs despite lack of evidence and exists with or without religion.
items.ww: The chapter gives faith that all people are good as an example of faith without religion.

alt.q: Faith, as a construct of spirituality, is limited to people who belong to an organized religion.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Although many associate faith with religion, faith also exists without religious beliefs.
alt.ww: Faith is not limited to religion; nonreligious people can hold firm beliefs too.

items.q: How does the chapter define spiritual well-being?
items.a: Feelings of contentment coming from the inner self
items.ex: Spiritual well-being is feelings of contentment from the inner self and is related to quality of life.
w: Regular participation in religious rituals and worship
Rituals and worship describe religious practice.
An energizing source oriented toward future goals
This describes hope.
Absence of any physical or mental illness
Spiritual well-being can coexist with illness; it comes from inner contentment.

alt.q: Which patient statement best reflects spiritual well-being?
alt.a: “I’ve forgiven my brother, and I can accept that my life will end someday.”
alt.ex: Spiritually healthy people can forgive themselves and others and accept hardship and mortality.
w: “I can’t forgive myself for the mistakes that led to this illness.”
Inability to forgive oneself suggests poor spiritual well-being.
“I don’t see any purpose in my life since the diagnosis.”
Lack of purpose suggests spiritual distress.
“I feel alone and disconnected from everyone I love.”
Spiritual well-being involves feeling connected to others.

items.q: Which are domains of spiritual well-being? Select all that apply.
o: Spiritual belief system
The spiritual belief system is one of the six domains.
Integration with a spiritual community
Integration with a spiritual community is a domain.
Ritualized practices and restrictions
Ritualized practices and restrictions is a domain.
Terminal events planning
Terminal events planning is a domain.
Financial and estate planning
Financial planning is not one of the six domains.
Physical fitness and nutrition
Fitness and nutrition are not domains of spiritual well-being.
items.ex: The six domains are belief system, personal spirituality, community, rituals and restrictions, implications for medical care, and terminal events planning.

alt.q: A nurse uses the domains of spiritual well-being to guide an assessment. Which topics belong to these domains? Select all that apply.
o: Personal spirituality
Personal spirituality is one of the six domains.
Implications for medical care
Implications for medical care is a domain.
Integration with a spiritual community
Integration with a spiritual community is a domain.
Level of formal education
Education level is not a domain of spiritual well-being.
Political affiliation
Political affiliation is not a domain of spiritual well-being.
alt.ex: Assessing all six domains shows how a patient’s spirituality may affect medical care and end-of-life planning.

items.q: Spiritual well-being is associated with which positive health outcomes? Select all that apply.
o: Decreased pain
Spiritual well-being is associated with decreased pain.
Reduced stress
Spiritual well-being is associated with reduced stress.
Lower risk of depression and suicide
Spiritual well-being lowers the risk of depression and suicide.
Improved tolerance to poor environmental conditions
Spiritual well-being improves tolerance to poor environmental conditions.
Higher risk of anxiety disorders
Spiritual well-being is associated with positive, not negative, outcomes.
No further need for medical treatment
Spiritual well-being supports health but does not replace treatment.
items.ex: Spiritual well-being shows the positive side of spirituality and is linked to less pain, stress, depression, and suicide risk.

alt.q: Which characteristics describe a person who is spiritually healthy? Select all that apply.
o: Experiences joy
Spiritually healthy people experience joy.
Can forgive self and others
Forgiveness of self and others reflects spiritual health.
Accepts hardship and mortality
Accepting hardship and mortality reflects spiritual health.
Feels isolated from others
Spiritual well-being involves feeling connected to others.
Avoids thinking about death
Spiritually healthy people accept mortality rather than avoid it.
alt.ex: Spiritually healthy people experience joy, forgive, accept hardship and mortality, and report enhanced quality of life.

items.q: Faith as a relationship with a higher power includes reasoning faith and trusting faith. What is reasoning faith?
items.a: Confidence in something for which there is no proof
items.ex: Reasoning faith (belief) is confidence in something unproven, accepting what reasoning cannot explain.
w: The actions a person takes to live out beliefs
Action describes trusting faith.
Formal membership in an institutional religion
This is faith as a cultural or institutional religion.
Belief based on scientific evidence and proof
Reasoning faith involves confidence without proof.

alt.q: In the chapter’s description of faith as a relationship with a higher power, trusting faith refers to what?
alt.a: Action
alt.ex: Faith incorporates a reasoning faith (belief) and a trusting faith (action), allowing a person to act on beliefs.
w: Belief
Belief describes reasoning faith.
Proof
Faith involves confidence without proof.
Doubt
Doubt is a feature of spiritual distress, not trusting faith.

items.q: A system of organized beliefs and worship that a person practices to outwardly express spirituality is called [[religion]].
items.ex: Religion is the “state of doing,” a system of practices tied to a denomination, sect, or form of worship.

alt.q: A patient outwardly expresses spirituality through [[religion|organized religion]], a specific system of practices tied to a particular denomination or form of worship.
alt.ex: Religion is the “state of doing,” a system of practices tied to a denomination, sect, or form of worship.

items.q: Which statement reflects a difference in how a Buddhist and a Christian view spirituality, as described in the chapter?
items.a: A Buddhist turns inward and values self-control; a Christian looks to God’s love for direction
items.ex: The chapter contrasts the Buddhist’s inward focus on self-control with the Christian’s reliance on God’s love for enlightenment.
w: A Buddhist looks to God’s love for direction; a Christian turns inward to self-control
This reverses the two views described in the chapter.
Both view suffering as caused by karma and disturbing emotions in the same way
Karma as the cause of suffering is a Buddhist teaching, not a shared view.
Both reject personal spirituality in favor of strict outward religious ritual
Both traditions include personal spirituality; neither is described this way.

alt.q: According to the Buddhist Four Noble Truths described in the chapter, what causes suffering?
alt.a: Karma and disturbing emotions
alt.ex: The second Noble Truth states suffering is caused by karma (past actions) and disturbing emotions.
w: Failure to attend worship services
Worship attendance is not named as a cause of suffering.
Lack of faith in a Supreme Being
Buddhists turn inward; suffering is attributed to karma and emotions.
Illness sent as a punishment
The Noble Truths attribute suffering to karma and disturbing emotions.

items.q: Religious practices encompass spirituality, but spirituality does not need to include religious practice.
items.a: True
items.ex: Religion and spirituality are closely associated but not synonymous; spirituality can exist without religion.
items.ww: The chapter states spirituality does not need to include religious practice.

alt.q: The terms religion and spirituality are synonymous and can be used interchangeably when providing spiritual care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Although often used interchangeably, religion and spirituality are not synonymous.
alt.ww: Nurses need to understand the differences; spirituality is broader than religion.

items.q: Which nursing goal is an example of religious care rather than spiritual care?
items.a: Helping the patient maintain faithfulness to belief systems and worship practices
items.ex: Religious care helps patients stay faithful to their belief systems and worship practices.
w: Helping the patient identify meaning and purpose in life
Identifying meaning and purpose is spiritual care.
Helping the patient look beyond the present situation
Looking beyond the present is spiritual care.
Helping the patient maintain personal relationships
Maintaining relationships is part of spiritual care.

alt.q: A nurse helps a patient look beyond the present and find meaning in an illness. Which type of care is the nurse providing?
alt.a: Spiritual care
alt.ex: Spiritual care helps people identify meaning and purpose, look beyond the present, and maintain relationships.
w: Religious care
Religious care supports faithfulness to belief systems and worship practices.
Sacramental care
Sacraments are religious rituals, not the focus described here.
Restorative care
Restorative care is a level of health care, not a type of spiritual support.

items.q: Lisa, a patient receiving chemotherapy, says, “I hope to keep going to church with my family, and with God’s help I can help my children cope.” Which concept is most evident in her statement?
items.a: Hope, an energizing sense of having something to live for and look forward to
items.ex: Hope is present when a person has something to live for and look forward to; it is closely tied to faith.
w: Spiritual distress, a loss of meaning and of hope for the future
Lisa expresses hope and meaning, not their absence.
Agnosticism, the belief that no ultimate reality is known
Lisa expresses faith in God, which is not agnosticism.
Self-transcendence, a sense of connecting to one’s inner self
Lisa’s statement focuses on future goals, which reflects hope.

alt.q: Which statement about hope is accurate?
alt.a: Hope motivates people to achieve goals, such as adopting healthy behaviors
alt.ex: Hope is energizing and motivates people to achieve goals, including healthy behaviors.
w: Hope is unrelated to faith and does not affect coping
Hope is closely associated with faith and helps people cope.
Hope focuses mainly on reviewing past life events
Hope is oriented toward future goals and outcomes.
Hope is present only in people who practice a religion
People express hope in all aspects of life, regardless of religion.

items.q: An 80-year-old patient whose spouse died last year spends much of the week volunteering at a food bank and visiting grandchildren. How should the nurse interpret this behavior?
items.a: It reflects a common way older adults express their spirituality
items.ex: Older adults often express spirituality by turning to important relationships and giving of themselves to others.
w: It suggests avoidance of grief that needs intervention
Giving to others and valuing relationships is a typical spiritual expression in older adults.
It shows a loss of connection with a higher power
Nothing suggests lost connection; spiritual health in older adults often reflects lifelong connection.
It shows that spiritual development has stopped
Spirituality continues to grow throughout adulthood.

alt.q: According to the chapter, spiritual health in older adults often provides what?
alt.a: Peace and acceptance of the self
alt.ex: Spiritual health in older adults gives peace and self-acceptance, often from a lifelong connection with a higher power.
w: Freedom from all illness and loss
Illness and loss can still threaten spiritual development in older adults.
Rejection of past spiritual experiences
Adults develop appreciation of past spiritual experiences.
Independence from relationships with others
Older adults value love and interactions with others.

items.q: Which construct of spirituality provides a dynamic and creative sense of strength to use when making difficult decisions?
items.a: Inner strength and peace
items.ex: Spirituality gives people a dynamic, creative inner strength for difficult decisions and influences health-related quality of life.
w: Self-transcendence
Self-transcendence is authentic connection to one’s inner self and new perspectives.
Connectedness
Connectedness is being connected within oneself, with others, and with a higher power.
Meaning and purpose in life
This construct helps people find meaning in positive and negative events.

alt.q: A patient in the intensive care unit says, “Even with all the noise and fear around me, I feel calm inside.” Which construct of spirituality does this reflect?
alt.a: Inner strength and peace
alt.ex: Inner peace fosters calm, positive feelings despite chaos, fear, and uncertainty.
w: Faith and hope
Faith and hope concern belief and future orientation, not calm amid chaos.
Interpersonal connectedness
Interpersonal connectedness is connection with others and the environment.
Transcendence
Transcendence is belief in a greater force beyond the material world.

items.q: Researchers and scholars agree on a single universal definition of spirituality.
items.a: False
items.ex: Because spirituality is subjective, multidimensional, and personal, no universal definition exists; five overlapping constructs define it.
items.ww: The chapter states scholars cannot agree on a universal definition of spirituality.

alt.q: Spirituality is an inherent human characteristic that exists in all people, regardless of their religious beliefs.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Spirituality is unique to everyone and exists in all people, regardless of religious beliefs.
alt.ww: The chapter describes spirituality as inherent in all people, not only the religious.

items.q: Which description best defines spiritual distress?
items.a: Absence of inner peace and connectedness, with inability to accept events or find meaning or hope
items.ex: Spiritual distress is the absence of inner peace and connectedness and inability to find meaning or hope.
w: Temporary sadness that follows any change in a person’s daily routine
Spiritual distress involves loss of meaning and connectedness, not routine sadness.
Disagreement among family members about which religion a patient follows
Family disagreement is not the definition of spiritual distress.
Lack of membership in an organized religious community or congregation
Spirituality and spiritual distress do not depend on religious membership.

alt.q: A patient with a new diagnosis says, “I don’t know who I am anymore. I feel abandoned, and I’ve lost my faith.” Which problem do these cues suggest?
alt.a: Spiritual distress
alt.ex: Spiritual distress causes people to question identity, feel doubt, lose faith, and feel alone or abandoned.
w: Spiritual well-being
Spiritual well-being involves contentment and connectedness, not abandonment.
Self-transcendence
Self-transcendence is a positive connection with one’s inner self.
Effective spiritual status
The patient’s loss of faith and identity indicates distress, not effective status.

items.q: In which situations is spiritual distress likely to develop? Select all that apply.
o: A patient’s beliefs conflict with a prescribed health regimen
Conflict between beliefs and prescribed regimens causes spiritual distress.
A patient is unable to practice usual religious rituals
Inability to practice usual rituals, as during COVID-19 closures, causes distress.
A patient fails to use spiritual resources during a major loss
Spiritual needs develop when people fail to use their spiritual resources.
A patient draws strength from prayer during treatment
Using prayer as a resource supports coping rather than causing distress.
A patient feels connected to family throughout illness
Connectedness is a feature of spiritual well-being.
items.ex: Spiritual distress arises from belief–treatment conflicts, inability to practice rituals, and failure to use spiritual resources.

alt.q: Terminal illness commonly causes which fears? Select all that apply.
o: Physical pain
Fear of physical pain is common in terminal illness.
Loss of independence
Terminal illness causes fear of losing independence.
Isolation
Fear of isolation is common in terminal illness.
The unknown
Terminal illness creates fear of the unknown and uncertainty about death.
Excessive social contact
Patients fear isolation, not too much social contact.
Losing interest in material wealth
Decreased desire for wealth is reported after a near-death experience, not a fear.
alt.ex: Terminal illness causes fears of pain, loss of independence, isolation, the unknown, and dying.

items.q: A 20-year-old patient injured in a motor vehicle crash shouts, “Why would God let this happen? None of you even care!” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “You sound very angry. I’m here to listen to what this has been like for you.”
items.ex: Anger at God and caregivers is common in sudden illness; acknowledging feelings and listening supports spiritual care.
w: “You shouldn’t blame God or the staff for your injuries.”
This judges the patient’s anger instead of accepting a common response.
“I’ll come back later when you are calmer and ready to talk.”
Leaving withdraws presence when the patient needs support.
“Let me call the chaplain so you can talk to someone about God.”
Referral may help later, but the nurse should first acknowledge and listen.

alt.q: A 50-year-old patient who just had a heart attack begins praying more often and reflecting on the positive aspects of life. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: A common way of remaining faithful to beliefs during sudden illness
alt.ex: People with sudden illness often pray, attend services more, or reflect on positives to stay faithful to their beliefs.
w: A sign of spiritual distress that requires a referral
Praying and reflecting are healthy coping responses, not signs of distress.
Denial of how serious the heart attack has been
Reflecting on beliefs is a way of coping, not denial.
An unusual response seen mainly in chronic illness
This response is described for sudden, acute illness.

items.q: A patient with advanced multiple sclerosis now depends on staff for bathing and feeding and says, “I can’t do anything for myself anymore.” Which feeling, linked to spiritual distress in chronic illness, is the patient expressing?
items.a: Powerlessness
items.ex: Dependence on others for routine self-care in chronic illness often creates feelings of powerlessness.
w: Denial
The patient openly acknowledges the dependence rather than denying it.
Hope
The statement expresses loss of ability, not an orientation toward future goals.
Inner peace
Inner peace fosters calm feelings; the statement expresses distress.

alt.q: Why does chronic illness often lead to spiritual distress?
alt.a: It threatens independence, and dependence on others creates powerlessness
alt.ex: Chronic illness threatens independence; powerlessness and loss of purpose impair coping.
w: It always ends in death within a short period of time
Chronic illness is long term; this describes terminal illness inaccurately.
It prevents patients from using any spiritual resources
Patients often use spirituality to adapt to chronic illness.
It removes any need for long-term adaptation
Adapting to chronic illness sometimes requires a long-term plan.

items.q: Which spiritual challenge is associated with Acute illness?
items.a: Sudden crisis forcing an unanticipated scramble to cope with new realities
items.ex: Each situation threatens spiritual health differently, from sudden crisis to long-term dependence to facing death.
w: Threat to independence, with dependence creating powerlessness
That goes with Chronic illness.
Uncertainty about what death means, prompting review of life’s meaning
That goes with Terminal illness.
Close brush with death that is often transformational
That goes with Near-death experience.

alt.q: Which spiritual challenge is associated with Chronic illness?
alt.a: Threat to independence, with dependence creating powerlessness
alt.ex: Each situation threatens spiritual health differently, from sudden crisis to long-term dependence to facing death.
w: Sudden crisis forcing an unanticipated scramble to cope with new realities
That goes with Acute illness.

That goes with Terminal illness.
Close brush with death that is often transformational
That goes with Near-death experience.

alt.a: Uncertainty about what death means, prompting review of life’s meaning
alt.ex: Each situation threatens spiritual health differently, from sudden crisis to long-term dependence to facing death.
w: Sudden crisis forcing an unanticipated scramble to cope with new realities
That goes with Acute illness.
Threat to independence, with dependence creating powerlessness
That goes with Chronic illness.
Close brush with death that is often transformational
That goes with Near-death experience.

alt.q: Which spiritual challenge is associated with Near-death experience?
alt.a: Close brush with death that is often transformational
alt.ex: Each situation threatens spiritual health differently, from sudden crisis to long-term dependence to facing death.
w: Sudden crisis forcing an unanticipated scramble to cope with new realities
That goes with Acute illness.

That goes with Chronic illness.
Uncertainty about what death means, prompting review of life’s meaning

alt.q: Which situation is associated with this spiritual challenge: “Sudden crisis forcing an unanticipated scramble to cope with new realities”?
alt.a: Acute illness
alt.ex: Each situation threatens spiritual health differently, from sudden crisis to long-term dependence to facing death.
w: Chronic illness
Chronic illness: Threat to independence, with dependence creating powerlessness.
Terminal illness
Terminal illness: Uncertainty about what death means, prompting review of life’s meaning.
Near-death experience
Near-death experience: Close brush with death that is often transformational.

alt.q: Which situation is associated with this spiritual challenge: “Threat to independence, with dependence creating powerlessness”?
alt.a: Chronic illness
alt.ex: Each situation threatens spiritual health differently, from sudden crisis to long-term dependence to facing death.
w: Acute illness
Acute illness: Sudden crisis forcing an unanticipated scramble to cope with new realities.
Terminal illness
Terminal illness: Uncertainty about what death means, prompting review of life’s meaning.
Near-death experience
Near-death experience: Close brush with death that is often transformational.

alt.q: Which situation is associated with this spiritual challenge: “Uncertainty about what death means, prompting review of life’s meaning”?
alt.a: Terminal illness

w: Acute illness
Acute illness: Sudden crisis forcing an unanticipated scramble to cope with new realities.
Chronic illness
Chronic illness: Threat to independence, with dependence creating powerlessness.
Near-death experience
Near-death experience: Close brush with death that is often transformational.

alt.q: Which situation is associated with this spiritual challenge: “Close brush with death that is often transformational”?
alt.a: Near-death experience
alt.ex: Each situation threatens spiritual health differently, from sudden crisis to long-term dependence to facing death.
w: Acute illness
Acute illness: Sudden crisis forcing an unanticipated scramble to cope with new realities.
Chronic illness
Chronic illness: Threat to independence, with dependence creating powerlessness.
Terminal illness
Terminal illness: Uncertainty about what death means, prompting review of life’s meaning.

mt.q: Match each health situation with the spiritual challenge the chapter associates with it.
pairs: Sudden crisis forcing an unanticipated scramble to cope with new realities
Threat to independence, with dependence creating powerlessness
Uncertainty about what death means, prompting review of life’s meaning
Close brush with death that is often transformational
mt.ex: Each situation threatens spiritual health differently, from sudden crisis to long-term dependence to facing death.

items.q: A patient with terminal cancer asks, “What have I done to deserve this?” Which nursing approach does the chapter recommend when caring for dying patients?
items.a: Help the patient gain a greater sense of control over the illness
items.ex: When caring for dying patients, help them gain greater control over their illness in the hospital or at home.
w: Avoid discussing meaning so the patient does not become upset
Questioning life’s meaning is common; avoiding it leaves spiritual needs unmet.
Redirect the patient to focus only on physical comfort measures
Dying involves spiritual health as well as physical comfort.
Explain that such questions are a sign of mental illness
Questions like this are common in terminal illness, not signs of mental illness.

alt.q: Which statement about terminal illness and spirituality is accurate?
alt.a: Some patients have a spiritual sense of peace that lets them face death without fear
alt.ex: Although terminal illness makes patients susceptible to distress, some find spiritual peace and face death without fear.
w: All dying patients experience spiritual distress
Some patients have a spiritual sense of peace about death.
Terminal illness affects the patient but rarely the family
Terminal illness also leads family members to question its meaning.
Patients near death seldom review or question their lives
Terminally ill patients often review life and question its meaning.

items.q: Which statement accurately describes a near-death experience (NDE)?
items.a: A psychological phenomenon in people close to clinical death, not linked to mental disorder
items.ex: An NDE occurs in people close to clinical death or revived after being declared dead and is not a mental disorder.
w: A hallucination that signals an underlying psychiatric disorder
NDEs are not associated with mental disorders.
A dream that reflects the patient’s specific religious expectations
NDEs are shared across cultures and religions, so they are unlikely to reflect specific religious expectations.
A side effect of sedative medications given during resuscitation
The chapter does not attribute NDEs to medications.

alt.q: A patient resuscitated after cardiac arrest describes a near-death experience. Which description is the nurse most likely to hear?
alt.a: Feeling at peace, moving through a dark tunnel, and seeing bright lights
alt.ex: Patients commonly describe peace, an out-of-body experience, a dark tunnel, bright lights, and meeting people who died before.
w: Hearing voices that command the patient to harm others
Command voices are not part of the typical NDE description.
Being unable to remember anything since childhood
Memory loss is not a typical NDE feature.
Seeing only images tied to one specific religion
NDEs are shared across cultures and religions.

items.q: A patient recovering from cardiopulmonary arrest hesitantly tells the nurse, “I saw myself floating above the bed while you were all working on me.” Which response is best?
items.a: “That sounds powerful. Would you like to tell me more about it?”
items.ex: Remaining open and giving the patient a chance to explore the NDE promotes spiritual well-being.
w: “That was probably a reaction to the medications we gave you.”
Explaining it away discourages sharing; acceptance affects how much the patient shares.
“Try not to think about it right now; you need your rest.”
Shutting down the discussion leaves the patient reluctant to share.
“I’ll ask for a psychiatric evaluation just to be safe.”
NDEs are not associated with mental disorders.

alt.q: Why is the nurse’s response to a patient’s report of a near-death experience important?
alt.a: It affects how much the patient shares about the experience
alt.ex: Patients may be reluctant to discuss an NDE; the nurse’s acceptance influences how much they share.
w: It determines whether the patient needs psychiatric care
NDEs are not mental disorders requiring psychiatric care.
It confirms whether the experience actually occurred
The nurse’s role is acceptance, not verifying the experience.
It decides whether the family should be told
Nurses support patients in sharing with significant others if they wish.

items.q: Which changes do patients often report after discussing a near-death experience openly? Select all that apply.
o: No longer being afraid of death
Patients who discuss an NDE are often no longer afraid of death.
Decreased desire to achieve material wealth
Patients report less desire for material wealth after an NDE.
Increased sensitivity to alcohol and medications
Patients report increased sensitivity to chemicals such as alcohol and medications.
Greater fear of dying
Patients are often no longer afraid of death.
Stronger desire for material wealth
The desire for material wealth decreases after an NDE.
items.ex: Patients who openly share an NDE find acceptance and meaning, lose fear of death, and value wealth less.

alt.q: Which nursing actions promote spiritual well-being after a patient survives a near-death experience? Select all that apply.
o: Remaining open to the patient’s account
Openness encourages the patient to share the experience.
Giving the patient a chance to explore what happened
Exploring the experience helps the patient find meaning.
Supporting the patient in sharing it with significant others
Sharing with family helps patients find acceptance and meaning.
Explaining that the experience was caused by low oxygen
Explaining it away discourages the patient from sharing.
Advising the patient not to tell family to avoid worry
Patients who discuss NDEs with family find acceptance and meaning.
alt.ex: After an NDE, the nurse remains open, lets the patient explore what happened, and supports sharing with significant others.

items.q: Because near-death experiences are reported across a broad range of cultures and religions, they are unlikely to reflect specific religious expectations.
items.a: True
items.ex: The commonality of NDEs across cultures suggests they may reflect brain changes near death, not specific religious expectations.
items.ww: Research cited in the chapter notes NDEs are shared across cultures and religions.

alt.q: Near-death experiences mainly reflect the specific religious expectations a patient held before the event.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: NDEs are shared across a broad range of cultures and religions, so they are unlikely to reflect specific religious expectations.
alt.ww: Shared features across cultures argue against NDEs being shaped by specific religious beliefs.

items.q: A psychological phenomenon of people who have been close to clinical death or have recovered after being declared dead is a [[near-death experience|NDE|near death experience]].
items.ex: An NDE is a powerfully close brush with the physical, emotional, and spiritual experiences of death, not a mental disorder.

alt.q: A patient revived after being declared dead who describes bright lights and a dark tunnel has had a [[near-death experience|NDE|near death experience]].
alt.ex: An NDE is a powerfully close brush with the physical, emotional, and spiritual experiences of death, not a mental disorder.

items.q: What do The Joint Commission standards require regarding spiritual care?
items.a: Acknowledging patients’ rights to spiritual care and assessing their beliefs and practices
items.ex: TJC requires organizations to acknowledge rights to spiritual care, provide for spiritual needs, and assess beliefs and practices.
w: Assigning a chaplain to perform every patient’s spiritual assessment
TJC requires nurses to assess beliefs; it does not assign this only to chaplains.
Providing spiritual care only to patients who request a specific religion
TJC requires acknowledging all patients’ rights to spiritual care.
Including prayer in the plan of care for all hospitalized patients
Routinely implementing prayer for everyone is coercive and unethical.

alt.q: Under The Joint Commission standards, through whom may health care organizations provide for patients’ spiritual needs?
alt.a: Pastoral care or others who are certified, ordained, or lay individuals
alt.ex: TJC allows spiritual needs to be met through pastoral care or certified, ordained, or lay individuals.
w: Only ordained clergy of the patient’s own faith
Lay and certified individuals may also provide spiritual care.
Only registered nurses with spiritual care certification
TJC names pastoral care and others, not only certified nurses.
Only family members chosen by the patient
TJC refers to pastoral care and certified, ordained, or lay providers.

items.q: Routinely implementing standard nursing interventions such as prayer or meditation for every patient is coercive and unethical.
items.a: True
items.ex: Nurses must determine which interventions are compatible with each patient’s beliefs, based on patient input, before selecting them.
items.ww: The chapter explicitly calls routine prayer or meditation coercive and unethical.

alt.q: Because prayer has documented benefits, nurses should include it routinely in every patient’s plan of care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Routine prayer is coercive; interventions must be chosen based on patient input and compatibility with beliefs.
alt.ww: Benefits do not justify imposing prayer; the ANA Code requires respect for each patient’s beliefs.

items.q: A nurse’s religious beliefs conflict with a patient’s choice to rely on faith practices during illness. Which behavior demonstrates the critical thinking attitude of integrity?
items.a: Refraining from voicing personal opinions about religion to the patient
items.ex: Nurses show integrity by not voicing opinions about religion or spirituality when their beliefs conflict with patients’.
w: Sharing personal beliefs so the patient can consider other options
Voicing conflicting beliefs violates integrity and may bias the patient.
Asking to be reassigned to a patient with similar beliefs
Integrity involves respecting differences, not avoiding them.
Documenting that the patient’s beliefs interfere with care
This lets personal bias form incorrect conclusions about patient needs.

alt.q: Why is humility essential when providing spiritual care, especially to patients from diverse cultural backgrounds?
alt.a: It helps the nurse recognize limits in knowledge of patients’ beliefs and practices
alt.ex: Humility means recognizing personal limitations in knowledge about patients’ spiritual beliefs and religious practices.
w: It allows the nurse to avoid discussing spirituality with patients
Humility supports, rather than avoids, spiritual assessment.
It ensures the nurse’s beliefs guide the patient’s choices
Nurses should not let personal beliefs guide patient choices.
It means deferring all spiritual questions to family members
Humility does not mean handing off spiritual care to family.

items.q: An oncologist strongly encourages a second round of chemotherapy rather than recommending palliative care. What does this example from the chapter illustrate?
items.a: A provider’s beliefs can affect how treatment options are discussed with patients
items.ex: Beliefs of a health care provider affect discussions of treatment options and ultimately patients’ health care choices.
w: Palliative care is inappropriate for patients who have cancer
The example is about provider influence, not the suitability of palliative care.
Patients’ spiritual beliefs rarely influence their treatment choices
The example shows provider beliefs matter; patient beliefs also shape choices.
Providers must always recommend the most aggressive therapy
The example warns about provider bias, not a rule to choose aggressive therapy.

alt.q: When a health care provider’s beliefs might shape a patient’s treatment choices, what does focusing on the patient’s spiritual health require of the nurse?
alt.a: Advocating for the patient’s ability to exercise their own beliefs
alt.ex: Focusing on patients’ spiritual health means advocating for their ability to exercise their beliefs.
w: Supporting the provider’s recommendation regardless of beliefs
The nurse advocates for the patient’s beliefs, not the provider’s preferences.
Encouraging the patient to adopt the nurse’s view of treatment
Nurses must not let personal biases shape patient decisions.
Avoiding any discussion of treatment choices with the patient
Advocacy requires engaging with the patient’s beliefs and choices.

items.q: Which types of knowledge help a nurse provide appropriate spiritual care? Select all that apply.
o: Concepts of spirituality
Knowledge of spirituality concepts helps anticipate patients’ personal issues.
Understanding of ethics
Ethics knowledge supports appropriate spiritual care.
The patient’s faith and belief systems
Knowing the patient’s faith and beliefs guides appropriate care.
The nurse’s own religious doctrine as the standard
Using the nurse’s doctrine as a standard imposes personal beliefs.
Diagnosis codes used for billing
Billing codes do not guide spiritual care.
items.ex: Knowledge of spirituality concepts, ethics, and the patient’s faith and beliefs helps the nurse provide appropriate spiritual care.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with a chronic illness. Which statements about chronic illness and spirituality are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Dependence on others often creates feelings of powerlessness
Dependence for routine self-care creates powerlessness.
Loss of a sense of purpose impairs the ability to cope
Powerlessness and loss of purpose impair coping with changed functioning.
Successful adaptation provides spiritual growth
Adapting to lifestyle changes strengthens a person spiritually.
Spiritual well-being has little effect on accepting the illness
Spiritual well-being helps patients cope with and accept chronic illness.
Adaptation is always achieved quickly without long-term planning
Adaptation sometimes takes a long-term plan.
alt.ex: Chronic illness can cause powerlessness, but spiritual well-being and successful adaptation support coping and growth.

items.q: Which nurses are more likely to care for their patients’ spiritual needs?
items.a: Nurses who are comfortable with their own spirituality
items.ex: Nurses comfortable with their own spirituality are more likely to care for patients’ spiritual needs.
w: Nurses who share the same religion as their patients
Comfort with one’s own spirituality, not shared religion, is the key factor.
Nurses who avoid reflecting on their own beliefs
Knowing one’s own spirituality helps nurses assist patients.
Nurses who work only in palliative care settings
Spiritual care is part of holistic practice in every setting.

alt.q: Nurses who foster their own spiritual health become resources for patients when they do what?
alt.a: Listen to patients’ stories and use their own spirituality as a tool
alt.ex: Nurses who foster their own spiritual health help patients by listening to stories and using spirituality as a tool.
w: Teach patients to adopt the nurse’s faith practices
Nurses should not impose their beliefs on patients.
Make spiritual decisions on patients’ behalf
Patients’ autonomy guides spiritual decisions.
Limit spiritual care to scheduled chaplain visits
Nurses provide spiritual care directly, not only through chaplains.

items.q: Which intellectual standards of critical thinking help the nurse explore the issues most meaningful to the patient and most likely to affect spiritual well-being?
items.a: Significance and relevance
items.ex: Significance and relevance let the nurse explore issues most meaningful to patients and most likely to affect spiritual well-being.
w: Clarity and precision
These standards matter, but the chapter names significance and relevance for this purpose.
Breadth and depth
The chapter names significance and relevance, not breadth and depth, here.
Logic and fairness
The chapter identifies significance and relevance for exploring meaningful issues.

alt.q: A nurse wants specific, significant, and relevant information when assessing a patient’s spiritual needs. Which element of critical thinking ensures this?
alt.a: Applying intellectual standards
alt.ex: Intellectual standards ensure specific, significant, and relevant information when assessing spiritual needs.
w: Applying personal religious beliefs
Personal beliefs can bias conclusions about patient needs.
Relying on environmental factors
Environmental factors affect care delivery, not the quality of information gathered.
Using delegation principles
Delegation principles do not ensure relevant assessment data.

items.q: Jeff notes that Lisa, who has breast cancer, can openly discuss her cancer and her treatment plan. What does this cue suggest, and what should Jeff do?
items.a: Lisa shows acceptance; offer her chances to share feelings and discuss the future
items.ex: As patients accept a life-threatening diagnosis, the nurse offers opportunities to share feelings and discuss the future.
w: Lisa is in denial; avoid discussing the future with her for now
Openly discussing the cancer and treatment shows acceptance, not denial.
Lisa has spiritual distress; refer her to a chaplain right away
Her open discussion does not suggest spiritual distress.
Lisa needs no support; focus only on her chemotherapy side effects
Accepting patients still benefit from chances to share feelings.

alt.q: As a patient begins to accept the diagnosis of a life-threatening disease, which nursing action is most appropriate?
alt.a: Offer opportunities to share feelings and discuss the future
alt.ex: Offering chances to share feelings and discuss the future supports patients as they accept the diagnosis.
w: Postpone discussions until treatment is completed
Delaying discussion misses the opportunity acceptance provides.
Focus conversation on physical symptoms only
Spiritual and emotional needs also require attention.
Encourage the patient to keep feelings private
Sharing feelings supports coping with a life-threatening disease.

items.q: The strength of a patient’s spirituality influences the ability to cope with and recover from a sudden illness or injury.
items.a: True
items.ex: Sudden illness creates crises that threaten spiritual health; spiritual strength influences coping and recovery.
items.ww: The chapter directly links the strength of spirituality to coping and recovery after sudden illness.

alt.q: Sudden, unexpected illness rarely affects spiritual health because patients focus on physical recovery.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Sudden, unexpected illness often creates spiritual distress and conflicts about beliefs and life’s meaning.
alt.ww: Acute illness is described as a common cause of spiritual distress, not something that spares spiritual health.

items.q: To avoid interruptions, the nurse can set aside specific time for spiritual assessment during routine care, such as when giving medications or setting up a meal tray.
items.a: True
items.ex: Setting aside time during routine care helps avoid time conflicts and interruptions during spiritual assessment.
items.ww: The chapter gives giving medications and setting up a meal tray as examples of set-aside time.

alt.q: Spiritual assessment should never be combined with routine care, such as giving medications, because it requires a separate scheduled visit.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The chapter suggests using routine care times, such as giving medications, to set aside time with the patient.
alt.ww: Routine care moments are recommended opportunities, not forbidden ones.

items.q: Which assessment question fits the area Faith, belief, fellowship, and community?
items.a: How does your faith help you cope?
items.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.
w: How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?
That goes with Life and self-responsibility.
Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?
That goes with Life satisfaction.
What feelings do you have after you pray or meditate?
That goes with Connectedness.

alt.q: Which assessment question fits the area Life and self-responsibility?
alt.a: How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?
alt.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.
w: How does your faith help you cope?
That goes with Faith, belief, fellowship, and community.
Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?
That goes with Life satisfaction.
What feelings do you have after you pray or meditate?
That goes with Connectedness.

alt.q: Which assessment question fits the area Life satisfaction?
alt.a: Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?
alt.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.
w: How does your faith help you cope?
That goes with Faith, belief, fellowship, and community.
How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?
That goes with Life and self-responsibility.
What feelings do you have after you pray or meditate?
That goes with Connectedness.

alt.q: Which assessment question fits the area Connectedness?
alt.a: What feelings do you have after you pray or meditate?
alt.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.
w: How does your faith help you cope?
That goes with Faith, belief, fellowship, and community.
How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?
That goes with Life and self-responsibility.
Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?
That goes with Life satisfaction.

alt.q: Which assessment question fits the area Vocation?
alt.a: How has your illness affected the way you live spiritually at home or work?
alt.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.
w: How does your faith help you cope?
That goes with Faith, belief, fellowship, and community.
How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?
That goes with Life and self-responsibility.
Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?
That goes with Life satisfaction.

alt.q: Which area of spiritual assessment does this question address: “How does your faith help you cope?”?
alt.a: Faith, belief, fellowship, and community
alt.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.
w: Life and self-responsibility
Life and self-responsibility: How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?.
Life satisfaction
Life satisfaction: Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?.
Connectedness

alt.q: Which area of spiritual assessment does this question address: “How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?”?
alt.a: Life and self-responsibility
alt.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.
w: Faith, belief, fellowship, and community
Faith, belief, fellowship, and community: How does your faith help you cope?.
Life satisfaction
Life satisfaction: Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?.
Connectedness
Connectedness: What feelings do you have after you pray or meditate?.

alt.q: Which area of spiritual assessment does this question address: “Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?”?
alt.a: Life satisfaction
alt.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.
w: Faith, belief, fellowship, and community
Faith, belief, fellowship, and community: How does your faith help you cope?.
Life and self-responsibility
Life and self-responsibility: How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?.
Connectedness
Connectedness: What feelings do you have after you pray or meditate?.

alt.q: Which area of spiritual assessment does this question address: “What feelings do you have after you pray or meditate?”?
alt.a: Connectedness
alt.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.
w: Faith, belief, fellowship, and community
Faith, belief, fellowship, and community: How does your faith help you cope?.
Life and self-responsibility
Life and self-responsibility: How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?.
Life satisfaction
Life satisfaction: Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?.

alt.q: Which area of spiritual assessment does this question address: “How has your illness affected the way you live spiritually at home or work?”?
alt.a: Vocation
alt.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.
w: Faith, belief, fellowship, and community
Faith, belief, fellowship, and community: How does your faith help you cope?.
Life and self-responsibility
Life and self-responsibility: How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?.
Life satisfaction
Life satisfaction: Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?.

mt.q: Match each area of spiritual assessment from Box 35.1 with an example assessment question.
pairs: How does your faith help you cope?
How do you feel about the changes this illness has caused?
Which accomplishments help you feel satisfied with your life?
What feelings do you have after you pray or meditate?
How has your illness affected the way you live spiritually at home or work?
mt.ex: Box 35.1 groups open-ended assessment questions by area so the nurse covers each aspect of spirituality.

items.q: A patient who is a Jehovah’s Witness has a critically low hemoglobin, and a blood transfusion is being considered. Which assessment finding is most important for the nurse to communicate to the health care provider?
items.a: The patient’s faith does not accept blood products as treatment
items.ex: Assess for faith-based guidance that conflicts with treatment; for Jehovah’s Witnesses, blood products are not acceptable.
w: The patient attends worship services every week
Attendance does not affect the treatment decision the provider must make.
The patient avoids alcohol as part of their faith
Avoiding alcohol is a dietary practice, not a conflict with transfusion.
The patient would like a visit from a congregation elder
A visit may be supportive, but the treatment conflict is the priority.

alt.q: During a faith assessment, a nurse learns that a patient is a Christian Scientist. Why is this information important to the plan of care?
alt.a: The patient may refuse medical interventions, believing faith heals
alt.ex: Christian Scientists may refuse any medical intervention because they believe their faith heals them.
w: The patient will require a strict vegetarian diet
Vegetarian diets are associated with some Hindus and Buddhists.
The patient must pray five times daily facing Mecca
Praying five times daily toward Mecca is the Islamic practice of Salah.
The patient will need to fast on Holy Days
Fasting on Holy Days is described for some Buddhists.

items.q: A patient’s admission record lists a church affiliation. The nurse is thinking about calling the church’s pastor to visit. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Ask the patient about their relationship with the pastor and faith community
items.ex: Do not assume a network offers desired support; a pastor’s visit is inappropriate if the patient has little fellowship there.
w: Call the pastor, because church members usually want to visit
Assuming support exists may lead to an unwanted, inappropriate visit.
Ask the family to contact the pastor without involving the patient
Involving others requires the patient’s permission and wishes.
Document the affiliation and request a pastoral visit at discharge
This still assumes the patient wants this pastor’s support.

alt.q: Which statement about assessing a patient’s fellowship and community is accurate?
alt.a: Do not assume a support network offers the type of support the patient desires
alt.ex: The nurse explores the extent and nature of support networks rather than assuming they provide wanted support.
w: A listed religious affiliation confirms strong ties to that community
Affiliation alone does not show the patient has fellowship there.
Fellowship includes only members of the patient’s place of worship
Fellowship also includes family, friends, coworkers, and neighbors.
Faith-based social support has little effect on health outcomes
Faith-based social support protects against negative health outcomes.

items.q: A 32-year-old patient who has had a second miscarriage stares out the window and says, “I don’t know why God did this to me again. How am I going to go on?” Which nursing diagnosis do these cues most support?
items.a: Spiritual Distress
items.ex: Expressing anger toward God and lack of hope or meaning are cues for Spiritual Distress after a recent loss.
w: Decreased Spiritual Distress
This diagnosis reflects effective resources and meaning, not hopelessness.
Effective Spiritual Status
The patient’s anger at God and hopelessness do not reflect effective status.
Impaired Family Process
No cues describe changes in family functioning.

alt.q: Which assessment finding supports the nursing diagnosis Decreased Spiritual Distress?
alt.a: The patient finds satisfaction while volunteering in community service
alt.ex: Decreased Spiritual Distress shows meaning and purpose through connectedness, such as satisfaction in volunteering.
w: The patient expresses anger toward God about the illness
Anger toward God is a cue for Spiritual Distress.
The patient states that life no longer has any meaning
Loss of meaning is a cue for Spiritual Distress.
The patient verbalizes conflicts about personal beliefs
Conflicts about beliefs suggest Spiritual Distress.

items.q: Which patients are likely to experience spiritual distress? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with poor relationships
Poor relationships increase the likelihood of spiritual distress.
A patient who recently experienced a loss
A recent loss makes spiritual distress more likely.
A patient suffering from a mental or physical illness
Mental or physical illness increases the risk of spiritual distress.
A patient who reports strong connectedness with family
Strong connectedness reflects spiritual well-being.
A patient who finds purpose in volunteer work
Finding purpose supports Decreased Spiritual Distress.
items.ex: Patients with poor relationships, recent loss, or mental or physical illness are likely to experience spiritual distress.

alt.q: Which assessment findings reflect the nursing diagnosis Spiritual Distress? Select all that apply.
o: Expressing lack of hope
Lack of hope reflects a poor state of spiritual well-being.
Expressing anger toward God
Anger toward God is a cue for Spiritual Distress.
Verbalizing conflicts about personal beliefs
Conflicts about beliefs suggest Spiritual Distress.
Interacting with friends and family during hard times
This supports Decreased Spiritual Distress.
Expressing inner strength and a source of guidance
Inner strength supports Decreased Spiritual Distress.
alt.ex: Spiritual Distress shows patterns of sadness, such as lack of hope or meaning, anger at God, or conflicting beliefs.

items.q: Which nursing diagnoses are commonly associated with spiritual health–related problems? Select all that apply.
o: Hopelessness
Hopelessness is listed among spiritual health–related diagnoses.
Powerlessness
Powerlessness is listed among spiritual health–related diagnoses.
Conflicting Spiritual Belief
Conflicting Spiritual Belief is a listed diagnosis.
Risk for Spiritual Distress
Risk for Spiritual Distress is a listed diagnosis.
Impaired Gas Exchange
Impaired Gas Exchange is a respiratory diagnosis.
Risk for Falls
Risk for Falls is a safety diagnosis, not a spiritual one.
items.ex: Common spiritual diagnoses include Risk for Spiritual Distress, Effective Spiritual Status, Hopelessness, Powerlessness, and Conflicting Spiritual Belief.

alt.q: Jeff analyzed assessment data for Lisa, a patient receiving chemotherapy for breast cancer. Which problems did he identify? Select all that apply.
o: Decreased Spiritual Distress
Lisa’s strong belief in God, church attendance, and prayer support this diagnosis.
Impaired Family Process
Lisa’s illness changed family dynamics, with less time together.
Anxiety
Lisa worries about the future and her chemotherapy symptoms.
Hopelessness
Lisa expresses hope and faith, so hopelessness was not identified.
Powerlessness
Jeff did not identify powerlessness among Lisa’s three problems.
alt.ex: Jeff identified Decreased Spiritual Distress, Impaired Family Process, and Anxiety, with Decreased Spiritual Distress as the priority.

items.q: A patient in acute distress after a new diagnosis says, “Everything is out of my control now.” Which nursing action best addresses this concern?
items.a: Let the patient decide whether to have morning care now or later
items.ex: When a patient is in acute distress, providing a sense of control minimizes powerlessness.
w: Complete all morning care quickly so the patient can rest
Doing care without input does not restore the patient’s sense of control.
Postpone spiritual care until physical priorities are met
Spiritual priorities do not need to be sacrificed for physical priorities.
Ask the family to make care decisions for the patient
Shifting decisions to family increases powerlessness.

alt.q: When a patient is terminally ill, what does the chapter identify as often the most important nursing intervention in supporting the patient and family in grief?
alt.a: Spiritual care
alt.ex: For terminally ill patients, spiritual care is often the most important intervention supporting patients and families in grief.
w: Discharge teaching
Teaching has a role, but spiritual care is often most important in terminal illness.
Hygiene care
Physical care continues, but spiritual care is often most important for grief.
Nutritional support
Nutrition matters, but spiritual care is identified as most important here.

items.q: Spiritual priorities do not need to be sacrificed for physical care priorities.
items.a: True
items.ex: Spiritual care is personalized, and the patient identifies what is most important in a mutually agreed-on plan.
items.ww: The chapter states spiritual priorities need not be sacrificed for physical care.

alt.q: Spiritual care should be postponed until a patient’s physical care priorities have been fully resolved.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Spiritual priorities do not need to be sacrificed for physical care priorities.
alt.ww: Postponing spiritual care contradicts the chapter’s guidance on setting priorities.

items.q: A hospitalized patient is active in a local church that has a faith community nurse. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: With the patient’s permission, involve the faith community nurse in the plan of care
items.ex: With the patient’s permission, the nurse involves clergy or church members, such as a faith community nurse, in care.
w: Contact the faith community nurse and share the patient’s diagnosis
Sharing health information requires the patient’s permission first.
Avoid involving church members to protect the patient’s privacy
Church resources can support the patient when the patient permits.
Ask the faith community nurse to complete the spiritual assessment
The nurse remains responsible for assessing the patient’s spirituality.

alt.q: What role can a faith community (parish) nurse serve for patients?
alt.a: A support and link to help with health care needs and spiritual health
alt.ex: Faith community nurses support spiritual health and link patients, especially older adults, with health care needs.
w: A replacement for the hospital pastoral care department
Pastoral care remains a separate, valuable hospital resource.
A provider who prescribes treatments for church members
Faith community nurses support and link patients; they are not prescribers.
A clergy member who performs sacraments and rites
Clergy and pastoral care provide sacraments, not faith community nurses.

items.q: A patient who just learned that her cancer has spread begins to cry. Which nursing action best establishes presence?
items.a: Sit with the patient, listen attentively, and accept her need to cry
items.ex: Presence is established by sitting with the patient, listening, accepting the need to cry, and offering time.
w: Leave the room to give the patient time to cry alone
Leaving removes presence, which helps prevent emotional isolation.
Hand her tissues and quickly change the subject
Changing the subject does not accept or support the need to cry.
Explain all of the treatment options available to her
Giving information is “doing for”; presence is “being with.”

alt.q: Which statement best describes the nursing concept of presence?
alt.a: “Being with” a patient rather than “doing for” a patient
alt.ex: Presence is being with a patient physically, psychologically, and spiritually, which prevents isolation and provides hope.
w: “Doing for” a patient by completing care tasks quickly
Presence emphasizes being with, not doing for.
Remaining physically in the room while charting
Presence requires attentive connection, not just physical proximity.
Making decisions for the patient to reduce stress
Presence supports patients as they make their own decisions.

items.q: Which factor is evident when a healing relationship develops between a nurse and a patient?
items.a: Realistically mobilizing hope for the nurse and patient
items.ex: A healing relationship includes realistic hope, an acceptable interpretation of the illness, and use of social, emotional, and spiritual resources.
w: The nurse deciding which beliefs best fit the patient
Imposing beliefs does not build a healing relationship.
The patient relying fully on the nurse for decisions
Healing relationships help patients use their own resources.
Avoiding any interpretation of the patient’s illness
Finding an acceptable interpretation of the illness is part of healing.

alt.q: An adult daughter becoming a caregiver for her older parent hopes to protect the parent from injury. Which nursing action helps make her hope realistic?
alt.a: Teaching the daughter basic care skills
alt.ex: Instructing the daughter in basic care skills makes her hope realistic, which is central to a healing relationship.
w: Assuring her that the parent will not be injured
False assurance does not make hope realistic.
Advising her to give up caregiving to avoid harm
This removes her hope rather than supporting it.
Suggesting she rely on prayer instead of training
Hope becomes realistic through skills, not by replacing training.

Planning and outcomes identification

Evaluation

items.q: When spiritual care involves helping a patient adjust to loss or a stressful life situation, expected outcomes are usually long term.
items.a: True
items.ex: Adjusting to loss takes time, so outcomes are long term, with short-term outcomes marking progress.
items.ww: The chapter states outcomes for adjusting to loss or stressful situations are long term.

alt.q: Renewing participation in religious practices is too small a step to serve as an expected outcome of spiritual care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Short-term outcomes such as renewing participation in religious practices help patients progressively reach spiritual health.
alt.ww: The chapter gives renewed religious participation as an example of a useful short-term outcome.
