items.q: In the Muslim faith, food that is permitted to eat is called [[halal]], while forbidden food is called haram.
items.ex: Islam divides food into halal (permitted) and haram (forbidden); pork and alcohol are haram.

alt.q: A Muslim patient asks whether a hospital meal is [[halal]], meaning that it is permitted to eat.
alt.ex: Islam divides food into halal (permitted) and haram (forbidden); pork and alcohol are haram.

items.q: The nurse teaches a patient with anxiety about meditation. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I’ll sit comfortably with my back straight and meditate 10 to 20 minutes twice a day.”
items.ex: Box 35.6 teaches sitting comfortably with a straight back and meditating 10 to 20 minutes twice a day.
w: “I’ll meditate for 60 minutes once a week when I have spare time.”
Meditation is recommended twice daily, not once weekly.
“I’ll meditate for 2 minutes with the television on in the background.”
Sessions should be 10 to 20 minutes in a space with minimal interruptions.
“I’ll meditate 10 times a day, stopping whenever my mind wanders.”
Meditation is twice daily; intrusive thoughts are disregarded, not a reason to stop.

alt.q: Which physiological changes may occur in people who meditate regularly?
alt.a: Decreased metabolism and heart rate with easier breathing
alt.ex: Regular meditation may decrease metabolism and heart rate, ease breathing, and slow brain waves.
w: Increased heart rate and faster brain waves
Meditation slows heart rate and brain waves.
Higher metabolism and more rapid breathing
Meditation decreases metabolism and eases breathing.
Elevated blood pressure and muscle tension
Meditation creates a relaxation response that reduces stress.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse that prayer has always helped her cope. Which action best supports the patient’s prayer?
items.a: Offer privacy and ask whether she would like the nurse to participate
items.ex: Support prayer by giving privacy if desired and learning whether the patient wants the nurse to participate.
w: Lead the patient in a prayer from the nurse’s own tradition
Imposing the nurse’s tradition does not respect the patient’s beliefs.
Schedule prayer only during visits from the chaplain
Prayer can be private, with family, or with the nurse, not only with clergy.
Discourage prayer during the hospital stay to promote rest
Prayer is an effective coping resource to be supported.

alt.q: A patient does not wish to pray but would like spiritual comfort. Which alternative does the chapter suggest?
alt.a: Listening to calming music or reading a text the patient selects
alt.ex: Alternatives to prayer include listening to calming music or reading a text selected by the patient.
w: Reading a scripture passage chosen by the nurse
The text should be selected by the patient, not the nurse.
Attending a group prayer service in the chapel
The patient does not wish to pray, so a prayer service does not fit.
Watching an educational video about the diagnosis
Teaching about the illness is not an alternative spiritual comfort measure.

items.q: During assessment, a patient expressed hopelessness. Which action is most appropriate when the nurse evaluates outcomes?
items.a: Ask the patient whether feelings of hope have been restored
items.ex: Spiritual evaluation data are usually subjective and are compared with the behaviors noted at assessment.
w: Review the patient’s vital sign trends for improvement
Vital signs are objective and do not show whether hope is restored.
Rely on the chaplain’s notes as objective evidence
The nurse evaluates by asking the patient directly about hope.
Check whether the patient attended a religious service
Attendance does not directly show whether hopelessness has resolved.

alt.q: Which statement about evaluating spiritual care outcomes is accurate?
alt.a: Evaluation data are usually subjective and compared with the initial assessment
alt.ex: The nurse compares the patient’s spiritual health with assessment findings using mostly subjective data.
w: Evaluation data are mostly objective measurements such as vital signs
Spiritual evaluation data are usually subjective.
Family and friends should be excluded from the evaluation
Include family and friends as appropriate when evaluating.
Spiritual health is expected to be fully achieved by discharge
Attaining spiritual health is a lifelong process.

items.q: Which statements about spirituality in older adults are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Older adults often use prayer as the primary coping mechanism during illness
Prayer is often the older adult’s primary coping mechanism.
Beliefs in the afterlife increase as adults age
Beliefs in the afterlife increase with age.
Greater social support positively affects spiritual well-being
Social support improves older adults’ spiritual well-being.
Leaving a legacy has little spiritual meaning for older adults
A legacy helps older adults leave the world with a sense of meaning.
Older adults rarely benefit from scripture reading or meditation
These practices can enhance wellness and coping in older adults.
items.ex: Box 35.5 links older adults’ spirituality with inner strength, prayer, afterlife beliefs, legacy, and social support.

alt.q: A nurse plans spiritual care for an older adult nearing the end of life. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Offer to coordinate visits from clergy, lawyers, and financial advisers
These visits help the patient complete unfinished business.
Help the patient leave a legacy such as an oral history or photographs
A legacy gives meaning and keeps connection for loved ones.
Listen actively to concerns and be present
Active listening and presence enhance connectedness.
Discourage talk about the afterlife to avoid distress
Afterlife beliefs increase with age and should be supported.
Limit visits from friends to conserve energy
Greater social support positively affects spiritual well-being.
alt.ex: Older adults benefit from completing unfinished business, leaving a legacy, presence, and social support.

items.q: Which situation is an example of a maturational loss?
items.a: A toddler showing separation anxiety when starting preschool
items.ex: Maturational losses are normally expected life changes, such as a toddler separating from a parent at preschool.
w: A factory worker losing a hand in a machinery accident
A sudden, unpredictable external event causes a situational loss.
A teenager grieving the theft of a new bicycle
Theft is a loss of a possession, not an expected developmental change.
A woman losing confidence after a friend rejects her
Rejection by a friend is an example of a perceived loss.

alt.q: Which description best defines a maturational loss?
alt.a: A necessary loss that includes all normally expected life changes across the life span
alt.ex: Maturational loss is a form of necessary loss made up of the expected changes of normal development.
w: A loss brought about by sudden, unpredictable external events in a person’s life
Losses caused by sudden, unpredictable external events are situational losses.
A loss uniquely defined by the person and less obvious to other people
A loss defined internally by the person and hard for others to see is a perceived loss.
A loss of a person who is physically present but psychologically unavailable
A person present but psychologically unavailable describes ambiguous loss.

items.q: A 24-year-old sustains permanent injuries in a car crash and cannot return to college or work. Which type of loss does this best illustrate?
items.a: Situational loss
items.ex: Sudden, unpredictable external events such as an automobile accident bring about situational loss.
w: Maturational loss
Maturational losses are normal, expected life changes, not sudden injuries.
Necessary loss
Necessary losses are part of expected change; situational losses seem unnecessary.
Ambiguous loss
Ambiguous loss involves uncertainty about a person who is missing or psychologically absent.

alt.q: Which feature distinguishes a situational loss from a maturational loss?
alt.a: It results from a sudden, unpredictable external event
alt.ex: Situational losses come from unpredictable external events, whereas maturational losses are expected life changes.
w: It is a normally expected change across the life span
Expected changes across the life span describe maturational loss.
It helps a person build coping skills for later losses
Building coping skills for later losses is a benefit of maturational losses.
It is usually replaced by something different or better
Being replaced by something different or better describes most necessary losses.

items.q: Maturational losses help people develop coping skills that they use later when they face unplanned or unexpected losses.
items.a: True
items.ex: Maturational losses linked to normal life transitions build coping skills for later unexpected losses.
items.ww: The text states that maturational losses help people develop coping skills, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Because maturational losses are expected, they do not affect a person’s ability to cope with later unexpected losses.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Maturational losses help people develop coping skills for unplanned, unwanted, or unexpected losses.
alt.ww: It is not true, because expected life transitions are exactly what build later coping skills.

items.q: Which situation is an example of a perceived loss?
items.a: Losing confidence after being rejected by a close friend
items.ex: A perceived loss is uniquely defined by the person, such as a loss of confidence after a friend’s rejection.
w: Losing a parent who dies after a long illness
Death of a family member is an actual loss that others can clearly recognize.
Losing a leg after a crush injury at work
Loss of a body part is an actual loss.
Losing a job when the company closes its plant
Loss of a job is listed as an example of an actual loss.

alt.q: Which definition of an actual loss is accurate?
alt.a: A loss in which a person can no longer feel, hear, see, or know a person or object
alt.ex: An actual loss occurs when the person or object can no longer be felt, heard, seen, or known.
w: A loss uniquely defined by the person and less obvious to other people
This defines a perceived loss, which others easily overlook.
A loss that occurs as part of normally expected life changes
Expected life changes across the life span are maturational losses.
A loss marked by uncertainty and a lack of finality
Uncertainty and lack of finality describe ambiguous loss.

items.q: Perceived losses are as painful as actual losses and are grieved in the same way.
items.a: True
items.ex: Although perceived losses are experienced internally and easy for others to overlook, they are as painful as actual losses.
items.ww: The text states perceived losses are grieved in the same way as actual losses, so they are not less painful.

alt.q: Because perceived losses are less obvious to others, they are usually less painful and grieved less intensely than actual losses.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Perceived losses are easy for others to overlook but are as painful as actual losses and grieved in the same way.
alt.ww: Being less visible to others does not make a perceived loss less painful to the person.

items.q: A patient says, “I know it sounds silly, but losing my grandmother’s ring in the fire hurts as much as when she died.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “That ring holds a lot of meaning for you. Tell me more about it.”
items.ex: Loss of an object can cause the same distress as loss of a person, depending on the value placed on it.
w: “At least no one was hurt in the fire, and jewelry can be replaced.”
This minimizes the loss and ignores the value the patient places on the ring.
“It is unusual to grieve an object as much as you grieved a person.”
Grieving a treasured object as much as a person is within the range of normal responses.
“You should focus your energy on rebuilding your home instead.”
Redirecting the patient blocks expression of grief over a meaningful loss.

alt.q: Why can the loss of a treasured object cause as much distress as the loss of a person?
alt.a: The level of distress depends on the value the person places on the object.
alt.ex: The extent of grieving over an object depends on its value, attached sentiment, or usefulness to the person.
w: Object losses are always situational, which makes them more intense.
Object losses can be actual losses of many kinds; being situational does not explain the distress.
Object losses are perceived losses that others readily recognize.
Perceived losses are easy for others to overlook, not readily recognized.
Object losses become more distressing when the object is easy to replace.
Grief depends on value and sentiment; easy replacement would not increase distress.

items.q: Which are examples of loss of an aspect of self? Select all that apply.
o: Loss of a body part
A body part is a valued aspect of self whose loss alters identity and self-concept.
Loss of a job
Loss of a job is listed as a loss of an aspect of self.
Loss of a physiological function
Loss of psychological or physiological function is a loss of an aspect of self.
Moving out of a rehabilitation unit
Moving out of a rehabilitation unit is a loss of a known environment.
Divorce from a spouse
Divorce is a loss of a significant other.
Theft of a car
Theft is a loss of possessions or objects.
items.ex: Illness, injury, or developmental changes can cause loss of a body part, job, or function, altering identity and self-concept.

alt.q: Which are examples of loss of a known environment? Select all that apply.
o: Leaving home
Leaving home is listed as a loss of a known environment.
Being hospitalized
Hospitalization places a person in an unfamiliar setting, a loss of known environment.
Starting a new job
A new job is listed as a loss of a known environment.
Moving out of a rehabilitation unit
Leaving a familiar rehabilitation unit is a loss of a known environment.
Death of a co-worker
Death of a co-worker is a loss of life.
Death of a family pet
A pet is a significant other that meets love and belonging needs.
alt.ex: Loss of a known environment comes from maturational or situational events, injury, or illness that place a person in unfamiliar settings.

items.a: Grief depends on the object’s value, sentiment, or usefulness
items.ex: Each type of loss in Table 36.1 has different implications for the person’s needs, identity, and grief.

That goes with Loss of known environment.
People or pets that met love and belonging needs are gone

items.q: A patient is admitted to a long-term care agency. Which losses does the nurse anticipate the patient may experience on entering the agency? Select all that apply.
o: Access to familiar people
Patients entering an agency lose access to familiar people and environments.
Privacy
Loss of privacy is common when patients enter an agency for care.
Control over body functions
Patients often lose control over body functions in an agency.
Control over daily routines
Agency schedules replace the patient’s own daily routines.
The need for social support
The need for support continues and often increases with loss.
The right to make health care decisions
Patients keep their decision rights; the text lists no such loss.
items.ex: Entering an agency for care causes losses of familiar people and environments, privacy, and control over body functions and routines.

alt.q: A patient has a chronic disabling illness. Which additional losses or changes does the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Financial hardship
Chronic illness or disability adds financial hardship for most people.
Changes in lifestyle
Chronic illness often brings about changes in lifestyle.
Dependence on others
Chronic illness and disability often increase dependence on others.
A guaranteed return to the previous family role
Illness changes functioning and often alters family role, not restoring it.
A reduced need for support from others
Increased dependence means support needs typically rise, not fall.
alt.ex: Chronic illness and disability produce multiple losses, including financial hardship, lifestyle changes, and dependence on others.

items.q: Which statement about necessary losses is accurate?

Sudden, unpredictable external events cause situational losses.

Necessary losses, such as maturational losses, occur across the entire life span.

alt.q: A nurse teaches that normal life changes always involve which kind of loss?
alt.a: Necessary loss
alt.ex: As people age, they learn that change always involves a necessary loss.
w: Situational loss
Situational losses come from unexpected external events, not every life change.
Ambiguous loss
Ambiguous losses are marked by uncertainty, not part of every normal change.
Perceived loss
Perceived losses are uniquely defined by the person, not a feature of every life change.

items.q: Two neighbors lose their homes in the same flood. One copes well, while the other is deeply distressed months later. Which explanation best accounts for the difference?
items.a: Each person’s previous experience with and perception of loss shape the grief response.
items.ex: The type of loss and a person’s prior experience with and perception of loss influence depth and duration of grief.
w: Only one of them experienced an actual loss from the flood.
Both lost homes, which is an actual loss for each person.
Loss of a home is a maturational loss for one of them.
A flood is a sudden external event, not an expected maturational change.
Grief over objects is always mild, so one is overreacting.
Loss of an object can generate as much distress as loss of a person.

alt.q: Which factors influence the depth and duration of a person’s grief response?
alt.a: The type of loss and the person’s previous experience with and perception of loss
alt.ex: Each person responds to loss differently based on the type of loss and prior experience with and perception of loss.
w: The person’s age and the length of any related hospital stay
Age and length of stay are not the factors the text names for depth and duration of grief.
Whether other people view the loss as welcome or unwelcome
How others view the loss does not set its depth; the person’s own perception does.
The number of visitors and cards the person receives afterward
Counting visitors or cards does not determine the depth and duration of grief.

items.q: Which statement about death as a loss is accurate?
items.a: It creates a permanent separation and represents the unknown for many people.
items.ex: Death is the ultimate loss; it represents the unknown and permanently separates people, causing fear, sadness, and regret.
w: Because it is expected, it rarely generates anxiety or fear.
Although expected, death often generates anxiety, fear, and uncertainty.
It causes grief for the dying person but rarely for caregivers.
Death can cause fear, sadness, and regret for family, friends, and caregivers too.
It is a maturational loss that mainly builds coping skills.
Death is described as the ultimate loss, not a maturational loss.

alt.q: A nurse plans to explore how a dying patient is approaching death. Which factors should the nurse assess?
alt.a: Culture, spirituality, values, previous experiences with death, and social support
alt.ex: Culture, spirituality, beliefs and values, prior experiences with death, and social support influence how a person approaches death.
w: Income level, insurance coverage, education, occupation, and housing
Financial and educational factors are not the influences the text names for approaching death.
Age at diagnosis, length of illness, and number of hospital stays
Illness timeline details do not describe how a person approaches death.
Blood pressure trends, oxygen saturation, and daily pain scores
Physiological data guide symptom care but do not reveal how a person approaches death.

items.q: Loss of self-esteem, a personal relationship, or a dream is an example of an intangible loss.
items.a: True
items.ex: Intangible losses include self-esteem, a personal relationship, confidence, or a dream.
items.ww: These losses cannot be touched or held, so they are intangible rather than tangible.

alt.q: Loss of a pet, a possession, or a body part is an example of an intangible loss.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A body part or function, a pet, and a possession are examples of tangible losses.
alt.ww: These are concrete things a person had, so they are tangible losses, not intangible ones.

items.q: A [[perceived]] loss is uniquely defined by the person experiencing it and is less obvious to other people.
items.ex: Perceived losses are experienced internally and individually, so others easily overlook them.

alt.q: Feeling a loss of status in a social group after a friend’s rejection is an example of a [[perceived]] loss.
alt.ex: Perceived losses are experienced internally and individually, so others easily overlook them.

items.q: A [[maturational]] loss is a form of necessary loss that includes all normally expected life changes across the life span.
items.ex: Maturational losses, such as starting school or leaving home, are expected parts of development.

alt.q: A college student’s sadness at leaving the campus community is an example of a [[maturational]] loss.
alt.ex: Maturational losses, such as starting school or leaving home, are expected parts of development.

items.q: After a back injury, a patient can no longer work as a firefighter and says, “I don’t even know who I am anymore.” Which type of loss does this statement best illustrate?
items.a: Loss of an aspect of self
items.ex: Injury that causes loss of a job or function alters a person’s identity and self-concept, a loss of an aspect of self.
w: Loss of known environment
Loss of known environment involves leaving familiar settings, not changes in identity.
Loss of a significant other
Loss of a significant other involves people or pets who meet love and belonging needs.
Loss of possessions or objects
Loss of possessions involves objects that are stolen, misplaced, or destroyed.

alt.q: Which implication is associated with loss of an aspect of self?
alt.a: Altered personal identity and self-concept
alt.ex: Illness, injury, or developmental change can remove a valued aspect of self and alter identity and self-concept.
w: Unmet love and belonging needs from friends or pets
Unmet love and belonging needs follow loss of a significant other.
Loneliness and uncertainty in an unfamiliar setting
Loneliness in an unfamiliar setting follows loss of a known environment.
Grief based on an object’s sentiment or usefulness
Grief tied to sentiment or usefulness follows loss of possessions.

items.q: A nursing student asks why a patient admitted for 2 days with pneumonia might experience loss. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
items.a: Even brief hospitalizations cause temporary changes in family roles, activities, and relationships.
items.ex: Even brief illnesses or hospitalizations temporarily change family role functioning, daily activities, and relationships.
w: Short stays permanently change a person’s identity and self-concept.
Brief hospitalizations cause temporary, not permanent, changes.
Brief illnesses cause loss only if the patient needs surgery.
Any illness can be a source of loss; surgery is not required.
Short hospital stays are maturational losses expected at every age.
Hospitalization is not a normally expected developmental change.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of loss related to a brief illness?
alt.a: “Even a short hospital stay can temporarily change my patient’s family role and routines.”
alt.ex: Even brief illnesses or hospitalizations cause temporary changes in family roles, daily activities, and relationships.
w: “A brief illness causes no loss as long as the patient fully recovers.”
Temporary changes in roles and routines are still losses even with full recovery.
“A brief hospital stay causes loss only when the patient has surgery.”
Surgery is not required for illness or hospitalization to cause loss.
“Only chronic illnesses cause changes in family roles and relationships.”
Brief illnesses also cause temporary changes in family roles and relationships.

items.q: Which life changes are welcome changes that can still involve loss? Select all that apply.
o: Marriage
Marriage is a welcome change that still involves loss.
Birth of a child
The birth of a child is a welcome change that still involves loss.
Divorce
Divorce is an example of an unwelcome change.
Loss of a job
Losing a job is an example of an unwelcome change.
A sudden accident
A sudden accident is an unexpected and unwelcome change.

alt.q: Which changes are expected changes related to loss? Select all that apply.

A child growing older and moving out is an expected change.

Starting preschool is a normal, expected maturational change.
A sudden car accident
A sudden accident is an unexpected change.

A sudden death is an unexpected loss.

Destruction by a tornado is a sudden, unexpected external event.
alt.ex: Losses can be expected, like a child moving out, or unexpected, like a sudden accident or death.

items.q: A patient has a below-knee amputation after a motorcycle crash and cannot return to work as a mail carrier. Which statement best guides the nurse’s plan of care?

Sudden external events cause situational, not maturational, losses.

Grief is individual; there is no rule that it waits until discharge.

alt.q: Which losses can follow a situational loss such as a permanent injury from an automobile accident?

w: Loss of a favorite teacher, classroom, and school friends
Leaving a teacher and classroom is an example of maturational loss.
Separation anxiety from a parent when starting preschool
Preschool separation anxiety is a maturational loss.
Leaving the campus community after college graduation
Leaving campus after graduation is an expected maturational loss.

items.q: Which factors determine how a person grieves?
items.a: Cultural norms, belief systems, support systems, and personal faith
items.ex: How one grieves depends on cultural norms, belief systems, support systems, and personal faith.

Income level, insurance status, and type of housing
Financial factors are not named as what determines how a person grieves.

Health habits are not the factors that determine how a person grieves.

Support affects how people grieve but does not prevent grief.

items.q: Which definition of grief is most accurate?

Grief is a process, not a state, and is rarely orderly or predictable.

An individualized response to loss is grief itself.

The time of sadness after a death is bereavement.

mt.q: Match each term with its meaning.
pairs: Individualized response to a perceived, real, or anticipated loss

items.q: Grief is a process rather than a state, and it is rarely orderly or predictable.
items.a: True
items.ex: The grief experience is a process, not a state, and grief work is rarely orderly and predictable.
items.ww: The text describes grief as a process that is rarely orderly, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Grief is a predictable state that most people move through in the same orderly way.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Grief is a personal process; no two people grieve the same loss in the same way.
alt.ww: Grief is not a predictable state, because it is a process that differs for each person.

items.q: Most grieving individuals recover adequately within 1 year after a loss.
items.a: True
items.ex: Most people recover adequately within 1 year, although some develop complicated or prolonged grief.
items.ww: The text states that most people recover within 1 year, so this is not false.

alt.q: Once a person recovers from a loss, grief work is fully completed, and anniversaries no longer cause surges of grief.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Objects, memories, and anniversaries can cause surges of loss, so grief work is never fully completed.
alt.ww: Grief can lessen and healing can occur, but reminders can still trigger grief, so grief work is never fully completed.

items.q: A woman whose husband died 2 weeks ago tells the nurse she plans to sell her house and move across the country next month. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Encourage her to postpone major decisions while she is grieving.
items.ex: During bereavement, nurses reassure people that feelings are normal and encourage them to postpone major decisions.
w: Help her find a real estate agent so the sale can begin soon.
Supporting a rushed major decision conflicts with advice to postpone major decisions.
Tell her that moving away will help her forget the loss.
Moving does not erase grief, and the advice discourages talking about the loss.
Explain that her feelings are abnormal this early in grief.
Bereaved people should be reassured that their feelings are normal.

alt.q: Which set of nursing actions is recommended for people experiencing bereavement?
alt.a: Let them talk about the loss, reassure them that feelings are normal, and encourage postponing major decisions
alt.ex: Bereaved people benefit from talking about the loss, reassurance their feelings are normal, and delaying major decisions.
w: Redirect talk away from the loss, focus on the future, and encourage quick decisions to regain control
Avoiding talk of the loss and rushing decisions conflict with recommended bereavement care.
Limit discussion of the loss, set a timeline for grieving, and encourage an early move to a new home
Grief has no set timeline, and major decisions should be postponed.
Discourage expressing sadness, assure them grief ends in weeks, and suggest returning to work at once
Expressing grief should be allowed, and most people need up to a year to recover.

items.q: The Jewish ritual of shivah, when normal activities stop and friends visit the home to honor the dead, is an example of which concept?
items.a: Mourning
items.ex: Shivah is a culturally influenced mourning ritual, an outward way of expressing and managing grief.
w: Bereavement
Bereavement is the time of sadness after a death, during which mourning rituals take place.
Anticipatory grief
Anticipatory grief occurs before an actual loss or death.
Disenfranchised grief
Disenfranchised grief involves a loss that cannot be openly shared, unlike shivah.

alt.q: Which statement about mourning is accurate?
alt.a: Most mourning rituals are culturally influenced, learned behaviors.
alt.ex: Mourning rituals, such as shivah, are mostly learned behaviors influenced by culture.
w: Mourning is an inner feeling that cannot be observed by others.
Mourning is the outward expression of grief, so it is observable.
Mourning rituals are biologically determined and the same everywhere.
Mourning rituals are learned and vary with culture.
Mourning refers only to the time period that follows a death.
The time period after a death is bereavement; mourning is the expression of grief.

items.q: Which feelings are normal in uncomplicated grief? Select all that apply.
o: Disbelief
Disbelief is a normal feeling of grief.
Yearning
Yearning is a normal feeling of grief.
Anger
Anger is a normal feeling of grief.
Depression
Depression is listed among normal feelings of grief.
Self-destructive behavior and obsessions
Self-destructive behavior and obsessions suggest exaggerated grief, a complicated grief type.
Preoccupation with the deceased and no interest in life for over a year
Prolonged preoccupation and loss of interest in life indicate complicated grief.
items.ex: Normal grief includes feelings such as disbelief, yearning, anger, and depression.

alt.q: Which coping mechanisms are helpful for people who are grieving? Select all that apply.
o: Hardiness and resilience
Hardiness and resilience are helpful coping mechanisms in grief.
A personal sense of control
A sense of personal control helps people cope with grief.
Making sense of the loss and seeing positive possibilities
Finding meaning and positive possibilities after a loss aids coping.
Suppressing all emotions to appear strong for others
Suppressing feelings is not a helpful mechanism; nurses help people express feelings.
Avoiding full realization of the loss for as long as possible
Avoiding realization of the loss is linked to delayed grief.
alt.ex: Hardiness and resilience, a sense of control, and making sense of the loss are helpful coping mechanisms.

items.q: The daughter of a patient with amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) says, “I feel like I’m already losing her, and I keep picturing the funeral.” The nurse recognizes this as which type of grief?
items.a: Anticipatory grief
items.ex: Anticipatory grief occurs before the actual death in prolonged or predicted loss and may include rehearsing the death.
w: Masked grief
In masked grief, a person is unaware that behaviors or symptoms result from a loss.
Delayed grief
Delayed grief is postponed after a loss, not experienced before it.
Disenfranchised grief
Disenfranchised grief involves a loss that is not socially acknowledged.

alt.q: A spouse caring for a partner with advanced dementia is experiencing anticipatory grief. Which nursing action is best?
alt.a: Help the spouse express feelings and suggest a caregiver support group.
alt.ex: Nurses help people express anticipatory grief feelings, and caregiver support groups often help them cope.
w: Advise the spouse to avoid thinking about the death until it occurs.
Nurses help people express, not avoid, feelings of anticipatory grief.
Explain that grieving before a death is a sign of complicated grief.
Anticipatory grief is a recognized grief type, not complicated grief.
Recommend that the spouse limit visits to lessen emotional strain.
Limiting contact does not address grief and is not a recommended action.

items.q: Which are phases that a person may experience as part of anticipatory grief? Select all that apply.
o: Accepting that death is inevitable
Accepting the inevitability of death is a phase of anticipatory grief.
Feeling concern for the dying person
Concern for the dying person is a phase of anticipatory grief.
Rehearsing the death
Rehearsing the death is a phase of anticipatory grief.
Imagining the future
Imagining the future without the person is a phase of anticipatory grief.
Bargaining to prevent the death
Bargaining is a stage in Kübler-Ross’s stages of dying, not an anticipatory grief phase.
Numbing to block the impact of the loss
Numbing is a phase of Bowlby’s attachment theory.
items.ex: Anticipatory grief may involve accepting inevitability, concern for the dying person, rehearsing the death, and imagining the future.

alt.q: When anticipatory grief extends over a long period, which responses may family members experience? Select all that apply.
o: Shock before the death occurs
Intense responses such as shock can occur before the actual death.
Denial before the death occurs
Denial is one of the intense responses that may come before the death.
Tearfulness before the death occurs
Tearfulness may occur as the family absorbs the loss gradually.
Relief when the death finally happens
People often feel relief when a long-anticipated death finally occurs.
Freedom from all stress because the death is expected
Preparing for death increases stress for some people.
No grief responses at all until after the death
Anticipatory grief occurs before the actual loss or death.
alt.ex: With prolonged anticipatory grief, people absorb the loss gradually, may feel shock, denial, and tearfulness, and often feel relief at the death.

items.q: Preparing for an expected death through anticipatory grief helps some people but increases stress for others.
items.a: True
items.ex: Anticipatory grief gives time to prepare, but for some it creates an emotional roller coaster of highs and lows.
items.ww: The text states that preparing for death increases stress for some people, so this is not false.

alt.q: Anticipatory grief reliably lowers stress for all family members because it gives them time to prepare.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Although preparing for death helps some individuals, it increases stress for others.
alt.ww: Time to prepare does not lower stress for everyone; some experience emotional highs and lows.

items.q: Which situation is most likely to lead to disenfranchised grief?
items.a: A woman grieves the death of her former spouse.
items.ex: Disenfranchised grief occurs when the relationship seems socially unacceptable or less significant, such as with a former spouse.
w: A husband grieves his wife after her long illness.
The loss of a current spouse is socially acknowledged and supported.
Adult children grieve a parent who died in hospice.
The death of a parent is a socially accepted loss with expected support.
A widow grieves her husband after a heart attack.

items.q: A patient with terminal cancer says, “If I can just live long enough to see my grandson’s wedding, I’ll be ready.” Which of Kübler-Ross’s stages does this statement reflect?
items.a: Bargaining
items.ex: In bargaining, the person cushions and postpones awareness of the loss by trying to prevent it from happening.
w: Denial
In denial, the person cannot accept the fact of the loss at all.
Anger
In anger, the person expresses resistance or intense anger at God, others, or the situation.
Acceptance
In acceptance, the person has incorporated the loss into life without conditions.

alt.q: Which statement by a dying patient reflects Kübler-Ross’s bargaining stage?
alt.a: “Please let me live until my daughter graduates, and I’ll never ask for anything else.”
alt.ex: Bargaining postpones awareness of the loss by trying to prevent it from happening.
w: “The lab must have mixed up my results with someone else’s.”
Refusing to accept the fact of the loss reflects denial.
“Why did God let this happen to me and not to someone else?”
Intense anger at God or the situation reflects the anger stage.
“I have made my peace and want to spend time with my family.”
Incorporating the loss into life reflects acceptance.

items.q: A patient recently told of a terminal diagnosis shouts at the nurse, “None of you know what you’re doing!” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Recognize the anger as a grief response and invite the patient to share feelings.
items.ex: Anger at others or the situation is a recognized stage of grief, and knowing this helps the nurse respond supportively.
w: Tell the patient that staying angry will keep them from reaching acceptance.
Grief is not linear, and lecturing the patient blocks expression of feelings.
Leave the room and avoid the patient until the patient becomes calmer.
Avoiding the patient withdraws support during a normal grief reaction.
Explain that the patient’s anger is a sign of complicated grief.
Anger is a normal grief feeling, not a sign of complicated grief.

alt.q: In Kübler-Ross’s stages of dying, which description matches the depression stage?
alt.a: The person realizes the full impact of the loss.
alt.ex: In the depression stage, the person realizes the full impact of the loss.
w: The person incorporates the loss into life.
Incorporating the loss into life describes acceptance.
The person tries to postpone the loss by preventing it.
Trying to prevent the loss describes bargaining.
The person cannot accept the fact of the loss.
Inability to accept the fact of the loss describes denial.

items.q: According to Kübler-Ross’s stages of dying, what purpose does denial serve?
items.a: It protects the person psychologically from a loss the person cannot yet bear.
items.ex: Denial is a form of psychological protection from a loss that the person cannot yet bear.
w: It shows that the person has incorporated the loss into life.
Incorporating the loss into life describes acceptance, not denial.
It shows that the person realizes the full impact of the loss.
Realizing the full impact of the loss describes depression.
It postpones the loss by trying to keep it from happening.
Trying to prevent the loss from happening describes bargaining.

alt.q: A patient just told of a spouse’s sudden death says, “No, that can’t be right. He was fine this morning.” How should the nurse interpret this reaction?
alt.a: As a protective response to a loss the patient cannot yet bear
alt.ex: Denial is a form of psychological protection from a loss the person cannot yet bear.
w: As a sign of complicated grief that requires immediate referral
Early disbelief is a normal response, not complicated grief.
As evidence that the patient has already reached acceptance
Refusing to accept the fact of the loss is denial, not acceptance.
As a sign of exaggerated grief with a high risk of suicide
Exaggerated grief involves self-destructive behavior, not initial disbelief.

items.ex: Yearning and searching brings tearful sobbing, acute distress, and physical symptoms such as chest tightness and insomnia.
w: Numbing
Numbing protects the person from the full impact of the loss.
Disorganization and despair
Disorganization and despair involve endless examination of how and why the loss occurred.
Reorganization
Reorganization involves accepting change and building new roles and relationships.

alt.q: One week after her husband’s death, a widow has episodes of tearful sobbing, chest tightness, loss of appetite, and insomnia. Which phase of Bowlby’s attachment theory does this reflect?
alt.a: Yearning and searching
alt.ex: Emotional outbursts with chest tightness, lethargy, insomnia, and appetite loss are common in yearning and searching.
w: Numbing
Numbing shields the person from the full impact rather than causing outbursts.
Disorganization and despair
This phase centers on examining why the loss occurred or anger at those responsible.
Reorganization
Reorganization is marked by acceptance and new roles, not acute distress.

items.q: A widower, a year after his wife’s death, has learned to cook, joined a community group, and speaks fondly of his wife. Which phase of Bowlby’s attachment theory does this reflect?
items.a: Reorganization
items.ex: In reorganization, the person accepts change, acquires new skills and relationships, and separates without lessening the relationship’s importance.
w: Numbing
Numbing protects the person from the full impact of the loss.
Yearning and searching
Yearning and searching involves tearful outbursts and acute distress.
Disorganization and despair
Disorganization and despair involves endless questioning about how and why the loss occurred.

alt.q: In Bowlby’s reorganization phase, how does the person separate from the lost relationship?
alt.a: Without feeling that the relationship’s importance is being lessened
alt.ex: Reorganization involves separating from the lost relationship without feeling its importance is lessened.
w: By forgetting the relationship so the pain goes away
Reorganization does not require forgetting; the relationship keeps its importance.
By endlessly examining how and why the loss occurred
Endless examination of the loss describes disorganization and despair.
By expressing anger at whoever seems responsible
Anger at those responsible describes disorganization and despair.

items.q: Which are tasks in Worden’s grief tasks model? Select all that apply.
o: Accepting the reality of the loss
Accepting the reality of the loss is a Worden grief task.
Experiencing the pain of grief
Experiencing the pain of grief is a Worden grief task.
Adjusting to a world in which the deceased is missing
Adjusting to life without the deceased is a Worden grief task.
Emotionally relocating the deceased and moving on with life
Emotionally relocating the deceased is a Worden grief task.
Bargaining to keep the loss from happening
Bargaining is a stage in Kübler-Ross’s stages of dying.
Numbing to block the full impact of the loss
Numbing is a phase of Bowlby’s attachment theory.
items.ex: Worden’s model lists four tasks: accept the reality, experience the pain, adjust to the world without the deceased, and emotionally relocate the deceased.

alt.q: A nurse uses Worden’s grief tasks model with a daughter whose mother has died. Which goals fit this model? Select all that apply.
o: Acknowledge that her mother has died
Accepting the reality of the loss is a Worden task.
Allow herself to feel the pain of the loss
Experiencing the pain of grief is a Worden task.
Adjust to daily life without her mother
Adjusting to a world without the deceased is a Worden task.
Move through the anger stage before bargaining
Anger and bargaining are Kübler-Ross stages, not Worden tasks.
Avoid thinking of her mother so the pain fades
Worden’s model calls for experiencing the pain of grief, not avoiding it.
alt.ex: Worden’s tasks include accepting the loss, experiencing its pain, and adjusting to a world without the deceased.

items.q: Which are restoration-oriented activities in the dual process model? Select all that apply.
o: Attending to life changes
Attending to life changes is a restoration-oriented activity.
Finding new roles or relationships
Finding new roles or relationships is a restoration-oriented activity.
Coping with finances
Coping with finances is a restoration-oriented activity.
Participating in distractions
Distractions are restoration-oriented and balance the loss-oriented state.
Dwelling on the loss
Dwelling on the loss is a loss-oriented activity.
Doing grief work
Grief work is a loss-oriented activity.
items.ex: Restoration-oriented activities address life changes, roles, finances, and distractions, balancing loss-oriented activities.

alt.q: Which are loss-oriented activities in the dual process model? Select all that apply.
o: Doing grief work
Grief work is a loss-oriented activity.
Dwelling on the loss
Dwelling on the loss is a loss-oriented activity.
Breaking connections with the deceased person
Breaking connections with the deceased is a loss-oriented activity.
Resisting activities to move past the grief
Resisting moving past the grief is a loss-oriented activity.
Coping with finances
Coping with finances is a restoration-oriented activity.
Finding new roles or relationships
Finding new roles or relationships is a restoration-oriented activity.
alt.ex: Loss-oriented activities focus on grief work, dwelling on the loss, breaking connections, and resisting moving past grief.

items.q: Which statements reflect processes in Rando’s R process model? Select all that apply.
o: Recognize the loss
Recognizing the loss is a process in Rando’s model.
React to the pain of separation
Reacting to the pain of separation is a process in Rando’s model.
Relinquish old attachments
Relinquishing old attachments is a process in Rando’s model.
Reinvest emotional energy into new people
Reinvesting emotional energy is a process in Rando’s model.
Resist activities to move past the grief
Resisting moving past grief is a loss-oriented activity in the dual process model.
Repress memories of the relationship
Rando’s model calls for recollecting and reexperiencing the relationship, not repressing it.
items.ex: Rando’s six processes are recognize, react, recollect and reexperience, relinquish, readjust, and reinvest.

alt.q: A grief counselor uses Rando’s R process model. Which behaviors of a widow reflect processes in this model? Select all that apply.
o: She shares memories of trips she took with her husband.
Sharing memories reflects recollecting and reexperiencing the relationship.
She cries openly about missing her husband.
Crying over the separation reflects reacting to its pain.
She begins volunteering and forming new friendships.
New friendships reflect reinvesting emotional energy into new people.
She insists that her husband has not really died.
Rando’s first process is to recognize the loss, not deny it.
She refuses to invest any energy in new relationships.
Rando’s model ends with reinvesting energy into new people.
alt.ex: Rando’s model includes recollecting the relationship, reacting to separation, and reinvesting in new people.

items.q: How do newer grief theories differ from early grief theories?
items.a: They view people as creating their own meanings and truths when facing loss.
items.ex: Newer theories hold that each person is unique and makes his or her own meanings when confronted with loss and death.
w: They describe a fixed series of stages that all grievers complete.
Moving through set stages or tasks describes early grief theories.
They state that grief ends once a person completes all of the tasks.
Grief work is never fully completed, and newer theories stress individuality.
They apply only to grief after death, not to other losses.
Grief theories also help explain responses to other significant losses.

alt.q: According to newer grief theories, which factors shape an individual’s grief experience?
alt.a: Social and personal context, family structure, meaning of relationships, and thought processes
alt.ex: Differences in context, family structure, relationship meaning, and thought processes shape each person’s grief experience.
w: Age, sex, number of prior hospitalizations, and level of education
These are not the factors newer theories name as shaping grief experience.
Only the cause of death and the setting in which the person died
Newer theories emphasize personal context and meaning, not just cause and setting.
Only the stage of grief that the person has reached at the time
Newer theories reject fixed stages and emphasize individual meaning.

items.q: Grief is cyclical, with movement forward and backward, rather than linear.
items.a: True
items.ex: Grief is not linear; it is cyclical, with movement forward and backward.
items.ww: The text states grief is cyclical rather than linear, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Grief follows a linear path, so once a person moves past a painful phase, the person does not return to it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Grief is cyclical, and people can move backward to strong grief reactions after better days.
alt.ww: Grief is not linear; strong reactions can return even after weeks of feeling better.

items.q: A woman whose husband died 6 months ago tells the nurse, “I was doing better, but I fell apart when a caller asked to speak to him. Am I going backward?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Grief comes and goes, so strong feelings can return even after better days.”
items.ex: Grief is cyclical; preparing grievers for difficult days among better days helps them understand and plan self-care.
w: “That reaction means you are developing complicated grief.”
A surge of grief at a reminder is normal and does not signal complicated grief.
“You should be past the hardest part of grieving by now.”
Grief has no fixed timeline, and this response dismisses her feelings.
“Try to avoid anything that reminds you of your husband.”
Avoidance is not recommended; reminders will occur, and planning for them supports self-care.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a newly bereaved family about the cyclical nature of grief. Which statement by a family member shows understanding of the teaching?
alt.a: “We should expect some hard days even after we start feeling better.”
alt.ex: Educating grievers about the cyclical pattern prepares them for difficult days among the better days.
w: “Once we start feeling better, the sadness should not come back.”
Grief is cyclical, so sadness can return after better days.
“If we have a bad day later, it means we are grieving wrong.”
Returning grief reactions are a normal part of the cyclical pattern.
“We will move through each stage of grief only one time.”
Grief is not linear; people move forward and backward.

items.q: A widow knows that her late husband’s birthday is approaching. Which plan best shows self-care based on the cyclical nature of grief?
items.a: Planning dinner with family that evening to share happy memories of him
items.ex: Knowing grief feelings will come and go lets the griever plan self-care, such as a family dinner sharing memories.
w: Staying busy at work all day so she will not think about the date
Avoiding the date does not prepare her for the expected surge of grief.
Removing all of her husband’s photos from the house before the date
Removing reminders does not prevent grief and is not the planned self-care described.
Spending the day alone so that she does not upset her family members
Isolating herself removes the support that helps on difficult days.

alt.q: Why does a nurse teach grievers about the cyclical pattern of grief?
alt.a: It prepares them for difficult days among the better days.
alt.ex: Educating grievers about the cyclical pattern prepares them for difficult days and allows necessary self-care.
w: It shortens the grieving period to less than a year.
Teaching about the cyclical pattern prepares grievers but does not shorten grief.
It prevents grief from returning on anniversaries.
Anniversaries can still cause surges of grief; teaching helps people prepare for them.
It helps them complete the stages in the correct order.
Grief is not linear, so there is no correct order to complete.

items.q: Although most grief theories describe how people cope with death, they also help explain responses to other significant losses.
items.a: True
items.ex: Grief theories help nurses understand responses to other significant losses as well as death.
items.ww: The text states grief theories also apply to other significant losses, so this is not false.

alt.q: Grief theories apply only to death and do not help explain responses to losses such as divorce or amputation.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Although most grief theories describe coping with death, they also help explain responses to other significant losses.
alt.ww: Grief theories are not limited to death; they help explain responses to other significant losses too.

items.q: The wide variety of grief theories reflects the complexity and individuality of grief responses.
items.a: True
items.ex: The variety of theories supports the complexity and individuality of grief responses.
items.ww: The text links the many theories to how complex and individual grief is, so this is not false.

alt.q: Because there are many grief theories, nurses can expect patients’ reactions to grief to be fairly uniform.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Reactions to grief vary widely, and the variety of theories reflects this individuality.
alt.ww: Many theories exist because reactions vary widely, not because they are uniform.

items.q: In the dual process model, [[restoration-oriented|restoration oriented|restoration]] activities, such as coping with finances and finding new roles, provide balance to the loss-oriented state.
items.ex: Restoration-oriented activities attend to life changes and balance the loss-oriented focus on grief work.

alt.q: Grief work and dwelling on the loss are [[loss-oriented|loss oriented]] activities in the dual process model.
alt.ex: Restoration-oriented activities attend to life changes and balance the loss-oriented focus on grief work.

items.q: A widower alternates between days of looking through photos and crying and days of learning to pay bills and going out with friends. Which grief theory best explains this pattern?
items.a: Dual process model
items.ex: The dual process model describes loss-oriented activities balanced by restoration-oriented activities such as managing finances and socializing.
w: Stages of dying
The stages of dying describe denial through acceptance, not alternating activities.
Attachment theory
Attachment theory describes phases from numbing to reorganization.
Grief tasks model
The grief tasks model describes four tasks rather than two balancing types of activity.

alt.q: In the dual process model, what is the purpose of restoration-oriented activities?
alt.a: They provide balance to the loss-oriented state.
alt.ex: Restoration-oriented activities such as coping with finances and distractions provide balance to the loss-oriented state.
w: They replace the need for any loss-oriented grief work.
The model balances the two types of activity rather than replacing grief work.
They involve breaking connections with the deceased person.
Breaking connections with the deceased is a loss-oriented activity.
They keep the person focused on dwelling on the loss.
Dwelling on the loss is a loss-oriented activity.

items.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of how to use grief theories in practice?
items.a: “I’ll use the theories as a guide, knowing each patient’s grief follows its own path.”
items.ex: Grief theories help nurses understand grief, but every individual’s grief experience follows a different path.
w: “I’ll expect each patient to move through the stages in the same order.”
Grief is not linear, and reactions vary widely among individuals.
“I’ll tell patients which stage of grief they should have reached by now.”
There is no expected timeline or stage, because grief is individual and cyclical.
“I’ll apply one theory to all patients so that my care is consistent.”
The variety of theories reflects the individuality of grief, so one theory does not fit all.

alt.q: Why is knowledge of grief theories useful to the nurse?
alt.a: It helps the nurse understand grief and make clinical judgments about helping.
alt.ex: Knowing grief theories and normal responses helps nurses understand grief and make clinical judgments to help grieving people.
w: It allows the nurse to predict exactly how long a patient’s grief will last.
Grief is individual and cyclical, so its length cannot be predicted exactly.
It identifies the single correct way for each patient to grieve a loss.
Reactions to grief vary widely; there is no single correct way to grieve.
It replaces the need to assess each patient’s individual reactions.
Theories support, not replace, assessment of each person’s unique grief.

items.q: The parent of a 2-year-old whose grandmother recently died asks how the toddler might show grief. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: “Your toddler may become fussier and have changes in eating, sleeping, and toileting.”
items.ex: Toddlers cannot understand death; grief shows as fussiness, eating and sleep changes, and bowel or bladder disturbances.
w: “Your toddler will understand that death is permanent but may not know its cause.”
Understanding permanence and irreversibility describes school-age children, not toddlers.
“Your toddler will likely ask detailed questions about why the death happened.”
Toddlers cannot understand loss or death, so detailed questions about causes are not expected.
“Your toddler is too young to be affected by the loss in any way.”
Toddlers do react, often with anxiety over separation from parents and loss of objects.

alt.q: Which finding in a toddler is a common expression of grief?
alt.a: Increased fussiness with changes in sleep patterns
alt.ex: Toddlers express grief through fussiness, eating and sleeping changes, and bowel or bladder disturbances.
w: Stated worry about what caused the death
Toddlers cannot understand loss or its causes; this reflects an older child.
Talking about the permanence of the loss
Grasping permanence and irreversibility develops in school-age children.
Worry about disrupted plans for the future
Disruption of future dreams describes developmental losses of young adults.

items.q: Which statement describes how school-age children typically understand loss?
items.a: They understand that death is permanent and irreversible but may not understand its causes.
items.ex: School-age children grasp permanence and irreversibility but do not always understand the causes of a loss.
w: They cannot understand death but feel anxiety over separation from parents.
This describes toddlers, who cannot understand loss or death.
They view death mainly as a disruption of plans for an independent future.
Disruption of future dreams and autonomy describes young adults.
They show resilience to loss because of many prior experiences with it.
Resilience from prior experiences and coping skills describes older adults.

alt.q: A nurse caring for an 8-year-old whose sibling died notices periods of intense crying and changes in eating, sleeping, and social engagement. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
alt.a: They are expected grief expressions for a school-age child.
alt.ex: Some school-age children have intense periods of emotional expression with changes in eating, sleeping, and social engagement.
w: They indicate the child does not understand that death is permanent.
School-age children understand permanence; these behaviors are typical grief expressions.
They are signs of complicated grief that require urgent referral.
These changes are common grief expressions in school-age children, not by themselves complicated grief.
They suggest the child is too young to be affected by the loss.
These behaviors show the child is affected by the loss and is grieving.

Major transitions such as caring for aging parents

Grasps the permanence of death but not always its causes

That goes with Toddler.

Loss disrupts future dreams and an autonomous sense of self

alt.a: School-age child

w: Toddler
Toddler: Anxiety over loss of objects and separation from parents.
Young adult

w: Toddler

alt.a: Older adult
alt.ex: Age and stage of development affect how a person understands and responds to loss.

pairs: Anxiety over loss of objects and separation from parents
