items.q: Which statements about grief in older adults are supported by the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Older adults are more likely to have faced multiple losses.
Increased age raises the likelihood of multiple losses, such as friends dying in communal living.
Complicated grief in older adults is associated with higher mortality, heart disease, and cancer.
Box 36.1 links complicated grief in older adults to these serious health outcomes.
Relieving depression and maintaining physical function are therapeutic goals.
These are named therapeutic goals for older adults experiencing grief.
Older adults rarely show resilience after a loss.
Many older adults show resilience, and others can learn from their courage.
Older adults do not benefit from the techniques used with younger people.
Older adults benefit from the same therapeutic techniques as people in other age-groups.
items.ex: Older adults face cumulative losses and risk complicated grief, yet many are resilient and benefit from standard therapies.

alt.q: An 82-year-old resident of an assisted-living community recently lost a close friend. Which factors place this resident at risk for complicated grieving? Select all that apply.
o: Multiple losses as friends in the community die
Multiple losses are a key risk for complicated grieving in older adults.
Fewer available resources
Fewer resources contribute to the risk of complicated grieving.
Decreased coping
Decreased coping increases the risk of complicated grieving.
Resilience developed from prior experiences
Resilience is a strength that helps older adults respond to loss, not a risk.
Being older than 80 years by itself
Age alone is not a risk; responses relate to the loss and individual differences.
alt.ex: Older adults risk complicated grieving because of multiple losses, fewer resources, and decreased coping.

items.q: There is little evidence that grief experiences differ because of age alone.
items.a: True
items.ex: Responses to loss relate more to the nature of the specific loss and individual differences than to age.
items.ww: The book states age by itself is not shown to change grief; the loss and the individual matter more.

alt.q: Older adults grieve differently from younger adults chiefly because of their advanced age.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Grief differences relate to the nature of the specific loss and individual differences, not age alone.
alt.ww: The statement is false because the textbook finds little evidence that age alone changes grief.

items.q: A 74-year-old patient recently diagnosed with heart disease is grieving the loss of health. Which statement by the patient reflects positive reappraisal?
items.a: “This diagnosis is my chance to start eating better and exercising.”
items.ex: Positive reappraisal (cognitive restructuring) reframes a loss, such as seeing a cardiac diagnosis as a chance to become healthy.
w: “I would rather not think about my heart until I have to.”
This reflects avoidance, not reframing the loss as an opportunity.
“My life is basically over now that my heart is failing.”
This is a negative view of the future, the opposite of positive reappraisal.
“I will let my children make my health decisions from now on.”
Handing over control is not cognitive restructuring of the loss.

alt.q: Which technique does evidence show helps older adults adapt to significant losses?
alt.a: Positive reappraisal, also called cognitive restructuring
alt.ex: Evidence indicates that positive reappraisal (cognitive restructuring) helps older adults adapt to significant losses.
w: Avoiding discussion of the loss until grief resolves
Avoidance is not the evidence-based technique; reappraisal helps adaptation.
Therapies designed only for older age-groups
Older adults benefit from the same therapeutic techniques as other age-groups.
Encouraging dependence on family for daily decisions
Dependence is not recommended; maintaining physical function is a therapeutic goal.

items.q: Which situation does the textbook identify as hampering grief work after a death?
items.a: Regret and unfinished business in a close relationship that was strained at the time of death
items.ex: Grief work is hampered by regret and unfinished business when people were close but did not have a good relationship at death.
w: Having many highly satisfying friendships to lean on during grief
Satisfying relationships and supportive friends reduce depression in grievers.
Being able to accept practical help from relatives and neighbors
Accepting help from others is a critical variable that supports recovery.
Receiving consistent social support from a faith community
Social support is a critical variable in recovery, not a barrier.

alt.q: Which variables does the textbook describe as critical to recovery from loss and grief?
alt.a: Social support and the ability to accept help from others
alt.ex: Social support and accepting help are critical recovery variables; satisfying relationships lessen depression in grievers.
w: Avoiding reminders of the deceased and staying busy
Avoidance is not identified as a critical recovery variable.
A high income and a stable job to return to
Socioeconomic status influences grief, but social support and accepting help are the critical variables.
A younger age and good physical health
Age alone has little effect on grief; social support and accepting help are critical.

items.q: A patient whose leg was amputated yesterday shouts at the nurse and refuses to talk with visitors. How should the nurse interpret this behavior?
items.a: It may be a normal response to loss that should be assessed without assumptions.
items.ex: Some patients ignore, lash out, plead with, or withdraw from others as part of a normal response to loss.
w: It shows the patient is not grieving appropriately and needs sedation.
Lashing out and withdrawing can be normal; avoid assumptions about how patients should react.
It means the patient has accepted the loss and needs no further support.
Anger and withdrawal do not indicate acceptance; the patient still needs support.
It indicates complicated grief that requires immediate psychiatric referral.
One day after a loss, such behavior is commonly a normal reaction, not complicated grief.

alt.q: When using critical thinking to assess a grieving patient, which approach should the nurse avoid?
alt.a: Making assumptions about how the patient should respond to the loss
alt.ex: Critical thinking requires the nurse to avoid assumptions about how patients should respond to a loss.
w: Drawing on past clinical experiences with grieving patients
Prior clinical experience helps the nurse support grieving patients and families.
Reflecting on personal responses to a past loss
Reflecting on one’s own losses helps the nurse recognize patient responses.
Exploring the issues most meaningful to the patient
The standards of significance and relevance direct the nurse to meaningful issues.

items.q: A nurse is caring for one patient who had a miscarriage and another whose home was destroyed by a tornado. Which consideration about the patient who had a miscarriage is most accurate?
items.a: She is likely to receive less support from others because the loss is private.
items.ex: Highly visible losses usually stimulate helping responses, whereas private losses such as miscarriage bring less support.
w: She will grieve less because the loss was not highly visible.
A private loss draws less outside support; it does not mean less grief.
She is likely to receive community and government assistance.
Community and governmental support typically follows highly visible losses like a tornado.
She will need less nursing support than the tornado survivor.
Less outside support means the nurse should explore her needs, not assume they are fewer.

alt.q: Which type of loss typically stimulates the greatest helping response from others?
alt.a: Loss of a home in a tornado
alt.ex: Highly visible losses, such as a home destroyed by a tornado, often bring community and governmental support.
w: A miscarriage early in pregnancy
Miscarriage is a private loss that brings less support from others.
An infertility diagnosis shared with no one
Private losses generally attract less support than highly visible ones.
A gradual loss of hearing with aging
A gradual, less visible loss does not draw the helping response a visible disaster does.

items.q: When a death is sudden and unexpected, survivors face the challenge of not having time to say goodbye.
items.a: True
items.ex: Sudden death removes the chance to say goodbye, whereas chronic illness leaves memories of prolonged suffering.
items.ww: The textbook names lack of time to say goodbye as a specific challenge of sudden, unexpected death.

alt.q: Survivors of a death after a long, debilitating illness mainly struggle with not having had time to say goodbye.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: After chronic illness, survivors have memories of prolonged suffering, pain, and loss of function; no goodbye fits sudden death.
alt.ww: Lacking time to say goodbye characterizes sudden, unexpected death, not death after prolonged illness.

items.q: A patient’s brother died by suicide. Which feeling should the nurse anticipate as particularly common for this survivor?
items.a: Guilt over whether something was missed that could have prevented the death
items.ex: Suicide survivors may feel guilt, wondering whether they missed something or could have prevented the death.
w: Relief that the brother’s prolonged physical suffering has ended
Memories of prolonged suffering are associated with death after chronic illness.
Comfort from an outpouring of community and government support
This describes highly visible losses such as natural disasters.
Indifference because the death was the brother’s own choice
Suicide complicates grief in unique ways; indifference is not described.

alt.q: Which losses does the textbook say complicate the grieving process in unique ways by their very nature?
alt.a: Death by violence or suicide and multiple losses
alt.ex: Death by violence or suicide and multiple losses by their nature complicate grieving in unique ways.
w: Expected deaths after a long hospice stay
Expected deaths in hospice are not singled out as uniquely complicating grief.
Highly visible losses such as natural disasters
Visible losses tend to stimulate helping responses from others.
Developmental losses that come with aging
Expected developmental losses are not described as uniquely complicating grief.

items.q: Which coping strategies does the textbook describe as healthy and effective responses to loss? Select all that apply.
o: Talking about the loss
Talking is a healthy, effective coping strategy.
Journaling
Journaling is a healthy, effective coping strategy.
Sharing emotions with others
Sharing emotions with others is a healthy, effective coping strategy.
Using alcohol to help with sleep
Alcohol and drug use are unhealthy, ineffective coping strategies.
Acting out in violence
Violent acting out is an unhealthy, ineffective coping strategy.
items.ex: Talking, journaling, and sharing emotions are healthy strategies; alcohol, drugs, and violence are unhealthy ones.

alt.q: A nurse is supporting a man whose wife recently died. Which nursing actions support his coping? Select all that apply.
o: Assess his grief response and coping strategies
Nurses support patients by assessing grief responses and coping strategies.
Provide education about grief
Patient education is one way nurses support grieving patients.
Encourage the use of healthy coping strategies
Nurses encourage healthy strategies such as talking and journaling.
Suggest a nightly drink to help him relax
Using alcohol is an unhealthy, ineffective coping strategy.
Advise him to keep his feelings to himself
Sharing emotions with others is a healthy coping strategy.
alt.ex: Nurses support grieving people by assessing grief and coping, providing education, and encouraging healthy coping.

items.q: Which factor does the textbook identify as influencing the coping skills an adult uses when facing a major loss?
items.a: The losses the person faced as a child
items.ex: Losses faced in childhood often influence the coping skills used for larger, more painful losses in adulthood.
w: The number of years of formal education
Education level is not identified; childhood loss experiences shape adult coping.
The person’s birth order in the family
Birth order is not identified as shaping coping with loss.
The setting where the loss took place
The setting is not identified; earlier losses in childhood shape coping skills.

alt.q: A nurse wants to understand how an adult patient is likely to cope with a spouse’s death. Which assessment question best addresses the factor the textbook links to adult coping skills?
alt.a: “What losses did you experience as a child, and how did you handle them?”
alt.ex: Childhood losses often influence the coping skills a person uses for larger losses in adulthood.
w: “Which hospital unit was your spouse admitted to?”
The admitting unit does not reveal how the patient copes with loss.
“How many years of school have you completed?”
Education level is not the factor linked to adult coping with loss.
“Would you prefer a male or a female nurse?”
Caregiver preference does not reveal how the patient learned to cope.

items.q: A newly widowed mother of three now works two jobs to cover expenses. Which statement best describes how socioeconomic status may affect her grief?
items.a: She may lack the time to grieve her loss or to care for herself.
items.ex: A widowed mother working several jobs may not find time for self-care or to grieve the loss of her spouse.
w: She will grieve more quickly because work keeps her busy.
Working several jobs leaves no time to grieve; it does not speed grief.
Her income level will have no effect on how she grieves.
Socioeconomic status influences grief in both direct and indirect ways.
She is unlikely to experience any change in family roles.
A newly widowed mother faces changing roles in the family.

alt.q: Which practical effect of limited finances on grief does the textbook describe?
alt.a: Being unable to take time off work to attend a funeral
alt.ex: Limited finances may prevent taking time off for a funeral or traveling to visit a dying family member.
w: Being required by law to have an autopsy performed
Autopsy requirements depend on circumstances of death, not finances.
Receiving more community support than other grievers
Limited resources do not bring extra support; they can limit grief activities.
Feeling the loss less deeply than other grievers
Finances affect the ability to grieve, not the depth of the loss.

items.q: After a patient’s death, family members begin loud public wailing in the hallway. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: Recognize the behavior as a possible cultural expression of respect for the dead
items.ex: In some cultures, public wailing and physical demonstrations of grief show respect for the dead.
w: Ask the family to keep their grief private to avoid upsetting others
The nurse tries to understand and appreciate cultural values rather than suppress them.
Document the behavior as a sign of complicated grief
Public displays of grief can be culturally normal, not complicated grief.
Request a psychiatric consultation for the family members
The behavior can reflect cultural practice; no psychiatric evaluation is indicated.

alt.q: A nurse notices that a patient’s family members show little outward emotion after a death. What is the best interpretation?
alt.a: Some cultures value stoicism and holding back public displays of emotion.
alt.ex: Expressions of grief vary by culture; some people are stoic and hold back public displays of emotion.
w: The family did not have a close relationship with the patient.
Stoicism reflects cultural values and does not show a lack of closeness.
The family is in denial and should be confronted about it.
Holding back emotion can be a cultural norm; confrontation is not appropriate.
The family’s grief is unhealthy and needs a referral.
Stoic grief can be culturally appropriate and is not by itself unhealthy.

items.q: When assessing cultural influences on grief, the nurse considers sexual and gender orientation, socioeconomic status, and family makeup.
items.a: True
items.ex: Culture extends beyond geographical location, so these factors shape grief practices and death rituals.
items.ww: The textbook directs nurses to consider these influences because culture is broader than geography.

alt.q: Cultural influence on grief practices is determined mainly by the geographical region a person comes from.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Culture extends beyond geography to include sexual and gender orientation, socioeconomic status, and family makeup.
alt.ww: Geography is only part of culture; the textbook names several other influences to assess.

items.q: A nurse encourages a dying patient to draw on spiritual resources. Which resources does the textbook identify? Select all that apply.
o: Faith in a higher power
Faith in a higher power is a spiritual resource.
Communities of support
Communities of support are a spiritual resource.
A sense of hope and meaning in life
Hope and meaning in life are spiritual resources.
Religious practices
Religious practices are a spiritual resource patients can draw on.
Avoiding beliefs that differ from the nurse’s own
Nurses remain open to views and beliefs that contrast with their own.
Increased use of sedating medications
Sedating medications are not a spiritual resource.
items.ex: Spiritual resources include faith in a higher power, support communities, friends, hope and meaning, and religious practices.

alt.q: Which decisions or responses does the textbook say a person’s faith often influences? Select all that apply.
o: Response to illness and treatment
Faith often influences a person’s response to illness and treatment.
Choices about advanced life-support options
Faith often influences decisions about advanced life support.
Decisions about autopsy and organ donation
Faith often influences autopsy and organ donation decisions.
Eligibility for hospice benefits
Hospice eligibility relates to prognosis and caregiver availability, not faith.
The rate at which drugs are cleared from the body
Drug clearance depends on renal and liver function, not faith.
alt.ex: Faith often influences responses to illness and treatment, life support, autopsy, organ donation, and beliefs about death.

items.q: A patient with advanced cancer tells the nurse, “I can’t see anything good coming. Nothing will get better.” The nurse recognizes this statement as a cue for which problem?
items.a: Spiritual distress related to an inability to feel hopeful
items.ex: Spiritual distress often arises from an inability to feel hopeful or to foresee any favorable outcomes.
w: Acute pain related to tumor growth
The statement expresses a lack of hope, not physical pain.
Expected acceptance of the dying process
Acceptance does not involve being unable to foresee any favorable outcome.
Deficient knowledge about treatment options
The patient is expressing loss of hope, not a lack of information.

alt.q: Which factor does the textbook identify as helping a person maintain a sense of hope?
alt.a: Strong relationships and emotional connectedness to others
alt.ex: Maintaining hope depends in part on strong relationships and emotional connectedness to others.
w: Avoiding conversations about the illness
Avoidance is not identified as a source of hope.
Focusing only on a cure for the disease
Hope can center on meaning and purpose, not only cure.
Limiting visits from friends and family
Limiting connections works against the relationships that sustain hope.

items.q: [[Hope]] is a multidimensional concept, considered a component of spirituality, that energizes and comforts people facing personal challenges.
items.ex: Hope helps patients move from weakness and powerlessness to living as fully as possible.

alt.q: Considered a component of spirituality, [[hope]] gives a person the ability to see life as having meaning or purpose.
alt.ex: Hope helps patients move from weakness and powerlessness to living as fully as possible.

items.q: A dying patient asks the nurse directly, “Am I dying?” Which right in the Dying Person’s Bill of Rights most directly guides the nurse’s response?
items.a: The right to have questions answered honestly
items.ex: The Dying Person’s Bill of Rights includes the right to have questions answered honestly and to hear the truth.
w: The right to be free from pain
Freedom from pain is a right, but it does not address answering the patient’s question.
The right to respect for the body after death
This right concerns care of the body after death, not answering questions.
The right to discuss religious experiences
This right concerns spiritual experiences, not truthful answers to questions.

alt.q: Which statement is included in the Dying Person’s Bill of Rights?
alt.a: The right to participate in decisions concerning care
alt.ex: The bill gives the dying person the right to participate in decisions concerning care.
w: The right to have the family make all care decisions
The dying person has the right to participate in care decisions personally.
The right to stop receiving nursing attention near death
The bill states the right to expect continuing medical and nursing attention.
The right to have the truth withheld to protect hope
The bill includes the right to hear the truth and have questions answered honestly.

items.q: On arriving for an initial assessment, the nurse finds a patient with end-stage heart failure short of breath and anxious. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Offer available measures for symptom relief, then return to complete the assessment
items.ex: Comfort is a priority in end-of-life care; offer symptom relief, determine its efficacy, and then return to assess.
w: Complete the full grief assessment before addressing the symptoms
A thorough assessment is difficult when a patient is short of breath or anxious; relieve symptoms first.
Ask the family to answer all of the assessment questions instead
Family input is valuable, but the patient’s distressing symptoms need relief first.
Postpone the assessment until the next scheduled home visit
Delaying is unnecessary; relieve symptoms, check their effect, and return to assess.

alt.q: Why does the nurse prioritize identifying distressing symptoms during the initial assessment of a patient at the end of life?
alt.a: A thorough assessment is difficult when the patient is in pain or short of breath.
alt.ex: Pain, nausea, anxiety, depression, or dyspnea make a thorough assessment difficult, so symptoms are addressed first.
w: Symptom data are required before family members can be interviewed.
Family can be interviewed anytime; the issue is the patient’s ability to participate.
Symptoms must be documented before advance directives are discussed.
No such rule exists; symptom relief comes first because distress limits assessment.
Grief assessment is unnecessary once the symptoms are controlled.
Grief assessment continues throughout the illness and into bereavement.

items.q: A patient reports loneliness, crying spells, and trouble sleeping, signs the nurse would expect after a recent loss. The nurse learns the patient’s husband died 2 years ago. How should the nurse interpret these findings?
items.a: The response most likely indicates a complicated, chronic grief experience.
items.ex: Signs expected of a recent loss that persist 2 years later most likely indicate complicated, chronic grief.
w: The findings reflect normal grief expected to last several years.
Signs typical of a recent loss persisting 2 years later suggest complicated, chronic grief.
The findings are unrelated to the loss and need no grief assessment.
The nurse considers all factors surrounding the loss in context.
The patient is experiencing anticipatory grief.
Anticipatory grief occurs before a loss, not 2 years after it.

alt.q: A grieving patient reports loneliness and difficulty falling asleep. Which assessment approach does the textbook recommend?
alt.a: Consider the loss in context: what it was, when it occurred, and its meaning
alt.ex: A single behavior can occur in all types of grief, so the nurse considers the loss in context.
w: Assume the insomnia is unrelated to grief and treat it separately
Symptoms are analyzed in context because they may be related to the loss.
Compare the patient’s behavior with how the nurse thinks a griever should act
Focus on how the patient is reacting, not how the nurse believes the patient should react.
Base a nursing diagnosis on these two findings alone
Accurate nursing diagnoses cannot rest on just one or two findings.

items.q: Which findings are common symptoms of grief listed in the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Tightness in the chest and throat
Chest and throat tightness is a common physical sensation of grief.
Feeling the presence of the deceased
Sensing the deceased’s presence is a common grief cognition.
Oversensitivity to noise
Oversensitivity to noise is a common physical sensation of grief.
Wearing objects that belonged to the deceased
Wearing the deceased’s belongings is a common grief behavior.
High fever with chills
Fever is not a grief symptom and suggests a physical cause such as infection.
Sudden one-sided facial drooping
One-sided drooping suggests a neurological problem, not grief.
items.ex: Grief produces feelings, cognitions, physical sensations, and behaviors such as chest tightness, sensing the deceased, and keeping belongings.

alt.q: A widow describes how she has felt since her husband’s death. Which statements reflect common grief cognitions or behaviors? Select all that apply.
o: “I keep forgetting where I put things and can’t concentrate.”
Memory problems and inability to concentrate are common grief cognitions.
“I have been dreaming about him almost every night.”
Dreams of the deceased are a common grief behavior.
“I can’t bring myself to change anything in his room.”
Keeping the deceased’s room intact is a common grief behavior.
“I hear a voice telling me to hurt myself.”
Command voices urging self-harm are not a normal grief symptom and need urgent follow-up.
“My skin has turned yellow over the past week.”
Yellow skin is a physical finding unrelated to grief.
alt.ex: Memory and concentration problems, dreams of the deceased, and keeping the deceased’s room intact are common grief responses.

items.q: A dying patient cries often, has angry outbursts, and reports nightmares. The nurse suspects Dysfunctional Grief. Which action should the nurse take before selecting this diagnosis?
items.a: Clarify whether the patient is having pain
items.ex: These cues can indicate Pain, Dysfunctional Grief, or Spiritual Distress; clarifying pain prevents an inaccurate diagnosis.
w: Select the diagnosis because this cluster confirms it
The same cues fit other diagnoses; validate assumptions before diagnosing.
Ask the family which diagnosis they prefer
Diagnoses come from validated assessment data, not family preference.
Choose Spiritual Distress because nightmares rule out grief
Nightmares do not rule out grief; further assessment is needed.

alt.q: Why can a nurse not make an accurate nursing diagnosis for a grieving patient from just one or two assessment findings?
alt.a: A single behavior can occur with several different problems and types of grief.
alt.ex: Because one behavior can reflect several problems, the nurse reviews data clusters and validates before diagnosing.
w: Nursing diagnoses must first be approved by the health care provider.
Nurses make nursing diagnoses from clustered, validated assessment data.
Grief-related diagnoses can be made only after the patient’s death.
Grief diagnoses apply before death, such as Anticipatory Grief.
One or two findings are enough only for physical diagnoses.
No diagnosis should rest on one or two findings; look for clusters of cues.

items.q: A nursing diagnosis of Dysfunctional Grief related to permanent loss of mobility requires different interventions than Dysfunctional Grief related to infertility after an ectopic pregnancy.
items.a: True
items.ex: Identifying the related-to factor ensures the nurse selects interventions that fit the cause of the problem.
items.ww: Different related factors call for different interventions even when the diagnosis label is the same.

alt.q: Once the nursing diagnosis label is chosen, the related-to factor has little effect on which interventions the nurse selects.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Clarifying the related factor ensures appropriate interventions, because different causes need different interventions.
alt.ww: The related factor directly guides intervention selection, so it is far from irrelevant.

items.q: Two patients have the nursing diagnosis Powerlessness. One often asks for clarification about the treatment plan; the other is depressed about having treatment for metastatic cancer. Which expected outcome is most realistic for the depressed patient?
items.a: Patient will identify a minimum of three effective coping skills.
items.ex: Realistic outcomes consider the patient’s resources and coping style; coping skills fit a depressed patient who feels powerless.
w: Patient will describe the expected course of the disease.
This fits the patient who seeks information and participates in educational discussions.
Patient will teach family members about the treatment plan.
Teaching others is unrealistic for a patient who is depressed and feels powerless.
Patient will independently manage all daily care activities.
This ignores the patient’s limited resources; outcomes must fit energy and coping.

alt.q: Which approach is most important when the nurse establishes expected outcomes with a patient who is dying?
alt.a: Collaborate closely with the patient, considering the patient’s own resources
alt.ex: Outcomes for dying patients are mutually set and consider physical energy, activity tolerance, family support, and coping style.
w: Use the standard outcomes listed for the diagnosis without changes
Outcomes are individualized to the patient’s preferences, beliefs, and culture.
Let the health care provider set the outcomes without the patient
The nurse partners with the patient and family to set outcomes.
Choose outcomes that focus mainly on curing the disease
Dying patients often prioritize comfort, social, or spiritual needs over cure.

items.q: A dying patient’s expected outcomes include pain control and promoting self-esteem. The patient is currently experiencing acute physical discomfort. Which should the nurse address first?
items.a: Pain control
items.ex: Pain control takes priority when the patient has acute physical discomfort; other issues follow once comfort is achieved.
w: Promoting self-esteem
Self-esteem is important, but acute physical discomfort takes priority.
Funeral planning
Planning can wait until the patient’s comfort needs are met.
Advance directive review
Comfort needs are met first, and then other issues can be addressed.

alt.q: Which statement about setting priorities for patients at the end of life is accurate?
alt.a: Once comfort needs are met, other issues important to the patient can be addressed.
alt.ex: Prioritize urgent physical or psychological needs, then address other issues important to the patient and family.
w: Patients at the end of life usually prefer medical cures over comfort.
They are often more likely to want comfort, social, or spiritual needs met.
The plan of care is set once and rarely needs revision.
Conditions change quickly, so reassess often and revise the plan.
Independence should be promoted even when it is unrealistic.
Autonomy takes priority only when independence is realistic for the patient.

items.q: Palliative care is appropriate only after a patient stops pursuing curative treatment.
items.a: False
items.ex: Patients receiving aggressive curative treatment and those who stopped life-extending treatment both benefit from palliative care.
items.ww: Limiting palliative care to after cure is abandoned is a common misconception that the textbook corrects.

alt.q: Palliative care is appropriate for patients of any age, with any diagnosis, at any time, and in any setting.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Palliative care relieves symptoms throughout the entire course of an illness, not only at the end of life.
alt.ww: Palliative care is not restricted by age, diagnosis, timing, or setting, so the statement is true.

items.q: Which are core beliefs or services of hospice programs? Select all that apply.
o: The patient and family are the unit of care
Hospice treats the patient and family together as the unit of care.
Bereavement follow-up after the patient’s death
Hospice provides bereavement follow-up to the family.
Trained volunteers for visitation and respite support
Hospice uses trained volunteers for visits and respite.
Medical and nursing services available at all times
Hospice offers 24-hour access to medical and nursing services.
Services provided only in the patient’s home
Hospice is available in home, hospital, extended care, and nursing home settings.
Care priorities set mainly by the health care team
Patients are active participants, and care is prioritized by patient wishes.
items.ex: Hospice core services include family-centered care, round-the-clock services, bereavement follow-up, and trained volunteers.

alt.q: A family asks the nurse about home hospice for their mother. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: “Patients accepted into hospice usually have less than 6 months to live.”
Hospice patients usually have a life expectancy of less than 6 months.
“A family caregiver must be available when she can no longer function alone.”
Home hospice eligibility requires a family caregiver.
“She may go to an inpatient hospice unit for symptom stabilization or respite.”
Home hospice patients may enter an inpatient unit for stabilization or caregiver respite.
“Hospice will stop her pain medications so she stays alert.”
Hospice gives priority to pain and symptom management.
“Hospice support for your family ends at the moment of death.”
Hospice provides bereavement visits to help the family grieve.
alt.ex: Home hospice usually serves patients with under 6 months to live, requires a family caregiver, and offers inpatient stabilization and respite.

items.q: During [[respite care|respite]], a patient temporarily receives care from others so that family caregivers can get away to rest and relax.
items.ex: Home caregiving is often exhausting, so hospice benefits include some days of respite care.

alt.q: A home hospice patient may enter an inpatient hospice unit for symptom stabilization or for caregiver [[respite]].
alt.ex: Home caregiving is often exhausting, so hospice benefits include some days of respite care.

items.q: The daughter of a dying patient angrily accuses the nurse of ignoring her mother. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “I see that you’re upset, and that’s understandable. I’m here to talk if you want.”
items.ex: Remain supportive by letting family members know that feelings such as anger are normal and offering to talk.
w: “There is no reason to be angry; we are doing all we can.”
This dismisses the feeling; anger during grief is normal and should be acknowledged.
“Why are you speaking to me in that tone of voice?”
A defensive question blocks communication instead of acknowledging feelings.
“I will come back later once you have calmed down.”
Leaving conveys rejection; the nurse should remain supportive and available.

alt.q: A grieving patient tells the nurse, “I don’t want to talk about it.” Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
alt.a: Express willingness to be available whenever the patient is ready
alt.ex: If a patient chooses not to share feelings, express willingness to be available at any time.
w: Keep asking questions until the patient shares feelings
Pressuring disrespects privacy; some patients resolve grief privately first.
Switch to closed-ended questions that are easier to answer
Closed-ended questions limit what the nurse learns; respect readiness instead.
Document that the patient refuses all psychosocial care
Declining to talk now is not refusing care; the nurse remains available.

items.q: The husband of a patient in the last days of life keeps urging her to finish her meals, though she says food makes her nauseated. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Explain that forcing food can cause discomfort, and help him find other ways to help
items.ex: As the body shuts down, nutrients cannot be absorbed and eating causes discomfort, so forcing food does more harm than good.
w: Encourage him to keep offering large meals to maintain her strength
Caloric needs fall near death; forcing large meals causes discomfort.
Suggest that he insist on nutritional supplements between meals
Forcing intake conflicts with the comfort goal of palliative care.
Tell him a feeding tube will be placed so she gets enough calories
Artificial nutrition is a patient and family decision, and nutrients are not absorbed as the body shuts down.

alt.q: Why do patients in the last days of life often develop anorexia?
alt.a: Illness, decreased activity, treatments, and fatigue lower their caloric needs and appetite.
alt.ex: Illness, excess respiratory secretions, decreased activity, treatments, and fatigue decrease caloric needs and appetite.
w: Family members usually serve foods that the patient dislikes.
Food choice is not the cause; the dying process lowers caloric needs.
Opioids raise the metabolic rate and suppress hunger signals.
This is not the textbook’s explanation; illness and fatigue reduce needs and appetite.
Patients deliberately refuse food in order to hasten death.
Anorexia results from the dying process, not a deliberate choice.

items.q: The son of a dying patient asks the nurse to hold his father’s morphine because he fears his father will become addicted. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Explain that true addiction is rare and that pain relief at the end of life takes priority
items.ex: The incidence of true addiction is very low, and a patient’s need for pain relief at the end of life takes priority.
w: Agree to hold doses unless his father specifically asks for them
Dying patients often cannot communicate needs; reassure the family about pain control.
Give the morphine only when the pain becomes severe
Around-the-clock dosing is preferred over waiting for pain to become severe.
Tell him addiction is likely but cannot be avoided at this stage
The incidence of true addiction to opioids is very low.

alt.q: A nurse teaches the family of a hospice patient about pain management. Which statement by a family member shows understanding?
alt.a: “We should keep treating his pain even if he doesn’t seem uncomfortable.”
alt.ex: Reassure the family of the need for pain control even when the patient does not appear to be in pain.
w: “We should save the medicine until his pain gets really bad.”
Waiting for severe pain is less effective than around-the-clock dosing.
“He will get addicted, so we should use as little as we can.”
True addiction is rare, and pain relief at the end of life takes priority.
“If he can’t tell us he hurts, he must not be in pain.”
Dying patients often cannot communicate; assess nonverbal cues of pain.

items.q: Which physical changes should the nurse teach a family to expect in the hours or days before death? Select all that apply.
o: Mottling and coolness of the extremities
Circulatory changes cause coolness and color changes such as mottling.
Decreased urine output with dark-colored urine
Urine output decreases and urine darkens near death.
Irregular breathing such as a Cheyne-Stokes pattern
Altered breathing, including apnea and Cheyne-Stokes respirations, is common.
Relaxed jaw muscles and a sagging mouth
Decreased muscle tone causes a relaxed jaw and sagging mouth.
Increased appetite and thirst
Intake of food and fluids decreases, and swallowing may become impossible.
Increased muscle tone and rigidity
Muscle tone decreases in the hours or days before death.
items.ex: Before death, patients often show circulatory changes, decreased urine output, altered breathing, and decreased muscle tone.

alt.q: The family of a dying patient asks the nurse what changes to expect. Which statements by the nurse are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: “Mottling is an expected sign as a body begins shutting down.”
This compassionate wording is the textbook’s example for describing mottling.
“He may sleep more and become harder to wake.”
Increased sleep and unresponsiveness are common before death.
“Congestion may make his breathing sound noisy near the end.”
Increased pulmonary secretions cause noisy respirations (death rattle).
“Based on these signs, he will die within 6 hours.”
Do not try to predict the time of death; explain what is happening instead.
“Every one of these changes will happen before he dies.”
Patients usually experience some but not all of these changes.
alt.ex: Describe expected changes compassionately, without predicting the time of death, since patients show some but not all signs.

items.q: Which nursing implication fits the symptom Corneal irritation?
items.a: Apply optical lubricants or artificial tears
items.ex: Table 36.3 links each end-of-life symptom to comfort measures that address its cause.
w: Elevate the head and turn at least every 2 hours
That goes with Noisy breathing (death rattle).
Reduce triggers such as strong smells and give antiemetics
That goes with Nausea.
Offer ice chips or a moist cloth to the lips
That goes with Dehydration.

alt.q: Which nursing implication fits the symptom Noisy breathing (death rattle)?
alt.a: Elevate the head and turn at least every 2 hours
alt.ex: Table 36.3 links each end-of-life symptom to comfort measures that address its cause.
w: Apply optical lubricants or artificial tears
That goes with Corneal irritation.
Reduce triggers such as strong smells and give antiemetics
That goes with Nausea.
Offer ice chips or a moist cloth to the lips
That goes with Dehydration.

alt.q: Which nursing implication fits the symptom Nausea?
alt.a: Reduce triggers such as strong smells and give antiemetics
alt.ex: Table 36.3 links each end-of-life symptom to comfort measures that address its cause.
w: Apply optical lubricants or artificial tears
That goes with Corneal irritation.
Elevate the head and turn at least every 2 hours
That goes with Noisy breathing (death rattle).
Offer ice chips or a moist cloth to the lips
That goes with Dehydration.

alt.q: Which nursing implication fits the symptom Dehydration?
alt.a: Offer ice chips or a moist cloth to the lips
alt.ex: Table 36.3 links each end-of-life symptom to comfort measures that address its cause.
w: Apply optical lubricants or artificial tears
That goes with Corneal irritation.
Elevate the head and turn at least every 2 hours
That goes with Noisy breathing (death rattle).
Reduce triggers such as strong smells and give antiemetics
That goes with Nausea.

alt.q: Which nursing implication fits the symptom Constipation?
alt.a: Give stool softeners or laxatives as needed
alt.ex: Table 36.3 links each end-of-life symptom to comfort measures that address its cause.
w: Apply optical lubricants or artificial tears
That goes with Corneal irritation.
Elevate the head and turn at least every 2 hours
That goes with Noisy breathing (death rattle).
Reduce triggers such as strong smells and give antiemetics
That goes with Nausea.

alt.q: Which nursing implication fits the symptom Urinary incontinence?
alt.a: Avoid using a brief when a catheter is in place
alt.ex: Table 36.3 links each end-of-life symptom to comfort measures that address its cause.
w: Apply optical lubricants or artificial tears
That goes with Corneal irritation.
Elevate the head and turn at least every 2 hours
That goes with Noisy breathing (death rattle).
Reduce triggers such as strong smells and give antiemetics
That goes with Nausea.

alt.q: Which symptom is managed by this action: “Apply optical lubricants or artificial tears”?
alt.a: Corneal irritation
alt.ex: Table 36.3 links each end-of-life symptom to comfort measures that address its cause.
w: Noisy breathing (death rattle)
Noisy breathing (death rattle): Elevate the head and turn at least every 2 hours.
Nausea
Nausea: Reduce triggers such as strong smells and give antiemetics.
Dehydration
Dehydration: Offer ice chips or a moist cloth to the lips.

alt.q: Which symptom is managed by this action: “Elevate the head and turn at least every 2 hours”?
alt.a: Noisy breathing (death rattle)
alt.ex: Table 36.3 links each end-of-life symptom to comfort measures that address its cause.
w: Corneal irritation
Corneal irritation: Apply optical lubricants or artificial tears.
Nausea
Nausea: Reduce triggers such as strong smells and give antiemetics.
Dehydration
Dehydration: Offer ice chips or a moist cloth to the lips.

alt.q: Which symptom is managed by this action: “Reduce triggers such as strong smells and give antiemetics”?

items.q: A woman whose husband died 3 years ago calls the hospice nurse, upset that she feels intensely sad again as the anniversary of his death approaches. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Acknowledge the loss, reassure her the reaction is normal, and encourage her to reminisce
items.ex: Anniversary reactions are common; openly acknowledge the loss, reassure that it is normal, and encourage reminiscing.
w: Tell her this reaction shows that her grief was never resolved
Renewed grief around the anniversary is common and does not mean grief was unresolved.
Suggest that she avoid reminders of her husband until the date passes
The textbook advises openly acknowledging the loss and reminiscing, not avoidance.
Advise her to ask her health care provider for a sleep aid
Excessive use of sleep aids is a warning sign of harmful coping.

alt.q: What does the term “anniversary reaction” mean?
alt.a: Renewed grief around the time of the loss in later years
alt.ex: Anniversary reactions are renewed grief around the time of the loss in subsequent years and are common.
w: Grief experienced before an expected loss occurs
Grief before a loss describes anticipatory grief.
Grief that lasts far longer than expected without resolving
Prolonged unresolved grief describes complicated, chronic grief.
Grief that cannot be openly acknowledged or shared
Grief that is not openly acknowledged describes disenfranchised grief.

items.q: During a home visit months after her mother’s death, a daughter describes several changes. Which finding indicates a long-term outcome of recovery from the loss rather than a short-term one?
items.a: Return of her sense of humor
items.ex: Long-term achievements include return of humor and normal life patterns, renewed relationships, and decreased inner pain.
w: Normalized sleep and eating patterns
Normalized sleep and dietary patterns are a short-term outcome.
Talking about the loss without feeling overwhelmed
This is a short-term outcome showing that grief interventions are effective.
Improved ability to make decisions
Improved decision making is a short-term outcome.

alt.q: Which finding is a short-term outcome indicating that grief interventions are effective?
alt.a: Talking about the loss without feeling overwhelmed
alt.ex: Short-term outcomes include talking about the loss without feeling overwhelmed, improved energy, and normalized sleep and eating.
w: Return of a sense of humor
Return of humor is a long-term achievement.
Renewed or new personal relationships
New or renewed relationships are a long-term achievement.
A decrease of inner pain
Decreased inner pain is a long-term achievement.

w: Exhaustion stage
That's stage 3 of 3.

w: Alarm stage

alt.a: Resistance stage
alt.ex: Selye’s GAS moves from initial alarm, to resistance as the body compensates, to exhaustion if adaptation fails or stress stays unrelieved.
w: Alarm stage
That's stage 1 of 3.

ord.q: Put the stages of the general adaptation syndrome (GAS) in the order in which they occur.
items: Alarm stage
Resistance stage
Exhaustion stage
ord.ex: Selye’s GAS moves from initial alarm, to resistance as the body compensates, to exhaustion if adaptation fails or stress stays unrelieved.

items.q: Which statement best describes allostasis?
items.a: The body’s attempt to return to a state of balance after a stressor
items.ex: A fundamental concept underlying the GAS is that the body tries to return to balance, a process called allostasis.
w: The excessive wear and tear on organs caused by chronic arousal
Wear and tear from chronic arousal and stress hormones is allostatic load, not allostasis.
The person’s evaluation of what a stressful event means personally
Evaluating the personal meaning of an event is primary appraisal.
The progressive breakdown of the body’s compensatory mechanisms
Breakdown of compensatory mechanisms describes the exhaustion stage of the GAS.

alt.q: A nurse explains that after an injury the body works to restore its physiological balance. Which term describes this process?
alt.a: Allostasis
alt.ex: Allostasis is the body’s attempt to return to a balanced state, the fundamental concept underlying the GAS.
w: Allostatic load
Allostatic load is the wear and tear on organs from chronic arousal, not the return to balance.
Secondary appraisal
Secondary appraisal is considering available coping strategies or resources.
Fight-or-flight response
Fight-or-flight is the arousal of the alarm stage, which mobilizes defenses rather than restores balance.

items.q: A patient arrives in the emergency department minutes after a motor vehicle crash. The nurse notes a rapid heart rate, dilated pupils, and heightened alertness. Which stage of the general adaptation syndrome do these findings reflect?
items.a: Alarm stage
items.ex: In the alarm stage the CNS is aroused and defenses mobilize, raising heart rate and alertness and dilating pupils.
w: Resistance stage
In resistance, heart rate and hormone levels should return toward normal as the body compensates.
Exhaustion stage
Exhaustion follows prolonged stress when compensatory mechanisms break down, not minutes after a stressor.
Recovery stage
Recovery is not one of Selye’s three GAS stages; immediate arousal reflects the alarm stage.

alt.q: During which stage of the general adaptation syndrome does the fight-or-flight response first mobilize the body’s defenses?
alt.a: Alarm stage
alt.ex: The alarm stage arouses the central nervous system and mobilizes body defenses; this is the fight-or-flight response.
w: Resistance stage
Resistance follows alarm, as the body stabilizes and compensates for changes the alarm stage induced.
Exhaustion stage
Exhaustion is the final stage, when energy for adaptation is depleted.
Appraisal stage
Appraisal is a cognitive process of evaluating stressors, not a stage of the GAS.

items.q: Which physiological changes occur during the alarm stage of the general adaptation syndrome? Select all that apply.
o: Increased blood glucose level
Rising glucocorticoid levels such as cortisol increase blood glucose to fuel the response.
Increased blood flow to muscles
Blood flow to muscles increases to prepare the body for fight or flight.
Dilation of the pupils
Pupils dilate to produce a greater visual field.
Increased blood volume
Hormonal effects in the alarm stage increase blood volume.
Decreased oxygen intake
Oxygen intake increases, not decreases, during the alarm stage.
Decreased mental alertness
Mental alertness increases during the alarm stage.
items.ex: Alarm-stage hormones raise blood volume, glucose, catecholamines, heart rate, muscle blood flow, oxygen intake, and alertness, and dilate the pupils.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching about the fight-or-flight response of the alarm stage. Which effects should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Increased heart rate
Catecholamines and other hormones increase the heart rate in the alarm stage.
Increased epinephrine and norepinephrine
Epinephrine and norepinephrine levels rise as the sympathetic system and adrenal medulla respond.
Increased oxygen intake
Oxygen intake increases to meet the demands of fight or flight.
Constriction of the pupils
Pupils dilate, not constrict, to widen the visual field.
Decreased blood glucose level
Blood glucose rises, not falls, because of glucocorticoids such as cortisol.
alt.ex: Fight-or-flight raises heart rate, catecholamines, and oxygen intake, increases glucose, and dilates the pupils.

items.q: During the resistance stage of the general adaptation syndrome, hormone levels, heart rate, blood pressure, and cardiac output should return to normal as the body begins to repair damage.
items.a: True
items.ex: In resistance, the body stabilizes and compensates for alarm-stage changes, and it begins to repair damage.
items.ww: Ongoing intensification of the physiological response with failing adaptation describes exhaustion, not resistance.

alt.q: During the resistance stage, compensation is effortless and uses no additional energy or bodily resources.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Compensation attempts during resistance consume energy and other bodily resources.
alt.ww: The book states that the body’s compensation attempts use up energy and bodily resources, which is why exhaustion can follow.

items.q: Which statement best describes the exhaustion stage of the general adaptation syndrome?
items.a: Continuous stress causes progressive breakdown of compensatory mechanisms
items.ex: Exhaustion occurs when the body can no longer resist the stressor and has depleted the energy needed for adaptation.
w: The central nervous system is aroused and body defenses are mobilized
Arousal and mobilization of defenses describe the alarm stage.
Hormone levels and heart rate return to normal as tissues are repaired
Return toward normal and repair describe the resistance stage.
The person evaluates which coping resources are available to manage
Considering coping resources is secondary appraisal, not a GAS stage.

alt.q: A patient has experienced unrelieved stress for months and can no longer maintain adaptation. Which stage of the general adaptation syndrome is the patient in?
alt.a: Exhaustion stage
alt.ex: When stress remains unrelieved and adaptive energy is depleted, the person progresses to the exhaustion stage.
w: Alarm stage
The alarm stage is the initial mobilization of defenses, not depletion after prolonged stress.
Resistance stage
Resistance is the attempt to compensate; exhaustion follows when that attempt fails.
Allostasis stage
Allostasis is the return to balance, not a stage of the GAS.

items.q: What is allostatic load?
items.a: Excessive wear and tear on organs from chronic arousal and stress hormones
items.ex: Chronic arousal with powerful hormones causes excessive wear and tear on organs, which is called allostatic load.
w: The body’s return to physiological balance after a stressor ends
Returning to balance is allostasis, not allostatic load.
The total number of stressors a person can tolerate at one time
Allostatic load refers to physiological wear and tear, not a tolerance limit.
The immediate surge of catecholamines during the fight-or-flight reaction
The catecholamine surge is part of the alarm stage, not long-term wear and tear.

alt.q: A patient has had chronic job stress for years and now has persistent hypertension and sleep deprivation. Which concept best explains the link?
alt.a: Allostatic load
alt.ex: Persistent allostatic load from chronic arousal can cause chronic hypertension, depression, sleep deprivation, and autoimmune disorders.
w: Allostasis
Allostasis is the return to balance; the problems arise from wear and tear, or allostatic load.
Primary appraisal
Primary appraisal is evaluating personal meaning of an event, not long-term organ damage.
Compensation
Compensation is an ego-defense mechanism, not a physiological cause of chronic disease.

items.q: A persistent allostatic load can lead to which long-term physiological problems? Select all that apply.
o: Chronic hypertension
Chronic arousal and stress hormones can cause chronic hypertension.
Depression
Depression is listed among the long-term problems of persistent allostatic load.
Chronic fatigue syndrome
Chronic fatigue syndrome can result from persistent allostatic load.
Autoimmune disorders
Autoimmune disorders are among the long-term effects of chronic arousal.
Enhanced immune function
Prolonged stress impairs immunity rather than enhancing it.
items.ex: A persistent allostatic load can cause chronic hypertension, depression, sleep deprivation, chronic fatigue syndrome, and autoimmune disorders.

alt.q: A nurse reviews the health risks of chronic stress with a patient. Which conditions should the nurse identify as linked to increasing stress? Select all that apply.
o: Infection
Stress impairs immunity, increasing the risk for infection.
High blood pressure
As stress increases, the risk for high blood pressure increases.
Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is listed among health changes linked with increasing stress.
Cancer
Impaired immunity from stress increases susceptibility to cancer.
Improved sleep quality
Chronic stress is linked with sleep deprivation, not improved sleep.
alt.ex: Increasing stress raises the risk for infection, high blood pressure, diabetes mellitus, and cancer through impaired immunity.

items.q: A patient caring for a parent with dementia says, “I’ve been so stressed this year, and I keep catching every cold that goes around.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Prolonged stress can weaken your immune system and make infections more likely.”
items.ex: The stress response causes prolonged changes in the immune system, impairing immunity and increasing infection risk.
w: “Stress affects only your mood, so the colds are probably unrelated.”
Stress has physical effects; impaired immunity makes infections more likely.
“Stress strengthens your immune system, so the colds must have another cause.”
Prolonged stress impairs, not strengthens, the immune response.
“Colds are caused by viruses, so stress has nothing to do with them.”
Although viruses cause colds, stress-impaired immunity increases susceptibility to infection.

alt.q: Why is a person under prolonged stress more susceptible to infection?
alt.a: The stress response causes prolonged changes that impair immunity
alt.ex: The neuroendocrine stress response produces prolonged immune system changes that impair immunity.
w: Stress hormones increase lymphocyte counts and overwork the immune system
Cortisol decreases, not increases, lymphocytes and immune responses.
Stress increases eosinophils and allergic responses that block immunity
Cortisol decreases eosinophils and allergic responses.
Stress lowers blood glucose so immune cells lack an energy source
Stress hormones raise blood glucose; impaired immunity comes from immune system changes.

items.q: A patient is told she needs surgery and thinks, “This could mean I lose my job.” Which process is the patient using?
items.a: Primary appraisal
items.ex: Primary appraisal is evaluating an event in terms of its personal meaning, such as harm, loss, threat, or challenge.
w: Secondary appraisal
Secondary appraisal considers available coping strategies or resources, not the event’s meaning.
Displacement
Displacement transfers emotions to a less threatening substitute.
Allostasis
Allostasis is the body’s physiological return to balance, not a mental evaluation.

alt.q: What is primary appraisal?
alt.a: Evaluating an event in terms of its personal meaning
alt.ex: A person experiences stress only if an event is appraised as significant; this evaluation of meaning is primary appraisal.
w: Considering the coping strategies and resources available
Considering coping options and resources is secondary appraisal.
Refusing to acknowledge an event that causes emotional pain
Refusing to acknowledge painful events is denial, an ego-defense mechanism.
Returning the body to physiological balance after a threat
The return to balance is allostasis, a physiological process.

items.q: After learning his wife needs chemotherapy, a patient tells the nurse, “I can use my vacation time, and my brother said he would help drive her.” Which process does this statement reflect?
items.a: Secondary appraisal
items.ex: Secondary appraisal is the process of considering possible available coping strategies or resources.
w: Primary appraisal
Primary appraisal is evaluating what the event means personally, not identifying resources.
Regression
Regression is coping through behaviors of an earlier developmental period.
Conversion
Conversion transforms emotional conflict into nonorganic physical symptoms.

alt.q: Which statement about primary and secondary appraisal is accurate?
alt.a: They occur at the same time as an ongoing perceptual process
alt.ex: Secondary appraisal of coping resources occurs at the same time as primary appraisal, and appraisal is ongoing.
w: Secondary appraisal begins only after primary appraisal has ended
The book states that secondary appraisal occurs at the same time as primary appraisal.
Each occurs once, when the stressor is first noticed
Appraisal is ongoing; feedback cues lead to reappraisals of the original perception.
Both are unconscious processes that protect against anxiety
Unconscious protection from anxiety describes ego-defense mechanisms, not appraisal.

items.q: A person’s cognitive and behavioral efforts to manage a stressor are called [[coping]].
items.ex: Coping is important to physical and psychological health because stress is linked with many health outcomes.

alt.q: When a person makes cognitive and behavioral efforts to manage a stressor, the person is [[coping]].
alt.ex: Coping is important to physical and psychological health because stress is linked with many health outcomes.

items.q: A patient with a new diagnosis of diabetes reads about meal planning and signs up for a class while also talking with a friend to calm her worries. How should the nurse interpret this behavior?
items.a: She is combining problem-focused and emotion-focused coping
items.ex: Most people combine strategies: gathering information and acting (problem-focused) while regulating emotions (emotion-focused).
w: She is using denial to avoid acknowledging the diagnosis
She is actively engaging with the diagnosis, which is the opposite of denial.
She is relying only on emotion-focused coping
Learning meal planning and taking a class are problem-focused actions.
She is showing ineffective coping that needs to be stopped
Using both problem- and emotion-focused strategies is a typical, healthy approach.

alt.q: A nursing student stops thinking about an upcoming exam to feel less anxious but keeps studying for it. Which statement best describes this?
alt.a: The student uses emotion-focused and problem-focused coping together
alt.ex: Avoiding thinking about the exam regulates emotion, while continuing to study takes action on the situation.
w: The student uses only problem-focused coping
Not thinking about the exam to ease stress is an emotion-focused strategy.
The student is in the exhaustion stage of the GAS
Exhaustion is physiological breakdown after prolonged stress, not a coping choice.
The student is using regression to avoid the stressor
Regression involves behaviors from an earlier developmental period.

items.q: Which patient is most likely to have the greatest difficulty coping with a stressor?
items.a: A patient with no social support who is unexpectedly told of a serious diagnosis
items.ex: Unexpected stressors are harder to cope with, and lack of social support weakens the response to a stressor.
w: A patient with supportive family who has planned an elective surgery for months
An anticipated stressor and social support both make coping easier.
A patient who feels competent managing a chronic illness for years
Feelings of competence help a person respond to stressors.
A patient who has a strong sense of personal control over treatment choices
A high level of personal control improves the response to a stressor.

alt.q: Which personal characteristic is likely to improve a person’s response to a psychological stressor?
alt.a: A strong social support system
alt.ex: Personal control, social support, and feelings of competence all influence the response to a stressor.
w: A stressor that arrives without warning
Unexpected stressors are often more difficult to cope with.
Several other stressors occurring at the same time
Additional simultaneous stressors make the response more difficult.
A stressor of high intensity and long duration
Greater intensity and duration of a threat worsen the response.

items.q: Which are personal resources that help determine how a person responds to stress? Select all that apply.
o: Problem-solving skills
Problem-solving skills are a personal resource for managing stress.
Financial status
Financial status is listed among personal resources.
Support from family and friends
Support from family and friends is a key personal resource.
Optimism and mindfulness
Optimism and mindfulness are personal stress-management techniques.

items.q: After a heated argument with his supervisor, a patient slams and yells at the hospital television when it will not turn on. Which ego-defense mechanism is the patient most likely using?
items.a: Displacement
items.ex: Displacement transfers emotions from a stressful situation to a less anxiety-producing substitute, such as a malfunctioning device.
w: Compensation
Compensation emphasizes an asset to make up for a perceived deficiency.
Identification
Identification is patterning behavior after another person and assuming that person’s qualities.
Conversion
Conversion changes emotional conflict into nonorganic physical symptoms, not redirected anger.

alt.q: A patient whose spouse died last month refuses to discuss the death and changes the subject whenever it is mentioned. Which ego-defense mechanism is the patient using?
alt.a: Denial
alt.ex: Denial avoids emotional conflict by refusing to consciously acknowledge something that causes intolerable emotional pain.
w: Displacement
Displacement redirects emotions to a substitute target rather than refusing to acknowledge the loss.
Regression
Regression involves behaviors from an earlier developmental period.
Dissociation
Dissociation is a subjective sense of numbing and reduced awareness of surroundings.

items.q: Ego-defense mechanisms are used unconsciously by everyone and, when activated by short-term stressors, usually do not result in psychiatric disorders.
items.a: True
items.ex: Everyone uses ego-defense mechanisms unconsciously for protection from anxiety; short-term use usually does not cause psychiatric disorders.
items.ww: The book describes ego-defense mechanisms as normal, spontaneous, and generally helpful, though occasionally one becomes distorted.

alt.q: Ego-defense mechanisms are deliberate, conscious strategies that a person chooses to solve problems directly.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Ego-defense mechanisms are unconscious and help a person cope with stress indirectly.
alt.ww: Direct, task-oriented problem solving is a separate adaptive behavior; defense mechanisms work indirectly and unconsciously.

items.q: The general adaptation syndrome can be triggered indirectly by a psychological event as well as directly by a physical event.
items.a: True
items.ex: The GAS is triggered directly by a physical event or indirectly by a psychological event.
items.ww: Psychological threats indirectly activate the GAS, so the stress response is not limited to physical injury.

alt.q: The general adaptation syndrome is activated only by physical injuries, not by psychological threats.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Psychological events indirectly activate the GAS, in addition to direct physical triggers.
alt.ww: The book states that psychological threats indirectly activate the GAS.

items.q: During the stress response, the hypothalamus releases corticotropin-releasing hormone (CRH). What is the next step in this hormonal pathway?
items.a: The anterior pituitary secretes increased adrenocorticotropic hormone (ACTH)
items.ex: CRH stimulates the anterior pituitary to secrete ACTH, which then stimulates the adrenal cortex.
w: The posterior pituitary secretes increased antidiuretic hormone (ADH)
Posterior pituitary ADH release is a separate pathway, not the response to CRH.
The adrenal medulla secretes increased aldosterone (mineralocorticoid)
Aldosterone comes from the adrenal cortex; the adrenal medulla releases catecholamines.
The kidneys secrete increased cortisol (glucocorticoid)
Cortisol is secreted by the adrenal cortex after ACTH stimulation.

alt.q: A nurse explains how stress increases blood volume. Which hormone effect contributes to this increase?
alt.a: Increased ADH secretion causing water retention
alt.ex: Stress stimulates the posterior pituitary to increase ADH, causing antidiuresis and water retention that raise blood volume.
w: Decreased aldosterone secretion causing sodium loss
Stress moderately increases aldosterone, which promotes sodium and water reabsorption.
Decreased cortisol secretion causing fluid shifts
Cortisol secretion markedly increases, not decreases, during the stress response.
Increased urine output causing fluid redistribution
ADH causes antidiuresis, which decreases urine output.

items.q: Which patient is experiencing chronic stress?

items.ex: Chronic stress occurs in stable conditions and from stressful roles, such as family duties, full-time work, and long-term illness.
w: A student who feels anxious during a 1-hour final examination
A brief, time-limited threat provokes acute stress.
A driver who swerves to avoid a deer on the highway
A sudden, brief threat produces acute rather than chronic stress.
A patient waiting 30 minutes for a minor procedure to begin
A short, time-limited event provokes acute stress.

alt.q: Which situation is most likely to provoke acute stress?
alt.a: A time-limited event that threatens a person for a brief period
alt.ex: Acute stress is provoked by time-limited events that threaten a person for a relatively brief period.
w: Living for years with a long-term illness
Living with a long-term illness produces chronic stress.
Carrying family responsibilities along with a full-time job
Ongoing stressful roles cause chronic stress.
Remaining in a stable but demanding role for many years
Chronic stress occurs in stable conditions and from stressful roles.

items.q: The same stimulus can be seen as a challenge that leads to growth by one person and as a threat that leads to stagnation by another.
items.a: True
items.ex: How a person views a stimulus determines whether it leads to mastery and growth or to stagnation and loss.
items.ww: Stress depends on individual perception, so the same stimulus does not affect everyone the same way.

alt.q: A given stimulus produces the same degree of stress and the same outcome in every person who experiences it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: One person sees a stimulus as a challenge and grows, while another sees it as a threat and stagnates.
alt.ww: Perception and appraisal make responses to the same stimulus differ between people.

items.q: Which is an example of a recurrent daily hassle that can further complicate chronic or acute stress?

w: Being involved in a violent personal assault
A violent assault is a traumatic event that can lead to PTSD.
Experiencing a major natural disaster
A natural disaster creates an adventitious crisis.
Being diagnosed with a severe illness
A severe illness provokes a situational crisis, not a daily hassle.

alt.q: A patient says, “Between the traffic every morning, keeping up the house, and paying the bills, I never get a break.” How should the nurse classify these stressors?
alt.a: Recurrent daily hassles
alt.ex: Commuting, maintaining a house, and managing money are recurrent daily hassles that add to chronic or acute stress.
w: Adventitious crises
Adventitious crises are major disasters or crimes of violence.
Developmental crises
Developmental crises arise from moving through life stages such as marriage or parenthood.
Traumatic events
Traumatic events such as assaults or disasters can lead to PTSD, not routine hassles.

items.q: When does posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) begin?
items.a: When a person experiences or witnesses a traumatic event and responds with intense fear or helplessness
items.ex: PTSD begins when a person experiences or witnesses trauma and responds with intense fear or helplessness.
w: When a person faces several recurrent daily hassles at work and home over many months
Daily hassles complicate chronic stress but do not define the onset of PTSD.
When a person moves into a new developmental stage such as marriage or parenthood
A new life stage creates a developmental crisis, not PTSD.
When a person cares for others for long periods and slowly loses empathy for them
Gradual loss of empathy from caregiving relates to compassion fatigue.

alt.q: A patient was a bystander at a mass shooting and felt intense fear and helplessness. Weeks later he has nightmares and feels emotionally detached. Which condition do these findings suggest?
alt.a: Posttraumatic stress disorder
alt.ex: Witnessing a traumatic event with intense fear or helplessness, followed by nightmares and detachment, suggests PTSD.
w: Developmental crisis
Developmental crises come from moving through life stages, not traumatic events.
Chronic stress
Chronic stress arises from stable conditions and stressful roles, not a single trauma.
Alarm stage of the GAS
The alarm stage is the immediate fight-or-flight response, not symptoms weeks later.

Flashbacks

Depression
Depression and PTSD commonly occur together.
Increased desire to discuss the event with strangers
PTSD is marked by intrusive memories and detachment, not eagerness to discuss the trauma.
items.ex: PTSD anxiety can appear as nightmares, emotional detachment, and flashbacks, and depression commonly occurs with PTSD.

alt.q: Which groups or events does the book identify as commonly linked with PTSD? Select all that apply.

alt.ex: PTSD is common among military personnel, veterans, and police and follows events such as accidents, disasters, and violent assaults.

These workers often witness suffering and commonly develop it.

The book identifies it as a component of compassion fatigue.
It occurs only in people who were physically injured
It comes from witnessing others’ suffering, not from personal injury.
It improves a person’s ability to relate to family

alt.ex: Secondary traumatic stress comes from witnessing suffering, is common in health care workers and first responders, and is part of compassion fatigue.

Situational crises are provoked by external sources such as job change, accidents, or severe illness.
Adventitious crisis
Adventitious crises come from major disasters or crimes of violence.
Secondary traumatic stress
Secondary traumatic stress comes from witnessing others’ suffering.

alt.a: Situational crisis
alt.ex: External sources such as a job change, a motor vehicle accident, or severe illness provoke situational crises.
w: Developmental crisis
Developmental crises arise from entering a new life stage, such as marriage.
Adventitious crisis

Posttraumatic stress disorder
PTSD follows a traumatic event met with intense fear, not a job loss.

items.a: False

alt.q: Developmental crises occur as a person moves through the stages of life, such as marriage or the birth of a child.

alt.ww: External events such as accidents provoke situational crises, which differ from developmental crises.

items.q: A nurse is beginning crisis intervention with a patient whose spouse was just seriously injured. Which question is most important for the nurse to ask?
items.a: “What does this mean to you?”
items.ex: In person-centered crisis care, the person’s view is the frame of reference, so the vital question is what the event means to them.
w: “Why are you so upset about this?”
“Why” questions can sound judgmental and do not explore the person’s own meaning.
“Have you had a crisis like this before?”
Past history may help later, but the person’s current perception is the vital starting point.
“Wouldn’t most people handle this better?”
Comparing the person to others dismisses the person’s perception, which frames the crisis.

alt.q: Why does the nurse ask a patient in crisis, “How is it going to affect your life?”
alt.a: The person’s own view of the crisis is the frame of reference for care
alt.ex: Person-centered crisis care uses the person’s perception as the frame of reference, because stressors affect people differently.
w: The same event causes the same level of stress in everyone
What causes extreme stress for one person is not always stressful for another.
It helps the nurse decide which GAS stage is present
The question explores personal meaning, not the physiological stage.
It shows the patient that the crisis is not serious
The question respects the patient’s perception rather than minimizing it.

items.q: Which factors influence a person’s return to equilibrium after a crisis?

w: Age at the time of the event, gender, and level of income

Pupil size, heart rate, and blood glucose during the alarm stage
These are physiological alarm-stage findings, not crisis resolution factors.
Number of daily hassles, commute time, and housework load
Daily hassles complicate stress but are not the listed factors for regaining equilibrium.

alt.q: Which statement about the outcome of a crisis is accurate?
alt.a: A person either grows or regresses, depending on how the situation is managed
alt.ex: Depending on how the person manages the situation, a person either grows or regresses because of a crisis.
w: A person always regresses to an earlier developmental level after a crisis
Growth is also possible when the person manages the crisis effectively.
A crisis has no lasting effect once the stressor is removed
A crisis is a turning point leading to growth or regression.
A person’s previous coping methods resolve every crisis
In a crisis, previous ways of coping are ineffective.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “Ever since the assault, I wake up from nightmares, I feel numb around my family, and I keep reliving it as if it were happening again.” How should the nurse interpret these findings?
items.a: They suggest posttraumatic stress disorder and need follow-up
items.ex: Nightmares, emotional detachment, and flashbacks after a violent assault are characteristic of PTSD.
w: They are expected daily hassles that will resolve on their own
Daily hassles are routine stressors like commuting, not trauma-related symptoms.
They show a developmental crisis related to a new life stage
Developmental crises arise from life-stage transitions, not traumatic events.
They show healthy problem-focused coping with the event
Intrusive recollections and detachment are PTSD symptoms, not problem-focused coping.

alt.q: Which patient statement most strongly suggests flashbacks related to posttraumatic stress disorder?
alt.a: “I keep reliving the crash in my mind even when I don’t want to.”
alt.ex: Flashbacks are recurrent and intrusive recollections of the traumatic event.
w: “I worry about paying my bills and fixing the house.”
Worry about bills and house upkeep reflects daily hassles.
“I feel nervous before my driving test next week.”
Brief anxiety about an upcoming event reflects acute stress.
“I have been tired since starting my new job.”
Fatigue after a job change reflects situational stress, not intrusive recollections.

items.q: Posttraumatic stress disorder is common among military personnel, veterans, and police.
items.a: True
