items.ex: PTSD is common in military personnel, veterans, and police, especially soldiers in combat and police involved in violent acts.
items.ww: These groups often witness or take part in disturbing events, which places them at high risk for PTSD.

alt.q: Posttraumatic stress disorder develops only in people who were physically injured during a traumatic event.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: PTSD begins when a person experiences or witnesses a traumatic event and responds with intense fear or helplessness.
alt.ww: Witnessing trauma, not only being injured, can lead to PTSD.

items.q: Which are the types of crises described in the book? Select all that apply.
o: Maturational or developmental crises
Developmental crises occur as a person moves through the stages of life.
Situational crises
Situational crises are provoked by external sources such as job change or severe illness.
Adventitious crises
Adventitious crises come from disasters or crimes of violence.
Allostatic crises
Allostatic load is wear and tear from chronic stress, not a type of crisis.
Secondary crises
Secondary traumatic stress is a stress type, but secondary crisis is not a crisis category.
items.ex: The three types of crises are maturational or developmental, situational, and adventitious crises.

alt.q: Which events would provoke a situational crisis? Select all that apply.
o: A job change
A job change is an external source that provokes a situational crisis.
A motor vehicle accident
A motor vehicle accident is listed as a situational crisis trigger.
A severe illness
Severe illness is an external source that provokes a situational crisis.
Getting married
Marriage is a new developmental stage, causing a developmental crisis.
A major hurricane
A major natural disaster creates an adventitious crisis.
alt.ex: External sources such as job change, motor vehicle accidents, and severe illness provoke situational crises.

items.q: John Edwards was recently diagnosed with stage 3 pancreatic cancer, and he and Sandra are struggling to cope. Which type of crisis does this diagnosis represent?
items.a: Situational crisis
items.ex: Severe illness is an external source that provokes a situational crisis.
w: Developmental crisis
Developmental crises come from moving into new life stages, such as marriage or parenthood.
Adventitious crisis
Adventitious crises result from major disasters or crimes of violence.
Maturational crisis
Maturational crisis is another name for a developmental crisis, not one caused by illness.

alt.q: A patient’s sudden diagnosis of a severe illness leaves the family unable to cope in their usual ways. How should the nurse classify this crisis?
alt.a: Situational crisis
alt.ex: External events such as severe illness provoke situational crises, in which previous coping becomes ineffective.
w: Developmental crisis
A developmental crisis comes with life stages, not an unexpected diagnosis.
Adventitious crisis
Adventitious crises are created by disasters or violent crime.
Secondary traumatic stress
Secondary traumatic stress results from witnessing others’ suffering over time.

sections.name: Nursing theory and the role of stress

items.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows correct understanding of the Neuman Systems Model?
items.a: “When one family member faces a stressor, the rest of the family can be affected.”
items.ex: A systems approach holds that a stressor at one place in a system, such as a family, affects other parts.
w: “Each person’s stress affects only that person, so I assess patients separately.”
The systems approach views people within interconnected systems, not in isolation.
“The model mainly tells me to dim lights and reduce noise for patients.”
Modifying peripheral stimuli reflects Roy’s adaptation model.
“The model is mostly about planning diet and exercise for wellness.”
Diet and exercise interventions reflect Pender’s health promotion model.

alt.q: Which statement about the Neuman Systems Model is accurate?
alt.a: A system may be a person, a family, or a community
alt.ex: In Neuman’s systems approach, a system is a person, family, or community.
w: A system refers only to one organ of the body
Neuman’s system is a person, family, or community, not an organ.
A system stays fixed regardless of its environment
Neuman views the system as constantly changing in response to the environment and stressors.
A system is affected by only one cause at a time
Events are multidimensional and not caused or affected by only one thing.

items.q: Sandra Edwards has had hypertension for 7 years and has been working late on a stressful project. If Matt uses Pender’s health promotion model with her, which approach fits best?
items.a: Help Sandra assess her own assets and plan activity, nutrition, and stress management
items.ex: Pender’s model has people assess their abilities and assets and uses activity, nutrition, and stress management to promote health.
w: Dim the lights and close the door during her clinic visit
Modifying peripheral stimuli reflects Roy’s adaptation model, not health promotion.
Analyze how John’s illness affects the family as a whole system
Analyzing effects across a family system reflects the Neuman Systems Model.
Determine which stage of the general adaptation syndrome she is in
Identifying a GAS stage reflects Selye’s theory, not Pender’s health promotion model.

alt.q: A nurse working from Pender’s health promotion model asks a stressed patient, “What strengths do you have that could help you stay healthy?” What is the rationale for this question?
alt.a: The model holds that people can assess their own abilities and assets
alt.ex: In Pender’s model, people assess their abilities and assets and want to live as healthily as possible.
w: The model holds that the nurse alone sets health goals
Pender’s model relies on the person’s own self-assessment and motivation.
The model holds that stimuli must be modified for adaptation
Modifying stimuli for adaptation is Roy’s model.
The model holds that each person has a normal line of defense
The normal line of defense is a Neuman Systems Model concept.

items.q: Which nursing theory uses a systems approach to explain how patients, families, and communities respond to stressors?
items.a: Neuman Systems Model
items.ex: The Neuman Systems Model uses a systems approach to understand responses of patients, families, and communities to stressors.
w: Roy’s adaptation model
Roy’s model focuses on modifying external stimuli so the person can adapt.
Pender’s health promotion model
Pender’s model focuses on promoting health, managing stress, and increasing well-being.
Selye’s general adaptation syndrome
The GAS is a physiological stress theory, not a nursing systems model.

alt.q: The concept of a “normal line of defense” belongs to which nursing model?
alt.a: Neuman Systems Model
alt.ex: In the Neuman Systems Model, each person’s set of responses to stress forms the normal line of defense.
w: Roy’s adaptation model
Roy’s model centers on modifying stimuli to promote adaptation.
Pender’s health promotion model
Pender’s model centers on health promotion and self-assessment of abilities.
Erikson’s developmental theory
Erikson’s theory describes developmental stages, not lines of defense.

items.q: According to a systems approach, what happens when a stressor affects one part of a system?
items.a: Other parts of the system are also affected
items.ex: A systems approach explains that a stressor at one place in a system affects other parts of the system.
w: Only the part directly exposed to the stressor is affected
Systems thinking holds that effects spread to other parts of the system.
The system ignores the stressor until it becomes severe
The model views the system as constantly changing in response to stressors.
The stressor is always traced to one single cause
Events are multidimensional and not caused by only one thing.

alt.q: A father loses his job, and soon his teenage daughter’s grades drop and his wife reports trouble sleeping. Which Neuman Systems Model concept does this best illustrate?
alt.a: A stressor in one part of a system affects other parts
alt.ex: In the Neuman model, the family is a system, so one member’s stressor affects the whole family.
w: Each family member has a separate, unrelated stress response
The systems approach views family members as interconnected parts of one system.
Stress occurs only when an event has a single cause
Neuman views events as multidimensional, not caused by one thing.
The family is modifying peripheral stimuli to adapt
Modifying stimuli to promote adaptation reflects Roy’s model.

items.q: In the Neuman Systems Model, what is the “normal line of defense”?
items.a: The set of responses to stress that a person develops to maintain health
items.ex: Every person develops a set of responses to stress that constitute the normal line of defense, maintaining health and wellness.
w: A physical barrier such as the skin that blocks harmful microorganisms
The normal line of defense is a set of stress responses, not an anatomical barrier.
The point at which the body’s compensatory mechanisms break down
Breakdown of compensation is the exhaustion stage of the GAS.
The nurse’s actions that modify noise and light in the room
Modifying environmental stimuli reflects Roy’s adaptation model.

alt.q: What is the purpose of the normal line of defense in the Neuman Systems Model?
alt.a: To maintain health and wellness
alt.ex: The normal line of defense, a person’s set of responses to stress, maintains health and wellness.
w: To block all stressors from reaching the person
Stressors still affect the system; the line of defense is a set of responses to them.
To trigger the alarm stage of the stress response
Triggering alarm is part of the physiological GAS, not the line of defense.
To identify one single cause of each stressful event
Neuman views events as multidimensional, not caused by one thing.

items.q: In the Neuman Systems Model, the set of responses to stress that each person develops to maintain health and wellness is called the [[normal line of defense|line of defense]].
items.ex: Every person develops responses to stress that constitute the normal line of defense, which maintains health and wellness.

alt.q: Neuman describes a person’s usual set of stress responses that protects health and wellness as the [[normal line of defense|line of defense]].
alt.ex: Every person develops responses to stress that constitute the normal line of defense, which maintains health and wellness.

items.q: According to the Neuman Systems Model, which influences buffer stress? Select all that apply.
o: Physiological
Physiological influences are one of the buffers of stress.
Psychological
Psychological influences buffer stress.
Sociocultural
Sociocultural influences buffer stress.
Developmental
Developmental influences buffer stress.
Spiritual
Spiritual influences buffer stress.
Allostatic
Allostatic load is wear and tear from chronic stress, not one of Neuman’s buffering influences.
items.ex: Neuman lists physiological, psychological, sociocultural, developmental, and spiritual influences as buffers against stress.

alt.q: A nurse uses the Neuman Systems Model to plan care for a stressed patient. Which dimensions should the nurse consider? Select all that apply.
o: Spiritual beliefs
Spiritual influences buffer stress and are a dimension interventions address.
Sociocultural background
Sociocultural influences buffer stress.
Developmental stage
Developmental influences buffer stress in Neuman’s model.
Only the physical injury
Neuman’s model is multidimensional, not limited to physical factors.
Only the single cause of the stressor
Events are multidimensional and not caused or affected by only one thing.
alt.ex: The Neuman model helps nurses consider the physiological, psychological, sociocultural, developmental, and spiritual dimensions that interventions must address.

items.q: The Neuman Systems Model views a patient, family, or community as constantly changing in response to the environment and stressors.
items.a: True
items.ex: Neuman views the patient, family, or community as constantly changing in response to the environment and stressors.
items.ww: The model describes a dynamic system, not a fixed one that stays the same regardless of stressors.

alt.q: In the Neuman Systems Model, the “system” refers only to the individual patient and not to families or communities.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: In Neuman’s systems approach, a system is a person, family, or community.
alt.ww: The book explicitly defines the system as a person, family, or community.

items.q: Why is the Neuman Systems Model useful for planning nursing care for a patient under stress?
items.a: It allows nurses to consider the dimensions that interventions must address
items.ex: Because stress is buffered by many influences, the Neuman model lets nurses consider all dimensions interventions must address.
w: It focuses only on the physiological stages of the stress response
The model is multidimensional, not limited to physiological stages.
It assumes each stressful event has a single identifiable cause
Neuman views events as multidimensional, not caused by only one thing.
It requires the nurse to remove every stressor from the patient’s life
The model is about understanding responses and buffers, not eliminating all stressors.

alt.q: Which statement reflects the Neuman Systems Model view of events?
alt.a: Events are multidimensional and not caused or affected by only one thing
alt.ex: The systems approach holds that events are multidimensional, so care must address multiple dimensions.
w: Each event has one cause that the nurse must identify and remove
Neuman rejects single-cause explanations of events.
Events affect only the person directly involved
A stressor at one place in the system affects other parts.
Events matter only when they cause physical symptoms
Psychological, sociocultural, developmental, and spiritual dimensions also matter.

items.q: A patient on a busy medical unit cannot sleep because of hallway noise. The nurse turns down the lights and closes the door. Which nursing theory does this action best reflect?
items.a: Roy’s adaptation model
items.ex: Roy’s model has the nurse modify and regulate peripheral stimuli, such as light and noise, to promote adaptation and healing.
w: Neuman Systems Model
Neuman’s model emphasizes systems and the normal line of defense, not modifying environmental stimuli.
Pender’s health promotion model
Pender’s model emphasizes health promotion through activity, nutrition, and stress management.
Selye’s general adaptation syndrome
The GAS describes the physiological stress response, not nursing interventions.

alt.q: According to Roy’s adaptation model, how does a nurse promote a patient’s adaptation to stressors?
alt.a: By helping the patient modify and regulate peripheral stimuli
alt.ex: Roy’s model states a person can modify external stimuli to allow adaptation, and the nurse assists with this.
w: By having the patient rate personal assets and plan healthy habits
Self-assessment of abilities and assets reflects Pender’s health promotion model.
By strengthening the patient’s normal line of defense
The normal line of defense is a Neuman Systems Model concept.
By moving the patient quickly through the alarm stage
The alarm stage is a physiological GAS concept, not Roy’s intervention focus.

items.q: According to Roy’s adaptation model, a person can modify external stimuli to allow adaptation to occur.
items.a: True
items.ex: Roy’s theory describes how individuals effectively respond to environmental stressors by modifying external stimuli to adapt.
items.ww: Roy’s model specifically holds that external stimuli can be modified to support adaptation.

alt.q: Roy’s adaptation model holds that environmental stimuli cannot be changed, so nursing care should focus only on the patient’s internal responses.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Roy’s model has the nurse help modify and regulate peripheral stimuli to create a supportive healing environment.
alt.ww: The book’s Roy example shows the nurse changing light and noise to promote relaxation and sleep.

items.q: A nurse applies Roy’s adaptation model to promote rest for an anxious hospitalized patient. Which actions reflect this model? Select all that apply.
o: Dimming the room lights
Turning down the lights modifies peripheral stimuli to promote relaxation.
Closing the door to decrease noise
Closing the door reduces noise, a peripheral stimulus, to promote sleep.
Creating a supportive healing environment
Roy’s model aims to regulate stimuli to promote a supportive healing environment.
Asking the patient to assess personal assets for healthy living
Self-assessment of abilities and assets reflects Pender’s health promotion model.
Analyzing how the stressor affects the whole family system
Examining effects across a system reflects the Neuman Systems Model.
items.ex: In Roy’s model, the nurse modifies and regulates peripheral stimuli, such as lights and noise, to support adaptation and healing.

alt.q: Which statements describe Roy’s adaptation model? Select all that apply.
o: It describes how a person can effectively respond to environmental stressors
Roy’s model explains effective response to stressors in the environment.
The nurse assists in modifying and regulating peripheral stimuli
The nurse helps modify stimuli such as light and noise.
A person can modify external stimuli to allow adaptation
Modifying external stimuli to allow adaptation is central to Roy’s theory.
Each person’s stress responses form a normal line of defense
The normal line of defense is a Neuman Systems Model concept.
Health is achieved mainly through diet and exercise plans
Diet and activity interventions are emphasized in Pender’s health promotion model.
alt.ex: Roy’s model focuses on effective response to environmental stressors through modifying and regulating external stimuli.

items.q: Which nursing model focuses on promoting health, managing stress, and increasing the level of well-being?
items.a: Pender’s health promotion model
items.ex: Pender’s HPM focuses on promoting health, managing stress, and increasing well-being.
w: Roy’s adaptation model
Roy’s model focuses on modifying external stimuli to allow adaptation.
Neuman Systems Model
Neuman’s model uses a systems approach and the normal line of defense.
Erikson’s developmental theory
Erikson’s theory describes developmental stages and related stressors.

alt.q: What is the primary focus of Pender’s health promotion model?
alt.a: Promoting health, managing stress, and increasing well-being
alt.ex: Pender’s HPM focuses on promoting health, managing stress, and increasing level of well-being.
w: Modifying peripheral stimuli to allow adaptation
Modifying stimuli is the focus of Roy’s adaptation model.
Describing a system’s normal line of defense
The normal line of defense belongs to the Neuman Systems Model.
Explaining the three stages of the stress response
The three stages describe Selye’s general adaptation syndrome.

items.q: A patient with work-related stress tells the nurse, “I want to figure out what I’m good at and change my habits so I can be as healthy as possible.” Which nursing model best guides the nurse’s response?
items.a: Pender’s health promotion model
items.ex: In Pender’s model, people assess their own abilities and assets and want to live as healthily as possible.
w: Roy’s adaptation model
Roy’s model guides modifying environmental stimuli rather than self-assessment of assets.
Neuman Systems Model
Neuman’s model analyzes how stressors affect a system and its lines of defense.
Selye’s general adaptation syndrome
The GAS explains the physiological stress response, not health-promotion planning.

alt.q: A nurse uses Pender’s health promotion model with a patient who reports high stress. Which intervention best fits this model?
alt.a: Helping the patient plan to increase physical activity
alt.ex: Pender’s model uses interventions such as increasing physical activity, improving nutrition, and stress management to promote health.
w: Closing the door and dimming the lights at bedtime
Modifying peripheral stimuli reflects Roy’s adaptation model.
Mapping how the stressor affects each family member
Examining effects across a family system reflects the Neuman model.
Identifying which stage of the GAS the patient is in
Staging the stress response reflects Selye’s GAS, not health promotion.

items.q: Which interventions does Pender’s health promotion model use to help a person become and remain healthy? Select all that apply.
o: Increasing physical activity
Increasing physical activity is a health-promotion intervention in this model.
Improving diet and nutrition
Improving diet and nutrition helps the individual become and remain healthy.
Using stress-management strategies
Stress-management strategies are part of Pender’s health-promotion interventions.
Avoiding self-assessment of abilities
In Pender’s model, people assess their own abilities and assets.
Waiting for illness before making changes
The model focuses on promoting health and well-being, not reacting to illness.
items.ex: Pender’s HPM uses physical activity, improved diet and nutrition, and stress-management strategies to help people become and remain healthy.

alt.q: A nurse develops a wellness plan for a stressed office worker using Pender’s model. Which elements fit this approach? Select all that apply.
o: A daily walking program
Increasing physical activity promotes health in Pender’s model.
Healthier meal choices
Improving diet and nutrition is a health-promotion intervention.
A relaxation or stress-management technique
Stress-management strategies help the person remain healthy.
Having the nurse decide all goals without the patient’s input
Pender’s model has people assess their own abilities and assets.
Reducing room noise to improve sleep in the hospital
Modifying peripheral stimuli reflects Roy’s adaptation model.
alt.ex: Pender’s model pairs the person’s own self-assessment with activity, nutrition, and stress-management interventions.

items.q: In Pender’s health promotion model, people can assess their own abilities and assets and want to live in ways that keep them as healthy as possible.
items.a: True
items.ex: Pender’s HPM holds that people assess their own abilities and assets and want to be as healthy as possible.
items.ww: The model is built on the person’s own self-assessment and motivation for health.

alt.q: Pender’s health promotion model focuses mainly on modifying peripheral stimuli such as lighting and noise.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Modifying peripheral stimuli is the focus of Roy’s adaptation model; Pender’s model focuses on health promotion.
alt.ww: Pender’s HPM focuses on promoting health, managing stress, and increasing well-being through lifestyle interventions.

items.q: What is the key idea of Neuman Systems Model?
items.a: A stressor in one part of a system affects other parts
items.ex: Neuman uses a systems approach, Roy focuses on modifying stimuli for adaptation, and Pender focuses on health promotion.
w: Modifying external stimuli allows adaptation to occur
That goes with Roy’s adaptation model.
Promoting health and well-being through activity, nutrition, and stress management
That goes with Pender’s health promotion model.

alt.q: What is the key idea of Roy’s adaptation model?
alt.a: Modifying external stimuli allows adaptation to occur
alt.ex: Neuman uses a systems approach, Roy focuses on modifying stimuli for adaptation, and Pender focuses on health promotion.
w: A stressor in one part of a system affects other parts
That goes with Neuman Systems Model.
Promoting health and well-being through activity, nutrition, and stress management
That goes with Pender’s health promotion model.

alt.q: What is the key idea of Pender’s health promotion model?
alt.a: Promoting health and well-being through activity, nutrition, and stress management
alt.ex: Neuman uses a systems approach, Roy focuses on modifying stimuli for adaptation, and Pender focuses on health promotion.
w: A stressor in one part of a system affects other parts
That goes with Neuman Systems Model.
Modifying external stimuli allows adaptation to occur
That goes with Roy’s adaptation model.

alt.q: Which nursing model holds that “A stressor in one part of a system affects other parts”?
alt.a: Neuman Systems Model
alt.ex: Neuman uses a systems approach, Roy focuses on modifying stimuli for adaptation, and Pender focuses on health promotion.
w: Roy’s adaptation model
Roy’s adaptation model: Modifying external stimuli allows adaptation to occur.
Pender’s health promotion model
Pender’s health promotion model: Promoting health and well-being through activity, nutrition, and stress management.

alt.q: Which nursing model holds that “Modifying external stimuli allows adaptation to occur”?
alt.a: Roy’s adaptation model
alt.ex: Neuman uses a systems approach, Roy focuses on modifying stimuli for adaptation, and Pender focuses on health promotion.
w: Neuman Systems Model
Neuman Systems Model: A stressor in one part of a system affects other parts.
Pender’s health promotion model
Pender’s health promotion model: Promoting health and well-being through activity, nutrition, and stress management.

alt.q: Which nursing model holds that “Promoting health and well-being through activity, nutrition, and stress management”?
alt.a: Pender’s health promotion model
alt.ex: Neuman uses a systems approach, Roy focuses on modifying stimuli for adaptation, and Pender focuses on health promotion.
w: Neuman Systems Model
Neuman Systems Model: A stressor in one part of a system affects other parts.
Roy’s adaptation model
Roy’s adaptation model: Modifying external stimuli allows adaptation to occur.

mt.q: Match each nursing model with its key idea about stress.
pairs: A stressor in one part of a system affects other parts
Modifying external stimuli allows adaptation to occur
Promoting health and well-being through activity, nutrition, and stress management
mt.ex: Neuman uses a systems approach, Roy focuses on modifying stimuli for adaptation, and Pender focuses on health promotion.

items.q: A nurse caring for a patient after a stroke notes that the patient’s spouse, adult children, and church community are all affected by the illness. Which model best helps the nurse address responses across the patient, family, and community?
items.a: Neuman Systems Model
items.ex: Neuman’s systems approach helps nurses understand stressor responses of patients, families, and communities as interconnected systems.
w: Roy’s adaptation model
Roy’s model focuses on modifying environmental stimuli for an individual’s adaptation.
Pender’s health promotion model
Pender’s model focuses on individual health promotion and well-being.
Selye’s general adaptation syndrome
The GAS explains an individual’s physiological response, not family or community responses.

alt.q: A community health nurse wants to understand how a factory closure affects families and local organizations. Which model is most suited to this analysis?
alt.a: Neuman Systems Model
alt.ex: Neuman’s model applies to persons, families, and communities and explains how a stressor affects other parts of a system.
w: Roy’s adaptation model
Roy’s model centers on modifying peripheral stimuli for adaptation.
Pender’s health promotion model
Pender’s model centers on individuals assessing their assets and promoting health.
Erikson’s developmental theory
Erikson’s theory describes individual developmental stages.

items.q: A nurse is comparing nursing models for a teaching session. Which statement correctly contrasts Roy’s and Pender’s models?
items.a: Roy focuses on modifying stimuli for adaptation; Pender focuses on promoting health and well-being
items.ex: Roy’s model regulates stimuli so adaptation can occur, whereas Pender’s HPM promotes health, stress management, and well-being.
w: Roy focuses on promoting well-being; Pender focuses on the normal line of defense
Health promotion is Pender’s focus, and the normal line of defense is Neuman’s concept.
Roy focuses on family systems; Pender focuses on modifying external stimuli
Systems are Neuman’s focus, and modifying stimuli is Roy’s.
Roy focuses on the stages of stress; Pender focuses on ego-defense mechanisms
Stages of stress belong to Selye’s GAS, and neither model centers on ego-defense mechanisms.

alt.q: Which statement correctly contrasts the Neuman and Roy models?
alt.a: Neuman uses a systems approach; Roy focuses on modifying stimuli for adaptation
alt.ex: Neuman’s model explains stress through systems, while Roy’s model has the nurse modify stimuli to promote adaptation.
w: Neuman focuses on diet and exercise; Roy focuses on systems
Diet and exercise fit Pender’s model, and systems are Neuman’s focus.
Neuman focuses on modifying stimuli; Roy focuses on the line of defense
These concepts are reversed: modifying stimuli is Roy’s and line of defense is Neuman’s.
Neuman focuses on developmental stages; Roy focuses on health promotion
Developmental stages are Erikson’s, and health promotion is Pender’s.

items.q: Matt, the nurse practitioner, learns that John’s cancer diagnosis is affecting Sandra’s health and her ability to support him. Applying the Neuman Systems Model, how should Matt view this situation?
items.a: As a family system in which John’s illness affects Sandra
items.ex: In the Neuman model, a stressor at one place in a system, such as one spouse’s illness, affects other parts.
w: As two separate patients whose stress responses are unrelated
The systems approach views family members as interconnected parts of one system.
As a situation requiring only changes in room light and noise
Modifying peripheral stimuli reflects Roy’s model and would not address the family system.
As a single-cause problem that will resolve when the cancer is treated
Neuman views events as multidimensional, not caused by only one thing.

alt.q: Using the Neuman Systems Model, which assessment approach best fits a couple coping with one spouse’s new cancer diagnosis?
alt.a: Assessing how the stressor affects both spouses across several dimensions
alt.ex: Neuman’s model views the family as a system and considers physiological, psychological, sociocultural, developmental, and spiritual dimensions.
w: Assessing only the patient’s physical response to chemotherapy
The model is multidimensional and includes the family system, not only physical responses.
Assessing only the noise and lighting in the clinic room
Environmental stimuli are the focus of Roy’s model.
Assessing only the spouse’s diet and exercise habits
Diet and exercise interventions reflect Pender’s model and omit other dimensions.

items.q: Which factor places a person at higher risk for prolonged stress?
items.a: Experiencing social determinants of health
items.ex: Situational and social stressors increase the risk for prolonged stress, especially with any social determinants of health.
w: Having strong social support from family
Social support helps people cope; it does not increase risk for prolonged stress.
Having used effective coping strategies before
Previous effective coping helps reduce, not increase, stress.
Facing a stressor that was anticipated
Anticipated stressors are generally easier to cope with than unexpected ones.

alt.q: Which statement about factors that influence how a person reacts to a stressor is accurate?
alt.a: Appraisal, social support, and coping strategies all depend on previous life experiences
alt.ex: A person’s appraisal of stressors, social support, and coping strategies depend on previous life experiences and affect reactions.
w: Stressors and coping mechanisms stay the same across the life span
Stressors and coping mechanisms vary across the life span.
Social determinants of health lower the risk for prolonged stress
Social determinants of health increase the risk for prolonged stress.
Previous life experiences have little effect on coping strategies
Coping strategies depend on previous life experiences.

items.q: Which is a situational stressor in the health care workplace that affects nurses?
items.a: Conflicting priorities during a high-acuity patient load
items.ex: Workplace situational stressors include high-acuity patient loads, conflicting priorities, distractions, and fear of disease transmission.
w: Losing autonomy because of general frailty
Loss of autonomy from frailty is a maturational stressor of older adults.
Searching for identity within peer groups
Searching for identity with peers is a stressor of adolescence.
Adjusting to the birth of a first child
The birth of a child is a developmental change, not a workplace stressor.

alt.q: Which is a situational stressor for patients and family caregivers?
alt.a: Difficulty paying for treatment of an illness
alt.ex: Adjusting to illness, uncertainty about treatment, difficulty paying for treatment, and limited access to providers are situational stressors.
w: Searching for identity apart from family
Separating from family to form identity is a maturational stressor of adolescents.
Constant distractions during a nursing shift
Constant distractions are a workplace stressor for nurses, not patients.
Teaching a child impulse control
Teaching impulse control relates to the initiative versus guilt developmental stage.

items.q: A nurse who functions best in the morning is considering a permanent night-shift position. Which response by the occupational health nurse is best?
items.a: “Morning-oriented people often have the most difficulty with night work, so let’s talk about how it may affect you.”
items.ex: Morning people have the greatest difficulty with night work and should be counseled about its potentially negative effects.
w: “Morning-oriented people adjust to night work more easily than others, so this is a good fit.”
Morning people have the greatest, not least, difficulty with night work.
“Your circadian rhythm will not affect how you tolerate night work, so it is fine.”
Knowing one’s circadian rhythm is a way to cope with shift work.
“Night work only causes problems for younger nurses, so you have nothing to worry about.”
Age makes people more morning oriented, so it does not protect against night-work difficulty.

alt.q: Which person is likely to have the greatest difficulty adjusting to night work and changing shifts?
alt.a: A nurse who functions best in the morning
alt.ex: People who function best in the morning have the greatest difficulty with night work and changing shifts.
w: A nurse who functions best in the evening
Evening-oriented people are not identified as having the most difficulty with night work.
A nurse who keeps a consistent meal schedule
A consistent sleep and mealtime schedule helps shift workers cope.
A nurse who knows his own circadian rhythm
Knowing one’s circadian rhythm helps nurses cope with shift work.

items.q: Which teaching should the nurse give to a colleague who works rotating shifts?
items.a: Keep sleep and mealtimes as consistent as possible
items.ex: People doing shift work need to maintain as consistent a sleep and mealtime schedule as possible.
w: Vary sleep times daily to stay flexible
Varying sleep times works against the consistency shift workers need.
Skip meals on night shifts to stay alert
Shift workers should keep a consistent mealtime schedule, not skip meals.
Change shifts often to avoid boredom
Changing shifts increases fatigue and work-related stress.

alt.q: A nurse working rotating shifts reports fatigue and stress. Which factor is most likely contributing?
alt.a: Changing shifts, which increases fatigue and work stress
alt.ex: Changing shifts increases fatigue and work-related stress for nurses.
w: Keeping a regular sleep and meal schedule
A consistent sleep and meal schedule helps reduce shift-work stress.
Understanding her own circadian rhythm
Knowing one’s circadian rhythm helps nurses cope with shift work.
Working in a unit with a lower acuity level
High, not low, acuity is a workplace stressor.

items.q: A daughter caring for her father after his stroke tells the nurse she feels overwhelmed. Which statement about family caregiver stress is supported by the book?
items.a: The actions of competent health care providers often help minimize caregiver stress
items.ex: Caregiving for someone with illness is stressful, but competent health care providers often help minimize that stress.
w: Family caregivers rarely experience stress when the illness is chronic
Being a family caregiver for someone with acute or chronic illness is stressful.
Caregivers of stroke survivors use only positive coping strategies
Caregivers of stroke survivors used both negative and positive coping strategies.
Uncertainty about treatment reduces stress for most family caregivers
Uncertainty about treatment and illness triggers stress in patients and caregivers.

alt.q: Which factors trigger situational stress for patients and family caregivers adjusting to illness?
alt.a: Physical limitations of the disease and uncertainty about treatment
alt.ex: Physical limitations of a disease and uncertainty about treatment and illness trigger stress in patients and caregivers.
w: Searching for identity apart from family and peers
Identity searching is a maturational stressor of adolescence.
Changing shifts and constant distractions at work
These are workplace stressors for nurses and other providers.
Teaching impulse control and cooperative behaviors
These are developmental tasks of the initiative versus guilt stage.

items.q: As people age, they tend to become more morning oriented.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states that people tend to become more morning oriented as they age.
items.ww: Aging shifts people toward a morning orientation, which can make night work harder.

alt.q: As people age, they tend to become more evening oriented and adjust more easily to night work.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: With age, people become more morning oriented, and morning people have the most difficulty with night work.
alt.ww: The book describes a shift toward morning orientation with aging, not toward evening orientation.

items.q: Which stressor is linked to Erikson’s stage of Initiative versus guilt?
items.a: Physical appearance, families, friends, and school
items.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.
w: Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family
That goes with Industry versus inferiority.
Preoccupation with appearance and body image
That goes with Identity versus role confusion.
Children leaving home and accepting physical aging
That goes with Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation.

alt.q: Which stressor is linked to Erikson’s stage of Industry versus inferiority?
alt.a: Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family
alt.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.
w: Physical appearance, families, friends, and school
That goes with Initiative versus guilt.
Preoccupation with appearance and body image
That goes with Identity versus role confusion.
Children leaving home and accepting physical aging
That goes with Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation.

alt.q: Which stressor is linked to Erikson’s stage of Identity versus role confusion?
alt.a: Preoccupation with appearance and body image
alt.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.
w: Physical appearance, families, friends, and school
That goes with Initiative versus guilt.
Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family
That goes with Industry versus inferiority.
Children leaving home and accepting physical aging
That goes with Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation.

alt.q: Which stressor is linked to Erikson’s stage of Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation?
alt.a: Children leaving home and accepting physical aging
alt.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.
w: Physical appearance, families, friends, and school
That goes with Initiative versus guilt.
Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family
That goes with Industry versus inferiority.
Preoccupation with appearance and body image
That goes with Identity versus role confusion.

alt.q: Which stressor is linked to Erikson’s stage of Integrity versus despair?
alt.a: Loss of autonomy from frailty or health problems
alt.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.
w: Physical appearance, families, friends, and school
That goes with Initiative versus guilt.
Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family
That goes with Industry versus inferiority.
Preoccupation with appearance and body image
That goes with Identity versus role confusion.

alt.q: Which Erikson stage is linked to the stressor “Physical appearance, families, friends, and school”?
alt.a: Initiative versus guilt
alt.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.
w: Industry versus inferiority
Industry versus inferiority: Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family.
Identity versus role confusion
Identity versus role confusion: Preoccupation with appearance and body image.
Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation
Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation: Children leaving home and accepting physical aging.

alt.q: Which Erikson stage is linked to the stressor “Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family”?
alt.a: Industry versus inferiority
alt.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.
w: Initiative versus guilt
Initiative versus guilt: Physical appearance, families, friends, and school.
Identity versus role confusion
Identity versus role confusion: Preoccupation with appearance and body image.
Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation
Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation: Children leaving home and accepting physical aging.

alt.q: Which Erikson stage is linked to the stressor “Preoccupation with appearance and body image”?
alt.a: Identity versus role confusion
alt.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.
w: Initiative versus guilt
Initiative versus guilt: Physical appearance, families, friends, and school.
Industry versus inferiority
Industry versus inferiority: Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family.
Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation
Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation: Children leaving home and accepting physical aging.

alt.q: Which Erikson stage is linked to the stressor “Children leaving home and accepting physical aging”?
alt.a: Generativity versus self-absorption and stagnation
alt.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.
w: Initiative versus guilt
Initiative versus guilt: Physical appearance, families, friends, and school.
Industry versus inferiority
Industry versus inferiority: Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family.
Identity versus role confusion
Identity versus role confusion: Preoccupation with appearance and body image.

alt.q: Which Erikson stage is linked to the stressor “Loss of autonomy from frailty or health problems”?
alt.a: Integrity versus despair
alt.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.
w: Initiative versus guilt
Initiative versus guilt: Physical appearance, families, friends, and school.
Industry versus inferiority
Industry versus inferiority: Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family.
Identity versus role confusion
Identity versus role confusion: Preoccupation with appearance and body image.

mt.q: Match each of Erikson’s developmental stages with a stressor the book links to it.
pairs: Physical appearance, families, friends, and school
Self-esteem issues, hospitalization, or divorce in the family
Preoccupation with appearance and body image
Children leaving home and accepting physical aging
Loss of autonomy from frailty or health problems
mt.ex: Stressors vary with Erikson’s life stages, from appearance and school in childhood to loss of autonomy in older adulthood.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a 5-year-old in the stage of initiative versus guilt who is stressed about starting school. What is imperative for the nurse and family to teach during this stage?
items.a: Impulse control and cooperative behaviors
items.ex: During initiative versus guilt, teaching impulse control and cooperative behaviors is imperative.
w: Independent career decision making
Career choices are stressors of adolescence, not early childhood.
Acceptance of physical aging
Accepting physical aging is a middle-age stressor.
Separation from family to join peers
Separating from family to form identity occurs in adolescence.

alt.q: Preadolescents in the stage of industry versus inferiority may develop a sense of inferiority if what occurs?
alt.a: They do not receive proper support for learning new skills
alt.ex: Erikson asserts preadolescents can develop inferiority if they lack proper support for learning new skills.
w: They separate from family to join peer groups
Separating from family to join peers is expected in adolescence, not a cause of inferiority.
They are taught impulse control and cooperation
Teaching impulse control is imperative in initiative versus guilt and is not a cause of inferiority.
They question career choices and sexuality
Career and sexuality questions are stressors of adolescence.

items.q: A 16-year-old patient hospitalized after an injury is very upset about a facial scar. Which statement best explains this reaction?
items.a: Adolescents often experience stress from preoccupation with appearance and body image
items.ex: In identity versus role confusion, adolescents search for identity, and preoccupation with appearance and body image causes stress.
w: Adolescents usually experience stress mainly from the loss of autonomy
Loss of autonomy from frailty is a stressor of older adults.
Adolescents typically feel stressed mostly about children leaving home
Children leaving home is a stressor for middle-age adults.
Adolescents most often feel stressed about impulse control at school
Impulse control is emphasized in the initiative versus guilt stage of early childhood.

alt.q: Which stressors are typical for adolescents in the stage of identity versus role confusion?
alt.a: Questions about sex, jobs, school, career choices, and mind-altering substances
alt.ex: Adolescents searching for identity face stressful questions about sex, jobs, school, careers, and substance use.
w: Loss of autonomy and mastery due to frailty and illness
Loss of autonomy from frailty affects older adults in integrity versus despair.
Beginning a family and a career and losing parents
These milestones affect younger and middle-age adults.
Physical appearance, families, friends, and early school
These stressors are identified in the initiative versus guilt stage.

items.q: An 82-year-old patient becomes withdrawn and has trouble concentrating after moving to a long-term care facility. Which action by the nurse is most important when assessing these changes?
items.a: Differentiate signs of stress and crisis from dementia and acute confusion
items.ex: Nurses must differentiate stress and crisis in older adults from dementia and acute confusion.
w: Document the changes as expected signs of normal aging
Changes should be assessed, not assumed normal; stress, crisis, dementia, or confusion may be present.
Assume the patient has dementia and request a memory unit
Assuming dementia skips the needed differentiation from stress and acute confusion.
Wait several months to see whether the changes resolve
Delaying assessment could miss acute confusion, crisis, or depression.

alt.q: Which stressor is typical for older adults in Erikson’s stage of integrity versus despair?
alt.a: Loss of autonomy and mastery from frailty or health problems
alt.ex: Older adults may face loss of autonomy and mastery from frailty or problems limiting stamina, strength, and cognition.
w: Searching for identity among peer groups
Searching for identity with peers is typical of adolescence.
Beginning a family and a career
Starting a family and career are stressors of younger adulthood.
Developing impulse control and cooperation
Impulse control and cooperation are emphasized in early childhood.

items.q: According to the book, what is stress in older adults most often related to?
items.a: A loss, such as retirement, health, or a loved one
items.ex: Older adults’ stress is most often related to a loss such as retirement, health or function, or a loved one.
w: Peer pressure, such as fitting in with a group
Peer pressure and fitting in are adolescent stressors.
Career building, such as seeking promotion
Building a career is a stressor of younger adulthood.
School demands, such as tests and grades
School-related stressors are typical of children and adolescents.

alt.q: Which statement about daily hassles in older adults is accurate?
alt.a: Older adults have more hassles with home maintenance and health than younger people do
alt.ex: Ordinary daily hassles are a source of stress, and older adults have more hassles with home maintenance and health.
w: Older adults have fewer daily hassles than younger people in every area
Older adults have more hassles with home maintenance and health.
Daily hassles do not cause stress in older adults
Ordinary hassles of daily living are a source of stress for older adults.
Older adults mainly have hassles with school and career planning
School and career stressors belong to younger age-groups.

items.q: An older adult who recently lost her spouse tells the nurse, “I just feel so empty and sad all the time.” Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Ask the patient whether she has thoughts of harming herself
items.ex: Because depression is common in older adults, it is important to assess for suicidal thoughts and intent.
w: Suggest that she start gardening to keep busy
Activities such as gardening can help, but safety assessment for suicide comes first.
Recommend that she listen to relaxing music each day
Music reduces stress, but suicide risk must be assessed first.
Reassure her that sadness after a loss always passes quickly
False reassurance dismisses her feelings and skips the needed safety assessment.

alt.q: Why is it important for the nurse to assess older adults under stress for suicidal thoughts and intent?
alt.a: Older adults have a high incidence of depression
alt.ex: The high incidence of depression in older adults makes assessment for suicidal thoughts and intent important.
w: Older adults rarely use any coping strategies
Older adults use coping strategies such as prayer, music, and gardening.
Impaired coping affects older adults less than younger adults
Impaired coping affects overall health in older adults more than in younger adults.
Older adults seldom experience losses that cause stress
Older adults’ stress is most often related to loss.

items.q: Which coping strategies are older adults likely to use during periods of stress? Select all that apply.
o: Prayer and religious practices
Older adults often use prayer and religious practices to cope with stress and anxiety.
Listening to music
Music helps older adults relax and reduces stress.
Activities such as gardening
Older adults often self-manage stress through activities like gardening.
Reappraising a stressor in a positive way
Positive reappraisal is a passive, emotion-focused strategy older adults often use.
Avoiding all social relationships
Social support and relationships are important in helping older adults cope.
items.ex: Older adults often use emotion-focused coping, prayer, music, and activities such as gardening, and benefit from social support.

alt.q: Which statements about stress and coping in older adults are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They often use passive, emotion-focused forms of coping
Older adults often use passive, intrapersonal, emotion-focused coping such as distraction.
Impaired coping affects their overall health more than in younger adults
Impaired coping has a greater effect on health in older adults.
Social support helps them cope with stress
Social support and relationships are important for older adults’ coping.
They rely mainly on confronting stressors through direct action
Older adults more often use passive, emotion-focused coping.
Their stress rarely relates to loss
Older adults’ stress is most often related to loss.
alt.ex: Older adults favor emotion-focused coping, are more affected by impaired coping, and benefit from social support.

items.q: Impaired coping affects overall health in older adults more than it does in younger adults.
items.a: True
items.ex: Box 37.2 states that impaired coping affects overall health in older adults more than in younger adults.
items.ww: Older adults are more vulnerable to the health effects of impaired coping, not less.

alt.q: Impaired coping has a smaller effect on overall health in older adults than in younger adults because of their life experience.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Impaired coping affects overall health in older adults more than in younger adults.
alt.ww: Life experience does not protect older adults; impaired coping has a greater effect on their health.

items.q: Which are risk factors for social isolation and loneliness in older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Family members who live at a distance
Distant family members increase the risk for social isolation and loneliness.
Decreased income and mobility
Reduced income and mobility are risk factors.
Loss of loved ones
Losing loved ones increases the risk for isolation and loneliness.
Living in a community with low cohesiveness
Communities with lower cohesiveness increase the risk.
Frequent visits with close friends
Close, meaningful relationships promote social connectedness rather than isolation.
items.ex: Risk factors include distant family, decreased income and mobility, loss of loved ones, and low community cohesiveness.

alt.q: Social isolation and loneliness contribute to which poor health outcomes in older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Depression
Social isolation and loneliness contribute to depression.
Decreased resistance to infection
They contribute to decreased resistance to infection.
Impaired cognitive function and dementia
Impaired cognition and dementia are linked to isolation and loneliness.
Cardiovascular disease
Cardiovascular disease is among the poor outcomes listed.
Increased self-esteem and hope
Isolation and loneliness lead to low self-esteem and decreased hope.
alt.ex: Isolation and loneliness contribute to depression, lower infection resistance, impaired cognition and dementia, poor function, and cardiovascular disease.

items.q: A distressing feeling of a perceived or actual lack of close relationships, emptiness, or lack of belonging to a larger group is called [[loneliness]].
items.ex: Social isolation frequently leads to loneliness, which varies in intensity, frequency, and duration.

alt.q: Social isolation frequently leads to [[loneliness]], a distressing feeling of emptiness or of lacking close relationships and belonging.
alt.ex: Social isolation frequently leads to loneliness, which varies in intensity, frequency, and duration.

items.q: A nurse in a long-term care facility plans interventions for residents who feel isolated. Which goal best reflects the book’s guidance?
items.a: Promote social connectedness through meaningful, close relationships
items.ex: Planned interventions should promote social connectedness, a feeling of meaningful relationships, caring, and belonging.
w: Limit visitors so residents can rest without disruption
Limiting visitors would increase isolation rather than promote connectedness.
Encourage residents to spend most of their time alone
Time alone increases social isolation, a common stressor for older adults.
Focus only on physical care because loneliness is expected
Loneliness harms mental and physical health and should be addressed.

alt.q: For older adults, what is social connectedness?
alt.a: A subjective feeling of having meaningful, close relationships
alt.ex: Social connectedness is a subjective, positive feeling of meaningful and close relationships with individuals, groups, or the community.
w: An objective count of how many people live in the home
Connectedness is a subjective feeling, not a count of household members.
A distressing feeling of emptiness and lack of belonging
A distressing feeling of emptiness defines loneliness.
Limited or no social interaction with others
Limited or no interaction describes social isolation.

items.q: Which child is at increased risk for stress-related developmental problems?
items.a: A child whose parent has a substance abuse disorder
items.ex: Children are at increased risk when parents have mental illness or substance abuse disorders or when they lose caregivers.
w: A child who has stable housing and supportive caregivers
Stable housing and supportive caregivers protect against stress.
A child who is learning cooperative behaviors in preschool
Learning cooperation is an expected developmental task, not a risk factor.
A child who lives in a cohesive, safe neighborhood
Disintegrated, violent neighborhoods, not cohesive ones, increase risk.

alt.q: Which sociocultural stressors are especially stressful for young people?
alt.a: Prolonged poverty and physical disability
alt.ex: Prolonged poverty and physical disability affect any age but are especially stressful for young people.
w: Retirement and loss of function
Retirement and loss of function are stressors of older adults.
Career promotion and job change
Career changes are adult situational stressors.
Home maintenance and health hassles
These hassles are more common in older adults.

items.q: What is perceived as a major stressor in one culture may be viewed as only a minor problem in another culture.
items.a: True
items.ex: Culture defines what is stressful, so a major stressor in one culture may be minor in another.
items.ww: Because culture shapes stress perception, the same event does not carry the same weight across cultures.

alt.q: Because stress is a universal physiological response, culture has little influence on what a person perceives as stressful.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A patient’s culture defines what is stressful and the ways of coping with stress.
alt.ww: The book states culture shapes which situations produce stress and how people perceive and cope with it.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient whose cultural background differs from the nurse’s. Which action best reflects person-centered care related to stress and coping?
items.a: Assess how the patient’s culture influences the patient’s appraisal of stress
items.ex: Person-centered care includes assessing culture’s influence on appraisal and finding culturally based resources that help coping.
w: Teach the patient the coping strategies that work best for the nurse
The nurse should identify strategies within the patient’s own culture, not impose personal ones.
Assume the patient prefers to express emotions openly about the illness
Some cultures value controlling emotions; preferences must be assessed, not assumed.
Avoid asking about cultural practices to prevent any offense
Nurses should identify individualized cultural practices related to stress management.

alt.q: Which statement about culture and coping is accurate?
alt.a: Cultures vary in their use of social support as a coping strategy
alt.ex: Coping strategies are influenced by culture, including the importance and use of social support.
w: All cultures encourage open expression of emotions under stress
Some cultures stress controlling emotions, while others favor expressing them.
Culture affects what is stressful but not how people cope
Culture influences both what is stressful and the coping strategies used.
Cultures provide the same resources for coping with stress
Cultures provide different resources, such as rituals, advice givers, and support groups.

items.q: Which statement best describes compassion fatigue?
items.a: A state of burnout combined with secondary traumatic stress
items.ex: Compassion fatigue describes a state of burnout and secondary traumatic stress in health care providers.
w: A deliberate pattern of harmful behavior toward a co-worker
Deliberate harmful behavior toward a co-worker is lateral violence, a possible result of compassion fatigue.
Psychological harm after an error that injures a patient
Harm after a medical error that injures a patient is second victim syndrome.
A protective stress response that sharpens a nurse’s focus
Compassion fatigue leaves nurses unable to focus; it is not a protective response.

alt.q: A hospice nurse reports feeling burned out and distressed from repeatedly witnessing patients suffer and die. Which term describes this combined state?
alt.a: Compassion fatigue
alt.ex: Burnout plus the secondary traumatic stress of witnessing suffering is compassion fatigue.
w: Second victim syndrome
Second victim syndrome follows a medical error that significantly harms a patient.
Lateral violence
Lateral violence is harmful behavior by one employee toward another.
General adaptation syndrome
General adaptation syndrome is the body’s physiological response to any stressor.

items.q: What is secondary traumatic stress?
items.a: Stress providers feel when witnessing and caring for others who suffer
items.ex: Secondary traumatic stress arises from witnessing and caring for patients who are suffering.
w: Stress a patient feels after a second traumatic injury
The term refers to health care providers, not to a patient’s repeated injury.
Stress a provider feels after making an error that harms a patient
Distress after a harmful medical error is second victim syndrome.
Stress that occurs when perceived demands exceed perceived resources
Demands outweighing resources defines burnout, the other component of compassion fatigue.

alt.q: Which nurse’s work is the clearest example of a setting for secondary traumatic stress?
alt.a: A hospice nurse who mainly cares for patients who are dying
alt.ex: Caring mainly for dying patients exposes the nurse repeatedly to others’ suffering, the source of secondary traumatic stress.
w: A nurse educator who teaches a skills laboratory course
Teaching skills does not involve repeatedly witnessing patient suffering.
A clinic nurse who gives routine immunizations to healthy adults
Routine immunizations for healthy adults rarely involve witnessing intense suffering.
A school nurse who performs annual vision screening
Vision screening is not a setting of ongoing exposure to suffering.

items.q: Burnout occurs when perceived [[demands]] outweigh perceived resources.
items.ex: Burnout results when what is asked of the nurse seems greater than the resources available to meet it.

alt.q: Burnout occurs when perceived demands outweigh perceived [[resources]].
alt.ex: Burnout results when what is asked of the nurse seems greater than the resources available to meet it.

items.q: Which findings in a nurse suggest the emotional exhaustion of compassion fatigue? Select all that apply.
o: Irritability
Emotional exhaustion from intense caring leaves nurses irritable.
Restlessness
Restlessness is a described effect of emotional exhaustion.
Inability to focus
Exhausted nurses are often unable to focus.
Difficulty engaging with patients
Compassion fatigue leaves nurses unable to engage with patients.
Eagerness to take on additional patients
Exhausted nurses withdraw rather than seek more patient contact.
Improved concentration over long shifts
Concentration declines rather than improves with emotional exhaustion.
items.ex: Giving of oneself in intense caring environments can cause emotional exhaustion with irritability, restlessness, poor focus, and poor engagement.

alt.q: Which conditions make compassion fatigue more likely to develop? Select all that apply.
o: The nurse is unable to practice self-care
Compassion fatigue often occurs when the nurse cannot practice self-care.
Social support for the nurse is lacking
Lack of social support contributes to this failure to cope.
Organizational pressures are affecting staffing levels
Organizational pressures on staffing are a described contributing situation.
The nurse keeps a regular daily exercise routine
Regular exercise is a recommended strategy that helps protect against stress.
The unit has a supportive work environment
A supportive work environment helps identify and prevent compassion fatigue.
alt.ex: Compassion fatigue is viewed as a failure to cope when self-care, social support, and adequate staffing are lacking.

items.q: Why is compassion fatigue sometimes viewed as a failure to cope?
items.a: It often arises when self-care, social support, and staffing are inadequate
items.ex: It often occurs when the nurse cannot practice self-care, lacks social support, and faces staffing pressures.
w: It occurs only in nurses who have a prior psychiatric diagnosis
The book links it to work conditions, not to a prior psychiatric diagnosis.
It develops only after a nurse makes a serious medication error
A harmful error leads to second victim syndrome, not compassion fatigue.
It appears mainly in nurses who have little patient contact
It develops from intense caring environments with heavy patient contact.

alt.q: A nurse on a short-staffed unit has had no time for self-care and has few people to talk to. Why is this nurse at risk for compassion fatigue?
alt.a: Lack of self-care, support, and adequate staffing impairs coping
alt.ex: Compassion fatigue often occurs when self-care is impossible, support is lacking, and staffing is strained.
w: Short staffing gives the nurse too little contact with patients
Short staffing increases, rather than decreases, the demands on the nurse.
Compassion fatigue is caused mainly by a lack of clinical knowledge
The book links it to exhaustion from caring, not to a knowledge deficit.
Having few people to talk to protects the nurse’s confidentiality
Lack of social support is a risk, not a protection.

items.q: A nurse manager on a critical care unit learns that an exhausted nurse has been belittling and threatening co-workers. Which term describes this behavior?
items.a: Lateral violence
items.ex: Lateral violence is deliberate, harmful workplace behavior by one employee toward another, a negative coping behavior linked to compassion fatigue.
w: Secondary traumatic stress
Secondary traumatic stress is the stress of witnessing suffering, not a behavior toward co-workers.
Second victim syndrome
Second victim syndrome is distress after a harmful medical error.
Caregiver burden
Caregiver burden describes the strain on a person caring for an ill family member.

alt.q: Which statement defines lateral violence?
alt.a: Deliberate, harmful behavior by one employee toward another at work
alt.ex: Lateral violence refers to deliberate and harmful workplace behavior between co-workers, including bullying.
w: Aggressive behavior a patient directs toward a nurse at work
Lateral violence occurs between employees, not from patients toward staff.
Accidental harm to a patient caused by a medication error
Harm from an error is not lateral violence; it can lead to second victim syndrome.
Harsh feedback that a supervisor gives during an annual review
Lateral violence is deliberate harmful behavior, not routine performance feedback.

items.q: Feelings of fear, hopelessness, and anxiety from compassion fatigue commonly lead to feelings of inadequacy and low self-esteem.
items.a: True
items.ex: These feelings usually result in inadequacy and low self-esteem, which can lead to negative coping such as lashing out.
items.ww: The book describes inadequacy and low self-esteem as usual results, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Compassion fatigue affects a nurse’s emotional health but does not cause physical health problems.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Compassion fatigue can cause physical, mental, and emotional health issues in health care providers.
alt.ww: The book states that physical health issues can result, so the statement cannot be true.

items.q: Lateral violence can include bullying and potentially assaultive behavior between co-workers.
items.a: True
items.ex: Lateral violence includes health care providers bullying and potentially assaulting co-workers.
items.ww: Bullying and assaultive behavior between co-workers are named examples, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Lateral violence refers to aggressive behavior that a patient directs toward a nurse.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Lateral violence is deliberate harmful behavior by one employee toward another, not by a patient.
alt.ww: Patient aggression is not lateral violence, which occurs between co-workers, so the statement cannot be true.

items.q: Why did nurses experience extreme stress and compassion fatigue early in the COVID-19 pandemic?
items.a: Little was known about the virus or how to care for very ill patients
items.ex: Uncertainty about the virus and caring for extremely ill patients caused fear, anxiety, helplessness, and powerlessness.
w: Most patients had mild illness and needed little nursing care
Many patients were extremely ill and required intense care.
Staffing levels on most units were higher than usual
Organizational pressures on staffing contribute to, rather than relieve, compassion fatigue.
Nurses had complete information about treatment from the start
Little was known about the virus, which contributed to fear and helplessness.

alt.q: Which group of nurses was particularly affected by compassion fatigue during the COVID-19 pandemic?
alt.a: Critical care nurses
alt.ex: Stress and compassion fatigue were particularly high in critical care nurses caring for extremely ill patients.
w: School nurses
School nurses were not identified as the most affected group.
Nurse educators
Nurse educators were not described as the group most affected.
Outpatient clinic nurses
Outpatient nurses were not identified as the most affected group.

items.q: Which strategies help nurses manage their own mental health during stressful times such as a pandemic? Select all that apply.
o: Accessing legitimate information to stay informed
Legitimate information helps nurses stay informed during stressful times.
Talking about stressors with co-workers
Sharing stressors with co-workers is a recommended strategy.
Using social media to stay connected with family and friends
Staying connected with loved ones supports mental health.
Practicing deep breathing and relaxation exercises
Deep breathing and relaxation are recommended self-care strategies.
Stopping exercise to save energy for work
Maintaining a regular daily exercise routine is recommended.
Keeping all worries private to avoid upsetting others
Talking about stressors with co-workers is encouraged.
items.ex: Recommended strategies include legitimate information, talking with co-workers, staying connected, self-care, relaxation, and daily exercise.

alt.q: Which actions outside of work help reduce compassion fatigue? Select all that apply.
o: Strengthening friendships outside the workplace
Friendships outside work help reduce compassion fatigue.
Taking part in creative activities to recharge emotional energy
Creative activities provide personal recharging of emotional energy.
Keeping a clear separation between work and home life
A clear separation between work and home life is crucial.
Bringing unfinished charting home to complete at night
Taking work home blurs the needed separation between work and home life.
Picking up extra shifts on days off to help the unit
Extra shifts reduce time for self-care and recharging.
alt.ex: Separating work and home, friendships outside work, and creative or interesting activities when off duty help reduce compassion fatigue.

items.q: A nurse tells the charge nurse, “I’ve worked extra shifts for months. I’m irritable and I can’t focus on my patients anymore.” Which response by the charge nurse is best?
items.a: “Let’s talk about what self-care you’ve had time for and who supports you.”
items.ex: The nurse shows signs of compassion fatigue; exploring self-care and support addresses its causes.
w: “Everyone is tired right now; you just need to push through it.”
Dismissing the feelings ignores early signs that need recognition and support.
“Try not to discuss this with co-workers so the stress doesn’t spread.”
Talking about stressors with co-workers is a recommended coping strategy.
“Focus harder on your tasks so your patients don’t notice.”
Pushing harder without support worsens exhaustion and does not address the cause.

alt.q: A charge nurse notices that a colleague has become irritable, restless, and withdrawn from patients after months of short staffing. What should the charge nurse recognize?
alt.a: These are early signs of compassion fatigue that need prompt attention
alt.ex: Early recognition of compassion fatigue is essential; irritability, restlessness, and poor engagement are signs of emotional exhaustion.
w: These are normal signs that the nurse is adjusting to the unit
These are signs of emotional exhaustion, not normal adjustment.
These are signs that the nurse needs more clinical skills training
The behaviors reflect exhaustion from caring, not a skills deficit.
These are signs of second victim syndrome after a medical error
No harmful error occurred; the findings fit compassion fatigue.

items.q: Research with palliative care workers found that good self-care was linked with which outcome?
items.a: Less compassion fatigue and more compassionate patient care
items.ex: Palliative care workers who practiced good self-care had less compassion fatigue and burnout and gave more compassionate care.
w: Less compassion fatigue but more emotional distance from patients
Self-care was linked with more, not less, compassionate care.
More burnout but greater efficiency in completing tasks
Good self-care was linked with less burnout.
No change in fatigue but higher rates of staff turnover
Self-care reduced compassion fatigue rather than leaving it unchanged.

alt.q: A hospice nurse asks why the agency encourages staff self-care. Which explanation is accurate?
alt.a: Staff who practice good self-care have less fatigue and give more compassionate care
alt.ex: Good self-care among palliative care workers reduced compassion fatigue and burnout and improved compassionate care.
w: Self-care is mainly required to meet agency accreditation standards
The reason given is reduced fatigue and better care, not accreditation.
Self-care allows nurses to care for more patients during each shift
The benefit described is less fatigue and more compassionate care, not higher workload.
Self-care helps nurses avoid forming relationships with dying patients
Self-care supports, rather than prevents, compassionate relationships with patients.

items.q: How does a supportive work environment help a nursing unit address compassion fatigue?
items.a: It guides the unit in designing communication to identify, prevent, and adapt to it
items.ex: A supportive work environment helps a unit design communication techniques to identify, prevent, and adapt to compassion fatigue situations.
w: It removes the need for nurses to practice their own self-care
Self-care remains essential even in a supportive environment.
It ensures nurses never care for patients who are suffering
Caring for suffering patients is part of nursing; the aim is early recognition and support.
It replaces early recognition with formal discipline for lashing out
Early recognition of risk is essential; discipline does not address the cause.

alt.q: A nurse manager wants to address compassion fatigue on a palliative care unit. Which step reflects the book’s emphasis?
alt.a: Recognize the risk early and build communication to identify and prevent it
alt.ex: Early recognition of risk is essential, and a supportive environment helps design communication to identify and prevent compassion fatigue.
w: Wait until staff show lateral violence before taking any action
Waiting for harmful behavior misses the essential early recognition of risk.
Rotate staff off the unit only after they request a transfer
Waiting for transfer requests is not early recognition or prevention.
Limit staff discussions about difficult patient situations
Talking about stressors with co-workers is a recommended strategy.

items.q: A nurse manager wants to reduce burnout related to shift work. Which strategy is supported by evidence?
items.a: Allowing nurses to use self-scheduling
items.ex: Self-scheduling improves job satisfaction, work-life balance, health, and perceived quality of care while decreasing turnover.
w: Rotating nurses to new shifts weekly without staff input
Unpredictable schedules without input add to the stress of shift work.
Eliminating work breaks to cover staffing gaps
Work breaks are used by agencies to reduce job-related stress.
Discouraging social sharing among colleagues
Social sharing among colleagues is a relationship-building strategy that reduces burnout.

alt.q: Which outcome has been linked with nurse self-scheduling?
alt.a: Improved work-life balance and decreased nurse turnover
alt.ex: Self-scheduling has been found to improve job satisfaction and work-life balance while decreasing turnover.
w: Increased turnover and decreased job satisfaction
Self-scheduling improved satisfaction and decreased turnover.
Improved work-life balance but lower perceived quality of care
Perceived quality of care improved with self-scheduling.
No effect on job satisfaction or on nurses’ health
Job satisfaction and health both improved with self-scheduling.

items.q: Recognizing which areas you control and can change, and which you are not responsible for, is a vital insight for managing work stress.
items.a: True
items.ex: Separating what you can control from what you cannot is described as a vital insight for reducing compassion fatigue.
items.ww: The book calls this a vital insight, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: To prevent compassion fatigue, nurses should blend work and home life so they can keep processing patient situations at home.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Making a clear separation between work and home life is crucial for reducing compassion fatigue.
alt.ww: Blending work into home life removes the separation the book calls crucial, so the statement cannot be true.

items.q: An oncology nurse has been taught about compassion fatigue. Which statement by the nurse shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I’ll keep work separate from home and make time for my painting class.”
items.ex: Separating work and home and doing creative activities to recharge emotional energy help reduce compassion fatigue.
w: “I’ll pick up extra shifts so I don’t have time to dwell on things.”
Extra shifts increase demands and reduce time for self-care.
“I’ll keep my feelings to myself so I don’t burden my co-workers.”
Talking about stressors with co-workers is a recommended strategy.
“I’ll stop my daily walks so I have more energy for work.”
A regular daily exercise routine helps manage stress.
