alt.q: An oncology nurse asks how to reduce compassion fatigue. Which suggestion is most appropriate?
alt.a: Strengthen friendships outside work and take part in interesting activities off duty
alt.ex: Friendships outside work and pursuing interesting or creative activities when off duty help reduce compassion fatigue.
w: Spend days off reviewing patient charts to stay prepared for work
This blurs the separation between work and home life.
Limit contact with friends so there is more time to rest alone
Social support and friendships help reduce compassion fatigue.
Take responsibility for every outcome on the unit to stay in control
Recognizing what is outside your control is a vital insight.

items.q: A nurse is experiencing burnout from chronic work stress. Which manifestations of burnout should the nurse recognize? Select all that apply.
o: Emotional exhaustion
Burnout is manifested as emotional exhaustion.
Poor decision making
Poor decision making is a manifestation of burnout.
Loss of a sense of personal identity
Burnout includes loss of a sense of personal identity.
Feelings of failure
Feelings of failure are a manifestation of burnout.
A heightened sense of accomplishment
Burnout brings feelings of failure, not accomplishment.
Improved clinical judgment
Burnout impairs decision making rather than improving it.
items.ex: Burnout results from chronic stress and appears as emotional exhaustion, poor decision making, loss of identity, and feelings of failure.

alt.q: Which strategies do health care agencies use to manage job-related stress and reduce burnout and turnover? Select all that apply.
o: Mindfulness exercises
Agencies use mindfulness exercises to manage job-related stress.
Resilience training
Resilience training is used to reduce burnout.
Social sharing among colleagues
Staff relationship-building such as social sharing reduces burnout.
Work breaks
Work breaks help manage job-related stress.
Mandatory overtime to cover vacancies
Overtime increases demands and contributes to burnout.
Limiting staff interaction during shifts
Relationship-building among staff is encouraged.
alt.ex: Agencies use mindfulness, resilience training, social sharing, and work breaks to reduce burnout and nursing staff turnover.

items.q: Which strategy do health care agencies use to reduce nurse burnout and turnover?
items.a: Resilience training for nursing staff
items.ex: Agencies use resilience training, mindfulness, social sharing, and work breaks to manage job-related stress.
w: Mandatory overtime to cover vacancies
Mandatory overtime increases demands, which drives burnout.
Removing scheduled work breaks
Work breaks are a strategy used to reduce job-related stress.
Limiting conversations among colleagues
Social sharing among colleagues helps reduce burnout.

alt.q: A hospital starts weekly social sharing sessions among nursing colleagues. What is the purpose of this strategy?
alt.a: To build staff relationships and reduce burnout
alt.ex: Relationship-building activities such as social sharing help manage job-related stress and reduce burnout and turnover.
w: To evaluate each nurse’s clinical competence
Social sharing builds relationships; it is not a competency evaluation.
To report co-workers who show lateral violence
The purpose is relationship-building, not reporting.
To replace the need for individual self-care
Self-care remains important alongside agency strategies.

items.q: What is second victim syndrome?
items.a: Distress in a provider involved in an error that significantly harms a patient
items.ex: Second victim syndrome affects health care providers when a medical error results in significant harm to a patient and family.
w: Distress in a provider from caring for many suffering patients
Stress from witnessing suffering is secondary traumatic stress, part of compassion fatigue.
Distress in a family member caring for a chronically ill relative
Strain on a family caregiver is caregiver burden or caregiver stress.
Distress in a patient injured by a second health care provider
The second victim is the provider involved in the error, not the patient.

alt.q: A nurse gave a medication in error that seriously harmed a patient. Weeks later, the nurse has guilt, nightmares, and fear of returning to work. Which condition is the nurse most likely experiencing?
alt.a: Second victim syndrome
alt.ex: Psychological harm in a provider after a harmful medical error, with PTSD-like symptoms, is second victim syndrome.
w: Compassion fatigue
Compassion fatigue results from burnout and witnessing suffering, not a specific harmful error.
Lateral violence
Lateral violence is harmful behavior toward a co-worker.
Caregiver burden
Caregiver burden affects family members caring for an ill relative.

items.q: A nurse involved in a medical error that harmed a patient is reluctant to return to work. Which reasons for this reluctance are described? Select all that apply.
o: Fear of isolation from the organization
Nurses fear being isolated from the organization after the error.
Loss of confidence
Loss of confidence keeps nurses from returning to work.
Humiliation
Humiliation is a described reason for reluctance.
Guilt and remorse
Guilt and remorse are described responses.
Expectation of a promotion
Nothing about a harmful error leads to expected promotion.
Belief that the error caused no harm
The syndrome follows an error that caused significant harm.
items.ex: Fear of isolation, loss of confidence, remorse, depression, humiliation, and guilt make second victims reluctant to return to work.

alt.q: Which feelings are common in a nurse experiencing second victim syndrome? Select all that apply.
o: Remorse
Remorse is a common response after a harmful error.
Depression
Depression is a described response.
Humiliation
Humiliation is a described response.
Indifference to the patient’s outcome
Second victims are haunted by the error, not indifferent to it.
Increased confidence in clinical skills
Loss of confidence, not increased confidence, is described.
alt.ex: Second victims commonly experience remorse, depression, humiliation, guilt, and loss of confidence.

items.q: Second victim syndrome can lead to symptoms similar to posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD).
items.a: True
items.ex: Harmful errors can haunt nurses throughout their lives, producing symptoms similar to PTSD.
items.ww: The book describes PTSD-like symptoms, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Psychological harm from second victim syndrome is short-lived and resolves once the incident report is filed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Fatal errors can haunt nurses throughout their lives and cause complex psychological harm.
alt.ww: The harm can last a lifetime and even lead to suicide, so the statement cannot be true.

items.q: When should a health care agency begin supporting a nurse involved in an error that significantly harmed a patient?
items.a: At the moment the event occurs
items.ex: Awareness of second victim syndrome allows agencies to provide support the moment such an event occurs.
w: After the root cause analysis is completed
Waiting for an analysis delays support that should begin immediately.
Only after the nurse requests help in writing
Support should be offered at once, not only on written request.
After the patient’s family has been discharged
Support for the second victim begins when the event occurs.

alt.q: How long should a health care agency continue to support a nurse experiencing second victim syndrome?
alt.a: For as long as it is deemed necessary
alt.ex: Agencies need to provide support for as long as deemed necessary.
w: For the first 24 hours after the event
Support is not limited to a fixed short period.
Until the nurse returns to the next scheduled shift
Many second victims need support well beyond returning to work.
Until the incident report has been reviewed
Support continues as long as needed, not until paperwork is done.

items.q: A nurse who was involved in a harmful medication error says, “I can’t come back. Everyone must think I’m incompetent.” Which response by the charge nurse is best?
items.a: “You deserve support right now. Let’s talk about how you’re feeling and the help available.”
items.ex: Second victims have a right to understanding, compassion, and support from peers and the organization.
w: “Mistakes happen to everyone, so try not to think about it anymore.”
Minimizing the event ignores the complex psychological harm second victims experience.
“Right now you need to focus on the patient’s family, not on yourself.”
Patients and families are a priority, but the second victim also has a right to support.
“A long break from nursing is probably the best solution for you.”
Encouraging withdrawal adds to isolation rather than offering peer and organizational support.

alt.q: A nurse manager is developing a program for staff involved in serious medical errors. Which element should the program include?
alt.a: Peer and organizational support with understanding and compassion
alt.ex: Second victims have a right to respect, dignity, and support from peers and the organization, including understanding and compassion.
w: Immediate suspension of the nurse until all reviews are completed
Second victims are entitled to just treatment and support, not automatic punishment.
A policy that staff not discuss the event with involved nurses
Isolation is a fear of second victims; peer support is needed.
Support only for nurses whose errors caused patient death
Support is needed whenever an error causes significant harm.

items.q: Although care of the patient and family is a priority after a harmful error, the involved nurse has a right to be treated with respect and dignity.
items.a: True
items.ex: The second victim has a right to respect, dignity, and support from peers and the organization.
items.ww: The book states this right explicitly, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Because the patient and family are the priority after a harmful error, the involved nurse should not receive support until the family’s needs are resolved.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Agencies should support the second victim the moment the event occurs, alongside caring for the patient and family.
alt.ww: Support begins immediately for the second victim, so delaying it is not correct.

items.q: A nurse who was involved in an error that caused a patient’s death tells a colleague, “I don’t see the point in going on anymore.” Which action should the colleague take first?
items.a: Ask directly whether the nurse is thinking of hurting themselves
items.ex: Second victim syndrome can lead to suicide; safety comes first, so ask directly about thoughts of self-harm.
w: Suggest that the nurse take a few days off to rest
Rest does not address the immediate safety concern raised by the statement.
Reassure the nurse that the error was not really their fault
Reassurance does not assess the safety risk the statement suggests.
Encourage the nurse to review the policy that was not followed
Reviewing policy ignores the possible risk of suicide.

alt.q: Why should nursing leaders take second victim syndrome seriously?
alt.a: The psychological harm can lead to outcomes as severe as suicide
alt.ex: Often overlooked, the complex psychological harm of second victim syndrome can lead to detrimental outcomes such as suicide.
w: The syndrome mainly affects the agency’s legal liability
The concern described is harm to the nurse, including suicide.
The syndrome is rare and usually resolves within a day
It can haunt nurses throughout their lives.
The syndrome affects patients more than involved staff
The syndrome affects the health care provider involved in the error.

items.q: Which describes a potential positive outcome for a nurse after involvement in a harmful medical error?
items.a: Gaining added knowledge and skills to prevent future errors
items.ex: One outcome is that nurses move on and work on gaining knowledge and skills to prevent future errors.
w: Avoiding reporting future errors to prevent blame
Hiding errors is unsafe and is not a described positive outcome.
Leaving the profession to avoid causing further harm
Leaving nursing reflects loss of confidence, not a positive outcome.
Denying that the error ever occurred
Denial does not help the nurse learn or prevent future errors.

alt.q: A nurse involved in a harmful error enrolls in a medication safety course a few months later. How should this behavior be interpreted?
alt.a: The nurse is moving on by building skills to prevent future errors
alt.ex: Gaining additional knowledge and skills to prevent errors is one way second victims move on.
w: The nurse is showing signs of worsening second victim syndrome
Seeking knowledge is a constructive response, not a sign of worsening.
The nurse is avoiding the feelings related to the error
Learning to prevent errors is a described healthy way of moving on.
The nurse is showing lateral violence toward co-workers
Taking a course is not harmful behavior toward co-workers.

items.q: Second victim syndrome affects health care providers involved in a medical [[error]] that results in significant harm to a patient.
items.ex: The provider involved in a harmful error becomes the second victim and may need ongoing support.

alt.q: A nurse who develops guilt and PTSD-like symptoms after a harmful medical error is experiencing [[second victim syndrome|second victim]].
alt.ex: The provider involved in a harmful error becomes the second victim and may need ongoing support.

Analyze cues
That's step 2 of 6.

ord.q: Put the steps of clinical judgment (NCSBN Clinical Judgment Measurement Model) used in the stress and coping critical thinking model in order.
items: Recognize cues
Analyze cues
Prioritize hypotheses
Generate solutions
Take action
Evaluate outcomes
ord.ex: Clinical judgment moves from recognizing and analyzing cues, to prioritizing hypotheses and generating solutions, to taking action and evaluating outcomes.

items.q: A nurse learns that a patient’s usual coping skills have not helped and the patient’s support system has failed. Which approach should the nurse use?
items.a: Crisis intervention counseling
items.ex: When usual coping skills have not helped or support systems have failed, use crisis intervention counseling.
w: Watchful waiting until the patient adapts
Waiting is inappropriate when coping and support have already failed.
Written stress-management handouts only
Handouts alone do not meet the needs of a patient whose coping has failed.
Focusing only on the patient’s physical symptoms
The patient needs help with coping, not only physical care.

alt.q: Which situation indicates that the nurse should use crisis intervention counseling?
alt.a: The patient’s usual coping skills and support systems have failed
alt.ex: Crisis intervention counseling is used when usual coping skills have not helped or support systems have failed.
w: The patient reports mild stress that is relieved by daily walks
Effective coping does not call for crisis intervention.
The patient has strong family support and copes well with illness
Intact coping and support do not indicate a crisis.
The patient asks for information about a scheduled procedure
An information request is met with teaching, not crisis counseling.

items.q: Which critical thinking attitude allows the nurse to respect a patient’s perception of a stressor?
items.a: Integrity
items.ex: Integrity is an essential attitude that allows the nurse to respect a patient’s perception of the stressor.
w: Perseverance
Perseverance helps in redesigning interventions during evaluation, not in respecting perception.
Independence
Independence helps the nurse seek resources, not respect the patient’s view.
Discipline
Discipline is not the attitude the book links with respecting the patient’s perception.

alt.q: Why should a nurse convey confidence that a patient can effectively manage stress?
alt.a: Patients gain confidence from the nurse’s belief in their ability to move past the event
alt.ex: Overwhelmed patients rely on the nurse as an expert and gain confidence from the nurse’s belief in them.
w: Confidence lets the nurse skip assessing the patient’s perception
Assessment of the patient’s perception is still essential.
Confidence shows the patient that their stressor is not serious
Confidence is about the patient’s ability to cope, not dismissing the stressor.
Confidence allows the nurse to make all decisions for the patient
The aim is to build the patient’s own ability to move past the event.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to help a patient who is very stressed by a new diagnosis. According to the psychiatric mental health nursing practice standards, what should the nurse do before intervening?
items.a: Assess the patient’s stress, coping mechanisms, and support system
items.ex: Practice standards guide assessment of a patient’s stress, coping mechanisms, and support system before intervening.
w: Refer the patient to a psychiatrist for medication
Referral is not the first step; assessment comes before intervention.
Teach the patient progressive muscle relaxation
Teaching is an intervention that follows assessment.
Enroll the patient in a mindfulness program
Selecting a program is an intervention that should follow assessment.

alt.q: A nursing student wants to teach relaxation techniques to a stressed patient right away. What should the instructor remind the student to do first?
alt.a: Assess the patient’s stress, coping, and support system
alt.ex: Standards for psychiatric mental health nursing guide assessment of stress, coping, and support before intervening.
w: Begin teaching while the patient is most distressed
Assessment must come before teaching or other interventions.
Ask the family to decide which technique to use
The patient’s own perception and coping must be assessed first.
Document that the patient refused relaxation teaching
Nothing indicates refusal; assessment is the first step.

items.q: Personal experience with stress and coping increases a nurse’s ability to empathize with a patient who is temporarily immobilized by stress.
items.a: True
items.ex: Personal experiences with stress and coping increase the nurse’s ability to empathize with stressed patients.
items.ww: The book states that personal experience increases empathy, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Experience with stressed patients teaches nurses that most people respond to the same stressor in the same way.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Experience teaches the nurse to understand each patient’s unique perspective because no two people are alike.
alt.ww: Experience shows that no two people are alike, so the statement cannot be true.

items.q: Matt reads about the relationship between stress and hypertension before caring for the Edwards family. What is the purpose of this preparation?
items.a: To target interventions that help Sandra control her blood pressure
items.ex: Matt studies the stress–hypertension link so he can target interventions to keep Sandra’s blood pressure under control.
w: To change John’s chemotherapy regimen to lower stress
Chemotherapy is prescribed by the oncologist and is unrelated to Sandra’s blood pressure.
To diagnose hypertension in John before chemotherapy starts
Matt’s concern is Sandra’s blood pressure, and nurses do not make medical diagnoses.
To explain to Sandra why she should avoid all exercise
Exercise helps reduce stress and is encouraged for Sandra.

alt.q: Why does Matt research local support groups before meeting with Sandra and John?
alt.a: The couple has no local family, so social isolation is a concern
alt.ex: Because Sandra and John have no family nearby, Matt is concerned about social isolation and looks for support groups.
w: Support groups can replace John’s chemotherapy appointments
Support groups add support but do not replace medical treatment.
The couple asked to stop attending their church
The couple values church attendance, which Matt plans to honor.
Support groups are required before chemotherapy can begin
Support groups are offered for coping, not required for treatment.

items.q: Which knowledge does the nurse integrate when assessing a patient’s stress and coping? Select all that apply.
o: Neurophysiological changes in each stage of the general adaptation syndrome
Knowing changes in the alarm, resistance, and exhaustion stages is part of the knowledge base.
Communication principles that help in assessing behavior
Communication principles contribute to assessing a patient’s behaviors.
Cultural influences on the stress response
Cultural influences are part of the knowledge base for assessing stress.
Basic coping mechanisms
Basic coping mechanisms are included in the knowledge base.
The nurse’s personal opinion of the patient’s lifestyle
Assessment should be fair and unbiased, not shaped by personal opinion.
The billing codes for the patient’s mental health visits
Billing codes are not part of the knowledge used to assess stress.
items.ex: The knowledge base includes stress responses, GAS changes, coping mechanisms, cultural influences, and communication principles.

alt.q: Which attitudes support the nurse’s assessment of a patient’s stress and coping? Select all that apply.
o: Exhibiting confidence that stress can be managed
Confidence is a key attitude when assessing stress.
Collecting data fairly and without bias
Fairness and integrity ensure unbiased data collection.
Conveying that patient information remains confidential
Confidentiality is part of approaching assessment with integrity.
Skepticism toward the patient’s description of the stressor
The nurse respects the patient’s perception rather than doubting it.
Emotional detachment to avoid influencing the patient
Empathy and caring presence, not detachment, support assessment.
alt.ex: Assessment attitudes include confidence that stress can be managed, fairness and integrity, and maintaining confidentiality.

items.q: Why must a nurse be especially aware of ethical responsibility when caring for a patient under severe stress?
items.a: Stress can reduce the patient’s autonomy
items.ex: Be especially aware of ethical responsibility when caring for someone whose autonomy is reduced by stress.
w: Stress removes the patient’s legal right to consent
Stress can reduce autonomy, but it does not remove legal rights.
Stress makes patient information exempt from confidentiality
Confidentiality must be respected for all patient information.
Stress increases the patient’s ability to make decisions
Stress reduces, rather than increases, decision-making ability.

alt.q: A patient overwhelmed by a sudden loss cannot decide what to do next. Which nursing approach is most appropriate at first?
alt.a: Provide direct intervention or guidance until the patient can act on their own
alt.ex: Patients overwhelmed by life events are often initially unable to act on their own behalf and need direct intervention or guidance.
w: Wait for the patient to request help before offering guidance
Overwhelmed patients often cannot act on their own behalf at first.
Ask the patient to make all care decisions without input
The patient’s reduced capacity calls for guidance, not full independence.
Postpone any support until the patient’s stress decreases
Support is needed now, while the patient is overwhelmed.

items.q: A nurse is assessing a patient from a different cultural background who is describing stress about a diagnosis. Which action best helps the nurse understand the patient’s perception?
items.a: Use linguistically and culturally effective communication skills
items.ex: Linguistically and culturally effective communication helps the nurse understand the patient’s perception of stress clearly and precisely.
w: Interpret the patient’s nonverbal cues using the nurse’s own norms
Cultural components must be considered when interpreting nonverbal behavior.
Ask the patient’s family to describe the patient’s feelings instead
The patient’s own perception of the stressor must be assessed.
Limit the interview to closed questions to save time
Open-ended questions and sufficient time help the patient share perceptions.

alt.q: What should guide the nurse’s focus when assessing a stressed patient’s perception of the situation?
alt.a: Factors that are relevant to the patient’s well-being
alt.ex: Focus on factors relevant to the patient’s well-being while using culturally effective communication.
w: Factors that are most interesting to the health care team
The focus is the patient’s well-being, not the team’s interests.
Factors that are easiest to document in the record
Ease of documentation does not determine relevance to the patient.
Factors that match the nurse’s own past stressors
Each patient is unique; the nurse focuses on the patient’s needs.

items.q: A health care agency is creating a support program for second victims. Which components should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Just treatment
Just treatment is a component of support for second victims.
Understanding and compassion
Understanding and compassion are part of support.
Transparency
Transparency is a described component of support.
Opportunity to contribute
Second victims should have the opportunity to contribute.
Automatic suspension pending investigation
Second victims are entitled to just treatment, not automatic punishment.
Restricting peer contact with the involved nurse
Second victims should be supported by peers, not isolated.
items.ex: Support for second victims includes just treatment, understanding and compassion, supportive care, transparency, and the opportunity to contribute.

alt.q: Which actions by a nurse manager show appropriate support for a nurse who made an error that harmed a patient? Select all that apply.
o: Offering support immediately after the event
Support should be provided the moment the event occurs.
Treating the nurse with respect and dignity
Second victims have a right to respect and dignity.
Being transparent about the review process
Transparency is part of support for second victims.
Ending support once the nurse returns to work
Support continues for as long as deemed necessary.
Telling co-workers to avoid the nurse for now
Isolation is feared by second victims; peer support is needed.
alt.ex: Appropriate support begins immediately, respects the nurse’s dignity, includes transparency, and continues as long as needed.

items.q: Which statement about second victim syndrome in nurses is accurate?
items.a: It is often overlooked even though it can cause complex psychological harm
items.ex: Second victim syndrome is often overlooked, yet involved nurses can sustain complex psychological harm.
w: It is always recognized and treated by the employing agency
The syndrome is described as often overlooked.
It affects only nurses who were disciplined for an error
It affects providers involved in a harmful error regardless of discipline.
It occurs only when the error causes no harm to the patient
It follows errors that cause significant harm to a patient.

alt.q: A nurse manager believes staff involved in harmful errors recover quickly without help. Which fact should change the manager’s view?
alt.a: Second victims can sustain lasting harm and may need long-term support
alt.ex: Harmful errors can haunt nurses throughout their lives, so support is needed for as long as necessary.
w: Second victims rarely remember the details of the error
Errors can haunt nurses throughout their lives.
Second victims recover once the patient’s family forgives them
Recovery is not described as depending on forgiveness.
Second victims usually prefer to be isolated from peers
Fear of isolation is a reason nurses avoid returning to work.

items.q: Why must the nurse first establish a trusting nurse-patient relationship before assessing a patient’s stress and coping?
items.a: The patient is being asked to share personal and sensitive information
items.ex: Assessment of stress and coping requires trust first because the patient shares personal and sensitive information.
w: Trust allows the nurse to skip observing nonverbal behavior
The nurse still observes nonverbal behavior and the environment.
Trust ensures the patient will agree with every intervention
Trust supports honest sharing; it does not guarantee agreement.
Trust removes the need to ask the patient about suicide
Suicide and homicide risk must still be assessed directly.

alt.q: A patient seems hesitant to discuss what is bothering them. Which nursing action best helps the patient share what is most bothersome?
alt.a: Take time to listen within a trusting nurse-patient relationship
alt.ex: Patients often cannot express what bothers them most until someone with time to listen offers the chance.
w: Give the patient a written checklist and leave the room
A checklist without presence does not build the trust needed to share.
Tell the patient what most people find stressful in this situation
Each patient’s perception is unique and must come from the patient.
Move quickly through questions to keep the interview short
Sufficient, uninterrupted time is needed for the patient to open up.

items.q: A nurse is beginning an assessment of a patient who came to the clinic feeling overwhelmed. Which question is the best way to begin?
items.a: “What is happening in your life that caused you to come today?”
items.ex: Begin with an open-ended question that requires the patient to focus on the problem.
w: “Are you feeling stressed today?”
A yes-or-no question does not help the patient focus and describe the problem.
“Have you tried any relaxation techniques?”
Asking about interventions comes after understanding the problem.
“Do you have family who can help you?”
Situational supports are assessed after the opening question.

alt.q: Why does the nurse begin a stress assessment with an open-ended question such as “What happened in your life that is different?”
alt.a: It requires the patient to focus on the problem
alt.ex: An open-ended opening question requires the patient to focus on what is happening.
w: It lets the nurse avoid asking about suicide risk
Suicide and homicide risk must still be asked about directly.
It allows the patient to answer with a simple yes or no
Open-ended questions invite description rather than yes or no.
It replaces the need to observe nonverbal behavior
Observation of nonverbal behavior remains part of assessment.

items.q: During a stress assessment, a patient says, “I just don’t see a way out of this.” Which question should the nurse ask?
items.a: “Are you thinking of hurting yourself or someone else?”
items.ex: Determine whether a person is suicidal or homicidal by asking directly.
w: “You’re not thinking of doing anything drastic, are you?”
This leading question discourages an honest answer.
“Why would you feel that way about your situation?”
A why question can feel judgmental and does not assess safety.
“Have you told your family how you feel about this?”
Safety must be assessed directly before exploring support.

alt.q: A patient answers yes when the nurse asks directly about thoughts of self-harm. What should the nurse determine next?
alt.a: Whether the patient has a plan and how lethal it is
alt.ex: If the patient is suicidal or homicidal, determine in a caring way whether there is a plan and its lethality.
w: Whether the patient has health insurance for therapy
Safety assessment takes priority over insurance coverage.
Whether the patient has tried mindfulness exercises
Coping techniques are not the priority when self-harm is possible.
Whether the patient’s family has noticed the feelings
Assessing the plan and lethality comes first for safety.

items.q: How should the nurse arrange the setting when interviewing a patient about stress?
items.a: Chairs side by side or at a 90-degree angle, at the patient’s height
items.ex: Sitting at the same height with chairs at 90 degrees or side by side lets both maintain or avoid eye contact comfortably.
w: Chairs directly facing each other, 1 foot apart
Directly facing chairs make it hard to avoid eye contact comfortably.
The nurse standing while the patient sits at a 90-degree angle
The nurse should sit at the same height as the patient.
Chairs on opposite sides of a desk, 6 feet apart
A desk barrier and distance do not create a comfortable, nonthreatening setting.

alt.q: Why does the nurse place the chairs at a 90-degree angle or side by side during a stress assessment?
alt.a: So both can maintain or avoid eye contact comfortably
alt.ex: This arrangement allows the nurse and patient to maintain or avoid eye contact comfortably.
w: So the nurse can see the clock and limit the interview time
Sufficient, uninterrupted time should be set aside.
So the patient cannot leave the room during the interview
The arrangement is for comfort, not restraint.
So the nurse can document without the patient noticing
The purpose is comfortable eye contact, not hidden documentation.

items.q: Which assessment questions address maladaptive coping in a patient experiencing stress? Select all that apply.
o: “Have you started using alcohol or tobacco to deal with your stress?”
Alcohol and tobacco use are maladaptive coping.
“Do you use any over-the-counter or herbal medications to manage your stress?”
OTC and herbal medication use for stress is assessed as maladaptive coping.
“Do you use any street drugs to cope?”
Street drug use is a maladaptive coping behavior.
“What is relaxing for you?”
This question assesses available coping resources.
“How long ago did you see your health care provider?”
This question assesses adherence to healthy practices.
items.ex: Maladaptive coping questions ask about alcohol, tobacco, OTC or herbal medications, and street drugs.

alt.q: Which assessment questions address patient safety in a patient experiencing stress? Select all that apply.
o: “Tell me how you sleep at night.”
Sleep patterns are assessed under patient safety.
“Are you having trouble staying awake during the day?”
Daytime sleepiness is a safety concern.
“Have you had any accidents at home, in the car, or on the job?”
Accidents are assessed as a safety issue.
“Do you have any thoughts of harming yourself or others?”
Thoughts of harm are a key safety question.
“Which strategies have you used in the past to deal with stress?”
This question assesses available coping resources.
alt.ex: Safety questions cover sleep, daytime sleepiness, eating changes, accidents, and thoughts of harming self or others.

items.q: When should the nurse obtain basic vital signs during a stress and coping assessment?
items.a: Before or at the end of the interview, depending on the patient’s anxiety
items.ex: Vital signs are obtained before or after the interview, depending on anxiety level, to assess physiological signs of stress.
w: Only after the patient’s stress has fully resolved
Vital signs are needed now to detect physiological signs of stress.
During the most emotional part of the interview
Timing depends on anxiety level, before or after the interview, not mid-discussion.
Only if the patient reports chest pain or dizziness
Vital signs are a routine part of assessing physiological stress.

alt.q: Which vital sign findings indicate a physiological response to stress?
alt.a: Elevated blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate
alt.ex: Physiological signs of stress include elevated blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate.
w: Decreased blood pressure, heart rate, and respiratory rate
Stress raises, rather than lowers, these vital signs.
Decreased temperature with a slowed heart rate
A slowed heart rate is not a sign of the stress response.
Slowed respirations with low blood pressure
Stress increases respiratory rate and blood pressure.

items.q: A nurse can make an accurate nursing diagnosis of Difficulty Coping from a single finding such as poor sleep.
items.a: False
items.ex: Accurate nursing diagnoses cannot be based on just one or two findings; the nurse clusters data and validates assumptions.
items.ww: One finding is not enough to support an accurate diagnosis, so the statement cannot be true.

alt.q: Making an accurate nursing diagnosis for a stressed patient requires clustering data rather than relying on one or two findings.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Clustering data and applying knowledge and experience lead to individualized nursing diagnoses.
alt.ww: The book states that one or two findings are not enough, so the statement is not false.

items.q: Which assessment findings are major findings for the nursing diagnosis Difficulty Coping?
items.a: Verbalizing an inability to cope and an inability to ask for help
items.ex: Major assessment findings of Difficulty Coping include verbalization of an inability to cope and inability to ask for help.
w: Elevated blood glucose and weight gain over 1 month
These are physiological findings, not the major findings for Difficulty Coping.
Requests for information about a planned surgery
Seeking information is an adaptive behavior, not a major finding.
Steady sleep patterns and regular meals each day
Normal sleep and eating do not suggest ineffective coping.

alt.q: A nurse must choose interventions for two patients with Difficulty Coping, one related to chronic back pain and one related to loss of a spouse. Why does the related factor matter?
alt.a: It ensures the nurse selects interventions that fit the cause
alt.ex: Clarifying the related factor ensures appropriate interventions because different causes need different interventions.
w: It determines which patient receives care first
The related factor guides interventions, not the order of care.
It is needed only for billing the patient’s insurance
The related factor guides the choice of interventions.
It replaces the need to validate data with the patient
Validating assumptions with the patient is still required.

items.q: Which are the three primary modes of intervention for stress? Select all that apply.
o: Decreasing stress-producing situations
Decreasing stress-producing situations is a primary mode of intervention.
Increasing resistance to stress
Increasing resistance to stress is a primary mode.
Learning skills that reduce the physiological response to stress
Learning skills to reduce the physiological response is a primary mode.
Avoiding all discussion of the stressor
Discussing the stressor helps the patient understand and cope with it.
Eliminating the need for support systems
Support systems benefit patients experiencing stress.
items.ex: The three primary modes are decreasing stress-producing situations, increasing resistance to stress, and learning skills that reduce the physiological response.

alt.q: A nurse plans stress-management interventions for a patient. Which choices reflect the primary modes of intervention for stress? Select all that apply.
o: Teaching time management to reduce stress-producing situations
Prioritizing tasks decreases stress-producing situations.
Encouraging regular exercise and rest to increase resistance to stress
Exercise and rest increase resistance to stress.
Teaching progressive muscle relaxation to reduce physical tension
Relaxation skills reduce the physiological response to stress.
Advising the patient to withdraw from social contact
Social support and contact help reduce stress.
Suggesting a glass of wine at bedtime to relax
Alcohol use to manage stress is a maladaptive coping behavior.
alt.ex: Time management, exercise and rest, and relaxation skills match the three primary modes of stress intervention.

items.q: Which nursing intervention fits Primary prevention?
items.a: Identifying individuals and populations at risk for stress
items.ex: Interventions for stress are designed within the framework of primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.
w: Acting on symptoms, such as protecting the patient from self-harm
That goes with Secondary prevention.
Helping the patient readapt with relaxation and time-management training
That goes with Tertiary prevention.

alt.q: Which nursing intervention fits Secondary prevention?
alt.a: Acting on symptoms, such as protecting the patient from self-harm
alt.ex: Interventions for stress are designed within the framework of primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.
w: Identifying individuals and populations at risk for stress
That goes with Primary prevention.
Helping the patient readapt with relaxation and time-management training
That goes with Tertiary prevention.

alt.q: Which nursing intervention fits Tertiary prevention?
alt.a: Helping the patient readapt with relaxation and time-management training
alt.ex: Interventions for stress are designed within the framework of primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.
w: Identifying individuals and populations at risk for stress
That goes with Primary prevention.
Acting on symptoms, such as protecting the patient from self-harm
That goes with Secondary prevention.

alt.q: Which level of prevention is “Identifying individuals and populations at risk for stress”?
alt.a: Primary prevention
alt.ex: Interventions for stress are designed within the framework of primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.
w: Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention: Acting on symptoms, such as protecting the patient from self-harm.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention: Helping the patient readapt with relaxation and time-management training.

alt.q: Which level of prevention is “Acting on symptoms, such as protecting the patient from self-harm”?
alt.a: Secondary prevention
alt.ex: Interventions for stress are designed within the framework of primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention: Identifying individuals and populations at risk for stress.
Tertiary prevention
Tertiary prevention: Helping the patient readapt with relaxation and time-management training.

alt.q: Which level of prevention is “Helping the patient readapt with relaxation and time-management training”?
alt.a: Tertiary prevention
alt.ex: Interventions for stress are designed within the framework of primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.
w: Primary prevention
Primary prevention: Identifying individuals and populations at risk for stress.
Secondary prevention
Secondary prevention: Acting on symptoms, such as protecting the patient from self-harm.

mt.q: Match each level of prevention with the nursing intervention for stress.
pairs: Identifying individuals and populations at risk for stress
Acting on symptoms, such as protecting the patient from self-harm
Helping the patient readapt with relaxation and time-management training
mt.ex: Interventions for stress are designed within the framework of primary, secondary, and tertiary prevention.

items.q: A single parent caring for two young children and an ill parent at home is overwhelmed but denies thoughts of suicide or harming others. What should the nurse assess next?
items.a: Whether the people under the patient’s care are safe
items.ex: If suicide or homicide is not an issue, identify potential threats to the safety of people in the patient’s care.
w: Whether the patient wants to join a mindfulness class
Safety of dependents comes before teaching coping techniques.
Whether the patient’s siblings will share caregiving
Exploring family help follows ensuring dependents are safe.
Whether the patient keeps a regular exercise routine
Health practices are assessed after safety has been ensured.

alt.q: After ensuring the safety of a stressed patient and those in the patient’s care, what should the nurse do next to set priorities?
alt.a: Use problem solving with the patient to set priorities
alt.ex: After ensuring safety, use problem solving with the patient to set priorities.
w: Set the priorities alone and inform the patient later
Priorities are set with the patient, considering the patient’s perspective.
Let the family set the priorities for the patient
The patient’s own perspective guides priority setting.
Address all stressors at once to save time
Problem solving sets priorities rather than tackling everything at once.

items.q: Which mind-body therapies should the nurse familiarize a patient with when teaching stress management? Select all that apply.
o: Meditation
Meditation is a mind-body therapy listed for stress management.
Progressive muscle relaxation
Progressive muscle relaxation is a listed mind-body therapy.
Guided imagery
Guided imagery is a listed mind-body therapy.
Tai chi
Tai chi is a listed mind-body therapy.
Nightly alcohol to promote sleep
Alcohol use to cope with stress is maladaptive.
Over-the-counter sleep aids
OTC medication use for stress is assessed as maladaptive coping.
items.ex: Mind-body therapies for stress include meditation, progressive muscle relaxation, guided imagery, hypnosis, yoga, and tai chi.

alt.q: After teaching about stress management, which statements by the patient show understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “I’ll fit 15 to 30 minutes of exercise into my daily activities.”
Teaching includes adding 15 to 30 minutes of exercise daily.
“I’ll keep a journal of my thoughts and feelings.”
Journaling is a recommended relaxation technique.
“I’ll listen to music that I enjoy when I feel tense.”
Listening to enjoyable music is a recommended relaxation technique.
“Now that I meditate, I can stop taking my prescribed medicine.”
Stress-management techniques are used in addition to, not instead of, current treatment.
“I’ll fill my free time with extra chores to stay busy.”
Unnecessary activities should be replaced with pleasurable or interesting ones.
alt.ex: Teaching includes daily exercise, journaling, enjoyable music, and adding stress techniques to, not replacing, prescribed treatment.

items.q: A 48-year-old patient with hypertension wants to start a running program to reduce stress. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Please discuss your exercise plan with your health care provider before starting.”
items.ex: Patients with chronic illness or older than 35 years should begin exercise only after discussing the plan with a health care provider.
w: “Start running daily at a high intensity to get the most benefit.”
High-intensity exercise without provider review is unsafe for this patient.
“Exercise will not help stress, so focus on medication instead.”
Regular exercise reduces tension and promotes relaxation.
“You can begin right away because running lowers blood pressure.”
This patient’s age and chronic illness require provider discussion first.

alt.q: Which patient should discuss a new exercise program with a health care provider before starting it?
alt.a: A 40-year-old with no chronic illness
alt.ex: Anyone older than 35 years, at risk for illness, or with chronic illness should first discuss exercise with a provider.
w: A 22-year-old with no chronic illness or risks
This patient does not meet the age or illness criteria.
A 28-year-old who exercised regularly last year
This patient is under 35 with no stated illness or risk.
A 30-year-old with no known risk factors
This patient is under 35 with no illness or risk factors.

items.q: A patient seeks help for a crisis. When did the precipitating event most likely occur?
items.a: About 1 to 2 weeks before the patient sought help
items.ex: The precipitating event usually occurs about 1 to 2 weeks before seeking help, though sometimes within 24 hours.
w: About 2 to 3 months before the patient sought help
Crises usually resolve within about 6 weeks, so months earlier is unlikely.
About 6 to 12 months before the patient sought help
The event usually occurs about 1 to 2 weeks before help is sought.
About 1 to 2 years before the patient sought help
A crisis is a short-term state; the event is usually recent.

alt.q: Within about how long does a person generally resolve a crisis in some way?
alt.a: About 6 weeks
alt.ex: Generally, a person resolves a crisis in some way within approximately 6 weeks.
w: About 48 hours
Resolution generally takes about 6 weeks, not 2 days.
About 6 months
Crises usually resolve within about 6 weeks.
About 1 year
A crisis is generally resolved within about 6 weeks.

items.q: A nurse is using crisis intervention with a patient who says, “I have pills saved up and I plan to take them tonight.” Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Immediately implement interventions to protect the patient
items.ex: The first goal of crisis intervention is patient safety, so protective interventions are implemented immediately.
w: Teach the patient deep-breathing exercises to reduce anxiety
Anxiety reduction is the second goal; safety comes first.
Help the patient identify new ways of coping with stress
Exploring coping follows ensuring the patient is safe.
Explore the patient’s feelings of anger and guilt
Exploring feelings comes after the immediate safety risk is addressed.

alt.q: Once a patient in crisis is safe, what is the second goal of crisis intervention?
alt.a: Reducing anxiety by putting the patient’s inner resources into effect
alt.ex: The second goal of crisis intervention is anxiety reduction using techniques that activate the patient’s inner resources.
w: Exploring the patient’s childhood experiences in depth
Crisis intervention focuses only on the problem presented by the crisis.
Beginning long-term traditional psychotherapy
Crisis intervention is brief and more directive than traditional therapy.
Transferring all decision making to the family
Patients value being partners in decision making during a crisis.

items.q: Crisis intervention is more directive than traditional psychotherapy and can be used by any trained member of the health care team.
items.a: True
items.ex: Crisis intervention is a brief, directive psychotherapy that any trained team member can use.
items.ww: The book states that any trained team member can use it, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Only psychiatrists may provide crisis intervention because it is a long-term form of psychotherapy.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Crisis intervention is brief, problem-focused, and usable by any trained health care team member.
alt.ww: It is brief and any trained team member can use it, so the statement cannot be true.

items.q: [[Mindfulness]] is a moment-to-moment awareness of the present with a nonjudgmental attitude of acceptance and openness.
items.ex: Mindfulness-based stress reduction uses this awareness to reduce psychological and physical symptoms.

alt.q: Moment-to-moment, nonjudgmental awareness of the present with acceptance and openness is called [[mindfulness]].
alt.ex: Mindfulness-based stress reduction uses this awareness to reduce psychological and physical symptoms.

items.q: A patient with rheumatoid arthritis says, “Since mindfulness has helped my stress so much, I can stop my arthritis medicine.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Mindfulness is used along with your current treatment, not instead of it.”
items.ex: Reinforce that stress-management techniques are used in addition to, not instead of, the patient’s current treatment.
w: “That’s a good plan if your stress level is now under control.”
Stopping prescribed treatment is unsafe; mindfulness is an add-on.
“You can stop it as long as you meditate twice each day.”
Meditation frequency does not replace prescribed treatment.
“Mindfulness works only in the short term, so it won’t help you.”
Mindfulness helps manage symptoms and distress in chronic conditions.

alt.q: A patient cannot attend in-person mindfulness sessions because of transportation problems. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
alt.a: Suggest an online mindfulness intervention
alt.ex: Consider an online mindfulness intervention if the patient cannot attend sessions in person.
w: Tell the patient mindfulness is not an option for them
Online mindfulness interventions have been effective.
Replace mindfulness with an over-the-counter sleep aid
OTC use for stress is a maladaptive coping behavior.
Advise the patient to wait until transportation is available
An online option avoids delaying the intervention.

items.q: A patient recovering from chronic stress usually improves gradually, whereas a patient recovering from acute stress often reports feeling better once the stressor is gone.
items.a: True
items.ex: Recovery from acute stress is often spontaneous once the stressor is gone, while chronic stress resolves more gradually.
items.ww: The book contrasts quick relief in acute stress with gradual recovery in chronic stress, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Patients recovering from chronic stress typically feel better right away once the stressor is removed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Recovery from chronic stress occurs gradually as the patient emerges from the strain.
alt.ww: Quick relief describes acute stress, not chronic stress, so the statement cannot be true.

items.q: A nurse’s contact with a patient will end before the patient’s stress-related outcomes have been met. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Refer the patient to resources such as a counselor or support group
items.ex: If contact ends before outcomes are achieved, refer the patient to appropriate resources so progress is not interrupted.
w: Document that the outcomes were met to close the plan of care
Documenting unmet outcomes as met is inaccurate.
Tell the patient to return only if a new crisis develops
Waiting for a new crisis delays and interrupts progress.
Discontinue the plan because the outcomes were not realistic
Unmet outcomes call for referral, not abandoning the plan.

alt.q: During evaluation, a patient reports continued acute stress. Which action should the nurse take first?
alt.a: Assess safety by asking about recent stressors at home or at work
alt.ex: If a patient reports continued acute stress, assess for safety by asking about recent stressors at home or work.
w: Redefine the original stressor with the patient
Redefining the stressor is used for continued chronic stress.
End the plan of care because it has failed
The nurse reassesses and revises rather than ending care.
Add a new relaxation technique without reassessing
Safety assessment comes before adding interventions.

items.q: Which statement best defines the term body mechanics?
items.a: The coordinated efforts of the musculoskeletal and nervous systems
items.ex: Body mechanics describes how the musculoskeletal and nervous systems work together in a coordinated way to produce movement.
w: The positioning of joints, tendons, ligaments, and muscles at rest
This describes body alignment, or posture, not body mechanics.
The force exerted on a body by the pull of gravity
This is the definition of weight, not body mechanics.
The ability to maintain a static position such as sitting
This describes balance, not the coordinated system effort called body mechanics.

alt.q: A nurse explains that body mechanics involves the coordinated efforts of two body systems. Which systems are they?
alt.a: Musculoskeletal and nervous systems
alt.ex: Movement is a complex process requiring coordination between the musculoskeletal and nervous systems, which is what body mechanics describes.
w: Cardiovascular and respiratory systems
These systems supply oxygen for activity but are not the systems body mechanics describes.
Integumentary and lymphatic systems
Skin and lymph tissue do not coordinate to produce body movement.
Endocrine and renal systems
Hormonal and kidney function do not make up the coordinated effort of body mechanics.

items.q: Why are the musculoskeletal and nervous systems often considered a single functional unit?
items.a: They work together dynamically to produce coordinated body movement
items.ex: Coordinated movement integrates musculoskeletal and nervous system function so closely that they are viewed as one unit.
w: They develop from the same tissue and share one blood supply
The text bases the single-unit view on how the systems work together, not on shared origin.
The nervous system can produce movement without the muscles
Nerves initiate and coordinate movement but cannot move the body without muscles and bones.
The skeleton directs movement while nerves only supply nutrients
Nerves control and coordinate movement; they do not merely nourish tissue.

alt.q: A student asks why movement is described as a complex process. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: It requires coordination between the musculoskeletal and nervous systems
alt.ex: Movement depends on the dynamic integration of the musculoskeletal and nervous systems, which is why it is complex.
w: It depends mainly on the strength of the large leg muscles
Strong muscles matter, but movement requires nervous system coordination as well.
It is controlled entirely by voluntary conscious thought
Much of movement, such as walking patterns, is learned and coordinated automatically.
It occurs only when the cardiovascular system is conditioned
Conditioning affects endurance, not the basic coordination that makes movement possible.

items.q: Using only the principles of body mechanics when lifting patients is enough to protect nurses from injury.
items.a: False
items.ex: Because a person’s center of gravity shifts during movement, relying only on body mechanics when lifting patients often injures staff.
items.ww: Historical body mechanics lifting techniques often caused debilitating musculoskeletal injuries to nurses and other staff.

alt.q: The body mechanics applied in historical nursing lifting techniques often caused debilitating musculoskeletal injuries to nurses.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Traditional lifting based on body mechanics alone caused many disabling musculoskeletal injuries, leading to evidence-based safe handling methods.
alt.ww: Body mechanics alone does not account for a patient’s shifting center of gravity, so staff injuries were common.

items.q: Nurses apply evidence-based information about alignment, balance, gravity, and friction in which nursing activities? Select all that apply.
o: Transferring patients
Knowledge of movement physics guides safe transfer of patients.
Assisting patients with ambulation
Alignment, balance, and gravity affect how nurses support patients who walk.
Determining a patient’s risk of falls
Balance and center of gravity are central to judging fall risk.
Selecting the safest way to move a patient
Friction and gravity knowledge help the nurse choose devices and methods for moving patients.
Calculating a patient’s medication dosage
Dosage calculation does not rely on the physics of body movement.
items.ex: Nurses use evidence about alignment, balance, gravity, and friction when transferring, ambulating, assessing fall risk, and choosing how to move patients.

alt.q: Which nursing decisions draw directly on an understanding of the physics of movement? Select all that apply.
o: Choosing a friction-reducing device to move a patient up in bed
Friction knowledge guides selection of devices that reduce resistance and skin damage.
Deciding how to support a patient who is walking
Ambulation assistance depends on balance and center of gravity.
Identifying that a patient is at risk for falling
Falls occur when the center of gravity becomes unbalanced.
Selecting the size of a blood pressure cuff
Cuff sizing depends on arm circumference, not movement physics.
Planning a low-sodium diet for heart failure
Diet planning does not rely on alignment, balance, gravity, or friction.
alt.ex: Movement physics guides friction-reducing device choice, ambulation support, fall risk assessment, and safe patient moves.

items.q: Which patient-handling tasks are identified as high risk for injury to health care workers? Select all that apply.
o: Transferring a patient from toilet to chair
Toilet-to-chair transfers are listed as high-risk handling tasks.
Repositioning a patient from side to side in bed
Side-to-side repositioning in bed is a high-risk task.
Making a bed with a patient in it
Making an occupied bed is listed among high-risk handling tasks.
Repositioning a patient in a chair
Repositioning a patient in a chair places strain on the caregiver.
Handing a patient a cup of water at the bedside
This task does not involve moving or supporting a patient’s weight.
Documenting a patient’s activity tolerance
Documentation involves no patient handling.
items.ex: High-risk tasks include toilet-to-chair, chair-to-bed, and bathtub-to-chair transfers; repositioning in bed or chair; lifting in bed; and making an occupied bed.

alt.q: A unit manager reviews tasks that most often injure staff. Which tasks belong on the high-risk list? Select all that apply.
o: Transferring a patient from chair to bed
Chair-to-bed transfers are high-risk patient-handling tasks.
Transferring a patient from bathtub to chair
Bathtub-to-chair transfers are listed as high risk.
Lifting a patient in bed
Lifting a patient in bed is a high-risk task for injury.
Reading a patient’s chart before a transfer
Reviewing the chart involves no physical handling.
Explaining a procedure to a seated patient
Patient teaching does not place a physical load on the caregiver.
alt.ex: Transfers between chair, bed, toilet, and bathtub and lifting or repositioning a patient in bed are high-risk handling tasks.

items.q: A nursing student asks, “Why do I need to understand physics to give patient care?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “It helps you understand how patients initiate movement and how to move safely yourself.”
items.ex: A basic grasp of the physics of body mechanics helps nurses understand patients’ movements and their own.
w: “It is needed mainly to calculate how much weight you can lift alone.”
Manual lifting is a last resort; physics knowledge is not used to justify solo lifting.
“It is only needed by physical therapists who plan exercise programs.”
Nurses use movement physics daily for transfers, ambulation, and fall risk.
“It lets you rely on body mechanics instead of using lift equipment.”
Body mechanics alone often injures staff; physics knowledge supports using devices.

alt.q: Which statement by a new nurse shows understanding of why knowledge of body mechanics physics matters in practice?
alt.a: “It helps me understand how patients start to move and how I move.”
alt.ex: Knowing how patients initiate movement and understanding your own movements requires a basic grasp of movement physics.
w: “It means I will no longer need to use mechanical lifts.”
Physics knowledge supports, rather than replaces, safe patient-handling equipment.
“It matters only when I care for patients with fractures.”
Movement physics applies to transfers, ambulation, and fall risk for all patients.
“It tells me exactly how much weight I can safely carry.”
The text does not use physics to set a safe solo lifting weight.

items.q: A nurse must transfer a patient who cannot bear weight from the bed to a chair. Which approach best reflects current evidence-based practice?
items.a: Assess the patient and use a mechanical lift with enough staff
items.ex: Today nurses use SPHM assessment, lifts, and assistive devices instead of relying on body mechanics alone to move patients.
w: Lift the patient manually using a wide base of support
Good body mechanics alone often leads to injury; manual lifting is a last resort.
Ask one colleague to help lift the patient by the arms
Manual lifting of a dependent patient strains staff and can injure the patient.
Have the patient pull up on the nurse’s neck to stand
A non–weight-bearing patient cannot stand, and pulling on the nurse risks injury to both.

alt.q: Which practice reflects the current evidence-based approach to moving dependent patients?
alt.a: Selecting transfer equipment and staffing based on patient assessment
alt.ex: SPHM uses assessment tools and algorithms to choose the right equipment and number of staff for each task.
w: Relying on correct body mechanics for all manual lifts
Body mechanics alone has historically caused debilitating staff injuries.
Lifting most of a patient’s weight with a team of two
Manual lifting should not involve lifting most or all of the patient’s weight.
Avoiding lift equipment to keep transfers quick
Lift equipment reduces injury; speed does not justify unsafe manual lifting.

items.q: What is the goal of the American Nurses Association’s safe patient-handling programs and nurse advocacy?
items.a: Complete elimination of manual patient handling
items.ex: The ANA is developing programs and advocacy aimed at safe environments with the complete elimination of manual patient handling.
w: Training all nurses to lift patients with correct posture
Good posture alone does not prevent injury; the goal is to remove manual handling.
Limiting each nurse to lifting a set number of patients daily
The goal is elimination of manual handling, not a daily lifting quota.
Assigning all transfers to physical therapy staff
The goal is safer methods for everyone, not shifting tasks to another discipline.

alt.q: The goal of eliminating all manual patient handling is associated with which organization’s programs and advocacy?
alt.a: American Nurses Association
alt.ex: The ANA promotes safe environments for nurses with the goal of completely eliminating manual patient handling.
w: American Physical Therapy Association
The text attributes this goal to the nursing professional organization, the ANA.
American Hospital Association
The text links the elimination goal to the ANA, not a hospital association.
American Heart Association
The heart association focuses on cardiovascular health, not patient-handling policy.

items.q: [[Body mechanics]] is a term that describes the coordinated efforts of the musculoskeletal and nervous systems.
items.ex: Body mechanics refers to how the musculoskeletal and nervous systems coordinate to produce movement.

alt.q: The coordinated effort of the musculoskeletal and nervous systems during movement is called [[body mechanics]].
alt.ex: Body mechanics refers to how the musculoskeletal and nervous systems coordinate to produce movement.

items.q: A colleague says, “I have always used good body mechanics, so I don’t need the lift for this patient.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Body mechanics alone doesn’t protect us, because a person’s center of gravity shifts.”
items.ex: A person’s center of gravity shifts during movement, so using only body mechanics to lift patients often injures staff.
w: “That’s fine as long as you bend your knees and keep your back straight.”
Correct posture does not make manual lifting of a patient safe.
“You’re right, lifts are only required for patients over 100 kg.”
SPHM bases equipment choice on assessment, not a single weight cutoff.
“Let’s lift together so that each of us carries half the weight.”
Manual lifting should not involve lifting most or all of the patient’s weight.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows understanding of why traditional lifting techniques injure staff?
alt.a: “A patient’s center of gravity moves, so body mechanics alone can’t keep me safe.”
alt.ex: Because people’s centers of gravity shift during movement, body mechanics alone often leads to injury.
w: “Injuries happen only when nurses forget to bend their knees.”
Even correct technique fails because patients are not stable, symmetrical loads.
“Patients are symmetrical, so their weight is easy to predict.”
People are not geometrically perfect, and their centers of gravity shift.
“Lifting is safe if I keep my feet together for control.”
A narrow base reduces stability, and manual lifting remains high risk.

items.q: Which injuries do health care workers frequently experience when they move or lift patients incorrectly?
items.a: Back injuries and overexertion
items.ex: Incorrect moving and lifting of patients commonly causes back injuries and overexertion in health care workers.
w: Needlestick injuries and blood exposure
These are sharps hazards, not injuries from moving or lifting patients.
Chemical burns and skin irritation
These relate to chemical exposure, not patient handling.
Hearing loss and eye strain
These are not the injuries associated with lifting and moving patients.

alt.q: A nurse who lifts patients without assistive devices is at greatest risk for which type of work-related injury?
alt.a: Musculoskeletal back injury
alt.ex: Manual lifting and transferring contributes to a high incidence of work-related musculoskeletal problems and back injuries.
w: Latex allergy
Latex allergy results from glove exposure, not from lifting patients.
Respiratory infection
Infection exposure is not the hazard of manual patient lifting.
Radiation exposure
Radiation is an imaging hazard, not a patient-handling hazard.

items.q: Which conditions during patient-handling tasks increase the risk of musculoskeletal injury to nurses? Select all that apply.
o: Lifting with the arms extended
Lifting with extended arms increases strain on the caregiver’s back.
Lifting when near the floor
Lifting near the floor is a recognized hazard in patient care.
Lifting with the trunk twisted
Twisting the trunk increases the risk of injury.
Lifting with one hand in a restricted space
One-handed lifting or working in a tight space increases injury risk.
Keeping the load close to the body
Keeping the load close reduces horizontal reach and back stress.
items.ex: Lifting with extended arms, near the floor, while sitting or kneeling, with a twisted trunk, or one-handed in a tight space raises injury risk.

alt.q: A nurse observes colleagues during patient care. Which actions place them at increased risk for injury? Select all that apply.
o: Lifting a patient’s legs while kneeling beside the bed
Lifting while kneeling or sitting is a hazardous posture.
Holding the load off to the side of the body
An off-center load increases strain on the back.
Pulling a patient up in bed without a device
Pulling or pushing during care contributes to injury.
Tightening the abdominal muscles before moving a load
Tightening the abdominal muscles reduces risk of injury to the lumbar spine.
Using a ceiling-mounted lift to transfer a patient
Lifts reduce muscular strain on the caregiver.
alt.ex: Kneeling, off-center loads, and pulling or pushing without devices raise injury risk; abdominal bracing and lifts reduce it.

items.q: The health care industry has one of the highest rates of work-related injuries and illnesses.
items.a: True
items.ex: Moving and lifting patients exposes health care workers to frequent injuries, making health care a high-injury industry.
items.ww: Health care work-related injury and illness rates are high and continue to rise, not low.

alt.q: Because of modern equipment, nursing is now considered a low-risk occupation for work-related injury.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Health care has one of the highest rates of work-related injuries and illnesses, and the rate continues to rise.
alt.ww: Equipment is not used consistently, and patient handling still causes many staff injuries.

items.q: A nurse prepares to help a patient with an intravenous line and an indwelling catheter move from bed to chair. Which action should the nurse take before beginning the transfer?
items.a: Arrange the tubing and lines so they will not interfere with the move
items.ex: Tubes and devices tether patients and complicate moves, so equipment is arranged before the transfer begins.
w: Clamp and disconnect the intravenous line for the transfer
Disconnecting lines is not required; they are arranged so they do not interfere.
Ask the patient to hold the catheter bag on the abdomen
Raising the drainage bag is unsafe and does not keep lines clear during the move.
Begin the transfer and adjust the lines if they pull
Equipment should be arranged before moving, not after it pulls.

alt.q: Why does a nurse arrange intravenous lines, feeding tubes, and catheters before transferring a patient?
alt.a: Devices that tether a patient complicate the move and can interfere with the transfer
alt.ex: Tubes that tether patients add physical effort and hazards, so they are arranged to stay out of the way.
w: Lines must be removed before any patient leaves the bed
Lines are arranged, not removed, for a transfer.
Arranging lines replaces the need for transfer equipment
Line management does not reduce the need for SPHM devices.
Tubing makes the patient lighter and easier to lift
Tubing adds complexity; it does not change the patient’s weight.

items.q: Why does a nurse need a knowledge base about the anatomy, physiology, and regulation of body movement?
items.a: To understand how a patient’s health condition affects activity
items.ex: This knowledge helps the nurse understand the impact of a health condition on activity and make sound clinical decisions.
w: To diagnose musculoskeletal disorders independently
Nurses use this knowledge for clinical judgment about activity, not medical diagnosis.
To prescribe the patient’s physical therapy program
Prescribing therapy is not the purpose the text gives for this knowledge.
To calculate the exact weight a nurse may lift alone
The text does not define a safe solo lifting weight from this knowledge.

alt.q: Knowledge of the anatomy and regulation of movement is essential to which nursing function?
alt.a: Making clinical judgments to select activity and exercise interventions
alt.ex: Understanding movement lets the nurse recognize patient problems and select appropriate activity and exercise interventions.
w: Writing medical orders for activity restrictions
Activity orders are not written by nurses based on this knowledge.
Determining the patient’s insurance coverage for therapy
Insurance decisions are unrelated to movement physiology.
Performing surgical repair of injured joints
Surgery is outside the nursing role.

items.q: According to the guidelines for preventing lift injuries, when should a nurse perform manual lifting?
items.a: As a last resort and only when it does not involve lifting most of the patient’s weight
items.ex: Lifting is a high-risk activity, so manual lifting is reserved as a last resort that does not involve most or all of the weight.
w: Whenever the patient weighs less than the nurse does
Patient weight relative to the nurse does not make manual lifting safe.
Whenever two nurses are available to share the patient’s full weight
Manual lifting should not involve lifting most or all of the patient’s weight.
As the first choice when the patient can bear partial weight
Manual lifting is never the first choice; equipment and patient help come first.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows correct understanding of manual lifting?
alt.a: “I lift by hand only as a last resort, and never most of the patient’s weight.”
alt.ex: Manual lifting is performed only as a last resort and only if it does not involve lifting most or all of the patient’s weight.
w: “Manual lifting is safe if I keep my back straight the whole time.”
Good posture does not remove the high biomechanical stress of lifting a patient.
“I lift manually first and use equipment if the patient is heavy.”
Equipment comes first; manual lifting is the last resort.
“Two of us can lift the patient’s full weight if we count to three.”
Lifting most or all of a patient’s weight manually should be avoided.

items.q: Which statement best describes safe patient handling and mobility (SPHM) techniques?
items.a: Standardized methods for handling and moving patients based on individual patient characteristics
items.ex: SPHM techniques are standardized methods for deciding how to handle, move, and mobilize patients according to their characteristics and conditions.
w: Lifting methods that rely only on the nurse’s correct posture and strength
Posture and strength alone are the older approach that caused injuries.
Rules that restrict patients to bed until they can walk independently
SPHM supports safe mobility; it does not restrict patients to bed.
Exercise routines that build the nurse’s back and leg muscle strength
SPHM concerns handling methods and equipment, not staff exercise programs.

alt.q: A nurse uses a standardized assessment of a patient’s condition and characteristics to decide how to move the patient. Which approach is the nurse using?
alt.a: Safe patient handling and mobility
alt.ex: SPHM uses standardized methods based on patient characteristics and conditions to determine how to handle and move patients.
w: Traditional body mechanics
Traditional body mechanics relies on lifting technique, not standardized patient assessment.
Progressive resistance training
Resistance training is an exercise method, not a patient-handling approach.
Range-of-motion exercise
ROM exercise moves joints; it does not determine how to transfer patients.

items.q: Safe patient handling and mobility techniques benefit health care staff but do not change patient outcomes.
items.a: False
items.ex: SPHM techniques also improve patient outcomes, including fewer pressure injuries and falls and fewer immobility complications.
items.ww: The text lists reduced pressure injuries, falls, and immobility complications as patient benefits of SPHM.

alt.q: Using SPHM techniques reduces pressure injuries and falls in patients as well as injuries to staff.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Besides protecting staff, SPHM improves patient outcomes such as fewer pressure injuries, falls, and immobility complications.
alt.ww: SPHM benefits are not limited to staff; patients also have fewer pressure injuries and falls.

items.q: A nurse manager finds that staff trained in lift use still lift patients manually. Which factor has research identified as limiting staff use of lift equipment?
items.a: Equipment that is not functioning properly or is hard to retrieve
items.ex: Lift use is often limited by availability of help, equipment function, and supplies that are unavailable or hard to retrieve.
w: Patients consistently refusing to be moved by a lift
Patient refusal is not among the factors the text identifies.
Lift equipment causing more staff injuries than manual lifting
SPHM equipment reduces, rather than increases, staff injuries.
Regulations that prohibit lifts in patient rooms
