alt.q: Which situation commonly leads nurses to skip available lift equipment despite training?
alt.a: The lift’s slings or supplies are stored far away and are hard to get
alt.ex: Research shows staff use of lifts is limited when equipment, supplies, or helpers are not readily available.
w: The patient’s health care provider has ordered the lift
An order supports, rather than limits, use of a lift.
The unit has a peer leader who trains staff on lifts
Peer leaders improve equipment competency and use.
The patient room has a ceiling-mounted lift installed
Ceiling lifts in rooms make equipment more available.

items.q: Which description best defines body alignment?
items.a: Positioning of the joints, tendons, ligaments, and muscles while standing, sitting, and lying
items.ex: Body alignment, or posture, refers to how joints, tendons, ligaments, and muscles are positioned in standing, sitting, and lying.
w: Coordination between the musculoskeletal and nervous systems during movement
This describes body mechanics, not body alignment.
The force that opposes movement when an object slides across a surface
This describes friction, not body alignment.
The pull of gravity on the body that is always directed downward
This describes weight, not body alignment.

alt.q: Which term refers to the positioning of the joints, tendons, ligaments, and muscles while standing, sitting, and lying?
alt.a: Body alignment
alt.ex: Body alignment, also called posture, is the positioning of joints, tendons, ligaments, and muscles in any position.
w: Body mechanics
Body mechanics is the coordinated effort of the musculoskeletal and nervous systems.
Proprioception
Proprioception is awareness of body position, not the positioning itself.
Muscle tone
Muscle tone is the normal state of balanced muscle tension.

items.q: Which are benefits of correct body alignment? Select all that apply.
o: Reduces strain on musculoskeletal structures
Correct alignment lessens strain on muscles, ligaments, and bones.
Maintains adequate muscle tone
Proper alignment helps maintain adequate muscle tone.
Promotes comfort
Correct alignment promotes patient comfort.
Contributes to conservation of energy
Proper alignment contributes to balance and energy conservation.
Increases the muscular work needed to stay upright
Optimal posture requires the least muscular work, not more.
Moves the center of gravity outside the base of support
Correct alignment keeps the center of gravity stable over the base of support.
items.ex: Correct alignment reduces musculoskeletal strain, maintains muscle tone, promotes comfort, and contributes to balance and energy conservation.

alt.q: A nurse repositions a bedbound patient into correct body alignment. Which outcomes does this support? Select all that apply.
o: Greater comfort
Correct alignment promotes comfort.
Less strain on muscles and ligaments
Alignment reduces strain on musculoskeletal structures.
A stable center of gravity
Body alignment means the center of gravity is stable.
Loss of muscle tone from reduced tension
Correct alignment maintains adequate muscle tone rather than reducing it.
Higher energy use to hold the position
Proper alignment conserves energy and needs the least muscular work.
alt.ex: Proper alignment promotes comfort, reduces musculoskeletal strain, keeps the center of gravity stable, and preserves muscle tone and energy.

items.q: When a person’s body is in proper alignment, the center of gravity is stable.
items.a: True
items.ex: Body alignment means that an individual’s center of gravity is stable.
items.ww: Proper alignment stabilizes the center of gravity; it does not make it unstable.

alt.q: When a person loses balance control, the center of gravity stays in its normal position.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Without balance control, the center of gravity is displaced, which can lead to a fall.
alt.ww: Loss of balance control displaces the center of gravity rather than keeping it in place.

items.q: Under which conditions does body balance occur?
items.a: Proper alignment with a relatively low center of gravity over a wide, stable base of support
items.ex: Body balance occurs when a properly aligned person has a relatively low center of gravity balanced over a wide, stable base of support.
w: Proper alignment with a high center of gravity over a narrow base of support
A high center of gravity over a narrow base reduces stability.
Rigid posture with a low center of gravity over a narrow base of support
A narrow base decreases stability, and rigid posture is not the goal.
Forward lean with a high center of gravity over a wide base of support
Leaning and a high center of gravity shift weight away from the base.

alt.q: A nurse wants to be most stable while helping a patient. Which combination provides the greatest balance?
alt.a: A low center of gravity over a wide base of support
alt.ex: Balance is greatest when a relatively low center of gravity is centered over a wide, stable base of support.
w: A high center of gravity over a wide base of support
Raising the center of gravity reduces stability even with a wide base.
A low center of gravity over a narrow base of support
A narrow base of support decreases stability.
A high center of gravity over a narrow base of support
This is the least stable combination.

items.q: When a person is standing in balance, where does a vertical line from the center of gravity fall?
items.a: Through the base of support
items.ex: In standing balance, a vertical line falls from the center of gravity through the base of support.
w: In front of the toes
A line falling outside the base of support means the person is unbalanced.
Behind the heels
A line behind the base of support indicates the body is falling backward.
To the side of one foot
A line outside the base of support means the center of gravity is displaced.

alt.q: A patient leans so far forward that a line from the center of gravity falls in front of the feet. What does the nurse conclude?
alt.a: The patient is unbalanced and at risk of falling
alt.ex: Balance requires the line from the center of gravity to fall through the base of support; outside it, the patient may fall.
w: The patient is balanced because both feet are on the floor
Both feet on the floor do not ensure balance if the line falls outside the base.
The patient has a lower center of gravity than normal
Leaning forward displaces the center of gravity; it does not make it lower.
The patient has widened the base of support
Leaning forward does not widen the base of support.

items.q: Through which structures does the nervous system control balance? Select all that apply.
o: Inner ear
Mechanoreceptors in the inner ear’s vestibule and semicircular canals sense balance.
Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates and stores learned patterns of movement.
Vision
Visual input gives feedback about whether you or the environment is moving.
Thyroid gland
The thyroid regulates metabolism, not balance.
Spleen
The spleen filters blood and has no role in balance.
items.ex: The nervous system controls balance through the inner ear, the cerebellum, and vision.

alt.q: A patient has an inner ear disorder and poor eyesight. Which systems involved in balance may be affected? Select all that apply.
o: Vestibular sense organs in the semicircular canals
Inner ear disorders can affect these balance receptors.
Visual feedback about movement
Poor vision reduces feedback about whether the person or environment is moving.
Dynamic equilibrium during head rotation
The ears and eyes together maintain balance during rotation or sudden movement.
Kidney regulation of fluid balance
Renal fluid balance is unrelated to physical balance control.
Pancreatic insulin release
Insulin release does not control balance.
alt.ex: The inner ear and eyes work together in dynamic equilibrium, so disorders of either impair balance.

items.q: Where in the ear are the sense organs for balance located?
items.a: Vestibule and semicircular canals
items.ex: Specialized hair cells in the vestibule and semicircular canals create impulses the brain perceives as sound or balance.
w: Tympanic membrane and ear canal
The eardrum and canal conduct sound; they do not hold balance receptors.
Auricle and earlobe
The external ear collects sound and does not sense balance.
Eustachian tube and middle ear bones
These structures equalize pressure and conduct sound, not sense balance.

alt.q: Mechanoreceptors in the vestibule and semicircular canals of the inner ear produce impulses perceived as which sensations?
alt.a: Sound or balance
alt.ex: Hair cells in the inner ear are stimulated to create nerve impulses the brain perceives as either sound or balance.
w: Pain or temperature
Pain and temperature are sensed by skin and tissue receptors.
Taste or smell
Taste and smell are sensed in the mouth and nose.
Touch or pressure
Touch and pressure are sensed by receptors in the skin.

items.q: A nurse notes that an older adult walks with small steps and keeps the feet close together. Which interpretation is correct?
items.a: The narrow stance decreases the base of support and alters balance
items.ex: Older adults often take smaller steps with feet closer together, which decreases the base of support and alters balance.
w: The narrow stance widens the base of support and improves balance
Keeping feet close together narrows, not widens, the base of support.
The narrow stance lowers the center of gravity and prevents falls
Foot position does not lower the center of gravity; it reduces stability.
The narrow stance is a normal pattern that does not affect balance
This gait pattern decreases the base of support and alters balance.

alt.q: Which change in an older adult’s gait decreases the base of support and alters balance?
alt.a: Taking smaller steps with the feet closer together
alt.ex: Smaller steps with the feet close together narrow the base of support and alter body balance.
w: Taking longer steps with the feet farther apart
A wider stance increases, not decreases, the base of support.
Walking with the knees slightly bent and feet apart
Bending the knees with feet apart improves stability.
Standing with feet separated a comfortable distance
Separating the feet widens the base of support.

items.q: A nurse prepares to change a dressing on a patient in a low hospital bed. Which action best protects the nurse’s balance and alignment?
items.a: Raise the bed to a comfortable working height
items.ex: Raising the bed prevents bending too far at the waist and shifting the base of support during a procedure.
w: Bend at the waist with the knees locked
Bending far at the waist shifts the base of support and strains the back.
Kneel on the floor beside the bed
Working near the floor while kneeling is a recognized injury hazard.
Stand with the feet close together
A narrow stance decreases the base of support and stability.

alt.q: Why does a nurse raise the height of the hospital bed before performing a procedure such as a dressing change?
alt.a: To prevent bending too far at the waist and shifting the base of support
alt.ex: A raised bed keeps the nurse from bending at the waist, protecting balance and alignment.
w: To make it easier for the patient to get out of bed afterward
A raised bed is lowered for patient exit; height is raised for the nurse’s work.
To increase friction between the patient and the sheets
Bed height does not change friction against the sheets.
To raise the patient’s center of gravity above the nurse’s
The purpose is the nurse’s posture, not the patient’s center of gravity.

items.q: A nurse prepares to lift a heavy object from the floor. Which action increases the nurse's stability?
items.a: Separating the feet a comfortable distance to widen the base of support
items.ex: A wider base of support, a center of gravity brought closer to that base, and bending the knees with an erect trunk all increase stability.
w: Keeping the feet close together to stay steady
Feet close together narrow the base of support and reduce stability.
Bending at the waist with the knees straight
Bending at the waist strains the back; the knees and hips are flexed with the trunk erect.
Holding the object at arm's length from the body
Holding objects away from the body moves the center of gravity away from the base.

alt.q: Why does a nurse bend the knees and flex the hips with the trunk erect when lifting?
alt.a: It lowers the center of gravity toward the base of support
alt.ex: Squatting with an erect trunk brings the center of gravity closer to the base of support, improving balance and protecting the back.
w: It narrows the base of support for better control
Stability comes from a wider, not narrower, base of support.
It moves the line of gravity outside the base of support
Balance requires the line of gravity to stay within the base of support.
It lets the back muscles do most of the work
Correct body mechanics spare the back by using the legs.

items.q: Which statement best describes optimal posture?
items.a: It favors function, requires the least muscular work, and places the least strain on tissues
items.ex: Posture means maintaining optimal alignment that favors function with the least muscular work and least strain on muscles, ligaments, and bones.
w: It holds the body rigid so the muscles stay tense and ready to move
Rigid, tense positioning increases muscular work and is not the goal.
It shifts the center of gravity forward to prepare for walking
Optimal posture keeps the center of gravity stable over the base of support.
It requires constant muscular effort to keep joints locked straight
Optimal posture requires the least, not constant, muscular effort.

alt.q: A patient asks what “good posture” means. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “It is body alignment that helps you function while putting the least strain on your body.”
alt.ex: Optimal posture favors function, requires the least muscular work, and places the least strain on muscles, ligaments, and bones.
w: “It means keeping your muscles tight so that you stand as straight as possible.”
Tense, rigid positioning increases work; good posture requires the least effort.
“It means leaning slightly forward so that your weight is over your toes.”
Leaning forward moves the line of gravity outside the base of support.
“It is a position you only need to think about while you are standing.”
Alignment applies while standing, sitting, and lying.

items.q: Which factors can compromise a person’s ability to remain balanced? Select all that apply.
o: Pain
Pain compromises the ability to remain balanced.
Pregnancy
Life changes such as pregnancy affect balance.
Medications that cause dizziness
Dizziness from medications impairs balance.
Prolonged immobility
Prolonged immobility affects balance.
Regular balance exercise
Exercise improves coordination and reduces fall risk rather than compromising balance.
A wide base of support
A wide base of support increases stability.
items.ex: Disease, injury, pain, age, pregnancy, dizziness-causing medications, and prolonged immobility can all compromise balance.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a patient’s history for threats to balance. Which findings are relevant? Select all that apply.
o: Recent leg injury
Injury compromises the ability to remain balanced.
Two weeks of bed rest
Prolonged immobility affects balance.
New antihypertensive that causes dizziness
Medications that cause dizziness affect balance.
Normal vision with corrective lenses
Corrected normal vision supports balance by giving visual feedback.
Daily walking program
Regular activity improves coordination and stability.
alt.ex: Injury, immobility, and dizziness-causing medications threaten balance; normal vision and regular activity support it.

items.q: A patient with impaired balance tells the nurse, “I just stay in my chair all day so I won’t fall.” Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: Fear of falling is leading the patient to restrict activity
items.ex: Impaired balance contributes to fear of falling and self-imposed activity restrictions, which threaten mobility.
w: The patient is making a safe choice that will improve balance
Self-imposed restriction leads to immobility, which further impairs balance.
The patient’s balance problem is caused by sitting too long
The patient restricts activity because of impaired balance, not the reverse.
The patient has no real risk because the chair prevents falls
Impaired balance remains a major threat to mobility and safety.

alt.q: Which consequence of impaired balance should a nurse anticipate in an older adult?
alt.a: Fear of falling and self-imposed activity restrictions
alt.ex: Impaired balance is a major threat to mobility and safety and contributes to fear of falling and self-limited activity.
w: Increased confidence and greater daily activity
Impaired balance tends to reduce, not increase, activity and confidence.
Improved muscle tone from extra effort to stay upright
Impaired balance threatens mobility; it does not improve muscle tone.
A wider base of support and lower fall risk
Older adults often narrow their base of support, increasing fall risk.

items.q: What role does the cerebellum play in body movement and balance?
items.a: It coordinates and stores learned patterns of muscle movement
items.ex: The cerebellum coordinates muscle movement patterns with the cerebrum’s motor areas and stores learned sequences such as walking.
w: It senses changes in sound waves to create balance impulses
Inner ear mechanoreceptors, not the cerebellum, respond to sound waves.
It supplies calcium to keep the long bones rigid
Bone firmness comes from calcium and phosphate in the bone matrix.
It provides visual feedback about the environment’s movement
Vision, not the cerebellum, gives feedback about environmental movement.

alt.q: The sequence of leg movements needed for walking is learned and stored in which part of the nervous system?
alt.a: Cerebellum
alt.ex: Coordinated movement patterns such as walking are learned and stored in the cerebellum.
w: Semicircular canals
The semicircular canals sense balance; they do not store movement patterns.
Spinal cord
The text locates learned movement patterns in the cerebellum.
Retina
The retina receives visual input, not stored movement patterns.

items.q: How does normal vision help a person maintain balance?
items.a: It gives feedback about whether the person or the environment is moving
items.ex: Visual input from the eyes provides feedback about whether you or your surroundings are moving.
w: It lowers the center of gravity when the eyes are open
Vision provides feedback; it does not change the center of gravity.
It widens the base of support by adjusting foot position
Vision informs balance but does not widen the stance directly.
It stores learned patterns of walking movement
Learned movement patterns are stored in the cerebellum.

alt.q: A patient with poor eyesight has more trouble keeping balance. Which explanation is accurate?
alt.a: Reduced visual input limits feedback about movement of the body and surroundings
alt.ex: Normal vision aids balance by telling the brain whether the person or the environment is moving.
w: Poor eyesight displaces the inner ear’s hair cells
Vision loss does not affect inner ear structures.
Poor eyesight raises the patient’s center of gravity
Vision does not change the location of the center of gravity.
Poor eyesight weakens the antigravity muscles directly
Vision loss reduces feedback; it does not directly weaken muscles.

items.q: Together, the ears and eyes function in dynamic equilibrium to maintain balance when the head or body rotates or moves suddenly.
items.a: True
items.ex: Dynamic equilibrium, from the ears and eyes working together, maintains balance during turning or bending over.
items.ww: The ears and eyes do work together, and dynamic equilibrium applies to rotation and sudden movement.

alt.q: Dynamic equilibrium refers to maintaining balance only while the body is completely still.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Dynamic equilibrium maintains balance when the head or body rotates or suddenly moves, such as when bending over.
alt.ww: Dynamic equilibrium is needed during movement such as turning in circles or bending, not only at rest.

items.q: A nurse is about to assess a patient’s body alignment. Which approach is best?
items.a: Help the patient feel at ease and assess standing, sitting, and then lying
items.ex: The nurse avoids having the patient assume an unnatural, rigid position and assesses alignment standing, sitting, then lying as able.
w: Ask the patient to stand rigidly at attention during the assessment
A rigid, unnatural position does not show the patient’s usual alignment.
Assess alignment only while the patient lies supine in bed
Alignment is assessed standing, sitting, and lying as the patient is able.
Have the patient walk briskly before observing posture
Brisk walking first is not part of alignment assessment.

alt.q: Which objective is part of a nurse’s assessment of body alignment?
alt.a: Identifying deviations in alignment caused by incorrect posture
alt.ex: Alignment assessment identifies deviations from incorrect posture, along with growth changes, learning needs, and contributing factors.
w: Determining the patient’s maximum lifting capacity
Lifting capacity is not an objective of alignment assessment.
Measuring the patient’s resting heart rate
Heart rate relates to activity tolerance, not alignment.
Calculating the patient’s body mass index
BMI is not an objective of body alignment assessment.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient the tripod position before crutch walking. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of why this stance is used?
items.a: “Putting the crutches out in front and to the side gives me a wider base to balance on.”
items.ex: The tripod position maintains balance by providing a wider base of support.
w: “Putting the crutches close to my feet lets me lean my armpits on them.”
The axillae should not bear weight on crutches.
“Keeping the crutches together in front of me lowers my center of gravity.”
The tripod places crutches to the side to widen the base, not lower the center of gravity.
“Bending forward at the hips over the crutches keeps me from falling.”
Correct tripod alignment includes extended hips and knees and an erect head.

alt.q: Why does the crutch tripod position help a patient maintain balance?
alt.a: It provides a wider base of support
alt.ex: Placing crutches in front of and to the side of each foot widens the base of support, improving balance.
w: It raises the patient’s center of gravity
A higher center of gravity reduces, rather than improves, stability.
It shifts body weight onto the axillae
The axillae should not bear any weight.
It narrows the stance for better control
A narrow stance decreases the base of support.

items.q: Body balance occurs when a person is properly aligned with a relatively low center of gravity balanced over a wide, stable [[base of support]].
items.ex: A wide, stable base of support with a low center of gravity over it provides balance.

alt.q: Separating the feet a comfortable distance widens the [[base of support]], which increases stability.
alt.ex: A wide, stable base of support with a low center of gravity over it provides balance.

items.q: Older adults who take smaller steps and keep their feet closer together widen their base of support and improve balance.
items.a: False
items.ex: Smaller steps with the feet close together decrease the base of support and alter balance.
items.ww: A narrow stance decreases stability, so older adults with this gait are at greater risk of falls.

alt.q: Keeping the feet closer together while walking decreases the base of support and alters body balance.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: A narrower stance reduces the base of support, which alters balance, as often seen in older adults.
alt.ww: Narrowing the stance does not improve balance; it reduces the base of support.

items.q: Which statement best defines weight?
items.a: The force exerted on a body by gravity
items.ex: Weight is the force gravity exerts on a body, and it is always directed downward.
w: The force that occurs in a direction opposing movement
This defines friction, not weight.
The force against skin while bony structures move
This defines shear, not weight.
The coordinated effort of muscles and nerves
This defines body mechanics, not weight.

alt.q: Why do patients fall when their center of gravity becomes unbalanced?
alt.a: Gravity pulls their weight downward
alt.ex: The force of weight is always directed downward, so an unbalanced body falls under gravity’s pull.
w: Friction pulls the body sideways
Friction opposes movement along a surface; it does not cause falls from imbalance.
Shear moves the skin away from bone
Shear damages tissue; it is not why an unbalanced body falls.
The base of support moves upward
The base of support does not move upward; gravity acts downward.

items.q: Where is the center of gravity usually located in a standing person?
items.a: At 55% to 57% of standing height, in the midline
items.ex: A person’s center of gravity is usually at 55% to 57% of standing height in the midline, and it shifts during movement.
w: At 35% to 37% of standing height, in the midline
This is too low; the center of gravity is at 55% to 57% of height.
At 75% to 77% of standing height, over the chest
This is too high; the center of gravity is at 55% to 57% of height.
At 55% to 57% of standing height, over the dominant hip
The center of gravity lies in the midline, not over one hip.

alt.q: A nurse explains where a person’s center of gravity usually lies. Which statement is accurate?
alt.a: It lies in the midline at about 55% to 57% of standing height and shifts with movement
alt.ex: People are not geometrically perfect; their center of gravity is about 55% to 57% of height in the midline and shifts.
w: It lies at the exact center of the body and stays fixed with movement
Only symmetrical objects have a fixed exact center; people’s centers shift.
It lies at about 25% to 27% of standing height near the knees
The center of gravity is at 55% to 57% of standing height.
It lies at about 55% to 57% of standing height to one side of the spine
The center of gravity is in the midline, not to one side.

items.q: The force exerted against the skin while the skin remains stationary and the bony structures move is called [[shear|shearing|shear force]].
items.ex: Shear occurs when the skeleton moves while the skin stays in place, stretching and damaging underlying vessels.

alt.q: When the head of the bed is raised beyond 60 degrees and the skeleton slides down while the skin stays against the sheets, [[shear|shearing|shear force]] occurs.
alt.ex: Shear occurs when the skeleton moves while the skin stays in place, stretching and damaging underlying vessels.

items.q: A person’s center of gravity remains fixed in one position during movement.
items.a: False
items.ex: A person’s center of gravity shifts during movement, which is why body mechanics alone often fails when lifting patients.
items.ww: Only symmetrical inanimate objects have a fixed center; people’s centers of gravity shift as they move.

alt.q: A person’s center of gravity shifts during movement, which is why lifting patients with body mechanics alone often injures nurses.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Because people are not geometrically perfect and their centers shift, body mechanics alone does not make lifting safe.
alt.ww: The center of gravity does not stay fixed; its shifting makes manual lifting of patients risky.

items.q: To lift an object safely, what must the lifter do?
items.a: Overcome the object’s weight and know its center of gravity
items.ex: Safe lifting requires overcoming the weight of the object and knowing where its center of gravity lies.
w: Overcome the object’s friction and keep the arms extended
Lifting with extended arms increases injury risk.
Lift quickly while twisting the trunk toward the target
Twisting increases the risk of injury to the lumbar spine.
Narrow the stance and lift with the back muscles
A narrow stance reduces stability, and the back should not do the lifting.

alt.q: A nurse explains why lifting a patient is harder to do safely than lifting a box of supplies. Which explanation is accurate?
alt.a: A patient’s center of gravity is not at an exact center and shifts during movement
alt.ex: A symmetrical object’s center of gravity is at its exact center, but a person’s is not and it shifts during movement.
w: A patient’s weight is directed upward rather than downward
Weight is always directed downward for patients and objects alike.
A box has no center of gravity, so its weight is easy to predict
Every object has a center of gravity; a box’s is at its exact center.
A patient produces less friction than a box on a surface
Friction does not explain the difference in lifting safety.

items.q: Which statement best defines friction?
items.a: A force that occurs in a direction to oppose movement
items.ex: Friction is a force that acts in the direction opposite to movement.
w: A force that always acts downward toward the earth
This describes gravity acting as weight, not friction.
A force that pulls the skin toward the head of the bed
This is not a definition of friction.
A force that keeps the center of gravity over the base
This describes balance, not friction.

alt.q: Which term describes a force that occurs in a direction opposing movement?
alt.a: Friction
alt.ex: Friction acts in the opposite direction to movement, creating resistance when a patient is moved across a surface.
w: Weight
Weight is the force of gravity on a body, directed downward.
Balance
Balance is the ability to maintain a position or move without falling.
Alignment
Alignment is the positioning of joints, tendons, ligaments, and muscles.

items.q: The greater the surface area of an object being moved, the greater the friction.
items.a: True
items.ex: Friction increases with surface area, so a larger object produces greater resistance to movement.
items.ww: Larger surface area increases rather than decreases friction and resistance.

alt.q: A larger object being moved across a surface produces less resistance to movement than a smaller one.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A larger object has more surface area, which produces greater friction and resistance to movement.
alt.ww: More surface area means more friction, not less, so larger objects resist movement more.

items.q: A nurse finds a patient with the head of the bed elevated to 75 degrees who has slid toward the foot of the bed. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Lower the head of the bed and reposition the patient with a friction-reducing sheet
items.ex: Elevation beyond 60 degrees causes shear; lowering the bed and using a friction-reducing device protects skin and staff.
w: Raise the head of the bed higher to keep the patient sitting up
Higher elevation increases gravitational pull and shear.
Pull the patient up in bed by grasping under the arms
Pulling causes friction and shear on the skin and strains the nurse.
Ask the patient to dig in the heels and push up the bed
Dragging the body along the sheets creates friction and shear.

alt.q: A patient sitting in bed with the head elevated beyond 60 degrees is at risk for which skin problem?
alt.a: Shear injury to deep tissues
alt.ex: Above 60 degrees, gravity pulls the skeleton toward the foot of the bed while the skin stays against the sheets, causing shear.
w: Moisture damage from perspiration
Moisture damage is not the mechanism described for high head-of-bed elevation.
Allergic contact rash from the sheets
An allergic rash is unrelated to bed elevation and gravity.
Superficial burn from friction-reducing sheets
Friction-reducing sheets protect the skin; they do not burn it.

items.q: A patient’s head of bed is elevated beyond 60 degrees and the patient slides down in bed. Which events occur in the tissues as a result of shear? Select all that apply.
o: Blood vessels in the underlying tissue are stretched and damaged
Shear stretches and damages the vessels beneath the skin.
Blood flow to the deep tissues is impeded
Damaged vessels impede blood flow to deep tissue.
Pressure injuries develop within the undermined tissue
Pressure injuries often form in the deep, undermined tissue.
The surface skin shows the most severe damage first
The surface tissue appears less affected than the deep tissue.
The bony skeleton moves toward the head of the bed
Gravity pulls the skeleton toward the foot of the bed.
items.ex: Shear stretches and damages underlying vessels, impedes deep blood flow, and causes pressure injuries in undermined tissue while the surface looks less affected.

alt.q: Which statements about shear injury are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The skin stays against the sheets while the skeleton moves
Shear occurs when skin stays stationary and the bony structures move.
Deep tissue damage may be greater than the surface suggests
Pressure injuries develop in undermined tissue while the surface appears less affected.
Gravity contributes when the head of the bed is raised high
Gravity pulls the skeleton toward the foot of the bed when the head is raised beyond 60 degrees.
Shear affects only the outer layer of skin
Shear damages vessels and deep tissue, not just the surface.
Raising the head of the bed higher helps prevent shear
Elevating the head of the bed beyond 60 degrees promotes shear.
alt.ex: In shear, the skeleton moves while skin stays put, often under gravity, damaging deep tissue more than the surface shows.

items.q: In shear injury from high head-of-bed elevation, which event comes right after “Gravity pulls the skeleton toward the foot of the bed while the skin stays against the sheets”?
items.a: Blood vessels in the underlying tissue are stretched and damaged
items.ex: That's event 3 of 5. High elevation lets gravity move the skeleton under stationary skin, damaging vessels, reducing deep blood flow, and causing pressure injury.
w: Blood flow to the deep tissues is impeded
That's event 4 of 5.
Head of bed is elevated beyond 60 degrees
That's event 1 of 5.
A pressure injury develops within the undermined tissue
That's event 5 of 5.

alt.q: Which event comes first in shear injury from high head-of-bed elevation?
alt.a: Head of bed is elevated beyond 60 degrees
alt.ex: That's event 1 of 5. High elevation lets gravity move the skeleton under stationary skin, damaging vessels, reducing deep blood flow, and causing pressure injury.
w: Gravity pulls the skeleton toward the foot of the bed while the skin stays against the sheets
That's event 2 of 5.
Blood vessels in the underlying tissue are stretched and damaged
That's event 3 of 5.
Blood flow to the deep tissues is impeded
That's event 4 of 5.

alt.q: Which event comes last in shear injury from high head-of-bed elevation?
alt.a: A pressure injury develops within the undermined tissue
alt.ex: That's event 5 of 5. High elevation lets gravity move the skeleton under stationary skin, damaging vessels, reducing deep blood flow, and causing pressure injury.
w: Blood flow to the deep tissues is impeded
That's event 4 of 5.
Blood vessels in the underlying tissue are stretched and damaged
That's event 3 of 5.
Gravity pulls the skeleton toward the foot of the bed while the skin stays against the sheets
That's event 2 of 5.

items.q: How do friction-reducing sheets make it easier and safer to move a patient up in bed?
items.a: They decrease surface area and reduce friction
items.ex: Ergonomic devices such as friction-reducing sheets decrease surface area and reduce friction when moving patients.
w: They increase surface area so the patient grips the bed
More surface area increases friction, which these devices aim to reduce.
They raise the patient’s center of gravity above the bed
A sling lifts the patient; a sheet works by reducing friction.
They add weight so gravity holds the patient in place
Adding weight would increase resistance, not ease movement.

alt.q: A nurse uses a friction-reducing sheet to move a patient up in bed. Which explanation of its benefit is accurate?
alt.a: It minimizes shearing forces that can damage the patient’s skin
alt.ex: A friction-reducing sheet lowers friction and minimizes shear, protecting the skin and reducing the nurse’s effort.
w: It raises the head of the bed to prevent sliding
The sheet does not change bed position.
It increases friction so the patient does not slip
These sheets reduce friction rather than increase it.
It removes the need for more than one caregiver
Staffing depends on patient assessment, not on the sheet alone.

items.q: A patient with a stage 3 pressure injury on the sacrum needs to be moved up in bed. Which approach should the nurse use?
items.a: Use a full-body sling lift or friction-reducing device to avoid shear
items.ex: For stage 3 or 4 pressure injuries, the nurse takes care to avoid shear, and lifts or devices prevent friction and tearing.
w: Slide the patient up on the bottom sheet without a device
Sliding on a plain sheet creates friction and shear on the wound.
Raise the head of the bed fully before moving the patient
High head elevation increases gravitational pull and shear.
Have the patient push up with the heels on the mattress
Pushing along the mattress produces friction and shear on the sacrum.

alt.q: Which precaution is most important when transferring a patient who has a stage 4 pressure injury?
alt.a: Avoiding shearing force against the skin
alt.ex: Clinical judgment for patients with stage 3 or 4 pressure injuries includes taking care to avoid shearing force.
w: Keeping the head of the bed above 60 degrees
Elevation beyond 60 degrees promotes shear.
Increasing friction between skin and sheets
Friction contributes to skin damage and should be reduced.
Pulling the patient by the arms to limit contact
Pulling causes friction and shear and risks injury.

items.q: A nurse inspects the skin of a patient who has repeatedly slid down in bed with the head elevated. Which understanding should guide the assessment?
items.a: Deep tissue damage may be greater than the surface skin suggests
items.ex: In shear injury, pressure injuries develop in undermined deep tissue while the surface tissue appears less affected.
w: Intact surface skin rules out underlying tissue damage
The surface can look less affected even when deep tissue is damaged.
Shear injury appears first as a blister on the surface
Shear damage begins in deep tissue, not as surface blistering.
Damage from sliding is limited to the outer skin layer
Shear stretches deep vessels and damages underlying tissue.

alt.q: Why can a shear-related pressure injury be more serious than it first appears?
alt.a: The undermined deep tissue is damaged while the surface looks less affected
alt.ex: Shear damages vessels and deep tissue, so pressure injuries develop beneath a surface that appears less affected.
w: The surface skin always shows the full depth of injury
The surface often looks less affected than the deep tissue.
Shear damages only bone, not soft tissue
Shear stretches and damages blood vessels in soft tissue.
The injury heals faster than it looks
Undermined tissue indicates deeper, not lesser, damage.

items.q: In a symmetrical inanimate object, the center of gravity is at the exact center of the object.
items.a: True
items.ex: Symmetrical objects have a center of gravity at their exact center, unlike people, whose centers shift.
items.ww: The book states that a symmetrical object’s center of gravity is at its exact center.

alt.q: Like a symmetrical box, a standing patient has a center of gravity fixed at the exact geometric center of the body.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: People are not geometrically perfect; their center of gravity is about 55% to 57% of height and shifts.
alt.ww: A person’s center of gravity is not fixed at an exact center; it shifts during movement.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient about crutch safety. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I’ll dry the rubber tips if they get wet, because water makes them slip.”
items.ex: Rubber tips increase surface friction to prevent slipping, and water decreases friction, raising slipping risk.
w: “I’ll remove the worn rubber tips so the crutches glide more smoothly.”
Rubber tips increase friction; worn tips should be replaced, not removed.
“Wet tips are safer because water helps them grip the floor.”
Water decreases surface friction and increases slipping risk.
“I’ll use my brother’s crutches if mine get wet at the tips.”
Crutches are measured for each patient and should not be shared.

alt.q: Why are rubber tips securely attached to crutches?
alt.a: They increase surface friction and help prevent slipping
alt.ex: Rubber crutch tips increase friction against the floor, which helps prevent slipping.
w: They decrease surface friction so the crutches glide
Reducing friction would increase the risk of slipping.
They absorb water to keep the floor dry
Wet tips decrease friction; they should be kept dry.
They raise the crutch height for better alignment
Tips are for traction, not for adjusting crutch height.

items.q: Which are benefits of using a full-body sling to move a patient? Select all that apply.
o: Mechanically lifts the patient off the bed surface
A sling lifts the patient off the bed rather than dragging them.
Prevents friction against the patient’s skin
Lifting off the surface prevents friction.
Prevents tearing or shearing of the skin
A sling protects the skin from tearing and shear.
Protects nurses from injury
Lifts reduce the physical strain on nurses and staff.
Increases the surface area in contact with the bed
Slings lift the patient off the surface, eliminating rather than increasing contact.
Eliminates the need to assess the patient before moving
Assessment still guides choice of equipment and staff.
items.ex: A full-body sling lifts the patient off the bed, preventing friction, tearing, and shear, and protects staff from injury.

alt.q: A nurse explains to a family why a sling lift is used to move their father up in bed. Which reasons are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It keeps his skin from being dragged across the sheets
Lifting off the surface prevents friction on the skin.
It helps prevent shear damage to his tissues
A sling prevents shearing of the skin.
It reduces the risk of injury to the staff
Slings protect nurses and staff from lifting injuries.
It lets the staff raise the head of the bed past 60 degrees safely
Elevation beyond 60 degrees promotes shear regardless of the lift.
It increases friction so he does not slip off the bed
The sling works by preventing friction, not increasing it.
alt.ex: Sling lifts prevent friction and shear on the patient’s skin and protect staff from injury.

items.q: Why do guidelines for preventing lift injuries direct nurses to slide a patient using a friction-reducing sheet rather than lift?
items.a: Sliding requires less effort than lifting and the sheet minimizes shear
items.ex: Sliding takes less effort than lifting, and a friction-reducing sheet minimizes shearing forces on the patient’s skin.
w: Sliding increases friction, which keeps the patient from falling
The sheet reduces friction; increasing it would raise effort and skin damage.
Sliding lets one nurse move any patient without help
Staffing depends on patient assessment; sliding does not remove the need for help.
Sliding keeps the patient’s center of gravity fixed in place
A person’s center of gravity shifts regardless of the method used.

alt.q: When transferring a patient from a bed onto a stretcher, which device is most appropriate according to the guidelines?
alt.a: Slide board
alt.ex: A slide board provides a slippery surface that reduces friction and is more appropriate for bed-to-stretcher transfers.
w: Gait belt
A gait belt is for ambulation assistance and is not used to lift or carry patients.
Walker
A walker supports ambulation, not lateral transfer to a stretcher.
Cane
A cane supports walking for minor balance problems.

items.q: Nurses use an air-assisted transfer device to move a patient from bed to stretcher. Which precaution is most important?
items.a: Guard against the patient sliding beyond or off the stretcher
items.ex: Reduced friction increases momentum, making the transfer hard to stop, so staff ensure the patient does not slide too far.
w: Inflate the device only after the patient is on the stretcher
The device is inflated before the transfer to reduce friction.
Raise the stretcher above the level of the bed mattress
The stretcher is positioned slightly lower than the mattress for a smooth transfer.
Unlock the stretcher brakes so it can move with the patient
Brakes are locked to prevent the stretcher from moving.

alt.q: What is the limitation of air-assisted transfer devices?
alt.a: Their friction reduction increases momentum, making a transfer harder to stop
alt.ex: Once a transfer begins, low friction adds momentum, so the patient could slide beyond or off the receiving surface.
w: Their high friction makes the patient harder to slide
These devices reduce friction rather than increase it.
Their inflation raises the patient’s risk of shear
Air-assisted devices reduce friction and shear during transfer.
Their weight requires a manual lift to position them
The limitation the text identifies is increased momentum, not device weight.

items.q: Why should a nurse take a position close to the patient before moving them?
items.a: It keeps the patient close to the caregiver’s center of gravity and reduces horizontal reach
items.ex: Staying close keeps the load in the same plane and near the caregiver’s center of gravity, reducing reach and back stress.
w: It increases friction between the patient and the bed for better control
The goal is to reduce friction, not increase it.
It raises the caregiver’s center of gravity for greater lifting power
A lower, not higher, center of gravity improves stability.
It lets the caregiver twist the trunk more easily during the move
Twisting increases the risk of injury and should be avoided.

alt.q: A nurse stands far from the bed and reaches out with extended arms to move a patient. What is the main risk?
alt.a: Increased stress on the nurse’s back from horizontal reach
alt.ex: Working away from the body increases horizontal reach and moves the load from the caregiver’s center of gravity, stressing the back.
w: Increased friction protecting the patient’s skin
Distance does not protect the skin; friction damages it.
Lower center of gravity improving the nurse’s balance
Reaching out does not lower the center of gravity.
Wider base of support reducing fall risk
Reaching with extended arms does not widen the base of support.

items.q: Which components of the bone matrix give bones their firmness?
items.a: Calcium and phosphate
items.ex: Calcium and phosphate in the bone matrix make bone firm and rigid enough to stay straight and bear weight.
w: Collagen and elastin
These fibers relate to flexibility of connective tissue, not the firmness the book attributes to bone matrix minerals.
Sodium and potassium
These electrolytes govern nerve and muscle excitability, not bone firmness.
Glucose and oxygen
Glucose and oxygen supply ATP for muscle contraction, not firmness of bone.

alt.q: A patient’s bone matrix has lost much of its calcium and phosphate. Which bone property is most directly reduced?
alt.a: Firmness that allows weight bearing
alt.ex: Firmness from calcium and phosphate keeps long bones straight and lets bones withstand weight bearing.
w: Elasticity that allows flexing
Elasticity and flexibility change mainly with age, not with matrix calcium and phosphate.
Ability to be stimulated by nerves
Responding to nerve signals is a property of skeletal muscle cells, not bone.
Supply of ATP for movement
ATP for movement is produced in muscle fibers using glucose and oxygen.

items.q: Which type of joint is freely movable and the most numerous and anatomically complex in the body?
items.a: Synovial joint
items.ex: Synovial, or true, joints such as the hinge joint of the elbow are freely movable and the most mobile and numerous.
w: Fibrous joint
Fibrous joints fit closely and are fixed, permitting little if any movement.
Cartilaginous joint
Cartilaginous joints are elastic but have little movement.
Ossified joint
Ossification occurs in cartilaginous joints when bone growth is complete, making them less movable.

alt.q: The joint between the tibia and fibula fits closely together and permits little if any movement. How is this joint classified?
alt.a: Fibrous joint
alt.ex: Fibrous joints, such as the tibia–fibula joint, are fixed and permit little if any movement.
w: Synovial joint
Synovial joints, such as the elbow, are freely movable.
Cartilaginous joint
Cartilaginous joints unite bones with cartilage, such as the ribs to the costal cartilage.
Hinge joint
A hinge joint, such as the elbow, is a freely movable type of synovial joint.

items.q: Which structure connects muscle to bone and is strong, flexible, and inelastic?
items.a: Tendon
items.ex: Tendons are glistening white fibrous bands that connect muscle to bone; the Achilles tendon is the thickest and strongest.
w: Ligament
Ligaments connect bone to bone and have some elasticity because of their elastic fibers.
Cartilage
Cartilage is a firm gel-based tissue that absorbs shock between articulating bones.
Synovial membrane
The synovial membrane lines the joint capsule; it does not connect muscle to bone.

alt.q: Which statement correctly describes a ligament?
alt.a: It binds joints and connects bone to bone
alt.ex: Ligaments are flexible bands of dense fibrous tissue that bind joints and connect bones and cartilage.
w: It connects muscle to bone and is inelastic
This describes a tendon, which links muscle to bone.
It covers the articular surfaces of bones
Hyaline cartilage covers articular surfaces of bones.
It gives shape to the external ear
Elastic cartilage gives shape to the external ear.

items.q: A patient who had a myocardial infarction (MI) 3 days ago has a new exercise plan. Which exercise type in the plan should the nurse question?
items.a: Isometric exercises that tighten and hold muscle groups
items.ex: Isometric work raises energy expenditure, respiratory rate, and cardiac workload, so it is sometimes contraindicated after MI.
w: Isotonic exercises that move joints gently
The book identifies isometric, not isotonic, work as the type sometimes contraindicated after MI.
Ankle pumping exercises done while in bed
Ankle pumping is a mild movement exercise, not the high-energy isometric work the book cautions against.
Short walks in the hallway with assistance
Walking is isotonic activity; the specific caution in the text concerns isometric contractions.

alt.q: A nurse explains why isometric exercises may be unsafe for a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). Which explanation is accurate?
alt.a: They increase energy expenditure and work on the heart
alt.ex: Isometric contractions do not shorten muscle but raise respiratory rate and cardiac work, like racing an engine in neutral.
w: They cause muscle shortening and joint strain
Isometric contractions cause no muscle shortening or active movement.
They reduce circulation to the exercised body part
Isometric exercise actually increases circulation to the involved body part.
They decrease osteoblastic activity in bone
Isometric exercise increases osteoblastic activity rather than reducing it.

items.q: A patient uses an overhead trapeze to pull up in bed and then slowly lowers back down to the mattress. Which type of muscle tension controls the slow lowering?
items.a: Eccentric tension
items.ex: Eccentric tension lengthens muscles to control the speed and direction of movement, such as lowering slowly from a trapeze.
w: Concentric tension
Concentric tension shortens the muscle, as when the patient pulls up on the trapeze.
Isometric tension
Isometric contraction increases tension without any change in muscle length or movement.
Muscle tonus
Tonus is the normal resting state of balanced muscle tension, not a movement contraction.

alt.q: A patient grasps an overhead trapeze and pulls up toward the head of the bed. Which type of muscle tension produces this movement?
alt.a: Concentric tension
alt.ex: In concentric tension, increased contraction shortens the muscle and produces movement, as in pulling up on a trapeze.
w: Eccentric tension
Eccentric tension lengthens the muscle to control lowering, not pulling up.
Isometric tension
Isometric contraction holds a stable position without shortening the muscle.
Stretch reflex
The stretch reflex maintains muscle length against a load; it is not a type of isotonic tension.

items.q: After 3 weeks of bed rest, a patient’s thigh muscles are visibly smaller. Which term should the nurse use to document this finding?
items.a: Disuse atrophy
items.ex: During prolonged inactivity, muscles usually shrink, a condition called disuse atrophy.
w: Hypertrophy
Hypertrophy is an increase in muscle size from active use during exercise.
Contracture
A contracture is a fixed shortening that limits joint motion, not a loss of muscle size.
Resorption
Resorption refers to bone loss, not shrinking of muscle.

alt.q: A patient’s leg muscles enlarge after weeks of regular resistance training. Which term describes this change?
alt.a: Hypertrophy
alt.ex: Active use of muscles during exercise increases muscle size and leads to hypertrophy.
w: Disuse atrophy
Disuse atrophy is shrinking of muscle from prolonged inactivity.
Ossification
Ossification is hardening of cartilage into bone, not muscle growth.
Proprioception
Proprioception is the muscle sense of body position, not a change in muscle size.

items.q: Which neuromuscular disorder impairs movement by disrupting transfer of the impulse from the neurotransmitter to the muscle?
items.a: Myasthenia gravis
items.ex: Myasthenia gravis disrupts transfer from the neurotransmitter to the muscle, impairing movement.
w: Parkinson disease
Parkinson disease alters neurotransmitter production.
Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis impairs muscle activity.
Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis hardens cartilage and impairs joint mobility, not nerve-to-muscle transmission.

alt.q: A patient’s movement problems are caused by altered production of neurotransmitters. Which disorder does the nurse recognize as working this way?
alt.a: Parkinson disease
alt.ex: Parkinson disease alters neurotransmitter production, which impairs movement.
w: Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis disrupts transfer from the neurotransmitter to the muscle.
Multiple sclerosis
Multiple sclerosis impairs muscle activity.
Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is a bone disorder that weakens bone integrity.

items.q: A patient with diabetes has lost sensation in the soles of both feet and walks unsteadily. Which explanation of the unsteadiness is most accurate?
items.a: Foot proprioceptors cannot relay pressure changes that guide posture and stepping
items.ex: Proprioceptors on the soles monitor pressure and signal antigravity muscles, supporting upright posture and automatic stepping.
w: The cerebellum can no longer store learned walking patterns
The cerebellum stores movement patterns; loss of foot sensation does not erase them.
The motor strip can no longer send voluntary impulses to the legs
Motor strip damage causes voluntary weakness; this patient’s problem is sensory input from the feet.
The inner ear can no longer detect rotation of the head
Inner ear mechanoreceptors sense head and body movement, not pressure on the soles.

alt.q: With eyes closed, a patient bends an elbow and correctly states where the hand is. Which function does this demonstrate?
alt.a: Proprioception
alt.ex: Proprioception is the muscle sense that tells the position of body parts in space without seeing them.
w: Dynamic equilibrium
Dynamic equilibrium maintains balance when the head or body rotates or suddenly moves.
Muscle tone
Muscle tone is the normal state of balanced muscle tension.
Stretch reflex
The stretch reflex keeps muscle length constant when a load is applied.

items.q: A nurse is about to change a dressing on a patient lying in a low bed. Which action best protects the nurse’s balance and back during the procedure?
items.a: Raise the bed to a working height before starting
items.ex: Raising the bed prevents bending too far at the waist and shifting the base of support.
w: Bend forward at the waist to reach the wound
Bending far at the waist shifts the center of gravity away from the base of support.
Stand with feet close together beside the bed
A narrow stance reduces the base of support and balance.
Keep the knees locked straight while working
The book advises bending the knees and flexing the hips while keeping the trunk erect.

alt.q: When is a person’s body balanced?
alt.a: When aligned with a low center of gravity over a wide, stable base of support
alt.ex: Body balance occurs with proper alignment and a relatively low center of gravity balanced over a wide, stable base.
w: When aligned with a high center of gravity over a narrow base of support
A high center of gravity over a narrow base reduces stability.
When the trunk is flexed forward with the feet placed close together
Flexing the trunk and narrowing the stance displace the center of gravity.
When the center of gravity falls outside the base of support
In standing balance a vertical line from the center of gravity falls through the base of support.

items.q: Where are coordinated patterns of movement, such as the sequence of leg movements for walking, learned and stored?
items.a: Cerebellum
items.ex: The cerebellum coordinates muscle movement with cerebral motor areas and stores learned movement patterns such as walking.
w: Precentral gyrus
The precentral gyrus, or motor strip, is the major voluntary motor area, not where patterns are stored.
Medulla
Most motor fibers cross at the level of the medulla; it does not store movement patterns.
Semicircular canals
The semicircular canals of the inner ear contribute to balance.

alt.q: Which brain area is the major voluntary motor area in the cerebral cortex?
alt.a: Precentral gyrus
alt.ex: The precentral gyrus, or motor strip, is the major voluntary motor area; most motor fibers descend from it.
w: Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates and stores patterns of movement.
Medulla
The medulla is where most descending motor fibers cross over.
Vestibule
The vestibule of the inner ear contains balance sense organs.

items.q: Which type of cartilage is strong and rigid and is found in the intervertebral disks and pubic symphysis?
items.a: Fibrocartilage
items.ex: Fibrocartilage is strong and rigid and is found in the pubic symphysis and intervertebral disks.
w: Hyaline cartilage
Hyaline, the most common type, covers articular surfaces of bones, costal cartilages, and tracheal rings.
Elastic cartilage
Elastic cartilage shapes the external ear, epiglottis, and eustachian tube.
Articular cartilage
Articular surfaces are covered by hyaline cartilage, which is not the type found in intervertebral disks.

alt.q: Which type of cartilage is the most common and covers the articular surfaces of bones?
alt.a: Hyaline cartilage
alt.ex: Hyaline cartilage is the most common type and covers articular surfaces, costal cartilages, and tracheal rings.
w: Fibrocartilage
Fibrocartilage is found in the pubic symphysis and intervertebral disks.
Elastic cartilage
Elastic cartilage gives shape to the external ear, epiglottis, and eustachian tube.
Costal ligament
Ligaments are fibrous bands that bind joints, not a type of cartilage.

items.q: Through which structures does the nervous system control balance? Select all that apply.
o: Inner ear
Mechanoreceptors in the vestibule and semicircular canals help create the sense of balance.
Cerebellum
The cerebellum coordinates muscle movement patterns needed to stay balanced.
Vision
Visual input tells whether you or the environment is moving.
Medulla
The medulla is where most motor fibers cross; it is not named as a balance control.
Precentral gyrus
The precentral gyrus is the major voluntary motor area, not one of the named balance controls.
items.ex: The book names the inner ear, the cerebellum, and vision as the nervous system’s balance controls.

alt.q: Which factors can compromise a person’s ability to remain balanced? Select all that apply.
o: Pregnancy
Life changes such as pregnancy compromise balance.
Medications that cause dizziness
Dizziness-producing medications affect balance.
Prolonged immobility
Prolonged immobility affects balance.
Pain
Pain is listed among the factors that compromise balance.
A wide, stable base of support
A wide base of support improves balance rather than compromising it.
alt.ex: Disease, injury, pain, development, pregnancy, dizziness-causing drugs, and prolonged immobility can all impair balance.

items.q: A nurse prepares to help lift a patient. Which actions help the nurse achieve balance and alignment? Select all that apply.
o: Separate the feet to a comfortable distance
Separating the feet widens the base of support.
Bring the center of gravity closer to the base of support
A center of gravity closer to the base increases balance.
Bend the knees and flex the hips while keeping the trunk erect
Squatting with proper back alignment keeps the trunk erect and reduces strain.
Bend forward from the waist with straight knees
Bending far at the waist shifts the base of support and strains the back.
Keep the feet close together for better control
A narrow stance shrinks the base of support and reduces balance.
items.ex: Widening the base, lowering the center of gravity, and squatting with an erect trunk promote balance and alignment.

alt.q: Which statements about posture are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Proper posture enhances body balance
The book states proper posture enhances balance.
Good posture requires the least muscular work to maintain
Optimal alignment requires the least muscular work and places the least strain on tissues.
Poor posture leads to muscle fatigue
Poor posture makes muscles work harder against gravity, causing fatigue.
Posture is unrelated to mood or discomfort
Posture often reflects personality, discomfort, and mood, such as slouching when tired or depressed.
Muscles hold posture only during active movement
Muscles hold posture through a low level of sustained contraction against gravity.
alt.ex: Proper posture favors function, needs the least muscular work, and enhances balance; poor posture causes fatigue.

items.q: Which statements about skeletal muscle are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Muscle fibers contract when an impulse crosses the neuromuscular junction
An electrochemical impulse travels from nerve to muscle across the neuromuscular junction.
ATP for contraction requires glucose and oxygen
Continued use of ATP requires glucose and oxygen delivered by capillaries.
During contraction one bone usually stays fixed while the other moves
Muscles attach to both articulating bones; one usually remains fixed.
Skeletal muscles usually act alone rather than in groups
Skeletal muscles usually act in groups, some contracting while others relax.
A lighter load generally produces a stronger contraction
Generally, the heavier the load, the stronger the contraction.
items.ex: Skeletal muscle contracts via neuromuscular impulses, uses ATP from glucose and oxygen, and works in coordinated groups.

alt.q: A nurse reviews how muscles produce movement. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Muscles coordinate movement through a system of levers
Bones such as the humerus, ulna, and radius act as levers to move loads.
Tendon attachment and joint type help determine the extent of movement
Load, tendon attachment, and joint type determine the type and extent of movement.
Voluntary movement combines isotonic and isometric contractions
The book states voluntary movement is a combination of both.
A prime mover can never act as an antagonist
A prime mover during flexion may be an antagonist during extension.
Isometric contractions use no extra energy
Isometric contractions increase energy expenditure even without muscle shortening.
alt.ex: Movement depends on levers, tendon attachment, joint type, and combined isotonic and isometric contractions.

items.q: A toddler’s bones are more pliable than an older adult’s bones and are better able to withstand traumatic injury.
items.a: True
items.ex: Bone elasticity changes with age; toddlers’ pliable bones withstand trauma better than older adults’ bones.
items.ww: Older adults, especially women, lose bone and develop osteoporosis, which increases fracture risk.

alt.q: Older adults’ bones withstand traumatic injury better than toddlers’ bones because they are more rigid.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Older adults are more susceptible to bone resorption and osteoporosis, increasing fracture risk.
alt.ww: Toddlers’ more pliable bones are the ones better able to withstand traumatic injury.

items.q: During an isometric contraction, muscle tension increases while muscle length stays the same.
items.a: True
items.ex: Isometric contraction raises tension without shortening, holding the body in a stable position, as in quadriceps sets.
items.ww: A change in muscle length with constant tension describes an isotonic contraction.

alt.q: During an isometric contraction, the muscle shortens while its tension stays the same, causing the body to move.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: This describes an isotonic contraction; isometric contraction increases tension with no change in length.
alt.ww: Isometric contraction holds a stable position with no shortening, so movement does not occur.

items.q: When a load becomes heavy enough to threaten injury, the body ignores the stretch reflex and the muscles relax.
items.a: True
items.ex: The stretch reflex keeps muscle length constant, but a dangerously heavy load causes relaxation, so you drop the object.
items.ww: The stretch reflex is overridden when the load threatens muscle injury.

alt.q: The stretch reflex keeps a muscle contracting against any load, however heavy, to maintain constant muscle length.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: When a load threatens injury, the body ignores the reflex and the muscle relaxes.
alt.ww: The reflex normally maintains length, but it is overridden by loads heavy enough to cause injury.

items.q: The muscle sense that tells a person the position of the body and its parts in space is called [[proprioception]].
items.ex: Proprioceptors in muscles, joint capsules, and tendons monitor contraction and stretch to signal body position.

alt.q: Stretch receptors in muscles, joint capsules, and tendons provide [[proprioception|proprioceptive sense]], awareness of body position and movement.
alt.ex: Proprioceptors in muscles, joint capsules, and tendons monitor contraction and stretch to signal body position.

items.q: The normal state of balanced muscle tension is called muscle tone, or [[tonus]].
items.ex: Muscle tone maintains functional positions such as sitting or standing and is kept up by continued muscle use, including ADLs.

alt.q: Activities of daily living help maintain [[muscle tone|tonus|tone]], which decreases during prolonged bed rest.
alt.ex: Muscle tone maintains functional positions such as sitting or standing and is kept up by continued muscle use, including ADLs.

items.ex: Muscles work in groups; the same muscle can act in different roles depending on the movement.
w: Opposes the prime mover and relaxes while it contracts
That goes with Antagonist.
Contracts with the prime mover to make movement more effective
That goes with Synergist.
Stabilizes joints to maintain posture and balance

w: Directly performs a specific movement

Opposes the prime mover and relaxes while it contracts
That goes with Antagonist.
Stabilizes joints to maintain posture and balance
That goes with Fixator.

w: Directly performs a specific movement
That goes with Prime mover.
Opposes the prime mover and relaxes while it contracts
That goes with Antagonist.
Contracts with the prime mover to make movement more effective
That goes with Synergist.

w: Antagonist

w: Prime mover

Synergist: Contracts with the prime mover to make movement more effective.
Fixator
Fixator: Stabilizes joints to maintain posture and balance.

alt.a: Synergist

Prime mover: Directly performs a specific movement.
Antagonist
Antagonist: Opposes the prime mover and relaxes while it contracts.
