mt.q: Match each functional classification of muscle action with its description.
pairs: Opposes the prime mover and relaxes while it contracts
Contracts with the prime mover to make movement more effective
Stabilizes joints to maintain posture and balance
mt.ex: Muscles work in groups; the same muscle can act in different roles depending on the movement.

items.q: Which characteristic distinguishes exercise from general physical activity?
items.a: It is structured and planned to develop and maintain fitness
items.ex: Exercise is a component of physical activity that is specifically planned and structured to develop and maintain fitness.
w: It is any energy expenditure from skeletal muscle movement
This defines physical activity in general, not exercise.
It always requires maximal exertion to be effective
Physical activity ranges from low resting levels to maximal exertion; exercise is not defined by intensity.
It is performed only as therapy after surgery
Exercise is sometimes therapeutic, but that is not what defines it.

alt.q: Which statement defines physical activity?
alt.a: Any energy expenditure brought about by skeletal muscle movement
alt.ex: Physical activity is any bodily movement by skeletal muscles that expends energy, from resting levels to maximal exertion.
w: A structured program planned to build physical fitness
This describes exercise, a planned component of physical activity.
The amount of exercise a patient is able to perform
This describes activity tolerance.
A therapeutic routine prescribed during rehabilitation
Therapeutic exercise is one use of exercise, not the definition of physical activity.

items.q: What does the term activity tolerance mean?
items.a: The type and amount of exercise or activity a patient is able to perform
items.ex: A patient’s individualized exercise program depends on activity tolerance, the type and amount of activity the patient can perform.
w: The maximum heart rate a patient reaches during exercise
Activity tolerance is not defined by a heart rate value.
The structured fitness plan a patient agrees to follow
A structured fitness plan is exercise, not tolerance.
The range of motion available in a patient’s joints
Range of motion describes joint movement, not overall activity tolerance.

alt.q: Which group of factors does the book identify as influencing a patient’s activity tolerance?
alt.a: Physiological, emotional, and developmental factors
alt.ex: Physiological, emotional, and developmental factors influence activity tolerance.
w: Genetic, financial, and educational factors
These are not the factor groups the book lists for activity tolerance.
Cultural, legal, and occupational factors
These are not the factor groups the book lists for activity tolerance.
Nutritional, spiritual, and environmental factors
These are not the factor groups the book lists for activity tolerance.

items.q: A patient is immobilized in bed after a pelvic injury and cannot tolerate increased activity. Which type of exercise is most appropriate to begin?
items.a: Isometric exercises
items.ex: Isometric exercise is ideal for patients who do not tolerate increased activity, such as those immobilized in bed.
w: Isotonic exercises such as walking
Walking requires the activity the immobilized patient cannot yet tolerate.
Resistive push-ups from a chair
Chair push-ups require sitting and pushing up, which this bed-bound patient cannot do.
Bicycling on a stationary cycle
Bicycling is isotonic activity that requires more mobility than the patient has.

alt.q: A patient asks which type of exercise best enhances circulatory and respiratory functioning. Which example should the nurse give?
alt.a: Brisk walking
alt.ex: Isotonic exercises such as walking, swimming, and bicycling enhance circulatory and respiratory functioning.
w: Quadriceps setting
Quadriceps sets are isometric exercises, used mainly when activity is not tolerated.
Pelvic floor tightening
Pelvic floor tightening is an isometric exercise, not the isotonic type that enhances cardiopulmonary function.
Pushing against a wall
Pushing against a stationary object is a resistive isometric exercise.

items.q: What is the main clinical use of having a patient perform resistive isometric exercise?
items.a: Assessing muscle strength
items.ex: Resistive isometric exercise is the main method used to assess muscle strength in the clinical setting.
w: Measuring range of joint motion
Range of motion is observed through joint movement, not resistive contraction.
Testing balance and coordination
Balance and coordination are tested with other tasks, not resistive contraction.
Evaluating cardiopulmonary endurance
Endurance is enhanced by isotonic activity; resistive isometrics are used to assess strength.

alt.q: Which activity is an example of a resistive isometric exercise?
alt.a: Sitting and pushing the hands against the chair seat to raise the hips
alt.ex: Hip lifting, pushing against a chair seat to raise the hips, is a resistive isometric exercise, like push-ups.
w: Walking at a steady pace around the hospital unit
Walking is an isotonic exercise.
Swimming laps at a moderate pace in a pool
Swimming is an isotonic exercise.
Riding a stationary bicycle for ten minutes
Bicycling is an isotonic exercise.

items.q: A patient with low bone density asks how isotonic exercise such as walking helps the bones. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “It promotes bone-building activity that combats osteoporosis.”
items.ex: Isotonic exercise promotes osteoblastic activity that combats osteoporosis, along with increasing muscle mass, tone, and strength.
w: “It lowers the calcium content of your bones.”
Reduced bone mineral would weaken bone; exercise is meant to strengthen it.
“It replaces the need for any other exercise.”
The best program combines isotonic, isometric, and resistive exercises.
“It mainly stretches your ligaments and tendons.”
The book links isotonic exercise to osteoblastic activity, not ligament stretching.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient shows understanding of teaching about resistive isometric exercise?
alt.a: “Pushing against resistance strengthens my muscles and stresses my bones to build them.”
alt.ex: Resistive isometric exercise promotes muscle strength and stresses bone to promote osteoblastic activity.
w: “Holding the contraction for a shorter time will build more endurance.”
Gradually increasing the hold time and resistance builds strength and endurance.
“This exercise works because it makes my muscles move my joints.”
Isometric contraction produces no muscle shortening or joint movement.
“I should start with the most resistance I can manage and then decrease it.”
Resistance should be increased gradually over time.

items.q: A patient has osteoporosis. Which description of the condition is accurate?
items.a: Bone density is reduced, though bone is biochemically normal
items.ex: In osteoporosis, bone remains biochemically normal but has reduced density and difficulty maintaining support, leading to fractures.
w: Bones are short, bowed, and deformed from birth
This describes osteogenesis imperfecta, an inherited disorder.
The spine curves structurally with vertebral rotation
This describes scoliosis, a congenital structural curvature.
Articular cartilage changes with bony overgrowth
This describes arthritis affecting the articular ends of bone.

alt.q: A child has an inherited disorder in which bones become short, bowed, and deformed, causing spinal curvature and short stature. Which condition is this?
alt.a: Osteogenesis imperfecta
alt.ex: Osteogenesis imperfecta is an inherited congenital defect that makes bones short, bowed, and deformed.
w: Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is reduced bone density in biochemically normal bone.
Osteoarthritis
Osteoarthritis is a degenerative joint disease affecting articular cartilage.
Scoliosis
Scoliosis is a structural spinal curvature with vertebral rotation, not bowed long bones.

items.q: A patient has a traumatic head injury with damage to the motor strip of the cerebrum. The family asks how much weakness to expect. Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: “The degree of weakness relates to how much of the motor strip was damaged.”
items.ex: The amount of voluntary motor impairment is directly related to the amount of destruction of the motor strip.
w: “Weakness will affect only the areas below the level of the injury.”
Loss of function below the level of injury describes spinal cord injury.
“Weakness will always be temporary after a head injury.”
The book does not describe head injury weakness as always temporary.
“Weakness occurs only when the cerebellum is also damaged.”
Voluntary motor impairment results from motor strip damage, not only cerebellar damage.

alt.q: A patient has a spinal cord injury. Which finding does the nurse expect?
alt.a: Loss of motor and sensory function below the level of injury
alt.ex: Spinal cord injury causes permanent or temporary loss of motor and sensory function below the injury level.
w: Loss of motor and sensory function above the level of injury
Function is lost below, not above, the level of the injury.
Loss of only sensory function with intact movement
Spinal cord injury affects both motor and sensory function.
Loss of function proportional to motor strip destruction
This describes traumatic head injury, not spinal cord injury.

items.q: A patient who is obese needs to be transferred from bed to chair. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Use an algorithm to choose the number of staff and the assistive device
items.ex: Patients who are obese need adapted approaches, and algorithms guide staff numbers and devices for transfers.
w: Transfer the patient manually with one other nurse
Manual transfer without assessment risks injury; algorithms determine staff and equipment needs.
Ask the patient to stand and pivot without assistance
Independent pivoting without assessment is unsafe for a patient needing adaptations.
Use the same transfer method used for other patients
Patients who are obese require adapted approaches rather than the usual method.

alt.q: Why do patients who are obese require adaptations in the approaches used for walking, transfer, and positioning?
alt.a: Excess weight burdens joints and muscles and impairs musculoskeletal health
alt.ex: Obesity places increased weight burden on joints and muscles, so mobility approaches must be adapted for safety.
w: Obesity prevents muscles from responding to nerve signals
Obesity does not stop muscles from responding to nerve impulses.
Obesity eliminates the need for weight-bearing activity
Weight-bearing activity remains important; obesity changes how it is assisted.
Obesity causes loss of sensation below the waist
Loss of sensation is not a described effect of obesity.

items.q: A patient has articular disruption from trauma to a joint capsule. Which injury represents the severe end of this range?
items.a: A separation leading to dislocation
items.ex: Articular disruption ranges from a mild tear causing a sprain to a severe separation leading to dislocation.
w: A tear resulting in a sprain
A tear causing a sprain is the mild end of articular disruption.
A bruise of the overlying skin
A bruise is a soft tissue injury, not articular capsule disruption.
A simple disruption of bone continuity
Disruption of bone tissue continuity is a fracture.

alt.q: A patient twisted an ankle, causing a tear in the articular capsule. How does the nurse classify this injury?
alt.a: A sprain, the mild form of articular disruption
alt.ex: A tear in the articular capsule resulting in a sprain is the mild form of articular disruption.
w: A dislocation, the severe form of articular disruption
Dislocation results from separation, the severe form.
A fracture, a disruption of bone tissue continuity
A fracture involves bone, not the articular capsule.
A contracture, a shortening of muscle tissue
A contracture is not the injury described for a capsule tear.

items.q: A nurse is planning activity for a patient with arthritis of both hips who needs help with ADLs. Which knowledge about arthritis is most relevant to the plan?
items.a: Degenerative changes commonly affect weight-bearing joints
items.ex: Arthritis changes articular cartilage with bony overgrowth and commonly affects weight-bearing joints, such as the hips.
w: It is an inherited disorder that bows the long bones
This describes osteogenesis imperfecta.
It causes loss of sensation below the affected joint
Loss of sensation below a level describes spinal cord injury.
It reduces bone density while bone stays normal
This describes osteoporosis.

alt.q: Which pathological change describes arthritis?
alt.a: Changes in articular cartilage with overgrowth of bone at the articular ends
alt.ex: Arthritis involves changes in articular cartilage combined with bony overgrowth at the articular ends.
w: Reduction of bone mass in biochemically normal bone
This describes osteoporosis.
Structural curvature of the spine with vertebral rotation
This describes scoliosis.
Loss of voluntary movement from motor strip damage
This describes traumatic head injury.

items.q: A patient has scoliosis. Why is the patient’s balance and mobility affected?
items.a: Muscles, ligaments, and soft tissues become shortened
items.ex: Scoliosis is a structural spinal curvature with vertebral rotation that shortens soft tissues and affects balance and mobility.
w: Bones lose density and fracture easily
Loss of bone density with fractures describes osteoporosis.
The synovial membrane becomes inflamed
Synovial inflammation describes inflammatory joint disease.
Motor fibers no longer cross at the medulla
Scoliosis is a congenital musculoskeletal defect, not a nerve pathway problem.

alt.q: Which condition is a structural curvature of the spine associated with vertebral rotation?
alt.a: Scoliosis
alt.ex: Scoliosis is a congenital structural spinal curvature with vertebral rotation that shortens soft tissues.
w: Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is reduced bone density leading to fractures.
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Osteogenesis imperfecta causes short, bowed, deformed bones.
Articular disruption
Articular disruption is trauma to articular capsules, such as sprains.

items.q: Which serious diseases and health conditions are associated with obesity? Select all that apply.
o: Type 2 diabetes mellitus
Obesity increases the risk of type 2 diabetes.
Hypertension
Hypertension is listed among obesity-related conditions.
Sleep apnea
Sleep apnea and breathing problems are associated with obesity.
Gallbladder disease
Gallbladder disease is listed among obesity-related conditions.
Osteogenesis imperfecta
Osteogenesis imperfecta is an inherited bone disorder, not caused by obesity.
High HDL cholesterol
Obesity is linked to low, not high, HDL cholesterol.
items.ex: Obesity raises risk for hypertension, dyslipidemia, type 2 diabetes, heart disease, stroke, gallbladder disease, sleep apnea, and more.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a community group about health risks of obesity. Which conditions should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Coronary heart disease
Coronary heart disease is linked to obesity.
Stroke
Stroke risk increases with obesity.
Depression and anxiety
Mental illness such as depression and anxiety is associated with obesity.
Cancer
Cancer is listed among obesity-related conditions.
Scoliosis
Scoliosis is a congenital spinal curvature, not an obesity-related condition.
alt.ex: Obesity is linked to heart disease, stroke, cancer, osteoarthritis, mental illness, and higher death rates from all causes.

items.q: Which musculoskeletal problems are associated with obesity? Select all that apply.
o: Low back pain
Excess weight burden on joints and muscles is associated with low back pain.
Gait disturbances
Obesity is associated with gait disturbances.
Gout
Gout is listed among obesity-associated problems.
Soft tissue damage
Obesity is associated with soft tissue damage.
Osteogenesis imperfecta
This is an inherited disorder, not a result of obesity.
Spinal cord injury
Spinal cord injury results from trauma, not obesity.
items.ex: Obesity burdens joints and muscles and is linked to low back pain, gait problems, soft tissue damage, gout, and more.

alt.q: A patient who is obese asks how weight affects the musculoskeletal system. Which conditions may the nurse mention? Select all that apply.
o: Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is listed among obesity-associated conditions.
Fibromyalgia
Fibromyalgia is associated with obesity.
Rheumatoid arthritis
Connective tissue disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis are associated with obesity.
Scoliosis
Scoliosis is a congenital structural curvature, not an obesity effect.
Myasthenia gravis
Myasthenia gravis is a neuromuscular transmission disorder, not linked to obesity in the text.
alt.ex: Obesity is associated with osteoporosis, fibromyalgia, gout, and connective tissue disorders such as rheumatoid arthritis.

items.q: Which are benefits of isometric exercise for a patient on bed rest? Select all that apply.
o: Increased muscle mass, tone, and strength
Isometric exercise increases muscle mass, tone, and strength.
Decreased potential for muscle wasting
Building muscle mass reduces the potential for muscle wasting.
Increased circulation to the involved body part
Isometric exercise increases circulation to the exercised part.
Increased osteoblastic activity
Isometric exercise increases osteoblastic activity.
Decreased energy expenditure
Isometric contractions increase energy expenditure despite no muscle shortening.
items.ex: Isometric exercise builds muscle, reduces wasting, boosts local circulation, and increases osteoblastic activity.

alt.q: Which are benefits of isotonic exercises such as walking, swimming, and bicycling? Select all that apply.
o: Enhanced circulatory and respiratory functioning
Isotonic exercise enhances circulatory and respiratory function.
Increased muscle mass, tone, and strength
Isotonic exercise increases muscle mass, tone, and strength.
Osteoblastic activity that combats osteoporosis
Isotonic exercise promotes osteoblastic activity.
Muscle contraction without any joint movement
Contraction without movement describes isometric exercise.
Ideal for patients who cannot tolerate increased activity
Isometric, not isotonic, exercise is ideal for those who cannot tolerate more activity.
alt.ex: Isotonic exercises improve cardiopulmonary function, build muscle, and promote osteoblastic activity against osteoporosis.

items.q: The best program of physical activity combines isotonic, isometric, and resistive exercises.
items.a: True
items.ex: Each exercise type produces different physiological and psychological benefits, so a combination works best.
items.ww: Relying on one exercise type misses benefits the others provide.

alt.q: The best program of physical activity focuses on a single type of exercise, such as isotonic exercise only.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book recommends combining isotonic, isometric, and resistive exercises for different benefits.
alt.ww: No single exercise type provides all the physiological and psychological benefits.

items.q: Push-ups are an example of an isotonic exercise.
items.a: False
items.ex: Push-ups are a resistive isometric exercise; walking, swimming, and bicycling are isotonic examples.
items.ww: Push-ups involve contracting against resistance, which the book classifies as resistive isometric exercise.

alt.q: Push-ups and hip lifting are examples of resistive isometric exercises.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Both involve contracting muscles while pushing against a surface, which defines resistive isometric exercise.
alt.ww: Isotonic examples in the book are walking, swimming, and bicycling, not push-ups.

items.q: Gradually increasing the resistance and the length of time a muscle contraction is held increases muscle strength and endurance.
items.a: True
items.ex: Progressive increases in resistance and hold time build strength and endurance in resistive isometric exercise.
items.ww: Resistance and hold time should increase gradually, not stay fixed or decrease.

alt.q: Muscle strength and endurance increase most when resistance is kept constant and contractions are held only briefly.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Strength and endurance increase with a gradual increase in resistance and contraction hold time.
alt.ww: Constant resistance and brief holds do not provide the progressive challenge the book describes.

items.q: The type and amount of exercise or activity that a patient is able to perform is called [[activity tolerance]].
items.ex: An individualized exercise program depends on activity tolerance, which physiological, emotional, and developmental factors influence.

alt.q: A nurse bases a patient’s individualized exercise program on the patient’s [[activity tolerance|tolerance for activity]].
alt.ex: An individualized exercise program depends on activity tolerance, which physiological, emotional, and developmental factors influence.

items.q: Isotonic, isometric, and resistive exercises all promote [[osteoblastic]] activity, which helps build bone.
items.ex: Exercise stresses bone and promotes osteoblastic activity, which combats osteoporosis.

alt.q: Walking combats osteoporosis by promoting [[osteoblastic|bone-building|osteoblast]] activity.
alt.ex: Exercise stresses bone and promotes osteoblastic activity, which combats osteoporosis.

items.q: Which category does Osteogenesis imperfecta belong to?
items.a: Congenital defect
items.ex: Pathological conditions affecting alignment and mobility include congenital, bone/joint/muscle, inflammatory, CNS, and traumatic disorders.
w: Bone, joint, and muscle disorder
That goes with Osteoporosis.
Inflammatory joint disease
That goes with Arthritis.
Central nervous system disorder
That goes with Spinal cord injury.

alt.q: Which category does Osteoporosis belong to?
alt.a: Bone, joint, and muscle disorder
alt.ex: Pathological conditions affecting alignment and mobility include congenital, bone/joint/muscle, inflammatory, CNS, and traumatic disorders.
w: Congenital defect
That goes with Osteogenesis imperfecta.
Inflammatory joint disease
That goes with Arthritis.
Central nervous system disorder
That goes with Spinal cord injury.

alt.q: Which category does Arthritis belong to?
alt.a: Inflammatory joint disease
alt.ex: Pathological conditions affecting alignment and mobility include congenital, bone/joint/muscle, inflammatory, CNS, and traumatic disorders.
w: Congenital defect
That goes with Osteogenesis imperfecta.
Bone, joint, and muscle disorder
That goes with Osteoporosis.
Central nervous system disorder
That goes with Spinal cord injury.

alt.q: Which category does Spinal cord injury belong to?
alt.a: Central nervous system disorder
alt.ex: Pathological conditions affecting alignment and mobility include congenital, bone/joint/muscle, inflammatory, CNS, and traumatic disorders.

items.q: Which statement best defines safe patient handling and mobility (SPHM) techniques?
items.a: Standardized methods to handle and move patients based on their characteristics
items.ex: SPHM techniques are standardized methods for determining how to handle, move, and mobilize patients based on individual characteristics and conditions.
w: Lifting techniques based only on the nurse’s body mechanics
Body mechanics alone often lead to injury; SPHM adds assessment and equipment.
Policies requiring two nurses for every manual patient lift
SPHM uses algorithms and equipment, not a rule of two nurses for manual lifting.
Exercise programs that strengthen nurses’ back muscles
SPHM concerns how patients are moved, not nurse fitness programs.

alt.q: A nurse uses standardized methods, based on a patient’s characteristics and conditions, to decide how to move and mobilize the patient. What is this approach called?
alt.a: Safe patient handling and mobility
alt.ex: SPHM uses standardized methods that are individualized to patient characteristics and conditions.
w: Proprioceptive positioning
Proprioception is the body’s sense of position, not a patient-handling approach.
Manual lift technique
SPHM reduces reliance on manual lifting through assessment and equipment.
Range-of-motion therapy
Range-of-motion therapy is exercise for joints, not a method for moving patients.

items.q: Which statement defines ergonomics?
items.a: The design of work tasks to best suit the capabilities of workers
items.ex: Ergonomics designs work tasks to fit workers’ capabilities; in SPHM it includes assessment, transfer devices, lifts, and safety procedures.
w: The study of how muscles generate force during contraction
This describes muscle physiology, not ergonomics.
The training of workers to lift heavier loads safely
Ergonomics changes the task to fit the worker rather than training workers to lift more.
The evaluation of a patient’s ability to bear weight
Evaluating a patient’s mobility is done with tools such as the BMAT 2.0.

alt.q: A hospital redesigns its patient-transfer tasks around the physical capabilities of its staff. Which principle is it applying?
alt.a: Ergonomics
alt.ex: Ergonomics is the design of work tasks to best suit workers’ capabilities.
w: Body alignment
Body alignment is the positioning of joints and muscles, not task design.
Proprioception
Proprioception is a muscle sense of body position.
Activity tolerance
Activity tolerance is the amount of activity a patient can perform.

items.q: A nurse is assigned a patient who needs to be moved up in bed and repositioned. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess the patient’s mobility level with a standardized tool
items.ex: SPHM begins with standardized mobility assessment, which guides selection of equipment and staff for the task.
w: Ask a coworker to help lift the patient manually
Manual lifting contributes to nurse injuries; assessment comes first to select safe equipment.
Raise the head of the bed above 60 degrees
Elevating the head of the bed beyond 60 degrees promotes shear as the patient slides.
Instruct the patient to push up with the heels
Directing the patient before assessing mobility may be unsafe and skips assessment.

alt.q: Which tool does an SPHM program use to identify a patient’s mobility level?
alt.a: Bedside Mobility Assessment Tool 2.0
alt.ex: SPHM programs use standardized assessment tools such as the BMAT 2.0 to identify patient mobility level.
w: Braden Scale for pressure injury risk
The Braden Scale predicts pressure injury risk, not mobility level for handling tasks.
Glasgow Coma Scale
The Glasgow Coma Scale measures level of consciousness.
Numeric pain rating scale
A pain scale rates pain severity, not mobility level.

items.q: A nurse calculates that a transfer will require lifting more than 15.9 kg (35 lb) of a patient’s weight. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Use a mechanical lift or transfer aid with two or three caregivers
items.ex: When a caregiver must lift more than 35 lb, the chapter calls for a mechanical lift or aid with at least two or three caregivers.
w: Use a manual lift with one additional caregiver (2 people total)
Manual lifting of more than 35 lb risks injury; equipment is required.
Lift the patient alone using a wide base of support (1 person)
Body mechanics alone cannot make a heavy manual lift safe.
Ask the patient to stand without help (0 caregivers)
Expecting independent standing ignores the patient’s assessed needs and risks a fall.

alt.q: A caregiver would have to lift more than what amount of a patient’s weight before a mechanical lift or transfer aid is required?
alt.ex: If a caregiver must lift more than 15.9 kg (35 lb), use a mechanical lift or transfer aid.
w: This is lower than the 35-lb threshold given in the chapter.
This exceeds the 35-lb threshold given in the chapter.
This far exceeds the 35-lb threshold given in the chapter.

items.q: A newly hired nurse is unsure how the ceiling lift in a patient’s room works. Which action is best?

w: Try the lift with the patient and learn as it is used

Manual lifting increases injury risk and bypasses SPHM practice.

alt.q: What role do unit peer leaders play in an SPHM program?

items.q: What is the purpose of safety huddles in an SPHM program?

Huddles supplement, not replace, standardized assessment tools.
To decide which staff can skip equipment training

alt.q: A unit holds brief staff meetings to share information about patient-handling risks for the shift. Which SPHM program element is this?

alt.q: A nurse manager reports that a new SPHM program has reduced patient falls. Which other patient benefit is the manager likely to see?

w: More frequent need for bed rest
SPHM promotes mobility rather than increasing bed rest.
Greater reliance on manual lifting

Fewer mobility assessments per shift

items.q: A nurse manager finds that staff trained in SPHM rarely use the available lifts. According to research, which factor commonly limits equipment use?

items.ex: Use of lifts is often limited by availability of help, equipment function, and easy access to supplies.

Patient refusal is not a barrier identified in the research described.

alt.q: Which situation would most likely reduce nursing staff use of a mechanical lift despite training?

Move the patient manually to avoid using equipment

Only after a patient has fallen or nearly fallen on the unit

items.q: Adolescent girls usually grow and develop earlier than adolescent boys.
items.a: True
items.ex: Girls usually grow and develop earlier; hips widen and fat deposits in the upper arms, thighs, and buttocks.
items.ww: The book states that adolescent girls, not boys, usually grow and develop earlier.

alt.q: Adolescent boys usually grow and develop earlier than adolescent girls.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Adolescent girls usually grow and develop earlier than boys.
alt.ww: Boys’ shape changes from long-bone growth and muscle mass typically come after girls’ earlier development.

items.q: A 55-year-old patient with asthma and heart failure says she cannot keep up a walking routine because she gets breathless. How should the nurse interpret this?
items.a: Symptoms of one chronic condition are limiting exercise needed for another
items.ex: With multiple chronic conditions, symptoms of one (asthma-related breathlessness) can prevent exercise needed for another (heart failure).
w: She lacks intrinsic motivation and needs external rewards
Nothing suggests low motivation; her barrier is a symptom of a chronic condition.
Adults her age normally lack full musculoskeletal function
Middle-age adults should normally have full musculoskeletal function.
Her exercise guidelines can match those of a healthy peer
Preexisting heart disease requires different exercise types and tolerance monitoring than in a peer without disease.

alt.q: Why does a patient with preexisting heart disease need an individualized exercise plan rather than one designed for a healthy peer?
alt.a: Heart disease changes the exercises chosen and how tolerance is monitored
alt.ex: A patient with heart disease has different guidelines for the type of exercise and for monitoring exercise tolerance than a peer without disease.
w: Heart disease prevents any form of regular exercise
Exercise is still needed; chronic disease changes how it is individualized, not whether it occurs.
Heart disease mainly affects fine motor skills
Heart disease affects exercise tolerance, not fine motor development.
Heart disease removes the need to monitor exercise tolerance
Heart disease increases, not removes, the need to monitor tolerance.

items.q: A nurse is developing an exercise program with a patient recovering from surgery. Which action best supports the patient’s need for autonomy?
items.a: Asking the patient to help choose the type and timing of exercise
items.ex: Autonomy means the patient is involved in deciding on the course of exercise.
w: Demonstrating each exercise until the patient performs it correctly
Building skill in performing the exercise supports competence, not autonomy.
Arranging for a friend to join the patient for each session
A sense of belonging with others supports relatedness, not autonomy.
Giving the patient a printed program the nurse designed alone
A program designed without the patient’s input does not involve the patient in deciding.

alt.q: A nurse is supporting a patient’s motivation to exercise. Which action best supports the patient’s need for competence?
alt.a: Coaching the patient until each exercise is performed correctly
alt.ex: Competence means the patient is able to perform the exercise successfully.
w: Letting the patient select preferred activities
Involving the patient in choosing activities supports autonomy.
Encouraging the patient to join a walking group
Belonging to a group supports relatedness.
Offering the patient a reward for each session
External rewards are not one of the three basic psychological needs.

items.q: Which basic psychological needs are proposed as the focus for promoting a patient’s exercise adherence? Select all that apply.
o: Autonomy
The patient needs to be involved in deciding on a course of exercise.
Competence
The patient needs to be competent in performing the exercise.
Relatedness
A feeling of belonging to a group is a basic need that improves motivation.
Financial security
Income affects access to resources but is not one of the three basic psychological needs.
External rewards
Intrinsic motivation works without external rewards; rewards are not a basic psychological need.
items.ex: Exercise adherence may be promoted by focusing on three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness.

alt.q: A nurse wants to strengthen a patient’s motivation to keep exercising. Which approaches reflect the three basic psychological needs? Select all that apply.
o: Involving the patient in deciding on the exercise
This addresses autonomy.
Making sure the patient can perform the exercise
This addresses competence.
Helping the patient feel part of a supportive group
This addresses relatedness.
Setting the program without patient input to save time
Excluding the patient undermines autonomy.
Paying the patient for each completed session
Payment is an external reward, not one of the basic psychological needs.
alt.ex: Supporting autonomy, competence, and relatedness promotes a patient’s motivation toward exercise adherence.

items.q: The drive to exercise that comes purely from within, without external rewards, because it is enjoyable and gives a sense of accomplishment is called [[intrinsic motivation|intrinsic]].
items.ex: Intrinsic motivation comes from within and is driven by enjoyment and a sense of accomplishment rather than external rewards.

alt.q: A patient who walks every day only because she enjoys it and feels accomplished is showing [[intrinsic motivation|intrinsic]].
alt.ex: Intrinsic motivation comes from within and is driven by enjoyment and a sense of accomplishment rather than external rewards.

items.q: A patient who works two jobs says there is no time to get to a fitness center. Which suggestion is most likely to help this patient adhere to exercise?
items.a: Build a home-based routine into existing daily activities
items.ex: Integrating exercise into daily routines is key to adherence, and home-based exercise avoids some barriers of center-based programs.
w: Join a center-based class that meets twice a week
Center-based programs are harder to integrate into daily living than home-based exercise.
Wait to start exercising until work demands ease
Delaying does not address the barrier and postpones the benefits of exercise.
Focus on diet changes instead of exercise for now
This avoids rather than solves the time barrier to exercise.

alt.q: Why may home-based exercise be easier for patients to integrate into daily living than center-based exercise?
alt.a: Some barriers can be avoided when exercising at home
alt.ex: Research shows home-based exercise can be easier to integrate because some barriers are avoided; older adults find it convenient.
w: Home programs need more equipment and supervision
Home exercise is perceived as convenient, not as requiring more equipment or supervision.
Center-based programs are not open to older adults
Center programs are available; home exercise is simply perceived as more convenient.
Home programs remove the need for motivation
Motivation remains important, especially when lifestyle offers little convenient time.

items.q: Individuals with lower levels of education and those in minority racial/ethnic groups tend to show which pattern of physical activity?
items.a: Higher work activity but lower nonwork activity
items.ex: These groups tend to be more active at work but less active outside work, which may limit health benefits.
w: Lower work activity but higher nonwork activity
The pattern is reversed: work activity tends to be higher and nonwork activity lower.
Higher work activity and higher nonwork activity
Nonwork physical activity tends to be lower, not higher, in these groups.
Lower work activity and lower nonwork activity
Work-related physical activity tends to be higher in these groups.

alt.q: Why might a patient with a physically demanding job still not gain the expected health benefits from activity?
alt.a: Nonwork activity has a stronger positive link to health
alt.ex: Nonwork physical activity has a stronger positive association with health than work physical activity.
w: Work activity counts only when done outdoors
The book contrasts work and nonwork activity, not indoor and outdoor settings.
Work activity always causes musculoskeletal injury
The book does not say work activity always causes injury.
Work activity has no effect on the body at all
Work activity has some effect, but nonwork activity is more strongly linked to health.

items.q: A community nurse wants to motivate members of a Spanish-speaking community to join an exercise program. Which strategy is most likely to succeed?
items.a: Have providers of the same language background offer support and advice
items.ex: Support and advice from health care providers of the same cultural or language background often motivates patients to become involved in exercise.
w: Use one standard program designed for the general population
Interventions should be culturally relevant and targeted to the group’s values and beliefs.
Focus teaching on increasing physical activity at work
Nonwork activity has a stronger positive association with health than work activity.
Distribute English-only handouts with exercise statistics
Materials that ignore language background are less likely to motivate participation.

alt.q: Which nursing action best reflects culturally appropriate promotion of physical activity?
alt.a: Targeting exercise plans to the patient’s values and beliefs
alt.ex: Exercise and fall prevention interventions should be culturally appropriate and targeted to a patient’s values and beliefs.
w: Applying the same plan to every patient for fairness
A uniform plan ignores cultural beliefs that affect motivation and adherence.
Avoiding discussion of the patient’s cultural beliefs
Cultural beliefs about exercise should be assessed, not avoided.
Recommending only activities the nurse personally enjoys
Activities should be appropriate and enjoyable for the patient, not the nurse.

items.q: Which employer strategies help employees overcome barriers to physical activity at the work site? Select all that apply.
o: Providing an on-site walking path
A walking path addresses lack of time, neighborhood safety concerns, and lack of social support.
Posting signs encouraging use of the stairs
Work-site reminders such as stair signs are useful.
Offering free or discounted parking in distant lots
Parking rewards motivate employees to walk from distant lots.
Reserving the closest parking spots for all staff
Close parking removes walking opportunities rather than rewarding activity.
Installing extra elevators to replace stairwells
This discourages stair use, the opposite of recommended reminders.
items.ex: Employers help by offering on-site activity opportunities, reminders, and rewards such as discounted parking.

alt.q: A nurse is consulting with an employer on a workplace wellness program. Which elements reflect the evidence on work-site physical activity? Select all that apply.
o: Rewarding employees committed to physical fitness
Rewards are an effective strategy for employees committed to fitness.
Posting reminders to take the stairs
Reminders such as stair signs are useful.
Expecting improved productivity and morale
Work-site activity programs improve worker productivity and morale.
Removing stairwell signs to reduce clutter
Stair signs are helpful reminders that encourage activity.
Limiting activity opportunities to off-site gyms
On-site opportunities help overcome time constraints.
alt.ex: Work-site opportunities, reminders, and rewards help employees be active and improve productivity and morale.

items.q: How much physical activity is nationally recommended for children each day?
items.a: 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous activity
items.ex: Schools can help children attain the nationally recommended 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity daily.
w: 30 minutes or more of light activity
The recommendation is longer and at moderate-to-vigorous, not light, intensity.
20 minutes of vigorous activity only
Twenty minutes falls well short of the 60-minute daily recommendation.
90 minutes or more of light activity
The recommendation specifies moderate-to-vigorous intensity, not light activity.

alt.q: A school nurse is planning a program to help students reach the daily activity recommendation. What is the daily target for children?
alt.a: At least 60 minutes of moderate-to-vigorous activity
alt.ex: Children should get 60 minutes or more of moderate-to-vigorous physical activity every day.
w: At least 30 minutes of moderate activity
Thirty minutes is half of the daily recommendation for children.
At least 150 minutes of light activity
The 150-minute figure is a weekly adult guideline for moderate-intensity activity.
At least 15 minutes of vigorous activity
Fifteen minutes falls far short of the 60-minute daily recommendation.

items.q: Relatedness is the feeling of belonging to a group and is a basic psychological need that improves motivation.
items.a: True
items.ex: Relatedness is the feeling of belonging to a group, including friends, coaches, or therapists, and supports motivation.
items.ww: The book defines relatedness exactly this way and links it to motivation.

alt.q: Relatedness and social support mean the same thing, so assessing one covers the other.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Relatedness is a feeling of belonging; social support is support accessible through social ties. Both matter for motivation.
alt.ww: The book distinguishes the two concepts and says both are important for motivation.

items.q: Women’s physical activity levels are more likely than men’s to be influenced by general social support.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book notes that women’s physical activity is more likely than men’s to be influenced by general social support.
items.ww: The book specifically identifies women, not men, as more influenced by general social support.

alt.q: Men’s physical activity levels are more likely than women’s to be influenced by general social support.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Women’s, not men’s, activity levels are more likely to be influenced by general social support.
alt.ww: The book identifies women as more influenced, so this reverses the finding.

items.q: A patient with obesity wants to start exercising. Which outcome is most appropriate for the nurse and patient to set together?
items.a: Walk 20 minutes on 4 days each week, reviewed in 2 weeks
items.ex: Outcomes should be specific, measurable, achievable, realistic, relevant, timed, and regularly reevaluated.
w: Lose 30 pounds within the next month
Losing significant weight over a short time is an unrealistic expectation that causes frustration.
Try to be more active over the next 12 months
This is vague, not specific or measurable, and has no regular reevaluation.
Run 5 miles every day starting tomorrow
This is not achievable or realistic for a patient just starting to exercise.

alt.q: A patient states, “I want to lose 40 pounds before my reunion in 3 weeks.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Let’s set a smaller, specific goal we can review every 2 weeks.”
alt.ex: The nurse partners with the patient to avoid unrealistic expectations and sets specific, measurable, timed outcomes that are regularly reevaluated.
w: “That is a great goal for the next 3 weeks.”
Supporting an unrealistic short-term weight goal sets the patient up for frustration.
“You will need to exercise 3 hours every day.”
This endorses an unrealistic goal with an unsafe, unachievable plan.
“Goals do not matter if you exercise 1 hour daily.”
Goal setting promotes adherence, so dismissing it is not appropriate.

items.q: An older adult would like to exercise more. Which barriers to exercise did research identify among adults over age 60? Select all that apply.
o: Caregiving duties
Caregiving responsibilities were an identified barrier.
Low motivation
Low motivation was an identified barrier.
Lack of affordable and attractive options
Lack of affordable, attractive options was an identified barrier.
Misperceptions of physical activity and aging
Misperceptions about activity and aging were an identified barrier.
Perceiving that exercise supports independence
This perception makes participation more likely, not less.
Having too many community exercise choices
The barrier identified was a lack, not an excess, of options.
items.ex: Poor health, lifetime inactivity, caregiving, low motivation, misperceptions, and lack of affordable, attractive options were barriers for adults over 60.

alt.q: Which findings are associated with a higher prevalence of physical inactivity? Select all that apply.
o: A lower level of education
Inactivity increased as education level decreased.
A higher body mass index
Inactivity increased as body mass index increased.
Lifetime physical inactivity in an adult over 60
Lifetime inactivity was a barrier to exercise in older adults.
A higher level of education
Inactivity rises with decreasing, not increasing, education.
Perceiving exercise as promoting independence
This perception increases, rather than decreases, participation.
alt.ex: Physical inactivity is more common with lower education, higher BMI, and, in older adults, a history of lifetime inactivity.

items.q: Which statement by the nurse is most likely to increase an older adult’s participation in exercise?
items.a: “Regular exercise can help you stay independent at home.”
items.ex: When older adults perceive that exercise contributes to independence, participation in exercise is more likely.
w: “Exercise mainly benefits younger people.”
Exercise benefits everyone, and this message would discourage participation.
“High-impact workouts build bone fastest.”
Older adults should avoid high-impact programs that can lead to fractures.
“You should rest more now that you are older.”
Rest does not build the endurance, coordination, and stability that exercise provides.

alt.q: An older adult says, “At my age, exercise won’t make a difference.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Exercise can lower your fall risk and help you stay independent.”
alt.ex: Exercise improves endurance, coordination, and stability, reduces falls, and supports independence, which motivates older adults.
w: “You are right; it is too late to start now.”
Older adults should be taught it is never too late to begin exercising.
“Exercise will mostly help you lose weight fast.”
Promising rapid weight loss sets unrealistic expectations.
“Just do what your friends do at the gym.”
Exercise should be individualized to the patient’s abilities and preferences.

items.q: When assessing a patient’s community environment, which finding suggests limited access to safe places to exercise?
items.a: The patient lives in a rural area without parks or trails
items.ex: People from rural areas and racial and ethnic minority groups are less likely to have access to safe spaces to exercise.
w: The town offers greenways and fitness classes
Greenways and classes are community supports that promote physical fitness.
A safe walking path is near the patient’s home
A nearby safe path indicates good access to activity.
Local agencies sponsor regular community walks
Community programs support, rather than limit, safe physical activity.

alt.q: Which group does the book identify as less likely to have access to safe spaces to exercise?
alt.a: People living in rural areas
alt.ex: Many people from rural areas and from racial and ethnic minority groups have less access to safe exercise spaces.
w: People living near greenways
Greenways are community resources that increase access to safe activity.
People with work-site walking paths
Work-site paths provide safe opportunities to walk.
People in towns with fitness classes
Community fitness classes increase, not limit, access.

items.q: To build competence in skills such as assisting with ambulation, using assistive devices, and transferring patients, a nurse should collaborate most with which professional?
items.a: Physical therapist
items.ex: Physical therapists’ education focuses on these skills, so collaborating with them helps nurses grow in competency.
w: Registered dietitian
Dietitians recommend dietary changes that may improve energy, not transfer techniques.
Respiratory therapist
Respiratory therapists focus on breathing care rather than ambulation and transfer skills.
Pharmacist
Pharmacists focus on medications, not mobility skills.

alt.q: Whose education is focused on skills such as using assistive devices, assisting with ambulation, and transferring patients?
alt.a: Physical therapists
alt.ex: The book recommends collaborating with physical therapists, whose education focuses on these movement skills.
w: Registered dietitians
Dietitians focus on nutrition and energy for exercise.
Occupational health nurses
The book does not identify them as the experts in these movement skills.
Health care providers
Providers prescribe therapy and activity limits; PTs focus on the movement skills themselves.

items.q: A patient at a rehabilitation center describes a plan to start walking every morning after discharge. Which stage of change best describes this patient?
items.a: Preparation
items.ex: A patient who describes a concrete plan to exercise after discharge is in the preparation stage.
w: Contemplation
Contemplation is thinking about or trying exercise inconsistently without commitment to start.
Action
Action means the patient has been actively exercising weekly for the past several months.
Precontemplation
Precontemplation means no intention to start exercising in the next 6 months.

alt.q: A patient says, “I keep thinking I should exercise, and I tried a few times, but I never stick with it.” Which stage of change best describes this patient?
alt.a: Contemplation
alt.ex: Patients who have been thinking about exercising or try it inconsistently are likely in the contemplation stage.
w: Preparation
Preparation involves a concrete plan for action in the immediate future.
Maintenance
Maintenance means action has been sustained for at least 6 months.
Precontemplation
Precontemplation means the person does not intend to change in the foreseeable future.
