items.q: During the BMAT 2.0 assessment, a patient pivots to the edge of the bed but becomes light-headed and diaphoretic within the first minute. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Keep the patient at Level 1 and use SPHM equipment for transfers
items.ex: Patients who cannot sit without becoming tachycardic, diaphoretic, or light-headed stay at Level 1 and need SPHM equipment.
w: Proceed to the Stretch task to test leg strength
A patient advances only after passing the current level’s task.
Have the patient stand to see whether symptoms resolve
Standing an unstable patient risks a fall; the patient failed seated tolerance.
Record Level 2 because the patient reached the bed’s edge
Reaching the edge is not passing; the patient must sit symptom-free and shake hands.

alt.q: Which finding allows a patient to advance from BMAT 2.0 Level 1 to Level 2?
alt.a: Sits unsupported and reaches across midline to shake hands without symptoms
alt.ex: Passing Sit and Shake requires unsupported seated balance and reaching across the midline with each hand without tachycardia, diaphoresis, or light-headedness.
w: Marches in place using small steps for three repetitions
Marching in place is part of the Level 4 Step task.
Pumps each ankle at least three times while seated
Ankle pumps are part of the Level 2 Stretch task.
Rises from sitting to standing with feet shoulder-width apart
Rising to stand is the Level 3 Stand task.

items.q: After exercise, heart rate and blood pressure should increase and then return to resting level within 1 to 5 minutes.
items.a: True
items.ex: Comparing post-activity vital signs with baseline shows activity tolerance; both should return to resting level within 1 to 5 minutes.
items.ww: The book sets 1 to 5 minutes as the expected return to resting level after exercise.

alt.q: After exercise, a patient’s heart rate is expected to stay above resting level for at least 30 minutes.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Heart rate and BP should return to resting level within 1 to 5 minutes after exercise.
alt.ww: A prolonged elevation is not the expected response; the book cites a 1- to 5-minute return.

items.q: A patient is tired and weak after exertion, exercises less, and rests more. Further assessment shows an abnormal heart rate and mild shortness of breath after exercise. Which nursing diagnosis is most accurate?
items.a: Activity Intolerance
items.ex: Fatigue-type cues plus abnormal heart rate and mild dyspnea after exercise lead to a definitive diagnosis of Activity Intolerance.
w: Fatigue
Tiredness alone could suggest Fatigue, but abnormal heart rate and dyspnea after exercise point to Activity Intolerance.
Impaired Mobility
Impaired Mobility is supported by cues such as slow gait, reduced joint motion, and difficulty standing.
Lack of Play Activity
Nothing in these cues relates to play activity.

alt.q: Why must a nurse identify the related factor for Activity Intolerance, such as excess weight gain versus prolonged bed rest?
alt.a: Different related factors require very different interventions
alt.ex: Related factors direct the choice of interventions; Activity Intolerance from weight gain needs different interventions than from bed rest.
w: Related factors determine the diagnosis label itself
The label stays Activity Intolerance; the related factor directs interventions.
Related factors are needed only for risk diagnoses
Related factors apply to problem-focused diagnoses; risk diagnoses use risk factors.
Related factors replace the need for patient outcomes
Outcomes are still set with the patient after diagnosis.

items.q: A 50-year-old patient is cleared by the health care provider to begin exercising at 60% of maximum heart rate. Which target heart rate should the nurse teach?
items.a: 102 beats/min
items.ex: Maximum heart rate is 220 minus age (170); 60% of 170 is 102 beats/min.
w: 96 beats/min
This is 60% of 160, the maximum for a 60-year-old.
119 beats/min
This is 70% of 170, higher than the prescribed 60%.
136 beats/min
This is 80% of 170, well above the prescribed starting target.

alt.q: A 70-year-old patient beginning an exercise program is to start at 60% of maximum heart rate. What is the target heart rate?
alt.a: 90 beats/min
alt.ex: 220 minus 70 gives a maximum of 150; 60% of 150 is 90 beats/min.
w: 84 beats/min
This is below 60% of the 150 beats/min maximum.
105 beats/min
This is 70% of 150, above the prescribed starting target.
120 beats/min
This is 80% of 150, far above a 60% starting target.

items.q: While monitoring a patient’s heart rate during exercise, the nurse should have the patient stop the activity when which findings occur? Select all that apply.
o: Heart rate rises above the targeted heart rate
Exceeding the target heart rate is a reason to stop.
Heart rate falls more than 20% from the resting value
A decrease of more than 20% from resting is a reason to stop.
Heart rate drops below 40 beats/min
A heart rate under 40 beats/min is a reason to stop.
Heart rate rises modestly but stays below target
A modest rise within target is an expected response to exercise.
Heart rate returns to resting level 3 minutes afterward
Return to resting within 1 to 5 minutes is a normal response.
items.ex: Stop activity if HR is above target, decreases more than 20% from resting, or is below 40 beats/min.

alt.q: A patient’s resting heart rate is 80 beats/min and the target rate is 100 beats/min. Which heart rates during exercise mean the patient should stop? Select all that apply.
o: 108 beats/min
This exceeds the target heart rate of 100.
60 beats/min
This is a 25% decrease from the resting value of 80.
92 beats/min
This is an expected rise that remains below target.
66 beats/min
This is about an 18% decrease, which does not exceed 20%.
98 beats/min
This remains within the target heart rate.
alt.ex: With a resting rate of 80 and target of 100, stop for rates above 100 or below 64 (more than a 20% drop).

items.q: A patient on prolonged bed rest sits on the side of the bed for the first time. After 90 seconds he still reports dizziness, and his systolic BP has dropped 24 mm Hg. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Return the patient to bed and recheck the blood pressure
items.ex: If dizziness lasts more than 60 seconds or systolic BP drops at least 20 mm Hg within 3 minutes of sitting, return the patient to bed.
w: Apply the gait belt and help him to stand
Standing a patient with orthostatic hypotension risks syncope and a fall.
Have him dangle 5 more minutes, then walk
These findings meet the criteria to return to bed, not to proceed with ambulation.
Encourage brisk walking to raise his blood pressure
Ambulating a symptomatic, hypotensive patient is unsafe.

alt.q: Which finding meets the book’s definition of orthostatic hypotension?
alt.a: Systolic BP drop of 22 mm Hg within 3 minutes of rising
alt.ex: Orthostatic hypotension is a systolic drop of at least 20 mm Hg or diastolic drop of at least 10 mm Hg within 2 to 5 minutes of rising.
w: Systolic BP drop of 8 mm Hg within 3 minutes of rising
An 8 mm Hg systolic drop is below the 20 mm Hg threshold.
Diastolic BP drop of 6 mm Hg within 3 minutes of rising
A 6 mm Hg diastolic drop is below the 10 mm Hg threshold.
Systolic BP rise of 20 mm Hg within 3 minutes of rising
Orthostatic hypotension is a drop, not a rise, in blood pressure.

items.q: Which patients are at higher risk for orthostatic hypotension? Select all that apply.
o: A patient on prolonged bed rest
Immobilization and prolonged bed rest increase the risk.
An older adult
Older adults are at higher risk.
A patient receiving antihypertensive drugs
Antihypertensive drugs increase the risk.
A patient who is dehydrated
Depleted intravascular volume lowers BP on standing.
A young adult who has no chronic illness
The book lists older age and chronic illness, not healthy young adults, as risks.
A patient who ambulates independently daily
Immobility, not regular ambulation, raises the risk.
items.ex: Risk is higher with immobility or bed rest, older age, antihypertensives, dehydration, and chronic illnesses such as diabetes and cardiovascular disease.

alt.q: A nurse is monitoring a patient for orthostatic hypotension when the patient first stands. Which symptoms may occur? Select all that apply.
o: Dizziness or light-headedness
These are common symptoms of orthostatic hypotension.
Syncope
Fainting can occur with orthostatic hypotension.
Muscle ache in the neck and shoulders
Neck and shoulder aching is a listed symptom.
Flushed, warm skin
Flushing is not a listed symptom of orthostatic hypotension.
Increased appetite
Appetite change is not a listed symptom.
alt.ex: Orthostatic hypotension may be asymptomatic or cause dizziness, light-headedness, syncope, neck and shoulder ache, and even angina.

items.q: A gait belt is a safe tool for lifting or carrying a patient by the waist if the patient begins to fall.
items.a: False
items.ex: A gait belt stabilizes balance; it is not used to lift or carry a patient, and trying to catch a patient can injure the nurse.
items.ww: The book states a gait belt is not to be used to lift or carry a patient by the waist.

alt.q: A gait belt is placed snugly below the belly button so that two fingers fit between the belt and the patient’s body.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Correct placement is snug, below the belly button, with two fingers fitting under it, avoiding incisions, tubes, and IV lines.
alt.ww: This is the placement the book describes for a gait belt.

items.q: While ambulating with a gait belt in place, a patient says, “I feel faint,” and her knees begin to buckle. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Extend one leg, let her slide down it, and protect her head
items.ex: With a wide base of support, the nurse extends a leg, lets the patient slide to the floor, and protects the head.
w: Grab her under the arms and lift her upright
Trying to stop a fall by lifting can injure the nurse and the patient.
Pull up firmly on the gait belt to keep her standing
A gait belt is not for lifting; trying to catch a patient risks back injury.
Release the belt and step away to avoid injury
The nurse should guide the patient safely to the floor, not let her fall unassisted.

alt.q: Which stance does the book describe for supporting a patient who begins to fall during ambulation?
alt.a: Wide base of support with one foot in front of the other
alt.ex: A wide base of support with one foot forward supports the patient’s weight as the nurse guides the patient to the floor.
w: Feet together with the knees locked straight
A narrow base with locked knees gives poor stability and increases injury risk.
Behind the patient with arms around the chest
The book describes holding the gait belt and lowering the patient, not a chest hold.
Kneeling beside the patient to catch the hips
Kneeling does not provide a stable base for guiding the patient down.

items.q: A nurse is ambulating a patient who had a stroke and has right-sided weakness. Where should the nurse stand?
items.a: On the patient’s right (affected) side
items.ex: For patients with neurological deficits such as stroke, the nurse stands on the affected side.
w: On the patient’s left (unaffected) side
The unaffected side is used for patients with orthopedic problems.
Directly in front of the patient (facing)
Standing in front blocks the walking path and is not the recommended position.
Directly behind the patient (holding shoulders)
The nurse stands at the side holding the gait belt, not behind holding shoulders.

alt.q: A patient with a fractured left ankle is ambulating with assistance. On which side should the nurse stand?
alt.a: On the patient’s right (unaffected) side
alt.ex: For patients with orthopedic problems, the nurse stands on the unaffected side.
w: On the patient’s left (affected) side
The affected side is used for neurological deficits, not orthopedic problems.
Directly in front of the patient (facing)
Standing in front blocks the path and is not the recommended position.
Directly behind the patient (holding shoulders)
The nurse stands at the side holding the gait belt.

items.q: In walking with a cane, which step comes right after “Place the cane a small stride (15 to 25 cm) forward”?
items.a: Move the weaker leg forward to the cane
items.ex: The cane goes forward first, then the weaker leg, then the stronger leg, so two points of support stay on the floor.
w: Advance the stronger leg past the cane
That's step 3 of 3.

alt.q: Which step comes first in walking with a cane?
alt.a: Place the cane a small stride (15 to 25 cm) forward
alt.ex: The cane goes forward first, then the weaker leg, then the stronger leg, so two points of support stay on the floor.
w: Move the weaker leg forward to the cane
That's step 2 of 3.
Advance the stronger leg past the cane
That's step 3 of 3.

alt.q: Which step comes last in walking with a cane?
alt.a: Advance the stronger leg past the cane
alt.ex: The cane goes forward first, then the weaker leg, then the stronger leg, so two points of support stay on the floor.
w: Move the weaker leg forward to the cane
That's step 2 of 3.
Place the cane a small stride (15 to 25 cm) forward
That's step 1 of 3.

alt.q: In walking with a cane, which step comes right after “Move the weaker leg forward to the cane”?
alt.a: Advance the stronger leg past the cane
alt.ex: The cane goes forward first, then the weaker leg, then the stronger leg, so two points of support stay on the floor.
w: Place the cane a small stride (15 to 25 cm) forward
That's step 1 of 3.

alt.q: In walking with a cane, which step comes right before “Move the weaker leg forward to the cane”?
alt.a: Place the cane a small stride (15 to 25 cm) forward
alt.ex: The cane goes forward first, then the weaker leg, then the stronger leg, so two points of support stay on the floor.
w: Advance the stronger leg past the cane
That's step 3 of 3.

alt.q: In walking with a cane, which step comes right before “Advance the stronger leg past the cane”?
alt.a: Move the weaker leg forward to the cane
alt.ex: The cane goes forward first, then the weaker leg, then the stronger leg, so two points of support stay on the floor.
w: Place the cane a small stride (15 to 25 cm) forward
That's step 1 of 3.

ord.q: Put the steps for walking with a cane in order, starting from standing with weight on both legs.
items: Place the cane a small stride (15 to 25 cm) forward
Move the weaker leg forward to the cane
Advance the stronger leg past the cane
ord.ex: The cane goes forward first, then the weaker leg, then the stronger leg, so two points of support stay on the floor.

items.q: Which description fits the Four-point alternating gait?
items.a: Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor
items.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.
w: All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first
That goes with Three-point gait.
Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg
That goes with Two-point gait.
Often used by people with paraplegia who wear weight-supporting braces
That goes with Swing-through gait.

alt.q: Which description fits the Three-point gait?
alt.a: All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first
alt.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.
w: Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor
That goes with Four-point alternating gait.
Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg
That goes with Two-point gait.
Often used by people with paraplegia who wear weight-supporting braces
That goes with Swing-through gait.

alt.q: Which description fits the Two-point gait?
alt.a: Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg
alt.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.
w: Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor
That goes with Four-point alternating gait.
All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first
That goes with Three-point gait.
Often used by people with paraplegia who wear weight-supporting braces
That goes with Swing-through gait.

alt.q: Which description fits the Swing-through gait?
alt.a: Often used by people with paraplegia who wear weight-supporting braces
alt.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.
w: Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor
That goes with Four-point alternating gait.
All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first
That goes with Three-point gait.
Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg
That goes with Two-point gait.

alt.q: Which description fits the Tripod position?
alt.a: Basic stance with crutches 15 cm in front of and beside each foot
alt.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.
w: Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor
That goes with Four-point alternating gait.
All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first
That goes with Three-point gait.
Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg
That goes with Two-point gait.

alt.q: Which crutch gait or stance is this: “Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor”?
alt.a: Four-point alternating gait
alt.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.
w: Three-point gait
Three-point gait: All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first.
Two-point gait
Two-point gait: Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg.
Swing-through gait
Swing-through gait: Often used by people with paraplegia who wear weight-supporting braces.

alt.q: Which crutch gait or stance is this: “All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first”?
alt.a: Three-point gait
alt.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.
w: Four-point alternating gait
Four-point alternating gait: Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor.
Two-point gait
Two-point gait: Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg.
Swing-through gait
Swing-through gait: Often used by people with paraplegia who wear weight-supporting braces.

alt.q: Which crutch gait or stance is this: “Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg”?
alt.a: Two-point gait
alt.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.
w: Four-point alternating gait
Four-point alternating gait: Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor.
Three-point gait
Three-point gait: All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first.
Swing-through gait
Swing-through gait: Often used by people with paraplegia who wear weight-supporting braces.

alt.q: Which crutch gait or stance is this: “Often used by people with paraplegia who wear weight-supporting braces”?
alt.a: Swing-through gait
alt.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.
w: Four-point alternating gait
Four-point alternating gait: Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor.
Three-point gait
Three-point gait: All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first.
Two-point gait
Two-point gait: Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg.

alt.q: Which crutch gait or stance is this: “Basic stance with crutches 15 cm in front of and beside each foot”?
alt.a: Tripod position
alt.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.
w: Four-point alternating gait
Four-point alternating gait: Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor.
Three-point gait
Three-point gait: All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first.
Two-point gait
Two-point gait: Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg.

mt.q: Match each crutch gait or stance with its description.
pairs: Each leg moves with the opposite crutch; three points always on the floor
All weight borne on one foot; affected leg kept off the ground at first
Partial weight on each foot; crutch moves with the opposite leg
Often used by people with paraplegia who wear weight-supporting braces
Basic stance with crutches 15 cm in front of and beside each foot
mt.ex: Crutch gaits differ in how much weight each leg bears; the tripod position is the basic stance assumed before walking.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient with a sprained right ankle to use crutches on stairs. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “Going up, my left leg leads; going down, my right leg leads.”
items.ex: Going up stairs the stronger leg leads; going down the affected leg leads with the crutch.
w: “Going up, my right leg leads; going down, my left leg leads.”
This reverses the rule: the strong leg leads going up, the affected leg going down.
“My left leg leads both going up and going down.”
The affected leg, not the strong leg, leads when descending.
“I can hop down the stairs on my left leg to go faster.”
Patients are cautioned not to hop while descending stairs.

alt.q: A patient with a weak left leg is going down stairs with crutches. Which leg should lead?
alt.a: The left (affected) leg, with the crutch
alt.ex: When descending, the patient lowers the crutch and the weak or affected leg first, then brings down the strong leg.
w: The right (strong) leg, before the crutch
The strong leg leads going up, not going down.
Both legs together (in a small hop)
Patients are cautioned not to hop while descending stairs.
The right (strong) leg, with the crutch
The strong leg comes down last, after the crutch and affected leg.

items.q: For which patient conditions is active range-of-motion (AROM) exercise contraindicated? Select all that apply.
o: A healing fracture site
A healing fracture is a contraindication to AROM.
A healing surgical site
A healing surgical site is a contraindication to AROM.
Severe, acute soft tissue trauma
Severe acute soft tissue trauma contraindicates AROM.
Joint instability
An unstable joint is a contraindication to AROM.
Voluntary control of muscle movement
Voluntary control is the indication for AROM, not a contraindication.
Mild muscle weakness needing strengthening
AROM is chosen based on muscle weakness and the activity needing strengthening.
items.ex: AROM is contraindicated with healing fractures or surgical sites, severe acute soft tissue trauma, joint pain, limited movement, instability, deformity, and contractures.

alt.q: Which findings should lead the nurse to withhold active range-of-motion exercise for a joint? Select all that apply.
o: Joint pain
Joint pain is a contraindication to AROM.
Contractures
Contractures are a contraindication to AROM.
Joint deformity
Deformity is a contraindication to AROM.
The patient can contract and coordinate the movement
This ability is the reason AROM is used.
The patient is alert and follows directions
Alertness supports, rather than prevents, AROM.
alt.ex: Withhold AROM for joint pain, contractures, deformity, instability, limited movement, and healing fractures, surgical sites, or severe soft tissue trauma.

items.q: Adults should do at least 150 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week plus muscle-strengthening activities on 2 or more days.
items.a: True
items.ex: The DHHS guidelines recommend 150 to 300 minutes of moderate aerobic activity weekly and muscle strengthening of all major groups 2 or more days.
items.ww: This matches the Physical Activity Guidelines for Americans described in the chapter.

alt.q: Older adults who cannot reach 150 minutes of moderate activity because of chronic conditions should avoid exercise.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: These older adults should be as physically active as their abilities and conditions allow.
alt.ww: The guidelines encourage activity within the person’s abilities rather than avoidance.

items.q: Which activity can the nurse appropriately delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Assisting a stable patient with ambulation
items.ex: Assisting with ambulation can be delegated when a patient’s condition is stable, with direction about BP checks and symptoms.
w: Promoting early exercise in the outpatient setting
The book states promoting early activity and exercise in the outpatient setting cannot be delegated.
Choosing the crutch gait the patient will use
A PT with the health care provider determines the appropriate crutch gait.
Setting the patient’s target heart rate for exercise
Target heart rate is set by the health care provider and nurse, not AP.

alt.q: A nurse delegates ambulation of a stable patient to AP. Which instruction should the nurse give?
alt.a: Return the patient to bed or chair if dizziness occurs
alt.ex: AP should immediately return the patient to bed or chair for diaphoresis, nausea, dizziness, or blurred vision and report it.
w: Skip the BP check if the patient walked yesterday
AP should assess BP before ambulation and when sitting on the side of the bed.
Keep walking if the patient becomes nauseated
Nausea is a reason to stop and return the patient to bed or chair.
Let the patient walk in regular socks
Nonskid shoes or socks are required before ambulating.

sections.name: Skill 38.1 · Using safe and effective transfer techniques

items.q: A nurse is planning bed-to-chair transfers for several patients. Which transfer requires the nurse to assist and supervise rather than simply delegate it to AP?
items.a: The first transfer of a patient after extensive surgery
items.ex: The nurse assists and supervises patients transferred for the first time after prolonged bed rest, extensive surgery, critical illness, or spinal cord trauma.
w: A routine transfer of a stable patient who transfers daily
Routine transfers of stable patients can be delegated to trained AP.
A transfer of a patient who stands and pivots on his own
An independent patient needs only standby; trained AP can do this.
A return to bed for a patient with a documented transfer plan
An established, documented transfer can be delegated to trained AP.

alt.q: Who is responsible for initially assessing a patient’s readiness and functional ability to transfer?
alt.a: The nurse
alt.ex: Transfers can be delegated to trained AP, but the nurse is responsible for the initial assessment of readiness and functional ability.
w: The assistive personnel
AP can perform transfers but do not do the initial assessment.
The family caregiver
Family caregivers may learn transfers but do not assess readiness in the hospital.
The patient, by self-report
Do not rely on self-report; obtain an objective assessment.

items.q: When delegating a transfer to AP, what information should the nurse provide? Select all that apply.
o: The patient’s mobility restrictions
AP need to know mobility restrictions for a safe transfer.
Changes in blood pressure to look for
AP should watch for BP changes during position changes.
Sensory alterations, such as being medicated or confused
These alterations may affect a safe transfer.
To report dizziness or the patient’s inability to assist
AP should report these observations to the nurse.
How to adjust the patient’s analgesic dose
Adjusting medication is outside the AP role.
items.ex: The nurse explains mobility restrictions, BP changes, sensory alterations, and what to observe and report, such as dizziness or ability to assist.

alt.q: After a delegated transfer, which observations should AP report back to the nurse? Select all that apply.
o: The patient became dizzy
Dizziness is a key observation to report.
The patient was unable to assist
The patient’s inability to assist should be reported.
The patient was able to assist
The book asks AP to report the patient’s ability or inability to assist.
The patient’s dietary preferences
Food preferences are unrelated to transfer safety.
The number of visitors in the room
Visitor count is unrelated to the patient’s transfer response.
alt.ex: AP report what they observe about transfer safety, such as dizziness and the patient’s ability or inability to assist.

items.q: When preparing to transfer a patient from bed to chair, how should the nurse position the chair?
items.a: At a 45-degree angle against the bed, facing the foot of the bed
items.ex: A chair at about 45 degrees with one side against the bed, facing the foot, gives easy access for the pivot.
w: At a 90-degree angle to the bed, facing the head of the bed
Facing the head of the bed would make the patient pivot farther and awkwardly.
Parallel to the bed at 0 degrees, facing the wall
A chair facing the wall does not allow a smooth pivot into the seat.
At a 45-degree angle, 1 meter away from the bed
The chair should be against the bed to shorten the transfer distance.

alt.q: Before a bed-to-wheelchair transfer, which wheelchair preparation is correct?
alt.a: Lock the brakes and remove the footrests
alt.ex: Lock the wheelchair brakes and remove footrests, and lock the bed brakes, before transferring.
w: Unlock the brakes so the chair can move
An unlocked chair can roll away and cause a fall.
Leave the footrests down for the feet
Footrests should be removed so they do not obstruct the transfer.
Raise the armrests out of the way
The patient uses the armrests for support while easing into the chair.

items.q: The daughter of a patient admitted with pneumonia says, “She walks fine at home, so she can get up to the chair by herself.” Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Perform the BMAT 2.0 before deciding how to transfer her
items.ex: Do not rely on patient or family self-report; obtain an objective assessment to determine capability.
w: Let the patient transfer alone as the daughter suggests
Family report is not an objective assessment of current ability.
Ask the patient whether she agrees she can transfer
Patient self-report is also not a reliable measure of ability.
Use a full-body lift without further assessment
Equipment should be chosen from an objective mobility assessment, not assumed.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid relying on a patient’s self-report of the ability to sit, stand, or walk?
alt.a: An objective assessment is needed to determine capability accurately
alt.ex: The book directs nurses to obtain an objective assessment, such as the BMAT 2.0, rather than rely on self-report.
w: Patients always overstate their abilities on purpose
The issue is accuracy, not intentional deception.
Self-report is useful only for pain ratings
The book does not limit self-report to pain; it warns against using it for mobility.
Family members should make the decision instead
Family report is self-report too and is equally unreliable.

items.q: A patient fails the BMAT 2.0 Stretch task but can bear weight on at least one leg. Which device is recommended for transfer?
items.a: Sit-to-stand lift
items.ex: At Level 2, use a sit-to-stand lift if the patient can bear weight on at least one leg, or a total lift if not.
w: Total lift with a sling
A total lift is for a Level 2 patient who cannot bear weight on at least one leg.
Standby assist only
Standby is for patients who can bear weight and balance independently.
A cane or walker only
Assistive devices are options for patients who fail Stand or Step.

alt.q: A patient fails the BMAT 2.0 Sit and Shake task. Which transfer approach is recommended?
alt.a: Total lift with sling or a lateral transfer device
alt.ex: Level 1 patients need a total lift with sling, positioning sheet, or straps, or lateral devices such as a friction-reducing or air-assisted device.
w: Sit-to-stand lift with one caregiver
Sit-to-stand lifts are for patients who can bear weight on at least one leg.
Stand-and-pivot with a gait belt
A patient without seated balance cannot safely stand and pivot.
Ambulation with a walker
Assistive devices are options for patients who fail Stand or Step.

items.q: A patient with left hemiplegia ignores objects and people on her left side. When teaching her to transfer, what should the nurse instruct her to do?

Look only toward her stronger right side
Looking only to the right worsens inattention to the neglected left side.

alt.q: What does “neglect” mean for a patient with hemiplegia?

Peripheral sensation loss decreases proprioception but is not neglect.
Fear of falling during transfers and walking

items.q: A patient rates pain at 7 on a 0-to-10 scale before a planned transfer to a chair. Which action is best?

Five minutes is too short; the book specifies 30 minutes.
Postpone all transfers until pain is 0 out of 10
Transfers need not wait for zero pain; premedicate and proceed.

alt.q: A patient received a prescribed analgesic 30 minutes before a transfer. What does the patient now require?

The analgesic is timed to allow the transfer, not delay it.

items.q: A patient with right-sided hemiparesis is moving from bed to chair. Where should the nurse place the chair?

alt.q: Which rule from the safe patient-handling algorithm guides the direction of a transfer?

items.q: Why should a patient with a new hip replacement and posterior hip precautions not be transferred with a Hoyer lift?
