ord.ex: The sling is placed by rolling the patient, the lift is positioned and attached, the patient sits up, is raised, then lowered into the chair.

items.q: Which outcome results from maintaining correct body alignment?
items.a: Reduced strain on musculoskeletal structures
items.ex: Correct alignment reduces musculoskeletal strain, maintains muscle tone, promotes comfort, and aids balance and energy conservation.
w: Increased friction between the skin and the bed
Friction is a force opposing movement; alignment does not increase it.
Displacement of the center of gravity
Displacement of the center of gravity occurs when balance control is lost, not with correct alignment.
Greater energy use during daily activities
Correct alignment contributes to conservation of energy, not greater energy use.

alt.q: A nurse explains to a student why patients are positioned in correct body alignment. Which benefit should the nurse include?
alt.a: It helps maintain muscle tone and promotes comfort
alt.ex: Correct body alignment helps maintain muscle tone, promotes comfort, and contributes to balance.
w: It increases the weight the body exerts downward
Weight is the force of gravity on the body; alignment does not change it.
It eliminates the need to reposition the patient
Aligned patients still need regular repositioning to prevent complications of immobility.
It replaces the need for friction-reducing devices
Alignment does not remove the need for safe patient-handling devices when moving patients.

items.q: Where is the center of gravity usually located in a person who is standing?
items.a: At 55% to 57% of standing height, in the midline
items.ex: People are not geometrically perfect; their center of gravity is usually at 55% to 57% of standing height in the midline.
w: At 35% to 37% of standing height, in the midline
This is too low; the center of gravity lies at 55% to 57% of standing height.
At 75% to 77% of standing height, at chest level
This is too high; the center of gravity lies at 55% to 57% of standing height.
At 50% of standing height, at the exact center
Only symmetrical inanimate objects have a center of gravity at their exact center.

alt.q: Why does relying only on body mechanics to lift patients often injure nurses?
alt.a: A person’s center of gravity is not at the body’s exact center
alt.ex: Unlike symmetrical objects, people’s centers of gravity sit at 55% to 57% of standing height, so lifting them by body mechanics alone causes injury.
w: A patient’s weight is directed upward when lying in bed
Weight is always directed downward by gravity.
Friction decreases as the patient’s surface area increases
Friction increases, not decreases, as surface area increases.
A patient’s center of gravity is always at the feet
The center of gravity is in the midline at 55% to 57% of standing height.

items.q: A nurse must move a patient who is unable to assist up in bed. Which approach best prevents friction and shear on the patient’s skin?
items.a: Use a full-body hydraulic lift to raise the patient off the bed
items.ex: A full-body lift moves the patient off the bed surface, preventing friction, tearing, and shearing of skin and protecting staff.
w: Slide the patient up by pulling under the patient’s arms
Dragging the patient across the sheets creates friction and shear and risks staff injury.
Have two staff members lift the patient using body mechanics
Patient lifting is discouraged; body mechanics alone often injure staff.
Raise the head of the bed above 60 degrees before moving
Elevating the head of the bed beyond 60 degrees promotes shear as the skeleton slides down.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with obesity who cannot help with moving up in bed. Which action is best?
alt.a: Use an ergonomic assistive device such as a full-body lift
alt.ex: A larger patient produces more friction, and an ergonomic lift removes the patient from the bed surface to protect skin and staff.
w: Ask the patient to push with the heels while staff pull
The patient cannot assist, and pulling the patient across the bed increases friction.
Lift the patient using a wide base of support
Lifting patients is discouraged because body mechanics alone often cause staff injury.
Move the patient quickly to limit time spent against the sheets
Speed does not prevent friction; a lift that removes the patient from the surface does.

items.q: Which statement about friction is accurate?
items.a: Friction increases as the surface area of the moved object increases
items.ex: Friction opposes movement, and the greater the surface area of the object moved, the greater the friction.
w: Friction is a force that acts in the direction of movement
Friction acts in a direction that opposes movement.
Friction decreases as the size of the moved object increases
A larger object produces greater, not less, resistance to movement.
Friction is the force of gravity acting on body weight
That describes weight; friction is a force opposing movement.

alt.q: Two patients need repositioning in bed: one of normal weight and one with obesity. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: The patient with obesity will produce more resistance against the bed
alt.ex: A larger body has more surface area against the bed and therefore produces greater friction and resistance to movement.
w: Both patients will produce the same resistance against the bed
Resistance increases with the surface area and size of the object moved.
The patient of normal weight will produce more resistance
The smaller patient produces less, not more, resistance.
Resistance depends only on how high the bed is raised
Resistance to movement depends on surface area and size, not bed height.

items.q: A patient sits with the head of the bed elevated to 75 degrees and repeatedly slides toward the foot of the bed. Which explanation of the risk is accurate?
items.a: Deep tissue is damaged by shear even if the skin looks less affected
items.ex: Shear stretches and damages blood vessels in deeper tissue, so pressure injuries develop in undermined tissue while surface tissue looks less affected.
w: The skin surface is damaged first, so redness shows the full extent
Surface tissue appears less affected; the damage is in the undermined deep tissue.
Only friction is present because the skin moves with the skeleton
In shear the skin stays against the sheets while the skeleton moves.
Gravity lifts the bony skeleton toward the head of the bed
Gravity pulls the skeleton toward the foot of the bed, not the head.

alt.q: Which situation is a common example of shear?
alt.a: The head of the bed is raised beyond 60 degrees and the patient slides down
alt.ex: With the head of the bed above 60 degrees, gravity pulls the skeleton down while the skin stays against the sheets.
w: A full-body hydraulic lift raises the patient off the mattress
A lift removes the patient from the bed surface, which prevents shear.
The patient stands with weight evenly spread over both feet
Standing balanced does not move bone against stationary skin.
The head of the bed is flat and the patient turns using a lift sheet
Keeping the bed flat avoids the gravity pull that causes shear.

items.q: What gives bones their firmness?
items.a: Inorganic salts such as calcium and phosphate in the bone matrix
items.ex: Firmness comes from inorganic salts such as calcium and phosphate in the bone matrix, giving rigidity for weight bearing.
w: Cartilage that lines the outer surface of long bones
Cartilage is a supporting connective tissue mainly in joints, not the source of bone firmness.
Red blood cells produced in the bone marrow
Marrow produces red blood cells; firmness comes from mineral salts.
Tendons that attach muscle tightly to the bone
Tendons connect muscle to bone; they do not make bone firm.

alt.q: A patient asks why bones can bear weight without bending. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: Calcium and phosphate salts in bone make it rigid enough to bear weight
alt.ex: Bone firmness from inorganic salts keeps long bones straight and enables them to withstand weight bearing.
w: Ligaments wrap around each bone and keep it from bending
Ligaments bind joints and connect bones and cartilages; they do not make bone rigid.
Skeletal muscles stay contracted to hold bones straight
Muscles contract and relax for movement; rigidity comes from bone minerals.
Bone marrow fills the bone and stiffens it with blood
Marrow produces red blood cells and stores blood; it does not provide rigidity.

items.q: A patient with diminished red blood cell production from altered bone marrow function reports tiring easily. Which nursing concern is most important?
items.a: Increased risk of falling related to fatigue
items.ex: Reduced hemoglobin lowers oxygen-carrying ability, causing fatigue that decreases mobility and increases fall risk.
w: Increased risk of shear related to high body weight
Shear relates to sliding in bed, not to reduced red blood cell production.
Increased bone firmness related to calcium release
Calcium release weakens bone; it does not increase firmness.
Increased muscle tone related to low hemoglobin
Low hemoglobin causes fatigue, not increased muscle tone.

alt.q: Why do patients with reduced red blood cell production tire easily?
alt.a: Their hemoglobin and oxygen-carrying ability are reduced
alt.ex: Long bone marrow produces red blood cells; less production means less hemoglobin and oxygen delivery, causing fatigue.
w: Their bones release too much phosphate into the blood
Phosphate release is not the cause; fatigue comes from reduced oxygen-carrying ability.
Their tendons lose elasticity and become stiff
Tendons are normally inelastic, and this does not explain fatigue from marrow disorders.
Their motor fibers no longer cross at the medulla
Motor fiber crossing is a nervous system feature unrelated to red blood cell production.

items.q: Which structure connects muscle to bone?
items.a: Tendon
items.ex: Tendons are white, glistening fibrous bands that connect muscle to bone and are strong, flexible, and inelastic.
w: Ligament
Ligaments bind joints together and connect bones and cartilages.
Cartilage
Cartilage is a nonvascular supporting connective tissue mainly in joints and the thorax.
Bone marrow
Bone marrow participates in red blood cell production and stores blood.

alt.q: Which description fits a tendon?
alt.a: A strong, flexible, inelastic band that attaches muscle to bone
alt.ex: Tendons connect muscle to bone and are strong, flexible, and inelastic.
w: A flexible band that binds joints and connects bones to cartilages
This describes a ligament.
A nonvascular tissue found chiefly in joints, trachea, and ear
This describes cartilage.
A contractile tissue that is the working element of movement
This describes skeletal muscle.

items.q: Which area of the brain is the major voluntary motor area?
items.a: The precentral gyrus of the cerebral cortex
items.ex: The precentral gyrus, or motor strip, in the cerebral cortex is the major voluntary motor area.
w: The medulla of the brainstem
Most motor fibers cross at the level of the medulla, but it is not the main voluntary motor area.
The cerebellum at the back of the brain
Cerebellar damage causes balance problems; it is not the motor strip.
The basal ganglia deep in the brain
Basal ganglia abnormalities are linked to dystonia and Parkinson posture, not the motor strip.

alt.q: A nurse reviews neuroanatomy before caring for a patient with a stroke. Where do most motor fibers from the motor strip cross?
alt.a: At the level of the medulla
alt.ex: Most motor fibers descend from the motor strip and cross at the medulla, so one side of the brain controls the opposite side of the body.
w: At the level of the cerebellum
The cerebellum is involved in balance; motor fibers cross at the medulla.
At the level of the lumbar spinal cord
The crossing occurs in the brainstem at the medulla, not in the lumbar cord.
At the level of the precentral gyrus
The precentral gyrus is where the fibers start, not where they cross.

items.q: An older adult started a new medication that causes dizziness and asks to walk to the bathroom. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess the patient’s balance and steadiness before walking
items.ex: Medications that cause dizziness affect balance, and impaired balance threatens safety, so assessment comes before ambulation.
w: Let the patient walk alone to promote independence
Walking alone with an unassessed balance problem risks a fall.
Tell the patient to remain on bed rest until discharge
Prolonged immobility itself impairs balance and causes deconditioning.
Lift the patient from the bed to a chair using body mechanics
Patient lifting is discouraged, and balance should be assessed first.

alt.q: A patient taking a medication that causes dizziness states, “I just stay in my chair all day now because I’m scared I’ll fall.” How should the nurse interpret this statement?
alt.a: Impaired balance has led to fear of falling and self-imposed activity restriction
alt.ex: Impaired balance contributes to a fear of falling and self-imposed activity restrictions.
w: The patient has adapted well and needs no further assessment
Self-imposed restriction is a mobility problem that needs assessment and intervention.
The patient’s balance problem has been resolved by sitting
Sitting avoids the problem; it does not resolve impaired balance.
The patient’s fear is unrelated to the medication taken
Medications that cause dizziness affect balance and can drive this fear.

items.q: Which disorder would most directly impair movement at the level of the nervous system?
items.a: A disorder that alters the transfer of impulses from nerve to muscle
items.ex: Movement is impaired by disorders altering neurotransmitter production, nerve-to-muscle impulse transfer, or activation of muscle activity.
w: A disorder that increases calcium and phosphate in bone matrix
Bone minerals give firmness; this is not a nervous system impairment.
A disorder that increases red blood cell production
Red blood cell production is a bone marrow function, not a nervous system process.
A disorder that makes tendons more inelastic
Tendons are normally inelastic; this is not a nervous system disorder.

alt.q: Which process, if altered, impairs movement by affecting the nervous system?
alt.a: Production of neurotransmitters
alt.ex: Disorders that alter neurotransmitter production, impulse transfer to muscle, or muscle activation impair movement.
w: Storage of calcium in bone
Calcium storage is a skeletal function, not a nervous system process.
Binding of joints by ligaments
Ligament binding is a structural function, not a nervous system process.
Production of red blood cells
Red blood cell production occurs in bone marrow, not the nervous system.

items.q: Which factors can compromise a person’s ability to remain balanced? Select all that apply.
o: Pregnancy
Life changes such as pregnancy compromise balance.
Pain
Pain is listed among the factors that compromise balance.
Medications that cause dizziness
Dizziness-producing medications affect balance.
Prolonged immobility
Prolonged immobility affects balance.
Correct body alignment
Correct alignment contributes to balance rather than compromising it.
Use of a full-body hydraulic lift
A lift is a safe-handling device; it does not compromise balance.
items.ex: Disease, injury, pain, age, pregnancy, dizziness-causing medications, and prolonged immobility compromise balance.

alt.q: A nurse is screening a patient for problems with balance. Which findings place the patient at risk? Select all that apply.
o: A recent injury
Injury compromises the ability to remain balanced.
Advanced age
Physical development such as age compromises balance.
A chronic disease
Disease compromises balance.
Regular walking for exercise
Physical activity is not listed as a threat to balance.
Sitting in correct body alignment
Correct alignment supports balance.
alt.ex: Age, disease, and injury are among the factors that compromise balance and threaten mobility and safety.

items.q: Which are functions of the skeletal system? Select all that apply.
o: Protecting vital organs such as the brain, heart, and lungs
The skull and ribs protect vital organs.
Storing calcium and releasing it into circulation
Bones store calcium and release it as needed, aiding calcium regulation.
Participating in red blood cell production
The marrow of long bones participates in red blood cell production.
Acting as a reservoir for blood
The internal structure of long bones acts as a blood reservoir.
Contracting and relaxing to produce movement
Skeletal muscle, not bone, contracts and relaxes.
Regulating balance and posture
The nervous system regulates movement, balance, and posture.
items.ex: Bones protect organs, regulate calcium, produce red blood cells, and store blood.

alt.q: A patient asks what bones do besides support the body. Which functions should the nurse describe? Select all that apply.
o: They release calcium into the blood when needed
Bones store calcium and release it into circulation as needed.
Long bones help produce red blood cells
Long bone marrow participates in red blood cell production.
The ribs protect the heart and lungs
The skeletal system protects vital organs.
They connect muscles to each other
Tendons connect muscle to bone; bones do not connect muscles together.
They send motor impulses to muscles
Motor impulses come from the nervous system.
alt.ex: The skeleton protects organs, regulates calcium, and its long-bone marrow helps produce red blood cells.

items.q: Which statements about ligaments, tendons, and cartilage are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Ligaments bind joints together and connect bones and cartilages
Ligaments bind joints and aid joint flexibility and support.
Tendons are strong, flexible, and inelastic
Tendons connecting muscle to bone are strong, flexible, and inelastic.
Cartilage has no blood vessels
Cartilage is nonvascular supporting connective tissue.
Cartilage becomes thicker and more elastic with aging
With aging cartilage becomes thinner and calcified.
Ligaments connect muscle directly to bone
Tendons, not ligaments, connect muscle to bone.
items.ex: Ligaments bind joints, tendons attach muscle to bone, and cartilage is nonvascular tissue that thins and calcifies with age.

alt.q: Which descriptions of connective tissues are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Cartilage is located chiefly in joints, thorax, trachea, larynx, nose, and ear
These are the main locations of cartilage.
Ligaments aid joint flexibility and support
Ligaments are flexible bands that support joints.
Tendons are white, glistening fibrous bands
This is how tendons are described.
Cartilage has a rich blood supply
Cartilage is nonvascular.
Tendons stretch easily like elastic
Tendons are inelastic.
alt.ex: Ligaments support joints, tendons are glistening inelastic bands, and cartilage is nonvascular tissue in specific locations.

items.q: Using only the principles of body mechanics is a safe way for nurses to lift patients.
items.a: False
items.ex: Patient lifting is discouraged, and relying only on body mechanics to lift patients often injures nurses and other staff.
items.ww: People’s centers of gravity are not at their exact center, so body mechanics alone does not make lifting safe.

alt.q: Patients at risk for being unsteady require safe patient-handling and mobility (SPHM) techniques.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Unsteady patients fall when their center of gravity is unbalanced, so SPHM techniques are required.
alt.ww: Relying on lifting or body mechanics alone often injures staff and does not protect unsteady patients.

items.q: With shear injury, the surface tissue can appear less affected than the damaged deeper tissue.
items.a: True
items.ex: Shear stretches and damages vessels in underlying tissue, so pressure injuries develop in undermined tissue while the surface looks less affected.
items.ww: Shear damage is mainly in deep tissue, so a normal-looking skin surface does not rule it out.

alt.q: Damage from shear is always most severe at the skin surface, where it is easy to see.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Shear damages blood vessels in deeper tissue, and the surface tissue appears less affected.
alt.ww: Pressure injuries from shear develop within undermined deep tissue, so the surface can underestimate damage.

items.q: Cartilage is a highly vascular tissue that becomes thicker with aging.
items.a: False
items.ex: Cartilage is nonvascular, and with aging it shows reduced thickness and calcification.
items.ww: Cartilage lacks blood vessels and thins rather than thickens with age.

alt.q: Cartilage is nonvascular, and aging reduces its thickness and causes calcification.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Cartilage has no blood vessels, and its characteristics change with aging, resulting in thinning and calcification.
alt.ww: Cartilage does not have a rich blood supply or thicken with age.

items.q: The force exerted against the skin while the skin remains stationary and the bony structures move is called [[shear|shearing]].
items.ex: In shear, skin stays against the sheets while the skeleton slides, stretching and damaging deep blood vessels.

alt.q: When a patient slides down in bed and the skin stays against the sheet while the skeleton moves, the force involved is [[shear|shearing]].
alt.ex: In shear, skin stays against the sheets while the skeleton slides, stretching and damaging deep blood vessels.

items.q: A fracture caused by weakened bone tissue is called a [[pathological fracture|pathologic fracture]].
items.ex: Immobile patients with decreased calcium regulation are at risk for osteoporosis and pathological fractures.

alt.q: An immobile patient with osteoporosis whose weakened bone breaks has sustained a [[pathological|pathologic]] fracture.
alt.ex: Immobile patients with decreased calcium regulation are at risk for osteoporosis and pathological fractures.

items.q: What is a Ligament?
items.a: Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages
items.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.
w: Connects muscle to bone
That goes with Tendon.
Nonvascular supporting connective tissue
That goes with Cartilage.
Region where two or more bones attach
That goes with Joint.

alt.q: What is a Tendon?
alt.a: Connects muscle to bone
alt.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.
w: Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages
That goes with Ligament.
Nonvascular supporting connective tissue
That goes with Cartilage.
Region where two or more bones attach
That goes with Joint.

alt.q: What is a Cartilage?
alt.a: Nonvascular supporting connective tissue
alt.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.
w: Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages
That goes with Ligament.
Connects muscle to bone
That goes with Tendon.
Region where two or more bones attach
That goes with Joint.

alt.q: What is a Joint?
alt.a: Region where two or more bones attach
alt.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.
w: Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages
That goes with Ligament.
Connects muscle to bone
That goes with Tendon.
Nonvascular supporting connective tissue
That goes with Cartilage.

alt.q: What is a Precentral gyrus?
alt.a: Major voluntary motor area of the cerebral cortex
alt.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.
w: Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages
That goes with Ligament.
Connects muscle to bone
That goes with Tendon.
Nonvascular supporting connective tissue
That goes with Cartilage.

alt.q: Which structure is the “Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages”?
alt.a: Ligament
alt.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.
w: Tendon
Tendon: Connects muscle to bone.
Cartilage
Cartilage: Nonvascular supporting connective tissue.
Joint
Joint: Region where two or more bones attach.

alt.q: Which structure is the “Connects muscle to bone”?
alt.a: Tendon
alt.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.
w: Ligament
Ligament: Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages.
Cartilage
Cartilage: Nonvascular supporting connective tissue.
Joint
Joint: Region where two or more bones attach.

alt.q: Which structure is the “Nonvascular supporting connective tissue”?
alt.a: Cartilage
alt.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.
w: Ligament
Ligament: Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages.
Tendon
Tendon: Connects muscle to bone.
Joint
Joint: Region where two or more bones attach.

alt.q: Which structure is the “Region where two or more bones attach”?
alt.a: Joint
alt.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.
w: Ligament
Ligament: Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages.
Tendon
Tendon: Connects muscle to bone.
Cartilage
Cartilage: Nonvascular supporting connective tissue.

alt.q: Which structure is the “Major voluntary motor area of the cerebral cortex”?
alt.a: Precentral gyrus
alt.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.
w: Ligament
Ligament: Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages.
Tendon
Tendon: Connects muscle to bone.
Cartilage
Cartilage: Nonvascular supporting connective tissue.

mt.q: Match each structure with its description.
pairs: Binds joints together and connects bones and cartilages
Region where two or more bones attach
Major voluntary motor area of the cerebral cortex
mt.ex: Each structure has a distinct role in movement: binding, attaching, supporting, articulating, or initiating voluntary motion.

items.q: What causes most disorders of stance or posture?
items.a: Unequal tone in muscle groups from loss of normal postural reflexes
items.ex: Postural disorders result from an inequality of tone in muscle groups caused by a loss of normal postural reflexes.
w: Excess calcium deposited in the joints from immobility
Calcium imbalance relates to bone resorption, not to the cause of postural disorders.
Too much friction between the patient and the bed
Friction affects skin during movement; it does not cause postural disorders.
Increased red blood cell production in long bones
Red blood cell production is unrelated to posture.

alt.q: A nurse explains postural abnormalities to a student. Which statement is accurate?
alt.a: They can be congenital, such as scoliosis, or idiopathic
alt.ex: Postural abnormalities may be congenital, like scoliosis, or idiopathic, meaning the cause is unknown.
w: They are always caused by trauma to the spine
Many postural abnormalities are congenital or idiopathic.
They improve balance by lowering the center of gravity
Equilibrium and balance are disrupted by postural abnormalities.
They never affect range of motion
Some postural abnormalities limit range of motion.

items.q: A patient with a postural abnormality has limited range of motion (ROM) in the affected joints. Which nursing action is best?
items.a: Maintain maximum ROM in unaffected joints and collaborate with the physical therapist
items.ex: Nurses maintain maximum ROM in unaffected joints and work with PTs, who design interventions to strengthen affected muscles and joints.
w: Restrict all movement of the unaffected joints to prevent strain
Restricting movement causes stiffness; ROM in unaffected joints should be maintained.
Force the affected joints past their limit during each bath
Forcing joints risks injury; PTs design safe strengthening interventions.
Delay any exercise until the posture corrects on its own
Waiting allows further loss; active interventions with the PT are needed.

alt.q: Which health care team member is the expert in designing interventions that improve a patient’s posture and strengthen affected muscles?
alt.a: Physical therapist
alt.ex: PTs are experts at designing interventions that strengthen affected muscles and joints and improve posture.
w: Registered dietitian
Dietitians provide insight on nutrition, not posture-strengthening exercise.
Assistive personnel
Assistive personnel help move and position patients but do not design therapy plans.
Pharmacist
Pharmacists manage medications, not posture-strengthening interventions.

items.q: A patient who had a cerebrovascular accident has upper extremities flexed at the elbows and held close to the body, with lower extremities externally rotated and extended. How should the nurse document this posture?
items.a: Decorticate posture
items.ex: Decorticate (hemiplegic) posture shows flexed arms held close to the body with extended, externally rotated legs and is seen after stroke.
w: Decerebrate posture
Decerebrate posture shows increased tone in extensor and trunk muscles with tonic neck reflexes.
Basal ganglion posture
Basal ganglion posture is stooped and hyperflexed with a short-stepped gait.
Dystonia
Dystonia is an abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions lasting seconds to weeks.

alt.q: Which cause is associated with decerebrate posture?
alt.a: Severe injury to the brain and brainstem
alt.ex: Decerebrate posture follows severe brain and brainstem injury, overstimulating postural righting and vestibular reflexes.
w: A congenital curve of the lumbar spine
A congenital lumbar curve describes lordosis, not decerebrate posture.
Too much dopamine in the basal ganglia
Excess dopamine is linked to chorea, not decerebrate posture.
Osteoporosis of the thoracic spine
Osteoporosis is a cause of kyphosis.

items.q: A patient with Parkinson disease has a stooped, hyperflexed posture and a narrow-based, short-stepped gait. Which nursing priority is most important?
items.a: Protecting the patient from falls during ambulation
items.ex: In basal ganglion posture the patient cannot adjust to tilting or loss of balance and falls instead, so fall prevention is the priority.
w: Restricting the patient’s fluid intake
Fluid restriction does not address the safety risk of this gait.
Encouraging the patient to walk faster
Faster walking does not restore lost postural reflexes and increases fall risk.
Teaching the patient to keep the arms flexed
Flexed arms are a feature of the disorder, not a safety measure.

alt.q: Why does a patient with basal ganglion posture tend to fall?
alt.a: The patient cannot make postural adjustments to tilting or loss of balance
alt.ex: Loss of normal postural reflexes leaves the patient unable to adjust to tilting, so the patient loses stability and falls.
w: The patient has a lateral S-shaped spine with unequal hips
This describes scoliosis, not basal ganglion posture.
The patient has excessive extensor muscle tone
Increased extensor tone describes decerebrate posture.
The patient has a wide-based gait with long steps
Basal ganglion posture has a narrow-based, short-stepped gait.

items.q: Which statement describes normal muscle tone?
items.a: Slight, smooth, and even resistance to passive joint movement
items.ex: Normal tone involves a slight resistance to passive movement that is smooth, constant, and even through the ROM.
w: No resistance at all to passive joint movement
Little or no resistance describes hypotonia.
Jerky resistance that changes throughout the ROM
Normal resistance is smooth, constant, and even.
Rigid resistance that prevents full joint movement
Normal tone allows the joint to move smoothly through its ROM.

alt.q: A nurse moves a patient’s elbow passively and feels little or no resistance. Which term describes this finding?
alt.a: Hypotonia
alt.ex: Hypotonia is decreased muscle tone with little or no resistance during passive movement.
w: Dystonia
Dystonia is an abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions.
Chorea
Chorea is a movement disorder related to too much dopamine.
Contracture
A contracture is a permanent muscle shortening that prevents full ROM.

items.q: A patient with cerebellar damage has hypotonia. Which finding should the nurse expect?
items.a: Difficulty rising from a chair without using arm support
items.ex: Patients with hypotonia tire easily, feel weak, and struggle to rise, sit without arm support, and use stairs.
w: Strong resistance when the nurse moves the patient’s joints
Hypotonia produces little or no resistance to passive movement.
Arms held flexed close to the body with legs extended
This describes decorticate posture.
A foot fixed permanently in plantar flexion
This describes foot drop, a contracture.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient with hypotonia is consistent with this condition?
alt.a: “I get tired fast and have trouble going up and down stairs.”
alt.ex: Hypotonia causes easy fatigue, weakness, and difficulty with stairs and rising from sitting.
w: “My muscles feel stiff and tight when you move my arm.”
Stiffness and resistance are not features of decreased tone.
“My curved upper back has gotten worse since my bones thinned.”
This describes kyphosis from osteoporosis.
“My head and neck keep twisting into the same position for hours.”
Sustained abnormal posture describes dystonia.

items.q: Which statement about movement disorders and dopamine is accurate?
items.a: Akinesia results from too little dopamine and chorea from too much
items.ex: Some movement disorders such as akinesias result from too little dopamine, and others such as chorea from too much.
w: Akinesia results from too much dopamine and chorea from too little
This reverses the relationship.
Both akinesia and chorea result from too much dopamine
Akinesia results from too little dopamine.
Both akinesia and chorea result from too little dopamine
Chorea results from too much dopamine.

alt.q: A patient has chorea. Which change in dopamine is associated with this movement disorder?
alt.a: Too much dopamine
alt.ex: Chorea is associated with too much dopamine stimulating muscle activity.
w: Too little dopamine
Too little dopamine is linked to akinesias.
Normal dopamine with low calcium
Chorea is linked to excess dopamine, not calcium.
Normal dopamine with high sodium
Chorea is linked to excess dopamine, not sodium.

items.q: A patient is admitted with a right-sided cerebral hemorrhage with necrosis. Which finding should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: Left-sided hemiplegia
items.ex: Destruction of the right motor strip results in left-sided hemiplegia because motor fibers cross at the medulla.
w: Right-sided hemiplegia
Motor fibers cross, so right-sided brain damage affects the left side.
Bilateral loss of motor control below the waist
Bilateral loss below a level occurs with complete spinal cord transection.
Isolated loss of balance with normal strength
Isolated balance problems suggest cerebellar damage, not motor strip destruction.

alt.q: A patient has left-sided hemiplegia after a stroke. Which area was most likely damaged?
alt.a: The right motor strip
alt.ex: Motor fibers cross at the medulla, so destruction of the right motor strip causes left-sided hemiplegia.
w: The left motor strip
Left motor strip damage causes right-sided weakness.
The cerebellum
Cerebellar damage mainly causes problems with balance.
The lumbar spinal cord
Lumbar cord injury does not produce one-sided hemiplegia of the body.

items.q: A patient has a complete transection of the spinal cord. Which effect on mobility should the nurse expect?
items.a: Bilateral loss of voluntary motor control below the level of injury
items.ex: A complete transection cuts motor fibers, causing bilateral loss of voluntary motor control below the level of trauma.
w: Loss of voluntary motor control on one side of the body only
One-sided loss describes hemiplegia from brain damage, not complete transection.
Loss of balance with intact voluntary motor control
Balance problems with intact strength suggest cerebellar damage.
Loss of voluntary motor control above the level of injury
Motor control is lost below, not above, the level of trauma.

alt.q: Why does a complete spinal cord transection cause loss of voluntary movement below the injury?
alt.a: The motor fibers that carry signals down the cord are cut
alt.ex: Motor fibers descending through the cord are severed, so voluntary control below the injury is lost on both sides.
w: Too much dopamine reaches the muscles below the injury
Dopamine excess is linked to chorea, not cord transection.
The cerebellum can no longer coordinate balance
Cerebellar damage affects balance; transection cuts motor fibers.
The bones below the injury lose calcium immediately
Bone loss develops with immobility over time; it is not why motor control is lost.

items.q: Why do young children usually have few complications after a fracture?
items.a: They are usually able to form new bone more easily than adults
items.ex: Young children usually form new bone more easily than adults, so they have few complications after a fracture.
w: Their bones contain no calcium or phosphate
Children’s bones contain minerals; the advantage is easier new bone formation.
Their fractures do not need to be immobilized
Fracture treatment often includes alignment and immobilization at any age.
Their fractures are usually pathological rather than traumatic
Fractures most commonly result from direct external trauma.

alt.q: Which condition can cause a pathological fracture?
alt.a: Metastatic cancer
alt.ex: Pathological fractures result from bone deformity such as osteoporosis, Paget disease, or metastatic cancer.
w: A sprained ankle ligament
A sprain is a soft-tissue injury, not a cause of pathological fracture.
A bruise over the thigh
A bruise is soft-tissue trauma, not a bone deformity.
Hypotonia from cerebellar damage
Hypotonia is decreased muscle tone, not a bone deformity.

items.q: Which statement distinguishes rheumatoid arthritis from osteoarthritis?
items.a: Rheumatoid arthritis is a systemic autoimmune disease that can affect organs
items.ex: Rheumatoid arthritis is a chronic, systemic, inflammatory autoimmune disease that can also inflame the lungs, heart, and kidneys.
w: Rheumatoid arthritis is the most common age-related joint disease
Osteoarthritis is the most common form of age-related joint disease.
Rheumatoid arthritis causes Heberden and Bouchard nodes of the hands
Heberden and Bouchard nodes are shown with osteoarthritis.
Rheumatoid arthritis never causes pain or changes in mobility
All forms of joint disease create pain and alter mobility.

alt.q: Which description fits osteoarthritis?
alt.a: The most common age-related joint disease of the synovial joints
alt.ex: Osteoarthritis is the most common age-related disease of synovial joints, causing chronic disability from pain and altered joint function.
w: A systemic autoimmune disease that inflames the heart and kidneys
This describes rheumatoid arthritis.
An abnormal posture held by sustained muscular contractions
This describes dystonia.
A disruption of bone tissue continuity from external trauma
This describes a fracture.

items.q: A patient with osteoarthritis of both knees tells the nurse she has stopped walking for exercise. How should the nurse interpret this?
items.a: It reflects the functional limitation that osteoarthritis commonly causes
items.ex: People with osteoarthritis experience functional limitations and gradual loss of activities such as walking for exercise.
w: It shows the arthritis has been cured by rest
Osteoarthritis causes chronic disability; rest does not cure it.
It is unrelated to joint disease and needs no follow-up
Loss of walking is a known effect of osteoarthritis and warrants assessment.
It indicates an autoimmune flare affecting the lungs
Organ inflammation is a feature of rheumatoid arthritis, not osteoarthritis.

alt.q: Among adults, in which group is the prevalence of arthritis highest?
alt.a: Adults who report no leisure time physical activity
alt.ex: Arthritis prevalence is highest among adults reporting no leisure time physical activity compared with more active adults.
w: Adults who meet physical activity recommendations
Adults who meet activity recommendations have lower prevalence.
Adults who are insufficiently but somewhat active
Insufficiently active adults have lower prevalence than those with no leisure activity.
Adults who are younger than 30 years of age
Arthritis prevalence rises with age, reaching more than half of adults over 75.

items.q: Which joints are typically affected by osteoarthritis? Select all that apply.
o: Knees
Osteoarthritis typically affects the knees.
Hips
Osteoarthritis typically affects the hips.
Hands
Osteoarthritis typically affects the hands, as with Heberden and Bouchard nodes.
Spine
Osteoarthritis typically affects the spine.
Lungs
Lungs are not joints; lung inflammation is linked to rheumatoid arthritis.
Kidneys
Kidneys are not joints; kidney inflammation is linked to rheumatoid arthritis.
items.ex: Osteoarthritis typically affects the knees, hips, hands, and spine.

alt.q: A patient has rheumatoid arthritis. Which joints are most commonly affected? Select all that apply.
o: Fingers
Fingers are among the joints most commonly affected.
Wrists
Wrists are commonly affected.
Ankles
Ankles are commonly affected.
Skull sutures
Skull sutures are not listed among affected joints.
Ribs and sternum
These are not listed among the joints most commonly affected.
alt.ex: Rheumatoid arthritis most commonly affects the fingers, feet, wrists, elbows, ankles, and knees.

items.q: A patient’s fractured forearm has been immobilized in a cast for several weeks. Which effects of this temporary immobilization should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Some muscle atrophy
Even temporary immobilization causes some muscle atrophy.
Loss of muscle tone
Temporary immobilization causes loss of muscle tone.
Joint stiffness
Joint stiffness results from temporary immobilization.
Increased muscle strength in the arm
Immobilization decreases, not increases, muscle strength.
Permanent loss of motor control in the hand
Motor control loss comes from nerve or CNS damage, not temporary casting.
items.ex: Even temporary immobilization of a fracture results in some muscle atrophy, loss of muscle tone, and joint stiffness.

alt.q: Which statements about fractures are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: A fracture is a disruption of bone tissue continuity
This is the definition of a fracture.
Most fractures result from direct external trauma
Fractures most commonly result from direct external trauma.
Treatment often includes alignment and immobilization
Positioning in alignment and immobilizing promotes healing and restores function.
Adults form new bone more easily than young children
Young children form new bone more easily than adults.
Immobilization of a fracture causes no muscle changes
Even temporary immobilization causes atrophy and loss of tone.
alt.ex: A fracture disrupts bone continuity, usually from trauma, and is treated by alignment and immobilization.

items.q: Which findings are expected in a patient with hypotonia? Select all that apply.
o: Tiring easily
Patients with hypotonia tire easily.
Feeling weak
Weakness is a feature of hypotonia.
Difficulty walking up and down stairs
Stairs are difficult with hypotonia.
Increased resistance to passive movement
Hypotonia has little or no resistance to passive movement.
Increased tone in extensor muscles
Increased extensor tone describes decerebrate posture.
items.ex: Hypotonia causes fatigue, weakness, and difficulty rising, sitting without arm support, and using stairs.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing a patient with cerebellar damage. Which findings suggest hypotonia? Select all that apply.
o: Little or no resistance when the nurse moves the patient’s knee
Hypotonia has little or no resistance during passive movement.
Needing arm support to sit down in a chair
Patients with hypotonia have difficulty sitting down without arm support.
Difficulty rising from a sitting position
Rising from sitting is difficult with hypotonia.
Smooth, constant, even resistance through the ROM
This describes normal muscle tone.
Arms flexed at the elbows and held close to the body
This describes decorticate posture.
alt.ex: Decreased tone with little resistance and difficulty rising or sitting without arm support are signs of hypotonia.

items.q: Scoliosis is a lateral S- or C-shaped spinal column with vertebral rotation and unequal heights of the hips and shoulders.
items.a: True
items.ex: Scoliosis is a lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation and unequal hip and shoulder heights.
items.ww: An exaggerated anterior lumbar curve is lordosis, and increased thoracic convexity is kyphosis, not scoliosis.

alt.q: Scoliosis is an exaggeration of the anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: An exaggerated anterior convex lumbar curve is lordosis; scoliosis is a lateral S- or C-shaped spine.
alt.ww: Scoliosis is a lateral curve with vertebral rotation, which differs from the lumbar curve of lordosis.

items.q: Damage to the cerebellum causes problems with balance.
items.a: True
items.ex: Trauma, stroke, or infection that damages the cerebellum causes problems with balance.
items.ww: The cerebellum is involved in balance, so its damage does disrupt balance.

alt.q: Motor impairment after damage to the motor strip is unrelated to how much of the motor strip is destroyed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Motor impairment is directly related to the amount of destruction of the motor strip.
alt.ww: Greater destruction of the motor strip produces greater motor impairment.

items.q: Prolonged bed rest can cause sensorimotor dysfunction that shows up as postural instability and a poor sense of balance.
items.a: True
items.ex: Prolonged bed rest causes neurobehavioral changes such as sensorimotor dysfunction, postural instability, and dysregulated balance.
items.ww: These changes, plus loss of muscle mass and strength, increase the risk of falls after bed rest.

alt.q: Prolonged bed rest improves postural stability and sense of balance by resting the nervous system.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Prolonged bed rest causes postural instability and dysregulated balance, raising fall risk.
alt.ww: Bed rest causes neurobehavioral changes and loss of strength that worsen, not improve, balance.

items.q: [[Osteoarthritis|OA]] is the most common form of age-related joint disease involving the synovial joints.
items.ex: Osteoarthritis causes chronic disability through pain and altered joint function, typically in knees, hips, hands, and spine.

alt.q: The age-related synovial joint disease that commonly causes Heberden and Bouchard nodes of the hands is [[osteoarthritis|OA]].
alt.ex: Osteoarthritis causes chronic disability through pain and altered joint function, typically in knees, hips, hands, and spine.

items.q: What is Lordosis?
items.a: Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine
items.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.
w: Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine
That goes with Kyphosis.
Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation
That goes with Scoliosis.
Abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions
That goes with Dystonia.

alt.q: What is Kyphosis?
alt.a: Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine
alt.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.
w: Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine
That goes with Lordosis.
Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation
That goes with Scoliosis.
Abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions
That goes with Dystonia.

alt.q: What is Scoliosis?
alt.a: Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation
alt.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.
w: Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine
That goes with Lordosis.
Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine
That goes with Kyphosis.
Abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions
That goes with Dystonia.

alt.q: What is Dystonia?
alt.a: Abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions
alt.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.
w: Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine
That goes with Lordosis.
Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine
That goes with Kyphosis.
Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation
That goes with Scoliosis.

alt.q: What is Basal ganglion posture?
alt.a: Stooped, hyperflexed posture with short-stepped gait
alt.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.
w: Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine
That goes with Lordosis.
Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine
That goes with Kyphosis.
Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation
That goes with Scoliosis.

alt.q: Which postural disorder is the “Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine”?
alt.a: Lordosis
alt.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.
w: Kyphosis
Kyphosis: Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine.
Scoliosis
Scoliosis: Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation.
Dystonia
Dystonia: Abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions.

alt.q: Which postural disorder is the “Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine”?
alt.a: Kyphosis
alt.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.
w: Lordosis
Lordosis: Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine.
Scoliosis
Scoliosis: Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation.
Dystonia
Dystonia: Abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions.

alt.q: Which postural disorder is the “Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation”?
alt.a: Scoliosis
alt.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.
w: Lordosis
Lordosis: Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine.
Kyphosis
Kyphosis: Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine.
Dystonia
Dystonia: Abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions.

alt.q: Which postural disorder is the “Abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions”?
alt.a: Dystonia
alt.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.
w: Lordosis
Lordosis: Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine.
Kyphosis
Kyphosis: Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine.
Scoliosis
Scoliosis: Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation.

alt.q: Which postural disorder is the “Stooped, hyperflexed posture with short-stepped gait”?
alt.a: Basal ganglion posture
alt.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.
w: Lordosis
Lordosis: Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine.
Kyphosis
Kyphosis: Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine.
Scoliosis
Scoliosis: Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation.

mt.q: Match each postural disorder with its description.
pairs: Exaggerated anterior convex curve of the lumbar spine
Increased convexity in the curvature of the thoracic spine
Lateral S- or C-shaped spine with vertebral rotation
Abnormal posture maintained by muscular contractions
Stooped, hyperflexed posture with short-stepped gait
mt.ex: Postural disorders differ by spinal curve or by abnormal muscle tone and reflexes.

items.q: A healthy adult of average weight is placed on bed rest. At about what rate does muscle strength decline from baseline?
items.a: About 3% a day
items.ex: An average adult without chronic illness on bed rest loses muscle strength at about 3% a day, so deconditioning appears within days.
w: About 3% a month
This is far too slow; deconditioning is apparent in a matter of days.
About 10% a day
This overstates the rate; the loss is about 3% a day.
About 1% a week
This is far too slow; the loss is about 3% a day.

alt.q: Which statement about deconditioning syndrome is accurate?
alt.a: Its effects on muscle are often apparent within a matter of days
alt.ex: Muscular deconditioning from inactivity is often apparent in days, with strength falling about 3% a day on bed rest.
w: It develops only after several months of bed rest
Effects appear in a matter of days, not months.
It affects only physical function, not social function
Deconditioning includes physical, psychological, social, and functional decline.
It occurs more slowly in older adults than in younger adults
Older adults lose function more severely and rapidly due to decreased reserve.

items.q: An immobile patient eats little and excretes more nitrogen than is taken in as protein. Which term describes this state?
items.a: Negative nitrogen balance
items.ex: When excreted nitrogen exceeds protein intake, negative nitrogen balance results, causing tissue catabolism, weight loss, and weakness.
w: Positive nitrogen balance
Positive balance means intake exceeds loss, the opposite of this situation.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia is excess blood calcium from bone resorption.
Orthostatic hypotension
Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in blood pressure on standing.

alt.q: Which findings result from tissue catabolism in a patient in negative nitrogen balance?
alt.a: Weight loss, decreased muscle mass, and weakness
alt.ex: Tissue breakdown in negative nitrogen balance produces weight loss, decreased muscle mass, and weakness.
w: Weight gain, increased muscle mass, and strength
Catabolism breaks tissue down; it does not build mass or strength.
Increased appetite, faster peristalsis, and diarrhea
Immobility decreases appetite and slows peristalsis.
Higher metabolic rate, fever, and edema
Immobility decreases, not increases, the metabolic rate.

items.q: A patient on prolonged bed rest has had no formed stool for 5 days and now has small amounts of liquid stool. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
items.a: Liquid stool may be passing around a fecal impaction
items.ex: Pseudodiarrhea is liquid stool passing around a fecal impaction, not true diarrhea, and is common with immobility.
w: The patient has normal diarrhea from an infection
With immobility this pattern suggests pseudodiarrhea around an impaction.
The patient’s constipation has resolved on its own
Liquid stool around hardened feces means the impaction remains.
Peristalsis has increased because of the bed rest
Immobility slows peristalsis; it does not speed it up.

alt.q: What can happen if a fecal impaction in an immobile patient is left untreated?
alt.a: A mechanical bowel obstruction can develop
alt.ex: Untreated impaction can cause mechanical obstruction, distention, dehydration, and worsening fluid and electrolyte disturbances.
w: Peristalsis speeds up and clears the impaction
Intestinal function becomes depressed over time.
Absorption of fluid from the bowel increases
Absorption ceases as the obstruction progresses.
Calcium is reabsorbed into the bones
Calcium is unrelated to impaction; immobility releases calcium from bone.

items.q: A patient on bed rest has a supine blood pressure of 128/78 mm Hg. Which reading taken 2 minutes after standing indicates orthostatic hypotension?
items.a: 104/74 mm Hg
items.ex: A systolic drop of at least 20 mm Hg or a diastolic drop of at least 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing defines orthostatic hypotension.
w: 122/76 mm Hg
A 6 mm Hg systolic and 2 mm Hg diastolic drop does not meet the criteria.
116/72 mm Hg
A 12 mm Hg systolic and 6 mm Hg diastolic drop does not meet the criteria.
130/80 mm Hg
Blood pressure rose slightly, which is not orthostatic hypotension.

alt.q: Which definition of orthostatic hypotension is accurate?
alt.a: A systolic drop of at least 20 mm Hg or diastolic drop of at least 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing
alt.ex: Orthostatic hypotension is defined by these blood pressure drops within 3 minutes of rising to an upright position.
w: A systolic drop of at least 10 mm Hg or diastolic drop of at least 5 mm Hg within 10 minutes of standing
The thresholds are 20 and 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes.
A systolic rise of at least 20 mm Hg or diastolic rise of at least 10 mm Hg within 3 minutes of standing
Orthostatic hypotension is a drop, not a rise, in pressure.
A systolic drop of at least 40 mm Hg or diastolic drop of at least 20 mm Hg within 1 minute of lying down
It occurs on rising upright, with drops of 20 and 10 mm Hg.

items.q: A patient on bed rest for 6 days after surgery suddenly reports shortness of breath and sharp chest pain when breathing. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Report the findings to the health care provider immediately
items.ex: Dyspnea followed by pleuritic chest pain is the most common presentation of pulmonary embolus, which can lead to shock or death.
w: Encourage the patient to ambulate in the hallway
Ambulating does not treat a suspected pulmonary embolus and delays care.
Massage the patient’s calves to improve circulation
Massaging a leg with a possible clot could dislodge it.
Document the findings and reassess in 4 hours
A suspected pulmonary embolus needs immediate reporting, not delayed reassessment.

alt.q: Which is the most common presenting symptom of a pulmonary embolus?
alt.a: Dyspnea
alt.ex: The most common presenting symptom of pulmonary embolus is dyspnea, followed by pleuritic chest pain and cough.
w: Flank pain
Flank and groin pain suggests a renal calculus blocking a ureter.
Fever
Fever is not listed as the most common presenting symptom of pulmonary embolus.
Calf cramping
Pulmonary embolus presents with respiratory symptoms, most often dyspnea.

items.q: Why do pathologic joint contractures tend to leave joints in flexed positions?
items.a: Flexor muscles for joints are stronger than extensor muscles
items.ex: Because flexors are stronger than extensors, disuse and muscle shortening tend to pull joints into flexion.
w: Extensor muscles for joints are stronger than flexor muscles
This reverses the relationship; flexors are stronger.
Ligaments shorten faster than muscles during bed rest
Contractures involve abnormal and permanent muscle shortening.
Bone resorption pulls the joint into flexion
Bone resorption causes disuse osteoporosis, not joint flexion.

alt.q: Which definition describes a pathologic joint contracture?
alt.a: Abnormal, permanent muscle shortening with fixation of a joint
alt.ex: A pathologic joint contracture is an abnormal and permanent muscle shortening from spasm or weakness with joint fixation.
w: Temporary muscle soreness that resolves with rest
Contractures are permanent, not temporary.
A disruption of bone tissue continuity at the joint
This describes a fracture.
Collapse of alveoli from blocked bronchioles
This describes atelectasis.

items.q: A patient had knee replacement surgery and the nurse notes the patient cannot dorsiflex the foot or lift the toes off the floor. Which complication is the patient most at risk for?
items.a: Stumbling and falling during ambulation
items.ex: With foot drop the foot is fixed in plantar flexion, the toes cannot clear the ground, and the patient is at risk for stumbling and falling.
w: Orthostatic hypotension when sitting up
Foot drop affects the ankle and gait, not blood pressure.
Hypostatic pneumonia from pooled secretions
Pneumonia results from pooled lung secretions, not foot drop.
Renal calculi from concentrated urine
Renal calculi result from hypercalcemia and urinary stasis, not foot drop.

alt.q: Which patient is at risk for foot drop?
alt.a: A patient with peroneal nerve compression after hip surgery
alt.ex: Compression of the peroneal nerve after hip or knee replacement, CVA, and multiple sclerosis place patients at risk for foot drop.
w: A patient with a healed forearm fracture who walks daily
A healed arm fracture with normal walking does not affect the foot.
A patient with mild hypercalcemia who walks daily
Hypercalcemia is linked to renal calculi, not foot drop.
A patient with a minor scalp laceration who walks daily
A scalp injury does not affect the nerves or muscles of the foot.

items.q: A patient immobilized for 2 weeks reports moderate to severe flank and groin pain with nausea. Which complication should the nurse suspect?
items.a: A renal calculus obstructing the ureter
items.ex: Immobilized patients often have hypercalcemia, and a stone obstructing a ureter causes flank and groin pain with nausea.
w: A pulmonary embolus blocking the pulmonary artery
Pulmonary embolus usually presents with dyspnea and pleuritic chest pain.
Foot drop from peroneal nerve compression
Foot drop causes inability to dorsiflex the foot, not flank pain.
Atelectasis from blocked bronchioles
Atelectasis affects the lungs and causes hypoventilation, not flank pain.

alt.q: Why are immobilized patients at risk for renal calculi?
alt.a: They frequently have hypercalcemia and urinary stasis
alt.ex: Calcium released from bone and urine pooling in the renal pelvis promote calcium stone formation.
w: They frequently have increased peristalsis of the ureters
Ureteral peristalsis is insufficient to overcome gravity when recumbent.
They frequently have dilute urine from high fluid intake
Fluid intake often falls, making urine concentrated.
They frequently have a positive nitrogen balance
Immobility causes negative, not positive, nitrogen balance.

items.q: On about which day after immobilization does urinary output typically begin to decline?
items.a: The fifth or sixth day
items.ex: As fluid intake diminishes, output declines on about the fifth or sixth day after immobilization and urine becomes concentrated.
w: The first or second day
Output decline typically occurs later, about the fifth or sixth day.
The tenth or eleventh day
Output decline typically occurs earlier, about the fifth or sixth day.
The twentieth or twenty-first day
Output decline typically occurs much earlier, about the fifth or sixth day.

alt.q: A patient debilitated by prolonged immobility has concentrated urine. Which intervention is essential?
alt.a: Providing adequate hydration
alt.ex: Concentrated urine raises the risk of calculi and infection, so adequate hydration is essential in a debilitated patient.
w: Restricting oral fluids
Restricting fluid worsens concentration and increases calculi and infection risk.
Keeping the patient flat at all times
Lying flat promotes urinary stasis.
Inserting an indwelling urinary catheter
Indwelling catheters are a cause of urinary tract infection.

items.q: A nurse caring for an older adult recovering from surgery wants to maintain the patient’s highest level of mobility. Which action is best?
items.a: Encourage the patient to do as many self-care activities as possible
items.ex: Encouraging self-care maintains mobility, while unnecessary help with bathing and transferring can contribute to immobility.
w: Complete the patient’s bath and transfers to save energy
Unnecessary help inadvertently contributes to the patient’s immobility.
Keep the patient on bed rest until discharge
Bed rest should be limited and activity begun as soon as possible.
Remove the patient’s walker to prevent tripping
Assistive devices should be available to encourage mobility and prevent falls.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse shows understanding of preventing functional decline in a hospitalized older adult?
alt.a: “I’ll let her bathe herself and help only where she needs it.”
alt.ex: Promoting independence in self-care maintains mobility; unnecessary help contributes to immobility.
w: “I’ll do all of her care so she can rest and recover.”
Doing everything for the patient contributes to immobility and decline.
“I’ll keep her glasses in the drawer so they don’t get lost.”
Glasses and hearing aids should be in use to encourage mobility.
“I’ll wait until discharge to start walking with her.”
Activity should begin as soon as possible to prevent deconditioning.

items.q: Why can the external appearance of a pressure injury underestimate the extent of tissue damage?
items.a: Superficial skin is less susceptible to pressure damage than deeper tissue
items.ex: Deeper tissues are more susceptible to pressure-induced damage than superficial skin, so the surface may look less injured.
w: Superficial skin is more susceptible to pressure damage than deeper tissue
This reverses the relationship; deeper tissue is more susceptible.
Pressure injuries form only on intact skin away from bony prominences
Pressure injuries typically develop over bony prominences or under devices.
Pressure injuries heal quickly once a patient becomes mobile
Any break in skin integrity is difficult to heal.

alt.q: Where is the rate of hospital-acquired pressure injuries highest?
alt.a: Adult intensive care units
alt.ex: Overall prevalence of pressure injuries is highest in long-term care, but hospital-acquired rates are highest in adult ICUs.
w: Pediatric outpatient clinics
Outpatient clinics are not identified as having the highest rates.
Maternity units
Maternity units are not identified as having the highest rates.
Same-day surgery centers
Same-day surgery centers are not identified as having the highest rates.

items.q: Which factors make up the Virchow triad for venous thrombus formation? Select all that apply.
o: Damage to the vessel wall
Vessel wall injury, such as during surgery, contributes to thrombus formation.
Alterations of blood flow
Stasis or turbulence in calf veins contributes to thrombus formation.
Hypercoagulability of the blood
Changes in clotting factors or platelet activity contribute to thrombus formation.
Increased red blood cell production
This is not one of the three Virchow triad factors.
Low blood calcium
Immobility raises, not lowers, blood calcium, and calcium is not a triad factor.
items.ex: The Virchow triad is vessel wall damage, altered blood flow, and hypercoagulability.

alt.q: A postoperative patient on bed rest is at risk for deep vein thrombosis. Which situations contribute to thrombus formation? Select all that apply.
o: Injury to a vein during surgery
Vessel wall damage is part of the Virchow triad.
Stasis of blood in the calf veins from lying still
Altered blood flow is part of the Virchow triad.
Increased platelet activity
Hypercoagulability is part of the Virchow triad.
Regular ambulation in the hallway
Movement reduces stasis rather than contributing to thrombus formation.
Decreased hemoglobin from low red blood cell production
This is not one of the Virchow triad factors.
alt.ex: Vessel injury, blood flow stasis, and increased clotting tendency together promote venous thrombus formation.

items.q: Which approaches are recommended to reduce functional decline in hospitalized older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Conduct an interprofessional geriatric assessment at admission
A comprehensive assessment of physical, psychosocial, and functional status is recommended at admission.
Ensure hearing aids, glasses, and walkers are in use
Assistive devices encourage mobility and prevent falls.
Implement early mobilization based on established protocols
Early mobilization is recommended even for acutely and critically ill patients.
Include a nutritional assessment before planning care
Nutrition affects reconditioning, rehabilitation success, and fall risk.
Provide full assistance with bathing to conserve energy
Unnecessary help contributes to immobility; independence should be encouraged.
Keep hallways furnished with extra chairs and equipment
Uncluttered hallways are recommended for age-friendly care.
items.ex: Recommended approaches include geriatric assessment, assistive devices, early mobilization, and nutritional assessment.

alt.q: A nurse plans care to prevent functional decline in a hospitalized 82-year-old patient. Which interventions should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Encourage walking coordinated with rehabilitation therapies
Activity including walking and strength training is recommended during hospitalization.
Provide large clocks and calendars in the environment
Environmental enhancements support age-friendly care.
Ensure the patient wears appropriate footwear
Appropriate footwear encourages mobility and prevents falls.
Limit help with meals to promote weight loss
Insufficient assistance with eating leads to malnutrition, which worsens immobility problems.
Use an indwelling urinary catheter for convenience
Protocols aim to minimize adverse effects of procedures such as urinary catheterization.
alt.ex: Walking, age-friendly environments, and proper footwear help prevent functional decline in hospitalized older adults.

items.q: Which are risk factors for deconditioning in patients who are hospitalized? Select all that apply.
o: Age
Age is a risk factor, and older adults decline faster due to decreased reserve.
Nutritional status
Nutritional status is a risk factor for deconditioning.
Preadmission functional status
Functional status before admission is a risk factor.
Cognitive impairment and depression
Cognitive impairment and depression are risk factors.
Normal body weight
Normal weight is not listed as a risk factor for deconditioning.
Early mobilization
Early mobilization helps prevent deconditioning.
items.ex: Age, nutrition, mobility, preadmission function, cognitive impairment, and depression are risk factors for deconditioning.

alt.q: A nurse identifies hospitalized patients at high risk for deconditioning. Which patient findings indicate risk? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced mobility before admission
Mobility and preadmission functional status are risk factors.
Poor nutritional status
Nutritional status is a risk factor.
Depression
Depression is a risk factor for deconditioning.
Walking independently three times a day
Regular independent walking reduces deconditioning risk.
Young age with no chronic illness
Older age, not youth, increases deconditioning risk.
alt.ex: Low preadmission mobility, poor nutrition, and depression increase a hospitalized patient’s risk for deconditioning.

items.q: A hospitalized patient must be on prescribed bed rest to become physically inactive.
items.a: False
items.ex: Hospitalized patients need not be on bed rest to be inactive; critically ill patients often cannot be active, and older adults often limit activity voluntarily.
items.ww: Inactivity occurs without bed rest orders, so nurses must watch for it in all patients.

alt.q: Older adults in the hospital often limit their activity voluntarily, for example because of a fear of bothering staff.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Reasons include fear of bothering staff, not wanting to overburden staff, viewing help negatively, and not wanting to feel dependent.
alt.ww: Inactivity in older adults is often self-imposed rather than ordered, so it does occur voluntarily.

items.q: An immobilized patient who also has primary osteoporosis is at high risk for accelerated bone loss.
items.a: True
items.ex: Disuse osteoporosis differs in origin from primary osteoporosis, but immobilized patients with primary osteoporosis are at high risk for accelerated bone loss.
items.ww: Bone resorption from immobility adds to existing primary osteoporosis, so bone loss accelerates rather than staying stable.

alt.q: Disuse osteoporosis from immobility and primary osteoporosis have the same origin, so immobility does not add to bone loss.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: They differ in origin, and immobilized patients with primary osteoporosis are at high risk for accelerated bone loss.
alt.ww: Immobility causes bone resorption that adds to primary osteoporosis and increases pathological fracture risk.

items.q: Prolonged immobilization of a toddler can delay gross-motor skills, intellectual development, and musculoskeletal development.
items.a: True
items.ex: Prolonged immobilization delays a young child’s gross-motor skills, intellectual development, and musculoskeletal development.
items.ww: Immobility affects development in the very young, so these delays are a real risk.

alt.q: Immobility affects only the physical systems of young children and does not delay their intellectual development.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Prolonged immobilization delays intellectual development as well as gross-motor and musculoskeletal development in young children.
alt.ww: The text lists intellectual development among the areas delayed by prolonged immobilization.

items.q: Collapse of alveoli that occurs when secretions block a bronchiole or bronchus is called [[atelectasis]].
items.ex: In atelectasis, distal alveoli collapse as trapped air is absorbed, producing hypoventilation.

alt.q: An immobile patient whose mucus plug causes the distal alveoli to collapse has developed [[atelectasis]].
alt.ex: In atelectasis, distal alveoli collapse as trapped air is absorbed, producing hypoventilation.

items.q: The pathological reduction in the normal size of muscle fibers after prolonged inactivity is called [[disuse atrophy]].
items.ex: Disuse atrophy follows inactivity from bed rest, trauma, casting of a body part, or local nerve damage.

alt.q: When a casted leg’s muscle fibers shrink from prolonged inactivity, the patient has developed [[disuse atrophy|atrophy]].
alt.ex: Disuse atrophy follows inactivity from bed rest, trauma, casting of a body part, or local nerve damage.

items.q: In mobility assessment, which level comes right after “Sitting up in bed”?
items.a: Transferring to a chair
items.ex: That's level 3 of 4. Begin in the most supported position and progress to higher levels as tolerated; progressive assessment promotes patient safety.
w: Walking
That's level 4 of 4.
Moving while lying down in bed
That's level 1 of 4.

alt.q: Which level comes first in mobility assessment?

alt.ex: That's level 1 of 4. Begin in the most supported position and progress to higher levels as tolerated; progressive assessment promotes patient safety.
w: Sitting up in bed
That's level 2 of 4.

That's level 3 of 4.
Walking
That's level 4 of 4.

w: Transferring to a chair
