ord.q: When the nurse is unsure of a patient’s physical abilities, in what order is mobility assessed?
items: Moving while lying down in bed
Sitting up in bed
Transferring to a chair
Walking
ord.ex: Begin in the most supported position and progress to higher levels as tolerated; progressive assessment promotes patient safety.

items.q: What is the first step in assessing a patient’s activity tolerance?
items.a: Collect a baseline heart rate, respiratory rate, and blood pressure
items.ex: Baseline vital signs are collected first and used to evaluate tolerance during later activity.
w: Have the patient walk the length of the hallway
Walking a short distance comes after baseline vital signs are recorded.
Ask the patient to rate fatigue after morning care
Fatigue reports are useful, but the book names baseline vital signs as the first step.
Measure oxygen saturation after climbing stairs
Stair climbing is not the starting point; baseline heart rate, respirations, and BP come first.

alt.q: A patient’s recovery time after walking has shortened from 10 minutes to 4 minutes over a week. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: Activity tolerance is improving
alt.ex: Decreasing recovery time after activity indicates improving activity tolerance.
w: Activity tolerance is declining
Declining tolerance would lengthen, not shorten, the time needed to recover.
The patient is developing orthostatic hypotension
Orthostatic hypotension is assessed with BP changes on position change, not recovery time.
The activity is too easy and should be stopped
Shorter recovery is a sign of progress, not a reason to stop activity.

items.q: A patient on bed rest after hip surgery reports cramping pain in the right calf, which is warm, swollen, and tender. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Keep the patient quiet in bed and notify the health care provider
items.ex: With a suspected DVT, keep the patient calm and quiet in bed, do not massage, and notify the provider immediately.
w: Massage the calf gently to relieve the cramping
Massaging the area can dislodge the clot and must never be done.
Assist the patient to walk in the hallway to improve flow
Activity is not started when a DVT is suspected; the patient stays quiet in bed.
Apply a sequential compression sleeve to the right leg
Manipulating a leg with signs of DVT could dislodge the clot, so compression is contraindicated.

alt.q: A patient’s left thigh is newly swollen, warm, and painful. Which instruction should the nurse give the family?
alt.a: Do not rub or massage the swollen leg
alt.ex: Massage could dislodge a thrombus, so patient, family, and staff are told not to massage the area.
w: Help the patient walk to loosen the leg
Walking is avoided when a DVT is suspected; the patient is kept quiet in bed.
Rub lotion firmly into the sore area
Firm rubbing is a form of massage and risks dislodging the clot.
Keep the leg crossed over the other leg
Crossing the legs compresses leg veins and is something patients are taught to avoid.

items.q: Where does the nurse mark each calf before measuring daily calf circumference for a patient at risk for DVT?
items.a: 10 cm below the mid-patella
items.ex: Mark each calf 10 cm (4 inches) down from the mid-patella and use that mark for every daily measurement.
w: 5 cm below the mid-patella
The book specifies 10 cm, not 5 cm, below the mid-patella.
10 cm above the mid-patella
A point above the knee is on the thigh; the calf mark is below the patella.
2 cm above the ankle bone
The calf mark is measured from the mid-patella, not from the ankle.

alt.q: Daily calf measurements show the right calf has increased by 3 cm while the left is unchanged. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: A possible early sign of thrombosis
alt.ex: A unilateral increase in calf circumference is an early indication of thrombosis.
w: Expected muscle growth from leg exercises
Muscle growth would not appear as a sudden one-sided increase in an immobile patient.
Normal dependent edema from bed rest
Dependent edema is not one-sided; a unilateral increase suggests thrombosis.
A measuring error to ignore
A unilateral increase must be treated as a possible DVT and reported, not dismissed.

items.q: A patient receiving active cancer treatment has been bedridden for 4 days and now has an entirely swollen leg; no other diagnosis is more likely. What is the Wells score interpretation?
items.a: 3 points, high probability of DVT
items.ex: Active cancer, bedridden 3 days or more, and entire leg swollen each score 1 point; 3 to 8 points is high probability.
w: 3 points, moderate probability of DVT
Moderate probability is 1 to 2 points; 3 points falls in the high range.
2 points, moderate probability of DVT
Each of the three findings scores 1 point, for a total of 3, not 2.
1 point, low probability of DVT
Low probability is −2 to 0 points, and this patient scores 3 points.

alt.q: A patient’s Wells score totals 1 point. How is the probability of DVT classified?
alt.a: 1 point, moderate probability
alt.ex: On the Wells score, 1 to 2 points indicates a moderate probability of DVT.
w: 1 point, low probability
Low probability is −2 to 0 points.
1 point, high probability
High probability requires 3 to 8 points.
1 point, DVT is ruled out
The Wells score estimates probability; it does not rule a DVT out.

items.q: Which intervention best reduces the risk of orthostatic hypotension for a patient who has been on bed rest?
items.a: Dangle the legs at the bedside as soon as condition allows
items.ex: Mobilizing as soon as possible, even just dangling, maintains muscle tone and increases venous return.
w: Teach isometric exercises to do while lying flat
Isometric exercises improve activity tolerance but have no beneficial effect on orthostatic hypotension.
Keep the patient flat until able to walk alone
Longer immobility raises the risk of orthostatic hypotension when the patient stands.
Stand the patient up quickly to shorten the dizzy spell
Patients are moved gradually and monitored for dizziness during position changes.

alt.q: A patient on bed rest asks whether tightening the leg muscles in bed will stop dizziness when getting up. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: They build activity tolerance but will not prevent the dizziness
alt.ex: Isometric exercises improve activity tolerance but do not prevent orthostatic hypotension; early mobilization does.
w: Yes, they are the best way to prevent dizziness
Isometric exercises have no beneficial effect on preventing orthostatic hypotension.
No, they raise the risk of a blood clot in the leg
Muscle activity promotes venous return; it does not raise clot risk.
Yes, as long as they are done every 15 minutes
No schedule of isometric exercise prevents orthostatic hypotension.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient with heart disease how to move up in bed. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will breathe out while I push myself up in bed.”
items.ex: Breathing out while moving avoids the Valsalva maneuver and the sudden pressure changes it causes.
w: “I will take a deep breath and hold it while I push up.”
Holding the breath and straining is the Valsalva maneuver, which the patient should avoid.
“I will bear down hard so I can move in one push.”
Bearing down raises intrathoracic pressure and can cause reflex bradycardia.
“I will hold my breath only when I lift my hips.”
Any breath holding with straining is the Valsalva maneuver and should be avoided.

alt.q: Why is the Valsalva maneuver dangerous for a patient with heart disease?
alt.a: It can cause reflex bradycardia and sudden cardiac death
alt.ex: Release of the strain sharply raises venous return and BP, producing reflex bradycardia that can cause sudden cardiac death.
w: It causes a blood clot to form in the lungs
Pulmonary emboli come from deep vein clots, not from breath holding.
It steadily lowers intrathoracic pressure and oxygen
Straining raises intrathoracic pressure; it does not lower it.
It causes fluid to collect in the dependent lungs
Secretion pooling results from immobility, not from the Valsalva maneuver.

items.q: Which patient best fits the nursing diagnosis Risk for Disuse Syndrome rather than Impaired Mobility?
items.a: A patient who is immobile and at risk for multisystem problems
items.ex: Risk for Disuse Syndrome applies to an immobile patient at risk for multisystem problems from inactivity.
w: A patient who walks with a cane but tires on stairs
Some limitation without complete immobility fits Impaired Mobility.
A patient who can turn in bed but needs help to stand
This patient has some limitations but is not completely immobile, which fits Impaired Mobility.
A patient whose weak leg limits walking distance
A partial limitation in walking fits Impaired Mobility, not disuse syndrome.

alt.q: A patient can turn in bed and transfer with help but cannot walk independently. Which nursing diagnosis fits best?
alt.a: Impaired Mobility
alt.ex: Impaired Mobility applies to a patient with some limitations who is not completely immobile.
w: Risk for Disuse Syndrome
Risk for Disuse Syndrome is for a patient who is immobile and at risk for multisystem problems.
Confined to Bed
This patient can transfer with help, so the patient is not confined to bed.
Social Isolation
Nothing in the data points to isolation; the data describe limited movement.

items.q: An 84-year-old patient on bed rest, oriented yesterday, is suddenly confused and inattentive today. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess for a physiological cause such as infection or fever
items.ex: Abrupt behavior changes often have a physiological cause; acute confusion may be the main sign of a UTI or fever in older adults.
w: Document the confusion as expected with aging
Delirium in older adults is not normal and requires a thorough assessment.
Turn on the television to increase stimulation
Stimulation helps orientation, but a sudden change must first be assessed for a cause.
Arrange a screening for clinical depression
Depression develops gradually; an abrupt change suggests a physiological cause.

alt.q: Which finding in an immobile older adult most strongly suggests a physiological rather than psychosocial cause?
alt.a: A sudden change in attention and orientation
alt.ex: Psychosocial changes usually develop gradually; abrupt behavior changes often signal surgery effects, drug reactions, PE, or infection.
w: Gradually increasing boredom over two weeks
Gradual boredom is a common psychosocial reaction to immobilization.
Frequent call-bell use for minor requests
Calling for minor help often reflects a need for socialization.
Mild anger about being confined to bed
Anger is a common emotional reaction to immobility, not a sign of a physiological cause.

items.q: The nurse assesses a patient who has been immobile for 5 days. Which finding is most important to report immediately?
items.a: Absent left pedal pulse that was present yesterday
items.ex: The absence of a lower-extremity pulse, especially one present before, must be documented and reported immediately.
w: Blanchable redness over the sacrum
Blanchable erythema needs monitoring and repositioning but is not an emergency.
Decreased appetite at breakfast and lunch
Anorexia is common with immobility and is addressed through nutrition planning.
Reports that the days feel very long
Boredom is a common psychosocial reaction, not an urgent physiological change.

alt.q: Which assessment finding in an immobile older adult is an early indication of heart failure?
alt.a: A third heart sound heard at the apex
alt.ex: Bed rest increases cardiac workload; an S3 at the apex is an early indication of heart failure in older adults.
w: A slightly elevated heart rate when lying down
Lying down normally increases cardiac workload and pulse rate somewhat.
Blanchable redness over both heels
Blanchable redness relates to skin pressure, not cardiac function.
Decreased bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Decreased bowel sounds reflect slowed peristalsis from immobility.

items.q: An assistive personnel (AP) is walking a patient who uses a walker. Which action by the AP requires the nurse to intervene?
items.a: Walking beside the patient while holding the patient’s arm
items.ex: Holding the arm makes it hard to lower a patient who faints and can dislocate the shoulder in a fall.
w: Applying a gait belt before the patient stands
A gait belt is always used when helping a patient walk with an assistive device.
Standing slightly behind and to the side of the patient
Standing slightly behind and to the side is the correct position.
Clearing equipment from the path before walking
A clear pathway free of equipment is needed before ambulation.

alt.q: A patient with a fractured left ankle is walking with a walker. Where should the nurse stand?
alt.a: Slightly behind the patient on the strong right side
alt.ex: With an orthopedic condition, the nurse stands slightly behind and off to the strong, unaffected side, using a gait belt.
w: Slightly behind the patient on the weak left side
The weak side is used for nonorthopedic weakness; orthopedic conditions call for the strong side.
Directly in front of the patient, walking backward
Standing in front blocks the walker and does not allow the nurse to lower the patient safely.
Several steps behind the patient to give independence
The nurse stays close behind and to the side with a gait belt in place.

items.q: Which technique is correct when the nurse performs passive range-of-motion exercises?
items.a: Move each joint slowly just to the point of resistance
items.ex: Passive ROM is done slowly and smoothly to the point of resistance; never force a joint and never cause pain.
w: Push each joint gently past resistance to gain range
A joint is never forced beyond the point of resistance.
Start with the small hand joints and move to larger ones
Use a head-to-toe sequence moving from larger to smaller joints.
Stand on the side of the bed opposite the joint
Stand on the side of the bed closest to the joint being exercised.

alt.q: How often are passive ROM exercises typically performed for a patient who cannot move an extremity?
alt.a: Each movement five times, two to three sessions a day
alt.ex: Repeat each joint movement five times per session, with sessions two to three times a day.
w: Each movement two times, one session a day
This is too few repetitions and sessions per the book’s guidance.
Each movement ten times, once every hour
The book recommends five repetitions per session, two to three sessions daily.
Each movement five times, one session a week
Weekly sessions are far too infrequent to prevent contractures.

items.q: Which findings are signs of a deep vein thrombosis (DVT)? Select all that apply.
o: Swelling in the affected leg
Swelling of the affected extremity is a sign of DVT.
Warm, cyanotic skin over the area
A DVT can make the skin of the extremity warm and cyanotic.
Itching of the affected extremity
Itching is listed among the signs of DVT.
Pain or tenderness in the extremity
Pain, tenderness, cramping, or soreness can accompany a DVT.
Equal swelling in both legs at once
A DVT usually occurs on one side of the body at a time.
Cool, pale skin with absent sensation
DVT skin is warm and cyanotic, not cool and pale.
items.ex: DVT signs include unilateral swelling, warm cyanotic skin, itching, and pain or tenderness in the affected extremity.

alt.q: An AP caring for a patient with SCDs should report which findings to the nurse? Select all that apply.
o: One calf looks larger than the other
Unequal calf or thigh size can signal a DVT and must be reported.
A calf that is red, hot, and tender
Redness, heat, and tenderness of the calf suggest a possible DVT.
Redness, itching, or irritation on the legs
These can be signs of an allergic reaction to elastic.
The patient routinely takes the device off
The AP reports when a patient routinely removes the compression device.
The green light shows the unit is running
A green light indicates normal functioning and needs no report.
alt.ex: The AP reports possible DVT signs, skin reactions to elastic, and routine removal of the device to the nurse.

items.q: Which conditions are risk factors for developing a deep vein thrombosis? Select all that apply.
o: Fracture of the pelvis or hip
Fractures of the pelvis, hips, or long bones are DVT risk factors.
Pregnancy and the 4 to 6 weeks after birth
Pregnancy and the postpartum weeks increase DVT risk.
Use of oral contraceptives
Oral contraceptives and estrogen use are listed risk factors.
Smoking
Smoking is a listed risk factor for DVT.
Young adult age
Increasing age, not young age, is the listed risk factor.
Regular daily walking
Activity promotes venous return; long periods of inactivity are the risk.
items.ex: DVT risk factors include fractures, pregnancy and postpartum, estrogen use, smoking, inactivity, cancer, obesity, and increasing age.

alt.q: Which patients have risk factors for DVT? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with metastatic cancer receiving therapy
Cancer, especially metastatic, and cancer therapy raise DVT risk.
A patient after a long airplane trip
Long periods of sitting during travel are a risk factor.
A patient with a central venous catheter
Having a tube in a main vein is a listed risk factor.
A patient with a past history of DVT
A previous DVT increases the risk of another.
A patient of normal weight who jogs daily
Normal weight and regular activity are not DVT risk factors.
alt.ex: Cancer, long travel, a catheter in a main vein, and prior DVT are all listed DVT risk factors.

items.q: The nurse prepares to apply graduated compression stockings. Which findings are contraindications? Select all that apply.
o: Dermatitis on the area to be covered
Dermatitis or open lesions under the stocking are contraindications.
A recent skin graft to the lower leg
A recent skin graft to the lower leg is a contraindication.
Cool, cyanotic feet with gangrenous toes
Decreased arterial circulation means stockings could further compromise circulation.
A warm, swollen calf suggesting DVT
Manipulating a leg with DVT signs could dislodge the clot.
Recent major abdominal surgery
Compression is recommended after major surgery to prevent DVT.
Bed rest after a hip fracture repair
Immobility after a fracture is a reason for, not against, mechanical prophylaxis.
items.ex: Skin lesions, recent grafts, poor arterial circulation, and signs of DVT are contraindications to compression stockings.

alt.q: Which patients should NOT have graduated compression stockings applied? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with a recent vein ligation
A local leg condition such as recent vein ligation can be compromised by the stocking.
A patient with open sores on the shins
Open skin lesions in the covered area are a contraindication.
A patient with gangrene of the foot
A gangrenous condition reflects poor arterial flow, so stockings are contraindicated.
A patient on bed rest after knee surgery
This patient is at risk for DVT and is a candidate for prophylaxis.
A patient with obesity awaiting surgery
Obesity is a DVT risk factor, not a contraindication to stockings.
alt.ex: Local leg conditions such as vein ligation, open lesions, and gangrene contraindicate stockings because they can compromise circulation.

items.q: Sequential compression devices are preferred over graduated compression stockings because of their improved efficacy and better patient adherence.
items.a: True
items.ex: SCDs are preferred for their better efficacy and adherence in preventing VTE.
items.ww: The book states SCDs are preferred to graduated stockings, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Adding graduated compression stockings to sequential compression devices gives a patient greater protection against VTE than SCDs alone.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Using SCDs plus graduated compression stockings offers no additive benefit for VTE outcomes.
alt.ww: There is no added VTE benefit from combining the two devices, so the statement cannot be true.

items.q: The prone position is considered first-line therapy for critically ill patients with severe acute respiratory distress syndrome.
items.a: True
items.ex: Prone positioning improves reopening of collapsed alveoli and ventilation-perfusion matching, enhancing oxygenation in severe ARDS.
items.ww: The book names prone positioning as first-line therapy for severe ARDS, so it is not false.

alt.q: Prone positioning should be avoided in severe acute respiratory distress syndrome because lying face-down worsens oxygenation.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Prone positioning improves oxygenation and can decrease mortality in severe ARDS.
alt.ww: Lying face-down up to 16 hours a day improves oxygenation, so it does not worsen it.

items.q: When auscultating the lungs of a patient with restricted activity, the nurse focuses on the dependent lung fields.
items.a: True
items.ex: Pulmonary secretions collect in the dependent lower regions, which can lead to pneumonia.
items.ww: Secretions pool in dependent areas, so focusing there is correct, not wrong.

alt.q: In a patient on bed rest, pulmonary secretions tend to collect in the upper lung lobes, so auscultation should focus there.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Secretions accumulate in the dependent lower lung regions, where auscultation should be focused.
alt.ww: Secretions settle by gravity into dependent areas, not the upper lobes, so the statement is false.

items.q: Unless contraindicated, an adult who is immobile needs to drink at least [[1100 to 1400|1100-1400|1100–1400]] mL of noncaffeinated fluids daily.
items.ex: Adequate hydration keeps secretions thin, supports elimination, and helps prevent renal calculi and UTIs.

alt.q: Normal hydration of [[1100 to 1400|1100-1400|1100–1400]] mL of noncaffeinated fluid a day helps an immobile patient keep pulmonary secretions thin.
alt.ex: Adequate hydration keeps secretions thin, supports elimination, and helps prevent renal calculi and UTIs.

items.q: What is the purpose of a Trochanter roll?
items.a: Prevents external rotation of the hips when supine
items.ex: Positioning aids maintain alignment and function and protect the skin of patients with limited mobility.
w: Keeps the foot in dorsiflexion to prevent foot drop
That goes with Foot boot.
Keeps the thumb slightly adducted and opposed to the fingers
That goes with Hand roll.
Lets the patient raise the trunk and reduces shear
That goes with Trapeze bar.

w: Prevents external rotation of the hips when supine

w: Prevents external rotation of the hips when supine

Trapeze bar

Hand roll

Trapeze bar

Trapeze bar

Foot boot

Hand roll

mt.q: Match each positioning aid with its purpose.
pairs: Prevents external rotation of the hips when supine

sections.name: Skill 39.1 · Moving and positioning patients in bed

items.q: The nurse delegates repositioning of a patient with a spinal cord injury to assistive personnel (AP). Which instruction is most appropriate?
items.a: Explain the movement restrictions and the SPHM devices to use
items.ex: The nurse directs AP by explaining positioning restrictions and the type of safe patient handling devices needed.
w: Reposition the patient whenever the patient asks for it
The nurse designates specific times during the shift for the AP to reposition the patient.
Decide how many helpers are needed once you begin
The nurse tells the AP how many caregivers are needed before the task starts.
Logroll the patient alone using the drawsheet
Logrolling requires three caregivers and RN supervision, never one person.

alt.q: Which part of moving and positioning a patient in bed can the nurse delegate to AP?
alt.a: Turning the patient and maintaining body alignment
alt.ex: Moving, positioning, and maintaining correct body alignment can be delegated to AP with direction.
w: Checking orders for movement restrictions
Reviewing provider orders for restrictions is a nursing responsibility.
Obtaining the Braden score to set turning frequency
Skin and risk assessment to plan care is done by the nurse.
Choosing the SPHM device the patient needs
The nurse determines the devices needed and explains them to AP.

items.q: A patient who weighs 102 kg (225 lb) cannot independently assist with moving up in bed. Which approach is safest?
items.a: Use a friction-reducing device with at least three caregivers
items.ex: Patients over 91 kg (200 lb) need an FRD and at least three caregivers to reduce caregiver strain.
w: Use a friction-reducing device with two caregivers
Two to three caregivers is the guideline for patients under 91 kg.
Use a pull sheet with two caregivers and no device
Pulling a migrated patient with a pull sheet carries an extremely high risk of injury.
Have one caregiver help while the patient uses a trapeze
This is not a one-person task unless the patient can reposition independently.

alt.q: A patient who weighs 68 kg (150 lb) cannot independently assist with moving up in bed. Which approach is recommended?
alt.a: Use a friction-reducing device with two to three caregivers
alt.ex: For patients under 91 kg (200 lb), use an FRD and two to three caregivers.
w: Have one nurse pull the patient up by the drawsheet
Moving a dependent patient is not a one-person task, and pull sheets risk injury.
Lift the patient under the arms with two nurses
Caregivers do not lift patients; an FRD lets the patient slide without lifting.
Use a friction-reducing device with one caregiver
A dependent patient needs two to three caregivers even with an FRD.

items.q: Why does the nurse raise the bed to elbow level before repositioning a patient?
items.a: It brings the work toward the nurse’s center of gravity, reducing back injury
items.ex: Working at elbow height keeps the load near the nurse’s center of gravity and lowers the risk of back injury.
w: It lets the patient push more easily with the feet
Bed height is set for the caregiver’s body mechanics, not the patient’s push.
It keeps the patient from rolling off the far side
Side rails, not bed height, prevent falls during positioning.
It reduces shear on the patient’s heels and sacrum
Friction-reducing devices and heel lifting reduce shear, not bed height.

alt.q: Before repositioning a patient in bed, to what height does the nurse raise the bed?
alt.a: Level with the nurse’s elbows
alt.ex: A working height level with the elbows reduces strain on the nurse’s back.
w: Level with the nurse’s hips
Hip level is lower than recommended; the book specifies elbow level.
Level with the nurse’s shoulders
Shoulder level is too high for safe body mechanics.
The lowest locked position
The lowest position is used after repositioning, not during it.

items.q: A patient after hip surgery rates pain at 8 out of 10 and asks not to be turned. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Offer the ordered analgesic about 30 minutes before repositioning
items.ex: When pain is enough to avoid movement, give an ordered analgesic 30 minutes beforehand to enhance participation.
w: Turn the patient right away to protect the skin
Turning a patient in severe pain first reduces participation; pain relief comes first.
Document the refusal and skip this turn
Skipping turns raises pressure injury risk; the barrier of pain should be treated.
Ask AP to turn the patient quickly to limit discomfort
Speed does not relieve pain and risks injury; an analgesic is offered first.

alt.q: The nurse gives an ordered analgesic to a patient who avoids moving because of pain. When should repositioning take place?
alt.a: After the medication has had time to take effect
alt.ex: Allowing pain medication to take effect before repositioning ensures comfort and cooperation.
w: Immediately, while giving the medication
Moving before the drug works defeats the purpose of premedicating.
Only after the patient reports no pain at all
Complete pain relief is not required; the patient needs enough comfort to move.
At the next routine turn, several hours later
Delaying the turn adds pressure risk; reposition once the drug takes effect.

items.q: A patient’s Braden Scale score is 18. How should the nurse interpret this score?
items.a: The patient is at risk for pressure injury development
items.ex: A Braden Scale score of 18 indicates the patient is at risk for pressure injury development.
w: The patient has no risk for pressure injury
A score of 18 is identified as at risk, not risk free.
The patient already has a stage 2 pressure injury
The Braden scale predicts risk; it does not stage existing injuries.
The patient no longer needs scheduled repositioning
An at-risk score supports, rather than removes, the need for repositioning.

alt.q: A patient’s total Braden score shows low risk, but the activity subscale shows risk. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Plan care that addresses the activity subscale risk
alt.ex: Even with a low-risk total, any area of risk on a subscale needs a corresponding plan of care.
w: Rely on the total score and plan no changes
Subscale risks must be addressed even when the total score is low.
Repeat the Braden score in 1 week
Waiting delays care; the identified subscale risk needs a plan now.
Discontinue the Braden scale for this patient
The Braden scale remains the most predictive tool and continues to be used.

items.q: In the supported semi-Fowler position, why does the nurse place pillows lengthwise under each leg from mid-thigh to ankle?
items.a: To keep the knees slightly flexed and let the heels float
items.ex: This placement prevents knee hyperextension and popliteal artery occlusion and keeps heels off the mattress.
w: To keep the knees fully extended to prevent contractures
Full extension risks hyperextension; the knees are kept in slight flexion.
To press the heels firmly into the mattress for support
Heels should not touch the bed, to avoid prolonged pressure.
To rotate the hips outward to relieve sacral pressure
External hip rotation is a trouble point to prevent, not a goal.

alt.q: Which leg pillow placement is correct in the supported supine position?
alt.a: Lengthwise from mid-thigh to ankle under each leg
alt.ex: Lengthwise pillows support slight knee flexion, prevent popliteal pressure, and float the heels.
w: One firm pillow directly under both knees
A pillow under the knees places pressure on the popliteal area and circulation.
A small pillow under the heels only
Pillows under the heels keep pressure on them instead of letting them float.
No pillows, with legs flat on the mattress
Unsupported legs leave the heels on the mattress and the knees unprotected.

items.q: Why does the nurse support the affected arm of a patient with hemiplegia away from the body with the elbow on a pillow?
items.a: Paralyzed muscles cannot resist gravity, so the shoulder may sublux
items.ex: Without normal muscle resistance to gravity, the shoulder can sublux, causing pain and edema.
w: Support stimulates the return of voluntary movement
Support prevents complications; it does not restore voluntary movement.
It keeps the arm against the chest to stop abduction
The arm is placed away from the side, not held against the chest.
It keeps the elbow hyperextended to stop contractures
The elbow is supported on a pillow, not held in hyperextension.

alt.q: A patient with left hemiplegia is in semi-Fowler position with the left arm hanging unsupported. Which complication is the nurse most trying to prevent by supporting the arm?
alt.a: Shoulder subluxation, pain, and edema
alt.ex: Paralyzed muscles do not resist gravity, so an unsupported arm can lead to shoulder subluxation, pain, and edema.
w: Plantar flexion contracture and footdrop
Footdrop is prevented by supporting the feet in dorsiflexion.
Flexion contracture of the cervical spine
Neck flexion is prevented by avoiding too many pillows under the head.
External rotation of the affected hip
Hip rotation is prevented with a trochanter roll alongside the legs.

items.q: An AP is helping two nurses logroll a patient after spinal surgery. Which action by the AP requires the nurse to intervene?
items.a: Turning the patient’s shoulders first and then the hips
items.ex: Logrolling moves all body parts together as one unit to prevent twisting of the spinal column.
w: Placing a small pillow between the patient’s knees
A pillow between the knees prevents spinal tension and hip adduction.
Crossing the patient’s arms on the chest
Crossing the arms on the chest prevents injury to the arms.
Rolling the patient on a count of three
Rolling smoothly on a count of three keeps the body moving as one unit.

alt.q: Why is a small pillow placed between the patient’s knees before logrolling?
alt.a: To prevent spinal tension and adduction of the hip
alt.ex: The pillow keeps the legs aligned so the spine and hip are not strained during the roll.
w: To prevent injury to the patient’s arms
Crossing the arms on the chest is what protects the arms.
To provide a handle for gripping the patient
The fanfolded drawsheet provides the handles for gripping.
To prevent foot drop after the turn
Therapeutic boots or splints are used to prevent foot drop.

items.q: After a week of repositioning, the nurse finds a localized area of erythema with early breakdown over a patient’s sacrum. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Increase the frequency of repositioning
items.ex: Localized erythema and breakdown call for more frequent repositioning, a different FRD, and appropriate skin care.
w: Keep the same turning interval and recheck in 1 week
Waiting allows the injury to progress; the frequency must be increased.
Raise the head of the bed above 60 degrees
Raising the head above 60 degrees increases shear on the sacrum.
Reduce ROM exercises to rest the skin
ROM exercises address joints; reducing them does not relieve skin pressure.

alt.q: Which intervention is recommended when a patient’s skin shows localized erythema after repositioning?
alt.a: Post a turning schedule above the patient’s bed
alt.ex: A turning schedule above the bed helps ensure the more frequent repositioning that skin breakdown requires.
w: Turn the patient less often so the skin can rest
Breakdown requires more frequent, not less frequent, repositioning.
Replace the FRD with a pull sheet
Pull sheets increase shear and caregiver injury risk; a different FRD is used instead.
Limit fluid intake to reduce skin moisture
Fluids are not restricted; hydration supports skin integrity.

items.q: Two nurses are moving a patient up in bed using a friction-reducing device. Which additional action protects the patient’s heels from shear?
items.a: Have another caregiver lift the heels during the move
items.ex: Lifting the heels while the patient is moved up protects them from shearing force.
w: Have the patient push down firmly with the heels
Pushing the heels into the mattress adds friction and shear.
Raise the head of the bed to 60 degrees first
The head of the bed is kept flat when moving a patient up with an FRD.
Slide the patient quickly to limit contact time
Speed does not protect the heels and increases injury risk.

alt.q: How is the bed positioned before nurses move a dependent patient up in bed with a friction-reducing device?
alt.a: Head of bed flat with the patient supine
alt.ex: A flat bed with the patient supine allows the patient to slide up without lifting and limits shear.
w: Head of bed in high Fowler position
An elevated head of bed makes the patient slide down and adds shear.
Head of bed raised to 30 degrees
The head of the bed is kept flat, not raised, for this move.
Patient side-lying with the bed tilted
The patient is returned to supine before being moved up.

items.q: Which patient factors indicate the need for more frequent repositioning? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced sensation from a spinal cord injury
Reduced sensation lowers awareness of pressure, so the patient cannot protect the area.
Arterial insufficiency in the legs
Impaired circulation predisposes the patient to pressure injury.
Prematurely born infant
Very young infants have fragile skin and need frequent turning.
Leg in skeletal traction
Traction impairs mobility and can decrease ROM.
Alert adult who shifts position independently
A patient who moves independently perceives and relieves pressure.
Full range of motion with intact sensation
Normal ROM and sensation are not risk factors for immobility complications.
items.ex: Reduced sensation, impaired mobility, impaired circulation, and very young or older age all increase the need for repositioning.

alt.q: Which patients have risk factors that require repositioning more often? Select all that apply.
o: An older adult recovering from a stroke
Age-related changes and stroke-related loss of function increase immobility risks.
A patient with diabetic neuropathy of the feet
Neuropathy reduces sensation, so pressure is not perceived.
A patient after joint surgery with limited ROM
Joint surgery impairs mobility and can decrease ROM.
A young adult with a sprained wrist who walks freely
A mobile patient with normal sensation changes position on their own.
A patient with normal pedal pulses who walks daily
Intact circulation and mobility are not risk factors.
alt.ex: Older age, neuropathy, and joint surgery all add to the risk of immobility complications and the need for frequent turning.

items.q: Which actions are part of completing the supported prone position? Select all that apply.
o: Turn the head to one side on a small pillow
A small pillow supports the head turned to the side for comfort and ventilation.
Place a small pillow under the abdomen
A pillow under the abdomen reduces lumbar strain.
Raise the legs on pillows with heels flexed out over the edge
This avoids pressure on the toes and sides of the feet.
Support the arm on the same side up with elbow flexed
A supported flexed elbow lifts pressure off the rib cage.
Place a thick pillow under the chest to lift the neck
Hyperextension of the neck is a prone trouble point to prevent.
Rest the toes flat against the mattress
The toes are kept off the mattress to avoid pressure.
items.ex: Supported prone positioning uses small pillows for the head, abdomen, arm, and legs to ease breathing and protect pressure points.

alt.q: Which statements about placing a patient in the prone position are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Three to four nurses are used to turn the patient
Prone positioning requires three to four nurses.
All tubing and drains are cleared before rolling
Clearing tubing prevents accidental removal and pressure injury.
An FRD or lift can take up to 70% of the load off caregivers
A lift or FRD under the patient greatly reduces strain on those pulling.
The patient is lifted straight up and flipped by two nurses
The patient is rolled laterally then onto the abdomen using an FRD or lift by three to four nurses.
Pulling with the lower back muscles is the recommended technique
Leg muscles, not the lower back, should do the work to reduce injury.
alt.ex: Prone positioning needs three to four nurses, cleared tubing, and an FRD or lift to protect caregivers.

items.q: Which items does the nurse document or report after moving and positioning a patient in bed? Select all that apply.
o: The position change and time of the change
Documentation includes the position change and its time.
The friction-reducing device used
The FRD used is part of the documentation.
Observations of skin, joint movement, and ventilation
Observations of skin, joints, and ventilation are documented.
Respiratory, skin, or joint complications to the provider
Complications are reported to the health care provider.
Only the patient’s pain score after each turn
Documentation is broader than pain alone and includes position, time, device, and observations.
The names of visitors present during the turn
Visitors are not part of positioning documentation.
items.ex: Document the position change, time, FRD, observations, and learning; report complications to the provider and tolerance at shift change.

alt.q: Before discharge, what should the nurse teach the family caregiver of a patient who needs help moving in bed? Select all that apply.
o: Signs and symptoms of pressure injury to watch for
Caregivers are taught to observe for signs of PI at home.
Signs of developing contractures
Caregivers are taught to observe for contractures.
How to position the patient correctly
Teach the family caregiver how to position the patient.
To get help from another person when the patient’s weight requires it
The caregiver needs assistance from another person if weight dictates.
To pull the patient up in bed by the arms
Pulling by the arms risks shoulder injury and shear; it is not taught.
alt.ex: Home teaching covers PI and contracture signs, correct positioning, and getting a second helper when the patient’s weight requires it.

items.q: Pulling a patient who has migrated down in bed with a pull sheet carries an extremely high risk of caregiver injury.
items.a: True
items.ex: Pull sheets cause high caregiver injury risk; FRDs and lifts are used instead.
items.ww: The book warns of extremely high injury risk with pull sheets, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: Moving a dependent patient up in bed is a safe one-person task as long as a drawsheet is used.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Moving up in bed is not a one-person task unless the patient can reposition independently.
alt.ww: A drawsheet does not make one-person moving safe for a dependent patient, so the statement is false.

items.q: When a patient with hemiplegia lies supine, the affected knee is flexed about 30 degrees because extensor spasticity is most severe in this position.
items.a: True
items.ex: Slight knee flexion breaks up the abnormal extension pattern, which is strongest when supine.
items.ww: The book directs 30-degree knee flexion for this reason, so the statement is correct.

alt.q: For a supine patient with hemiplegia and extensor spasticity, a firm board pressed against the ball of the foot reduces muscle tone.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hard surfaces against the ball of the foot tend to increase muscle tone; a soft foot boot is used.
alt.ww: Stimulation of the ball of the foot by a hard surface increases tone, so the statement is false.

items.q: After repositioning a patient, the nurse raises side rails as appropriate and lowers the bed to its lowest locked position.
items.a: True
items.ex: A low, locked bed with side rails as appropriate prevents falls after positioning.
items.ww: These safety steps are required to prevent falls, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: After repositioning a patient, the bed is best left at elbow height so the next caregiver can reach the patient easily.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The bed is returned to the lowest locked position after repositioning to prevent falls.
alt.ww: Elbow height is only for working; leaving the bed high increases fall risk.

items.q: If a caregiver would have to lift more than [[35]] lb (15.9 kg) of a patient’s weight, the patient is considered fully dependent and assistive devices are used.
items.ex: The 35-lb (15.9-kg) limit marks when manual lifting is unsafe and SPHM devices are required.

alt.q: A patient is treated as fully dependent for positioning when a caregiver would lift more than [[15.9]] kg (35 lb) of the patient’s weight.
alt.ex: The 35-lb (15.9-kg) limit marks when manual lifting is unsafe and SPHM devices are required.

items.q: In 30-degree lateral positioning, which step comes right after “Roll the patient onto the side using knee and shoulder for leverage”?
items.a: Place a pillow under the patient’s head and neck
items.ex: That's step 5 of 9. The patient is moved over, rolled using leverage, then realigned at shoulder and hip and supported with pillows.
w: Bring the dependent shoulder blade slightly forward
That's step 6 of 9.
Keep the near leg straight, flex the other knee, and place hands on knee and shoulder
That's step 3 of 9.
Bring the dependent hip forward so the upper hip is about 30 degrees to the mattress
That's step 7 of 9.

alt.q: Which step comes first in 30-degree lateral positioning?
alt.a: Lower the head of the bed as far as tolerated with a nurse on each side
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 9. The patient is moved over, rolled using leverage, then realigned at shoulder and hip and supported with pillows.
w: Place an FRD under the drawsheet and move the patient toward the side opposite the turn
That's step 2 of 9.
Keep the near leg straight, flex the other knee, and place hands on knee and shoulder
That's step 3 of 9.
Roll the patient onto the side using knee and shoulder for leverage
That's step 4 of 9.

alt.q: Which step comes last in 30-degree lateral positioning?
alt.a: Place a pillow under the semiflexed upper leg from groin to foot
alt.ex: That's step 9 of 9. The patient is moved over, rolled using leverage, then realigned at shoulder and hip and supported with pillows.
w: Place a tuck-back pillow behind the patient’s back
That's step 8 of 9.
Bring the dependent hip forward so the upper hip is about 30 degrees to the mattress
That's step 7 of 9.
Bring the dependent shoulder blade slightly forward
That's step 6 of 9.

alt.q: In 30-degree lateral positioning, which step comes right after “Lower the head of the bed as far as tolerated with a nurse on each side”?
alt.a: Place an FRD under the drawsheet and move the patient toward the side opposite the turn
alt.ex: That's step 2 of 9. The patient is moved over, rolled using leverage, then realigned at shoulder and hip and supported with pillows.

items.q: Which layer of the skin contains the sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles?
items.a: Dermis
items.ex: Nerve fibers, blood vessels, sweat glands, sebaceous glands, and hair follicles run through the dermal layers.
w: Epidermis
The epidermis is the outer layer that shields against water loss and generates new cells.
Subcutaneous tissue
Subcutaneous tissue holds fat cells, provides insulation, and anchors skin to muscle.
Stratum corneum
The stratum corneum is the outermost surface of the epidermis, not the glandular layer.

alt.q: Which skin layer provides heat insulation and anchors the skin loosely to underlying structures such as muscle?
alt.a: Subcutaneous tissue
alt.ex: The subcutaneous tissue, filled with fat cells, insulates and loosely anchors the skin to muscle.
w: Dermis
The dermis is collagen and elastic fibers supporting the epidermis and housing glands.
Epidermis
The epidermis is the outer protective layer that sheds and replaces cells.
Stratum corneum
The stratum corneum is the surface layer whose loss raises pressure injury risk.

items.q: According to the textbook, what is the most important property of sebum?
items.a: It has bactericidal action.
items.ex: Sebum softens skin and slows water loss, but the book stresses its bactericidal action as more important.
w: It promotes heat loss by evaporation.
Sweat, not sebum, promotes heat loss by evaporation.
It generates new epidermal cells.
The epidermis itself generates new cells to replace those shed.
It carries oxygen to the dermis.
Blood vessels in the dermis deliver oxygen; sebum is an oily secretion.

alt.q: Which skin secretion lubricates skin and hair, slows water loss in low humidity, and kills bacteria?
alt.a: Sebum
alt.ex: Sebaceous glands secrete sebum into hair follicles, where it lubricates and has bactericidal action.
w: Sweat
Sweat cools the body through evaporation; it does not lubricate skin and hair.
Cerumen
Cerumen is earwax produced in the ear canal, not a general skin secretion.
Serous fluid
Serous fluid weeps from abrasions; it is not a normal lubricating secretion.

items.q: Why does the textbook caution against using alkaline soaps on the skin?
items.a: They neutralize the protective acid condition of the skin.
items.ex: The skin’s acidic pH retards bacterial growth, and alkaline soaps neutralize this protection.
w: They block sweat glands and prevent heat loss.
The book links alkaline soaps to loss of acidity, not to blocked sweat glands.
They thicken the stratum corneum and cause calluses.
Calluses result from friction or pressure, not from soap.
They increase sebum production and cause acne.
Acne involves bacterial breakdown of sebum; alkaline soap is not named as a cause.

alt.q: Which property of normal skin helps slow bacterial growth on its surface?
alt.a: Its acidic pH
alt.ex: The skin’s acidic pH, along with relative dryness and sebum, further retards bacterial growth.
w: Its alkaline pH
Normal skin is acidic; alkaline soaps neutralize this protective condition.
Its constant moisture
Relative dryness, not moisture, inhibits bacterial growth; moisture causes MASD.
Its lack of resident flora
Normal flora resides on skin and actually helps inhibit pathogens.

items.q: Mrs. White, 78, has dry, itchy skin on her arms and legs. Which bathing approach should the nurse use?
items.a: Use warm water, blot the skin dry, and apply moisturizer right after drying.
items.ex: Warm water, blotting, and immediate moisturizer reduce dryness in aging skin that produces fewer lubricating substances.
w: Use hot water and rub the skin briskly with a towel to stimulate circulation.
Hot water dries skin, and rubbing adds friction to fragile aging skin.
Bathe her twice daily with deodorant soap to reduce itching.
Frequent bathing and harsh soaps increase dryness and itching.
Leave the bathroom door open and let the skin air-dry fully.
Closing the door keeps humidity; moisturizer should be applied right after drying.

alt.q: An older adult with dry skin is taught about bathing. Which statement shows understanding of the teaching?
alt.a: “I’ll use warm water, pat my skin dry, and put lotion on right away.”
alt.ex: Warm water, patting dry, and prompt moisturizer help maintain fluid within aging skin.
w: “A long hot bath every day will soothe my itching.”
Hot water and frequent bathing worsen dryness and itching.
“I’ll leave a little soap on my skin to keep it soft.”
Soap residue irritates skin; the body should be rinsed of all soap.
“I’ll wait an hour after drying before using lotion.”
Moisturizer works best applied immediately after towel drying.

items.q: A nurse prepares to bathe a patient with paraplegia from a spinal cord injury. Which action is most important for skin safety?
items.a: Check the bath water temperature before it touches the patient’s skin.
items.ex: Patients with paralysis do not perceive temperature or burning, so the nurse must ensure water is not too hot.
w: Ask the patient to report whether the water feels too hot on the legs.
The patient cannot perceive heat or burning in paralyzed areas.
Use extra soap on the legs to remove oils that harbor bacteria.
Excess soap causes chemical irritation and dryness.
Rub the legs firmly to stimulate sensation during the bath.
Firm rubbing adds friction, which weakens the epidermis.

alt.q: Why must a nurse be especially careful with bath water temperature for a patient with advanced dementia?
alt.a: The patient may not perceive pain, burning, or temperature.
alt.ex: Patients with cognitive disorders or dementia may not perceive pain, burning, temperature, or pressure.
w: The patient’s skin produces too much sebum.
Sebum production is not the reason for temperature caution.
The patient’s skin is more acidic than normal.
Skin acidity protects against bacteria; it does not explain burn risk.
The patient sweats less and cannot cool down.
The danger is unrecognized burning, not reduced sweating.

items.q: A patient has frequent episodes of urinary and fecal incontinence. Which skin finding is most important for the nurse to report?
items.a: Erythema and edema of the perineal skin with areas of erosion
items.ex: Incontinence-associated dermatitis shows erythema and edema and can progress to erosion and infection.
w: Smooth, warm, supple perineal skin with good turgor
Smooth, warm, supple skin with good turgor is a normal finding.
Slight body odor before the morning bath
Mild odor is addressed with hygiene; it is not a skin injury.
Dry, flaky skin on the outer forearms
Dry skin needs care but is less urgent than eroded, inflamed perineal skin.

alt.q: Which condition is the most common form of moisture-associated skin damage?
alt.a: Incontinence-associated dermatitis
alt.ex: IAD is the most common MASD, marked by erythema and edema that may progress to erosion.
w: Allergic contact dermatitis
Contact dermatitis is caused by a substance such as adhesive or soap, not moisture.
Medical adhesive–related skin injury
MARSI results from repeated adhesive removal, not moisture exposure.
Acne vulgaris
Acne is inflammation of the sebaceous glands, not moisture damage.

items.q: A patient with a fever is lying under three heavy blankets. Why should the nurse remove the extra coverings?
items.a: Excess coverings conserve heat and interfere with heat loss by radiation and conduction.
items.ex: Bed coverings promote heat conservation, interfering with normal heat loss in a febrile patient.
w: Excess coverings increase heat loss by evaporation of sweat.
Coverings conserve heat; wet linen, not blankets, increases heat loss.
Excess coverings stimulate sebum production and acne.
Blankets are not linked to sebum or acne in the text.
Excess coverings lower the skin’s acidic pH.
Skin pH is altered by alkaline soaps, not blankets.

alt.q: A patient’s gown and sheets are soaked with perspiration. What effect does this have on body temperature regulation?
alt.a: Wet bed linen and gowns increase heat loss.
alt.ex: Wet linen increases heat loss, so keeping linen dry helps temperature regulation and prevents moisture damage.
w: Wet bed linen and gowns conserve body heat.
Wet linen promotes heat loss; dry coverings conserve heat.
Wet bed linen and gowns have no effect on heat loss.
The book lists wet linen as increasing heat loss.
Wet bed linen and gowns stop evaporation of sweat.
Moisture promotes evaporative and conductive heat loss.

items.q: Which nursing practice is most likely to weaken the epidermis?
items.a: Removing tape quickly from the same area of skin each day
items.ex: Scraping or stripping the skin surface, such as tape removal, weakens the epidermis.
w: Applying an emollient after the bath
Emollients soften skin and prevent moisture loss.
Smoothing wrinkles out of the bed linen
Smoothing linen removes sources of mechanical irritation.
Using warm rather than hot bath water
Warm water protects against dryness; it does not strip the epidermis.

alt.q: When repositioning a patient in bed, why should the nurse avoid dragging the patient across the sheets?
alt.a: Friction removes the stratum corneum and increases risk for pressure injuries.
alt.ex: Minimizing friction preserves the stratum corneum and lowers pressure injury risk.
w: Friction makes the skin too acidic and promotes bacteria.
An acid pH protects skin; friction strips its surface layer.
Friction increases sebum and causes acne flares.
Acne relates to sebaceous gland activity, not repositioning.
Friction blocks heat loss by radiation and conduction.
Heat loss is affected by coverings and moisture, not friction.

items.q: What role do the bacteria that normally reside on the outer epidermis play?
items.a: They inhibit the growth of disease-causing microorganisms.
items.ex: Resident normal flora is helpful because it inhibits the growth of pathogens.
w: They break down sebum and cause most skin infections.
Normal flora is protective, not the main cause of skin infection.
They generate new cells to replace shed skin cells.
The epidermis generates new cells; bacteria do not.
They regulate body temperature through evaporation.
Sweat evaporation, not bacteria, aids heat loss.

alt.q: A student says daily bathing should remove all bacteria from the skin. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Normal flora on the skin is helpful because it keeps harmful organisms from growing.”
alt.ex: Resident flora inhibits pathogen growth, so the goal is cleanliness, not sterile skin.
w: “Yes, any bacteria left on the skin will cause an infection.”
Bacteria commonly reside on skin, and normal flora is protective.
“Hot water and alkaline soap are needed to sterilize the skin.”
Hot water dries skin, and alkaline soap removes its protective acidity.
“Bathing several times daily is best for all older adults.”
Older adults are bathed only once or twice a week to protect skin oils.

items.q: A patient with obesity is being bathed. Which area requires the nurse’s particular attention?
items.a: Skinfolds, which must be separated, inspected, and kept dry
items.ex: Skinfolds trap moisture and limit air circulation; they must be separated, inspected, and dried, especially in patients who are overweight.
w: The palms, which are prone to callus formation
Calluses form from friction on palms or soles; skinfolds are the key concern here.
The scalp, which needs daily medicated shampoo
Medicated shampoo treats dandruff; it is not routine for obesity.
The forearms, which need daily alkaline soap
Alkaline soap neutralizes the skin’s protective acid condition.

alt.q: Why does obesity increase a patient’s risk for skin problems?
alt.a: Adipose tissue increases moisture and pressure and limits air circulation.
alt.ex: Excess adipose tissue adds pressure, traps moisture, and reduces air circulation, raising pressure injury risk.
w: Adipose tissue makes the skin more acidic and brittle.
Obesity is linked to moisture and pressure, not acidity.
Adipose tissue greatly increases sebum and hair growth.
The book does not link obesity to sebum or hair growth.
Adipose tissue makes the skin overly sensitive to pain.
The concern is moisture and pressure, not heightened pain sensitivity.

items.q: A patient’s skin is flaky and rough on the hands and legs. Which instruction about dry skin is correct?
items.a: Rinse all soap off the body because residue can irritate the skin.
items.ex: Soap residue irritates skin and can cause breakdown, so thorough rinsing is part of dry skin care.
w: Increase bathing frequency to remove dead skin cells.
Dry skin calls for bathing less frequently, not more.
Limit fluid intake to reduce sweating that dries skin.
Increasing fluid intake helps hydrate dry skin.
Wait until the skin is fully air-dried before applying cream.
Moisturizing cream is applied immediately after towel drying.

alt.q: A patient with dry skin is taught self-care. Which statement shows a need for further teaching?
alt.a: “I’ll take a hot bath every evening to soften my skin.”
alt.ex: Dry skin calls for less frequent bathing with warm, not hot, water.
w: “I’ll use a humidifier to add moisture to the air.”
Adding moisture to the air is a correct dry skin intervention.
“I’ll pat my skin dry instead of rubbing it.”
Patting skin dry is correct for dry skin.
“I’ll drink more fluids during the day.”
Increasing fluid intake is a correct intervention.

items.q: Which functions does the skin perform? Select all that apply.
o: Protection against microorganisms
The relatively impermeable epidermis prevents entry of microorganisms.
Body temperature regulation
Radiation, evaporation, conduction, and convection from skin control temperature.
Cutaneous sensation
Skin contains sensory organs for touch, pain, heat, cold, and pressure.
Excretion and secretion
Sweat and sebum are excreted and secreted through the skin.
Production of red blood cells
Red blood cell production is not a skin function listed in the text.
Production of antibodies
Antibody production is not listed among the skin’s functions.
items.ex: The skin protects, secretes, excretes, regulates temperature, and provides cutaneous sensation.

alt.q: Which statements correctly describe how the skin carries out its functions? Select all that apply.
o: Sweat promotes heat loss by evaporation.
Sweat evaporation is a skin mechanism for heat loss.
Sebum lubricates the skin and hair.
Sebum softens and lubricates skin and hair.
Sensory organs detect touch, pain, heat, cold, and pressure.
These sensory organs provide cutaneous sensation.
Constant moisture strengthens the epidermal barrier.
Constant moisture causes moisture-associated skin damage.
Alkaline soaps reinforce the skin’s acid protection.
Alkaline soaps neutralize the protective acid condition.
alt.ex: Sweat, sebum, and sensory organs carry out heat loss, lubrication, and sensation; moisture and alkaline soap harm the skin.

items.q: Which practices contribute to dry, flaky skin? Select all that apply.
o: Bathing too frequently
Too-frequent bathing removes protective oils.
Bathing in hot water
Hot water leads to dry, flaky skin.
Living in a low-humidity environment
Low humidity increases dryness and itching.
Applying moisturizer right after drying
Moisturizer helps maintain fluid within the skin.
Bathing with warm water
Warm, not hot, water is recommended for dry skin.
items.ex: Frequent bathing, hot water, and low humidity strip protective oils and moisture from the skin.

alt.q: Which actions help prevent dry skin? Select all that apply.
o: Bathe less frequently
Less frequent bathing preserves protective oils.
Use a humidifier
A humidifier adds moisture to the air.
Increase fluid intake
Fluids help hydrate the skin.
Use hot water to open pores
Hot water dries the skin.
Leave soap residue on the skin
Soap residue irritates skin and can cause breakdown.
alt.ex: Less frequent bathing, a humidifier, and more fluids reduce dryness; hot water and soap residue worsen it.

items.q: Which patients need especially careful skin assessment because of increased risk for impaired skin integrity? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with reduced sensation after a stroke
Reduced sensation means skin injury goes unnoticed.
A patient with a cast on the lower leg
External devices exert pressure and friction on the skin.
A patient with delirium who is incontinent
Altered cognition and excretions on skin increase risk.
A patient with poor protein intake and dehydration
Poor nutrition and hydration impair tissue synthesis and turgor.
An alert, mobile adult with normal intake
This patient has none of the listed risk factors.
items.ex: Reduced sensation, devices, altered cognition, incontinence, and poor nutrition all raise risk for impaired skin integrity.

alt.q: Which conditions does the textbook identify as risk factors for skin problems? Select all that apply.
o: Immobilization
Inability to change position exposes dependent parts to pressure.
Vascular insufficiency
Decreased circulation leads to ischemia and breakdown.
Excessive secretions such as wound drainage
Moisture irritates skin and causes maceration.
Regular use of emollients
Emollients soften skin and prevent moisture loss.
Intact sensation and full mobility
These protect against, rather than cause, skin injury.
alt.ex: Immobility, poor circulation, and excess moisture are skin risk factors; emollients and normal function protect the skin.

items.q: Constant exposure of the skin to moisture strengthens the epidermis and protects it from injury.
items.a: False
items.ex: Constant moisture causes moisture-associated skin damage, so linen and clothing should be kept dry.
items.ww: The book states relative dryness inhibits bacteria and constant moisture leads to skin injury.

alt.q: Keeping bed linen and clothing dry helps prevent moisture-associated skin damage.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Dry linen and clothing limit constant moisture exposure that leads to MASD.
alt.ww: It is not false; the book directly recommends dry linen to prevent moisture exposure.

items.q: Too-frequent bathing and the use of hot water often lead to dry, flaky skin.
items.a: True
items.ex: These practices remove protective oils, leaving skin dry and flaky.
items.ww: It is not false; the book names frequent bathing and hot water as causes of dryness.

alt.q: The more often older adults bathe, the better their skin retains its protective oils.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Older adults are bathed only once or twice a week to avoid removing protective oils.
alt.ww: Frequent bathing strips oils; aging skin already produces fewer lubricating substances.

items.q: Patients with paralysis can be relied on to report bath water that is too hot on affected areas.
items.a: False
items.ex: Patients with paralysis do not perceive pressure, pain, temperature, or burning sensations.
items.ww: The patient cannot feel heat in paralyzed areas, so the nurse must check temperature.

alt.q: Patients with cognitive disorders or dementia may not perceive pain, burning, temperature, or pressure.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Impaired perception means the nurse must protect these patients from burns and pressure.
alt.ww: It is not false; the book states these patients may not perceive such sensations.

items.q: Constant exposure of the skin to moisture causes [[moisture-associated skin damage|MASD|moisture associated skin damage]].
items.ex: Wet linen, perspiration, and incontinence keep skin moist and lead to MASD and skin injury.

alt.q: Incontinence-associated dermatitis is the most common form of [[moisture-associated skin damage|MASD|moisture associated skin damage]].
alt.ex: Wet linen, perspiration, and incontinence keep skin moist and lead to MASD and skin injury.

items.q: Sebaceous glands secrete [[sebum]], an oily fluid that lubricates the skin and has bactericidal action.
items.ex: Sebum is secreted into hair follicles, softens skin, slows water loss, and kills bacteria.

alt.q: The oily, odorous secretion that slows water loss from skin when humidity is low is called [[sebum]].
alt.ex: Sebum is secreted into hair follicles, softens skin, slows water loss, and kills bacteria.

items.q: What does Epidermis describe?
items.a: Outer layer that prevents water loss and generates new cells
items.ex: Each skin layer and gland has a distinct role in protection, support, and lubrication.
w: Collagen and elastic layer holding glands and hair follicles
That goes with Dermis.
Fat-filled layer that insulates and anchors skin to muscle
That goes with Subcutaneous tissue.
Structures that secrete sebum into hair follicles
That goes with Sebaceous glands.

alt.q: What does Dermis describe?
alt.a: Collagen and elastic layer holding glands and hair follicles
alt.ex: Each skin layer and gland has a distinct role in protection, support, and lubrication.
w: Outer layer that prevents water loss and generates new cells
That goes with Epidermis.
Fat-filled layer that insulates and anchors skin to muscle
That goes with Subcutaneous tissue.
Structures that secrete sebum into hair follicles
That goes with Sebaceous glands.

alt.q: What does Subcutaneous tissue describe?
alt.a: Fat-filled layer that insulates and anchors skin to muscle
alt.ex: Each skin layer and gland has a distinct role in protection, support, and lubrication.
w: Outer layer that prevents water loss and generates new cells
That goes with Epidermis.
Collagen and elastic layer holding glands and hair follicles
That goes with Dermis.
Structures that secrete sebum into hair follicles
That goes with Sebaceous glands.

alt.a: Structures that secrete sebum into hair follicles
