w: Outer layer that prevents water loss and generates new cells
That goes with Epidermis.
Collagen and elastic layer holding glands and hair follicles
That goes with Dermis.
Fat-filled layer that insulates and anchors skin to muscle
That goes with Subcutaneous tissue.

alt.q: Which structure is the “Outer layer that prevents water loss and generates new cells”?
alt.a: Epidermis
alt.ex: Each skin layer and gland has a distinct role in protection, support, and lubrication.
w: Dermis
Dermis: Collagen and elastic layer holding glands and hair follicles.
Subcutaneous tissue
Subcutaneous tissue: Fat-filled layer that insulates and anchors skin to muscle.
Sebaceous glands
Sebaceous glands: Structures that secrete sebum into hair follicles.

alt.q: Which structure is the “Collagen and elastic layer holding glands and hair follicles”?
alt.a: Dermis
alt.ex: Each skin layer and gland has a distinct role in protection, support, and lubrication.
w: Epidermis
Epidermis: Outer layer that prevents water loss and generates new cells.
Subcutaneous tissue
Subcutaneous tissue: Fat-filled layer that insulates and anchors skin to muscle.
Sebaceous glands
Sebaceous glands: Structures that secrete sebum into hair follicles.

alt.q: Which structure is the “Fat-filled layer that insulates and anchors skin to muscle”?
alt.a: Subcutaneous tissue
alt.ex: Each skin layer and gland has a distinct role in protection, support, and lubrication.
w: Epidermis
Epidermis: Outer layer that prevents water loss and generates new cells.
Dermis
Dermis: Collagen and elastic layer holding glands and hair follicles.
Sebaceous glands
Sebaceous glands: Structures that secrete sebum into hair follicles.

alt.q: Which structure is the “Structures that secrete sebum into hair follicles”?
alt.a: Sebaceous glands
alt.ex: Each skin layer and gland has a distinct role in protection, support, and lubrication.
w: Epidermis
Epidermis: Outer layer that prevents water loss and generates new cells.
Dermis
Dermis: Collagen and elastic layer holding glands and hair follicles.
Subcutaneous tissue
Subcutaneous tissue: Fat-filled layer that insulates and anchors skin to muscle.

mt.q: Match each skin structure with its description.
pairs: Outer layer that prevents water loss and generates new cells
Collagen and elastic layer holding glands and hair follicles
Fat-filled layer that insulates and anchors skin to muscle
Structures that secrete sebum into hair follicles
mt.ex: Each skin layer and gland has a distinct role in protection, support, and lubrication.

items.q: Which patient is at greatest risk for developing a serious foot problem?
items.a: A patient with diabetes mellitus and peripheral neuropathy
items.ex: Diabetes, peripheral neuropathy, and PVD reduce blood flow and sensation, so foot injuries quickly become serious.
w: A patient with seasonal allergies and asthma
Allergies and asthma do not reduce blood flow or sensation to the feet.
A young adult with a healed wrist fracture
A healed wrist fracture does not affect foot circulation or sensation.
A patient with a recent upper respiratory infection
A respiratory infection does not impair foot circulation or nerves.

alt.q: Why are patients with peripheral vascular disease at high risk for serious foot problems?
alt.a: Reduced blood flow to the feet impairs healing and promotes infection.
alt.ex: PVD reduces blood flow to the extremities, which impairs healing and raises infection risk.
w: Increased blood flow causes swelling and blisters.
PVD reduces, rather than increases, blood flow.
Excess sebum production softens the skin of the soles.
Older feet are dry from decreased sebaceous secretion.
Heightened sensation makes minor injuries very painful.
These disorders cause loss of sensation, not heightened sensation.

items.q: A patient with diabetes develops a foot ulcer after stepping on a tack. In the three contributing factors for diabetic foot ulcers, what does stepping on the tack represent?
items.a: The pivotal event causing the injury
items.ex: Diabetic foot ulcers involve neuropathy, ischemia, and a pivotal event such as stepping on a foreign object.
w: Peripheral neuropathy from nerve damage
Neuropathy is the change in nerve function, not the injuring event.
Ischemia from arterial plaque formation
Ischemia is decreased blood flow from plaque in the arteries.
Gangrene from an infected ulcer
Gangrene is a possible outcome of infected ulcers, not a contributing factor.

alt.q: Among the contributing factors for diabetic foot ulcers, what does ischemia refer to?
alt.a: Decreased blood flow related to plaque formation in arteries
alt.ex: Ischemia is reduced blood flow from arterial plaque, one of three factors in diabetic foot ulcers.
w: Changes in the function and efficiency of the nerves
This defines peripheral neuropathy.
Trauma such as banging the toe on furniture
This describes the pivotal event that causes injury.
Fungal infection of the skin between the toes
This describes athlete’s foot, not ischemia.

items.q: Which finding is characteristic of a normal, healthy nail?
items.a: Transparent, smooth, and convex with a pink nail bed
items.ex: A healthy nail is transparent, smooth, and convex, with a pink nail bed and translucent white tip.
w: Thickened and horny, separating from the nail bed
This suggests inflammatory lesions or fungus of the nail bed.
Opaque and concave with a pale blue nail bed
Normal nails are transparent and convex with a pink bed.
Brittle and ridged with an inflamed cuticle
An inflamed cuticle results from incorrect or infrequent nail care.

alt.q: A nurse inspects a patient’s toenails. Which finding is abnormal and should be documented?
alt.a: Thickened, horny nails separating from the nail bed
alt.ex: Inflammatory lesions and fungus of the nail bed cause thickened, horny nails that separate from the bed.
w: Pink nail beds with translucent white tips
Pink beds and translucent white tips are normal.
Smooth, convex nail surfaces
Smooth and convex nails are normal.
Transparent nail plates
Normal nails appear transparent.

items.q: A patient with diabetes says, “I soak my feet in warm water every night to keep them soft.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Soaking softens the skin and can lead to ulcers or infection, so wash and dry your feet instead.”
items.ex: Long soaks cause maceration that leads to ulceration or infection; patients with diabetes should not soak their feet.
w: “That is a good habit, but add Epsom salts to prevent infection.”
Soaking itself is the problem; the book says do not soak the feet.
“Soak your feet longer so the calluses can be cut off at home.”
Calluses should be referred to a podiatrist, not self-treated.
“Use hot water instead of warm so you can feel the temperature.”
Hot water risks burns because neuropathy reduces heat sensation.

alt.q: A nurse reviews foot care with a patient who has diabetes. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
alt.a: “I’ll wash my feet in lukewarm water and dry well between my toes.”
alt.ex: Daily washing in lukewarm water and thorough drying between the toes prevents maceration and infection.
w: “I’ll soak my feet for 20 minutes each evening.”
Soaking macerates tissue and increases risk of ulceration.
“I’ll use a heating pad when my feet feel cold.”
Heating pads are avoided because reduced sensation risks burns.
“I’ll go barefoot at home so my feet can breathe.”
Patients with diabetes should never go barefoot.

items.q: A patient with diabetes asks how to trim toenails safely at home. Which instruction is correct?
items.a: Trim the nails straight across and file the edges smooth.
items.ex: Trimming straight across and square filing the edges prevents ingrown nails and skin cuts.
w: Trim the nails in a deep curve at the corners.
Cutting into the corners promotes ingrown nails.
Soak the feet for an hour, then cut the nails short.
Soaking causes maceration and is avoided in diabetes.
Cut the cuticles back with scissors after trimming.
Cutting skin around the nail predisposes to infection.

alt.q: Improper nail trimming can lead to which common problem?
alt.a: Ingrown nails
alt.ex: Ingrown nails grow into the soft tissue and result from improper trimming, poor shoe fit, or heredity.
w: Plantar warts
Plantar warts are caused by papillomavirus.
Athlete’s foot
Athlete’s foot is a fungal infection linked to constricting footwear.
Calluses
Calluses result from local friction or pressure.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient with diabetes about skin care for the feet. Which statement by the patient shows a need for further teaching?
items.a: “I rub lotion between my toes to keep that skin soft.”
items.ex: Emollient lotion is applied over the feet but not between the toes, where moisture promotes maceration.
w: “I check inside my shoes before I put them on.”
Checking shoes for rough areas or objects is correct.
“I wear clean, dry socks with my shoes.”
Clean, dry socks at all times are recommended.
“I use a mirror to look at the bottoms of my feet.”
Using a mirror for daily inspection is correct.

alt.q: Where should a patient with diabetes avoid applying emollient lotion?
alt.a: Between the toes
alt.ex: Lotion keeps foot skin soft but is not applied between the toes, which must be kept dry.
w: On the heels
Lotion over all foot surfaces, including heels, keeps skin soft.
On the tops of the feet
The tops of the feet can receive lotion.
On the soles of the feet
Dry soles benefit from emollient lotion.

items.q: A nurse assesses the legs of a patient with diabetes. Which finding suggests vascular insufficiency rather than peripheral neuropathy?
items.a: Decreased hair growth on the legs and feet
items.ex: Decreased hair growth is a sign of vascular insufficiency, along with absent pulses and shiny skin.
w: Muscle wasting of the lower extremities
Muscle wasting is listed as a sign of peripheral neuropathy.
Absent deep tendon reflexes
Decreased or absent reflexes indicate peripheral neuropathy.
An abnormal gait
Abnormal gait is listed as a sign of peripheral neuropathy.

alt.q: Which assessment finding suggests peripheral neuropathy rather than vascular insufficiency?
alt.a: Decreased response to vibration and touch
alt.ex: Absent or decreased reflexes and response to vibration, touch, or pain indicate peripheral neuropathy.
w: Shiny appearance of the skin
Shiny skin is a sign of vascular insufficiency.
Blanching of skin on elevation
Blanching on elevation indicates vascular insufficiency.
Thickened nails
Thickened nails are listed under vascular insufficiency.

items.q: A patient with diabetes has a painful, swollen ingrown toenail. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?
items.a: Refer the patient to a podiatrist for treatment.
items.ex: Warm soaks are an exception for patients with diabetes, so referral to a podiatrist is appropriate.
w: Teach the patient to use frequent warm antiseptic soaks.
Warm soaks are contraindicated for patients with diabetes or vascular disease.
Trim the nail corners in a curve to relieve pressure.
Curved corner trimming promotes ingrown nails.
Apply an oval corn pad around the affected toe.
Oval corn pads increase pressure on the toes.

alt.q: For which patient would warm soaks for paronychia be contraindicated?
alt.a: A patient with diabetes mellitus
alt.ex: Warm compresses or soaks treat paronychia, except in patients with diabetes.
w: A healthy teenager who bites the nails
Warm soaks are appropriate for a patient without diabetes.
An adult who frequently uses polish remover
Polish remover causes nail dryness but does not contraindicate soaks.
A young adult with athlete’s foot
Athlete’s foot is fungal; it is not a stated exception to soaks.

items.q: A patient has a painful corn on the fifth toe. Which recommendation is consistent with the textbook?
items.a: Wear wider, softer shoes and see a podiatrist.
items.ex: Corns are aggravated by tight shoes; wider, softer shoes and podiatrist referral are recommended.
w: Apply an oval corn pad over the toe.
Oval corn pads increase pressure on the toes.
Cut the corn down with a razor blade at home.
Patients should not self-treat corns or calluses.
Wear snug shoes to keep the toe from moving.
Tight shoes aggravate corn pain.

alt.q: A patient asks how to treat a thick, painless callus on the sole of the foot. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “See a podiatrist; orthotic devices can help relieve the pressure.”
alt.ex: Calluses are referred to a podiatrist and not self-treated; orthotics redistribute weight to relieve pressure.
w: “Shave the callus off with a razor after soaking.”
Patients should not self-treat calluses.
“Apply antifungal powder twice daily until it fades.”
Calluses come from friction or pressure, not fungus.
“Wear tighter shoes so the area is not rubbed.”
Tight-fitting shoes make callus discomfort worse.

items.q: Mrs. White has arthritic deformity in both hands. What should the nurse do first when planning her hygiene care?
items.a: Observe her performing a hygiene task to determine the help she needs.
items.ex: Watching the patient brush her teeth or comb her hair shows the level of assistance needed.
w: Complete all of her hygiene care to save her energy.
Doing all care ignores her abilities and does not foster independence.
Teach her granddaughter to take over all hygiene care.
Family involvement follows assessment of what help is needed.
Delay hygiene care until her arthritis pain resolves.
Chronic arthritis will not resolve; care is adapted to her abilities.

alt.q: Why does a condition such as arthritis or multiple sclerosis affect hygiene care?
alt.a: It interferes with hand movement and impairs self-care abilities.
alt.ex: The hand has wide dexterity; conditions that interfere with hand movement impair a patient’s self-care.
w: It causes thickened, horny fingernails.
Thick, horny nails result from nail bed inflammation or fungus.
It leads to plantar warts on the hands.
Plantar warts are viral lesions on the sole of the foot.
It increases skin sensation and pain during bathing.
The concern is lost dexterity, not heightened skin sensation.

items.q: An older adult reports aching feet when walking. Why is this complaint a safety concern?
items.a: Foot pain is a source of falls in older adults.
items.ex: Foot pain changes gait and is a source of falls; footwear changes can reduce this risk.
w: Foot pain usually signals a plantar wart.
Foot pain has many causes; warts are only one.
Foot pain increases sebaceous secretion and maceration.
Older feet are dry from decreased sebaceous secretion.
Foot pain prevents the nails from growing.
Nail growth is not described as affected by foot pain.

alt.q: How does foot pain affect a patient’s body mechanics?
alt.a: It changes the gait, straining other joints and muscle groups.
alt.ex: Foot pain often changes a patient’s gait, causing strain on different joints and muscles.
w: It strengthens the muscles of the lower leg.
Pain limits activity rather than strengthening muscles.
It increases balance by slowing walking speed.
Altered gait from pain increases fall risk.
It has no effect on standing or walking.
Discomfort while standing or walking limits self-care.

items.q: A nurse teaches foot care to a patient with diabetes. Which instructions should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Inspect the feet daily, using a mirror if needed.
Daily inspection of all surfaces detects problems early.
Never walk barefoot.
Shoes protect feet that may have reduced sensation.
Check inside shoes before putting them on.
Rough areas or objects can rub and injure the foot.
Wiggle the toes and move the ankles several times a day.
These movements keep blood flowing to the feet.
Use an electric blanket to warm cold feet.
Electric blankets and heating pads are avoided due to burn risk.
Soak the feet daily to soften calluses.
Soaking causes maceration, ulceration, or infection.
items.ex: Daily inspection, footwear protection, and circulation exercises protect the feet; heat sources and soaking cause injury.

alt.q: Which practices should a patient with diabetes avoid? Select all that apply.
o: Crossing the legs for long periods
Crossing the legs impairs blood flow to the feet.
Using a heating pad on the feet
Heating pads risk burns in feet with reduced sensation.
Walking barefoot on hot pavement
Shoes should always be worn on hot surfaces.
Drying thoroughly between the toes
Thorough drying between the toes is recommended.
Wearing clean, dry socks
Clean, dry socks are worn at all times.
alt.ex: Crossing legs, heat sources, and going barefoot endanger the feet; drying between toes and clean socks protect them.

items.q: Which signs indicate vascular insufficiency of the lower extremities? Select all that apply.
o: Absent or decreased pulses
Weak or absent pulses reflect poor arterial supply.
Shiny appearance of the skin
Shiny skin is a sign of vascular insufficiency.
Blanching of skin on elevation
Blanching on elevation indicates poor circulation.
Poor wound healing
Reduced blood flow impairs healing.
Absent deep tendon reflexes
Absent reflexes indicate peripheral neuropathy.
Muscle wasting of the lower legs
Muscle wasting is a sign of peripheral neuropathy.
items.ex: Absent pulses, shiny skin, blanching on elevation, and poor healing reflect inadequate circulation.

alt.q: Which signs indicate peripheral neuropathy? Select all that apply.
o: Foot deformities
Foot deformities are a sign of peripheral neuropathy.
Abnormal gait
Abnormal gait is listed under peripheral neuropathy.
Decreased response to painful stimuli
Reduced response to stimuli reflects nerve damage.
Decreased hair growth on the legs
Decreased hair growth indicates vascular insufficiency.
Thickened nails
Thickened nails are listed under vascular insufficiency.
alt.ex: Deformities, abnormal gait, and decreased response to stimuli indicate neuropathy; hair loss and thick nails indicate vascular problems.

items.q: Which actions are part of a thorough foot assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Inspect between the toes and over the entire sole
All skin surfaces, including between toes and the sole, are examined.
Palpate the dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses
Pulses show adequacy of circulation.
Test sensation to light touch, pinprick, and temperature
Sensation testing detects neuropathy.
Observe the patient’s gait
Pain or decreased sensation causes limping or an unnatural gait.
Inspect only the tops of the feet to save time
Lesions often occur on the sole and between the toes.
items.ex: A complete foot assessment covers all skin surfaces, pulses, sensation, and gait.

alt.q: A nurse assesses the feet of a patient with diabetes. Which findings indicate increased risk for diabetic foot ulcers? Select all that apply.
o: Calluses
Calluses indicate increased risk for diabetic foot ulcers.
Toe deformity
Foot or toe deformity indicates increased ulcer risk.
Signs of trauma
Trauma to the foot indicates increased ulcer risk.
Pink nail beds
Pink nail beds are a normal finding.
Palpable pedal pulses
Palpable pulses indicate adequate circulation.
alt.ex: Trauma, calluses, ulceration, and deformity signal increased risk for diabetic foot ulcers.

items.q: Patients with diabetic neuropathy may be unable to feel heat, cold, pain, or pressure in their feet.
items.a: True
items.ex: Loss of sensory nerve function means foot injuries can go unnoticed and quickly become serious.
items.ww: It is not false; the book states these disorders cause loss of sensation.

alt.q: Patients with diabetic neuropathy usually notice foot injuries quickly because pain sensation increases.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Neuropathy reduces sensation, so patients may not feel injuries and need daily foot inspection.
alt.ww: Neuropathy causes loss, not heightening, of pain sensation.

items.q: Plantar warts are fungal lesions that are never contagious.
items.a: False
items.ex: Plantar warts are caused by papillomavirus and are sometimes contagious.
items.ww: The book identifies a virus, not a fungus, and notes warts can be contagious.

alt.q: Plantar warts are caused by papillomavirus and are sometimes contagious.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Plantar warts appear on the sole, are sometimes contagious, and are referred to a podiatrist.
alt.ww: It is not false; the book names papillomavirus as the cause.

items.q: Which finding describes normal oral mucosa?
items.a: Pink, moist, smooth, and glistening without lesions
items.ex: Normal oral mucosa glistens and is pink, soft, moist, smooth, and without lesions.
w: Pale, dry, and coated with a white film
Dryness and coating suggest xerostomia or poor hygiene.
Bright red, swollen, and tender to touch
Redness and swelling suggest inflammation such as stomatitis.
Rough, cracked, and dull in appearance
Cracked, dull tissue is not normal mucosa.

alt.q: Which oral finding is abnormal and should be reported to the health care provider?
alt.a: Red, swollen mucosa with ulcerations
alt.ex: Normal mucosa is pink, moist, and smooth; ulcerations and inflammation are reported.
w: Pink, glistening mucosa
Pink, glistening mucosa is normal.
Soft, moist mucosa
Soft, moist mucosa is normal.
Smooth mucosa without lesions
Smooth mucosa without lesions is normal.

items.q: Why can trauma to the floor of the mouth or underside of the tongue cause significant bleeding?
items.a: These areas are richly supplied with blood vessels.
items.ex: The floor of the mouth and undersurface of the tongue are highly vascular, so trauma bleeds heavily.
w: These areas lack a mucous membrane lining.
The mucous membrane lines the entire oral cavity.
These areas are covered by the hard palate.
The hard palate forms the roof, not the floor, of the mouth.
These areas produce enzymes that prevent clotting.
Saliva contains enzymes for digestion, not anticoagulation.

alt.q: A nurse provides oral care to a patient with a cut on the underside of the tongue. What should the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: The area may bleed significantly because it is highly vascular.
alt.ex: The undersurface of the tongue is richly supplied with blood vessels, so trauma often bleeds heavily.
w: The area will bleed little because it has few vessels.
This area is richly vascular, not poorly supplied.
The area will heal without care because saliva is sterile.
Saliva removes debris but is not sterile.
The area cannot be inspected because it lacks mucosa.
Mucous membrane lines the whole oral cavity.

items.q: Which statement describes a function of saliva?
items.a: It dissolves food chemicals to promote taste.
items.ex: Saliva cleanses the mouth, dissolves food chemicals for taste, moistens food, and contains enzymes.
w: It forms plaque that protects the gum line.
Plaque is harmful and is removed by brushing and flossing.
It stimulates new tooth growth in adults.
Saliva does not stimulate tooth growth.
It thickens secretions to protect the airway.
Thick secretions are a risk for airway clearance problems.

alt.q: Why does decreased saliva increase a patient’s risk for oral infection?
alt.a: Saliva normally removes cellular and bacterial debris.
alt.ex: Saliva removes cellular and bacterial debris that can cause infection, particularly fungal infection.
w: Saliva normally adds bacteria that fight fungi.
Saliva removes debris; it does not add bacteria.
Saliva normally keeps the mouth alkaline and sterile.
The book describes debris removal, not sterility.
Saliva normally coats teeth with fluoride.
Fluoride comes from toothpaste and rinses, not saliva.

items.q: Which patient is at greatest risk for xerostomia?
items.a: A patient receiving head and neck radiation who breathes through the mouth
items.ex: Radiation exposure and mouth breathing both impair salivary secretion, causing dry mouth.
w: A patient who drinks 2 liters of fluid daily and breathes through the nose
Good hydration and nasal breathing support saliva.
A patient who brushes twice daily with fluoride toothpaste
Brushing prevents caries but does not affect saliva production.
A patient who chews sugar-free gum after meals
Chewing is not named as a cause of dry mouth.

alt.q: A patient takes diuretics and antidepressants. Which oral problem should the nurse assess for?
alt.a: Xerostomia
alt.ex: Medications such as diuretics and antidepressants impair salivary secretion and cause dry mouth.
w: Glossitis
Glossitis is inflammation of the tongue, not the expected drug effect.
Cheilitis
Cheilitis is cracked lips, not reduced saliva.
Pediculosis
Pediculosis is lice infestation, unrelated to oral medications.

items.q: A patient receiving chemotherapy has stomatitis. Which instruction is appropriate?
items.a: Rinse with normal saline on waking, after meals, and at bedtime.
items.ex: Saline rinses clean the mouth; alcohol, commercial mouthwash, and vigorous flossing irritate inflamed tissue.
w: Rinse with an alcohol-based mouthwash after each meal.
Patients with stomatitis avoid alcohol and commercial mouthwash.
Floss vigorously at the gum line to remove plaque.
Gentle flossing prevents gum bleeding; it may need to be suspended.
Use lemon-glycerin swabs to moisten the mouth.
Lemon-glycerin dries mucous membranes and erodes enamel.

alt.q: A patient with stomatitis is taught oral care. Which statement shows understanding?
alt.a: “I’ll use a soft toothbrush and floss gently.”
alt.ex: A soft brush and gentle flossing prevent gum bleeding in inflamed oral mucosa.
w: “I’ll use a firm brush to scrub off the sores.”
Firm brushing traumatizes inflamed tissue.
“I’ll rinse with my regular mouthwash every hour.”
Commercial mouthwash is avoided with stomatitis.
“A glass of wine will help numb the burning.”
Patients with stomatitis are advised to avoid alcohol.

items.q: A nurse prepares to give oral care to an unconscious patient. How should the patient be positioned?
items.a: Semi-Fowler position with the head turned toward the nurse
items.ex: Turning the head and raising the bed to semi-Fowler position protects against choking and aspiration.
w: Flat supine with the head midline
Flat supine positioning lets secretions pool and be aspirated.
High Fowler with the neck hyperextended
Hyperextension does not help secretions drain away from the airway.
Prone with the face in the pillow
Prone positioning prevents access and risks airway obstruction.

alt.q: While cleaning the mouth of an unconscious patient, how should the nurse hold the mouth open?
alt.a: With a padded tongue blade or small oral airway
alt.ex: A padded tongue blade or small oral airway is used; fingers are never used because a human bite carries pathogens.
w: With two gloved fingers between the teeth
Never use fingers; a human bite contains many pathogens.
With a metal spoon placed between the molars
A padded blade or oral airway is specified, not a metal spoon.
With a rolled washcloth held by the nurse’s hand
The book specifies a padded tongue blade or small oral airway.

items.q: A nurse delegates oral hygiene to assistive personnel (AP). Which task must the nurse perform rather than delegate?
items.a: Assessing the patient’s gag reflex for aspiration risk
items.ex: Oral hygiene may be delegated, but the nurse assesses the gag reflex to judge aspiration risk.
w: Brushing the patient’s teeth
Toothbrushing can be delegated to AP.
Raising the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees
AP are instructed to keep the HOB raised 30 to 45 degrees.
Helping the patient rinse and spit
Rinsing is part of delegated oral hygiene.

alt.q: While brushing a patient’s teeth, assistive personnel note the patient is coughing and choking. What should the AP do?
alt.a: Report it to the nurse immediately.
alt.ex: AP must immediately report excessive coughing, drooling, or choking during or after oral hygiene.
w: Finish brushing, then mention it at shift end.
Choking signals aspiration risk and needs immediate reporting.
Lower the head of the bed flat and continue.
Lowering the bed increases aspiration risk.
Give the patient a large drink of water.
Extra water may worsen choking and aspiration.

items.q: A nurse sees assistive personnel caring for a patient’s dentures. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?
items.a: Wrapping the dentures in a napkin on the meal tray
items.ex: Dentures left on a napkin are easily thrown away; they belong in a labeled, enclosed cup.
w: Storing the dentures in tepid water in a labeled cup
Covered, labeled storage in water prevents warping and loss.
Lining the sink with a washcloth before cleaning
A washcloth in the sink cushions dentures if dropped.
Rinsing the dentures in tepid water
Tepid water avoids cracking or warping the dentures.

alt.q: Why should dentures be rinsed in tepid rather than hot water?
alt.a: Hot water can warp dentures so they no longer fit.
alt.ex: Hot water warps dentures and very cold water can crack them, so tepid water is used.
w: Hot water dissolves the denture adhesive.
The concern is warping of the denture itself.
Hot water makes dentures too slippery to hold.
The book cites warping, not slipperiness.
Hot water increases fungal growth on dentures.
Fungal stomatitis relates to hygiene and constant wear, not water temperature.

items.q: Why is oral care especially important for a patient who is unconscious?
items.a: Pooled secretions grow gram-negative bacteria that cause pneumonia if aspirated.
items.ex: Saliva pooling at the back of the throat grows gram-negative bacteria that cause pneumonia if aspirated.
w: Unconscious patients produce more saliva that rinses the mouth.
These patients have decreased salivation and dry mucosa.
Unconscious patients have a stronger gag reflex during care.
Unconscious patients often have a reduced gag reflex.
Unconscious patients cannot develop dental plaque.
Dryness increases plaque formation in these patients.

alt.q: Which factor makes a patient who is debilitated more susceptible to oral infection?
alt.a: Decreased salivation and increased plaque from mouth dryness
alt.ex: Changed normal flora, dryness-related plaque, and decreased salivation make these patients susceptible to infection.
w: Increased salivation that washes away normal flora
These patients have decreased, not increased, salivation.
A heightened gag reflex that causes vomiting
Debilitated or unconscious patients often lack a gag reflex.
Thin respiratory secretions that drain freely
Secretions are often thick and require oral suction.

items.q: Which oral rinse does the textbook recommend for a patient on mechanical ventilation?
items.a: 0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) rinse
items.ex: A 0.12% CHG oral care protocol reduces oral infections and ventilator-associated pneumonia in critically ill patients.
w: 4% chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) bath solution
4% CHG is used in bathing programs, not oral rinses.
50/50 hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) and saline
This mixture is listed for removing blood from hair.
2% lemon-glycerin (LG) swab solution
Lemon-glycerin dries mucous membranes and erodes enamel.

alt.q: A nurse uses 0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate during oral care in the ICU. What is the main goal?
alt.a: Reducing ventilator-associated pneumonia
alt.ex: 0.12% CHG oral care reduces oral infections, VAP, and non–ventilator-associated pneumonia.
w: Whitening discolored teeth
CHG is used for infection prevention, not cosmetic whitening.
Increasing saliva production
CHG is antimicrobial; it does not stimulate saliva.
Loosening dentures for removal
CHG has no role in denture removal.

items.q: A patient taking an anticoagulant asks about flossing. Which instruction is correct?
items.a: Use unwaxed floss and avoid vigorous flossing near the gum line.
items.ex: Patients on anticoagulants, chemotherapy, or radiation use unwaxed floss gently to prevent bleeding.
w: Stop all oral hygiene until the medication ends.
Oral hygiene continues; flossing is done gently.
Floss vigorously twice daily to remove all tartar.
Vigorous flossing near the gum line causes bleeding.
Rinse with lemon-glycerin after flossing to stop bleeding.
Lemon-glycerin dries mucosa and erodes enamel.

alt.q: A patient with diabetes asks how often to see a dentist. What is the best response?
alt.a: “Every 3 to 4 months, because diabetes often causes gum disease.”
alt.ex: Patients with diabetes or on chemotherapy often have periodontal disease and should see a dentist every 3 to 4 months.

This is too infrequent for a patient at risk for periodontal disease.
“Every 12 months, the same as everyone else.”
Patients with diabetes need more frequent dental visits.
“Every 6 weeks, to have your teeth cleaned.”
The book recommends every 3 to 4 months.

items.q: Which factors can impair salivary secretion and lead to xerostomia? Select all that apply.

Mouth breathing

Difficulty swallowing
Dry mouth affects swallowing.
Poor denture fit

Increased risk for oral ulcerations
Dry mouth increases risk for ulceration and trauma.
Excessive drooling
Xerostomia means too little, not too much, saliva.
Improved digestion
Dry mouth impairs, rather than improves, digestion.
alt.ex: Xerostomia affects taste, swallowing, digestion, nutrition, and denture fit and increases ulceration risk.

items.q: Which instructions should the nurse give to assistive personnel performing oral hygiene? Select all that apply.
o: Report any ulcerations, bleeding, or open sores.
AP report oral lesions and bleeding to the nurse.
Immediately report coughing, drooling, or choking.
These signs suggest aspiration risk.
Keep the head of the bed raised 30 to 45 degrees.
Raising the HOB helps prevent aspiration.

Assessing the gag reflex is the nurse’s responsibility.
Keep the patient flat to make brushing easier.

items.ex: AP report lesions, bleeding, and choking and position the patient to prevent aspiration; the nurse assesses the gag reflex.

alt.q: Which statements about delegating denture care to assistive personnel are correct? Select all that apply.

Dentures go in an enclosed, labeled cup.
alt.ex: Denture care can be delegated; AP avoid temperature extremes and report cracks or oral abnormalities.

items.q: Which teaching points about routine oral hygiene are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Brush at least twice a day with fluoride toothpaste.
This is the guideline for effective oral hygiene.
Replace the toothbrush every 3 months or after a cold.
This limits microorganism growth on the brush.
Do not share toothbrushes with family members.
Sharing toothbrushes risks cross-contamination.
Floss once a day.
Daily flossing is sufficient per the guidelines.
Give fluoride rinse to children age 6 or under.
Young children may swallow the rinse.
Drink directly from the mouthwash bottle to save time.
This risks cross-contamination.
items.ex: Twice-daily fluoride brushing, daily flossing, regular brush replacement, and not sharing items support oral health.

alt.q: Which practices are discouraged in oral hygiene? Select all that apply.
o: Using foam swabs as the main way to remove plaque
Foam swabs are ineffective at removing plaque.
Using lemon-glycerin sponges
They dry mucous membranes and erode enamel.
Sharing a toothbrush with a spouse
Sharing toothbrushes spreads microorganisms.
Using a soft-bristled toothbrush
Soft bristles stimulate gums without abrasion.
Using an enlarged handle for weak grip
Enlarged handles help patients with decreased dexterity.
alt.ex: Foam swabs, lemon-glycerin, and shared brushes are discouraged; soft bristles and adapted handles are recommended.

w: Tears that have drained into the ear canal
Tears drain through the nasolacrimal duct, not into the ear canal.
Excess clear discharge from the nasal mucosa
Clear, watery nasal discharge suggests allergies, not a cause of muffled hearing.
Soap residue that has irritated the cornea
Corneal irritation affects the eye, not hearing.

items.q: A nurse is cleaning the eyes of a patient during a bed bath. Which technique is correct?
items.a: Use plain warm water and wipe from the inner to the outer canthus
items.ex: Eyes are washed with plain warm water from inner to outer canthus, using a clean section of cloth for each eye.
w: Use mild soap and wipe from the outer to the inner canthus
Soap irritates the eye, and wiping toward the inner canthus pushes secretions toward the nasolacrimal duct.
Use a CHG cloth and wipe both eyes with the same section
CHG is never used on the eyes, and each eye needs a separate section of cloth.
Press gently on the closed eyeball to loosen secretions
Direct pressure over the eyeball causes serious injury.

alt.q: Why does the nurse wipe each eye from the inner canthus toward the outer canthus?
alt.a: It keeps secretions from entering the nasolacrimal duct
alt.ex: Bathing from inner to outer canthus prevents secretions from entering the nasolacrimal duct.
w: It stimulates the blink reflex to lubricate the cornea
Wiping direction is chosen to keep secretions out of the duct, not to trigger blinking.
It spreads tears evenly across the sclera
The direction is chosen to move secretions away from the nasolacrimal duct.
It allows one cloth section to be used for both eyes
A different section of the washcloth is used for each eye to reduce infection transmission.

items.q: A confused patient is admitted and cannot say whether they wear contact lenses. How should the nurse check for lenses?
items.a: Stand to the side and observe the corneas and the sclera
items.ex: Standing to the side shows a lens on the cornea; the sclera is also checked because a lens may shift off the cornea.
w: Shine a penlight into each pupil from directly in front
The book directs the nurse to stand to the side of the eyes to see a lens.
Press on each closed eyelid to feel for a lens
Pressure over the eyeball can cause serious injury.
Wait until the patient is alert enough to answer
Delay is unsafe because a lens left in too long causes corneal injury.

alt.q: Why is it important to determine promptly whether an unresponsive patient is wearing contact lenses?
alt.a: A lens left in place too long can injure the cornea
alt.ex: An undetected contact lens left in place too long causes corneal injury.
w: A lens left in place stops all tear production
The book identifies corneal injury, not loss of tears, as the risk.
A lens left in place causes impacted cerumen
Cerumen is an ear problem unrelated to contact lenses.
A lens left in place blocks the nasolacrimal duct
The risk the book names is corneal injury.

items.q: A nurse prepares to irrigate the ear of a 45-year-old patient with impacted cerumen. How should the nurse position the pinna?
items.a: Pull the pinna up and back
items.ex: For adults and children over 3 years of age, the pinna is pulled gently up and back to straighten the canal.
w: Pull the pinna down and back
Down and back is used for children 3 years of age or younger.
Pull the pinna down and forward
This does not straighten the adult ear canal and is not the book’s technique.
Leave the pinna in its natural position
The pinna is retracted to straighten the canal for irrigation.

alt.q: A nurse prepares to irrigate the ear of a 2-year-old child. How should the nurse position the pinna?
alt.a: Pull the pinna down and back
alt.ex: In children 3 years of age or younger, the pinna is pulled down and back.
w: Pull the pinna up and back
Up and back is used for adults and children over 3 years of age.
Pull the pinna up and forward
This is not a technique described for ear irrigation.
Press the tragus inward over the canal
Pressing the tragus would occlude the canal rather than straighten it.

items.q: During an ear irrigation the patient reports nausea and vertigo. What do these symptoms indicate?
items.a: The solution is too hot or too cold or is under too much pressure
items.ex: Pain, nausea, or vertigo during irrigation signal that the solution temperature or pressure is wrong.
w: The cerumen has loosened and the irrigation is complete
Completion is judged by inspecting the canal, not by nausea or vertigo.
The tympanic membrane is intact and responding normally
These are warning symptoms, not signs of a normal response.
The syringe tip is not occluding the canal tightly enough
The canal must not be occluded, because occlusion puts pressure on the tympanic membrane.

alt.q: What temperature should the irrigating solution be for ear irrigation?
alt.ex: The ear canal is washed gently with warm solution at 37°C (98.6°F) to avoid pain, nausea, or vertigo.
w: Solution this cool can cause vertigo and nausea.
Solution warmer than body temperature can cause discomfort and vertigo.
Solution this hot can cause pain, vertigo, and injury.

items.q: Which finding in a patient’s history contraindicates ear irrigation?
items.a: A perforated tympanic membrane
items.ex: A perforated tympanic membrane contraindicates irrigation, so the nurse asks about it before the procedure.
w: Impacted cerumen in the affected ear
Impacted cerumen is the usual reason for irrigation, not a contraindication.
Age older than 65 years
Older adults commonly have impacted cerumen that can be removed by irrigation.
Use of a behind-the-ear hearing aid
Wearing a hearing aid is not listed as a contraindication to irrigation.

alt.q: Before irrigating a patient’s ear, which question is the priority to ask?
alt.a: Have you ever had a perforated eardrum?
alt.ex: Irrigation is contraindicated with a perforated tympanic membrane, so this history is obtained first.
w: Do you wear soft or rigid contact lenses?
Contact lens use does not affect whether ear irrigation is safe.
How often do you shampoo your hair?
Shampoo frequency is unrelated to the safety of ear irrigation.
Do you have a clear, watery nasal discharge?
Nasal discharge relates to allergies, not to irrigation safety.

items.q: Which instructions about routine ear hygiene are correct according to the textbook? Select all that apply.
o: Clean the outer ear with a washcloth and warm water
Routine ear care involves cleaning the outer ear with a washcloth and warm water.
Gently rotate the end of a moistened washcloth into the canal
The outer canal is cleansed with the end of a moistened washcloth rotated gently into it.
Use gentle downward retraction at the canal entrance to loosen visible wax
Gentle downward retraction usually causes visible cerumen to loosen and slip out.
Use a cotton-tipped applicator to remove deep earwax
Cotton-tipped applicators can injure the canal, rupture the eardrum, or impact cerumen.
Carefully lift out hardened wax with a bobby pin
Bobby pins can injure the canal and rupture the tympanic membrane.
Irrigate impacted wax at home without a provider’s order
Irrigation requires a health care provider’s order.
items.ex: Routine ear care uses a washcloth and warm water; sharp or narrow objects can injure the canal or push cerumen deeper.

alt.q: A patient asks how to remove earwax at home. Which objects should the nurse teach the patient never to use? Select all that apply.
o: Toothpicks
Toothpicks can injure the ear canal and rupture the tympanic membrane.
Paper clips
Paper clips can injure the canal and impact cerumen.
Cotton-tipped applicators
Cotton-tipped applicators can push cerumen deeper and injure the canal.
Bobby pins
Bobby pins can injure the canal and rupture the tympanic membrane.
A washcloth moistened with warm water
A moistened washcloth is the recommended way to clean the outer ear and canal entrance.
alt.ex: Objects such as bobby pins, toothpicks, paper clips, and cotton-tipped applicators can injure the canal, rupture the eardrum, or impact cerumen.

items.q: Chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) cloths may be used to clean the eyes and face during daily CHG bathing.
items.a: False
items.ex: The textbook states never to use CHG solution or cloths to clean the eyes, ears, or face.
items.ww: CHG is safe for the body and perineum, but the book specifically excludes the eyes, ears, and face.

alt.q: The eyes are cleaned with a washcloth moistened in plain water, and CHG is never used on the eyes, ears, or face.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Basic eye care uses a clean washcloth moistened in water; CHG is not used on the eyes, ears, or face.
alt.ww: Soap and CHG can irritate the eyes, so plain water is the correct cleansing agent.

items.q: Patients who are unconscious need more frequent eye care because they have lost the protective blink reflex.
items.a: True
items.ex: Without the corneal blink reflex, unconscious patients are at risk for corneal drying, abrasions, and infection.
items.ww: The book states unconscious patients require more frequent eye care because blinking normally protects and lubricates the eye.

alt.q: Gentle direct pressure over the eyeball is an acceptable way to loosen crusted eye secretions.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Crusts are soaked with a warm, damp cloth for 2 to 3 minutes; pressure over the eyeball causes serious injury.
alt.ww: The book warns never to apply direct pressure over the eyeball because it causes injury.

items.q: Which description fits the Completely-in-canal (CIC) hearing aid?
items.a: Smallest and least visible; plugged by cerumen more than other models
items.ex: Hearing aids differ in size, visibility, power, and the dexterity needed to use them.
w: Fits the external canal; not for people with moisture or skin problems in the canal
That goes with In-the-ear (ITE).
Largest aid; useful for patients with manual dexterity difficulties
That goes with Behind-the-ear (BTE).
Analyzes sounds to remove background noise; programmed by an audiologist
That goes with Digital.

alt.q: Which description fits the In-the-ear (ITE) hearing aid?
alt.a: Fits the external canal; not for people with moisture or skin problems in the canal
alt.ex: Hearing aids differ in size, visibility, power, and the dexterity needed to use them.
w: Smallest and least visible; plugged by cerumen more than other models
That goes with Completely-in-canal (CIC).
Largest aid; useful for patients with manual dexterity difficulties
That goes with Behind-the-ear (BTE).
Analyzes sounds to remove background noise; programmed by an audiologist
That goes with Digital.

alt.q: Which description fits the Behind-the-ear (BTE) hearing aid?
alt.a: Largest aid; useful for patients with manual dexterity difficulties
alt.ex: Hearing aids differ in size, visibility, power, and the dexterity needed to use them.
w: Smallest and least visible; plugged by cerumen more than other models
That goes with Completely-in-canal (CIC).
Fits the external canal; not for people with moisture or skin problems in the canal
That goes with In-the-ear (ITE).
Analyzes sounds to remove background noise; programmed by an audiologist
That goes with Digital.

alt.q: Which description fits the Digital hearing aid?
alt.a: Analyzes sounds to remove background noise; programmed by an audiologist
alt.ex: Hearing aids differ in size, visibility, power, and the dexterity needed to use them.
w: Smallest and least visible; plugged by cerumen more than other models
That goes with Completely-in-canal (CIC).
Fits the external canal; not for people with moisture or skin problems in the canal
That goes with In-the-ear (ITE).
Largest aid; useful for patients with manual dexterity difficulties
That goes with Behind-the-ear (BTE).

alt.q: Which type of hearing aid is described as “Smallest and least visible; plugged by cerumen more than other models”?
alt.a: Completely-in-canal (CIC)
alt.ex: Hearing aids differ in size, visibility, power, and the dexterity needed to use them.
w: In-the-ear (ITE)
In-the-ear (ITE): Fits the external canal; not for people with moisture or skin problems in the canal.
Behind-the-ear (BTE)
Behind-the-ear (BTE): Largest aid; useful for patients with manual dexterity difficulties.
Digital
Digital: Analyzes sounds to remove background noise; programmed by an audiologist.

alt.q: Which type of hearing aid is described as “Fits the external canal; not for people with moisture or skin problems in the canal”?
alt.a: In-the-ear (ITE)
alt.ex: Hearing aids differ in size, visibility, power, and the dexterity needed to use them.
w: Completely-in-canal (CIC)
Completely-in-canal (CIC): Smallest and least visible; plugged by cerumen more than other models.
Behind-the-ear (BTE)
Behind-the-ear (BTE): Largest aid; useful for patients with manual dexterity difficulties.
Digital
Digital: Analyzes sounds to remove background noise; programmed by an audiologist.

alt.q: Which type of hearing aid is described as “Largest aid; useful for patients with manual dexterity difficulties”?
alt.a: Behind-the-ear (BTE)
alt.ex: Hearing aids differ in size, visibility, power, and the dexterity needed to use them.
w: Completely-in-canal (CIC)
Completely-in-canal (CIC): Smallest and least visible; plugged by cerumen more than other models.
In-the-ear (ITE)
In-the-ear (ITE): Fits the external canal; not for people with moisture or skin problems in the canal.
Digital
Digital: Analyzes sounds to remove background noise; programmed by an audiologist.

alt.q: Which type of hearing aid is described as “Analyzes sounds to remove background noise; programmed by an audiologist”?
alt.a: Digital
alt.ex: Hearing aids differ in size, visibility, power, and the dexterity needed to use them.
w: Completely-in-canal (CIC)
Completely-in-canal (CIC): Smallest and least visible; plugged by cerumen more than other models.
In-the-ear (ITE)
In-the-ear (ITE): Fits the external canal; not for people with moisture or skin problems in the canal.
Behind-the-ear (BTE)
Behind-the-ear (BTE): Largest aid; useful for patients with manual dexterity difficulties.

mt.q: Match each type of hearing aid with its description.
pairs: Smallest and least visible; plugged by cerumen more than other models
Fits the external canal; not for people with moisture or skin problems in the canal
Largest aid; useful for patients with manual dexterity difficulties
Analyzes sounds to remove background noise; programmed by an audiologist
mt.ex: Hearing aids differ in size, visibility, power, and the dexterity needed to use them.

items.q: A patient’s hearing aid makes a whistling sound. What does this most likely indicate?
items.a: Incorrect earmold insertion, poor fit, or earwax buildup
items.ex: Whistling indicates incorrect earmold insertion, improper fit of the aid, or buildup of earwax or fluid.
w: A fully charged battery working as intended
Whistling is a problem signal, not a sign of normal battery function.
A volume set at one-third to one-half
One-third to one-half volume is the recommended starting setting after insertion.
Normal filtering of background noise
Filtering background noise does not produce whistling.

alt.q: A patient is starting to use a new hearing aid. How long should the patient wear it at first?
alt.a: 15 to 20 minutes, gradually increasing to 10 to 12 hours
alt.ex: A new aid is worn 15 to 20 minutes at first, with time gradually increased to 10 to 12 hours.
w: 1 to 2 hours, gradually increasing to 24 hours
The book recommends starting at 15 to 20 minutes and working up to 10 to 12 hours.
4 to 6 hours on the first day, then all day
This starts too long; wearing time is increased gradually from 15 to 20 minutes.
10 to 12 hours, starting on the first day
10 to 12 hours is the goal reached gradually, not the starting time.

items.q: Which teaching points about hearing aid care are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid hairspray and perfume while wearing the aid
Spray residue makes the aid oily and greasy.
Remove or disconnect the battery when the aid is not in use
Box 40.13 directs removing or disconnecting the battery when not in use.
Clean the aid with a soft cloth as the manufacturer directs
Hearing aids are usually cleaned with a soft cloth.
Keep batteries where pets and small children cannot reach them
Batteries are stored securely so pets or curious children do not ingest them.
Wear the aid while using a hair dryer to check sound quality
Hearing aids are not worn under heat lamps or hair dryers.
Turn the volume to maximum right after insertion
The aid is turned slowly to one-third to one-half volume, then adjusted.
items.ex: Box 40.13 guides patients to protect the aid from heat, moisture, and residue and to keep it and its batteries clean and safe.

alt.q: Which situations should a patient avoid while wearing a hearing aid? Select all that apply.
o: Sitting under a heat lamp
Heat lamps can damage the aid.
Using a hair dryer
Hearing aids are not worn under a hair dryer.
Being outdoors in very wet, cold weather
Very wet, cold weather can damage the aid.
Applying hairspray
Hairspray residue makes the aid oily and greasy.
Having a conversation in a quiet room
Conversation is the purpose of the aid; volume is adjusted to a comfortable level for talking.
alt.ex: Heat, moisture, and spray residue damage hearing aids, so the aid is removed in these situations.

items.q: Contact lens wearers are taught the acronym RSVP: Redness, [[Sensitivity]], Vision problems, and Pain, which signal the need to remove the lenses.
items.ex: If any RSVP problem occurs, contact lenses are removed immediately, and a vision care specialist is contacted if problems continue.

alt.q: If a contact lens wearer notices redness, sensitivity, vision problems, or [[pain|eye pain]] (RSVP), the lenses should be removed immediately.
alt.ex: If any RSVP problem occurs, contact lenses are removed immediately, and a vision care specialist is contacted if problems continue.

items.q: The nurse teaches a patient about contact lens care. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I will keep my lenses moist or wet whenever I am not wearing them.”
items.ex: Box 40.12 teaches patients to keep lenses moist or wet when not worn.
w: “I can rinse my soft lenses with tap water to save solution.”
Tap water is not used to clean soft lenses.
“I will reuse yesterday’s storage solution if it still looks clean.”
Fresh solution is used daily for storing and disinfecting lenses.
“If debris sticks to a lens, I will scrape it off with my fingernail.”
Fingernails are never used on a lens to remove dirt or debris.

alt.q: Which statement by a contact lens wearer indicates a need for further teaching?
alt.a: “I keep my lenses in the same storage solution for a few days.”
alt.ex: Fresh solution must be used daily for storing and disinfecting lenses.
w: “I always start with the same lens when inserting or removing.”
Starting with the same lens avoids mix-ups and is correct practice.
“I wash, rinse, and air-dry my lens case every day.”
Daily washing, rinsing, and air-drying of the case is correct practice.
“If I drop a lens, I pick it up with a finger moistened in solution.”
A moistened finger is the correct way to pick up a dropped lens.

items.q: A patient cannot clear dried nasal secretions. Which action by the nurse is correct?
items.a: Use an applicator moistened in saline, inserted no farther than the cotton tip
items.ex: A cotton-tipped applicator moistened in water or saline may be used, but never beyond the length of the cotton tip.
w: Insert a dry applicator deep into the nostril to reach secretions
Applicators are moistened and never inserted beyond the cotton tip.
Have the patient blow forcefully with both nostrils occluded
The book recommends a wet washcloth, a moist applicator, or gentle suctioning.
Flush the nostril with warm tap water using a bulb syringe
Nasal irrigation is not described; excess secretions are removed by gentle suctioning.

alt.q: When using a moistened cotton-tipped applicator for nasal care, how far may it be inserted?
alt.a: No farther than the length of the cotton tip
alt.ex: The applicator is never inserted beyond the length of the cotton tip, to protect the nasal tissues.
w: About 2.5 cm (1 inch) past the cotton tip
Inserting beyond the cotton tip risks injury to nasal tissues.
Until resistance is felt at the back of the nose
Deep insertion is unsafe; the limit is the cotton tip.
Halfway up the length of the applicator stick
Only the cotton tip is inserted.

items.q: A patient has a nasogastric tube taped to the nose, and the tape is damp from nasal secretions. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Change the tape, because moist tape can macerate the skin and mucosa
items.ex: Tape becomes moist from secretions and macerates skin and mucosa, so it is changed at least daily and as needed.
w: Leave the tape until its scheduled weekly change
Tape is changed at least once a day, and moist tape threatens tissue integrity.
Add another layer of tape over the damp tape
Adding tape traps moisture against the skin and does not prevent maceration.
Remove the tape and let the tube hang freely
Tubing must be anchored to minimize tension and friction on the nares.

alt.q: How often does the textbook direct the nurse to change the tape anchoring a nasogastric or feeding tube?
alt.a: At least once a day
alt.ex: Tape anchoring nasal tubes is changed at least once a day because moist tape can macerate the skin.
w: At least once a week
Weekly changes allow moisture and maceration to develop.
Only when the tube is replaced
Tape needs daily changes regardless of tube replacement.
Every 3 days
The book directs changing the tape at least once a day.

items.q: A patient has a nasogastric tube. Which findings should the nurse look for where the tubing contacts the nares? Select all that apply.
o: Edema
Edema at the contact site is listed as a finding to observe.
Skin ulceration
Pressure and friction from tubing can cause ulceration.
Localized tenderness
Localized tenderness suggests device-related tissue injury.
Bleeding
Bleeding at the nares is listed as a finding to observe.
Pink, moist mucosa with little discharge
This is the normal appearance of the nasal mucosa, not a complication.
items.ex: Tubing in the nose can cause edema, ulceration, tenderness, inflammation, drainage, and bleeding where it contacts the nares.

alt.q: Which statements about assessment of the nose are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Normal nasal mucosa is pink and clear
Healthy nasal mucosa is pink and clear.
A healthy nose has little or no discharge
Normal nasal mucosa has little or no discharge.
Allergies cause a clear, watery discharge
The book links clear, watery discharge with allergies.
Skin under devices on the nose is assessed and cleaned at least twice daily
Skin around and beneath medical devices is assessed and cleaned at least twice daily.
Thick, crusted discharge is expected in healthy adults
Healthy nasal mucosa has little or no discharge.
alt.ex: Normal nasal mucosa is pink and clear with little discharge, and skin under nasal devices needs frequent assessment to prevent MDRPI.

items.q: During assessment, the nurse notes redness and crusty drainage in one of a patient’s eyes. Which interpretation is most accurate?
items.a: Possible conjunctivitis that is contagious and can spread to the other eye
items.ex: Redness indicates allergic or infectious conjunctivitis, and its crusty drainage easily spreads from one eye to the other.
w: Normal tearing that cleanses and protects the eye
The healthy eye is not inflamed and has no drainage.
Expected dryness from age-related loss of tears
Dryness does not explain redness with crusty drainage.
Irritation from wearing eyeglasses for long periods
Eyeglasses are not described as causing red, draining eyes.

alt.q: Why does the nurse wear clean gloves and perform hand hygiene before and after examining a patient’s red, draining eyes?
alt.a: Allergic or infectious conjunctivitis can be highly contagious
alt.ex: Redness may indicate conjunctivitis, which is highly contagious, so gloves and hand hygiene prevent spread.
w: Gloves keep cerumen from transferring to the eye
Cerumen is an ear secretion; the concern is spreading conjunctivitis.
Gloves prevent fingerprints on the patient’s contact lenses
The reason given is the contagious nature of conjunctivitis.
Gloves keep soap residue off the patient’s cornea
Soap is avoided on the eyes; gloves protect against spreading infection.

items.q: Glass eyeglass lenses can be cleaned with cool water and dried with a soft cloth.
items.a: True
items.ex: Cool water cleans glass lenses, and a soft cloth prevents scratching.
items.ww: The book recommends cool water and a soft cloth, not harsher methods, for glass lenses.

alt.q: Paper towels are a good choice for drying plastic eyeglass lenses because they absorb water quickly.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Paper towels scratch lenses; plastic lenses scratch easily and need special cleaning solutions and drying tissues.
alt.ww: The book says to use a soft cloth, not paper towels, to prevent scratching.

items.q: Which factor plays the major role in determining a person’s hygiene practices during childhood?
items.a: Family customs
items.ex: During childhood, family customs largely determine bathing frequency, time of day, and practices such as brushing and flossing.
w: Peer groups
Peer groups and media influence hygiene mainly in adolescence.
Work groups
Work groups shape expectations about appearance during the adult years.
Media advertising
Media influence becomes prominent as children enter adolescence.

alt.q: As children enter adolescence, which influences often shape their hygiene practices?
alt.a: Peer groups and media
alt.ex: In adolescence, peer groups and media often influence hygiene practices, making health education important.
w: Family customs alone
Family customs dominate in childhood; adolescents are increasingly influenced by peers and media.
Work groups and friends
Work groups influence appearance expectations during adulthood.
Changes in living conditions
Changes in living conditions commonly affect hygiene in older adults and people with limited resources.

items.q: A patient with diabetic neuropathy and paresthesia of both feet wants to take a tub bath. Which action is the nurse’s priority?
items.a: Check the bath water temperature before the patient gets in
items.ex: Patients with paresthesia cannot feel water that is too hot and can burn themselves, so safety comes first.
w: Teach the patient to test the water with the toes
Reduced sensation in the feet makes this an unreliable and unsafe test.
Add bath oil to the water to soothe dry skin
Bath oil makes tub surfaces slippery and does not address burn risk.
Let the patient bathe alone to promote independence
Safety is the priority for a patient with a sensory deficit.

alt.q: Why does decreased sensation place a patient at special risk during hygiene care?
alt.a: The patient may not feel pressure or water that is too hot
alt.ex: Decreased sensation places a patient at risk for pressure or thermal injuries, such as burns from hot bath water.
w: The patient cannot grasp a washcloth or toothbrush
A weakened grasp results from conditions such as arthritis or stroke, not sensory loss.
The patient forgets to attend to basic hygiene
Forgetting hygiene needs is linked to cognitive impairment such as dementia.
The patient becomes short of breath during bathing
Shortness of breath relates to chronic cardiac or pulmonary illness.

items.q: Which actions reflect culturally congruent hygiene care as described in Box 40.1? Select all that apply.
o: Provide a gender-congruent caregiver when the patient requests one
Privacy and gender-congruent caregivers are provided as requested.
Adapt the hygiene schedule so family members can participate if desired
Families may participate in care by adapting the schedule.
Ask whether bathing needs to occur before or after prayers
Cultural practices may affect the timing of hygiene activities.
Discuss with the patient or family before cutting or shaving hair
Hair is not cut or shaved without prior discussion.
Require daily bathing so all patients receive the same standard
Care is individualized; uniform rules ignore cultural preferences.
items.ex: Box 40.1 calls for privacy, family participation, attention to timing and touch preferences, and respect for hair and toileting practices.

alt.q: Which statements about cultural influences on hygiene are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Some cultures prohibit or restrict touching
The book directs nurses to recognize differing preferences about touch and personal space.
Toileting practices vary by culture
Box 40.1 notes that toileting practices vary by culture.
Hygiene care can become a source of conflict and stress
Culture influences hygiene, and care can become a potential source of conflict.
Menstrual hygiene practices are based on person-centered care and preference
Menstrual hygiene is provided according to personal preference.
Water temperature preferences are the same across cultures
Box 40.1 asks about preferences for hot or cold water.
alt.ex: Culturally congruent hygiene care respects preferences about touch, timing, water temperature, menstrual and toileting practices, and hair.

items.q: A patient from a cultural group that prefers less frequent bathing and does not use deodorant has no hygiene-related health problem. Which approach by the nurse is best?
items.a: Respect the practice and avoid expressing disapproval
items.ex: Nurses avoid expressing disapproval or forcing changes in hygiene practices unless the practices affect the patient’s health.
w: Explain that daily bathing is required during hospitalization
Forcing changes is inappropriate when the practice does not affect health.
Provide deodorant and encourage its use each morning
This imposes the nurse’s norms on a practice that does not affect health.
Document the practice as a self-care deficit
A cultural preference is not a self-care deficit.

alt.q: A patient’s cultural hygiene practice is contributing to a skin problem. Which approach does the textbook recommend?
alt.a: Use tact, provide information, and allow choices
alt.ex: When practices affect health, the nurse uses tact, provides information, and allows choices.
w: Insist that the patient adopt the agency’s routine
Insisting removes patient choice and is not the recommended approach.
Avoid discussing it to prevent cultural conflict
Practices that affect health need to be addressed tactfully.
Ask the family to change the patient’s routine
The nurse works directly with the patient using tact and offering choices.

items.q: How does the textbook define body image?
items.a: A person’s subjective concept of their body’s appearance, structure, or function
items.ex: Body image is a person’s subjective concept of their body, including physical appearance, structure, or function.
w: An objective measure of a person’s weight relative to height
This describes a measurement such as BMI, not body image.
A person’s knowledge about the importance of hygiene
This describes health beliefs, which also influence hygiene.
The cultural rules a person follows for grooming
Cultural variables are a separate factor influencing hygiene.

alt.q: A patient who is usually neatly groomed now appears unkempt and uninterested in hygiene. What does the textbook suggest the nurse do?
alt.a: Assess the patient’s ability to participate in hygiene further
alt.ex: Patients who appear unkempt or uninterested may need further assessment of their ability to participate or education about hygiene.
w: Perform complete hygiene care without involving the patient
The patient’s abilities and preferences need assessment first.
Document that the patient prefers not to bathe
The change needs assessment, not assumption of a preference.
Remind the patient that appearance reflects self-respect
This is judgmental and does not identify the cause.

items.q: A home care nurse visits a patient with limited finances who lives alone. Which socioeconomic consideration affects this patient’s hygiene?
items.a: The patient may lack basic supplies such as soap and toothpaste
items.ex: Economic status influences access to bathing facilities and basic supplies such as deodorant, shampoo, and toothpaste.
w: The patient will prefer showers to tub baths
Shower or bath choice reflects personal preference, not finances.
The patient will not value personal cleanliness
Limited resources do not mean a person does not value hygiene.
The patient will need more frequent shampooing
Socioeconomic status does not determine shampoo frequency.

alt.q: Which home modification does the textbook mention to help a patient perform hygiene self-care safely?
alt.a: Nonskid surfaces and grab bars in the bath
alt.ex: The home environment may need safety devices such as nonskid surfaces and grab bars in the bath.
w: Bath oil added to the tub water
Bath oil makes tub surfaces slippery and increases fall risk.
A heating pad placed beside the tub
Heating pads pose a burn risk and are not listed as safety devices.
Removal of the bathroom door for access
This is not a modification the book describes.

items.q: A patient says, “I know brushing matters, but I don’t think I’ll ever get gum disease.” Which factor explains why this patient is unlikely to change behavior?
items.a: The patient does not perceive susceptibility to the problem
items.ex: Motivation depends on perceived susceptibility, seriousness, and benefit; knowledge alone is not enough to change behavior.
w: The patient lacks knowledge about hygiene
The patient states awareness that brushing matters; perception of risk is missing.
The patient’s family customs prohibit brushing
Nothing in the statement suggests family customs are involved.
The patient cannot afford dental supplies
The statement reflects perceived risk, not finances.

alt.q: According to the textbook, when are patients most likely to adopt a healthy hygiene behavior?
alt.a: When they recognize a risk and can act affordably without negative effects
alt.ex: Patients adopting behaviors recognize a risk and see reasonable, cost-effective action without negative consequences.
w: When they receive written information about the behavior
Knowledge alone is not enough; motivation is also key.
When the nurse explains the behavior is required
Being told a behavior is required does not build motivation.
When family members perform the behavior for them
Motivation depends on the patient’s own perception of risk and benefit.

items.q: Which skin characteristic describes the Neonate?
items.a: Epidermis and dermis loosely bound; friction causes bruising
items.ex: Skin matures from fragile neonatal skin through adolescence, then becomes drier and thinner with aging.
w: Skin layers more tightly bound, giving greater resistance to infection
That goes with Toddler.
More active sebaceous glands, predisposing to acne
That goes with Adolescent.
Dryness, thinning, and decreased elasticity
That goes with Older adult.
