pairs: Epidermis and dermis loosely bound; friction causes bruising
Skin layers more tightly bound, giving greater resistance to infection
More active sebaceous glands, predisposing to acne
mt.ex: Skin matures from fragile neonatal skin through adolescence, then becomes drier and thinner with aging.

items.q: Which measures does the textbook recommend to reduce skin dryness in an older adult? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid frequent bathing
Frequent bathing increases dryness and itching.
Use warm water
Warm, not hot, water reduces drying of the skin.
Close the bathroom door to maintain humidity
Low humidity increases dryness, so humidity is kept in the room.
Blot the skin dry
Blotting avoids friction on fragile, thin skin.
Rub the skin briskly with a towel to stimulate oils
Older skin is fragile and bruises easily; it is blotted dry.
Wait several hours after bathing to apply moisturizer
Moisturizer is applied immediately after drying the skin.
items.ex: Older skin is dry and fragile, so bathing is limited, water is warm, humidity is kept, skin is blotted, and moisturizer is applied promptly.

alt.q: Which age-related skin changes explain why older adults need caution during bathing, turning, and repositioning? Select all that apply.
o: Epidermal cell replacement slows and the skin thins
Thinner skin with slower cell replacement is easily injured.
Moisture leaves the skin, increasing bruising risk
Loss of moisture increases the risk for bruising and injury.
Skin glands produce less lubricating substances
Less lubrication makes the skin dry and itchy.
Sebaceous glands become overactive and cause acne
Increased sebaceous activity and acne occur in adolescence.
Epidermis and dermis are loosely bound as in neonates
Loosely bound layers describe neonatal skin.
alt.ex: Aging skin thins, loses moisture and resiliency, and produces less lubrication, so it bruises and tears easily.

items.q: Sweat glands become fully functional during puberty, so adolescents often need more frequent bathing.
items.a: True
items.ex: Sweat glands become fully functional at puberty, and more frequent bathing and shampooing reduce body odor and oily hair.
items.ww: The book states sweat glands mature at puberty, increasing the need for bathing.

alt.q: In adolescent girls, estrogen causes the skin to become thinner and less vascular.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Estrogen causes the skin of adolescent girls to become soft, smooth, and thicker, with increased vascularity.
alt.ww: The book describes thicker, more vascular skin in adolescent girls, not thinner skin.

items.q: An older adult reports foot pain when walking. Why is this complaint especially important to address?
items.a: Foot pain is a source of falls in older adults
items.ex: Older adults often complain of foot pain, which is a source of falls; footwear changes can reduce this risk.
w: Foot pain is the earliest sign of Morton’s neuroma
Morton’s neuroma is a condition of middle-aged women, not a general warning sign.
Foot pain always indicates a fungal infection
Foot pain has many causes, including corns, calluses, and bunions.
Foot pain means the patient needs daily foot soaks
Soaking is not recommended as a response to foot pain.

alt.q: What causes the dry, scaly feet common in older adults?
alt.a: Decreased sebaceous secretion and dehydration of epidermal cells
alt.ex: Dry, scaly feet result from decreased sebaceous gland secretion and dehydration of epidermal cells.
w: Increased sweat gland activity and fungal growth
Sweat gland activity does not cause dryness; fungal infection is a separate problem.
Excess friction from properly fitting footwear
Properly fitting footwear reduces problems; it does not cause dryness.
Accelerated replacement of epidermal cells
Epidermal cell replacement slows, rather than speeds up, with aging.

items.q: At about what age do the first permanent (secondary) teeth erupt?
items.a: About 6 years
items.ex: Infants begin teething at about 6 to 8 months, and the first permanent teeth erupt at about 6 years of age.
w: About 6 to 8 months
This is when infants begin teething with primary teeth.
About 2 years
This is too early for permanent teeth to erupt.
About 12 years
Permanent teeth begin erupting years earlier, at about 6 years.

alt.q: At about what age do infants begin teething?
alt.a: 6 to 8 months
alt.ex: Infants begin teething at approximately 6 to 8 months of age.
w: 1 to 2 months
This is too early for teething to begin.
12 to 14 months
Teething usually begins earlier, at about 6 to 8 months.
About 6 years
About 6 years is when the first permanent teeth erupt.

items.q: Active inflammation of the sebaceous glands accompanied by pimples, common in adolescence, is called [[acne]].
items.ex: Sebaceous glands become more active in adolescence, predisposing teens to acne.

alt.q: Because their sebaceous glands become more active, adolescents are predisposed to [[acne]], an inflammation with pimples.
alt.ex: Sebaceous glands become more active in adolescence, predisposing teens to acne.

items.q: Why do dentures often fit poorly as a person ages?
items.a: The gums lose vascularity and tissue elasticity
items.ex: With aging, gums lose vascularity and tissue elasticity, which may cause dentures to fit poorly.
w: The permanent teeth continue to erupt
Permanent teeth are in place from adolescence; they do not keep erupting.
Saliva production increases with age
Saliva secretion declines with age, causing dry mouth.
The jawbone grows larger after middle age
This is not a cause the book describes.

alt.q: Which factors contribute to poor oral health as a person ages?
alt.a: Chronic disease, reduced hand grasp, and medications with oral side effects
alt.ex: Age-related mouth changes, chronic disease, reduced grasp, inattention to oral care, and medications contribute to poor oral health.
w: Increased saliva, stronger gums, and fewer medications
Saliva decreases and gums weaken with age; medication use often increases.
Regular brushing, flossing, and limiting sticky sweets
These habits protect teeth and gums rather than harming them.
Eruption of new teeth and thicker gum tissue
Neither occurs with aging; gums lose elasticity.

items.q: A patient with dementia becomes fearful and agitated when the nurse begins morning hygiene. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Modify the hygiene approach to fit the patient’s individual needs
items.ex: Person-centered care considers the effect of cognitive impairment and provides individualized modifications to hygiene care.
w: Complete the bath quickly before agitation increases
Rushing increases fear; care is adapted to the patient’s needs.
Postpone all hygiene until the patient asks for it
Patients with dementia often forget hygiene needs and will not ask.
Have two staff members hold the patient still
Restraint increases fear and aggression and is not person-centered.

alt.q: Why might a patient with cognitive impairment become aggressive during hygiene care?
alt.a: The patient is unaware of hygiene needs and becomes fearful
alt.ex: People with cognitive impairment may be unaware of hygiene needs and become fearful and agitated, resulting in aggression.
w: The patient has a strong preference for showers
Personal preference does not explain fear-related aggression.
The patient’s sensation to hot water is increased
Cognitive impairment does not increase thermal sensation.
The patient has too much energy after resting
Aggression stems from fear and confusion, not excess energy.

items.q: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease becomes short of breath partway through a bath. Which plan reflects the textbook’s guidance?
items.a: Include rest periods so the patient can still participate
items.ex: Patients who tire or become short of breath may need complete care; rest periods allow them to participate.
w: Finish the bath quickly without stopping
Pushing through increases fatigue; rest periods are planned.
Have the patient complete the bath alone to build endurance
Fatigued patients need assistance, not more exertion.
Omit hygiene until the patient is discharged
Hygiene is still needed; it is paced rather than omitted.

alt.q: Which critical thinking attitude helps the nurse care for a patient with decreased activity tolerance during hygiene?
alt.a: Flexibility, pacing activities and planning rest periods
alt.ex: Flexibility lets the nurse pace activities and plan rest periods during bathing for patients with decreased activity tolerance.
w: Strict adherence to the unit’s bathing schedule
Rigid schedules do not accommodate variation in tolerance.
Rigid use of the same routine for every patient
Hygiene care is individualized, not routine.
Speed in completing care before fatigue begins
Rushing does not address activity intolerance.

items.q: Which factors does the textbook list as causes of limited mobility that reduce a patient’s ability to perform hygiene? Select all that apply.
o: Obesity
Obesity is listed as a cause of limited mobility.
Pain
Pain limits ROM and mobility.
Medication effect
Medication effects can limit mobility.
Presence of an indwelling catheter or IV line
Medical devices such as catheters, feeding tubes, and IV lines limit mobility.
Preference for showers over tub baths
Bathing preference is a personal choice, not a cause of limited mobility.
items.ex: Limited mobility from obesity, injury, weakness, surgery, pain, inactivity, medications, or medical devices reduces safe hygiene self-care.

alt.q: Which conditions does the textbook name as causes of a weakened grasp that makes using a toothbrush or washcloth difficult? Select all that apply.
o: Arthritis
Arthritis weakens grasp, as with Mrs. White’s rheumatoid arthritis.
Stroke
Stroke can weaken grasp.
Muscular disorders
Muscular disorders can weaken grasp.
Allergic rhinitis
Allergies cause nasal discharge, not a weakened grasp.
Conjunctivitis
Conjunctivitis affects the eyes, not grasp strength.
alt.ex: A weakened grasp from arthritis, stroke, or muscular disorders makes hygiene tools difficult to use.

items.q: The nurse must fully assess a patient’s hygiene needs and functional ability before delegating hygiene care.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states the nurse fully assesses hygiene needs and functional ability prior to delegating this care.
items.ww: Assessment cannot be skipped; it determines what care is needed before delegation.

alt.q: Because bathing can be delegated, assistive personnel may assess a patient’s functional ability before the nurse sees the patient.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Bathing can be delegated, but assessment of hygiene needs and functional ability is the nurse’s responsibility before delegation.
alt.ww: The book requires the nurse to assess hygiene needs before delegating; assessment is not delegated.

items.q: Which is an example of an environmental factor the nurse considers when planning hygiene care?
items.a: Frequent interruptions from other health care providers on a busy unit
items.ex: Environmental factors include roommates’ needs and interruptions from other providers that affect the timing of care.
w: The patient’s knowledge of the importance of hygiene
Knowledge relates to health beliefs, not the environment.
The patient’s family customs about bathing
Family customs are a social factor.
The patient’s subjective view of their appearance
This describes body image.

alt.q: Before assessing a patient for hygiene, why does the nurse review the EHR for new orders for equipment or therapies?
alt.a: To avoid time conflicts and plan for extra time or personnel
alt.ex: Reviewing the EHR helps the nurse avoid time conflicts and determine whether extra personnel or time is needed.
w: To decide whether the patient prefers a shower or a bath
Preferences are learned by asking the patient.
To determine the patient’s cultural hygiene practices
Cultural practices are learned through the nursing history with the patient.
To find out whether the patient values cleanliness
Health beliefs are assessed with the patient, not from equipment orders.

items.q: As scalp hair becomes thinner and drier with aging, shampooing is usually performed less frequently.
items.a: True
items.ex: With aging, scalp hair thins and dries, so shampooing is usually needed less often.
items.ww: The book links thinner, drier hair in older adults with less frequent shampooing.

alt.q: Because hair becomes oilier with aging, older adults usually need to shampoo more frequently.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hair becomes thinner and drier with aging, so shampooing is usually performed less often.
alt.ww: Oily hair needing frequent shampooing is linked to adolescence, not aging.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to give hygiene care to a patient with diabetes mellitus. How should the nurse approach the assessment?
items.a: Do a brief history to identify priority areas, such as the feet
items.ex: Not every body region is assessed routinely; a brief history directs attention to priority areas such as the feet in diabetes.
w: Do a full head-to-toe assessment of every body region first
The book states not to routinely assess all body regions before hygiene.
Skip the assessment because the bath will reveal any problems
A focused history and assessment are needed to plan individualized care.
Assess only the skin areas the patient reports as painful
Patients may be unaware of problems, such as diabetic foot changes.

alt.q: For which patient is assessment of the skinfolds a priority area during hygiene care?
alt.a: A patient who is obese
alt.ex: Brief history identifies priority areas, such as skinfolds in a patient who is obese, where moisture collects.
w: A patient with diabetes who has well-fitting shoes
In diabetes, the feet are the priority area.
A patient who is ambulatory with no skin complaints
This patient has no specific skinfold risk.
A patient receiving a short course of oral antibiotics
Antibiotic therapy directs attention to the oral cavity.

items.q: Which is the most common form of moisture-associated skin damage (MASD)?
items.a: Incontinence-associated dermatitis (IAD)
items.ex: IAD is the most common MASD; it causes erythema and edema and can progress to erosion and infection.
w: Medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI)
MARSI results from adhesive removal, not prolonged moisture.
Medical device–related pressure injury (MDRPI)
MDRPI results from device pressure or friction.
Contact dermatitis (CD)
Contact dermatitis is a reaction to a causative agent such as soap or adhesive.

alt.q: A patient with fecal incontinence has red, swollen perineal skin that could progress to erosion. Which problem do these findings suggest?
alt.a: Incontinence-associated dermatitis
alt.ex: IAD is characterized by erythema and edema on the skin surface and can evolve into erosion and secondary infection.
w: Medical adhesive–related skin injury
MARSI occurs where adhesives are applied and removed.
Athlete’s foot
Athlete’s foot is a fungal infection of the feet.
Pediculosis corporis
Body lice cause itching, scratches, and hemorrhagic spots.

items.q: Medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI) is defined by erythema or other skin abnormality that persists 30 minutes or more after an adhesive is removed.
items.a: True
items.ex: MARSI is erythema or another cutaneous abnormality that persists 30 minutes or more after removing a device or adhesive.
items.ww: The book’s definition of MARSI uses the 30-minute persistence threshold.

alt.q: Erythema that resolves within 30 minutes after an adhesive is removed is the defining sign of MARSI.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: MARSI is defined by abnormalities that persist 30 minutes or more after adhesive removal, not ones that resolve.
alt.ww: Redness that resolves within 30 minutes does not meet the book’s definition of MARSI.

items.q: Which factors place a patient at risk for oral problems according to Table 40.3? Select all that apply.
o: Chemotherapeutic drugs
Chemotherapy kills rapidly dividing cells in the oral lining, causing ulcers and inflammation.
Radiation therapy to the head and neck
Head and neck radiation reduces saliva and lowers its pH.
Frequent use of lozenges or cough drops
These contain large amounts of sugar that promote caries.
Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes predisposes to dry mouth, gingivitis, periodontal disease, and tooth loss.
Brushing twice a day with fluoride toothpaste
This is a recommended practice that reduces oral problems.
items.ex: Table 40.3 lists medications, therapies, devices, and diseases that increase the risk for oral problems.

alt.q: Which statements about oral risk factors in Table 40.3 are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Being NPO causes excess drying and fragility of the mucosa
Dehydration and NPO status dry the mucosa and increase secretions on the tongue.
Mechanical ventilation creates a risk for ventilator-associated pneumonia
Intubated, ventilated patients are at risk for VAP.
Patients with cognitive impairment often overlook oral hygiene
These patients are at higher risk for periodontitis and tooth loss.
Antacids and chewable vitamins protect the teeth from caries
Their sugar or acid content increases dental caries.
Immunosuppression protects the gums from bleeding
Immunosuppression predisposes to inflammation and bleeding gums.
alt.ex: Dehydration, ventilation, cognitive impairment, sugary medications, and immunosuppression all increase oral risk.

items.q: Mrs. White rates her abdominal pain as 7/10 on her second postoperative day, and her bed bath is planned. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Give the prescribed analgesic and wait 20 to 30 minutes before the bath
items.ex: A prn analgesic is given before the bath, which begins 20 to 30 minutes later, so the patient can participate comfortably.
w: Begin the bath now and give pain medication afterward
Bathing in severe pain limits participation and comfort.
Cancel the bath until the next day
Hygiene can proceed once pain is controlled.
Have the patient bathe herself to distract from the pain
Distraction does not replace pain control and she cannot grasp a washcloth.

alt.q: After giving Mrs. White an analgesic before her bath, what does the nurse do next?
alt.a: Reassess her pain about 30 minutes later
alt.ex: Jamie returned 30 minutes later to rate pain, which had improved to 2/10, before continuing.
w: Begin the bath immediately after giving the analgesic
The medication needs time to work, and its effect is evaluated first.
Wait 2 hours to make sure the drug has peaked
Waiting this long delays care; the bath begins 20 to 30 minutes later.
Document the pain rating and end the assessment
Pain relief is reassessed before proceeding with care.

items.q: A patient has limited ROM, cannot grasp a washcloth, cannot regulate the faucet, and cannot wash all body parts. Which nursing diagnosis do these findings support?
items.a: Self-Care Deficit: Impaired Ability to Bath
items.ex: Difficulty using hygiene items, regulating water, and washing all body parts clusters into Self-Care Deficit: Impaired Ability to Bath.
w: Impaired Oral Mucous Membrane
This diagnosis relates to findings in the oral cavity.
Risk for Infection
These findings describe functional limits in bathing, not infection risk.
Low Self Esteem
The findings describe physical inability to bathe rather than self-esteem.

alt.q: Mrs. White has redness under her buttocks, thighs, and breasts, but her skin is intact. Which nursing diagnosis is most appropriate?
alt.a: Risk for Impaired Skin Integrity
alt.ex: Redness over intact skin is an early cue for pressure injury, supporting a risk diagnosis.
w: Impaired Tissue Integrity
Her skin is intact, so an actual tissue integrity problem is not present.
Self-Care Deficit: Impaired Ability to Bath
This diagnosis is supported by her inability to grasp items, not by skin redness.
Activity Intolerance
Redness under skinfolds does not indicate activity intolerance.

items.q: Two patients have Impaired Oral Mucous Membrane: one related to malnutrition and one related to chemotherapy. Which intervention is specific to the malnourished patient?
items.a: Consult a registered dietitian for dietary supplements
items.ex: When poor nutrition is the related factor, the nurse consults a dietitian; the related factor guides intervention selection.
w: Follow cancer nursing guidelines for oral mucositis
This addresses mucosal injury from chemotherapy.
Rinse with a bland rinse and limit diet to soft foods
These are oral mucositis measures for chemotherapy.
Apply water-based moisturizer to the lips after chemotherapy
This is part of the chemotherapy mucositis guidelines.

alt.q: A patient’s oral mucosa is inflamed from chemotherapy. Which measures follow cancer nursing guidelines for oral mucositis?
alt.a: Gentle brushing with a soft toothbrush and a soft-food diet
alt.ex: Mucositis care includes gentle brushing with a soft toothbrush, flossing, bland rinses, soft foods, and water-based lip moisturizer.
w: Lemon-glycerin swabs and a high-fiber diet
Lemon-glycerin dries mucous membranes and erodes enamel.
Alcohol-based mouthwash and spicy foods
Alcohol and irritating foods worsen inflamed mucosa.
Vigorous brushing with a firm toothbrush
Firm bristles and vigorous brushing traumatize inflamed tissue.

items.q: What does a Complete bed bath involve?
items.a: Given to a patient who is totally dependent in bed

That goes with Partial bed bath.
Patient sits in a chair, does part of the bath, and gets help with hard-to-reach areas
That goes with Sponge bath at the sink.
Premoistened no-rinse cloths with surfactant cleaner and emollient

Sponge bath at the sink

alt.q: Which type of bath is described as “Continuous stream of water; thorough but can be tiring”?
alt.a: Shower
alt.ex: Box 40.4 describes bath types by how dependent the patient is and how thorough or tiring the method is.
w: Complete bed bath
Complete bed bath: Given to a patient who is totally dependent in bed.
Partial bed bath
Partial bed bath: Washes only parts that would cause discomfort if unbathed, plus the back.
Sponge bath at the sink
Sponge bath at the sink: Patient sits in a chair, does part of the bath, and gets help with hard-to-reach areas.

mt.q: Match each type of bath with its description from Box 40.4.
pairs: Given to a patient who is totally dependent in bed
Washes only parts that would cause discomfort if unbathed, plus the back
Patient sits in a chair, does part of the bath, and gets help with hard-to-reach areas
Premoistened no-rinse cloths with surfactant cleaner and emollient
Continuous stream of water; thorough but can be tiring
mt.ex: Box 40.4 describes bath types by how dependent the patient is and how thorough or tiring the method is.

items.q: A patient with a Stage 4 pressure injury is receiving daily CHG bathing. How should the nurse use CHG near the wound?
items.a: Bathe with CHG only around the dressing or wound
items.ex: CHG is safe on superficial wounds, but with open or deep wounds such as Stage 3 or 4 pressure injuries it is used only around them.
w: Apply CHG directly into the wound bed
CHG is not used in open or deep wounds.
Stop all CHG bathing until the wound heals
CHG bathing continues, avoiding only the wound itself.
Rinse the wound with CHG and then with saline
CHG is not applied to open or deep wounds.

alt.q: On which areas is CHG considered safe to use during bathing?
alt.a: Superficial wounds, abrasions, rashes, and the perineum
alt.ex: CHG is safe on superficial wounds, abrasions, rashes, and for perineal care, but not on the eyes, ears, or face.
w: The eyes, ears, and face
CHG is never used on the eyes, ears, or face.
Stage 3 and 4 pressure injury wound beds
With deep wounds, CHG is used only around the wound.
Deep surgical wounds with exposed tissue
Open or deep wounds are bathed around, not with, CHG.

items.q: After a bath basin is cleaned, it may be used to store the patient’s hygiene supplies.
items.a: False
items.ex: Bath basins are air-dried completely and never used for storage, because they can harbor biofilm and bacteria.
items.ww: Basins are a reservoir for bacteria, so the book directs reserving them only for bathing.

alt.q: Bath basins should be air-dried completely and reserved only for bathing, not for storing supplies.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Basins can form biofilm and transmit HAIs, so they are air-dried and not used to store supplies.
alt.ww: Using basins for storage contributes to bacterial reservoirs, which the book warns against.

items.q: A patient with dementia becomes frightened and resists during a bath. Which action is best?
items.a: Ask permission and offer choices, such as soap and timing
items.ex: Asking permission and offering choices reduces feelings of loss of control, a common trigger of aggression during bathing.
w: Complete the bath quickly to limit the patient’s distress
Rushing increases distress; the book advises not rushing.
Keep the room cool to help the patient stay calm
Being cold is a trigger; the patient is kept warm.
Use a loud, firm voice so the patient follows directions
A low, pleasant voice is recommended.

alt.q: Which factor is a common trigger of aggressive behavior during bathing in a patient with cognitive impairment?
alt.a: Feeling cold, exposed, or vulnerable
alt.ex: Unmanaged pain, being cold, feeling exposed or vulnerable, and loss of control often trigger aggression during bathing.
w: Being offered a choice of soap
Offering choices reduces triggers by restoring control.
Receiving an analgesic 30 minutes before
Pain control before bathing reduces triggers.
Hearing comforting words during the bath
Comforting words enhance relaxation.

items.q: Assistive personnel plan to massage a reddened area over a patient’s sacrum after a bath. Which instruction should the nurse give?
items.a: Do not massage reddened areas, especially over bony prominences
items.ex: Massaging reddened areas breaks surface capillaries, which can promote pressure injury formation.
w: Massage the area firmly to restore circulation
Massage damages capillaries over reddened areas.
Massage with lotion for at least 10 minutes
Reddened areas are not massaged for any length of time.
Massage the area only if the patient requests it
Reddened areas are not massaged even at the patient’s request.

alt.q: Which situation does the textbook list as a contraindication to a back rub?
alt.a: Fractured ribs
alt.ex: The EHR is checked for contraindications to massage such as fractured ribs, burns, or heart surgery.
w: Muscle tension after bathing
Back rubs relieve muscular tension.
Mild anxiety before sleep
Effleurage is associated with reduced anxiety.
Recent completion of a bed bath
Following a bath is a good time for a back rub.

items.q: Which foot care guidelines should the nurse teach a patient with diabetes mellitus? Select all that apply.
o: Inspect the feet daily, using a mirror if needed
Daily inspection of all surfaces detects problems early.
Wash feet daily in lukewarm water and dry between the toes
Lukewarm water and thorough drying prevent injury and maceration.
Apply emollient lotion but not between the toes
Lotion softens skin, but moisture between toes promotes maceration.
Trim visible toenails straight across and file edges smooth
Straight trimming with smooth edges prevents injury.
Soak the feet daily to soften calluses
Soaking causes maceration that can lead to ulceration or infection.
Use a heating pad to warm cold feet at night
Patients avoid heating pads and electric blankets to prevent burns.
items.ex: Diabetic foot care stresses daily inspection, gentle washing and drying, lotion except between toes, safe trimming, and protection from heat.

alt.q: Which statements by a patient with diabetes show correct understanding of foot care? Select all that apply.
o: “I will check inside my shoes before putting them on.”
Checking shoes detects rough areas or objects that rub the foot.
“I will wear shoes on hot pavement and at the beach.”
Feet are protected from hot and cold surfaces.
“I will wiggle my toes and move my ankles a few times a day.”
This promotes blood flow to the feet.
“I will walk barefoot at home so my feet can breathe.”
Patients should never go barefoot.
“I will cross my legs when sitting to stay comfortable.”
Crossing the legs for long periods impairs blood flow.
alt.ex: Patients with diabetes protect their feet from injury and heat and promote circulation.

items.q: Which oral hygiene product does the textbook recommend for patients at increased risk for poor oral hygiene, such as those on mechanical ventilation?
items.a: 0.12% chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) oral rinse
items.ex: Antimicrobial toothpaste and 0.12% CHG rinse are used for high-risk patients and reduce VAP and oral infections.
w: Lemon-glycerin sponges (swabs)
Lemon-glycerin sponges dry mucous membranes and erode tooth enamel.
Commercial foam swabs (sponges)
Foam swabs are ineffective in removing plaque.
Fluoride rinse (any strength)
Fluoride rinses help prevent decay; CHG is recommended for high-risk patients.

alt.q: Why does the textbook advise against using lemon-glycerin sponges for oral care?
alt.a: They dry mucous membranes and erode tooth enamel
alt.ex: Lemon-glycerin sponges dry the mucous membranes and erode tooth enamel.
w: They are too effective at removing plaque
Effective plaque removal is desirable, not a reason to avoid a product.
They contain fluoride that children may swallow
The fluoride caution applies to rinses in children 6 and under.
They increase saliva and the risk of aspiration
The concern is drying of the mucosa, not increased saliva.

items.q: A nurse is providing oral care to an unconscious patient. Which action is safest?
items.a: Hold the mouth open with a padded tongue blade
items.ex: A small oral airway or padded tongue blade holds the mouth open; fingers are never used because a human bite carries pathogens.
w: Hold the mouth open with two gloved fingers
Fingers are never used to hold the mouth open.
Place the patient flat with the head midline
The head is turned toward the nurse with the bed in semi-Fowler position.
Skip explaining steps since the patient is not awake
The nurse explains steps and sensations even when the patient is unresponsive.

alt.q: Why does the nurse turn an unconscious patient’s head toward the nurse and use suction during oral care?
alt.a: To prevent aspiration of secretions that can cause pneumonia
alt.ex: Unconscious patients have a reduced gag reflex, and pooled secretions contain gram-negative bacteria that cause pneumonia if aspirated.
w: To make the mouth easier to see with a penlight
The main reason is aspiration prevention, not visibility.
To stimulate the patient to wake up
Positioning is for airway protection, not arousal.
To allow fluoride rinse to coat the back teeth
Positioning protects against aspiration of secretions.

items.q: A patient is going to surgery and wears dentures. Which action by the nurse best protects the dentures?
items.a: Give them to a family member and document who received them
items.ex: Dentures are expensive; giving them to a family member and documenting it prevents loss if the patient changes rooms.
w: Wrap them in a tissue on the bedside stand
Dentures in tissues or napkins are easily thrown away.
Store them dry in an unlabeled cup in the drawer
Dentures are stored in water in a labeled, enclosed cup.
Send them to surgery in a soaking cup on the stretcher
The patient may not return to the same room, risking loss.

alt.q: A nurse is cleaning a patient’s dentures. Which water temperature is appropriate, and why?
alt.a: Tepid water, because hot water warps and cold water cracks them
alt.ex: Dentures are rinsed in tepid water; water that is too hot warps them and water that is too cold can crack them.
w: Hot water, because heat disinfects the dentures fully
Hot water warps dentures so they no longer fit.
Ice water, because cold firms the denture material
Very cold water can crack dentures.
Boiling water, because it removes all plaque
Boiling water would warp dentures.

items.q: In the nursing process for hygiene, which step comes right after “Analysis and nursing diagnosis”?

w: Implementation
That's step 4 of 5.
Assessment

w: Planning and outcomes identification

w: Planning and outcomes identification
That's step 3 of 5.

ord.q: Place the steps of the nursing process for hygiene in order.
items: Assessment
Analysis and nursing diagnosis
Planning and outcomes identification
Implementation
Evaluation
ord.ex: The nursing process moves from assessment through diagnosis and planning to implementation and evaluation.

items.q: Which guidelines apply regardless of the type of bath a patient receives? Select all that apply.
o: Expose only the body part being washed
Proper draping provides privacy and warmth.
Keep the nurse call system within reach if leaving the bedside
This maintains safety even during a brief absence.
Keep the room warm and control drafts
Wet skin loses heat rapidly through evaporation.
Encourage the patient to do as much as possible
Promoting independence is a bathing guideline.
Open a window to remove odors during the bath
Windows are kept closed to prevent chilling.
items.ex: Bathing guidelines are privacy, safety, warmth, promoting independence, and anticipating needs.

alt.q: Which actions help maintain a patient’s warmth during a bath? Select all that apply.
o: Keep windows closed
Closing windows controls drafts.
Keep the patient covered except the part being washed
Limiting exposure reduces heat loss.
Keep the room warm
A warm room prevents chilling of wet skin.
Leave wet skin to air-dry under a fan
Wet skin loses heat rapidly through evaporation; a fan increases chilling.
Uncover the whole body to wash it quickly
Exposure causes chilling and violates privacy.
alt.ex: Wet skin loses heat rapidly through evaporation, so the room is warmed and only the part being washed is exposed.

items.q: A patient receiving anticoagulants or with a low platelet count should be shaved with an electric razor.
items.a: True
items.ex: Patients prone to bleeding must use a personal electric razor to prevent cuts and bleeding.
items.ww: Blade razors can cause cuts that bleed excessively in patients with clotting problems.

alt.q: A new disposable blade razor is the safest choice for shaving a patient who takes a blood thinner.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients on blood thinners or with low platelet counts use an electric razor to avoid bleeding from cuts.
alt.ww: The book specifies an electric razor, not a blade, for patients at risk for bleeding.

items.q: Long, slow, gliding massage strokes that are associated with reduced anxiety, heart rate, and respiratory rate are called [[effleurage]].
items.ex: Effleurage during a back rub promotes relaxation and is linked to lower anxiety, heart rate, and respiratory rate.

alt.q: A back rub using [[effleurage]], or long, slow, gliding strokes, promotes relaxation after a bath.
alt.ex: Effleurage during a back rub promotes relaxation and is linked to lower anxiety, heart rate, and respiratory rate.

items.q: Which part of Skill 40.1 must the nurse perform rather than delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Assessing the patient’s skin, pain level, and ROM
items.ex: Bathing can be delegated to AP, but assessment of skin, pain level, and ROM cannot be delegated.
w: Bathing the patient’s arms and trunk
Bathing itself can be delegated to AP.
Applying a clean gown after the bath
Changing the gown is part of bathing, which AP may perform.
Changing the bath water when it cools
Changing bath water is part of the delegated bathing task.

alt.q: A nurse delegates a bed bath to assistive personnel. Which instruction is appropriate?
alt.a: Report any fatigue, shortness of breath, or pain
alt.ex: AP are instructed to report patient fatigue, shortness of breath, or pain to the nurse.
w: Massage any reddened skin areas during bathing
AP are told to avoid massaging reddened areas.
Soak the patient’s feet to soften calluses
AP avoid soaking feet unless directed by the nurse.
Adjust the IV flow rate after changing the gown
Regulation of IV flow rate is not delegated to AP.

items.q: Which instructions should the nurse give assistive personnel who will bathe a patient? Select all that apply.
o: Avoid massaging reddened skin areas
Massage of reddened areas can promote pressure injury.
Avoid soaking the patient’s feet unless directed by the nurse
Soaking can cause maceration.
Report any signs of impaired skin integrity
Skin findings are reported for nurse assessment.
Properly position a patient with an indwelling catheter or IV tubing
Correct positioning protects equipment and the patient.
Regulate the IV flow rate if it changes during gown removal
IV flow regulation is not delegated to AP.
items.ex: AP may bathe patients but must avoid harmful actions and report skin changes, fatigue, dyspnea, or pain to the nurse.

alt.q: Which findings should assistive personnel report to the nurse during a bed bath? Select all that apply.
o: Shortness of breath
Dyspnea indicates activity intolerance and is reported.
Patient fatigue
Fatigue is reported so the nurse can adjust care.
Pain
Pain is reported for nurse assessment.
A new break in the skin
Signs of impaired skin integrity are reported.
The patient’s choice of lotion
Product preference is honored by AP and does not need to be reported.
alt.ex: AP report signs of impaired skin integrity, fatigue, shortness of breath, or pain because the nurse must assess them.

items.q: Before a CHG bath, the nurse reviews the EHR for allergy or sensitivity to CHG and selects another cleanser if one is present.
items.a: True
items.ex: Skill 40.1 directs the nurse to check for CHG allergy or sensitivity and choose another cleansing solution if present.
items.ww: Assessment step 3 specifically reviews the EHR for CHG allergy before bathing.

alt.q: Because sensitivity to CHG is rare, the nurse does not need to check for CHG allergy before bathing.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Although sensitivity is rare, the EHR is reviewed for CHG allergy and another cleanser is chosen if one exists.
alt.ww: The skill lists reviewing for CHG allergy as an assessment step before bathing.

items.q: A patient with dementia becomes agitated whenever told it is bath time. Which approach does Skill 40.1 suggest?
items.a: Use an alternative method such as a bath bag or cloth wipes
items.ex: For patients with dementia who become agitated, alternative bathing such as bath bags or cloth wipes is considered.
w: Bathe the patient in a tub to promote relaxation
Tub bathing is more exertion and change, not an alternative for agitation.
Bathe the patient at a new time each day
Keeping the patient’s established routine may reduce agitation.
Delay all bathing until the agitation resolves
Hygiene is adapted rather than withheld.

alt.q: Why does the nurse assess a patient’s bathing preferences, such as time of day and products used, before a bath?
alt.a: Using the patient’s routine may reduce agitation in dementia
alt.ex: Assessing preferences allows participation and comfort, and an established routine may reduce agitation in dementia.
w: It allows the nurse to schedule baths by unit routine
Preferences individualize care rather than fitting unit routine.
It determines whether the patient is allergic to CHG
Allergy is checked separately in the EHR.
It replaces the need to assess the patient’s skin
Skin assessment is still required.

items.q: A nurse needs to leave the bedside briefly to get fresh bath water for a patient at moderate fall risk. Which action is correct?
items.a: Raise the appropriate number of side rails and lower the bed
items.ex: The nurse raises the number of side rails required by the fall risk assessment and lowers the bed before leaving.
w: Raise all four side rails to keep the patient safe
Having all side rails raised is considered a restraint.
Leave the side rails down so the patient can reach items
Leaving the bedside without appropriate side rails is unsafe.
Leave the bed at working height for quick return
The bed is lowered when the nurse leaves the bedside.

alt.q: Why should the nurse avoid raising all side rails when leaving a patient’s bedside during a bath?
alt.a: Having all side rails raised is considered a restraint
alt.ex: The number of side rails depends on fall risk, but raising all of them is considered a restraint.
w: It prevents the nurse from reaching the over-bed table
The concern is restraint, not reach.
It makes the patient feel colder during the bath
Side rails do not affect warmth.
It increases the risk of CHG spills
Side rails are unrelated to CHG use.

items.q: A patient has an IV line in the left arm and a gown with no snaps. How should the nurse remove the gown?
items.a: Remove it from the right arm first, then slide the IV bag and tubing through the sleeve
items.ex: The gown comes off the arm without the IV first; the IV bag and tubing are then passed through the sleeve without disconnecting.
w: Disconnect the IV tubing, remove the gown, then reconnect
The book states not to disconnect IV tubing to remove a gown.
Remove it from the left arm first, pulling the tubing gently
The arm without the IV is freed first to avoid pulling the line.
Cut the gown sleeve off the left arm with scissors
The skill describes sliding the bag and tubing through the sleeve.

alt.q: A patient has a casted right arm. How should the nurse change the patient’s gown?
alt.a: Remove it from the left arm first and put the clean gown on the right arm first
alt.ex: Undressing the unaffected side first and dressing the affected side first eases manipulation of the gown over the injured limb.
w: Remove it from the right arm first and dress the left arm first
This reverses the correct order and strains the injured limb.
Remove and replace the gown on the right arm first both times
The affected side is undressed last, not first.
Remove and replace the gown on the left arm first both times
The affected side is dressed first, not last.

items.q: A patient becomes excessively tired during a bed bath. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Reschedule bathing to a time when the patient is more rested
Bathing is moved to a time of better tolerance.
Perform hygiene in stages between scheduled rest periods
Staging care reduces exertion.
Notify the health care provider about changes in fatigue
Changes in fatigue level are reported.
Elevate the head of the bed for a patient with breathing difficulty
Patients with cardiopulmonary conditions need an elevated head of bed.
Lay the patient flat to finish the bath more quickly
Lying flat worsens breathing difficulty and rushing increases fatigue.
items.ex: Skill 40.1 lists rescheduling, staging care with rest periods, elevating the head of bed, and notifying the provider for excessive fatigue.

alt.q: Which assessments in Skill 40.1 measure a patient’s tolerance of bathing? Select all that apply.
o: Asking the patient to rate fatigue on a 0-to-10 scale
Rating tiredness measures tolerance to bathing activity.
Reviewing prior nurses’ notes for activity tolerance
Prior notes reveal tolerance, comfort, and shortness of breath.
Asking the patient to rate comfort on a 0-to-10 scale
Comfort rating shows changes during bathing and ROM.
Checking the bath water with a thermometer
Water temperature checks prevent burns, not activity intolerance.
Confirming allergies to bath products
Allergy checks prevent reactions, not activity intolerance.
alt.ex: Fatigue and comfort ratings and review of prior notes help the nurse judge how well a patient tolerates bathing.

items.q: Why does the nurse fold the washcloth into a mitt when bathing a patient?
items.a: It retains water and heat and keeps cold edges off the patient
items.ex: A mitt retains water and heat better than a loose cloth, keeps cold edges from brushing the patient, and prevents splashing.
w: It allows one cloth to be used for the entire bath
Clean sections and separate cloths are still needed to limit transmission.
It increases friction to remove dead skin cells
Force and friction on the skin are avoided during bathing.
It allows CHG to be rinsed off more completely
CHG is not rinsed off; it is left to dry on the skin.

alt.q: Why does the nurse test the bath water and have the patient place fingers in it before bathing?
alt.a: To prevent burns to the skin
alt.ex: Testing water temperature prevents burns, especially in patients with reduced sensation.
w: To check whether the CHG has dissolved
Testing temperature is for burn prevention, not mixing.
To soften the cuticles before nail care
Hand soaking for nail care is a separate step.
To assess the patient’s grasp strength
Grasp is assessed separately during assessment.

items.q: For an unconscious patient without a blink reflex, the nurse gently closes the eyelid, applies an eye patch or shield, and tapes the patch rather than the eyelid.
items.a: True
items.ex: Keeping eyelids closed maintains moisture; tape is placed over the patch or shield, never on the eyelid.
items.ww: Skill 40.1 directs closing the eye with the back of a fingertip and taping the patch, not the eyelid.

alt.q: For an unconscious patient without a blink reflex, the nurse tapes the eyelid directly closed to protect the cornea.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The eyelid is closed gently and covered with a patch or shield; the tape goes over the patch, not on the eyelid.
alt.ww: The skill states “Do not tape eyelid”; tape is placed over the patch or shield.

items.q: Assistive personnel are bathing a patient with 4% CHG solution in a basin. Which observation requires the nurse to intervene?
items.a: Rinsing the CHG off the patient’s skin after washing
items.ex: CHG is not rinsed; it is allowed to dry on the skin to achieve its antimicrobial effect.
w: Using a new washcloth for each major body part
A separate cloth for each body part is correct with CHG.
Keeping the CHG basin water for the whole bath
One bottle of CHG is enough for the whole bath, so the water is kept.
Avoiding CHG on the patient’s face and eyes
CHG is never used on the eyes or face.

alt.q: Why does the nurse use a new washcloth for each body part when bathing with CHG in a basin?
alt.a: Dipping a used cloth back into the basin contaminates the solution
alt.ex: Re-dipping a cloth contaminates the CHG solution and makes it less effective.
w: CHG dissolves washcloths after a single use
Cloths are changed to avoid contaminating the solution.
A new cloth rinses CHG off each area
CHG is not rinsed; it is left to dry.
A new cloth makes the skin feel less sticky
Stickiness is expected; the reason is preventing contamination.

items.q: When washing a patient’s arm, why does the nurse use long, firm strokes from the fingers toward the axilla?
items.a: Moving distal to proximal promotes venous return
items.ex: Long, firm strokes stimulate circulation, and moving distal to proximal promotes venous return.
w: Moving proximal to distal removes more bacteria
Direction is chosen to promote venous return.
Short, light strokes reduce patient fatigue
The skill specifies long, firm strokes.
Starting at the axilla keeps the hand cleanest
The skill begins at the fingers and moves toward the axilla.

alt.q: In which direction does the nurse wash a patient’s leg during a bed bath?
alt.a: From ankle to knee and from knee to thigh
alt.ex: Washing ankle to knee and knee to thigh, distal to proximal, promotes circulation and venous return.
w: From thigh to knee and from knee to ankle
Washing toward the foot does not promote venous return.
In circular motions starting at the thigh
The skill uses long, firm strokes moving upward.
From the foot to the hip in one stroke
The skill divides the leg into ankle to knee and knee to thigh.

items.q: While washing a patient’s lower leg, the nurse notes calf warmth, redness, swelling, and tenderness. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Avoid massaging the leg and report the findings
items.ex: These may be early signs of DVT; massaging the legs is contraindicated because a clot could dislodge.
w: Massage the calf firmly to improve venous return
Massaging could dislodge a possible blood clot.
Soak the leg in warm water to ease tenderness
Soaking does not address a possible DVT and delays reporting.
Apply lotion with vigorous strokes and continue
Vigorous strokes on the leg are contraindicated with a possible clot.

alt.q: Why is massaging a patient’s legs contraindicated during bathing?
alt.a: A blood clot, if present, could become dislodged
alt.ex: Massaging the legs is contraindicated because a possible blood clot could become dislodged.
w: Massage causes excessive drying of leg skin
The contraindication relates to clots, not dryness.
Massage spreads CHG onto the eyes and face
This is unrelated to leg massage.
Massage increases the risk of foot fungus
The concern is dislodging a blood clot.

items.q: When bathing a patient with diabetes mellitus, the nurse avoids soaking the patient’s hands and gently cleans under the nails instead.
items.a: True
items.ex: Soaking the hands of a patient with diabetes can cause maceration and risk for infection.
items.ww: Skill 40.1 specifically says not to soak the fingers of a patient with diabetes.

alt.q: Soaking the hands of a patient with diabetes for several minutes is recommended to soften cuticles before nail care.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Soaking can macerate the skin of a patient with diabetes, so dirt is gently cleared from under the nails instead.
alt.ww: Soaking is reserved for patients without diabetes; the skill warns against it in diabetes.

items.q: In female perineal care, which step comes right after “Wash the labia majora, wiping from perineum to rectum”?
items.a: Separate the labia and wash downward from the pubic area toward the rectum
items.ex: That's step 4 of 7. Female perineal care moves from positioning and draping to cleansing front to back, catheter care, rinsing, and re-covering.
w: Provide catheter care as needed
That's step 5 of 7.
Fold the lower corner of the bath blanket up and wash and dry the upper thighs
That's step 2 of 7.

items.q: A nurse is providing perineal care to an uncircumcised male patient with decreased sensation in his lower extremities. Which step is most important to prevent injury?
items.a: Return the foreskin to its natural position after cleaning
items.ex: A retracted foreskin can tighten around the shaft, causing edema; patients with reduced sensation cannot feel this.
w: Clean the shaft before the tip of the penis
Cleaning starts at the meatus, the least contaminated area.
Use vigorous strokes to clean the shaft quickly
Vigorous massage may cause an erection; gentle handling is used.
Keep the legs together to protect the scrotum
Abducting the legs gives easier access to scrotal tissues.

alt.q: When cleaning the penis during perineal care, where does the nurse begin and in what motion?
alt.a: At the urethral meatus, using a circular motion outward
alt.ex: Cleaning moves from least to most contaminated, so the nurse starts at the meatus and cleans outward in circles.
w: At the base of the shaft, moving toward the tip
This moves contamination toward the urethral meatus.
At the scrotum, then moving up to the tip
The scrotum is cleaned after the penis.
At the tip, wiping back and forth across it
A circular motion from the meatus outward is used.

items.q: If a male patient has an erection during perineal care, the nurse defers the procedure until later.
items.a: True
items.ex: Skill 40.1 directs deferring perineal care if an erection occurs; gentle, firm handling reduces the chance of one.
items.ww: The skill states to defer the procedure, not to continue, if the patient has an erection.

alt.q: If a male patient has an erection during perineal care, the nurse uses vigorous strokes to finish the procedure quickly.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Vigorous massage of the penis may cause an erection; if one occurs, the nurse defers care until later.
alt.ww: The skill directs deferring care and handling gently, not using vigorous strokes.

items.q: Which actions promote safety when a patient takes a tub bath? Select all that apply.
o: Place a rubber mat on the tub bottom
Mats prevent slipping and falling.
Have the patient demonstrate the safety bars and call system before leaving
The patient must be able to use these devices if weak or faint.
Tell the patient not to stay in the tub longer than 10 to 15 minutes
Prolonged warm water exposure can cause dizziness.
Drain the tub before an unsteady patient tries to get out
Draining first prevents accidental falls.
Add bath oil to the water to protect dry skin
Oil makes tub surfaces slippery.
items.ex: Tub safety includes mats, demonstrated use of safety devices, time limits, frequent checks, and draining the tub before exit.

alt.q: Which actions are appropriate when a patient takes a shower in the hospital? Select all that apply.
o: Turn the shower on and adjust the temperature before the patient enters
Adjusting water first prevents burns.
Use a shower seat if the patient is weak
A shower seat supports patients with weakness or poor balance.
Place an “occupied” sign on the bathroom door
The sign maintains privacy.
Knock before entering when the patient signals
Knocking provides privacy.
Let the patient adjust the hot water after stepping in
Water temperature is adjusted before entering to prevent burns.
alt.ex: Showers are prepared in advance for safe temperature and privacy, with a seat for patients who need support.

items.q: Why does the nurse instruct a patient not to remain in a warm tub longer than 10 to 15 minutes?
items.a: Prolonged warm water causes vasodilation and light-headedness
items.ex: Prolonged exposure to warm water causes vasodilation and pooling of blood, leading to light-headedness or dizziness.
w: Prolonged warm water causes vasoconstriction and chills
Warm water dilates blood vessels.
Prolonged soaking removes CHG from the skin after 5 minutes
The time limit relates to vasodilation and dizziness.
Prolonged soaking raises the water temperature over 20 minutes
Water cools over time; the concern is vasodilation.

alt.q: How often should the nurse check on a patient taking a tub bath?
alt.a: Every 5 minutes
alt.ex: The nurse checks on the patient every 5 minutes and limits tub time to 10 to 15 minutes.
w: Every 15 minutes
This is too infrequent; the skill directs checks every 5 minutes.
Every 30 minutes
This leaves the patient unattended too long.
Only when the patient signals
The nurse checks every 5 minutes as well as responding to the call system.

items.q: CHG used in daily bathing reduces bacteria on the skin for up to [[24]] hours.
items.ex: CHG continues antimicrobial activity for up to 24 hours, which helps reduce hospital-acquired infections.

alt.q: Because CHG keeps reducing bacteria for up to [[24|twenty-four]] hours, it is left to dry on the skin rather than rinsed off.
alt.ex: CHG continues antimicrobial activity for up to 24 hours, which helps reduce hospital-acquired infections.

sections.name: Skill 40.2 · Performing nail and foot care

items.q: A nurse delegates foot care for a patient without diabetes or circulatory problems to assistive personnel (AP). Which instruction should the nurse give the AP?
items.a: Do not trim the patient’s nails unless agency policy or the provider permits it
items.ex: AP are instructed not to trim nails unless the agency or health care provider permits it.
w: Soak both feet in hot water for 20 minutes before washing them
Water must be warm and tested; prolonged hot soaks risk burns and maceration.
Round the corners of the toenails with a file after washing
Toenail corners are never filed or shaped because this damages tissue.
Apply extra lotion between the toes to prevent cracking
Excess lotion must not be left between the toes.

alt.q: Which patient’s nail and foot care can the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?
alt.a: A patient recovering from knee surgery who has no circulatory problems
alt.ex: Nail and foot care can be delegated for patients without diabetes, PVD, or circulatory compromise.
w: A patient with type 2 diabetes mellitus and thick toenails
Diabetes increases the risk of injury and infection, so this care is not delegated.
A patient with peripheral vascular disease and cool feet
PVD reduces blood flow, so this patient’s foot care is not delegated to AP.
A patient with circulatory compromise and leg edema
Circulatory compromise excludes delegation of nail and foot care to AP.

items.q: After foot care, which findings should assistive personnel report to the nurse? Select all that apply.
o: A break in the skin on the heel
Breaks in skin are to be reported because they create a route for infection.
Redness over the side of the foot
Redness can signal pressure or irritation and must be reported.
Numbness in the toes
Numbness suggests reduced sensation and is reported to the nurse.
Swelling of the feet
Swelling is one of the findings AP are told to report.
Feet that feel warm and dry after drying
Warm, thoroughly dried feet are an expected finding after care.
Nails filed even with the tops of the toes
Nails even with the tops of the digits are the intended result.
items.ex: AP report breaks in skin, redness, numbness, swelling, or pain to the nurse.

alt.q: Which conditions mean a patient’s nail and foot care should not be delegated to assistive personnel? Select all that apply.
o: Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes reduces blood flow and sensation, raising the risk of injury and infection.
Peripheral vascular disease
PVD reduces blood flow to the feet, so care is not delegated.
Circulatory compromise
Any circulatory compromise excludes delegation of this skill.
Seasonal allergies
Allergies do not affect foot circulation or delegation of foot care.
A healed appendectomy incision
A healed abdominal incision does not affect foot care delegation.
alt.ex: Delegation applies only to patients without diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, or circulatory compromise.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to provide foot care for a patient with diabetes mellitus. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Wash the feet without soaking them in the basin
items.ex: Patients with diabetes or PVD do not soak feet because soaking causes maceration, drying, and tissue breakdown.
w: Soak the feet for 3 to 5 minutes to soften calluses
Soaking is skipped for diabetes; it leads to maceration and infection.
Cut thick corns with sterile scissors to relieve pressure
Cutting corns breaks skin integrity and risks infection, especially with diabetes.
Apply an oval corn pad to protect a painful toe
Oval pads press on toes and decrease circulation to surrounding tissue.

alt.q: A patient with peripheral vascular disease asks the nurse to soak the feet for comfort. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Soaking can soften and dry your skin too much, so I will wash your feet instead.”
alt.ex: Soaking feet with PVD can cause maceration and drying, leading to tissue breakdown and infection.
w: “I will soak your feet for 10 minutes so the calluses come off easily.”
Soaking is skipped entirely for PVD because of maceration risk.
“I will use very warm water so your circulation will improve.”
Water must be tested; heat does not justify soaking with PVD.
“Soaking is fine as long as I dry between your toes afterward.”
Drying afterward does not remove the risk; soaking is avoided.

items.q: Soaking the feet of a patient with diabetes mellitus is recommended because it softens calluses and prevents infection.
items.a: False
items.ex: Soaking diabetic feet can cause maceration and drying of the skin, leading to tissue breakdown and infection.
items.ww: Softening calluses does not outweigh the maceration risk; the book says to skip soaking with diabetes.

alt.q: For a patient with diabetes mellitus or peripheral vascular disease, the nurse skips soaking and goes straight to scrubbing callused areas with a washcloth.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Step 5 directs the nurse to skip soaking for diabetes, neuropathy, or PVD and proceed to foot care.
alt.ww: Soaking is not required first; it is harmful for these patients because of maceration.

items.q: Excessive softening of the skin from soaking is called [[maceration]].
items.ex: Maceration from soaking the feet of patients with diabetes or PVD leads to tissue breakdown and infection.

alt.q: Thorough drying of the fingers prevents [[maceration]] of tissues and impedes fungal growth.
alt.ex: Maceration from soaking the feet of patients with diabetes or PVD leads to tissue breakdown and infection.

items.q: Why does the nurse advise a patient not to use oval corn pads on the toes?
items.a: They exert pressure on the toes and decrease circulation to surrounding tissue
items.ex: Oval pads press on the toes, reducing circulation to nearby tissues.
w: They contain acids that cause chemical burns and ulceration
Burns and ulcers are the risk of liquid corn-removal preparations.
They tear thin skin and cause medical adhesive–related skin injury
Tearing and MARSI are the risk of applying adhesive tape.
They dry the nails because of the chemicals they contain
Excessive nail drying comes from nail polish and polish remover.

alt.q: Which home foot remedy decreases circulation by exerting pressure on the toes?
alt.a: Oval corn pads
alt.ex: Oval pads press on toes, decreasing circulation to the surrounding tissues.
w: Liquid corn-removal preparations
Liquid preparations cause burns and ulcerations rather than pressure.
Adhesive tape applied to the foot
Adhesive tape risks skin tearing and MARSI when removed.
Cutting calluses with a razor blade
Razor cutting breaks skin integrity and causes infection.

items.q: While assessing a patient’s foot care practices, which home remedies should the nurse identify as placing the patient at risk for injury? Select all that apply.
o: Over-the-counter liquid corn removers
Liquid preparations cause burns and ulcerations.
Cutting calluses with scissors
Cutting breaks skin integrity and can cause infection.
Applying adhesive tape to the foot
Older adult skin tears when tape is removed, risking MARSI.
Using oval corn pads on the toes
Oval pads exert pressure and decrease circulation.
Wearing clean, properly fitting shoes
Proper footwear reduces the risk of infection, friction, and ulcers.
Drying thoroughly between the toes
Thorough drying impedes fungal growth and prevents maceration.
items.ex: These remedies can cause more injury to soft tissue than the original foot problem.

alt.q: When assessing a patient’s footwear, which questions should the nurse ask? Select all that apply.
o: Do you wear socks or compression hose?
Sock and hose use is part of the footwear assessment.
Are your shoes tight or ill fitting?
Ill-fitting shoes cause friction, ulcerations, and infection.
Do you wear garters or knee-high nylons?
Garters and knee-highs are specifically assessed.
Is your footwear clean?
Cleanliness of footwear is part of the assessment.
Which shoe brand do you usually prefer?
Brand preference is not a factor in foot and nail risk.
alt.ex: Properly fitting, clean footwear reduces risk for infection, friction, and ulcerations.

items.q: An older adult covers a sore spot on the foot with adhesive tape. Why is this practice a concern?
items.a: Thin, delicate skin may tear when the tape is removed
items.ex: Older adult skin is thin and tears easily, raising the risk of medical adhesive–related skin injury.
w: The tape reduces circulation by pressing on the toes
Pressure that decreases circulation is the problem with oval corn pads.
The tape causes chemical burns of the surrounding skin
Chemical burns are a risk of liquid corn-removal preparations.
The tape dries the toenails and makes them brittle
Nail drying is linked to nail polish and polish remover.

alt.q: Medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI) is a particular risk of which foot care practice in an older adult?
alt.a: Applying adhesive tape to the foot
alt.ex: Removing tape from thin, delicate older adult skin can tear it, causing MARSI.
w: Using oval corn pads on the toes
Oval pads cause pressure and reduced circulation, not adhesive injury.
Filing nails straight across
Filing straight across prevents sharp edges and is recommended.
Soaking the hands in warm water
Soaking softens debris under nails and does not involve adhesive.

items.q: Frequent use of nail polish and polish remover can cause excessive drying of the nails.
items.a: True
items.ex: Chemicals in polish and remover dry the nails, so the nurse asks about their use.
items.ww: These products are not harmless; their chemicals dry the nails excessively.

alt.q: Nail polish remover moisturizes the nail plate, so frequent use helps prevent brittle nails.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Polish remover chemicals cause excessive drying of the nails.
alt.ww: Remover does not moisturize; its chemicals are the reason the nurse asks about frequent use.

items.q: Why does Older adult increase the risk for foot or nail problems?
items.a: Poor vision, poor coordination, or inability to bend over
items.ex: Each condition raises foot and nail risk through circulation, self-care ability, gait, or infection resistance.
w: Reduced peripheral blood flow and sensation in the feet
That goes with Diabetes mellitus or PVD.
Edema in dependent areas that reduces tissue blood flow
That goes with Heart failure or renal disease.
Altered gait that increases friction and pressure on the feet
That goes with Cerebrovascular accident.

alt.ex: Each condition raises foot and nail risk through circulation, self-care ability, gait, or infection resistance.
w: Poor vision, poor coordination, or inability to bend over
That goes with Older adult.
Edema in dependent areas that reduces tissue blood flow
That goes with Heart failure or renal disease.
Altered gait that increases friction and pressure on the feet
That goes with Cerebrovascular accident.

w: Poor vision, poor coordination, or inability to bend over
That goes with Older adult.

That goes with Diabetes mellitus or PVD.
Altered gait that increases friction and pressure on the feet
That goes with Cerebrovascular accident.

alt.q: Why does Cerebrovascular accident increase the risk for foot or nail problems?
alt.a: Altered gait that increases friction and pressure on the feet
alt.ex: Each condition raises foot and nail risk through circulation, self-care ability, gait, or infection resistance.
w: Poor vision, poor coordination, or inability to bend over
That goes with Older adult.
Reduced peripheral blood flow and sensation in the feet
That goes with Diabetes mellitus or PVD.
Edema in dependent areas that reduces tissue blood flow
That goes with Heart failure or renal disease.

alt.q: Why does Immunosuppression increase the risk for foot or nail problems?
alt.a: Reduced ability of the body to fight infection
alt.ex: Each condition raises foot and nail risk through circulation, self-care ability, gait, or infection resistance.

That goes with Older adult.
Reduced peripheral blood flow and sensation in the feet
That goes with Diabetes mellitus or PVD.
Edema in dependent areas that reduces tissue blood flow
That goes with Heart failure or renal disease.

alt.q: Which condition increases foot risk because of “Poor vision, poor coordination, or inability to bend over”?
alt.a: Older adult
alt.ex: Each condition raises foot and nail risk through circulation, self-care ability, gait, or infection resistance.
w: Diabetes mellitus or PVD
Diabetes mellitus or PVD: Reduced peripheral blood flow and sensation in the feet.
Heart failure or renal disease
Heart failure or renal disease: Edema in dependent areas that reduces tissue blood flow.
Cerebrovascular accident
Cerebrovascular accident: Altered gait that increases friction and pressure on the feet.

alt.q: Which condition increases foot risk because of “Reduced peripheral blood flow and sensation in the feet”?
alt.a: Diabetes mellitus or PVD
alt.ex: Each condition raises foot and nail risk through circulation, self-care ability, gait, or infection resistance.
w: Older adult
Older adult: Poor vision, poor coordination, or inability to bend over.
Heart failure or renal disease
Heart failure or renal disease: Edema in dependent areas that reduces tissue blood flow.
Cerebrovascular accident
Cerebrovascular accident: Altered gait that increases friction and pressure on the feet.

alt.q: Which condition increases foot risk because of “Edema in dependent areas that reduces tissue blood flow”?
alt.a: Heart failure or renal disease
alt.ex: Each condition raises foot and nail risk through circulation, self-care ability, gait, or infection resistance.
w: Older adult
Older adult: Poor vision, poor coordination, or inability to bend over.
Diabetes mellitus or PVD
Diabetes mellitus or PVD: Reduced peripheral blood flow and sensation in the feet.
Cerebrovascular accident
Cerebrovascular accident: Altered gait that increases friction and pressure on the feet.

alt.q: Which condition increases foot risk because of “Altered gait that increases friction and pressure on the feet”?
alt.a: Cerebrovascular accident
alt.ex: Each condition raises foot and nail risk through circulation, self-care ability, gait, or infection resistance.
w: Older adult
Older adult: Poor vision, poor coordination, or inability to bend over.
Diabetes mellitus or PVD
Diabetes mellitus or PVD: Reduced peripheral blood flow and sensation in the feet.
Heart failure or renal disease
Heart failure or renal disease: Edema in dependent areas that reduces tissue blood flow.

alt.q: Which condition increases foot risk because of “Reduced ability of the body to fight infection”?
alt.a: Immunosuppression
alt.ex: Each condition raises foot and nail risk through circulation, self-care ability, gait, or infection resistance.
w: Older adult
Older adult: Poor vision, poor coordination, or inability to bend over.
Diabetes mellitus or PVD
Diabetes mellitus or PVD: Reduced peripheral blood flow and sensation in the feet.
Heart failure or renal disease
Heart failure or renal disease: Edema in dependent areas that reduces tissue blood flow.

mt.q: Match each condition with the reason it increases a patient’s risk for foot or nail problems.
pairs: Poor vision, poor coordination, or inability to bend over
Reduced peripheral blood flow and sensation in the feet
Edema in dependent areas that reduces tissue blood flow
Altered gait that increases friction and pressure on the feet
Reduced ability of the body to fight infection
mt.ex: Each condition raises foot and nail risk through circulation, self-care ability, gait, or infection resistance.

items.q: During assessment for nail and foot care, which pulse does the nurse palpate on each foot?
items.a: Dorsalis pedis pulse
items.ex: The nurse palpates the dorsalis pedis pulse and radial and ulnar pulses to assess blood flow to extremities.
w: Popliteal pulse
The popliteal pulse is behind the knee and is not the foot pulse named.
Femoral pulse
The femoral pulse is in the groin, not the foot.
Brachial pulse
The brachial pulse is in the arm, not the foot.

alt.q: Why does the nurse assess color, temperature, capillary refill, and pulses before nail and foot care?
alt.a: To assess adequacy of blood flow to the extremities
alt.ex: Circulatory alterations change nail integrity and raise infection risk when skin breaks.
w: To determine the patient’s level of health literacy
Health literacy is assessed by other means, not by circulation checks.
To decide how long the feet should soak in the basin
Soak time is fixed; circulation findings may mean no soaking at all.
To choose the type of lotion to apply to the feet
Lotion is applied to retain moisture; circulation checks assess blood flow.

items.q: A patient receiving chemotherapy has thickened, discolored toenails. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Wash the feet and defer nail care until a foot specialist evaluates the patient
items.ex: Immunosuppressed patients often need specialist nail care; defer care beyond washing until evaluated.
w: Trim the toenails short and file the corners to a rounded shape
Corners are never shaped, and specialist evaluation is needed first.
Soak the feet for 20 minutes and then trim the nails
Prolonged soaking and nurse trimming are inappropriate before specialist evaluation.
Delegate trimming of the toenails to assistive personnel
AP do not trim nails, and this patient needs a specialist.

alt.q: Which patient’s nail care, other than washing the feet, should be deferred until a foot specialist evaluates the patient?
alt.a: An older adult with peripheral vascular disease
alt.ex: Patients with PVD or diabetes, older adults, and immunosuppressed patients often need specialist nail care.
w: A young adult with a sprained wrist
A sprain does not affect foot circulation or infection risk.
A middle-aged adult after an appendectomy
Abdominal surgery does not require specialist foot care.
A teenager with seasonal allergies
Allergies do not increase the risk of foot tissue injury.

items.q: Which tool does the nurse use to clean gently under the fingernails?
items.a: The end of a plastic applicator stick
items.ex: A plastic applicator stick removes debris; orange sticks and cotton swabs splinter and injure the nail bed.
w: An orange stick
Orange sticks splinter and can injure the nail or nail bed.
The end of a cotton swab
Cotton swab ends splinter and can cause injury to the nail.
The tip of the nail clippers
Clippers are for trimming nails, not cleaning beneath them.

alt.q: Why should the nurse avoid using an orange stick to clean under a patient’s nails?
alt.a: It can splinter and injure the nail or nail bed
alt.ex: Orange sticks and cotton swab ends splinter, so a plastic applicator stick is used.
w: It pushes the cuticle back too far
Pushing back the cuticle is done with a soft nail brush; splintering is the concern.
It removes too little debris to be useful
The concern is injury from splintering, not effectiveness.
It cannot be used while fingers are immersed
Cleaning is done while fingers are immersed; splintering is the concern.

items.q: How should the nurse shape a patient’s fingernails during nail care?
items.a: File them straight across and even with the tops of the fingers
items.ex: Filing straight across removes sharp edges so the nail cannot injure adjacent tissue.
w: File them into a curve that follows the fingertip
Shaping the corners damages tissue and increases infection risk.
Clip them well below the tops of the fingers
Nails are cut even with the tops of the fingers, not below them.
Clip them diagonally at the corners
Clipping corners shapes them, which damages tissue.

alt.q: Why does the nurse file nails straight across rather than shaping the corners?
alt.a: Shaping the corners damages tissue and increases the risk for infection
alt.ex: Straight-across filing eliminates sharp edges without damaging adjacent tissue.
w: Straight edges make the nails grow faster
Filing technique is about preventing injury, not nail growth.
Rounded corners trap more lotion under the nails
Lotion is not the reason; corner shaping damages tissue.
Straight edges help the cuticle grow over the nail
The cuticle should be pushed back, not encouraged to overgrow.

items.q: When trimming toenails, the nurse files the corners of the toenails to a rounded shape.
items.a: False
items.ex: The nurse does not file toenail corners because shaping them damages tissue and raises infection risk.
items.ww: Rounding corners is the misconception; straight-across trimming avoids tissue injury.

alt.q: The nurse trims toenails straight across and does not file the corners of the toenails.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Toenails are trimmed using the straight-across procedure, and the corners are not filed.
alt.ww: Filing the corners damages tissue and increases the risk for infection.

items.q: How long does the nurse allow the fingernails and feet to soak before cleaning them, for a patient who may soak?
items.a: 3 to 5 minutes
items.ex: A 3- to 5-minute soak softens debris beneath nails so it can be removed easily.
w: 15 to 20 minutes
The skill directs a 3- to 5-minute soak, not 15 to 20 minutes.
30 to 40 minutes
Soaks this long are not part of the skill and risk maceration.
45 to 60 minutes
An hour-long soak is far beyond the time directed in the skill.

alt.q: What is the purpose of soaking the fingernails and feet for 3 to 5 minutes?
alt.a: To soften debris beneath the nails so it can be removed easily
alt.ex: Soaking softens debris under the nails before the nurse cleans them.
w: To dry the cuticles so they can be trimmed
Soaking softens rather than dries; cuticles are pushed back with a brush.
To improve circulation in a patient with PVD
Patients with PVD skip soaking because of maceration risk.
To sterilize the skin before nail trimming
Warm water softens debris; it does not sterilize the skin.

items.q: In nail and foot care, which step comes right after “Dry the fingers thoroughly”?
items.a: File the fingernails straight across
items.ex: That's step 5 of 9. Fingernails are soaked, cleaned, dried, and filed before the feet are scrubbed, dried, trimmed, and moisturized.
w: Scrub callused areas of the feet with a washcloth
That's step 6 of 9.
Clean around the cuticles with a soft brush
That's step 3 of 9.
Dry the feet and clean under the toenails
That's step 7 of 9.

alt.q: Which step comes first in nail and foot care?
alt.a: Allow the feet and fingernails to soak
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 9. Fingernails are soaked, cleaned, dried, and filed before the feet are scrubbed, dried, trimmed, and moisturized.
w: Clean under the fingernails with a plastic applicator stick
That's step 2 of 9.
Clean around the cuticles with a soft brush
That's step 3 of 9.
Dry the fingers thoroughly
That's step 4 of 9.

alt.q: Which step comes last in nail and foot care?
alt.a: Apply lotion to the feet and hands
alt.ex: That's step 9 of 9. Fingernails are soaked, cleaned, dried, and filed before the feet are scrubbed, dried, trimmed, and moisturized.
w: Trim the toenails
That's step 8 of 9.
Dry the feet and clean under the toenails
That's step 7 of 9.
Scrub callused areas of the feet with a washcloth
That's step 6 of 9.

alt.q: In nail and foot care, which step comes right after “Allow the feet and fingernails to soak”?
alt.a: Clean under the fingernails with a plastic applicator stick
alt.ex: That's step 2 of 9. Fingernails are soaked, cleaned, dried, and filed before the feet are scrubbed, dried, trimmed, and moisturized.
w: Clean around the cuticles with a soft brush
That's step 3 of 9.
Dry the fingers thoroughly
That's step 4 of 9.
File the fingernails straight across
That's step 5 of 9.

alt.a: Clean around the cuticles with a soft brush

w: Dry the fingers thoroughly
That's step 4 of 9.

alt.a: Dry the fingers thoroughly
alt.ex: That's step 4 of 9. Fingernails are soaked, cleaned, dried, and filed before the feet are scrubbed, dried, trimmed, and moisturized.
w: File the fingernails straight across
That's step 5 of 9.

That's step 2 of 9.
Scrub callused areas of the feet with a washcloth
That's step 6 of 9.

alt.a: Scrub callused areas of the feet with a washcloth

w: Dry the feet and clean under the toenails
That's step 7 of 9.
Dry the fingers thoroughly
That's step 4 of 9.
Trim the toenails
That's step 8 of 9.

alt.q: In nail and foot care, which step comes right after “Scrub callused areas of the feet with a washcloth”?
alt.a: Dry the feet and clean under the toenails
alt.ex: That's step 7 of 9. Fingernails are soaked, cleaned, dried, and filed before the feet are scrubbed, dried, trimmed, and moisturized.
w: Trim the toenails
That's step 8 of 9.
File the fingernails straight across
That's step 5 of 9.
Apply lotion to the feet and hands
That's step 9 of 9.
