alt.a: Trim the toenails
alt.ex: That's step 8 of 9. Fingernails are soaked, cleaned, dried, and filed before the feet are scrubbed, dried, trimmed, and moisturized.
w: Apply lotion to the feet and hands
That's step 9 of 9.
Scrub callused areas of the feet with a washcloth

alt.a: Apply lotion to the feet and hands

That's step 5 of 9.

alt.a: Clean under the fingernails with a plastic applicator stick

Allow the feet and fingernails to soak

File the fingernails straight across

ord.q: Put these implementation steps of nail and foot care in order.
items: Allow the feet and fingernails to soak
Clean under the fingernails with a plastic applicator stick
Clean around the cuticles with a soft brush
Dry the fingers thoroughly
File the fingernails straight across
Scrub callused areas of the feet with a washcloth
Dry the feet and clean under the toenails
Trim the toenails
Apply lotion to the feet and hands
ord.ex: Fingernails are soaked, cleaned, dried, and filed before the feet are scrubbed, dried, trimmed, and moisturized.

items.q: The nurse observes assistive personnel finishing foot care for a patient without diabetes. Which action requires the nurse to intervene?
items.a: Leaving a thick layer of lotion between the patient’s toes
items.ex: Lotion is rubbed in thoroughly, and excess must not be left between the toes.
w: Scrubbing callused areas of the feet with a washcloth
Friction from a washcloth properly removes dead skin layers.
Drying the feet thoroughly before applying lotion
Thorough drying impedes fungal growth and prevents maceration.
Placing a disposable bathmat under the patient’s feet
A bathmat protects the feet from soil and microorganisms on the floor.

alt.q: Why does the nurse apply lotion to the feet and hands after nail and foot care?
alt.a: To lubricate dry skin by helping it retain moisture
alt.ex: Lotion lubricates dry skin and helps it retain moisture; excess is not left between toes.
w: To soften debris beneath the toenails
Debris is softened by soaking, not by lotion.
To dry the skin between the toes
Lotion moisturizes; drying between toes is done with a towel.
To remove dead skin layers from calluses
Dead skin is removed by friction from a washcloth.

items.q: After foot care, a patient has tender calluses at a point of friction and an ulcer on one toe. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Refer the patient to a podiatrist
Podiatry referral is indicated for painful calluses or corns.
Discuss a change in footwear
A change in footwear may be needed to improve calluses or corns.
Institute wound care policies for the ulcer
Remaining ulcerations require wound care policies.
Increase the frequency of assessment and hygiene
More frequent assessment and hygiene are indicated for ulcerations.
Teach the patient to trim the corns with a razor
Cutting corns breaks skin integrity and causes infection.
Soak the foot daily for 30 minutes
Prolonged soaking causes maceration and is not an intervention for ulcers.
items.ex: Painful calluses call for footwear change and podiatry; ulcers call for wound care and specialist consultation.

alt.q: A patient’s cuticles and surrounding tissues are inflamed and tender after nail care. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Repeat the nail care
Repeating nail care is a listed intervention for inflamed cuticles.
Evaluate the need for an antifungal or antibiotic cream
Inflamed cuticles may need antifungal or antibiotic cream.
Cut the inflamed cuticles away with scissors
Cutting tissue breaks skin integrity and increases infection risk.
Apply adhesive tape around each inflamed nail
Adhesive tape can tear skin and cause MARSI.
Use an orange stick to clean under the nails
Orange sticks splinter and injure the nail bed.
alt.ex: Inflamed cuticles call for repeated nail care and evaluation for antifungal or antibiotic cream.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient with diabetes about foot care at home. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will wear closed shoes and avoid walking barefoot.”
items.ex: Patients are encouraged not to go barefoot or wear open-toed shoes to prevent foot injury.
w: “I will wear open-toed sandals so my feet can breathe.”
Open-toed shoes are discouraged because they leave the feet exposed to injury.
“I will cut my corns with a clean razor blade.”
Cutting corns breaks skin and greatly raises infection risk with diabetes.
“I will soak my feet every evening to soften them.”
Soaking diabetic feet causes maceration and tissue breakdown.

alt.q: Which home care recommendation should the nurse include when teaching foot care to a patient at home?
alt.a: Remove rugs and objects that block pathways
alt.ex: The home is assessed for rugs, blocked pathways, and uneven flooring that could injure the feet.
w: Walk barefoot indoors to strengthen the feet
Patients are encouraged not to go barefoot.
Wear open-toed shoes to reduce friction
Open-toed shoes are discouraged because they expose the feet.
Use oval corn pads to cushion the toes
Oval pads decrease circulation by pressing on the toes.

sections.name: Skill 40.3 · Performing mouth care for a patient who is unconscious or debilitated

items.q: A nurse delegates mouth care for a patient who is unconscious to assistive personnel (AP). Which task must the nurse perform rather than delegate?
items.a: Assessing the patient’s gag reflex
items.ex: The nurse is responsible for assessing the gag reflex, which determines aspiration risk.
w: Positioning the patient for mouth care
AP can position the patient, with another AP helping.
Using an oral suction catheter to clear secretions
AP are directed to use an oral suction catheter to clear secretions.
Brushing the patient’s teeth with a soft toothbrush
Oral hygiene for an unconscious patient can be delegated to AP.

alt.q: Which part of oral care for a patient who is debilitated remains the nurse’s responsibility?
alt.a: Determining aspiration risk by checking the gag reflex
alt.ex: Gag reflex assessment is the nurse’s responsibility because it determines aspiration risk.
w: Cleaning the lips and mucosa with a toothette
Cleaning the mouth is part of the oral care that can be delegated.
Applying moisturizer to the patient’s lips
Lip moisturizing is part of the delegable oral care.
Placing a towel under the patient’s head
Placing towels is a simple step AP can perform.

items.q: Which instructions should the nurse give assistive personnel who will provide mouth care for a patient who is unconscious? Select all that apply.
o: Have another AP help position the patient
A second AP helps position the patient properly.
Follow special precautions such as aspiration precautions
AP must be aware of aspiration precautions.
Use an oral suction catheter to clear secretions
Oral suctioning clears secretions and reduces aspiration risk.
Report bleeding gums or excessive coughing or choking
These signs of impaired mucosa or aspiration are reported to the nurse.
Hold the mouth open with your fingers during brushing
Fingers are never placed in an unconscious patient’s mouth.
Assess the gag reflex before starting care
Gag reflex assessment is the nurse’s responsibility.
items.ex: AP get help positioning, follow aspiration precautions, suction secretions, and report bleeding, coughing, or choking.

alt.q: Which findings during mouth care should assistive personnel report to the nurse? Select all that apply.
o: Bleeding of the gums
Bleeding indicates impaired integrity of the oral mucosa.
Excessive coughing
Excessive coughing may signal aspiration.
Choking during rinsing
Choking suggests aspiration and must be reported.
Moist, pink oral mucosa
Moist, pink mucosa is a normal finding.
Lips that are soft after moisturizer
Soft lips after moisturizer are an expected result.
alt.ex: AP report signs of impaired oral mucosa, such as bleeding, and excessive coughing or choking.

items.q: How does the nurse assess for the presence of a gag reflex before mouth care?
items.a: Place a tongue blade on the back half of the tongue
items.ex: Touching the back half of the tongue with a tongue blade tests the gag reflex to judge aspiration risk.
w: Place a tongue blade on the tip of the tongue
The tongue blade goes on the back half of the tongue, not the tip.
Shine a penlight on the roof of the mouth
A penlight is used to inspect the oral cavity, not to test the gag reflex.
Instill a small amount of water into the mouth
Instilling water before assessing the gag reflex risks aspiration.

alt.q: Why does the nurse assess the gag reflex of a patient who is unconscious before mouth care?
alt.a: To determine the patient’s risk for aspiration
alt.ex: Patients with an impaired gag reflex cannot clear secretions and have a higher aspiration risk.
w: To decide whether the patient needs dentures
Denture needs are not determined by the gag reflex.
To check whether the patient can hear instructions
Hearing is not assessed by the gag reflex.
To measure the patient’s oxygen saturation
Oxygen saturation is assessed separately with respirations.

items.q: A nurse finds that a patient who is unconscious has an impaired gag reflex. Which action is most important before beginning mouth care?
items.a: Keep suction equipment available and working at the bedside
items.ex: An impaired gag reflex means secretions pool in the back of the mouth, so suction must be ready.
w: Place the patient flat and supine for easier access
Supine positioning lets secretions collect in the pharynx and raises aspiration risk.
Rinse the mouth with a large amount of water
Large volumes of fluid increase aspiration risk.
Hold the mouth open with a gloved finger
Fingers are never placed in an unconscious patient’s mouth.

alt.q: Why is a patient with an impaired gag reflex at higher risk for aspiration during mouth care?
alt.a: The patient cannot clear secretions, which collect in the back of the oral cavity
alt.ex: Without a gag reflex, secretions pool in the back of the mouth and can be aspirated.
w: The patient bites down hard on the toothbrush and the nurse’s fingers
Biting is a bite reflex concern, managed with an oral airway.
The patient produces less saliva, so the oral mucosa becomes dry
Reduced saliva does not explain aspiration risk.
The patient’s lips dry and crack during care and begin to bleed
Dry lips are prevented with moisturizer and are unrelated to aspiration.

items.q: A nurse is about to give mouth care to a patient who is unconscious and has no head or neck injury. How should the nurse position the patient?
items.a: Side-lying with the head turned toward the mattress and HOB elevated at least 30 degrees
items.ex: Side-lying with the head dependent lets secretions drain from the mouth instead of the pharynx.
w: Supine with the head midline and HOB elevated 10 degrees
Supine positioning lets secretions collect in the back of the pharynx.
Prone with the head turned to one side and HOB flat
Prone with a flat bed is not the position used for safe mouth care.
Supine with the neck hyperextended and HOB flat
Hyperextension and a flat bed increase the risk of aspiration.

alt.q: Why does the nurse turn the head of an unconscious patient toward the mattress during mouth care?
alt.a: To let secretions drain from the mouth instead of collecting in the pharynx
alt.ex: The dependent head position allows drainage from the mouth and prevents aspiration.
w: To make it easier for the patient to hear the nurse
Positioning is for drainage, not hearing.
To keep the patient’s teeth apart during brushing
An oral airway, not head position, keeps the teeth apart.
To stimulate the gag reflex during brushing
The nurse avoids stimulating the gag reflex during care.

items.q: For mouth care, the unconscious patient is placed side-lying with the head of the bed elevated at least [[30|thirty]] degrees.
items.ex: Side-lying with HOB at least 30 degrees lets secretions drain from the mouth and prevents aspiration.

alt.q: A patient with no head or neck injury is positioned in the [[side-lying|side lying|lateral]] position with the head turned toward the mattress for mouth care.
alt.ex: Side-lying with HOB at least 30 degrees lets secretions drain from the mouth and prevents aspiration.

items.q: A nurse may place gloved fingers in the mouth of an unconscious patient to hold the mouth open during brushing.
items.a: False
items.ex: Fingers are never placed in the mouth because they could occlude the airway and the patient may bite down.
items.ww: Gloves do not prevent airway occlusion or bite injury; an oral airway is used instead.

alt.q: Never place fingers into the mouth of a patient who is unconscious, because this could occlude the airway and the patient may bite down.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The book warns against placing fingers in the mouth because of airway occlusion and bite injury.
alt.ww: Gloves do not make finger placement safe; an oral airway keeps the teeth apart instead.

items.q: A patient who is debilitated keeps clenching the teeth during mouth care. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Insert an oral airway when the patient is relaxed, without using force
items.ex: An oral airway keeps the teeth apart and prevents biting; it is inserted gently when the patient is relaxed.
w: Pry the teeth apart with a tongue blade
Force is not used and could injure the patient.
Hold the jaw open with the fingers
Fingers are never placed in the mouth of an unconscious or debilitated patient.
Skip brushing and rinse the mouth with water
Mechanical brushing is required; rinsing alone does not remove plaque.

alt.q: How does the nurse insert an oral airway for a patient who has a bite reflex during mouth care?
alt.a: Insert it upside down, then turn it sideways and over the tongue
alt.ex: Inserting upside down and turning it over the tongue keeps the teeth apart without force.
w: Insert it right side up and push it straight to the back
The airway is inserted upside down and then turned, not pushed straight.
Insert it sideways along the cheek and leave it sideways
The airway is turned over the tongue, not left sideways.
Insert it with force while the patient is biting down
Do not use force; insert when the patient is relaxed if possible.

items.q: When brushing the teeth of a patient who is unconscious, at what angle does the nurse hold the toothbrush bristles to the gum line?
items.a: 45 degrees
items.ex: A 45-degree angle lets bristle tips rest against and penetrate under the gum line to remove plaque.
w: 90 degrees
A 90-degree angle does not place bristle tips under the gum line.
15 degrees
A 15-degree angle is too flat to reach under the gum line.
180 degrees
A 180-degree angle would hold the brush parallel and not reach the gum line.

alt.q: Which brushing technique does the nurse use on the inner and outer surfaces of the teeth?
alt.a: Brush from the gum to the crown of each tooth
alt.ex: Brushing from gum to crown with bristles at 45 degrees removes plaque above and below the gum line.
w: Brush from the crown down to the gum of each tooth
Brushing moves from gum to crown, not crown to gum.
Brush in wide circles across all teeth at once
Inner and outer surfaces are brushed gum to crown, tooth by tooth.
Brush only the biting surfaces back and forth
Back-and-forth brushing is for biting surfaces, not all surfaces.

items.q: A patient who is unconscious has a low platelet count and bleeds easily. Which equipment should the nurse use to clean the mouth?
items.a: Toothette sponge
items.ex: A toothette sponge is used if the patient has a bleeding tendency or toothbrushing is contraindicated.
w: Firm-bristled adult toothbrush
Firm bristles could injure the gums; a soft brush or sponge is used.
Lemon-glycerin sponge
Lemon-glycerin sponges dry mucous membranes and erode enamel.
Orange stick wrapped in gauze

CHG protocols are used together with brushing, not instead of it.

Removing dentures does not by itself require sponges instead of brushing.

items.q: Why is a patient who is intubated and on mechanical ventilation at risk for ventilator-associated pneumonia (VAP)?
items.a: The artificial airway bypasses normal defenses and changes the oral flora
items.ex: Intubation bypasses normal airway defenses and rapidly changes oral flora, raising VAP risk.
w: The patient’s gag reflex becomes overly sensitive
VAP risk comes from bypassed defenses, not an overactive gag reflex.
The ventilator dries the lips and causes cracking
Lip drying is prevented by moisturizer and does not explain VAP.
The patient receives too much oral moisture
Excess oral moisture is not the described cause of VAP.

alt.ex: Daily brushing and CHG significantly reduce VAP in critically ill patients.

Lemon-glycerin dries mucosa; brushing with CHG is the described combination.
Foam swabs used alone without brushing
Foam swabs do not remove plaque; mechanical brushing is required.

Lip moisturizer protects lips but does not reduce VAP alone.

items.ww: Brushing and CHG work together; brushing alone does not replace the CHG protocol.

alt.ww: Omitting CHG removes one of the two measures shown to reduce VAP.

items.q: During mouth care, a patient who is unconscious begins coughing and the nurse suspects aspiration of secretions. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

Suctioning maintains airway patency when secretions accumulate.
Elevate the head of the bed
Elevating the HOB facilitates breathing.
Notify the health care provider
Suspected aspiration is reported to the health care provider.
Prepare the patient for a chest x-ray
A chest x-ray may be ordered to evaluate suspected aspiration.
Rinse the mouth with a large amount of water
Large volumes of fluid increase the risk of further aspiration.
Lower the head of the bed flat
A flat position worsens breathing and aspiration risk.
items.ex: Suspected aspiration calls for suctioning, raising the HOB, notifying the provider, and preparing for a chest x-ray.

alt.q: Which assessments help the nurse recognize aspiration early during mouth care for a patient who is unconscious? Select all that apply.

Oxygen saturation helps detect aspiration early.
Excessive coughing or choking
Coughing or choking may signal aspiration.
Color of the fingernails’ cuticles
Cuticle color is not used to detect aspiration.
Presence of dentures in the mouth
Dentures are removed for access, not assessed for aspiration.
alt.ex: Respirations, oxygen saturation, and coughing or choking help identify aspiration early.

Lemon-glycerin dries mucosa, and firm bristles can injure inflamed tissue.
Hot water rinses and a firm toothbrush
Room temperature rinses and soft bristles are used for mucositis.
Foam swabs alone with no rinsing

alt.q: What is mucositis?

Lung infection after aspiration is aspiration pneumonia, not mucositis.

Mucositis is inflammation, not increased saliva.

Lip moisturizer prevents cracking but does not prepare for emergencies.

Asking about comfort evaluates care, not emergency readiness.

A flat position lets secretions collect in the pharynx.

A straw cannot suction secretions effectively.

items.q: Which term describes the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide during cellular metabolism?
items.a: Respiration
items.ex: Respiration is gas exchange during cellular metabolism; it is often confused with ventilation, the movement of air in and out of the lungs.
w: Ventilation
Ventilation is the movement of gases into and out of the lungs, not cellular gas exchange.
Perfusion
Perfusion is the cardiovascular system’s pumping of blood to the tissues and back to the lungs.
Compliance
Compliance is the ability of the lungs to distend in response to increased intraalveolar pressure.

alt.q: Which term describes the process of moving gases into and out of the lungs during inhalation and exhalation?
alt.a: Ventilation
alt.ex: Ventilation is air flowing into the lungs on inspiration and out on expiration, coordinating muscular and elastic properties of lungs and thorax.
w: Respiration
Respiration is the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide during cellular metabolism.
Diffusion
Diffusion moves respiratory gases from one area to another by concentration gradients.
Perfusion
Perfusion is the pumping of oxygenated blood to tissues and return of deoxygenated blood to the lungs.

items.q: Which nerve innervates the diaphragm, the major inspiratory muscle?
items.a: Phrenic nerve
items.ex: The diaphragm is innervated by the phrenic nerve, which exits the spinal cord at the fourth cervical vertebra.
w: Vagus nerve
Vagus nerve fibers slow the heart rate; they do not drive the diaphragm.
Intercostal nerve
Intercostal nerves supply the intercostal muscles of the rib cage, not the diaphragm.
Spinal accessory nerve
The accessory nerve does not innervate the diaphragm; the phrenic nerve does.

alt.q: The phrenic nerve, which innervates the diaphragm, exits the spinal cord at which level?
alt.a: Fourth cervical vertebra
alt.ex: The phrenic nerve exits at the fourth cervical vertebra, so high cervical injuries can paralyze the diaphragm.
w: Seventh cervical vertebra
Injury below C5 usually spares the phrenic nerve, so it does not exit as low as C7.
First thoracic vertebra
The phrenic nerve exits in the cervical region, not the thoracic region.
Second lumbar vertebra
The lumbar spine is far below the cervical origin of the phrenic nerve.

items.q: Intrapleural pressure is normally negative, meaning it is less than atmospheric pressure.
items.a: True
items.ex: Intrapleural pressure is less than atmospheric pressure (760 mm Hg at sea level), and becomes more negative to draw air in.
items.ww: Air flow depends on intrapleural pressure being below atmospheric pressure, so calling it positive is incorrect.

alt.q: For air to flow into the lungs, intrapleural pressure must become less negative than at rest.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: For inspiration, intrapleural pressure becomes more negative, creating a pressure gradient from the atmosphere to the alveoli.
alt.ww: A more negative pleural pressure, created by diaphragm and external intercostal contraction, is what draws air into the lungs.

items.q: Expiration is normally a passive process that depends on the elastic recoil of the lungs.
items.a: True
items.ex: Expiration requires little or no muscle work because it relies on the elastic recoil properties of the lungs.
items.ww: Inspiration is the active phase; expiration in a healthy person is passive.

alt.q: Inspiration is a passive process, whereas expiration requires active contraction of the diaphragm.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Inspiration is active, stimulated by chemoreceptors; expiration is passive and depends on elastic recoil.
alt.ww: The diaphragm contracts during inspiration and relaxes to let air escape, so the roles are reversed in this statement.

items.q: What is the function of surfactant in the lungs?
items.a: Maintaining alveolar surface tension so the alveoli do not collapse
items.ex: Surfactant is produced in the lungs to maintain alveolar surface tension and prevent alveolar collapse.
w: Moving respiratory gases across the membrane by concentration gradients
Moving gases by concentration gradients is diffusion, not the role of surfactant.
Binding oxygen in red blood cells so it can reach the tissues
Hemoglobin, not surfactant, binds and carries oxygen to the tissues.
Sensing changes in pH and carbon dioxide to adjust breathing
Chemoreceptors, not surfactant, monitor pH, PaCO2, and PaO2.

alt.q: A patient with a pulmonary disease has decreased surfactant production. Which complication should the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: Atelectasis
alt.ex: Without enough surfactant, alveoli collapse (atelectasis), preventing normal exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
w: Polycythemia
Polycythemia is increased red blood cells in response to chronic hypoxemia, not a result of low surfactant.
Increased lung compliance
Increased compliance is seen in emphysema and aging, not as a result of lost surfactant.
Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation is excess CO2 removal from anxiety, fever, drugs, or acidosis, not low surfactant.

items.q: [[Atelectasis]] is a collapse of the alveoli that prevents normal exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide.
items.ex: Atelectasis can develop when surfactant production is decreased in certain pulmonary diseases.

alt.q: When alveoli collapse and can no longer exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide, the condition is called [[atelectasis]].
alt.ex: Atelectasis can develop when surfactant production is decreased in certain pulmonary diseases.

items.q: During assessment of a patient with emphysema, the nurse notes that the patient’s clavicles elevate with each inspiration. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
items.a: It can indicate ventilatory fatigue, air hunger, or decreased lung expansion
items.ex: Clavicle elevation on inspiration reflects accessory muscle use and can signal ventilatory fatigue, air hunger, or reduced lung expansion.
w: It shows the patient is breathing quietly with minimal effort
Healthy breathing is quiet and effortless; clavicle elevation signals increased work of breathing.
It shows the diaphragm is descending fully with each breath
Clavicle elevation reflects accessory muscle use, not effective diaphragm movement.
It shows lung compliance has returned to the normal range
Clavicle elevation is a sign of respiratory distress, not of restored compliance.

alt.q: A patient with COPD has been using the accessory muscles of respiration for several days. Which outcome should the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: Fatigue, because prolonged accessory muscle use does not ventilate effectively
alt.ex: Prolonged accessory muscle use does not promote effective ventilation and eventually causes fatigue.
w: Improved gas exchange, because accessory muscles replace the diaphragm
The diaphragm remains the major inspiratory muscle; accessory muscles cannot ventilate effectively long term.
Lower oxygen needs, because accessory muscles use very little energy
Accessory muscle use increases work of breathing and energy expenditure.
Easier exhalation, because accessory muscles restore elastic recoil
Accessory muscles do not restore the elastic recoil lost in advanced COPD.

items.q: The amount of energy a person spends on breathing depends on which factors? Select all that apply.
o: Rate and depth of breathing
Faster or deeper breathing requires more energy.
Lung compliance
The ease with which the lungs expand affects how much work breathing takes.
Airway resistance
Narrowed airways raise the pressure needed to move air, increasing work.
The intrinsic rate of the SA node
The SA node sets the heart’s rhythm and does not determine the work of breathing.
The length of the PR interval
The PR interval is an ECG measure of conduction, not a determinant of breathing effort.
items.ex: Work of breathing depends on the rate and depth of breathing, lung compliance, and airway resistance.

alt.q: Which changes increase a patient’s work of breathing (WOB)? Select all that apply.
o: Increased use of accessory muscles
Accessory muscle use increases energy expenditure for breathing.
Decreased lung compliance
Stiffer lungs need more effort to expand.
Increased airway resistance
Narrowed airways from bronchoconstriction or mucus make breathing harder.
Normal elastic recoil during expiration
Normal passive recoil makes expiration require little or no muscle work.
Adequate surfactant production
Surfactant keeps alveoli open and does not increase work of breathing.
alt.ex: Accessory muscle use, decreased compliance, and increased airway resistance raise WOB, energy expenditure, and oxygen demand.

items.q: In which condition is lung compliance increased?
items.a: Emphysema
items.ex: Compliance increases in degenerative lung tissue diseases such as emphysema and in the older adult population.
w: Pulmonary edema
Pulmonary edema decreases compliance by making the lungs harder to distend.
Pleural fibrosis
Interstitial and pleural fibrosis decrease compliance.
Kyphosis
Structural abnormalities such as kyphosis decrease compliance.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for four patients. Which patient is most likely to have decreased lung compliance?
alt.a: A patient with several fractured ribs
alt.ex: Traumatic structural abnormalities such as fractured ribs decrease the lungs’ ability to distend.
w: A patient with long-standing emphysema
Emphysema is a degenerative lung disease that increases compliance.
An older adult with degenerative lung tissue
Degenerative changes in older adults increase compliance.
A patient with iron-deficiency anemia
Anemia lowers oxygen-carrying capacity but does not alter lung compliance.

items.q: A patient with asthma has wheezing from bronchoconstriction and thick mucus in the airways. The nurse recognizes that these changes will have which effect?
items.a: Increase airway resistance and decrease oxygen delivered to the alveoli
items.ex: Bronchoconstriction or excess mucus narrows the airways, raising resistance and reducing oxygen delivery to the alveoli.
w: Decrease airway resistance and increase oxygen delivered to the alveoli
Narrowed airways raise, not lower, airway resistance.
Increase lung compliance and decrease the work of breathing
Narrowed airways increase the work of breathing; they do not improve compliance.
Thicken the alveolocapillary membrane and slow carbon dioxide transport
Membrane thickening occurs with edema, infiltrates, or effusion, not with bronchoconstriction.

alt.q: Which situation increases airway resistance?
alt.a: Excess mucus narrowing the diameter of the airways
alt.ex: Any further decrease in airway diameter from bronchoconstriction or excess mucus increases airway resistance.
w: Relaxation of the diaphragm at the end of inspiration
Diaphragm relaxation allows passive exhalation; it does not narrow the airways.
Production of surfactant in the alveoli
Surfactant prevents alveolar collapse and does not narrow the airways.
A larger tidal volume during exercise
Tidal volume changes with activity but does not by itself narrow the airways.

items.q: Approximately what percentage of oxygen is transported by hemoglobin?
items.ex: Hemoglobin carries most oxygen, about 97%; the rest is dissolved in plasma.
w: Hemoglobin carries far more than half of the oxygen in the blood.
Hemoglobin transports nearly all oxygen, about 97%, not three quarters.
Only a small portion is dissolved in plasma; hemoglobin carries about 97%.

alt.q: When hemoglobin combines with oxygen, which compound forms?
alt.a: Oxyhemoglobin
alt.ex: Hemoglobin combines with oxygen to form oxyhemoglobin, a reversible bond that frees oxygen to enter tissues.
w: Deoxyhemoglobin
Deoxyhemoglobin is reduced hemoglobin after oxygen has dissociated.
Carbonic acid
Carbonic acid forms when carbon dioxide is hydrated in red blood cells.
Bicarbonate
Bicarbonate is formed when carbonic acid dissociates; it diffuses into plasma.

items.q: Which factors influence the capacity of the blood to carry oxygen? Select all that apply.
o: Amount of oxygen dissolved in the plasma
Dissolved plasma oxygen is one of the three influences on carrying capacity.
Amount of hemoglobin
Hemoglobin carries about 97% of oxygen, so its amount is critical.
Ability of hemoglobin to bind with oxygen
Hemoglobin must bind oxygen to carry it to the tissues.
Number of chemoreceptors in the carotid body
Chemoreceptors regulate ventilation; they do not determine how much oxygen blood carries.
Amount of surfactant in the alveoli
Surfactant prevents alveolar collapse; it is not part of blood’s carrying capacity.
items.ex: Oxygen-carrying capacity depends on dissolved plasma oxygen, the amount of hemoglobin, and hemoglobin’s ability to bind oxygen.

alt.q: Which patients have a decreased ability of the blood to carry oxygen to the tissues? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with sepsis whose pH is 7.28
Acidosis (pH below 7.35) decreases the ability to carry oxygen.
A patient with COPD who has an elevated PaCO2
Hypercapnia decreases the blood’s ability to carry and deliver oxygen.
A patient with anemia after excess blood loss
Low hemoglobin leaves fewer carriers for oxygen.
A patient with a pH of 7.40 and normal hemoglobin
A normal pH and hemoglobin do not reduce carrying capacity.
A patient with a PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg
A PaCO2 of 40 mm Hg is within normal limits, not hypercapnic.
alt.ex: Acidosis, hypercapnia, and low hemoglobin each reduce the blood’s ability to carry and deliver oxygen.

items.q: The nurse reviews data for four patients. Which patient’s blood has the most reduced ability to carry oxygen to the tissues?
items.a: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis with a pH of 7.21
items.ex: Acidosis (pH below 7.35), as in diabetic ketoacidosis, decreases the blood’s ability to carry and deliver oxygen.
w: A patient after knee surgery with a pH of 7.38
A pH of 7.38 is not acidotic, so carrying capacity is not reduced.
A patient with a sprained ankle and a pH of 7.42
A pH of 7.42 is within normal limits.
A patient with a migraine and a PaCO2 of 38 mm Hg
A PaCO2 of 38 mm Hg is normal, so the patient is not hypercapnic.

alt.q: A patient has pulmonary edema. Why does this condition reduce oxygen delivery to the tissues?
alt.a: The alveolocapillary membrane thickens, slowing diffusion of gases
alt.ex: A thickened membrane makes gases take longer to transfer, slowing exchange and decreasing oxygen delivery.
w: The surface area of the membrane is surgically removed
Loss of surface area occurs with processes such as lobectomy, not edema.
The hemoglobin molecule can no longer form oxyhemoglobin
Edema affects membrane thickness, not hemoglobin’s ability to bind oxygen.
The phrenic nerve can no longer stimulate the diaphragm
Phrenic nerve damage results from cervical injury, not pulmonary edema.

items.q: Most carbon dioxide is carried back to the lungs in venous blood, partly bound to reduced hemoglobin (deoxyhemoglobin).
items.a: True
items.ex: Deoxyhemoglobin combines with carbon dioxide, and venous blood transports most carbon dioxide back to the lungs to be exhaled.
items.ww: Venous blood, with reduced hemoglobin, is the route by which most carbon dioxide returns to the lungs.

alt.q: In red blood cells, hemoglobin buffers the bicarbonate ion while the hydrogen ion diffuses into the plasma.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Carbonic acid dissociates into hydrogen and bicarbonate; hemoglobin buffers the hydrogen ion, and bicarbonate diffuses into plasma.
alt.ww: The roles are reversed: hemoglobin buffers hydrogen, and bicarbonate moves into the plasma.

items.q: Where are the chemoreceptors that respond to changes in blood oxygen, carbon dioxide, and hydrogen ion levels located?
items.a: Medulla, aortic body, and carotid body
items.ex: Chemoreceptors in the medulla, aortic body, and carotid body stimulate neural regulators to adjust rate and depth of ventilation.
w: Cerebral cortex, pons, and cerebellum
The cerebral cortex provides voluntary control of breathing; it is not the chemoreceptor site.
Alveoli, bronchioles, and trachea
These are airway structures, not the chemoreceptor sites.
SA node, AV node, and bundle of His
These are parts of the cardiac conduction system.

alt.q: Which part of the central nervous system regulates the voluntary control of respiration?
alt.a: Cerebral cortex
alt.ex: The cerebral cortex delivers impulses to the respiratory motor neurons by way of the spinal cord for voluntary control.
w: Carotid body
The carotid body contains chemoreceptors that respond to blood gas changes, not voluntary control.
Aortic body
The aortic body contains chemoreceptors involved in chemical, not voluntary, regulation.
Phrenic nerve
The phrenic nerve innervates the diaphragm; it is not the CNS center for voluntary control.

items.q: Blood flow through the pulmonary circulation depends on the pumping ability of which chamber?
items.a: Right ventricle
items.ex: The pulmonary artery receives poorly oxygenated mixed venous blood from the right ventricle, whose pumping drives pulmonary flow.
w: Left ventricle
The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the systemic circulation.
Left atrium
The left atrium receives oxygen-rich blood returning from the pulmonary veins.
Right atrium
The right atrium receives blood from the vena cava; the right ventricle pumps it to the lungs.

alt.q: After gas exchange in the pulmonary capillaries, oxygen-rich blood returns to which chamber of the heart?
alt.a: Left atrium
alt.ex: Oxygen-rich blood flows through the pulmonary venules and veins and returns to the left atrium.
w: Right atrium
The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the vena cava.
Right ventricle
The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary artery.
Pulmonary artery
The pulmonary artery carries poorly oxygenated blood away from the heart to the lungs.

items.q: A patient with COPD who is using accessory muscles to breathe asks the nurse why breathing leaves him so tired. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “The extra effort to breathe uses energy and raises your body’s need for oxygen.”
items.ex: Increased WOB raises energy expenditure, metabolic rate, and oxygen demand, creating a vicious cycle in impaired ventilation.
w: “Breathing out takes strong muscle work, even in healthy lungs.”
Expiration is normally passive and requires little or no muscle work.
“Your lungs are making too much surfactant, which tires you.”
Surfactant keeps alveoli open; certain lung diseases decrease, not increase, it.
“Your neck muscles move air better than your diaphragm does.”
The diaphragm is the major inspiratory muscle; prolonged accessory use is ineffective.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient with COPD shows understanding of why breathing harder makes symptoms worse?
alt.a: “Working harder to breathe makes my body need even more oxygen.”
alt.ex: Increased WOB raises metabolic rate, oxygen need, and carbon dioxide production, worsening respiratory status.
w: “Working harder to breathe lowers the oxygen my body needs.”
Increased WOB raises, not lowers, the body’s oxygen demand.
“Working harder to breathe helps my body get rid of less CO2.”
Increased WOB raises the need for carbon dioxide elimination.
“Working harder to breathe restores the stretch of my lungs.”
Extra effort does not restore elastic recoil lost in advanced COPD.

items.q: A patient has a condition, such as COPD or cystic fibrosis, that alters the structure and function of the pulmonary system. Which findings may the nurse observe? Select all that apply.
o: Increased respiratory rate
Altered pulmonary function often increases respiratory rate.
Decreased oxygen saturation
Impaired gas exchange lowers oxygen saturation levels.
Decreased lung expansion
Pulmonary diseases can limit lung expansion.
Adventitious lung sounds
Abnormal breath sounds can occur with these conditions.
Decreased work of breathing
These conditions increase, not decrease, the work of breathing.
items.ex: Pulmonary conditions such as COPD, asthma, lung cancer, and cystic fibrosis can raise RR, lower SpO2, limit expansion, and cause adventitious sounds.

alt.q: Which conditions does the text identify as changing the structure and function of the pulmonary system? Select all that apply.
o: Asthma
Asthma alters pulmonary structure and function, affecting respiration.
Lung cancer
Lung cancer alters pulmonary structure and function.
Cystic fibrosis
Cystic fibrosis alters pulmonary structure and function.
Iron-deficiency anemia
Anemia reduces oxygen-carrying capacity of blood rather than pulmonary structure.
Severe dehydration
Dehydration causes hypovolemia, a circulatory rather than pulmonary structural problem.
alt.ex: COPD, asthma, lung cancer, and cystic fibrosis are examples of conditions that change pulmonary structure and function.

items.q: Which chamber pumps oxygenated blood through the systemic circulation?
items.a: Left ventricle
items.ex: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aorta into the systemic circulation.
w: Right ventricle
The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary circulation.
Right atrium
The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood returning from the vena cava.
Left atrium
The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the lungs and passes it to the left ventricle.

alt.q: Which chamber pumps deoxygenated blood through the pulmonary circulation?
alt.a: Right ventricle
alt.ex: The right ventricle pumps deoxygenated blood into the pulmonary artery and lungs.
w: Left ventricle
The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the systemic circulation.
Left atrium
The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins.
Right atrium
The right atrium receives blood from the vena cava; it does not pump blood to the lungs.

items.q: What is the normal stroke volume for a healthy adult?
items.a: 50 to 75 mL per contraction
items.ex: Stroke volume, the blood ejected from the ventricle with each contraction, is normally 50 to 75 mL in a healthy adult.
w: 10 to 25 mL per contraction
This is far below the normal adult stroke volume of 50 to 75 mL.
150 to 200 mL per contraction
This exceeds the normal adult stroke volume of 50 to 75 mL.
4 to 8 L per contraction
4 to 8 L/min is the normal cardiac output, not the volume per contraction.

alt.q: What is the normal cardiac output for a healthy adult at rest?
alt.a: 4 to 8 L/min
alt.ex: Cardiac output, the blood ejected from the left ventricle each minute, is normally 4 to 8 L/min at rest.
w: 1 to 2 L/min
This is well below the normal resting cardiac output of 4 to 8 L/min.
10 to 14 L/min
This exceeds normal resting cardiac output of 4 to 8 L/min.
50 to 75 L/min
50 to 75 mL is the normal stroke volume per contraction, not liters per minute.

items.q: Cardiac output equals [[stroke volume|SV]] multiplied by heart rate.
items.ex: Cardiac output = stroke volume × heart rate, so a change in either alters the blood ejected each minute.

items.q: Which principle states that the more the myocardium stretches during filling, the stronger the next contraction?
items.a: Starling’s law of the heart
items.ex: Starling’s (Frank-Starling) law: in a healthy heart, increased myocardial stretch increases the strength of contraction.
w: Afterload
Afterload is the resistance to ejection of blood from the left ventricle.
Myocardial contractility
Contractility is the heart’s ability to squeeze blood from the ventricles, not the stretch principle.
Normal sinus rhythm
Normal sinus rhythm describes the electrical impulse path starting at the SA node.

alt.q: In a patient with cardiomyopathy, why does Starling’s law no longer apply?
alt.a: Myocardial stretch is beyond the heart’s physiological limits
alt.ex: In cardiomyopathy, stretch exceeds physiological limits, stroke volume is insufficient, and blood backs up into the circulation.
w: Ventricular filling time is too long to cause stretch
The problem is excessive stretch beyond limits, not inadequate filling time.
The SA node fires too slowly to trigger contraction
Cardiomyopathy affects the muscle’s stretch response, not SA node firing.
The coronary arteries fill only during ventricular systole
Coronary arteries fill during diastole; this is unrelated to Starling’s law failing.

items.q: A patient who is hemorrhaging receives fluid therapy and blood replacement. Which effect does the nurse expect from this treatment?
items.a: Increased preload, stroke volume, and cardiac output
items.ex: Replacing circulating volume increases preload, which increases stroke volume and, in turn, cardiac output.
w: Decreased preload, stroke volume, and cardiac output

Respiratory center depression is linked to opioids, not to CO’s mechanism.

alt.q: Carbon monoxide poisoning creates which type of problem with hemoglobin?
alt.a: A functional anemia
alt.ex: Because CO occupies hemoglobin and does not easily dissociate, hemoglobin is unavailable for oxygen, creating a functional anemia.
w: A polycythemia
Polycythemia is increased red cells in response to chronic hypoxemia, not CO toxicity.
A hypovolemia
Hypovolemia is reduced circulating blood volume, as in shock or dehydration.
A hypercapnia
Hypercapnia is elevated PaCO2, not the effect of CO on hemoglobin.

items.q: A patient comes to the emergency department with headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and dyspnea. The patient’s spouse, who lives in the same home, has the same symptoms. Which condition should the nurse consider?
items.a: Carbon monoxide poisoning
items.ex: CO is colorless and odorless, people are often unaware of exposure, and its symptoms mimic other illnesses.
w: Obesity-hypoventilation syndrome
This syndrome develops in some morbidly obese patients and would not strike two household members at once.
Flail chest
Flail chest results from multiple rib fractures, not from a shared exposure.
Guillain-Barré syndrome
This neuromuscular disease causes hypoventilation, not shared headache and nausea in a household.

alt.q: Why is carbon monoxide poisoning often missed?
alt.a: Its symptoms mimic other illnesses, and people are often unaware of exposure
alt.ex: CO is colorless and odorless, so people often do not know they were exposed, and headache, dizziness, and nausea mimic other illnesses.
w: Its symptoms appear only years after the exposure has ended
CO symptoms such as headache, dizziness, and nausea occur with toxicity, not years later.
It causes no symptoms until the hemoglobin level reaches zero
CO causes headache, dizziness, nausea, vomiting, and dyspnea.
It has a strong odor that people quickly become used to
CO is odorless, which is why exposure goes unnoticed.

items.q: A patient with severe dehydration has a heart rate of 118 beats/min and cool extremities. The nurse recognizes these findings as which response?
items.a: The body’s attempt to return more blood to the heart and raise cardiac output
items.ex: With significant fluid loss, the body adapts through peripheral vasoconstriction and increased heart rate to increase cardiac output.
w: The body’s attempt to remove excess carbon dioxide produced by fever
Fever raises CO2 and breathing; this patient’s problem is fluid loss.
A sign that the patient’s oxygen-carrying capacity has increased
Hypovolemia causes tissue hypoxia; it does not increase carrying capacity.
A sign that the phrenic nerve has been damaged by dehydration
Phrenic nerve damage results from cervical trauma, not dehydration.

alt.q: A patient in shock has reduced circulating blood volume. Which effect on the tissues does the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: Hypoxia from decreased circulating blood volume
alt.ex: Hypovolemia from shock or severe dehydration reduces circulating blood volume, resulting in tissue hypoxia.
w: Polycythemia from increased red cell production
Polycythemia is an adaptation to chronic hypoxemia, not the immediate effect of hypovolemia.
Improved perfusion from peripheral vasodilation
The body responds with vasoconstriction, and perfusion is reduced.
Hypercapnia from increased surfactant production
Hypovolemia is not linked to surfactant or hypercapnia in the text.

items.q: A patient has an opiate overdose. Through which mechanism is the fraction of inspired oxygen (FiO2) reaching the alveoli decreased?
items.a: Hypoventilation
items.ex: Decreased FiO2 can result from hypoventilation, such as occurs in opiate overdoses.
w: Upper airway obstruction
Airway obstruction also lowers FiO2, but an opiate overdose does so through hypoventilation.
High altitude
High altitude lowers environmental oxygen; it is not the mechanism in an overdose.
Anemia
Anemia lowers hemoglobin, not the inspired oxygen concentration.

alt.q: A hiker becomes short of breath at a high altitude. Why is less oxygen reaching the hiker’s alveoli?
alt.a: The environmental oxygen is decreased
alt.ex: At high altitudes, decreased environmental oxygen lowers the inspired oxygen concentration.
w: The airway is obstructed by mucus
Airway obstruction is a different cause of decreased FiO2.
The hemoglobin is bound to carbon monoxide
CO binding reduces carrying capacity, not inspired oxygen concentration.
The respiratory center is depressed by opiates
Opiate depression causes hypoventilation, not the hiker’s problem.

items.q: An increased metabolic rate is normal during pregnancy, wound healing, and exercise, and most people can meet the extra oxygen demand.
items.a: True
items.ex: Most people meet the higher oxygen demand; oxygenation declines only when the cardiopulmonary systems cannot keep up.
items.ww: Increased metabolic rate in these states is normal and usually does not cause oxygen deprivation.

alt.q: Most healthy people with an increased metabolic rate from exercise or wound healing show signs of oxygen deprivation.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Most people can meet the increased oxygen demand and do not display signs of oxygen deprivation.
alt.ww: Oxygen deprivation appears only when cardiopulmonary systems are unable to meet the demand.

items.q: Why does a persistent fever increase a patient’s risk for hypoxemia?
items.a: Protein breakdown weakens respiratory muscles while CO2 production rises
items.ex: Persistent fever breaks down protein and wastes respiratory muscles while CO2 rises, increasing WOB until hypoxemia develops.
w: Fever lowers the metabolic rate and slows carbon dioxide production
Fever raises the metabolic rate and carbon dioxide production.
Fever thickens the alveolocapillary membrane and blocks diffusion
Membrane thickening is linked to edema, infiltrates, or effusion, not fever.
Fever causes the body to build muscle mass in the diaphragm
Persistent fever causes muscle wasting, including the diaphragm.

alt.q: A patient has had a fever for several days. Which patient is at greatest risk for hypoxemia from this fever?
alt.a: A patient who also has a chronic pulmonary disease
alt.ex: Patients with pulmonary diseases are at greater risk for hypoxemia when fever increases oxygen demand and CO2 production.
w: A patient who also has a healed ankle fracture
A healed fracture does not limit the cardiopulmonary response to fever.
A patient who also has well-controlled acne
Skin conditions do not impair the cardiopulmonary response to fever.
A patient who also has corrected nearsightedness
Vision problems do not affect the ability to meet oxygen demand.

items.q: A woman in the last trimester of pregnancy reports becoming short of breath when climbing stairs. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
items.a: “The growing uterus pushes up on your diaphragm, so you can’t take in as much air.”
items.ex: In the last trimester, the enlarging uterus pushes abdominal contents against the diaphragm, reducing inspiratory capacity and causing dyspnea on exertion.
w: “Pregnancy lowers your metabolic rate, so your body needs less oxygen.”
Pregnancy increases, not lowers, the metabolic rate.
“Pregnancy lowers your heart’s output, so less blood reaches your lungs.”
Cardiac output increases during pregnancy.
“Pregnancy makes your lungs produce extra surfactant, so they stiffen.”
Surfactant prevents alveolar collapse; it does not cause dyspnea in pregnancy.

alt.q: Which change in the last trimester of pregnancy leads to dyspnea on exertion and increased fatigue?
alt.a: Decreased inspiratory capacity
alt.ex: The enlarging uterus pushes against the diaphragm, so inspiratory capacity declines in the last trimester.
w: Increased lung compliance
Pressure on the diaphragm reduces, not increases, lung expansion.
Decreased metabolic rate
Pregnancy increases the metabolic rate.
Increased residual volume
The text attributes dyspnea to declining inspiratory capacity, not residual volume.

items.q: Which respiratory effects of morbid obesity should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced lung volumes, especially in the supine position
The heavy lower thorax and abdomen reduce lung volumes when recumbent or supine.
Obstructive sleep apnea
Reduced lung volumes in the recumbent position often cause obstructive sleep apnea.
Reduced lung and chest wall compliance
The abdomen encroaches on the chest, decreasing compliance.
Increased work of breathing
Morbid obesity increases WOB.
Better lung expansion when lying flat
Lung volumes are reduced, not improved, in the supine position.
items.ex: Morbid obesity reduces lung volumes and compliance, increases WOB, and often causes obstructive sleep apnea.

alt.q: Which statements about obesity-hypoventilation syndrome are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Oxygenation is decreased.
In this syndrome, oxygenation decreases.
Carbon dioxide is retained.
Hypoventilation causes carbon dioxide retention.
It develops in some patients with morbid obesity.
It develops in some morbidly obese patients.
It causes excessive removal of carbon dioxide.
Excess CO2 removal is hyperventilation; this syndrome retains CO2.
It increases lung and chest wall compliance.
Morbid obesity decreases compliance.
alt.ex: In obesity-hypoventilation syndrome, oxygenation decreases and carbon dioxide is retained.

items.q: A morbidly obese patient returns from abdominal surgery. The nurse recognizes this patient is at increased risk for which complication?
items.a: Atelectasis or pneumonia from incomplete lung expansion
items.ex: After surgery, obese patients’ lungs do not expand fully and lower lobes retain secretions, raising risk for atelectasis or pneumonia.
w: Polycythemia from reduced oxygen demand
Polycythemia responds to chronic hypoxemia; obesity does not reduce oxygen demand.
Increased lung compliance from abdominal pressure
Abdominal encroachment decreases compliance.
Hyperventilation from excess CO2 removal
Obesity is linked to hypoventilation and CO2 retention, not hyperventilation.

alt.q: Why is a patient with morbid obesity susceptible to pneumonia after surgery?
alt.a: The lungs do not expand fully, and the lower lobes retain secretions
alt.ex: Incomplete lung expansion with retained secretions in the lower lobes predisposes to atelectasis or pneumonia.
w: The lungs overexpand, and the upper lobes produce excess surfactant
Lungs in obesity are underexpanded, and surfactant is not the cited cause.
The heart rate slows, and cardiac output rises to abnormal levels
These cardiac changes are not the reason given for postoperative pneumonia.
The hemoglobin binds carbon monoxide, and oxygen transport stops
CO binding relates to carbon monoxide exposure, not obesity.

items.q: Which musculoskeletal abnormality affects the rib cage and can impair oxygenation?
items.a: Pectus excavatum
items.ex: Pectus excavatum is a structural abnormality of the rib cage that can reduce oxygenation.
w: Kyphosis
Kyphosis is an abnormality of the vertebral column, not the rib cage.
Scoliosis
Scoliosis is an abnormality of the vertebral column.
Lordosis
Lordosis is an abnormality of the vertebral column.

alt.q: Which group lists abnormal structural configurations of the vertebral column that can impair oxygenation?
alt.a: Kyphosis, lordosis, and scoliosis
alt.ex: Kyphosis, lordosis, and scoliosis are vertebral column abnormalities that impair oxygenation.
w: Pectus excavatum, flail chest, and rib fractures
These involve the rib cage or chest trauma, not the vertebral column.
Emphysema, asthma, and cystic fibrosis
These are pulmonary diseases, not vertebral abnormalities.
Myasthenia gravis, muscular dystrophy, and Guillain-Barré
These are neuromuscular diseases, not structural vertebral abnormalities.

items.q: Which statement accurately describes flail chest?
items.a: Multiple rib fractures cause chest wall instability, so the lung beneath contracts on inspiration and bulges on expiration
items.ex: In flail chest, instability from multiple rib fractures makes the injured area move paradoxically, resulting in hypoxia.
w: A single bruised rib causes the lung beneath it to expand more fully on inspiration and deflate on expiration
Flail chest involves multiple fractures, and the injured area moves paradoxically, not normally.
Air trapping in the alveoli increases the anteroposterior diameter of the chest wall over several years
This describes barrel chest from chronic lung disease, not flail chest.
Damage to the phrenic nerve keeps the diaphragm from descending properly during each inspiration
This describes cervical trauma at C3 to C5, not flail chest.

alt.q: A trauma patient has a section of chest wall that moves inward on inspiration and outward on expiration. Which condition does the nurse suspect?
alt.a: Flail chest
alt.ex: Multiple rib fractures create chest wall instability, so the lung under the injury contracts on inspiration and bulges on expiration.
w: Barrel chest
Barrel chest is an increased anteroposterior diameter from chronic lung disease.
Pectus excavatum
Pectus excavatum is a structural rib cage abnormality, not a traumatic instability.
Kyphosis
Kyphosis is a curvature of the vertebral column.

items.q: A patient who had upper abdominal surgery is receiving opioids for pain. Which assessment finding is most important for the nurse to report?
items.a: Respiratory rate of 8 breaths/min with shallow breaths
items.ex: Opioids depress the respiratory center, and shallow postoperative breathing further decreases chest wall movement and ventilation.
w: Pain rated 4 on a 0-to-10 scale when coughing
Some incisional pain with coughing is expected and less urgent than respiratory depression.
Oxygen saturation of 96% on room air
An SpO2 of 96% is within the normal range of 95% or higher.
Heart rate of 88 beats/min at rest
A heart rate of 88 is within normal limits.

alt.q: Why does a patient with a thoracic surgical incision often have reduced ventilation?
alt.a: The patient takes shallow breaths to avoid pain
alt.ex: Patients with thoracic or upper abdominal incisions breathe shallowly to avoid pain, which decreases chest wall movement.
w: The patient takes deep breaths to clear pain
Patients avoid deep breaths because they cause incisional pain.
The patient produces excess surfactant
Surgery is not linked to excess surfactant; pain-related shallow breathing is the cause.
The patient has an increased lung compliance
Pain causing shallow respirations, not compliance changes, reduces ventilation.

items.q: A patient has a cervical spinal cord injury at the C3 to C5 level. Which respiratory effect does the nurse anticipate?
items.a: Paralysis of the phrenic nerve, so the diaphragm does not descend properly
items.ex: Trauma at C3 to C5 usually paralyzes the phrenic nerve, reducing inspiratory volumes and causing hypoxemia.
w: Loss of the intercostal nerves, with the phrenic nerve left intact
This pattern occurs with injury below C5, not at C3 to C5.
Loss of the chemoreceptors that sense carbon dioxide in the blood
Chemoreceptors are in the medulla, aortic body, and carotid body, not the cervical cord.
Increased airway resistance from bronchoconstriction and mucus
Airway resistance is unrelated to cervical spinal cord trauma.

alt.q: A patient has a spinal cord injury below the C5 vertebra. Which respiratory effect is most likely?
alt.a: Intercostal muscle loss that prevents anteroposterior chest expansion
alt.ex: Injury below C5 usually spares the phrenic nerve but damages intercostal nerves, preventing anteroposterior chest expansion.
w: Phrenic nerve paralysis that prevents the diaphragm from descending
Phrenic paralysis is typical of C3 to C5 injury, not injury below C5.
Loss of the medulla’s neural regulation of ventilation
Medulla involvement causes abnormal breathing patterns; this injury is in the spinal cord.
Paradoxical chest wall motion from multiple rib fractures
Paradoxical motion is flail chest from rib fractures.

items.q: Neuromuscular diseases such as myasthenia gravis and Guillain-Barré syndrome can cause hypoventilation by decreasing the ability to expand and contract the chest wall.
items.a: True
items.ex: Neuromuscular diseases impair chest wall movement, leading to atelectasis, hypercapnia, and hypoxemia.
items.ww: These diseases are named examples of conditions that cause hypoventilation.

alt.q: Neuromuscular diseases such as myasthenia gravis reduce oxygenation mainly by lowering the blood’s hemoglobin level.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Neuromuscular diseases reduce oxygenation by decreasing the ability to expand and contract the chest wall.
alt.ww: Low hemoglobin is the mechanism of anemia, not of neuromuscular disease.

items.q: A barrel chest in COPD or cystic fibrosis results from overuse of accessory muscles and air trapping.
items.a: True
items.ex: Overuse of accessory muscles and air trapping change the anteroposterior diameter of the chest wall, producing a barrel chest.
items.ww: The barrel chest is linked to accessory muscle overuse and air trapping in chronic lung disease.

alt.q: A barrel chest in COPD results mainly from multiple rib fractures that make the chest wall unstable.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Barrel chest results from accessory muscle overuse and air trapping; unstable rib fractures cause flail chest.
alt.ww: Chest wall instability from multiple rib fractures is flail chest, not barrel chest.

items.q: Which are the three primary alterations in respiratory functioning? Select all that apply.
o: Hypoventilation
Hypoventilation is one of the three primary alterations.
Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation is one of the three primary alterations.
Hypoxia
Hypoxia is one of the three primary alterations.
Hypovolemia
Hypovolemia is reduced circulating blood volume, a circulatory problem.
Polycythemia
Polycythemia is an adaptive increase in red cells to chronic hypoxemia.
items.ex: The three primary alterations in respiratory functioning are hypoventilation, hyperventilation, and hypoxia.

alt.q: Illnesses that affect ventilation or oxygen transport produce which primary respiratory alterations? Select all that apply.
o: Inadequate alveolar ventilation with CO2 retention
This describes hypoventilation.
Removal of CO2 faster than it is produced
This describes hyperventilation.
Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level
This describes hypoxia.
Increased red blood cell production
This is polycythemia, an adaptation, not a primary alteration.
Decreased circulating blood volume
This is hypovolemia, a circulatory problem.
alt.ex: Hypoventilation, hyperventilation, and hypoxia are the three primary alterations in respiratory functioning.

items.q: The goal of ventilation is a normal arterial carbon dioxide tension (PaCO2) of [[35 to 45|35-45|35 and 45]] mm Hg.
items.ex: A normal PaCO2 is 35 to 45 mm Hg; ventilation aims to keep CO2 in this range.

alt.q: Hypoventilation and hyperventilation move the PaCO2 outside its normal range of [[35 to 45|35-45|35 and 45]] mm Hg.
alt.ex: A normal PaCO2 is 35 to 45 mm Hg; ventilation aims to keep CO2 in this range.

items.q: What is the normal arterial oxygen tension (PaO2)?
items.a: 80 to 100 mm Hg
items.ex: The goal of ventilation is a normal PaO2 between 80 and 100 mm Hg.
w: 35 to 45 mm Hg
35 to 45 mm Hg is the normal PaCO2, not PaO2.
60 to 70 mm Hg
A PaO2 near 60 mm Hg is the level that stimulates the hypoxic drive in COPD, not normal.
100 to 120 mm Hg
The normal PaO2 range is 80 to 100 mm Hg.

alt.q: What is the normal arterial oxygen saturation (SpO2) measured by pulse oximetry?
alt.a: 95% or higher
alt.ex: Normal SpO2, monitored noninvasively with a pulse oximeter, is greater than or equal to 95%.
w: 85% or higher
An SpO2 below 95% is below the normal value.
90% or higher
The normal SpO2 is 95% or higher, not 90%.
75% or higher
This is far below the normal SpO2 of 95% or higher.

items.q: What does Hypoventilation mean?
items.a: Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide
items.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.
w: Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it
That goes with Hyperventilation.
Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level
That goes with Hypoxia.
Decrease in the amount of arterial oxygen
That goes with Hypoxemia.

alt.q: What does Hyperventilation mean?
alt.a: Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it
alt.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.
w: Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide
That goes with Hypoventilation.
Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level
That goes with Hypoxia.
Decrease in the amount of arterial oxygen
That goes with Hypoxemia.

alt.q: What does Hypoxia mean?
alt.a: Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level
alt.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.
w: Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide
That goes with Hypoventilation.
Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it
That goes with Hyperventilation.
Decrease in the amount of arterial oxygen
That goes with Hypoxemia.

alt.q: What does Hypoxemia mean?
alt.a: Decrease in the amount of arterial oxygen
alt.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.
w: Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide
That goes with Hypoventilation.
Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it
That goes with Hyperventilation.
Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level
That goes with Hypoxia.

alt.q: What does Cyanosis mean?
alt.a: Blue discoloration from desaturated hemoglobin in the capillaries
alt.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.
w: Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide
That goes with Hypoventilation.
Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it
That goes with Hyperventilation.
Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level
That goes with Hypoxia.

alt.q: Which term means “Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide”?
alt.a: Hypoventilation
alt.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.
w: Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation: Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it.
Hypoxia
Hypoxia: Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level.
Hypoxemia
Hypoxemia: Decrease in the amount of arterial oxygen.

alt.q: Which term means “Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it”?
alt.a: Hyperventilation
alt.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.
w: Hypoventilation
Hypoventilation: Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide.
Hypoxia
Hypoxia: Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level.
Hypoxemia
Hypoxemia: Decrease in the amount of arterial oxygen.

alt.q: Which term means “Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level”?
alt.a: Hypoxia
alt.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.
w: Hypoventilation
Hypoventilation: Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide.
Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation: Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it.
Hypoxemia
Hypoxemia: Decrease in the amount of arterial oxygen.

alt.q: Which term means “Decrease in the amount of arterial oxygen”?
alt.a: Hypoxemia
alt.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.
w: Hypoventilation
Hypoventilation: Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide.
Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation: Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it.
Hypoxia
Hypoxia: Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level.

alt.q: Which term means “Blue discoloration from desaturated hemoglobin in the capillaries”?
alt.a: Cyanosis
alt.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.
w: Hypoventilation
Hypoventilation: Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide.
Hyperventilation
Hyperventilation: Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it.
Hypoxia
Hypoxia: Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level.

mt.q: Match each term with its definition.
pairs: Alveolar ventilation inadequate to meet oxygen demand or eliminate carbon dioxide
Lungs remove carbon dioxide faster than cellular metabolism produces it
Inadequate tissue oxygenation at the cellular level
Decrease in the amount of arterial oxygen
Blue discoloration from desaturated hemoglobin in the capillaries
mt.ex: These terms describe alterations in ventilation and oxygenation that nurses assess for.

items.q: As alveolar ventilation decreases in hypoventilation, what happens to carbon dioxide?
items.a: It is retained in the body
items.ex: Hypoventilation means alveolar ventilation is inadequate, so the body retains carbon dioxide.
w: It is exhaled faster than it is produced
Exhaling CO2 faster than it is produced is hyperventilation.
It is converted into oxyhemoglobin
Oxyhemoglobin forms from hemoglobin and oxygen, not carbon dioxide.
It is unaffected by the change
Reduced alveolar ventilation directly causes CO2 retention.

alt.q: A patient has increasing atelectasis. Why does this lead to hypoventilation?
alt.a: As more alveoli collapse, less of the lung is ventilated
alt.ex: Atelectasis collapses alveoli, preventing gas exchange; as more collapse, less lung is ventilated and hypoventilation occurs.
w: As more alveoli collapse, more surfactant is produced
Atelectasis is linked to decreased, not increased, surfactant.
As more alveoli collapse, compliance greatly increases
Collapsed alveoli do not increase compliance or ventilation.
As more alveoli collapse, CO2 is removed more quickly
Collapsed alveoli reduce ventilation, so CO2 is retained.

items.q: A patient with COPD has been receiving oxygen at a high flow rate and becomes drowsy and confused with slow, shallow respirations. The nurse recognizes this is most likely caused by which problem?
items.a: Loss of the hypoxic drive to breathe, causing carbon dioxide retention
items.ex: In COPD, excess oxygen keeps PaO2 above the level that stimulates breathing, causing hypoventilation and CO2 retention.
w: Hyperventilation from anxiety, causing excess carbon dioxide loss
Slow, shallow breathing with drowsiness reflects hypoventilation, not hyperventilation.
Carbon monoxide binding to hemoglobin, causing a functional anemia
CO toxicity results from exposure to carbon monoxide, not high-flow oxygen.
Increased surfactant from oxygen, causing alveolar collapse
Surfactant prevents alveolar collapse; oxygen is not described as increasing it.

alt.q: For a patient with COPD who relies on a hypoxic drive to breathe, administering oxygen above which concentration can cause hypoventilation?
alt.a: 24% to 28% (1 to 3 L/min)
alt.ex: Oxygen above 24% to 28% (1 to 3 L/min) can prevent PaO2 from falling to the level that stimulates breathing.
w: 50% to 60% (8 to 10 L/min)
The risk begins at a much lower concentration, above 24% to 28%.
35% to 40% (5 to 6 L/min)
The text sets the threshold lower, above 24% to 28% (1 to 3 L/min).
Hypoventilation can occur at far lower concentrations, above 24% to 28%.

items.q: In a patient with COPD who has adapted to high carbon dioxide levels, which PaO2 level stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors to increase ventilation?
items.a: 60 mm Hg
items.ex: In COPD, the stimulus to breathe is a PaO2 falling to about 60 mm Hg, which stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors.
w: 100 mm Hg
100 mm Hg is the top of the normal PaO2 range and would not trigger the hypoxic drive.
80 mm Hg
80 mm Hg is the low end of normal PaO2, not the hypoxic drive trigger.
45 mm Hg
45 mm Hg is the upper limit of normal PaCO2, not the PaO2 trigger.

alt.q: In a patient with COPD, the peripheral chemoreceptors that drive breathing are located where?
alt.a: Aortic arch and carotid bodies
alt.ex: The peripheral chemoreceptors of the aortic arch and carotid bodies are primarily sensitive to low oxygen in COPD.
w: Cerebral cortex and spinal cord
The cerebral cortex controls voluntary breathing; it is not the peripheral chemoreceptor site.
Alveoli and pulmonary capillaries
These are gas exchange sites, not chemoreceptor locations.
SA node and AV node
These are parts of the cardiac conduction system.

items.q: Which signs and symptoms are associated with hypoventilation? Select all that apply.
o: Mental status changes
CO2 retention in hypoventilation causes mental status changes.
Dysrhythmias
Hypoventilation can cause dysrhythmias.
Potential cardiac arrest
Untreated hypoventilation can lead to cardiac arrest.
Numbness and tingling of the hands and feet
Numbness and tingling are signs of hyperventilation.
Sighing breaths
Sighing breaths are a sign of hyperventilation.
items.ex: Hypoventilation causes mental status changes, dysrhythmias, and potential cardiac arrest; untreated, it leads to convulsions and death.

alt.q: If hypoventilation is left untreated, which outcomes can occur? Select all that apply.
o: Convulsions
Untreated hypoventilation can progress to convulsions.
Unconsciousness
Rapid decline leads to unconsciousness.
Death
Untreated hypoventilation can be fatal.
Respiratory alkalosis
Hypoventilation retains CO2, which leads to respiratory acidosis, not alkalosis.
Polycythemia within minutes
Polycythemia is a chronic adaptation, not an acute outcome of hypoventilation.
alt.ex: Untreated hypoventilation causes rapid decline with convulsions, unconsciousness, and death.

items.q: Which signs and symptoms are associated with hyperventilation? Select all that apply.
o: Rapid respirations
Hyperventilation involves an increased rate of breathing.
Sighing breaths
Sighing breaths are a sign of hyperventilation.
Numbness and tingling of the hands and feet
Excess CO2 loss causes numbness and tingling of extremities.
Light-headedness
Light-headedness occurs with hyperventilation.
Slow, shallow respirations
Slow, shallow breathing describes hypoventilation.
Retention of carbon dioxide
CO2 retention occurs in hypoventilation; hyperventilation removes excess CO2.
items.ex: Hyperventilation causes rapid respirations, sighing breaths, numbness and tingling, light-headedness, and possibly loss of consciousness.

alt.q: Which conditions can induce hyperventilation? Select all that apply.
o: Severe anxiety
Acute anxiety leads to exhalation of excessive carbon dioxide.
Salicylate (aspirin) poisoning
Salicylate poisoning produces excess CO2, stimulating faster, deeper breathing.
Diabetic ketoacidosis
The body overbreathes to compensate for metabolic acidosis.
Fever
Fever increases metabolic rate and CO2 production, increasing rate and depth of breathing.
Opiate overdose
Opiate overdose causes hypoventilation.
Excess oxygen in a patient with COPD
Excess oxygen in COPD causes hypoventilation.
alt.ex: Severe anxiety, infection, fever, drugs such as salicylates and amphetamines, and metabolic acidosis can induce hyperventilation.

items.q: A patient in diabetic ketoacidosis has deep, rapid respirations. What is the purpose of this breathing pattern?
items.a: To reduce the carbon dioxide available to form carbonic acid
items.ex: The respiratory system overbreathes to compensate for metabolic acidosis by reducing CO2 available to form carbonic acid.
w: To increase the carbon dioxide available to form bicarbonate
Overbreathing lowers, not raises, carbon dioxide levels.
To raise the PaO2 to the level that stimulates the hypoxic drive
The hypoxic drive applies to COPD, not compensation for ketoacidosis.
To slow the metabolic rate and lower ketone production
Overbreathing corrects acid-base balance; it does not slow metabolism.

alt.q: A patient with salicylate (aspirin) poisoning is hyperventilating. Which mechanism explains this?
alt.a: Excess carbon dioxide production stimulates the respiratory center
alt.ex: Salicylate poisoning and amphetamine use cause excess CO2 production, and the respiratory center compensates with faster, deeper breathing.
w: Decreased carbon dioxide production depresses the respiratory center
Salicylates increase CO2 production and stimulate, not depress, breathing.
Carbon monoxide binds hemoglobin and blocks oxygen transport
This describes CO poisoning, not salicylate toxicity.
Phrenic nerve damage keeps the diaphragm from descending
Phrenic nerve damage results from C3 to C5 trauma.
