sections.name: Skill 41.3 · Care of patients with chest tubes

items.q: Which task can the nurse assign to assistive personnel caring for a patient with a chest tube?
items.a: Helping the patient ambulate with the drainage system in place
items.ex: Managing chest tubes cannot be delegated, but AP can ambulate, reposition, and transfer patients with the system.
w: Adjusting the suction-control dial to the prescribed level
Setting suction is part of chest tube management, which cannot be delegated.
Evaluating the tubing for an air leak by clamping it
Locating an air leak requires nursing assessment and judgment.
Milking the tubing when a clot is visible
Milking is done only by the nurse and only when a clot risks harm.

alt.q: Which instruction should the nurse give to assistive personnel caring for a patient with a chest tube?
alt.a: Report sudden shortness of breath or excessive bubbling in the water seal right away
alt.ex: AP must immediately report vital sign changes, chest pain, sudden dyspnea, or excessive water-seal bubbling.
w: Clamp the chest tube whenever the patient walks in the hallway
Hemostats go with the patient but the tube is not clamped for ambulation.
Raise the drainage system to chest level when moving the patient
The system must stay upright and below the chest to prevent backflow.
Empty the drainage chamber at the end of each shift
Drainage is measured by marking levels, and management stays with the nurse.

items.q: A nurse notes vigorous bubbling in the suction-control chamber of a patient’s water-seal chest drainage system. Which action is appropriate?
items.a: Turn down the suction source until bubbling is gentle and continuous
items.ex: Vigorous bubbling does not add suction to the chest; it only evaporates water faster, so gentle bubbling is the goal.
w: Leave the suction as set because more bubbling means better lung expansion
Increased bubbling does not increase suction to the pleural space.
Clamp the chest tube near the chest wall to stop the bubbling
Clamping is for specific situations such as locating an air leak, not suction-control bubbling.
Add sterile water to the water-seal chamber to quiet the bubbling
The water-seal chamber is separate; suction-control bubbling is set by the suction source.

alt.q: In a three-chamber water-seal system, what determines the highest negative pressure that can be applied to the pleural space?
alt.a: The depth of fluid in the suction-control chamber
alt.ex: The fluid level in the suction-control chamber dictates the maximum negative pressure; 20 cm of water is about −20 cm H2O.
w: The vigor of bubbling in the suction-control chamber
Stronger bubbling only evaporates water faster and does not add suction.
The amount of drainage in the collection chamber
Drainage volume reflects fluid output, not the suction limit.
The height of the system below the patient’s chest
Position below the chest promotes gravity drainage, not suction pressure.

items.q: A dry suction chest drainage system is being set up. Within what range does the suction-control dial typically deliver suction?
items.a: −10 to −40 cm of water pressure
items.ex: Dry suction systems are adjusted by dial to the prescribed level, which ranges from −10 to −40 cm of water.
w: −50 to −80 cm of water pressure
This exceeds the range of a dry suction-control dial and risks lung tissue damage.
−1 to −5 cm of water pressure
This is below the range used to evacuate air and fluid from the pleural space.
+10 to +40 cm of water pressure
Chest drainage uses negative pressure; positive pressure would push air into the chest.

alt.q: What is the function of the automatic control valve on a dry suction-control device?
alt.a: It adjusts to air leaks and suction-source changes to deliver prescribed suction
alt.ex: The valve compensates for patient air leaks and suction fluctuations to keep suction at the prescribed level.
w: It acts as the one-way valve that lets air escape from the pleural space
The water-seal chamber, not the suction-control valve, acts as the one-way valve.
It collects drainage from the pleural space for measurement
Drainage collects in the collection chamber.
It replaces the need to fill the water-seal chamber with sterile solution
The water-seal chamber of a dry suction system is still filled with sterile solution.

items.q: A nurse notes that the fluid in the water-seal chamber of a patient with a chest tube no longer rises and falls with breathing. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Check the tubing for kinks, dependent loops, or clots
items.ex: Tidaling stops when the lung is fully expanded or the system is obstructed, so the nurse first rules out obstruction.
w: Increase the suction to restart the fluctuation
More suction does not correct an obstruction and can harm pleural tissue.
Prepare the patient for removal of the chest tube
Lung reexpansion is only one cause; obstruction must be excluded first.
Clamp the chest tube and observe for one hour
Clamping is limited to specific purposes and does not treat absent tidaling.

alt.q: Which two conditions can cause fluctuation (tidaling) in the water-seal chamber to stop?
alt.a: Full lung reexpansion or an obstruction in the drainage system
alt.ex: Tidaling stops when the lung has fully reexpanded or when the system is obstructed.
w: An upright drainage unit or securely taped connections
These are signs of a correctly maintained system, not causes of absent tidaling.
Intermittent bubbling or straw-colored drainage
Intermittent expiratory bubbling and straw-colored drainage are expected findings.
Mechanical ventilation or deep breathing exercises
Ventilated patients still tidal, though in the opposite pattern.

items.q: To locate an air leak, the nurse clamps a patient’s chest tube close to the chest wall, and the bubbling in the water-seal chamber stops. What should the nurse conclude?
items.a: The leak is inside the thorax or at the insertion site; notify the provider
items.ex: If bubbling stops with clamps at the chest wall, the leak is in the patient or at the insertion site and the provider is notified.
w: The leak is in the drainage system, which should be replaced
A leak in the drainage system continues bubbling until clamps are near the unit.
The leak is in the tubing between the patient and the chamber
A tubing leak stops bubbling only when the clamps bracket that tubing section.
There is no leak, and the clamps can be left in place
Stopping of bubbling localizes the leak; the clamps are not left on the tube.

alt.q: A patient with a pneumothorax has intermittent bubbling in the water-seal chamber only during expiration. How should the nurse interpret this?
alt.a: It is expected as air is evacuated from the pleural cavity
alt.ex: Intermittent bubbling on expiration is normal; continuous bubbling on inspiration and expiration indicates a leak.
w: It indicates a leak at one of the tubing connections
A leak produces continuous bubbling during both inspiration and expiration.
It means the lung has fully reexpanded
An absence of bubbling, not intermittent bubbling, may indicate full reexpansion.
It means the suction-control chamber needs more water
Water-seal bubbling reflects air leaving the pleura, not suction-control water level.

items.q: A patient’s chest tube becomes disconnected from the drainage system while the patient is turning. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Submerge the distal end of the tube 2 to 4 cm in sterile water
items.ex: Placing the tube end 2 to 4 cm below the surface of a 250-mL bottle of sterile water or NS creates a temporary water seal.
w: Leave the tube end open to air until a new unit arrives
An open tube lets atmospheric air enter the pleural space.
Place the tube end 15 to 20 cm below the water surface
The distal end is submerged only 2 to 4 cm below the surface of sterile water or NS.
Wrap the tube end in dry gauze for 2 to 4 hours
Dry gauze does not create a seal and air can still enter the chest.

alt.q: A patient’s chest tube is accidentally pulled out of the chest. Which action should the nurse take?
alt.a: Apply pressure over the site, then a petroleum gauze dressing as the patient exhales
alt.ex: Immediate pressure and a sealed petroleum gauze dressing applied on exhalation limit air entry; then the provider is notified.
w: Reinsert the tube into the insertion site using sterile technique
Inserting chest tubes is done by the health care provider, not the nurse.
Cover the site with dry gauze taped loosely on all four sides
A petroleum gauze dressing with a tight seal is needed to keep air out.
Place the patient flat and wait for the chest x-ray results
The site must be sealed immediately; waiting allows air to enter the chest.

items.q: Four hours after thoracic surgery, which chest tube drainage finding is most important for the nurse to report to the health care provider?
items.a: 250 mL of bloody drainage from a posterior chest tube in the past hour
items.ex: More than 200 mL of bloody drainage per hour from a posterior tube indicates possible hemorrhage.
w: A sudden gush of dark blood from a posterior tube after the patient turned
A gush with position change is often pooled old blood, not active bleeding.
Little or no output from an anterior tube placed for a pneumothorax
An anterior tube for a pneumothorax drains air, so little fluid output is expected.
40 mL of drainage from a mediastinal tube in the past hour
Less than 100 mL per hour from a mediastinal tube is expected after surgery.

alt.q: A patient has a mediastinal chest tube after cardiac surgery. Which drainage pattern does the nurse expect?
alt.a: Less than 100 mL per hour, and no more than 500 mL in the first 24 hours
alt.ex: Mediastinal tubes drain less than 100 mL/h early on and no more than 500 mL in the first 24 hours.
w: 200 to 300 mL per hour, and about 1000 mL in the first 24 hours
Bloody drainage over 100 to 200 mL per hour suggests hemorrhage and must be reported.
No drainage at all during the first 24 hours after surgery
Some drainage is expected; no drainage may signal obstruction.
Bright red drainage that increases in amount each hour
Drainage should decrease gradually; increasing bright red output suggests bleeding.

items.q: A patient has just had a chest tube inserted to drain a hemothorax. In which position should the nurse place the patient to promote drainage?
items.a: High Fowler position
items.ex: After tube placement, high Fowler position is used to drain fluid from a hemothorax.
w: Trendelenburg position
A head-down position would not promote gravity drainage of fluid from the pleural space.
Prone position
Lying prone would compress the tube and does not promote fluid drainage.
Flat supine position
A flat position does not use gravity to drain fluid from the lower chest.

alt.q: After a chest tube is placed to evacuate air from a pneumothorax, which position promotes optimal drainage?
alt.a: Semi-Fowler or high Fowler position
alt.ex: Semi-Fowler or high Fowler position is used after placement to evacuate air from a pneumothorax.
w: Trendelenburg or reverse Trendelenburg position
Head-down positions do not promote air evacuation or lung expansion.
Prone or lateral position on the tube side
Lying on the tube can compress it and impede drainage.
Flat supine position with legs elevated
A flat position does not facilitate lung expansion or chest tube drainage.

items.q: Two rubber-tipped hemostats are kept at the bedside of a patient with a chest tube. For which purpose is double clamping of the chest tube appropriate?
items.a: To assess whether the patient is ready to have the tube removed
items.ex: Clamping is limited to assessing for air leaks, changing systems, testing readiness for removal, or accidental disconnection.
w: To prevent backflow whenever the patient ambulates
Hemostats go with the patient, but keeping the system below the chest prevents backflow.
To stop continuous gentle bubbling in the suction-control chamber
Gentle continuous bubbling in the suction-control chamber is expected.
To reduce drainage when the output exceeds 200 mL in an hour
Excess bloody drainage is reported to the provider, not stopped by clamping.

alt.q: Where should the nurse keep the rubber-tipped hemostats for a patient with a chest tube?
alt.a: In an easily accessible spot that goes with the patient when ambulating
alt.ex: Two hemostats per tube are kept accessible, such as taped to the headboard, and stay with the patient when walking.
w: Locked in the medication room until the provider orders clamping
Hemostats must be immediately available in case of disconnection.
Clamped on the tubing at all times as a safety precaution
Routine clamping would block drainage and risk tension pneumothorax.
In the supply room, since clamping is only done during removal
Clamping has several purposes, including accidental disconnection, so they stay nearby.

items.q: Before connecting a newly inserted chest tube to a drainage system, why does the nurse turn off the suction source?
items.a: Sudden negative pressure on connection could damage the pleural tissues
items.ex: Suction is turned back on after connection to avoid a sudden increase in negative pressure on the pleura.
w: Suction would draw sterile water out of the water-seal chamber
The concern is pleural injury, not loss of water-seal fluid.
Suction must be off for the health care provider to order a chest x-ray
The x-ray verifies tube placement and is unrelated to suction during connection.
Suction prevents the drainage tubing from being taped securely
Connections are taped or zip-tied regardless of whether suction is on.

alt.q: While setting up a chest drainage system before insertion, the nurse clamps the drainage tubing, connects to suction, and turns suction on. What is the purpose of these steps?
alt.a: To verify the system is airtight and patent before connection
alt.ex: Checking the system before connecting the patient ensures it is airtight and prevents air from leaking into the pleural space.
w: To pre-fill the pleural space with negative pressure
The patient is not yet connected; suction is turned off before connection.
To measure how much drainage the system can hold
Collection chamber capacity is not tested this way.
To remove sterile water from the suction-control chamber
Fluid in the suction-control chamber sets the suction limit and is not removed.

items.q: A chest tube was inserted 30 minutes ago. How often should the nurse assess the patient’s vital signs, breath sounds, insertion site, and drainage at this time?
items.a: Every 15 minutes for the first 2 hours
items.ex: Frequent checks in the first 2 hours detect early complications such as respiratory distress, leakage, or bleeding.
w: Every 1 hour for the first 8 hours
Hourly checks are too infrequent to detect early procedure-related complications.
Every 4 hours for the first 24 hours
Assessments begin every 15 minutes, then continue at least every shift.
Once at the end of the shift
Waiting until shift end could miss hemorrhage or tension pneumothorax.

alt.q: A patient has had a chest tube for several hours. How should the expected character of the drainage change over time?
alt.a: It decreases gradually and changes from bloody to pink to straw colored
alt.ex: Drainage should gradually decrease and progress from bloody to pink to straw colored.
w: It increases gradually and changes from straw colored to bright red
Increasing bloody drainage suggests hemorrhage, not expected healing.
It stays the same amount and remains dark red throughout
Drainage is expected to decrease and lighten in color over time.
It stops abruptly and changes from serous to cloudy
Abrupt cessation may mean obstruction, and cloudy drainage is not the expected pattern.

items.q: A patient is being assessed before chest tube insertion. Which findings indicate increased respiratory distress and hypoxia? Select all that apply.
o: Asymmetrical chest movement
Uneven chest movement reflects a collapsed or compressed lung.
Displaced trachea
Tracheal shift indicates rising pressure in the chest, as in tension pneumothorax.
New confusion
Confusion is a sign of inadequate oxygen to the brain.
Marked cyanosis
Cyanosis indicates poor tissue oxygenation.
Equal breath sounds over both lungs
Distress causes decreased breath sounds over affected and unaffected lungs.
Slowed heart rate with rising blood pressure
Tension pneumothorax causes tachycardia and hypotension, not bradycardia and hypertension.
items.ex: Decreased breath sounds, cyanosis, asymmetrical chest movement, tracheal displacement, dyspnea, and confusion indicate distress and hypoxia.

alt.q: A patient with a chest tube develops sharp, stabbing chest pain. Which additional findings would suggest a tension pneumothorax? Select all that apply.
o: Hypotension
A drop in blood pressure accompanies tension pneumothorax.
Tachycardia
Increased heart rate accompanies tension pneumothorax.
Mediastinal shift
Mediastinal shift is a critical sign of a severe change such as tension pneumothorax.
Gradual change of drainage from pink to straw colored
This is the expected progression of chest tube drainage.
Intermittent bubbling in the water seal on expiration
Intermittent expiratory bubbling is normal as air leaves the pleura.
alt.ex: Sharp chest pain with hypotension, tachycardia, and mediastinal shift indicates a tension pneumothorax.

items.q: Which actions help maintain a patent, freely draining chest tube system? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the drainage system upright and below the level of the chest
This promotes gravity drainage and prevents backflow into the pleural space.
Coil excess tubing horizontally on the mattress without dependent loops
Dependent loops collect drainage and can cause tension pneumothorax.
Lift the tubing every 15 minutes if looping cannot be avoided
Lifting helps gravity move drainage when looping is unavoidable.
Keep the water-seal and suction-control vents unoccluded
Open vents let displaced air and excess negative pressure escape.
Strip the tubing every hour to prevent clots
Routine stripping raises intrathoracic pressure and can damage lungs and pleura.
Let excess tubing hang over the edge of the bed
Hanging tubing forms a dependent loop that can occlude drainage.
items.ex: An upright system below the chest, no dependent loops, open vents, and lifting looped tubing keep drainage flowing.

alt.q: A nurse reviews care for a patient with a chest tube after trauma. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Tape all connections in a double-spiral pattern or use zip ties
Secured connections prevent air from leaking into the system and pleural space.
Hang the tubing in a straight line from chest tube to chamber
A straight line promotes drainage and prevents accumulation in the pleural cavity.
Lift the drain frequently when drainage is heavy
Gentle lifting lets gravity move blood and viscous material to the chamber.
Place the drainage unit on the bed beside the patient’s chest
The unit must stay below chest level to prevent backflow.
Cover the suction-control vent to prevent fluid evaporation
Vents must not be occluded so excess negative pressure can escape.
alt.ex: Secured connections, straight tubing, frequent lifting with heavy drainage, and a unit below the chest support drainage.

items.q: A patient with a chest tube suddenly develops respiratory distress, chest pain, hypotension, and tachycardia. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Notify the health care provider immediately
These are critical signs of severe change such as tension pneumothorax or hemorrhage.
Obtain a set of vital signs and SpO2
Current vital signs and SpO2 guide treatment of the change in status.
Provide oxygen as ordered
Oxygen supports tissue oxygenation during distress.
Elevate the head of the bed to 45 degrees
Head elevation to 45 degrees eases breathing during distress.
Clamp the chest tube until the provider arrives
Clamping can trap air and worsen a tension pneumothorax.
Lower the head of the bed flat to raise blood pressure
A flat position impairs lung expansion; the head of bed is elevated 45 degrees.
items.ex: For critical changes, notify the provider, obtain VS and SpO2, give oxygen, elevate the head of bed 45 degrees, and prepare for x-ray.

alt.q: A patient with a chest tube has new subcutaneous emphysema at the neck, decreased breath sounds, and marked cyanosis. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Prepare for a chest x-ray
An x-ray helps evaluate lung status and tube position.
Notify the health care provider immediately
These are critical findings indicating a severe change in status.
Collect vital signs and SpO2
Vital signs and SpO2 document the patient’s current status.
Wait 1 hour and reassess before calling
Critical findings require immediate notification, not delayed reassessment.
Milk the tubing vigorously along its full length
Routine milking raises intrathoracic pressure and is not a response to distress.
alt.ex: Critical distress findings require immediate notification, vital signs and SpO2, oxygen, head elevation, and preparation for x-ray.

items.q: Routine stripping or milking of chest tubes is recommended to keep the tubing free of clots.
items.a: False
items.ex: Routine stripping raises intrathoracic pressure and can damage lungs or pleura; gentle milking is reserved for a harmful visible clot.
items.ww: Routine stripping is not recommended practice because of the pressure it creates.

alt.q: Gentle milking of chest tubing may be indicated only when a visible clot puts the patient at risk of further harm.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Milking is reserved for visible clots that threaten harm, such as tension pneumothorax.
alt.ww: Milking is not routine because it can increase pressure and injure lung or pleural tissue.

items.q: In a patient who is breathing spontaneously, fluid in the water-seal chamber rises with inspiration and falls with expiration.
items.a: True
items.ex: This tidaling pattern shows the system is functioning; the pattern reverses with mechanical ventilation.
items.ww: The rise-on-inspiration pattern is the expected finding in spontaneous breathing.

alt.q: In a patient receiving mechanical ventilation, fluid in the water-seal chamber rises with inspiration and falls with expiration.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: With mechanical ventilation, tidaling is the opposite of spontaneous breathing.
alt.ww: Rise on inspiration describes spontaneous breathing, not positive-pressure ventilation.

items.q: A sudden flow of dark bloody drainage after a patient changes position usually indicates active hemorrhage.
items.a: False
items.ex: A sudden gush of dark blood with position change is often old pooled blood rather than active bleeding.
items.ww: Active hemorrhage is suggested by sustained hourly bloody output above set limits, not a gush with turning.

alt.q: A sudden flow of dark bloody drainage after a patient changes position is often old blood that had pooled in the chest.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Coughing or repositioning can release collected blood, so a gush of dark drainage is often old blood.
alt.ww: Active hemorrhage shows as large, continuing hourly volumes of bloody drainage, not a single gush.

items.q: A crackling sensation felt when palpating around a chest tube insertion site is called [[crepitus]] and indicates subcutaneous emphysema.
items.ex: Crepitus reflects air trapped under the skin; small amounts are absorbed, but large amounts must be reported.

alt.q: Air trapped in the subcutaneous tissue around a chest tube produces [[crepitus|crackling]] on palpation.
alt.ex: Crepitus reflects air trapped under the skin; small amounts are absorbed, but large amounts must be reported.

items.q: In chest tube insertion and connection, which step comes right after “Tape connections and check the system for patency with suction”?
items.a: Turn off suction and unclamp the drainage tubing
items.ex: That's step 4 of 7. The system is prepared and tested, suction is turned off, the tube is inserted and connected, then suction resumes and connections are secured.
w: Assist the provider with insertion of the chest tube
That's step 5 of 7.
Set up the drainage system and add sterile solution
That's step 2 of 7.
Help attach the drainage tube to the chest tube and turn on suction
That's step 6 of 7.

items: Review the order, confirm consent, and complete a Time Out
Set up the drainage system and add sterile solution
Tape connections and check the system for patency with suction
Turn off suction and unclamp the drainage tubing
Assist the provider with insertion of the chest tube
Help attach the drainage tube to the chest tube and turn on suction
Tape or zip-tie all connections between the chest tube and drainage tube
ord.ex: The system is prepared and tested, suction is turned off, the tube is inserted and connected, then suction resumes and connections are secured.

items.q: What is the function of the Collection chamber?
items.a: Receives fluid draining from the pleural space
items.ex: Fluid drains to the first chamber, the water seal blocks air reentry, and suction control limits negative pressure.
w: Acts as a one-way valve so air cannot reenter the pleura
That goes with Water-seal chamber.
Its fluid depth sets the maximum negative pressure
That goes with Suction-control chamber.
Lets air escape on a dry suction system
That goes with Positive-pressure relief valve.

items.q: Which task related to home oxygen therapy may the nurse delegate to assistive personnel?
items.a: Informing the nurse of concerns about oxygen use or storage
items.ex: Teaching home oxygen use cannot be delegated, but AP report concerns about oxygen use or storage.
w: Teaching the family to refill the portable liquid oxygen tank
Teaching patients and families about home oxygen cannot be delegated to AP.
Changing the prescribed oxygen flow rate as symptoms change
Flow rate is set by order and is not changed by AP or the patient.
Assessing the home for fire, trip, and fall hazards
Risk assessment of the home is a nursing assessment responsibility.

alt.q: A home health aide visits a patient who uses home oxygen. Which instruction from the nurse is appropriate?
alt.a: Tell me if you see oxygen being used or stored unsafely
alt.ex: AP inform the nurse of concerns about use or storage; teaching remains the nurse’s responsibility.
w: Teach the patient how to read the oxygen cylinder gauge
Teaching home oxygen use cannot be delegated to AP.
Raise the flow rate if the patient seems short of breath
Flow rate changes are not made without an order.
Explain the emergency plan for a power failure to the family
Discussing emergency plans is part of nurse-led teaching.

items.q: A family caregiver asks why the patient’s oxygen concentrator alarm sounded for a few seconds after it was turned on. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “That is expected; it stops once the right pressure builds inside.”
items.ex: The concentrator alarm sounds briefly at startup and turns off when the desired internal pressure is reached.
w: “Unplug it right away; the alarm means the motor is failing.”
A brief startup alarm is normal and does not indicate motor failure.
“Switch to the spare tank and call 9-1-1 immediately.”
A brief startup alarm is not an emergency.
“The alarm means the flow rate is set too high for you.”
The startup alarm relates to internal pressure, not the flow setting.

alt.q: What happens to the alarm when an oxygen concentrator is first turned on?
alt.a: It sounds for a few seconds, then stops when pressure is reached
alt.ex: A brief alarm at startup is expected until the concentrator reaches its desired internal pressure.
w: It sounds continuously until the caregiver resets it
The alarm turns off by itself once the desired pressure is reached.
It stays silent unless the tubing is disconnected
The alarm normally sounds briefly at every startup.
It sounds only when the cylinder pressure gauge is low
Concentrators do not use cylinders; the startup alarm reflects internal pressure.

items.q: While refilling a portable liquid oxygen unit, the patient’s spouse finds that the unit will not separate from the stationary reservoir. Which instruction should the nurse give?
items.a: Wait 5 to 10 minutes for the valves to warm, and do not touch frosted areas
items.ex: The valves have frozen together; waiting lets them warm, and touching frosted areas can cause frostbite.
w: Pull firmly with both hands to break the connection
Forcing frozen valves apart risks damage and contact with frosted, frostbite-causing parts.
Pour warm water over the frosted valves to loosen them
The book directs waiting 5 to 10 minutes for valves to warm, not adding water.
Leave the fill valve open until the unit releases
Leaving the fill valve open overfills the unit and can cause malfunction.

alt.q: Why does the nurse caution a patient not to touch frosted areas of a liquid oxygen system after filling?
alt.a: Skin contact with frosted areas can cause frostbite
alt.ex: Liquid oxygen parts become extremely cold during filling, and touching frosted areas damages skin through frostbite.
w: Frosted areas indicate an oxygen leak that can ignite on contact
The danger from frost is skin damage from cold, not ignition.
Touching frost transfers bacteria into the oxygen supply
The risk is frostbite; connectors are wiped dry to remove moisture.
Frosted areas carry an electrical charge from the reservoir
Liquid oxygen reservoirs do not produce an electrical hazard at frosted areas.

items.q: When should a patient disconnect a portable liquid oxygen unit from the stationary reservoir during filling?
items.a: When the hissing noise changes and a vapor cloud forms
items.ex: A change in hissing and a vapor cloud signal the unit is full; overfilling causes malfunction from high tank pressure.
w: When the hissing noise first begins after the valve opens
Hissing begins as filling starts; the unit is not yet full.
After a full 10 minutes of continuous filling
The tank usually fills in about 2 minutes, so 10 minutes would overfill it.
When frost first appears on the stationary reservoir
Ice often forms during filling and does not mean the tank is full.

alt.q: Why should a patient avoid overfilling a portable liquid oxygen unit?
alt.a: High pressure in the tank causes the unit to malfunction
alt.ex: Overfilling creates high pressure in the ambulatory tank, which causes the unit to malfunction.
w: Extra oxygen raises the delivered flow rate above the order
The flow rate is set by the flow selector, not by how full the tank is.
The extra liquid freezes the patient’s nasal cannula
Freezing occurs at the filling connection, not at the cannula.
Overfilling empties the stationary reservoir completely
The concern is pressure in the ambulatory unit, not depletion of the reservoir.

items.q: A patient with COPD on home oxygen at 2 L/min tells the nurse, “When I feel more short of breath, I turn the oxygen up to 5.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Please keep it at 2; more oxygen than prescribed can be harmful with COPD.”
items.ex: Patients are taught not to change the flow rate because exceeding the prescribed amount can harm a patient with COPD.
w: “That is fine as long as you turn it back down within an hour.”
Any increase beyond the prescribed rate can be harmful in COPD.
“Turning it up is safe because extra oxygen cannot hurt you.”
Exceeding the prescribed amount of oxygen is sometimes harmful.
“You should turn it up only at night while you are sleeping.”
The flow rate is never changed without a prescription.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient receiving home oxygen shows understanding of the teaching about flow rate?
alt.a: “I will keep the flow at the rate my provider ordered.”
alt.ex: The patient is taught not to change the flow rate, since too much oxygen can be harmful.
w: “I will double the flow whenever I walk to the mailbox.”
Changing the flow rate without an order can be harmful, especially with COPD.
“I will lower the flow when I feel fine to save oxygen.”
Lowering the rate on one’s own risks hypoxia; the ordered rate is maintained.
“I will set the flow based on how my chest feels each day.”
Flow is set to the prescribed rate, not adjusted by symptoms.

items.q: A home care patient reports increased fatigue, dizziness, and trouble concentrating while using oxygen at the prescribed rate. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Check whether the oxygen source and delivery device are working properly
items.ex: When hypoxia signs occur, the nurse first verifies that the source and device are delivering oxygen properly.
w: Increase the flow rate until the symptoms resolve
The flow rate is not changed without an order; equipment problems are checked first.
Tell the patient to rest and reassess at the next weekly visit
Signs of hypoxia need prompt assessment, not delay.
Replace the oxygen tubing with a longer length for easier movement
Long tubing is a possible cause of hypoxia, not a remedy.

alt.q: A home oxygen patient develops signs of hypoxia. Which possible cause should the nurse investigate?
alt.a: Poor tubing connections or very long oxygen tubing
alt.ex: Poor connections, long tubing, or a worsening physical problem can cause hypoxia at home.
w: Storing the oxygen tank upright in the bedroom
Upright storage is a recommended safety practice and does not cause hypoxia.
Posting “Oxygen in Use” signs on each door
Signs are a safety measure and do not affect oxygen delivery.
Having a second set of cannula and tubing at home
A spare set is recommended for cleaning and malfunctions.

items.q: Why does the home care nurse advise a patient who uses an oxygen concentrator to notify local emergency medical services (EMS)?
items.a: EMS will call the home during a power outage and may help prioritize power restoration
items.ex: Many municipalities require notification so EMS can check on the patient and the home may be placed on a priority list.
w: EMS will deliver replacement concentrators when the motor fails
Equipment is supplied by the DME vendor, not EMS.
EMS will adjust the oxygen flow rate during routine home visits
Flow rate follows the provider’s order and is monitored by the nurse.
EMS will inspect the home for smoking before oxygen arrives
The nurse completes the home risk assessment for smoking and hazards.

alt.q: A patient receiving oxygen through a concentrator asks what to have ready in case the power goes out. Which response is best?
alt.a: “Keep a spare oxygen tank available for emergency use.”
alt.ex: A spare tank provides backup oxygen because a concentrator stops working during a power failure.
w: “Keep extra nasal cannulas so you can switch devices.”
A spare cannula does not supply oxygen when the concentrator has no power.
“Plug the concentrator into an extension cord in the closet.”
Equipment is never placed in a closet, and this does not provide backup.
“Turn the flow rate up now to store oxygen in your lungs.”
Oxygen cannot be stored this way, and the flow rate is not changed.

items.q: Why does the nurse make sure a patient on home oxygen has two sets of delivery devices and tubing?
items.a: One set is used while the other is cleaned or if a set malfunctions
items.ex: An extra set allows continuous therapy during cleaning or equipment malfunction.
w: Each set is used with a different oxygen flow rate
The patient uses one prescribed flow rate and does not change it.
The second set lets two family members use the oxygen
Home oxygen is prescribed for the patient only.
Using both sets at once doubles the oxygen delivered
Only one delivery device is worn at a time at the ordered rate.

alt.q: A patient asks why the DME supplier left an extra nasal cannula and tubing. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “It lets you keep using oxygen while one set is cleaned or broken.”
alt.ex: Extra equipment is used when the first set is being cleaned or malfunctions.
w: “It is for use at a higher flow rate during activity.”
Patients are taught not to change the prescribed flow rate.
“It should be connected to the backup tank at all times.”
The spare set is for cleaning or malfunction, not constant connection.
“It is meant for a visitor who feels short of breath.”
Oxygen is prescribed for the patient and is not shared.

items.q: During the first home visit, which method may the nurse use as one of two patient identifiers?
items.a: Confirming the address of the home
items.ex: In the home setting, confirmation of the address can serve as one of the two identifiers.
w: Recognizing the patient’s face from the hospital chart
Facial recognition may be used only for ongoing visits, not the first visit.
Checking the label on the oxygen concentrator
Equipment labels are not an accepted patient identifier.
Asking a neighbor to confirm the patient’s name
Identifiers come from the patient and agency records, not neighbors.

alt.q: On which home visits may the nurse use facial recognition as one of the two patient identifiers?
alt.a: On ongoing visits after the patient has been identified
alt.ex: Facial recognition is acceptable for ongoing visits; address confirmation can be used during the first visit.
w: On the first visit, before any other identifier is checked
On the first visit, identifiers such as address confirmation are used.
On every visit, as the only identifier required
Two identifiers are always required.
Only when the patient’s address cannot be confirmed
Facial recognition depends on prior contact, not on address problems.

items.q: A nurse is planning where to teach a patient to use home oxygen equipment. Which setting is best?
items.a: The well-lit room where the patient will most often use the oxygen
items.ex: Practicing where the skill is routinely performed improves learning, and good lighting helps visualization.
w: The kitchen near the stove so the family can gather easily
Oxygen must be at least 8 feet from heat sources, and kitchens have distractions.
A dim bedroom where the patient can rest during the lesson
Good lighting improves visualization of the skill.
A busy living room with the television on for comfort
Noise and distractions reduce the patient’s attention to teaching.

alt.q: Why does the nurse teach home oxygen skills in the room where the patient will use the equipment?
alt.a: Practicing in the same environment improves comprehension and learning
alt.ex: Learning in the environment where the skill is routinely performed facilitates comprehension.
w: The DME vendor requires all teaching to occur in that room
The rationale is learning effectiveness, not vendor requirements.
It allows the nurse to skip teaching about other rooms
The choice of setting does not replace safety teaching for the whole home.
Oxygen equipment cannot be moved from room to room
Ambulatory systems are portable; the setting is chosen to aid learning.

items.q: During a home visit, the nurse finds a patient smoking a cigarette while wearing a nasal cannula connected to oxygen. After making the situation safe, which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Reinforce teaching, include the family, and plan problem-solving exercises
items.ex: Unsafe oxygen practices call for reinforced education, family involvement, problem-solving exercises, and follow-up reassessment.
w: Remove the oxygen equipment from the home permanently
The book’s response is reinforced teaching and follow-up, not withdrawing prescribed therapy.
Lower the flow rate so that less oxygen is near the flame
Any oxygen near a flame is a fire hazard, and the flow rate is not changed.
Document the event and wait for the next scheduled visit
Unsafe practice requires reinforced teaching now and follow-up reassessment.

alt.q: A patient who lives alone cannot fill the portable liquid oxygen unit independently. Which action should the nurse take?
alt.a: Identify and teach a family caregiver who can help fill the tank
alt.ex: When a patient cannot fill the ambulatory system, the nurse instructs a family caregiver who can help.
w: Tell the patient to use only the stationary reservoir at home
Limiting the patient to the reservoir restricts mobility and does not solve the problem.
Instruct the patient to leave the fill valve open overnight
Overfilling causes malfunction, and the patient must stay with the unit while filling.
Switch the patient’s prescription to a higher flow rate
Flow rate is unrelated to the inability to fill the tank.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient and family to recognize hypoxia at home. Which signs should they report to the health care provider? Select all that apply.
o: Increased anxiety or apprehension
Apprehension and anxiety are early signs of hypoxia.
Decreased ability to concentrate
Reduced concentration reflects inadequate oxygen to the brain.
Increased pulse and respiratory rate
The body compensates for hypoxia by increasing heart and breathing rates.
Pallor or cyanosis
Skin color changes indicate poor tissue oxygenation.
Slower pulse and respiratory rate
Hypoxia increases, rather than decreases, pulse and respiratory rate.
Improved energy and alertness
Hypoxia causes increased fatigue and decreased alertness.
items.ex: Apprehension, poor concentration, fatigue, dizziness, behavior changes, faster pulse and breathing, pallor, and cyanosis suggest hypoxia.

alt.q: Which findings in a patient using home oxygen suggest a respiratory tract infection that should be reported? Select all that apply.
o: Fever
Fever is a listed sign of respiratory tract infection.
Increased sputum
Increased sputum is a sign of infection.
A change in sputum color
Sputum color change suggests infection.
Foul-smelling sputum
A foul sputum odor suggests infection.
Clear sputum unchanged from baseline
Unchanged sputum does not suggest a new infection.
alt.ex: Fever and increased, discolored, or foul sputum suggest a respiratory tract infection that raises oxygen demand.

items.q: Which home oxygen safety practices should the nurse teach? Select all that apply.
o: Store oxygen tanks upright
Upright storage is part of safe home oxygen practice.
Keep oxygen at least 8 feet from open flames
A distance of 2.4 meters (8 feet) reduces fire risk.
Post “No Smoking/Oxygen in Use” signs at each entrance
Signs alert everyone entering that oxygen is in use.
Watch for trip hazards from tubing and cylinders
Tubing and cylinders create fall risks in the home.
Keep the concentrator in a closet to muffle its noise
Oxygen equipment must not be placed in a closet; it needs ventilation.
Apply petroleum jelly near the equipment to protect tubing
Grease, oil, and petroleum are kept away from oxygen equipment.
items.ex: Safe practice includes upright storage, distance from flames, no-smoking signs, and awareness of trip hazards.

alt.q: During a home visit, which observations show the patient is using oxygen safely? Select all that apply.
o: The concentrator sits in a clutter-free, well-ventilated area
Equipment belongs in a clutter-free, well-ventilated location.
Equipment is turned off when not in use
Turning off equipment when not in use is recommended.
No one smokes or vapes inside the home
Smoking, including e-cigarettes, is not allowed in the home.
The oxygen tank is stored beside the space heater
Oxygen must be at least 8 feet from heat sources.
Tubing is draped under bedding and curtains
Equipment is kept away from drapes, curtains, and bedding.
alt.ex: Safe use includes a clutter-free, ventilated location, turning equipment off when unused, and no smoking or vaping.

items.q: A home care nurse is completing a risk assessment before a patient begins home oxygen therapy. Which elements should the assessment include? Select all that apply.
o: Smoking status of the patient and household members
Smoking by anyone in the home creates a fire risk with oxygen.
Fire hazards in the home
Identifying fire risks ensures safe delivery of oxygen.
Trip and fall hazards
Tubing and cylinders add to existing fall risks.
The patient’s and caregiver’s health literacy
Health literacy guides how the nurse teaches oxygen use.
The brand of cooking oil used in the kitchen
The concern is keeping grease and oil away from equipment, not oil brands.
items.ex: The nurse assesses household smoking, fire, trip, and fall risks along with health literacy and learning readiness.

alt.q: Which factors should the nurse assess to determine a patient’s readiness to learn about home oxygen? Select all that apply.
o: Presence of pain, nausea, or fatigue
Physical symptoms can reduce the ability to concentrate on teaching.
Interest in the instruction
Interest affects readiness to learn.
Confusion or frailty
Confusion or frailty may require relying on a family caregiver.
The number of rooms in the home
Home size does not determine learning readiness.
The patient’s preferred oxygen supplier brand
Supplier brand does not indicate readiness to learn.
alt.ex: Pain, nausea, fatigue, interest, illness, frailty, and confusion affect a patient’s readiness and ability to learn.

items.q: Long oxygen tubing and poor tubing connections are possible causes of hypoxia in a patient using home oxygen.
items.a: True
items.ex: Poor connections and long tubing can reduce the oxygen that reaches the patient.
items.ww: Tubing length and connections do affect delivery, so they are checked when hypoxia occurs.

alt.q: Using longer oxygen tubing improves oxygen delivery because the patient can move more freely.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Long oxygen tubing is listed as a possible cause of hypoxia at home.
alt.ww: Greater mobility does not improve delivery; long tubing can reduce the oxygen reaching the patient.

items.q: Using e-cigarettes inside the home is acceptable for a patient on home oxygen because they produce no open flame.
items.a: False
items.ex: The no-smoking rule includes e-cigarettes, or vaping, for the safety of all occupants.
items.ww: Vaping is specifically included in the teaching not to smoke within the home.

alt.q: The teaching not to smoke inside a home where oxygen is used also applies to e-cigarettes.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Patients and families are taught that the smoking risk includes e-cigarettes, commonly called vaping.
alt.ww: E-cigarettes are not exempt; vaping is named in the no-smoking teaching.

sections.name: Location and movement of water and electrolytes

items.q: In an adult, approximately what proportion of total body water is intracellular fluid (ICF)?
items.a: About two-thirds
items.ex: In adults, ICF makes up about two-thirds of total body water and ECF about one-third.
w: About one-third
One-third of total body water is extracellular fluid, not intracellular fluid.
About one-half
The book places ICF at about two-thirds, not half, of total body water.
About three-fourths
ICF is about two-thirds of total body water; three-fourths overstates it.

alt.q: Which fluid compartment holds the largest share of total body water in an adult?
alt.a: Intracellular fluid
alt.ex: ICF holds about two-thirds of body water (about 28 L in Fig. 42.1), more than all ECF combined.
w: Interstitial fluid
Interstitial fluid is a major division of ECF, which totals only about one-third of body water.
Intravascular plasma
Plasma is the smallest major compartment, about 3 L in Fig. 42.1.
Transcellular fluid
Transcellular fluids are only a minor division of the ECF.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Diffusion of electrolytes across a cell membrane requires which of the following?
items.a: Protein ion channels in the membrane
items.ex: Diffusion is passive, but electrolytes cross cell membranes only through proteins that serve as ion channels.
w: Energy supplied by ATP
ATP is required for active transport, not for passive diffusion.
Movement against a concentration gradient
Diffusion moves particles down a gradient; moving against it is active transport.
Blood proteins exerting oncotic pressure
Oncotic pressure from blood proteins affects filtration across capillaries, not ion diffusion.

alt.q: When a sodium channel in a cell membrane opens, why does Na+ diffuse into the cell?
alt.a: Na+ concentration is lower in the ICF than in the ECF
alt.ex: Diffusion is passive movement from higher to lower concentration, and Na+ is lower inside cells.
w: Na+ concentration is higher in the ICF than in the ECF
Na+ is higher in the ECF; the sodium-potassium pump keeps ICF sodium low.
The sodium-potassium pump uses ATP to push Na+ inward
The pump moves Na+ out of the cell, not into it.
Osmotic pressure in the cell pulls Na+ across the membrane
Osmotic pressure moves water by osmosis, not electrolytes by diffusion.

items.q: Plasma is the intravascular portion of the extracellular fluid.
items.a: True
items.ex: Intravascular fluid is the liquid part of the blood, or plasma, one of the two major ECF divisions.
items.ww: Plasma is outside cells and inside blood vessels, so it is intravascular ECF, not ICF or interstitial fluid.

alt.q: Interstitial fluid is the liquid portion of the blood that circulates within the blood vessels.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Interstitial fluid lies between the cells and outside the blood vessels; plasma is the intravascular fluid.
alt.ww: The liquid part of blood is intravascular fluid (plasma); interstitial fluid is outside the vessels.

w: A lean young adult man
A lean adult man has about 60% body water, the highest of these groups.
A muscular young adult woman
Muscle holds more water than fat, and youth also favors a higher proportion of water.
A lean middle-aged man
Lean men have relatively high body water because muscle contains more water than fat.

alt.q: Why does a person who is obese have a lower percentage of body water than a lean person?
alt.a: Fat tissue contains less water than muscle
alt.ex: The book explains that people who are obese have less body water because fat contains less water than muscle.
w: Fat cells actively pump water out of the body
Fat cells do not pump water out; the difference is the low water content of fat.
Obesity greatly increases insensible water loss
The book attributes the difference to tissue water content, not increased insensible loss.
Adipose tissue moves water into the lymph vessels
Lymph removes excess interstitial fluid; it does not explain lower water content in obesity.

items.q: Which ions are cations found in body fluids? Select all that apply.

Sodium is a positively charged ion, a cation.
Potassium (K+)
Potassium carries a positive charge, so it is a cation.
Calcium (Ca2+)
Calcium carries a 2+ charge, making it a cation.
Magnesium (Mg2+)
Magnesium carries a 2+ charge, making it a cation.
Chloride (Cl−)
Chloride is negatively charged, so it is an anion.
Bicarbonate (HCO3−)
Bicarbonate is negatively charged, so it is an anion.
items.ex: Cations are positively charged ions; in body fluids they are sodium, potassium, calcium, and magnesium.

items.q: Why are electrolyte measurements commonly reported in milliequivalents per liter (mEq/L)?
items.a: One mEq of an electrolyte combines with one mEq of another
items.ex: Milliequivalents account for ionic charge, so one mEq of one electrolyte combines with one mEq of another.
w: They measure intracellular as well as serum levels
Laboratory electrolyte values are measured in serum and do not reflect intracellular levels.
They ignore the electrical charge of each ion
mEq/L are calculated by multiplying millimoles by the ion’s charge, so charge is included.
They equal milligrams of electrolyte per deciliter
Milligrams per deciliter is a different unit; mEq/L are based on millimoles and charge.

alt.q: How are milliequivalents per liter calculated from millimoles per liter?
alt.a: Multiply millimoles per liter by the ion’s charge
alt.ex: mEq/L equal mmol/L multiplied by the electrolyte charge, such as 1 for Na+ and 2 for Ca2+.
w: Divide millimoles per liter by the ion’s charge
The charge is multiplied, not divided, to convert mmol/L to mEq/L.
Multiply millimoles per liter by the molecular weight
Molecular weight is used to get mmol from milligrams, not mEq from mmol.
Divide milligrams per liter by the ion’s charge
Milligrams are divided by molecular weight to give millimoles; charge then multiplies millimoles.

items.q: Which particles determine the tonicity (effective concentration) of a body fluid?
items.a: Particles that cannot easily cross cell membranes, such as Na+
items.ex: Tonicity depends on particles like sodium that do not cross cell membranes easily.
w: Particles that easily cross cell membranes, such as urea
Urea passes easily through cell membranes, so it does not determine tonicity.
Only large blood proteins, such as albumin and globulin
Blood proteins create colloid osmotic pressure in capillaries; tonicity is set by impermeant particles like Na+.
Water molecules moving freely between compartments, such as in osmosis
Water is the solvent that moves; tonicity reflects dissolved particles, not the water itself.

alt.q: A solution that is more concentrated than normal blood is described as which of the following?
alt.a: Hypertonic
alt.ex: A hypertonic solution is more concentrated than blood; hypotonic is more dilute, and isotonic matches blood.
w: Hypotonic
A hypotonic solution is more dilute than blood.
Isotonic
An isotonic solution has the same tonicity as normal blood.
Hypo-osmolar
Hypo-osmolar describes fluid that is too dilute, the opposite of more concentrated.

items.q: Osmolality is a measure of the number of particles per kilogram of water.
items.a: True
items.ex: Osmolality counts particles per kilogram of water, so more dissolved particles mean a more concentrated fluid.
items.ww: Osmolality is defined by particle number per kilogram of water, so the statement is accurate.

alt.q: Urea, which crosses cell membranes easily, is a main determinant of a fluid’s tonicity.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Tonicity is determined by particles that cannot easily cross cell membranes, such as Na+, not urea.
alt.ww: Urea passes easily through membranes, so it adds to osmolality but not to tonicity.

items.q: Which statement accurately describes the sodium-potassium pump?
items.a: It uses ATP to move Na+ out of cells and K+ into cells
items.ex: This active transport pump keeps ICF low in Na+ and high in K+ compared with the ECF.
w: It uses ATP to move K+ out of cells and Na+ into cells
The direction is reversed; the pump moves Na+ out and K+ in.
It moves Na+ into cells passively through open channels
Passive movement through channels is diffusion, not the ATP-driven pump.
It moves water into cells toward higher osmotic pressure
Water moves by osmosis; the pump moves electrolytes.

alt.q: Which process uses ATP to move electrolytes against their concentration gradient?
alt.a: Active transport
alt.ex: Active transport requires ATP to move electrolytes from lower to higher concentration, as in the sodium-potassium pump.
w: Diffusion
Diffusion is passive movement down a concentration gradient and uses no ATP.
Osmosis
Osmosis moves water, not electrolytes, across a semipermeable membrane.
Filtration
Filtration moves fluid between capillaries and interstitial space by pressure differences.

items.q: A patient is receiving an IV infusion of a hypotonic solution. Which statement by a nursing student shows correct understanding of its effect on the patient’s cells?

w: Water will move out of the cells, and they will shrink.
Water leaving cells and shrinking them is the effect of a hypertonic solution.

alt.q: A patient is receiving an IV infusion of a hypertonic solution. Which effect on the cells does the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: Water leaves the cells by osmosis, and they shrink.
alt.ex: A hypertonic infusion concentrates interstitial fluid, so water leaves cells to equalize osmolality.
w: Water enters the cells by osmosis, and they swell.
Cells swell when a hypotonic solution dilutes the interstitial fluid.
Water stays in place, and cell size is unchanged.
Cell size stays the same with an isotonic solution.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which force is the main outward-pushing force that moves fluid from capillaries into the interstitial area?
items.a: Capillary hydrostatic pressure
items.ex: Capillary hydrostatic pressure is a relatively strong outward force, strongest at the arterial end of the capillary.
w: Blood colloid osmotic pressure
Blood colloid osmotic (oncotic) pressure pulls fluid into capillaries, not out.
Interstitial fluid hydrostatic pressure
This weaker force pushes fluid back into the capillaries.
Intracellular osmotic pressure
ICF osmotic pressure pulls water into cells; it is not one of the capillary filtration forces.

alt.q: Which force, created by albumin and other blood proteins, pulls fluid from the interstitial area back into capillaries?
alt.a: Oncotic pressure
alt.ex: Blood colloid osmotic pressure, or oncotic pressure, comes from proteins too large to leave the capillaries.
w: Capillary hydrostatic pressure
Capillary hydrostatic pressure pushes fluid out of capillaries.
Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure
Interstitial colloid osmotic pressure is a very small force opposing oncotic pressure.
Intracellular osmotic pressure
ICF osmotic pressure pulls water into cells, not into capillaries.

items.q: At the venous end of a normal capillary, fluid moves from the interstitial area into the capillary, removing metabolic wastes.
items.a: True
items.ex: At the venous end, hydrostatic pressure is weaker and blood colloid osmotic pressure is stronger, so fluid returns to the capillary.
items.ww: Fluid moves into the capillary at the venous end because oncotic pressure exceeds the weaker hydrostatic pressure there.

alt.q: Capillary hydrostatic pressure is strongest at the venous end of a capillary, where it pushes nutrients out to the cells.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Capillary hydrostatic pressure is strongest at the arterial end, where fluid carrying nutrients moves into the interstitial area.
alt.ww: At the venous end hydrostatic pressure is weaker, so fluid moves into the capillary, carrying wastes.

The fluid inside your cells is moving out into your bloodstream too quickly.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Where is angiotensin I converted to angiotensin II?
items.a: Lung capillaries
items.ex: Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) in the lung capillaries converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II.
w: Juxtaglomerular cells
Juxtaglomerular cells release renin, which forms angiotensin I.
Adrenal cortex
The adrenal cortex releases aldosterone in response to angiotensin II.
Posterior pituitary
The posterior pituitary releases ADH, not ACE.

alt.q: What is the role of renin in the RAAS?
alt.a: It converts angiotensinogen to angiotensin I
alt.ex: Renin, released by juxtaglomerular cells, converts the inactive protein angiotensinogen to angiotensin I.
w: It converts angiotensin I to angiotensin II
This step is performed by ACE in the lung capillaries.
It resorbs sodium and water in the distal tubules
Aldosterone causes sodium and water resorption in the distal tubules.
It stimulates the posterior pituitary to release ADH
ADH release is not the function of renin described in the RAAS.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which statements about the renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system (RAAS) are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Angiotensin II vasoconstricts some vascular beds.
Vasoconstriction is one of the functions of angiotensin II.
Aldosterone causes sodium and water resorption in the distal renal tubules.
Aldosterone resorbs sodium and water in isotonic proportion, increasing ECV.
Aldosterone increases urinary excretion of potassium and hydrogen ions.
This effect links aldosterone to electrolyte and acid-base balance.
Aldosterone increases sodium and water loss in the urine.
Increasing sodium and water loss is the effect of ANP, which opposes aldosterone.
Renin is released by the adrenal cortex.
Renin comes from juxtaglomerular cells in the kidneys; the adrenal cortex releases aldosterone.
items.ex: The RAAS regulates ECV and blood pressure through angiotensin II vasoconstriction and aldosterone-driven sodium and water retention.

alt.q: Which statements about aldosterone are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It is released from the adrenal cortex.
Angiotensin II stimulates aldosterone release from the adrenal cortex.
It resorbs sodium and water in isotonic proportion.
Aldosterone returns sodium and water to the blood in isotonic proportion.
It increases the volume of the ECF.
Returning sodium and water to the blood increases ECV.
It acts on collecting ducts to resorb water alone.
Resorbing water alone in the collecting ducts is the action of ADH.
It is released when atrial cells are stretched.
Stretched atrial cells release ANP, which opposes aldosterone.
alt.ex: Aldosterone from the adrenal cortex resorbs sodium and water to raise ECV and increases potassium and hydrogen excretion.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient has lost a large amount of blood after trauma. Which compensatory response does the nurse expect?
items.a: Increased renin release, leading to sodium and water retention
items.ex: Hemorrhage lowers renal blood flow, increasing renin and RAAS activity to retain sodium and water and restore ECV.
w: Decreased renin release, leading to sodium and water excretion
Low renal blood flow increases, not decreases, renin release.
Increased ANP release, leading to sodium and water excretion
ANP is released when atria are stretched by increased ECV, not after blood loss.
Decreased ADH release, leading to large volumes of dilute urine
Severely decreased blood volume increases ADH, reducing urine volume.

alt.q: A patient has been vomiting for 2 days. Which hormonal response does the nurse expect?
alt.a: Increased ADH and RAAS activity with decreased urine volume
alt.ex: Fluid loss from vomiting increases ADH and RAAS activity, so urine volume decreases to conserve fluid.
w: Decreased ADH and RAAS activity with increased urine volume
These changes would worsen fluid loss; the body conserves fluid after vomiting.
Increased ANP activity with increased sodium and water loss
ANP rises with increased ECV, not after fluid loss.
Decreased aldosterone activity with potassium retention
Lower ECV increases aldosterone through the RAAS.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: What stimulates the release of atrial natriuretic peptide (ANP)?
items.a: Stretching of atrial cells by increased ECV
items.ex: Atrial cells release ANP when stretched, such as by increased extracellular fluid volume.
w: Decreased blood flow through the renal arteries
Decreased renal blood flow increases renin release.
Increased plasma osmolality sensed in the brain
Increased osmolality stimulates thirst and ADH release.
Decreased atrial stretch from low blood volume
ANP is released with increased stretch, not decreased stretch.

alt.q: A patient has ECV excess. Which hormonal response helps restore fluid balance?
alt.a: ANP release increases sodium and water loss in urine
alt.ex: Increased ECV stretches the atria, and ANP increases urinary sodium and water loss to lower ECV.
w: Aldosterone release increases sodium and water retention
Retaining sodium and water would worsen ECV excess.
ADH release increases water resorption in the kidneys
More water resorption would add to the excess volume.
Renin release increases angiotensin II formation
Increased renin leads to sodium and water retention, worsening the excess.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: ANP is a weak hormone that opposes the effect of aldosterone.
items.a: True
items.ex: ANP increases sodium and water loss in urine, opposing aldosterone’s sodium and water retention.
items.ww: The book describes ANP as a weak hormone that opposes aldosterone, so the statement is accurate.

alt.q: ANP is released from the adrenal cortex and causes the kidneys to retain sodium and water.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: ANP is released from stretched atrial cells and increases sodium and water excretion.
alt.ww: Retaining sodium and water is aldosterone’s effect; ANP comes from the heart and promotes their loss.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Antidiuretic hormone is also called [[vasopressin]].
items.ex: ADH, or vasopressin, regulates body fluid osmolality by controlling how much water is excreted in urine.

alt.q: [[Vasopressin]] is another name for the hormone released from the posterior pituitary that causes renal water resorption.
alt.ex: ADH, or vasopressin, regulates body fluid osmolality by controlling how much water is excreted in urine.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which are normal routes of fluid output? Select all that apply.
o: Skin
Skin loses fluid through insensible loss and sweat.
Lungs
Lungs continuously lose water through insensible loss.
GI tract
The GI tract normally excretes about 100 to 200 mL daily.
Kidneys
Kidneys produce urine and are the major regulator of output.
Vomiting
Vomiting is an abnormal route of fluid output.
Wound drainage
Wound drainage is an abnormal route of fluid output.
items.ex: Fluid output normally occurs through four organs: the skin, lungs, GI tract, and kidneys.

alt.q: Which are examples of abnormal fluid output? Select all that apply.
o: Vomiting
Vomiting is listed as an abnormal route of fluid output.
Wound drainage
Drainage from a wound is abnormal fluid output.
Hemorrhage
Blood loss is an abnormal route of fluid output.
Urine
Urine is normal output through the kidneys.
Insensible loss through the lungs
Insensible lung loss is a normal, continuous output.
alt.ex: Vomiting, wound drainage, and hemorrhage are abnormal outputs, unlike normal losses through skin, lungs, GI tract, and kidneys.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: What distinguishes a volume imbalance from an osmolality imbalance?
items.a: Volume imbalances alter the amount of ECF; osmolality imbalances alter body fluid concentration
items.ex: Volume imbalances disturb how much fluid is in the ECF; osmolality imbalances disturb how concentrated body fluids are.
w: Volume imbalances alter body fluid concentration; osmolality imbalances alter the amount of ECF
The definitions are reversed.
Volume imbalances affect only the ICF; osmolality imbalances affect only the ECF
Volume imbalances involve the extracellular compartment, and osmolality shifts water across cell membranes.
Volume imbalances never occur with osmolality imbalances; each always occurs alone
Volume and osmolality imbalances may occur separately or together, as in clinical dehydration.

alt.q: A disturbance in the concentration of body fluids is classified as which type of fluid imbalance?
alt.a: Osmolality imbalance
alt.ex: Osmolality imbalances are disturbances in concentration, such as hypernatremia and hyponatremia.
w: Volume imbalance
Volume imbalances disturb the amount, not the concentration, of ECF.
Extracellular volume deficit
ECV deficit is too little isotonic fluid with normal osmolality.
Extracellular volume excess
ECV excess is too much isotonic fluid with normal osmolality.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: In ECV deficit, body fluids have decreased volume but normal osmolality.
items.a: True
items.ex: ECV deficit is an isotonic loss of sodium and water, so volume falls while concentration stays normal.
items.ww: Because water and sodium are lost in isotonic proportion, osmolality remains normal in ECV deficit.

alt.q: In ECV deficit, the extracellular fluid becomes too concentrated because more water than sodium is lost.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Losing more water than salt causes hypernatremia; ECV deficit alone is an isotonic loss with normal osmolality.
alt.ww: Too-concentrated fluid describes hypernatremia or clinical dehydration, not isolated ECV deficit.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which assessment findings are consistent with ECV deficit? Select all that apply.
o: Postural hypotension
Low vascular volume causes blood pressure to drop on standing.
Tachycardia with a thready pulse
The heart rate rises and the pulse weakens with low vascular volume.
Flat neck veins when supine
Neck veins stay flat even lying down when vascular volume is low.
Crackles in the lungs
Crackles are a sign of ECV excess.
Full neck veins when upright
Full neck veins when upright indicate ECV excess.
Edema in dependent areas
Dependent edema is a sign of ECV excess.
items.ex: ECV deficit causes signs of low vascular and interstitial volume, such as postural hypotension, thready pulse, and flat neck veins.

alt.q: Which assessment findings are consistent with ECV excess? Select all that apply.
o: Sudden overnight weight gain
Isotonic fluid gain shows quickly as weight gain.
Edema in dependent areas
Excess interstitial fluid collects in dependent areas.
Crackles in the lungs
Excess fluid can collect in the lungs, causing crackles.
Poor skin turgor
Poor skin turgor is a sign of ECV deficit.
Slow vein filling
Slow vein filling reflects low vascular volume in ECV deficit.
alt.ex: ECV excess shows as sudden weight gain, dependent edema, full neck veins when upright, and crackles.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with ECV deficit from several days of vomiting is being monitored. Which new finding is most important to report?
items.a: Restlessness and confusion
items.ex: Restlessness and confusion are signs of severe ECV deficit, which can progress to hypovolemic shock.
w: Dry oral mucous membranes
Dry mucous membranes are an expected sign of ECV deficit, not a sign of severity.
Dark yellow urine
Dark yellow urine is expected with ECV deficit and does not indicate severe deficit.
Poor skin turgor
Poor skin turgor is an expected sign rather than an indicator of severe deficit.

alt.q: Which finding indicates that a patient’s ECV deficit has become severe?
alt.a: Urine output below 30 mL/h
alt.ex: Oliguria, defined here as urine output below 30 mL/h, is listed as a sign of severe ECV deficit.
w: Urine specific gravity of 1.015
A specific gravity of 1.015 is not the concentrated urine expected in ECV deficit.
Heart rate of 76 beats/min
A heart rate of 76 beats/min is not tachycardia and does not suggest severe deficit.
Weight loss of 0.5 kg over 1 week
Gradual small weight loss does not reflect sudden fluid loss or severe deficit.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which set of laboratory findings is consistent with ECV deficit without a renal cause?
items.a: Increased hematocrit, BUN above 20 mg/dL, urine specific gravity above 1.030
items.ex: Hemoconcentration raises hematocrit and BUN, and the kidneys produce concentrated urine unless the cause is renal.
w: Decreased hematocrit, BUN below 10 mg/dL, urine specific gravity below 1.005
Decreased hematocrit and low BUN reflect hemodilution in ECV excess.
Serum sodium below 136 mEq/L, serum osmolality below 285 mOsm/kg, normal hematocrit
Low sodium and osmolality indicate hyponatremia, an osmolality imbalance.
Serum sodium above 145 mEq/L, serum osmolality above 295 mOsm/kg, normal hematocrit
High sodium and osmolality define hypernatremia, not isotonic ECV deficit.

alt.q: Which laboratory findings are consistent with ECV excess?
alt.a: Decreased hematocrit and BUN below 10 mg/dL
alt.ex: In ECV excess, excess isotonic fluid dilutes the blood, lowering hematocrit and BUN.
w: Increased hematocrit and BUN above 20 mg/dL
These reflect hemoconcentration in ECV deficit.
Urine specific gravity above 1.030 and increased hematocrit
Concentrated urine and high hematocrit fit ECV deficit.
Serum sodium above 145 mEq/L and osmolality above 295 mOsm/kg
These values define hypernatremia, not ECV excess.

items.a: ECV excess
items.ex: Sudden overnight weight gain and crackles are signs of ECV excess, and heart failure causes renal sodium and water retention.
w: ECV deficit
ECV deficit causes sudden weight loss and flat neck veins, not weight gain and crackles.
Hypernatremia
Hypernatremia causes cerebral signs such as decreased level of consciousness, not weight gain and crackles.
Hyponatremia
Hyponatremia causes cerebral dysfunction from swollen brain cells, not crackles and weight gain.

alt.q: A patient has dependent edema, full neck veins when semi-upright, and crackles. Which cause is consistent with these findings?

alt.ex: Too much sodium-containing isotonic IV fluid causes ECV excess with edema, full neck veins, and crackles.
w: Excessive infusion of 5% dextrose in water
Excessive D5W adds relatively more water than salt, causing hyponatremia.
Diabetes insipidus without increased water intake
Diabetes insipidus causes loss of more water than salt, leading to hypernatremia.
Massive sweating without water and salt intake
Massive sweating without replacement causes ECV deficit, not excess.
