items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why do signs of cerebral dysfunction develop in hypernatremia?
items.a: Water leaves brain cells by osmosis, and the cells shrivel
items.ex: Hypertonic interstitial fluid draws water out of cells by osmosis; shriveling brain cells cause cerebral signs.
w: Water enters brain cells by osmosis, and the cells swell
Cell swelling and cerebral edema occur in hyponatremia.
Sodium enters brain cells by active transport, and the cells burst
Sodium does not move in to burst cells; water leaves the cells instead.
Fluid leaks from brain capillaries, and interstitial edema forms
Hypernatremia acts by osmotic water shifts out of cells, not capillary leakage.

alt.q: Which change in brain cells produces the signs of hyponatremia?
alt.a: Water enters the cells by osmosis, causing cerebral edema
alt.ex: Dilute interstitial fluid causes water to enter cells, and swelling of brain cells produces cerebral dysfunction.
w: Water leaves the cells by osmosis, and they shrivel
Cells shrivel in hypernatremia, when interstitial fluid is hypertonic.
Potassium leaves the cells, and they shrink in size
The problem in hyponatremia is water moving into cells, not potassium loss.
Cell volume stays normal because only ECV changes
Osmolality imbalances shift water across cell membranes, changing cell volume.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Hyponatremia, a hypotonic condition, is also called water excess or water [[intoxication]].
items.ex: Hyponatremia means body fluids are too dilute, from gaining relatively more water than salt or losing more salt than water.

alt.q: Another name for water excess, in which body fluids are too dilute, is water [[intoxication]].
alt.ex: Hyponatremia means body fluids are too dilute, from gaining relatively more water than salt or losing more salt than water.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which pair of serum values indicates hyponatremia?
items.a: Na+ 130 mEq/L and osmolality 275 mOsm/kg
items.ex: Hyponatremia is serum Na+ below 136 mEq/L with osmolality below 285 mOsm/kg.
w: Na+ 150 mEq/L and osmolality 305 mOsm/kg
Values above 145 mEq/L and 295 mOsm/kg indicate hypernatremia.
Na+ 140 mEq/L and osmolality 290 mOsm/kg
Both values are within normal ranges.
Na+ 147 mEq/L and osmolality 298 mOsm/kg
These values are above normal, indicating hypernatremia.

alt.q: Hypernatremia is present when serum sodium rises above which level?
alt.a: 145 mEq/L
alt.ex: Hypernatremia is serum Na+ above 145 mEq/L with osmolality above 295 mOsm/kg.
w: 136 mEq/L
136 mEq/L is the lower limit of normal; values below it indicate hyponatremia.
140 mEq/L
140 mEq/L is a normal serum sodium level.
155 mEq/L
Hypernatremia begins above 145 mEq/L, not 155 mEq/L.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with several days of diarrhea has been replacing the losses by drinking only plain water and is now confused. Which imbalance does the nurse suspect?
items.a: Hyponatremia
items.ex: Replacing large fluid output with water but no salt causes loss of relatively more salt than water, producing hyponatremia.
w: Hypernatremia
Hypernatremia results from losing more water than salt or gaining more salt than water.
ECV excess
ECV excess is a gain of isotonic sodium-containing fluid, not water alone.
Clinical dehydration
Clinical dehydration involves poor water intake; this patient has been drinking plenty of water.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a patient with gastroenteritis about replacing fluid losses. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
alt.a: I will drink fluids that contain some sodium, not only plain water.
alt.ex: Replacing vomiting and diarrhea losses with sodium-containing fluids helps prevent both hyponatremia and clinical dehydration.
w: I will replace my losses with as much plain water as possible.
Replacing large losses with water but no salt can cause hyponatremia.
I will stop drinking until the vomiting and diarrhea are over.
Inadequate intake during GI losses leads to clinical dehydration.
I will take salt tablets with only small sips of water.
Salt tablets with little water add more salt than water, causing hypernatremia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which conditions can cause hyponatremia? Select all that apply.
o: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH secretion
Excessive ADH causes retention of relatively more water than salt.
Psychogenic polydipsia
Excessive water intake adds relatively more water than salt.
Excessive IV infusion of 5% dextrose in water
D5W provides water without salt, diluting body fluids.
Repeated tap-water enemas
Tap-water enemas add water that dilutes body fluids.
Diabetes insipidus
ADH deficiency causes loss of more water than salt, leading to hypernatremia.
Administration of salt tablets
Salt tablets add relatively more salt than water, causing hypernatremia.
items.ex: Hyponatremia results from gaining relatively more water than salt or losing relatively more salt than water.

alt.q: Which conditions can cause hypernatremia? Select all that apply.
o: Diabetes insipidus
ADH deficiency causes loss of relatively more water than salt.
Osmotic diuresis
Osmotic diuresis causes loss of more water than salt.
Tube feedings without enough water
Tube feedings can add relatively more salt than water.
Inability to respond to thirst due to aphasia
Patients who cannot respond to thirst may not replace water losses.
Use of hypotonic irrigating solutions
Hypotonic irrigating solutions add water and cause hyponatremia.
Excessive ADH secretion
Excess ADH retains water and causes hyponatremia.
alt.ex: Hypernatremia results from losing relatively more water than salt or gaining relatively more salt than water.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: An immobile patient with aphasia receives continuous tube feedings and now has a serum sodium of 151 mEq/L. Which finding should the nurse assess for?
items.a: Decreased level of consciousness
items.ex: Hypernatremia causes cerebral dysfunction such as confusion, lethargy, or coma, with seizures if rapid or severe.
w: Edema in dependent areas
Dependent edema is a sign of ECV excess, not hypernatremia.
Crackles in the lungs
Crackles indicate ECV excess with fluid in the lungs.
Full neck veins when upright
Full neck veins when upright reflect ECV excess.

alt.q: Which patient is at greatest risk for hypernatremia?
alt.a: An immobile patient with aphasia receiving tube feedings
alt.ex: Tube feedings add relatively more salt than water, and immobility and aphasia prevent response to thirst.
w: A patient receiving large volumes of IV D5W
Excess D5W adds water without salt, causing hyponatremia.
A patient with SIADH after a head injury
Excess ADH retains water, causing hyponatremia.
A patient who received several tap-water enemas
Tap-water enemas add water and cause hyponatremia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which conditions can cause ECV deficit? Select all that apply.
o: Laxative overuse
Increased GI output from laxatives causes isotonic fluid loss.
Drainage from a fistula
Fistula drainage increases GI output of isotonic fluid.
Burns
Burns cause loss of plasma, an isotonic fluid.
Diuretic use
Diuretics increase renal output of sodium and water.
Cirrhosis
Cirrhosis causes renal sodium and water retention, leading to ECV excess.
Glucocorticoid excess
Glucocorticoid excess causes renal sodium and water retention, leading to ECV excess.
items.ex: ECV deficit occurs when output of isotonic fluid exceeds intake of sodium-containing fluid, as with GI, renal, or blood losses.

alt.q: Which conditions can cause ECV excess? Select all that apply.
o: Heart failure
Heart failure causes renal retention of sodium and water.
Aldosterone excess
Excess aldosterone causes renal sodium and water retention.
Acute oliguric renal disease
Oliguric renal disease retains sodium and water.
Adrenal insufficiency
Deficits of cortisol and aldosterone increase renal output, causing ECV deficit.
Hemorrhage
Blood loss causes ECV deficit.
alt.ex: ECV excess occurs when intake or renal retention of isotonic sodium and water exceeds output.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: After a very salty restaurant meal with plenty of water, a patient notices swollen ankles and tight rings the next morning. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
items.a: Mild ECV excess from gaining isotonic sodium and water
items.ex: Eating extra salty food and drinking water can produce mild ECV excess with swelling and overnight weight gain.
w: Mild ECV deficit from losing isotonic sodium and water
ECV deficit causes weight loss and flat neck veins, not swelling.
Hyponatremia from gaining more water than salt
Hyponatremia causes cerebral signs, and salty food plus water adds isotonic fluid.
Clinical dehydration from losing more water than salt
Clinical dehydration involves low volume and concentrated fluids, not swelling.

alt.q: Which weight change does the nurse associate with the mild ECV excess that can follow a salty meal with water?
alt.a: Gain of 1 kg (2.2 lb) or more overnight
alt.ex: The book notes a gain of 1 kg (2.2 lb) or more overnight as a manifestation of mild ECV excess.
w: Loss of 1 kg (2.2 lb) or more overnight
Sudden overnight weight loss is a sign of ECV deficit.
Gain of 0.1 kg (0.2 lb) over 1 week
A tiny gradual gain does not reflect sudden fluid gain.
Loss of 0.5 kg (1.1 lb) over 1 week
Gradual weight loss does not indicate ECV excess.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: The signs and symptoms of both hypernatremia and hyponatremia are those of cerebral dysfunction, such as a decreased level of consciousness.
items.a: True
items.ex: Both imbalances shift water across brain cell membranes, causing confusion, lethargy, coma, or seizures.
items.ww: Table 42.3 lists decreased level of consciousness and possible seizures for both osmolality imbalances.

alt.q: Hypernatremia and hyponatremia can be told apart at the bedside because only hyponatremia decreases level of consciousness.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Both imbalances cause decreased level of consciousness, so laboratory sodium and osmolality values distinguish them.
alt.ww: Hypernatremia also causes confusion, lethargy, or coma because brain cells shrivel.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: The term hypovolemia means decreased vascular volume and often is used when discussing ECV deficit.
items.a: True
items.ex: Hypovolemia refers to low vascular volume, which occurs with an ECV deficit.
items.ww: The book defines hypovolemia as decreased vascular volume and links it to ECV deficit.

alt.q: Hypovolemia refers to body fluids that are too concentrated while fluid volume remains normal.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hypovolemia means decreased vascular volume; too-concentrated fluid with normal volume describes hypernatremia.
alt.ww: Concentration problems are osmolality imbalances; hypovolemia is a volume problem.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Increased hematocrit and BUN in a patient with ECV deficit reflect which process?
items.a: Hemoconcentration
items.ex: Loss of plasma volume concentrates the blood, raising hematocrit and BUN.
w: Hemodilution
Hemodilution lowers hematocrit and BUN in ECV excess.
Cerebral edema
Cerebral edema is brain cell swelling in hyponatremia.
Osmotic diuresis
Osmotic diuresis is a cause of hypernatremia, not a lab finding.

alt.q: Decreased hematocrit and BUN below 10 mg/dL in a patient with ECV excess reflect which process?
alt.a: Hemodilution
alt.ex: Excess isotonic fluid in the vascular space dilutes the blood, lowering hematocrit and BUN.
w: Hemoconcentration
Hemoconcentration raises hematocrit and BUN in ECV deficit.
Water intoxication
Water intoxication is another name for hyponatremia, an osmolality imbalance.
Osmotic diuresis
Osmotic diuresis causes water loss and hypernatremia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with ECV excess related to heart failure. Which new finding is most important to report?
items.a: Confusion with worsening lung crackles
items.ex: Confusion and pulmonary edema signal severe ECV excess, which needs prompt reporting.
w: Mild swelling of both ankles
Ankle edema is an expected finding of ECV excess, not a sign of severity.
Rings feeling slightly tight
Tight rings reflect mild ECV excess and are less urgent.
Weight gain of 0.2 kg
A 0.2-kg gain is small and does not signal severe excess.

alt.q: Which findings indicate that ECV excess has become severe?
alt.a: Confusion and pulmonary edema
alt.ex: Table 42.3 lists confusion and pulmonary edema as signs of severe ECV excess.
w: Thirst and oliguria
Thirst and oliguria are signs of severe ECV deficit.
Flat neck veins and tachycardia
These are signs of ECV deficit.
Cold, clammy skin and hypotension
These are signs of severe ECV deficit and hypovolemic shock.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which patient is most likely to develop clinical dehydration?
items.a: A patient with gastroenteritis and fever who cannot keep fluids down
items.ex: Clinical dehydration is common when vomiting and diarrhea losses are not replaced, often with fever increasing water loss.
w: A patient with SIADH who is receiving IV 5% dextrose in water
SIADH and D5W both add relatively more water than salt, causing hyponatremia.
A patient with heart failure who has been eating salty foods
Heart failure and salty foods lead to ECV excess, not dehydration.
A patient with psychogenic polydipsia who drinks excessive water
Excessive water intake causes hyponatremia, not clinical dehydration.

alt.q: Clinical dehydration is the combination of which two imbalances?
alt.a: ECV deficit and hypernatremia
alt.ex: Clinical dehydration means the ECV is too low and body fluids are too concentrated.
w: ECV deficit and hyponatremia
Hyponatremia means body fluids are too dilute, not too concentrated.
ECV excess and hypernatremia
ECV excess means too much volume, not too little.
ECV excess and hyponatremia
This combination involves too much volume and dilute fluid, the opposite of dehydration.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why is sodium discussed separately from the other electrolytes in the electrolyte balance section?
items.a: Serum sodium imbalances are the osmolality imbalances
items.ex: Hypernatremia and hyponatremia are the osmolality imbalances, so sodium is covered with fluid imbalances.
w: Sodium is not considered an electrolyte
Sodium is an electrolyte; it is excluded only because its imbalances are osmolality imbalances.
Sodium is measured only inside the cells
Laboratory values measure serum, not intracellular, electrolyte levels.
Sodium is unaffected by intake and output
Sodium balance depends on intake and output, as with ECV imbalances.

alt.q: Serum sodium imbalances are classified as which type of imbalance?
alt.a: Osmolality imbalances
alt.ex: Hypernatremia and hyponatremia are disturbances in body fluid concentration, so they are osmolality imbalances.
w: Extracellular volume imbalances
ECV imbalances involve isotonic gain or loss with normal osmolality.
Acid-base imbalances
Acid-base imbalances involve hydrogen ion concentration, not serum sodium.
Electrolyte distribution imbalances
The book groups serum sodium imbalances with osmolality imbalances.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with renal disease has oliguria. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of teaching about potassium intake?
items.a: I need to limit potatoes and fruits because my kidneys excrete less potassium.
items.ex: Oliguria decreases renal potassium excretion, so potassium intake must decrease to maintain balance.
w: I should eat more potatoes and fruits because I make little urine.
Increasing potassium intake when excretion is reduced would cause potassium to accumulate.
My urine output does not affect how much potassium stays in my body.
Oliguria decreases renal potassium excretion, so it does affect potassium balance.
I should add Brazil nuts and molasses to keep my potassium up.
These are potassium sources; intake should decrease when renal excretion falls.

alt.q: Why must a patient with oliguria decrease electrolyte intake such as potassium?
alt.a: Oliguria decreases renal excretion of potassium
alt.ex: When output decreases, as with oliguria, intake must also decrease to keep electrolytes balanced.
w: Oliguria increases renal excretion of potassium
Polyuria, not oliguria, increases renal potassium excretion.
Oliguria shifts potassium into cells
Insulin, epinephrine, and alkalosis shift potassium into cells.
Oliguria increases fecal excretion of potassium
Diarrhea, not oliguria, increases fecal potassium excretion.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which items are listed as dietary sources of potassium? Select all that apply.
o: Fruits

Potatoes
Potatoes are a listed potassium source.
Brazil nuts
Brazil nuts are a listed potassium source.
Molasses
Molasses is a listed potassium source.
Aluminum antacids
Aluminum antacids prevent phosphate absorption; they are not a potassium source.
Black licorice
Black licorice increases renal potassium excretion rather than supplying potassium.
items.ex: Table 42.4 lists fruits, potatoes, instant coffee, molasses, and Brazil nuts as potassium sources; potassium absorbs easily.

alt.q: Which items are listed as dietary sources of calcium? Select all that apply.
o: Dairy products
Dairy products are a listed calcium source.
Canned fish with bones
Canned fish with bones is a listed calcium source.
Broccoli
Broccoli is a listed calcium source.
Black licorice
Black licorice affects potassium excretion and is not a calcium source.
Aluminum antacids
Aluminum antacids prevent phosphate absorption; they are not a calcium source.
alt.ex: Table 42.4 lists dairy products, canned fish with bones, broccoli, and oranges as calcium sources.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which factor shifts potassium from the ECF into cells?
items.a: Insulin
items.ex: Insulin, epinephrine, and alkalosis shift potassium into cells.
w: Some types of acidosis
Some types of acidosis shift potassium out of cells.
Black licorice
Black licorice increases renal excretion of potassium; it does not shift it into cells.
Oliguria
Oliguria decreases renal potassium excretion; it does not shift potassium into cells.

alt.q: Which factor shifts potassium out of cells into the ECF?
alt.a: Some types of acidosis
alt.ex: Some types of acidosis shift potassium out of cells, whereas alkalosis shifts it in.
w: Insulin
Insulin shifts potassium into cells.
Epinephrine
Epinephrine shifts potassium into cells.
Alkalosis
Alkalosis shifts potassium into cells, not out of them.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which medication class decreases renal excretion of calcium?
items.a: Thiazide diuretics
items.ex: Table 42.4 lists thiazide diuretics as decreasing renal excretion of calcium.
w: Aluminum antacids
Aluminum antacids prevent phosphate absorption.
Magnesium-containing laxatives
These are a source of magnesium intake, not a factor reducing calcium excretion.
Insulin
Insulin shifts potassium and phosphate into cells.

alt.q: A patient taking a thiazide diuretic asks how the drug affects calcium. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: It decreases the amount of calcium your kidneys excrete.
alt.ex: Thiazide diuretics decrease renal excretion of calcium.
w: It increases the amount of calcium your kidneys excrete.
Thiazides decrease, rather than increase, renal calcium excretion.
It shifts calcium out of your bones into your blood.
Parathyroid hormone, not a thiazide, shifts calcium out of bone.
It blocks calcium absorption from the dairy foods you eat.
Undigested fat, not thiazides, prevents calcium absorption.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which hormone shifts calcium out of bone into the blood?
items.a: Parathyroid hormone
items.ex: Parathyroid hormone shifts calcium out of bone, whereas calcitonin shifts calcium into bone.
w: Calcitonin
Calcitonin shifts calcium into bone, the opposite effect.
Aldosterone
Aldosterone affects sodium, water, potassium, and hydrogen ion excretion.
Insulin
Insulin shifts potassium and phosphate into cells.

alt.q: What is the effect of calcitonin on calcium distribution?
alt.a: It shifts calcium into bone
alt.ex: Calcitonin moves calcium into bone, opposing parathyroid hormone.
w: It shifts calcium out of bone
Parathyroid hormone shifts calcium out of bone.
It shifts phosphate out of cells
Calcitonin’s listed effect is on calcium distribution into bone.
It shifts potassium into cells
Insulin, epinephrine, and alkalosis shift potassium into cells.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Potassium is absorbed easily from the GI tract.
items.a: True
items.ex: Table 42.4 notes that potassium absorbs easily, so dietary sources readily affect potassium balance.
items.ww: The book states potassium absorbs easily, unlike calcium and magnesium, whose absorption undigested fat can block.

alt.q: Potassium is poorly absorbed from the GI tract, so dietary sources have little effect on its balance.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Potassium absorbs easily, so intake from foods such as fruits and potatoes affects balance.
alt.ww: Because potassium is absorbed easily, dietary intake must be adjusted when output changes.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Electrolyte values on laboratory reports are measured in blood serum and do not measure intracellular levels.
items.a: True
items.ex: Laboratory reports measure serum electrolytes, even though K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, and phosphate are concentrated in cells and bone.
items.ww: Serum values reflect only the low plasma concentrations, not the much higher intracellular levels.

alt.q: A normal serum potassium value directly measures the potassium concentration inside the patient’s cells.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Serum values do not measure intracellular levels, where most potassium is located.
alt.ww: Laboratory electrolyte values are measured in serum, so they do not measure intracellular concentration.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient who eats large amounts of black licorice also takes a diuretic. The nurse monitors for loss of which electrolyte through increased renal excretion?
items.a: Potassium
items.ex: Black licorice and diuretics both increase renal excretion of potassium.
w: Calcium
Thiazide diuretics decrease renal calcium excretion, and licorice is not listed for calcium.
Phosphate
Phosphate renal excretion is linked to oliguria in the table, not licorice or diuretics.
Sodium
Licorice causes sodium retention; the shared effect of licorice and diuretics is potassium loss.

alt.q: Which pair of factors increases renal excretion of potassium?
alt.a: Aldosterone and hypomagnesemia
alt.ex: Aldosterone, black licorice, diuretics, hypomagnesemia, and polyuria increase renal potassium excretion.
w: Oliguria and insulin
Oliguria decreases renal potassium excretion, and insulin shifts potassium into cells.
Insulin and epinephrine
These shift potassium into cells rather than increasing its excretion.
Oliguria and alkalosis
Oliguria decreases excretion, and alkalosis shifts potassium into cells.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient has chronic diarrhea with undigested fat in the stool. Which electrolytes are at risk because undigested fat prevents their absorption and increases fecal excretion?
items.a: Calcium and magnesium
items.ex: Undigested fat prevents absorption and, with chronic diarrhea, increases fecal excretion of calcium and magnesium.
w: Potassium and phosphate
Undigested fat is not listed as affecting potassium or phosphate absorption.
Sodium and potassium
The table links undigested fat to calcium and magnesium, not sodium and potassium.
Phosphate and sodium
Aluminum antacids, not undigested fat, prevent phosphate absorption.

alt.q: Which substance prevents absorption of phosphate from the GI tract?
alt.a: Aluminum antacids
alt.ex: Table 42.4 lists aluminum antacids as preventing phosphate absorption.
w: Magnesium-containing antacids
Magnesium-containing antacids are a source of magnesium.
Processed foods
Processed foods are a source of phosphate.
Milk
Milk is a source of phosphate.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with heavy alcohol use has rising blood ethanol levels. Increased renal excretion of which electrolyte does the nurse anticipate?
items.a: Magnesium
items.ex: Rising blood ethanol increases renal excretion of magnesium.
w: Calcium
Rising ethanol is not listed as affecting calcium excretion.
Phosphate
Phosphate renal excretion is linked to oliguria, not ethanol, in the table.
Chloride
Chloride is not among the electrolytes the table links to rising blood ethanol.

alt.q: A patient has oliguria. How does this affect magnesium balance?
alt.a: Renal excretion of magnesium decreases
alt.ex: Oliguria decreases renal excretion of magnesium, so magnesium can accumulate.
w: Renal excretion of magnesium increases
Rising blood ethanol, not oliguria, increases renal magnesium excretion.
Fecal excretion of magnesium increases
Chronic diarrhea and undigested fat increase fecal excretion.
Magnesium shifts out of bone into blood
Oliguria affects renal excretion, not bone distribution of magnesium.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient receives IV insulin. Which electrolyte change should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: Potassium and phosphate shift into cells, lowering serum levels
items.ex: Insulin shifts both potassium and phosphate from the ECF into cells.
w: Potassium and phosphate shift out of cells, raising serum levels
Insulin moves these electrolytes into cells, not out of them.
Calcium shifts out of bone, raising serum calcium levels
Parathyroid hormone shifts calcium out of bone.
Magnesium excretion in the urine increases sharply
Rising blood ethanol increases renal magnesium excretion, not insulin.

alt.q: Which hormones shift both potassium and phosphate into cells?
alt.a: Insulin and epinephrine
alt.ex: Table 42.4 lists insulin and epinephrine as shifting potassium and phosphate into cells.
w: Parathyroid hormone and calcitonin
These hormones shift calcium out of and into bone.
Aldosterone and ADH
These hormones regulate renal sodium, water, and potassium excretion.
ANP and renin
These regulate sodium and water balance, not cellular shifts of electrolytes.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Through which routes does electrolyte output occur? Select all that apply.
o: Urine
Urine is a normal route of electrolyte excretion.
Feces
Feces are a normal route of electrolyte excretion.
Sweat
Sweat contains electrolytes such as sodium.
Drainage from fistulas
Fistula drainage is an abnormal route of electrolyte output.
Exhaled water vapor
Insensible lung loss is water, not an electrolyte output route listed in the book.
Shift into intracellular fluid
Movement into cells is electrolyte distribution, not output.
items.ex: Electrolytes are normally excreted in urine, feces, and sweat and are also lost by vomiting, drainage tubes, or fistulas.

alt.q: A patient has a nasogastric tube to suction and a draining fistula. Which are sources of electrolyte output for this patient? Select all that apply.
o: Nasogastric drainage
Drainage tubes are a route of electrolyte output.
Fistula drainage
Fistulas are a route of electrolyte output.
Urine
Urine is a normal route of electrolyte output.
IV fluid infusion
IV fluids are a route of intake, not output.
Oral fluid intake
Oral fluids are intake, not output.
alt.ex: Electrolyte output includes normal routes plus abnormal losses such as vomiting, drainage tubes, and fistulas.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which statements about electrolyte distribution are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Plasma levels of K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, and phosphate are low compared with cells and bone.
These electrolytes are concentrated in cells and bone, not plasma.
Concentration differences between plasma and cells are necessary for normal muscle and nerve function.
The book links these gradients to normal muscle and nerve function.
Only ionized calcium in the blood is active.
Some blood calcium is bound and inactive; only ionized calcium is active.
Most body calcium is in the ECF.
Calcium is low in ECF; most is in bones.
Potassium is higher in the ECF than in the ICF.
Potassium is low in ECF and high in ICF.
items.ex: K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, and phosphate are low in plasma and high in cells and bone, gradients needed for muscle and nerve function.

alt.q: Which electrolytes have plasma concentrations that are very low compared with their concentrations in cells and bone? Select all that apply.
o: Potassium (K+)
K+ is low in ECF and high in ICF.
Calcium (Ca2+)
Ca2+ is low in ECF and mostly in bones.
Magnesium (Mg2+)
Mg2+ is low in ECF and mostly in bones and cells.
Phosphate
Phosphate is low in ECF and higher in ICF and bones.
Sodium (Na+)
Na+ is higher in the ECF than in the ICF.
Chloride (Cl−)
Cl− is higher in the ECF than in the ICF.
alt.ex: Plasma levels of K+, Ca2+, Mg2+, and phosphate are very low compared with cells and bone.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Some calcium in the blood is bound and inactive; only [[ionized]] calcium is active.
items.ex: Laboratory tables list total and ionized calcium separately because only ionized calcium is physiologically active.

alt.q: The physiologically active form of calcium in the blood is [[ionized]] calcium.
alt.ex: Laboratory tables list total and ionized calcium separately because only ionized calcium is physiologically active.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: When electrolyte output increases, electrolyte intake must increase to maintain electrolyte balance.
items.a: True
items.ex: Balance requires intake to match output, so higher losses require higher intake.
items.ww: Without increased intake, increased output would deplete electrolytes.

alt.q: A patient with oliguria should increase electrolyte intake to make up for the reduced urine output.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: When output decreases, as with oliguria, electrolyte intake must also decrease to maintain balance.
alt.ww: Oliguria reduces electrolyte excretion, so more intake would cause accumulation.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Where is most of the body’s calcium located?
items.a: In bones, with some inside cells
items.ex: Calcium is low in the ECF, mostly in bones, and some is intracellular.
w: In the ECF, bound to plasma proteins
Calcium is low in the ECF; only part of blood calcium is bound.
In plasma as ionized calcium
Ionized calcium is the active blood form, but plasma calcium is low overall.
In interstitial fluid around cells
Calcium is low in all ECF, including interstitial fluid.

alt.q: Where is most of the body’s magnesium located?
alt.a: In bones and inside cells
alt.ex: Magnesium is low in the ECF and found mostly in bones and inside cells.
w: In plasma, bound to proteins
Some blood magnesium is bound, but plasma magnesium is low overall.
In interstitial fluid
Magnesium is low in the ECF, which includes interstitial fluid.
In the ECF as free magnesium
Free magnesium is the active blood form, but ECF levels are low.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with oliguria from renal disease takes magnesium-containing antacids and laxatives daily. Which is the nurse’s greatest concern?
items.a: Magnesium accumulation from high intake and low renal excretion
items.ex: Magnesium-containing products add intake while oliguria decreases renal excretion, so magnesium can build up.
w: Magnesium loss because oliguria increases renal excretion
Oliguria decreases, rather than increases, renal magnesium excretion.
Calcium loss because antacids block calcium absorption
Undigested fat blocks calcium absorption; aluminum antacids block phosphate.
Potassium loss because laxatives shift potassium into cells
Insulin, epinephrine, and alkalosis shift potassium into cells, not laxatives.

alt.q: Which patient has the greatest risk of magnesium accumulation?
alt.a: A patient with oliguria who takes magnesium-containing laxatives
alt.ex: High magnesium intake combined with decreased renal excretion from oliguria leads to accumulation.
w: A patient with chronic diarrhea and undigested fat in stool
Chronic diarrhea and undigested fat increase fecal magnesium loss.
A patient with heavy alcohol use and rising blood ethanol
Rising ethanol increases renal magnesium excretion, causing loss.
A patient with polyuria who takes aluminum-containing antacids
Aluminum antacids affect phosphate, and polyuria increases excretion.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with oliguria has a rising serum phosphate level. Which change in serum calcium should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: Serum calcium decreases
items.ex: Calcium decreases in the blood when phosphate rises, and phosphate decreases when calcium rises.
w: Serum calcium increases
Calcium and phosphate move in opposite directions, so calcium falls when phosphate rises.
Serum calcium stays the same
Calcium is affected because its blood level falls as phosphate rises.
Calcium shifts out of bone and rises
Parathyroid hormone shifts calcium out of bone; rising phosphate lowers blood calcium.

alt.q: A patient’s serum calcium level is rising. Which change in serum phosphate does the nurse expect?
alt.a: Serum phosphate decreases
alt.ex: Phosphate decreases in the blood when calcium rises, reflecting their inverse relationship.
w: Serum phosphate increases
Phosphate and calcium vary inversely, so phosphate falls when calcium rises.
Serum phosphate stays the same
Rising calcium lowers blood phosphate.
Phosphate shifts out of cells and rises
Rising calcium lowers phosphate; insulin and epinephrine shift phosphate into cells.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which serum potassium level meets the laboratory definition of hypokalemia?
items.a: 3.2 mEq/L
items.ex: Hypokalemia is a serum potassium level below 3.5 mEq/L (3.5 mmol/L).
w: 3.8 mEq/L
A level of 3.8 mEq/L is above the 3.5 mEq/L cutoff, so it is not hypokalemia.
4.6 mEq/L
A level of 4.6 mEq/L is between 3.5 and 5 mEq/L, which is not an imbalance.
5.4 mEq/L
A level above 5 mEq/L indicates hyperkalemia, not hypokalemia.

alt.q: Which serum potassium level indicates hyperkalemia?
alt.a: 5.6 mEq/L
alt.ex: Hyperkalemia is a serum potassium level above 5 mEq/L (5 mmol/L).
w: 3.3 mEq/L
A level below 3.5 mEq/L indicates hypokalemia.
4.1 mEq/L
A level of 4.1 mEq/L is not above 5 mEq/L, so it is not hyperkalemia.
4.8 mEq/L
A level of 4.8 mEq/L is still below the 5 mEq/L cutoff for hyperkalemia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with oliguria has a new prescription for an IV solution containing potassium chloride. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Check the patient’s recent urine output
items.ex: Decreased urine output lowers potassium output, so oliguria creates high risk of hyperkalemia when potassium is given.
w: Start the infusion at the prescribed rate
Starting potassium before checking urine output risks hyperkalemia in a patient with oliguria.
Encourage potassium-rich foods at meals
Adding potassium intake increases hyperkalemia risk when output is decreased.
Obtain a sample for a serum calcium level
Calcium does not determine whether potassium can be safely given; urine output does.

alt.q: Before hanging an IV bag with added potassium, the nurse reviews the record. Which finding should the nurse clarify with the health care provider before starting it?
alt.a: Urine output of 80 mL over the past 8 hours
alt.ex: Low urine output decreases potassium excretion, so giving IV potassium could cause life-threatening hyperkalemia.
w: Serum potassium level of 3.2 mEq/L
A low potassium level is the reason for replacement, not a reason to hold it.
Bilateral weakness of the quadriceps muscles
Quadriceps weakness is a sign of hypokalemia, which supports potassium replacement.
Recent use of a potassium-wasting diuretic
Potassium-wasting diuretics cause potassium loss, which supports replacement.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient taking a potassium-wasting diuretic has a serum potassium of 2.9 mEq/L and bilateral quadriceps weakness. Which finding is most important for the nurse to report immediately?
items.a: Shallow, weak respirations
items.ex: Hypokalemic weakness can ascend to the respiratory muscles, which is life threatening.
w: Abdominal distention
Abdominal distention is an expected GI sign of hypokalemia and not an immediate threat to breathing.
Decreased bowel sounds
Decreased bowel sounds are expected with hypokalemia but are less urgent than respiratory weakness.
Constipation for 2 days
Constipation reflects GI effects of hypokalemia and is not life threatening.

alt.q: When does the muscle weakness of hypokalemia become life threatening?
alt.a: When it ascends to involve the respiratory muscles
alt.ex: Hypokalemic weakness begins in the quadriceps and is life threatening once it reaches the respiratory muscles.
w: When it remains limited to the quadriceps muscles
Quadriceps weakness is the usual starting point and is not itself life threatening.
When it occurs together with constipation
Constipation is a GI sign of hypokalemia, not what makes weakness life threatening.
When it occurs together with abdominal distention
Abdominal distention is a GI sign of hypokalemia, not what makes weakness life threatening.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which patient is at highest risk for hyperkalemia?
items.a: A patient with crushing trauma to both legs
items.ex: Massive cellular damage such as crushing trauma shifts potassium out of cells into the ECF.
w: A patient receiving insulin for diabetic ketoacidosis
Insulin treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis shifts potassium into cells, causing hypokalemia.
A patient with prolonged nasogastric drainage
Nasogastric drainage increases potassium output, causing hypokalemia.
A patient taking a potassium-wasting diuretic
Potassium-wasting diuretics increase potassium output, causing hypokalemia.

alt.q: Which condition causes hyperkalemia by decreasing potassium output?
alt.a: Use of a potassium-sparing diuretic
alt.ex: Potassium-sparing diuretics, oliguria, and adrenal insufficiency all decrease potassium output.
w: Cell damage from cytotoxic chemotherapy
Chemotherapy-related cell damage causes hyperkalemia by shifting potassium out of cells, not by decreasing output.
Rapid infusion of stored blood
Rapid infusion of stored blood causes hyperkalemia through increased potassium intake.
Excess ingestion of potassium salt substitutes
Salt substitutes cause hyperkalemia through increased potassium intake.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: After rapid transfusion of several units of stored blood, a patient reports numbness and tingling around the mouth and in the fingers. Which imbalance should the nurse suspect?
items.a: Ionized hypocalcemia
items.ex: Citrate in stored blood binds ionized calcium, and circumoral and finger tingling are signs of hypocalcemia.
w: Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia decreases neuromuscular excitability and causes lethargy, not tingling.
Hypokalemia
Transfusion of stored blood does not cause hypokalemia, and hypokalemia causes weakness rather than circumoral tingling.
Hypermagnesemia
Hypermagnesemia causes lethargy and hypoactive reflexes; citrated blood lowers rather than raises active magnesium.

alt.q: Why can rapid administration of citrated stored blood cause symptomatic hypocalcemia?
alt.a: Citrate binds ionized calcium, shifting it to an inactive form
alt.ex: Citrate binding shifts calcium from the active ionized form to an inactive bound form.
w: Citrate increases calcium excretion by the kidneys
Citrate acts in the blood by binding calcium, not by increasing renal excretion.
Citrate moves calcium out of the blood into bone
Citrate binds calcium in the blood; it does not shift calcium into bone.
Citrate blocks calcium absorption from the intestine
Transfused citrate binds calcium already in the blood rather than blocking intestinal absorption.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why do people with acute pancreatitis frequently develop hypocalcemia?
items.a: Calcium binds to undigested fat in the feces and is excreted
items.ex: Calcium bound to fecal fat is lost, decreasing dietary absorption and preventing reabsorption from GI fluids.
w: Pancreatic enzymes destroy parathyroid hormone in the blood
The book attributes the hypocalcemia to fecal fat binding, not to destroyed parathyroid hormone.
Vomiting removes calcium-rich gastric fluid from the body
The mechanism in pancreatitis is calcium loss with undigested fat in stools.
Inflamed pancreatic cells release citrate that binds calcium
Citrate binding occurs with transfusion of stored blood, not pancreatitis.

alt.q: A patient with acute pancreatitis has fatty stools. How does the undigested fat contribute to hypocalcemia?
alt.a: It reduces dietary calcium absorption and GI calcium reabsorption
alt.ex: Calcium binds the fat and is excreted, so less is absorbed from food and GI fluids.
w: It increases calcium excretion by the kidneys
The calcium is lost in feces, not through increased renal excretion.
It shifts calcium from the blood into bone
Fecal fat binds calcium in the GI tract; it does not move calcium into bone.
It converts ionized calcium into protein-bound calcium
Protein binding is not the mechanism; calcium binds fat in the feces and is excreted.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with metastatic breast cancer reports increasing fatigue, nausea, and constipation and is lethargic. Which electrolyte imbalance should the nurse suspect?
items.a: Hypercalcemia
items.ex: Some cancer cells secrete chemicals that shift calcium out of bone; hypercalcemia decreases neuromuscular excitability, causing lethargy.
w: Hypocalcemia
Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability, causing tingling, spasms, and tetany rather than lethargy.
Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia causes abdominal cramps and diarrhea, not constipation and lethargy.
Hypomagnesemia
Hypomagnesemia increases neuromuscular excitability, causing hyperactive reflexes and tetany.

alt.q: A patient with lung cancer has hypercalcemia because tumor chemicals shift calcium out of bone. Which complication should the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: Pathological fractures
alt.ex: Calcium leaving bone weakens it, so bones can break with forces that would not break healthy bone.
w: Tetany and laryngospasm
Tetany and laryngospasm result from the increased excitability of hypocalcemia.
Positive Chvostek sign
A positive Chvostek sign reflects increased excitability seen with hypocalcemia or hypomagnesemia.
Peaked T waves
Peaked T waves are an ECG change of hyperkalemia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why do the signs and symptoms of hypomagnesemia resemble those of hypocalcemia?
items.a: Both imbalances increase neuromuscular excitability
items.ex: Hypomagnesemia, like hypocalcemia, increases neuromuscular excitability, producing tetany, twitching, and hyperactive reflexes.
w: Both imbalances decrease neuromuscular excitability
Decreased excitability is the basis of hypercalcemia and hypermagnesemia signs.
Both imbalances result from excess antacid use
Magnesium-containing antacids cause hypermagnesemia, not these deficits.
Both imbalances shift potassium out of cells
Shifts of potassium out of cells cause hyperkalemia and are not the shared mechanism.

alt.q: Which pair of imbalances share signs such as lethargy and diminished reflexes because both decrease neuromuscular excitability?
alt.a: Hypercalcemia and hypermagnesemia
alt.ex: Both hypercalcemia and hypermagnesemia decrease neuromuscular excitability, causing lethargy and hypoactive reflexes.
w: Hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia
These deficits increase neuromuscular excitability, causing hyperactive reflexes.
Hypocalcemia and hypermagnesemia
Hypocalcemia increases excitability, so this pair does not share decreased excitability.
Hypercalcemia and hypomagnesemia
Hypomagnesemia increases excitability, so this pair does not share decreased excitability.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with oliguric end-stage renal disease has been taking a magnesium-containing antacid daily. Which assessment finding is most important to report immediately?
items.a: Decreased rate and depth of respirations
items.ex: Decreased rate and depth of respirations signals severe hypermagnesemia, which can progress to cardiac arrest.
w: Flushing and a sensation of warmth
Flushing and warmth occur with an acute rise in magnesium but are not immediately life threatening.
Lethargy and drowsiness
Lethargy is a common sign of hypermagnesemia but is less urgent than respiratory depression.
Hypoactive deep tendon reflexes
Hypoactive reflexes are expected with hypermagnesemia but do not threaten the airway or breathing.

alt.q: Which set of findings would the nurse expect in a patient with hypermagnesemia?
alt.a: Hypoactive reflexes, bradycardia, and hypotension
alt.ex: Hypermagnesemia decreases neuromuscular excitability, producing hypoactive reflexes, bradycardia, and hypotension.
w: Hyperactive reflexes, tachycardia, and hypertension
These findings reflect hypomagnesemia, which increases excitability.
Positive Chvostek sign, tetany, and seizures
These findings reflect increased excitability from hypocalcemia or hypomagnesemia.
Peaked T waves, diarrhea, and abdominal cramps
These findings are associated with hyperkalemia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which form of calcium in the blood is physiologically active?
items.a: Ionized calcium
items.ex: Ionized calcium is the physiologically active form; protein- and anion-bound calcium are inactive.
w: Protein-bound calcium
Calcium bound to plasma proteins is an inactive form.
Citrate-bound calcium
Calcium bound to small anions such as citrate is inactive.
Calcium stored in bone
Bone calcium is not circulating active calcium; it can shift into the ECF.

alt.q: Which statement about total blood calcium is accurate?
alt.a: It includes active ionized calcium and inactive bound forms
alt.ex: Total blood calcium contains ionized calcium plus inactive forms bound to plasma proteins and small anions.
w: It consists only of active ionized calcium
Total calcium also contains inactive protein- and anion-bound calcium.
It consists only of protein-bound calcium
Total calcium also includes ionized calcium and anion-bound calcium.
It excludes calcium bound to anions such as citrate
Calcium bound to small anions such as citrate is part of total blood calcium.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with chronic alcoholism and malnutrition has muscle twitching, insomnia, and tachycardia. Which imbalance is most likely?
items.a: Hypomagnesemia
items.ex: Chronic alcoholism and malnutrition decrease magnesium intake and absorption; twitching, insomnia, and tachycardia are signs of hypomagnesemia.
w: Hypermagnesemia
Hypermagnesemia causes lethargy, bradycardia, and hypotension rather than twitching and tachycardia.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia decreases excitability, causing lethargy and diminished reflexes.
Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia is linked to decreased output or cell damage, not alcoholism, and causes cramps and diarrhea.

alt.q: Which serum magnesium level indicates hypomagnesemia?
alt.a: 1.1 mEq/L
alt.ex: Hypomagnesemia is a serum magnesium level below 1.3 mEq/L (0.65 mmol/L).
w: 1.6 mEq/L
A level of 1.6 mEq/L is above the 1.3 mEq/L cutoff for hypomagnesemia.
1.9 mEq/L
A level of 1.9 mEq/L is not below 1.3 mEq/L or above 2.1 mEq/L.
2.4 mEq/L
A level above 2.1 mEq/L indicates hypermagnesemia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which conditions can cause hypokalemia? Select all that apply.
o: Prolonged vomiting
Vomiting increases potassium output from the GI tract.
Nasogastric or fistula drainage
GI drainage removes potassium-containing fluid.
Potassium-wasting diuretic therapy
Potassium-wasting diuretics increase renal potassium output.
Insulin treatment of diabetic ketoacidosis
Insulin shifts potassium from the ECF into cells.
Potassium-sparing diuretic therapy
Potassium-sparing diuretics decrease potassium output and cause hyperkalemia.
Crushing trauma to a limb
Massive cell damage shifts potassium out of cells, causing hyperkalemia.
items.ex: Hypokalemia results from decreased intake, shift into cells, or increased output such as GI losses and potassium-wasting diuretics.

alt.q: Which conditions can cause hyperkalemia? Select all that apply.
o: Oliguria from end-stage kidney disease
Oliguria decreases potassium output.
Excess use of potassium salt substitutes
Salt substitutes increase potassium intake.
Adrenal insufficiency
Deficient aldosterone and cortisol decrease potassium output.
Cytotoxic chemotherapy causing massive cell damage
Cell damage shifts potassium out of cells into the ECF.
Glucocorticoid therapy
Glucocorticoid therapy increases potassium output and causes hypokalemia.
Aldosterone excess
Excess aldosterone increases potassium output and causes hypokalemia.
alt.ex: Hyperkalemia results from increased intake, shift out of cells, or decreased output such as oliguria and adrenal insufficiency.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which findings would the nurse expect in a patient with hypocalcemia? Select all that apply.
o: Positive Chvostek sign
Facial muscle contraction when the facial nerve is tapped reflects increased excitability.
Numbness and tingling around the mouth
Circumoral numbness and tingling are signs of hypocalcemia.
Hyperactive reflexes
Increased neuromuscular excitability produces hyperactive reflexes.
Carpal and pedal spasms
Carpal and pedal spasms and tetany reflect increased excitability.
Diminished reflexes
Diminished reflexes occur with hypercalcemia, which decreases excitability.
Anorexia and constipation
Anorexia and constipation are signs of hypercalcemia.
items.ex: Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability, causing tingling, a positive Chvostek sign, hyperactive reflexes, spasms, and tetany.

alt.q: Which findings would the nurse expect in a patient with hypercalcemia? Select all that apply.
o: Anorexia, nausea, and vomiting
GI signs are part of hypercalcemia’s presentation.
Constipation
Constipation is a sign of hypercalcemia.
Diminished reflexes
Decreased neuromuscular excitability causes diminished reflexes.
Confusion and personality change
Hypercalcemia can cause confusion, personality change, and decreased level of consciousness.
Positive Chvostek sign
A positive Chvostek sign reflects increased excitability seen with hypocalcemia.
Laryngospasm
Laryngospasm results from the increased excitability of hypocalcemia.
alt.ex: Hypercalcemia decreases neuromuscular excitability, causing lethargy, diminished reflexes, GI symptoms, and confusion.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which conditions can cause hypercalcemia? Select all that apply.
o: Prolonged immobilization
Immobilization shifts calcium out of bone into the ECF.
Hyperparathyroidism
Hyperparathyroidism shifts calcium out of bone.
Thiazide diuretic use
Thiazide diuretics decrease calcium output.
Milk-alkali syndrome
Milk-alkali syndrome increases calcium intake and absorption.
Vitamin D deficiency
Vitamin D deficiency decreases calcium absorption and causes hypocalcemia.
Hypoparathyroidism
Hypoparathyroidism shifts calcium into bone and causes hypocalcemia.
items.ex: Hypercalcemia results from increased intake, shift of calcium out of bone, or decreased output.

alt.q: Which conditions can cause hypomagnesemia? Select all that apply.
o: Malnutrition
Malnutrition decreases magnesium intake.
Chronic alcoholism
Chronic alcoholism decreases magnesium intake and absorption.
Loop diuretic use
Thiazide and loop diuretics increase magnesium output.
Rapid administration of citrated blood
Citrate shifts magnesium to an inactive bound form.
Overuse of magnesium-containing antacids
Magnesium-containing antacids increase intake and cause hypermagnesemia.
Oliguric end-stage renal disease
Decreased renal output causes hypermagnesemia.
alt.ex: Hypomagnesemia results from decreased intake and absorption, shift to an inactive form, or increased output.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Hypercalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability, which explains its common sign of lethargy.
items.a: False
items.ex: Hypercalcemia decreases neuromuscular excitability; lethargy is its most common sign.
items.ww: Increased excitability is the basis of hypocalcemia and hypomagnesemia, not hypercalcemia.

alt.q: Hypocalcemia increases neuromuscular excitability, which is the basis for its signs and symptoms.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Increased excitability explains tingling, hyperactive reflexes, spasms, tetany, and seizures in hypocalcemia.
alt.ww: Decreased excitability belongs to hypercalcemia; hypocalcemia does the opposite.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A shift of an electrolyte from cells or bone into the ECF can cause a plasma electrolyte excess.
items.a: True
items.ex: Plasma excess results from intake greater than output or a shift from cells or bone into the ECF.
items.ww: Shifts out of cells or bone add electrolyte to the plasma, so they can produce an excess.

alt.q: A shift of an electrolyte from the ECF into cells or bone causes a plasma electrolyte excess.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A shift from the ECF into cells or bone removes electrolyte from plasma, causing a deficit.
alt.ww: Moving electrolyte out of the plasma lowers its concentration, so it cannot create an excess.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: As serum magnesium continues to rise, symptoms of hypermagnesemia progress from weakness and drowsiness to somnolence and paralysis.
items.a: True
items.ex: Rising magnesium increasingly decreases neuromuscular excitability, progressing to somnolence and paralysis.
items.ww: Hypermagnesemia worsens as levels rise; it does not cause excitability signs such as tetany.

alt.q: As serum magnesium continues to rise, symptoms of hypermagnesemia progress from muscle twitching to tetany and seizures.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Twitching, tetany, and seizures reflect increased excitability from hypomagnesemia; rising magnesium causes drowsiness, somnolence, and paralysis.
alt.ww: Hypermagnesemia decreases neuromuscular excitability, so it does not progress to tetany.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Contraction of the facial muscles when the facial nerve is tapped is called a positive [[Chvostek|Chvostek’s|Chvostek's]] sign.
items.ex: A positive Chvostek sign reflects increased neuromuscular excitability in hypocalcemia or hypomagnesemia.

alt.q: A nurse taps the facial nerve of a patient with hypocalcemia and sees the facial muscles contract; this is a positive [[Chvostek|Chvostek’s|Chvostek's]] sign.
alt.ex: A positive Chvostek sign reflects increased neuromuscular excitability in hypocalcemia or hypomagnesemia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Hypocalcemia is a total serum calcium level below [[9.0|9]] mg/dL.
items.ex: Total serum calcium below 9.0 mg/dL (2.25 mmol/L) indicates hypocalcemia; above 10.5 mg/dL indicates hypercalcemia.

alt.q: Hypercalcemia is a total serum calcium level above [[10.5]] mg/dL.
alt.ex: Total serum calcium below 9.0 mg/dL (2.25 mmol/L) indicates hypocalcemia; above 10.5 mg/dL indicates hypercalcemia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which statement about metabolic acids is accurate?
items.a: They include all acids other than carbonic acid, such as lactic acid
items.ex: Metabolic acids are any acids that are not carbonic acid, including citric acid and lactic acid.
w: They are excreted mainly by the lungs as carbon dioxide and water
The lungs excrete carbonic acid; the kidneys excrete metabolic acids.
They form when carbon dioxide combines with water in the blood
Carbon dioxide plus water forms carbonic acid, not metabolic acids.
They are produced by cells only during disease states
Cellular metabolism constantly creates both carbonic and metabolic acids.

alt.q: Which organ system excretes metabolic acids?
alt.a: The kidneys
alt.ex: The kidneys excrete all acids except carbonic acid, which the lungs excrete.
w: The lungs
The lungs excrete carbonic acid as CO2 and water, not metabolic acids.
The liver
The liver is not one of the body’s two acid-excretion systems.
The skin
The skin is not one of the body’s two acid-excretion systems.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient’s arterial blood gas report shows a base excess of −6 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret this value?
items.a: The blood contains excessive metabolic acids
items.ex: Base excess below −2 indicates excessive metabolic acids overwhelming normal buffering capacity.
w: The blood contains excessive bicarbonate
Excessive bicarbonate is shown by a base excess above +2.
The lungs are retaining carbon dioxide
CO2 retention is shown by an increased PaCO2, not base excess.
Gas exchange in the alveoli is poor
Poor alveolar gas exchange is shown by a low PaO2.

alt.q: A patient’s arterial blood gas report shows a base excess of +5 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret this value?
alt.a: The blood contains excessive bicarbonate
alt.ex: Base excess above +2 indicates excessive amounts of bicarbonate.
w: The blood contains excessive metabolic acids
Excessive metabolic acids produce a base excess below −2.
The lungs are retaining carbon dioxide
CO2 retention is shown by an increased PaCO2, not base excess.
Gas exchange in the alveoli is poor
Poor alveolar gas exchange is shown by a low PaO2.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient’s PaCO2 is 52 mm Hg. Which interpretation is correct?
items.a: CO2 is accumulating in the blood because of hypoventilation
items.ex: Increased PaCO2 means CO2 (carbonic acid) is accumulating because the lungs are hypoventilating.
w: CO2 is being excreted excessively through hyperventilation
Hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 below 35 mm Hg.
The kidneys are retaining too many metabolic acids
Metabolic acid excess is reflected by a decreased HCO3−, not PaCO2.
The blood contains too few metabolic acids
Too few metabolic acids is reflected by an increased HCO3−.

alt.q: A patient’s PaCO2 is 30 mm Hg. Which interpretation is correct?
alt.a: CO2 is being excreted excessively through hyperventilation
alt.ex: Decreased PaCO2 indicates excessive CO2 excretion and less carbonic acid from hyperventilation.
w: CO2 is accumulating in the blood because of hypoventilation
Hypoventilation raises PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg.
The kidneys are retaining too many metabolic acids
Metabolic acid excess is reflected by a decreased HCO3−, not PaCO2.
The blood contains too few metabolic acids
Too few metabolic acids is reflected by an increased HCO3−.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient’s PaO2 has fallen from 75 mm Hg to 58 mm Hg over the past hour. What change in SaO2 should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: A rapid drop in oxygen saturation
items.ex: SaO2 drops rapidly once PaO2 falls below 60 mm Hg.
w: A slight rise in oxygen saturation
Falling PaO2 lowers, not raises, oxygen saturation.
No change until PaO2 falls below 40 mm Hg
SaO2 begins to drop rapidly below 60 mm Hg, well before 40 mm Hg.
A gradual drop only after the pH falls
The rapid drop is tied to PaO2 falling below 60 mm Hg, not to a pH change first.

alt.q: Below approximately which PaO2 level does SaO2 begin to drop rapidly?
alt.a: 60 mm Hg
alt.ex: SaO2 drops rapidly when PaO2 falls below 60 mm Hg (8 kPa).
w: 80 mm Hg
80 mm Hg is the lower end of normal PaO2, not the point of rapid desaturation.
90 mm Hg
90 mm Hg is within the normal PaO2 range of 80 to 100 mm Hg.
40 mm Hg
Rapid desaturation already begins below 60 mm Hg, before PaO2 reaches 40 mm Hg.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which is the major buffer system in the extracellular fluid?
items.a: Bicarbonate buffer system
items.ex: The bicarbonate buffer system is the major ECF buffer and buffers metabolic acids.
w: Hemoglobin buffer system
Hemoglobin is one of the other buffers, not the major ECF buffer.
Phosphate buffer system
Phosphate buffers are other buffers, notably in renal tubular fluid.
Protein buffer system
Protein buffers contribute but are not the major ECF buffer.

alt.q: In the bicarbonate buffer system, what is the normal ratio of bicarbonate to carbonic acid?
alt.ex: The buffer pair normally has a lot of bicarbonate and a small amount of carbonic acid, a 20:1 ratio.
w: This reverses the ratio; bicarbonate, not carbonic acid, is present in the larger amount.
The normal ratio is 20:1, not 10:1.
The pair is not balanced equally; bicarbonate greatly exceeds carbonic acid.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: During heavy exercise a patient’s cells release lactic acid into the blood. How does the bicarbonate buffer keep the blood pH from falling?
items.a: Bicarbonate takes up the free H+, forming carbonic acid
items.ex: When bicarbonate combines with H+ from a metabolic acid, the H+ is no longer free and does not lower pH.
w: Bicarbonate releases H+, forming carbonic acid
Bicarbonate takes up H+; it is carbonic acid that can release H+.
Carbonic acid takes up the free H+, forming bicarbonate
Carbonic acid releases H+ when there are too few; it does not take up excess H+.
Bicarbonate combines with lactic acid, forming ammonia
Ammonia is secreted by renal tubular cells; it is not a product of buffering.

alt.q: How quickly do body buffers respond to a change in the amount of free H+?
alt.a: Within seconds
alt.ex: Buffers work rapidly, within seconds, taking up or releasing H+ as needed.
w: Within a few minutes
A few minutes describes the start of compensatory hyperventilation, not buffering.
Within about 24 hours
About 24 hours is when renal compensation begins to show clinical effect.
Over 3 to 5 days
Three to 5 days is when renal compensation reaches a steady state.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which acids do the kidneys excrete?
items.a: All acids except carbonic acid
items.ex: The kidneys excrete all acids except carbonic acid; the lungs excrete carbonic acid as CO2 and water.
w: Only carbonic acid
Carbonic acid is the one acid the lungs, not the kidneys, excrete.
Only lactic acid and citric acid
These are examples, but the kidneys excrete all metabolic acids.
Carbonic acid and ketoacids only
The kidneys do not excrete carbonic acid; they excrete all other acids.

alt.q: When there are too many H+ ions in the blood, how do renal cells respond?
alt.a: They secrete more H+ into the tubules and retain more HCO3−
alt.ex: Renal cells move more H+ into the tubular fluid for excretion and return more HCO3− to the blood.
w: They secrete fewer H+ into the tubules and retain less HCO3−
Renal cells excrete fewer H+ only when there are too few H+ in the blood.
They excrete more HCO3− into the urine with the H+
Renal cells put HCO3− back into the blood as they secrete H+.
They convert the excess H+ into carbon dioxide for exhalation
Converting carbonic acid to CO2 for exhalation is the lungs’ role, not the kidneys’.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: When a patient’s PaCO2 rises, what response do the central chemoreceptors trigger?
items.a: Faster and deeper respirations
items.ex: Rising PaCO2 lowers CSF pH, and central chemoreceptors trigger faster, deeper breathing to remove CO2.
w: Slower and shallower respirations
Slower, shallower breathing is triggered when PaCO2 falls.
Increased renal secretion of ammonia
Ammonia secretion is a renal response, not a chemoreceptor-driven one.
Increased renal retention of bicarbonate
Bicarbonate retention is a slower renal process, not a chemoreceptor response.

alt.q: A rising PaCO2 stimulates the central chemoreceptors by changing the pH of which fluid?
alt.a: Cerebrospinal fluid, whose pH decreases
alt.ex: When PaCO2 rises, CSF pH decreases, and central chemoreceptors trigger faster, deeper respirations.
w: Cerebrospinal fluid, whose pH increases
Added CO2 makes CSF more acidic, so its pH decreases.
Renal tubular fluid, whose pH decreases
Tubular fluid pH relates to renal acid excretion, not chemoreceptor stimulation.
Interstitial fluid, whose pH increases
The central chemoreceptors respond to CSF pH, which falls as PaCO2 rises.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why do renal tubular cells secrete ammonia when the kidneys must excrete a large amount of H+?
items.a: Ammonia combines with H+ to form ammonium so urine is not too acidic
items.ex: Ammonia binds tubular H+ as ammonium (NH4+), allowing metabolic acid excretion without overly acidic urine.
w: Ammonia releases H+ into the blood to raise bicarbonate
Ammonia takes up H+ in the tubules; it does not release H+ into the blood.
Ammonia neutralizes carbonic acid in the alveoli of the lungs
Ammonia acts in renal tubular fluid, not in the lungs.
Ammonia binds bicarbonate so that it can be excreted in urine
The kidneys return bicarbonate to the blood while excreting H+.

alt.q: What is the role of phosphate buffers in renal tubular fluid?
alt.a: Keeping urine from becoming too acidic as H+ is excreted
alt.ex: Phosphate buffers in tubular fluid limit urine acidity when the kidneys excrete H+.
w: Carrying carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs
Transport of CO2 to the lungs is not the role of tubular phosphate buffers.
Releasing H+ to make the blood more acidic
Tubular phosphate buffers take up excreted H+ in urine; they do not acidify blood.
Preventing bicarbonate from returning to the blood
Renal cells return bicarbonate to the blood as they secrete H+.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with chronic kidney disease cannot excrete metabolic acids normally, and the acids are accumulating in the blood. Which compensatory finding would the nurse expect?
items.a: Increased rate and depth of respirations
items.ex: When the kidneys cannot correct the acid excess, respiratory rate and depth increase to excrete more carbonic acid.
w: Decreased rate and depth of respirations
Slower, shallower breathing would retain carbonic acid and worsen the acidity.
Increased renal excretion of H+
The diseased kidneys are unable to excrete metabolic acids normally.
Rising serum bicarbonate level
Accumulating metabolic acids use up bicarbonate, so it decreases rather than rises.

alt.q: A patient’s lungs cannot adequately remove CO2, and increasing the respiratory rate has not corrected the problem. Which compensation should the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: The kidneys excrete more metabolic acid
alt.ex: If increased respirations cannot correct CO2 retention, the kidneys begin compensatory excretion of metabolic acid.
w: The kidneys excrete more bicarbonate
Renal compensation for acidity retains bicarbonate rather than excreting it.
The lungs excrete more metabolic acid
The lungs excrete only carbonic acid, not metabolic acids.
The buffers excrete the excess carbon dioxide
Buffers bind or release H+; they do not excrete acids.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why is keeping arterial blood pH within 7.35 to 7.45 essential?
items.a: Outside this range, cell enzymes and hemoglobin do not function properly
items.ex: Abnormal pH impairs enzyme function and hemoglobin’s handling of oxygen, causing serious problems and possibly death.
w: Outside this range, the kidneys stop producing urine
The book links abnormal pH to enzyme and hemoglobin dysfunction, not to urine production stopping.
Outside this range, cells stop producing carbon dioxide
Cells constantly produce CO2; abnormal pH impairs enzymes and hemoglobin.
Outside this range, all buffers are permanently destroyed
Buffers are not destroyed; enzyme and hemoglobin function is impaired.

alt.q: A patient’s arterial pH is 7.25. Which consequence of this pH is the nurse most concerned about?
alt.a: Impaired cell enzyme function and oxygen handling by hemoglobin
alt.ex: A pH outside 7.35 to 7.45 disrupts enzymes and hemoglobin oxygen handling and can be fatal.
w: Increased production of carbonic acid by the lungs
The lungs excrete carbonic acid; they do not produce it.
Permanent loss of the body’s bicarbonate buffers
Buffers are used up and replenished, not permanently lost.
Excessively alkaline cerebrospinal fluid
A pH of 7.25 is acidic, so body fluids are too acidic, not alkaline.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which arterial blood gas values are within the normal adult range? Select all that apply.
o: Normal arterial pH is 7.35 to 7.45.
PaCO2 43 mm Hg
Normal PaCO2 is 35 to 45 mm Hg.
HCO3− 23 mEq/L
Normal HCO3− is 21 to 28 mEq/L.
PaO2 74 mm Hg
Normal PaO2 is 80 to 100 mm Hg, so 74 mm Hg indicates poor oxygenation.
SaO2 91%
Normal SaO2 is 95% to 100%.
Base excess −4 mEq/L
Normal base excess is −2 to +2 mEq/L; −4 indicates excess metabolic acids.
items.ex: Normal adult ABGs: pH 7.35–7.45, PaCO2 35–45 mm Hg, HCO3− 21–28 mEq/L, PaO2 80–100 mm Hg, SaO2 95%–100%.

alt.q: Which arterial blood gas values are outside the normal adult range? Select all that apply.
o: PaCO2 50 mm Hg
PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg indicates CO2 accumulation from hypoventilation.
HCO3− 19 mEq/L
HCO3− below 21 mEq/L indicates too many metabolic acids.
SaO2 92%
SaO2 below 95% is below the normal range.
A pH of 7.44 is within 7.35 to 7.45.
PaO2 88 mm Hg
A PaO2 of 88 mm Hg is within 80 to 100 mm Hg.
Base excess +1 mEq/L
A base excess of +1 is within −2 to +2 mEq/L.
alt.ex: Values outside the normal ABG ranges signal acid-base or oxygenation problems that need follow-up.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which substances act as buffers in the body? Select all that apply.
o: Bicarbonate
The bicarbonate buffer system is the major ECF buffer.
Hemoglobin
Hemoglobin is one of the other body buffers.
Plasma proteins
Protein buffers help maintain normal pH.
Phosphate
Phosphate buffers act in body fluids, including renal tubular fluid.
Sodium chloride
Sodium chloride is not described as a buffer pair.
Glucose
Glucose is not a buffer that takes up or releases H+.
items.ex: Buffers include the bicarbonate system plus hemoglobin, protein, phosphate, cellular, and bone buffers.

alt.q: Which processes make up acid-base homeostasis? Select all that apply.
o: Acid production
Cellular metabolism constantly produces carbonic and metabolic acids.
Acid buffering
Buffers take up or release H+ to keep pH normal.
Acid excretion
The lungs and kidneys excrete acids to match production.
Acid storage in adipose tissue
Storage in fat tissue is not one of the three processes.
Acid absorption from the intestine
Intestinal absorption is not one of the three processes.
alt.ex: Acid-base homeostasis is the dynamic interplay of acid production, acid buffering, and acid excretion.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse is reviewing how the lungs regulate acid-base balance. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Exhaling removes CO2 from the body
Exhalation excretes carbonic acid as CO2 and water.
Changing the rate and depth of breathing changes carbonic acid levels
Altered ventilation changes CO2 and therefore carbonic acid concentration.
A falling PaCO2 triggers slower, shallower respirations
Central chemoreceptors slow breathing when PaCO2 falls.
The lungs excrete metabolic acids such as lactic acid
The kidneys, not the lungs, excrete metabolic acids.
Rising PaCO2 raises the pH of cerebrospinal fluid
Rising PaCO2 lowers CSF pH, which stimulates faster breathing.
items.ex: The lungs excrete carbonic acid as CO2, adjusting rate and depth of breathing in response to PaCO2.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing how the kidneys regulate acid-base balance. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: They secrete H+ into renal tubular fluid
Renal cells secrete H+ for excretion in urine.
They return HCO3− to the blood while secreting H+
HCO3− goes back into the blood as H+ is secreted.
They secrete ammonia to bind H+ when acid excretion is high
Ammonia forms ammonium with H+, keeping urine from being too acidic.
They excrete carbonic acid as carbon dioxide
The lungs excrete carbonic acid as CO2 and water.
They excrete more H+ when there are too few H+ in the blood
Renal cells excrete fewer H+ when blood H+ is low.
alt.ex: The kidneys excrete metabolic acids by secreting H+, retaining HCO3−, and using phosphate and ammonia to limit urine acidity.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A pH of 7.0 is neutral, and the more free H+ ions a solution contains, the more acidic it is.
items.a: True
items.ex: The pH scale runs from 1.0 (very acid) to 14.0 (very alkaline), and more H+ means more acidity.
items.ww: More H+ ions make a solution more acidic, not more alkaline, and 7.0 is the neutral point.

alt.q: Bases release H+ ions, while acids take up H+ ions.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Acids release H+ ions; bases (alkaline substances) take up H+ ions.
alt.ww: This reverses the definitions: acids are the H+ donors and bases are the H+ acceptors.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Because pH is a logarithmic measure, a small change in blood pH reflects only a minor change in H+ concentration.
items.a: False
items.ex: Small changes in pH denote large changes in H+ concentration and are clinically important.
items.ww: pH is a negative logarithm, so even small pH shifts represent large changes in free H+.

alt.q: Small changes in arterial pH denote large changes in H+ concentration and are clinically important.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: pH is a negative logarithm of free H+ concentration, so small pH changes reflect large H+ changes.
alt.ww: Treating small pH changes as minor ignores the logarithmic scale and large underlying H+ change.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Normal acid-base balance is maintained when acid excretion equals acid production.
items.a: True
items.ex: When the lungs and kidneys excrete acid at the rate cells produce it, pH stays normal.
items.ww: If excretion fell below production, acids would accumulate and blood would become too acidic.

alt.q: Because buffers bind free H+ permanently, normal acid-base balance can be maintained without acid excretion.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Buffers only hold acids temporarily until they reach the lungs and kidneys; excretion must equal production.
alt.ww: Buffers keep blood from becoming too acidic while acids circulate to the lungs and kidneys for excretion.
