items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why are there two different types of acidosis, respiratory and metabolic?
items.a: Cells produce two types of acid: carbonic acid and metabolic acids
items.ex: Because cells produce carbonic acid and metabolic acids, acidosis can arise from excess of either type.
w: The blood contains two separate pH ranges for lungs and kidneys
There is one normal arterial pH range, 7.35 to 7.45.
Acidosis is classified by whether it is acute or chronic
Types of acidosis are named for the acid involved, not duration.
Only the lungs and the skin can excrete acids from the body
The two acid-excretion systems are the lungs and kidneys.

alt.q: A condition makes the blood too acidic because of excess carbonic acid. Which imbalance is this?
alt.a: Respiratory acidosis
alt.ex: Excess carbonic acid from alveolar hypoventilation is respiratory acidosis.
w: Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic acidosis results from excess metabolic acids or loss of bicarbonate.
Respiratory alkalosis
Respiratory alkalosis is a deficit of carbonic acid from hyperventilation.
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis is excess bicarbonate or loss of metabolic acid.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which statement best describes compensation in an acid-base imbalance?
items.a: It moves pH toward normal but does not correct the cause
items.ex: Compensatory mechanisms help normalize pH and survival but leave the underlying problem uncorrected.
w: It corrects the underlying cause of the imbalance
Only the system with the problem can correct it; compensation does not.
It returns pH to normal permanently without treatment
If the cause is not corrected, compensatory mechanisms eventually fail.
It always involves the same organ that caused the imbalance
The opposite system compensates: kidneys for respiratory, lungs for metabolic.

alt.q: A patient’s respiratory acidosis is being compensated by the kidneys. What will happen if the underlying respiratory problem is not corrected?
alt.a: The compensatory mechanisms will eventually fail
alt.ex: Compensation helps survival temporarily, but without correcting the cause the mechanisms eventually fail.
w: The kidneys will eventually correct the respiratory problem
Only the lungs can correct a respiratory acid-base imbalance.
The pH will be held permanently in the normal range
Compensation limits pH change only temporarily if the cause persists.
The lungs will begin compensating for the kidneys
The lungs are the source of this problem and cannot also compensate for it.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which system compensates for a respiratory acid-base imbalance?
items.a: The kidneys, by changing the amount of metabolic acid in the blood
items.ex: The kidneys compensate for respiratory imbalances; only the lungs can correct them.
w: The lungs, by changing the amount of carbonic acid in the blood
The lungs are the source of a respiratory imbalance; they compensate for metabolic imbalances.
The liver, by converting carbonic acid into bicarbonate
The liver is not described as a compensating system.
The buffers, by excreting excess acid in the urine
Buffers bind or release H+; they do not excrete acid.

alt.q: Which system compensates for a metabolic acid-base imbalance?
alt.a: The lungs, by changing the amount of carbonic acid in the blood
alt.ex: The respiratory system compensates for metabolic imbalances; only the kidneys can correct them.
w: The kidneys, by changing the amount of metabolic acid in the blood
The kidneys correct metabolic imbalances and compensate for respiratory ones.
The liver, by converting metabolic acids into carbon dioxide
The liver is not described as a compensating system.
The buffers, by excreting excess bicarbonate through the skin
Buffers bind or release H+; they do not excrete substances.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with chronic bronchitis has respiratory acidosis. How long does renal compensation typically take to reach a steady state?
items.a: 3 to 5 days
items.ex: Renal compensation is slow, often taking 24 hours to show effect and 3 to 5 days to reach a steady state.
w: A few seconds
Seconds describes the speed of buffers.
A few minutes
A few minutes describes the start of respiratory compensation for metabolic acidosis.
About 6 hours
Renal compensation often needs 24 hours just to show clinical effect.

alt.q: How long does renal compensation for respiratory acidosis often take to begin showing clinical effect?
alt.a: About 24 hours
alt.ex: Renal compensation often takes 24 hours to show effect and 3 to 5 days to reach steady state.
w: Within seconds
Seconds describes the speed of buffers, not renal compensation.
Within a few minutes
Minutes describes the onset of compensatory hyperventilation.
About 10 days
Renal compensation reaches steady state within 3 to 5 days, well before 10 days.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why do the kidneys usually not compensate for respiratory alkalosis?
items.a: Respiratory alkalosis is usually short lived
items.ex: Respiratory alkalosis is usually short lived, so the slow renal compensation does not have time to act.
w: The kidneys can only compensate for metabolic imbalances
The kidneys compensate for respiratory imbalances; they correct metabolic ones.
Respiratory alkalosis does not change the blood pH
Falling PaCO2 creates a carbonic acid deficit that raises pH.
The lungs correct respiratory alkalosis within seconds
The book attributes the absent compensation to the imbalance being short lived.

alt.q: A patient’s respiratory alkalosis from acute anxiety is short lived. Which HCO3− finding would the nurse expect?
alt.a: HCO3− within the normal range of 21 to 28 mEq/L
alt.ex: Short-lived respiratory alkalosis does not allow renal compensation, so HCO3− stays normal.
w: HCO3− below 21 mEq/L from renal compensation
HCO3− falls below 21 only if the kidneys have had time to compensate.
HCO3− above 28 mEq/L from bicarbonate retention
Retaining bicarbonate would worsen alkalosis and is not compensation for it.
HCO3− below 15 mEq/L from metabolic acid excess
Metabolic acid excess describes metabolic acidosis, not acute respiratory alkalosis.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: How is the anion gap calculated?
items.a: Plasma Na+ minus the sum of plasma Cl− and HCO3−
items.ex: The anion gap is the sodium concentration minus the sum of chloride and bicarbonate concentrations.
w: Plasma Cl− minus the sum of plasma Na+ and HCO3−
Chloride is subtracted, not used as the starting value.
Plasma HCO3− minus the sum of plasma Na+ and Cl−
Sodium is the starting value from which the anions are subtracted.
Plasma Na+ plus the sum of plasma Cl− and HCO3−
The anion gap subtracts the measured anions from sodium.

alt.q: A patient’s plasma Na+ is 140 mEq/L, Cl− is 104 mEq/L, and HCO3− is 14 mEq/L. What is the anion gap, and how is it classified?
alt.a: 22 mEq/L, a high anion gap
alt.ex: 140 − (104 + 14) = 22 mEq/L, which is greater than 12 mEq/L and therefore high.
w: 36 mEq/L, a high anion gap
36 is Na+ minus Cl− only; HCO3− must also be subtracted.
10 mEq/L, a normal anion gap
The correct calculation gives 22 mEq/L, not 10 mEq/L.
22 mEq/L, a normal anion gap
A gap above 12 mEq/L is classified as high, not normal.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient has metabolic alkalosis from prolonged gastric suctioning. What may limit the degree of respiratory compensation?
items.a: The body’s need for oxygen
items.ex: Compensation requires hypoventilation, and the need for oxygen limits how much breathing can slow.
w: The kidneys’ need to retain bicarbonate
Retaining bicarbonate is not what limits the lungs’ compensation.
The rapid onset of renal compensation
Renal compensation is slow and does not limit respiratory compensation.
The buffers’ need to release hydrogen ions
Buffer activity is not identified as a limit on respiratory compensation.

alt.q: Which respiratory compensation would the nurse expect in a patient with metabolic alkalosis from vomiting?
alt.a: Slower, shallower breathing that raises PaCO2
alt.ex: Hypoventilation lets carbonic acid accumulate, raising PaCO2 and moving pH toward normal.
w: Faster, deeper breathing that lowers PaCO2
Hyperventilation is the compensation for metabolic acidosis.
Faster, deeper breathing that raises HCO3−
Hyperventilation lowers carbonic acid and does not raise HCO3−.
Slower, shallower breathing that lowers PaCO2
Hypoventilation raises PaCO2; it does not lower it.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient admitted after an opioid overdose has a respiratory rate of 8 breaths/min. ABGs: pH 7.29, PaCO2 56 mm Hg, HCO3− 26 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret these results?
items.a: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
items.ex: Low pH with PaCO2 above 45 and normal HCO3− indicates respiratory acidosis without renal compensation.
w: Compensated respiratory acidosis
Renal compensation would raise HCO3− above 28 mEq/L.
Uncompensated metabolic acidosis
Metabolic acidosis has HCO3− below 21 mEq/L.
Compensated metabolic alkalosis
A pH below 7.35 is acidic, not alkaline.

alt.q: A patient with long-standing COPD has ABGs of pH 7.34, PaCO2 60 mm Hg, and HCO3− 33 mEq/L. How should the nurse interpret these results?
alt.a: Respiratory acidosis with renal compensation
alt.ex: PaCO2 above 45 with HCO3− above 28 shows respiratory acidosis that the kidneys are compensating.
w: Uncompensated respiratory acidosis
HCO3− above 28 shows that renal compensation has occurred.
Metabolic alkalosis with respiratory compensation
A pH of 7.34 is acidic, so the primary problem is not alkalosis.
Metabolic acidosis with respiratory compensation
Metabolic acidosis has HCO3− below 21, not 33 mEq/L.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient is sobbing and very anxious after receiving bad news. ABGs: pH 7.52, PaCO2 29 mm Hg, HCO3− 24 mEq/L. Which imbalance do these results show?
items.a: Respiratory alkalosis
items.ex: High pH with PaCO2 below 35 and normal HCO3− indicates respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation.
w: Respiratory acidosis
Respiratory acidosis has a low pH and PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg.
Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis has HCO3− above 28 mEq/L.
Metabolic acidosis
Metabolic acidosis has a low pH and HCO3− below 21 mEq/L.

alt.q: A patient is hyperventilating from acute anxiety. Which finding would the nurse expect?
alt.a: Numbness and tingling of the fingers and around the mouth
alt.ex: Respiratory alkalosis increases cell membrane excitability, causing paresthesias of fingers, toes, and circumoral region.
w: Decreased rate and depth of respirations
Slower, shallower breathing causes respiratory acidosis, not alkalosis.
Headache with lethargy from carbonic acid buildup
Carbonic acid buildup describes respiratory acidosis.
Diminished reflexes with constipation
Diminished reflexes and constipation are signs of hypercalcemia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with severe diarrhea develops metabolic acidosis. Which anion gap finding would the nurse expect?
items.a: Normal anion gap because bicarbonate is lost
items.ex: Diarrhea removes bicarbonate directly, producing metabolic acidosis with a normal anion gap.
w: High anion gap because ketoacids accumulate
Ketoacid accumulation occurs with diabetic ketoacidosis or starvation.
High anion gap because lactic acid accumulates
Lactic acid accumulates with circulatory shock or extreme exercise.
High anion gap because salicylates accumulate
Salicylate overdose adds an unusual organic acid, not seen with diarrhea.

alt.q: Which patient with metabolic acidosis would the nurse expect to have a high anion gap?
alt.a: A patient with diabetic ketoacidosis
alt.ex: An increase of acids other than HCl, such as ketoacids, produces a high anion gap.
w: A patient with severe diarrhea
Diarrhea causes bicarbonate loss with a normal anion gap.
A patient with a pancreatic fistula
Pancreatic fistula drainage removes bicarbonate, giving a normal anion gap.
A patient with renal tubular acidosis
Renal tubular acidosis is a normal anion gap cause.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient has had continuous nasogastric suction for several days. Which arterial blood gas results would the nurse expect if respiratory compensation is occurring?
items.a: pH 7.51, PaCO2 48 mm Hg, HCO3− 34 mEq/L
items.ex: Gastric suction removes metabolic acid; high pH and HCO3− with PaCO2 above 45 show compensated metabolic alkalosis.
w: pH 7.29, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, HCO3− 15 mEq/L
Low pH and HCO3− with low PaCO2 indicate compensated metabolic acidosis.
pH 7.52, PaCO2 28 mm Hg, HCO3− 23 mEq/L
High pH with low PaCO2 and normal HCO3− indicates respiratory alkalosis.
pH 7.30, PaCO2 58 mm Hg, HCO3− 26 mEq/L
Low pH with high PaCO2 indicates respiratory acidosis.

alt.q: A patient has diabetic ketoacidosis with compensatory hyperventilation. Which arterial blood gas results would the nurse expect?
alt.a: pH 7.29, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, HCO3− 15 mEq/L
alt.ex: Metabolic acidosis lowers pH and HCO3−, and compensatory hyperventilation lowers PaCO2 below 35 mm Hg.
w: pH 7.51, PaCO2 48 mm Hg, HCO3− 34 mEq/L
High pH and HCO3− with high PaCO2 indicate compensated metabolic alkalosis.
pH 7.52, PaCO2 28 mm Hg, HCO3− 23 mEq/L
High pH with low PaCO2 indicates respiratory alkalosis.
pH 7.30, PaCO2 58 mm Hg, HCO3− 26 mEq/L
High PaCO2 with normal HCO3− indicates uncompensated respiratory acidosis.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why does acute respiratory alkalosis cause excitement, confusion, and paresthesias?
items.a: A rising pH increases cell membrane excitability
items.ex: When blood, CSF, and ICF pH rise acutely, cell membrane excitability increases, producing neurological symptoms.
w: A rising pH decreases cell membrane excitability
Decreased excitability would cause depression, not excitement and paresthesias.
A rising PaCO2 lowers the pH of brain cells
In respiratory alkalosis PaCO2 falls, and pH rises.
A falling HCO3− causes acid buildup in the brain
Respiratory alkalosis is a carbonic acid deficit, not acid buildup.

alt.q: Why does respiratory acidosis cause a decreased level of consciousness?
alt.a: Decreased CSF pH and brain-cell pH depress neurological function
alt.ex: In respiratory acidosis, decreased CSF and intracellular brain pH cause decreased level of consciousness.
w: Increased CSF pH and brain-cell pH excite neurons
Respiratory acidosis lowers, not raises, CSF and brain-cell pH.
Decreased PaCO2 removes carbonic acid from the brain
Respiratory acidosis involves increased PaCO2, not decreased.
Increased HCO3− from renal compensation sedates neurons
Renal compensation raises HCO3− to help pH; it does not cause the altered consciousness.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which conditions can cause respiratory acidosis? Select all that apply.
o: Overdose of a respiratory depressant drug
Brainstem respiratory depression causes alveolar hypoventilation.
Chronic bronchitis (type B COPD)
Impaired gas exchange causes CO2 retention.
Chest wall surgery causing pain with breathing
Painful respiration limits ventilation and causes hypoventilation.
Respiratory muscle weakness from hypokalemia
Impaired neuromuscular function reduces ventilation.
Anxiety with sobbing
Anxiety and sobbing cause hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis.
Acute pain without chest involvement
Acute pain causes hyperventilation and respiratory alkalosis.
items.ex: Respiratory acidosis results from alveolar hypoventilation due to impaired gas exchange, neuromuscular function, or brainstem control.

alt.q: Which conditions can cause respiratory alkalosis? Select all that apply.
o: Hypoxemia early in an asthma episode
Hypoxemia from any cause stimulates hyperventilation.
Anxiety and psychological distress
Anxiety causes alveolar hyperventilation.
Gram-negative sepsis
Sepsis stimulates brainstem respiratory control.
Inappropriate mechanical ventilator settings
Excessive ventilator settings can cause hyperventilation.
Drug overdose with a respiratory depressant
Respiratory depressants cause hypoventilation and respiratory acidosis.
Airway obstruction
Airway obstruction impairs gas exchange and causes respiratory acidosis.
alt.ex: Respiratory alkalosis results from alveolar hyperventilation caused by hypoxemia, pain, anxiety, brainstem stimulation, or ventilator settings.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which conditions can cause high anion gap metabolic acidosis? Select all that apply.
o: Diabetic ketoacidosis
Ketoacids are added metabolic acids that raise the anion gap.
Circulatory shock
Shock produces lactic acidosis with a high anion gap.
Ingestion of methanol or ethylene glycol
These are metabolized to acids that raise the anion gap.
Oliguric acute kidney injury
Excess normal metabolic acids accumulate when the kidneys cannot excrete them.
Severe diarrhea
Diarrhea causes bicarbonate loss with a normal anion gap.
Renal tubular acidosis
Renal tubular acidosis causes a normal anion gap.
items.ex: A high anion gap reflects added acids other than HCl, such as ketoacids, lactic acid, and toxic organic acids.

alt.q: Which conditions can cause metabolic alkalosis? Select all that apply.
o: Excessive vomiting
Vomiting removes metabolic acid.
Excessive administration of sodium bicarbonate
Sodium bicarbonate directly increases base.
Massive blood transfusion
The liver converts the citrate in stored blood to HCO3−.
Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia is listed as a cause of metabolic acid loss.
Diarrhea
Diarrhea removes bicarbonate and causes metabolic acidosis.
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Ketoacidosis adds metabolic acids and causes metabolic acidosis.
alt.ex: Metabolic alkalosis results from increased bicarbonate or loss of metabolic acid, as with vomiting or gastric suction.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which findings would the nurse expect in a patient with uncompensated metabolic acidosis? Select all that apply.
o: pH below 7.35
Excess metabolic acids lower the pH.
HCO3− below 21 mEq/L
Bicarbonate falls as it buffers metabolic acids or is lost.
PaCO2 within 35 to 45 mm Hg
Without compensation, PaCO2 remains normal.
Decreased level of consciousness
Metabolic acidosis causes lethargy, confusion, or coma.
HCO3− above 28 mEq/L
Elevated HCO3− indicates metabolic alkalosis or compensated respiratory acidosis.
PaCO2 above 45 mm Hg
Elevated PaCO2 indicates respiratory acidosis or compensated metabolic alkalosis.
items.ex: Uncompensated metabolic acidosis shows low pH, low HCO3−, normal PaCO2, and decreased level of consciousness.

alt.q: Which findings would the nurse expect in a patient with metabolic alkalosis? Select all that apply.
o: pH above 7.45
Loss of metabolic acid or excess base raises pH.
HCO3− above 28 mEq/L
Bicarbonate rises in metabolic alkalosis.
Numbness and tingling of fingers and around the mouth
Paresthesias are signs of metabolic alkalosis.
Muscle cramps
Muscle cramps are listed signs of metabolic alkalosis.
Increased rate and depth of respirations
The respiratory compensation for metabolic alkalosis is hypoventilation.
HCO3− below 21 mEq/L
Low HCO3− indicates metabolic acidosis.
alt.ex: Metabolic alkalosis shows high pH and HCO3−, paresthesias, cramps, and possibly confusion and dysrhythmias.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: The kidneys compensate for respiratory acid-base imbalances, and the respiratory system compensates for metabolic acid-base imbalances.
items.a: True
items.ex: Each system compensates for imbalances originating in the other, while only the originating system can correct the problem.
items.ww: A system cannot compensate for its own failure, so compensation comes from the other system.

alt.q: The lungs can correct a metabolic acidosis by excreting more carbonic acid.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Only the kidneys can correct a metabolic imbalance; increased ventilation only compensates by limiting the pH change.
alt.ww: Hyperventilation moves pH toward normal but leaves the excess metabolic acid in place.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: In metabolic acidosis, respiratory compensation is slow and takes 3 to 5 days to reach a steady state.
items.a: False
items.ex: Compensatory hyperventilation for metabolic acidosis begins within a few minutes.
items.ww: The 3-to-5-day time frame describes renal compensation for respiratory acidosis, not respiratory compensation.

alt.q: Compensatory hyperventilation in metabolic acidosis begins within a few minutes.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Low pH stimulates chemoreceptors, and hyperventilation starts within minutes to remove carbonic acid.
alt.ww: Days-long timing applies to renal compensation; the lungs respond in minutes.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: In respiratory acidosis, the kidneys compensate by increasing excretion of metabolic acids, which increases blood bicarbonate.
items.a: True
items.ex: Renal compensation excretes more metabolic acid in the urine, raising blood HCO3− toward the compensated range above 28 mEq/L.
items.ww: The kidneys retain bicarbonate as they excrete acid, so HCO3− rises rather than falls.

alt.q: In respiratory acidosis, the kidneys compensate by excreting bicarbonate, which lowers blood HCO3−.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The kidneys compensate for respiratory acidosis by excreting metabolic acid, which raises HCO3−.
alt.ww: Excreting bicarbonate would make the blood more acidic and worsen the acidosis.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: The [[anion gap]] is a reflection of unmeasured anions in plasma, used to help identify the cause of metabolic acidosis.

alt.q: An anion gap greater than [[12]] mEq/L is classified as a high anion gap.
alt.ex: The anion gap equals Na+ minus (Cl− + HCO3−); a normal value is about 8 to 12 mEq/L.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why do older adults have an increased risk of extracellular fluid volume (ECV) deficit and dehydration?

alt.q: About what percentage of body weight is water in older adults?

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Robert is caring for Mrs. Mendoza, age 77, who has been vomiting and has had diarrhea for 24 hours. Which electrolyte imbalance is a risk with both vomiting and diarrhea?

Hypercalcemia

Hypermagnesemia

alt.q: Mrs. Mendoza has had both vomiting and diarrhea for 24 hours. Which fluid imbalance should Robert anticipate as a risk of both?

w: ECV excess
ECV excess is linked to a sodium-rich diet, heart failure, or oliguric renal disease.
Hyperkalemia
GI losses lower potassium; hyperkalemia is not a risk of vomiting and diarrhea.
Hypercalcemia

w: Metabolic alkalosis
Metabolic alkalosis is linked to vomiting or gastric suction.
Respiratory acidosis

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: An 84-year-old patient who is confused has had poor oral intake for 3 days. When asked, the patient says, “I’m not thirsty at all.” Which action by the nurse is best?

items.q: An older adult with urinary incontinence tells the nurse, “I don’t drink much during the day so I don’t have accidents.” Which risk should the nurse recognize?
items.a: Hypernatremia and ECV deficit
items.ex: Restricting fluid because of bladder control or mobility problems increases risk of hypernatremia and ECV deficit.
w: Hyponatremia and ECV excess
Fluid restriction leads to deficits, not excess volume or diluted sodium.
Hyperkalemia and metabolic alkalosis
Restricting fluid is not linked to these imbalances in the book.
Hypercalcemia and respiratory acidosis
These imbalances are not caused by voluntary fluid restriction.

alt.q: Which older adult is at increased risk of hypernatremia because of voluntary fluid restriction?
alt.a: A patient with impaired mobility who limits drinking to avoid walking to the bathroom
alt.ex: Impaired mobility or bladder control can lead patients to restrict fluids, risking hypernatremia and ECV deficit.
w: A patient with heart failure who follows a sodium-rich diet
A sodium-rich diet with heart failure is linked to ECV excess.
A patient with chronic alcoholism who drinks heavily on weekends
Chronic alcoholism is linked to hypomagnesemia, not fluid restriction.
A patient with cancer who takes calcium supplements every morning
Cancer and calcium intake relate to calcium imbalance, not fluid restriction.

items.q: Why do the kidney changes of normal aging increase an older adult’s risk of metabolic acidosis?
items.a: They make it more difficult to excrete a large acid load
items.ex: Aging kidneys have more difficulty excreting a large acid load, so metabolic acids can accumulate.
w: They cause the lungs to retain carbon dioxide
CO2 retention by the lungs causes respiratory, not metabolic, acidosis.
They cause excessive excretion of hydrogen ions
Excess H+ excretion would lower, not raise, acid in the blood.
They increase bicarbonate retention in the blood
Increased bicarbonate would tend toward alkalosis, not acidosis.

alt.q: An older adult with a severe infection is producing extra metabolic acids. Which age-related factor increases the risk that metabolic acidosis will develop?

alt.ex: Normal aging makes it harder for the kidneys to excrete large acid loads, increasing metabolic acidosis risk.
w: Increased percentage of body weight as water
Body water decreases with aging, and it is not the acid-excretion factor.
Increased thirst sensation with aging
Thirst decreases with aging and does not affect acid excretion.
Improved urine-concentrating ability with aging
Urine-concentrating ability decreases, and it relates to hypernatremia, not acid excretion.

items.q: Which age-related factors increase an older adult’s risk of fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base imbalances? Select all that apply.

Decreased thirst increases risk of hypernatremia and dehydration.
Decreased percentage of body weight as water
Body water falls to about 50%, increasing ECV deficit risk.
Combined effects of chronic diseases and multiple medications
Disease and medications together challenge fluid and electrolyte balance.
Reduced ability of diseased kidneys to concentrate urine
Chronic renal disease increases risk of hypernatremia, ECV deficit, and dehydration.

Cardiovascular illness decreases the ability to adapt, raising pulmonary edema risk.

alt.q: A nurse is planning care for an older adult at risk of dehydration. Which precautions are appropriate? Select all that apply.

Thirst is unreliable in older adults because it decreases with age.
Have the patient rise slowly during orthostatic blood pressure checks

Cardiovascular illness increases pulmonary edema risk with rapid infusion.

Restricting fluids increases risk of hypernatremia and ECV deficit.
Assume the patient’s body water is the same as a young adult’s
Older adults have a lower percentage of body water, about 50%.
alt.ex: Safe care of older adults avoids relying on thirst, prevents falls from postural hypotension, and monitors IV fluid tolerance.

sections.name: Nursing process: fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient with heart failure weighed 70 kg yesterday morning and weighs 71.5 kg this morning on the same scale. About how much fluid has the patient retained?
items.ex: Each kilogram of weight gained or lost overnight equals about 1 L of fluid retained or lost.
w: This underestimates the gain; a 1.5-kg overnight change reflects about 1.5 L.
3 L
This doubles the true value; 1 kg of overnight change equals 1 L, not 2 L.
150 mL
Overnight weight change reflects liters of fluid, not small volumes like this.

alt.q: An adult patient with vomiting weighs 2 kg less this morning than yesterday morning. How should the nurse interpret this change?
alt.a: About 2 L of fluid has been lost
alt.ex: An overnight loss of 1 kg equals about 1 L of fluid; a 2-kg loss suggests about 2 L lost and ECV deficit.
w: About 200 mL of fluid has been lost
Each kilogram represents about 1 L, so 2 kg is about 2 L, not 200 mL.
About 4 L of fluid has been lost
This doubles the estimate; 1 kg equals about 1 L of fluid.
Fluid has shifted into the cells
Daily weights show changes in total body fluid, not shifts between compartments.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse delegates daily weights to assistive personnel (AP) for a patient with ECV excess. Which instruction is correct?
items.a: Have the patient void, then weigh at the same time on the same scale
items.ex: Accurate daily weights require voiding first, the same time each day, the same scale, and the same clothing or linens.
w: Weigh the patient after breakfast so the patient has energy to stand
Weighing after a meal adds the weight of food and fluid, which distorts the comparison.
Use whichever scale is closest, as long as the weight is recorded
Switching scales introduces error; the same scale must be used each day.
Weigh at any time of day, but always before the patient voids
The patient should void first and be weighed at the same time each day.

alt.q: An AP reports a patient’s weights for 3 days, each taken on a different scale at different times. What is the main problem with these data?
alt.a: The weights cannot be compared reliably to detect fluid changes
alt.ex: Comparing day-to-day weight requires the same scale, time, and clothing; otherwise changes may not reflect fluid gain or loss.
w: The weights should have been estimated visually instead
Measured weights are needed; visual estimates are not accurate for fluid status.
The weights should be compared only with the admission weight
Each day is compared with the previous day, and trends are reviewed over several days.
The weights are only useful if taken every 4 hours
Daily weights, taken once a day under the same conditions, are the standard.

items.q: A patient on intake and output (I&O) measurement eats 240 mL of ice chips during the shift. How much intake should the nurse record?
items.a: 120 mL
items.ex: Ice chips are recorded as one-half of their volume in I&O measurement.
w: 240 mL
Recording the full volume overestimates intake; ice chips melt to about half their volume.
60 mL
This is one-quarter of the volume; the book specifies recording one-half.
0 mL
Ice chips are a fluid and count as intake.

alt.q: A patient eats 300 mL of ice chips. Which amount does the nurse document as intake?
alt.a: 150 mL
alt.ex: Document one-half the volume of ice chips; 300 mL of ice chips is recorded as 150 mL.
w: 300 mL
Ice chips are not recorded at full volume; half the volume is documented.
75 mL
This is one-quarter of the volume, not one-half.
200 mL
This is two-thirds of the volume; ice chips are recorded at one-half.

items.q: A parent of an infant with diarrhea asks how to rehydrate the baby at home. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Give an oral rehydration fluid that contains sodium, such as Pedialyte
items.ex: With ECV deficit from GI losses, replace fluid with sodium-containing fluids; infants become imbalanced quickly.
w: Give whole milk often, because it provides both fluid and calories
Liquids containing lactose are inappropriate when a patient has diarrhea.
Give plain water often, because it is gentle on the stomach
Low-sodium liquids do not replace the sodium lost in diarrhea.
Hold all fluids for 24 hours so the bowel can rest
Withholding fluids worsens ECV deficit; infants need prompt rehydration.

alt.q: Which statement by a parent shows understanding of teaching about an infant’s vomiting and diarrhea?
alt.a: “I will give a sodium-containing rehydration drink or call for care right away.”
alt.ex: GI losses quickly cause serious imbalances in infants, so parents should promptly rehydrate with sodium-containing fluid or seek care.
w: “I will wait 2 or 3 days to see whether it stops on its own.”
Waiting is unsafe; infants develop serious imbalances quickly from GI losses.
“I will give apple juice because it has a lot of fluid.”
Low-sodium liquids are inappropriate for replacing diarrheal losses.
“I will give extra formula mixed with more water than usual.”
Diluted formula supplies water without the sodium needed to restore ECV.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient has an order for 1000 mL D5 ½NS with 20 mEq KCl at 125 mL/h. Which assessment should the nurse confirm before starting the infusion?
items.a: Adequate kidney function and urine output
items.ex: Verify adequate kidney function and urine output before giving IV potassium, because hyperkalemia can cause fatal dysrhythmias.
w: Normal serum calcium level
Calcium is not the safety check for potassium-containing fluids; renal function is.
Presence of bowel sounds
Bowel sounds do not determine whether the kidneys can excrete potassium.
Normal capillary refill time
Capillary refill reflects perfusion, not the ability to excrete potassium.

alt.q: Which method of giving potassium chloride (KCl) is never acceptable?
alt.a: IV push through a port in the IV tubing
alt.ex: Under no circumstances should KCl be given by IV push, because hyperkalemia can cause fatal cardiac dysrhythmias.
w: Added to an IV solution such as D5 ½NS
Adding KCl to IV solutions is common and acceptable when kidney function is adequate.
Diluted in an IV solution at an ordered hourly rate
A controlled, diluted infusion is the acceptable way to give IV potassium.
Added to IV fluids for a patient who is NPO
Patients with normal renal function who are NPO should have potassium added to IV fluids.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient has hypernatremia that cannot be treated with oral water. Which IV solution does the nurse anticipate?
items.a: 0.45% sodium chloride
items.ex: A hypotonic solution such as 0.45% NaCl dilutes the ECF and rehydrates cells in hypernatremia.
w: 3% sodium chloride
Hypertonic saline raises osmolality and pulls water out of cells, worsening hypernatremia.
Lactated Ringer solution
LR is isotonic; it expands ECV but does not enter cells to rehydrate them.
0.9% sodium chloride
Normal saline is isotonic and does not enter cells, so it will not dilute body fluids.

alt.q: A patient has ECV deficit from vomiting and diarrhea. Which IV solution is indicated to expand extracellular volume?
alt.a: 0.9% sodium chloride
alt.ex: Sodium-containing isotonic solutions such as normal saline are indicated to prevent or treat ECV deficit.
w: 3% sodium chloride
Hypertonic saline draws water from cells and is not routine ECV replacement.
Dextrose 5% in water
D5W becomes hypotonic in the body; most of its water enters cells rather than staying in the ECF.
Dextrose 10% in water
D10W leaves free water that moves into cells; it does not expand ECV effectively.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient takes furosemide daily for heart failure. Which electrolyte imbalance should the nurse monitor for?
items.a: Hypokalemia
items.ex: Potassium-wasting diuretics such as furosemide cause hypokalemia, along with ECV deficit and hypomagnesemia.
w: Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia is linked to potassium-sparing diuretics and ACE inhibitors, not furosemide.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia is linked to calcium carbonate antacids and cancer, not furosemide.
Hypermagnesemia
Furosemide causes magnesium loss; hypermagnesemia is linked to magnesium hydroxide.

alt.q: A patient reports using baking soda several times a day as an antacid. Which imbalance is the patient at risk for?
alt.a: ECV excess
alt.ex: Baking soda has a high sodium content that holds water in the extracellular compartment, causing ECV excess.
w: ECV deficit
Sodium retains water; baking soda leads to excess, not deficit, of ECV.
Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia is linked to diuretics, vomiting, and laxatives, not baking soda.
Hypermagnesemia
Hypermagnesemia is linked to magnesium hydroxide, such as Milk of Magnesia.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient’s IV site is swollen, pale, and cool to the touch, and the infusion has slowed. The fluid contains no additives. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Stop the infusion
items.ex: These are signs of infiltration; stop the infusion first, then discontinue the IV, elevate the extremity, and restart in another extremity.
w: Apply firm pressure over the swollen area
Pressure can force the solution into contact with more tissue.
Raise the IV container to increase flow
Increasing flow pushes more fluid into the subcutaneous tissue.
Flush the catheter to clear a possible clot
Flushing an infiltrated line sends more fluid into the tissue.

alt.q: After stopping an infiltrated additive-free infusion and removing the catheter, which action is appropriate?
alt.a: Elevate the affected extremity
alt.ex: Elevating the affected extremity is a listed intervention for infiltration after stopping the infusion.
w: Massage the area firmly
Avoid pressure over the site; it forces solution into more tissue.
Restart the IV just above the swelling in the same vein
The new IV line is started in the other extremity.
Resume the infusion at a slower rate
An infiltrated catheter is no longer in the vein and must be discontinued.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: During a tubing change, a patient suddenly develops dyspnea, coughing, chest pain, and hypotension. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Clamp or cover the leak to stop air entering
items.ex: These are signs of air embolism; first prevent further air from entering the system by clamping or covering the leak.
w: Increase the infusion rate to flush the line
Running fluid faster does not stop air entry and could push in more air.
Obtain a full set of vital signs
Assessment matters, but the emergency action is to stop more air from entering first.
Document the time symptoms began
Documentation is done after the patient is safe.

alt.q: After the leak is clamped in a suspected air embolism, how should the nurse position the patient?
alt.a: On the left side
alt.ex: The book directs placing the patient on the left side, preferably with the head of bed raised, to trap air.
w: On the right side
The book specifies the left side to trap air, not the right.
Prone with the head flat
Prone positioning is not the recommended position for air embolism.
Supine with the legs elevated
This is not the position the book gives for trapping air.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Ten minutes into a transfusion of packed RBCs, a patient develops chills, flank pain, tachycardia, and hypotension. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Stop the transfusion
items.ex: These suggest an acute hemolytic reaction; stop the transfusion immediately, then keep the line open with new tubing and get help.
w: Slow the transfusion and recheck vital signs in 15 minutes
A suspected hemolytic reaction requires stopping the blood, not slowing it.
Give an antipyretic and continue the transfusion
Continuing the blood can worsen the reaction; even small amounts are harmful.
Turn on the saline connected to the Y-tubing
Using the existing Y-tubing infuses the blood left in the line into the patient.

alt.q: Why does the nurse replace the IV tubing down to the catheter hub instead of opening the saline on the Y-tubing set when a hemolytic reaction is suspected?
alt.a: Blood left in the tubing would otherwise infuse
alt.ex: Opening the saline on the Y-set flushes the remaining blood into the patient; even a small amount can worsen the reaction.
w: New tubing filters out the antibodies causing the reaction
Tubing does not filter antibodies; it is changed to avoid giving more blood.
The Y-tubing cannot carry normal saline safely
Y-tubing is primed with saline; the issue is the blood remaining in it.
New tubing allows the blood to be restarted faster
The blood is not restarted in a suspected hemolytic reaction.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse is planning care for a patient on a 1200 mL/day oral fluid restriction. How should the fluid usually be distributed?
items.a: Half from 7 a.m. to 3 p.m.; the rest over evening and night
items.ex: Half the total is allotted to the day shift, when patients are active, eat two meals, and take most medications.
w: Most of it at night, when the patient is least active
The larger share is given during the day, when activity, meals, and medications occur.
Equal amounts every hour around the clock
The book allots half to the day period, not equal hourly portions.
All of it with meals, none between meals
Fluid is planned across meals, between meals, bedtime, and medications.

alt.q: A patient on fluid restriction complains of a very dry mouth. Which intervention is most appropriate?
alt.a: Provide frequent mouth care
alt.ex: Frequent mouth care moistens mucous membranes, prevents drying and cracking, and maintains comfort during fluid restriction.
w: Offer unlimited ice chips, since they are not fluid
Ice chips are fluids and count toward the restriction.
Give extra gelatin between meals
Gelatin is a fluid and counts toward the restricted amount.
Allow an extra glass of water at bedtime
Exceeding the ordered amount defeats the purpose of the restriction.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which findings suggest extracellular fluid volume (ECV) deficit? Select all that apply.
o: Orthostatic hypotension
Hypotension or orthostatic hypotension is a vascular marker of ECV deficit.
Rapid, thready pulse
A rapid, thready pulse reflects low vascular volume.
Neck veins flat when supine
Flat or collapsing neck veins when supine indicate ECV deficit.
Dry mucous membranes between cheek and gum
Dryness between cheek and gum is an interstitial marker of ECV deficit.
Bounding pulse
A bounding pulse is a sign of ECV excess.
Crackles in dependent lung lobes
Crackles with progressive dyspnea suggest ECV excess.
items.ex: ECV deficit lowers vascular and interstitial volume, causing hypotension, weak rapid pulse, flat neck veins, and dry mucosa.

alt.q: Which findings suggest ECV excess? Select all that apply.
o: Bounding pulse
A bounding pulse reflects increased vascular volume.
Neck veins distended when semi-upright
Full neck veins when upright or semi-upright indicate ECV excess.
Edema of the ankles or sacrum
Dependent edema is an interstitial marker of ECV excess.
Weight gain of 1 kg or more in 24 hours
A gain of 1 kg or more overnight indicates ECV excess in adults.
Sluggish capillary refill
Sluggish capillary refill suggests ECV deficit.
Small volume of dark yellow urine
Concentrated low urine output is a sign of ECV deficit.
alt.ex: ECV excess raises vascular and interstitial volume, causing bounding pulse, distended neck veins, edema, and rapid weight gain.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which factors increase a patient’s risk for phlebitis? Select all that apply.
o: Hypertonic or acidic IV solution
Acidic or hypertonic solutions irritate the vein wall.
Rapid IV infusion rate
A rapid rate is a listed risk factor for phlebitis.
Catheter inserted in an area of flexion
Flexion areas move the catheter and irritate the vein.
Poorly secured catheter
Catheter movement in the vein can cause phlebitis.
Use of a transparent semipermeable dressing
Transparent dressings secure the device and allow inspection; they are not a risk factor.
Thorough hand hygiene before handling the line
Good hand hygiene reduces risk; poor hand hygiene increases it.
items.ex: Phlebitis risk rises with irritating solutions, fast rates, irritating drugs, flexion sites, poor securement, and poor asepsis.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing a patient’s IV therapy. Which features place this patient at risk for phlebitis? Select all that apply.
o: Infusion of potassium chloride
IV drugs such as KCl are listed risk factors for phlebitis.
Vancomycin given through the catheter
Vancomycin is an irritating drug that increases phlebitis risk.
Lack of aseptic technique during care
Poor aseptic technique raises the risk of phlebitis.
Catheter well secured with a securement device
Good securement prevents catheter movement and reduces phlebitis.
Catheter placed in a forearm vein away from joints
Avoiding areas of flexion lowers the risk.
alt.ex: Irritating drugs such as KCl and vancomycin and lapses in asepsis raise phlebitis risk; good securement and site choice lower it.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: For a stable patient receiving IV fluids, which tasks may the nurse delegate to assistive personnel (AP)? Select all that apply.
o: Measuring daily weights
Daily weights can be delegated to AP when the patient is stable.
Measuring and recording oral intake and urine output
AP often document oral intake and urine, diarrhea, and vomitus output.
Providing direct physical care such as hygiene
Direct physical care can be delegated when the patient is stable.
Administering the IV fluid
Administration of IV fluid is not delegated to AP.
Performing hemodynamic assessment
Hemodynamic assessment is a nursing responsibility that is not delegated.
Recording intake given through the feeding tube
Intake through feeding or IV tubes is a nursing responsibility in many agencies.
items.ex: When the patient is stable, daily weights, I&O, and physical care can be delegated; IV administration and hemodynamic assessment cannot.

alt.q: Which tasks must the nurse keep rather than delegate to AP for a patient with an IV infusion? Select all that apply.
o: Administering the IV fluid
IV fluid administration is not delegated to AP.
Assessing hemodynamic status
Hemodynamic assessment is not delegated to AP.
Documenting drainage through tubes
AP often document urine, diarrhea, and vomitus but not drainage through tubes.
Measuring the patient’s daily weight
Daily weights may be delegated when the patient is stable.
Emptying and measuring a urinal
AP commonly measure and document urine output.
alt.ex: IV fluid administration, hemodynamic assessment, and tube intake or drainage stay with the nurse; weights and basic I&O can be delegated.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Skin turgor is not a reliable indicator of fluid status in older adults.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book notes that skin turgor testing is not reliable for older adults.
items.ww: Age-related skin changes make turgor misleading, so other markers such as weight and mucous membranes are used.

alt.q: Thirst is a reliable way to detect dehydration in older adults.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Older adults have decreased thirst sensation, so thirst is not relied on to assess dehydration or hypernatremia.
alt.ww: Reduced thirst in aging means a patient can be dehydrated without feeling thirsty.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: People who are Rh negative receive only Rh-negative blood components.
items.a: True
items.ex: Rh-negative people lack the Rh antigen and receive only Rh-negative blood components.
items.ww: Giving Rh-positive blood to an Rh-negative person can trigger an immune response against the Rh antigen.

alt.q: People with type AB-positive blood are called universal blood donors.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Type O-negative people are universal donors; type AB-positive people are universal recipients.
alt.ww: AB-positive red cells carry A, B, and Rh antigens, so they cannot be given to every recipient.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Older adults are at increased risk of pulmonary edema when isotonic IV fluids are infused rapidly, especially with cardiovascular illness.
items.a: True
items.ex: Cardiovascular illness reduces the ability to adapt to a sudden rise in vascular volume, raising the risk of pulmonary edema.
items.ww: Rapid isotonic infusion expands vascular volume, which a weakened heart cannot handle.

alt.q: Because isotonic fluids do not enter cells, they can be infused rapidly in older adults without risk of overload.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Isotonic fluids stay in the ECF, so rapid infusion can cause circulatory overload and pulmonary edema in older adults.
alt.ww: Fluid that stays in the vascular space is exactly what overloads a heart that cannot adapt.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: When IV fluid containing a tissue-damaging (vesicant) drug enters the subcutaneous tissue, the complication is called [[extravasation]].
items.ex: Infiltration is IV fluid entering tissue; extravasation is the term used when the fluid contains a vesicant drug.

alt.q: Leakage of a vesicant such as chemotherapy into tissue around the venipuncture site is called [[extravasation]].
alt.ex: Infiltration is IV fluid entering tissue; extravasation is the term used when the fluid contains a vesicant drug.
