items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse is about to insert a peripheral IV, and an AP is helping with the patient. Which instruction to the AP is appropriate?
items.a: Tell me if the IV dressing becomes wet
items.ex: AP cannot insert IVs but should report wet dressings, site redness, pain, swelling, leaking, low fluid, or pump alarms.
w: Try inserting the IV if my first attempt fails
Inserting a peripheral IV device cannot be delegated to AP.
Adjust the pump rate if the alarm sounds
AP report alarms to the nurse; they do not regulate infusions.
Remove the catheter if the site looks red
AP report site redness; the nurse assesses and decides on removal.

alt.q: Which statement about delegating short peripheral IV insertion is accurate?
alt.a: AP may not insert it; LPN delegation depends on state law
alt.ex: Insertion cannot be delegated to AP, and delegation to LPNs varies by state nurse practice act.
w: AP may insert it after a competency check
Insertion of a peripheral IV device is never delegated to AP.
AP may insert it if the nurse stays nearby
Supervision does not make IV insertion an AP task.
LPNs may insert it in every state
LPN delegation varies by state nurse practice act.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse is preparing to start an IV on an 82-year-old patient. Which catheter gauge is most appropriate?
items.a: 22- to 24-gauge
items.ex: Neonates, children, and older adults use 22- to 24-gauge catheters; the smallest gauge that fits the therapy is chosen.
w: 14- to 16-gauge
These large catheters are not listed for routine use and would damage fragile veins.
18- to 20-gauge
A larger catheter such as 20-gauge is chosen for rapid fluid replacement, not routine use in older adults.
26- to 28-gauge
These gauges are not among the catheter sizes the skill lists.

alt.q: An adult trauma patient needs rapid fluid replacement. Which catheter does the nurse select?
alt.a: 20-gauge
alt.ex: A larger catheter, such as 20-gauge, is selected when rapid fluid replacement is required.
w: 22-gauge
22-gauge is smaller and used for routine adult or older adult therapy.
24-gauge
24-gauge is the smallest listed size and would limit rapid flow.
26-gauge
This size is not listed and is too small for rapid replacement.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Where should the nurse apply the tourniquet before selecting a vein in the forearm?
items.a: 10 to 15 cm above the proposed site
items.ex: Place the tourniquet 10–15 cm (4–6 inches) above the site, tight enough to impede venous flow while keeping arterial flow.
w: 2 to 3 cm above the proposed site
This is too close to the site; the book specifies 10–15 cm above.
25 to 30 cm above the proposed site
This is farther than the 10–15 cm the book specifies.
5 to 8 cm below the proposed site
A tourniquet below the site would not distend the vein at the insertion point.

alt.q: After applying a tourniquet, the nurse cannot feel the radial pulse. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Loosen the tourniquet until a distal pulse is present
alt.ex: The tourniquet should impede venous flow but maintain arterial circulation; check for a distal pulse.
w: Leave it in place to maximize vein distention
Blocking arterial flow prevents venous filling and is unsafe.
Tighten it further to make the vein visible
Tightening would further impair arterial circulation.
Move it to the wrist below the insertion site
The tourniquet belongs 10–15 cm above the proposed site.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: When selecting a vein for a short peripheral IV in an adult, which sites should the nurse avoid? Select all that apply.
o: Arm on the side of breast surgery with axillary node dissection
This increases risk of infection, lymphedema, or vessel damage.
Arm with an arteriovenous fistula or graft
Extremities with dialysis grafts or fistulas are avoided.
Wrist or antecubital area
Areas of flexion increase risk of infiltration, phlebitis, and dislodgement.
Veins of the lower extremities
Leg veins are not used routinely in adults because of thrombophlebitis risk.
Forearm vein on the nondominant arm
Forearm veins on the nondominant side are preferred sites.
Most distal suitable site on the nondominant arm
Using the most distal site in the nondominant arm is recommended.
items.ex: Avoid compromised limbs, flexion areas, and lower extremities; prefer distal forearm veins on the nondominant arm.

alt.q: Which sites are appropriate to consider for a short peripheral IV in an adult? Select all that apply.
o: Cephalic vein on the forearm
Forearm veins such as the cephalic are preferred in adults.
Basilic vein on the forearm
The basilic vein is a preferred forearm vein.
Most distal suitable site on the nondominant arm
Distal sites on the nondominant arm preserve self-care.
Ventral surface of the wrist
The ventral wrist is painful and risks nerve damage.
Site distal to a previous infiltration
Sites distal to infiltration can cause new infiltration and vessel damage.
Arm affected by a stroke
Extremities affected by stroke are avoided.
alt.ex: Forearm veins on the nondominant arm are preferred; avoid the ventral wrist, previously damaged veins, and affected limbs.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse cleans the IV insertion site with alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG). Which technique is correct?
items.a: Use a back-and-forth motion and let it dry completely
items.ex: CHG is applied with a back-and-forth motion and must dry completely, at least 20 seconds, for full antisepsis.
w: Use concentric circles from the site outward, then blot dry
Concentric circles are used for alcohol or povidone-iodine; blotting prevents full antisepsis.
Wipe once quickly and insert while the skin is still wet
The antiseptic must fully dry to be effective.
Scrub vigorously in circles and fan the site to dry it
Vigorous friction can tear fragile skin, and circles are for other agents.

alt.q: After cleaning the site with CHG, the nurse needs to palpate the vein again. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Wear sterile gloves to palpate or repeat the antisepsis
alt.ex: Touching the cleaned area introduces microorganisms, so use sterile gloves or clean the site again.
w: Palpate with a clean gloved finger and proceed
A clean glove contaminates the prepared site; sterile gloves or reantisepsis are needed.
Wipe the fingertip with alcohol before palpating
This does not make the finger sterile; the site would be contaminated.
Palpate quickly with a bare fingertip for accuracy
A bare finger introduces microorganisms to the cleaned site.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why must the nurse never reinsert the stylet into the catheter after advancing the catheter into the vein?
items.a: The catheter can shear off and embolize
items.ex: Reinserting the stylet can cut the catheter, and the fragment can travel in the vein as an embolus.
w: The stylet loses sterility once withdrawn
Sterility is a concern, but the specific danger is catheter shearing and embolism.
It causes the vein to spasm and collapse
Vasospasm is not the reason given; catheter shearing is.
It triggers the safety device to lock the hub
The safety device covers the stylet; the hazard is shearing the catheter.

alt.q: Why should the nurse avoid advancing the entire stylet into the vein during venipuncture?
alt.a: It may pierce the vein wall and cause a hematoma
alt.ex: Advancing the whole stylet can penetrate the back wall of the vein, resulting in a hematoma.
w: It may shear the catheter off inside the vein
Shearing results from reinserting the stylet, not from advancing it.
It may cause the drip chamber to overfill
The drip chamber is unrelated to stylet advancement.
It may contaminate the catheter hub
Hub contamination comes from touching the open hub, not stylet depth.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Right after a successful venipuncture and flush, the nurse notes swelling at the insertion site. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Remove the catheter
items.ex: Swelling at the site indicates infiltration, which requires immediate catheter removal.
w: Apply the dressing and recheck in an hour
Infiltration requires immediate removal, not delayed reassessment.
Flush again with more saline to open the vein
Further flushing pushes more fluid into the tissue.
Raise the IV container to improve flow
Raising the container increases flow into the tissue.

alt.q: A nurse finds that a patient’s new IV catheter is occluded and will not flush easily. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Remove the catheter and do not force a flush
alt.ex: Occluded catheters should not be flushed; determine the cause and remove the occluded catheter.
w: Flush forcefully with a 3-mL syringe
Occluded catheters should not be flushed.
Increase the pump pressure to clear it
Forcing fluid through an occluded catheter is unsafe.
Leave it in place and recheck at the next shift
An occluded catheter cannot deliver therapy and should be removed.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse is flushing a short extension set that has a positive pressure displacement needleless connector. Which sequence is correct?
items.a: Flush, disconnect the syringe, then clamp
items.ex: For positive pressure displacement connectors, flush, disconnect the syringe, and then clamp to prevent blood reflux.
w: Flush, clamp while pushing, then disconnect
This is the sequence for negative pressure displacement connectors.
Clamp, flush, then disconnect the syringe
Clamping first would prevent the flush from entering the catheter.
Disconnect, flush, then clamp
The syringe must be attached to flush the line.

alt.q: A needleless connector uses negative pressure displacement. Which flush sequence prevents blood reflux into the catheter?
alt.a: Flush, clamp while pushing, then disconnect
alt.ex: With negative displacement, clamp while maintaining pressure on the syringe, then disconnect.
w: Flush, disconnect the syringe, then clamp
This sequence is for positive pressure displacement connectors.
Clamp, disconnect, then flush
The flush must occur before clamping and disconnecting.
No sequence is needed for this connector
Neutral displacement connectors have no set sequence; negative ones do.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which information does the nurse include on the label of a new peripheral IV dressing?
items.a: Insertion date and time, catheter gauge and length, and initials
items.ex: Labeling the date, time, gauge, length, and initials shows the device type and how long it has been in place.
w: Ordered solution, rate, and total volume to infuse
Solution and rate go in the record and on the container, not the dressing label.
Patient’s name, room number, and allergies
Identifiers and allergies belong on the ID band, not the dressing label.
Next dressing change date and the vein used
The required label items are insertion date and time, gauge, length, and initials.

alt.q: Why does the nurse label the primed IV tubing with the date?
alt.a: To show how long it has been in use and when to change it
alt.ex: Dating the tubing lets staff recognize how long it has been used and when it is due for change.
w: To show which solution is running through it
The solution is identified on the container, not by the tubing date.
To record the ordered infusion rate
The infusion rate is programmed and documented, not dated on the tubing.
To identify the nurse who will remove the IV
The tubing date marks use time, not who removes the catheter.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse is having difficulty finding a distended vein in a patient’s forearm. Which action helps distend the vein?
items.a: Position the arm lower than the heart
items.ex: Gravity promotes venous distention; slow fist clenching, light downward stroking, and controlled warming also help.
w: Raise the arm above the heart for 2 minutes
Raising the arm drains blood from the veins and reduces distention.
Tap the vein firmly several times
Repeated tapping can damage veins, especially fragile veins in older adults.
Tighten the tourniquet until the pulse disappears
Blocking arterial flow prevents venous filling.

alt.q: Which intervention has been found to increase successful peripheral catheter insertion?
alt.a: Controlled warming of the extremity
alt.ex: Warming the extremity for several minutes increases successful peripheral catheter insertion.
w: Shaving the site with a razor
Shaving may increase infection risk; clip hair instead.
Multiple vigorous taps on the vein
Repeated tapping can damage the vein.
Applying the tourniquet as tightly as possible
An overly tight tourniquet blocks arterial flow and venous filling.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why does the nurse prime the short extension tubing and needleless connector with normal saline before venipuncture?
items.a: To replace air so it does not enter the vein
items.ex: Priming replaces the air in the extension set with saline, preventing air from entering the vein during insertion.
w: To dilute the IV solution before it reaches the vein
Priming is done to remove air, not to dilute the solution.
To warm the tubing to body temperature
Priming with saline does not serve to warm the tubing.
To test the vein for patency before insertion
Patency is tested after insertion by blood return and flushing.

alt.q: After connecting the extension set, why does the nurse aspirate with the saline syringe before flushing?
alt.a: To remove air and confirm blood return
alt.ex: Aspirating removes air to prevent embolism, and blood return that looks like whole blood confirms the catheter is in the vein.
w: To obtain a blood sample for laboratory tests
The purpose is to remove air and confirm placement, not to collect a specimen.
To clear the stylet from the catheter
The stylet is already removed before the extension set is attached.
To check the pump’s pressure settings
Aspiration checks the catheter, not the pump.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Why does the nurse loop the IV tubing alongside the dressing and tape it to the arm?
items.a: The loop comes apart before the catheter dislodges
items.ex: If the tubing is pulled, the taped loop gives way first, reducing the risk of dislodging the catheter.
w: The loop slows the infusion to the ordered rate
Looping tubing secures it; it is not used to control rate.
The loop keeps air bubbles out of the catheter
Air is removed by priming, not by looping the tubing.
The loop allows the dressing to be changed less often
Dressing change frequency depends on dressing type and integrity.

alt.q: A patient is at risk for MARSI. Which action does the nurse take when securing the IV?
alt.a: Apply a polymer-based skin protectant before the dressing
alt.ex: A skin barrier applied and allowed to dry before adhesive devices decreases the risk of MARSI.
w: Use extra nonsterile tape to hold the catheter firmly
Excess tape increases skin injury risk; nonsterile tape is avoided.
Stretch the dressing tightly over the site
TSM dressings are applied without tension or stretching.
Apply the dressing while the skin is still damp
The skin protectant must dry completely before the dressing is applied.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse reviews a patient’s record for risk of medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI). Which factors increase risk? Select all that apply.
o: Advanced age
Age is a common risk factor for MARSI.
Dehydration
Dehydration is a listed MARSI risk factor.
Malnutrition
Malnutrition increases skin vulnerability to adhesive injury.
Prior radiation therapy to the area
Exposure to radiation therapy is a listed risk factor.
Regular aerobic exercise
Exercise is not listed as a MARSI risk factor.
Use of a polymer-based skin protectant
Skin protectants decrease, not increase, MARSI risk.
items.ex: MARSI risk factors include age, dehydration, malnutrition, radiation exposure, and chronic conditions such as diabetes or edema.

alt.q: Which findings at an IV dressing site indicate medical adhesive–related skin injury? Select all that apply.
o: Skin stripping
Mechanical trauma such as skin stripping is a form of MARSI.
Blistering
Blistering is a mechanical injury from adhesive.
Irritation from the adhesive
Dermatitis in response to adhesive is a form of MARSI.
Maceration or folliculitis
Maceration and folliculitis are listed MARSI complications.
Palpable venous cord
A palpable venous cord is a sign of phlebitis, not MARSI.
alt.ex: MARSI includes mechanical trauma, dermatitis from the adhesive, and maceration or folliculitis.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which items does the nurse document after inserting a short peripheral IV? Select all that apply.
o: Number of insertion attempts, successful and unsuccessful
All attempts are documented, not just the successful one.
Precise site, vein, and catheter gauge and length
Documentation includes location, vessel, brand, length, and gauge.
Type of solution, additives, and rate
The infusing solution, additives, rate, and method are recorded.
Patient’s response to the insertion
The patient’s response, such as what the patient reports, is documented.
Only the attempt that was successful
Both successful and unsuccessful attempts must be documented.
Name of the visitor present during insertion
Visitor names are not part of IV insertion documentation.
items.ex: Document attempts, exact site and device, solution and rate, method of infusion, and the patient’s response.

alt.q: Which events after catheter placement should the nurse report to the health care provider? Select all that apply.
o: Persistent pain or suspected nerve damage
Adverse events such as suspected nerve damage are reported.
Hematoma formation
Hematoma after placement is a reportable adverse event.
Arterial puncture
Arterial puncture is a reportable adverse event.
Patient asks what fluid is infusing
This is a teaching need, not an adverse event.
Dressing applied without wrinkles
A properly applied dressing is an expected finding.
alt.ex: Adverse events on placement, such as persistent pain, suspected nerve damage, hematoma, or arterial puncture, are reported.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Hair at a planned IV site should be clipped with scissors or clippers rather than shaved with a razor.
items.a: True
items.ex: Shaving may increase infection risk, so hair is clipped if removal is needed.
items.ww: Razors can cause tiny skin breaks that allow microorganisms to enter.

alt.q: Shaving the IV site with a razor is preferred because it lowers infection risk.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Shaving may increase the risk of infection; clip hair with scissors or clippers instead.
alt.ww: Clipping, not shaving, is the method that avoids raising infection risk.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: When priming IV tubing, the nurse squeezes the drip chamber so it fills one-third to one-half full.
items.a: True
items.ex: A partly filled drip chamber prevents air from entering the tubing and lets the nurse see the drops.
items.ww: A completely filled chamber hides drops, and an empty one lets air enter the tubing.

alt.q: When priming IV tubing, the drip chamber should be filled completely to keep out air.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The drip chamber is filled one-third to one-half full; a full chamber prevents observing the drip rate.
alt.ww: A partly filled chamber already prevents air entry while keeping drops visible.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A transparent semipermeable membrane (TSM) dressing is preferred over gauze because it allows the insertion site to be inspected.
items.a: True
items.ex: TSM and ISD dressings are preferred; gauze prevents assessment of the site and is reserved for drainage, sweating, or sensitivity.
items.ww: Gauze hides the site, so it is only used when TSM or ISD dressings cannot be used.

alt.q: A gauze dressing is the preferred dressing for a new IV site because it lets the nurse see the insertion site.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Gauze prevents assessment of the insertion site; TSM or ISD dressings are preferred.
alt.ww: Gauze is reserved for drainage, excessive perspiration, or sensitivity to transparent dressings.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Before starting an IV, the nurse learns the patient had a reaction to chlorhexidine (CHG) in the past. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Place an allergy ID band and use a different skin antiseptic
items.ex: Assess for allergy to iodine, adhesive, latex, or CHG; place an allergy band and choose an alternative such as 70% alcohol.
w: Use CHG anyway because it is the preferred antiseptic
Agents used during insertion can cause serious allergic reactions if an allergy exists.
Skip skin antisepsis to avoid any reaction
Skin antisepsis is still required; an alternative agent such as 70% alcohol is used.
Postpone the IV until the allergy can be tested
An allergy does not prevent insertion; the nurse substitutes a safe antiseptic.

alt.q: An older adult with fragile veins that bruise easily needs a peripheral IV. How should the nurse use the tourniquet?
alt.a: Apply it loosely or not at all
alt.ex: For fragile veins or easy bruising, apply the tourniquet loosely or not at all to prevent vein damage and bruising.
w: Apply it as tightly as possible to distend the vein
Tight pressure damages fragile veins and causes bruising.
Leave it on throughout the entire procedure
The tourniquet is released after access; prolonged pressure harms fragile veins.
Apply it directly over the planned insertion site
The tourniquet goes 10–15 cm above the site, not over it.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A single clinician should make no more than [[two|2]] attempts at starting a peripheral IV.
items.ex: Limiting attempts protects veins; after two unsuccessful attempts, escalate to a more skilled clinician, with no more than four in total.

alt.q: Total attempts at initiating peripheral IV access should be limited to no more than [[four|4]].
alt.ex: Limiting attempts protects veins; after two unsuccessful attempts, escalate to a more skilled clinician, with no more than four in total.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A health care provider orders 1000 mL of 0.9% sodium chloride to infuse over 8 hours. What hourly rate does the nurse program?
items.a: 125 mL/h
items.ex: Divide total volume by hours of infusion: 1000 mL ÷ 8 h = 125 mL/h.
w: 100 mL/h
100 mL/h would take 10 hours to infuse 1000 mL.
150 mL/h
150 mL/h would finish 1000 mL in under 7 hours.
80 mL/h
80 mL/h would take 12.5 hours to infuse 1000 mL.

alt.q: An order reads 3 L of IV fluid over 24 hours. What is the hourly rate?
alt.a: 125 mL/h
alt.ex: Convert to milliliters and divide by hours: 3000 mL ÷ 24 h = 125 mL/h.
w: 100 mL/h
100 mL/h for 24 hours delivers only 2400 mL.
150 mL/h
150 mL/h for 24 hours delivers 3600 mL.
300 mL/h
300 mL/h would infuse 3 L in 10 hours.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: An IV is ordered at 125 mL/h by gravity using tubing with a drop factor of 15 drops/mL. What drip rate does the nurse set?
items.a: 31 drops/min
items.ex: 125 mL/h × 15 drops/mL ÷ 60 min = 31.25, rounded to 31 drops/min.
w: 21 drops/min
21 drops/min results from using a drop factor of 10, not 15.
125 drops/min
125 drops/min would be correct only for microdrip (60 drops/mL) tubing.
47 drops/min
This overestimates the rate; 125 × 15 ÷ 60 is about 31.

alt.q: An IV is ordered at 50 mL/h by gravity using microdrip tubing. What drip rate does the nurse set?
alt.a: 50 drops/min
alt.ex: Microdrip delivers 60 drops/mL, so 50 mL/h × 60 ÷ 60 min = 50 drops/min.
w: 8 drops/min
This uses a drop factor of 10, which is macrodrip, not microdrip.
13 drops/min
This uses a drop factor of 15; microdrip is 60 drops/mL.
100 drops/min
This doubles the correct rate.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: An order reads 1000 mL over 10 hours by gravity, and the macrodrip tubing delivers 10 drops/mL. What drip rate should the nurse set?
items.a: 17 drops/min
items.ex: 1000 mL ÷ 10 h = 100 mL/h; 100 × 10 ÷ 60 = 16.7, rounded to 17 drops/min.
w: 10 drops/min
This is the drop factor, not the calculated drip rate.
25 drops/min
25 drops/min would apply with a drop factor of 15.
100 drops/min
100 is the hourly rate in mL/h, not drops per minute with this tubing.

alt.q: An order reads 1000 mL over 8 hours by gravity with tubing that delivers 10 drops/mL. What drip rate should the nurse set?
alt.a: 21 drops/min
alt.ex: 1000 mL ÷ 8 h = 125 mL/h; 125 × 10 ÷ 60 = 20.8, rounded to 21 drops/min.
w: 31 drops/min
31 drops/min would apply with a drop factor of 15.
13 drops/min
This underestimates; 125 × 10 ÷ 60 is about 21.
125 drops/min
125 drops/min would apply only with microdrip tubing.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: For a gravity infusion in an adult, how high above the IV site should the nurse hang the container?
items.a: At least 76.2 cm (30 inches)
items.ex: Gravity pressure must overcome venous pressure and resistance from the tubing and catheter, requiring at least 76.2 cm (30 inches).
w: At least 30 cm (12 inches)
This height is too low to overcome venous pressure and tubing resistance.
At least 45 cm (18 inches)
The book specifies at least 76.2 cm (30 inches) for adults.
At least 15 cm (6 inches)
This is far too low for reliable gravity flow.

alt.q: A gravity infusion of a more viscous fluid is running slowly. Which adjustment fits the book’s guidance?
alt.a: Raise the container higher above the IV site
alt.ex: Height increases driving pressure; increase container height for more viscous fluids.
w: Lower the container to the level of the IV site
Lowering the container reduces driving pressure and slows flow.
Fill the drip chamber completely
A full drip chamber prevents counting drops and does not improve flow.
Close the roller clamp halfway
Partly closing the clamp slows the infusion further.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: How does the nurse count the drip rate of a gravity infusion?
items.a: Hold a watch at drip-chamber level and count for 1 minute
items.ex: Holding a timing device at the level of the drip chamber and counting for a full minute gives an accurate rate.
w: Count drops for 10 seconds and multiply by 10
Multiplying a 10-second count by 10 is the wrong math; the book counts for 1 minute.
Estimate the rate from the level in the IV bag
The bag level is checked hourly but does not give the minute drip rate.
Read the rate from the roller clamp markings
Roller clamps have no rate markings; drops must be counted.

alt.q: How often should the nurse monitor the drip rate of a gravity infusion?
alt.a: At least hourly
alt.ex: Many factors influence drip rate, so frequent monitoring, at least hourly, ensures the fluid infuses as prescribed.
w: Once per shift
Once a shift is too infrequent; gravity rates change with position and other factors.
Only when the bag is empty
Waiting until the bag empties would miss rate errors.
Every 4 hours
Gravity drip rates are monitored at least hourly.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: An EID alarm sounds in a patient’s room. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess the IV system from the container to the insertion site
items.ex: An alarm signals a problem; trace the system from the container to the VAD site to find causes such as kinks, air, or infiltration.
w: Silence the alarm and restart the pump
Restarting without assessment could continue an infusion despite a complication.
Increase the programmed rate
Changing the rate does not address the cause of the alarm.
Remove the tubing and run the fluid by gravity
Removing tubing from the pump risks free flow and ignores the cause.

alt.q: Which condition can trigger an EID alarm?
alt.a: A clotted catheter
alt.ex: Occlusion from a clotted catheter, as well as kinks, closed clamps, air, empty containers, and low battery, triggers EID alarms.
w: A drip chamber one-third full
One-third to one-half full is the correct drip chamber level.
A roller clamp fully open below the pump
The drip regulator is opened completely while an EID is in use.
A dated label on the container
Labeling the container does not affect pump function.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient’s IV runs in rapidly by accident. The patient now has dyspnea, crackles in the lungs, and edema of the legs. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Slow the infusion rate
items.ex: These signs indicate fluid volume excess; slow the infusion first, then notify the provider immediately.
w: Place the patient flat in bed
The patient is placed in high Fowler position, not flat, to ease breathing.
Increase the rate to finish the bag quickly
More fluid would worsen the fluid volume excess.
Document the findings and recheck in 1 hour
Fluid volume excess needs immediate action and provider notification.

alt.q: After slowing the infusion for a patient with signs of fluid volume excess, how should the nurse position the patient?
alt.a: High Fowler position
alt.ex: High Fowler position eases breathing in fluid volume excess while the nurse notifies the provider and anticipates oxygen and diuretics.
w: Trendelenburg position
Lowering the head worsens dyspnea from fluid in the lungs.
Flat supine position
Lying flat increases breathing difficulty with pulmonary fluid.
Prone position
Prone positioning is not the recommended action for fluid volume excess.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient’s gravity IV is running slower than ordered. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Check for kinks, position changes, or container height
items.ex: When an IV runs slow, check position, container height, kinks, or obstruction and inspect the VAD site before seeking a new order.
w: Open the roller clamp fully to catch up
Catching up risks fluid overload; find and correct the cause.
Flush the catheter with a 3-mL syringe
Forcing a flush before finding the cause may harm the vein or catheter.
Remove the IV and restart it in a new site
Simple causes such as kinks should be checked first.

alt.q: A patient’s IV container ran empty and the line is no longer patent. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Discontinue the IV and restart a catheter in a new site
alt.ex: When patency is lost after the container runs empty, discontinue the infusion and restart a new peripheral catheter.
w: Flush the catheter forcefully to clear it
Forcing a flush is unsafe; the catheter is replaced.
Hang a new bag and open the clamp fully
A catheter that has lost patency will not deliver fluid.
Leave the catheter capped for later use
A nonpatent catheter cannot be used and must be removed.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: An AP is caring for a patient with an IV infusion. Which task related to the infusion is appropriate for the AP?
items.a: Report when the fluid container is nearly empty
items.ex: Regulating flow rates cannot be delegated; AP inform the nurse about alarms, near-empty containers, and patient discomfort.
w: Adjust the roller clamp to the ordered rate
Regulating IV flow rates cannot be delegated to AP.
Reprogram the pump when it alarms
AP report alarms; the nurse responds and programs the pump.
Calculate the drip rate for a gravity infusion
Calculating and setting flow rates is a nursing responsibility.

alt.q: A patient tells the AP that the IV site is burning. What should the AP do?
alt.a: Report the complaint to the nurse
alt.ex: AP are directed to report patient discomfort such as pain, burning, bleeding, or swelling to the nurse.
w: Slow the infusion until the burning stops
AP do not regulate infusions.
Remove the IV catheter
AP do not discontinue IVs; the nurse assesses the site.
Tell the patient this is a normal sensation
Burning may signal a complication and must be reported.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse programs a smart pump for an IV medication, and the pump alarms and shuts down immediately. What does this most likely mean?
items.a: The settings were outside the unit’s parameters
items.ex: Smart pumps have medication libraries and dose limits; an immediate alarm and shutdown means settings fell outside unit parameters.
w: The IV catheter has infiltrated
Infiltration may trigger alarms later, but an immediate shutdown points to programming limits.
The battery is fully charged
A charged battery does not cause the pump to shut down.
The tubing is the correct type for the pump
Correct tubing would not cause a shutdown.

alt.q: What is the purpose of the anti–free flow safeguard on an EID?
alt.a: To prevent a bolus if the tubing is removed
alt.ex: Anti–free flow protection prevents bolus infusion during malfunction or when tubing is removed from the pump.
w: To warm fluid to body temperature
Anti–free flow protection controls flow, not temperature.
To filter particles from the solution
Filters remove particles; anti–free flow prevents uncontrolled flow.
To calculate drops per minute
The pump delivers an hourly rate; this feature prevents free flow.

items.q: The health care provider writes “D5W with 20 mEq KCl 125 mL/h continuous.” How should the nurse interpret this order?

items.ex: An abbreviated continuous order implies the IV continues at this rate until a new order changes or discontinues it.
w: Infuse one 1000-mL bag and then stop
“Continuous” means the infusion continues until a new order is written.
Infuse at 125 mL/h for 8 hours only
No time limit is stated; it continues until changed or stopped.
Change the rate to KVO when the first bag ends
A KVO rate requires its own order with a specific rate.

alt.q: Which item must the nurse document when an IV runs on an EID?

alt.ex: When an EID is used, document the type and rate of infusion and the device identification number.
w: The color of the IV pole and pump
Equipment color is not part of IV documentation.
The pump’s battery charge level each hour
Battery level is not a documentation requirement.
The name of the pump manufacturer’s sales representative
This is unrelated to the patient’s infusion record.

items.q: A nurse reviews the record to decide how closely to control an IV volume. Which patients have increased risk for fluid and electrolyte imbalance? Select all that apply.

Neonates are listed as high risk, so volume control must be strict.
Older adult
Older adults are listed as high risk for imbalance.
Patient with a history of heart disease
Cardiac disease increases the risk of fluid overload.
Patient with renal disease
Renal disease impairs fluid and electrolyte excretion.
Healthy 30-year-old after minor surgery
This patient has none of the listed risk factors.
Adolescent with a sprained ankle
A minor injury does not make volume control critical.
items.ex: Neonates, older adults, and patients with cardiac or renal disease need strict volume control, which guides the choice of infusion device.

alt.q: Which patients need an infusion pump rather than gravity flow? Select all that apply.

Patient at risk for volume overload

Patient with impaired renal function
Impaired renal function is an indication for a pump.

Medications needing a specific hourly volume require a pump.

Pumps attach to IV poles; patient preference is not the indication.
alt.ex: Pumps are needed for low rates, risk of overload, renal impairment, and solutions requiring a specific hourly volume.

items.q: When should the nurse change a patient’s IV solution container?
items.a: When about 50 mL remains in the neck of the container
items.ex: Change the container when fluid remains only in its neck, a new solution is ordered, or the hang time has expired.
w: When about 250 mL remains in the container
Changing this early wastes solution; wait until only the neck holds fluid.
After the container has run completely dry
Letting the container empty risks loss of patency and air entering the tubing.
Every 4 hours regardless of the volume left
Change timing depends on volume, new orders, or hang time, not a set 4 hours.

alt.q: A nurse notes that the current IV bag still has 400 mL left, but the provider has ordered a different solution. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Change the container to the newly ordered solution
alt.ex: A container is changed when a new type of solution has been ordered, even if fluid remains.
w: Wait until only 50 mL remains, then hang the new solution
Once a new solution is ordered, the change should not wait for the old bag to empty.
Add the new solution to the current bag
Medications or solutions are not added to infusing containers.
Hang the new solution on a separate pole without connecting it
The new solution must replace the old one to be delivered.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: While moving the spike from the old IV bag into the new bag, the nurse accidentally touches the spike to the bedside table. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Obtain a new IV tubing set
items.ex: A spike contaminated by touching an unsterile object requires a new IV tubing set.
w: Wipe the spike with alcohol and insert it
Wiping does not restore sterility; the tubing must be replaced.
Insert the spike quickly to limit exposure
Speed does not undo contamination of the spike.
Rinse the spike with sterile saline
Rinsing does not make a contaminated spike sterile.

alt.q: Why does the nurse remove the spike from the old container and insert it into the new one quickly, without touching the tip?
alt.a: To keep the drip chamber from emptying and maintain sterility
alt.ex: Moving quickly keeps the drip chamber from emptying, and not touching the tip maintains sterility.
w: To reduce the need for a time label
Speed does not replace labeling the new container.
To increase the infusion rate during the change
The roller clamp is closed during the change; flow is not increased.
To avoid having to check the solution label
The solution is always checked before it is hung.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: After hanging a new IV bag, the nurse notices the drip chamber is completely full. Why is this a problem?
items.a: The nurse cannot observe or regulate the drip rate
items.ex: A completely full drip chamber hides the drops, so the rate cannot be observed or regulated; it should be one-third to one-half full.
w: It causes air to enter the tubing
A full chamber hides drops; an empty chamber is what lets air in.
It increases the infusion rate automatically
Chamber level does not set the rate; it prevents seeing the drops.
It makes the solution incompatible with the tubing
Chamber level has no effect on compatibility.

alt.q: How does the nurse lower the fluid level in an overfilled drip chamber?
alt.a: Pinch the tubing, invert the bag, squeeze the chamber, then right the bag
alt.ex: Removing the bag, pinching the tubing below the chamber, inverting, squeezing, and turning upright lowers the level.
w: Open the roller clamp fully and let fluid run out
This infuses fluid rapidly into the patient and does not fix the chamber.
Disconnect the tubing and drain the chamber
Disconnecting breaks the system and risks contamination.
Tap the chamber until the fluid level drops
Tapping removes small bubbles in the tubing, not excess chamber fluid.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Before attaching new tubing to a saline lock, how long should the nurse scrub the injection cap with an antiseptic swab?
items.a: At least 15 seconds, then let it dry
items.ex: Scrubbing the injection cap for at least 15 seconds and allowing it to dry completely ensures effective disinfection.
w: At least 3 seconds, then connect while wet
A brief wipe and connecting while wet do not disinfect effectively.
At least 2 minutes, then blot it dry
The book specifies at least 15 seconds and air drying, not blotting.
No scrub is needed if the cap is capped
Every access requires the cap to be scrubbed first.

alt.q: After scrubbing the injection cap, how much normal saline does the nurse inject through the cap into the extension set?
alt.a: 3 to 5 mL
alt.ex: A syringe with 3–5 mL of normal saline is injected to maintain catheter patency.
w: 0.5 to 1 mL
This is less than the volume the book specifies.
10 to 20 mL
This is more than the 3–5 mL used at this step.
25 to 30 mL
This large volume is not used to flush a short extension set.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse is about to discontinue a peripheral IV for a patient who takes warfarin. How should the nurse adjust the procedure?
items.a: Hold pressure longer, 5 to 10 minutes, and assess bleeding
items.ex: Anticoagulants, platelet inhibitors, or low platelets require steady pressure for 5–10 minutes and assessment for bleeding.
w: Apply pressure for only 30 seconds to avoid bruising
Short pressure is unsafe with anticoagulants; longer pressure is needed.
Withdraw the catheter quickly to limit bleeding
The catheter is withdrawn slowly; speed does not control bleeding.
Skip the dressing so bleeding can be watched
A sterile folded gauze dressing is applied after bleeding stops.

alt.q: Before discontinuing a peripheral IV, why does the nurse ask whether the patient takes an anticoagulant?
alt.a: It increases the time pressure must be applied
alt.ex: Anticoagulants or a coagulopathy increase bleeding, so more time is needed to apply pressure after removal.
w: It changes the type of antiseptic used
The antiseptic choice does not depend on anticoagulant use.
It means the catheter must be cut to remove it
Catheters are never cut; they are withdrawn slowly.
It requires a health care provider to remove the IV
Removal is done by the nurse with an order; pressure time changes.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: After withdrawing a peripheral IV catheter, why does the nurse inspect the end of the catheter?
items.a: To be sure the tip is intact and did not break off
items.ex: A tip that breaks off can embolize, which is an emergency; inspection confirms the catheter is intact.
w: To decide whether to culture the catheter
Culture is for suspected infection; routine inspection checks the tip.
To see whether the catheter can be reused
Catheters are single use and never reinserted.
To measure the gauge for documentation
The gauge is documented at insertion; inspection checks integrity.

alt.q: Why does the nurse avoid using scissors when removing an IV dressing before discontinuing the IV?
alt.a: Scissors might damage the catheter or injure the patient
alt.ex: Scissors can accidentally cut the catheter or the patient’s skin, so they are not used.
w: Scissors are too slow to remove the dressing
The concern is damage and injury, not speed.
Scissors would contaminate the gloves
The reason given is catheter damage and skin injury.
Scissors cannot cut a transparent dressing
Transparent dressings can be cut, but doing so risks harm.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient receiving IV therapy asks to take a shower. The IV is due to be discontinued soon, and another will be started later. What is the best plan?
items.a: Schedule the shower after the IV is removed and before the new one is placed
items.ex: Coordinate hygiene after discontinuing an IV and before another venipuncture; never disconnect tubing for hygiene.
w: Disconnect the tubing during the shower, then reconnect it
Disconnecting tubing breaks the system and leads to contamination.
Let the patient shower with the IV site uncovered
The IV site and dressing must be kept dry and protected.
Delay the shower until the IV therapy ends for good
Coordination allows hygiene between IV sites without waiting.

alt.q: A patient with an infusing IV needs a gown change, and the infusion cannot be stopped. Which approach is best?
alt.a: Use a special IV gown with snaps if available
alt.ex: If the infusion cannot be discontinued, use an IV gown and never disconnect the tubing to change clothing.
w: Disconnect the tubing briefly to change the gown
Disconnecting tubing to change a gown leads to contamination.
Cut the old gown sleeve off over the IV
The book recommends IV gowns or threading the bag through the sleeve.
Leave the patient in the soiled gown until discharge
The patient’s hygiene needs can be met safely with an IV gown.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Before discontinuing a patient’s peripheral IV, what does the nurse tell the patient to expect?
items.a: Hold the arm still; you may feel burning; it takes about 5 minutes
items.ex: The patient is told to hold the extremity still, that a burning sensation may occur, and that the procedure takes about 5 minutes.
w: Move the arm freely; there will be no sensation; it takes 1 minute
The patient must hold still, and a burning sensation is possible.
Make a tight fist; you will feel cold; it takes about 15 minutes
These are not the instructions or time given in the book.
Lift the arm overhead; you may feel pressure; it takes about 30 minutes
The arm is held still, and the procedure takes about 5 minutes.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient shows understanding of teaching before IV removal?
alt.a: “I need to keep my arm still, and I may feel some burning.”
alt.ex: Patients are told to hold the extremity still and that a burning sensation may be felt during removal.
w: “I should pull my arm away if it stings.”
Moving the arm can cause trauma; the arm is kept still.
“This will take about an hour.”
The procedure takes about 5 minutes.
“I won’t feel anything at all.”
A burning sensation may be felt as the catheter is removed.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse labels a new plastic IV bag with the time hung and the hourly levels. How should the label be applied?
items.a: Write only on the time label placed on the bag
items.ex: With plastic bags, mark only on the label and not on the container itself.
w: Write directly on the plastic with a marker
Marking directly on plastic bags is avoided; use the label.
Write the times on the tubing below the drip chamber
The tubing label shows tubing change date, not hourly volume levels.
Write the times on the patient’s dressing label
The dressing label shows insertion data, not container times.

alt.q: What is the purpose of the time label on an IV container?
alt.a: To compare the volume infused with the prescribed rate
alt.ex: A time label gives a visual comparison of volume infused with the prescribed rate.
w: To show when the tubing must be changed
The tubing has its own date label for change timing.
To identify when the catheter was inserted
Insertion time is on the dressing label.
To record the nurse’s initials only
The label shows time hung, time of completion, and hourly intervals.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Which instructions may the nurse give to AP caring for a patient with an IV system? Select all that apply.
o: Tell me when the IV container is nearly empty
AP inform the nurse when a container is near completion.
Report any cloudiness or precipitate in the solution
AP report cloudiness or precipitate in the IV solution.
Report if the tubing has been lying on the floor
Contaminated tubing must be reported to the nurse.
Protect the IV dressing during hygiene
AP protect the dressing during hygiene and ADLs.
Change the IV container when it runs low
Changing IV containers cannot be delegated to AP.
Discontinue the IV when the order is written
Discontinuing an IV cannot be delegated to AP.
items.ex: AP report problems and protect the dressing, but changing containers or tubing and discontinuing IVs cannot be delegated.

alt.q: Which IV maintenance tasks must the nurse perform rather than delegate to AP? Select all that apply.
o: Changing the IV fluid container
Changing IV containers is not delegated to AP.
Changing the IV tubing
Changing IV tubing is not delegated to AP.
Discontinuing the peripheral IV
Discontinuing an IV is not delegated to AP.
Reporting a pump alarm
AP can report pump alarms to the nurse.
Reporting leakage around the tubing
AP are instructed to report leakage.
alt.ex: Container changes, tubing changes, and IV removal stay with the nurse; AP report alarms and leaks.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Before hanging a new IV solution, which checks should the nurse perform? Select all that apply.
o: Verify the expiration date
The solution expiration date is verified before hanging.
Observe for precipitate, discoloration, and leakage
Solutions are inspected for precipitate, discoloration, and leaks.
Allow a refrigerated solution to warm to room temperature
Refrigerated solutions are warmed to room temperature first.
Follow any light sensitivity restrictions
Light-sensitive solutions must be protected as directed.
Add the newly ordered medication to the bag that is infusing
Medications are not added to infusing containers.
Write the hang time directly on the plastic bag
Mark only the label on plastic bags, not the container.
items.ex: Check the seven rights, expiration date, appearance, temperature, and light sensitivity before hanging the next solution.

alt.q: A nurse inspects an IV solution delivered from pharmacy. Which findings mean the bag should not be used? Select all that apply.
o: Cloudy solution
Cloudiness suggests contamination or incompatibility.
Visible precipitate
Solutions with precipitates are not used.
Leak in the bag
A leaking bag has compromised integrity and infection risk.
Past the expiration date
Expired solutions are not used.
Label matching the order
A matching label is an expected finding.
Clear, colorless solution
A clear solution without discoloration is acceptable.
alt.ex: Do not use solutions that are cloudy, discolored, contain precipitate, leak, or are expired.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A nurse finds that a patient’s infusion is 150 mL behind the expected volume. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Notify the health care provider per agency policy
Notify the provider if the infusion is 100–200 mL off the anticipated amount.
Assess for signs of fluid volume deficit
Evaluate for adverse effects such as FVD or FVE.
Find and correct the cause, such as a kink
Determine and correct causes like position change, kinks, or loss of patency.
Use an EID if accurate flow is critical
An EID is used when accurate flow rate is critical.
Open the clamp fully to catch up the volume
Catching up risks fluid overload; the cause is corrected and the provider notified.
Flush the catheter forcefully
Forceful flushing is unsafe and does not address the cause.
items.ex: For an incorrect flow rate, notify the provider per policy, assess for FVD or FVE, correct the cause, and use an EID when needed.

alt.q: A nurse finds that a patient received about 200 mL more IV fluid than expected. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Assess for signs of fluid volume excess
Evaluate for adverse effects such as FVE.
Notify the health care provider per agency policy
A variance of 100–200 mL is reported per policy.
Determine why the rate was incorrect
Identify causes such as position change or tubing problems.
Stop all IV fluids permanently
The provider decides on changes to therapy; the nurse does not stop it permanently.
Remove the tubing from the pump and run by gravity
An EID is preferred when accurate rate is critical.
alt.ex: With too much fluid infused, assess for FVE, report per policy, and correct the cause of the rate error.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: The short extension tubing stays attached to the peripheral catheter and is changed when the catheter is changed.
items.a: True
items.ex: The extension set remains on the short peripheral catheter and is replaced with the catheter.
items.ww: Changing it separately would require extra manipulation of the catheter hub.

alt.q: The short extension tubing should be replaced every time the administration set is changed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The extension tubing remains attached to the catheter and is changed only when the catheter is changed.
alt.ww: Replacing it with each tubing change adds unnecessary catheter manipulation.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: IV tubing changes should be coordinated with solution container changes when possible.
items.a: True
items.ex: Coordinating changes reduces the number of times the system is opened, lowering infection risk.
items.ww: Each separate opening of the system adds a chance for contamination.

alt.q: IV tubing should be changed at a different time from the solution container to spread out the work.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Tubing changes are scheduled with container changes to reduce how often the system is opened.
alt.ww: Separate changes open the system more often and increase contamination risk.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: Primary continuous IV tubing for routine solutions is replaced no more often than every 96 hours but at least every 7 days.
items.a: True
items.ex: For solutions other than PN, lipids, or blood, continuous primary tubing is changed no more often than 96 hours and at least every 7 days.
items.ww: Changing too often opens the system unnecessarily; leaving it beyond 7 days raises risk.

alt.q: Primary continuous IV tubing for routine solutions should be replaced every 24 hours.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Every-24-hour changes apply to intermittent infusions and lipids; continuous primary tubing is changed every 96 hours to 7 days.
alt.ww: Frequent changes of continuous tubing open the system without added benefit.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: A patient is receiving IV fluids with added potassium. During the maintenance assessment, why does the nurse review the patient’s serum potassium in the EHR?
items.a: To compare with baseline and judge response to the solution

items.q: A nurse is assigning morning care for a patient with a peripheral IV to assistive personnel (AP). Which instruction to the AP is appropriate?
items.a: Tell me if the patient says the IV dressing feels damp or is coming loose.
items.ex: AP cannot change IV dressings but should report moistness or loosening of the dressing to the nurse.
w: Change the IV dressing if it comes loose during the patient’s bath.
Changing a peripheral IV dressing cannot be delegated to AP; they report a loose dressing to the nurse.
Take off the IV dressing for the bath and put it back when the arm is dry.
AP protect the dressing during hygiene; removing and replacing it is a nursing skill.
Check the IV site every 4 hours and record any complications you find.
Assessing the VAD site for complications is a nursing responsibility, not an AP task.

alt.q: Which task related to a peripheral IV dressing may the nurse delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
alt.a: Protecting the IV dressing during hygiene and daily activities
alt.ex: AP are directed to protect the IV dressing during hygiene and ADLs and to report moistness or loosening.
w: Replacing a loosened TSM dressing over the IV site
Changing a peripheral IV dressing cannot be delegated to AP.
Applying skin barrier protectant around the IV site
Skin barrier protectant is applied by the nurse as part of the dressing change.
Labeling the new dressing with the date and catheter gauge
Labeling is part of the dressing change, which the nurse performs.

items.q: For an adult patient, how often should an intact transparent semipermeable membrane (TSM) dressing over a peripheral IV be changed?
items.a: At least every 7 days, or immediately if its integrity is disrupted
items.ex: TSM dressings and ISDs are changed at least every 7 days, or at once if lifted, soiled, wet, or bloody.
w: At least every 24 hours, or immediately if its integrity is disrupted
Daily changes are not required; each change increases the risk of catheter displacement.
At least every 2 days, or immediately if its integrity is disrupted
A 2-day interval applies to gauze dressings, not TSM dressings or ISDs.
At least every 14 days, or immediately if its integrity is disrupted
Fourteen days exceeds the 7-day maximum interval for TSM dressings and ISDs.

alt.q: A patient’s peripheral IV is covered with a gauze dressing that remains clean, dry, and intact. How often may the nurse change it?
alt.a: Every 2 days, or sooner if the dressing is compromised
alt.ex: Gauze dressings may be changed every 2 days, or sooner if compromised; gauze also hides the site from view.
w: Every 7 days, or sooner if the dressing is compromised
Seven days is the interval for TSM dressings and ISDs, not gauze.
Every 8 hours, or sooner if the dressing is compromised
Changing every shift is unnecessary and increases the risk of catheter displacement.
Every 14 days, or sooner if the dressing is compromised
Fourteen days is far longer than the 2-day interval for gauze dressings.

items.q: A nurse checks a TSM dressing over a peripheral IV. Which findings mean the dressing must be changed now rather than at the scheduled time? Select all that apply.
o: One border edge of the dressing has lifted away from the skin
A lifted or detached edge disrupts dressing integrity and requires an immediate change.
Blood has collected under the transparent portion of the dressing
Blood under the dressing disrupts its integrity and calls for an immediate change.
The dressing is visibly soiled with food from breakfast
A visibly soiled dressing must be changed immediately.
The skin under the adhesive shows a small tear
Compromised skin integrity under the dressing is an indication for an immediate change.
The intact dressing was applied 3 days ago
An intact TSM dressing can stay up to 7 days; extra changes risk catheter displacement.
The health care provider changed the infusion rate
A change in infusion rate does not affect dressing integrity.
items.ex: TSM dressings are changed immediately when lifted, soiled, wet, bloody, or covering damaged skin; otherwise at least every 7 days.

alt.q: A TSM dressing was applied to a patient’s IV site 2 days ago. Which observations require the nurse to change it now? Select all that apply.
o: Moisture is visible under the transparent window
Moisture under the dressing disrupts integrity and causes skin maceration.
Drainage is present at the insertion site under the film
Drainage under the dressing is an indication for an immediate change.
The edge closest to the catheter hub has detached
Any lifted or detached border edge means dressing integrity is disrupted.
The insertion site is clearly visible through the film
Visibility of the site is the intended benefit of a TSM dressing, not a problem.
The film is wrinkled but sealed on every edge
A sealed, clean, dry dressing remains intact and does not need an early change.
alt.ex: Moisture, drainage, or a detached edge disrupts TSM dressing integrity and requires an immediate change.

items.q: Before changing a peripheral IV dressing, the nurse reviews the EHR for risk of medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI). Which findings increase this risk? Select all that apply.
o: Dehydration
Dehydration is a listed risk factor for MARSI.
Malnutrition
Malnutrition is a listed risk factor for MARSI.
Recent radiation therapy
Exposure to radiation therapy increases the risk for MARSI.
Edema of the extremity with the IV
Edema of the extremity is a listed MARSI risk factor.
Intact skin with normal turgor
Intact skin with normal turgor reflects good skin condition, not a MARSI risk.
Adequate daily oral fluid intake
Adequate hydration is protective; dehydration is the risk factor.
items.ex: MARSI risk factors include age, dehydration, malnutrition, radiation therapy, chronic conditions such as diabetes, and extremity edema.

alt.q: Which patient conditions place a patient at increased risk for MARSI when adhesive IV dressings are used? Select all that apply.
o: Diabetes mellitus
Chronic conditions such as diabetes mellitus increase MARSI risk.
Immunosuppression
Immunosuppression is a chronic condition listed as a MARSI risk factor.
Malnutrition
Malnutrition is a listed risk factor for MARSI.
Normal hydration status
Normal hydration is not a risk; dehydration is the listed risk factor.
Well-balanced nutritional intake
Good nutrition is not a risk; malnutrition is the listed risk factor.
alt.ex: Chronic conditions like diabetes and immunosuppression, plus malnutrition, raise the risk for adhesive-related skin injury.

items.q: While stabilizing the catheter with the nondominant hand, how should the nurse remove an old TSM dressing to reduce skin injury?
items.a: Stretch a loosened corner horizontally in the opposite direction while supporting the skin
items.ex: The stretch-and-relax technique stretches the film horizontally while one hand supports the skin, preventing MARSI.
w: Lift a loosened corner straight up and peel the film off quickly in one motion
Pulling up quickly traumatizes skin; the book uses a low horizontal stretch while supporting skin.
Grasp the center of the film over the hub and lift it straight off the catheter
Lifting from the center risks dislodging the catheter; loosen edges and stretch horizontally.
Soak the film with antiseptic swabs until it floats free from the skin surface
Sterile adhesive remover, not antiseptic, is used to loosen the adhesive bond if needed.

alt.q: A nurse is removing an integrated securement device (ISD) from a peripheral IV site. Which technique is correct?
alt.a: Open the strip perforations, then peel low and slow from the tubing exit toward the insertion site
alt.ex: For an ISD, open the perforations and peel back slowly from where tubing exits toward the insertion site.
w: Open the strip perforations, then pull the dressing straight up starting at the insertion site
Pulling up from the skin causes trauma; the ISD is peeled back toward the insertion site.
Lift the dressing straight up from the catheter hub first, then open the strip perforations
Perforations are opened first, and the dressing is peeled back rather than lifted up.
Peel the dressing quickly from the insertion site outward toward where the tubing exits
Removal is low and slow and moves from the tubing exit toward the insertion site.

items.q: When removing a gauze IV dressing, the nurse takes off the old dressing one layer at a time, pulling toward the insertion site.
items.a: True
items.ex: Removing gauze one layer at a time toward the insertion site avoids tugging the catheter out of the vein.
items.ww: The skill directs removing gauze one layer at a time by pulling toward the insertion site, watching for tangled tubing.

alt.q: When removing tape strips from a gauze IV dressing, the nurse pulls each strip from the center of the dressing outward toward its ends.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Tape strips are lifted from each side toward the center; once both sides are loose, the strip is lifted from the center.
alt.ww: Working from the sides toward the center while stabilizing the hub prevents pulling the catheter out of position.

items.q: A peripheral IV will remain in place after its dressing is removed. How should the nurse cleanse the site with an alcohol-based 2% chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG) swab?
items.a: Scrub with back-and-forth friction for 30 seconds and let it dry completely
items.ex: CHG is applied with back-and-forth friction for 30 seconds and must dry completely for full antisepsis.
w: Wipe in concentric circles from the site outward for 10 seconds and blot it dry
Concentric circles apply to alcohol or povidone-iodine; blotting prevents the complete drying antisepsis requires.
Scrub with back-and-forth friction for 5 seconds and apply the dressing while damp
Five seconds is too short, and a damp site reduces antisepsis and dressing adhesion.
Wipe in concentric circles from the outer edge inward for 30 seconds and let it dry
Moving inward drags organisms toward the site; CHG uses back-and-forth friction.

alt.q: A nurse uses a povidone-iodine swab for skin antisepsis during an IV dressing change. Which technique is correct?
alt.a: Clean in concentric circles from the insertion site outward, then let it dry completely
alt.ex: Alcohol or povidone-iodine is applied in concentric circles moving outward from the site and allowed to dry fully.
w: Clean in concentric circles from the outer edge toward the insertion site, then let it dry
Cleaning moves from the insertion site outward, not toward it.
Clean in concentric circles from the insertion site outward, then apply the dressing at once
The antiseptic must dry completely before the dressing is applied.
Scrub back and forth across the insertion site, then blot off the excess with gauze
Back-and-forth friction is the CHG method; blotting prevents complete drying.

items.src: Ch 42 · Fluid, electrolyte, and acid-base balance

items.q: With 2% CHG antisepsis, scrub the IV insertion site using back-and-forth friction for [[30|thirty]] seconds, then allow it to dry completely.
items.ex: Thirty seconds of friction followed by complete drying is needed for effective CHG skin antisepsis.

alt.q: Before applying the new dressing, the antiseptic must be allowed to [[dry completely|dry|air dry|fully dry]] because drying is necessary for complete antisepsis.
alt.ex: Thirty seconds of friction followed by complete drying is needed for effective CHG skin antisepsis.

items.q: A nurse is changing the TSM dressing on a confused patient who keeps pulling the IV arm away. Which action is best?
items.a: Ask another nurse or AP to help hold the extremity still during the change
items.ex: For a restless or uncooperative patient, having another nurse or AP help keeps the catheter stable and secure.
w: Apply the new dressing without skin antisepsis to shorten the procedure
Skipping antisepsis increases the risk of catheter-related infection.
Remove the catheter and restart the IV once the patient becomes calm
A functioning catheter without complications does not need removal for restlessness.
Cover the site with a BAND-AID until the patient is calmer later
BAND-AIDs are not occlusive and should not be used over catheter insertion points.

alt.q: During a peripheral IV dressing change, which action best prevents accidental dislodgement of the catheter?
alt.a: Keep one finger over the catheter until the new dressing secures the hub
alt.ex: One finger stays over the catheter until the dressing secures the hub to prevent dislodgement.
w: Secure the hub with nonsterile tape before removing the old film
Nonsterile tape over the insertion point increases the risk of insertion site infection.
Ask the patient to hold the catheter hub with the other hand
The patient’s hand would contaminate the site; the nurse stabilizes the catheter.
Remove the old film quickly so the hub is uncovered only briefly
Fast removal traumatizes skin and can pull the catheter; use slow, supported removal.

items.q: A BAND-AID is an acceptable covering for a peripheral catheter insertion point when a TSM dressing is not available.
items.a: False
items.ex: BAND-AIDs are not occlusive, so they are never used over catheter insertion points.
items.ww: The insertion site needs a sterile dressing such as a TSM dressing or ISD to protect it and lower infection risk.

alt.q: Nonsterile tape should not be placed over a peripheral catheter insertion point because it increases the risk for insertion site infection.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Nonsterile tape over an insertion point raises infection risk, so only a sterile dressing covers the site.
alt.ww: Tape is used to anchor tubing alongside the dressing, never as a covering over the insertion point.

items.q: After skin antisepsis, the nurse applies skin barrier protectant where the tape, dressing, or stabilization device will go and lets it dry before applying the dressing.
items.a: True
items.ex: Skin barrier protectant maintains skin integrity, prevents adhesive irritation, and promotes adhesion once dry.
items.ww: The skill applies the protectant to areas where adhesives will be reapplied and allows it to dry before dressing.

alt.q: Skin barrier protectant is applied under an IV dressing mainly to weaken adhesion so the dressing is easier to remove at the next change.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Skin barrier protectant promotes dressing adhesion while protecting skin from adhesive irritation.
alt.ww: It coats skin to maintain integrity and promote adhesion; sterile adhesive remover is what loosens adhesive at removal.

items.q: Which information should the nurse write on the label of a newly applied peripheral IV dressing?
items.a: Date and time of IV insertion, VAD gauge and length, and nurse’s initials
items.ex: The label shows insertion date and time, VAD gauge size and length, and the nurse’s initials.
w: Date of the dressing change, type of IV fluid, and patient’s room number
IV fluid type and room number are not dressing label items; insertion date and VAD size are.
Patient’s name, ordered infusion rate, and health care provider’s name
Infusion rate and provider name belong in orders and records, not on the dressing label.
Time of the last flush, antiseptic used, and the AP’s initials
AP do not change dressings; the label carries the nurse’s initials and VAD details.

alt.q: Why does the nurse label a newly applied peripheral IV dressing according to agency policy?
alt.a: It communicates the device type and the interval for dressing change and site rotation
alt.ex: The label tells caregivers what device is in place and when the dressing change and site rotation are due.
w: It replaces documentation of the dressing change in the electronic health record
The dressing change must still be documented; the label does not replace the record.
It tells the assistive personnel when they may change the dressing themselves
AP cannot change peripheral IV dressings, so the label is not for that purpose.
It identifies the ordered IV solution and the prescribed infusion rate
The label describes the VAD and its timing, not the solution or rate.

items.q: After removing a peripheral IV dressing, the nurse finds redness, warmth, and swelling at the catheter entry point with purulent drainage. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Determine whether the VAD needs removal and notify the health care provider
items.ex: Signs of local infection may require VAD removal; the catheter is removed if ordered and the provider is notified.
w: Cleanse the site, apply a new TSM dressing, and reassess at the next routine change
Local infection must not be covered and left; early treatment prevents bloodstream infection.
Apply a site protection device over a new dressing to limit further irritation
A protection device prevents bumping and dislodgement; it does not treat a local infection.
Increase the infusion rate to keep the catheter patent while monitoring the site
Raising the rate does not address infection and is not an ordered intervention.

alt.q: During a peripheral IV dressing change, the catheter slips out of the patient’s vein. The patient still needs IV therapy. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Start a new peripheral IV in the other extremity or above the previous site
alt.ex: If the VAD is dislodged and therapy continues, restart a new line in the other extremity or above the old site.
w: Reinsert the same catheter after cleansing it with a CHG swab
A dislodged catheter is never reinserted; a new peripheral IV is started.
Start a new IV just below the previous insertion site in the same vein
A new site is chosen in the other extremity or above, not below, the previous site.
Cover the site and wait 24 hours before inserting a new IV
Continued therapy is necessary, so a new line is restarted rather than delayed.

items.q: A nurse observes a newly hired nurse finishing a peripheral IV dressing change with a TSM dressing. Which action requires correction?
items.a: Placing a strip of tape across the TSM dressing to hold the tubing
items.ex: Tape should not be placed over a TSM dressing or ISD; tubing is taped alongside the dressing.
w: Anchoring the extension tubing alongside the dressing on the arm
Anchoring tubing alongside the dressing is correct and prevents accidental dislodgement.
Placing tape directly over the tubing on the skin beside the dressing
Taping directly over the tubing next to the dressing is the correct method.
Labeling the dressing with the insertion date, gauge, and initials
Labeling the dressing per agency policy is a correct step in the procedure.

alt.q: How should the nurse secure the IV extension tubing after applying a new TSM dressing?
alt.a: Anchor the tubing alongside the dressing with tape placed directly over the tubing
alt.ex: Taping the tubing alongside the dressing prevents dislodgement without placing tape over the TSM film.
w: Loop the tubing over the dressing and tape it across the transparent film
Tape is not placed over a TSM dressing or ISD.
Tuck the tubing beneath the edge of the TSM dressing to hold it flat
Lifting the edge to tuck tubing disrupts the dressing seal and its integrity.
Wrap tape around the arm and over the dressing to hold the tubing
Tape over the dressing is avoided; the tubing is anchored alongside it.

items.q: A patient going home with a peripheral IV has received teaching about the IV site. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “If the catheter comes out, I’ll press gauze on the site and call the home health nurse.”
items.ex: If the catheter comes out, a gauze pressure dressing is applied and the home health nurse is notified.
w: “I can shower without covering the site because the clear dressing is waterproof.”
The site is protected in a plastic bag taped occlusively to keep it dry during bathing.
“If the dressing gets loose, I’ll press it down and wait for the weekly change.”
A compromised dressing needs prompt action; it is not left until the scheduled change.
“If the catheter slips partway out, I’ll gently push it back into the vein.”
A dislodged catheter is never pushed back in; this risks infection and vein injury.

alt.q: Which instruction should the nurse include when teaching a home care patient how to bathe with a peripheral IV?
alt.a: Wrap the IV site in a plastic bag and tape it closed to keep it dry
alt.ex: Wrapping the site in a plastic bag taped occlusively keeps the dressing dry and intact during bathing.
w: Remove the dressing before showering and put on a new one afterward
Patients do not remove the sterile dressing; it is protected and kept dry instead.
Let the water run over the clear dressing, then pat it dry afterward
Moisture disrupts dressing integrity and causes skin maceration, so the site is kept dry.
Soak the IV arm in the tub briefly to loosen the old adhesive
Soaking wets the dressing and site; the site must be kept dry.

items.q: Why does the nurse evaluate the IV flow rate right after changing a peripheral IV dressing?
items.a: Manipulating the catheter and tubing can change the rate of infusion
items.ex: Handling the catheter and tubing during the change can alter the infusion rate, so patency and rate are rechecked.
w: A new dressing requires a new infusion rate order from the provider
The dressing change does not require a new rate order; the ordered rate is verified.
The current infusion rate must be written on the new dressing label
The label lists insertion date and time, VAD gauge and length, and initials, not the rate.
Checking the flow rate replaces later assessments of the IV site
The site is still evaluated at set intervals for IV-related complications.

alt.q: A nurse has just finished applying a new TSM dressing to a peripheral IV. Which evaluation should the nurse perform next?
alt.a: Check the function, patency, and flow rate of the IV system
alt.ex: Evaluating function, patency, and flow rate confirms the IV line is working correctly after the change.
w: Remove the stabilization device again to inspect the skin beneath it
Removing the new device would disturb the secured catheter without reason.
Replace the IV tubing and the solution container with new ones
A dressing change does not require new tubing or a new solution container.
Restart the IV in the opposite arm to prevent future phlebitis
A functioning IV is not restarted; site rotation follows signs or policy, not the dressing change.

Lot number of the antiseptic swab that was used
The swab lot number is not among the documentation items listed for this skill.
Name of the AP who protected the dressing during the bath
The AP’s name is not a documentation item for an IV dressing change.

alt.q: After a peripheral IV dressing change that revealed phlebitis, which information should the nurse document or report? Select all that apply.

The complication and the interventions performed
Any complications and interventions are documented and reported to the health care provider.
The patient’s response to treatment of the complication
Response to treatment is documented and reported to the health care provider.
Brand name of the adhesive remover used
The adhesive remover brand is not a listed documentation item.
The patient’s food intake at the last meal
Meal intake is unrelated to IV dressing change documentation.
alt.ex: IV-related complications, the interventions taken, and the patient’s response are documented and reported to the health care provider.
