items.q: Which structure controls the rhythm of the sleep-wake cycle and coordinates it with other circadian rhythms?
items.a: The suprachiasmatic nucleus in the hypothalamus
items.ex: Nerve cells of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN) in the hypothalamus control the sleep-wake rhythm.
w: The reticular activating system in the upper brainstem
The RAS maintains alertness and wakefulness; it does not set the rhythm of the cycle.
The medulla oblongata in the lower brainstem
The medulla controls functions such as breathing; the SCN of the hypothalamus sets the sleep-wake rhythm.
The motor cortex in the frontal lobe of the cerebrum
Cortical activity can stimulate the RAS, but the cortex does not control the sleep-wake rhythm.

alt.q: Nerve cells of the suprachiasmatic nucleus (SCN), which control the sleep-wake rhythm, are located in which brain structure?
alt.a: Hypothalamus
alt.ex: The SCN nerve cells in the hypothalamus control the sleep-wake rhythm; the hypothalamus is also the major sleep center.
w: Upper brainstem
The upper brainstem contains the RAS, which maintains wakefulness.
Cerebral cortex
The cortex shows electrical activity measured by EEG but does not house the SCN.
Cerebellum
The cerebellum is not described as part of sleep-wake regulation.

items.q: A new graduate nurse began working night shifts 3 weeks ago and now reports a poor appetite and a 2.3-kg (5-lb) weight loss. Which explanation is most accurate?
items.a: Disruption of the sleep-wake cycle has changed other physiological functions
items.ex: When the sleep-wake cycle is disrupted, as with rotating shifts, other physiological functions such as appetite usually change as well.
w: Night work raises the basal metabolic rate during sleep periods
The basal metabolic rate lowers during sleep; the change reflects a disrupted cycle.
The weight loss signals an illness unrelated to the work schedule
The book uses this exact situation as a typical effect of a disrupted sleep-wake cycle.
Working nights increases slow-wave sleep and suppresses hunger
Shift work disrupts sleep; it does not increase slow-wave sleep.

alt.q: A nurse working rotating shifts reports irritability and difficulty making sound decisions. Which response by a colleague is most accurate?
alt.a: “Changes in your sleep-wake cycle often cause irritability and impaired judgment.”
alt.ex: Anxiety, restlessness, irritability, and impaired judgment are common symptoms of sleep cycle disturbances.
w: “These symptoms mean you are developing narcolepsy and need medication.”
Narcolepsy is a specific disorder; these symptoms commonly follow any sleep cycle disturbance.
“Shift changes affect only appetite and weight, not mood or thinking.”
Sleep cycle disturbances commonly cause anxiety, irritability, and impaired judgment.
“Irritability occurs only after you have been awake for 48 hours.”
Symptoms follow disruption of the usual cycle, not a set number of hours awake.

items.q: An older adult patient who normally sleeps at night and is awake during the day has slept most of today and is restless tonight. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Perform a focused assessment for a change in health status
items.ex: Reversals in the sleep-wake cycle sometimes indicate a serious illness, so the nurse assesses before intervening.
w: Keep the patient awake all day tomorrow to reset the cycle
Intervening before assessing could miss a serious illness causing the reversal.
Ask the health care provider for a nightly sedative
A sedative treats a symptom and could mask an underlying illness that needs assessment.
Document the change as an expected effect of hospitalization
A reversal can signal serious illness and should not be dismissed as expected.

alt.q: A patient who normally sleeps at night begins falling asleep during the day. How should the nurse interpret this change?
alt.a: It may indicate a serious illness and needs further assessment
alt.ex: A reversal in the sleep-wake cycle sometimes indicates a serious illness.
w: It is a normal adaptation to hospital routines and needs no follow-up
Although routines disrupt sleep, a reversal can signal serious illness and must be assessed.
It reflects normal aging and is expected in all older adults
A sleep-wake reversal is not an expected change of aging.
It shows the patient is getting enough deep sleep at night
Daytime sleep with nighttime wakefulness suggests a problem, not adequate deep sleep.

items.q: A nurse explains circadian rhythms to a patient. When does body temperature normally peak?
items.a: In the afternoon
items.ex: Normally body temperature peaks in the afternoon, decreases gradually, and drops sharply after a person falls asleep.
w: In the early morning hours
Temperature is low during sleep; it peaks in the afternoon.
Shortly after falling asleep
Temperature drops sharply after a person falls asleep.
During the last REM period
The book links the temperature peak to the afternoon, not to a sleep stage.

alt.q: Which statement describes the normal relationship between body temperature and sleep?
alt.a: Temperature declines gradually from its afternoon peak and drops sharply after sleep onset
alt.ex: Changes in body temperature correlate with sleep: it peaks in the afternoon and drops sharply once a person falls asleep.
w: Temperature stays level all day and then rises sharply after sleep onset
Temperature varies across the day and falls, not rises, after sleep onset.
Temperature is lowest in the afternoon and peaks during deep sleep
This reverses the pattern; temperature peaks in the afternoon and is lower during sleep.
Temperature varies with meals and is unrelated to the sleep-wake cycle
Temperature follows the 24-hour circadian cycle and correlates with sleep patterns.

items.q: Which substances secreted by the hypothalamus promote wakefulness and REM sleep?
items.a: Hypocretins, acetylcholine, and glutamate
items.ex: The hypothalamus secretes hypocretins (orexins), acetylcholine, and glutamate, which promote wakefulness and REM sleep.
w: Adenosine, melatonin, and serotonin
These substances help control sleep rather than promote wakefulness.
Prostaglandin D2, L-tryptophan, and growth factors
These substances help control sleep, not wakefulness.
Insulin, glucagon, and thyroxine
These hormones are not the hypothalamic substances that regulate wakefulness and REM sleep.

alt.q: Which substance helps control sleep rather than promote wakefulness?
alt.a: Adenosine
alt.ex: Prostaglandin D2, adenosine, melatonin, serotonin, L-tryptophan, and growth factors control sleep.
w: Glutamate
Glutamate is secreted by the hypothalamus to promote wakefulness and REM sleep.
Acetylcholine
Acetylcholine promotes wakefulness and REM sleep.
Hypocretin
Hypocretins (orexins) promote wakefulness and REM sleep.

items.q: How does the ascending reticular activating system (RAS) maintain arousal and wakefulness?
items.a: Its neurons release catecholamines such as norepinephrine
items.ex: Arousal, wakefulness, and consciousness result from RAS neurons releasing catecholamines such as norepinephrine.
w: Its neurons release melatonin in response to darkness
Melatonin helps control sleep; the RAS maintains wakefulness through catecholamines.
Its neurons release adenosine as sensory input increases
Adenosine helps control sleep rather than maintain wakefulness.
Its neurons suppress all activity of the cerebral cortex
Cortical activity such as thoughts actually stimulates the RAS.

alt.q: A postoperative patient in pain cannot fall asleep. Which explanation best describes the physiology involved?
alt.a: Pain stimuli reach the RAS, which maintains alertness and wakefulness
alt.ex: The RAS receives visual, auditory, pain, and tactile stimuli and keeps the person alert and awake.
w: Pain lowers body temperature and delays the afternoon peak
Pain keeps a person awake by stimulating the RAS, not by changing temperature timing.
Pain blocks the hypothalamus from secreting hypocretins
Hypocretins promote wakefulness, so blocking them would not keep a patient awake.
Pain shortens the presleep period to less than 10 minutes
A shorter presleep period would mean falling asleep faster, not staying awake.

items.q: Which can stimulate the reticular activating system (RAS) and promote wakefulness? Select all that apply.
o: Visual stimuli
The RAS receives visual sensory stimuli.
Auditory stimuli
The RAS receives auditory sensory stimuli such as noise.
Pain
Pain is one of the sensory stimuli the RAS receives.
Emotions and thought processes
Activity from the cerebral cortex, such as emotions or thoughts, stimulates the RAS.
Rising adenosine levels
Adenosine is one of the substances that control sleep.
items.ex: The RAS receives visual, auditory, pain, and tactile stimuli, and cortical activity such as emotions also stimulates it.

alt.q: A nurse wants to reduce stimulation of a patient’s reticular activating system (RAS) at bedtime. Which factors could keep the patient awake? Select all that apply.
o: Loud conversation in the hallway
Auditory stimuli reach the RAS and maintain wakefulness.
Bright overhead lights in the room
Visual stimuli reach the RAS and maintain wakefulness.
Unrelieved incisional pain
Pain stimuli reach the RAS and keep the patient alert.
Worry about the next day’s surgery
Emotions and thought processes in the cortex stimulate the RAS.
A dark, quiet room
Reducing light and noise decreases sensory input to the RAS.
A familiar bedtime routine
A familiar routine does not add the sensory or emotional stimulation that activates the RAS.
alt.ex: Noise, light, pain, and worry all stimulate the RAS, which maintains alertness and wakefulness.

items.q: Which characteristics describe REM sleep? Select all that apply.
o: Vivid, full-color dreaming
Vivid, full-color dreaming occurs during REM sleep.
Fluctuating heart and respiratory rates
REM is typified by fluctuating heart and respiratory rates and fluctuating or increased blood pressure.
Loss of skeletal muscle tone
Muscle atonia, or loss of skeletal muscle tone, occurs during REM sleep.
Increased gastric secretions
Gastric secretions increase during REM sleep.
Easy arousal by sounds such as noise
Easy arousal by noise describes N1; it is very difficult to arouse a sleeper in REM.
Feeling of having daydreamed if awakened
This feeling describes awakening from N1, the lightest stage.
items.ex: REM sleep brings vivid dreams, rapid eye movements, fluctuating vital signs, loss of muscle tone, and increased gastric secretions.

alt.q: Which characteristics describe NREM stage N3 sleep? Select all that apply.
o: It is called slow-wave sleep
N3, formerly stages 3 and 4, is called slow-wave sleep.
The sleeper is difficult to arouse and rarely moves
N3 is the deepest stage; the sleeper is difficult to arouse and rarely moves.
Vital signs are lower than during waking hours
Brain and muscle activity and vital signs are significantly decreased in N3.
Vivid, full-color dreaming occurs
Vivid, full-color dreaming characterizes REM sleep.
It lasts only a few minutes and is the lightest stage
This describes N1, the lightest level of sleep.
alt.ex: N3 is the deepest, slow-wave stage with low vital signs, little movement, and difficult arousal.

items.q: Which statements about the normal adult sleep cycle are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: A person usually passes through four to six complete cycles each night
Once asleep, a person usually passes through four to six complete sleep cycles.
Each cycle lasts a total of 90 to 110 minutes
Each cycle of three NREM stages and a REM period lasts 90 to 110 minutes.
A sleeper may fluctuate between NREM stages 2 and 3 before entering REM
Not everyone progresses consistently; fluctuation between stages 2 and 3 is described.
REM sleep shortens with each successive cycle
REM sleep lengthens with each cycle, lasting up to 60 minutes in the last one.
Stage 3 NREM sleep lengthens with each successive cycle
Stage 3 shortens with each successive cycle.
items.ex: Adults typically have four to six 90- to 110-minute cycles; stage 3 shortens and REM lengthens as the night goes on.

alt.q: Which changes occur as an adult moves through successive sleep cycles during the night? Select all that apply.
o: NREM stage 3 becomes shorter
With each successive cycle, stage 3 of NREM sleep shortens.
REM periods become longer
With each successive cycle, REM sleep lengthens.
REM may last up to 60 minutes in the last cycle
REM sleep lasts up to 60 minutes during the last sleep cycle.
NREM stage 3 becomes longer
Stage 3 shortens, rather than lengthens, as the night goes on.
A new presleep period begins before each cycle
The presleep period occurs once, before sleep begins.
alt.ex: As cycles repeat, deep NREM stage 3 shortens and REM lengthens, reaching up to 60 minutes in the last cycle.

items.q: NREM sleep makes up about 75% of a night’s sleep.
items.a: True
items.ex: NREM sleep accounts for about 75% of the night, and REM sleep for about 25%.
items.ww: REM sleep is the smaller share, about 25% of the night.

alt.q: REM sleep makes up about 75% of a night’s sleep.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: REM sleep accounts for about 25% of the night; NREM sleep accounts for about 75%.
alt.ww: NREM, not REM, sleep makes up the larger share of the night.

items.q: During NREM stage N1, sensory stimuli such as noise easily arouse the sleeper.
items.a: True
items.ex: N1 is the lightest level of sleep, so noise easily arouses the sleeper.
items.ww: Difficult arousal describes N3 and REM sleep, not N1.

alt.q: During REM sleep, sensory stimuli such as noise easily arouse the sleeper.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: It is very difficult to arouse a sleeper during REM sleep.
alt.ww: Easy arousal by noise describes the lightest stage, N1, not REM sleep.

items.q: In the two-process model of sleep regulation, the homeostatic process (Process S) rises during waking and declines during sleep.
items.a: True
items.ex: Process S rises while a person is awake and declines during sleep; it regulates the length and depth of sleep.
items.ww: Process S builds during wakefulness, which is why it declines once sleep begins.

alt.q: In the two-process model of sleep regulation, the homeostatic process (Process S) declines during waking and rises during sleep.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Process S rises during waking and declines during sleep.
alt.ww: This reverses the direction of Process S, which builds up while awake.

items.q: NREM stage N3, the deepest stage of sleep, is called [[slow-wave sleep|slow wave sleep]].
items.ex: N3 (formerly stages 3 and 4) is slow-wave sleep, from which a person is more difficult to arouse.

alt.q: A sleeper in [[slow-wave sleep|slow wave sleep]], NREM stage N3, is difficult to arouse and rarely moves.
alt.ex: N3 (formerly stages 3 and 4) is slow-wave sleep, from which a person is more difficult to arouse.

items.q: Which instrument measures muscle tone during a sleep study?
items.a: Electromyogram (EMG)
items.ex: The electromyogram measures muscle tone, which changes across sleep stages.
w: Electroencephalogram (EEG)
The EEG measures electrical activity in the cerebral cortex.
Electrooculogram (EOG)
The EOG measures eye movements.
Electrocardiogram (ECG)
The ECG records heart rhythm, not muscle tone during sleep.

alt.q: What does the electrooculogram (EOG) measure during a sleep study?
alt.a: Eye movements
alt.ex: The EOG measures eye movements, which help identify REM sleep.
w: Muscle tone
Muscle tone is measured by the electromyogram (EMG).
Cortical electrical activity
Electrical activity in the cerebral cortex is measured by the EEG.
Heart rhythm
Heart rhythm is not what the EOG records.

items.q: About how long after sleep begins does the first REM period usually start?
items.a: About 90 minutes
items.ex: REM sleep usually begins about 90 minutes after sleep has begun, at the end of the first cycle.
w: About 10 minutes
REM within minutes of sleep onset is abnormal; it is seen in narcolepsy.
About 30 minutes
Thirty minutes is the upper end of the normal presleep period, not REM onset.
About 4 hours
Several complete cycles, each ending in REM, occur within 4 hours.

alt.q: What is the average length of a REM period?
alt.a: About 20 minutes
alt.ex: REM duration increases with each cycle and averages 20 minutes.
w: About 2 minutes
REM periods average about 20 minutes, not 2.
About 45 minutes
REM averages 20 minutes, although it can last up to 60 minutes in the last cycle.
About 90 minutes
Ninety minutes is the length of a typical whole sleep cycle.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “Every night it takes me more than an hour to fall asleep.” Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: The patient stays in the presleep period longer than the normal 10 to 30 minutes
items.ex: The presleep period normally lasts 10 to 30 minutes; people who have trouble falling asleep often stay in it an hour or more.
w: The patient has a normal presleep period, which lasts 60 to 90 minutes
A normal presleep period lasts 10 to 30 minutes, not 60 to 90.
The patient enters REM sleep too early, which normally begins at 10 minutes
REM normally begins about 90 minutes after sleep onset.
The patient stays in N3 sleep too long, which normally lasts 10 to 30 minutes
The patient has not yet fallen asleep, so N3 is not involved.

alt.q: How long does the presleep period normally last in an adult?
alt.a: 10 to 30 minutes
alt.ex: The presleep period, when a person is aware only of growing sleepiness, normally lasts 10 to 30 minutes.
w: 1 to 5 minutes
The normal presleep period is longer, 10 to 30 minutes.
45 to 60 minutes
Staying this long in presleep suggests trouble falling asleep.
90 to 110 minutes
This is the length of a full sleep cycle.

items.q: A patient admitted to a medical unit usually goes to bed at 2300 and wakes at 0800 at home. Which nursing action best supports the patient’s sleep?
items.a: Plan care around the patient’s usual bedtime and wake time when possible
items.ex: Failure to maintain a patient’s usual sleep-wake cycle negatively affects overall health, so care is adapted to the patient’s pattern.
w: Have the patient follow the unit’s standard 2100 lights-out time
Agency routines that ignore personal sleep-wake patterns lead to poor sleep quality.
Give a prescribed sleep aid at 2100 so the patient sleeps earlier
Forcing an earlier bedtime changes the patient’s usual cycle and lowers sleep quality.
Wake the patient at 0530 with the other patients for routine care
Interrupting the usual cycle for routine care prevents adequate sleep.

alt.q: Why does hospitalization commonly lead to poor sleep quality?
alt.a: Hospital routines change the patient’s usual sleep-wake cycle
alt.ex: Typical hospital routines interrupt sleep or prevent patients from falling asleep at their usual time.
w: Hospital lighting greatly increases slow-wave sleep
Hospital routines disrupt sleep; they do not increase slow-wave sleep.
Patients spend more of each night in REM sleep
The problem is a changed sleep-wake cycle, not extra REM sleep.
Illness removes the body’s need for regular sleep
Ill patients still need their usual sleep-wake cycle maintained.

items.q: In the two-process model of sleep regulation, what defines the time of wake-up?
items.a: The intersection of Process S and Process C
items.ex: Process S and Process C operate together, and the time of wake-up is defined by where they intersect.
w: The highest point of Process S
Process S peaks at the end of waking and declines during sleep; its peak does not mark wake-up.
The lowest point of Process C
Wake-up is defined by both processes together, not one curve alone.
The end of the fourth REM period
Wake-up is not tied to a fixed number of REM periods.

alt.q: Which statement correctly describes Process C in the two-process model?
alt.a: It influences the timing and duration of sleep-wake cycles
alt.ex: Circadian rhythms (Process C) influence the internal organization of sleep and the timing and duration of sleep-wake cycles.
w: It primarily regulates the length and depth of sleep
Regulating sleep length and depth is the role of Process S.
It rises during waking and declines during sleep
This pattern describes the homeostatic Process S.
It measures muscle tone during each sleep stage
Muscle tone is measured by the EMG, not a sleep process.

items.q: Which set best describes the main functions of sleep?
items.a: Restoration, memory consolidation, and preparation for wakefulness
items.ex: Sleep is a time of restoration, memory consolidation, and preparation for the next period of wakefulness.
w: Raising metabolism, increasing heart rate, and building muscle tone
During sleep metabolism, heart rate, and muscle tone decrease.
Raising body temperature, digesting meals, and releasing catecholamines
Temperature drops during sleep; catecholamine release by the RAS supports wakefulness.
Erasing all memories, increasing alertness, and storing extra glucose
Sleep consolidates memory rather than erasing it.

alt.q: A student asks why people need sleep. Which response best reflects the functions of sleep?
alt.a: “Sleep restores the body, consolidates memory, and readies you for waking.”
alt.ex: Sleep functions as restoration, memory consolidation, and preparation for the next period of wakefulness.
w: “Sleep mainly raises your metabolism so you burn more energy.”
The basal metabolic rate lowers during sleep, conserving energy.
“Sleep mainly raises your heart rate to strengthen the heart.”
Heart rate falls during sleep, which preserves cardiac function.
“Sleep mainly lets you dream so you can forget the day.”
Dreaming is only part of sleep; restoration and memory consolidation are main functions.

items.q: During NREM sleep, a healthy adult’s heart rate typically falls to what level?
items.a: 60 beats/min or less
items.ex: Heart rate decreases from an average of 70 to 80 beats/min to 60 beats/min or less, preserving cardiac function.
w: 40 beats/min or less
The book describes a fall to 60 beats/min or less, not 40.
70 to 80 beats/min
This is the normal average waking heart rate.
90 beats/min or more
Heart rate decreases, not increases, during NREM sleep.

alt.q: A healthy adult’s heart rate is 76 beats/min while awake and 58 beats/min during the night while asleep. What is the nurse’s best interpretation?
alt.a: An expected decrease during sleep that helps preserve cardiac function
alt.ex: During NREM sleep heart rate normally drops to 60 beats/min or less, which preserves cardiac function.
w: Bradycardia that must be reported to the health care provider at once
A rate near 60 during sleep is an expected NREM change in a healthy adult.
Evidence that the patient is in REM sleep with fluctuating vital signs
A steady fall in heart rate reflects NREM sleep; REM brings fluctuating rates.
A medication effect that means the next scheduled dose must be held
Nothing suggests a drug effect; this decrease is a normal function of sleep.

items.q: Which body functions decrease during NREM sleep? Select all that apply.
o: Respirations
Respirations decrease during sleep.
Blood pressure
Blood pressure decreases during sleep.
Muscle tone
Muscle tone decreases during sleep.
Body temperature
Temperature decreases during sleep.
Release of human growth hormone
Growth hormone is released during NREM stage 3 for repair of cells.
Cortical activity and oxygen consumption
These increase during REM sleep and are linked to memory and learning.
items.ex: During NREM sleep heart rate, respirations, temperature, blood pressure, and muscle tone all decrease.

alt.q: A patient asks what happens in the body during deep NREM sleep. Which changes should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Growth hormone is released for repair of cells
During NREM stage 3 the body releases human growth hormone for repair and renewal of cells.
The basal metabolic rate lowers, conserving energy
A lower basal metabolic rate during sleep conserves the body’s energy supply.
Heart rate falls to 60 beats/min or less
Heart rate drops from 70 to 80 to 60 beats/min or less, preserving cardiac function.
Cerebral blood flow and cortical activity increase
These brain changes are associated with REM sleep.
Muscle tone and blood pressure increase
Muscle tone and blood pressure decrease during NREM sleep.
alt.ex: Deep NREM sleep slows the body: heart rate and metabolism fall, energy is conserved, and growth hormone supports repair.

items.q: A patient recovering from extensive burns asks why the nurse is trying to protect long periods of uninterrupted deep sleep. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “During deep sleep your body releases growth hormone to repair and renew cells.”
items.ex: During NREM stage 3 the body releases human growth hormone for the repair and renewal of epithelial and specialized cells.
w: “During deep sleep your heart rate rises to send more oxygen to the wounds.”
Heart rate decreases during NREM sleep.
“During deep sleep vivid dreams help you cope with the stress of the injury.”
Vivid, elaborate dreams are linked to REM sleep, not deep NREM sleep.
“During deep sleep your metabolism rises so your body burns more energy.”
The basal metabolic rate lowers during sleep to conserve energy.

alt.q: Which processes for renewing tissues occur during rest and sleep?
alt.a: Protein synthesis and cell division
alt.ex: Protein synthesis and cell division for the renewal of tissues occur during rest and sleep.
w: Protein catabolism and nitrogen loss
Altered nitrogen balance and protein catabolism are effects of sleep deprivation.
Rising metabolism and energy use
Basal metabolic rate lowers during sleep, conserving energy.
Catecholamine release and muscle tension
Catecholamines from the RAS maintain wakefulness, and muscle tone decreases in sleep.

items.q: REM sleep appears to be important for which functions?
items.a: Early brain development, cognition, and memory
items.ex: REM sleep appears important for early brain development, cognition, and memory, with changes tied to memory storage and learning.
w: Growth hormone release, protein synthesis, and cell division
These restorative processes are linked to NREM stage 3 and rest.
Lowering heart rate, blood pressure, and metabolic rate
These decreases describe NREM sleep.
Muscle repair, energy storage, and temperature control
The book links REM sleep to brain development, cognition, and memory.

alt.q: Which sleep phase appears most important for early brain development?

alt.ex: REM sleep appears to be important for early brain development, cognition, and memory.

N1 is the lightest stage of sleep and is not linked to brain development.

N2 is a stage of sound sleep with slowing brain activity.

The presleep period is the time of growing sleepiness before sleep begins.

items.q: A patient in the intensive care unit has been awakened frequently for 3 nights and now says the staff are plotting against him. Which explanation should the nurse consider?

items.ex: A loss of REM sleep often leads to confusion and suspicion.
w: Excess slow-wave sleep often leads to suspicious thinking
Frequent awakenings reduce sleep; excess slow-wave sleep is not linked to suspicion.
Increased growth hormone often leads to mood changes
Growth hormone supports cell repair; it is not linked to suspicion.
A lowered metabolic rate often leads to paranoid thoughts
A lowered metabolic rate during sleep conserves energy and does not cause suspicion.

alt.q: Which effect commonly results from a loss of REM sleep?
alt.a: Confusion and suspicion
alt.ex: A loss of REM sleep often leads to confusion and suspicion.
w: Increased muscle tone
Muscle tone is not described as an effect of losing REM sleep.
Lower blood pressure
Lower blood pressure is a normal change during NREM sleep.
Improved memory storage
REM sleep supports memory; losing it would not improve memory.

items.q: Which effects can result from prolonged sleep loss? Select all that apply.
o: Impaired immune function
Sleep deprivation affects immune function.
Altered mood and memory
Prolonged sleep loss alters mood and memory.
Poorer motor performance and equilibrium
Prolonged sleep loss alters motor performance and equilibrium.
Altered nitrogen balance and protein catabolism
Sleep deprivation affects metabolism, nitrogen balance, and protein catabolism.
Greater release of growth hormone
Growth hormone is released during deep sleep, so sleep loss would not increase it.
Lower risk of hypertension
People with sleep problems are more likely to have hypertension.
items.ex: Sleep deprivation affects immune function, metabolism, nitrogen balance, and protein catabolism, and alters mood, motor performance, memory, and equilibrium.

alt.q: People with sleep problems are more likely to have which chronic conditions? Select all that apply.
o: Hypertension
Individuals with sleep problems are more likely to have hypertension.
Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes mellitus is more common in people with sleep problems.
Obesity
Obesity is linked with sleep problems.
Depression
Depression is more common in people with sleep problems.
Cataracts
Cataracts are not among the chronic diseases linked to sleep problems.
alt.ex: Sleep problems are associated with hypertension, cardiovascular disease, diabetes mellitus, obesity, and depression.

items.q: Which indirect costs are associated with sleep deprivation? Select all that apply.
o: Motor vehicle accidents
Motor vehicle accidents are an indirect cost of sleep deprivation.
Industrial accidents
Industrial accidents are linked to sleep deprivation.
Medical errors
Medical errors are an indirect cost of sleep deprivation.
Fewer hospital admissions
Hospitalization is listed as a cost of sleep deprivation, not a saving.
Improved workplace productivity
People with sleep problems have poorer productivity.
items.ex: Millions of health care dollars go to indirect costs of sleep deprivation, such as accidents, litigation, hospitalization, medical errors, and death.

alt.q: A nurse educator explains why sleep deprivation is a public health concern. Which consequences should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Poorer quality of life
People with sleep problems may have poorer quality of life.
Decreased productivity
Sleep problems are linked with lower productivity.
Litigation and property damage
Litigation and property damage are indirect costs of sleep deprivation.
Lower overall health care spending
Sleep deprivation adds millions of dollars in indirect health care costs.
Faster reaction times while driving
Sleep deprivation contributes to motor vehicle accidents.
alt.ex: Sleep deprivation lowers quality of life and productivity and drives costs such as accidents, litigation, and property damage.

items.q: Dreams occur during both NREM and REM sleep, but REM dreams are more vivid and elaborate.
items.a: True
items.ex: Dreams occur in both phases; REM dreams are more vivid and elaborate and may aid learning, memory, and stress adaptation.
items.ww: Dreaming is not limited to one phase, though REM dreams are the most vivid.

alt.q: Dreams occur only during REM sleep.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Dreams occur during both NREM and REM sleep, although REM dreams are more vivid.
alt.ww: NREM sleep also includes dreaming, so dreams are not limited to REM sleep.

items.q: People who recall their dreams vividly usually awaken just after a period of REM sleep.
items.a: True
items.ex: Vivid dream recall usually follows awakening just after a REM period.
items.ww: Awakening right after REM, when vivid dreams occur, favors recall.

alt.q: People who recall their dreams vividly usually awaken during NREM stage 3 sleep.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: People with vivid dream recall usually awaken just after a period of REM sleep.
alt.ww: N3 is deep slow-wave sleep; vivid recall is linked to awakening after REM.

items.q: The basal metabolic rate lowers during sleep, which conserves the body’s energy supply.
items.a: True
items.ex: A lower basal metabolic rate during sleep conserves the body’s energy.
items.ww: Sleep slows biological functions, including metabolism.

alt.q: The basal metabolic rate rises during sleep to fuel tissue repair.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The basal metabolic rate lowers during sleep, conserving energy.
alt.ww: Tissue repair occurs through growth hormone and protein synthesis, while metabolism slows.

items.q: During NREM stage 3 sleep, the body releases [[human growth hormone|growth hormone|HGH|GH]] for the repair and renewal of epithelial and specialized cells such as brain cells.
items.ex: Growth hormone released in deep NREM sleep restores biological processes by repairing and renewing cells.

alt.q: Repair and renewal of epithelial cells and brain cells depend on [[human growth hormone|growth hormone|HGH|GH]], which is released during NREM stage 3 sleep.
alt.ex: Growth hormone released in deep NREM sleep restores biological processes by repairing and renewing cells.

items.q: How does the content of REM dreams typically change through the night?
items.a: From current events to emotional dreams of childhood or the past
items.ex: REM dreams progress from dreams about current events to emotional dreams of childhood or the past.
w: From childhood memories to dreams about current events
This reverses the progression described in the book.
From vivid dreams to no dreams at all by the morning
Dreams continue and change in content through the night.
From emotional dreams to calm images of future plans
Content moves toward the past, not toward future plans.

alt.q: What do most people dream about?
alt.a: Immediate concerns such as an argument or worries over work
alt.ex: Most people dream about immediate concerns such as an argument with a spouse or worries over work.
w: Future events they have never experienced
Dreams usually reflect immediate concerns, not unknown future events.
Detailed memories from early infancy
Emotional childhood dreams appear late in the night but are not what most dreams are about.
Random images with no link to their lives
Most dreams relate to current concerns of the person.

items.q: How does personality influence the quality of dreams?
items.a: A depressed person tends to dream of helplessness
items.ex: Personality influences dreams: a creative person has elaborate, complex dreams, whereas a depressed person dreams of helplessness.
w: A creative person tends to have brief, simple dreams
Creative people tend to have elaborate and complex dreams.
An anxious person tends not to dream at all
The book does not say anxiety stops dreaming; dreams occur in both NREM and REM sleep.
A depressed person tends to dream of success
A depressed person dreams of helplessness.

alt.q: Which person is most likely to report elaborate and complex dreams?
alt.a: A creative artist
alt.ex: A creative person has elaborate and complex dreams.
w: A person with depression
A depressed person tends to dream of helplessness.
A person who rarely recalls dreams
Poor recall reflects forgetting dreams, not dream complexity.
A person who wakes during N3
Waking from deep NREM sleep is not linked to elaborate dreams.

items.q: A patient in psychotherapy wants to remember dreams to discuss with the therapist. Which suggestion by the nurse is most helpful?
items.a: Think about the dream consciously as soon as you wake up
items.ex: To remember a dream, a person has to consciously think about it on awakening.
w: Wait until the therapy session to think about the dream
Most people forget dreams unless they think about them on awakening.
Sleep longer to increase your amount of stage 3 sleep
Vivid dream recall is linked to awakening after REM, not to more stage 3 sleep.
Take a long nap each afternoon to increase dreaming
Napping does not help a person recall nighttime dreams.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient shows understanding of how to improve dream recall?
alt.a: “I will think about my dream right when I wake up.”
alt.ex: Consciously thinking about a dream on awakening is needed to remember it.
w: “I will think about my dreams later in the day.”
Most dreams are forgotten unless thought about on awakening.
“I will try to wake up during my deepest sleep.”
Recall is best after REM sleep, not during deep NREM sleep.
“I will take a sleeping pill so I dream more.”
Recall depends on thinking about the dream on awakening, not on medication.

items.q: Why do clinical psychologists sometimes analyze patients’ dreams during psychotherapy?
items.a: Describing and interpreting a dream sometimes helps resolve fears
items.ex: The ability to describe a dream and interpret its significance sometimes helps resolve personal concerns or fears.
w: Dream content reliably diagnoses a sleep disorder
Sleep disorders are diagnosed with sleep laboratory studies, not dream content.
Dream analysis increases the amount of REM sleep
Analyzing dreams is a psychotherapy tool; it does not change sleep stages.
Recalling dreams lowers the basal metabolic rate
Metabolic rate lowers with sleep itself, not with dream recall.

alt.q: Besides learning, memory processing, and stress adaptation, which other theory about the function of dreams does the text describe?
alt.a: Dreams erase certain fantasies or nonsensical memories
alt.ex: Another theory suggests that dreams erase certain fantasies or nonsensical memories.
w: Dreams raise body temperature to prepare for waking
Temperature drops during sleep; dreams are not linked to raising it.
Dreams trigger the release of human growth hormone
Growth hormone is released during NREM stage 3, not by dreaming.
Dreams occur only in people with sleep disorders
Dreams occur in everyone during NREM and REM sleep.

items.q: A nurse who often works double shifts says, “I only sleep about 4 hours a night, but I’m fine.” Which response best reflects the effects of sleep loss?
items.a: “Ongoing sleep loss can impair memory and motor performance and contribute to errors.”
items.ex: Prolonged sleep loss alters mood, motor performance, memory, and equilibrium, and sleep deprivation contributes to medical errors.
w: “Sleep loss affects only mood, so your work will not suffer.”
Sleep loss also affects motor performance, memory, and equilibrium.
“Your body fully adapts to short sleep after a few weeks.”
The benefits of sleep go unnoticed until problems from deprivation develop.
“Short sleep is harmful only if you also skip REM sleep.”
Any prolonged sleep loss alters body functions, not only loss of REM sleep.

alt.q: Which finding in a patient with prolonged sleep loss reflects the effect of sleep deprivation on body function?
alt.a: Impaired equilibrium and slowed motor performance
alt.ex: Prolonged sleep loss alters mood, motor performance, memory, and equilibrium.
w: Sharper short-term memory and recall
Sleep loss impairs memory rather than improving it.
Stronger immune response to infection
Sleep deprivation affects immune function negatively.
Steadier mood and greater patience
Prolonged sleep loss alters mood, often negatively.

items.q: Which brain change during REM sleep is associated with memory storage and learning?
items.a: Increased cerebral blood flow and cortical activity
items.ex: REM sleep brings increased cerebral blood flow, cortical activity, oxygen consumption, and epinephrine release, linked to memory and learning.
w: Decreased cortical activity and oxygen use
Cortical activity and oxygen consumption increase during REM sleep.
Release of growth hormone for cell repair
Growth hormone release occurs in NREM stage 3.
Lowered epinephrine release and brain activity
Epinephrine release and brain activity increase during REM sleep.

alt.q: During REM sleep, which change in body chemistry is associated with memory storage?
alt.a: Increased epinephrine release
alt.ex: Increased oxygen consumption and epinephrine release during REM sleep are associated with memory storage and learning.
w: Decreased oxygen consumption
Oxygen consumption increases during REM sleep.
Increased growth hormone release
Growth hormone is released during NREM stage 3 for cell repair.
Decreased cerebral blood flow
Cerebral blood flow increases during REM sleep.

items.q: A patient says, “I never dream.” Which response by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: “Most people forget their dreams, and some believe they don’t dream at all.”
items.ex: Most people forget their dreams, and few have dream recall or believe they dream at all.
w: “Not dreaming means you are getting no REM sleep at night.”
Failing to recall dreams reflects forgetting, not an absence of REM sleep.
“Only people under a lot of stress have any dreams.”
Everyone dreams during NREM and REM sleep.
“Not dreaming is an early warning sign of narcolepsy.”
Narcolepsy involves vivid dreams at sleep onset, not an absence of dreams.

alt.q: Which statement about dream recall is accurate?
alt.a: Most people forget their dreams
alt.ex: Most people forget their dreams, and few have dream recall.
w: Most people recall nearly all of their dreams
Most people forget their dreams.
Dreams are recalled best after waking from N3
Vivid recall follows awakening just after REM sleep.
Recall improves when you avoid thinking of them
A dream must be consciously thought about on awakening to be remembered.

items.q: What function does this serve: Release of growth hormone in NREM stage 3?
items.a: Repair and renewal of epithelial and brain cells
items.ex: Sleep restores the body through growth hormone, conserves energy and cardiac function, and supports memory through REM sleep.
w: Memory storage and learning
That goes with Increased cortical activity during REM sleep.
Conservation of the body’s energy supply
That goes with Lowered basal metabolic rate during sleep.
Preservation of cardiac function
That goes with Slowed heart rate during NREM sleep.

alt.q: What function does this serve: Increased cortical activity during REM sleep?
alt.a: Memory storage and learning
alt.ex: Sleep restores the body through growth hormone, conserves energy and cardiac function, and supports memory through REM sleep.
w: Repair and renewal of epithelial and brain cells
That goes with Release of growth hormone in NREM stage 3.
Conservation of the body’s energy supply
That goes with Lowered basal metabolic rate during sleep.
Preservation of cardiac function
That goes with Slowed heart rate during NREM sleep.

A large neck circumference increases OSA risk.
Menopause
Women experiencing menopause have a higher incidence of OSA.
Smoking
Smoking increases the risk of OSA.
Age younger than 30 years
Increasing age, especially over 65, raises OSA risk.
Low blood pressure
Hypertension, not low blood pressure, is a major factor in OSA.
items.ex: Obesity and hypertension are major OSA factors; smoking, age over 65, heart failure, alcohol, large neck, and menopause also increase risk.

alt.q: Which structural abnormalities can predispose a patient to obstructive sleep apnea? Select all that apply.
o: Deviated septum
A deviated septum can predispose a patient to OSA.
Nasal polyps
Nasal polyps can predispose a patient to OSA.
Enlarged tonsils
Enlarged tonsils can predispose a patient to OSA.
Broad, prominent lower jaw
A narrow, not broad, lower jaw predisposes to OSA.
Small neck circumference
A large neck circumference is the OSA risk factor.
alt.ex: A deviated septum, nasal polyps, a narrow lower jaw, or enlarged tonsils can predispose a patient to OSA.

items.q: A patient with obesity and hypertension reports loud snoring, morning headaches, and falling asleep at work. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Report findings suggesting sleep apnea to the health care provider
items.ex: These symptoms suggest OSA, which is diagnosed in a sleep laboratory and increases cardiovascular risk if untreated.
w: Suggest a sleep aid at bedtime to improve sleep quality
A sleep aid does not address blocked airflow and delays diagnosis.
Suggest a glass of wine at bedtime to promote relaxation
Alcohol increases the risk of OSA.
Suggest a 2-hour afternoon nap to reduce the sleepiness
Napping treats a symptom and does not address a possible breathing disorder.

alt.q: Which finding in a patient with suspected obstructive sleep apnea is most consistent with the disorder?
alt.a: Morning headaches and excessive daytime sleepiness
alt.ex: EDS, fatigue, morning headaches, irritability, depression, poor concentration, and decreased sex drive are common OSA symptoms.
w: Sudden muscle weakness when laughing
Muscle weakness with intense emotion is cataplexy, a symptom of narcolepsy.
Itching deep in the leg muscles at bedtime
Deep itching in the muscles before sleep describes restless legs syndrome.
Sleepwalking in the first hours of sleep
Sleepwalking is a parasomnia, not a symptom of OSA.

items.q: Obstructive sleep apnea causes a serious decline in arterial oxygen saturation. Which complications is the patient at risk for? Select all that apply.
o: Cardiac dysrhythmias
OSA puts patients at risk for cardiac dysrhythmias.
Right-sided heart failure
OSA puts patients at risk for right-sided heart failure.
Pulmonary hypertension
OSA puts patients at risk for pulmonary hypertension.
Stroke
OSA puts patients at risk for stroke.
Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism affects sleep onset but is not a complication of OSA.
Iron deficiency anemia
Iron deficiency anemia is linked to restless legs syndrome, not caused by OSA.
items.ex: Low oxygen saturation in OSA risks dysrhythmias, right-sided heart failure, pulmonary hypertension, angina, stroke, and hypertension.

alt.q: Untreated sleep apnea increases the risk of which conditions? Select all that apply.
o: Hypertension
Untreated sleep apnea increases the risk of hypertension.
Diabetes mellitus
Untreated sleep apnea increases the risk of diabetes mellitus.
Heart failure
Untreated sleep apnea increases the risk of heart disease and heart failure.
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism affects the last sleep stage; it is not a result of sleep apnea.
Narcolepsy
Narcolepsy is a separate dysfunction of sleep-wake regulation.
alt.ex: Untreated sleep apnea increases the risk of hypertension, diabetes mellitus, heart disease, and heart failure.

items.q: A patient with obesity is newly diagnosed with obstructive sleep apnea and asks what can be done. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Weight reduction and CPAP are among the treatment options.”
items.ex: OSA treatment options include weight reduction, sleep hygiene, BiPAP, CPAP, surgery, hypoglossal nerve stimulation, and oral devices.
w: “Stimulants such as modafinil are the main treatment.”
Modafinil and similar stimulants are used for narcolepsy.
“Antidepressants will stop the episodes of apnea.”
Antidepressants suppress cataplexy in narcolepsy, not apnea.
“Iron supplements will keep your airway from closing.”
Iron relates to restless legs syndrome, not airway obstruction.

alt.q: Which is a treatment option for obstructive sleep apnea?
alt.a: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation
alt.ex: Hypoglossal nerve stimulation is listed among OSA treatment options along with CPAP, BiPAP, surgery, and oral devices.
w: Sodium oxybate
Sodium oxybate is a wakefulness-promoting agent used for narcolepsy.
Iron replacement
Iron deficiency is linked to restless legs syndrome.
Supine infant positioning
Supine positioning is recommended for infants to reduce SIDS risk.

items.q: Which symptom differentiates narcolepsy type 1 from narcolepsy type 2?
items.a: Cataplexy
items.ex: Cataplexy, sudden muscle weakness during intense emotions, is a symptom of narcolepsy type 1 that differentiates it from type 2.
w: Excessive daytime sleepiness
EDS is the most common complaint in narcolepsy generally.
Loud snoring
Loud snoring is typical of obstructive sleep apnea.
Sleepwalking
Sleepwalking is a parasomnia, a disorder of arousal.

alt.q: What is cataplexy?
alt.a: Sudden muscle weakness during intense emotions
alt.ex: Cataplexy is sudden muscle weakness during intense emotions such as anger, sadness, or laughter.
w: Inability to move or talk just before waking
This describes sleep paralysis.
Vivid dreams while falling asleep
Vivid dreams at sleep onset are another narcolepsy symptom, not cataplexy.
Sudden stopping of airflow during sleep
Cessation of airflow describes sleep apnea.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient with narcolepsy about managing symptoms. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will keep my daytime naps to 20 minutes or less.”
items.ex: Brief daytime naps no longer than 20 minutes help reduce subjective feelings of sleepiness in narcolepsy.
w: “I will take a 2-hour nap after lunch every day.”
Naps should be brief, no longer than 20 minutes.
“A large lunch will help me stay alert all afternoon.”
Heavy meals increase drowsiness; light, high-protein meals are advised.
“Long drives are safe as long as I take my medicine.”
Medications only partly increase wakefulness; long-distance driving should be avoided.

alt.q: A patient with narcolepsy should avoid which factor because it increases drowsiness?
alt.a: Sitting for long periods in hot, stuffy rooms
alt.ex: Patients with narcolepsy avoid alcohol, heavy meals, exhausting activities, long-distance driving, and long periods in hot, stuffy rooms.
w: Chewing gum during the day
Chewing gum is a management method that helps patients with narcolepsy.
Eating light meals high in protein
Light, high-protein meals are recommended in narcolepsy.
Following a regular exercise program
Regular exercise helps manage narcolepsy.

items.q: A teacher tells the school nurse that a 15-year-old student keeps falling asleep suddenly in class and is “just lazy.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “These sudden sleep attacks could be narcolepsy and should be evaluated.”
items.ex: Narcolepsy usually begins in adolescence, and sleep attacks are easily mistaken for laziness or lack of interest.
w: “Teenagers need very little sleep, so this is a behavior problem.”
Narcolepsy sleep attacks are often mistaken for laziness.
“The student is probably drinking and should be disciplined.”
A sleep attack is easily mistaken for drunkenness.
“Sudden sleep in class at this age always means sleep apnea.”
Uncontrollable sleep attacks starting in adolescence suggest narcolepsy.

alt.q: Why is narcolepsy often missed when symptoms first appear?
alt.a: Its symptoms are confused with normal teenage sleepiness
alt.ex: Narcolepsy symptoms first appear in adolescence and are often confused with the EDS common in that age group.
w: It first appears only in adults over age 65
Symptoms typically begin in adolescence.
It causes no noticeable symptoms during the day
Excessive daytime sleepiness is its most common complaint.
Its sleep attacks happen only during the night
Sleep attacks occur at inappropriate times during the day.

items.q: Which findings are symptoms of sleep deprivation? Select all that apply.
o: Ptosis and blurred vision
Ptosis and blurred vision are listed symptoms of sleep deprivation.
Slowed response time
Slowed response time is a symptom of sleep deprivation.
Increased sensitivity to pain
Sleep deprivation increases sensitivity to pain.
Decreased motivation
Decreased motivation is a symptom of sleep deprivation.
Heightened reflexes
Sleep deprivation decreases reflexes.
Improved fine-motor skill
Sleep deprivation causes fine-motor clumsiness.
items.ex: Sleep deprivation causes symptoms such as ptosis, blurred vision, slowed responses, pain sensitivity, irritability, and decreased motivation.

alt.q: A patient in the intensive care unit has been awakened every hour for 3 nights. Which findings suggest sleep deprivation? Select all that apply.
o: Confusion and disorientation
Confusion and disorientation are symptoms of sleep deprivation.
Cardiac arrhythmias
Cardiac arrhythmias are listed among sleep-deprivation symptoms.
Fine-motor clumsiness
Fine-motor clumsiness is a symptom of sleep deprivation.
Increased auditory alertness
Sleep deprivation decreases auditory and visual alertness.
Faster reaction time
Sleep deprivation slows response time.
alt.ex: Frequent interruptions lead to sleep deprivation, shown by confusion, arrhythmias, clumsiness, decreased alertness, and slowed responses.

items.q: A hospitalized patient shows signs of sleep deprivation from frequent nighttime care. Which nursing intervention is most effective?
items.a: Reduce environmental disturbances and interruptions from nighttime care
items.ex: The most effective treatment for sleep deprivation is to eliminate or correct the environmental factors and care activities that disrupt sleep.
w: Request a sleeping medication for nightly use
Medication does not remove the disruptions causing the deprivation.
Encourage several long daytime naps to catch up
Correcting the disruptive factors is the most effective treatment.
Increase nighttime vital sign checks for fatigue
More nighttime checks would add to the interruptions causing the problem.

alt.q: What is the most effective treatment for sleep deprivation?
alt.a: Eliminating the factors that disrupt the sleep pattern
alt.ex: Eliminating or correcting environmental factors and care activities that disrupt sleep is the most effective treatment.
w: Prescribing a hypnotic for nightly use
Medication does not address the causes of disrupted sleep.
Increasing total sleep time to 12 hours
Long sleep duration is itself linked to obesity, diabetes, and other problems.
Tracking sleep with a smartphone app
Sleep apps still need study to validate their accuracy and do not treat deprivation.

items.q: Which sleep study measures sleepiness during at least four napping opportunities spread throughout the day?
items.a: Multiple Sleep Latency Test (MSLT)
items.ex: The MSLT measures eye movements, muscle tone, and brain activity during at least four daytime naps and takes 8 to 10 hours.
w: Overnight polysomnogram
A polysomnogram monitors sleep stages during nighttime sleep.
Actigraphy (wrist device)
Actigraphy measures sleep-wake patterns over an extended period such as 1 week.
Electrooculogram (EOG)
The EOG measures eye movements but is not itself a daytime nap test.

alt.q: A patient will wear a device on the wrist for 1 week to measure sleep-wake patterns. What is this device called?
alt.a: Actigraph
alt.ex: An Actigraph worn on the wrist measures sleep-wake patterns, sleep time, efficiency, and awakenings over about 1 week.
w: Polysomnogram
A polysomnogram uses EEG, EMG, and EOG during nighttime sleep in a laboratory.
Electromyogram
An electromyogram measures muscle tone.
Multiple Sleep Latency Test
The MSLT measures sleepiness during daytime naps over 8 to 10 hours.

items.q: Which description fits Hypersomnias?

items.ex: The ICSD classifies sleep disorders into categories such as insomnias, breathing disorders, hypersomnias, circadian disorders, parasomnias, and movement disorders.

Parasomnias: Undesirable behaviors that usually occur during sleep.

items.q: Parasomnias are more common in children than in adults.
items.a: True
items.ex: Parasomnias are more common in children; in children they are usually benign and outgrown.
items.ww: The book states that parasomnias occur more often in children than adults.

alt.q: When adults have parasomnias, the problems are usually benign and outgrown, just as they are in children.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: When adults have parasomnias, it often indicates more serious disorders.
alt.ww: Children usually outgrow parasomnias, but in adults they often signal a more serious disorder.

items.q: A nurse teaches the parents of a newborn how to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS). Which instruction is correct?
items.a: Place the infant on the back to sleep
items.ex: Because the prone position is associated with SIDS, the AAP recommends placing infants supine during sleep.
w: Place the infant on the stomach to sleep
The prone position is associated with SIDS.
Place the infant prone after each feeding
Prone positioning is associated with SIDS at any time.
Place the infant in any position that settles her
The AAP specifically recommends the supine position for sleep.

alt.q: Which statement by a parent shows understanding of the teaching about safe infant sleep?
alt.a: “I will lay my baby down to sleep on her back.”
alt.ex: Placing infants supine during sleep reduces the risk of SIDS.
w: “I will lay my baby down to sleep on her stomach.”
The prone position is associated with SIDS.
“I will lay my baby face-down after her feedings.”
Face-down is the prone position, which is associated with SIDS.
“I will let my baby sleep in whatever position she likes.”
The AAP recommends the supine position for infant sleep.

items.q: A [[polysomnogram|polysomnography]] uses EEG, EMG, and EOG to monitor stages of sleep and wakefulness during nighttime sleep.
items.ex: Sleep laboratory studies such as the polysomnogram diagnose sleep disorders.

alt.q: Monitoring nighttime sleep stages with EEG, EMG, and EOG together is called a [[polysomnogram|polysomnography]].
alt.ex: Sleep laboratory studies such as the polysomnogram diagnose sleep disorders.

items.q: In sleep apnea, airflow through the nose and mouth stops for periods ranging from 10 seconds to 1 to 2 minutes.
items.a: True
items.ex: Sleep apnea involves a lack of airflow through the nose and mouth for 10 seconds to 1 to 2 minutes.
items.ww: The book defines apnea periods as lasting from 10 seconds up to 1 to 2 minutes.

alt.q: In sleep apnea, pauses in airflow typically last less than 5 seconds.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Apnea periods last from 10 seconds to 1 to 2 minutes.
alt.ww: Pauses shorter than 10 seconds do not fit the book’s description of apnea.

items.q: Which description best fits a person who is at rest?
items.a: Mentally relaxed, free from anxiety, and physically calm
items.ex: The textbook describes people at rest as mentally relaxed, free from anxiety, and physically calm.
w: Physically inactive and lying quietly in bed
Rest does not imply inactivity; a person can rest while walking or reading.
Asleep with reduced awareness of surroundings
Rest is not the same as sleep; people rest while awake by reading or listening to music.
Free of all mental and physical activity
Rest is a state of mental, physical, and spiritual activity, not an absence of activity.

alt.q: Which statement about rest is accurate?
alt.a: Rest leaves a person refreshed and ready to resume the day’s activities
alt.ex: Rest is a state of mental, physical, and spiritual activity that leaves people refreshed, rejuvenated, and ready to resume activities.
w: Rest requires lying in bed or sitting in a comfortable chair
This is a common assumption, but rest does not require settling into a bed or chair.
Rest occurs only when a person is in light stages of sleep
Rest is a waking state of relaxation and refreshment, not a sleep stage.
Rest is achieved only by eliminating all physical activity
Rest does not imply inactivity; a long walk can be restful.

items.q: Rest always means that a person is physically inactive.
items.a: False
items.ex: Rest does not imply inactivity; people rest by taking a long walk or practicing a relaxation exercise.
items.ww: Although many people picture rest as lying in bed, the textbook states rest is a state of mental, physical, and spiritual activity.

alt.q: A person can be at rest while taking a long walk.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The textbook lists taking a long walk among the ways people rest, because rest is about feeling relaxed and refreshed.
alt.ww: Rest does not require inactivity, so walking can be a restful activity.

items.q: Which activities does the textbook identify as ways people commonly rest? Select all that apply.
o: Reading a book
Reading is one of the habits people use to obtain rest.
Listening to music
Listening to music helps people relax and rest.
Taking a long walk
A long walk is restful even though it involves physical activity.
Practicing a relaxation exercise
Relaxation exercises are a common way to obtain rest.
Finishing office work in bed
Working in bed is mentally stimulating and interferes with relaxation.
Drinking coffee to stay alert
Caffeine is a stimulant and does not promote rest.
items.ex: People rest by reading, practicing relaxation exercises, listening to music, taking a long walk, or sitting quietly.

alt.q: A nurse asks a patient about personal habits for obtaining rest. Which responses describe restful activities? Select all that apply.
o: “I sit quietly on my porch.”
Sitting quietly is a way people obtain rest.
“I do a relaxation exercise.”
Relaxation exercises promote a calm, restful state.
“I listen to music I enjoy.”
Listening to music is a common way to rest.
“I resolve family arguments late at night.”
Resolving family problems before bedtime is stimulating and discouraged.
“I play video games until I feel tired.”
Electronic devices near bedtime stimulate the person and disrupt sleep.
alt.ex: Sitting quietly, relaxation exercises, and music are restful habits; stimulating activities interfere with rest.

items.q: A patient on bed rest after a heart attack says, “I just lie here worrying that I will never get back to work.” Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: The patient is on bed rest but is not necessarily feeling rested.
items.ex: Patients on bed rest may have emotional distress, such as fear about returning to their usual lifestyle, that prevents relaxation.
w: The patient is getting adequate rest because activity is restricted.
Restricted activity alone does not produce rest when emotional distress prevents relaxation.
The patient’s worry shows that bed rest is working as intended.
Worry is a sign of stress that interferes with rest, not a sign of benefit.
The patient needs more hours in bed to begin feeling rested.
More time in bed does not relieve the worry that is preventing rest.

alt.q: Why might a patient on bed rest fail to feel rested?
alt.a: Emotional distress about physical limitations prevents relaxation.
alt.ex: Concern over physical limitations or fear of not returning to a usual lifestyle causes stress that prevents complete relaxation.
w: Bed rest increases the physical demands placed on the body.
Bed rest is used to reduce, not increase, physical demands.
Lying in bed always produces too much deep sleep.
Bed rest does not cause excess deep sleep; the barrier is emotional distress.
Bed rest removes all psychological demands on the patient.
If it removed psychological demands, the patient would feel rested; distress persists.

items.q: For what main reason do nurses care for patients on bed rest?
items.a: To reduce physical and psychological demands on the body
items.ex: Bed rest is used in many health care settings to reduce physical and psychological demands on the body.
w: To increase the percentage of REM sleep each night
Bed rest is not prescribed to alter sleep stages.
To guarantee that patients feel refreshed and relaxed
Patients on bed rest do not necessarily feel rested.
To increase physical stimulation needed for healing
Bed rest lowers demands on the body rather than adding stimulation.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student about bed rest needs correction?
alt.a: “Patients on bed rest always feel rested because they are inactive.”
alt.ex: Patients on bed rest do not necessarily feel rested; emotional distress can prevent relaxation.
w: “Bed rest reduces the physical demands on the body.”
This is accurate; bed rest reduces physical demands.
“Bed rest reduces the psychological demands on the body.”
This is accurate; bed rest is used to reduce psychological demands too.
“Patients on bed rest may feel stressed about their limitations.”
This is accurate; concern over limitations causes stress.

items.q: According to the textbook, what can happen when a person lacks rest for long periods?
items.a: Illness develops or an existing illness worsens.
items.ex: A lack of rest for long periods causes illness or worsening of existing illness, so nurses must stay aware of rest needs.
w: The body adapts and needs less rest in the future.
The textbook warns of harm from prolonged lack of rest, not adaptation.
Only a brief, harmless decrease in daytime energy occurs.
Prolonged lack of rest has serious health effects, not just brief tiredness.
Rest needs are fully met by sleeping longer on weekends.
Sleeping long hours on weekends disturbs the sleep-wake cycle and is discouraged.

alt.q: A nurse explains why she always considers each patient’s need for rest. Which rationale is best?
alt.a: Prolonged lack of rest causes illness or worsens existing illness.
alt.ex: You must always be aware of a patient’s need for rest because a long-term lack of rest causes or worsens illness.
w: Rest needs matter only for patients who are on bed rest.
All patients need rest, not only those on bed rest.
Rest is important mainly for the comfort of the nursing staff.
Rest is assessed for the patient’s health, not staff comfort.
Lack of rest affects mood but has no physical effects.
Prolonged lack of rest causes illness, which includes physical effects.

items.q: Illness and unfamiliar health care routines easily affect the usual rest and sleep patterns of people entering a hospital.
items.a: True
items.ex: Illness and unfamiliar routines in a health care setting readily disrupt a patient’s usual rest and sleep patterns.
items.ww: Hospital routines are new to patients and commonly disrupt rather than preserve their usual patterns.

alt.q: Patients entering a hospital usually keep their normal rest and sleep patterns because they are less active.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Illness and unfamiliar health care routines easily disrupt the rest and sleep patterns of patients entering a hospital.
alt.ww: Being less active does not protect patients from the disruption that illness and unfamiliar routines cause.

items.q: A newly admitted patient tells the nurse, “I just can’t seem to relax here.” Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Ask the patient what usually helps them rest at home.
items.ex: People have their own habits for obtaining rest; assessing these first lets the nurse bring them into care.
w: Ask the health care provider for a sleeping medication.
Sleep medications are a last resort; assessment comes before intervention.
Turn on the television to distract the patient.
Television stimulates some people and is chosen only if the patient finds it restful.
Explain that patients adjust after the first week.
This dismisses the concern and skips assessment of the patient’s habits.

alt.q: A hospitalized patient says, “At home I always read before I fall asleep.” Which nursing action best supports this patient’s rest?
alt.a: Offer reading material at bedtime.
alt.ex: Incorporating a patient’s usual habit, such as reading before sleep, helps promote rest and sleep.
w: Encourage the patient to break the reading habit.
Reading is a beneficial habit for this patient and should be supported.
Turn off all lights promptly at 2100.
This ignores the patient’s routine and preferences.
Offer a sedative so reading is not needed.
Sedatives are not a substitute for a patient’s effective rest habits.

items.q: A patient hospitalized for several days of diagnostic tests cannot rest because of uncertainty about the results. Which nursing action is most helpful?
items.a: Explain the purpose of each procedure and answer the patient’s questions.
items.ex: Giving information and some control over care minimizes uncertainty and anxiety so the patient can rest.
w: Avoid discussing the tests so the patient does not worry more.
Withholding information increases uncertainty; information gives peace of mind.
Give a sedative at the first sign of restlessness.
Sedatives are used cautiously and only after other measures; they do not address uncertainty.
Remind the patient that worrying will slow recovery.
This adds pressure and does not reduce the uncertainty causing the anxiety.

alt.q: A patient on bed rest is too anxious about upcoming procedures to rest. Which approach best promotes rest?
alt.a: Give the patient information and a voice in decisions about care.
alt.ex: Providing information and giving patients control over their care reduces the uncertainty and anxiety that block rest.
w: Limit conversation so the patient can lie still.
Stillness without addressing anxiety does not produce rest.
Tell the patient that procedures are routine and not to worry.
False reassurance does not relieve uncertainty the way information does.
Ask the family to stay away until testing ends.
Isolating the patient does not reduce uncertainty and may increase distress.

items.q: Which nursing actions help hospitalized patients obtain rest? Select all that apply.
o: Combine several needed tasks into one visit to the room
Clustering care reduces the number of disturbances.
Draw blood samples at a time when the patient is awake
Scheduling procedures during waking hours avoids interrupting rest.
Plan for 2 to 3 hours of uninterrupted sleep during the night
The textbook advises always trying to provide this uninterrupted period.
Give baths during the night when the unit is quieter
Baths and routine hygiene are not given at night for nursing convenience.
Return to the room every few minutes to check each tube
