items.q: Which statement about using a 100-mm visual analogue scale to assess sleep is accurate?
items.a: It is useful for tracking one patient over time, not for comparing patients.
items.ex: The visual analogue scale gives a numerical value for sleep satisfaction and is used repeatedly for one individual.
w: It is best used to compare sleep quality among patients.
The scale assesses an individual patient, not comparisons between patients.
It measures the exact number of minutes a patient slept.
It measures perceived satisfaction with the night’s sleep, not minutes.
It screens surgical patients for obstructive sleep apnea.
OSA screening uses the STOP-Bang tool.

alt.q: A nurse asks a patient to mark a line between “best night’s sleep” and “worst night’s sleep.” How is the result used?
alt.a: The mark’s distance in millimeters shows change in the patient’s sleep over time.
alt.ex: Measuring the mark in millimeters gives a numerical satisfaction value that is repeated to show change.
w: The mark ranks the patient against others on the unit.
The scale is not used to compare patients.
The mark determines the dose of a sleep medication.
The scale assesses perceived sleep, not drug dosing.
The mark diagnoses the type of sleep disorder present.
It measures satisfaction with sleep, not the specific disorder.

items.q: For how long does the textbook suggest that a patient and bed partner keep a sleep-wake log?
items.a: 1 to 4 weeks
items.ex: A sleep-wake log kept for 1 to 4 weeks shows day-to-day variations in sleep-wake patterns.
w: 1 to 2 days
A day or two cannot show variations over extended periods.
3 to 6 months
The textbook recommends 1 to 4 weeks.
Exactly 24 hours
The log covers 24-hour information each day but is kept for weeks.

alt.q: Which factor is necessary for a sleep-wake log to be useful?
alt.a: The patient must be motivated to complete it daily.
alt.ex: Although the log is helpful, the patient needs to be motivated to complete it each day.
w: The log must be completed by the nurse each night.
The patient completes the log daily, with help from a partner.
The log must record only nighttime events.
Entries include 24-hour data such as meals, naps, and activities.
The log must be kept for at least 6 months.
The textbook suggests keeping the log for 1 to 4 weeks.

items.q: Which assessment questions help identify sleep apnea? Select all that apply.
o: “Do you snore loudly?”
Loud snoring is a key sleep apnea question.
“Has anyone told you that you stop breathing for short periods during sleep?”
Breathing pauses reported by a partner suggest apnea.
“Do you have headaches after awakening?”
Morning headaches are asked about for sleep apnea.
“Do you have difficulty staying awake during the day?”
Daytime sleepiness is part of the apnea assessment.
“Do you have episodes of losing muscle control or falling?”
This question screens for narcolepsy.
“Do you have vivid, lifelike dreams when falling asleep?”
This question screens for narcolepsy.
items.ex: Sleep apnea questions focus on loud snoring, breathing pauses, morning headaches, and daytime sleepiness.

alt.q: Which assessment questions are used to screen for narcolepsy? Select all that apply.
o: “Do you fall asleep at the wrong times?”
Falling asleep at the wrong times suggests narcolepsy.
“Have you felt unable to move or talk just before waking or falling asleep?”
This describes sleep paralysis, a narcolepsy question.
“Do you have episodes of losing muscle control or falling to the floor?”
Sudden loss of muscle control is asked about for narcolepsy.
“Does anyone in your family snore loudly?”
Family snoring is a sleep apnea question.
“Do you have headaches when you wake up?”
Morning headaches are a sleep apnea question.
alt.ex: Narcolepsy questions ask about sleep attacks, loss of muscle control, sleep paralysis, and vivid dreams.

items.q: The STOP-Bang tool is used to screen for obstructive sleep apnea and is frequently part of preoperative assessments.
items.a: True
items.ex: STOP-Bang is a reliable, evidence-based OSA screening tool often used in preanesthesia and preoperative assessments.
items.ww: The textbook identifies STOP-Bang as an OSA screening tool.

alt.q: The STOP-Bang tool measures a patient’s daytime sleepiness with eight items scored from 0 to 3.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Eight items scored 0 to 3 describe the Epworth Sleepiness Scale; STOP-Bang screens for obstructive sleep apnea.
alt.ww: Daytime sleepiness scoring belongs to the Epworth scale, not STOP-Bang.

items.q: Which behaviors should the nurse observe for as signs of sleep deprivation? Select all that apply.
o: Irritability
Irritability is a behavior of sleep deprivation.
Disorientation similar to a drunken state
Disorientation resembling intoxication can occur.
Frequent yawning
Frequent yawning is a sign of sleep deprivation.
Slurred speech
Slurred speech is a behavior of sleep deprivation.
Improved concentration
Sleep deprivation impairs concentration.
Increased alertness
Sleep deprivation reduces alertness.
items.ex: Sleep deprivation shows as irritability, disorientation, frequent yawning, and slurred speech.

alt.q: A nurse visits a caregiver who has slept poorly for weeks. Which findings suggest sleep deprivation? Select all that apply.
o: She yawns frequently during the visit.
Frequent yawning signals sleep deprivation.
She has dark circles under her eyes.
Dark circles under the eyes were noted as a physical sign in Julie.
She shifts position in the chair repeatedly.
Frequent position changes are a sign of sleep problems.
She sits calmly without yawning.
Absence of yawning and position changes suggests adequate sleep.
She reports feeling well rested.
Feeling rested indicates sleep needs are met.
alt.ex: Frequent yawning, dark circles, and repeated position changes point to sleep deprivation.

items.q: A hospitalized patient who has slept little for many nights reports seeing strange colors in the room and acts afraid when the nurse enters. Which explanation should the nurse consider?
items.a: Prolonged sleep deprivation can cause psychotic behavior such as delusions and paranoia.
items.ex: When sleep deprivation lasts a long time, psychotic behavior such as delusions and paranoia sometimes develops.
w: These findings are expected effects of a single sleepless night.
Psychotic behavior is linked to long-lasting, not brief, sleep deprivation.
These findings indicate the patient is getting too much REM sleep.
The patient is sleep deprived, not getting excess REM sleep.
These findings show the patient is adapting to the hospital.
Seeing strange objects and fear are warning signs, not adaptation.

alt.q: Which finding suggests that a patient’s sleep deprivation has lasted a long time?
alt.a: Delusions and paranoia
alt.ex: Psychotic behaviors such as delusions and paranoia sometimes develop when sleep deprivation is prolonged.
w: Mild drowsiness after lunch
Mild drowsiness does not indicate long-term deprivation.
Taking 20 minutes to fall asleep
Falling asleep within 20 minutes was an improvement outcome for Julie.
Waking once during the night
Waking once nightly was reported after Julie’s sleep improved.

items.q: A nurse notes that a patient yawned once during the admission interview. Which conclusion is most appropriate?
items.a: More data are needed; a diagnosis requires a cluster of findings.
items.ex: Accurate nursing diagnoses cannot be made from just one or two findings; the nurse looks for clusters of data.
w: The patient has Sleep Deprivation.
One finding is not enough to support a nursing diagnosis.
The patient has Impaired Sleep related to noise.
Neither the problem nor its related factor is supported by one yawn.
The patient has Fatigue and needs a hypnotic.
One finding cannot support a diagnosis, and hypnotics are a last resort.

alt.q: Why does the nurse specify the related factor in a diagnosis of Impaired Sleep?
alt.a: Different causes require different interventions.
alt.ex: Impaired Sleep related to chronic pain needs different therapies than Impaired Sleep related to an unfamiliar hospital environment.
w: All causes of Impaired Sleep are treated the same way.
Interventions are chosen to target the specific related factor.
The related factor determines the patient’s medical diagnosis.
Related factors guide nursing interventions, not medical diagnoses.
The related factor is needed only for billing purposes.
If the cause is defined incorrectly, the patient does not benefit from care.

items.q: Which expected outcomes are appropriate and measurable for a patient with a sleep disturbance? Select all that apply.
o: Patient falls asleep within 30 minutes of going to bed.
This is a measurable patient outcome from the textbook.
Patient reports fewer awakenings during the night.
Fewer reported awakenings is a measurable outcome.
Patient expresses feeling rested after sleep.
The patient’s report of feeling rested is an outcome.
Patient reports sleeping 8 hours each night.
Hours of sleep reported is a measurable outcome.
Nurse will dim the lights at 2200 each night.
This is a nursing intervention, not a patient outcome.
Patient will understand sleep better.
“Understand better” is vague and not measurable.
items.ex: Outcomes describe measurable patient results such as sleep onset time, awakenings, feeling rested, and hours slept.

alt.q: A nurse and Julie set outcomes for her Impaired Sleep. Which outcomes are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Julie reports waking up less frequently and feeling rested within 4 weeks.
This was a mutually agreed-on, time-limited outcome.
Julie verbalizes adherence to a regular bedtime routine within 4 weeks.
This measurable outcome was set with Julie.
Julie falls asleep within 30 minutes of going to bed.
Time to fall asleep is a measurable sleep outcome.
The nurse will teach relaxation techniques at the next visit.
This describes a nursing intervention, not a patient outcome.
Julie will never have a poor night of sleep again.
This outcome is unrealistic; outcomes should be realistic and measurable.
alt.ex: Realistic, measurable, time-limited patient outcomes set with the patient guide sleep care.

items.q: A patient with a painful hip fracture tells the nurse she cannot sleep. Which nursing priority is most appropriate?
items.a: Manage the pain first, then focus on sleep therapies.
items.ex: When physical symptoms interfere with sleep, managing them is the priority; sleep therapies follow once symptoms are relieved.
w: Teach sleep-hygiene habits before addressing the pain.
Sleep hygiene will not work while pain keeps the patient awake.
Ask for a hypnotic so she sleeps through the pain.
Hypnotics are a last resort and do not relieve the underlying pain.
Refer her to a sleep center for an evaluation.
Referral is for chronic sleep problems; the cause here is pain.

alt.q: A patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease has trouble breathing when lying flat and cannot sleep. Which intervention addresses the priority?
alt.a: Position the patient semi-sitting and give prescribed bronchodilators before sleep.
alt.ex: Controlling the physical symptom that disrupts sleep comes first; semi-sitting and bronchodilators ease breathing.
w: Teach the patient to avoid electronic devices before bed.
Device use is not the cause of this patient’s sleep problem.
Place the patient flat with one pillow to promote rest.
Lying flat increases the effort to breathe.
Ask for a sedative to help the patient fall asleep.
Sedatives are not the priority when a physical symptom disrupts sleep.

items.q: A patient with obstructive sleep apnea received general anesthesia and opioid analgesics after surgery. Which finding is most important to report to the health care provider immediately?
items.a: The patient is difficult to arouse.
items.ex: Anesthesia and analgesics reduce defenses against airway obstruction; a patient with OSA who is difficult to arouse needs immediate reporting.
w: The patient rates incisional pain 4 out of 10.
Moderate pain is managed cautiously but is not the immediate airway concern.
The patient asks for an extra pillow.
Extra pillows help prevent a supine position and are not a concern.
The patient wants to use the home CPAP machine.
Using home CPAP is encouraged if agency policy allows.

alt.q: Which postoperative finding in a patient with obstructive sleep apnea requires immediate notification of the health care provider?
alt.a: Trouble breathing while sleeping
alt.ex: Postoperative patients with OSA are at risk for airway obstruction; trouble breathing must be reported immediately.
w: Request to sleep on the side
Side-lying is recommended for patients with OSA.
Request to elevate the head of the bed
Elevating the head of the bed is recommended for OSA.
Report of feeling tired after surgery
Tiredness alone is expected and not an airway emergency.

items.q: An older adult is taught about promoting sleep at home. Which statement shows understanding of the teaching about naps?
items.a: “If I nap, I’ll keep it to 30 minutes early in the day.”
items.ex: Older adults should eliminate naps unless routine, and any naps should be limited to 30 minutes early in the day.
w: “I’ll take a 2-hour nap late in the afternoon.”
Long, late naps disrupt nighttime sleep.
“I’ll nap whenever I feel sleepy, for as long as I need.”
Naps should be limited to 30 minutes and timed early.
“I’ll nap right after dinner so I fall asleep easier.”
Naps are timed early in the day, not in the evening.

alt.q: A resident in a long-term care facility naps for hours each afternoon. Which nursing action best supports nighttime sleep?
alt.a: Limit daytime naps to 30 minutes or less and engage the resident in activities.
alt.ex: Limiting naps to 30 minutes or less and keeping residents active and involved improves nighttime sleep.
w: Encourage the resident to stay in bed most of the day.
Time in bed is limited whenever possible.
Allow unlimited naps as long as the resident is comfortable.
Long naps interfere with nighttime sleep.
Serve meals in bed to help the resident conserve energy.
Residents should be up in a chair and in the dining area for meals.

items.q: Which sleep-hygiene teaching points from the textbook should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Get out of bed and do a quiet activity if not asleep within 30 minutes.
Staying in bed awake strengthens the link between bed and wakefulness.
Stop using electronic devices about 30 minutes before going to bed.
Devices emit blue light that affects sleep and circadian rhythms.
Avoid heavy meals 3 hours before bedtime.
Heavy meals before bedtime interfere with sleep; a light snack may help.
Avoid sleeping long hours on weekends or holidays.
Long weekend sleep disturbs the normal sleep-wake cycle.
Do vigorous exercise right before bed to become tired.
Vigorous exercise within 2 hours of bedtime is avoided.
Use the bedroom for studying and watching television.
The bedroom is used only for sleep and sex.
items.ex: Sleep hygiene includes leaving bed when awake, limiting devices, avoiding late heavy meals, and keeping a regular schedule.

alt.q: Which statements by a patient show understanding of sleep-hygiene teaching? Select all that apply.
o: “I’ll limit my caffeine to morning coffee.”
Caffeine should be limited to morning coffee.
“I’ll try earplugs and an eyeshade if my room is noisy and bright.”
Earplugs and eyeshades may help the sleep environment.
“I’ll exercise in the morning or afternoon.”
Daily exercise is preferred in the morning or afternoon.
“I’ll lie in bed until I fall asleep, however long it takes.”
If not asleep within 30 minutes, the patient should get up.
“I’ll catch up on sleep by sleeping in all weekend.”
Long weekend sleep disrupts the sleep-wake cycle.
alt.ex: Morning caffeine only, earplugs and eyeshades, and daytime exercise reflect correct sleep hygiene.

items.q: What dose and timing of melatonin does the textbook recommend?
items.a: 0.3 to 3 mg taken 2 hours before bedtime
items.ex: The recommended melatonin dose is 0.3 to 3 mg taken 2 hours before bedtime.
w: 5 to 10 mg taken at the moment of lying down
This exceeds the recommended dose and timing.
0.3 to 3 mg taken upon awakening in the morning
Melatonin is taken before bedtime to promote sleep.
10 to 20 mg taken 30 minutes before bedtime
This is far above the recommended 0.3 to 3 mg.

alt.q: An older adult asks about melatonin. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “Take 0.3 to 3 mg about 2 hours before bedtime.”
alt.ex: Melatonin, which is decreased in many older adults, is recommended at 0.3 to 3 mg 2 hours before bedtime.
w: “Take 10 to 20 mg right before bedtime.”
This dose is far above the recommended range.
“Take 0.3 to 3 mg when you wake during the night.”
The recommended timing is 2 hours before bedtime.
“Take 5 mg with breakfast to reset your clock.”
Melatonin is taken before bedtime, not with breakfast.

items.q: An older adult who was continent, ambulatory, and alert becomes confused and incontinent after starting a benzodiazepine for sleep. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Report the benzodiazepine to the health care provider as a possible cause.
items.ex: Benzodiazepines stay active longer in older adults; new confusion, incontinence, or impaired mobility should raise concern about the drug.
w: Document the changes as normal aging and continue the drug.
Sudden confusion and incontinence are not expected aging changes.
Give an extra dose so the patient sleeps through the night.
Patients should not take more than the prescribed dose.
Apply a safety belt so the patient stays in bed.
Safety belts are considered restraints and are not used.

alt.q: Why is benzodiazepine use potentially dangerous for older adults?
alt.a: The drugs remain active longer, increasing next-day sedation and fall risk.
alt.ex: Benzodiazepines stay active longer in older adults, causing respiratory depression, next-day sedation, amnesia, and impaired coordination.
w: The drugs are eliminated faster, causing no effect.
Older adults metabolize drugs more slowly, so effects last longer.
The drugs increase REM sleep, causing vivid nightmares.
The textbook stresses prolonged action and falls, not nightmares.
The drugs are safe for unlimited long-term nightly use.
Benzodiazepines are intended for short-term use.

items.q: Older adults should be cautioned about over-the-counter antihistamines for sleep because their long duration of action can cause confusion and falls.
items.a: True
items.ex: OTC antihistamines have a long duration of action that can cause confusion, constipation, urinary retention, and falls in older adults.
items.ww: These drugs are not safe sleep aids for older adults because of their long action and adverse effects.

alt.q: Over-the-counter antihistamines are a preferred sleep aid for older adults because of their short duration of action.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: OTC antihistamines have a long duration of action and increase the risk of confusion and falls in older adults.
alt.ww: Nonprescription sleep medications are not recommended, and these drugs act long, not briefly.

items.q: Medications that induce sleep are called [[hypnotics|hypnotic]], whereas sedatives produce a calming or soothing effect.
items.ex: Hypnotics induce sleep; sedatives produce calm. Both are used cautiously, at the lowest dose, and short term.

alt.q: A drug given specifically to induce sleep is classified as a [[hypnotic|hypnotics]].
alt.ex: Hypnotics induce sleep; sedatives produce calm. Both are used cautiously, at the lowest dose, and short term.

items.q: Experts recommend a low dose of a short-acting benzodiazepine-like drug such as zolpidem for no longer than 2 to 3 weeks.
items.a: True
items.ex: Zolpidem at a low dose for 2 to 3 weeks or less is recommended because it causes fewer dependence and rebound problems.
items.ww: The recommendation is specifically short-term, low-dose use.

alt.q: Benzodiazepine-like drugs such as zolpidem are intended for indefinite nightly use to treat insomnia.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Zolpidem is recommended at a low dose for short-term use of no longer than 2 to 3 weeks.
alt.ww: Regular use of any sleep medication leads to tolerance and withdrawal, so use is short-term.

items.q: Parents who practice bed-sharing for cultural reasons ask the nurse about infant sleep. Which response is best?
items.a: “I respect your tradition. Sharing a room but not a bed is safer for your baby.”
items.ex: Nurses discuss co-sleeping risks while remaining culturally respectful and recommend room-sharing without bed-sharing.
w: “Bed-sharing is safe as long as you use a special device.”
Devices to make bed-sharing safe have not been shown to reduce suffocation or SIDS.
“Your tradition is wrong and you must stop immediately.”
This is not culturally sensitive or respectful of the parents’ views.
“Bed-sharing is fine if one of you drinks only at night.”
Parents who co-sleep should avoid alcohol or drugs that impair arousal.

alt.q: Which infant would be at greatest risk if the parents practiced bed-sharing?
alt.a: A premature infant whose father smokes
alt.ex: Bed-sharing is not recommended for premature infants or with parents who smoke or use alcohol or drugs because of SIDS risk.
w: A term infant sleeping in a crib in the parents’ room
Room-sharing without bed-sharing is the recommended practice.
A term infant in a sleeper with no loose blankets
Light sleepers and removing blankets are recommended safety measures.
A term infant placed in a crib with a fitted sheet
A fitted sheet on a safe mattress is recommended.

items.q: Which statement best describes the nature of pain?
items.a: It is subjective, and only the patient knows whether it is present and how it feels
items.ex: Pain is subjective and highly individualized; only the patient knows whether pain is present and what it feels like.
w: It is a single physiological sensation that a specific stimulus reliably produces
The book stresses pain is more than a single sensation from a specific stimulus.
It is objective, so a skilled nurse can confirm its presence by observation alone
A nurse cannot see or feel a patient’s pain; it is purely subjective.
It is uniform, so two people with the same injury feel the same amount of it
No two people experience pain in the same way, even with similar injuries.

alt.q: A nurse is deciding whose information is most reliable for determining whether a patient has pain. Which source is most reliable?
alt.a: The patient’s own report of the pain
alt.ex: Only the patient knows whether pain is present and how it feels, so the self-report is the most reliable source.
w: The patient’s heart rate and blood pressure
Vital signs often return to baseline as people adapt, so they cannot confirm or rule out pain.
The family’s impression of the patient’s comfort
Family observations help, but they cannot replace the patient’s subjective report.
The nurse’s judgment of the injury’s severity
The nurse cannot see or feel pain; the same injury causes different pain in different people.

items.q: A patient rates abdominal pain as 8 on a 0-to-10 scale while chatting and laughing with visitors. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: Accept the rating as valid and plan interventions to relieve the pain
items.ex: Pain is whatever the person experiencing it says it is, so the nurse accepts the report and acts to relieve it.
w: Document that the rating seems exaggerated given the patient’s behavior
Behavior varies widely; labeling the report as exaggerated ignores the subjective nature of pain.
Wait until the visitors leave and ask the patient to rate the pain again
Delaying treatment to re-test the report leaves the pain untreated and implies disbelief.
Tell the patient that laughing shows the pain is probably mild right now
Telling the patient the pain is mild disputes the patient’s report, which is the authority on pain.

alt.q: A nursing student says, “The patient says the pain is severe, but the vital signs are normal, so it can’t be that bad.” Which reply by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Pain is whatever the patient says it is, so we treat the reported pain.”
alt.ex: The patient’s report defines pain; vital signs may stay normal because many people adapt to pain.
w: “You’re right; we should hold analgesics until the vital signs change.”
Waiting for vital sign changes leaves pain untreated; many people in pain have normal vital signs.
“Let’s ask the family whether the patient tends to exaggerate symptoms.”
Seeking to discredit the report conflicts with respecting the subjective nature of pain.
“Normal vital signs mean the patient is coping well, so pain isn’t a priority.”
Normal vital signs do not mean pain is absent or less important to relieve.

items.q: Which definition of pain does the International Association for the Study of Pain (IASP) use?
items.a: An unpleasant, subjective sensory and emotional experience linked to actual or potential tissue damage
items.ex: The IASP defines pain as an unpleasant, subjective sensory and emotional experience associated with actual or potential tissue damage.
w: An objective nerve signal that occurs only when tissue has actually been damaged
Pain is subjective and may relate to potential, not only actual, tissue damage.
A purely emotional reaction to stress that occurs without any sensory component
The definition includes both sensory and emotional components.
A measurable response of the autonomic nervous system to a harmful stimulus
Autonomic responses may accompany pain, but the definition centers on a subjective experience.

alt.q: According to the IASP definition, pain can be associated with which kind of tissue damage?
alt.a: Actual or potential tissue damage
alt.ex: The IASP definition includes experiences associated with, or resembling those associated with, actual or potential tissue damage.
w: Only actual tissue damage that can be seen
The definition also includes potential damage, so visible damage is not required.
Only tissue damage confirmed by imaging
Diagnostic confirmation is not part of the definition; pain is a subjective experience.
Only damage that has lasted at least 3 months
Duration distinguishes acute from chronic pain; it is not part of the definition of pain.

items.q: Which statement explains the protective purpose of pain?
items.a: It is a physiological mechanism that protects a person from a harmful stimulus
items.ex: Pain is a physiological mechanism that protects an individual from a harmful stimulus.
w: It is a learned behavior that helps a person gain attention from others
Pain is a physiological protective mechanism, not a learned bid for attention.
It is a cognitive process that develops only after tissue has healed
Pain warns of actual or potential damage; it does not arise only after healing.
It is an emotional state that motivates a person to rest more often
Pain has emotional components, but its protective function is warning of harmful stimuli.

alt.q: A person touches a hot pan and feels pain. Which function of pain does this illustrate?
alt.a: Protection from a harmful stimulus
alt.ex: Pain is a physiological mechanism that warns of and protects a person from harmful stimuli.
w: Conservation of energy for healing
Pain actually reduces energy and causes fatigue rather than conserving it.
Improvement of interpersonal relationships
Pain interferes with relationships rather than improving them.
Stimulation of emotional resilience
Pain has emotional effects, but its protective role is warning of harm.

items.q: Mrs. Mays, who has osteoarthritis and resolving pneumonia, is preparing for discharge. Which statement she makes is most important for the nurse to address in discharge planning?
items.a: “My hip and knee pain wakes me two or three times a night.”
items.ex: Her unrelieved pain limits walking, self-care, and sleep, threatening her ability to manage at home.
w: “My pneumonia is getting better every day.”
A resolving pneumonia is improvement, not a new problem needing priority attention.
“I know how to manage my diabetes at home.”
She reports confidence in diabetes management, and her glucose is more stable.
“My husband helps me with my daily activities.”
Family support is a strength, not a problem to address first.

alt.q: A patient being discharged says, “My breathing is better, but my hand pain is so bad I can’t button my shirt.” Which nursing concern should guide discharge teaching?
alt.a: Unrelieved pain is limiting the patient’s ability to care for self
alt.ex: Pain interferes with function and quality of life, so it must be addressed for safe self-care at home.
w: The patient’s respiratory status is likely to worsen at home
The patient reports breathing is better; the cue points to pain-limited function.
The patient needs a referral for a new clothing wardrobe
Changing clothing ignores the underlying cue of unrelieved pain affecting function.
The patient is focusing on minor symptoms to delay discharge
Dismissing the report as minor disregards the subjective nature of pain.

items.q: A patient with long-standing joint pain says, “I’m worn out all the time.” Which explanation is consistent with the nature of pain?
items.a: Pain reduces a person’s energy and often causes fatigue
items.ex: Pain reduces energy and often causes fatigue, along with affecting relationships and quality of life.
w: Pain increases energy but disrupts concentration
Pain reduces energy; it does not increase it.
Fatigue is unrelated to pain and suggests another illness
Fatigue is a recognized effect of pain, so it should not be attributed elsewhere automatically.
Fatigue occurs only when pain is caused by cancer
Pain of any cause can reduce energy and cause fatigue.

alt.q: Which physical effect is commonly caused by pain?
alt.a: Fatigue from reduced energy
alt.ex: The book notes pain reduces a person’s energy and often causes fatigue.
w: Improved sleep from exhaustion
Pain more often disrupts sleep, as seen when Mrs. Mays wakes at night.
Increased stamina from stress hormones
Pain drains energy rather than building stamina.
Heightened appetite from activity
Pain is not described as increasing appetite; chronic pain is linked to anorexia.

items.q: How does the book describe a nurse’s responsibility for assessing and managing a patient’s pain?
items.a: It is both a legal and an ethical responsibility
items.ex: Nurses are legally and ethically responsible for assessing and managing pain.
w: It is an optional task if a pain specialist is involved
Nurses remain responsible for pain assessment and management in all settings.
It is an ethical ideal but not a legal duty
The responsibility is legal as well as ethical.
It is a legal duty limited to postoperative patients
Pain occurs in all health care settings, and the duty is not limited to surgery.

alt.q: A nurse says, “Pain management is the health care provider’s job, not mine.” Which response by the charge nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “Nurses are legally and ethically responsible for pain care.”
alt.ex: Assessing and managing pain is a legal and ethical responsibility of nurses.
w: “That’s correct; nurses only document pain ratings.”
Nurses do more than document; they assess and manage pain.
“Only nurses on surgical units are responsible for pain.”
Patients have pain in all settings, and the nurse’s duty applies everywhere.
“Pain care is ethical but carries no legal duty.”
The responsibility is both legal and ethical.

items.q: In the Declaration of Montreal, the IASP declared that access to pain management is which of the following?
items.a: A fundamental human right
items.ex: The IASP declared that access to pain management is a fundamental human right.
w: A privilege reserved for terminal illness
The declaration applies to everyone, not only patients who are dying.
A benefit determined by insurance status
Calling it a human right means access should not depend on coverage.
An optional goal after curing disease
Pain relief is a right in itself, not secondary to cure.

alt.q: A nurse advocates for pain relief for a patient without insurance, citing the IASP. Which principle supports this?
alt.a: Access to pain management is a fundamental human right
alt.ex: The IASP’s Declaration of Montreal states that access to pain management is a fundamental human right.
w: Pain relief is reserved for patients with cancer
The right to pain management is not limited to a diagnosis.
Pain relief should follow treatment of the cause
The principle does not make pain relief secondary to curing the cause.
Pain relief depends on the facility’s resources
A fundamental right does not depend on an agency’s resources.

items.q: Which nursing behavior best reflects person-centered pain management?
items.a: Advocating for relief based on the patient’s own description of the pain
items.ex: Person-centered care recognizes that pain can and should be relieved and calls for advocacy, compassion, and respect.
w: Limiting pain relief until the cause of the pain is fully diagnosed
Person-centered care recognizes pain should be relieved, not delayed for diagnosis.
Basing interventions mainly on what the family believes the patient feels
Family input helps, but the patient’s report is central to person-centered care.
Treating every patient with the same pain protocol regardless of reports
Every pain experience is unique, so care must be individualized.

alt.q: A nurse wants to practice person-centered pain management. Which attitude is essential?
alt.a: Recognizing that pain can and should be relieved
alt.ex: Person-centered pain management requires recognizing that pain can and should be relieved.
w: Accepting that some pain is an expected part of being ill
Accepting pain as inevitable conflicts with the goal that pain should be relieved.
Believing that patients tolerate pain better with less medicine
This belief leads to undertreatment rather than person-centered relief.
Trusting objective signs over the patient’s description of pain
Pain is subjective; the patient’s description is the basis of care.

items.q: A patient with chronic hip pain receives teaching about the effects of unmanaged pain. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “If my pain isn’t treated, it can affect my mood, my relationships, and even my finances.”
items.ex: Untreated pain may lead to serious physical, psychological, social, and financial consequences.
w: “Untreated pain only affects my body, so my emotions won’t be involved.”
Pain has emotional and cognitive components, and untreated pain has psychological effects.
“As long as I keep busy, untreated pain won’t affect my quality of life.”
Pain influences quality of life and interferes with relationships.
“Pain is just a warning signal, so it is safe to ignore it once I know the cause.”
Leaving pain untreated can lead to serious physical, psychological, social, and financial harm.

alt.q: Which outcome is a possible consequence of leaving pain untreated?
alt.a: Serious psychological, social, and financial problems
alt.ex: Untreated pain can lead to serious physical, psychological, social, and financial consequences.
w: Improved coping and stronger interpersonal relationships
Pain interferes with interpersonal relationships rather than strengthening them.
Increased energy and greater daily activity
Pain reduces energy and often causes fatigue.
Faster recovery because the body rests more
Unrelieved pain slows recovery and limits activity.

items.q: Which statement about how pain is handled in health care settings reflects the chapter?
items.a: Pain is often underrecognized, misunderstood, and inadequately treated
items.ex: Although pain often causes people to seek care, it is often underrecognized, misunderstood, and inadequately treated.
w: Pain is usually overtreated because it is easy to measure objectively
Pain is subjective and is more often undertreated than overtreated.
Pain is rarely a reason that people seek health care services
Pain often causes patients to seek health care.
Pain is seen mainly in hospital settings rather than in the community
Nurses encounter patients with pain in all health care settings.

alt.q: Why does the book describe pain as a public health problem that needs better coordination of care?
alt.a: Pain is common and is often inadequately treated
alt.ex: Pain affects everyone, is often inadequately treated, and is complicated by the opioid crisis, making it a public health concern.
w: Pain is rare but very costly when it occurs
Pain is experienced by everyone, not rare.
Pain is easy to treat once it is diagnosed
Pain is described as difficult to manage and understand.
Pain is mainly a concern for older adults
Pain affects people of all ages in all health care settings.

items.q: Pain has which components? Select all that apply.
o: Physical
Pain includes physical components such as the sensation itself.
Emotional
Pain is an emotional as well as a sensory experience.
Cognitive
Pain has cognitive components, such as how the person interprets it.
Solely reflexive
Pain is more than a reflex; it is a complex subjective experience.
Purely objective
Pain is subjective; nurses cannot see or feel it.
items.ex: Pain is more than a single physiological sensation; it has physical, emotional, and cognitive components.

alt.q: A nurse explains to a patient why pain can affect more than the body. Which aspects of a person does pain involve? Select all that apply.
o: How the person thinks about the pain
Pain has cognitive components.
How the person feels emotionally
Pain has emotional components.
The physical sensation of discomfort
Pain has physical components.
Only the reflex withdrawal from the stimulus
Reflex withdrawal is only a protective response, not the whole pain experience.
Only measurable changes in vital signs
Vital signs often stay at baseline; pain is mainly a subjective experience.
alt.ex: Pain involves physical, emotional, and cognitive components rather than a single sensation.

items.q: Which effects can pain have on a person? Select all that apply.
o: Fatigue
Pain reduces energy and often causes fatigue.
Strained interpersonal relationships
Pain interferes with interpersonal relationships.
Reduced quality of life
Pain influences a patient’s quality of life.
Financial consequences when untreated
Untreated pain can have serious financial consequences.
Increased energy for daily tasks
Pain reduces energy rather than increasing it.
items.ex: Pain reduces energy, interferes with relationships, and affects quality of life; untreated, it has physical, psychological, social, and financial consequences.

alt.q: A home care nurse visits a patient with poorly controlled pain. Which problems should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Tiredness and low energy
Pain reduces energy and often causes fatigue.
Withdrawal from family and friends
Pain interferes with interpersonal relationships.
Worry about money and work
Untreated pain can cause financial consequences.
Better sleep from physical exhaustion
Pain often disrupts sleep rather than improving it.
Improved mood from being at home
Untreated pain carries psychological consequences rather than improved mood.
alt.ex: Poorly controlled pain causes fatigue, strains relationships, and creates psychological, social, and financial problems.

items.q: Which outcomes result from effective pain management? Select all that apply.
o: Earlier mobilization
Relieved pain lets patients get moving sooner.
Decreased hospital length of stay
Effective pain management shortens hospital stays.
Fewer hospital and clinic visits
Patients with controlled pain need fewer visits.
Lower health care costs
Effective pain management reduces health care costs.
Reduced activity to protect healing tissue
Effective pain management improves activity levels rather than reducing them.
Longer recovery from surgery
Relieved pain speeds recovery and mobilization.
items.ex: Effective pain management leads to earlier mobilization, more activity, fewer visits, shorter stays, and lower costs.

alt.q: A nurse manager presents the benefits of improving pain control on a surgical unit. Which benefits can the manager expect? Select all that apply.
o: Patients walking sooner after surgery
Effective pain management results in earlier mobilization.
Improvement in patient activity levels
Relieved pain improves activity levels.
Shorter hospital stays
Effective pain management decreases length of stay.
More readmissions for pain
Effective pain management leads to fewer hospital and clinic visits.
Higher overall costs of care
Effective pain management lowers health care costs.
alt.ex: Good pain control improves mobilization and activity while reducing visits, length of stay, and costs.

items.q: A nurse cannot see or feel a patient’s pain, because pain is purely subjective.
items.a: True
items.ex: Pain is purely subjective; only the patient knows whether it is present and how it feels.
items.ww: Pain is not objective; nurses rely on the patient’s report rather than direct observation.

alt.q: If a person has had the same type of injury twice, the two painful events will produce identical responses.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: No two painful events create identical responses or feelings, even in the same person.
alt.ww: Each pain experience is unique, so identical responses cannot be assumed.

items.q: Pain is a single physiological sensation caused by a specific stimulus.
items.a: False
items.ex: Pain is more than a single sensation; it has physical, emotional, and cognitive components.
items.ww: Calling pain only a sensation ignores its emotional and cognitive components.

alt.q: In addition to its physical sensation, pain has emotional and cognitive components.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Pain is a protective physiological mechanism with physical, emotional, and cognitive components.
alt.ww: Pain is not purely physical; emotions and thinking shape the experience.

items.q: Pain exists whenever the person experiencing it says it exists.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book reminds nurses that pain is whatever the person says it is and exists whenever the person says it does.
items.ww: Nurses cannot confirm pain independently; the patient’s report is the authority.

alt.q: Pain should be treated only when the nurse can observe signs such as grimacing or a rise in heart rate.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Pain is subjective; a patient’s report is enough, and many people in pain show no obvious signs.
alt.ww: Requiring observable signs would leave many patients in pain untreated.

items.q: Which factor is essential for assessing a patient’s pain effectively and achieving adequate pain management?
items.a: Effective communication among the patient, family, and caregivers
items.ex: Effective communication among the patient, family, and professional caregivers is essential to assess pain and manage it adequately.
w: Reliance on vital sign changes to confirm the pain
Vital signs often return to baseline, so they cannot confirm pain.
A standard pain protocol applied the same way to all
Each person’s pain experience is unique, so care must be individualized.
Observation of the patient by the nurse without asking
Pain is subjective, so the nurse must communicate with the patient.

alt.q: A nurse caring for a patient with severe arthritis pain wants an accurate pain assessment. Which action best supports this goal?
alt.a: Talking with the patient and family about the pain experience
alt.ex: Effective communication among the patient, family, and professional caregivers is essential for effective pain assessment.
w: Comparing the pain with that of other patients with arthritis
No two people experience pain the same way, so comparison is misleading.
Waiting for the patient to show grimacing before asking
Many patients do not show obvious signs or report pain unless asked.
Relying on the health care provider’s estimate of severity
Only the patient knows how the pain feels; others cannot judge it alone.

items.q: Only the [[patient]] knows whether pain is present and how the experience feels.
items.ex: Pain is subjective and highly individualized, so the patient is the authority on the pain.

alt.q: Because pain is subjective, the [[patient]] is the only one who truly knows whether pain is present.
alt.ex: Pain is subjective and highly individualized, so the patient is the authority on the pain.

items.q: Pain is described as a highly individualized and [[subjective]] experience.
items.ex: Pain is subjective; no two people experience it in the same way.

alt.q: Because nurses cannot see or feel pain, it is called a [[subjective]] experience.
alt.ex: Pain is subjective; no two people experience it in the same way.

items.q: A patient steps on a nail and immediately feels a sharp, well-localized pain in the sole of the foot. Which nerve fibers transmit this first pain?
items.a: Myelinated A-delta fibers
items.ex: Fast myelinated A-delta fibers transmit sharp, localized first pain.
w: Unmyelinated C fibers
C fibers relay dull, achy, poorly localized second pain a few seconds later.
Efferent motor fibers
Efferent motor fibers carry impulses to muscles in the reflex arc, not pain sensation.
Large-diameter touch fibers
Large-diameter fibers inhibit pain transmission in gate-control theory.

alt.q: A few seconds after stepping on a nail, a patient reports that the whole foot aches. Which fibers transmit this second pain?
alt.a: Unmyelinated C fibers
alt.ex: Small unmyelinated C fibers relay dull, achy, poorly localized impulses, producing second pain.
w: Myelinated A-delta fibers
A-delta fibers transmit the initial sharp, localized first pain.
Efferent motor fibers
Motor fibers carry impulses away from the spinal cord to muscles.
Spinal motor neurons
Spinal motor neurons trigger reflex withdrawal; they do not transmit pain sensation.

items.q: What happens during pain transduction?
items.a: Energy from a noxious stimulus is converted into electrical impulses
items.ex: Transduction converts thermal, mechanical, or chemical stimulus energy into electrical impulses that begin in the periphery.
w: Impulses travel from the dorsal horn to the brain via spinothalamic tracts
Movement of impulses to the spinal cord and brain is pain transmission.
The cerebral cortex interprets the quality and meaning of the pain
Interpreting the pain is pain perception.
Endorphins and serotonin hinder impulses in the dorsal horn
Descending inhibitory mediators act during pain modulation.

alt.q: A nurse explains that a burn activates nociceptors that change heat energy into electrical impulses. Which process is the nurse describing?
alt.a: Pain transduction
alt.ex: Pain transduction converts the energy of thermal, mechanical, or chemical stimuli into electrical impulses.
w: Pain transmission
Transmission begins after transduction and carries the impulse to the spinal cord and brain.
Pain perception
Perception is the point at which the person becomes aware of the pain.
Pain modulation
Modulation involves descending mediators and sensitization that alter pain.

items.q: Which term describes a sensory peripheral nerve fiber that responds to pain-producing stimuli?
items.a: Nociceptor
items.ex: A nociceptor is a sensory peripheral pain nerve fiber that carries the impulse from a pain-producing stimulus.
w: Interneuron
Local interneurons are dorsal horn neurons, not the peripheral receptor fiber.
Motor neuron
Motor neurons carry impulses to muscles, as in the withdrawal reflex.
Mast cell
Mast cells produce histamine; they are not nerve fibers.

alt.q: A nociceptor that responds to thermal, mechanical, and chemical stimuli is classified as which type?
alt.a: Polymodal nociceptor
alt.ex: Some nociceptors respond to multiple types of stimuli and are called polymodal nociceptors.
w: Projection nociceptor
Projection neurons are dorsal horn neurons that ascend to the brain, not a nociceptor type.
Efferent nociceptor
Nociceptors carry sensory (afferent) impulses, not efferent ones.
Propriospinal nociceptor
Propriospinal neurons are dorsal horn neurons, not a class of nociceptor.

items.q: After a crush injury, inflammatory mediators lower the threshold needed to activate nociceptors. What is this process called?
items.a: Peripheral sensitization
items.ex: Mediators such as prostaglandins and bradykinin lower nociceptor activation thresholds, a process called peripheral sensitization.
w: Pain modulation by endorphins
Endorphins reduce pain transmission rather than lowering the activation threshold.
Protective reflex withdrawal
The reflex arc causes muscle withdrawal and does not change nociceptor thresholds.
Pain perception in the cortex
Perception is awareness of pain in the brain, not a change at peripheral nerve fibers.

alt.q: Which effect does peripheral sensitization have on nociceptors?
alt.a: It lowers the threshold needed to trigger an action potential
alt.ex: Peripheral sensitization lowers the threshold for activating nociceptors, so less stimulation produces pain impulses.
w: It raises the threshold needed to trigger an action potential
Sensitization makes nerves easier, not harder, to activate.
It blocks impulses from reaching the dorsal horn
Blocking impulses would reduce pain; sensitization increases pain input.
It converts nociceptors into motor fibers
Nociceptors remain sensory fibers; only their activation threshold changes.

items.q: A patient recovering from a burn reports severe pain when the bedsheet lightly touches the skin near the wound. Which term describes this finding?
items.a: Allodynia
items.ex: Allodynia is pain in response to normally non-noxious stimuli, such as light touch from a sheet, and reflects central sensitization.
w: Hyperalgesia
Hyperalgesia is an exaggerated response to a stimulus that is already noxious.
Referred pain
Referred pain is felt at a site distant from its source, such as a tumor.
Second pain
Second pain is the dull ache carried by C fibers after an injury.

alt.q: A patient with ongoing pain reports that a minor pinprick now feels excruciating. Which term describes this exaggerated response to a noxious stimulus?
alt.a: Hyperalgesia
alt.ex: Hyperalgesia is an exaggerated response to noxious stimuli and is a manifestation of central sensitization.
w: Allodynia
Allodynia is pain from a normally non-noxious stimulus, such as light touch.
Analgesia
Analgesia is the absence or relief of pain.
Nociception
Nociception is the normal nervous system process that allows detection of pain.

items.q: Where in the brain is the location and intensity of pain identified?
items.a: Somatosensory cortex
items.ex: The somatosensory cortex identifies where pain is and how intense it is.
w: Limbic system
The limbic system, part of the association cortex, determines how a person feels about pain.
Medullary reticular formation
This is one destination of ascending projection neurons, not the site that identifies location and intensity.
Dorsal root ganglion
The dorsal root ganglion is part of the peripheral pathway to the spinal cord, not the brain.

alt.q: Which brain structure primarily determines how a person feels emotionally about pain?
alt.a: Limbic system
alt.ex: The association cortex, primarily the limbic system, determines how a person feels about pain.
w: Somatosensory cortex
The somatosensory cortex identifies location and intensity of pain.
Pons
The pons receives ascending pain fibers but is not described as setting feelings about pain.
Spinal motor neurons
Spinal motor neurons drive the reflex withdrawal response.

items.q: A patient accidentally touches a hot iron and pulls the hand away before feeling burning pain. Which explanation is accurate?
items.a: A-delta fibers synapse with spinal motor neurons in a reflex arc that bypasses the brain
items.ex: In the protective reflex, A-delta impulses synapse with spinal motor neurons, and efferent fibers trigger withdrawal without going through the brain.
w: The somatosensory cortex signals the arm muscles once it identifies the burn
The reflex arc bypasses the brain, so the cortex does not initiate the withdrawal.
Endorphins released in the brainstem stimulate the arm to pull away
Endorphins produce analgesia; they do not trigger muscle withdrawal.
C fibers carry a dull ache to the thalamus, which triggers movement
C fibers carry second pain; the withdrawal reflex uses A-delta fibers and spinal motor neurons.

alt.q: Which nerve fibers carry the impulse from the spinal cord back to the muscle in the protective withdrawal reflex?
alt.a: Efferent motor nerve fibers
alt.ex: Motor impulses travel along efferent nerve fibers back to a muscle near the stimulus, causing withdrawal.
w: Afferent sensory nerve fibers
Afferent fibers carry sensory impulses toward the spinal cord, not to the muscle.
Unmyelinated C fibers
C fibers are afferent fibers that carry dull, achy pain.
Spinothalamic tract fibers
The spinothalamic tract carries pain impulses up to the brain.

items.q: A patient asks why the pain has spread beyond the original injury site after weeks of unrelieved pain. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: “Continuous pain signals can sensitize your spinal cord, which makes pain spread.”
items.ex: Continuous nociceptive input causes central sensitization, which can expand pain beyond its initial location.
w: “Your nerves have adapted and are sending fewer pain signals than before.”
Spreading pain reflects increased, not decreased, nociceptive input.
“Your body has stopped producing prostaglandins in the injured tissue.”
Prostaglandins increase pain sensitivity; their loss would not cause spreading pain.
“Your pain reflex is now traveling through the brain instead of the cord.”
The reflex arc is unrelated to the spread of pain caused by sensitization.

alt.q: Which clinical finding indicates central sensitization?
alt.a: Pain that expands beyond the location of the original injury
alt.ex: Central sensitization causes pain to expand beyond the initial location, hyperalgesia, and allodynia.
w: Sharp pain that is well localized to the injury site
Sharp, localized pain is normal first pain carried by A-delta fibers.
Pain that decreases when the injured area is rubbed
Pain relief from rubbing is explained by gate-control theory.
Rapid withdrawal of a limb from a painful stimulus
Withdrawal is the normal protective reflex.

items.q: Which statement about endogenous neuromodulators such as endorphins is accurate?
items.a: They are present at higher levels in people who have less pain from a similar injury
items.ex: Endorphins are natural morphine-like substances, and higher levels occur in people with less pain than others with similar injuries.
w: They are released only after a person takes opioid analgesics
These substances are produced naturally and are activated by stress and pain.
They increase pain transmission by binding to receptors in the skin
They cause analgesia by attaching to opiate receptors in the brain.
They are found only in the brain and nowhere else in the body
They are located in the brain, spinal cord, and gastrointestinal tract.

alt.q: What activates the body’s natural morphine-like neuromodulators?
alt.a: Stress and pain
alt.ex: Inhibitory neuromodulators are activated by stress and pain and cause analgesia at opiate receptors.
w: Inflammation and edema only
Edema results from substance P and histamine; neuromodulators respond to stress and pain.
Rest and sleep
The book lists stress and pain, not rest, as the activators.
Rubbing the injured area
Rubbing activates large-diameter fibers that close the pain gate.

items.q: Which action of substance P contributes to pain?
items.a: It is needed to transmit pain impulses from the periphery to higher brain centers
items.ex: Substance P is an excitatory peptide in dorsal horn neurons required to transmit pain impulses and causes vasodilation and edema.
w: It inhibits pain transmission in the dorsal horn
Inhibiting transmission describes serotonin and endorphins, not substance P.
It is released by mast cells to dilate capillaries
Mast cells release histamine.
It forms from the breakdown of cell membrane phospholipids
Prostaglandins form from phospholipid breakdown.

alt.q: A patient’s injured ankle becomes swollen. Which excitatory neurotransmitter causes vasodilation and edema while also transmitting pain impulses?
alt.a: Substance P
alt.ex: Substance P transmits pain impulses from the periphery to higher centers and causes vasodilation and edema.
w: Serotonin
Serotonin is released to inhibit pain transmission.
Endorphin
Endorphins are inhibitory and produce analgesia.
GABA
GABA is a descending inhibitory mediator that helps produce analgesia.

items.q: After nociceptive impulses reach the dorsal horn, which pathway carries them to the thalamus and higher brain centers?
items.a: Spinothalamic tracts
items.ex: A-delta impulses travel from the dorsal horn to deeper laminae and higher brain centers by way of the spinothalamic tracts.
w: Efferent motor nerves
Efferent motor nerves carry reflex impulses back to muscles, not up to the brain.
Dorsal root ganglia
Dorsal root ganglia are on the peripheral path into the spinal cord, before the dorsal horn.
Peripheral afferent fibers
Peripheral afferent fibers carry impulses from the periphery to the spinal cord, not up to the brain.

alt.q: Many dorsal horn projection neurons have axons that cross the midline and ascend. Which areas do they reach?
alt.a: The thalamus, cerebral cortex, pons, and medullary reticular formation
alt.ex: Projection neurons cross the midline and ascend to the thalamus, cortical gray matter, pons, and parts of the medullary reticular formation.
w: The peripheral muscles near the site of the stimulus
Impulses to peripheral muscles travel along efferent fibers in the reflex arc.
The mast cells and blood vessels at the injury site
Mast cells and vessels are peripheral sources of inflammatory mediators.
The dorsal root ganglia on the opposite side of the cord
Dorsal root ganglia lie on the incoming peripheral pathway, not the ascending destination.

items.q: Which substances act as endogenous descending inhibitory mediators during pain modulation? Select all that apply.
o: Endorphins
Endorphins are endogenous opioids that help produce analgesia.
Serotonin
Serotonin is released to inhibit pain transmission.
Gamma-aminobutyric acid
GABA is a descending inhibitory mediator that hinders nociceptive impulses.
Bradykinin
Bradykinin increases pain stimuli by binding to receptors on peripheral nerves.
Substance P
Substance P is excitatory and transmits pain impulses.
Histamine
Histamine is a pronociceptive mediator released by mast cells.
items.ex: During modulation, projection neurons activate endorphins, serotonin, and GABA to hinder nociceptive impulses in the dorsal horn.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching about substances that reduce pain transmission in the dorsal horn. Which substances should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Endogenous opioids
Endorphins are endogenous opioids that produce analgesia.
Serotonin
Serotonin inhibits pain transmission.
GABA
GABA helps produce analgesia as a descending inhibitory mediator.
Prostaglandins
Prostaglandins increase sensitivity to pain.
Bradykinin
Bradykinin increases pain stimuli.
alt.ex: Endorphins, serotonin, and GABA are inhibitory mediators that reduce transmission of pain impulses.

items.q: Which mediators released during inflammation lower the threshold for activating nociceptors? Select all that apply.
o: Prostaglandins
Prostaglandins are pronociceptive and increase sensitivity to pain.
Bradykinin
Bradykinin binds to peripheral nerve receptors and increases pain stimuli.
Substance P
Substance P is a pronociceptive mediator released in inflammation.
Histamine
Histamine is listed among vasoactive, pronociceptive mediators.
Endorphins
Endorphins are inhibitory and produce analgesia.
GABA
GABA is a descending inhibitory mediator.
items.ex: Inflammation releases prostaglandins, bradykinin, substance P, and histamine, which cause peripheral sensitization.

alt.q: Which substances contribute to peripheral sensitization after tissue injury? Select all that apply.
o: Histamine from mast cells
Histamine is a vasoactive mediator released in inflammation.
Bradykinin from leaking plasma
Bradykinin increases pain stimuli at peripheral nerves.
Prostaglandins from cell membranes
Prostaglandins increase sensitivity to pain.
Serotonin from the brainstem
Serotonin inhibits pain transmission.
Endorphins from the brain
Endorphins are natural analgesics.
alt.ex: Pronociceptive mediators such as histamine, bradykinin, and prostaglandins lower nociceptor thresholds.

items.q: Which factors commonly disrupt the pain process? Select all that apply.
o: Trauma
Trauma is a common factor that disrupts the pain process.
Drugs
Drugs can disrupt the pain process.
Tumor growth
Tumor growth can disrupt the pain process.
Metabolic disorders
Metabolic disorders disrupt the pain process.
Rubbing the skin
Rubbing modifies pain through the gate mechanism; it is not listed as a disrupting factor.
items.ex: Pain perception requires consciousness and an intact CNS; trauma, drugs, tumor growth, and metabolic disorders commonly disrupt it.

alt.q: A patient’s ability to perceive pain may be impaired. Which conditions could account for this? Select all that apply.
o: Loss of consciousness
Pain perception requires consciousness.
Spinal cord trauma
Trauma can disrupt the intact CNS needed for perception.
A metabolic disorder
Metabolic disorders commonly disrupt the pain process.
Light physical activity
Activity does not disrupt the nervous system pathway for pain.
Mild anxiety
Anxiety is not listed as disrupting the pain process.
alt.ex: Perception requires consciousness and an intact CNS; trauma and metabolic disorders can disrupt the pain process.

items.q: A patient experiencing pain can tell which physiological process of nociception is occurring.
items.a: False
items.ex: A patient in pain cannot discriminate among transduction, transmission, perception, and modulation.
items.ww: The processes occur without the person being able to separate them.

alt.q: Understanding the processes of nociception helps a nurse recognize the rationale for selected pain therapies.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Knowing each process helps the nurse recognize causes, accompanying symptoms, and the rationale for therapies.
alt.ww: Even though patients cannot tell the processes apart, nurses use this knowledge to plan care.

items.q: The brain has a single pain center that both locates pain and determines how a person feels about it.
items.a: False
items.ex: The somatosensory cortex and the limbic system play different roles, and there is no single pain center.
items.ww: Pain perception involves several brain areas, not one center.

alt.q: There is no single pain center in the brain.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Different cortical areas locate pain and assign its emotional meaning, so there is no single center.
alt.ww: Pain is processed in multiple brain areas, including the somatosensory cortex and limbic system.

items.q: Pain perception requires consciousness and an intact central nervous system.
items.a: True
items.ex: A person must be conscious with an intact CNS to become aware of nociceptive impulses.
items.ww: Without consciousness or an intact CNS, impulses cannot be perceived as pain.

alt.q: The protective withdrawal reflex requires the brain to perceive pain before the muscle contracts.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The reflex arc travels from A-delta fibers to spinal motor neurons and back to the muscle, bypassing the brain.
alt.ww: Withdrawal happens at the spinal level before conscious awareness.

items.q: The observable nervous system activity that allows people to detect pain is called [[nociception]].
items.ex: Pain is subjective, but nociception is the observable activity in the nervous system that allows detection of pain.

alt.q: Transduction, transmission, perception, and modulation are the four processes of [[nociception]].
alt.ex: Pain is subjective, but nociception is the observable activity in the nervous system that allows detection of pain.

items.q: According to gate-control theory, why does rubbing an injured area reduce pain?
items.a: It stimulates large-diameter fibers that close the gate to pain transmission
items.ex: Rubbing promotes large-diameter fiber input, which inhibits transmission of pain signals from small-diameter fibers to the brain.
w: It stimulates small-diameter fibers that open the gate to pain transmission
Small-diameter fibers open the gate, increasing rather than reducing pain.
It releases histamine that numbs nerve endings near the injury
Histamine dilates capillaries and promotes pain; it does not numb nerves.
It triggers a reflex arc that moves the limb away from the injury
The reflex arc causes withdrawal and does not explain relief from rubbing.

alt.q: A child bumps an elbow and rubs it. The parent asks why rubbing helps. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Rubbing sends touch signals that help block pain signals to the brain.”
alt.ex: Rubbing activates large-diameter fibers that close the gate and inhibit pain signals from small fibers.
w: “Rubbing pushes the pain chemicals away from the elbow.”
Gate-control theory explains relief through nerve fibers, not moving chemicals.
“Rubbing opens the nerve gate so the pain passes quickly.”
Opening the gate increases pain transmission; rubbing closes it.
“Rubbing causes the brain to release a numbing hormone.”
The theory attributes relief to large-diameter fiber input at the gate.

items.q: In gate-control theory, which fibers open the gate to pain transmission?
items.a: Small-diameter fibers activated by noxious stimuli
items.ex: Small-diameter fibers activated by noxious stimuli open the gate, while large-diameter fibers inhibit and close it.
w: Large-diameter proprioceptive fibers
Large-diameter fibers have inhibitory effects that shut the gate.
Efferent motor fibers
Motor fibers carry reflex impulses to muscles and are not part of the gate mechanism.
Descending inhibitory fibers
Descending inhibitory pathways reduce pain transmission.

alt.q: In gate-control theory, what effect do large-diameter fibers have?
alt.a: They inhibit pain transmission and shut the gate
alt.ex: Large-diameter fibers have inhibitory effects that shut the gate to pain signals from small fibers.
w: They open the gate to pain transmission
Small-diameter fibers activated by noxious stimuli open the gate.
They carry sharp first pain to the brain
Sharp first pain is carried by A-delta fibers in the nociception pathway.
They trigger protective withdrawal reflexes
The reflex arc involves A-delta fibers and spinal motor neurons.

items.q: What was significant about the gate-control theory when it was first proposed?
items.a: It first suggested that pain has emotional and cognitive components
items.ex: The gate-control theory was the first to suggest pain has emotional and cognitive components in addition to physical sensation.
w: It first identified the four processes of nociception
Nociception’s four processes are a separate physiological description.
It first proved that pain is purely a physical sensation
The theory moved away from pain as purely physical.
It first described a genetically determined neural matrix
A genetically determined neural matrix is the later neuromatrix theory.

alt.q: A nurse considers a patient’s fear and beliefs when planning pain care. Which theory first supported viewing pain this way?
alt.a: Gate-control theory
alt.ex: Gate-control theory was the first to suggest that pain has emotional and cognitive components, not just physical ones.
w: Neuromatrix theory
Neuromatrix theory came later and centers on a genetically determined neural matrix.
General adaptation syndrome
The general adaptation syndrome describes the stress response, not pain components.
Peripheral sensitization
Peripheral sensitization is a physiological process, not a theory of pain components.

items.q: Which statement describes the neuromatrix theory of pain?
items.a: A genetically determined neural matrix, shaped by sensory input, makes each person’s pain unique
items.ex: The neuromatrix theory holds that a genetically determined neural matrix develops and is modulated by sensory input, so pain perception is unique.
w: Large fibers close a spinal gate that small fibers open, which controls pain signals
Opening and closing a gate describes gate-control theory.
Pain is a single sensation that follows a specific stimulus in the same way for all
The neuromatrix theory emphasizes that each person’s perception is unique.
Pain results only from activation of the sympathetic branch of the nervous system
Sympathetic stimulation is a physiological response, not the neuromatrix theory.

alt.q: A patient asks why a friend with the same injury reports far less pain. Which theory best explains individual differences in pain perception?
alt.a: Neuromatrix theory
alt.ex: Neuromatrix theory proposes a genetically determined, sensory-modulated neural matrix that makes pain perception unique to each person.
w: Gate-control theory
Gate-control theory mainly explains how large-fiber input such as rubbing reduces pain.
Reflex arc theory
The reflex arc explains withdrawal from a painful stimulus, not individual perception.
Specificity theory
Pain is not a single sensation produced uniformly by a specific stimulus.

items.q: What is the purpose of Dilation of bronchial tubes during a sympathetic response to pain?

That goes with Increased heart rate.
Provides additional energy

Controls body temperature during stress
That goes with Diaphoresis.

w: Provides increased oxygen intake

alt.a: Dilation of bronchial tubes

w: Increased heart rate
Increased heart rate: Provides increased oxygen transport.
Increased blood glucose level
Increased blood glucose level: Provides additional energy.
Diaphoresis

w: Dilation of bronchial tubes
Dilation of bronchial tubes: Provides increased oxygen intake.
Increased blood glucose level
Increased blood glucose level: Provides additional energy.
Diaphoresis
Diaphoresis: Controls body temperature during stress.

alt.a: Increased blood glucose level
alt.ex: Table 44.1 links each sympathetic response to low-to-moderate or superficial pain with its protective purpose.
w: Dilation of bronchial tubes
Dilation of bronchial tubes: Provides increased oxygen intake.
Increased heart rate
Increased heart rate: Provides increased oxygen transport.
Diaphoresis
Diaphoresis: Controls body temperature during stress.

alt.q: Which sympathetic response to pain “Controls body temperature during stress”?
alt.a: Diaphoresis

w: Dilation of bronchial tubes
Dilation of bronchial tubes: Provides increased oxygen intake.
Increased heart rate
Increased heart rate: Provides increased oxygen transport.

Increased blood glucose level: Provides additional energy.

alt.q: Which sympathetic response to pain “Affords better vision”?
alt.a: Dilation of pupils

Dilation of bronchial tubes: Provides increased oxygen intake.
Increased heart rate
Increased heart rate: Provides increased oxygen transport.
Increased blood glucose level
