alt.a: Decreased gastrointestinal motility
alt.ex: Table 44.1 links each sympathetic response to low-to-moderate or superficial pain with its protective purpose.
w: Dilation of bronchial tubes
Dilation of bronchial tubes: Provides increased oxygen intake.
Increased heart rate
Increased heart rate: Provides increased oxygen transport.
Increased blood glucose level
Increased blood glucose level: Provides additional energy.

mt.q: Match each sympathetic response to pain with its cause or effect.
pairs: Frees energy for more immediate activity
mt.ex: Table 44.1 links each sympathetic response to low-to-moderate or superficial pain with its protective purpose.

items.q: A patient is admitted with severe, continuous pain from a renal stone. Which finding should the nurse expect from the body’s response to this type of pain?
items.a: Decreased heart rate and blood pressure with nausea
items.ex: Severe, deep visceral pain such as renal colic activates the parasympathetic system, causing nausea, vomiting, and decreased heart rate and blood pressure.
w: Increased heart rate with dilated pupils
These are sympathetic responses to low-to-moderate or superficial pain.
Increased muscle tension with dilated bronchi
These sympathetic responses prepare for action in less severe, superficial pain.
Increased blood glucose with diaphoresis
These are sympathetic responses, not the parasympathetic response to deep visceral pain.

alt.q: Which type of pain is most likely to stimulate the sympathetic branch of the autonomic nervous system?
alt.a: Superficial pain of low-to-moderate intensity
alt.ex: Low-to-moderate and superficial pain elicit the fight-or-flight reaction through sympathetic stimulation.
w: Continuous, severe visceral pain
Severe, deep visceral pain activates the parasympathetic system.
Deep pain from a myocardial infarction
Deep pain from conditions such as myocardial infarction activates the parasympathetic system.
Colic from a gallbladder stone
Gallbladder colic is deep visceral pain that activates the parasympathetic system.

items.q: On postoperative day 3, a patient rates incision pain as 7 on a 0-to-10 scale. Vital signs are at the patient’s baseline. Which interpretation by the nurse is correct?
items.a: Most people adapt to pain, so baseline vital signs do not rule out significant pain
items.ex: Except with severe traumatic pain, most people adapt to pain reflexively and their vital signs return to baseline.
w: Baseline vital signs show the rating is inaccurate and should be repeated
Vital signs often normalize as people adapt, so they cannot disprove a pain report.
Baseline vital signs show the pain has resolved and analgesia can stop
The patient reports 7/10 pain, which still needs treatment.
Baseline vital signs show the patient is in early shock from the pain
Shock occurs with severe traumatic pain and does not present as stable baseline vital signs.

alt.q: Which statement about vital signs in patients with pain is accurate?
alt.a: Patients in pain do not always have changes in their vital signs
alt.ex: Most people adapt to pain and their physical signs return to baseline, so vital signs are not a reliable pain indicator.
w: Patients in pain always have an increased heart rate
Adaptation means heart rate often returns to baseline.
Patients in pain always have a decreased blood pressure
Blood pressure may rise, fall, or stay at baseline depending on pain type and adaptation.
Patients in pain always have rapid, irregular breathing
Rapid, irregular breathing occurs with prolonged severe pain, not in every patient.

items.q: Which effect of a short-term increase in cortisol occurs as part of the sympathetic response to pain?
items.a: Heightened memory, a burst of immunity, and lower pain sensitivity
items.ex: Table 44.1 lists heightened memory functions, a burst of increased immunity, and lower sensitivity to pain as short-term cortisol effects.
w: Decreased memory, lower immunity, and higher pain sensitivity
The short-term effects are the opposite: heightened memory, more immunity, and less pain sensitivity.
Slowed heart rate, low blood pressure, and nausea
These are parasympathetic responses to severe or deep pain.
Increased gastrointestinal motility, hunger, and fatigue
Sympathetic stimulation decreases gastrointestinal motility.

alt.q: Which sympathetic response to pain lowers sensitivity to pain for a short time?
alt.a: Increased cortisol level
alt.ex: A short-term rise in cortisol heightens memory, boosts immunity, and lowers sensitivity to pain.
w: Increased blood glucose level
Increased blood glucose provides additional energy.
Peripheral vasoconstriction
Vasoconstriction elevates blood pressure and shifts blood to muscles and brain.
Dilation of pupils
Pupil dilation affords better vision.

items.q: A patient with severe abdominal pain begins vomiting. Which explanation for this parasympathetic response is accurate?
items.a: The vagus nerve sends impulses to the chemoreceptor trigger zone in the brain
items.ex: Severe or deep pain stimulates the parasympathetic system; vagal impulses to the chemoreceptor trigger zone cause nausea and vomiting.
w: Increased gastrointestinal motility forces stomach contents upward
The book attributes vomiting to vagal impulses, not to increased motility.
Increased cortisol irritates the lining of the stomach
Short-term cortisol effects listed are memory, immunity, and lower pain sensitivity.
Dilated bronchial tubes trigger a reflex that causes retching
Bronchial dilation is a sympathetic response that increases oxygen intake.

alt.q: Which finding results from vagal stimulation in a patient with severe, deep pain?
alt.a: Decreased heart rate and blood pressure
alt.ex: Parasympathetic responses to severe or deep pain include decreased heart rate and blood pressure from vagal stimulation.
w: Increased heart rate and respiratory rate
Increased heart and respiratory rates are sympathetic responses that improve oxygen intake and transport.
Dilated pupils and diaphoresis
Pupil dilation and sweating are sympathetic responses to low-to-moderate pain.
Increased muscle tension and blood glucose
These sympathetic responses prepare muscles for action and provide energy.

items.q: A patient on a surgical unit cries out loudly with each position change. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Accept the patient’s way of expressing pain and assess the need for relief
items.ex: Nurses should be open to how patients express pain and not ignore a person’s need to cry out or be verbally expressive.
w: Ask the patient to stay quiet so other patients are not disturbed
Discouraging expression ignores the patient’s individual response to pain.
Document that the patient appears to have a low tolerance and is complaining
Patients with low tolerance are often inaccurately labeled as complainers.
Delay repositioning until the patient can stop crying out
Delaying care does not address the pain the patient is expressing.

alt.q: Which nursing approach best supports assessment of a patient’s unique response to pain?
alt.a: Remaining open to how the patient chooses to express pain
alt.ex: Assessing therapy success requires recognizing each patient’s unique response, including verbal expression.
w: Expecting all patients to show grimacing when in pain
Behavioral responses vary with culture, beliefs, and experience.
Relying mainly on changes in vital signs
Vital signs often return to baseline as patients adapt.
Discouraging loud or emotional expressions of pain
Nurses should not ignore a patient’s need to cry out or be expressive.

items.q: A patient after hip surgery says, “I don’t want to bother the nurses by asking for pain medicine.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Please tell us when pain starts so we can control it and help you stay active.”
items.ex: Teach patients to report pain when it occurs to allow better control and optimal function.
w: “That’s thoughtful; try to wait until the pain becomes severe.”
Waiting until pain is severe makes control harder and limits function.
“We will check on you at the end of the shift for pain.”
Delaying assessment leaves the patient enduring pain without relief.
“Most patients find that pain goes away if they ignore it.”
Ignoring pain can lead to unrelieved pain and reduced activity.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient shows understanding of teaching about reporting pain?
alt.a: “I should let the nurse know as soon as my pain begins.”
alt.ex: Reporting pain when it occurs facilitates better control and optimal functional status.
w: “I should wait until the pain is unbearable before calling.”
Waiting allows pain to worsen and reduces control.
“Asking for pain relief shows I have lost self-control.”
Some patients avoid reporting for this reason, which leads to unrelieved pain.
“I should not mention pain because it inconveniences the staff.”
Fear of inconveniencing others is a barrier to reporting, not a correct belief.

items.q: Which term describes pain that significantly alters quality of life and restricts the ability to perform daily activities or work?
items.a: High-impact chronic pain
items.ex: Untreated or unrelieved pain that greatly alters quality of life and restricts daily activities or work is called high-impact chronic pain.
w: Breakthrough pain
Breakthrough pain is a separate key term related to cancer pain, not this functional definition.
Referred pain
Referred pain is felt at a site distant from its source.
First pain
First pain is the sharp, localized pain carried by A-delta fibers.

alt.q: A patient with unrelieved back pain can no longer work or complete daily activities. Which term describes this phenomenon?
alt.a: High-impact chronic pain
alt.ex: When unrelieved pain restricts work and daily activities and alters quality of life, it is called high-impact chronic pain.
w: Second pain
Second pain is the dull ache transmitted by C fibers after injury.
Allodynia
Allodynia is pain from a normally non-noxious stimulus.
Acute pain
Acute pain is short-term and self-limiting rather than a long-term restriction of function.

items.q: A patient with advanced dementia cannot describe pain. Which nursing action is most appropriate for identifying pain in this patient?
items.a: Observe for behaviors such as grimacing, guarding, and changes in activity
items.ex: Nurses often recognize behavioral patterns that reflect pain even when patients cannot report it verbally, such as those with dementia.
w: Assume pain is absent unless the patient asks for medicine
Patients with cognitive changes may be unable to ask, so absence of requests does not mean absence of pain.
Rely on an increase in heart rate to confirm the pain
Vital signs often return to baseline, so they cannot confirm pain.
Wait until the family visits to ask whether the patient hurts
Delaying assessment leaves pain unrecognized; the nurse observes behavior now.

alt.q: Which statement about recognizing pain in patients with cognitive changes is accurate?
alt.a: Nurses can recognize behavioral patterns that reflect pain without a verbal report
alt.ex: Nurses often recognize behavioral patterns reflecting pain even when patients cannot report it verbally.
w: Patients with dementia do not perceive pain, so assessment is unnecessary
Cognitive changes affect reporting, not the presence of pain.
Pain can only be identified when the patient gives a verbal rating
Behavioral cues help identify pain when verbal reports are not possible.
Changes in vital signs are the only reliable indicator of pain
Many people in pain have vital signs at baseline.

alt.q: Which findings are sympathetic responses to pain? Select all that apply.

items.q: Except with severe traumatic pain that causes shock, most people adapt to pain and their physical signs return to baseline.

items.q: Continuous, severe, or deep pain involving visceral organs typically activates the parasympathetic nervous system.

items.q: Patients who have a low pain tolerance are sometimes inaccurately perceived as complainers.

Anorexia and weight loss are associated with chronic pain.
Hopelessness
Hopelessness is associated with chronic pain.
Weight gain from increased appetite
Chronic pain is associated with anorexia and weight loss.
Increased energy
Chronic pain causes physical and mental exhaustion.
items.ex: Symptoms of chronic pain include fatigue, insomnia, anorexia, weight loss, apathy, hopelessness, depression, and anger.

alt.q: A nurse assesses a patient who has had chronic arthritis pain for years. Which findings should the nurse anticipate? Select all that apply.
o: Apathy
Apathy is a symptom associated with chronic pain.
Anger
Anger is associated with chronic pain.
Depression
Depression is associated with chronic pain.
Obvious grimacing at all times
A person with chronic pain often does not show obvious symptoms.
Complete adaptation to the pain
A person with chronic noncancer pain often does not adapt to the pain.
alt.ex: Chronic pain is associated with apathy, anger, and depression, often without obvious outward signs.

items.q: Which factors contribute to undertreatment of cancer pain? Select all that apply.
o: Inadequate education of health care providers
Inadequate provider education leads to undertreatment.
Fear of addiction
Fear of addiction contributes to undertreatment.
Delay in referral to hospice
Delayed hospice referral leads to undertreatment.
Short staffing and time constraints
Agency barriers such as short staffing contribute to undertreatment.
Most cancer pain cannot be relieved
About 90% of patients with cancer pain manage it with simple interventions.
items.ex: Provider education gaps, fear of addiction, cultural and religious beliefs, hospice delays, and agency barriers cause undertreatment of cancer pain.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing barriers to relieving pain in patients with cancer. Which barriers should the nurse identify? Select all that apply.
o: Cultural and religious beliefs
Cultural and religious beliefs can lead to undertreatment.
Lack of communication within the agency
Agency barriers such as poor communication contribute.
Fear of addiction
Fear of addiction contributes to undertreatment.
Too many effective treatment options
Undertreatment stems from barriers, not an excess of options.
Most patients with cancer have no pain
Not all patients have pain, but this is not a barrier to treating those who do.
alt.ex: Cultural and religious beliefs, agency communication problems, and fear of addiction contribute to undertreatment of cancer pain.

items.q: Which consequences can result from chronic pain? Select all that apply.
o: Job loss
Chronic pain is a major cause of disability leading to job loss.
Social isolation
Chronic pain can lead to social isolation.
Sexual dysfunction
Sexual dysfunction is a consequence of chronic pain.
Inability to perform simple daily activities
Chronic pain can prevent simple daily activities.
Faster healing of the original injury
Chronic pain often continues after healing and does not speed it.
items.ex: Chronic pain is a major cause of psychological and physical disability, leading to job loss, isolation, and sexual dysfunction.

alt.q: A nurse plans care for a patient disabled by chronic pain. Which problems should the nurse address? Select all that apply.
o: Loss of employment
Chronic pain commonly leads to job loss.
Withdrawal from social contacts
Social isolation is a consequence of chronic pain.
Difficulty with daily activities
Chronic pain limits simple daily activities.
Excess energy at night
Chronic pain is associated with exhaustion and fatigue.
Rapid adaptation to pain
Persons with chronic noncancer pain often do not adapt to the pain.
alt.ex: Chronic pain leads to job loss, social isolation, and inability to perform daily activities.

items.q: If acute pain is not adequately controlled, it can progress to chronic pain.
items.a: True
items.ex: Unrelieved acute pain can progress to chronic pain, so adequate control is important.
items.ww: Uncontrolled acute pain does not always resolve harmlessly; it may become chronic.

alt.q: Acute pain that is not treated always resolves without lasting effects once the tissue heals.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Unrelieved acute pain slows recovery, causes complications, and can progress to chronic pain.
alt.ww: Acute pain usually resolves with healing, but poorly controlled pain can have lasting effects.

items.q: All patients with cancer experience pain.
items.a: False
items.ex: Not all patients with cancer have pain, and 90% of those who do can manage it with simple interventions.
items.ww: Pain is common but not universal in cancer.

alt.q: Most patients with cancer who have pain can manage it with simple interventions.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: About 90% of patients with cancer pain manage their pain with simple interventions.
alt.ww: Cancer pain is often manageable, though undertreatment still occurs.

items.q: A patient with chronic pain who consults many health care providers is usually a drug seeker.
items.a: False
items.ex: Such a patient is sometimes labeled a drug seeker when actually seeking adequate pain relief.
items.ww: The label is often inaccurate; the patient is commonly seeking relief, and referral to a specialist helps.

alt.q: A patient with chronic pain who visits numerous providers is often seeking adequate pain relief.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Patients with chronic pain who see many providers are often seeking relief but may be mislabeled as drug seekers.
alt.ww: Assuming drug-seeking behavior ignores unrelieved pain; referral to a specialist is the appropriate response.

items.q: Pain felt at a site distant from a tumor is called [[referred]] pain.
items.ex: A patient with cancer may sense pain at the tumor site or distant from it, which is referred pain.

alt.q: When a patient senses pain away from the actual site of a tumor, the nurse documents it as [[referred]] pain.
alt.ex: A patient with cancer may sense pain at the tumor site or distant from it, which is referred pain.

items.q: Which factor was among the most frequently reported barriers to effective pain assessment and management?
items.a: Nurses’ lack of knowledge of pain assessment tools
items.ex: Lack of knowledge of assessment tools was one of the most reported barriers, along with communication problems and missing protocols.
w: Verbal reporting of patients’ pain scores during report
Verbal reporting of pain scores during report is a facilitator, not a barrier.
Attention to a patient’s ability to self-report pain
Attention to the patient’s ability to self-report facilitates successful pain management.
More effective collaboration between health care providers
Better collaboration between providers facilitates, rather than blocks, pain management.

alt.q: Which factor was found to facilitate successful pain assessment and management?
alt.a: Verbal reporting of patients’ pain scores during report
alt.ex: Sharing pain scores verbally during report, along with education and collaboration, facilitated successful pain management.
w: Prescriptions that are not guided by pain scores
Prescriptions not guided by pain scores were one of the most reported barriers.
Absence of standard pain-control protocols
Missing guidelines and protocols for pain control were a commonly reported barrier.
Communication barriers between nurses and patients
Communication barriers with patients were among the most reported barriers.

items.q: Which barriers to pain assessment and management were among the most commonly reported? Select all that apply.
o: Nurses’ lack of knowledge of pain assessment tools
Knowledge gaps about assessment tools were a leading barrier.
Communication barriers with patients
Difficulty communicating with patients was a leading barrier.
Prescriptions not guided by pain scores
Orders that ignore pain scores were a leading barrier.
Absence of standard guidelines and protocols for pain control
Missing guidelines and protocols were a leading barrier.
Education and training in pain management
Education and training facilitated pain assessment and management.
Attention to the patient’s ability to self-report pain
Attention to self-report ability was a facilitator, not a barrier.
items.ex: Lack of tool knowledge, communication barriers, prescriptions not tied to pain scores, and absent protocols were the most reported barriers.

alt.q: A unit is planning ways to improve pain management. Which strategies were shown to facilitate successful pain assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Providing more education and training on pain assessment
Education and training facilitated pain assessment and management.
Improving collaboration between health care providers
More effective collaboration among providers was a facilitator.
Reporting patients’ pain scores verbally during report
Verbal reporting of pain scores during report was a facilitator.
Writing analgesic prescriptions without reference to pain scores
Prescriptions not guided by pain scores were a major barrier.
Leaving pain evaluation out of unit protocols
The absence of protocols addressing pain control and evaluation was a major barrier.
alt.ex: Education, collaboration, verbal reporting of pain scores, and attention to self-report ability facilitated successful pain management.

items.q: A patient with chronic low back pain rates pain at 8 on a 0-to-10 scale while calmly watching television. A colleague says, “He can’t hurt that much; nothing shows up on his imaging.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “His report is what counts, so I will treat his pain based on his rating.”
items.ex: Nurses must accept patients’ reports of pain; requiring objective signs reflects a bias that limits pain relief.
w: “You’re right. I’ll wait until he shows signs of distress before treating.”
Waiting for objective signs reflects the misconception that pain exists only when it is visible.
“Let’s ask the provider for a placebo to see whether he is really in pain.”
Deceptive placebo use is discouraged and damages trust between patients and caregivers.
“I’ll recheck his vital signs before I decide whether he has pain.”
Vital signs do not confirm or rule out pain; the patient’s self-report is the most reliable indicator.

alt.q: A nurse notices that she privately thinks of a patient with neuropathic pain as a “complainer.” Which action best reflects her professional responsibility?
alt.a: Accept the patient’s report and follow evidence-based pain guidelines
alt.ex: Despite personal beliefs, nurses must accept reports of pain, follow professional standards, and provide evidence-based care.
w: Withhold analgesics until an objective cause for the pain is found
Requiring an obvious source of pain stereotypes the patient and limits relief.
Describe the patient as difficult during hand-off report
Labeling patients as difficult spreads bias and worsens access to treatment.
Offer pain relief only when the patient grimaces or cries
Believing pain only when patients appear to hurt is a misconception that limits relief.

items.q: Administering analgesics on a regular schedule leads to drug addiction.
items.a: False
items.ex: This is listed as a common misconception; regular analgesic dosing does not in itself lead to addiction.
items.ww: Fear of causing addiction is a bias that leads nurses to avoid acknowledging pain and undertreat it.

alt.q: Fear of contributing to medication addiction leads some nurses to avoid acknowledging patients’ pain.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Some nurses avoid acknowledging pain because they fear contributing to addiction, which limits pain relief.
alt.ww: The text identifies this fear as a real influence on nurses that limits pain relief.

items.q: The amount of tissue damage in an injury accurately indicates how intense the patient’s pain is.
items.a: False
items.ex: This is a common misconception; pain is subjective, and tissue damage does not reliably predict pain intensity.
items.ww: Pain is unique to each person, so the extent of injury cannot be used to judge pain intensity.

alt.q: The extent of tissue damage is not a reliable gauge of a patient’s pain intensity.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Believing tissue damage accurately indicates pain intensity is a misconception; the patient’s report is what counts.
alt.ww: Pain is a subjective experience, so visible injury cannot measure how much a patient hurts.

items.q: Health care personnel are the best authorities on the nature of a patient’s pain.
items.a: False
items.ex: This is a common misconception; the patient’s self-report is the single most reliable indicator of pain.
items.ww: Patients know the most about their own pain, so clinicians are not the best authority on it.

alt.q: The patient, rather than the health care provider, is the best authority on the patient’s pain.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Patients know the most about their pain, and self-report is the most reliable indicator of its existence and intensity.
alt.ww: Treating clinicians as the authority on a patient’s pain is a recognized misconception.

items.q: Which beliefs about pain are misconceptions? Select all that apply.
o: Psychogenic pain is not real.
This is a false belief; psychogenic pain is real pain.
Chronic pain is psychological.
This is a false belief; chronic pain is not simply psychological.
Patients with minor illnesses have less pain than those with severe physical alteration.
This is a false belief; severity of illness does not predict pain.
Patients who cannot speak do not feel pain.
This is a false belief; nonverbal patients feel pain and need behavioral assessment.
A patient’s self-report is the most reliable indicator of pain.
This is accurate; self-report is the single most reliable indicator of pain.
Bias can cause nurses to underestimate a patient’s pain.
This is accurate; bias is a recognized source of error in pain assessment.
items.ex: Box 44.2 lists false beliefs, including that psychogenic pain is not real and that nonverbal patients do not feel pain.

alt.q: A nurse educator reviews biases about pain. Which statements should the educator identify as false? Select all that apply.
o: Patients who abuse substances overreact to discomfort.
This is a listed misconception about patients who use drugs or alcohol.
Administering analgesics regularly leads to drug addiction.
This is a listed misconception that leads to undertreatment.
Health care personnel are the best authorities on a patient’s pain.
This is a listed misconception; the patient is the authority.
Nurses should accept a patient’s report of pain.
This is a professional obligation, not a misconception.
Patient expectations influence pain-management outcomes.
This is accurate and essential to person-centered care.
alt.ex: Beliefs that substance users overreact, regular analgesics cause addiction, and clinicians know best are all false per Box 44.2.

items.q: Nurses’ mistrust of patients’ pain reports and fear of addiction are associated with which patient outcome?
items.a: Increased recovery time
items.ex: These beliefs and fears lead to mistrust, longer recovery, complications, mortality, psychological problems, and higher costs.
w: Shorter hospital stays
Undertreated pain increases recovery time rather than shortening stays.
Lower health care costs
These beliefs are linked to increased, not lower, health care costs.
Fewer complications
These beliefs are associated with more complications, not fewer.

alt.q: According to research, how do clinician-based bias and discrimination affect patients in pain?
alt.a: They worsen pain and disability by reducing access to treatment
alt.ex: Bias and discrimination reduce access to treatment and increase pain-related injustice, depression, and perceived stress.
w: They prevent opioid misuse without changing pain outcomes
Bias worsens pain and disability; it is not a safe way to prevent misuse.
They lower perceived stress by limiting medication use
Bias increases, rather than lowers, patients’ perceived stress.
They have no measurable effect on pain or disability
Research shows bias and discrimination worsen pain and disability.

items.q: When a patient has pain with no obvious source, such as neuropathy, how do some health care providers mistakenly view the patient?
items.a: As a malingerer or complainer
items.ex: Providers who believe pain requires objective signs stereotype such patients as malingerers, complainers, or difficult patients.
w: As an opioid-tolerant patient
Opioid tolerance is a drug adaptation, not a stereotype about pain without a visible source.
As a patient with referred pain
Referred pain is a location classification, not a biased label.
As a stoic patient
Stoicism means suffering without complaint, the opposite of the stereotype described.

alt.q: Which patient is most at risk of being stereotyped as “difficult” because of providers’ preconceptions about pain?
alt.a: A patient with chronic low back pain and no visible injury
alt.ex: When there is no obvious source of pain, some providers stereotype the patient as a malingerer, complainer, or difficult patient.
w: A patient with an open fracture of the tibia
An open fracture is an obvious source of pain, so it rarely triggers this stereotype.
A patient with a fresh abdominal surgical incision
A fresh incision is an obvious source of pain.
A patient with a visible second-degree burn
A visible burn is an obvious source of pain.

items.q: A nurse realizes she was raised to believe people should “tough out” pain. Which action best supports person-centered pain care?
items.a: Acknowledge her own beliefs so they do not shape her pain care
items.ex: Acknowledging personal values and beliefs about pain is essential to person-centered care and to viewing pain through the patient’s eyes.
w: Share her belief so the patient learns to endure the pain
Imposing personal beliefs ignores the patient’s preferences, values, and needs.
Rely on vital signs rather than the patient’s self-report
Vital signs do not replace self-report, the most reliable indicator of pain.
Request patients who are not experiencing pain
Avoiding patients with pain does not address the bias or meet professional standards.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student shows understanding of person-centered pain management?
alt.a: “I need to view the pain experience through the patient’s eyes.”
alt.ex: Viewing pain through the patient’s eyes and recognizing patient expectations are essential to person-centered care.
w: “My own pain experiences tell me how much this patient hurts.”
Personal experience cannot measure another person’s pain; pain is unique and subjective.
“If the patient looks comfortable, the rating is probably exaggerated.”
Doubting reports based on appearance is a misconception that limits pain relief.
“Patient expectations have little effect on pain outcomes.”
Patient expectations influence outcomes related to pain management.

items.q: Whatever their personal beliefs, nurses must accept patients’ [[reports|report|self-reports|self-report]] of pain.
items.ex: Nurses must accept reports of pain and act according to professional guidelines, standards, and evidence-based care.

alt.q: A nurse’s professional duty is to accept a patient’s [[report|reports|self-report|self-reports]] of pain even when personal beliefs differ.
alt.ex: Nurses must accept reports of pain and act according to professional guidelines, standards, and evidence-based care.

items.q: Barriers and facilitators of pain assessment were categorized as nurse-related, patient-related, physician-related, and which fourth category?
items.a: System-related
items.ex: Barriers and facilitators were grouped as nurse-, system-, patient-, and physician-related.
w: Family-related
Family factors were not one of the four categories identified.
Pharmacy-related
Pharmacy factors were not one of the four categories identified.
Insurance-related
Insurance factors were not one of the four categories identified.

alt.q: Into which set of categories were barriers and facilitators of pain assessment and management grouped?
alt.a: Nurse-, system-, patient-, and physician-related
alt.ex: The study grouped barriers and facilitators as nurse-, system-, patient-, and physician-related.
w: Physical, emotional, spiritual, and social
These are dimensions of the pain experience, not the barrier categories.
Acute, chronic, cancer, and noncancer
These are types of pain, not the barrier categories.
Cultural, genetic, developmental, and economic
These are factors influencing pain, not the barrier categories.

items.q: A patient is aphasic after a stroke and cannot rate pain. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Observe behaviors and use an appropriate tool to assess for pain
items.ex: Believing that patients who cannot speak do not feel pain is a misconception; the nurse assesses behaviors with a suitable tool.
w: Assume no pain because the patient has not asked for medication
Many patients do not report pain; absence of a request is not absence of pain.
Record a pain score of 0 because no rating is possible
A missing self-report does not mean the patient has no pain.
Wait for the family to request analgesia for the patient
Assessing pain is a nursing responsibility and should not wait for family requests.

alt.q: A postoperative patient who drinks alcohol daily reports severe pain. A colleague says, “People who drink always overreact.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “That is a misconception; I will assess and treat his pain like anyone else’s.”
alt.ex: The belief that patients who use substances overreact to discomfort is false and must not limit pain treatment.
w: “Agreed. I’ll give the lowest dose available regardless of his rating.”
Ignoring the pain rating reflects bias rather than individualized assessment.
“We should hold all analgesics because he may be drug seeking.”
Labeling patients as drug seeking is poorly defined and causes bias and prejudice.
“Let’s wait and see whether he settles down without medication.”
Delaying treatment because of bias leaves pain unrelieved and increases complications.

items.q: Nurses who are knowledgeable about the concepts of pain can analyze a patient’s pain experience more objectively.
items.a: True
items.ex: Knowledgeable nurses analyze pain more objectively and make judgments that respect patients’ preferences, values, and needs.
items.ww: Knowledge of pain concepts directly improves the nurse’s clinical judgments about pain treatment.

alt.q: A nurse’s knowledge of pain concepts has little effect on clinical judgments about pain treatment.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Knowledge of pain concepts helps nurses analyze pain objectively and choose effective treatment.
alt.ww: Lack of knowledge is one of the most reported barriers, showing that knowledge strongly affects care.

items.q: How does believing that patients have pain only when they show objective signs affect patient care?
items.a: It limits the interventions offered to relieve pain
items.ex: This belief negatively influences pain assessment and seriously limits the interventions offered for relief.
w: It improves the accuracy of pain assessment
Relying on objective signs introduces bias and reduces assessment accuracy.
It reduces opioid misuse without affecting relief
This belief reduces pain relief; it is not a safe misuse-prevention strategy.
It has no effect once a pain scale is used
Bias still shapes how nurses respond to pain scores and offer relief.

alt.q: A nurse believes a patient’s report of pain only if the patient appears to be in pain. What is the most likely result?
alt.a: The patient’s pain is underassessed and undertreated
alt.ex: Assumptions and biases about patients in pain seriously limit nurses’ ability to offer pain relief.
w: The patient receives safer, more accurate pain care
Bias makes pain care less accurate, not safer.
The patient’s recovery time is shortened
Undertreated pain increases recovery time.
The patient develops trust in the health care team
These beliefs lead to mistrust between patients and caregivers.

items.q: Which actions reflect a nurse’s professional responsibilities when personal beliefs about pain differ from the patient’s? Select all that apply.
o: Accept the patient’s report of pain
Nurses must accept patients’ reports of pain.
Act according to professional guidelines and position statements
Nurses act according to professional guidelines, standards, and position statements.
Individualize policies, procedures, and protocols
Nurses individualize appropriate policies, procedures, and protocols.
Provide evidence-based care
Nurses provide evidence-based pain care.
Wait for objective signs before giving analgesics
Requiring objective signs is a bias that limits pain relief.
Limit analgesics to avoid causing addiction
Fear of addiction is a misconception that leads to undertreatment.
items.ex: Personal beliefs aside, nurses accept pain reports, follow professional standards, individualize protocols, and provide evidence-based care.

alt.q: A preceptor explains to a new graduate how to keep biases out of pain care. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Having personal beliefs is normal, but patients’ reports must be accepted.
Nurses have personal beliefs but must still accept reports of pain.
Patient expectations influence pain-management outcomes.
Recognizing patient expectations is essential to person-centered care.
Acknowledging your own values about pain is part of person-centered care.
Acknowledging personal values helps prevent bias in pain care.
A patient with no visible injury is probably exaggerating.
Pain without an obvious source is real; this is a harmful stereotype.
Nurses’ beliefs rarely affect how pain is managed.
Nurses’ knowledge, attitudes, and beliefs affect their approach to pain management.
alt.ex: Nurses acknowledge their own values, recognize patient expectations, and accept patients’ reports of pain.

items.q: A patient with chronic neuropathic pain says, “The last nurse told me my tests are normal, so I shouldn’t hurt this much.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “I believe you. Tell me about your pain and what helps it.”
items.ex: Accepting the report and exploring the pain through the patient’s eyes counters bias and supports effective relief.
w: “Severe pain usually shows up on tests, so let’s repeat them.”
Pain with no obvious source is still real; tests are not needed to validate it.
“Try not to focus on it, and it may go away on its own.”
This dismisses the report rather than accepting and assessing it.
“Your pain may be psychological since nothing was found.”
Believing chronic pain is psychological is a listed misconception.

alt.q: Which statement by a nurse to a patient with chronic pain best demonstrates acceptance of the patient’s pain report?
alt.a: “You know your pain best; let’s plan relief around what you tell me.”
alt.ex: The nurse accepts the report and partners with the patient, recognizing the patient as the authority on the pain.
w: “Your scans are normal, so the pain should be mild.”
Tying pain to test results reflects bias; pain without an obvious source is real.
“I’ll believe the rating once I see you grimacing.”
Requiring visible signs of pain is a misconception that limits relief.
“Most patients with your condition need far less medication.”
Comparing patients ignores that each person’s pain experience is unique.

items.q: Some providers stereotype patients whose pain has no obvious source as [[malingerers|malingerer]], complainers, or difficult patients.
items.ex: This preconception negatively influences pain assessment and seriously limits interventions offered to relieve pain.

alt.q: Calling a patient with neuropathic pain a [[malingerer|malingerers]] reflects a common bias about pain with no obvious source.
alt.ex: This preconception negatively influences pain assessment and seriously limits interventions offered to relieve pain.

items.q: Why is it essential for the nurse to recognize a patient’s expectations about pain management?
items.a: Patient expectations influence outcomes related to pain management
items.ex: Recognizing that expectations influence outcomes is essential to person-centered care.
w: Patient expectations determine the opioid dose to prescribe
Dosing is individualized by the provider from assessment, not set by expectations alone.
Patient expectations replace the need for a pain assessment
A thorough assessment is always needed; expectations are one part of it.
Patient expectations show whether the pain report is honest
Expectations do not test honesty; nurses accept patients’ reports of pain.

alt.q: Which nursing approach best reflects person-centered care for a patient in pain?
alt.a: Considering the patient’s preferences, values, and needs in treatment
alt.ex: Knowledgeable nurses make clinical judgments that recognize a patient’s preferences, values, and needs.
w: Applying the same pain plan to all patients with a diagnosis
Pain is unique, so standard plans must be individualized.
Basing treatment on the nurse’s personal beliefs about pain
Personal beliefs must not override the patient’s report and preferences.
Giving relief only when objective signs confirm the pain
Requiring objective signs is a bias that limits relief.

items.q: A nurse assumes that a patient having a minor outpatient procedure will need much less pain relief than a patient after major surgery. What does this assumption reflect?
items.a: A common misconception about pain
items.ex: Believing patients with minor illnesses have less pain than those with severe alterations is listed as a false belief.
w: An evidence-based pain standard
No standard predicts pain from the size of the illness or procedure.
Accurate prediction from tissue damage
Tissue damage does not accurately indicate pain intensity.
A sound application of the gate-control theory
Gate-control theory explains pain modulation, not this assumption.

alt.q: Which statement about pain is accurate?
alt.a: A patient with a minor illness may have as much pain as one with a severe condition
alt.ex: Assuming minor illness means less pain is a misconception; pain is subjective and unique to each person.
w: Pain intensity can be predicted from the extent of tissue damage
This is a listed misconception; tissue damage does not indicate pain intensity.
Chronic pain is mainly psychological in origin
This is a listed misconception about chronic pain.
Patients who cannot speak do not experience pain
This is a listed misconception; nonverbal patients feel pain.

items.q: Which factor influencing pain is nonmodifiable?
items.a: Age
items.ex: Age is a nonmodifiable factor; nursing interventions target modifiable factors such as fear and anxiety.
w: Fear
Fear is modifiable through teaching and coping skills.
Anxiety
Anxiety is a modifiable factor nurses target with interventions.
Knowledge about pain
Knowledge can be improved through patient and family education.

alt.q: Which factors do nursing interventions primarily target when helping patients cope with pain?
alt.a: Modifiable factors such as fear and anxiety
alt.ex: Nurses target modifiable factors like fear and anxiety by giving patients and families knowledge and coping skills.
w: Nonmodifiable factors such as age
Age cannot be changed, so it is not the target of interventions.
Inherited factors such as pain threshold
Genetic influences are not modified by nursing interventions.
Neurological factors such as spinal cord injury
Neurological damage is not a modifiable factor nurses change through teaching.

items.q: Term neonates have the same sensitivity to pain as older children and adults.
items.a: True
items.ex: Term neonates are as sensitive to pain as older children and adults; preterm neonates are even more sensitive.
items.ww: Believing infants are less sensitive to pain is a listed misconception.

alt.q: Preterm neonates are less sensitive to pain than term neonates.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Preterm neonates have greater sensitivity to pain than term neonates or older children.
alt.ww: The text corrects the misconception that infants are less sensitive; preterm neonates are more sensitive.

items.q: Before a heel stick, a parent says, “My newborn has never felt pain, so this won’t really hurt her.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Babies feel pain even during their very first painful experience.”
items.ex: Pain requires no prior experience; infants do not need to learn it from earlier painful events.
w: “That’s right. Infants learn to feel pain gradually over time.”
Infants do not need to learn pain from previous experience.
“Newborns feel pain but are less sensitive than older children.”
Term neonates are as sensitive as older children; preterm neonates are more sensitive.
“We have no reliable way to know whether infants feel pain.”
Behavioral cues and physiological indicators assess infant pain reliably and validly.

alt.q: Which statement about pain in infants is accurate?
alt.a: Pain does not need to be learned from earlier painful experiences
alt.ex: Pain occurs with the first pain experience; infants have the anatomy for pain processing by mid- to late gestation.
w: Infants lack the anatomy needed to process pain
Infants have the anatomical and functional requirements for pain processing by mid- to late gestation.
Preterm neonates feel less pain than term neonates
Preterm neonates are more sensitive to pain than term neonates.
Infant pain cannot be assessed reliably by nurses
Behavioral cues and physiological indicators assess infant pain reliably.

items.q: An 82-year-old resident with dementia and arthritis is asleep in a chair. Her son says, “She’s sleeping, so she must not be in pain.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Sleep can be a way of coping or a sign of exhaustion, not pain relief.”
items.ex: Do not assume absence of pain from behavior; older adults may sleep as a coping strategy or from exhaustion.
w: “You’re right. People who are asleep do not have pain.”
Assuming a sleeping or distracted older adult has no pain is a listed misconception.
“Older adults feel less pain as they age, so she is likely fine.”
No scientific basis exists for a decrease in pain perception with age.
“Her pain reports would not be valid anyway because of dementia.”
Reports from cognitively impaired adults are not less valid; accept them and use relevant tools.

alt.q: An older adult with osteoarthritis denies pain but moves slowly and stiffly. Which reason commonly explains why older adults underreport pain?
alt.a: Not wanting to alarm loved ones or bother caregivers
alt.ex: Older adults underreport pain to avoid alarming loved ones or bothering caregivers, and because they expect pain with age.
w: Pain perception decreases naturally with aging
There is no scientific basis that pain perception decreases with age.
Older adults have fewer painful conditions
Older adults have a higher incidence of painful conditions such as arthritis.
Older adults cannot use pain rating scales
Many older adults can use scales; underreporting reflects beliefs and fears.

items.q: Which reasons explain why older adults commonly underreport pain? Select all that apply.
o: Expecting to have pain with increasing age
Many older adults believe pain is expected with aging.
Fear of losing their independence
Fear of losing independence leads some older adults to hide pain.
Believing caregivers already know and are doing all they can
Some assume caregivers know about the pain and are already treating it.
Not wanting to distract, anger, or bother caregivers
Older adults may avoid reporting pain to avoid bothering caregivers.
Decreased pain perception that comes with age
No scientific basis exists for decreased pain perception with age.
Fewer painful conditions than younger adults
Older adults have more painful conditions such as arthritis and osteoporosis.
items.ex: Older adults underreport pain because of expectations, fears, and beliefs, not because they feel less pain.

alt.q: A nurse teaches staff why older patients may not report pain. Which reasons should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: They grew up valuing the ability to “grin and bear it.”
Many older adults were raised to endure pain silently.
They do not want to alarm loved ones.
Not wanting to alarm loved ones is a common reason for underreporting.
They believe showing pain is unacceptable.
Many older patients believe it is unacceptable to show pain.
Age dulls their sensitivity to pain.
The claim that age dulls pain sensitivity has no scientific basis and is unsafe.
Their reports of pain are usually unreliable.
Older adults’ reports are valid, including those with cognitive impairment.
alt.ex: Stoic upbringing, not wanting to alarm family, and beliefs that pain should not be shown lead older adults to underreport pain.

items.q: An older adult who eats poorly has a low serum albumin level. Why does this increase the risk of toxic effects from many analgesics?
items.a: Less drug is protein bound, leaving more free active drug
items.ex: Many analgesics are highly protein bound; low albumin leaves more free drug available, raising the risk of side effects.
w: Less drug is absorbed from the gastrointestinal tract
Low albumin affects protein binding, not oral absorption.
More drug is excreted rapidly by the kidneys
Declining renal function reduces, rather than increases, drug excretion.
More drug is stored in increased body fat
Increased body fat affects fat-soluble drugs, not protein binding.

alt.q: Why does a normal dose of morphine produce a higher drug concentration in an older adult?
alt.a: The percentage of body water decreases with aging
alt.ex: With aging, body water decreases, increasing the concentration of water-soluble drugs such as morphine.
w: Body fat decreases with aging
Body fat increases with aging, which affects fat-soluble drugs such as fentanyl.
Muscle mass increases with aging
Muscle mass decreases with aging.
Serum albumin rises with aging
Poor nutrition may lower, not raise, serum albumin.

items.q: Because liver and renal function decline with age, older adults often experience a greater peak effect and longer duration of analgesics.
items.a: True
items.ex: Reduced hepatic metabolism and renal excretion prolong and intensify analgesic effects in older adults.
items.ww: Age-related organ decline slows drug clearance, so effects are stronger and last longer, not weaker or shorter.

alt.q: Age-related decline in liver and kidney function shortens the duration of analgesic effects in older adults.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Reduced metabolism and excretion lead to a greater peak effect and longer duration of analgesics.
alt.ww: Slower drug clearance prolongs, rather than shortens, analgesic effects.

items.q: Based on current evidence about genetic influences on pain, what may help a patient with a persistent pain syndrome?
items.a: Seeking genetic counseling
items.ex: Genes may influence pain sensitivity and drug metabolism, so genetic counseling may help patients with persistent pain syndromes.
w: Avoiding all opioid analgesics
Genetics may affect opioid metabolism, but the text does not advise avoiding all opioids.
Taking routine placebo trials
Placebos are discouraged and are not linked to genetic influences on pain.
Increasing daily fluid intake
Fluid intake is unrelated to genetic influences on pain.

alt.q: Genetic differences may help explain which aspect of a patient’s pain experience?
alt.a: How the patient metabolizes opioid medications
alt.ex: Genetic influences may explain sensitivity to pain as well as metabolism of pain medications such as opioids.
w: How the patient’s culture shapes pain expression
Pain expression is shaped by culture, not explained by genes in the text.
Whether the patient has an internal locus of control
Locus of control is a coping style, a psychological factor.
Whether the patient’s family is present for support
Family presence is a social factor, not a genetic one.

items.q: A patient who has never had surgery is scheduled for abdominal surgery tomorrow. Which preoperative action by the nurse best reduces the patient’s perception of postoperative pain?
items.a: Explain the type of pain to expect and the methods available to relieve it
items.ex: Without prior experience, new pain can seem like a complication; preparing the patient reduces pain perception and improves coping.
w: Avoid discussing pain so the patient does not become anxious
Not preparing the patient makes postoperative pain seem like a serious complication.
Wait until pain begins before teaching relief methods
Teaching belongs in the preoperative and anticipatory phase, before pain begins.
Tell the patient that severe incisional pain is uncommon
Severe incisional pain for several days after abdominal surgery is common.

alt.q: A patient on the second day after abdominal surgery says, “This pain is terrible. Did something go wrong?” The patient received no preoperative teaching about pain. What best explains the patient’s reaction?
alt.a: First-time pain without preparation often seems like a complication
alt.ex: When a patient has no experience with a painful condition, the first perception of pain often impairs coping.
w: Prior painful experiences have made the patient overly sensitive
This patient has no previous experience with this type of pain.
Severe pain after abdominal surgery is a rare finding
Severe incisional pain for several days after abdominal surgery is common.
The patient has an external locus of control
Locus of control affects coping style but does not explain fear of a complication.

items.q: A person who has experienced pain before will accept pain more easily in the future.
items.a: False
items.ex: Prior experience does not mean a person accepts pain more easily; unrelieved or severe past pain causes anxiety or fear.
items.ww: Previous frequent pain without relief causes anxiety or fear rather than easier acceptance.

alt.q: Previous frequent episodes of pain without relief can cause anxiety or fear about future pain.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Repeated unrelieved or severe pain causes anxiety or fear, which shapes future pain experiences.
alt.ww: Prior experience does not make pain easier to accept; unrelieved pain increases fear.

items.q: A postoperative patient never asks for pain medication but grimaces and guards the incision. The patient says, “The nurses know when I need something.” Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Offer the prescribed prn analgesic on time without waiting to be asked
items.ex: A patient with an external locus of control is passive in managing pain, so the nurse is more responsive in offering prn medications.
w: Wait until the patient specifically requests the analgesic
This passive patient may never ask, leaving pain unrelieved.
Document that the patient has no pain because none was reported
Behavioral signs of discomfort indicate pain even without a request.
Teach the patient to manage pain alone before offering medication
Delaying analgesia ignores current pain and the patient’s coping style.

alt.q: Which behavior is characteristic of a patient with an internal locus of control?
alt.a: Asks questions, wants information, and makes treatment choices
alt.ex: People with internal loci of control see themselves as controlling outcomes such as pain, so they seek information and choices.
w: Follows directions and is passive in managing pain
Passive direction-following describes an external locus of control.
Believes the nurse is responsible for relieving the pain
Relying on others for outcomes describes an external locus of control.
Avoids information about the pain and its treatment
Internal-locus patients desire information rather than avoid it.

items.q: A critically ill patient feels a lack of control over the environment and is anxious. The patient reports severe pain. Which statement guides the nurse’s action?
items.a: Anxiety may be treated, but anxiolytics never substitute for analgesia
items.ex: Pharmacological and nonpharmacological anxiety management is appropriate, but anxiolytic medications are not a substitute for analgesia.
w: An anxiolytic can be given instead of the analgesic
Anxiolytics do not relieve pain and cannot replace analgesics.
Analgesia should be delayed until the anxiety resolves
Pain and anxiety feed each other, so delaying analgesia worsens both.
Only the anxiety needs treatment since it causes the pain
Pain and anxiety are intertwined; the pain itself requires analgesia.

alt.q: Which statement about the relationship between pain and anxiety is accurate?
alt.a: Anxiety increases pain perception, and pain causes anxiety
alt.ex: The relationship is complex; anxiety and fear increase pain perception, and pain causes anxiety and fear.
w: Anxiety and pain are easy to separate and treat alone
It is difficult to separate the two sensations.
Anxiety decreases pain perception by distracting the patient
Anxiety increases, rather than decreases, pain perception.
Pain has no effect on a patient’s level of anxiety
Pain causes feelings of anxiety and fear.

items.q: Why do interventions such as guided imagery and relaxation reduce a patient’s perception of pain?
items.a: They focus the patient’s attention on stimuli other than pain
items.ex: Increased attention increases pain, whereas focusing attention on other stimuli diminishes pain perception.
w: They block opioid receptors in the spinal cord
Attention-based interventions do not act on opioid receptors.
They increase the patient’s focus on the pain site
Increased attention to pain is associated with increased pain.
They eliminate the source of tissue damage
These techniques change perception; they do not remove the pain source.

alt.q: Which relationship between attention and pain is accurate?
alt.a: Greater attention to pain is linked with greater pain
alt.ex: The degree to which a patient focuses on pain influences perception; distraction diminishes the pain response.
w: Greater attention to pain is linked with less pain
Increased attention is associated with increased, not decreased, pain.
Distraction is linked with an increased pain response
Distraction is associated with a diminished pain response.
Attention has no effect on how pain is perceived
Attention strongly influences the patient’s perception of pain.

items.q: Which actions reflect culturally sensitive pain assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Use culturally appropriate tools such as the Wong-Baker FACES scale
Culturally appropriate tools improve pain assessment across cultures.
Assess the patient’s health literacy
Health literacy affects the nurse’s ability to teach about pain management.
Use a professional translator when the patient does not speak English
Professional translators help patients describe their pain accurately.
Develop awareness of your own values and beliefs about pain
Personal awareness reduces bias in responding to pain reports.
Assume every patient will ask for pain medication when needed
Some patients believe asking is inappropriate and expect the nurse to bring medication.
Judge pain intensity mainly by the patient’s facial expressions
Facial expression varies by culture; some people conceal pain by smiling.
items.ex: Culturally sensitive care uses appropriate tools, assesses literacy, uses professional translators, and builds self-awareness of personal values.

alt.q: Which cultural beliefs might keep a patient from asking for pain medication? Select all that apply.
o: Asking for help shows a lack of respect
Some patients believe asking for help indicates disrespect.
Acknowledging pain is a sign of weakness
Some patients view acknowledging pain as weakness.
The nurse will bring medication if it is appropriate
Some patients assume the nurse will bring needed medication, so asking is inappropriate.
Suffering is part of life to be endured
Some cultures consider suffering something to endure, linked to religious beliefs.
Pain must be reported promptly to get relief
This belief would encourage, not prevent, asking for medication.
alt.ex: Beliefs about respect, weakness, nurses’ role, and enduring suffering may stop patients from requesting pain relief.

items.q: A postoperative patient from a culture in which negative emotions are often concealed smiles and nods while the nurse prepares the patient to walk. Which action by the nurse is best?
items.a: Ask directly about pain rather than relying on facial expression
items.ex: In some cultures pain is concealed by smiling, so the nurse explores the patient’s pain experience directly.
w: Conclude the patient is comfortable because of the smile
Facial expressions vary by culture and may hide pain.
Wait for the patient to request pain medication
Some patients consider asking for medication inappropriate.
Record the facial expression as the pain rating
A smile is not a pain rating; the patient’s report is needed.

alt.q: Which statement about culture and pain expression is accurate?
alt.a: Some people conceal pain, even by smiling
alt.ex: Facial expressions vary with culture; some people use less expression, and some conceal pain by smiling.
w: Everyone uses facial expressions to show pain
Use of facial expression to show pain varies with culture.
Pain is expressed the same way across cultures
Different meanings and attitudes about pain exist across cultural groups.
Lack of facial expression means pain is mild
Less expressive patients may still have significant pain.

items.q: Spirituality is an active search for [[meaning]] in situations, and it affects how patients view and cope with pain.
items.ex: Spiritual beliefs affect how patients cope with pain, and supporting spiritual practices is essential to pain management.

alt.q: Because spirituality involves a search for [[meaning]], it shapes the way a patient views pain.
alt.ex: Spiritual beliefs affect how patients cope with pain, and supporting spiritual practices is essential to pain management.

items.q: A patient with persistent pain asks, “Why has God let this happen to me?” Which response by the nurse is most supportive?
items.a: “Tell me how your faith has helped you cope with difficult times.”
items.ex: Supporting patients’ spiritual practices is essential; positive spiritual coping improves adjustment to pain and mental health.
w: “Let’s focus on your medication instead of those questions.”
Dismissing spiritual concerns ignores an important part of the pain experience.
“Everything happens for a reason, so try not to worry.”
This cliché closes communication rather than supporting coping.
“Pain is physical, so faith does not really affect it.”
Pain has physical and emotional components, and spiritual beliefs affect coping.

alt.q: Which outcome is associated with positive spiritual coping, such as looking to a higher being for strength, in patients with persistent pain?
alt.a: Better adjustment to pain and better mental health
alt.ex: Patients using positive spiritual coping adjust better to pain and have significantly better mental health.
w: Greater need for opioid analgesics
The text does not link spiritual coping with higher analgesic needs.
Increased social isolation
Social isolation is an effect of pain, not of positive spiritual coping.
Higher pain intensity ratings
Positive spiritual coping is linked with better adjustment, not higher pain.

items.q: A nurse is assessing how a patient’s chronic pain affects the family. Which effect on the family is described?
items.a: The family caregiver’s quality of life may be negatively affected
items.ex: Pain affects family members too; a caregiver of a patient with chronic pain may have reduced quality of life.
w: Family relationships typically become less stressful
Irritability and anger in patients with pain increase family stress.
Family members are rarely affected by the pain
When a person has pain, family members are also affected.
Social contacts usually increase for the family
Pain often restricts social contacts, and isolation is common.

alt.q: Which school-related effect is common in children with chronic pain?
alt.a: Higher levels of absenteeism
alt.ex: Children with chronic pain have higher levels of school absenteeism.
w: Improved academic performance
Pain interferes with, rather than improves, school performance.
Fewer missed school days than peers
Children with chronic pain miss more school, not less.
Increased participation in sports
Pain limits physical and social activities.

items.q: Persistent pain in older adults may be associated with which problems? Select all that apply.
o: Falls
Persistent pain is associated with falls in older adults.
Diminished appetite
Persistent pain is associated with diminished appetite.
Impaired sleep
Persistent pain is associated with impaired sleep.
Delirium
Persistent pain is associated with delirium and reduced cognition.
Increased activity tolerance
Pain reduces mobility and activity tolerance.
Improved cognitive function
Persistent pain is associated with reduced cognitive function.
items.ex: Persistent pain in older adults is linked with falls, poor appetite, impaired sleep, depression, delirium, and reduced cognition.

alt.q: Chronic pain commonly limits which activities of daily living? Select all that apply.
o: Instrumental activities such as shopping and house cleaning
Pain often limits IADLs such as shopping and cleaning.
Exercise and walking
Chronic pain limits the ability to exercise and walk.
Participation in social activities
Pain often restricts leisure and social activities.
Risk of falling
Chronic pain increases, rather than limits, fall risk.
Need for social support
Pain increases the need for support from family and friends.
alt.ex: Chronic pain reduces physical activity and increases disability, limiting IADLs, exercise, chores, and social activities.

items.q: Which is the single most reliable indicator of the existence and intensity of a patient’s pain?
items.a: The patient’s self-report
items.ex: A patient’s self-report of pain is the single most reliable indicator of its existence and intensity.
w: Changes in vital signs
Vital signs are not reliable proof of pain; pain cannot be measured objectively.
Nonverbal behaviors
Behaviors suggest pain but are less reliable than self-report.
The nurse’s judgment
Nurse bias can lead to overestimating or underestimating pain.

alt.q: A patient says, “I feel like I have to prove to everyone that I’m hurting.” Which principle should guide the nurse?
alt.a: The nurse must accept that pain exists when the patient reports it
alt.ex: It is not the patient’s responsibility to prove pain; it is the nurse’s responsibility to accept that it exists.
w: The patient must show objective signs before pain is treated
Pain is subjective and cannot be measured objectively.
The health care provider must confirm the pain on examination
Pain is accepted on the patient’s report, not provider confirmation.
The nurse must verify the pain with a diagnostic test
No test can measure pain; it is a subjective experience.

items.q: A patient returns from surgery grimacing and reporting severe pain. How should the nurse approach the pain assessment at this time?
items.a: Assess location, severity, and quality now; gather details later
items.ex: During acute pain, streamline assessment to location, severity, and quality, and collect a detailed assessment once the patient is comfortable.
w: Complete a full pain history before giving analgesia
Patients in acute severe pain have difficulty giving detailed descriptions.
Ask first how the pain affects work and daily activities
Effects on function are assessed later in a more detailed assessment.
Monitor only vital signs until the pain subsides
Vital signs cannot replace assessment of pain location, severity, and quality.

alt.q: For a patient with chronic pain rather than an acute episode, what should a thorough pain assessment include?
alt.a: Affective, cognitive, behavioral, spiritual, and social dimensions
alt.ex: A thorough assessment of chronic pain includes affective, cognitive, behavioral, spiritual, and social dimensions.
w: Only the location, severity, and quality of the pain
A streamlined assessment fits acute pain episodes, not chronic pain.
Only the patient’s vital signs and facial expression
Physiological and facial cues alone miss the many dimensions of chronic pain.
Only the medications the patient takes at home
Medications are one part of a much broader chronic pain assessment.

items.q: A nurse uses the PAINAD tool for a patient with advanced dementia and obtains a score of 6. How should the nurse interpret this score?
items.a: It is a behavior score showing pain is present, not its intensity
items.ex: Behavioral tools identify the presence of pain but not its intensity, so the number is a behavior score.
w: It equals a rating of 6 on a 0-to-10 intensity scale
A behavior score is not a pain-intensity rating.
It measures how much pain the patient can tolerate
Pain tools identify how much pain exists, not how much a patient tolerates.
It shows the patient does not need an analgesic
A behavior score indicating pain calls for treatment, not withholding it.

alt.q: A patient with severe dementia is resisting care and has fearful expressions. After ruling out infection and constipation, what should the nurse do?
alt.a: Assume pain is present and treat it
alt.ex: Patients who are nonverbal often show atypical pain signs; after ruling out other problems, assume pain is present.
w: Assume the behavior is caused only by dementia
Combativeness and resistance to care may be atypical signs of pain.
Wait until the patient can give a pain rating
A patient with severe dementia may never provide a rating.
Document the patient as pain free
Behavior changes are potential indicators of pain, not evidence of comfort.

items.q: Which are possible sources of error in pain assessment? Select all that apply.
o: Nurse bias that leads to overestimating or underestimating pain
Bias consistently distorts pain estimates.
Vague or closed-ended assessment questions
Unclear or closed questions produce unreliable data.
Tools not validated for the specific patient population
Tools must be evidence based and validated for the population.
Medical terms the patient with low health literacy cannot understand
Jargon prevents patients from giving accurate information.
Using the same validated scale consistently for a patient
Consistent use of a validated scale reduces error.
Asking open-ended questions about the pain
Open-ended questions support reliable assessment data.
items.ex: Bias, unclear questions, unvalidated tools, jargon, incomplete patient information, and cognitive impairment can all cause assessment errors.

alt.q: A nurse wants to reduce errors when assessing pain. Which practices help? Select all that apply.
o: Using a tool validated for the patient’s population
Validated tools ensure accurate assessment in that population.
Asking clear, open-ended questions
Clear questions avoid unreliable data.
Using words the patient can understand
Avoiding medical terms helps patients with low health literacy.
Applying a child-validated tool to all adults by default
A tool validated for one population may not be reliable in another.
Relying on the nurse’s impression of pain severity
Nurse bias is a source of error in pain assessment.
alt.ex: Validated tools, clear questions, and plain language reduce errors in pain assessment.

items.q: Which practice reflects correct use of pain rating scales?
items.a: Use the same scale consistently for each patient
items.ex: Once you find the scale that works best for a patient, use it consistently so changes over time can be evaluated.
w: Compare one patient’s rating with another patient’s
Pain scales must not be used to compare one patient’s pain with another’s.
Rotate among different scales each shift
Switching scales prevents accurate tracking of trends.
Rely on the severity number as the full assessment
Relying solely on a number fails to capture pain’s multidimensionality.

alt.q: A nurse says, “Bed 2 rated her pain a 6, but she seems to hurt less than Bed 4, who rated a 5.” What is the problem with this reasoning?
alt.a: Pain scales should not compare one patient with another
alt.ex: Pain ratings reflect each person’s own perception over time and must not be compared between patients.
w: The nurse should have used a visual analogue scale
Changing the scale would not make comparisons between patients valid.
Ratings of 5 and 6 indicate identical pain levels
The issue is comparing patients, not the numbers themselves.
Behavior is more accurate than the patients’ ratings
Self-report is the most reliable indicator of pain.

items.q: Neuropathic pain is usually described with words such as shooting, burning, tingling, or electric-like.
items.a: True
items.ex: Neuropathic pain is typically sharp shooting, stabbing, burning, tingling, or electric-like, which guides treatment choices.
items.ww: These descriptors are characteristic of neuropathic pain, which is treated differently from nociceptive pain.

alt.q: Pain from a surgical incision is typically described as burning and electric-like, indicating neuropathic pain.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Incisional pain is usually described as dull, aching, and throbbing, indicating nociceptive pain.
alt.ww: Burning and electric-like descriptors point to neuropathic pain, not typical incisional pain.

items.q: A nurse delegates a back massage to assistive personnel (AP). Which task related to this patient must the nurse keep?
items.a: Performing the patient’s pain assessment
items.ex: Massage can be delegated to AP, but assessment of a patient’s pain cannot be delegated.
w: Giving the back massage
The skill of massage can be delegated to AP.
Dimming the room lights
Preparing the environment is within the AP’s role during massage.
Warming the lotion before use
Warming lotion is part of the delegated massage skill.

alt.q: Which instruction should the nurse give to AP who will perform a back massage?
alt.a: Report any worsening of the patient’s pain
alt.ex: The nurse directs AP to report worsening pain and explains when massage works best and how to adapt it to restrictions.
w: Assess the pain intensity before and after massage
Pain assessment cannot be delegated to AP.
Massage over any bruised or swollen areas
Massage is contraindicated over bruised, swollen, or inflamed areas.
Use firm massage with patients who cannot communicate
Use very gentle massage with patients who cannot communicate.

items.q: Distraction works best for short, intense pain lasting a few minutes, such as during an invasive procedure.
items.a: True
items.ex: Distraction works best for brief, intense pain, such as during a procedure or while waiting for an analgesic to work.
items.ww: Distraction is most effective for short, intense pain rather than prolonged pain.

alt.q: If distraction relieves a patient’s pain, it shows that the pain was not severe.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Relief from distraction does not mean pain was mild; this doubt is a disadvantage of the technique.
alt.ww: Distraction reduces awareness of real pain, so its success does not disprove the pain.

items.q: Which actions help control painful stimuli in the patient’s environment? Select all that apply.
o: Tighten and smooth wrinkled bed linen
Wrinkled linen creates pressure and discomfort.
Reposition the patient to avoid lying on tubing
Lying on IV or chest tubing causes painful pressure.
Loosen constricting bandages that are not pressure dressings
Constricting bandages cause pain unless purposely applied for pressure.
Lift the patient in bed rather than pulling
Lifting with safe handling devices avoids friction and pain.
Leave wet dressings until the next scheduled change
Wet dressings and linens should be changed to promote comfort.
Allow wound drainage to remain on the skin until bathing
Avoid exposing skin to irritants such as drainage, urine, or stool.
items.ex: Removing or preventing painful stimuli is a simple, effective way to promote comfort, especially in immobilized patients.

alt.q: A patient who is immobilized after a stroke has abdominal distention and cramping from constipation. Which nursing actions address this painful stimulus? Select all that apply.
o: Increase the patient’s fluid intake
Increasing fluids helps restore normal elimination.
Ambulate the patient as able
Activity promotes bowel elimination.
Request a stool softener or laxative
Stool softeners or laxatives may be needed to relieve constipation.
Restrict fluids to reduce abdominal fullness
Restricting fluids worsens constipation.
Keep the patient on bed rest until cramping stops
Immobility contributes to constipation and discomfort.
alt.ex: Preventing constipation with fluids, activity, and stool softeners or laxatives removes a painful stimulus.

This order would indicate 5 mg acetaminophen and 325 mg oxycodone.

APAP stands for acetaminophen, not ibuprofen.

alt.ex: Exceeding 4 g in 24 hours risks hepatotoxicity, the major adverse effect of acetaminophen.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient receiving opioids. Which finding is the earliest warning of opioid-induced respiratory depression?

items.ex: Sedation always occurs before respiratory depression, so nurses closely monitor sedation in patients taking opioids.
w: Pupil dilation
Opioids cause pupil constriction; dilation is a withdrawal sign.
Pruritus
Pruritus is a common side effect, not a warning of respiratory depression.
Constipation
Constipation is a common side effect that does not precede respiratory depression.

alt.q: Why do nurses closely monitor sedation level in patients receiving opioids?
alt.a: Sedation always occurs before respiratory depression

Sedation is an adverse effect, not a measure of pain relief.
Sedation shows the patient is opioid tolerant
Tolerance is a reduced response requiring more drug, not sedation.
Sedation occurs only after respiratory depression
Sedation precedes, rather than follows, respiratory depression.

items.q: After naloxone reverses an adult patient’s opioid-induced respiratory depression, why does the nurse continue to evaluate the patient every 15 minutes for 2 hours?

w: Naloxone itself causes delayed respiratory depression
Naloxone reverses, rather than causes, respiratory depression.
The opioid’s potency increases after naloxone is given
Naloxone does not increase opioid potency.
Naloxone must be repeated every 15 minutes by protocol

alt.q: How should the nurse give IV naloxone to an adult with opioid-induced respiratory depression?

items.q: A patient using a transdermal fentanyl patch should avoid heating pads, hot baths, and sunbathing.

Dependence is the body adjusting to regular use, causing withdrawal when the drug stops.
Opioid use disorder
OUD is a problematic pattern of use causing impairment or distress.
Pseudoaddiction
Pseudoaddiction describes behaviors of a patient seeking adequate relief of undertreated pain.

alt.q: A patient develops chills, diarrhea, and “gooseflesh” after suddenly stopping long-term opioids. Which term describes the underlying state?

Hyperalgesia is increased pain sensitivity, not withdrawal.

items.q: A nurse gives a patient an oral analgesic at 0900. At what time should the nurse ask whether the medication has relieved the pain?

IV push drugs peak in 15 to 30 minutes; oral drugs take about 1 hour.
At about 1300, when the oral drug peaks
Waiting 4 hours misses the peak effect of the oral analgesic.
At about 1500, at the next scheduled dose
Evaluation should occur at peak effect, not at the next dose.

alt.q: A nurse gives morphine by IV push at 1400. When is the best time to ask the patient about pain relief?

The drug has not yet reached peak effect immediately after injection.
Between 1500 and 1530
Oral drugs peak in about 1 hour; IV push drugs peak sooner.
At 1800, before the next dose
