items.q: Which instruction should the nurse give to assistive personnel (AP) caring for a patient who has patient-controlled analgesia (PCA)?
items.a: Report it if anyone other than the patient presses the button

AP must never administer a PCA dose for the patient.
Increase the dose if the patient reports more pain
AP cannot program or adjust PCA; the skill cannot be delegated.
Silence pump alarms and reposition the patient
AP should notify the nurse of problems rather than manage the pump.

alt.q: Which PCA-related activity is appropriate for assistive personnel (AP)?

Programming the pump is a nursing responsibility that cannot be delegated.
Changing the analgesic cartridge when it is empty
Handling and administering PCA medication cannot be delegated to AP.
Evaluating whether the PCA is relieving the pain
Evaluation of PCA effectiveness requires nursing assessment.

items.q: A patient’s health record lists a morphine allergy with the reaction “itching.” The patient is scheduled to start a morphine PCA. Which conclusion by the nurse is correct?

w: Itching is an allergy, so morphine PCA must be canceled
Pruritus alone does not indicate allergy or contraindicate PCA.
Itching signals impending anaphylaxis, so the PCA is held
Pruritus is a common opioid side effect, not a sign of anaphylaxis.
Itching shows the patient is opioid tolerant
Pruritus is a side effect unrelated to opioid tolerance.

alt.q: Why does the nurse assess a patient for obstructive sleep apnea syndrome before starting PCA?

OSAS affects breathing during sleep, not the ability to use the button.
It increases the dose of opioid the patient will need

ord.q: Put these steps for starting patient-controlled analgesia in the correct order.
items: Check the MAR against the health care provider’s written order

items.q: When the nurse compares the MAR with the name of the medication on the PCA drug cartridge at the bedside, which check for accuracy is this?
items.a: The third check
items.ex: Checking the label when removed from storage and after assembly are the first two checks; the bedside comparison is the third.
w: The first check
The first check occurs when the module is removed from storage.
The second check
The second check occurs after assembly.
The fourth check
The skill describes three checks; the bedside comparison is the third.

alt.q: When does the nurse perform the first and second checks of the PCA medication label?
alt.a: When removed from storage and after assembly
alt.ex: The label is checked when removed from storage and after assembly; the bedside comparison is the third check.
w: When removed from storage and at hand-off report
Hand-off is when pump programming is reconciled, not the second label check.
At the bedside and after the loading dose
The bedside comparison is the third check, and checks occur before dosing.
When reviewing the EHR and when priming tubing
EHR review assesses history and allergies, not the drug label.

items.q: Why are basal (continuous) PCA infusions not recommended for opioid-naïve patients after surgery?
items.a: They increase the risk of respiratory depression
items.ex: Background basal infusions are associated with more nausea, vomiting, and respiratory depression in opioid-naïve patients.
w: They cause opioid withdrawal in naïve patients
Withdrawal is a concern for opioid-tolerant patients who are undertreated.
They prevent the patient from using demand doses
Patients can still press for demand doses when a basal rate runs.
They automatically shorten the lockout interval
A basal rate does not change the programmed lockout interval.

alt.q: For which patient may a background basal PCA infusion be necessary?
alt.a: An opioid-tolerant patient with cancer pain
alt.ex: In opioid-tolerant patients, a basal infusion may be needed to prevent undertreatment and possible opioid withdrawal.
w: An opioid-naïve patient after abdominal surgery
Basal doses are not recommended for opioid-naïve postoperative patients.
A patient with untreated obstructive sleep apnea
OSAS raises the risk of respiratory depression from opioids.
An older adult with no recent opioid use
Older, opioid-naïve patients are at higher risk for adverse events.

items.q: Which points should the nurse include when teaching a patient about PCA? Select all that apply.
o: The lockout interval prevents an overdose
Explaining the lockout relieves anxiety about overdosing.
Only the patient should press the PCA button
Verbal and written instruction warns against anyone else pressing the button.
Using doses helps with repositioning, walking, and deep breathing
Self-dosing aids activity, coughing, and deep breathing.
Notify the nurse if the alarm sounds or pain changes
Patients report alarms, problems gaining relief, and changes in pain.
Family members may press the button while the patient sleeps
PCA by proxy bypasses the safety feature requiring an awake patient.
The pump delivers a dose every time the button is pressed
The pump delivers doses only after the programmed lockout interval.
items.ex: Teaching covers lockout safety, patient-only activation, use of doses for activity, and reporting problems to the nurse.

alt.q: When is PCA teaching best done, and how is it reinforced? Select all that apply.
o: Before the procedure, so the patient can use it after anesthesia
Preoperative teaching prepares the patient to use PCA on awakening.
With a demonstration of the pump
Demonstrating the pump helps the patient learn to use it.
With teach-back to confirm understanding
Teach-back confirms the patient and family understand PCA use.
Only after the patient is sedated in recovery
Teaching must occur before the patient becomes sedated.
Only in writing, with no verbal explanation
Instruction should be verbal and written and include demonstration.
alt.ex: Teach before the procedure, demonstrate the pump, and reinforce with teach-back before the patient becomes sedated.

items.q: A nurse finds a patient’s daughter pressing the PCA button while the patient is asleep. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Only your mother should press it, because it is a safety feature.”
items.ex: PCA by proxy bypasses the safety feature that requires an awake patient to activate the device.
w: “Thank you for helping keep her pain under control.”
Pressing the button for the patient is dangerous and must be stopped.
“Press it only once per lockout interval while she sleeps.”
Family should not press the button at all, regardless of timing.
“That is fine if she grimaced before falling asleep.”
Earlier grimacing does not make PCA by proxy safe.

alt.q: Why is PCA by proxy dangerous?
alt.a: It bypasses the need for an awake patient to activate a dose
alt.ex: A sedated patient cannot press the button, which protects against overdose; proxy dosing removes that safeguard.
w: It shortens the programmed lockout interval
Proxy dosing does not change the pump’s lockout settings.
It changes the basal rate on the pump
Pressing the button delivers demand doses only.
It disconnects the tubing from the IV line
Pressing the button does not affect the tubing connection.

items.q: Where does the nurse connect the PCA tubing to the patient’s IV system?
items.a: The injection port nearest the patient
items.ex: Inserting the adapter at the port nearest the patient establishes the route and prevents use of PCA tubing for other IV push drugs.
w: The injection port farthest from the patient
The adapter is inserted into the port nearest the patient.
Directly into the primary IV solution bag
PCA tubing connects at an injection port, not into the IV bag.
Any port, so the PCA line can be used for IV push drugs
PCA tubing must not be used to give other drugs by IV push.

alt.q: How long should the nurse scrub the injection port with an antiseptic swab before connecting PCA tubing?
alt.a: 15 seconds, then allow it to dry
alt.ex: Scrubbing vigorously for 15 seconds and allowing it to dry reduces the risk of catheter-related bloodstream infection.
w: 5 seconds, then blow on it to dry
A brief wipe is inadequate, and blowing contaminates the port.
30 seconds, then wipe it dry with gauze
Wiping dry removes the antiseptic’s effect; allow it to air dry.
2 seconds, then connect immediately
The port must be scrubbed for 15 seconds and allowed to dry.

items.q: Which equipment should the nurse gather for starting PCA? Select all that apply.
o: Opioid reversal agent such as naloxone
A reversal agent must be available for respiratory depression.
Pulse oximetry and capnography equipment
These monitor for oversedation and respiratory distress.
Needleless connector
A needleless connector attaches PCA tubing to the IV line.
Antiseptic swab
The injection port is scrubbed before connection.
Sterile gloves
Clean gloves, when applicable, are listed for PCA setup.
Sterile suture removal kit
Suture removal has no role in setting up PCA.
items.ex: PCA equipment includes the pump and tubing, analgesic cartridge, needleless connector, antiseptic swab, naloxone, and monitoring devices.

alt.q: Before starting PCA, which elements of the order does the nurse check on the MAR? Select all that apply.
o: Medication name and dosage
The drug and dose are verified against the order.
Lockout period
The lockout period must match the order.
Frequency: demand, continuous, or both
The nurse verifies whether doses are demand, continuous, or both.
Route of administration
The route is checked against the provider’s order.
The patient’s preferred pain scale
Pain scale choice is an assessment decision, not part of the medication order.
alt.ex: The nurse checks the patient’s name, drug and dose, route, lockout period, and dosing frequency against the order.

items.q: A patient using PCA after surgery is difficult to arouse and responds minimally to physical stimulation. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Stop the PCA and notify the health care provider immediately
items.ex: A sedated patient who is not easily aroused is at risk of respiratory depression; stop the PCA and notify the provider at once.
w: Encourage the patient to press the button more often
More opioid would worsen sedation and respiratory depression.
Document the finding and reassess in 4 hours
Oversedation requires immediate action and monitoring every 10 minutes or more.
Lengthen the lockout interval and continue the PCA
The PCA must be stopped, not adjusted, when the patient is not easily aroused.

alt.q: A patient on PCA is somnolent and minimally responsive. After stopping the PCA, how often should the nurse monitor vital signs and oxygen saturation?
alt.a: Every 10 minutes or more often
alt.ex: For a sedated patient who is not easily aroused, monitor VS, oxygen saturation, and/or capnography every 10 minutes or more often.
w: Every 30 minutes
Every 30 minutes is too infrequent for a patient at risk of respiratory depression.
Every 1 to 2 hours
Every 1 to 2 hours is routine postoperative monitoring, not care for oversedation.
Every 4 hours
Every 4 hours is far too infrequent for an oversedated patient.

items.q: A patient on PCA is sedated and not easily aroused. After stopping the PCA and notifying the provider, which additional actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Elevate the head of the bed 30 degrees unless contraindicated
Elevating the head of the bed supports breathing.
Ask family members if they pressed the button
PCA by proxy is a possible cause of oversedation.
Review the MAR for other sedating drugs
Other sedating drugs add to opioid sedation.
Prepare to administer naloxone
An opioid reversal agent may be needed.
Let the patient sleep undisturbed until fully awake
The patient needs frequent monitoring and stimulation to breathe deeply.
Lower the head of the bed flat to rest
The head of the bed is elevated 30 degrees unless contraindicated.
items.ex: For oversedation, elevate the head of bed, encourage deep breaths, apply ordered oxygen, look for causes, and prepare naloxone.

alt.q: Which actions help determine why a patient on PCA became oversedated? Select all that apply.
o: Evaluate the amount of opioid delivered in the past 4 to 8 hours
Reviewing recent opioid delivery shows whether dosing caused sedation.
Ask family whether they pressed the button without the patient’s knowledge
PCA by proxy can cause oversedation.
Review the MAR for other sedating medications
Other sedating drugs can add to opioid effects.
Ask the patient to rate pain before taking any action
Safety comes first; the PCA is stopped and the provider notified.
Increase the demand dose to test the response
More opioid would worsen oversedation.
alt.ex: Reviewing recent opioid amounts, possible proxy dosing, and other sedating drugs helps identify the cause of oversedation.

items.q: A patient is at highest risk for oversedation and respiratory distress during the first 24 hours of PCA administration.
items.a: True
items.ex: Risk is highest in the first 24 hours, so monitoring is more frequent at the start and at night.
items.ww: The first 24 hours carry the greatest risk, which is why monitoring is most frequent then.

alt.q: Hypoventilation during PCA is least likely at night while the patient sleeps.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hypoventilation and hypoxia tend to occur during sleep, so monitor more often at night.
alt.ww: Opioid-induced respiratory depression is regulated by sleep-wake mechanisms and tends to occur during sleep.

items.q: Which documentation entry best records a patient’s response to PCA?
items.a: Pain 3 of 10 after walking; POSS 1; RR 16
items.ex: Documenting “PCA in use” or “PCA effective” is inadequate; record pain ratings, sedation scores, and vital signs.
w: PCA in use; patient resting
“PCA in use” is not an adequate record of the patient’s pain level.
PCA effective; no complaints
“PCA effective” does not document the actual pain rating.
Patient comfortable with PCA
A vague statement does not capture pain intensity or sedation level.

alt.q: How does the nurse calculate the total infused PCA dose for documentation?
alt.a: Add the demand and continuous doses together
alt.ex: The infused dose is calculated by adding demand and continuous doses and entering the total on the flow sheet.
w: Multiply the number of attempts by the demand dose
Attempts include presses during lockout that delivered no drug.
Count only the demand doses delivered
Continuous (basal) doses must be included in the total.
Subtract the basal dose from the demand doses
Basal and demand doses are added, not subtracted.

items.q: When PCA is discontinued, two RNs must witness the [[wastage|waste|wasting]] of remaining opioid and sign the record.
items.ex: Two-RN witnessing meets Controlled Substances Act requirements for documenting Schedule II drugs.

alt.q: To meet the Controlled Substances Act, opioid [[wastage|waste|wasting]] from a PCA must be witnessed by two RNs.
alt.ex: Two-RN witnessing meets Controlled Substances Act requirements for documenting Schedule II drugs.

items.q: During the first 12 hours after surgery, how often does the nurse monitor a patient using PCA for sedation and respiratory status, per the skill?
items.a: Every 1 to 2 hours
items.ex: Monitor every 1 to 2 hours for the first 12 hours, and more often at the start and at night.
w: Every 4 hours
Every 4 hours is too infrequent during the highest-risk period.
Every 8 hours
Every 8 hours is far too infrequent after starting PCA.
Once each shift
Once a shift misses early signs of oversedation.

alt.q: Which monitoring approach has been found superior for earlier identification of respiratory depression and oversedation in patients on PCA?
alt.a: Nurse observation using the POSS
alt.ex: Studies report nurse observation with the POSS is superior for early detection; oximetry and capnography add information.
w: Pulse oximetry while on supplemental oxygen
Oximetry has low sensitivity for hypoventilation when oxygen is used.
Capnography as the only monitoring
Evidence is insufficient to firmly recommend capnography alone.
Trending blood pressure readings
Blood pressure is not the best early indicator of oversedation.

items.q: A patient using PCA reports pain at 8 on a 0-to-10 scale despite pressing the button often. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Perform a complete pain reassessment and inspect the IV site
items.ex: For continued pain, reassess pain, look for other complications, inspect the IV site for occlusion or infiltration, and check pump function.
w: Press the button for the patient after each lockout
Anyone other than the patient pressing the button is dangerous.
Shorten the lockout interval without an order
Pump settings follow the provider’s order and require a second RN check.
Tell the patient that some pain is expected with PCA
Continued pain requires reassessment, not reassurance alone.

alt.q: A patient with severe hand arthritis cannot press the PCA button well enough to keep pain controlled. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Consult the provider about another route or a basal dose
alt.ex: If the patient cannot manipulate the device, consult the provider about an alternative route or possibly a basal dose.
w: Have a family member press the button for the patient
Proxy dosing by family is not recommended in adults.
Press the button for the patient every lockout period
Nurse activation requires specific authorized criteria, not routine dosing.
Continue the PCA and reassess the patient tomorrow
Unrelieved pain needs prompt action, not delayed reassessment.

items.q: PCA can be used at home by patients who are in hospice or who have moderate to severe pain caused by cancer.
items.a: True
items.ex: Home PCA is used in hospice and for moderate to severe cancer pain after the patient’s and caregiver’s abilities are assessed.
items.ww: The skill’s home care considerations specifically describe PCA use in these patients at home.

alt.q: Because PCA pumps are locked, the patient’s and family caregiver’s understanding need not be assessed before home use.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Before home PCA, thoroughly assess the patient’s and caregiver’s understanding, safety measures, and dosing approach.
alt.ww: Locked pumps prevent tampering but do not replace assessment of the caregivers’ ability to use PCA safely.

sections.name: Nutrients: The biochemical units of nutrition

items.q: Which term describes the energy needed at rest to maintain life-sustaining activities such as breathing, circulation, heart rate, and temperature for a specific amount of time?
items.a: Basal metabolic rate
items.ex: The basal metabolic rate (BMR) is the energy needed at rest to maintain life-sustaining activities for a specific time.
w: Nutrient density
Nutrient density is the proportion of essential nutrients to the number of kilocalories.
Nitrogen balance
Nitrogen balance means nitrogen intake and output are equal; it is not an energy measure.
Gluconeogenesis
Gluconeogenesis is the conversion of amino acids and glycerol into glucose for energy.

alt.q: What does the resting energy expenditure (REE) represent?
alt.a: The energy consumed over 24 hours to maintain the body’s resting internal working function
alt.ex: REE, or resting metabolic rate, is the energy needed over a 24-hour period to maintain resting internal body function.
w: The energy a person uses during 1 hour of moderate to intense exercise
REE describes energy used at rest over 24 hours, not during exercise.
The proportion of essential nutrients compared with the kilocalories in a food
That describes nutrient density, not energy expenditure.
The kilocalories stored as glycogen in the liver and muscle after a meal
Glycogen is a small energy reserve; REE is the energy consumed at rest.

items.q: A patient’s daily kilocalorie intake has consistently exceeded the body’s energy demands for several months. Which outcome should the nurse expect?
items.a: Weight gain
items.ex: Weight gain occurs when kilocalories exceed energy demands; weight is stable only when intake meets requirements.
w: Weight loss
Weight loss results when kilocalories fall below energy requirements.
Stable body weight
Weight stays stable only when food intake matches energy requirements.
Negative nitrogen balance
Negative nitrogen balance comes from tissue loss in conditions such as burns or starvation, not excess kilocalories.

alt.q: A patient eats fewer kilocalories than the body requires each day for several weeks. Which change in body weight does the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: A gradual loss of body weight
alt.ex: Decreasing kilocalories below energy requirements results in weight loss.
w: A gradual gain in body weight
Weight gain occurs when kilocalories exceed energy demands.
No change in body weight
Weight is stable only when intake meets energy requirements.
An increase in lean muscle mass
Adding lean muscle (anabolism) requires adequate nutrients and positive nitrogen balance.

items.q: Which nutrient is the main source of energy in the diet and supplies glucose as the main fuel for the brain?
items.a: Carbohydrates
items.ex: Carbohydrates are the main dietary energy source and supply glucose for the brain, exercising muscles, and blood cell production.
w: Proteins
Protein’s essential role is growth, maintenance, and repair; it is spared when carbohydrate intake is adequate.
Fats
Fats are the most calorie-dense nutrient, but carbohydrates are the main energy source and brain fuel.
Minerals
Minerals are inorganic elements that stimulate biochemical reactions; they do not provide energy.

alt.q: A nurse explains why carbohydrates are needed even during a weight-loss plan. Which body function relies on carbohydrate (glucose) as its main fuel?
alt.a: Brain function
alt.ex: Glucose from carbohydrates is the main fuel for the brain, exercising skeletal muscles, blood cell production, and the renal medulla.
w: Storage of fat-soluble vitamins
Fat-soluble vitamins are stored in the body’s fatty compartments; this does not depend on glucose fuel.
Maintenance of nitrogen balance
Nitrogen balance depends on protein intake and output, not glucose fuel.
Synthesis of vitamin K by colon bacteria
Colon bacteria synthesize vitamin K; this is not a glucose-fueled body function.

items.q: What is a Monosaccharide?
items.a: A simple sugar such as glucose or fructose
items.ex: Carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, disaccharides, or polysaccharides; fiber is a polysaccharide that digestive enzymes cannot break down.
w: Two simple sugars plus water, such as lactose or sucrose
That goes with Disaccharide.
A complex carbohydrate such as starch that is not water soluble
That goes with Polysaccharide.
The structural part of plants not broken down by digestive enzymes
That goes with Fiber.

alt.q: What is a Disaccharide?
alt.a: Two simple sugars plus water, such as lactose or sucrose
alt.ex: Carbohydrates are classified as monosaccharides, disaccharides, or polysaccharides; fiber is a polysaccharide that digestive enzymes cannot break down.
w: A simple sugar such as glucose or fructose
That goes with Monosaccharide.
A complex carbohydrate such as starch that is not water soluble
That goes with Polysaccharide.
The structural part of plants not broken down by digestive enzymes
That goes with Fiber.

items.q: Insoluble fiber is not digestible and does not contribute calories to the diet.
items.a: True
items.ex: Insoluble fiber passes through without being digested, so it adds no calories.
items.ww: Only digestible nutrients supply calories; insoluble fiber is not broken down by digestive enzymes.

alt.q: Insoluble fiber is slowly digested in the colon and supplies a steady source of calories.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Insoluble fiber is not digestible and contributes no calories to the diet.
alt.ww: Digestive enzymes cannot break fiber down, so it provides no calories.

items.q: Which functions in the body require protein? Select all that apply.
o: Growth, maintenance, and repair of body tissue
This is protein’s essential role.
Blood clotting and fluid regulation
Blood clotting and fluid regulation both require proteins.
Acid-base balance
Proteins are needed to maintain acid-base balance.
Transport of nutrients and many drugs in the blood
Proteins carry nutrients and many drugs in the bloodstream.
Main fuel for the brain
Glucose from carbohydrates, not protein, is the brain’s main fuel.
Main form of reserve energy stored in adipose tissue
Fat stored as adipose tissue is the major energy reserve; protein is stored in muscle.
items.ex: Proteins build and repair tissue and are needed for clotting, fluid regulation, acid-base balance, and transport in the blood.

alt.q: Which body substances are made of protein? Select all that apply.
o: Collagen
Collagen is a structural protein.
Hormones and enzymes
Hormones and enzymes are made of protein.
Immune cells
Immune cells are made of protein.
Albumin and insulin
Albumin and insulin are simple proteins made only of amino acids or their derivatives.
Glycogen
Glycogen is synthesized from glucose and stored in the liver and muscle.
Triglycerides
Triglycerides are fats composed of fatty acids.
alt.ex: Collagen, hormones, enzymes, immune cells, and simple proteins such as albumin and insulin are made of protein.

items.q: Which statement best describes a complete protein?
items.a: It contains all essential amino acids to support growth and maintain nitrogen balance
items.ex: A complete protein supplies all essential amino acids needed for growth and nitrogen balance.
w: It combines a simple protein with a nonprotein substance such as a lipid
That describes a complex protein, such as lipoprotein.
It is missing one or more of the nine indispensable amino acids
That describes an incomplete protein, found in grains, nuts, legumes, and vegetables.
It contains only amino acids or their derivatives, such as albumin
That describes a simple protein, such as albumin or insulin.

alt.q: A patient who eats no animal products asks which plant food provides a complete protein. Which food should the nurse identify?
alt.a: Soy
alt.ex: Most complete proteins come from animal sources, but plant sources such as soy are also complete.
w: Oats
Grains are incomplete proteins missing one or more indispensable amino acids.
Peanuts
Nuts and legumes are incomplete proteins.
Carrots
Vegetables are incomplete proteins.

items.q: What are complementary proteins?
items.a: Pairs of incomplete proteins that together supply the protein of a complete source
items.ex: Combining complementary incomplete proteins supplies the total protein provided by complete protein sources.
w: Animal proteins that contain every one of the essential amino acids
Proteins containing all essential amino acids are complete proteins.
Simple proteins bonded to a nonprotein substance such as a lipid
A simple protein combined with a nonprotein substance is a complex protein.
Proteins that spare carbohydrate from being used as an energy source
Carbohydrate spares protein, not the reverse; this does not define complementary proteins.

alt.q: A patient follows a plant-based diet built on grains, legumes, and nuts. Why does the nurse encourage combining these foods?
alt.a: Pairing incomplete proteins provides the amino acids found in complete proteins
alt.ex: Grains, legumes, and nuts are incomplete proteins; combined as complementary proteins they supply complete protein.
w: Combining them lowers the total kilocalories of each meal
The goal of complementary proteins is amino acid completeness, not fewer kilocalories.
Combining them increases absorption of fat-soluble vitamins
Fat-soluble vitamin absorption is unrelated to combining protein sources.
Combining them converts plant fiber into digestible calories
Insoluble fiber stays indigestible and contributes no calories.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient admitted with extensive burns. Which nitrogen state does the nurse expect, and why?
items.a: Negative nitrogen balance, because tissue destruction causes more nitrogen loss than gain
items.ex: Burns, infection, fever, starvation, head injury, and trauma cause negative nitrogen balance through tissue destruction or fluid loss.
w: Positive nitrogen balance, because tissue repair raises nitrogen intake above output
Positive balance is needed for healing, but burns cause tissue loss that produces negative balance.
Nitrogen balance, because intake and output of nitrogen remain equal after injury
Balance means intake equals output; burns increase nitrogen loss.
Positive nitrogen balance, because fever increases the use of nitrogen for energy
Fever is a cause of negative nitrogen balance, not positive.

alt.q: Which patient is expected to be in positive nitrogen balance?
alt.a: A woman with a normal pregnancy
alt.ex: Positive nitrogen balance is required for growth, normal pregnancy, maintaining lean mass and organs, and wound healing.
w: A man with a head injury after a fall
Head injury causes negative nitrogen balance.
A child with a high fever from an infection
Fever and infection cause negative nitrogen balance.
An older adult with prolonged starvation
Starvation causes negative nitrogen balance and tissue wasting.

items.q: Which conditions place a patient at risk for negative nitrogen balance? Select all that apply.
o: Infection
Infection increases nitrogen loss through tissue destruction.
Burns
Burns cause tissue destruction and loss of nitrogen-containing fluids.
Starvation
Starvation leads to wasting of body tissues and nitrogen loss.
Trauma
Trauma increases nitrogen loss from tissue destruction.
Normal pregnancy
Normal pregnancy requires positive nitrogen balance.
Normal childhood growth
Growth requires positive nitrogen balance.
items.ex: Negative nitrogen balance occurs with infection, burns, fever, starvation, head injury, and trauma, when nitrogen loss exceeds gain.

alt.q: Which situations require positive nitrogen balance? Select all that apply.
o: Wound healing
The body uses nitrogen to build and repair tissue during healing.
Normal pregnancy
Pregnancy requires positive nitrogen balance.
Maintaining lean muscle mass and vital organs
Maintenance of lean mass and organs requires positive balance.
Starvation
Starvation causes tissue wasting and negative nitrogen balance.
Head injury
Head injury causes negative nitrogen balance.
alt.ex: Positive nitrogen balance supports growth, normal pregnancy, maintenance of lean mass and organs, and wound healing.

items.q: A patient recovering from surgery has a large healing wound. The nurse teaches that the diet must include enough carbohydrates and fats along with protein. What is the rationale?
items.a: Adequate nonprotein kilocalories spare protein for tissue growth and repair
items.ex: When carbohydrate meets energy needs, protein is spared as an energy source and can be used for repair.
w: Carbohydrates and fats supply the nitrogen needed for wound repair
Nitrogen comes from protein metabolism, not from carbohydrates or fats.
Protein cannot be used for energy under any circumstances
Protein does provide energy; the goal is to spare it for repair.
Carbohydrates contain the essential amino acids missing from protein foods
Amino acids come from protein, not carbohydrates.

alt.q: Why does a diet need to provide adequate kilocalories from nonprotein sources?
alt.a: So that protein can be used for growth, maintenance, and repair rather than energy
alt.ex: Protein’s essential role is growth, maintenance, and repair; sufficient carbohydrate spares protein as an energy source.
w: So that fat-soluble vitamins can be stored in adipose tissue
Vitamin storage is not the reason for nonprotein kilocalories.
So that the body can stay in negative nitrogen balance
Negative nitrogen balance reflects tissue loss and is not a goal.
So that insoluble fiber can be converted into usable glucose
Insoluble fiber is not digestible and supplies no calories.

items.q: [[Linoleic acid|linoleic]] is an unsaturated fatty acid and the only essential fatty acid in humans.
items.ex: Linoleic acid is the only essential fatty acid; unsaturated fatty acids are important for metabolic processes.

alt.q: The only fatty acid that is essential in humans is [[linoleic acid|linoleic]], which is unsaturated.
alt.ex: Linoleic acid is the only essential fatty acid; unsaturated fatty acids are important for metabolic processes.

items.q: Which nutrient is the most calorie-dense?
items.a: Fat
items.ex: Fats (lipids), composed of triglycerides and fatty acids, are the most calorie-dense nutrient.
w: Carbohydrate
Carbohydrate is the main energy source, but fat provides more kilocalories per gram.
Protein
Protein provides energy but is less calorie-dense than fat.
Fiber
Insoluble fiber is not digestible and contributes no calories.

alt.q: Which nutrient, composed of triglycerides and fatty acids, provides the most kilocalories for its amount?
alt.a: Fat
alt.ex: Fats (lipids) are made of triglycerides and fatty acids and are the most calorie-dense nutrient.
w: Carbohydrate
Carbohydrate is the main dietary energy source but is less calorie-dense than fat.
Protein
Protein is made of amino acids and is less calorie-dense than fat.
Water
Water supplies no kilocalories.

items.q: Infants have the greatest percentage of total body water, and older adults have the least.
items.a: True
items.ex: Infants have the most body water because of greater surface area; older adults have the least.
items.ww: Body water percentage is highest in infancy and declines to its lowest in older adulthood.

alt.q: Older adults have a greater percentage of total body water than infants because they have more body surface area.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Infants have the greatest percentage of total body water because of their greater surface area.
alt.ww: Older adults have the least total body water, which raises their risk for dehydration.

items.q: Which patient is expected to have the lowest percentage of total body water?
items.a: An older adult with a large amount of adipose tissue
items.ex: Adipose tissue repels water and older people have the least body water, so this patient has the lowest percentage.
w: A healthy full-term newborn infant
Infants have the greatest percentage of total body water.
A young adult with a high proportion of lean muscle
Lean muscle contains more water than any tissue except blood.
A school-age child with a normal body weight
Children have more body water than older adults, especially those with more fat.

alt.q: Which body tissue contains more water than any other tissue except blood?
alt.a: Lean muscle
alt.ex: Lean muscle contains more water than any other tissue except blood.
w: Adipose tissue
Adipose tissue repels water, decreasing the percentage of total body water.
Bone
Bone is not identified as the most water-rich tissue.
Skin
Skin is not identified as the most water-rich tissue after blood.

items.q: Water makes up approximately what percentage of total body weight?
items.ex: Water makes up 60% to 70% of total body weight, and proper cellular function depends on an adequate fluid environment.
w: This underestimates body water; water makes up 60% to 70% of body weight.
This underestimates body water; water makes up 60% to 70% of body weight.
This overestimates body water; water makes up 60% to 70% of body weight.

alt.q: A nurse explains why adequate fluid intake matters for cellular function. Which statement about body water is accurate?
alt.a: Water makes up 60% to 70% of total body weight
alt.ex: Water makes up 60% to 70% of total body weight, and cells depend on an adequate fluid environment.
w: Water makes up 20% to 30% of total body weight
This underestimates body water, which is 60% to 70% of body weight.
Water makes up 40% to 50% of total body weight
This underestimates body water, which is 60% to 70% of body weight.
Water makes up 85% to 95% of total body weight
This overestimates body water, which is 60% to 70% of body weight.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “I take extra vitamin A and vitamin E capsules every day because extra vitamins just wash out.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Vitamins A and E are stored in body fat, so taking too much can lead to toxicity.”
items.ex: Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K are stored in fatty compartments, and the high storage capacity makes toxicity possible.
w: “That is correct; any vitamin you do not use is excreted in the urine.”
Fat-soluble vitamins are stored, not readily excreted, so excess can build up.
“Vitamins A and E must be taken daily because the body cannot store them.”
That describes water-soluble vitamins B complex and C, not A and E.
“Vitamins A and E can be safely taken in any amount because they are antioxidants.”
Antioxidant action does not prevent toxicity from excess fat-soluble vitamins.

alt.q: Which group lists only fat-soluble vitamins?
alt.a: Vitamins A, D, E, and K
alt.ex: The fat-soluble vitamins are A, D, E, and K; they are stored in the body’s fatty compartments.
w: Vitamins B, C, D, and K
Vitamins B complex and C are water soluble.
Vitamins A, B, C, and E
Vitamins B complex and C are water soluble.
Vitamins C, D, E, and K
Vitamin C is water soluble.

items.q: Because the body does not store water-soluble vitamins, toxicity from these vitamins cannot occur.
items.a: False
items.ex: Water-soluble vitamins are not stored, but toxicity can still occur.
items.ww: Not being stored does not make excess intake harmless; toxicity is still possible.

alt.q: Because the body does not store water-soluble vitamins, daily food intake needs to include adequate amounts to meet requirements.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Vitamins C and B complex are not stored, so daily intake must meet requirements.
alt.ww: Without body stores, missed intake is not covered by reserves as fat-soluble vitamins are.

items.q: Which nutrients have antioxidant properties that neutralize free radicals? Select all that apply.
o: Vitamin A
Vitamin A is an antioxidant.
Vitamin C
Vitamin C is an antioxidant.
Vitamin E
Vitamin E is an antioxidant.
Selenium
Selenium is a trace element with antioxidant properties.
Vitamin K
Vitamin K is fat soluble but is not listed as an antioxidant.
Sodium
Sodium is not identified as an antioxidant.
items.ex: Vitamins A, C, and E, beta-carotene, and the trace element selenium act as antioxidants against oxidative cell damage.

alt.q: A nurse teaches about foods that help protect cells from oxidative damage. Which nutrients act as antioxidants? Select all that apply.
o: Beta-carotene
Beta-carotene is an antioxidant.
Vitamin C
Vitamin C is an antioxidant.
Vitamin E
Vitamin E is an antioxidant.
Vitamin D
Vitamin D is fat soluble and comes from the sun and diet, but is not listed as an antioxidant.
Cadmium
Cadmium is a trace element that can have toxic effects.
alt.ex: Beta-carotene and vitamins A, C, and E neutralize the free radicals that cause oxidative damage to cells and tissues.

items.q: How do macrominerals differ from microminerals (trace elements)?
items.a: Macrominerals have a daily requirement of 100 mg or more; microminerals, less than 100 mg
items.ex: Macrominerals are required in amounts of 100 mg or more daily; microminerals (trace elements) are required in amounts under 100 mg.
w: Macrominerals have a daily requirement of 10 mg or more; microminerals, less than 10 mg
The dividing line is 100 mg per day, not 10 mg.
Macrominerals have a daily requirement of 1000 mg or more; microminerals, less than 1000 mg
The dividing line is 100 mg per day, not 1000 mg.
Macrominerals have a daily requirement of less than 100 mg; microminerals, 100 mg or more
This reverses the definitions; macrominerals are needed in the larger amounts.

alt.q: A mineral has a daily requirement of 150 mg. How is it classified?
alt.a: Macromineral
alt.ex: Minerals required in amounts of 100 mg or more per day are macrominerals.
w: Micromineral
Microminerals are required in amounts under 100 mg per day.
Trace element
Trace elements are microminerals, required in amounts under 100 mg per day.
Antioxidant vitamin
Minerals are inorganic elements; vitamins are organic substances.

items.q: Which statement correctly describes the pH of digestive secretions?
items.a: Saliva is relatively neutral, gastric juice is highly acidic, and small intestine secretions are alkaline

w: Saliva is highly acidic, gastric juice is alkaline, and small intestine secretions are relatively neutral
Gastric juice is acidic, not alkaline, and intestinal secretions are alkaline.
Saliva is alkaline, gastric juice is relatively neutral, and small intestine secretions are highly acidic
Gastric juice is highly acidic and intestinal secretions are alkaline.
Saliva, gastric juice, and small intestine secretions all have the same relatively neutral pH
The secretions differ in pH, matching the enzymes that act in each area.

alt.q: As chyme moves through the small intestine and mixes with its secretions, what happens to the activity of gastric enzymes?
alt.a: It is inhibited as the mixture becomes increasingly alkaline
alt.ex: The increasingly alkaline mixture inhibits gastric enzymes and promotes the action of duodenal secretions.
w: It increases as the mixture becomes increasingly acidic
The mixture becomes more alkaline, not acidic, in the small intestine.
It is unchanged because enzymes work at any pH
Most enzymes work best at a specific pH.
It increases because bile activates pepsinogen
Bile emulsifies fat; it does not activate gastric enzymes.

items.q: A patient asks why it matters to chew food thoroughly. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
items.a: Longer chewing allows more starch digestion by salivary amylase in the mouth
items.ex: Salivary amylase begins converting cooked starch to maltose; the longer food is chewed, the more starch digestion occurs.
w: Longer chewing allows salivary enzymes to break down proteins and fats chemically
Mouth enzymes do not react with proteins and fats, which are only broken down physically.
Longer chewing releases intrinsic factor needed to absorb vitamin B12
Intrinsic factor is secreted by parietal cells in the stomach.
Longer chewing triggers secretion of bile from the gallbladder into the mouth
Bile enters the small intestine, not the mouth, and emulsifies fat.

alt.q: Which nutrient begins chemical digestion in the mouth?
alt.a: Cooked starch
alt.ex: Salivary amylase acts on cooked starch to begin its conversion to maltose.
w: Protein
Proteins are broken down physically in the mouth but remain chemically unchanged.
Fat
Fats remain chemically unchanged in the mouth because mouth enzymes do not act on them.
Fiber
Fiber is not broken down by digestive enzymes.

items.q: Stimulation by the parasympathetic nervous system, such as through the vagus nerve, increases gastrointestinal tract action.
items.a: True
items.ex: Parasympathetic nerve stimulation, for example by the vagus nerve, increases GI tract activity.
items.ww: Vagal (parasympathetic) input stimulates rather than slows digestive secretion and motility.

alt.q: Stimulation of the vagus nerve slows gastrointestinal secretion and motility.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The vagus nerve is parasympathetic, and parasympathetic stimulation increases GI tract action.
alt.ww: Vagal stimulation increases, not decreases, GI activity.

items.q: A patient has lost the parietal cells of the stomach lining. The nurse anticipates a problem absorbing which nutrient?
items.a: Vitamin B12
items.ex: Parietal cells secrete intrinsic factor, which is necessary for absorption of vitamin B12 in the ileum.
w: Vitamin K
Vitamin K is synthesized by colon bacteria and does not depend on intrinsic factor.
Vitamin C
Vitamin C is water soluble and absorbed easily without intrinsic factor.
Calcium
Calcium absorption does not depend on intrinsic factor.

alt.q: Which substance do the parietal cells of the stomach secrete?
alt.a: Hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor
alt.ex: Parietal cells secrete hydrochloric acid and intrinsic factor, which is needed for vitamin B12 absorption.
w: Pepsinogen and gastrin
Pepsinogen and gastrin are secreted by the chief cells and trigger parietal cell secretion.
Secretin and cholecystokinin
Secretin and CCK are hormones secreted by the small intestine.
Bile and bicarbonate

alt.ww: Activity, not strict intake restriction, is emphasized for adolescents.

items.q: Which findings are diagnostic criteria for bulimia nervosa? Select all that apply.
o: Recurrent episodes of binge eating
Binge eating is a core criterion for bulimia nervosa.
A feeling of lack of control over eating during binges
Loss of control during binges is a criterion.
Self-induced vomiting or laxative use to prevent weight gain
These are inappropriate compensatory behaviors.
Binge eating and compensatory behaviors at least once a week for 3 months
This frequency and duration is required.
Significantly low body weight from restricting energy intake
This is a criterion for anorexia nervosa.
items.ex: Bulimia nervosa involves recurrent binges, lack of control, compensatory behaviors at least weekly for 3 months, and self-evaluation tied to shape.

alt.q: Which findings are diagnostic criteria for anorexia nervosa? Select all that apply.
o: Restriction of energy intake leading to significantly low body weight
This is a criterion for anorexia nervosa.
Intense fear of gaining weight despite a significantly low weight
This is a criterion for anorexia nervosa.
Claiming to feel fat even when emaciated
This shows disturbance in how body weight or shape is experienced.
Binge eating with compensatory behaviors weekly for 3 months
This is a criterion for bulimia nervosa.
Steady weight gain from regular large meals
Weight gain does not match anorexia nervosa criteria.
alt.ex: Anorexia nervosa involves restriction causing significantly low weight, intense fear of weight gain, and disturbed body image.

items.q: A nurse is counseling a pregnant 16-year-old about nutrition during pregnancy. Which approach is likely to be best tolerated?
items.a: Offering suggestions rather than rigid directions
items.ex: Teenagers better tolerate suggestions than rigid directions, and many do not want to gain weight.
w: Giving a strict meal plan with no room for food choices
Rigid directions are less well tolerated by teenagers.
Telling her to limit weight gain by skipping snacks
Limiting weight gain is not the goal; adequate nutrition protects mother and fetus.
Delaying nutrition counseling until the third trimester
Malnutrition at conception increases risk, so counseling should not be delayed.

alt.q: A pregnant 15-year-old tells the nurse, “I don’t want to gain weight.” Which nursing response is most likely to be well tolerated?
alt.a: “Here are a few snack ideas you might try that support your baby’s growth.”
alt.ex: Most teens do not want to gain weight, and suggestions are better tolerated than rigid directions.
w: “You must follow this exact meal plan every day without changes.”
Rigid directions are less well tolerated by teenagers.
“Skipping snacks is a good way to keep your weight down.”
Skipping meals or snacks contributes to nutrient deficiency, risking mother and fetus.
“We can talk about nutrition later in your pregnancy.”
Malnutrition at conception increases risk, so counseling should not wait.

items.q: Women of childbearing age need [[400]] mcg of folic acid daily, increasing to [[600]] mcg daily during pregnancy.
items.ex: Folic acid supports DNA synthesis and red blood cell growth; low intake can cause neural tube defects.

alt.q: During pregnancy, folic acid intake should increase to [[600]] mcg daily to help prevent fetal neural tube defects.
alt.ex: Folic acid supports DNA synthesis and red blood cell growth; low intake can cause neural tube defects.

items.q: A nurse teaches a woman who is breastfeeding. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I need about 500 extra kilocalories a day and should avoid caffeine and alcohol.”
items.ex: Lactation requires 500 kcal/day above usual intake, and caffeine, alcohol, and drugs are excreted in breast milk.
w: “I need fewer calories now because I am no longer pregnant.”
Milk production increases energy requirements by about 500 kcal/day.
“My protein needs are lower now than they were during pregnancy.”
Protein needs during lactation are greater than during pregnancy.
“I should drink as much fluid as possible, even beyond my thirst.”
Fluid intake should be adequate but not excessive.

alt.q: How much additional energy does a lactating woman need above the usual allowance?
alt.a: 500 kcal/day
alt.ex: Milk production increases energy requirements, so lactating women need 500 kcal/day above the usual allowance.
w: 100 kcal/day
This underestimates the energy cost of milk production.
1000 kcal/day
This overestimates; the recommendation is 500 kcal/day.
250 kcal/day
This underestimates; the recommendation is 500 kcal/day.

items.q: Although older adults need less energy because their metabolic rate slows, their vitamin and mineral requirements remain unchanged from middle adulthood.
items.a: True
items.ex: Adults 65 and older need less energy, but vitamin and mineral needs stay the same as in middle adulthood.
items.ww: Lower energy needs do not lower vitamin and mineral needs, so nutrient-dense foods become more important.

alt.q: Because their metabolic rate slows, older adults need fewer vitamins and minerals than middle-aged adults.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Vitamin and mineral requirements of older adults remain unchanged from middle adulthood.
alt.ww: Only energy needs decline with age; vitamin and mineral needs do not.

items.q: Which age-related gastrointestinal changes affect nutrition in older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced saliva production
Less saliva affects chewing and swallowing.
Increased taste threshold
A higher taste threshold alters food flavor and may decrease intake.
Decreased thirst sensation
Diminished thirst can lead to dehydration.
Decreased esophageal and colonic peristalsis
Slower peristalsis is an age-related GI change.
Increased gag reflex
The gag reflex is reduced, not increased, with aging.
Increased number of taste cells
Older adults often experience a decrease in taste cells.
items.ex: Aging brings tooth and gum changes, less saliva, oral mucosal atrophy, higher taste threshold, less thirst, reduced gag reflex, and slower peristalsis.

alt.q: Which adverse medication effects can impair nutrition in older adults? Select all that apply.
o: Anorexia
Medications can cause loss of appetite.
Xerostomia
Dry mouth from medications affects eating.
Early satiety
Feeling full early reduces intake.
Impaired smell and taste perception
Altered smell and taste reduce enjoyment of food.
Increased saliva production
Medications commonly cause dry mouth, not increased saliva.
alt.ex: Medication effects such as anorexia, GI bleeding, xerostomia, early satiety, and altered smell and taste impair older adults’ nutrition.

items.q: An 82-year-old patient is confused and weak, with hot, dry skin, a furrowed tongue, and a rapid pulse. Which condition should the nurse suspect first?
items.a: Dehydration
items.ex: Diminished thirst in older adults leads to dehydration, with confusion, weakness, hot dry skin, furrowed tongue, and rapid pulse.
w: Milk anemia
Milk anemia occurs in toddlers who drink excess milk.
Fluid overload
Hot, dry skin and a furrowed tongue indicate fluid deficit, not excess.
Osteoporosis
Osteoporosis is decreased bone mass density and does not cause these signs.

alt.q: Why are older adults at increased risk for dehydration?
alt.a: Thirst sensation diminishes, leading to inadequate fluid intake
alt.ex: Diminished thirst sensation in older adults leads to inadequate fluid intake or dehydration.
w: Older adults have the highest percentage of total body water
Older adults have the least total body water.
Saliva production increases, causing excess fluid loss
Saliva production decreases with aging.
The colon absorbs more water as people age
Colon water absorption is not the cause; reduced thirst is.

items.q: How do special diets based on religion, culture, or personal preference compare nutritionally with diets based on MyPlate guidelines?
items.a: They are not necessarily more or less nutritious, because good nutrition depends on a balanced intake of all nutrients
items.ex: Any eating pattern can be adequate or inadequate; what matters is a balanced intake of all required nutrients.
w: They are usually less nutritious, because they restrict foods recommended in national guidelines
Restrictions do not automatically make a diet inadequate; careful choices can still meet nutrient needs.
They are usually more nutritious, because they were developed long before federal guidelines existed
Age of a dietary tradition does not determine its nutritional value; balance of nutrients does.
They are nutritionally equal only when the patient also takes a daily multivitamin supplement
The book does not require supplements; balanced food choices determine adequacy.

alt.q: A student says, “Religious diets are always nutritionally inferior to MyPlate.” Which reply by the nurse is most accurate?
alt.a: A special diet can meet nutrient needs if it provides a balanced intake of all required nutrients.
alt.ex: Special diets are not inherently better or worse; balanced intake of all required nutrients is the key.
w: A special diet is always healthier because it limits processed and animal foods.
Special diets are not automatically healthier; adequacy still depends on balance.
A special diet can meet nutrient needs only if a dietitian prescribes it.
Adequacy depends on balanced food choices, not on who prescribes the diet.
A special diet should be replaced with MyPlate during any hospital stay.
Nurses respect religious and cultural food patterns rather than replacing them.

Drinks milk but avoids eggs

Avoids meat, fish, and poultry but eats eggs and milk

items.q: A parent tells the nurse that their 6-year-old follows a strict vegan diet. Which nutrient deficiency is the nurse most concerned about?
items.a: Vitamin B12
items.ex: Children on vegetarian diets are especially at risk for protein and vitamin deficiencies such as a lack of vitamin B12.
w: Vitamin C
Vitamin C is plentiful in fruits and vegetables, which a vegan diet includes.
Dietary fiber
Plant-based diets are naturally high in fiber, so fiber is not the concern.
Carbohydrate
Grains, fruits, and vegetables supply ample carbohydrate in a vegan diet.

alt.q: Which statement by a parent of a child following a vegetarian diet shows understanding of the nurse’s teaching?
alt.a: “I need to plan my child’s meals carefully so they get enough protein and vitamin B12.”
alt.ex: Careful planning helps vegetarian children avoid protein and vitamin deficiencies such as B12.
w: “Because plant foods are healthy, my child’s diet needs no special planning.”
Vegetarian children are especially at risk for deficiencies, so planning is needed.
“My child’s main risk is getting too much protein from beans and nuts.”
The risk is too little protein, not an excess.
“A vegetarian diet means my child will not need any vitamin B12 at all.”
Children still need vitamin B12; a lack of it is a key risk of vegetarian diets.

items.q: A Muslim patient tells the nurse that their religious observance is approaching. According to Table 45.3, which dietary practice should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: Fasting from sunrise to sunset for a month during Ramadan
items.ex: Muslim dietary practices include Ramadan fasting from sunrise to sunset for a month, and avoiding pork and alcohol.
w: Fasting for 24 hours on Yom Kippur, a day of atonement
Yom Kippur fasting is a Jewish practice, not a Muslim one.
Avoiding leavened bread for 8 days during Passover
Avoiding leavened bread during Passover is a Jewish practice.
Observing meatless days, commonly during the season of Lent
Meatless days during Lent are observed by some Christian faiths.

alt.q: A patient’s religion forbids pork and alcohol, requires ritualized animal slaughter for meat, and includes a month of daytime fasting. Which religion does this describe?
alt.a: Muslim
alt.ex: Table 45.3 lists pork, alcohol, ritualized slaughter, and Ramadan sunrise-to-sunset fasting for Muslims.
w: Hinduism
Hinduism restricts all meats, not only pork, and does not include Ramadan fasting.
Seventh-Day Adventist
Seventh-Day Adventists avoid pork and alcohol but do not observe Ramadan.
Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints
Latter-Day Saints restrict alcohol, tobacco, and caffeine, not pork or Ramadan fasting.

items.q: A hospitalized patient who keeps kosher receives a meal tray. Which item should the nurse question before serving it?
items.a: A cheeseburger with a glass of milk
items.ex: Jewish dietary law prohibits mixing milk or dairy products with meat dishes.
w: A baked fish fillet with scales and steamed rice
Fish with scales is permitted; only shellfish and scaleless fish are restricted.
A garden salad with oil and vinegar dressing
A plain salad contains no restricted meat, shellfish, blood, or meat–dairy mix.
A vegetable soup with a slice of bread
Neither vegetables nor ordinary bread are restricted outside Passover.

alt.q: A Jewish patient who follows kosher dietary laws asks for a snack. Which choice is consistent with these laws?
alt.a: A fruit cup and a slice of plain bread
alt.ex: Fruit and bread contain no pork, shellfish, blood, or meat–dairy mixing, so they fit kosher rules.
w: A ham and cheese sandwich
Pork is prohibited, and mixing meat with dairy is also not allowed.
A shrimp cocktail with sauce
Shellfish are restricted; only fish with scales are permitted.
A rare roast beef with a milkshake
Rare meat and blood are restricted, and meat may not be mixed with dairy.

items.q: A patient is a member of the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints. According to Table 45.3, which items does this faith restrict? Select all that apply.
o: Alcohol
Alcohol is restricted by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints.
Tobacco
Tobacco is listed as a restriction for Latter-Day Saints.
Caffeine, such as in teas, coffees, and sodas
Caffeine-containing beverages are restricted for Latter-Day Saints.
All meats
Restriction of all meats is listed for Hinduism, not Latter-Day Saints.
Mixing milk products with meat dishes
Avoiding milk with meat is a Jewish dietary law.
items.ex: Table 45.3 lists alcohol, tobacco, and caffeine (teas, coffees, sodas) for the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-Day Saints.

alt.q: A patient practices Judaism. According to Table 45.3, which dietary restrictions may apply? Select all that apply.
o: Pork
Pork is prohibited in Judaism.
Shellfish; only fish with scales are eaten
Judaism restricts shellfish and permits only fish with scales.
Mixing milk or dairy products with meat dishes
Kosher law forbids combining dairy with meat.
Blood, such as blood sausage, and rare meats
Blood and rare meats are restricted in Judaism.
Caffeine, such as in teas, coffees, and sodas
Caffeine restriction is listed for Latter-Day Saints and Seventh-Day Adventists.
All meats, including poultry and fish
Restricting all meats is a Hindu practice, not a Jewish one.
alt.ex: Judaism restricts pork, shellfish, predatory fowl, blood and rare meats, and mixing dairy with meat.

items.q: According to Table 45.3, Hinduism restricts all meats.
items.a: True
items.ex: Table 45.3 lists all meats, along with alcohol, as restrictions in Hinduism.
items.ww: The restriction of all meats is a key Hindu dietary practice, so the statement is correct.

alt.q: According to Table 45.3, Hinduism restricts pork but permits beef and other meats.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hinduism restricts all meats, not just pork.
alt.ww: Restricting only pork describes Muslim, Jewish, and Seventh-Day Adventist practice, not Hinduism.

items.q: Box 45.5 describes lactose intolerance in several ethnic groups. What is lactose intolerance, and what nutritional problem often results?
items.a: A deficiency of the intestinal enzyme lactase, which often leads to calcium deficiency
items.ex: Lactose intolerance affects nutrient absorption, so calcium deficiency and decreased bone mass density often result.
w: A deficiency of the pancreatic enzyme lipase, which often leads to vitamin K deficiency
Lipase digests fat; lactose intolerance involves the intestinal enzyme lactase.
An allergy to the protein in cow’s milk, which often leads to iron deficiency
Lactose intolerance is an enzyme deficiency, not a milk protein allergy.
A deficiency of the gastric enzyme pepsin, which often leads to protein deficiency
Pepsin digests protein; lactose intolerance is a lactase deficiency.

alt.q: A patient of Asian-Pacific descent has lactose intolerance and avoids dairy products. Which long-term problem should the nurse plan to help prevent?
alt.a: Decreased bone mass density from calcium deficiency
alt.ex: Lactose intolerance limits absorption and calcium intake, causing calcium deficiency and decreased bone mass density.
w: Iron-deficiency anemia from blood loss in the stool
Lactose intolerance is linked to calcium deficiency, not GI blood loss.
Elevated LDL cholesterol from a high-fat diet
Avoiding dairy does not raise LDL cholesterol; the concern is calcium.
Vitamin B12 deficiency from avoiding all meats
This patient avoids dairy, not meat; the book links lactose intolerance to calcium deficiency.

items.q: A patient whose culture follows the hot and cold theory of foods has pneumonia, which the patient views as a “cold” illness. Which meal is most consistent with the patient’s beliefs?
items.a: Beef with rice and eggs
items.ex: Cold illnesses such as pneumonia require hot foods; beef, rice, and eggs are classified as hot foods.
w: Chicken with beans and citrus fruit
Chicken, beans, and citrus fruits are classified as cold foods.
Fish with tropical fruit and honey
Fish, tropical fruits, and honey are cold foods.
Most vegetables with raisins and dairy
Most vegetables, raisins, and dairy products are cold foods.

alt.q: A patient who follows the hot and cold theory of foods has a fever, which is viewed as a “hot” condition. Which meal is most consistent with the patient’s beliefs?
alt.a: Fish with beans and citrus fruit
alt.ex: Hot conditions such as fever require cold foods; fish, beans, and citrus fruits are cold foods.
w: Lamb with chili peppers and rice
Lamb, chili peppers, and rice are hot foods.
Pork with onions and radishes
Pork, onions, and radishes are hot foods.
Eggs with peas and cheese
Eggs, peas, and cheese are classified as hot foods.

items.q: In the hot and cold theory of foods, which conditions are considered “cold” illnesses that require hot foods? Select all that apply.
o: Pneumonia
Pneumonia is a cold illness, so hot foods are used.
Earache
Earache is listed among the cold illnesses.
Rheumatism
Rheumatism is a cold illness requiring hot foods.
Cancer
Cancer is listed as a cold illness.
Pregnancy
Pregnancy is a hot condition that requires cold foods.
Diarrhea
Diarrhea is a hot condition that requires cold foods.
items.ex: Cold illnesses include menstruation, cancer, pneumonia, earache, colds, paralysis, headache, and rheumatism.

alt.q: In the hot and cold theory of foods, which conditions are considered “hot” conditions that require cold foods? Select all that apply.
o: Fever
Fever is a hot condition treated with cold foods.
Sore throat
Sore throat is listed among the hot conditions.
Constipation
Constipation is a hot condition requiring cold foods.
Headache
Headache is a cold illness that calls for hot foods.
Colds
Colds are cold illnesses that call for hot foods.
alt.ex: Hot conditions include pregnancy, fever, infections, diarrhea, rashes, ulcers, liver and kidney problems, constipation, and sore throat.

items.q: Judaism includes 24 hours of fasting on Yom Kippur, a day of atonement.
items.a: True
items.ex: Table 45.3 lists a 24-hour fast on Yom Kippur as a Jewish dietary practice.
items.ww: Yom Kippur fasting is listed in the table, so calling it false would be incorrect.

alt.q: During Passover, observant Jewish patients avoid unleavened bread for 8 days.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: During the 8 days of Passover, leavened bread is avoided, not unleavened bread.
alt.ww: Unleavened bread is eaten during Passover; it is leavened bread that is restricted.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient whose family brings traditional foods to the hospital. Which nursing action best reflects the person-centered implications in Box 45.5?
items.a: Ask the patient and family what meaning the foods they commonly eat have for them
items.ex: Box 45.5 directs the nurse to ask patients or family caregivers to identify the meaning of foods they commonly eat.
w: Explain that hospital meals are designed to meet all nutritional needs
Dismissing family foods ignores the cultural meaning food holds for the patient.
Ask the family to bring only foods that appear on the MyPlate guidelines
Imposing MyPlate disregards the patient’s cultural food patterns.
Document the foods and refer the family to the dietitian for correction
Assessing the meaning of food comes first; correction implies the foods are wrong.

alt.q: Box 45.5 notes that culture influences the meaning of food beyond nutrition. Which example from the box illustrates this?
alt.a: Children rewarded with candy for “being good” come to link candy with being good
alt.ex: Eating carries feelings such as “good” and “bad”; candy given as a reward becomes tied to being good.
w: Children who drink milk daily develop higher bone mass density as adults
This describes a nutritional effect, not a cultural meaning of food.
Children who skip breakfast have lower energy levels during school hours
This describes physiology, not the meaning culture gives to food.
Children who eat vegetables regularly have fewer vitamin deficiencies
This is a nutritional outcome rather than a cultural meaning.

items.q: Mrs. Cooper takes warfarin 2.5 mg daily. Which statement by Mrs. Cooper shows understanding of the nurse’s teaching about her diet?
items.a: “I will keep track of how many green leafy vegetables I eat.”
items.ex: Because she takes warfarin, Mrs. Cooper needs to watch her intake of green leafy vegetables.
w: “I will drink extra milk each day to help my warfarin work.”
Milk is not linked to warfarin in the book; leafy greens are.
“I will avoid all fruit while I am taking warfarin.”
Fruit is not restricted with warfarin; green leafy vegetables are the concern.
“I will add extra salt to my food to improve my appetite.”
She has hypertension and heart failure, so she must watch her sodium intake.

alt.q: Mrs. Cooper takes warfarin. Which food should the nurse teach her to monitor in her diet because of this medication?
alt.a: Spinach and other green leafy vegetables
alt.ex: Green leafy vegetables are the foods Mrs. Cooper must watch because she takes warfarin.
w: Bananas and other tropical fruits
Tropical fruits are not identified as a warfarin concern in the book.
Oatmeal and other whole grains
Whole grains are not linked to warfarin in the book.
Eggs and other protein sources
Mrs. Cooper needs adequate protein; eggs are not a warfarin concern.

items.q: What effect has research shown from consuming a vegetarian diet?
items.a: It can significantly improve LDL cholesterol and cardiometabolic outcomes
items.ex: Research shows vegetarian diets can significantly improve low-density lipoprotein cholesterol and cardiometabolic outcomes.
w: It reliably prevents protein deficiency in children and older adults
Vegetarian children are actually at higher risk for protein and B12 deficiency.
It eliminates the need for vitamin B12 from any food source
Vitamin B12 is still needed; its lack is a key risk of vegetarian diets.
It raises HDL cholesterol enough to replace lipid-lowering drugs
The book reports LDL improvement, not replacement of medications.

alt.q: A patient asks whether a vegetarian diet can meet protein needs. Which response by the nurse is accurate?

items: Recognize cues

items.q: Which critical thinking attitude does the book identify as important when obtaining a patient’s nutritional assessment?
items.a: Being open-minded about the patient’s nutritional practices
items.ex: The critical thinking model calls for being open-minded about the patient’s nutritional practices during assessment.
w: Being skeptical of the patient’s self-reported food intake
Skepticism is not listed; open-mindedness and confidence are the attitudes named.
Being directive about replacing cultural foods with standard foods
Replacing cultural foods conflicts with person-centered, open-minded assessment.
Being brief to avoid tiring the patient with personal questions
The model calls for confidence in collecting culture, preference, and restriction data.

alt.q: In the critical thinking model for nutrition assessment, which attitude involves comfortably collecting data about culture, socioeconomic status, and dietary restrictions?
alt.a: Displaying confidence
alt.ex: The model directs nurses to display confidence when collecting data on culture, socioeconomic status, and personal preferences.
w: Displaying humility
Humility is not the attitude the model links to collecting these data.
Displaying discipline
Discipline is cited for evaluation, not for collecting assessment data here.
Displaying risk taking
Risk taking is not identified for collecting these nutritional data.

items.q: In the critical thinking model for nutrition assessment, which item is an example of a professional standard?
items.a: Dietary reference intakes, MyPlate, and Healthy People 2030
items.ex: DRIs, MyPlate, Healthy People 2030, and the Dietary Guidelines for Americans are standards used to assess nutrition.
w: Caring for patients with altered nutrition
This is an example of experience in the critical thinking model.
Interruptions during the assessment process
This is an environmental factor in the critical thinking model.
Effects of medications on nutrition
This is part of the knowledge base in the critical thinking model.

alt.q: In the critical thinking model for nutrition assessment, “observation of nutritional practices of friends and family” belongs to which component?
alt.a: Experience
alt.ex: Experience includes caring for patients with altered nutrition, observing others’ nutritional practices, and personal assessment.
w: Standards
Standards include DRIs, MyPlate, Healthy People 2030, and agency policies.
Environment
Environment includes resources from other professionals and interruptions.
Attitudes
Attitudes include open-mindedness and confidence.

items.q: A person who consumes only plant foods is called a [[vegan]].
items.ex: Vegans eat only plant foods, unlike ovolactovegetarians and lactovegetarians, who include milk.

alt.q: A vegetarian who avoids meat, fish, and poultry but eats eggs and milk is an [[ovolactovegetarian|ovo-lacto-vegetarian|lacto-ovo vegetarian|lactoovovegetarian]].
alt.ex: Vegans eat only plant foods, unlike ovolactovegetarians and lactovegetarians, who include milk.

items.q: Ryan reviews diet therapy for Mrs. Cooper, who has diabetes mellitus, hypertension, heart failure, and takes warfarin. Which dietary components does he note she needs to watch? Select all that apply.
o: Sodium
Sodium intake matters for her hypertension and heart failure.
Cholesterol
Cholesterol is listed among the intakes she must watch.
Carbohydrate and sugar
Carbohydrate and sugar intake matter for her diabetes mellitus.
Green leafy vegetables
Green leafy vegetables must be watched because she takes warfarin.
Protein
Adequate protein is important for her; protein is not something to limit.
Fluid
Adequate fluid intake is emphasized for older adults with her conditions.
items.ex: Mrs. Cooper must watch sodium, cholesterol, carbohydrate, sugar, and green leafy vegetables while keeping calories, protein, and fluids adequate.

alt.q: When planning meals with an older adult, which factors does the book say can affect food choice and meal planning? Select all that apply.
o: Food preferences
Preferences affect what the patient will eat.
Finances
Finances affect the patient’s ability to buy food.
Culture
Culture shapes food choices and meanings.
Religion
Religious practices can restrict certain foods.
Blood type
Blood type is not identified as a factor affecting food choice.
Eye color
Eye color has no bearing on food choice or meal planning.
alt.ex: Preferences, finances, culture, and religion all affect food choice and meal planning.

items.q: Children who follow a vegetarian diet are especially at risk for protein and vitamin deficiencies.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book singles out vegetarian children as especially at risk for protein and vitamin deficiencies such as vitamin B12.
items.ww: Because children’s needs are high and B12 comes mainly from animal foods, the risk is real.

alt.q: Because plant foods supply all essential nutrients, children who follow a vegetarian diet need no special meal planning.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Vegetarian children are especially at risk for protein and B12 deficiency, so careful planning is needed.
alt.ww: Careful planning helps ensure a balanced diet; without it, deficiencies can develop.

items.q: What is the purpose of nutrition screening during an initial assessment?
items.a: To quickly identify malnutrition or risk of malnutrition using simple tools
items.ex: Screening is a quick method of identifying malnutrition or its risk using simple tools.
w: To calculate a patient’s exact daily calorie and protein requirements
Calculating requirements is done by the RD and health care provider, not by screening.
To prescribe a therapeutic diet for the patient’s medical diagnosis
RDs use detailed data to prescribe therapeutic diets; screening only identifies risk.
To measure plasma proteins that confirm a diagnosis of malnutrition
Laboratory tests are separate from screening, which uses simple tools.

alt.q: A patient’s screening reveals unintentional weight loss and ongoing nausea and diarrhea. What is the nurse’s best next action?
alt.a: Request a nutritional consultation
alt.ex: Risk factors such as unintentional weight loss or altered nutritional symptoms require nutritional consultation.
w: Repeat the screening in 1 week
Identified risk factors require consultation now, not repeat screening.
Begin an enteral tube feeding
Tube feeding requires an order and fuller assessment, not just screening.
Place the patient on a clear liquid diet
Changing the diet is not the response to a positive screen; consultation is.

items.q: A patient with renal failure weighed 70 kg yesterday and weighs 70.9 kg this morning on the same scale. What does the nurse recognize about this finding?
items.a: It is significant because it usually indicates retention of about 1 L of fluid
items.ex: Each 0.45 kg (1 lb) equals about 500 mL of fluid, so a 0.9-kg gain in 24 hours reflects about 1 L retained.
w: It is insignificant because daily weight normally varies by about 1 kg
A 0.9-kg gain in 24 hours in renal failure is significant, not normal variation.
It is significant because it usually indicates a gain of about 1 kg of fat
Rapid weight changes usually reflect fluid shifts, not changes in body fat.
It is significant because it usually indicates retention of about 250 mL of fluid
A 0.9-kg gain equals about 1000 mL, not 250 mL, of fluid.

alt.q: A nurse explains why patients are weighed daily. One pint (500 mL) of retained fluid equals approximately how much body weight?
alt.ex: One pint or 500 mL of fluid equals 0.45 kg (1 lb).
w: 0.9 kg (2 lb)
A 0.9-kg change reflects about 1 L of fluid, not 500 mL.
This underestimates the weight of 500 mL of fluid.
1.4 kg (3 lb)
This overestimates; 1.4 kg reflects about 1.5 L of fluid.

items.q: A patient is considered obese when the body mass index is greater than [[30]] kg/m2.
items.ex: Overweight is a BMI of 25 to 30 kg/m2; a BMI over 30 kg/m2 defines obesity.

alt.q: Body mass index is calculated by dividing weight in kilograms by height in [[meters squared|meters squared (m2)|m2|square meters]].
alt.ex: Overweight is a BMI of 25 to 30 kg/m2; a BMI over 30 kg/m2 defines obesity.
