ord.q: Place these key steps for inserting a small-bore feeding tube in the correct order.
items: Position the patient upright in high-Fowler position
Apply pulse oximeter or capnograph and measure vital signs
Measure the tube length and mark it
Insert the tube through the nostril to the posterior nasopharynx
Have the patient flex the head toward the chest
Advance the tube as the patient swallows to the marked length
Check the tube position behind the throat with penlight and tongue blade
Aspirate contents to measure pH, then anchor and mark the tube
Obtain an x-ray to confirm placement
ord.ex: Positioning and monitoring precede measuring and insertion; position checks, pH testing, anchoring, and x-ray confirmation follow.

items.q: What is the most accurate method for confirming the placement of a newly inserted small-bore feeding tube?
items.a: Radiographic examination of the tube position
items.ex: Radiographic confirmation remains the gold standard and is required before the first feeding.
w: Auscultation of injected air over the stomach
Air insufflation with auscultation is not a reliable method.
pH testing of fluid aspirated from the tube
pH testing supports placement on an ongoing basis but is not the gold standard.
Measurement of the external tube length
External length helps detect displacement but does not confirm tip position.

alt.q: A nurse has inserted a small-bore feeding tube and obtained gastric aspirate with pH 3. What must happen before the first feeding is given?
alt.a: Placement must be confirmed by x-ray
alt.ex: Confirmation by x-ray is mandatory before any feeding or medication through a newly inserted tube.
w: The stylet must be reinserted to stiffen the tube
A stylet is never reinserted while the tube is in place.
The tube must be advanced another 10 cm
Advancing further is not required; x-ray confirmation is.
The nurse must inject air while listening over the stomach
Air insufflation is an unreliable method of verification.

items.q: After inserting a small-bore feeding tube, the nurse notices the stylet has been partially pulled out. The x-ray has not been read yet. What is the correct action?
items.a: Do not reinsert the stylet; report the situation and await x-ray results
items.ex: A partially or fully removed stylet must never be reinserted, because it can perforate the tube and injure the patient.
w: Reinsert the stylet fully so the tube remains stiff
Reinserting a stylet can perforate the tube and injure the patient.
Remove the tube and reinsert it with the stylet
Removal is not indicated; the stylet simply must not be reinserted.
Flush the tube with 30 mL of air to straighten it
Air does not reposition a stylet and is not part of this step.

alt.q: When is the stylet removed from a newly inserted small-bore feeding tube?
alt.a: After x-ray verification confirms correct placement
alt.ex: The stylet stays in place until x-ray confirms position, because adjustment may still be needed.
w: As soon as the tube reaches the marked length
Removing it before x-ray prevents adjustment if placement is wrong.
Immediately after the pH of the aspirate is checked
pH testing alone does not confirm placement before stylet removal.
Before the tube is anchored to the patient’s nose
The stylet remains until x-ray verification, after anchoring.

items.q: Which patient factors increase the risk of a medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI) from tape or adhesive tube fixation devices? Select all that apply.
o: Older age
Age is a common risk factor for MARSI.
Dehydration
Dehydration increases MARSI risk.
Malnutrition
Malnutrition is a listed risk factor.
Exposure to radiation therapy
Radiation therapy increases skin vulnerability to adhesives.
Adequate hydration and nutrition
These are protective, not risk factors.
Recent use of a hypoallergenic tape
Hypoallergenic tape is not listed as a MARSI risk factor.
items.ex: MARSI risk factors include age, dehydration, malnutrition, radiation therapy, chronic conditions such as diabetes, and edema.

alt.q: Which findings are signs of a medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI)? Select all that apply.
o: Erythema
Redness is a sign of MARSI.
Blistering
Blistering reflects the skin’s reaction to adhesive.
Excoriation
Excoriation is a listed sign of MARSI.
Pale, cool, intact skin under the tape
Intact skin without redness or blisters is not a MARSI sign.
Clear aspirate with pH below 5
This relates to tube placement, not skin injury.
alt.ex: Erythema, blistering, and excoriation are signs of MARSI related to the skin’s reaction to adhesive.

items.q: How should the nurse secure the end of a newly placed small-bore feeding tube to the patient’s gown?
items.a: With a clip or a piece of tape
items.ex: A clip or tape reduces traction on the naris; safety pins can come open and injure patients.
w: With a safety pin through the tube
Safety pins can become unfastened and cause injury.
With a rubber band around the tube
The skill specifies a clip or tape, not a rubber band.
With a knot tied in the tube
Knotting would occlude the tube and is not a securement method.

alt.q: Why does the nurse use a fixation device or taping method that lets the tube float free of the naris?
alt.a: It reduces pressure on the naris and prevents a medical device–related pressure injury
alt.ex: Allowing the tube to float free reduces pressure on the naris and the risk of MDRPI.
w: It allows the tube to advance into the intestine on its own
Securement is not meant to let the tube migrate.
It makes the tube easier to remove if the patient pulls on it
Securement aims to prevent dislodgment, not ease removal.
It keeps the stylet in place until the x-ray is taken
Securement does not hold the stylet in place.

items.q: After inserting a nasointestinal feeding tube, how should the nurse position the patient until radiographic confirmation of placement?
items.a: On the right side when possible
items.ex: Placing the patient on the right side promotes passage of the tube into the small intestine.
w: On the left side when possible
The right side, not the left, promotes intestinal passage.
Flat and supine when possible
Lying flat increases aspiration risk.
Prone when possible
Prone positioning is not recommended for this purpose.

alt.q: A nurse places a patient on the right side after inserting a nasointestinal tube. What is the rationale?
alt.a: It promotes passage of the tube into the small intestine
alt.ex: Right-side positioning helps the nasointestinal tube move past the pylorus into the small intestine.
w: It prevents the tube from coiling in the esophagus
Right-side positioning promotes intestinal passage, not esophageal straightening.
It reduces pressure on the naris used for insertion
Pressure on the naris is reduced by securement, not side-lying.
It makes aspirating gastric fluid for pH easier
The rationale is tube advancement into the intestine.

items.q: A nurse is removing a small-bore feeding tube. Which action prevents aspiration of gastric contents during removal?
items.a: Have the patient take a deep breath and hold it while the kinked tube is withdrawn
items.ex: Holding the breath and kinking the tube prevent aspiration and leakage as the tube is pulled out.
w: Have the patient lie flat and breathe deeply while the tube is withdrawn slowly
Lying flat increases aspiration risk; high-Fowler is used.
Flush the tube with 30 mL of air and then withdraw it while the patient talks
Air flush and talking do not protect the airway during removal.
Leave the tube open and withdraw it while the patient swallows water
An open tube can leak, and swallowing water during removal is not directed.

alt.q: Which action is part of removing a small-bore feeding tube?
alt.a: Position the patient in high-Fowler position unless contraindicated
alt.ex: High-Fowler position reduces the risk of pulmonary aspiration should the patient vomit during removal.
w: Place the patient supine with the head of bed flat
Lying flat increases aspiration risk during removal.
Remove the tube quickly in short, jerking pulls
The tube is withdrawn steadily and smoothly.
Leave the feeding administration set connected
The tube is disconnected from the set and clamped or capped first.

items.q: Water-soluble lubricant may be used to ease insertion of a small-bore feeding tube.
items.a: True
items.ex: Dipping the tube in water-soluble lubricant per manufacturer directions eases passage into the naris and GI tract.
items.ww: The skill lists water-soluble lubricant as an option and forbids only petroleum-based lubricant.

alt.q: Petroleum-based lubricant is the preferred choice for easing insertion of a small-bore feeding tube.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Petroleum-based lubricant should never be used for feeding tube insertion.
alt.ww: Only water-soluble lubricant is used, per manufacturer directions.

items.q: Injecting air into the feeding tube while auscultating the abdomen is a reliable way to confirm the tube tip position.
items.a: False
items.ex: Air insufflation with auscultation is not reliable; x-ray confirms new placement and pH supports ongoing checks.
items.ww: A whooshing sound can be heard even when the tube is not in the stomach.

alt.q: Listening for insufflated air over the abdomen is an unreliable method to determine feeding tube tip position.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The skill states that auscultation of insufflated air does not reliably show where the tube tip lies.
alt.ww: X-ray confirmation and pH testing are used instead of air insufflation.

items.q: Fasting gastric fluid aspirated from a correctly placed tube usually has a pH less than [[5|five]].
items.ex: Gastric aspirate in a fasting patient is acidic; fluid with pH above 6 suggests intestinal or respiratory placement.

alt.q: Fluid aspirated from a tube in the small intestine of a fasting patient usually has a pH greater than [[6|six|6.0]].
alt.ex: Gastric aspirate in a fasting patient is acidic; fluid with pH above 6 suggests intestinal or respiratory placement.

items.q: After inserting a small-bore feeding tube, which findings suggest the tube may be in the respiratory tract? Select all that apply.
o: Coughing and dyspnea
These symptoms may indicate placement in the respiratory tract.
Cyanosis
Cyanosis suggests impaired oxygenation from airway placement.
Decrease in oxygen saturation
Lowered SpO2 may detect the tip in the trachea or lung.
Increase in end-tidal CO2
Rising end-tidal CO2 may detect the tube in the airway.
Aspirate with a pH of 3
A pH of 3 is consistent with gastric placement.
Patient speaks clearly without distress
Normal speech without distress does not suggest airway placement.
items.ex: Coughing, dyspnea, cyanosis, falling SpO2, or rising end-tidal CO2 may indicate airway placement.

alt.q: Which information should the nurse document after inserting a small-bore feeding tube? Select all that apply.
o: Type and size of tube placed
Tube type and size are documented.
Length of tube inserted
The inserted length is documented.
Confirmation of tube position by radiographic film
X-ray confirmation of position is documented.
Condition of the naris and patient tolerance
Naris condition and tolerance are documented.
Sound heard when air was injected into the tube
Air insufflation is unreliable and is not part of documentation.
alt.ex: Document tube type and size, tip location, length inserted, tolerance, naris condition, and x-ray confirmation.

items.q: A patient with a small-bore feeding tube in the duodenum vomits forcefully. Afterward, the external tube marking has moved. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Aspirate GI contents and measure the pH to check for displacement
items.ex: Coughing or vomiting can displace the tube; the nurse aspirates contents and checks pH, replacing the tube if displaced.
w: Push the tube back in to the original marking
A displaced tube is not pushed back; it is removed and a new tube is verified.
Resume the feeding at the previous rate
Feeding before verifying position risks aspiration.
Inject air and listen over the abdomen
Air insufflation is not reliable for checking placement.

alt.q: A patient develops crackles, dyspnea, and fever after a feeding tube was placed. Which actions are expected?
alt.a: Report to the provider, position the patient on the side, and suction as needed
alt.ex: Aspiration calls for reporting, side-lying to protect the airway, suctioning, and possible antibiotics.
w: Increase the feeding rate, raise the head of bed, and recheck in 4 hours
Feeding should not be increased when aspiration is suspected.
Remove the stylet, flush with water, and continue the feeding
These steps do not address suspected aspiration.
Place the patient supine, give fluids by mouth, and monitor
Supine positioning and oral fluids increase aspiration risk.

sections.name: Skill 45.3 · Administering enteral nutrition: Nasogastric, nasointestinal, gastrostomy, or jejunostomy tube

items.q: Agency policy allows assistive personnel (AP) to administer nasoenteric tube feedings. What must happen before the AP starts a feeding?
items.a: An RN or LPN verifies tube placement and patency
items.ex: The AP may give the feeding only after a licensed nurse (RN or LPN) has verified placement and patency.
w: The AP checks the pH of the gastric aspirate
Verifying placement is a licensed nurse task, not something the AP is directed to do.
The AP measures the gastric residual volume
GRV checks are part of the nurse’s assessment, not an AP direction in this skill.
The health care provider confirms the infusion rate
The order sets the rate, but placement and patency are what the nurse must verify first.

alt.q: A nurse delegates an ordered continuous tube feeding to assistive personnel (AP). Which instruction should the nurse give the AP?
alt.a: Keep the feeding at the ordered rate and do not adjust it
alt.ex: AP are directed to maintain the ordered feeding rate without adjusting it and to report problems.
w: Speed up the rate if the feeding falls behind schedule
AP must not adjust the rate; catching up risks intolerance and aspiration.
Lower the head of the bed flat while the feeding runs
The head of the bed stays elevated 30 to 45 degrees to prevent aspiration.
Check the tube’s pH before each new bag is hung
Checking placement is done by the RN or LPN, not delegated to AP.

items.q: A patient receiving a continuous tube feeding suddenly develops dyspnea, a fever, and new crackles in the lungs. Which action should the nurse take immediately?
items.a: Position the patient on the side
items.ex: These findings suggest aspiration; the nurse immediately positions the patient on the side, reports the change, and suctions as needed.
w: Lower the head of the bed to flat
Lying flat increases aspiration risk; the side-lying position protects the airway.
Increase the feeding rate slightly
Infusing more formula would worsen aspiration of tube feeding.
Check the gastric residual volume
GRV does not treat aspiration; airway protection and reporting come first.

alt.q: A nurse auscultates wheezes and notes dyspnea in a patient who is receiving a nasogastric tube feeding. Which set of actions does the textbook direct?
alt.a: Report the change at once, turn the patient to the side, and suction
alt.ex: For suspected aspiration, immediately report to the health care provider, position on the side, and suction nasotracheally or orotracheally.
w: Recheck the pH, flush with water, and resume the feeding
Resuming the feeding ignores signs that formula has entered the airway.
Place the patient supine, raise the legs, and recheck in an hour
Supine positioning increases aspiration, and waiting delays needed care.
Give an extra water flush, document, and continue to observe
Extra fluid in the stomach adds risk; aspiration needs immediate reporting.

items.q: A nurse measures a gastric residual volume (GRV) of 300 mL in a patient receiving tube feedings. The abdomen is soft and nondistended, and the patient denies pain or nausea. Which action is best?
items.a: Continue the feeding and take measures to reduce aspiration risk
items.ex: A GRV of 200 to 500 mL raises concern, but feedings should not be stopped automatically below 500 mL without other signs of intolerance.
w: Stop the feeding automatically until the next shift
Automatic cessation is not recommended for GRV under 500 mL without other signs of intolerance.
Discard the aspirate and recheck the GRV in 30 minutes
Discarding loses nutrients and electrolytes, and frequent checks delay feeding and clog tubes.
Increase the rate to make up for the delay in feeding
An elevated GRV is a reason for caution, not for speeding up the infusion.

alt.q: Why is routine checking of gastric residual volume (GRV) no longer recommended?
alt.a: GRV correlates poorly with pneumonia, regurgitation, and aspiration
alt.ex: GRV is a poor predictor of pneumonia, regurgitation, and aspiration and should not be the single measure of tolerance.
w: GRV readings are accurate only when feedings are given by bolus
The concern is poor correlation with complications, not the feeding method.
Aspirating GRV is the most common cause of tube displacement
The book links frequent GRV checks to tube occlusion and delayed feeding, not displacement.
GRV must be measured by a dietitian rather than by a nurse
Nurses check GRV per agency policy; the issue is how little it predicts.

items.q: A nurse aspirates fluid from a patient’s jejunostomy tube. The fluid looks like gastric secretions and tests acidic on the pH strip. What does this finding suggest?
items.a: The tube may have moved into the stomach
items.ex: Intestinal fluid normally has a pH greater than 6, so acidic, gastric-looking fluid suggests displacement into the stomach.
w: The tube is correctly placed in the small intestine
Correct jejunal placement yields intestinal fluid with a pH greater than 6.
The tube tip has entered the respiratory tract
Respiratory secretions are not acidic like gastric fluid.
The tube is blocked by precipitated formula
A clog prevents aspiration or flushing; it does not change the pH of fluid returned.

alt.q: A nurse checks residual volume from a patient’s nasointestinal feeding tube and obtains 45 mL. What should the nurse suspect?
alt.a: The tube has displaced into the stomach
alt.ex: Intestinal residual is usually very small; a volume greater than 10 mL suggests the tube has moved into the stomach.
w: The feeding is being absorbed normally
Normal intestinal residual is very small, so 45 mL is not an expected finding.
The tube has advanced further into the colon
The book links a residual over 10 mL to displacement into the stomach.
The patient needs a faster feeding rate
A large intestinal residual signals possible displacement, not a need for more formula.

items.q: In a patient who has fasted for at least 4 hours, what pH is usually expected for gastric fluid aspirated from a feeding tube?
items.a: pH 1.0 to 4.0
items.ex: Fasting gastric fluid is acidic, usually pH 1.0 to 4.0; intestinal fluid has a pH greater than 6.
w: pH 6.0 to 7.0
A pH greater than 6 suggests intestinal rather than gastric placement.
This is the normal pH of blood, not of gastric aspirate.
Gastric fluid is acidic; values this high do not indicate stomach placement.

alt.q: A patient receives continuous feedings into the stomach. When does the textbook direct the nurse to check the pH of aspirate?
alt.a: When feedings are held for at least 1 hour
alt.ex: With continuous feedings, pH is checked when the feeding has been held at least 1 hour, such as for diagnostic tests.
w: Every 15 minutes during the infusion
Such frequent aspiration is not recommended and would delay feeding.
Only once, on the day the tube is inserted
Placement must be rechecked at least every 4 hours or per policy.
Whenever the patient asks for oral care
Oral hygiene needs do not trigger a pH check of the aspirate.

items.q: Why should enteral formula be at room temperature before it is administered?
items.a: Cold formula can cause gastric cramping and discomfort
items.ex: Formula given by tube bypasses the mouth and esophagus, so cold formula is not warmed and causes cramping.
w: Cold formula is more likely to clog small-bore tubing
The rationale given is cramping and discomfort, not clogging.
Warm formula is less likely to grow bacteria in the bag
Warm temperatures do not reduce growth; aseptic handling limits contamination.
Cold formula changes the pH reading of the aspirate
Formula temperature is not linked to pH readings in this skill.

alt.q: A nurse finds a container of reconstituted formula in the refrigerator that was mixed 30 hours ago. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Discard it because the 24-hour limit has passed
alt.ex: Unused reconstituted and refrigerated formula is discarded within 24 hours of preparation.
w: Warm it to room temperature and hang it
Warming does not make formula safe after the 24-hour discard limit.
Use it if the container still looks intact
Appearance does not extend the 24-hour limit for prepared formula.
Dilute it with water and hang it right away
Diluting expired formula does not remove contamination risk.

items.q: A patient receiving tube feedings must remain supine because of a spinal injury. How should the nurse position the patient during feedings?
items.a: In reverse Trendelenburg position
items.ex: For a patient who must stay supine, reverse Trendelenburg raises the head to help prevent aspiration.
w: In Trendelenburg position
Trendelenburg lowers the head, which increases aspiration risk.
In flat supine position
Lying flat is a risk factor for aspiration during feedings.
In prone position
Prone positioning is not the textbook’s option for a supine-only patient.

alt.q: A patient on mechanical ventilation who is heavily sedated is receiving tube feedings. What head-of-bed elevation is recommended?
alt.a: 45 degrees
alt.ex: Researchers recommend 45 degrees for ventilated or heavily sedated patients, lowering to 30 degrees periodically for comfort or pressure injury risk.
w: 15 degrees
This is below the minimum of 30 degrees needed to help prevent aspiration.
20 degrees
Elevation should be at least 30 degrees during feedings.
0 degrees
A flat position is a risk factor for aspiration.

items.q: A nurse reviews the evaluation data of a patient receiving continuous tube feedings. Which finding is most important to report?
items.a: Weight gain of 1.4 kg (3 lb) in 24 hours
items.ex: A sudden gain of more than 0.9 kg (2 lb) in 24 hours usually indicates fluid retention.
w: Gastric aspirate pH of 4 (fasting)
A pH of 4 or less in a fasting patient is expected with gastric placement.
Bowel sounds present in all quadrants (active)
Present bowel sounds are an expected finding, not a sign of intolerance.
Gastric residual volume of 40 mL (one check)
A small GRV is not a sign of intolerance or aspiration risk.

alt.q: A patient has just started continuous tube feedings. How often should the nurse weigh the patient?
alt.a: Daily until the goal rate holds 24 hours, then 3 times weekly
alt.ex: Daily weights continue until the maximum rate is reached and maintained for 24 hours, then the patient is weighed 3 times per week.
w: Once weekly from the first day of feedings
Weekly weights would miss sudden gains that signal fluid retention early on.
Every 4 hours until the tube is removed
Every 4 hours is the interval for placement checks, not weights.
Only at admission and again at discharge
Weights are needed to evaluate nutritional status and fluid balance during feeding.

items.q: A nurse finds that a patient’s feeding tube is clogged. Which action should the nurse try first?
items.a: Attempt to flush the tube with water
items.ex: The first intervention for a clogged tube is a water flush; special unclogging products are also available.
w: Instill a carbonated beverage into the tube
Carbonated beverages are not to be used to unclog feeding tubes.
Flush the tube with cranberry juice
Juices are not to be used to unclog feeding tubes.
Lay the patient flat and pull back hard
The patient stays in semi-Fowler position, and force risks tube damage.

alt.q: The spouse of a patient with a home gastrostomy tube asks whether cola can be used to clear a clogged tube. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: Use water first; avoid soft drinks and juices for clogs
alt.ex: Water flushes or special products are used; carbonated beverages and juices are not to be used for clogged tubes.
w: Yes, cola is the most effective way to clear a clog
The book specifically says not to use carbonated beverages.
Use orange juice instead because it is more acidic
Juices are also not to be used to unclog feeding tubes.
Replace the tube yourself whenever it becomes clogged
Hold the feeding and notify the health care provider if flushing fails.

items.q: A patient receiving tube feedings has had five loose stools in the past 24 hours. When looking for a cause, which factor should the nurse investigate?
items.a: A medication that contains sorbitol
items.ex: Causes of diarrhea to rule out include Clostridium difficile infection, contaminated feeding, and sorbitol-containing medications.
w: A head-of-bed elevation of 45 degrees
Elevating the head of the bed prevents aspiration; it does not cause diarrhea.
Water flushes given every 4 hours
Routine 30-mL flushes provide free water and clear the tube.
A formula given at room temperature
Room-temperature formula is recommended and prevents cramping.

alt.q: According to the textbook, which pattern defines a large amount of diarrhea in a patient receiving tube feedings?
alt.a: More than three loose stools in 24 hours
alt.ex: More than three loose stools in 24 hours is the unexpected outcome that prompts notifying the provider and consulting the dietitian.
w: More than one loose stool in 24 hours
A single loose stool does not meet the textbook threshold.
More than three formed stools in 24 hours
The definition refers to loose stools, not formed stools.
Any loose stool in a 72-hour period
The threshold is more than three loose stools within 24 hours.

items.q: During hand-off report on a patient receiving a continuous tube feeding, why does the nurse trace the administration set tubing to the enteral tube connection?
items.a: To confirm the feeding is infusing by the enteral route
items.ex: Tracing tubing to the connection point ensures the feeding is infused enterally and not by a wrong route such as IV.
w: To measure how much formula remains in the bag
Volume is read from the container, not by tracing tubing.
To check the pH of formula left inside the tubing
pH is checked on aspirate from the tube, not on formula in the set.
To decide when to change to a new formula type
Formula type is set by the order, not by tracing tubing at hand-off.

alt.q: Which practice helps prevent tube feeding from being given through an IV line?
alt.a: Using ENFit connectors and feeding-only pumps
alt.ex: ENFit devices do not fit Luer-Lok connections, and tube feedings use pumps designated for enteral feeding, not IV fluids.
w: Using Luer-Lok syringes for all water flushes
ENFit is designed to be incompatible with Luer-Lok, preventing misconnections.
Hanging feeding bags on the same IV pole as fluids
Shared poles do not prevent misconnection; correct connectors do.
Running the feeding through an IV infusion pump
The book says to use pumps designated for tube feeding, not IV pumps.

items.q: A nurse assesses a patient before starting tube feedings. Which factors increase the patient’s risk for aspiration? Select all that apply.
o: Sedation
Sedation reduces airway clearance and is a listed risk factor.
Mechanical ventilation
Mechanical ventilation is a listed aspiration risk factor.
Neurological compromise
Neurological compromise impairs airway protection.
Lying flat
A flat position allows reflux of formula into the airway.
Sitting upright in a chair
Sitting up is a recommended position that lowers aspiration risk.
Walking independently in the hall
Independent mobility is not a listed risk factor.
items.ex: Sedation, mechanical ventilation, nasotracheal suctioning, neurological compromise, lying flat, and sepsis increase aspiration risk.

alt.q: Before a tube feeding, a nurse examines the abdomen. Which findings suggest the patient may not tolerate the feeding? Select all that apply.
o: Expanding abdominal girth
Increasing girth is an objective sign of intolerance.
Firmness on palpation
Firmness and tenderness suggest intolerance.
Increasing nasogastric output
Rising NG output is an objective sign of intolerance.
Vomiting
Vomiting indicates the feeding is not being tolerated.
Soft, nontender abdomen
A soft, nontender abdomen is an expected finding.
Stable abdominal girth
Unchanged girth does not suggest intolerance.
alt.ex: Changes in bowel sounds, expanding girth, tenderness, firmness, increasing NG output, and vomiting suggest intolerance and are reported.

items.q: A nurse evaluates a patient on continuous tube feedings for aspiration. Which findings may indicate that formula has entered the respiratory tract? Select all that apply.
o: Coughing
Coughing is a respiratory change that may signal aspiration.
Tachypnea
A rapid respiratory rate may indicate aspiration.
Hoarseness
Hoarseness is a listed respiratory change.
Crackles in the lungs
Crackles suggest fluid or formula in the airways.
Stable oxygen saturation
Aspiration is suggested by a change in oxygen saturation, not stability.
Active bowel sounds
Bowel sounds reflect GI function, not respiratory status.
items.ex: Coughing, dyspnea, tachypnea, change in oxygen saturation, hoarseness, or crackles may indicate aspiration of tube feeding.

alt.q: Assistive personnel are helping with a patient’s tube feeding. Which observations should the AP report to the nurse? Select all that apply.
o: Gagging
AP are directed to report gagging.
Paroxysms of coughing
Coughing fits may indicate aspiration and must be reported.
Choking
Choking must be reported right away.
Discomfort voiced by the patient
AP report any discomfort the patient voices during feeding.
Patient asking for mouth care
AP provide frequent oral hygiene; this request is routine care.
Patient sitting up in a chair
Sitting up is a recommended position, not a problem to report.
alt.ex: AP report gagging, coughing paroxysms, choking, difficulty infusing, and patient discomfort, all of which may signal problems.

items.q: A nurse labels a bag for an intermittent tube feeding. Which information belongs on the label? Select all that apply.
o: Patient identifiers
Identifiers confirm the right patient is receiving the feeding.
Formula type
Formula type is a critical element of the EN order.
Enteral delivery site (route and access)
The route and access are listed label elements.
Volume and frequency of water flushes
Water flush orders belong on the EN label.
The patient’s health literacy level
Health literacy is assessed for teaching, not placed on the bag.
The most recent gastric residual volume
GRV is documented in the record, not on the bag label.
items.ex: Critical EN order elements go on the label, plus date, time, and initials, which also show when to change the set.

alt.q: A nurse hangs a new feeding container. Which entries are part of correct labeling? Select all that apply.
o: Administration method
The method of administration is a listed label element.
Date, time, and nurse’s initials
These show when the feeding was hung and when to change the set.
Patient identifiers
Identifiers confirm the right patient receives the feeding.
The patient’s last bowel movement
Bowel patterns are documented in the record, not on the bag.
The aspirate pH from the last check
pH results are documented, not written on the bag label.
alt.ex: Labels carry EN order elements and the date, time, and initials of the nurse who hung the feeding.

items.q: Frequent gastric residual volume checks can raise the risk of tube occlusion because acidic gastric contents cause protein in the formula to precipitate in the tube.
items.a: True
items.ex: Acid causes formula protein to precipitate in the lumen, so frequent GRV checks increase occlusion risk and reduce nutrition delivered.
items.ww: The book warns that frequent GRV measurement increases, not decreases, the risk of tube occlusion.

alt.q: Checking gastric residual volume frequently helps keep small-bore feeding tubes open by clearing formula from the lumen.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Frequent GRV checks increase the risk of tube occlusion because gastric acid makes formula protein precipitate.
alt.ww: GRV checks are limited to standard intervals precisely because they promote clogging and delay feeding.

items.q: In the hospital, formula in an open enteral feeding system should hang no longer than 4 to 8 hours.
items.a: True
items.ex: Open systems are limited to 4 to 8 hours of infusion (12 hours at home); closed systems follow the manufacturer.
items.ww: Open systems are exposed to contamination, so their hang time is limited to 4 to 8 hours.

alt.q: Formula poured into an open feeding bag may hang safely for up to 48 hours, the same as a closed system.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Open systems are limited to 4 to 8 hours; closed-system containers may hold a 24- to 48-hour supply.
alt.ww: Only intact closed systems run longer, following the manufacturer’s recommendations.

items.q: A continuous tube feeding can usually begin with full-strength formula, with the rate advanced gradually as ordered.
items.a: True
items.ex: Feedings usually start full strength, and the rate is advanced gradually based on age, condition, and expected tolerance.
items.ww: The book states that tube feeding can usually begin with full-strength formula rather than diluted formula.

alt.q: Every new tube feeding must start with formula diluted to half strength to prevent intolerance.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Tube feeding can usually begin with full-strength formula; the rate is then advanced gradually as ordered.
alt.ww: Dilution is not required to start; conservative advancement depends on the patient’s condition.

items.q: [[ENFit|ENFit connectors|ENFit connector]] devices are not compatible with Luer-Lok connections, which helps prevent enteral feeding from being given by the wrong route.
items.ex: ENFit connectors fit only enteral devices, so feedings cannot be connected to IV tubing.

alt.q: To prevent misconnection with IV lines, feeding tubing is attached to the feeding tube with an [[ENFit|ENFit connector|ENFit connection system]] connector.
alt.ex: ENFit connectors fit only enteral devices, so feedings cannot be connected to IV tubing.

items.q: In administering a tube feeding, which step comes right after “Fill the administration tubing and hang the container”?
items.a: Elevate the head of the bed at least 30 degrees
items.ex: That's step 5 of 9. Formula is checked and prepared, the patient positioned, placement verified, and the feeding connected and followed by a flush.
w: Verify tube placement by checking aspirate pH
That's step 6 of 9.
Prepare the formula at room temperature
That's step 3 of 9.
Check gastric residual volume per agency policy
That's step 7 of 9.

alt.q: Which step comes first in administering a tube feeding?
alt.a: Perform hand hygiene and apply clean gloves
alt.ex: That's step 1 of 9. Formula is checked and prepared, the patient positioned, placement verified, and the feeding connected and followed by a flush.
w: Reverify the formula and check its expiration date
That's step 2 of 9.
Prepare the formula at room temperature
That's step 3 of 9.
Fill the administration tubing and hang the container
That's step 4 of 9.

alt.q: Which step comes last in administering a tube feeding?
alt.a: Flush the tube with water after the feeding
alt.ex: That's step 9 of 9. Formula is checked and prepared, the patient positioned, placement verified, and the feeding connected and followed by a flush.
w: Connect the tubing using the ENFit connector
That's step 8 of 9.
Check gastric residual volume per agency policy
That's step 7 of 9.
Verify tube placement by checking aspirate pH
That's step 6 of 9.

alt.q: In administering a tube feeding, which step comes right after “Perform hand hygiene and apply clean gloves”?
alt.a: Reverify the formula and check its expiration date
alt.ex: That's step 2 of 9. Formula is checked and prepared, the patient positioned, placement verified, and the feeding connected and followed by a flush.
w: Prepare the formula at room temperature
That's step 3 of 9.
Fill the administration tubing and hang the container
That's step 4 of 9.
Elevate the head of the bed at least 30 degrees
That's step 5 of 9.

alt.q: In administering a tube feeding, which step comes right after “Reverify the formula and check its expiration date”?
alt.a: Prepare the formula at room temperature
alt.ex: That's step 3 of 9. Formula is checked and prepared, the patient positioned, placement verified, and the feeding connected and followed by a flush.
w: Fill the administration tubing and hang the container
That's step 4 of 9.
Perform hand hygiene and apply clean gloves
That's step 1 of 9.
Elevate the head of the bed at least 30 degrees
That's step 5 of 9.

alt.q: In administering a tube feeding, which step comes right after “Prepare the formula at room temperature”?
alt.a: Fill the administration tubing and hang the container
alt.ex: That's step 4 of 9. Formula is checked and prepared, the patient positioned, placement verified, and the feeding connected and followed by a flush.
w: Elevate the head of the bed at least 30 degrees
That's step 5 of 9.
Reverify the formula and check its expiration date
That's step 2 of 9.
Verify tube placement by checking aspirate pH
That's step 6 of 9.

alt.q: In administering a tube feeding, which step comes right after “Elevate the head of the bed at least 30 degrees”?
alt.a: Verify tube placement by checking aspirate pH
alt.ex: That's step 6 of 9. Formula is checked and prepared, the patient positioned, placement verified, and the feeding connected and followed by a flush.
w: Check gastric residual volume per agency policy
That's step 7 of 9.
Fill the administration tubing and hang the container
That's step 4 of 9.
Connect the tubing using the ENFit connector
That's step 8 of 9.

alt.q: In administering a tube feeding, which step comes right after “Verify tube placement by checking aspirate pH”?
alt.a: Check gastric residual volume per agency policy
alt.ex: That's step 7 of 9. Formula is checked and prepared, the patient positioned, placement verified, and the feeding connected and followed by a flush.
w: Connect the tubing using the ENFit connector
That's step 8 of 9.
Elevate the head of the bed at least 30 degrees
That's step 5 of 9.
Flush the tube with water after the feeding
That's step 9 of 9.

alt.q: In administering a tube feeding, which step comes right after “Check gastric residual volume per agency policy”?
alt.a: Connect the tubing using the ENFit connector
alt.ex: That's step 8 of 9. Formula is checked and prepared, the patient positioned, placement verified, and the feeding connected and followed by a flush.
w: Flush the tube with water after the feeding
That's step 9 of 9.
Verify tube placement by checking aspirate pH
That's step 6 of 9.
Elevate the head of the bed at least 30 degrees

items.q: A nurse delegates blood glucose testing for a stable patient to assistive personnel (AP). Which direction should the nurse give the AP?
items.a: Which puncture sites to use and when to obtain levels
items.ex: The nurse directs AP on appropriate puncture sites and testing times and reviews expected glucose levels and when to report.
w: How to adjust the insulin dose based on the result
Insulin decisions require nursing judgment and orders, not AP action.
How to assess the patient for signs of hypoglycemia
Assessment of the patient’s condition cannot be delegated to AP.
How to decide whether the test should be skipped
Test timing is set by the provider’s order, not by AP judgment.

alt.q: Assistive personnel report a blood glucose result that is far outside the patient’s expected range. What should happen next?
alt.a: The nurse retakes the blood glucose level per policy
alt.ex: AP report unexpected levels so the nurse can retake the blood glucose level according to agency policy.
w: The AP repeats the test and reports only the lower value
The nurse, not the AP, retakes an unexpected value.
The AP documents the value and waits for the next check
Unexpected values must be reported, not left until the next check.
The AP gives orange juice before telling the nurse
Treatment follows nursing assessment and orders, not AP decisions.

items.q: A patient’s order reads “blood glucose before insulin doses.” Why must the nurse confirm such conditions before collecting the sample?
items.a: Carbohydrate intake and glucose preparations change blood glucose
items.ex: Dietary carbohydrate and concentrated glucose preparations alter levels, so timing such as fasting or before insulin matters.
w: The meter cannot read samples taken right after meals
Meters read any sample; the issue is that intake alters the value.
Insulin causes the test strip code to change
Strip codes are unrelated to insulin; timing affects the glucose level.
Skin punctures are not permitted after a patient eats
Eating does not prevent puncture; it changes the result’s meaning.

alt.q: Which condition might a nurse need to confirm before collecting a blood glucose sample?
alt.a: Whether the patient has been fasting
alt.ex: Before sampling, the nurse checks conditions such as fasting, postprandial timing, certain medications, or upcoming insulin doses.
w: Whether the patient has showered today
Bathing is not a condition for timing the glucose sample.
Whether the patient has had a recent chest x-ray
Imaging does not affect when glucose is sampled.
Whether the patient slept on the right side
Sleep position is not a testing condition for glucose.

items.q: A patient asks why the nurse is pricking the side of the finger instead of the center of the fingertip. Which response is best?
items.a: The side has fewer nerve endings, so it hurts less
items.ex: Sides of fingers have fewer nerve endings, while the central tip has a denser nerve supply.
w: The center has fewer blood vessels to sample from
The reason for choosing the side is pain, not a lack of blood flow.
The side heals faster than the center of the finger
Healing speed is not the rationale given for site choice.
The meter reads only blood from the finger’s side
Meters read blood from any proper site; the side is chosen to reduce pain.

alt.q: Which area should a nurse avoid when puncturing a stable adult’s finger for glucose testing?
alt.a: The central tip of the finger
alt.ex: The central fingertip has a denser nerve supply, so the lateral side of the finger is used instead.
w: The lateral side of the finger
The lateral side is the recommended site in stable adults.
A finger free of cuts or sores
Intact skin is appropriate for puncture.
A finger with no recent punctures
Unpunctured skin is preferred over recently punctured sites.

items.q: A patient’s left hand is edematous, and two fingers on the right hand have recent puncture marks. Which site should the nurse choose for a glucose test?
items.a: Side of an unpunctured, intact right finger
items.ex: Edematous, inflamed, or recently punctured sites add interstitial fluid that mixes with blood and raises infection risk.
w: Side of a swollen left finger
Edema adds interstitial fluid to the sample and is avoided.
Side of a recently punctured right finger
Recently punctured sites are avoided because of tissue fluid and infection risk.
Center of a swollen left fingertip
This site combines edema with the dense nerve supply of the central tip.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid a puncture site that is edematous, inflamed, or recently punctured?
alt.a: Interstitial fluid mixes with blood and infection risk rises
alt.ex: Such sites have increased interstitial fluid that mixes with the blood sample and carry more risk for infection.
w: The meter cannot detect blood from these sites
The concern is sample dilution and infection, not detection.
These sites always bleed too heavily to sample
Heavy bleeding is linked to clotting problems, not to edema.
Such sites have more nerve endings than normal
The rationale is fluid mixing and infection, not nerve supply.

items.q: Before a fingerstick, the nurse asks the patient to wash the hands with soap and water. What is the rationale?
items.a: It cleans the skin and promotes vasodilation at the site
items.ex: Hand hygiene with soap and water cleanses the skin, promotes vasodilation, and reduces transmission of microorganisms.
w: It removes the need to use an antiseptic swab later
The site is still wiped with an antiseptic swab before puncture.
It raises the glucose level to the patient’s baseline
Washing does not change blood glucose; it prepares the skin.
It numbs the finger so the lancet causes less pain
Washing is for cleansing and vasodilation, not numbing.

alt.q: A nurse wipes the patient’s finger with an antiseptic swab before the puncture. What should the nurse do next?
alt.a: Allow the site to dry before puncturing
alt.ex: The site is wiped lightly with antiseptic and allowed to dry, which removes microorganisms from the skin surface.
w: Puncture right away while the site is still wet
The book directs the nurse to let the antiseptic dry first.
Blow on the site to make the antiseptic dry faster
Blowing on the site adds contamination; the site air-dries.
Wipe the site again with a dry cotton ball
The direction is to let the site dry, not to wipe it off.

items.q: Why does the nurse remove a test strip from the vial and then tightly seal the cap?
items.a: To protect strips from discoloration by air or light
items.ex: Sealing the vial protects remaining strips from discoloration caused by exposure to air or light.
w: To keep the meter battery from draining
The vial cap has no effect on the meter’s battery.
To prevent the lancet from becoming dull
Lancets are separate single-use items unrelated to the vial cap.
To keep the code on the vial from fading
The vial is sealed to protect the strips, not the printed code.

alt.q: A nurse’s glucose meter displays a code on its screen. What must the nurse confirm before applying blood?
alt.a: The code matches the code on the test strip vial
alt.ex: The code on the strip vial must match the meter’s code for the meter to operate accurately.
w: The code matches the patient’s medical record number
Strip codes relate to the strip lot, not to patient identifiers.
The code matches the lancet package lot number
Lancet lots are unrelated to the meter’s strip code.
The code matches the last result shown on the meter
The code is matched to the strip vial, not to prior results.

items.q: A student nurse is about to puncture a patient’s finger and first rubs and milks the finger vigorously. Which response by the instructor is best?
items.a: Hold the finger in a dependent position instead
items.ex: A dependent position increases blood flow; milking may hemolyze the specimen and introduce excess tissue fluid.
w: Keep milking it to get the largest drop possible
Milking the site may hemolyze the specimen and add tissue fluid.
Raise the hand above the heart before puncture
The hand is held in a dependent position to increase blood flow.
Soak the finger in alcohol to bring blood to it
The site is wiped lightly with antiseptic and allowed to dry.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid milking or massaging the finger before a glucose puncture?
alt.a: It may hemolyze the specimen and add tissue fluid
alt.ex: Milking the site may hemolyze the sample and introduce excess tissue fluid, which affects accuracy.
w: It causes the meter code to stop matching the vial
Milking affects the sample, not the meter’s code.
It makes the lancet go deeper than its setting
Lancet depth is set by cocking the device, not by massage.
It always causes bruising in older adults
The concern given is hemolysis and tissue fluid, not bruising.

items.q: A nurse observes a student obtaining a blood glucose sample. Which action by the student requires correction?
items.a: Scraping the blood drop onto the test strip
items.ex: Scraping blood onto the strip or applying it to the wrong side prevents accurate glucose measurement.
w: Bringing the strip in the meter to the blood drop
Touching the strip to the drop lets blood wick in correctly.
Wiping the site with antiseptic and letting it dry
Cleansing and drying the site is the correct technique.
Cocking the lancet device to the proper depth
Adjusting depth for the patient is a correct step.

alt.q: How should blood be applied to the test strip for an accurate glucose reading?
alt.a: Touch the strip to the drop and let it wick in
alt.ex: The strip in the meter is brought to the blood drop and blood is wicked onto the strip.
w: Scrape the drop onto the strip with its edge
Scraping blood onto the strip prevents accurate measurement.
Smear the drop over both sides of the strip
Applying blood to the wrong side prevents accurate results.
Squeeze the drop onto the strip before inserting it
The strip is already in the meter when blood is applied.

items.q: A nurse’s glucose meter malfunctions during a test. After reviewing troubleshooting instructions, what should the nurse do?
items.a: Repeat the test using a different puncture site
items.ex: When the meter malfunctions, review troubleshooting, then repeat the test without reusing the same puncture site.
w: Repeat the test at the same puncture site
The same puncture site is not used for a repeat test.
Record an estimated value based on symptoms
Estimated values are not a substitute for a measured result.
Skip the test until the next scheduled time
The test is repeated after troubleshooting, not skipped.

alt.q: A patient whose meter gave an error message says, “I’ll just stick the same spot again so I don’t make a new hole.” Which response is best?
alt.a: Use a new site for the repeat test
alt.ex: A repeat test after a malfunction should not use the same puncture site.
w: That is fine because the site is already open
Reusing the puncture site is specifically avoided for repeat tests.
Squeeze the old site hard until it bleeds again
The repeat test uses a different site, not the old one.
Wait 24 hours before testing again at any site
The test is repeated after troubleshooting, not delayed a day.

items.q: After a fingerstick, a patient who takes an anticoagulant continues to bleed from the puncture site. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Apply pressure to the puncture site
items.ex: Bleeding at the site is managed first with pressure; anticoagulants can prolong bleeding, and the provider is notified if it continues.
w: Notify the health care provider immediately
Pressure is applied first; the provider is notified if bleeding continues.
Hold the hand in a dependent position
A dependent position increases blood flow to the finger.
Puncture another finger to recheck glucose
Another puncture adds bleeding risk and does not stop the bleeding.

alt.q: A nurse applies pressure to a puncture site that keeps bleeding in a patient on anticoagulant therapy. The bleeding continues. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Notify the health care provider
alt.ex: If bleeding continues despite pressure, the nurse notifies the health care provider.
w: Massage the site firmly to stop bleeding
Massage does not stop bleeding and can injure tissue.
Document it and recheck at the next test
Continued bleeding must be reported, not left until later.
Hold the next dose of anticoagulant
Changing medications requires a provider order.

items.q: A patient’s blood glucose result is above the target range. Which action is appropriate for the nurse?
items.a: Check for medication orders that cover glucose deviations
items.ex: For results outside target, the nurse keeps monitoring, checks orders, notifies the provider, and gives insulin or carbohydrate as ordered.
w: Give insulin in an amount the nurse thinks is right
Insulin is given as ordered, not by the nurse’s own estimate.
Recheck the result only at the next scheduled time
Out-of-range results need follow-up and reporting, not waiting.
Discard the result because the meter is likely wrong
The result is acted on and reported unless the meter malfunctions.

alt.q: A patient with diabetes is learning blood glucose monitoring before discharge. Which statement shows understanding of the teaching?
alt.a: “I can check my blood sugar more often than ordered if needed.”
alt.ex: Patients are taught the frequency of monitoring and that they may test more often than prescribed if necessary.
w: “I can reuse my lancets for a week if I wipe them.”
Lancets are never reused because of infection risk.
“I can throw used lancets into my kitchen trash bag.”
Sharps go in a nonpermeable, puncture-resistant container.
“I should check only when I feel unwell or shaky.”
Patients follow the prescribed frequency and may test more often if needed.

items.q: A nurse reviews a patient’s EHR before a fingerstick. Which findings increase the risk for bleeding or bruising at the puncture site? Select all that apply.
o: Low platelet count
Abnormal clotting increases risk of bleeding and ecchymosis.
Anticoagulant therapy
Anticoagulants increase bleeding at the puncture site.
Bleeding disorder
Bleeding disorders impair clotting at the site.
Fasting since midnight
Fasting affects the glucose value, not bleeding risk.
Insulin dose due before lunch
Insulin timing affects test timing, not bleeding risk.
items.ex: Low platelets, anticoagulants, and bleeding disorders impair clotting, increasing the risk of local ecchymosis and bleeding.

alt.q: Which patients are at increased risk for prolonged bleeding after a glucose fingerstick? Select all that apply.
o: A patient receiving an anticoagulant
Anticoagulants prolong bleeding at the puncture site.
A patient with a very low platelet count
Low platelets impair clotting at the site.
A patient with a known bleeding disorder
Bleeding disorders raise the risk of bleeding and bruising.
A patient who just ate a meal
A recent meal changes the glucose value, not bleeding risk.
A patient who washed the hands first
Hand washing promotes cleansing and vasodilation, not bleeding risk.
alt.ex: Clotting problems from low platelets, anticoagulants, or bleeding disorders increase bleeding and ecchymosis at the puncture site.

items.q: A nurse is teaching a patient and family caregiver about home blood glucose monitoring. Which points should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Dispose of lancets in a puncture-resistant container
Sharps go in a nonpermeable, puncture-resistant container.
Family should be able to test if the patient is ill
Caregivers should perform the test when the patient cannot.
Testing may be done more often than prescribed if needed
Patients may test more frequently than ordered if necessary.
Record findings and know how to retrieve results
Recording and retrieving results is part of home teaching.
Reuse a lancet if it is wiped with alcohol
Lancets are never reused because of infection risk.
Use any brand of strip that fits the meter
Use only test strips recommended for the meter.
items.ex: Home teaching covers sharps disposal, caregiver backup, testing frequency, and recording results.

alt.q: A family caregiver will help with glucose testing at home. Which statements by the caregiver show correct understanding? Select all that apply.
o: “I will put used lancets in a hard, puncture-proof container.”
Sharps belong in a nonpermeable, puncture-resistant container.
“I can do the test when my father is too ill to do it.”
Caregivers should be able to test when the patient cannot.
“We will write down each result in a log.”
Patients and families are taught to record findings.
“We can use a lancet twice if it looks clean.”
Lancets are never reused because of infection risk.
“We should never test more often than ordered.”
Testing can be done more often than prescribed if necessary.
alt.ex: Caregivers should dispose of sharps safely, test when the patient cannot, and record results; extra testing is allowed if needed.

items.q: A nurse documents a blood glucose test. Which items should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: The glucose level
The glucose value is a required entry.
Appearance of the puncture site
Site appearance is documented after the test.
Patient’s response to the procedure
The patient’s response is part of the documentation.
Action taken for an abnormal result
Interventions for out-of-range values are documented and reported.
The meter battery’s remaining charge
Battery status is not part of the patient record.
The AP’s opinion of the patient’s diet
Opinions do not belong in documentation.
items.ex: Document the procedure, patient response, site appearance, glucose level, actions for abnormal values, and teaching provided.

alt.q: A patient’s glucose result is below the target range. Which should the nurse document or report? Select all that apply.
o: The abnormal glucose level
Abnormal blood glucose levels are reported.
Interventions given to correct the level
Interventions to correct high or low levels are reported and documented.
Any patient education provided
Education provided is described in documentation.
Evaluation of the patient’s learning
The nurse documents evaluation of patient and caregiver learning.
The cost of the test strips used
Supply cost is not part of clinical documentation.
alt.ex: Abnormal levels, corrective interventions, education, and learning evaluation are documented and reported.

items.q: A lancet must never be reused because of the risk of infection.

items.ex: A new lancet is used for each puncture because reuse risks infection.
items.ww: Cleaning does not make a lancet safe to reuse; the book says never reuse it.

alt.q: A lancet can be reused on the same patient if it is wiped with alcohol between uses.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Lancets are never reused because of infection risk, even on the same patient.
alt.ww: Alcohol wiping does not change the rule; each puncture requires a new lancet.

items.q: Blood glucose measurements from alternative sites such as the forearm are meter specific and may differ from fingertip results.

items.ex: Alternative-site readings depend on the meter and may differ from traditional sites.
items.ww: The book warns that alternative-site results can differ, so they are not interchangeable with fingersticks.

alt.q: Forearm blood glucose readings are always identical to fingertip readings, regardless of the meter used.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Alternative-site measurements are meter specific and may differ from those at traditional sites.
alt.ww: Readings can vary by site and meter, so results are not guaranteed to match.

items.q: Assessment of a patient’s condition may be delegated to assistive personnel when the patient is stable.
items.a: False
items.ex: Assessment cannot be delegated; AP may only obtain and test the sample when the patient is stable.
items.ww: Patient stability allows delegation of the testing skill, never of assessment.

alt.q: When a patient’s condition is stable, obtaining and testing a blood glucose sample can be delegated to assistive personnel.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: With a stable patient, AP may perform the fingerstick and test, while assessment remains with the nurse.
alt.ww: The textbook explicitly permits delegating the testing skill for stable patients.

Touch the test strip to the blood drop

Press the lancet device against the lateral finger

alt.ex: That's step 2 of 9. The patient and meter are prepared, the site is cleansed and punctured, blood is applied, and results are shared.
w: Insert the test strip into the meter
That's step 3 of 9.
Wipe the site with antiseptic and let it dry
That's step 4 of 9.
Hold the site in a dependent position

w: Wipe the site with antiseptic and let it dry

items.q: Where are the kidneys located in relation to the peritoneum?
items.a: Retroperitoneally, on either side of the vertebral column against the deep back muscles
items.ex: The kidneys lie behind the peritoneum, beside the spine and against the deep muscles of the back.
w: Intraperitoneally, on either side of the vertebral column below the diaphragm
The kidneys lie behind the peritoneum, not within the peritoneal cavity.
Anterior to the peritoneum, beside the liver and stomach in the upper abdomen
The kidneys are posterior structures, lying against the deep muscles of the back.
Within the pelvic cavity, directly behind the symphysis pubis
The empty bladder, not the kidneys, lies behind the symphysis pubis.

alt.q: Why is the left kidney normally positioned higher than the right kidney?

w: The heart occupies space on the left side and pulls the left kidney upward.
The heart does not determine kidney position; the liver lowers the right kidney.
The left kidney is larger and needs more room beneath the diaphragm.
Kidney size is not the reason; the liver displaces the right kidney downward.
The spleen occupies space on the left side and lifts the left kidney upward.
The book attributes the difference to the liver on the right, not the spleen.

items.q: What is the functional unit of the kidney that removes waste products from the blood?
items.a: Nephron
items.ex: Nephrons remove wastes from the blood and play a major role in regulating fluid and electrolyte balance.
w: Glomerulus
The glomerulus is the capillary cluster within each nephron, not the whole functional unit.
Renal pelvis
The renal pelvis collects urine and is where the ureter attaches.
Juxtaglomerular cell
Juxtaglomerular cells release renin during renal ischemia; they are not the functional unit.

alt.q: Within each nephron, what is the cluster of capillaries that filters the blood called?
alt.a: Glomerulus
alt.ex: The glomerulus filters water, glucose, amino acids, urea, uric acid, creatinine, and major electrolytes.
w: Loop of Henle
The loop of Henle is a tubule segment that resorbs filtrate, not a capillary cluster.
Distal tubule
The distal tubule resorbs filtrate; it is not the filtering capillary cluster.
Proximal convoluted tubule
The proximal convoluted tubule resorbs filtrate rather than filtering blood.

items.q: Which substances are normally filtered through the glomerulus? Select all that apply.
o: Glucose
Glucose is filtered by the glomerulus and is normally resorbed in the tubules.
Creatinine
Creatinine, a waste product, is filtered through the glomerulus.
Urea
Urea is a metabolic waste filtered by the glomerulus.
Large proteins
Large proteins do not normally pass the glomerulus; their presence in urine suggests glomerular injury.
Red blood cells
Blood cells do not normally filter through the glomerulus; hematuria suggests injury.
Major electrolytes
The glomerulus filters major electrolytes, which are then selectively resorbed.
items.ex: The glomerulus filters water, glucose, amino acids, urea, uric acid, creatinine, and electrolytes, but not large proteins or blood cells.

alt.q: Which substances should NOT normally pass through a healthy glomerulus into the filtrate? Select all that apply.
o: Large proteins
Large proteins are normally held back by the glomerulus.
Blood cells
Blood cells are normally too large to filter through the glomerulus.
Uric acid
Uric acid is normally filtered by the glomerulus.
Amino acids
Amino acids are normally filtered by the glomerulus.
Water
Water is normally filtered, and most of it is resorbed in the tubules.
alt.ex: Only large proteins and blood cells are normally kept out of the filtrate; their appearance in urine points to glomerular injury.

items.q: A patient’s urinalysis shows both protein and red blood cells. What should the nurse suspect?
items.a: Injury to the glomerulus
items.ex: Large proteins and blood cells do not normally filter through the glomerulus, so proteinuria and hematuria suggest glomerular injury.
w: Normal concentration of morning urine
Concentrated urine does not contain protein or blood cells.
Overactive resorption in the loop of Henle
Resorption problems do not let large proteins and blood cells into the filtrate.
Excess fluid intake diluting the urine
Dilution changes concentration but does not add protein or blood cells to urine.

alt.q: A nurse suspects glomerular injury in a patient with a kidney disorder. Which urinalysis result supports this suspicion?

alt.ex: Proteinuria and hematuria indicate that large molecules and cells are passing an injured glomerulus.
w: Clear, light yellow urine with no sediment
This describes normal, dilute urine, not glomerular injury.
Urine that becomes cloudy after standing
Urine standing several minutes normally becomes cloudy.
Acidic urine pH in the morning
An acid pH is normal and helps protect against bacterial growth.

items.q: Approximately what percentage of glomerular filtrate is resorbed into the plasma rather than excreted as urine?

alt.q: Approximately what percentage of glomerular filtrate is excreted as urine?

items.q: It is the resorption process in the nephron that maintains the delicate balance of fluid and electrolytes.

items.ex: Selective resorption of about 99% of filtrate in the tubules and loop of Henle keeps fluids and electrolytes balanced.
items.ww: Balance depends on resorption; if most filtrate were excreted, fluids and electrolytes would be lost rapidly.

alt.ww: Fluid balance comes from resorbing nearly all filtrate, not from excreting most of it.

Angiotensin II
Angiotensin II: Causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone release.
Aldosterone
Aldosterone: Causes water retention, increasing blood volume.

Erythropoietin: Stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow.
Angiotensin II
Angiotensin II: Causes vasoconstriction and stimulates aldosterone release.
Aldosterone
Aldosterone: Causes water retention, increasing blood volume.

alt.a: Angiotensin II
alt.ex: The kidneys support red cell production and blood pressure through erythropoietin, the renin-angiotensin system, and vasodilating prostaglandins.
w: Erythropoietin
Erythropoietin: Stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow.
Renin
Renin: Converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.
Aldosterone
Aldosterone: Causes water retention, increasing blood volume.

alt.a: Aldosterone
alt.ex: The kidneys support red cell production and blood pressure through erythropoietin, the renin-angiotensin system, and vasodilating prostaglandins.
w: Erythropoietin
Erythropoietin: Stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow.
Renin
Renin: Converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.

alt.a: Prostaglandin E2 and prostacyclin

Erythropoietin: Stimulates red blood cell production in bone marrow.
Renin
Renin: Converts angiotensinogen into angiotensin I.
