Orthotopic neobladder
Orthotopic neobladder: Ileal pouch in the bladder’s position; patient voids through the urethra.
Ileal conduit
Ileal conduit: Continuous urine flow without control, collected in an external pouch.

mt.q: Match each type of urinary diversion or drainage device with its feature.
pairs: Emptied by inserting a catheter through the stoma 4 to 6 times a day
Ileal pouch in the bladder’s position; patient voids through the urethra
Continuous urine flow without control, collected in an external pouch
Tube tunneled through the skin to drain an obstructed renal pelvis
mt.ex: Diversions differ in continence and emptying: catheterized reservoir, urethral voiding neobladder, pouched ileal conduit, or nephrostomy drainage.

items.q: A patient is scheduled for a continent urinary reservoir. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the self-care required?
items.a: “I will need to put a catheter into my stoma 4 to 6 times a day.”
items.ex: The reservoir’s one-way valve holds urine, so patients must catheterize the pouch 4 to 6 times daily for life.
w: “I will wear a pouch to collect urine that drains all the time.”
Continuous drainage into a pouch describes an ileal conduit.
“I will empty my new bladder by bearing down on the toilet.”
Voiding with a Valsalva technique describes an orthotopic neobladder.
“I will need to catheterize myself once or twice a week.”
Weekly catheterization is far too infrequent; it is 4 to 6 times a day.

alt.q: In a continent urinary reservoir, what structure acts as the one-way valve that keeps urine in the pouch?
alt.a: The ileocecal valve
alt.ex: The ileocecal valve creates a one-way valve; urine is removed by catheter through the stoma.
w: The external urethral sphincter
The reservoir drains through an abdominal stoma, not the urethra.
The bladder trigone
The bladder has been removed, so the trigone is not present.
The ureterovesical junction
The ureters are embedded in the reservoir; they do not form its outlet valve.

items.q: Mixed urinary incontinence is present when a patient has both stress- and urgency-type symptoms.
items.a: True
items.ex: Mixed UI combines the effort-related leakage of stress UI with the urgency of urge UI.
items.ww: The book defines mixed UI as the presence of both stress- and urgency-type symptoms.

alt.q: Multifactorial incontinence is the term for incontinence in which a patient has both stress- and urgency-type symptoms.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Combined stress and urgency symptoms define mixed UI; multifactorial UI has many interacting risk factors.
alt.ww: Multifactorial incontinence involves multiple interacting factors such as chronic illnesses, medications, and environment.

items.q: A patient taking phenazopyridine calls the clinic worried that the urine is bright orange. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “This medication commonly turns urine orange.”
items.ex: Box 46.1 notes that some drugs change urine color; phenazopyridine turns urine orange.
w: “Stop the medication and go to the emergency department.”
Orange urine is an expected drug effect, not an emergency.
“Orange urine means you are severely dehydrated.”
The color change is caused by the drug, not by dehydration.
“Orange urine is an early sign of kidney failure.”
This is a known medication effect, not a sign of kidney failure.

alt.q: Which medication class increases the risk for urinary retention by inhibiting bladder contractility?
alt.a: Anticholinergics
alt.ex: Anticholinergic agents such as atropine inhibit bladder contractility and increase retention risk.
w: Diuretics
Diuretics increase urine output by preventing resorption of water and electrolytes.
Hypnotics
Hypnotics and sedatives reduce the ability to recognize the urge to void.
Vitamins
Riboflavin changes urine color but does not inhibit bladder contraction.

items.q: Which type of aseptic technique does the nurse use when performing perineal care or examining the genitalia?
items.a: Medical asepsis, including proper hand hygiene
items.ex: Perineal care and genital examination are not invasive, so medical asepsis with hand hygiene is required.
w: Sterile technique with sterile gloves and drapes
Sterile technique is reserved for invasive procedures such as catheterization.
No special technique beyond wearing a gown
Medical asepsis, including hand hygiene, is required for perineal care.
Protective isolation with a mask and gown
Protective isolation is not the required asepsis for routine perineal care.

alt.q: Which type of aseptic technique does the nurse use when inserting a urinary catheter?
alt.a: Sterile aseptic technique
alt.ex: Any invasive procedure into the sterile urinary tract, such as catheterization, requires sterile aseptic technique.
w: Medical asepsis with clean gloves
Medical asepsis is for perineal care, not invasive entry into the sterile bladder.
Clean technique with hand hygiene only
Clean technique is not enough for an invasive urinary procedure.
Standard precautions with a mask only
A mask alone does not provide sterile technique for catheter insertion.

items.q: The urinary tract is normally sterile, so infection control principles are used to prevent UTIs.
items.a: True
items.ex: Because the urinary tract is sterile, introducing organisms through care or procedures can cause infection.
items.ww: The book states the urinary tract is sterile and directs use of infection control to prevent UTIs.

alt.q: Because the urinary tract normally contains bacteria, clean technique is sufficient for inserting a urinary catheter.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The urinary tract is sterile, and catheterization requires sterile aseptic technique.
alt.ww: Clean technique is used for perineal care; invasive catheterization of the sterile bladder requires sterile technique.

items.q: According to the chapter, perineal hygiene becomes an especially essential part of care in which situation?
items.a: When the usual pattern of urinary elimination is altered
items.ex: Perineal hygiene is essential when elimination is altered, such as with incontinence or an indwelling catheter.
w: Only when the patient requests a bath
Perineal hygiene is a planned part of care, not only provided on request.
Only after a urine specimen is collected
Hygiene is needed whenever elimination is altered, not just after specimens.
Only when a patient has a fever
Fever is not the trigger; altered elimination patterns are.

alt.q: A patient with an indwelling urinary catheter has just had a bowel movement. Which action should the nurse take?
alt.a: Provide perineal hygiene right away
alt.ex: Regular perineal hygiene, especially after a bowel movement, reduces the risk for CAUTI.
w: Wait until the scheduled 8-hour catheter care
Soiling near the catheter needs prompt cleansing, not delay.
Remove the catheter and insert a new one
Soiling calls for hygiene, not routine catheter replacement.
Clamp the catheter until the bed is changed
Clamping obstructs urine flow and does not reduce contamination.

items.q: A nurse is preparing to insert an indwelling urinary catheter. Which action best reduces the patient’s risk for CAUTI?
items.a: Use sterile equipment and sterile insertion technique
items.ex: Aseptic insertion with sterile equipment is an evidence-based CAUTI prevention measure.
w: Use the largest catheter available
The smallest catheter possible is recommended to reduce trauma and infection.
Use clean gloves to save sterile supplies
Catheter insertion is invasive and requires sterile technique.
Leave the catheter unsecured to allow movement
Catheters should be secured to prevent movement and pulling.

alt.q: Which catheter size choice is recommended to help prevent CAUTI?
alt.a: The smallest catheter possible for the patient
alt.ex: Box 46.9 recommends the smallest catheter possible, individualized to the patient.
w: The largest catheter that fits the urethra
Larger diameters increase urethral trauma and are reserved for special situations.
A 30-mL balloon catheter for all adults
Large balloons increase discomfort, trauma, and incomplete emptying.
Whichever size is stocked on the unit
Catheter size should be individualized to the patient, not chosen for convenience.

items.q: Which actions help prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the drainage bag below the level of the bladder
This prevents urine backflow into the bladder.
Secure the catheter to prevent movement and pulling
Securing reduces urethral trauma from catheter movement.
Maintain a sterile, closed drainage system
A closed system keeps pathogens from entering the tubing.
Remove the catheter as soon as possible
CAUTI risk rises with each day the catheter remains.
Change the catheter at routine fixed intervals
The IDSA advises changing catheters based on clinical indicators, not routine intervals.
Disconnect the tubing to collect a specimen
Specimens are taken from the sampling port without opening the system.
items.ex: Key CAUTI measures include a closed sterile system, dependent drainage, securement, unobstructed flow, and early removal.

alt.q: Which actions by a nurse emptying a urinary drainage bag follow CAUTI prevention guidelines? Select all that apply.
o: Use a separate measuring container for each patient
Separate receptacles prevent cross-contamination between patients.
Keep the drainage spigot from touching the container
Spigot contact can introduce organisms into the bag.
Empty the bag when it is about half full
An overfull bag pulls on the catheter and increases CAUTI risk.
Raise the bag above the bladder to drain the tubing
Raising the bag causes urine backflow into the bladder.
Share one graduated container among patients in a room
Shared containers spread organisms between patients.
alt.ex: When emptying the bag, use a separate container per patient, avoid spigot contact, and empty at half full.

items.q: A nurse sees a patient with an indwelling catheter walking in the hall while holding the drainage bag at chest level. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Have the patient carry the bag below the level of the bladder
items.ex: Keeping the bag below the bladder prevents backflow of urine into the bladder and reduces CAUTI risk.
w: Clamp the catheter for the rest of the walk
Clamping obstructs urine flow and is not a backflow-prevention measure.
Let the patient keep it at chest level
Holding the bag above the bladder allows urine to flow back into the bladder.
Rest the bag on the floor while the patient stands
The bag must never touch the floor to prevent contamination.

alt.q: Which drainage bag may be worn without keeping it dependent to the bladder?
alt.a: A belly bag worn across the abdomen
alt.ex: A belly bag has a one-way valve that prevents backflow, so it need not be dependent.
w: A standard bedside drainage bag
Standard bags must always hang below the bladder.
A leg bag worn on the thigh
A leg bag must still stay below the bladder.
A bag hung on the bed rail
A bed-hung bag must stay below bladder level to prevent backflow.

items.q: How should the nurse collect a urine specimen from a patient with an indwelling catheter and closed drainage system?
items.a: Aspirate urine from the sampling port in the tubing
items.ex: Specimens are collected from a special port so the closed drainage system is never opened.
w: Disconnect the catheter from the tubing and drain urine
Separating connections introduces pathogens into the closed system.
Pour urine from the drainage bag into a specimen cup
Urine in the bag is not fresh and the bag is a contamination site.
Remove the catheter and collect the next voided urine
Removing a needed catheter only to get a specimen is unnecessary.

alt.q: Why should the connection between the catheter and drainage tubing not be separated?
alt.a: Separating it can introduce pathogens into the closed system
alt.ex: The closed sterile drainage system protects the bladder; opening connections introduces organisms.
w: Separating it deflates the catheter balloon
The balloon is inflated through its own lumen and is not affected.
Separating it stops urine production
Urine production is a kidney function, not affected by the connection.
Separating it causes the bag to overfill
Opening the connection causes contamination, not bag overfilling.

items.q: A urinary drainage bag may rest on the floor as long as it stays below the level of the bladder.
items.a: False
items.ex: The bag hangs below the bladder on the bedframe or chair and should never touch the floor.
items.ww: The book states the bag must never touch the floor to prevent accidental contamination during emptying.

alt.q: A urinary drainage bag should hang below the level of the bladder and should never touch the floor.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Dependent drainage prevents backflow, and keeping the bag off the floor prevents contamination.
alt.ww: Resting the bag on the floor risks contamination, even if it is below the bladder.

items.q: A nurse teaches a female patient how to prevent urinary tract infections. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I will wipe from front to back after using the toilet.”
items.ex: Wiping front to back keeps bacteria from the perineal area away from the short female urethra.
w: “I will use a perfumed spray to keep the area fresh.”
Perfumed washes and sprays should be avoided.
“I will take bubble baths to keep myself extra clean.”
Bubble baths are among the products to avoid.
“I will drink less so I don’t have to void as often.”
Adequate fluid intake helps flush the urinary tract.

alt.q: Which practice should the nurse teach a female patient to avoid to reduce her risk for UTI?
alt.a: Wearing tight clothing
alt.ex: Patients are taught to avoid tight clothing, perfumed perineal washes and sprays, and bubble baths.
w: Wearing cotton undergarments
Cotton undergarments are recommended to help prevent UTIs.
Voiding at regular intervals
Regular voiding is a key UTI prevention measure.
Drinking enough to pass pale urine
Adequate fluid intake to produce pale yellow urine is recommended.

items.q: Which teaching points help a patient prevent urinary tract infections? Select all that apply.
o: Drink enough fluid to pass pale yellow urine
Adequate fluids flush the urinary system.
Void at regular intervals
Regular voiding is a key UTI prevention intervention.
Females should wipe front to back
This keeps perineal bacteria away from the urethra.
Wear cotton undergarments
Cotton undergarments are recommended in Box 46.7.
Use perfumed perineal washes daily
Perfumed washes and sprays should be avoided.
Hold urine as long as possible
Patients should void regularly, not delay voiding.
items.ex: UTI prevention includes adequate fluids, regular voiding, front-to-back cleansing, and avoiding irritating products.

alt.q: A patient has urine leakage. Which measures help protect the patient from UTI and skin problems? Select all that apply.
o: Stress frequent perineal hygiene
Perineal hygiene is especially stressed when urine leakage occurs.
Use containment products designed for urine
Urine-specific products are recommended.
Choose products that wick wetness from the skin
Wicking products limit prolonged wetness.
Limit changes to once daily to save supplies
Prolonged periods of urine wetness should be avoided.
Use any absorbent pad, such as a menstrual pad
Products should be designed for urine and wick wetness away.
alt.ex: With leakage, stress perineal hygiene and use urine-specific, wicking products to avoid prolonged wetness.

items.q: In many health care agencies, patients with indwelling catheters receive catheter care every [[8|eight]] hours as the minimal standard of care.
items.ex: Routine catheter care at least every 8 hours, plus perineal hygiene after soiling, reduces CAUTI risk.

alt.q: The minimal standard in many agencies is to provide catheter care at least once every [[8|eight]] hours.
alt.ex: Routine catheter care at least every 8 hours, plus perineal hygiene after soiling, reduces CAUTI risk.

items.q: Why should a urinary drainage bag be emptied when it is about half full?
items.a: An overfull bag pulls on the catheter, causing urethral trauma
items.ex: Tension from an overfull bag can traumatize the urethra or meatus and increase CAUTI risk.
w: A half-full bag is needed for an accurate culture
Specimens come from the sampling port, not from the bag.
A half-full bag causes the balloon to deflate
Bag volume does not affect balloon inflation.
A full bag stops the kidneys from making urine
Bag fullness does not affect urine production by the kidneys.

alt.q: A nurse finds a patient’s drainage bag nearly full and pulling on the catheter. What risk does this create?
alt.a: Urethral trauma and increased risk for CAUTI
alt.ex: Tension on the catheter can injure the urethra and meatus, raising the risk for CAUTI.
w: Autonomic dysreflexia and severe hypotension
Autonomic dysreflexia causes hypertension and is linked to spinal cord injury.
Urinary diversion leakage and stoma damage
This patient has a urethral catheter, not a diversion stoma.
Increased urine production and diuresis
A full bag does not increase urine production.

items.q: A patient with an indwelling catheter has had no urine drain into the bag for 2 hours. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Check the tubing and catheter for kinks or occlusion
items.ex: With no drainage, first check for kinks or obvious occlusion of the tubing or catheter.
w: Irrigate the catheter with sterile saline
Irrigation is not first and risks flushing debris and causing UTI.
Remove the catheter and reinsert a new one
Simple causes such as kinks should be checked before replacement.
Give the patient extra fluids to drink
A blocked system will not drain no matter how much the patient drinks.

alt.q: Which nursing action helps keep an indwelling catheter drainage system patent?
alt.a: Avoid positioning the patient on the drainage tubing
alt.ex: Lying on tubing kinks it and obstructs flow; keeping flow unobstructed also reduces CAUTI risk.
w: Coil the tubing below the bag outlet
Dependent loops of tubing let urine pool and obstruct drainage.
Clamp the tubing between bag emptyings
Clamping stops urine flow and obstructs drainage.
Hang the bag above the bladder level
Raising the bag causes backflow into the bladder.

items.q: The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends changing indwelling urinary catheters at regular fixed intervals to prevent infection.
items.a: False
items.ex: The IDSA advises changing catheters based on clinical indicators such as obstruction, infection, or a break in the system.
items.ww: The book states the IDSA does not recommend routine-interval catheter changes.

alt.q: Indwelling catheters should be changed based on clinical indicators such as obstruction, infection, or a break in the closed drainage system.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The IDSA recommends clinical indicators, not fixed schedules, to decide when to change a catheter.
alt.ww: Routine fixed-interval changes are not recommended by the IDSA.

items.q: Why should incontinent patients use containment products designed for urine that wick wetness away from the body?
items.a: Prolonged urine wetness on the skin should be avoided
items.ex: Urine-specific wicking products limit prolonged wetness, protecting skin and lowering infection risk.
w: They allow the nurse to check on the patient less often
Products do not replace prompt toileting help and hygiene.
They keep the bladder from filling with urine
Containment products do not affect bladder filling.
They replace the need for perineal hygiene
Perineal hygiene is especially stressed when leakage occurs.

alt.q: Why should nurses avoid incontinence-containment products unless they are needed for uncontrolled leakage?
alt.a: They can promote skin maceration and delay toilet access
alt.ex: Some products are hard to remove, promote skin maceration, and interfere with prompt toilet access.
w: They increase the kidneys’ production of urine
Containment products have no effect on urine production.
They cause bladder overdistention and retention
Products do not cause retention.
They require sterile technique to apply
Applying a containment product is not a sterile procedure.

items.q: Which strategies can a nurse advocate as alternatives to an indwelling urinary catheter? Select all that apply.
o: Using a bladder scanner to measure urine volume
A bladder scanner assesses volume without invasive instrumentation.
Starting a voiding schedule for an incontinent patient
A voiding schedule is a noninvasive alternative.
Using an external device such as a condom catheter
Alternative drainage devices are recommended when possible.
Inserting a catheter to manage routine incontinence
Inappropriate catheter use should be reduced to prevent CAUTI.
Leaving a catheter in place until hospital discharge
Catheters should be removed as soon as they are no longer needed.
items.ex: Nurses advocate noninvasive options such as bladder scanning, voiding schedules, and external devices to avoid CAUTI.

alt.q: Which statements describe the nurse’s role in CAUTI prevention? Select all that apply.
o: Advocate for the patient if catheter indications do not meet guidelines
Nurses should question inappropriate catheter use.
Collaborate with providers to remove catheters early
Early removal when indications end reduces CAUTI.
Use evidence-based nurse-driven CAUTI protocols
Nurse-driven protocols are a recommended practice.
Allow any available staff member to insert catheters
Only trained, dedicated personnel should insert catheters.
Accept catheter orders without reviewing indications
Nurses should evaluate indications and advocate as needed.
alt.ex: Nurses review catheter indications, advocate, collaborate on early removal, and use protocols and trained personnel.

items.q: A long-term indwelling catheter becomes occluded with sediment. In general, which approach is best?
items.a: Change the catheter rather than flush it
items.ex: Changing an occluded catheter avoids the infection risk of flushing debris into the bladder.
w: Irrigate it forcefully with tap water
Irrigation uses sterile solution and risks UTI; tap water is not used.
Disconnect the tubing and milk the catheter
Opening the closed system introduces pathogens.
Leave it in place and recheck in a day
An occluded catheter will not drain and needs prompt action.

alt.q: When the health care provider orders irrigation to keep a catheter patent, which principle must the nurse follow?
alt.a: Maintain a closed urinary drainage system
alt.ex: Irrigation can cause UTI, so it must be done without breaking the closed system.
w: Use clean tap water for each irrigation
Irrigation uses sterile solution, not tap water.
Open the catheter-tubing connection to irrigate
Opening the connection breaks the closed system.
Irrigate every hour whether or not needed
Irrigation is done only when ordered, not routinely each hour.

items.q: A patient on day 3 after surgery is alert, walking independently, and no longer has a medical indication for the indwelling catheter. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Collaborate with the health care provider to remove the catheter
items.ex: Prompt removal when indications no longer exist is a key intervention to reduce CAUTI.
w: Keep the catheter until the patient is discharged
Each catheter day adds 3% to 7% to CAUTI risk.
Change the catheter to a new sterile one
A new catheter keeps the infection risk; removal is indicated.
Clamp the catheter to retrain the bladder
Clamping is not the recommended step when the catheter is no longer needed.

alt.q: Each day an indwelling urinary catheter remains in place, by approximately how much does the patient’s risk of acquiring a CAUTI increase?
alt.ex: Box 46.9 reports a 3% to 7% increased risk of CAUTI for each catheter day.
w: The daily increase reported is higher than this range.
12% to 16% is the share of inpatients who have a catheter at some point.
This range is much higher than the reported daily increase.

items.q: An indwelling catheter was removed this morning. Which finding during later voids suggests a possible infection?
items.a: Painful urination that continues after the first few voids
items.ex: Some discomfort with the first few voids is expected, but continued painful urination indicates possible infection.
w: Mild discomfort with the first void only
Discomfort with the first few voids after removal is expected.
Voiding about 300 mL every 3 to 4 hours
Regular, adequate voids show normal bladder function.
Pale yellow, clear urine in each void
Clear, pale yellow urine is a normal finding.

alt.q: After an indwelling catheter is removed, for how long should the nurse monitor the patient’s voiding with a voiding record or bladder diary?
alt.a: At least 24 to 48 hours
alt.ex: Voiding is monitored for at least 24 to 48 hours after removal, recording the time and amount of each void.
w: At least 2 to 4 hours
This is too short to detect retention or infection after removal.
At least 7 to 10 days
The recommended monitoring period is 24 to 48 hours.
At least 4 to 6 weeks
Four to six weeks is the change interval for long-term catheters.

items.q: Because many drainage systems have an antireflux valve, the nurse does not need to keep the drainage bag below the level of the bladder.
items.a: False
items.ex: Even with an antireflux valve, the nurse prevents urine pooling in the tubing and keeps the bag below the bladder.
items.ww: The book says to monitor the system and keep the bag below the bladder despite antireflux valves.

alt.q: Even when a drainage system has an antireflux valve, the nurse prevents pooling of urine in the tubing and keeps the bag below the bladder.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Preventing backflow from tubing and bag into the bladder is a key CAUTI intervention regardless of valves.
alt.ww: An antireflux valve does not replace monitoring for pooling and keeping the bag dependent.

items.q: By what age is a child’s neurological system usually developed enough to associate the sensation of bladder filling with urination?
items.a: 2 to 3 years
items.ex: The neurological system is not well developed until 2 to 3 years, so younger children cannot link filling to urination.
w: 6 to 9 months
Infants cannot yet associate bladder filling and urge with urination.
12 to 15 months
At this age the neurological system is not yet developed enough.
5 to 6 years
The neurological system is usually developed earlier, by 2 to 3 years.

alt.q: A parent asks why their 14-month-old cannot be toilet trained yet. Which explanation is most accurate?
alt.a: The child cannot yet connect bladder filling with the need to void
alt.ex: Until neurological development at 2 to 3 years, a child cannot associate filling and urge with urination.
w: The child’s kidneys do not yet produce urine steadily
Infants produce large volumes of urine; kidney output is not the barrier.
The child’s urethra is too short to stay closed
Urethral length is not the reason toilet training is delayed.
The child lacks a bladder sphincter until age 4
The barrier is neurological development, not absence of a sphincter.

items.q: Which signs show that a toddler is ready for toilet training? Select all that apply.
o: Recognizes the feeling of urge to void
Recognizing urge is required for successful training.
Can hold urine for 1 to 2 hours
Holding urine 1 to 2 hours is a readiness sign.
Can communicate the need to void
Communicating needs is required for toilet training.
Stays dry through the entire night
Continence starts during the day; nighttime dryness comes later.
Has reached 12 months of age
Children cannot control voiding until 18 to 24 months.
items.ex: Toilet training succeeds when the child recognizes urge, holds urine 1 to 2 hours, and communicates needs.

alt.q: Which findings suggest that a 15-month-old is not yet ready for toilet training? Select all that apply.
o: Cannot tell the parent when he needs to void
Communicating need is required for readiness.
Wets the diaper every 20 to 30 minutes
He cannot yet hold urine for 1 to 2 hours.
Shows no awareness of bladder fullness
Recognizing urge is a required readiness sign.
Is still wet after naps or overnight
Daytime continence comes first; night wetting does not rule out readiness.
Produces light yellow, dilute urine
Dilute urine is normal in young children and unrelated to readiness.
alt.ex: A child not yet ready cannot sense urge, hold urine for 1 to 2 hours, or communicate needs.

items.q: A parent of a 26-month-old asks about starting toilet training. Which statement by the parent shows understanding of readiness?
items.a: “She is ready when she can tell me she needs to go and stay dry for an hour or two.”
items.ex: Readiness requires recognizing urge, holding urine for 1 to 2 hours, and communicating needs.
w: “She is ready as soon as she stays dry all night long.”
Continence starts during the day; nighttime dryness comes later.
“She should be trained by her first birthday at the latest.”
Children cannot voluntarily control voiding until 18 to 24 months.
“She is ready when she can hold her urine for a whole morning.”
Holding urine 1 to 2 hours, not a whole morning, signals readiness.

alt.q: A 30-month-old can hold urine for 1 to 2 hours and tells the parent when he needs to void. What should the nurse expect?
alt.a: Toilet training will likely be successful, starting in the daytime
alt.ex: When a child recognizes urge, holds urine 1 to 2 hours, and communicates, training succeeds, with daytime continence first.
w: He will be continent at night before the daytime
Continence starts during daytime hours, not at night.
He is too young for toilet training to succeed
He shows all the signs of readiness for toilet training.
He will need a urinary catheter to train
Toilet training does not involve catheterization.

items.q: A child who wets the bed at night without waking from sleep has [[nocturnal enuresis|enuresis]].
items.ex: Nocturnal enuresis is nighttime wetting without waking and can continue until late childhood.

alt.q: Nighttime incontinence in a child who does not wake from sleep is called [[nocturnal enuresis|enuresis]].
alt.ex: Nocturnal enuresis is nighttime wetting without waking and can continue until late childhood.

items.q: During toilet training, continence is usually achieved first during daytime hours.
items.a: True
items.ex: Continence starts during the day; nighttime wetting may continue, sometimes until late childhood.
items.ww: The book states continence starts during daytime hours, not at night.

alt.q: Children usually achieve nighttime continence before they become continent during the day.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Daytime continence comes first; nocturnal enuresis can persist until late childhood.
alt.ww: Continence begins in the daytime, so nighttime continence does not come first.

items.q: A parent notes that their 4-month-old’s urine is very light yellow, almost clear. How should the nurse explain this finding?
items.a: Infants cannot effectively concentrate urine
items.ex: Infants and young children cannot concentrate urine well, so it appears light yellow or clear.
w: The infant is likely developing a UTI
Clear, light urine is normal in infants and not a sign of infection.
The infant is not taking in enough fluid
Inadequate intake would produce darker, more concentrated urine.
Infant urine contains no waste products
Infant urine contains wastes; it is simply less concentrated.

alt.q: Why is an infant’s urine typically light yellow or clear?
alt.a: Immature kidneys cannot concentrate urine effectively
alt.ex: Infants cannot concentrate urine, so their urine looks light yellow or clear.
w: Infants excrete only small volumes of urine
Infants excrete large volumes for their body size.
Breast milk lacks any pigment or solute
The color reflects limited urine concentration, not milk composition.
Infants void only once or twice daily
Infants void often and produce large volumes, not rare voids.

items.q: A 6-month-old infant weighs 7 kg. About how much urine should the nurse expect the infant to excrete daily?
items.a: 400 to 500 mL
items.ex: A 6-month-old weighing 6 to 8 kg excretes about 400 to 500 mL daily, a large volume for body size.
w: 50 to 100 mL
This is far too little; infants excrete large volumes relative to body size.
150 to 200 mL
This underestimates the 400 to 500 mL expected at this age and size.
This approaches adult-range output and is too much for a 7-kg infant.

alt.q: Compared with adults, how does an infant’s urine output relate to body size?
alt.a: Infants excrete large volumes of urine for their size
alt.ex: Relative to small body size, infants and children excrete large urine volumes, about 400 to 500 mL daily at 6 months.
w: Infants excrete very little urine for their size
Infant output is large, not small, relative to body size.
Infants excrete the same per kilogram as adults
Infants excrete more relative to size than adults.
Infants excrete urine only after weaning
Infants produce urine from birth.

items.q: A patient in the first trimester of pregnancy reports needing to urinate more often. What explains this change?
items.a: Hormonal changes and fetal pressure increase urine production and reduce bladder capacity
items.ex: In early and late pregnancy, hormones and fetal pressure cause increased urine production and decreased bladder capacity.
w: The pregnant uterus blocks the ureters and causes retention
Frequency results from increased production and reduced capacity, not ureteral blockage.
Pregnancy causes the kidneys to stop concentrating urine at all
The book does not attribute frequency to loss of urine concentration.
Frequency in pregnancy is usually caused by a bladder infection
Frequency is a common normal change of pregnancy, not usually infection.

alt.q: During which periods of pregnancy is urinary frequency most common?
alt.a: Early and late pregnancy
alt.ex: Urinary frequency is common in early and late pregnancy as bladder capacity decreases.
w: Only in the second trimester
Frequency is described in early and late pregnancy, not only mid-pregnancy.
Only after the baby is delivered
Frequency is a change during pregnancy, not only postpartum.
Only in pregnancies with twins
Frequency is common in all pregnancies, not only multiples.

items.q: Normal aging is the cause of bladder dysfunction in older adults.
items.a: False
items.ex: Age-related changes do not cause bladder dysfunction, but they increase its risk and incidence.
items.ww: The book states aging changes are not the cause of bladder dysfunction; they only raise the risk.

alt.q: Age-related changes in the urinary tract do not cause bladder dysfunction, but they increase its risk and incidence.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Aging increases the risk and incidence of bladder dysfunction without directly causing it.
alt.ww: Aging itself is not the cause of bladder dysfunction, so this statement is accurate.

items.q: What is the most common type of urinary incontinence in older adult males and females?
items.a: Urgency urinary incontinence
items.ex: Box 46.2 identifies urgency urinary incontinence as the most common type in older adults of both sexes.
w: Stress urinary incontinence
Stress UI is common in females but is not identified as the most common type in older adults.
Functional urinary incontinence
Functional UI is significant in older adults but is not the most common type.
Transient urinary incontinence
Transient UI has reversible causes and is not named as most common.

alt.q: What are the most common reasons for urgency urinary incontinence in older males and females, respectively?
alt.a: Prostate hypertrophy and atrophic urethral mucosa
alt.ex: In older males prostate hypertrophy, and in older females atrophic urethral mucosa, most often cause urgency UI.
w: Kidney stones and pelvic organ prolapse
These are not the reasons Box 46.2 lists for urgency UI.
Urethral strictures and childbirth trauma
Childbirth trauma is linked to stress UI, not the listed urgency causes.
Spinal cord injury and multiple sclerosis
These neurological causes are not the most common reasons in older adults.

items.q: Which urinary characteristic is typical of the Infant life stage?
items.a: Cannot concentrate urine, so urine is light yellow or clear
items.ex: Bladder control and urine characteristics change across the life span, from infancy through pregnancy and older adulthood.
w: Nervous system matures enough to link bladder filling with voiding
That goes with Toddler of 2 to 3 years.
Fetal pressure and hormones cause frequency and reduced bladder capacity
That goes with Pregnancy.
Decreased ability to delay voiding after the first urge
That goes with Older adult.

alt.q: Which urinary characteristic is typical of the Toddler of 2 to 3 years life stage?
alt.a: Nervous system matures enough to link bladder filling with voiding
alt.ex: Bladder control and urine characteristics change across the life span, from infancy through pregnancy and older adulthood.
w: Cannot concentrate urine, so urine is light yellow or clear
That goes with Infant.
Fetal pressure and hormones cause frequency and reduced bladder capacity
That goes with Pregnancy.
Decreased ability to delay voiding after the first urge
That goes with Older adult.

alt.q: Which urinary characteristic is typical of the Pregnancy life stage?
alt.a: Fetal pressure and hormones cause frequency and reduced bladder capacity
alt.ex: Bladder control and urine characteristics change across the life span, from infancy through pregnancy and older adulthood.
w: Cannot concentrate urine, so urine is light yellow or clear
That goes with Infant.
Nervous system matures enough to link bladder filling with voiding
That goes with Toddler of 2 to 3 years.
Decreased ability to delay voiding after the first urge
That goes with Older adult.

alt.q: Which urinary characteristic is typical of the Older adult life stage?
alt.a: Decreased ability to delay voiding after the first urge
alt.ex: Bladder control and urine characteristics change across the life span, from infancy through pregnancy and older adulthood.
w: Cannot concentrate urine, so urine is light yellow or clear
That goes with Infant.
Nervous system matures enough to link bladder filling with voiding
That goes with Toddler of 2 to 3 years.
Fetal pressure and hormones cause frequency and reduced bladder capacity
That goes with Pregnancy.

alt.q: Which life stage is described by “Cannot concentrate urine, so urine is light yellow or clear”?
alt.a: Infant
alt.ex: Bladder control and urine characteristics change across the life span, from infancy through pregnancy and older adulthood.
w: Toddler of 2 to 3 years
Toddler of 2 to 3 years: Nervous system matures enough to link bladder filling with voiding.
Pregnancy
Pregnancy: Fetal pressure and hormones cause frequency and reduced bladder capacity.
Older adult
Older adult: Decreased ability to delay voiding after the first urge.

alt.q: Which life stage is described by “Nervous system matures enough to link bladder filling with voiding”?
alt.a: Toddler of 2 to 3 years
alt.ex: Bladder control and urine characteristics change across the life span, from infancy through pregnancy and older adulthood.
w: Infant
Infant: Cannot concentrate urine, so urine is light yellow or clear.
Pregnancy
Pregnancy: Fetal pressure and hormones cause frequency and reduced bladder capacity.
Older adult
Older adult: Decreased ability to delay voiding after the first urge.

alt.q: Which life stage is described by “Fetal pressure and hormones cause frequency and reduced bladder capacity”?
alt.a: Pregnancy
alt.ex: Bladder control and urine characteristics change across the life span, from infancy through pregnancy and older adulthood.
w: Infant
Infant: Cannot concentrate urine, so urine is light yellow or clear.
Toddler of 2 to 3 years
Toddler of 2 to 3 years: Nervous system matures enough to link bladder filling with voiding.
Older adult
Older adult: Decreased ability to delay voiding after the first urge.

alt.q: Which life stage is described by “Decreased ability to delay voiding after the first urge”?
alt.a: Older adult
alt.ex: Bladder control and urine characteristics change across the life span, from infancy through pregnancy and older adulthood.
w: Infant
Infant: Cannot concentrate urine, so urine is light yellow or clear.
Toddler of 2 to 3 years
Toddler of 2 to 3 years: Nervous system matures enough to link bladder filling with voiding.
Pregnancy
Pregnancy: Fetal pressure and hormones cause frequency and reduced bladder capacity.

mt.q: Match each life stage with a urinary elimination characteristic described in the chapter.
pairs: Cannot concentrate urine, so urine is light yellow or clear
Nervous system matures enough to link bladder filling with voiding
Fetal pressure and hormones cause frequency and reduced bladder capacity
Decreased ability to delay voiding after the first urge
mt.ex: Bladder control and urine characteristics change across the life span, from infancy through pregnancy and older adulthood.

items.q: An 80-year-old patient was recently started on an antimuscarinic medication for overactive bladder. Which finding is most important to report?
items.a: New confusion and disorientation
items.ex: Antimuscarinics can cause cognitive impairment in older adults, so mental status changes must be assessed and reported.
w: Fewer episodes of urgency
Fewer urgency episodes show the medication is working as intended.
Voiding about every 3 hours
Voiding every 3 to 4 hours is a normal pattern.
Pale yellow urine
Pale yellow urine indicates adequate hydration.

alt.q: Why should the nurse carefully assess mental status in an older adult who has recently started an antimuscarinic medication?
alt.a: This drug class can cause cognitive impairment in older adults
alt.ex: Box 46.2 warns that antimuscarinics have the potential to cause cognitive impairment in older adults.
w: This drug class commonly causes severe hypoglycemia
Hypoglycemia is not the listed concern with antimuscarinics.
This drug class causes the urine to turn orange
Orange urine is linked to phenazopyridine, not antimuscarinics.
This drug class increases urine output sharply
Increased output describes diuretics, not antimuscarinics.

items.q: A nursing home resident with dementia has frequent incontinence episodes. Which intervention should the nurse implement?
items.a: Remind the resident to void more frequently
items.ex: Box 46.2 recommends reminding older adults with cognitive impairment to void more often to improve continence.
w: Insert an indwelling urinary catheter
A catheter adds CAUTI risk and is not indicated to manage incontinence.
Restrict the resident’s fluid intake all day
Older adults need adequate hydration; thirst sensation already declines.
Apply briefs and check them once a shift
Containment alone delays toileting and causes prolonged wetness.

alt.q: An older adult with arthritis and impaired mobility has new incontinence. Which plan best maximizes self-care and continence?
alt.a: A toileting program with mobility aids and help with hygiene
alt.ex: Box 46.2 recommends toileting programs, mobility aids, and hygiene help for older adults with impaired mobility.
w: An indwelling catheter to prevent wet linens
Catheters increase CAUTI risk and do not promote self-care.
Bed rest with a bedpan at fixed times only
Bed rest further limits mobility and independence.
Limiting fluids after breakfast each day
Fluid limits risk dehydration; only 2 hours before bed is advised.

items.q: Which nursing actions are recommended for older adults with urinary elimination concerns? Select all that apply.
o: Encourage adequate water intake because thirst decreases with age
Adequate hydration promotes bladder health.
Teach pelvic muscle exercises to older women with stress incontinence
There is no age limit on their effectiveness.
Evaluate new medications as a cause of new-onset incontinence
New drugs can affect cognition, mobility, or voiding.
Accept new incontinence as part of normal aging
Treating UI as normal aging is why it often goes untreated.
Limit fluids throughout the day to reduce voiding
Only restrict fluids 2 hours before bedtime to reduce nocturia.
items.ex: Box 46.2 emphasizes hydration, pelvic muscle exercises, and evaluating all causes of new incontinence in older adults.

alt.q: Which statements about urinary changes in older adults are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Bladder capacity may decrease
Box 46.1 lists decreased bladder capacity in older adults.
The ability to delay voiding after the first urge decreases
Older adults have less time between the first desire and urgent need.
The sensation of thirst decreases
Decreased thirst makes encouraging water intake important.
Bladder contractions during filling decrease
Contractions during filling increase, along with bladder irritability.
Pelvic muscle exercises no longer work after age 70
There is no age limit on the effectiveness of pelvic muscle exercises.
alt.ex: Aging brings decreased capacity, more bladder irritability, less ability to delay voiding, and reduced thirst.

items.q: An older adult reports getting up several times each night to void. Which instruction should the nurse give?
items.a: Restrict fluid intake for 2 hours before bedtime
items.ex: Restricting fluids for 2 hours before bedtime decreases nocturia while daytime hydration continues.
w: Restrict fluid intake for 8 hours before bedtime
Long restriction risks dehydration; only 2 hours is advised.
Restrict fluid intake to 500 mL per day
Severe restriction risks dehydration and irritates the bladder.
Drink 1000 mL of water right before bedtime
Large bedtime intake would increase, not decrease, nocturia.

alt.q: A nurse teaches an older adult about reducing nocturia. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
alt.a: “I will stop drinking fluids 2 hours before I go to bed.”
alt.ex: Stopping fluids 2 hours before bedtime reduces nighttime voiding without limiting daytime hydration.
w: “I will stop drinking fluids after lunch each day.”
Long restriction risks dehydration; thirst already decreases with age.
“I will drink most of my fluids in the evening.”
Evening fluids increase nighttime voiding.
“I will drink only when I feel very thirsty.”
Thirst decreases with aging, so relying on thirst risks dehydration.

items.q: There is no age limit on the effectiveness of pelvic muscle exercises for older women with stress incontinence.
items.a: True
items.ex: Box 46.2 directs nurses to teach pelvic muscle exercises to older women because they remain effective at any age.
items.ww: The book explicitly states there is no age limit on the effectiveness of pelvic muscle exercises.

alt.q: Pelvic muscle exercises lose their effectiveness in older women and are not recommended for stress incontinence after menopause.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Pelvic muscle exercises remain effective at any age and are recommended for older women with stress UI.
alt.ww: The book states there is no age limit on the effectiveness of these exercises.

items.q: A 78-year-old man reports urgency, frequency, a slow stream, and dribbling. Which condition should the nurse assess for first?
items.a: Urinary retention from prostate enlargement
items.ex: Box 46.2 directs assessment of older men with these voiding changes for retention from age-related prostate enlargement.
w: Functional incontinence from poor mobility
These symptoms point to an outlet problem, not toilet access barriers.
Stress incontinence from a weak pelvic floor
Stress UI causes leakage with exertion, not a slow stream.
Transient incontinence from dehydration
Dehydration is not linked to slow stream and dribbling in the text.

alt.q: Why are older men with a slow stream and decreased output at risk for urinary retention?
alt.a: Age-related prostate enlargement can obstruct the bladder outlet
alt.ex: Prostatic enlargement can obstruct the bladder outlet, causing retention.
w: Aging shortens the male urethra significantly
Aging does not shorten the urethra.
Aging stops the kidneys from producing urine
Kidney production does not stop with normal aging.
Aging removes the sensation of thirst
Thirst decreases, but this does not explain retention.

items.q: Why does age-related urinary incontinence often remain untreated in older adults?
items.a: It is often considered a part of normal aging
items.ex: Because UI is seen as normal aging, it often goes untreated even though it is not a normal change.
w: It cannot be treated after age 65
Treatments such as pelvic muscle exercises work at any age.
It always resolves on its own
Age-related UI does not reliably resolve without intervention.
It is too rare to require screening
Urinary elimination problems are common in older adults.

alt.q: An older adult says, “Leaking urine is just part of getting old, so there’s no point mentioning it.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Incontinence is not a normal part of aging, and it can often be treated.”
alt.ex: Aging increases risk but does not cause incontinence; treating it as normal leaves it untreated.
w: “You’re right, so we will just order more absorbent briefs.”
This accepts a treatable problem as normal aging.
“It only matters if you also have a fever.”
Incontinence warrants evaluation regardless of fever.
“Most people your age need a catheter for this.”
Catheters are not routine treatment for incontinence and add CAUTI risk.

items.q: What is the term for the use of multiple medications, which is more common in older adults and can affect urinary elimination?
items.a: Polypharmacy
items.ex: Polypharmacy is common in older adults, and many of these drugs alter the bladder’s ability to hold or empty urine.
w: Polyuria
Polyuria means excessive urine production, not the use of many medications.
Polydipsia
Polydipsia means excessive thirst, not the use of many medications.
Pharmacokinetics
Pharmacokinetics is how the body handles drugs, not the use of many drugs.

alt.q: Why is polypharmacy a concern for urinary elimination in older adults?
alt.a: Many medications alter the bladder’s ability to hold or empty urine
alt.ex: Drugs such as antihypertensives, antidepressants, and sedatives can affect holding or emptying of urine.
w: Many medications turn the urine an unusual color
Some drugs change urine color, but that is not the stated concern.
Many medications make the urethra shorter
Medications do not change urethral length.
Many medications prevent urine production entirely
The concern is bladder holding and emptying, not stopping urine production.

items.q: According to the factors influencing urinary elimination, until what age are children unable to voluntarily control voiding?
items.a: 18 to 24 months
items.ex: Box 46.1 states children cannot voluntarily control voiding until 18 to 24 months of age.
w: 6 to 9 months
Voluntary control is not possible this early in infancy.
9 to 12 months
Voluntary control is not expected before 18 to 24 months.
4 to 5 years
Voluntary control begins well before this age.

alt.q: Why are older adults at increased risk for urinary incontinence?
alt.a: Chronic illnesses and factors that limit mobility, cognition, and manual dexterity
alt.ex: Box 46.1 links increased UI risk in older adults to chronic illness and impaired mobility, cognition, and dexterity.
w: Kidneys that stop concentrating urine with normal aging
Inability to concentrate urine is described in infants, not as the cause in older adults.
A urethra that lengthens and narrows with normal aging
Urethral lengthening is not described as an age-related change.
Increased thirst that leads to very large fluid intake
Thirst decreases, not increases, with aging.

items.q: Which components are part of a person’s self-concept? Select all that apply.
o: Body image
Body image is a component of self-concept.
Self-esteem
Self-esteem is a component of self-concept.
Roles
Roles are part of self-concept.
Identity
Identity is a component of self-concept.
Urine output
Urine output is a physiological measure, not part of self-concept.
Bladder capacity
Bladder capacity is anatomical, not part of self-concept.
items.ex: Self-concept includes body image, self-esteem, roles, and identity, and elimination problems can affect each.

alt.q: A patient with new incontinence avoids social events and says, “I feel like I’m no longer the person I was.” Which aspects of self-concept are affected? Select all that apply.
o: Identity
Feeling no longer the same person reflects a change in identity.
Self-esteem
Incontinence can be devastating to self-esteem.
Roles
Avoiding social events affects the patient’s roles.
Renal function
Renal function is physiological, not a component of self-concept.
Fluid balance
Fluid balance is physiological, not part of self-concept.
alt.ex: Incontinence can affect identity, self-esteem, and roles, which are components of self-concept.

items.q: A child who is learning toileting skills refuses to let the parent flush the toilet. What is the most likely reason?
items.a: The child sees urine and feces as extensions of self
items.ex: Children achieving bladder control may view urine and feces as extensions of self and not want them flushed.
w: The child has a urinary tract infection
Refusal to flush is a developmental behavior, not a sign of infection.
The child has nocturnal enuresis
Enuresis is nighttime wetting without waking, unrelated to flushing.
The child is not yet ready to void
The child is already toileting; the behavior reflects attachment to wastes.

alt.q: A parent says their 3-year-old cries when the toilet is flushed after voiding. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Young children often see their urine as part of themselves, so this is common.”
alt.ex: Children learning toileting may see wastes as extensions of self and resist flushing them away.
w: “This means your child is not ready for toilet training at all.”
The behavior is common during learning and does not mean training should stop.
“This is a sign of a bladder problem that needs testing.”
This developmental behavior does not indicate bladder pathology.
“You should punish this so the habit doesn’t continue.”
Punishment is not appropriate for a normal developmental response.

items.q: An older adult with incontinence tells the nurse, “I hate having to ask for help to go to the bathroom. I feel like a baby.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Needing help with something so personal can feel hard. Tell me more.”
items.ex: Asking for toileting help can feel embarrassing or childlike; acknowledging feelings supports self-esteem and self-determination.
w: “Everyone needs help sometimes, so don’t worry about it.”
This dismisses the patient’s feelings rather than exploring them.
“I can put a catheter in so you won’t need to ask.”
A catheter adds CAUTI risk and does not address the feelings expressed.
“If you wear briefs, you won’t have to call me at all.”
Briefs delay toilet access and can further harm self-image.

alt.q: A patient who needs help toileting is quiet and avoids eye contact after an incontinent episode. Which nursing interpretation is most accurate?
alt.a: The episode may be threatening the patient’s self-esteem
alt.ex: Incontinence and needing help can be embarrassing, feel childlike, and threaten self-determination.
w: The patient is showing early signs of a UTI
The behavior follows the episode and reflects emotional impact, not infection.
The patient does not care about continence
Embarrassment suggests the patient cares deeply about continence.
The patient is trying to limit fluid intake today
Avoiding eye contact reflects embarrassment, not fluid behavior.

items.q: When patients ask for help with toileting, they may perceive it as embarrassing or as being treated like a child.
items.a: True
items.ex: Toileting is private and personal, so needing help can feel embarrassing and threaten self-determination.
items.ww: The book states that asking for toileting help can be perceived as embarrassing or childlike.

alt.q: Because voiding is a basic body function, patients seldom feel embarrassed when they need help with toileting.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Toileting is private; needing help can feel embarrassing, childlike, and threaten self-determination.
alt.ww: The book describes help with toileting as potentially embarrassing and threatening to self-determination.

items.q: A patient with a new ileal conduit says, “My partner won’t want to be close to me anymore.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Tell me more about your concerns about intimacy with your partner.”
items.ex: A urinary diversion affects body image and can feel like a threat to a sexual relationship; the nurse explores these concerns.
w: “Your partner will get used to it, so try not to worry.”
False reassurance dismisses the patient’s concern.
“Most patients stop worrying about that after surgery.”
This minimizes a known psychosocial impact of diversions.
“Let’s focus on learning to change the pouch first.”
Deferring the concern ignores the psychosocial need the patient raised.

alt.q: Which psychosocial concern should the nurse anticipate in a patient who has had a urinary diversion?
alt.a: Altered body image and a perceived threat to sexual relationships
alt.ex: A diversion influences body image and can be perceived as a threat to a healthy sexual relationship.
w: Loss of interest in all food and fluids
This is not the psychosocial impact described for diversions.
Fear that the stoma will stop producing urine
This is not identified as the main concern.
Desire to resume toilet training
Toilet training relates to children, not diversion patients.

items.q: A patient needs to use a bedside commode. Which actions protect the patient’s privacy? Select all that apply.
o: Close the room door and bedside curtain
Closing doors and curtains creates privacy.
Ask visitors to leave the room
Visitors should leave when a commode, bedpan, or urinal is used.
Run water to mask voiding sounds
Running water masks sounds and also promotes relaxation.
Leave the door open so staff can monitor
This exposes the patient during a private act.
Discuss the urine output with the roommate present
Elimination matters are private and should not be discussed openly.
items.ex: Elimination is a private act; close doors and curtains, ask visitors to leave, and mask voiding sounds.

alt.q: Which statements explain why privacy matters during urinary elimination? Select all that apply.
o: Micturition is often a culturally private event
Many cultures consider voiding a private act.
Privacy and adequate time help the bladder empty completely
Box 46.1 notes privacy and time influence emptying.
Lack of privacy can cause embarrassment
Elimination is personal and exposure can embarrass patients.
Privacy is needed only for female patients
Privacy is needed for all patients regardless of gender.
Privacy matters only when the patient is confused
All patients need privacy for this private act.
alt.ex: Voiding is culturally private; privacy prevents embarrassment and supports complete bladder emptying.

items.q: A female patient’s cultural background emphasizes female modesty and prohibits touching by unrelated males. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Arrange a female caregiver for elimination care when possible
items.ex: Box 46.4 recommends a same-gender caregiver for patients whose culture emphasizes modesty and prohibits such touching.
w: Assign whichever nurse is available
This ignores the patient’s cultural preferences regarding gender.
Have a male nurse provide care quickly
A male caregiver conflicts with the patient’s stated cultural norms.
Ask a family member to insert a catheter
Catheter insertion requires trained personnel and sterile technique.

alt.q: A nurse is caring for patients from many cultures. Which principle guides culturally sensitive elimination care?
alt.a: Assess each patient as an individual, since variation within cultures is common
alt.ex: Variations within cultural groups are common, so each patient is assessed and cared for individually.
w: Apply one standard approach to everyone from a given culture
Assuming group norms ignores individual variation.
Avoid asking about elimination to prevent embarrassment
Ask questions in a sensitive, straightforward manner.
Assume that patients readily discuss incontinence
Incontinence is often not discussed with professionals.

items.q: Which psychological factor can impair bladder emptying because of inadequate relaxation of the pelvic floor muscles and urinary sphincter?
items.a: Anxiety
items.ex: Anxiety can prevent relaxation of the pelvic floor and sphincter, affecting bladder emptying.
w: Depression
Depression can decrease the desire for continence, not block muscle relaxation.
Boredom
Boredom is not listed as a factor affecting bladder emptying.
Contentment
Contentment is not a factor that impairs bladder emptying.

alt.q: Which psychological factor can decrease a patient’s desire for urinary continence?
alt.a: Depression
alt.ex: Box 46.1 states that depression can decrease the desire for urinary continence.
w: Anxiety
Anxiety affects urgency, frequency, and bladder emptying rather than desire for continence.
Stress
Stress affects urgency and voiding frequency.
Excitement
Excitement is not listed as affecting desire for continence.

items.q: Depression can decrease a patient’s desire for urinary continence.
items.a: True
items.ex: Box 46.1 lists depression as a psychological factor that decreases the desire for continence.
items.ww: The book directly identifies decreased desire for continence as an effect of depression.

alt.q: Anxiety and stress typically decrease the frequency of voiding.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Anxiety and stress can heighten the sense of urgency and increase voiding frequency.
alt.ww: Box 46.1 states anxiety and stress increase, not decrease, voiding frequency.

items.q: Which critical thinking attitude helps the nurse obtain a complete picture during an assessment of a sensitive area such as incontinence?
items.a: Establishing trust with the patient
items.ex: Trust helps the patient reveal the full picture of a potentially sensitive area of assessment.
w: Relying on the chart alone
The chart cannot replace a trusting dialogue about sensitive symptoms.
Limiting the interview time
Rushing the interview discourages disclosure of sensitive information.
Avoiding direct questions
Questions should be sensitive yet straightforward, not avoided.

alt.q: A nurse recognizes the limits of her knowledge about a new continence device and asks a continence nurse for guidance. Which critical thinking attitude does this show?
alt.a: Humility
alt.ex: Displaying humility in recognizing limitations in knowledge is a critical thinking attitude in Fig. 46.4.
w: Discipline
Discipline refers to obtaining complete and correct assessment data.
Perseverance
Perseverance is persisting with a plan to manage elimination problems.
Independence
Asking for guidance reflects humility about limits, not independent thinking.

items.ex: Fig. 46.4 links knowledge, experience, environment, standards, and attitudes to clinical judgment about urinary elimination.

That goes with Experience.
Interruptions and resources such as catheter equipment

alt.a: Caring for patients at risk for urinary infection

That goes with Environment.

Experience: Caring for patients at risk for urinary infection.

Experience: Caring for patients at risk for urinary infection.
