Environment: Interruptions and resources such as catheter equipment.

mt.q: Match each element of the critical thinking model for urinary elimination with an example.
pairs: Caring for patients at risk for urinary infection
Interruptions and resources such as catheter equipment
Displaying respect for patients’ cultural preferences
mt.ex: Fig. 46.4 links knowledge, experience, environment, standards, and attitudes to clinical judgment about urinary elimination.

items.q: A nurse caring for an incontinent patient suggests a voiding schedule instead of the indwelling catheter the team is considering. What role is the nurse demonstrating?
items.a: Patient advocate
items.ex: Nurses advocate by suggesting noninvasive alternatives to catheterization, such as voiding schedules or bladder scanners.
w: Case manager
Case management coordinates services, not advocacy for noninvasive care.
Researcher
The nurse is applying, not generating, evidence.
Educator
The action is advocating for the patient, not teaching.

alt.q: Which action is an example of a nurse advocating for a noninvasive alternative to catheterization?
alt.a: Using a bladder scanner to assess urine volume
alt.ex: A bladder scanner measures urine volume without invasive instrumentation, avoiding unnecessary catheterization.
w: Inserting a straight catheter to check volume
Straight catheterization is an invasive procedure.
Requesting an indwelling catheter for comfort
This adds an invasive device rather than avoiding one.
Irrigating the catheter to keep it patent
Irrigation is an invasive catheter intervention.

items.q: How can a nurse’s personal experience of having had a UTI help in patient care?
items.a: It helps the nurse understand a patient’s frustration and embarrassment
items.ex: Personal experience with frequency, urgency, and dysuria helps the nurse understand a patient’s frustration and embarrassment.
w: It allows the nurse to prescribe antibiotics
Personal experience does not expand the nurse’s scope of practice.
It replaces the need for a full assessment
A complete, correct assessment is still required.
It shows that all patients have the same symptoms
Each patient is unique and must be assessed individually.

alt.q: Which source of experience in the critical thinking model helps a nurse anticipate toileting needs of older adults?
alt.a: Caring for older adults with functional disabilities
alt.ex: Caring for older adults with functional disabilities helps the nurse anticipate toileting needs.
w: Reading the agency’s visitor policy
Visitor policies do not build experience with toileting needs.
Memorizing laboratory reference ranges
This is knowledge, not experience with patient toileting needs.
Completing a course on wound dressings
Wound care training does not address toileting needs.

items.q: Which sociocultural factors can influence urinary elimination? Select all that apply.
o: Norms about private versus communal toilet facilities
Cultures differ in expecting private or communal facilities.
Religious norms about who may help with elimination
Religious or cultural norms may dictate acceptable helpers.
School recess or work break schedules
Social expectations can interfere with timely voiding.
Diuretic medication use
Diuretics are a medication factor, not a sociocultural one.
Prostatic enlargement
Prostatic enlargement is a pathological condition.
items.ex: Box 46.1 lists cultural norms, religious norms on helpers, and social expectations as sociocultural factors.

alt.q: A nurse assesses cultural influences on a patient’s elimination care. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Ask questions in a sensitive, straightforward manner
Sensitive, direct questioning is recommended.
Ask whether the patient prefers a same-gender caregiver
Culture may dictate gender-specific roles in elimination care.
Attend carefully to closing doors and draping
Privacy is important in many cultures.
Assume all members of a culture share the same practices
Variation within cultural groups is common.
Skip the topic of incontinence to avoid offense
Incontinence must be assessed, though it is often not raised by patients.
alt.ex: Culturally sensitive care uses straightforward questions, honors gender preferences and privacy, and treats each patient individually.

items.q: The nurse uses the critical thinking attitude of [[perseverance|persistence]] to create a plan leading to successful management of urinary elimination problems.
items.ex: Perseverance helps the nurse keep working with a patient until elimination problems are successfully managed.

alt.q: Continuing to revise a continence plan until it works shows the critical thinking attitude of [[perseverance|persistence]].
alt.ex: Perseverance helps the nurse keep working with a patient until elimination problems are successfully managed.

items.q: Because of the personal nature of elimination, urinary problems such as incontinence often are not discussed with medical professionals.
items.a: True
items.ex: Box 46.4 notes that the private nature and cultural practices around elimination often keep patients from raising incontinence.
items.ww: The book states incontinence often goes undiscussed because elimination is personal and culturally shaped.

alt.q: Patients usually raise incontinence with their health care providers without prompting, so nurses rarely need to ask about it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Incontinence is often not discussed with professionals, so nurses must sensitively ask about it.
alt.ww: Because elimination is private, patients often do not bring up incontinence on their own.

items.q: Which example illustrates how intrinsic and extrinsic factors create unique urinary problems for patients?
items.a: A male develops stress UI after prostate cancer surgery due to sphincter trauma
items.ex: The chapter notes males may develop stress UI after prostate surgery because of trauma to the urinary sphincter.
w: A male develops urgency UI because the female urethra is short
The short urethra is a female trait and relates to UTI risk.
A female develops functional UI because of a kidney stone
Functional UI arises from access barriers, not kidney stones.
A child develops stress UI from drinking too much water
Water intake does not cause stress UI.

alt.q: A patient who drinks a large amount of coffee daily reports a frequent, urgent need to void. Which explanation is most accurate?
alt.a: Caffeine can increase urinary urgency and frequency
alt.ex: People with high caffeine intake or taking diuretics may have increased urgency and frequency.
w: Caffeine causes the bladder to lose all sensation
Caffeine is a bladder irritant; it does not abolish sensation.
Caffeine weakens the pelvic floor muscles
Pelvic floor weakness causes stress UI, not caffeine-related urgency.
Caffeine blocks urine from leaving the kidneys
Caffeine does not block urine flow from the kidneys.

items.q: A hospitalized patient presses the call light and asks for help to the bathroom. Which nursing action best protects the patient’s dignity?
items.a: Respond to the request for toileting help as quickly as possible
items.ex: Prompt response to toileting requests avoids embarrassing accidents, protecting self-esteem.
w: Apply an incontinence brief so the patient can wait
Containment products interfere with toilet access and are used only when needed.
Ask the patient to wait until the next scheduled round
Delays lead to embarrassing accidents.
Tell the patient to void in the bed and call afterward
This causes an avoidable, embarrassing accident.

alt.q: A patient with poor balance needs supervision while on the toilet and says this feels demeaning. Which approach is best?
alt.a: Discuss with the patient how to balance safety and self-care
alt.ex: Balancing safety and supporting self-care can be challenging and needs to be discussed with the patient.
w: Leave the patient alone to preserve dignity
Poor balance requires supervision on the toilet for safety.
Insert a catheter so supervision is not needed
A catheter adds CAUTI risk and does not address self-care.
Insist on a bedpan for every void instead
This removes independence without discussing the patient’s needs.

items.q: A male patient who is unable to walk to the bathroom needs to void. He is able to stand safely. Which approach best respects his usual voiding position?
items.a: Help him stand at the bedside to use a urinal
items.ex: Most males stand to void and void more easily standing, so assist him to stand at the bedside with a urinal.
w: Place him on a bedpan in a flat supine position
Lying flat is not the normal voiding position and hinders emptying.
Have him sit on a bedpan with the head of bed raised
Most males void more easily standing when they can do so safely.
Insert a straight catheter to empty his bladder
Catheterization is invasive and not needed when he can void.

alt.q: Why should the nurse consider gender preferences in positioning when assisting patients who cannot use a bathroom?
alt.a: Most males stand to void, whereas females sit
alt.ex: Gender differences in voiding position affect how the nurse assists patients who cannot use a bathroom.
w: Most females stand to void, whereas males sit
This reverses the usual positions; most males stand and females sit.
Both males and females void best lying flat
Lying flat is not a normal voiding position for either.
Position preference only matters for children
Position preferences matter for adults who need help voiding.

items.q: A nurse is planning toileting care for a patient with mild cognitive impairment. Which approach is most appropriate?
items.a: Involve the patient in planning and decisions about toileting care
items.ex: Nurses should not assume a patient with cognitive impairment cannot understand or participate in care.
w: Make all toileting decisions without the patient
Excluding the patient assumes incapacity and undermines self-determination.
Keep the patient in briefs to avoid discussions
Containment products delay toileting and harm dignity.
Ask only the family about the patient’s habits
The patient can often participate and should be asked directly.

alt.q: Which assumption should the nurse avoid when assessing the self-care ability of a patient diagnosed with cognitive impairment?
alt.a: That the patient cannot understand or take part in care
alt.ex: The book cautions against assuming a cognitively impaired patient cannot understand or participate in care.
w: That the patient may need help with some activities
Some patients with cognitive problems need individualized help.
That the patient may have personal toileting routines
Integrating a patient’s habits into care is recommended.
That the patient may feel embarrassed by supervision
Supervision on the toilet can feel embarrassing or demeaning.

items.q: A patient returned from abdominal surgery 4 hours ago and has an indwelling catheter. Hourly urine output was 22 mL and then 25 mL over the past 2 hours. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess the patient for signs of blood loss
items.ex: Hourly output after surgery reflects circulating blood volume; output under 30 mL/h calls for immediate assessment for bleeding and provider notification.
w: Irrigate the catheter to clear possible clots
Irrigation is not ordered and risks infection; low output first points to possible blood loss.
Encourage oral fluids and recheck in 4 hours
Output under 30 mL/h needs immediate assessment, not a delayed recheck.
Document the output as expected after surgery
Output below 30 mL/h for 2 hours is a cause for concern, not an expected finding.

alt.q: Which urine output finding in an adult should prompt further assessment and notification of the health care provider?
alt.a: Less than 30 mL/h for more than 2 consecutive hours
alt.ex: Output under 30 mL/h for more than 2 hours may signal fluid imbalance, kidney dysfunction, or decreased blood volume.
w: About 35 mL/h for 3 consecutive hours
35 mL/h is above the 30 mL/h threshold the book uses.
About 50 mL/h for 8 consecutive hours
50 mL/h is well above the 30 mL/h threshold.
About 40 mL/h for 4 consecutive hours
40 mL/h is above the 30 mL/h threshold the book uses.

items.q: A patient who had knee surgery has received IV fluids and has not voided for 6 hours. The patient feels an urge to void but cannot start a stream. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess the lower abdomen and scan the bladder for retention
items.ex: Patients who have not voided in 3 to 6 hours despite documented intake should be evaluated for urinary retention.
w: Insert an indwelling catheter to drain the bladder
Catheterization needs an order and comes after assessment confirms retention.
Apply manual pressure over the bladder to empty it
The Credé method is not used until the health care provider is consulted.
Restrict fluids until the patient is able to void
Limiting fluids does not treat retention; the bladder must be assessed first.

alt.q: When palpating the abdomen of an adult with urinary retention, where does the nurse expect to feel the distended bladder?
alt.a: Above the symphysis pubis along the midline
alt.ex: A distended bladder rises above the symphysis pubis along the midline and can reach the umbilicus.
w: Below the symphysis pubis deep in the pelvis
This is where the bladder rests when it is not distended.
In the left lower quadrant near the iliac crest
The distended bladder rises along the midline, not to one side.
At the costovertebral angle along the back
The costovertebral angle is percussed for kidney tenderness, not bladder fullness.

items.q: A patient taking phenazopyridine for painful urination calls the nurse, upset that the urine is bright orange. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “This color is an expected effect of your medication.”
items.ex: Phenazopyridine, a urinary analgesic, turns urine bright orange, so patients should expect this change.
w: “This color suggests bleeding from your bladder.”
Bleeding from the bladder or urethra usually causes bright red urine, not orange.
“This color means you may have liver disease.”
Liver disease causes dark amber urine from bilirubin, not bright orange urine.
“This color shows you are very dehydrated.”
Concentrated urine is darker amber; bright orange is the drug’s effect.

alt.q: A patient’s urine is bright red. The nurse knows this color usually indicates bleeding from which site?
alt.a: The bladder or urethra
alt.ex: Bleeding from the bladder or urethra usually causes bright red urine; bleeding higher in the tract makes it dark red.
w: The kidneys or ureters
Bleeding from the kidneys or ureters usually makes urine dark red.
The liver or bile ducts
Liver disease darkens urine to amber from bilirubin; it is not bleeding.
The renal pelvis or glomeruli
These are kidney structures; kidney bleeding usually produces dark red urine.

items.q: The nurse teaches a patient with stress incontinence how to keep the bladder healthy. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I will stop drinking fluids 2 hours before bedtime.”
items.ex: Avoiding fluids 2 hours before bedtime reduces nocturia without limiting total daily intake.
w: “I will cut back on water so I leak less often.”
Limiting fluids concentrates urine, which irritates the bladder and worsens symptoms.
“I will hover over the toilet seat when I void.”
Females should sit well back on the seat with feet flat; hovering hinders emptying.
“I will wait to void until my urge is very strong.”
Voiding at regular intervals, usually every 3 to 4 hours, is recommended.

alt.q: A patient learning pelvic muscle (Kegel) exercises describes how to do them. Which statement shows correct understanding?
alt.a: “I squeeze as if holding in gas, keeping my belly and thighs relaxed.”
alt.ex: The pelvic muscle is found by squeezing as if to hold in gas, without contracting the abdomen, buttocks, or thighs.
w: “I tighten my abdomen and buttocks hard during each squeeze.”
Patients are taught not to contract the abdomen, buttocks, or thighs.
“I hold my breath while I keep each squeeze held tight.”
Counting out loud is taught to prevent breath holding during the exercises.
“I do one long set of these exercises once a week.”
The exercises are done 3 to 4 times a day on a daily schedule.

items.q: A cognitively intact patient with urge incontinence begins bladder retraining. The bladder diary shows voiding every hour. Which schedule should the nurse reinforce first?
items.a: Attempt to void every 1 hour and 15 minutes
items.ex: Patients add 15 minutes to their current interval and void at that time even without an urge.
w: Attempt to void every 30 minutes
Shortening the interval reinforces frequency; retraining slowly lengthens it.
Attempt to void every 3 to 4 hours
Three to 4 hours is the end goal, reached gradually, not the starting interval.
Attempt to void every 2 hours and 30 minutes
Retraining adds 15 minutes to the current interval, not a large jump.

alt.q: What is the goal interval between voidings for a patient who completes a bladder retraining program?
alt.a: 3 to 4 hours
alt.ex: Patients gradually lengthen the time between voidings, aiming for 3 to 4 hours.
w: 30 to 60 minutes
Short intervals are the pattern retraining aims to lengthen.
1 to 2 hours
One to 2 hours is shorter than the book’s goal.
6 to 8 hours
Holding urine this long exceeds the goal; voiding every 3 to 4 hours is advised.

items.q: To check a patient with fever and suspected kidney infection for tenderness, which technique should the nurse use?
items.a: Gently percuss the costovertebral angle
items.ex: Infected or inflamed kidneys are tender; gentle percussion at the costovertebral angle checks for flank tenderness.
w: Deeply palpate the right lower quadrant
Deep abdominal palpation does not assess the kidneys for tenderness.
Auscultate the flank with the diaphragm
Auscultation with the bell checks for a renal bruit and is usually an APRN skill.
Lightly palpate above the symphysis pubis
Suprapubic palpation assesses bladder fullness, not kidney tenderness.

alt.q: Which landmarks form the costovertebral angle that the nurse percusses to assess the kidneys?
alt.a: The spine and the twelfth rib
alt.ex: The costovertebral angle is formed along the back by the spine and the twelfth rib.
w: The spine and the iliac crest
The iliac crest is part of the pelvis, below the kidneys.
The sternum and the twelfth rib
The sternum is on the front of the chest, not the back.
The scapula and the eighth rib
These landmarks are too high on the back to assess the kidneys.

items.q: A patient who has vomited for 2 days has a urine specific gravity of 1.035. How should the nurse interpret this result?
items.a: Concentrated urine consistent with dehydration
items.ex: Normal specific gravity is 1.005–1.030; a high value reflects concentrated urine, as in dehydration.
w: Dilute urine consistent with overhydration
Overhydration lowers specific gravity; 1.035 is above normal.
Normal concentration for an adult
1.035 is above the normal range of 1.005–1.030.
Dilute urine consistent with early renal disease
Early renal disease lowers specific gravity rather than raising it.

alt.q: What is the normal range for urine specific gravity on a routine urinalysis?
alt.ex: Specific gravity measures particle concentration; the normal range is 1.005–1.030.
w: These values are below normal and reflect very dilute urine.
These values are above normal and reflect concentrated urine.
These values are well above the normal range.

items.q: Which balloon size is recommended for an adult indwelling catheter?
items.a: A 5-mL balloon filled with 10 mL
items.ex: The recommended adult balloon is 5 mL, which needs 10 mL of fluid to fill completely.
w: A 30-mL balloon filled with 30 mL
30-mL balloons are for continuous bladder irrigation and cause problems with long-term use.
A 3-mL balloon filled with 3 mL
A 3-mL balloon is sized for a child.
A 10-mL balloon filled with 20 mL
The recommended adult size is a 5-mL balloon filled with 10 mL.

alt.q: Why is long-term use of a 30-mL balloon on an indwelling catheter discouraged?
alt.a: It increases urethral trauma, expulsion, and pooling of urine
alt.ex: Large balloons cause discomfort, urethral irritation and trauma, expulsion, and urine pooling below the drainage eyes.
w: It holds too little fluid to anchor the catheter
A 30-mL balloon is the largest size; the problems come from its large size.
It cannot be used with a closed drainage system
Balloon size does not affect use of a closed drainage system.
It blocks the sampling port used for specimens
The sampling port is on the tubing and is not affected by balloon size.

items.q: A nurse notes that no urine has drained into a patient’s indwelling catheter bag for the past hour. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Check the catheter and tubing for kinks or occlusion
items.ex: With no drainage, the nurse first checks for kinks or obvious occlusion of the tubing or catheter.
w: Irrigate the catheter with sterile normal saline
Irrigation risks infection and is not the first step; look for simple causes first.
Replace the catheter with a new sterile catheter
Changing the catheter is premature before the tubing is checked.
Notify the health care provider of absent output
Check for kinks or occlusion first, then report if drainage is still absent.

alt.q: When should the nurse empty a patient’s urinary drainage bag?
alt.a: When the bag is half full
alt.ex: Drainage bags are emptied when half full because an overfull bag pulls on the catheter.
w: When the bag is completely full
An overfull bag creates tension on the catheter, causing urethral trauma and CAUTI risk.
Only once at the end of each 12-hour shift
Emptying is based on volume, half full, not only on shift timing.
When urine backs up into the tubing
Urine backing up means the bag is overfull and risks backflow and traction.

items.q: A patient starts oxybutynin for urinary urgency. Which adverse effect should the nurse monitor for?
items.a: Constipation
items.ex: Antimuscarinics commonly cause dry mouth, constipation, and blurred vision, so the bowel record is monitored.
w: Diarrhea
Antimuscarinics slow the bowel; constipation, not diarrhea, is common.
Excess salivation
Dry mouth, not excess saliva, is a common antimuscarinic effect.
Orange urine
Orange urine is caused by phenazopyridine, not antimuscarinics.

alt.q: A patient is prescribed mirabegron for urgency. Which assessment is most important for the nurse to monitor?
alt.a: Blood pressure
alt.ex: Mirabegron, a beta3-adrenergic agonist, can raise blood pressure, so blood pressure is monitored.
w: Blood glucose
Mirabegron is not linked to changes in blood glucose in the book.
Urine color
Color change is a known effect of phenazopyridine, not mirabegron.
Oxygen saturation
Mirabegron is not linked to changes in oxygenation in the book.

items.q: For which patient is a condom-type external catheter most appropriate?
items.a: A male with incontinence who empties his bladder completely
items.ex: Condom catheters suit incontinent males with complete, spontaneous bladder emptying and carry less UTI risk than indwelling catheters.
w: A male with urinary retention from prostate enlargement
An external catheter only collects voided urine; it cannot drain a retained bladder.
A male with broken, irritated skin on the penile shaft
Condom catheters are applied only when penile skin is intact.
A male whose hourly output must be measured after surgery
Accurate hourly postoperative output is measured with an indwelling catheter and urometer.

alt.q: Why is a condom-type external catheter an excellent option for many males with urinary incontinence?
alt.a: It carries less risk for UTI than an indwelling catheter
alt.ex: External catheters are noninvasive and are associated with less UTI risk than indwelling catheters.
w: It allows accurate measurement of residual urine
Postvoid residual is measured with a bladder scanner or straight catheter.
It drains a bladder that cannot empty on its own
It only collects urine the patient voids; it does not drain the bladder.
It needs no skin checks once it has been applied
The penis is inspected within 15 to 30 minutes and at least daily.

items.q: Which interventions help prevent catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)? Select all that apply.
o: Use the smallest catheter suited to the patient
Using the smallest possible catheter is an evidence-based CAUTI measure.
Keep the drainage bag below the level of the bladder
This prevents backflow of urine into the bladder.
Remove the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed
Each catheter day raises CAUTI risk, so prompt removal is key.
Secure the catheter to prevent movement and pulling
Securement reduces movement and traction on the catheter.
Disconnect the tubing to collect urine specimens
Specimens come from the sampling port; the closed system must stay intact.
Change the catheter routinely every 3 days
Routine scheduled changes are not recommended; clinical indicators guide changes.
items.ex: CAUTI prevention includes appropriate catheter size, a closed dependent system, securement, and prompt removal.

alt.q: A nurse reviews care of patients with indwelling catheters. Which practices increase the risk for CAUTI? Select all that apply.
o: Letting urine pool in loops of the drainage tubing
Pooled urine can flow back toward the bladder.
Resting the drainage bag on the floor
A bag on the floor can become contaminated.
Letting the drainage spigot touch the measuring container
Spigot contact can introduce bacteria into the system.
Using a separate measuring container for each patient
A dedicated container prevents cross-contamination.
Performing perineal hygiene daily and after soiling
Routine perineal hygiene lowers CAUTI risk.
alt.ex: Pooling urine, floor contact, and spigot contamination raise CAUTI risk; dedicated containers and hygiene lower it.

items.q: After an indwelling catheter is removed, which findings suggest incomplete bladder emptying that needs intervention? Select all that apply.
o: Abdominal pain and distention
These suggest urine is being retained in the bladder.
Constant dribbling of urine
Dribbling can indicate an overfull bladder that is not emptying.
Voiding very small amounts
Small frequent voids can signal incomplete emptying.
A sensation of incomplete emptying
This symptom points to retained urine.
Mild discomfort with the first void
Some discomfort with the first few voids after removal is expected.
Voiding 300 mL every 3 to 4 hours
This reflects a normal voiding pattern.
items.ex: Pain, distention, dribbling, small voids, incontinence, and incomplete emptying after removal indicate retained urine.

alt.q: A nurse monitors a patient after indwelling catheter removal. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Record the time and amount of each void in a bladder diary
A bladder diary documents voiding and any incontinence.
Monitor voiding for at least 24 to 48 hours
This is the minimum monitoring period after removal.
Measure postvoid residual with a bladder scanner
A bladder scan shows how well the bladder empties.
Restrict fluids so the patient voids less often
Adequate fluid intake is needed; restriction does not aid assessment.
Treat continued painful urination as expected
Continued pain on urination suggests possible infection.
alt.ex: After removal, monitor voiding 24 to 48 hours with a bladder diary and PVR, and report continued dysuria.

items.q: Which instructions belong in patient education for a healthy bladder? Select all that apply.
o: Drink six to eight glasses of water spread through the day
Steady hydration keeps urine dilute and less irritating.
Keep the bowels regular
A rectum full of stool can irritate the bladder.
Stop smoking
Smoking raises bladder cancer risk and causes cough that worsens stress incontinence.
Females should wipe from front to back
Front-to-back cleansing helps prevent UTIs.
Strain to empty the bladder more quickly
Patients should avoid straining and take time to empty fully.
Drink most fluids in the late evening
Avoiding fluids 2 hours before bedtime reduces nocturia.
items.ex: Healthy bladder teaching covers hydration, regular bowels, good voiding habits, UTI prevention, and smoking cessation.

alt.q: Which items should the nurse teach a patient with urinary urgency to limit because they irritate the bladder? Select all that apply.
o: Caffeine
Caffeine is an especially common bladder irritant.
Artificial sweeteners
Artificial sweeteners are listed bladder irritants.
Spicy foods
Spicy foods can increase frequency and urgency.
Citrus products
Citrus is a common bladder irritant.
Plain water
Adequate water intake is encouraged, not limited.
alt.ex: Caffeine, artificial sweeteners, spicy foods, and citrus irritate the bladder; water should not be limited.

items.q: Urine left standing for several hours becomes alkaline because of bacterial growth.
items.a: True
items.ex: Standing urine grows bacteria, which raises pH and alters test accuracy.
items.ww: Standing urine does not become more acidic or stay unchanged; bacterial growth makes it alkaline.

alt.q: Urine that stands at room temperature for several hours becomes more acidic, which preserves it for testing.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Standing urine becomes alkaline from bacterial growth, so specimens must reach the laboratory promptly or be preserved.
alt.ww: Standing urine changes, so delay harms accuracy rather than preserving the specimen.

items.q: The Infectious Diseases Society of America recommends changing indwelling urinary catheters on a fixed routine schedule.
items.a: False
items.ex: IDSA advises changing catheters based on clinical indicators such as obstruction, infection, or breaks in the closed system.
items.ww: Routine interval changes are not recommended; changes depend on clinical indicators.

alt.q: Indwelling catheters are changed based on clinical indicators such as obstruction, infection, or a break in the closed system.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: IDSA does not recommend routine interval changes; clinical indicators determine when to change.
alt.ww: A fixed schedule is not the recommended basis for changing catheters.

items.q: Placing a patient on intake and output (I&O) monitoring can be a nursing judgment, not only a health care provider’s order.
items.a: True
items.ex: Although often ordered, placing a patient on I&O is also a nursing judgment.
items.ww: Nurses may start I&O measurement on their own judgment to evaluate bladder emptying and fluid balance.

alt.q: Only a health care provider can decide to place a patient on intake and output measurement.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: I&O is often ordered, but nurses can also place a patient on I&O as a nursing judgment.
alt.ww: Nurses are not limited to provider orders when deciding to measure I&O.

items.q: Being awakened from sleep by the urge to void is called [[nocturia]].
items.ex: Nocturia means waking at night with the urge to void; ask how many times it happens each night.

alt.q: A patient who gets up three times each night because of the urge to pass urine has [[nocturia]].
alt.ex: Nocturia means waking at night with the urge to void; ask how many times it happens each night.

sections.name: Skill 46.1 · Urine specimen collection: Midstream (clean-voided) urine; sterile urinary catheter

items.q: A nurse delegates collection of a clean-voided urine specimen to assistive personnel (AP). Which finding should the AP be told to report to the nurse?
items.a: The patient has burning on urination
items.ex: AP report pain or burning, inability to start a stream, and urine that is not clear.
w: The patient prefers to cleanse their own perineum
Patients often prefer self-cleansing; this is expected, not a finding to report.
The urine sample is clear and pale yellow
Clear urine is normal; AP report urine that is not clear.
The patient asks to collect it in the bathroom
Mobile patients may collect clean-voided specimens in the bathroom.

alt.q: Which part of urine specimen collection can the nurse delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
alt.a: Collecting the specimen at the ordered time
alt.ex: Specimen collection can be delegated; the nurse identifies the specimen type and technique and evaluates results.
w: Interpreting the culture and sensitivity report
Evaluating results and reporting findings remain nursing responsibilities.
Deciding which specimen type the patient needs
The nurse identifies the specimen type and technique for the AP.
Teaching about the antibiotic that is ordered
Patient teaching about medications is a nursing responsibility.

items.q: Why does the nurse have the patient begin voiding into the toilet before passing the container into the stream?
items.a: The first urine flushes out organisms that collect at the meatus
items.ex: The initial stream flushes out microorganisms that normally accumulate at the urethral meatus.
w: The first urine has the bacteria needed for culture
The first urine carries meatal contaminants, which is why it is not collected.
The first urine is too concentrated for accurate results
Concentration is not the reason; contamination at the meatus is.
The first urine dilutes the specimen to the right volume
The first urine goes into the toilet, not the specimen.

alt.q: Why does the nurse remove the specimen container before the urine flow stops?
alt.a: It keeps skin flora and bladder sediment out of the specimen
alt.ex: Removing the container before flow stops and before releasing the labia or penis prevents flora and sediment contamination.
w: It keeps the container from overflowing onto the bed
Volume control is not the stated reason; contamination is.
It ensures the specimen contains the most concentrated urine
The last urine may carry sediment; it is avoided, not wanted.
It allows the antiseptic solution to dry on the skin
Antiseptic drying is unrelated to when the container is removed.

items.q: How much urine does the nurse collect for a midstream clean-voided specimen?
items.a: 90 to 120 mL
items.ex: Once the stream starts, the container is passed into it to collect 90 to 120 mL.
w: 5 to 10 mL
This is too little urine for a midstream specimen.
20 to 30 mL
This is the volume collected during catheter insertion, not a midstream specimen.
250 to 300 mL
This exceeds the volume needed for a midstream specimen.

alt.q: A patient asks how much urine to catch in the cup for a midstream specimen. Which instruction is correct?
alt.a: “Catch about 90 to 120 mL after your stream has started.”
alt.ex: A midstream specimen is 90 to 120 mL collected after the stream is established.
w: “Catch about 10 mL from the very first part of your stream.”
The first urine flushes the meatus and goes into the toilet.
“Catch about 500 mL, all the urine you pass at once.”
Only a midstream portion is collected, not the whole void.
“Catch about 30 mL from the very end of your stream.”
The container is removed before the flow stops to avoid sediment.

items.q: A nurse sees a student preparing to fill a sterile culture cup from the spigot of a patient’s urinary drainage bag. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Have the student draw urine from the catheter sampling port
items.ex: Urine in a drainage bag is not sterile; specimens are aspirated from the sampling port without opening the system.
w: Allow it if the spigot is wiped with alcohol first
Bag urine is not sterile no matter how the spigot is cleaned.
Have the student disconnect the catheter from the tubing
Opening the closed system introduces pathogens; specimens come from the port.
Allow it if the urine in the bag was collected today
Urine in the drainage bag is never considered sterile for culture.

alt.q: Before aspirating a specimen from a catheter sampling port, the nurse clamps the drainage tubing. Where and for how long?
alt.a: Below the sampling port, for up to 15 minutes
alt.ex: Clamping below the port for as long as 15 minutes lets fresh urine collect in the tubing for sampling.
w: Above the sampling port, for up to 15 minutes
Clamping above the port would keep urine from reaching it.
Below the sampling port, for 1 to 2 hours
The book limits clamping to about 10 to 15 minutes.
At the drainage bag outlet, for 5 minutes
Clamping the bag outlet does not collect fresh urine at the port.

items.q: A nurse is collecting a urine culture from a patient’s indwelling catheter. How much urine should be withdrawn from the sampling port?
items.a: 3 mL
items.ex: A 3-mL safety Luer-Lok syringe is used to withdraw 3 mL for culture.
w: 20 mL
Twenty mL is withdrawn for a routine urinalysis, not a culture.
60 mL
This is far more than needed for a culture.
0.5 mL
This is too little; the proper volume is needed to perform the test.

alt.q: A nurse needs a routine urinalysis specimen from a patient’s indwelling catheter. How much urine should be withdrawn?
alt.a: 20 mL
alt.ex: A 20-mL Luer-Lok syringe is used to withdraw 20 mL for routine urinalysis.
w: 3 mL
Three mL is the volume for a culture.
100 mL
This is more than the test requires.
1 mL
This is too little to perform a routine urinalysis.

items.q: A patient’s urine culture shows more than 10,000 organisms per milliliter. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Report the findings to the health care provider
items.ex: A colony count above 10,000/mL shows bacterial growth, which is reported so treatment can be ordered.
w: Repeat the clean-voided specimen collection
Repeating collection is for a contaminated specimen, not a positive culture.
Insert a catheter to drain the bladder
A positive culture does not indicate a need for catheterization.
Encourage the patient to limit fluid intake
Limiting fluids is not an intervention for bacterial growth.

alt.q: After reporting a urine culture that shows bacterial growth, which ongoing assessment should the nurse perform?
alt.a: Monitor the patient for fever and dysuria
alt.ex: After reporting and giving ordered medications, the nurse monitors for fever and dysuria.
w: Monitor the patient for orange-colored urine
Orange urine is a phenazopyridine effect, not a sign of infection.
Monitor the patient for weight gain and edema
These are not the listed follow-up assessments for bacterial growth.
Monitor the patient for blurred vision
Blurred vision is an antimuscarinic side effect, not an infection sign.

items.q: When inspecting a clean-voided specimen, the nurse finds toilet paper in the cup. Which action is best?
items.a: Repeat the instructions and collect a new specimen
items.ex: Contaminants prevent a specimen from being used, so the nurse re-teaches and repeats collection.
w: Remove the paper and send the specimen
The specimen is already contaminated and cannot be used.
Send it with a note on the requisition
A contaminated specimen gives inaccurate results even if noted.
Insert an indwelling catheter right away
Catheterization is considered only if a clean-voided specimen cannot be obtained.

alt.q: A patient cannot provide an uncontaminated clean-voided specimen even after repeated instruction. What does the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: Catheterization to obtain the specimen
alt.ex: If a clean-voided specimen cannot be obtained, the patient may need catheterization.
w: Sending the contaminated specimen anyway
Contaminated specimens cannot be used.
Canceling the ordered urine culture
The test is still needed; the collection method changes.
Collecting urine from a bedpan with stool
Stool contaminates the specimen and makes it unusable.

items.q: A nurse collects a urine specimen but cannot send it to the laboratory right away. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Refrigerate the specimen until it can be sent
items.ex: Specimens go to the lab within 20 minutes; if delay is unavoidable, refrigerate to limit changes.
w: Leave it at the bedside at room temperature
Urine standing at room temperature grows bacteria and alters results.
Add sterile saline to keep the urine fresh
Adding fluid dilutes and alters the specimen.
Warm it in a basin to body temperature
Warmth speeds bacterial growth and changes results.

alt.q: A patient will collect a urine specimen at home for culture. Which instruction is correct?
alt.a: Keep the specimen on ice until it reaches the laboratory
alt.ex: Keeping the sample on ice minimizes bacterial growth before it is cultured.
w: Keep the specimen warm so the bacteria stay alive
Warmth promotes overgrowth and inaccurate results.
Store the specimen at room temperature overnight
Standing urine grows bacteria and alters test results.
Leave the cup uncapped so moisture can escape
The lid must be tight to prevent contamination and spillage.

items.q: A nurse teaches an uncircumcised male patient to collect a clean-voided specimen. Which instruction is correct?
items.a: Retract the foreskin, keep it back while voiding, then return it
items.ex: Retraction allows effective cleansing and keeps the stream clean; returning the foreskin prevents constriction.
w: Leave the foreskin in place and cleanse over it
The foreskin must be retracted to cleanse the meatus effectively.
Retract the foreskin and leave it retracted afterward
The foreskin must be returned to prevent constriction and swelling.
Cleanse from the edge of the glans toward the meatus
Cleansing moves from the meatus outward, least to most contaminated.

alt.q: How should a male patient cleanse the urethral meatus before a midstream specimen?
alt.a: In circles from the meatus outward, three times with new towelettes
alt.ex: Circular cleansing from center outward with a new towelette each time moves from least to most contaminated.
w: In circles from the outside toward the meatus, one time
Moving toward the meatus carries organisms onto it.
Back and forth across the meatus with one towelette
A single towelette rubbed back and forth spreads contamination.
From the base of the shaft to the tip, one time
The meatus is cleansed with circular strokes, three times.

items.q: When cleansing a female patient before a midstream specimen, which stroke does the nurse perform last?
items.a: Down the center over the urethral meatus
items.ex: Cleanse the far labial fold, the near fold, then down the center, front to back, with a fresh swab each time.
w: Along the labial fold farthest from the nurse
The far fold is cleansed first.
Along the labial fold closest to the nurse
The near fold is cleansed second, before the center.
From the anus up toward the urethral meatus
Cleansing moves front to back to keep fecal material from the meatus.

alt.q: Why does the nurse cleanse a female patient’s urethral area from front to back?
alt.a: To keep fecal material away from the urinary meatus
alt.ex: Front-to-back cleansing prevents contamination of the meatus with fecal material.
w: To spread the antiseptic evenly over the labia
Even spreading is not the purpose; direction prevents fecal contamination.
To make the labia easier to hold apart
Labial separation is done with the nondominant hand, regardless of direction.
To rinse away the antiseptic before voiding
Rinsing, if required, is done with sterile water afterward.

items.q: How should the nurse label a urine specimen?
items.a: On the container, not the lid, in the patient’s presence
items.ex: Labeling the container in the patient’s presence with two identifiers ensures correct identification.
w: On the lid, in the patient’s presence
Lids can be separated from containers, so the label goes on the container.
On the container, later at the nurses’ station
Labels are confirmed in the patient’s presence to prevent errors.
On the biohazard bag only, at the laboratory
The container itself must be labeled before it leaves the room.

alt.q: A female patient is menstruating when her urine specimen is collected. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Note on the label that she is menstruating
alt.ex: Menstrual blood can appear in the specimen, so the label indicates menstruation.
w: Discard the specimen and send nothing
The specimen is still sent; menstruation is noted on the label.
Rinse the cup with sterile water first
Rinsing the cup does not address possible blood from menses.
Send the specimen with no notation
Without a note, blood from menses could be misread as hematuria.

items.q: Before collecting a urine specimen, the nurse assesses for urinary tract infection. Which findings are consistent with UTI? Select all that apply.
o: Frequency and urgency
These are listed indicators of UTI.
Dysuria
Painful urination is an indicator of UTI.
Flank pain and fever
These suggest infection that may involve the kidneys.
Cloudy, malodorous urine
Cloudy, foul-smelling urine is a UTI indicator.
Clear, pale straw-colored urine
This is a normal urine finding.
Bright orange urine with phenazopyridine
This is an expected drug effect, not an infection sign.
items.ex: UTI indicators include frequency, urgency, dysuria, hematuria, flank pain, fever, and cloudy, malodorous urine.

alt.q: Which findings should assistive personnel (AP) collecting a urine specimen report to the nurse? Select all that apply.
o: Urine that contains blood
Urine that is not clear, such as with blood, is reported.
Cloudy urine or excess sediment
Cloudiness and sediment are reportable findings.
Inability to start a urine stream
This may indicate retention or obstruction.
Pain or burning on urination
These may indicate infection.
Urine that is clear and pale yellow
Clear urine is normal and does not need to be reported.
alt.ex: AP report urine that is not clear, inability to initiate a stream, and pain or burning on urination.

items.q: A nurse is collecting a sterile urine specimen from an indwelling catheter. Which actions are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Clamp the tubing below the sampling port
This lets fresh urine collect at the port.
Scrub the port with a disinfectant swab for 15 seconds
Cleansing the port prevents microorganisms from entering the catheter.
Attach a needleless Luer-Lok syringe to the port
A needleless system prevents needlestick injury.
Unclamp the tubing after the specimen is drawn
Unclamping prevents urine stasis in the bladder.
Disconnect the catheter from the drainage tubing
Opening the closed system introduces pathogens.
Pour urine from the drainage bag into the cup
Urine in the drainage bag is not sterile.
items.ex: Catheter specimens are aspirated from a cleansed port while the tubing is briefly clamped, keeping the system closed.

alt.q: Which actions would contaminate a sterile urine specimen from an indwelling catheter? Select all that apply.
o: Taking urine from the drainage bag
Bag urine is not considered sterile.
Attaching the syringe before the port is cleansed
An uncleansed port can carry microorganisms into the sample.
Separating the catheter from the drainage tubing
Breaking the closed system introduces pathogens.
Transferring urine into a sterile container for culture
This is the correct step to keep a culture specimen sterile.
Placing the lid tightly on the container
A tight lid prevents contamination and spillage.
alt.ex: Bag urine, an uncleansed port, and opening the system contaminate specimens; sterile transfer and a tight lid protect them.

items.q: Which information does the nurse confirm on a urine specimen label in the patient’s presence? Select all that apply.
o: Two patient identifiers
Two identifiers ensure the specimen is matched to the correct patient.
The specimen source
The source, such as clean-voided or catheter, is on the label.
The collection date and time
Date and time are confirmed on the label.
The nurse’s interpretation of the urine color
Characteristics are documented in the record, not on the label.
The antibiotic the nurse expects to be ordered
Expected treatment does not belong on a specimen label.
items.ex: Labels carry two identifiers, specimen source, and collection date and time, confirmed in the patient’s presence.

alt.q: Which items should the nurse document after collecting a urine specimen? Select all that apply.
o: Method used to obtain the specimen
The collection method is documented.
Characteristics of the specimen
Urine characteristics are documented.
Time the specimen was sent to the laboratory
Timing affects accuracy and is documented.
Patient’s tolerance of the procedure
The patient’s response is documented.
The organism the nurse expects the culture to grow
Predictions are not documented; the laboratory identifies organisms.
alt.ex: Document method, date and time, test ordered, laboratory, characteristics, tolerance, and time sent.

items.q: When agency procedure calls for it, the nurse rinses the cleansed perineum with sterile water so antiseptic does not contaminate the specimen.
items.a: True
items.ex: Rinsing with sterile water and drying prevents antiseptic solution from entering the specimen.
items.ww: Antiseptic left on the skin can contaminate the specimen, so rinsing is done when agency procedure indicates.

alt.q: Antiseptic solution left on the perineum improves a urine culture by killing bacteria in the stream.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Antiseptic in the specimen is a contaminant; agencies may require rinsing with sterile water to prevent it.
alt.ww: Antiseptic contaminates the specimen rather than improving the culture.

items.q: After drawing a specimen from the catheter port, the nurse unclamps the tubing so urine drains by gravity and does not stagnate in the bladder.
items.a: True
items.ex: Unclamping allows gravity drainage and prevents stasis of urine in the bladder.
items.ww: Leaving the tubing clamped would cause urine stasis, so it is released after sampling.

alt.q: The catheter tubing may stay clamped until the specimen results return, so fresh urine is available for repeat testing.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The tubing is clamped only up to about 15 minutes and is released right after the specimen is drawn.
alt.ww: Prolonged clamping causes urine stasis in the bladder.

items.q: The nurse may touch the inside of the specimen cap once the patient has finished voiding.
items.a: False
items.ex: The cap is placed sterile side up and only its outside is touched when recapping.
items.ww: Touching the inside contaminates the container, the most frequent reason for inaccurate culture results.

alt.q: The nurse places the specimen cap with the sterile inside facing up and touches only its outside when recapping.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Keeping the inside of the cap and container untouched maintains sterility of the specimen.
alt.ww: Touching the inside of the cap would contaminate the specimen.

sections.name: Skill 46.2 · Insertion of a straight (intermittent) or indwelling

items.q: A nurse is preparing to insert an indwelling urinary catheter. Which task can the nurse delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Holding a light to illuminate the perineum
items.ex: AP may assist with positioning, lighting, privacy, and perineal care, but cannot insert catheters.
w: Inserting a straight catheter to check residual
Straight catheter insertion cannot be delegated to AP.
Inflating the balloon after insertion
Balloon inflation is part of catheter insertion, which the nurse performs.
Cleansing the meatus with sterile antiseptic
Sterile cleansing is part of the insertion skill the nurse performs.

alt.q: Which instruction should the nurse give assistive personnel (AP) caring for a patient after indwelling catheter insertion?
alt.a: Report fever or discomfort after the procedure
alt.ex: AP report postprocedure discomfort or fever, and abnormal urine, leaking, or pain.
w: Reinsert the catheter if it slips out
Catheter insertion cannot be delegated to AP.
Partly deflate the balloon if pain occurs
Manipulating the balloon is not an AP task; pain is reported.
Add fluid to the balloon if urine leaks
Leaking is reported to the nurse; AP do not adjust the balloon.

items.q: Before inserting an indwelling catheter held with an adhesive securement device, the nurse reviews risk factors. Which finding increases the risk of medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI)?
items.a: History of radiation therapy
items.ex: Age, dehydration, malnutrition, radiation exposure, chronic conditions, and skin edema are common MARSI risk factors.
w: History of hay fever and asthma
These suggest latex allergy risk, not MARSI risk.
Recent urinary tract infection
UTI is not listed as a risk factor for adhesive skin injury.
Need for a Coudé-tip catheter
Catheter tip shape is unrelated to adhesive skin injury.

alt.q: Which signs at a catheter securement site indicate medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI)?
alt.a: Erythema, blistering, and excoriation
alt.ex: MARSI reflects the skin’s reaction to adhesive and shows as erythema, blistering, and excoriation.
w: Pallor, coolness, and absent pulses
These reflect impaired circulation, not adhesive injury.
Purulent drainage from the meatus
Meatal drainage suggests infection, not adhesive injury.
Pink, moist, and intact skin
This describes healthy tissue, not injury.

items.q: A nurse prepares to insert a short-term indwelling catheter in an 82-year-old patient with no hematuria. Which catheter size is most appropriate?
items.a: 12 to 14 Fr
items.ex: Use the smallest catheter possible; older adults usually need 12 to 14 Fr.
w: 20 to 22 Fr
Larger sizes are for special cases such as gross hematuria or urological surgery.
5 to 6 Fr
This size is for infants.
8 to 10 Fr
This size is for children.

alt.q: Which situation calls for a larger catheter of 20 to 22 Fr?
alt.a: Gross hematuria after urological surgery
alt.ex: Larger catheters are reserved for special circumstances such as urological surgery or gross hematuria.
w: Routine output monitoring in an adult
Most adults need 14 to 16 Fr; the smallest size possible is used.
Straight catheterization to measure residual
Straight catheterization kits use 12 to 14 Fr single-lumen catheters.
A patient who has had a vaginoplasty
Surgery involving the urethra may call for a smaller catheter, not a larger one.

items.q: Why does the nurse use the smallest catheter size possible?
items.a: Large diameters increase the risk for urethral trauma
items.ex: Larger catheters increase urethral trauma, while small catheters allow drainage of the periurethral glands.
w: Small catheters drain urine from the bladder faster
Drainage speed is not the stated reason; trauma prevention is.
Small catheters do not need a balloon to stay in
Indwelling catheters of any size use a balloon to stay in place.
Large catheters cannot be secured to the thigh
Securement is possible for any size; size choice is about trauma.

alt.q: A transgender female patient who had a vaginoplasty needs an indwelling catheter. Which consideration is correct?
alt.a: A smaller catheter may be needed, and a urologist may be consulted
alt.ex: After gender-confirming surgery involving the urethra, a smaller catheter and consultation may be necessary.
w: A Coudé-tip catheter is always required
Coudé tips are for passing an enlarged prostate, not routine after vaginoplasty.
A 20 to 22 Fr catheter prevents leakage
Large catheters raise trauma risk; a smaller size may be needed.
Catheterization is never done after this surgery
Catheters can be placed; size and expert consultation are considered.

items.q: While a nurse cleanses a female patient’s urethral meatus before catheterization, the labia slip closed. What should the nurse do?

w: Continue and insert the catheter quickly
Inserting through a contaminated area raises CAUTI risk.
Reopen the labia with the sterile dominant hand
This contaminates the hand that must stay sterile for the catheter.
Apply more lubricant to the catheter tip
Lubricant does not correct contamination of the meatus.

alt.q: Why does the nurse keep the nondominant hand separating the labia throughout female catheterization?

w: It keeps the nondominant hand sterile
The nondominant hand is considered contaminated once it touches the patient.
It prevents the balloon from inflating early
Hand position does not affect balloon inflation.
It stops urine from flowing too quickly
The hand exposes the meatus; it does not control urine flow.

The nondominant hand is already contaminated; this is not the reason.
To keep the foreskin from retracting
The foreskin is intentionally retracted if uncircumcised.
To prevent swelling of the glans

alt.q: How does the nurse hold the penis during catheter insertion, and why?

Bearing down, not angle, relaxes the external sphincter.
At 0 degrees, flat on the abdomen, to prevent leakage
The penis is lowered only after insertion.
At 60 degrees toward the thigh, to open the meatus
The penis is held perpendicular, not angled toward the thigh.

200 to 250 mL

w: Advance it another 12.5 to 15 cm (5 to 6 inches)
This is far more than needed for the short female urethra.
Withdraw it 2.5 cm (1 inch) before inflating
Withdrawing could leave the balloon in the urethra.
Inflate it at once, advancing 0 cm (0 inches)
The catheter is advanced farther before the balloon is inflated.

items.q: While the nurse inflates the balloon of an indwelling catheter, the patient reports sudden pain. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Stop inflating and let the fluid flow back into the syringe
items.ex: Pain or resistance suggests the balloon is in the urethra; stop, deflate, advance farther, and reinflate.
w: Finish inflating quickly to shorten the discomfort
Inflating in the urethra can cause injury.
Pull the catheter out with the balloon inflated
Removing an inflated balloon traumatizes the urethra.
Inject the remaining fluid more slowly
Slower inflation still expands the balloon in the urethra.

alt.q: After deflating, advancing, and reinflating the balloon, the patient still has pain. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Remove the catheter and notify the health care provider
alt.ex: If pain continues after repositioning, the catheter is removed and the provider is notified.
w: Leave it in place and give an analgesic
Ongoing pain may mean injury and needs removal and reporting.
Add extra fluid to the balloon
Overfilling does not fix a malpositioned balloon.
Tape the catheter tightly to the thigh
Securing it does not address the cause of pain.

items.q: After inflating the balloon, the nurse gently pulls the catheter until resistance is felt and then advances it slightly. Why?
items.a: To avoid pressure on the bladder neck
items.ex: Moving the catheter slightly back into the bladder avoids pressure of the balloon on the bladder neck.
w: To check whether the balloon is underinflated
Underinflation is prevented by injecting the full designated amount.
To release trapped air from the balloon
The balloon is filled with sterile water, not checked for air this way.
To flush urine from the drainage eyes
The maneuver positions the balloon, not the drainage eyes.

alt.q: Why must the nurse inflate the balloon with the full amount of fluid designated by the manufacturer?
alt.a: Underinflation distorts the balloon and can damage the bladder
alt.ex: An underinflated balloon becomes distorted and may cause bladder damage.
w: Overfilling is needed to prevent expulsion
The designated amount is used, not extra fluid.
Partial filling makes later removal harder
Removal difficulty is not the stated reason.
The full amount sterilizes the balloon lumen
Sterile water inflates the balloon; it does not sterilize it.

items.q: Where does the nurse secure an indwelling catheter in a male patient?
items.a: Upper thigh or lower abdomen, with the penis directed toward the chest
items.ex: Anchoring to the upper thigh or lower abdomen reduces traction on the urethra and minimizes injury.
w: Inner thigh, with the penis directed toward the feet
Securing to the inner thigh is the method for females.
To the side rail, with tape around the tubing
Side rails move and can pull or dislodge the catheter.
Lower leg below the knee, with the tubing taut
Taut tubing creates tension; slack must be allowed.

alt.q: Where does the nurse attach a catheter securement device on the catheter, and why?
alt.a: Just above the bifurcation, to avoid occluding the catheter
alt.ex: Attaching the device just above the bifurcation prevents catheter occlusion while reducing movement.
w: Over the balloon port, to keep the port closed
Covering the port is not the purpose of securement.
At the bag end of the tubing, to prevent kinks
The device is placed near the bifurcation, not at the bag.
At the meatus, to stop leakage of urine
Securement at the meatus would cause pressure injury.

items.q: After inserting an indwelling catheter, a nurse sees the drainage bag hooked to the lowered side rail. Which action is best?
items.a: Move the bag to the bedframe below bladder level
items.ex: Bags on movable side rails can pull or dislodge the catheter; the bedframe keeps the bag below the bladder.
w: Leave it, because the lowered rail is below the bladder
Side rails move and increase urethral trauma and dislodgement.
Place the bag on the floor beside the bed
Bags should never rest on the floor because of contamination.
Hang the bag on the IV pole above the bed
A bag above the bladder allows backflow and raises CAUTI risk.

alt.q: Why is the drainage bag kept below the level of the bladder at all times?
alt.a: To prevent backflow of urine into the bladder
alt.ex: Keeping the bag dependent prevents backflow, which can cause CAUTI.
w: To increase the speed of urine production
Bag position does not change urine production.
To keep the balloon fully inflated
Bag position does not affect balloon volume.
To make measuring hourly output easier
Measurement is not the reason; preventing backflow is.

items.q: During catheterization of a female patient, the catheter enters the vagina. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Leave it in place and insert a new sterile catheter into the meatus
items.ex: Leave the misplaced catheter, cleanse again, insert a new sterile catheter, then remove the vaginal one.
w: Remove it, wipe it, and reinsert it into the meatus
The catheter is contaminated and must not be reinserted.
Remove it and reinsert the same catheter higher
A contaminated catheter would introduce organisms into the bladder.
Leave it in place and inflate its balloon
The catheter is not in the bladder; inflating it is inappropriate.

alt.q: When is a catheter that was mistakenly placed in the vagina removed?
alt.a: After the second catheter is placed in the urethra
alt.ex: The misplaced catheter stays as a landmark until a new sterile catheter is successfully inserted.
w: Before the meatus is cleansed again
Removing it early loses the landmark that prevents a repeat error.
As soon as the error is noticed
It is left in place until the second catheter is inserted.
At the end of the nurse’s shift
It is removed right after successful insertion of the second catheter.

items.q: A patient with a newly placed indwelling catheter reports bladder discomfort, and urine is draining well. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Check the catheter for traction
items.ex: With a patent catheter, first check for traction, then notify the provider and monitor the urine.
w: Irrigate the catheter with sterile saline
The catheter is patent; irrigation is not indicated.
Partially deflate the catheter balloon
Underinflation distorts the balloon and can damage the bladder.
Clamp the catheter for 1 hour
Clamping causes urine stasis and does not address discomfort.

alt.q: A patient’s indwelling catheter drains well with no traction, but bladder discomfort persists. What should the nurse suspect and report?
alt.a: Bladder spasms or a urinary tract infection
alt.ex: Persistent discomfort with a patent catheter may mean bladder spasms or UTI; notify the provider.
w: A drainage bag that is too empty
Bag volume does not cause bladder discomfort.
Normal pressure from the insertion
Insertion pressure goes away quickly; persistent pain is reported.
A balloon that is correctly placed
Correct placement does not explain ongoing discomfort.

items.q: A patient with a spinal cord injury will perform chronic intermittent self-catheterization at home. Which statement shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “Clean technique is acceptable for catheterizing myself at home.”
items.ex: In nonacute settings, clean technique is an acceptable, practical alternative for chronic intermittent catheterization.
w: “I should drain about 1,000 mL each time I catheterize.”
The goal for intermittent catheterization is about 400 mL per drainage.
“I can cut back on fluids so I catheterize less often.”
Adequate fluid intake is taught to reduce infection risk.
“I only need to watch for infection the first week.”
Signs of infection are monitored for as long as catheterization continues.

alt.q: A patient changing from a large bedside bag to a leg bag at home asks what to do. Which instruction is correct?
alt.a: Wash your hands and cleanse the connection ports with alcohol
alt.ex: Handwashing and alcohol cleansing of the ports reduce contamination when changing bags.
w: Rinse the connection ports with tap water first
Tap water does not disinfect the ports.
Wear the leg bag at night and the large bag by day
Leg bags are worn by day; larger bags are used at night.
Hang the leg bag above the knee for good flow
Bags must stay below bladder level to prevent backflow.

items.q: Which evaluation steps follow insertion of an indwelling catheter? Select all that apply.
o: Palpate the bladder or use a bladder scanner for distention
This shows whether distention is relieved.
Ask whether the feeling of bladder fullness was relieved
The patient’s report confirms relief of discomfort.
Check the catheter and tubing connections for leaks
No leaks protects skin and keeps the system closed.
Observe the character and amount of urine
This shows adequate flow and changes suggesting CAUTI.
Pull firmly on the catheter to test the balloon
Traction can injure the urethra and bladder neck.
Disconnect the tubing to check the flow
Disconnecting breaks the closed sterile system.
items.ex: Evaluation checks relief of distention and fullness, urine character and amount, leaks, and patient understanding.

alt.q: Which information does the nurse document after inserting an indwelling catheter? Select all that apply.
o: Type and size of the catheter
Type and size guide future care and reinsertion.
Amount of fluid used to inflate the balloon
Balloon volume is needed for safe removal.
Characteristics and amount of urine
Urine findings are documented.
Patient’s response to the procedure
The patient’s response is documented.
The nurse’s opinion of the patient’s cooperation
Personal opinions do not belong in documentation.
alt.ex: Document the reason, catheter type and size, balloon volume, specimen, urine, response, and learning.

items.q: During catheter insertion, which situations require the nurse to replace items or start over? Select all that apply.
o: A sterile glove touches the patient’s thigh
Contaminated gloves are replaced and the procedure restarted.
The catheter tip touches the bed linen
A contaminated catheter must be replaced with a sterile one.
Supplies on the sterile field become contaminated
Contaminated supplies are replaced or a new kit is used.
The patient touches a corner of the field away from supplies
If supplies stay sterile, the nurse avoids touching that area.
The patient feels pressure as the catheter is inserted
Pressure is a normal sensation that passes quickly.
items.ex: Contaminated gloves, catheter, or supplies are replaced; if only an unused part of the field is touched, avoid that area.

alt.q: Which statements about maintaining sterility during catheter insertion are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The nondominant hand that touches the patient is contaminated
Once it separates labia or holds the penis, it is no longer sterile.
The dominant gloved hand stays sterile to handle the catheter
Only the sterile hand handles swabs and the catheter.
Coiling the catheter in the palm keeps its end off nonsterile surfaces
Coiling prevents the distal end from touching unsterile areas.
The contaminated hand may guide the catheter tip
The contaminated hand must not touch the sterile catheter.
Gloves that touch the thigh can be wiped and reused
Contaminated gloves are replaced.
alt.ex: The nondominant hand is contaminated, the dominant hand stays sterile, and the coiled catheter is kept off unsterile surfaces.

items.q: Which teaching points are appropriate for a patient going home with an indwelling catheter? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the drainage bag below the level of the bladder
This prevents backflow and CAUTI.
Watch urine color, clarity, odor, and amount
Observing urine helps detect problems early.
Know the signs of urinary tract infection
Patients and caregivers are taught UTI signs.
Keep an extra catheter, kit, and drainage bag at home
At least one spare set should always be available.
Rest the drainage bag on the floor at night
Floor contact contaminates the bag.
Disconnect the tubing to empty the bag
The bag is emptied through its drain without opening the system.
items.ex: Home teaching covers bag position and emptying, urine observation, UTI signs, leak troubleshooting, and spare supplies.

alt.q: Which actions help keep urine flowing through an indwelling catheter? Select all that apply.
o: Coil excess tubing on the bed
Coiling prevents kinks and dependent loops.
Check the tubing for kinks
Kinks obstruct urine flow.
Avoid lying on the drainage tubing
Body weight on tubing blocks flow.
Let the tubing hang in a loop below the bed
Dependent tubing lets urine pool instead of draining.
Keep the tubing clamped while walking
Clamping stops drainage; the bag is carried below the bladder.
alt.ex: Keeping tubing free of kinks, pressure, and dependent loops maintains flow and may reduce CAUTI risk.

items.q: When inserting a straight catheter, the nurse stops advancing it once urine appears.
items.a: True
items.ex: A straight catheter has no balloon, so advancing stops when urine flows.
items.ww: Further advancing is needed only for an indwelling catheter so the balloon reaches the bladder.

alt.q: With a straight catheter, the nurse advances another 2.5 to 5 cm after urine appears so the balloon is in the bladder.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Straight catheters have no balloon; the nurse stops advancing when urine appears.
alt.ww: Extra advancement applies to indwelling catheters, which have a balloon.

items.q: Asking the patient to bear down gently during catheter insertion relaxes the external urinary sphincter.
items.a: True
items.ex: Bearing down relaxes the external sphincter and, in females, helps show the meatus.
items.ww: Bearing down eases insertion rather than tightening the sphincter.

alt.q: Bearing down tightens the external sphincter, so patients are told to hold their breath and stay still during insertion.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Bearing down relaxes the external urinary sphincter and aids catheter insertion.
alt.ww: The book asks patients to bear down because it eases, not hinders, insertion.

items.q: The nurse allows the bladder to empty fully during catheterization unless agency policy limits the volume drained.
items.a: True
items.ex: There is no definitive evidence that limiting volume helps, so the bladder empties fully unless policy restricts it.
items.ww: No strong evidence requires clamping after a set volume; agency policy guides any limit.

alt.q: Strong evidence requires clamping the catheter after 500 mL to prevent complications during catheterization.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: No definitive evidence shows benefit in limiting the volume drained; follow agency policy.
alt.ww: The book states there is no definitive evidence for a maximum drainage volume.

items.q: Leaving an uncircumcised male patient’s foreskin retracted after catheterization can cause dangerous swelling of the penis called [[paraphimosis]].
items.ex: The foreskin is replaced over the glans after catheterization to prevent paraphimosis.

alt.q: A retracted foreskin that is not returned over the glans can lead to [[paraphimosis]].
alt.ex: The foreskin is replaced over the glans after catheterization to prevent paraphimosis.

items.a: Inflate the balloon with the full designated amount
items.ex: That's step 5 of 8. The meatus is cleansed, the catheter inserted and advanced, the balloon inflated and seated, then the catheter and bag secured.
w: Pull gently until resistance is felt, then advance slightly
That's step 6 of 8.
Ask the patient to bear down and insert the catheter
That's step 3 of 8.
Attach a securement device to the catheter
That's step 7 of 8.

sections.name: Skill 46.3 · Care and removal of an indwelling catheter

items.q: Agency policy allows assistive personnel (AP) to remove indwelling catheters. A nurse plans to have an AP remove a patient’s catheter. What must the nurse do before delegating this task?
items.a: Assess the patient’s status and verify the health care provider’s order for removal
items.ex: Removal can be delegated per agency policy, but the nurse must first assess the patient and verify the order.
w: Measure a postvoid residual volume with a bladder scanner before removal
A PVR is measured after the patient voids following removal, and only if ordered.
Obtain a sterile urine specimen from the catheter port before removal
A urine specimen is not a required step before delegating catheter removal.
Deflate the catheter balloon so that the AP only needs to pull the catheter out
The AP who removes the catheter deflates the balloon; the nurse’s required step is assessment and order verification.

alt.q: Which statement about delegating indwelling catheter care and removal to assistive personnel (AP) is accurate?
alt.a: Both routine catheter care and catheter removal can be delegated, after the nurse assesses the patient and verifies the order for removal
alt.ex: Routine catheter care can be delegated; removal can be delegated per agency policy after nurse assessment and order verification.
w: Routine catheter care can be delegated, but catheter removal can be performed only by a registered nurse in every agency
The book states removal can be delegated to AP according to agency policy.
Neither routine catheter care nor catheter removal can be delegated, because both require sterile technique and assessment
Catheter care uses clean gloves and soap and water, and both tasks can be delegated.
Catheter removal can be delegated, but routine catheter care must be performed by the nurse because it requires assessment
Routine catheter care is a delegable skill; the nurse retains assessment.

items.q: A nurse directs assistive personnel caring for a patient after catheter removal to report findings that may indicate an upper urinary tract infection (kidney infection). Which findings should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Fever and chills
Fever and chills are systemic signs listed for an upper UTI such as kidney infection.
Flank pain
Flank pain suggests kidney involvement, an upper UTI.
Back pain
Back pain is listed among signs that may indicate an upper UTI.
Blood in the urine
Blood in the urine is included among the reportable signs of an upper UTI.
Mild burning with the first voiding that soon subsides
Mild burning with the first voiding is an expected, temporary result of urethral irritation.
Clear, straw-colored urine
Clear, straw-colored urine is a normal finding, not a sign of infection.
items.ex: AP should report fever, chills, burning, flank pain, back pain, and blood in the urine, which may indicate an upper UTI.

alt.q: An AP reports several complaints from a patient whose catheter was removed yesterday. Which complaints point to an upper UTI (kidney infection) rather than a lower UTI? Select all that apply.
o: Flank pain
Flank pain is grouped with signs of an upper UTI such as kidney infection.
Fever and chills
Fever and chills are listed with upper UTI signs.
Back pain
Back pain is included among signs of an upper UTI.
Urgency and frequency
Urgency and frequency are grouped with signs of a lower UTI (bladder infection).
Lower abdominal pain
Lower abdominal pain is listed with signs of a lower UTI.
alt.ex: Fever, chills, flank pain, back pain, and blood in the urine may indicate an upper UTI such as kidney infection.

items.q: What is the rationale for this action: Retract the labia or foreskin and keep the hand in position?
items.a: Gives full view of the urethral meatus and prevents contamination during cleansing
items.ex: Each step of catheter care and removal protects the urethra, limits microorganisms, or prevents discomfort.
w: Prevents traction on the catheter that could damage the urethra and bladder neck
That goes with Hold the catheter with two fingers of the nondominant hand.
Moves from an area with more microorganisms to an area with fewer
That goes with Clean the catheter starting at the meatus and moving away from the body.
Keeps movement from creating tension on the catheter
That goes with Allow slack when reapplying the securement device.
