items.q: Which equipment is used to deflate the balloon when removing an indwelling catheter?
items.a: A 10-mL or larger syringe without a needle
items.ex: A needleless syringe of 10 mL or more is attached to the inflation valve to withdraw the balloon fluid.
w: A 3-mL syringe with a 25-gauge needle
A needle is not used, and a 3-mL syringe is too small for the usual balloon volume.
A 1-mL tuberculin syringe without a needle
A 1-mL syringe cannot hold the balloon volume; a 10-mL or larger syringe is required.
A pair of scissors to cut the inflation valve
The inflation valve is never cut to drain the balloon.

alt.q: Before removing a catheter, how does the nurse determine the size of the inflation balloon and the syringe needed?
alt.a: By looking at the balloon size printed on the balloon inflation valve
alt.ex: Balloon size in mL is printed on the inflation valve, which tells the syringe size and expected fluid volume.
w: By measuring the length of the catheter from the meatus to the drainage bag
Catheter length does not indicate balloon volume.
By reading the volume marked on the side of the urine drainage bag
The drainage bag shows urine volume, not balloon size.
By estimating the volume from the French size of the catheter tip
French size refers to catheter diameter; balloon volume is printed on the valve.

items.q: Why does a recent history of bowel incontinence increase a catheterized patient’s risk for catheter-associated urinary tract infection (CAUTI)?
items.a: Escherichia coli, the most common cause of CAUTI, is a major colonizer of the bowel
items.ex: E. coli is a major bowel colonizer and the most common CAUTI organism, so fecal incontinence raises CAUTI risk.
w: Staphylococcus aureus, the most common cause of CAUTI, lives mainly on the skin of the perineum
The book names E. coli, a bowel organism, as the most common cause of CAUTI.
Liquid stool dislodges the catheter balloon, allowing urine to leak around the catheter
Stool does not deflate the balloon; the risk comes from bowel bacteria.
Bowel incontinence causes dehydration, which concentrates urine and promotes encrustation
The risk is contamination by bowel bacteria, not urine concentration.

alt.q: A catheterized patient has had several episodes of fecal incontinence. Why should the nurse consider this patient at increased risk for CAUTI?
alt.a: Bowel organisms such as Escherichia coli are the most common cause of CAUTI
alt.ex: E. coli colonizes the bowel and is the most common CAUTI bacterium, so soiling increases risk.
w: Repeated cleansing removes protective oils from the urethral meatus
The book links the risk to bowel bacteria, not to cleansing.
Stool in the drainage bag raises the pH of the collected urine
Stool does not enter a closed drainage bag; bowel bacteria reaching the meatus are the risk.
Abdominal straining with incontinence pushes the catheter deeper into the bladder
Straining does not cause CAUTI; contamination with bowel organisms does.

items.q: Indwelling catheters left in place for more than a few days carry a higher risk for catheter encrustation and CAUTI.
items.a: True
items.ex: Duration matters; the nurse reviews how long the catheter has been in place and may prompt removal.
items.ww: Risk rises, rather than falls, the longer a catheter remains in place.

alt.q: The risk for catheter encrustation and CAUTI decreases after a catheter has been in place for several days because the urethra adapts to it.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Catheters in place more than a few days carry higher risk for encrustation and CAUTI.
alt.ww: The urethra does not adapt to lower risk; longer duration increases encrustation and infection risk.

items.q: A nurse prepares to provide perineal hygiene for a patient with an indwelling catheter. Which cleansing agent does the book describe as appropriate?
items.a: Mild soap and warm water, with a chlorhexidine 2% cloth as an option
items.ex: Antiseptics have not been shown to definitively decrease CAUTI, so mild soap and water is appropriate; CHG 2% cloth is optional.
w: Povidone-iodine solution applied around the meatus each shift
Antiseptic cleansers have not been shown to definitively reduce CAUTI and are not required.
Antibiotic ointment applied to the meatus after each cleansing
The book does not recommend applying antibiotic ointment during catheter care.
Sterile normal saline poured over the meatus from a sterile basin
Catheter care is a clean procedure using mild soap and warm water.

alt.q: A family caregiver asks whether a strong antiseptic must be used for daily catheter care at home to prevent infection. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Mild soap and warm water is appropriate; antiseptics have not been shown to clearly lower infection rates.”
alt.ex: There is no clear evidence that antiseptics reduce CAUTI more than nonantiseptics, so mild soap and water is appropriate.
w: “Use an alcohol-based cleanser, because soap and water cannot remove bacteria from the catheter.”
Soap and water removes residue containing microorganisms; alcohol cleansers are not recommended.
“Use povidone-iodine at each cleansing, because it is proven to prevent catheter infections.”
Antiseptic cleansers have not been shown to definitively decrease CAUTI.
“Avoid washing near the catheter, because cleansing pushes bacteria into the bladder.”
Perineal hygiene and cleaning along the catheter are part of routine catheter care.

items.q: During catheter care, clean the catheter in a circular motion starting close to the urinary meatus and moving away from the body for about [[10|ten]] cm (4 inches).
items.ex: Cleaning outward from the meatus removes residue containing microorganisms that can ascend the catheter.

alt.q: Starting at the meatus, the nurse cleans along the catheter length for about [[4|four]] inches (10 cm), moving away from the body.
alt.ex: Cleaning outward from the meatus removes residue containing microorganisms that can ascend the catheter.

items.q: Before removing a catheter securement device, the nurse reviews risk factors for medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI). Which factors increase risk? Select all that apply.
o: Older age
Patient age is among the common risk factors assessed for MARSI.
History of dehydration or malnutrition
Dehydration and malnutrition are listed MARSI risk factors.
Exposure to radiation therapy
Radiation exposure affects skin integrity and increases MARSI risk.
Diabetes mellitus or immunosuppression
Chronic conditions such as diabetes and immunosuppression are listed risk factors.
Recent fecal incontinence
Fecal incontinence increases CAUTI risk, not adhesive-related skin injury.
Dark amber urine in the drainage bag
Urine color is assessed for infection or hydration, not as a MARSI risk factor.
items.ex: Common MARSI risk factors include age, dehydration, malnutrition, radiation therapy, chronic conditions, and skin edema.

alt.q: A nurse reviews the history of a patient whose catheter securement device will be removed. Which findings place the patient at greater risk for MARSI? Select all that apply.
o: Edema of the skin
Skin edema is a listed risk factor for medical adhesive–related skin injury.
Long-term immunosuppression
Immunosuppression is an underlying chronic condition that raises MARSI risk.
Poor nutritional intake for several weeks
Malnutrition is a common risk factor for MARSI.
Use of a 16 Fr catheter with a 10-mL balloon
Catheter and balloon size determine syringe size, not MARSI risk.
Recent episodes of bowel incontinence
Bowel incontinence raises CAUTI risk, not adhesive-related skin injury.
alt.ex: Age, dehydration, malnutrition, radiation exposure, chronic conditions, and skin edema are common MARSI risk factors.

ord.q: Place these steps for removing an indwelling catheter in order.
items: Remove the catheter securement device while keeping the drainage tubing connected
Perform catheter care around the meatus and along the catheter
Let the balloon fluid drain into the syringe by gravity and confirm the full volume is removed
Pull the catheter out slowly and smoothly, and examine it to ensure it is whole
Wrap the catheter in the waterproof pad and unhook the bag and tubing from the bed
Empty, measure, and document the urine in the drainage bag
Initiate a voiding record or bladder diary
ord.ex: Catheter care precedes removal; the balloon is fully deflated before the catheter is withdrawn, and urine is measured afterward.

items.q: While removing an indwelling catheter, the nurse feels resistance as the catheter is withdrawn. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Stop pulling and repeat balloon deflation to remove any remaining fluid
items.ex: The catheter should slide out easily; resistance means fluid may remain, so repeat deflation and never use force.
w: Apply firm, steady traction until the catheter slides out
Force can traumatize the urethral wall when the balloon is partially inflated.
Cut the balloon inflation valve so the remaining fluid drains
The inflation valve must never be cut to drain the balloon.
Ask the patient to bear down while the nurse pulls the catheter
Bearing down does not deflate the balloon; remaining fluid must be removed first.

alt.q: Why does the nurse confirm that the volume of fluid in the syringe matches the balloon inflation volume before pulling out the catheter?
alt.a: A partially inflated balloon can traumatize the urethral wall during removal
alt.ex: Comparing removed fluid with the inflation volume ensures the balloon is fully deflated before withdrawal.
w: A full syringe confirms that the catheter has not become encrusted
Syringe volume reflects balloon deflation, not encrustation.
Balloon fluid must be measured and recorded as part of urine output
Balloon fluid is not urine and is not counted as output.
A full syringe shows that the drainage bag has been completely emptied
The drainage bag is emptied separately; the syringe shows balloon fluid removed.

items.q: A nurse attempts to remove an indwelling catheter, but the fluid used for balloon inflation does not return into the syringe. Which action is appropriate first?
items.a: Reposition the patient and make sure the catheter is not pinched or kinked
items.ex: The first related intervention is repositioning and checking that the catheter is not pinched or kinked.
w: Cut the balloon inflation valve to allow the fluid to drain out
Never cut the inflation valve; notify the health care provider if the balloon will not deflate.
Pull firmly on the catheter to dislodge the balloon from the bladder neck
Force with an inflated balloon traumatizes the urethra and bladder neck.
Inject 10 mL of air into the inflation valve to break up the balloon
Injecting more into the balloon is not a listed intervention and can cause injury.

alt.q: A catheter balloon still will not deflate after the nurse repositions the patient, attaches a new syringe for passive emptying, and gently pulls back on the plunger. What should the nurse do next?
alt.a: Notify the health care provider and leave the inflation valve intact
alt.ex: If the balloon does not deflate, do not cut the inflation valve; notify the health care provider.
w: Cut the inflation valve with sterile scissors so the water drains
Cutting the inflation valve is specifically prohibited.
Remove the catheter slowly while the patient takes deep breaths
An inflated balloon must not be pulled through the urethra.
Ask assistive personnel to try deflating the balloon with a larger syringe
Unresolved deflation is reported to the provider, not handed off to AP.

items.q: After removing an indwelling catheter, the nurse examines it and finds that the tip is not intact. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Notify the health care provider immediately
items.ex: A catheter that is not whole means pieces may still be in the bladder, which requires immediate provider notification.
w: Document the finding and reassess at the next scheduled catheter check
Retained catheter pieces need immediate provider notification, not routine follow-up.
Encourage fluids so the fragment passes with the first voiding
The book directs immediate notification, not waiting for the fragment to pass.
Reinsert a new catheter to retrieve the missing piece
Retrieving fragments is not a nursing intervention; notify the provider.

alt.q: Why does the nurse inspect a catheter immediately after removing it?
alt.a: To ensure it is whole, because missing pieces may remain in the bladder
alt.ex: A non-whole catheter means fragments may be in the bladder, and the provider must be notified immediately.
w: To estimate how much urine was in the bladder at the time of removal
Urine volume is measured from the drainage bag, not by inspecting the catheter.
To decide whether the same catheter can be cleaned and reinserted later
A removed catheter is wrapped in a waterproof pad and discarded, not reused.
To check the balloon size printed on the inflation valve for documentation
Balloon size is checked before removal to choose the syringe.

items.q: Seven hours after catheter removal, a patient has not voided and reports lower abdominal discomfort. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess for bladder distention
items.ex: Assessment comes first; the related interventions begin with assessing for bladder distention.
w: Reinsert an indwelling catheter to drain the bladder
Recatheterization requires an order and is not the first action before assessment.
Restrict fluids until the patient is able to void
Fluid intake is encouraged after removal unless contraindicated.
Document the finding and reassess at the end of the shift
Inability to void with abdominal pain within 6 to 8 hours must be addressed and reported, not deferred.

alt.q: A patient whose catheter was removed this morning reports straining to void and passing small amounts frequently with a feeling of not emptying. Which action is most appropriate?
alt.a: Perform a bladder scan to assess for excessive urine volume in the bladder
alt.ex: A bladder ultrasound or scan identifies excessive retained urine when a patient has signs of incomplete emptying.
w: Reassure the patient that frequent small voidings mean the bladder is emptying well
Small frequent voidings with a sense of fullness suggest incomplete emptying.
Ask the patient to limit fluids to reduce the frequency of voiding
Fluid intake should be maintained or increased after removal unless contraindicated.
Insert a new indwelling catheter without an order to relieve the symptoms
An order is required for catheterization; assessment comes first.

items.q: The nurse notifies the health care provider if a patient is unable to void within 6 to 8 hours after catheter removal and/or has abdominal pain.
items.a: True
items.ex: Failure to void within 6 to 8 hours or abdominal pain suggests retention and is reported to the provider.
items.ww: Waiting longer risks bladder overdistention; the book sets a 6- to 8-hour limit.

alt.q: After catheter removal, the nurse waits up to 24 hours for the first voiding before notifying the health care provider, because the bladder needs a full day to regain tone.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The provider is notified if the patient cannot void within 6 to 8 hours of removal or has abdominal pain.
alt.ww: A 24-hour wait is too long; inability to void within 6 to 8 hours requires notification.

items.q: When ordered, a postvoid residual (PVR) volume is measured after catheter removal. When does the book state the most reliable PVR reading is obtained?
items.a: Within 5 to 15 minutes after helping the patient void
items.ex: Measuring PVR within 5 to 15 minutes of voiding provides the most reliable reading.
w: Within 30 to 60 minutes after helping the patient void
Waiting this long allows new urine to collect, so the reading overestimates residual.
Within 2 to 4 hours after the catheter is removed, before any voiding
PVR measures urine left after voiding, so the patient must void first.
Within 1 to 2 minutes before the patient attempts to void
A measurement before voiding is a bladder volume, not a postvoid residual.

alt.q: A patient voids 250 mL after catheter removal, and a PVR has been ordered. When should the nurse perform the bladder scan?
alt.a: Within 5 to 15 minutes after the patient voids
alt.ex: The most reliable PVR reading is obtained 5 to 15 minutes after voiding.
w: At least 1 hour after the patient voids
An hour allows urine to reaccumulate, making the residual inaccurate.
Within 6 to 8 hours after the patient voids
This is the window for the first voiding after removal, not the timing of a PVR.
Just before the patient’s next expected voiding
PVR is measured shortly after voiding to show the urine left behind.

items.q: A urinary drainage bag should be emptied when it is one-half full.
items.a: True
items.ex: An overfull bag pulls on the catheter, causing urethral or meatal trauma, and impedes urine flow.

alt.q: A urinary drainage bag can safely be left until it is completely full, because emptying it often opens the closed system to infection.
alt.a: False

alt.ww: An overfull bag pulls on the catheter and traumatizes the urethra and meatus.

items.q: During routine checks of a patient’s indwelling catheter drainage system, which findings show the system is set up correctly? Select all that apply.
o: The catheter is secured to the upper thigh
Securing the catheter to the upper thigh maintains unobstructed urine flow.
The tubing has no loops or kinks and is not clamped
Unobstructed tubing assists in preventing CAUTI.
The drainage bag hangs below the level of the bladder
A bag below the bladder lets urine flow freely and helps prevent CAUTI.
The drainage bag is about two-thirds full
The bag should be emptied at one-half full to prevent tension on the catheter.
The drainage bag rests on the bed beside the patient’s hip
A bag at bladder level impedes drainage; it must hang below the bladder.
items.ex: Correct setup includes a secured catheter, straight unclamped tubing, a bag below the bladder, and a bag less than half full.

alt.q: A nurse finds several problems with a patient’s catheter drainage system. Which findings need correction? Select all that apply.
o: The tubing has a dependent loop hanging below the bag inlet
Tubing should lie without loops or kinks to keep urine flowing.
The drainage bag is hooked to the raised side rail above the bladder
The bag must stay below bladder level to prevent backflow and CAUTI.
The drainage bag is more than half full
An overfull bag pulls on the catheter and should be emptied at one-half full.
The securement device holds the catheter with some slack
Slack is intended so movement does not create tension on the catheter.
Urine is flowing freely into the bag
Free flow of urine into the bag is the expected finding.
alt.ex: Loops, a bag above the bladder, and an overfull bag all obstruct flow or raise CAUTI and trauma risk.

items.q: A nurse removes a patient’s indwelling catheter and provides discharge teaching. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “Some mild burning the first time I urinate is common and should soon go away.”
items.ex: Mild burning, discomfort, or small-volume first voiding results from urethral irritation and soon subsides.
w: “I should drink less fluid today so my bladder is not overloaded.”
Patients are encouraged to maintain or increase fluid intake unless contraindicated.
“Burning that continues with fever and back pain is normal for a few days.”
Fever, back pain, and persistent burning may indicate UTI and should be reported.
“I do not need to save or measure my urine after the catheter is out.”
All urine is measured and recorded on a voiding record or bladder diary.

alt.q: After catheter removal, a patient asks why it burns slightly to urinate. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Mild burning is common with the first voiding from urethral irritation and usually soon subsides.”
alt.ex: The nurse explains that mild burning with the first voiding results from urethral irritation and soon subsides.
w: “Burning always means a bladder infection, so I will get an antibiotic order.”
Mild burning with the first voiding is expected and not by itself a sign of infection.
“Burning means the catheter tore your urethra, so I will notify the surgeon now.”
Mild burning reflects urethral irritation, not tissue tearing.
“Burning means your bladder is not emptying, so I will reinsert the catheter.”

items.q: Before removing the catheter, the nurse moves the syringe plunger up and down, pulls it back to 0.5 mL, and lets balloon fluid drain into the syringe by gravity. What is the purpose of passive drainage?

A partially inflated balloon traumatizes the urethra; full deflation is the goal.
It prevents air from entering the bladder during catheter removal
The balloon port does not open into the bladder; the concern is balloon ridges.

alt.q: What problem does the nurse avoid by allowing the catheter balloon to empty passively rather than by forcefully aspirating it?
alt.a: Formation of balloon ridges that cause discomfort or trauma during removal
alt.ex: Forceful aspiration can create ridges in the balloon; passive drainage prevents them.
w: Backflow of urine from the drainage bag into the bladder
Backflow is prevented by keeping the bag below the bladder.
Loss of the balloon fluid needed to culture for infection
Balloon fluid is not cultured; it is removed to deflate the balloon.
Kinking of the drainage tubing below the catheter junction
Tubing position is checked separately; passive drainage concerns the balloon.

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient receiving continuous bladder irrigation (CBI). Which task can the nurse delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?

Hanging a new bag of sterile irrigation solution and priming the tubing
Setting up irrigation is part of the skill, which cannot be delegated.
Instilling irrigant through the catheter port with a sterile syringe
Closed intermittent irrigation cannot be delegated to AP.

alt.q: Which statement about delegating closed catheter irrigation is accurate?

w: The skill can be delegated after the nurse sets up the irrigation equipment

items.q: A nurse directs assistive personnel caring for a patient receiving closed catheter irrigation. Which findings should the AP be told to report? Select all that apply.

Drainage that is lightly pink and free flowing

Output in the bag that is greater than irrigant infused
More output than irrigant is expected because of urine production.
items.ex: AP report pain, leakage, decreased urine output, and changes in urine color or blood clots.

alt.q: An AP caring for a patient on continuous bladder irrigation asks which observations need to be reported to the nurse. Which should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

items.q: Before starting closed catheter irrigation, which assessments does the nurse perform? Select all that apply.

Stopping flow allows clots to form and block the catheter.

A slower rate permits clotting; the book directs increasing the rate.

Opening the closed system is not the intervention described for clots.

Remove the syringe and clamp so the solution drains into the bag
ord.ex: The irrigant is prepared, the tubing clamped, and the port cleansed before slow instillation and release for drainage.

items.q: During closed intermittent catheter irrigation, why does the nurse clamp the catheter tubing below the soft injection port before instilling the solution?
items.a: It allows the irrigating solution to enter the catheter and flow into the bladder
items.ex: Occluding the tubing below the injection point directs the irrigant up into the bladder instead of the bag.
w: It prevents urine from leaking around the catheter at the meatus
Clamping directs irrigant into the bladder; it does not address leakage.
It keeps the irrigating solution from cooling before it reaches the bladder
Solution temperature is not affected by the clamp.
It holds the catheter in place so the balloon does not slip
The securement device, not the clamp, anchors the catheter.

alt.q: Why does the nurse instill intermittent irrigation solution using slow, even pressure?
alt.a: It minimizes trauma to the bladder mucosa
alt.ex: Gentle instillation of the solution minimizes trauma to the bladder mucosa.
w: It prevents the syringe from separating from the port
A twisting motion secures the syringe tip in the lumen.
It allows medication to be absorbed before draining
Absorption depends on dwell time with the catheter clamped, not injection speed.
It keeps air from entering the drainage bag
Air prevention relates to priming continuous irrigation tubing.

items.q: Some medicated irrigants must dwell in the bladder for a prescribed period, so the catheter is clamped temporarily before being allowed to drain.
items.a: True
items.ex: Medications must stay long enough to be absorbed by the bladder lining, but a clamped system must not be left unattended.
items.ww: The book specifically notes that certain medicated irrigants require temporary clamping for a dwell time.

alt.q: Once a medicated irrigant is instilled, the drainage tubing can be left clamped unattended until the next scheduled irrigation.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A clamped drainage tubing and bag should not be left unattended.
alt.ww: Clamping is temporary for the prescribed dwell period; leaving it unattended risks bladder distention.

items.q: During closed intermittent irrigation, the irrigating solution does not return into the drainage bag. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Examine the drainage tubing for clots, sediment, and kinks
Clots, sediment, or kinks commonly block return of irrigant.
Evaluate the patient for pain and bladder distention
Retained irrigant can distend the bladder and cause pain.
Inspect the urine for presence of or increase in clots and sediment
Increasing clots or sediment may explain obstruction.
Notify the health care provider
Irrigant that does not flow freely from the bladder is reported to the provider.
Instill another 50 mL of irrigant with firm pressure
Adding fluid to an obstructed bladder worsens distention and trauma.
Leave the tubing clamped and recheck at the end of the shift
A clamped system must not be left unattended.
items.ex: When irrigant does not return, check tubing and urine for clots or kinks, evaluate pain and distention, and notify the provider.

alt.q: A patient reports pain during catheter irrigation. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Examine the drainage tubing for clots, sediment, or kinks
Obstruction is a common cause of pain during irrigation.
Evaluate the patient for bladder distention
Pain may reflect overdistention when irrigant cannot drain.
Notify the health care provider
Pain with irrigation is reported to the health care provider.
Speed up instillation to finish the procedure quickly
Rapid instillation can traumatize the bladder mucosa and worsen pain.
Remove the catheter to relieve the discomfort
Removal requires an order and is not a listed intervention for pain.
alt.ex: Pain with irrigation calls for checking for clots or kinks, evaluating distention, and notifying the provider.

items.q: A patient receiving continuous bladder irrigation reports a strong sensation of bladder fullness and lower abdominal spasms. The drainage bag has had little new output in the past hour. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Examine the drainage tubing for clots, sediment, or kinks
items.ex: Pain with reduced outflow suggests obstruction; first check the tubing for clots or kinks, and if outflow stays blocked, stop the inflow and notify the provider.
w: Increase the irrigation rate to flush out the clots
Adding more irrigant to a blocked system increases distention and injury.
Administer a prescribed analgesic and reassess in 1 hour
Treating pain without finding the cause misses a possible obstruction.
Teach the patient that spasms are expected with irrigation
Pain with poor outflow is an unexpected outcome that needs assessment.

alt.q: A patient on continuous bladder irrigation has a distended bladder and the irrigant is not flowing at the prescribed rate. After checking the tubing for kinks and clots, which action is required?
alt.a: Notify the health care provider
alt.ex: The provider is notified when irrigant does not flow freely, the patient has pain, or bladder distention occurs.
w: Increase the infusion until the bag begins to fill
More inflow worsens distention when outflow is blocked.
Clamp the drainage tubing to measure the retained volume
Clamping the outflow increases distention and is unsafe.
Remove the catheter and apply a new one without an order
Catheter changes require an order and are not the listed intervention.

items.q: Why might a drainage bag for a patient on continuous bladder irrigation need to be emptied every 1 to 2 hours?
items.a: Continuous irrigant inflow fills the bag rapidly
items.ex: Irrigant plus urine fills the bag quickly; emptying keeps outflow unobstructed and prevents bladder overdistention.
w: Irrigant left in the bag for 3 hours becomes contaminated
The reason is rapid filling, not a time limit for contamination.
A sample must be sent from the bag every 1 to 2 hours
Routine hourly specimens are not part of this skill.
The weight of 1 to 2 hours of urine pulls the catheter out
Rapid filling from irrigant is the stated reason for frequent emptying.

alt.q: What can happen if continuous bladder irrigant cannot adequately flow out of the bladder?
alt.a: Discomfort, bladder distention, and possible injury from overdistention
alt.ex: When irrigant cannot drain, the bladder overdistends, causing discomfort and possible injury.
w: Dehydration from loss of fluid through the drainage bag
Blocked outflow retains fluid; it does not cause fluid loss.
Hypothermia from cooling of the retained irrigating solution
Irrigant is at room temperature; the risk is overdistention.
Hematuria from the irrigant diluting the patient’s urine
Dilution does not cause bleeding; the risk is distention and injury.

items.q: Which statement best describes the role of the mouth in digestion?
items.a: It breaks nutrients down mechanically and chemically into a usable size and form
items.ex: The mouth both mechanically and chemically breaks down nutrients so they reach a usable size and form.
w: It absorbs most nutrients and electrolytes before food is swallowed
Most nutrients and electrolytes are absorbed in the duodenum and jejunum, not the mouth.
It secretes intrinsic factor so that vitamin B12 can be absorbed
Intrinsic factor is secreted by the stomach, not the mouth.
It propels the food bolus toward the stomach by mass movements
Peristalsis moves the bolus down the esophagus; mass movements occur in the colon.

alt.q: A student says, “The mouth only prepares food mechanically by chewing.” Which correction is accurate?
alt.a: The mouth also begins the chemical breakdown of nutrients
alt.ex: The mouth breaks down nutrients both mechanically (teeth) and chemically, not by chewing alone.
w: The mouth also absorbs water, alcohol, and some fatty acids
Limited absorption of water, alcohol, and some fatty acids is a stomach function.
The mouth also produces gastrin to regulate digestion
Gastrin is a hormone produced by the stomach.
The mouth also destroys pathogenic bacteria with acid
Destroying swallowed pathogenic bacteria is a protective function of the stomach.

items.q: What is the main purpose of chewing food?
items.a: Breaking food into a size suitable for swallowing
items.ex: The teeth chew food, breaking it down into pieces small enough to swallow.
w: Mixing food with gastric juices to form small particles
Churning food and mixing it with gastric juices is done by the stomach.
Preventing air from entering the esophagus during meals
The upper esophageal sphincter prevents air from entering the esophagus.
Absorbing water and some fatty acids from the food
The stomach, not the mouth, absorbs limited water and some fatty acids.

alt.q: Which structure breaks food down into a size suitable for swallowing?
alt.a: The teeth
alt.ex: Chewing by the teeth reduces food to a size that can be swallowed.
w: The salivary glands
The salivary glands produce saliva, which dilutes and softens food rather than cutting it up.
The upper esophageal sphincter
This circular muscle keeps air out of the esophagus and prevents reflux into the throat.
The lower esophageal sphincter
This sphincter prevents stomach contents from refluxing into the esophagus.

items.q: Which function does saliva serve in digestion?
items.a: It dilutes and softens food for easier swallowing
items.ex: Saliva from the salivary glands dilutes and softens food in the mouth so it is easier to swallow.
w: It destroys pathogenic bacteria swallowed with food
Destroying swallowed bacteria is a protective function of the stomach.
It stimulates the appetite by releasing ghrelin
Ghrelin is a stomach hormone that increases appetite.
It carries bile salts to the ileum for absorption
Bile comes from the liver, and the ileum absorbs bile salts; saliva has no such role.

alt.q: A patient with a very dry mouth says food is hard to swallow. The nurse explains that saliva normally helps by doing what?
alt.a: Diluting and softening food in the mouth
alt.ex: Saliva dilutes and softens food, so a dry mouth makes swallowing harder.
w: Neutralizing stomach acid before it reaches the throat
Preventing reflux of stomach contents is the job of the esophageal sphincters.
Churning food into small particles
Churning food into small particles is a stomach function.
Propelling food down by peristalsis
Peristalsis, a muscular contraction, propels the bolus down the esophagus.

items.q: An 80-year-old patient reports eating less because “my dentures hurt when I chew.” Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Inspect the patient’s teeth, gums, and the fit of the dentures
items.ex: Assessment comes first; poor dentition or poorly fitting dentures affect the ability to chew.
w: Advise the patient to swallow food in larger bites
Partially chewed food is not digested as easily, so larger bites would worsen digestion.
Tell the patient to remove the dentures for all meals
This skips assessment and would further reduce chewing ability.
Recommend a low-fiber diet to make chewing easier
Reducing fiber promotes constipation and does not address the cause found on assessment.

alt.q: An older adult with loose dentures has been swallowing food in large pieces. Which explanation should the nurse give about why this matters?
alt.a: Partially chewed food is not digested as easily
alt.ex: Decreased chewing ability is common in older adults, and partially chewed food is harder to digest.
w: Large pieces of food are absorbed faster in the stomach
The stomach absorbs only limited substances; larger pieces are not absorbed faster.
Saliva fully digests food that is not chewed well
Saliva only dilutes and softens food; it cannot make up for poor chewing.
Unchewed food speeds esophageal emptying in older adults
Esophageal emptying actually slows with age; unchewed food does not speed it.

items.q: Why does the nurse inspect the mouth when assessing a patient with an elimination problem?
items.a: Poor dentition, ill-fitting dentures, and sores affect chewing and eating
items.ex: Problems with teeth, dentures, or mouth sores interfere with chewing and make eating difficult and painful.
w: Mouth sores are the most common cause of acute diarrhea
The book links mouth sores to difficult, painful eating, not to diarrhea.
The color of the tongue shows whether stools are formed
Stool consistency is assessed by inspecting feces, not the tongue.
Saliva samples are used to screen for occult blood
Occult blood testing uses fecal specimens, not saliva.

alt.q: A patient has several painful sores on the tongue and gums. Which effect on intake does the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: Eating becomes difficult and painful
alt.ex: Sores in the mouth make eating not only difficult but also painful, which can reduce intake.
w: Saliva production stops completely
Mouth sores make eating painful; the book does not say they stop saliva production.
Food is chewed more thoroughly
Painful sores make chewing and eating harder, not more thorough.
Stomach absorption of nutrients increases
Mouth sores do not increase absorption in the stomach.

items.q: A patient with an NG tube for gastric decompression says the mouth feels very dry. Which intervention is best?
items.a: Provide frequent mouth care and offer water-moistened swabs
items.ex: Frequent mouth care and water-moistened swabs or lozenges relieve mouth dryness caused by mouth breathing.
w: Clamp the tube so the patient can drink large amounts
Clamping a decompression tube stops drainage and does not address the cause of dryness.
Remove the tube and reinsert it in the other naris
Dryness comes from mouth breathing, not from which naris is used.
Limit oral care to once daily to prevent gagging
Frequent, not limited, mouth care is recommended to minimize discomfort.

alt.q: Why does a patient with an NG tube often develop a dry mouth?
alt.a: One nostril is occluded, so the patient breathes through the mouth
alt.ex: With one nostril occluded by the tube, the patient mouth-breathes, which dries the mouth.
w: The tube suctions saliva directly out of the mouth
The tube drains stomach secretions, not saliva from the mouth.
Lidocaine jelly used at insertion stops saliva production
Lidocaine reduces insertion discomfort; it is not the cause of ongoing dryness.
Gastric acid travels up the tube and irritates the mouth
The tube drains gastric contents away; mouth breathing causes the dryness.

items.q: Which group lists accessory organs of the GI tract that are found in the mouth?
items.a: Teeth, tongue, and salivary glands
items.ex: The accessory organs include the teeth, tongue, and salivary glands, as well as the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder.
w: Esophagus, stomach, and duodenum
These are parts of the alimentary canal itself, not accessory organs.
Cecum, appendix, and rectum
These are parts of the large intestine, not accessory organs of the mouth.
Pharynx, sphincters, and esophagus
These form part of the passage for food, not the accessory organs listed in the book.

alt.q: The alimentary canal is a single tube that begins at which structure?
alt.a: The mouth
alt.ex: The alimentary canal extends from the mouth to the anus.
w: The esophagus
The esophagus is part of the canal but comes after the mouth.
The stomach
The stomach lies partway along the canal, below the diaphragm.
The duodenum
The duodenum is the first section of the small intestine, well past the start of the canal.

items.q: Which age-related change involving the mouth can impair digestion in older adults?
items.a: Decreased chewing ability
items.ex: Older adults may have decreased chewing ability, and partially chewed food is not digested as easily.
w: Increased secretion of gastric acids
Increased gastric acid secretion is described in adolescents.
More rapid intestinal peristalsis
Rapid intestinal peristalsis is a characteristic of infants.
Smaller stomach capacity
Smaller stomach capacity is a characteristic of infants.

alt.q: Which consequence of decreased chewing ability in older adults does the book describe?
alt.a: Partially chewed food is not digested as easily
alt.ex: Poorly chewed food is harder to digest, which matters because peristalsis and absorption also decline with age.
w: Unchewed food speeds peristalsis and causes diarrhea
Peristalsis declines in older adults; the book does not link poor chewing to diarrhea.
Large food pieces are absorbed directly in the esophagus
The esophagus transports food by peristalsis; it does not absorb nutrients.
Unchewed food bypasses the stomach and enters the colon
All swallowed food passes through the stomach and small intestine first.

items.q: A patient with a new ileostomy asks whether popcorn is allowed. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Eat small amounts, chew it well, and drink fluids with it.”
items.ex: Eating high-fiber foods in small amounts, chewing well, and drinking fluids makes a food blockage unlikely.
w: “Avoid it for life because it always blocks the stoma.”
Food blockage is infrequent and unlikely when the food is eaten carefully.
“Swallow it quickly with little chewing to limit gas.”
Thorough chewing, not quick swallowing, helps prevent a food blockage.
“Eat as much as you like; an ileostomy has no diet concerns.”
Foods with indigestible fiber, like popcorn, can cause a food blockage.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient with an ileostomy shows understanding of how to prevent a food blockage?
alt.a: “I’ll chew fresh pineapple well and eat small amounts with fluids.”
alt.ex: Chewing well, eating small amounts, and drinking fluids with fibrous foods help prevent a food blockage.
w: “I’ll eat large servings of corn to bulk up my stool.”
Sweet corn has indigestible fiber; large servings raise the risk of blockage.
“I’ll avoid drinking fluids with high-fiber meals.”
Drinking fluids with fibrous foods helps prevent blockage and replaces lost fluid.
“I’ll swallow raw mushrooms whole so they pass quickly.”
Raw mushrooms can cause a blockage; they need to be chewed well.

items.q: A patient with an NG tube reports a persistent sore throat. Which measure might the health care provider order to relieve it?
items.a: Gargles with topical Xylocaine jelly
items.ex: Sore throat is common with an NG tube, and gargles with topical Xylocaine jelly may be ordered to minimize irritation.
w: Clamping the air vent of the sump tube
The air vent of a Salem sump tube must never be clamped.
Increasing suction to high continuous
Low intermittent suction is used because it decreases gastric irritation.
Removing the tube’s fixation device
The fixation device prevents tube migration and is changed, not removed, as needed.

alt.q: Which comfort measure relieves mouth and throat dryness in a patient with an NG tube?
alt.a: Lozenges or water-moistened swabs to suck on
alt.ex: Water-moistened swabs or lozenges may relieve mouth and throat dryness caused by mouth breathing.
w: Limiting mouth care to prevent gagging
Frequent mouth care is recommended to minimize discomfort from a dry mouth.
Lowering the head of the bed flat
The head of the bed is kept elevated to reduce aspiration risk; it does not relieve dryness.
Clamping the tube between suction periods
Clamping does not affect mouth dryness, which comes from mouth breathing.

items.q: Intestinal gas normally escapes from the body by which routes?
items.a: Through the mouth by belching and through the anus as flatus
items.ex: Normally intestinal gas escapes through the mouth (belching) or the anus (passing flatus).
w: Through the lungs by exhalation and through the skin
Intestinal gas leaves through the mouth or anus, not the lungs or skin.
Through the bloodstream and then out in the urine
The book describes gas escaping by belching or passing flatus, not in urine.
Through the stomach wall and the abdominal cavity
Gas trapped in the bowel distends it; it does not pass through the wall.

alt.q: Belching is the escape of intestinal gas through which structure?
alt.a: The mouth
alt.ex: Belching is intestinal gas escaping through the mouth; flatus is gas passed through the anus.
w: The anus
Gas escaping through the anus is passing flatus, not belching.
The nose
The book names the mouth, not the nose, as the route for belching.
The stoma
A stoma is a surgical opening for fecal diversion, not the route for belching.

items.q: A parent reports that a 10-month-old infant has had diarrhea all day. Which finding when the nurse inspects the mouth suggests dehydration?
items.a: Dry mouth and tongue
items.ex: Dry mouth and tongue is a sign of dehydration in infants and young children.
w: Moist pink gums
Moist mucous membranes suggest adequate hydration.
Excessive drooling
Drooling indicates saliva production, not dehydration.
Swollen gums from teething
Teething causes gum swelling but is not a sign of dehydration.

alt.q: Which finding is most important for the nurse to report in an infant with diarrhea?
alt.a: Dry mouth and no tears when crying
alt.ex: Dry mouth and tongue and no tears when crying are signs of dehydration, which infants are especially susceptible to.
w: Yellow stools in a breastfed infant
Yellow is the normal stool color for an infant.
A wet diaper every 2 to 3 hours
Regular wet diapers suggest adequate hydration; no wet diapers for 3 hours is the concern.
Drooling and chewing on toys
These are common infant behaviors, not signs of dehydration.

items.q: Which findings affect a patient’s ability to chew and eat? Select all that apply.
o: Poor dentition
Poor dentition influences the ability to chew.
Poorly fitting dentures
Ill-fitting dentures make chewing difficult.
Sores in the mouth
Mouth sores make eating difficult and painful.
Normal saliva production
Saliva helps by softening food; normal production does not impair eating.
Regular daily food intake
Regular intake helps maintain peristalsis; it does not impair chewing.
items.ex: Teeth, dentures, and the condition of the mouth all influence chewing and eating.

alt.q: When assessing the mouth of a patient with an elimination problem, which findings should the nurse note? Select all that apply.
o: Condition of the teeth
Poor dentition affects chewing.
Fit of the dentures
Poorly fitting dentures affect chewing.
Sores on the tongue or gums
Sores make eating difficult and painful.
Contour and symmetry of the abdomen
Abdominal contour is part of the abdominal assessment, not the mouth.
Presence of hemorrhoids
Hemorrhoids are noted when inspecting the rectal area.
alt.ex: The nurse inspects the teeth, tongue, and gums because they influence chewing and eating.

items.q: Which statements about the mouth and saliva are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The salivary glands produce saliva
Saliva is produced by the salivary glands in the mouth.
Saliva dilutes and softens food
This makes food easier to swallow.
The mouth breaks down nutrients mechanically and chemically
Both types of breakdown begin in the mouth.
Saliva secretes intrinsic factor for vitamin B12
Intrinsic factor comes from the stomach.
The mouth is an accessory organ, not part of the alimentary canal
The alimentary canal begins at the mouth; the teeth, tongue, and salivary glands are accessory organs.
items.ex: The mouth starts mechanical and chemical breakdown, and saliva dilutes and softens food for swallowing.

alt.q: Which structures are accessory organs of the GI tract? Select all that apply.
o: Teeth
The teeth are listed as accessory organs.
Tongue
The tongue is listed as an accessory organ.
Salivary glands
The salivary glands are accessory organs that produce saliva.
Liver
The liver is an accessory organ that supplies bile.
Esophagus
The esophagus is part of the alimentary canal.
Stomach
The stomach is part of the alimentary canal.
alt.ex: Accessory organs are the teeth, tongue, salivary glands, liver, pancreas, and gallbladder; the esophagus and stomach form the canal.

items.q: A patient has an NG tube connected to suction. Which measures help keep the mouth, nose, and throat comfortable? Select all that apply.
o: Frequent mouth care
Frequent mouth care minimizes discomfort from a dry mouth.
Water-moistened swabs or lozenges
These may relieve mouth and throat dryness.
Frequent lubrication of the nares
Lubrication may minimize nasal discomfort from the tube.
Clamping the blue air vent
The air vent of a Salem sump tube must never be clamped.
Leaving soiled tape in place to avoid moving the tube
Soiled or loose tape is changed as needed to reduce pressure and prevent migration.
items.ex: Frequent mouth care, moist swabs or lozenges, and lubricating the nares relieve the discomfort an NG tube causes.

alt.q: Which problems should the nurse anticipate in a patient who has an NG tube? Select all that apply.
o: Dry mouth from mouth breathing
With one nostril occluded, the patient breathes through the mouth.
Sore throat
Patients often complain of a sore throat.
Irritation or pressure injury of the nasal mucosa
The tube irritates the mucosa and pressure can cause a device-related injury.
Improved sense of taste
Nothing in the book suggests an NG tube improves taste.
Increased appetite from ghrelin release
Ghrelin is a normal stomach hormone; the tube does not increase its release.
alt.ex: An NG tube commonly causes a dry mouth, sore throat, and irritation of the nasal mucosa.

items.q: The teeth break food down into a size suitable for swallowing.
items.a: True
items.ex: Chewing by the teeth reduces food to pieces that can be swallowed.
items.ww: Breaking food into a swallowable size is the job of the teeth.

alt.q: The main role of saliva is to cut food into pieces small enough to swallow.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Saliva dilutes and softens food; the teeth break it into a swallowable size.
alt.ww: Saliva softens food but cannot cut it; chewing by the teeth does that.

items.q: Partially chewed food is digested just as easily as well-chewed food.
items.a: False
items.ex: Partially chewed food is not digested as easily, a concern for older adults with decreased chewing ability.
items.ww: Chewing prepares food for digestion, so poorly chewed food is harder to digest.

alt.q: Decreased chewing ability in older adults can make food harder to digest.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Older adults may chew less effectively, and partially chewed food is not digested as easily.
alt.ww: Chewing matters to digestion, so reduced chewing ability does affect it.

items.q: The salivary glands are accessory organs of the GI tract.
items.a: True
items.ex: The teeth, tongue, and salivary glands are accessory organs, along with the liver, pancreas, and gallbladder.
items.ww: They are not part of the alimentary canal itself but are accessory organs.

alt.q: The mouth is an accessory organ rather than part of the alimentary canal.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The alimentary canal extends from the mouth to the anus, so the mouth is part of the canal.
alt.ww: The book places the mouth in the alimentary canal; its teeth, tongue, and salivary glands are accessory organs.

items.q: Saliva, produced by the [[salivary glands|salivary gland]], dilutes and softens food for easier swallowing.
items.ex: The salivary glands in the mouth produce saliva, which dilutes and softens food.

alt.q: The [[salivary glands|salivary gland]] secrete the fluid that softens food in the mouth.
alt.ex: The salivary glands in the mouth produce saliva, which dilutes and softens food.

items.q: What is the role of the Teeth?
items.a: Break food into a size suitable for swallowing
items.ex: Each structure from the mouth to the stomach has a distinct job in preparing and moving food.
w: Dilutes and softens food
That goes with Saliva.
Keeps air out of the esophagus
That goes with Upper esophageal sphincter.
Prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus
That goes with Lower esophageal sphincter.

alt.q: What is the role of the Saliva?

alt.ex: Each structure from the mouth to the stomach has a distinct job in preparing and moving food.
w: Break food into a size suitable for swallowing
That goes with Teeth.
Keeps air out of the esophagus
That goes with Upper esophageal sphincter.
Prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus
That goes with Lower esophageal sphincter.

alt.q: What is the role of the Upper esophageal sphincter?

w: Break food into a size suitable for swallowing
That goes with Teeth.
Dilutes and softens food
That goes with Saliva.
Prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus
That goes with Lower esophageal sphincter.

alt.q: What is the role of the Lower esophageal sphincter?
alt.a: Prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus
alt.ex: Each structure from the mouth to the stomach has a distinct job in preparing and moving food.
w: Break food into a size suitable for swallowing
That goes with Teeth.
Dilutes and softens food
That goes with Saliva.
Keeps air out of the esophagus
That goes with Upper esophageal sphincter.

alt.q: What is the role of the Stomach?
alt.a: Churns food and mixes it with gastric juices
alt.ex: Each structure from the mouth to the stomach has a distinct job in preparing and moving food.
w: Break food into a size suitable for swallowing
That goes with Teeth.
Dilutes and softens food
That goes with Saliva.
Keeps air out of the esophagus
That goes with Upper esophageal sphincter.

alt.q: Which structure or substance “Break food into a size suitable for swallowing”?
alt.a: Teeth
alt.ex: Each structure from the mouth to the stomach has a distinct job in preparing and moving food.
w: Saliva
Saliva: Dilutes and softens food.
Upper esophageal sphincter

alt.q: Which structure or substance “Dilutes and softens food”?
alt.a: Saliva
alt.ex: Each structure from the mouth to the stomach has a distinct job in preparing and moving food.
w: Teeth
Teeth: Break food into a size suitable for swallowing.
Upper esophageal sphincter
Upper esophageal sphincter: Keeps air out of the esophagus.
Lower esophageal sphincter
Lower esophageal sphincter: Prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus.

alt.q: Which structure or substance “Keeps air out of the esophagus”?
alt.a: Upper esophageal sphincter
alt.ex: Each structure from the mouth to the stomach has a distinct job in preparing and moving food.
w: Teeth
Teeth: Break food into a size suitable for swallowing.
Saliva
Saliva: Dilutes and softens food.
Lower esophageal sphincter
Lower esophageal sphincter: Prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus.

alt.q: Which structure or substance “Prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus”?
alt.a: Lower esophageal sphincter
alt.ex: Each structure from the mouth to the stomach has a distinct job in preparing and moving food.
w: Teeth
Teeth: Break food into a size suitable for swallowing.
Saliva
Saliva: Dilutes and softens food.
Upper esophageal sphincter
Upper esophageal sphincter: Keeps air out of the esophagus.

alt.q: Which structure or substance “Churns food and mixes it with gastric juices”?
alt.a: Stomach
alt.ex: Each structure from the mouth to the stomach has a distinct job in preparing and moving food.
w: Teeth
Teeth: Break food into a size suitable for swallowing.
Saliva
Saliva: Dilutes and softens food.
Upper esophageal sphincter
Upper esophageal sphincter: Keeps air out of the esophagus.

mt.q: Match each upper GI structure or substance with its role.
pairs: Break food into a size suitable for swallowing
Keeps air out of the esophagus
Prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus
Churns food and mixes it with gastric juices
mt.ex: Each structure from the mouth to the stomach has a distinct job in preparing and moving food.

items.q: Which description of the esophagus is accurate?
items.a: A collapsible, muscular tube lined with mucosa
items.ex: The esophagus is a collapsible, muscular, mucosa-lined tube that carries food toward the stomach.
w: A rigid tube held open by rings of cartilage
The esophagus is collapsible, not rigid.
A pouchlike organ located just below the diaphragm
This describes the stomach.
A 6- to 8-meter tube where most nutrients are absorbed
This describes the small intestine.

alt.q: A collapsible, muscular, mucosa-lined tube that carries food from the throat to the stomach is which structure?
alt.a: The esophagus
alt.ex: The esophagus is the collapsible, muscular tube between the throat and the stomach.
w: The duodenum
The duodenum is the first section of the small intestine, after the stomach.
The ileum
The ileum is the last section of the small intestine.
The colon
The colon is the large intestine, far below the stomach.

items.q: What is the function of the upper esophageal sphincter?
items.a: Keeping air out of the esophagus and esophageal contents out of the throat
items.ex: This circular muscle prevents air from entering the esophagus and esophageal contents from refluxing into the throat.
w: Keeping stomach contents from refluxing back into the esophagus
That is the function of the lower esophageal sphincter.
Keeping colon contents from returning to the small intestine
That is the function of the ileocecal valve.
Pushing the bolus down the esophagus with wavelike contractions
Peristalsis, not the sphincter, propels the bolus.

alt.q: Which structure prevents air from entering the esophagus?
alt.a: The upper esophageal sphincter
alt.ex: The upper esophageal sphincter, a circular muscle, keeps air out of the esophagus.
w: The lower esophageal sphincter
The lower sphincter prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus.
The ileocecal valve
The ileocecal valve prevents regurgitation from the colon into the small intestine.
The internal anal sphincter
The internal anal sphincter helps control defecation.

items.q: Where is the lower esophageal sphincter located?
items.a: Between the esophagus and the upper end of the stomach
items.ex: The lower esophageal sphincter lies between the esophagus and the top of the stomach.
w: Between the throat and the top of the esophagus
This is the location of the upper esophageal sphincter.
Between the ileum and the beginning of the colon
This is the location of the ileocecal valve.
Between the rectum and the outside of the body
The anal sphincters control the outlet at the anus.

alt.q: A patient asks what normally keeps stomach contents from flowing back into the esophagus. Which structure does the nurse name?
alt.a: The lower esophageal sphincter
alt.ex: The lower esophageal sphincter prevents reflux of stomach contents back into the esophagus.
w: The upper esophageal sphincter
The upper sphincter prevents esophageal contents from refluxing into the throat.
The ileocecal valve
The ileocecal valve prevents regurgitation back into the small intestine.
The external anal sphincter
The external anal sphincter helps control defecation.

items.q: How does a bolus of food move down the esophagus?
items.a: By peristalsis, contractions that propel food along the GI tract
items.ex: Peristalsis is the contraction that propels food through the length of the GI tract, including the esophagus.
w: By gravity alone, without any muscle contraction
The esophagus is muscular, and peristalsis moves the bolus.
By mass movements that occur 3 or 4 times daily
Mass movements push contents through the colon.
By suction created as the stomach churns its contents
Churning mixes food in the stomach; it does not pull food down.

alt.q: Which term describes the contraction that propels food through the length of the GI tract?
alt.a: Peristalsis
alt.ex: Peristalsis is the wavelike contraction that propels food from the esophagus onward.
w: Chyme
Chyme is the liquid material that enters the small intestine.
Reflux
Reflux is backward flow, which the sphincters prevent.
Ileus
An ileus is a temporary stop in peristalsis.

items.q: A newly inserted NG tube must be used to give a medication. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Confirm tube placement by x-ray before giving anything
items.ex: X-ray is the gold standard and must confirm initial placement before any medication or liquid is given.
w: Give the medication if the patient is not coughing
Absence of coughing does not confirm that the tip is in the stomach.
Mark the tube at the naris and give the medication
Marking the tube is done after placement is confirmed.
Irrigate the tube with saline and then give the drug
Instilling fluid before placement is confirmed risks entry into the lungs.

alt.q: Why must the tip of an NG tube reach the stomach rather than end in the esophagus?
alt.a: A tip in the esophagus raises the risk for pulmonary aspiration
alt.ex: Tubes that terminate in the esophagus place the patient at risk for pulmonary aspiration.
w: A tip in the esophagus makes the stomach secrete more acid
Tip position in the esophagus is dangerous because of aspiration, not acid secretion.
A tip in the esophagus blocks intrinsic factor secretion
Intrinsic factor secretion is unaffected by tube position.
A tip in the esophagus prevents the patient from swallowing
The danger the book stresses is pulmonary aspiration.

items.q: While awaiting x-ray confirmation, the nurse aspirates clear, saliva-like fluid from a newly inserted NG tube. What does this finding suggest?
items.a: The tube tip may be in the esophagus
items.ex: Saliva-like aspirate suggests esophageal placement; gastric contents are usually green, off-white, tan, bloody, or brown.
w: The tube tip is in the stomach
Gastric aspirate is usually green, off-white, tan, bloody, or brown.
The tube tip is in the duodenum
Duodenal placement usually gives yellow or bile-stained aspirate.
The tube is ready for feedings
Placement must be confirmed by x-ray, and this finding suggests a misplaced tube.

alt.q: Which bedside aspirate finding is most consistent with an NG tube tip in the stomach?
alt.a: Green aspirate with a pH of 4
alt.ex: Gastric aspirate is usually green, and a pH between 1.0 and 5.0 supports stomach placement.
w: Saliva-like aspirate with a pH of 7
Saliva-like aspirate suggests the esophagus, and pH 7 is above the gastric range.
Yellow, bile-stained aspirate with a pH of 7
Bile-stained aspirate suggests duodenal placement.
Clear aspirate with a pH of 8
A pH of 8 is well above the 1.0 to 5.0 gastric range.

items.q: Which age-related change in the upper GI tract can impair absorption in older adults?
items.a: Peristalsis declines and esophageal emptying slows
items.ex: In older adults peristalsis declines and esophageal emptying slows, which impairs absorption by the intestinal mucosa.
w: Peristalsis speeds up and esophageal emptying quickens
Both peristalsis and esophageal emptying slow with age.
Gastric acid secretion increases to digest fiber
Increased gastric acid secretion is described in adolescents.
Stomach capacity shrinks to infant size
Smaller stomach capacity is described in infants, not older adults.

alt.q: Which statement by a nursing student about older adults’ upper GI function is accurate?
alt.a: “Esophageal emptying slows, which can impair absorption.”
alt.ex: Slower esophageal emptying and declining peristalsis in older adults impair absorption.
w: “Esophageal emptying speeds up, causing diarrhea.”
Esophageal emptying slows with age rather than speeding up.
“The lower esophageal sphincter stops working.”
The book does not describe loss of the lower sphincter with aging.
“Chewing ability usually improves with age.”
Older adults may have decreased chewing ability.

items.q: Which test uses a swallowed contrast medium to examine the structure and motility of the esophagus?
items.a: Barium swallow
items.ex: A barium swallow uses swallowed opaque contrast to show the structure and motility of the pharynx, esophagus, and stomach.
w: Colonoscopy
A colonoscopy directly views the large intestine.
Anorectal manometry
Anorectal manometry measures pressure in the anal sphincters.
Colonic transit study
A colonic transit study tracks swallowed markers through the colon over 5 days.

alt.q: A barium swallow is ordered for a patient. Which structures will it examine?
alt.a: Pharynx, esophagus, and stomach
alt.ex: A barium swallow examines the upper GI tract, including the pharynx, esophagus, and stomach.
w: Cecum, colon, and rectum
Barium given by enema is used to view the lower GI tract.
Liver, gallbladder, and pancreas
These accessory organs are assessed with other tests, such as liver function tests.
Anal canal and anal sphincters
Anorectal manometry assesses the anal sphincters.

items.q: A patient scheduled for an upper endoscopy to view the esophagus and stomach asks about the procedure. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “You’ll usually have clear liquids the day before, and you’ll be sedated.”
items.ex: Endoscopy is done under sedation, and patients are usually on a clear liquid diet the day before.
w: “No sedation is used, so you can drive yourself home.”
Endoscopic examinations are done under sedation.
“You’ll swallow a capsule and eat normally for 5 days.”
This describes a colonic transit study.
“You’ll lie very still while magnets take pictures.”
This describes an MRI.

alt.q: Which test gives direct visualization of the esophagus using a lighted fiberoptic tube?
alt.a: Upper endoscopy
alt.ex: Upper endoscopy uses a lighted fiberoptic tube to directly view the upper GI tract.
w: Barium swallow
A barium swallow is an x-ray that gives indirect visualization.
Plain film of the abdomen
A KUB is a simple x-ray film, not direct visualization.
Ultrasound imaging
Ultrasound uses sound waves and is a form of indirect visualization.

items.q: A patient with upper GI bleeding is to have a Sengstaken-Blakemore tube inserted. The spouse asks what the tube does. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “It uses an inflated balloon to apply pressure and prevent bleeding.”
items.ex: Compression tubes such as the Sengstaken-Blakemore use an inflated balloon to prevent esophageal or GI hemorrhage.
w: “It removes gas and secretions to relieve distention.”
Decompression is done with tubes such as the Salem sump or Levin.
“It delivers liquid feedings because swallowing is impaired.”
Enteral feeding uses tubes such as the Dobhoff.
“It washes out the stomach after a poisoning.”
Lavage uses tubes such as the Ewald or Levin.

alt.q: Which purpose of nasogastric intubation involves internal pressure from an inflated balloon to prevent esophageal hemorrhage?
alt.a: Compression
alt.ex: Compression uses an inflated balloon to apply internal pressure and prevent esophageal or GI hemorrhage.
w: Decompression
Decompression removes secretions and gas to prevent or relieve distention.
Lavage
Lavage is irrigation of the stomach for bleeding, poisoning, or gastric dilation.
Enteral feeding
Enteral feeding instills liquid nutrition into the stomach or small intestine.

items.q: A nurse estimates NG tube length with the XEN + 10 method. Which risk does the book link to a length that is too long?
items.a: The tube may coil in the stomach and migrate up toward the esophagus
items.ex: In some people XEN + 10 is too long, so the tube coils and migrates back toward the esophagus or advances into the duodenum.
w: The tip may stop in the pharynx and cause constant gagging
A tube that is too short, not too long, would stop higher up.
The tube may be unable to pass the lower esophageal sphincter
An overly long measurement does not stop the tube at the sphincter.
The tube may kink in the nose and block the air vent
The book’s concern is coiling and migration, not nasal kinking.

alt.q: Why is x-ray confirmation required right after an NG tube is inserted?
alt.a: No method of estimating tube length is 100% successful
alt.ex: Because none of the length-estimating techniques is fully reliable, immediate x-ray confirmation is required.
w: Aspirate color is never useful for checking placement
Observing aspirate is useful for initial placement while awaiting the x-ray.
pH testing is the gold standard but takes too long
Radiography, not pH testing, is the gold standard.
The tube must be repositioned after every x-ray
The tube is marked at the naris once placement is confirmed, not routinely moved.

items.q: Which statements about the esophageal sphincters are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: The upper esophageal sphincter is a circular muscle
The book describes it as a circular muscle.
The upper sphincter prevents air from entering the esophagus
It keeps air out and prevents reflux into the throat.
The lower sphincter prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus
That is its function.
The lower sphincter lies between the esophagus and the duodenum
It lies between the esophagus and the upper end of the stomach.
The upper sphincter pushes food toward the stomach
Peristalsis propels the bolus.
items.ex: The upper sphincter keeps air out of the esophagus, and the lower sphincter keeps stomach contents out of it.

alt.q: Which functions belong to the upper esophageal sphincter? Select all that apply.
o: Preventing air from entering the esophagus
This is a function of the upper sphincter.
Preventing esophageal contents from refluxing into the throat
This is a function of the upper sphincter.
Preventing stomach contents from refluxing into the esophagus
This is the lower sphincter’s function.
Preventing regurgitation back into the small intestine
This is the ileocecal valve’s function.
Propelling the bolus toward the stomach
Peristalsis propels the bolus.
alt.ex: The upper esophageal sphincter keeps air out of the esophagus and keeps esophageal contents from refluxing into the throat.

items.q: Which tests can be used to examine the esophagus? Select all that apply.
o: Barium swallow
It examines the structure and motility of the pharynx, esophagus, and stomach.
Upper endoscopy
It directly visualizes the upper GI tract.
Colonoscopy
A colonoscopy views the large intestine.
Anorectal manometry
This measures anal sphincter pressures.
Colonic transit study
This tracks markers through the colon.
items.ex: A barium swallow and an upper endoscopy examine the upper GI tract, including the esophagus.

alt.q: A patient is scheduled for a barium swallow. Which statements about this test are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It uses a swallowed opaque contrast medium
Barium is swallowed for this x-ray study.
It examines structure and motility of the upper GI tract
That is the purpose of the test.
It includes the pharynx, esophagus, and stomach
These are the structures examined.
It allows polyps to be removed during the test
Polyps are removed during endoscopy, not an x-ray study.
It requires removing all metal because magnets are used
That is a requirement for MRI.
alt.ex: A barium swallow is an x-ray study using swallowed contrast to view the pharynx, esophagus, and stomach.

items.q: Which statements about peristalsis are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It propels food through the length of the GI tract
This is the book’s definition of peristalsis.
It moves the bolus down the esophagus
The bolus travels down the esophagus with the aid of peristalsis.
It declines in older adults
Peristalsis declines and esophageal emptying slows with age.
It is temporarily stopped by general anesthesia
General anesthetics cause temporary cessation of peristalsis.
It occurs only in the large intestine
Peristalsis occurs along the whole GI tract, including the esophagus.
It is increased by opioid analgesics
Opioids slow peristalsis.
items.ex: Peristalsis moves food along the entire GI tract and is slowed by aging, anesthesia, and opioids.

alt.q: Which factors slow or stop peristalsis? Select all that apply.
o: Opioid analgesics
Opioids slow peristalsis and contractions.
General anesthesia
General anesthetics temporarily stop peristalsis.
Immobilization
Immobilization slows peristalsis.
Physical activity
Physical activity promotes peristalsis.
Acute emotional stress
During emotional stress, peristalsis increases.
alt.ex: Opioids, general anesthesia, and immobility slow peristalsis, whereas activity and emotional stress increase it.

items.q: The lower esophageal sphincter prevents stomach contents from refluxing into the esophagus.
items.a: True
items.ex: The lower esophageal sphincter lies at the top of the stomach and blocks reflux into the esophagus.
items.ww: Preventing reflux of stomach contents is exactly this sphincter’s function.

alt.q: The upper esophageal sphincter lies between the esophagus and the stomach.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The lower esophageal sphincter lies between the esophagus and the stomach; the upper one is at the throat end.
alt.ww: The sphincter at the stomach end is the lower esophageal sphincter.

items.q: Peristalsis occurs only in the intestines, not in the esophagus.
items.a: False
items.ex: The bolus travels down the esophagus with the aid of peristalsis.
items.ww: Peristalsis propels food through the whole GI tract, including the esophagus.

alt.q: Peristalsis helps move a bolus of food down the esophagus.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Peristalsis is the contraction that propels food, including down the esophagus.
alt.ww: The esophagus is muscular and uses peristalsis to move food.

items.q: Aspirating saliva-like fluid confirms that an NG tube is in the stomach.
items.a: False
items.ex: Saliva-like aspirate suggests the tube may be in the esophagus.
items.ww: Gastric contents are usually green, off-white, tan, bloody, or brown, not saliva-like.

alt.q: An NG tube whose tip ends in the esophagus places the patient at risk for pulmonary aspiration.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The tip must reach the stomach because tubes ending in the esophagus risk pulmonary aspiration.
alt.ww: The book warns specifically about aspiration when the tip is in the esophagus.

items.q: The [[lower esophageal sphincter|LES]] lies between the esophagus and the upper end of the stomach.
items.ex: The lower esophageal sphincter prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus.

alt.q: Reflux of stomach contents back into the esophagus is prevented by the [[lower esophageal sphincter|LES]].
alt.ex: The lower esophageal sphincter prevents reflux of stomach contents into the esophagus.

items.q: The contraction that propels food through the length of the GI tract is called [[peristalsis]].
items.ex: Peristalsis moves the bolus down the esophagus and contents through the intestines.

alt.q: A bolus of food travels down the esophagus with the aid of [[peristalsis|peristaltic contractions]].
alt.ex: Peristalsis moves the bolus down the esophagus and contents through the intestines.

items.q: In the passage of swallowed food, which structure comes right after “Esophagus”?
items.a: Lower esophageal sphincter
items.ex: That's structure 3 of 5. Food passes the upper sphincter, travels down the esophagus, crosses the lower sphincter into the stomach, then enters the small intestine.
w: Stomach
That's structure 4 of 5.
Upper esophageal sphincter
That's structure 1 of 5.
Small intestine
That's structure 5 of 5.

alt.q: Which structure comes first in the passage of swallowed food?
alt.a: Upper esophageal sphincter
alt.ex: That's structure 1 of 5. Food passes the upper sphincter, travels down the esophagus, crosses the lower sphincter into the stomach, then enters the small intestine.
w: Esophagus
That's structure 2 of 5.
Lower esophageal sphincter
That's structure 3 of 5.
Stomach
That's structure 4 of 5.

alt.q: Which structure comes last in the passage of swallowed food?
alt.a: Small intestine
alt.ex: That's structure 5 of 5. Food passes the upper sphincter, travels down the esophagus, crosses the lower sphincter into the stomach, then enters the small intestine.
w: Stomach
That's structure 4 of 5.
Lower esophageal sphincter
That's structure 3 of 5.
Esophagus
That's structure 2 of 5.
