items.q: A patient says breathing feels harder after eating an unusually large meal. Which explanation by the nurse is best?
items.a: A large meal enlarges the stomach and makes it hard for the diaphragm to descend
items.ex: The stomach lies just below the diaphragm, and a very large meal can enlarge it enough to hinder diaphragm descent.
w: Food in the stomach presses on the trachea and narrows it
The stomach lies below the diaphragm and does not press on the trachea.
Gastrin released after a meal constricts the airways
Gastrin regulates digestion; it does not constrict airways.
The lower esophageal sphincter closes and blocks the lungs
This sphincter prevents reflux into the esophagus; it is not part of the airway.

alt.q: Which statement about the stomach’s location and shape is accurate?
alt.a: It is an elongated pouch lying just below the diaphragm
alt.ex: The stomach is an elongated, pouchlike structure located just below the diaphragm.
w: It is a narrow tube lying just above the diaphragm
The esophagus is the tube above the diaphragm; the stomach lies below it.
It is a long coiled tube filling the lower abdomen
This describes the small intestine.
It is a fixed organ that never changes position
The stomach’s position can change during inspiration and expiration.

items.q: Which substance secreted by the stomach facilitates vitamin B12 absorption?
items.a: Intrinsic factor
items.ex: The stomach secretes intrinsic factor to facilitate vitamin B12 absorption.
w: Gastrin
Gastrin is a stomach hormone that regulates digestion.
Ghrelin
Ghrelin is a stomach hormone that increases appetite.
Bile
Bile comes from the liver and enters the small intestine.

alt.q: What is the function of intrinsic factor?
alt.a: Facilitating vitamin B12 absorption
alt.ex: Intrinsic factor, secreted by the stomach, facilitates absorption of vitamin B12.
w: Increasing the appetite before meals
Ghrelin is the stomach hormone that increases appetite.
Regulating the process of digestion
Gastrin is the stomach hormone that regulates digestion.
Destroying swallowed pathogenic bacteria
Destroying swallowed pathogens is a protective stomach function, not the role of intrinsic factor.

items.q: Which hormone produced by the stomach increases appetite?
items.a: Ghrelin
items.ex: The stomach produces ghrelin, which increases appetite.
w: Gastrin
Gastrin regulates digestion rather than increasing appetite.
Intrinsic factor
Intrinsic factor facilitates vitamin B12 absorption and is not a hormone.
Lipase
Lipase is measured in blood to assess for pancreatitis; it is not a stomach hormone.

alt.q: What is the role of gastrin?
alt.a: Regulating digestion
alt.ex: Gastrin is a hormone produced by the stomach that regulates digestion.
w: Increasing appetite
Ghrelin is the stomach hormone that increases appetite.
Facilitating vitamin B12 absorption
Intrinsic factor facilitates vitamin B12 absorption.
Softening food for swallowing
Saliva softens food in the mouth.

items.q: Which substances can the stomach absorb in limited amounts?
items.a: Certain drugs, water, alcohol, and some fatty acids
items.ex: The stomach performs only limited absorption of certain drugs, water, alcohol, and some fatty acids.
w: Most dietary carbohydrates and proteins
The jejunum absorbs carbohydrates and proteins.
Bile salts, fats, and certain vitamins
The ileum absorbs these substances.
Large volumes of sodium and chloride
The colon resorbs large amounts of sodium and chloride daily.

alt.q: A student says, “The stomach is the main site of nutrient absorption.” Which correction is best?
alt.a: Its absorption is limited; the duodenum and jejunum absorb most nutrients
alt.ex: The stomach absorbs only limited substances, while the duodenum and jejunum absorb most nutrients and electrolytes.
w: The stomach absorbs nothing and only stores food
The stomach does perform a limited amount of absorption.
The colon absorbs most nutrients after the stomach
The colon mainly absorbs water, sodium, and chloride.
The esophagus absorbs most nutrients before the stomach
The esophagus transports food; it does not absorb nutrients.

items.q: How does the stomach help protect the body from infection?
items.a: By destroying pathogenic bacteria swallowed with food or mucus
items.ex: The stomach destroys pathogenic bacteria swallowed with food or with mucus from the respiratory tract.
w: By producing antibodies that coat all swallowed food
The book describes destruction of bacteria, not antibody coating of food.
By secreting saliva that kills microorganisms in food
Saliva is produced by salivary glands in the mouth and dilutes and softens food.
By absorbing bacteria before they reach the intestines
The stomach destroys pathogens; it does not absorb them.

alt.q: Adolescents have increased secretion of gastric acids. Besides digesting food fibers, what does this acid do?
alt.a: Acts as a bactericide against swallowed organisms
alt.ex: Gastric acid in adolescents helps digest food fibers and acts as a bactericide against swallowed organisms.
w: Increases appetite by releasing ghrelin
Ghrelin is a hormone; gastric acid is not described as releasing it.
Speeds emptying of the esophagus
Gastric acid is not described as affecting esophageal emptying.
Slows peristalsis in the colon
Gastric acid secretion is not linked to colonic peristalsis in the book.

items.q: What happens when the stomach churns food?
items.a: Food is broken into small particles and mixed with gastric juices
items.ex: Churning breaks food into small particles and mixes them with gastric juices.
w: Food is diluted and softened by saliva
Saliva acts on food in the mouth.
Food is propelled through the whole GI tract
Peristalsis propels food through the length of the GI tract.
Water is absorbed so stool becomes formed
Water absorption that forms stool occurs in the colon.

alt.q: Which stomach function describes its role as a food reservoir?
alt.a: Storing food until it can be partially digested and moved on
alt.ex: As a reservoir, the stomach stores food until it is partially digested and moved along the GI tract.
w: Holding feces until just before defecation
The rectum holds feces just before defecation.
Storing vitamin B12 for later release
The stomach secretes intrinsic factor; it does not store B12.
Collecting bile from the liver between meals
Bile enters the small intestine from the liver.

items.q: Before irrigating an NG tube, the nurse checks the pH of the aspirate. Which result indicates that the tube is in the stomach?
items.a: pH 4.0
items.ex: Gastric aspirate pH must measure between 1.0 and 5.0 to confirm the tube is in the stomach.
w: pH 6.5
A pH of 6.5 is above the 1.0 to 5.0 gastric range.
pH 7.5
A pH of 7.5 is above the gastric range and does not confirm stomach placement.
pH 9.0
A pH of 9.0 is far above the gastric range.

alt.q: Which pH range of aspirate confirms NG tube placement in the stomach before irrigation?
alt.ex: The book states gastric aspirate pH must measure between 1.0 and 5.0 to ensure stomach placement.
w: This range is above the acidic gastric range.
This range is too high to confirm gastric placement.
This range is alkaline and does not indicate gastric contents.

items.q: An NG tube in a patient who had gastric surgery yesterday has stopped draining. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: Notify the health care provider instead of repositioning the tube
items.ex: An NG tube is never repositioned after gastric surgery because moving it can rupture the suture line.
w: Advance the tube a few centimeters to reach gastric fluid
Advancing the tube after gastric surgery can rupture the suture line.
Withdraw the tube slightly and reconnect the suction
Any repositioning after gastric surgery risks rupturing the suture line.
Clamp the blue air vent to strengthen the suction
The air vent of a Salem sump tube must never be clamped.

alt.q: Why must the nurse never reposition an NG tube in a patient after gastric surgery?
alt.a: Moving the tube can rupture the gastric suture line
alt.ex: Repositioning an NG tube after gastric surgery can rupture the suture line.
w: Moving the tube increases loss of intrinsic factor
The concern is mechanical damage to the suture line.
Moving the tube permanently blocks its air vent
Repositioning does not block the air vent.
Placement cannot be confirmed by x-ray after surgery
X-ray verification remains the gold standard after surgery.

items.q: A patient has a Salem sump tube connected to suction. The nurse finds the blue pigtail clamped. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Unclamp it and keep it above the level of the stomach
items.ex: The air vent must never be clamped, and keeping it above stomach level prevents siphoning that clogs the tube.
w: Leave it clamped to increase the suction strength
Clamping the vent prevents free, continuous drainage of secretions.
Connect the pigtail directly to the suction source
The pigtail is an air vent and is never connected to suction.
Use the pigtail to irrigate the tube with saline
The air vent is never used for irrigation.

alt.q: Why is the blue pigtail of a Salem sump tube kept above the level of the stomach?
alt.a: To prevent a siphoning action that clogs the tube
alt.ex: Keeping the air vent above the stomach prevents siphoning that would clog the tube.
w: To let gastric contents drain out through the vent
Gastric contents drain through the main lumen, not the vent.
To keep gastric acid from reaching the esophagus
The lower esophageal sphincter, not the vent position, prevents reflux.
To allow irrigation through the air lumen
The air vent is never used for irrigation.

items.q: Why does the nurse use normal saline when irrigating an NG tube?
items.a: It minimizes loss of electrolytes from stomach fluids
items.ex: Using saline for irrigation minimizes loss of electrolytes from stomach fluids.
w: It neutralizes gastric acid to protect the mucosa
Saline is used to limit electrolyte loss, not to neutralize acid.
It stimulates ghrelin release to restore appetite
Ghrelin is not affected by the irrigating solution.
It is sterile, and NG tube care requires sterile technique
NG tube insertion and care use clean technique, not sterile technique.

alt.q: A nursing student asks why the skill calls for normal saline to irrigate an NG tube that drains stomach fluids. Which reply is accurate?
alt.a: “Saline limits the electrolytes lost from the stomach.”
alt.ex: Normal saline minimizes electrolyte loss from stomach fluids during irrigation.
w: “Saline dissolves the tape that anchors the tube.”
Irrigation clears the tube; it has nothing to do with the tape.
“Saline confirms that the tube is in the stomach.”
Placement is confirmed by aspirate pH and x-ray, not by irrigating.
“Saline restores the intrinsic factor removed by suction.”
Irrigating solution does not replace intrinsic factor.

items.q: Which suction setting is usually ordered for an NG tube, and why?
items.a: Low intermittent, because it decreases gastric irritation
items.ex: Suction is usually ordered at a low intermittent setting, which decreases gastric irritation from the tube.
w: High continuous, because it drains secretions fastest
High suction is not the usual order and increases irritation.
High intermittent, because it keeps the tube from clogging
A higher setting is considered only if thick secretions cannot be cleared by irrigation.
Low continuous, because it keeps the air vent open
The usual order is low intermittent; the vent is kept open by never clamping it.

alt.q: What is the rationale for using a low intermittent suction setting with an NG tube?
alt.a: It decreases gastric irritation from the tube
alt.ex: Low intermittent suction is chosen because it decreases gastric irritation.
w: It increases intrinsic factor secretion
Suction settings do not affect intrinsic factor.
It removes the need for placement checks
Placement is still verified, for example before irrigation.
It allows the air vent to be clamped safely
The air vent is never clamped.

items.q: Which are functions of the stomach? Select all that apply.
o: Storing food until it is partially digested
The stomach acts as a food reservoir.
Secreting intrinsic factor
Intrinsic factor facilitates vitamin B12 absorption.
Producing gastrin and ghrelin
Gastrin regulates digestion, and ghrelin increases appetite.
Destroying swallowed pathogenic bacteria
This is a protective function of the stomach.
Absorbing most carbohydrates and proteins
The jejunum absorbs carbohydrates and proteins.
Producing bile to break down nutrients
Bile comes from the liver.
items.ex: The stomach stores, churns, and begins digesting food, secretes intrinsic factor, makes gastrin and ghrelin, and destroys pathogens.

alt.q: Which statements about the stomach are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Its position can change during inspiration and expiration
The book notes that its position can change with breathing.
It churns food into small particles
It mixes the particles with gastric juices.
It secretes gastric acids and enzymes
These aid in food digestion.
It absorbs large volumes of water to form stool
The colon absorbs water and forms stool.
It is located just above the diaphragm
The stomach lies just below the diaphragm.
alt.ex: The stomach lies below the diaphragm, can shift with breathing, churns food, and secretes acids and enzymes.

items.q: While awaiting x-ray confirmation, the nurse aspirates from a new NG tube. Which aspirate colors are typical of gastric contents? Select all that apply.
o: Green
Gastric contents are usually green.
Off-white
Gastric contents are sometimes off-white.
Tan
Gastric contents are sometimes tan.
Brown
Gastric contents are sometimes brown.
Yellow or bile stained
This suggests duodenal placement.
Clear and saliva-like
This suggests the tube is in the esophagus.
items.ex: Gastric contents are usually green and sometimes off-white, tan, bloody, or brown.

alt.q: Which aspirate findings suggest that an NG tube tip is not in the stomach? Select all that apply.
o: Yellow, bile-stained aspirate
This suggests duodenal placement.
Saliva-like aspirate
This suggests esophageal placement.
Aspirate pH of 8
Gastric pH should be between 1.0 and 5.0.
Green aspirate with a pH of 3
This is consistent with gastric contents.
Tan aspirate with a pH of 4
This is consistent with gastric contents.
alt.ex: Bile-stained or saliva-like aspirate, or a pH above 5.0, suggests the tip is outside the stomach.

items.q: Which characteristics of infants affect their digestion? Select all that apply.
o: Smaller stomach capacity
Infants have a smaller stomach capacity.
Less secretion of digestive enzymes
Infants secrete fewer digestive enzymes.
More rapid intestinal peristalsis
Intestinal peristalsis is more rapid in infants.
Voluntary control of defecation from birth
Control of defecation does not develop until 2 to 3 years of age.
Increased gastric acid secretion to digest fiber
This is described in adolescents.
items.ex: Infants have a smaller stomach, fewer digestive enzymes, and faster intestinal peristalsis.

alt.q: Which age-related GI changes are matched correctly with the age group? Select all that apply.
o: Infants: smaller stomach capacity
Infants have a smaller stomach capacity.
Adolescents: increased secretion of gastric acids
Adolescents secrete more gastric acid.
Older adults: slower esophageal emptying
Esophageal emptying slows in older adults.
Infants: full control of defecation
Defecation control develops at 2 to 3 years.
Older adults: stronger anal sphincter tone
Anal sphincter tone weakens with age.
alt.ex: Stomach capacity, gastric acid secretion, and esophageal emptying change in predictable ways across the life span.

items.q: The position of the stomach can change during inspiration and expiration.

items.q: What are the approximate dimensions of the adult small intestine?
items.a: 2.4 cm (1 inch) wide and 6 to 8 m (20–26 feet) long
items.ex: The small intestine is about 2.4 cm (1 inch) in diameter and 6 to 8 m (20–26 feet) long.
w: 6 cm (2½ inches) wide and 1.5 to 1.8 m (5–6 feet) long
These are the dimensions of the large intestine.
2.4 cm (1 inch) wide and 1.5 to 1.8 m (5–6 feet) long
The small intestine is much longer, 6 to 8 m.
6 cm (2½ inches) wide and 6 to 8 m (20–26 feet) long
The small intestine is narrower, about 2.4 cm wide.

alt.q: Compared with the large intestine, how does the small intestine differ in size?
alt.a: It is narrower but much longer
alt.ex: The small intestine is about 2.4 cm wide and 6 to 8 m long; the colon is 6 cm wide and 1.5 to 1.8 m long.
w: It is wider and much longer
The large intestine has the larger diameter.
It is wider but much shorter
The small intestine is narrower and longer.
It is narrower and much shorter
The small intestine is much longer than the colon.

items.q: Which section of the small intestine absorbs carbohydrates and proteins?
items.a: Jejunum
items.ex: The jejunum, about 2.5 m long, absorbs carbohydrates and proteins.
w: Duodenum
The duodenum continues to process fluid from the stomach.
Ileum
The ileum absorbs water, fats, and bile salts.
Cecum
The cecum is the first part of the large intestine.

alt.q: What does the jejunum absorb?
alt.a: Carbohydrates and proteins
alt.ex: The jejunum is the section of the small intestine that absorbs carbohydrates and proteins.
w: Water, fats, and bile salts
These are absorbed by the ileum.
Large volumes of sodium and chloride
The colon resorbs large amounts of sodium and chloride.
Alcohol and some fatty acids
The stomach absorbs limited amounts of these.

items.q: A patient has had most of the ileum surgically removed. Absorption of which substances is most likely affected?
items.a: Fats, bile salts, and certain vitamins
items.ex: The ileum absorbs water, fats, bile salts, and certain vitamins.
w: Carbohydrates and proteins
These are absorbed by the jejunum.
Alcohol and certain drugs
The stomach absorbs limited amounts of these.
Large volumes of sodium and chloride
The colon resorbs large amounts of sodium and chloride.

alt.q: Which section of the small intestine absorbs bile salts?
alt.a: Ileum
alt.ex: The ileum, the last and longest section, absorbs water, fats, and bile salts.
w: Duodenum
The duodenum continues to process fluid from the stomach.
Jejunum
The jejunum absorbs carbohydrates and proteins.
Sigmoid colon
The sigmoid colon is part of the large intestine.

items.q: Which statement about the duodenum is accurate?
items.a: It is about 20 to 28 cm long and continues to process fluid from the stomach
items.ex: The duodenum, about 20 to 28 cm (8–11 inches) long, continues to process fluid from the stomach.
w: It is about 2.5 m long and absorbs carbohydrates and proteins
This describes the jejunum.
It is about 3.7 m long and absorbs water, fats, and bile salts
This describes the ileum.
It is about 17 to 20 cm long and holds feces until defecation
This describes the rectum.

alt.q: Which section is the shortest part of the small intestine?
alt.a: Duodenum
alt.ex: The duodenum is about 20 to 28 cm long, much shorter than the jejunum (2.5 m) or ileum (3.7 m).
w: Jejunum
The jejunum is about 2.5 m long.
Ileum
The ileum is about 3.7 m long, the longest section.
Cecum
The cecum belongs to the large intestine, not the small intestine.

items.q: Which sections of the small intestine absorb most nutrients and electrolytes?
items.a: Duodenum and jejunum
items.ex: The duodenum and jejunum absorb most nutrients and electrolytes in the small intestine.
w: Jejunum and ileum
The ileum mainly absorbs water, fats, bile salts, and certain vitamins.
Ileum and cecum
The cecum is part of the large intestine.
Duodenum and ileum
The jejunum, not the ileum, joins the duodenum in absorbing most nutrients.

alt.q: A patient asks where most nutrients and electrolytes are absorbed. Which response by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “In the first two sections of the small intestine.”
alt.ex: The duodenum and jejunum, the first two sections, absorb most nutrients and electrolytes.
w: “In the stomach, before food reaches the intestine.”
The stomach performs only limited absorption.
“In the large intestine, as stool is formed.”
The colon mainly absorbs water, sodium, and chloride.
“In the last section of the small intestine.”
The ileum absorbs mainly water, fats, bile salts, and certain vitamins.

items.q: Digestive enzymes and bile enter the small intestine from which organs?
items.a: The pancreas and the liver
items.ex: Digestive enzymes and bile enter the small intestine from the pancreas and the liver.
w: The stomach and the esophagus
The esophagus transports food; it does not supply enzymes or bile.
The salivary glands and the stomach
Salivary glands act in the mouth; bile comes from the liver.
The colon and the rectum
These lie after the small intestine and do not supply enzymes or bile.

alt.q: What is the role of the digestive enzymes and bile that enter the small intestine?
alt.a: Further breaking down nutrients into a form the body can use
alt.ex: Enzymes and bile from the pancreas and liver further break down nutrients into a usable form.
w: Propelling chyme toward the large intestine
Peristalsis moves chyme along.
Preventing reflux of contents into the stomach
Sphincters, not enzymes, prevent reflux.
Absorbing water to form solid stool
The colon absorbs water to form stool.

items.q: What is the consistency of intestinal contents by the time they reach the end of the small intestine?
items.a: A thick liquid with some semisolid particles
items.ex: Resorption is so efficient that contents at the end of the small intestine are a thick liquid with semisolid particles.
w: A soft, formed solid mass
Formed stool develops in the colon as water is absorbed.
A hard, dry mass of stool
Hard stool results when colonic contents move slowly.
A thin liquid unchanged from entry
Efficient resorption thickens the contents along the small intestine.

alt.q: In what form does chyme enter the small intestine?
alt.a: As a liquid material
alt.ex: Chyme comes into the small intestine as a liquid and mixes with digestive enzymes.
w: As a soft, formed mass

This exceeds the amount the colon is described as resorbing daily.

alt.q: Besides water, which substances does the colon resorb in significant amounts each day?
alt.a: Sodium and chloride
alt.ex: The colon resorbs up to 1.5 L of water plus significant amounts of sodium and chloride daily.
w: Carbohydrates and proteins
These are absorbed in the jejunum of the small intestine.
Fats and bile salts
The ileum absorbs fats and bile salts.
Iron and vitamin B12
Iron and certain vitamins are absorbed in the small intestine.

items.q: A patient has abnormally fast peristalsis through the colon. Which stool characteristic should the nurse expect?
items.a: Watery stool
items.ex: Fast peristalsis leaves less time for water absorption, so the stool is watery.
w: Hard, dry stool
Hard stool forms when peristalsis slows and water keeps being absorbed.
Soft, formed stool
Soft, formed stool is the normal result of normal transit time.
Small, pebble-like stool
Small, hard stool reflects slow transit and excess water absorption.

alt.q: A patient’s colonic contents are moving through the colon very slowly. Which outcome should the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: Constipation with a hard stool mass
alt.ex: When peristalsis slows, water continues to be absorbed and a hard mass of stool forms, causing constipation.
w: Diarrhea with watery stool
Watery stool results from abnormally fast peristalsis.
Normal soft, formed stool
Soft, formed stool reflects normal transit, not slowed movement.
Increased flatus with loose stool
Loose stool reflects rapid transit, not slowed movement.

items.q: The amount of water the colon absorbs depends on how quickly colonic contents move through it.
items.a: True
items.ex: Faster movement leaves less time for absorption; slower movement allows more water to be absorbed.
items.ww: Transit time directly determines water absorption, which is why stool can be watery or hard.

alt.q: The colon absorbs the same amount of water regardless of how quickly its contents move.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Water absorption depends on transit speed: fast peristalsis yields watery stool, slow peristalsis yields hard stool.
alt.ww: If absorption were fixed, transit speed would not change stool consistency, but it does.

items.q: A patient on bed rest after surgery has slowed peristalsis. The patient asks why this matters for bowel movements. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “When stool moves slowly, the colon keeps absorbing water, so the stool becomes hard.”
items.ex: Slowed peristaltic contractions let water continue to be absorbed, forming a hard stool mass and constipation.
w: “When stool moves slowly, the colon secretes extra water, so the stool becomes loose.”
Slow transit increases water absorption, making stool hard, not loose.
“When stool moves slowly, the small intestine absorbs the stool’s fat, so it becomes pale.”
Slow colonic transit changes water content, not fat absorption or color.
“When stool moves slowly, the rectum fills with gas, so the stool becomes watery.”
Watery stool results from rapid, not slow, peristalsis.

alt.q: A patient with diarrhea asks why the stools are so watery. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “The stool is moving through the colon too fast for water to be absorbed.”
alt.ex: With abnormally fast peristalsis there is less time for water absorption, so stool is watery.
w: “The stool is moving through the colon too slowly for water to be absorbed.”
Slow movement allows more absorption and causes hard stool.
“The colon has stopped absorbing sodium and chloride completely.”
The book links watery stool to rapid transit, not a total loss of electrolyte absorption.
“The ileocecal valve is letting stool flow back into the small intestine.”
The ileocecal valve prevents backflow; it does not explain watery stool.

items.q: How often do mass peristaltic movements normally occur in the colon?
items.a: 3 or 4 times daily
items.ex: Mass peristalsis pushes undigested food toward the rectum only 3 or 4 times daily, strongest in the hour after meals.
w: 1 time every 2 to 3 days
Mass movements occur several times daily, not once every few days.
10 to 12 times daily
Mass movements are infrequent, occurring only 3 or 4 times daily.
1 time every hour
Hourly movement describes ongoing peristalsis, not the 3 or 4 daily mass movements.

alt.q: When is the strongest mass peristaltic movement of the colon usually seen?
alt.a: During the hour after mealtime
alt.ex: Mass movements occur 3 or 4 times daily, with the strongest during the hour after a meal.
w: During the hour before mealtime
The strongest mass movement follows, not precedes, a meal.
During the first hours of sleep
The book ties the strongest movement to the hour after meals.
During periods of fasting
Food intake, not fasting, precedes the strongest mass movement.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient with irregular bowel movements how to plan a toileting routine. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will sit on the toilet within an hour after breakfast.”
items.ex: The strongest mass peristalsis occurs in the hour after a meal, so this is the best time to attempt defecation.
w: “I will sit on the toilet right before I eat breakfast.”
Mass movements are strongest after, not before, a meal.
“I will wait until the urge has passed several times.”
Ignoring the urge disrupts habits and can lead to constipation.
“I will sit on the toilet at a different time each day.”
A regular schedule timed to when the urge usually occurs supports normal elimination.

alt.q: A patient wants to establish regular bowel habits. When should the nurse suggest the patient attempt defecation?
alt.a: About an hour after a meal
alt.ex: Mass peristalsis is strongest in the hour after mealtime, making defecation more likely then.
w: Just before going to bed
The book links the strongest colonic movement to the hour after meals, not bedtime.
About an hour before a meal
Mass movements are strongest after eating, not before.
Only when abdominal cramping begins
Waiting for cramping is not a routine; timing after meals uses mass peristalsis.

items.q: In a healthy person, the rectum normally contains fecal matter at all times.
items.a: False
items.ex: The rectum is normally empty of fecal matter until just before defecation.
items.ww: Stool enters the rectum just before defecation, and the resulting distention signals the need to defecate.

alt.q: The rectum is normally empty of fecal matter until just before defecation.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Stool moves into the rectum only shortly before defecation, where its distention triggers awareness of the urge.
alt.ww: A rectum that always held stool could not signal the urge to defecate through distention.

items.q: What is the role of the vertical and transverse folds of tissue in the rectum?
items.a: They help control expulsion of fecal contents
items.ex: Rectal folds help control the expulsion of fecal contents during defecation.
w: They absorb most of the water in the stool
The colon as a whole resorbs water; the folds help control expulsion.
They prevent backflow into the small intestine
The ileocecal valve prevents regurgitation into the small intestine.
They secrete enzymes that digest fiber
Rectal folds are not described as secreting digestive enzymes.

alt.q: Each fold of tissue in the rectum contains veins. Why is this clinically important?
alt.a: The veins can distend with straining and form hemorrhoids
alt.ex: Pressure from straining distends the veins in the rectal folds, resulting in hemorrhoid formation.
w: The veins can rupture with eating and cause diverticula
Diverticula are saclike outpouchings of the intestinal wall, not distended rectal veins.
The veins can absorb drugs and cause rectal toxicity
The book does not describe drug absorption by rectal fold veins.
The veins can clot with exercise and cause an ileus
An ileus is a temporary stop in peristalsis, often after bowel surgery.

items.q: A patient reports straining hard during most bowel movements. The nurse explains the patient’s increased risk for which condition?
items.a: Hemorrhoids
items.ex: Straining distends the veins in the rectal folds, resulting in hemorrhoid formation.
w: Ileus
An ileus is a temporary cessation of peristalsis, usually after bowel surgery.
Diverticula
Diverticula risk is linked to age over 50, not to straining in the rectum.
Ileocecal reflux
The ileocecal valve prevents backflow; straining does not cause this.

alt.q: A patient with new hemorrhoids asks what caused them. Which explanation by the nurse is most accurate?
alt.a: “Pressure from straining stretched the veins in the folds of your rectum.”
alt.ex: The rectal folds contain veins that distend under pressure from straining, forming hemorrhoids.
w: “Fast peristalsis kept water from being absorbed in your colon.”
Rapid peristalsis causes watery stool, not hemorrhoids.
“Gas from foods like beans stretched the walls of your colon.”
Gas increases colonic motility; it is not described as causing hemorrhoids.
“Your ileocecal valve allowed stool to flow back into your small bowel.”
Backflow through the ileocecal valve is not the cause of hemorrhoids.

items.q: Which statements about the rectum are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It makes up the last 17 to 20 cm of the intestinal tube
The rectum is the final 17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches) of the intestinal tube.
It is normally empty until just before defecation
Fecal matter enters the rectum shortly before defecation.
It contains folds of tissue with veins that can distend
Straining distends these veins and forms hemorrhoids.
It is the first part of the large intestine
The cecum is the first part; the rectum is the final part.
It absorbs most of the bile salts from stool
The ileum absorbs bile salts.
items.ex: The rectum is the final 17 to 20 cm of the large intestine, normally empty until defecation, with vein-containing folds.

alt.q: A student reviews the anatomy of the lower GI tract. Which statements about the rectum should the student include? Select all that apply.
o: It is the final part of the large intestine
The rectum is the last part of the large intestine before the anus.
Its folds help control expulsion of stool
Vertical and transverse folds help control expulsion during defecation.
It measures about 7 or 8 inches in length
The rectum is the last 17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches) of the intestinal tube.
It stores stool continuously between bowel movements
The rectum is normally empty until just before defecation.
It connects directly to the ileocecal valve
The ileocecal valve joins the ileum to the cecum, at the start of the colon.
alt.ex: The rectum is the final 7 or 8 inches of the large intestine; its folds help control expulsion.

items.q: What is the normal value for the Diameter of the colon?
items.a: About 6 cm (2½ inches)
items.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.
w: That goes with Length of the colon.
17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches)
That goes with Length of the rectum.
Up to 1.5 L
That goes with Daily water resorbed by the colon.

alt.q: What is the normal value for the Length of the colon?
alt.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.
w: About 6 cm (2½ inches)
That goes with Diameter of the colon.
17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches)
That goes with Length of the rectum.
Up to 1.5 L
That goes with Daily water resorbed by the colon.

alt.q: What is the normal value for the Length of the rectum?
alt.a: 17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches)
alt.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.
w: About 6 cm (2½ inches)
That goes with Diameter of the colon.
That goes with Length of the colon.
Up to 1.5 L
That goes with Daily water resorbed by the colon.

alt.q: What is the normal value for the Daily water resorbed by the colon?
alt.a: Up to 1.5 L
alt.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.
w: About 6 cm (2½ inches)
That goes with Diameter of the colon.
That goes with Length of the colon.
17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches)
That goes with Length of the rectum.

alt.q: What is the normal value for the Daily mass peristaltic movements?
alt.a: 3 or 4 times
alt.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.
w: About 6 cm (2½ inches)
That goes with Diameter of the colon.
That goes with Length of the colon.
17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches)
That goes with Length of the rectum.

alt.q: Which feature of the large intestine has the value “About 6 cm (2½ inches)”?
alt.a: Diameter of the colon
alt.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.
w: Length of the colon
Length of the colon: 1.5 to 1.8 m (5–6 feet).
Length of the rectum
Length of the rectum: 17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches).
Daily water resorbed by the colon
Daily water resorbed by the colon: Up to 1.5 L.

alt.q: Which feature of the large intestine has the value “1.5 to 1.8 m (5–6 feet)”?
alt.a: Length of the colon
alt.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.
w: Diameter of the colon
Diameter of the colon: About 6 cm (2½ inches).
Length of the rectum
Length of the rectum: 17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches).
Daily water resorbed by the colon
Daily water resorbed by the colon: Up to 1.5 L.

alt.q: Which feature of the large intestine has the value “17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches)”?
alt.a: Length of the rectum
alt.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.
w: Diameter of the colon
Diameter of the colon: About 6 cm (2½ inches).
Length of the colon
Length of the colon: 1.5 to 1.8 m (5–6 feet).
Daily water resorbed by the colon
Daily water resorbed by the colon: Up to 1.5 L.

alt.q: Which feature of the large intestine has the value “Up to 1.5 L”?
alt.a: Daily water resorbed by the colon
alt.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.
w: Diameter of the colon
Diameter of the colon: About 6 cm (2½ inches).
Length of the colon
Length of the colon: 1.5 to 1.8 m (5–6 feet).
Length of the rectum
Length of the rectum: 17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches).

alt.q: Which feature of the large intestine has the value “3 or 4 times”?
alt.a: Daily mass peristaltic movements
alt.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.
w: Diameter of the colon
Diameter of the colon: About 6 cm (2½ inches).
Length of the colon
Length of the colon: 1.5 to 1.8 m (5–6 feet).
Length of the rectum
Length of the rectum: 17 to 20 cm (7 or 8 inches).

mt.q: Match each feature of the large intestine with its normal value.
pairs: Daily water resorbed by the colon
mt.ex: The colon is wide but short, ends in a 17- to 20-cm rectum, resorbs up to 1.5 L of water, and has 3 or 4 mass movements daily.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient about the GI tract. Which organ should the nurse identify as the primary organ of bowel elimination?
items.a: The large intestine
items.ex: The large intestine, or colon, is the primary organ of bowel elimination.
w: The small intestine
The small intestine mainly digests and absorbs nutrients.
The stomach
The stomach stores, churns, and partially digests food.
The pancreas
The pancreas is an accessory organ that secretes digestive enzymes.

alt.q: Which part of the GI tract normally changes digestive fluid into a soft, formed solid or semisolid mass?
alt.a: The colon
alt.ex: As the colon resorbs water, fecal matter normally becomes a soft, formed solid or semisolid mass.
w: The jejunum
The jejunum absorbs carbohydrates and proteins; contents remain liquid.
The duodenum
The duodenum continues to process fluid from the stomach.
The stomach
The stomach mixes food with gastric juices to form liquid chyme.

items.q: Waves of peristalsis move digestive fluid from the small intestine into the large intestine through the ileocecal valve.
items.a: True
items.ex: Digestive fluid enters the colon by waves of peristalsis through the ileocecal valve.
items.ww: The ileocecal valve is the entry point to the colon, and peristalsis drives contents through it.

alt.q: Digestive fluid enters the large intestine by gravity because peristalsis stops at the end of the ileum.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Peristaltic waves push digestive fluid through the ileocecal valve into the colon.
alt.ww: Peristalsis continues into and through the colon, including mass movements toward the rectum.

items.q: A nurse reviews how stool consistency is determined in the colon. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Normal fecal matter becomes a soft, formed solid or semisolid mass
Normal colonic water absorption produces soft, formed stool.
Abnormally fast peristalsis produces watery stool
Rapid transit leaves less time for water absorption.
Slowed peristalsis produces a hard stool mass
Slow transit lets water keep being absorbed, causing constipation.
Slowed peristalsis produces watery stool
Slow transit increases absorption and hardens stool.
Stool consistency is set in the stomach and does not change in the colon
Colonic water absorption determines final stool consistency.
items.ex: Transit speed through the colon determines how much water is absorbed and therefore stool consistency.

alt.q: Which statements correctly link colonic movement to stool form? Select all that apply.
o: Less time in the colon means less water is absorbed
Fast peristalsis shortens absorption time, making stool watery.
More time in the colon means more water is absorbed
Slow peristalsis allows continued absorption and hard stool.
Constipation can result when peristaltic contractions slow
A hard stool mass forms when contractions slow.
Watery stool results when peristaltic contractions slow
Watery stool results from abnormally fast peristalsis.
Hard stool results when peristalsis is abnormally fast
Fast peristalsis causes watery, not hard, stool.
alt.ex: Fast colonic transit yields watery stool; slow transit yields hard stool and constipation.

items.q: What does the body expel from the rectum through the anus?
items.a: Feces and flatus
items.ex: The body expels feces and flatus (gas) from the rectum through the anus.
w: Bile and chyme
Bile and chyme are processed in the small intestine before reaching the colon.
Urine and feces
Urine is eliminated through the urinary tract, not the anus.
Gastric juice and mucus
Gastric juice acts in the stomach; the anus expels feces and gas.

alt.q: Through which structure are feces and flatus expelled from the rectum?
alt.a: The anus
alt.ex: Feces and flatus leave the rectum through the anus.
w: The cecum
The cecum is the first part of the large intestine, where contents enter.
The ileocecal valve
The ileocecal valve controls entry from the small intestine into the colon.
The sigmoid colon
The sigmoid colon lies above the rectum and passes stool into it.

items.q: Which nerves innervate the internal and external anal sphincters?
items.a: Sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves
items.ex: The anal sphincters are innervated by sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves, and their contraction and relaxation aid control of defecation.
w: Only sympathetic nerves
The sphincters receive both sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation.
Only parasympathetic nerves
The sphincters receive both parasympathetic and sympathetic innervation.
Only cranial nerves
The book describes sympathetic and parasympathetic innervation of the sphincters.

alt.q: Contraction and relaxation of which structures aid in controlling defecation?
alt.a: The internal and external anal sphincters
alt.ex: The internal and external sphincters, innervated by sympathetic and parasympathetic nerves, aid control of defecation.
w: The upper and lower esophageal sphincters
These control the movement of food into and out of the esophagus.
The ileocecal and pyloric valves
These control movement between parts of the upper GI tract and colon, not defecation.
The ascending and descending colon
These colon segments move contents; the anal sphincters control defecation.

items.q: What does the rich supply of sensory nerves in the anal canal allow a person to do?
items.a: Tell whether solid, liquid, or gas needs to be expelled
items.ex: Sensory nerves in the anal canal distinguish solid, liquid, and gas, which helps maintain continence.
w: Tell whether the stomach is ready for the next meal
Anal sensory nerves sense rectal contents, not stomach capacity.
Tell whether the colon has absorbed enough water
The book does not describe anal nerves sensing colonic water absorption.
Tell whether peristalsis in the small intestine has stopped
Anal sensory nerves sense what is in the anal canal, not small-bowel motility.

alt.q: The sensory nerves of the anal canal mainly help a person maintain which function?
alt.a: Continence
alt.ex: By sensing solid, liquid, or gas, the anal canal’s sensory nerves help maintain continence.
w: Peristalsis
Peristalsis is muscular movement through the GI tract, not a function of anal sensation.
Digestion
Digestion takes place mainly in the stomach and small intestine.
Absorption
Absorption of water and electrolytes occurs in the colon, not through anal sensation.

items.q: Which structures or features aid in controlling defecation at the anus? Select all that apply.
o: Internal anal sphincter
Its contraction and relaxation help control defecation.
External anal sphincter
Its contraction and relaxation help control defecation.
Sensory nerves of the anal canal
They sense solid, liquid, or gas and help maintain continence.
Lower esophageal sphincter
This sphincter prevents gastric reflux into the esophagus.
Ileocecal valve
This valve prevents regurgitation into the small intestine.
items.ex: The internal and external sphincters and the anal canal’s sensory nerves work together to control defecation and continence.

alt.q: A patient asks what helps a person “hold it” until reaching a toilet. Which structures should the nurse mention? Select all that apply.
o: Muscles of the anal sphincters
Contraction of the internal and external sphincters helps control defecation.
Sensory nerves in the anal canal
These nerves sense what needs to be expelled and help maintain continence.
Muscles of the pelvic floor
Pelvic floor and anal sphincter tone help control defecation; weakening makes control harder.
The ileocecal valve
This valve sits between the small intestine and colon.
The upper esophageal sphincter
This sphincter keeps air out of the esophagus.
alt.ex: Sphincter muscles, anal sensory nerves, and pelvic floor tone all help control defecation.

items.q: The anal canal has a rich supply of sensory nerves that help maintain continence.
items.a: True
items.ex: These sensory nerves let a person tell whether solid, liquid, or gas needs to be expelled.
items.ww: The book specifically describes the anal canal as richly supplied with sensory nerves that aid continence.

alt.q: The anal canal has few sensory nerves, so a person cannot sense whether gas or stool is present.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A rich supply of sensory nerves lets people distinguish solid, liquid, and gas in the anal canal.
alt.ww: This sensory ability is what helps people maintain continence.

items.q: Before giving a prescribed enema, the nurse separates the patient’s buttocks and observes a rectal prolapse. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Withhold the enema and notify the health care provider
items.ex: Rectal prolapse contraindicates an enema, so the nurse holds it and reports the finding.
w: Insert the enema tip slowly using extra lubricant
Extra lubricant helps with hemorrhoids, but prolapse contraindicates the enema.
Give the enema with the patient seated on the toilet
Prolapse contraindicates an enema, and the toilet position can injure the rectal wall.
Give a smaller volume of enema solution
Reducing volume does not make an enema safe when prolapse is present.

alt.q: During perianal inspection before an enema, the nurse notes hemorrhoids but no prolapse. Which action is most appropriate?
alt.a: Apply extra water-soluble lubricant to the enema tip
alt.ex: With hemorrhoids present, extra lubricant provides added comfort during insertion.
w: Cancel the enema and notify the health care provider
Hemorrhoids are not listed as a contraindication; prolapse is.
Insert the tip quickly to limit discomfort
Gentle, slow insertion prevents trauma to the rectal mucosa.
Insert the tip directed toward the patient’s spine
The tip is directed toward the umbilicus to follow the rectal curve.

items.q: A patient is tense as the nurse prepares to insert an enema tip. Which instruction by the nurse best relaxes the external anal sphincter?
items.a: “Breathe out slowly through your mouth.”
items.ex: Breathing out slowly through the mouth promotes relaxation of the external anal sphincter.
w: “Hold your breath and bear down.”
Bearing down increases pressure and tension rather than relaxing the sphincter.
“Squeeze your buttocks together.”
Tightening the buttocks contracts rather than relaxes the sphincter.
“Take a deep breath and hold it.”
Holding a breath increases tension; slow exhalation relaxes the sphincter.

alt.q: While inserting a rectal tube for an enema, the nurse touches the patient’s skin next to the anus with the tube tip first. What is the purpose?
alt.a: To promote relaxation of the external anal sphincter
alt.ex: Touching the skin with the tube and having the patient exhale slowly helps relax the external anal sphincter.
w: To check the temperature of the enema solution
Solution temperature is checked before the procedure, not by touching the skin.
To stimulate the vagus nerve and slow peristalsis
Vagal stimulation is a risk of rectal manipulation, not a goal.
To lubricate the perianal skin before insertion
Lubricant is applied to the tube tip, not by touching the skin.

items.q: A patient who has poor anal sphincter control needs an enema. How should the nurse position the patient?
items.a: In a side-lying position in bed with a bedpan under the buttocks
items.ex: Patients with poor sphincter control are given the enema on a bedpan; the toilet position can let the tubing abrade the rectal wall.
w: Sitting upright on the toilet during instillation
Sitting on the toilet is unsafe because the curved rectal tubing can injure the rectal wall.
Standing at the bedside leaning over the bed
Standing is not a recommended enema position and does not address poor sphincter control.
Prone in bed with a waterproof pad under the hips
The side-lying position is used; prone positioning is not described for enemas.

alt.q: A patient asks to sit on the toilet while receiving an enema because of weak sphincter control. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Sitting on the toilet can let the tubing injure your rectum, so I’ll place a bedpan under you in bed.”
alt.ex: The curved rectal tubing can abrade the rectal wall when a patient sits on the toilet; a bedpan is used instead.
w: “Sitting on the toilet is best because it helps you hold the solution longer.”
Sitting on the toilet during instillation is unsafe because of rectal wall injury.
“You can sit on the toilet as long as I insert the tube very slowly.”
Slow insertion does not remove the risk the toilet position creates.
“We will skip the enema because of your weak sphincter control.”
Poor sphincter control is managed with a bedpan; it does not cancel the enema.

items.q: While the nurse inserts a rectal tube for an enema, the tube does not pass easily. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Let a small amount of fluid infuse, then try reinserting slowly
items.ex: Instilled fluid relaxes the sphincter and adds lubrication, so the tube can then be reinserted slowly without force.
w: Push the tube firmly past the resistance
Forcing the tube can traumatize the rectal mucosa or perforate the bowel.
Ask the patient to bear down to open the anus
Bearing down tightens rather than relaxes; slow exhalation and fluid help relax the sphincter.
Insert the tube farther toward the patient’s spine
The tube is directed toward the umbilicus, and forcing it farther risks perforation.

alt.q: Why does allowing a small amount of enema fluid to flow help when the rectal tube meets resistance?
alt.a: The fluid relaxes the sphincter and adds lubrication
alt.ex: Instilled fluid relaxes the anal sphincter and provides extra lubrication for slow reinsertion.
w: The fluid softens the sphincter muscle permanently
Any relaxation is temporary and used only to ease reinsertion.
The fluid stimulates the vagus nerve to open the anus
Vagal stimulation slows the heart rate; it is a risk, not a goal.
The fluid flushes hemorrhoids out of the anal canal
Fluid does not remove hemorrhoids; it relaxes the sphincter and lubricates.

items.q: Which statement best defines fecal incontinence?
items.a: The inability to control the passage of feces and gas from the anus
items.ex: Fecal incontinence is the inability to control passage of feces and gas from the anus.
w: The inability to pass stool despite a strong urge to defecate
This describes difficulty with evacuation, not loss of control.
The passage of fewer than three stools in a week
Infrequent stool relates to constipation, not incontinence.
The passage of large amounts of gas through the mouth
Gas escaping through the mouth is belching, a normal route for intestinal gas.

alt.q: A patient soils clothing several times a day because gas and stool pass without warning. The nurse recognizes which problem?
alt.a: Fecal incontinence
alt.ex: Uncontrolled passage of feces and gas from the anus is fecal incontinence.
w: Fecal impaction
Impaction is a hardened stool mass retained in the rectum.
Flatulence
Flatulence is gas causing fullness and cramping, not loss of control of stool.
Hemorrhoids
Hemorrhoids are dilated rectal veins, not uncontrolled passage of stool.

items.q: Which conditions often contribute to fecal incontinence? Select all that apply.
o: Conditions that impair anal sphincter function
Physical conditions affecting the sphincter often cause incontinence.
Large-volume liquid stools such as diarrhea

Peristalsis declines, rather than speeds up, in older adults.
Reduced number of diverticula in the colon

w: Stronger perineal floor tone
Perineal floor tone weakens rather than strengthens with age.
Faster esophageal emptying

Increased chewing ability

items.q: During digital removal of an impacted stool, the patient’s pulse drops significantly. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Stop the procedure
items.ex: Rectal manipulation stimulates the vagus nerve and can slow the heart rate; stop if the pulse drops significantly or rhythm changes.
w: Speed up removal to finish quickly
Continued manipulation further stimulates the vagus nerve and can worsen bradycardia.
Give an enema to soften the mass
Stopping manipulation takes priority over further rectal intervention.
Ask the patient to bear down
Bearing down does not address the falling pulse; the procedure must stop.

alt.q: Why does the nurse periodically reassess the pulse during digital removal of stool?
alt.a: Rectal manipulation can stimulate the vagus nerve and slow the heart rate
alt.ex: Excess rectal manipulation stimulates the vagus nerve, which sometimes causes a reflex slowing of the heart rate.
w: Rectal manipulation can stimulate the sympathetic nerves and raise blood pressure
The book warns of vagal stimulation and slowing of the heart rate.
Rectal manipulation can cause fluid shifts and rapid dehydration
The concern described is a reflex drop in heart rate, not fluid loss.
Rectal manipulation can release toxins that cause tachycardia
Vagal stimulation slows, rather than speeds, the heart rate.

items.q: [[Anorectal manometry|anal manometry]] measures the pressure activity of the internal and external anal sphincters and reflexes during rectal distention.
items.ex: Anorectal manometry also measures relaxation during straining and rectal sensation.

items.q: Weakened abdominal and pelvic floor muscles impair a person’s ability to control the external anal sphincter.

items.ex: Weak abdominal and pelvic floor muscles impair the ability to increase intraabdominal pressure and control the external sphincter.
items.ww: Muscle tone used in defecation, lost through illness or nerve damage, affects sphincter control.

alt.a: False

items.q: A patient with painful swollen hemorrhoids receives teaching. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “My goal is soft, formed bowel movements that don’t hurt.”
items.ex: The primary goal for a patient with hemorrhoids is soft-formed, painless bowel movements, helped by diet, fluids, and exercise.

Straining increases venous pressure and worsens hemorrhoids.

Adequate fluids keep stools soft; hard stools cause bleeding and irritation.

Suppressing the urge leads to constipation and hard, irritating stools.

alt.q: Which measure can the nurse suggest for temporary relief of swollen hemorrhoids?

Proper diet and fluids keep stools soft; restricting them leads to hard stools.
Strict bed rest until the swelling is gone
Regular exercise improves the likelihood of soft stools.
A daily stimulant laxative
Regular stimulant laxative use is avoided because the bowel becomes dependent.

items.q: The embarrassment of soiling clothes from fecal incontinence often leads to social isolation.

alt.q: Fecal incontinence is a physical problem that seldom affects a patient’s body image.
alt.a: False

items.q: Before inserting an enema tip, the nurse inspects the perianal region. Which abnormalities is the nurse looking for? Select all that apply.

Anal fissure
Fissures are among the perianal abnormalities inspected for.
Rectal prolapse
Prolapse contraindicates an enema.
Diverticula
Diverticula are outpouchings of the intestinal wall and are not seen on perianal inspection.
Ileus
An ileus is a cessation of peristalsis, not a visible perianal finding.
items.ex: Perianal inspection checks for hemorrhoids, anal fissure, and rectal prolapse, which influence or contraindicate the enema.

Anal fissure

Intact perianal skin with no lesions

Soft, formed stool on the perianal skin

alt.ex: Findings on perianal inspection, such as prolapse, hemorrhoids, or fissure, guide whether and how to insert the tip.

items.q: Which physiological factors are essential to normal bowel function and defecation? Select all that apply.
o: Normal GI tract function
Normal GI function is one of the essential physiological factors.

Awareness of rectal distention signals the need to defecate.
Voluntary sphincter control
Voluntary control of the sphincter allows defecation at an appropriate time.
Adequate rectal capacity and compliance
The rectum must be able to hold and stretch with stool.
Continuous presence of stool in the rectum
The rectum is normally empty until just before defecation.
Rapid peristalsis through the colon
Abnormally fast peristalsis causes watery stool, not normal defecation.
items.ex: Normal defecation requires normal GI function, rectal sensory awareness, voluntary sphincter control, and adequate rectal capacity and compliance.

Sensing rectal distention and contents is essential to defecation.

Voluntary sphincter control is an essential factor.
Rectal capacity and compliance
Adequate rectal capacity and compliance are essential.
Production of intrinsic factor
Intrinsic factor aids B12 absorption in digestion, not defecation.
Function of the lower esophageal sphincter
This sphincter prevents gastric reflux and is not part of defecation.
alt.ex: Rectal sensation, voluntary sphincter control, and rectal capacity and compliance are essential components of defecation.

items.q: Where does normal defecation begin?
items.a: With movement in the left colon
items.ex: Normal defecation begins with movement in the left colon, moving stool toward the anus.
w: With movement in the cecum
The cecum is where contents enter the colon; defecation begins in the left colon.
With relaxation of the external sphincter
External sphincter relaxation occurs later, at the time of defecation.
With contraction of the abdominal muscles
Abdominal contraction occurs at the time of expulsion, after stool reaches the rectum.

alt.q: Movement in which part of the colon starts the process of normal defecation?
alt.a: The left colon
alt.ex: Normal defecation begins with movement in the left colon, pushing stool toward the anus.
w: The right colon
The book identifies the left colon as where defecation begins.
The cecum
The cecum receives contents from the ileum and is not where defecation begins.
The ileum
The ileum is part of the small intestine.

items.q: What causes the internal anal sphincter to relax during normal defecation?
items.a: Distention of the rectum when stool reaches it
items.ex: When stool reaches the rectum, distention relaxes the internal sphincter and creates awareness of the need to defecate.
w: Voluntary contraction of the abdominal muscles
Abdominal contraction increases intrarectal pressure at the time of expulsion.
Movement of food into the stomach
The book links internal sphincter relaxation to rectal distention, not stomach filling.
Relaxation of the external sphincter
External sphincter relaxation follows internal relaxation at the time of defecation.

alt.q: What happens when stool reaches and distends the rectum?
alt.a: The internal sphincter relaxes and the person becomes aware of the urge
alt.ex: Rectal distention relaxes the internal sphincter and produces awareness of the need to defecate.
w: The external sphincter contracts and the urge disappears
Distention produces awareness of the urge, and the internal sphincter relaxes.
The ileocecal valve opens and stool moves backward
The ileocecal valve prevents backflow into the small intestine.
The abdominal muscles relax and peristalsis stops
Abdominal muscles contract at the time of defecation to raise intrarectal pressure.

items.q: At the time of defecation, what increases intrarectal pressure to force stool out?
items.a: Contraction of the abdominal muscles
items.ex: As the external sphincter relaxes, abdominal muscles contract, increasing intrarectal pressure and forcing stool out.
w: Contraction of the external sphincter
The external sphincter relaxes, not contracts, at the time of defecation.
Relaxation of the abdominal muscles
The abdominal muscles must contract to raise intrarectal pressure.
Closure of the ileocecal valve
The ileocecal valve prevents backflow into the small intestine and does not expel stool.

alt.q: A patient with weakened abdominal muscles after long-term illness has difficulty passing stool. Which part of defecation is most affected?
alt.a: Increasing intrarectal pressure to expel stool
alt.ex: Abdominal muscle contraction raises intrarectal pressure; weakened muscles impair this and increase the risk for constipation.
w: Sensing that stool is in the rectum
Sensory awareness depends on nerves, not abdominal muscle strength.
Moving stool through the left colon
Colonic movement is peristaltic, not driven by abdominal muscles.
Relaxing the internal sphincter
Internal sphincter relaxation is triggered by rectal distention.

items.q: When stool reaches the rectum, distention causes the internal sphincter to relax.
items.a: True
items.ex: Rectal distention relaxes the internal sphincter and creates awareness of the need to defecate.
items.ww: The book links internal sphincter relaxation directly to rectal distention by stool.

alt.q: When stool first reaches the rectum, the external sphincter relaxes automatically and stool is expelled.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Rectal distention relaxes the internal sphincter; the external sphincter relaxes later, at the time of defecation.
alt.ww: External sphincter relaxation is under voluntary control and occurs only when the person defecates.

items.q: A patient tells the nurse, “I have to strain to have a bowel movement most days.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Let’s review what you eat and drink, because straining can mean changes are needed.”
items.ex: Straining suggests a need for changes in diet or fluid intake or an underlying GI disorder, so assessment comes first.
w: “Straining is normal, so there is no need to change anything.”
Normal defecation is painless and passes soft stool; straining is not normal.
“You should take a stimulant laxative every day to stop straining.”
Regular stimulant laxative use causes dependence; fiber laxatives are tried first.
“Straining harder will help train your bowel to work faster.”
Straining raises venous pressure and can cause hemorrhoids.

alt.q: A home health nurse learns that an older adult has been straining with bowel movements. What should the nurse conclude from this finding?
alt.a: Diet or fluid changes may be needed or a GI disorder may be present
alt.ex: Straining indicates the patient may need diet or fluid changes or that there is an underlying disorder in GI function.
w: Normal bowel function with healthy abdominal muscles
Straining is not part of normal, painless defecation.
Rapid peristalsis with large-volume liquid stools
Liquid stools from rapid transit do not require straining.
Expected aging that needs no further assessment
Straining warrants assessment of diet, fluids, and GI function.

items.q: Which description reflects normal defecation?
items.a: Painless passage of soft, formed stool
items.ex: Normally defecation is painless and results in the passage of soft, formed stool.
w: Passage of hard stool with mild pain
Hard stool and pain suggest constipation or another problem, not normal defecation.
Passage of liquid stool with cramping
Liquid stool with cramping suggests rapid transit or diarrhea.
Passage of formed stool with straining
Straining indicates a need for dietary change or an underlying disorder.

alt.q: Which bowel elimination finding would the nurse document as normal?
alt.a: A soft, formed stool passed without discomfort
alt.ex: Normal defecation is painless and produces soft, formed stool.
w: A hard, dry stool passed after straining
Hard stool with straining indicates constipation.
A watery stool passed with urgency
Watery stool reflects abnormally fast transit.
Small, hard pieces of stool passed with pain
Pain and hard stool are not normal defecation.

items.q: A patient with a spinal cord injury does not feel when stool fills the rectum. Which essential component of defecation is impaired?
items.a: Sensory awareness of rectal distention
items.ex: Sensory awareness of rectal distention and contents is essential; without it, the patient cannot recognize the need to defecate.
w: Adequate rectal capacity and compliance
Capacity and compliance refer to the rectum’s ability to hold stool, not to sensation.
Normal small intestine absorption
The patient’s problem is sensing rectal contents, not absorbing nutrients.
Ileocecal valve function
The ileocecal valve prevents backflow into the small intestine.

alt.q: A patient can feel the urge to defecate but cannot hold stool until reaching the toilet. Which essential component of defecation is most likely impaired?
alt.a: Voluntary sphincter control
alt.ex: Voluntary sphincter control allows a person to delay defecation until an appropriate time.
w: Sensory awareness of rectal contents
The patient feels the urge, so sensory awareness is present.
Movement of stool in the left colon
Stool is reaching the rectum, so colonic movement is occurring.
Normal gastric acid secretion
Gastric acid aids digestion and is not involved in holding stool.

items.q: Normally, defecation is painless and results in the passage of [[soft, formed|soft formed|soft and formed]] stool.
items.ex: Normal colonic water absorption and an intact defecation process produce soft, formed stool without pain.

alt.q: Straining or pain is not expected, because normal bowel movements produce [[soft, formed|soft formed|soft and formed]] stool.
alt.ex: Normal colonic water absorption and an intact defecation process produce soft, formed stool without pain.

items.q: Which anal sphincter does a person relax voluntarily at the time of defecation?
items.a: The external sphincter
items.ex: The external sphincter relaxes at the time of defecation and is under voluntary control.
w: The internal sphincter
The internal sphincter relaxes in response to rectal distention, before the person chooses to defecate.

items.q: Chavela, age 78, has frequent constipation and tells the home health nurse that she strains with every bowel movement. Which action should the nurse take first?
