alt.q: A patient remains inactive and is unable to eat after bowel surgery. How will this affect the patient’s ileus?
alt.a: Return of normal bowel elimination will be further delayed
alt.ex: Inactivity and not eating after surgery further delay the return of normal bowel elimination.
w: Normal bowel elimination will return sooner than usual
Inactivity and lack of intake slow, not speed, recovery.
The ileus will turn into diarrhea within 24 hours
Inactivity and no intake prolong the ileus rather than cause diarrhea.
Inactivity and diet will have no effect on the ileus
The book states both further delay return of bowel function.

items.q: What is the effect or role of Opioid analgesics?
items.a: Slow peristalsis, often causing constipation
items.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.
w: Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea
That goes with Antibiotics.
Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum
That goes with Fiber laxatives.
Used next if fiber does not relieve constipation
That goes with Osmotic laxatives.

alt.q: What is the effect or role of Antibiotics?
alt.a: Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea
alt.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.
w: Slow peristalsis, often causing constipation
That goes with Opioid analgesics.
Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum
That goes with Fiber laxatives.
Used next if fiber does not relieve constipation
That goes with Osmotic laxatives.

alt.q: What is the effect or role of Fiber laxatives?
alt.a: Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum
alt.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.
w: Slow peristalsis, often causing constipation
That goes with Opioid analgesics.
Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea
That goes with Antibiotics.
Used next if fiber does not relieve constipation
That goes with Osmotic laxatives.

alt.q: What is the effect or role of Osmotic laxatives?
alt.a: Used next if fiber does not relieve constipation
alt.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.
w: Slow peristalsis, often causing constipation
That goes with Opioid analgesics.
Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea
That goes with Antibiotics.
Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum
That goes with Fiber laxatives.

alt.q: What is the effect or role of Stimulant laxatives?
alt.a: Avoid regular use because the bowel becomes dependent
alt.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.
w: Slow peristalsis, often causing constipation
That goes with Opioid analgesics.
Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea
That goes with Antibiotics.
Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum
That goes with Fiber laxatives.

alt.q: Which medication type is described as “Slow peristalsis, often causing constipation”?
alt.a: Opioid analgesics
alt.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.
w: Antibiotics
Antibiotics: Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea.
Fiber laxatives
Fiber laxatives: Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum.
Osmotic laxatives
Osmotic laxatives: Used next if fiber does not relieve constipation.

alt.q: Which medication type is described as “Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea”?
alt.a: Antibiotics
alt.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.
w: Opioid analgesics
Opioid analgesics: Slow peristalsis, often causing constipation.
Fiber laxatives
Fiber laxatives: Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum.
Osmotic laxatives
Osmotic laxatives: Used next if fiber does not relieve constipation.

alt.q: Which medication type is described as “Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum”?
alt.a: Fiber laxatives
alt.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.
w: Opioid analgesics
Opioid analgesics: Slow peristalsis, often causing constipation.
Antibiotics
Antibiotics: Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea.
Osmotic laxatives
Osmotic laxatives: Used next if fiber does not relieve constipation.

alt.q: Which medication type is described as “Used next if fiber does not relieve constipation”?
alt.a: Osmotic laxatives
alt.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.
w: Opioid analgesics
Opioid analgesics: Slow peristalsis, often causing constipation.
Antibiotics
Antibiotics: Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea.
Fiber laxatives
Fiber laxatives: Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum.

alt.q: Which medication type is described as “Avoid regular use because the bowel becomes dependent”?
alt.a: Stimulant laxatives
alt.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.
w: Opioid analgesics
Opioid analgesics: Slow peristalsis, often causing constipation.
Antibiotics
Antibiotics: Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea.
Fiber laxatives
Fiber laxatives: Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum.

mt.q: Match each medication with its effect on bowel elimination.
pairs: Decrease intestinal flora, often causing diarrhea
Used first for regular evacuation of the rectum
Used next if fiber does not relieve constipation
Avoid regular use because the bowel becomes dependent
mt.ex: Opioids constipate, antibiotics cause diarrhea, and laxatives progress from fiber to osmotic, avoiding regular stimulant use.

items.q: A patient who needs a laxative for regular evacuation of the rectum asks which type to try. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “A fiber laxative is usually tried first.”
items.ex: Fiber laxatives are used first; an osmotic laxative is used next if fiber does not relieve constipation.
w: “A stimulant laxative is usually tried first.”
Regular stimulant use is avoided because the intestine becomes dependent.
“An osmotic laxative should always be tried first.”
Osmotic laxatives are used after fiber laxatives fail.
“An enema should be given daily before any laxative.”
Fiber laxatives are the first step; daily enemas are not the first choice.

alt.q: A patient taking a fiber laxative still has constipation. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the next step?
alt.a: “The next type to try is an osmotic laxative.”
alt.ex: An osmotic laxative is used next if fiber laxatives do not relieve constipation.
w: “The next type to try is a daily stimulant laxative.”
Regular stimulant laxative use causes dependence.
“The next step is to stop drinking extra fluids.”
Reduced fluid hardens stool and worsens constipation.
“The next step is to double my opioid dose.”
Opioids slow peristalsis and cause constipation.

items.q: Which factors increase a patient’s risk for constipation? Select all that apply.
o: Taking opioid analgesics
Opioids slow peristalsis and contractions, often causing constipation.
Prolonged immobilization
Immobility slows peristalsis.
Low fluid and fiber intake
Reduced fluid and fiber harden stool and slow transit.
Ignoring the urge to defecate
Suppressing the urge disrupts habits and causes constipation.
Taking antibiotics
Antibiotics decrease intestinal flora and often cause diarrhea.
Prolonged emotional stress
Stress increases peristalsis and tends to cause diarrhea.
items.ex: Opioids, immobility, low fluid and fiber, and ignoring the urge all promote constipation.

alt.q: A nurse reviews several patients’ histories. Which patients are at increased risk for constipation? Select all that apply.
o: A patient in the third trimester of pregnancy
Slowed peristalsis and fetal pressure on the rectum cause constipation.
A patient with depression
Depression may slow autonomic impulses and peristalsis.
A patient with weakened pelvic floor muscles after a spinal cord injury
Weak abdominal and pelvic floor muscles increase constipation risk.
A patient taking antibiotics for an infection
Antibiotics tend to cause diarrhea.
A patient who walks several times a day
Physical activity promotes peristalsis.
alt.ex: Late pregnancy, depression, and weakened abdominal and pelvic floor muscles all increase constipation risk.

items.q: A patient had a colonoscopy this morning and reports increased gas and loose stools. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “These changes are common and usually resolve once you resume your normal eating pattern.”
items.ex: After GI visualization procedures, increased gas or loose stools often occur until normal eating resumes.
w: “These changes mean the bowel was injured and need immediate surgery.”
Gas and loose stools are expected after bowel preparation and visualization.
“These changes mean you should not eat for another 24 hours.”
Resuming a normal eating pattern helps elimination return to normal.
“These changes mean you need a stimulant laxative tonight.”
Loose stools do not call for a laxative; regular stimulant use is avoided.

alt.q: Why do patients need a prescribed bowel preparation before examinations such as a colonoscopy?
alt.a: To ensure that the bowel is empty for visualization
alt.ex: Visualization of GI structures requires a bowel preparation, such as laxatives and/or enemas, so the bowel is empty.
w: To increase intestinal flora for accurate results
Bowel prep empties the bowel; antibiotics, not prep, alter flora.
To slow peristalsis during the examination
The purpose is to empty the bowel, not to slow peristalsis.
To harden stool so it can be seen more clearly
The bowel must be empty, not filled with hard stool.

items.q: Which bowel pattern is listed as a sign of constipation?
items.a: Fewer than three bowel movements per week
items.ex: Infrequent bowel movements, fewer than three per week, are a sign of constipation.
w: Fewer than three bowel movements per day
Several stools per day is not a sign of constipation; adults may normally go up to three times daily.
Fewer than one bowel movement every 2 days
Going every 2 days can still be within the normal adult range of twice daily to three times a week.
Fewer than seven bowel movements per week
Fewer than seven per week is not the cutoff; the book uses fewer than three per week.

alt.q: A patient reports having two bowel movements in the past 7 days. Based on frequency alone, how should the nurse interpret this pattern?
alt.a: It is consistent with constipation
alt.ex: Fewer than three bowel movements per week is a sign of constipation.
w: It is consistent with diarrhea
Diarrhea is an increase in the number of liquid, unformed stools, not fewer stools.
It is consistent with fecal impaction
Impaction is an inability to expel hardened retained feces, identified by palpating a mass, not by frequency alone.
It is a normal adult pattern
A normal adult pattern ranges from twice daily to three times a week, so two per week is below normal.

items.q: Why does slowed intestinal motility lead to a hard, dry stool?
items.a: The fecal mass stays in contact with the intestinal wall longer, so most of its water is absorbed
items.ex: When motility slows, exposure to the intestinal wall lets most fecal water be absorbed, leaving little to soften the stool.
w: The colon secretes extra mucus that binds the fecal mass into a firm, dry stool
Increased mucus secretion is linked to colonic irritation and watery diarrhea, not hard stool.
The small intestine stops absorbing nutrients, so dense undigested food fills the colon
The problem is excess water absorption from the slow-moving mass, not loss of nutrient absorption.
The anal sphincter tightens with each delay, compressing the stool into a dry mass
Sphincter tightening does not dry stool; prolonged contact with the bowel wall removes the water.

alt.q: A patient asks why constipation makes stools so painful to pass. Which explanation is accurate?
alt.a: When stool moves slowly, the bowel absorbs most of its water, leaving a dry, hard mass
alt.ex: Slow motility leaves little water to soften and lubricate the stool, and passing dry, hard stool often causes rectal pain.
w: When stool moves slowly, the bowel adds fluid to it, making a bulky, swollen mass
The bowel removes water from slow-moving stool; it does not add fluid.
When stool moves quickly, the bowel cannot absorb water, so it forms a sharp mass
Rapid passage leaves stool watery, as in diarrhea, not hard.
When stool moves quickly, mucus coats it heavily, so the rectum becomes irritated
Rapid passage with increased mucus describes diarrhea rather than constipation.

items.q: A patient who had abdominal surgery yesterday is receiving opioids for pain. Which bowel elimination intervention should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: A stool softener or laxative to prevent constipation
items.ex: Patients receiving opioids for pain after surgery often require a stool softener or laxative to prevent constipation.
w: An antidiarrheal agent to slow peristalsis
Opioids already slow motility; an antidiarrheal would worsen the risk of constipation.
A low-fiber diet to reduce intestinal gas
A low-fiber diet is listed as a cause of constipation, not a preventive measure.
Fluid restriction to limit liquid stools
Low fluid intake contributes to constipation and hard stools.

alt.q: Which medication class does the textbook single out as an especially common cause of constipation?
alt.a: Opiates
alt.ex: Box 47.1 lists medications, especially opiates, among the common causes of constipation.
w: Antibiotics
Antibiotics alter normal flora and are linked to diarrhea, including C. difficile infection.
Topical hemorrhoid medications
Topical medications relieve hemorrhoid swelling and pain; they are not a listed cause of constipation.
Stool softeners
Stool softeners are used to prevent constipation, not cause it.

items.q: Which factors are common causes of constipation? Select all that apply.
o: Ignoring the urge to defecate
Irregular bowel habits and ignoring the urge are listed causes of constipation.
Physical inactivity
Lack of exercise slows bowel elimination and is a listed cause.
Low-fiber diet high in animal fats
A low-fiber diet high in animal fats is a common cause.
Spinal cord injury
Neurological conditions that block nerve impulses to the colon cause constipation.
High fluid intake
Low fluid intake, not high intake, contributes to constipation.
Recent antibiotic therapy
Antibiotics alter GI flora and are associated with diarrhea, not constipation.
items.ex: Box 47.1 lists irregular habits, chronic illness, low-fiber diet, low fluids, stress, inactivity, opiates, life changes, and neurological conditions.

alt.q: A nurse reviews the histories of several patients. Which patients have a risk factor for constipation? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with Parkinson disease
Chronic illnesses such as Parkinson disease are listed causes of constipation.
A patient grieving the recent death of a spouse
Stress, such as the death of a loved one, can cause constipation.
A patient who has been traveling for 2 weeks
Changes in routine, such as travel, are listed causes.
A patient who drinks about 3 L of fluid daily
Adequate fluid intake helps keep stool soft rather than causing constipation.
A patient who walks briskly for 45 minutes daily
Regular exercise stimulates peristalsis; inactivity is the risk factor.
alt.ex: Chronic illness, stress, and changes in routine are among the common causes of constipation in Box 47.1.

items.q: Constipation is a symptom rather than a disease.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states constipation is a symptom, not a disease, with many possible causes such as diet, fluids, inactivity, and medications.
items.ww: Calling constipation a disease ignores that it results from many different underlying causes.

alt.q: Constipation is a disease with a single underlying cause that is treated the same way in every patient.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Constipation is a symptom with many possible causes, so the nurse assesses each patient for the likely cause.
alt.ww: Because constipation has many causes, treatment depends on the cause in each patient.

items.q: Which patients are most at risk for developing a fecal impaction?
items.a: Patients who are debilitated, confused, or unconscious
items.ex: Debilitated, confused, or unconscious patients may be dehydrated, too weak, or unaware of the need to defecate.
w: Patients who are ambulatory, alert, and eating a high-fiber diet
Mobility, alertness, and fiber all help prevent hard, retained stool.
Patients who are taking antibiotics for a urinary tract infection
Antibiotics are a risk factor for diarrhea and C. difficile, not impaction.
Patients who are recovering at home after a minor outpatient procedure
Minor procedures do not place patients in the highest-risk group for impaction.

alt.q: Why are unconscious patients at high risk for fecal impaction?
alt.a: They are unaware of the urge to defecate, so stool becomes too hard and dry to pass
alt.ex: Patients unaware of the need to defecate retain stool until it is too hard and dry to pass.
w: They produce more intestinal mucus, so stool becomes too sticky to pass
Increased mucus is associated with colonic irritation and diarrhea, not impaction.
They absorb less water from the colon, so stool becomes too bulky to pass
Impaction involves stool that has lost water and become hard, not bulky watery stool.
They have faster peristalsis, so stool reaches the rectum before it softens
Faster peristalsis produces liquid stool, not a hardened mass.

items.q: A confused older adult in long-term care has not passed a formed stool for 5 days and now has a continuous ooze of liquid stool. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Gently perform a digital examination of the rectum to palpate for a mass
items.ex: Continuous oozing of liquid stool suggests impaction; the nurse gently performs a digital rectal examination to palpate for the impacted mass.
w: Give an antidiarrheal agent to slow the liquid stool
The liquid is seeping around an impacted mass; slowing motility would not relieve the impaction.
Collect a stool specimen and wait for culture results
Waiting for a culture delays recognizing the likely impaction behind the ooze.
Apply a fecal collector and document the diarrhea
Treating the ooze as diarrhea misses the impaction causing it.

alt.q: A nurse notes that a debilitated patient has a continuous seepage of liquid stool after several days without a bowel movement. What does this finding most likely indicate?
alt.a: Liquid feces from higher in the colon is seeping around an impacted mass
alt.ex: Suspect an impaction when continuous oozing of liquid stool occurs, because liquid feces seeps around the hardened mass.
w: An infection is causing large-volume diarrhea from the small intestine
Several days without a stool followed by oozing points to impaction rather than infectious diarrhea.
The anal sphincter has lost tone, so normal stool cannot be retained
Loss of sphincter control causes incontinence of normal stool, not oozing after days without a bowel movement.
Hemorrhoids are producing a watery discharge from the rectal veins
Hemorrhoids are dilated veins; they do not produce liquid stool.

items.q: The parent of an infant with diarrhea calls the clinic. Which finding reported by the parent is a sign of dehydration?
items.a: No wet diapers for the past 4 hours
items.ex: No wet diapers for 3 hours or more is a sign of dehydration in infants and young children.
w: Tears present when the infant cries
No tears when crying is the dehydration sign; tears suggest adequate hydration.
A moist mouth and tongue
A dry mouth and tongue, not a moist one, indicates dehydration.
Alert and responsive behavior
Listlessness or irritability, not alertness, is a sign of dehydration.

alt.q: Which finding in a 9-month-old with diarrhea most indicates dehydration?
alt.a: Sunken soft spot on the skull
alt.ex: A sunken soft spot, eyes, or cheeks is a sign of dehydration in infants and young children.
w: Bulging soft spot on the skull
The soft spot sinks, rather than bulges, with dehydration.
Frequent wet diapers
Absence of wet diapers for 3 hours or more signals dehydration.
Tears with crying
Absence of tears when crying signals dehydration.

items.q: Which findings are signs of dehydration in an adult with diarrhea? Select all that apply.
o: Dark-colored urine
Dark urine is a listed sign of dehydration in adults.
Less frequent urination than usual
Decreased urination reflects fluid loss.
Dizziness or light-headedness
Dizziness and light-headedness are listed adult signs.
Thirst
Thirst is a sign of dehydration in adults.
Moist, supple skin
Dry skin, not moist skin, is a sign of dehydration.
Pale, dilute urine
Dilute urine suggests adequate hydration rather than fluid loss.
items.ex: Box 47.2 lists thirst, less frequent urination, dark urine, dry skin, fatigue, dizziness, and light-headedness as adult dehydration signs.

alt.q: A nurse teaches an older adult with diarrhea which signs of dehydration to report. Which signs should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Dry skin
Dry skin is a listed sign of dehydration in adults.
Fatigue
Fatigue is a listed sign of dehydration in adults.
Urinating less often than usual
Less frequent urination signals fluid loss.
Increased urine output
Dehydration decreases, rather than increases, urination.
Pale yellow urine
Dark-colored urine, not pale urine, signals dehydration.
alt.ex: Adults with dehydration may have thirst, dry skin, fatigue, dizziness, less frequent urination, and dark urine.

items.q: Meticulous skin care and containment of fecal drainage are necessary for a patient with repeated diarrhea stools.
items.a: True
items.ex: Repeated diarrhea exposes perineal and buttock skin to irritating intestinal contents, so skin care and containment prevent breakdown.
items.ww: Diarrhea is irritating to the skin, so skipping careful skin care risks skin breakdown.

alt.q: Because diarrhea stools are mostly water, they rarely irritate the skin of the perineum and buttocks.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Diarrhea stools contain irritating intestinal contents that can cause skin breakdown without meticulous skin care.
alt.ww: Watery stool still carries irritating contents, so the risk to skin is high, not rare.

items.q: A nurse is leaving the room of a patient with Clostridium difficile infection. Which hand hygiene action is best?
items.a: Wash hands with soap and water
items.ex: Only hand hygiene with soap and water is effective to physically remove C. difficile spores from the hands.
w: Use an alcohol-based hand rub
Alcohol rubs do not physically remove C. difficile spores; soap and water are required.
Remove gloves without further hand hygiene
Hand hygiene is still needed after glove removal to prevent spreading spores.
Wipe hands with a disinfectant cloth
The book specifies soap and water as the only effective way to remove spores from hands.

alt.q: A nursing student asks why soap and water are used instead of hand gel after caring for a patient with C. difficile. Which response is accurate?
alt.a: Only soap and water physically removes C. difficile spores from the hands
alt.ex: Soap-and-water hand hygiene is the only method effective for physically removing C. difficile spores.
w: Only soap and water kills the bacteria that remain on the gloves
The point is removing spores from the hands, not treating the gloves.
Hand gel causes skin irritation that lets the spores enter the body
Skin irritation is not the reason; gel does not remove the spores.
Hand gel is reserved for patients on airborne precautions
C. difficile hand hygiene is about spore removal, not the type of precautions.

items.q: A patient with a positive test for C. difficile is being admitted. Which room assignment is preferred?
items.a: A private room with a dedicated toilet, on contact/enteric precautions
items.ex: Patients with C. difficile are placed on contact/enteric isolation precautions, preferably in a private room with a dedicated toilet.
w: A semiprivate room with a shared toilet, on standard precautions
A shared toilet allows transmission; contact/enteric precautions are required.
A private room with negative airflow, on airborne precautions
C. difficile spreads by contact with hands and surfaces, not through the air.
A semiprivate room with a bedside commode, on droplet precautions
Droplet precautions do not address contact spread of C. difficile.

alt.q: Why is a private room with a dedicated toilet preferred for a patient with C. difficile?
alt.a: It helps prevent transmission of the organism to other patients
alt.ex: Patients are exposed to C. difficile through hands and contaminated surfaces, so a dedicated toilet helps prevent spread.
w: It allows the patient to receive antibiotics without interruption
Room assignment does not affect antibiotic administration.
It lets the nurse measure liquid stool output more accurately
Measuring output is not the reason for the private room and toilet.
It protects the patient from airborne organisms carried by visitors
The goal is preventing contact spread of C. difficile to others.

items.q: Which factors place a patient most at risk for Clostridium difficile infection? Select all that apply.
o: Clindamycin therapy
Antibiotics such as clindamycin alter normal flora and allow C. difficile overgrowth.
Long stay in a health care setting
Long stays in health care settings increase exposure and risk.
Immunocompromising condition
Immunocompromising conditions are a listed risk factor.
Advanced age
Advanced age places patients most at risk.
High-fiber diet
Diet is not a listed risk factor for C. difficile.
Regular aerobic exercise
Exercise is not related to C. difficile risk.
items.ex: Antibiotic use, GI surgery or manipulation, long health care stays, immunocompromise, and advanced age put patients most at risk for C. difficile.

alt.q: A nurse reviews the records of several patients with new diarrhea. Which patients have a risk factor for C. difficile? Select all that apply.
o: A patient receiving a third-generation cephalosporin
Third- or fourth-generation cephalosporins are high-risk antibiotics.
A patient who recently had gastrointestinal surgery
GI surgery or manipulation increases risk.
A patient receiving a fluoroquinolone
Fluoroquinolones are listed high-risk antibiotics.
A patient who is newly lactose intolerant
Lactose intolerance causes diarrhea from milk sugar, not C. difficile risk.
A patient who recently started a stool softener
Stool softeners are not a listed risk factor for C. difficile.
alt.ex: High-risk antibiotics and GI surgery or manipulation are listed risk factors for C. difficile infection.

items.q: An alcohol-based hand rub is sufficient to remove Clostridium difficile spores from the hands.
items.a: False
items.ex: Only hand hygiene with soap and water physically removes C. difficile spores.
items.ww: Alcohol rubs do not physically remove spores, so soap and water are required.

alt.q: Washing with soap and water is the only hand hygiene method that physically removes C. difficile spores.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The book states only soap-and-water hand hygiene is effective against C. difficile spores on the hands.
alt.ww: Relying on hand rub alone would leave spores on the hands and spread infection.

items.q: A patient has diarrhea caused by a foodborne pathogen. What is usually the goal of treatment?
items.a: To rid the GI system of the pathogen rather than slow peristalsis
items.ex: With foodborne pathogens, the goal is usually to rid the GI tract of the organism rather than slow peristalsis.
w: To slow peristalsis so the pathogen stays in the colon longer
Slowing motility would keep the pathogen in the bowel, which is not the goal.
To add fiber so the pathogen is bound into formed stool
Fiber is not the treatment goal for foodborne diarrhea.
To restrict fluids so the volume of watery stool decreases
Restricting fluids risks dehydration; fluid replacement is needed with diarrhea.

alt.q: A patient with diarrhea from contaminated food asks why the health care provider did not order a drug to stop it. Which explanation is best?
alt.a: The goal is usually to clear the pathogen from the bowel, not to slow it down
alt.ex: When diarrhea results from a foodborne pathogen, the aim is to rid the GI system of the pathogen rather than slow peristalsis.
w: The goal is to let the pathogen reach the small intestine and be absorbed
Absorbing the pathogen is not the aim; clearing it from the GI tract is.
Antidiarrheal drugs are never used for any type of diarrhea
Antidiarrheals are used for some conditions; they are just not the goal here.
Diarrhea from food always resolves without fluid replacement
Diarrhea can cause dehydration, so fluid replacement may be needed.

items.q: A patient reports abdominal pain, bloating, gas, and diarrhea within a few hours of drinking cow’s milk. Which condition do these findings suggest?
items.a: Lactose intolerance
items.ex: People who cannot digest milk sugar often have pain, nausea, bloating, gas, and diarrhea after drinking cow’s milk.
w: Celiac disease
Celiac disease is an immune disease in which eating gluten damages the small intestine.
Fecal impaction
Impaction is retained hardened feces, not a reaction within hours of drinking milk.
Hemorrhoids
Hemorrhoids are dilated rectal veins and do not cause food-related diarrhea.

alt.q: A patient states, “Every time I eat bread or pasta, my small intestine gets damaged.” Which condition is the patient describing?
alt.a: Celiac disease
alt.ex: Celiac disease is an immune disease in which eating gluten damages the small intestine.
w: Lactose intolerance
Lactose intolerance is a reaction to milk sugar, not gluten.
Flatulence
Flatulence is gas accumulation in the intestines, not immune damage from gluten.
C. difficile infection
C. difficile is an infection linked to antibiotics and contact with the organism.

items.q: In which situation does flatulence most often cause abdominal distention and severe, sharp pain?
items.a: When intestinal motility is reduced by opiates, anesthesia, surgery, or immobility
items.ex: Flatulence causes distention and severe, sharp pain when motility is reduced by opiates, general anesthetics, abdominal surgery, or immobilization.
w: When gas escapes freely by belching or passing flatus after meals
Gas that escapes normally does not stretch the bowel wall.
When peristalsis increases after eating a food the person tolerates
Increased motility of tolerated food is not the described cause of painful gas.
When the patient walks frequently and drinks adequate fluids daily
Activity and fluids promote motility rather than gas retention.

alt.q: A patient on the first day after abdominal surgery reports sharp, cramping abdominal pain and a distended abdomen. Which explanation fits these findings?
alt.a: Reduced intestinal motility is letting gas accumulate and stretch the bowel wall
alt.ex: After surgery and anesthesia, reduced motility allows gas to accumulate, distending the bowel and causing sharp pain.
w: Increased intestinal motility is moving gas out too quickly through the anus
Gas passing out quickly would relieve distention rather than cause it.
Dilated rectal veins are pressing against the bowel and causing distention
Hemorrhoids are rectal veins and do not distend the abdomen.
Excess colonic mucus is coating the bowel and preventing absorption of fluid
Excess mucus is linked to diarrhea, not gas distention.

items.q: A nurse inspects a patient’s anal area and sees an external hemorrhoid with purplish discoloration. What does this discoloration indicate?
items.a: Thrombosis, a hardening of the underlying vein
items.ex: Purplish discoloration of an external hemorrhoid indicates thrombosis, which increases pain and sometimes requires excision.
w: Inflammation, a swelling of the internal anal canal
Inflamed, distended hemorrhoids in the anal canal are internal, not purplish external ones.
Infection, an invasion of the skin by fecal bacteria
The book links the purplish color to a hardened vein, not infection.
Impaction, a hardened fecal mass behind the vein
Impaction is retained stool, not discoloration of a hemorrhoid.

alt.q: Which factor frequently causes hemorrhoids by increasing venous pressure?
alt.a: Straining at defecation
alt.ex: Increased venous pressure from straining at defecation, pregnancy, heart failure, and chronic liver disease frequently causes hemorrhoids.
w: Frequent ambulation
Activity is not a listed cause; it helps keep stools soft.
High-fiber diet
Fiber softens stool and reduces straining.
Antibiotic therapy
Antibiotics are linked to diarrhea and C. difficile, not hemorrhoids.

items.q: Fecal [[impaction]] results from unrelieved constipation when a patient cannot expel hardened feces retained in the rectum.
items.ex: Impaction is hardened, retained stool; if unresolved, severe impaction leads to intestinal obstruction.

alt.q: Suspect fecal [[impaction]] when a patient who has not passed stool for days has a continuous ooze of liquid stool.
alt.ex: Impaction is hardened, retained stool; if unresolved, severe impaction leads to intestinal obstruction.

items.q: What determines whether a surgically created stoma is called a colostomy or an ileostomy?
items.a: The part of the intestinal tract used to create the stoma
items.ex: A colostomy or ileostomy is named for the part of the intestine brought through the abdominal wall to form the stoma.
w: Whether the stoma is temporary or permanent
Both colostomies and ileostomies can be temporary or permanent.
Whether the stoma has one or two openings
Number of openings distinguishes loop from end ostomies, not colostomy from ileostomy.
The type of pouching system the patient wears
The pouch is chosen to fit the stoma; it does not name it.

alt.q: A stoma is created by bringing the ileum through the abdominal wall. What is this surgical opening called?
alt.a: An ileostomy
alt.ex: The stoma is named for the part of the intestine used; a stoma from the ileum is an ileostomy.
w: A colostomy
A colostomy uses part of the colon, not the ileum.
A Hartmann pouch
A Hartmann pouch is the closed intestine distal to an end colostomy.
An ileoanal pouch
An ileoanal pouch is attached to the anus, not brought out as a stoma.

items.q: Which type of ostomy produces the most formed stool?
items.a: Sigmoid colostomy
items.ex: The location determines stool consistency; a sigmoid colostomy, farthest along the colon, has the most formed stool.
w: Transverse colostomy
Transverse colostomy output is thick liquid to soft.
Ileostomy
Ileostomy effluent leaves before entering the colon, so it is frequent and liquid.
Continent ileostomy
This pouch is created from small intestine, so contents have not passed through the colon.

alt.q: A nurse cares for a patient with a new transverse colostomy. Which output consistency should the nurse expect?
alt.a: Thick liquid to soft
alt.ex: Output from a transverse colostomy is thick liquid to soft in consistency.
w: Firm and well formed
More formed stool is expected from a sigmoid colostomy.
Frequent and watery
Frequent liquid stools are expected from an ileostomy.
Mucus only
Mucus alone drains from the distal opening of a loop ostomy.

items.q: A patient with a new ileostomy is worried that the output is liquid and frequent. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “This is expected, because the stool leaves your body before it reaches the colon.”
items.ex: With an ileostomy, effluent leaves the body before entering the colon, so stools are frequent and liquid.
w: “This is expected for now, and the stool will become firm once the stoma heals.”
Ileostomy output stays liquid because the colon is bypassed, not because of healing.
“This is unusual, so I will report it as diarrhea to your health care provider.”
Liquid, frequent output is the expected result of an ileostomy.
“This is unusual, and it means the stoma was placed too low in the colon.”
An ileostomy is formed from the ileum, not the colon.

alt.q: Why is ileostomy effluent frequent and liquid?
alt.a: It exits the body before entering the colon, where water is normally absorbed
alt.ex: An ileostomy diverts effluent before the colon, so stools are frequent and liquid.
w: It passes through the entire colon too quickly to absorb water
The effluent does not pass through the colon at all.
It is mixed with mucus from the distal part of the stoma
Mucus from a distal opening describes a loop ostomy, not the reason ileostomy output is liquid.
It is diluted by fluid the patient drinks when emptying the pouch
Drinking fluid replaces losses; it does not make the output liquid.

items.q: Why might a surgeon place a plastic rod or bridge under the bowel loop when creating a loop colostomy?
items.a: To keep the loop of intestine from slipping back into the abdomen
items.ex: The rod, bridge, or rubber catheter is placed temporarily under the bowel loop to keep it from slipping back.
w: To separate the proximal opening from the distal opening permanently
The device is temporary and supports the loop; it does not create permanent separation.
To drain mucus from the distal part of the loop into the pouch
The distal opening drains mucus on its own; the rod supports the loop.
To keep the stoma closed until the patient is ready to irrigate
The bowel is opened and sutured to the skin; the rod does not close the stoma.

alt.q: A nurse notes a plastic rod under the stoma of a patient who just had a loop colostomy. What is the purpose of this device?
alt.a: It temporarily supports the loop so it does not retract into the abdomen
alt.ex: The rod or bridge temporarily keeps the bowel loop from slipping back into the abdomen.
w: It anchors the pouch so the skin barrier does not loosen
The rod supports the bowel loop, not the pouching system.
It marks the stoma as permanent for future surgical reversal
Loop colostomies are reversible stomas; the rod does not mark permanence.
It drains effluent from the proximal end directly into a bag
The proximal end drains fecal effluent on its own; the rod supports the loop.

items.q: A nurse observes that one opening of a patient’s loop colostomy drains stool and the other drains only mucus. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
items.a: It is expected, because the distal part drains mucus and the proximal end drains effluent
items.ex: A loop ostomy has two openings: the proximal end drains fecal effluent and the distal part drains mucus.
w: It is unexpected, because both openings should drain fecal effluent
Only the proximal end drains fecal effluent; the distal part drains mucus.
It is unexpected, because the mucus indicates infection of the distal bowel
Mucus from the distal part is the normal drainage of a loop ostomy.
It is expected, because the proximal end drains mucus and the distal end drains effluent
This reverses the openings; the proximal end drains effluent.

alt.q: A patient with a loop colostomy asks why there are two openings in the stoma. Which explanation is accurate?
alt.a: One opening drains stool from the proximal bowel and the other drains mucus from the distal bowel
alt.ex: In a loop ostomy, the proximal end drains fecal effluent and the distal part drains mucus.
w: One opening drains stool and the other is used to irrigate the colostomy
Irrigation uses a cone in the stoma; the second opening is the distal bowel draining mucus.
Both openings drain stool so the pouch fills evenly from each side
Only the proximal end drains stool.
One opening drains stool and the other drains urine from the bladder
Bowel diversions do not drain urine.

items.q: For which conditions is an ileoanal pouch anastomosis performed?
items.a: Ulcerative colitis or familial adenomatous polyposis
items.ex: The ileoanal pouch anastomosis is for patients needing a colectomy for ulcerative colitis or familial adenomatous polyposis (FAP).
w: Fecal impaction or chronic constipation
These are managed with diet, laxatives, enemas, or digital removal, not colectomy.
Spina bifida or myelomeningocele
These conditions may lead to an antegrade continence enema procedure in children.
Hemorrhoids or anal fissure
These are anal conditions, not indications for colectomy.

alt.q: Which patient is a candidate for an ileoanal pouch anastomosis?
alt.a: A patient needing a colectomy for familial adenomatous polyposis
alt.ex: Ileoanal pouch anastomosis is performed for patients who need a colectomy for ulcerative colitis or FAP.
w: A child with refractory constipation from spina bifida
Children with this problem may have an antegrade continence enema procedure.
A patient with a temporary diversion for perianal wounds
Transverse or sigmoid colostomies are used temporarily to divert stool from perianal wounds.
A patient with lactose intolerance and chronic diarrhea
Food intolerance is managed by diet, not colectomy.

items.q: When an ileal pouch is created, why does the patient also have a temporary ileostomy?
items.a: To divert effluent while the suture lines in the pouch heal
items.ex: A temporary ileostomy diverts effluent and allows the pouch suture lines to heal.
w: To drain mucus from the rectum until it is removed later
The colon and rectum are removed; the ileostomy diverts effluent for healing.
To let the patient practice catheterizing the stoma
Catheterizing a stoma describes a continent ileostomy, not the temporary ileostomy.
To provide a route for antegrade enemas after discharge
Antegrade enemas are given through an ACE continence valve.

alt.q: A patient asks why the ileostomy created with the ileoanal pouch is only temporary. Which explanation is accurate?
alt.a: It protects the new pouch while it heals, after which stool passes through the anus
alt.ex: The temporary ileostomy diverts flow while the pouch heals; afterward the patient is continent and evacuates via the anus.
w: It drains mucus until the remaining colon begins to absorb water
The entire colon is removed in this procedure.
It is replaced by a permanent colostomy once the pouch heals
After healing, stool is evacuated through the anus, not a colostomy.
It is closed once the patient learns to irrigate the pouch
Irrigation is not part of this procedure; closure follows healing.

items.q: How does a patient empty a continent ileostomy?
items.a: By placing a large catheter into the stoma to drain the pouch
items.ex: A continent ileostomy has a valve that is drained only when the patient places a large catheter into the stoma.
w: By attaching a drainable pouch that collects effluent continuously
The continent stoma has a valve, so it does not drain continuously into a pouch.
By evacuating stool through the anus several times a day
Evacuation through the anus describes an ileoanal pouch anastomosis.
By instilling an enema through a valve created from the appendix
This describes the antegrade continence enema procedure.

alt.q: A patient with a continent ileostomy describes self-care. Which statement shows understanding?
alt.a: “I put a large catheter into my stoma to empty the pouch several times a day.”
alt.ex: The continent stoma has a valve that drains only when a large catheter is inserted; the pouch is emptied several times daily.
w: “I empty the bag attached to my stoma when it is one-third full.”
A continent ileostomy does not use an external collection pouch that fills continuously.
“I pass stool through my anus because the pouch is attached there.”
Passing stool through the anus describes the ileoanal pouch anastomosis.
“I give an enema through my stoma and stool comes out my anus.”
This describes the antegrade continence enema procedure.

items.q: After an antegrade continence enema (ACE) is given, when does colonic evacuation usually begin?
items.a: About 10 to 20 minutes after the enema fluid is given
items.ex: Colonic evacuation begins about 10 to 20 minutes after a patient receives the ACE fluid.
w: About 2 to 5 minutes after the enema fluid is given
Two to 5 minutes is the usual retention time for a prepackaged hypertonic enema.
About 6 to 8 hours after the enema fluid is given
Six to 8 hours is the onset for stimulant cathartics.
About 12 to 24 hours after the enema fluid is given
Twelve to 24 hours is the onset for bulk-forming laxatives.

alt.q: Which structure does the surgeon use to create the continence valve for an antegrade continence enema?
alt.a: The appendix or cecum
alt.ex: In the ACE procedure the surgeon uses the child’s appendix or cecum to create a continence valve on the abdomen.
w: The ileum or jejunum
Ileum is used for ileostomies and ileal pouches, not the ACE valve.
The sigmoid or rectum
The enema is given from above; the valve is made from the appendix or cecum.
The transverse colon
Transverse colon is used for transverse colostomies.

items.q: For which purposes are transverse and sigmoid colostomies performed? Select all that apply.
o: To divert stool temporarily from an area of trauma
These ostomies are done as a temporary means to divert stool from trauma.
To divert stool from perianal wounds
They are used to divert stool from perianal wounds.
As a palliative diversion when a tumor obstructs the bowel
They may be a palliative diversion for tumor obstruction.
To allow continent evacuation through the anus
Continent anal evacuation is the goal of an ileoanal pouch anastomosis.
To create a valve for antegrade enemas
A continence valve for enemas is the ACE procedure.
items.ex: Transverse and sigmoid colostomies are the easiest to perform and are used temporarily for trauma or perianal wounds or palliatively for tumor obstruction.

alt.q: A nurse explains why a temporary sigmoid or transverse colostomy may be created. Which reasons should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Relief of obstruction caused by a tumor
A colostomy may be a palliative diversion when a tumor causes obstruction.
Protection of a healing perianal wound
Diverting stool keeps it away from perianal wounds.
Diversion of stool from traumatized bowel
Temporary diversion from an area of trauma is a listed purpose.
Treatment of lactose intolerance
Food intolerance is managed by diet, not ostomy surgery.
Prevention of fecal impaction in older adults
Impaction is prevented with fluids, fiber, exercise, and bowel routines.
alt.ex: These colostomies divert stool temporarily from trauma or perianal wounds, or palliate obstruction from a tumor.

items.q: Which outcomes do patients often experience after an antegrade continence enema (ACE) procedure? Select all that apply.
o: Less fecal soiling
Patients often experience less fecal soiling.
Better appetite
A better appetite is a reported benefit.
Reduced abdominal pain
Patients often have reduced abdominal pain.
Scheduled bowel movements
The ACE allows scheduled bowel movements.
Stool output through an abdominal pouch
Enema fluid and stool come out through the anus, not a pouch.
No further need for enemas
The procedure creates a route for regular enemas.
items.ex: After an ACE procedure, patients often experience less soiling, better appetite, reduced abdominal pain, and scheduled bowel movements.

alt.q: The parent of a child with spina bifida asks what an ACE procedure may accomplish. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: “Your child will likely have fewer soiling accidents.”
Less fecal soiling is a common result.
“Bowel movements can happen on a schedule.”
Scheduled bowel movements are a reported benefit.
“You can give the enema through a valve on the abdomen.”
The caregiver inserts a tube into the abdominal continence valve.
“Stool will drain into a bag on your child’s abdomen.”
The enema evacuates through the anus, not into an abdominal bag.
“The procedure removes the colon so constipation cannot recur.”
The ACE uses the appendix or cecum for a valve; the colon is not removed.
alt.ex: An ACE lets caregivers give enemas through an abdominal valve, leading to less soiling and scheduled bowel movements through the anus.

items.q: Which statements describe the ileoanal pouch anastomosis? Select all that apply.
o: The surgeon removes the colon
The procedure removes the colon.
A pouch is created from the end of the small intestine
The pouch is formed from the end of the small intestine.
The pouch is attached to the anus
The pouch is attached to the patient’s anus and simulates the rectum.
The patient remains continent of stool
Stool is evacuated via the anus, so the patient is continent.
The patient wears a permanent abdominal pouch
Only a temporary ileostomy is used while the pouch heals.
It is always completed in a single surgery
The procedure requires one to three surgeries.
items.ex: In ileoanal pouch anastomosis, the colon is removed and a small-intestine pouch attached to the anus collects stool, simulating the rectum.

alt.q: A patient scheduled for ileoanal pouch anastomosis asks what to expect. Which statements by the nurse are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: “The new pouch will act like your rectum.”
The pouch simulates the function of the rectum.
“You will have a temporary ileostomy while the pouch heals.”
A temporary ileostomy diverts effluent while suture lines heal.
“You may need one to three surgeries.”
The procedure requires one to three surgeries.
“You will drain the pouch with a catheter through your abdomen.”
Catheter drainage describes a continent ileostomy.
“Part of your colon will remain to absorb water.”
The colon is removed in this procedure.
alt.ex: The ileal pouch simulates the rectum; a temporary ileostomy protects it during healing, and one to three surgeries may be needed.

items.q: Loop colostomies are reversible stomas.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book describes loop colostomies as reversible stomas constructed in the ileum or colon.
items.ww: Loop stomas are made to be reversed, so describing them as permanent is wrong.

alt.q: End ostomies are always permanent and cannot be reversed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: End ostomies may be permanent or reversible, and the rectum may be left intact or removed.
alt.ww: Some end ostomies are reversible, so “always permanent” is inaccurate.

items.q: With an ileostomy, fecal effluent leaves the body before it enters the colon.
items.a: True
items.ex: An ileostomy diverts effluent from the ileum, so it leaves before reaching the colon and is frequent and liquid.
items.ww: Ileostomy effluent bypasses the colon, so it does not pass through the colon first.

alt.q: With an ileostomy, fecal effluent passes through the colon before leaving through the stoma.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Ileostomy effluent exits before entering the colon, which is why it is liquid.
alt.ww: If effluent passed through the colon, water would be absorbed and stool would be more formed.

items.q: A patient with an ileoanal pouch anastomosis is continent of stool because stool is evacuated through the anus.
items.a: True
items.ex: The pouch is attached to the anus and simulates the rectum, so the patient is continent of stool.
items.ww: This procedure preserves anal evacuation, so the patient does not depend on an external pouch.

alt.q: After an ileoanal pouch anastomosis heals, the patient must wear a permanent abdominal pouch to collect stool.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Only a temporary ileostomy is used during healing; afterward stool is evacuated via the anus.
alt.ww: The point of the procedure is continence through the anus, not a permanent abdominal pouch.

items.q: A patient with an ileostomy is preparing for discharge. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of fluid needs?
items.a: “I will drink 8 ounces of fluid each time I empty my pouch.”
items.ex: Ileostomy patients lose fluid and salt through the stoma; drinking 240 mL (8 oz) at each pouch emptying helps meet greater fluid needs.
w: “I will limit fluids so my pouch does not fill so quickly.”
Limiting fluids risks dehydration because fluid and salt are lost through the stoma.
“I will avoid salt because it makes my output more watery.”
Salt is lost through the stoma and needs to be replaced, not avoided.
“I will drink extra fluid only when the output looks formed.”
Ileostomy output is liquid; fluid replacement is needed routinely.

alt.q: Why do patients with ileostomies need to pay special attention to fluid and salt intake?
alt.a: They lose both fluid and salt through the stoma and risk dehydration
alt.ex: Patients with ileostomies digest food completely but lose fluid and salt through the stoma, so they must replace them.
w: They cannot digest food completely, so salt is needed for absorption
Ileostomy patients digest food completely; the losses are fluid and salt.
They retain extra fluid in the pouch, so salt helps draw it out
Fluid is lost through the stoma, not retained.
They absorb extra salt through the stoma, so fluid dilutes it
The stoma loses salt; it does not absorb it.

items.q: A patient with an ileostomy asks whether eating popcorn is safe. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Eat it in small amounts, chew it well, and drink fluids with it.”
items.ex: Foods with indigestible fiber can cause a food blockage, but small amounts eaten with fluids and chewed well rarely cause trouble.
w: “Avoid it completely, because it always causes a food blockage.”
Food blockage is infrequent, and these foods are usually fine in small, well-chewed amounts.
“Eat as much as you like, because the stoma cannot become blocked.”
Indigestible fiber can cause a food blockage in people with ileostomies.
“Eat it only without fluids, so it does not swell in your intestine.”
Drinking fluids with these foods helps prevent blockage.

alt.q: Which food can cause a food blockage in a patient with an ileostomy?
alt.a: Fresh pineapple
alt.ex: Foods with indigestible fiber, such as sweet corn, popcorn, raw mushrooms, fresh pineapple, and Chinese cabbage, can cause blockage.
w: White rice
White rice is a low-residue food, not one with indigestible fiber.
Applesauce
Applesauce is a low-residue food recommended during diarrhea.
Mashed potatoes
Potatoes are a low-residue food, not a listed cause of blockage.

items.q: Before meeting Chavela, a home care nurse reviews her history of constipation and her opioid prescription after knee surgery. Which assessment should the nurse recognize as a priority?
items.a: How often she has bowel movements and the quality of her stools
items.ex: Knowing that pain medications cause constipation and that she has a history of it, the nurse prioritizes bowel movement frequency and stool quality.
w: Whether she has a family history of colorectal cancer
Family cancer history is part of a full history but is not the priority cue here.
Whether she has had any recent foreign travel
Travel history relates to diarrhea assessment, not opioid-related constipation.
How many bathrooms she shares with other people
Bathroom sharing affects habits but is less urgent than her bowel pattern on opioids.

alt.q: A nurse plans care for a postoperative patient who takes opioids and has a history of constipation. Which knowledge guides the nurse to assess bowel patterns as a priority?
alt.a: Many pain medications cause constipation
alt.ex: Recognizing that many pain medications cause constipation helps the nurse anticipate needed assessment data.
w: Opioids usually cause diarrhea after surgery
Opioids slow motility and cause constipation, not diarrhea.
Knee surgery directly damages the colon
Knee surgery does not directly damage the bowel; the medications affect it.
Constipation history protects against new problems
A history of constipation increases, not decreases, the risk.

items.q: What is meant by Loop colostomy?
items.a: Reversible stoma with two openings, often supported by a temporary rod
items.ex: Bowel diversions differ in where the stool exits, whether the stoma is reversible, and how the patient empties the bowel.
w: Intestine brought out and turned down like a turtleneck; distal bowel removed or sewn closed
That goes with End colostomy.
Colon removed and a small-intestine pouch attached to the anus
That goes with Ileoanal pouch anastomosis.
Small-intestine pouch with a valved abdominal stoma drained by catheter
That goes with Continent ileostomy.

alt.q: What is meant by End colostomy?
alt.a: Intestine brought out and turned down like a turtleneck; distal bowel removed or sewn closed
alt.ex: Bowel diversions differ in where the stool exits, whether the stoma is reversible, and how the patient empties the bowel.
w: Reversible stoma with two openings, often supported by a temporary rod
That goes with Loop colostomy.
Colon removed and a small-intestine pouch attached to the anus
That goes with Ileoanal pouch anastomosis.
Small-intestine pouch with a valved abdominal stoma drained by catheter
That goes with Continent ileostomy.

alt.q: What is meant by Ileoanal pouch anastomosis?
alt.a: Colon removed and a small-intestine pouch attached to the anus
alt.ex: Bowel diversions differ in where the stool exits, whether the stoma is reversible, and how the patient empties the bowel.
w: Reversible stoma with two openings, often supported by a temporary rod
That goes with Loop colostomy.
Intestine brought out and turned down like a turtleneck; distal bowel removed or sewn closed
That goes with End colostomy.
Small-intestine pouch with a valved abdominal stoma drained by catheter
That goes with Continent ileostomy.

items.q: When the intestine distal to an end colostomy is sewn closed and left in the abdominal cavity, it is called a [[Hartmann pouch|Hartmann’s pouch|Hartmann's pouch]].
items.ex: In an end colostomy the distal intestine is either removed or sewn closed as a Hartmann pouch.

alt.q: A sewn-closed segment of bowel left in the abdomen distal to an end colostomy is known as a [[Hartmann pouch|Hartmann’s pouch|Hartmann's pouch]].
alt.ex: In an end colostomy the distal intestine is either removed or sewn closed as a Hartmann pouch.

items.q: Which assessment tool provides an accurate picture of a patient’s current bowel elimination pattern?
items.a: A bowel elimination diary completed by the patient or family caregiver
items.ex: Having the patient or family caregiver complete a bowel elimination diary gives an accurate assessment of the current pattern.
w: A single abdominal x-ray film taken on admission
A plain film shows structures at one moment, not the ongoing bowel pattern.
A serum amylase and lipase level drawn on admission
These tests assess hepatobiliary disease and pancreatitis, not bowel patterns.
A one-time nurse estimate based on bowel sounds
Bowel sounds do not record frequency and timing of defecation.

alt.q: A nurse wants an objective measure of a patient’s stool characteristics. Which tool should the nurse use?
alt.a: The Bristol Stool Form Scale
alt.ex: A scale such as the Bristol Stool Form Scale provides an objective measure of stool characteristics.
w: The fecal occult blood test
The FOBT detects microscopic blood, not stool form.
The colonic transit study
A transit study tracks radiopaque markers over 5 days, not stool form.
Anorectal manometry
Manometry measures sphincter pressures and reflexes.

items.q: During a nursing history, a patient reports cramping abdominal pain, nausea, and no bowel movements. Which problem should the nurse recognize these findings may indicate?
items.a: Intestinal obstruction
items.ex: Cramping pain, nausea, and the absence of bowel movements sometimes indicate an intestinal obstruction.
w: Lactose intolerance
Lactose intolerance causes diarrhea after milk, not absent bowel movements.
Hemorrhoids
Hemorrhoids cause rectal pain and bleeding, not nausea and no bowel movements.
C. difficile infection
C. difficile causes diarrhea, not an absence of bowel movements.

alt.q: A nurse auscultates a patient’s abdomen and hears high-pitched, hyperactive bowel sounds. Which condition is associated with this finding?
alt.a: Small-intestine obstruction
alt.ex: High-pitched and hyperactive bowel sounds occur with small-intestine obstruction and inflammatory disorders.
w: Postoperative ileus
Ileus causes absent or hypoactive bowel sounds.
Chronic constipation
Constipation is not the condition linked to high-pitched sounds in the text.
Fecal incontinence
Incontinence is not associated with high-pitched, hyperactive sounds.

items.q: Normal bowel sounds occur every [[5 to 15|5-15]] seconds and last a second to several seconds.
items.ex: Absent or hypoactive sounds occur with ileus; high-pitched hyperactive sounds occur with small-intestine obstruction.

alt.q: When auscultating the abdomen, the nurse expects normal bowel sounds to occur about every [[5 to 15|5-15]] seconds.
alt.ex: Absent or hypoactive sounds occur with ileus; high-pitched hyperactive sounds occur with small-intestine obstruction.

items.q: A patient is to collect a stool specimen for ova and parasites. Which action is most important after the specimen is obtained?
items.a: Send the labeled specimen to the laboratory promptly while it is still warm
items.ex: Tests for ova and parasites require warm stool, and delays at room temperature cause changes that alter results.
w: Refrigerate the specimen until the next scheduled laboratory pickup
Ova and parasite tests need warm stool; waiting delays delivery.
Leave the specimen at the bedside so the patient can add more stool
Specimens are sealed and sent promptly; adding later stool delays results.
Mix the specimen with water so it is easier for the laboratory to test
Patients are taught to avoid mixing feces with urine or water.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a patient how to collect a stool specimen at home. Which instruction is correct?
alt.a: Avoid mixing the stool with urine or toilet water
alt.ex: Teach the patient to avoid mixing feces with urine or water and to defecate into a clean, dry container.
w: Add a small amount of water to keep the stool moist
Mixing feces with water is to be avoided.
Collect the stool from the toilet bowl after flushing
Stool is collected in a clean, dry container, not from toilet water.
Include some toilet paper so the laboratory can see wiping
Specimens should be free of toilet paper.

items.q: A patient is scheduled for a guaiac-based fecal occult blood test (gFOBT). Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will not eat red meat for 3 days before the test.”
items.ex: Patients avoid red meat for 3 days before a gFOBT to prevent false-positive results.
w: “I will drink extra orange juice for 3 days before the test.”
Citrus fruits and juices are avoided for 3 days because they cause false-negative results.
“I will start taking a vitamin C supplement before the test.”
Vitamin C supplements are avoided because they cause false-negative results.
“I will take ibuprofen for my back pain the week of the test.”
NSAIDs are stopped for 7 days, if approved, because they can cause false-positive results.

alt.q: Why should a patient avoid vitamin C supplements and citrus juices for 3 days before a gFOBT?
alt.a: They can cause a false-negative result
alt.ex: Vitamin C supplements and citrus fruits and juices can cause a false-negative gFOBT result.
w: They can cause a false-positive result
Red meat and NSAIDs, not vitamin C, can cause false-positive results.
They can cause bleeding in the colon
The concern is test interference, not bleeding.
They can cause the stool to turn blue
A blue color on the guaiac paper indicates occult blood.

items.ex: After developing solution is applied, a blue color indicates a positive guaiac test.

alt.ex: After developing solution is applied, a blue color indicates a positive guaiac test.

items.q: According to the American Cancer Society guidelines, at what age should people at average risk begin regular colorectal cancer screening?
items.a: 45 years
items.ex: People at average risk who are 45 years old should begin regular screening.
w: 40 years
Forty is younger than the age set for average-risk screening.
50 years
Screening now starts at 45 rather than 50 to detect cancer earlier.
55 years
Fifty-five is later than the recommended starting age.

alt.q: A 60-year-old patient at average risk had a normal colonoscopy. According to the screening guidelines, when should the next colonoscopy be done?
alt.a: In 10 years
alt.ex: For average-risk people, colonoscopy is repeated every 10 years.
w: In 1 year
Annual testing applies to gFOBT and FIT, not colonoscopy.
In 3 years
Every 3 years applies to the DNA stool test.
In 5 years
Every 5 years applies to flexible sigmoidoscopy and CT colonography.

items.q: Which findings are warning signs of colorectal cancer? Select all that apply.
o: Narrowing of stool lasting more than a few days
A change in bowel habits such as narrowing of stool is a warning sign.
Rectal bleeding or blood in the stool
Blood ranging from bright red to dark brown or black is a warning sign.
Sensation of incomplete evacuation
Feeling of incomplete emptying is a listed warning sign.
Unintended weight loss and fatigue
Weakness, fatigue, or unintended weight loss is a warning sign.
Soft, formed stool every day
Daily soft, formed stool is a normal pattern.
Brief gas after eating beans
Occasional flatulence after certain foods is not a warning sign.
items.ex: Box 47.7 lists changes in bowel habits, rectal bleeding, incomplete evacuation, unexplained pain, and weakness, fatigue, or weight loss as warning signs.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a community group which symptoms to report as possible signs of colorectal cancer. Which should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Unexplained abdominal or back pain
Unexplained abdominal or back pain is a listed warning sign.
Diarrhea or constipation lasting more than a few days
A persistent change in bowel habits is a warning sign.
Dark brown or black blood in the stool
Blood in stool from bright red to black is a warning sign.
Stool shaped like the diameter of the rectum
Stool resembling the rectal diameter is normal; narrow stool is abnormal.
Brown stool with a typical odor
Brown stool with usual odor is a normal finding.
alt.ex: Warning signs include persistent bowel habit changes, blood in the stool, unexplained abdominal or back pain, and weight loss.

items.q: Virtual colonoscopy (CT colonography) can replace colonoscopy because it allows polyps to be removed.
items.a: False
items.ex: Virtual colonoscopy does not replace colonoscopy because it does not allow polyp removal or biopsy.
items.ww: Only direct endoscopy allows removal of polyps and biopsies.

alt.q: Virtual colonoscopy requires bowel preparation but cannot be used to remove polyps or obtain biopsies.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: CT colonography requires bowel prep and does not allow polyp removal or biopsy, so it does not replace colonoscopy.
alt.ww: Imaging alone cannot remove tissue, so polyps found still need colonoscopy.

items.q: A nurse is placing a patient who is immobile on a bedpan. Which technique is correct?
items.a: Roll the patient onto the side, place the bedpan firmly against the buttocks, then roll the patient back onto it
items.ex: When patients are immobile or cannot safely raise their hips, rolling them onto the bedpan is safest for patient and caregiver.
w: Lift the patient’s hips off the mattress and slide the bedpan underneath them
The nurse never lifts a patient onto a bedpan; this risks injury.
Keep the bed flat and push the bedpan under the hips while the patient lies supine
Forcing the pan under a supine patient causes back hyperextension and discomfort.
Have the patient bridge the hips while the nurse holds the bedpan flat beneath them
An immobile patient cannot safely raise the hips; rolling is used instead.

alt.q: To reduce back strain, what is the proper head-of-bed elevation for a patient sitting on a bedpan?
alt.a: 30 to 45 degrees
alt.ex: The proper position on a bedpan is with the head of the bed elevated 30 to 45 degrees to reduce back strain.
w: 0 to 10 degrees
Leaving the bed flat forces the patient to hyperextend the back.
10 to 20 degrees
This is nearly flat and still strains the back.
80 to 90 degrees
Sitting fully upright is not the described bedpan position.

Pulls fluid into the bowel to soften stool and distend the bowel
