items.q: Which enema solution is the only type given to infants and children?
items.a: Normal saline
items.ex: Infants and children receive only normal saline because they are at greater risk for fluid imbalance.
w: Tap water
Hypotonic tap water can cause water toxicity or circulatory overload if absorbed.
Hypertonic solution
Hypertonic enemas are contraindicated in young infants and dehydrated patients.
Soapsuds solution
Soapsuds can cause electrolyte imbalance or mucosal damage.

alt.q: Why is normal saline considered the safest enema solution?
alt.a: It exerts the same osmotic pressure as fluid in the interstitial spaces
alt.ex: Normal saline is isotonic with interstitial fluid, which lessens the danger of excess fluid absorption.
w: It pulls fluid out of the interstitial spaces into the colon
Pulling fluid into the colon describes hypertonic solutions.
It irritates the colon mucosa to stimulate peristalsis
Mucosal irritation describes soapsuds enemas.
It lubricates the feces so they are easier to pass
Lubrication describes oil-retention enemas.

items.q: During digital removal of an impacted stool, the patient’s pulse drops significantly. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Stop the procedure
items.ex: Rectal manipulation can stimulate the vagus nerve and slow the heart; the nurse stops if the pulse drops significantly or rhythm changes.
w: Continue more quickly to finish
Continuing increases vagal stimulation and risk.
Insert a second lubricated finger
More manipulation increases vagal stimulation.
Give an enema to finish clearing
The immediate response to a significant pulse drop is to stop the procedure.

alt.q: Why does the nurse reassess pulse rate periodically during digital removal of stool?
alt.a: Rectal manipulation can stimulate the vagus nerve and slow the heart rate
alt.ex: Excess rectal manipulation stimulates the vagus nerve and sometimes causes reflex slowing of the heart rate.
w: Rectal manipulation can stimulate the sympathetic system and raise the heart rate
The concern is vagal stimulation causing a slower, not faster, heart rate.
Pain from the procedure can cause an irregular rhythm from dehydration
The rhythm concern is vagal stimulation, not dehydration.
Fatigue from lying on the left side can cause a drop in blood volume
Positioning does not reduce blood volume; vagal stimulation is the risk.

items.q: A patient with a nasogastric tube connected to suction complains of nausea. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess both placement and patency of the tube
items.ex: When a patient with an NG tube is nauseated or vomits, assess both placement and patency, then reposition and irrigate as needed.
w: Remove the tube and notify the health care provider
Removing the tube is not indicated before assessing placement and patency.
Clamp the blue air vent to increase suction
The air vent of a Salem sump must not be clamped when connected to suction.
Give an antiemetic and recheck in 1 hour
Nausea may mean the tube is displaced or blocked, which must be assessed first.

alt.q: A Salem sump tube is connected to suction. What should the nurse do with the blue “pigtail” air vent?
alt.a: Leave it open to permit free, continuous drainage
alt.ex: The air vent allows free, continuous drainage when the main lumen is on suction, so it is not clamped.
w: Clamp it to increase the suction pressure
Clamping the vent prevents free, continuous drainage.
Connect it to a second suction source
The vent is for air; the main lumen goes to suction.
Use it to give tube feedings
Large-bore Salem sump tubes are used for decompression.

items.q: Which measures should be included in a bowel training program for a patient with chronic constipation? Select all that apply.
o: Choosing a defecation time based on the patient’s pattern
The time is chosen from the patient’s usual elimination pattern.
Offering a hot drink or prune juice before the defecation time
Fluids that stimulate peristalsis are offered before the set time.
Helping the patient to the toilet at the designated time
Taking the patient to the toilet at the same time daily builds the habit.
Teaching the patient to lean forward and bear down without straining
Leaning forward, applying abdominal pressure, and bearing down promote emptying.
Rotating the defecation time each day to prevent dependence
The program depends on attempting defecation at the same time each day.
Limiting exercise to keep the patient rested
Maintaining normal exercise within the patient’s ability is part of the program.
items.ex: Bowel training uses a consistent daily time based on the patient’s pattern, stimulating fluids, privacy, proper position, and regular exercise.

alt.q: A nurse sets up a bowel training program for an older adult with fecal incontinence from cognitive impairment. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Document times when the patient is incontinent
Assessing the pattern and incontinence times guides the schedule.
Provide privacy and an unhurried environment
Privacy and an unhurried, nonjudgmental caregiver are part of a successful program.
Ensure a family caregiver can devote time to the program
A patient with cognitive impairment needs a caregiver able to devote the time.
Give a stimulant laxative daily to set the schedule
Daily stimulant laxatives cause dependence and are not part of habit training.
Use the bedpan only when the patient asks for it
Training uses scheduled toileting at a designated time.
alt.ex: A successful program includes assessing the pattern, a consistent time, privacy, an unhurried caregiver, and family caregiver commitment.

items.q: A patient is incontinent of diarrhea. Which skin care measures should the nurse use? Select all that apply.
o: Clean the skin with a no-rinse cleanser
A no-rinse cleanser is recommended after each episode.
Apply a barrier ointment after each episode
A barrier ointment protects skin from digestive enzymes in stool.
Change absorbent products immediately after cleansing
Prompt changes limit contact between stool and skin.
Check on the patient frequently
Frequent checks allow prompt removal of fecal drainage.
Wipe vigorously with dry toilet tissue
Repeated wiping with toilet tissue further irritates the skin.
Leave the brief in place until the next scheduled change
Stool left on the skin causes rapid breakdown.
items.ex: Digestive enzymes in liquid stool break down skin rapidly, so gentle cleansing, barrier ointment, and prompt changes are needed.

alt.q: Why is a patient with diarrhea or fecal incontinence at high risk for skin breakdown? Select all that apply.
o: Digestive enzymes in liquid stool damage the skin
The enzymes in liquid stool cause rapid skin breakdown.
Repeated wiping with toilet tissue irritates the skin
Frequent wiping further irritates the skin.
Fecal contents may remain on the skin
Breakdown occurs when fecal contents remain on the skin.
Liquid stool cools the skin and reduces blood flow
The cause is enzymes and contact with stool, not cooling.
Barrier ointments trap moisture against the skin
Barrier ointments protect the skin and are recommended.
alt.ex: Enzymes in liquid stool, stool left on the skin, and repeated wiping all contribute to rapid skin breakdown.

items.q: There are no blood tests that specifically diagnose most GI disorders.
items.a: True
items.ex: The book states no blood tests specifically diagnose most GI disorders; hemoglobin and hematocrit assess anemia when bleeding is suspected.
items.ww: Blood tests support assessment but do not specifically diagnose most GI disorders.

alt.q: A hemoglobin and hematocrit level is ordered to diagnose the cause of a patient’s constipation.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hemoglobin and hematocrit are ordered when GI bleeding is suspected, to determine the extent of anemia.
alt.ww: These tests measure anemia from bleeding, not the cause of constipation.

items.q: A patient had abdominal surgery 1 day ago and rates pain as 8 out of 10. The nurse also needs to teach about high-fiber foods. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Manage the patient’s pain before teaching about dietary changes
items.ex: If pain is not controlled, the patient is not ready to learn about nutrition, so pain management comes first.
w: Teach about high-fiber foods while the patient is awake
Uncontrolled pain prevents the patient from being ready to learn.
Give a printed list of high-fiber foods to read later
Handing over materials does not address the priority need of pain control.
Postpone ambulation until the teaching is complete
Early ambulation helps prevent constipation and should not be delayed for teaching.

alt.q: After abdominal surgery, which combination of interventions does the textbook identify as priorities to aid recovery?
alt.a: Pain management, increasing fluids, and early ambulation
alt.ex: Priorities after abdominal surgery are managing pain and preventing constipation through increased fluids and early ambulation.
w: Fiber teaching, bed rest, and fluid restriction
Bed rest and fluid restriction promote constipation; fiber teaching waits for pain control.
Daily laxatives, bed rest, and low-fiber meals
Inactivity and low fiber promote constipation; laxatives are not for routine maintenance.
Fluid restriction, ambulation, and fiber teaching
Fluid restriction promotes hard stools and constipation.

items.q: A nurse is delegating enemas for several patients. Which enema must the nurse administer rather than delegate to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate) enema for high potassium
items.ex: Enema administration can usually be delegated, but a medicated enema must be administered by a nurse.
w: Tap-water enema (bag) before a diagnostic test
A cleansing tap-water enema can usually be delegated per agency policy.
Prepackaged (Fleet) enema for constipation
A prepackaged hypertonic enema is not a medicated enema and can usually be delegated.
Normal saline enema (bag) for constipation
A saline cleansing enema can usually be delegated per agency policy.

alt.q: Which statement about delegating enema administration to assistive personnel (AP) is accurate?
alt.a: AP can give enemas in most agencies, but a nurse must give medicated enemas
alt.ex: The skill can be delegated in most agencies after checking policy, but medicated enemas must be given by a nurse.
w: AP can give any enema, including medicated enemas, after training
Medicated enemas must be administered by a nurse.
AP cannot give any enema because it requires sterile technique
Enemas are clean procedures and can usually be delegated.
AP can give medicated enemas but not cleansing enemas
This reverses the rule; medicated enemas are the ones a nurse must give.

items.q: Assistive personnel (AP) report on four patients who received enemas. Which report requires the nurse’s immediate attention?
items.a: Blood around the rectal area after the enema
items.ex: AP are told to inform the nurse immediately about blood in the stool or around the rectal area or new abdominal pain.
w: Mild cramping during the enema
Cramping is the listed exception; some cramping is normal with an enema.
Brown liquid stool after the enema
Expelled stool and solution is the expected result of the enema.
An urge to defecate after 3 minutes
An urge to defecate after a few minutes is the expected response.

alt.q: Which instruction should the nurse give assistive personnel (AP) who will administer an enema?
alt.a: “Tell me right away if the patient has new abdominal pain other than cramping.”
alt.ex: AP report new abdominal pain (except cramping), rectal bleeding, blood in stool, or vital sign changes immediately.
w: “Tell me right away if the patient feels mild cramping during the enema.”
Cramping is the listed exception and is a normal sensation.
“Tell me right away if the patient needs the bedpan after the enema.”
Needing to defecate is the expected result, not an urgent report.
“Tell me right away if the patient expels the solution with stool.”
Expelling solution and stool is the intended outcome.

items.q: Why is an adult placed in the left side-lying position with the right knee flexed to receive an enema?
items.a: Solution flows by gravity along the natural curve of the sigmoid colon and rectum
items.ex: Left side-lying lets the solution flow downward along the natural curve of the sigmoid colon and rectum, improving retention.
w: Solution flows by gravity into the small intestine for faster absorption
The enema targets the rectum and colon, not small intestine absorption.
Solution is kept away from the sigmoid colon to reduce cramping
The position directs solution along the sigmoid colon rather than away from it.
Solution is held in the rectum only, which prevents distention of the colon
Solution flows into the sigmoid colon; retention there stimulates peristalsis.

alt.q: Which position should the nurse use when administering an enema to a young child?
alt.a: Dorsal recumbent
alt.ex: The skill notes that a child is placed in the dorsal recumbent position for an enema.
w: Left side-lying with right knee flexed
This is the adult position; children are placed dorsal recumbent.
Sitting on the toilet
Giving an enema on the toilet is unsafe because the tubing can abrade the rectal wall.
Prone with a pillow under the hips
Prone positioning is not described for enema administration.

items.q: Giving an enema while the patient sits on the toilet is a safe option for a patient with poor sphincter control.
items.a: False
items.ex: Giving an enema on the toilet is unsafe because curved rectal tubing can abrade the rectal wall; a bedpan is placed under the buttocks instead.
items.ww: The toilet position causes the tubing to injure the rectal wall, so it is never the safe option.

alt.q: A patient with poor sphincter control should receive an enema with a bedpan placed under the buttocks.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Patients with poor sphincter control need a bedpan under the buttocks, because the toilet position is unsafe.
alt.ww: Using the toilet instead risks rectal wall injury from the curved tubing.

items.q: While examining the perianal region before an enema, the nurse sees rectal prolapse. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Withhold the enema and notify the health care provider
items.ex: Rectal prolapse contraindicates an enema, so the nurse withholds it and reports the finding.
w: Give the enema using a smaller rectal tube
Changing the tube size does not remove the contraindication.
Give the enema with extra lubricant on the tip
Extra lubricant helps with hemorrhoids, but prolapse contraindicates the enema.
Give a prepackaged enema in place of an enema bag
Any enema is contraindicated when prolapse is present.

alt.q: A nurse finds hemorrhoids while inspecting a patient’s perianal area before an enema. Which adjustment is appropriate?
alt.a: Apply extra water-soluble lubricant to the enema tip
alt.ex: With hemorrhoids present, extra lubricant provides added comfort during insertion.
w: Cancel the enema because hemorrhoids contraindicate it
Prolapse, not hemorrhoids, contraindicates an enema.
Insert the tip quickly to limit contact with the hemorrhoids
Insertion must be slow and gentle to prevent mucosal trauma.
Use cold solution to shrink the hemorrhoids during the enema
Cold solution causes cramping and is difficult to retain.

items.q: In giving a prepackaged enema, which step comes right after “Separate the buttocks, locate the anus, and have the patient breathe out slowly”?
items.a: Hold the container upright and expel any air
items.ex: That's step 3 of 5. The tip is lubricated, the patient relaxes, air is expelled, the tip is inserted toward the umbilicus, and the bottle is rolled to instill all solution.
w: Gently insert the lubricated tip into the anal canal toward the umbilicus
That's step 4 of 5.
Remove the plastic cap and apply more water-soluble lubricant as needed
That's step 1 of 5.
Squeeze and roll the bottle from bottom to tip until all solution has entered
That's step 5 of 5.

That's step 3 of 5.
Separate the buttocks, locate the anus, and have the patient breathe out slowly

Remove the plastic cap and apply more water-soluble lubricant as needed
That's step 1 of 5.

ord.q: Put the steps for giving a prepackaged disposable enema in order.
items: Remove the plastic cap and apply more water-soluble lubricant as needed
Separate the buttocks, locate the anus, and have the patient breathe out slowly
Hold the container upright and expel any air
Gently insert the lubricated tip into the anal canal toward the umbilicus
Squeeze and roll the bottle from bottom to tip until all solution has entered
ord.ex: The tip is lubricated, the patient relaxes, air is expelled, the tip is inserted toward the umbilicus, and the bottle is rolled to instill all solution.

items.q: When inserting the rectal tube or enema tip, the nurse points it toward the patient’s [[umbilicus|navel|belly button]].
items.ex: Directing the tip toward the umbilicus follows the rectal anatomy and prevents trauma to the rectal mucosa.

alt.q: To follow the natural direction of the rectum, the enema tip is inserted gently toward the [[umbilicus|navel|belly button]].
alt.ex: Directing the tip toward the umbilicus follows the rectal anatomy and prevents trauma to the rectal mucosa.

items.q: How far should the nurse insert the rectal tube when giving an enema to an adult?
items.a: 7.5 to 10 cm (3 to 4 inches)
items.ex: For adults and adolescents, the tube is inserted 7.5 to 10 cm (3 to 4 inches); deeper insertion can cause bowel perforation.
w: 2.5 to 3.75 cm (1 to 1½ inches)
This is the insertion depth for an infant.
5 to 7.5 cm (2 to 3 inches)
This is the insertion depth for a child.
15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 inches)
Inserting beyond the proper limit can cause bowel perforation.

alt.q: A nurse is giving an enema to a school-age child. How far should the nurse insert the rectal tube?
alt.a: 5 to 7.5 cm (2 to 3 inches)
alt.ex: For a child, the rectal tube is inserted 5 to 7.5 cm (2 to 3 inches).
w: 7.5 to 10 cm (3 to 4 inches)
This is the depth for adults and adolescents.
2.5 to 3.75 cm (1 to 1½ inches)
This is the depth for an infant.
10 to 12.5 cm (4 to 5 inches)
This exceeds the recommended depth for any age and risks perforation.

items.q: While inserting a rectal tube, the nurse feels resistance. Which action is appropriate?
items.a: Stop advancing and do not force the tube
items.ex: If resistance is felt, the nurse does not force insertion; the nurse stops and may let a small amount of fluid infuse or consult the provider.
w: Push the tube firmly past the resistance
Forcing the tube can traumatize or perforate the rectal wall.
Raise the enema bag to 60 cm to clear it
Raising the bag that high causes rapid instillation and possible bowel rupture.
Withdraw the tube and insert it on the toilet
Giving an enema on the toilet is unsafe because tubing can abrade the rectal wall.

alt.q: A rectal tube does not pass easily during an enema. Why may the nurse allow a small amount of fluid to infuse before slowly trying again?
alt.a: The fluid relaxes the sphincter and provides additional lubrication
alt.ex: Instilling a small amount of fluid relaxes the sphincter and provides lubrication so the tube can be reinserted slowly.
w: The fluid dissolves any fecal impaction in the rectum
An impaction must be removed before the enema; fluid does not dissolve it.
The fluid stretches the rectal wall to allow faster insertion
The goal is relaxation and lubrication, not faster insertion.
The fluid confirms the tube is in the sigmoid colon
The small infusion is not a placement check.

items.q: During an enema from an enema bag, the patient complains of cramping. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Lower the container or clamp the tubing for a short time
items.ex: Temporarily stopping the infusion minimizes cramping and helps the patient retain the solution.
w: Raise the container higher to finish the infusion quickly
Raising the container causes rapid instillation and more painful distention.
Remove the tube and end the procedure immediately
Cramping alone is managed by slowing or pausing the flow.
Ask the patient to sit up so the solution flows downward
Repositioning is not the described response to cramping.

alt.q: Fluid begins to escape around the rectal tube during an enema. Which action should the nurse take?
alt.a: Lower the container or clamp the tubing briefly
alt.ex: The nurse lowers the container or clamps the tubing if fluid escapes around the tube or cramping occurs.
w: Push the tube farther into the rectum
Inserting beyond the proper limit can cause bowel perforation.
Raise the bag above 45 cm to increase flow
High pressure can cause painful distention or bowel rupture.
Switch to a larger rectal tube right away
Changing tube size is not the described response.

items.q: For a regular enema given with an enema bag, how high above the anus should the nurse raise the container?
items.a: 30 cm (12 inches)
items.ex: The container is raised 30 cm (12 inches) for a regular enema; raising it too high causes rapid instillation and possible bowel rupture.
w: 7.5 cm (3 inches)
This height is for a low enema.
15 cm (6 inches)
This height is not one of the listed levels.
60 to 75 cm (24 to 30 inches)
This height would cause rapid instillation and risk bowel rupture.

alt.q: A health care provider orders a high enema. How high above the anus should the nurse raise the container?
alt.a: 30 to 45 cm (12 to 18 inches)
alt.ex: For a high enema the container is raised 30 to 45 cm (12 to 18 inches) to cleanse more of the colon.
w: 7.5 cm (3 inches)
This height is for a low enema that cleanses only the rectum and sigmoid colon.
15 cm (6 inches)
This height is not one of the listed levels.
60 to 90 cm (24 to 36 inches)
This height would cause rapid instillation and risk bowel rupture.

items.q: Why does the nurse warm the enema solution and test it on the inner wrist before administration?
items.a: Hot water burns the intestinal mucosa, and cold water causes cramping and is hard to retain
items.ex: Warmed, tepid solution avoids burning the mucosa with hot water and avoids cramping from cold water.
w: Warm water dissolves stool, and cold water hardens it into an impaction
Temperature is chosen to avoid injury and cramping, not to dissolve stool.
Warm water kills bacteria, and cold water lets bacteria grow in the colon
Enemas are not sterile because the colon normally contains bacteria.
Warm water is absorbed faster, and cold water stays in the rectum longer
Faster absorption is not the reason for warming the solution.

alt.q: A family caregiver will give enemas at home. Which instruction about the solution is correct?
alt.a: Give warmed fluid slowly and do not exceed the recommended volume
alt.ex: Home care teaching includes slow administration of warmed fluid and not exceeding recommended volumes or number of enemas.
w: Give hot fluid quickly so the colon empties faster
Hot water burns the mucosa, and rapid infusion causes cramping.
Give cold fluid slowly so the patient can retain it longer
Cold water causes cramping and is difficult to retain.
Give extra fluid if the first enema does not work
Caregivers must not exceed recommended volumes or number of enemas.

items.q: A patient has an order for “enemas until clear.” What is the maximum number of consecutive enemas the patient should receive?
items.a: Three
items.ex: Patients should receive no more than three consecutive enemas to prevent fluid and electrolyte imbalance.
w: Two
Two is within the limit, but the stated maximum is three.
Five
Five exceeds the limit and risks fluid and electrolyte imbalance.
Unlimited
Repeated enemas risk fluid and electrolyte imbalance, so there is a limit.

alt.q: A nurse gives “enemas until clear.” Which finding indicates the goal has been met?
alt.a: The returned solution may be tinted but has no solid fecal material
alt.ex: With enemas until clear, the expelled water may be tinted but should not contain solid fecal material.
w: The returned solution is completely colorless like tap water
The return may still be tinted when the goal is met.
The patient has received five enemas without stool return
No more than three consecutive enemas are given.
The returned solution contains small pieces of formed stool
Solid fecal material means the return is not yet clear.

items.q: A patient has just expelled an enema into the bedside toilet. Which instruction should the nurse give?
items.a: “Please don’t flush, so I can look at the stool and solution.”
items.ex: The nurse observes the character of stool and solution to determine whether the enema was effective.
w: “Please flush right away, so the odor does not bother you.”
Flushing before inspection prevents the nurse from evaluating the results.
“Please stand up quickly, so the rest of the fluid drains out.”
Rushing a patient after an enema increases fall risk and is not described.
“Please wipe with dry tissue only, so the skin stays dry.”
Washing the anal area with warm soap and water protects the skin from fecal contents.

alt.q: After giving a prepackaged hypertonic enema, how long should the nurse expect the patient to retain the solution before the urge to defecate occurs?
alt.a: Usually 2 to 5 minutes
alt.ex: The patient retains a prepackaged enema until the urge to defecate occurs, usually in 2 to 5 minutes.
w: Usually 10 to 20 minutes
Ten to 20 minutes is when evacuation begins after an antegrade continence enema.
Usually 30 to 60 minutes
This is far longer than the usual retention for a hypertonic enema.
Usually several hours
Retention for several hours is the goal of an oil-retention enema.

items.q: Severe abdominal cramping and bleeding develop during an enema and are not relieved by slowing the flow. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Stop the enema
Severe cramping or bleeding unrelieved by slowing the flow requires stopping the enema.
Notify the health care provider
The provider is notified of this unexpected outcome.
Obtain vital signs
Vital signs are obtained to assess the patient’s response.
Raise the container to finish quickly
Raising the container increases pressure and risk of bowel rupture.
Insert the tube farther to bypass the cramp
Deeper insertion can cause bowel perforation.
items.ex: For severe cramping, bleeding, or sudden pain unrelieved by slowing the flow, stop the enema, notify the provider, and obtain vital signs.

alt.q: A patient receiving an enema suddenly reports severe abdominal pain that continues after the flow is stopped. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Discontinue the enema
Sudden severe pain unrelieved by stopping the flow requires ending the enema.
Check the patient’s vital signs
Vital signs are obtained for this unexpected outcome.
Report the pain to the health care provider
The provider is notified.
Resume the enema at a faster rate
Faster infusion causes more cramping and distention.
Encourage the patient to retain the solution longer
Severe unrelieved pain is a reason to stop, not to prolong retention.
alt.ex: Sudden severe pain unrelieved by slowing the flow is an unexpected outcome: stop the enema, obtain vital signs, and notify the provider.

items.q: Which assessments should the nurse complete before administering an enema? Select all that apply.
o: Last bowel movement and recent bowel pattern
These establish a baseline and explain the need for the enema.
Presence of hemorrhoids
Hemorrhoids may obscure the rectal opening and cause discomfort or bleeding.
Ability to turn and lie on the side
Mobility determines whether help is needed to position the patient.
Allergy to ingredients of a prepackaged enema
Checking allergies reduces the risk of an allergic reaction.
Ability to sit on the toilet for the procedure
Enemas are not given on the toilet because tubing can injure the rectal wall.

FOBT results are not part of the pre-enema assessment.
items.ex: Before an enema, the nurse checks bowel pattern, hemorrhoids, abdominal pain, mobility, allergies, and abdominal distention.

Dilating the rectum is not part of pre-enema assessment.

alt.a: False

alt.a: True

sections.name: Skill 47.2 · Insertion, maintenance, and removal of a nasogastric tube for gastric decompression

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with an NG tube to suction. Which tasks can the nurse delegate to assistive personnel (AP)? Select all that apply.
o: Measuring and documenting the NG drainage
Measuring and recording NG drainage is an appropriate AP task.
Providing oral and nasal hygiene
AP can perform oral and nasal hygiene for a patient with an NG tube.
Anchoring the tube to the gown during routine care
AP can secure the tube to the gown to prevent accidental displacement.
Irrigating the NG tube with normal saline
Maintaining the NG tube, including irrigation and placement checks, cannot be delegated to AP.
Checking the pH of gastric aspirate to confirm placement
Verifying tube placement is a nursing responsibility and cannot be delegated.
items.ex: Inserting and maintaining an NG tube cannot be delegated, but AP can measure drainage, give hygiene, and help secure the tube.

alt.q: The nurse instructs AP caring for a patient with an NG tube. Which findings should the AP report to the nurse immediately? Select all that apply.
o: Patient complaint of abdominal pain
Abdominal pain may signal that decompression is not working and must be reported at once.
Patient complaint of burning
Burning complaints must be reported immediately to the nurse.
Redness or irritation of the nares
Redness or irritation of the nares can signal a developing device-related pressure injury.
Measured drainage that matches the previous shift
Stable drainage is documented as usual and does not need immediate reporting.
Patient request for ice chips that are allowed
AP may offer permitted ice chips as a comfort measure.
alt.ex: AP should immediately report abdominal pain, burning, and signs of redness or irritation of the nares.

items.q: Why is a 14-Fr or 16-Fr tube chosen for gastric decompression in an adult rather than a smaller-lumen tube?
items.a: The tube must be able to remove thick secretions
items.ex: Smaller-lumen catheters are not used for adult decompression because they cannot remove thick gastric secretions.
w: A larger tube passes more easily through the nares
Lubrication, swallowing, and head flexion ease passage; size is chosen for drainage.
A larger tube does not need placement verification
Every NG tube needs placement verified, with x-ray as the gold standard.
A larger tube is less likely to cause pressure injury
Any medical device, including an NG tube, puts the patient at risk for MDRPI.

alt.q: A nurse is gathering equipment for NG insertion for gastric decompression in an adult. Which tube size is appropriate?
alt.a: 16 Fr
alt.ex: A 14-Fr or 16-Fr tube is used so thick secretions can be removed during decompression.
w: 8 Fr
An 8-Fr tube has too small a lumen to remove thick secretions in an adult.
10 Fr
A 10-Fr tube is a smaller-lumen catheter not used for adult decompression.
6 Fr
A 6-Fr tube is far too narrow to drain thick gastric secretions.

items.q: A nurse prepares to insert an NG tube in a patient who is disoriented and cannot follow commands. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Get help from another staff member to insert the tube
items.ex: When a patient is confused or unable to follow commands, another staff member should help with insertion.
w: Postpone the insertion until the patient is fully oriented
The ordered decompression is still needed; getting help makes insertion safe.
Delegate the insertion to experienced assistive personnel
NG tube insertion cannot be delegated to AP.
Insert the tube with the patient lying flat and supine
The head of bed should be raised to promote swallowing and reduce aspiration risk.

alt.q: Which patient assessment finding indicates that the nurse should obtain a second staff member before inserting an NG tube?
alt.a: The patient is confused and unable to follow commands
alt.ex: A confused or disoriented patient cannot cooperate, so another staff member should help with insertion.
w: The patient reports nasal congestion on one side
Congestion is handled by using the uninvolved nasal passage.
The patient had an NG tube during a prior admission
Previous experience helps prepare the patient and does not require extra staff.
The patient has hypoactive bowel sounds on auscultation
Diminished bowel sounds are baseline data and do not require extra staff.

items.q: How is the XEN + 10 method used to estimate NG tube insertion length in an adult?
items.a: Measure from xiphoid process to earlobe to tip of nose and add 10 cm
items.ex: XEN + 10 measures xiphoid to earlobe to nose tip, then adds 10 cm to approximate the distance to the stomach.
w: Measure from tip of nose to earlobe to mid-umbilicus and add 10 cm
Nose to earlobe to mid-umbilicus is the NEMU method, with nothing added.
Measure from tip of nose to earlobe to xiphoid process and add 5 cm
XEN + 10 starts at the xiphoid and adds 10 cm, not 5 cm.
Measure from earlobe to mid-umbilicus to xiphoid process and add 10 cm
The xiphoid, earlobe, and nose tip are the landmarks for XEN + 10.

alt.q: Which length-estimation method is described as most used in the neonatal intensive care unit and is the option for children?
alt.a: Nose to earlobe to mid-umbilicus (NEMU)
alt.ex: NEMU, measured from nose to earlobe to mid-umbilicus, is the child option and most used in the NICU.
w: Xiphoid to earlobe to nose plus 10 cm (XEN + 10)
XEN + 10 is an adult option that may be too long in some people.
Corrected nose-earlobe-xiphoid formula (CoNEX)
CoNEX is an adult option that corrects the NEX length with a formula or table.
Nose to earlobe to xiphoid without correction (NEX)
NEX is the most widely used adult method despite its low accuracy.

items.q: While the nurse advances an NG tube, the patient begins to cough and oxygen saturation drops. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Withdraw the tube into the posterior nasopharynx until normal breathing resumes
items.ex: Coughing and falling oxygen saturation suggest the tube entered the airway, so pull it back until breathing normalizes.
w: Advance the tube quickly while the patient is coughing
The tube is never advanced during coughing or inspiration because it will likely enter the respiratory tract.
Instill 30 mL of normal saline to check the tube position
Nothing is instilled before placement is confirmed; fluid could enter the lungs.
Tape the tube in place and request a chest x-ray
Securing a tube that may be in the airway delays the urgent need to withdraw it.

alt.q: During NG insertion, capnography shows a rising end-tidal CO2 and the patient starts coughing. What is the nurse’s best action?
alt.a: Pull the tube back into the posterior nasopharynx and wait for normal breathing
alt.ex: Rising CO2 and coughing suggest airway entry; withdraw the tube into the nasopharynx until breathing returns to normal.
w: Force the tube past the resistance to reach the marked length
An NG tube must never be forced.
Have the patient take a deep breath and advance the tube
Advancing during inspiration makes entry into the respiratory tract more likely.
Aspirate with a syringe and test the pH of the return
Placement checks come after insertion; airway compromise needs immediate withdrawal.

items.q: Radiography is the gold standard for verifying initial NG tube placement and must be done before any medication or liquid is given through the tube.
items.a: True
items.ex: No length-estimation method is 100% accurate, so x-ray confirmation is required immediately after insertion.
items.ww: Aspirate color and pH help, but x-ray is the most accurate way to confirm the tube is in the stomach.

alt.q: A gastric aspirate pH of 4 is the most accurate way to confirm initial NG tube placement, so an x-ray is not needed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: pH testing is a supportive indicator, but radiography remains the gold standard for initial placement.
alt.ww: Because no bedside method is fully reliable, x-ray confirmation of initial placement is required.

items.q: Before irrigating an NG tube, the nurse confirms placement because the pH of gastric aspirate must measure between 1.0 and [[5.0|5]].
items.ex: A gastric aspirate pH of 1.0 to 5.0 supports that the NG tube is in the stomach.

alt.q: An aspirate pH no higher than [[5.0|5]] supports gastric placement of the NG tube before irrigation.
alt.ex: A gastric aspirate pH of 1.0 to 5.0 supports that the NG tube is in the stomach.

items.q: A patient has a Salem sump tube connected to suction. Which actions regarding the blue “pigtail” are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Keep the pigtail above the level of the stomach
Keeping it above the stomach prevents a siphoning action that clogs the tube.
Place 10 mL of air into the pigtail after irrigation
Injecting 10 mL of air ensures the air vent stays patent.
Clamp the pigtail between drainage checks
The air vent must never be clamped off.
Instill normal saline through the pigtail to irrigate
Saline is never introduced through the air vent; irrigation goes through the main lumen.
Connect the pigtail to a second suction source
The air vent is never connected to suction.
items.ex: The pigtail is an air vent that allows continuous drainage; keep it above the stomach and never clamp, suction, or irrigate it.

alt.q: Which statements describe the purpose and handling of the Salem sump air vent? Select all that apply.
o: It connects with the tube’s second lumen
The blue pigtail is the air vent connected to the second lumen.
It permits free, continuous drainage while the main lumen is on suction
The vent lets secretions drain freely when the main lumen is on suction.
It is kept above the stomach to prevent siphoning
Positioning above the stomach prevents siphoning that clogs the tube.
It is the preferred port for saline irrigation
Saline is never instilled through the air vent.
It should be clamped during patient transport
The air vent is never clamped off.
alt.ex: The air vent links to the second lumen, keeps drainage continuous, and must stay above the stomach and unclamped.

items.q: Why does the nurse use normal saline rather than water to irrigate an NG tube?
items.a: Saline minimizes loss of electrolytes from stomach fluids
items.ex: Using normal saline for irrigation minimizes electrolyte loss from the stomach fluids being removed.
w: Saline dissolves thick secretions faster than water
The book’s reason for saline is electrolyte preservation, not dissolving secretions.
Saline is less harmful than water if it enters the lungs
Placement is verified first precisely so no solution enters the lungs.
Saline raises gastric pH and protects the stomach lining
Irrigation is not done to change gastric pH.

alt.q: A nurse prepares to irrigate an NG tube. Which solution and amount does the nurse draw up?
alt.a: 30 mL of normal saline
alt.ex: The nurse draws up 30 mL of normal saline, which minimizes electrolyte loss from stomach fluids.
w: 30 mL of sterile water
Water is not used because saline minimizes electrolyte loss.
100 mL of normal saline
The skill specifies 30 mL of saline for irrigation.
10 mL of air
Ten milliliters of air is placed in the pigtail vent after irrigation, not used to irrigate.

items.q: While irrigating an NG tube, the nurse meets resistance. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Check for kinks in the tubing and turn the patient onto the left side
items.ex: The tube tip may lie against the stomach lining; checking kinks and turning left may free it.
w: Push the saline in with firmer, steady pressure
Solution is never forced because pressure causes gastric trauma.
Instill the saline through the blue pigtail instead
Saline is never introduced through the air vent of a Salem sump tube.
Remove the tube and prepare to insert a new one
Removal requires an order; kinks and repositioning are checked first.

alt.q: A nurse has checked for kinks and turned the patient to the left side, but resistance during NG irrigation keeps recurring. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Report the repeated resistance to the health care provider
alt.ex: Repeated resistance after troubleshooting should be reported to the health care provider.
w: Increase the suction to a high continuous setting
Suction changes require consulting the health care provider.
Advance the tube a few centimeters further
The tube is not repositioned without confirming placement, and never after gastric surgery.
Irrigate with a larger volume under more pressure
Forcing solution causes gastric trauma.

items.q: A nurse instills 30 mL of normal saline into an NG tube and then aspirates 45 mL. How should the nurse document this?
items.a: Record 15 mL as output
items.ex: When more is aspirated than instilled, the difference is documented as output.
w: Record 15 mL as intake
The difference is intake only when less fluid returns than was instilled.
Record 45 mL as intake
The aspirated amount exceeds what was instilled, so the difference is output.
Record 75 mL as output
Only the difference between aspirated and instilled amounts is recorded.

alt.q: After instilling 30 mL of normal saline into an NG tube, the nurse can aspirate only 20 mL. How is this recorded?
alt.a: Record 10 mL as intake
alt.ex: When less is aspirated than instilled, the difference is documented as intake.
w: Record 10 mL as output
The difference is output only when more returns than was instilled.
Record 20 mL as output
Only the difference between instilled and aspirated amounts is recorded.
Record 50 mL as intake
The two amounts are not added together.

items.q: For a patient who has had gastric surgery, the nurse should never reposition the NG tube.
items.a: True
items.ex: Repositioning an NG tube after gastric surgery can rupture the suture line.
items.ww: Moving the tube after gastric surgery risks rupturing the suture line, so it is never repositioned.

alt.q: If the NG tube of a patient who had gastric surgery stops draining, the nurse should gently advance or rotate the tube to restore drainage.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: An NG tube is never repositioned after gastric surgery because it can rupture the suture line.
alt.ww: Manipulating the tube after gastric surgery threatens the suture line, so the nurse does not reposition it.

w: Have the patient inhale and hold the breath
That's step 6 of 8.

Clamp the tube and pull it out steadily into a towel

ord.q: Place these steps for removing an NG tube in order.
items: Verify the order in the EHR to remove the tube
Briefly stop suction to auscultate for bowel sounds
Explain that removal is less distressing than insertion
Turn off suction and disconnect the tube
Insert 20 mL of air into the tube lumen
Have the patient inhale and hold the breath
Clamp the tube and pull it out steadily into a towel
Inspect the tube for intactness
ord.ex: Removal starts with the order and bowel sound check, clears the tube with air, then withdraws it while the patient holds the breath.

items.q: Why does the nurse instruct the patient to inhale and hold the breath while the NG tube is being pulled out?
items.a: Holding the breath helps prevent aspiration
items.ex: Temporary airway obstruction occurs during removal, and breath-holding helps prevent aspiration.
w: Holding the breath reduces burning in the nasopharynx
Breath-holding protects the airway; clamping and steady pulling reduce mucosal trauma.
Holding the breath keeps the tube from kinking
Kinking is not the reason; the goal is preventing aspiration.
Holding the breath lets the nurse hear bowel sounds
Bowel sounds are checked before removal with suction briefly stopped.

alt.q: As the nurse is about to pull out an NG tube, which instruction should the nurse give the patient?
alt.a: Take a breath in and hold it while I remove the tube
alt.ex: Holding the breath during removal helps prevent aspiration while the airway is temporarily obstructed.
w: Breathe in deeply and steadily while I remove the tube
Inhaling during withdrawal is unsafe; the patient holds the breath to prevent aspiration.
Swallow sips of water while I remove the tube
Swallowing aids insertion; fluids may not be allowed for up to 24 hours after removal.
Cough forcefully several times while I remove the tube
Coughing is not requested; breath-holding protects the airway.

items.q: A patient with an NG tube to low intermittent suction reports nausea, and the abdomen is distended and painful. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess the tube’s patency and verify its placement
items.ex: The tube may be occluded or out of the stomach, so patency and placement are checked first.
w: Notify the health care provider of unrelieved nausea
The provider is notified if nausea or distention continues after troubleshooting.
Increase the suction to a high continuous setting
Suction settings are changed only after consulting the health care provider.
Remove the tube and offer the patient ice chips
Removal needs an order and would not relieve the distention.

alt.q: A patient with an NG tube becomes nauseated with a distended abdomen. The nurse confirms placement and patency and verifies suction is on, but symptoms continue after irrigation. What should the nurse do next?
alt.a: Notify the health care provider
alt.ex: Unrelieved nausea or distention after troubleshooting is reported to the health care provider.
w: Advance the tube 10 cm further
The tube is not advanced without an order; unrelieved symptoms are reported.
Clamp the tube for several hours
Clamping would stop decompression and worsen distention.
Instill saline through the blue pigtail
Saline is never instilled through the air vent of a Salem sump tube.

items.q: The nurse is caring for several patients with NG tubes. Which finding is most important to report to the health care provider?
items.a: Fever, shortness of breath, and pulmonary congestion
items.ex: Fever, shortness of breath, and pulmonary congestion are signs of pulmonary aspiration and require prompt reporting.
w: A sore throat and pharyngeal irritation
A sore throat is a normal result of tube irritation.
Green gastric aspirate with a pH of 4
Green aspirate with an acidic pH is expected with gastric placement.
A burning sensation in the nose during insertion
Burning in the nasopharynx is an expected part of insertion.

alt.q: A patient with an NG tube develops a fever and shortness of breath. After completing a respiratory assessment and notifying the health care provider, what does the nurse anticipate?
alt.a: Obtaining a chest x-ray as ordered
alt.ex: For suspected pulmonary aspiration, the nurse assesses breathing, notifies the provider, and obtains a chest x-ray as ordered.
w: Irrigating the tube with 30 mL of saline
Irrigation addresses a clogged tube, not aspiration.
Switching the tube to the other naris
Changing naris addresses skin irritation, not aspiration.
Lowering the head of the bed to flat
Head-of-bed elevation reduces aspiration risk, so it is not lowered.

items.q: It is normal for a patient with an NG tube to have a sore throat or irritation in the pharynx.
items.a: True
items.ex: Sore throat and pharyngeal irritation result from tube irritation and are expected.
items.ww: Pharyngeal soreness is an expected effect of the tube, not a sign of a complication.

alt.q: A sore throat in a patient with an NG tube indicates that the tube has entered the trachea and must be removed.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A sore throat is a normal result of tube irritation; airway entry shows as coughing or changes in oxygen saturation.
alt.ww: The nurse explains that a sore throat is normal with an NG tube.

items.q: The nurse uses the CLEAN mnemonic to prevent medical device–related pressure injury from an NG tube. Which actions are part of CLEAN? Select all that apply.
o: Correct tube position
C stands for correct tube position.
Stabilize the tube
L comes from stabiLize the tube.
Evaluate the area near and under the tube
E stands for evaluate the area near and under the tube.
Alleviate pressure
A stands for alleviate pressure.
Apply alcohol-based skin prep under the tape
Alcohol-based skin preps dry the skin and are avoided in patients at risk for MARSI.
Leave the tape in place until the tube is removed
A schedule is set to remove the tape and assess skin and mucosa.
items.ex: CLEAN stands for Correct tube position, stabiLize tube, Evaluate the area, Alleviate pressure, and Note date and time.

alt.q: A patient has had an NG tube for several days. Which factors can contribute to device-related injury of the nares? Select all that apply.
o: Rigidity of the device rubbing against the mucosa
A rigid tube rubbing on mucosa can cause injury.
Increased moisture around the tubing
Moisture around the tubing increases risk of tissue injury.
Securing the device too tightly
Tight securement contributes to device-related injury.
Poor positioning or fixation of the device
Poor positioning or fixation can injure skin and mucosa.
Assessing the nares at least twice a day
Assessing the nares twice a day is a preventive measure, not a cause.
alt.ex: Rigidity, moisture, tight securement, and poor positioning or fixation all contribute to MDRPI from NG tubes.

items.q: Unless contraindicated, how high should the nurse keep the head of the bed for a patient with an NG tube?
items.a: 30 to 45 degrees, preferably 45 degrees
items.ex: Elevating the head of bed 30 to 45 degrees, preferably 45, reduces the risk of aspirating stomach contents.
w: 10 to 15 degrees, preferably 15 degrees
This elevation is too low to reduce aspiration risk effectively.
15 to 20 degrees, preferably 20 degrees
The recommended elevation is 30 to 45 degrees.
60 to 90 degrees, preferably 90 degrees
High Fowler position is used during insertion; ongoing care calls for 30 to 45 degrees.

alt.q: A nurse finds a patient with an NG tube lying flat in bed. Why should the nurse raise the head of the bed to 30 to 45 degrees?
alt.a: To reduce the risk of aspirating stomach contents
alt.ex: Head-of-bed elevation reduces the risk of aspiration of stomach contents.
w: To increase the speed of gastric drainage
The reason given for elevation is aspiration prevention.
To prevent pressure injury at the nares
Fixation and the CLEAN mnemonic address nares pressure injury.
To make bowel sounds easier to hear
Bowel sounds are auscultated with suction turned off, not by repositioning.

sections.name: Skill 47.3 · Pouching a colostomy or an ileostomy

items.q: Which ostomy care task may be delegated to assistive personnel (AP) in some agencies?
items.a: Pouching an established ostomy that is 3 weeks old
items.ex: Care of an established ostomy, 2 to 3 weeks or more after surgery, can be delegated in some agencies.
w: Pouching a new ostomy on the first postoperative day
Pouching a new ostomy should not be delegated to AP.
Selecting a new skin barrier for a retracted stoma
Barrier selection requires nursing or WOCN assessment.
Teaching a patient self-care for a new colostomy
Patient education is done by the nurse or WOCN, not AP.

alt.q: A nurse is assigning care. For which patient should the nurse NOT delegate the pouch change to AP?
alt.a: A patient with a new ileostomy created 2 days ago
alt.ex: Pouching a new ostomy should not be delegated; only established ostomies (2–3 weeks or more) may be delegated in some agencies.
w: A patient with a colostomy created 4 weeks ago
A 4-week-old ostomy is established, so delegation may be allowed per agency policy.
A patient with a colostomy created 6 months ago
A long-established ostomy may be pouched by AP in some agencies.
A patient with an ileostomy created 3 weeks ago
A 3-week-old ostomy meets the established-ostomy time frame.

items.q: How often should an ostomy pouching system usually be changed?
items.a: Every 3 to 7 days
items.ex: Pouches are changed every 3 to 7 days, not daily, to minimize skin irritation from unnecessary changes.
w: Every 12 to 24 hours
Daily changes cause unnecessary skin irritation.
Every 1 to 2 days
Changing this often traumatizes peristomal skin unnecessarily.
Every 10 to 14 days
The recommended interval is 3 to 7 days.

alt.q: A patient with a colostomy says, “I plan to change my whole pouch every morning so it stays fresh.” Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Changing it every 3 to 7 days is enough and is easier on your skin.”
alt.ex: Pouches are changed every 3 to 7 days because unnecessary changes of the whole system irritate skin.
w: “Changing it every morning is the best way to protect your skin.”
Daily removal causes unnecessary skin irritation.
“Changing it once every 2 weeks will keep the seal strongest.”
The usual interval is 3 to 7 days.
“Changing it only when it feels heavy is enough for most people.”
A heavy pouch is emptied, not changed; changes occur every 3 to 7 days or with leaks.

items.q: Why should a patient empty an ostomy pouch when it is one-third to one-half full?
items.a: The weight of the pouch may disrupt the adhesive seal
items.ex: Emptying at one-third to one-half full keeps the pouch’s weight from breaking the adhesive seal on the skin.
w: A fuller pouch interferes with return of peristalsis
Peristalsis is not affected by pouch volume.
Effluent changes color if left in the pouch
Color change is not the reason for emptying at this level.
Measuring output is accurate only at this volume
Output can be measured at any volume; the concern is the seal.

alt.q: When should the nurse teach a patient with an ileostomy to empty the pouch?
alt.a: When it is one-third to one-half full
alt.ex: Emptying at one-third to one-half full prevents the pouch’s weight from disrupting the seal.
w: When it is three-quarters full
Waiting this long lets the weight disrupt the adhesive seal.
When it is completely full
A full pouch is heavy and likely to break the seal and leak.
When it is one-tenth full
Emptying this often is unnecessary; the guideline is one-third to one-half full.

mt.q: Match each ostomy care term with its meaning.
pairs: Output that drains from the ostomy into the pouch
Barrier often needed for a flush or retracted stoma
Product that eases barrier removal and reduces MARSI
Wound, ostomy, and continence nurse who helps select barriers and teach self-care

items.q: A nurse finds that a patient’s ostomy pouch is leaking stool at the edge of the barrier. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Change the pouching system
items.ex: A leaking pouch is changed because taping or patching leaves the skin exposed to chemical or enzymatic irritation.
w: Tape the edge of the wafer to contain the effluent
Taping over a leak leaves skin exposed to irritating effluent.
Wait until the scheduled day to change the pouch
Effluent on skin causes more trauma than early removal of the wafer.
Apply a patch over the leak and empty the pouch
Patching a leak leaves the peristomal skin exposed to irritation.

alt.q: A patient’s ostomy pouch has leaked repeatedly over the past week. What does this most likely indicate?
alt.a: A different type of pouch or added products are needed
alt.ex: Repeated leaking may mean a different pouch or products such as stoma paste or seal are needed.
w: The pouch should be changed every day from now on
Daily changes cause skin irritation; the system itself needs adjusting.
The patient should stop eating solid foods
Diet change is not the book’s response to repeated leaking.
The edges of the wafer should be taped routinely
Taping leaves skin exposed to effluent and is not the solution.

items.q: The nurse cleans peristomal skin with mild soap and water to remove all effluent before applying a new pouch.
items.a: False
items.ex: Peristomal skin is cleaned gently with warm tap water only because soap leaves a residue that may irritate skin.
items.ww: Soap residue can irritate skin, so warm tap water alone is used.

alt.q: The nurse gently cleans peristomal skin with warm tap water and a washcloth, without scrubbing, and pats it dry.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Warm tap water avoids soap residue, and drying is needed because the pouch does not adhere to wet skin.
alt.ww: Soap is avoided because its residue may irritate skin, and scrubbing traumatizes skin.

items.q: After cleaning peristomal skin, why does the nurse pat the skin dry before applying the new pouch?
items.a: The pouch does not adhere to wet skin
items.ex: A pouch will not stick to wet skin, so the skin is patted dry before application.
w: Moisture causes the stoma to shrink
Stoma size changes are related to postoperative swelling, not moisture.
Wet skin hides signs of a necrotic stoma
Stoma color and texture are assessed directly; drying is for adhesion.
Drying prevents minor bleeding from the stoma
Minor bleeding when the stoma is touched is normal and unrelated to drying.

alt.q: A nurse applies a new skin barrier while the peristomal skin is still damp from cleaning. Which problem is most likely?
alt.a: The pouch will not adhere to the skin
alt.ex: A pouch does not adhere to wet skin, so the skin must be patted dry first.
w: The stoma will retract below the skin
Retraction is a stoma characteristic, not a result of damp skin.
The stoma will stop bleeding when touched
Minor bleeding with touch is normal and unrelated to skin moisture.
The effluent will become more liquid
Effluent consistency depends on the type of ostomy, not skin moisture.

items.q: Minor bleeding when the nurse touches the stoma during cleaning is normal.
items.a: True
items.ex: The stoma bleeds slightly when touched; failure to bleed when washed gently is a sign of necrosis.
items.ww: A small amount of bleeding with touch is expected, not a complication.

alt.q: A stoma that does not bleed when gently washed is a healthy sign that should simply be documented.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Failure to bleed when washed gently is a sign of a necrotic stoma that must be reported.
alt.ww: A healthy stoma bleeds slightly when touched, so absence of bleeding is a warning sign.

items.q: During a pouch change, which stoma finding is most important for the nurse to report to the nurse in charge or health care provider?
items.a: Purple-black color with a dry texture
items.ex: A purple or black, dry stoma indicates necrosis and must be reported and documented.
w: Moist red tissue that bleeds slightly
A moist stoma that bleeds slightly when touched is expected.
Mild swelling 1 week after surgery
Swelling is a normal postoperative response in the first 4 to 6 weeks.
Liquid output from a new ileostomy
Normal ileostomy effluent is liquid.

alt.q: Which assessment of a new colostomy suggests the stoma is necrotic?
alt.a: It does not bleed when gently washed
alt.ex: Failure to bleed when washed gently, along with dark color, dryness, or sloughing, suggests necrosis.
w: It is moist and red when cleaned
A moist, red stoma is a normal finding.
It is slightly swollen around the edges
Postoperative swelling is expected in the first weeks.
It is passing flatus during the change
Flatus during a pouch change suggests returning peristalsis.

items.q: The nurse expects the size of a new stoma to change during the first [[4 to 6|4-6]] weeks after surgery.
items.ex: Postoperative swelling makes the stoma change size for 4 to 6 weeks, so it is remeasured at pouch changes.

alt.q: Because of normal postoperative swelling, a stoma is measured at each pouch change for the first [[4 to 6|4-6]] weeks.
alt.ex: Postoperative swelling makes the stoma change size for 4 to 6 weeks, so it is remeasured at pouch changes.

items.q: In pouching an ostomy, which step comes right after “Trace the stoma pattern on the barrier backing”?
items.a: Cut the opening in the skin barrier wafer
items.ex: That's step 5 of 8. The old system is removed and skin cleaned before the new barrier is measured, cut, applied, and closed.
w: Remove the protective backing from the wafer
That's step 6 of 8.
Measure the stoma
That's step 3 of 8.
Apply the pouch over the stoma and press firmly
That's step 7 of 8.

alt.q: Which step comes first in pouching an ostomy?
