ord.q: Place these steps for pouching an ostomy in order.
items: Remove the used pouch and skin barrier
Clean the peristomal skin with warm tap water and pat dry
Measure the stoma
Trace the stoma pattern on the barrier backing
Cut the opening in the skin barrier wafer
Remove the protective backing from the wafer
Apply the pouch over the stoma and press firmly
Close the end of the pouch with a clip or closure
ord.ex: The old system is removed and skin cleaned before the new barrier is measured, cut, applied, and closed.

items.q: After applying a new ostomy pouch, why does the nurse have the patient hold a hand over the pouch?
items.a: Pouch adhesives are heat sensitive and hold better at body temperature
items.ex: Heat and pressure activate pouch adhesives, which hold more securely at body temperature.
w: Pressure from the hand reduces stoma swelling
Hand pressure secures the seal; swelling is a normal postoperative response.
The hand keeps effluent from entering the new pouch
The pouch is meant to collect effluent; the hand secures the seal.
Holding the pouch helps the patient accept the stoma
Acceptance is assessed separately; this step is for adhesion.

alt.q: Which instruction helps secure the seal of a newly applied ostomy pouch?
alt.a: Hold your hand over the pouch for a while to warm it
alt.ex: Adhesives are heat and pressure sensitive, so warmth from the hand secures the seal.
w: Blow cool air from a hair dryer over the pouch
Adhesives hold better with warmth, not cooling.
Stand up right away and walk to set the seal
Activity does not secure the seal; heat and pressure do.
Tape over the edges of the wafer immediately
Taping is not how the seal is secured.

items.q: How should the nurse remove a used skin barrier to reduce peristomal skin trauma?
items.a: Push the skin away from the barrier in the direction of hair growth
items.ex: Gently pushing skin away from the barrier, with adhesive releaser, reduces skin trauma and MARSI.
w: Pull the barrier quickly upward against the direction of hair growth
Rapid removal against hair growth causes skin irritation or breakdown.
Peel the barrier off while scrubbing the skin with soap
Skin is never scrubbed, and soap leaves an irritating residue.
Soak the barrier in alcohol until it lifts off the skin
Alcohol-based products are avoided because they irritate skin.

alt.q: A nurse is teaching a caregiver to remove an ostomy barrier. Which caregiver action shows correct technique?
alt.a: Lifting the edge with one hand while pressing down on the skin with the other
alt.ex: Lifting the edge while pressing the skin down, working top to bottom, reduces skin trauma during removal.
w: Pulling the barrier off in one quick motion from the bottom
Quick removal traumatizes skin; working top down lets the pouch catch output.
Rubbing the edges with acetone to dissolve the adhesive
Acetone-based products are avoided; adhesive releaser is used.
Tugging the pouch while the patient pulls the skin taut
Tugging the pouch strips skin; the skin is pressed away from the barrier.

items.q: Which factors place a patient with an ostomy at risk for medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI)? Select all that apply.
o: Dehydration
Dehydration is a common risk factor for MARSI.
Malnutrition
Malnutrition increases the risk for MARSI.
Exposure to radiation therapy
Radiation therapy is a listed MARSI risk factor.
Edema of the skin
Skin edema raises the risk for MARSI.
Use of a transparent pouch
A transparent pouch lets the stoma be observed and is not a MARSI risk.
Formed colostomy effluent
Soft or formed stool is normal colostomy effluent, not a MARSI risk.
items.ex: Age, dehydration, malnutrition, radiation, chronic conditions such as diabetes or immunosuppression, and edema raise MARSI risk.

alt.q: A nurse reviews the EHR before changing an ostomy pouch. Which patient conditions should raise the nurse’s level of observation for MARSI? Select all that apply.
o: Diabetes
Chronic conditions such as diabetes are MARSI risk factors.
Immunosuppression
Immunosuppression is a MARSI risk factor.
Older age
Age is a common risk factor for MARSI.
A pouch changed every 5 days
Changing every 3 to 7 days is the recommended interval.
Use of warm tap water for skin cleaning
Warm tap water is the recommended cleanser and is not a risk factor.
alt.ex: Chronic conditions such as diabetes or immunosuppression and older age raise the risk for MARSI with adhesive stoma products.

items.q: A patient’s peristomal skin is irritated and blistered. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Remove the pouch more carefully
Careful removal reduces skin stripping from adhesive.
Use only water to cleanse the skin
Water alone avoids irritating residue on the skin.
Consult a WOCN
A WOCN can help assess skin and select a better pouching system.
Pat the skin dry after washing
Patting rather than rubbing protects irritated skin.
Clean the skin with an alcohol-based product
Alcohol or acetone-based products should be avoided.
Rub the skin briskly to remove adhesive residue
Skin is patted dry, not rubbed.
items.ex: Irritated peristomal skin calls for gentle removal, water-only cleansing, patting dry, avoiding alcohol or acetone, and WOCN consultation.

alt.q: Which factors can cause irritation, blistering, or a rash on the skin around a stoma? Select all that apply.
o: Fecal contents undermining the pouch seal
Effluent under the seal causes irritant dermatitis.
Adhesive exposure and removal
Adhesive exposure and removal can strip skin.
Fungal skin eruption
Fungal or other skin eruptions can cause a peristomal rash.
Changing the pouch every 3 to 7 days
This is the recommended interval and minimizes irritation.
Cleaning with warm tap water only
Water-only cleansing is recommended to avoid irritation.
alt.ex: Peristomal skin problems come from effluent undermining the seal, adhesive stripping, or fungal and other eruptions.

items.q: A patient with a new colostomy turns away and refuses to look at the stoma during a pouch change. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “This is a big change. Tell me how you are feeling about it.”
items.ex: When a patient refuses to view the stoma, the nurse allows expression of feelings, encourages family support, and refers to a WOCN.
w: “You need to look now, because you will go home soon.”
Pressuring the patient ignores the need to express feelings first.
“Fine, your family can take over all the care at home.”
Family support is encouraged, but it does not replace exploring the patient’s feelings.
“Most people get used to it, so it is not a big deal.”
Minimizing the change discourages the patient from expressing feelings.

alt.q: A patient refuses to view the new ileostomy or participate in care. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
alt.a: Obtain a referral for a WOCN
alt.ex: Refusal to view the stoma calls for a WOCN referral, a chance to express feelings, and family support.
w: Document the refusal and stop all teaching
Teaching is replanned, not stopped, and support is offered.
Perform all ostomy care until discharge without discussion
The patient needs support and an opportunity to express feelings.
Tell the patient the stoma will be reversed later
Promising reversal is inaccurate and does not address the patient’s feelings.

items.q: The nurse teaches a patient with an ostomy about home care. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I can shower without covering my pouch.”
items.ex: A patient may shower without covering the pouch.
w: “I will store my extra pouches in my car’s glove box.”
Extreme heat or cold affects barrier and adhesive materials.
“I only need to carry the clamp that is on my pouch.”
Patients carry an extra clamp in case one breaks or gets lost.
“I must wash my washcloths separately from other laundry.”
Washable items used for skin care may be washed with household laundry.

alt.q: Which statement by a patient with a colostomy indicates a need for more teaching about home care?
alt.a: “I will keep my spare pouches in the hot garage.”
alt.ex: Pouches should not be stored in extremely hot or cold places because temperature affects barrier and adhesive.
w: “I will carry plastic bags to throw away used pouches.”
Carrying plastic bags for disposal when away from home is correct.
“I will keep an extra clamp with me when I go out.”
Carrying a spare clamp is correct teaching.
“I can shower with my pouch on without covering it.”
Showering without covering the pouch is permitted.

items.q: Patients should avoid storing ostomy pouches in extremely hot or cold locations.
items.a: True
items.ex: Temperature affects the barrier and adhesive materials of a pouching system.
items.ww: Heat and cold damage barrier and adhesive materials, so storage temperature matters.

alt.q: Because pouches are sealed in packaging, storing them in a very hot car or a freezing garage does not affect them.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Extreme temperatures affect barrier and adhesive materials, so pouches are not stored in very hot or cold places.
alt.ww: Packaging does not protect barrier and adhesive materials from temperature damage.

items.q: During a pouch change on a postoperative patient, the nurse notes flatus passing from the stoma. What does this finding indicate?
items.a: Peristalsis is returning
items.ex: Noting flatus during a pouch change helps determine that peristalsis is returning.
w: The pouch seal is leaking
Leaks are detected by observing the barrier and its adherence to the abdomen.
The stoma is becoming necrotic
Necrosis shows as a purple or black, dry stoma that does not bleed.
The stoma has retracted
Retraction is a stoma characteristic that may call for a convex barrier.

alt.q: Which observation during a pouch change suggests that bowel function is returning after ostomy surgery?
alt.a: Flatus passing from the stoma
alt.ex: The presence of flatus during a pouch change helps determine that peristalsis is returning.
w: No output at the first pouch change
There may be no output at the first change; this does not show returning peristalsis.
Mild swelling of the stoma
Swelling is a normal postoperative response, not a sign of peristalsis.
Minor bleeding when the stoma is touched
Minor bleeding when the stoma is touched is normal and unrelated to peristalsis.

items.q: Why does the nurse have the patient assume a semi-reclining or supine position for a pouch change?
items.a: There are fewer skinfolds, which eases pouch application
items.ex: A semi-reclining position reduces skinfolds, which makes applying the pouching system easier.
w: Output from the stoma slows, which prevents leakage
Position is chosen for the skin surface, not to change output.
The stoma bleeds less, which keeps the skin clean
Minor bleeding when the stoma is touched is normal regardless of position.
The patient cannot see the stoma, which lowers anxiety
A mirror is offered if possible so the patient can observe.

alt.q: A patient with an established ostomy asks whether lying in bed is required for pouch changes. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “Some people with established ostomies prefer to stand; lying back reduces skinfolds.”
alt.ex: A semi-reclining or supine position reduces skinfolds, but some patients with established ostomies prefer to stand.
w: “You must always lie completely flat to keep the seal from failing.”
Some patients with established ostomies prefer to stand for pouch changes.
“You should sit fully upright so stool drains away from the stoma.”
Sitting upright creates skinfolds; semi-reclining or supine is preferred.
“You should lie on your side so the pouch hangs straight down.”
Side-lying is not the position described for pouching.

items.q: Which description fits the stratum corneum?
items.a: The thin outermost epidermal layer of flattened, dead, keratinized cells
items.ex: The stratum corneum is the thin top layer of the epidermis, made of flattened, dead, keratinized cells.
w: The innermost epidermal layer where cells actively divide and multiply
That describes the basal layer (stratum basale), where new epidermal cells originate.
The inner skin layer made mostly of connective tissue and collagen
That describes the dermis, which lies beneath the epidermis.
The membrane that separates the epidermis from the underlying dermis
That is the dermal-epidermal junction, not the stratum corneum.

alt.q: From which layer do the cells of the stratum corneum originate?
alt.a: The basal layer (stratum basale) of the epidermis
alt.ex: Cells form in the basal layer, then divide, migrate toward the surface, flatten, and die in the stratum corneum.
w: The reticular region (deep layer) of the dermis
The dermis is mostly connective tissue with few cells; it does not produce surface epidermal cells.
The papillary region (upper layer) of the dermis
The papillary region is part of the dermis, not the epidermal layer that generates new cells.
The dermal-epidermal junction (separating membrane)
The junction separates the two layers; it is not where epidermal cells divide.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which function does the thin stratum corneum perform?
items.a: Protects underlying cells and tissues from dehydration
items.ex: The stratum corneum protects underlying tissues from dehydration and blocks entry of certain chemical agents.
w: Provides tensile strength and mechanical support
Tensile strength and mechanical support are functions of the dermis.
Produces collagen to restore structural integrity
Collagen is formed by fibroblasts in the dermis, not by the stratum corneum.
Supplies blood vessels and nerves to the skin
Blood vessels and nerves are found in the dermal layer.

alt.q: A topical medication applied to intact skin is absorbed. Which skin layer permits this absorption?
alt.a: The stratum corneum of the epidermis
alt.ex: The stratum corneum allows water evaporation and permits absorption of certain topical medications.
w: The reticular region of the dermis
The dermis lies beneath the epidermis; the outer barrier the drug meets first is the stratum corneum.
The subcutaneous fat beneath the dermis
Subcutaneous tissue lies below the skin and is not the absorbing surface layer.
The fibroblast layer of the dermis
Fibroblasts are collagen-forming cells in the dermis, not a surface absorptive layer.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: How does the dermis differ from the epidermis?
items.a: It contains mostly connective tissue and few skin cells
items.ex: The dermis is mainly connective tissue with collagen, blood vessels, and nerves, and few skin cells.
w: It consists mostly of flattened, dead, keratinized cells
Dead keratinized cells make up the stratum corneum of the epidermis.
It sheds its surface cells through normal desquamation
Desquamation is shedding of epidermal surface cells, not dermal tissue.
It contains layered strata of constantly dividing cells
Layered strata and dividing basal cells belong to the epidermis.

alt.q: Which structures are found in the dermal layer of the skin?
alt.a: Collagen, blood vessels, and nerves
alt.ex: The dermis contains collagen, blood vessels, and nerves, giving strength and support to the skin.
w: Keratinized cells, melanocytes, and basal cells
These are found in the epidermis, not the dermis.
Stratum lucidum, granulosum, and spinosum
These strata are layers of the epidermis.
Skeletal muscle, bone, and cartilage
The dermis protects muscles and bones; it does not contain them.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which cells are the only distinctive cell type within the dermis?
items.a: Fibroblasts, which form collagen
items.ex: Fibroblasts are responsible for collagen formation and are the only distinctive dermal cell type.
w: Melanocytes, which produce pigment
Melanocytes are shown in the epidermis, not described as the distinctive dermal cell.
Basal cells, which divide and migrate
Basal cells are in the innermost epidermal layer.
Keratinocytes, which flatten and die
Flattened, dead keratinized cells form the stratum corneum of the epidermis.

alt.q: What is the main role of fibroblasts in the skin?
alt.a: Forming collagen in the dermis
alt.ex: Fibroblasts form collagen, the tough fibrous protein that gives the dermis its strength.
w: Forming keratin in the stratum corneum
Keratinized cells arise from basal cells migrating to the surface, not from fibroblasts.
Shedding surface cells by desquamation
Desquamation is the normal shedding of epidermal surface cells.
Carrying sensation from the skin surface
Sensation is carried by nerves in the dermis, not by fibroblasts.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: When skin is injured, what is the role of the epidermis in healing?
items.a: It resurfaces the wound and restores the barrier against organisms
items.ex: The epidermis resurfaces the wound and restores the barrier; the dermis restores structural integrity.
w: It restores collagen and the structural integrity of the skin
Restoring collagen and structural integrity is the dermis’s role.
It supplies new blood vessels and nerves to the wound bed
Blood vessels and nerves are dermal structures, not the epidermis’s healing role.
It provides tensile strength to hold the wound edges closed
Tensile strength is provided by the dermis.

alt.q: During healing of an injured area, which layer restores the structural integrity (collagen) of the skin?
alt.a: The dermis
alt.ex: The dermis responds to injury by restoring collagen and the physical properties of the skin.
w: The stratum corneum
The stratum corneum is a thin dead-cell layer; the epidermis resurfaces but does not rebuild collagen.
The basal epidermal layer
Epidermal cells resurface the wound; collagen restoration is a dermal function.
The dermal-epidermal junction
The junction is a separating membrane, not the layer that restores collagen.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Why does the skin of older adults tear easily during mechanical trauma such as tape removal?
items.a: The attachment between the epidermis and dermis becomes flattened
items.ex: A flattened dermal-epidermal attachment lets the layers separate easily with mechanical trauma.
w: The stratum corneum becomes thicker and more rigid
The book describes thinning and reduced elasticity, not a thicker, rigid stratum corneum.
Epidermal turnover speeds up and weakens new cells
Aging decreases epidermal turnover; it does not speed up.
The dermis gains extra collagen that stiffens the skin
Aging decreases collagen, which reduces skin strength.

alt.q: A 90-year-old patient develops a skin tear when a strip of tape is removed. Which age-related change best explains this injury?
alt.a: Flattening of the dermal-epidermal junction
alt.ex: When the dermal-epidermal attachment flattens, the epidermis tears away easily with tape removal.
w: Increased subcutaneous padding over the bones
Aging decreases subcutaneous tissue; it does not increase padding.
Faster inflammatory response at the tape site
Aging diminishes, rather than speeds, the inflammatory response.
Increased collagen production in the dermis
Aging decreases collagen, which is part of why skin is fragile.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse must remove an adhesive dressing from an older adult. Which technique is best?
items.a: Use two hands to slowly remove it parallel to the skin while supporting the skin-tape interface
items.ex: Slow, parallel removal with skin supported at the skin-tape interface limits tearing of fragile older skin.
w: Pull it off quickly in one motion at a right angle to the skin surface
Quick, perpendicular pulling stresses the weak dermal-epidermal attachment and causes tears.
Lift one corner and peel it straight up while the patient holds still
Peeling straight up without supporting the skin increases the risk of skin tears.
Moisten the dressing and pull it briskly toward the patient’s head
Brisk pulling without skin support is unsafe for aging skin with decreased barrier function.

alt.q: A nursing student describes removing tape from an older adult’s arm. Which statement shows correct understanding?
alt.a: “I will release the skin from the tape slowly, keeping the tape parallel to the skin.”
alt.ex: Releasing skin slowly, with the tape kept low and parallel and the skin supported, protects fragile skin.
w: “I will pull the tape off quickly so the discomfort lasts only a moment.”
Rapid removal causes skin tears in older adults, whose epidermis separates easily.
“I will lift the tape straight up from the skin to avoid dragging it.”
Lifting straight up stresses the skin; the book directs removal parallel to the skin.
“I will hold the tape with one hand and peel it back as fast as I can.”
The book directs using two hands and removing tape slowly while supporting the skin.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: An older adult with dementia and hemiplegia has frequent urinary incontinence. Which nursing action is most important to protect the skin?
items.a: Provide prompt skin hygiene to keep the skin clean and dry
items.ex: Co-morbidities raise the risk of incontinence and MASD, so prompt hygiene to keep skin dry is essential.
w: Wait to cleanse the skin until the next scheduled bath
Delaying hygiene leaves moisture on fragile skin and raises the risk of MASD.
Apply extra layers of linen under the patient to absorb urine
Extra linen holds moisture against skin and does not replace prompt hygiene.
Limit fluid intake so the patient voids less often
Restricting fluids is not a recommended skin-protection measure and risks dehydration.

alt.q: Which factor most increases an older adult’s risk for moisture-associated skin damage (MASD)?
alt.a: Incontinence related to dementia, immobility, or medications
alt.ex: Co-morbidities, decreased mobility, and medications increase incontinence risk and subsequent MASD.
w: Increased epidermal turnover related to aging
Aging decreases epidermal turnover; it is not the cause of MASD.
Thickened subcutaneous tissue over the hips
Aging decreases subcutaneous tissue; MASD is linked to moisture from incontinence.
A heightened inflammatory response in the skin
Aging diminishes the inflammatory response; MASD is caused by prolonged moisture.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: The daughter of a thin older adult asks why her mother is at risk for skin injury over her hips and tailbone. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Less fat under the skin means less padding over the bones, raising the risk of shear injury.”
items.ex: Decreased subcutaneous tissue reduces padding over bony prominences and increases the risk of shear injury.
w: “Older skin turns over faster, so it wears thin over the bones more quickly.”
Aging decreases epidermal turnover; the risk comes from less subcutaneous padding.
“Older adults have more collagen, which makes the skin rigid over the bones.”
Aging decreases collagen; the risk over bony areas is reduced padding.
“Her stronger inflammatory response makes the skin over her bones swell.”
Aging diminishes the inflammatory response; it does not increase swelling over bones.

alt.q: Which age-related change reduces protection over an older adult’s bony prominences?
alt.a: Decreased subcutaneous tissue
alt.ex: Less subcutaneous tissue means less padding over bony prominences, increasing the risk of shear injury.
w: Increased skin elasticity
Aging reduces skin elasticity.
Thickened epidermal layers
Aging skin has decreased epidermal turnover and becomes more fragile, not thicker.
Increased dermal collagen
Aging decreases collagen.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Why do wounds of older adults heal more slowly?
items.a: A diminished inflammatory response slows epithelialization
items.ex: Aging diminishes the inflammatory response, resulting in slow epithelialization and slower wound healing.
w: An exaggerated inflammatory response damages new tissue
Aging diminishes, rather than exaggerates, the inflammatory response.
Faster epidermal turnover exhausts the basal cells
Aging decreases epidermal turnover; it does not speed it up.
Extra subcutaneous fat blocks blood flow to wounds
Aging decreases subcutaneous tissue; slow healing relates to inflammation and turnover.

alt.q: Besides aging itself, which factors does the book identify as interfering with wound healing in older adults?
alt.a: Existing medical conditions and polypharmacy
alt.ex: Existing medical conditions and polypharmacy interfere with wound healing in older adults.
w: Increased mobility and frequent exercise
Decreased mobility, not increased activity, is a risk factor in older adults.
Thicker skin and greater elasticity
Aging reduces skin elasticity and thickness.
Faster epidermal turnover and repair
Aging skin has decreased epidermal turnover.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: What is desquamation?
items.a: Normal shedding of surface skin cells
items.ex: Desquamation is the normal shedding of surface cells, which are replaced by cells migrating up from the basal layer.
w: Division of cells in the basal layer
Cell division in the basal layer produces new cells; shedding is desquamation.
Formation of collagen by fibroblasts
Collagen formation by fibroblasts occurs in the dermis.
Separation of the dermis from the epidermis
That is the mechanism of skin tears, not normal shedding.

alt.q: Why is the constant upward movement of epidermal cells important?
alt.a: It replaces surface cells lost during desquamation
alt.ex: Constant migration from the basal layer replaces surface cells sloughed during normal shedding.
w: It produces collagen for dermal strength
Collagen is formed by dermal fibroblasts, not migrating epidermal cells.
It carries nerves toward the skin surface
Nerves are found in the dermis and do not migrate with epidermal cells.
It thickens the dermal-epidermal junction
Cell migration does not thicken the junction; it renews the surface layer.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which age-related changes increase an older adult’s risk for skin tears and pressure injuries? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced skin elasticity
Reduced elasticity is an age-related change that increases risk for skin tears and PIs.
Decreased collagen
Less collagen weakens skin and increases risk of breakdown.
Thinning of underlying muscle and tissues
Thinner underlying tissue reduces protection and increases risk.
Flattened attachment between epidermis and dermis
A flattened junction lets the skin tear easily with mechanical trauma.
Increased epidermal turnover
Aging decreases epidermal turnover.
Stronger inflammatory response
Aging diminishes the inflammatory response.
items.ex: Reduced elasticity, decreased collagen, thinning tissues, and a flattened junction make older skin fragile.

alt.q: A nurse reviews why aging skin is more vulnerable. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Barrier function against moisture, shear, friction, and pressure is decreased
Older adults’ skin has decreased barrier function and less protection.
Healing takes more time
Decreased epidermal turnover means healing requires more time.
Subcutaneous padding over bony prominences is reduced
Less subcutaneous tissue increases the risk of shear injury.
Skin elasticity increases with age
Aging reduces skin elasticity.
Collagen production rises to compensate for thinning skin
Aging decreases collagen.
alt.ex: Aging skin has a weaker barrier, slower healing, and less padding over bony prominences.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which are functions of the stratum corneum? Select all that apply.
o: Protects underlying tissues from dehydration
The thin stratum corneum protects underlying cells and tissues from dehydration.
Prevents entrance of certain chemical agents
It blocks entry of certain chemical agents.
Allows evaporation of water from the skin
The stratum corneum permits water to evaporate from the skin.
Permits absorption of certain topical medications
Certain topical medications are absorbed through it.
Provides tensile strength for underlying organs
Tensile strength is a function of the dermis.
Houses the nerves that sense pressure and pain
Nerves are found in the dermis.
items.ex: The stratum corneum protects against dehydration and chemicals while allowing evaporation and some drug absorption.

alt.q: Which are functions of the dermis? Select all that apply.
o: Provides tensile strength
The dermis provides tensile strength.
Gives mechanical support
The dermis provides mechanical support.
Protects underlying muscles, bones, and organs
The dermis protects underlying muscles, bones, and organs.
Resurfaces a wound to restore the barrier
Resurfacing and restoring the barrier is the epidermis’s role.
Sheds dead surface cells by desquamation
Shedding of surface cells occurs in the epidermis.
alt.ex: The dermis provides strength, support, and protection for deeper structures.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which nursing actions are recommended for older adults to reduce skin injury? Select all that apply.
o: Frequently assess pressure points related to bed or chair position
Box 48.1 directs frequent assessment of pressure points related to position.
Check skin under medical devices for pressure
Pressure from medical devices should be assessed frequently.
Provide prompt hygiene after incontinence
Prompt hygiene keeps skin dry and prevents MASD.
Remove tape slowly while supporting the skin
Slow removal with skin support prevents skin tears.
Remove adhesive dressings quickly to limit discomfort
Quick removal tears fragile older skin.
Assess pressure points only once a week
Pressure points should be assessed frequently, not weekly.
items.ex: Frequent pressure checks, prompt hygiene, and gentle tape removal protect fragile older skin.

alt.q: An older adult with a nasal cannula sits in a chair most of the day. Which assessments should the nurse perform frequently? Select all that apply.
o: Pressure points related to the sitting position
Pressure points related to chair position need frequent assessment.
Skin under the oxygen tubing
Pressure from medical devices must be assessed frequently.
Skin over the bony prominences
Reduced padding over bony prominences increases risk of injury.
Hair texture on the scalp
Hair texture is not a pressure-related skin risk for this patient.
Nail length on the fingers
Nail length is not related to pressure from position or devices.
alt.ex: Older adults need frequent checks of positional pressure points and skin under devices.

items.a: False

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

alt.q: Epidermal turnover speeds up with age, so older adults heal superficial wounds faster than younger adults.
alt.a: False

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which statement best defines a pressure injury (PI)?
items.a: Localized damage to skin and underlying soft tissue, usually over a bony prominence or from a device
items.ex: A PI is localized damage to skin and soft tissue, usually over a bony prominence or related to a device.
w: Generalized inflammation of the skin from prolonged contact with urine or stool
That describes incontinence-associated dermatitis, a type of MASD, not a PI.
Superficial loss of the epidermis caused by skin dragged across bed linens
That is a friction injury, which should not be classified as a PI.
Erythema persisting 30 minutes after an adhesive is removed from the skin
That is the definition of medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI).

alt.q: Which factors cause a pressure injury to form?
alt.a: Intense and/or prolonged pressure, or pressure combined with shear
alt.ex: PIs result from intense and/or prolonged pressure or pressure in combination with shear.
w: Prolonged exposure of the skin to wound drainage or stool
Moisture exposure causes MASD; it raises PI risk but is not the defining cause.
Skin dragged across coarse linens during position changes
Dragging causes friction injury to the epidermis, which is not classified as a PI.
Repeated removal of tape from the same area of skin
Repeated tape removal causes MARSI, not a PI.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse presses a finger over a reddened area on a patient’s hip. The area turns lighter, and redness returns when the finger is removed. How should the nurse interpret this?
items.a: Blanchable hyperemia, a transient response to an ischemic episode
items.ex: Skin that blanches and then reddens again shows transient blanchable hyperemia as the tissue overcomes ischemia.
w: Nonblanchable erythema, indicating probable deep tissue damage
Nonblanchable erythema does not lighten with pressure; this area did blanch.
A Stage 1 pressure injury requiring a pressure injury report
Stage 1 requires nonblanchable erythema; this redness blanched.
Deep tissue pressure injury from damage at the bone-muscle interface
DTPI shows persistent nonblanchable deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration.

alt.q: A reddened area over a patient’s sacrum stays red when the nurse presses on it. What does this finding most likely indicate?
alt.a: Nonblanchable erythema, meaning deep tissue damage is probable
alt.ex: Erythema that does not blanch under pressure suggests deep tissue damage is probable.
w: Blanchable hyperemia, a normal response once pressure is relieved
Blanchable hyperemia lightens with finger pressure; this area did not.
Vasodilation that will resolve without any tissue damage
Persistent nonblanching redness indicates probable damage, not harmless vasodilation.
A friction injury limited to the outer layer of the skin
Friction causes denuded red, painful skin; nonblanching redness points to pressure damage.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: While turning a patient, the nurse finds intact skin over the sacrum with a localized area of nonblanchable redness. How should the nurse document this finding?
items.a: Stage 1 pressure injury
items.ex: Intact skin with localized nonblanchable erythema is a Stage 1 PI.
w: Stage 2 pressure injury
Stage 2 has partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis; this skin is intact.
Deep tissue pressure injury
DTPI shows deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration or a blood-filled blister.
Unstageable pressure injury
Unstageable injuries are full-thickness losses obscured by slough or eschar.

alt.q: A patient has an intact, serum-filled blister over the heel with a pink surrounding area and no visible fat. How should the nurse classify it?
alt.a: Stage 2 pressure injury
alt.ex: Stage 2 is partial-thickness skin loss that can present as an intact or ruptured serum-filled blister.
w: Stage 1 pressure injury
Stage 1 is intact skin with nonblanchable erythema and no blister.
Stage 3 pressure injury
Stage 3 is full-thickness loss with visible adipose tissue.
Deep tissue pressure injury
A DTPI blister is blood-filled, not serum-filled.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is inspecting the sacrum of a patient with a dark skin tone for early pressure injury. Which action is best?
items.a: Use natural or halogen light and compare the area with the patient’s baseline skin color
items.ex: Dark skin may not visibly blanch, so use good lighting and compare with baseline color and adjacent areas.
w: Use bright fluorescent overhead lighting to get the clearest view of the area
Fluorescent light can cast a bluish tint on dark skin and should be avoided.
Rely on the blanch test alone to decide whether nonblanchable erythema exists
Dark skin tones may not show a visible blanch response.
Assess skin color only, because temperature and moisture are unreliable here
Skin temperature and moisture must also be assessed by palpation in dark skin.

alt.q: On a patient with dark skin, which finding over the sacrum should the nurse recognize as a possible sign of deep tissue injury?
alt.a: A purple or maroon area that does not change when pressure is applied
alt.ex: In dark skin, purple or maroon discoloration that stays unchanged under pressure may indicate deep tissue injury.
w: An area that is the same color as the patient’s surrounding skin
Color matching the patient’s baseline is not a sign of injury.
An area that lightens and quickly returns to its usual color
Lightening and prompt return suggests a transient response, not deep injury.
A soft area that feels the same temperature as nearby skin
Changes in temperature and consistency, not sameness, suggest injury.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: When the head of a patient’s bed is elevated, the patient slides down. Which force is acting, and where does its damage occur?
items.a: Shear, causing damage at the deeper fascial level over a bony prominence
items.ex: With shear, skin stays fixed while bone slides, stretching capillaries and causing deep necrosis at the fascial level.
w: Friction, causing damage limited to the epidermis over the sacrum
Friction injures the top layer; sliding with the skin fixed is shear, which damages deep tissue.
Moisture, causing softening and erosion of the surface skin
Moisture softens skin but is not the force created by sliding down in bed.
Mechanical load, causing damage only where tubing touches skin
Mechanical load is external force from an object; sliding with fixed skin is shear.

alt.q: Which action best prevents shear injury when moving a patient from bed to stretcher?
alt.a: Use a friction-relief device so the skin is not pulled across the bed
alt.ex: Shear occurs when skin is pulled across the bed during transfer; friction-relief devices help prevent it.
w: Raise the head of the bed fully before moving the patient across
Elevating the head of the bed causes the skeleton to slide and creates shear.
Slide the patient across the bed sheet in one smooth motion
Pulling skin across the bed is exactly what creates shear and friction.
Have the patient push with the heels to scoot onto the stretcher
Scooting drags skin across the surface, causing shear and friction.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A restless patient has red, painful, denuded skin on the elbows from rubbing against the bed linens. How should this injury be classified?
items.a: A friction injury, which should not be classified as a pressure injury
items.ex: Friction damages the epidermis (sometimes called a sheet burn) and should not be classified as a PI.
w: A Stage 2 pressure injury from partial-thickness skin loss
Friction injuries are not PIs, so they are not staged.
A shear injury causing necrosis deep in the tissue layers
Shear damages deep fascial tissue; this is superficial skin loss from rubbing.
A deep tissue pressure injury from pressure at the bone
DTPI is persistent deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration from pressure and shear.

alt.q: Which layer of the skin does a friction injury affect?
alt.a: The epidermis, causing superficial skin loss
alt.ex: Unlike shear, friction affects only the epidermis, producing red, painful, denuded skin.
w: The deep fascia over a bony prominence
Damage at the deep fascial level is caused by shear.
The bone-muscle interface beneath the skin
Damage at the bone-muscle interface leads to deep tissue PI.
The full thickness of skin and muscle
Full-thickness loss describes Stage 3 or 4 PIs, not friction injury.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A pressure injury on a patient’s sacrum has exposed bone visible in the wound bed. How should the nurse stage it?
items.a: Stage 4 pressure injury
items.ex: Exposed or directly palpable fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage, or bone defines Stage 4.
w: Stage 3 pressure injury
Stage 3 shows visible fat, but fascia, muscle, tendon, and bone are not exposed.
Stage 2 pressure injury
Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis only.
Unstageable pressure injury
An injury is unstageable only when slough or eschar hides the depth.

alt.q: A full-thickness wound shows visible fat and rolled edges (epibole), but no exposed muscle, tendon, or bone. How should it be staged?
alt.a: Stage 3 pressure injury
alt.ex: Stage 3 is full-thickness skin loss with visible adipose tissue but no exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, or bone.
w: Stage 2 pressure injury
Fat is not visible in a Stage 2 PI.
Stage 4 pressure injury
Stage 4 requires exposed or palpable fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage, or bone.
Deep tissue pressure injury
Visible fat indicates a full-thickness PI, not a DTPI.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient has a heel pressure injury covered by dry, adherent, intact eschar without redness or fluctuance. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: Leave the eschar in place without softening or removing it
items.ex: Stable eschar on the heel or an ischemic limb should not be softened or removed.
w: Apply a moist dressing to soften the eschar for removal
Softening stable heel eschar is contraindicated.
Arrange debridement so the wound depth can be staged
Stable heel eschar is left in place even though the wound stays unstageable.
Gently lift the eschar edges to inspect the wound bed
Disturbing stable heel eschar removes its protective cover.

alt.q: Why can a pressure injury covered with necrotic tissue not be staged?
alt.a: The necrotic tissue hides the true depth of the injury
alt.ex: Staging depends on depth, which necrotic tissue obscures until the base is exposed.
w: Necrotic tissue means the injury is healing too quickly
Necrotic tissue does not indicate rapid healing; it hides the depth.
Necrotic tissue appears only in deep tissue injuries
Necrotic tissue can cover Stage 3 or 4 wounds, which become unstageable.
Necrotic tissue proves the wound is a friction injury
Friction injuries are superficial; necrotic tissue obscures full-thickness depth.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient has intact skin over the coccyx with a persistent, nonblanchable maroon discoloration. The patient reports pain in the area. Which classification is most accurate?
items.a: Deep tissue pressure injury
items.ex: Persistent nonblanchable deep red, maroon, or purple discoloration of intact or nonintact skin is a DTPI.
w: Stage 1 pressure injury
Stage 1 color changes do not include purple or maroon discoloration.
Stage 2 pressure injury
Stage 2 has partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis, not intact maroon skin.
Moisture-associated skin damage
MASD is inflammation and erosion from moisture, not maroon discoloration from pressure.

alt.q: Where does a deep tissue pressure injury originate?
alt.a: At the bone-muscle interface from intense or prolonged pressure and shear
alt.ex: DTPI results from intense and/or prolonged pressure and shear at the bone-muscle interface.
w: At the skin surface from friction against the bed linens
Surface friction damages the epidermis and is not classified as a PI.
In the epidermis from prolonged contact with urine or stool
Moisture causes MASD, not deep tissue injury.
In the stratum corneum from repeated adhesive tape removal
Repeated tape removal causes MARSI.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient’s Stage 3 pressure injury is now filling in with granulation tissue and getting shallower. How should the nurse document it?
items.a: Healing Stage 3 pressure injury
items.ex: Once staged, the stage endures as it heals; a Stage 3 showing healing is a healing Stage 3 PI.
w: Stage 2 pressure injury
PIs are not reverse staged; a healing Stage 3 does not become Stage 2.
Stage 1 pressure injury
A Stage 3 PI does not progress back to Stage 1 as it heals.
Unstageable pressure injury
Unstageable applies when slough or eschar hides the depth, not to healing.

alt.q: A nurse documents “Stage 4 pressure injury, now Stage 2.” Which response by the charge nurse is best?
alt.a: “A healing Stage 4 is still documented as a healing Stage 4 pressure injury.”
alt.ex: PI staging describes depth at assessment, and the original stage endures as the wound heals.
w: “That is correct, since the wound is now shallower than before.”
Reverse staging is not used; the stage endures as it heals.
“Document it as unstageable until it is completely closed.”
Unstageable means slough or eschar obscures the depth, not healing.
“Change it to Stage 3 first, then to Stage 2 next week.”
A PI does not progress backward through stages while healing.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which factors are systemic factors that reduce the tissue’s tolerance to externally applied pressure?
items.a: Poor nutrition, aging, hydration status, and low blood pressure
items.ex: Systemic factors such as nutrition, aging, hydration, and low blood pressure affect tissue tolerance.
w: Shear, friction, and moisture at the skin surface
Shear, friction, and moisture are extrinsic, not systemic, factors.
Pressure intensity, pressure duration, and position
These relate to pressure itself, not to systemic tissue tolerance.
Tubing, bed linens, and other external surfaces
These are sources of mechanical load, not systemic factors.

alt.q: Which extrinsic factors make skin more susceptible to damage from pressure?
alt.a: Shear, friction, and moisture
alt.ex: The greater the shear, friction, and moisture present, the more susceptible the skin is to pressure damage.
w: Nutrition, hydration, and blood pressure
These are systemic factors affecting tissue tolerance.
Aging, co-morbidities, and medications
These are patient-related factors, not extrinsic skin factors.
Collagen, blood vessels, and fibroblasts
These are dermal structures that help redistribute pressure.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which patients are at risk for developing pressure injuries? Select all that apply.
o: An older adult with a fractured hip
Older adults and people with fractured hips are listed as at risk.
A patient with a spinal cord injury
People with SCIs have decreased or absent motor and sensory function.
A patient with diabetes mellitus and peripheral vascular disease
These conditions are listed risks for PI.
A patient receiving hospice care
People in hospice settings are listed as at risk.
An alert young adult who walks independently after a dental visit
This person has normal mobility and sensation and no listed risk factor.
items.ex: Decreased mobility, decreased sensation, incontinence, and poor nutrition place these patients at risk.

alt.q: Which patient conditions place a patient at risk for pressure injury? Select all that apply.
o: Decreased sensory perception
Patients who cannot feel pressure cannot respond to relieve it.
Fecal or urinary incontinence
Moisture from incontinence increases PI risk.
Poor nutrition
Poor nutrition is a contributing factor and reduces tissue tolerance.
Comatose or confused mental state
Altered consciousness prevents patients from protecting themselves.
Ability to change position independently
Independent repositioning protects against PIs; inability to do so is the risk.
alt.ex: Impaired sensation, incontinence, poor nutrition, and altered consciousness all raise PI risk.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which findings in a patient with a dark skin tone may indicate a pressure injury? Select all that apply.
o: Localized purple, blue, or violet discoloration that does not change with pressure
In dark skin, these colors may appear instead of red; purple may mean deep injury.
A circumscribed area that is warm, later becoming cool to touch
Warmth, then coolness as tissue changes color, suggests injury.
Taut, shiny edema with induration more than 15 mm across
Edema with induration over 15 mm may occur.
Pain over a bony prominence or under a medical device
Pain in suspected areas should be assessed.
A visible blanch response confirming normal tissue
Dark skin may not show a visible blanch response, so blanching is unreliable.
items.ex: Use color change, temperature, edema, consistency, and pain, not blanching alone, to detect PIs in dark skin.

alt.q: Which techniques are recommended when assessing dark skin for pressure injury? Select all that apply.
o: Compare the area of concern with the patient’s baseline color
Compare color with the patient’s baseline and unaffected areas.
Palpate for temperature and tissue consistency changes
Temperature and consistency must be assessed by palpation.
Slightly moisten the skin to assess subepidermal moisture
Dark skin is higher in lipid content; slight moistening aids detection.
Use fluorescent lighting to highlight color differences
Fluorescent light casts a bluish tint on dark skin.
Rely on skin color alone to determine risk
Patients with dark skin cannot be assessed by skin color alone.
alt.ex: Good lighting, baseline comparison, palpation, and subepidermal moisture checks improve detection.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which features describe a Stage 2 pressure injury? Select all that apply.
o: Partial-thickness skin loss with exposed dermis
Stage 2 is partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis.
Viable, pink or red, moist wound bed
The wound bed is viable, pink or red, and moist.
Intact or ruptured serum-filled blister
Stage 2 may present as a serum-filled blister.
Visible adipose tissue in the wound
Visible fat indicates full-thickness loss (Stage 3).
Slough or eschar in the wound bed
Slough and eschar are not present in Stage 2.
items.ex: Stage 2 is shallow, viable partial-thickness loss without fat, granulation tissue, slough, or eschar.

alt.q: Which features describe a Stage 4 pressure injury? Select all that apply.
o: Exposed or palpable bone, tendon, or muscle
Stage 4 has exposed or directly palpable deep structures.
Full-thickness skin and tissue loss
Stage 4 is full-thickness skin and tissue loss.
Undermining, tunneling, or epibole
These often occur in Stage 4 PIs.
Intact skin with nonblanchable redness
Intact skin with nonblanchable erythema is Stage 1.
Serum-filled blister with no exposed tissue
A serum-filled blister describes Stage 2.
alt.ex: Stage 4 is full-thickness loss with exposed deep structures, often with undermining or tunneling.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Deep pressure injuries initially form at the bone–soft tissue interface and extend outward toward the skin.
items.a: True
items.ex: Muscle damage is more significant because deep PIs start at the bone–soft tissue interface and extend outward.
items.ww: Superficial damage starts at the surface, but deep PIs begin at the bone and move outward.

alt.q: All pressure injuries begin at the skin surface and progress inward toward the bone.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Damage can begin at the surface and progress inward or begin at the muscle and progress outward.
alt.ww: Bottom-up deep damage starts at the bone–soft tissue interface, so not all PIs start at the surface.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A healing Stage 3 pressure injury is redocumented as a Stage 2 pressure injury once it becomes shallower.
items.a: False
items.ex: Once staged, the stage endures; it is documented as a healing Stage 3 PI.
items.ww: Reverse staging is not used; a Stage 3 does not progress to a lower stage.

alt.q: Once a pressure injury is staged, that stage endures even as the wound heals.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Staging describes depth at assessment, and the original stage is kept, described as healing.
alt.ww: A healing PI is not reverse staged; the original stage remains with the word healing.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Low pressure applied over a prolonged period can damage tissue, just as high-intensity pressure over a short period can.
items.a: True
items.ex: Both low pressure over a long time and high-intensity pressure over a short time cause tissue damage.
items.ww: The book names both patterns as concerns, so low pressure is not harmless if prolonged.

alt.q: Only high-intensity pressure causes tissue damage; low pressure is harmless regardless of how long it lasts.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Prolonged low pressure also occludes blood flow and contributes to cell death.
alt.ww: Duration matters: extended low pressure damages tissue as well.

alt.q: An adverse [[microclimate]] (heat and humidity at the skin) reduces soft tissue tolerance to pressure and shear.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which statement best defines a medical device–related pressure injury (MDRPI)?
items.a: Injury from sustained pressure or shear over nonbony areas due to a poorly fitting or misused device
items.ex: MDRPIs result from sustained pressure or shear from an ill-fitting, poorly positioned, or misused device, often over nonbony areas.
w: Injury that persists 30 minutes after removal of an adhesive securing a device
That is the definition of MARSI, not MDRPI.
Injury limited to bony prominences caused by lying in one position too long
MDRPIs occur over nonbony locations from devices, not only over bony prominences.
Injury caused by prolonged exposure of skin to moisture beneath a dressing
Moisture exposure causes MASD, not MDRPI.

alt.q: A nurse explains MDRPIs to a new graduate. Which statement is accurate?
alt.a: “They can form over nonbony areas wherever a device presses on skin or tissue.”
alt.ex: MDRPIs occur over nonbony locations from sustained pressure or shear by a device.
w: “They form only over bony prominences such as the sacrum and heels.”
MDRPIs specifically occur over nonbony locations under devices.
“They are caused by adhesive pulling the epidermis away from the dermis.”
Adhesive stripping of the epidermis is MARSI.
“They are caused mainly by stool or urine left on the patient’s skin.”
Skin damage from urine or stool is incontinence-associated dermatitis, a type of MASD.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Where do most medical device–related pressure injuries occur?
items.a: Face and head, especially the ears
items.ex: Most MDRPIs occur in the face and head region, specifically the ears.
w: Sacrum and coccyx, especially when lying supine
These are classic sites for PIs over bony prominences, not most MDRPIs.
Heels and ankles, especially under heavy blankets
Heels can be injured by mattresses, but most MDRPIs are on the face and head.
Hands and wrists, especially under restraints
Restraints can cause MDRPIs, but the face and ears are the most common sites.

alt.q: Which devices are most commonly linked with MDRPIs?
alt.a: Oxygen tubing and masks
alt.ex: Oxygen tubing and masks are the devices most commonly linked with MDRPIs.
w: Pulse oximetry devices and probes
Pulse oximeters are at-risk devices but not the most common.
Compression stockings and braces
These are at-risk devices but not the most common source.
Indwelling urinary catheters and bags
Catheters are at-risk devices, but oxygen equipment is most common.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Why are proactive assessment and prevention especially critical for medical device–related pressure injuries?
items.a: MDRPIs form faster than Stage 1 or Stage 2 pressure injuries
items.ex: Because MDRPIs form faster than Stage 1 or 2 PIs, proactive assessment and prevention are critical.
w: MDRPIs heal faster than other pressure injuries once found
The book stresses rapid formation, not rapid healing, as the reason for prevention.
MDRPIs occur only in neonates and critically ill patients
These groups are especially vulnerable, but MDRPIs occur across settings and ages.
MDRPIs are easy to treat with dressings after they occur
It is difficult and sometimes impossible to apply a dressing to an MDRPI.

alt.q: Which patient groups are particularly vulnerable to MDRPIs?
alt.a: Critically ill patients and neonates
alt.ex: Critically ill patients and neonates are particularly vulnerable to MDRPIs.
w: Ambulatory adults and adolescents
Ambulatory patients are not identified as especially vulnerable.
Postpartum patients and athletes
These groups are not identified as especially vulnerable.
Outpatients and home-care visitors
These are not the groups the book names as most vulnerable.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: During skin assessment, a nurse notes a reddened area on a patient’s thigh in the exact shape of the urinary catheter tubing. What does this pattern indicate?
items.a: A medical device–related pressure injury from the tubing
items.ex: An MDRPI generally conforms to the pattern or shape of the device that caused it.
w: Moisture-associated skin damage from urine leakage
MASD causes inflamed skin with irregular borders, not a device-shaped mark.
Medical adhesive–related skin injury from tape
MARSI occurs where adhesive was removed, not in the shape of tubing.
A friction injury from rubbing against bed linens
Friction produces denuded skin from dragging, not a device-shaped imprint.

alt.q: A patient has a wound on the cheek that matches the outline of the oxygen mask edge. Which conclusion is most accurate?
alt.a: The mask caused a medical device–related pressure injury
alt.ex: MDRPIs generally conform to the pattern or shape of the device.
w: The patient has a friction injury from moving in bed
A wound matching a device outline indicates device pressure.
The patient has dermatitis from mucus or saliva
Moisture damage does not take the shape of a device.
The patient has a Stage 1 PI over a bony prominence
This injury is from a device, and its stage depends on depth, not location.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient receives oxygen by nasal cannula. Which intervention best prevents a medical device–related pressure injury?
items.a: Apply a dressing to the external ears and periodically remove the cannula to inspect
items.ex: Table 48.1 recommends a dressing on the external ear and periodic removal of the cannula to relieve pressure and inspect.
w: Tighten the cannula tubing so it cannot slide on the face
Tighter tubing increases pressure on the ears and nose.
Leave the cannula in place continuously to avoid hypoxia
Periodic brief removal is needed to relieve pressure and inspect skin.
Tape the tubing firmly to both cheeks to stabilize it
Extra adhesive adds MARSI risk and does not relieve ear pressure.

alt.q: Why might the nurse consider silicone oxygen tubing for a patient using a nasal cannula?
alt.a: Its flexibility decreases the risk of pressure injury
alt.ex: Silicone oxygen tubing decreases the risk of PI formation because it is flexible.
w: It delivers a higher oxygen concentration
Silicone tubing is chosen for flexibility, not oxygen delivery.
It stays in place without any securement
Its benefit is flexibility, not eliminating securement.
It does not need to be removed for inspection
Periodic removal and inspection are still required.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse repositions a patient’s endotracheal tube laterally to relieve pressure on the lips. Which check is most important?
items.a: Confirm that the depth of the tube has not changed
items.ex: When moving the ET tube laterally, ensure the depth does not change.
w: Confirm that the tube is now centered in the mouth
Moving laterally rotates pressure points; a centered tube is not the goal.
Confirm that the tongue is resting on the tube
Pressure on the tongue is what lateral movement aims to relieve.
Confirm that the tube tape has been removed
Tape removal is not the key safety check; tube depth is.

alt.q: Why is an endotracheal tube moved laterally from side to side?
alt.a: To relieve pressure over different portions of the lips and tongue
alt.ex: Lateral movement relieves pressure over different areas of the lips and tongue.
w: To improve air movement through the tube
Lateral movement is for pressure relief, not airflow.
To allow the tube to advance to a deeper position
Tube depth must not change when moving it laterally.
To prevent the tube from rubbing against the nares
An endotracheal tube’s pressure areas are the lips and tongue.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient wears a hard cervical collar and perspires heavily. Which plan is most appropriate?
items.a: Perform collar care more often than daily, and seek to switch to a softer collar as soon as possible
items.ex: Remove hard collars as soon as possible; do collar care at least daily and more often with heavy perspiration.
w: Perform collar care once a week, since cleaning the pads disturbs the neck
Collar care is needed at least daily, and more often with perspiration.
Keep the hard collar on and add padding without removing it for skin checks
The collar is removed for skin care and pad changes; padding alone is not enough.
Inspect the scalp only when the patient reports discomfort under the collar
The scalp should be inspected daily, not only when symptoms occur.

alt.q: What does daily cervical collar care include?
alt.a: Removing the collar, cleansing the skin, and changing the soft pads
alt.ex: Collar care includes removing the collar, cleansing skin, and changing pads so they can be washed and dried.
w: Loosening the collar and leaving the same pads in place
Pads are changed so they can be washed and dried.
Wiping the outside of the collar while it stays on
The collar is removed so skin can be cleansed and inspected.
Applying lotion under the collar without removing it
The collar must be removed for skin cleansing and pad changes.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: How often should compression stockings be removed to reduce the risk of a medical device–related pressure injury?
items.a: Twice daily for at least 1 hour
items.ex: Table 48.1 recommends removing stockings twice daily for at least 1 hour.
w: Once daily for 10 minutes
This is less often and shorter than recommended.
Every 2 days for at least 4 hours
Stockings should be removed twice each day, not every 2 days.
Once weekly for 30 minutes
Weekly removal does not allow adequate pressure relief or inspection.

alt.q: Which areas are at risk for pressure injury from compression stockings?

alt.ex: Compression stockings put pressure on the calf, behind the knee, heel, and toes.
w: Thigh, groin, hip, and buttock
These are not the listed pressure areas for compression stockings.
Ankle, wrist, elbow, and shoulder
Wrists and ankles are pressure areas for immobilization devices.
Neck, scalp, ear, and chin
These areas relate to collars and oxygen devices.

Devices should be the correct size for the individual.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient has a wound drainage tube after surgery. Which instruction to the patient best prevents a medical device–related pressure injury?

w: Only when the drain is emptied

items.q: Which actions help prevent medical device–related pressure injuries? Select all that apply.
o: Choose the correct size of device for the individual
Correct sizing, especially of endotracheal tubes and oxygen equipment, reduces pressure.
Cushion high-risk areas such as ears and nasal bridge with foam or dressings
Cushioning protects the skin at high-risk areas.
Remove or move removable devices to assess skin at least daily
Daily removal or movement allows inspection under the device.
Avoid placing devices over sites of prior or existing PI
Placing devices over prior PIs increases injury risk.
Place devices under an immobile patient for stability
Devices should not be placed directly under a bedridden or immobile patient.
Tighten securement so the device cannot shift
Overtightening increases pressure; devices must fit correctly.
items.ex: Correct sizing, cushioning, daily inspection, and careful placement reduce MDRPI risk.

alt.q: A nurse cares for an immobile patient with several devices. Which actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Confirm that no tubing or device is lying under the patient
Devices should not be placed directly under an immobile patient.
Inspect skin under, around, and at the edges of each device
Assessment under, around, and at the edges of devices is critical.
Base the frequency of checks on how the skin responds
Individualize the frequency of pressure checks based on skin response.
Position a device over the patient’s healed Stage 2 site
Devices should not be placed over sites of prior PI.
Assume skin under a cast does not need inspection
Pressure can develop under casts; inspect when not contraindicated.
alt.ex: Keep devices off the patient’s body surface, inspect all around them, and individualize checks.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient has an indwelling urinary catheter. Which interventions prevent a device-related pressure injury? Select all that apply.
o: Provide meticulous perineal care

Anchor and secure the catheter to reduce pressure
Securing the catheter reduces pressure.
Ensure there is no tension on the catheter
Tension on the catheter increases pressure on the urethra or penis.
Run the drainage tubing under the patient’s thigh
Tubing under the thigh creates pressure on the skin.
Pull the catheter taut so it does not move
There should be no tension on the catheter.
items.ex: Perineal care, secure anchoring, and avoiding tension protect the thighs, labia, urethra, and penis.

alt.q: Which areas are at risk for pressure from an indwelling urinary catheter? Select all that apply.
o: Thighs
Catheter tubing can press on the thighs.
Urethra and labia in females

Tip of the penis in males
This is the listed pressure area for males.
Occipital region

Nasal bridge
The nasal bridge is at risk from NG tubes, nasotracheal tubes, and masks.
alt.ex: Catheter-related pressure affects the thighs, female urethra and labia, and the male penile tip.

o: A critically ill adult receiving mechanical ventilation

A patient placed prone for ventilatory support

A patient with edema under a cast

o: Nasal cannulas

Cervical collars
Cervical collars are at-risk devices.
Pulse oximetry devices
Pulse oximetry devices are at-risk devices.
