items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which wound is classified as a closed wound?
items.a: A contusion over the thigh
items.ex: In a closed wound the skin surface stays intact while underlying tissues may be damaged, as in a contusion.
w: A laceration of the forearm
A laceration splits the skin and exposes underlying tissue, so it is an open wound.
A Stage 3 pressure injury
A Stage 3 pressure injury is a full-thickness open wound.
An abrasion of the knee
An abrasion removes surface skin, so it is an open partial-thickness wound.

alt.q: Which wound is an example of an open wound?
alt.a: A puncture wound from a nail
alt.ex: Open wounds have split, incised, or cracked skin that exposes underlying tissues to the outside environment.
w: A hematoma under the skin
A hematoma is a closed wound; the skin surface remains intact.
A Stage 1 pressure injury
A Stage 1 pressure injury has intact skin, so it is a closed wound.
A bruise over the shin
A bruise (contusion) leaves the skin intact and is a closed wound.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient’s appendectomy incision is closed with staples. By which process will this wound heal?
items.a: Primary intention
items.ex: A closed, approximated incision heals by primary intention through epithelialization, quickly and with minimal scarring.
w: Secondary intention
Secondary intention applies to wounds with tissue loss whose edges are left open to fill with granulation tissue.
Tertiary intention
Tertiary intention delays closure until infection risk resolves; this incision was closed right away.
Regeneration of the dermis
Deeper structures such as the dermis do not regenerate; a closed incision heals by primary intention.

alt.q: A severe laceration with tissue loss is left open to fill in on its own. By which process will it heal?
alt.a: Secondary intention
alt.ex: Wounds with tissue loss are left open and heal by granulation tissue formation, contraction, and epithelialization.
w: Primary intention
Primary intention requires closed, approximated wound edges.
Tertiary intention
Tertiary intention means the wound is closed later once infection risk resolves.
Regeneration of the dermis
The dermis does not regenerate; tissue loss is replaced by granulation and scar tissue.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A partial-thickness wound kept moist can resurface in about 4 days, compared with 6 to 7 days if left open to air. What explains this difference?
items.a: Epidermal cells migrate only across a moist surface
items.ex: In a dry wound the epithelial cells must travel down to a moist level before they can migrate, slowing resurfacing.
w: Moisture keeps the inflammatory response from starting
The inflammatory response still occurs in moist wounds; it is a beneficial part of healing.
Moist wounds heal by scar formation instead
Partial-thickness wounds heal by regeneration, not by scar formation.
Air exposure speeds collagen deposition
Air exposure slows resurfacing; partial-thickness repair relies on epithelial migration, not collagen.

alt.q: About how long can a partial-thickness wound that is kept moist take to resurface?
alt.a: About 4 days
alt.ex: Because epidermal cells migrate only across moist surfaces, a moist partial-thickness wound can resurface in about 4 days.
w: About 6 to 7 days
Six to 7 days is the time for a wound left open to air.
About 2 to 3 weeks
This is far longer than the text describes for moist partial-thickness wounds.
About 24 hours
The first 24 hours is the usual length of the inflammatory response, not resurfacing.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which cells are described as the “garbage cells” that clean a wound of bacteria, dead cells, and debris?
items.a: Macrophages
items.ex: Monocytes transform into macrophages, which clear bacteria, dead cells, and debris by phagocytosis.
w: Fibroblasts
Fibroblasts synthesize collagen; they do not clean debris from the wound.
Platelets
Platelets gather to stop bleeding during hemostasis.
Melanocytes
Melanocytes are pigmented cells; scar tissue usually has fewer of them.

alt.q: During the inflammatory phase, macrophages release growth factors that attract which cells?
alt.a: Fibroblasts that synthesize collagen
alt.ex: Macrophage growth factors attract fibroblasts, the cells that synthesize collagen, the main component of scar tissue.
w: Platelets that form a fibrin clot
Platelets act during hemostasis to stop bleeding, before macrophages arrive.
Melanocytes that pigment new skin
Melanocytes are not the cells attracted by macrophage growth factors.
Mast cells that release histamine
Mast cells release histamine early in inflammation; they are not attracted by macrophages.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: When does the proliferation and new tissue formation phase of full-thickness wound healing begin?
items.a: 3 to 4 days after injury, lasting up to 2 weeks
items.ex: Proliferation begins 3 to 4 days after injury and can last as long as 2 weeks.
w: Within minutes of injury, lasting a few hours
This describes hemostasis, which controls bleeding right after injury.
Several weeks after injury, lasting over a year
This describes remodeling and maturation, the final phase.
10 to 12 days after injury, lasting 3 days
Proliferation starts much earlier, at 3 to 4 days, and lasts up to 2 weeks.

alt.q: Which activities characterize the proliferation phase of full-thickness wound healing?
alt.a: Granulation tissue filling, wound contraction, and epithelialization
alt.ex: In proliferation the wound fills with granulation tissue, contracts, and resurfaces by epithelialization.
w: Vessel constriction, platelet clumping, and clot formation
These events make up hemostasis.
Histamine release, vasodilation, and WBC migration
These events make up the inflammatory phase.
Collagen reorganization and scar strengthening over months
These events make up remodeling and maturation.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: On postoperative day 6, a patient’s abdominal incision separates completely and loops of bowel protrude. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Cover the protruding organs with sterile saline–soaked gauze
items.ex: Evisceration is an emergency; saline-soaked sterile gauze reduces bacterial invasion and drying of the exposed tissues.
w: Gently push the organs back into the abdomen
Evisceration requires surgical repair; the nurse never replaces the organs.
Offer sips of water to calm the patient
The patient must be kept NPO in preparation for emergency surgery.
Apply a dry sterile dressing and tape it firmly
A dry dressing lets exposed tissue dry out; the gauze must be saline-soaked.

alt.q: Why does the nurse cover eviscerated tissue with sterile gauze soaked in sterile saline?
alt.a: To reduce bacterial invasion and drying of the tissues
alt.ex: Moist sterile gauze protects protruding organs from contamination and drying while the surgical team is contacted.
w: To push the organs gently back into place
The organs are not replaced by the nurse; surgical repair is required.
To promote closure by granulation tissue
Evisceration is an emergency requiring surgery, not healing by granulation.
To stimulate bleeding that cleans the wound
Saline gauze is not used to stimulate bleeding.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: On postoperative day 5 after abdominal surgery, an obese patient coughs and then says, “It felt like something gave way.” Which complication should the nurse suspect?
items.a: Dehiscence
items.ex: Dehiscence often follows a sudden strain such as coughing, and patients often report a feeling that something has given way.
w: Hematoma
A hematoma is a localized collection of blood with swelling and bluish discoloration.
Evisceration
Evisceration requires protrusion of visceral organs through the wound, which is not described.
Hemorrhage
Hemorrhage presents with bleeding or signs of hypovolemia, not a sensation of something giving way.

alt.q: In the first few days after surgery, which wound finding should alert the nurse to potential dehiscence?
alt.a: An increase in serosanguineous drainage
alt.ex: An increase in serosanguineous drainage in the first few days after surgery signals possible dehiscence.
w: Mild redness along the incision edges
Some redness at incision edges is normal for the first few days.
A palpable healing ridge under the incision
A healing ridge is a sign of normal healing; its absence by day 9 is abnormal.
Minimal serous drainage on the first day
Minimal drainage immediately after surgery is expected.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Eight hours after hip surgery, which finding is most important for the nurse to report as possible internal hemorrhage?
items.a: Thigh swelling with a sudden rise in bloody drain output
items.ex: Internal bleeding shows as distention or swelling of the area, a change in drain output, or signs of hypovolemic shock.
w: Slight redness along the incision edges
Mild redness at the edges is a normal inflammatory response early after surgery.
Small amount of serosanguineous drainage
Minimal serosanguineous drainage is expected immediately after surgery.
Incisional pain rated 4 on a 0-to-10 scale
Moderate incisional pain is expected and is not a sign of hemorrhage.

alt.q: During which period after surgery or injury is the risk of wound hemorrhage greatest?
alt.a: The first 24 to 48 hours
alt.ex: Observe surgical wounds closely because hemorrhage risk is greatest in the first 24 to 48 hours.
w: Days 5 to 12 after suturing
Days 5 to 12 is when dehiscence can occur, not peak hemorrhage risk.
Within 30 days after surgery
Thirty days is the time frame for surgical site infections.
Several weeks after the injury
Several weeks after injury is when remodeling begins.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Within what time frame after surgery do surgical site infections (SSIs) occur?
items.a: Within 30 days
items.ex: SSIs occur within 30 days of surgery, so a patient can develop one after discharge.
w: Within 24 hours
SSIs are not limited to the first day; they can appear up to 30 days later.
Within 72 hours
Some contaminated wounds show infection in 2 to 3 days, but SSIs can occur up to 30 days.
Within 6 months
The text defines the SSI window as 30 days, not 6 months.

alt.q: Three weeks after emergency abdominal surgery, a patient has fever and a tender, inflamed incision with odorous drainage. Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
alt.a: “These signs fit a surgical site infection, which can occur up to 30 days after surgery.”
alt.ex: SSIs occur within 30 days of surgery and cause fever, tenderness, inflamed edges, and odorous purulent drainage.
w: “An infection this late cannot be related to your surgery.”
SSIs can appear up to 30 days after surgery.
“Incisions normally stay inflamed and tender for several weeks.”
Inflammation at wound edges normally fades after the first 2 to 3 days.
“Odorous drainage is a normal part of the remodeling phase.”
Odorous, purulent drainage signals infection, not normal remodeling.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which solution does the text describe as sufficient for cleansing most clean wounds?
items.a: Water or normal saline
items.ex: In most cases water or saline is sufficient for cleansing a clean wound.
w: Full-strength povidone-iodine
Povidone-iodine is cytotoxic and is not used in clean, granulating wounds.
Routine hydrogen peroxide
Opinions differ about the safety of hydrogen peroxide and its risk of tissue damage.
Dakin solution
Dakin solution is cytotoxic and is used for chemical debridement, not routine cleansing.

alt.q: A wound is contaminated with debris, necrotic tissue, and heavy drainage. Which type of cleaner should be used?
alt.a: A cleaner that is noncytotoxic to healthy tissue
alt.ex: Contaminated wounds need a cleaner that removes debris without harming healthy tissue.
w: A cleaner that is cytotoxic to all wound cells
Cytotoxic cleaners damage healthy tissue and fibroblasts needed for healing.
An alcohol-based antiseptic skin cleaner
Harsh antiseptics are not recommended for wound beds; a noncytotoxic cleaner is used.
Dry gauze rubbed firmly across the wound
Vigorous dry rubbing causes bleeding and further injury.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient’s contaminated abdominal incision was left open after surgery. The patient asks, “Why didn’t they close it?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “It will be closed once the infection risk resolves and it is free of debris.”
items.ex: Contaminated wounds are managed by delayed primary closure (tertiary intention) once infection risk resolves and debris is gone.
w: “Open wounds always heal faster and with less scarring.”
Open wounds take longer to heal and carry more infection and scarring risk.
“It will never be closed and must fill in with scar.”
This describes secondary intention; delayed closure is planned here.
“Leaving it open shows the wound is not infected.”
The wound was left open because it is contaminated and needs observation.

alt.q: Which type of wound healing is frequently used for abdominal incisions complicated by infection?
alt.a: Tertiary intention
alt.ex: Tertiary intention, or delayed primary closure, waits until infection risk is resolved and the wound is free of debris.
w: Primary intention
Primary intention closes clean wounds right away; infected incisions are not closed immediately.
Secondary intention
Secondary intention leaves the wound open permanently to fill with scar tissue.
Regeneration
Regeneration is how partial-thickness wounds heal, not infected incisions.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which findings are local clinical signs of wound infection? Select all that apply.
o: Erythema around the wound
Erythema is a local sign of wound infection.
Thick drainage with a change in color and odor
A change in drainage appearance, such as thickening, color change, or odor, suggests infection.
Periwound warmth, pain, or edema
Warmth, pain, and edema around the wound are local signs of infection.
Increased amount of wound drainage
An increased amount of drainage is a local sign of infection.
Dry pink tissue across the wound surface
Dry pink tissue reflects reestablished epidermis in a healing partial-thickness wound.
Clear, watery drainage in small amounts
Small amounts of serous drainage are not a sign of infection.
items.ex: Local infection signs include erythema, more drainage, changed drainage appearance, and periwound warmth, pain, or edema.

alt.q: Which factors increase a patient’s risk for a surgical site infection? Select all that apply.
o: Hyperglycemia
Hyperglycemia is a listed SSI risk factor.
Smoking
Smoking is a listed SSI risk factor.
Obesity
Obesity is a listed SSI risk factor.
Emergency abdominal surgery
Emergency and abdominal surgery are listed SSI risk factors.
Use of surgical staples
Staples are a common skin closure and are not listed as an SSI risk factor.
Elective surgery on an extremity
Emergency and abdominal surgery, not elective limb surgery, are listed risks.
alt.ex: SSI risk factors include hyperglycemia, smoking, untreated peripheral vascular disease, cancer, obesity, age, and emergency and abdominal surgery.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which patients are at increased risk for wound dehiscence? Select all that apply.
o: A patient with poor nutritional status
Poor nutrition impairs wound healing and increases dehiscence risk.
A patient with a wound infection
About half of dehiscence occurrences are associated with wound infection.
A patient with diabetes mellitus
Diabetes is an underlying disease that impairs healing and raises dehiscence risk.
A patient with obesity
Obesity strains the wound, and adipose tissue heals poorly.
A patient with a minor scalp laceration
Dehiscence is a complication of surgical incisions, especially abdominal ones.
A patient who splints the incision when coughing
Splinting supports the incision and helps prevent dehiscence.
items.ex: Poor nutrition, infection, diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, and obesity all raise the risk for dehiscence.

alt.q: A patient has total separation of an abdominal wound with organs protruding. Which actions should the nurse take? Select all that apply.
o: Place sterile saline-soaked gauze over the tissues
Moist sterile gauze reduces bacterial invasion and drying of the tissues.
Contact the surgical team
Evisceration is an emergency that requires surgical repair.
Keep the patient NPO
The patient is kept NPO in preparation for emergency surgery.
Observe for signs and symptoms of shock
Monitor for shock while preparing the patient for surgery.
Ask the patient to cough to assess the wound
Coughing raises abdominal pressure and worsens wound separation.
Push the organs back inside with sterile gloves
The nurse does not replace organs; surgical repair is required.
alt.ex: For evisceration, cover with saline-soaked gauze, call the surgical team, keep NPO, watch for shock, and prepare for surgery.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which findings may indicate internal hemorrhage from a surgical wound? Select all that apply.
o: Distention or swelling of the affected body part
Swelling or distention can signal bleeding into the tissues.
A change in the type and amount of drain output
A change in drain drainage can reveal internal bleeding.
Signs of hypovolemic shock
Hypovolemic shock signs indicate significant blood loss.
Bluish swelling with a change in sensation or warmth
This describes a hematoma, a localized collection of blood.
Dry, intact dressing with no drainage
A dry dressing does not rule out internal bleeding, but it is not a sign of it.
A well-approximated incision with mild redness
Mild redness at approximated edges is normal early healing.
items.ex: Internal bleeding may show as swelling, changes in drain output, signs of hypovolemic shock, or a hematoma.

alt.q: A hematoma forms near a major artery after surgery. Which statements are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: A hematoma is a localized collection of blood under the tissues
This is the definition of a hematoma.
It often takes on a bluish discoloration
Hematomas often appear bluish with swelling.
An expanding hematoma can obstruct blood flow
Pressure from an expanding hematoma near a major vessel obstructs blood flow.
It is harmless wherever it forms
A hematoma near a major artery or vein is dangerous.
It always produces visible bleeding on the dressing
Internal bleeding may show no visible blood.
alt.ex: A hematoma is a localized blood collection that is dangerous near major vessels because it can obstruct blood flow.

items.q: In individuals with darkly pigmented skin, scar tissue may be more highly pigmented than the surrounding skin.
items.a: True
items.ex: Scar tissue usually has fewer melanocytes and looks lighter, but in darkly pigmented skin it may be darker.
items.ww: The text states scar tissue in darkly pigmented skin may be more highly pigmented than surrounding skin.

alt.q: Once remodeling is complete, a healed wound has the same tensile strength as the tissue it replaced.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: A healed wound usually does not regain the tensile strength of the original tissue, even after months of remodeling.
alt.ww: Although the collagen scar gains strength for months, it usually remains weaker than the original tissue.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: During the inflammatory phase, the nurse should cool the area to reduce swelling unless the swelling is within a closed compartment.
items.a: False
items.ex: Inflammation is beneficial; cooling or reducing swelling has no value unless swelling occurs in a closed compartment.
items.ww: The rule is reversed: intervene only when swelling occurs within a closed compartment such as the neck or ankle.

alt.q: The redness, edema, and warmth of the inflammatory phase are beneficial, so cooling the area is generally of no value.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The inflammatory response helps establish a clean wound bed, so there is no value in cooling it except in a closed compartment.
alt.ww: Cooling is not routinely needed because inflammation is a beneficial part of healing.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A partial-thickness wound heals by regeneration, whereas a full-thickness wound heals by forming new tissue.
items.a: True
items.ex: Partial-thickness wounds regenerate; full-thickness wounds form new tissue and scar because deeper structures do not regenerate.
items.ww: The text distinguishes these mechanisms: regeneration for partial-thickness and new tissue formation for full-thickness wounds.

alt.q: Full-thickness wounds, such as Stage 3 and 4 pressure injuries, heal by regeneration of the lost dermis and subcutaneous tissue.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Full-thickness wounds heal by scar formation because deeper structures do not regenerate.
alt.ww: Only partial-thickness wounds heal by regeneration; full-thickness wounds must fill with new tissue and scar.

items.ex: Zinc supplements are based on serum deficiency, limited to 10 to 14 days, and large doses can be toxic.
w: “Take as much zinc as you like; it is harmless.”
Large doses of zinc can be toxic and impair immune function.
“Zinc should be taken for at least 6 months.”
Supplementation should be limited to 10 to 14 days.
“Zinc speeds healing by boosting copper use.”
Zinc may inhibit, not improve, copper metabolism.

alt.q: What is a risk of taking large doses of zinc to promote wound healing?
alt.a: Toxicity and inhibited copper metabolism
alt.ex: Large zinc doses can be toxic, may inhibit copper metabolism, and can impair immune function.
w: Excess collagen and hypertrophic scar
The text does not link zinc to excess scar; toxicity is the concern.
Reversal of steroid effects on skin
Reversing steroid effects is a benefit of vitamin A.
Faster wound contraction and closure
Large doses do not speed healing; they carry toxicity risks.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient with diabetes mellitus and peripheral vascular disease has a foot wound. Why is this patient at risk for poor healing?
items.a: Poor circulation limits oxygen delivery to the tissues
items.ex: Diabetes and peripheral vascular disease impair circulation, and chronic tissue hypoxia impairs collagen synthesis and infection resistance.
w: Excess oxygen in the blood damages new collagen
The concern is too little, not too much, oxygen in the tissues.
These conditions speed up macrophage activity
Poor perfusion slows healing; it does not speed macrophage activity.
These conditions raise protein needs only
The main problem described is poor tissue perfusion and hypoxia.

alt.q: What effect does chronic tissue hypoxia have on wound healing?
alt.a: It impairs collagen synthesis and lowers resistance to infection
alt.ex: Oxygen fuels cellular functions; chronic hypoxia impairs collagen synthesis and reduces tissue resistance to infection.
w: It speeds collagen synthesis and scar formation
Hypoxia slows, rather than speeds, collagen synthesis.
It shortens the inflammatory phase
Hypoxia impairs healing; it does not shorten inflammation.
It has no effect once granulation begins
Oxygen is needed throughout healing, though needs vary by phase.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which phase of wound healing does a wound infection prolong?
items.a: The inflammatory phase
items.ex: Infection prolongs inflammation, delays collagen synthesis, prevents epithelialization, and increases tissue-destroying cytokines.
w: The hemostasis phase
Hemostasis is impaired by anticoagulants and clotting disorders, not mainly by infection.
The remodeling phase
The text says infection prolongs the inflammatory phase, not remodeling.
The coagulation phase only
Coagulation is hemostasis; infection prolongs inflammation.

alt.q: About how much more does treatment of an infected wound cost than treatment of an uninfected wound?
alt.a: 70% more
alt.ex: Infected wounds cost about 70% more to treat, so preventing infection is a major goal of wound care.
w: 10% more
The cost difference is much larger than 10%.
25% more
The cost difference is much larger than 25%.
200% more
The text reports 70%, not 200%.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: An 82-year-old patient’s surgical wound is healing more slowly than expected. Which age-related change best explains this?
items.a: Decreased macrophage function delays inflammation and collagen synthesis
items.ex: In aging, reduced macrophage function delays the inflammatory response and collagen synthesis and slows epithelialization.
w: Increased melanocytes darken and weaken the scar
Melanocytes affect scar color, not the speed of healing in older adults.
Faster epithelialization causes early wound closure
Aging slows, not speeds, epithelialization.
Heightened inflammation overwhelms the wound bed
Aging causes a delayed, not exaggerated, inflammatory response.

alt.q: Which phases of wound healing are affected by the physiological changes of aging?
alt.a: All phases of wound healing
alt.ex: Aging affects all phases of healing, largely through decreased macrophage function.
w: Only the hemostasis phase
Aging affects more than hemostasis.
Only the remodeling phase
Aging also delays inflammation and collagen synthesis.
No phases, only scar color
Aging slows inflammation, collagen synthesis, and epithelialization.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient with a draining leg wound says, “I don’t want my grandchildren to visit because of the smell.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Tell me more about how this wound is affecting you.”
items.ex: Odor from drainage affects a patient’s perception of the wound; the nurse first explores the impact on self-concept.
w: “The smell is not that noticeable to others.”
This dismisses the patient’s concern rather than assessing it.
“You should not worry about the visitors.”
This offers false reassurance instead of exploring feelings.
“The odor shows the wound is healing well.”
Strong odor can signal infection and is not a sign of healing.

alt.q: Which factor is identified as affecting a patient’s perception of a wound?
alt.a: Odor from wound drainage
alt.ex: Location, scars, stitches or drains, odor from drainage, and prosthetic devices affect how patients perceive wounds.
w: The brand of dressing tape used
Tape brand is not listed as a factor in wound perception.
The time of the dressing change
Timing of care is not listed as a perception factor.
The nurse’s years of experience
Nurse experience is not listed as a factor in wound perception.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Two days after surgery, a patient’s incision has induration, local warmth, and purulent drainage, and the patient has a fever. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Report the findings as signs of wound infection
items.ex: Erythema, warmth, edema, induration, pain, purulent drainage, and fever indicate wound infection and must be reported.
w: Document them as normal early inflammation
Purulent drainage and fever are not part of normal inflammation.
Apply an ice pack to reduce the swelling
Cooling does not treat infection; the findings require reporting.
Reassess the wound at the next dressing change
Signs of infection need prompt reporting, not delay.

alt.q: Which finding in a surgical wound most strongly suggests infection rather than normal healing?
alt.a: A change in odor and amount of drainage
alt.ex: A change in odor, volume, or character of drainage is an indication of wound infection.
w: Mild redness at the edges on day 1
Some redness at incision edges is normal for the first few days.
Dry pink tissue across the surface
Dry pink tissue reflects normal reepithelialization.
Minimal serosanguineous drainage on day 1
Minimal serosanguineous drainage is expected right after surgery.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse assesses a patient with diabetes mellitus differently from a patient lying in skeletal traction. What is the basis for this difference?
items.a: Knowledge of underlying disease and pressure injury pathology
items.ex: Knowing the pathophysiology of underlying diseases and pressure injuries gives a scientific basis for individualizing assessment.
w: Agency policy forbids using one tool for both
The difference comes from knowledge of each patient’s condition, not a tool ban.
Patients in traction never develop pressure injuries
Immobility in traction creates pressure injury risk.
Patients with diabetes need no skin assessment
Diabetes impairs perfusion and healing, so assessment is essential.

alt.q: Because chronic wounds are difficult to heal, what does the text emphasize in evaluating them?
alt.a: Diligently evaluating responses and modifying ineffective interventions
alt.ex: Be diligent in evaluating the patient’s response and determining which interventions work and which need modification.
w: Keeping the same plan unchanged until discharge
Ineffective interventions should be modified, not continued unchanged.
Evaluating only when the wound has fully closed
Ongoing evaluation is needed throughout healing.
Relying only on the patient’s own report
Evaluation includes objective wound assessment, not only patient report.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Physiological processes of wound healing depend on the availability of which nutrients? Select all that apply.
o: Protein
Protein supplies the amino acids fibroblasts use to form collagen.
Vitamin A
Vitamin A supports epithelialization and reverses steroid effects.
Vitamin C
Vitamin C is necessary for collagen synthesis.
Zinc and copper
These trace minerals support epithelialization, collagen synthesis, and fiber linking.
Caffeine
Caffeine is not a healing nutrient; noncaffeinated fluids are recommended.
Alcohol
Alcohol is not a healing nutrient; nonalcoholic fluids are recommended.
items.ex: Healing depends on protein, vitamins (especially A and C), and the trace minerals zinc and copper.

alt.q: Which statements about nutrition and wound healing are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: A deficiency in any needed nutrient can delay healing
Deficiencies in any of the nutrients impair or delay healing.
Protein needs increase in patients with wounds
Protein needs especially are increased for tissue repair.
Patients at risk of malnutrition need a nutrition team consult
Consult a nutritional team for individualized dietary prescriptions.
Collagen forms without dietary protein
Fibroblasts form collagen from amino acids acquired from ingested protein.
Calories are unnecessary if protein is adequate
Calories are needed as fuel for cellular healing activity.
alt.ex: Healing needs balanced intake of calories, protein, vitamins, and minerals, with nutrition team input for at-risk patients.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which findings indicate a wound infection? Select all that apply.
o: Induration
Induration is an indication of wound infection.
Local warmth and edema
Warmth and edema are local signs of wound infection.
Purulent drainage
Purulent drainage indicates infection.
Fever
Fever can accompany wound infection.
Blanchable erythema that fades quickly
Blanchable erythema is normal reactive hyperemia.
Dry pink epithelium at the edges
Dry pink epithelium is a sign of healing.
items.ex: Infection signs include erythema, warmth, edema, induration, pain, purulent or changed drainage, surrounding redness, and fever.

alt.q: A nurse teaches a family caregiver what to report about a home wound. Which signs of infection should be included? Select all that apply.
o: Change in the odor of drainage
A change in odor suggests infection.
Increase in the volume of drainage
A change in drainage volume suggests infection.
Redness spreading into surrounding tissue
Redness in the surrounding tissue indicates infection.
Wound edges slowly getting smaller
Shrinking wound size indicates healing.
Red, moist granulation tissue in the base
Granulation tissue indicates progress toward healing.
alt.ex: Report changes in odor, volume, or character of drainage, surrounding redness, warmth, pain, or fever.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: How does a wound infection interfere with healing? Select all that apply.
o: It prolongs the inflammatory phase
Infection prolongs inflammation.
It delays collagen synthesis
Infection delays collagen synthesis.
It prevents epithelialization
Infection prevents the wound from resurfacing.
It increases proinflammatory cytokines
More proinflammatory cytokines lead to further tissue destruction.
It speeds wound contraction
Infection impairs, not speeds, healing activities.
It shortens the time to closure
Infection lengthens healing time.
items.ex: Infection prolongs inflammation, delays collagen, prevents epithelialization, and raises cytokines that destroy tissue.

alt.q: Which statements explain why infected wounds heal poorly? Select all that apply.
o: Infected wounds compete for available calorie intake
The increased metabolic needs of infection compete for calories.
Excess inflammation prolongs healing
Too much inflammation prolongs healing because arriving cells compete for nutrients.
Epithelialization is prevented
Infection prevents epithelialization.
Infection strengthens new collagen
Infection delays collagen synthesis.
Infection lowers the wound’s metabolic needs
Infection increases metabolic energy needs.
alt.ex: Infection raises metabolic demand, prolongs inflammation, and blocks collagen formation and resurfacing.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

sections.name: Nursing process: skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse finds a reddened area over a patient’s sacrum. When the nurse presses on it, the redness persists. What does this finding indicate?
items.a: Damage to the capillary bed consistent with a Stage 1 injury
items.ex: Nonblanchable erythema persists under pressure and indicates structural damage to the capillary bed, a Stage 1 pressure injury.
w: Normal reactive hyperemia that will fade in hours
Reactive hyperemia blanches with pressure; this redness did not.
Inflammatory erythema with an intact capillary bed
Inflammatory erythema with intact capillaries blanches with pressure.
A Stage 2 injury with partial loss of skin
Stage 2 involves an open or blistered area; this skin is intact.

alt.q: When the nurse presses on a reddened sacral area, it turns pale and then reddens again when pressure is released. How should this be interpreted?
alt.a: Blanchable erythema with an intact capillary bed
alt.ex: Blanchable erythema, such as normal reactive hyperemia, indicates that the underlying capillary bed is intact.
w: Nonblanchable erythema of a Stage 1 injury
Nonblanchable redness persists under pressure.
Deep tissue injury requiring debridement
Blanching redness does not indicate deep tissue injury.
Hematoma formation beneath the skin
A hematoma appears as swelling with bluish discoloration.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse observes an assistive personnel (AP) caring for an immobile patient with a reddened sacrum. Which action by the AP requires the nurse to intervene?
items.a: Massaging the reddened area to improve circulation
items.ex: Never massage reddened areas; massage breaks down underlying capillaries and increases the risk of pressure injury.
w: Using a lift sheet to reposition the patient
A lift sheet reduces friction and shear and is correct.
Keeping the head of the bed at 30 degrees
Elevating the head of the bed 30 degrees or less reduces shear.
Applying moisture barrier after incontinence
A moisture barrier protects skin from urine and stool.

alt.q: Why should a nurse never massage a reddened area over a bony prominence?
alt.a: It breaks down capillaries and increases tissue injury risk
alt.ex: Massage of reddened areas damages underlying capillaries and can lead to pressure injury formation.
w: It causes the area to blanch permanently
Massage does not cause permanent blanching; it damages capillaries.
It removes the protective moisture barrier
The main concern is capillary damage, not removing the barrier.
It hides signs of infection in the area
The reason given is capillary breakdown and tissue injury.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse teaches a wheelchair user about preventing pressure injuries. Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I will shift my weight every 15 minutes while sitting.”
items.ex: Shifting weight every 15 minutes gives short-term relief to the ischial tuberosities, which bear more pressure when sitting.
w: “A donut cushion will protect my tailbone best.”
Donut-shaped cushions reduce blood supply and widen areas of ischemia.
“I can sit up to 4 hours before changing position.”
Sitting should be limited to 2 hours or less at any one time.
“A firm, rigid cushion keeps my weight off my hips.”
Rigid cushions are contraindicated; foam, gel, or air cushions are recommended.

alt.q: For a patient at risk for skin breakdown who can sit in a chair, what is the maximum time to sit at one time?
alt.a: 2 hours or less
alt.ex: Limit chair sitting to 2 hours or less because pressure on the ischial tuberosities is greater than when supine.
w: 4 hours or less
Four hours exceeds the recommended limit for sitting.
6 hours or less
Six hours greatly exceeds the recommended limit.
15 minutes or less
Fifteen minutes is the interval for weight shifting, not the sitting limit.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A person arrives at a clinic with a knife blade embedded in the thigh. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Leave the blade in place and apply pressure around it
items.ex: A penetrating object provides pressure that controls bleeding; removal can cause massive, uncontrolled bleeding.
w: Remove the blade, then apply direct pressure
Removing the object can cause massive, uncontrolled bleeding.
Apply firm pressure directly on the blade
Pressure is applied around, not on, the penetrating object.
Irrigate the wound with saline around the blade
The priority is controlling bleeding and transporting the patient.

alt.q: Why is a penetrating object such as a knife blade left in place until the patient reaches an emergency department?
alt.a: The object provides pressure that controls some bleeding
alt.ex: Leaving the object in place controls some bleeding; removing it can cause massive, uncontrolled hemorrhage.
w: The object keeps tetanus bacteria out of the wound
Leaving it in place is about controlling bleeding, not tetanus.
The object prevents the wound from becoming dirty
Penetrating objects often carry contaminants into wounds.
The object speeds clot formation inside the tissue
The reason is pressure control of bleeding, not clot formation.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient’s Jackson-Pratt drain has drained 40 mL each shift, but over the past 4 hours there has been no drainage through the tubing. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Notify the health care provider of a possible blocked drain
items.ex: A sudden decrease in drainage through the tubing may indicate a blocked drain, so the health care provider is notified.
w: Document the finding as expected healing
A sudden stop in drainage suggests blockage rather than expected healing.
Pull the drain out a few centimeters to reposition it
Pulling or advancing a drain is usually the health care provider’s responsibility.
Remove the drain and apply a dry dressing
Nurses do not remove a drain because of a suspected blockage.

alt.q: A Hemovac evacuator can no longer hold a vacuum on its own. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Notify the surgeon, who may order a secondary vacuum system
alt.ex: When an evacuator cannot maintain vacuum, the surgeon is notified and may order wall suction.
w: Remove the evacuator and leave the tubing open
Leaving the tubing open loses suction and risks contamination.
Clamp the tubing until the next shift
Clamping allows fluid to collect in tissues, slowing healing.
Squeeze the device every hour without reporting
The problem must be reported so a secondary vacuum can be ordered.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is obtaining a wound culture by swab. Which action is correct?
items.a: Clean the wound with normal saline before collecting the specimen
items.ex: Old drainage contains resident skin flora that may not be the causative organism, so the wound is cleaned first.
w: Swab the old drainage on the removed dressing
Never culture old drainage; it contains resident flora.
Swab necrotic tissue in the wound base
Culturing necrotic tissue leads to false-positive results.
Collect the specimen after antibiotics are started
Collect the culture before starting antibiotics.

alt.q: When obtaining a wound swab culture, where should the nurse rotate the swab?
alt.a: Within 1 to 2 cm2 of clean, viable wound tissue
alt.ex: Infection resides in viable tissue; rotating with pressure over clean tissue elicits tissue fluid.
w: Across the periwound skin around the edges
Culturing periwound skin gives false-positive results.
Over black necrotic eschar in the wound
Culturing necrotic tissue gives false-positive results.
In the drainage collected on the old dressing
Old drainage contains resident flora, not the true pathogen.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which equipment does the text describe as delivering wound irrigation at a pressure that cleans without damaging healthy tissue?
items.a: A 35-mL syringe with a 19-gauge angiocatheter
items.ex: A 35-mL syringe with a 19-gauge angiocatheter delivers saline at about 8 psi, a safe and effective pressure.
w: A 3-mL syringe with a 25-gauge needle
A small syringe and fine needle do not produce the described irrigation pressure.
A 60-mL piston syringe pressed into the wound
The syringe tip should never occlude the wound opening.
A bulb syringe inserted into the drain site
Irrigate over, not in, the drainage site.

alt.q: Why should a nurse never occlude a wound opening with the syringe tip during irrigation?
alt.a: It raises pressure and can force bacteria deeper into the wound
alt.ex: Occluding the opening pushes fluid into a closed space, causing tissue damage, discomfort, and possible spread of bacteria.
w: It prevents the solution from warming to body temperature
Temperature of the solution is not the reason given.
It makes the irrigation fluid flow too slowly to clean
The concern is excess pressure, not slow flow.
It contaminates the syringe for the next irrigation
The concern is tissue damage and bacteria in the wound bed.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient receiving negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT) reports severe pain. Which pressure range can be used to reduce pain without compromising effectiveness?
items.a: 75 to 80 mm Hg
items.ex: For patients with severe pain, lower NPWT pressures of 75 to 80 mm Hg reduce discomfort without compromising effectiveness.
w: 125 to 150 mm Hg
125 mm Hg is the standard setting; raising pressure would not reduce pain.
200 to 250 mm Hg
These pressures are far above the levels described for NPWT.
10 to 15 mm Hg
These pressures are below the lower range described in the text.

alt.q: At what pressure does evidence show improved microvascular blood flow and granulation with intermittent NPWT?
alt.a: 125 mm Hg
alt.ex: Intermittent therapy at 125 mm Hg improves microvascular blood flow and granulation tissue formation.
w: 50 mm Hg
50 mm Hg is below the range discussed in the text.
75 mm Hg
75 to 80 mm Hg is the lower range used for patients with severe pain.
250 mm Hg
250 mm Hg is far above the pressure discussed.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: For which patient should the nurse question an order for warm moist compresses?
items.a: A patient with suspected acute appendicitis
items.ex: Heat is contraindicated in acute localized inflammation such as appendicitis because it could cause rupture.
w: A patient with chronic low back muscle strain
Heat is used to relieve muscle strain and spasm.
A patient with arthritis joint pain
Heat improves blood flow and relieves pain in arthritis.
A patient with menstrual cramping
Heat is a recognized treatment for menstrual cramping.

alt.q: For which patient should the nurse question an order for a cold pack?
alt.a: A patient with arteriosclerosis and diminished pedal pulses
alt.ex: Cold further reduces blood supply in impaired circulation; the nurse questions the order if circulatory inadequacy is present.
w: A patient who sprained an ankle 2 hours ago
Cold is used immediately after sprains and strains.
A patient with a minor burn
Cold therapy is used for minor burns.
A patient just after an injection
Cold is listed as useful after injections.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: When removing an intermittent suture, which technique prevents infection?
items.a: Cut close to the skin on one side and pull through from the other
items.ex: Never pull the contaminated visible part of a suture through tissue; cut close to the skin and pull from the other side.
w: Cut the knot and pull the visible suture through
This drags the contaminated exposed suture through tissue.
Pull the suture out without cutting it first
Sutures are cut before removal to avoid trauma and contamination.
Cut both sides far from the skin before pulling
Cutting far from the skin pulls exposed suture material through tissue.

alt.q: Why should the visible part of a suture never be pulled through underlying tissue during removal?
alt.a: Surface suture harbors microorganisms that could cause infection
alt.ex: Sutures on the skin harbor microorganisms and debris, while the part beneath the skin is sterile.
w: The visible part is absorbable and will dissolve
Skin sutures being removed are nonabsorbable.
The buried part harbors bacteria that must stay inside
The part beneath the skin is sterile.
Pulling it through speeds removal of the remaining staples
The concern is contamination, not speed.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is packing a deep wound with saline-moistened gauze. Which action is correct?
items.a: Pack lightly until the gauze reaches the level of the wound surface
items.ex: Pack loosely to contact the whole wound surface, stopping at the wound surface to avoid pressure and maceration.
w: Pack tightly so the gauze fills every space firmly
Overpacking causes pressure on the wound bed tissue.
Let the gauze overlap onto the wound edges
Packing that overlaps the edges causes periwound maceration.
Pack the gauze folded to keep it compact
Gauze is unfolded so it can wick drainage and contact the surface.

alt.q: Why should wound packing never extend above the wound surface onto the edges?
alt.a: Packing that overlaps the edges macerates periwound skin
alt.ex: Packing on the wound edges causes periwound skin maceration, and overpacking puts pressure on the wound bed.
w: It stops the dressing from wicking drainage
Overlap is a problem because it macerates the periwound skin.
It makes the dressing too dry to work
The concern is maceration of surrounding skin, not dryness.
It increases the frequency of dressing orders
Order frequency is not the reason given.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is planning care to prevent pressure injuries in a bedbound patient. Which interventions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Position the patient in a 30-degree lateral position
A 30-degree lateral position avoids direct pressure on the hip.
Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or less
Limiting head elevation reduces sliding and shear.
Use a friction-reducing sheet to reposition
Lifting rather than dragging prevents friction and shear injury.
Apply a moisture barrier after each incontinence episode
Barrier ointment protects the skin from urine and stool.
Raise the head of the bed to 45 degrees for comfort
Head elevation above 30 degrees increases shear on the sacrum.
Massage reddened bony prominences
Massage damages capillaries and increases tissue injury risk.
items.ex: Prevention combines skin care and incontinence management, proper positioning and support surfaces, and education.

alt.q: Which statements about repositioning to prevent pressure injuries are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Turning intervals should be based on patient assessment
Repositioning intervals must be based on individual assessment.
Support surfaces do not eliminate the need for turning
Repositioning is still required when a support surface is in use.
Positioning devices should protect bony prominences
Use positioning devices to protect bony prominences.
A 2-hour turning schedule always prevents injury
A standard 1.5- to 2-hour interval does not always prevent injury.
Dragging the patient up in bed is acceptable
Dragging causes friction and shear; a transfer device is used to lift.
alt.ex: Repositioning is individualized, continues with support surfaces, uses lifting devices, and protects bony prominences.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which conditions are contraindications to negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT)? Select all that apply.
o: Necrotic tissue with eschar
Eschar must be removed; necrotic tissue is a contraindication.
Untreated osteomyelitis
Untreated osteomyelitis is a contraindication.
Malignancy in the wound
Malignancy in the wound is a contraindication.
Exposed blood vessels or organs
Exposed vasculature, nerves, anastomotic sites, or organs are contraindications.
A dehisced surgical wound
Dehisced wounds are an indication for NPWT.
A partial-thickness burn
Partial-thickness burns are an indication for NPWT.
items.ex: NPWT is contraindicated with eschar, untreated osteomyelitis, unexplored fistulas, malignancy, and exposed vessels, nerves, or organs.

alt.q: Which wounds are indications for negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT)? Select all that apply.
o: A dehisced abdominal wound
Dehisced wounds are an indication for NPWT.
A diabetic foot injury
Diabetic injuries are an indication for NPWT.
A high-risk sternal incision
Select high-risk postoperative incisions, such as sternal ones, are indications.
A wound covered with eschar
Necrotic tissue with eschar is a contraindication.
A wound containing malignancy
Malignancy in the wound is a contraindication.
alt.ex: NPWT is used for chronic, acute, traumatic, and dehisced wounds, burns, diabetic and pressure injuries, flaps, grafts, and high-risk incisions.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which safety measures should the nurse follow when applying heat or cold therapy? Select all that apply.
o: Check the patient and skin every 20 minutes
Check every 20 minutes for excess redness, pain, or tingling.
Instruct the patient to report sensation changes at once
Patients report changes in sensation or discomfort immediately.
Place the nurse call system within reach
The patient must be able to call for help.
Follow agency policy for safe temperatures
Agency policy defines safe temperatures.
Let the patient adjust the temperature setting
Patients should not adjust temperature settings.
Leave a patient who cannot sense heat unattended
Never leave unattended a patient who cannot sense temperature changes.
items.ex: Box 48.12 stresses prevention, frequent checks, patient reporting, safe temperatures, and never leaving a vulnerable patient alone.

alt.q: Which patients are at increased risk for injury from heat or cold applications? Select all that apply.
o: An older adult with reduced pain sensitivity
Older adults may not perceive pain from heat or cold.
A patient with a spinal cord injury
Altered nerve pathways prevent reception of sensory stimuli.
A patient who is confused
Confused patients may not move away from or report discomfort.
A patient with an area of edema
Edema reduces sensation to temperature stimuli.
An alert adult with intact sensation
Intact sensation and alertness allow the patient to sense and report problems.
alt.ex: Very young or old age, open wounds, edema, scar, vascular disease, confusion, and spinal cord injury raise risk.

items.q: Exposure to gastric and pancreatic drainage carries the highest risk for skin breakdown.
items.a: True
items.ex: Gastric and pancreatic fluids have digestive qualities that irritate and break down the skin quickly.
items.ww: Saliva and serosanguineous drainage are low risk; urine and stool are moderate; gastric and pancreatic drainage is highest.

alt.q: Saliva and serosanguineous drainage carry the highest risk for skin breakdown among body fluids.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Saliva and serosanguineous drainage are not very caustic and carry a low risk of skin breakdown.
alt.ww: The highest risk comes from gastric and pancreatic drainage, which have digestive qualities.

items.q: The hand check method is a reliable way to assess whether a patient has bottomed out on a support surface.
items.a: False

items.ww: Bottoming out is reduced by proper surface selection, patient placement, and avoiding extra layers of bedding.

alt.q: The hand check method for detecting bottoming out on a support surface is no longer recommended.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The hand check is unreliable; proper selection, placement, and minimal bedding layers reduce bottoming out.
alt.ww: Guidelines no longer recommend the hand check because it is not reliable.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Chronic pressure injury wounds usually require clean technique for dressing changes.
items.a: True

items.ww: Sterile technique is used for fresh surgical wounds, not routinely for chronic pressure injuries.

alt.q: Chronic pressure injury wounds require sterile gloves and sterile technique at every dressing change.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Chronic pressure injuries require clean technique; sterile technique is for wounds such as fresh surgical incisions.
alt.ww: Clean medical asepsis is appropriate for chronic nonsurgical wounds such as pressure injuries.

sections.name: Skill 48.1 · Risk assessment, skin assessment, and prevention strategies for pressure injury

items.q: A nurse is caring for an immobile older adult at risk for pressure injury (PI). Which task can the nurse assign to assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Repositioning the patient on the individualized turning schedule
items.ex: AP may reposition patients and keep skin clean and dry; PI risk assessment remains the nurse’s responsibility.
w: Scoring the patient’s PI risk with the agency’s risk tool
PI risk assessment cannot be delegated to AP.
Deciding whether the patient needs a specialty mattress
Selecting interventions from assessment data is nursing judgment, not an AP task.
Evaluating whether a reddened area over the sacrum blanches
Assessing skin for blanching is part of skin assessment, which the nurse performs.

alt.q: Which instruction should the nurse give AP caring for a patient with a nasal cannula and an indwelling catheter?
alt.a: Report any redness or abrasion you notice from the medical devices
alt.ex: AP are told to report skin changes and any redness or abrasion from medical devices to the nurse.
w: Complete the PI risk score if the patient’s condition changes
Risk assessment cannot be delegated; the nurse rescores when condition changes.
Massage any reddened skin under the tubing to restore circulation
Reddened areas must not be massaged because massage can damage underlying tissue.
Remove the cannula overnight if the ears look red
Oxygen therapy is not stopped by AP; they report device-related redness to the nurse.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: While inspecting a patient’s sacrum, the nurse presses a reddened area with a gloved finger and releases it. The area stays red. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
items.a: Abnormal reactive hyperemia suggesting a possible Stage 1 PI
items.ex: Tissue that does not blanch when palpated indicates abnormal reactive hyperemia and possible Stage 1 PI.
w: Normal reactive hyperemia showing that the tissue is not at risk
Normal reactive hyperemia blanches (lightens) when pressed; this area did not.
Moisture-associated skin damage caused by incontinence
MASD results from moisture exposure; a nonblanching area over a bony prominence suggests pressure injury.
A full-thickness PI with exposed subcutaneous tissue
Intact, nonblanching red skin is an early sign, not a full-thickness wound.

alt.q: When the nurse presses a reddened area over a patient’s heel, the redness lightens in color. What does this indicate?
alt.a: Normal reactive hyperemia; the tissue is not at risk for injury
alt.ex: Redness that blanches on palpation is normal reactive hyperemia, indicating the tissue is not at risk.
w: Abnormal reactive hyperemia; a Stage 1 PI is likely
Abnormal reactive hyperemia does not blanch when pressed.
Deep tissue injury; the heel must be debrided
Blanching skin indicates normal circulation, not deep tissue injury.
Mottling from persistent tissue hypoxia; refer to WOCN
Mottling and pallor are abnormal responses; blanching redness is normal.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: After a patient is turned off the sacrum, the nurse notes blanchable erythema over the area. Within what time should this redness resolve after off-loading?
items.a: 30 minutes
items.ex: Blanchable erythema should resolve within 30 minutes of off-loading; if it persists, consider a support surface or new schedule.
w: 2 hours
Two hours is far too long; persistence beyond 30 minutes calls for changes in care.
8 hours
Waiting 8 hours would delay needed changes to the support surface or turning schedule.
24 hours
Redness lasting a day signals tissue injury; normal hyperemia fades within 30 minutes.

alt.q: During daily skin inspection, a nurse finds a reddened area over the trochanter that does not blanch. When should the nurse recheck the area?
alt.a: In 30 minutes to 1 hour
alt.ex: If a reddened area does not blanch, suspect tissue injury and recheck it in 30 minutes to 1 hour.
w: In 4 to 6 hours
The book directs a recheck within 30 minutes to 1 hour, not hours later.
In 12 hours
A 12-hour delay could allow suspected tissue injury to progress unnoticed.
In 24 hours
Rechecking the next day is too late for suspected tissue injury.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient is admitted to an acute care medical unit. According to the skill’s guidance, when must the nurse complete the initial PI risk assessment?
items.a: Within 8 hours of admission, then reassess every 24 hours or with a change in condition
items.ex: In acute care, perform the initial assessment within 8 hours of admission and reassess every 24 hours or as condition changes.
w: Within 24 hours of admission, then reassess once weekly
Weekly reassessment is the long-term care schedule, and 24 hours is too late for the initial acute care assessment.
Within 48 hours of admission, then reassess every 72 hours
Acute care requires assessment within 8 hours and daily reassessment.
Within 8 hours of admission, then reassess only at discharge
Risk must be reassessed every 24 hours or as condition changes, not only at discharge.

alt.q: A nurse works in a long-term care facility. After the admission PI risk assessment, how often should the nurse reassess the resident?
alt.a: Weekly, then per agency standards or when condition changes
alt.ex: In long-term care, assess on admission, reassess weekly, then according to agency standards or when condition changes.
w: Every 8 hours, then daily after the first week
Every-8-hour reassessment is not the long-term care schedule in the book.
Every 24 hours for the length of the stay
Daily reassessment is the acute and critical care schedule.
Only with every registered nurse visit
Reassessment with every RN visit is the home care schedule.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse uses the Braden Scale for a patient in the intensive care unit. Which cutoff score identifies ICU patients at risk for PI?
items.a: A score less than 18
items.ex: For intensive care patients, a Braden score less than 18 identifies risk for PI.
w: A score less than 9
A cutoff this low would miss many at-risk ICU patients; the ICU cutoff is less than 18.
A score greater than 20
Higher Braden scores indicate lower risk, not higher risk.
A score of 23 or higher
23 is the highest possible Braden score and reflects minimal risk.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing an older adult with the Braden Scale. Which score indicates risk for PI in this population?
alt.a: A score of 14 or lower
alt.ex: For older adults, a Braden score of 14 or lower identifies risk for PI.
w: A score of 20 or higher
Higher Braden scores reflect lower risk.
A score of 23
23 is the top Braden score and indicates minimal risk.
A score of 19 or higher
Scores this high fall above the older-adult cutoff of 14.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is turning an immobile patient onto the side. Which position should the nurse use to reduce PI risk?
items.a: 30-degree lateral position supported with pillows
items.ex: A 30-degree lateral position reduces direct contact of the trochanter with the support surface; avoid the 90-degree position.
w: 90-degree lateral position directly on the hip
The 90-degree lateral position places full weight on the trochanter and should be avoided.
Prone position with the forehead on the mattress
Prone positioning increases PI risk because the forehead and chest have little soft tissue padding.
High-Fowler’s position with the knees flat
Elevating the head of bed high increases sliding and shear injury.

alt.q: Why does the nurse use a 30-degree rather than a 90-degree lateral position for a patient at risk for PI?
alt.a: It reduces direct contact of the trochanter with the support surface
alt.ex: The 30-degree tilt keeps the trochanter off the surface, while 90 degrees places body weight on it.
w: It allows the patient to eat without risk of aspiration
Aspiration risk relates to head-of-bed elevation, not the degree of lateral tilt.
It prevents contractures of the knees and hips
Contracture prevention is not the stated reason for the 30-degree position.
It increases moisture under the sacrum to protect the skin
Moisture increases breakdown risk; the 30-degree position reduces trochanter pressure.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient at risk for shear injury has no risk for aspiration. How should the nurse position the head of the bed (HOB)?
items.a: At 30 degrees or lower, or the lowest elevation the condition allows
items.ex: Keeping the HOB at 30 degrees or lower decreases sliding toward the foot of the bed and shear injury.
w: At 45 degrees or higher, to ease breathing at all times
Higher elevation increases sliding and shear injury.
At 60 degrees, raised and lowered every 2 hours
Raising the HOB to 60 degrees promotes sliding and shear.
Flat at 0 degrees for all patients, including tube feedings
The HOB is not lowered for patients at risk for aspiration.

alt.q: A patient at risk for shear injury is receiving continuous tube feedings and is at risk for aspiration. Which action is correct regarding the head of the bed?
alt.a: Do not lower the HOB below what is needed to prevent aspiration
alt.ex: The HOB is kept at 30 degrees or lower to limit shear, but it is not lowered for patients at risk for aspiration.
w: Keep the HOB flat to eliminate all shear forces
Lowering the HOB is contraindicated when the patient is at risk for aspiration.
Keep the HOB at 15 degrees during the feeding
Lowering the HOB during feedings increases aspiration risk.
Lower the HOB to 30 degrees only during the night
Aspiration risk persists at night; the HOB is not lowered for at-risk patients.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which action best protects the heels of a patient on bed rest from PI?
items.a: Use a pillow under the calves so the heels float off the bed
items.ex: Floating the heels off-loads them completely and redistributes leg weight along the calf.
w: Place a folded towel directly under each heel
A towel under the heel still allows the heel to bear weight on the bed.
Massage each heel with lotion once a shift
Massage can damage underlying tissue and does not off-load the heel.
Position a pillow under the Achilles tendon only
Heel suspension supports the calf without placing pressure on the Achilles tendon.

alt.q: Why does a heel suspension device or pillow placed under the calves help prevent heel PIs?
alt.a: It off-loads the heel and spreads the leg’s weight along the calf
alt.ex: Heels are the second most common PI site; floating them removes pressure without loading the Achilles tendon.
w: It raises the legs to reduce edema in the feet
Edema reduction is not the stated purpose; the goal is complete heel off-loading.
It keeps the heels warm to improve local perfusion
Warmth is not the mechanism; removing pressure from the heel is.
It places firm pressure on the Achilles tendon instead
Correct heel off-loading avoids pressure on the Achilles tendon.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: An AP tells the nurse, “I’m going to rub lotion into that red spot on his hip to get the blood flowing.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Please don’t massage reddened areas; massage can damage the tissue underneath.”
items.ex: Reddened areas are not massaged because massage has the potential to damage underlying tissues.
w: “Good idea; massage for 5 minutes and then reposition him.”
Massage of reddened areas can damage deeper tissue and is not recommended.
“Use a heat pack first so the massage works better.”
Neither heat nor massage is an approved intervention for reddened areas.
“Massage only if the redness is still there in 4 hours.”
Massage is avoided regardless of how long redness lasts.

alt.q: During skin inspection, a nurse finds persistent redness over a patient’s coccyx. Which action should the nurse avoid?
alt.a: Massaging the reddened area to increase circulation
alt.ex: Massage of reddened areas can damage underlying tissue, so it is avoided.
w: Repositioning the patient off the reddened area
Repositioning off the area reduces pressure and is appropriate.
Rechecking the area in 30 minutes to 1 hour
Rechecking nonblanching redness in 30 minutes to 1 hour is recommended.
Reevaluating the patient’s positioning plan
Skin changes call for reevaluating the positioning plan.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is assessing a patient with darkly pigmented skin for early PI. Which approach is most appropriate?
items.a: Look for color that differs from the patient’s usual skin color and assess warmth and edema
items.ex: Dark skin may not blanch, so look for color differing from normal and assess temperature, edema, and tissue consistency.
w: Rely on the blanch test, because dark skin blanches like light skin
Darkly pigmented skin may not blanch, so the blanch test alone is unreliable.
Assess only for open areas, because redness cannot occur in dark skin
Color changes can occur; they appear as a change from the patient’s usual color.
Wait for the Braden score to fall before inspecting the skin
Skin inspection is ongoing and does not wait for a score change.

alt.q: Which finding over a bony prominence is a warning sign of PI development in a patient with darkly pigmented skin?
alt.a: Localized heat, edema, and induration
alt.ex: Localized heat, edema, and induration are warning signs used because color changes are hard to see in dark skin.
w: Redness that blanches quickly when pressed
Blanching redness is normal reactive hyperemia, and dark skin may not blanch at all.
Skin that matches the surrounding skin tone
Skin matching the usual color is not a warning sign.
Cool, soft tissue with normal turgor
Cool, soft tissue does not suggest pressure damage; warmth and induration do.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient who uses a wheelchair can shift weight independently. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of PI prevention teaching?
items.a: “I’ll do a chair push-up or lean forward about every 15 minutes.”
items.ex: Patients who can reposition while sitting should relieve pressure every 15 minutes with push-ups, leaning, or side-to-side movement.
w: “I’ll shift my weight about once every 4 hours.”
Every 4 hours is far too infrequent; shifts are encouraged every 15 minutes.
“I can sit as long as I like because the cushion relieves pressure.”
A cushion does not replace pressure relief; time in the chair is limited.
“I only need to shift my weight once I feel sore.”
Waiting for discomfort is unsafe, especially with sensory loss; relief is scheduled.

alt.q: A home care nurse teaches the family of a patient who sits in a chair most of the day. How often should they help the patient make small position shifts?
alt.a: Every 15 minutes
alt.ex: Small shifts, such as moving the legs, every 15 minutes redistribute pressure over bony prominences.
w: Every 2 hours
Two-hour intervals are often cited for bed turning; seated shifts are every 15 minutes.
Every 4 hours
Four hours without pressure relief while sitting is too long.
Every 8 hours
Eight hours between shifts would allow prolonged pressure on the ischial area.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient has a nasogastric tube, a nasal cannula, and an indwelling urinary catheter. How often should the nurse assess the skin around and beneath these devices?
items.a: At least twice daily and after repositioning
items.ex: Skin around and under medical devices is assessed at least twice daily and after repositioning.
w: Once daily during the bath
Once a day is too infrequent for skin under medical devices.
Once weekly when the risk score is updated
Weekly checks would miss device-related injury that can develop quickly.
Only when the device is replaced
Device sites need frequent assessment whether or not the device is changed.

alt.q: A nurse removes a cervical collar and finds an area of injury on the neck. Which feature most strongly suggests a medical device–related PI (MDRPI)?
alt.a: The injury matches the size and shape of the device
alt.ex: An MDRPI typically conforms to the same size and shape as the device that caused it.
w: The injury lies directly over the sacrum
MDRPIs can occur away from bony prominences, wherever a device presses.
The injury is a moist, macerated area
Maceration points to moisture-associated skin damage rather than device pressure.
The injury has an irregular, spreading border
A device injury typically mirrors the device’s shape rather than spreading irregularly.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: While reviewing the EHR, the nurse notes several patient factors. Which factors increase the patient’s risk for PI? (Select all that apply.)
o: Fever with diaphoresis
Fever raises tissue metabolic demand, and diaphoresis leaves skin moist.
Anemia
Low hemoglobin reduces oxygen delivery to tissues.
Heavy sedation
A sedated patient is not alert and does not change position independently.
Generalized edema
Edematous tissue is less tolerant of pressure, friction, and shear.
Ability to turn independently in bed
Independent movement relieves pressure; immobility is the risk factor.
Intact sensation in all extremities
Intact sensation lets the patient feel discomfort and move; sensory loss is the risk.
items.ex: Fever, anemia, heavy sedation, and edema each impair tissue tolerance or the patient’s ability to relieve pressure.

alt.q: A nurse is screening patients for PI risk. Which patients have a risk factor described in the skill? (Select all that apply.)
o: A patient with hemiplegia after a stroke
Sensory loss prevents the patient from feeling pressure and changing position.
A patient placed in prone position for ventilation
Prone positioning loads the forehead and chest, which have little padding.
A patient with a history of a healed sacral PI
Healed PI skin has decreased tensile strength and tolerates less pressure.
A patient receiving vasopressor medications
Vasopressors reduce tissue perfusion, increasing PI risk.
A well-nourished adult who walks hourly
Good nutrition and mobility are protective, not risk factors.
alt.ex: Sensory loss, prone positioning, prior PI, and circulatory problems such as vasopressor use all raise PI risk.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient is incontinent of urine and stool. Which interventions should the nurse include in the plan to reduce PI risk? (Select all that apply.)
o: Clean and dry the skin as soon as possible after each episode
Prompt cleansing limits skin exposure to body fluids that cause maceration.
Apply moisture barrier ointment to the perineum after each episode
Barrier ointment protects skin from stool and urine.
Apply a protective barrier after each episode if the skin is denuded
A barrier between skin and stool or urine allows denuded skin to heal.
Cleanse the skin once at the end of each shift
Waiting until shift end prolongs moisture exposure; clean after each episode.
Massage the perineal skin firmly to stimulate circulation
Massage can damage underlying tissue and is avoided.
items.ex: Moisture from incontinence causes maceration, so skin is cleaned promptly and protected with barriers after each episode.

alt.q: Friction and shear are identified as risk factors for a bedbound patient. Which interventions are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)
o: Use a slide board to transfer the patient to a stretcher
A slide board provides a slippery surface that reduces friction.
Use a lift team to raise the patient off the sheets
Lifting rather than dragging prevents shear.
Keep the head of the bed at 30 degrees or lower if not contraindicated
Low HOB elevation reduces sliding toward the foot of the bed.
Pull the patient up in bed by the arms
Dragging the patient along sheets creates shear.
Keep the head of the bed at 60 degrees
High HOB elevation increases sliding and shear injury.
alt.ex: Safe handling equipment and low HOB elevation keep the patient from dragging or sliding, which produces friction and shear.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: During skin assessment, a nurse checks for PI caused by medical devices. Which site and device pairs are at risk? (Select all that apply.)
o: Nares, from a nasogastric tube and its tape
Tape and materials securing the NG tube press on the nares.
Ears, from an oxygen nasal cannula
Cannula tubing places pressure on the ears and tips of the nares.
Lips and tongue, from an endotracheal tube
Devices securing artificial airways press on oral mucosa and can cause ulceration.
Urinary meatus, from an indwelling catheter
The meatus is at risk, especially when the tubing pulls.
Forehead, from a properly fitted hospital gown
A gown is not a medical device; a pulse oximetry device can injure the forehead.
items.ex: Any device that presses on skin or mucosa can cause an MDRPI, including NG tubes, cannulas, airways, and catheters.

alt.q: Which actions are appropriate when assessing skin under medical devices? (Select all that apply.)
o: Completely remove compression stockings to inspect the feet, heels, and legs
Stockings must be fully removed to assess the skin adequately.
Verify that each device is correctly sized, positioned, and secured
Incorrect size or placement causes excess pressure and rubbing.
Remove the device, if not contraindicated, to view the skin beneath it
Removing the device allows tissue under and around it to be observed.
Roll compression stockings down to the ankle to check the calves
Rolled-down stockings cause pressure and do not allow full assessment.
Inspect device sites only when the patient reports pain
Device sites are assessed routinely; many patients cannot report discomfort.
alt.ex: Device-related injury is found by removing devices when allowed, removing stockings fully, and checking fit and placement.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Skin over a previously healed PI has decreased tensile strength and cannot tolerate pressure as well as undamaged skin.
items.a: True
items.ex: Healed PI tissue is weaker, so a history of PI is itself a risk factor for a new injury.
items.ww: The healed area does not regain full strength; it is more vulnerable to pressure than undamaged skin.

alt.q: Once a PI has fully healed, the scar tissue tolerates pressure as well as surrounding undamaged skin.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The tensile strength of skin from a previously healed PI is decreased, so it tolerates less pressure.
alt.ww: Healed PI skin remains weaker than undamaged skin, so the area needs extra protection.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: In neonates and very young children, the head is the most common site of PI.
items.a: True
items.ex: Neonates and very young children are at high risk for PI, and the head is the most common site.
items.ww: Pediatric PI most often occurs on the head, not the sacrum or heels as in adults.

alt.q: In neonates, the sacrum is the most common site of PI, just as in older adults.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: For neonates and very young children, the head is the most common PI site.
alt.ww: The head, not the sacrum, is the most common PI site in neonates and very young children.

items.q: A nurse may delegate the PI risk assessment to AP as long as the AP uses the agency-approved risk tool.
items.a: False
items.ex: PI risk assessment cannot be delegated; AP may reposition, keep skin dry, and report skin changes.
items.ww: Using an approved tool does not make risk assessment delegable; it requires the nurse’s clinical judgment.

alt.q: PI risk assessment is a nursing responsibility, while AP may reposition patients and report skin changes.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The nurse performs risk assessment; AP help with repositioning, hygiene, and reporting changes.
alt.ww: Risk assessment is not delegated to AP, even with a standardized tool.

items.ex: Frequent small shifts while sitting relieve pressure on sacral and ischial areas.

alt.q: A patient who can reposition while seated is encouraged to do chair push-ups or lean forward every [[15]] minutes.
alt.ex: Frequent small shifts while sitting relieve pressure on sacral and ischial areas.
