sections.name: Skill 48.2 · Treating pressure injuries and wounds

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient with a Stage 3 PI. Which instruction should the nurse give the AP?
items.a: Report to me right away if the dressing is soiled by stool
items.ex: AP report potential contamination of the dressing, such as incontinence or dislodgement, because treating PIs cannot be delegated.
w: Reapply hydrogel to the wound if the dressing comes off
Treating PIs and wounds cannot be delegated to AP.
Measure the wound’s length and width after the bath
Wound measurement is part of nursing wound assessment.
Cleanse the wound with saline if the dressing gets wet
Wound cleansing is part of treatment, which AP cannot perform.

alt.q: Which statement by the AP about a patient with a sacral PI requires the nurse to clarify the AP’s role?
alt.a: “If the alginate dressing gets soiled, I’ll replace it myself.”
alt.ex: Treating PIs and wounds is not delegated; the AP should report contamination of the dressing to the nurse.
w: “I’ll tell you right away if the patient has a fever.”
AP are instructed to report fever immediately; this is correct.
“I’ll let you know if the dressing slips off when I turn him.”
Reporting a dislodged dressing is an appropriate AP action.
“I’ll report any new drainage I see on his sheets.”
AP should report any wound drainage immediately; this is correct.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient rates PI pain as 6 on a 0-to-10 scale before a scheduled dressing change, and a prn analgesic is ordered. When should the nurse give it?
items.a: 30 minutes before the treatment
items.ex: Giving ordered prn analgesia 30 minutes before treatment helps keep the dressing change from being traumatic.
w: Immediately after the treatment is completed
Medicating afterward leaves the patient in pain during the procedure.
2 hours before the treatment
The skill specifies 30 minutes before treatment, not 2 hours.
5 minutes before the treatment
Five minutes does not allow the medication time to take effect.

alt.q: Why does the nurse assess the patient’s pain before, during, and after PI treatment?
alt.a: Dressing changes should not be traumatic for the patient
alt.ex: Wound pain is assessed throughout care so treatment can be adjusted and remain nontraumatic.
w: Pain scores are used to stage the PI
Staging is based on the depth of tissue destruction, not pain.
Pain is the most reliable sign of wound healing
Healing is judged by wound measurements and tissue type, not pain alone.
Pain ratings replace the need for wound measurements
Pain ratings supplement, but never replace, wound measurement.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse assesses the nutritional status of a patient with a PI. Which finding indicates clinically significant malnutrition according to the skill?
items.a: Loss of 5% of body weight in 30 days
items.ex: Clinically significant malnutrition includes weight loss of 5% in 30 days (or 10% in 180 days), anemia, low albumin, or BMI under 22.
w: Loss of 2% of body weight in 30 days
A 2% loss is below the 5%-in-30-days criterion.
Loss of 5% of body weight in 180 days
The 180-day criterion is a 10% loss, not 5%.
Gain of 5% of body weight in 30 days
Weight gain is not a malnutrition criterion in the skill.

alt.q: Which body mass index (BMI) meets the skill’s criterion for clinically significant malnutrition in a patient with a PI?
alt.a: BMI of 21
alt.ex: A BMI less than 22 is one criterion for clinically significant malnutrition.
w: BMI of 23
A BMI of 23 is above the cutoff of less than 22.
BMI of 25
A BMI of 25 does not meet the malnutrition criterion.
BMI of 28
A BMI of 28 is well above the cutoff of less than 22.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse assesses a PI wound bed and finds that most of the tissue is black. What does this finding most likely indicate?
items.a: The wound may require debridement
items.ex: A high percentage of black (necrotic) tissue in the wound bed may require debridement.
w: The wound is moving toward healing
Granulation tissue, not black tissue, shows progress toward healing.
The wound is fully epithelialized
Epithelialized wounds are covered with new skin, not black tissue.
The wound needs a transparent film dressing
Black tissue indicates possible debridement, not a film dressing.

alt.q: A nurse notes yellow slough covering much of a PI wound bed. How should the nurse interpret this finding?
alt.a: It may indicate infection or colonization
alt.ex: Yellow tissue or slough may indicate the presence of infection or colonization.
w: It shows the wound is moving toward healing
Granulation tissue indicates healing; slough does not.
It is a normal finding in a Stage 1 PI
Stage 1 PI involves intact skin, so slough is not part of it.
It means the periwound skin is macerated
Maceration is a periwound finding, not a wound bed tissue type.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is measuring a PI that has undermining along one edge. Which tool should the nurse use to measure the depth of the undermining?
items.a: A sterile cotton-tipped applicator
items.ex: A sterile cotton-tipped applicator measures depth, undermining, and sinus tracts; a disposable guide measures length and width.
w: A disposable paper measuring guide
The paper guide is used for length and width, not depth or undermining.
A gloved fingertip pressed into the tunnel
A gloved finger is used to examine wound edges, not to measure depth.
A tape measure placed across the wound
A flat tape cannot measure depth or undermining beneath the edges.

alt.q: Why does the nurse measure the length, width, and depth of a PI at consistent points with each assessment?
alt.a: Wound size changes as healing progresses and guides therapy
alt.ex: Consistent measurements give objective data on wound size, which changes over time and influences needed therapies.
w: Measurements determine which topical antibiotic to order
Antibiotic choice is not determined by measurements alone.
Measurements identify the type of exudate present
Exudate is described by amount, color, odor, and characteristics.
Measurements replace the need to describe tissue type
Tissue type is assessed separately and is still required.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is cleaning a PI before applying a new dressing. Which technique should the nurse use?
items.a: Clean from the least-contaminated to the most-contaminated area
items.ex: Cleaning from least to most contaminated removes exudate and surface bacteria without introducing organisms into cleaner areas.
w: Clean from the most-contaminated to the least-contaminated area
This direction carries organisms from dirty areas into cleaner tissue.
Scrub the wound bed briskly with dry gauze
Brisk scrubbing traumatizes the wound; cleansing uses saline or an ordered cleanser.
Use one gauze pad back and forth across the wound
Reusing gauze back and forth spreads contamination across the wound.

alt.q: A patient has a deep PI that requires cleansing. How should the nurse clean it as ordered?
alt.a: With saline delivered with an irrigating syringe
alt.ex: For deep injuries, clean with saline delivered by an irrigating syringe as ordered.
w: With dry sterile gauze packed and removed
Dry gauze does not cleanse a deep wound and may injure tissue.
With a cotton ball soaked in povidone-iodine
Saline irrigation is the ordered method for deep injuries.
With warm tap water from a basin
Deep PIs are cleansed with saline or a prescribed wound-cleaning agent.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient with a necrotic PI has an order for collagenase ointment. Which wound-cleansing order should the nurse question?
items.a: Cleanse with Dakin solution before each application
items.ex: Iodine, silver-based products, and Dakin solution inactivate collagenase and other enzymatic debriding agents.
w: Cleanse with normal saline before each application
Normal saline is compatible with enzymatic debriding agents.
Cleanse from least to most contaminated area
This cleansing direction is correct and does not affect enzymes.
Cover with moist gauze after application
A moist gauze cover is consistent with enzyme application.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid cleansing a wound with a silver-based product when an enzymatic debriding agent is in use?
alt.a: The cleansing agent renders the enzyme ineffective
alt.ex: Collagenase and other enzymes are incompatible with iodine, silver, and Dakin solution, which make them ineffective.
w: Silver causes the enzyme to digest healthy tissue
The problem is enzyme inactivation, not damage to healthy tissue.
Silver increases the risk of wound bleeding
Bleeding is not the stated reason for avoiding silver products.
Silver stains the wound and hides necrosis
Staining is not the concern; inactivation of the enzyme is.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is applying an enzymatic debriding ointment to a PI. Which technique is correct?
items.a: Apply a small amount only to the necrotic areas of the wound
items.ex: A thin layer acts more effectively, and enzyme on surrounding skin can irritate or macerate it.
w: Spread a thick layer over the wound and surrounding skin
Excess ointment irritates surrounding skin, and a thick layer is less effective.
Apply ointment to the periwound skin to prevent spread
Enzyme on surrounding skin may macerate it.
Rub the ointment into granulation tissue at the wound base
The enzyme is applied directly to necrotic areas, not healthy tissue.

alt.q: After applying an enzyme ointment to a PI, how should the nurse cover the wound?
alt.a: Place moist, not wet, gauze over the injury and tape it in place
alt.ex: Moist gauze protects the wound and keeps the ointment from being removed during turning and repositioning.
w: Leave the wound open to air so the enzyme can dry
An uncovered wound loses ointment during repositioning and is unprotected.
Place soaking-wet gauze over the injury and tape it
The gauze should be moist, not wet, to avoid excess moisture.
Apply a dry adherent dressing pressed into the wound
Dry gauze can adhere to tissue and cause injury on removal.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is applying a calcium alginate dressing to a heavily draining PI. Why does the nurse pack the wound lightly?
items.a: The dressing swells, and tight packing can compromise blood flow
items.ex: Alginate absorbs exudate and swells into a gel, so tight packing could compromise tissue blood flow.
w: The dressing shrinks, and loose packing keeps it in contact
Alginate swells rather than shrinks as it absorbs fluid.
Light packing allows the alginate to adhere to the wound bed
Alginate forms a nonadhesive gel; adherence is not the goal.
Light packing keeps the wound bed from becoming moist
Alginate maintains a moist gel environment in the wound.

alt.q: After lightly packing a wound with calcium alginate, what should the nurse do next?
alt.a: Apply a secondary dressing and tape it in place
alt.ex: Alginate is placed with a sterile applicator or gloved finger and then covered with a secondary dressing.
w: Leave the alginate uncovered so it can absorb air
Alginate requires a secondary dressing to hold it in place.
Apply a layer of enzyme ointment over the alginate
Enzyme is not layered over alginate as part of this step.
Pack additional alginate until it is tightly filled
Tight packing can compromise blood flow as the alginate swells.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: For a patient with a PI, when should topical antibiotics be considered according to the skill?
items.a: If no healing is noted after 2 to 4 weeks of optimal care
items.ex: Topical antibiotics decrease bioburden and should be considered if no healing occurs after 2 to 4 weeks of optimal care.
w: If no healing is noted after 2 to 4 days of optimal care
Two to four days is too short to judge whether healing has stalled.
If no healing is noted after 6 to 9 months of optimal care
Waiting months would delay treatment of a nonhealing wound.
At the first dressing change for every new PI
Topical antibiotics are not routine for every PI.

alt.q: A patient’s PI has shown no healing after 3 weeks of optimal care. Which treatment option might be considered to reduce bioburden?
alt.a: A topical antibiotic
alt.ex: Topical antibiotics decrease wound bioburden and are considered when no healing occurs after 2 to 4 weeks of optimal care.
w: A dry gauze dressing
Dry gauze can adhere to tissue and does not reduce bioburden.
A transparent film dressing
Film dressings suit superficial wounds with minimal exudate, not bioburden control.
A higher head-of-bed angle
Head-of-bed position affects shear, not wound bioburden.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: The skin around a patient’s PI has become macerated since the last dressing change. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Select a dressing with greater moisture-absorbing capacity
items.ex: For maceration, reduce periwound exposure to moisture and choose a dressing that absorbs more moisture.
w: Apply a thicker layer of hydrogel over the wound
Hydrogel donates moisture and would worsen maceration.
Cover the periwound skin with wet saline gauze
Adding moisture to periwound skin worsens maceration.
Apply enzyme ointment to the surrounding skin
Enzyme on surrounding skin may itself macerate it.

alt.q: A nurse reviews a new wound care order and finds that it does not match established wound care guidelines for the patient’s PI. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Review the order with the health care team
alt.ex: If an order is inconsistent with guidelines or the identified outcome, the nurse reviews it with the health care team.
w: Carry out the order exactly as written
Following an order inconsistent with guidelines without review could harm the patient.
Change the treatment to match the guidelines
Nurses do not change wound orders independently; they review with the team.
Ask the AP to carry out the order
Treating PIs cannot be delegated, and the order needs review first.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse inspects the skin under a dressing’s adhesive. Which findings are signs of medical adhesive–related skin injury (MARSI)? (Select all that apply.)
o: Erythema
Erythema is a sign of the skin’s reaction to adhesive.
Blistering
Blistering under adhesive is a sign of MARSI.
Excoriation
Excoriation is a sign of MARSI.
Healthy granulation tissue
Granulation tissue is found in the wound bed and indicates healing.
Periwound rash with erosion from moisture
Erosion of periwound skin or rash from moisture indicates MASD.
items.ex: Erythema, blistering, and excoriation are signs of MARSI, a reaction of the skin to an adhesive.

alt.q: A nurse is assessing the skin around a draining PI. Which findings indicate moisture-associated skin damage (MASD)? (Select all that apply.)
o: Erosion of the superficial periwound skin
Erosion of underlying or superficial periwound skin indicates MASD.
A rash in the periwound area
A periwound rash is an indication of MASD.
Macerated skin at the wound margins
Maceration results from excess moisture exposure.
Granulation tissue in the wound base
Granulation is a healing tissue type, not skin damage.
Dry, intact skin around the wound
Dry, intact periwound skin indicates no MASD.
alt.ex: MASD appears as periwound erosion, rash, and maceration from prolonged exposure to moisture.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient’s PI has extended beyond its original margins. Which actions are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)
o: Monitor laboratory results such as WBC count, hemoglobin, and albumin
Abnormal labs are systemic signs of poor wound healing.
Assess and revise the current turning schedule
An enlarging PI suggests ongoing pressure that turning must address.
Consider other pressure-redistribution devices
A different support surface may better relieve pressure.
Monitor for weight loss and fluid imbalances
Weight loss and fluid imbalance are systemic signs of poor healing.
Massage the wound edges to stimulate blood flow
Massage can damage underlying tissue.
items.ex: An enlarging PI calls for checking systemic signs of poor healing and improving pressure relief.

alt.q: A patient’s PI has become deeper with increased drainage and new necrotic tissue. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Review current wound care management
Deterioration means the current plan must be reexamined.
Consult the interprofessional team about changing the regimen
The team decides on changes in the wound care regimen.
Obtain wound cultures if ordered
Cultures help identify infection when ordered.
Continue the same plan for another month before reassessing
Waiting allows further deterioration; changes are needed now.
Pack the wound tightly with dry gauze
Tight dry packing can injure tissue and does not address deterioration.
alt.ex: A deteriorating PI requires review of care, interprofessional consultation, and cultures if ordered.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

Fever
Fever is a systemic sign of infection.
Elevated white blood cell count
An elevated WBC count is a sign of infection.

New necrosis may accompany wound infection.
Pink granulation tissue filling the base
Granulation tissue indicates healing, not infection.
items.ex: Drainage, foul odor, necrosis, fever, and elevated WBC count signal possible PI infection.

alt.q: A home care nurse is planning PI care with a family caregiver. Which considerations are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)

Caregiver time influences dressing choice at home.

Medicare limits reimbursement for some support surfaces.
alt.ex: Home planning considers caregiver time, supply storage and availability, equipment needs, and reimbursement limits.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.ww: Dry gauze does adhere, which is why moist gauze is preferred for many wounds.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Albumin levels can fall in inflammatory conditions and liver dysfunction, so a specific albumin level is not an indicator of impaired nutrition.

items.ww: Albumin is influenced by inflammation and liver disease, so it is not a specific nutrition marker.

alt.q: A single low serum albumin level reliably confirms that a patient with a PI is malnourished.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Albumin decreases in inflammation, liver dysfunction, and other conditions, so one value is not a nutrition indicator.
alt.ww: Many non-nutritional conditions lower albumin, so it cannot confirm malnutrition alone.

sections.name: Skill 48.3 · Applying dry and moist dressings

items.q: A nurse is planning care for several patients. Which dressing task may be delegated to AP according to agency policy?
items.a: A dry dressing change on a chronic wound
items.ex: Dry and moist dressing changes can be delegated to AP when the wound is chronic, per agency policy.
w: A first dressing change on a new surgical incision
Care of acute new wounds remains the nurse’s responsibility.
A dressing change that requires sterile technique
Wound care requiring sterile technique is not delegated.
Evaluation of how well a wound is healing
Evaluation of wound healing is a nursing responsibility.

alt.q: AP are changing a dry dressing on a patient’s chronic wound. Which finding should the AP report to the nurse immediately?
alt.a: Bleeding from the wound
alt.ex: AP are instructed to report pain, fever, bleeding, or wound drainage to the nurse immediately.
w: A dressing that was dated by the previous shift
A dated dressing is expected and does not require immediate reporting.
Use of the special tape noted in the care plan
Using the planned tape technique is expected, not a finding to report.
Intact skin around the wound edges
Intact periwound skin is a normal finding.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is removing tape from a dressing on a patient with fragile skin. Which technique reduces the risk of skin tears?
items.a: Pull the tape slowly at a low angle, parallel to the skin, while supporting the skin
items.ex: Removing tape low and parallel to the skin with support at the skin–tape interface reduces skin tears.
w: Pull the tape quickly straight up at a 90-degree angle from the skin
Pulling straight up stresses the skin and increases tearing.
Pull the tape quickly against the direction of hair growth
Tape over hair is removed in the direction of hair growth.
Pull the tape quickly at a low angle without supporting the skin
Tape is removed slowly while the skin is supported at the skin–tape interface.

alt.q: A dressing is taped over a hairy area of a patient’s forearm. How should the nurse remove the tape?
alt.a: In the direction of hair growth
alt.ex: Removing tape in the direction of hair growth reduces skin trauma; clip hair only with permission and per policy.
w: Against the direction of hair growth
Removing against hair growth pulls hair and traumatizes skin.
By shaving the area before removing the tape
Shaving or clipping requires patient permission and is not the removal technique.
With a quick upward pull perpendicular to the skin
Tape is removed slowly at a low angle, not with a quick upward pull.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A dry gauze dressing has stuck to a wound that is not meant to be debrided. What should the nurse do before removing it?
items.a: Moisten it with normal saline, wait 1 to 2 minutes, then remove
items.ex: Moistening the adhered dry dressing with saline for 1 to 2 minutes allows nontraumatic removal.
w: Pull it off quickly in one motion to limit pain over 1 to 2 seconds
Quick removal of adhered gauze can injure the wound surface.
Soak it with povidone-iodine, wait 10 minutes, then remove
The skill specifies normal saline and a 1-to-2-minute wait.
Leave it in place for 24 hours until it loosens
Leaving the old dressing delays wound care; saline loosens it within minutes.

alt.q: When the bottom layer of a moist dressing has adhered to a wound being debrided, what should the nurse do?
alt.a: Gently free the dressing while alerting the patient to discomfort
alt.ex: Gently freeing the adhered moist dressing debrides the wound while preventing trauma to healing tissue.
w: Soak the dressing in saline until it floats free
For a wound being debrided, the moist layer is freed gently, not soaked off.
Pull the dressing off rapidly in one motion
Rapid removal can traumatize the healing wound surface.
Leave the bottom layer in place and add new gauze
Old gauze is removed so all dressing material leaves the wound.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

w: Remove the glue with adhesive remover before cleansing
The glue should not be removed.
Moisten the glue with saline and peel it away gently
The glue is not removed, even gently.
Pack moist gauze over the glue to soften it
The glue is left intact; only the top dressing is replaced.

alt.q: A transparent film dressing covers a patient’s wound. How should the nurse remove it?
alt.a: Gently pull the edge and allow the film to release and lift
alt.ex: Gently pulling the film’s edge lets it release and lift from the skin with less trauma.
w: Peel the film rapidly straight upward from one corner
Rapid upward peeling stresses the skin and can cause tears.
Cut through the film and lift it off in pieces
Cutting the film risks injuring the wound and is not the method described.
Soak the film in saline for 10 minutes before pulling
The book describes gently pulling the edge so the film releases.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient has a surgical wound with a drain. How should the nurse clean around the drain site?
items.a: Use circular strokes starting near the drain and moving outward
items.ex: Cleaning in circles from the drain outward and away from the insertion site prevents contamination.
w: Use circular strokes starting at the outer edge and moving inward
Moving inward carries organisms toward the drain site.
Use back-and-forth strokes across the drain site
Back-and-forth strokes spread contamination over the insertion site.
Clean only the skin farthest from the drain
The area around the drain must be cleaned, starting near the drain.

alt.q: Why does the nurse use a separate saline-moistened gauze for each cleaning stroke when cleaning a wound?
alt.a: To prevent transfer of organisms from an area already cleaned
alt.ex: A fresh gauze or swab for each stroke prevents organisms from moving back into areas already cleaned.
w: To keep the wound bed as dry as possible during cleansing
Drying is done afterward by blotting with sterile gauze.
To remove the antiseptic ointment from the wound edges
Ointment is applied after cleaning, not removed during it.
To reduce the amount of saline needed for the procedure
Using new gauze for each stroke is about asepsis, not saline use.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is preparing gauze for a moist dressing. Which action is correct?
items.a: Wring out excess solution so the gauze is moist, not wet
items.ex: Inner gauze should be moist, not wet, so it absorbs drainage and adheres to debris without macerating skin.
w: Leave the gauze dripping so the wound stays saturated
Wet gauze lets moisture escape and macerate the periwound skin.
Apply the gauze dry and moisten it after it is in place
Gauze is moistened in solution and wrung out before application.
Soak the gauze in tap water to keep costs down
Gauze is moistened in the prescribed sterile solution.

alt.q: Why should the inner gauze of a moist dressing be damp rather than wet?
alt.a: Damp gauze absorbs drainage and traps debris as it dries
alt.ex: Damp gauze absorbs drainage and, when allowed to dry, traps debris; excess moisture macerates the periwound.
w: Wet gauze cannot be cut with sterile scissors
Ease of cutting is not the reason the gauze must be damp.
Damp gauze prevents the dressing from absorbing drainage
Damp gauze increases, not prevents, absorption of drainage.
Wet gauze sticks to the outer cover dressing
The concern with wet gauze is periwound maceration, not sticking to the cover.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is packing a deep wound with moist fine-mesh gauze. Which technique is correct?
items.a: Loosely fill all wound surfaces without packing above skin level
items.ex: Packing loosely contacts all surfaces, including tunnels, without overpacking above the skin or touching periwound skin.
w: Tightly fill the wound so the gauze rises above skin level
Overpacking above the skin is avoided; packing should be loose.
Place gauze only on the wound base and leave tunnels empty
Dead spaces from sinus tracts, tunnels, and undermining must be filled.
Extend the moist gauze onto the periwound skin for coverage
Moist gauze must not touch periwound skin because it causes maceration.

alt.q: Why must moist packing gauze not touch the periwound skin?
alt.a: Moisture escaping the dressing can macerate the periwound area
alt.ex: Moisture that reaches surrounding skin often macerates the periwound area.
w: The gauze will stick to the skin and hold the dressing in place
Holding the dressing is done with tape or ties, not gauze on skin.
Periwound contact prevents the gauze from wicking drainage
Wicking is promoted by loose packing; the concern is skin maceration.
Periwound contact stimulates excess granulation tissue
Excess granulation is not the concern described for periwound contact.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse packs a deep wound with several pieces of moist gauze. What should the nurse do before completing the dressing?
items.a: Count and document the number of gauze pieces placed
items.ex: Counting and documenting the pieces ensures that all gauze is removed with each dressing change.
w: Moisten the outer cover dressing with saline
The outer layer is dry and moisture-retentive, not moistened.
Cut the gauze so it extends onto the periwound skin
Gauze must not touch the periwound skin.
Apply a transparent film directly over the packing
The book covers moist gauze with a dry moisture-retentive layer and a surface dressing.

alt.q: Why does the nurse document the number of gauze pieces packed into a deep wound?
alt.a: It ensures that all gauze is removed at the next dressing change
alt.ex: A documented count lets the next nurse confirm that every piece of packing has been removed.
w: It is used to calculate the patient’s fluid output
The count tracks removal of packing, not fluid output.
It determines how often the AP can change the dressing
Dressing frequency is set by the order, not the gauze count.
It replaces measurement of the wound’s depth
Wound depth is still measured; the count serves a different purpose.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is securing a dressing with nonallergenic tape. How far beyond the dressing should the tape extend?
items.a: 2.5 to 5 cm (1 to 2 inches)
items.ex: Tape is applied over the gauze and 2.5 to 5 cm (1–2 inches) beyond the dressing to keep it stable.
w: 0.5 to 1 cm (0.25 to 0.5 inch)
Such a short extension may not hold the dressing securely.
10 to 15 cm (4 to 6 inches)
Excess tape increases skin exposure to adhesive and MARSI risk.
15 to 20 cm (6 to 8 inches)
This much tape is unnecessary and increases adhesive injury risk.

alt.q: Why does the nurse use nonallergenic tape to secure a gauze dressing?
alt.a: It reduces the risk for MARSI
alt.ex: Nonallergenic tape reduces the risk of medical adhesive–related skin injury.
w: It absorbs drainage from the wound
Tape secures the dressing; it does not absorb drainage.
It keeps the dressing moist
Moisture is maintained by the dressing layers, not the tape.
It removes necrotic tissue
Tape has no debriding action.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient has a small wound on fragile skin that needs frequent dressing changes. Which method of securing the dressing reduces skin irritation from tape?
items.a: A protective window made from four hydrocolloid strips
items.ex: A protective window frames small wounds; tape attaches to the strips instead of the skin, causing less irritation.
w: A double layer of tape applied directly to the skin
More tape on skin increases irritation and MARSI risk.
Roller gauze wrapped tightly around the trunk
Roller gauze is used to secure dressings on extremities.
Moist gauze extended onto the skin to hold the dressing
Moist gauze on the periwound skin causes maceration.

alt.q: A nurse makes a protective window around a wound. Where does the nurse attach the tape ends of the new dressing?
alt.a: To the hydrocolloid strips surrounding the wound
alt.ex: In a protective window, the dressing’s tape ends are secured to the hydrocolloid or stomahesive strips, not the skin.
w: Directly to the periwound skin
Taping to skin is what the window is designed to avoid.
To the patient’s gown
Tape is secured to the strips, not to clothing.
To the wound packing
Tape secures the outer dressing to the frame, not to packing.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient 4 days after abdominal surgery says, “It feels like something gave way under my dressing.” The nurse finds evisceration. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Cover the wound with a sterile dressing moistened with saline
items.ex: If dehiscence or evisceration occurs, protect the wound first by covering it with a sterile moist saline dressing.
w: Leave the patient to call the health care provider
The nurse stays with the patient; another person can notify the provider.
Gently push the protruding tissue back into the wound
Viscera are protected, not replaced, by the nurse.
Cover the wound with a dry gauze pad
Dry gauze can stick to exposed tissue; a sterile moist saline dressing is used.

alt.q: A nurse has covered a patient’s eviscerated wound with a sterile moist saline dressing. Which action is appropriate next?
alt.a: Instruct the patient to lie still and stay to monitor vital signs
alt.ex: The nurse keeps the patient still, stays to monitor vital signs, and has the provider notified immediately.
w: Help the patient walk to the bathroom to urinate
Movement can worsen the separation; the patient should lie still.
Remove the dressing every 15 minutes to inspect it
Repeated removal disturbs the protective covering over the wound.
Leave to document the event before calling for help
The nurse stays with the patient, and the provider is notified immediately.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: During a dressing change, a nurse notes new drainage and an odor coming from the wound. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Verify with the health care provider about obtaining a wound culture
items.ex: Drainage or odor from the wound calls for verifying with the provider whether to obtain a wound culture.
w: Change to a dry dressing to help debride the wound
Dry dressings are not appropriate for debriding wounds.
Apply additional antiseptic ointment without an order
Ointment is applied only as ordered.
Document the finding and recheck it next week
New drainage and odor need prompt follow-up, not a week’s delay.

alt.q: A patient’s wound is inflamed and tender, with yellow necrotic tissue. Which action is most appropriate?
alt.a: Notify the provider and consult the WOCN about debridement
alt.ex: For yellow, tan, or brown necrotic tissue, notify the provider and consult the WOCN about the need for debridement.
w: Pack the wound tightly with dry gauze
Tight dry packing injures tissue and does not address necrosis.
Remove the necrotic tissue at the bedside with scissors
The need for debridement is determined with the provider and WOCN.
Apply a transparent film to hide the odor
Covering the wound does not treat inflammation or necrosis.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A dressing change reveals a wound that is inflamed and tender, with drainage and odor. Which actions should the nurse take? (Select all that apply.)
o: Monitor for additional signs of infection such as fever and elevated WBC count
Systemic signs help confirm wound infection.
Notify the health care provider
Signs of infection are reported to the provider.
Obtain wound cultures as ordered
Cultures identify the organism when ordered.
Switch to a dry dressing so the wound will dry out
Dry dressings dry out, adhere, and are linked to higher infection rates.
Wait until the next scheduled change to recheck the wound
Signs of infection need prompt action, not delay.
items.ex: An inflamed, draining, odorous wound suggests infection, so the nurse monitors, notifies the provider, and obtains cultures as ordered.

alt.q: A wound begins to bleed during a dressing change. Which actions are appropriate? (Select all that apply.)

Color and amount show how severe the bleeding is.
Inspect the area under the patient for blood
Blood can pool under the patient, so this area is checked.
Obtain vital signs as needed
Vital signs show the effect of blood loss.
Notify the health care provider
Bleeding during a dressing change is reported to the provider.
Remove all packing quickly to locate the source
Rapid removal can traumatize tissue and increase bleeding.
alt.ex: Bleeding is assessed by amount, color, pooling under the patient, and vital signs, and the provider is notified.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which statements describe disadvantages of dry dressings? (Select all that apply.)

Adherence causes pain and trauma when the dressing is removed.
Moisture evaporates quickly, so they dry out
Rapid drying is a disadvantage of dry dressings.
They usually need frequent changes
Because they dry out, dry dressings typically need frequent changes.
They are linked to higher infection rates than semi-occlusive dressings
Infection rates are higher compared with semi-occlusive dressings.
They are the best choice for debriding wounds
Dry dressings are not appropriate for debriding wounds.
items.ex: Dry dressings adhere, dry out, need frequent changes, and have higher infection rates than semi-occlusive dressings.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing a patient’s EHR before a dressing change. Which factors place the patient at risk for poor wound healing? (Select all that apply.)

Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes is a chronic illness that impairs healing.
Recent radiation therapy
Radiation therapy can affect wound healing.
Obesity

Normal nutrition with no chronic illness
Good nutrition without chronic disease supports healing.
alt.ex: Aging, chronic illness, poor nutrition, medications such as steroids, and cancer treatments affect wound healing.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient with a moist dressing is at risk for moisture-associated skin damage (MASD). Which products may the nurse use to protect the periwound skin? (Select all that apply.)

Skin sealants are moisture barriers for periwound skin.

Barrier ointments protect periwound skin from moisture.
Solid-wafer skin barrier
Solid-wafer barriers protect periwound skin.

Wet gauze on the periwound skin adds moisture and causes maceration.
Extra layers of moist packing extending onto the skin
Packing must not touch periwound skin.
items.ex: Moisture barriers such as sealants, ointments, paste, and solid wafers protect periwound skin from MASD.

alt.q: Which findings should the nurse report after a dressing change? (Select all that apply.)
o: Unexpected appearance of wound drainage
Unexpected drainage may signal a complication.
Accidental removal of a drain
Accidental drain removal must be reported.
Bright red bleeding
Bright red bleeding is reported promptly.
Signs of MARSI in the periwound skin
Periwound changes and signs of MARSI or MASD are reported.
A clean, dry outer dressing
A clean, dry dressing is an expected finding.
alt.ex: Unexpected drainage, drain removal, bright red bleeding, and periwound skin changes are reported.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.a: True

items.ww: Dry dressings adhere and traumatize tissue, so they are not used for debridement.

alt.q: A dry gauze dressing is the dressing of choice when a wound needs debridement.
alt.a: False

alt.ww: Moist dressings, not dry ones, gently free adhered material and debride the wound.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.ww: Waiting longer than a shift could miss changes in drainage.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

sections.name: Skill 48.4 · Implementation of negative-pressure wound therapy (NPWT)

items.q: A nurse is caring for a patient receiving NPWT. Which instruction should the nurse give the AP?
items.a: Report any alarm from the NPWT unit to me
items.ex: NPWT cannot be delegated, but AP report alarms, leakage, dressing changes, and changes in temperature or comfort.
w: Reset the pressure level if the alarm sounds
Adjusting NPWT settings is part of the skill, which AP cannot perform.
Patch any leaks with tape before calling me
Managing the dressing seal is a nursing responsibility.
Turn the unit off during bathing and back on later
Operating NPWT therapy is not delegated to AP.

alt.q: Which statement by the AP shows correct understanding of caring for a patient with NPWT?
alt.a: “I’ll tell you if I see fluid leaking around the drape.”
alt.ex: AP report wound fluid leakage around the adhesive drape edges to the nurse.
w: “I’ll replace the foam if the dressing looks flat.”
Replacing NPWT dressings is not delegated; AP report changes in dressing shape.
“I’ll lower the pressure if he says it hurts.”
Changing pressure settings is a nursing action; AP report comfort changes.
“I’ll position him lying on the tubing to keep it secure.”
AP use caution to avoid pressure from tubing or displacing it.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Before starting NPWT, the nurse reviews the health care provider’s order. Besides directing care, why is this order necessary?
items.a: It is required for reimbursement
items.ex: The order specifies dressing frequency and pressure settings and is also needed for reimbursement.
w: It allows the AP to perform the dressing change
NPWT cannot be delegated, with or without an order.
It replaces the need for wound measurement
Wound measurements are still required for each change.
It lets the nurse choose any pressure setting
The order specifies the amount of negative pressure.

alt.q: Which information should the nurse look for when reviewing the EHR before an NPWT dressing change?
alt.a: The ordered negative pressure, pressure cycle, and dressing change frequency
alt.ex: The EHR review identifies frequency of changes, pressure amount, foam or gauze used, cycle type, and prior wound appearance.
w: The AP who last changed the NPWT dressing
AP do not change NPWT dressings, so this is not relevant information.
The color of the canister used at the last change
Canister color does not guide the dressing change.
The brand of tape the patient prefers at home
Tape preference is not part of the NPWT order review.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: When preparing to change an NPWT dressing, the nurse turns off the unit. Why does the nurse close the clamp on the dressing tubing?
items.a: To prevent drainage from backflowing into the wound when reconnected
items.ex: Clamping the dressing tubing prevents drainage from flowing back into the wound when the system is reconnected.
w: To keep the foam dressing from drying out during removal
Clamping manages drainage flow, not foam moisture.
To increase the negative pressure in the canister
The unit is off; clamping does not raise pressure.
To allow the AP to remove the dressing safely
NPWT dressing changes are not delegated to AP.

alt.q: A nurse has turned off an NPWT unit and closed the clamps on the dressing and pump tubing. What should the nurse do next?
alt.a: Disconnect the tubes and let fluid in the pump tubing drain into the collection device
alt.ex: After clamping, the tubes are disconnected so fluid in the pump tubing drains into the collection device.
w: Pull off the transparent film quickly to expose the foam
Film is removed by gently stretching and slowly pulling it away from the skin.
Irrigate the wound through the tubing before disconnecting it
Irrigation, if ordered, is done after the dressing is removed.
Empty the canister into the wound to moisten the foam
Drainage must never flow back into the wound.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient has a wound with exposed tendon. Which NPWT foam is most appropriate?
items.a: White soft foam
items.ex: White foam is denser with smaller pores and is used over tendons, muscle, bone, and tunnels to restrict granulation.
w: Black polyurethane foam
Black foam stimulates granulation and contraction and is not used over tendon.
Dry woven gauze packed tightly
Gauze can be an NPWT filler, but white foam is used over tendons.
Calcium alginate rope
Alginate is not the NPWT foam described for exposed structures.

alt.q: Which NPWT foam has larger pores and is most effective in stimulating granulation tissue and wound contraction?
alt.a: Black polyurethane (PU) foam
alt.ex: Black PU foam has larger pores and best stimulates granulation tissue and wound contraction.
w: White soft (dense) foam
White foam is denser and used when granulation must be restricted.
Silver-impregnated (antimicrobial) gauze
Silver products reduce bioburden; they are not the granulation-stimulating foam.
Hydrocolloid (wafer) dressing
Hydrocolloid protects periwound skin but is not an NPWT filler foam.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is applying the connecting pad to an NPWT dressing. How should the nurse create the opening in the transparent dressing?
items.a: Cut a round hole at least 2 cm (0.8 inch) across
items.ex: A round hole of at least 2 cm allows drainage; a slit or X may seal off the opening.
w: Cut an X about 2 cm (0.8 inch) across
An X-shaped cut may seal off the opening.
Cut a slit about 1 cm (0.4 inch) long
A slit may close and seal off the opening.
Cut a round hole about 0.5 cm (0.2 inch) across
The hole must be at least 2 cm to allow drainage.

alt.q: Why does the nurse avoid cutting a slit or an X in the transparent dressing when applying the NPWT connecting pad?
alt.a: The cut may seal off the opening for drainage
alt.ex: A slit or X can close and seal off the opening, so a round hole of at least 2 cm is cut.
w: The cut may cause the foam to dry out
Foam moisture is not the concern; blocked drainage is.
The cut is too large to maintain negative pressure
The problem is that a slit closes, not that it is too large.
The cut exposes the patient’s skin to adhesive
Adhesive exposure is not related to the shape of the cut.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is trimming the NPWT transparent dressing. How far onto the periwound skin should the dressing extend?
items.a: About 2.5 to 5 cm (1 to 2 inches)
items.ex: The transparent dressing is trimmed to cover the wound and foam and extend about 2.5 to 5 cm onto periwound skin.
w: About 0.5 cm (0.2 inch)
This margin is too small to maintain an airtight seal.
About 10 to 12 cm (4 to 5 inches)
This much adhesive is unnecessary and increases MARSI risk.
About 15 cm (6 inches)
Such a wide margin is not recommended.

alt.q: A nurse places the NPWT transparent dressing over the foam. Which application technique maintains negative pressure?
alt.a: Apply it snugly and wrinkle-free to form an airtight seal
alt.ex: The dressing must be snug, airtight, and free of wrinkles or tunnels to keep a negative-pressure environment.
w: Apply it loosely with folds so the foam can expand
Wrinkles and folds create leaks that break the seal.
Apply it only over the foam without touching the skin
The film must extend onto the periwound skin to seal.
Apply it in overlapping strips with gaps between them
Gaps let air in and prevent a negative-pressure seal.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse places three pieces of foam into a tunneled wound during an NPWT dressing change. What should the nurse do with this information?
items.a: Document the number of pieces in the patient’s chart
items.ex: Counting and documenting filler pieces tells the next nurse how many must be removed at the next change.
w: Tell the patient so they can remove the foam at home
Removal of foam is part of the dressing change, not a patient task.
Write it on the canister so the AP can track it
The count is documented in the chart, not left to the AP.
Nothing, because foam dissolves before the next change
Foam does not dissolve; every piece must be removed.

alt.q: During an NPWT dressing change, the nurse removes the old foam. Which action is most important?
alt.a: Make sure all pieces of foam are removed
alt.ex: All foam pieces are removed, using the documented count to confirm that none remain in the wound.
w: Save one piece of foam to place back in the wound
Old foam is discarded; new filler is cut for the wound.
Pull the foam off quickly in one motion
Foam is removed one layer at a time with care.
Leave foam in tunnels to protect the tissue
Retained foam is not acceptable; all pieces must be removed.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient receiving NPWT suddenly has bright red blood filling the tubing and canister. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Stop NPWT immediately and notify the health care provider
items.ex: If the wound hemorrhages, stop NPWT immediately and notify the provider.
w: Increase the negative pressure to control the bleeding
Higher suction would worsen bleeding.
Change the canister and continue the therapy
Therapy must stop when the wound hemorrhages.
Document the drainage and reassess in 1 hour
Hemorrhage requires immediate action, not delayed reassessment.

alt.q: Which finding in a patient receiving NPWT should the nurse report to the health care provider immediately?
alt.a: Brisk, bright-red bleeding from the wound
alt.ex: Brisk bright-red bleeding, dehiscence, evisceration, poor healing, or possible infection is reported immediately.
w: Patient ambulating with the portable unit
Patients may ambulate with NPWT; this is expected.
A display screen showing “Therapy On”
This verifies the system is on, which is an expected finding.
Serous drainage collecting in the canister
Serous canister drainage is expected and is measured regularly.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient receiving NPWT reports increasing wound pain. Which action is appropriate?
items.a: Decrease the pressure setting
items.ex: For increased pain, consider lowering pressure, moistening the filler, changing to continuous cycling, and reviewing analgesia.
w: Increase the pressure setting
Higher pressure would likely increase pain.
Change from continuous to intermittent cycling
The recommended change is from intermittent to continuous cycling.
Remove the dry foam quickly to limit pain
Foam is moistened with saline so it loosens from granulation tissue.

alt.q: A patient with NPWT reports pain when the foam is removed. Which action should the nurse take?
alt.a: Instill normal saline to moisten the foam before removing it
alt.ex: Instilling saline moistens foam and filler so they loosen from granulation tissue, reducing pain.
w: Pull the foam off rapidly in one motion
Rapid removal of adhered foam traumatizes granulation tissue.
Increase negative pressure before removal
Higher pressure does not loosen the foam and may add pain.
Switch from continuous to intermittent cycling
The book suggests changing from intermittent to continuous, not the reverse.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: During an NPWT dressing change, the nurse notes copious drainage that looks purulent and has a foul odor. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Obtain a wound culture
items.ex: Copious, purulent, or foul-smelling drainage calls for a wound culture and may mean NPWT needs to be discontinued.
w: Increase the pressure to remove the drainage faster
Changing pressure does not address possible infection.
Reapply the old foam to save supplies
Old foam is discarded; reusing it would add contamination.
Decrease the frequency of dressing changes
Signs of infection call for more frequent dressing changes.

alt.q: An NPWT wound appears inflamed and tender, with increased drainage and odor. Which action is appropriate?
alt.a: Increase the frequency of dressing changes
alt.ex: For inflammation, increased drainage, and odor, notify the provider, obtain a culture, and change dressings more often.
w: Decrease the frequency of dressing changes
Infection signs call for more frequent, not fewer, changes.
Turn off the unit until the next change
Leaving the unit off does not treat infection and loses therapy.
Switch to a higher pressure setting
Pressure changes do not treat infection.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: After applying a new NPWT dressing, how should the nurse secure the tubing?
items.a: Several centimeters away from the dressing, avoiding pressure points
items.ex: Tubing over bony prominences can cause medical device–related PIs, so it is secured away from pressure points.
w: Directly over the nearest bony prominence for stability
Tubing over bony prominences can cause MDRPI.
Under the patient’s hip to keep it from moving
Tubing lying under the body creates pressure on the skin.
Tightly coiled on top of the dressing
Tubing is secured away from the dressing, not on top of it.

alt.q: Why does the nurse avoid placing NPWT drainage tubing over bony prominences?
alt.a: It can cause a medical device–related pressure injury
alt.ex: Drainage tubes over bony prominences can cause MDRPIs.
w: It can break the airtight seal of the dressing
The reason given is device-related pressure injury, not seal loss.
It can cause drainage to flow back into the wound
Backflow is prevented by clamping, not tubing placement.
It can increase the pressure setting on the unit
Tubing placement does not change the unit’s pressure setting.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient will continue NPWT at home. What should the wound specialist assess before discharge?
items.a: The home environment and the patient’s ability to see controls and hear alarms
items.ex: Home NPWT requires checking stairways and outlets and whether the patient can see device controls and hear alarms.
w: Whether the patient can change the pressure setting without an order
Pressure settings require a health care provider’s order.
Whether the canister can be emptied into the household sink
This is not among the home considerations in the skill.
Whether the family can perform sterile debridement at home
Debridement is done by a WOCN or provider, not family.

alt.q: Which teaching should the nurse include for a family caregiver managing NPWT at home?
alt.a: How to attach the device to a wall outlet to recharge the battery
alt.ex: Home teaching includes recharging the battery at a wall outlet and giving analgesics so dressing changes are tolerated.
w: How to raise the pressure setting if drainage increases
Pressure settings require an order and are not adjusted by family.
How to turn the unit off overnight to save battery
Therapy is not stopped overnight to save battery.
How to reuse old foam to reduce cost
Old foam is discarded at each change.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is preparing the periwound skin before applying an NPWT dressing. Which actions help maintain an airtight seal? (Select all that apply.)
o: Apply skin protectant or barrier film to the periwound skin
Barrier products help maintain the airtight seal and protect against MASD.
Fill creases and skinfolds with a skin barrier paste or strip
Filling uneven surfaces creates a level surface for the seal.
Gently blot the periwound with gauze to dry it thoroughly
Dry skin allows the adhesive drape to seal.
Apply moisturizing lotion to the periwound skin
Lotion would interfere with adhesion and the seal.
Leave scars and creases uncovered
Uneven surfaces must be filled to maintain the seal.
items.ex: A dry, protected, level periwound surface allows the drape to form an airtight seal.

alt.q: After applying an NPWT dressing, which actions should the nurse take to inspect the system? (Select all that apply.)
o: Verify that the system is on
The unit must be on, such as a display showing therapy on.
Verify that all clamps are open and tubing is patent
Closed clamps or kinks block negative pressure.
Check that a tight seal is present
Negative pressure is achieved only with a tight seal.
Patch any leak with strips of transparent film
Film strips patch leaks around the wound edges.
Cut a slit in the drape to release excess pressure
A slit would break the seal and may block the opening.
alt.ex: System checks confirm the unit is on, clamps are open, tubing is patent, and the seal is intact or patched.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which information should the nurse document after an NPWT dressing change? (Select all that apply.)
o: Type of foam used, black or white
Documentation includes the type of dressing.
Number of pieces of foam placed
The count ensures all pieces are removed later.
Pressure mode and setting
Mode and pressure setting are documented.
Appearance of the wound and drainage characteristics
Wound appearance and drainage are documented.
Brand of tape used at the previous change
Tape brand is not among the NPWT documentation items.
items.ex: NPWT documentation covers wound appearance, drainage, dressing type and count, pressure settings, and patient response.

alt.q: Which assessments should the nurse perform when evaluating a patient receiving NPWT? (Select all that apply.)
o: Inspect the wound, wound bed, and periwound for drainage and odor
Ongoing inspection shows wound healing status.
Ask the patient to rate pain on a 0-to-10 scale
Pain ratings show comfort after the procedure.
Verify the airtight seal and the pressure setting
This confirms effective negative pressure.
Measure canister drainage on a regular basis
Measuring output monitors fluid balance.
Remove the drape each shift to look at the foam
Removing the drape would break the seal; inspection is done without disrupting therapy.
alt.ex: Evaluation checks wound status, pain, seal and settings, and canister output.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which statements about NPWT dressing changes are accurate? (Select all that apply.)
o: Fresh sterile wounds require sterile gloves
Fresh sterile wounds require sterile technique.
Chronic wounds require clean technique
Clean technique is used for chronic wounds.
Filler must contact the entire wound base and margins
Contact with the whole wound maintains negative pressure.
Foam should be cut larger than the wound to overlap the skin
Foam is cut to fit the exact size and shape of the wound.
Old foam may be left in tunnels if it is hard to remove
All pieces of foam must be removed at each change.
items.ex: Glove type depends on wound type, and the filler must fit and contact the entire wound.

alt.q: Which actions are correct when applying an NPWT filler dressing? (Select all that apply.)
o: Cut the foam with sterile scissors to the exact shape of the wound
Exact fit maintains negative pressure to the entire wound.
Fill tunneled and undermined areas
Filler must contact tunnels and undermined areas.
Count the pieces of filler placed
The count guides removal at the next change.
Leave undermined areas unfilled to reduce pain
Filler must reach tunneled and undermined areas to maintain negative pressure.
Leave the wound base uncovered for drainage
Filler must contact the entire wound base.
alt.ex: Filler is cut to the wound’s exact size and shape, fills all spaces, and is counted.
