items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is planning care for several patients with open wounds. Which wound irrigation could the nurse delegate to nursing assistive personnel (AP)?
items.a: Irrigation of an established chronic wound on a patient’s sacrum
items.ex: Wound irrigation is not delegated to AP unless the wound is an established chronic wound; the nurse still assesses the wound.
w: Irrigation of a newly dehisced abdominal surgical incision
A new open wound needs the nurse’s assessment and irrigation; it is not an established chronic wound.
Irrigation of a fresh traumatic laceration in the emergency department
A fresh traumatic wound is not an established chronic wound, so the nurse performs the irrigation.
Irrigation of a deep postoperative wound with a very small opening
A new deep postoperative wound requires the nurse’s skill and assessment, so it is not delegated.

alt.q: A nurse delegates irrigation of an established chronic leg ulcer to an AP. Which instruction should the nurse give the AP?
alt.a: Notify the nurse when the wound is exposed so it can be assessed
alt.ex: Assessing and documenting wound characteristics remain the nurse’s responsibility, so the AP calls the nurse when the wound is exposed.
w: Measure the wound and document its characteristics in the record
Assessing and documenting wound characteristics is the nurse’s responsibility, not the AP’s.
Increase the irrigation pressure if any blood appears in the wound
The AP reports blood to the nurse; bleeding calls for less pressure, not more.
Obtain a wound culture whenever the drainage looks different
Wound cultures are obtained by the nurse when indicated; the AP reports drainage changes.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A wound is estimated to hold about 40 mL. How much irrigation solution should the nurse prepare?
items.a: 60 to 80 mL, which is 1.5 to 2 times the wound volume
items.ex: The equipment list calls for an irrigant volume of 1.5 to 2 times the estimated wound volume.
w: 40 mL, which is equal to the wound volume
A volume equal to the wound is too little; the book calls for 1.5 to 2 times the wound volume.
20 to 30 mL, which is about half the wound volume
Half the wound volume would not flush the wound adequately; use 1.5 to 2 times its volume.
160 to 200 mL, which is 4 to 5 times the wound volume
The recommended amount is 1.5 to 2 times the estimated wound volume, not 4 to 5 times.

alt.q: What volume of irrigation solution does the book recommend relative to the estimated volume of the wound?
alt.a: 1.5 to 2 times the estimated wound volume
alt.ex: Preparing 1.5 to 2 times the estimated wound volume provides enough irrigant to flush the wound.
w: 0.5 to 1 times the estimated wound volume
This amount is too small to flush the wound; the book recommends 1.5 to 2 times its volume.
3 to 4 times the estimated wound volume
The book recommends 1.5 to 2 times the estimated wound volume, not 3 to 4 times.
5 to 6 times the estimated wound volume
The book recommends 1.5 to 2 times the estimated wound volume, not 5 to 6 times.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Why does the nurse use a 35-mL syringe with a 19-gauge angiocatheter to irrigate an open wound?
items.a: It delivers irrigation pressures between 4 and 15 psi to remove debris safely
items.ex: This syringe and catheter combination gives an ideal pressure of 4 to 15 psi for mechanical cleaning and debris removal.
w: It delivers irrigation pressures between 20 and 30 psi to dissolve necrotic tissue
Pressures of 20 to 30 psi are too high; the syringe and 19-gauge catheter deliver 4 to 15 psi.
It delivers irrigation pressures between 1 and 2 psi to avoid any mechanical force
Irrigation intentionally uses mechanical force; the target range is 4 to 15 psi.
It delivers irrigation pressures between 50 and 60 psi to sterilize the wound bed
Irrigation does not sterilize a wound, and 50 to 60 psi would damage tissue.

alt.q: A nurse irrigates an open wound with a 35-mL syringe and a 19-gauge angiocatheter. Which pressure range does this deliver?
alt.a: 4 to 15 psi
alt.ex: A 35-mL syringe with a 19-gauge angiocatheter delivers 4 to 15 psi for mechanical debridement.
w: 0.5 to 2 psi
This pressure is too low to separate debris; the syringe and catheter deliver 4 to 15 psi.
20 to 35 psi
This range exceeds the 4 to 15 psi that the syringe and catheter deliver.
40 to 60 psi
This range is far above the 4 to 15 psi used for safe wound irrigation.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: When irrigating an open wound with a syringe, where should the nurse hold the syringe tip?
items.a: 2.5 cm (1 inch) above the upper end of the wound
items.ex: Holding the tip 2.5 cm above the upper end prevents syringe contamination and unsafe pressure of the flowing solution.
w: Touching the wound bed at the lower end of the wound
Touching the wound contaminates the syringe; the tip is held above the upper end.
15 cm (6 inches) above the center of the wound
At 15 cm the stream loses its controlled pressure; the book specifies 2.5 cm above the upper end.
2.5 cm (1 inch) below the lower end of the wound
Solution flows from top to bottom and clean to contaminated, so the tip goes above the upper end.

alt.q: A nurse holds the irrigating syringe 2.5 cm (1 inch) above the upper end of an open wound. What is the reason for this placement?
alt.a: It prevents syringe contamination and unsafe pressure of the flowing solution
alt.ex: Correct placement keeps the syringe sterile and keeps the stream at a safe pressure.
w: It allows the nurse to measure wound depth with the syringe tip
The syringe tip never touches the wound; depth is measured during wound assessment.
It warms the irrigant to body temperature before it reaches the wound
Irrigant is warmed to room temperature beforehand; tip placement does not change its temperature.
It increases the pressure of the stream above 15 psi for deeper cleaning
Pressures above 15 psi are unsafe; tip placement is meant to prevent unsafe pressure.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is irrigating a deep wound with a very small opening using a soft catheter attached to the syringe. How far should the nurse insert the catheter tip?
items.a: Gently, about 1.3 cm (0.5 inch), without forcing it
items.ex: Inserting the catheter about 1.3 cm prevents the tip from touching the fragile inner wall; forcing it causes tissue damage.
w: Firmly, until resistance is felt at the base of the wound
Forcing the catheter into the wound causes tissue damage; insert it gently about 1.3 cm.
Gently, about 5 cm (2 inches), to reach the deepest tissue
Inserting 5 cm risks contact with the fragile inner wall; the book specifies about 1.3 cm.
Not at all, holding the catheter 2.5 cm (1 inch) above the opening
For a deep wound with a small opening, the catheter is inserted so irrigant flows directly into the wound.

alt.q: During irrigation of a deep wound with a small opening, a nurse feels resistance while inserting the soft catheter. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Stop advancing and avoid forcing the catheter into the wound
alt.ex: Forcing the catheter causes tissue damage; it is inserted gently only about 1.3 cm (0.5 inch).
w: Push the catheter past the resistance to reach the wound base
Pushing past resistance forces the catheter and damages fragile tissue.
Switch to a 19-gauge needle so it passes through more easily
A needle would be more damaging; the soft catheter is used for small deep openings.
Increase the plunger pressure to open the wound tract
Slow, continuous pressure is used; extra force can damage tissue and cause bleeding.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A patient receiving an anticoagulant has an order for wound irrigation with a pulsatile lavage device. Which action by the nurse is most appropriate?
items.a: Use caution and monitor closely for bleeding during the irrigation
items.ex: Irrigation can cause bleeding, so caution is needed in patients on anticoagulants or with coagulopathy.
w: Use the highest pressure setting to finish the procedure quickly
High pressure increases bleeding risk; settings follow the order, usually 4 to 15 psi.
Hold the anticoagulant for 24 hours before the irrigation
The nurse does not stop prescribed anticoagulants on their own; the book calls for caution.
Proceed without changes because anticoagulants do not affect wounds
Anticoagulants increase bleeding tendency, and irrigation could cause bleeding.

alt.q: Before irrigating a wound, why does the nurse assess whether the patient takes an anticoagulant or has a coagulopathy?
alt.a: Irrigation could cause bleeding in a patient with a bleeding tendency
alt.ex: A bleeding tendency calls for caution because the force of irrigation can cause bleeding.
w: Anticoagulants react chemically with normal saline irrigant
Normal saline does not react with anticoagulants; the concern is bleeding.
Anticoagulants make the wound unable to heal by secondary intention
Anticoagulants do not prevent secondary intention healing; the concern is bleeding during irrigation.
Patients with coagulopathy need a wound culture before irrigation
Cultures are based on signs of infection, not on coagulation status.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: During wound irrigation, fresh bleeding begins to ooze from the wound bed. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Apply pressure to the wound with sterile gauze to stop the bleeding
items.ex: Stopping the bleeding with sterile gauze pressure comes first; the nurse then notifies the provider and uses less pressure next time.
w: Continue irrigating with more pressure to clear the blood
More pressure worsens bleeding; future irrigations should use less pressure.
Document the bleeding and complete the dressing change
Documentation follows care; fresh bleeding must be controlled and reported first.
Obtain a wound culture of the bloody drainage
Bleeding is not an indication for a culture; the immediate need is to stop the bleeding.

alt.q: A nurse applies sterile gauze pressure to stop bleeding that appeared during wound irrigation. Which change should the nurse plan for the next irrigation?
alt.a: Flush the wound using less pressure
alt.ex: When bleeding appears, the next irrigation uses less pressure to avoid further trauma to the wound bed.
w: Flush the wound using a 23-gauge needle for more force
A smaller gauge raises pressure; the book calls for less pressure after bleeding.
Flush the wound with cold solution to constrict vessels
Irrigant should be at room temperature for comfort and to reduce vascular constriction.
Flush the wound for a longer time at the same pressure
The intervention for bleeding is to reduce pressure, not to lengthen irrigation.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Partway through a wound irrigation, the patient reports that the pain has increased from 3 to 7 on a 0-to-10 scale. Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Decrease the force of pressure used for the irrigation
items.ex: Increased pain during irrigation calls for less pressure and assessment of the need for more analgesia before wound care.
w: Increase the pressure so the procedure ends sooner
More force increases discomfort; the book calls for decreasing pressure.
Continue at the same pressure because pain is expected
Pain should not increase as a result of irrigation, so the technique must change.
Switch to a colder irrigant to numb the wound
Room-temperature irrigant increases comfort; cold solution causes vascular constriction.

alt.q: After a wound irrigation, a patient reports pain was much worse during the procedure. What should the nurse plan before the next wound care?
alt.a: Assess the need for additional analgesia before wound care
alt.ex: Increased pain calls for evaluating extra analgesia before wound care and using less irrigation pressure.
w: Skip the analgesic so pain can guide the irrigation pressure
Analgesia is given at least 30 minutes before irrigation to promote comfort.
Irrigate with a higher pressure so the procedure is shorter
Higher pressure worsens discomfort; the book calls for decreasing pressure.
Ask the provider to discontinue all wound irrigation
The first steps are to reduce pressure and assess analgesic needs, not to stop treatment.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Why does the nurse make sure the irrigation solution is at room temperature before irrigating an open wound?
items.a: It increases comfort and reduces the vascular constriction response in tissues
items.ex: Room-temperature irrigant is more comfortable and reduces vascular constriction in wound tissues.
w: It kills surface bacteria more effectively than cold solution
Temperature does not make saline antibacterial; mechanical force removes surface bacteria.
It increases the irrigation pressure delivered by the syringe
Pressure depends on the syringe and catheter, not on the solution temperature.
It prevents the solution from becoming contaminated in the basin
Sterile technique prevents contamination; temperature is chosen for comfort and blood flow.

alt.q: A home care patient keeps homemade saline in the refrigerator. What should the patient do before using it to irrigate the wound?
alt.a: Let the saline reach room temperature
alt.ex: Room-temperature saline increases comfort and reduces vascular constriction in the wound tissues.
w: Boil the saline and use it while still hot
Hot solution can injure tissue; the book says to let saline reach room temperature.
Use the saline straight from the refrigerator
Cold solution causes vascular constriction and discomfort.
Add more salt to the saline before use
Adding salt changes the solution; the recipe is 8 teaspoons of salt per gallon.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is teaching a family caregiver to make normal saline for home wound irrigation. Which statement by the caregiver shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “I will mix 8 teaspoons of salt into 1 gallon of distilled water.”
items.ex: The book’s home recipe is 8 teaspoons of salt in 1 gallon of distilled water.
w: “I will mix 2 teaspoons of salt into 1 gallon of tap water.”
The recipe uses 8 teaspoons of salt and distilled water, not tap water.
“I will mix 8 tablespoons of salt into 1 quart of distilled water.”
This is far too concentrated; the recipe is 8 teaspoons per gallon.
“I will mix 1 teaspoon of salt into 1 gallon of distilled water.”
One teaspoon is too little salt; the recipe uses 8 teaspoons per gallon.

alt.q: A caregiver has made normal saline at home for wound irrigation. Which statement shows correct understanding of its storage?
alt.a: “I can keep it refrigerated for up to 1 month.”
alt.ex: Homemade saline can be refrigerated for 1 month and is warmed to room temperature before use.
w: “I can keep it on the counter for up to 6 months.”
Homemade saline is refrigerated and kept for only 1 month.
“I must make a new batch every 2 hours.”
Refrigerated homemade saline can be kept for 1 month.
“I can keep it frozen for up to 1 year.”
The book says to refrigerate it for up to 1 month, not freeze it for a year.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: After irrigating a wound with a syringe or pulsatile device, why does the nurse observe for retained irrigant?
items.a: Retained irrigant is a medium for bacterial growth and infection
items.ex: Irrigant left in the wound can support bacterial growth and lead to infection.
w: Retained irrigant dilutes the wound culture results
Cultures are taken after cleaning; the concern with retained fluid is bacterial growth.
Retained irrigant raises the pressure of the next irrigation
Irrigation pressure depends on the device; retained fluid is a risk for infection.
Retained irrigant cools the wound and slows the dressing change
The main concern with retained fluid is that it promotes bacterial growth.

alt.q: Which finding after a wound irrigation should the nurse report immediately to the health care provider?
alt.a: Retention of irrigant in the wound
alt.ex: The book lists retention of irrigant, fresh bleeding, a sharp increase in pain, or signs of shock for immediate reporting.
w: Clear irrigant draining into the basin
Clear return shows that debris has been removed and is the goal of irrigation.
A dry, intact dressing labeled with the date
A dry, labeled dressing is the expected outcome after irrigation.
Pain rated the same as before irrigation
Pain should not increase with irrigation, so unchanged pain is acceptable.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse is irrigating a wound with a handheld shower. Which technique is correct?
items.a: Use a gentle, warm spray for 5 to 10 minutes with the showerhead 30 cm (12 inches) away
items.ex: The shower runs for 5 to 10 minutes with a gentle warm flow 30 cm from the wound to clean it thoroughly.
w: Use a forceful, hot spray for 1 to 2 minutes with the showerhead 5 cm (2 inches) away
The spray should be gentle and warm, kept 30 cm away for 5 to 10 minutes.
Use a gentle, cold spray for 20 to 30 minutes with the showerhead 60 cm (24 inches) away
The water should be warm and the shower lasts 5 to 10 minutes at 30 cm.
Use a forceful, warm spray for 15 to 20 minutes with the showerhead touching the wound
A forceful spray touching the wound can injure tissue; use a gentle flow 30 cm away.

alt.q: Which patient is the best candidate for wound cleaning with a handheld shower?
alt.a: A patient who can shower independently or with help, including at home
alt.ex: Handheld showering suits patients able to shower with help or independently and can be done at home.
w: A patient on bed rest who cannot be moved from bed
A shower requires sitting in a shower chair or standing, so a bed-bound patient is not a candidate.
A patient with a deep wound with a very small opening
A deep wound with a small opening is irrigated with a syringe and soft catheter.
A patient who is unconscious and receiving mechanical ventilation
This patient cannot sit or stand in a shower; shower cleaning is for patients able to shower.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which findings after a wound irrigation should the nurse report to the health care provider immediately? Select all that apply.
o: Fresh bleeding from the wound
Fresh bleeding is listed for immediate reporting to the provider.
A sharp increase in the patient’s pain
A sharp increase in pain is reported immediately.
Irrigant retained in the wound
Retained irrigant is a medium for bacterial growth and is reported immediately.
Signs of shock
Signs of shock are reported to the provider immediately.
Clear return in the collection basin
Clear return shows that debris has been removed, which is the expected result.
Pain rated the same as before irrigation
Pain should not increase with irrigation, so unchanged pain is not urgent.
items.ex: Fresh bleeding, a sharp increase in pain, retention of irrigant, or signs of shock must be reported immediately.

alt.q: Which items should the nurse document after a wound irrigation? Select all that apply.
o: Amount and type of solution used
The amount and type of irrigant are part of the documentation.
Irrigation device and pressure used
The device and pressure are documented.
Patient’s tolerance of the procedure
Tolerance of the procedure is documented.
Type of dressing applied after irrigation
The dressing applied after irrigation is documented.
Name of the AP who stocked the supplies
Supply stocking is not part of wound irrigation documentation.
The nurse’s opinion of the provider’s order
Personal opinions about orders do not belong in the record.
alt.ex: Documentation includes wound assessment before and after, drainage, solution, device and pressure, tolerance, and the new dressing.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Which findings would indicate the need to obtain a wound culture? Select all that apply.
o: Inflammation around the wound
Periwound inflammation is an indication for a wound culture.
Purulent odor or drainage
Purulent odor or drainage suggests infection and indicates a culture.
New drainage from the wound
New drainage is listed as an indication for a culture.
A febrile patient
Fever is an indication for obtaining a wound culture.
Pink granulation tissue in the wound bed
Pink granulation tissue is a sign of healing, not infection.
Decreasing amount of exudate
Exudate should decrease as a wound heals, so this is expected.
items.ex: Inflammation, purulent odor or drainage, new drainage, or fever indicate that a wound culture should be obtained.

alt.q: A nurse is reviewing a patient’s wound before irrigation. Which findings suggest infection that should prompt a culture? Select all that apply.
o: Warm, red periwound skin
Warm red periwound skin is a sign of infection.
A temperature of 38.6°C (101.5°F)
A febrile patient is an indication for a wound culture.
Purulent drainage on the removed dressing
Purulent drainage indicates a culture is needed.
Wound edges that are dry and intact
Dry, intact edges are not a sign of infection.
Steadily decreasing wound drainage
Decreasing drainage is expected in a healing wound.
alt.ex: Signs of infection such as periwound redness and warmth, fever, or purulent drainage prompt a culture.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: On which tissues should pulsatile high-pressure lavage NOT be used? Select all that apply.
o: Skin grafts
Pulsatile lavage should not be used on skin grafts.
Exposed blood vessels
Exposed blood vessels can be injured by pulsatile lavage.
Exposed tendon or bone
Pulsatile lavage should not be used on exposed tendon or bone.
A wound bed with necrotic tissue
Pulsatile lavage is often the irrigation of choice for necrotic wounds.
Periwound skin that is intact
The restrictions apply to grafts and exposed vessels, muscle, tendon, and bone, not intact skin.
items.ex: Pulsatile lavage is avoided on skin grafts and exposed blood vessels, muscle, tendon, or bone.

alt.q: Which statements about pulsatile high-pressure lavage are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: It is often the irrigation of choice for necrotic wounds.
Pulsatile lavage is often chosen for necrotic wounds.
Pressure settings follow the provider’s order, usually 4 to 15 psi.
Settings are per order, usually between 4 and 15 psi.
It should be used with caution in patients taking anticoagulants.
Anticoagulants or coagulation disorders increase the risk of bleeding.
It is the preferred method for cleaning skin grafts.
Pulsatile lavage should not be used on skin grafts.
It is always used without suction.
It may be used with or without suction.
alt.ex: Pulsatile lavage suits necrotic wounds at ordered pressures, but avoid it on grafts and exposed structures and use caution with anticoagulants.

alt.ww: Culturing an uncleaned wound would not follow the recommended technique.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

sections.name: Skill 48.6 · Applying roller gauze or elastic bandage

items.q: A nurse is reviewing bandaging tasks for the shift. Which task may be delegated to assistive personnel (AP), according to agency policy?
items.a: Applying roller gauze to secure a nonsterile dressing
items.ex: Applying bandages to secure nonsterile dressings can be delegated to AP per agency policy.
w: Applying an elastic bandage for compression of a leg
Applying an elastic bandage for compression cannot be delegated to AP.
Assessing a wound before a bandage is applied over it
The nurse assesses the condition of any wound or dressing before bandaging.
Applying roller gauze for compression of a sprained wrist
Roller gauze or elastic bandage for compression cannot be delegated to AP.

alt.q: Which bandaging task must the nurse perform rather than delegate to AP?
alt.a: Applying an elastic bandage to provide compression
alt.ex: Applying roller gauze or elastic bandage for compression cannot be delegated to AP.
w: Applying roller gauze to hold a nonsterile dressing
Securing nonsterile dressings with a bandage can be delegated per agency policy.
Reporting a patient’s tingling after a bandage is applied
AP are instructed to report tingling to the nurse, so this is an AP task.
Reporting a change in skin color below a bandage
Reporting color changes below a bandage is an expected AP responsibility.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: An AP reports that a patient says the toes have felt numb and tingly since an elastic bandage was applied to the lower leg. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Assess circulation distal to the elastic bandage
items.ex: For pain or numbness, the nurse first assesses distal circulation, then releases and reapplies the bandage with less pressure.
w: Notify the health care provider of the numbness
The provider is notified if findings are abnormal or complaints continue, after assessment.
Raise the leg and recheck the toes in 2 hours
Numbness signals possible impaired circulation and needs prompt assessment, not a 2-hour delay.
Give the ordered analgesic for leg discomfort
Medicating masks a sign of impaired circulation; distal circulation is assessed first.

alt.q: A nurse releases an elastic bandage after a patient reports leg pain and numbness. Distal pulse, temperature, and capillary refill are normal. What should the nurse do next?
alt.a: Reapply the bandage with less pressure
alt.ex: After releasing the bandage and finding normal circulation, the nurse reapplies it with less pressure.
w: Reapply the bandage with more tension
More tension worsens pressure; the bandage is reapplied with less pressure.
Leave the bandage off until the next day
The ordered bandage is reapplied with less pressure rather than left off.
Wrap the bandage from proximal to distal
Bandages are always wrapped from distal to proximal to promote venous return.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Why does the nurse begin applying an elastic bandage at the distal point and wrap toward the proximal boundary?
items.a: It exerts even pressure and promotes venous return
items.ex: Wrapping distal to proximal with even tension conforms evenly to the body part and promotes venous return.
w: It traps venous blood in the distal extremity
Distal-to-proximal wrapping promotes, rather than blocks, venous return.
It hides the toes so they stay warm
Toes and fingertips are left uncovered for circulatory assessment.
It lets the bandage end be taped to skin
The end is secured to the outside layer of bandage, not to the skin.

alt.q: A nurse is applying an elastic bandage to a patient’s forearm. Where should the nurse begin the wrap?
alt.a: At the wrist, the distal point, wrapping toward the elbow
alt.ex: Bandaging starts at the distal point and moves to the proximal boundary to promote venous return.
w: At the elbow, the proximal point, wrapping toward the wrist
Starting proximally and wrapping distally impairs venous return.
At the middle of the forearm, wrapping in both directions
The book directs a single direction, from distal to proximal.
At the fingertips, covering them completely
Fingertips are left uncovered so circulation can be assessed.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: By how much should each turn of a roller gauze or elastic bandage overlap the previous turn?
items.a: One-half to two-thirds the width of the bandage
items.ex: Overlapping by one-half to two-thirds the width prevents uneven tension and circulatory impairment.
w: One-tenth to one-quarter the width of the bandage
Too little overlap leaves gaps and uneven tension; overlap one-half to two-thirds.
The full width of the bandage on every turn
Full overlap adds bulk without coverage; overlap one-half to two-thirds.
No overlap, so that the edges just touch
Each layer must overlap the previous one by one-half to two-thirds.

alt.q: A nurse sees an elastic bandage whose turns barely overlap, with gaps between them. What problem can this cause?
alt.a: Uneven bandage tension and circulatory impairment
alt.ex: Overlapping turns by one-half to two-thirds width prevents uneven tension and circulatory impairment.
w: Better venous return because of reduced bulk
Gaps cause uneven tension, which impairs circulation rather than improving it.
Even pressure along the whole extremity
Without proper overlap, the pressure is uneven.
Improved immobilization of the injured joint
Poor overlap weakens support; a snug figure-eight gives joint immobilization.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: An elastic bandage is ordered to provide simple compression of a patient’s lower leg. When should the nurse measure the leg circumference to select the bandage width?
items.a: Before or shortly after the patient gets out of bed in the morning
items.ex: Measuring in the morning or after at least 15 minutes in bed avoids the swelling that develops when the leg is dependent.
w: At the end of the day after the patient has been walking
Dependent swelling later in the day overestimates the leg size.
Right after the patient has sat in a chair for 2 hours
Sitting causes dependent swelling; measure after time in bed instead.
Only after the bandage has been in place for 8 hours
Circumference is assessed before application to choose the correct width.

alt.q: A patient has been up walking in the hall. The nurse needs to measure the leg circumference for an elastic compression bandage. What should the nurse do?
alt.a: Have the patient lie in bed for at least 15 minutes first
alt.ex: Circumference is measured in the morning or after the patient has been in bed for at least 15 minutes.
w: Measure right away while the patient is standing
Standing after walking increases swelling, giving an inaccurate size.
Wait until the patient has sat in a chair for 1 hour
Sitting keeps the leg dependent; the patient should be in bed at least 15 minutes.
Measure the opposite leg and choose a smaller width
A bandage that is too small may compromise circulation to the distal extremity.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Before applying roller gauze to secure a dressing on a dependent extremity, why does the nurse elevate the extremity for 15 minutes?
items.a: It promotes venous return and decreases swelling
items.ex: Elevating a dependent extremity for 15 minutes before bandaging promotes venous return and reduces swelling.
w: It warms the skin so the tape adheres better
Elevation is meant to reduce swelling, not warm the skin.
It increases arterial pressure in the distal part
Elevation aids venous return; it does not increase distal arterial pressure.
It dries any wound drainage before bandaging
Drainage is managed with the dressing; elevation reduces swelling.

alt.q: For how long should the nurse elevate a dependent extremity before applying a bandage to secure a dressing?
alt.a: 15 minutes
alt.ex: Elevating for 15 minutes before bandaging promotes venous return and decreases swelling.
w: 2 minutes
Two minutes is too short; the book calls for 15 minutes of elevation.
60 minutes
The book specifies 15 minutes, not 60 minutes.
4 hours
The book specifies 15 minutes of elevation before bandaging.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: A nurse finishes wrapping an elastic bandage around a patient’s ankle. How should the nurse secure the end of the bandage?
items.a: Tape or clip it to the outside layer of bandage
items.ex: The bandage ends with two circular turns and is secured to the outside layer, not to the skin.
w: Tape it directly to the patient’s skin
Taping to skin risks medical adhesive–related skin injury; secure to the bandage.
Tuck it under the first anchoring turn
Tucking does not hold securely; the end is fixed with tape or clips.
Tie it in a knot over the ankle bone
A knot over a bony prominence creates pressure; use tape or clips.

alt.q: How does the nurse anchor the beginning of a roller gauze or elastic bandage?
alt.a: With two circular turns
alt.ex: Application begins with two circular turns to anchor the bandage and ends with two circular turns.
w: With a figure-eight turn
Figure-eight turns cover joints; anchoring is done with two circular turns.
With a strip of tape on the skin
The bandage is anchored with two circular turns and later secured to the bandage itself.
With a spiral turn
Spiral turns cover cylindrical parts after the bandage is anchored.

items.src: Ch 48 · Skin integrity and wound care

items.q: Why does the nurse leave the toes uncovered when applying an elastic bandage to the foot and ankle, unless the toes themselves are being treated?
items.a: So the toes can be checked for circulation

items.q: Which three components make up any sensory experience?
items.a: Reception, perception, and reaction
items.ex: Every sensory experience involves receiving a stimulus, becoming aware of and interpreting it, and then reacting to it.
w: Stimulation, transmission, and adaptation
Transmission and adaptation describe parts of nerve function, but the three named components are reception, perception, and reaction.
Detection, storage, and recall
Storage of sensory information is one way the brain avoids bombardment, not a component of every sensory experience.
Reception, integration, and modulation
Integration is part of perception, and modulation is not one of the three named components.

alt.q: A stimulus reaches a receptor, the person becomes aware of it, and then responds. Which component of the sensory experience is the response?
alt.a: Reaction
alt.ex: After interpreting the significance of a sensation, the person reacts to the stimulus, the final component of the sensory experience.
w: Reception
Reception is the first component, when a receptor nerve cell is stimulated.
Perception
Perception is the awareness, integration, and interpretation of the stimulus, before the response.
Transmission
Transmission describes the impulse traveling along nerve pathways, not the person’s response.

items.q: Which statement describes a typical sensory receptor?
items.a: It usually responds to only one type of stimulus, such as light or sound
items.ex: Reception begins with stimulation of a receptor, which is usually for only one type of stimulus such as light, touch, taste, or sound.
w: It responds equally to light, touch, taste, and sound
Receptors are usually specific to a single type of stimulus, not all types.
It interprets the meaning of a stimulus before sending it on
Interpretation of stimuli occurs in specialized neurons of the cerebral cortex, not in the receptor.
It sends impulses only to the same side of the brain
Sensory pathways usually cross over to the opposite side of the brain.

alt.q: Why are the special senses described as having grouped receptors?
alt.a: Their receptors lie close together or in specialized organs such as the retina or taste buds
alt.ex: For the special senses, receptors are grouped closely or located in specialized organs such as the taste buds or retina.
w: Their receptors respond to every type of stimulus at the same time
Receptors usually respond to only one type of stimulus.
Their receptors are spread evenly over the entire skin surface
Special sense receptors are concentrated in specialized organs, not spread across the skin.
Their receptors bypass nerve pathways to reach the brain
Impulses travel along nerve pathways to the spinal cord or directly to the brain.

items.q: Where does the actual perception or awareness of a unique sensation take place?
items.a: In the receiving region of the cerebral cortex
items.ex: Specialized neurons in the receiving region of the cerebral cortex interpret the quality and nature of sensory stimuli.
w: In the sensory receptor that first detects the stimulus
The receptor only begins reception; awareness depends on the cerebral cortex.
In the spinal cord where impulses first arrive
The spinal cord relays impulses; it does not interpret their quality and nature.
In the reticular activating system of the brainstem
The reticular activating system mediates stimuli to the cortex; the cortex interprets them.

alt.q: Specialized neurons in the receiving region of the cerebral cortex interpret the quality and nature of a stimulus. Which component of the sensory experience does this describe?
alt.a: Perception
alt.ex: Perception is the conscious awareness, integration, and interpretation of stimuli by the cerebral cortex.
w: Reception
Reception is stimulation of the receptor nerve cell, not interpretation in the cortex.
Reaction
Reaction is the person’s response after the sensation has been interpreted.
Adaptation
Adaptation is when a person stops responding to a continued, unchanging stimulus.

items.q: Sound waves stimulate hair cell receptors in the organ of Corti. Along which nerve do the resulting impulses travel to the brain?
items.a: The eighth cranial nerve
items.ex: Hair cells in the organ of Corti send impulses along the eighth cranial nerve to the acoustic area of the temporal lobe.
w: The second cranial nerve
The second cranial nerve is the optic nerve, which carries visual impulses.
The fifth cranial nerve
The fifth cranial nerve is not the pathway for hearing impulses.
The seventh cranial nerve
The seventh cranial nerve is not the pathway for hearing impulses; the eighth is.

alt.q: Impulses from the hair cells of the organ of Corti travel along the eighth cranial nerve to which area of the brain?
alt.a: The acoustic area of the temporal lobe
alt.ex: Auditory impulses reach the acoustic area of the temporal lobe, where they are interpreted.
w: The visual area of the occipital lobe
The occipital lobe receives visual, not auditory, impulses.
The motor area of the frontal lobe
The frontal motor area controls movement; it does not receive hearing impulses.
The vestibular nuclei of the cerebellum
Hearing impulses go to the acoustic area of the temporal lobe.

items.q: A patient received a sedative 30 minutes ago and is now drowsy. Which conclusion by the nurse about the patient’s sensory function is accurate?
items.a: The lowered level of consciousness is likely to impair the patient’s sensory perception
items.ex: A person’s level of consciousness influences perception, and any factor that lowers consciousness impairs sensory perception.
w: Sedation sharpens perception by reducing distracting stimuli
Lowered consciousness impairs perception rather than sharpening it.
Perception is unaffected because the sensory receptors are intact
Intact receptors are not enough; perception depends on consciousness and cortical interpretation.
Only the sense of pain is affected by the patient’s drowsiness
Factors that lower consciousness impair sensory perception in general, not only pain.

alt.q: Which factor directly influences a person’s perception and interpretation of stimuli?
alt.a: The person’s level of consciousness
alt.ex: Perception requires that a person become conscious of a stimulus, so a lowered level of consciousness impairs perception.
w: The number of receptors in the skin
The text links perception to consciousness and past experience, not receptor count.
The person’s body temperature
Body temperature is not described as a factor in sensory perception.
The time of day the stimulus occurs
Time of day is not named as an influence on perception.

items.q: A patient with blurred vision reaches for a cup and knocks it over. Which explanation best accounts for this inappropriate reaction to a stimulus?
items.a: The patient cannot experience the visual sensation completely, so the reaction is inaccurate
items.ex: When patients cannot experience sensations completely, as with blurred vision, they can react inappropriately to sensory stimuli.
w: The patient has adapted to the visual stimulus and stopped responding to it
Adaptation means not noticing a continued stimulus; it does not explain a misjudged reach.
The patient’s receptors are sending impulses to the wrong sense organ
Receptors send impulses along nerve pathways to the brain, not to other sense organs.
The patient is experiencing sensory overload from the cup
A single object does not create overload; the problem is incomplete visual sensation.

alt.q: A young child who has never felt a burn touches a hot pan and does not pull away quickly. Which concept explains the child’s reaction?
alt.a: Perception depends on past experiences that help a person understand a stimulus
alt.ex: Perception includes interpretation based on experience, so a person without past experience of a stimulus such as pain may react inappropriately.
w: Pain is a stimulus to which people quickly adapt
Pain is the stimulus to which adaptation usually does not occur.
Children lack sensory receptors for temperature
The issue is interpretation without past experience, not absence of receptors.
The child’s level of consciousness must be lowered
Nothing suggests lowered consciousness; lack of past experience explains the reaction.

items.q: After a person is exposed to the same stimulus for a while, the sensation goes unnoticed. Which stimulus is the exception to this adaptation?
items.a: Pain
items.ex: Adaptation occurs with most sensory stimuli except pain, which continues to be noticed.
w: Background music
Background music is the book’s example of a stimulus a person stops noticing.
Light touch of clothing
Constant light touch is a typical stimulus that goes unnoticed with continued exposure.
A steady odor in a room
A constant odor is a typical stimulus to which a person adapts.

alt.q: A patient states, “When I first got here the hum of the air system bothered me, but now I don’t even notice it.” Which concept explains this?
alt.a: Adaptation, in which a person stops responding to a continued, unchanging stimulus
alt.ex: After continued reception of the same stimulus, a person stops responding and the sensory experience goes unnoticed.
w: Sensory deprivation, in which stimuli lack enough quality and quantity
Deprivation involves insufficient stimuli and produces symptoms such as boredom or confusion.
Sensory overload, in which the brain cannot ignore stimuli
In overload the person cannot disregard stimuli, the opposite of what the patient describes.
Sensory deficit, in which reception and perception are impaired
The patient’s hearing is not impaired; the brain is simply filtering a familiar sound.

items.q: A patient with an inner ear disorder reports both reduced hearing and episodes of imbalance. Which explanation should the nurse give?
items.a: The inner ear labyrinth unites the parts for hearing and balance
items.ex: The union of the vestibular and cochlear parts of the labyrinth explains the combined hearing and balance symptoms of inner ear disorders.
w: The middle ear ossicles control both hearing and balance
The ossicles transfer sound; balance end organs are in the inner ear labyrinth.
The external ear canal regulates both sound and body position
The external canal shelters the eardrum and maintains temperature and humidity.
The optic nerve carries both hearing and balance impulses
The optic nerve carries visual impulses; hearing travels along the eighth cranial nerve.

alt.q: Why do disorders of the inner ear commonly cause a combination of hearing and balance symptoms?
alt.a: The membranous labyrinth contains the end organs of both hearing and balance
alt.ex: The labyrinth unites the vestibular (balance) and cochlear (hearing) parts, so one disorder affects both functions.
w: The eardrum maintains both hearing and balance
The eardrum transmits sound vibrations; it does not contain balance organs.
The middle ear air space controls both hearing and balance
The middle ear contains the ossicles that transfer sound, not the balance organs.
The temporal lobe receives no balance information from the ear
This does not explain the combined symptoms; the shared labyrinth does.

items.q: What is the function of the external ear canal?
items.a: It shelters the eardrum and maintains constant temperature and humidity to preserve its elasticity
items.ex: The external canal protects the eardrum and keeps temperature and humidity steady so the eardrum stays elastic.
w: It contains three small bones that transfer sound to the inner ear
The three ossicles are located in the air-containing middle ear.
It holds the fluid that bathes the end organs of hearing and balance
Fluid bathing the membranous labyrinth is in the inner ear.
It contains the hair cells that send impulses to the eighth cranial nerve
Hair cell receptors are in the organ of Corti of the inner ear.

alt.q: Which ear structure keeps the eardrum elastic by maintaining relatively constant temperature and humidity?
alt.a: The external ear canal
alt.ex: The external ear canal shelters the eardrum and maintains steady temperature and humidity to keep it elastic.
w: The middle ear
The middle ear is the air-containing space holding the ossicles.
The oval window
The oval window is where stapes movement creates vibrations in inner ear fluid.
The membranous labyrinth
The labyrinth contains the end organs of hearing and balance.

items.q: A patient who is deaf in one ear reports difficulty telling which direction a sound is coming from. Which explanation is accurate?
items.a: Two ears provide stereophonic hearing, which is needed to judge sound direction
items.ex: The ears transmit the direction from which sounds originate, and two ears provide stereophonic hearing to judge that direction.
w: The external canal of the hearing ear cannot maintain humidity
Humidity in the canal preserves eardrum elasticity; it does not determine sound direction.
The eighth cranial nerve carries only low-pitched sounds
The eighth cranial nerve carries hearing impulses in general, not only low pitches.
Sound direction is judged by the ossicles of one ear alone
Judging direction depends on stereophonic hearing from two ears.

alt.q: What is the purpose of having two ears?
alt.a: To provide stereophonic hearing that allows a person to judge sound direction
alt.ex: Two ears provide stereophonic hearing, which lets a person judge the direction from which sounds originate.
w: To double the number of ossicles available to amplify sound
Each middle ear has its own ossicles; having two ears is about judging direction.
To allow one ear to rest while the other hears
Both ears work together to provide stereophonic hearing.
To supply separate nerves for hearing and for balance
Hearing and balance share the labyrinth in each ear; two ears serve sound direction.

items.q: How does the brain prevent sensory bombardment?
items.a: By discarding or storing sensory information and reacting to the most meaningful stimuli
items.ex: It is impossible to react to all stimuli, so the brain discards or stores information and responds to what is most significant at the time.
w: By shutting down receptors when too many stimuli arrive
Receptors keep receiving; the brain manages input by discarding or storing it.
By reacting to every stimulus as soon as it arrives
Trying to react to every stimulus leads to sensory alteration, not protection.
By sending all stimuli directly to conscious awareness
Conscious awareness of all stimuli would cause overload; the brain filters them.

alt.q: A person absorbed in a good book does not notice music playing in the background. Which process explains this?
alt.a: The brain responds to the most meaningful stimuli and lets a continued stimulus go unnoticed
alt.ex: A person reacts to stimuli most meaningful at the time, and a continued stimulus such as background music goes unnoticed.
w: The person is experiencing sensory deprivation from the music
Deprivation involves insufficient stimuli, not a filtered background sound.
The person has an acute hearing deficit
Hearing is intact; the brain is filtering a less meaningful stimulus.
The music has caused sensory overload
Overload occurs when a person cannot ignore stimuli, the opposite of this situation.

items.q: Which statements about normal sensory perception are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Perception includes integration and interpretation of stimuli based on past experience
Perception draws on a person’s experiences to integrate and interpret stimuli.
Sensory nerve pathways usually cross over to the opposite side of the brain
Sensory pathways usually send stimuli to the opposite side of the brain.
The nervous system must be intact for a person to perceive a sensation
Stimuli must reach the appropriate brain centers through an intact nervous system.
Factors that lower consciousness impair sensory perception
Level of consciousness influences perception, so lowered consciousness impairs it.
Most receptors respond to many different types of stimuli
A receptor is usually for only one type of stimulus.
A person continues to notice every stimulus as long as it is present
With continued exposure most stimuli go unnoticed, except pain.
items.ex: Perception requires an intact nervous system, consciousness, and experience, and pathways usually cross to the opposite side of the brain.

alt.q: A student explains how sensations are perceived. Which statements by the student are correct? Select all that apply.
o: “Specialized neurons in the cerebral cortex interpret the nature of the stimulus.”
The receiving region of the cerebral cortex interprets the quality and nature of stimuli.
“Impulses travel along pathways to the spinal cord or directly to the brain.”
Once created, a nerve impulse travels to the spinal cord or directly to the brain.
“A person must become conscious of the stimulus for perception to occur.”
Perception takes place when a person becomes conscious of a stimulus.
“Perception happens inside the receptor before impulses are sent.”
Receptors begin reception; perception occurs in the cerebral cortex.
“People adapt to pain just as they adapt to background noise.”
Adaptation occurs with most stimuli except pain.
alt.ex: Perception occurs when impulses reach the cortex and the person becomes conscious of the stimulus; pain is the exception to adaptation.

items.q: Which statements describe the middle ear? Select all that apply.
o: It is an air-containing space between the eardrum and the oval window
The middle ear is the air-filled space between the eardrum and oval window.
It contains three small bones called ossicles
The three ossicles are located in the middle ear.
With the eardrum, it transfers sound to the fluid-filled inner ear
The eardrum and ossicles transfer sound to the inner ear.
It contains the hair cells of the organ of Corti
The organ of Corti is in the inner ear.
It is filled with perilymph that bathes the end organs of hearing
Perilymph is in the inner ear; the middle ear contains air.
items.ex: The middle ear is an air space holding the ossicles, which with the eardrum carry sound to the fluid-filled inner ear.

alt.q: Which structures are located in the inner ear? Select all that apply.
o: The membranous labyrinth
The fluid-bathed membranous labyrinth contains the end organs of hearing and balance.
Perilymph that transmits vibrations from the oval window
Vibrations at the oval window travel in the perilymph of the inner ear.
Hair cells that send impulses to the eighth cranial nerve
Inner ear hair cells send impulses along the eighth cranial nerve.
The three ossicles
The ossicles are in the air-containing middle ear.
The structure that maintains eardrum humidity
The external ear canal maintains temperature and humidity for the eardrum.
alt.ex: The inner ear holds the fluid-filled labyrinth and hair cells; the ossicles are in the middle ear.

items.q: According to the chapter, sensory alterations occur when which conditions are present? Select all that apply.
o: A person attempts to react to every stimulus in the environment
Reacting to every stimulus upsets the balance and causes sensory alteration.
The variety of stimuli is insufficient
Insufficient variety of stimuli disturbs the balance that maintains well-being.
The quality of stimuli is insufficient
Insufficient quality of stimuli also leads to sensory alteration.
The brain discards some sensory information
Discarding or storing information is the normal way the brain prevents bombardment.
A person stops noticing a continued background stimulus
Adaptation to a continued stimulus is a normal phenomenon.
items.ex: Well-being depends on a balance of stimuli; reacting to everything, or too little variety or quality, causes sensory alteration.

alt.q: Which situations maintain the balance of sensory input that supports well-being? Select all that apply.
o: The brain stores some sensory information for future use
Storing information is one way the brain prevents sensory bombardment.
A person reacts mainly to the most meaningful stimuli
Reacting to the most significant stimuli is the normal way to avoid bombardment.
A person stops noticing a constant background sound
Adaptation to a continued stimulus is normal and protects against bombardment.
A person tries to respond to every stimulus at once
Trying to react to every stimulus causes sensory alteration.
A patient’s environment offers little variety of stimuli
Insufficient variety of stimuli causes sensory alteration.
alt.ex: Filtering, storing, and adapting keep sensory input balanced; reacting to everything or receiving too little variety disrupts it.

items.q: Sensory nerve pathways usually cross over to send stimuli to the opposite side of the brain.
items.a: True
items.ex: Sensory nerve pathways usually cross over, so stimuli from one side reach the opposite side of the brain.
items.ww: Pathways usually cross over; they do not typically stay on the same side.

alt.q: Sensory nerve pathways usually send stimuli to the same side of the brain as the receptor.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Sensory nerve pathways usually cross over to the opposite side of the brain.
alt.ww: Saying stimuli stay on the same side ignores the usual crossing of sensory pathways.

items.q: Adaptation, in which a continued stimulus goes unnoticed, occurs with pain just as it does with other stimuli.
items.a: False
items.ex: Adaptation occurs with most sensory stimuli except pain, which continues to be noticed.
items.ww: Pain is specifically named as the exception to the adaptability phenomenon.

alt.q: Pain is the exception to the adaptation that occurs with most continued sensory stimuli.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: A person stops responding to most continued stimuli, but not to pain.
alt.ww: Claiming people adapt to pain like other stimuli contradicts the textbook.

items.q: A person can perceive a sensation only if the nervous system is intact so that stimuli reach the appropriate brain centers.
items.a: True
items.ex: The nervous system must be intact for stimuli to reach brain centers and for the person to perceive the sensation.
items.ww: Intact receptors alone are not enough; impulses must reach and be interpreted by the brain.

alt.q: As long as the sensory receptor is working, a person perceives a sensation even if the nerve pathway to the brain is interrupted.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Perception requires an intact nervous system so stimuli reach the appropriate brain centers.
alt.ww: Perception occurs in the cerebral cortex, so an interrupted pathway prevents it.

items.q: Sound waves stimulate hair cell receptors within the organ of [[Corti]] in the ear.
items.ex: The organ of Corti holds the hair cells that turn sound into impulses carried by the eighth cranial nerve.

alt.q: Hair cells in the organ of [[Corti]] send impulses along the eighth cranial nerve to the temporal lobe.
alt.ex: The organ of Corti holds the hair cells that turn sound into impulses carried by the eighth cranial nerve.

items.q: In sound transmission, which step comes right after “Stapes movement at the oval window creates vibrations in inner ear fluid”?
items.a: Vibrations in the perilymph stimulate hair cells

w: Hair cells send impulses along the eighth cranial nerve
That's step 5 of 6.
Vibration transmits through the bony ossicles
That's step 2 of 6.
Impulses reach the acoustic area of the temporal lobe
That's step 6 of 6.

ord.ex: Sound passes from eardrum to ossicles to oval window and perilymph, stimulating hair cells that signal the brain through the eighth cranial nerve.

items.q: In vision, which step comes right after “Light rays are adjusted as they pass through the pupil and lens”?
items.a: A change in lens shape focuses light on the retina
items.ex: That's step 3 of 5. Light is bent by the cornea, adjusted by the pupil and lens, focused on the retina, and converted by photoreceptors into signals for the optic nerve.
w: Rods and cones in the sensory retina are stimulated by light
That's step 4 of 5.
Light rays enter the convex cornea and begin to converge
That's step 1 of 5.
Photoreceptor cells send electrical potentials by way of the optic nerve to the brain
That's step 5 of 5.

items.q: Which term describes a deficit in the normal function of sensory reception and perception?
items.a: Sensory deficit
items.ex: A sensory deficit is a deficit in the normal function of sensory reception and perception, such as declining visual or hearing acuity.
w: Sensory deprivation
Sensory deprivation results from stimuli of insufficient quality or quantity to maintain awareness.
Sensory overload
Sensory overload occurs when a person cannot disregard or selectively ignore multiple stimuli.
Sensory adaptation
Adaptation is the normal process of no longer noticing a continued stimulus.

alt.q: Which situation is an example of a sensory deficit?
alt.a: An older adult whose visual acuity has gradually declined
alt.ex: A decline in visual or hearing acuity is a deficit in the normal function of sensory reception and perception.
w: A patient on prolonged bed rest in a quiet private room
Bed rest is a restrictive environment that causes sensory deprivation.
A patient in a busy critical care unit with constant alarms
Constant alarms and activity can cause sensory overload.
A patient who no longer notices a ticking clock
Not noticing a continued stimulus is normal adaptation.

items.q: When is a patient’s ability to function and relate effectively within the environment most seriously impaired?
items.a: When the patient has more than one sensory alteration
items.ex: A patient’s ability to function and relate effectively is seriously impaired when more than one sensory alteration is present.
w: When the patient’s sensory deficit developed gradually
A gradual deficit allows a person to learn to rely on unaffected senses.
When the patient has adapted to a constant background stimulus
Adaptation to a continued stimulus is a normal process.
When the patient relies on unaffected senses to compensate
Relying on unaffected senses is an adaptive response to a deficit.

alt.q: An older adult has both a hearing deficit and severe cataracts and is now hospitalized in a busy unit. Which conclusion by the nurse is most accurate?
alt.a: Having more than one sensory alteration seriously impairs the patient’s ability to function in the environment
alt.ex: Multiple sensory alterations together seriously impair a patient’s ability to function and relate within the environment.
w: The hearing deficit will make the visual deficit less noticeable
Combined alterations compound each other rather than cancel out.
The patient’s senses will quickly sharpen to compensate in the hospital
Compensation develops over time and does not offset multiple alterations in a new setting.
Only the most severe of the alterations needs to be considered
Each alteration adds to the impairment, so all must be considered.

items.q: A patient reports a slow loss of peripheral vision, difficulty adapting to darkness, and halos around lights. Which condition do these findings suggest?
items.a: Glaucoma
items.ex: Glaucoma raises intraocular pressure against the optic nerve, causing peripheral vision loss, poor dark adaptation, and halos around lights.
w: Macular degeneration
Macular degeneration affects central vision, with blurred reading matter and distorted vertical lines.
Presbyopia
Presbyopia is a decline in the lens’s ability to focus on near objects.
Myopia
Myopia is nearsightedness, an inability to see distant objects clearly.

alt.q: A patient with untreated glaucoma is most likely to report which visual change?
alt.a: Loss of peripheral vision
alt.ex: Rising intraocular pressure against the optic nerve in glaucoma causes peripheral visual loss.
w: Distortion of vertical lines
Distorted vertical lines are an early sign of macular degeneration.
Inability to see near objects only
Difficulty seeing near objects is typical of presbyopia.
Sudden painful redness and tearing
These are not listed glaucoma findings in the chapter.

items.q: An older adult reports that reading matter has become blurred and the center of the visual field looks distorted, including vertical lines. Which condition should the nurse suspect?
items.a: Macular degeneration
items.ex: Macular degeneration affects the macula, which provides central vision; early signs include blurred reading matter and distorted vertical lines.
w: Glaucoma
Glaucoma causes peripheral, not central, vision loss and halos around lights.
Cataract
A cataract causes glare and blurred vision from a cloudy lens, not distorted vertical lines.
Diabetic retinopathy
Diabetic retinopathy results from retinal blood vessel changes with hemorrhage and macular edema.

alt.q: What is the macula responsible for?
alt.a: Central vision
alt.ex: The macula is the specialized part of the retina responsible for central vision.
w: Peripheral vision
Loss of peripheral vision is associated with glaucoma and the optic nerve.
Focusing on near objects
Focusing on near objects is the lens’s accommodation, lost in presbyopia.
Producing tears
Tear glands, not the macula, produce tears.

items.q: Which description of a cataract is accurate?
items.a: Cloudy or opaque areas in the lens that cause glare and blurred vision, usually developing gradually without pain
items.ex: A cataract is clouding of the lens that interferes with light passage, causing glare and blurring and usually developing painlessly.
w: Increased pressure in the eye that damages the optic nerve and causes halos
This describes glaucoma, not a cataract.
Changes in retinal blood vessels that cause hemorrhage and macular edema
This describes diabetic retinopathy.
Too few tears produced by tear glands, causing itching and burning
This describes dry eyes.

alt.q: Ms. Long has a cataract in her left eye. Which symptoms should the nurse expect her to report?
alt.a: Blurred vision and problems with glare
alt.ex: Cataracts interfere with passage of light through the lens, causing glare and blurred vision.
w: Sudden eye pain with redness and tearing
Cataracts usually develop gradually without pain, redness, or tearing.
Loss of central vision with distorted vertical lines
These are signs of macular degeneration.
Numbness and tingling around the eye
Numbness and tingling describe peripheral neuropathy, not cataracts.

items.q: A patient had a stroke affecting the right hemisphere of the brain. Which finding should the nurse anticipate?
items.a: Inattention to and neglect of the left side
items.ex: A right-hemisphere stroke causes left-sided symptoms, which may include loss of half the visual field and left-sided neglect.
w: Difficulty with speech
Speech difficulty is typical of a left-hemisphere stroke.
Neglect of the right side of the body
Symptoms appear on the side opposite the affected hemisphere, so right-hemisphere damage affects the left.
Loss of sensation in both legs equally
Stroke affects extremities controlled by the affected area, not both sides equally.

alt.q: A patient’s stroke affected the left hemisphere of the brain. Which finding is most likely?
alt.a: Difficulty with speech and right-sided symptoms
alt.ex: A left-hemisphere stroke produces symptoms on the right side, such as difficulty with speech.
w: Neglect of the left visual field
Left-sided neglect follows a right-hemisphere stroke.
Left-sided weakness with visual-spatial alterations
Left-sided and visual-spatial changes follow right-hemisphere strokes.
No change in proprioception or coordination
Stroke can alter proprioception with marked incoordination and imbalance.

items.q: A patient has been on strict bed rest in a quiet private room for 2 weeks and reports boredom and restlessness. Which type of sensory deprivation does this represent?
items.a: A restrictive environment that produces monotony and boredom
items.ex: Restrictive environments such as bed rest are one of three types of sensory deprivation and produce monotony and boredom.
w: Reduced sensory input from visual or hearing loss
Reduced input refers to sensory deficits such as vision or hearing loss.
Elimination of patterns or meaning from input
This type refers to exposure to strange environments.
Excessive stimulation from multiple sources
Excessive stimulation causes overload, not deprivation.

alt.q: A patient is admitted to an unfamiliar hospital unit full of strange sights and sounds. Which type of sensory deprivation is the patient at risk for?
alt.a: Elimination of patterns or meaning from input
alt.ex: Exposure to strange environments removes the patterns and meaning from sensory input.
w: Reduced sensory input from vision or hearing loss
Reduced sensory input refers to a sensory deficit such as vision or hearing loss.
A restrictive environment such as bed rest
Restrictive environments such as bed rest produce monotony and boredom.
Sensory adaptation to a continued stimulus
Adaptation is the normal process of not noticing a continued stimulus.

items.q: An older adult with a neurocognitive disorder who is in a private isolation room becomes increasingly confused. Which nursing consideration is most appropriate?
items.a: Assess the patient’s existing sensory function and the quality of stimuli in the environment
items.ex: Deprivation symptoms resemble mental illness or electrolyte imbalance, and isolated older adults with neurocognitive disorders are prone to delirium.
w: Conclude that the patient is developing a new mental illness
Deprivation can mimic mental illness, so sensory function and stimuli must be assessed first.
Reduce stimulation further by darkening the room
Further reducing stimuli worsens deprivation in an isolated patient.
Attribute the confusion to normal aging
Confusion in this setting suggests deprivation-related delirium, not normal aging.

alt.q: Why must the nurse always be aware of a patient’s sensory function and environmental stimuli when an adult becomes confused?
alt.a: Deprivation symptoms resemble mental illness or electrolyte imbalance
alt.ex: Because deprivation can mimic other causes of confusion, assessing sensory function and stimuli prevents misinterpretation.
w: Sensory deprivation always causes permanent cognitive damage
The text does not describe deprivation effects as always permanent.
Confusion in adults is caused only by sensory deficits
Confusion has other causes, such as electrolyte imbalance or psychotropic drugs.
Sensory deprivation occurs only in children
Deprivation affects adults, especially isolated older adults.

items.q: A patient in the critical care unit has racing thoughts, scattered attention, and anxiety and keeps pulling at the dressings and tubes. Which interpretation by the nurse is most accurate?
items.a: The patient is showing signs of sensory overload
items.ex: Racing thoughts, scattered attention, restlessness, anxiety, and playing with tubes and dressings are signs of sensory overload.
w: The patient is showing signs of sensory deprivation
The busy, stimulus-rich CCU setting and racing thoughts point to overload, not deprivation.
The patient is having simple mood swings
Overload behaviors are easily confused with mood swings, so the nurse should look for overload signs.
The patient has a new sensory deficit
A deficit is a loss of reception and perception, not racing thoughts and scattered attention.

alt.q: Which nursing measures become important parts of care for a patient experiencing sensory overload?
alt.a: Constant reorientation and control of excessive stimuli
alt.ex: The text states that constant reorientation and control of excessive stimuli are important in caring for patients with overload.
w: Adding more stimuli to hold the patient’s attention
More stimuli worsen overload.
Leaving the patient alone for long periods without contact
Overload calls for reorientation and stimulus control, not isolation.
Increasing the frequency of bedside assessments
Frequent monitoring and bedside assessment add to overload risk.

items.q: How does sensory overload differ from sensory deprivation?
items.a: Overload is individualized; the stimuli needed for health vary by person
items.ex: In contrast to deprivation, overload is individualized; tolerance varies with fatigue, attitude, and emotional and physical well-being.
w: Overload produces a state completely unlike deprivation
Overload causes a state similar to sensory deprivation.
Overload occurs only in patients with sensory deficits
Overload can occur in anyone who cannot selectively ignore multiple stimuli.
Overload depends only on the loudness of the environment
Tolerance varies with fatigue, attitude, and emotional and physical well-being.

alt.q: Which factor influences a person’s tolerance to sensory overload?
alt.a: The person’s level of fatigue
alt.ex: Tolerance to sensory overload varies with fatigue, attitude, and emotional and physical well-being.
w: The person’s eye color
Eye color is not a factor in tolerance to overload.
The number of sensory receptors the person has
Tolerance depends on fatigue, attitude, and well-being, not receptor count.
The person’s height and weight
Height and weight are not named as influences on overload tolerance.

items.q: Why are patients able to receive sensory stimuli even while sleeping deeply?
items.a: The reticular activating system in the brainstem mediates all sensory stimuli to the cerebral cortex
items.ex: Because the reticular activating system mediates all sensory stimuli to the cortex, patients receive stimuli even in deep sleep.
w: The eighth cranial nerve remains active only during sleep
The eighth cranial nerve carries hearing impulses awake or asleep; the RAS explains reception during sleep.
The cerebral cortex stores all stimuli until the person awakens
Storage is one way the brain prevents bombardment, not the reason stimuli are received in sleep.
Sensory receptors become more sensitive during sleep
The text attributes reception during sleep to the reticular activating system.

alt.q: Which structure mediates all sensory stimuli to the cerebral cortex?
alt.a: The reticular activating system
alt.ex: The reticular activating system in the brainstem mediates all sensory stimuli to the cerebral cortex.
w: The organ of Corti
The organ of Corti contains hearing receptors only.
The optic nerve
The optic nerve carries visual impulses only.
The membranous labyrinth
The labyrinth contains the end organs of hearing and balance.

items.q: Which behavior by a patient with a hearing impairment is a maladaptive response to the sensory deficit?
items.a: Avoiding social gatherings out of embarrassment
items.ex: Withdrawing from people out of embarrassment is the book’s example of a maladaptive response to hearing loss.
w: Turning the unaffected ear toward the speaker
Turning the better ear toward the speaker is an adaptive behavior.
Relying more on vision to follow conversations
Relying on unaffected senses is an adaptive response.
Asking others to face the patient when speaking
Seeking face-to-face communication helps the patient hear and is adaptive.

alt.q: Which behavior by a patient with a hearing impairment is an adaptive response to the deficit?
alt.a: Turning the unaffected ear toward the speaker to hear better
alt.ex: Turning the unaffected ear toward the speaker is the book’s example of adapting to a hearing deficit.
w: Avoiding people because of embarrassment
Avoiding people is a maladaptive response.
Refusing to communicate with family members
Withdrawing from communication is maladaptive.
Staying home from social events to hide the loss
Avoiding socialization is a maladaptive coping response.

items.ex: Box 49.1 lists common visual, hearing, taste, and neurological deficits and how each affects the person.
w: Inability to see distant objects clearly

Common progressive hearing disorder in older adults

Hardened earwax in the canal causing conduction deafness
