items.q: Which findings are effects of sensory deprivation? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced capacity to learn
Reduced learning capacity is a cognitive effect of sensory deprivation.
Disorientation and confusion
Disorientation and confusion are cognitive effects of deprivation.
Emotional lability
Emotional lability is an affective effect of deprivation.
Reduced color perception
Reduced color perception is a perceptual effect of deprivation.
Increased tactile accuracy
Deprivation produces less tactile accuracy, not more.
Improved problem solving
Deprivation causes inability to think or problem solve.
items.ex: Box 49.2 groups deprivation effects as cognitive, affective, and perceptual, all reflecting worsened function.

alt.q: A patient has been isolated for a long period. Which findings would the nurse recognize as affective effects of sensory deprivation? Select all that apply.
o: Boredom
Boredom is an affective effect of deprivation.
Increased anxiety
Increased anxiety is an affective effect of deprivation.
Depression
Depression is an affective effect of deprivation.
Changes in spatial and time judgment
Changes in spatial and time judgment are perceptual effects.
Poor task performance
Poor task performance is a cognitive effect.
alt.ex: Affective effects of deprivation include boredom, restlessness, anxiety, emotional lability, depression, and panic.

items.q: Which patients does the chapter identify as at risk for sensory overload? Select all that apply.
o: A patient in an emergency room for an acute illness
Acutely ill patients in an emergency room easily experience overload.
A patient with dementia
Patients with dementia are at risk for sensory overload.
A patient who is in constant pain
Constant pain places a patient at risk for overload.
A patient who requires frequent monitoring and bedside assessment
Frequent monitoring and bedside assessment add stimuli that can cause overload.
A patient on prolonged bed rest in a quiet private room
A quiet, restrictive environment places a patient at risk for deprivation.
A patient with a gradual, long-standing hearing loss
A gradual hearing loss is a sensory deficit, and the person usually learns to rely on other senses.
items.ex: Acute illness in busy settings, dementia, constant pain, and frequent monitoring all increase the risk of overload.

alt.q: A nurse in a critical care unit lists sources of stimuli that contribute to sensory overload. Which items belong on the list? Select all that apply.
o: Lights that are usually left on
In a CCU the lights are usually on, adding to overload.
Sounds from monitoring equipment and alarms
Monitor sounds and equipment alarms contribute to overload.
Staff conversations
Staff conversations add to the constant activity in a CCU.
A monotonous environment with little activity
A monotonous environment leads to deprivation, not overload.
Absence of visitors
Absence of visitors contributes to isolation and deprivation.
alt.ex: Constant lighting, equipment sounds and alarms, staff talk, and people entering the unit combine to cause overload in a CCU.

items.q: Which behaviors suggest that a patient is experiencing sensory overload? Select all that apply.
o: Racing thoughts
Racing thoughts are a symptom of sensory overload.
Scattered attention
In overload, attention scatters in many directions.
Restlessness and anxiety
Anxiety and restlessness occur with overload.
Constantly playing with tubes and dressings
Some patients in overload constantly play with tubes and dressings.
An increased need for physical stimulation
An increased need for physical stimulation is an effect of deprivation.
Boredom from a monotonous setting
Boredom from monotony reflects sensory deprivation.
items.ex: Overload causes racing thoughts, scattered attention, restlessness, anxiety, and fidgeting with tubes and dressings.

alt.q: A nurse suspects a patient has sensory deprivation rather than overload. Which findings support deprivation? Select all that apply.
o: Boredom
Boredom is an affective effect of deprivation.
Increased need for socialization
An increased need for socialization is a cognitive effect of deprivation.
Increased need for physical stimulation
An increased need for physical stimulation is an affective effect of deprivation.
Racing thoughts in a busy environment
Racing thoughts amid many stimuli suggest overload.
Playing with tubes in a noisy unit
Fidgeting with tubes in a noisy setting suggests overload.
alt.ex: Deprivation produces boredom and increased needs for socialization and stimulation, whereas overload produces racing thoughts and fidgeting.

items.q: When a sensory deficit develops gradually, some of a person’s other senses may become more acute to compensate.
items.a: True
items.ex: A person learns to rely on unaffected senses, and some senses become more acute, as with heightened hearing in a person who is blind.
items.ww: The book gives the example of a person who is blind developing an acute sense of hearing.

alt.q: When a sensory deficit develops gradually, a person tends to rely less on the unaffected senses.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: With a gradual deficit, a person learns to rely more on unaffected senses, which may become more acute.
alt.ww: The person relies more, not less, on unaffected senses to compensate for the loss.

items.q: Patients are unable to receive any sensory stimuli while sleeping deeply.
items.a: False
items.ex: The reticular activating system mediates all sensory stimuli to the cortex, so patients receive stimuli even in deep sleep.
items.ww: The chapter states that patients receive stimuli even while sleeping deeply.

alt.q: Because the reticular activating system mediates sensory stimuli to the cortex, patients can receive stimuli even while sleeping deeply.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The reticular activating system allows stimuli to reach the cortex even during deep sleep.
alt.ww: Saying sleep blocks all stimuli ignores the role of the reticular activating system.

items.q: Sensory overload produces a state similar to sensory deprivation.
items.a: True
items.ex: Because overload prevents meaningful response by the brain, it causes a state similar to sensory deprivation.
items.ww: Although caused by too many stimuli, overload leads to a state resembling deprivation.

alt.q: Because sensory overload is the opposite of deprivation, its effects on a patient bear no resemblance to deprivation.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Overload prevents meaningful response by the brain and causes a state similar to deprivation.
alt.ww: The textbook states overload causes a state similar to deprivation, not an unrelated one.

items.q: Sensory [[overload]] occurs when a person receives multiple stimuli and cannot perceptually disregard or selectively ignore some of them.
items.ex: Excessive stimulation prevents the brain from ignoring stimuli, so the person cannot make sense of the environment.

alt.q: A patient in a noisy critical care unit who cannot selectively ignore the many alarms and voices is experiencing sensory [[overload]].
alt.ex: Excessive stimulation prevents the brain from ignoring stimuli, so the person cannot make sense of the environment.

items.q: Which sounds are easiest for an older adult with age-related hearing changes to hear?
items.a: Low-pitched vowel sounds
items.ex: Low-pitched sounds and low-pitched vowels are easiest for older adults to hear.
w: High-frequency sounds such as s, sh, ph, and k
High-frequency sounds are difficult for older adults to hear.
Consonants such as z, t, f, and g
These consonants are difficult for older adults to discriminate.
Conversation over background noise
Hearing conversation over background noise is difficult with aging.

alt.q: Which sounds are most difficult for an older adult with age-related hearing changes to hear?
alt.a: High-frequency sounds such as s, sh, ph, and k
alt.ex: Aging makes high-frequency sounds and certain consonants difficult to hear and discriminate.
w: Low-pitched vowel sounds
Low-pitched vowels are the easiest sounds for older adults to hear.
Low-pitched tones such as a buzzer
Low-pitched sounds are easiest to hear.
Slow, low-pitched speech in a quiet room
Low pitch and a quiet setting make speech easier to hear.

items.q: An older adult answers questions inappropriately and seems inattentive, and the family worries about dementia. Which nursing consideration is most important?
items.a: Assess the patient’s hearing, because age-related sensory deficits are sometimes mistaken for dementia
items.ex: Older adults with normal age-related sensory deficits are sometimes inappropriately diagnosed with dementia.
w: Reassure the family that these behaviors are expected with dementia
Concluding dementia without assessing hearing risks a wrong diagnosis.
Avoid speaking with the patient to reduce stimulation
Avoiding communication would increase isolation and not clarify the cause.
Explain that hearing does not change until after age 70
Hearing changes begin as early as age 30.

alt.q: Why is it a concern when an older adult has normal age-related sensory changes?
alt.a: The older adult with a deficit is sometimes inappropriately diagnosed with dementia
alt.ex: Age-related deficits can mimic cognitive impairment, so older adults may be misdiagnosed with dementia.
w: Sensory changes always lead to permanent blindness or deafness
Normal age-related changes do not always lead to total loss.
Sensory changes prevent the use of hearing aids or glasses
Assistive devices can help with age-related changes.
Sensory changes occur only in patients with dementia
Sensory changes are normal with aging and occur without dementia.

items.q: Which age-related eye changes increase the risk of glaucoma?
items.a: Loss of pigment from the iris and buildup of collagen fibers in the anterior chamber
items.ex: These changes decrease resorption of intraocular fluid, which increases the risk of glaucoma.
w: A flatter, thicker cornea that alters light refraction
A flatter, thicker cornea often leads to astigmatism.
A decline in the lens’s ability to focus on near objects
This is presbyopia, the need for reading glasses.
A decrease in the number of sensory cells in the nasal lining
This is an olfactory change, not an eye change.

alt.q: A buildup of collagen fibers in the anterior chamber of an older adult’s eye increases the risk of glaucoma. What is the reason?
alt.a: It decreases the resorption of intraocular fluid
alt.ex: Collagen buildup and iris pigment loss decrease resorption of intraocular fluid, raising glaucoma risk.
w: It flattens and thickens the cornea
Corneal flattening and thickening lead to astigmatism.
It clouds the lens and causes glare
Lens clouding describes a cataract.
It damages the macula and central vision
Loss of central vision describes macular degeneration.

items.q: During adulthood the cornea becomes flatter and thicker. Which visual problem often results?
items.a: Astigmatism
items.ex: The aging cornea, which helps refract light to the retina, becomes flatter and thicker, often leading to astigmatism.
w: Glaucoma
Glaucoma risk rises from iris pigment loss and collagen buildup in the anterior chamber.
Macular degeneration
Macular degeneration is loss of central vision from the macula.
Cataract
A cataract is clouding of the lens.

alt.q: Which age-related change commonly leads to astigmatism?
alt.a: The cornea becomes flatter and thicker
alt.ex: A flatter, thicker cornea alters light refraction to the retina and often leads to astigmatism.
w: Pigment is lost from the iris
Iris pigment loss contributes to glaucoma risk.
The lens loses its ability to focus on near objects
Loss of near focus is presbyopia.
Taste buds decrease in number
Fewer taste buds is a gustatory change.

items.q: A nurse assesses the environment of a hospitalized patient. Which finding most likely contributes to sensory overload?
items.a: A roommate who keeps the television on and the lights on constantly
items.ex: A roommate who constantly watches television, persistently talks, or keeps lights on contributes to sensory overload.
w: Pictures of family members on the bedside table
Family pictures are meaningful stimuli that reduce deprivation.
A calendar and clock on the wall
A calendar and clock are meaningful stimuli recommended in health care settings.
Short daily visits from the patient’s spouse
The presence of visitors offers positive stimulation.

alt.q: Which items in a patient’s hospital room provide meaningful stimuli that reduce the incidence of sensory deprivation?
alt.a: A calendar, a clock, and pictures of family members
alt.ex: Meaningful stimuli such as pictures of family, a calendar, and a clock should be present in health care settings.
w: A roommate’s television playing all day
A constantly playing television contributes to overload.
Lights left on all night
Continuous lighting contributes to overload.
A bed placed next to the elevator
Repetitive noise from an elevator contributes to overload.

items.q: Which patient is at greatest risk for sensory overload?
items.a: A patient in skeletal traction with pain whose room is next to the nurses’ station
items.ex: Pain, restriction by traction, and a room near loud or repetitive noise all contribute to overstimulation.
w: An ambulatory patient in a quiet private room far from the nurses’ station
A quiet room without pain or restriction poses little overload risk.
A patient awaiting discharge who walks in the halls with family
This patient has no listed overload factors such as pain, traction, or noise.
A patient on bed rest in an isolation room with few visitors
Isolation with few visitors places a patient at risk for deprivation.

alt.q: Which room location places a hospitalized patient at greater risk for sensory overload?
alt.a: A room next to an elevator or stairwell
alt.ex: A room near repetitive or loud noises, such as an elevator, stairwell, or nurses’ station, contributes to overload.
w: A room at the quiet end of the hall
A quiet location reduces overload risk.
A room with a window view of a garden
A window view is not a source of excessive stimuli.
A private room with the door closed
A closed private room reduces noise rather than adding to it.

items.q: Which patient should the nurse identify as needing screening for noise-induced hearing loss?
items.a: An airport ground crew worker
items.ex: Occupations with high noise levels, such as factory or airport work, carry a risk for noise-induced hearing loss.
w: A welder
Welders are at risk for eye injuries from chemicals or flying objects.
An office worker who types all day
Repetitive wrist movements put this worker at risk for carpal tunnel syndrome.
A school librarian
A quiet library is not an occupation with high noise exposure.

alt.q: Which worker should the nurse identify as needing screening for visual impairment because of the risk of eye injury?
alt.a: A welder exposed to flying objects and chemicals
alt.ex: Occupations with exposure to chemicals or flying objects, such as welding, place workers at risk for eye injuries.
w: A factory worker exposed to loud machinery
Loud machinery places the worker at risk for hearing loss.
An assembly line worker doing repetitive wrist motions
Repetitive wrist motion causes carpal tunnel syndrome.
An airport worker near jet engines
Airport noise places a worker at risk for hearing loss.

items.q: According to the chapter, blindness from glaucoma is about how many times more common in African Americans than in people of other ethnicities?
items.a: About 6 times
items.ex: Blindness from glaucoma is about six times more common in African Americans than in those from other ethnicities.
w: About 2 times
The book states about six times, not two.
About 10 times
The book states about six times, not ten.
About 3 times
The book states about six times, not three.

alt.q: Which population has about six times the rate of blindness from glaucoma compared with other ethnicities?
alt.a: African Americans
alt.ex: Blindness from glaucoma is about six times more common in African Americans.
w: Non-Hispanic White Americans
The higher glaucoma blindness rate is reported in African Americans.
Asian Americans
The text identifies African Americans as having the higher rate.
American Indians
American Indians are named as having higher rates of diabetic retinopathy, not glaucoma blindness.

items.q: Which statement about disparities in eye care is accurate according to the chapter?
items.a: Hispanic and Black patients have fewer outpatient ophthalmic visits than non-Hispanic White patients
items.ex: Box 49.3 reports fewer outpatient ophthalmic visits among Hispanic and Black patients, complicating preventive care and treatment.
w: Hispanic and Black patients have more outpatient ophthalmic visits than non-Hispanic White patients
The disparity runs the other way; they have fewer visits.
Children in states with more Medicaid-insured patients have shorter waits for eye surgery
These children experience extended wait times for visits and surgery.
Diabetic retinopathy is less common in American Indians than in other populations
American Indians are more likely to have diabetes and diabetic retinopathy.

alt.q: Which populations are more likely to have diabetes and diabetic retinopathy, according to Box 49.3?
alt.a: Hispanics, American Indians, and African Americans
alt.ex: These populations are more likely to have diabetes and diabetic retinopathy, yet not all receive needed vision services.
w: Non-Hispanic White Americans only
Box 49.3 names Hispanics, American Indians, and African Americans.
Children younger than 5 years
Children are discussed regarding wait times, not diabetic retinopathy rates.
Adults with private insurance only
Insurance type is not named as a risk factor for diabetic retinopathy.

items.q: A patient in an intensive care unit with restricted visiting becomes withdrawn and anxious. Which explanation is most accurate?
items.a: The absence of meaningful conversation with loved ones leads to isolation, loneliness, anxiety, and depression
items.ex: Restricted visiting removes an important coping mechanism, and the lack of meaningful conversation causes isolation, anxiety, and depression.
w: Visitor restrictions reduce stimuli and therefore protect against sensory alterations
Absent visitors increase isolation and contribute to deprivation.
Withdrawal is a normal part of critical illness that needs no attention
Behavioral changes signal the effects of isolation and need attention.
The patient’s anxiety is caused only by the medical condition
The amount and quality of social contact also influence sensory function.

alt.q: Why is the ability to discuss concerns with loved ones important to a patient’s sensory function?
alt.a: It is an important coping mechanism, and its absence results in isolation and loneliness
alt.ex: Discussing concerns with loved ones helps people cope, and its absence causes isolation, loneliness, anxiety, and depression.
w: It increases stimuli to the point of sensory overload
Supportive social contact is a positive influence, not a cause of overload.
It has little effect because sensory function depends only on the sense organs
The amount and quality of social contact influence sensory function.
It replaces the need for meaningful stimuli in the room
Social contact and meaningful stimuli both matter.

items.q: A nurse cares for a toddler who was born with a hearing deficit and lives at home with the parents. What should the nurse focus on first?
items.a: Assessing the toddler’s safety risks as the child becomes more mobile
items.ex: For this toddler, the nurse focuses on assessing safety risks, then helping the family adapt the home environment.
w: Helping the toddler accept the need to start wearing hearing aids
Acceptance of hearing aids is the focus for an older adult with new-onset hearing loss.
Determining whether Medicare will pay for hearing aids
Medicare coverage is a concern for the older adult example.
Referring the parents for a fireworks safety class
This is not the focus described for the toddler with a hearing deficit.

alt.q: A nurse cares for an older adult with new-onset, age-related hearing loss. What is the nurse’s focus?
alt.a: Helping the patient accept the need for hearing aids and work out how to pay for them
alt.ex: For new age-related hearing loss, the nurse helps the patient accept hearing aids and determine coverage or costs.
w: Assessing safety risks as the patient becomes more mobile
This focus applies to the toddler with a congenital hearing deficit.
Teaching the patient sign language as the first step
The chapter’s example focuses on hearing aid acceptance and cost.
Placing the patient in a quiet private room
Room placement is not the focus described for this patient.

items.q: Which hospitalized patient is at greatest risk for sensory deprivation?
items.a: A patient in a private isolation room after a bone marrow transplant
items.ex: Patients isolated for immunocompromise are in private rooms and often cannot enjoy normal interactions with visitors.
w: A patient in a semi-private room with frequent family visits
Frequent visits provide positive stimulation.
A patient with pain in traction near the nurses’ station
Pain, traction, and noise place this patient at risk for overload.
A patient in the emergency department with an acute illness
Acutely ill patients in an emergency department are at risk for overload.

alt.q: Why are patients isolated for active tuberculosis at risk for sensory alterations?
alt.a: They are in private rooms and often cannot enjoy normal interactions with visitors
alt.ex: Isolated patients are in private rooms and lack normal interactions with visitors, which places them at risk.
w: Tuberculosis directly damages the eighth cranial nerve
The risk described comes from isolation, not nerve damage.
Isolation rooms are usually louder than other rooms
The concern is lack of interaction, not added noise.
Isolated patients receive more frequent bedside assessments
The text links isolation to lack of normal social contact.

items.q: Which visual changes are normal with aging? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced visual fields
Reduced visual fields are a normal age-related visual change.
Increased glare sensitivity
Older adults are more sensitive to glare.
Impaired night vision
Impaired night vision is a normal aging change.
Reduced depth perception
Depth perception declines with aging.
Enhanced color discrimination
Color discrimination is reduced, not enhanced, with aging.
Sharper near vision after age 40
Presbyopia reduces near vision, usually from ages 40 to 50.
items.ex: Normal aging reduces visual fields, depth perception, and color discrimination and increases glare sensitivity and night vision problems.

alt.q: An older adult asks which vision changes are expected with age. Which changes should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Needing glasses for reading
Presbyopia and the need for reading glasses usually occur from ages 40 to 50.
Reduced color discrimination
Color discrimination declines with aging.
More difficulty with glare
Glare sensitivity increases with aging.
Wider visual fields
Visual fields are reduced with aging.
Improved vision in the dark
Night vision is impaired with aging.
alt.ex: Expected age-related changes include presbyopia, reduced color discrimination, glare sensitivity, and impaired night vision.

items.q: Which recreational activities can weaken hearing ability? Select all that apply.
o: Target shooting
Target shooting is a noisy activity that weakens hearing.
Hunting
Hunting involves loud noise that can weaken hearing.
Woodworking
Woodworking is named as a noisy recreational activity.
Listening to loud music
Loud music weakens hearing ability.
Watercolor painting
Painting is not a noisy activity that harms hearing.
Reading in a quiet library
A quiet setting does not expose a person to hazardous noise.
items.ex: Target shooting, hunting, woodworking, and loud music are noisy recreational activities that weaken hearing.

alt.q: Which activities place a person at risk for eye injury? Select all that apply.
o: Using consumer fireworks
Consumer fireworks place individuals at risk for eye injuries.
Playing sports
Sports activities place individuals at risk for eye injuries.
Welding
Welders are exposed to chemicals or flying objects.
Listening to music through speakers at moderate volume
This is not a risk for eye injury.
Taking a quiet walk in the park
A quiet walk carries no listed risk for eye injury.
alt.ex: Sports, consumer fireworks, and jobs with flying objects or chemicals such as welding place people at risk for eye injuries.

items.q: A nurse plans to make a hospital room more meaningful for a patient at risk for sensory deprivation. Which items are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Pictures of family members
Family pictures are meaningful stimuli.
A calendar and a clock
A calendar and clock provide meaningful stimuli and orientation.
The patient’s favorite music
Music is listed among meaningful stimuli.
Visits from family and friends
The presence of others offers positive stimulation.
A roommate who persistently tries to talk
A roommate who talks persistently contributes to overload.
A bed near the noisy stairwell for more activity
Repetitive noise from a stairwell contributes to overload.
items.ex: Meaningful stimuli such as family pictures, music, a calendar, a clock, and visitors reduce deprivation and promote alertness.

alt.q: Which factors in the hospital environment contribute to sensory overload? Select all that apply.
o: Frequent observations and numerous procedures
Frequent observations and many procedures are often stressful and overstimulating.
A room near the elevator
Repetitive noise from an elevator contributes to overload.
A roommate who keeps lights on continuously
Continuous lighting from a roommate contributes to overload.
A family photograph on the windowsill
Family photographs are meaningful stimuli that reduce deprivation.
A wall calendar
A calendar is a meaningful stimulus.
alt.ex: Frequent procedures, nearby noise, and a disruptive roommate add excessive stimuli and contribute to overload.

items.q: Proprioceptive changes after age 60 include decreased balance and a reduced automatic response to brace oneself when falling.
items.a: True
items.ex: After 60, proprioceptive changes reduce balance, spatial orientation, coordination, and the protective bracing response, increasing fall risk.
items.ww: These changes are common after 60 and increase the risk of falling.

alt.q: Age-related proprioceptive changes result only from changes in the peripheral nervous system.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Proprioceptive changes after 60 result from changes in both the peripheral and central nervous systems.
alt.ww: The central nervous system also contributes, not only the peripheral system.

items.q: The prevalence of age-related macular degeneration is lower for non-Hispanic African American people than for other ethnic or racial groups.
items.a: True
items.ex: National survey data showed lower prevalence of age-related macular degeneration in non-Hispanic African American people.
items.ww: African Americans have higher rates of glaucoma blindness, but lower rates of macular degeneration.

alt.q: Age-related macular degeneration is more prevalent among non-Hispanic African American people than among other groups.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: AMD prevalence was lower for non-Hispanic African American people than for other groups.
alt.ww: This confuses AMD with glaucoma, for which African Americans have higher blindness rates.

items.q: Early intense visual and auditory stimulation can adversely affect the visual and auditory pathways of high-risk neonates.
items.a: True
items.ex: In high-risk neonates, early intense stimulation can harm visual and auditory pathways and alter other sensory organ development.
items.ww: The book warns that intense early stimulation can harm, not help, these pathways.

alt.q: Intense visual and auditory stimulation early in life promotes healthy development of sensory pathways in high-risk neonates.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Early intense stimulation can adversely affect visual and auditory pathways in high-risk neonates.
alt.ww: The chapter describes harm, not benefit, from intense early stimulation.

items.q: At what age does the following usually begin: Hearing changes?
items.a: About age 30
items.ex: Hearing changes begin first, around 30; presbyopia appears at 40 to 50; taste and smell around 50; proprioception after 60.
w: Ages 40 to 50
That goes with Presbyopia and need for reading glasses.
About age 50
That goes with Taste and smell changes.
After age 60
That goes with Proprioceptive changes.

alt.q: At what age does the following usually begin: Presbyopia and need for reading glasses?
alt.a: Ages 40 to 50
alt.ex: Hearing changes begin first, around 30; presbyopia appears at 40 to 50; taste and smell around 50; proprioception after 60.
w: About age 30
That goes with Hearing changes.
About age 50
That goes with Taste and smell changes.
After age 60
That goes with Proprioceptive changes.

alt.q: At what age does the following usually begin: Taste and smell changes?
alt.a: About age 50
alt.ex: Hearing changes begin first, around 30; presbyopia appears at 40 to 50; taste and smell around 50; proprioception after 60.
w: About age 30
That goes with Hearing changes.
Ages 40 to 50
That goes with Presbyopia and need for reading glasses.
After age 60
That goes with Proprioceptive changes.

alt.q: At what age does the following usually begin: Proprioceptive changes?
alt.a: After age 60
alt.ex: Hearing changes begin first, around 30; presbyopia appears at 40 to 50; taste and smell around 50; proprioception after 60.
w: About age 30
That goes with Hearing changes.
Ages 40 to 50
That goes with Presbyopia and need for reading glasses.
About age 50
That goes with Taste and smell changes.

alt.q: Which age-related change usually begins at “About age 30”?
alt.a: Hearing changes
alt.ex: Hearing changes begin first, around 30; presbyopia appears at 40 to 50; taste and smell around 50; proprioception after 60.
w: Presbyopia and need for reading glasses
Presbyopia and need for reading glasses: Ages 40 to 50.
Taste and smell changes
Taste and smell changes: About age 50.
Proprioceptive changes
Proprioceptive changes: After age 60.

alt.q: Which age-related change usually begins at “Ages 40 to 50”?
alt.a: Presbyopia and need for reading glasses
alt.ex: Hearing changes begin first, around 30; presbyopia appears at 40 to 50; taste and smell around 50; proprioception after 60.
w: Hearing changes
Hearing changes: About age 30.
Taste and smell changes
Taste and smell changes: About age 50.
Proprioceptive changes
Proprioceptive changes: After age 60.

alt.q: Which age-related change usually begins at “About age 50”?
alt.a: Taste and smell changes
alt.ex: Hearing changes begin first, around 30; presbyopia appears at 40 to 50; taste and smell around 50; proprioception after 60.
w: Hearing changes
Hearing changes: About age 30.
Presbyopia and need for reading glasses
Presbyopia and need for reading glasses: Ages 40 to 50.
Proprioceptive changes
Proprioceptive changes: After age 60.

alt.q: Which age-related change usually begins at “After age 60”?
alt.a: Proprioceptive changes
alt.ex: Hearing changes begin first, around 30; presbyopia appears at 40 to 50; taste and smell around 50; proprioception after 60.
w: Hearing changes
Hearing changes: About age 30.
Presbyopia and need for reading glasses
Presbyopia and need for reading glasses: Ages 40 to 50.
Taste and smell changes
Taste and smell changes: About age 50.

mt.q: Match each age-related sensory change with the age at which it usually begins.
pairs: Presbyopia and need for reading glasses
mt.ex: Hearing changes begin first, around 30; presbyopia appears at 40 to 50; taste and smell around 50; proprioception after 60.

items.q: Repetitive wrist or finger movements put pressure on the [[median]] nerve, resulting in carpal tunnel syndrome.
items.ex: The median nerve runs from the forearm into the palm; repetitive motion compresses it and alters tactile sensation.

alt.q: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from pressure on the [[median]] nerve, which runs from the forearm into the palm of the hand.
alt.ex: The median nerve runs from the forearm into the palm; repetitive motion compresses it and alters tactile sensation.

items.q: A nurse is speaking with an older adult who has a hearing impairment, and the patient is struggling to understand. The nurse needs to raise the voice. Which technique is best?
items.a: Speak in lower tones rather than shouting
items.ex: Loud sounds are higher pitched and conceal consonants, so if you must raise your voice, speak in lower tones.
w: Shout so that every word is clearly heard
Shouting raises pitch, accentuates vowels, and conceals consonants, impeding hearing.
Speak in a higher-pitched voice
Higher-pitched sounds are harder for older adults with hearing loss to hear.
Speak from the doorway so the voice carries
Speaking from another room or at a distance makes hearing harder.

alt.q: Why should a nurse avoid shouting at a patient with a hearing impairment?
alt.a: Loud sounds are higher pitched and conceal consonants
alt.ex: Shouting accentuates vowel sounds and conceals consonants, which impedes hearing.
w: Loud sounds damage hearing aids
The text explains shouting impedes hearing by distorting pitch.
Patients with hearing loss hear only whispers
Patients with hearing loss do not hear only whispers; lower tones help.
Loud sounds cause sensory deprivation
Shouting distorts speech sounds; it does not cause deprivation.

items.q: A patient with expressive aphasia after a stroke understands questions but cannot answer them in words. Which nursing approach is most appropriate?
items.a: Ask questions that require simple yes-or-no answers and offer a communication board
items.ex: For patients who have problems speaking, ask yes-or-no questions and offer pictures or a communication board for pointing.
w: Speak loudly so the patient can process the question
Aphasia is not hearing loss, so loud speech is not helpful.
Use childish phrases to keep messages simple
Patronizing and childish phrases should be avoided.
Ask several open-ended questions at once
Multiple open-ended questions require speech the patient cannot produce and add pressure.

alt.q: A patient with aphasia has trouble comprehending what is said. Which approach should the nurse use?
alt.a: Use simple, short questions and facial gestures to give additional clues
alt.ex: For comprehension problems, simple short questions and facial gestures provide additional clues.
w: Speak loudly and quickly to hold the patient’s attention
Speak slowly and do not shout; hearing loss is not the problem.
Avoid talking about familiar topics
Speaking of familiar things of interest to the patient is recommended.
Hurry the patient to answer before fatigue sets in
Give the patient time and do not pressure or tire the patient.

items.q: A patient who is deaf uses sign language as the preferred method of communication and needs intravenous (IV) therapy. Which action by the nurse is appropriate?
items.a: Avoid placing IV lines in both of the patient’s hands
items.ex: Do not restrict the hands of a patient who is deaf; never have IV lines in both hands if sign language is preferred.
w: Place IV lines in both hands so either can be used for infusions
IV lines in both hands restrict signing, the patient’s means of communication.
Restrain the patient’s hands to protect the IV sites
Restricting the hands prevents communication by sign language.
Communicate only by shouting while the IV is in place
Shouting impedes hearing and does not replace sign language.

alt.q: Which practice supports communication for a patient who is deaf and communicates by sign language?
alt.a: Keeping the patient’s hands free and unrestricted
alt.ex: Patients who sign need free hands, so the nurse avoids restricting them or placing IV lines in both hands.
w: Inserting IV lines in both hands
IV lines in both hands prevent signing.
Speaking from another room
Speaking from another room should be avoided.
Approaching from behind to avoid distraction
Approaching from behind startles the patient; get the patient’s attention first.

items.q: A patient receiving gentamicin reports new ringing in the ears and difficulty hearing. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
items.a: Report the findings, because gentamicin is ototoxic and can permanently damage the auditory nerve
items.ex: Some antibiotics, including gentamicin, streptomycin, and tobramycin, are ototoxic and permanently damage the auditory nerve.
w: Reassure the patient that the symptoms are expected and harmless
Ototoxic damage can be permanent, so the finding must be reported.
Increase the volume of the television for the patient
This ignores a possible medication-related injury to hearing.
Irrigate the ear canal to remove cerumen
Assuming cerumen without addressing the ototoxic drug could miss permanent nerve damage.

alt.q: Which medication in a patient’s history is most important to note as a risk for permanent hearing damage?
alt.a: Tobramycin
alt.ex: Tobramycin, streptomycin, and gentamicin are ototoxic antibiotics that can permanently damage the auditory nerve.
w: Chloramphenicol
Chloramphenicol sometimes irritates the optic nerve, not the auditory nerve.
Acetaminophen
Acetaminophen is not named as an ototoxic drug.
Erythromycin ointment
Erythromycin ointment is used for newborn eye prophylaxis.

items.q: A patient completes the Revised Hearing Handicap Inventory–Screening (RHHI-S). How should the nurse interpret a high score?
items.a: The higher the score, the greater the handicapping effect of the hearing impairment
items.ex: The RHHI-S is a 10-item questionnaire on the social and emotional effects of hearing loss; higher scores mean greater handicap.
w: A high score means the patient’s hearing is excellent
A higher score reflects greater handicapping effects, not better hearing.
A high score means the patient has cerumen impaction
The RHHI-S measures perceived social and emotional effects, not cerumen.
A high score rules out the need for audiological intervention
The tool identifies patients who need audiological intervention.

alt.q: What does the RHHI-S measure?
alt.a: Perceived social and emotional effects of hearing loss
alt.ex: The 5-minute, 10-item RHHI-S assesses perceived social and emotional effects of hearing loss.
w: The pitch range of sounds a person can hear
Pitch testing is not what the RHHI-S assesses.
The amount of cerumen in the ear canal
Cerumen is assessed by inspecting the ear canal.
A person’s cognitive function
Cognitive function is assessed with tools such as the Mini-Mental State Examination.

items.q: A nurse orients a patient who is blind to a hospital room. Which action is most appropriate?
items.a: Have the patient walk the room touching walls; keep objects in place
items.ex: Patients who are blind establish direction by feeling room boundaries, and moved objects no longer exist for them, creating hazards.
w: Rearrange furniture daily to provide new sensory stimulation
Moving objects, even a chair, creates a safety hazard for a patient who is blind.
Approach from behind quietly to avoid disturbing the patient
Approach from the front to avoid startling the patient.
Describe the room once and expect the patient to remember it
Absorbing the room takes time, and the patient often needs reorientation.

alt.q: Why should the nurse keep all objects in the same position for a patient who is blind?
alt.a: A moved object no longer exists for the patient and becomes a hazard
alt.ex: Moving an object, even a chair, creates a safety hazard because the patient relies on knowing its location.
w: Moving objects causes sensory overload
The concern is safety from unknown object locations, not overload.
Patients who are blind cannot learn a new room arrangement
Patients can learn arrangements with time and explanation.
Agency policy forbids moving furniture
The rationale is patient safety, not policy.

items.q: A patient is being discharged from an outpatient surgery department after cataract removal. Which priority of care is most appropriate?
items.a: Learning about self-care restrictions
items.ex: The priority for a patient discharged after cataract removal is learning about self-care restrictions.
w: Reducing anxiety and preventing further injury to the eye
This is the priority for a patient entering the emergency department with eye trauma.
Long-term adaptation to permanent visual loss
Long-term goals apply to permanent loss, not routine cataract surgery discharge.
Frequent reorientation and pleasant stimuli such as a back rub
These are temporary measures for short-term overload in an ICU.

alt.q: Dilyana identifies Risk for Injury, Risk for Fall, Fear, and Anxiety for Ms. Long. Why are Risk for Injury and Risk for Fall her priority diagnoses?
alt.a: They directly affect Ms. Long’s safety, which is always a top priority
alt.ex: Safety is always a top priority, so diagnoses that directly affect safety come first.
w: They are the easiest diagnoses to resolve
Priority is based on safety, not ease.
Fear and Anxiety cannot be addressed by nursing
Fear and Anxiety are applicable diagnoses that also improve as safety improves.
Ms. Long did not express any fear
Ms. Long expressed fear of falling on the stairs and of losing her vision.

items.q: A patient in the intensive care unit is showing signs of sensory overload. Which intervention should the nurse implement?
items.a: Combine the dressing change, bath, and vital sign measurements in one visit
items.ex: Organizing care by combining activities in one visit conserves energy, prevents fatigue, and reduces sensory overload.
w: Spread care activities evenly across the shift to keep the patient engaged
Spreading activities increases interruptions and stimuli.
Leave suction and oxygen equipment running in case they are needed
Turn off bedside equipment not in use to minimize noise.
Keep the room lights on so the patient stays oriented
Dimming lights during quiet time reduces excessive stimuli.

alt.q: Which measures are part of a “quiet time” intervention on a hospital unit?
alt.a: Dimming the lights, closing the shades, and shutting the doors
alt.ex: “Quiet time” includes dimming lights throughout the unit, closing shades, and shutting doors.
w: Scheduling laboratory draws during the quiet period
Coordination with laboratory departments should minimize interruptions.
Turning up the television volume to mask noise
Added noise defeats the purpose of quiet time.
Holding staff conversations outside patient rooms
Staff need to control conversation outside rooms.

items.q: How often does the chapter state that individuals at higher risk for glaucoma should have a dilated eye examination?
items.a: Every 2 years
items.ex: Individuals at higher risk for glaucoma should have a dilated eye examination every 2 years.
w: Every year
Annual dilated eye examinations are recommended for people with diabetes mellitus.
Every 5 years
Every 5 years is too infrequent for those at higher risk.
Every 6 months
The recommended interval for higher-risk individuals is every 2 years.

alt.q: How often should a patient with diabetes mellitus have a dilated eye examination?
alt.a: Every year
alt.ex: People with diabetes mellitus are advised to have a dilated eye examination every year.
w: Every 2 years
Every 2 years applies to individuals at higher risk for glaucoma.
Every 5 years
Every 5 years is too infrequent for people with diabetes.
Only when vision changes occur
Routine annual examinations detect problems early.

items.q: A nurse teaches an office worker about preventing digital eyestrain. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?
items.a: “Every 20 minutes I will look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.”
items.ex: The 20-20-20 rule recommends a 20-second break to view something 20 feet away every 20 minutes.
w: “Every 20 minutes I will close my eyes for 2 minutes.”
The rule involves looking 20 feet away for 20 seconds, not closing the eyes.
“Every 2 hours I will look at something 20 feet away for 20 seconds.”
The distance break is every 20 minutes; the 15-minute rest is every 2 hours.
“Every 20 minutes I will look at something 2 feet away for 20 seconds.”
The rule calls for viewing something 20 feet away to allow refocusing.

alt.q: A patient who uses a computer all day asks how to position the screen. Which advice is consistent with the chapter?
alt.a: Place the screen 15 to 20 degrees below eye level and 20 to 28 inches from the eyes
alt.ex: Box 49.6 recommends a screen 15 to 20 degrees below eye level and 51 to 71 cm (20 to 28 inches) from the eyes.
w: Place the screen 15 to 20 degrees above eye level and 10 to 12 inches from the eyes
The screen belongs below eye level and farther away.
Place the screen at eye level and 40 to 48 inches from the eyes
The recommended distance is 20 to 28 inches, slightly below eye level.
Place the screen 30 to 40 degrees below eye level and 6 to 8 inches from the eyes
This angle is too steep and the screen too close.

items.q: A nurse evaluates whether teaching on hearing aid care has been effective. Which evaluation method is most effective?
items.a: Ask the patient to explain or demonstrate how to clean and check the hearing aid
items.ex: Asking a patient to explain or demonstrate self-care skills is an effective evaluative measure.
w: Assume learning occurred because the patient nodded during teaching
Smiling and nodding can mask a hearing deficit and do not confirm learning.
Ask the patient whether the teaching was interesting
Interest does not show whether the skill was learned.
Document that teaching was completed and end the plan
Evaluation must confirm learning before ending interventions.

alt.q: Who is the source for evaluating whether a patient’s sensory care expectations were met?
alt.a: The patient
alt.ex: Only patients can tell whether their sensory abilities are improving and which interventions are most successful.
w: The health care provider alone
The patient is the source for evaluating whether expectations were met.
The nurse’s observations alone
Observations help, but the nurse must ask the patient whether needs were met.
The agency’s quality improvement committee
The patient, not a committee, judges whether personal expectations were met.

items.q: Which techniques should the nurse use when communicating with a patient who has a hearing impairment? Select all that apply.
o: Rephrase rather than repeat when not understood
Rephrasing gives the patient different words to understand.
Talk toward the patient’s better ear
Speaking toward the better or normal ear improves hearing.
Keep hands away from the mouth with the face illuminated
A visible, well-lit face supports lipreading.
Make sure a hearing aid is in place and working
A working hearing aid is necessary for communication.
Approach the patient quietly from behind
Approaching from behind startles the patient; get the patient’s attention first.
Shout each word slowly and clearly
Shouting conceals consonants and impedes hearing.
items.ex: Get attention, face the patient in good light, use a working aid, speak toward the better ear, and rephrase.

alt.q: A family asks how to talk with a relative who has hearing loss. Which suggestions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.
o: Move away from background noise
Background noise makes it harder to hear.
Avoid dropping the voice at the end of a sentence
Keeping the voice up at sentence ends helps the person hear.
Speak slightly slower
People with hearing loss may need more time to process messages.
Speak while walking away to save time
Avoid speaking from another room or while walking away.
Repeat the same sentence louder each time
Rephrase rather than repeat, and do not shout.
alt.ex: Families should reduce background noise, speak slightly slower, keep the voice up, rephrase, and be patient.

items.q: A nurse assesses the home of a patient with sensory alterations. Which findings are safety hazards? Select all that apply.
o: Loose area rugs placed over carpeting
Loose rugs and runners are common trip hazards.
Extension cords in the main walking route
Cords in walking paths are hazards.
Water faucets not marked hot and cold
Unmarked faucets are a hazard, especially with reduced sensation.
Unlit stairways without handrails
Unlit stairways and lack of handrails are hazards.
Low-pile carpeting throughout the home
Low-pile carpeting is recommended for patients with visual alterations.
A handrail extending the full length of the stairs
A securely fastened full-length handrail is a recommended safety feature.
items.ex: Common home hazards include loose rugs, cords in pathways, unmarked faucets, missing grab bars, and poorly lit stairways.

alt.q: A nurse walks into a hospitalized patient’s room to check for safety hazards. Which findings require correction? Select all that apply.
o: The nurse call system is out of the patient’s reach
The call system must be within easy, safe reach.
The bedside table is cluttered
Bedside tables and areas should be clutter free.
A drainage bag is positioned so the patient cannot rise easily
Equipment should allow the patient to rise from bed or chair easily.
The pathway from the bed to the bathroom is clear
A clear path to the bathroom is the desired safe condition.
The IV pole is on wheels and easy to move
An easily moved IV pole on wheels is the desired condition.
alt.ex: In the hospital, check that the call system is reachable, areas are clutter free, and equipment and pathways allow safe movement.

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient and family caregiver about effective use of a hearing aid. Which instructions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Store batteries in a dry, secure place away from pets and children
Batteries should be stored dry and out of reach.
Clean the ear canal daily
Daily ear canal cleaning is part of hearing aid care.
Do not use hair spray while the hearing aid is in place
Hair products should not be used with the aid in place.
Report static or sound distortion to the hearing aid laboratory
Static, distortion, and poor volume should be reported.
Check the volume by turning the dial to its lowest setting
Volume is checked by turning the dial to maximum gain.
Discard spare batteries so old and new ones are not mixed
An extra set of unused batteries should be kept available.
items.ex: Box 49.7 teaches daily integrity checks, battery care, ear canal cleaning, avoiding hair products, and reporting problems.

alt.q: A patient asks how to check the volume of a hearing aid. Which steps and checks are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Turn the dial to maximum gain
Volume is checked by turning the dial to maximum gain.
Listen to see whether the voice is clear
The check confirms whether the voice is clear.
Inspect the earmold, cord, and connection plugs for cracks or fraying
Daily integrity checks include sites where damage is likely.
Turn the dial to the lowest setting and listen
The check uses maximum gain, not the lowest setting.
Spray the device with hair spray to protect it
Hair products should not be used with the hearing aid.
alt.ex: To check function, turn to maximum gain, confirm a clear voice, and inspect the parts most likely to be damaged.

items.q: When helping a patient with a visual impairment eat, the nurse arranges food according to the numbers on a clock face and uses the same arrangement each time.
items.a: True
items.ex: Arranging food by clock positions and being consistent each time helps patients with visual impairments eat independently.
items.ww: The book stresses consistency each time the clock method is used.

alt.q: When using the clock method for meals, the nurse should vary food positions at each meal to stimulate the patient’s cognition.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The nurse should be consistent each time the clock method is used.
alt.ww: Varying positions defeats the purpose of a consistent frame of reference.

items.q: Federal regulations require a medical examination before hearing aids are purchased for patients younger than 18 years.
items.a: True
items.ex: A medical examination is required before purchase for patients younger than 18; over-the-counter aids are for adults 18 or older.
items.ww: Over-the-counter hearing aids are limited to people 18 or older with mild to moderate loss.

alt.q: Over-the-counter hearing aids are appropriate for adults with severe to profound hearing loss.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Over-the-counter hearing aids are available for people 18 or older with mild to moderate hearing loss.
alt.ww: Severe loss falls outside the mild-to-moderate range for which over-the-counter aids are intended.

items.q: When acting as a sighted guide, the nurse walks a half step ahead while the patient lightly grasps the nurse’s arm just above the elbow.
items.a: True
items.ex: The person being guided holds the guide’s arm just above the elbow, and the guide walks a half step ahead.
items.ww: This positioning lets the patient follow the guide’s movements safely.

alt.q: When acting as a sighted guide, the nurse walks a half step behind the patient while holding the patient’s elbow.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The guide walks a half step ahead, and the patient grasps the guide’s arm, not the reverse.
alt.ww: Guides should not push, pull, or grab the person; the patient holds the guide’s arm.

items.q: Excessive cerumen occluding the ear canal causes [[conductive|conduction]] hearing loss.
items.ex: With aging, cerumen thickens and builds up, blocking sound conduction through the ear canal.

alt.q: Impacted earwax in an older adult produces a [[conductive|conduction]] type of hearing loss.
alt.ex: With aging, cerumen thickens and builds up, blocking sound conduction through the ear canal.

items.q: For a patient with reduced tactile sensation, the home water heater should be set no higher than [[120]] degrees Fahrenheit (48.8°C).
items.ex: Reduced sensation in the extremities increases the risk of burns from hot water.

Cannot understand language or communicate orally

items.q: A patient arrives in the emergency department with a perforated appendix and is taken directly to surgery. How is this surgery classified by urgency?
items.a: Emergency
items.ex: Emergency surgery must be done immediately to save life or preserve function; repair of a perforated appendix is the textbook example.
w: Urgent
Urgent surgery is necessary for health but is not necessarily an emergency, such as removing a gallbladder for stones.
Elective
Elective surgery is based on the patient’s choice and is not essential for health.
Palliative
Palliative describes purpose, not urgency; it relieves symptoms without producing a cure.

alt.q: Which description defines an emergency surgical procedure?
alt.a: Must be done immediately to save life or preserve function of a body part
alt.ex: Emergency procedures, such as controlling internal hemorrhage, cannot be delayed without threatening life or function.
w: Necessary for health and prevents additional problems, but not immediately
This describes urgent surgery, such as excising a cancerous tumor.
Performed on the basis of the patient’s choice and not essential for health
This describes elective surgery, such as a bunionectomy.
Involves extensive alteration of body parts and poses great risk
This describes major surgery, a classification of seriousness rather than urgency.

items.q: A patient is scheduled for a colon resection to remove a malignant tumor. Which set of classifications applies to this procedure?
items.a: Major, urgent, and ablative
items.ex: The book uses this example: the resection is major in seriousness, urgent in urgency, and ablative because a diseased part is removed.
w: Minor, elective, and diagnostic
Colon resection involves extensive alteration and is necessary for health, so it is neither minor nor elective.
Major, emergency, and palliative
Tumor removal is urgent rather than immediately lifesaving, and removing diseased tissue is ablative.
Minor, urgent, and reconstructive
Colon resection is major in seriousness and removes diseased tissue rather than restoring function.

alt.q: A gastrectomy is performed on one patient to resect a bleeding ulcer and on another to remove a malignant tumor. How does its urgency classification differ?
alt.a: Emergency for the bleeding ulcer and urgent for the tumor
alt.ex: The same procedure is classified differently depending on the reason; bleeding needs immediate control, whereas tumor removal is urgent.
w: Urgent for the bleeding ulcer and elective for the tumor
Bleeding must be controlled immediately, and tumor removal is necessary for health, not elective.
Elective for both because the procedure is the same
Classification depends on the reason for surgery, not only on the procedure performed.
Emergency for the tumor and urgent for the bleeding ulcer
This reverses the classifications; hemorrhage is the immediate threat to life.

items.q: A surgical procedure relieves or reduces the intensity of disease symptoms but does not produce a cure. How is it classified by purpose?
items.a: Palliative
items.ex: Palliative surgery, such as debridement of necrotic tissue or resection of nerve roots, eases symptoms without curing the disease.
w: Ablative
Ablative surgery excises or removes a diseased body part, such as an appendectomy.
Diagnostic
Diagnostic surgery confirms a diagnosis, often by removing tissue for testing.
Constructive
Constructive surgery restores function lost or reduced because of congenital anomalies.

alt.q: Which procedure does the textbook list as an example of palliative surgery?
alt.a: Resection of nerve roots
alt.ex: Resection of nerve roots relieves symptoms such as pain without curing the underlying disease, which makes it palliative.
w: Internal fixation of a fracture
Fracture fixation restores function to traumatized tissue, so it is reconstructive or restorative.
Repair of a cleft palate
Cleft palate repair corrects a congenital anomaly, so it is constructive.
Removal of the gallbladder
Removing a diseased organ such as the gallbladder is ablative.

items.q: An infant is scheduled for repair of a cleft palate. How is this surgery classified by purpose?
items.a: Constructive
items.ex: Constructive surgery restores function lost or reduced as a result of congenital anomalies, such as cleft palate or atrial septal defect.
w: Reconstructive
Reconstructive or restorative surgery repairs traumatized or malfunctioning tissue, such as a fracture, not a congenital defect.
Cosmetic
Cosmetic surgery improves personal appearance, such as a rhinoplasty, rather than restoring lost function.
Ablative
Ablative surgery removes a diseased body part, which a cleft palate repair does not do.

alt.q: A patient with a fractured femur has internal fixation of the fracture. How is this surgery classified by purpose?
alt.a: Reconstructive/restorative
alt.ex: Reconstructive or restorative surgery restores function or appearance to traumatized or malfunctioning tissues, such as fractures or scars.
w: Constructive
Constructive surgery corrects function lost because of congenital anomalies, not trauma.
Palliative
Palliative surgery relieves symptoms without cure; fixation restores function to the bone.
Diagnostic
Diagnostic surgery confirms a diagnosis; fixation treats a known injury.

items.q: A surgeon performs an exploratory laparotomy to inspect the abdominal organs and confirm a diagnosis. How is this surgery classified by purpose?
items.a: Diagnostic
items.ex: Diagnostic surgery is exploration to confirm a diagnosis and often removes tissue for further testing.
w: Ablative
Ablative surgery removes a diseased part; an exploratory laparotomy is done to inspect and confirm.
Palliative
Palliative surgery relieves symptoms of a known disease rather than establishing the diagnosis.
Procurement
Procurement removes organs or tissues for transplantation into another person.

alt.q: A woman is scheduled for a biopsy of a breast mass. What is the purpose of this procedure?
alt.a: To confirm a diagnosis by removing tissue for testing
alt.ex: A breast mass biopsy is diagnostic surgery: tissue is removed so the diagnosis can be confirmed.
w: To relieve symptoms without curing the disease
This is palliative surgery, such as debridement of necrotic tissue.
To restore appearance to malfunctioning tissue
This is reconstructive surgery, such as a scar revision.
To remove an entire diseased organ
This is ablative surgery, such as a cholecystectomy.

items.q: A preoperative patient has hypertension that is well controlled with medication and is a current smoker. No other conditions are present. Which ASA physical status class fits this patient?
items.a: ASA II
items.ex: ASA II is mild systemic disease without substantive functional changes, including current smoking and well-controlled hypertension.
w: ASA I
ASA I is a normal healthy, nonsmoking patient; smoking and hypertension exclude this class.
ASA III
ASA III requires severe systemic disease, such as poorly controlled hypertension or COPD.
ASA IV
ASA IV is severe disease that is a constant threat to life, such as a recent myocardial infarction.

alt.q: A patient with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) is scheduled for surgery. Which ASA physical status class fits?
alt.a: ASA III
alt.ex: ASA III is severe systemic disease with substantive functional changes, such as poorly controlled diabetes or COPD.
w: ASA I
ASA I is a normal healthy patient without systemic disease.
ASA II
ASA II covers well-controlled diabetes and mild lung disease, not poorly controlled diabetes and COPD.
ASA V
ASA V is a moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation.

items.q: A patient who had a myocardial infarction 2 months ago now needs surgery. Which ASA physical status class applies?
items.a: ASA IV
items.ex: A myocardial infarction within the past 3 months is severe systemic disease that is a constant threat to life, which is ASA IV.
w: ASA II
ASA II is mild disease without substantive functional changes, not a recent myocardial infarction.
ASA III
ASA III includes conditions such as a pacemaker or moderately reduced ejection fraction, not a recent infarction.
ASA VI
ASA VI is a patient declared brain dead whose organs are being removed for donation.

alt.q: A patient with a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm is rushed to surgery. Which ASA physical status class applies?
alt.a: ASA V
alt.ex: ASA V is a moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation, such as one with a ruptured aneurysm.
w: ASA III
ASA III is severe systemic disease with functional change, not an immediately fatal condition.
ASA IV
ASA IV is a constant threat to life, but a ruptured aneurysm means death is expected without surgery.
ASA VI
ASA VI applies only to a brain-dead patient whose organs are being removed for donation.

items.q: On what basis does the American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) assign a physical status classification?
items.a: The patient’s physiological condition, independent of the procedure
items.ex: The ASA classification describes the condition of the patient facing surgery, regardless of which operation is planned.
w: The seriousness of the planned surgical procedure
Seriousness classifies the procedure as major or minor, not the patient’s physical status.
The urgency with which surgery must be performed
Urgency classifies the procedure as elective, urgent, or emergency.
The type of anesthesia the patient will receive
The ASA class reflects the patient’s physiology, not the anesthetic chosen.

alt.q: How do surgeons and anesthesia providers use the ASA physical status classification?
alt.a: As a risk assessment guideline for how surgery will be performed
alt.ex: The ASA class gives the surgical team a risk assessment guideline for factors that influence how surgery is performed.
w: To decide whether the surgery is elective or urgent
Urgency is a separate classification based on how soon the procedure is needed.
To determine whether the procedure is major or minor
Major and minor describe the procedure’s seriousness, not the patient’s condition.
To confirm the diagnosis before the incision is made
Diagnostic surgery confirms a diagnosis; the ASA class rates physiological risk.

items.q: A patient scheduled for a cataract extraction says, “Everyone keeps calling this minor surgery, so I feel silly being this nervous.” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Any surgery can feel major to you. What worries you the most?”
items.ex: Any procedure can be considered major from the patient’s perspective, so the nurse validates the feeling and explores the concern.
w: “Cataract surgery is minor, so there is really nothing to worry about.”
This dismisses the patient’s feelings; minor procedures can still feel major to patients and families.
“Try not to think about it until the day of surgery.”
Avoidance does not address the concern or allow the nurse to assess the patient’s anxiety.
“Your surgeon can explain why the risk is so low.”
Deferring to the surgeon misses the nurse’s chance to assess and respond to the patient’s worry.

alt.q: A family member says, “The doctor told us it is only a minor procedure, but we are all very anxious.” What principle should guide the nurse’s response?
alt.a: Any procedure can be considered major from the family’s perspective
alt.ex: Classification of seriousness does not dictate how patients and families experience surgery, so their anxiety deserves attention.
w: Minor procedures do not require psychological preparation
Patients and families may experience any surgery as major and still need support.
Anxiety is expected only before major or emergency surgery
Any procedure can feel major to the patient and family, whatever its classification.
Families should be told that minor surgery has no risk
Minor surgery involves minimal, not zero, risk to well-being.

items.q: Which patient’s surgery is classified as urgent rather than elective or emergency?
items.a: Removal of the gallbladder for stones
items.ex: Urgent surgery is necessary for health and prevents additional problems but is not necessarily an emergency; gallbladder removal for stones fits.
w: Repair of a traumatic amputation
Traumatic amputation requires immediate surgery to save life or function, making it an emergency.
Bunionectomy for foot discomfort
A bunionectomy is elective, performed by patient choice and not essential for health.
Rhinoplasty to reshape the nose
Rhinoplasty is cosmetic in purpose and elective in urgency.

alt.q: A patient chooses to have a hernia repaired at a convenient time. Which term describes this surgery’s urgency?
alt.a: Elective
alt.ex: Elective surgery is performed on the basis of the patient’s choice and is not always necessary for health; hernia repair is an example.
w: Urgent
Urgent surgery is necessary for health, such as excision of a cancerous tumor.
Emergency
Emergency surgery must be done immediately to save life or preserve function.
Ablative
Ablative describes purpose, removing a diseased part, not urgency.

items.q: A preoperative patient has a body mass index (BMI) of 42 kg/m² and no other health problems. Which ASA physical status class is most consistent with this finding?
items.a: ASA III
items.ex: Morbid obesity, a BMI of 40 kg/m² or greater, is listed as severe systemic disease, which is ASA III.
w: ASA I
ASA I is a normal healthy patient; morbid obesity is a systemic disease.
ASA II
ASA II includes obesity with a BMI of 30 to 40 kg/m², not 40 or greater.
ASA V
ASA V is a moribund patient not expected to survive without the operation.

alt.q: A healthy pregnant patient with a BMI of 34 kg/m² needs surgery. Which ASA physical status class is most consistent with these findings?
alt.a: ASA II
alt.ex: Pregnancy and obesity with a BMI of 30 to 40 kg/m² are examples of mild systemic disease, which is ASA II.
w: ASA I
ASA I is a normal healthy patient; pregnancy and obesity are listed under ASA II.
ASA III
ASA III includes morbid obesity with a BMI of 40 kg/m² or greater.
ASA IV
ASA IV is severe systemic disease that constantly threatens life.

items.q: Which procedures does the textbook give as examples of major surgery? Select all that apply.
o: Coronary artery bypass
Bypass surgery involves extensive alteration of body parts and poses great risk.
Resection of a lung lobe
Lung lobe resection is extensive and poses great risks to well-being.
Removal of the larynx
Laryngectomy involves extensive alteration of body parts.
Cataract extraction
Cataract extraction involves minimal alteration and risk, so it is minor.
Tooth extraction
Tooth extraction is an example of minor surgery.
items.ex: Major surgery involves extensive reconstruction or alteration of body parts and poses great risks to well-being.

alt.q: Which procedures are examples of emergency surgery? Select all that apply.
o: Control of internal hemorrhaging
Hemorrhage must be controlled immediately to save life.
Repair of a perforated appendix
A perforated appendix requires immediate surgery.
Repair of a traumatic amputation
Traumatic amputation needs immediate surgery to save life or function.
Excision of a cancerous tumor
Tumor excision is urgent: necessary for health but not necessarily an emergency.
Breast reconstruction
Breast reconstruction is listed as elective surgery.
alt.ex: Emergency surgery must be done immediately to save life or preserve the function of a body part.

items.q: Which characteristics place a patient in ASA physical status class II? Select all that apply.
o: Current smoker
Current smoking is listed as mild systemic disease.
Well-controlled diabetes mellitus
Well-controlled diabetes is mild disease without substantive functional changes.
Social alcohol drinker
Social drinking is an ASA II example.
Implanted pacemaker
An implanted pacemaker is listed under ASA III.
Active hepatitis
Active hepatitis is severe systemic disease, ASA III.
items.ex: ASA II is a patient with mild systemic disease without substantive functional changes.

alt.q: Which characteristics place a patient in ASA physical status class III? Select all that apply.
o: Poorly controlled hypertension
Poorly controlled hypertension is severe systemic disease.
Alcohol dependence
Alcohol dependence or abuse is listed under ASA III.
Moderate reduction of cardiac ejection fraction
A moderately reduced ejection fraction is an ASA III example.
Pregnancy
Pregnancy is listed under ASA II.
Sepsis
Sepsis is a constant threat to life, which is ASA IV.
alt.ex: ASA III is a patient with severe systemic disease with substantive functional changes.

items.q: Which statements about the classification of surgical procedures are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Procedures are classified by seriousness, urgency, and purpose.
These three categories make up the classification of surgical procedures.
One procedure can fall into more than one classification.
A colon resection, for example, is major, urgent, and ablative.
Urgent procedures are major in seriousness.
The classifications intersect; urgent procedures are major.
A procedure always carries the same urgency classification.
A gastrectomy can be an emergency for bleeding or urgent for a tumor.
Minor procedures carry no risk to well-being.
Minor surgery involves minimal, not absent, risk to well-being.
items.ex: Knowing how classifications intersect and vary by patient helps the nurse plan appropriate perioperative care.

alt.q: A nurse reviews how surgical procedures are classified. Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Knowing the classifications assists in planning perioperative care.
Classification guides the nurse in anticipating patient needs.
The same procedure may be done for different reasons in different patients.
Different reasons can change a procedure’s urgency classification.
Any procedure can be considered major from the patient’s perspective.
Patients and families may experience any surgery as major.
Seriousness classifies surgery as elective or emergency.
Elective and emergency are urgency classifications; seriousness is major or minor.
Cosmetic surgery is classified by urgency.
Cosmetic is a purpose classification.
alt.ex: Surgery is classified by seriousness, urgency, and purpose, and the categories frequently overlap.

items.q: An urgent surgical procedure is always an emergency that must be performed immediately.
items.a: False
items.ex: Urgent surgery is necessary for health and often prevents further problems, but it is not necessarily an emergency.
items.ww: Only emergency surgery must be done immediately; urgent surgery such as tumor excision can be scheduled.

alt.q: Urgent surgery is necessary for the patient’s health but is not necessarily an emergency.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Urgent procedures, such as removing a gallbladder for stones, prevent further problems without requiring immediate surgery.
alt.ww: Equating urgent with emergency is wrong; emergency surgery is reserved for immediate threats to life or function.

items.q: The ASA physical status class depends on which surgical procedure the patient will have.
items.a: False
items.ex: The ASA assigns the class from the patient’s physiological condition, independent of the proposed procedure.
items.ww: Seriousness and urgency describe the procedure; the ASA class describes the patient.

alt.q: A patient’s ASA physical status class is assigned independent of the proposed surgical procedure.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The ASA class reflects the patient’s physiological condition, such as the severity of systemic disease.
alt.ww: Basing the ASA class on the procedure confuses it with seriousness or urgency classifications.

items.q: Healthy patients with no systemic disease face no risk from anesthesia.
items.a: False
items.ex: Anesthesia involves risks even in healthy patients, although patients with metabolic or cardiac dysfunction are at higher risk.
items.ww: Even an ASA I patient faces some anesthetic risk, so no patient is risk free.

alt.q: Anesthesia involves risks even in healthy patients, and the risk is higher in patients with cardiac or metabolic dysfunction.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The textbook notes anesthetic risk in all patients, with higher risk in those with metabolic and cardiac dysfunction.
alt.ww: Assuming healthy patients have no anesthetic risk ignores that anesthesia itself carries risk.

items.q: ASA physical status class V describes a [[moribund]] patient who is not expected to survive without the operation.
