items.q: The stress of surgery activates the endocrine system in every surgical patient. Which physiological changes does the nurse anticipate as a result?
items.a: Increased blood pressure, heart rate, and respiration
items.ex: Hormone and catecholamine release during the surgical stress response raises blood pressure, heart rate, and respiration.
w: Decreased blood pressure, heart rate, and respiration
Catecholamines stimulate rather than depress these vital signs.
Increased heart rate with decreased blood pressure
The stress response raises blood pressure along with heart rate.
Decreased platelet aggregation and respiration
Platelet aggregation increases during the stress response, and respiration rises.

alt.q: What causes the rise in blood pressure, heart rate, and respiration seen with the surgical stress response?
alt.a: Release of hormones and catecholamines
alt.ex: Surgery activates the endocrine system, releasing hormones and catecholamines that drive these vital sign changes.
w: Reduced platelet aggregation
Platelet aggregation increases with stress and does not raise vital signs.
Inhibition of the endocrine system
The endocrine system is activated, not inhibited, by surgical stress.
Vasodilation from general anesthesia
Anesthetic vasodilation causes heat loss; it does not explain the stress response.

items.q: A patient who smokes a pack of cigarettes daily is scheduled for abdominal surgery. Which postoperative complication is this patient at higher risk for because of smoking?
items.a: Pneumonia
items.ex: Smoking thickens and increases airway secretions, making them harder to clear after surgery and contributing to pneumonia.
w: Urinary retention
Urinary retention risk relates to age, sex, procedure, and anesthesia factors, not smoking.
Postoperative nausea and vomiting
Nonsmoking status, not smoking, is a risk factor for PONV.
Hypoglycemia
Smoking is not linked to hypoglycemia; it affects the airway and wound healing.

alt.q: Why does a patient who smokes have a higher risk of delayed wound healing after surgery?
alt.a: Smoking decreases oxygen reaching the cells in the wound
alt.ex: Less oxygen at the surgical wound means it heals more slowly and is more likely to become infected.
w: Smoking increases protein breakdown in the wound
Protein breakdown is part of the stress response, not the smoking effect described.
Smoking causes excess fluid to collect in the wound
The textbook links smoking to reduced wound oxygenation, not fluid collection.
Smoking speeds the metabolism of anesthetic agents
Anesthetic metabolism is not how smoking delays healing.

items.q: Why are older adult patients at increased risk for unintended hypothermia during surgery?
items.a: General anesthetics inhibit shivering and cause vasodilation
items.ex: Anesthetic effects on shivering and vessel tone cause heat loss, which combines with age-related changes to raise hypothermia risk.
w: General anesthetics raise the basal metabolic rate
Older adults have a lower basal metabolic rate, and anesthetics cause heat loss.
General anesthetics cause vasoconstriction in the skin
Anesthetics cause vasodilation, which increases heat loss.
General anesthetics increase oxygen consumption
Older adults have reduced oxygen consumption; this does not cause hypothermia.

alt.q: Besides temperature control problems, which surgical risk does the textbook describe for infants?
alt.a: Difficulty maintaining normal circulatory blood volume
alt.ex: Infants have trouble keeping a normal circulatory volume, so they are at risk for both dehydration and overhydration.
w: Reduced baroreceptor function causing falls
Reduced baroreceptor function is an older adult risk.
Stiffened lung tissue reducing oxygenation
Stiffened lung tissue is an age-related change in older adults.
Increased pain tolerance masking complications
Increased pain tolerance is an older adult neurological change.

items.q: A 79-year-old patient becomes dizzy when standing up after surgery. Which age-related change best explains this finding?
items.a: Insufficient baroreceptor function
items.ex: Baroreceptors regulate blood pressure; when insufficient, they cause postural hypotension and dizziness, raising fall risk.
w: Decreased cough reflex
A decreased cough reflex raises aspiration and infection risk, not dizziness.
Reduced bladder capacity
Reduced bladder capacity causes urgency and retention, not postural dizziness.
Delayed gastric emptying
Delayed gastric emptying increases reflux and indigestion risk.

alt.q: A postoperative older adult has a decreased reaction time and is at risk for falls. Which nursing intervention does the textbook recommend?
alt.a: Perform fall risk screening and institute fall precautions
alt.ex: Older adults face confusion and falls after anesthesia, so fall screening, precautions, and frequent orientation are recommended.
w: Keep the patient on bed rest until discharge
Early mobility is encouraged; bed rest increases pulmonary and clotting complications.
Withhold all pain medication to keep the patient alert
Adequate pain control is needed so the patient can take part in exercises.
Rush tasks to reduce the time the patient spends standing
Older adults need adequate time to respond, process information, and perform tasks.

items.q: After surgery, what minimum daily caloric intake does a patient need to maintain energy reserves?
items.a: 1500 kcal/day
items.ex: At least 1500 kcal/day is needed to maintain energy reserves, which is hard to reach when intake is limited or PONV occurs.
w: 800 kcal/day
800 kcal/day is below the textbook’s minimum for maintaining postoperative energy reserves.
1000 kcal/day
1000 kcal/day is below the 1500 kcal/day minimum after surgery.
3000 kcal/day
3000 kcal/day exceeds the stated minimum; the textbook sets at least 1500 kcal/day.

alt.q: A malnourished patient is scheduled for surgery. Which outcome is this patient more likely to have?
alt.a: Negative nitrogen balance and delayed wound healing
alt.ex: Malnourished patients have poor anesthesia tolerance, negative nitrogen balance, delayed recovery, infection, and delayed wound healing.
w: Faster recovery because of a lower metabolic rate
Malnutrition delays, rather than speeds, postoperative recovery.
Improved tolerance of anesthetic agents
Malnourished patients have poor tolerance for anesthesia.
Lower risk of infection because of reduced tissue mass
Tissue repair and infection resistance depend on adequate nutrition.

items.q: Why does obesity increase a patient’s risk of wound infection, dehiscence, and evisceration after surgery?
items.a: Fatty tissue has a poor blood supply
items.ex: Poor blood flow in fatty tissue slows delivery of the nutrients and antibodies needed for wound healing.
w: Fatty tissue releases excess catecholamines
Catecholamines come from the stress response, not from adipose tissue.
Fatty tissue speeds protein breakdown
Protein breakdown results from surgical trauma, not from fatty tissue.
Fatty tissue increases the oxygen reaching the wound
Adipose tissue reduces, rather than increases, delivery to the wound.

alt.q: A patient with obesity has impaired physical mobility before surgery and pain and fatigue afterward. Which complication does this combination place the patient at risk for?
alt.a: Venous thromboembolism
alt.ex: Preexisting impaired mobility plus postoperative pain and fatigue delays activity and increases the risk of VTE.
w: Hypoglycemia
Reduced mobility in obese patients is linked to clot formation, not hypoglycemia.
Postoperative nausea and vomiting
PONV risk factors include female sex and nonsmoking status, not immobility.
Hyperkalemia
The textbook links this combination to VTE, not potassium excess.

items.q: A patient with obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) received opioid analgesics after surgery and is sleeping on the back. Which finding is most important for the nurse to report?
items.a: Repeated pauses in breathing with oxygen saturation of 84%
items.ex: Opioids and the supine position worsen OSA; apnea with desaturation can progress to severe hypoxemia and death.
w: Pain rating of 4 on a 0-to-10 scale with grimacing on turning
A moderate pain rating is not as urgent as apnea with oxygen desaturation.
Blood pressure of 136/82 mm Hg while the patient sleeps
This blood pressure is not an immediate threat compared with hypoxemia.
Heart rate of 88 beats per minute and regular rhythm
A regular heart rate of 88 is within normal limits and less urgent than desaturation.

alt.q: Which situation places a patient with obstructive sleep apnea at the highest risk after surgery?
alt.a: Being sedated while lying on the back
alt.ex: Sedatives, opioids, and anesthesia relax the upper airway, and the risk is highest when the patient is sedated and supine.
w: Sitting upright while fully awake
Upright and awake is the opposite of the high-risk situation described.
Ambulating in the hallway with assistance
Ambulation while awake does not relax the upper airway like sedation does.
Receiving no sedatives or opioids
Absence of sedation lowers, not raises, airway relaxation risk.

items.q: A patient completed radiation therapy to shrink a tumor before surgical removal. Ideally, how long should the surgeon wait after radiation before operating?
items.a: 4 to 6 weeks
items.ex: Waiting 4 to 6 weeks after radiation allows for its effects on normal tissue and reduces wound-healing problems.
w: 24 to 48 hours
Operating this soon would expose the patient to serious wound-healing problems.
1 to 2 weeks
This is shorter than the recommended 4 to 6 weeks after radiation.
6 to 12 months
The textbook recommends 4 to 6 weeks, not months, after radiation.

alt.q: Why should surgery be delayed after a patient completes radiation treatments?
alt.a: Radiation thins the skin, destroys collagen, and impairs perfusion
alt.ex: These effects on normal tissue cause serious wound-healing problems if surgery is not delayed.
w: Radiation increases the risk of postoperative nausea
PONV risk factors do not include radiation in the textbook.
Radiation causes the body to retain potassium
Potassium is lost, not retained, after surgery; radiation affects skin and collagen.
Radiation thickens the skin and blocks anesthetics
Radiation thins rather than thickens the skin.

items.q: During the first 2 to 5 days after surgery, how does the adrenocortical stress response affect fluid and electrolyte balance?
items.a: The body retains sodium and water and loses potassium
items.ex: The adrenocortical stress response causes sodium and water retention with potassium loss after surgery.
w: The body loses sodium and water and retains potassium
This reverses the response; sodium and water are retained and potassium is lost.
The body retains sodium, water, and potassium
Potassium is lost, not retained, after surgery.
The body loses sodium, water, and potassium
Sodium and water are retained in the first days after surgery.

alt.q: A preoperative patient’s laboratory results show a significant potassium imbalance. Why is this finding important to report before surgery?
alt.a: Potassium excess or depletion increases the chance of dysrhythmias
alt.ex: Either too much or too little potassium raises the risk of dysrhythmias during or after surgery.
w: Potassium imbalance increases the risk of hypothermia
Hypothermia risk relates to anesthesia and age, not potassium.
Potassium imbalance causes obstructive sleep apnea
OSA is an airway disorder unrelated to potassium.
Potassium imbalance delays the effect of antibiotics
The textbook links potassium imbalance to dysrhythmias, not antibiotic action.

items.q: A patient had a hernia repair and has not voided 4 hours after surgery. A bladder scan shows 650 mL of urine. Which action does the nurse anticipate?
items.a: A single-time urinary catheterization
items.ex: A single-time catheterization is recommended when the bladder scan measures greater than 600 mL.
w: Insertion of an indwelling urinary catheter
The recommendation is a single-time catheterization, not an indwelling catheter.
Repeating the bladder scan in 8 hours
A volume over 600 mL already meets the threshold for catheterization.
Restricting oral fluids until the patient voids
Restricting fluids does not empty an overdistended bladder.

alt.q: A patient is being discharged after ambulatory surgery without having voided. Which instruction should the nurse give?
alt.a: Seek medical assistance if unable to void 8 hours after discharge
alt.ex: Ambulatory surgery patients may not void before discharge, so they seek help if unable to void within 8 hours.
w: Seek medical assistance if unable to void 24 hours after discharge
The textbook sets 8 hours after discharge, not 24 hours.
Limit fluid intake until the first void at home
Limiting fluids is not the textbook instruction for postoperative retention.
Seek medical assistance if unable to void 2 hours after discharge
The threshold is 8 hours after discharge, not 2 hours.

items.q: Which patient has the highest risk for postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV)?
items.a: A young nonsmoking woman with motion sickness having gynecological surgery
items.ex: Female sex, younger age, nonsmoking status, motion sickness history, and gynecological surgery are all PONV risk factors.
w: An older male smoker having cataract extraction under local anesthesia
Older age, male sex, and smoking are not PONV risk factors.
A middle-aged male smoker having a hand procedure with no opioids
This patient has few risk factors and no opioid use.
An older woman who smokes having a brief skin biopsy
Older age, smoking, and a brief procedure lower PONV risk.

alt.q: Why is postdischarge nausea and vomiting (PDNV) particularly problematic after ambulatory surgery?
alt.a: Patients at home lack fast-onset intravenous antiemetics
alt.ex: Once home, patients no longer have access to fast-onset IV antiemetic medications to control nausea and vomiting.
w: Ambulatory surgery patients have more PONV than inpatients
Ambulatory surgery patients generally have less PONV.
Home oral fluids always trigger vomiting
The problem is lack of IV antiemetics, not oral fluids.
PDNV usually causes urinary retention
PDNV risks include aspiration and dehydration, not urinary retention.

items.q: Which patient is most at risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE) based on surgical factors?
items.a: A patient having hip surgery under general anesthesia lasting 75 minutes
items.ex: VTE risk is highest with general anesthesia and surgery over 90 minutes, or over 60 minutes for pelvis or lower limb surgery.
w: A patient having abdominal surgery under general anesthesia lasting 70 minutes
Non-pelvic, non-limb surgery reaches the risk threshold at 90 minutes.
A patient having cataract extraction under local anesthesia lasting 30 minutes
Local anesthesia and a short procedure do not meet the risk criteria.
A patient having a skin biopsy under local anesthesia lasting 20 minutes
This brief procedure under local anesthesia is not a high VTE risk.

alt.q: For surgery involving the pelvis or lower limb under general anesthesia, which surgical time places a patient at highest risk for VTE?
alt.a: More than 60 minutes
alt.ex: The threshold is more than 60 minutes for pelvis or lower limb surgery and more than 90 minutes for other surgery.
w: More than 30 minutes
The textbook threshold for pelvis or lower limb surgery is 60 minutes, not 30.
More than 90 minutes
90 minutes is the threshold for surgery not involving the pelvis or lower limb.
More than 180 minutes
The risk threshold is far shorter: 60 minutes for pelvic or lower limb surgery.

items.q: Which patient-related factors increase the risk for postoperative nausea and vomiting (PONV)? Select all that apply.
o: Female sex
Women are at greater risk for PONV.
History of motion sickness
A history of PONV or motion sickness is a risk factor.
Nonsmoking status
Nonsmokers have a higher PONV risk.
Younger age
Younger age is a listed risk factor.
Current smoking
Nonsmoking, not smoking, raises PONV risk.
Older age
Younger age, not older age, increases PONV risk.
items.ex: Screening for these factors lets nurses take precautions; patients with four or more risk factors have a higher incidence of PONV.

alt.q: Which anesthesia- and surgery-related factors increase the risk for PONV? Select all that apply.
o: Use of volatile anesthetics
Volatile anesthetics such as nitrous oxide raise PONV risk.
Longer duration of anesthesia
Duration of anesthesia is an anesthesia-related risk factor.
Perioperative opioid use
Opioids given around surgery raise PONV risk.
Cholecystectomy
Abdominal procedures such as cholecystectomy are associated with PONV.
Ambulatory surgery setting
Ambulatory surgery patients generally have less PONV.
Avoidance of opioids
Avoiding opioids removes, rather than adds, a risk factor.
alt.ex: Volatile anesthetics, longer anesthesia, opioids, and abdominal or gynecological surgery are associated with PONV.

items.q: Which factors increase a patient’s risk for postoperative urinary retention (POUR)? Select all that apply.
o: Older age
Older age is a patient-specific risk factor.
Male gender
Male gender is a patient-specific risk factor.
Anorectal surgery
Anorectal surgery is a procedure-specific risk factor.
Excessive intraoperative fluid administration
Excess intraoperative fluid is an anesthesia-specific risk factor.
Female gender
The textbook lists male, not female, gender as a risk factor.
Short duration of anesthesia
Prolonged, not short, anesthesia raises POUR risk.
items.ex: POUR risk factors are grouped as patient-specific, procedure-specific, and anesthesia-specific.

alt.q: A nurse screens surgical patients for POUR risk. Which findings are risk factors? Select all that apply.
o: Planned joint arthroplasty
Joint arthroplasty is a procedure-specific risk factor.
History of prior pelvic surgery
Prior pelvic surgery is a patient-specific risk factor.
Use of anticholinergic agents
Anticholinergic agents are a medication-related risk factor.
Neurological disease
Neurological disease is a patient-specific risk factor.
Younger age
Older, not younger, age is a POUR risk factor.
Avoidance of opioids
Opioid use, not avoidance, increases POUR risk.
alt.ex: Patients with these risk factors need bladder scanning if they cannot void by 4 hours after surgery.

items.q: Which conditions place a surgical patient at higher risk for venous thromboembolism (VTE)? Select all that apply.
o: Prior VTE
A previous VTE is a listed risk factor.
Use of steroids
Steroid use increases VTE risk.
Dehydration
Dehydration is a listed VTE risk factor.
Body mass index of 40 kg/m² or greater
Obesity at this level is a VTE risk factor.
Body mass index of 22 kg/m²
A normal BMI is not a VTE risk factor.
Expected early return to full mobility
Significant reduction in mobility, not early mobility, raises VTE risk.
items.ex: Older age, diabetes, prior VTE, cardiovascular or lung disease, recent surgery, dehydration, clotting disorders, steroids, and obesity increase VTE risk.

alt.q: A nurse reviews the history of a patient scheduled for surgery. Which findings increase the patient’s VTE risk? Select all that apply.
o: Diabetes mellitus
Diabetes is a listed VTE risk factor.
Peripheral arterial disease
Peripheral arterial disease is a listed risk factor.
Recent surgery
Recent surgery increases VTE risk.
A blood clotting disorder causing hypercoagulability
Hypercoagulable states increase clot risk.
Surgery under local anesthesia lasting 20 minutes
General anesthesia and longer surgical time raise VTE risk.
Age of 30 years
Older adults, not young adults, are listed as high risk.
alt.ex: Identifying VTE risk factors before surgery lets the team plan prevention for a largely preventable complication.

items.q: Chronic smoking increases the amount and thickness of airway secretions, which increases the risk of aspiration.
items.a: True
items.ex: Thick, abundant secretions are harder to clear after surgery, raising aspiration and pneumonia risk in smokers.
items.ww: Claiming smoking reduces secretions is wrong; it increases their amount and thickness.

alt.q: Chronic smoking decreases airway secretions, which lowers a patient’s risk of aspiration during surgery.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Smoking increases the amount and thickness of airway secretions, so aspiration risk rises.
alt.ww: This statement reverses the effect; smoking makes secretions thicker and more plentiful.

items.q: Patients who have ambulatory surgery generally have more postoperative nausea and vomiting than other surgical patients.
items.a: False
items.ex: Ambulatory surgery patients generally have less PONV, although nausea can occur after they leave the surgical setting.
items.ww: Ambulatory patients are not at greater PONV risk; the concern is that symptoms may begin after discharge.

alt.q: Patients who have ambulatory surgery generally have less PONV, but nausea and vomiting may still occur after discharge.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: PONV is less common after ambulatory surgery, but postdischarge nausea and vomiting can still develop at home.
alt.ww: Saying ambulatory patients have more PONV contradicts the textbook.

items.q: An older adult’s reduced tactile sense and increased pain tolerance decrease the ability to respond to early warning signs of surgical complications.
items.a: True
items.ex: Sensory losses mean older adults may not notice pressure or pain, so nurses inspect bony prominences and watch for nonverbal pain.
items.ww: Older adults’ sensory losses blunt, rather than sharpen, their awareness of early complications.

alt.q: Because of sensory changes with aging, older adults are more likely than younger adults to report early warning signs of surgical complications.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Reduced tactile sense and increased pain tolerance decrease older adults’ ability to respond to early warning signs.
alt.ww: Sensory changes make older adults less, not more, likely to recognize early complications.

items.q: Obstructive sleep apnea causes pauses in breathing (apnea) that last at least [[10]] seconds during sleep.
items.ex: Most apneic episodes last 10 to 30 seconds, and some last a minute or longer, causing significant oxygen desaturation.

alt.ex: Most apneic episodes last 10 to 30 seconds, and some last a minute or longer, causing significant oxygen desaturation.

Decreased respiratory muscle strength and cough reflex
Teach coughing, deep breathing, and spirometer use
Delayed gastric emptying and decreased saliva
Elevate the head of the bed at least 45 degrees
Screen for delirium and orient frequently to surroundings
mt.ex: Age-related changes reduce an older adult’s ability to maintain homeostasis, so each system needs targeted perioperative nursing care.

items.q: The WHO Surgical Safety Checklist promotes effective communication during which three perioperative periods?
items.a: Before anesthesia, before skin incision, and before leaving the operative area
items.ex: The WHO checklist targets these three points to ensure communication and safe practice during surgery.
w: At admission, before anesthesia, and at hospital discharge
Admission and hospital discharge are not checklist periods.
Before skin incision, during wound closure, and on PACU discharge
Wound closure and PACU discharge are not among the three periods.
At preadmission testing, before skin incision, and on PACU arrival
Preadmission testing and PACU arrival are not checklist periods.

alt.q: Which point in surgery is one of the three periods covered by the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist?
alt.a: Prior to skin incision
alt.ex: The checklist covers prior to anesthesia, prior to skin incision, and prior to the patient leaving the operative area.
w: During preadmission testing
Preadmission testing occurs days before surgery and is not a checklist period.
At discharge from the PACU
The last checklist period is before the patient leaves the operative area, not the PACU.
During the first postoperative dressing change
Dressing changes occur after surgery and are not checklist periods.

items.q: Why do transitions from one care provider to another place surgical patients at risk?
items.a: They can lead to injuries, missed care, and errors in translating information
items.ex: Each hand-off is a chance for information to be lost or misunderstood, so smooth hand-offs are needed to reduce medical errors.
w: They increase the patient’s risk of surgical site infection
Infection risk relates to factors such as glycemic control and skin antisepsis.
They require the patient to repeat informed consent
Consent is verified, not repeated, at each transition.
They lengthen the duration of general anesthesia
Transitions affect communication, not the length of anesthesia.

alt.q: What is the main purpose of a smooth communication hand-off between perioperative caregivers?
alt.a: To ensure continuity of care and reduce the risk of medical errors
alt.ex: Because different nurses usually care for the patient in each phase, clear hand-offs keep care continuous and safe.
w: To shorten the patient’s length of stay in the PACU
The purpose described is continuity and safety, not shorter stays.
To replace documentation in the electronic health record
Hand-offs supplement, not replace, accurate documentation.
To allow one nurse to care for the patient in every phase
Hand-offs are needed precisely because different nurses usually care for the patient.

items.q: A preoperative nurse has completed the patient’s preparation and documentation, and the patient is ready to go to the operating room. Which action best communicates the patient’s status to the receiving team?
items.a: Give a verbal SBAR hand-off with the patient present
items.ex: A written or electronic record alone is inadequate; AORN and TJC recommend the hand-off occur with the patient present.
w: Rely on the completed preoperative checklist in the EHR
Once the patient is ready for the OR, a written or electronic record is inadequate alone.
Call the OR with a report after the patient is transported
The hand-off should happen with the patient, not after transport.
Leave a written note on the front of the paper chart
A written note does not allow the dialogue an effective hand-off requires.

alt.q: Why do AORN and TJC recommend that hand-off reports occur with the patient present?
alt.a: To ensure the right patient receives the right surgery at the right site
alt.ex: Including the patient in the hand-off allows verification of identity, procedure, and site.
w: To allow the patient to approve the nurse’s documentation
The purpose is verification of patient, procedure, and site.
To reduce the time needed to transport the patient
Hand-off with the patient is about safety, not speed.
To let the patient choose the anesthesia provider
Choice of provider is not the purpose of the bedside hand-off.

items.q: In a preoperative-to-intraoperative hand-off using SBAR, under which component does the nurse report the patient’s allergies and NPO status?
items.a: Background
items.ex: Background includes pertinent history, medical clearance, allergies, NPO status, vital signs, medications, laboratory results, and code status.
w: Situation
Situation covers the patient’s name, date of birth, procedure, and pertinent documents.
Assessment
Assessment covers understanding of surgery, special needs, cultural factors, and anesthesia requests.
Recommendations
Recommendations cover whether the patient was seen by the surgeon and anesthesia provider and is ready.

alt.q: In the SBAR preoperative hand-off, under which component does the nurse report the patient’s current level of understanding of the surgery?
alt.a: Assessment
alt.ex: Assessment includes understanding of the surgery, special needs or precautions, cultural or emotional factors, and anesthesia requests.
w: Situation
Situation identifies the patient, the procedure, and pertinent documents.
Background
Background includes history, allergies, NPO status, vital signs, and medications.
Recommendations
Recommendations state readiness for surgery and invite questions.

items.q: During an SBAR hand-off to the operating room team, what does the nurse include in the Recommendations component?
items.a: Whether the patient is ready for surgery
items.ex: Recommendations state whether the surgeon and anesthesia provider saw the patient, whether the patient is ready, and invite questions.
w: The patient’s name and date of birth
Name and date of birth belong in the Situation component.
The patient’s code status
Code status is reported under Background.
Pertinent cultural or emotional factors
Cultural and emotional factors are reported under Assessment.

alt.q: A nurse begins an SBAR hand-off to the OR. Which information belongs in the Situation component?
alt.a: The operative procedure, including site and modifiers
alt.ex: Situation identifies the patient, the procedure with its site and modifiers, and whether documents are present and consistent.
w: The patient’s medication profile
Medications are reported under Background.
Special patient needs or precautions
Special needs and precautions are part of Assessment.
A chance for staff to voice concerns
Inviting questions and concerns is part of Recommendations.

items.q: Under the Universal Protocol, who is responsible for marking the operative site?
items.a: The individual who will perform the surgery
items.ex: The person performing and accountable for the procedure personally marks the site and involves the patient if possible.
w: The circulating nurse in the operating room
The circulating nurse does not mark the site; the operating surgeon does.
The preoperative nurse during admission
Site marking is not delegated to the admitting nurse.
The anesthesia provider before induction
The anesthesia provider is not the one accountable for the procedure site.

alt.q: In the holding area, a surgeon asks the nurse to mark the operative site because the surgeon is running late. Which response by the nurse is best?
alt.a: “The person performing the surgery must personally mark the site.”
alt.ex: The Universal Protocol requires the individual performing and accountable for the surgery to personally mark the site.
w: “I will mark it now and you can confirm it at the time-out.”
A nurse marking the site does not meet the Universal Protocol requirement.
“The patient can mark the site while we wait for you.”
The patient is involved if possible, but the surgeon must mark the site.
“We can skip the mark because we will do a time-out.”
Site marking and the time-out are separate required principles.

items.q: A patient in the holding area refuses to have the operative site marked. What should the nurse do?
items.a: Document the refusal on the procedure checklist
items.ex: If the patient refuses a site mark, the Universal Protocol directs documentation of the refusal on the procedure checklist.
w: Mark the site after the patient is anesthetized
Marking against the patient’s refusal disregards the patient’s involvement in the process.
Cancel the surgery until the patient agrees
The textbook directs documentation of the refusal, not cancellation.
Ask a family member to mark the site instead
Only the individual performing the surgery marks the site.

alt.q: A patient tells the nurse, “I don’t want anyone drawing on my skin.” How is this handled under the Universal Protocol?
alt.a: The refusal is documented on the procedure checklist
alt.ex: The protocol includes the patient in the process, and a refused mark is documented on the procedure checklist.
w: The surgeon marks the site once the patient is sedated
Marking after sedation ignores the patient’s refusal.
The time-out is skipped because there is no mark
All team members still perform the time-out before the procedure.
The circulating nurse marks the site with tape instead
The protocol calls for indelible ink by the surgeon, or documented refusal.

items.q: When is the Universal Protocol time-out performed?
items.a: Just before the procedure starts
items.ex: The time-out is the final verification of the correct patient, procedure, site, and implants just before starting the procedure.
w: At the preadmission testing visit
Preadmission testing is part of preoperative verification, not the time-out.
When the patient arrives in the PACU
The time-out happens before, not after, the procedure.
Immediately after wound closure
Verification after closure would be too late to prevent wrong-site surgery.

alt.q: Who participates in the Universal Protocol time-out?
alt.a: All members of the surgical or procedure team
alt.ex: All members of the surgical team perform the time-out to verify the correct patient, procedure, site, and implants.
w: Only the surgeon and the circulating nurse
The time-out involves every member of the team, not only two people.
Only the anesthesia provider
The anesthesia provider takes part, but all team members perform the time-out.
Only the preoperative nurse in the holding area
The time-out is a team activity, not a single nurse’s task.

items.q: During preoperative verification, a patient states the surgery will be on the left knee, but the consent form lists the right knee. Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Report the discrepancy to the surgeon before the procedure proceeds
items.ex: Verification ensures the scheduled surgery matches the patient’s expectations; a mismatch must be reported before surgery continues.
w: Reassure the patient that the consent form is correct
The nurse cannot assume which is correct; the discrepancy must be resolved first.
Correct the consent form to match the patient’s statement
The nurse does not change the consent; the surgeon must clarify the procedure.
Send the patient to the operating room as scheduled
Proceeding with an unresolved site discrepancy risks wrong-site surgery.

alt.q: Which element is part of preoperative verification under the Universal Protocol?
alt.a: Confirming that the scheduled surgery matches the patient’s expectations
alt.ex: Verification ensures documents and results are available and that the scheduled surgery is consistent with what the patient expects.
w: Marking the operative site with indelible ink
Site marking is the second principle, separate from verification.
Pausing just before incision for final confirmation
That final pause is the time-out, the third principle.
Counting sponges before the incision is closed
Sponge counts are an intraoperative safety task, not a Universal Protocol principle.

items.q: A PACU nurse receives a hand-off report from the surgical team. How does this report help the PACU nurse plan care?
items.a: It helps anticipate how quickly the patient will regain consciousness
items.ex: Hand-off data let the recovery nurse anticipate time to regain consciousness, likely complications, and analgesic needs.
w: It replaces the nurse’s own initial assessment
The PACU nurse still performs an assessment after receiving the hand-off.
It tells the nurse which family member gave consent
Consent details are not the focus of the PACU hand-off.
It allows the nurse to skip vital sign checks
Vital signs are still monitored closely in the PACU.

alt.q: During the PACU hand-off, the anesthesia provider reports the IV fluids and blood products given during surgery. What does this information alert the PACU nurse to?
alt.a: The patient’s fluid and electrolyte balance
alt.ex: A report of IV fluids or blood products given alerts the recovery nurse to the patient’s fluid and electrolyte status.
w: The patient’s readiness for discharge home
Discharge readiness is judged later, using scoring criteria.
The patient’s level of surgical understanding
Understanding of surgery is part of the preoperative hand-off.
The patient’s risk for wrong-site surgery
Wrong-site risk is addressed before surgery through the Universal Protocol.

items.q: A PACU nurse is transferring a patient to the acute nursing unit. What must the PACU nurse and the receiving nurse do during the bedside hand-off?
items.a: Verify the patient’s identity using two identifiers
items.ex: During the PACU-to-unit hand-off, nurses verify identity with two identifiers before reviewing the patient’s status.
w: Verify identity by checking the room number
A room number is not a patient identifier.
Postpone the report until the family arrives
Families are informed promptly, but the hand-off is not delayed for them.
Complete the report by text message to save time
The hand-off happens at the bedside with time to ask questions.

alt.q: Where does the hand-off between the surgical team and the PACU nurse take place?
alt.a: At the patient’s bedside
alt.ex: The PACU hand-off is interactive, interprofessional, and done at the bedside so caregivers can dialogue and ask questions.
w: At the nurses’ station after the patient settles
The hand-off occurs at the bedside, not away from the patient.
By phone from the operating room
A bedside hand-off allows face-to-face questions with the patient present.
In the waiting room with the family
The family is updated separately; the hand-off is between caregivers at the bedside.

items.q: TJC, AORN, and WHO recommend a formal hand-off before surgery. Which items should it include at a minimum? Select all that apply.
o: Patient name and date of birth
Patient identification is a minimum hand-off element.
Allergies and nothing by mouth status
Allergies and NPO status are required elements.
Laboratory data and code status
Both are minimum hand-off elements.
Whether the patient has seen the surgeon and anesthesiologist
This confirms readiness and is a minimum element.
The patient’s insurance authorization
Insurance information is not a clinical hand-off element.
The patient’s preferred postoperative menu
Diet preferences are not among the minimum elements.
items.ex: A formal hand-off covers identity, procedure and site, history, allergies, NPO status, vital signs, labs, code status, medications, understanding, and cultural needs.

alt.q: A preoperative nurse prepares a formal hand-off for the surgical team. Which items belong in it? Select all that apply.
o: Operative procedure, including the site
Procedure and site are minimum hand-off elements.
Current medications taken the day of surgery
Day-of-surgery medications must be communicated.
Patient’s level of surgical understanding
Understanding of surgery is a minimum element.
Cultural implications
Cultural implications are part of the formal hand-off.
The surgeon’s preferred discharge time
Discharge timing is not a minimum hand-off element.
The patient’s parking arrangements
Logistics like parking are not clinical hand-off content.
alt.ex: A standard hand-off ensures the intraoperative team receives the information needed for safe, person-centered care.

items.q: Which are principles of TJC’s Universal Protocol for preventing wrong site and wrong procedure surgery? Select all that apply.
o: Preoperative verification of documents and test results
Verification is the first principle.
Marking the operative site with indelible ink
Site marking is the second principle.
A time-out just before starting the procedure
The time-out is the third principle.
A sponge count before wound closure
Sponge counts are intraoperative safety checks, not a Universal Protocol principle.
A postoperative debriefing in the PACU
Debriefing in the PACU is not one of the three principles.
items.ex: The Universal Protocol has three principles: preoperative verification, site marking, and a time-out.

alt.q: Site marking under the Universal Protocol is used to identify which features? Select all that apply.
o: Left and right distinction
Marking distinguishes left from right.
Multiple structures such as fingers
Marking identifies the correct structure among several.
Levels of the spine
Marking identifies the correct spinal level.
The patient’s allergy status
Allergies are verified in documentation, not marked on the site.
The planned type of anesthesia
Anesthesia type is not shown by site marking.
alt.ex: Indelible ink marks left and right distinction, multiple structures, and spinal levels to prevent wrong-site surgery.

items.q: When the surgical team gives a hand-off to the PACU nurse, which topics does the report include? Select all that apply.
o: Type of anesthesia provided
Anesthesia type helps predict recovery of consciousness.
Vital sign trends during surgery
VS trends are part of the surgical team’s report.
Estimated blood and urine loss
Estimated losses inform fluid balance assessment.
Dressings, tubes, and drains at the wound
Wound information is included in the report.
The patient’s insurance coverage
Insurance is not part of the clinical hand-off.
The patient’s menu choices for dinner
Meal choices are not hand-off content.
items.ex: The report covers anesthesia, VS trends, intraoperative medications, IV fluids, estimated losses, and wound details.

alt.q: When the PACU nurse gives a hand-off to the nurse on the acute care unit, which items are reviewed? Select all that apply.
o: Level of consciousness
Level of consciousness is reviewed at transfer.
Medications given during surgery and in the PACU
All medications given are reviewed.
IV lines, drainage tubes, and dressings
Lines, tubes, and dressings are reviewed.
Type of surgery and anesthesia performed
Surgery and anesthesia type are reviewed.
The patient’s room number only, as identification
Nurses verify identity with two identifiers, not a room number.
A summary of the patient’s billing
Billing is not part of the clinical hand-off.
alt.ex: The PACU report helps the receiving nurse anticipate needs and obtain equipment; uninterrupted time for questions is important.

items.q: Once a patient is ready for the operating room, a complete written or electronic record is enough to communicate the patient’s status to the receiving team.
items.a: False
items.ex: A written or electronic record is inadequate alone; an effective verbal hand-off is required when the patient transfers.
items.ww: Relying on the record skips the interactive hand-off needed to verify the right patient, surgery, and site.

alt.q: Even with complete documentation, an effective hand-off is required when a patient is transferred to the operating room team.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The transfer of patient information between providers requires an effective hand-off, not documentation alone.
alt.ww: Documentation alone cannot replace the interactive exchange of a hand-off.

items.q: Hospitals and surgical outpatient centers may modify or add to the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist based on their practice guidelines.
items.a: True
items.ex: The WHO checklist can be adapted by agencies to fit their own practice guidelines.
items.ww: The checklist is not fixed; agencies may modify or add to it.

alt.q: Agencies must use the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist exactly as written, without changes.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Hospitals and outpatient centers can modify or add to the checklist based on their practice guidelines.
alt.ww: The textbook explicitly allows agencies to adapt the checklist.

items.q: The Universal Protocol applies only to procedures performed in a hospital operating room.
items.a: False
items.ex: The protocol is implemented for any invasive surgical procedure, whether in a hospital, ASC, or health care provider office.
items.ww: Location does not exempt a procedure; any invasive procedure requires the protocol.

alt.q: The Universal Protocol is implemented for invasive procedures in a health care provider’s office as well as in hospitals.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The protocol applies whenever an invasive surgical procedure is performed, no matter the location.
alt.ww: Limiting the protocol to hospitals ignores invasive procedures in ASCs and offices.

items.q: The final verification of the correct patient, procedure, site, and implants just before the procedure begins is called the [[time-out|time out|timeout]].
items.ex: All members of the surgical team perform the time-out, which commonly occurs in the holding area or just before the procedure.

alt.q: Just before starting a procedure, all team members pause for a [[time-out|time out|timeout]] to confirm patient, procedure, site, and implants.
alt.ex: All members of the surgical team perform the time-out, which commonly occurs in the holding area or just before the procedure.

alt.q: In the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist, which period comes right before “Prior to the patient leaving the operative area”?

w: Prior to administration of anesthesia

ord.q: Put the three perioperative periods covered by the WHO Surgical Safety Checklist in order.

Prior to skin incision
Prior to the patient leaving the operative area
ord.ex: The checklist follows the course of surgery, from before anesthesia through incision to leaving the operative area.

items.q: Why is monitoring blood glucose imperative for a surgical patient with diabetes or prediabetes?
items.a: Hyperglycemia increases the risk of wound infection and mortality
items.ex: Poor glucose control, specifically hyperglycemia, during and after surgery raises the risk of wound infection and death.
w: Hyperglycemia increases the risk of urinary retention
The textbook links hyperglycemia to wound infection and mortality, not urinary retention.
Hypoglycemia is the only glucose risk after surgery
Hyperglycemia is the specific risk linked to infection and mortality.
Hyperglycemia shortens wound healing time
High glucose impairs, rather than speeds, wound healing.

alt.q: In which patients does controlling blood glucose perioperatively reduce mortality?
alt.a: Patients with or without diabetes having general or cardiac surgery
alt.ex: Evidence shows perioperative glucose control reduces mortality in general and cardiac surgery patients, with or without diabetes.
w: Only patients with type 1 diabetes mellitus
Benefits extend to patients without diabetes as well.
Only patients having ambulatory surgery
The evidence cited involves general and cardiac surgery patients.
Only patients with a history of wound infection
Glucose control benefits a broader group of surgical patients.

items.q: A patient with diabetes is in the surgical care unit after an abdominal procedure. Which finding is most important for the nurse to report?
items.a: Blood glucose of 245 mg/dL
items.ex: Postoperative hyperglycemia above 180 mg/dL is associated with wound infections and longer hospital stays.
w: Blood glucose of 150 mg/dL
This value is below the 180 mg/dL threshold for postoperative hyperglycemia.
Oral temperature of 37.0°C (98.6°F)
A normal temperature does not need urgent reporting.
Pain rating of 3 on a 0-to-10 scale
Mild pain is less urgent than significant hyperglycemia.

alt.q: What blood glucose goal does the textbook recommend for patients after surgery?
alt.a: Less than 180 mg/dL
alt.ex: Maintaining glucose below 180 mg/dL and reducing glucose variability is recommended evidence-based practice.
w: Less than 250 mg/dL
Levels above 180 mg/dL are already associated with wound infection.
Less than 70 mg/dL
This level would represent hypoglycemia, not a safe target.
Greater than 200 mg/dL
Levels this high are hyperglycemia, linked to infection and longer stays.

items.q: A patient with diabetes asks why the insulin dose is different after surgery. Which explanation by the nurse is accurate?
items.a: “Insulin needs can rise from surgical stress or fall from eating less.”
items.ex: Insulin requirements fluctuate after surgery: stress may raise needs, while decreased nutritional intake may lower them.
w: “Insulin needs always fall after surgery because you are resting.”
Some patients need more insulin because of the surgical stress response.
“Insulin needs always rise after surgery and stay high afterward.”
Some patients need less insulin because of decreased intake.
“Insulin is not needed after surgery until you go home.”
Glucose monitoring and appropriate insulin continue throughout the perioperative period.

alt.q: Why are insulin dosages usually adjusted before surgery?
alt.a: Food intake is reduced before surgery
alt.ex: Insulin doses are usually adjusted because of the reduced food intake before surgery.
w: Insulin interacts with anesthetics to cause bradycardia
Bradycardia with anesthesia is linked to antihypertensives, not insulin.
Insulin prolongs bleeding time during surgery
Prolonged bleeding is linked to NSAIDs and anticoagulants.
Insulin potentiates the action of anesthetic agents
Antibiotics, not insulin, are described as potentiating anesthetics.

items.q: Why does diabetes mellitus increase a patient’s surgical risk?
items.a: It increases infection risk and impairs wound healing
items.ex: Altered glucose metabolism and associated circulatory impairment increase susceptibility to infection and impair healing.
w: It alters the excretion of anesthetic drugs
Altered drug excretion is the risk described for renal disease.
It increases the risk of hemorrhage
Bleeding disorders, not diabetes, increase hemorrhage risk.
It reduces the ability to compensate for acid-base changes
This is the risk described for chronic respiratory disease.

alt.q: How does the stress of surgery commonly affect blood glucose levels?
alt.a: It often results in hyperglycemia
alt.ex: Surgical stress and protein breakdown often cause hyperglycemia, which decreases tissue healing and increases infection risk.
w: It usually causes hypoglycemia
The stress response raises, rather than lowers, blood glucose.
It has no effect on blood glucose
Surgical stress commonly results in hyperglycemia.
It lowers glucose only in patients without diabetes
Stress hyperglycemia can occur in surgical patients generally.

items.q: A surgeon orders a prophylactic antibiotic for a patient having surgery. Which timing is associated with reduced wound infection rates?
items.a: Given 60 minutes before incision and stopped within 24 hours
items.ex: Infection rates fall when the antibiotic is given 60 minutes before incision and stopped within 24 hours after surgery.
w: Given 6 hours before incision and stopped within 24 hours
The recommended timing is 60 minutes, not 6 hours, before incision.
Given 60 minutes before incision and continued for 7 days
Antibiotics are stopped within 24 hours after surgery.
Given after incision and stopped within 72 hours
The antibiotic is given before incision and stopped within 24 hours.

alt.q: A preoperative patient has an antibiotic ordered before surgery. Who determines the specific time the antibiotic is given?
alt.a: The surgeon, who orders a specific time before surgery
alt.ex: The surgeon orders a specific time before surgery for the oral or IV antibiotic to be given.
w: The patient, who chooses a convenient time
Timing is ordered by the surgeon to maximize infection prevention.
The pharmacist, after the surgery ends
The antibiotic is ordered for a time before surgery, by the surgeon.
The PACU nurse, on the patient’s arrival

alt.q: For which patients is research evidence strong supporting preoperative decolonization?

Patients having diagnostic biopsy

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient about bathing before abdominal surgery. Which statement by the patient shows understanding of the teaching?

alt.q: Why is skin antisepsis performed before surgeries involving the chest, abdomen, or major joint replacements?

items.q: A patient’s abdominal surgical site has hair that does not interfere with exposure, closure, or dressing of the site. Which action should the nurse take?

Clip the hair the evening before surgery

Remove the hair with a depilatory cream
The textbook recommends leaving hair unless it interferes; then clipping is preferred.

alt.q: Hair at a surgical site must be removed because it interferes with wound closure. Which method does the nurse use?

w: Shaving with a razor the evening before surgery
Razors cause micro-nicks, and hair is removed close to surgery.
Clipping with a reused clipper head the night before
Clipper heads are single-use and hair removal is done close to surgery.
Shaving with a razor right before the incision
Razor removal is associated with more SSIs than clipping.

items.q: How does the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services (CMS) classify a surgical site infection (SSI)?

The never-event classification applies regardless of patient age.
