items.ex: Pressure above 32 mm Hg blocks arterial flow; during prolonged unrelieved pressure capillary pressure may reach 150 mm Hg.

alt.q: Ischemic tissue injury can develop once capillary pressure rises above [[32 mm Hg|32]], because arterial blood flow is impeded.
alt.ex: Pressure above 32 mm Hg blocks arterial flow; during prolonged unrelieved pressure capillary pressure may reach 150 mm Hg.

items.q: During prolonged, unrelieved pressure without a position change, capillary pressure can rise to as much as which level?
items.a: 150 mm Hg
items.ex: Capillary pressures may increase to as much as 150 mm Hg during prolonged pressure, far above the 32 mm Hg threshold.
w: 32 mm Hg
32 mm Hg is the threshold at which arterial flow is impeded, not the peak reached.
60 mm Hg
The book states pressure can reach 150 mm Hg, much higher than 60.
250 mm Hg
The book gives 150 mm Hg as the possible peak, not 250.

alt.q: A patient lies in a fixed position for hours during surgery. What happens when capillary pressure exceeds 32 mm Hg?
alt.a: Arterial blood flow is impeded and ischemic injury can develop
alt.ex: Above 32 mm Hg, arterial flow to tissue is blocked, which leads to ischemia and pressure injury.
w: Venous return increases and tissue oxygenation improves
High external pressure impairs, rather than improves, tissue perfusion.
Capillaries dilate and protect the tissue from damage
Sustained pressure compresses capillaries; it does not protect tissue.
Lymphatic flow speeds up and removes tissue edema
The concern is impeded arterial flow and ischemia, not faster lymph flow.

items.q: During the preoperative skin assessment, which areas does the nurse inspect with particular care? Select all that apply.
o: Heels
Heels are a bony prominence named for careful inspection.
Sacrum
The sacrum is a bony prominence at high risk for PI.
Back of the head
The back of the head is listed among bony prominences to inspect.
Scapulae
The scapula is a listed bony prominence.
Anterior abdomen
The abdomen is not a bony prominence listed for PI inspection.
Palms of the hands
The palms are not among the bony prominences the book lists.
items.ex: Inspect skin over bony prominences such as the heels, elbows, sacrum, back of head, and scapula.

alt.q: Which preoperative skin assessment actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Separate body folds in a patient who is obese
Separating folds ensures the skin is examined thoroughly.
Inspect the skin over the elbows and heels
These bony prominences are at risk during fixed OR positions.
Note any existing lesions or wounds
Current skin alterations such as lesions or wounds are identified preoperatively.
Consider the position the patient will need on the OR table
The planned OR position shows which areas are at risk.
Inspect only the planned incision site
The whole skin surface, especially bony prominences, must be assessed.
Skip skin checks in patients under age 65
All surgical patients need a skin assessment, not only older adults.
alt.ex: A thorough skin assessment covers bony prominences, body folds, existing lesions, and areas at risk from the planned OR position.

items.q: A nurse reviews four patients scheduled for surgery today. Which patient should be monitored most carefully for intraoperative pressure injury?
items.a: A 79-year-old with a hematocrit of 32% and a 7-hour procedure
items.ex: Older age, hematocrit below 35%, and an expected OR time over 6.15 hours each call for careful monitoring.
w: A 34-year-old with a hematocrit of 44% and a 1-hour procedure
Normal hematocrit, young age, and a short case carry lower risk.
A 46-year-old with an albumin of 4.1 g/dL and arthroscopy
Normal albumin and a short procedure suggest lower PI risk.
A 25-year-old athlete having a 40-minute hernia repair
Young, healthy, and a brief case make this the lowest-risk patient.

alt.q: Which laboratory finding identifies a surgical patient who should be monitored carefully for pressure injury?
alt.a: Hematocrit level less than 35%
alt.ex: AORN guidance lists hematocrit under 35% among findings that call for careful PI monitoring.
w: Hematocrit level greater than 45%
A low, not high, hematocrit is the listed risk finding.
Platelet count of 250,000/mm3
This normal platelet count is not a listed PI risk finding.
Serum sodium of 140 mEq/L
This sodium level is normal and not a PI risk marker.

items.q: Postoperative pressure injuries often do not appear until 48 hours or more after surgery, so assessment must continue during the hospital stay.
items.a: True
items.ex: Because PIs can take 48 hours or more to appear, skin assessment continues throughout the postoperative stay.
items.ww: A normal skin check right after surgery does not rule out a PI that appears days later.

alt.q: If a patient’s skin is intact on return from the PACU, pressure injury assessment can be stopped.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Postoperative PIs often do not appear for 48 hours or more, so assessment continues during the stay.
alt.ww: Intact skin on arrival does not mean no injury occurred; deep tissue damage can surface later.

items.q: A patient on the surgical unit had no surgery-specific pressure injury scale used during the perioperative period. Which tool may the nurse use to assess current postoperative risk?
items.a: Braden Scale
items.ex: Postoperatively, if no surgical PI scale was used, the Braden Scale can assess current risk factors.
w: STOP-Bang questionnaire
STOP-Bang screens for obstructive sleep apnea, not PI risk.
Scott Triggers tool
The Scott Triggers tool is a single preoperative measure, not a postoperative reassessment.
Glasgow Coma Scale
The Glasgow Coma Scale measures level of consciousness, not PI risk.

alt.q: A postoperative patient refuses to turn because of incisional pain. Which concern should the nurse recognize?
alt.a: Development of a pressure injury
alt.ex: When a patient is unable or unwilling to turn because of incisional pain, PI development is a concern.
w: Wound dehiscence from turning
Turning with support is encouraged; the risk named here is PI from immobility.
Opioid tolerance from frequent dosing
The concern from refusing to turn is skin breakdown, not tolerance.
Malignant hyperthermia
Malignant hyperthermia is an anesthesia reaction, unrelated to refusal to turn.

items.q: Why does morbid obesity increase a patient’s risk for pressure injury on the operating table?
items.a: Excess weight over bony prominences restricts blood flow
items.ex: Excess weight placed on skin over bony prominences restricts blood flow, allowing PIs to form during surgery.
w: Fatty tissue produces too much moisture under drapes
The book’s reason is restricted blood flow from weight, not fat-produced moisture.
Obese patients need less padding on the OR bed
Obese patients need careful positioning and padding, not less.
Adipose tissue speeds the metabolism of anesthetics
This is not a stated mechanism for PI in obesity.

alt.q: A circulating nurse is preparing the OR bed for a patient with morbid obesity. What caution about positioning devices does the textbook give?
alt.a: PIs can develop from wrinkles and misplaced foam devices
alt.ex: Pressure-redistributing surfaces help, but wrinkles and incorrectly placed foam devices can themselves cause PIs.
w: Gel pads should be avoided in patients who are obese
Gel pads are listed among available pressure-redistribution surfaces.
Padding is unnecessary when an air mattress is used
Padding and devices are still needed; the risk is incorrect placement.
Foam devices remove all pressure risk once placed
Foam devices placed incorrectly can cause PIs rather than prevent them.

items.q: According to Table 50.3, how often should the skin of an older adult having surgery be assessed?
items.a: Every 4 hours
items.ex: Older adults have fragile skin and less subcutaneous tissue, so the table directs skin assessment every 4 hours.
w: Every 8 hours
An 8-hour interval is longer than the 4 hours the table recommends.
Every 12 hours
Twice daily checks are too infrequent for fragile older skin.
Once every 24 hours
Daily checks would miss early pressure damage in older adults.

alt.q: For an older adult with decreased subcutaneous tissue and fragile skin, how often does Table 50.3 direct the nurse to turn or reposition the patient?
alt.a: At least every 2 hours
alt.ex: The table directs turning or repositioning at least every 2 hours, plus padding of all bony prominences during surgery.
w: At least every 4 hours
Every 4 hours is the skin assessment interval, not the turning interval.
At least every 6 hours
Six hours far exceeds the 2-hour turning interval.
Only when the patient requests it
Turning must be scheduled, because older adults may not sense pressure.

items.q: The Munro Scale is a cumulative tool that assesses pressure injury risk factors in each of the operative phases.
items.a: True
items.ex: The Munro Scale has preoperative, intraoperative, and postoperative components, which increases how often risk is assessed.
items.ww: The Munro Scale is not a one-time screen; it adds risk factors across all phases.

alt.q: The Scott Triggers tool reassesses a patient’s pressure injury risk in each operative phase.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The Scott Triggers tool is a single preoperative measure; the Munro Scale is the cumulative phase-by-phase tool.
alt.ww: Only the Munro Scale is described as cumulative across operative phases.

items.q: Which item is part of the intraoperative component of the Munro Scale?
items.a: Hypotension
items.ex: The intraoperative scale includes ASA class, anesthesia type, moisture, surface/motion, hypotension, and body temperature.
w: Weight loss
Weight loss belongs to the preoperative component.
Occurrence of hemorrhage
Hemorrhage belongs to the postoperative component.
Nutritional state
Nutritional state belongs to the preoperative component.

alt.q: Which item is assessed in the postoperative component of the Munro Scale?
alt.a: Length of the surgical procedure
alt.ex: The postoperative component includes length of the procedure and occurrence of hemorrhage.
w: Body temperature during surgery
Body temperature is part of the intraoperative component.
Preoperative body mass index
BMI is part of the preoperative component.
Mobility before the operation
Mobility is part of the preoperative component.

items.q: A patient returns to the nursing unit after a 5-hour procedure in the lithotomy position. Which action best addresses pressure injury prevention?
items.a: Inspect skin over areas that bore pressure in the OR position
items.ex: After surgery, perform a careful skin assessment, focusing on areas at risk from the surgical position, and use pressure-reduction strategies.
w: Delay the first skin check until 48 hours after surgery
Assessment starts on return; PIs may appear late, so checks continue, not start, later.
Keep the patient in one position to limit incisional pain
Immobility increases PI risk; repositioning is needed.
Massage reddened bony areas to restore circulation
Massage is not a recommended pressure-reduction strategy in the text.

alt.q: A patient is transferred from the OR after a long procedure. Which nursing action reflects postoperative pressure injury prevention?
alt.a: Perform a careful skin assessment and use pressure-reduction strategies
alt.ex: The book directs a careful postoperative skin assessment and appropriate pressure-reduction strategies.
w: Rely on the intraoperative record instead of inspecting the skin
The nurse must inspect the skin directly, not rely only on records.
Inspect only the dressing and incision during the first day
The whole skin surface, especially pressure points, must be checked.
Avoid repositioning until the patient can turn alone
Waiting for independent turning prolongs pressure on tissues.

items.q: Which expected outcome for pressure injury prevention is written correctly?
items.a: Patient remains free of PI 24 hours after surgery
items.ex: Outcomes are patient-centered, measurable, and include a time frame, as in the book’s example.
w: Nurse turns the patient every 2 hours after surgery
This is a nursing intervention, not a patient outcome.
Patient will have healthier skin after surgery
This lacks a measurable criterion and time frame.
Patient will understand skin care while hospitalized
This is vague and not measurable as stated.

alt.q: A nurse writes the outcome “Patient will be free of pressure injury.” What does this outcome lack?
alt.a: A time frame for achievement
alt.ex: Each outcome needs a time frame, such as “free of PI 24 hours after surgery.”
w: A nursing intervention
Outcomes describe patient results; interventions are written separately.
A medical diagnosis
Outcomes do not require a medical diagnosis.
A health care provider order
Nursing outcomes do not need a provider’s order.

items.q: Jeff reviews his assessment of Mr. Cooper before colon surgery. Which finding should Jeff recognize as an intrinsic risk factor for pressure injury?
items.a: A 10-lb weight loss with decreased appetite
items.ex: Recent weight loss and decreased appetite suggest altered nutrition, an intrinsic risk that lowers tolerance to pressure.
w: Clear breath sounds with no dyspnea
Normal respiratory findings are not a PI risk factor.
Walking 2 miles four to five times a week
Regular activity reflects good mobility, which lowers risk.
A temperature of 36.8°C (98.2°F)
This temperature is normal and not a risk finding.

alt.q: How do RNs help prevent pressure injuries during surgery?
alt.a: Careful positioning and pressure-relieving surfaces
alt.ex: RNs prevent intraoperative PIs by carefully positioning patients and using pressure-relieving surfaces.
w: Massaging bony prominences during the case
Massage is not the prevention strategy described.
Keeping the patient in one fixed position
Fixed positioning for hours increases PI risk.
Limiting skin checks to the PACU
Risk screening starts preoperatively and continues after surgery.

items.q: Which result does current evidence associate with preoperative patient education?
items.a: Reduced length of hospital stay
items.ex: Preoperative education is linked to shorter stays, less anxiety, and fewer postoperative complications.
w: Greater need for postoperative analgesia
Education is linked to less postoperative pain, not more analgesic need.
Higher anxiety before surgery
Education reduces, rather than raises, anxiety.
More postoperative complications
Evidence shows a reduced risk of complications.

alt.q: A hospital reviews its preoperative teaching program. Which outcome would the evidence lead them to expect?
alt.a: Less postoperative depression
alt.ex: Preoperative education has been shown to lessen postoperative pain, depression, and agency costs.
w: Higher overall agency costs
Education reduces, not raises, agency costs.
Lower patient satisfaction
Education increases patient satisfaction.
Slower return to functioning
Education speeds recovery and return to functioning.

items.q: Which outcomes are linked to preoperative education? Select all that apply.
o: Reduced anxiety
Patients who receive preoperative education show lower anxiety levels.
More realistic postoperative expectations
Education gives patients realistic expectations.
Reduced agency costs
Education has been shown to reduce agency costs.
Lessened postoperative pain
Education is linked to less postoperative pain.
No need for postoperative analgesics
Pain is expected after surgery; education reduces, not eliminates, analgesic need.
Longer hospital stays
Education is associated with shorter, not longer, stays.
items.ex: Preoperative education reduces anxiety, pain, costs, and length of stay and improves knowledge and satisfaction.

alt.q: Structured teaching throughout the perioperative period influences which areas? Select all that apply.
o: Ventilatory function
Teaching improves the ability and willingness to deep-breathe and cough.
Physical functional capacity
Teaching increases willingness to ambulate and resume ADLs.
Length of hospital stay
Being informed helps prevent complications and shortens stays.
Sense of well-being
Prepared patients report less anxiety and greater well-being.
Choice of anesthetic agent
The anesthesia provider chooses the agent; this is not a listed teaching effect.
Need for informed consent
Consent is required regardless of teaching.
alt.ex: Structured teaching influences ventilatory function, functional capacity, well-being, length of stay, and anxiety about pain.

items.q: Which statement about methods of preoperative education is accurate?
items.a: Videos are less effective than verbal communication
items.ex: Videos let patients reflect, but verbal communication is more effective because it allows questions and clarification.
w: Videos are more effective than face-to-face teaching
The book states the reverse: videos are less effective than verbal communication.
Brochures should replace individual nurse meetings
Brochures are one method among several, not a replacement for meetings.
Group classes are discouraged before admission
Preadmission group classes are a commonly used method.

alt.q: Why is verbal communication more effective than videos for preoperative education?
alt.a: It lets the patient ask questions and clarify concerns
alt.ex: Verbal communication allows the patient to ask questions and clarify concerns about the surgical process.
w: It takes less of the nurse’s time than a video
Its value is interaction, not time savings.
It removes the need for written materials
Printed materials are still used to reinforce teaching.
It lets the patient replay the content at home
Replaying content is an advantage of videos, not of verbal teaching.

items.q: Preoperative education supports collaborative decision making that helps patients make better choices.
items.a: True
items.ex: Education allows preoperative collaborative decision making so the patient can make better choices.
items.ww: Education does more than inform; it lets the patient share in decisions about care.

alt.q: Preoperative education mainly helps the surgical team and has little effect on the choices patients make.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The book states education allows collaborative decision making that lets patients make better choices.
alt.ww: Education directly supports patient participation in decisions, not only staff efficiency.

items.q: A nurse has just explained and demonstrated deep-breathing exercises to a patient scheduled for surgery. Which action best confirms the patient’s understanding?
items.a: Ask the patient to perform a return demonstration
items.ex: After explaining and demonstrating, use teach-back and a return demonstration to reinforce the skill and build confidence.
w: Ask the patient whether there are any questions
A yes/no question does not confirm the patient can perform the skill.
Give the patient a brochure to read later
Printed material reinforces but does not confirm understanding.
Have the patient watch the video one more time
Watching again does not show that the patient can do the exercise.

alt.q: After teaching leg exercises, the nurse wants to confirm learning. Which nursing action fits the teach-back approach?
alt.a: Have the patient explain the exercise in their own words
alt.ex: Teach-back asks patients to explain or show what they learned so the nurse can confirm understanding.
w: Repeat the explanation a second time more slowly
Repeating the content does not check what the patient learned.
Document that the teaching was completed
Documenting teaching does not confirm understanding.
Ask the family to confirm they were listening
The patient’s own understanding must be confirmed.

items.q: A patient preparing for abdominal surgery says, “I want to be sure I understand the pain teaching.” Which statement by the patient shows understanding?
items.a: “I’ll rate my pain on the scale and ask for medicine before it gets severe.”
items.ex: Patients are taught to use a pain scale and to take analgesics before pain becomes excruciating.
w: “I’ll wait until the pain is unbearable before asking for medicine.”
Unrelieved pain becomes excruciating and harder to control at ordered doses.
“I’ll avoid all pain medicine so I don’t get addicted.”
Pain must be controlled for the patient to take part in recovery activities.
“If I have pain after surgery, something went wrong.”
Pain after surgery is expected and is managed.

alt.q: A patient will use patient-controlled analgesia (PCA) after surgery. Which statement shows the patient understood the teaching?
alt.a: “I’ll press the button as soon as my pain becomes persistent.”
alt.ex: Patients are taught to give PCA medication as soon as pain becomes persistent.
w: “I’ll press the button only when my pain reaches 10.”
Waiting for severe pain makes it hard to control.
“My wife can press the button whenever I seem restless.”
PCA is for the patient to control their own pain.
“I’ll save the button for nighttime so I can sleep.”
PCA is used whenever pain becomes persistent, not only at night.

items.q: Why does the nurse tell a patient before surgery that the OR is bright and cold and that the BP cuff will hum and tighten?
items.a: Reducing anxiety lowers the anesthetic dose needed for induction
items.ex: Sensory information reduces anxiety before anesthesia, which helps reduce the amount of anesthetic needed for induction.
w: It meets the legal requirement for informed consent
Consent covers the procedure’s risks and benefits, not sensory preparation.
It lets the patient choose the room temperature
The OR environment is not set by patient choice.
It prevents the need for prewarming blankets
Patients are still often prewarmed or given warm blankets.

alt.q: A patient will be intubated for general anesthesia. Which statement by the nurse provides sensory preparation for after surgery?
alt.a: “Your throat may feel sore from the breathing tube.”
alt.ex: Postoperative sensations include sore throat from an endotracheal tube, dry mouth, tight dressings, and blurred vision from ointment.
w: “You will not feel any pain at the incision.”
Pain at the surgical site is expected and should not be denied.
“The operating room will be warm and dimly lit.”
The OR is described as very bright and cold.
“Your vision will be sharper than usual on waking.”
Ophthalmic ointment causes blurred vision after surgery.

items.q: Why is including family members in preoperative teaching advisable?
items.a: Family members often retain teaching better and coach the patient
items.ex: Family often coaches postoperative exercises and remembers teaching better than the patient, which supports recovery.
w: Family members can sign the consent if the patient refuses
A patient’s refusal is respected; family does not override it.
Family members are required to give medications in the hospital
Nurses give medications in the hospital, not family members.
Family members replace the need to teach the patient
The patient still needs teaching; family supports it.

alt.q: The anxious spouse of a patient keeps asking what the drains and monitors will be for after surgery. Why should the nurse prepare the spouse?
alt.a: An anxious relative’s worry can heighten the patient’s fear
alt.ex: If relatives do not understand routine postoperative events, their anxiety heightens the patient’s fear; preparing them lessens it.
w: The spouse is legally responsible for postoperative monitoring
Monitoring is a nursing responsibility, not the spouse’s.
The spouse must approve each postoperative treatment
The patient, not the spouse, consents to care.
Teaching the spouse means the patient needs no teaching
The patient still needs explanations; family teaching adds to it.

items.q: When preadmission nurses call patients up to 1 week before surgery, which topic do they typically cover?
items.a: The extent and purpose of food and fluid restrictions
items.ex: Calls cover arrival and surgery times, food and fluid restrictions, physical preparation, and holding-area procedures.
w: The exact time the surgery will be finished
Surgery times are only approximate and cannot be promised.
The pathology results from the planned surgery
Pathology results come after surgery, not before.
The discharge prescriptions the patient will need
Discharge prescriptions are not part of the preadmission call content listed.

alt.q: A nurse is making preadmission calls for next week’s surgical patients. Which instruction fits the purpose of these calls?
alt.a: Explain bathing or showering with antiseptic
alt.ex: Preadmission calls teach physical preparation such as bowel preparation and antiseptic bathing.
w: Explain how the surgeon will close the incision
Surgical technique is explained by the surgeon, not in preadmission calls.
Explain how to remove skin staples at home
Staple removal is not a preadmission teaching topic.
Explain the results of intraoperative lab tests
Intraoperative results are not available before surgery.

items.q: A patient scheduled for surgery tomorrow says, “I’m not really sure what operation I’m having.” Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Notify the surgeon that the patient needs further explanation
items.ex: If a patient has little or no understanding of the surgery, notify the surgeon, who is responsible for explaining it.
w: Explain the procedure using precise medical terms
Technical terms add to confusion, and explaining the procedure is the surgeon’s role.
Proceed with preparation because the consent is signed
A signed form does not replace real understanding.
Reassure the patient that the details are not important
Understanding the procedure is essential to informed consent.

alt.q: A patient asks the nurse more questions about the steps of a surgery the surgeon already explained. What should the nurse do first?
alt.a: Clarify what the patient discussed with the surgeon
alt.ex: First clarify what the surgeon told the patient, avoid technical terms, and never contradict the surgeon’s explanation.
w: Describe a different approach the nurse prefers
The nurse must avoid contradicting the surgeon’s explanation.
Tell the patient to ask the anesthesia provider
The nurse first clarifies what the patient already learned.
Give a detailed technical description of the steps
Technical medical terms add to a patient’s confusion.

items.q: The nurse should tell the patient and family that the scheduled operative time is exact.
items.a: False
items.ex: The scheduled time is only a rough estimate; surgery may start sooner or later.
items.ww: Delays happen for many reasons unrelated to the patient, so the time cannot be promised.

alt.q: The nurse tells the family that delays in surgery happen for various reasons and do not necessarily mean there is a problem.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: Families should know delays are common and do not necessarily indicate a problem; excessive delays are communicated.
alt.ww: Telling families that delays mean trouble would cause needless anxiety.

items.q: Why should the nurse avoid overpreparing or underpreparing a patient about postoperative monitoring and therapies?
items.a: Contradictions between explanations and reality cause anxiety
items.ex: Patients who know what monitoring to expect are less apprehensive, but explanations that don’t match reality cause anxiety.
w: Detailed teaching is legally limited to the surgeon
Nurses teach about routine monitoring and therapies.
Patients forget all information given before surgery
Teaching is effective; the concern is mismatched information.
Postoperative care is the same for every patient
Care varies, which is why not every requirement can be predicted.

alt.q: Which situation makes it easier for the nurse to prepare a patient appropriately for postoperative care?
alt.a: An elective case with an ERAS protocol and adequate teaching time
alt.ex: Preparation is easier in elective cases when the surgeon uses guidelines such as ERAS and there is time for education.
w: An emergency case with no time before surgery
Emergencies leave little time to prepare the patient.
A case in which the surgeon has no care guidelines
Care guidelines make expected care more predictable.
A case in which teaching is done during sedation
Sedated patients cannot learn effectively.

items.q: Which topics does a patient having inpatient surgery need to understand to facilitate recovery? Select all that apply.
o: Pain control
Pain control is listed among inpatient recovery topics.
Early ambulation
Early ambulation prevents pulmonary and vascular complications.
Diet progression
Diet progression is a listed recovery topic.
Wound care
Wound care is part of inpatient recovery teaching.
Adjusting the IV infusion rate
Patients do not adjust their own IV rates.
Staying on bed rest for several days
Early mobility, not prolonged bed rest, is promoted.
items.ex: Inpatients need to understand pain control, early ambulation, diet progression, wound care, and postoperative exercises.

alt.q: Which postoperative exercises should be taught before an inpatient surgery? Select all that apply.
o: Diaphragmatic breathing
Diaphragmatic breathing is a listed postoperative exercise.
Incentive spirometry
Incentive spirometry is taught to promote lung expansion.
Turning
Turning is part of the exercise teaching.
Leg exercises
Leg exercises help prevent DVT.
Keeping the legs still to protect the incision
Leg exercises, not immobility, prevent vascular complications.
Breath holding instead of coughing
Coughing is taught; breath holding is not a listed exercise.
alt.ex: Postoperative exercises include diaphragmatic breathing, incentive spirometry, coughing, turning, and leg exercises.

items.q: Which sensations should the nurse prepare a patient to expect after general anesthesia with an endotracheal tube? Select all that apply.
o: Blurred vision from eye ointment
Ophthalmic ointment blurs vision after surgery.
Sore throat
An endotracheal tube can cause a sore throat.
Dryness of the mouth
Dry mouth is a listed postoperative sensation.
Tightness of dressings
Dressings may feel tight after surgery.
Complete absence of incisional pain
Pain at the surgical site is expected.
A warm, dimly lit recovery area
Patients are told the OR is bright and cold; this is not a listed sensation.
items.ex: Postoperative sensations include blurred vision, pain at the site and pressure areas, tight dressings, dry mouth, and sore throat.

alt.q: Which sensations should the nurse describe to a patient about the operating room before induction? Select all that apply.
o: The room is very bright
Patients are warned the OR is very bright.
The room is cold
Patients are warned the OR is cold and may be prewarmed.
The BP monitor hums and beeps
The noninvasive BP monitor makes a hum and a beep.
The BP cuff tightens to take a reading
The cuff tightening is a sensation patients are told about.
The surgeon will wake the patient during the incision
This is not a sensation described for the OR.
The room will be completely silent
Monitors make sounds, so the room is not silent.
alt.ex: Telling patients the OR is bright and cold and describing monitor sounds reduces anxiety before anesthesia.

items.q: Patients who learn about pain and ways to relieve it before surgery tend to require less analgesia afterward.
items.a: True
items.ex: Patients taught about pain are less anxious, ask for what they need, and require less analgesia.
items.ww: Pain teaching lowers, rather than raises, the need for analgesics.

alt.q: Patients who receive pain-management teaching before surgery tend to need more analgesia afterward because they ask for it more often.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Patients taught about pain before surgery are less anxious and require less analgesia after surgery.
alt.ww: Asking for what they need does not raise total analgesic use; teaching lowers it.

items.q: After explaining each postoperative exercise, the nurse demonstrates it and uses [[teach-back|teach back]] to confirm understanding.
items.ex: Teach-back confirms understanding, and a return demonstration reinforces the skill and builds confidence.

alt.q: The nurse asks the patient to perform a [[return demonstration|return-demonstration]] of each exercise to reinforce it and build confidence.
alt.ex: Teach-back confirms understanding, and a return demonstration reinforces the skill and builds confidence.

items.q: Before surgery, teach patients how to use a [[pain scale|pain rating scale]] so they are prepared to rate their pain afterward.
items.ex: Learning the pain scale before surgery prepares patients to report pain accurately after surgery.

alt.q: So that patients can rate their pain after surgery, the nurse teaches use of a [[pain scale|pain rating scale]] preoperatively.
alt.ex: Learning the pain scale before surgery prepares patients to report pain accurately after surgery.

items.q: A patient scheduled for a colectomy refuses to take any opioids after surgery because of fear of addiction. Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “Tell me your concerns. Pain control helps you take part in recovery.”
items.ex: Listen to concerns and encourage ordered analgesics, because uncontrolled pain prevents participation in postoperative therapy.
w: “You have no choice; the surgeon has ordered the opioids.”
This dismisses the patient’s concern and right to discuss care.
“Opioids carry no risk of addiction after surgery.”
This is inaccurate reassurance about a real concern.
“Then you will just have to tolerate the pain.”
Unrelieved pain hinders recovery; alternatives should be discussed.

alt.q: A patient expected to have severe postoperative pain worries about becoming dependent on opioids. What should the nurse discuss before surgery?
alt.a: How providers will taper opioids and switch to less addictive drugs
alt.ex: When severe pain is expected, discuss gradual opioid reduction and switching to less addictive medication as the patient progresses.
w: That opioids will be avoided entirely for safety
Opioids may be needed; the plan is to taper, not avoid them entirely.
That analgesics should be taken only at bedtime
Analgesics are taken at ordered intervals to keep pain controlled.
That pain is untreatable after major surgery
Pain is expected but manageable with a multimodal plan.

items.q: Jeff plans time with Mr. Cooper and his wife to discuss the planned colectomy. How should Jeff begin the teaching session?
items.a: Ask Mr. Cooper to describe what he thinks the procedure involves
items.ex: Starting with the patient’s understanding, concerns, and wanted information lets the nurse individualize teaching.
w: Show a standard video before asking any questions
Assessing the patient’s understanding comes before choosing teaching content.

alt.q: Which intake requires fasting for at least “6 hours” before surgery?
alt.a: Infant formula or nonhuman milk
alt.ex: ASA fasting guidelines reduce aspiration risk, but always follow the health care provider’s orders.
w: Clear liquids
Clear liquids: 2 hours.
Breast milk
Breast milk: 4 hours.
Meat or fried foods
Meat or fried foods: 8 hours.

alt.q: Which intake requires fasting for at least “8 hours” before surgery?
alt.a: Meat or fried foods
alt.ex: ASA fasting guidelines reduce aspiration risk, but always follow the health care provider’s orders.
w: Clear liquids
Clear liquids: 2 hours.
Breast milk
Breast milk: 4 hours.
Infant formula or nonhuman milk
Infant formula or nonhuman milk: 6 hours.

mt.q: Match each intake with the ASA-recommended minimum fasting time before a nonemergent procedure.
mt.ex: ASA fasting guidelines reduce aspiration risk, but always follow the health care provider’s orders.

items.q: In the Universal Protocol, which principle comes right after “Preoperative verification of documents and procedure”?
items.a: Marking the operative site
items.ex: Verification confirms documents and expectations, the site is marked, and a final time-out occurs just before the procedure.
w: Time-out just before starting the procedure
That's principle 3 of 3.

alt.q: Which principle comes first in the Universal Protocol?
alt.a: Preoperative verification of documents and procedure
alt.ex: Verification confirms documents and expectations, the site is marked, and a final time-out occurs just before the procedure.
w: Marking the operative site
That's principle 2 of 3.
Time-out just before starting the procedure
That's principle 3 of 3.

alt.q: Which principle comes last in the Universal Protocol?
alt.a: Time-out just before starting the procedure
alt.ex: Verification confirms documents and expectations, the site is marked, and a final time-out occurs just before the procedure.
w: Marking the operative site
That's principle 2 of 3.
Preoperative verification of documents and procedure
That's principle 1 of 3.

alt.q: In the Universal Protocol, which principle comes right after “Marking the operative site”?
alt.a: Time-out just before starting the procedure
alt.ex: Verification confirms documents and expectations, the site is marked, and a final time-out occurs just before the procedure.
w: Preoperative verification of documents and procedure
That's principle 1 of 3.

alt.q: In the Universal Protocol, which principle comes right before “Marking the operative site”?
alt.a: Preoperative verification of documents and procedure
alt.ex: Verification confirms documents and expectations, the site is marked, and a final time-out occurs just before the procedure.
w: Time-out just before starting the procedure
That's principle 3 of 3.

alt.q: In the Universal Protocol, which principle comes right before “Time-out just before starting the procedure”?
alt.a: Marking the operative site
alt.ex: Verification confirms documents and expectations, the site is marked, and a final time-out occurs just before the procedure.
w: Preoperative verification of documents and procedure
That's principle 1 of 3.

ord.q: Put the three principles of TJC’s Universal Protocol in order.
items: Preoperative verification of documents and procedure
Marking the operative site
Time-out just before starting the procedure
ord.ex: Verification confirms documents and expectations, the site is marked, and a final time-out occurs just before the procedure.

items.q: A nurse uses the STOP-Bang questionnaire to screen a surgical patient. Which findings are risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea? Select all that apply.
o: Loud snoring heard through closed doors
Loud snoring is the S in STOP-Bang.
Someone observed the patient stop breathing during sleep
Observed apnea is the O in STOP-Bang.
BMI greater than 35 kg/m2
A BMI over 35 is a Bang risk factor.
Neck circumference greater than 40 cm
Neck circumference over 40 cm is a risk factor.
Age over 35 years
The age criterion is over 50 years, not 35.
Female gender
Male gender is the STOP-Bang risk factor.
items.ex: Any STOP-Bang item answered yes is a risk factor for OSA.

alt.q: Which findings count as STOP-Bang risk factors for obstructive sleep apnea? Select all that apply.
o: Often feeling tired during the daytime
Daytime tiredness is the T in STOP-Bang.
Being treated for high blood pressure
High blood pressure is the P in STOP-Bang.
Male gender
Male gender is a Bang risk factor.
Age over 50 years
Age over 50 is a Bang risk factor.
BMI of 28 kg/m2
The BMI criterion is greater than 35 kg/m2.
Neck circumference of 35 cm
The neck criterion is greater than 40 cm (16 inches).
alt.ex: STOP-Bang covers snoring, tiredness, observed apnea, blood pressure, BMI over 35, age over 50, neck over 40 cm, and male gender.

items.q: Which patients are most at risk for a latex allergy? Select all that apply.
o: A child with spina bifida
Children with spina bifida are at high risk for latex allergy.
A patient with a history of multiple surgeries
Multiple surgeries increase latex exposure and risk.
A health care professional
Health care workers are among those most at risk.
A patient with a spinal cord injury and long-term catheter use
Long-term urinary catheter use increases latex exposure.
A patient allergic to penicillin
Penicillin allergy is not a listed latex risk factor.
A patient with controlled hypertension
Hypertension is not a latex allergy risk factor.
items.ex: Latex allergy risk is highest with genetic predisposition, spina bifida, long-term catheter use, multiple surgeries, and health care or rubber work.

alt.q: A patient reports food allergies. Which foods suggest possible cross-sensitivity to latex? Select all that apply.
o: Bananas
Bananas are listed as cross-sensitive with latex.
Kiwifruit
Kiwifruit is listed as cross-sensitive with latex.
Avocados
Avocados are listed as cross-sensitive with latex.
Chestnuts
Chestnuts are listed as cross-sensitive with latex.
Shellfish
Shellfish is not among the foods listed for latex cross-sensitivity.
Peanuts
Peanuts are not among the foods listed for latex cross-sensitivity.
alt.ex: Foods linked to latex cross-sensitivity include bananas, chestnuts, kiwifruit, avocados, potatoes, tomatoes, and wheat.

items.q: On the morning of surgery, which items should the nurse have the patient remove? Select all that apply.
o: Hairpins and clips
Metal pins can become an exit source for electrocautery current and cause burns.
Polish from at least one fingernail
Nail polish and shellac can cause false pulse oximetry readings.
Contact lenses and false eyelashes
Anything in or around the eye can irritate or injure it during surgery.
Partial or complete dentures
Removable prostheses can be lost or damaged during surgery.
Hospital gown
A clean hospital gown is worn; personal nightwear is removed.
Identification band
The ID band must stay on to verify the patient’s identity.
items.ex: Removing metal, makeup, polish, eye items, and prostheses prevents burns, false readings, eye injury, and loss of devices.

alt.q: A patient has valuables on the morning of surgery. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
o: Document a ring as silver with a red stone
Describe items by color and metal, not by assumed gem type.
Give valuables to a family member or secure location
Valuables go to family or a secure designated location.
Remove a wedding band before hand surgery
Remove rings when swelling of the hand or fingers is likely.
Remove metal piercings
Metal items are removed to reduce the risk of burns.
Document the red stone as a ruby
Naming the gem can lead to disputes; describe only what is seen.
Tape all rings in place as the preferred practice
Taping a band is possible but not the preferred practice.
alt.ex: Describe valuables objectively, secure them or give them to family, and remove rings or metal that pose swelling or burn risks.

items.q: A patient scheduled for elective surgery in 2 hours has an oral temperature of 38.4°C (101.1°F). Which action should the nurse take first?
items.a: Notify the surgeon of the elevated temperature
items.ex: An elevated temperature may signal infection and alters drug metabolism; notify the surgeon immediately, as elective surgery is often postponed.
w: Give an antipyretic and continue preparation
Masking the fever without notifying the surgeon could hide an infection.
Document the reading and send the patient to surgery
Abnormal findings must be reported before surgery.
Recheck the temperature after the surgery
Waiting delays a finding that may postpone elective surgery.

alt.q: During the preoperative assessment, a nurse auscultates wheezing in a patient’s airways. Why is it important to report this finding?
alt.a: The patient is at risk for further airway narrowing during and after surgery
alt.ex: Wheezing before surgery signals risk of further narrowing during surgery and after extubation; notify the health care provider.
w: Wheezing shows the patient is well hydrated for anesthesia
Wheezing reflects airway narrowing, not hydration.
Wheezing means the patient needs no incentive spirometry
Respiratory risk increases the need for pulmonary hygiene.
Wheezing confirms the patient has obstructive sleep apnea
OSA is screened with tools like STOP-Bang, not wheezing.

items.q: A patient scheduled for surgery has just received a preoperative opioid and sedative, and the nurse discovers the consent form is unsigned. Which statement about consent is correct?
items.a: Consent must be obtained before any sedation is given
items.ex: Consent is obtained before sedation to ensure a clear level of consciousness; report the problem rather than have the sedated patient sign.
w: The patient can sign now because the drugs do not induce sleep
Sedating drugs alter consciousness; consent must precede them.
The nurse may sign the form on the patient’s behalf
The nurse cannot consent for the patient.
A person with general power of attorney can sign instead
Persons with only general power of attorney cannot sign surgical consents.

alt.q: Who is responsible for explaining the procedure, risks, benefits, alternatives, and possible complications before surgery?
alt.a: The surgeon
alt.ex: Explaining the procedure and obtaining informed consent is the surgeon’s responsibility; the nurse reports concerns about understanding.
w: The preoperative nurse
The nurse confirms understanding and reports concerns but does not explain the procedure for consent.
The surgical technologist
Surgical technologists do not obtain consent.
The patient’s family member
Family may support the patient but do not explain surgical risks.

items.q: TJC recommends that consent materials be written at a [[fifth-grade|fifth grade|5th-grade|5th grade]] or lower reading level.
items.ex: Writing consent materials at a fifth-grade or lower level helps ensure the patient understands the surgery.

alt.q: To support understanding, surgical consent materials should not exceed a [[fifth-grade|fifth grade|5th-grade|5th grade]] reading level.
alt.ex: Writing consent materials at a fifth-grade or lower level helps ensure the patient understands the surgery.

items.q: When is a prophylactic antibiotic given to reduce surgical site infection rates?
items.a: 60 minutes before the incision, stopped within 24 hours after surgery
items.ex: Wound infection rates fall when the antibiotic is given 60 minutes before incision and stopped within 24 hours.
w: 6 hours before the incision, continued for 7 days after surgery
The book specifies 60 minutes before and stopping within 24 hours.
At skin closure, continued for 72 hours after surgery
Antibiotics are given before the incision, not at closure.
12 hours before the incision, stopped at hospital discharge
Timing is 60 minutes before incision, stopped within 24 hours.

alt.q: A patient is scheduled for orthopedic surgery. Which decolonization regimen does strong evidence support?
alt.a: Intranasal mupirocin twice daily and daily CHG bathing for up to 5 days
alt.ex: Decolonization with mupirocin and chlorhexidine gluconate reduces S. aureus colonization, including MRSA, before orthopedic or cardiothoracic surgery.
w: Oral vancomycin daily and povidone-iodine shampoo for 10 days
The regimen described uses intranasal mupirocin and CHG bathing.
Intranasal mupirocin once and a single alcohol wipe of the site
Mupirocin is given twice daily with daily CHG bathing for up to 5 days.
Daily CHG bathing alone for 2 days before the operation
Decolonization includes intranasal mupirocin as well as CHG.

items.q: Hair at a patient’s surgical site will interfere with closure of the incision. Which action by the nurse is correct?
items.a: Clip the hair close to surgery using a single-use clipper head
items.ex: When hair removal is needed, clipping causes fewer SSIs than razors; use single-use heads close to surgery.
w: Shave the site with a razor the night before
Razors cause micro-nicks, and removal should be close to surgery.
Shave the site with a new razor just before surgery
Razors cause micro-nicks in the skin that increase SSI risk.
Clip the hair the evening before with a shared clipper
Clipper heads are single-use, and removal is done close to surgery.

alt.q: Why is clipping preferred over shaving when hair at a surgical site must be removed?
alt.a: Razors cause micro-nicks in the skin
alt.ex: Micro-nicks from razors raise SSI risk, so clipping is preferred when hair must be removed.
w: Clipping removes resident flora from the scalp
Shampooing, not clipping, reduces resident scalp flora.
Clipping makes skin antisepsis unnecessary
Skin antisepsis is still performed before surgery.
Razors leave hair that blocks the incision
The issue with razors is skin injury, not leftover hair.

items.q: A surgeon orders “enemas until clear” before colon surgery. How does the nurse know the order has been met?
items.a: The return solution contains no solid fecal material
items.ex: Enemas until clear means giving enemas until the return contains no solid stool, usually limited to three in succession.
w: The return solution is completely colorless
Clear refers to no solid fecal material, not a colorless return.
The patient has received five enemas in a row
Most agencies limit successive enemas, usually to three.
The patient reports no further urge to defecate
The endpoint is the content of the return, not the patient’s urge.

alt.q: A patient has completed a bowel preparation with several enemas and cathartics before colon surgery. Which laboratory value should the nurse verify?
alt.a: Potassium level
alt.ex: Diarrhea from bowel preparation can cause hypokalemia, so verify the potassium level afterward.
w: Hemoglobin level
Bowel preparation does not directly lower hemoglobin.
Platelet count
Platelets are not affected by bowel cleansing.
Serum albumin level
Albumin is a nutrition marker, not the value to check after bowel prep.

items.q: A nurse is about to give ordered preoperative medications to a patient. Which action should the nurse complete first?
items.a: Have the patient void and finish other nursing care
items.ex: Complete all other care and have the patient void before giving preoperative drugs, which cause drowsiness and dizziness.
w: Give the drugs, then help the patient to the bathroom
Walking after sedating drugs increases fall risk.
Give the drugs, then remove dentures and jewelry
Other care is completed before medications are given.
Give the drugs, then obtain the signed surgical consent
Consent must be signed before drugs that alter consciousness.

alt.q: After receiving preoperative medications, a patient says, “I feel fine; I’ll walk to the bathroom myself.” Which response is best?
alt.a: “Please stay in bed and use the call light so I can help you.”
alt.ex: Preoperative drugs cause drowsiness and dizziness, so the patient stays in bed and calls for help to prevent falls.
w: “That’s fine, since these drugs do not cause sleep.”
Even without sleep, drowsiness and dizziness make falls likely.
“Go ahead, but walk slowly and hold the wall.”
The patient should not get up unassisted after preoperative drugs.
“You can walk alone once the side rails are down.”
Side rails stay up and the bed low for safety.

items.q: During Jeff’s assessment, Mr. Cooper has a heart rate of 106 beats/min, BP 150/90, reduced eye contact, and states, “This surgery will change my entire life.” Which nursing diagnosis is the priority?
items.a: Anxiety related to insufficient information about surgery
items.ex: Mr. Cooper’s elevated vital signs, reduced eye contact, and stated worries about the colostomy support Anxiety as the primary diagnosis.
w: Risk for Perioperative Position Injury related to obesity
Mr. Cooper is not obese, and his data center on anxiety.
Impaired Airway Clearance related to secretions
His breath sounds are clear with no dyspnea.
Impaired Skin Integrity related to incontinence
No skin breakdown or incontinence is reported.

alt.q: A patient awaiting emergency surgery suddenly has a drop in blood pressure while the nurse is teaching about postoperative exercises. What becomes the priority?
alt.a: Hemodynamic stabilization
alt.ex: When BP drops, hemodynamic stabilization takes priority over education and stress management.
w: Completing the exercise teaching
Teaching is deferred when the patient becomes unstable.
Stress management techniques
Physiological stability comes before stress management.
Reviewing advance directives
Stabilizing the patient comes first in an urgent change.

items.q: In an SBAR preoperative-to-intraoperative hand-off, which information belongs in the Background section?
items.a: Patient allergies and NPO status
items.ex: Background includes pertinent history, medical clearance, allergies, NPO status, vital signs, medications, and code status.
w: Patient’s current understanding of the surgery
Understanding of surgery belongs in Assessment.
Whether the patient is ready for surgery
Readiness for surgery belongs in Recommendations.
Name of the procedure, including site
The procedure and site belong in Situation.

alt.q: In an SBAR preoperative-to-intraoperative hand-off, which information belongs in the Assessment section?
alt.a: Pertinent cultural or emotional factors
alt.ex: Assessment includes understanding of surgery, special needs or risks, cultural or emotional factors, and anesthesia requests.
w: Patient name and date of birth
Identifying data belong in Situation.
Medications taken today
The medication profile belongs in Background.
Chance for staff to voice concerns
Allowing questions belongs in Recommendations.

items.q: Which preoperative finding is a contraindication to applying antiembolism devices?
items.a: History of peripheral arterial bypass grafting
items.ex: Antiembolism devices are not used with material allergy, unusual leg size or shape, peripheral arterial disease or bypass, or neuropathy.
w: Planned orthopedic surgery this morning
Orthopedic surgery is an indication for mechanical VTE prophylaxis.
Family history of deep vein thrombosis
DVT risk supports, rather than contraindicates, prophylaxis.
Scheduled 3-hour abdominal surgery
GI surgery commonly includes mechanical VTE prophylaxis.

alt.q: A patient scheduled for GYN surgery has an order for sequential compression devices. Which assessment finding should the nurse report before applying them?
alt.a: Peripheral neuropathy in both legs
alt.ex: Peripheral neuropathy is a contraindication to antiembolism devices, so the nurse reports it before applying them.
w: A normal leg size and shape
Only an unusual leg size or shape is a contraindication.
A planned surgery lasting several hours
Longer surgery increases the need for VTE prevention.
A history of smoking 1 pack per day
Smoking is not a contraindication to compression devices.

items.q: For an inpatient, all prescription medications taken before surgery are discontinued automatically after surgery unless reordered.
items.a: True
items.ex: Preoperative prescriptions stop automatically after inpatient surgery unless reordered, which is why medication reconciliation at hand-off matters.
items.ww: Medications do not resume on their own; they must be reordered.

alt.q: For an inpatient, prescription medications taken before surgery resume automatically after surgery unless the surgeon cancels them.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Prescription medications are discontinued automatically after inpatient surgery unless reordered.
alt.ww: The default is discontinuation, not automatic resumption.

items.q: The person who will perform the surgery must personally mark the operative site, involving the patient if possible.
items.a: True
items.ex: Under the Universal Protocol, the individual performing and accountable for the procedure personally marks the site.
items.ww: Site marking is not delegated to other team members.

alt.q: Under the Universal Protocol, the circulating nurse may mark the operative site on behalf of the surgeon.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: The person performing the surgery must personally mark the site and involve the patient if possible.
alt.ww: Delegating the mark to a nurse is not allowed; the accountable surgeon marks it.

items.q: A patient who habitually uses alcohol and must stay in the hospital longer than 24 hours is at risk for acute alcohol withdrawal.
items.a: True
items.ex: Habitual alcohol users hospitalized more than 24 hours are at risk for withdrawal and its severe form, delirium tremens.
items.ww: Withdrawal risk is real once alcohol intake stops during a hospital stay.

alt.q: Patients who regularly use alcohol or drugs usually need lower-than-usual doses of anesthetics and analgesics.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: Cross-tolerance in these patients often results in a need for higher-than-usual doses.
alt.ww: Cross-tolerance raises, rather than lowers, dose requirements.

items.q: Per Table 50.5, how long before surgery are anticoagulants such as warfarin or aspirin discontinued?
items.a: At least 48 hours
items.ex: Per Table 50.5, anticoagulants are stopped at least 48 hours before surgery; in current practice warfarin is often held about 5 days, so follow the prescriber’s plan.
w: At least 6 hours
Six hours is too short to reverse anticoagulant effects.
At least 12 hours
The table specifies at least 48 hours.
At least 24 hours
The table specifies at least 48 hours, not 24.

alt.q: A patient has taken prednisone daily for years. What does the nurse anticipate about corticosteroid dosing around surgery?
alt.a: Doses are often increased temporarily
alt.ex: Prolonged corticosteroid use causes adrenal atrophy, reducing stress response, so doses are often increased temporarily.
w: Doses are stopped 1 week before surgery
Stopping abruptly would worsen the inability to respond to stress.
Doses are halved on the day of surgery
The body needs more, not less, steroid support during stress.
Doses are held until the patient eats
Holding steroids risks an inadequate stress response.

items.q: Which statement best describes the preanesthesia care unit (PCU)?
items.a: An area outside the OR where preoperative preparations are completed
items.ex: The PCU, or holding area, sits outside the OR and is where final preoperative preparations are finished.
w: A unit where patients recover until they meet anesthesia discharge criteria
That describes the postanesthesia care unit (PACU), not the PCU.
A clinic where patients complete preadmission testing days before surgery
The PCU is used on the day of surgery, just before the patient enters the OR.
A sterile area inside the OR suite where the team scrubs and gowns
The PCU is located outside the OR, not inside the sterile suite.

alt.q: A patient is moved to an area just outside the operating room where the IV is started and preoperative medications are given. What is this area called?
alt.a: Preanesthesia care unit
alt.ex: Final preoperative preparations, including IV access and preoperative medications, take place in the preanesthesia care unit.
w: Postanesthesia care unit
The PACU receives patients after surgery, not before it.
Phase II recovery area
Phase II recovery is a postoperative level of care that progresses the patient home.
Convalescent nursing unit
Phase III convalescent care takes place after surgery for hospitalized patients.

items.q: A patient in the preanesthesia care unit received preoperative medications and asks the nurse, “Why am I getting so sleepy?” Which response by the nurse is best?
items.a: “The medicine you were just given before surgery can make you feel drowsy.”
items.ex: The nurse explains that preoperative medications may cause drowsiness so the patient understands the expected effect.
w: “You are probably just tired from waiting so long for your surgery.”
This dismisses the expected medication effect the nurse should explain.
“Sleepiness means the general anesthetic has already started working.”
General anesthesia is given later by the anesthesia provider; drowsiness here comes from preoperative medication.
“Try to stay awake so the anesthesia provider can finish assessing you.”
Drowsiness is expected after preoperative medication and does not need to be resisted.

alt.q: A nurse in the preanesthesia care unit has just administered a patient’s preoperative medications. What should the nurse explain to the patient?
alt.a: Why the patient may begin to feel drowsy
alt.ex: Patients who receive preoperative medications should be told why they may begin to feel drowsy.
w: Why the patient will need to stay in the unit for several hours
The patient stays in the PCU only briefly.
Why the patient must sign the surgical consent after the medication
Consent is not obtained after sedating medications have been given.
Why the patient will lose all sensation and reflexes in the unit
Loss of sensation and reflexes occurs with general anesthesia, not with preoperative medication.

items.q: While waiting in the preanesthesia care unit, a patient says, “It is freezing in here.” Which action should the nurse take?
items.a: Offer the patient an extra blanket or a warming blanket
items.ex: The PCU and nearby OR suites are kept cool, so the nurse offers extra or warming blankets.
w: Explain that the cold is needed and blankets are not allowed
Blankets are encouraged; prewarming helps prevent perioperative hypothermia.
Ask the health care provider to delay surgery until the patient warms
A cool room is expected; warming measures are used rather than delaying surgery.
Move the patient into the OR early because the OR is warmer
The OR suites are also usually cool.

alt.q: Why does the nurse in the preanesthesia care unit routinely offer patients an extra or warming blanket?
alt.a: The PCU and the adjacent OR suites are usually kept cool
alt.ex: A cool PCU and OR environment makes warmth important, and prewarming helps prevent hypothermia.
w: Preoperative medications cause a high fever that must be masked
Preoperative medications are not described as causing fever.
Blankets hide the IV site to prevent the patient from touching it
Blankets are offered for warmth, not to conceal IV sites.
Warm blankets replace the need for any intraoperative warming
Active intraoperative warming is still used to prevent hypothermia.

items.q: Which statements about the preanesthesia care unit (PCU) are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Nurses working there are members of the OR staff
PCU nurses are OR staff and dress in scrub attire per infection control policy.
The patient usually stays there only briefly
The PCU is a short stop where final preparations are completed.
The temperature there is usually cool
The PCU and nearby OR suites are typically cool, so extra blankets are offered.
It is located inside the sterile OR suite
The PCU is outside the OR.
Patients remain there until they meet anesthesia discharge criteria
Discharge criteria apply to postanesthesia recovery, not to the preoperative PCU.
items.ex: The PCU is a brief, cool holding area outside the OR staffed by OR nurses in scrub attire.

alt.q: A nursing student is oriented to the presurgical care unit (PSCU). Which statements are correct? Select all that apply.
o: It is sometimes called the holding area
PCU, PSCU, and holding area name the same preoperative area.
Nurses there wear scrub suits, hats, and footwear
PSCU nurses follow OR infection control dress policies.
Preoperative preparations are completed there
Final preoperative preparations happen in this area before the OR.
It is where phase II recovery teaching begins
Postoperative teaching begins in phase II recovery after surgery.
Patients typically spend most of the surgical day there
The patient stays only briefly in this area.
alt.ex: The PSCU, or holding area, is where OR-staff nurses complete final preoperative preparations.

items.q: In some ambulatory surgical settings, one perioperative primary nurse admits the patient, circulates during the procedure, and manages recovery and discharge.
items.a: True
items.ex: Some ambulatory settings use a perioperative primary nurse who follows the patient through all phases.
items.ww: This single-nurse model is described for some ambulatory settings, so the statement is not false.

alt.q: In ambulatory surgical settings, a nurse who admits a patient may never also circulate during that patient’s procedure.
alt.a: False
alt.ex: In some ambulatory settings, the same perioperative primary nurse admits, circulates, and manages recovery and discharge.
alt.ww: The book describes nurses who admit, circulate, and discharge the same patient, so no such rule exists.

items.q: In the preanesthesia care unit, which member of the team usually performs the patient assessment before anesthesia?
items.a: The anesthesia provider
items.ex: The anesthesia provider usually assesses the patient in the PCU before giving anesthesia.
w: The scrub nurse
The scrub nurse prepares to work in the sterile field with the surgeon.
The RN first assistant
The RNFA assists the surgeon with tissue handling, hemostasis, and suturing.
The PACU nurse
The PACU nurse cares for the patient after surgery.

alt.q: A patient in the holding area asks why another clinician has come to examine them after the nurse finished. Who is this most likely to be?
alt.a: The anesthesia provider performing the usual preanesthesia assessment
alt.ex: In the PCU, the anesthesia provider usually performs a patient assessment.
w: The scrub nurse completing a final skin assessment
The scrub nurse works in the sterile field and does not assess the patient in the PCU.
The PACU nurse confirming postoperative orders
The PACU nurse receives the patient after surgery.
The surgical technologist checking the surgical counts
Counts are managed in the OR, not by examining the patient in the PCU.

items.q: If an IV catheter is not already in place, only the anesthesia provider may insert one in the preanesthesia care unit.
items.a: False
items.ex: Either a nurse or an anesthesia provider inserts an IV catheter in the PCU if one is not present.
items.ww: Nurses also insert IV catheters in the PCU, so limiting it to anesthesia providers is wrong.

alt.q: Either a nurse or an anesthesia provider may insert an IV catheter in the preanesthesia care unit if one is not already present.
alt.a: True
alt.ex: The book states a nurse or anesthesia provider establishes IV access in the PCU when needed.
alt.ww: Insertion is not restricted to one role; both nurses and anesthesia providers may do it.

items.q: A nurse inserts an IV catheter for a patient in the preanesthesia care unit. What is the main purpose of this IV access?
items.a: To establish a route for fluid replacement, IV drugs, or blood products
items.ex: PCU IV access provides a route for fluids, IV drugs, and blood products during and after surgery.
w: To obtain blood samples for preadmission laboratory testing
Preadmission testing is done before the day of surgery.
To deliver total parenteral nutrition throughout the procedure
The book does not describe PCU IV access for parenteral nutrition.
To measure core body temperature continuously during surgery
Core temperature is measured with bladder, esophageal, or rectal probes.

alt.q: Which situation does the IV catheter placed in the preanesthesia care unit prepare the team to manage?
alt.a: Replacing fluids or giving blood products if needed during surgery
alt.ex: The PCU IV line establishes a route for fluid replacement, IV drugs, and blood products.
w: Draining urine continuously during a long procedure
Urine is drained by a urinary catheter, not an IV line.
Measuring end-tidal carbon dioxide during anesthesia
End-tidal carbon dioxide is measured with capnography.
Returning electrosurgical current safely to the generator
A grounding pad on the skin returns electrosurgical current.

items.q: Evidence shows that preventing hypothermia by prewarming surgical patients helps reduce which complication?
items.a: Surgical site infection
items.ex: Prewarming helps reduce shivering, cardiac arrest, blood loss, SSI, pressure injuries, and mortality.
w: Postoperative urinary retention
Urinary retention is linked to anesthesia, opioids, and positioning, not listed among prewarming benefits.
Paralytic ileus
Ileus results from handling of the intestines, not from hypothermia in this list.
Malignant hyperthermia
MH is a genetic reaction to certain anesthetics, not prevented by prewarming.

items.q: A patient has an indwelling urinary catheter after surgery and has no indication for continued use. When should the catheter be removed?

alt.q: Which statement about delegating perioperative teaching to assistive personnel (AP) is accurate?

AP may not take part in postoperative exercises in any way

items.q: Why does the nurse check the nursing history for the patient’s height and age before preoperative teaching?

alt.q: A nurse preparing to teach incentive spirometry reviews the patient’s record. Which data does the nurse need to set the target volume?

items.q: During preoperative assessment, which question by the nurse best evaluates the patient’s understanding of the planned surgery?

A yes-or-no question does not show what the patient actually understands.

“Are you comfortable with the surgery plan?”

Ask the family caregiver whether the patient understands

items.q: A nurse arrives to do preoperative teaching and finds the patient grimacing and rating abdominal pain as 7 out of 10. Which action should the nurse take?

A patient in pain cannot focus on learning, so teaching would be ineffective.
Have assistive personnel do the teaching later in the day
Preoperative teaching cannot be delegated to assistive personnel.
Give written handouts in place of the teaching session
Handouts do not replace teaching and demonstration of postoperative exercises.

Pain means the surgery must be rescheduled

items.q: A nurse teaches a patient about preoperative showers with chlorhexidine gluconate (CHG). Which instructions are correct? Select all that apply.

Rinsing removes residual antiseptic that may irritate the skin.
Dry off with a fresh, clean, dry towel after each shower
Used towels hold microorganisms that grow with moisture.
Put on clean clothing after each shower
Clean clothing minimizes reintroducing microorganisms to clean skin.
Reuse the same towel for every shower to limit lint
Used towels contain microorganisms; a fresh towel is needed each time.
Leave the antiseptic on the skin without rinsing
Residual antiseptic can cause skin irritation, so the skin is rinsed thoroughly.

alt.q: Which statements by a patient show correct understanding of preoperative chlorhexidine shower teaching? Select all that apply.

A fresh towel each time avoids reintroducing microorganisms.
“I’ll rinse the soap off well before I dry off.”
Rinsing removes residual antiseptic that can irritate the skin.
“I’ll put on clean clothes after I shower.”
Clean clothing helps keep the skin free of microorganisms.
“I’ll hang my towel up and use it again tomorrow.”
Damp used towels harbor microorganisms that grow in moisture.
“I can skip the shower count; one is always enough.”
The number of showers follows medical orders and agency policy.

items.q: A nurse teaches leg exercises to a patient at risk for thromboembolic disease. Which exercises are included? Select all that apply.
o: Ankle rotation, drawing circles with the big toe
Ankle circles promote joint mobility.
Alternating dorsiflexion and plantar flexion
Calf pumping promotes venous return to prevent thrombus formation.
Quadriceps setting, pressing the knee toward the mattress
Quadriceps setting maintains knee mobility and improves venous return.
Straight leg raises from the bed surface
Raising the straight leg contracts the quadriceps and promotes venous return.
Massaging the calves firmly several times a day
Calf massage is not one of the taught leg exercises.
Keeping the legs crossed at the knee while in bed
Crossing the legs is not a taught exercise and does not promote venous return.
items.ex: Leg exercises are done every 1 to 2 hours while awake to promote venous return and reduce the risk of DVT.

alt.q: A patient asks how often to perform leg exercises and which ones to do. Which instructions are correct? Select all that apply.
o: Do them every 1 to 2 hours while awake
Leg exercises are encouraged every 1 to 2 hours while awake.
Repeat each exercise 5 times
Ankle circles, calf pumping, quadriceps setting, and leg raises are each repeated 5 times.
Lie on your back to do them
The patient is positioned supine for leg exercises.
Do them only once a day before bedtime
Once a day is far too infrequent to prevent venous stasis.
Hold each straight leg raise for 5 minutes
The leg is raised and drawn up 5 times, not held for minutes.
alt.ex: Leg exercises are done supine, each repeated 5 times, every 1 to 2 hours while awake.

items.q: According to the skill, the ideal exercise to promote venous return and improve lung vital capacity after surgery is early mobility.
items.a: True
items.ex: Leg exercises help patients in bed or resting, but early mobility is the ideal exercise.
items.ww: In-bed leg exercises are useful but are not described as superior to early mobility.

alt.ex: Early mobility is the ideal exercise; leg exercises are for patients restricted to bed or resting.
